title: Microstructural development of human newborn cerebral white matter assessed in vivo by diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging.
text: Alterations in the architecture of white matter in the developing human brain can impact cortical development and result in functional disabilities. A line scan diffusion-weighted MRI sequence with diffusion tensor analysis was used to measure the apparent diffusion coefficient, calculate relative anisotropy, and delineate three-dimensional fiber architecture in white matter in preterm (n = 17) and full-term infants (n = 7). To investigate the effects of prematurity on white matter development, early gestation preterm infants (n = 10) were studied again at term. In the central white matter, the mean apparent diffusion coefficient at 28 weeks was higher, at 1.8 microm2/ms, and decreased towards term to 1.2 microm2/ms. In contrast, the posterior limb of the internal capsule showed similar mean apparent diffusion coefficients at both times, at 1.2 and 1.1 microm2/ms, respectively. Relative anisotropy was found to be higher in areas closer to term, with greater absolute values in the internal capsule than in the central white matter. At term, preterm infants showed higher mean diffusion coefficients in the central white matter (1.4 +/- 0.24 versus 1.15 +/- 0.09 microm2/ms, p = 0.016) and lower relative anisotropy in both areas compared to full-term infants (white matter, 10.9 +/- 0.6 versus 22.9 +/- 3.0%, p = 0.001; internal capsule, 24.0 +/- 4.44 versus 33.1 +/- 0.6%, p = 0.006). Nonmyelinated fibers in the corpus callosum were visible by diffusion tensor MRI as early as 28 weeks, and full-term and preterm infants at term showed distinct differences in white matter fiber organization. These findings suggest that quantitative assessment of water diffusion by diffusion tensor MRI provides valuable insights into the microstructural development of white matter in living infants.

title: Induction of myelodysplasia by myeloid-derived suppressor cells.
text: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are age-related stem cell malignancies characterized by shared features of an activated adaptive immune response and ineffective hematopoiesis. In this study, we found that myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), which are typically linked to immunosuppression and cancer, were significantly expanded in the bone marrow of MDS patients. These clonally distinct MDSC overproduce suppressive cytokines and function as potent apoptotic effectors targeting autologous hematopoietic progenitors. Using multiple transfected cell models, we discovered that MDSC expansion is driven by the interaction of the proinflammatory molecule S100A9 with CD33. This ligand-receptor interaction recruits components to CD33's immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motif (ITIM), leading to the secretion of suppressive cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β by immature myeloid cells. In S100A9 transgenic mice, we observed bone marrow accumulation of MDSC, accompanied by development of progressive multilineage cytopenias and cytological dysplasia. Importantly, early maturation of MDSC by either all-trans-retinoic acid treatment or active ITAM-bearing adapter protein (DAP12) interruption of CD33 signaling rescued the hematologic phenotype. These findings suggest that primary bone marrow expansion of MDSC driven by the S100A9/CD33 pathway disrupts hematopoiesis and contributes to the development of MDS.

title: BC1 RNA, the transcript from a master gene for ID element amplification, is able to prime its own reverse transcription.
text:
ID elements, also known as short interspersed elements (SINEs), are found in high copy number in many rodent genomes. These elements are known to be amplified through a process called retroposition, which involves several regulatory steps. One of these steps is the priming of the RNA transcript for reverse transcription and integration. This study specifically focuses on the priming of the BC1 RNA gene transcript for reverse transcription.
The BC1 RNA gene is a master gene for ID element amplification in rodent genomes, and its transcripts are capable of efficient self-primed reverse transcription. This self-priming ability is due to the secondary structure of the 3'-unique region of the BC1 RNA gene transcript. The observation that a gene actively amplified throughout rodent evolution makes a RNA capable of efficient self-primed reverse transcription suggests that self-priming is a key feature in establishing the BC1 RNA gene as a master gene for ID element amplification.

title: The DNA Methylome of Human Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
text:
DNA methylation plays a crucial role in various biological processes in human health and disease, and recent technological advancements have enabled the analysis of the entire genome (methylome) of human cells with unprecedented resolution. In this study, we used whole-genome bisulfite sequencing at 24.7-fold coverage (12.3-fold per strand) to generate a comprehensive methylome dataset of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a single Asian individual. We found that approximately 68% of CpG sites and less than 0.2% of non-CpG cytosine sites were methylated, indicating that non-CpG cytosine methylation is relatively rare in human PBMCs.
Our analysis of the PBMC methylome revealed a rich epigenomic landscape, including 20 distinct genomic features such as regulatory, protein-coding, non-coding, RNA-coding, and repeat sequences. Integration of our methylome data with the individual's genome sequence enabled the identification of 599 haploid differentially methylated regions (hDMRs) covering 287 genes. Of these, 76 genes had hDMRs within 2 kilobases of their transcriptional start sites, and over 80% of these genes displayed allele-specific expression (ASE). These findings demonstrate that allele-specific methylation (ASM) is a recurrent phenomenon in human PBMCs and is highly correlated with ASE. This study provides a comprehensive resource for future epigenomic research and confirms the use of new sequencing technology as a paradigm for large-scale epigenomics studies.

title: The human myelin basic protein gene is included within a 179-kilobase transcription unit: expression in the immune and central nervous systems.
text: Two human Golli (gene expressed in the oligodendrocyte lineage) - MBP (myelin basic protein) cDNAs have been isolated from a human oligodendroglioma cell line, allowing for the determination of the entire structure of the human Golli-MBP gene. The Golli-MBP gene, which consists of 10 exons, including seven that make up the MBP gene, is approximately 179 kilobases (kb) in length and contains two transcription start sites, resulting in the production of alternatively spliced transcripts. These transcripts are expressed in various tissues, including the fetal thymus, spleen, and human B-cell and macrophage cell lines, as well as in fetal spinal cord. These findings suggest that the expression of exons encoding the autoimmunogen/encephalitogen MBP in the central nervous system is linked to cells and tissues of the immune system through the normal expression of the Golli-MBP gene. Additionally, the conservation of this genetic locus among species implies that the MBP transcription unit is an integral part of the Golli transcription unit and that this structural arrangement is important for the genetic function and/or regulation of these genes.

title: Targeting A20 Decreases Glioma Stem Cell Survival and Tumor Growth
text: Glioblastomas, a deadly form of cancer, are maintained by a functional cellular hierarchy controlled by self-renewing glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs). GSCs are regulated by unique molecular pathways compared to the bulk tumor, making them potential therapeutic targets. We discovered that A20 (TNFAIP3), a regulator of cell survival and the NF-κB pathway, is overexpressed in GSCs at both the mRNA and protein levels compared to non-stem glioblastoma cells. To investigate the functional significance of A20 in GSCs, we used lentiviral-mediated delivery of short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to target A20 expression. Inhibiting A20 expression decreased GSC growth and survival by mechanisms involving decreased cell-cycle progression and decreased phosphorylation of p65/RelA. Elevated levels of A20 in GSCs contributed to their resistance to apoptosis, as GSCs were less susceptible to TNFalpha-induced cell death than matched non-stem glioma cells, but A20 knockdown sensitized GSCs to TNFalpha-mediated apoptosis. The decreased survival of GSCs upon A20 knockdown also impaired their ability to self-renew in primary and secondary neurosphere formation assays. Furthermore, mice bearing human glioma xenografts had increased survival when A20 was targeted. In silico analysis of a glioma patient genomic database revealed that A20 overexpression and amplification are inversely correlated with survival. These findings suggest that A20 contributes to glioma maintenance through its effects on the GSC subpopulation. Although inactivating mutations in A20 are found in lymphoma, similar mutations have not been identified in glioma genomic sequencing, and our data suggest that A20 may function as a tumor enhancer in glioma through promotion of GSC survival. Therefore, A20 anticancer therapies should be approached with caution, as their effects may differ depending on the tumor type.

title: Efficient targeting of expressed and silent genes in human ESCs and iPSCs using zinc-finger nucleases
text:
Harnessing the full potential of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) requires efficient methods for genetic modification. However, current techniques for generating cell type–specific lineage reporters and reliable tools for disrupting, repairing, or overexpressing genes through gene targeting are limited and seldom used. To address this challenge, we have developed a highly efficient method for targeting three genes in human pluripotent cells using zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN)–mediated genome editing.
First, we used ZFNs specific to the OCT4 (POU5F1) locus to generate OCT4-eGFP reporter cells that allow for monitoring the pluripotent state of hESCs. Next, we introduced a transgene into the AAVS1 locus to create a robust drug-inducible overexpression system in hESCs. Finally, we demonstrated the ability to target non-expressed genes in hESCs and hiPSCs by using ZFNs to generate reporter cells for the PITX3 gene.
In summary, our findings provide a significant improvement in the efficiency of genetic modification in hESCs and hiPSCs, paving the way for further research and potential therapeutic applications.

title: Empirical Bayesian models for analysing molecular serotyping microarrays
text:
Microarrays offer a promising platform for molecular diagnostics, allowing for the simultaneous detection of numerous biomarkers in highly multiplexed assays. In the context of infectious diseases, microarrays can be used to identify the presence of specific biomarkers, such as pneumococcal serotypes, in clinical samples. In this study, we applied a microarray designed for molecular serotyping of Streptococcus pneumoniae to identify the presence of any one of 91 known pneumococcal serotypes in DNA extracts. The microarray incorporated oligonucleotide probes for all known capsular polysaccharide synthesis genes, and a statistical analysis of the microarray intensity data was performed to determine the presence of specific serotypes or combinations of serotypes in each sample.
To address the challenges of analyzing microarray data in the context of infectious diseases, we propose an empirical Bayesian model for calculating the probabilities of combinations of serotypes based on the microarray data. This model takes into account the dependencies between serotypes, which are induced by genes they have in common, as well as by homologous genes that are similar in sequence. To improve the accuracy of the analysis, additional probes are included on the microarray for serotypes that are very similar in capsular gene composition. The proposed model is applied to experimental data from samples containing individual serotypes and samples containing combinations of serotypes with known levels of abundance. The results demonstrate the ability of the model to accurately detect the presence of individual serotypes and combinations of serotypes, as well as to estimate the relative abundance of each serotype within a combination.
The proposed model is based on an empirical Bayesian approach, which allows for the incorporation of prior knowledge about the relative abundance of serotypes in a sample. This prior knowledge can be used to inform the analysis and improve the accuracy of the results. The model also takes into account the dependencies between serotypes, which can affect the accuracy of the analysis. By accounting for these dependencies, the model can provide a more accurate estimate of the relative abundance of each serotype within a combination.
The results of the analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in detecting the presence of individual serotypes and combinations of serotypes in microarray data. In all but two cases, the model was able to uniquely determine the presence of individual serotypes in experimental samples. Additionally, the model was able to detect the presence of combinations of serotypes, and provide an approximate measure of the percentage abundance of each serotype within the combination. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed model for analyzing microarray data in the context of infectious diseases.

title: Bayesian measures of model complexity and fit
text: In this work, we address the problem of comparing complex hierarchical models, where the number of parameters is not explicitly defined. By employing an information-theoretic argument, we derive a measure, pD, for the effective number of parameters in a model, which represents the difference between the posterior mean of the deviance and the deviance at the posterior means of the parameters of interest. Specifically, pD approximates the trace of the product of Fisher's information and the posterior covariance, which in normal models corresponds to the trace of the 'hat' matrix projecting observations onto fitted values. We explore the properties of pD in exponential families and demonstrate its use as a Bayesian measure of fit or adequacy. Moreover, we propose a diagnostic plot of deviance residuals against leverages, which provides insight into the contributions of individual observations to the fit and complexity of the model. Finally, we introduce a deviance information criterion, which combines pD with the posterior mean deviance, and provide an approximate decision-theoretic justification for this measure. The procedure is illustrated through examples, and comparisons are made with alternative Bayesian and classical proposals. Throughout, we emphasize that the quantities required are trivial to compute in a Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis.

title: Simplifying likelihood ratios
text: Likelihood ratios are a valuable tool for assessing the accuracy of diagnostic tests, yet they are often overlooked due to the complexity of interpreting them. Converting between "probability" and "odds" of disease requires a calculator, which can be a barrier for clinicians at the bedside. This article proposes a simpler method of interpreting likelihood ratios, eliminating the need for calculators, nomograms, or conversions to "odds" of disease. With this approach, clinicians can make more informed diagnostic decisions in real-time. Several examples demonstrate how this method can be applied in practice.

title: induction of early IFN-inducible genes in the absence of type
text: Upon recognition of influenza virus by TLR7, plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) produce copious amounts of type I interferon (IFN-alpha). Synthetic TLR7 ligands, such as Flu and CL097, can induce the maturation of pDCs, as evidenced by the upregulation of costimulatory molecules and the production of proinflammatory cytokines, although they only elicit low-level production of IFN-alpha. To elucidate the TLR7 signaling mechanisms in pDCs and how these differing profiles are generated, we investigated the effects of 2 TLR7 ligands on the activation of blood-isolated pDCs and the human GEN2.2 pDC cell line. Type I IFN production by pDCs is closely correlated with the translocation of interferon regulatory factor 7 (IRF7) into the nucleus, which is distinctly influenced by the 2 TLR7 ligands. Notably, despite the rapid expression of IFN-inducible genes, such as mxa, cxcl10, and trail, within 4 hours of stimulation, this expression is independent of type I IFN and is instead controlled by STAT1 phosphorylation, which is strictly dependent on the PI3K-p38MAPK signaling pathway. This novel signaling pathway enables pDCs to promptly respond to viral infection during the early stages of the innate immune response.

title: Arteriolar function in visceral adipose tissue is impaired in human obesity.
text:
Objective:
This study aimed to investigate the relationship between adipose tissue phenotype and depot-specific microvascular function in obese individuals.
Methods and Results:
In 30 obese subjects (age 42±11 years, body mass index 46±11 kg/m(2)) undergoing bariatric surgery, we collected visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue and characterized depot-specific adipose phenotypes. We evaluated the vasomotor function of the adipose microvasculature using videomicroscopy of small arterioles (75-250 μm) isolated from different fat compartments. Endothelium-dependent, acetylcholine-mediated vasodilation was significantly impaired in visceral arterioles compared to the subcutaneous depot (P<0.001 by ANOVA). Nonendothelium-dependent responses to papaverine and nitroprusside were similar. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase inhibition with N(ω)-nitro-l-arginine methyl ester reduced subcutaneous vasodilation, but had no effect on severely blunted visceral arteriolar responses. Visceral fat exhibited greater expression of proinflammatory, oxidative stress-related, hypoxia-induced, and proangiogenic genes; increased activated macrophage populations; and had a higher capacity for cytokine production ex vivo.
Conclusions:
Our findings provide clinical evidence that the visceral microenvironment may be intrinsically toxic to arterial health, providing a potential mechanism by which visceral adiposity burden is linked to atherosclerotic vascular disease. Our findings also support the evolving concept that both adipose tissue quality and quantity may play significant roles in shaping cardiovascular phenotypes in human obesity.

title: Common Carotid Intima Media Thickness and Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index Correlate with Local but Not Global Atheroma Burden: A Cross Sectional Study Using Whole Body Magnetic Resonance Angiography
text:
BACKGROUND: Common carotid intima media thickness (CIMT) and ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI) are commonly used as surrogate markers of atherosclerosis, but their correlation with global atherosclerotic burden has not been well-established. In this study, we compare CIMT and ABPI with atheroma burden as measured by whole body magnetic resonance angiography (WB-MRA) in patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease (PAD).
METHODS: We recruited 50 patients with symptomatic PAD and measured CIMT using ultrasound during rest and exercise. We also performed ABPI using the ankle-brachial pressure index. WB-MRA was performed in a 1.5T MRI scanner using 4 volume acquisitions with a divided dose of intravenous gadolinium gadoterate meglumine (Dotarem, Guerbet, FR). The WB-MRA data was divided into 31 anatomical arterial segments, and each segment was scored according to the degree of luminal narrowing. The segment scores were summed to calculate a standardized atheroma score.
RESULTS: Our results showed a high standardized atheroma score of 39.5±11, indicating significant atherosclerotic burden. CIMT showed a positive correlation with the whole body atheroma score (β = 0.32, p = 0.045), but this was primarily due to its strong correlation with the neck and thoracic segments (β = 0.42, p = 0.01). In contrast, ABPI correlated with the whole body atheroma score (β = -0.39, p = 0.012), which was due to a strong correlation with the ilio-femoral vessels (β = -0.45, p = 0.005). On multiple linear regression analysis, no correlation was found between CIMT and global atheroma burden (β = 0.13, p = 0.45), while the correlation between ABPI and atheroma burden persisted (β = -0.45, p = 0.005).
CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that ABPI, but not CIMT, correlates with global atheroma burden as measured by WB-MRA in patients with symptomatic PAD. This correlation is primarily due to the strong correlation between ABPI and ilio-femoral atheroma burden. These results suggest that ABPI may be a more useful marker than CIMT for assessing global atherosclerotic burden in patients with PAD.

title: Loss of immune escape mutations during persistent HCV infection in pregnancy enhances replication of vertically transmitted viruses
text: Globally, approximately 1% of pregnant women are persistently infected with the hepatitis C virus (HCV). Mother-to-child transmission of HCV occurs in 3-5% of pregnancies and accounts for most new childhood infections. HCV-specific CD8(+) cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) play a crucial role in clearing acute HCV infections, but in the majority of persistent infections, these cells become dysfunctional or recognize mutant viruses that evade immune recognition. Increased HCV replication during pregnancy may further impair HCV-specific CTLs, limiting their ability to selectively pressure persistent viruses. To investigate this possibility, we analyzed the circulating viral quasispecies during and after consecutive pregnancies in two women. Our findings revealed a loss of escape mutations in HLA class I epitopes during pregnancy, which was associated with the emergence of more fit viruses. CTL selective pressure was reimposed after childbirth, at which point escape mutations in these epitopes predominated in the quasispecies, and viral load decreased significantly. Importantly, the viruses transmitted perinatally were those with enhanced fitness due to the reversion of escape mutations. Our results suggest that the immunoregulatory changes of pregnancy reduce CTL selective pressure on HCV class I epitopes, thereby facilitating vertical transmission of viruses with optimized replicative fitness.

title: The journey of developing hematopoietic stem cells.
text: During embryonic development, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) undergo a complex process of maturation and self-renewal, involving multiple anatomical sites. HSC precursors emerge from mesoderm and must mature into functional HSCs through a series of divisions, while migrating through various embryonic niches that provide essential signals for their establishment and self-renewal ability. To generate HSCs from embryonic stem cells, these processes must be recapitulated in vitro. Understanding the interactions between developing HSCs and their niches is crucial for expanding and generating HSCs in the laboratory, with potential clinical applications.

title: The sacroiliac joint in the spondyloarthropathies.
text: The term "spondyloarthropathy" (SpA) encompasses a group of related inflammatory joint diseases that share common clinical features and a unique association with the major histocompatibility complex class I molecule HLA-B27. Five subgroups can be distinguished: ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and undifferentiated SpA. The sacroiliac joints are predominantly affected in SpA, with the most prominent involvement in ankylosing spondylitis, where early disease often affects the joints. Advanced imaging techniques, such as dynamic magnetic resonance imaging, have helped to overcome diagnostic challenges in the early stages of sacroiliac joint inflammation. Recent studies have also examined the inflammatory infiltrates in the sacroiliac joints, revealing the presence of T cells, macrophages, and various cytokines. Biopsy specimens obtained through guided computed tomography have shown the absence of reactive arthritis-associated bacteria. The underlying pathogenesis of SpA and the reason for its preference for the sacroiliac joints remain unclear, and the genetic background of SpA and its relationship to initial bacterial infections are still being investigated. In chronic disease, autoimmune mechanisms may play a more significant role.

title: A rapid method for extraction of cotton (Gossypium spp.) genomic DNA suitable for RFLP or PCR analysis
text: Isolation of high-quality genomic DNA from Gossypium (cotton) species can be challenging due to the presence of high levels of polysaccharides, oxidizable quinones, and other interfering compounds. We have developed a procedure that consistently yields genomic DNA of adequate size and quality for RFLP (restriction fragment length polymorphism) and PCR (polymerase chain reaction) analysis, as well as for most common cloning applications. To achieve this, we employ a combination of antioxidants, phenol-binding reagents, and phenol oxidase inhibitors throughout the procedure. Additionally, we eliminate most polysaccharides by isolating the nuclei early in the process.

title: Cross sectional stature and weight reference curves for the UK, 1990.
text: The existing reference curves for stature and weight in the UK, first published in 1966, have been in use for decades despite growing concerns that they may not accurately reflect the growth patterns of contemporary British children. To address these concerns, we have estimated new reference curves using the most recent data from seven sources, covering the age range of birth to 20 years. These curves are nationally representative and were created using Cole's LMS method, which provides efficient estimates of conventional centiles and a good fit to the data. Our analysis reveals significant differences between the new curves and the currently used curves at key ages for both stature and weight. Given the concerns expressed about the existing curves and the differences between them and the new curves, we propose that the curves presented here should replace the existing UK reference curves.

title: The suture provides a niche for mesenchymal stem cells of craniofacial bones
text: Bone tissue undergoes constant renewal, supported by stem cells, with recent studies revealing that perivascular mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) contribute to the turnover of long bones. However, the identity and regulatory environment of craniofacial-bone MSCs, which are flat bones derived from a distinct embryonic origin than long bones, remain unknown. In this study, we identify Gli1+ cells within the suture mesenchyme as the primary MSC population for craniofacial bones. These cells are not associated with blood vessels, give rise to all craniofacial bones in the adult, and are activated during injury repair. Gli1+ cells are typical MSCs in vitro, and ablation of these cells leads to craniosynostosis and arrested skull growth, indicating that they are an essential stem cell population. Our findings suggest that craniofacial sutures provide a unique niche for MSCs for craniofacial bone homeostasis and repair.

title: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to the dormant multipotent stem cell in the mammalian heart
text:
Cardiac neural crest-derived cells (cNCCs) have the ability to form clonal spheroids in serum-free medium, which express markers of undifferentiated neural precursor cells, including nestin, Musashi-1, and multi-drug resistance transporter gene 1. Following differentiation, these markers are lost and replaced by the expression of neuron-, glial-, smooth muscle cell–, or cardiomyocyte-specific proteins. cNCCs transplanted into chick embryos migrate to the truncus arteriosus and cardiac outflow tract and contribute to the development of dorsal root ganglia, spinal nerves, and aortic smooth muscle cells.
Using double transgenic mice encoding protein 0–Cre/Floxed-EGFP, the lineage of cNCCs in the fetal myocardium was investigated. Undifferentiated cells expressed GATA-binding protein 4 and nestin, but not actinin, whereas differentiated cells were identified as cardiomyocytes. These findings suggest that cNCCs migrate into the heart, where they remain as dormant multipotent stem cells, and under the right conditions, differentiate into cardiomyocytes and typical neural crest-derived cells, including neurons, glia, and smooth muscle.

title: The mammalian target of rapamycin signaling pathway mediates epileptogenesis in a model of temporal lobe epilepsy.
text: Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying epileptogenesis is crucial for developing more effective treatments for epilepsy. Recently, we discovered that the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling pathway plays a role in epileptogenesis, and mTOR inhibitors can prevent epilepsy in a mouse model of tuberous sclerosis complex. To investigate the potential role of mTOR in a rat model of temporal lobe epilepsy induced by status epilepticus, we examined the expression of phospho-S6 (P-S6) in the hippocampus and neocortex after acute kainate-induced seizures. Our results showed that there was a biphasic activation of the mTOR pathway, with an initial rise in P-S6 expression starting 1 hour after seizure onset, peaking 3-6 hours later, and returning to baseline by 24 hours in both the hippocampus and neocortex. However, a second increase in P-S6 expression was observed in the hippocampus only, starting at 3 days after seizure onset, peaking 5-10 days later, and persisting for several weeks. This second phase of mTOR activation correlated with the development of chronic epileptogenesis in the hippocampus. Treatment with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin before kainate injection blocked both the acute and chronic phases of seizure-induced mTOR activation and reduced kainate-induced neuronal cell death, neurogenesis, mossy fiber sprouting, and the development of spontaneous epilepsy. Late treatment with rapamycin after termination of status epilepticus blocked the chronic phase of mTOR activation and reduced mossy fiber sprouting and epilepsy but not neurogenesis or neuronal death. These findings suggest that mTOR signaling plays a critical role in epileptogenesis in the kainate rat model and that mTOR inhibitors have potential antiepileptogenic effects in this model.

title: Acute administration of recombinant Angiopoietin-1 ameliorates multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome and improves survival in murine sepsis.
text:
Introduction:
Endothelial activation leading to vascular barrier breakdown plays a crucial role in the pathophysiology of multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in sepsis. Recent evidence suggests that the function of the vessel-protective factor Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1), a ligand of the endothelial-specific Tie2 receptor, is inhibited by its antagonist Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2) during sepsis. To investigate whether reversing the effects of sepsis-induced suppression of Ang-1 and elevation of Ang-2 could protect against MODS, we aimed to evaluate the efficacy of intravenous injection of recombinant human (rh) Ang-1 in a murine sepsis model.
Methods:
Polymicrobiological abdominal sepsis was induced in mice through cecal ligation and puncture (CLP). Mice were treated with either 1 μg of intravenous rhAng-1 or control buffer immediately after CLP induction and every 8 hours thereafter. Sham-operated animals served as time-matched controls.
Results:
Compared to buffer-treated controls, rhAng-1-treated septic mice exhibited significant improvements in various hematologic and biochemical indicators of MODS. Additionally, rhAng-1 stabilized endothelial barrier function, as evidenced by inhibition of protein leakage from lung capillaries into the alveolar compartment. Histological analysis revealed that rhAng-1 treatment attenuated leukocyte infiltration in lungs and kidneys of septic mice, likely due to reduced endothelial adhesion molecule expression in rhAng-1-treated mice. Finally, the protective effects of rhAng-1 treatment were reflected by an improved survival time in a lethal CLP model.
Conclusion:
In a clinically relevant murine sepsis model, intravenous rhAng-1 treatment alone was sufficient to significantly improve a variety of sepsis-associated organ dysfunctions and survival time, likely by preserving endothelial barrier function. Further studies are needed to pave the road for clinical application of this therapy concept.

title: Mechanisms linking obesity to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes
text: Obesity is intricately linked to an elevated risk of developing insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. In obese individuals, the adipose tissue produces and releases an excessive amount of non-esterified fatty acids, glycerol, hormones, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and other factors that contribute to the emergence of insulin resistance. When insulin resistance is concurrent with dysfunction of the pancreatic islet β-cells, which are responsible for secreting insulin, the inability to regulate blood glucose levels inevitably ensues. The dysfunction of β-cells is a crucial factor in the development and progression of type 2 diabetes. This understanding has prompted extensive research into the molecular and genetic underpinnings of the disease, as well as the development of novel approaches to its prevention and treatment.

title: Tracking the fate of glomerular epithelial cells in vivo using serial multiphoton imaging in novel mouse models with fluorescent lineage tags
text: Podocytes play a crucial role in maintaining the health of the glomerular filter, but their study in the intact kidney has been challenging due to technical limitations. Here, we report the development of serial multiphoton microscopy (MPM) to visualize the motion of podocytes and parietal epithelial cells (PECs) in vivo over several days. In podocin-GFP mice, we observed sporadic multicellular clusters of podocytes and their migration into the parietal Bowman's capsule after unilateral ureteral ligation. Using cell-specific expression of CFP, GFP, YFP, or RFP in podocin-confetti mice, we tracked the simultaneous migration of multiple podocytes. In PEPCK-GFP mice, serial MPM revealed PEC-to-podocyte migration and nanotubule connections. Our findings support a highly dynamic glomerular environment and cellular composition, highlighting the potential of this new approach to advance our understanding of glomerular injury and regeneration.

title: CTCF binding at the H19 imprinting control region mediates maternally inherited higher-order chromatin conformation to restrict enhancer access to Igf2.
text: The H19 imprinting control region (ICR) is believed to regulate the silencing of the maternally inherited Igf2 allele through a CTCF-dependent chromatin insulator. The ICR has been shown to interact with a silencer region in Igf2, as well as a differentially methylated region (DMR)1, but the mechanisms by which CTCF influences this chromatin loop and prevents the physical access of distal enhancers to Igf2 are not fully understood. To investigate, we performed systematic chromosome conformation capture (3C) analysis across the Igf2/H19 region spanning over 160 kb, identifying sequences that interact physically with the distal enhancers and the ICR. Our findings reveal that, on the paternal chromosome, enhancers interact with the Igf2 promoters, whereas on the maternal allele, CTCF binding within the H19 ICR prevents this interaction. CTCF binding in the maternal ICR regulates its interaction with matrix attachment region (MAR)3 and DMR1 at Igf2, forming a tight loop around the maternal Igf2 locus, which may contribute to its silencing. Mutation of CTCF binding sites in the H19 ICR leads to loss of CTCF binding and de novo methylation of a CTCF target site within Igf2 DMR1, suggesting that CTCF can coordinate regional epigenetic marks. This comprehensive 3C analysis of an imprinting cluster reveals that CTCF plays a crucial role in the epigenetic regulation of higher-order chromatin structure and gene silencing over long distances in the genome.

title: De novo assembly of a PML nuclear subcompartment occurs through multiple pathways and induces telomere elongation.
text:
Telomerase-negative tumor cells employ an alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) mechanism, which involves DNA recombination and repair to maintain their proliferative potential. A distinctive cytological feature of this process is the accumulation of promyelocytic leukemia (PML) nuclear protein at telomeric DNA, forming ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs). In this study, we investigated the de novo formation of telomeric PML nuclear subcompartments by recruiting APB protein components. Our findings reveal that functionally distinct proteins can efficiently initiate the formation of bona fide APBs through a self-organizing and self-propagating manner. These proteins include:
1. PML and Sp100, which are the constitutive components of PML nuclear bodies.
2. Telomere repeat binding factors 1 and 2 (TRF1 and TRF2, respectively), which are involved in telomere maintenance.
3. The DNA repair protein NBS1 and the SUMO E3 ligase MMS21, as well as the isolated SUMO1 domain, which interacts with another protein factor.
By contrast, repair factors Rad9, Rad17, and Rad51 were less efficient in APB nucleation but were recruited to preassembled APBs. The artificially created APBs induced telomeric extension through a DNA repair mechanism, as inferred from their colocalization with sites of non-replicative DNA synthesis and histone H2A.X phosphorylation, and an increase in telomere repeat length. These activities were absent after recruitment of the APB factors to a pericentric locus, indicating that APBs are functional intermediates of the ALT pathway.

title: Effects of an opal termination codon preceding the nsP4 gene sequence in the O'Nyong-Nyong virus genome on Anopheles gambiae infectivity.
text: The RNA of the alphavirus encodes four nonstructural proteins, nsP1, nsP2, nsP3, and nsP4. When translation terminates at an opal termination codon between nsP3 and nsP4, the polyprotein P123 is produced. However, when translational readthrough occurs or the opal termination codon is replaced by a sense codon in the virus genome, the polyprotein P1234 is produced instead. Evolutionary pressures have maintained the genomic sequence encoding both the stop codon (opal) and an open reading frame (arginine) in the O'nyong-nyong virus (ONNV) genome, suggesting that both are important. ONNV can replicate in both vertebrate and invertebrate hosts, and the predominance of a particular codon at this locus in the viral quasispecies may be determined by alternate replication in these hosts. To investigate the functional significance of the opal stop codon in ONNV, we created mutants with an opal, ochre, or amber stop codon replacing the arginine between nsP3 and nsP4. The presence of the opal stop codon nearly doubled the infectivity of ONNV in mosquitoes, and dissemination began earlier in mosquitoes infected with the opal virus. Although sequence analysis indicated that the codon usage at this position corresponded with that of the virus administered in the blood meal, these results suggest that the primary fitness advantage provided to ONNV by the presence of the opal codon is related to mosquito infectivity.

title: Down-regulation of a host microRNA by a Herpesvirus saimiri noncoding RNA.
text:
Herpesvirus saimiri-transformed T cells express seven uncharacterized viral non-coding RNAs (HSURs). We identified conserved sequences in HSURs 1 and 2 that may serve as binding sites for three host-cell microRNAs (miRNAs). Using coimmunoprecipitation experiments, we confirmed that HSURs 1 and 2 interact with the predicted miRNAs in virally transformed T cells. Surprisingly, we found that the abundance of one of these miRNAs, miR-27, is significantly reduced in transformed cells, leading to altered expression of miR-27 target genes. Our results demonstrate that HSUR 1 directs the degradation of mature miR-27 in a sequence-specific and binding-dependent manner, illustrating a novel viral strategy for manipulating host-cell gene expression via the miRNA pathway.

title: HTRF: A Technology Tailored for Drug Discovery –A Review of Theoretical Aspects and Recent Applications
text: Homogeneous Time-Resolved Fluorescence (HTRF) is the most commonly employed generic assay technology for measuring analytes in a homogeneous format, making it the ideal platform for drug target studies in high-throughput screening (HTS). This technology combines Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) with Time-Resolved measurement (TR). In TR-FRET assays, a signal is generated when a donor and acceptor molecule are in close proximity, resulting in fluorescence resonance energy transfer. By using dual-wavelength detection, buffer and media interference are significantly reduced, and the final signal is proportional to the extent of product formation. HTRF is known for its sensitivity and robustness, allowing it to be miniaturized into 384 and 1536-well plate formats. This technology has been applied to various antibody-based assays, including GPCR signaling (cAMP and IP-One), kinases, cytokines, and biomarkers, as well as protein-protein, protein-peptide, and protein-DNA/RNA interactions. Since its introduction to the drug-screening field over a decade ago, HTRF has been used to expedite the study of GPCRs, kinases, new biomarkers, protein-protein interactions, and other targets of interest. Additionally, it has been utilized as an alternative method for bioprocess monitoring. The first-generation HTRF technology, which uses Europium cryptate as a fluorescence donor, was improved in 2008 with the introduction of a second-generation donor, Terbium cryptate (Tb), enhancing screening performance. Tb possesses different photophysical properties compared to Europium, including increased quantum yield and a higher molar extinction coefficient. Moreover, it can serve as a donor fluorophore to green-emitting fluors due to its multiple emission peaks, including one at 490 nm. All Terbium HTRF assays can be read on the same HTRF-compatible instruments as Europium HTRF assays. In summary, HTRF is a highly sensitive and robust technology for detecting molecular interactions in vitro, making it widely used for both primary and secondary screening phases of drug development. This review covers the general principles of HTRF and its current applications in drug discovery.

title: Chk1 inhibits replication factory activation but allows dormant origin firing in existing factories
text: Replication origins are licensed for entry into S phase by the loading of MCM2-7 hexamers prior to the S phase. However, only approximately 10% of licensed origins are normally utilized in S phase, with the remaining ones remaining dormant. When DNA replication is inhibited, dormant origins nearby initiate to ensure that all DNA is eventually replicated. In contrast, replicative stress activates ataxia telangiectasia and rad-3-related (ATR) and Chk1 checkpoint kinases, which inhibit origin firing. In this study, we demonstrate that at low levels of replication stress, ATR/Chk1 predominantly suppresses the initiation of new replication factories by inhibiting the activation of new replication factories, thereby reducing the number of active factories. Concurrently, inhibition of replication fork progression allows dormant origins to initiate within existing replication factories. The inhibition of new factory activation by ATR/Chk1 therefore redirects replication towards active factories where forks are inhibited and away from regions that have yet to start replication. This minimizes the deleterious consequences of fork stalling and prevents similar problems from arising in unreplicated regions of the genome.

title: Fra-1 protooncogene regulates IL-6 expression in macrophages and promotes the generation of M2d macrophages
text:
The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a pivotal role in the growth and progression of tumor cells. As the primary source of inflammation within the TME, M2d macrophages are influenced by the TME to adopt an immunosuppressive role that fosters tumor metastasis and progression. Fra-1, a transcription factor, forms heterodimers with Jun partners and regulates gene expression. Fra-1 has been implicated in tumorigenesis and progression, yet its function in the differentiation of M2d macrophages remains poorly understood. Our study aimed to investigate the role of Fra-1 in the differentiation of M2d macrophages.
We co-cultured 4T1 mammary carcinoma cells with RAW264.7 macrophage cells and observed that the 4T1 cells directed the differentiation of RAW264.7 cells into M2d macrophages. We found that the 4T1 cells induced the overexpression of Fra-1 in RAW264.7 cells, which then bound to the interleukin 6 (IL-6) promoter to increase the production of IL-6. IL-6 acted in an autocrine manner to further skew the differentiation of RAW264.7 macrophages into M2d macrophages.
Our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying the generation of M2d macrophages and offer potential strategies for reversing their immune-suppressive effects to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapeutic approaches.

title: Analysis of SiO2 nanoparticles binding proteins in rat blood and brain homogenate
text: A variety of nanoparticles, including titanium oxide (TiO2), zinc oxide, aluminum oxide, gold oxide, silver oxide, iron oxide, and silica oxide, are commonly used in various products such as chemicals, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and electronics. Recently, SiO2 nanoparticles have gained attention due to their inert toxicity profile and lack of association with irreversible toxicological changes in animal models. As a result, exposure to SiO2 nanoparticles is increasing. SiO2 nanoparticles are used in a wide range of applications, including strengthening fillers for construction materials and non-toxic platforms for biomedical applications such as drug delivery and theragnostics. However, recent in vitro experiments have suggested that SiO2 nanoparticles may be cytotoxic. To investigate this further, we analyzed the protein corona on the surface of SiO2 nanoparticles in the blood and brain of rats. We found that higher numbers of proteins were adsorbed onto smaller SiO2 nanoparticles (20 nm) than larger ones (100 nm) regardless of charge. Additionally, more proteins were found on arginine-coated positively charged SiO2 nanoparticles than on negatively charged ones. The proteins identified in the corona were further analyzed using ClueGO, a Cytoscape plugin for protein ontology and biological interaction pathways. These findings suggest that proteins bound to the surface of nanoparticles may play a role in complex biological processes and affect functional and conformational properties.

title: Inferring nucleosome positions with their histone mark annotation from ChIP data
text:
MOTIVATION
The nucleosome is the fundamental repeating unit of chromatin, consisting of two copies each of the four core histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4, and approximately 147 base pairs of DNA. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) of the histone proteins, such as methylation or acetylation, play a crucial role in chromatin dynamics and gene regulation. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) is a powerful tool for genome-wide analysis of histone modifications, but its interpretation requires sophisticated computational methods.
RESULTS
We present NucHunter, an algorithm that leverages ChIP-seq data for multiple histone modifications to predict positioned nucleosomes and their associated histone modification patterns. NucHunter provides annotations of nucleosomes with histone modification intensities, enabling the inference of nucleosomal states and their correlations with underlying genomic features and chromatin-related processes, such as transcriptional start sites, enhancers, RNA polymerase II elongation, and chromatin-mediated repression. As a versatile tool, NucHunter can be used to predict positioned nucleosomes from a panel of histone modification ChIP-seq experiments and identify distinct histone modification patterns associated with different chromatin states.
AVAILABILITY
The software is freely available at <http://epigen.molgen.mpg.de/nuchunter/>.

title: Generation of large numbers of dendritic cells from mouse bone marrow cultures supplemented with granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor
text: Bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DCs) are known to arise from the bone marrow, but the process of their development is not fully understood. Recently, a method was described for inducing DC growth from MHC class II-negative precursors in marrow. The study found that removing nonadherent, newly formed granulocytes by gentle washes during the first 2-4 days of culture leaves behind proliferating clusters of cells that are loosely attached to a more firmly adherent "stroma." These clusters can be dislodged and isolated by 1-g sedimentation, and upon reculture, large numbers of DCs are released. The DCs are identified based on their distinct cell shape, ultrastructure, and repertoire of antigens, as detected with a panel of monoclonal antibodies. The DCs express high levels of MHC class II products and act as powerful accessory cells for initiating the mixed leukocyte reaction. The study also found that GM-CSF, but not macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF), is required for the generation of all three lineages of myeloid cells (granulocytes, macrophages, and DCs) from marrow precursors. This finding suggests that marrow progenitors can act as a major source of DCs, which could be useful for future molecular and clinical studies of this otherwise trace cell type.

title: Insulin action and resistance in obesity and type 2 diabetes
text: Nutritional excess is a significant predictor of type 2 diabetes, as it enhances insulin secretion but impairs insulin's metabolic actions in the liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue. However, the timing and mechanisms of these events during the development of obesity and diabetes remain poorly understood, highlighting a crucial knowledge gap in the field of metabolic disease. This Perspective reviews alternative viewpoints and recent findings on the temporal and mechanistic connections between hyperinsulinemia, obesity, and insulin resistance. Although significant attention has been focused on early stages of the insulin signaling cascade, insulin resistance in obesity appears to be primarily mediated downstream of these steps. New discoveries also reveal extensive metabolic cross-talk between the liver, adipose tissue, pancreas, and skeletal muscle, providing exciting opportunities for therapeutic intervention but also daunting challenges. Over the past 5 years, numerous advances have emerged, offering hope for the development of novel treatment strategies for type 2 diabetes.

title: Effect of lowering blood pressure on cardiovascular events and mortality in patients on dialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
text:
BACKGROUND: Patients undergoing dialysis are at a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular mortality and morbidity compared to the general population. Despite the known benefits of lowering blood pressure in the general population, there is limited evidence on the efficacy and safety of blood pressure reduction in dialysis patients. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effect of blood pressure lowering on cardiovascular outcomes in patients on dialysis.
METHODS: We systematically searched major medical databases, including Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, for randomized controlled trials published between 1950 and November 2008, without language restrictions. We extracted data from eligible trials that reported cardiovascular outcomes in patients on dialysis. A random effects model was used for meta-analysis.
FINDINGS: Our search yielded eight relevant trials, which provided data for 1679 patients and 495 cardiovascular events. We found that actively treated patients had a mean reduction of 4.5 mm Hg in systolic blood pressure and 2.3 mm Hg in diastolic blood pressure compared to controls. Blood pressure lowering treatment was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92; p=0.009), all-cause mortality (RR 0.80, 0.66-0.96; p=0.014), and cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.71, 0.50-0.99; p=0.044) compared to control regimens. These findings were consistent across various patient subgroups included in the studies.
INTERPRETATION: Our findings suggest that treatment with blood pressure-lowering agents should be considered a standard of care for individuals undergoing dialysis to reduce their high risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. These results provide strong evidence to support the use of blood pressure-lowering therapy in this population, and highlight the need for further research to determine the optimal blood pressure target and treatment approach.

title: Interaction of an adenovirus E3 14.7-kilodalton protein with a novel tumor necrosis factor alpha-inducible cellular protein containing leucine zipper domains.
text: Early region 3 (E3) of group C human adenoviruses (Ad) encodes several proteins that inhibit tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha) cytolysis, including the 14.7-kDa E3 protein (E3-14.7K) and a heterodimer consisting of two polypeptides of 10.4 and 14.5 kDa. To elucidate the mechanism by which these viral proteins inhibit TNF-alpha functions, the E3-14.7K protein was employed in a yeast two-hybrid screen to identify interacting proteins in HeLa cell cDNA library. A novel protein, designated FIP-2 (for 14.7K-interacting protein), was identified, which contains multiple leucine zipper domains without significant homology to known proteins. FIP-2 interacted with E3-14.7K both in vitro and in vivo, colocalized with Ad E3-14.7K in the cytoplasm, particularly near the nuclear membrane, and caused redistribution of the viral protein. FIP-2, by itself, does not induce cell death; however, it can reverse the protective effect of E3-14.7K on cell killing induced by overexpression of the intracellular domain of the 55-kDa TNF receptor or by RIP, a death protein involved in the TNF-alpha and Fas apoptosis pathways. Deletion analysis revealed that the reversal effect of FIP-2 depends on its interaction with E3-14.7K. Three major mRNA forms of FIP-2 have been detected in multiple human tissues, and expression of the transcripts was induced by TNF-alpha treatment in a time-dependent manner in two different cell lines. FIP-2 harbors consensus sequences for potential posttranslational modifications. These findings suggest that FIP-2 is one of the cellular targets for Ad E3-14.7K, and its mechanism of affecting cell death involves the TNF receptor, RIP, or a downstream molecule affected by either of these two molecules.

title: PML induces compaction, TRF2 depletion and DNA damage signaling at telomeres and promotes their alternative lengthening.
text: The alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) mechanism enables cancer cells to evade senescence and apoptosis in the absence of active telomerase. A distinctive feature of this pathway is the formation of ALT-associated promyelocytic leukemia (PML) nuclear bodies (APBs) at telomeres. To investigate the role of APBs in a human ALT cell line, we conducted an RNA interference (RNAi) screen using an automated 3D fluorescence microscopy platform and advanced 3D image analysis. We identified 29 proteins involved in APB formation, including those involved in telomere and chromatin organization, protein sumoylation, and DNA repair. By integrating and extending these findings, we found that APBs induce clustering of telomere repeats, telomere compaction, and depletion of the shelterin protein TRF2 (also known as TERF2). These changes correlate with the activation of a DNA damage response at telomeres in APBs, as evidenced by a significant enrichment of the phosphorylated form of the ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase. Therefore, we propose that APBs maintain telomere stability by inducing a DNA damage response in ALT-positive tumor cells through altering the telomeric chromatin state to activate ATM phosphorylation.

title: Gr-1+CD11b+ myeloid cells tip the balance of immune protection to tumor promotion in the premetastatic lung.
text: The mechanisms by which a primary tumor influences a distant organ before the arrival of tumor cells are still unclear. This study shows that the number of Gr-1+CD11b+ immature myeloid cells increases in the lungs of mice with mammary adenocarcinomas before tumor cell arrival. In the premetastatic lungs, these cells significantly reduce the production of interferon-gamma and increase pro-inflammatory cytokines. They also produce large amounts of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) and promote vascular remodeling. Deleting MMP9 normalizes the abnormal vasculature in the premetastatic lung and reduces lung metastasis. Our findings reveal a novel protumor mechanism for Gr-1+CD11b+ cells, which transforms the premature lung environment into an inflammatory and proliferative state, weakens immune protection, and promotes metastasis through aberrant vasculature formation. Therefore, inhibiting Gr-1+CD11b+ cells could normalize the premature lung environment, enhance host immunosurveillance, and inhibit tumor metastasis.

title: Activin/Nodal signalling in stem cells.
text: Activin/Nodal growth factors play a crucial role in regulating various biological processes throughout development, including early cell fate decisions, organogenesis, and adult tissue homeostasis. In this overview, we will delve into the mechanisms by which the Activin/Nodal signaling pathway influences stem cell function in these different stages of development. We will also explore recent findings that link Activin/Nodal signaling to pathological conditions, such as cancer stem cells and their potential as a therapeutic target. Furthermore, we will discuss open questions and future directions in understanding the role of Activin/Nodal signaling in stem cell self-renewal, differentiation, and proliferation.

title: Distinct RNA-dependent RNA polymerases are required for RNAi triggered by double-stranded RNA versus truncated transgenes in Paramecium tetraurelia
text: In many eukaryotes, RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs) play crucial roles in the RNA interference (RNAi) pathway. These enzymes are involved in the recognition and processing of aberrant transcripts, leading to the amplification of the silencing response. We have investigated the functions of RdRP genes from the ciliate Paramecium tetraurelia in both experimentally induced and endogenous mechanisms of gene silencing. In this organism, RNAi can be triggered by either high-copy, truncated transgenes or by directly feeding cells with double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Interestingly, the putatively functional RDR1 and RDR2 genes are required for the accumulation of both primary small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and a distinct class of small RNAs suggestive of secondary siRNAs. In contrast, a third gene with a highly divergent catalytic domain, RDR3, is necessary for siRNA accumulation when RNAi is triggered by truncated transgenes. Our data further suggest that RDR3 is involved in the accumulation of endogenous siRNAs and in the regulation of the surface antigen gene family. Notably, while only one of these genes is normally expressed in any clonal cell line, the knockdown of RDR3 leads to the co-expression of multiple antigens. These findings provide evidence for a functional specialization of Paramecium RdRP genes in distinct RNAi pathways operating during vegetative growth.

title: Mechanisms of Renal Cell Apoptosis Induced by Cyclosporine A: A Systematic Review of in vitro Studies
text: Background: Chronic cyclosporine A (CsA) nephrotoxicity (CCN) is a significant cause of chronic renal dysfunction, with no effective clinical interventions available. Objective: To investigate the mechanisms of renal cell apoptosis in CCN, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of all in vitro studies on this topic. Methods: We systematically searched Medline, Embase, and ISI databases from 1966 to July 2010, and evaluated the quality of in vitro studies using standardized criteria. We extracted data using the PICOS principles and synthesized the findings. Results: Our analysis revealed four main pathways involved in renal cell apoptosis induced by CsA in different cell species: 1) Upregulation of Fas and Fas-L expression, increase in FADD and apoptosis enzymes (caspase-2, -3, -4, -7, -8, -9, and -10); 2) Induction of oxidative stress and damage to the antioxidant defense system; 3) Downregulation of Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL; and 4) Increase in the expression of HERP, GRP78, and CHOP. Additionally, CsA was found to induce renal cell apoptosis and increase the expression of iNOS and p53 in cultured cells. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that at least four pathways may contribute to renal cell apoptosis induced by CsA in vitro, and these pathways may provide potential targets for interventions. However, these findings need to be confirmed in vivo.

title: Blood stem cells emerge from aortic endothelium by a novel type of cell transition
text:
The developmental history of haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) during embryonic development remains a topic of debate, particularly their potential relationship with vascular endothelial cells. The first anatomical site from which cells with long-term HSC potential have been isolated is the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM), specifically the vicinity of the dorsal aortic floor. However, there is ongoing debate about whether HSCs arise directly from the aortic floor into the dorsal aortic lumen or emerge within the underlying mesenchyme.
Using non-invasive, high-resolution imaging of live zebrafish embryos, we have shown that HSCs emerge directly from the aortic floor through a stereotyped process that does not involve cell division but rather the strong bending and egress of single endothelial cells from the aortic ventral wall into the sub-aortic space. These cells undergo a transformation into haematopoietic cells, which is polarized in both the dorso-ventral and rostro-caudal versus medio-lateral directions. Our results demonstrate that the aortic floor is haemogenic and that HSCs emerge from it into the sub-aortic space through a novel type of cell behavior, which we term an endothelial haematopoietic transition.
In contrast to the prevailing view that HSCs arise from the mesodermal layer, our findings suggest that they may instead originate from the endothelium of the aorta. This novel mechanism of HSC emergence has important implications for our understanding of haematopoiesis and the development of blood cells.

title: Probable person to person transmission of novel avian influenza A (H7N9) virus in Eastern China, 2013: epidemiological investigation
text:
Objective: To investigate the transmission of novel avian influenza H7N9 virus from person to person and its efficiency.
Design: Epidemiological investigations conducted after a family cluster of two patients with avian H7N9 infection in March 2013.
Setting: Wuxi, Eastern China.
Participants: Two patients, their close contacts, and relevant environments.
Methods: Samples from the patients and environments were collected and tested using real-time reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR), viral culture, and haemagglutination inhibition assay. Any contacts who developed illness had samples tested for avian H7N9 by rRT-PCR. Paired serum samples were obtained from contacts for serological testing by haemagglutination inhibition assays.
Main Outcomes Measures: Clinical data, exposure history before the onset of illnesses, and results of laboratory testing of pathogens and further analysis of sequences and phylogenetic tree to isolated strains.
Results: The index patient became ill five to six days after his last exposure to poultry. The second patient, his daughter aged 32, who provided unprotected bedside care in the hospital, had no known exposure to poultry. She developed symptoms six days after her last contact with her father. Two strains were isolated successfully from the two patients. Genome sequence and analyses of phylogenetic trees showed that both viruses were almost genetically identical. Forty-three close contacts of both patients were identified. One had mild illness but had negative results for avian H7N9 by rRT-PCR. All 43 close contacts tested negative for haemagglutination inhibition antibodies specific for avian H7N9.
Conclusions: The infection of the daughter probably resulted from contact with her father (the index patient) during unprotected exposure, suggesting that in this cluster the virus was able to transmit from person to person. The transmissibility was limited and non-sustainable.

title: Genetic Variation in the Interleukin-28B Gene Is Associated with Spontaneous Clearance and Progression of Hepatitis C Virus in Moroccan Patients
text:
Background: Genetic variations in the IL28B gene have been extensively linked to treatment outcomes, spontaneous clearance, and progression of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. The present study aimed to investigate the role of IL28B polymorphisms in predicting treatment outcomes and disease progression in a Moroccan population.
Methods: The study cohort consisted of 438 individuals, including 232 patients with persistent HCV infection (115 with mild chronic hepatitis and 117 with advanced liver disease), 68 individuals who had spontaneously cleared HCV, and 138 healthy controls. The IL28B SNPs rs12979860 and rs8099917 were genotyped using a TaqMan 5' allelic discrimination assay.
Results: The study found that the protective rs12979860-C and rs8099917-T alleles were more common in individuals who had spontaneously cleared HCV (77.9% and 95.6%, respectively). Individuals who had cleared HCV were found to be 4.69 times more likely to have the C/C genotype for the rs12979860 polymorphism and 3.55 times more likely to have the T/T genotype at rs8099917. Patients with advanced liver disease carried the rs12979860-T/T genotype more frequently than patients with mild chronic hepatitis C (odds ratio [OR] = 1.89, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.99-3.61, p = 0.0532) and this risk was even more pronounced when compared to healthy controls (OR = 4.27, 95% CI = 2.08-8.76, p = 0.0005). The rs8099917-G allele was also associated with advanced liver disease (OR = 2.34, 95% CI = 1.40-3.93, p = 0.0100).
Conclusions: The study findings suggest that polymorphisms near the IL28B gene play a significant role in both spontaneous clearance and progression of HCV infection in the Moroccan population. These results provide valuable insights into the genetic factors that contribute to HCV disease progression and may help inform personalized treatment strategies in the future.

title: CD127 expression inversely correlates with FoxP3 and suppressive function of human CD4+ T reg cells
text: Regulatory T (T reg) cells are crucial regulators of immune tolerance. While most T reg cells are defined by the expression of CD4, CD25, and the transcription factor FoxP3, these markers have proven challenging in identifying this specialized T cell subset in humans. Our study found that the IL-7 receptor (CD127) is down-regulated on a subset of CD4+ T cells in peripheral blood. We discovered that the majority of these cells are FoxP3+, including those with low or no CD25 expression. Using a combination of CD4, CD25, and CD127, we were able to obtain a highly purified population of T reg cells, accounting for significantly more cells than previously identified through other surface marker criteria. These cells were highly suppressive in functional suppressor assays, with cells separated based solely on CD4 and CD127 expression showing anergic properties. In fact, cells from this subset were as suppressive as the "classic" CD4+CD25hi T reg cell subset. Finally, our findings suggest that CD127 can be used as a biomarker for human T reg cells, supporting its use in quantifying T reg cell subsets in individuals with type 1 diabetes.

title: Environmental factors that influence the cutaneous production of vitamin D
text: Most vertebrates, including humans, derive the majority of their daily vitamin D requirements from incidental exposure to sunlight. During this exposure, the solar ultraviolet B photons (290-315 nm) penetrate the skin, where they catalyze the photolysis of 7-dehydrocholesterol into precholecalciferol. Subsequently, precholecalciferol undergoes a thermally induced rearrangement of its double bonds to form cholecalciferol. However, factors such as skin pigmentation, aging, and the application of sunscreen can diminish the cutaneous production of cholecalciferol. Moreover, the number of solar ultraviolet B photons that reach the earth's surface is influenced by factors such as latitude, season, and time of day, as well as the presence of ozone pollution in the atmosphere, which can alter the cutaneous production of cholecalciferol. In Boston, for instance, exposure to sunlight during the months of November through February results in insignificant amounts of cholecalciferol production in the skin. Additionally, windowpane glass absorbs ultraviolet B radiation, rendering exposure to sunlight through glass windows ineffective for cholecalciferol production. It is now recognized that vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency are prevalent in elderly individuals, particularly those who are immobile or reside in latitudes that do not provide adequate sunlight-mediated cholecalciferol during the winter months. These deficiencies can exacerbate osteoporosis, cause osteomalacia, and increase the risk of skeletal fractures. Fortunately, encouraging responsible sun exposure or consuming a multivitamin tablet containing 10 micrograms (400 IU) vitamin D can prevent vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency.

title: Genomic imprinting in development, growth, behavior and stem cells.
text: Mammalian genes that are subject to genomic imprinting are preferentially expressed from a single parental allele, which is essential for normal development. A small number of these imprinted genes play crucial roles in regulating fetal growth, and recent research has also shown that they have intricate roles in the brain, with significant consequences for behavior and neuronal function. Furthermore, new studies have highlighted the importance of proper expression of specific imprinted genes in induced pluripotent stem cells and adult stem cells. These findings underscore the complex nature and developmental importance of imprinted genes.

title: Quantitative Detection of Hepatitis C Virus RNA by Light Cycler PCR and Comparison with Two Different PCR Assays
text: The novel Light Cycler technology was applied to the detection of hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA in clinical samples. Serum samples from 81 patients were tested using Light Cycler PCR, AMPLICOR HCV Monitor assay, and an in-house PCR method. Our findings show that Light Cycler is a rapid and reliable method for both detecting and quantifying HCV RNA.

title: Targeting arginine metabolism pathway to treat arginine-dependent cancers.
text: The substantial differences in metabolism between cancerous and healthy cells have prompted the development of metabolism-based anti-tumor treatments. Arginine, a semi-essential amino acid, is of particular interest due to the unique metabolic characteristics of cancer cells. Unlike normal cells, which can synthesize arginine de novo and also take up extracellular arginine, many tumors have defects in enzymes involved in arginine metabolism, making them reliant on external arginine sources. This dependency is known as arginine auxotrophy. Exploiting this characteristic, arginine deprivation therapy has been investigated as a novel cancer treatment. By depriving tumors of arginine, the growth and survival of cancer cells are inhibited. This approach has shown promise in preclinical studies, particularly when combined with other cancer therapies. By integrating insights from both clinical oncologists and laboratory scientists, this review aims to highlight the potential of arginine deprivation as a promising anticancer strategy.

title: Rank Signaling Links the Development of Invariant γδ T Cell Progenitors and Aire+ Medullary Epithelium
text: During the embryonic-neonatal period, the thymic medulla provides a specialized microenvironment that enables the negative selection of T cells. The presence of autoimmune regulator (Aire)-expressing medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) during this stage is both necessary and sufficient to establish long-lasting tolerance. Our study revealed that the emergence of the first cohorts of Aire(+) mTECs before the selection of the αβ T cell repertoire is directed by Rankl(+) lymphoid tissue inducer cells and invariant Vγ5(+) dendritic epidermal T cell (DETC) progenitors. These early thymocytes expressing gene products of rearranged genes are the first to undergo maturation. Subsequently, the generation of Aire(+) mTECs fosters Skint-1-dependent, but Aire-independent, DETC progenitor maturation, leading to the emergence of an invariant DETC repertoire. Our findings attribute a functional importance to the temporal development of Vγ5(+) γδ T cells during thymus medulla formation for αβ T cell tolerance induction and demonstrate a Rank-mediated reciprocal link between DETC and Aire(+) mTEC maturation.

title: Long-term immune deficiency after allogeneic stem cell transplantation: B-cell deficiency is associated with late infections.
text: In this study, the immune reconstitution of 140 patients who underwent myeloablative allogeneic transplantation was analyzed. The patients were disease-free for 2 years before the transplantation. The study found that there was a defect in CD4 and CD8 cells, involving naive, terminally differentiated, memory, and activated subsets. Specifically, natural killer cells normalized at six months, while CD19(+)/CD5(+) B cells expanded after three months and memory B cells persisted with a defect. Chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) did not significantly impact CD8 subsets, but naive and competent CD4 subsets were strongly affected. However, the most significant impact of chronic GVHD was on B-cell subsets, particularly on the memory B population. The study also found that the cumulative incidence of late severe infections was low (14% at four years). Using Cox's models, low B-cell counts at 12 and 24 months were associated with the hazard of developing late infections, particularly if patients did not develop chronic GVHD.

title: The stimulatory potency of T cell antigens is influenced by the formation of the immunological synapse.
text: T cell activation is contingent upon the interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR) and peptide-major histocompatibility (pMHC) ligands. Despite understanding the factors that contribute to the stimulatory potency of a pMHC molecule, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Our findings demonstrate that a peptide displaying characteristics of a weak agonist stimulates T cell proliferation more than the wild-type agonist ligand. An in silico approach suggested that the inability to form the central supramolecular activation cluster (cSMAC) could underlie the increased proliferation. This conclusion was corroborated by experiments that showed that enhancing cSMAC formation diminished the stimulatory capacity of the weak peptide. Our research underscores the intricate interplay of factors that determine the quality of a T cell antigen.

title: Control of glutamate clearance and synaptic efficacy by glial coverage of neurons.
text: A study on excitatory synaptic transmission in the rat hypothalamic supraoptic nucleus found that the clearance of glutamate from the extracellular space is closely linked to the degree of astrocytic coverage of neurons. Specifically, reduced glutamate clearance, either through pharmacological intervention or decreased glial coverage in the synaptic area, can modulate presynaptic metabotropic glutamate receptors and impact transmitter release. These findings suggest that astrocytic wrapping of neurons plays a critical role in regulating synaptic efficiency in the central nervous system.

title: Duration of androgen suppression in the treatment of prostate cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: The combination of radiotherapy and long-term medical suppression of androgens has been shown to improve overall survival in patients with locally advanced prostate cancer. In this study, we compared the use of radiotherapy plus short-term androgen suppression with the use of radiotherapy plus long-term androgen suppression in the treatment of locally advanced prostate cancer.
METHODS: We randomly assigned patients with locally advanced prostate cancer who had received external-beam radiotherapy and 6 months of androgen suppression to two groups: one receiving no further treatment (short-term suppression) and the other receiving 2.5 years of further treatment with a luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone agonist (long-term suppression). The noninferiority of short-term androgen suppression was evaluated using an outcome of overall survival, with a hazard ratio of more than 1.35 required for noninferiority. An interim analysis showed futility, and the results were presented with an adjusted one-sided alpha level of 0.0429.
RESULTS: A total of 1113 patients were registered, of whom 970 were randomly assigned, 483 to short-term suppression and 487 to long-term suppression. After a median follow-up of 6.4 years, 132 patients in the short-term group and 98 in the long-term group had died, with 47 deaths due to prostate cancer in the short-term group and 29 in the long-term group. The 5-year overall mortality for short-term and long-term suppression was 19.0% and 15.2%, respectively, with a hazard ratio of 1.42 (95.71% upper confidence limit, 1.79; P=0.65 for noninferiority). Adverse events in both groups included fatigue, diminished sexual function, and hot flushes.
CONCLUSIONS: The combination of radiotherapy plus 6 months of androgen suppression did not demonstrate noninferiority compared to radiotherapy plus 3 years of androgen suppression in the treatment of locally advanced prostate cancer. (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00003026.)

title: A Functional Neuroimaging Study of Sound Localization: Visual Cortex Activity Predicts Performance in Early-Blind Individuals
text: Blind individuals often demonstrate heightened nonvisual perceptual abilities, yet the neural basis of this enhanced performance remains largely unexplored. A prior behavioral study revealed that some early-blind individuals localize sounds more accurately than sighted controls using monaural cues. To investigate the neural basis of these differences in humans, we conducted functional imaging studies using positron emission tomography (PET) and a speaker array that allowed for pseudo-free-field presentations within the scanner.
