title: DNA Deamination Mediates Innate Immunity to Retroviral Infection
text: CEM15/APOBEC3G is a cellular protein that plays a crucial role in resistance to infection by virion infectivity factor (Vif)-deficient human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Using a murine leukemia virus (MLV)-based system, our study provides evidence that CEM15/APOBEC3G functions as a DNA deaminase, which is incorporated into virions during viral production and leads to the deamination of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine within the retroviral minus (first)-strand cDNA. This deamination event likely triggers the destruction of the viral DNA, thereby providing a mechanism of innate immunity against retroviruses. Furthermore, our findings suggest that HIV Vif can protect MLV from this CEM15/APOBEC3G-dependent restriction, implying that targeted DNA deamination is a major strategy of innate immunity against retroviruses. These observations also suggest that this mechanism may contribute to the sequence variation observed in many viruses, including HIV.

title: Global, regional, and national disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) for 315 diseases and injuries and healthy life expectancy (HALE), 1990–2015: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015
text:
Background: Healthy life expectancy (HALE) and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) provide comprehensive measures of health across geographies and time, allowing for assessments of epidemiological patterns and health system performance, as well as informing investments in research and development and monitoring progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In this study, we aimed to provide updated HALE and DALYs for geographies worldwide and evaluate how disease burden changes with development.
Methods: We utilized results from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2015 (GBD 2015) to derive HALE and DALYs by sex for 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2015, taking into account all-cause mortality, cause-specific mortality, and non-fatal disease burden. We calculated DALYs by summing years of life lost (YLLs) and years of life lived with disability (YLDs) for each geography, age group, sex, and year, and estimated HALE using the Sullivan method. We then assessed how observed levels of DALYs and HALE differed from expected trends calculated with the Socio-demographic Index (SDI), a composite indicator constructed from measures of income per capita, average years of schooling, and total fertility rate.
Findings: Total global DALYs remained relatively unchanged from 1990 to 2015, with decreases in communicable, neonatal, maternal, and nutritional (Group 1) disease DALYs offset by increased DALYs due to non-communicable diseases (NCDs). This epidemiological transition was largely driven by changes in population growth and ageing, but was accelerated by widespread improvements in SDI that also correlated strongly with the increasing importance of NCDs. Both total DALYs and age-standardised DALY rates due to most Group 1 causes significantly decreased by 2015, and although total burden climbed for the majority of NCDs, age-standardised DALY rates due to NCDs declined. However, age-standardised DALY rates due to several high-burden NCDs (including osteoarthritis, drug use disorders, depression, diabetes, congenital birth defects, and skin, oral, and sense organ diseases) either increased or remained unchanged, leading to increases in their relative ranking in many geographies. From 2005 to 2015, HALE at birth increased by an average of 2·9 years (95% uncertainty interval 2·9-3·0) for men and 3·5 years (3·4-3·7) for women, while HALE at age 65 years improved by 0·85 years (0·78-0·92) and 1·2 years (1·1-1·3), respectively. Rising SDI was associated with consistently higher HALE and a somewhat smaller proportion of life spent with functional health loss; however, rising SDI was related to increases in total disability. Many countries and territories in central America and eastern sub-Saharan Africa had increasingly lower rates of disease burden than expected given their SDI. At the same time, a subset of geographies recorded a growing gap between observed and expected levels of DALYs, a trend driven mainly by rising burden due to war, interpersonal violence, and various NCDs.
Interpretation: Health is improving globally, but this means more populations are spending more time with functional health loss, an absolute expansion of morbidity. The proportion of life spent in ill health decreases somewhat with increasing SDI, a relative compression of morbidity, which supports continued efforts to elevate personal income, improve education, and limit fertility. Our analysis of DALYs and HALE and their relationship to SDI represents a robust framework on which to benchmark geography-specific health performance and SDG progress. Country-specific drivers of disease burden, particularly for causes with higher-than-expected DALYs, should inform financial and research investments, prevention efforts, health policies, and health system improvement initiatives for all countries along the development continuum. Funding: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

title: Adverse drug events: database construction and in silico prediction.
text:
Adverse drug events (ADEs) are harmful reactions that occur when individuals take medications at the recommended dosages. These events are crucial for a drug's approval in clinical use or continued market presence. Unfortunately, many ADEs are not discovered until after a drug is approved and can lead to significant morbidity and mortality. To address this issue, identifying methods to avoid or reduce ADEs is a critical aspect of drug discovery and development.
In this study, we present a comprehensive database of adverse drug events, known as MetaADEDB, which contains over 520,000 drug-ADE associations among 3059 unique compounds (including 1330 drugs) and 13,200 ADE items. The database was created through data integration and text mining, and all compounds and ADEs were annotated with the most commonly used concepts defined in Medical Subject Headings (MeSH).
To further enhance the prediction of potential ADEs, we developed a computational method called the phenotypic network inference model (PNIM). This method was tested using the MetaADEDB database and achieved an area under the receive operating characteristic curve (AUC) of over 0.9 through 10-fold cross-validation. In external validation, the AUC value was 0.912 for an US-FDA Adverse Events Reporting System dataset, indicating the reliability of the prediction method.
MetaADEDB is now available for free use at http://www.lmmd.org/online_services/metaadedb/. This database and prediction method provide a valuable tool for searching for known side effects or predicting potential side effects for a given drug or compound.

title: Genetic Tests for Ecological and Allopatric Speciation in Anoles on an Island Archipelago
text: From Darwin's studies of the Galapagos and Wallace's studies of Indonesia, islands have played a significant role in evolutionary investigations, and radiations within archipelagos are often interpreted as supporting the traditional view of allopatric speciation. Even during the current paradigm shift towards other modes of speciation, island radiations, such as the Lesser Antillean anoles, are thought to exemplify this process. Geological and molecular phylogenetic evidence suggests that, in the archipelago of Martinique, anole populations provide several examples of secondary contact between island species. Four precursor island species, with up to 8 million years of divergence, met when their islands coalesced to form the current island of Martinique. Moreover, adjacent anole populations also show marked adaptation to distinct habitat zonation, allowing both allopatric and ecological speciation to be tested in this system. We take advantage of this opportunity for replicated island coalescence and independent ecological adaptation to conduct an extensive population genetic study of hypervariable neutral nuclear markers. Our findings show that, even after substantial periods of spatial isolation, putative allospecies exhibit less reproductive isolation than conspecific populations in adjacent habitats in all three cases of subsequent island coalescence. The degree of genetic interchange suggests that while there is always a significant genetic signature of past allopatry, and this may be quite strong if the selection regime allows, there is no case of complete allopatric speciation, despite a strong prima facie case for it. Importantly, there is greater genetic isolation across the xeric/rainforest ecotone than is associated with any secondary contact. This rejection of the development of reproductive isolation in allopatric divergence supports the potential for ecological speciation, even though full speciation has not been achieved in this case. Additionally, this explanation accounts for the paucity of anole species in the Lesser Antilles compared to the Greater Antilles.

title: Deficiency and pharmacological stabilization of mast cells reduce diet-induced obesity and diabetes in mice
text: Although mast cells have traditionally been associated with allergic responses, recent research suggests that these cells play a role in various other diseases, including multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, aortic aneurysm, and cancer. This study uncovers evidence that mast cells are also involved in diet-induced obesity and diabetes. For instance, white adipose tissue (WAT) from obese humans and mice contain more mast cells than WAT from lean individuals. Moreover, genetic or pharmacological deficiency of mast cells or their stabilization in mice on a Western diet leads to reduced body weight gain, lower levels of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and proteases in serum and WAT, along with improved glucose homeostasis and energy expenditure. Mechanistic studies reveal that mast cells contribute to WAT and muscle angiogenesis, as well as cell apoptosis and cathepsin activity. Transferring cytokine-deficient mast cells into mice shows that these cells produce interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma), which promote mouse adipose tissue cysteine protease cathepsin expression, apoptosis, and angiogenesis, thereby exacerbating diet-induced obesity and glucose intolerance. Our findings suggest the potential of developing novel therapies for these common human metabolic disorders, as clinically available mast cell-stabilizing agents reduce obesity and diabetes in mice.

title: Familial aphasic episodes: another variant of partial epilepsy with simple inheritance?
text: We report on a family with partial epilepsy that exhibits simple inheritance patterns. Affected members commonly experience aphasic episodes with secondary generalization, which typically occur during adolescence or adulthood. The response to medication has varied significantly among patients. Notably, no neurological defects or decline in intelligence were observed. This case represents a distinct variety of rare familial partial epilepsy with neocortical epilepsy features.

title: Endosome-ER Contacts Control Actin Nucleation and Retromer Function through VAP-Dependent Regulation of PI4P
text: VAP (VAPA and VAPB) is an evolutionarily conserved protein that resides in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and plays a crucial role in regulating the exchange of lipids across adjacent bilayers. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms by which VAP influences the function of endosomes, which are membranous organelles that facilitate the transport of proteins and lipids between the ER and other cellular compartments. Our findings reveal that VAP regulates the levels of phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) on endosomes, which in turn affects the actin nucleation process mediated by the WASH protein complex. VAP is recruited to retromer budding sites on endosomes through an interaction with the retromer SNX2 subunit, and the loss of VAP leads to an accumulation of PI4P, actin comets, and trans-Golgi proteins on endosomes. These defects can be mimicked by downregulating OSBP, a protein that interacts with VAP and transports PI4P. Our results demonstrate the importance of PI4P in retromer-/WASH-dependent budding from endosomes, highlighting the ER's ability to control the dynamics of budding and association with the cytoskeleton of another membrane through direct contacts leading to bilayer lipid modifications.

title: Anaphase-Promoting Complex/Cyclosome–Dependent Proteolysis of Human Cyclin a Starts at the Beginning of Mitosis and Is Not Subject to the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint
text:
Cyclin A is a stable protein in the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, but its stability is disrupted when cells enter mitosis. Specifically, cyclin A is almost completely degraded before the metaphase to anaphase transition. Microinjection of antibodies against subunits of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) or against human Cdc20 (fizzy) arrested cells at metaphase and stabilized both cyclins A and B1. Interestingly, cyclin A was efficiently polyubiquitylated by Cdc20 or Cdh1-activated APC/C in vitro, whereas the proteolysis of cyclin B1 was delayed by the spindle assembly checkpoint. In contrast, the degradation of cyclin A was not delayed by the spindle assembly checkpoint. These findings suggest that the APC/C is activated as cells enter mitosis and immediately targets cyclin A for degradation, whereas the spindle assembly checkpoint delays the degradation of cyclin B1 until the metaphase to anaphase transition.
Notably, the "destruction box" (D-box) of cyclin A is longer than that of cyclin B, by 10-20 residues. Overexpression of wild-type cyclin A delayed the metaphase to anaphase transition, whereas expression of cyclin A mutants lacking a D-box arrested cells in anaphase. These results provide further insight into the regulation of the cell cycle and the role of cyclin A in this process.

title: Human T Cell Leukemia Virus Reactivation with Progression of Adult T-Cell Leukemia-Lymphoma
text:
Background: Adult T-cell leukemia-lymphoma (ATLL) has a dismal prognosis, despite various treatment regimens being trialed. Virus expression is often limited or absent at the time of diagnosis, suggesting that secondary genetic or epigenetic changes play a significant role in disease pathogenesis.
Methods and Findings: In this phase II clinical trial, we prospectively investigated the efficacy of combination chemotherapy followed by antiretroviral therapy in ATLL patients. Nineteen patients were enrolled between 2002 and 2006 at five medical centers and received infusional chemotherapy with etoposide, doxorubicin, and vincristine, daily prednisone, and bolus cyclophosphamide (EPOCH) for two to six cycles until maximum clinical response. Following chemotherapy, patients received antiviral therapy with daily zidovudine, lamivudine, and alpha interferon-2a for up to one year. Seven patients discontinued treatment due to progressive disease or chemotherapy toxicity, while eleven patients achieved an objective response with a median duration of response of thirteen months, and two complete remissions. During chemotherapy induction, viral RNA expression increased (median 190-fold), and virus replication occurred, concurrent with disease progression.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that EPOCH chemotherapy followed by antiretroviral therapy is an active therapeutic regimen for ATLL. However, the reactivation of virus during induction chemotherapy may contribute to treatment failure. Alternative therapies that can simultaneously prevent virus expression and are cytocidal for malignant cells are urgently needed in this disease.

title: Montelukast and fluticasone compared with salmeterol and fluticasone in protecting against asthma exacerbation in adults: one year, double blind, randomised, comparative trial.
text: Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of adding montelukast or salmeterol to inhaled fluticasone propionate in patients with uncontrolled asthma symptoms, as measured by the percentage of patients experiencing at least one asthma exacerbation over a 52-week period. Design: A 52-week, double-blind, multicentre trial randomly assigning patients to receive either montelukast or salmeterol in addition to inhaled fluticasone propionate. Setting: Multiple clinical centres. Participants: Adults and children aged 15-72 years with a history of chronic asthma for over a year, baseline FEV1 value between 50-90% predicted, and a beta agonist improvement of >12% in FEV1. Main Outcome Measures: The primary endpoint was the percentage of patients experiencing at least one asthma exacerbation during the 52-week trial. Secondary outcomes included changes in FEV1, morning peak expiratory flow, asthma-specific quality of life, and nocturnal awakenings. Results: The addition of montelukast to inhaled fluticasone resulted in a 1% reduction in the percentage of patients experiencing an asthma exacerbation compared to the addition of salmeterol (19.1% vs 20.1%). The difference was found to be non-inferior to salmeterol (risk ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.86-1.29). Salmeterol and fluticasone significantly improved FEV1 before a beta agonist was used and morning peak expiratory flow compared to montelukast and fluticasone (P < 0.001), while improvements in asthma-specific quality of life and nocturnal awakenings were similar between the groups. Montelukast and fluticasone significantly reduced peripheral blood eosinophil counts compared to salmeterol and fluticasone (P = 0.011). Both treatments were generally well tolerated. Conclusion: The addition of montelukast to inhaled fluticasone propionate may provide equivalent clinical control to salmeterol in patients with uncontrolled asthma symptoms, with the added benefit of reducing peripheral blood eosinophil counts.

title: Control of assembly and function of glutamate receptors by the amino-terminal domain.
text: The extracellular amino-terminal domains (ATDs) of ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits play a crucial role in controlling a diverse range of receptor functions, including subunit assembly, receptor trafficking, channel gating, agonist potency, and allosteric modulation. These functions are exerted by the ATDs, which reside distal to the membrane and are a common feature of all glutamate receptors. The many different features of the ionotropic glutamate receptor classes and subunits may be regulated by the ATDs, leading to differential modulation of receptor function. Recent advances in understanding the structure and function of the ATDs may provide a means to target this region for the therapeutic modulation of glutamatergic signaling. For example, NMDA receptor antagonists that interact with the GluN2B ATD have shown promise in animal models of ischemia, neuropathic pain, and Parkinson's disease.

title: Fission yeast and other yeasts as emergent models to unravel cellular aging in eukaryotes.
text: In recent years, simple organisms such as yeasts and worms have made significant contributions to aging research. Studies conducted in Saccharomyces cerevisiae have helped elucidate numerous molecular mechanisms underlying cellular aging and uncovered novel longevity genes. These genes have been found to be conserved in more complex eukaryotes, leading to the extension of these discovery approaches to other yeast models, including Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Candida albicans, Kluyveromyces lactis, and Cryptococcus neoformans. In fission yeast, researchers have identified links between asymmetrical cell division and nutrient signaling pathways with aging. This review aims to summarize the current state of knowledge on the mechanisms controlling both replicative and chronological aging in S. pombe and the other emerging yeast models.

title: Centrifugal elutriation as a method for isolation of large numbers of functionally intact human peripheral blood monocytes.
text: Centrifugal elutriation was used to isolate human peripheral blood monocytes (HPBM) from mononuclear cells collected as a secondary component after platelet concentration. The HPBM were separated into two populations: small monocytes (SM) and large monocytes (LM), with a purity of 95% and 93%, respectively. The elutriation process did not affect the viability of the HPBM, as demonstrated by trypan blue exclusion. The HPBM populations were histochemically and functionally purified from the lymphocyte population, as shown by the lack of reactivity to leu-1 and leu-7 and the depletion of NK cell activity. The HPBM populations were also enriched in HLA-Dr, OKM-1, OKM-5, MY-8, and leu M-3 monoclonal antibody marker staining. There were no differences in the percent positive cells for any of the monocyte-specific monoclonal antibodies between the SM and LM populations. All three HPBM populations were able to mediate antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity to human red blood cells, with LM mediating more lysis than SM.

title: Asthma in United States Olympic athletes who participated in the 1996 Summer Games.
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate the prevalence of asthma among highly competitive athletes participating in the 1996 Summer Olympic Games in Atlanta. We analyzed data from the United States Olympic Committee (USOC) Medical History Questionnaire completed by 699 athletes. Our findings revealed that 15.3% of the athletes had a previous diagnosis of asthma, and 13.9% reported taking asthma medications in the past. Additionally, 16.7% of the athletes reported using an asthma medication, having a diagnosis of asthma, or both. Of the athletes, 73 (10.4%) were currently taking an asthma medication at the time of the study. The prevalence of asthma was highest among athletes who participated in cycling and mountain biking (50%), compared to other sports such as diving and weight lifting, where no athletes had asthma. Our study suggests that the prevalence of asthma among athletes in the 1996 Summer Games was higher than in the general population or in those who participated in the 1984 Summer Games. Furthermore, our findings suggest that asthma may influence the sport chosen by an athlete.

title: Relapse specific mutations in NT5C2 in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia
text: Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) that has relapsed carries a poor prognosis, even after intensive retreatment, due to the presence of intrinsic drug resistance. The underlying biological mechanisms are not well understood. In this study, we analyzed the transcriptomes of bone marrow specimens from ten children with pediatric B-lymphoblastic leukemia at diagnosis and relapse using RNA sequencing. We identified 20 novel, nonsynonymous mutations in genes that were not present at initial diagnosis, with two individuals harboring relapse-specific mutations in the NT5C2 gene, which encodes a 5'-nucleotidase. Full-exon sequencing of NT5C2 was conducted in 61 additional relapse specimens, revealing additional mutations in five cases. Enzymatic analysis of mutant proteins showed that base substitutions conferred increased enzymatic activity and resistance to treatment with nucleoside analog therapies. Notably, all individuals who harbored NT5C2 mutations relapsed early, within 36 months of initial diagnosis (P = 0.03). These findings suggest that mutations in NT5C2 are associated with the outgrowth of drug-resistant clones in ALL.

title: Relationship between Sloan-Kettering virus expression and mouse follicular development
text: The Sloan-Kettering virus gene product (Ski) is a unique nuclear oncoprotein that belongs to the ski/sno proto-oncogene family. Ski exhibits multiple functions in various cell types, including the ability to induce both oncogenic transformation and terminal muscle differentiation when expressed at high levels. As important transcription regulators of the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily, Ski/SnoN form heterodimers and play a crucial role in follicle development. To investigate the relationship between Ski expression and mouse follicular development, this study employed immunohistochemical and real-time PCR techniques in ovaries of neonatal and gonadotropin-induced immature mice. In postnatal mice, Ski was highly expressed in oocyte nuclei at postnatal day 1, which then shifted to the perinuclear space and decreased in total levels with follicular development. During the estrous cycle, Ski expression was observed at proestrus and estrus, with a decrease at metestrus and a subsequent increase at diestrus. Following gonadotropin injection, Ski was found in the perinuclear space and weak in oocyte nuclei. After luteinization, Ski expression was detected in the corpus luteum. Real-time PCR results also showed that Ski mRNA expression was inversely correlated with ovulation-related genes during cumulus expansion, with a decrease in expression as follicle development progressed. Ski is specifically expressed during follicle development, ovulation, and luteinization, suggesting that it plays essential roles in these processes, particularly during early follicular development.

title: Involvement of CB1 cannabinoid receptors in emotional behaviour
text:
Background: The endogenous cannabinoid system, particularly the CB1 cannabinoid receptor, has been implicated in the regulation of various behavioral and neuroendocrine functions, including emotional responses and learning and memory processes. Recently, CB1 knockout mice have been generated, providing a valuable tool for investigating the neurophysiology of the endogenous cannabinoid system.
Objectives: To investigate the role of the CB1 cannabinoid receptor in emotional-related behavioral responses, including aggressiveness, anxiety, depression, and learning models, using CB1 knockout mice.
Methods: Behavioral tests, including the light/dark box, chronic unpredictable mild stress, resident–intruder test, and active avoidance paradigm, were used to evaluate the spontaneous responses of CB1 knockout mice and wild-type controls.
Results: Our findings revealed that CB1 knockout mice exhibited increased aggressive behavior in the resident–intruder test and anxiogenic-like responses in the light/dark box. Additionally, CB1 knockout mice showed a higher susceptibility to develop depressive-like responses in the chronic unpredictable mild stress procedure, suggesting an increased vulnerability to anhedonia. Furthermore, CB1 knockout mice displayed a significant increase in conditioned responses in the active avoidance model, indicating improved learning and memory processes.
Conclusions: These findings suggest that endogenous cannabinoids, acting through the CB1 receptor, play a crucial role in the regulation of emotional behavior and contribute to the physiological processes of learning and memory.

title: Exosomal levels of miRNA-21 from cerebrospinal fluids associated with poor prognosis and tumor recurrence of glioma patients
text: Glioma, the most common type of primary brain tumors, is known to communicate with other cells through extracellular vesicles, such as exosomes, which transport cell-derived proteins and nucleic acids, including microRNAs (miRNAs). In this study, we analyzed the levels of cancer-related miRNAs in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with recurrent glioma and compared them to those in serum and exosomes. We found that the levels of exosomal miR-21 in the CSF were significantly higher in glioma patients than in non-tumor control groups, and this correlation was only observed in the CSF and not in serum. Additionally, we found that the levels of miR-21 in the CSF correlated with the metastasis of the tumor to the spinal cord and the recurrence of the tumor in specific anatomical sites. Furthermore, we verified that miR-21 levels were associated with tumor grade and negatively correlated with patient overall survival time. To further investigate the role of miR-21 in glioma, we suppressed its expression in U251 cells using a lentiviral inhibitor and found that the levels of miR-21 target genes, such as PTEN, RECK, and PDCD4, were up-regulated at the protein level. Our results suggest that the levels of exosomal miR-21 in the CSF could be a promising indicator for glioma diagnosis and prognosis, particularly in predicting tumor recurrence or metastasis.

title: Age‐associated microRNA expression in human peripheral blood is associated with all‐cause mortality and age‐related traits
text: Recent studies have uncovered connections between DNA methylation and the expression of protein-coding genes in the aging process. However, the relationship between microRNA expression and age has not been thoroughly investigated. To address this gap, we analyzed the expression of 127 microRNAs in whole blood from 5221 adults and found that most microRNAs were underexpressed in older individuals. Integrative analysis of microRNA and mRNA expression revealed changes in age-associated mRNA expression that may be driven by age-associated microRNAs involved in RNA processing, translation, and immune function. We developed a linear model to predict microRNA age based on the expression levels of 80 microRNAs and found that microRNA age correlated modestly with predicted age from DNA methylation and mRNA expression. We also identified a biomarker of accelerated aging, the difference between microRNA age and chronological age (Δage), which was associated with all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, including coronary heart disease, hypertension, blood pressure, and glucose levels. Based on these findings, we constructed a microRNA age prediction model that could potentially detect accelerated aging and predict risks for age-related diseases.

title: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) in frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
text:
AIMS: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is clinically and pathologically diverse, with variations in MAPT, GRN, and C9ORF72 associated with the disease. However, the underlying mechanisms of these genetic and non-genetic forms of FTLD remain unclear. Epigenetic factors, such as histone regulation by histone deacetylases (HDACs), may play a role in the dysregulation of transcriptional activity, which is thought to contribute to the neurodegenerative process.
METHODS: We analyzed the distribution and intensity of HDACs 4, 5, and 6 in immunostained sections of temporal cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum from 33 pathologically confirmed cases of FTLD and 27 controls.
RESULTS: Our results showed a significant increase in cytoplasmic HDAC4 and HDAC6 immunostaining in granule cells of the dentate gyrus in cases of FTLD compared to controls, with a more pronounced effect in cases of FTLD tau-Picks compared to FTLD tau-MAPT and controls. No differences were observed between FTLD-TDP subtypes or between genetic and non-genetic forms of FTLD. Additionally, no changes were seen in HDAC5 in any FTLD or control cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that dysregulation of HDAC4 and/or HDAC6 may play a role in the pathogenesis of FTLD-tau associated with Pick bodies, although the lack of immunostaining in Pick bodies implies that such changes do not directly contribute to their formation.

title: Evolution and Impact of Subclonal Mutations in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
text: Clonal evolution is a crucial aspect of cancer progression and relapse. In a comprehensive study of 149 chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) cases, we integrated whole-exome sequencing and copy number analysis to determine the proportion of cancer cells harboring specific somatic mutations. We identified driver mutations as either predominantly clonal (e.g., MYD88, trisomy 12, and del(13q)) or subclonal (e.g., SF3B1 and TP53), corresponding to earlier and later stages of CLL development. To further investigate clonal evolution in CLL, we sampled leukemia cells from 18 patients at two time points. Remarkably, 10 of the 12 CLL cases treated with chemotherapy (but only one of six without treatment) exhibited clonal evolution, primarily involving subclones with driver mutations (e.g., SF3B1 and TP53) that expanded over time. Additionally, the presence of a subclonal driver mutation was found to be an independent risk factor for rapid disease progression. Our study uncovers the patterns of clonal evolution in CLL, providing insights into its stepwise transformation, and highlights the link between the presence of subclones and poor clinical outcomes.

title: The transcriptional program of sporulation in budding yeast
text: In the developmental program of budding yeast, diploid cells give rise to haploid cells through the process of sporulation, which involves meiosis and spore morphogenesis. To investigate changes in gene expression during this process, DNA microarrays containing nearly every yeast gene were used to analyze gene expression patterns. Seven distinct temporal patterns of gene induction were observed. The transcription factor Ndt80 was found to be important in inducing a large group of genes at the end of meiotic prophase. By analyzing coordinately expressed genes, consensus sequences were identified that are responsible for temporal regulation. These sequences provided clues about the potential functions of hundreds of previously uncharacterized genes, some of which have vertebrate homologs that may be involved in gametogenesis.

title: Grass plants bind, retain, uptake, and transport infectious prions.
text: Prions, the protein-based infectious agents responsible for prion diseases, can bind and retain infectious prion protein (PrP(Sc)) in plants. Our study found that small amounts of PrP(Sc) in diluted brain homogenate or excretory materials (urine and feces) can bind to wheat grass roots and leaves. Infectious prions from diverse sources, including chronic wasting disease, can interact with plants, leading to efficient transmission of the disease to wild-type hamsters through ingestion of prion-contaminated plants. Additionally, leaves sprayed with a prion-containing preparation retained infectious PrP(Sc) for several weeks, indicating that plants can act as long-term carriers of prion infectivity. Furthermore, our findings suggest that plants can uptake prions from contaminated soil and transport them to aerial parts of the plant, including the stem and leaves. These results demonstrate that plants can efficiently bind and transmit infectious prions, providing evidence for the possible role of environmental prion contamination in the horizontal transmission of the disease.

title: Innate lymphoid cells mediate influenza-induced airway hyper-reactivity independently of adaptive immunity
text: Patients with asthma, a significant public health concern, are at a heightened risk of developing serious disease from influenza virus infection, but the specific mechanisms by which influenza A causes airway disease and asthma are not yet fully understood. In a mouse model, we found that influenza infection acutely triggers airway hyper-reactivity (AHR), a defining characteristic of asthma, in a manner that is independent of T helper type 2 (TH2) cells and adaptive immunity. Instead, influenza infection induces AHR through a previously unidentified pathway that relies on the interleukin 13 (IL-13)–IL-33 axis and a unique subset of immune cells called "natural helper cells." Influenza A virus infection, which activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, leads to a substantial increase in the production of IL-33 by alveolar macrophages, which in turn activates natural helper cells to produce large amounts of IL-13.

title: The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions
text:
Improving the design and implementation of evidence-based practices relies on successful behavior change interventions. This requires a suitable framework for characterizing interventions and linking them to an analysis of the targeted behavior. While various frameworks of behavior change interventions exist, their effectiveness in meeting this purpose is unclear. This paper evaluates existing frameworks and develops a new framework to address their limitations.
METHODS:
We conducted a systematic search of electronic databases and consulted with behavior change experts to identify frameworks of behavior change interventions. These were evaluated based on three criteria: comprehensiveness, coherence, and a clear link to an overarching model of behavior. A new framework was developed to meet these criteria. The reliability of the new framework was examined in two domains of behavior change: tobacco control and obesity.
RESULTS:
Nineteen frameworks were identified, covering nine intervention functions and seven policy categories that could enable those interventions. However, none of the frameworks reviewed covered the full range of intervention functions or policies, and only a minority met the criteria of coherence or linkage to a model of behavior. At the center of the proposed new framework is a 'behaviour system' involving three essential conditions: capability, opportunity, and motivation (what we term the 'COM-B system'). This forms the hub of a 'behaviour change wheel' (BCW) around which are positioned the nine intervention functions aimed at addressing deficits in one or more of these conditions; around this are placed seven categories of policy that could enable those interventions to occur. The BCW was used reliably to characterize interventions within the English Department of Health's 2010 tobacco control strategy and the National Institute of Health and Clinical Excellence's guidance on reducing obesity.
CONCLUSIONS:
Interventions and policies to change behavior can be usefully characterized by means of a BCW comprising: a 'behaviour system' at the hub, encircled by intervention functions and then by policy categories. Further research is needed to determine how far the BCW can lead to more efficient design of effective interventions.

title: Intermittent prophylaxis with oral truvada protects macaques from rectal SHIV infection.
text: HIV continues to disseminate globally, primarily through sexual contact. Despite advances in treatment and care, preventing transmission through vaccines or microbicides has proven challenging. A promising strategy to prevent transmission is prophylactic treatment with antiretroviral drugs before exposure to HIV. Clinical trials are currently underway evaluating the efficacy of daily treatment with reverse transcriptase inhibitors such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or Truvada (TDF plus emtricitabine). We hypothesized that intermittent prophylactic treatment with long-acting antiviral drugs would be as effective as daily dosing in blocking the earliest stages of viral replication and preventing mucosal transmission. To test this hypothesis, we administered prophylactic Truvada to macaque monkeys intermittently and then exposed them rectally to simian-human immunodeficiency virus (SHIV) once a week for 14 weeks. We found that a simple regimen with an oral dose of Truvada given 1, 3, or 7 days before exposure followed by a second dose 2 hours after exposure was as protective as daily drug administration, possibly due to the long intracellular persistence of the drugs. Additionally, a two-dose regimen initiated 2 hours before or after virus exposure was effective, and full protection was obtained by doubling the Truvada concentration in both doses. Conversely, no protection was observed if the first dose was delayed until 24 hours after exposure, highlighting the importance of blocking initial replication in the mucosa. Our results demonstrate that intermittent prophylactic treatment with an antiviral drug can be highly effective in preventing SHIV infection, with a wide window of protection. These findings strengthen the possibility of developing practical and cost-effective strategies to prevent HIV transmission in humans.

title: RNA is favourable for analysing EGFR mutations in malignant pleural effusion of lung cancer.
text: Malignant pleural effusion (MPE) can be a valuable sample type for evaluating the EGFR status of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, direct sequencing of genomic DNA from MPE samples is not very sensitive for detecting EGFR mutations. To determine whether RNA-based EGFR analysis is less susceptible to interference from non-tumor cells with lower EGFR expression, we compared three methods (RNA-based sequencing versus DNA-based sequencing and mass spectrometry) in a cohort of 150 lung adenocarcinoma patients receiving first-line tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Our results showed that EGFR mutations were significantly more frequently identified by RNA-based sequencing than by DNA-based sequencing and mass spectrometry (for all mutations, 67.3% versus 44.7% and 46.7%, respectively; for L858R or exon 19 deletions, 61.3% versus 41.3% and 46.7%, respectively). Moreover, RNA-based sequencing provided better prediction of clinical efficacy of first-line TKIs. In patients with acquired resistance, EGFR sequencing from RNA yielded satisfactory detection of T790M (54.2%). These findings demonstrate that using RNA as a template for EGFR sequencing greatly improves sensitivity for detecting EGFR mutations in MPE samples from NSCLC, highlighting RNA as the preferred source for analyzing EGFR mutations in heterogeneous MPE specimens.

title: Pharmacological correction of a defect in PPARγ signaling ameliorates disease severity in Cftr-deficient mice
text: Cystic fibrosis is caused by genetic mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (Cftr) gene, which impairs its function as an apical chloride channel that supports bicarbonate transport in the body. Individuals with cystic fibrosis exhibit characteristic abnormalities, including thickened and retained mucus in airways and organs, inflammation, altered lipid metabolism, and insulin resistance. In this study, we investigate the role of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-gamma) in the pathophysiology of cystic fibrosis. We find that colonic epithelial cells and whole lung tissue from Cftr-deficient mice exhibit a defect in PPAR-gamma function, which contributes to an abnormal gene expression program. Specifically, we identify reduced levels of the endogenous PPAR-gamma ligand 15-keto-prostaglandin E(2) (15-keto-PGE(2)) as a contributing factor to this defect. Treatment of Cftr-deficient mice with the synthetic PPAR-gamma ligand rosiglitazone partially normalizes the altered gene expression pattern and reduces disease severity. Interestingly, rosiglitazone has no effect on chloride secretion in the colon but increases expression of genes encoding carbonic anhydrases 4 and 2 (Car4 and Car2), bicarbonate secretion, and reduces mucus retention. These findings reveal a reversible defect in PPAR-gamma signaling in Cftr-deficient cells that can be pharmacologically corrected to alleviate the severity of the cystic fibrosis phenotype in mice.

title: Visualization of volatile substances in different organelles with an atmospheric-pressure mass microscope.
text: We have developed a cutting-edge mass microscope (mass spectrometry imager with spatial resolution higher than the naked eye) equipped with an atmospheric pressure ion-source chamber for laser desorption/ionization (AP-LDI) and a quadrupole ion trap time-of-flight (QIT-TOF) analyzer. This optical microscope combined with the mass spectrometer allowed us to precisely identify and analyze the relevant tissue region before performing imaging mass spectrometry (IMS). To achieve high spatial resolution, we used an ultraviolet laser tightly focused with a triplet lens. The atmospheric pressure ion-source chamber enables us to analyze fresh samples with minimal loss of intrinsic water or volatile compounds. By employing mass-microscopic AP-LDI imaging of freshly cut ginger rhizome sections, we were able to localize the compounds related to pungency and flavor, including 6-gingerol ([M + K](+) at m/z 333.15, positive mode; [M - H](-) at m/z 293.17, negative mode) and the monoterpene ([M + K](+) at m/z 191.09), within oil drop-containing organelles. Subsequent AP-LDI-tandem MS/MS analyses allowed us to compare authentic signals from freshly cut ginger directly with the standard reagent, enabling us to monitor the quality of plants at the organelle level.

title: Coding of Sweet, Bitter, and Umami Tastes Different Receptor Cells Sharing Similar Signaling Pathways
text: Mammals are capable of detecting a diverse range of chemical stimuli through their taste system, which is mediated by two distinct families of receptors (T1Rs and T2Rs). These receptors respond to sweet, amino acid, and bitter compounds, respectively. In this study, we investigate the role of TRPM5, a taste transient receptor potential ion channel, and PLCbeta2, a phospholipase C selectively expressed in taste tissue, in taste reception. Our results demonstrate that knockouts of TRPM5 and PLCbeta2 abolish sweet, amino acid, and bitter taste perception, while leaving sour and salty tastes unaffected. This suggests that, despite utilizing different receptors, sweet, amino acid, and bitter taste transduction converge on a common signaling pathway. Using PLCbeta2 taste-blind animals, we then explore a fundamental question in taste perception: how different taste modalities are encoded at the cellular level. By engineering mice that rescue PLCbeta2 function exclusively in bitter-receptor expressing cells, we find that bitter taste is encoded independently of sweet and amino acids, and that taste receptor cells are not broadly tuned across these modalities.

title: Green synthesis of silver nanoparticles and characterization of their inhibitory effects on AGEs formation using biophysical techniques
text: Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) resulting from non-enzymatic glycation are a significant factor in the secondary complications of diabetes. Researchers are focusing on discovering new compounds that can inhibit AGEs without affecting the normal structure and function of biomolecules. A number of natural and synthetic compounds have been proposed as AGE inhibitors. In this study, we investigated the inhibitory effects of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) on AGEs formation. AgNPs (~30.5 nm) synthesized from Aloe Vera leaf extract were characterized using UV-Vis spectroscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and dynamic light scattering (DLS) techniques. The inhibitory effects of AgNPs on AGEs formation were evaluated by assessing the degree of reactivity of free amino groups (lysine and arginine residues), protein-bound carbonyl and carboxymethyl lysine (CML) content, and the effects on protein structure using various physicochemical techniques. The results showed that AgNPs significantly inhibit AGEs formation in a concentration-dependent manner and have a positive effect on protein structure. These findings suggest that AgNPs may play a therapeutic role in diabetes-related complications.

title: Myosin Light Chain–activating Phosphorylation Sites Are Required for Oogenesis in Drosophila
text: The Drosophila spaghetti squash (sqh) gene encodes the regulatory myosin light chain (RMLC) of nonmuscle myosin II. Biochemical analysis of vertebrate nonmuscle and smooth muscle myosin II has shown that phosphorylation of specific amino acids on the RMLC greatly enhances the actin-dependent myosin ATPase and motor activity in vitro. To investigate the in vivo importance of these sites in Drosophila, we created transgenes in which these amino acids were altered and examined their phenotypes in an sqh null mutant background during oocyte development in female Drosophila. We found that germ line cystoblasts lacking a functional sqh gene exhibit severe defects in proliferation and cytokinesis, with abnormal ring canals and accumulation of myosin heavy chain aggregates. Interestingly, mutant sqh transgenes in which both serine-21 and threonine-20 were replaced by alanines (sqh -A20, A21) behave similarly to the null allele, with no heavy chain aggregates observed. In contrast, expression of sqh -A21, which only alters the primary phosphorylation target serine-21 site, partially restores functionality to germ line myosin II, allowing cystoblast division and oocyte development, although with some cytokinesis failure and abnormalities in rapid cytoplasmic transport. Substituting a glutamate for serine-21 (sqh -E21) allows oogenesis to be completed with minimal defects, producing eggs that can develop normally to produce fertile adults. Flies expressing sqh -A20, in which only the secondary phosphorylation site is absent, appear to be entirely wild type. These genetic findings suggest that phosphorylation at serine-21 is critical for RMLC function in vivo, but that the function can be partially provided by phosphorylation at threonine-20.

title: Stages of the pathologic process in Alzheimer disease: age categories from 1 to 100 years.
text: Two thousand three hundred and thirty-two non-selected brains from individuals aged 1 to 100 years were examined using immunocytochemistry (AT8) and Gallyas silver staining for abnormal tau, and immunocytochemistry (4G8) and Campbell-Switzer staining for β-amyloid. Of these, 342 cases were negative in the Gallyas stain, but when re-staged using AT8, only 10 were immunonegative. Fifty-eight cases had subcortical tau predominantly in the locus coeruleus, with no abnormal cortical tau (subcortical Stages a-c). Cortical involvement (abnormal tau in neurites) was first identified in the transentorhinal region (Stage 1a, 38 cases), where pretangle material was observed (Stage 1b, 236 cases). Pretangles gradually evolved into argyrophilic neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) that progressed in parallel with NFT Stages I to VI. Pretangles predominantly occurred in subcortical regions at younger ages. Of the total cases, 1,031 (44.2%) had β-amyloid plaques. The first plaques appeared in the neocortex after the onset of tauopathy in the brainstem. Plaques generally developed in the 40s in 4% of all cases, culminating in their tenth decade (75%). There was a significant correlation between β-amyloid plaques and NFTs (p < 0.0001). These findings suggest that tauopathy associated with sporadic Alzheimer's disease may begin earlier than previously thought and possibly in the lower brainstem rather than in the transentorhinal region.

title: Coronary bypass graft patency in patients with diabetes in the Bypass Angioplasty Revascularization Investigation (BARI).
text:
Background: Few studies have investigated the long-term status of bypass grafts in patients with and without diabetes after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Therefore, the relationship between diabetes and the patency of internal mammary artery (IMA) and vein grafts over a prolonged follow-up period remains uncertain.
Methods and Results: In this study, we analyzed the angiographic data of 1526 patients who underwent CABG as initial revascularization in the Bari Atrial Fibrillation and Cardiac Death (BARI) study. Of these patients, 99 (34%) had treated diabetes mellitus (TDM), and 469 (38%) did not. The average follow-up time was 3.9 years, during which time 89% of IMA grafts and 71% of vein grafts were free of stenoses > or =50%. After statistical adjustment, TDM was unrelated to having a graft stenosis > or =50% (adjusted odds ratio, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.58 to 1.32).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that diabetes does not adversely affect the patency of IMA or vein grafts over a mean follow-up period of 4 years. This suggests that previously observed differences in survival between CABG-treated patients with and without diabetes may be largely due to differential risk of mortality from noncardiac causes rather than any specific adverse effect of diabetes on graft patency.

title: A novel ATAC-seq approach reveals lineage-specific reinforcement of the open chromatin landscape via cooperation between BAF and p63
text:
Background:
Open chromatin regions are closely linked with active regulatory elements during development and are often disrupted in diseases. The BAF (SWI/SNF) complex is crucial for development and has been shown to remodel chromatin in vitro and control access to specific regions in vivo. However, the mechanisms by which BAF regulates the open chromatin landscape to control developmental processes, such as human epidermal differentiation, remain unclear.
Results:
Using a novel "on-plate" ATAC-sequencing approach that profiles open chromatin landscapes with minimal adherent cells, we demonstrate that the BAF complex is essential for maintaining 11.6% of open chromatin regions in epidermal differentiation. These BAF-dependent regions are highly cell-type-specific and are enriched for p63 binding sites, a master transcription factor in epidermal cells. The DNA sequences surrounding p63 binding sites intrinsically favor nucleosome formation and are inaccessible in other cell types without p63, preventing ectopic activation. In epidermal cells, BAF and p63 mutually recruit each other to maintain 14,853 open chromatin regions. We further show that BAF and p63 cooperate to position nucleosomes away from p63 binding sites and recruit transcriptional machinery to control tissue differentiation.
Conclusions:
Our findings reveal that BAF exhibits high specificity in regulating the open chromatin landscape during epidermal differentiation by collaborating with p63 to maintain lineage-specific open chromatin regions. This study provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying the regulation of developmental processes and the role of chromatin remodeling complexes in maintaining cell-type-specific gene expression.

title: Aging, habitual exercise, and dynamic arterial compliance.
text: Background: A decline in the flexibility of the large-sized cardiothoracic (central) arteries with advancing age is an independent risk factor for the development of cardiovascular disease. Methods and Results: We investigated the role of regular exercise in preserving central arterial compliance, or the ability of the arteries to stretch and recoil, in middle-aged and older men. We conducted cross-sectional and interventional studies. In the first study, we analyzed the central arterial compliance of 151 healthy men aged 18 to 77 years, dividing them into three groups based on their level of physical activity: sedentary, recreationally active, and endurance exercise-trained. We found that central arterial compliance was significantly lower in middle-aged and older men compared to young men in all three groups. However, the difference between sedentary and recreationally active men was not significant, while the endurance-trained men had 20% to 35% higher central arterial compliance than the other two groups. In the second study, we examined the effects of a 3-month aerobic exercise intervention on central arterial compliance in 20 middle-aged and older sedentary men. Regular exercise significantly increased central arterial compliance to levels similar to those of middle-aged and older endurance-trained men, independent of changes in body mass, adiposity, arterial blood pressure, or maximal oxygen consumption. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that regular aerobic-endurance exercise can attenuate age-related reductions in central arterial compliance and restore levels in previously sedentary healthy middle-aged and older men, which may be one mechanism by which habitual exercise lowers the risk of cardiovascular disease in this population.

title: A comparison of cancer screening practices in cancer survivors and in the general population: the Korean national health and nutrition examination survey (KNHANES) 2001–2007
text: This study aimed to investigate cancer screening rates among cancer survivors in Korea and compare them to those of two control groups: individuals with other chronic diseases but no history of cancer, and individuals without any chronic diseases or cancer history. The study analyzed data from 15,556 adults aged 30 or older who participated in the 2001, 2005, and 2007 Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (KNHANES). The study found that cancer survivors had higher screening rates for all four cancer sites (breast, cervical, gastric, and colorectal) compared to both control groups, but the difference was only statistically significant for breast cancer after adjusting for gender, age, marital status, education, income, working status, health insurance, smoking and drinking status, and self-reported health status. Cancer survivors were more likely than individuals without a cancer history to obtain screening examinations according to recommended guidelines, but even among survivors, screening rates were suboptimal, highlighting the need for a more systematic approach to second primary cancer screening and prevention.

title: Negative effect of the transcriptional activator GAL4
text: The transcriptional activator GAL4 binds specific sites on DNA to regulate gene expression by activating adjacent genes. The distinct activating regions of GAL4 are enriched in acidic residues, which are thought to interact with other proteins in the transcriptional machinery, such as TATA-binding protein or RNA polymerase II. The DNA-binding region of GAL4 positions the activating region near the target gene. Our findings show that GAL4 derivatives with high expression levels in yeast inhibit the transcription of genes lacking GAL4 binding sites, with more efficient activators causing stronger inhibition. Inhibition does not depend on the DNA-binding domain, suggesting that it reflects a titration effect of the activating region of GAL4.

title: The Bayh–Dole Act and university research and development
text: This study investigates the connection between university research and development (R&D) activities and the Bayh-Dole Act. The Act significantly simplified the process for universities to obtain patents on research funded by the federal government, which may have encouraged universities to alter their R&D focus. The Act may incentivize a shift away from basic research (which does not generate licensing fees) and towards applied research (which does generate patents and licensing fees). Furthermore, the Act may make it more appealing for industry to fund university R&D projects, as the results would now be easier to patent. This study diverges from existing literature, which relies on patent data (a measure of research output) to examine the Act's impact, by using research and development data (a measure of inventive input) to explore the Act's effects.

title: The relation between past exposure to fine particulate air pollution and prevalent anxiety: observational cohort study
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between exposure to particulate air pollution and the prevalence of high symptoms of anxiety in a large cohort of women.
Design: Observational cohort study.
Setting: Nurses' Health Study.
Participants: 71,271 women residing throughout the contiguous United States who had valid estimates of exposure to particulate matter and data on anxiety symptoms.
Main Outcome Measures: Meaningfully high symptoms of anxiety, defined as a score of 6 points or greater on the phobic anxiety subscale of the Crown-Crisp index, assessed in 2004.
Results: The study population had a prevalence of high anxiety symptoms of 15%. Exposure to particulate matter was characterized using estimated average exposure to PM2.5 and PM2.5-10 in the one month, three months, six months, one year, and 15 years prior to assessment of anxiety symptoms, and residential distance to the nearest major road two years prior to assessment. Significantly increased odds of high anxiety symptoms were observed with higher exposure to PM2.5 for multiple averaging periods, with the association being stronger for more recent exposures. There was no association between anxiety and exposure to PM2.5-10, and residential proximity to major roads was not related to anxiety symptoms in a dose-dependent manner.
Conclusions: Exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) was associated with high symptoms of anxiety, with more recent exposures potentially more relevant than more distant exposures. Reducing exposure to ambient PM2.5 may reduce the population-level burden of clinically relevant symptoms of anxiety, warranting further research in this area.

title: A mitochondrially targeted compound delays aging in yeast through a mechanism linking mitochondrial membrane lipid metabolism to mitochondrial redox biology☆
text: A recent study has uncovered a natural compound that slows down aging in yeast by altering mitochondrial redox processes. This mechanism involves the introduction of lithocholic bile acid into yeast cells, which accumulates primarily in the inner mitochondrial membrane. As yeast cells age, the bile acid triggers a remodeling of phospholipid synthesis and movement within both mitochondrial membranes. This age-related remodeling of mitochondrial phospholipid dynamics leads to significant changes in the composition of mitochondrial membrane phospholipids, altering mitochondrial abundance and morphology. These changes, in turn, impact the age-related chronology of redox processes in mitochondria, including mitochondrial respiration, membrane potential, and the balance of mitochondrially produced reactive oxygen species. The study suggests that this mechanism may hold the key to understanding and promoting healthy aging.

title: Isolation from African Sykes' monkeys (Cercopithecus mitis) of a lentivirus related to human and simian immunodeficiency viruses.
text: An analysis of serum samples from 100 wild-caught or colony-born Sykes' monkeys (Cercopithecus mitis) in Kenya revealed that 59 animals had antibodies cross-reactive to human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) and to simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs). Among the seropositive animals, a lentivirus, designated SIVsyk, was isolated from five of six animals, but isolation was only possible in four cases after depleting the CD8+ lymphocytes and cocultivating the CD4(+)-enriched cell population with peripheral blood mononuclear cells from seronegative Sykes' monkeys. SIVsyk shared morphological and biochemical characteristics with other SIVs and HIVs, including an Mg2(+)-dependent reverse transcriptase enzyme and the ability to replicate in and be cytopathic for CEMx174 and Sup-T1 cells. However, SIVsyk differed significantly from other SIVs in that it failed to replicate in normal human, mangabey, and macaque peripheral blood mononuclear cells and serum from seropositive Sykes' monkeys immunoprecipitated env antigens from HIV-1 as well as from HIV-2, SIVsmm, and SIVagm. These findings indicate a high prevalence of natural infection in Sykes' monkeys in Kenya with a unique lentivirus that appears to have a limited host range and cross-reactivity to HIV-1 and other SIVs.

title: Role of the Single-Stranded DNA–Binding Protein SsbB in Pneumococcal Transformation: Maintenance of a Reservoir for Genetic Plasticity
text: Bacteria possess a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein called SSB, which plays a crucial role in genome maintenance. In Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae, an alternative SSB called SsbB is specifically expressed during periods of genetic transformation, but its exact function has been unclear. To investigate, we compared a null mutant (ssbB(-)) and a C-ter truncation (ssbBΔ7) of SsbB in S. pneumoniae, the latter constructed because the acidic tail of SSBs is important for interactions with partner proteins. Our findings demonstrate that SsbB directly protects internalized ssDNA, and we show that it is highly abundant, potentially binding up to half a genome equivalent of ssDNA. Additionally, we find that SsbB participates in the processing of ssDNA into recombinants and is essential for chromosomal transformation at high DNA concentrations, while inhibiting plasmid transformation. Our results suggest that SsbB creates a reservoir of ssDNA, allowing for successive recombination cycles, and that the C-ter of SsbB is not necessary for this function. We propose that the evolutionary purpose of SsbB is to maintain this reservoir, which enhances the genetic plasticity of S. pneumoniae by increasing the likelihood of multiple transformation events in the same cell.

title: Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly
text: The intricate nature of the human brain has hindered researchers' ability to study various brain disorders in simpler organisms, highlighting the need for an in vitro model of human brain development. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel three-dimensional culture system using human pluripotent stem cells, termed cerebral organoids, which recapitulate the formation and organization of different brain regions. These regions include a cerebral cortex with progenitor populations that give rise to mature cortical neuron subtypes. Notably, cerebral organoids exhibit features similar to those observed during human cortical development, such as a well-organized progenitor zone with abundant outer radial glial stem cells. To further demonstrate the utility of this system, we used RNA interference and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells to model microcephaly, a disorder that has proven challenging to recapitulate in mice. Our findings reveal premature neuronal differentiation in patient organoids, a defect that may contribute to the disease phenotype. Overall, these results demonstrate the potential of three-dimensional organoids to recapitulate both development and disease in the most complex human tissue.

title: Localization of a gene for partial epilepsy to chromosome 10q
text: There is convincing evidence that genetics play a role in epilepsy, but it is commonly believed that this genetic contribution is limited to "generalized" epilepsies, and that most forms of "partial" epilepsy are non-genetic. However, in a study of a single family with 11 affected individuals, we found strong evidence for the localization of a gene for partial epilepsy through linkage analysis. This susceptibility gene is located on chromosome 10q, with a maximum two-point lod score of 3.99 at θ=0.0. All affected individuals share a single haplotype for seven tightly linked contiguous markers, with a maximum lod score of 4.83 at θ=0.0. Our results also indicate that the susceptibility locus is located within a 10 centimorgan interval.

title: Metastatic colonization requires the repression of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition inducer Prrx1.
text: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) plays a crucial role in embryonic development, where it facilitates the formation of tissues despite the cells' origin far from their final destination. However, cancer cells have hijacked this process for tumor dissemination. The significance of EMT in cancer is still a topic of debate due to the unclear mechanisms by which migratory cells colonize distant tissues to form macrometastases. We have discovered that the homeobox factor Prrx1 acts as an EMT inducer, conferring migratory and invasive properties to cancer cells. The loss of Prrx1 function is essential for cancer cells to metastasize in vivo, and the cells revert to an epithelial phenotype upon the acquisition of stem cell properties. Unlike traditional EMT transcription factors, Prrx1 uncouples EMT and stemness, and serves as a biomarker associated with patient survival and lack of metastasis.

title: A cohort study of the risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 in relation to papillomavirus infection.
text:
Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) has been linked to cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), but the exact timing of the infection and the development of CIN is unclear. Additionally, the specific type of HPV, other sexually transmitted diseases, and other risk factors may play a role in the development of CIN.
Methods: We conducted a prospective study of 241 women who presented for evaluation of sexually transmitted diseases and had negative cervical cytology tests. The women were followed every four months with cytology and colposcopy examinations of the uterine cervix and tests for HPV DNA and other sexually transmitted diseases.
Results: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 was confirmed by biopsy in 28 women. Using survival analysis, the cumulative incidence of CIN at two years was 28% among women with a positive HPV test and 3% among those without detectable HPV DNA. The risk was highest among those with HPV types 16 or 18 infection (adjusted relative risk compared to those without HPV infection: 11; 95% confidence interval: 4.6-26; attributable risk: 52%). All 24 cases of CIN grade 2 or 3 among HPV-positive women were detected within 24 months after the first positive HPV test. After adjusting for the presence of HPV infection, the development of CIN was also associated with younger age at first intercourse, the presence of serum antibodies to Chlamydia trachomatis, the presence of serum antibodies to cytomegalovirus, and cervical infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Conclusions: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is a common and early manifestation of cervical infection with HPV, particularly types 16 and 18. The development of CIN is also associated with other risk factors, including younger age at first intercourse, the presence of serum antibodies to Chlamydia trachomatis, the presence of serum antibodies to cytomegalovirus, and cervical infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

title: Investigating survival prognosis of glioblastoma using evolutional properties of gene networks
text: In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in applying graph theory techniques to the analysis of biologically-informed gene networks derived from cancer cell line data. While much of the current research has focused on constructing and analyzing static, topological representations of these networks, there has been limited investigation into the use of graph theoretical methods for evolutionary studies of cancer. Our study aims to address this gap by leveraging graph theory metrics, such as degree, betweenness, and closeness centrality, to identify important hub genes across different stages of the disease. Previous work has identified four subtypes of glioblastoma in adults based on signature genes, and we find that these subtypes correspond to distinct survival times, with the most aggressive subtype having a median survival time of 11.3 months and the least aggressive subtype having a median survival time of 13.1 months. By applying evolutionary graph theory methods to survival data categorization, we confirm the importance of genes associated with different survival times and extend the application of graph theory approaches to evolutionary studies of cancer cell line data.

title: Compound heterozygous ZMPSTE24 mutations reduce prelamin A processing and result in a severe progeroid phenotype.
text:
Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS; OMIM 176670) is a rare and rapidly progressive disorder that mimics premature aging in affected children. Typically, these children appear normal at birth but develop failure to thrive and other characteristic features, such as alopecia, micrognathia, loss of subcutaneous fat, abnormal dentition, sclerodermatous skin changes, and osteolysis of the clavicles and distal phalanges, by the age of two. The mean age of death is around 13 years, primarily due to atherosclerosis. HGPS is primarily sporadic in occurrence, but recent studies have identified de novo heterozygous mutations in the LMNA gene in the majority of HGPS patients. A single family with autosomal recessive inheritance of homozygous LMNA mutations has also been reported.
LMNA encodes lamins A and C, which are components of the nuclear lamina, a meshwork underlying the nuclear envelope that provides structural support and regulates chromatin organization and gene expression. Mutations in LMNA have been associated with at least eight inherited disorders, known as laminopathies, which affect various tissues, including muscle, neurons, skin, bone, and adipose tissue. These disorders share common genetic defects and exhibit overlapping phenotypes, suggesting that they may represent a spectrum of related diseases. HGPS shares phenotypic similarities with other laminopathies, such as atypical Werner's syndrome and mandibuloacral dysplasia. These diseases are often associated with lipodystrophy, which is a prominent feature of another laminopathy, familial partial lipodystrophy of the Dunnigan variety. Mandibuloacral dysplasia has been further classified into two subtypes, one of which is characterized by a distinctive facial appearance.

title: Reliability of patient responses in pay for performance schemes: analysis of national General Practitioner Patient Survey data in England
text:
The objective of this study was to assess the robustness of patient responses to a new national survey of patient experience as a basis for providing financial incentives to doctors. The study analyzed the representativeness of the respondents to the GP Patient Survey compared to those sampled (5.5 million patients registered with 8273 general practices in England in January 2009) and to the general population. Additionally, the study looked at non-response bias by examining the relation between practice response rates and scores on the survey, and analyzed the reliability of the survey to estimate the proportion of variance of practice scores attributable to true differences between practices.
The overall response rate was found to be 38.2% (2.2 million responses), which is comparable to similar surveys in the UK. However, men, young adults, and people living in deprived areas were found to be under-represented among respondents. When it came to questions related to pay for performance, there was no systematic association between response rates and questionnaire scores. Two questions that triggered payments to general practitioners were found to be reliable measures of practice performance, with average practice-level reliability coefficients of 93.2% and 95.0%. Less than 3% and 0.5% of practices had fewer than the number of responses required to achieve conventional reliability levels of 90% and 70%.
A change to the payment formula in 2009 resulted in an increase in the average impact of random variation in patient scores on payments to general practitioners compared with payments made in 2007 and 2008.
The study's findings suggest that there is little evidence to support the concern of some general practitioners that low response rates and selective non-response bias have led to systematic unfairness in payments attached to questionnaire scores. The study raises issues relating to the validity and reliability of payments based on patient surveys and provides lessons for the UK and for other countries considering the use of patient experience as part of pay for performance schemes.

title: Impact of low alcohol verbal descriptors on perceived strength: An experimental study
text: The study examines how consumers perceive the strength and appeal of alcoholic beverages based on verbal descriptors such as "low," "lighter," and "reduced." The research used a within-subjects experimental design, where participants rated the strength and appeal of 18 terms denoting different levels of alcohol content (wine or beer) based on their drinking preferences. The results show that verbal descriptors form two clusters: one for lower strength products and another for high strength products. The study found that the term "Regular" was the most appealing, while the low and high intensifier descriptors were the least appealing. The findings suggest that the perceived strength and appeal of alcohol products decrease as the verbal descriptors imply a deviation from the "Regular" category. The study's implications are discussed in terms of policy implications for lower strength alcohol labeling and public health outcomes.

title: Transgenic Interleukin 10 Prevents Induction of Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
text: The effectiveness of interleukin 10 (IL-10) in treating autoimmune-mediated central nervous system inflammation is controversial. Research using the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model, which involves various routes, regimens, and delivery methods of IL-10, suggests that these variables may impact its immunoregulatory function. To investigate the impact of these factors on IL-10's regulation of EAE pathogenesis, we analyzed transgenic mice expressing a human IL-10 (hIL-10) gene under the control of a class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) promoter. These mice were highly resistant to EAE induced by active immunization, and this resistance was mediated by the suppression of autoreactive T cell function. In contrast, myelin-reactive T helper 1 cells were induced but remained nonpathogenic in the IL-10 transgenic mice. Antibody depletion confirmed that EAE resistance was dependent on the presence of the transgenic IL-10. Mice expressing the hIL-10 transgene but not the endogenous murine IL-10 gene demonstrated that transgenic IL-10 from MHC class II–expressing cells was sufficient to block induction of EAE. These findings demonstrate that IL-10 can completely prevent EAE if present at appropriate levels and times during disease induction.

title: Autosomal dominant immune dysregulation syndrome in humans with CTLA4 mutations
text: The protein cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) plays a critical role in regulating immune responses, and its dysfunction can lead to autoimmune disorders. We studied a large family with a rare genetic disorder characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, recurrent infections, and multiple autoimmune features. We identified a unique nonsense mutation in the CTLA-4 gene in these individuals, and screened 71 unrelated patients with similar clinical symptoms for additional mutations. Our findings revealed five additional families with previously undescribed splice site and missense mutations in CTLA-4. While some individuals with CTLA-4 mutations remained asymptomatic, others exhibited impaired regulatory T cell function, decreased B cell numbers, and disrupted T and B cell homeostasis. Our study suggests that mutations in CTLA-4 can result in a complex immune dysregulation syndrome, highlighting the critical role of this protein in maintaining immune balance.

title: Specific inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 by PD 0332991 and associated antitumor activity in human tumor xenografts.
text: PD 0332991 is a highly selective inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (Cdk4/6), with an IC50 value of 0.011 micromolar for Cdk4 and 0.016 micromolar for Cdk6, indicating negligible activity against a panel of 36 additional protein kinases. In vitro, PD 0332991 exhibits potent antiproliferative activity against Rb-positive tumor cells, resulting in an exclusive G1 cell cycle arrest and a concomitant decrease in phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein at Ser780/Ser795. Following oral administration to mice bearing the Colo-205 human colon carcinoma, PD 0332991 displays marked tumor regression. At therapeutic doses, PD 0332991 eliminates phosphorylation of Rb and the proliferative marker Ki-67 in tumor tissue, as well as down-regulates the expression of genes under the transcriptional control of E2F.
