These findings suggest that inhibition of Cdk4/6 activity alone is sufficient to induce tumor regression and reduce tumor burden in some tumors.

title: Neutrophils support lung colonization of metastasis-initiating breast cancer cells
text: Despite progress in developing drugs that target cancer cells, treatments for metastatic tumors often fail. The established dependence of cancer cells on their microenvironment suggests targeting the non-cancer cell component of the tumor as a potential therapeutic approach. However, the poorly characterized role of host responses during tumor growth and metastasis limits the effectiveness of this approach. Here, we identify neutrophils as the primary driver of metastatic establishment in the pre-metastatic lung microenvironment of mouse breast cancer models. Neutrophils play a fundamental role in inflammatory responses, and their contribution to tumorigenesis is still controversial. By blocking neutrophil recruitment to the pre-metastatic site, we demonstrate that neutrophils specifically support metastatic initiation. Importantly, we find that neutrophil-derived leukotrienes expand the sub-pool of cancer cells with high tumorigenic potential, allowing them to colonize distant tissues. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of the leukotriene-generating enzyme arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase (Alox5) abrogates neutrophil pro-metastatic activity and reduces metastasis. Our results highlight the efficacy of targeted therapy against a specific tumor microenvironment component and suggest that neutrophil Alox5 inhibition may limit metastatic progression.

title: Effect of Previous Miscarriage on Depressive Symptoms During Subsequent Pregnancy and Postpartum in the First Baby Study
text: Our study aimed to investigate the hypothesis that nulliparous women with a history of miscarriage are at increased risk of depression during late pregnancy and in the postpartum period compared to women without such a history. We conducted a secondary analysis of a longitudinal cohort study, the First Baby Study, and compared 448 pregnant women with a history of miscarriage to 2,343 pregnant women without a history of miscarriage in terms of their risk of probable depression (score >12 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). Our results showed that women with a history of miscarriage were not more likely than women without a history of miscarriage to score in the probable depression range during the third trimester or at 6 or 12 months postpartum. However, we found that women with a history of miscarriage were more likely to score in the probable depression range at 1 month postpartum, after adjusting for sociodemographic factors (odds ratio [OR] 1.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03–2.69). Our findings suggest that women with a history of miscarriage may be more vulnerable to depression during the first month postpartum than women without prior miscarriage, but this effect does not appear to persist beyond this time period. We recommend promoting awareness surrounding this issue and planning further research to identify risk factors that may position a woman with a history of miscarriage to be at higher risk for depression.

title: IL-1β, IL-4 and IL-12 control the fate of group 2 innate lymphoid cells in human airway inflammation in the lungs
text: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) secrete type 2 cytokines, which play a crucial role in protecting against parasitic infections but can also contribute to a diverse array of inflammatory airway diseases. In this study, we investigate the direct activation of human ILC2s by interleukin 1β (IL-1β) and the conversion of these activated ILC2s into interferon-γ (IFN-γ)-producing ILC1s in response to IL-12. Furthermore, we observe that the plasticity of ILCs is evident in the diseased tissues of patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), which exhibit IL-12 or IL-4 signatures and the accumulation of ILC1s or ILC2s, respectively. Notably, eosinophils are a prominent cellular source of IL-4, revealing a complex interplay between IL-5-producing ILC2s and IL-4-producing eosinophils. Our findings suggest that IL-12 and IL-4 play a pivotal role in determining the functional identity of ILC2s and that an imbalance between these cytokines can perpetuate either type 1 or type 2 inflammation.

title: Summary
text: Steroid receptor RNA activator (SRA), the sole known RNA coactivator, enhances transactivation by nuclear receptors (NRs). Through our investigation, we discovered that SLIRP (SRA stem-loop interacting RNA binding protein), a protein expressed in both normal and tumor tissues, binds to a specific substructure of SRA, known as STR7. SLIRP harbors an RNA recognition motif (RRM), which represses NR transactivation in a SRA- and RRM-dependent manner, and also enhances the effect of Tamoxifen. Furthermore, SLIRP modulates the association of SRC-1 with SRA. Additionally, we found that SHARP, a RRM-containing corepressor, also binds to STR7, thereby augmenting repression in a SRA- and RRM-dependent manner. Interestingly, SLIRP colocalizes with SKIP (Chr14q24.3), another NR coregulator, and reduces SKIP-potentiated NR signaling. Our results demonstrate that SLIRP regulates NR transactivation, suggest it may play a role in mitochondrial function, and provide insight into the interactions between SRA, SLIRP, SRC-1, and NCoR.

title: Naringenin inhibits allergen-induced airway inflammation and airway responsiveness and inhibits NF-kappaB activity in a murine model of asthma.
text: Naringenin, a flavonoid with anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, was investigated for its potential to attenuate allergen-induced airway inflammation in a murine model of asthma. Mice were sensitized and challenged with ovalbumin, and some were administered naringenin before the challenge. The development of airway inflammation and airway reactivity were evaluated by measuring inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and total IgE in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and serum. Additionally, the degradation of IκBα and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in the lungs, as well as NF-κB binding activity, were measured by Western blot and electrophoretic mobility shift assay, respectively. The mRNA levels of iNOS, CCL5, and CCL11 were also detected by real-time PCR. The results showed that naringenin significantly attenuated ovalbumin-induced airway inflammation and airway reactivity in experimental mice, associated with lower levels of IL-4 and IL-13 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and lower serum total IgE. Naringenin also inhibited pulmonary IκBα degradation and NF-κB DNA-binding activity, as well as the expression of its target genes CCL5, CCL11, and iNOS. These findings suggest that naringenin may play a protective role in the asthma process by inhibiting NF-κB and reducing the expression of its target genes.

title: The evolution of Fox genes and their role in development and disease
text: The forkhead box (Fox) family of transcription factors, which emerged in unicellular eukaryotes, has undergone an extensive evolutionary expansion through multiple duplication events and occasional gene loss, resulting in a diverse array of over 40 members in mammals. Fox genes have evolved to assume specialized functions in various crucial biological processes. Mutations in Fox genes have a profound impact on human disease, leading to a wide range of phenotypes, including cancer, glaucoma, and language disorders. We provide an overview of the key features of the Fox gene family's evolution and highlight the diverse contributions of various Fox subfamilies to developmental processes, from embryonic organogenesis to speech acquisition.

title: Emergent structures and dynamics of cell colonies by contact inhibition of locomotion
text: Cells within tissues can organize into a wide range of structures based on their function, with dramatic changes in organization often occurring during tissue development or cancer progression. To investigate these processes, we use computer simulations of self-propelled particles with generic cell-like interactions. By adjusting the parameters of cell softness, cell-cell adhesion, and contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL), we can reproduce a variety of tissue structures and collective dynamics observed in nature, including regular distributions of cells, dynamic cell clusters, gel-like networks, collectively migrating monolayers, and 3D aggregates. We provide analytical predictions for transitions between noncohesive, cohesive, and 3D cell arrangements, and show how CIL influences these transitions. Specifically, we find that CIL promotes cell dispersal and hinders the formation of cohesive tissues, while in continuous monolayers, CIL leads to collective cell motion, ensures tensile intercellular stresses, and opposes cell extrusion. Our work highlights the key role of CIL in determining the emergent structures and dynamics of cell colonies.

title: Failure of cell cleavage induces senescence in tetraploid primary cells
text: Tetraploidy can arise in mammalian cells due to various mitotic or cleavage defects, leading to aneuploidy when tetraploid cells continue to divide. The arrest of the tetraploid cell cycle is a crucial cellular control mechanism. We investigated the effects of tetraploidy on primary rat embryo fibroblasts (REF52) and human foreskin fibroblasts. Our results show that these cells become senescent in G1 phase after drug- or siRNA-induced failure of cell cleavage. In contrast, T-antigen-transformed REF52 and p53+/+ HCT116 tumor cells rapidly become aneuploid by continuing to cycle after cleavage failure. Tetraploid primary cells quickly enter a quiescent state, as evidenced by the loss of the Ki-67 proliferation marker and the fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator/late cell cycle marker geminin. The arrest is not due to DNA damage, as the γ-H2AX DNA damage marker remains at normal levels after tetraploidy induction. The arrested tetraploid cells eventually become senescent, as determined by SA-β-galactosidase activity. Our findings suggest that tetraploid primary cells can become senescent without DNA damage and that the induction of senescence is essential for tetraploidy arrest. Additionally, we found that the expression of p16INK4a is necessary for tetraploid arrest, as siRNA suppression of p16INK4a allows primary cells to become aneuploid.

title: Cell death: the significance of apoptosis.
text:
Cell death can be classified based on morphological or biochemical criteria, or on the circumstances under which it occurs. Currently, the only unequivocal evidence of cell death is the presence of irreversible structural alterations. While biochemical indicators of cell death have been proposed, their definition and application can be challenging. Moreover, studies of cell function or reproductive capacity do not always allow for a clear distinction between death and dormant states, which may be reversible.
Two distinct patterns of morphological change have been identified in dying cells: coagulative necrosis and condensation with maintained organelle integrity. Coagulative necrosis is characterized by swelling and rupture of plasma and organelle membranes, leading to dissolution of organized structure and evoking exudative inflammation in vivo. In contrast, condensation with maintained organelle integrity results in the formation of surface protuberances that separate as membrane-bounded globules, which are phagocytosed and digested by resident cells in tissues, without associated inflammation.
These two patterns of morphological change are associated with different underlying mechanisms and have distinct clinical implications. Understanding the classification of cell death is essential for the development of effective therapeutic strategies for various diseases and conditions.

title: The mitochondrial RNA-binding protein GRSF1 localizes to RNA granules and is required for posttranscriptional mitochondrial gene expression.
text: RNA-binding proteins play a crucial role in posttranscriptional gene regulation, controlling the processing, storage, and handling of cellular RNAs. Our findings reveal that GRSF1, previously linked to the selective translation of influenza mRNAs, is targeted to mitochondria, where it forms granules in close proximity to newly synthesized mtRNA foci near mitochondrial nucleoids. GRSF1 preferentially binds RNAs transcribed from three adjacent genes on the light strand of mtDNA, including the ND6 mRNA and long noncoding RNAs for cytb and ND5, each containing multiple binding sites. By knocking down GRSF1 through RNA interference, we observe alterations in mitochondrial RNA stability, impaired loading of mRNAs and lncRNAs onto the mitochondrial ribosome, and defects in ribosome assembly. These changes lead to a specific protein synthesis defect and a failure to produce normal amounts of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, highlighting GRSF1 as a key regulator of posttranscriptional mitochondrial gene expression.

title: Identification and purification of a 62,000-dalton protein that binds specifically to the polypyrimidine tract of introns.
text: A protein of molecular size 62,000 daltons (p62) was detected in nuclear extracts of HeLa cells through UV cross-linking to mRNA precursors. p62 selectively binds to the polypyrimidine tract of the 3' splice site region of introns. Following purification to homogeneity, p62 binds specifically to the polypyrimidine tract of pre-mRNAs without requiring the AG dinucleotide at the 3' splice site. Alterations in the polypyrimidine tract that reduce p62 binding lead to a corresponding decrease in the efficiency of forming a U2 snRNP/pre-mRNA complex and splicing. p62 remains bound to the pre-mRNA within the spliceosome. This protein, termed polypyrimidine tract binding protein (pPTB), is proposed to play a critical role in recognizing the 3' splice site during splicing.

title: Capsule endoscopy in acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage: a prospective cohort study.
text:
Background and Study Aims:
Capsule endoscopy may play a crucial role in the evaluation of patients presenting with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage in the emergency department. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of capsule endoscopy with nasogastric tube aspiration and esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) in identifying the source of bleeding, inflammatory lesions, and patient satisfaction.
Patients and Methods:
The study enrolled 49 adult patients with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage presenting to two academic emergency departments. Participants ingested a wireless video capsule, followed by nasogastric tube aspiration and later EGD. The presence of blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract was compared between capsule endoscopy and nasogastric tube aspiration, while the identification of peptic/inflammatory lesions and safety were compared between capsule endoscopy and EGD.
Results:
The study found that capsule endoscopy identified gross blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract, including the duodenum, significantly more often than nasogastric tube aspiration (15/18 vs. 6/18; P = 0.035). However, there was no significant difference in the identification of peptic/inflammatory lesions between capsule endoscopy (27/40 vs. 35/40; P = 0.10, OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.11-1.15). Capsule endoscopy reached the duodenum in 45/46 patients (98%). One patient experienced self-limited shortness of breath and another had coughing during capsule ingestion.
Conclusions:

In an emergency department setting, capsule endoscopy appears safe and feasible for evaluating patients with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Capsule endoscopy identifies gross blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract more accurately than nasogastric tube aspiration and identifies inflammatory lesions, as well as EGD. However, capsule endoscopy should not be considered a substitute for EGD in the evaluation of acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

title: Electroporation of Cas9 protein/sgRNA into early pronuclear zygotes generates non-mosaic mutants in the mouse.
text:
The CRISPR/Cas9 system is a powerful tool for investigating the functions of genes in a wide range of organisms, including mice. To produce genetically modified embryos or mice using this method, Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA (sgRNA) are typically introduced into zygotes through microinjection or electroporation. However, the resulting mutants are often genetically mosaic, consisting of multiple cell types with different mutations, which can complicate the analysis of phenotypes in founder embryos or mice. To overcome this limitation and simplify the analysis of gene function, we have developed a method for generating non-mosaic mouse mutant embryos.
We achieved this by introducing Cas9 protein and sgRNA into in vitro fertilized (IVF) zygotes through electroporation, allowing the genome editing to occur before the first replication of the mouse genome. As a result, all cells in the mutant embryo carry the same set of mutations, eliminating the problem of mosaicism/allele complexity in founder mutant embryos or mice generated by the CRISPR/Cas9 system. This innovative approach enables researchers to more easily elucidate the roles of genes in developmental processes, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms of embryonic development and disease.

title: Molecular Basis for Target RNA Recognition and Cleavage by Human RISC
text: The RNA-Induced Silencing Complex (RISC) is a ribonucleoprotein particle consisting of a short interfering RNA (siRNA) and an active Argonaute protein. RISC is capable of cleaving target messenger RNAs (mRNAs) that are complementary to the siRNA. While the mechanism of cleavage is well understood, the process of target recognition remains enigmatic. Our study shows that the accessibility of the target site directly correlates with the efficiency of cleavage, indicating that RISC is unable to cleave structured RNA. During target recognition, RISC transiently interacts with single-stranded RNA nonspecifically and promotes siRNA-target RNA annealing. Additionally, the 5' part of the siRNA within RISC creates a thermodynamic threshold that determines the stable association of RISC and the target RNA. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into the importance of RISC and target RNA features for achieving efficiency and specificity in RNA interference.

title: Cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in tumor microenvironment.
text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are a vital component of the tumor microenvironment, promoting the growth and invasion of cancer cells through various mechanisms. Despite their heterogeneity, CAFs have been found to exhibit distinct morphological features and physiological functions. The crosstalk between cancer cells and CAFs plays a crucial role in cancer progression, and understanding this relationship may lead to the development of new cancer therapies by targeting CAFs. In this review, we will discuss the latest findings on the role of CAFs in tumorigenesis and metastasis, as well as the potential therapeutic implications of targeting CAFs.

title: Cold Exposure Promotes Atherosclerotic Plaque Growth and Instability via UCP1-Dependent Lipolysis
text: The molecular mechanisms underlying the increased cardiovascular risk associated with cold exposure remain unclear. However, our study reveals that cold exposure triggers food-intake-independent lipolysis, leading to a significant increase in plasma levels of small low-density lipoprotein (LDL) remnants, which accelerates the development of atherosclerotic lesions in mice. In two genetic mouse knockout models (apolipoprotein E(-/-) [ApoE(-/-)] and LDL receptor(-/-) [Ldlr(-/-)] mice), persistent cold exposure stimulates atherosclerotic plaque growth by increasing lipid deposition. Moreover, we observed a marked increase in inflammatory cells and plaque-associated microvessels in the cold-acclimated ApoE(-/-) and Ldlr(-/-) mice, leading to plaque instability. Deletion of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), a key mitochondrial protein involved in thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue (BAT), in the ApoE(-/-) strain completely protected mice from the cold-induced atherosclerotic lesions. Cold acclimation also reduced plasma levels of adiponectin, and systemic delivery of adiponectin protected ApoE(-/-) mice from plaque development. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying low-temperature-associated cardiovascular risks.

title: Mild overexpression of MeCP2 causes a progressive neurological disorder in mice.
text: Mutations in the X-linked gene encoding the transcriptional repressor protein MeCP2 are responsible for Rett syndrome and other neurodevelopmental disorders. While the majority of mutations associated with disease are loss-of-function mutations, the specific aspect of MeCP2 function that leads to these phenotypes remains unclear. To investigate, we overexpressed wild-type human MeCP2 in transgenic mice using a large genomic clone containing the entire human MECP2 locus. Surprisingly, these mice displayed enhanced motor and contextual learning and improved synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus at 10 weeks of age. However, after 20 weeks, they developed seizures, became hypoactive, and approximately 30% died by 1 year of age. These findings suggest that MeCP2 levels must be tightly regulated in vivo, and that even mild overexpression of this protein can be detrimental. Additionally, these results support the possibility that duplications or gain-of-function mutations in MECP2 may underlie some cases of X-linked delayed-onset neurobehavioral disorders.

title: Alcohol Sales and Risk of Serious Assault
text:
BACKGROUND: Alcohol consumption has been linked to an increased risk of unintentional injuries, including motor vehicle crashes. Prior research on the association between alcohol use and violent injuries was limited by the use of survey-based data and the inclusion of cases from a single trauma center, without adequate controls. Furthermore, these studies were unable to comprehensively capture most alcohol sales. In Ontario, most alcohol is sold through retail outlets run by the provincial government, and hospitals are financed under a provincial healthcare system. To address these limitations, we conducted a population-based case-crossover analysis to assess the risk of hospitalization due to assault in association with retail alcohol sales across Ontario.
METHODS AND FINDINGS: We analyzed all hospitalizations for assault in Ontario between April 1, 2002, and December 1, 2004. On the day prior to each assault case's hospitalization, we compared the volume of alcohol sold at the store in closest proximity to the victim's home to the volume of alcohol sold at the same store 7 days earlier. We used conditional logistic regression analysis to determine the associated relative risk (RR) of assault per 1,000 liters higher daily sales of alcohol. Our findings showed that nearly 25% of the 3,212 persons admitted to hospital for assault were between the ages of 13 and 20, and 83% were male. A total of 1,150 assaults (36%) involved the use of a sharp or blunt weapon, and 1,532 (48%) arose during an unarmed brawl or fight. We found that for every 1,000 liters more of alcohol sold per store per day, the relative risk of being hospitalized for assault was 1.13 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02-1.26). The risk was higher among males (1.18, 95% CI 1.05-1.33), youth aged 13 to 20 (1.21, 95% CI 0.99-1.46), and those living in urban areas (1.19, 95% CI 1.06-1.35).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that there is a positive association between retail alcohol sales and the risk of serious assault, particularly among young urban men. Given the potential to reduce the risk of alcohol-related violence, consideration should be given to novel methods of prevention.

title: miR-375 inhibits autophagy and reduces viability of hepatocellular carcinoma cells under hypoxic conditions.
text:
Background and Aims:
Tumor cells often survive under hypoxic conditions by inducing autophagy, a process by which cells degrade and recycle damaged or dysfunctional cellular components. We investigated the role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in regulating autophagy of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells under hypoxic conditions.
Methods:
We used gain- and loss-of-function approaches to evaluate the effect of miRNAs on autophagy in human HCC cell lines (Huh7 and Hep3B) under hypoxic conditions. Autophagy was quantified using immunoblot, immunofluorescence, and transmission electron microscopy analyses, as well as after incubation of cells with bafilomycin A1. We used a luciferase reporter assay to confirm associations between miRNAs and their targets. We also analyzed the growth of HCC xenograft tumors in nude mice.
Results:
Our results showed that miR-375 was down-regulated in HCC cells and tissues, and it inhibited autophagy under hypoxic conditions by suppressing the conversion of LC3I to LC3II and thereby autophagic flux. The ability of miR-375 to inhibit autophagy was independent of its ability to regulate 3'-phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase-1-AKT-mammalian target of rapamycin signaling, but instead involved suppression of ATG7, an autophagy-associated gene. miR-375 bound directly to a predicted site in the 3' untranslated region of ATG7. Up-regulating miR-375 or down-regulating ATG7 inhibited mitochondrial autophagy of HCC cells, reduced the elimination of damaged mitochondria under hypoxia, increased release of mitochondrial apoptotic proteins, and reduced viability of HCC cells. In mice, xenograft tumors that expressed miR-375 had fewer autophagic cells, larger areas of necrosis, and grew more slowly than tumors from HCC cells that expressed lower levels of miR-375.
Conclusions:
Our findings suggest that miR-375 inhibits autophagy by reducing expression of ATG7 and impairs viability of HCC cells under hypoxic conditions in culture and in mice. These results suggest that miRNAs that inhibit autophagy of cancer cells might be developed as therapeutics.

title: Pseudouridine profiling reveals regulated mRNA pseudouridylation in yeast and human cells
text: Post-transcriptional modification of RNA nucleosides is a ubiquitous process in living organisms, with pseudouridine being the most abundant modified nucleoside in non-coding RNAs. Pseudouridine enhances the function of transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA by stabilizing their RNA structure. However, mRNAs were previously thought to be devoid of pseudouridine, but artificial pseudouridylation has been shown to significantly impact mRNA function by facilitating non-canonical base pairing in the ribosome decoding center. Although the physiological relevance of mRNA pseudouridylation was unclear, our study presents a comprehensive analysis of pseudouridylation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and human RNAs using a genome-wide, single-nucleotide-resolution method called Pseudo-seq. Pseudo-seq accurately identifies known modification sites as well as novel sites in non-coding RNAs, and reveals hundreds of pseudouridylated sites in mRNAs. Through genetic analysis, we were able to assign most of the new modification sites to one of seven conserved pseudouridine synthases, Pus1-4, 6, 7, and 9. Interestingly, the majority of pseudouridines in mRNA are regulated in response to environmental signals, such as nutrient deprivation in yeast and serum starvation in human cells. These findings suggest a mechanism for the rapid and regulated rewiring of the genetic code through inducible mRNA modifications. Our study reveals unanticipated roles for pseudouridylation and provides a resource for identifying the targets of pseudouridine synthases implicated in human disease.

title: The descent of memory T-cell subsets
text: The immune system has evolved to become increasingly complex over time, providing the host with a significant advantage in the fight against infectious agents. The development of immunological memory, which confers long-lasting protection and prolongs the host's lifespan, is a key aspect of this complexity. The generation of diverse subsets of memory T cells, each with distinct homing and functional properties, has greatly enhanced our defensive capabilities. However, the relationship between these subsets is still a topic of debate. In this Opinion article, we revisit recent findings and propose that it is likely that two distinct lineages make up the memory CD8+ T-cell population that develops in response to infection.

title: Differential distribution of IL28B.rs12979860 single-nucleotide polymorphism among Egyptian healthcare workers with and without a hepatitis C virus-specific cellular immune response
text: In this study, we investigated the distribution and correlation of the IL28B.rs12979860 single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) with HCV-specific cell-mediated immune (CMI) responses among Egyptian healthcare workers (HCWs). We enrolled 402 HCWs in four groups: seronegative aviremic subjects (n = 258), seronegative viremic subjects (n = 25), subjects with spontaneously resolved HCV infection (n = 41), and chronic HCV patients (n = 78). We tested all subjects for an HCV-specific CMI response using an ex-vivo interferon-gamma (IFNγ) ELISpot assay with nine HCV genotype-4a overlapping 15-mer peptide pools corresponding to all of the HCV proteins. We also tested the subjects for IL28B.rs12979860 SNP by real-time PCR. Our results showed that ~27 % of the seronegative aviremic HCWs (group 1) demonstrated an HCV-specific CMI, suggesting clearance of infection after low-level exposure to HCV. The frequency of IL28B.rs12979860 C allele homozygosity was 49 %, 48 %, 49 %, and 23 % in the four groups, while the frequency of the T allele was 14 %, 16 %, 12 and 19 %, respectively. These findings suggest differential distributions of the IL28B.rs12979860 genotype among subjects with different HCV status. However, we did not find any relationship between the IL28B genotypes and the outcome of HCV-specific CMI responses in the four groups (p > 0.05). In conclusion, our data show that the IL28B.rs12979860 genotype distribution differs among Egyptian HCWs with different HCV status, but it cannot predict the outcome of HCV-specific CMI responses.

title: TCR ligand density and affinity determine peripheral induction of Foxp3 in vivo
text: T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation is essential for the extrathymic differentiation of forkhead box p3(+) (Foxp3(+)) regulatory T cells. Various lines of evidence suggest that weak TCR stimulation favors the induction of Foxp3 in the periphery, but the influence of TCR ligand potency on this process remains unclear. To investigate, we characterized the density and affinity of TCR ligands that promote Foxp3 induction in vivo and found that a low dose of a strong agonist resulted in optimal induction of Foxp3. Initial Foxp3 induction by weak agonist peptide can be enhanced by disrupting TCR-peptide major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) interactions or altering peptide dose. However, time-course experiments revealed that Foxp3-positive cells induced by weak agonist stimulation are deleted, along with their Foxp3-negative counterparts, whereas Foxp3-positive cells induced by low doses of the strong agonist persist. Our findings suggest that the cumulative quantity of TCR stimulation, defined by pMHC ligand potency, density, and duration of TCR interactions, determines initial peripheral Foxp3 induction. However, the route to peripheral tolerance is influenced by noninterchangeable factors, including TCR ligand potency and density, in the persistence of induced Foxp3(+) T cells.

title: Electromagnetic interference from radio frequency identification inducing potentially hazardous incidents in critical care medical equipment.
text:
Introduction:
Advances in autoidentification technologies, such as radio frequency identification (RFID), have been proposed to improve patient safety and the tracking and tracing of medical equipment. However, there have been no reports of electromagnetic interference (EMI) caused by RFID on critical care equipment. This study aimed to assess and classify incidents of EMI caused by RFID on critical care equipment.
Methods:
This study was conducted in May 2006 at the Academic Medical Centre, University of Amsterdam, Amsterdam, The Netherlands. The study included 41 medical devices from 22 different manufacturers in 17 categories. EMI tests were conducted without a patient being connected to the devices, and the tests were conducted according to an international test protocol. The incidents of EMI were classified according to a critical care adverse events scale as hazardous, significant, or light.
Results:
The study found that RFID induced 34 EMI incidents, with 22 incidents classified as hazardous, 2 incidents classified as significant, and 10 incidents classified as light. The passive 868-MHz RFID signal induced a higher number of incidents (26 incidents in 41 EMI tests; 63%) compared with the active 125-kHz RFID signal (8 incidents in 41 EMI tests; 20%). The passive 868-MHz RFID signal induced EMI in 26 medical devices, including 8 devices that were also affected by the active 125-kHz RFID signal. The median distance between the RFID reader and the medical device in all EMI incidents was 30 cm (range, 0.1-600 cm).
Conclusion:
The study found that RFID can potentially cause hazardous incidents in critical care equipment. Implementation of RFID in the critical care environment should require on-site EMI tests and updates of international standards. Further research is needed to determine the frequency and severity of EMI caused by RFID in different clinical settings.

title: Potent RNAi by short RNA triggers.
text: RNA interference (RNAi) is a gene silencing mechanism where a ribonucleoprotein complex, called the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), targets a complementary messenger RNA (mRNA) for site-specific degradation. While longer double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) are processed into shorter interfering RNAs (siRNAs) or microRNAs (miRNAs) in cells, RNAi studies in human cells typically use synthetic 19- to 20-nucleotide (nt) siRNA duplexes with 2-nt overhangs at the 3'-end of both strands. Here, we report that systematic synthesis and analysis of siRNAs with deletions at the passenger and/or guide strand revealed a short RNAi trigger, 16-nt siRNA, which induces potent RNAi in human cells. Our results indicate that the minimum requirement for dsRNA to trigger RNAi is an approximately 42 A-form helix with approximately 1.5 helical turns. The 16-nt siRNA more effectively knocked down mRNA and protein levels than 19-nt siRNA when targeting the endogenous CDK9 gene, suggesting that 16-nt siRNA is a more potent RNAi trigger. In vitro kinetic analysis of RISC programmed in HeLa cells indicates that 16-nt siRNA has a higher RISC-loading capacity than 19-nt siRNA. These results suggest that RISC assembly and activation during RNAi does not necessarily require a 19-nt duplex siRNA and that 16-nt duplexes can be designed as more potent triggers to induce RNAi.

title: IL-23–responsive innate lymphoid cells are increased in inflammatory bowel disease
text:
Experimental and genetic studies have shown that the IL-23/IL-17 axis plays a key role in the development of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). While Th17 cells are the primary focus of IL-23-driven inflammation, recent discoveries have uncovered a novel population of innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) in mice that produce IL-17, IL-22, and IFN-γ in response to IL-23 and contribute to innate colitis. However, the role of ILC populations in human health and disease is still poorly understood.
In this study, we investigated the role of IL-23-responsive ILCs in the human intestine, both in control and IBD patients. Our findings revealed increased expression of Th17-associated cytokine genes, such as IL17A and IL17F, among intestinal CD3⁻ cells in IBD patients. Notably, IL17A and IL17F expression was restricted to CD56⁻ ILCs, while IL-23 induced IL22 and IL26 in the CD56⁺ ILC compartment. Furthermore, we observed a significant and selective increase in CD127⁺CD56⁻ ILCs in the inflamed intestine of Crohn's disease (CD) patients, but not in ulcerative colitis patients.
These results suggest that IL-23-responsive ILCs are present in the human intestine and that intestinal inflammation in CD is associated with the selective accumulation of a distinct ILC population characterized by inflammatory cytokine expression. ILCs may contribute to intestinal inflammation through cytokine production, lymphocyte recruitment, and organization of the inflammatory tissue, and may represent a novel tissue-specific target for subtypes of IBD.

title: Scaling of Dorsal-Ventral Patterning by Embryo Size-Dependent Degradation of Spemann’s Organizer Signals
text: Spemann's organizer plays a crucial role in dorsal-ventral (DV) patterning during amphibian embryonic development by secreting diffuse proteins, such as Chordin, which counteracts ventralizing bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). This robust DV patterning is so effective that an embryo with its ventral half removed can still develop into a smaller but proportionally patterned larva. Here, we reveal that this patterning relies on the facilitated degradation of Chordin and the expression of the Chordin-proteinase inhibitor Sizzled on the opposite side. Sizzled, which is stable and widely diffuses along the DV axis, stabilizes Chordin and expands its distribution in the ventral direction, thereby limiting BMP-dependent Sizzled production and forming an axis-wide feedback loop for shaping Chordin's activity. Using bisection assays, we demonstrate that Chordin degradation is dynamically controlled by embryo-size-coupled Sizzled accumulation. We propose a scaling model that enables the DV pattern to adjust proportionally to embryonic axis size.

title: Augmenting Antitumor Immune Responses with Epigenetic Modifying Agents
text: Epigenetic silencing of immune-related genes is a fundamental aspect of tumorigenesis, where cancer cells evade the immune system by suppressing the expression of genes involved in antigen processing and presentation. This phenomenon hinders the immune system's ability to recognize and attack cancer cells, allowing them to proliferate and progress. By modulating the tumor microenvironment through epigenetic mechanisms, the potential for immune recognition and tumor lysis can be restored. Preclinical studies have identified various immune cells and pathways that can be targeted through epigenetic modifications, leading to enhanced antigen presentation, T-cell function, and breakdown of suppressive mechanisms. Recent clinical trials are exploring the use of epigenetic therapies in combination with immunotherapies to improve treatment outcomes.

title: Activation of proteinase-activated receptor 2 in human osteoarthritic cartilage upregulates catabolic and proinflammatory pathways capable of inducing cartilage degradation: a basic science study
text: Proteinase-activated receptors (PARs) are a family of G protein-coupled receptors that are activated by a serine-dependent cleavage, generating a tethered activating ligand. In this study, we investigated the expression and modulation of PAR-2 in human normal and osteoarthritis (OA) cartilage/chondrocytes. We found that PAR-2 is produced by human chondrocytes and is significantly upregulated in OA compared to normal chondrocytes. The receptor levels were significantly upregulated by interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) as well as by a specific PAR-2-activating peptide (PAR-2-AP). The study also showed that PAR-2 activation significantly induced the synthesis of major catabolic factors in OA cartilage, including metalloproteinase (MMP)-1 and MMP-13, and the inflammatory mediator cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2). Furthermore, we identified p38 as the major signalling pathway regulating the synthesis of these factors. Our results suggest that PAR-2 may be a potential new therapeutic target for the treatment of OA.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps enriched in oxidized mitochondrial DNA are interferogenic and contribute to lupus-like disease
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) have been implicated in autoimmune disorders, but their exact mechanisms of generation and role in sterile inflammation are still unclear. Research has shown that ribonucleoprotein immune complexes (RNP ICs), which induce NETosis, require mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) for optimal NET stimulation. After RNP IC stimulation of neutrophils, mitochondria become hypopolarized and move to the cell surface. The extracellular release of oxidized mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is pro-inflammatory in vitro and, when injected into mice, stimulates type I interferon (IFN) signaling through a STING-dependent pathway. Mitochondrial ROS are also necessary for spontaneous NETosis of low-density granulocytes from individuals with systemic lupus erythematosus and chronic granulomatous disease, despite the absence of NADPH oxidase activity. In vivo inhibition of mitochondrial ROS reduces disease severity and type I IFN responses in a mouse model of lupus. These findings highlight the role of mitochondria in the generation of NETs and pro-inflammatory oxidized mtDNA in autoimmune diseases.

title: Microenvironment rigidity modulates responses to the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor lapatinib via YAP and TAZ transcription factors.
text:
Stiffness, a biophysical property of the extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in modulating cellular functions, including proliferation, invasion, and differentiation. Moreover, stiffness may also influence therapeutic responses in cancer treatments. However, the underlying mechanisms for the lack of durability in cancer treatments, particularly for chemotherapies and pathway-targeted drugs, remain poorly understood.
Tumor progression is often accompanied by changes in the biophysical properties of the tissue, and we aimed to investigate the role of matrix rigidity in modulating the sensitive versus resistant states of HER2-amplified breast cancer cells in response to the HER2-targeted kinase inhibitor lapatinib. Our findings revealed that the antiproliferative effect of lapatinib was inversely proportional to the elastic modulus of the adhesive substrata.
We further explored the mechanisms underlying lapatinib resistance by examining the role of mechanosensitive transcription coactivators, YAP and TAZ. Down-regulation of these proteins, either through siRNA or with the small-molecule YAP/TEAD inhibitor verteporfin, eliminated modulus-dependent lapatinib resistance. In vivo experiments in mice also revealed a trend of increasing sensitivity to lapatinib as YAP levels decreased, suggesting a critical role for stiffness in modulating the efficacy of HER2 pathway-targeted therapies.
Our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying resistance to cancer therapies and highlight the potential of targeting the mechanotransduction arm of the Hippo pathway to improve therapeutic outcomes. By modulating the stiffness of the extracellular matrix, we may be able to enhance the efficacy of HER2 pathway-targeted therapies and improve treatment outcomes in cancer patients.

title: Effective population size and patterns of molecular evolution and variation
text: The size of a population, Ne, plays a crucial role in determining the rate of change in a population's composition due to genetic drift, which is the random sampling of genetic variants in a finite population. Ne also influences the level of variability in a population and the effectiveness of selection relative to drift. This article examines the properties of Ne in various biological contexts and the factors that impact it. Specifically, selection can lead to variations in Ne across the genome, and advances in genomic techniques are providing new insights into how selection shapes Ne.

title: Is emotional dysregulation part of the psychopathology of ADHD in adults?
text: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common condition in adulthood, characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. However, some researchers argue that these symptoms may not fully capture the psychopathology of ADHD in adults. While the current International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV) do not include symptoms of emotional dysregulation as a core aspect of ADHD, some authors (e.g., Wender, 1995) propose a more differentiated understanding of adult ADHD that takes into account the subjective experiences of the adult patient. This approach suggests that emotional symptoms, such as irritability, anxiety, and depression, are an integral part of the disorder. Empirical studies have shown that these symptoms have sufficient reliability and validity, and can be considered as distinct factors in the psychopathology of adult ADHD. Pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions can help alleviate these symptoms. This review highlights the importance of considering emotional symptoms in the diagnosis and treatment of ADHD, which should be given more attention in future research.

title: A neural basis for melanocortin-4 receptor regulated appetite
text:
The hypothalamus's arcuate nucleus (ARC) contains neurons that express pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP), which have opposing effects on homeostatic satiety. When calorie intake is low, these neurons stimulate satiety, but when calorie intake is high, they inhibit it. The actions of these ligands on downstream melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4R) in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH) are antagonistic, with activation of these receptors leading to increased feeding. Despite the importance of these neurons in energy balance, the underlying neural circuitry remains unknown.
Using mice with Cre recombinase in MC4R neurons, we demonstrate bidirectional control of feeding by activating or inhibiting PVH(MC4R) neurons. These cells are found to be a functional exponent of ARC(AgRP) neuron-driven hunger. Furthermore, we reveal that this function is mediated by a PVH(MC4R)→lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPBN) pathway. Activation of this circuit encodes positive valence, but only in calorically depleted mice. This suggests that the satiating and appetitive nature of PVH(MC4R)→LPBN neurons supports the principles of drive reduction and highlights this circuit as a promising target for antiobesity drug development.

title: Lymph node T cell responses predict the efficacy of live attenuated SIV vaccines
text: Live attenuated simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) vaccines (LAVs) continue to demonstrate the most effective protection against HIV and AIDS in nonhuman primate models, yet the underlying mechanisms of this protection remain poorly understood. Our study reveals that the degree of protection against intravenous challenge with wild-type SIVmac239 correlates with the magnitude and function of SIV-specific, effector-differentiated T cells in the lymph node, but not with responses in the blood or other immune parameters. We found that maintaining protective T cell responses is linked to persistent LAV replication in the lymph node, primarily in follicular helper T cells. These findings suggest that effective LAVs maintain a pool of lymphoid tissue-based, effector-differentiated, SIV-specific T cells that can intercept and suppress early wild-type SIV amplification, and in sufficient frequencies, completely control and potentially clear infection. This discovery provides a rationale for the development of safe, persistent vectors that can elicit and maintain these protective responses.

title: Activation of Serotonin 2C Receptors in Dopamine Neurons Inhibits Binge-like Eating in Mice
text:
Background:
Neural networks that regulate binge eating remain to be identified, and effective treatments for binge eating are limited.
Methods:
We employed a multidisciplinary approach combining neuroanatomic, pharmacologic, electrophysiological, Cre-lox, and chemogenetic techniques to investigate the functions of 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) 2C receptor (5-HT2CR) expression in dopamine (DA) neurons in the regulation of binge-like eating behavior in mice.
Results:
Our findings demonstrated that 5-HT activates DA neural activity through a 5-HT2CR-mediated mechanism, and activation of this midbrain 5-HT→DA neural circuit inhibits binge-like eating behavior in mice. Furthermore, we found that 5-HT medications, including fluoxetine, d-fenfluramine, and lorcaserin (a selective 5-HT2CR agonist), act on 5-HT2CRs expressed by DA neurons to inhibit binge-like eating in mice.
Conclusions:
We identified the 5-HT2CR population in DA neurons as a potential target for antibinge therapies, and provided preclinical evidence that 5-HT2CR agonists could be used to treat binge eating.

title: Restoration of chaperone-mediated autophagy in aging liver improves cellular maintenance and hepatic function
text: Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA), a selective degradation mechanism for cytosolic proteins in lysosomes, plays a crucial role in the cellular quality control system. Our previous research has shown that CMA activity declines with age, leading to the accumulation of altered proteins, disrupted cellular homeostasis, and ultimately, the functional impairment characteristic of aged organisms. To investigate whether preserving autophagic activity could prevent these negative consequences of aging, we generated a double transgenic mouse model in which the abundance of the lysosomal receptor for CMA, which decreases with age, can be modulated. In this study, we examined the effects of preventing the age-dependent decrease in receptor abundance on cellular and organ function in aged rodents. Our results demonstrate that maintaining efficient CMA activity until late in life is associated with lower intracellular accumulation of damaged proteins, improved protein damage handling capacity, and enhanced organ function. These findings suggest that preserving autophagic activity may be a promising strategy for preventing or delaying the negative consequences of aging.

title: The Incidence and Repetition of Hospital-Treated Deliberate Self Harm: Findings from the World's First National Registry
text:
Suicide is a pressing public health concern, with approximately one million deaths by suicide occurring annually worldwide. Deliberate self-harm (DSH) is the most significant risk factor for suicide, yet few countries have reliable data on DSH. To address this gap, we developed a national DSH registry in the Republic of Ireland to determine the incidence of hospital-treated DSH at the national level and to characterize the spectrum and pattern of presentations with DSH and repetition.
Methods and Findings:
Between 2003 and 2009, the Irish National Registry of Deliberate Self-Harm collected data on DSH presentations to all 40 hospital emergency departments in the country. Data were collected by trained data registration officers using standardized methods of case ascertainment and definition. The Registry recorded 75,119 DSH presentations involving 48,206 individuals. The total incidence rate decreased from 209 (95% CI: 205-213) per 100,000 in 2003 to 184 (95% CI: 180-189) per 100,000 in 2006 and increased again to 209 (95% CI: 204-213) per 100,000 in 2009. Noteworthy annual changes included successive 10% increases in the male rate in 2008 and 2009. There was significant variation by age, with peak rates observed in women in the 15-19 year age group (620 (95% CI: 605-636) per 100,000) and in men in the 20-24 age group (427 (95% CI: 416-439) per 100,000). Repetition rates varied significantly by age, method of self-harm, and number of previous episodes.
Conclusions:
Population-based data on hospital-treated DSH represent a crucial indicator of the burden of mental illness and suicide risk in the community. The increased DSH rate in Irish men in 2008 and 2009 coincided with the onset of the economic recession in Ireland, highlighting the need for effective interventions to reduce DSH repetition rates as a key priority for health systems.

title: A Common Mechanism of Cellular Death Induced by Bactericidal Antibiotics
text: Antibiotic mode of action classification is determined by the interaction between the drug and the bacterial target, with lethal effects on bacterial function being a key factor. Here, we reveal that the three primary classes of bactericidal antibiotics, regardless of their target interaction, stimulate the production of highly harmful hydroxyl radicals in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, ultimately leading to cell death. In contrast, bacteriostatic drugs do not produce hydroxyl radicals. Our findings demonstrate that the mechanism of hydroxyl radical formation induced by bactericidal antibiotics involves an oxidative damage cellular death pathway involving the tricarboxylic acid cycle, a temporary depletion of NADH, destabilization of iron-sulfur clusters, and stimulation of the Fenton reaction. Our results suggest that all three major classes of bactericidal drugs can be enhanced by targeting bacterial systems that remediate hydroxyl radical damage, including proteins involved in triggering the DNA damage response, such as RecA.

title: Increased atherosclerosis in mice reconstituted with apolipoprotein E null macrophages.
text: Macrophages derived from macrophage-derived foam cells express abundant apolipoprotein E (apoE) in atherosclerotic lesions. To investigate the physiological role of apoE secretion by macrophages in atherogenesis, bone marrow transplantation was employed to reconstitute C57BL/6 mice with macrophages that were either apoE-deficient or contained the wild-type apoE gene. After 13 weeks on an atherogenic diet, C57BL/6 mice reconstituted with apoE-deficient bone marrow developed significantly more atherosclerosis than controls, despite similar serum cholesterol levels and lipoprotein profiles. Conversely, apoE expression was absent in the macrophage-derived foam cells of C57BL/6 mice reconstituted with apoE-deficient bone marrow, suggesting that the lack of apoE expression by macrophages promotes foam cell formation. These findings support a protective role for apoE expression by macrophages in early atherogenesis.

title: Endothelium-mediated relaxation of porcine collateral-dependent arterioles is improved by exercise training.
text:
BACKGROUND: The endothelium plays a crucial role in regulating coronary tone through the production of nitric oxide (NO). However, the endothelium-dependent modulation of coronary tone is impaired in the collateral-dependent coronary microcirculation. We aimed to investigate the effect of exercise training on endothelium-mediated relaxation and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (ecNOS) mRNA levels in the collateral-dependent coronary microvasculature.
METHODS: We used a porcine model of chronic coronary occlusion and collateral development to evaluate the hypothesis that exercise training enhances endothelium-mediated relaxation and increases ecNOS mRNA levels in the collateral-dependent microvasculature. Adult female miniature swine were subjected to chronic, progressive ameroid occlusion of the proximal left circumflex coronary artery (LCx); after 2 months, animals were randomly exposed to 16-week exercise-training (EX group; treadmill running) or sedentary (SED group; cage confinement) protocols. After completion of the EX or SED programs, coronary arterioles (approximately 100 microm in diameter) were isolated from the collateral-dependent LCx (distal to occlusion) and nonoccluded left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD) regions of each heart. Arterioles were studied using in vitro videomicroscopy or frozen for ecNOS mRNA analysis (RT-PCR techniques).
RESULTS: Relaxation to the endothelium-dependent vasodilator bradykinin was decreased in arterioles isolated from the collateral-dependent LCx versus nonoccluded LAD regions of SED animals (P < 0.05). However, bradykinin-mediated relaxation was not different in LCx versus LAD arterioles isolated from EX animals. Nitroprusside-induced relaxation was unaffected by either chronic occlusion or exercise. Importantly, ecNOS mRNA expression was significantly decreased in arterioles isolated from the LCx versus LAD regions of SED animals. After training, ecNOS mRNA expression was not different between LAD and LCx arterioles.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that exercise training enhances bradykinin-mediated relaxation of collateral-dependent LCx arterioles isolated after chronic coronary occlusion, likely due to effects on ecNOS mRNA expression and increased NO production. These data provide evidence for the importance of endothelial function in the regulation of coronary tone and suggest that exercise training may be a useful strategy for improving endothelial function in individuals with impaired coronary circulation.

title: Loss of the RhoGAP SRGP-1 promotes the clearance of dead and injured cells in Caenorhabditis elegans
text: Multicellular organisms exhibit an efficient mechanism for removing dying cells from their bodies. This process is conserved throughout evolution and involves various pathways. In this study, we identify a negative regulator of cell clearance, SRGP-1, in both Caenorhabditis elegans and mammalian cells. Our findings reveal that loss of SRGP-1 function leads to enhanced engulfment of apoptotic cells, while overexpression of SRGP-1 inhibits the removal of apoptotic cell corpses. We demonstrate that SRGP-1 functions as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for CED-10 (Rac1) and plays a crucial role in engulfing cells. Interestingly, loss of SRGP-1 function not only promotes the clearance of already dead cells but also enhances the removal of cells that have been weakened through sublethal apoptotic, necrotic, or cytotoxic insults. In contrast, impaired engulfment allows damaged cells to evade clearance, leading to increased long-term survival. Our findings suggest that C. elegans employs an evolutionarily conserved survey mechanism that identifies and eliminates unfit cells within a tissue.

title: Abnormalities in the myeloid progenitor compartment in Down syndrome fetal liver precede acquisition of GATA1 mutations.
text: Children with Down syndrome (DS) are at a higher risk of developing acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) in early childhood. At least two genetic events occurring in utero are required for the development of DS-AMKL, including trisomy 21 (T21) and N-terminal-truncating GATA1 mutations. To investigate the role of T21 in DS-AMKL, we compared the second-trimester hemopoiesis in DS individuals without GATA1 mutations to gestation-matched normal controls. We found that in all DS fetal livers (FLs), but not marrows, the frequency of megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors was significantly increased (55.9% ± 4% vs 17.1% ± 3%, CD34(+)CD38(+) cells; P < .001), while common myeloid progenitors and granulocyte-monocyte (GM) progenitors were commensurately reduced. Additionally, the clonogenicity of DS-FL CD34(+) cells was markedly increased (78% ± 7% vs 15% ± 3%), with a 7-fold higher frequency of megakaryocyte-erythroid and GM progenitors. Replating efficiency of colony-forming unit-granulocyte, erythrocyte macrophage, megakaryocyte (CFU-GEMM) progenitors was also significantly increased. These findings suggest that T21 alone has a profound impact on fetal liver hemopoiesis, providing a testable hypothesis to explain the increased susceptibility to GATA1 mutations in DS-AMKL and DS-associated transient myeloproliferative disorder.

title: Regulatory and metabolic rewiring during laboratory evolution of ethanol tolerance in E. coli
text:
Understanding the genetic basis of adaptation is a fundamental challenge in biology, as changes in fitness can result from minute perturbations to multiple pathways, making it difficult to identify the underlying molecular mechanisms. To address this problem, we have developed a combined experimental/computational framework that allows us to investigate the genetic basis of ethanol tolerance in Escherichia coli.
We used fitness profiling to measure the consequences of single-locus perturbations in the context of ethanol exposure, revealing the contributing loci organized into cellular processes and regulatory pathways such as osmoregulation and cell-wall biogenesis. Surprisingly, we found that a dominant component of adaptation involves metabolic rewiring, boosting intracellular ethanol degradation and assimilation.
To further investigate the mechanisms of ethanol tolerance, we used phenotypic and metabolomic analysis of laboratory-evolved ethanol-tolerant strains. Remarkably, these strains exhibited the same adaptive paths as predicted from our coarse-grained search of the fitness landscape, providing strong evidence for the role of metabolic rewiring in adaptation.
In summary, our study demonstrates the power of a combined experimental/computational framework for understanding the genetic basis of adaptation, and highlights the importance of metabolic rewiring in the adaptation of Escherichia coli to ethanol stress.

title: Familial risk of lymphoproliferative tumors in families of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia: results from the Swedish Family-Cancer Database.
text: The genetic factors contributing to the development of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) are highlighted by family and population studies. However, the extent to which other malignancies share these genetic factors and the impact of sex and age on inherited risk remain unclear. To investigate, we analyzed data from the Swedish Family-Cancer Database, comprising 14,336 first-degree relatives of 5,918 CLL cases and 28,876 first-degree relatives of 11,778 controls. We found that relatives of CLL cases were significantly more likely to develop CLL (relative risk [RR] = 7.52, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.63-15.56), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (RR = 1.45, 95% CI = 0.98-2.16), and Hodgkin lymphoma (RR = 2.35, 95% CI = 1.08-5.08). No significant differences in risk were observed between parents, siblings, and offspring, or between males and females. Additionally, the age of the case at diagnosis did not affect the inherited risk. Using life table methods, we did not find evidence of anticipation. Our findings suggest that the genetic factors underlying CLL are shared with other lymphoproliferative malignancies, indicating a common genetic pathway. However, due to the relatively low incidence of clinically diagnosed CLL, the absolute excess risk to relatives is small.

title: Collagen/Polypropylene composite mesh biocompatibility in abdominal wall reconstruction.
text:
Background: Intraperitoneal placement of polypropylene mesh can lead to extensive visceral adhesions, making it contraindicated. To address this issue, different coatings are being developed to enhance the properties of polypropylene mesh. Collagen is a protein with unique biocompatibility and cell ingrowth enhancement potential. A novel acetic acid extracted collagen coating was developed to enable direct contact between the mesh and viscera. The aim of this study was to evaluate the long-term effects of this coating on surgical aspects and biomechanical properties of polypropylene mesh implanted in direct contact with viscera, including complications, adhesions, mesh strength, and inflammatory response.
Methods: Forty adult Wistar rats were divided into two groups: experimental (polypropylene mesh with acetic acid extracted collagen coating) and control (polypropylene mesh only). A standardized procedure of mesh implantation was performed. The animals were killed 3 months after surgery, and their bodies were analyzed for complications, mesh area covered by adhesions, adhesion severity, mesh strength, and inflammatory response.
Results: The mean adhesion area was significantly lower in the experimental group (14.5% vs 69.9%, p < 0.001). Adhesion severity was also reduced in the experimental group, with grades 0 and 1 being more common (p < 0.04 and p < 0.002, respectively), and grade 3 being less common (p < 0.0001). An association between adhesion area and severity was found (p < 0.0001). Complications, mesh strength, and inflammatory response to the mesh were similar in both groups.
Conclusions: The acetic acid extracted collagen coating significantly reduces visceral adhesions to polypropylene mesh. The coating does not increase complications or affect mesh incorporation.

title: Microvessel Density and Status of p53 Protein as Potential Prognostic Factors for Adjuvant Anthracycline Chemotherapy in Retrospective Analysis of Early Breast Cancer Patients Group
text:
A significant proportion of patients with early-stage breast cancer do not benefit from anthracycline-based chemotherapy. The aim of this retrospective study was to investigate the impact of microvessel density (MVD) and p53 protein status on 5-year disease-free survival (DFS) in breast cancer patients treated with anthracyclines in the adjuvant setting. The study analyzed immunohistochemically the MVD and p53 status of 172 breast cancer tumors in clinical stages T1-2, N1-N2, and M0.
The study found that 123 tumors (71.5%) had low MVD (≤ 214.8 microvesells/mm(2)), while 49 tumors (28.5%) had high MVD (>214.8 microvesells/mm(2)). The proportion of high MVD tumors significantly increased in tumors with N2 involvement (P = 0.000) and in estrogen or progesterone receptor-negative tumors (P = 0.029). p53 positivity was detected in 50 tumors (29.1%) and was significantly associated with higher tumor grade (P = 0.000), steroid receptor negativity (P = 0.000), cytokeratin 5/6 positivity (P = 0.026), topoisomerase IIα overexpression (P = 0.005), and higher proliferation rate (P = 0.001).
In univariate analysis, higher MVD (P = 0.016) and p53 negativity (P = 0.023) were significantly related to longer DFS (median follow-up 36 months). In multivariate Cox regression analysis, MVD was independently associated with DFS. These findings suggest that higher MVD is a favorable prognostic factor for early-stage breast cancer patients after adjuvant anthracycline-based chemotherapy.

title: Ranking of elimination feasibility between malaria-endemic countries
text: The Global Malaria Eradication Program (1955-1972) revealed a set of common technical and operational factors that enabled certain countries to successfully combat malaria. These factors were mapped for all malaria-endemic countries and combined to create an objective, relative ranking of countries based on their feasibility of eliminating malaria. The analysis was conducted separately for Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, and the limitations of the approach were discussed. The rankings showed that malaria elimination would be most feasible in countries in the Americas and Asia, and least feasible in countries in central and west Africa. The results differed when measuring feasibility based on technical or operational factors, highlighting the unique challenges faced by each country. The findings are not meant to be prescriptive, predictive, or provide absolute assessments of feasibility, but they demonstrate the value of spatial information in facilitating evidence-based assessments of relative malaria elimination feasibility for individual countries that can be quickly updated.

title: Genetics of obesity in adult adoptees and their biological siblings.
text: An adoption study investigating the genetic effects on obesity in adulthood was conducted, comparing adoptees separated from their biological parents at a young age with their biological full and half siblings raised by their natural parents. The adoptees were categorized into four groups based on their weight, with 115 full siblings of 57 adoptees and 850 half siblings of 341 adoptees participating in the study. The results showed that the body mass index (BMI) of full siblings increased significantly with the weight of the adoptees, while the BMI of half siblings showed a weaker increase across the four weight groups. There were no significant interactions with sex, sex of the siblings, or sex of the common parent. In contrast to previous findings in half siblings and natural parents, there was a striking and significant increase in BMI between full siblings of overweight and obese adoptees, suggesting that genetic factors independent of sex may influence the degree of fatness in adults living in the same environment.

title: 2010 rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria: an American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism collaborative initiative.
text:
Objective: The 1987 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) have been criticized for their lack of sensitivity in detecting early disease. This study aimed to develop new classification criteria for RA that prioritize early detection and prevention of persistent and/or erosive disease.
Methods: A joint working group from the ACR and the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) developed a new approach to classifying RA in three phases. The focus was on identifying factors that distinguish patients with high risk of persistent and/or erosive disease from those with less severe disease. The new criteria set is based on the confirmed presence of synovitis in at least one joint, absence of an alternative diagnosis that better explains the synovitis, and achievement of a total score of 6 or greater (out of a possible 10) from individual scores in four domains: number and site of involved joints (range 0-5), serological abnormality (range 0-3), elevated acute-phase response (range 0-1), and symptom duration (with two levels: range 0-1).
Results: The new classification system redefines the current paradigm of RA by emphasizing early detection of features associated with persistent and/or erosive disease. The criteria prioritize the identification of patients at high risk of developing severe disease, rather than solely relying on late-stage features to define the disease construct.
Conclusion: This new classification system has the potential to refocus attention on the importance of early diagnosis and effective disease management to prevent or minimize the undesirable sequelae that are currently associated with the RA paradigm. By prioritizing early detection and prevention, the new criteria aim to improve patient outcomes and reduce the burden of the disease.

title: A role for fibroblasts in mediating the effects of tobacco-induced epithelial cell growth and invasion.
text: Cigarette smoke and smokeless tobacco contain harmful compounds that can cause cancer, but the mechanisms by which these compounds lead to tumor growth and progression are not fully understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of smokeless tobacco extracts on human oral fibroblasts. We found that exposure to these extracts increased levels of reactive oxygen species, oxidative DNA damage, and DNA breaks in a dose-dependent manner. Prolonged exposure to the extracts caused fibroblasts to enter a senescence-like growth arrest, accompanied by changes in their secretory phenotype. When we cocultured fibroblasts exposed to smokeless tobacco extracts with immortalized but non-tumorigenic keratinocytes, we found that factors secreted by the modified fibroblasts increased the proliferation and invasiveness of partially transformed epithelial cells, but not their normal counterparts. Additionally, smokeless tobacco extracts-exposed fibroblasts caused partially transformed keratinocytes to lose the expression of E-cadherin and ZO-1, as well as involucrin, changes that are indicative of compromised epithelial function and commonly associated with malignant progression. Our results suggest that fibroblasts may play a role in tumorigenesis by increasing the aggressiveness of epithelial cells. Therefore, tobacco may not only initiate mutagenic changes in epithelial cells but also promote their growth and invasion by creating a procarcinogenic stromal environment.

title: ImmTAC-redirected tumour cell killing induces and potentiates antigen cross-presentation by dendritic cells
text: The ability of dendritic cells (DCs) to cross-present antigens plays a pivotal role in eliciting a polyclonal and long-lasting T cell response against cancer. Therefore, the capacity of emerging immunotherapeutic agents to orchestrate tumor eradication may depend on their ability to induce antigen cross-presentation. ImmTACs (immune-mobilizing monoclonal TCRs against cancer) are a novel class of soluble bi-specific anti-cancer agents that combine pico-molar affinity TCR-based antigen recognition with T cell activation via a CD3-specific antibody fragment. ImmTACs specifically recognize HLA-restricted tumor-associated antigens presented by cancer cells, leading to T cell redirection and a potent anti-tumor response. Using an ImmTAC specific for a HLA-A*02-restricted peptide derived from the melanoma antigen gp100 (termed IMCgp100), we demonstrate that ImmTAC-mediated melanoma cell death leads to cross-presentation of melanoma antigens by DCs. These cross-presented antigens can activate both melanoma-specific T cells and polyclonal T cells redirected by IMCgp100, with the former showing enhanced activation in the presence of cross-presenting DCs. The mechanism of DC cross-presentation involves the rapid and direct capture of membrane fragments from dying tumor cells by DCs, leading to the presentation of gp100-peptide-HLA complexes to T cells. Using a fluorescently labeled soluble TCR, we visualized and quantified DC cross-presentation of gp100-peptide-HLA complexes, demonstrating how ImmTACs interact with both the innate and adaptive components of the immune system to enhance the prospect of eliciting an effective and durable anti-tumor response in patients.

title: Basal keratinocyte tetrasomy in low-grade squamous intra-epithelial lesions of the cervix is restricted to high and intermediate risk HPV infection but is not type-specific
text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection appears to be an early event in the development of cervical cancer, with additional genetic alterations being required for the progression to cancer. In this study, we analyzed 179 low-grade cervical squamous intra-epithelial lesions (SILs) and 15 normal cervices for the presence of HPV using both in situ hybridization and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). PCR was performed using primers specific for low-risk HPV types 6, 11, 40, 42, 43, 44, as well as intermediate-risk HPV types 31, 33, 35, 39, 51, 52, 58, 59, 66, and 68. Interphase cytogenetic analysis using pericentromeric probes for chromosomes 1, 3, 4, 6, 10, 11, 17, 18, and X was also performed to identify numerical chromosomal abnormalities. Our findings indicate that the induction of tetrasomy, characterized by the presence of four copies of each chromosome, is a property restricted to high-risk and intermediate-risk HPV types, but not low-risk HPV types. This abnormality was identified in 17 of 46 epithelia infected with high-risk HPVs and 23 of 83 epithelia infected with intermediate-risk HPVs, but not in any of the epithelia infected with low-risk HPVs (n = 62). The factors underlying which lesions will develop this abnormality are currently unknown. © 2000 Cancer Research Campaign.

title: “Rapid-Impact Interventions”: How a Policy of Integrated Control for Africa's Neglected Tropical Diseases Could Benefit the Poor
text:
Over the past two decades, significant progress has been made in controlling a select group of major human tropical infections. These achievements include substantial reductions in the prevalence and incidence of so-called neglected diseases, such as lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, guinea worm, leprosy, and trachoma (Box 1). These neglected diseases are primarily found in rural areas of low-income countries and are often associated with poverty and stigma. In fact, these diseases have been a burden on humanity for millennia, as they are mentioned in ancient texts such as the Bible. However, with the implementation of aggressive regional vertical interventions, there is a possibility that some of these neglected tropical infections could be eventually controlled or even eliminated in certain areas of endemicity (Box 2). In the case of guinea worm infection, the possibility of disease eradication is also on the horizon (Box 2).
Box 1: Neglected Tropical Diseases
• Lymphatic filariasis
• Onchocerciasis
• Guinea worm
• Leprosy
• Trachoma

Box 2: Common Features of the Neglected Tropical Diseases

• Ancient afflictions that have burdened humanity for centuries
• Poverty-promoting conditions
• Associated with stigma
• Rural areas of low-income countries and fragile states
• No commercial markets for products that target these diseases
• Interventions, when applied, have a history of success

title: FTY720 (fingolimod) is a neuroprotective and disease-modifying agent in cellular and mouse models of Huntington disease.
text: Huntington's disease (HD) is a genetic neurodegenerative disorder without a current cure or means to slow or stop the brain changes it causes. In this study, we aimed to investigate whether FTY720, the first approved oral therapy for multiple sclerosis, may be effective in HD models and serve as an alternative therapeutic approach for the disease. We employed preclinical target validation paradigms and examined the in vivo efficacy of chronic FTY720 administration in R6/2 HD mouse models. Our findings indicate that FTY720 improved motor function, extended survival, and reduced brain atrophy in R6/2 mice. The beneficial effect of FTY720 administration was associated with a significant enhancement of neuronal activity and connectivity, as well as a reduction of mutant huntingtin aggregates. Additionally, there was an increase in phosphorylation of mutant huntingtin at serine 13/16 residues, which are predicted to attenuate protein toxicity.

title: Specificity Residues Determine Binding Affinity for Two-Component Signal Transduction Systems
text:
Introduction:
Two-component systems (TCS) are ubiquitous in bacteria, comprising histidine kinases (HKs) and their cognate response regulators (RRs). These systems allow bacteria to sense and respond to a wide variety of signals, including environmental changes and cellular signals. The Myxococcus xanthus genome encodes one of the largest repertoires of signaling proteins in bacteria, including 127 HKs and 143 RRs. Of these, 27 are bona fide NtrC-family response regulators, many of which are encoded adjacent to their predicted cognate kinases.
System-wide profiling methods were used to determine the kinetic preferences of HK-NtrC RR pairs in M. xanthus. Isothermal titration calorimetry measurements revealed that cognate HK-RR pairs interact with dissociation constants (Kd) of approximately 1 µM, while noncognate pairs had no measurable binding.
Results:
To investigate the specificity of HK-RR pairs in M. xanthus, a chimera was generated between the histidine kinase, CrdS, and HK1190. Residues conferring phosphotransfer and phosphatase specificity were identified and found to dictate binding affinity, thereby establishing discrete protein-protein interactions that prevent cross-talk.
Discussion:
