text: In cancer cachexia, weight loss is primarily caused by a combination of decreased food intake and increased energy expenditure. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we studied the roles of uncoupling proteins (UCPs) UCPI, -2, and -3 in a murine model of cachexia, the MAC16 adenocarcinoma. We found that weight loss in MAC16-bearing mice reached 24% below that of non-tumor-bearing controls within 18 days, with significant reductions in fat-pad mass and muscle mass. Food intake was 26-60% lower than in controls on days 17-18. Interestingly, pair-feeding non-tumor-bearing mice to match the hypophagia induced by the tumor resulted in less weight loss and smaller decreases in fat-pad mass. Core temperature in MAC16 mice was significantly lower than in controls, and pair-feeding had no effect. We found that MAC16 mice had higher levels of UCP1 mRNA in brown adipose tissue (BAT) than controls, and this increase was not affected by pair-feeding. UCP2 and -3 expression in BAT did not differ significantly between groups. However, UCP2 mRNA levels were comparably increased in both MAC16 and pair-fed groups in skeletal muscle, with no significant difference between the two groups. Similarly, UCP3 mRNA was significantly higher than controls in both MAC16 and pair-fed groups, with no significant difference between the two groups. Our findings suggest that overexpression of UCP1 in BAT in MAC16-bearing mice may be an adaptive response to hypothermia induced by tumor products, leading to increased thermogenesis and total energy expenditure. Increased UCP2 and -3 expression in muscle may be involved in lipid utilization during lipolysis in MAC16-induced cachexia.

title: In vitro Anti-Tumor Effects of Statins on Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Systematic Review
text:
BACKGROUND Statins, commonly used to treat arteriosclerosis, have also been found to have anti-cancer properties. This systematic review aims to investigate the in vitro effects of statins on head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).
METHODS We conducted a comprehensive search of Cochrane, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and PubMed up until May 9, 2015, without any time or language restrictions. We selected in vitro studies that examined the effect of statins on HNSCC cells.
RESULTS Of the 153 identified studies, 14 met our inclusion criteria. These studies demonstrated that statins have a significant impact on HNSCC cell lines, affecting cell viability, cell cycle, cell death, and protein expression levels involved in carcinogenic pathways. These findings corroborate the potential anti-tumor effects of statins in vitro. The study highlights the biological mechanisms of statins when used alone or in combination with traditional cancer therapies, such as chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy.
CONCLUSIONS Although limited research has been conducted, the available evidence suggests that statins may have potential as an adjuvant agent in cancer treatment, particularly in the management of HNSCC. Further clinical assessment is warranted to confirm these findings.

title: Circulating Mitochondrial DNA in Patients in the ICU as a Marker of Mortality: Derivation and Validation
text:
Background: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has been shown to play a critical role in activating inflammation and the innate immune system. However, its potential as a biomarker in the intensive care unit (ICU) has not been fully explored. We hypothesized that circulating cell-free mtDNA levels would be associated with mortality and improve risk prediction in ICU patients.
Methods and Findings: We analyzed mtDNA levels in blood samples from two prospective observational cohort studies of ICU patients, including 200 patients in the Brigham and Women's Hospital Registry of Critical Illness (BWH RoCI) and 243 patients in the Molecular Epidemiology of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ME ARDS) cohort. mtDNA levels were measured using quantitative real-time PCR, and the results were compared between medical and non-medical ICU patients. We found that ICU patients with an elevated mtDNA level (≥3,200 copies/μl plasma) had significantly increased odds of dying within 28 days of ICU admission in both cohorts. Additionally, the addition of an elevated mtDNA level improved the net reclassification index (NRI) of 28-day mortality among medical ICU patients when added to clinical models in both cohorts. In the BWH RoCI cohort, patients with an elevated mtDNA level had an increased risk of death, even when analyzed in patients with sepsis or acute respiratory distress syndrome. Study limitations included the lack of data on the pathological roles of mtDNA in the patients and the limited number of measurements for some biomarkers.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that increased mtDNA levels are associated with ICU mortality and could serve as a viable plasma biomarker in medical ICU patients. The inclusion of mtDNA level improves risk prediction in medical ICU patients, and further research is warranted to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and potential clinical applications.

title: Fructosamine Is a Useful Indicator of Hyperglycaemia and Glucose Control in Clinical and Epidemiological Studies – Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Experience from the AMORIS Cohort
text: The study aimed to evaluate the utility of fructosamine as a glycemic biomarker in the diagnosis and monitoring of diabetes. The study analyzed data from the AMORIS cohort, which consisted of 10,987 subjects with serum glucose, fructosamine, and HbA1c measurements. The study found that fructosamine was strongly correlated with HbA1c in both fasting and non-fasting subjects with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.67 to 0.75. The study also found that fructosamine levels were similar over time in fasting patients with type 2 diabetes, and that fructosamine levels could accurately discriminate between subjects with and without diabetes (area under curve ranging from 0.91 to 0.95). The study concluded that fructosamine may be a useful biomarker of hyperglycaemia and glucose control in clinical and epidemiological studies.

title: Lifeact: a versatile marker to visualize F-actin
text: Live imaging of the actin cytoskeleton is essential for understanding various biological processes, but current methods for visualizing actin have several drawbacks. Here, we present Lifeact, a 17-amino-acid peptide that selectively stains filamentous actin (F-actin) structures in eukaryotic cells and tissues. Importantly, Lifeact does not interfere with actin dynamics in vitro and in vivo, and its chemically modified form allows for visualization of actin dynamics in non-transfectable cells.

title: Robustness of Random Forest-based gene selection methods
text:
Gene selection is a crucial step in microarray data analysis as it provides valuable insights into the underlying biological mechanisms. However, due to the noisy nature of microarray data, selecting the right genes can be a challenging task. Machine learning methods, including Random Forest-based feature selection, have been widely used to address this challenge. In this study, we compared four state-of-the-art Random Forest-based feature selection methods in a gene selection context, focusing on the stability of selection and post-selection accuracy.
Our results showed that all methods were equivalent in terms of post-selection accuracy, but they differed significantly in the number of selected genes and stability of selection. The Boruta algorithm predicted the most genes as potentially important, while the post-selection classifier error rate, a commonly used measure of gene selection quality, was found to be a potentially deceptive measure. When considering the number of consistently selected genes, the Boruta algorithm was the best performer, despite being the most computationally intensive method. To reduce computational demands, we replaced Random Forest importance with a similar measure from Random Ferns, resulting in computational levels comparable to other algorithms. Interestingly, the minimal optimal selection methods, which were designed to select a minimum number of genes, were found to select a high fraction of false positives.
In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of careful gene selection in microarray data analysis and the need to consider stability and post-selection accuracy when selecting genes. The Boruta algorithm was found to be the most effective method in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency, while the post-selection classifier error rate was found to be a potentially deceptive measure of gene selection quality. These findings have important implications for the analysis of microarray data and the interpretation of gene selection results.

title: Improved variant discovery through local re-alignment of short-read next-generation sequencing data using SRMA
text: A crucial aspect of next-generation sequencing (NGS) analysis is the process of aligning short reads to a reference genome. This involves mapping each read independently to the reference genome, taking into account the unique characteristics of each read. However, reads that observe the same non-reference DNA sequence are highly correlated, meaning they share similar features. By leveraging this correlation, a novel algorithm called SRMA (Short-Read Micro Realigner) can generate a more accurate consensus of the underlying DNA sequence of the targeted genome. SRMA uses this correlation to better model the true variation in the target genome, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the genetic material.

title: Functional elements within the dynein microtubule-binding domain
text: Dynein interacts with microtubules through an ATP-sensitive linkage localized to a structurally complex region of the heavy chain, following the fourth P-loop motif. Currently, little is known regarding the mechanisms by which binding affinity is achieved and modulated during ATP hydrolysis. To investigate this, we have conducted a detailed analysis of the microtubule contact site through the use of fragment expression, alanine substitution, and peptide competition. Our findings identify three clusters of amino acids crucial for physical contact with microtubules, with two of these clusters sharing sequence homology with MAP1B, and the third located downstream. Amino acid substitutions within any one of these regions can abrogate or weaken microtubule binding, suggesting that these activities are highly coordinated. Furthermore, we have discovered a peptide that disrupts MAP1B binding to microtubules, supporting previous evidence for similar interaction sites. Additionally, we have identified four amino acids whose substitutions affect the release of the motor from the microtubule, suggesting that nucleotide-sensitive affinity may be locally regulated at the site of contact. Our work represents the first comprehensive description of dynein-tubulin interactions and provides a framework for understanding the mechanisms underlying affinity modulation.

title: The Transcription Factors Egr2 and Egr3 Are Essential for the Control of Inflammation and Antigen-Induced Proliferation of B and T Cells
text:
Lymphocytes exhibit optimal responses against pathogens with minimal inflammation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored. In this study, we investigated the role of transcription factors Egr2 and Egr3 in regulating lymphocyte function. Surprisingly, we found that deleting both Egr2 and Egr3 in lymphocytes led to a lethal autoimmune syndrome characterized by excessive serum proinflammatory cytokines and impaired antigen receptor-induced cell proliferation in both B and T cells.
Further investigation revealed that Egr2- and Egr3-defective B and T cells displayed hyperactive STAT1 and STAT3 signaling, while antigen receptor-induced activation of transcription factor AP-1 was significantly impaired. We discovered that Egr2 and Egr3 directly regulate the expression of suppressor of cytokine signaling-1 (SOCS1) and SOCS3, which inhibit STAT1 and STAT3, and also block the function of Batf, an AP-1 inhibitor, in B and T cells.
Our findings demonstrate that Egr2 and Egr3 play a crucial role in regulating B and T cell function in adaptive immune responses and homeostasis by promoting antigen receptor signaling and controlling inflammation.

title: Effect of hyperosmolality on alkaline phosphatase and stress-response protein 27 of MCF-7 breast cancer cells
text: MCF-7, a continuous cell line derived from a human breast carcinoma, exhibits minimal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity. The enzyme is heat-stable and is inhibited by L-phenylalanine and L-phenylalanylglycylglycine, but not by L-homoarginine, 1-bromotetramisole, or levamisole. These findings suggest that MCF-7 cells produce term-placental ALP, the oncodevelopmental enzyme form inappropriately expressed by a variety of human tumors. In contrast to human cancer cells that produce this enzyme monophenotypically, ALP activity of MCF-7 cells is not significantly increased by glucocorticoids or sodium butyrate. Notably, exposure to hyperosmolality leads to a pronounced increase in enzyme activity, which can be blocked by cycloheximide. The results obtained in cell-free assays were confirmed by cytochemical and immunocytochemical assays on whole cells. To investigate the potential effects of the agents tested on other cellular processes, the expression of two stress-response proteins (srp 27 and srp 72) was examined using specific immunocytochemical assays. The results showed that neither protein is affected by glucocorticoids, while sodium butyrate has no effect on srp 27 but alters the intracellular distribution of srp 72. Furthermore, hyperosmolality leads to an increase in srp 27, but not srp 72.

title: The Bile Acid Chenodeoxycholic Acid Increases Human Brown Adipose Tissue Activity.
text: Interest in brown adipose tissue (BAT) as a potential treatment for metabolic disorders has been renewed with the discovery of functional BAT in humans. In animal studies, BAT can be activated by bile acids, which activate type 2 iodothyronine deiodinase (D2) in BAT through the G-protein-coupled receptor TGR5, leading to increased oxygen consumption and energy expenditure. To investigate the potential of bile acids as a BAT activator in humans, we examined the effects of oral supplementation with the bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) on human BAT activity. Our study found that treatment of 12 healthy female subjects with CDCA for two days resulted in increased BAT activity and whole-body energy expenditure. In vitro studies showed that CDCA or specific TGR5 agonists increased mitochondrial uncoupling and D2 expression in primary human brown adipocytes, but this effect was absent in primary white adipocytes. These findings suggest that bile acids may be a target for activating BAT in humans, providing a potential new approach for treating metabolic disorders.

title: RNase H and Postreplication Repair Protect Cells from Ribonucleotides Incorporated in DNA
text: The integrity of the genome is challenged when ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs) are incorporated into DNA during replication, instead of the usual deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs). DNA replicases have a selective process to limit misincorporation, but the accumulation of ribonucleoside monophosphates (rNMPs) in the genome can cause replication stress and toxic effects, particularly in the absence of RNase H1 and RNase H2, which remove rNMPs. Postreplication repair (PRR) pathways, such as MMS2-dependent template switch and Pol ζ-dependent bypass, are crucial for tolerating the presence of rNMPs in the chromosomes. Pol ζ can efficiently replicate over 1-4 rNMPs, and cells lacking RNase H accumulate mono- and polyubiquitylated PCNA and have a constitutively activated PRR. These findings highlight the importance of RNase H1, RNase H2, template switch, and translesion DNA synthesis in overcoming rNTPs misincorporated during DNA replication, and may provide insights into the pathogenesis of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome.

title: Selective elimination of high constitutive activity or chemokine binding in the human herpesvirus 8 encoded seven transmembrane oncogene ORF74.
text:
Human herpesvirus 8-encoded Open reading frame 74 (ORF74) is a highly active seven transmembrane (7TM) receptor that is stimulated by angiogenic chemokines, such as growth-related oncogene-alpha, and inhibited by angiostatic chemokines, such as interferon-gamma-inducible protein. Transgenic mice expressing ORF74 under the control of the CD2 promoter develop highly vascularized Kaposi's sarcoma-like tumors. To better understand the molecular mechanism of ORF74's transforming activity, we created three distinct mutant forms of the receptor: one with normal constitutive signaling but lacking binding and action of chemokines due to a 22-amino acid deletion in the N-terminal extension; another with high constitutive activity but selective elimination of stimulatory regulation by angiogenic chemokines due to substitution of basic residues at the extracellular ends of TM-V or TM-VI; and a third lacking constitutive activity but preserving the ability to be stimulated by agonist chemokines due to the introduction of an Asp residue on the hydrophobic, presumed membrane-exposed face of TM-II. These mutant forms can be used in transgenic animals to identify the molecular mechanism of ORF74's transforming activity.
In summary, by carefully modifying the ORF74 receptor through targeted mutagenesis, we can eliminate either agonist or inverse agonist modulation, as well as high constitutive activity, and gain insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying its transforming potential.

title: An insulin-like signaling pathway affects both longevity and reproduction in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: Mutations in the genes daf-2 and age-1 in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans lead to a significant increase in lifespan as well as a developmental arrest at the dauer stage. daf-2 and age-1 encode components of an insulin signaling pathway, which regulates the activity of the daf-16 gene. Mutations in daf-16 result in a dauer-defective phenotype and are epistatic to the diapause arrest and life span extension phenotypes of daf-2 and age-1 mutants. Additionally, we find that weak daf-2 alleles and maternally rescued age-1 alleles that extend lifespan but do not arrest at the dauer stage also reduce fertility and viability. Interestingly, age-1(hx546) has reduced maternal and zygotic age-1 activity. daf-16 mutations suppress all of the daf-2 and age-1 phenotypes, including dauer arrest, life span extension, reduced fertility, and viability defects. These findings suggest that the insulin signaling pathway, mediated by DAF-2 through the AGE-1 phosphatidylinositol-3-OH kinase, regulates reproduction and embryonic development, as well as dauer diapause and life span, and that DAF-16 transduces these signals. The regulation of fertility, life span, and metabolism by an insulin-like signaling pathway is similar to the endocrine regulation of metabolism and fertility by mammalian insulin signaling.

title: Estimating prion concentration in fluids and tissues by quantitative PMCA
text: Prions, the protein-based infectious agents responsible for prion diseases, can be accurately detected with high sensitivity through protein misfolding cyclic amplification (PMCA) technology. In this study, we present a quantitative PMCA procedure to measure the concentration of very low levels of prions in biological samples. By applying this method, we determined the amounts of misfolded prion protein (PrPSc) in the brains, spleens, blood, and urine of scrapie-infected hamsters.

title: Positional cloning of the APECED gene
text: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type I (APS 1, also known as APECED) is an autosomal-recessive disorder that maps to human chromosome 21q22.3 between markers D21S49 and D21S171 through linkage studies. Researchers have recently isolated a novel gene from this region, called AIRE (autoimmune regulator), which encodes a protein containing transcription factor-like motifs, including two zinc-finger (PHD-finger) motifs, a proline-rich region, and three LXXLL motifs. Analysis of mutations in this gene in Swiss and Finnish APECED patients revealed two mutations: a C→T substitution that changes the Arg 257 (CGA) to a stop codon (TGA) and an A→G substitution that changes the Lys 83 (AAG) to a Glu codon (GAG). The predominant mutation in Finnish APECED patients is the Arg257stop (R257X), which was found in 10/12 alleles studied. These findings suggest that the gene defective in APECED is responsible for the pathogenesis of the disease. The identification of the gene responsible for APECED should facilitate genetic diagnosis and potential treatment of the disease, and further enhance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying autoimmune diseases.

title: AMP-Activated Protein Kinase: An Ubiquitous Signaling Pathway With Key Roles in the Cardiovascular System
text: The AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular and systemic energy homeostasis, functioning as a key regulator of energy metabolism. Over the past two decades, research has revealed that AMPK's scope extends beyond energy metabolism, with significant impacts on various cellular processes. In particular, AMPK exerts important roles in cardiovascular tissues, where it regulates cardiac metabolism and contractile function, while also promoting anti-inflammatory, anti-atherogenic, and anti-contractile actions in blood vessels. This review aims to delve into the intricate mechanisms by which AMPK influences the cardiovascular system, including the molecular basis of genetic mutations that affect cardiac function and the proposed pathways through which AMPK regulates vascular function under both normal and abnormal conditions.

title: Differentiation of trophoblast stem cells into giant cells is triggered by p57/Kip2 inhibition of CDK1 activity.
text: During mammalian development, genome endoreduplication is a rare event for which the underlying mechanism remains unknown. This process is first observed when fibroblast growth factor 4 (FGF4) deprivation induces the differentiation of trophoblast stem (TS) cells into non-proliferating trophoblast giant (TG) cells, which are essential for embryo implantation. Our study shows that inhibition of cyclin-dependent protein kinase 1 (CDK1) by RO3306 leads to differentiation of TS cells into TG cells. In contrast, RO3306 induces abortive endoreduplication and apoptosis in embryonic stem cells, highlighting that inactivation of CDK1 triggers endoreduplication only in cells programmed to differentiate into polyploid cells. Similarly, FGF4 deprivation results in CDK1 inhibition through overexpression of two CDK-specific inhibitors, p57/KIP2 and p21/CIP1. TS cell mutants reveal that p57 is essential to trigger endoreduplication by inhibiting CDK1, while p21 suppresses the expression of the checkpoint protein kinase CHK1, thereby preventing induction of apoptosis. Additionally, CDK2(-/-) TS cells demonstrate that CDK2 is required for endoreduplication when CDK1 is inhibited. Interestingly, p57 is expressed exclusively in G-phase nuclei to allow CDK activation of S phase. Therefore, endoreduplication in TS cells is triggered by p57 inhibition of CDK1, accompanied by suppression of the DNA damage response by p21.

title: Atg5-independent autophagy regulates mitochondrial clearance and is essential for iPSC reprogramming
text: The generation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is accompanied by a significant metabolic shift from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis during the reprogramming process. However, the underlying mechanism of this metabolic transformation remains unclear. Our findings indicate that an Atg5-independent autophagic process plays a crucial role in mitochondrial clearance, a key event involved in the metabolic switch. We discovered that blocking this autophagy, but not canonical autophagy, impedes mitochondrial clearance, thereby preventing iPSC induction. Additionally, our results suggest that AMPK, an upstream regulator of autophagy, can be targeted by small molecules to modulate mitochondrial clearance during metabolic reprogramming. Our study not only reveals the importance of Atg5-independent autophagy in establishing pluripotency, but also suggests that the metabolic switch observed in iPSC generation is also present in tumorigenesis.

title: A mutation in Orai1 causes immune deficiency by abrogating CRAC channel function
text: Antigen stimulation of immune cells triggers an increase in intracellular calcium ions (Ca2+) through the activation of Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels, leading to the immune response to pathogens by activating the transcription factor NFAT. We have previously shown that immune cells from patients with a severe combined immune deficiency (SCID) syndrome are defective in store-operated Ca2+ entry and CRAC channel function. To identify the genetic defect in these patients, we employed two unbiased genome-wide approaches: a modified linkage analysis with single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays and a Drosophila RNA interference screen designed to identify regulators of store-operated Ca2+ entry and NFAT nuclear import. Our findings converged on a novel protein called Orai1, which contains four putative transmembrane segments. The SCID patients were found to be homozygous for a single missense mutation in ORAI1, and expression of wild-type Orai1 in SCID T cells restored store-operated Ca2+ influx and the CRAC current (ICRAC). We propose that Orai1 is a critical component or regulator of the CRAC channel complex.

title: Estimates of global prevalence of childhood underweight in 1990 and 2015.
text: The United Nations Millennium Development Goals aim to reduce the prevalence of underweight among children under the age of 5 by half between 1990 and 2015. To estimate trends in childhood underweight by geographic regions, we conducted a time series analysis of prevalence data from 1965 to 2002, drawn from the World Health Organization's Global Database on Child Growth and Malnutrition. Our findings indicate that worldwide, the prevalence of underweight is expected to decline from 26.5% in 1990 to 17.6% in 2015, a decrease of 34% (95% CI: -43% to -23%). However, the developing regions are projected to fall short of meeting the Millennium Development Goals, with the exception of Northern Africa. In contrast, the prevalence of underweight is expected to increase in sub-Saharan Africa, Eastern Africa, Middle Africa, and Western Africa. The number of underweight children is expected to decline globally, but this decrease is not expected to be significant in all subregions. Overall, while there is an improvement in the global situation, the developing regions are not expected to meet the Millennium Development Goals, with the exception of Northern Africa.

title: Canonical Wnt signaling regulates organ-specific assembly and differentiation of CNS vasculature.
text: Each organ in the body relies on a network of blood vessels, known as the vasculature, to supply it with oxygen and nutrients. However, the blood vessels associated with individual organs can have distinct structural and molecular characteristics. For instance, the vasculature of the central nervous system (CNS) is characterized by a tightly sealed endothelium that forms a barrier between the blood and brain, known as the blood-brain barrier. In contrast, blood vessels of other organs are more porous. Two ligands, Wnt7a and Wnt7b, are produced by the neuroepithelium of the developing CNS during vascular invasion. Using genetic mouse models, we found that these ligands directly target the vascular endothelium and that the CNS utilizes the canonical Wnt signaling pathway to promote the formation and differentiation of the organ's vasculature in a way that is specific to the CNS.

title: Bone progenitor dysfunction induces myelodysplasia and secondary leukemia
text: Mesenchymal cells play a crucial role in the 'stroma' of both normal and malignant tissues, with specific mesenchymal cell types involved in the regulatory niches of stem cells. By investigating how mesenchymal osteolineage cells modulate haematopoiesis, we found that deleting Dicer1 specifically in mouse osteoprogenitors, but not in mature osteoblasts, disrupts the integrity of haematopoiesis. Myelodysplasia resulted, and acute myelogenous leukaemia emerged with acquired genetic abnormalities, despite intact Dicer1. Analyzing gene expression altered in osteoprogenitors due to Dicer1 deletion revealed reduced expression of Sbds, the gene mutated in Schwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome, a human bone marrow failure and leukaemia predisposition condition. Deleting Sbds in mouse osteoprogenitors induced bone marrow dysfunction with myelodysplasia. These findings demonstrate that perturbation of specific mesenchymal subsets of stromal cells can disrupt differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis of heterologous cells and disrupt tissue homeostasis. Moreover, primary stromal dysfunction can lead to secondary neoplastic disease, supporting the concept of niche-induced oncogenesis.

title: Generating diploid embryos from Xenopus tropicalis.
text: Xenopus tropicalis offers a remarkable advantage for researchers: the ability to easily generate diploid embryos throughout the year with minimal effort. By administering a simple treatment of human chorionic gonadotropin, investigators can produce a large number of synchronized embryos through in vitro fertilization or a substantial number of embryos from a mating pair. This capability allows for the induction of ovulations on demand, opening up a wide range of opportunities for experiments, including experimental embryology, molecular manipulation of gene products, and genetics.

title: Oct4-Induced Pluripotency in Adult Neural Stem Cells
text: The transcription factors Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc can induce pluripotency in both mouse and human fibroblasts. Previously, we described the direct reprogramming of adult mouse neural stem cells (NSCs) using Oct4 and either Klf4 or c-Myc. Interestingly, these NSCs endogenously express Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4, as well as several intermediate reprogramming markers. Our current findings reveal that exogenous expression of the germline-specific transcription factor Oct4 is sufficient to generate pluripotent stem cells from adult mouse NSCs. These one-factor induced pluripotent stem cells (1F iPS) are comparable to embryonic stem cells in vitro and in vivo. Not only can these cells be efficiently differentiated into NSCs, cardiomyocytes, and germ cells in vitro, but they are also capable of teratoma formation and germline transmission in vivo. Our results demonstrate that Oct4 is both necessary and sufficient for direct reprogramming of NSCs to pluripotency.

title: Getting started with yeast.
text:
Yeast, specifically Saccharomyces cerevisiae, has emerged as a model organism due to its simplicity and ease of genetic manipulation. With a genetic complexity slightly higher than that of bacteria, yeast shares many technical advantages that facilitated rapid progress in molecular genetics of prokaryotes and their viruses. Some key properties that make yeast suitable for biological studies include:
1. Rapid growth and dispersed cells, allowing for easy replica plating and mutant isolation.
2. A well-defined genetic system, including a highly versatile DNA transformation system.
3. Nonpathogenic nature, allowing for safe handling with minimal precautions.
4. Commercial availability of large quantities of normal baker's yeast, providing a cost-effective source for biochemical studies.
5. The development of DNA transformation has made yeast particularly accessible to gene cloning and genetic engineering techniques.
6. Structural genes corresponding to virtually any genetic trait can be identified through complementation from plasmid libraries.
7. Plasmids can be introduced into yeast cells either as replicating molecules or by integration into the genome.
8. Unique to yeast, integrative recombination of transforming DNA occurs exclusively through homologous recombination, allowing for directed insertion of cloned sequences into specific locations in the genome.
9. Cloned yeast sequences, accompanied by foreign sequences on plasmids, can be targeted to specific locations in the genome.

By leveraging these properties, researchers have been able to make significant advances in understanding the genetic and molecular basis of various biological processes, including metabolism, cell signaling, and gene regulation. The versatility of yeast as a model system has contributed significantly to the development of genetic engineering techniques and has paved the way for the manipulation of complex eukaryotic organisms.

title: PCNA functions as a molecular platform to trigger Cdt1 destruction and prevent re-replication
text: Ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis of the replication licensing factor Cdt1 (Cdc10-dependent transcript 1) in the S phase of the cell cycle is a crucial mechanism that restricts DNA replication to a single round per cell cycle in metazoans. In Xenopus egg extracts, Cdt1 is degraded on chromatin during DNA replication. Our findings indicate that replication-dependent proteolysis of Cdt1 requires its interaction with proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), a homotrimeric processivity factor for DNA polymerases. Cdt1 binds to PCNA through a conserved PCNA-interaction motif in Cdt1 across all metazoans, and removal of PCNA from egg extracts inhibits replication-dependent Cdt1 degradation. Mutation of the PCNA-interaction motif leads to a stabilized Cdt1 protein that induces re-replication. Additionally, we found that DDB1, a component of the Cul4 E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediates human Cdt1 proteolysis in response to DNA damage, is also required for replication-dependent Cdt1 degradation. Cdt1 and DDB1 interact in extracts, and DDB1 chromatin loading is dependent on the binding of Cdt1 to PCNA, which suggests that PCNA functions as a platform for Cdt1 destruction, ensuring efficient and temporally restricted inactivation of a key cell-cycle regulator.

title: Meiosis in Drosophila: seeing is believing.
text: Recent breakthroughs have significantly advanced our comprehension of Drosophila meiosis through the integration of cytological and genetic approaches. New techniques have enabled the characterization of chromosome positioning and spindle formation during female meiosis I. The proteins encoded by the nod and ncd genes, which are essential for proper chromosome segregation without exchange events, have been identified as kinesin-like motors. The effects of mutations in these genes on the spindle and chromosomes, along with the localization of these proteins, have provided a mechanistic model for female meiosis I. In male meiosis I, the genomic regions responsible for homologous pairing have been resolved to specific DNA sequences, offering a foundation for elucidating the molecular basis of meiotic pairing. The cytological techniques available in Drosophila have also facilitated investigations into the regulation of sister-chromatid segregation. Recently, the products of two genes (mei-S332 and ord) essential for sister-chromatid cohesion have been identified. Moreover, significant progress has been made in understanding Drosophila meiosis through the delineation of a functional centromere using minichromosome derivatives and the identification of several regulatory genes for the meiotic cell cycle.

title: Effect of physical activity on cognitive function in older adults at risk for Alzheimer disease: a randomized trial.
text: Background: Many observational studies have shown that physical activity is associated with a reduced risk of cognitive decline in older adults. However, the evidence from randomized controlled trials is limited. Objective: To determine whether a 24-week physical activity intervention can reduce the rate of cognitive decline among older adults at risk of cognitive impairment. Design and Setting: Randomized controlled trial conducted between 2004 and 2007 in metropolitan Perth, Western Australia. Participants: Volunteers aged 50 years or older who reported memory problems but did not meet criteria for dementia were recruited. Methods: Participants were randomly assigned to either an education and usual care group or a 24-week home-based physical activity program. The primary outcome measure was the change in Alzheimer Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog) scores over 18 months. Results: In an intent-to-treat analysis, participants in the intervention group showed a modest improvement of 0.26 points (95% CI: -0.89 to 0.54) in ADAS-Cog scores at the end of the intervention, while those in the usual care group showed a deterioration of 1.04 points (95% CI: 0.32 to 1.82). The absolute difference between the groups was -1.3 points (95% CI: -2.38 to -0.22) at the end of the intervention. At 18 months, the intervention group showed a further improvement of 0.73 points (95% CI: -1.27 to 0.03) in ADAS-Cog scores, while the usual care group showed a slight improvement of 0.04 points (95% CI: -0.46 to 0.88). Conclusion: The results of this randomized controlled trial suggest that a 6-month program of physical activity may provide a modest improvement in cognition among older adults with subjective memory impairment over an 18-month follow-up period.

title: Variants at 6q21 implicate PRDM1 in the etiology of therapy-induced second malignancies after Hodgkin's lymphoma
text: Individuals who survived childhood Hodgkin's lymphoma are at risk of developing second malignant neoplasms (SMNs) as a result of radiation therapy. Our study identified two variants at chromosome 6q21 that are associated with SMNs in survivors of Hodgkin's lymphoma who were treated with radiation therapy as children, but not in those treated as adults. These variants are linked to decreased basal expression of the PRDM1 gene (which encodes a protein called PR domain containing 1, with ZNF domain) and impaired induction of the PRDM1 protein after radiation exposure. These findings suggest a new interaction between genetic factors and radiation exposure that may contribute to the development of SMNs in survivors of childhood Hodgkin's lymphoma.

title: Long non-coding RNA profiling of human lymphoid progenitor cells reveals transcriptional divergence of B cell and T cell lineages
text: To gain insights into the transcriptional landscape that regulates human lymphoid cell development during postnatal life, we employed RNA sequencing to generate a comprehensive picture of the long non-coding transcriptome across human bone marrow and thymic progenitor cells at various stages of B lymphoid and T lymphoid differentiation. Through this analysis, we identified over 3,000 novel long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) that were previously uncharacterized. Our findings revealed that lncRNAs play a crucial role in lymphoid commitment, with unique expression patterns that are highly stage-specific and more lineage-specific than those of protein-coding genes. Interestingly, protein-coding genes that co-express with neighboring lncRNA genes exhibited enrichment for ontologies related to lymphoid differentiation. Our study also uncovered new developmental relationships among the earliest progenitor cells in the human bone marrow and thymus, highlighting the exquisite cell-type specificity of global lncRNA expression patterns.

title: The VTI family of SNARE proteins is necessary for plant viability and mediates different protein transport pathways.
text: The Arabidopsis genome harbors a family of v-SNAREs, specifically VTI11, VTI12, and VTI13, wherein only VTI11 and VTI12 are expressed at appreciable levels. Although these two proteins share 60% sequence similarity, they complement distinct transport pathways when co-expressed in the yeast vti1 mutant, with VTI11 being the recently identified mutated gene in the shoot gravitropic mutant zig, and exhibiting defects in vascular patterning and auxin transport upon mutation. In contrast, an Arabidopsis T-DNA insertion mutant, vti12, displayed a normal phenotype under nutrient-rich growth conditions, but showed an accelerated senescence phenotype upon nutrient-poor conditions, suggesting a possible role in the plant autophagy pathway. Notably, VTI11 and VTI12 were able to substitute for each other in their respective SNARE complexes, and a double-mutant cross between zig and vti12 was embryo lethal, implying that some VTI1 protein is essential for plant viability, and that the two proteins exhibit partial functional redundancy.

title: CLASPs link focal adhesion-associated microtubule capture to localized exocytosis and adhesion site turnover
text: In migrating human keratinocytes, the turnover of integrin-based focal adhesions (FAs) with the extracellular matrix (ECM) is crucial for coordinated cell movement. FAs form near the leading edge of the cell, mature through contractile forces, and disassemble as the cell body advances. We have found that the clustering of microtubule-associated proteins CLASP1 and CLASP2 around FAs occurs at specific times during FA turnover. These proteins, along with LL5β (also known as PHLDB2), help facilitate the disassembly of FAs by recruiting enzymes that degrade the ECM. Additionally, CLASPs are required for the degradation of ECM components, and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases slows FA disassembly to a similar extent as depletion of CLASPs or LL5β. Furthermore, we have discovered that CLASPs establish a local secretion pathway near FAs by tethering microtubules, which facilitates the delivery, docking, and fusion of exocytic vesicles. This pathway plays a crucial role in FA turnover by severing cell-matrix connections. In summary, our findings demonstrate that CLASPs couple microtubule organization, vesicle transport, and cell interactions with the ECM to facilitate FA turnover and coordinated cell movement.

title: CHD4 Is a RanGTP-Dependent MAP that Stabilizes Microtubules and Regulates Bipolar Spindle Formation
text:
Background: The production of GTP-bound Ran GTPase (RanGTP) around chromosomes triggers the assembly of spindle fibers by activating nuclear localization signal (NLS)-containing proteins. While several NLS proteins have been identified as spindle assembly factors, the complexity of the process prompted us to investigate additional proteins with distinct roles in spindle assembly.
Results: Our investigation uncovered a chromatin-remodeling ATPase, CHD4, as a RanGTP-dependent microtubule (MT)-associated protein (MAP). The MT-binding region of CHD4 contains an NLS, and chromatin-binding domains enable its localization to the spindle. In Xenopus egg extracts and cultured cells, CHD4 dissociates from mitotic chromosomes and partially localizes to the spindle. Depletion of CHD4 from egg extracts significantly reduces the quantity of MTs produced around chromatin and impedes spindle assembly. Similarly, RNAi-mediated depletion of CHD4 in HeLa and Drosophila S2 cells leads to defects in spindle assembly and chromosome alignment in early mitosis, resulting in chromosome missegregation. Additional analysis in egg extracts and HeLa cells reveals that CHD4 functions as a RanGTP-dependent MT stabilizer. Furthermore, the CHD4-containing NuRD complex promotes the organization of MTs into bipolar spindles in egg extracts, a function that is independent of chromatin remodeling.
Conclusions: Our findings uncover a novel role for CHD4 as a MAP required for MT stabilization and involved in generating spindle bipolarity.

title: Myocardial muscarinic receptor upregulation and normal response to isoproterenol in denervated hearts by familial amyloid polyneuropathy.
text:
Background:
Patients with familial amyloid polyneuropathy, a rare hereditary form of amyloidosis, experience progressive autonomic neuropathy. While the disease does not typically lead to heart failure, it is associated with sudden death, conduction disturbances, and an increased risk of complications during anesthesia. Despite cardiac sympathetic denervation being well-established, the post-synaptic status of the cardiac autonomic nervous system remains unclear.
Methods and Results:
Twenty-one patients (age: 39±11 years; normal coronary arteries; left ventricular ejection fraction: 68±9%) were studied using positron emission tomography (PET) with (11)C-MQNB (methylquinuclidinyl benzilate), a specific hydrophilic antagonist, to evaluate the density and affinity constants of myocardial muscarinic receptors. Cardiac beta-receptor functional efficiency was assessed by measuring the heart rate (HR) response to intravenous infusion of isoproterenol (5 minutes after 2 mg of atropine, 5, 10, and 15 ng/kg per minute during 5 minutes per step). Compared to control subjects, patients had higher mean muscarinic receptor density (B'(max): 35.5±8.9 vs. 26.1±6.7 pmol/mL, P=0.003), without changes in receptor affinity. The decrease in HR after injection of atropine, as well as after MQNB, was lower in patients compared to control subjects, despite similar basal HR (DeltaHR after atropine: 11±21% vs. 62±17%; P<0.001), indicating parasympathetic denervation. Incremental infusion of isoproterenol induced a similar increase in HR in patients and control subjects.
Conclusions:
Cardiac autonomic denervation in familial amyloid polyneuropathy leads to an upregulation of myocardial muscarinic receptors without changes in cardiac beta-receptor responsiveness to catecholamines.

title: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase links oxidative PPP, lipogenesis and tumor growth by inhibiting LKB1-AMPK signaling
text:
The oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) has been implicated in tumor growth, with the third enzyme, 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (6PGD), playing a particular role in tumorigenesis. However, the specific contribution of 6PGD to cancer development remains unclear. Our study aimed to investigate the role of 6PGD in cancer cell proliferation and tumor growth, and to identify potential inhibitors of this enzyme as anticancer agents.
We found that suppression of 6PGD led to decreased lipogenesis and RNA biosynthesis, as well as increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cancer cells. These changes in cellular metabolism and redox balance attenuated cell proliferation and tumor growth. Our results suggest that 6PGD-mediated production of ribulose-5-phosphate (Ru-5-P) inhibits the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) by disrupting the active LKB1 complex, thereby activating acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 and lipogenesis. Ru-5-P and NADPH are thought to be precursors in RNA biosynthesis and lipogenesis, respectively, and our findings provide an additional link between the oxidative PPP and lipogenesis through Ru-5-P-dependent inhibition of LKB1-AMPK signaling.
Furthermore, we identified and developed two 6PGD inhibitors, physcion and its derivative S3, which effectively inhibited 6PGD, cancer cell proliferation, and tumor growth in nude mice xenografts without obvious toxicity. These findings suggest that 6PGD could be a promising anticancer target.

title: Plant Nuclear RNA Polymerase IV Mediates siRNA and DNA Methylation-Dependent Heterochromatin Formation
text: All eukaryotic organisms possess three nuclear DNA-dependent RNA polymerases, specifically Pol I, II, and III. Notably, plants exhibit an additional nuclear polymerase, Pol IV, which possesses a distinct catalytic subunit. Genetic and biochemical evidence indicates that Pol IV does not overlap functionally with Pol I, II, or III and is nonessential for viability. However, disruption of the Pol IV catalytic subunit genes NRPD1 or NRPD2 leads to impaired association of heterochromatin with chromocenters, concurrent with losses in cytosine methylation at pericentromeric 5S gene clusters and AtSN1 retroelements. Loss of CG, CNG, and CNN methylation in Pol IV mutants suggests a partnership between Pol IV and the methyltransferase responsible for RNA-directed de novo methylation. Consistently, 5S gene and AtSN1 siRNAs are significantly reduced in Pol IV mutants. The data imply that Pol IV plays a crucial role in producing siRNAs that target de novo cytosine methylation events required for facultative heterochromatin formation and higher-order heterochromatin associations.

title: Sema3A regulates bone-mass accrual through sensory innervations
text: Semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) is a diffuse axonal chemorepellent that plays a crucial role in axon guidance. Previous studies have shown that Sema3a-deficient mice exhibit multiple developmental defects due to abnormal neuronal innervations. In this study, we found that Sema3A is abundantly expressed in bone and affects osteoblast differentiation in a cell-autonomous manner, leading to decreased bone mass in Sema3a-deficient mice. However, osteoblast-specific Sema3A-deficient mice (Sema3acol1-/-) and Sema3aosx-/-) had normal bone mass despite decreased Sema3A expression in bone. In contrast, mice lacking Sema3A in neurons (Sema3asynapsin-/-) and Sema3anestin-/-) had low bone mass similar to Sema3a-deficient mice, indicating that neuron-derived Sema3A is responsible for the observed bone abnormalities. We also found that the number of sensory innervations of trabecular bone was significantly decreased in Sema3asynapsin-/-) mice, while sympathetic innervations of trabecular bone were unchanged. Moreover, ablating sensory nerves in wild-type mice decreased bone mass, while it did not reduce the low bone mass in Sema3anestin-/-) mice, suggesting that the sensory nervous system plays an essential role in normal bone homeostasis. Additionally, we identified neuronal abnormalities in Sema3a-deficient mice, including olfactory development, in Sema3asynapsin-/-) mice, which suggests that neuron-derived Sema3A regulates neural development in an autocrine manner. This study demonstrates that Sema3A regulates bone remodeling indirectly by modulating sensory nerve development, but not directly by acting on osteoblasts.

title: Direct lineage reprogramming: strategies, mechanisms, and applications.
text: The direct conversion of one specialized cell type into another using defined factors has revolutionized traditional concepts of epigenetic stability in differentiated cells. With the rapid expansion of cell types generated through direct conversion in recent years, this approach has emerged as a promising means of producing functional cells. In this review, we will examine recent advances in lineage reprogramming, including the discovery of new reprogramming factors, the underlying molecular mechanisms, strategies for generating functionally mature cells, and methods for evaluating induced cells. Additionally, we will discuss the progress made towards applying lineage reprogramming and the major challenges that remain to be overcome for this strategy to reach its full potential.

title: Converging Intracranial Markers of Conscious Access
text: In this study, we employed a visual masking procedure while recording intracranial electroencephalogram (iEEG) in ten patients to investigate the differences between conscious and nonconscious processing of briefly flashed words. We found that nonconscious processing of masked words was observed in various cortical areas within an early time window (less than 300 milliseconds), accompanied by gamma-band activity without long-distance neural activity, suggesting a quickly dissipating feedforward wave. In contrast, conscious processing of unmasked words was characterized by the convergence of four distinct neurophysiological markers: sustained voltage changes in the prefrontal cortex, large increases in spectral power in the gamma band, increases in long-distance phase synchrony in the beta range, and increases in long-range Granger causality. Our findings provide new insights into the neural correlates of conscious access and have important implications for current theoretical discussions in the field.

title: Hyperglycemia is associated with increased bone mineral density and decreased trabecular bone score in elderly Japanese men: The Fujiwara-kyo osteoporosis risk in men (FORMEN) study.
text:
Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) exhibit an increased risk of fractures despite having higher areal bone mineral density (aBMD). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between glycemic and insulin resistance status and bone microarchitecture, as well as the potential roles of pentosidine and bone turnover markers in this association.
Methods: A total of 2012 community-dwelling men aged ≥65 years underwent baseline measurements of spine aBMD, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), serum insulin, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), osteocalcin, type I procollagen N-terminal propeptide, type I collagen C-terminal crosslinking telopeptide, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase isoenzyme 5b, pentosidine, height, and weight, and underwent an interview regarding past disease history. Homeostasis model assessment-insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was also calculated. T2DM was defined based on physician diagnosis or biochemical test results. Trabecular bone score (TBS) was calculated at the same vertebrae as those used for aBMD measurement.
Results: After excluding participants with a disease history and/or taking medications affecting bone metabolism, 1683 men (age, 72.9 ± 5.2 years) were analyzed. Compared to those without T2DM, men with T2DM had significantly higher aBMD. However, there was no significant difference in TBS. Furthermore, FPG, HbA1c, and HOMA-IR levels were significantly inversely correlated with TBS after adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), and aBMD. Multivariate linear regression analyses revealed that glycemic indices (FPG and HbA1c) were significantly associated with increased aBMD and decreased TBS, and that HOMA-IR was associated only with TBS. These associations did not change after further adjusting for bone turnover markers and pentosidine levels.
Conclusions: Hyperglycemia and elevated insulin resistance were associated with low TBS independently of bone turnover and pentosidine levels. These findings suggest that glycemic and insulin resistance status may play a significant role in the development of low bone density in patients with T2DM.

title: Matrix Remodeling Promotes Pulmonary Hypertension through Feedback Mechanoactivation of the YAP/TAZ-miR-130/301 Circuit.
text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a complex and lethal vascular disorder characterized by an enigmatic molecular etiology. Recent findings have elucidated the early and ubiquitous nature of vascular extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and stiffening in the development of PH. In multiple pulmonary vascular cell types, we discovered that ECM stiffening induces the microRNA-130/301 family through the activation of the co-transcription factors YAP and TAZ. This microRNA family regulates a PPARγ-APOE-LRP8 signaling axis, which promotes collagen deposition and LOX-dependent remodeling, further upregulating YAP/TAZ via a mechanosensitive feedback loop. Concomitantly, ECM remodeling controls pulmonary vascular cell-to-cell communication via mechanotransduction, modulation of secreted vasoactive mediators, and regulation of associated microRNA pathways. In vivo, pharmacological inhibition of microRNA-130/301, APOE, or LOX activity ameliorates ECM remodeling and PH. These findings reveal that ECM remodeling, as controlled by the YAP/TAZ-miR-130/301 feedback circuit, serves as an early trigger of PH and offers combinatorial therapeutic targets for this devastating disease.

title: Exosomal transfer of stroma-derived miR21 confers paclitaxel resistance in ovarian cancer cells through targeting APAF1
text: Advanced ovarian cancer typically spreads to the visceral adipose tissue of the omentum, but the molecular mechanisms that govern the growth and progression of cancer cells in this microenvironment have remained largely unexplored. In this study, we employed next-generation sequencing technology to investigate the molecular determinants of ovarian cancer growth in the omental tissue. Our findings revealed significantly higher levels of microRNA-21 (miR21) isomiRNAs in exosomes and tissue lysates isolated from cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) and fibroblasts (CAFs) compared to ovarian cancer cells. Functional studies showed that miR21 is transferred from CAAs or CAFs to the cancer cells, where it suppresses ovarian cancer apoptosis and confers chemoresistance by binding to its direct novel target, APAF1. These results suggest that the malignant phenotype of metastatic ovarian cancer cells can be altered by miR21 delivered by exosomes derived from neighboring stromal cells in the omental tumor microenvironment. Moreover, inhibiting the transfer of stromal-derived miR21 may represent an alternative therapeutic strategy for the treatment of metastatic and recurrent ovarian cancer.

title: Age-related changes in kynurenic acid production in rat brain.
text: Two separate in vitro assays were conducted to investigate the biosynthesis of the broad-spectrum excitatory amino acid receptor antagonist kynurenic acid (KYNA) throughout the lifespan of the adult rat. The enzyme kynurenine aminotransferase, which plays a crucial role in KYNA's anabolism, was found to exhibit steady increases in activity between 3 and 24 months of age in all five brain regions examined. Contrary to these increases, no changes were observed in the liver. The most pronounced changes were observed in the cortex and striatum, where enzyme activity increased threefold during the period studied. Additionally, tissue slice experiments revealed that KYNA production from its bioprecursor L-kynurenine was significantly enhanced in the cortex and hippocampus of old animals. Depolarizing agents or sodium replacement had virtually the same effect on tissues from young and old rats. These findings, which are in agreement with previous reports on an age-dependent increase in KYNA concentration in brain tissue, suggest that the aged brain exhibits an enhanced KYNA tone. This, combined with the reported decline in cerebral excitatory amino acid receptor densities with age, may contribute to cognitive and memory dysfunction in old animals.

title: The polycomb group protein Suz12 is required for embryonic stem cell differentiation.
text:
Polycomb group (PcG) proteins form multiprotein complexes, known as Polycomb repressive complexes (PRCs), which play a crucial role in regulating gene expression during cellular differentiation. PRC2, in particular, contains the PcG proteins EZH2, SUZ12, and EED, and is responsible for repressing transcription through the methylation of lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3). SUZ12 is a critical component of PRC2, and its inactivation leads to early embryonic lethality in mice.
Interestingly, we have demonstrated that Suz12-deficient mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells can be established and expanded in tissue culture. These cells exhibit global loss of H3K27me3 and increased expression levels of differentiation-specific genes. Moreover, Suz12-deficient ES cells show impaired proper differentiation, resulting in the lack of repression of ES cell markers and the activation of differentiation-specific genes.
Furthermore, we have found that the PcGs are actively recruited to several genes during ES cell differentiation, despite an increase in H3K27me3 levels. This suggests that PcGs have different mechanisms to regulate transcription during cellular differentiation.
In summary, our findings demonstrate that Suz12 is essential for the establishment of specific expression programs required for ES cell differentiation. Additionally, we provide evidence that PcGs have diverse mechanisms to regulate transcription during cellular differentiation.

title: The 1.9 A structure of a proteasome-11S activator complex and implications for proteasome-PAN/PA700 interactions.
text: Proteasomes are cylindrical structures that play a crucial role in various cellular processes by degrading a wide range of cytosolic and nuclear proteins. The degradation process occurs through axial pores that are opened by activator complexes, allowing substrate access and product release from the enclosed catalytic chamber. In this study, we present high-resolution structures of wild-type and mutant archaeal proteasomes bound to the activator PA26. These structures provide insight into the mechanism of proteolysis, which involves an ordered open conformation that can be triggered by the displacement of surrounding residues. Our findings also reveal the binding mechanism of PA26, which involves an interaction between its C-terminal region and a conserved lysine. Interestingly, our biochemical observations suggest that an equivalent interaction occurs between the unrelated ATP-dependent activators PAN and PA700.

title: Innate Immune and Chemically Triggered Oxidative Stress Modifies Translational Fidelity
text: Accurate transfer RNA (tRNA) aminoacylation is crucial for protein and cell function, and purified aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases exhibit a fidelity of one error per 10,000 to 100,000 couplings. However, the accuracy of tRNA aminoacylation in vivo is uncertain and might be significantly lower. Our study reveals that in mammalian cells, approximately 1% of methionine (Met) residues used in protein synthesis are misacylated to non-methionyl-tRNAs. Remarkably, this misacylation increases up to tenfold upon exposure to live or non-infectious viruses, toll-like receptor ligands, or chemically induced oxidative stress. Met is misacylated to specific non-methionyl-tRNA families, and these Met-misacylated tRNAs are used in translation. The misacylation is blocked by an inhibitor of cellular oxidases, implicating reactive oxygen species (ROS) as the misacylation trigger. Our findings demonstrate an unexpected conditional aspect of decoding mRNA and highlight the importance of considering alternative iterations of the genetic code.

title: Yeast sirtuins and the regulation of aging.
text: The sirtuins are a family of evolutionarily conserved enzymes that rely on NAD+ to deacetylate proteins. Each deacetylation reaction requires one molecule of NAD+. This reliance on NAD+ makes sirtuins susceptible to changes in NAD+ levels or biosynthesis, which can impact their function. The Sir2 protein from Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the founding member of the sirtuin family and has been well characterized as a histone deacetylase involved in transcriptional silencing of heterochromatin domains and as a pro-longevity factor for replicative life span (RLS), which is the number of times a mother cell divides (buds) before senescing. Deleting SIR2 shortens RLS, while increased gene dosage extends it. Sir2 has also been implicated in mediating the beneficial effects of caloric restriction (CR) on life span in both yeast and higher eukaryotes, although there has been some debate in the field. S. cerevisiae has four additional sirtuins, Hst1, Hst2, Hst3, and Hst4. This review discusses the function of Sir2 and the Hst homologs in replicative aging and chronological aging, as well as how the sirtuins are regulated in response to environmental stresses such as CR.

title: The effect of combination treatment with aliskiren and blockers of the renin-angiotensin system on hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Objective: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to evaluate the safety of combining aliskiren with agents that block the renin-angiotensin system.
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Data sources: Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and two trial registries, up to 7 May 2011.
Study selection: Published and unpublished randomized controlled trials that compared combined treatment with aliskiren and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers with monotherapy using these agents for at least four weeks and provided numerical data on the adverse event outcomes of hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury.
Methods: A random effects model was used to calculate pooled risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals for these outcomes.
Results: 10 randomized controlled studies (4814 participants) were included in the analysis. Combination therapy with aliskiren and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers significantly increased the risk of hyperkalaemia compared with monotherapy using angiotensin converting enzymes or angiotensin receptor blockers (relative risk 1.58, 95% confidence interval 1.24 to 2.02) or aliskiren alone (1.67, 1.01 to 2.79). The risk of acute kidney injury did not differ significantly between the combined therapy and monotherapy groups (1.14, 0.68 to 1.89).
Conclusion: The use of aliskiren in combination with angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers is associated with an increased risk for hyperkalaemia. The combined use of these agents warrants careful monitoring of serum potassium levels.

title: The ins and outs of DNA transfer in bacteria.
text:
Transformation and conjugation enable the transfer of genetic information between bacterial cells or between bacteria and eukaryotic cells through dominant mechanisms. These processes rely on the recognition of double-stranded DNA, followed by the transfer of single strands. Sophisticated molecular machines facilitate the passage of large DNA molecules through the layers of the cell surface. These machines have been largely identified, and here we present detailed models of their roles in DNA transport.
Transformation and conjugation are crucial for the spread of beneficial traits, including antibiotic resistance. They allow bacteria to share genetic material, enabling the transfer of desirable characteristics between cells. These processes involve the recognition of double-stranded DNA, followed by the transfer of single strands. Specialized molecular machines are responsible for navigating the passage of large DNA molecules through the cell surface. These machines have been extensively identified, and here we present detailed models of their functions in DNA transport.

title: Synaptic islands defined by the territory of a single astrocyte.
text: In the mammalian brain, astrocytes play a crucial role in modulating neuronal function by synchronizing neuronal firing and coordinating synaptic networks. However, the structural basis of this process remains poorly understood. To investigate the three-dimensional relationships between cortical astrocytes and neurons, we used a transgenic and viral approach to label astrocytes with enhanced green fluorescent protein. By performing a three-dimensional reconstruction of astrocytes from tissue sections or live animals in vivo, we found that cortical astrocytes occupy nonoverlapping territories similar to those described in the hippocampus. On average, a single astrocyte enwraps four to eight neuronal somata, and one astrocyte contacts 300 to 600 neuronal dendrites. These findings, combined with recent studies showing that glial Ca2+ signaling is restricted to individual astrocytes in vivo and leads to gliotransmission, suggest the concept of functional islands of synapses in which groups of synapses are modulated by the gliotransmitter environment controlled by a single astrocyte. This new structural-based conceptual framework provides a novel way to interpret functional data involving interactions between neurons and astrocytes in the mammalian brain.

title: Role of DNA Methylation and Epigenetic Silencing of HAND2 in Endometrial Cancer Development
text:
Background: Endometrial cancer incidence has been steadily increasing due to the growing aging and obesity populations. The environment and lifestyle play a significant role in the development of endometrial cancer, and recent evidence suggests that epigenetic factors, such as DNA methylation, play a crucial role in this process. This study aimed to investigate the functional role of epigenetic factors in endometrial cancer development.
Methods and Findings: We conducted an epigenome-wide methylation analysis of over 27,000 CpG sites in endometrial cancer tissue samples (n = 64) and control samples (n = 23). Our results revealed that HAND2, a gene encoding a transcription factor expressed in the endometrial stroma, is one of the most commonly hypermethylated and silenced genes in endometrial cancer. Using a novel integrative epigenome-transcriptome-interactome analysis, we identified HAND2 as the hub of the most highly ranked differential methylation hotspot in endometrial cancer. These findings were validated using candidate gene methylation analysis in multiple clinical sample sets of tissue samples from a total of 272 additional women. We found that increased HAND2 methylation was a feature of premalignant endometrial lesions and was associated with a decrease in RNA and protein levels. Furthermore, women with high endometrial HAND2 methylation in their premalignant lesions were less likely to respond to progesterone treatment. HAND2 methylation analysis of endometrial secretions collected using high vaginal swabs taken from women with postmenopausal bleeding specifically identified those patients with early stage endometrial cancer with both high sensitivity and high specificity (receiver operating characteristics area under the curve = 0.91 for stage 1A and 0.97 for higher than stage 1A). Finally, mice harboring a Hand2 knock-out specifically in their endometrium developed precancerous endometrial lesions with increasing age, and these lesions also demonstrated a lack of PTEN expression.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that HAND2 methylation is a common and crucial molecular alteration in endometrial cancer, which could potentially be employed as a biomarker for early detection of endometrial cancer and as a predictor of treatment response. However, further validation in prospective studies is required to confirm the clinical utility of HAND2 DNA methylation.

title: Socioeconomic factors, material inequalities, and perceived control in self-rated health: cross-sectional data from seven post-communist countries.
text: This study investigated the relationship between perceived control and various socioeconomic factors, as well as self-rated health, in seven post-communist countries (Russia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic). The study used questionnaire interviews to collect data on self-rated health, education, marital status, perceived control based on nine questions, and material deprivation (availability of food, clothing, and heating). Two ecological measures of material inequality were also collected: an inequality score estimated from the survey data and the Gini coefficient from published sources. Data from 5,330 men and women aged 20-60 were analyzed. The study found that the prevalence of poor health (worse than average) varied between 8% in the Czechs and 19% in the Hungarians. The age-sex-adjusted odds ratio for university versus primary education was 0.36 (0.26-0.49). The odds ratio per 1 standard deviation increase in perceived control and material deprivation was 0.58 (95% CI 0.48-0.69) and 1.51 (1.40-1.63), respectively. The odds ratio for an increase in inequality equivalent to the difference between the most and least unequal populations was 1.49 (0.88-2.52) using the material inequality score and 1.41 (0.91-2.20) using the Gini coefficient. After adjusting for individuals' deprivation or perceived control, there was no significant effect of either inequality measure. The study suggests that, as in Western populations, education and material deprivation are strongly related to self-rated health. Perceived control appeared to mediate some of the effects of material deprivation. The non-significant effects of both ecological measures of inequality were eliminated by controlling for individuals' characteristics.

title: Integrin αvβ3/c-src “Oncogenic Unit” Promotes Anchorage-independence and Tumor Progression
text:
Integrins play a crucial role in regulating the growth, survival, and invasion of tumor cells, with the expression of integrin alpha(v)beta(3) being associated with the progression of various human tumors. However, our study reveals a previously unappreciated adhesion-independent function of integrin alpha(v)beta(3) in pancreatic cancer and other carcinomas. Specifically, we found that alpha(v)beta(3) expressed in carcinoma cells enhanced anchorage-independent tumor growth in vitro and increased lymph node metastases in vivo, without relying on cell adhesion or focal adhesion kinase (FAK) activation. Instead, these effects were mediated by the recruitment of c-Src to the beta(3) integrin cytoplasmic tail, leading to c-Src activation, Crk-associated substrate (CAS) phosphorylation, and tumor cell survival. Interestingly, these findings suggest that an alpha(v)beta(3)-c-Src signaling module may contribute to the aggressive behavior of integrin alpha(v)beta(3)-expressing tumors in humans.
Our results provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying tumor progression and suggest that targeting the alpha(v)beta(3)-c-Src signaling module may be a promising strategy for inhibiting the growth and metastasis of integrin alpha(v)beta(3)-expressing tumors.

title: Genomewide Analysis of PRC1 and PRC2 Occupancy Identifies Two Classes of Bivalent Domains
text: In embryonic stem (ES) cells, bivalent chromatin domains with overlapping repressive (H3 lysine 27 trimethylation) and activating (H3 lysine 4 trimethylation) histone modifications mark the promoters of more than 2,000 genes. To gain insights into the structure and function of bivalent domains, we mapped key histone modifications and subunits of Polycomb-repressive complexes 1 and 2 (PRC1 and PRC2) genome-wide in human and mouse ES cells through chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by ultra-high-throughput sequencing. We found that bivalent domains can be segregated into two classes: the first occupied by both PRC2 and PRC1 (PRC1-positive) and the second specifically bound by PRC2 (PRC2-only). PRC1-positive bivalent domains appear functionally distinct as they more efficiently retain lysine 27 trimethylation upon differentiation, show stringent conservation of chromatin state, and associate with an overwhelming number of developmental regulator gene promoters. We also used computational genomics to search for sequence determinants of Polycomb binding. This analysis revealed that the genome-wide locations of PRC2 and PRC1 can be largely predicted from the locations, sizes, and underlying motif contents of CpG islands. We propose that large CpG islands depleted of activating motifs confer epigenetic memory by recruiting the full repertoire of Polycomb complexes in pluripotent cells.

title: Spatiotemporal regulation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition is essential for squamous cell carcinoma metastasis.
text: Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) has been implicated in the process of metastasis, where stationary epithelial tumor cells are converted into motile mesenchymal cells. However, the role of EMT in carcinoma metastasis remains controversial due to the lack of a mesenchymal phenotype in human carcinoma metastases. To investigate the role of EMT in carcinoma metastasis, we used a spontaneous squamous cell carcinoma mouse model. Our results show that activation of the EMT-inducing transcription factor Twist1 is sufficient to promote carcinoma cells to undergo EMT and disseminate into the blood circulation. Interestingly, we found that in distant sites, turning off Twist1 to allow reversion of EMT is essential for disseminated tumor cells to proliferate and form metastases. Our study provides in vivo evidence of the requirement of "reversible EMT" in tumor metastasis and may help resolve the controversy surrounding the importance of EMT in carcinoma metastasis.

title: Control of Apoptosis by Asymmetric Cell Division
text: Asymmetric cell division and programmed cell death (apoptosis) are crucial processes in the development and function of multicellular organisms. Our research has uncovered a fascinating link between these two processes: they are functionally interconnected. Specifically, we found that the pathway involving three genes - dnj-11 MIDA1, ces-2 HLF, and ces-1 Snail - in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans regulates the enzymatic machinery responsible for apoptosis. Interestingly, similar proteins, such as GlsA in the alga Volvox carteri and Snail, Escargot, and Worniu in Drosophila melanogaster, have been implicated in asymmetric cell division. These findings suggest that this pathway may be conserved across the plant and animal kingdoms. Moreover, based on our results, we propose that this pathway directly controls the apoptotic fate in C. elegans, and possibly other animals as well.

title: CXCR2 mediates NADPH oxidase–independent neutrophil extracellular trap formation in cystic fibrosis airway inflammation
text: Upon activation, neutrophils release DNA fibers coated with antimicrobial proteins, forming neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). While NETs are crucial for innate immune defense, excessive NET formation has been linked to autoinflammatory diseases. However, the mechanisms regulating NET formation, particularly during chronic inflammation, are poorly understood. Our study reveals that the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) CXCR2 mediates NET formation. We found that CXCR2-mediated NET formation is independent of NADPH oxidase and involves Src family kinases. We demonstrate the pathophysiological relevance of this mechanism in cystic fibrosis lung disease, characterized by chronic neutrophilic inflammation. Our results show abundant NETs in airway fluids from individuals with cystic fibrosis and mouse cystic fibrosis lung disease, and NET amounts correlate with impaired obstructive lung function. Inhibiting CXCR2 using small-molecule antagonists in the lungs of mice improves lung function without affecting neutrophil recruitment, proteolytic activity, or antibacterial host defense. These findings establish CXCR2 as a receptor mediating NADPH oxidase-independent NET formation and provide evidence that this GPCR pathway is operative and druggable in cystic fibrosis lung disease.

title: Modelling the Impact of Artemisinin Combination Therapy and Long-Acting Treatments on Malaria Transmission Intensity
text:
The article investigates the potential impact of different antimalarial drugs on transmission of Plasmodium falciparum malaria in endemic areas. The study uses a mathematical model to estimate the reduction in transmission that may be achieved by introducing various types of treatment for symptomatic malaria, including artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), and other drugs with different pharmacodynamics. The study areas are located in Tanzania and have varying transmission intensities.
The results show that ACTs have the potential to significantly lower patient infectiousness and reduce population-level transmission of the parasite, with the highest transmission settings showing the greatest impact.
