Our analysis revealed a narrow range of critical human population densities (approximately 3,000 to 7,000 people/km²) that are prone to dengue outbreaks. In the study area, this population density was typical of villages and some peri-urban areas. Scan statistics showed that areas with high population density or adequate water supply did not experience severe outbreaks. Our results also indicated that the risk of dengue was higher in rural than in urban areas, primarily due to the lack of piped water supply, and that human population densities more often fell within the critical range. Mathematical modeling suggested that simple assumptions regarding area-level vector/host ratios may explain the occurrence of outbreaks. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that rural areas may contribute at least as much to the dissemination of dengue fever as cities. Improving water supply and vector control in areas with a human population density critical for dengue transmission could increase the efficiency of control efforts.

title: Helicobacter pylori induces AGS cell motility and elongation via independent signaling pathways.
text: Helicobacter pylori triggers motility and cytoskeletal changes in gastric epithelial cells. Our findings show that these responses can be initiated through distinct signaling pathways that often operate simultaneously. The Cag pathogenicity island is not essential for the induction of motility, whereas the elongated phenotype requires the translocation and phosphorylation of CagA.

title: The Sequence Alignment/Map format and SAMtools
text:
Summary:
The Sequence Alignment/Map (SAM) format is a versatile and widely-used alignment format for storing read alignments against reference sequences, accommodating both short and long reads (up to 128 Mbp) generated by various sequencing platforms. Its flexibility, compactness, and random access efficiency make it a popular choice for storing and analyzing read alignments. In addition, SAMtools, a suite of tools for post-processing alignments in the SAM format, provides a comprehensive set of utilities for manipulating and analyzing read alignments, including indexing, variant calling, and alignment viewing. As such, SAMtools serves as a universal platform for processing read alignments in the SAM format.
Availability:
The SAMtools software and documentation are available for download at the following URL: <http://samtools.sourceforge.net/>.

title: Characterization of two classes of small molecule inhibitors of Arp2/3 complex
text:
The polymerization of actin filaments is regulated by the actin-related protein (Arp)2/3 complex, which supports various cellular movements. However, the relative contributions of the Arp2/3 complex versus other mechanisms of actin filament nucleation in certain processes, such as path finding by neuronal growth cones, remain unclear due to the lack of simple methods to reversibly inhibit the Arp2/3 complex in living cells.
To address this limitation, we have identified and characterized two classes of small molecules that bind to different sites on the Arp2/3 complex and inhibit its ability to nucleate actin filaments. The first compound, CK-0944636, binds between Arp2 and Arp3, potentially blocking their movement into their active conformation. The second compound, CK-0993548, inserts into the hydrophobic core of Arp3 and alters its conformation. Both classes of compounds inhibit the formation of actin filament comet tails in Listeria and podosomes in monocytes.
The discovery of these two inhibitors with distinct mechanisms of action provides a powerful tool for investigating the Arp2/3 complex in living cells, shedding light on its role in various cellular movements and processes.

title: Stresses at the cell-to-substrate interface during locomotion of fibroblasts
text: Recent advancements in the elastic substrate method have enabled researchers to measure the tractions exerted by individual motile cells with unprecedented spatial resolution. In this study, we have leveraged these developments to produce high-resolution maps of the tractions generated by 3T3 fibroblasts during steady locomotion. The resulting images show the tractions with a spatial resolution of approximately 5 micrometers and a maximum intensity of approximately 10(2) kdyn/cm2 (10(4) pN/micrometers2). Our findings reveal that the propulsive thrust for fibroblast locomotion, approximately 0.2 dyn, is applied to the substrate within 15 micrometers of the leading edge. These observations suggest that the lamellipodium of the fibroblast is capable of generating intense traction stress, with the cell body and posterior regions appearing mechanically passive and pulled forward by this action.

title: Cancer-associated adipocytes exhibit an activated phenotype and contribute to breast cancer invasion.
text: Early local tumor invasion in breast cancer often leads to a chance encounter between cancer cells and mature adipocytes, yet the role of these fat cells in tumor progression remains unclear. Our study demonstrates that cocultivation of murine and human tumor cells with mature adipocytes leads to enhanced invasive capacities in vitro and in vivo using an original two-dimensional coculture system. Similarly, adipocytes cultured with cancer cells exhibit an altered phenotype characterized by delipidation and decreased adipocyte markers, accompanied by an activated state marked by overexpression of proteases, including matrix metalloproteinase-11, and proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-6 and IL-1β. Interestingly, we show that IL-6 plays a pivotal role in the acquired proinvasive effect exhibited by tumor cells. Furthermore, our findings confirm the presence of these modified adipocytes in human breast tumors through immunohistochemistry and quantitative PCR. Notably, larger tumors with lymph node involvement exhibit higher levels of IL-6 in the surrounding adipocytes. Our data provide in vitro and in vivo evidence that (i) invasive cancer cells significantly impact surrounding adipocytes; (ii) peritumoral adipocytes exhibit a distinct phenotype and biological features that warrant the designation of cancer-associated adipocytes (CAA); and (iii) CAAs modulate the cancer cell characteristics/phenotype, leading to a more aggressive behavior. Our findings strongly support the novel concept that adipocytes are integral to a complex vicious cycle orchestrated by cancer cells to promote tumor progression, a phenomenon that may be exacerbated in obese individuals.

title: Prevalence of cardiovascular disease risk factor in the Chinese population: the 2007-2008 China National Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders Study.
text:
Introduction:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) has emerged as the most prevalent and debilitating health burden affecting the Chinese population. The present study aimed to investigate the prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors and non-fatal CVDs among a nationally representative sample of Chinese adults using data from the 2007-2008 China National Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders Study.
Methods:
A multistage stratified design method was used to randomly recruit 46,239 adults aged 20 years or older. Lifestyle factors, CVD diagnosis, stroke, diabetes, and family history were collected, and an oral glucose tolerance test or standard meal test was performed. Non-fatal CVDs were reported by the subjects. SUDAAN software was used for weighted statistical analyses, and a P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results:
The prevalence of coronary heart disease, stroke, and CVDs was 0.74%, 1.07%, and 1.78% in males, and 0.51%, 0.60%, and 1.10% in females, respectively. The presence of CVDs increased with age in both males and females. The prevalence of being overweight or obese, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or hyperglycaemia was 36.67%, 30.09%, 67.43%, and 26.69% in males, and 29.77%, 24.79%, 63.98%, and 23.62% in females, respectively. In the total sample of 46,239 patients, the prevalence of one subject having 1, 2, 3, or ≥4 of the 5 defined risk factors (smoking, overweight or obese, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, or hyperglycaemia) was 31.17%, 27.38%, 17.76%, and 10.19%, respectively. Following adjustment for gender and age, the odds ratio of CVDs for those who had 1, 2, 3, or ≥4 risk factors was 2.36, 4.24, 4.88, and 7.22, respectively, when compared with patients with no risk factors.
Conclusion:
The study found that the prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors was high among the Chinese population, with multiple risk factors present in the same individual. These findings highlight the need for reasonable prevention strategies to attenuate the rapid rise in cardiovascular morbidity.

title: Microvascular and Macrovascular Complications of Diabetes
text:
Diabetes is a group of chronic diseases characterized by elevated blood sugar levels. Modern medical care employs a wide range of lifestyle and pharmaceutical interventions aimed at preventing and controlling hyperglycemia. In addition to ensuring the adequate delivery of glucose to the body's tissues, treatment of diabetes seeks to minimize the harmful effects of hyperglycemia on the body. The importance of protecting the body from hyperglycemia cannot be overstated, as the direct and indirect effects on the vascular system are the primary source of morbidity and mortality in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
Diabetic retinopathy is a common microvascular complication of diabetes, responsible for approximately 10,000 new cases of blindness annually in the United States alone.1 The risk of developing diabetic retinopathy or other microvascular complications depends on both the duration and severity of hyperglycemia. Studies have shown that both the severity of hyperglycemia and the presence of hypertension are associated with the development of diabetic retinopathy in patients with type 2 diabetes.2,3 In patients with type 1 diabetes, retinopathy typically develops within 20 years of diagnosis.1 Retinopathy may begin to develop as early as 7 years before the diagnosis of diabetes in patients with type 2 diabetes.1
Several pathological mechanisms have been proposed to explain how diabetes leads to retinopathy. These include:
1. Increased permeability of blood vessels in the retina, leading to leakage of fluid and protein.
2. Damage to the blood vessels in the retina, leading to inflammation and scarring.
3. Abnormalities in the growth and maintenance of blood vessels in the retina.
4. Increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can damage blood vessel walls and contribute to inflammation.
5. Impaired function of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), leading to the accumulation of lipids and the death of retinal cells.

In conclusion, diabetic retinopathy is a significant complication of diabetes that can lead to blindness if left untreated. Understanding the relationship between diabetes and vascular disease is crucial for physicians in the prevention and treatment of these complications. The clinical armamentarium for primary and secondary prevention of diabetic retinopathy is expanding, and early detection and treatment are essential for preserving vision in patients with diabetes.

title: Involvement of S-nitrosylation of actin in inhibition of neurotransmitter release by nitric oxide
text:
Background: The role of nitric oxide (NO) in pain transmission is still a topic of debate, with both pro-nociceptive and anti-nociceptive effects proposed. One mechanism by which NO acts as a signaling molecule is through S-nitrosylation, a reversible post-translational modification of selective cysteine residues in proteins. However, the specific targets and mechanisms of S-nitrosylation in the spinal cord remain unclear.
Methods: We employed the "biotin-switch" method and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry to identify S-nitrosylated proteins in the spinal cord.
Results: Our results show that actin is a major protein S-nitrosylated in the spinal cord by the NO donor, S-nitroso-N-acetyl-DL-penicillamine (SNAP). Interestingly, actin was found to be more S-nitrosylated in the S2 fraction than in the P2 fraction of the spinal homogenate. Treatment of PC12 cells with SNAP resulted in rapid S-nitrosylation of actin and inhibition of dopamine release from the cells. Similar to the actin cytoskeleton disruptor cytochalasin B, SNAP decreased the amount of filamentous actin cytoskeleton just beneath the membrane. Inhibitors of soluble guanylyl cyclase and cGMP-dependent protein kinase did not attenuate the inhibition of dopamine release.
Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that actin is a major S-nitrosylated protein in the spinal cord and suggests that NO directly regulates neurotransmitter release by S-nitrosylation, in addition to the well-known phosphorylation by cGMP-dependent protein kinase. These findings provide new insights into the complex role of NO in pain transmission and suggest that S-nitrosylation may play a key role in the regulation of neurotransmitter release.

title: Independent Association of Lobular Involution and Mammographic Breast Density With Breast Cancer Risk
text: BACKGROUND: Lobular involution, or age-related atrophy of breast lobules, has been found to be inversely associated with breast cancer risk, while mammographic breast density (MBD) is positively associated with breast cancer risk. To investigate whether these factors are independently associated with breast cancer risk in women with benign breast disease, we conducted a nested cohort study among women (n = 2666) with benign breast disease diagnosed at Mayo Clinic between 1985 and 1991 and a mammogram available within 6 months of diagnosis. Women were followed up for an average of 13.3 years to determine any breast cancer incidence. Lobular involution was categorized as none, partial, or complete, while parenchymal pattern was classified using the Wolfe classification as N1 (nondense), P1, P2 (ductal prominence occupying <25% or >25% of the breast, respectively), or DY (extremely dense). HAZARD RATIOS (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used to assess the associations of lobular involution and MBD with breast cancer risk using adjusted Cox proportional hazards models. All tests of statistical significance were two-sided. RESULTS: After adjusting for MBD, having no or partial lobular involution was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer compared to having complete involution (none: HR of breast cancer incidence = 2.62, 95% CI = 1.39 to 4.94; partial: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.61, 95% CI = 1.03 to 2.53; P(trend) = .002). Similarly, after adjusting for involution, having dense breasts was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer compared to having nondense breasts (for DY: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.67, 95% CI = 1.03 to 2.73; for P2: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.96, 95% CI = 1.20 to 3.21; for P1: HR of breast cancer incidence = 1.23, 95% CI = 0.67 to 2.26; P(trend) = .02). Having a combination of no involution and dense breasts was associated with a higher risk of breast cancer compared to having complete involution and nondense breasts (HR of breast cancer incidence = 4.08, 95% CI = 1.72 to 9.68; P = .006). CONCLUSION: Lobular involution and MBD are independently associated with breast cancer incidence, and combining these factors further increases the risk of breast cancer. These findings suggest that assessing both lobular involution and MBD may be important for breast cancer risk assessment in women with benign breast disease.

title: Pleiotropy as a mechanism to stabilize cooperation
text: Most genes influence multiple traits, a phenomenon known as pleiotropy, which poses a significant challenge to evolution as adaptive changes in one trait may be hindered by the potential impact on other traits controlled by the same genes. However, we have discovered an unexpected benefit of pleiotropy in the context of cooperation. In the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, a remarkable act of cooperation occurs when some cells sacrifice themselves to form a stalk that supports the reproductive spores of the others. We have identified a gene, dimA, that has two contrasting effects: it is required for the signalling molecule DIF-1 to induce differentiation into prestalk cells, but ignoring DIF-1 allows cells to cheat by avoiding the stalk. Surprisingly, we found that in populations containing wild-type cells, lacking the dimA gene results in exclusion from spores. This pleiotropic linkage between stalk and spore formation limits the potential for cheating in D. discoideum, as defecting on prestalk cell production leads to an even greater reduction in spores. Our findings suggest that the evolution of pleiotropic links between cheating and personal costs can stabilize cooperative adaptations.

title: The homeobox gene goosecoid controls cell migration in Xenopus embryos.
text: Goosecoid (Gsc), a homeobox gene specifically expressed in the dorsal blastopore lip of the Xenopus gastrula, has been implicated in the regulation of Spemann's organizer phenomenon. Using lineage tracing and time-lapse microscopy, the fate of embryonic cells microinjected with Gsc mRNA was investigated. The results revealed non-cell autonomous effects of microinjected Gsc, whereby neighboring uninjected cells were recruited into a twinned dorsal axis. Additionally, ectopic expression of Gsc mRNA in ventral blastomeres and overexpression of Gsc in dorsal blastomeres led to cell movement towards the anterior of the embryo. These findings suggest a role for Gsc in the control of gastrulation movements in groups of cells, rather than in dissociated cells, and demonstrate the ability of a vertebrate homeobox gene to regulate region-specific cell migration.

title: Epigenetic switch involved in activation of pioneer factor FOXA1-dependent enhancers.
text: Transcription factors (TFs) bind specifically to distinct regions of the mammalian genome called cis-regulatory elements, including enhancers, which play crucial roles in regulating gene expression during development and differentiation. Despite the well-established role of chromatin in controlling TF functions, there is still much to be learned about the chromatin structure of enhancers and how it is established. In this study, we analyzed enhancers on a genomic scale that recruit FOXA1, a pioneer transcription factor that activates transcriptional competency of these cis-regulatory sites. We found that FOXA1 binds to regions of the genome with local DNA hypomethylation, and its cell-type-specific recruitment to chromatin is linked to differences in DNA methylation levels at its binding sites. Using neural differentiation as a model, we showed that inducing FOXA1 expression and its subsequent recruitment to enhancers is associated with DNA demethylation. Concomitantly, histone H3 lysine 4 methylation is induced at these enhancers. These epigenetic changes may both stabilize FOXA1 binding and allow for the subsequent recruitment of transcriptional regulatory factors. Interestingly, when cloned into reporter constructs, FOXA1-dependent enhancers were able to recapitulate their cell type-specific activity. However, their activities were inhibited by DNA methylation. Therefore, these enhancers are intrinsic cell type-specific regulatory regions whose activities need to be potentiated by FOXA1 through the induction of an epigenetic switch that includes DNA demethylation.

title: Leptin treatment ameliorates anxiety in ob/ob obese mice.
text: We examined the impact of administered leptin on anxiety-like behavior in ob/ob mice. We administered leptin via repeated intraperitoneal injections for 5 days and assessed anxiety in a standard elevated plus maze. We also measured body weight daily. Our findings revealed that repeated leptin administrations significantly increased the proportion of total entries in the open arms and the total number of entries. Moreover, body weight was reduced by 13.2% after treatment. Our results suggest that leptin treatment not only improves obesity but also alleviates anxiety in ob/ob mice, implying that treating obesity may lead to a solution for psychological problems.

title: Predicting new molecular targets for known drugs
text: Although drugs are designed to target specific physiological systems, they often bind to multiple receptors or proteins, leading to unintended side effects and potential new therapeutic applications. To explore these interactions computationally, we analyzed 3,665 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved and experimental drugs against hundreds of targets, defined by their ligands. Using chemical similarity analysis, we predicted thousands of unanticipated drug-target associations. We experimentally validated 30 of these predictions, including the antagonism of the beta(1) receptor by the Prozac, the inhibition of the 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) transporter by Vadilex, and the antagonism of the histamine H(4) receptor by Rescriptor. Our study identified 23 new drug-target associations, five of which were found to be potent (<100 nM). The physiological relevance of one of these associations, N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) on serotonergic receptors, was confirmed in a knockout mouse. This systematic and comprehensive approach may lead to a better understanding of drug side effects and new therapeutic applications for many drugs.

title: Bone loss and vascular calcification: A bi-directional interplay?
text: Vascular calcification (VC) is a recognized predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Previously considered a passive and degenerative process, VC is now understood to be an active process that shares similarities with bone formation. Both VC and osteoporosis (OP) are influenced by oxidative stress and inflammation, and are regulated by a complex network of biochemical factors. These factors include vitamin D, osteoprotegerin, osteopontin, matrix Gla protein, cathepsin K, fibroblast growth factor-23, and fetuin-A. A deeper understanding of this regulatory network, with its multiple feedback loops and cross talk between organs, may help to reduce the prevalence of calcific vasculopathy and OP in the aging population, and to develop targeted preventive and therapeutic interventions for both conditions.

title: Immobilized chemokine fields and soluble chemokine gradients cooperatively shape migration patterns of dendritic cells.
text: Chemokines regulate immune cell migration by inducing either directed or random movement, and by activating integrins to promote cell adhesion. We investigated dendritic cell (DC) migration and found that the mode of chemokine presentation within tissues determines the cellular response. Surface-immobilized CCL21, which binds to the heparan sulfate on the surface of DCs through its receptor CCR7, causes random movement of DCs that is confined to the chemokine-presenting surface. This is because surface-immobilized CCL21 triggers integrin-mediated adhesion. In contrast, direct contact with CCL21 leads to the truncation of its anchoring residues, allowing it to be released from the solid phase. Soluble CCL21, which lacks anchoring residues, forms gradients and triggers chemotactic movement but not surface adhesion. The combination of adhesive random migration and directional steering enables DCs to move dynamically and spatially restricted within tissues, mimicking the cellular dynamics observed in secondary lymphoid organs.

title: Local proliferation dominates lesional macrophage accumulation in atherosclerosis
text: During the inflammatory response that leads to atherogenesis, macrophages accumulate progressively in the expanding arterial wall. The idea that circulating monocytes give rise to lesional macrophages has reinforced the notion that monocyte infiltration determines macrophage buildup. However, recent research has shown that macrophage accumulation does not always depend on monocyte recruitment in certain inflammatory contexts. To better understand the mechanism underlying macrophage accumulation in atherosclerosis, we revisited the process in murine atherosclerotic lesions. We found that macrophages in these lesions turn over rapidly, with replenishment occurring primarily through local macrophage proliferation rather than monocyte influx. The microenvironment plays a key role in macrophage proliferation, with the involvement of scavenger receptor A (SR-A). Our study highlights macrophage proliferation as a crucial event in atherosclerosis and identifies macrophage self-renewal as a potential therapeutic target for cardiovascular disease.

title: Enzymatically active lysosomal proteases are associated with amyloid deposits in Alzheimer brain.
text:
The formation of beta-amyloid in the brains of individuals with Alzheimer's disease involves the proteolytic cleavage of a membrane-associated precursor protein by unidentified proteases. Intracellular proteolytic enzymes called cathepsins were found to be present in high levels in senile plaques, which are characteristic lesions of Alzheimer's disease, when brain sections were stained with antibodies to cathepsin D and cathepsin B. In contrast, no extracellular cathepsin immunoreactivity was observed in control brains from non-neurologically diseased individuals or those with Huntington's disease or Parkinson's disease.
In situ enzyme histochemistry using synthetic peptides and protein substrates showed that senile plaques had the highest levels of enzymatically active cathepsin. At the ultrastructural level, cathepsin immunoreactivity in senile plaques was primarily localized to lysosomal dense bodies and lipofuscin granules, which were extracellular. These structures were abundant in degenerating neurons of Alzheimer's neocortex, and cathepsin-laden neuronal perikarya in various stages of disintegration could be seen within some senile plaques. The high levels of enzymatically competent lysosomal proteases abnormally localized in senile plaques provide evidence for candidate enzymes that may mediate the proteolytic formation of amyloid. Therefore, we propose that amyloid precursor protein within senile plaques is processed by lysosomal proteases derived from degenerating neurons, leading to an abnormal sequence of proteolytic cleavages and the accumulation of beta-amyloid.

title: Gastric juice miR-129 as a potential biomarker for screening gastric cancer
text:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play a crucial role in the occurrence and development of gastric cancer. Conventional serological tests for screening gastric cancer have limitations in sensitivity and specificity. However, miRNAs in peripheral blood have been used as biomarkers of gastric cancer. However, most of these miRNAs are shared by several types of cancer. Unlike these miRNAs, gastric juice miR-129-1/2 are aberrantly expressed in gastric cancer, making them potential biomarkers for screening gastric cancer.
A total of 141 gastric juice samples from gastric cancer, gastric ulcer, atrophic gastritis, and minimal gastritis patients or subjects with normal mucosa were collected via gastroscopy. The levels of gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p were detected using quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction. A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was constructed to differentiate patients with gastric cancer from patients with benign gastric diseases.
Our results showed that patients with gastric cancer had significantly lower levels of gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p compared to patients with benign gastric diseases. The areas under the ROC curve (AUC) were 0.639 and 0.651 for miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p, respectively. Using the parallel combination test, the AUC was up to 0.656. In summary, our findings suggest that gastric juice miR-129-1-3p and miR-129-2-3p are potential biomarkers for the screening of gastric cancer, and the detection of gastric juice miRNAs is a convenient non-invasive method for the diagnosis of gastric cancer.

title: Epidemiological expansion, structural studies, and clinical challenges of new β-lactamases from gram-negative bacteria.
text: The challenge of β-lactamase evolution in treating infections caused by multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria is a significant concern for the infectious disease community. With over 1,000 naturally occurring β-lactamases, attempts to understand the structure-function relationships have become daunting. Recent years have seen the emergence of new ESBLs, such as KPC serine carbapenemases and metallo-β-lactamases like VIM, IMP, and NDM-1, which have spread globally. The rapid appearance of these enzymes in single organisms makes the development of new β-lactamase inactivators or β-lactamase-stable β-lactams even more challenging. To combat the evolving nature of these enzymes, combination therapy is likely to be necessary.

title: Robust synchronization of coupled circadian and cell cycle oscillators in single mammalian cells
text: Circadian cycles and cell cycles, two fundamental periodic processes with a period within the range of 1 day, can exhibit synchronization through coupling. To investigate the mutual interactions between these oscillators, we employed time-lapse imaging of single mammalian NIH3T3 fibroblasts over several days. Our analysis of thousands of circadian cycles in dividing cells revealed that both oscillators operate in a 1:1 mode-locked state, with cell divisions occurring approximately 5 hours before the peak in circadian Rev-Erbα-YFP reporter expression. While both unidirectional and bidirectional coupling mechanisms have been proposed, our findings, combined with stochastic modeling, unequivocally demonstrate that the reverse coupling is the predominant mechanism in NIH3T3 cells. Furthermore, temperature, genetic, and pharmacological perturbations revealed that the two interacting cellular oscillators can adopt a synchronized state that is remarkably robust across a wide range of parameters. These findings have significant implications for the understanding of circadian function in proliferative tissues, including the epidermis, immune system, and cancer.

title: Identification of a Brainstem Circuit Controlling Feeding
text: Hunger, triggered by a negative energy balance, prompts the search and consumption of food. While the role of hypothalamus neurons in this process is partially understood, the function of specific brain cell types in other regions is less clear. Here, we investigate the role of neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), which express either vesicular GABA transporters (DRNVgat neurons) or vesicular glutamate transporters (DRNVGLUT3 neurons). We find that these neurons are reciprocally activated by changes in energy balance and that modulating their activity has opposing effects on feeding behavior. Increasing the number of DRNVgat neurons enhances food intake, while decreasing the number of DRNVGLUT3 neurons suppresses it. Moreover, modulating these neurons in obese mice (ob/ob) normalizes food intake and body weight and improves locomotor activity. Finally, we identify druggable targets in these neurons and show that local infusion of agonists for specific receptors on these neurons has significant effects on feeding behavior. These findings establish the DRN as a crucial node in the regulation of energy balance. PAPERCLIP.

title: Infection-induced NETosis is a dynamic process involving neutrophil multitasking in vivo
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are released by dying neutrophils in a process that takes hours, leaving a temporary gap that invading microorganisms can exploit. Neutrophils capable of migration, phagocytosis, and NETosis have not been documented. In vivo, we directly observed live polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs) rapidly releasing NETs to prevent systemic bacterial dissemination. NETosis occurred during crawling, resulting in the deposition of large areas of NETs. NET-releasing PMNs had decondensed nuclei and eventually lost their DNA, while cells with abnormal nuclei displayed erratic pseudopods and hyperpolarization, suggesting that the nucleus plays a crucial role in crawling. The release of NETs requires both Toll-like receptor 2 and complement-mediated opsonization, which are tightly regulated. In addition, live human PMNs injected into mouse skin developed decondensed nuclei and formed NETs in vivo, and intact anuclear neutrophils were abundant in Gram-positive human abscesses. Therefore, early in infection, NETosis involves neutrophils that can multitask without undergoing lysis.

title: Swim training suppresses tumor growth in mice.
text: The present study aimed to investigate the impact of physical training on the growth of cancer cells in mice. Male Swiss mice were divided into two groups: one group underwent swim training for 6 weeks (5 days/week, 1 hour per session, at 50% of maximum capacity), while the other group remained sedentary. After 6 weeks of training, the mice were injected with Ehrlich tumor cells and then euthanized. The researchers measured the size and weight of the tumors, as well as the number of macrophages and neutrophils present in the tumors. They found that the tumors in the sedentary mice were significantly larger than those in the trained mice, with an approximate 270% and 280% increase in tumor weight and volume, respectively. Additionally, the number of macrophages in the tumors was significantly lower in the trained mice, and neutrophil accumulation was slightly reduced. The trained mice also showed a substantial increase in exercise capacity, as measured by their ability to complete a 440% longer exercise session at 50% of maximum capacity. These findings suggest that physical training may be a useful approach to preventing the growth and progression of cancer, and may improve the outcome of cancer treatment.

title: Lung dendritic cells imprint T cell lung homing and promote lung immunity through the chemokine receptor CCR4
text: T cell migration into the lungs is crucial for immune defense, but the mechanisms that regulate this process are not well understood. In this study, we discovered that lung dendritic cells (DCs) play a key role in directing T cell migration into the lungs. We found that T cells activated by lung DCs are more efficient at homing to the lungs in response to inhaled antigens and at rest compared to T cells activated by DCs from other tissues. As a result, T cells activated by lung DCs provide better protection against influenza than T cells activated by DCs from other tissues. Lung DCs imprint the expression of the chemokine receptor CCR4 on T cells, which contributes to T cell lung imprinting. When we deleted the CCR4 gene in T cells activated by lung DCs, their ability to migrate into the lungs was significantly impaired. Therefore, our findings suggest that lung DCs are responsible for imprinting T cell lung homing and promoting lung immunity in part through the CCR4 receptor.

title: microRNAs: A Safeguard against Turmoil?
text: New findings indicate that microRNAs (miRNAs) play a crucial role in various stress responses beyond their previously recognized function in development. Contrary to their usual function of suppressing target gene expression, miRNAs may actually become activators of expression during times of stress. This unexpected phenomenon could be partially attributed to novel interactions between miRNA/Argonaute complexes and RNA-binding proteins that relocate to different subcellular regions during stress.

title: Vascular smooth muscle cell calcification is mediated by regulated exosome secretion.
text:
Matrix vesicles (MVs), produced by vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), serve as the initial site of mineralization, and fetuin-A, a potent circulating inhibitor of calcification, is specifically loaded into MVs. However, the mechanisms of fetuin-A intracellular trafficking and MV biogenesis in VSMC calcification are poorly understood.
The objective of this study is to investigate the regulation and role of MV biogenesis in VSMC calcification.
Methods and Results:
Alexa488-labeled fetuin-A was internalized by human VSMCs through the endosomal system and exocytosed from multivesicular bodies via exosome release. VSMC-derived exosomes were enriched with tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81, and their release was regulated by sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3. Comparative proteomics revealed that VSMC-derived exosomes were compositionally similar to exosomes from other cell sources but also shared components with osteoblast-derived MVs, including calcium-binding and extracellular matrix proteins. Elevated extracellular calcium induced sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 expression and the secretion of calcifying exosomes from VSMCs in vitro, and chemical inhibition of sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 prevented VSMC calcification. In vivo, multivesicular bodies containing exosomes were observed in vessels from chronic kidney disease patients on dialysis, and CD63 colocalized with calcification. Additionally, factors such as tumor necrosis factor-α and platelet-derived growth factor-BB were found to increase exosome production, leading to increased calcification of VSMCs in response to calcifying conditions.
Conclusions:
This study identifies MVs as exosomes and shows that factors that can increase exosome release can promote vascular calcification in response to environmental calcium stress. Modulation of the exosome release pathway may be a novel therapeutic target for prevention.

title: Vaccines against malaria
text: There is currently no licensed vaccine available to protect against any human parasitic disease, including Plasmodium falciparum malaria, a major cause of infectious mortality. This has led to a wide range of approaches being explored in the development of malaria vaccines, with the availability of a safe challenge model allowing for small-scale efficacy testing of vaccine candidates. Malaria vaccine development has been at the forefront of assessing new vaccine technologies, including novel adjuvants, vectored prime-boost regimes, and the concept of community vaccination to block malaria transmission. Most current vaccine candidates target a single stage of the parasite's life cycle, with vaccines against the early pre-erythrocytic stages showing the most success. A protein-based adjuvant vaccine and viral vector vaccines targeting the intracellular liver-stage parasite with cellular immunity have shown partial efficacy in humans, and an anti-sporozoite vaccine is currently in phase III trials. However, a more effective malaria vaccine suitable for widespread, cost-effective deployment is likely to require a multi-component vaccine targeting multiple life cycle stages. The most promising near-term approach to develop such a product is to combine existing partially effective pre-erythrocytic vaccine candidates.

title: MicroRNA-21 is Induced by Rapamycin in a Model of Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC) and Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
text: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a complex disease affecting women, is characterized by the proliferation of smooth muscle-like cells in the lung, leading to cystic lung destruction. In addition, women with LAM may develop renal angiomyolipomas. The underlying cause of LAM is mutations in the tuberous sclerosis complex genes (TSC1 or TSC2), which leads to hyperactive mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) signaling. Treatment with the mTOR inhibitor, Rapamycin, can stabilize lung function in LAM patients and reduce the size of renal angiomyolipomas. However, when treatment is discontinued, lung function declines, and angiomyolipomas regrow, suggesting that factors induced by mTORC1 inhibition may promote the survival of TSC2-deficient cells. The role of microRNA (miRNA) signaling in the response of LAM to mTORC1 inhibition is unknown. To investigate this, we used two separate screens to identify Rapamycin-dependent miRNAs in LAM patient-derived cells. We found that Rapamycin upregulated multiple miRNAs, including pro-survival miRNAs, in TSC2-deficient patient-derived cells. The most significantly increased miRNA was miR-21, a pro-survival miR. Our findings suggest that the induction of miRs may contribute to the response of LAM and TSC patients to Rapamycin therapy.

title: Reduced NF1 expression confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in lung cancer.
text: Activating mutations in the EGF receptor (EGFR) are linked to clinical sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as erlotinib and gefitinib. However, resistance often develops, usually due to a secondary EGFR mutation, most commonly T790M. Through a comprehensive genome-wide siRNA screen in a human lung cancer cell line and analysis of murine EGFR-driven lung adenocarcinomas, we discovered that erlotinib resistance was associated with decreased expression of neurofibromin, the RAS GTPase-activating protein encoded by the NF1 gene. Erlotinib failed to completely inhibit RAS-ERK signaling when neurofibromin levels were reduced. Treatment of neurofibromin-deficient lung cancers with a MAP-ERK kinase (MEK) inhibitor restored sensitivity to erlotinib. Low levels of NF1 expression were linked to primary and acquired resistance of lung adenocarcinomas to EGFR TKIs in patients. These findings identify a subpopulation of patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma who may benefit from combination therapy with EGFR and MEK inhibitors.

title: Human IRGM induces autophagy to eliminate intracellular mycobacteria.
text:
Immunity-related GTPases (IRGs) play a crucial role in protecting cells against intracellular pathogens. Our research has shown that murine Irgm1 (LRG-47) GTPase induces autophagy and generates large autolysosomal organelles as a mechanism for eliminating intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis. We have also discovered a function for a human IRG protein in controlling intracellular pathogens, and our findings suggest that the human Irgm1 ortholog, IRGM, plays a role in autophagy and in reducing the intracellular load of bacilli.
In this rewrite, I have tried to make the language more concise and clear, while still conveying the same information as the original text. I have also added some additional details to make the text more engaging and informative.

title: Implementation of a Clinical Pharmacy Education Program in a Teaching Hospital: Resident Oriented Documentation and Intervention
text: The purpose of this study was to develop a clinical pharmacy education program at Masih Daneshvari Hospital, a university-affiliated hospital located in Tehran, Iran. To achieve this goal, the researchers first identified the most common pharmacist-involved interventions and areas of potential education for pharmacy students and residents. Data on clinical pharmacy interventions and drug information forms were collected during the study period, from January 2006 to January 2007. A total of 772 interventions were conducted during the study year, with drug information accounting for 22.30% of all interventions, followed by dose adjustment and therapeutic reduction or addition. The average number of medications per patient was 8.62 ± 7.54. Based on these findings, the study concludes that while the challenge of pharmacy as a profession is still in its early stages in Iran compared to developed countries, there is a high demand for clinical pharmacy services among healthcare providers.

title: The surgical anatomy of the conduction tissues.
text: Based on our collective experience, we have reviewed the anatomy of the cardiac conduction tissues as observed by the surgeon in both normal and abnormal hearts. The sinus node is located subepicardially in the terminal sulcus, and due to its variable blood supply, the superior cavoatrial junction is a potential danger area. There are no distinct tracts extending through the atrial tissues between the sinus and atrioventricular nodes. The atrioventricular node, which forms the atrial part of the atrioventricular conduction axis, is confined within the triangle of Koch. The axis penetrates through the central fibrous body and branches on the muscular ventricular septum, immediately beneath the interventricular component of the membranous septum. The landmarks can be observed through the right atrium, left atrium, and aorta. We then consider the surgical anatomy of the abnormal muscular atrioventricular connections that are associated with ventricular pre-excitation syndromes. Finally, we develop rules for predicting the disposition of the conduction tissues in congenitally malformed hearts, taking into account alignment between the atrial and ventricular septal structures and the pattern of ventricular architecture present. The most important variables in this regard are alignment between the atrial and ventricular septal structures and the pattern of ventricular architecture present.

title: Agreement between an online dietary assessment tool (myfood24) and an interviewer-administered 24-h dietary recall in British adolescents aged 11-18 years.
text:
Introduction:
Myfood24 is an online 24-hour dietary assessment tool designed for use among British adolescents and adults. However, there is limited research on the validity of using new technology in assessing nutritional intake among adolescents. Therefore, a relative validation of myfood24 against a face-to-face interviewer-administered 24-hour multiple-pass recall (MPR) was conducted among 75 British adolescents aged 11-18 years. The study aimed to evaluate the agreement between myfood24 and the interviewer-administered MPR in terms of total energy intake (EI) and nutrients.
Methods:
Participants were asked to complete myfood24 and an interviewer-administered MPR on two non-consecutive days at school. Total energy intake (EI) and nutrients recorded by the two methods were compared using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman plots (using between and within-individual information), and weighted κ to assess the agreement.
Results:
Energy, macronutrients, and other reported nutrients from myfood24 demonstrated strong agreement with the interview MPR data, and ICC ranged from 0·46 for Na to 0·88 for EI. There was no significant bias between the two methods for EI, macronutrients, and most reported nutrients. The mean difference between myfood24 and the interviewer-administered MPR for EI was -230 kJ (-55 kcal) (95 % CI -490, 30 kJ (-117, 7 kcal); P=0·4) with limits of agreement ranging between 39 % (3336 kJ (-797 kcal)) lower and 34 % (2874 kJ (687 kcal)) higher than the interviewer-administered MPR. There was good agreement in terms of classifying adolescents into tertiles of EI (κ w =0·64). The agreement between day 1 and day 2 was as good for myfood24 as for the interviewer-administered MPR, reflecting the reliability of myfood24. myfood24 has the potential to collect dietary data of comparable quality with that of an interviewer-administered MPR.
Discussion:
The results of this study suggest that myfood24 is a valid tool for assessing dietary intake among British adolescents. The strong agreement between myfood24 and the interviewer-administered MPR in terms of total energy intake (EI) and nutrients suggests that myfood24 has the potential to collect dietary data of comparable quality with that of an interviewer-administered MPR. The lack of significant bias between the two methods for EI, macronutrients, and most reported nutrients also supports the validity of myfood24. The good agreement in terms of classifying adolescents into tertiles of EI further suggests that myfood24 is a reliable tool for assessing dietary intake.
Conclusion:

In conclusion, this study provides evidence that myfood24 is a valid tool for assessing dietary intake among British adolescents. The strong agreement between myfood24 and the interviewer-administered MPR in terms of total energy intake (EI) and nutrients suggests that myfood24 has the potential to collect dietary data of comparable quality with that of an interviewer-administered MPR. The lack of significant bias between the two methods for EI, macronutrients, and most reported nutrients also supports the validity of myfood24. myfood24 has the potential to be a useful tool for assessing dietary intake among adolescents in large-scale studies or surveillance systems.

title: Modulation of cancer chemotherapy by green tea.
text: Biochemical modulation has been instrumental in the development of cancer chemotherapy, and we have focused our attention on the consumption of common beverages to investigate their impact on the antitumor activity of doxorubicin. Specifically, we examined the effects of green tea and its components on the antitumor activity of doxorubicin in Ehrlich ascites carcinoma tumor-bearing mice. Our findings revealed that oral administration of green tea significantly enhanced the inhibitory effects of doxorubicin on tumor growth, resulting in a 2.5-fold increase in the antitumor activity. Moreover, the combination of green tea and doxorubicin led to an increase in the concentration of doxorubicin in the tumor, while the concentration of the drug in normal tissues remained unchanged. These results suggest that consuming green tea may complement cancer chemotherapy and potentially improve the quality of life of cancer patients. We also observed a similar enhancement of antitumor activity in M5076 ovarian sarcoma cells, which have low sensitivity to doxorubicin, further supporting the potential benefits of green tea in cancer treatment.

title: Histone deacetylase 5 interacts with Krüppel-like factor 2 and inhibits its transcriptional activity in endothelium.
text:
Introduction:
Vascular endothelial dysfunction and inflammation are hallmarks of atherosclerosis, a complex and multifactorial disease that affects the cardiovascular system. Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) is a key player in the anti-inflammatory and anti-atherosclerotic properties of the endothelium, but the molecular mechanisms underlying its transcriptional activation remain poorly understood.
Methods and Results:
In this study, we investigated the molecular mechanisms of KLF2 transcriptional activation and its regulation by histone deacetylase 5 (HDAC5). We found that HDAC5 associates with KLF2 in the nuclei of human umbilical cord vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and represses KLF2 transcriptional activation. Steady laminar flow attenuated the association of HDAC5 with KLF2 by stimulating HDAC5 phosphorylation-dependent nuclear export in HUVEC. We also mapped the KLF2-HDAC5-interacting domains and found that the N-terminal region of HDAC5 interacts with the C-terminal domain of KLF2. Chromatin immunoprecipitation and luciferase reporter assays showed that HDAC5 through a direct association with KLF2 suppressed KLF2 transcriptional activation. Overexpression of HDAC5 inhibited KLF2-dependent endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) promoter activity in COS7 cells and gene expression in both HUVECs and bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs). Conversely, silencing of HDAC5 enhanced KLF2 transcription and eNOS expression in HUVEC. Moreover, we observed that the level of eNOS protein in the thoracic aorta isolated from HDAC5 knockout mice was higher, whereas expression of pro-inflammatory vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 was lower, compared with those of HDAC5 wild-type mice.
Conclusion:
Our findings reveal a novel role of HDAC5 in modulating KLF2 transcriptional activation and eNOS expression. These results suggest that HDAC5, as a binding partner and modulator of KLF2, could be a new therapeutic target to prevent vascular endothelial dysfunction associated with cardiovascular diseases.

title: N348I in HIV-1 reverse transcriptase can counteract the nevirapine-mediated bias toward RNase H cleavage during plus-strand initiation.
text:
Drug resistance-associated mutations in HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) can impact the balance between polymerase and ribonuclease H (RNase H) activities within the enzyme. Recent research has shown that the N348I mutation in the connection domain leads to selective dissociation from RNase H-competent complexes, while the polymerase-competent complex remains largely unchanged. N348I has been linked to resistance to the non-nucleoside RT inhibitor (NNRTI), nevirapine; however, the underlying mechanism connecting changes in RNase H activity to NNRTI susceptibility remains unclear.
Recent findings suggest that NNRTIs may alter the orientation of RT on its nucleic acid substrate, enhancing RNase H activity. Our study demonstrates that RNase H-mediated primer removal is more efficient in the presence of NNRTIs, but the N348I mutant enzyme can counteract this effect. Notably, efavirenz, a tight binding inhibitor, restricts the influence of the mutation. These findings provide strong evidence that N348I can counteract the inhibitory effects of nevirapine during the initiation of (+)-strand DNA synthesis, revealing a novel mechanism of resistance. The data are consistent with clinical observations showing a greater impact of N348I on susceptibility to nevirapine compared to efavirenz.

title: Cancer survivorship research: the challenge of recruiting adult long term cancer survivors from a cooperative clinical trials group
text:
Introduction:
The growing number of adult cancer survivors highlights the need for information on the potential long-term effects of cancer treatments. While few adult cancer patients participate in clinical trials, those previously enrolled in these trials can provide valuable insights into treatment-related late effects.
Methods:
We conducted a study to investigate the late health outcomes and quality of life of long-term survivors of colorectal cancer, using data from five phase III randomized clinical trials from the National Surgical Adjuvant Breast & Bowel Project (NSABP). We aimed to recruit and enroll long-term survivors in the study, but faced challenges in doing so.
Results:
We invited 65 NSABP treatment sites to participate in the study, and 60 sites agreed to enroll patients. However, we were only able to recruit 976 patients (41% of the potential sample), of whom 744 (76%) expressed interest in participating and 708 completed interviews (95% of those expressing interest, and 29% of the total potential sample). Multiple barriers to recruitment were identified, including difficulty locating patients, lack of institutional commitment, and lack of patient interest.
Conclusions:
Patients treated on clinical trials can provide valuable insights into the late effects of cancer treatments. However, retrospective recruitment has significant limitations, and mechanisms should be established for prospective long-term follow-up to identify and understand the frequency and type of late effects associated with cancer treatments.
Implications for Cancer Survivors:
As cancer patients are living longer, it is important to learn from participants in clinical trials whether specific treatment regimens are associated with any serious late effects. This information can help cancer survivors make informed decisions about their care and manage their health over the long term.

title: Arylsulfatase B Improves Locomotor Function after Mouse Spinal Cord Injury
text: Bacterial chondroitinase ABC (ChaseABC) has been employed to remove the inhibitory chondroitin sulfate chains from chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, thereby enhancing regeneration after rodent spinal cord injury. In light of the potential benefits of mammalian enzymes, we hypothesized that the mammalian enzyme arylsulfatase B (ARSB) would also enhance recovery after mouse spinal cord injury. The use of ARSB offers an attractive alternative to ChaseABC, as it exhibits greater chemical stability and reduced immunogenicity. Our findings demonstrate that a single injection of human ARSB into injured mouse spinal cord eliminates immunoreactivity for chondroitin sulfates within five days, and up to 9 weeks after injury. Moreover, we observed improvements in locomotor recovery assessed by the Basso Mouse Scale (BMS) in ARSB-treated mice compared to control mice at 6 weeks after injection, and similar improvements were observed in mice treated with either ARSB or ChaseABC after a severe spinal cord injury. Additionally, serotonin and tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactive axons were more extensively present in spinal cords treated with ARSB and ChaseABC, and the immunoreactive axons penetrated further beyond the injury site in ARSB- or ChaseABC-treated mice than in control mice. These results indicate that mammalian ARSB improves functional recovery after central nervous system (CNS) injury, and the underlying structural/molecular mechanisms remain to be elucidated.

title: The World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS): a short screening scale for use in the general population.
text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) was developed in conjunction with the revision of the WHO Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI) to assess adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The current study examines the concordance between the ASRS and a short-form ASRS screener with blind clinical diagnoses in a community sample.
The ASRS includes 18 questions about the frequency of recent DSM-IV Criterion A symptoms of adult ADHD, while the ASRS screener consists of six of these questions selected based on stepwise logistic regression to optimize concordance with clinical classification. The study compared ASRS responses to blind clinical ratings of DSM-IV adult ADHD in a sample of 154 participants who previously participated in the US National Comorbidity Survey Replication (NCS-R), oversampling those who reported childhood ADHD and adult persistence.
The results showed that each ASRS symptom measure was significantly related to the comparable clinical symptom rating, but varied substantially in concordance (Cohen's kappa in the range 0.16-0.81). Optimal scoring to predict clinical syndrome classifications was to sum unweighted dichotomous responses across all 18 ASRS questions. However, due to the wide variation in symptom-level concordance, the unweighted six-question ASRS screener outperformed the unweighted 18-question ASRS in sensitivity (68.7% vs. 56.3%), specificity (99.5% vs. 98.3%), total classification accuracy (97.9% vs. 96.2%), and kappa (0.76 vs. 0.58).
The study concludes that until further calibration in larger samples is conducted, the unweighted six-question ASRS screener should be preferred to the full ASRS in community surveys and clinical outreach and case-finding initiatives.

title: Human milk proresolving mediators stimulate resolution of acute inflammation
text:
Human milk contains a unique blend of nutrients and bioactive compounds that support infant development and immune system maturation. In this study, we investigated the resolving properties of human milk and identified specific lipid mediators (LMs) that play a crucial role in the resolution of inflammation.
Using human milk lipid mediator isolates (HLMIs) and in vivo experiments, we found that HLMIs significantly reduced the number of neutrophils and shortened the resolution interval (Ri) by 54% compared to peritonitis. Our rigorous liquid-chromatography tandem-mass spectrometry (LC-MS-MS)-based lipid mediator (LM) metabololipidomics analysis revealed that human milk possesses a proresolving LM-specialized proresolving mediator (LM-SPM) signature profile, containing specialized proresolving mediators (SPMs) such as resolvins (Rv), protectins (PDs), maresins (MaRs), and lipoxins (LXs) at bioactive levels (pico-nanomolar concentrations).
Specifically, we identified D-series Rvs (e.g., RvD1, RvD2, RvD3, AT-RvD3, and RvD4), PD1, MaR1, E-series Rvs (e.g. RvE1, RvE2, and RvE3), and LXs (LXA4 and LXB4) in human milk. Of these SPMs, RvD2 and MaR1 (50 ng per mouse) individually shortened Ri by ∼75%. Interestingly, milk from mastitis had higher levels of leukotriene B4 and prostanoids and lower SPM levels, suggesting a potential link between milk quality and the resolution of inflammation.
Our findings provide strong evidence that human milk has proresolving actions via comprehensive LM-SPM profiling, highlighting a novel mechanism in maternal–infant biochemical imprinting. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the complex interplay between the mother and the infant during early life and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for inflammatory disorders.

title: Cerebral perfusion and stroke.
text: Stroke is a complex and multifaceted disorder that arises from various disease mechanisms, leading to a disruption of blood flow to the brain and subsequent tissue damage. This review aims to delve into the intricate mechanisms that regulate normal cerebral circulation and how they are disturbed in disease states. A crucial aspect of treating patients with acute ischemic stroke is the concept of an ischemic penumbra, a region of potentially salvageable tissue that can be saved through timely medical intervention. This review will examine the evidence for the existence of this penumbra in humans.

title: Epigenetic regulation of miR-184 by MBD1 governs neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
text:
Methyl-CpG binding protein 1 (MBD1) regulates gene expression through an epigenetic mechanism mediated by DNA methylation. Previous studies have shown that MBD1 deficiency impairs the differentiation and neurogenesis of adult neural stem/progenitor cells (aNSCs), but the underlying mechanism was unclear. This study aims to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which MBD1 regulates aNSC differentiation.
Our findings demonstrate that MBD1 regulates the expression of several microRNAs in aNSCs, with miR-184 being a key target. Specifically, we show that miR-184 is directly repressed by MBD1. High levels of miR-184 promote proliferation but inhibit differentiation of aNSCs, while inhibition of miR-184 rescues the phenotypes associated with MBD1 deficiency.
Furthermore, we identify Numbl (Numblike) as a target of miR-184. miR-184 binds to the 3'-UTR of Numbl mRNA and affects its translation, leading to a decrease in Numbl expression. Expression of exogenous Numbl can rescue the aNSC defects that result from either miR-184 overexpression or MBD1 deficiency.
Together, these findings suggest that MBD1, miR-184, and Numbl form a regulatory network that controls the balance between proliferation and differentiation of aNSCs. This network is critical for proper brain development, and dysregulation of this network may contribute to neurological disorders.
In summary, our study reveals a novel mechanism by which MBD1 regulates aNSC differentiation through the epigenetic regulation of microRNAs, including miR-184 and Numbl. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying brain development and neurological disorders, and highlight the importance of epigenetic regulation in these processes.

title: Landscape of genetic lesions in 944 patients with myelodysplastic syndromes
text: High-throughput DNA sequencing has significantly contributed to the diagnosis and prognosis of patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). In this study, we investigated the genetic and molecular profiles of 944 MDS patients using targeted deep sequencing and array-based genomic hybridization. We identified 89.5% of patients with at least one mutation, with 47 genes found to be significantly mutated in over 10% of cases. These mutations were associated with higher risk groups and/or blast elevation. By analyzing the survival of 875 patients, we found that 25 of 48 genes (including PRPF8) had a significant impact on survival (P<0.05). A novel prognostic model, 'Model-1,' was developed using 14 genes and conventional factors, which separated patients into four risk groups with 3-year survival rates of 95.2%, 69.3%, 32.8%, and 5.3% (P<0.001). Subsequently, a 'gene-only model,' 'Model-2,' was constructed using the same 14 genes, which also demonstrated significant prognostic value (P<0.001 in the validation cohort). Our findings demonstrate the importance of large-scale genetic and molecular profiling of multiple target genes for subclassification and prognostication in MDS patients.

title: Integrated molecular genetic profiling of pediatric high-grade gliomas reveals key differences with the adult disease.
text: Objective: To identify copy number alterations and gene expression signatures in pediatric high-grade gliomas (HGG). Methods: We performed a high-resolution analysis of genomic imbalances in 78 de novo pediatric HGGs, including 7 diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas, using single nucleotide polymorphism microarray analysis. Gene expression was analyzed using gene expression microarrays for 53 tumors, and results were compared to publicly available data from adult tumors. Results: Significant differences in copy number alterations were found between childhood and adult glioblastoma. PDGFRA was the predominant target of focal amplification in childhood HGG, including diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas, and gene expression analyses suggested an important role for deregulated PDGFRalpha signaling in pediatric HGG. No IDH1 hotspot mutations were found in pediatric tumors, highlighting molecular differences with adult secondary glioblastoma. Pediatric and adult glioblastomas were distinguished by frequent gain of chromosome 1q and lower frequency of chromosome 7 gain and 10q loss. PDGFRA amplification and 1q gain occurred at higher frequency in irradiation-induced tumors, suggesting that these are initiating events in childhood gliomagenesis. A subset of pediatric HGGs showed minimal copy number changes. Conclusion: Integrated molecular profiling revealed significant differences in the molecular features underlying pediatric and adult HGG, indicating that findings in adult tumors cannot be simply extrapolated to younger patients. PDGFRalpha may be a useful target for pediatric HGG, including diffuse pontine gliomas.

title: Gene set enrichment analysis: a knowledge-based approach for interpreting genome-wide expression profiles.
text: Although genome-wide RNA expression analysis has become a standard tool in biomedical research, extracting meaningful biological insights from these data remains a significant challenge. To address this issue, we present Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), a powerful analytical method for interpreting gene expression data. GSEA's strength lies in its focus on gene sets, which are groups of genes that share common biological functions, chromosomal locations, or regulatory mechanisms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GSEA by applying it to several cancer-related data sets, including leukemia and lung cancer. Interestingly, while single-gene analysis reveals little similarity between two independent studies of patient survival in lung cancer, GSEA identifies many common biological pathways. The GSEA method is available as a freely accessible software package, along with an initial database of 1,325 biologically defined gene sets.

title: The evolution of RNAs with multiple functions.
text:
Increasing evidence suggests that many genes in the eukaryotic genome encode both protein-coding and regulatory information. This observation challenges our understanding of the gene and raises questions about the extent to which this phenomenon occurs across the genome and how it has evolved. To investigate, we consider the early evolution of genes in microorganisms, where proteins likely evolved from a cellular machinery based on RNA. While protein-coding genes dominated the genomes of microorganisms, it is likely that RNA retained its other functions and capabilities, as evidenced by cis-acting riboswitches and untranslated regions (UTRs). Based on the complexity of regulatory systems in developmentally complex organisms, we hypothesize that:
1. mRNAs have been and continue to be subject to secondary selection to provide trans-acting regulatory capabilities in parallel with protein-coding functions.
2. Some protein-coding loci may have lost their protein-coding functions and acquired more sophisticated trans-regulatory functions through gene duplication.
3. Many transcripts have undergone secondary processing to release different products.

4. Novel proteins have emerged within loci that previously evolved functionality as regulatory RNAs.

We also review recent observations from transcriptomic surveys of complex eukaryotes, which suggest that many loci have the capacity to transact a multitude of overlapping and potentially independent functions as both regulatory and protein-coding RNAs. In conclusion, we propose that many eukaryotic loci have evolved the capacity to perform multiple functions as both regulatory and protein-coding RNAs, challenging our traditional view of the gene.

title: In Vitro–expanded Antigen-specific Regulatory T Cells Suppress Autoimmune Diabetes
text: The scarcity of CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), their anergic phenotype, and diverse antigen specificity pose significant challenges to harnessing this potent tolerogenic population for the treatment of autoimmunity and organ transplant rejection. In this investigation, we describe a robust method for expanding antigen-specific Tregs from autoimmune-prone nonobese diabetic mice. We found that purified CD4+ CD25+ Tregs can be expanded up to 200-fold within a period of less than 2 weeks in vitro using a combination of anti-CD3, anti-CD28, and interleukin 2. The expanded Tregs exhibit a classical cell surface phenotype and demonstrate both in vitro and in vivo suppressive functions over effector T cell functions. Most notably, a small number of antigen-specific Tregs can reverse diabetes after disease onset, suggesting a novel approach to cellular immunotherapy for autoimmune diseases.

title: Stathmin overexpression identifies high-risk patients and lymph node metastasis in endometrial cancer.
text:
Background: Overexpression of the oncogen Stathmin has been linked to aggressive endometrial carcinoma and a potential for PI3Kinase inhibitors in this disease. To validate the prognostic value of Stathmin expression in a large prospective multicenter setting, we aimed to investigate the biological tumor marker Stathmin in relation to clinicopathologic variables, including lymph node status and survival.
Methods: A total of 1,076 endometrial cancer patients were recruited from 10 centers to evaluate the expression of Stathmin in relation to lymph node metastasis and survival. Immunohistochemical staining was performed on 477 hysterectomy and 818 curettage specimens.
Results: Seventy-one percent of the patients (n = 763) underwent lymph node sampling, and 12% had metastatic nodes (n = 94). Stathmin overexpression was detected in 37% (302 of 818) of the curettage and 18% (84 of 477) of the hysterectomy specimens analyzed. Stathmin overexpression in curettage and hysterectomy specimens was highly correlated and significantly associated with nonendometrioid histology, high grade, and aneuploidy. Stathmin analysis in preoperative curettage samples significantly correlated with and was an independent predictor of lymph node metastases. High Stathmin expression was associated with poor disease-specific survival (P ≤ 0.002) in both curettage and hysterectomy specimens.
Conclusion: Stathmin immunohistochemical staining identifies endometrial carcinomas with lymph node metastases and poor survival. Further investigation is needed to determine the value of Stathmin as a predictive marker for response to PI3Kinase inhibition and as a tool to stratify patients for lymph node sampling in endometrial carcinomas.

title: Statin prophylaxis and inflammatory mediators following cardiopulmonary bypass: a systematic review
text:
Introduction:
Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is a common surgical procedure used to treat various heart conditions, but it can also lead to inflammatory complications. Statin drugs have been found to have potent anti-inflammatory effects, raising the possibility that they may influence an important mechanism of injury in CPB. However, there is limited evidence to confirm this. Our systematic review aimed to investigate whether pre-operative prophylactic statin therapy can decrease the inflammatory response in people undergoing heart surgery with CPB.
Methods:
We conducted a comprehensive literature search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of open heart surgery with CPB in adults or children who received prophylactic statin treatment prior to CPB. Two authors independently identified eligible studies, extracted data, and assessed study quality using standardized instruments. We pooled data using a random effects model and performed descriptive analysis when data could not be pooled.
Results:
Eight RCTs were included in the review, with limited data available for each inflammatory outcome. Pooled data demonstrated that statin therapy attenuated the post-CPB increase in interleukins 6 and 8 (IL-6, IL-8), peak high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) post-CPB (WMD [95% confidence interval (CI)] -23.5 pg/ml [-36.6 to -10.5]; -23.4 pg/ml [-35.8 to -11.0]; -15.3 mg/L [CI -26.9 to -3.7]; -2.10 pg/ml [-3.83 to -0.37] respectively). Limited RCT evidence also suggested that statin therapy may decrease adhesion molecules following CPB, including neutrophil CD11b and soluble P (sP)-selectin.
Conclusions:
While the RCT evidence suggests a reduction in post-CPB inflammation by statin therapy, the limitations of the current literature mean that the findings are not definitive. Several of the trials were not methodologically rigorous, and statin intervention was highly variable in this small number of studies. This systematic review highlights the significant gap in the current literature regarding the potential anti-inflammatory effect of statin therapy prior to CPB. Further high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and establish the optimal use of statin therapy in CPB patients.

title: Array-based Comparative Genomic Hybridization for Genome-Wide Screening of DNA Copy Number in Bladder Tumors
text: In a study of 41 primary bladder tumors, researchers used array-based comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH) to characterize genome-wide copy number profiles. In addition to previously identified alterations in large chromosomal regions, the study identified many small genomic regions with high-level amplifications or homozygous deletions. High-level amplifications were detected in 192 genomic clones, with the most frequent locations including 6p22.3 (E2F3), 8p12 (FGFR1), 8q22.2 (CMYC), 11q13 (CCND1, EMS1, INT2), and 19q13.1 (CCNE). Homozygous deletions were detected in 51 genomic clones, with four showing deletions in more than one case. Significant correlations were observed between copy number gain of clones containing CCNE1 and gain of ERBB2, and between gain of CCND1 and deletion of TP53. Additionally, there was a significant complementary association between gain of CCND1 and gain of E2F3. While there was no significant relationship between copy number changes and tumor stage or grade, the linked behavior among genomic loci suggests that array CGH will be increasingly important in understanding pathways critical to bladder tumor biology.

title: Tet2 is required to resolve inflammation by recruiting Hdac2 to specifically repress IL-6
text:
Epigenetic modifiers play a crucial role in establishing and maintaining unique cellular identities by regulating chromatin and methylation status. Tet proteins, a family of enzymes that catalyze DNA modifications such as 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), have been shown to regulate chromatin architecture and gene transcription independently of DNA methylation. However, the role of Tet proteins in regulating immunity and inflammation remains largely unexplored.
Our study reveals that Tet2 selectively mediates active repression of interleukin-6 (IL-6) transcription during inflammation resolution in innate myeloid cells, including dendritic cells and macrophages. Loss of Tet2 leads to increased production of inflammatory mediators, including IL-6, at late stages of the inflammatory response. Tet2-deficient mice are more susceptible to endotoxin shock and dextran-sulfate-sodium-induced colitis, displaying a more severe inflammatory phenotype and increased IL-6 production compared to wild-type mice.
We found that the transcription factor IκBζ, which is specific to IL-6, targets Tet2 to the Il6 promoter, indicating opposite regulatory roles of IκBζ at different stages of inflammation. Tet2 recruits histone deacetylase 2 (Hdac2) and represses Il6 transcription via histone deacetylation, providing mechanistic evidence for the gene-specific transcription repression activity of Tet2. Additionally, we demonstrate that Tet2 prevents constant transcription activation at the chromatin level, thereby resolving inflammation.
In conclusion, our findings reveal a novel mechanism by which Tet2 regulates immunity and inflammation, highlighting its importance in maintaining proper immune function.

title: Control of immunity by the TNFR-related molecule OX40 (CD134).
text: TNFR/TNF superfamily members play a crucial role in regulating various immune functions. Recent research has highlighted the significance of the interaction between OX40 (CD134) and its ligand OX40L (CD252) in this family. These molecules exert a profound influence on conventional CD4 and CD8 T cells, and more recent studies have demonstrated their ability to modulate NKT cell and NK cell function, as well as to facilitate cross-talk with professional antigen-presenting cells, such as mast cells, smooth muscle cells, and endothelial cells. Furthermore, OX40-OX40L interactions also impact the differentiation and activity of regulatory T cells. Blocking OX40L has shown promise in treating autoimmune and inflammatory diseases in animal models, and reagents that stimulate OX40 signaling are being explored as adjuvants for vaccination and cancer treatment.

title: The Drosophila DHR96 nuclear receptor binds cholesterol and regulates cholesterol homeostasis.
text: Maintaining proper cholesterol levels is crucial for normal cellular function and preventing the harmful effects of high cholesterol levels. Our research reveals that the Drosophila DHR96 nuclear receptor interacts with cholesterol and regulates the coordinated transcriptional response of genes involved in cholesterol uptake, transport, and storage. DHR96 mutants are sensitive to low levels of cholesterol and accumulate excess cholesterol when fed a high-cholesterol diet. The cholesterol accumulation phenotype can be attributed to the misregulation of npc1b, an ortholog of the mammalian Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 gene NPC1L1, which is essential for dietary cholesterol uptake. These findings establish DHR96 as a central regulator of cholesterol homeostasis.

title: A neuroimaging investigation of the association between aerobic fitness, hippocampal volume, and memory performance in preadolescent children.
text: Because children are becoming increasingly overweight, unhealthy, and unfit, understanding the neurocognitive benefits of an active lifestyle in childhood has significant public health and educational implications. Animal studies have shown that aerobic exercise is linked to increased cell growth and survival in the hippocampus, as well as enhanced learning and memory.
