Recent research in older adults has also found that high levels of aerobic fitness are associated with larger hippocampal volumes and better memory performance. The present study aimed to extend these findings to a sample of preadolescent children. Using magnetic resonance imaging, the study found that higher-fit children had larger bilateral hippocampal volumes and superior performance on a relational memory task compared to lower-fit children. Additionally, the study found that bilateral hippocampal volume mediated the relationship between fitness level (VO(2) max) and relational memory performance. Contrary to predictions, no relationship was found between aerobic fitness, nucleus accumbens volume, and memory. These findings suggest that aerobic fitness may have a specific effect on the structure and function of the preadolescent human brain, with important implications for public health and education.

title: Association between maternal serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level and pregnancy and neonatal outcomes: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
text:
Objective: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the association between serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD) levels during pregnancy and various pregnancy outcomes.
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
Data sources: Medline (1966 to August 2012), PubMed (2008 to August 2012), Embase (1980 to August 2012), CINAHL (1981 to August 2012), the Cochrane database of systematic reviews, and the Cochrane database of registered clinical trials.
Study selection: Studies reporting on the association between serum 25-OHD levels during pregnancy and the outcomes of interest (pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, bacterial vaginosis, caesarean section, small for gestational age infants, birth weight, birth length, and head circumference).
Data extraction: Two authors independently extracted data from original research articles, including key indicators of study quality. We pooled the most adjusted odds ratios and weighted mean differences. Associations were tested in subgroups representing different patient characteristics and study quality.
Results: 3357 studies were identified and reviewed for eligibility. 31 eligible studies were included in the final analysis. Insuficient serum levels of 25-OHD were associated with gestational diabetes (pooled odds ratio 1.49, 95% confidence interval 1.18 to 1.89), pre-eclampsia (1.79, 1.25 to 2.58), and small for gestational age infants (1.85, 1.52 to 2.26). Pregnant women with low serum 25-OHD levels had an increased risk of bacterial vaginosis and low birthweight infants but not delivery by caesarean section.
Conclusion: Vitamin D insufficiency is associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and small for gestational age infants. Pregnant women with low 25-OHD levels had an increased risk of bacterial vaginosis and lower birth weight infants, but not delivery by caesarean section.

title: β-Adrenergic receptor antagonism prevents anxiety-like behavior and microglial reactivity induced by repeated social defeat.
text: Repeated social defeat in mice leads to altered immune function and the development of psychological disorders, including anxiety and depression. In this study, we found that repeated social defeat increased c-Fos staining in brain regions associated with fear and threat appraisal, leading to anxiety-like behavior in a β-adrenergic receptor-dependent manner. Additionally, repeated social defeat resulted in a significant increase in the number of CD11b(+)/CD45(high)/Ly6C(high) macrophages that trafficked to the brain, as well as elevated levels of inflammatory markers on the surface of microglia and macrophages. Furthermore, repeated social defeat led to an increase in deramified microglia in the medial amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus. Interestingly, mRNA analysis of microglia revealed that repeated social defeat increased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β) and reduced levels of glucocorticoid responsive genes (GILZ and FKBP51). The stress-dependent changes in microglia and macrophages were prevented by propranolol, a β-adrenergic receptor antagonist. Microglia isolated from socially defeated mice and cultured ex vivo showed enhanced production of pro-inflammatory cytokines after stimulation with lipopolysaccharide. Notably, repeated social defeat increased c-Fos activation in IL-1 receptor type-1-deficient mice, but did not promote anxiety-like behavior or microglia activation in the absence of functional IL-1 receptor type-1. These findings suggest that repeated social defeat-induced anxiety-like behavior and enhanced reactivity of microglia are dependent on the activation of β-adrenergic and IL-1 receptors.

title: In vitro differentiation of transplantable neural precursors from human embryonic stem cells
text: The exceptional developmental potential and replicative capacity of human embryonic stem (ES) cells hold great promise for an almost limitless supply of specific cell types for transplantation therapies. In this study, we explore the in vitro differentiation, enrichment, and transplantation of neural precursor cells derived from human ES cells. Upon aggregation into embryoid bodies, the differentiating ES cells formed large numbers of neural tube-like structures in the presence of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF-2). We isolated and purified neural precursors within these formations using selective enzymatic digestion and differential adhesion. Following the withdrawal of FGF-2, these precursors differentiated into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. We then transplanted these neural precursors into neonatal mouse brains, where they incorporated into various brain regions and differentiated into both neurons and astrocytes. Importantly, no teratoma formation was observed in the transplant recipients, suggesting that human ES cell–derived neural precursors may serve as a viable source for nervous system repair.

title: Characterization of prostaglandin E2 production by Candida albicans.
text: Candida albicans produces lipid metabolites that are functionally comparable to host prostaglandins, as demonstrated through mass spectrometry analysis. These studies have shown that C. albicans produces authentic prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) from arachidonic acid, with maximal PGE2 production observed at 37 degrees Celsius in stationary-phase culture supernatants and cell-free lysates generated from stationary-phase cells. Interestingly, PGE2 production is inhibited by both non-specific cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase inhibitors but not by inhibitors specific to the cyclooxygenase 2 isoenzyme. The C. albicans genome lacks a cyclooxygenase homolog, but several genes potentially involved in prostaglandin production from C. albicans were investigated. The findings revealed that a C. albicans fatty acid desaturase homolog (Ole2) and a multicopper oxidase homolog (Fet3) play roles in prostaglandin production, with ole2/ole2 and fet3/fet3 mutant strains exhibiting reduced PGE2 levels compared to parent strains. This work demonstrates that the synthesis of PGE2 in C. albicans occurs via novel pathways.

title: A global role for KLF1 in erythropoiesis revealed by ChIP-seq in primary erythroid cells.
text: KLF1 regulates a wide range of genes to guide erythroid cell differentiation from bipotent progenitors. To investigate the local cis-regulatory contexts and transcription factor networks in which KLF1 operates, we performed KLF1 ChIP-seq in mice. Our findings revealed at least 945 sites in the genome of E14.5 fetal liver erythroid cells that are occupied by endogenous KLF1. Many of these sites are located near erythroid gene promoters, such as Hbb-b1, but the majority are distant from any known genes. Our data suggests that KLF1 directly regulates most aspects of terminal erythroid differentiation, including the production of alpha- and beta-globin protein chains, heme biosynthesis, coordination of proliferation and anti-apoptotic pathways, and construction of the red cell membrane and cytoskeleton. Additionally, we propose new mechanisms for KLF1 collaboration with other transcription factors, such as the erythroid transcription factor GATA1, to maintain homeostasis in the erythroid compartment.

title: KOBAS 2.0: a web server for annotation and identification of enriched pathways and diseases
text: High-throughput experimental technologies typically identify numerous genes associated with or affected by a biological or disease process. From these genes, researchers aim to identify the underlying biological pathways and potential diseases. To facilitate this process, we have developed a web server called KOBAS 2.0, which utilizes mapping to genes with known annotations to annotate an input set of genes with putative pathways and disease relationships. KOBAS 2.0 can perform both ID mapping and cross-species sequence similarity mapping, followed by statistical tests to identify significantly enriched pathways and diseases. This web server leverages knowledge from 1327 species across five pathway databases (KEGG PATHWAY, PID, BioCyc, Reactome, and Panther) and five human disease databases (OMIM, KEGG DISEASE, FunDO, GAD, and NHGRI GWAS Catalog). KOBAS 2.0 can be accessed at <http://kobas.cbi.pku.edu.cn>.

title: Translocation of sickle cell erythrocyte microRNAs into Plasmodium falciparum inhibits parasite translation and contributes to malaria resistance.
text: Erythrocytes bearing a variant hemoglobin allele (HbS) are implicated in sickle cell disease, while also exhibiting resistance to infection by the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. The multifaceted molecular basis of this resistance remains incompletely understood. Our study uncovers a novel mechanism of resistance in HbAS and HbSS erythrocytes, which involve dysregulated microRNA (miRNA) composition. During the intraerythrocytic life cycle of P. falciparum, a subset of erythrocyte miRNAs translocate into the parasite. Specifically, miR-451 and let-7i are highly enriched in HbAS and HbSS erythrocytes and negatively regulate parasite growth. Surprisingly, we found that these miRNAs have integrated into essential parasite messenger RNAs, leading to impaired ribosomal loading and translational inhibition. Our findings suggest that sickle cell erythrocytes exhibit cell-intrinsic resistance to malaria in part through an atypical miRNA activity, which may represent a unique host defense strategy against complex eukaryotic pathogens.

title: CD28 and ITK signals regulate autoreactive T cell trafficking
text: Activation of self-reactive T cells and their migration to target tissues leads to autoimmune organ damage. Mice lacking the co-inhibitory receptor cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) develop fatal autoimmunity characterized by lymphocytic infiltration into nonlymphoid tissues. We demonstrate that the CD28 co-stimulatory pathway regulates the trafficking of self-reactive Ctla4(-/-) T cells to tissues. Concurrent ablation of the CD28-activated Tec family kinase ITK does not block spontaneous T cell activation but instead causes self-reactive Ctla4(-/-) T cells to accumulate in secondary lymphoid organs. Despite excessive spontaneous T cell activation and proliferation in lymphoid organs, Itk(-/-); Ctla4(-/-) mice are otherwise healthy, mount antiviral immune responses, and exhibit a long lifespan. We propose that ITK specifically licenses autoreactive T cells to enter tissues to mount destructive immune responses. Notably, ITK inhibitors mimic the null mutant phenotype and also prevent pancreatic islet infiltration by diabetogenic T cells in mouse models of type 1 diabetes, highlighting their potential utility for the treatment of human autoimmune disorders.

title: Delayed and Accelerated Aging Share Common Longevity Assurance Mechanisms
text: Mutant dwarf and calorie-restricted mice exhibit healthy aging and an unusually long lifespan, whereas mouse models for DNA repair-deficient progeroid syndromes age and die prematurely. To identify mechanisms that regulate mammalian longevity, we compared the genome-wide expression profiles of these mice. Contrary to expectations, we found significant associations between the profiles of the progeroid and long-lived mice. Subsequent analysis revealed suppression of endocrine and energy pathways with increased stress responses in both delayed and premature aging. To validate these findings, we analyzed the transcriptomes of liver, lung, kidney, and spleen across the entire murine adult lifespan and confirmed the results on an independent aging cohort. The majority of genes showed similar expression changes in all four organs, indicating a systemic transcriptional response with aging. This systemic response included the same biological processes that are triggered in progeroid and long-lived mice. However, on a genome-wide scale, the transcriptomes of naturally aged mice showed a strong association to progeroid mice but not to long-lived mice. These findings suggest that endocrine and metabolic changes are "survival" responses to genotoxic stress or starvation, whereas genome-wide associations in gene expression with natural aging are indicative of biological age, which may delineate pro- and anti-aging effects of treatments aimed at health-span extension.

title: Arginine depletion as a mechanism for the immune privilege of corneal allografts
text: The cornea is a unique tissue that enjoys immune privilege, meaning it is protected from the immune system's attack. Recently, it was discovered that arginase, an enzyme that depletes the essential amino acid arginine, can modulate T-cell function. To investigate the expression of arginase in the cornea and its potential role in immune privilege, we used a mouse transplant model. Our findings revealed that both the endothelium and epithelium of mouse corneas express functional arginase I, which can suppress T-cell proliferation in a laboratory culture system. When we administered an arginase inhibitor to recipient mice, it accelerated the rejection of allogenic C57BL/6 (B6) corneal grafts. In contrast, inhibiting arginase activity had no effect on the rejection of primary skin grafts that express little or no arginase. Moreover, the inhibition of arginase did not affect systemic T-cell proliferation. These findings demonstrate that arginase is functional in the cornea and contributes to its immune privilege, and that modulating arginase can impact graft survival.

title: Once-a-day Concerta methylphenidate versus three-times-daily methylphenidate in laboratory and natural settings.
text: The study evaluates the efficacy and duration of action of an extended-release methylphenidate (MPH) preparation, Concerta, in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Sixty-eight children aged 6-12 years old were randomly assigned to receive placebo, immediate-release MPH three times a day (tid), or Concerta, a once-daily MPH formulation, at three different dosing levels. The study was conducted in both natural and laboratory settings, with children receiving each medication condition for 7 days. The results show that both Concerta and tid MPH were significantly different from placebo on various measures of behavior, including teacher ratings, parent ratings, and objective measures such as behavior frequency counts and academic problems completed. The study also found that Concerta was superior to tid MPH on two parent rating scores, and that children's sleep and appetite were similar for the two preparations. In the laboratory setting, both medications improved productivity and accuracy on arithmetic seatwork assignments, as well as disruptive and on-task behavior, and classroom rule following. The study suggests that the Concerta long-acting formulation of MPH is effective in providing medication benefits throughout the day and early evening, and that the use of background behavioral treatment in clinical trials can be useful in evaluating the efficacy of stimulant medication.

title: Leaderless genes in bacteria: clue to the evolution of translation initiation mechanisms in prokaryotes
text: The Shine-Dalgarno (SD) signal, long considered the primary translation initiation signal in prokaryotes, has been shown to be dominant in bacteria. However, recent studies have revealed that leaderless genes, which lack 5'-untranslated regions (5'-UTR) on their mRNAs, are abundant in archaea. Despite this, most large-scale in silico analyses on translation initiation mechanisms in bacteria are based on the SD-led initiation pathway, with little focus on leaderless genes. To address this knowledge gap, we analyzed the signals in translation initiation regions of over 950 bacterial and 72 archaeal genomes and constructed an evolutionary scenario for leaderless genes in bacteria. Using an algorithm to identify multi-signal in upstream regions of genes for a genome, we classified genes into SD-led, TA-led, and atypical genes based on the most probable signal in their upstream sequences. Our results show that leaderless genes are widespread, but not dominant, in various bacteria, with Actinobacteria and Deinococcus-Thermus having over 20% of genes as leaderless. Analyzing leaderless genes in closely related bacterial genomes revealed that the change in translation initiation mechanisms, which occurs between genes derived from a common ancestor, is linearly dependent on the phylogenetic relationship. Additionally, our analysis showed that the proportion of leaderless genes in bacteria has a decreasing trend in evolution.

title: Neuronal Sirt1 deficiency increases insulin sensitivity in both brain and peripheral tissues.
text: Sirtuin 1 (Sirt1) is a NAD(+)-dependent class III deacetylase that functions as a cellular energy sensor. Recent studies have suggested that Sirt1 may also play a role in the central regulation of energy balance and glucose metabolism, beyond its well-established effects in peripheral tissues. To investigate this idea, we generated Sirt1 neuron-specific knockout (SINKO) mice. On both standard chow and high-fat diet (HFD), SINKO mice were found to be more insulin sensitive than Sirt1(f/f) mice, as evidenced by lower fasting insulin levels, improved glucose tolerance and insulin tolerance, and enhanced systemic insulin sensitivity during hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp studies. Additionally, hypothalamic insulin sensitivity was found to be increased in SINKO mice compared to controls, as demonstrated by increased activation of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), phosphorylation of Akt and forkhead box protein O1 (FoxO1) following systemic insulin injection. Interestingly, intracerebroventricular injection of insulin led to a greater systemic effect to improve glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in SINKO mice compared to controls. In vitro studies using a cultured hypothalamic cell line revealed that inhibition of Sirt1 potentiated insulin-induced AKT and FoxO1 phosphorylation, which was traced to a reduced ability of Sirt1 to directly deacetylate and repress the insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS-1) function. The enhanced central insulin signaling in SINKO mice was accompanied by increased insulin receptor signal transduction in liver, muscle, and adipose tissue. In conclusion, our findings suggest that neuronal Sirt1 negatively regulates hypothalamic insulin signaling, leading to systemic insulin resistance. Interventions that reduce neuronal Sirt1 activity may have the potential to improve systemic insulin action and limit weight gain on an obesogenic diet.

title: Candidate Causal Regulatory Effects by Integration of Expression QTLs with Complex Trait Genetic Associations
text: The recent success of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has led to a new challenge: determining how the reported susceptibility variants actually mediate complex traits and diseases. Expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) have been implicated in disease associations through overlaps between eQTLs and GWAS signals. However, the sheer number of eQTLs and the strong correlation structure (LD) in the genome make it likely that some of these overlaps are coincidental and not driven by the same functional variants. To address this challenge, we propose an empirical methodology called Regulatory Trait Concordance (RTC), which accounts for local LD structure and integrates eQTLs and GWAS results to identify the subset of association signals that are due to cis eQTLs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RTC through simulations and apply it to prioritize relevant genes for each of the published GWAS loci. We detect several potential disease-causing regulatory effects, with a strong enrichment for immunity-related conditions, consistent with the nature of the cell line tested (LCLs). Additionally, we present an extension of the method in trans, where interrogating the whole genome for downstream effects of the disease variant can provide insight into its unknown primary biological effect. Our findings suggest that integrating cellular phenotype associations with organismal complex traits will facilitate the biological interpretation of the genetic effects on these traits.

title: Gender-dependent differences in outcome after the treatment of infection in hospitalized patients.
text: Context: While it is well established that gender can impact the outcome of various diseases, the role of gender in infection has not been adequately studied. Objective: To investigate the impact of gender on the outcome of hospitalized patients treated for infection. Design: Observational cohort study conducted over a 26-month period from December 1996 to January 1999 at a university-affiliated hospital. Setting: University-affiliated hospital. Participants: A total of 892 patients in the surgical units of the hospital with 1470 consecutive infectious episodes (782 in men and 688 in women). Main Outcome Measures: Mortality during hospitalization by gender for infection episodes overall and for specific infectious sites, including lung, peritoneum, bloodstream, catheter, urine, surgical site, and skin/soft tissue. Results: Among all infections, there was no significant difference in mortality based on gender (men, 11.1% vs women, 14.2%; P = .07). After logistic regression analysis, factors independently associated with mortality included higher APACHE II score, older age, malignancy, blood transfusion, and diagnosis of infection more than 7 days after admission, but not gender (female odds ratio [OR] for death, 1.32; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90-1.94; P = .16). Mortality was higher in women for lung (men, 18% vs women, 34%; P = .002) and soft tissue (men, 2% vs women, 10%; P < or = .05) infection; for other infectious sites, mortality did not differ by gender. Factors associated with mortality due to pneumonia by logistic regression included higher APACHE II score, malignancy, diabetes mellitus, diagnosis of infection more than 7 days after admission, older age, transplantation, and female gender (OR for death, 2.25; 95% CI, 1.17-4.32; P = .02). Conclusions: Although gender may not be a predictor of mortality among all infections, women appear to be at increased risk for death from hospital-acquired pneumonia, even after controlling for other comorbidities.

title: Comparative Safety of Targeted Therapies for Metastatic Colorectal Cancer between Elderly and Younger Patients: a Study Using the International Pharmacovigilance Database
text: Targeted therapies are increasingly used to treat metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), but their post-marketing safety in the elderly is understudied. This study aimed to compare the adverse drug reactions (ADRs) of targeted therapies used for mCRC in real-life settings, according to age. An analysis of VigiBase, a database of individual case safety reports (ICSRs), was performed, including ADR reports for aflibercept, bevacizumab, cetuximab, panitumumab, and regorafenib used in CRC. The study found that while some ADRs were more common in the elderly, such as cardiac disorders and respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders, the majority of PRRs were not different between the two age groups, except for encephalopathies, which were significantly associated with bevacizumab in the elderly only. These findings suggest that selected elderly patients can be treated with these targeted therapies.

title: CpG island methylation in premalignant stages of gastric carcinoma.
text: There is a limited number of studies on methylation analysis of premalignant lesions of gastric carcinoma, despite the fact that gastric carcinoma is one of the tumors with a high frequency of CpG island hypermethylation. To investigate the frequency and timing of hypermethylation during gastric carcinogenesis, we analyzed the methylation status of five genes (p16, human Mut L homologue 1 (hMLH1), death-associated protein (DAP)-kinase, thromobospondin-1 (THBS1), and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 3 (TIMP-3)) in non-neoplastic gastric mucosa (n = 118), adenomas (n = 61), and carcinomas (n = 64). We found three different classes of methylation behaviors in these five genes. DAP-kinase was methylated at a similar frequency in all four stages, while hMLH1 and p16 were methylated more frequently in cancer samples than in intestinal metaplasia or adenomas. However, hMLH1 and p16 were not methylated in chronic gastritis. THBS1 and TIMP-3 were methylated in all stages, but showed a marked increase in hypermethylation frequency from chronic gastritis to intestinal metaplasia and from adenomas to carcinomas. The average number of methylated genes was higher in adenomas and carcinomas than in non-metaplastic mucosa. These results suggest that CpG island hypermethylation occurs early in multistep gastric carcinogenesis and tends to accumulate along the multistep carcinogenesis.

title: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy: current and emerging treatment options for transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis
text: Transthyretin familial amyloid polyneuropathy (TTR-FAP) is a fatal disorder characterized by the deposition of abnormal fibrils derived from misfolded, normally soluble transthyretin (TTR) molecules. The disease is primarily caused by a point mutation in the TTR gene, which leads to the destabilization of the physiological TTR tetramer and the formation of monomers with a tendency to self-aggregate. The main clinical feature of TTR-FAP is progressive sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy, which primarily affects small unmyelinated nerve fibers and leads to disproportionate sensory loss, particularly in the perception of pain and temperature. Autonomic neuropathy, including orthostatic hypotension, constipation, diarrhea, erectile dysfunction, anhydrosis, and urinary retention or incontinence, typically accompanies sensory deficits early in the disease course. Later, involvement of motor fibers causes rapidly progressive weakness and gait disturbances. In addition to the peripheral nervous system, the heart and gut are frequently affected. The onset of symptoms in TTR-FAP is bimodal, with peaks at ages 33 and 60 years, and the course of the disease is uniformly progressive and fatal, with an average survival time of 10.8 years in Portuguese patients and 7.3 years in late-onset Japanese patients. Common causes of death include cachexia, cardiac failure, arrhythmia, and secondary infections. Liver transplantation is the standard therapy for patients who are in a good enough clinical condition to tolerate this intervention, as it stops the progression of neuropathy by removing the main source of mutant TTR. Recently, orally administered tafamidis meglumine has been approved by European authorities for the treatment of TTR-FAP, as it has been shown to stabilize the TTR tetramer and improve patient outcomes. Various other strategies have been studied in vitro to prevent TTR amyloidosis, including gene therapy, immunization, dissolution of TTR aggregates, and free radical scavengers, but none of them is ready for clinical use at present.

title: Invariant natural killer T cells: bridging innate and adaptive immunity
text: Cells of the innate immune system engage with pathogens through conserved pattern-recognition receptors, whereas cells of the adaptive immune system recognize pathogens through diverse, antigen-specific receptors generated through somatic DNA rearrangement. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, a subset of lymphocytes, bridge the innate and adaptive immune systems. Although iNKT cells express T cell receptors generated through somatic DNA rearrangement, these receptors are semi-invariant and recognize a limited set of lipid and glycolipid antigens, similar to the pattern-recognition receptors of the innate immune system. Functionally, iNKT cells resemble cells of the innate immune system in their rapid activation and lack of immunological memory. They can be activated by various stimuli and participate in the regulation of diverse immune responses. Activated iNKT cells produce cytokines that can modulate and jump-start adaptive immune responses. Identified glycolipid antigens can elicit distinct effector functions in iNKT cells, which have been employed to test the potential of harnessing iNKT cells for therapeutic purposes in human diseases. Here, we review the innate-like properties and functions of iNKT cells and their interactions with other immune cell types.

title: Olmesartan-based therapies: an effective way to improve blood pressure control and cardiovascular protection.
text: The primary objective of hypertension treatment is to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease. Among the various first-line antihypertensive drug classes, angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) stand out for their excellent efficacy and tolerability. The disruption of the renin-angiotensin cascade has been linked to several benefits in terms of target organ protection and cardiovascular prevention. Specifically, olmesartan, a type of ARB, has been extensively studied in trials of organ protection, demonstrating improvements in various disease markers, such as microinflammation, plaque volume reduction, vascular hypertrophy regression, and microalbuminuria prevention. Additionally, olmesartan has been evaluated in combination with either hydrochlorothiazide or amlodipine, as well as with both drugs in a single-pill triple combination, showing enhanced antihypertensive efficacy without significant tolerability issues. This treatment strategy, which leverages a drug with such characteristics and the availability of different combinations with other first-line drug classes, may represent an effective approach for achieving blood pressure control in the majority of hypertensive patients, which could also contribute to better cardiovascular disease prevention.

title: Manslaughter by Fake Artesunate in Asia—Will Africa Be Next?
text: Falciparum malaria is a deadly disease that disproportionately affects the rural poor. Artemisinin derivatives, such as artesunate, play a crucial role in the treatment and control of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, particularly in the face of growing antimalarial drug resistance worldwide. However, a concerning trend has emerged since 1998, where counterfeit "artesunate" tablets (containing no artesunate) have been flooding mainland Southeast Asia (as depicted in Figure S1). In some countries, the majority of available artesunate is counterfeit. Artemisinin derivatives are renowned for their rapid antimalarial effects and excellent tolerability, which has led to their popularity among patients. However, their relatively high cost has created a demand for cheaper alternatives, particularly among the most vulnerable populations, who have been preyed upon by counterfeiters with fatal consequences.

title: Workshop: endothelial cell dysfunction leading to diabetic nephropathy : focus on nitric oxide.
text: Clinical manifestations of diabetic nephropathy are directly linked to diabetic microangiopathy. This review re-examines the previously proposed Steno hypothesis and proposes a new concept that development of endothelial cell dysfunction is a common pathway for various diabetic complications. Specifically, glucose's ability to scavenge nitric oxide is suggested to be the initial stage of endothelial dysfunction. As diabetes progresses, the gradual accumulation of advanced glycated end products and the induction of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 lead to a decrease in endothelial nitric oxide synthase expression and a reduction in nitric oxide production, which are considered critical for the maintenance of endothelial dysfunction. This new perspective on the role of endothelial dysfunction in diabetic complications may lead to the development of novel strategies for their prevention.

title: A nuclear Argonaute promotes multi-generational epigenetic inheritance and germline immortality
text: Epigenetic information is typically erased at the onset of each new generation. However, in some cases, epigenetic information can be transmitted from parent to offspring through a process known as multigenerational epigenetic inheritance. A notable example of this phenomenon is the double-stranded RNA-mediated gene silencing mechanism in Caenorhabditis elegans, which can be inherited for more than five generations. To elucidate this process, we conducted a genetic screen for nematodes defective in transmitting RNAi silencing signals to future generations. This screen identified the heritable RNAi defective 1 (hrde-1) gene, which encodes an Argonaute protein that associates with small interfering RNAs in the germ cells of progeny exposed to double-stranded RNA. In these germ cells, HRDE-1 engages the nuclear RNAi defective pathway to direct the trimethylation of histone H3 at Lys 9 (H3K9me3) at RNAi-targeted genomic loci, thereby promoting RNAi inheritance. Under normal growth conditions, HRDE-1 associates with endogenously expressed short interfering RNAs to direct nuclear gene silencing in germ cells. In hrde-1- or nuclear RNAi-deficient animals, germline silencing is lost over generational time, leading to steadily worsening defects in gamete formation and function that ultimately result in sterility. These findings establish that the Argonaute protein HRDE-1 directs gene-silencing events in germ-cell nuclei, thereby driving multigenerational RNAi inheritance and promoting immortality of the germ-cell lineage. We propose that C. elegans utilizes the RNAi inheritance machinery to transmit epigenetic information accrued by past generations to regulate important biological processes in future generations.

title: Autophagic programmed cell death by selective catalase degradation.
text:
Autophagy plays a crucial role in regulating various cellular functions, including cell survival during starvation and control of infectious pathogens. However, recent studies have shown that autophagy can also induce cell death, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Our research has uncovered a novel mechanism of autophagic cell death, which involves the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), lipid oxidation of the plasma membrane, and loss of membrane integrity.
We found that inhibition of autophagy using chemical compounds or reducing the expression of key autophagy proteins, such as ATG7, ATG8, and receptor interacting protein (RIP), blocks ROS accumulation and cell death. Our findings reveal that the selective autophagic degradation of the major enzymatic ROS scavenger, catalase, leads to abnormal ROS accumulation. Intriguingly, caspase inhibition directly induces catalase degradation and ROS accumulation, which can be prevented by autophagy inhibitors.
These discoveries provide a molecular insight into the complex relationship between ROS and non-apoptotic programmed cell death, highlighting the critical role of autophagy in regulating cellular homeostasis. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the mechanisms of cell death in various diseases, including cancer and neurodegeneration, and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for these conditions.

title: Human epidermal stem cell function is regulated by circadian oscillations.
text:
Human skin is capable of withstanding harmful environmental factors that occur on a daily basis, yet the mechanisms by which circadian rhythms influence the function of human epidermal stem cells remain largely unexplored. Our study aimed to investigate the temporal patterns of core clock genes in both epidermal stem cells and their differentiated counterparts, and how these patterns impact the function of these cells.
Our findings reveal that in human epidermal stem cells and their differentiated counterparts, core clock genes exhibit a successive and phased expression pattern throughout the 24-hour day-night cycle. Each of these successive clock waves is associated with a peak in the expression of specific subsets of transcripts, which temporally segregate the predisposition of epidermal stem cells to respond to various cues that regulate their proliferation or differentiation, such as TGFβ and calcium.
Our results demonstrate that disruptions in the circadian rhythm have a profound impact on the function of epidermal stem cells in both culture and in vivo. We propose that this intricate mechanism provides epidermal stem cells with environmentally relevant temporal functional cues throughout the day, thereby ensuring homeostasis. Furthermore, we suggest that perturbations in this mechanism may contribute to the development of aging and carcinogenesis.

title: Engraftment of engineered ES cell–derived cardiomyocytes but not BM cells restores contractile function to the infarcted myocardium
text:
Cellular cardiomyoplasty is a promising treatment option for severe heart failure, but the most effective cell source remains unclear and controversial. To investigate this, we examined the fate and functional impact of bone marrow (BM) cells and embryonic stem cell (ES cell)–derived cardiomyocytes after transplantation into the infarcted mouse heart. However, the enrichment and long-term engraftment of ES cells are poorly understood, making it challenging to use them for cell therapy.
To overcome these limitations, we generated transgenic ES cells that expressed puromycin resistance and enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) cassettes under the control of a cardiac-specific promoter. Puromycin selection resulted in a highly purified (>99%) cardiomyocyte population, and the yield of cardiomyocytes increased 6–10-fold due to induction of proliferation during purification. Long-term engraftment (4–5 months) was observed when co-transplanting selected ES cell–derived cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts into the injured heart of syngeneic mice, and no teratoma formation was observed (n = 60).
Our results show that ES-based cell therapy is a promising approach for the treatment of impaired myocardial function, and it provides better results than BM-derived cells. Transplantation of ES cell–derived cardiomyocytes improved heart function, but BM cells had no positive effects. Additionally, no contribution of BM cells to cardiac, endothelial, or smooth muscle neogenesis was detected.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that ES cell-based therapy is a more effective approach than BM cell therapy for the treatment of heart failure. The use of ES cells allows for the generation of a highly purified cardiomyocyte population, which can be engrafted into the injured heart and improve its function. These findings provide valuable insights into the use of cellular cardiomyoplasty for the treatment of heart failure and highlight the potential of ES cell-based therapy in this area.

title: Hyaluronan impairs vascular function and drug delivery in a mouse model of pancreatic cancer
text: Objective: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is characterized by stromal desmoplasia and vascular dysfunction, which significantly hinder drug delivery. This study investigates the potential of hyaluronan (HA), a ubiquitous extracellular matrix component, as a novel therapeutic target in PDA. Methods: Using a genetically engineered mouse model of PDA, the authors employed a clinically formulated PEGylated human recombinant PH20 hyaluronidase (PEGPH20) to enzymatically deplete HA and evaluated tumor perfusion, vascular permeability, and drug delivery. The preclinical utility of PEGPH20 in combination with gemcitabine was assessed through short-term and survival studies. Results: PEGPH20 efficiently depleted HA, leading to the re-expansion of PDA blood vessels and increased intratumoral delivery of doxorubicin and gemcitabine. Moreover, PEGPH20 induced fenestrations and interendothelial junctional gaps in PDA tumor endothelia, resulting in a tumor-specific increase in macromolecular permeability. Combination therapy with PEGPH20 and gemcitabine showed inhibition of PDA tumor growth and prolonged survival compared to gemcitabine monotherapy, suggesting immediate clinical utility. Conclusions: The study demonstrates that HA impedes the intratumoral vasculature in PDA and suggests that its enzymatic depletion may improve drug delivery and response in patients with pancreatic cancer.

title: Ribose 2′-O-methylation provides a molecular signature for the distinction of self and non-self mRNA dependent on the RNA sensor Mda5
text:
The 5' cap structures of higher eukaryotic mRNAs are characterized by ribose 2'-O-methylation, a modification that has been conserved throughout evolution. Similarly, many viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes have evolved 2'-O-methyltransferases to autonomously modify their mRNAs. However, despite extensive research, a clear biological role for 2'-O-methylation of mRNA remains elusive.
Our study uncovers a critical role for 2'-O-methylation of viral mRNA in subverting the induction of type I interferon. We demonstrate that mutants of human and mouse coronavirus lacking 2'-O-methyltransferase activity exhibited higher expression of type I interferon and were more sensitive to type I interferon. Notably, the induction of type I interferon by these viruses was found to be dependent on the cytoplasmic RNA sensor Mda5. These findings suggest that RNA modifications such as 2'-O-methylation may serve as a molecular signature for the distinction between self and non-self mRNA, highlighting the importance of RNA modification in the immune response.

title: Relationship between activity levels, aerobic fitness, and body fat in 8- to 10-yr-old children.
text: The connections between children's physical activity, aerobic fitness, and body fatness are unclear, and indirect measurements, such as heart rate (HR), may obscure any relationships. To investigate these associations, we conducted a study using the Tritrac-R3D, a pedometer, and HR measurements. Thirty-four children aged 8-10 years participated in the study. The Tritrac and pedometer were worn for up to 6 days, and HR was measured for one day. Our findings revealed a positive correlation between activity measured by the Tritrac or pedometer and fitness in the entire group (Tritrac: r = 0.66; pedometer: r = 0.59; P < 0.01) and in boys and girls separately (P < 0.05). Additionally, we found a negative correlation between activity and body fatness in the entire group (r = -0.42; P < 0.05). In contrast, HR did not correlate significantly with fitness, and a high HR (>139 beats/min) was associated with a positive correlation with body fatness in girls (r = 0.64; P < 0.05). These findings suggest that HR is an unreliable measure of activity. Overall, our study supports a positive relationship between activity and fitness and suggests a negative relationship between body fatness and activity.

title: Junctional actin assembly is mediated by Formin-like 2 downstream of Rac1
text: Epithelial integrity is crucial, and its disruption can lead to early-stage cancer. The formation of new adherens junctions (AJ) between individual epithelial cells requires coordinated, spatial actin dynamics, but the mechanisms that regulate the initiation of actin polymerization for cell-cell adhesion are not well understood. To investigate the real-time assembly of actin during the formation of cell-cell adhesions in human breast epithelial cells in three-dimensional environments, we used live cell imaging. We found that formin-like 2 (FMNL2) is specifically required for actin assembly and turnover at newly formed cell-cell contacts, as well as for human epithelial lumen formation. FMNL2 associates with components of the AJ complex, including Rac1 activity and the FMNL2 C terminus. By using optogenetic control of Rac1 in living cells, we were able to rapidly drive FMNL2 to epithelial cell-cell contact zones. Our data show that Rac1-induced actin assembly and subsequent AJ formation critically depend on FMNL2, revealing FMNL2 as a key driver of human epithelial AJ formation downstream of Rac1.

title: Inhibition of HDM2 and activation of p53 by ribosomal protein L23.
text: For a long time, the interplay between cell growth and proliferation has been recognized as crucial for proper cellular function. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying this relationship have remained largely elusive. Our study uncovers a previously unknown interaction between the ribosomal protein L23 and the E3 ubiquitin ligase HDM2. We found that L23 and another HDM2-interacting protein, L11, can simultaneously yet distinctly interact with HDM2 to form a ternary complex. Interestingly, we discovered that overexpression of L23 inhibits HDM2-induced p53 polyubiquitination and degradation, leading to a p53-dependent cell cycle arrest. Conversely, reducing L23 levels causes nucleolar stress and triggers the translocation of B23 from the nucleolus to the nucleoplasm, resulting in p53 stabilization and activation. Our findings suggest that cells maintain a steady-state level of L23 during normal growth, and altering L23 levels could disrupt the HDM2-p53 pathway by affecting the integrity of the nucleolus.

title: Association of Blood Monocyte and Platelet Markers with Carotid Artery Characteristics: The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Carotid MRI Study
text:
Background: Atherosclerosis is characterized by the infiltration of inflammatory cells from the circulation into the arterial wall, which plays a crucial role in the formation of plaques. Blood cell activation has been implicated in the development of atherosclerosis, and this study aimed to investigate the relationship between blood cellular markers and quantitative measures of carotid wall components in a large cohort of participants.
Methods: We analyzed the correlation between blood cellular markers and quantitative measures of carotid wall components in 1,546 participants from the ARIC (Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities) Carotid MRI Study. Carotid imaging was performed using gadolinium contrast-enhanced MRI, and cellular phenotyping was conducted using flow cytometry.
Results: Our findings revealed that monocyte Toll-like receptor (TLR)-2 is associated with larger plaques, while CD14, myeloperoxidase, and TLR-4 are associated with smaller plaques. In addition, platelet CD40L is associated with smaller plaques and thinner caps, while P-selectin is associated with smaller core size.
Conclusions: Our study provides evidence that blood cell activation is significantly associated with atherosclerotic changes of the carotid wall. These findings suggest that blood cellular markers may serve as potential biomarkers for the early detection and monitoring of atherosclerosis.

title: Vascular endothelial cadherin controls VEGFR-2 internalization and signaling from intracellular compartments
text:
Receptor internalization is a crucial mechanism for regulating cell signaling events, and it plays a key role in controlling cell growth and proliferation. In the context of endothelial cells, the internalization of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) type 2 is a critical step in regulating cell growth and response to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Previous studies have shown that the association of vascular endothelial cadherin (VEC) with VEGFR2 contributes to density-dependent growth inhibition. In the present study, we investigate the mechanism by which VEC limits cell proliferation by retaining VEGFR2 at the membrane and preventing its internalization into signaling compartments.
Our findings reveal that VEGF induces clathrin-dependent internalization of VEGFR2, and this process is accelerated in the absence of VEC or when VEC is not associated with junctions. Surprisingly, internalization of VEGFR2 does not terminate its signaling, as the internalized receptor is phosphorylated, codistributes with active phospholipase C-γ, and activates p44/42 mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphorylation and cell proliferation. Inhibition of VEGFR2 internalization reestablishes contact inhibition of cell growth, while silencing the junction-associated density-enhanced phosphatase-1/CD148 phosphatase restores VEGFR2 internalization and signaling.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that VEC limits cell proliferation by retaining VEGFR2 at the membrane and preventing its internalization into signaling compartments. This mechanism provides a novel insight into the regulation of cell signaling events and highlights the importance of junctional adhesion molecules in controlling cell growth and proliferation.

title: Diversification in the HIV-1 Envelope Hyper-variable Domains V2, V4, and V5 and Higher Probability of Transmitted/Founder Envelope Glycosylation Favor the Development of Heterologous Neutralization Breadth
text: A recent study examining plasma neutralization breadth in HIV-1 infected individuals at nine International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) sites found that viral load, HLA-A*03 genotype, and subtype C infection were strongly associated with the development of neutralization breadth. In this study, we further analyze the impact of transmitted/founder (T/F) envelope (Env), early Env diversification, and autologous neutralization on plasma neutralization breadth in 21 participants identified during recent infection at two sites: Kigali, Rwanda (n = 9) and Lusaka, Zambia (n = 12). Using single-genome analysis of full-length T/F Env sequences, we found that all 21 individuals were infected with a highly homogeneous population of viral variants, which were categorized as subtype C (n = 12), A1 (n = 7), or recombinant AC (n = 2). An extensive amino acid sequence-based analysis of variable loop lengths and glycosylation patterns in the T/F Envs revealed that a lower ratio of NXS to NXT-encoded glycan motifs correlated with neutralization breadth. Additionally, we found that extensive diversification focused in the V2, V4, and V5 regions of gp120, accompanied by contemporaneous viral escape, significantly favored the development of breadth. These results suggest that more efficient glycosylation of subtype A and C T/F Envs through fewer NXS-encoded glycan sites is more likely to elicit antibodies that can transition from autologous to heterologous neutralizing activity following exposure to gp120 diversification. This initiates an Env-antibody co-evolution cycle that increases neutralization breadth, and is further augmented over time by additional viral and host factors. These findings suggest that understanding how variation in the efficiency of site-specific glycosylation influences neutralizing antibody elicitation and targeting could advance the design of immunogens aimed at inducing antibodies that can transition from autologous to heterologous neutralizing activity.

title: Glycolytic oligodendrocytes maintain myelin and long-term axonal integrity
text: Oligodendrocytes, the glial cells responsible for myelinating axons in the central nervous system, play a crucial role in maintaining the long-term integrity of axons. However, the underlying mechanisms behind this process are still unclear. To investigate, we generated conditional mutant mice lacking the Cox10 gene (protoheme IX farnesyltransferase), which is essential for the assembly of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase (COX), also known as mitochondrial complex IV. In the peripheral nervous system, Cox10 mutants exhibited severe neuropathy with dysmyelination, abnormal Remak bundles, muscle atrophy, and paralysis. Interestingly, disrupting mitochondrial respiration did not lead to glial cell death. In contrast, in the adult central nervous system, we found no signs of demyelination, axonal degeneration, or secondary inflammation. Unlike cultured oligodendrocytes, which are sensitive to COX inhibitors, post-myelination oligodendrocytes survived well in the absence of COX activity. Moreover, using in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we discovered that brain lactate concentrations were increased in mutants compared to controls, but were only detectable in mice exposed to volatile anaesthetics. This suggests that oligodendrocytes in the brain rapidly metabolize aerobic glycolysis products, which can be used by myelinated axons when energy-deprived. Our findings support a model in which axon-glia metabolic coupling serves a physiological function.

title: Siglec-1 Is a Novel Dendritic Cell Receptor That Mediates HIV-1 Trans-Infection Through Recognition of Viral Membrane Gangliosides
text:
Dendritic cells (DCs) play a crucial role in the induction of immunity against pathogens, but HIV-1 can exploit their functions to enhance its spread. Uninfected DCs can capture HIV-1 and transfer it to nearby CD4+ T cells through a process called trans-infection. Early studies identified DC-SIGN, a C-type lectin, as the HIV-1 binding factor on DCs, which interacts with the viral envelope glycoproteins. However, upon DC maturation, DC-SIGN is downregulated, and HIV-1 capture and trans-infection are enhanced via a glycoprotein-independent pathway that recognizes sialyllactose-containing membrane gangliosides.
Our findings reveal that the sialic acid-binding Ig-like lectin 1 (Siglec-1, CD169), which is highly expressed on mature DCs, specifically binds HIV-1 and vesicles carrying sialyllactose. Moreover, Siglec-1 is essential for trans-infection by mature DCs, highlighting a novel mechanism that mediates HIV-1 dissemination in activated tissues. These findings identify Siglec-1 as a key factor in HIV-1 spread via infectious DC/T-cell synapses.

title: The composition of the gut microbiota throughout life, with an emphasis on early life
text: The human gut microbiota has emerged as a crucial component of overall health. As the immune system develops, the microbiota plays a vital role in intestinal function and regulation. Recent research suggests that the gut microbiota is seeded before birth, with the mother's microbiota serving as the initial inoculum. From birth, the microbiota diversifies and matures by the end of the first 3-5 years of life, influenced by factors such as mode of delivery, diet, genetics, and mucin glycosylation. Once established, the gut microbiota remains relatively stable throughout adulthood, but can be altered by bacterial infections, antibiotic use, lifestyle changes, surgery, and long-term dietary shifts. These changes can increase the risk of disease, highlighting the importance of a proper establishment and maintenance of the gut microbiota throughout life. This review examines recent studies on early colonization and the factors that influence this process, with a focus on their impact on health.

title: Intrauterine protein restriction combined with early postnatal overfeeding was not associated with adult-onset obesity but produced glucose intolerance by pancreatic dysfunction
text: In this study, we investigated the effects of intrauterine protein restriction (IPR) combined with overfeeding during lactation on the development of adult-onset obesity and metabolic disorders. After birth, litters from dams fed control (17% protein) and low protein (6% protein) diets were adjusted to either four or eight pups. All offspring were fed a 12% protein diet from weaning until they were 90 days old. Compared to the control groups (CC and LC), the IPR and overfeeding groups (CO and LO) had higher food intakes, oxygen consumption, and carbon dioxide production, as well as lower brown adipose tissue weight and lipid content. In contrast, the LO rats had higher relative food intake, brown adipose tissue weight and lipid content, reduced oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, and spontaneous activity, as well as increased relative retroperitoneal adipose tissue weight and unaltered absolute white adipose tissue weight and lipid content. The fasting serum glucose levels were similar among the groups, but the area under the glucose curve was higher in the LO and CO rats than in the LC and CC rats. Additionally, the basal insulinemia and homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) were lower in the LO group than in the other groups. The total area under the insulin curve for the LO rats was similar to the CC rats, and both were lower than the CO and LC rats. The kitt (a measure of insulin sensitivity) was higher in the LO, LC, and CO groups than in the CC group. These findings suggest that IPR followed by overfeeding during lactation does not induce obesity in adulthood, but rather produces glucose intolerance by impairing pancreatic function.

title: Somatic coding mutations in human induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Defined transcription factors can reprogram adult mammalian cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) through epigenetic modification. Although some reprogramming methods involve DNA integration, it is unclear whether the genome remains unchanged at the single nucleotide level. To investigate, we analyzed 22 iPSC lines generated using five different methods and found an average of five protein-coding point mutations in the regions sampled. The majority of these mutations were non-synonymous, nonsense, or splice variants, and were enriched in genes associated with cancer. We also found that at least half of these reprogramming-associated mutations existed in the fibroblast progenitors at low frequencies, while the rest occurred during or after reprogramming. These findings suggest that iPSCs acquire genetic modifications in addition to epigenetic modifications. Therefore, extensive genetic screening should become a standard procedure to ensure the safety of iPSCs before clinical use.

title: Cell cycle, CDKs and cancer: a changing paradigm
text: Tumor-associated cell cycle defects are often caused by alterations in cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity. Uncontrolled CDKs can lead to unscheduled proliferation, as well as genomic and chromosomal instability. Current models suggest that mammalian CDKs are essential for driving each cell cycle phase, making it unlikely that therapeutic strategies targeting CDK activity will selectively target tumor cells. However, recent genetic evidence has revealed that while CDK1 is necessary for the cell cycle, interphase CDKs are only essential for the proliferation of specialized cells. Emerging evidence suggests that tumor cells may also require specific interphase CDKs for proliferation, making selective CDK inhibition a potential therapeutic strategy against certain human neoplasias.

title: Sudden infant death syndrome.
text: Despite a decline in prevalence over the past two decades, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) remains the leading cause of death for infants aged 1 month to 1 year in developed countries. Behavioral risk factors identified through epidemiological studies include sleeping in the prone or side position, exposure to smoke, the use of soft bedding and sleep surfaces, and overheating. Additionally, evidence suggests that using a pacifier at sleep time and room sharing without bed sharing are associated with a decreased risk of SIDS. While the exact cause of SIDS is unknown, immature cardiorespiratory autonomic control and a failure of arousal responsiveness from sleep are important factors. Gene polymorphisms related to serotonin transport and autonomic nervous system development may make affected infants more vulnerable to SIDS. Public health campaigns have successfully reduced SIDS incidence by 50-90%. However, more needs to be done to reduce prenatal smoke exposure and implement other recommended infant care practices to further lower the incidence of SIDS. Continued research is necessary to uncover the underlying pathophysiology of SIDS.

title: Regulation of heterochromatic silencing and histone H3 lysine-9 methylation by RNAi.
text: Eukaryotic heterochromatin is defined by an abundance of repetitive sequences and transposable elements, as well as altered histones, and has a profound impact on both gene expression and chromosome segregation. In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, we inhibited the function of genes encoding RNAi machinery, including argonaute, dicer, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. This led to an uncontrolled accumulation of complementary transcripts from centromeric heterochromatic repeats. Concomitant with this, we observed the de-repression of transgenes integrated at the centromere, a loss of histone H3 lysine-9 methylation, and impaired centromere function. We propose that double-stranded RNA generated from centromeric repeats acts as a key player in the formation and maintenance of heterochromatin through the RNAi pathway.

title: Conformational Changes during Pore Formation by the Perforin-Related Protein Pleurotolysin
text: Membrane attack complex/perforin-like (MACPF) proteins are the largest superfamily of pore-forming proteins, playing crucial roles in both immunity and pathogenesis. These proteins are composed of two parts: a soluble monomer that assembles into a large transmembrane pore via conformational changes that are not yet structurally and mechanistically characterized. In this study, we present an 11 Å resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the fungal toxin Pleurotolysin (Ply), along with crystal structures of both components (the lipid-binding PlyA protein and the pore-forming MACPF component PlyB). These data reveal a 13-fold pore 80 Å in diameter and 100 Å in height, with each subunit composed of a PlyB molecule atop a membrane-bound dimer of PlyA. The resolution of the EM map, combined with biophysical and computational experiments, allowed for confident assignment of subdomains in a MACPF pore assembly. The major conformational changes in PlyB involve a ∼70° opening of the bent and distorted central β-sheet of the MACPF domain, accompanied by extrusion and refolding of two α-helical regions into transmembrane β-hairpins (TMH1 and TMH2). We determined the structures of three different disulfide bond-trapped prepore intermediates, which were analyzed using molecular modeling and flexible fitting to generate a potential trajectory of β-sheet unbending. Our results suggest that MACPF conformational change is triggered by disruption of the interface between a conserved helix-turn-helix motif and the top of TMH2. Following the release of these regions, the transmembrane regions assemble into β-hairpins via top-down zippering of backbone hydrogen bonds to form the membrane-inserted β-barrel. The intermediate structures of the MACPF domain during refolding into the β-barrel pore establish a structural paradigm for the transition from soluble monomer to pore, which may be conserved across the whole superfamily. The TMH2 region is critical for the release of both TMH clusters, explaining why this region is targeted by endogenous inhibitors of MACPF function.

title: The widespread regulation of microRNA biogenesis, function and decay
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a diverse group of gene regulators that control various developmental and cellular processes in eukaryotic organisms by repressing target messenger RNAs (mRNAs) post-transcriptionally. These small RNAs are typically 21 nucleotides in length and play a crucial role in regulating gene expression. Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in understanding the mechanisms of miRNA biogenesis and function. Recent research has also uncovered the intricate regulation of miRNA regulators themselves, revealing a complex network of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions that control miRNA metabolism and function. These regulations play a crucial role in the context-specific functions of miRNAs.

title: The cytidine deaminase CEM15 induces hypermutation in newly synthesized HIV-1 DNA
text: High mutation frequency during reverse transcription plays a crucial role in the genetic diversity of primate lentiviral populations. It is the primary driver of drug resistance and immune evasion. One of the characteristic features of primate lentiviruses, including HIV-1, is G to A hypermutation during replication in vivo and in cell culture. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear. Our study demonstrates that CEM15 (also known as apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like 3G; APOBEC3G), an endogenous inhibitor of HIV-1 replication, is a cytidine deaminase that can induce G to A hypermutation in newly synthesized viral DNA. This effect can be counteracted by the HIV-1 virion infectivity factor (Vif). It appears that this viral DNA mutator is a viral defense mechanism in host cells that may induce either lethal hypermutation or instability of the incoming nascent viral reverse transcripts, which could account for the Vif-defective phenotype. Importantly, the accumulation of CEM15-mediated non-lethal hypermutation in the replicating viral genome could significantly contribute to the genetic variation of primate lentiviral populations.

title: Variants in the Toll-interacting protein gene are associated with susceptibility to sepsis in the Chinese Han population
text:
Introduction:
Deregulated or excessive host immune responses play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of sepsis. Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathways and their negative regulators are pivotal in modulating host immune responses and the development of sepsis. This study aimed to investigate the association between genetic variants in TLR signaling pathway genes and their negative regulators and susceptibility to sepsis in the Chinese Han population.
Methods:
We enrolled 378 patients with severe sepsis and 390 healthy control subjects. Five genes, including TLR2, TLR4, TLR9, MyD88, and TOLLIP, were analyzed for their association with sepsis susceptibility using a tag single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) strategy. Twelve tag SNPs were selected based on data from the Chinese Han population in Beijing from the HapMap project and were genotyped by direct sequencing. The mRNA expression levels of TOLLIP were determined using real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, and concentrations of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
Results:
Our findings showed that the minor C-allele of rs5743867 in TOLLIP was significantly associated with a decreased risk of sepsis after adjustment for covariates in multiple logistic regression analysis (Padj = 0.00062, odds ratio (OR)adj = 0.71, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.59 to 0.86). A 3-SNP haplotype block harboring the associated SNP rs5743867 also displayed strong association with sepsis susceptibility (omnibus test P value = 0.00049). Haplotype GTC showed a protective role against sepsis (Padj = 0.0012), while haplotype GCT showed an increased risk for sepsis (Padj = 0.00092). After exposure to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), TOLLIP mRNA expression levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from homozygotes for the rs5743867C allele were significantly higher than in heterozygotes and homozygotes for the rs5743867T allele (P = 0.013 and P = 0.01, respectively). Moreover, the concentrations of TNF-α and IL-6 in culture supernatants were significantly lower in the subjects of rs5743867CC genotype than in CT and TT genotype subjects (P = 0.016 and P = 0.003 for TNF-α; P = 0.01 and P = 0.002 for IL-6, respectively).

title: Children's estimates of food portion size: the development and evaluation of three portion size assessment tools for use with children.
text: A number of methods have been developed to help individuals estimate portion sizes, but their effectiveness in improving portion size estimation among children has not been thoroughly investigated. The aim of this study was to create portion size assessment tools specifically designed for children and to evaluate the accuracy of children's estimates of portion size using these tools. The tools included food photographs, food models, and an interactive portion size assessment system (IPSAS). A total of 201 children, aged 4-16 years, were provided with known amounts of food to eat in a school setting. The children were then asked to estimate the amount of each food using each tool, 24 hours after consuming the food. The portion sizes used in the study were based on national survey data. The results showed significant differences in accuracy between the three tools, with children performing best when using the IPSAS and food photographs. The accuracy and precision of estimates made using the food models were poor. Additionally, the study found that estimates of the amount of food served were more accurate than estimates of the amount consumed. Further research is needed to address issues related to the reporting of leftover food, which can impact estimates of actual food consumption. The IPSAS has shown potential for assessing dietary intake in children, but it would need to be expanded to cover a wider range of foods and validated in a real-life setting before practical application.

title: A 3D Map of the Yeast Kinetochore Reveals the Presence of Core and Accessory Centromere-Specific Histone
text:
The budding yeast kinetochore is approximately 68 nanometers in length with a diameter slightly larger than a 25 nanometer microtubule. The kinetochores from the 16 chromosomes are organized in a stereotypic cluster encircling central spindle microtubules. Quantitative analysis of the inner kinetochore cluster (Cse4, COMA) reveals structural features not apparent in singly attached kinetochores. Notably, the cluster of Cse4-containing kinetochores is physically larger perpendicular to the spindle axis compared to the cluster of Ndc80 molecules. If there were a single Cse4 molecule or nucleosome at the kinetochore attached to each microtubule plus end, the cluster of Cse4 would appear geometrically identical to Ndc80. Therefore, the structure of the inner kinetochore at the surface of the chromosomes remains unresolved.
To investigate the two-dimensional distribution of kinetochore components relative to the mitotic spindle in metaphase, we employed point fluorescence microscopy and statistical probability maps. Comparison of the experimental images with three-dimensional architectures derived from convolution of mathematical models revealed a pool of Cse4 radially displaced from Cse4 at the kinetochore and kinetochore microtubule plus ends. This pool of displaced Cse4 can be experimentally depleted in mRNA processing pat1Δ or xrn1Δ mutants. Moreover, the peripheral Cse4 molecules do not template outer kinetochore components.
Our study suggests the presence of an inner kinetochore plate at the centromere-microtubule interface in budding yeast, and provides insight into the number of Ndc80 molecules at the microtubule attachment site. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying kinetochore function and chromosome segregation during cell division.

title: American Society of Clinical Oncology policy statement: the role of the oncologist in cancer prevention and risk assessment.
text:
Oncologists have a unique opportunity to utilize risk assessment and cancer prevention strategies to prevent or slow the progression of cancer in both cancer survivors and individuals at high risk of developing cancer. By expanding their knowledge of the natural history and prognosis of various cancers, oncologists can advise patients on the risk of second malignancies and treatment-related cancers. As recognized leaders in the full spectrum of cancer care, oncologists are well-positioned to participate in community-based cancer prevention activities. However, economic barriers, such as inadequate or lack of insurance, can hinder patient access to these services. Additionally, insufficient reimbursement for existing and developing interventions may discourage oncologists from providing these services.
To address these challenges, the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), the leading medical society for cancer specialists involved in patient care and clinical research, is committed to supporting oncologists in their comprehensive involvement in cancer prevention. This statement highlights the current role of oncologists in risk assessment and prevention counseling, provides examples of risk assessment and prevention activities that should be offered by oncologists, identifies potential opportunities for collaboration between oncologists and primary care physicians in prevention education and coordination of care for cancer survivors, describes ASCO's efforts in educating and training oncologists regarding prevention, and proposes improvements in the payment environment to encourage patient access to these services.

title: The BLM helicase contributes to telomere maintenance through processing of late-replicating intermediate structures
text: Werner's syndrome (WS) and Bloom's syndrome (BS) are cancer predisposition disorders caused by the loss of function of the RecQ helicases WRN and BLM, respectively. Both disorders are characterized by defects in DNA replication, hyperrecombination events, and chromosomal aberrations, which are hallmarks of cancer. Interestingly, inefficient replication of the G-rich telomeric strand contributes to chromosome aberrations in WS cells, suggesting a link between WRN, telomeres, and genomic stability. Our findings also demonstrate that BLM also plays a role in chromosome-end maintenance, as telomere defects (TDs) are observed in BLM-deficient cells at an elevated frequency, similar to cells lacking a functional WRN helicase. Loss of both helicases exacerbates TDs and chromosome aberrations, indicating that BLM and WRN function independently in telomere maintenance. Furthermore, our results show that BLM localization changes in response to replication dysfunction, such as in WRN-deficient cells or after aphidicolin treatment. Exposure to replication challenge causes an increase in decatenated deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) structures and late-replicating intermediates (LRIs), which are visible as BLM-covered ultra-fine bridges (UFBs) in anaphase. A subset of UFBs originates from telomeric DNA, and their frequency correlates with telomere replication defects. Therefore, we propose that the BLM complex contributes to telomere maintenance through its activity in resolving LRIs.

title: Formation of a thymus from rat ES cells in xenogeneic nude mouse↔rat ES chimeras.
text: Researchers are actively investigating various conditions for differentiating embryonic stem (ES) cells or induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells into specific cell types. However, producing a functional organ with a three-dimensional structure in vitro remains challenging. In this paper, we describe the generation of a green fluorescent protein-expressing rat ES cell line and the production of mouse↔rat ES chimera by injecting rat ES cells into mouse blastocysts. The rat ES cells contributed to various organs in the chimera, including germ cells. Interestingly, when we injected ES cells into blastocysts of nu/nu mice lacking a thymus, the resulting chimeras produced thymus tissue derived from rat ES cells. These chimeric animals may provide a potential method for deriving various organs from ES or iPS cells.

title: Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is required for CNS, but not non-CNS, angiogenesis.
text:
Despite the pivotal role of central nervous system (CNS) blood vessels, the molecular mechanisms governing CNS angiogenesis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) formation remain largely unexplored. To investigate the role of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in these processes, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of Wnt signaling in CNS blood vessels.
Using TOP-Gal Wnt reporter mice, we first identified that canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling is specifically activated in CNS, but not non-CNS, blood vessels during development. This activation was found to correlate with the expression of distinct Wnt ligands by neural progenitor cells in specific regions of the CNS, including Wnt7a and Wnt7b in ventral regions and Wnt1, Wnt3, Wnt3a, and Wnt4 in dorsal regions.
In vivo blockade of Wnt/β-catenin signaling resulted in specific disruptions to CNS angiogenesis, leading to reduced vessel number, loss of capillary beds, and the formation of hemorrhagic vascular malformations that remained adherent to the meninges. Furthermore, we demonstrated that Wnt/β-catenin signaling regulates the expression of the BBB-specific glucose transporter glut-1.
Taken together, these findings provide compelling evidence for an essential role of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in driving CNS-specific angiogenesis and highlight the link between angiogenesis and BBB formation. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying CNS development and function, and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for CNS-related disorders.

title: Cyanidin-3-rutinoside, a natural polyphenol antioxidant, selectively kills leukemic cells by induction of oxidative stress.
text: Anthocyanins, a group of naturally occurring phenolic compounds found in various fruits and vegetables, have been shown to have a range of biological activities, including anti-mutagenic and anti-carcinogenic effects, which are attributed to their antioxidant properties. In this study, we investigated the effects and mechanisms of the most common type of anthocyanins, cyanidin-3-rutinoside, on leukemia and lymphoma cell lines. Our findings revealed that cyanidin-3-rutinoside, extracted and purified from the black raspberry cultivar Jewel, induced apoptosis in HL-60 cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner. Interestingly, this compound also induced the accumulation of peroxides, which are involved in the induction of apoptosis in HL-60 cells. Additionally, cyanidin-3-rutinoside treatment resulted in the activation of p38 MAPK and JNK signaling pathways, leading to cell death through the mitochondrial pathway mediated by Bim. We found that down-regulation of Bim or overexpression of Bcl-2 or Bcl-x(L) significantly blocked apoptosis. Notably, cyanidin-3-rutinoside treatment did not lead to increased ROS accumulation in normal human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and had no cytotoxic effects on these cells. These results suggest that cyanidin-3-rutinoside has the potential to be used in leukemia therapy, as it is widely available and selective against tumors.

title: Gout-associated uric acid crystals activate the NALP3 inflammasome
text: The development of acute and chronic inflammatory responses, known as gout and pseudogout, respectively, are linked to the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) or calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in joints and surrounding tissues.
