Although MSU crystals were first identified as the causative agent of gout in the 18th century and more recently as a 'danger signal' released from dying cells, the molecular mechanisms underlying MSU- or CPPD-induced inflammation are still not well understood. Our study shows that MSU and CPPD activate the caspase-1-activating NALP3 (also known as cryopyrin) inflammasome, leading to the production of active interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18. Macrophages from mice lacking various components of the inflammasome, such as caspase-1, ASC, and NALP3, are defective in crystal-induced IL-1β activation. Additionally, an impaired neutrophil influx is observed in an in vivo model of crystal-induced peritonitis in inflammasome-deficient mice or mice lacking the IL-1β receptor (IL-1R). These findings provide insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying the inflammatory conditions of gout and pseudogout, and further support a crucial role of the inflammasome in several autoinflammatory diseases.

title: Hematopoietic stem cell quiescence promotes error-prone DNA repair and mutagenesis.
text: Most adult stem cells, including hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), are maintained in a dormant or resting state in the body. This dormancy is believed to be an important protective mechanism for stem cells, as it minimizes the harmful effects of cellular respiration and DNA replication. However, we have found that HSC quiescence can also have negative consequences. We discovered that HSCs have unique mechanisms to ensure their survival in response to ionizing radiation (IR), including increased expression of pro-survival genes and strong activation of the p53-mediated DNA damage response. We found that quiescent and proliferating HSCs are equally protected from radiation damage, but they use different types of DNA repair mechanisms. Specifically, quiescent HSCs rely on non-homologous end joining (NHEJ)-mediated DNA repair, which can lead to the acquisition of genetic rearrangements that can persist in vivo and contribute to hematopoietic abnormalities. Our results suggest that quiescence is a double-edged sword that makes HSCs intrinsically vulnerable to mutations following DNA damage.

title: Recruitment of Nck by CD3ϵ Reveals a Ligand-Induced Conformational Change Essential for T Cell Receptor Signaling and Synapse Formation
text: The process of how membrane receptors initiate signal transduction upon ligand binding is a subject of intense investigation. The T cell receptor complex (TCR-CD3) is composed of TCR alpha/beta ligand binding subunits bound to CD3 subunits responsible for signal transduction. Although it has been speculated that TCR-CD3 may undergo a conformational change upon ligand binding, confirmation is still lacking. Our study provides strong evidence that ligand engagement of TCR-CD3 induces a conformational change that exposes a proline-rich sequence in CD3 epsilon, leading to the recruitment of the adaptor protein Nck. This occurs prior to and independently of tyrosine kinase activation. Furthermore, by disrupting the association of Nck with CD3 epsilon in vivo, we demonstrate that TCR-CD3 recruitment of Nck is crucial for the maturation of the immune synapse and T cell activation.

title: Pseudo-Seq: Genome-Wide Detection of Pseudouridine Modifications in RNA.
text:
RNA molecules harbor a diverse array of chemically modified bases, with pseudouridine (Ψ) being the most abundant modified base found in cellular RNAs. Recent mapping studies have identified hundreds of Ψ sites in mRNAs, many of which are dynamically regulated. Although the pseudouridine landscape has been explored in only a limited number of cell types and growth conditions, the enzymes responsible for mRNA pseudouridylation are conserved across all organisms, suggesting that many novel pseudouridylated sites remain to be discovered.
To address this gap in knowledge, we have developed Pseudo-seq, a technique that enables the genome-wide identification of Ψ sites with single-nucleotide resolution. In this chapter, we provide a detailed description of Pseudo-seq, including protocols for RNA isolation from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Pseudo-seq library preparation, and data analysis. We also describe the computational methods used to process and map sequencing reads, identify sites of pseudouridylation, and assign them to specific pseudouridine synthases.
The approach presented here is easily adaptable to any cell or tissue type, allowing for the identification of novel Ψ sites in a wide range of organisms. The discovery of these sites is a crucial first step in elucidating the regulation and functions of these modifications, which are essential for understanding the complex mechanisms of post-transcriptional gene expression.

title: The Mammalian Epigenome
text: Chemical modifications to DNA and histone proteins interact in a complex network to regulate chromatin structure and genome function. This epigenetic landscape, encompassing all potentially heritable changes across the genome, is referred to as the epigenome. The composition of the epigenome within a given cell is influenced by a combination of genetic factors, cellular lineage, and environmental exposures. With the completion of the human genome sequence, researchers are now striving to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the epigenetic modifications that determine how genetic information is translated into diverse cellular phenotypes across a wide range of developmental stages, tissue types, and disease states. This review focuses on current research initiatives, including large-scale studies, emerging technologies, and the challenges that lie ahead.

title: Microtubule-associated histone deacetylase 6 supports the calcium store sensor STIM1 in mediating malignant cell behaviors.
text: Stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) is an endoplasmic reticulum Ca(2+) storage sensor that plays a crucial role in promoting cell growth, migration, and angiogenesis in breast and cervical cancers. In this study, we investigate the differential regulation of STIM1-mediated store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) between cervical cancer cells and normal cervical epithelial cells, with a focus on the microtubule-associated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6). Using confocal microscopy, we observe that microtubule integrity is essential for STIM1 trafficking to the plasma membrane and interaction with Orai1, an essential pore subunit of SOCE. Our findings reveal that cancer cells overexpress both STIM1 and Orai1 compared to normal cervical epithelial cells, and that HDAC6 upregulation in cancer cells is accompanied by hypoacetylated α-tubulin. Treatment of cancer cells with a specific HDAC6 inhibitor, tubastatin-A, inhibits STIM1 translocation to the plasma membrane and blocks SOCE activation, as demonstrated by total internal reflection fluorescent images and intracellular Ca(2+) determination. In contrast, HDAC6 inhibition does not affect interactions between STIM1 and the microtubule plus end-binding protein EB1. Our results suggest that HDAC6 is a promising target for disrupting STIM1-mediated SOCE as a general strategy to inhibit malignant cell behavior. Analysis of surgical specimens confirms that most cervical cancer tissues overexpress STIM1 and Orai1, accompanied by hypoacetylated α-tubulin, supporting the potential of targeting HDAC6 in cancer therapy.

title: The tumor necrosis factor family receptors RANK and CD40 cooperatively establish the thymic medullary microenvironment and self-tolerance.
text:
Medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) play a crucial role in establishing T cell self-tolerance by expressing autoimmune regulator (Aire) and peripheral tissue-specific self-antigens. However, the mechanisms underlying mTEC development are not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the regulatory role of receptor activator of NF-κB (RANK) and CD40 signals in mTEC development.
Our findings demonstrate that RANK signaling is essential for mTEC development during embryonic development, while in postnatal mice, cooperation between RANK and CD40 signals is necessary for mTEC development to establish the medullary microenvironment. When fetal thymic stroma cells were stimulated in vitro with RANK or CD40 ligands, mTEC development occurred in a TRAF6-, NF-κB inducing kinase (NIK)-, and IκB kinase beta (IKKβ)-dependent manner.
These results suggest that the developmental stage-dependent cooperation between RANK and CD40 signals is crucial for mTEC development, thereby establishing self-tolerance.

title: Rare and common variants: twenty arguments
text: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have significantly advanced our knowledge of the genetic factors contributing to disease risk. However, the observation that these studies typically identify only a small fraction of the total causal variants has led to a debate over whether the majority of the genetic variance is concealed as rare variants of large effect or as common variants of small effect. In this review, I present 20 arguments for and against each of these models and demonstrate that both can be reconciled.

title: DNA methylation status predicts cell type-specific enhancer activity.
text: The binding of cell-selective glucocorticoid receptors (GRs) to distal regulatory elements is associated with cell type-specific regions of accessible chromatin. These regions can either be pre-existing (pre-programmed) or induced by the receptor (de novo). The mechanisms underlying the formation and maintenance of these sites are currently unclear. Our study reveals a global enrichment of CpG density for pre-programmed elements, suggesting their demethylated state plays a role in maintaining open chromatin in a tissue-specific manner. In contrast, sites that are actively opened by GR (de novo) have low CpG density and form a unique class of enhancers devoid of suppressive effects of agglomerated methyl-cytosines. Treatment with glucocorticoids induces rapid changes in methylation levels at selected CpGs within de novo sites. Furthermore, we identify GR-binding elements with CpGs at critical positions, and demonstrate that methylation can affect GR-DNA interactions in vitro. Our findings establish a direct link between tissue-specific chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and transcription factor binding, highlighting the integral role of DNA methylation in gene regulation by nuclear receptors.

title: BLM helicase facilitates telomere replication during leading strand synthesis of telomeres
text: Based on its in vitro unwinding activity on G-quadruplex (G4) DNA, the Bloom syndrome-associated helicase BLM is proposed to play a role in telomere replication by facilitating the progression of replication forks through G-rich telomeric DNA. To investigate this, single molecule analysis of replicated DNA (SMARD) was used to assess the contribution of BLM helicase to telomere replication in BLM-deficient cells. The results showed that replication forks initiating from origins within the telomere, which copy the G-rich strand by leading strand synthesis, moved slower through the telomere compared to the adjacent subtelomere in BLM-deficient cells. Fork progression through the telomere was further slowed in the presence of a G4 stabilizer. Using a G4-specific antibody, the study found that deficiency in BLM or another G4-unwinding helicase, the Werner syndrome-associated helicase WRN, resulted in increased G4 structures in cells. Notably, deficiency in either helicase led to greater increases in G4 DNA detected in the telomere compared to G4 seen genome-wide. These findings suggest that BLM helicase facilitates telomere replication by resolving G4 structures formed during the copying of the G-rich strand by leading strand synthesis.

title: Reflecting on 25 years with MYC
text: Just over two decades ago, the human homologue of a retroviral oncogene, MYC, was first identified. Since then, MYC research has been a hotbed of intense scientific inquiry, with numerous groundbreaking advances made. Looking back, it is remarkable how each new discovery about MYC regulation and function has not only shed light on the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer development, but has also had far-reaching implications for various biological disciplines. In this article, we will recap the major breakthroughs in MYC biology and speculate on the future directions of MYC research.

title: Protective effects of exercise and phosphoinositide 3-kinase(p110alpha) signaling in dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
text: Regular physical activity protects against cardiovascular disease, and the associated physiological cardiac hypertrophy is typically beneficial, in contrast to pathological hypertrophy associated with disease. The p110alpha isoform of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) plays a crucial role in the induction of exercise-induced hypertrophy. However, it remains unclear whether genes activated in the athlete's heart, including p110alpha, may have an impact on cardiac function and survival in the setting of heart failure. To investigate the effects of progressive exercise training and PI3K(p110alpha) activity on survival and cardiac function in two models of heart disease, we subjected transgenic mice with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) to swim training, genetically crossed cardiac-specific transgenic mice with increased or decreased PI3K(p110alpha) activity to the DCM model, and examined the effects of PI3K(p110alpha) transgenics on acute pressure overload (ascending aortic constriction). Our findings showed that exercise training and increased cardiac PI3K(p110alpha) activity prolonged survival in the DCM model by 15-20%, while reduced PI3K(p110alpha) activity drastically shortened lifespan by approximately 50%. Increased PI3K(p110alpha) activity also had a favorable effect on cardiac function and fibrosis in the pressure-overload model and attenuated pathological growth. Furthermore, we found that PI3K(p110alpha) signaling negatively regulated G protein-coupled receptor stimulated extracellular signal-regulated kinase and Akt (via PI3K, p110gamma) activation in isolated cardiomyocytes. These results suggest that exercise and enhanced PI3K(p110alpha) activity may delay or prevent progression of heart disease, and that supraphysiologic activity can be beneficial. Identification of genes important for hypertrophy in the athlete's heart could lead to the development of new strategies for treating heart failure.

title: The effect of cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption and fruit and vegetable consumption on IVF outcomes: a review and presentation of original data
text:
Background: Lifestyle factors, including smoking, alcohol consumption, and nutritional habits, significantly impact health, wellness, and the risk of chronic diseases. In the realm of in-vitro fertilization (IVF) and pregnancy, these lifestyle factors also influence oocyte production, fertilization rates, pregnancy, and pregnancy loss, with chronic, low-grade oxidative stress potentially underpinning poor outcomes for some IVF cases.
Methods: We conducted a review of the current literature and presented original, previously unpublished data obtained from couples attending the PIVET Medical Centre in Western Australia.
Results: During the study, 80% of female and 70% of male partners completed a one-week diary documenting their smoking, alcohol, and fruit and vegetable intake. The subsequent clinical outcomes of their IVF treatment, including the quantity of oocytes collected, fertilization rates, pregnancy, and pregnancy loss, were subjected to multiple regression analysis to investigate the relationship between patients, treatment, and recorded lifestyle factors. Of significance, it was found that male smoking increased the risk of pregnancy loss (p = 0.029), while female smoking had an adverse effect on ovarian reserve. Both alcohol consumption (β = 0.074, p < 0.001) and fruit and vegetable consumption (β = 0.034, p < 0.001) exhibited positive effects on fertilization.
Conclusion: Our findings, combined with the current literature, demonstrate a substantial impact of lifestyle factors on IVF clinical outcomes. While conflicting results exist regarding other lifestyle factors, such as nutritional habits, it is evident that chronic oxidative stress induced by lifestyle factors and poor nutritional habits are associated with a lower rate of IVF success.

title: Efficient Mitochondrial Genome Editing by CRISPR/Cas9
text: The Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 system has been widely used for editing nuclear DNA to introduce mutations or correct specific disease alleles. However, its potential for editing mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has remained unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that the CRISPR/Cas9 system can be targeted to mitochondria to edit mtDNA with specific guide RNAs (sgRNAs). We show that the FLAG-Cas9 protein can localize to mitochondria and cleave specific mtDNA loci, leading to disruption of mitochondrial protein homeostasis. To improve the specificity of CRISPR/Cas9 in mitochondria, we developed a mitochondria-targeted Cas9 (mitoCas9) that localizes only to mitochondria. This new version of Cas9, when used in combination with gRNA targeting mtDNA, leads to specific cleavage of mtDNA and disruption of mitochondrial membrane potential. Our findings demonstrate that mtDNA editing is possible using CRISPR/Cas9, and the development of mitoCas9 provides a valuable tool for mitochondrial genome editing.

title: Histone Variant H2A.Z Marks the 5′ Ends of Both Active and Inactive Genes in Euchromatin
text: In the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae, histone variant H2A.Z is deposited at the edges of silent heterochromatin to prevent its unwanted spread. We discovered that H2A.Z nucleosomes are found at the promoter regions of nearly all genes in euchromatin. These nucleosomes typically consist of two positioned nucleosomes flanking a nucleosome-free region (NFR) containing the transcription start site. What's more, enrichment at the 5' ends is observed not only at actively transcribed genes but also at inactive loci. By mutating a typical promoter, we found that a 22-base-pair segment of DNA is sufficient to program the formation of a NFR flanked by two H2A.Z nucleosomes. This segment contains a binding site for the Myb-related protein Reb1 and an adjacent dT:dA tract. Efficient deposition of H2A.Z is further promoted by a specific pattern of histone H3 and H4 tail acetylation and the bromodomain protein Bdf1, a component of the Swr1 remodeling complex that deposits H2A.Z.

title: Exercise and respiratory training improve exercise capacity and quality of life in patients with severe chronic pulmonary hypertension.
text:
Background: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is associated with reduced physical capacity, decreased quality of life, and poor prognosis due to right heart failure. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of exercise and respiratory training on patients with severe symptomatic PH.
Methods and Results: Thirty patients with PH (21 women; mean age, 50±13 years; mean pulmonary artery pressure, 50±15 mm Hg; mean World Health Organization [WHO] class, 2.9±0.5; pulmonary arterial hypertension, n=23; chronic thromboembolic PH, n=7) on stable disease-targeted medication were randomly assigned to a control (n=15) and a primary training (n=15) group. Medication remained unchanged during the study period. Primary end points were the changes from baseline to week 15 in the distance walked in 6 minutes and in scores of the Short Form Health Survey quality-of-life questionnaire. Changes in WHO functional class, Borg scale, and parameters of echocardiography and gas exchange were also assessed. At week 15, patients in the primary and secondary training groups showed improved 6-minute walking distance; the mean difference between the control and the primary training group was 111 m (95% confidence interval, 65 to 139 m; P<0.001). Exercise training was well tolerated and improved scores of quality of life, WHO functional class, peak oxygen consumption, oxygen consumption at the anaerobic threshold, and achieved workload. Systolic pulmonary artery pressure values at rest did not change significantly after 15 weeks of exercise and respiratory training (from 61±18 to 54±18 mm Hg) within the training group.
Conclusions: This study suggests that respiratory and physical training may be a promising adjunct to medical treatment in severe PH. The results add to the beneficial effects of modern medical treatment.

title: HIV-1 regulation of latency in the monocyte-macrophage lineage and in CD4+ T lymphocytes.
text: In 1996, the introduction of HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy) raised expectations for the eradication of HIV-1. However, the discovery of latent HIV-1 reservoirs in CD4+ T cells and the monocyte-macrophage lineage thwarted these hopes. These long-lived reservoirs pose a significant obstacle to HIV-1 eradication. This review focuses on the establishment and maintenance of HIV-1 latency in these two major targets for HIV-1 infection: CD4+ T cells and the monocyte-macrophage lineage. Understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the establishment, maintenance, and reactivation of HIV-1 latency in these reservoirs is crucial for the development of effective therapeutic interventions. Achieving complete viral eradication, the ultimate goal for clinicians, may be attainable through strategic interventions targeting both latently and actively infected cells. We propose that novel approaches, such as combining different types of proviral activators, may significantly reduce the size of latent HIV-1 reservoirs in patients on HAART.

title: Effects of Electro-Acupuncture Therapy on Post-Stroke Depression in Patients with Different Degrees of Motor Function Impairments: a Pilot Study
text:
The current study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of electro-acupuncture therapy in reducing post-stroke depression (PSD) and the potential interaction between motor function impairments and the treatment outcome. Twenty-eight PSD patients were assigned to either a good or poor motor function group based on their motor grade. The Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS), and Manual Muscle Test (MMT) were administered at various time points throughout the study, including the screening and initial phases, and at 4, 8, 12, and 16 weeks of daily electro-acupuncture treatment.
The results of the study showed that electro-acupuncture therapy significantly reduced PSD in both the good and poor motor function groups. However, the treatment effect was more pronounced in the good motor function group, with a greater reduction in depression symptoms compared to the poor motor function group. Notably, the degree of motor function impairment did not change throughout the study in either group.
The findings of this study suggest that electro-acupuncture therapy can be an effective treatment for PSD, and that the treatment outcome may vary depending on the level of motor function impairment. These results provide valuable insights into the potential benefits and limitations of electro-acupuncture therapy for PSD, and highlight the importance of considering individual patient factors when tailoring treatment strategies.

title: T cell receptor ligation induces the formation of dynamically regulated signaling assemblies
text: T cell antigen receptor (TCR) activation triggers a cascade of events that lead to the formation of signaling complexes, including tyrosine kinase activation, assembly of signaling complexes, and immune synapse formation. In this study, we used fluorescently tagged signaling proteins to investigate the kinetics and mechanics of signaling complex formation in live Jurkat leukemic T cells. Upon TCR engagement, T cells rapidly formed small, dynamic clusters that were enriched in TCR, phosphotyrosine, ZAP-70, LAT, Grb2, Gads, and SLP-76 proteins. These clusters were distinct from lipid rafts and were capable of inducing calcium elevations. Interestingly, LAT, Grb2, and Gads were transiently associated with the TCR, while ZAP-70-containing clusters persisted for over 20 minutes. However, photobleaching studies revealed that ZAP-70 continuously dissociated from and reassociated with these complexes. Furthermore, SLP-76 translocated to a perinuclear structure after clustering with the TCR. Our findings highlight the dynamic nature of signaling complexes and demonstrate that they can form rapidly (within seconds) after TCR engagement, without the need for lipid raft aggregation or the formation of a central TCR-rich cluster.

title: Developmental heterogeneity of cardiac fibroblasts does not predict pathological proliferation and activation.
text:
RATIONALE: Fibrosis in the heart is mediated in part by extracellular matrix-depositing fibroblasts. Although these mesenchymal cells are believed to have multiple embryonic origins, the functional implications of this heterogeneity are currently unknown.
OBJECTIVE: To identify and characterize cardiac fibroblasts using a panel of surface markers.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We used flow cytometry, epifluorescence microscopy, confocal microscopy, and transcriptional profiling (using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and RNA-seq) to identify and characterize cardiac fibroblasts. We found that Thy1(+)CD45(-)CD31(-)CD11b(-)Ter119(-) cells constitute the majority of cardiac fibroblasts. Using lineage tracing, transplantation studies, and parabiosis, we showed that most adult cardiac fibroblasts derive from the epicardium, a minority arise from endothelial cells, and a small fraction from Pax3-expressing cells. We did not observe the generation of cardiac fibroblasts from bone marrow or circulating cells. Interestingly, we found that proliferation rates of fibroblast subsets on injury were identical, and the relative abundance of each lineage remained the same after injury. Additionally, RNA-seq analysis revealed that Tie2-derived and Tbx18-derived fibroblasts within each operation group exhibit similar gene expression profiles.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that the cellular expansion of cardiac fibroblasts after transaortic constriction surgery is not restricted to any single developmental subset. The parallel proliferation and activation of a heterogeneous population of fibroblasts on pressure overload may indicate that common signaling mechanisms stimulate their pathological response.

title: Pre-eclampsia: connecting angiogenic and metabolic pathways.
text: Pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy-related hypertensive disorder, affects 5-8% of pregnancies worldwide. This review focuses on recent advances in pre-eclampsia research, specifically in the areas of angiogenesis and metabolism. We first explore the 'angiogenic imbalance' theory, which proposes that pre-eclampsia results from an imbalance of factors that promote or inhibit angiogenesis, such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase (sFlt1), 2-methoxyestradiol (2-ME), and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). Next, we examine the connection between pre-eclampsia and dysfunctional metabolism of homocysteine and placental glycogen. Our goal is to shed light on the complex relationships between angiogenesis and metabolism in pre-eclampsia, in the hope of updating or reconsidering existing models of pathogenesis.

title: Protein Lysine Acetylated/Deacetylated Enzymes and the Metabolism-Related Diseases
text: Lysine acetylation is a reversible post-translational modification, classified as an epigenetic phenomenon, where an acetyl group is transferred from acetyl-CoA to the amino group of a targeted protein, modulated by enzymes called acetyltransferases (HATs/KATs) and deacetylases (HDACs/KDACs). This modification regulates various metabolic processes, including fatty acid oxidation, Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, angiogenesis, and more. Disorders of lysine acetylation have been linked to metabolic complications such as obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. As research on proteomic acetylation continues to expand, lysine acetylation has been found to play a role in cellular immune status and degenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease and Huntington's disease. This review aims to summarize the current studies on lysine acetylation in metabolism modulation and its relationship to metabolism-related diseases, such as cardiovascular disease and fat metabolism disorders.

title: Differential Specificity of Endocrine FGF19 and FGF21 to FGFR1 and FGFR4 in Complex with KLB
text:
Background: Recent studies have suggested that beta-Klotho (KLB) and endocrine fibroblast growth factor 19 (FGF19) and 21 (FGF21) redirect fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) signaling to regulate metabolic homeostasis and suppress obesity and diabetes. However, the identity of the predominant metabolic tissue in which a major FGFR-KLB complex resides that critically mediates the differential actions and metabolism effects of FGF19 and FGF21 remains unclear.
Methodology/Principal Findings: To determine the receptor and tissue specificity of FGF21 in comparison to FGF19, we used direct, sensitive, and quantitative binding kinetics, and downstream signal transduction and expression of early response genes upon administration of FGF19 and FGF21 in mice. Our results showed that FGF21 binds FGFR1 with much higher affinity than FGFR4 in the presence of KLB; while FGF19 binds both FGFR1 and FGFR4 in the presence of KLB with comparable affinity. The interaction of FGF21 with FGFR4-KLB is very weak even at high concentrations and could be negligible at physiological concentrations. Both FGF19 and FGF21, but not FGF1, exhibited binding affinity to KLB. The binding of FGF1 is dependent on the presence of FGFRs. Both FGF19 and FGF21 were unable to displace the binding of FGF1, and conversely, FGF1 cannot displace the binding of FGF19 and FGF21. These results indicate that KLB is an indispensable mediator for the binding of FGF19 and FGF21 to FGFRs, which is not required for FGF1 binding.
Conclusions: Our results indicate that unlike FGF19, FGF21 is unable to bind FGFR4-KLB complex with affinity comparable to FGFR1-KLB, and therefore, at physiological concentrations, less likely to directly and significantly target the liver where FGFR4-KLB predominantly resides. However, both FGF21 and FGF19 have the potential to activate responses of primarily the adipose tissue where FGFR1-KLB resides.

title: Therapeutic efficacy of a multi-epitope vaccine against Helicobacter pylori infection in BALB/c mice model.
text:
Epitope vaccine represents a promising therapeutic option for vaccination against Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection. In this study, we constructed a multi-epitope vaccine, HUepi-LTB, consisting of five epitopes and the mucosal adjuvant E. coli heat-labile enterotoxin B subunit (LTB). We evaluated the therapeutic effect of HUepi-LTB against H. pylori infection in a BALB/c mouse model.
HUepi-LTB was constructed by expressing three Th epitopes from UreB and two B cell epitopes from UreB and HpaA in E. coli. Oral therapeutic immunization with HUepi-LTB significantly reduced H. pylori colonization compared to oral immunization with PBS, and the protection was found to be correlated with antigen-specific CD4+ T cells, IgG, and mucosal IgA antibody responses.
Our findings suggest that HUepi-LTB may be a promising vaccine candidate for controlling H. pylori infection.

title: DNA fragments in the blood plasma of cancer patients: quantitations and evidence for their origin from apoptotic and necrotic cells.
text: Increased levels of DNA fragments have frequently been observed in the blood plasma of cancer patients. Previous studies have shown that only a small fraction of the DNA in blood plasma is derived from cancer cells, but the source of the remaining circulating DNA is unknown. To investigate this, we used quantitative methylation-specific PCR to measure the fraction of plasma DNA derived from tumor cells in 30 unselected cancer patients. We found that the amount of tumor DNA in the plasma ranged from 3% to 93% of the total circulating DNA. We also investigated the potential sources of non-tumor DNA in the plasma and found that T-cell DNA made up only a small contribution in a few cases. To determine whether plasma DNA originates from apoptotic or necrotic cells, we treated cells with apoptotic (staurosporine) or necrotic (staurosporine plus oligomycin) agents in vitro and induced apoptotic (anti-CD95) or necrotic (acetaminophen) liver injury in mice. We found that increasing amounts of DNA were released into the supernatants of cells and the blood plasma of treated animals, and we were able to distinguish between apoptotic and necrotic plasma DNA using gel electrophoresis. The same characteristic patterns of DNA fragments were observed in plasma derived from different cancer patients, suggesting that apoptotic and necrotic cells are a major source of plasma DNA in cancer patients.

title: Pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of eptifibatide in patients with acute coronary syndromes: prospective analysis from PURSUIT.
text:
Background: Platelet deposition and aggregation play a crucial role in the development of ischemic complications in acute coronary syndromes (ACS). However, the pharmacodynamic effects of the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonist eptifibatide have been studied primarily in healthy individuals, leaving its effects in patients with ACS unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of eptifibatide on ex vivo platelet aggregation in patients with ACS.
Methods and Results: Forty-eight patients with ACS were randomly assigned to receive an intravenous bolus of eptifibatide (180 μg/kg) followed by a 72-hour infusion (n=48) or placebo (n=50). Plasma eptifibatide levels were measured at various time points during and after treatment, and ex vivo platelet aggregation was assessed using thrombin receptor agonist peptide (TRAP) and adenosine diphosphate (ADP) stimulation. The results showed that eptifibatide produced profound and prolonged inhibition of platelet aggregation during treatment, which partially recovered by 4 hours after the bolus. The inhibition of platelet aggregation was greater with TRAP stimulation than with ADP stimulation, and the aggregation response was greater in blood samples anticoagulated with citrate than with D-phenylalanyl-L-prolyl-L-arginine chloromethylketone (PPACK). Plasma eptifibatide levels were found to significantly correlate with receptor occupancy but not with inhibition of platelet aggregation.
Conclusions: The study demonstrates that eptifibatide inhibits platelet aggregation profoundly in patients with ACS, followed by a brief partial recovery. These findings enhance our understanding of the relationship between the pharmacodynamic and clinical effects of eptifibatide in such patients and may have important implications for its use in percutaneous interventions.

title: Proinflammatory cytokines underlying the inflammation of Crohn's disease.
text: The purpose of this review is to summarize the current understanding of the proinflammatory cytokines responsible for the inflammation associated with Crohn's disease and to explore the potential for developing therapies that target these cytokines. Recent research has shed new light on the roles of both T helper cell (Th)1 and Th17 responses in the pathogenesis of Crohn's disease. Initial studies suggested that an interleukin-12-driven Th1 response was the primary cause of inflammation in Crohn's disease, leading to the production of interferon-gamma. However, more recent studies in mouse models have shown that a Th17 response is the main driver of inflammation through the production of interleukin-17. A more balanced view is now emerging, suggesting that interferon-gamma may arise from both Th1 and Th17-mediated responses at different stages of the inflammatory process. These findings support the idea that anti-interleukin-12p40, an antibody that inhibits both Th1 and Th17 responses, is the most potent anticytokine for treating Crohn's disease.

title: STATISTICAL METHODS FOR ASSESSING AGREEMENT BETWEEN TWO METHODS OF CLINICAL MEASUREMENT
text: In medical measurements, comparing a new technique with an established one is crucial to determine if they are compatible. However, many researchers make mistakes when analyzing these comparisons, relying excessively on correlation coefficients. This approach is misleading and can lead to incorrect conclusions. A better alternative is to use graphical techniques and simple calculations, which provide a more accurate assessment of the comparison. Additionally, this analysis is closely related to the evaluation of repeatability, which is an essential aspect of medical measurements.

title: The multidrug ABC transporter BmrC/BmrD of Bacillus subtilis is regulated via a ribosome-mediated transcriptional attenuation mechanism
text: The expression of specific drug transporters in response to antibiotic pressure is a crucial aspect of the development of multidrug resistance in bacteria, posing a significant threat to human health. To gain insights into the underlying regulatory mechanisms, we investigated the transcriptional activation of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter BmrC/BmrD in the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis. Using promoter-GFP fusions and live cell array technology, we found that bmrCD expression is temporally controlled and only occurs during the late-exponential and stationary growth stages, regardless of the timing of the antibiotic challenge. We discovered that this is due to the tight transcriptional control by the transition state regulator AbrB. Furthermore, our results showed that the bmrCD genes are co-transcribed with bmrB (yheJ), a small open reading frame located upstream of bmrC, which harbors three alternative stem-loop structures. These stem-loops are essential for antibiotic-induced bmrCD transcription. Interestingly, the antibiotic-induced bmrCD expression requires the translation of bmrB, which suggests that BmrB serves as a regulatory leader peptide. Our findings demonstrate for the first time that a ribosome-mediated transcriptional attenuation mechanism controls the expression of a multidrug ABC transporter.

title: The neural crest is a source of mesenchymal stem cells with specialized hematopoietic stem cell niche function
text:
Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and osteolineage cells play a crucial role in the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche in the bone marrow of long bones. However, their developmental relationships are not well understood. In this study, we investigate the distinct functions of different MSC populations in the developing marrow of long bones.
Proliferative mesoderm-derived nestin(-) MSCs are involved in fetal skeletogenesis and lose their MSC activity shortly after birth. In contrast, quiescent neural crest-derived nestin(+) cells maintain their MSC activity and differentiate into HSC niche-forming MSCs, which help establish the HSC niche by secreting Cxcl12. The migration of these cells to the bone marrow requires the ErbB3 receptor.
Interestingly, the neonatal Nestin-GFP(+) Pdgfrα(-) cell population also contains Schwann cell precursors, but does not comprise mature Schwann cells. This suggests that in the developing bone marrow HSC niche-forming MSCs share a common origin with sympathetic peripheral neurons and glial cells, and that ontogenically distinct MSCs have non-overlapping functions in endochondrogenesis and HSC niche formation.
In summary, our findings demonstrate that different MSC populations in the developing marrow of long bones have distinct functions, and that these functions are developmentally regulated. Understanding the developmental relationships between MSCs and other cell types in the HSC niche is crucial for the development of therapeutic strategies to enhance HSC function and promote hematopoiesis.

title: Hotspots of aberrant epigenomic reprogramming in human induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) hold great promise for regenerative medicine and research on disease and development. The process of somatic cell reprogramming involves reconfiguring epigenetic marks, giving iPSCs characteristics similar to embryonic stem (ES) cells. However, it is unknown how comprehensive the restoration of ES-cell-like DNA methylation patterns is across the genome. In this study, we present the first whole-genome profiles of DNA methylation at single-base resolution for five human iPSC lines, as well as methylomes of ES cells, somatic cells, and differentiated iPSCs and ES cells. Our findings reveal significant variability in iPSC reprogramming, including somatic memory and aberrant reprogramming of DNA methylation. iPSCs share large-scale differentially methylated regions near centromeres and telomeres that exhibit incomplete reprogramming of non-CG methylation, as well as differences in CG methylation and histone modifications. Moreover, we find that errors in reprogramming CG methylation are transmitted at a high frequency during differentiation, providing an iPSC reprogramming signature that persists after differentiation.

title: Inheritance of coronary artery disease in men: an analysis of the role of the Y chromosome
text:
Background: Coronary artery disease (CAD) affects men more frequently than women, and this disparity has been observed in various populations. To investigate the potential role of the Y chromosome in this phenomenon, we genotyped 11 markers in the male-specific region of the Y chromosome in 3233 unrelated British men from three cohorts. We then traced the Y chromosome back to one of 13 identified haplogroups and examined the association between these haplogroups and the risk of CAD in cross-sectional and prospective studies.
Methods: We genotyped 11 markers in the male-specific region of the Y chromosome in 3233 biologically unrelated British men from the British Heart Foundation Family Heart Study (BHF-FHS), West of Scotland Coronary Prevention Study (WOSCOPS), and Cardiogenics Study. Using these data, we identified 13 haplogroups and tracked the Y chromosome back to each of these haplogroups. We then examined the association between each haplogroup and the risk of CAD in cross-sectional and prospective studies. Finally, we performed functional analysis of Y chromosome effects on monocyte and macrophage transcriptome in British men from the Cardiogenics Study.
Findings: Of the 13 identified haplogroups, two (R1b1b2 and I) accounted for approximately 90% of Y chromosome variants among British men. Carriers of haplogroup I had a 50% higher age-adjusted risk of CAD compared to men with other Y chromosome lineages in BHF-FHS (odds ratio 1.75, 95% CI 1.20-2.54, p=0.004), WOSCOPS (1.45, 1.08-1.95, p=0.012), and joint analysis of both populations (1.56, 1.24-1.97, p=0.0002). The association between haplogroup I and increased risk of CAD was independent of traditional cardiovascular and socioeconomic risk factors. Analysis of macrophage transcriptome in the Cardiogenics Study revealed that 19 molecular pathways showing strong differential expression between men with haplogroup I and other lineages of the Y chromosome were interconnected by common genes related to inflammation and immunity, and some of them have a strong relevance to atherosclerosis.
Interpretation: Our findings suggest that the human Y chromosome is associated with the risk of CAD in men of European ancestry, possibly through interactions of immunity and inflammation. These findings have important implications for the understanding of the underlying mechanisms of CAD and may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies.
Funding: This study was supported by the British Heart Foundation, UK National Institute for Health Research, LEW Carty Charitable Fund, National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia, European Union 6th Framework Programme, and Wellcome Trust.

title: Cytoscape 2.8: new features for data integration and network visualization
text:
Cytoscape is a widely utilized bioinformatics software package for visualizing and integrating biological networks. Version 2.8 introduces two significant new features—Custom Node Graphics and Attribute Equations—which can be combined to significantly enhance Cytoscape's data integration and visualization capabilities. Custom Node Graphics enable the projection of an image onto a node, including dynamically generated or remote images. Attribute Equations provide Cytoscape with spreadsheet-like functionality, allowing the value of an attribute to be computed dynamically as a function of other attributes and network properties.
Cytoscape is a desktop Java application released under the Library Gnu Public License (LGPL). Binary install bundles and source code for Cytoscape 2.8 are available for download from the official Cytoscape website.

title: Detection of Histone Modifications at Specific Gene Loci in Single Cells in Histological Sections
text: Chromatin immunoprecipitation assays have significantly advanced our understanding of the role of histone modifications in gene regulation. However, they are limited in their ability to analyze gene expression at the single-cell level, which can lead to confusion when studying heterogeneous cell populations. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel method that enables visualization of histone modifications at specific genomic loci with single-cell resolution in formaldehyde-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections. This approach combines in situ hybridization and proximity ligation assays, allowing us to study the distribution of histone modifications in individual cells. Our results demonstrate that dimethylation of lysine 4 of histone H3 (H3K4me2) at the MYH11 locus is specifically enriched in smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in both human and mouse tissue sections. Moreover, we found that this mark persists even in SMCs that have undergone phenotypic modulation in atherosclerotic lesions, despite the lack of detectable expression of SMC marker genes. This method has the potential to be applied broadly in the study of epigenetic mechanisms in complex multicellular tissues during development and disease.

title: Mechanistic characterization of the sulfur-relay system for eukaryotic 2-thiouridine biogenesis at tRNA wobble positions
text: The modification of tRNAs, specifically 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl-2-thiouridine (mcm(5)s(2)U), is crucial for the proper decoding of NNR codons in eukaryotes. The 2-thio group in mcm(5)s(2)U confers conformational rigidity by stabilizing the C3'-endo ribose puckering, ensuring accurate codon-anticodon pairing. We have identified five genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, YIL008w (URM1), YHR111w (UBA4), YOR251c (TUM1), YNL119w (NCS2) and YGL211w (NCS6), that are essential for the 2-thiolation of mcm(5)s(2)U. An in vitro sulfur transfer experiment revealed that Tum1p stimulates the cysteine desulfurase of Nfs1p and accepts persulfide sulfurs from Nfs1p. URM1 is a ubiquitin-related modifier, and UBA4 is an E1-like enzyme involved in protein urmylation. The carboxy-terminus of Urm1p is activated as an acyl-adenylate (-COAMP), then thiocarboxylated (-COSH) by Uba4p. The activated thiocarboxylate can be utilized in the subsequent reactions for 2-thiouridine formation, mediated by Ncs2p/Ncs6p. We successfully reconstituted the 2-thiouridine formation in vitro using recombinant proteins, revealing that this process shares a common pathway and chemical reactions with protein urmylation. The sulfur flow of eukaryotic 2-thiouridine formation is distinct from the bacterial sulfur-relay system, which is based on persulfide chemistry.

title: High prevalence of asthma in cross country skiers.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the prevalence of asthma symptoms and bronchial hyperresponsiveness in elite cross-country skiers in Sweden compared to non-skiers, and to assess changes in these measures during the year.
Design:
Cross-sectional study conducted during the winter ski season and summer.
Setting:
Six ski clubs for élite skiers in two different areas of Sweden (total 47 skiers).
Subjects:
42 élite cross-country skiers and 29 non-skiing referents.
Main Outcome Measures:
Bronchial responsiveness, asthma symptoms, and lung function.
Results:
Bronchial responsiveness was significantly higher and asthma symptoms more prevalent in the skiers than in the referents. There was no difference in bronchial responsiveness within either group between winter and summer. 15 of the 42 skiers used antiasthmatic drugs regularly, and 23 had a combination of asthma symptoms and hyperresponsive airways or physician-diagnosed asthma, or both. Altogether 33 skiers had symptoms of asthma or bronchial hyperresponsiveness. One of the referents had symptoms of asthma and bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and none used antiasthmatic drugs regularly.
Conclusions:
Asthma, asthma-like symptoms, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness are significantly more common in elite cross-country skiers than in the general population and non-skiers. Strenuous exercise at low temperatures involving breathing large volumes of cold air is the most likely explanation for persistent asthma in skiers.

title: Characterization of biochemical properties of Bacillus subtilis RecQ helicase.
text: RecQ family helicases act as protectors of the genome. Unlike Escherichia coli, the Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis bacterium has two RecQ-like homologues, RecQ[Bs] and RecS, which are essential for repairing DNA double-strand breaks. RecQ[Bs] also ensures a smooth progression of the cell cycle by binding to forked DNA. In this study, we present the first biochemical analysis of recombinant RecQ[Bs]. RecQ[Bs] weakly binds to single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and blunt-ended double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), but strongly to forked dsDNA. The protein exhibits DNA-stimulated ATPase activity and ATP- and Mg(2+)-dependent DNA helicase activity with a 3' → 5' polarity. Molecular modeling reveals that RecQ[Bs] shares high sequence and structure similarity with E. coli RecQ. Interestingly, RecQ[Bs] resembles truncated Saccharomyces cerevisiae Sgs1 and human RecQ helicases more than RecQ[Ec] in its enzymatic activities. RecQ[Bs] unwinds forked dsDNA and DNA duplexes with a 3'-overhang, but is inactive on blunt-ended dsDNA and 5'-overhung duplexes. The protein also unwinds blunt-ended DNA with structural features, including nicks, gaps, 5'-flaps, Kappa joints, synthetic replication forks, and Holliday junctions. These findings shed light on the possible functions of RecQ[Bs] in maintaining genomic stability.

title: SOD1 Integrates Signals from Oxygen and Glucose to Repress Respiration
text: Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1) is an abundant enzyme that has been extensively studied as a regulator of antioxidant defense. Using the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model organism, our research has uncovered a novel mechanism by which SOD1 regulates respiration. Specifically, we have found that SOD1 signals from oxygen and glucose to repress respiration by stabilizing two casein kinase 1-gamma (CK1γ) homologs, Yck1p and Yck2p, which are essential for respiratory repression. Our findings indicate that SOD1 binds a C-terminal degron in Yck1p/Yck2p and promotes kinase stability by catalyzing superoxide conversion to peroxide. Remarkably, similar effects of SOD1 on CK1γ stability were observed in mammalian cells and a human cell line, suggesting that this signaling pathway may be conserved across species. These findings may provide important insights into how rapidly proliferating cells and many cancers accomplish glucose-mediated repression of respiration in favor of aerobic glycolysis.

title: The prognostic impact of the platelet distribution width-to-platelet count ratio in patients with breast cancer
text: In this retrospective analysis of 275 patients with breast cancer, we investigated the prognostic value of platelet volume indices (PVIs) in predicting disease-free survival (DFS). PVIs, including platelet distribution width (PDW), mean platelet volume (MPV), and platelet distribution width-to-platelet count ratio (PDW/P), were compared with clinicopathological variables and identified independent indicators associated with DFS using the Cox proportional hazards model. Our findings revealed that an elevated PDW/P was significantly correlated with age and HER2 status, and univariate analysis revealed that elevated PDW, MPV, and PDW/P, as well as tumor size, nuclear grade, and lymph node involvement, were associated with inferior DFS rates. On multivariate analysis, a large tumor size and elevated PDW/P were identified as significant prognostic factors for DFS, with hazard ratios of 3.24 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.24-8.47) and 2.99 (95% CI: 1.18-7.57), respectively (p<0.05). Our study is the first to demonstrate that an elevated PDW/P significantly reduces DFS in patients with breast carcinoma. The simplicity and relatively low cost of measuring PVIs using routine blood counts make it an attractive biomarker for improving risk assessment in breast cancer patients.

title: Persistent LCMV infection is controlled by blockade of type I interferon signaling.
text: During persistent viral infections, there is a correlation between various immune responses and disease progression. Specifically, elevated interferon signature, chronic immune activation, negative immune regulator expression, and lymphoid tissue destruction are all linked to disease progression. In a study using mice infected with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, we found that blocking type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling using an IFN-I receptor neutralizing antibody led to a reduction in immune system activation, decreased expression of negative immune regulatory molecules, and restored lymphoid architecture. Importantly, this effect was observed both before and after the establishment of persistent virus infection, and was found to be CD4 T cell-dependent. These findings provide strong evidence for a direct causal link between IFN-I signaling, immune activation, negative immune regulator expression, lymphoid tissue disorganization, and virus persistence. Our results suggest that targeting IFN-I may be a promising strategy for controlling persistent virus infections.

title: Lam6 Regulates the Extent of Contacts between Organelles
text: In eukaryotic cells, communication between organelles is essential for proper functioning as a unified unit. One key means of communication is through close proximity at membrane contact sites, allowing for the exchange of lipids and small molecules between organelles. These contact sites are dynamic and can change in response to environmental or cellular cues, but the regulatory mechanisms behind this are not well understood. Our study sheds light on this by revealing that the Saccharomyces cerevisiae protein Lam6 is involved in several central contact sites, including ERMES (ER/mitochondria encounter structure), vCLAMP (vacuole and mitochondria patch), and NVJ (nuclear vacuolar junction). We found that Lam6 is necessary for the expansion of contact sites under normal conditions and plays a crucial role in coordinating contact site size. Interestingly, Lam6 is part of a larger protein family and is conserved in vertebrates, suggesting that our findings may have broader implications for understanding the mechanisms of organelle communication.

title: Endocrine regulation of human fetal growth: the role of the mother, placenta, and fetus.
text: The environment in which the fetus develops plays a crucial role in its survival and long-term health. The growth and development of the fetus are regulated by complex interactions between the mother, placenta, and fetus. The mother provides the fetus with essential nutrients and oxygen through the placenta, while the fetus influences the mother's metabolism through the production of hormones that regulate nutrient supply. The placenta acts as a vital interface between the mother and fetus, regulating fetal growth through the production and metabolism of growth-promoting hormones such as insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) and glucocorticoids. Proper trophoblast invasion in early pregnancy and increased uteroplacental blood flow are essential for adequate fetal growth and development. The placenta can also respond to fetal endocrine signals to enhance nutrient transport by increasing placental growth, activating transport systems, and producing hormones that modulate maternal physiology and behavior. Poor fetal growth can have severe short-term and long-term consequences, including increased mortality and morbidity. The endocrine regulation of fetal growth involves intricate interactions between the mother, placenta, and fetus, which can have lasting effects on the fetus's physiology.

title: Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition contributes to cardiac fibrosis
text: Cardiac fibrosis, characterized by an excessive buildup of extracellular matrix, is often accompanied by a decrease in the number of microvasculature and disruption of normal myocardial structures. The origin of the fibroblasts responsible for this excessive matrix deposition is currently unknown, and there are no specific anti-fibrotic therapies available. Our study reveals that cardiac fibrosis is actually caused by the transformation of endothelial cells into fibroblasts through an endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) process, similar to the events that occur during the formation of the atrioventricular cushion in the embryonic heart. We found that transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) induces endothelial cells to undergo EndMT, while bone morphogenic protein 7 (BMP-7) preserves the endothelial phenotype. Importantly, we showed that the systemic administration of recombinant human BMP-7 (rhBMP-7) significantly inhibited EndMT and the progression of cardiac fibrosis in mouse models of pressure overload and chronic allograft rejection. Our findings suggest that EndMT plays a crucial role in the progression of cardiac fibrosis and that rhBMP-7 may be a potential therapeutic strategy to inhibit EndMT and slow down the progression of chronic heart disease associated with fibrosis.

title: Coupled local translation and degradation regulate growth cone collapse
text: Local protein synthesis plays a crucial role in mediating axonal responses to Semaphorin3A (Sema3A) and other guidance cues. However, only a subset of the axonal proteome is produced locally, while most proteins are transported from the soma. The reason for this selective local synthesis is still unclear. Our study reveals that local protein synthesis and degradation are intimately linked in growth cones. We find that growth cones exhibit high levels of ubiquitination, and local signaling pathways trigger the ubiquitination and degradation of RhoA, a key mediator of Sema3A-induced growth cone collapse. Inhibiting RhoA degradation is sufficient to eliminate the need for local protein synthesis in Sema3A-induced growth cone collapse. Additionally, we discover that growth cones are the primary targets of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and local protein degradation is a crucial feature of growth cones, requiring continuous replenishment of proteins through local translation to maintain growth cone responses.

title: Cdk11 is a RanGTP-dependent microtubule stabilization factor that regulates spindle assembly rate
text: Production of Ran-guanosine triphosphate (GTP) near chromosomes triggers local microtubule (MT) nucleation and stabilization. The nuclear protein TPX2 is essential for RanGTP-mediated MT nucleation. To identify the MT stabilizer, we purified NLS (nuclear localization signal)-containing proteins from Xenopus laevis egg extracts. This NLS protein fraction harbors the MT stabilization activity. Following purification, we employed mass spectrometry to detect proteins in the active fractions, including cyclin-dependent kinase 11 (Cdk11). Cdk11 localizes on spindle poles and MTs in Xenopus cell cultures and egg extracts. Recombinant Cdk11 exhibits RanGTP-dependent MT stabilization activity, whereas a kinase-dead mutant lacks this function. Inactivation of Cdk11 in egg extracts abrogates RanGTP-dependent MT stabilization and significantly reduces the spindle assembly rate. Simultaneous depletion of TPX2 completely inhibits centrosome-dependent spindle assembly. Our findings indicate that Cdk11 is responsible for RanGTP-dependent MT stabilization near chromosomes, and this local stabilization is crucial for maintaining normal spindle assembly and function.

title: Population dynamics of a pathogen: the conundrum of vivax malaria
text: Building a mathematical model of population dynamics of pathogens within their host involves considering factors similar to those in ecology, as pathogens can prey on cells in the host. However, within the multicellular host, infected cell types are integrated with other cellular systems that intervene in the infection process. For example, immune responses attempt to detect and eliminate or contain pathogens, while homeostatic mechanisms try to compensate for cell loss. This review focuses on modeling applied to malarias, diseases caused by single-celled eukaryote parasites that infect red blood cells, with a particular emphasis on vivax malaria, a disease often thought to be mild (if sometimes incapacitating) due to the parasite's limited attack on red blood cells. However, through mathematical modeling, I will argue that depletion of this cell pool can have severe consequences for the host if the parasite's growth is not effectively checked by host immune responses. Additionally, modeling can help elucidate recent field observations that suggest vivax malaria may be more dangerous than previously thought.

title: Identification and analysis of ribonuclease P and MRP RNA in a broad range of eukaryotes
text:
Ribonucleoprotein complexes RNases P and MRP are essential for the processing of transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA), respectively. The RNA subunits of these enzymes share a structural similarity and play a crucial role in the catalytic reaction. Both RNAs possess a highly conserved helical region, P4, which is vital for the enzymatic reaction.
Using a bioinformatics approach based on conserved elements, we analyzed available genomic sequences of eukaryotic organisms and identified a large number of novel nuclear RNase P and MRP RNA genes. For instance, this investigation increases the number of known MRP RNA sequences by a factor of three. We present secondary structure models of many of the predicted RNAs. Although all sequences are able to fold into the consensus secondary structure of P and MRP RNAs, a notable variation in size is observed, ranging from a 160-nt Nosema locustae MRP RNA to larger RNAs, such as a 696-nt Plasmodium knowlesi P RNA. The P and MRP RNA genes are often found in tandem in some protists, further highlighting the close evolutionary relationship between these RNAs.

title: Calcium absorption varies within the reference range for serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
text:
Background: Calcium absorption is often impaired when vitamin D levels are low, but the exact level of vitamin D repletion needed to fully normalize absorption is unknown for humans.
Objective: To determine the level of vitamin D repletion needed to fully normalize calcium absorption in humans using pharmacokinetic methods and commercially available calcium supplements.
Design: Two experiments were conducted one year apart in the spring, with participants receiving either 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD) pretreatment or no pretreatment.
Methods: Participants received a 500 mg oral calcium load as part of a standard low-calcium breakfast, and a low-calcium lunch was provided at mid-day. Blood samples were taken fasting and at frequent intervals for 10-12 hours after the load to measure serum total calcium levels. The area under the curve (AUC) for the load-induced increment in serum total calcium was used to estimate relative calcium absorption at the two 25OHD concentrations.
Results: The AUC(9) +/- SEM was 3.63 mg/hr/dL +/- 0.234 in participants pretreated with 25OHD and 2.20 +/- 0.240 in those not pretreated (P < 0.001). In brief, calcium absorption was 65% higher at serum 25OHD levels averaging 86.5 nmol/L than at levels averaging 50 nmol/L (both values within the nominal reference range for this analyte).
Conclusions: Although the mean serum 25OHD level in the experiment without supplementation was within the current reference ranges, calcium absorptive performance at 50 nmol/L was significantly reduced relative to that at a mean 25OHD level of 86 nmol/L. Therefore, individuals with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels at the low end of the current reference ranges may not be getting the full benefit from their calcium intake. We conclude that the lower end of the current reference range is set too low.

title: Evolution of virulence in opportunistic pathogens: generalism, plasticity, and control
text: Standard theories of virulence evolution propose that virulence factors are maintained because they enhance parasitic exploitation and transmission between hosts, leading to increased growth and fitness. However, a growing body of research has challenged this view, revealing that many opportunistic pathogens (OPs) do not conform to these assumptions. Instead, virulence factors are often maintained due to their advantages in non-parasitic contexts. In this review, we re-examine virulence evolution theory in the context of OPs and emphasize the importance of considering environments outside the focal virulence site. We demonstrate that virulence selection is influenced by correlations between these external and focal settings, and identify key drivers of these correlations, including generalist strategies and phenotypic plasticity. Finally, we highlight the remaining theoretical and empirical challenges that must be addressed to gain a more complete understanding of OPs.

title: Genome-Wide Profiling of H3K56 Acetylation and Transcription Factor Binding Sites in Human Adipocytes
text:
The growing prevalence of obesity and metabolic disorders underscores the need for a deeper understanding of adipocyte biology, particularly in regards to transcriptional regulation. Transcription factor binding and histone modifications are crucial factors influencing transcriptional outcomes, yet there is a lack of data on these epigenetic marks in human adipocytes. To address this gap, we investigated H3K56 acetylation sites in human adipocytes derived from mesenchymal stem cells. Our findings revealed that nearly half of the genome exhibits H3K56 acetylation, with the highest levels associated with transcription factors and genes involved in adipokine signaling and Type II Diabetes pathways.
To identify the transcription factors that recruit acetyltransferases and deacetylases to these regions, we analyzed the DNA sequences near H3K56 acetylated regions and found an enrichment of the E2F recognition sequence. Using chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by high-throughput sequencing, we confirmed that genes bound by E2F4, HSF-1, and C/EBPα have higher than expected levels of H3K56 acetylation, and that the transcription factor binding sites and acetylation sites often but rarely overlap. Additionally, we discovered a significant difference in the bound targets of C/EBPα in 3T3-L1 and human adipocytes, highlighting the need for species-specific epigenetic and transcription factor binding site maps. This study provides the first genome-wide profile of H3K56 acetylation, E2F4, C/EBPα, and HSF-1 binding in human adipocytes, and will serve as a valuable resource for elucidating the complex regulatory mechanisms governing adipocyte transcriptional regulation.

title: Detecting and characterizing circular RNAs
text: In the early 1990s, Circular RNA (circRNA) transcripts were first identified, yet knowledge of these species has remained limited due to the challenges associated with studying them through traditional methods of RNA analysis. However, recent advances in bioinformatic approaches, combined with biochemical enrichment strategies and deep sequencing, have enabled comprehensive studies of circRNAs. These studies have revealed a vast number of endogenous circRNAs in mammalian cells, with some exhibiting high abundance and conservation across species. Emerging evidence suggests that certain circRNAs may regulate microRNA (miRNA) function, and roles in transcriptional control have also been proposed. As such, the study of these noncoding RNAs holds significant potential for both therapeutic and research applications. Nevertheless, the primary challenge for the field will be to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms and functional roles of circRNAs.

title: A classification of unstable angina revisited.
text: Unstable angina is a critical phase of coronary heart disease characterized by unpredictable symptoms and varying prognosis. A decade ago, a clinical classification system was introduced based on symptoms to predict patient outcomes. This system was validated through prospective studies that correlated with angiographic and histological findings. It has been used in numerous large clinical trials. Recent research has elucidated the pathophysiological roles of platelet activation and inflammation in unstable angina, leading to the identification of improved markers of myocardial injury, acute-phase proteins, and hemostatic markers that predict clinical outcomes. Specifically, cardiac-specific troponin T and troponin I have been shown to be the best predictors of early risk in patients with angina at rest. Accordingly, it is suggested that the original classification be expanded by subclassifying one large group of unstable angina patients, those with angina at rest within the past 48 hours (class IIIB), into troponin-positive (T(pos)) and troponin-negative (T(neg)) patients. The 30-day risk of death and myocardial infarction is up to 20% in class IIIB-T(pos) patients but less than 2% in class IIIB-T(neg) patients. Initial results suggest that troponins can function as surrogate markers for thrombus formation and can guide therapy with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonists or low-molecular-weight heparins. These findings provide additional impetus for incorporating the measurement of these markers into the clinical classification and represent a novel approach to treating high-risk patients.

title: Alcohol Intake and Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review Implementing a Mendelian Randomization Approach
text:
BACKGROUND: Alcohol consumption has been identified as a modifiable risk factor for hypertension, but observational studies are prone to confounding by other lifestyle and demographic factors, while clinical trials are challenging to implement and have limited follow-up time. To provide robust evidence on the association between alcohol consumption and hypertension, we employed Mendelian randomization using a common genetic variant in aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2). ALDH2 encodes a key enzyme involved in alcohol metabolism, and individuals homozygous for the null variant (ALDH2*2*2) experience adverse symptoms when consuming alcohol, leading to lower alcohol consumption compared to wild-type homozygotes (ALDH2*1*1) or heterozygotes (surrogate for moderate drinkers). We hypothesized that this genetic variant may influence the risk of hypertension by affecting alcohol consumption behavior.
METHODS AND FINDINGS: We conducted fixed-effect meta-analyses of the ALDH2 genotype with blood pressure (n = 7,658) and hypertension (n = 4,219) using studies identified through a systematic review. In males, we found an overall odds ratio of 2.42 (95% CI 1.66-3.55, p = 4.8 x 10(-6)) for hypertension comparing ALDH2*1*1 with ALDH2*2*2 homozygotes and an odds ratio of 1.72 (95% CI 1.17-2.52, p = 0.006) comparing heterozygotes (surrogate for moderate drinkers) with ALDH2*2*2 homozygotes. Additionally, we found that systolic blood pressure was 7.44 mmHg (95% CI 5.39-9.49, p = 1.1 x 10(-12)) higher among ALDH2*1*1 than among ALDH2*2*2 homozygotes, and 4.24 mmHg (95% CI 2.18-6.31, p = 0.00005) higher among heterozygotes than among ALDH2*2*2 homozygotes.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide strong evidence that alcohol consumption has a significant impact on blood pressure and the risk of hypertension. Our study highlights the potential of Mendelian randomization as a powerful tool for investigating the relationship between modifiable lifestyle factors and disease risk.

title: Rapid and Sensitive RT-QuIC Detection of Human Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease Using Cerebrospinal Fluid
text:
Rapid and accurate diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is crucial for assessing patient care options and transmission risks. Currently, real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) assays of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and nasal-brushing specimens can identify CJD with varying degrees of sensitivity and specificity, taking 2.5 to 5 days. Here, we describe an improved RT-QuIC assay that can identify positive CSF samples within 4 to 14 hours with better analytical sensitivity. In a study of 11 CJD patients, 10 were positive using the new assay, while 7 were positive using the previous conditions. A total of 46 of 48 CSF samples from sporadic CJD patients were positive, while all 39 non-CJD patients were negative, giving 95.8% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity. This second-generation RT-QuIC assay significantly improves the speed and sensitivity of detecting prion seeds in CSF specimens from CJD patients, enhancing prospects for rapid and accurate ante mortem CJD diagnosis.
The early and accurate diagnosis of neurodegenerative protein misfolding diseases, such as CJD, is a long-standing challenge. This issue is particularly important with prion diseases, as they are deadly, transmissible, and resistant to decontamination. The recently developed RT-QuIC test has emerged as a highly sensitive and specific diagnostic tool for CJD, but its application can miss 11 to 23% of CJD cases due to its longer detection time. Our study demonstrates a significant improvement in RT-QuIC analysis of human CSF, allowing for the discrimination of CJD and non-CJD patients in a matter of hours rather than days with enhanced sensitivity. These findings provide a prototype for tests for misfolded protein aggregates that cause various amyloid diseases, such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and tauopathies, with broader implications for the diagnosis of these debilitating conditions.

title: Wortmannin, a phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitor, selectively enhances cytotoxicity of receptor-directed-toxin chimeras in vitro and in vivo.
text:
Background:
The resistance of some neoplastic cell lines to treatment with ligand-toxin chimeras has been attributed to an increased rate of lysosomal uptake and degradation following endocytosis of the chimera-receptor complex. Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) activity has been identified as a key player in intracellular trafficking, particularly from endosomes to lysosomes. Therefore, we hypothesized that co-exposing cells to a PI3K inhibitor might enhance the cytotoxicity of ligand-toxin chimeras.
Methods:
In vitro, the cytotoxicity of five receptor-directed toxin chimeras (bFGF-SAP, bFGF-PE, aFGF-PE, HBEGF-SAP, and bFGF-gelonin) and an immunotoxin (11A8-SAP) was examined in the presence or absence of the PI3K inhibitor wortmannin against a panel of human neoplastic cell lines (SK-MEL-5, PA-1, DU145, and MCF-7). In vivo, the antitumor activity of a treatment regimen combining wortmannin (1 or 2 mg/kg i.p.) and bFGF-SAP (10 micrograms/kg i.v.) once a week for 4 weeks was evaluated compared to administration of each agent alone in C3H/HeN mice implanted with the FSallC murine fibrosarcoma.
Results:
At concentrations greater than the reported Ki for PI3K inhibition (1-10 microM), wortmannin enhanced the cytotoxicity of saporin or gelonin chimeras, but produced subadditive cytotoxicity when combined with Pseudomonas exotoxin chimeras. When low nanomolar concentrations selective for PI3K inhibition (5-100 nM) were examined for effects on one receptor-directed toxin chimera, wortmannin dramatically enhanced bFGF-SAP cytotoxicity in three of the four cell lines. A different PI3K inhibitor, LY294002 (Ki approximately 1 microM), however, failed to potentiate bFGF-SAP. When administered to mice, wortmannin combined with bFGF-SAP resulted in a significant decrease in tumor volumes compared to vehicle-treated controls that was not observed in mice treated with either agent alone.
Conclusions:
Taken together, these results suggest that although wortmannin increases the cytotoxic efficacy of some receptor-directed chimeras, potentiation may occur through an alternative pathway not involving PI3K inhibition.

title: Chronic stress, glucocorticoid receptor resistance, inflammation, and disease risk.
text: We propose a model where chronic stress leads to glucocorticoid receptor resistance (GCR), which in turn hinders the body's ability to regulate inflammation. To test this model, we conducted two studies. In study 1, we assessed stressful life events, GCR, and various control variables, including baseline antibody to the challenge virus, age, body mass index (BMI), season, race, sex, education, and virus type, in 276 healthy adult volunteers. After they were quarantined and exposed to one of two rhinoviruses, we followed them for 5 days to assess viral isolation and symptoms of a common cold. In study 2, we assessed the same control variables and GCR in 79 subjects who were subsequently exposed to a rhinovirus and monitored at baseline and for 5 days after viral challenge for the production of local (in nasal secretions) proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6). Our findings provide support for the model, as we found that individuals with recent exposure to a long-term threatening stressful experience had lower GCR, which in turn reduced their risk of developing a cold. In study 2, we found that higher GCR levels among infected subjects were associated with increased production of local proinflammatory cytokines. These findings suggest that chronic stress may play a key role in the onset and progression of various diseases by disrupting the body's ability to regulate inflammation.

title: Pituitary Adenylate Cyclase-Activating Polypeptide (PACAP), a Neuron-Derived Peptide Regulating Glial Glutamate Transport and Metabolism
text:
In the brain, glutamatergic neurotransmission is primarily terminated through the rapid uptake of synaptically released glutamate into astrocytes, which is mediated by the Na+-dependent glutamate transporters GLT-1 and GLAST. These transporters are then converted into glutamine by the enzyme glutamine synthetase (GS). Recent studies have shown that various factors can alter glial glutamate uptake through post-translational modifications of glutamate transporters. However, the only known factor that affects the expression of glial glutamate transporters and GS is the coculturing of glia with neurons.
We now demonstrate that neurons regulate glial glutamate turnover through pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP). In the cerebral cortex, PACAP is produced by neurons and specifically affects a subpopulation of astroglia involved in glutamate turnover. Exposure of astroglia to PACAP increases the maximal velocity of [(3)H]glutamate uptake by promoting the expression of GLT-1, GLAST, and GS.
