In this study, we sequenced RNA from 69 lymphoblastoid cell lines derived from unrelated Nigerian individuals that have been extensively genotyped by the International HapMap Project. By combining data from all individuals, we generated a comprehensive map of the transcriptional landscape of these cells, revealing extensive use of unannotated untranslated regions and over 100 novel putative protein-coding exons.
Using the genotypes from the HapMap project, we identified over a thousand genes where genetic variation influences overall expression levels or splicing. Our findings demonstrate that eQTLs near genes typically act through a mechanism involving allele-specific expression, and that variation that affects the inclusion of an exon is enriched within and near the consensus splice sites.
Our results highlight the power of high-throughput sequencing for jointly analyzing variation in transcription, splicing, and allele-specific expression across individuals. This approach has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of the genetic mechanisms underlying natural variation in gene expression, with important implications for both medical and evolutionary genetics.

title: Mesenchymal and haematopoietic stem cells form a unique bone marrow niche
text: The cellular components of the haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche in the bone marrow are not fully understood, with studies suggesting involvement of osteoblasts, endothelial cells, and perivascular cells. However, our research reveals that mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) expressing the protein nestin play a crucial role in the HSC niche. Nestin+ MSCs account for the majority of bone-marrow colony-forming unit fibroblastic activity and can be cultured as non-adherent 'mesenspheres' that can self-renew and expand in serial transplantations. These cells are spatially associated with HSCs and adrenergic nerve fibers, and exhibit high expression of genes involved in HSC maintenance. Furthermore, we found that these genes, as well as others involved in osteoblastic differentiation, are selectively downregulated during enforced HSC mobilization or activation of β3 adrenoreceptors. Interestingly, parathyroid hormone administration increases the number of bone marrow nestin+ cells and promotes their osteoblastic differentiation, while in vivo depletion of nestin+ cells significantly reduces HSC content in the bone marrow. In addition, purified HSCs home near nestin+ MSCs in the bone marrow of lethally irradiated mice, and in vivo depletion of nestin+ cells reduces bone marrow homing of haematopoietic progenitors. These findings uncover a previously unknown partnership between two distinct somatic stem cell types and suggest the existence of a unique niche in the bone marrow composed of heterotypic stem cell pairs.

title: Response to self antigen imprints regulatory memory in tissues
text:
The balance between T-cell responses and tissue inhibition in maintaining immune homeostasis is critical for tissue health. Currently, the mechanisms by which tissues and the immune system communicate to establish and maintain this balance are not well understood. However, clinical evidence suggests that repeated exposure to self-antigens within tissues can lead to a decrease in pathological autoimmune responses, possibly to mitigate inflammatory damage and preserve function. Many organ-specific autoimmune diseases exhibit an initial severe presentation followed by less severe flares, and in some cases, spontaneous resolution. Antigen-specific immunotherapy, involving the repeated injection of allergens or self-antigens in the skin, has been shown to diminish the inflammatory response after each exposure. While these findings suggest that tissues can attenuate autoimmune reactions upon repeated exposure to antigens, the underlying mechanism remains unknown.
Our study reveals that upon expression of self-antigen in a peripheral tissue, thymus-derived regulatory T cells (Treg cells) become activated, proliferate, and differentiate into more potent suppressors, which mediate resolution of organ-specific autoimmunity in mice. After resolution of the inflammatory response, activated Treg cells are maintained in the target tissue and are primed to attenuate subsequent autoimmune reactions when antigen is re-expressed. Therefore, Treg cells confer 'regulatory memory' to the target tissue, providing a framework for understanding their response to self-antigens in peripheral tissues and offering mechanistic insight into how tissues regulate autoimmunity.

title: Reprogramming of human somatic cells to pluripotency with defined factors
text: Pluripotency refers to the ability of cells in early embryos to differentiate into any cell type in the organism. Embryonic stem cells are derived from the embryo and retain this pluripotency, making them valuable tools for researching tissue formation. Recently, scientists have reprogrammed adult cells, such as murine fibroblasts, into pluripotent cells using four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and Myc). This process, called induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) reprogramming, has been used to generate iPSCs from fetal, neonatal, and adult human primary cells, including dermal fibroblasts isolated from a skin biopsy of a healthy research subject. These iPSCs are similar in morphology and gene expression to embryonic stem cells and can form teratomas in immune-deficient mice, just like embryonic stem cells. These findings demonstrate that specific factors can reprogram adult cells into pluripotency, providing a method to generate patient-specific cells in culture.

title: Haematopoietic stem cells do not asymmetrically segregate chromosomes or retain BrdU
text:
Stem cells are proposed to segregate chromosomes asymmetrically during self-renewing divisions, resulting in the retention of older DNA strands in daughter stem cells while newly synthesized strands are transferred to differentiating cells. Additionally, stem cells are thought to retain DNA labels, such as 5-bromo-2-deoxyuridine (BrdU), either due to asymmetric chromosome segregation or slow division. However, the purity of stem cells among BrdU-label-retaining cells has not been thoroughly investigated in any tissue, and the 'immortal strand hypothesis' has not been tested in a system with definitive stem cell markers.
To address these questions, we investigated the retention of BrdU in haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) using well-characterized markers. We administered BrdU to newborn mice, mice treated with cyclophosphamide and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, and normal adult mice for 4-10 days, followed by 70 days without BrdU. Our results revealed that less than 6% of HSCs retained BrdU, and less than 0.5% of all BrdU-retaining haematopoietic cells were HSCs. These findings indicate that BrdU has poor specificity and sensitivity as a marker for HSCs.
To further investigate the segregation of chromosomes in HSCs, we performed sequential administration of 5-chloro-2-deoxyuridine and 5-iodo-2-deoxyuridine. Our results showed that HSCs segregate their chromosomes randomly, indicating that they do not retain older DNA strands during division. Additionally, division of individual HSCs in culture revealed no asymmetric segregation of the label. Taken together, these findings suggest that HSCs cannot be identified based on BrdU label retention and do not retain older DNA strands during division, challenging the 'immortal strand hypothesis' for stem cells.

title: Circadian Clocks in Human Red Blood Cells
text: Circadian (approximately 24-hour) clocks are fundamental to the coordinated physiology of organisms as diverse as cyanobacteria and humans. All current models of the molecular circadian clockwork in eukaryotic cells rely on transcription-translation feedback loops. However, studying non-transcriptional mechanisms in the clockwork has been challenging in mammalian systems. To overcome these difficulties, we developed innovative assays using human red blood cells, which lack a nucleus (and therefore DNA) and cannot perform transcription. Our findings reveal that transcription is not essential for circadian oscillations in humans, and that non-transcriptional events are sufficient to sustain cellular circadian rhythms. Using red blood cells, we discovered that peroxiredoxins, highly conserved antioxidant proteins, exhibit ∼24-hour redox cycles that persist for several days under constant conditions (i.e., in the absence of external cues). These rhythms are also entrainable (i.e., tunable by environmental stimuli) and temperature-compensated, two key features of circadian rhythms. Our findings are expected to enhance the sophistication of cellular clock models, highlighting the interdependence of transcriptional and non-transcriptional oscillations in all eukaryotic cells.

title: G-protein-coupled receptor of Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus is a viral oncogene and angiogenesis activator.
text:
Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV/HHV8), a gamma-2 herpesvirus, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) and primary effusion B-cell lymphomas (PELs). KSHV infects malignant and progenitor cells of KS and PEL, and encodes putative oncogenes and genes that may contribute to the development of these malignancies by stimulating angiogenesis.
One of the viral genes of interest is an open reading frame (ORF) 74, which encodes a G-protein-coupled receptor. This receptor is expressed in KS lesions and PEL, and its activation leads to constitutive signaling pathways linked to cell proliferation. In this study, we investigate the role of this receptor in KSHV-mediated oncogenesis.
Our findings demonstrate that activation of the KSHV G-protein-coupled receptor leads to cell transformation and tumorigenicity, and induces a switch to an angiogenic phenotype characterized by the production of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and Kaposi's spindle-cell growth factor (KSGF). We also show that this receptor can activate two protein kinases, JNK/SAPK and p38MAPK, which are involved in signaling cascades similar to those induced by inflammatory cytokines that promote angiogenesis and mitogenesis in KS cells and B cells.
Overall, our results suggest that the KSHV G-protein-coupled receptor is a viral oncogene that exploits cell signaling pathways to induce transformation and angiogenesis in KSHV-mediated oncogenesis.

title: Therapeutic potential of GSK-J4, a histone demethylase KDM6B/JMJD3 inhibitor, for acute myeloid leukemia
text:
Title: Targeting KDM6B as a Potential Therapeutic Strategy for Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Abstract:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a complex and aggressive disease with poor prognosis. Despite growing evidence implicating dysregulation of histone modification in AML, few targeted therapies have been developed. In this study, we investigated the therapeutic potential of targeting KDM6B, a demethylase of tri-methylated histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me3), in AML.
Methods: We treated primary AML cells and cell lines with a KDM6B-specific inhibitor, GSK-J4, and evaluated its effects on cell proliferation, apoptosis, and gene expression. We also used RNA sequencing to identify the underlying mechanisms of KDM6B inhibition in AML.
Results: Our results showed that KDM6B expression was up-regulated in AML and positively correlated with poor survival. Treatment with GSK-J4 increased global H3K27me3 levels and reduced cell proliferation and colony-forming ability in AML cells. GSK-J4 treatment also induced cell apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest in Kasumi-1 cells, and displayed a synergistic effect with cytosine arabinoside. In a human AML xenograft mouse model, injection of GSK-J4 attenuated disease progression. Treatment with GSK-J4 primarily down-regulated DNA replication and cell-cycle-related pathways, as well as abrogated the expression of critical cancer-promoting HOX genes. ChIP-qPCR validated increased H3K27me3 enrichment at the transcription start sites of these HOX genes.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that targeting KDM6B with GSK-J4 has therapeutic potential for AML. This study provides evidence for the role of KDM6B in AML and highlights the potential of targeting histone modification in AML treatment. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of KDM6B inhibition and to evaluate its efficacy in clinical settings.

title: Structure of the proton-gated urea channel from the gastric pathogen Helicobacter pylori
text:
Half of the world's population is infected with Helicobacter pylori, leading to gastritis, gastric ulcers, and an increased risk of gastric cancer. The bacterium's survival in the stomach depends on a proton-gated inner-membrane urea channel called HpUreI, which is essential for its acid tolerance. The channel is closed at neutral pH and opens at acidic pH, allowing urea to reach the cytoplasmic urease, which produces NH3 and CO2, neutralizing incoming protons and maintaining a pH of around 6.1 in the periplasm, even in acidic environments.
We have determined the structure of HpUreI, revealing a hexameric ring of six protomer assemblies surrounding a central plug of ordered lipids. Each protomer contains a channel formed by a twisted bundle of six transmembrane helices, with a unique two-helix hairpin motif repeated three times around the central axis of the channel. The channel and protomer interfaces contain conserved residues in the AmiS/UreI superfamily, indicating the preservation of channel architecture and oligomeric state in this family. Aromatic or aliphatic side chains line the entire channel and define two constriction sites in the middle, with mutation of Trp 153 in the cytoplasmic constriction site affecting urea selectivity.
Our discovery of the hexameric channel structure provides a new model for the permeation of urea and other small amide solutes in prokaryotes and archaea.

title: Drosophila oocyte localization is mediated by differential cadherin-based adhesion.
text: In the Drosophila follicle, the oocyte is always located in the posterior position among a group of 16 germline cells. Although the importance of this cell arrangement for the formation of the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo has been well-documented, the molecular mechanism behind the oocyte's posterior localization was previously unknown. Our study reveals that the homophilic adhesion molecule DE-cadherin is responsible for the oocyte's positioning. During follicle development, DE-cadherin is expressed in both germline and surrounding follicle cells, with the highest concentration found at the interface between the oocyte and posterior follicle cells. Mosaic analysis shows that DE-cadherin is required in both germline and follicle cells for proper oocyte localization, suggesting that interactions between germline and somatic cells may play a role in this process. By analyzing the behavior of the oocyte in chimaeric follicles, we found that the oocyte's position is determined by the position of DE-cadherin-expressing follicle cells, to which the oocyte selectively attaches itself. The oocyte preferentially contacts DE-cadherin-expressing follicle cells that have higher levels of DE-cadherin. Based on these findings, we propose that in wild-type follicles, the oocyte competes with its sister germline cells for contact with the posterior follicle cells, a process driven by differences in DE-cadherin expression. This is the first in vivo example of a cell-sorting process that relies on differential adhesion mediated by a cadherin.

title: Somatic sex identity is cell-autonomous in the chicken
text: In the mammalian model of sex determination, embryos are initially sexually indifferent until the action of a sex-determining gene triggers gonadal differentiation. While this model is thought to apply to all vertebrates, its validity has yet to be confirmed. To investigate the sex-determining mechanism in birds, we examined three lateral gynandromorph chickens, which are rare, naturally occurring individuals with both male and female characteristics on opposite sides of their body. Our findings showed that these birds are genuine male:female chimeras, suggesting that male and female avian somatic cells may have an inherent sex identity. To test this hypothesis, we transplanted presumptive mesoderm between embryos of reciprocal sexes, generating embryos with male:female chimaeric gonads. Unlike the outcome in mammalian mixed-sex chimaeras, where the donor cells are integrated into the functional structures of the host gonad, in chicken mixed-sex chimaeras, the donor cells were excluded from the host gonad. For example, when female tissue was transplanted into a male host, donor cells contributing to the developing testis retained a female identity and expressed a marker of female function. Our study demonstrates that avian somatic cells possess an inherent sex identity and that sexual differentiation in birds is cell autonomous.

title: Centrosome polarization delivers secretory granules to the immunological synapse
text: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) eliminate infected or cancerous cells by releasing specialized granules, called lytic granules, at the immunological synapse formed between the CTL and the target cell. Upon contact with the target, the microtubule organizing center of the CTL polarizes towards the target and granules move along microtubules in a minus-end direction towards the polarized microtubule organizing center. However, the final steps of secretion remained unclear. Our study reveals that CTLs do not require actin or plus-end microtubule motors for secretion, instead, the centrosome moves to and contacts the plasma membrane at the central supramolecular activation cluster of the immunological synapse. Actin and IQGAP1 are cleared away from the synapse, and granules are delivered directly to the plasma membrane. These findings demonstrate that CTLs employ a previously unreported mechanism for delivering secretory granules to the immunological synapse, with granule secretion controlled by centrosome delivery to the plasma membrane.

title: Deubiquitination of p53 by HAUSP is an important pathway for p53 stabilization
text: The p53 tumor suppressor protein is a short-lived molecule that is maintained at low levels in normal cells through the ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis pathway, primarily mediated by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Mdm2. The stabilization of p53 is crucial for its tumor suppressor function, but the in vivo regulation of ubiquitinated p53 levels remains poorly understood. Through mass spectrometry analysis of affinity-purified p53-associated factors, we have identified herpesvirus-associated ubiquitin-specific protease (HAUSP) as a novel p53-interacting protein. HAUSP exhibits strong stabilization of p53 even in the presence of excess Mdm2, and also induces p53-dependent cell growth repression and apoptosis. Interestingly, HAUSP possesses intrinsic deubiquitination activity that specifically targets p53 both in vitro and in vivo. In contrast, expression of a catalytically inactive point mutant of HAUSP in cells leads to increased p53 ubiquitination and destabilization of the protein. These findings reveal a novel mechanism by which p53 can be stabilized through direct deubiquitination, and suggest that HAUSP may function as a tumor suppressor in vivo by stabilizing p53.

title: Defective tryptophan catabolism underlies inflammation in mouse chronic granulomatous disease
text: Fifty years ago, chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) was first identified as a fatal condition in children, where their immune system struggled to fight off infections. Since then, significant discoveries have been made, including the inability of patients' white blood cells to effectively kill bacteria and fungi, due to underlying genetic abnormalities. In this inherited disorder, phagocytes lack the crucial NADPH oxidase activity, resulting in a lack of reactive oxygen species production, particularly superoxide anion. This leads to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, as well as chronic inflammatory conditions, including granuloma formation in internal organs. The reasons for the exaggerated inflammatory response have been unclear, but recent findings reveal a key role of a superoxide-dependent step in tryptophan metabolism along the kynurenine pathway. In CGD mice with lethal pulmonary aspergillosis, this blockade leads to unrestrained reactivity of Vγ1+ γδ T cells, dominant production of interleukin (IL)-17, defective regulatory T-cell activity, and acute inflammatory lung injury. Although beneficial effects are observed with IL-17 neutralization or γδ T-cell contraction, complete cure and reversal of the hyperinflammatory phenotype are achieved by replacement therapy with a natural kynurenine distal to the blockade in the pathway. Effective therapy involves co-administration of recombinant interferon-γ (IFN-γ), which restores production of downstream immunoactive metabolites and enables the emergence of regulatory Vγ4+ γδ and Foxp3+ αβ T cells. Surprisingly, the lack of reactive oxygen species contributes to the hyperinflammatory phenotype associated with NADPH oxidase deficiencies, through a dysfunctional kynurenine pathway of tryptophan catabolism. However, reactivating this pathway downstream of the superoxide-dependent step can reverse this condition.

title: Experimental and theoretical study of mitotic spindle orientation
text: The microenvironmental architecture and adhesiveness of a cell play a crucial role in regulating the orientation of the spindle in vivo. Through a combination of theoretical and experimental approaches, we have investigated spindle orientation in HeLa (human) cells. Our findings reveal that spindle orientation can be understood as a result of the interaction between cortical force generators and spindle microtubules, which are activated by cortical cues. We have developed a simple physical model of this spindle mechanics, allowing us to calculate the angular profiles of torque acting on the spindle and the angular distribution of spindle orientations. Our model accounts for the preferred spindle orientation and the full angular distribution of spindle orientations observed in various cellular microenvironment geometries. Additionally, it correctly describes asymmetric spindle orientations that occur under specific distributions of cortical cues. Our results demonstrate that, based on a few simple assumptions, a quantitative description of spindle orientation can be provided for adherent cells.

title: CHROMOTHRIPSIS FROM DNA DAMAGE IN MICRONUCLEI
text:
Recent advances in genome sequencing have uncovered a novel mutational phenomenon in cancer and congenital disorders, known as chromothripsis. This phenomenon is characterized by extensive genomic rearrangements and an oscillating pattern of DNA copy number levels, all of which are restricted to one or a few chromosomes. The underlying mechanism of chromothripsis remains elusive, but our previous work suggested that it could arise from the physical isolation of chromosomes in aberrant nuclear structures called micronuclei.
To investigate this hypothesis further, we employed a combination of live cell imaging and single-cell genome sequencing. Our findings demonstrate that micronucleus formation can indeed give rise to a spectrum of genomic rearrangements, some of which recapitulate all known features of chromothripsis. These events are confined to the mis-segregated chromosome and occur within a single cell division. Furthermore, our data suggest that the mechanism of chromothripsis may involve the fragmentation and subsequent reassembly of a single chromatid from a micronucleus.
Taken together, these experiments establish a new mutational process, with chromothripsis representing one extreme outcome. This work has significant implications for our understanding of the mechanisms underlying genetic instability in cancer and other diseases, and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

title: DNA-binding factors shape the mouse methylome at distal regulatory regions
text: Methylation of cytosines is a crucial epigenetic modification in mammalian genomes, yet the underlying rules and mechanisms remain largely unexplored. To gain a deeper understanding of this process, we generated high-resolution methylomes of mouse stem cells and neuronal progenitors using advanced quantitative analysis techniques. Our findings revealed low-methylated regions (LMRs) with an average methylation level of approximately 30%. These regions were found to be enriched in CpG-poor distal regulatory areas, as indicated by their location, DNase I hypersensitivity, and the presence of enhancer chromatin marks and enhancer activity in reporter assays. Furthermore, our results demonstrated that DNA-binding factors are necessary and sufficient to create LMRs, and that cell-type-specific LMRs are occupied by cell-type-specific transcription factors. This study provides valuable methylome references for the mouse and highlights the importance of DNA-binding factors in influencing DNA methylation patterns, enabling the identification of active regulatory regions.

title: Molecular basis of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase II activity
text:
RNA polymerase II (Pol II) plays a crucial role in gene transcription by catalyzing DNA-dependent RNA synthesis. However, recent evidence suggests that Pol II also possesses intrinsic RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) activity. This means that Pol II can use a homopolymeric RNA template to synthesize new RNA molecules without the presence of DNA.
In this study, we demonstrate the RdRP activity of Pol II using pure polymerase, an RNA template-product scaffold, and nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs). Crystallography reveals the template-product duplex in the site occupied by the DNA-RNA hybrid during transcription. Our findings show that RdRP activity resides at the active site used during transcription, but it is slower and less processive than DNA-dependent activity.
Interestingly, we also found that the complex of transcription factor IIS (TFIIS) with Pol II can cleave one HDV strand, create a reactive stem-loop in the hybrid site, and extend the new RNA 3' end. Short RNA stem-loops with a 5' extension suffice for activity, but their growth to a critical length apparently impairs processivity.
Our discovery provides a missing link in molecular evolution, suggesting that Pol II evolved from an ancient replicase that duplicated RNA genomes. This finding highlights the versatility and evolutionary history of Pol II, which plays a crucial role in gene expression and RNA synthesis.

title: Bacteria activate sensory neurons that modulate pain and inflammation
text: Nociceptor neurons are specialized to detect harmful stimuli and initiate the sensation of pain to protect the organism. Bacterial infections cause pain through unknown molecular mechanisms, although they are thought to be secondary to immune activation. Our study shows that bacteria directly activate nociceptors, and that the immune response mediated through TLR2, MyD88, T cells, B cells, and neutrophils and monocytes is not necessary for Staphylococcus aureus-induced pain in mice. We found that mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in mice are correlated with the live bacterial load rather than tissue swelling or immune activation. Bacteria activate calcium flux and action potentials in nociceptor neurons through distinct mechanisms involving bacterial N-formylated peptides and the pore-forming toxin α-haemolysin. Ablation of Nav1.8-lineage neurons, which include nociceptors, eliminated pain during bacterial infection, but concurrently increased local immune infiltration and lymphadenopathy of the draining lymph node. Our findings reveal an unexpected role for the nervous system in host-pathogen interactions, where bacterial pathogens produce pain by directly activating sensory neurons that modulate inflammation.

title: E2F1-3 Switch from Activators in Progenitor Cells to Repressors in Differentiating Cells
text: In the established model of mammalian cell cycle control, the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) functions to restrict cells from entering S phase by binding and sequestering E2f activators (E2f1, E2f2, and E2f3), which are typically depicted as the ultimate effectors of a transcriptional program that commits cells to enter and progress through S phase. Using a panel of tissue-specific cre-transgenic mice and conditional E2f alleles, we investigated the effects of E2f1, E2f2, and E2f3 triple deficiency in murine embryonic stem cells, embryos, and small intestines. Our findings reveal that in normal dividing progenitor cells, E2f1-3 function as transcriptional activators, contrary to the prevailing view, and are dispensable for cell division but are necessary for cell survival. In contrast, in differentiating cells, E2f1-3 function in a complex with Rb as repressors to silence E2f targets and facilitate exit from the cell cycle. The inactivation of Rb in differentiating cells led to a switch of E2f1-3 from repressors to activators, resulting in the superactivation of E2f responsive targets and ectopic cell divisions. Notably, loss of E2f1-3 completely suppressed these phenotypes caused by Rb deficiency, providing insight into the activator versus repressor functions of E2f1-3 in vivo and revealing distinct roles in dividing versus differentiating cells and in normal versus cancer-like cell cycles.

title: K-Ras(G12C) inhibitors allosterically control GTP affinity and effector interactions
text:
Somatic mutations in the small GTPase K-Ras are the most prevalent activating alterations found in human cancer, and are typically associated with poor responses to conventional therapies. Attempts to target this oncogene directly have been hindered by its picomolar affinity for GTP/GDP and the absence of known allosteric regulatory sites. Oncogenic mutations result in functional activation of Ras family proteins by impairing GTP hydrolysis, leading to diminished regulation by GTPase activity and increased dependence on the relative nucleotide affinity and concentration. This shift in nucleotide binding favors GTP over GDP, resulting in an increased proportion of active GTP-bound Ras.
We report the development of small molecules that irreversibly bind to a specific oncogenic mutant, K-Ras(G12C), which does not affect the wild-type protein. Crystallographic studies reveal the formation of a novel pocket beneath the effector binding switch-II region, which is exploited by these inhibitors for binding. The binding of these compounds to K-Ras(G12C) disrupts both switch-I and switch-II, thereby altering the native nucleotide preference to favor GDP over GTP and impairing binding to Raf. Our findings provide structure-based validation of a novel allosteric regulatory site on Ras that can be targeted in a mutant-specific manner.

title: Cyclin A Regulates Kinetochore-Microtubules to Promote Faithful Chromosome Segregation
text:
The most striking event in the cell cycle is the alignment of chromosomes during metaphase, which facilitates accurate chromosome segregation through the formation of bi-oriented attachments between kinetochores and spindle microtubules. However, errors in these attachments are common in early mitosis (prometaphase), and their persistence is a leading cause of chromosomal instability in aneuploid cancer cells. The mechanism by which error correction is achieved in prometaphase to ensure error-free mitosis is unknown.
Our study reveals that kinetochore-microtubule attachments in prometaphase cells are significantly less stable than in metaphase cells. The transition to more stable attachments in metaphase requires the degradation of cyclin A, which is mediated by the proteasome. Persistent expression of cyclin A hinders k-MT stabilization even in cells with properly aligned chromosomes. In contrast, k-MTs are prematurely stabilized in cyclin-A-deficient cells, leading to higher rates of chromosome mis-segregation. Therefore, the stability of k-MT attachments increases progressively among all chromosomes as cells transition from prometaphase to metaphase.
Cyclin A creates a cellular environment that promotes microtubule detachment from kinetochores in prometaphase, allowing for efficient error correction and faithful chromosome segregation. This study sheds light on the critical role of cyclin A in ensuring accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis.

title: Induced pluripotent stem cells from a spinal muscular atrophy patient
text: Spinal muscular atrophy is one of the most common inherited forms of neurological disorders leading to infant mortality. Patients experience selective loss of lower motor neurons, resulting in muscle weakness, paralysis, and often death. Although patient fibroblasts have been extensively studied to understand spinal muscular atrophy, motor neurons have a distinct anatomy and physiology that may contribute to their susceptibility to the disease process. In this study, we generated induced pluripotent stem cells from skin fibroblast samples taken from a child with spinal muscular atrophy. These cells grew robustly in culture, maintained the disease genotype, and produced motor neurons displaying selective deficits compared to those derived from the child's unaffected mother. This is the first investigation to demonstrate that human induced pluripotent stem cells can be used to model the specific pathology seen in a genetically inherited disease. As such, this represents a valuable resource for investigating disease mechanisms, screening new drug compounds, and developing novel therapies.

title: A role for mitochondria in NLRP3 inflammasome activation
text: The NLRP3 inflammasome is activated in response to various host "danger" signals, including infection and metabolic dysregulation. Previous studies have suggested that NLRP3 inflammasome activity is negatively regulated by autophagy and positively regulated by reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated by an unknown organelle. Our findings reveal that blocking mitophagy/autophagy leads to the accumulation of damaged, ROS-producing mitochondria, which in turn activates the NLRP3 inflammasome. Under normal conditions, resting NLRP3 localizes to endoplasmic reticulum structures, but upon inflammasome activation, both NLRP3 and its adaptor ASC redistribute to the perinuclear space, where they co-localize with endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria organelle clusters. Interestingly, suppression of mitochondrial activity by inhibiting the voltage-dependent anion channel reduces both ROS generation and inflammasome activation, suggesting that the NLRP3 inflammasome may detect mitochondrial dysfunction and play a role in the development of inflammatory diseases.

title: Break-induced telomere synthesis underlies alternative telomere maintenance
text:
Homology-directed DNA repair is crucial for maintaining the integrity of the genome through templated DNA synthesis. In approximately 10-15% of human cancers, alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) relies on homology-directed DNA repair to maintain telomere length. Despite progress in understanding how DNA damage triggers the assembly and execution of a DNA replication complex (break-induced replisome) at telomeres or other regions of the mammalian genome, the mechanisms underlying ALT telomere maintenance remain poorly understood.
Here, we delineate break-induced telomere synthesis and demonstrate that it relies on a specialized replisome, which is distinct from the canonical replisome components, ATM and ATR, or the homologous recombination protein Rad51. Our findings reveal that the inception of telomere damage recognition by the break-induced replisome triggers homology-directed telomere maintenance. Specifically, the loading of proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) by replication factor C (RFC) serves as the initial sensor of telomere damage, leading to the predominance of DNA polymerase δ (Pol δ) through its POLD3 subunit. This process is independent of other canonical replisome components, highlighting the unique nature of the break-induced replisome in ALT telomere maintenance.
In conclusion, our study sheds light on the mechanisms underlying ALT telomere maintenance, providing insights into the complex interplay between DNA damage, replication, and repair in maintaining genome stability. Further investigations into the break-induced replisome and its role in ALT telomere maintenance may lead to a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms of cancer development and progression.

title: Innate immunity induced by composition-dependent RIG-I recognition of hepatitis C virus RNA
text:
Innate immune defenses are crucial for controlling virus infections, and they are triggered by the recognition of viral macromolecular motifs known as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by host cells. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an RNA virus that infects approximately 200 million people worldwide, and its replication is regulated by hepatic immune defenses triggered by the cellular RIG-I helicase. RIG-I recognizes PAMP RNA by binding to it and signaling the activation of interferon regulatory factor 3, leading to the expression of interferon-α/β and antiviral/interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) that restrict infection.
In this study, we identify the polyuridine motif of the HCV genome 3' non-translated region and its replication intermediate as the PAMP substrate of RIG-I, and demonstrate that this and similar homopolyuridine or homopolyriboadenine motifs present in the genomes of RNA viruses are the primary features of RIG-I recognition and immune triggering in human and murine cells. We also show that the 5' terminal triphosphate on the PAMP RNA is necessary but not sufficient for RIG-I binding, which is primarily dependent on the homopolymeric ribonucleotide composition, linear structure, and length of the RNA motif.
Our findings provide a significant advance in understanding the mechanisms of RIG-I-mediated immune responses, as they demonstrate the specificity of RIG-I recognition of homopolymeric RNA motifs within the genome of HCV and other RNA viruses. These results also suggest that immunogenic features of the PAMP-RIG-I interaction could be exploited as an immune adjuvant for vaccine and immunotherapy approaches.

title: Generation of transgenic non-human primates with germline transmission
text: The common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) is gaining popularity as a non-human primate model in biomedical research due to its relatively high reproductive rate. This makes it a promising candidate for genetic modification through transgenic technology. Although several attempts have been made to create non-human primate transgenics, the expression of the transgene in live infants has been difficult to demonstrate through objective methods such as polymerase chain reaction with reverse transcription or western blots. Here, we report the successful use of a self-inactivating lentiviral vector in sucrose solution to produce transgenic common marmosets that express the transgene in multiple organs. Notably, we were able to transmit the transgene to the germline, resulting in normal development of the transgenic offspring. The creation of transgenic marmosets offers a valuable new animal model for studying human diseases, as they share a close genetic relationship with humans. This model will be useful in many areas of biomedical research.

title: Induction of human neuronal cells by defined transcription factors
text: Somatic cell nuclear transfer, cell fusion, or the expression of lineage-specific factors have been shown to induce cell fate changes in various somatic cell types. Recently, we observed that the forced expression of a combination of three transcription factors, Brn2 (also known as Pou3f2), Ascl1, and Myt1l, can efficiently convert mouse fibroblasts into functional induced neuronal (iN) cells. In this study, we demonstrate that the same three factors can generate functional neurons from human pluripotent stem cells as early as 6 days after transgene activation. When combined with the basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor NeuroD1, these factors can also convert fetal and postnatal human fibroblasts into iN cells exhibiting typical neuronal morphologies and expressing multiple neuronal markers, even after downregulation of the exogenous transcription factors. Notably, the vast majority of human iN cells were able to generate action potentials and matured to receive synaptic contacts when co-cultured with primary mouse cortical neurons. Our findings demonstrate that non-neural human somatic cells, as well as pluripotent stem cells, can be directly converted into neurons by lineage-determining transcription factors. These methods may provide a means to generate patient-specific human neurons for in vitro disease modeling or future applications in regenerative medicine.

title: PAAR-repeat proteins sharpen and diversify the Type VI secretion system spike
text: The bacterial type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a complex, dynamic machine composed of multiple components that play a crucial role in the ecology of many Gram-negative bacteria. T6SS is responsible for the translocation of a wide range of toxic effector molecules, allowing predatory cells to kill both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. The T6SS organelle is similar in function to the contractile tails of bacteriophages and is thought to attack cells by first penetrating them with a trimeric protein complex called the VgrG spike. While the exact composition of the T6SS organelle and the mechanisms of effector selection and delivery are unknown, our study reveals that proteins from the PAAR (proline-alanine-alanine-arginine) repeat superfamily form a sharp conical extension on the VgrG spike, which is involved in attaching effector domains to the spike. Crystal structures of PAAR-repeat proteins bound to VgrG-like partners show that these proteins sharpen the tip of the T6SS spike complex. Our results demonstrate that PAAR proteins are essential for T6SS-mediated secretion and target cell killing by Vibrio cholerae and Acinetobacter baylyi, and suggest a new model of the T6SS organelle in which the VgrG-PAAR spike complex is decorated with multiple effectors that are delivered simultaneously into target cells in a single contraction-driven translocation event.

title: Replication stress activates DNA repair synthesis in mitosis
text: Oncogenes have been implicated in causing DNA replication stress, which is believed to play a key role in the development of tumors. Many chromosomal rearrangements characteristic of human cancers originate from specific regions of the genome called common fragile sites (CFSs). These regions are difficult to replicate and often manifest as gaps or breaks on metaphase chromosomes, particularly when cells are exposed to replicative stress. The MUS81-EME1 structure-specific endonuclease is involved in the appearance of chromosome gaps or breaks at CFSs following replicative stress. Our study shows that entry of cells into mitotic prophase triggers the recruitment of MUS81 to CFSs, leading to the promotion of POLD3-dependent DNA synthesis at these regions. This process helps to minimize chromosome mis-segregation and non-disjunction. We propose that the attempted condensation of incompletely duplicated loci in early mitosis serves as the trigger for completion of DNA replication at CFS loci in human cells. Interestingly, this POLD3-dependent mitotic DNA synthesis is enhanced in aneuploid cancer cells that exhibit intrinsically high levels of chromosomal instability (CIN+) and replicative stress, suggesting that targeting this pathway could represent a new therapeutic approach.

title: A specific amyloid-β protein assembly in the brain impairs memory
text: As we age, our memory function often declines, and it is believed that this decline is initially caused by changes in synaptic function rather than a loss of neurons. However, some individuals go on to develop Alzheimer's disease, which is characterized by neurodegeneration. To investigate the cause of memory decline in the absence of neurodegeneration or amyloid-β protein accumulation, we used Tg2576 mice, which express a human amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) variant linked to Alzheimer's disease. Young Tg2576 mice have normal memory and lack neuropathology, while middle-aged mice develop memory deficits without any neuronal loss, and old mice form abundant neuritic plaques containing amyloid-β. We found that the memory deficits in middle-aged Tg2576 mice are caused by the extracellular accumulation of a 56-kDa soluble amyloid-β assembly, which we term Aβ*56 (Aβ star 56). Aβ*56 purified from the brains of impaired Tg2576 mice disrupts memory when administered to young rats, suggesting that Aβ*56 impairs memory independently of plaques or neuronal loss and may contribute to cognitive deficits associated with Alzheimer's disease.

title: Cleavage of GSDMD by inflammatory caspases determines pyroptotic cell death
text:
Inflammatory caspases, including caspase-1, -4, -5, and -11, play a crucial role in the innate immune response by inducing pyroptosis, a form of programmed necrosis. Despite their importance in immunity and endotoxic shock, the mechanism by which these caspases induce pyroptosis is not fully understood. To investigate this, researchers used genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 nuclease screens to identify the protein gasdermin D (Gsdmd) as a key player in pyroptosis induction.
Gsdmd-deficient cells were found to be resistant to the induction of pyroptosis by cytosolic lipopolysaccharide and known canonical inflammasome ligands. Additionally, interleukin-1β release was diminished in Gsdmd-deficient cells, despite intact processing by caspase-1. The study found that caspase-1 and caspase-4/5/11 specifically cleaved the linker between the amino-terminal gasdermin-N and carboxy-terminal gasdermin-C domains in GSDMD, which was required and sufficient for pyroptosis. The cleavage released the intramolecular inhibition on the gasdermin-N domain, which showed intrinsic pyroptosis-inducing activity.
Other gasdermin family members were not cleaved by inflammatory caspases, but shared the autoinhibition. Gain-of-function mutations in Gsdma3, which causes alopecia and skin defects, disrupted the autoinhibition, allowing the gasdermin-N domain to trigger pyroptosis. These findings provide new insights into inflammasome-mediated immunity/diseases and change our understanding of pyroptosis and programmed necrosis.

title: Role of corin in trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodelling in pregnancy
text: During pregnancy, trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodeling are crucial for reducing maternal vascular resistance and increasing uteroplacental blood flow. For a long time, impaired spiral artery remodeling has been linked to pre-eclampsia, a common pregnancy complication. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Corin (also known as atrial natriuretic peptide-converting enzyme) is a cardiac protease that activates atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), a hormone that regulates blood pressure. Surprisingly, corin is expressed in the pregnant uterus. Here, we uncover a new function of corin and ANP in promoting trophoblast invasion and spiral artery remodeling. We show that corin- or ANP-deficient mice develop high blood pressure and proteinuria, hallmarks of pre-eclampsia. In these mice, trophoblast invasion and uterine spiral artery remodeling are significantly impaired. Consistently, the ANP potently stimulates human trophoblasts to invade Matrigels. In patients with pre-eclampsia, uterine Corin mRNA and protein levels are significantly lower than in normal pregnancies. Moreover, we have identified Corin gene mutations in pre-eclamptic patients, which reduce corin activity in processing pro-ANP. These findings suggest that corin and ANP are essential for the physiological changes at the maternal-fetal interface, and defects in corin and ANP function may contribute to pre-eclampsia.

title: Metabolic rescue in pluripotent cells from patients with mtDNA disease
text:
Mitochondria play a crucial role in energy production through oxidative phosphorylation, which is dependent on the expression of specific genes encoded by mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Mutations in mtDNA can lead to severe and debilitating disorders with limited treatment options. The clinical manifestations of these disorders vary depending on the type of mutation and the level of mutant and wild-type mtDNA in each cell. Here, we generated genetically corrected pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) from patients with mtDNA disease using two different approaches: inducing pluripotency (iPS) and somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT).
We generated multiple iPS cell lines from patients with common heteroplasmic mutations, including 3243A>G, which causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), and 8993T>G and 13513G>A, implicated in Leigh syndrome. We also generated isogenic iPS cell lines containing exclusively wild-type or mutant mtDNA through spontaneous segregation of heteroplasmic mtDNA in proliferating fibroblasts. Additionally, we used SCNT to replace the mutant mtDNA in homoplasmic 8993T>G fibroblasts with wild-type mtDNA to generate corrected Leigh-NT1 PSCs.
Our results show that both reprogramming approaches offer complementary strategies for derivation of PSCs containing exclusively wild-type mtDNA. Through spontaneous segregation of heteroplasmic mtDNA in individual iPS cell lines, we were able to generate PSCs with normal mitochondrial function. Alternatively, through SCNT, we were able to replace the mutant mtDNA in homoplasmic mtDNA-based disease with wild-type mtDNA, resulting in PSCs with normal mitochondrial function. Our findings suggest that both approaches have the potential to be used in the treatment of mtDNA disease, providing a promising avenue for the development of new therapies.

title: The yeast Pif1p helicase removes telomerase from telomeric DNA
text:
Telomeres, the chromosomal ends of eukaryotic cells, are critical for maintaining genome stability and preventing chromosomal breakage. While genetic studies have established the baker's yeast Pif1p DNA helicase as a negative regulator of telomerase, the enzyme responsible for maintaining telomeric DNA, the molecular basis for this inhibition remained unclear. In this study, we investigate the biochemical mechanisms underlying the inhibition of telomerase by Pif1p.
Our findings reveal that in vitro, Pif1p reduces the processivity of telomerase and releases the enzyme from telomeric oligonucleotides. The released telomerase remains enzymatically active, as it is able to lengthen a challenge oligonucleotide. In vivo, overexpression of Pif1p leads to a reduction in telomerase association with telomeres, while depleting cells of Pif1p results in increased levels of telomere-bound Est1p, a subunit of telomerase that is present on the telomere when the enzyme is active.
Based on these findings, we propose that Pif1p helicase activity limits telomerase action both in vivo and in vitro by displacing active telomerase from DNA ends. This mechanism provides a novel insight into the regulation of telomerase and highlights the importance of Pif1p in maintaining genome stability.

title: Small regulatory RNAs inhibit RNA Polymerase II during the elongation phase of transcription
text: Eukaryotic cells harbor a diverse array of endogenous small regulatory RNAs that regulate various cellular processes, including heterochromatin formation, developmental timing, defense against parasitic nucleic acids, and genome rearrangement. Many of these small regulatory RNAs are thought to function within the nucleus. For example, in plants and fungi, short interfering RNAs (siRNAs) associate with nascent transcripts and direct chromatin and/or DNA modifications. To further elucidate the biological roles of small regulatory RNAs, we conducted a genetic screen to identify factors required for RNA interference (RNAi) in Caenorhabditis elegans nuclei. Our findings reveal that the gene nuclear RNAi defective-2 (nrde-2) encodes an evolutionarily conserved protein that is essential for siRNA-mediated silencing within nuclei. NRDE-2 interacts with the Argonaute protein NRDE-3 within nuclei and is recruited by NRDE-3/siRNA complexes to targeted nascent transcripts, where it facilitates an NRDE-2-dependent silencing of pre-messenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) 3' to sites of RNAi. Additionally, we observe an NRDE-2-dependent accumulation of RNA polymerase (RNAP) II at genomic loci targeted by RNAi, as well as NRDE-2-dependent decreases in RNAP II occupancy and transcriptional activity 3' to sites of RNAi. These results establish NRDE-2 as a component of the nuclear RNAi machinery and demonstrate that metazoan siRNAs can silence nuclear-localized RNAs co-transcriptionally. Furthermore, these findings reveal a novel mode of RNAP II regulation, where siRNA-directed recruitment of NRDE factors inhibits RNAP II during the elongation phase of transcription.

title: Cdk1 is sufficient to drive the mammalian cell cycle
text: Unicellular organisms, such as yeast, require a single cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk1) to drive cell division. In contrast, mammalian cells are thought to require the coordinated activation of at least four different Cdks (Cdk2, Cdk3, Cdk4, and Cdk6) to progress through interphase and mitosis. However, recent genetic evidence has challenged this model, showing that mice can survive without individual interphase Cdks. Moreover, most mouse cell types can proliferate in the absence of two or three interphase Cdks. Similarly, ablation of some of the activating subunits of Cdks, such as D-type and E-type cyclins, leads to similar results. Here, we demonstrate that mouse embryos lacking all interphase Cdks (Cdk2, Cdk3, Cdk4, and Cdk6) undergo organogenesis and develop to midgestation. In these embryos, Cdk1 binds to all cyclins, leading to the phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (pRb) and the expression of genes regulated by E2F transcription factors. Mouse embryonic fibroblasts derived from these embryos proliferate in vitro, although with an extended cell cycle due to inefficient inactivation of Rb proteins. However, they become immortal upon continuous passage. Moreover, embryos lacking Cdk1 fail to develop to the morula and blastocyst stages. These findings indicate that Cdk1 is the sole essential cell cycle Cdk and that it can execute all the necessary events to drive cell division in the absence of interphase Cdks.

title: Calorie restriction extends Saccharomyces cerevisiae lifespan by increasing respiration
text: Calorie restriction (CR) has been shown to increase lifespan across a wide range of organisms, making it the only proven method to lengthen the lifespan of mammals. To investigate the mechanisms behind this effect, we established a CR model in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Our findings reveal that limiting glucose or reducing the activity of the glucose-sensing cyclic-AMP-dependent kinase (PKA) can extend lifespan in this system. Interestingly, lifespan extension in a PKA mutant requires the presence of Sir2 and NAD (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide). In this study, we aim to uncover how CR activates Sir2 to extend lifespan. Our results show that the shift in carbon metabolism towards the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid cycle and the subsequent increase in respiration play a central role in this process. These findings suggest that this metabolic strategy may also apply to CR in animals, offering a promising avenue for increasing lifespan.

title: Mosaic PPM1D mutations are associated with predisposition to breast and ovarian cancer
text:
New advancements in sequencing technologies have opened up unprecedented opportunities to investigate the role of rare genetic variations in the development of common diseases. However, there are significant challenges associated with study design, data analysis, and replication. By using pooled next-generation sequencing of 507 genes involved in DNA repair in 1,150 samples, an analytical strategy focused on protein-truncating variants (PTVs), and a large-scale sequencing case-control replication experiment involving 13,642 individuals, we have found that rare PTVs in the p53-inducible protein phosphatase PPM1D are associated with an increased risk of breast cancer and ovarian cancer.
Our findings reveal that PPM1D PTV mutations were present in 25 out of 7,781 cases compared to 1 out of 5,861 controls (P = 1.12 × 10−5), with 18 mutations identified in 6,912 individuals with breast cancer (P = 2.42 × 10−4) and 12 mutations found in 1,121 individuals with ovarian cancer (P = 3.10 × 10−9). Notably, all of the identified PPM1D PTVs were mosaic in lymphocyte DNA and clustered within a 370-base-pair region in the final exon of the gene, carboxy-terminal to the phosphatase catalytic domain. Functional studies showed that the mutations result in enhanced suppression of p53 in response to ionizing radiation exposure, suggesting that the mutant alleles encode hyperactive PPM1D isoforms. Our findings have significant implications for the detection and management of breast and ovarian cancer risk, as well as for the broader understanding of the role of rare and mosaic genetic variants in common conditions. These results also highlight the potential of sequencing in identifying such variants.

title: Immunogenicity of induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), generated from somatic cells through the introduction of specific factors, hold great promise for regenerative medicine as a renewable source of autologous cells. However, it has not been thoroughly investigated whether these autologous cells are immune-tolerated by the recipient. We found that embryonic stem cells (ESCs) derived from inbred C57BL/6 (B6) mice can form teratomas in B6 mice without any evident immune rejection, while allogeneic ESCs from 129/SvJ mice fail to form teratomas in B6 mice due to rapid rejection by recipients. B6 mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) were reprogrammed into iPSCs using either a retroviral approach (ViPSCs) or an episomal approach (EiPSCs) that does not result in genomic integration. In contrast, teratomas formed by B6 ViPSCs were mostly immune-rejected by B6 recipients, and the majority of teratomas formed by B6 EiPSCs were immunogenic in B6 mice with T cell infiltration and apparent tissue damage and regression observed in a small fraction of teratomas. Global gene expression analysis of teratomas formed by B6 ESCs and EiPSCs revealed a number of genes overexpressed in EiPSC-derived teratomas, and several of these gene products were found to contribute directly to the immunogenicity of the B6 EiPSC-derived cells in B6 mice. These findings suggest that abnormal gene expression in some cells differentiated from iPSCs can induce a T-cell-dependent immune response in syngeneic recipients, highlighting the importance of evaluating the immunogenicity of therapeutically valuable cells derived from patient-specific iPSCs before any clinical application.

title: Direct conversion of human fibroblasts to multilineage blood progenitors
text: The limitations of reprogrammed human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) in terms of lineage specification are well-documented. However, our study demonstrates the ability to generate progenitors and mature cells of the haematopoietic lineage directly from human dermal fibroblasts without first establishing pluripotency. By ectopically expressing OCT4 (also known as POU5F1)-activated haematopoietic transcription factors, together with specific cytokine treatment, we were able to generate cells that express the pan-leukocyte marker CD45. These unique fibroblast-derived cells gave rise to granulocytic, monocytic, megakaryocytic, and erythroid lineages, and demonstrated in vivo engraftment capacity. Notably, the adult haematopoietic programs were activated in these cells, which is distinct from haematopoiesis involving pluripotent stem cells, where embryonic programs are activated. Our findings demonstrate the restoration of multipotency from human fibroblasts, and suggest an alternative approach to cellular reprogramming for autologous cell-replacement therapies that avoids the complications associated with the use of human pluripotent stem cells.

title: Mical links semaphorins to F-actin disassembly
text:
The precise mechanisms by which instructive cues on the cell surface, such as semaphorins, regulate the actin cytoskeleton are not well understood. Semaphorins are a large family of these cues that have been studied for their effects on cell movement, navigation, angiogenesis, immunology, and cancer. However, the molecules that connect semaphorins to the precise control of cytoskeletal elements remain unknown. Recently, a new family of proteins called Mical has been found to associate with plexin receptors on the cell surface and mediate axon guidance, synaptogenesis, dendritic pruning, and other cell morphological changes. Mical enzymes perform redox reactions and contain domains that regulate cell morphology, but their role in mediating morphological changes is unknown.
Our study shows that Mical directly links semaphorins and plexin receptors to the precise control of actin filament dynamics in vivo. We found that Mical is both necessary and sufficient for semaphorin-plexin-mediated F-actin reorganization in vivo. Additionally, we purified Mical protein and found that it directly binds F-actin and disassembles both individual and bundled actin filaments. We also discovered that Mical utilizes its redox activity to alter F-actin dynamics in vivo and in vitro, indicating a previously unknown role for specific redox signaling events in actin cytoskeletal regulation. Mical is therefore a novel F-actin-disassembly factor that provides a molecular conduit through which actin reorganization, a hallmark of cell morphological changes including axon navigation, can be precisely achieved spatiotemporally in response to semaphorins.

title: Novel Foxo1-dependent transcriptional programs control Treg cell function
text: Regulatory T (Treg) cells, characterized by the expression of the transcription factor forkhead box P3 (Foxp3), maintain immune homeostasis by suppressing self-destructive immune responses. Foxp3 acts as a late-acting differentiation factor controlling Treg cell homeostasis and function, while the early commitment of Treg cells is regulated by the Akt kinase and the forkhead box O (Foxo) family of transcription factors. However, the extent to which Foxo proteins regulate Treg cell homeostasis and function beyond the commitment stage remains unclear. Our study shows that Foxo1 is a crucial regulator of Treg cell function. Treg cells exhibit high levels of Foxo1 and display reduced T-cell receptor-induced Akt activation, Foxo1 phosphorylation, and Foxo1 nuclear exclusion. Mice lacking Foxo1 in Treg cells develop a fatal inflammatory disorder similar to that seen in Foxp3-deficient mice, but without the loss of Treg cells. Genome-wide analysis of Foxo1 binding sites reveals approximately 300 Foxo1-bound target genes, including the pro-inflammatory cytokine interferon gamma (Ifng), which are not directly regulated by Foxp3. These findings demonstrate that the evolutionarily ancient Akt–Foxo1 signaling module controls a novel genetic program essential for Treg cell function.

title: Functional screening identifies miRNAs inducing cardiac regeneration
text:
In mammals, the growth of the heart during embryonic development is primarily driven by an increase in the number of cardiomyocytes. After birth, cardiomyocytes cease to proliferate, and the heart grows through hypertrophic enlargement of existing myocytes. Due to the limited ability of cardiomyocytes to renew themselves in adulthood, repair of cardiac damage through myocardial regeneration is limited. However, we have found that the exogenous administration of selected microRNAs (miRNAs) significantly stimulates cardiomyocyte proliferation and promotes cardiac repair.
We used a high-content microscopy and high-throughput functional screening for human miRNAs that promote neonatal cardiomyocyte proliferation using a whole-genome miRNA library. Forty miRNAs were identified that strongly increased both DNA synthesis and cytokinesis in neonatal mouse and rat cardiomyocytes. Two of these miRNAs, hsa-miR-590 and hsa-miR-199a, were further tested and shown to promote cell cycle re-entry of adult cardiomyocytes ex vivo and to stimulate cardiomyocyte proliferation in both neonatal and adult animals. In mice after myocardial infarction, these miRNAs led to marked cardiac regeneration and almost complete recovery of cardiac functional parameters. The miRNAs identified have great potential for the treatment of cardiac pathologies resulting from cardiomyocyte loss.

title: Specificity of sensory–motor connections encoded by Sema3e–Plxnd1 recognition
text: Spinal reflexes are mediated by synaptic connections between sensory afferents and motor neurons, which demonstrate a hierarchical organization of specificity at multiple levels. Only certain classes of proprioceptive sensory neurons establish direct, monosynaptic connections with motor neurons, which are governed by rules of motor pool specificity, where they form strong connections with motor neurons supplying the same muscle while avoiding those supplying antagonistic muscles. This pattern of connectivity is initially established accurately and maintained in the absence of activity, suggesting that the specificity of wiring relies on the matching of recognition molecules on the surface of sensory and motor neurons. However, the fine specificity of synaptic connections in these reflex circuits remains unresolved, and to address this question, we have employed molecular genetic methods to manipulate recognition proteins expressed by subsets of sensory and motor neurons in mice. Our findings reveal that a recognition system involving the expression of class 3 semaphorin Sema3e by selected motor neuron pools and its high-affinity receptor plexin D1 (Plxnd1) by proprioceptive sensory neurons is a critical determinant of synaptic specificity in sensory–motor circuits. Modifying the profile of Sema3e–Plxnd1 signaling in sensory or motor neurons leads to functional and anatomical rewiring of monosynaptic connections without altering motor pool specificity, indicating that patterns of monosynaptic connectivity in this prototypic central nervous system circuit are constructed through a recognition program based on repellent signaling.

title: A chromatin remodelling complex involved in transcription and DNA processing.
text: The packaging of eukaryotic DNA within chromatin creates barriers that hinder the access of enzymes that process DNA, requiring cells to have specialized multi-protein complexes called chromatin remodeling complexes. These complexes, each containing an ATPase subunit from the SNF2/SWI2 superfamily, use ATP hydrolysis to increase nucleosome mobility and are essential for transcription. In this study, we analyzed SNF2/SWI2- and ISWI-related proteins to identify remodeling complexes that may assist other DNA transactions. We purified a complex from Saccharomyces cerevisiae containing the Ino80 ATPase, which is involved in chromatin remodeling, transcription, and DNA damage repair. The purified complex displays 3' to 5' DNA helicase activity and facilitates transcription in vitro. Mutants of ino80 are hypersensitive to agents that cause DNA damage and have defects in transcription, suggesting that chromatin remodeling driven by the Ino80 ATPase is connected to both transcription and DNA damage repair.

title: Oncogenic pathway signatures in human cancers as a guide to targeted therapies
text:
The process of developing cancer is a complex one, involving the accumulation of multiple mutations that disrupt the normal regulation of cell growth and fate. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of using DNA microarray-based gene expression signatures to define cancer subtypes, predict disease recurrence, and identify responses to specific therapies. These signatures can also be used to analyze oncogenic pathways and identify patterns of deregulation in tumors.
In this study, we show that gene expression signatures can be identified that reflect the activation status of several oncogenic pathways. When evaluated in large collections of human cancers, these signatures identify patterns of pathway deregulation in tumors and have clinically relevant associations with disease outcomes. By combining signature-based predictions across multiple pathways, we can identify coordinated patterns of pathway deregulation that distinguish between specific cancers and tumor subtypes. Clustering tumors based on pathway signatures further defines prognosis in respective patient subsets, highlighting the importance of oncogenic pathway deregulation in the development and progression of cancer.
In addition, we demonstrate that predictions of pathway deregulation in cancer cell lines can predict the sensitivity to therapeutic agents that target components of the pathway. By linking pathway deregulation with sensitivity to therapeutics, we can use these oncogenic pathway signatures to guide the use of targeted therapies. Overall, our findings provide a powerful tool for understanding the complex biology of cancer and for developing personalized therapies that target the underlying oncogenic pathways.

title: CTCF mediates methylation-sensitive enhancer-blocking activity at the H19/Igf2 locus.
text:
The Insulin-like Growth Factor 2 (Igf2) and H19 genes are imprinted, resulting in the silencing of the maternal and paternal alleles, respectively. This event is dependent on an imprinted control region located two kilobases upstream of H19 (References 1, 2). On the paternal chromosome, this element is methylated, leading to the silencing of H19 (References 2-4). On the maternal chromosome, the region remains unmethylated, which is necessary for the silencing of the Igf2 gene located 90 kilobases upstream (References 5, 6).
We have proposed that the unmethylated imprinted control region acts as a chromatin boundary, blocking the interaction of Igf2 with enhancers located 3' of H19 (References 5, 6). This enhancer-blocking activity is lost when the region is methylated, allowing paternal expression of Igf2.
Using transgenic mice and tissue culture, we have shown that the unmethylated imprinted control regions from mouse and human H19 exhibit enhancer-blocking activity (References 7, 8). Furthermore, we have found that the zinc finger protein CTCF binds to several sites in the unmethylated imprinted control region, which are essential for enhancer blocking (References 9, 10). Consistent with our model, CTCF binding is abolished by DNA methylation.
Our findings provide the first example of a regulated chromatin boundary in vertebrates, highlighting the importance of epigenetic markings in controlling gene expression.

title: Broad and potent neutralization of HIV-1 by a gp41-specific human antibody
text: Characterization of human monoclonal antibodies has provided significant insights into the mechanisms of broad HIV-1 neutralization. In this study, we report an HIV-1 gp41 membrane-proximal external region (MPER)-specific antibody, designated 10E8, which neutralizes approximately 98% of tested viruses. An analysis of sera from 78 healthy HIV-1-infected donors revealed that 27% contained MPER-specific antibodies and 8% contained 10E8-like specificities. In contrast to other neutralizing MPER antibodies, 10E8 did not bind phospholipids, was not autoreactive, and bound cell-surface envelope. The structure of 10E8 in complex with the complete MPER revealed a site of vulnerability consisting of a narrow stretch of highly conserved gp41-hydrophobic residues and a critical arginine or lysine prior to the transmembrane region. Analysis of resistant HIV-1 variants confirmed the importance of these residues for neutralization. The highly conserved MPER is a target of potent, non-self-reactive neutralizing antibodies, suggesting that HIV-1 vaccines should aim to induce antibodies to this region of HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein.

title: Disruption of the Hepcidin/Ferroportin Regulatory System Causes Pulmonary Iron Overload and Restrictive Lung Disease
text: New research suggests that excessive iron buildup in the lungs may play a role in a range of chronic lung diseases. However, the specific mechanisms involved in this process and the role of iron in the development of lung diseases are still not well understood. To investigate, we examined mice with a specific genetic mutation that affects the ferroportin gene, which is responsible for regulating iron levels in the body. We found that these mice had significantly higher levels of iron in their alveolar macrophages, epithelial cells lining the airways, and lung tissue compared to normal mice. This excess iron was associated with increased oxidative stress and a restrictive lung disease characterized by decreased total lung capacity and reduced blood oxygen saturation. These findings suggest that iron may play a role in the development of lung disease, which is not typically considered a classical iron-related disorder.

title: Genome-wide genetic analysis of polyploidy in yeast
text: Polyploidy, characterized by an increase in the number of chromosomes, is a common occurrence during development, cellular stress, and disease. Despite its prevalence, the physiological consequences of polyploidy are not well understood. Previous studies have identified 'ploidy-specific lethality', where gene deletions that are not lethal in haploid or diploid organisms can lead to lethality in triploid or tetraploid cells. To further elucidate the mechanisms underlying ploidy-specific lethality, we conducted a genome-wide screen to identify mutations that exhibit ploidy-specific lethality. Our screen identified 39 out of 3,740 mutations that exhibited ploidy-specific lethality, all of which affected genomic stability by impairing homologous recombination, sister chromatid cohesion, or mitotic spindle function. We uncovered defects in wild-type tetraploids predicted by the screen and elucidated mechanisms by which tetraploidization affects genomic stability. Specifically, we found that tetraploids have a high incidence of syntelic/monopolar kinetochore attachments to the spindle pole, which can be attributed to mismatches in the ability to scale the size of the spindle pole body, spindle, and kinetochores. These findings suggest that geometric constraints can have profound effects on genome stability, and may be relevant in a variety of biological contexts, including disease states such as cancer.

title: Diverse and heritable lineage imprinting of early haematopoietic progenitors
text:
The production of blood cells by haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and their progenitors is a complex process, with ongoing debates about the precise mechanisms involved. One model suggests that lymphoid and myeloid production branch off from a lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitor (LMPP), with both branches subsequently producing dendritic cells. However, this model has been primarily based on in vitro clonal assays and population-based tracking in vivo, which may overlook the in vivo single-cell complexity.
To address these limitations, we employed a novel version of 'cellular barcoding' to trace the in vivo fate of hundreds of LMPPs and HSCs at the single-cell level. Our findings reveal that LMPPs are highly heterogeneous in the cell types they produce, with some producing combinations of lymphoid-, myeloid-, and dendritic-cell-biased producers. Conversely, although we observe a known lineage bias of some HSCs, most cellular output is derived from a small number of HSCs that each generates all cell types.
Furthermore, our in vivo analysis of the output of sibling cells derived from single LMPPs shows that they often share a similar fate, suggesting that the fate of these progenitors was imprinted. This imprinting is also observed for dendritic-cell-biased LMPPs, which may indicate that dendritic cells constitute a distinct lineage with separate ancestry. These findings support a 'graded commitment' model of haematopoiesis, in which heritable and diverse lineage imprinting occurs earlier than previously thought.

title: Crowding induces live cell extrusion to maintain homeostatic cell numbers in epithelia
text:
Epithelial tissues rely on the maintenance of a delicate balance between cell proliferation and cell death to ensure proper function and prevent overcrowding. To maintain homeostasis, the number of dividing cells must be matched with the number of dying cells. While compensatory cell division can be triggered by cell death, the mechanisms underlying the relief of overcrowding due to proliferation remain unclear.
Our studies have shown that the extrusion of live cells from epithelial tissues is a critical mechanism for controlling cell numbers during homeostasis. When we induce cell death in epithelial tissues, dying cells are extruded through the formation of an actomyosin ring, which squeezes the cell out of the tissue. However, the drivers of cell death during normal homeostasis are not well understood.
To investigate this, we examined the effects of overcrowding on epithelial cell numbers in human, canine, and zebrafish tissues. Our results show that overcrowding induced by proliferation and migration leads to the extrusion of live cells from the tissue, with the highest levels of extrusion occurring at sites of highest crowding in vivo. In vitro, overcrowding can also induce extrusion of live cells, which requires sphingosine 1-phosphate signaling and Rho-kinase-dependent myosin contraction. Notably, the extrusion of live cells is distinct from apoptotic cell extrusion, as it involves signaling through stretch-activated channels.
Furthermore, we found that disruption of the stretch-activated channel Piezo1 in zebrafish prevents extrusion and leads to the formation of epithelial cell masses. These findings suggest that live cell extrusion may serve as a tumor-suppressive mechanism that prevents the accumulation of excess epithelial cells.
In summary, our studies reveal that overcrowding in epithelial tissues leads to the extrusion of live cells, which is a critical mechanism for maintaining homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of excess cells. Understanding the mechanisms underlying this process may provide insights into the development of new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of epithelial-related diseases.

title: Direct observation of ligand recognition by T cells
text: The activation of T cells through the interaction of their T-cell receptors with antigenic peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on the surface of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) is a critical step in the adaptive immune response. To investigate this process in single cells, we employed three-dimensional fluorescence microscopy to visualize individual peptide-MHC complexes labeled with the fluorescent protein phycoerythrin. Our goal was to characterize T-cell sensitivity and the requirements for forming an immunological synapse. We found that CD4-expressing T cells responded to even a single agonist peptide-MHC ligand with transient calcium signaling.
