The organization of molecules in the contact zone between the T cell and APC took on the characteristics of an immunological synapse when only about ten ligands were present. This sensitivity was highly dependent on CD4, as blocking this molecule with antibodies rendered T cells unable to detect fewer than about 30 ligands.

title: Crypt stem cells as the cells-of-origin of intestinal cancer
text: Intestinal cancer originates from mutations in genes such as adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) in the Wnt signaling pathway. Despite being a common occurrence in cancer, the cell of origin has remained elusive. To investigate this further, we established a tamoxifen-inducible Cre recombinase mouse model expressing Lgr5 (leucine-rich-repeat containing G-protein-coupled receptor 5) in long-lived intestinal stem cells. When we deleted Apc in these stem cells, they transformed into cancer cells within days, which then grew and formed microadenomas at the crypt bottoms. These microadenomas showed unimpeded growth and developed into macroscopic adenomas within 3-5 weeks. The distribution of Lgr5+ cells within the adenomas indicated that a stem cell/progenitor cell hierarchy was maintained in early neoplastic lesions. When Apc was deleted in short-lived transit-amplifying cells using a different Cre mouse, the growth of the induced microadenomas rapidly stalled. Even after 30 weeks, large adenomas were rare in these mice, indicating that stem-cell-specific loss of Apc leads to progressive growth of neoplasia.

title: Microbial engineering for the production of advanced biofuels
text: Advanced biofuels produced by microorganisms share similar properties with petroleum-based fuels and can seamlessly integrate into the existing transportation infrastructure. However, achieving high enough yields for practical use requires the genetic engineering of the microorganism's metabolism. This involves the use of data-driven and synthetic biology approaches to optimize both the host organism and the metabolic pathways for maximum fuel production. While there have been some promising developments, significant challenges must still be addressed to commercialize advanced biofuels and compete with conventional fuels.

title: Sperm chromatin proteomics identifies evolutionarily conserved fertility factors
text:
Male infertility has long been a mysterious medical issue of significant concern. The integrity of sperm chromatin is a crucial indicator of male fertility and potential for in vitro fertilization. Chromosome aneuploidy and DNA damage are associated with reproductive failure. Identifying conserved proteins essential for sperm chromatin structure and packaging can reveal common causes of infertility.
To address this, we combined proteomics, cytology, and functional analysis in Caenorhabditis elegans to identify spermatogenic chromatin-associated proteins crucial for fertility. Our approach involved several steps: purification of chromatin from comparable meiotic cell types, such as those undergoing spermatogenesis or oogenesis; proteomic analysis using multidimensional protein identification technology (MudPIT) to identify factors that co-purify with chromatin; prioritizing sperm proteins based on abundance; and eliminating general chromatin and meiotic factors through subtraction.
Our strategy reduced a list of 1,099 proteins co-purified with spermatogenic chromatin to 132 proteins for functional analysis. Through RNA interference and protein localization studies, we discovered conserved spermatogenesis-specific proteins essential for DNA compaction, chromosome segregation, and fertility. Unexpected roles in spermatogenesis were also found for factors involved in other processes. Our approach successfully identified fertility factors conserved from C. elegans to mammals, with 37% (7/19) of mouse gene knockouts corresponding to nematode proteins causing male sterility. Our list provides significant opportunities to uncover causes of male infertility and potential targets for male contraceptives.

title: Nanog safeguards pluripotency and mediates germline development
text: Nanog is a divergent homeodomain protein that plays a crucial role in the maintenance of pluripotency in mammalian pluripotent cells and developing germ cells. Deletion of Nanog leads to early embryonic lethality, while constitutive expression enables autonomous self-renewal of embryonic stem cells, making Nanog a core element of the pluripotent transcriptional network. However, our study reveals that Nanog fluctuates in mouse embryonic stem cells, with transient downregulation of Nanog appearing to predispose cells towards differentiation but not marking commitment. Genetic deletion of Nanog from embryonic stem cells shows that, although they are prone to differentiate, these cells can self-renew indefinitely in the absence of Nanog. Moreover, expanded Nanog null cells colonize embryonic germ layers and exhibit multilineage differentiation both in fetal and adult chimaeras. Interestingly, although Nanog-deficient primordial germ cells are recruited to the germ line, they fail to mature on reaching the genital ridge, a defect that can be rescued by repair of the mutant allele. These findings suggest that Nanog is dispensable for expression of somatic pluripotency but is specifically required for formation of germ cells. Therefore, Nanog acts primarily in the construction of inner cell mass and germ cell states rather than in the housekeeping machinery of pluripotency. Our study also suggests that Nanog stabilizes embryonic stem cells in culture by resisting or reversing alternative gene expression states.

title: Succinate is an inflammatory signal that induces IL-1β through HIF-1α
text: Macrophages activated by the Gram-negative bacterial product lipopolysaccharide shift their core metabolism from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis. Our findings show that inhibiting glycolysis with 2-deoxyglucose reduces lipopolysaccharide-induced interleukin-1β production but not tumour-necrosis factor-α in mouse macrophages. A comprehensive metabolic map of lipopolysaccharide-activated macrophages reveals upregulation of glycolytic genes and downregulation of mitochondrial genes, which correlates with the expression profiles of altered metabolites. Lipopolysaccharide significantly increases the levels of the tricarboxylic-acid cycle intermediate succinate, with glutamine-dependent anaplerosis being the primary source. The 'GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) shunt' pathway also plays a role in succinate production. Lipopolysaccharide-induced succinate stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, an effect that is inhibited by 2-deoxyglucose, with interleukin-1β being an important target. Additionally, lipopolysaccharide increases succinylation of several proteins. Therefore, we identify succinate as a key metabolite in innate immune signalling, which enhances interleukin-1β production during inflammation.

title: Planar cell polarity signalling couples cell division and morphogenesis during neurulation
text: Environmental and genetic aberrations can lead to neural tube closure defects (NTDs) in approximately 1 in every 1,000 births. Mouse and frog models have suggested that Van Gogh-like 2 (Vangl2, also known as Strabismus) and other components of planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling may play a crucial role in controlling neurulation by promoting the convergence of neural progenitors towards the midline. Our study reveals a novel function for PCP signaling during neurulation in zebrafish, where non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling polarizes neural progenitors along the anteroposterior axis. This polarity is transiently lost during cell division in the neural keel, but is re-established as daughter cells reintegrate into the neuroepithelium. Mutations in zebrafish Vangl2 (in trilobite mutants) abrogate the polarization of neural keel cells, disrupt re-intercalation of daughter cells into the neuroepithelium, and result in ectopic neural progenitor accumulations and NTDs. Notably, blocking cell division leads to the rescue of trilobite neural tube morphogenesis despite persistent defects in convergence and extension, revealing a previously unappreciated mechanism that may underlie NTDs.

title: The challenge of new drug discovery for tuberculosis
text: Tuberculosis (TB) is currently more prevalent globally than at any other time in human history, with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the pathogen responsible for the disease, employing various strategies to survive and evade the immune system within different host lesions. A pressing concern is the need to enhance the effectiveness of TB drug discovery approaches and identify new molecular scaffolds to combat the emergence of multi-drug-resistant strains of M. tuberculosis. The urgency of this situation has even led to the re-evaluation and repurposing of some old drug families. The success of any strategy will depend heavily on a thorough understanding of the intricate interactions between the pathogen and its human host. This review aims to discuss recent innovations in TB drug discovery and evolving strategies to accelerate the development and delivery of newer agents to patients.

title: Subunit Arrangement and Phenylethanolamine Binding in GluN1/GluN2B NMDA Receptors
text: Since the discovery that the anti-hypertensive agent ifenprodil has neuroprotective effects through its interaction with NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptors, there has been a concerted effort to understand the mechanism of action and develop improved therapeutic compounds based on this knowledge. Neurotransmission mediated by NMDA receptors is essential for normal brain development and function, and these receptors are composed of heteromeric ion channels that are activated by the simultaneous binding of glycine and glutamate to the GluN1 and GluN2 subunits, respectively. A unique feature of NMDA receptors is that their ion channel activity is allosterically regulated by the binding of small molecules to the amino-terminal domain (ATD) in a subtype-specific manner. Ifenprodil and related phenylethanolamine compounds, which specifically inhibit GluN1 and GluN2B NMDA receptors, have been extensively studied for their potential use in treating various neurological disorders and diseases, including depression, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease. However, the mechanisms underlying the recognition of phenylethanolamines and ATD-mediated allosteric inhibition are still poorly understood due to a lack of structural information. Here, we report that the GluN1 and GluN2B ATDs form a heterodimer, and that phenylethanolamine binds at the interface between these subunits, rather than within the GluN2B cleft. The crystal structure of the heterodimer formed between the GluN1b ATD from Xenopus laevis and the GluN2B ATD from Rattus norvegicus reveals the molecular determinants for phenylethanolamine binding. Furthermore, engineering of an inter-subunit disulfide bond in the bi-lobed structure of the GluN2B ATD significantly decreases sensitivity to ifenprodil, indicating that conformational freedom in the GluN2B ATD is essential for ifenprodil-mediated allosteric inhibition of NMDA receptors. These findings pave the way for the design of subtype-specific compounds with therapeutic value for neurological disorders and diseases.

title: Association of NOD2 leucine-rich repeat variants with susceptibility to Crohn's disease.
text: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, the two primary types of chronic inflammatory bowel disease, are complex conditions with unknown causes. Researchers have identified a genetic susceptibility locus for Crohn's disease on chromosome 16. To further investigate the genetic basis of the disease, the authors used a positional-cloning strategy, which involves linkage analysis followed by linkage disequilibrium mapping. This approach led to the identification of three independent associations with Crohn's disease: a frameshift variant and two missense variants of the NOD2 gene, which encodes a member of the Apaf-1/Ced-4 superfamily of apoptosis regulators. These variants affect either the leucine-rich repeat domain of the protein or the adjacent region. NOD2 activates nuclear factor NF-kB, and the carboxy-terminal leucine-rich repeat domain has an inhibitory role and acts as an intracellular receptor for microbial pathogens. These findings suggest that the NOD2 gene product confers susceptibility to Crohn's disease by altering the recognition of pathogens and/or by over-activating NF-kB in monocytes, providing a molecular model for the pathogenic mechanism of the disease that can now be further investigated.

title: Human cardiovascular progenitor cells develop from a KDR+ embryonic-stem-cell-derived population
text: The functional heart is composed of distinct mesoderm-derived lineages, including cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells. Studies in the mouse embryo and mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation model have shown that these three lineages originate from a common Flk-1+ (kinase insert domain protein receptor, also known as Kdr) cardiovascular progenitor, which represents an early stage in mesoderm specification towards the cardiovascular lineages. To investigate whether a similar progenitor exists during human cardiogenesis, we analyzed the development of cardiovascular lineages in human embryonic stem cell differentiation cultures. Our findings demonstrate that after induction with combinations of activin A, bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4), basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF, also known as FGF2), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF, also known as VEGFA), and dickkopf homolog 1 (DKK1) in serum-free media, human embryonic stem-cell-derived embryoid bodies generate a KDRlow/C-KIT(CD117)neg population that exhibits cardiac, endothelial, and vascular smooth muscle potential in vitro and, after transplantation, in vivo. When plated in monolayer cultures, these KDRlow/C-KITneg cells differentiate to generate populations consisting of over 50% contracting cardiomyocytes. Populations derived from the KDRlow/C-KITneg fraction give rise to colonies that contain all three lineages when plated in methylcellulose cultures. Results from limiting dilution studies and cell-mixing experiments support the interpretation that these colonies are clones, indicating that they originate from a human cardiovascular progenitor. Together, these findings identify a progenitor that defines one of the earliest stages of human cardiac development.

title: Cancer-related inflammation
text: The mediators and cellular effectors of inflammation play a crucial role in the local environment of tumors. In some cases, inflammatory conditions exist before the development of cancer, while in others, an oncogenic change triggers an inflammatory microenvironment that fosters tumor growth. Regardless of its origin, chronic inflammation within the tumor microenvironment has far-reaching consequences for cancer progression. It promotes the proliferation and survival of malignant cells, facilitates angiogenesis and metastasis, undermines adaptive immune responses, and alters responses to hormones and chemotherapeutic agents. As researchers continue to unravel the molecular pathways underlying cancer-related inflammation, new target molecules are being identified, paving the way for improved cancer diagnosis and treatment.

title: ESCRT-III recognition by VPS4 ATPases
text:
The ESCRT (endosomal sorting complex required for transport) pathway plays a crucial role in various biological processes, including endosomal intraluminal vesicle formation, HIV budding, and cytokinesis. VPS4 ATPases are essential for these processes by recognizing and disassembling ESCRT-III assemblies, which are involved in membrane fission events. Our study reveals that the MIT (microtubule interacting and transport) domains of human VPS4A and VPS4B proteins bind to conserved sequence motifs located at the carboxy terminus of the CHMP1–3 class of ESCRT-III proteins.
The structures of VPS4A MIT–CHMP1A and VPS4B MIT–CHMP2B complexes were determined, showing that the C-terminal CHMP motif forms an amphipathic helix that binds in a groove between the last two helices of the tetratricopeptide-like repeat (TPR) of the VPS4 MIT domain, but in an opposite orientation to a canonical TPR interaction. The MIT domain also contains distinct pockets that bind to three conserved leucine residues of the CHMP motif, which are essential for VPS4 recruitment and endosomal protein sorting. Mutations that disrupt these interactions impair VPS4 recruitment and relieve dominant-negative VPS4 inhibition of HIV budding, highlighting the importance of these interactions in the VPS4-CHMP interaction.
Our findings provide insight into how VPS4 ATPases recognize and interact with their ESCRT substrates to facilitate membrane fission events, which are crucial for the release of viruses, endosomal vesicles, and daughter cells. Overall, this study sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the ESCRT pathway and its role in various cellular processes.

title: Pif1 family helicases suppress genome instability at G-quadruplex motifs
text: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase serves as a prototype for the Pif1 DNA helicase family, which is conserved across a wide range of organisms, from bacteria to humans. Our findings indicate that Pif1 helicases exhibit exceptional potency in unwinding G-quadruplexes. Moreover, we have discovered that Pif1 helicases from diverse organisms, separated by over 3 billion years of evolution, are capable of suppressing DNA damage at G-quadruplex motifs in yeast. The resulting genetic and epigenetic changes are significant, as they can lead to the formation of new mutations. Interestingly, when expressed in yeast, human PIF1 was able to not only suppress G-quadruplex-induced DNA damage but also regulate telomere length.

title: Lysyl oxidase is essential for hypoxia-induced metastasis
text:
Metastasis is a complex process that accounts for the majority of cancer-related deaths, and it can be influenced by both the immediate microenvironment (cell-cell or cell-matrix interactions) and the broader tumor microenvironment (e.g., vascularization). Hypoxia (low oxygen levels) is clinically associated with metastasis and poor patient outcomes, although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. Microarray studies have shown that the expression of lysyl oxidase (LOX) is elevated in hypoxic human tumor cells. Interestingly, LOX expression is paradoxically associated with both tumor suppression and tumor progression, and its role in tumorigenesis appears to depend on cellular location, cell type, and transformation status.
Our study reveals that LOX expression is regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and is associated with hypoxia in human breast and head and neck tumors. Patients with high LOX-expressing tumors have poor distant metastasis-free and overall survival. In contrast, inhibition of LOX eliminates metastasis in mice with orthotopically grown breast cancer tumors. Mechanistically, secreted LOX is responsible for the invasive properties of hypoxic human cancer cells through focal adhesion kinase activity and cell-matrix adhesion. Furthermore, LOX may be required to create a niche permissive for metastatic growth. Our findings suggest that LOX is essential for hypoxia-induced metastasis and could be a promising therapeutic target for preventing and treating metastases.

title: Identification of human brain tumour initiating cells
text: The cancer stem cell (CSC) hypothesis proposes that malignant clones are maintained by a small fraction of cells with stem cell properties. Although the existence of CSCs in leukemia is well-established, limited evidence exists for CSCs in solid tumors, with the exception of breast cancer. Recently, we isolated a CD133+ cell subpopulation from human brain tumors that exhibited stem cell properties in vitro. However, the true measure of CSCs is their ability to self-renew and recapitulate the original tumor. Here, we report the development of a xenograft assay that identified human brain tumor initiating cells that initiate tumors in vivo. Only the CD133+ brain tumor fraction contained cells capable of tumor initiation in NOD-SCID (non-obese diabetic, severe combined immunodeficient) mouse brains. Injection of as few as 100 CD133+ cells produced a tumor that could be serially transplanted and was a phenocopy of the patient's original tumor, whereas injection of 105 CD133- cells engrafted but did not cause a tumor. This discovery provides insights into human brain tumor pathogenesis and strongly supports the CSC hypothesis as the basis for many solid tumors. Moreover, it identifies a previously unidentified cellular target for more effective cancer therapies.

title: Anthropometric reference data for international use: recommendations from a World Health Organization Expert Committee.
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) convened an Expert Committee to reassess the use of anthropometry at different ages for evaluating health, nutrition, and social wellbeing. The Committee's tasks included establishing reference data for anthropometric indexes when appropriate and providing guidelines on how to use the data. For fetal growth, the Committee recommended an existing sex-specific multiracial reference. However, due to significant technical limitations of the current National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS)/WHO reference and its inadequacy in assessing the growth of breastfed infants, the Committee recommended the development of a new reference for weight and length/height of infants and children, which would be a complex and costly endeavor. Proper interpretation of midupper arm circumference for preschoolers requires age-specific reference data. To evaluate adolescent height-for-age, the Committee recommended using the current NCHS/WHO reference. The use of NCHS body mass index (BMI) data, with their upper percentile elevations and skewness, is not ideal for setting health goals; however, these data were provisionally recommended for defining obesity based on a combination of elevated BMI and high subcutaneous fat. The NCHS values were provisionally recommended as reference data for subscapular and triceps skinfold thicknesses. Guidelines were also provided for adjusting adolescent anthropometric comparisons for maturational status. Currently, there is no need for adult reference data for BMI; interpretation should be based on practical BMI cutoffs. Finally, the Committee noted that few normative anthropometric data exist for the elderly, especially for those over 80 years of age. Proper definitions of health status, function, and biological age remain to be developed for this group.

title: Diverse interventions that extend mouse lifespan suppress shared age-associated epigenetic changes at critical gene regulatory regions
text:
Background: Age-related epigenetic alterations have been implicated in the aging process. Specifically, age-associated DNA methylation changes have been identified as a robust biomarker of aging, referred to as the "aging clock." However, the impact of longevity-promoting interventions, such as genetic, dietary, and drug interventions, on the epigenome is not well understood. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of age-associated DNA methylation changes at the whole-genome, single-nucleotide level in mouse liver and evaluated the effects of three longevity-promoting interventions: the Ames dwarf Prop1 df/df mutation, calorie restriction, and rapamycin.
Results: Our findings revealed age-associated hypomethylation in highly expressed genes critical for liver function in wild-type mice fed an unsupplemented ad libitum diet. These genes were enriched for those that exhibit changes in expression with age. In contrast, hypermethylation was observed at CpG islands marked with bivalent activating and repressing histone modifications, and resembled hypermethylation in liver cancer. Notably, age-associated methylation changes were suppressed in Ames dwarf and calorie-restricted mice, and to a lesser extent in rapamycin-treated mice.
Conclusions: Our study demonstrates that age-associated hypo- and hypermethylation events occur at distinct regulatory features of the genome. The longevity-promoting interventions examined in this study, including genetic, dietary, and drug interventions, suppress some age-associated methylation changes, suggesting that these interventions exert their beneficial effects, in part, by modulating the epigenome. This study provides a foundation for understanding the epigenetic contribution to healthy aging and longevity and the molecular basis of the DNA methylation clock.

title: Extracellular vesicles for drug delivery.
text: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are cell-derived membrane vesicles that facilitate intercellular communication through the transfer of biological information. Recent discoveries have piqued scientific interest in using EVs as drug delivery vehicles, as they may offer several advantages over existing delivery methods. These advantages include the ability to bypass natural barriers, target specific cells, and maintain stability in the circulation. However, the therapeutic potential of EVs has been limited due to challenges in scaling up their isolation and efficiently loading drugs. To achieve targeted drug delivery, the intrinsic cell-targeting properties of EVs must be engineered. Here, we provide an overview of recent progress and remaining challenges in the development of EVs as drug delivery vehicles.

title: Effects of soy isoflavones and phytate on homocysteine, C-reactive protein, and iron status in postmenopausal women.
text:
BACKGROUND: Soy protein or its components may offer protection against atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors, including total homocysteine (tHcy), C-reactive protein (CRP), and excess body iron, which tend to increase during menopause.
OBJECTIVE: The primary objective of this study was to determine the independent effect of soy protein components, isoflavones and phytate, on CVD risk factors in postmenopausal women. The secondary objective was to identify factors (blood lipids, oxidative stress indexes, serum ferritin, plasma folate, plasma vitamin B-12, and body mass index (BMI)) contributing to tHcy and CRP concentrations.
DESIGN: This double-blind, 6-week study randomly assigned 55 postmenopausal women aged 47-72 years to one of four soy protein (40 g/d) isolate treatments: native phytate and native isoflavone (n=14), native phytate and low isoflavone (n=13), low phytate and native isoflavone (n=14), or low phytate and low isoflavone (n=14). The study measured iron indexes, tHcy, CRP, and BMI.
RESULTS: Soy protein with native phytate significantly reduced tHcy (P=0.017), transferrin saturation (P=0.027), and ferritin (P=0.029), whereas soy protein with native isoflavones had no effect on any variables. At baseline, BMI was highly correlated with tHcy (r=0.39, P=0.003) and CRP (r=0.55, P<0.0001), whereas HDL cholesterol was correlated with CRP (r=-0.30, P=0.02). Multiple regression analysis showed that LDL cholesterol and BMI contributed significantly (R2=19.9%, P=0.003) to the overall variance in tHcy.
CONCLUSION: Consuming phytate-rich foods and maintaining a healthy weight may reduce atherosclerotic CVD risk factors in postmenopausal women.

title: Replication Fork Stability Confers Chemoresistance in BRCA-deficient Cells
text: Cells lacking the Brca1 and Brca2 genes have impaired capacity for DNA double-strand break repair through homologous recombination, making them more sensitive to DNA-damaging agents such as cisplatin and PARP inhibitors. In this study, we found that loss of the MLL3/4 complex protein, PTIP, protects Brca1/2-deficient cells from DNA damage and rescues the lethality of Brca2-deficient embryonic stem cells. However, PTIP deficiency does not restore homologous recombination activity at double-strand breaks. Instead, its absence inhibits the recruitment of the MRE11 nuclease to stalled replication forks, thereby protecting nascent DNA strands from extensive degradation. Our findings suggest that acquisition of PARP inhibitors and cisplatin resistance in Brca2-deficient tumor cells is associated with replication fork protection, which is independent of Brca2 reversion mutations. Disruption of multiple proteins, including PARP1 and CHD4, leads to the same outcome of replication fork protection, highlighting the complex mechanisms by which tumor cells evade chemotherapeutic interventions and acquire drug resistance.

title: Plasma Corin as a Predictor of Cardiovascular Events in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure.
text:
Objective: To investigate the prognostic value of plasma corin in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF).
Background: Corin, a protein produced by the cardiac ventricles, has been shown to play a crucial role in regulating blood pressure and cardiac function. However, its prognostic value in CHF patients has not been well-established.
Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study of 1,148 CHF patients and analyzed the association between plasma corin levels and clinical prognosis using multivariate Cox regression analysis.
Results: Our findings revealed that patients with low corin levels (<458 pg/ml) were more likely to be women and hypertensive, and were associated with increased New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, and decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Multivariate Cox regression analysis showed that log corin was an independent predictor of major adverse cardiac event(s) (MACE) (hazard ratio: 0.62; 95% confidence interval: 0.39 to 0.95), along with age, diabetes, NYHA functional class, LVEF, eGFR, and log NT-proBNP. Additionally, log corin was a significant predictor of cardiovascular death (p = 0.041) and heart failure rehospitalization (p = 0.015) after adjusting for clinical variables and established biomarkers of adverse prognosis. The Kaplan-Meier survival curves showed that low corin was a significant predictor of MACE in patients with NT-proBNP levels above and below the median.
Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that plasma corin is a valuable prognostic marker of MACE in patients with CHF, independent of established conventional risk factors.

title: Cryo-EM structures of Tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease brain
text:
Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, and currently, there are no disease-modifying therapies available. The condition is characterized by the presence of abundant neurofibrillary lesions and neuritic plaques in the cerebral cortex. Neurofibrillary lesions are composed of paired helical and straight tau filaments, which are distinct from the tau filaments found in other neurodegenerative diseases. However, high-resolution structures of these tau filaments have not been previously available.
In this study, we present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps at 3.4-3.5 Å resolution and corresponding atomic models of paired helical and straight filaments isolated from the brain tissue of an individual with Alzheimer's disease. Our findings reveal that the filament cores of these tau filaments are composed of two identical protofilaments, spanning residues 306-378 of the tau protein, which adopt a combined cross-β/β-helix structure. This structure serves as the seed for tau aggregation. Interestingly, paired helical and straight filaments differ in their inter-protofilament packing, indicating that they are ultrastructural polymorphs.
Our study demonstrates the potential of cryo-EM to atomic characterize amyloid filaments derived from patient-derived material, paving the way for investigating a range of neurodegenerative diseases. This work provides a crucial step towards understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying these devastating disorders and may ultimately lead to the development of mechanism-based therapies.

title: Modulation of the proteoglycan receptor PTPσ promotes recovery after spinal cord injury
text: Contusive spinal cord injury often leads to a range of disabilities due to limited neuronal regeneration and functional plasticity. It is well established that an increase in glial-derived chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans (CSPGs) within the glial scar and perineuronal net creates a barrier to axonal regrowth and sprouting. Recently, protein tyrosine phosphatase σ (PTPσ), along with its sister phosphatase leukocyte common antigen-related (LAR), and the nogo receptors 1 and 3 (NgR), have been identified as receptors for the inhibitory glycosylated side chains of CSPGs. Our study found that PTPσ plays a critical role in converting growth cones into a dystrophic state by stabilizing them within CSPG-rich substrates. We developed a membrane-permeable peptide mimetic of the PTPσ wedge domain that binds to PTPσ and relieves CSPG-mediated inhibition. Systemic delivery of this peptide over several weeks restored significant serotonergic innervation to the spinal cord below the level of injury and facilitated functional recovery of both locomotor and urinary systems. Our findings add a new layer of understanding to the critical role of PTPσ in mediating the growth-inhibited state of neurons due to CSPGs within the injured adult spinal cord.

title: A gp130–Src–YAP module links inflammation to epithelial regeneration
text: Inflammation fosters the regeneration of damaged tissues through mysterious mechanisms, some of which involve interleukin (IL)-6 family members, the expression of which is heightened in various diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases and colorectal cancer. We demonstrate in mice and human cells that gp130, a co-receptor for IL-6 cytokines, triggers the activation of YAP and Notch, transcriptional regulators that control tissue growth and regeneration, independently of the gp130 effector STAT3. Through YAP and Notch, intestinal gp130 signaling stimulates epithelial cell proliferation, leads to aberrant differentiation, and confers resistance to mucosal erosion. gp130 interacts with related tyrosine kinases Src and Yes, which are activated upon receptor engagement to phosphorylate YAP and induce its stabilization and nuclear translocation. This signaling module is significantly activated upon mucosal injury to promote healing and maintain barrier function.

title: Hemoglobin concentration in white, black, and Oriental children: is there a need for separate criteria in screening for anemia?
text: According to several large surveys, the concentration of hemoglobin in Black individuals was found to be 0.5 to 1.0 g/dl lower than that of income-matched Whites. It is unclear whether this difference is due to a genetic trait, such as thalassemia minor or hemoglobinopathies, or to environmental factors like iron deficiency. To investigate this further, we analyzed data from multiphasic examinations conducted on 1718 White, 741 Black, and 315 Oriental children between the ages of 5 and 14. Our findings revealed that the median hemoglobin concentration was 0.5 g/dl lower in Black children compared to White children of both sexes (P less than 0.001). After excluding individuals with abnormal hemoglobin by electrophoresis (Hgb S and C) and those with a mean corpuscular volume more than 5% below the normal mean for age (to exclude iron deficiency or thalassemia minor), the difference remained statistically significant at 0.5 g/dl (P less than 0.001). These findings suggest that Black individuals may have a natural hemoglobin concentration that is approximately 0.5 g/dl lower than that of Whites, which could result in approximately 10% of normal Black individuals being misdiagnosed as anemic if the same diagnostic criteria are applied.

title: Divergent reprogramming routes lead to alternative stem-cell states
text: Pluripotency is characterized by a cell's ability to differentiate into all three embryonic germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Pluripotent cells can be obtained through two methods: derivation from embryonic stem cells or reprogramming of somatic cells through the forced expression of key transcription factors. However, it is unknown whether there are additional classes of pluripotent cells or the full range of reprogrammed phenotypes. To investigate, we studied reprogrammed cells without preconceived notions of iPSC states and demonstrated that mouse embryonic fibroblasts can undergo unique epigenetic modifications to reach a stable, Nanog-positive alternative pluripotent state. This discovery expands our understanding of the pluripotent spectrum, revealing that it encompasses multiple unique cell states.

title: Autophagy mediates degradation of nuclear lamina
text:
Macroautophagy, commonly referred to as autophagy, is a cellular process that degrades various cellular components and is implicated in various human diseases. While significant research has focused on the degradation of cytoplasmic materials through autophagy, little is known about the role of autophagy in degrading nuclear components. Our study uncovers a novel function of autophagy in degrading nuclear lamina components in mammals.
The autophagy protein LC3/Atg8, which plays a crucial role in autophagy membrane trafficking and substrate delivery, is present in the nucleus and interacts with the nuclear lamina protein lamin B1. This interaction does not downregulate lamin B1 during starvation but mediates its degradation upon oncogenic insults, such as those caused by activated RAS. The degradation of lamin B1 is achieved through nucleus-to-cytoplasm transport that delivers lamin B1 to the lysosome.
Our findings suggest that this newly discovered function of autophagy acts as a protective mechanism against tumorigenesis. Inhibiting autophagy or the LC3-lamin B1 interaction prevents oncogene-induced lamin B1 loss and attenuates senescence in primary human cells.
In summary, our study uncovers a novel role of autophagy in degrading nuclear lamina components, providing a protective mechanism against tumorigenesis. The interaction between LC3 and lamin B1 is a key player in this process, and its inhibition can prevent oncogene-induced senescence in primary human cells.

title: Pro-resolving lipid mediators are leads for resolution physiology
text: Recent breakthroughs in our understanding of the mechanisms underlying the resolution of acute inflammation have led to the discovery of a new class of pro-resolving lipid mediators, known as specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs). This group includes the lipoxin, resolvin, protectin, and maresin families. These mediators have been found to have potent bioactions when administered in vivo, and have been shown to evoke anti-inflammatory and novel pro-resolving mechanisms, as well as enhance microbial clearance in animal models. Interestingly, while SPMs were first identified in the context of inflammation resolution, they are not limited to this function and have been found to play roles in a variety of other physiological processes, including host defense, pain, organ protection, and tissue remodeling. This review aims to provide an overview of the mechanisms of SPMs and the omega-3 essential fatty acid pathways that are involved in their physiological functions.

title: ZMYND11 links histone H3.3K36me3 to transcription elongation and tumour suppression
text:
The recognition of modified histones by 'reader' proteins plays a crucial role in the regulation of chromatin structure and gene expression. Specifically, the trimethylation of lysine 36 on histone H3 (H3K36me3) is deposited onto nucleosomes in transcribed regions after RNA polymerase II elongation in yeast, leading to the recruitment of epigenetic regulators that reset the chromatin to a relatively repressive state, thereby suppressing cryptic transcription. However, the role of H3K36me3 in transcription regulation in mammals is less well understood due to the incorporation of histone variant H3.3 during transcription elongation.
Our study shows that the candidate tumour suppressor ZMYND11 specifically recognizes H3K36me3 on H3.3 (H3.3K36me3) and regulates RNA polymerase II elongation. Structural analysis reveals that the recognition of H3.3K36me3 by ZMYND11 is mediated by the encapsulation of the H3.3-specific 'Ser 31' residue within a composite pocket formed by the tandem bromo-PWWP domains of ZMYND11. Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) analysis demonstrates a genome-wide co-localization of ZMYND11 with H3K36me3 and H3.3 in gene bodies, and its occupancy requires the pre-deposition of H3.3K36me3. Although ZMYND11 is associated with highly expressed genes, it functions as an unconventional transcription co-repressor by modulating RNA polymerase II at the elongation stage.
Our findings identify ZMYND11 as an H3.3-specific reader of H3K36me3 that links the histone-variant-mediated transcription elongation control to tumour suppression. Low expression levels of ZMYND11 in breast cancer patients are associated with worse prognosis, and overexpression of ZMYND11 suppresses cancer cell growth in vitro and tumour formation in mice. Together, these results demonstrate the critical role of ZMYND11 in regulating chromatin structure and gene expression, and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for cancer treatment.

title: Autocrine BDNF–TrkB signalling within a single dendritic spine
text: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its receptor TrkB play a crucial role in various forms of neuronal plasticity, including structural long-term potentiation (sLTP), which is linked to learning in animals. However, it is unknown whether BDNF release and TrkB activation occur during sLTP, and if so, when and where. To investigate this, we used a fluorescence resonance energy transfer-based sensor for TrkB and two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy to monitor TrkB activity in single dendritic spines of CA1 pyramidal neurons in cultured murine hippocampal slices. Our findings show that TrkB is activated rapidly (within 1 minute) and sustained (for over 20 minutes) in the stimulated spine, depending on N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDAR) and calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) signaling, as well as postsynaptically synthesized BDNF. We also demonstrate the presence of postsynaptic BDNF in dendrites and spines of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons using electron microscopy. Furthermore, we show that rapid, glutamate-induced BDNF release from single dendritic spines can be observed using BDNF fused to superecliptic pHluorin. Our findings reveal a spine-autonomous, autocrine signaling mechanism involving NMDAR-CaMKII-dependent BDNF release from stimulated dendritic spines and subsequent TrkB activation on these same spines, which is essential for both structural and functional LTP.

title: Whole genomes redefine the mutational landscape of pancreatic cancer
text: Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most aggressive and debilitating forms of cancer, with a significant impact on public health. To gain a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying this disease, we performed whole-genome sequencing and copy number variation (CNV) analysis on 100 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDACs). Our findings revealed a prevalence of chromosomal rearrangements leading to gene disruption, affecting both well-established cancer-related genes (TP53, SMAD4, CDKN2A, ARID1A, and ROBO2) and novel candidate drivers (KDM6A and PREX2). The analysis also revealed four distinct subtypes of PDACs based on patterns of structural variation (variation in chromosomal structure), which may have clinical implications. Notably, a significant proportion of PDACs harbored focal amplifications, many of which contained druggable oncogenes (ERBB2, MET, FGFR1, CDK6, PIK3R3, and PIK3CA), although at low individual patient prevalence. Furthermore, we found that genomic instability was associated with inactivation of DNA maintenance genes (BRCA1, BRCA2, or PALB2), and a mutational signature of DNA damage repair deficiency. Of the eight patients who received platinum therapy, four of five individuals with measures of defective DNA maintenance exhibited a response.

title: Human oocytes reprogram adult somatic nuclei of a type 1 diabetic to diploid pluripotent stem cells
text: The transfer of somatic cell nuclei into oocytes can result in the generation of pluripotent stem cells that are equivalent to embryonic stem cells, offering promise for autologous cell replacement therapy. Although methods to induce pluripotent stem cells from somatic cells using transcription factors are widely used in basic research, significant differences between induced pluripotent stem cells and embryonic stem cells have been reported, which may impact their clinical applicability. To investigate the parameters affecting the efficiency of blastocyst development and stem cell derivation from somatic cells, we systematically examined the effects of various protocol modifications. Our findings showed that improvements to the oocyte activation protocol, including the use of kinase and translation inhibitors, and cell culture in the presence of histone deacetylase inhibitors, enhanced the development to the blastocyst stage. We also found that the efficiency of development varied between oocyte donors, and was inversely related to the number of days of hormonal stimulation required for oocyte maturation. To overcome the issue of premature oocyte activation caused by concentrated Sendai virus, we used diluted Sendai virus in calcium-free medium. Using this modified nuclear transfer protocol, we successfully derived diploid pluripotent stem cell lines from somatic cells of a newborn and, for the first time, an adult, a female with type 1 diabetes.

title: A three-dimensional human neural cell culture model of Alzheimer’s disease
text:
Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, characterized by two primary pathological hallmarks: amyloid-β plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. The amyloid hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease posits that the excessive accumulation of amyloid-β peptide leads to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles composed of aggregated hyperphosphorylated tau. However, despite extensive research, no single disease model has successfully linked these two pathological events using human neuronal cells.
Mouse models with familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD) mutations exhibit amyloid-β-induced synaptic and memory deficits, but they do not fully recapitulate other key pathological events of Alzheimer's disease, including distinct neurofibrillary tangle pathology. In contrast, human neurons derived from Alzheimer's disease patients have shown elevated levels of toxic amyloid-β species and phosphorylated tau, but did not demonstrate amyloid-β plaques or neurofibrillary tangles.
To address this gap in our understanding, we used a human neural stem-cell-derived three-dimensional (3D) culture system to investigate the effects of FAD mutations in β-amyloid precursor protein and presenilin 1 on amyloid-β deposition. Our results showed that these mutations were able to induce robust extracellular deposition of amyloid-β, including amyloid-β plaques, in the 3D culture system. Furthermore, the 3D-differentiated neuronal cells expressing FAD mutations exhibited high levels of detergent-resistant, silver-positive aggregates of phosphorylated tau in the soma and neurites, as well as filamentous tau, as detected by immunoelectron microscopy.
Inhibition of amyloid-β generation with β- or γ-secretase inhibitors not only decreased amyloid-β pathology, but also attenuated tauopathy. Additionally, we found that glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) regulated amyloid-β-mediated tau phosphorylation. Our findings demonstrate that we have successfully recapitulated amyloid-β and tau pathology in a single 3D human neural cell culture model.
This innovative approach to recapitulating Alzheimer's disease pathology in a 3D neural cell culture model has significant implications for the development of more precise human neural cell models of other neurodegenerative disorders. By providing a platform for studying the complex interplay between amyloid-β and tau pathology, our findings may lead to the identification of new therapeutic targets and strategies for the prevention and treatment of these devastating diseases.

title: Mesenchymal-endothelial-transition contributes to cardiac neovascularization
text: Endothelial cells play a crucial role in cardiac repair by contributing to a subset of cardiac fibroblasts through endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition. However, it remains unclear whether cardiac fibroblasts can directly adopt an endothelial cell fate and contribute to neovascularization after cardiac injury. Using genetic fate map techniques, we have shown that cardiac fibroblasts can rapidly adopt an endothelial-cell-like phenotype after acute ischaemic cardiac injury. These fibroblast-derived endothelial cells exhibit the same anatomical and functional characteristics as native endothelial cells. We have found that the transcription factor p53 regulates this switch in cardiac fibroblast fate, with loss of p53 severely impairing the formation of fibroblast-derived endothelial cells and reducing post-infarct vascular density. Conversely, stimulation of the p53 pathway in cardiac fibroblasts enhances mesenchymal-to-endothelial transition, promotes vascularity, and improves cardiac function. These findings suggest that mesenchymal-to-endothelial transition contributes to neovascularization of the injured heart and represents a potential therapeutic target for enhancing cardiac repair.

title: Estimation of optimal serum concentrations of 25-hydroxyvitamin D for multiple health outcomes.
text: Recent research suggests that vitamin D intakes above the current recommendations may be associated with better health outcomes. However, the optimal serum concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] has not been defined. This review summarizes the evidence from studies that evaluated the thresholds for serum 25(OH)D concentrations in relation to bone mineral density (BMD), lower-extremity function, dental health, and risk of falls, fractures, and colorectal cancer. For all endpoints, the most advantageous serum concentrations of 25(OH)D begin at 75 nmol/L (30 ng/mL), with the best concentrations found between 90 and 100 nmol/L (36-40 ng/mL). In most individuals, these concentrations cannot be reached with the current recommended intakes of 200 and 600 IU vitamin D/d for younger and older adults, respectively. A comparison of vitamin D intakes with achieved serum concentrations of 25(OH)D revealed that, for bone health in younger adults and all studied outcomes in older adults, an increase in the recommended intake of vitamin D is warranted. An intake of at least 1000 IU (25 microg) vitamin D (cholecalciferol)/d is needed to bring vitamin D concentrations in at least 50% of the population up to 75 nmol/L. The implications of higher doses for the entire adult population should be addressed in future studies.

title: Cohesin-dependent globules and heterochromatin shape 3D genome architecture in S. pombe
text: Eukaryotic genomes are organized into complex three-dimensional structures, including self-associating topological domains, whose borders are enriched in cohesin and CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), which are essential for long-range interactions. Despite significant progress in understanding the local chromatin interactions that govern higher-order folding of chromatin fibers, the mechanisms by which cohesin contributes to this process remain poorly understood. To address this gap in knowledge, we performed genome-wide chromatin conformation capture (Hi-C) analysis on the Schizosaccharomyces pombe genome, a small eukaryote that exhibits fundamental features of higher-order chromosome organization. Our findings reveal key elements of chromosome architecture and genome organization in wild-type and mutant strains. On chromosome arms, we observed the formation of 'globules,' small regions of chromatin that interact locally and require a distinct function of cohesin from its role in sister chromatid cohesion. Cohesin is enriched at globule boundaries, and its loss leads to disruption of local globule structures and global chromosome territories. In contrast, heterochromatin, which loads cohesin at specific sites including pericentromeric and subtelomeric domains, is dispensable for globule formation but plays a crucial role in mediating chromatin fibre compaction at centromeres and promoting prominent inter-arm interactions within centromere-proximal regions. These interactions provide structural constraints that are essential for proper genome organization. Loss of heterochromatin leads to relaxation of these constraints, resulting in an increase in intra- and inter-chromosomal interactions. Our findings uncover fundamental genome folding principles that are crucial for coordinating nuclear functions.

title: A temporal shift in the circuits mediating retrieval of fear memory
text: Fear memories allow animals to avoid danger, increasing their chances of survival. However, little is known about how the circuits involved in retrieving these memories change over time. In this study, we investigated the role of the dorsal midline thalamus in the retrieval of auditory conditioned fear in rats. We found that the thalamus is required for the retrieval of fear memories at late time points (24 hours, 7 days, 28 days) but not at early time points (0.5 hours, 6 hours) after learning. Specifically, the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), a subregion of the dorsal midline thalamus, showed increased c-Fos expression only at late time points, indicating that the PVT is gradually recruited for fear retrieval. The prelimbic prefrontal cortex (PL), which is necessary for fear retrieval, sends dense projections to the PVT. Retrieval at late time points activated PL neurons projecting to the PVT, and optogenetic silencing of these projections impaired retrieval at late, but not early, time points. In contrast, silencing of PL inputs to the basolateral amygdala impaired retrieval at early, but not late, time points, indicating a time-dependent shift in retrieval circuits. Additionally, retrieval at late time points activated PVT neurons projecting to the central nucleus of the amygdala, and silencing these projections at late, but not early, time points induced a persistent attenuation of fear. These findings suggest that the PVT may play a crucial role as a thalamic node in cortico-amygdalar networks for the retrieval and maintenance of long-term fear memories.

title: Derivation of novel human ground state naive pluripotent stem cells
text: Mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells are isolated from the inner cell mass of blastocysts and can be maintained in a naive inner-cell-mass-like state in vitro by providing exogenous stimulation with leukaemia inhibitory factor (LIF) and inhibiting certain signaling pathways (termed 2i/LIF conditions). Naive ES cells display characteristics such as driving Oct4 (also known as Pou5f1) transcription by its distal enhancer, retaining a pre-inactivation X chromosome state, and reduced DNA methylation and H3K27me3 repressive chromatin mark deposition on developmental regulatory gene promoters. Upon withdrawal of 2i/LIF, naive mouse ES cells can transition towards a primed pluripotent state similar to that of the post-implantation epiblast. Although human ES cells share some molecular features with naive mouse ES cells, they also exhibit epigenetic differences with primed murine epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs). These include preferential use of a proximal enhancer element to maintain OCT4 expression, pronounced X chromosome inactivation in most female human ES cells, increased DNA methylation, and prominent deposition of H3K27me3 and bivalent domain acquisition on lineage regulatory genes. The feasibility of establishing human ground state naive pluripotency in vitro with equivalent molecular and functional features to those seen in mouse ES cells remains to be determined. Here, we describe conditions that allow the derivation of genetically unmodified human naive pluripotent stem cells from established primed human ES cells, somatic cells through induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell reprogramming, or directly from blastocysts. The novel naive pluripotent cells exhibit molecular characteristics and functional properties similar to those of mouse naive ES cells and distinct from conventional primed human pluripotent cells. For example, they demonstrate competence in generating cross-species chimaeric mouse embryos that undergo organogenesis following microinjection of human naive iPS cells into mouse morulas. Overall, our findings open up new avenues for regenerative medicine, patient-specific iPS cell disease modeling, and the study of early human development in vitro and in vivo.

title: Predicting immunogenic tumour mutations by combining mass spectrometry and exome sequencing
text:
Human tumors typically harbor a remarkable number of somatic mutations, which can make them recognized as "non-self" neo-antigens by the adaptive immune system. Recent studies have confirmed that mutant peptides can serve as T-cell epitopes, but the discovery of these epitopes has been a laborious process that requires the screening of patient tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes to recognize antigen libraries constructed following tumor exome sequencing. To simplify the discovery of immunogenic mutant peptides, we developed an approach that combines whole-exome and transcriptome sequencing analysis with mass spectrometry to identify neo-epitopes in two widely used murine tumor models.
We identified over 1,300 amino acid changes, of which approximately 13% were predicted to bind major histocompatibility complex class I (MHCI). A small fraction of these were confirmed by mass spectrometry. The peptides were then structurally modeled bound to MHCI. Mutations that were solvent-exposed and therefore accessible to T-cell antigen receptors were predicted to be immunogenic. Vaccination of mice with these predicted immunogenic peptides yielded therapeutically active T-cell responses. The predictions also enabled the generation of peptide-MHCI dextramers that could be used to monitor the kinetics and distribution of the anti-tumor T-cell response before and after vaccination. These findings suggest that a suitable prediction algorithm may provide an approach for pharmacodynamic monitoring of T-cell responses as well as for the development of personalized vaccines in cancer patients.

title: In vivo genome editing using Staphylococcus aureus Cas9
text: The RNA-guided endonuclease Cas9 has emerged as a powerful genome-editing tool, but its size limitations hinder its utility in certain applications, particularly when combined with the highly versatile AAV delivery vehicle. To address this challenge, we investigated six smaller Cas9 orthologues and found that Cas9 from Staphylococcus aureus (SaCas9) can edit the genome with comparable efficiency to SpCas9, while being significantly shorter. We packaged SaCas9 and its guide RNA into a single AAV vector and targeted the cholesterol regulatory gene Pcsk9 in the mouse liver, resulting in >40% gene modification and reduced serum Pcsk9 and total cholesterol levels within one week of injection. To assess the specificity of SaCas9 and SpCas9, we used the BLESS assay and demonstrated that SaCas9-mediated in vivo genome editing has the potential to be both efficient and specific.

title: Effects of exercise intensity on cardiovascular fitness, total body composition, and visceral adiposity of obese adolescents.
text: Little is known about how the intensity of exercise affects cardiovascular fitness and body composition in obese adolescents. To investigate this, we assigned 80 obese adolescents (ages 13-16) to one of three groups: lifestyle education (LSE) alone, LSE plus moderate-intensity physical training, or LSE plus high-intensity physical training. The intervention lasted 8 months, and physical training was offered 5 days a week. We found that high-intensity physical training significantly improved cardiovascular fitness compared to moderate-intensity physical training and LSE alone. However, there was no clear difference in the effectiveness of high-intensity and moderate-intensity physical training on body composition. Specifically, both types of physical training led to favorable changes in cardiovascular fitness, percentage of body fat (%BF), and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) in obese adolescents. These findings suggest that high-intensity physical training may be more effective than moderate-intensity physical training in improving cardiovascular fitness in obese adolescents, but there is no clear difference in their effectiveness on body composition.

title: Low methionine ingestion by rats extends life span.
text: Dietary energy restriction has been a widely studied means of increasing mammalian lifespan. Our research shows that reducing the concentration of the essential amino acid L-methionine in the diet from 0.86% to 0.17% in male Fischer 344 rats leads to a 30% increase in lifespan. Methionine restriction resulted in a complete loss of growth, despite increased food intake on a body weight basis. Early-life energy consumption studies revealed that the energy intake of 0.17% methionine-fed animals was near normal for their size, although their consumption per animal was lower than that of larger 0.86% methionine-fed rats. Increasing the energy intake of 0.17% methionine-fed rats did not enhance growth, while restricting the energy intake of 0.85% methionine-fed rats to that of 0.17% methionine-fed animals did not significantly reduce growth, suggesting that food restriction was not the primary factor in life span extension. The well-defined biochemical pathways of methionine metabolism and utilization offer the potential for uncovering the specific mechanism underlying this dietary restriction-related life span extension.

title: Epicatechin and a cocoa polyphenolic extract modulate gene expression in human Caco-2 cells.
text: We conducted a functional genomic analysis to investigate the effects of epicatechin and polyphenolic cocoa extract on human colon adenocarcinoma cells (Caco-2). We used a specific Human Hematology/Immunology cDNA array (Clontech) containing 406 genes in duplicate to analyze the differentially expressed genes. Treatment with epicatechin resulted in the downregulation of 21 genes and the upregulation of 24 genes, while incubation with the cocoa polyphenolic extract led to the underexpression of 24 genes and the overexpression of 28 genes. We validated the changes in expression of four genes (FTH1, MAPKK1, STAT1, and XRCC1) by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Western blotting was used to confirm the changes in protein expression of MAPKK1, STAT1, MRP1, and FTH1 genes. Our findings suggest that the antioxidant properties of cocoa flavonoids are involved in the cellular response to oxidative stress, and that flavonoids may have novel mechanisms of action at the molecular level. Specifically, the downregulation of genes involved in DNA repair (XRCC1) and the upregulation of genes involved in cellular stress response (STAT1) suggest that flavonoids may protect against oxidative stress-induced DNA damage. Additionally, the upregulation of genes involved in cellular transport (MRP1) and protein degradation (FTH1) may contribute to the anti-cancer effects of flavonoids.

title: An atlas of active enhancers across human cell types and tissues
text: Enhancers play a crucial role in the precise temporal and cell-type-specific activation of gene expression in multicellular eukaryotes. Understanding the properties, regulatory activity, and target genes of enhancers is essential to elucidate the mechanisms of cell differentiation and homeostasis. In this study, we leverage the FANTOM5 panel of samples, which covers a wide range of human tissues and cell types, to generate an atlas of active, in vivo-transcribed enhancers. Our findings reveal that enhancers share features with CpG-poor messenger RNA promoters but produce bidirectional, exosome-sensitive, and relatively short unspliced RNAs, the generation of which is highly correlated with enhancer activity. The atlas is used to compare regulatory programs between different cells at an unprecedented level of depth, identify disease-associated regulatory single nucleotide polymorphisms, and classify cell-type-specific and ubiquitous enhancers. Additionally, we explore the functional implications of enhancer redundancy, which explains gene expression strength rather than expression patterns. The online FANTOM5 enhancer atlas represents a unique resource for investigating cell-type-specific enhancers and gene regulation.

title: Precision microbiome reconstitution restores bile acid mediated resistance to Clostridium difficile
text:
The gastrointestinal tracts of mammals are home to hundreds of microbial species that contribute to overall health, including resistance to intestinal pathogens. However, many antibiotics can disrupt these microbial communities and increase susceptibility to pathogens like Clostridium difficile, leading to increased morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients. While some bacteria provide resistance to C. difficile infection, their in vivo inhibitory mechanisms are not well understood.
To investigate, we treated mice with different antibiotics that altered their microbiota in distinct ways, leading to varying susceptibility to C. difficile infection. By analyzing the microbiota of hospitalized patients and using mathematical modeling, we identified resistance-associated bacteria that are common to both mice and humans.
Surprisingly, we found that Clostridium scindens, a bile acid 7α-dehydroxylating intestinal bacterium, is associated with resistance to C. difficile infection. Moreover, we discovered that administration of C. scindens enhances resistance to infection in a secondary bile acid-dependent manner.
Our findings have significant implications for the development of targeted antimicrobials and microbiome-based diagnostics and therapeutics for individuals at risk of C. difficile infection. By identifying a probiotic candidate that corrects a clinically relevant microbiome deficiency, we may be able to prevent or treat C. difficile infections more effectively.

title: Transcription initiation complex structures elucidate DNA opening
text: Transcription of eukaryotic protein-coding genes begins with the assembly of the RNA polymerase (Pol) II initiation complex and the promoter DNA opening. In this process, we have used cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to determine the structures of yeast initiation complexes at resolutions of 8.8 Å and 3.6 Å, respectively. These structures reveal how DNA is positioned and retained over the Pol II cleft through interactions between the TATA-box-binding protein TBP and transcription factors TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, and TFIIF. DNA opening occurs at the tip of the Pol II clamp and the TFIIE 'extended winged helix' domain, and can occur in the absence of TFIIH. Additionally, we have found that loading of the DNA template strand into the active center may be facilitated by movements of obstructing protein elements triggered by allosteric binding of the TFIIE 'E-ribbon' domain. These findings suggest a unified model for transcription initiation, with a key event being the trapping of open promoter DNA by extended protein-protein and protein-DNA contacts.

title: Multiple mechanisms disrupt the let-7 microRNA family in neuroblastoma
text: Poor prognosis in neuroblastoma is linked to genetic amplification of the MYCN gene. MYCN, in turn, is targeted by let-7, a family of tumor suppressor microRNAs that play a role in various cancers. LIN28B, an inhibitor of let-7 production, is overexpressed in neuroblastoma and regulates MYCN. However, our findings show that LIN28B is not essential in MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cell lines, despite the de-repression of let-7. We also discovered that MYCN mRNA levels in amplified disease are unusually high, which is sufficient to absorb let-7, reconciling the dispensability of LIN28B. Furthermore, we found that genetic loss of let-7 is common in neuroblastoma, inversely associated with MYCN amplification, and independently associated with poor outcomes. These findings provide a rationale for the chromosomal loss patterns observed in neuroblastoma, suggesting that disruption of let-7 by LIN28B, MYCN sponging, or genetic loss is a unifying mechanism of neuroblastoma development with broader implications for cancer pathogenesis.

title: Radiation and Dual Checkpoint Blockade Activates Non-Redundant Immune Mechanisms in Cancer
text: Immune checkpoint inhibitors have shown impressive clinical responses, but optimal outcomes require combination with multiple therapies. This raises questions about the underlying mechanisms of non-redundancy and resistance. In this study, we observed significant tumor regression in a subset of patients with metastatic melanoma treated with an anti-CTLA4 antibody and radiation, and replicated this effect in mouse models. Although combined treatment improved responses in both irradiated and unirradiated tumors, resistance remained a common challenge. Unbiased analyses of mice revealed that resistance was due to the upregulation of PD-L1 on melanoma cells, leading to T-cell exhaustion. Therefore, optimal response in melanoma and other cancer types requires the combination of radiation, anti-CTLA4, and anti-PD-L1/PD-1. Anti-CTLA4 predominantly inhibits T-regulatory cells (Treg cells), leading to an increase in the CD8 T-cell to Treg (CD8/Treg) ratio. Radiation enhances the diversity of the T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire of intratumoral T cells. The combination of anti-CTLA4 and radiation promotes the expansion of T cells, while radiation shapes the TCR repertoire of the expanded peripheral clones. The addition of PD-L1 blockade reverses T-cell exhaustion, mitigates the depression in the CD8/Treg ratio, and further encourages oligoclonal T-cell expansion. Similarly, in patients with melanoma who showed high PD-L1 expression and did not respond to radiation plus anti-CTLA4, persistent T-cell exhaustion and rapid disease progression were observed. These findings suggest that PD-L1 expression on melanoma cells can evade anti-CTLA4-based therapy, and the combination of radiation, anti-CTLA4, and anti-PD-L1 promotes response and immunity through distinct mechanisms.

title: G-protein-independent coupling of MC4R to Kir7.1 in hypothalamic neurons
text:
The coordinated release of anorexigenic α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH) and orexigenic Agouti-related protein (AgRP) from distinct hypothalamic neurons in the arcuate region leads to the regulation of energy homeostasis in the central nervous system. Both peptides bind with high affinity to the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R), with α-MSH acting as an agonist that activates the Gαs signaling pathway, while AgRP competes with α-MSH for binding to the receptor and blocks the constitutive activity mediated by the ligand-mimetic amino-terminal domain of the receptor.
In mice, the regulation of firing activity of neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) by α-MSH and AgRP can be mediated through independent mechanisms. While α-MSH activates the Gαs signaling pathway, AgRP induces the closure of inwardly rectifying potassium channels, Kir7.1, leading to hyperpolarization of neurons. Furthermore, AgRP exhibits biased agonist activity, binding to MC4R and opening Kir7.1 channels, even in the absence of its inhibition of α-MSH binding. This suggests that Kir7.1 signaling plays a central role in melanocortin-mediated regulation of energy homeostasis within the PVN. The coupling of MC4R to Kir7.1 may help explain the unusual aspects of melanocortin signaling, such as the gene dosage effect of MC4R and the sustained effects of AgRP on food intake.

title: Role of ghrelin in the relationship between hyperphagia and accelerated gastric emptying in diabetic mice.
text:
Background and Aims:
Ghrelin is a peptide hormone that regulates appetite and gastric motility. Mice with streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetes exhibit hyperphagia and altered gastric emptying, which is associated with increased plasma ghrelin levels. To investigate the causative role of ghrelin in diabetic hyperphagia, we compared changes in ghrelin receptor knockout (GHS-R(-/-) and wild-type (GHS-R(+/+)) mice with STZ-induced diabetes.
Methods:
We measured gastric emptying using the [(13)C]octanoic acid breath test and quantified the mRNA expression of neuropeptide Y (NPY), agouti-related peptide (AgRP), and proopiomelanocortin by real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction. Neural contractions were elicited by electrical field stimulation in fundic smooth muscle strips.
Results:
Diabetes increased plasma ghrelin levels to a similar extent in both genotypes. Hyperphagia was more pronounced in GHS-R(+/+) than in GHS-R(-/-) mice between days 12 and 21. Increases in NPY and AgRP mRNA expression were less pronounced in diabetic GHS-R(-/-) than in GHS-R(+/+) mice from day 15 on, whereas decreases in proopiomelanocortin mRNA levels were similar in both genotypes. Gastric emptying was accelerated to a similar extent in both genotypes, starting on day 16. In fundic smooth muscle strips of diabetic GHS-R(+/+) and GHS-R(-/-) mice, neuronal relaxations were reduced, whereas contractions were increased; this increase was related to an increased affinity of muscarinic and tachykinergic receptors.

title: Human serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol response to extended oral dosing with cholecalciferol.
text:
The background information suggests that the amount of cholecalciferol (vitamin D) required to achieve or maintain a specific serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration is not well understood, particularly within the range of physiological supply. The objectives of the study were to determine the quantitative relationship between steady-state cholecalciferol input and resulting serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration, and to estimate the proportion of the daily requirement that is met by cholecalciferol reserves in body tissue stores during winter.
The study was conducted over 20 weeks during winter in Omaha, Nebraska, where the latitude is approximately 41.2 degrees north. Sixty-seven healthy male participants received daily oral doses of labeled cholecalciferol at 0, 25, 125, and 250 micrograms (mcg) cholecalciferol. Serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentrations were measured at regular intervals throughout the study.
The results showed that serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentrations increased directly proportional to the dose of cholecalciferol administered, with a slope of approximately 0.70 nmol/L for each additional 1 mcg cholecalciferol input. The calculated oral input required to maintain the serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration present before the study (i.e., in the autumn) was approximately 12.5 mcg (500 IU)/d, while the total amount from all sources (supplement, food, tissue stores) needed to sustain the starting 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration was estimated at approximately 96 mcg (approximately 3800 IU)/d. By difference, the tissue stores provided approximately 78-82 mcg/d.
The study concluded that healthy men appear to require 3000-5000 IU cholecalciferol/d, with the majority of this amount (approximately 80-82 mcg/d) coming from cutaneously synthesized accumulations from solar sources during the preceding summer months. The current recommended vitamin D inputs are inadequate to maintain serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol concentration in the absence of substantial cutaneous production of vitamin D.

title: Intratumor heterogeneity and branched evolution revealed by multiregion sequencing.
text:
Background: Intratumor heterogeneity, or the presence of genetic and molecular differences within a tumor, can pose challenges to personalized medicine approaches that rely on analysis of single tumor biopsy samples.
Methods: To investigate intratumor heterogeneity, we performed exome sequencing, chromosome aberration analysis, and ploidy profiling on multiple spatially separated samples from primary renal carcinomas and associated metastatic sites. We used immunohistochemical analysis, mutation functional analysis, and profiling of messenger RNA expression to characterize the consequences of intratumor heterogeneity.
Results: Phylogenetic reconstruction revealed a branched evolutionary tumor growth model, with approximately 63-69% of all somatic mutations not detectable across every tumor region. Intratumor heterogeneity was observed for a mutation within an autoinhibitory domain of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase, which correlated with S6 and 4EBP phosphorylation in vivo and constitutive activation of mTOR kinase activity in vitro. Mutational intratumor heterogeneity was observed for multiple tumor-suppressor genes, including SETD2, PTEN, and KDM5C, which underwent multiple distinct and spatially separated inactivating mutations within a single tumor, suggesting convergent phenotypic evolution. Gene-expression signatures of good and poor prognosis were detected in different regions of the same tumor. Additionally, allelic composition and ploidy profiling analysis revealed extensive intratumor heterogeneity, with 26 of 30 tumor samples from four tumors harboring divergent allelic-imbalance profiles and with ploidy heterogeneity in two of four tumors.
Conclusions: Intratumor heterogeneity can lead to an underestimation of the tumor genomics landscape portrayed from single tumor-biopsy samples and may present major challenges to personalized-medicine and biomarker development. Intratumor heterogeneity, associated with heterogeneous protein function, may foster tumor adaptation and therapeutic failure through Darwinian selection. (Funded by the Medical Research Council and others.)

title: Succession of microbial consortia in the developing infant gut microbiome.
text: The colonization of the infant gut microbiome has been characterized as chaotic, but this view may be due to a lack of understanding of the factors influencing its development. To investigate the assembly of the human infant gut microbiome, we conducted a 2.5-year case study, collecting 60 fecal samples from a healthy infant and documenting its diet and health status. Analysis of over 300,000 16S rRNA genes revealed that the phylogenetic diversity of the microbiome increased gradually over time, with changes in community composition following a smooth temporal gradient. In contrast, major taxonomic groups exhibited abrupt shifts in abundance in response to changes in diet or health. Our findings suggest that the assembly of the infant gut microbiome is non-random, with discrete steps of bacterial succession occurring in response to life events.
