Results: YANA-C showed good agreement with both standard methods in categorizing subjects as consumers or non-consumers (κ = 0.48-0.92 for study 1 and κ = 0.38-0.90 for study 2). Spearman's correlations for energy and nutrient intakes ranged between 0.44 and 0.79 for study 1 and between 0.44 and 0.86 for study 2. Nutrient and energy intakes were generally higher in YANA-C compared to the food record, but not compared to the interview (except for fiber). YANA-C showed fair to moderate agreement with the other methods in ranking portions/amounts in consumers only for most food groups (weighted κ = 0.11-0.55 for study 1 and 0.04-0.73 for study 2). Amounts in consumers only were significantly lower in YANA-C for cereals, and significantly higher for milk, soft drinks, sugar/sweets, and savory snacks compared to the food record, and for potatoes compared to the interview. Only a few pupils reported the program negatively.
Conclusion: YANA-C is a promising tool for collecting detailed dietary information from young adolescents with relatively low staff resources, making it useful for many nutrition research applications.

title: Antiretroviral Therapy for Prevention of Tuberculosis in Adults with HIV: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text:
Background: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is the most significant risk factor for developing tuberculosis, and the resurgence of the disease is largely attributable to the spread of HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. According to estimates from 2010, there were approximately 1.1 million new cases of tuberculosis among the 34 million people living with HIV worldwide. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has the potential to prevent HIV-associated tuberculosis, and we conducted a systematic review of studies that examined the impact of ART on tuberculosis incidence in adults with HIV infection.
Methods and Findings: We conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, the African Index Medicus, LILACS, and clinical trial registries for randomized controlled trials, prospective cohort studies, and retrospective cohort studies that compared tuberculosis incidence by ART status in HIV-infected adults in developing countries. The studies included in the meta-analyses were categorized based on the baseline CD4 count: less than 200 cells/μl, 200 to 350 cells/μl, greater than 350 cells/μl, and any CD4 count. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria. Our findings showed that ART is strongly associated with a reduction in tuberculosis incidence across all CD4 count strata, with hazard ratios ranging from 0.16 to 0.43. There was no significant evidence of hazard ratio modification with respect to baseline CD4 count category (p = 0.20).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that ART is strongly associated with a reduction in tuberculosis incidence in all CD4 count strata, and earlier initiation of ART may be a key component of global and national strategies to control the HIV-associated tuberculosis syndemic.
Editors' Summary: This systematic review found that antiretroviral therapy (ART) is strongly associated with a reduction in tuberculosis incidence in adults with HIV infection, across all CD4 count strata. The findings suggest that earlier initiation of ART may be a key component of global and national strategies to control the HIV-associated tuberculosis syndemic.

title: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and breast cancer: a review of the current evidence.
text: Over the past decades, there has been a significant increase in incidences of breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome due to the obesity epidemic, particularly in industrialized countries. The link between diabetes and breast cancer is complex, and various factors may contribute to the association. Insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and changes in the signaling of growth hormones and steroid hormones may play a role in the development of breast cancer. We reviewed epidemiologic studies to investigate the association between type 2 diabetes and the risk of breast cancer, as well as the available evidence on the potential hormonal mediators of this association. Our findings suggest a modest association between type 2 diabetes and breast cancer risk, with a stronger association among postmenopausal women. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear due to the shared risk factors between the two diseases, including obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and potentially, intake of saturated fat and refined carbohydrates. While the metabolic syndrome is closely related to diabetes and encompasses additional factors that may influence breast cancer risk, its role in breast carcinogenesis has not been studied, leaving a knowledge gap in this area.

title: Loss of TDP43 inhibits progression of triple-negative breast cancer in coordination with SRSF3
text: Aberrant alternative splicing has been identified as a key characteristic of cancer, and in this study, we have found that TDP43 (TAR DNA-binding protein 43) plays a crucial role in the unique splicing profile of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Our clinical data reveal that TDP43 is highly expressed in TNBC tumors with poor prognosis, and we have found that both knocking down and overexpressing TDP43 significantly impacts TNBC progression. Using deep sequencing analysis and functional experiments, we have discovered that TDP43 alters the majority of splicing events, particularly those regulated by the splicing factor SRSF3 (serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 3). The TDP43/SRSF3 complex controls specific splicing events, including downstream genes PAR3 and NUMB, and the knockdown or overexpression of these genes leads to changes in metastasis and proliferation. Our findings suggest that the TDP43/SRSF3 complex and downstream PAR3 isoform are potential therapeutic targets for TNBC treatment.

title: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture--pathologic basis of plaque stability and instability.
text:
Atherosclerosis remains a crucial area of research in pathology, due to its intricate pathogenesis and significant clinical implications. A large number of diseases with diverse clinical presentations, such as myocardial infarction, stroke, abdominal aneurysms, and lower limb ischemia, are ultimately linked to atherosclerosis. Despite their varying clinical manifestations, most acute atherosclerosis complications share a common pathogenetic feature: plaque rupture. Plaque disruptions can range from minor surface fissures to deep intimal tears that extend into the soft lipid core of lesions, leading to thrombus formation in all cases. The abdominal aorta is the most commonly affected arterial site, where plaque disruption and thrombosis can result in extensive surface ulcerations covering large areas of the aortic wall, as observed in many autopsy cases in older individuals. While atherosclerosis is undoubtedly involved in abdominal aneurysm formation, mural thrombosis in these patients surprisingly leads to a low rate of clinically significant complications, although cholesterol emboli can be found in their kidneys and skin at autopsy. However, the impact of the various biologically active mediators released from eroded aortic surfaces on the human body remains unclear. In contrast, occlusive thrombosis is a frequent and often fatal complication of plaque in small diameter vessels such as coronary arteries.

title: Pioneer factor Pax7 deploys a stable enhancer repertoire for specification of cell fate
text: Pioneer transcription factors play a crucial role in establishing new cell fates by triggering chromatin remodeling. However, the kinetics and stability of these processes remain inadequately understood. Our study demonstrates that Pax7, a pioneer transcription factor, is necessary and sufficient for the specification of one pituitary lineage. Pax7 rapidly binds to its targeted enhancers, but the associated chromatin remodeling and gene activation occur more slowly. The opened enhancers by Pax7 exhibit a loss of DNA methylation and retain stable epigenetic memory, as evidenced by the binding of non-pioneer factors after Pax7 withdrawal. This work shows that transient Pax7 expression is sufficient for stable specification of cell identity. Our analysis of Pax7 dynamics during pituitary lineage specification reveals that Pax7 binds rapidly to uniquely marked heterochromatin pioneer sites and initiates chromatin opening that persists after Pax7 withdrawal, accompanied by loss of DNA hypermethylation at pioneered enhancers.

title: Human cancer cells utilize mitotic DNA synthesis to resist replication stress at telomeres regardless of their telomere maintenance mechanism
text: Telomeres share similarities with common fragile sites (CFSs) in that they are challenging to replicate and exhibit fragility during mitosis in response to DNA replication stress. At CFSs, this fragility is associated with a delay in completing DNA replication until early mitosis, at which point cells are believed to switch to a RAD52-dependent form of break-induced replication. We have found that this mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) is also present in human telomeres. MiDAS at telomeres is not limited to those displaying overt fragility and is observed in a wide range of cell lines, regardless of whether their telomeres are maintained by telomerase or the alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) mechanism. MiDAS at telomeres requires RAD52 and is mechanistically similar to CFS-associated MiDAS, with the notable exception that telomeric MiDAS does not require the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease. According to our model, replication stress triggers a RAD52-dependent form of break-induced replication that bypasses the need for MUS81-EME1 to complete DNA synthesis in mitosis.

title: Low drug levels and thrombotic complications in high‐risk atrial fibrillation patients treated with direct oral anticoagulants
text: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) do not require routine laboratory monitoring, but a recent study found that measuring DOAC levels at steady state may be associated with a lower risk of thromboembolic events in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). The study included 565 consecutive naive patients with AF who were enrolled within the START Laboratory Registry. DOAC-specific measurements (diluted thrombin time or anti-activated factor II calibrated for dabigatran; anti-activated FX calibrated for rivaroxaban or apixaban) at trough were performed locally at steady state within 15-25 days after the start of treatment. The study found that thromboembolic complications occurred in 10 patients who had baseline C-trough levels in the lowest class of drug levels, with an incidence of 2.4%. In contrast, the incidence of thromboembolic events among patients with DOAC C-trough levels in the remaining classes was 0%. The patients with thrombotic complications also had a higher mean CHA2 DS2 -VASc score than the total patient population. These findings suggest that measuring DOAC levels at steady state may be useful in identifying patients at high risk of thromboembolic events and may help guide treatment decisions. However, larger studies are needed to confirm these preliminary observations.

title: Consensus guidelines for the detection of immunogenic cell death.
text: Apoptotic cells were once thought to be immune-tolerant or unable to trigger responses specific to their dead cell-associated antigens. However, research has shown that a unique type of apoptotic death, termed "immunogenic cell death" (ICD), can occur, which is not overlooked by the adaptive immune system. ICD is characterized by the release of a specific set of immunostimulatory damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) in a specific spatiotemporal configuration. Various cancer therapies, including chemotherapy and radiation, can induce ICD. Unfortunately, the current method for detecting ICD involves using immunocompetent mouse models and syngeneic cancer cells, which is not feasible for large-scale screening. To address this challenge, we have developed a high-content, high-throughput platform that allows for the detection of multiple DAMPs, such as cell surface-exposed calreticulin, extracellular ATP, and high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), as well as the processes that underlie their emission, including endoplasmic reticulum stress, autophagy, and necrotic plasma membrane permeabilization. We believe that this technology will facilitate the development of next-generation anticancer regimens that not only kill malignant cells but also convert them into a cancer-specific therapeutic vaccine.

title: Long-Term ERK Inhibition in KRAS-Mutant Pancreatic Cancer Is Associated with MYC Degradation and Senescence-like Growth Suppression.
text: Induction of compensatory mechanisms and ERK reactivation have limited the effectiveness of Raf and MEK inhibitors in RAS-mutant cancers. Our study found that direct pharmacological inhibition of ERK inhibited the growth of a subset of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer cell lines, and concurrent PI3K inhibition caused synergistic cell death. Additional combinations that enhanced ERK inhibitor action were also identified. Unexpectedly, long-term treatment of sensitive cell lines led to cellular senescence, which was mediated in part by MYC degradation and p16 reactivation. Enhanced basal PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling was associated with de novo resistance to ERK inhibitors, as were other protein kinases identified through kinome-wide siRNA screening and a genetic gain-of-function screen. Our findings highlight the diverse consequences of targeting this kinase cascade through ERK inhibition.

title: TRF2 Recruits RTEL1 to Telomeres in S Phase to Promote T-Loop Unwinding
text: The helicase RTEL1 plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of vertebrate telomeres by promoting t-loop unwinding and suppressing telomere fragility. However, the mechanism by which RTEL1 engages with the telomere to facilitate t-loop unwinding is not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the role of the shelterin protein TRF2 in recruiting RTEL1 to telomeres during S phase. We find that TRF2 interacts with RTEL1 through a metal-coordinating motif in RTEL1, and that this interaction is essential for preventing catastrophic t-loop processing by structure-specific nucleases. We also identify a mutation in RTEL1 (R1264H) that disrupts its interaction with TRF2, leading to aberrant t-loop excision, telomere length heterogeneity, and loss of the telomere as a circle. These findings implicate TRF2 in the recruitment of RTEL1 to facilitate t-loop disassembly at telomeres during S phase.

title: Macrophages Facilitate Electrical Conduction in the Heart
text: The functions of tissue-resident macrophages in the heart during the steady state are currently unknown. However, our study reveals that cardiac macrophages play a crucial role in electrical conduction through the distal atrioventricular node. We found that these macrophages are densely interspersed with elongated cells expressing connexin 43, a critical protein for electrical conduction. When connected to spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes via connexin-43-containing gap junctions, cardiac macrophages have a negative resting membrane potential and synchronize their depolarization with cardiomyocytes. In contrast, macrophages increase the resting membrane potential of cardiomyocytes, according to computational modeling, and accelerate their repolarization. Furthermore, photostimulation of channelrhodopsin-2-expressing macrophages improves atrioventricular conduction, while conditional deletion of connexin 43 in macrophages and congenital lack of macrophages delay atrioventricular conduction. In the Cd11bDTR mouse, macrophage ablation leads to progressive atrioventricular block, highlighting the importance of macrophages in both normal and abnormal cardiac conduction.

title: A Tunable Diffusion‐Consumption Mechanism of Cytokine Propagation Enables Plasticity in Cell‐to‐Cell Communication in the Immune System
text:
In the context of immune cell communication, cytokines play a crucial role in coordinating a context-appropriate response. However, the spatial extent of this communication remains poorly understood. To address this gap in knowledge, Oyler-Yaniv et al. (2017) employed theoretical considerations and experimental models of immune responses in vitro and in vivo to quantify the spatial distribution of cytokines in dense tissues. Their findings revealed that the diffusion of cytokines is countered by consumption, leading to the formation of spherical cytokine niches around cytokine-producing cells. The size of these niches was found to scale with the density of cytokine-consuming cells, providing a mechanistic basis for understanding the variability in immune responses. In vivo measurements revealed that cytokine niches were responsible for a high degree of cell-to-cell variance in cytokine exposure, highlighting the importance of considering the spatial distribution of diffusible factors in immune cell communication.
Key points:
* Cytokine communication is essential for immune cell coordination, but the distance over which this communication occurs is unknown.
* Oyler-Yaniv et al. (2017) used theoretical and experimental approaches to investigate the spatial distribution of cytokines in dense tissues.
* The diffusion of cytokines is countered by consumption, leading to the formation of spherical cytokine niches around cytokine-producing cells.
* The size of these niches scales with the density of cytokine-consuming cells, providing a mechanistic basis for understanding cell-to-cell variability in immune responses.
* In vivo measurements revealed that cytokine niches are responsible for a high degree of cell-to-cell variance in cytokine exposure.

title: Cardiac neural crest contributes to cardiomyogenesis in zebrafish.
text: In birds and mammals, cardiac neural crest is crucial for heart development and plays a key role in the formation of the conotruncal cushion and outflow tract septation. However, the presence of cardiac neural crest in zebrafish has been questioned due to the lack of outflow tract septation in the zebrafish embryo. This study aimed to investigate the existence of cardiac neural crest in zebrafish using three distinct lineage-labeling approaches. The results showed that cardiac neural crest cells do exist in zebrafish and have the ability to generate MF20-positive muscle cells in the myocardium of the major chambers during development. Fate-mapping revealed that cardiac neural crest cells originate from both neural tube regions similar to those found in birds and a novel region rostral to the otic vesicle. Unlike other vertebrates, cardiac neural crest invades the myocardium in all segments of the heart in zebrafish, including the outflow tract, atrium, atrioventricular junction, and ventricle. The study also identified three distinct groups of premigratory neural crest along the rostrocaudal axis, each with a unique propensity to contribute to different segments in the heart. Zebrafish will serve as a valuable model for understanding the interactions between cardiac neural crest and cardiovascular development.

title: Sodium Hydroxide Production from Seawater Desalination Brine: Process Design and Energy Efficiency.
text: The ability to raise pH is a crucial requirement for desalination pretreatment, particularly in reverse osmosis, as well as for other industries. However, conventional methods of pH adjustment often result in significant emissions and the consumption of non-renewable resources. An alternative approach is to utilize waste brine from desalination to produce sodium hydroxide through appropriate concentration and purification steps. In this study, an efficient process train (with variations) is developed and modeled for sodium hydroxide production from seawater desalination brine using membrane chlor-alkali electrolysis. The integrated system consists of nanofiltration, concentration through evaporation or mechanical vapor compression, chemical softening, further ion-exchange softening, dechlorination, and membrane electrolysis. The performance of the NaOH production process is evaluated in terms of system productivity, component performance, and energy consumption, and their dependencies on electrolyzer outlet conditions and brine recirculation are investigated. The analysis also includes an assessment of the energy efficiency of major components, estimation of system operating expenses, and comparison with similar processes. The brine-to-caustic process is shown to be technically feasible and offers several advantages, including reduced environmental impact through minimized brine discharge and increased overall water recovery ratio of the reverse osmosis facility. Additionally, optimal conditions are provided for producing caustic that can be used both within the plant and in excess for potential revenue.

title: High-Throughput Genetic Screens Identify a Large and Diverse Collection of New Sporulation Genes in Bacillus subtilis
text:
The differentiation of the bacterium Bacillus subtilis into a dormant spore is one of the most well-characterized developmental pathways in biology, with numerous genetic screens conducted over the past half-century identifying a large number of factors involved in every stage of this process. Recently, transcriptional profiling has uncovered additional sporulation-induced genes required for successful spore development. To investigate whether there are any sporulation genes left to be discovered, we employed transposon-sequencing (Tn-seq) and identified 133 out of the 148 genes with known sporulation defects. Surprisingly, we discovered 24 additional genes that had not been previously implicated in spore formation.
To investigate the functions of these newly identified genes, we conducted fluorescence microscopy surveys of early, middle, and late stages of differentiation of null mutants from the B. subtilis ordered knockout collection. This analysis revealed mutants that are delayed in the initiation of sporulation, defective in membrane remodeling, and impaired in spore maturation, as well as novel sporulation phenotypes. We performed in-depth characterization of two new factors that participate in cell-cell signaling pathways during sporulation, SpoIIT and SpoIIIL, with SpoIIT functioning in the activation of σE in the mother cell and SpoIIIL being required for σG activity in the forespore.
Our analysis also revealed that as many as 36 sporulation-induced genes with no previously reported mutant phenotypes are required for timely spore maturation. Furthermore, we discovered a large set of transposon insertions that trigger premature initiation of sporulation. These findings highlight the power of Tn-seq for the discovery of new genes and novel pathways in sporulation, and demonstrate the potential of this approach for investigating other, less well-characterized developmental processes.

title: Psychobiological mechanisms underlying the social buffering of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical axis: a review of animal models and human studies across development.
text:
Over the past century, discovering the stress-buffering effects of social relationships has been a significant finding in psychobiology. However, a deeper understanding of the underlying neurobiological and psychological mechanisms of this buffering is only now beginning to emerge. One key area of research involves investigating the neurocircuitry that regulates the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis, which is activated in response to stress.
This review aims to integrate animal models and human studies of social regulation of the HPA axis across the lifespan, focusing on the process known as social buffering. Social buffering refers to a dampened HPA axis stress response when an individual is exposed to a threat or challenge in the presence or with the assistance of a conspecific. This process has been observed across species and is thought to play a critical role in mitigating the negative effects of stress on the body.
While some aspects of the underlying neurobiology are better understood, significant gaps remain in our knowledge across all domains of the literature. To address these gaps, we propose a working conceptual model that highlights the role of oxytocinergic systems and prefrontal neural networks as potential biological mediators of social buffering. We also suggest that early experiences play a critical role in shaping later social buffering effects.
This synthesis identifies both general future directions and specific experiments that need to be conducted to develop a more comprehensive model of the HPA social buffering effect across the lifespan, incorporating multiple levels of analysis: neuroendocrine, behavioral, and social. By advancing our understanding of these mechanisms, we can better understand how social relationships can buffer the negative effects of stress and inform strategies for promoting resilience and well-being across the lifespan.

title: Elevation of circulating branched-chain amino acids is an early event in human pancreatic adenocarcinoma development
text: The majority of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are diagnosed with advanced disease and have a poor prognosis of less than 12 months. While obesity and glucose intolerance have been linked to PDAC, the relationship between circulating metabolites and early cancer progression is unclear. To investigate metabolic changes in early disease, we analyzed plasma metabolites from individuals with pancreatic cancer (cases) and matched controls from four prospective cohort studies. Our findings reveal that elevated levels of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) in prediagnostic plasma are associated with a more than twofold increased risk of future pancreatic cancer diagnosis, independent of known risk factors. The strongest association was observed among individuals with samples collected 2-5 years before diagnosis, suggesting that occult disease may be present at this stage. We also found that plasma BCAAs are elevated in mice with early-stage pancreatic cancers driven by mutant Kras expression, but not in mice with Kras-driven tumors in other tissues. Moreover, we discovered that breakdown of tissue protein accounts for the increase in plasma BCAAs that accompanies early-stage disease. These findings suggest that increased whole-body protein breakdown is an early event in the development of PDAC.

title: Effective Use of PI3K and MEK Inhibitors to Treat Mutant K-Ras G12D and PIK3CA H1047R Murine Lung Cancers
text: Somatic mutations in the p110-alpha catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), specifically in the helical domain (E545K and E542K) and the kinase domain (H1047R), have been identified. Although these mutations have been shown to be transforming in vitro, their oncogenic potential has yet to be assessed in genetically engineered mouse models. Recently, clinical trials of PI3K inhibitors have begun, and it remains to be seen if these treatments will be effective against a range of cancers or if they will be restricted to specific, genetically defined malignancies. To investigate this, we generated a mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma by expressing the H1047R mutation in p110-alpha. Treatment of these tumors with NVP-BEZ235, a dual pan-PI3K and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor in clinical development, led to significant tumor regression as observed by positron emission tomography-computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and microscopic examination. In contrast, lung cancers driven by mutant Kras did not respond substantially to single-agent NVP-BEZ235. However, when NVP-BEZ235 was combined with a mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK) inhibitor, ARRY-142886, there was significant synergy in shrinking these Kras-mutant cancers. These in vivo studies suggest that inhibitors of the PI3K-mTOR pathway may be effective against cancers with PIK3CA mutations, and when combined with MEK inhibitors, may effectively treat KRAS mutated lung cancers.

title: Transdifferentiation of glioblastoma cells into vascular endothelial cells.
text: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive brain tumor and exhibits significant resistance to combination and anti-VEGF therapies. To investigate the mechanisms of resistance, we examined the blood vessels of GBMs in tumors induced in p53(+/-) heterozygous mice using lentiviral vectors containing oncogenes and the marker GFP. Surprisingly, we observed GFP(+) vascular endothelial cells (ECs) in the tumors. When we transplanted mouse GBM cells, we found that the tumor-derived endothelial cells (TDECs) originated from tumor-initiating cells and were not the result of cell fusion between ECs and tumor cells. An in vitro differentiation assay revealed that hypoxia plays a crucial role in the differentiation of tumor cells into ECs, which is independent of VEGF. Interestingly, TDEC formation was not only resistant to an anti-VEGF receptor inhibitor in mouse GBMs but actually led to an increase in their frequency. We also observed the presence of TDECs in a xenograft model of human GBM spheres from clinical specimens and direct clinical samples from patients with GBM. Our findings suggest that TDECs are a crucial player in the resistance to anti-VEGF therapy and may be a promising target for GBM therapy.

title: Ribosomal DNA copy loss and repeat instability in ATRX-mutated cancers
text:
The ATRX (alpha thalassemia/mental retardation X-linked) protein complexes with DAXX to facilitate the deposition of histone variant H3.3 into repetitive heterochromatin. Recent genomic sequencing studies have revealed that mutations in ATRX are associated with the activation of alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) in cancers, which can lead to the loss of rDNA copy number. In this study, we investigate the effect of ATRX depletion on rDNA copy number in mouse embryonic stem cells and find that depletion leads to a selective loss of rDNA copy number. This loss of rDNA copy number is also observed in ATRX-mutated human ALT-positive tumors, which show a significantly lower rDNA copy number compared to ALT-negative tumors. Furthermore, we discover that the loss of rDNA copy number and repeat instability in the absence of ATRX are caused by a disruption in H3.3 deposition and the subsequent failure of heterochromatin formation at rDNA repeats. Additionally, we find that ATRX-depleted cells exhibit reduced ribosomal RNA transcription output and increased sensitivity to RNA polymerase I (Pol I) transcription inhibitor CX5461. Notably, human ALT-positive cancer cell lines are also more sensitive to CX5461 treatment, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for targeting Pol I transcription in ALT cancers.
In summary, this study uncovers the contribution of ATRX loss of function to tumorigenesis through the loss of rDNA stability and highlights the potential of targeting Pol I transcription in ALT cancers.

title: Combining indoor residual spraying and insecticide-treated nets for malaria control in Africa: a review of possible outcomes and an outline of suggestions for the future
text: Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS) are currently the primary methods of malaria vector control. In many cases, these methods are used in combination within the same households, particularly in holoendemic and hyperendemic settings. While there is limited evidence to suggest that co-application of ITNs and IRS provides greater protective benefits than either method used alone, the combination of these insecticide-based interventions may offer enhanced household-level protection if the candidate active ingredients have complementary effects on mosquitoes that enter or attempt to enter homes. Specifically, the use of highly deterrent IRS compounds in combination with highly toxic ITNs may lead to increased protection. To avoid the problem of insecticide resistance, it is important that ITNs and IRS products be of different insecticide classes, such as pyrethroid-based nets combined with organophosphate or carbamate based IRS. The overall community benefits of these interventions will also depend on factors such as the proportion of people covered by the interventions and the behavior of vector species. This article emphasizes the need for further basic and operational research, including mathematical modeling, to evaluate the effectiveness of IRS/ITN combinations in comparison to IRS alone or ITNs alone.

title: Membrane estrogen receptor-α levels in MCF-7 breast cancer cells predict cAMP and proliferation responses
text: 17β-estradiol (E2) can rapidly increase cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production, but the optimal conditions for measuring these levels and the signaling pathways involved in the proliferative effects on breast cancer cells are not fully understood. To address these questions, we compared cAMP responses in MCF-7 cell lines with low (mERlow) and high (mERhigh) expression of the membrane form of estrogen receptor (mER)-α. We found that the loss of cAMP at 37°C was not due to export and that 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX) only partially preserved cAMP, suggesting that multiple phosphodiesterases modulate its level. The accumulated cAMP was consistently higher in mERhigh cells than in mERlow cells, implicating mER-α levels in the process. The estrogen receptor modulator ICI172,780 blocked the E2-induced response, and 17α-estradiol did not elicit the response, suggesting that mER-α is involved in these responses. E2 dose-dependent cAMP production was biphasic in both cell types but was responsive to 50-fold higher E2 concentrations in mERhigh cells. Proliferation of mERlow cells was stimulated over the whole range of E2 concentrations, while the number of mERhigh cells was greatly decreased at concentrations above 1 nmol/l, suggesting that estrogen over-stimulation can lead to cell death. E2-mediated activation of adenylyl cyclase and downstream participation of protein kinase A were shown to be involved in these responses. These findings suggest that rapid mER-α-mediated nongenomic signaling cascades generate cAMP and downstream signaling events, which contribute to the regulation of breast cancer cell number.

title: The embryonic cell lineage of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: The developmental history of Caenorhabditis elegans has been traced from fertilization to newly hatched larva, revealing the complete cell lineage of this organism. During embryogenesis, 671 cells are generated, of which 113 (in the hermaphrodite) or 111 (in the male) undergo programmed cell death, while the remaining cells either differentiate into terminal cell types or become postembryonic blast cells. Despite the fixed relationship between cell ancestry and cell fate, the correlation between them lacks a clear pattern, with some neurons arising from the embryonic ectoderm, while others are produced by the mesoderm or are sisters to muscles. However, cell ablation experiments have shown that at least some sections of embryogenesis exhibit substantial cell autonomy. We conclude that the cell lineage plays an important role in determining cell fate, and discuss the origin of repeat units in the body wall, the generation of various orders of symmetry, the analysis of the lineage in terms of sublineages, and evolutionary implications.

title: Self-Reactive B Cells in the Germinal Center Reaction.
text: Maintaining immunological self-tolerance requires the selective prevention of lymphocytes carrying self-reactive antigen receptors from mounting harmful or inflammatory effector responses. Traditionally, self-tolerance is understood in terms of the removal, editing, or silencing of B and T cells that have developed self-reactive antigen receptors during their early development. However, activated B cells that encounter foreign antigens can enter germinal centers (GCs), where they modify their antigen receptor through somatic hypermutation (SHM) of their immunoglobulin genes. The emergence of activated, self-reactive GC B cells poses a unique challenge to self-tolerance that must be quickly addressed to prevent autoantibody production. This review focuses on the current understanding of the mechanisms that enforce B cell self-tolerance, particularly in relation to the control of self-reactive GC B cells. Additionally, we consider how self-reactive GC B cells can escape self-tolerance and initiate autoantibody production, or alternatively, undergo SHM to produce productive antibody responses.

title: Chronic inflammation (inflammaging) and its potential contribution to age-associated diseases.
text: Human aging is characterized by a persistent, low-grade inflammation, known as "inflammaging." This phenomenon is a significant risk factor for both morbidity and mortality in elderly individuals, as most age-related diseases share an inflammatory pathogenesis. However, the underlying causes of inflammaging and its contribution to adverse health outcomes are still not fully understood. Identifying the pathways that control age-related inflammation across various systems is crucial to determine whether modulating inflammaging through treatments may be beneficial in older individuals. The "Inflammation in Aging" session at the Advances in Gerosciences meeting held at the National Institutes of Health/National Institute on Aging in Bethesda on October 30 and 31, 2013, aimed to address these unanswered questions. This article summarizes the key findings from this session.

title: Cryptochromes Enabling Plants and Animals to Determine Circadian Time
text: Cryptochromes are specialized photoreceptors that are responsible for detecting blue light and playing a crucial role in regulating circadian rhythms in both plants and animals. Recent research has also identified cryptochromes in bacteria, expanding their known presence across the three domains of life. In plants, cryptochromes are involved in a range of functions, including the entrainment of circadian rhythms, while in animals, they serve a similar function and are also an essential component of the circadian clock. In Drosophila and mammals, cryptochromes are particularly important for maintaining the proper functioning of the circadian clock.

title: Neural crest-derived stem cells migrate and differentiate into cardiomyocytes after myocardial infarction.
text:
Objective:
In this study, we investigated the migration and differentiation potential of primitive neural crest-derived (NC) cells in the context of myocardial infarction (MI).
Methods and Results:
To examine the migration and differentiation potential of NC cells, we used a transgenic mouse model in which NC cells express enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP). In the neonatal heart, NC stem cells (NCSCs) were primarily localized in the outflow tract, but they were also distributed throughout the ventricular myocardium in a gradient from base to apex. Time-lapse video analysis revealed that NCSCs were migratory, and some persisted in the adult heart. Following MI, NCSCs accumulated at the ischemic border zone area (BZA), which expresses monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). Ex vivo cell migration assays demonstrated that MCP-1 induced NCSC migration, and this chemotactic effect was significantly depressed by an anti-MCP-1 antibody. Small NC cardiomyocytes first appeared in the BZA 2 weeks post-MI and gradually increased in number thereafter.
Conclusions:
These findings suggest that NCSCs migrate into the BZA via MCP-1/CCR2 signaling and contribute to the provision of cardiomyocytes for cardiac regeneration after MI. These results provide new insights into the role of NC cells in the regeneration of the heart following MI.

title: Mitochondria as sensors and regulators of calcium signalling
text: Over the past two decades, the accumulation of calcium (Ca2+) in energized mitochondria has gained significant attention as a crucial biological process with far-reaching physiological implications. Research has shown that mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake plays a central role in regulating intracellular Ca2+ signaling, cell metabolism, cell survival, and other cell-type specific functions by buffering cytosolic Ca2+ levels and modulating mitochondrial effectors. Recently, the discovery of mitochondrial Ca2+ transporters has provided new insights into the mechanisms underlying this process, paving the way for further investigation and potential molecular interventions.

title: Caspase-11 promotes the fusion of phagosomes harboring pathogenic bacteria with lysosomes by modulating actin polymerization.
text: Inflammasomes are complexes of multiple proteins, including members of the NLR (nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat containing) family and caspase-1. When bacterial molecules are detected within macrophages, the inflammasome assembles, leading to the activation of caspase-1. While caspase-11 mediates caspase-1 activation in response to lipopolysaccharide and bacterial toxins, its role during bacterial infection remains unclear. Our study demonstrated that caspase-11 is not essential for caspase-1 activation in response to Legionella, Salmonella, Francisella, and Listeria. Additionally, we found that active mouse caspase-11 is required for restricting L. pneumophila infection. Similarly, human caspase-4 and caspase-5, homologs of mouse caspase-11, cooperate to restrict L. pneumophila infection in human macrophages. Caspase-11 promotes the fusion of the L. pneumophila vacuole with lysosomes by modulating actin polymerization through cofilin. However, caspase-11 is dispensable for the fusion of lysosomes with phagosomes containing non-pathogenic bacteria, revealing a distinct difference in the trafficking of phagosomes based on their cargo.

title: Adipocyte inflammation is essential for healthy adipose tissue expansion and remodeling.
text: Chronic inflammation plays a crucial role in the relationship between obesity and its associated health problems. Contrary to the belief that inflammatory signals negatively impact metabolism, our research shows that proinflammatory signaling in adipocytes is necessary for proper adipose tissue remodeling and expansion. To investigate the role of inflammation in adipose tissue, we generated three mouse models with a reduced ability to produce proinflammatory signals in adipose tissue. These models showed a reduced capacity for adipogenesis in vivo, while their differentiation potential remained unchanged in vitro. When exposed to a high-fat diet, these mice exhibited impaired expansion of visceral adipose tissue, which was associated with decreased intestinal barrier function, increased hepatic steatosis, and metabolic dysfunction. The reduced local proinflammatory response in adipocytes led to increased ectopic lipid accumulation, glucose intolerance, and systemic inflammation. In essence, adipose tissue inflammation is an adaptive response that enables the safe storage of excess nutrients and contributes to a visceral depot barrier that effectively filters gut-derived endotoxin.

title: Chronic variable stress activates hematopoietic stem cells
text:
Exposure to psychosocial stress is a risk factor for various diseases, including atherosclerosis. Although the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood, there is evidence to suggest that the interaction between the mind and the immune system may play a role in the development and progression of these diseases. Known interactions between the brain and immune system include the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which regulates glucocorticoid production in the adrenal cortex, and the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary axis, which controls stress-induced catecholamine release in support of the fight-or-flight response. However, the impact of chronic stress on hematopoietic stem cell activity remains unclear.
Our study shows that stress leads to increased proliferation of the most primitive hematopoietic progenitors, resulting in higher levels of disease-promoting inflammatory leukocytes. We found that chronic stress induced monocytosis and neutrophilia in humans, and when investigating the source of leukocytosis in mice, we discovered that stress activates upstream hematopoietic stem cells. Under conditions of chronic variable stress in mice, sympathetic nerve fibers released excess noradrenaline, which signals bone marrow niche cells to decrease CXCL12 levels through the β3-adrenergic receptor. This leads to elevated hematopoietic stem cell proliferation, resulting in an increased output of neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes. When atherosclerosis-prone Apoe(-/-) mice were subjected to chronic stress, accelerated hematopoiesis promoted plaque features associated with vulnerable lesions that can cause myocardial infarction and stroke in humans.
In summary, our findings suggest that chronic psychosocial stress may contribute to the development and progression of atherosclerosis by altering hematopoietic stem cell activity, leading to increased inflammatory leukocyte production and promoting the formation of vulnerable plaques.

title: CNTF reverses obesity-induced insulin resistance by activating skeletal muscle AMPK
text: Ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) has been shown to promote weight loss and improve glucose tolerance in both humans and rodents. Research suggests that CNTF acts centrally by stimulating hypothalamic neurogenesis to regulate food intake, and peripherally by altering hepatic gene expression. Our findings reveal that CNTF signals through the CNTFRα–IL-6R–gp130β receptor complex to increase fatty-acid oxidation and reduce insulin resistance in skeletal muscle, independently of central signaling. These peripheral effects of CNTF are not suppressed by diet-induced or genetic models of obesity, making it a promising therapeutic approach for treating obesity-related diseases.

title: The Global Spread of Hepatitis C Virus 1a and 1b: A Phylodynamic and Phylogeographic Analysis
text: Background: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is estimated to affect approximately 130-180 million people globally. While the origin of HCV is unknown, genetic analysis suggests that genotype 1 likely originated in West Africa. Previous studies have suggested that HCV transmission began in the early 20th century and grew steadily until the late 1980s. However, epidemiological data suggest that the expansion of HCV may have occurred after World War II. Objective: To elucidate the timescale and route of the global spread of HCV. Methods: We analyzed a large dataset of newly obtained E2P7NS2 and NS5B sequences, along with all available global HCV sequences with information in both genomic regions. We employed phylodynamic methods to estimate the timescale and nature of the global expansion of the most prevalent HCV subtypes, 1a and 1b. Results: Our findings indicate that transmission of subtypes 1a and 1b "exploded" between 1940 and 1980, with the spread of 1b preceding that of 1a by at least 16 years (95% confidence interval 15-17). Phylogeographic analysis of all available NS5B sequences suggests that HCV subtypes 1a and 1b disseminated from the developed world to the developing countries. Conclusion: Our data suggest that the evolutionary rate of HCV is faster than previously suggested. The global spread of HCV coincided with the widespread use of transfused blood and blood products and with the expansion of intravenous drug use, but slowed prior to the wide implementation of anti-HCV screening. The differences in transmission routes associated with subtypes 1a and 1b provide an explanation for the relatively earlier expansion of 1b. Our findings indicate that the most plausible route of HCV dispersal was from developed countries to the developing world.

title: Pharmacological interventions for smoking cessation: an overview and network meta-analysis.
text:
The text provides an overview of the effectiveness and safety of various smoking cessation treatments, based on a review of Cochrane reviews. The treatments evaluated include nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), bupropion, varenicline, nortriptyline, clonidine, lobeline, dianicline, mecamylamine, nicotine vaccines, and silver acetate.
The review found that NRT, bupropion, and varenicline are effective in achieving long-term abstinence, with NRT and bupropion being superior to placebo, and varenicline being more effective than other forms of NRT and bupropion. Varenicline was also found to be more effective than nicotine patch, nicotine gum, and other forms of NRT, but was not more effective than combination NRT. Cytisine, a nicotine receptor partial agonist, also returned positive findings, with a risk ratio of 3.98 for quitting.
In terms of safety, the review found that bupropion was associated with a lower incidence of serious adverse events compared to placebo, but the manufacturer's estimate of six seizures in the bupropion arms versus none in the placebo arms was lower than expected. Varenicline was also found to have a similar incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events compared to placebo. Nortriptyline was found to increase the chances of quitting, but this was offset by a dose-dependent rise in adverse events. Clonidine, mecamylamine, and nicotine vaccines were found to have inconclusive evidence regarding their effectiveness and safety.
Overall, the review concluded that NRT, bupropion, varenicline, and cytisine are effective smoking cessation treatments, with minimal adverse events. However, further research is needed to fully understand the safety of varenicline and the potential of cytisine as an affordable and effective treatment.

title: A library of yeast transcription factor motifs reveals a widespread function for Rsc3 in targeting nucleosome exclusion at promoters.
text: The primary mechanism by which cells recognize and regulate gene expression is through the specific binding of DNA-binding proteins to specific genomic features. In this study, we systematically determined the DNA-binding specificities of 112 transcription factors in yeast, representing 19 distinct structural classes. One-third of these binding specificities had not been previously reported. We found that certain binding sequences, such as those containing the core CGCG motif, are enriched in specific genomic locations, including approximately 100 bp upstream of transcription start sites. Mutation of these sequences, known as Rsc3 binding elements, resulted in a significant increase in nucleosome occupancy in hundreds of proximal promoters, indicating that Rsc3 plays a crucial role in targeting nucleosome exclusion at yeast promoters. These findings highlight the importance of Rsc3 in regulating gene expression and suggest a broader role in promoter architecture.

title: EphA3 maintains tumorigenicity and is a therapeutic target in glioblastoma multiforme.
text: A significant amount of effort has been devoted to identifying functional therapeutic targets in glioblastoma (GBM) in order to halt the growth of this aggressive cancer. Our research has shown that the receptor tyrosine kinase EphA3 is overexpressed in GBM, particularly in the most aggressive mesenchymal subtype. Notably, EphA3 is highly expressed on the tumor-initiating cell population in glioma and plays a critical role in maintaining tumor cells in a less differentiated state by modulating mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling. By knocking down or depleting EphA3-positive tumor cells, we have found that their tumorigenic potential is significantly reduced, comparable to treatment with a therapeutic radiolabeled EphA3-specific monoclonal antibody. These findings identify EphA3 as a functional, targetable receptor in GBM.

title: Chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells for acute lymphoid leukemia.
text: Chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells with specificity for CD19 have shown promise in the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), but it remains to be established whether these cells have clinical activity in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). In a small study, two children with relapsed and refractory pre-B-cell ALL received infusions of T cells transduced with an anti-CD19 antibody and a T-cell signaling molecule (CTL019 chimeric antigen receptor T cells). The dose of CTL019 T cells ranged from 1.4 x 10^6 to 1.2 x 10^7 cells per kilogram of body weight. In both patients, the CTL019 T cells expanded to levels that were more than 1000 times higher than the initial engraftment level, and were identified in bone marrow and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Eight grade 3 or 4 adverse events were noted, including cytokine-release syndrome and B-cell aplasia. In one child, the cytokine-release syndrome was severe, but was effectively reversed with etanercept and tocilizumab. Complete remission was observed in both patients, with one patient remaining in remission at 11 months after treatment, while the other patient relapsed approximately 2 months after treatment. These findings suggest that chimeric antigen receptor-modified T cells are capable of killing even aggressive, treatment-refractory acute leukemia cells in vivo, and highlight the need to target other molecules in addition to CD19 in some patients with ALL.

title: Extended-connectivity fingerprints.
text: Extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs) represent a novel class of topological fingerprints for molecular characterization, which were developed specifically for structure-activity modeling. Unlike traditional topological fingerprints, which were initially designed for substructure and similarity searching, ECFPs offer several advantageous qualities. Firstly, they can be calculated rapidly, making them a time-efficient tool for analysis. Secondly, they are not predetermined and can capture an almost infinite number of distinct molecular features, including stereochemical information. This allows for more accurate interpretation of analysis results, as the features represented in the ECFPs correspond to the presence of specific substructures. Additionally, the ECFP algorithm can be tailored to generate different types of circular fingerprints, each optimized for specific applications. Despite their widespread adoption and validation, the implementation of ECFPs has not been comprehensively described in the literature until now.

title: Suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 inhibits antiviral IFN-beta signaling to enhance HIV-1 replication in macrophages.
text: HIV-1 replication within macrophages of the central nervous system (CNS) often leads to cognitive and motor impairments, known as HIV-associated dementia (HAD) in its most severe form. Initially, interferon-beta (IFN-beta) suppresses viral replication within these cells, but this protection is temporary, allowing HIV-1 to eventually overcome it and resume replication through an unknown mechanism, leading to the progression of HAD. Our study suggests that Suppressor of Cytokine Signaling (SOCS)3, a molecule that inhibits IFN signaling, may enable HIV-1 to evade the innate immune response within the CNS. We found that SOCS3 is elevated in an in vivo simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV)/macaque model of HAD and correlates with the recurrence of viral replication and onset of CNS disease. In vitro, the HIV-1 regulatory protein transactivator of transcription induces SOCS3 in human and murine macrophages in a nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)-dependent manner. SOCS3 expression attenuates the response of macrophages to IFN-beta at proximal levels of signaling pathway activation and downstream antiviral gene expression, allowing HIV-1 replication to overcome the inhibitory effect of IFN-beta. These findings indicate that SOCS3 expression, induced by stimuli present in the HIV-1-infected brain, such as transactivator of transcription, inhibits antiviral IFN-beta signaling to enhance HIV-1 replication in macrophages. This in vitro and in vivo correlation suggests that SOCS3 may allow HIV-1 to evade the protective innate immune response within the CNS, leading to the recurrence of viral replication and ultimately promoting progression toward HAD.

title: Molecular model of the human 26S proteasome.
text: The 26S proteasome plays a crucial role in maintaining homeostasis in eukaryotic cells by regulating the degradation of a wide range of proteins, including key regulators involved in cell cycle progression and apoptosis. In this study, we have used cryo-electron microscopy and single-particle analysis to determine the structure of the human 26S proteasome. Through the integration of this information with crystal structures, homology models, and other biochemical data, we have constructed a comprehensive molecular model of the complete 26S proteasome. This model provides a detailed understanding of the 20S proteolytic core region and the 19S regulatory particle, and allows for a redefinition of the subunit assignment within the 19S particle. The insights gained from this study offer a strong foundation for elucidating the mechanisms underlying the 26S proteasome's function.

title: Urinary bisphenol A concentrations and early reproductive health outcomes among women undergoing IVF.
text:
Study Question: Are urinary bisphenol A (BPA) concentrations associated with ovarian response and early reproductive outcomes in women undergoing IVF?
Summary Answer: Higher urinary BPA concentrations were found to be associated with decreased ovarian response, number of fertilized oocytes, and decreased blastocyst formation in women undergoing IVF.
What is Known Already: Experimental animal and in vitro studies have reported associations between BPA exposure and adverse reproductive outcomes. Previous studies have also shown an association between urinary BPA and decreased ovarian response in women undergoing IVF.
Study Design: Prospective preconception cohort study.
Participants/Materials: One hundred and seventy-four women aged 18-45 years undergoing 237 IVF cycles at the Massachusetts General Hospital Fertility Center, Boston, MA, USA, between November 2004 and August 2010.
Setting and Methods: Urinary BPA concentrations were measured by online solid-phase extraction-high-performance liquid chromatography-isotope dilution-tandem mass spectrometry. Mixed effect models, Poisson regression, and multivariate logistic regression models were used to evaluate the association between cycle-specific urinary BPA concentrations and measures of ovarian response, oocyte maturation, fertilization, embryo quality, and cleavage rate. Correlation among multiple IVF cycles in the same woman was accounted for using generalized estimating equations.
Main Results and the Role of Chance: The geometric mean (SD) for urinary BPA concentrations was 1.50 (2.22) µg/l. After adjustment for age and other potential confounders (Day 3 serum FSH, smoking, BMI), there was a significant linear dose-response association between increased urinary BPA concentrations and decreased number of oocytes (overall and mature), decreased number of normally fertilized oocytes, and decreased E(2) levels. The mean number of oocytes and normally fertilized oocytes decreased by 24 and 27%, respectively, for the highest versus the lowest quartile of urinary BPA (trend test P < 0.001). Women with urinary BPA above the lowest quartile had decreased blastocyst formation (trend test P-value = 0.08).
Limitations and Reasons for Caution: Potential limitations include exposure misclassification due to the very short half-life of BPA and its high variability over time; uncertainty about the generalizability of the results to the general population of women conceiving naturally and limited sample.
Wider Implications of the Findings: The results from this extended study, using IVF as a model to study early reproductive health outcomes in humans, indicate a negative dose-response association between urinary BPA concentrations and serum peak E(2) and oocyte yield, confirming previous findings. In addition, the study found significantly decreased metaphase II oocyte count and number of normally fertilizing oocytes and a suggestive association between BPA urinary concentrations and decreased blastocyst formation, thus indicating that BPA may alter reproductive function in susceptible women undergoing IVF.
Study Funding/Competing Interests: This work was supported by grants ES009718 and ES000002 from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences and grant OH008578 from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. None of the authors has actual or potential competing financial interests.
Disclaimer: The findings and conclusions in this report are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the views of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: Cost-effectiveness of options for the diagnosis of high blood pressure in primary care: a modelling study.
text:
Background:
Traditionally, the diagnosis of hypertension has relied on blood pressure measurements taken in a clinical setting. However, studies have shown that home and ambulatory measurements provide a more accurate picture of an individual's blood pressure and are better correlated with cardiovascular outcomes. In this study, we aimed to compare the cost-effectiveness of different diagnostic strategies for hypertension.
Methods:
We conducted a Markov model-based probabilistic cost-effectiveness analysis using a hypothetical primary care population aged 40 years or older with a screening blood pressure measurement greater than 140/90 mm Hg and risk factor prevalence equivalent to the general population. We compared three diagnostic strategies: further blood pressure measurement in the clinic, at home, and with an ambulatory monitor. We evaluated the strategies based on lifetime costs, quality-adjusted life years, and cost-effectiveness.
Findings:
Our results showed that ambulatory monitoring was the most cost-effective strategy for the diagnosis of hypertension for both men and women of all ages. Ambulatory monitoring was found to be cost-saving for all age groups, resulting in more quality-adjusted life years for men and women older than 50 years. This finding was robust when assessed with a wide range of deterministic sensitivity analyses around the base case, but was sensitive if home monitoring was judged to have equal test performance to ambulatory monitoring or if treatment was judged effective irrespective of whether an individual was hypertensive.
Interpretation:
Our findings suggest that ambulatory monitoring as a diagnostic strategy for hypertension after an initial raised reading in the clinic would reduce misdiagnosis and save costs. The additional costs associated with ambulatory monitoring are counterbalanced by cost savings from better targeted treatment. Therefore, ambulatory monitoring is recommended for most patients before the start of antihypertensive drugs.
Funding:
This study was funded by the National Institute for Health Research and the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence.

title: Folic acid improves endothelial function in coronary artery disease via mechanisms largely independent of homocysteine lowering.
text:
Background: Homocysteine is a risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD), although the exact relationship between the two remains unclear. It is important to determine the direct cause of homocysteine's association with CAD, as reducing plasma homocysteine levels can be safely and inexpensively achieved through folic acid supplementation.
Methods and Results: In this randomized, placebo-controlled study, 33 patients with CAD were given folic acid (5 mg/d) for 6 weeks. Endothelial function was assessed through flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) measurements taken before, at 2 and 4 hours after the first dose of folic acid, and after 6 weeks of treatment. Plasma folate levels significantly increased by 1 hour, with FMD improving at 2 and 4 hours and being largely complete by 4 hours. However, there was no significant change in total homocysteine (tHcy) levels acutely, although free homocysteine (fHcy) levels did show a slight reduction at 4 hours. The improvement in FMD did not correlate with reductions in either fHcy or tHcy at any time.
Conclusions: These findings suggest that folic acid improves endothelial function in CAD acutely through a mechanism largely independent of homocysteine.

title: Focal adhesion kinase links mechanical force to skin fibrosis via inflammatory signaling
text: Exuberant fibroproliferation is a common complication following injury, with the underlying mechanisms not fully understood. One crucial aspect of wound healing that is often overlooked is the role of mechanical force in regulating cell-matrix interactions. Intracellular focal adhesion components, including focal adhesion kinase (FAK), play a key role in this process. Our study reveals that FAK is activated after cutaneous injury and that this process is enhanced by mechanical loading. In mice lacking FAK in fibroblasts, there is significantly less inflammation and fibrosis in a model of hypertrophic scar formation compared to control mice. We found that FAK acts through extracellular-related kinase (ERK) to mechanically trigger the secretion of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1, also known as CCL2), a potent chemokine involved in human fibrotic disorders. Similarly, MCP-1 knockout mice exhibit minimal scarring, indicating that inflammatory chemokine pathways are a primary mechanism by which FAK mechanotransduction leads to fibrosis. Inhibition of FAK using small molecules reduces scar formation in vivo by attenuating MCP-1 signaling and inflammatory cell recruitment. These findings suggest that physical force regulates fibrosis through inflammatory FAK-ERK-MCP-1 pathways, and that targeting FAK with molecular strategies can effectively decouple mechanical force from pathological scar formation.

title: Prognostic Accuracy of the SOFA Score, SIRS Criteria, and qSOFA Score for In-Hospital Mortality Among Adults With Suspected Infection Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit
text:
The Sepsis-3 criteria have emphasized the importance of a change in Sequential [Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, introduced quick SOFA (qSOFA), and removed the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria from the sepsis definition. This study aimed to externally validate and assess the discriminatory capacities of an increase in SOFA score by 2 or more points, 2 or more SIRS criteria, or a qSOFA score of 2 or more points for outcomes among patients who are critically ill with suspected infection.
Retrospective cohort analysis of 184,875 patients with an infection-related primary admission diagnosis in 182 Australian and New Zealand intensive care units (ICUs) from 2000 to 2015 was conducted. The study found that SOFA demonstrated significantly greater discrimination for in-hospital mortality than SIRS criteria or qSOFA, with an incremental improvement of 0.164 (99% CI, 0.159-0.169) for SOFA vs SIRS criteria and 0.146 (99% CI, 0.142-0.151) for SOFA vs qSOFA (P <.001). SOFA (AUROC, 0.736 [99% CI, 0.733-0.739]) outperformed the other scores for the secondary end point (SIRS criteria: AUROC, 0.609 [99% CI, 0.606-0.612]; qSOFA: AUROC, 0.606 [99% CI, 0.602-0.609]). The findings were consistent for both outcomes in multiple sensitivity analyses.
The study suggests that SIRS criteria and qSOFA may have limited utility for predicting mortality in an ICU setting. The study highlights the importance of the SOFA score in predicting in-hospital mortality among critically ill patients with suspected infection.

title: Predictors of mammographic density: insights gained from a novel regression analysis of a twin study.
text: Understanding which factors influence mammographically dense and nondense areas is crucial because percent mammographic density adjusted for age is a strong, consistently distributed risk factor for breast cancer, particularly when adjusted for weight or body mass index. In this study, we measured mammographically dense areas in 571 monozygotic and 380 dizygotic Australian and North American twin pairs aged 40 to 70 years using computer-assisted methods. We employed a novel regression modeling approach, where each twin's measure of dense and nondense area was regressed against their own and their co-twin's covariates. By evaluating the changes in regression estimates with the inclusion of the twin and/or co-twin's covariates, we could assess the consistency of these associations with causal and/or other models. Our findings revealed that adjusting for the individual's weight attenuated the co-twin associations with weight, suggesting a causal effect of weight on mammographic measures. Specifically, the association between weight and mammographic density was thrice stronger for nondense than dense area. However, later age at menarche, greater height, and parity were associated with greater dense and lesser nondense areas in a manner inconsistent with causality. The associations between mammographic density measures and height were also observed, which may be due to shared early life environmental factors that predispose to both height and breast cancer risk.

title: Shaping the landscape of the Escherichia coli chromosome: replication-transcription encounters in cells with an ectopic replication origin
text: Each cell division involves the unwinding of millions of DNA base pairs to facilitate chromosome duplication and gene transcription. However, due to the shared template nature of DNA replication and transcription, conflicts between these processes are inevitable, and head-on collisions are thought to be particularly problematic. Contrary to expectations, a recent study reported unperturbed cell cycle progression in Escherichia coli cells with an ectopic replication origin containing highly transcribed rrn operons replicated opposite to normal. In this study, we have replicated the same strain and observed a doubling time twice that of normal cells. Replication profiles of this background revealed significant deviations, particularly in highly transcribed regions and the termination area, compared to wild-type profiles. These deviations were alleviated by mutations that either inactivate the termination area or destabilize RNA polymerase complexes, allowing for easier displacement by replication forks. Our findings demonstrate that head-on replication-transcription conflicts are highly problematic and support the idea that avoiding these collisions has significantly contributed to the distinct architecture of bacterial chromosomes. Interestingly, analysis of the replication profile of the previously published E. coli construct revealed a chromosomal rearrangement that alleviates replication-transcription conflicts in a simple yet intriguing manner.

title: Epithelial–mesenchymal transitions in tumour progression
text: Without epithelial-mesenchymal transitions (EMTs), multicellular organisms would be unable to progress beyond the blastula stage of embryonic development. However, this crucial developmental program has a darker side in the context of tumor progression. EMTs provide a new framework for understanding how carcinomas can transition towards more dedifferentiated and malignant states.

title: Platelets at the interface of thrombosis, inflammation, and cancer.
text:
Although historically associated with roles in hemostasis and thrombosis, the platelet has emerged as a multifaceted cell with far-reaching implications in various disease processes. Recent observations have highlighted the platelet's ability to influence a wide range of seemingly unrelated pathophysiological events, including inflammation. This shift in understanding the platelet's function is rooted in its evolutionary origins as a lower vertebrate cell type with both hemostatic and immunological roles.
In cancer biology, the platelet's involvement in the complex interplay between hemostasis, thrombosis, inflammation, and cancer is gaining increasing attention. By examining the hallmarks of cancer and the ways in which platelets can impact multistep tumor development, we can gain a deeper appreciation for the platelet's role in disease processes. The use of animal models of platelet dysfunction and current antiplatelet therapies provides a valuable framework for understanding the mechanistic insights into a wide range of pathophysiological events.
As a result, basic scientists studying platelet function can expand their focus beyond the traditional hemostasis and thrombosis paradigms, while hematologists must recognize the platelet's relevance in a variety of disease processes. By appreciating the platelet's multifaceted nature, we can uncover new avenues for disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

title: Cellular roles of DNA topoisomerases: a molecular perspective
text: DNA topoisomerases are the masterful manipulators of the DNA world, effortlessly facilitating the passage of DNA strands or double helices through one another to solve all topological challenges that arise during replication, transcription, and other cellular processes. Over the past three decades, extensive biochemical and structural research has provided a detailed understanding of how the different subfamilies of DNA topoisomerases manipulate DNA at the molecular level. In this review, we delve into the cellular functions of these enzymes from a molecular perspective.

title: MicroRNA sponges: progress and possibilities.
text:
Three years ago, the "sponge" method for microRNA (miRNA) loss of function was introduced. This method involves using RNAs called sponges, which contain complementary binding sites to a specific miRNA of interest. These sponges are produced within cells from transgenes, and they can effectively block a family of related miRNAs by binding to their seed region. This transgenic approach has proven to be a valuable tool for studying miRNA functions in various experimental systems.
In this article, we will explore ways to optimize sponge and related constructs, and review recent applications of this method with a particular focus on stable expression in cancer studies and in transgenic animals. We will discuss how sponges can be optimized for efficient and specific inhibition of miRNAs, and how they can be used to study the functional consequences of miRNA loss of function in different biological contexts.

title: Wip1 phosphatase regulates p53-dependent apoptosis of stem cells and tumorigenesis in the mouse intestine.
text: Colorectal cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths, and to gain a deeper understanding of its development, we investigated the role of Wip1 phosphatase in the mouse model of APC(Min)-driven polyposis. Our findings revealed that Wip1 removal increased the lifespan of APC(Min) mice by significantly reducing polyp formation. This protection was dependent on the p53 tumor suppressor, which plays a role in regulating apoptosis in intestinal stem cells. Interestingly, we found that activation of the Wnt pathway in Wip1-deficient mice led to increased apoptosis in stem cells, compared to wild-type APC(Min) mice. Based on these observations, we propose that Wip1 phosphatase regulates homeostasis in intestinal stem cells, and its loss suppresses APC(Min)-driven polyposis by lowering the threshold for p53-dependent apoptosis of stem cells, thereby preventing their transformation into tumor-initiating stem cells.

title: The shunt problem: control of functional shunting in normal and tumour vasculature
text: Networks of blood vessels in normal and tumor tissues exhibit heterogeneous structures, with varying blood flow pathway lengths. To ensure efficient blood flow distribution, mechanisms for vascular adaptation must be able to inhibit the formation of functional shunts, where short pathways become enlarged and flow bypasses long pathways. This adaptation requires the exchange of information about tissue metabolic status between feeding vessels and downstream vessels through conducted responses. We propose that impaired vascular communication in tumor microvascular networks, leading to functional shunting, is a primary cause of dysfunctional microcirculation and local hypoxia in cancer. We suggest that anti-angiogenic treatment of tumors may restore vascular communication and thereby improve or normalize flow distribution in tumor vasculature.

title: Pharmacological Blockade of ASCT2-dependent Glutamine Transport Leads To Anti-tumor Efficacy in Preclinical Models
text: The distinct metabolic requirements of cancer cells present a promising avenue for drug discovery in the era of precision medicine. However, therapeutic targeting of cancer metabolism has yielded a limited number of new drugs thus far. The neutral amino acid glutamine plays a crucial role in various metabolic processes exploited by cancer cells, including biosynthesis, cell signaling, and oxidative defense. Here, we report the preclinical development of V-9302, a competitive small molecule inhibitor of transmembrane glutamine flux that selectively targets the amino acid transporter ASCT2. Pharmacological blockade of ASCT2 with V-9302 resulted in impaired cancer cell growth and proliferation, increased cell death, and enhanced oxidative stress, thereby contributing to antitumor responses in vitro and in vivo. This study represents the first attempt to utilize a pharmacological inhibitor of glutamine transport in oncology, marking the emergence of a novel class of targeted therapy and paving the way for groundbreaking treatments that target cancer cell metabolism.

title: An Antidepressant Decreases CSF Aβ Production in Healthy Individuals and in Transgenic AD Mice
text: Serotonin signaling has been shown to inhibit the production of amyloid-β (Aβ) in both in vitro and animal models of Alzheimer's disease (AD). In a transgenic AD mouse model (APP/PS1 plaque-bearing mice), the antidepressant citalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, was found to decrease Aβ levels in brain interstitial fluid in a dose-dependent manner. The growth of individual amyloid plaques was assessed in plaque-bearing mice that were chronically administered citalopram, and the results showed that citalopram arrested the growth of preexisting plaques and reduced the appearance of new plaques by 78%. In a separate study, the effects of citalopram on Aβ production and concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were measured in healthy human volunteers using stable isotope labeling kinetics. The results showed that Aβ production in CSF was slowed by 37% in the citalopram group compared to the placebo group, and total CSF Aβ concentrations decreased by 38% in the drug-treated group. These findings suggest that citalopram may have potential as a preventive strategy for AD, and this study provides key target engagement data for future AD prevention trials.

title: Variations in the quality and sustainability of long-term glycaemic control with continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.
text:
Objective: To investigate the pattern of changes in HbA1c levels in individuals with Type 1 diabetes managed by long-term continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII).
Methods: We retrospectively analyzed computerized clinic records of 35 adults with Type 1 diabetes and elevated HbA1c (≥ 64 mmol/mol, 8.0%) on multiple daily insulin injections, who were switched to CSII for at least 5 years.
