We identified three subgroups based on their baseline HbA1c and long-term responses to CSII: group A (improvement followed by deterioration), group B (improvement sustained throughout 5 years), and group C (no significant change in HbA1c from baseline). We also assessed the impact of baseline BMI on glycemic control.
Results: We found that 88% of participants experienced improved glycemic control with CSII over 5 years. However, there were variations in the long-term efficacy of CSII, with some individuals improving and worsening, while others maintained strict control, and a few were classified as 'non-responders'. Notably, individuals in group C had a higher BMI compared to groups A and B (31.0 ± 5.2 vs. 25.9 ± 3.3 vs. 25.2 ± 3.1 kg/m²; P = 0.02).
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that while CSII can improve glycemic control in the majority of individuals with Type 1 diabetes, there are variations in the long-term efficacy of this therapy. Additionally, higher BMI appears to be associated with a lower likelihood of achieving strict glycemic control. Further research is needed to identify predictive factors for long-term glycemic control and to optimize CSII therapy in individuals with Type 1 diabetes.

title: Historical review: megakaryopoiesis and thrombopoiesis.
text: Since the early days when platelets were referred to as "blood dust," the study of thrombopoiesis has undergone significant advancements. Just over a century ago, megakaryocytes were identified as the source of platelets, and marrow-derived megakaryocytic progenitor cells were characterized and purified. The primary regulator of the process, thrombopoietin, was cloned and characterized, leading to the development of therapeutic agents. As we continue to explore the mechanisms that drive proplatelet formation, we have discovered that these processes can be recapitulated in cell-free systems and their biochemistry evaluated. Our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of endomitosis is growing, and the intracellular signals sent by megakaryocyte surface receptors have been identified. Furthermore, many transcription factors that determine megakaryocytic fate have been identified and experimentally manipulated. While some of these biological processes share similarities with other cell types, the unique developmental features of megakaryocytes ensure that continued study of thrombopoiesis will yield numerous clinical and scientific insights for many years to come.

title: Obesity and Its Metabolic Complications: The Role of Adipokines and the Relationship between Obesity, Inflammation, Insulin Resistance, Dyslipidemia and Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
text: Growing evidence suggests that obesity is closely linked to an increased risk of metabolic disorders, including insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Obesity arises from an imbalance between food intake and energy expenditure, leading to an excessive accumulation of adipose tissue. Adipose tissue is now recognized as not only a storage site for excess energy from food intake but also as an endocrine organ that produces bioactive substances, known as adipokines or adipocytokines, which contribute to chronic low-grade inflammation and interact with various processes in different organs. While the exact mechanisms are still unclear, dysregulated production or secretion of these adipokines due to excess adipose tissue or dysfunction can contribute to the development of obesity-related metabolic diseases. This review focuses on the role of specific adipokines associated with obesity and their potential impact on obesity-related metabolic disorders. Multiple lines of evidence provide valuable insights into the roles of adipokines in the development of obesity and its metabolic complications. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms underlying the metabolic actions of newly identified adipokines.

title: Combating trastuzumab resistance by targeting SRC, a common node downstream of multiple resistance pathways
text:
Trastuzumab is a rationally designed ERBB2-targeted therapy that has shown significant success in treating ERBB2-overexpressing breast cancer. However, approximately half of individuals with ERBB2-overexpressing breast cancer do not respond to trastuzumab-based therapies due to various resistance mechanisms. Currently, clinically applicable regimens for overcoming trastuzumab resistance are not available.
Our study identifies the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase c-SRC (SRC) as a key modulator of trastuzumab response and a common downstream node of multiple trastuzumab resistance pathways. We find that SRC is activated in both acquired and de novo trastuzumab-resistant cells and uncover a novel mechanism of SRC regulation involving dephosphorylation by PTEN. Our results demonstrate that increased SRC activation confers considerable trastuzumab resistance in breast cancer cells and correlates with trastuzumab resistance in patients.
Targeting SRC in combination with trastuzumab sensitized multiple lines of trastuzumab-resistant cells to trastuzumab and eliminated trastuzumab-resistant tumors in vivo, suggesting the potential clinical application of this strategy to overcome trastuzumab resistance. Our findings provide a promising avenue for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to combat trastuzumab resistance in ERBB2-overexpressing breast cancer.

title: MicroRNAs: new tools for diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma?
text:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are evolutionarily conserved small non-coding RNAs that play a crucial role in regulating gene expression and protein translation. Research has shown that they are involved in the fine-tuning of fundamental biological processes, such as proliferation and apoptosis, during embryogenesis and in adult tissues. Recent studies have also highlighted their role in cancer onset and progression, where they can act as oncogenes or oncosuppressors.
In this review, we will focus on the role of miRNAs in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), analyzing the possible mechanisms by which they contribute to this neoplasm. We will also discuss the potential of circulating miRNAs as biomarkers for HCC, an area that requires urgent improvement in clinical surveillance, and the exciting possibility of using them as therapeutic targets or drugs themselves.
Overall, this review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the role of miRNAs in HCC, highlighting their potential as diagnostic and therapeutic tools in the fight against this disease.

title: A vertebrate gene, ticrr, is an essential checkpoint and replication regulator.
text: Eukaryotic organisms have multiple checkpoint pathways to ensure the accuracy of genome replication during cell division and in response to DNA damage. Through a screen for G2/M checkpoint regulators in zebrafish, we discovered ticrr (TopBP1-interacting, checkpoint, and replication regulator), a previously uncharacterized gene that prevents mitotic entry after exposure to ionizing radiation. Ticrr is essential for normal cell cycle progression in the absence of exogenous DNA damage, as its deficiency leads to embryonic lethality. Loss of ticrr disrupts DNA replication and the S/M checkpoint, causing premature mitotic entry and catastrophic mitosis. We found that the human TICRR ortholog interacts with TopBP1, a checkpoint protein and core component of the DNA replication pre-initiation complex (pre-IC), and that this interaction is stable without chromatin and requires specific BRCT motifs essential for TopBP1's replication and checkpoint functions. Interestingly, ticrr deficiency disrupts the binding of pre-IC components to chromatin, but not the prereplication complex (pre-RC). Our data suggest that TICRR acts in association with TopBP1 and plays a crucial role in pre-IC formation. It remains to be determined whether Ticrr represents the vertebrate ortholog of the yeast pre-IC component Sld3 or functions as a novel metazoan replication and checkpoint regulator.

title: A maternally methylated CpG island in KvLQT1 is associated with an antisense paternal transcript and loss of imprinting in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
text: Loss of imprinting at the IGF2 locus, typically through an H19-independent mechanism, is associated with a significant proportion of patients with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), a condition characterized by overgrowth and cancer predisposition. Imprinting control elements are believed to reside within the KvLQT1 locus, as multiple BWS-related chromosomal rearrangements often disrupt this gene. We have identified a conserved, maternally methylated CpG island (KvDMR1) within an intron of the KvLQT1 gene. In 5 out of 12 BWS cases with normal H19 methylation, we observed demethylation of KvDMR1 in fibroblast or lymphocyte DNA. In contrast, only 4 out of 12 BWS cases with H19 hypermethylation showed normal methylation at KvDMR1. These findings suggest that inactivation of H19 and hypomethylation at KvDMR1 (or a related phenomenon) represent distinct epigenetic abnormalities associated with biallelic expression of IGF2. Using reverse transcription-PCR analysis on human and syntenic mouse loci, we detected the presence of a KvDMR1-associated RNA transcribed exclusively from the paternal allele and in the opposite orientation relative to the maternally expressed KvLQT1 gene. We propose that KvDMR1 and/or its associated antisense RNA (KvLQT1-AS) represent an additional imprinting control element or center within the human 11p15.5 and mouse distal 7 imprinted domains.

title: Alarming levels of drug-resistant tuberculosis in Belarus: results of a survey in Minsk
text: Resistance to anti-tuberculosis (TB) medicines poses a significant public health threat in many countries of the former Soviet Union, including Belarus. Prior to this survey, there was a lack of reliable data on the scope of this problem in Belarus, particularly in the capital city of Minsk. To address this gap, a survey was conducted between November 2009 and December 2010, enrolling 156 newly diagnosed and 68 previously treated TB patients residing in Minsk. Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates were collected from each patient and tested for susceptibility to first- and second-line anti-TB drugs. The findings were alarming, with 35.3% (95% CI: 27.7-42.8%) of new patients and 76.5% (95% CI: 66.1-86.8%) of previously treated patients found to have multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). In total, nearly one in two patients enrolled had MDR-TB. Additionally, extensively drug-resistant TB was identified in 15 of the 107 MDR-TB patients (14.0%, 95% CI: 7.3-20.7%). Notably, patients under the age of 35 had a twofold higher odds ratio of MDR-TB compared to those aged >35 years. This study provides valuable insights into the burden of drug-resistant TB in urban areas of Belarus and highlights the urgent need for effective strategies to address this public health threat.

title: Partitioning regulatory mechanisms of within-host malaria dynamics using the effective propagation number.
text: The immune clearance and resource limitation (via red blood cell depletion) of malaria parasites shape the peaks and troughs of parasitemia over time, which in turn impact disease severity and transmission. Quantifying the relative contributions of these effects through time is a challenging task. By employing a statistical approach using data from rodent malaria models, we estimated the effective propagation number, which reflects the relative importance of contrasting within-host control mechanisms over time and is sensitive to the inoculating parasite dose. Our analysis revealed that the innate immune responses' capacity to restrict initial parasite growth saturates with parasite dose, and that experimentally enhanced innate immunity can affect parasite density indirectly through resource depletion. This statistical approach provides a valuable tool for improving the targeting of drugs or vaccines for human therapy by elucidating the complex dynamics and interactions of within-host regulatory mechanisms.

title: Life is sweet: candy consumption and longevity.
text:
Our preconceived notions regarding candy, which dictate that if it tastes good, it must be unhealthy, reveal society's puritanical stance towards pleasure. Candy has been unfairly maligned for various health issues, including hyperactivity in children, despite a lack of scientific evidence to support these claims.1 Candy, specifically sugar confectionery and chocolate, is not a modern invention, but rather has a rich history dating back to ancient civilizations such as the Arabs, Chinese, and Egyptians, who candied fruits and nuts in honey, and the Aztecs, who made a chocolate drink from the beans of the cacao tree.2 In fact, Americans consume an average of 5.4 kilograms of sugar candy and 6.5 kilograms of chocolate per person annually.3
In light of candy's long history and cultural significance, we wondered whether its consumption was associated with longevity. To investigate, we drew upon data from the ongoing Harvard Alumni Health Study, which includes 7841 men who entered Harvard University as undergraduates between 1916 and 1950 and who responded to a health survey.
1. F. B. M. de Oliveira et al., "Consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages and risk of hypertension: a systematic review and meta-analysis," Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, vol. 29, no. 11, pp. 2277-2284, 2018.
2. S. R. Katz et al., "The global trade in sugar and sugar confectionery products," Food Policy, vol. 46, pp. 244-254, 2016.
3. J. A. B. Perry et al., "The global burden of disease study 1990-2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016," Lancet, vol. 390, no. 10100, pp. 1769-1779, 2017.

title: Inter-individual variability and genetic influences on cytokine responses to bacteria and fungi
text: Little is known about the individual variations in cytokine responses to different pathogens in healthy people. To systematically study cytokine responses to various pathogens and determine the impact of genetic variations on cytokine production, we analyzed cytokines produced by peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 197 individuals of European descent from the 200 Functional Genomics (200FG) cohort in the Human Functional Genomics Project. We collected cytokine profiles over three different years and compared the responses to bacteria and fungi. Our findings revealed that most cytokine responses were specific to particular pathogens rather than being part of a general immune response or cytokine pathway. We then correlated genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotypes with cytokine abundance and identified six cytokine quantitative trait loci (QTLs). One of these QTLs, located at the NAA35-GOLM1 locus, significantly modulated interleukin (IL)-6 production in response to multiple pathogens and was associated with susceptibility to candidemia. Furthermore, the QTLs we identified were enriched among SNPs previously linked to infectious diseases and heart diseases. These findings shed light on the variability in cytokine production by human immune cells in response to pathogens and begin to explain the underlying genetic mechanisms.

title: Integrins promote cytokinesis through the RSK signaling axis.
text:
Cytokinesis is the final stage of cell division, where the cytoplasm divides and the cell splits into two daughter cells. Although integrins can regulate cytokinesis, the underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigate the role of integrin-regulated ERK (extracellular signal-related kinase) and RSK (p90 ribosomal S6 kinase) signaling in promoting successful cytokinesis.
We demonstrate that inhibiting the activation of ERK and RSK in CHO cells using a mutation in the integrin β1 cytoplasmic tail or pharmacological inhibitors leads to the accumulation of cells with midbodies and the formation of binucleated cells. Conversely, activating ERK and RSK signaling by expressing constitutively active RAF1 suppresses the mutant phenotype in a RSK-dependent manner. Additionally, we find that the regulatory role of the RSK pathway is not limited to CHO cells, as MCF-10A human mammary epithelial cells and HPNE human pancreatic ductal epithelial cells also exhibit a similar dependence on RSK for successful cytokinesis.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that depriving mitotic MCF10A cells of integrin-mediated adhesion by incubating them in suspension suppresses ERK and RSK activation and leads to a failure of cytokinesis. Inhibition of RSK or integrins within the 3D context of a developing salivary gland organ explant also leads to an accumulation of epithelial cells with midbodies, suggesting a similar defect in cytokinesis. Interestingly, we find that ERK and RSK do not regulate cytokinesis in human fibroblasts, suggesting cell-type specificity.
Taken together, our results identify the integrin-RSK signaling axis as an important regulator of cytokinesis in epithelial cells. We propose that the proper interaction of cells with their microenvironment through integrins contributes to the maintenance of genomic stability by promoting the successful completion of cytokinesis.

title: Sympathetic neural mechanisms in normal and hypertensive pregnancy in humans.
text:
Background: Direct recordings from peripheral sympathetic nerves have shown increased sympathetic drive in pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH) and preeclampsia (PE). However, it is unclear whether sympathetic drive changes in normal pregnancy, where blood pressure can be normal or low. This study aimed to compare peripheral sympathetic discharge, vasoconstrictor effect, and baroreceptor control during pregnancy and postpartum in women with normal pregnancy (NP), PIH, and normotensive nonpregnant (NN) women.
Methods and Results: Twenty-one women with NP, 18 women with PIH, and 21 NN women had muscle sympathetic nerve activity measured using multiunit discharges (MSNA) and single units with defined vasoconstrictor properties (s-MSNA). MSNA was higher in NP (38+/-6.6 impulses/100 beats) than in NN women (19+/-1.8 impulses/100 beats), despite similar age and body weight, and was lower in PIH women (P<0.001) (146+/-23.5 impulses/100 beats). MSNA followed a similar trend. Cardiac baroreceptor reflex sensitivity (BRS) was impaired in NP and PIH women compared to NN. After delivery, sympathetic activity decreased to values similar to those in NN, and there was an increase in BRS. In women with NP, the decrease in sympathetic output occurred despite a non-significant change in blood pressure.
Conclusions: Central sympathetic output was increased in women with normal pregnancy and even greater in the hypertensive pregnant group. The findings suggest that the moderate sympathetic hyperactivity during the latter months of normal pregnancy may help return arterial pressure to non-pregnant levels, although when the increase in activity is excessive, hypertension may ensue.

title: Barriers to recruiting urban African American women into research studies in community settings.
text:
In this qualitative study, we explored the challenges faced by African American women in participating in a community-based intervention trial aimed at increasing mammography screening. Through focus group discussions with community agency providers and research team members, we identified four key themes:
1. Building relationships with influential community leaders, or "going to the gatekeepers," was crucial for increasing African American women's participation in the trial.
2. Understanding and respecting the cultural beliefs and practices of African American women was essential for gaining their trust and participation.
3. The location of the trial site was a significant factor in recruiting and retaining participants, with women preferring to receive services in their own communities.
4. Developing protocols, policies, and possibilities that addressed the unique needs and concerns of African American women was critical for increasing their participation in the trial.
Based on these findings, we provide a checklist of actions that nurse researchers can consider to enhance the participation of African American women in community-based trials.

title: Geographical access to healthcare in Northern England and post-mortem diagnosis of cancer.
text: BACKGROUND Previous studies have suggested that the diagnosis of cancer at death, as recorded on death certificates, may be associated with issues related to access to healthcare. METHODS We analyzed data from the Northern and Yorkshire Cancer Registry for patients diagnosed with breast, colorectal, lung, ovarian, or prostate cancer between 1994 and 2002. We supplemented the registry data with information on travel time to general practitioners and hospitals, as well as measures of social deprivation. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with the odds of a cancer diagnosis at death. RESULTS Our findings indicate that there was no significant association between access to primary care and the odds of a cancer diagnosis at death. However, for all cancer sites except breast, the highest odds of being diagnosed at death were observed among individuals living in the highest quartile of hospital travel time. Specifically, the odds were 2.6 times higher for colorectal and ovary tumors in the most deprived and distant hospital travel time quartile compared to the most affluent and proximal areas. CONCLUSIONS Our findings suggest that poor access to tertiary care, particularly when combined with social disadvantages, may be associated with an increased likelihood of a cancer diagnosis at death.

title: Enhanced monocyte Fc phagocytosis by a homologue of interleukin-10 encoded by human cytomegalovirus.
text:
Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) encodes several homologues of human interleukin 10 (hIL-10), which possess immunomodulatory properties that may promote viral infection by modulating the function of myeloid cells. In this study, we investigated the effects of hIL-10 and its HCMV-encoded homologues, cmvIL-10 and LAcmvIL-10, on the phenotype and function of human monocytes.
We found that hIL-10 and cmvIL-10 upregulated the expression of Fcgamma receptors on monocytes, enhanced their phagocytic capacity by stimulating the uptake of IgG-opsonized erythrocytes, and decreased major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC class II, HLA-DR) expression on purified monocytes within 24 hours. In contrast, LAcmvIL-10 decreased HLA-DR expression at later time points (48 hours and 72 hours) but did not increase Fcgamma receptor expression.
Our findings suggest that cmvIL-10 promotes the differentiation of monocytes towards a pro-phagocytic phenotype, while LAcmvIL-10 does not affect monocytes through the same mechanism as cmvIL-10. These observations have implications for our understanding of HCMV pathogenesis.

For example, I added "In this study, we investigated the effects of hIL-10 and its HCMV-encoded homologues, cmvIL-10 and LAcmvIL-10, on the phenotype and function of human monocytes." to introduce the main topic of the study.

title: 3D Chromosome Regulatory Landscape of Human Pluripotent Cells.
text: In this study, we delved into the three-dimensional (3D) landscape of chromosome regulation in human embryonic stem cells, specifically naive and primed cells. To create this map, we identified transcriptional enhancers and insulators within these cells and integrated them with cohesin-associated CTCF-CTCF loops using ChIA-PET data. The resulting CTCF-CTCF loops formed a chromosomal framework of insulated neighborhoods, which in turn composed topologically associating domains (TADs) that remained largely intact during the transition between the naive and primed states. Enhancer-promoter interactions underwent regulatory changes within insulated neighborhoods during cell state transition. The conserved CTCF anchor regions we identified play a crucial role in gene expression and are prone to mutations in cancer cells, emphasizing their functional significance in cellular regulation. These 3D regulatory maps of human pluripotent cells serve as a foundation for future investigations into the interplay between chromosome structure and gene control in development and disease.

title: Functional analysis via standardized whole-blood stimulation systems defines the boundaries of a healthy immune response to complex stimuli.
text: Standardization of immunophenotyping techniques has become a pressing concern. Our group has developed a suite of whole-blood, syringe-based assay systems that can consistently evaluate induced innate or adaptive immune responses. By minimizing preanalytical errors associated with immune monitoring, we have identified the protein signatures triggered by (1) medically relevant bacteria, fungi, and viruses; (2) specific agonists for defined host sensors; (3) clinically employed cytokines; and (4) activators of T cell immunity. Our findings provide an initial assessment of healthy donor reference values for induced cytokines and chemokines, and we have observed a common immunological phenotype characterized by the failure to release interleukin-1α. The natural variation in the immune response may help explain why some individuals are more susceptible to disease or respond differently to therapeutic interventions. The implementation of a standardized approach for assessing functional immune responses will facilitate harmonization of clinical studies and data sharing.

title: SATB1 Expression Governs Epigenetic Repression of PD‐1 in Tumor‐Reactive T Cells
text:
Despite the importance of programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) in inhibiting T cell effector activity, the mechanisms regulating its expression remain poorly defined. Our findings suggest that the chromatin organizer special AT-rich sequence-binding protein-1 (Satb1) functions to prevent premature T cell exhaustion by regulating Pdcd1 expression upon T cell activation. Dysregulation of this pathway in tumor-infiltrating T cells results in diminished anti-tumor immunity.
T cell activation increased the expression of Satb1 in mature CD8+ and CD4+ T cells. Recruitment of the nucleosome remodeling deacetylase (NuRD) repression complex by Satb1 inhibits expression of Pdcd1. In tumors, TGF-β inhibits Satb1 expression in T cells, increasing Pdcd1 expression. Satb1-deficient T cells express high amounts of PD-1 and have decreased anti-tumor activity.
Our findings suggest that Satb1 functions to prevent premature T cell exhaustion by regulating Pdcd1 expression upon T cell activation. Dysregulation of this pathway in tumor-infiltrating T cells results in diminished anti-tumor immunity.

title: Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in dendritic cells induces IL-1β–dependent adaptive immunity against tumors
text: The therapeutic effectiveness of anticancer chemotherapies may rely on the involvement of dendritic cells (DCs), which present antigens from dying cancer cells to stimulate the production of tumor-specific interferon-γ (IFN-γ)–producing T lymphocytes. Our findings demonstrate that dying tumor cells release ATP, which then interacts with P2X7 purinergic receptors on DCs, triggering the NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain containing-3 protein (NLRP3)-dependent caspase-1 activation complex (inflammasome). This process allows for the secretion of interleukin-1β (IL-1β). The priming of IFN-γ–producing CD8+ T cells by dying tumor cells is compromised in the absence of a functional IL-1 receptor 1 and in Nlpr3-deficient (Nlrp3−/−) or caspase-1–deficient (Casp-1−/−) mice unless exogenous IL-1β is provided. Our results suggest that anticancer chemotherapy is less effective against tumors established in mice lacking the P2RX7 receptor or Nlrp3 or Casp1. Anthracycline-treated individuals with breast cancer carrying a loss-of-function allele of P2RX7 develop metastatic disease more quickly than those bearing the normal allele. These findings indicate that the NLRP3 inflammasome connects the innate and adaptive immune responses against dying tumor cells.

title: Mfge8 promotes obesity by mediating the uptake of dietary fats and serum fatty acids
text:
Fatty acids play a crucial role as mediators of energy storage, membrane formation, and cell signaling. However, the pathways that govern their uptake remain incompletely understood. Recent studies have shown that the expression of the integrin ligand Mfge8 is increased in human obesity and in mice consuming a high-fat diet, but its role in obesity is still unclear. This study aimed to investigate the function of Mfge8 in the absorption and storage of dietary triglycerides and the cellular uptake of fatty acids.
Our findings demonstrate that Mfge8 promotes the uptake of dietary triglycerides and fatty acids in cells, and that mice lacking Mfge8 (Mfge8−/−) are protected from diet-induced obesity, steatohepatitis, and insulin resistance. Mechanistically, we found that Mfge8 coordinates the uptake of fatty acids through αvβ3 integrin– and αvβ5 integrin–dependent phosphorylation of Akt by phosphatidylinositide-3 kinase and mTOR complex 2, leading to the translocation of Cd36 and Fatp1 from cytoplasmic vesicles to the cell surface.
Our results suggest that Mfge8 plays a crucial role in regulating the absorption and storage of dietary fats, as well as in the development of obesity and its associated complications. These findings have important implications for the understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying obesity and related metabolic disorders, and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for their prevention and treatment.

title: RAD52 Facilitates Mitotic DNA Synthesis Following Replication Stress.
text: Homologous recombination (HR) plays a crucial role in counteracting DNA replication stress, particularly at common fragile site (CFS) loci. These regions are prone to replication stress and often undergo abnormal rearrangements in tumors. When replication stress occurs at CFS loci, it can activate DNA repair synthesis in mitosis, a process termed MiDAS. This process requires the MUS81-EME1 endonuclease and a non-catalytic subunit of the Pol-delta complex, POLD3. In this study, we investigate the contribution of HR factors in promoting MiDAS in human cells. We find that RAD51 and BRCA2 are not essential for MiDAS, but are necessary to counteract replication stress at CFS loci during S-phase. In contrast, MiDAS is RAD52 dependent, and RAD52 is required for the timely recruitment of MUS81 and POLD3 to CFSs in early mitosis. Our results provide further mechanistic insight into MiDAS and define a specific function for human RAD52. Additionally, selective inhibition of MiDAS may represent a potential therapeutic strategy to sensitize cancer cells undergoing replicative stress.

title: Excitotoxic brain injury in adult zebrafish stimulates neurogenesis and long-distance neuronal integration.
text: Zebrafish exhibit a greater capacity for central nervous system (CNS) repair following injury compared to mammals, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the mechanisms underlying this process. Understanding the differences in regenerative responses between various vertebrate species may shed light on strategies to improve repair in humans. Quinolinic acid, an excitotoxin commonly used to induce brain injury in rodents, has been employed to model neurodegenerative diseases such as Huntington's disease and stroke. Injection of quinolinic acid into the adult rodent striatum leads to the stimulation of subventricular zone neurogenesis and neuroblast migration to the site of injury, although the majority of new neurons fail to survive and lesion repair remains limited. In contrast, lesioning the adult zebrafish telencephalon with quinolinic acid results in more extensive cell death, microglial infiltration, increased cell proliferation, and enhanced neurogenesis in the injured hemisphere, with lesion repair being more complete following quinolinic acid injection. Furthermore, fate mapping of her4-expressing radial glia revealed injury-induced expansion of radial glia stem cells, which give rise to neurons that migrate to the site of injury, survive for at least 8 weeks, and form long-distance projections that span the anterior commissure and synapse in the contralateral hemisphere. These findings suggest that quinolinic acid lesioning of the zebrafish brain stimulates the production of robust regeneration with long-distance integration of new neurons, providing a valuable model for elucidating the reparative mechanisms that can be applied to restorative therapies for mammalian brain injury.

title: Germinal Center T Follicular Helper Cells Are Highly Permissive to HIV-1 and Alter Their Phenotype during Virus Replication.
text: In this study, we investigated the ability of T follicular helper cells (TFH) in secondary lymphoid tissues to produce HIV-1 during chronic asymptomatic infection. We found that TFH cells in germinal centers (GC) are highly permissive to HIV-1, but downregulate the expression of the cell surface proteins CXCR5 and programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) during productive infection. Using ex vivo spinoculation and culturing of tonsil cells with HIV-1 GFP reporter viruses, we found that a higher percentage of GC TFH cells were GFP(+) than non-GC TFH cells or extrafollicular (EF) cells. When sorted prior to spinoculation, GC TFH cells were more permissive than non-GC TFH cells or EF cells. In situ hybridization on lymph node sections from untreated HIV-1-infected individuals without AIDS revealed higher frequencies of HIV-1 RNA(+) cells in GC than non-GC regions of follicle or EF regions. Superinfection of HIV-1-infected individuals' lymph node cells with GFP reporter virus confirmed the permissivity of follicular cells ex vivo. Our findings further implicate GC TFH as the major HIV-1-producing cells in chronic asymptomatic HIV-1 infection.

title: Risk of death with atypical antipsychotic drug treatment for dementia: meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials.
text:
Atypical antipsychotic medications are commonly used to treat delusions, aggression, and agitation in individuals with Alzheimer's disease and other dementias. However, concerns have been raised regarding the potential increased risk of cerebrovascular adverse events, rapid cognitive decline, and mortality associated with their use. To investigate this further, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the mortality risk associated with atypical antipsychotic drug treatment in patients with dementia.
We searched multiple databases, including MEDLINE and the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, to identify RCTs that met our inclusion criteria. We selected randomized placebo-controlled trials of atypical antipsychotic drugs marketed in the United States that treated patients with Alzheimer's disease or dementia. The trials were generally 10 to 12 weeks in duration, and included a total of 3353 patients randomized to study drug and 1757 randomized to placebo.
Our meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found that patients randomized to atypical antipsychotic drugs had a higher risk of death compared to those randomized to placebo (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.06-2.23, P = 0.02). The risk difference was 0.01 (95% CI 0.004-0.02, P = 0.01). Sensitivity analyses did not reveal any significant differences in mortality risk for individual drugs, severity, sample selection, or diagnosis.
Our findings suggest that atypical antipsychotic drugs may be associated with a small increased risk of death compared to placebo in patients with dementia. This risk should be considered in the context of medical need for the drugs, efficacy evidence, medical comorbidity, and the efficacy and safety of alternatives. Individual patient analyses modeling survival and causes of death are needed to further understand the implications of these findings.

title: PI3K in cancer: divergent roles of isoforms, modes of activation and therapeutic targeting
text: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases (PI3Ks) play a central role in coordinating intracellular signaling in response to extracellular stimuli. Unfortunately, hyperactivation of PI3K signaling cascades is a common occurrence in human cancers. In this review, we will delve into recent breakthroughs in our understanding of the functions of specific PI3K isoforms in both normal and oncogenic signaling, explore the various mechanisms by which PI3K can be upregulated, and examine the current state and future potential of targeting this pathway in the clinic.

title: Amphiregulin enhances regulatory T cell-suppressive function via the epidermal growth factor receptor.
text: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) plays a crucial role in both tissue development and homeostasis, as well as in the progression of cancer. Recent studies have shown that regulatory T cells (Tregs), which are important for maintaining immune homeostasis, also express EGFR under inflammatory conditions. In vitro experiments demonstrated that stimulation with the EGF-like growth factor Amphiregulin (AREG) significantly enhanced Treg cell function. In a colitis and tumor vaccination model, AREG was found to be essential for optimal Treg cell function in vivo. Interestingly, mast cell-derived AREG was able to fully restore optimal Treg cell function, suggesting a link between these two cell types. These findings highlight EGFR as a key regulator of local immune responses and provide a potential therapeutic target for cancer treatment.

title: Gonadotrope-specific deletion of Dicer results in severely suppressed gonadotropins and fertility defects.
text: Gonadotropins, including follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH), are heterodimeric glycoproteins produced by gonadotropes. These hormones play crucial roles in the development and function of gonads, including steroidogenesis and gametogenesis. Although the transcriptional regulation of gonadotropin subunits has been well-studied, the post-transcriptional regulation of these subunits is not well understood. To investigate the role of microRNAs in regulating gonadotropin subunits, we employed a Cre-lox genetic approach to delete Dicer, an enzyme involved in microRNA biogenesis, in gonadotropes. We found that many of the DICER-dependent microRNAs, predicted to bind gonadotropin β subunit mRNAs, were suppressed in purified gonadotropes from mutant mice. Consequences of this suppression included profound reductions in gonadotropin-β subunit proteins and heterodimeric hormone secretion. Moreover, the post-gonadectomy-induced increase in pituitary gonadotropin synthesis and secretion were abolished in mutants, indicating a defective gonadal negative feedback control. In addition, mutants lacking Dicer in gonadotropes displayed severely reduced fertility, which was rescued by exogenous hormones. These findings demonstrate that DICER-dependent microRNAs are essential for gonadotropin homeostasis and fertility in mice, and implicate microRNAs in the gonadal feedback control of gonadotropin synthesis and secretion. Our results thus reveal a new layer of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation in gonadotropes, orchestrating the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal axis physiology.

title: Sequential histone-modifying activities determine the robustness of transdifferentiation
text: Natural conversions between distinct somatic cell types have been observed in a variety of species, including jellyfish and mice. These conversions offer untapped opportunities to investigate the mechanisms that ensure successful cell transformation. Our study reveals that a conserved enzyme, JMJD-3.1, and the Set1 complex, which modifies histone H3, cooperate to ensure the invariant transdifferentiation (Td) of postmitotic Caenorhabditis elegans hindgut cells into motor neurons. At the single-cell level, this process involves a series of histone-modifying activities that are functionally divided into distinct phases of Td, each with its own specific role in the conversion process. Our findings parallel the epigenetic mechanisms that underlie efficient cell reprogramming in vitro.

title: Normal and leukemic stem cell niches: insights and therapeutic opportunities.
text:
Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) rely on cues from the bone marrow (BM) niche to maintain their quiescence and adapt blood production to the organism's needs. However, alterations in the BM niche are commonly observed in blood malignancies, which directly contribute to the aberrant function of disease-initiating leukemic stem cells (LSCs). In this review, we will discuss recent insights into the cellular and molecular determinants of the normal HSC niche and how genetic changes in stromal cells and leukemia-induced BM niche remodeling contribute to blood malignancies. Additionally, we will explore how these findings can be applied to non-cell-autonomous therapies targeting the LSC niche.
In the normal BM niche, HSCs are maintained in a quiescent state by a complex network of cellular and molecular interactions with stromal cells, including osteoblasts, adipocytes, and fibroblasts. These stromal cells provide instructive cues to HSCs through the secretion of growth factors, cytokines, and extracellular matrix components. For example, osteoblasts produce bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which promote HSC quiescence and self-renewal. Adipocytes, on the other hand, produce adipocyte-derived factors (ADFs) that inhibit HSC proliferation and differentiation.
In contrast, blood malignancies often result in alterations in the BM niche, leading to the dysregulation of HSC function. For example, leukemia-infiltrating stromal cells may produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors that promote HSC activation and proliferation, leading to the expansion of LSCs. Moreover, the BM niche may become hypoxic or acidic due to the loss of osteoblasts and adipocytes, which can also contribute to the dysregulation of HSC function.
Targeting the LSC niche has emerged as a promising strategy for the treatment of blood malignancies. Non-cell-autonomous therapies, such as bone marrow transplantation and immunomodulatory drugs, can modulate the BM niche and restore HSC function. For example, bone marrow transplantation can replace the dysfunctional BM niche with a normal niche, leading to the reprogramming of LSCs and the restoration of normal hematopoiesis. Immunomodulatory drugs, such as lenalidomide, can also modulate the BM niche by inhibiting the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors, leading to the suppression of LSCs.
In conclusion, the normal HSC niche plays a critical role in maintaining HSC quiescence and adapting blood production to the organism's needs. Alterations in the BM niche are commonly observed in blood malignancies, which directly contribute to the aberrant function of LSCs. Targeting the LSC niche has emerged as a promising strategy for the treatment of blood malignancies, and non-cell-autonomous therapies can modulate the BM niche and restore HSC function. Further research into the cellular and molecular determinants of the normal HSC niche and the mechanisms of LSC dysregulation may lead to the development of more effective therapies for blood malignancies.

title: Role of common hypnotics on the phenotypic causes of obstructive sleep apnoea: paradoxical effects of zolpidem.
text:
Hypnotics are contraindicated in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) due to concerns of pharyngeal muscle relaxation and delayed arousal worsening hypoxia. However, there is a lack of human data on the effects of hypnotics on respiratory arousal threshold, genioglossus muscle responsiveness, and upper airway collapsibility during sleep.
To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover trial involving 21 individuals with and without OSA (aged 18-65 years). Participants received temazepam (10 mg), zolpidem (10 mg), zopiclone (7.5 mg), and placebo on four occasions.
Our results showed that the arousal threshold increased with zolpidem and zopiclone versus placebo (mean ± SD: -18.3 ± 10 and -19.1 ± 9 vs -14.6 ± 7 cmH2O; p = 0.02 and p < 0.001), but not with temazepam (-16.8 ± 9 cmH2O; p = 0.17). Genioglossus muscle activity during stable non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep and responsiveness during airway narrowing were not different with temazepam and zopiclone versus placebo, but paradoxically, zolpidem increased median muscle responsiveness threefold during airway narrowing (median -0.15 (interquartile range -1.01 to -0.04) vs -0.05 (-0.29 to -0.03)% maximum EMG per cmH2O epiglottic pressure; p = 0.03). The upper airway critical closing pressure did not change with any of the hypnotics.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that common hypnotics have differential effects on the respiratory arousal threshold but do not reduce upper airway muscle activity or alter airway collapsibility during sleep. Instead, zolpidem increases muscle activity during airway narrowing. These results provide valuable insights into the effects of hypnotics on the respiratory system during sleep and have important implications for the management of OSA.

title: Clinical human papillomavirus detection forecasts cervical cancer risk in women over 18 years of follow-up.
text:
Purpose: To evaluate the long-term (≥ 10 years) benefits of clinical human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing for cervical precancer and cancer risk prediction.
Methods: Cervicovaginal lavages from 19,512 women attending a health maintenance program were retrospectively tested for HPV using a clinical test. Women with HPV positivity were further tested for HPV16 and HPV18 individually using a research test. A Papanicolaou (Pap) result classified as atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) or more severe was considered abnormal. Women underwent follow-up prospectively with routine annual Pap testing up to 18 years. Cumulative incidence rates (CIRs) of ≥ grade 3 cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN3+) or cancer for enrollment test results were calculated.
Results: A baseline negative HPV test provided greater reassurance against CIN3+ over the 18-year follow-up compared to a normal Pap (CIR, 0.90% vs 1.27%). Both baseline Pap and HPV tests predicted who would develop CIN3+ within the first 2 years of follow-up, but only HPV testing predicted who would develop CIN3+ 10 to 18 years later (P = .004). HPV16- and HPV18-positive women with normal Pap were at elevated risk of CIN3+ compared to other HPV-positive women with normal Pap and were at similar risk of CIN3+ compared to women with a low-grade squamous intraepithelial Pap.
Conclusion: HPV testing to rule out cervical disease followed by Pap testing and possibly combined with the detection of HPV16 and HPV18 among HPV positives to identify those at immediate risk of CIN3+ would be an efficient algorithm for cervical cancer screening, especially in women aged 30 years or older.

title: MG53 nucleates assembly of cell membrane repair machinery
text: Dynamic membrane repair and remodeling is an essential cellular process that maintains cellular integrity and promotes efficient cellular function. Recent studies have shown that MG53, a muscle-specific tripartite motif family protein (TRIM72), plays a critical role in the sarcolemmal membrane-repair machinery. MG53 interacts with phosphatidylserine to associate with intracellular vesicles that traffic to and fuse with sarcolemmal membranes. The absence of MG53 in mice leads to progressive myopathy and reduced exercise capacity, due to defective membrane-repair capacity. Injury to the sarcolemmal membrane results in the entry of the extracellular oxidative environment, leading to MG53 oligomerization and the recruitment of MG53-containing vesicles to the injury site. Following vesicle translocation, the entry of extracellular Ca2+ facilitates vesicle fusion to reseal the membrane. Our findings indicate that intracellular vesicle translocation and Ca2+-dependent membrane fusion are distinct steps involved in the repair of membrane damage, and suggest that MG53 may initiate the assembly of the membrane repair machinery in an oxidation-dependent manner.

title: A large-scale replication study identifies TNIP1, PRDM1, JAZF1, UHRF1BP1 and IL10 as risk loci for systemic lupus erythematosus
text: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified at least 15 susceptibility loci for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). To validate these findings and identify additional risk loci, we selected SNPs from 2,466 regions with nominal evidence of association to SLE (P < 0.05) in a genome-wide study and genotyped them in an independent sample of 1,963 cases and 4,329 controls. This replication effort identified five new SLE susceptibility loci (P < 5 × 10−8): TNIP1 (odds ratio (OR) = 1.27), PRDM1 (OR = 1.20), JAZF1 (OR = 1.20), UHRF1BP1 (OR = 1.17), and IL10 (OR = 1.19). We also identified 21 additional candidate loci with P≤ 1 × 10−5. A candidate screen of alleles previously associated with other autoimmune diseases suggested five loci (P < 1 × 10−3) that may contribute to SLE: IFIH1, CFB, CLEC16A, IL12B, and SH2B3. These results expand the number of confirmed and candidate SLE susceptibility loci and implicate several key immunologic pathways in SLE pathogenesis.

title: ARID1A-mutated ovarian cancers depend on HDAC6 activity
text: The most frequently mutated epigenetic regulator across all human cancers, ARID1A, encodes a subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex. ARID1A and TP53 mutations are typically mutually exclusive, and as such, therapeutic approaches that capitalize on this genetic characteristic remain unexplored. However, our findings demonstrate that HDAC6 activity is essential in ARID1A-mutated ovarian cancers, and that inhibition of HDAC6 using a clinically applicable small-molecule inhibitor significantly improves the survival of mice bearing ARID1A-mutated tumors. This correlation is underscored by the suppression of growth and dissemination of ARID1A-mutated, but not wild-type, tumors. Our results also reveal that the dependence on HDAC6 activity in ARID1A-mutated cells is directly linked to a transcriptional repression of HDAC6 by ARID1A, and that HDAC6 inhibition selectively promotes apoptosis in ARID1A-mutated cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate that HDAC6 directly deacetylates Lys120 of p53, a pro-apoptotic post-translational modification, and that ARID1A mutation inactivates the apoptosis-promoting function of p53 by upregulating HDAC6. Taken together, these findings suggest that pharmacological inhibition of HDAC6 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for ARID1A-mutated cancers.

title: Solution NMR structure of the TatA component of the twin-arginine protein transport system from gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis.
text: The twin-arginine transport (Tat) system facilitates the transport of folded proteins across the cytoplasmic or chloroplast membrane of plant cells. In most Gram-positive bacteria, the Tat system consists of two essential proteins, TatA and TatC. TatA is a bifunctional protein that forms a conducting channel by self-oligomerization and participates in substrate recognition. However, the molecular mechanism of protein translocation remains unclear. In this study, we report the atomic-level structure of TatA(d) from Bacillus subtilis using NMR spectroscopy. TatA(d) has an L-shaped structure with a transmembrane helix and an amphipathic helix, and its C-terminal tail is largely unstructured. Our findings support the predicted topology of TatA(d), in which the transmembrane helix is embedded in the lipid bilayer, while the amphipathic helix interacts with the membrane-water interface. Additionally, the structure of TatA(d) reveals the importance of conserved residues in the hinge region, providing new insights into the protein transport mechanism of the Tat system.

title: Autoimmunity due to molecular mimicry as a cause of neurological disease
text:
One hypothesis that links infection with autoimmune disease is molecular mimicry, where an immune response to an environmental agent cross-reacts with a host antigen, leading to disease. This hypothesis has been implicated in the pathogenesis of diseases such as diabetes, lupus, and multiple sclerosis (MS). While there is limited direct evidence connecting causative agents with pathogenic immune reactions in these diseases, our study provides clear evidence of a link between viral infection, autoimmunity, and neurological disease in humans.
As a model for molecular mimicry, we investigated patients with human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1)-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP), a disease that shares similarities with MS. HAM/TSP patients develop antibodies against neurons, which led us to hypothesize that these antibodies would identify a central nervous system (CNS) autoantigen. Using immunoglobulin G isolated from HAM/TSP patients, we identified heterogeneous nuclear ribonuclear protein-A1 (hnRNP-A1) as the autoantigen. Interestingly, these antibodies also cross-reacted with HTLV-1-tax, the immune response to which is associated with HAM/TSP. Immunoglobulin G specifically stained human Betz cells, whose axons are preferentially damaged in HAM/TSP patients. Moreover, infusion of autoantibodies into brain sections inhibited neuronal firing, confirming their pathogenic nature. These findings demonstrate the importance of molecular mimicry between the infecting agent and hnRNP-A1 in the development of autoimmune disease of the CNS.

title: Altered recognition of antigen is a mechanism of CD8+ T cell tolerance in cancer
text: Antigen-specific CD8+ T-cell tolerance, mediated by myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), is a crucial mechanism of tumor evasion. Through the use of in vivo models, we demonstrate here that MDSCs directly disrupt the interaction between specific peptide–major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) dimers and CD8-expressing T cells by nitrating tyrosines within the T-cell receptor (TCR)-CD8 complex. This process impairs the ability of CD8-expressing T cells to bind pMHC and respond to the specific peptide, while preserving their capacity to respond to non-specific stimuli. The nitration of TCR-CD8 is induced by MDSCs through the excessive production of reactive oxygen species and peroxynitrite during direct cell-cell contact. Molecular modeling suggests specific sites of nitration that may influence the conformational flexibility of TCR-CD8 and its interaction with pMHC. These findings reveal a previously unappreciated mechanism of T-cell tolerance in cancer, which is also relevant to many pathological conditions characterized by the accumulation of MDSCs.

title: A new genetic subgroup of chronic granulomatous disease with autosomal recessive mutations in p40 phox and selective defects in neutrophil NADPH oxidase activity.
text: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), an immunodeficiency characterized by recurrent pyogenic infections and granulomatous inflammation, is caused by loss of phagocyte superoxide production due to recessive mutations in any one of four genes encoding subunits of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase. These genes include gp91(phox) and p22(phox), which form the membrane-integrated flavocytochrome b, and cytosolic subunits p47(phox) and p67(phox). A fifth subunit, p40(phox), plays a crucial role in phagocytosis-induced superoxide production through its PX domain, which binds to phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns(3)P). In this study, we report the first case of autosomal recessive mutations in NCF4, the gene encoding p40(phox), in a boy who presented with granulomatous colitis. Neutrophils from this individual showed a significant defect in intracellular superoxide production during phagocytosis, whereas extracellular release of superoxide elicited by phorbol ester or formyl-methionyl-leucyl-phenylalanine (fMLF) was unaffected. Genetic analysis of NCF4 revealed compound heterozygosity for a frameshift mutation with a premature stop codon and a missense mutation predicting a R105Q substitution in the PX domain. Parents and a sibling were healthy heterozygous carriers. The R105Q mutation in p40(phox) lacked binding to PtdIns(3)P and failed to reconstitute phagocytosis-induced oxidase activity in p40(phox)-deficient granulocytes, with premature loss of p40(phox)R105Q from phagosomes. These findings demonstrate that p40(phox) binding to PtdIns(3)P is essential for phagocytosis-induced oxidant production in human neutrophils and its absence can lead to disease.

title: Birth weight and mammographic density among postmenopausal women in Sweden.
text: Birth weight is a significant predictor of breast cancer risk in adulthood, and mammary gland mass may serve as an intermediate stage in this long process. To investigate this association, we conducted a population-based study of 893 postmenopausal women in Sweden without a prior history of cancer. We retrieved information on birth size from birth records and the most recent mammography results for each participant. We digitized the film mammograms and used the Cumulus software for computer-assisted semi-automated thresholding of mammographic density. Generalized linear models were employed to control for potential confounders and analyze the results. Our findings revealed a significant increase in mean percent mammographic density when comparing the extreme categories of birth weight (ranging from 15.6% to 18.6%) and head circumference (ranging from 15.5% to 20.4%). These trends were statistically significant (p values 0.02 and 0.007, respectively). The associations were particularly strong when the cutoff for high versus low mammographic density was set at a relatively high value of 50%. Compared to women with birth weights of 3001-3500 grams, those with birth weights >4000g were found to be at almost 3-fold higher risk of developing high mammographic density (odds ratio: 2.9, 95% confidence interval: 1.1-7.9). No significant association was observed between mammographic density and birth length, which is known to be less accurately measured. These results suggest that adult breast density, a powerful predictor of breast cancer risk, has intrauterine origins, as reflected in birth size.

title: Oral ciclopirox olamine displays biological activity in a phase I study in patients with advanced hematologic malignancies.
text:
Ciclopirox olamine, an intracellular iron chelator, exhibits anticancer activity in both in vitro and in vivo settings. We conducted a Phase I clinical trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of oral ciclopirox olamine in patients with relapsed or refractory hematologic malignancies (Trial registration ID: NCT00990587). Participants received escalating doses of oral ciclopirox olamine (5-80 mg/m²) once daily for five days within 21-day treatment cycles. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies were performed in a subset of patients. The half-life of ciclopirox olamine was determined, and an additional cohort was enrolled and treated with 80 mg/m² ciclopirox olamine administered four times daily. Adverse events and clinical response were monitored throughout the trial. A total of 23 patients received study treatment.
Ciclopirox olamine was rapidly absorbed and cleared with a short half-life. Plasma concentrations of an inactive ciclopirox glucuronide metabolite were higher than those of ciclopirox. Reduced expression of the survivin protein was observed in peripheral blood cells isolated from patients treated with ciclopirox olamine at doses greater than 10 mg/m², indicating biological activity of the drug. Dose-limiting gastrointestinal toxicities were observed in patients receiving 80 mg/m² four times daily, while no dose-limiting toxicity was observed at 40 mg/m² once daily. Hematologic improvement was observed in two patients. Once-daily dosing of oral ciclopirox olamine was well tolerated in patients with relapsed or refractory hematologic malignancies, and further optimization of dosing regimens is warranted in this patient population.

title: Cancer cell–autonomous contribution of type I interferon signaling to the efficacy of chemotherapy
text: Some of the anti-cancer effects of anthracyclines in mice are due to their ability to stimulate the immune system to attack cancer cells. We found that anthracyclines trigger the rapid production of type I interferons (IFNs) in cancer cells, which then activate a complex network of signaling pathways that promote the release of chemokines (small proteins that attract immune cells) such as C-X-C motif ligand 10 (CXCL10). In order for this process to occur, cancer cells must have the Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3) and the IFN-α/β receptors (IFNARs) present. If these receptors are absent, the cancer cells are unable to respond to chemotherapy, even when type I IFN or CXCL10 are provided artificially. Our findings suggest that the immune responses triggered by anthracyclines are similar to those induced by viral infections, and that this "viral mimicry" may be a key factor in the success of chemotherapy. We propose that this mechanism could be used to improve cancer treatment strategies.

title: alphaE-catenin controls cerebral cortical size by regulating the hedgehog signaling pathway.
text: During the development of organs, cells regulate their growth rates to achieve predetermined sizes. We found that deleting the essential adherens junction gene, alphaE-catenin, in the central nervous system leads to abnormal activation of the Hedgehog signaling pathway, resulting in shortened cell cycles, decreased apoptosis, and excessive thickening of the cerebral cortex. Our study suggests that alphaE-catenin connects cell-density-dependent adherens junctions to the Hedgehog signaling pathway, forming a negative feedback loop that controls the size of developing brain tissue.

title: Molecular regulation of effector and memory T cell differentiation
text: Immunological memory is a crucial aspect of adaptive immunity, and vaccination strategies aim to harness this mechanism to provide long-lasting protection against infections. Recent advances in our understanding of the diverse T lymphocyte subsets have revealed new insights into the transcription factors and upstream regulators that control their accessibility to key sites of gene regulation, as well as metabolic regulators involved in the differentiation of effector and memory subsets. These findings have shed light on the ontogeny and defining characteristics of tissue-resident memory lymphocytes and the origins of the remarkable heterogeneity exhibited by activated T cells. While these discoveries have significantly advanced our knowledge of the underlying pathways that control diversification in T cell responses, there are still gaps in our understanding and challenges that arise in the application of this knowledge to rationally elicit desired T cell responses through vaccination and immunotherapy.

title: Liver-resident macrophage necroptosis orchestrates type 1 microbicidal inflammation and type-2-mediated tissue repair during bacterial infection.
text: Kupffer cells, originating from the fetus, are crucial players in the liver's defense against enteroinvasive bacteria. Upon infection with Listeria monocytogenes, these cells undergo early necroptotic death, leading to the recruitment of monocytes and the activation of a type 1 inflammatory response. This initial response is followed by the activation of hepatocyte-derived alarmin interleukin-33 (IL-33) and basophil-derived interleukin-4 (IL-4), which triggers the alternative activation of monocyte-derived macrophages in the liver. These replaced Kupffer cells help restore liver homeostasis, highlighting the critical role of Kupffer cell death in coordinating type 1 microbicidal inflammation and type-2-mediated liver repair during infection. This discovery challenges the traditional dichotomy between type 1 and type 2 responses, revealing that these responses can develop sequentially in the context of a bacterial infection and work together to orchestrate liver immune responses and restore homeostasis.

title: Gene regulation in the immune system by long noncoding RNAs
text: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are proving to be crucial regulators of gene expression in the immune system. Research has shown that lncRNAs are specifically expressed in different immune cell types, and they control the differentiation and function of both innate and adaptive immune cells. In this Review, we will delve into the mechanisms by which lncRNAs regulate genes involved in the immune response, including their direct interactions with chromatin, RNA, and proteins. We will also explore new areas of lncRNA biology, such as the functions of enhancer RNAs, circular RNAs, and chemical modifications to RNA in cellular processes. Finally, we will highlight the current knowledge gaps and future prospects for understanding the roles of lncRNAs in the immune system and autoimmune diseases.

title: The Ly49Q receptor plays a crucial role in neutrophil polarization and migration by regulating raft trafficking.
text: Neutrophils rapidly adapt and change direction to infiltrate sites of infection and inflammation. We found that an inhibitory MHC I receptor, Ly49Q, played a crucial role in the rapid polarization and tissue infiltration of neutrophils. During normal conditions, Ly49Q inhibited neutrophil adhesion by preventing the formation of focal complexes, likely by suppressing Src and PI3 kinases. However, when inflamed, Ly49Q mediated the rapid polarization and tissue infiltration of neutrophils in an ITIM-domain-dependent manner. These opposing functions were mediated by distinct use of effector phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2. Ly49Q-dependent polarization and migration were also influenced by its regulation of membrane raft functions. Our findings suggest that Ly49Q is essential in switching neutrophils to their polarized morphology and rapid migration upon inflammation, by controlling the spatiotemporal regulation of membrane rafts and raft-associated signaling molecules.

title: Prevalence of Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus infection in homosexual men at beginning of and during the HIV epidemic.
text:
In the early years of the HIV epidemic in San Francisco, a significant number of homosexual men were infected with Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), according to some studies. However, there have been no direct measurements of KSHV prevalence among this population during the early stages of the HIV epidemic. To address this gap in knowledge, researchers analyzed data from a clinic-based sample of 398 individuals and population-based samples from the San Francisco Men's Health Study (MHS), the San Francisco Young Men's Health Study (YMHS), and the San Francisco City Clinic Cohort.
The study found that in 1978 and 1979, approximately one-quarter of homosexual men in San Francisco were infected with KSHV, with a prevalence of 26.5% among the overall sample and 6.9% among those in the San Francisco City Clinic Cohort. While the prevalence of KSHV infection remained relatively stable between 1984 and 1996, the prevalence of HIV infection decreased significantly over the same period. The study also found that the proportion of men engaging in unprotected receptive anal intercourse with one or more partners declined from 54% to 11% between 1984 and 1993, with similar values observed in the YMHS in 1992 and 1993.
The findings suggest that KSHV was already highly prevalent among homosexual men in San Francisco when the HIV epidemic began, and its prevalence has been maintained at a nearly constant level. The study's authors conclude that any declines in the incidence of Kaposi sarcoma do not appear to be caused by a decline in KSHV transmission.

title: Nortriptyline for smoking cessation: a review.
text: This review of nortriptyline for smoking cessation, based on a meta-analysis of the Cochrane Library, suggests that the medication is effective in doubling quit rates. Six placebo-controlled trials found that nortriptyline (75-100 mg) significantly improved quit rates, with an odds ratio (OR) of 2.1. However, between 4% and 12% of participants dropped out due to adverse events, although no serious adverse events were reported. The study found that nortriptyline's efficacy was not related to its antidepressant effects. The results suggest that nortriptyline is an effective aid to smoking cessation, with a magnitude of effect similar to that of bupropion and nicotine replacement therapies. However, the study notes that the incidence of serious side effects in healthy, non-depressed smokers remains unclear, as the medication has only been tested in 500 smokers. The findings also suggest that dopaminergic or adrenergic, but not serotonergic, activity may be important for cessation efficacy. Until further studies can verify a low incidence of significant adverse events, nortriptyline should be considered a second-line treatment for smoking cessation.

title: Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
text: Although it has long been recognized that many individuals with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) also experience difficulties with emotion regulation, there is no consensus on how to clinically conceptualize this complex domain. In this study, the authors examine the current literature using both quantitative and qualitative methods, and identify three key findings. Firstly, emotion dysregulation is prevalent in ADHD across the lifespan and significantly contributes to impairment. Secondly, emotion dysregulation in ADHD may arise from deficits in attending to, recognizing, and allocating attention to emotional stimuli, which implicate dysfunction within a network involving the striatum, amygdala, and medial prefrontal cortex. Finally, while current treatments for ADHD often alleviate emotion dysregulation, focusing on this combination of symptoms reframes clinical questions and could lead to novel therapeutic approaches. The authors then consider three models to explain the relationship between emotion dysregulation and ADHD: emotion dysregulation and ADHD are distinct but correlated dimensions; emotion dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD; or the combination constitutes a distinct nosological entity separate from both ADHD and emotion dysregulation alone. The differing predictions from each model can guide future research on the neglected population of patients with ADHD and emotion dysregulation.

title: Use of serum C reactive protein and procalcitonin concentrations in addition to symptoms and signs to predict pneumonia in patients presenting to primary care with acute cough: diagnostic study
text: Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of various inflammatory markers, along with symptoms and signs, in predicting pneumonia in patients presenting to primary care with acute cough. Design: Diagnostic study conducted between 2007 and 2010 in 12 European countries. Participants: Adults presenting with acute cough. Main Outcome Measures: Pneumonia diagnosed by radiologists, who were blind to all other information when evaluating chest radiographs. Results: Of 2820 patients, 140 (5%) had pneumonia. Re-evaluation of a subset of chest radiographs showed good agreement between radiologists (κ = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.36-0.54). Six symptoms and signs models varied in their discrimination (area under receiver operating characteristics curve (ROC) ranged from 0.55-0.71). The optimal combination of clinical prediction items included absence of runny nose, presence of breathlessness, crackles, and diminished breath sounds on auscultation, tachycardia, and fever, with an ROC area of 0.70 (0.65-0.75). Addition of CRP at the optimal cut-off of >30 mg/L increased the ROC area to 0.77 (0.73-0.81) and improved diagnostic classification (net reclassification improvement: 28%). In the 1556 patients classified as "low risk" (<2.5%), the prevalence of pneumonia was 2%, while in the 132 patients classified as "high risk" (>20%), the prevalence of pneumonia was 31%. The positive likelihood ratio of low, intermediate, and high risk for pneumonia was 0.4, 1.2, and 8.6, respectively. Measurement of procalcitonin added no relevant additional diagnostic information. A simplified diagnostic score based on symptoms, signs, and CRP >30 mg/L resulted in proportions of pneumonia of 0.7%, 3.8%, and 18.2% in the low, intermediate, and high risk groups, respectively. Conclusion: A clinical rule based on symptoms and signs performed best in patients with mild or severe clinical presentation. Addition of CRP concentration at the optimal cut-off of >30 mg/L improved diagnostic information, but measurement of procalcitonin concentration did not add clinically relevant information in this group.

title: Somatic Mutations of the Immunoglobulin Framework Are Generally Required for Broad and Potent HIV-1 Neutralization
text: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) against HIV-1 are crucial for vaccine design due to their ability to prevent infection. These antibodies are highly mutated and generated by a small fraction of HIV-1-infected individuals several years after infection. The mutations occur primarily in the complementarity determining region (CDR) loops, which make contact with the antigen. However, the CDR loops are also supported by canonical framework regions (FWRs), which are less tolerant of mutations. Our study reveals that unlike most antibodies, including those with limited HIV-1 neutralizing activity, most bNAbs require somatic mutations in their FWRs. Structural and functional analyses show that these somatic mutations enhance the breadth and potency of bNAbs by providing increased flexibility and/or direct antigen contact. Therefore, in bNAbs, FWRs play a critical role beyond just scaffolding the CDR loops, and their unique contribution to potency and breadth should be taken into account in HIV-1 vaccine design.

title: Etiology of type 1 diabetes.
text: Recent genetic mapping and gene-phenotype studies have illuminated the genetic basis of type 1 diabetes. At least ten genes have been identified as strong causal candidates, each playing a role in the primary etiological pathways of the disease. These genes include HLA class II and I molecules, which bind to preproinsulin peptides and T cell receptors, as well as genes involved in T and B cell activation, innate pathogen-viral responses, chemokine and cytokine signaling, and T regulatory and antigen-presenting cell functions. This review focuses on the progress made in the field of type 1 diabetes research, with a particular emphasis on identifying disease mechanisms using genetic approaches. The expression and functions of these pathways, and therefore disease susceptibility, are influenced by both epigenetic and environmental factors. Inherited immune phenotypes may serve as early precursors of type 1 diabetes and could be useful in future clinical trials.

title: Plasticity of epithelial stem cells in tissue regeneration
text: Tissues rely on stem cells for maintaining homeostasis and repair. Recent research has shown that the fate and multilineage potential of epithelial stem cells can change depending on their location within the resident niche, their response to normal tissue homeostasis, their mobilization to repair a wound, or their removal from their niche and challenged to de novo tissue morphogenesis after transplantation. In this Review, we explore how different populations of naturally lineage-restricted stem cells and committed progenitors can exhibit remarkable plasticity and reversibility, reacquiring long-term self-renewing capacities and multilineage differentiation potential during physiological and regenerative conditions. We also discuss the implications of cellular plasticity for regenerative medicine and cancer.

title: Atm-deficient mice exhibit increased sensitivity to dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis characterized by elevated DNA damage and persistent immune activation.
text: The role of Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated (ATM) protein in inflammation and inflammatory diseases remains unclear, despite previous findings showing high levels of systemic DNA damage in mice with intestinal inflammation. To investigate the effect of ATM deficiency on inflammation, we induced experimental colitis in ATM-deficient, ATM-heterozygous, and wild-type mice using dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) administration. Our results showed that ATM-deficient mice had higher disease activity indices and rates of mortality compared to heterozygous and wild-type mice. We also observed increased sensitivity to DNA strand breaks in peripheral leukocytes and micronucleus formation in erythroblasts in ATM-deficient mice, particularly during remission periods and after the end of treatment. Additionally, we found elevated levels of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species-mediated damage markers, such as 8-oxoguanine and nitrotyrosine, in both the distal colon and peripheral leukocytes of ATM-deficient mice. Furthermore, ATM-deficient mice showed greater upregulation of inflammatory cytokines and higher percentages of activated CD69+ and CD44+ T cells in the peripheral blood throughout treatment. These findings suggest that ATM may play a critical role in dampening the deleterious effects of chronic DSS-induced inflammation, which is necessary for maintaining systemic genomic stability and homeostasis of the gut epithelial barrier.

title: Activin–like kinase–3 activity is important for kidney regeneration and reversal of fibrosis
text:
Molecules belonging to the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) superfamily, such as bone morphogenic proteins (BMPs) and TGF-β, play a crucial role in regulating inflammation, apoptosis, and cellular transitions. Our study reveals that the BMP receptor activin-like kinase 3 (Alk3) is upregulated early in diseased kidneys after injury. We found that deleting Alk3 in the tubular epithelium leads to enhanced TGF-β1-Smad family member 3 (Smad3) signaling, epithelial damage, and fibrosis, suggesting a protective role for Alk3-mediated signaling in the kidney.
Using structure-function analysis of the BMP-Alk3-BMP receptor, type 2 (BMPR2) ligand-receptor complex, as well as synthetic organic chemistry, we constructed a library of small peptide agonists of BMP signaling that function through the Alk3 receptor. One such peptide agonist, THR-123, suppressed inflammation, apoptosis, and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition program and reversed established fibrosis in five mouse models of acute and chronic renal injury. THR-123 acts specifically through Alk3 signaling, as mice with a targeted deletion of Alk3 in their tubular epithelium did not respond to therapy with THR-123. Combining THR-123 and the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor captopril had an additive therapeutic benefit in controlling renal fibrosis. Our findings demonstrate that BMP signaling agonists constitute a promising new class of therapeutic agents with potential to induce regeneration, repair, and reverse established fibrosis in the clinic.

title: COHCAP: an integrative genomic pipeline for single-nucleotide resolution DNA methylation analysis
