text: COHCAP (City of Hope CpG Island Analysis Pipeline) is an algorithm designed to analyze single-nucleotide resolution DNA methylation data generated from either an Illumina methylation array or targeted bisulfite sequencing. The primary objective of COHCAP is to identify CpG islands that display a consistent pattern of methylation across CpG sites. Currently, COHCAP is the only DNA methylation package that integrates with gene expression data to identify a subset of CpG islands most likely to regulate downstream gene expression. COHCAP can also generate lists of differentially methylated CpG islands with a concordance of approximately 50% with gene expression data from both cell line and patient data. For example, this article highlights well-established breast cancer biomarkers (such as estrogen receptor) that exhibit a negative correlation between DNA methylation and gene expression. In addition to providing visualization tools for quality control metrics, regions of differential methylation, and correlations between methylation and gene expression, COHCAP is freely available for download at <https://sourceforge.net/projects/cohcap/>.

title: Subgrouping of patients with neuropathic pain according to pain-related sensory abnormalities: a first step to a stratified treatment approach.
text:
BACKGROUND: Patients with neuropathic pain exhibit diverse sensory abnormalities, which collectively form distinct patterns or mosaics, known as sensory profiles, in individual patients. One hypothesis suggests that the development of these profiles is attributed to the activation of distinct pathophysiological mechanisms of pain generation, resulting in specific sensory abnormalities. Despite the promise of new drugs, several controlled trials have yielded negative results, which may be attributed to the heterogeneity of the patient population. Subgrouping patients based on their sensory profiles could help mitigate this heterogeneity and improve clinical trial design.
RECENT DEVELOPMENTS: Recent studies have demonstrated the existence of subgroups of patients with neuropathic pain who perceive their pain differently, despite sharing similar sensory profiles. These findings suggest that a statistical categorization of patients based on their sensory profiles may lead to the identification of specific subgroups that respond better to particular treatments. The use of this approach in clinical trials could result in a more targeted and effective treatment strategy.
WHERE NEXT?: The development of a new classification system for neuropathic pain that takes into account sensory profiles has the potential to revolutionize the field. By incorporating sensory phenotyping into clinical trial design, researchers can enrich the study population with potential treatment responders, leading to a stratified treatment approach and ultimately personalized treatment. This approach may also help identify novel therapeutic targets and improve the efficiency of drug development.

title: The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3).
text:
In 2001, definitions and clinical criteria for sepsis and septic shock were last revised. However, significant advances have been made in the understanding of the pathobiology, management, and epidemiology of sepsis since then, suggesting the need for an update. To address this need, a task force of 19 experts in sepsis pathobiology, clinical trials, and epidemiology was convened by the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine. The task force developed new definitions and clinical criteria for sepsis and septic shock through a combination of meetings, Delphi processes, analysis of electronic health record databases, and voting. The new definitions and criteria were then circulated to international professional societies for peer review and endorsement.
The task force concluded that the term "severe sepsis" is redundant and that sepsis should be defined as "life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection." For clinical operationalization, organ dysfunction can be represented by an increase in the Sequential [Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or more, which is associated with an in-hospital mortality greater than 10%. Septic shock should be defined as a subset of sepsis in which particularly profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities are associated with a greater risk of mortality than with sepsis alone. Patients with septic shock can be clinically identified by a vasopressor requirement to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mm Hg or greater and serum lactate level greater than 2 mmol/L (>18 mg/dL) in the absence of hypovolemia. This combination is associated with hospital mortality rates greater than 40%. In out-of-hospital, emergency department, or general hospital ward settings, adult patients with suspected infection can be rapidly identified as being more likely to have poor outcomes typical of sepsis if they have at least 2 of the following clinical criteria that together constitute a new bedside clinical score termed quickSOFA (qSOFA): respiratory rate of 22/min or greater, altered mentation, or systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg or less.
The updated definitions and clinical criteria offer greater consistency for epidemiologic studies and clinical trials and facilitate earlier recognition and more timely management of patients with sepsis or at risk of developing sepsis.

title: Stem cell transplantation in patients with autonomic neuropathy due to primary (AL) amyloidosis.
text: OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to evaluate the outcomes of patients with autonomic neuropathy (AN) undergoing autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) for AL amyloidosis. METHODS: A case-control study was conducted among patients with AL amyloidosis and AN who underwent ASCT, and compared them to a large, matched cohort without AN. RESULTS: Thirteen patients with AN were identified, and their outcomes were compared to a control group of 95 patients without AN. The results showed that patients with AN had more organs involved and a reduced conditioning dose of melphalan compared to the control group. The median duration of hospitalization and engraftment kinetics were similar for both groups. Atrial fibrillation occurred in all patients with AN, but only in one control patient (p < 0.0001). The median overall survival (OS) for patients with AN was 29 months, compared to >60 months for controls (p < 0.0001). Univariate analysis revealed that cardiac involvement, AN, glomerular filtration rate, number of organs involved, and NT-pro-BNP were all associated with OS. Multivariate analysis confirmed that AN retained an independent, adverse impact on OS. CONCLUSIONS: The study findings suggest that patients with AN can undergo ASCT with relative safety. However, AN is an independent determinant of adverse survival outcomes in these patients.

title: MicroRNA-148a regulates LDL receptor and ABCA1 expression to control circulating lipoprotein levels
text: The hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) pathway plays a crucial role in removing excess circulating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) from the bloodstream. While the transcriptional regulation of LDLR is well understood, the post-transcriptional mechanisms that control LDLR expression are just being uncovered. In this study, we developed a high-throughput genome-wide screening assay to identify microRNAs (miRNAs) that regulate LDLR activity in human hepatic cells. From this screen, we identified and characterized miR-148a as a negative regulator of LDLR expression and activity. We also discovered a Sterol Regulatory Element–Binding Protein 1 (SREBP1)-mediated pathway through which miR-148a regulates LDL-C uptake. In mice, inhibition of miR-148a increased hepatic LDLR expression and decreased plasma LDL-C levels. Additionally, we found that miR-148a regulates hepatic expression of ATP-binding cassette, subfamily A, member 1 (ABCA1) and circulating high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels in vivo. These findings demonstrate the importance of miR-148a in regulating hepatic LDL-C clearance and suggest that inhibiting miR-148a may be a therapeutic strategy to reduce elevated LDL-C/HDL-C ratios, a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

title: BRACHYURY and CDX2 Mediate BMP-Induced Differentiation of Human and Mouse Pluripotent Stem Cells into Embryonic and Extraembryonic Lineages
text: BMP signaling is believed to steer human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) towards multiple lineages, including mesoderm and trophoblast. The BMP-induced trophoblast phenotype has long been a paradox in stem cell biology, and our study aimed to reassess BMP function in hESCs and mouse epiblast-derived cells. Through the use of BMP4 and FGF2 (in conjunction with ERK), we discovered that these factors cooperate to induce mesoderm and inhibit endoderm differentiation. The resulting cells exhibited high levels of BRACHYURY (BRA), which preceded the expression of CDX2. Both genes were essential for the expression of mesodermal genes, as well as trophoblast-associated genes. Maximal expression of the latter was observed in the absence of FGF, but these cells also coexpressed mesodermal genes and displayed distinct cell surface and epigenetic properties compared to placental trophoblasts. Our findings suggest that BMP primarily induces hESCs to form mesoderm, rather than trophoblast, by acting through BRA and CDX2.

title: Degradation of Cellular miR-27 by a Novel, Highly Abundant Viral Transcript Is Important for Efficient Virus Replication In Vivo
text: Cytomegaloviruses produce large amounts of viral miRNAs during lytic infection, yet they only modestly alter the cellular miRNA profile. The most significant change upon lytic murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection is the rapid degradation of cellular miR-27a and miR-27b. We found that this regulation is mediated by the ∼1.7 kb spliced and highly abundant MCMV m169 transcript. The specificity of this regulation is achieved through a single, optimized miRNA binding site located in the 3'-untranslated region (3'-UTR) of m169. This site can be easily and efficiently retargeted to other cellular and viral miRNAs through target site replacement. Expression of the 3'-UTR of m169 by an adenoviral vector was sufficient to mediate its function, indicating that no other viral factors are essential in this process. Degradation of miR-27a/b was found to be accompanied by 3'-tailing and -trimming. Interestingly, we discovered that this interaction is mutual, suggesting potential regulation of m169 by miR-27a/b. Moreover, three mutant viruses that could no longer target miR-27a/b, either due to miRNA target site disruption or target site replacement, showed significant attenuation in multiple organs as early as 4 days post infection, indicating that degradation of miR-27a/b is important for efficient MCMV replication in vivo.

title: Social and geographical factors affecting access to treatment of colorectal cancer: a cancer registry study
text:
Objective: To investigate the impact of deprivation and distance from hospital on cancer outcomes, specifically stage at diagnosis and receipt of treatment, in a large population-based study in the north of England.
Design: Analysis of a cancer registry database, including data on stage and treatment details from the first 6 months.
Setting: Population-based study of patients resident in a large area in the north of England.
Participants: 39,619 patients with colorectal cancer diagnosed between 1994 and 2002.
Outcomes measured: Stage of diagnosis and receipt of treatment in relation to deprivation and distance from hospital.
Results: Patients in the most deprived quartile were significantly more likely to be diagnosed at stage 4 for rectal cancer (OR 1.516, p<0.05) but less so for colonic cancer. There was a trend for both sites for patients in the most deprived quartile to be less likely to receive chemotherapy for stage 4 disease. Patients with colonic cancer were very significantly less likely to receive any treatment if they came from any but the most affluent area (ORs 0.639, 0.603 and 0.544 in increasingly deprived quartiles), this may have been exacerbated if the hospital was distant from their residence (OR for forth quartile for both travel and deprivation 0.731, not significant). The effect was less for rectal cancer and no effect of distance was seen.
Conclusions: Residing in a deprived area is associated with tendencies to higher stage at diagnosis and especially in the case of colonic cancer to reduced receipt of treatment. These observations are consistent with other findings and indicate that access to diagnosis requires further investigation.

title: Development of candidate genomic markers to select breast cancer patients for dasatinib therapy.
text: The selection of patients for targeted therapies is crucial, yet phase I/II trials are often underpowered to identify predictors of drug response. Our research aimed to develop genomic predictors of dasatinib sensitivity that could be tested in early-phase clinical trials. We compared gene expression profiles of dasatinib-sensitive and resistant cell lines (n = 23) to create a dasatinib sensitivity index (modified DS index). Additionally, we defined a Src pathway activity index (revised Src index) using genes induced by Src transfection of mammary epithelial cells and optimized its reproducibility across cell lines and human specimens. A dasatinib target index was developed by combining the weighted sum of 19 kinases that bind to dasatinib with variable affinity. The performance of these prediction models was evaluated in independent cell lines with known dasatinib sensitivity, and their feasibility was assessed in 133 biopsies of primary breast cancers. The modified DS index showed high accuracy (90%) in independent breast cancer cell lines (n = 12), and the target index, but not the revised Src index signature, distinguished dasatinib-sensitive and resistant cells (P = 0.0024). The genomic predictors demonstrated acceptable reproducibility in replicate cell line and human gene expression data. When all three predictors were applied to the same 133 patient samples, they identified different patient subsets as potentially sensitive. We identified three conceptually different potential predictors of dasatinib response that were reproducible across cell lines and human data, which are currently being tested in a clinical trial to determine their utility.

title: BEDTools: a flexible suite of utilities for comparing genomic features
text:
MOTIVATION:
In genomics research, testing correlations between different sets of genomic features is a crucial task. However, searching for overlaps between features using existing web-based methods can be challenging due to the vast amounts of data generated by current sequencing technologies. Therefore, fast and flexible tools are required to efficiently ask complex questions of these data.
RESULTS:
This article introduces a new software suite, BEDTools, for the comparison, manipulation, and annotation of genomic features in Browser Extensible Data (BED) and General Feature Format (GFF) format. BEDTools also supports the comparison of sequence alignments in BAM format to both BED and GFF features. The tools are highly efficient and enable the user to compare large datasets, such as those generated by next-generation sequencing, with both public and custom genome annotation tracks. BEDTools can be combined with other tools and standard UNIX commands, making it easy to perform routine genomics tasks and complex pipelines that can quickly answer intricate questions of large genomic datasets.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION:
BEDTools was developed in C++ and is available under an open-source license. The source code and a comprehensive user manual are freely available at <http://code.google.com/p/bedtools>.
CONTACT:
For inquiries, please contact Aaron Quinlan at aaronquinlan@gmail.com or Imran H. H. Husain at imh4y@virginia.edu.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Vegetarian diet improves insulin resistance and oxidative stress markers more than conventional diet in subjects with Type 2 diabetes
text:
The aim of this study was to compare the effects of a calorie-restricted vegetarian diet and a conventional diabetic diet, both with or without exercise training, on insulin resistance, visceral fat, and oxidative stress markers in patients with Type 2 diabetes.
METHODS: This 24-week randomized, open, parallel-design study enrolled 74 patients with Type 2 diabetes, randomly assigning them to either the experimental group (n=37) receiving a vegetarian diet or the control group (n=37) receiving a conventional diabetic diet. Both diets were isocaloric and calorie-restricted (-500 kcal/day), with all meals provided. After 12 weeks, the second 12 weeks of the diet were combined with aerobic exercise training. Participants were examined at baseline, 12 weeks, and 24 weeks. The primary outcomes were insulin sensitivity measured by hyperinsulinaemic isoglycaemic clamp, volume of visceral and subcutaneous fat measured by magnetic resonance imaging, and oxidative stress markers measured by thiobarbituric acid reactive substances. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis.
RESULTS: Forty-three percent of participants in the experimental group and 5% of participants in the control group reduced their diabetes medication (P < 0.001). Body weight decreased more in the experimental group than in the control group (-6.2 kg, 95% CI -6.6 to -5.3 vs. -3.2 kg, 95% CI -3.7 to -2.5; interaction group × time P = 0.001). A greater increase in insulin sensitivity was observed in the experimental group than in the control group (30%, 95% CI 24.5-39 vs. 20%, 95% CI 14-25, P = 0.04). Both visceral and subcutaneous fat decreased more in the experimental group than in the control group (P = 0.007 and P = 0.02, respectively). Plasma adiponectin increased (P = 0.02) and leptin decreased (P = 0.02) in the experimental group, with no change in the control group. Vitamin C, superoxide dismutase, and reduced glutathione increased in the experimental group (P = 0.002, P < 0.001, and P = 0.02, respectively). Differences between groups were greater after the addition of exercise training. Changes in insulin sensitivity and enzymatic oxidative stress markers correlated with changes in visceral fat.
CONCLUSIONS: A calorie-restricted vegetarian diet had greater capacity to improve insulin sensitivity compared with a conventional diabetic diet over 24 weeks. The greater loss of visceral fat and improvements in plasma concentrations of adipokines and oxidative stress markers with this diet may be responsible for the reduction of insulin resistance. The addition of exercise training further augmented the improved outcomes with the vegetarian diet.

title: Antidepressant use and risk of adverse outcomes in older people: population based cohort study
text: Objective: To investigate the association between antidepressant treatment and the risk of various adverse outcomes in older adults, including mortality, suicide attempts, cardiovascular events, falls, fractures, and drug reactions. Design: Cohort study of patients aged 65 and older diagnosed with depression in 570 general practices in the UK. Setting: Primary care database. Participants: 60,746 patients diagnosed with a new episode of depression between ages 65-100 years from 1996 to 2007 and followed up until 2008. Main Outcome Measures: Hazard ratios were calculated to assess the association between antidepressant use and the risk of various adverse outcomes, adjusted for potential confounding variables. Results: Of the 54,038 patients who received antidepressant prescriptions during follow-up, the most common classes were selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs, 54.7%), tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs, 31.6%), and other antidepressants (13.5%). The associations between antidepressant classes and adverse outcomes differed significantly, with SSRIs associated with the highest adjusted hazard ratios for falls (1.66, 95% CI 1.58-1.73) and hyponatraemia (1.52, 1.33-1.75), and the group of other antidepressants associated with the highest adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause mortality (1.66, 1.56-1.77), attempted suicide/self-harm (5.16, 3.90-6.83), stroke/transient ischaemic attack (1.37, 1.22-1.55), fracture (1.64, 1.46-1.84), and epilepsy/seizures (2.24, 1.60-3.15). TCAs did not have the highest hazard ratio for any of the outcomes. Absolute risks over 1 year for all-cause mortality were 7.04% for patients not taking antidepressants, 8.12% for TCAs, 10.61% for SSRIs, and 11.43% for other antidepressants. Conclusion: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and drugs in the group of other antidepressants were associated with an increased risk of several adverse outcomes compared to TCAs. Further research is needed to confirm these findings, but the risks and benefits of different antidepressants should be carefully evaluated when these drugs are prescribed to older people.

title: The benefits of statins in people without established cardiovascular disease but with cardiovascular risk factors: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
text:
Objective: To investigate the effectiveness of statins in reducing all-cause mortality and major coronary and cerebrovascular events in individuals without established cardiovascular disease, but with cardiovascular risk factors, and to determine if these effects are similar across different subgroups, including men and women, young and older individuals, and those with diabetes mellitus.
Design: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Data Sources: Cochrane controlled trials register, Embase, and Medline.
Data Abstraction: Two independent investigators identified studies that met the following criteria: (1) clinical effects of statins compared with a placebo or control group, (2) follow-up of at least one year, (3) at least 80% or more participants without established cardiovascular disease, and (4) outcome data on mortality and major cardiovascular disease events. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q and I(2) statistics, and publication bias was assessed by visual examination of funnel plots and the Egger regression test.
Results: A total of 10 trials enrolled 70,388 participants, of whom 23,681 (34%) were women and 16,078 (23%) had diabetes mellitus. The mean follow-up was 4.1 years. Treatment with statins significantly reduced the risk of all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.81-0.96), major coronary events (odds ratio 0.70, 95% confidence interval 0.61-0.81), and major cerebrovascular events (odds ratio 0.81, 95% confidence interval 0.71-0.93). No evidence of an increased risk of cancer was observed. There was no significant heterogeneity of the treatment effect in clinical subgroups.
Conclusion: In patients without established cardiovascular disease but with cardiovascular risk factors, statin use was associated with significantly improved survival and large reductions in the risk of major cardiovascular events. These findings suggest that statins may be beneficial for individuals with cardiovascular risk factors, regardless of their age, gender, or presence of diabetes mellitus.

title: Mechanical coupling between transsynaptic N-cadherin adhesions and actin flow stabilizes dendritic spines
text: The structure of neuronal dendritic spines is a crucial indicator of synaptic function, and it is regulated by various factors, including the intracellular actin/myosin cytoskeleton and transcellular N-cadherin adhesions. To investigate the mechanical relationship between these molecular components, we conducted quantitative live-imaging experiments in primary hippocampal neurons. Our findings revealed that actin turnover and structural motility were lower in dendritic spines compared to immature filopodia, and increased upon expression of a non-adhesive N-cadherin mutant, resulting in an inverse relationship between spine motility and actin enrichment. Additionally, pharmacological stimulation of myosin II led to the rearward motion of actin structures in spines, demonstrating that myosin II exerts tension on the actin network. Interestingly, the formation of stable, actin-rich structures was induced at contacts between dendritic filopodia and N-cadherin-coated beads or micropatterns. Finally, computer simulations of actin dynamics mimicked various experimental conditions, suggesting that the actin flow rate is a critical parameter controlling actin enrichment in dendritic spines. These findings demonstrate that a clutch-like mechanism between N-cadherin adhesions and the actin flow underlies the stabilization of dendritic filopodia into mature spines, a mechanism that may have important implications in synapse initiation, maturation, and plasticity in the developing brain.

title: Phosphate and R2D2 restrict the substrate specificity of Dicer-2, an ATP-driven ribonuclease.
text: Drosophila Dicer-2 produces small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) from long double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), whereas Dicer-1 generates microRNAs (miRNAs) from pre-miRNA. What distinguishes the two Dicers is their specificity for their biological substrates. While purified Dicer-2 can efficiently cleave pre-miRNA, inorganic phosphate and the Dicer-2 partner protein R2D2 inhibit pre-miRNA cleavage. Dicer-2 contains C-terminal RNase III domains that mediate RNA cleavage, an N-terminal helicase motif whose function is unclear, and is an ATP-stimulated dsRNA-hydrolyzing enzyme that hydrolyzes ATP to ADP. ATP hydrolysis is essential for Dicer-2 to process long dsRNA, but not pre-miRNA. Wild-type Dicer-2 can generate siRNAs faster than it can dissociate from a long dsRNA substrate, suggesting that the Dicer-2 helicase domain uses ATP to generate multiple siRNAs from a single molecule of dsRNA before dissociating from its substrate.

title: Therapeutic potential of mood stabilizers lithium and valproic acid: beyond bipolar disorder.
text: The mood stabilizers lithium and valproic acid (VPA) have been traditionally used to treat bipolar disorder (BD), a complex mental illness resulting from interactions between genetic and environmental factors that impair the brain's ability to adapt and recover. Recent studies have also highlighted the therapeutic potential of these drugs in other central nervous system (CNS) diseases. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms of action of lithium and VPA, gleaned from cellular and animal models of various neurological, neurodegenerative, and neuropsychiatric disorders. The article will discuss the primary targets of these drugs, including glycogen synthase kinase-3 for lithium and histone deacetylases for VPA, and how they induce the expression of neurotrophic, angiogenic, and neuroprotective proteins. Additionally, the review will explore the involvement of cell survival signaling cascades, oxidative stress pathways, and protein quality control mechanisms in the beneficial effects of lithium and VPA. The article will also discuss the potential of cotreatment to enhance neuroprotection and stem cell homing and migration, as well as the use of microRNAs as new therapeutic targets. Furthermore, preclinical findings have shown that the neuroprotective benefits of these agents can lead to anti-inflammation, angiogenesis, neurogenesis, blood-brain barrier integrity, and disease-specific neuroprotection. These mechanisms can be compared to dysregulated disease mechanisms to identify specific risk biomarkers, which could guide personalized medicine approaches for treating CNS diseases. Future clinical endeavors are warranted to fully explore the therapeutic potential of lithium and VPA across a wide range of CNS diseases.

title: The feasibility of malaria elimination in South Africa
text:
Background:
The last major malaria epidemic in South Africa occurred in 2000, resulting in a significant decline in malaria incidence. However, the country is now at a critical juncture, with the World Health Organization (WHO) threshold for malaria elimination being met. In light of the Millennium Development Goal of reversing the spread of malaria by 2015, South Africa is being encouraged to adopt an elimination agenda. This study aimed to assess the appropriateness of implementing a malaria elimination program in present-day South Africa.
Methods:
An assessment of South Africa's progress in implementing an integrated malaria control program across the three malaria-endemic provinces was conducted. Vector control and case management data were analyzed from 2000 to 2011.
Results:
Both malaria-related morbidity and mortality have shown a significant decline across all three malaria-endemic provinces since 2000. The greatest decline was observed in KwaZulu-Natal, where cases decreased from 42,276 in 2000 to 380 in 2010, and deaths dropped from 122 in 2000 to six in 2010. Although there has been a 49.2% (8,553 vs 4,214) decrease in malaria cases reported in Limpopo Province, it currently contributes the most to malaria incidence in South Africa. Despite average insecticide spray coverage of over 80% in all three provinces, malaria incidence remains above the elimination threshold in Mpumalanga and Limpopo. Locally transmitted case numbers have declined in all three malaria provinces, but imported case numbers have been increasing. Knowledge gaps in vector distribution, insecticide resistance status, and drug usage were also identified.
Conclusions:
Malaria elimination in South Africa is a feasible goal if certain criteria are met. Firstly, continued support for existing malaria control programs is crucial to sustain the gains made. Secondly, cross-border malaria control initiatives with neighboring countries must be strongly encouraged and supported to reduce malaria in the region and the importation of malaria into South Africa. Thirdly, operational research, particularly on vector distribution and insecticide resistance status, must be conducted urgently. Finally, surveillance systems must be refined to ensure the necessary information is collected to inform an elimination agenda.

title: The epidemiology of sexually transmitted co-infections in HIV-positive and HIV-negative African-Caribbean women in Toronto
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate the prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in African-Caribbean women in Toronto, Canada. We recruited 126 HIV-positive and 291 HIV-negative women through a community health centre and collected data on their socio-behavioural characteristics, HIV status, and serology for various infections, including HIV, hepatitis B, herpes simplex virus (HSV), human papillomavirus (HPV), and human cytomegalovirus (CMV). Our findings revealed that HIV-positive women were more likely to have active hepatitis B infection and a history of HBV vaccination compared to HIV-negative women. In addition, HSV-2 infection was significantly more common in HIV-positive women (86.3%) than in HIV-negative women (46.6%). Vaginal HPV infection was also more prevalent in HIV-positive women (50.8%) than in HIV-negative women (22.6%). However, classical STIs were rare in both groups. Our study highlights the importance of screening for HIV-associated infections, such as HBV and HSV, in this high-risk population.

title: Characterization of Programmed Death-1 Homologue-1 (PD-1H) Expression and Function in Normal and HIV Infected Individuals
text: Chronic immune activation that persists despite antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the strongest predictor of disease progression in HIV infection. In HIV-infected individuals, monocytes/macrophages are known to spontaneously secrete cytokines, although the underlying mechanism and molecules involved remain unknown. Our study reveals that overexpression of the newly identified co-stimulatory molecule, PD1 homologue (PD-1H), in human monocytes/macrophages leads to spontaneous cytokine secretion. This process requires signaling via PD-1H, as cytokine secretion can be abrogated by deleting the cytoplasmic domain. Interestingly, we found that overexpression of PD-1H is observed in monocytes from chronically HIV-infected individuals, which correlates with immune activation and CD4 depletion, but not viral load. Moreover, we discovered that antigen presentation by PD-1H-overexpressing monocytes leads to enhanced cytokine secretion by HIV-specific T cells, suggesting that PD-1H may play a crucial role in modulating immune activation and immune response in HIV infection.

title: A conserved mechanism for centromeric nucleosome recognition by centromere protein CENP-C.
text: During mitosis, the proper segregation of chromosomes relies on the assembly of the kinetochore complex at the centromere. This process is mediated by the recognition of the histone variant CENP-A in the centromeric nucleosome by the centromere protein C (CENP-C). By defining the determinants of this recognition mechanism, we have discovered that CENP-C binds to a hydrophobic region in the CENP-A tail and docks onto the acidic patch of histone H2A and H2B. Furthermore, our findings reveal a conserved mechanism for protein recruitment to centromeres and a histone recognition mode whereby a disordered peptide binds the histone tail through hydrophobic interactions facilitated by nucleosome docking.

title: Chemical tools for biomolecular imaging.
text: The visualization of biologically relevant molecules and processes within living cells has revolutionized cell biology into a quantitative science. While significant advancements have been made in some areas, the majority of cellular processes remain invisible, resistant to even the most advanced laser technologies. To overcome this limitation, further progress will depend on the development of novel fluorophores and fluorescent sensors to target these processes. In this review, we will discuss recent approaches to creating these sensors, methods for attaching them to specific biomolecules, and their applications to various biological challenges.

title: Reactive oxygen species, DNA damage, and error-prone repair: a model for genomic instability with progression in myeloid leukemia?
text: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of disorders characterized by inefficient blood cell production, with a heightened risk of developing acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The molecular mechanisms underlying MDS progression are unclear, but a key factor is the loss of genetic material (genomic instability). Using a mouse model of myeloid leukemia progression, we found that there is a stepwise increase in the frequency of DNA damage, leading to an increased frequency of error-prone repair of double-strand breaks (DSB) by nonhomologous end-joining. This is accompanied by a concomitant increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) in these transgenic mice. We discovered that RAC1, an essential component of the ROS-producing NADPH oxidase, is downstream of RAS and plays a role in ROS production in NRAS/BCL2 mice. In addition, we found that DNA damage and error-prone repair can be decreased or reversed in vivo by N-acetyl cysteine antioxidant treatment. Our findings provide a mechanism for the increase in the error rate of DNA repair with MDS disease progression and suggest potential treatment strategies that target RAS/RAC pathways and ROS production in human MDS/AML.

title: A link between inflammation and metastasis: serum amyloid A1 and A3 induce metastasis, and are targets of metastasis-inducing S100A4
text: S100A4 has been implicated in both metastasis and chronic inflammation, but its precise function remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which S100A4 contributes to tumor progression. Our findings reveal that S100A4 regulates the expression of acute-phase response proteins, such as serum amyloid A (SAA) 1 and SAA3, which in turn promote the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). We demonstrate for the first time that SAA proteins not only stimulate their own transcription but also enhance the transcription of other pro-inflammatory proteins, including S100A8 and S100A9. Furthermore, we show that SAA proteins promote tumor cell adhesion, migration, and invasion, and that intravenous injection of S100A4 protein leads to the expression of SAA proteins and cytokines in an organ-specific manner. In a breast cancer animal model, ectopic expression of SAA1 or SAA3 in tumor cells significantly promoted metastasis formation and immune cell infiltration. Coordinate expression of S100A4 and SAA in tumor samples from colorectal carcinoma patients was also found to be associated with reduced overall survival. These findings suggest that SAA proteins serve as effectors for the metastasis-promoting functions of S100A4, and provide a link between inflammation and tumor progression.

title: Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity and acetyl group accumulation during exercise after different diets.
text: In this study, the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDHa) and the accumulation of acetyl groups in human skeletal muscle were examined at rest and during exercise after different diets. Five male participants cycled at 75% of their maximum oxygen uptake (VO2 max) until exhaustion after consuming a low-carbohydrate diet (LCD) for 3 days and again 1-2 weeks later for the same duration after consuming a high-carbohydrate diet (HCD) for 3 days. Resting PDHa was lower after the LCD and coincided with a greater intramuscular acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio, acetyl-CoA content, and acetylcarnitine content. PDHa increased during exercise in both conditions, but at a lower rate in the LCD condition compared to the HCD condition. During exercise, muscle acetyl-CoA and acetylcarnitine content and the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio decreased in the LCD condition but increased in the HCD condition. Under resting conditions, PDHa was influenced by the availability of fat or carbohydrate fuels, which affected the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio. However, during exercise, the activation of PDHa occurred independently of changes in the acetyl-CoA-to-CoASH ratio, suggesting that other factors are more important.

title: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential and its distinction from myelodysplastic syndromes.
text: Recent genetic studies of large populations have revealed that mutations in hematopoietic cells during aging can lead to clonal expansion. Clonally restricted hematopoiesis is associated with an increased risk of developing myeloid or lymphoid neoplasia and higher mortality rates. Although myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are defined by cytopenias, abnormal blood and bone marrow cell morphology, and clonal hematopoiesis, most individuals who acquire clonal hematopoiesis during aging will never develop MDS. Therefore, the acquisition of somatic mutations that drive clonal expansion in the absence of cytopenias and dysplastic hematopoiesis can be considered clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), similar to monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis, which are precursor states for hematologic neoplasms but are usually benign and do not progress. Because mutations are frequently observed in healthy older persons, detecting an MDS-associated somatic mutation in a cytopenic patient without other evidence of MDS may cause diagnostic confusion. Here, we discuss the nature and prevalence of CHIP, the distinction between this state and MDS, and current areas of uncertainty regarding diagnostic criteria for myeloid malignancies.

title: DNA Methylation mediated down-regulating of MicroRNA-33b and its role in gastric cancer
text: The discovery of microRNAs (miRNAs) has opened up a new avenue for understanding the mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment of human cancers. Recent studies have shown that down-regulation of tumor-suppressive miRNAs due to CpG island hypermethylation is a common feature of cancer. In this study, we found that the down-regulation of miR-33b was associated with the advanced stage of gastric cancer (GC) patients. We also observed that ectopic expression of miR-33b in GC cells inhibited cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, and this effect may be due to miR-33b targeting the oncogene c-Myc. Additionally, we found that the methylation level of the CpG island upstream of miR-33b was enhanced in GC patients with down-regulated miR-33b, and this was confirmed by methylation-specific PCR (MSP) amplification. Furthermore, re-introduction of miR-33b significantly suppressed tumorigenesis of GC cells in nude mice. In conclusion, miR-33b acts as a tumor suppressor, and hypermethylation of the CpG island upstream of miR-33b is responsible for its down-regulation in gastric cancer.

title: Modulation of glucose metabolism in macrophages by products of nitric oxide synthase.
text: Nitric oxide (NO), a byproduct of L-arginine metabolism, inhibits cellular oxidative metabolism by suppressing enzymes in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and electron transport chain. The impact of NO synthase (NOS) activity on specific pathways of glucose metabolism in freshly harvested and overnight-cultured rat resident peritoneal macrophages, at rest and after stimulation with zymosan, was investigated using radiolabeled glucose. NOS activity was modulated by varying the L-arginine concentration in the culture media and using its specific inhibitor, NG-monomethyl-L-arginine. The results showed that NOS activity was associated with increased glucose disappearance, glycolysis, and hexose monophosphate shunt activity, and a decrease in the flux of glucose and butyrate carbon through the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Additionally, the enhanced glucose utilization that follows zymosan stimulation was augmented by suppressing NOS activity. These findings demonstrate that the metabolic characteristics of macrophages are significantly influenced by NO produced by NOS.

title: SOCS1/JAB is a negative regulator of LPS-induced macrophage activation.
text: Bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) activates the innate immune system through the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) pathway. Our findings demonstrate that the suppressor of cytokine-signaling-1 (SOCS1/JAB) is rapidly induced by LPS and negatively regulates LPS signaling. Using SOCS1(+/-) mice and SOCS1(-/-) mice with an interferon-gamma (IFNgamma)-deficient background, we found that these mice were more susceptible to LPS-induced lethal effects compared to wild-type littermates. Additionally, LPS-induced nitric oxide (NO(2)(-)) synthesis and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFalpha) production were augmented in SOCS1(-/-) macrophages. Furthermore, LPS tolerance, a mechanism that protects against endotoxin shock, was significantly reduced in SOCS1(-/-) cells. LPS-induced I-kappaB and p38 phosphorylation was upregulated in SOCS1(-/-) macrophages, and forced expression of SOCS1 suppressed LPS-induced NF-kappaB activation. These results demonstrate that SOCS1 directly regulates TLR4 signaling and modulates the innate immune response.

title: Bacteria-triggered CD4+ T Regulatory Cells Suppress Helicobacter hepaticus–induced Colitis
text: Previously, we demonstrated that mice lacking interleukin-10 (IL-10) develop colitis after infection with Helicobacter hepaticus, but not wild-type (WT) mice. In this study, we show that reconstituting IL-10-deficient (IL-10 KO) mice with CD4+ T cells from WT mice leads to the development of intestinal inflammation, while cotransferring CD4+ T cells from H. hepaticus-infected but not uninfected WT mice prevents this colitis. Surprisingly, the disease-protective WT CD4+ cells are found in both the CD25+ and CD25− subpopulations, with higher frequencies in the latter. Our data suggest that CD25+ and CD25− CD45RBlow CD4+ cells block colitis through IL-10 and not transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, as treatment with anti-IL-10R but not anti-TGF-β monoclonal antibody abrogated their protective effect. In vitro, CD45RBlow CD4+ cells from infected WT mice produce IL-10 and suppress interferon-γ production by IL-10 KO CD4+ cells in an H. hepaticus-specific manner. Our findings support the idea that H. hepaticus infection induces regulatory T cells in WT mice that prevent bacteria-induced colitis, which may be a mechanism protecting normal individuals against inflammatory bowel disease.

title: The NLRP12 Sensor Negatively Regulates Autoinflammatory Disease by Modulating Interleukin-4 Production in T Cells.
text: Missense mutations within the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptor pyrin domain containing gene 12 (Nlrp12) have been linked to periodic fever syndromes and atopic dermatitis in human populations. In this study, we have elucidated the crucial role of NLRP12 in negatively regulating harmful T cell responses. Nlrp12(-/-) mice exhibited exaggerated T cell responses to antigen immunization, characterized by hyperinflammation. Moreover, transfer of CD4(+)CD45RB(hi)Nlrp12(-/-) T cells into immunodeficient mice resulted in more severe colitis and atopic dermatitis. Contrary to expectations, NLRP12 deficiency did not exacerbate ascending paralysis during experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE); instead, Nlrp12(-/-) mice developed atypical neuroinflammatory symptoms marked by ataxia and loss of balance. Notably, enhanced T-cell-mediated interleukin-4 (IL-4) production played a pivotal role in the development of atypical EAE disease in Nlrp12(-/-) mice. These findings illuminate an unanticipated function of NLRP12 as an intrinsic negative regulator of T-cell-mediated immunity and identify altered NF-κB regulation and IL-4 production as key mediators of NLRP12-associated disease.

title: Shc coordinates signals from intercellular junctions and integrins to regulate flow-induced inflammation
text: Atherosclerotic plaque formation occurs in regions of the vasculature where chronic inflammation is present due to disturbed blood flow patterns. The integration of multiple mechanotransduction pathways is required for endothelial phenotype modulation by flow, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our study demonstrates that, in response to flow, the adaptor protein Shc is activated and interacts with cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesions. This activation is independent of the matrix and requires the involvement of tyrosine kinases such as vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 and Src. Furthermore, we found that Shc binding to integrins is dependent on VE-cadherin, but only occurs on specific matrices. Silencing Shc leads to a reduction in both matrix-independent and matrix-dependent signals. Additionally, Shc regulates flow-induced inflammatory signaling by activating nuclear factor kappaB-dependent signals that promote atherogenesis. In vivo, Shc is activated in regions of atherosclerosis-prone arteries, and its activation correlates with areas of atherosclerosis. Our findings support a model in which Shc coordinates signals from cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesions to elicit flow-induced inflammatory signaling.

title: SIRT1 Redistribution on Chromatin Promotes Genomic Stability but Alters Gene Expression during Aging
text: Genomic instability and alterations in gene expression are fundamental aspects of eukaryotic aging. The histone deacetylase Sir2 plays a crucial role in silencing transcription and stabilizing repetitive DNA in yeast, but during aging or in response to DNA damage, the Sir complex relocalizes to sites of genomic instability, leading to the desilencing of genes that contribute to sterility, a hallmark of yeast aging. Using embryonic stem cells, we have found that mammalian Sir2, SIRT1, and other chromatin-modifying proteins repress a diverse set of genes across the mouse genome, including repetitive DNA sequences. In response to DNA damage, SIRT1 dissociates from these loci and relocalizes to the sites of damage to promote repair, leading to transcriptional changes that parallel those observed in the aging mouse brain. Increased expression of SIRT1 has been shown to promote survival in a mouse model of genomic instability and suppress age-dependent transcriptional changes, suggesting that the redistribution of SIRT1 and other chromatin-modifying proteins in response to DNA damage may be a conserved mechanism of aging across eukaryotic species.

title: Bariatric Surgery in the United Kingdom: A Cohort Study of Weight Loss and Clinical Outcomes in Routine Clinical Care.
text:
The study aimed to investigate the long-term effects of contemporary bariatric surgery on a broad range of clinical outcomes in large populations treated in routine clinical practice. The study used an observational retrospective cohort design using data from the United Kingdom Clinical Practice Research Datalink, which included 3,882 patients who underwent bariatric surgery between 2010 and 2014 and were matched with 3,882 obese patients without surgery. The main outcome measures were changes in weight, body mass index (BMI), and obesity-related comorbidities, including type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, angina, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, fractures, obstructive sleep apnea, and cancer, as well as mortality.
The study found that bariatric surgery patients exhibited rapid weight loss in the first four months after surgery, with a rate of 4.98 kg/mo, which slowed down but remained significant to the end of 4 years. Gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy were associated with greater initial weight reduction than gastric banding. Bariatric surgery was also found to be associated with significant improvements in pre-existing T2DM, hypertension, angina, MI, and obstructive sleep apnea, as well as a reduced risk of incident T2DM, hypertension, angina, MI, and obstructive sleep apnea. However, no association was detected between bariatric surgery and fractures, cancer, or stroke. The study concluded that bariatric surgery as delivered in the UK healthcare system is associated with dramatic weight loss, sustained at least 4 years after surgery, which is accompanied by substantial improvements in pre-existing T2DM and hypertension, as well as a reduced risk of incident T2DM, hypertension, angina, MI, and obstructive sleep apnea. Widening the availability of bariatric surgery could lead to substantial health benefits for many people who are morbidly obese.

title: Notch signalling acts in postmitotic avian myogenic cells to control MyoD activation.
text:
During Drosophila myogenesis, Notch signaling functions at multiple stages of muscle differentiation. In contrast, the role of Notch signaling in vivo during chick myogenesis has been poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the in vivo role of Notch signaling in chicken myogenesis.
First, we demonstrate that the Notch1 receptor is expressed in postmitotic cells of the myotome and that the Notch ligands Delta1 and Serrate2 are detected in subsets of differentiating myogenic cells, positioning them to signal to Notch1 during myogenic differentiation. We also reexamine the expression of MyoD and Myf5 during avian myogenesis, finding that Myf5 is expressed earlier than MyoD, consistent with previous results in mice.
Next, we investigate the effect of forced expression of the Notch ligand Delta1 on myogenic differentiation. Using a retroviral system, we show that Delta1 overexpression has no effect on the expression of early myogenic markers Pax3 and Myf5, but strongly downregulates MyoD in infected somites. Although Delta1 overexpression results in a complete lack of differentiated muscles, we observe that initial formation of a myotome is not prevented, indicating that exit from the cell cycle has not been blocked. These findings suggest that Notch signaling acts in postmitotic myogenic cells to control a critical step of muscle differentiation.

title: Hepatitis C virus infection in a large cohort of homosexually active men: independent associations with HIV-1 infection and injecting drug use but not sexual behaviour.
text:
Objective: To determine the prevalence and risk factors for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in a cohort of homosexually active men, with a particular focus on assessing sexual transmission.
Design: A cross-sectional study using sera collected between 1984 and 1989 to determine the prevalence of HCV antibody, and a case-control analysis using questionnaire data from HCV positive and negative subjects to identify risk factors.
Subjects/Setting: 1038 homosexually active men participating in a prospective study established to identify risk factors for AIDS, recruited through private and public primary care and sexually transmissible disease (STD) services in central Sydney.
Main Outcome Measures: Prevalence of HCV antibody and its association with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection, other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), number of sexual partners, sexual practices, and recreational drug use.
Results: Overall, 7.6% of subjects tested were seropositive for HCV antibody. In univariate analysis, HCV infection was significantly associated with injecting drug use (IDU), HIV infection, and a history of syphilis, anogenital herpes, gonorrhoea, and hepatitis B. In case-control analysis, similar sexual behaviors were reported by HCV positive and HCV negative subjects, except that HCV negative subjects were less likely to engage in unprotected receptive anal intercourse without ejaculation, unprotected insertive and receptive oro-anal intercourse (rimming), and insertive fisting. In multiple logistic regression analyses, only HIV-1 infection and IDU in the previous six months remained significantly associated with the presence of HCV antibody.
Conclusions: Injecting drug use was the major behavioral risk factor for HCV infection, and if sexual transmission did occur, it may have been facilitated by concurrent HIV-1 infection.

title: Analysis of human cytomegalovirus-encoded microRNA activity during infection.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are expressed across a wide range of organisms, from plants to animals, and play a crucial role in regulating gene expression post-transcriptionally. Unique among miRNAs, those encoded by viruses have the potential to target both viral and host genes. We have previously demonstrated that a human cytomegalovirus (HCMV)-encoded miRNA, miR-UL112, downregulates the expression of a host immune gene, MICB, and its ectopic expression leads to reduced viral replication and titers. However, the targets of most viral miRNAs and their functions remain unknown. Here, we demonstrate that miR-UL112 also targets the UL114 gene and show that its reduction reduces the activity of UL114 as a uracil DNA glycosylase, with only minimal effects on virus growth. Additionally, we find that two other HCMV-encoded miRNAs, miR-US25-1 and miR-US25-2, reduce viral replication and DNA synthesis not only of HCMV but also of other viruses, suggesting that these miRNAs target cellular genes essential for virus growth. Therefore, we propose that in addition to miR-UL112, two additional HCMV miRNAs control the life cycle of the virus.

title: Anti-obesity drugs: past, present and future
text: The ideal anti-obesity drug should produce sustained weight loss with minimal side effects, while taking into account the complex mechanisms that regulate energy balance. These mechanisms involve redundant pathways, shared functions with other physiological processes, and influences from social, hedonic, and psychological factors, which limit the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions. Despite ongoing efforts, anti-obesity drug discovery programs have faced numerous challenges, including false starts, clinical trial failures, and withdrawals due to unforeseen adverse effects. Targeting pathways in metabolic tissues, such as adipocytes, liver, and skeletal muscle, has shown promise in preclinical studies, but none have advanced to clinical development. Recent advances in understanding the peptidergic signaling of hunger and satiety, including ghrelin, cholecystokinin (CCK), peptide YY (PYY), and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), as well as homeostatic mechanisms related to leptin and its upstream pathways in the hypothalamus, have opened new avenues for drug development. However, it remains uncertain whether these agents will meet regulatory requirements for licensing. GLP-1 receptor agonists have successfully treated diabetes and have shown promising body-weight-lowering effects in humans, potentially paving the way for other anti-obesity agents. To overcome the challenges of developing drugs that can match the effectiveness of surgical intervention, a new approach may be needed. In other therapeutic areas, such as diabetes and hypertension, combination therapies using peptides and small molecules are being explored in clinical trials, although regulatory experience suggests that significant challenges lie ahead. In the future, this polytherapeutic strategy could potentially rival surgery in terms of efficacy, safety, and sustainability of weight loss.

title: Cytochemical Analysis of Pollen Development in Wild-Type Arabidopsis and a Male-Sterile Mutant.
text: Microsporogenesis has been investigated in wild-type Arabidopsis thaliana and the nuclear male-sterile mutant BM3 using cytochemical staining. The mutant lacks adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, an enzyme involved in the purine salvage pathway that converts adenine to AMP. Comparisons between wild-type and mutant pollen development revealed that pollen development in the mutant began to deviate from wild type shortly after meiosis, as the tetrads of microspores were released from their callose walls. The first noticeable abnormality in pollen development was a darker staining of the microspore wall due to incomplete synthesis of the intine. Vacuole formation was delayed and irregular in the mutant, and the majority of the mutant microspores failed to undergo mitotic divisions. Additionally, enzyme activities of alcohol dehydrogenase and esterases decreased in the mutant soon after meiosis and were undetectable in mature pollen grains of the mutant. Furthermore, RNA accumulation was diminished in the mutant. These findings suggest that adenine salvage may play a crucial role in pollen development.

title: Prevalence, risk factors, and uptake of interventions for sexually transmitted infections in Britain: findings from the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal)
text:
The study conducted by the researchers aimed to assess the prevalence of four sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in Britain, specifically Chlamydia trachomatis, type-specific human papillomavirus (HPV), Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and HIV antibody, among a representative sample of women and men aged 16-74 years. The study also examined the uptake of interventions, such as testing and attendance at sexual health clinics, among the participants.
The study found that the prevalence of Chlamydia trachomatis was 1.5% in women and 1.1% in men, with the highest prevalence observed among individuals aged 16-24 years. The study also found that 60.4% of chlamydia infections in women and 43.3% in men were in individuals who had had one sexual partner in the past year. In addition, 54.2% of sexually active 16-24-year-olds in women and 34.6% in men reported testing for chlamydia in the past year, with higher testing rates observed among those with more partners.
The study also found that high-risk HPV was detected in 15.9% of women, similar to the findings in Natsal-2. Coverage of HPV catch-up vaccination was 61.5%, with lower coverage observed among older women. The prevalence of HPV types 16 and 18 in women aged 18-20 years was lower in Natsal-3 than in Natsal-2. Gonorrhoea and HIV were uncommon and restricted to participants with recognised high-risk factors.
The study's findings suggest that STIs are distributed heterogeneously, requiring general and infection-specific interventions. The increases in testing and attendance at sexual health clinics, especially among individuals at highest risk, are encouraging. However, STIs persist both in individuals accessing and those not accessing services. The study provides empirical evidence to inform future sexual health interventions and services.
The study was funded by grants from the UK Medical Research Council and the Wellcome Trust, with support from the Economic and Social Research Council and the Department of Health.

title: Cancer Pharmacogenomics and Pharmacoepidemiology: Setting a Research Agenda to Accelerate Translation
text:
Recent advances in genomic research have significantly contributed to predicting response to cancer therapies. Researchers in cancer pharmacogenomics and pharmacoepidemiology aim to understand why individuals respond differently to drug treatments, both in terms of adverse effects and treatment efficacy. To identify research priorities and necessary resources, the National Cancer Institute (NCI) organized a workshop titled "Cancer Pharmacogenomics: Setting a Research Agenda to Accelerate Translation" on July 21, 2009, in Bethesda, MD. This commentary summarizes and discusses five science-based recommendations and four infrastructure-based recommendations that emerged from the workshop. Key recommendations include:
1. Collecting germline and tumor biospecimens in NCI-sponsored clinical trials and some observational and population-based studies to support routine collection.
2. Incorporating pharmacogenomic markers into clinical trials.
3. Addressing the ethical, legal, social, and biospecimen- and data-sharing implications of pharmacogenomic and pharmacoepidemiologic research.
4. Establishing partnerships across NCI, with other federal agencies, and with industry to facilitate the discovery and validation of clinical, sociodemographic, lifestyle, and genomic markers related to cancer treatment response and adverse events. These recommendations will improve the speed and efficiency of translating new pharmacogenomic and pharmacoepidemiologic information into clinical practice.

title: Differential transcription of the orphan receptor RORbeta in nuclear extracts derived from Neuro2A and HeLa cells.
text: A crucial model system for investigating the processes leading to productive transcription is provided by the superfamily of nuclear receptors, which are predominantly regulated by ligands. Over the years, several 'orphan' nuclear receptors have been isolated, but their ligands remain unknown. Consequently, little is understood about how these 'orphan' receptors regulate transcription. In this study, we have investigated the biochemical and transcriptional properties of the neuronally expressed orphan nuclear receptor RORbeta (NR1F2) and compared them with the retinoic acid receptor heterodimer RXRalpha-RARalpha (NR2B1-NR1B1) and Gal-VP16 in vitro. Although RORbeta binds to its DNA-binding sites with relatively low affinity, it efficiently directs transcription in nuclear extracts derived from a neuronal cell line, Neuro2A, but not in nuclear extracts from non-neuronal HeLa cells. In contrast, RXRalpha-RARalpha and the acidic transcription factor Gal-VP16 support transcription in Neuro2A and HeLa nuclear extracts equally efficiently. These observations suggest that different (co)factors are required for transactivation by members of the NR1 subfamily of nuclear receptors.

title: Estrogens, progestogens, normal breast cell proliferation, and breast cancer risk.
text: Epidemiological studies suggest that ovarian hormones play a role in the development of breast cancer at all stages of life. Early menopause and premenopausal obesity may reduce the risk, while postmenopausal obesity and menopausal estrogen replacement therapy may increase the risk. Combined oral contraceptives and Depo-Provera do not appear to affect the risk. It is believed that estrogens and progestogens act through and with proto-oncogenes and growth factors to influence breast cell proliferation and breast cancer etiology. Animal studies have shown that estrogen can cause interlobular ductal cell division, while progesterone can cause increased terminal duct lobular unit cell division during the luteal phase. Most breast carcinomas originate from terminal duct lobular unit cells, which multiply rapidly during pregnancy and the luteal phase. However, there is significant interpersonal variation in breast cell division rates. No studies have compared breast cell division rates to serum hormone concentrations, but the peak of mitosis occurs around 3 days before breast cell death in the late luteal and early follicular phases. Other research suggests that breast stem cell proliferation is linked to breast cancer development, and endocrine therapy can reduce mitotic activity, indicating the estrogen and progesterone receptor content of breast cancers. Hormone-dependent breast cancer cell lines are all estrogen-dependent, and progesterone can block these cells, which behave like endometrial cells. The findings of various breast cell proliferation studies are unclear, and further research is needed to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying these observations.

title: Analysis of the interaction of primate retroviruses with the human RNA interference machinery.
text: The debate surrounding whether retroviruses, such as human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) and human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), interact with the cellular RNA interference machinery has been a topic of much discussion. In this study, we provide evidence that neither HIV-1 nor HTLV-1 produces significant levels of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) or microRNAs (miRNAs) in persistently infected T cells. Additionally, we demonstrate that the retroviral nuclear transcription factors HIV-1 Tat and HTLV-1 Tax, as well as the Tas transactivator encoded by primate foamy virus, are unable to inhibit RNA interference in human cells. Furthermore, stable expression of physiological levels of HIV-1 Tat did not globally inhibit microRNA production or expression in infected human cells. These findings suggest that HIV-1 and HTLV-1 do not induce the production of viral siRNAs or miRNAs, nor do they repress the cellular RNA interference machinery in infected cells.

title: Impact of diabetes on long-term prognosis in patients with unstable angina and non-Q-wave myocardial infarction: results of the OASIS (Organization to Assess Strategies for Ischemic Syndromes) Registry.
text:
Background: Unstable coronary artery disease is the most common cause of admission to a coronary care unit, but the long-term prognosis of patients with this diagnosis, particularly those with diabetes mellitus, remains uncertain.
Methods and Results: Prospectively collected data from 6 countries in the Organization to Assess Strategies for Ischemic Syndromes (OASIS) registry were analyzed to determine the 2-year prognosis of diabetic and nondiabetic patients hospitalized with unstable angina or non-Q-wave myocardial infarction. Of the 8013 registry patients, 1718 (21%) had diabetes. Diabetic patients had a higher rate of coronary bypass surgery compared to nondiabetic patients (23% vs 20%, P < 0.001), but similar rates of catheterization and angioplasty. Diabetes independently predicted mortality, cardiovascular death, new myocardial infarction, stroke, and new congestive heart failure. Interestingly, diabetic patients without prior cardiovascular disease had similar event rates for all outcomes as nondiabetic patients with established cardiovascular disease.
Conclusions: Hospitalization for unstable angina or non-Q-wave myocardial infarction is associated with a high 2-year morbidity and mortality, particularly for patients with diabetes. Notably, diabetic patients without prior cardiovascular disease have the same long-term morbidity and mortality as nondiabetic patients with established cardiovascular disease after hospitalization for unstable coronary artery disease.

title: Strain improvement by metabolic engineering: lysine production as a case study for systems biology.
text: A primary objective of systems biology is to elucidate cellular function and physiology through the integrated analysis of comprehensive genomic and physiological data. This holistic approach has been widely employed in the past, as it forms the foundation of metabolic flux analysis, the distribution of kinetic control in metabolic pathways, and the distinctive characteristic of metabolic engineering. As a case study, these tools have been applied to enhance lysine-producing strains of Corynebacterium glutamicum. A systematic examination of the physiology of this organism led to the identification of specific metabolic targets, resulting in substantial improvements in product yield and productivity. This case study serves as a blueprint for the development of systems biology tools to leverage large volumes of cellular and genome-wide transcriptional and physiological data.

title: Cognitive behavioral therapy vs zopiclone for treatment of chronic primary insomnia in older adults: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Insomnia is a common problem in older adults, with numerous negative consequences for their health, social interactions, and mental well-being. Prior research has shown that both psychological and pharmacological interventions can be effective in treating insomnia, but there is a lack of blinded, placebo-controlled trials comparing these approaches. This study aimed to investigate the short- and long-term clinical efficacy of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and pharmacological treatment in older adults with chronic primary insomnia.
The study was a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial conducted between 2004 and 2005 at a single university-based outpatient clinic in Norway. Participants were 46 adults aged 60.8 years on average (22 women), with chronic primary insomnia. The study included three groups: CBT (n=18), sleep medication (zopiclone, 7.5 mg per night; n=16), and placebo medication (n=12). All treatments lasted for 6 weeks, and the CBT group was followed up at 6 months.
The primary outcome measures were ambulatory clinical polysomnographic data and sleep diaries, which were used to assess total wake time, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and slow-wave sleep (measured only through polysomnography). The results showed that CBT was superior to zopiclone on three out of four outcome measures, with participants in the CBT group improving their sleep efficiency from 81.4% at pretreatment to 90.1% at 6-month follow-up, compared to a decrease from 82.3% to 81.9% in the zopiclone group. Additionally, participants in the CBT group spent more time in slow-wave sleep stages 3 and 4 and less time awake during the night compared to the other groups. Total sleep time was similar across all groups, but at 6 months, patients receiving CBT had better sleep efficiency using polysomnography than those taking zopiclone.
In conclusion, these findings suggest that interventions based on CBT are superior to zopiclone treatment both in short- and long-term management of insomnia in older adults. This study highlights the importance of CBT as a viable and effective treatment option for insomnia in this population.

title: Local changes in lipid environment of TCR microclusters regulate membrane binding by the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain
text:
The T cell receptor (TCR) CD3ε and ζ cytoplasmic domains interact with the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM), as revealed by a previous nuclear magnetic resonance structure. Specifically, both tyrosines of the CD3ε immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif are embedded in the PM bilayer. Previous studies have shown that electrostatic interactions between acidic phospholipids and clusters of basic CD3ε residues are crucial for CD3ε and ζ membrane binding. Phosphatidylserine (PS), the most abundant negatively charged lipid on the inner leaflet of the PM, plays a significant role in CD3ε cytoplasmic domain binding.
Our findings demonstrate that TCR triggering by peptide-MHC complexes leads to the dissociation of the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain from the PM. This release is accompanied by a significant reduction in negative charge and available PS in TCR microclusters. These changes in the lipid composition of TCR microclusters occur even when TCR signaling is blocked with a Src kinase inhibitor, indicating that local alterations in lipid composition render the CD3ε cytoplasmic domain accessible during early stages of T cell activation.

title: Humans and great apes share a large frontal cortex
text: Some of the exceptional cognitive abilities of humans are commonly attributed to an enlarged frontal lobe, which evolved disproportionately during human evolution. This theory is primarily based on comparisons between human and primate brains, excluding great apes. To investigate this claim, we used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to compare the relative size of the frontal cortices in living primate species, including all extant hominoids. Our findings revealed that the human frontal cortices were not significantly larger than those of great apes, challenging the notion of a frontal advantage responsible for special cognitive abilities. Instead, we propose that these abilities may be due to differences in the size and connectivity of individual cortical areas, rather than an overall increase in frontal lobe size during human evolution.

title: Virus-Plus-Susceptibility Gene Interaction Determines Crohn's Disease Gene Atg16L1 Phenotypes in Intestine
text: It is intriguing that disease often fails to manifest in individuals carrying common risk alleles of genes associated with disease susceptibility, despite the presence of these alleles. Our study reveals that a specific virus infection, combined with a mutation in the Crohn's disease susceptibility gene Atg16L1, can lead to intestinal abnormalities in mice. This virus-gene interaction triggers irregularities in granule packaging and unique gene expression patterns in Paneth cells, as well as alterations in the response to injury induced by the toxic substance dextran sodium sulfate. These pathologies are dependent on the presence of TNFalpha and IFNgamma and can be prevented by treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Our findings provide a concrete example of how a virus-gene interaction, in conjunction with additional environmental factors and commensal bacteria, can determine the phenotype of individuals carrying common risk alleles for inflammatory diseases.

title: CaMKII Triggers the Diffusional Trapping of Surface AMPARs through Phosphorylation of Stargazin
text: The Ca(2+)/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) plays a crucial role in the synaptic recruitment of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) during both development and plasticity. However, the underlying mechanism remains elusive. By employing single-particle tracking of AMPARs, our study reveals that CaMKII activation and postsynaptic translocation lead to the synaptic trapping of AMPARs that are diffusing in the membrane. This immobilization requires both phosphorylation of the auxiliary subunit Stargazin and its binding to PDZ domain scaffolds, without relying on the PDZ binding domain of the GluA1 AMPAR subunit or its phosphorylation at Ser831. Furthermore, CaMKII-dependent AMPAR immobilization regulates short-term plasticity, as NMDA-dependent Ca(2+) influx in the postsynapse triggers a CaMKII- and Stargazin-dependent decrease in AMPAR diffusional exchange at synapses, which in turn controls synaptic function.

title: Epigenetics in diabetic nephropathy, immunity and metabolism
text:
When it comes to the epigenome, there is a delicate balance between understanding and confusion. Walking this line can reveal a fascinating additional layer of transcriptional control. Above the genome level, there are rules for how chemical information is read, and epigenetic modifications show a different side of the genetic code, diverse and regulated. These modifications can result in short- to long-term changes in genetic transcription, offering exquisite control but also posing a significant challenge to understanding the mechanisms underlying complex diseases.
Recent technological and computational advances have improved the acquisition of epigenomic patterns, deepening our understanding of the complex chromatin landscape. Identifying the true physiological targets of regulatory proteins, such as reader proteins, writer proteins, and eraser proteins, is key to resolving distinct chromatin signatures of diabetic complications. However, how do diverse proteins regulate the diabetic landscape from an epigenomic perspective?
This review draws on an expanding compendium of experimental and clinical studies to detail the current state-of-play and provide a perspective on chromatin-dependent mechanisms implicated in diabetic complications, with a special focus on diabetic nephropathy. We hypothesize a codified signature of the diabetic epigenome and provide examples of prime candidates for chemical modification. Moreover, we explore future strategies to expedite and refine the search for clinically relevant discoveries, as well as the challenges associated with therapeutic strategies targeting epigenetic pathways.

title: Drinking pattern and mortality: the Italian Risk Factor and Life Expectancy pooling project.
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between a specific aspect of drinking pattern (i.e., drinking wine outside meals) and the risk of all-cause and cause-specific mortality.
Methods: The Risk Factors and Life Expectancy Study, a pooled analysis of several epidemiological studies conducted in Italy, included 8,647 men and 6,521 women aged 30-59 years at baseline, without history of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Participants were followed up for an average of 7 years, during which time mortality data was collected.
Results: Compared to drinkers of wine with meals, drinkers of wine outside meals showed higher mortality rates from all causes, non-CVD diseases, and cancer. This association was independent of CVD risk factors measured at baseline, amount of alcohol consumed, and was stronger in women than in men.
Conclusions: The present findings suggest that drinking patterns may have significant implications for health outcomes. The relationship between alcohol consumption and disease has been extensively studied, but most studies have limitations, including a focus on quantity of alcohol consumed without considering drinking patterns. The present study highlights the importance of examining the various components of alcohol consumption, particularly drinking patterns, in determining the health effects of alcohol.

title: Pointing in the right direction: new developments in the field of planar cell polarity
text: Planar cell polarity (PCP) is a widespread phenomenon observed in various developmental processes, characterized by collective cell movement and tissue organization. Disruptions in PCP can lead to severe developmental defects. Recent research in flies and vertebrates has expanded our understanding of PCP by identifying new functions and signalling components, and proposing novel mechanistic models. However, despite these advances, the quest to distill fundamental principles of PCP remains ongoing, and significant mechanistic uncertainties continue to pose significant challenges.
