title: ADAR1 Forms a Complex with Dicer to Promote MicroRNA Processing and RNA-Induced Gene Silencing
text: Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) play a crucial role in RNA editing, specifically converting adenosine residues to inosine in double-stranded RNAs. In this study, we investigated the interplay between the RNA editing mechanism and the RNA interference (RNAi) machinery and found that ADAR1 forms a complex with Dicer through direct protein-protein interaction. Notably, ADAR1 enhances the maximum rate (Vmax) of pre-microRNA (miRNA) cleavage by Dicer and facilitates the loading of miRNA onto RNA-induced silencing complexes, revealing a novel function of ADAR1 in miRNA processing and RNAi mechanisms. ADAR1 distinguishes its functions in RNA editing and RNAi by forming either ADAR1/ADAR1 homodimers or Dicer/ADAR1 heterodimers, respectively. Consistently, the absence of miRNAs in ADAR1(-/-) mouse embryos leads to a global inhibition of their target gene expression, which might contribute to their embryonic lethality.

title: Interchangeability of Biosimilars: A European Perspective
text: Many of the top-selling 'blockbuster' biological medicinal products are, or soon will be, facing competition from similar biological medicinal products (biosimilars) in the EU. Biosimilarity is based on the concept of comparability, which has been successfully used for several decades to ensure that a biological product is similar before and after a manufacturing change. Over the past 10 years, experience with biosimilars has shown that even complex biotechnology-derived proteins can be copied successfully. Most best-selling biologicals are used for long-term treatment. This has sparked intense debate on the interchangeability of a biosimilar with its reference product, with the main concern being immunogenicity. We examine the theoretical basis of the presumed risks of switching between a biosimilar and its reference product and the available data on switches. Our conclusion is that switching between comparable versions of the same active substance approved in accordance with EU legislation is not expected to trigger or enhance immunogenicity. Based on current knowledge, it is unlikely and difficult to demonstrate that two products, comparable on a population level, would have different safety or efficacy in individual patients upon a switch. Our conclusion is that biosimilars licensed in the EU are interchangeable.

title: Exome sequencing identifies somatic gain-of-function PPM1D mutations in brainstem gliomas
text: Gliomas originating in the brainstem and thalamus are exceptionally aggressive tumors that are challenging to surgically remove. To gain insights into the genetic and epigenetic characteristics of these tumors, we conducted exomic sequencing on 14 brainstem gliomas (BSGs) and 12 thalamic gliomas. We also performed targeted mutational analysis on an additional 24 such tumors and genome-wide methylation profiling of 45 gliomas. This study led to the discovery of tumor-specific mutations in PPM1D, encoding wild-type p53-induced protein phosphatase 1D (WIP1), in 37.5% of the BSGs that harbored hallmark H3F3A mutations encoding p. Lys27Met substitutions. PPM1D mutations were found to be mutually exclusive with TP53 mutations in BSGs and attenuated p53 activation in vitro. PPM1D mutations were identified as truncating alterations in exon 6, which enhanced the ability of PPM1D to suppress the activation of the DNA damage response checkpoint protein CHK2. These findings establish PPM1D as a frequently mutated target and a potential therapeutic target in brainstem gliomas.

title: Crystal structure of a nucleosome core particle containing the variant histone H2A.Z
text: The activation of transcription within chromatin is linked to the incorporation of the essential histone variant H2A.Z into nucleosomes. While H2A.Z and other histone variants may form distinct chromosomal domains, the molecular mechanism by which they function is largely unknown. In this study, we have determined the 2.6 Å crystal structure of a nucleosome core particle containing H2A.Z. The overall structure is similar to that of a previously reported 2.8 Å nucleosome structure containing major histone proteins, but localized changes result in a subtle destabilization of the interaction between the H2A.Z–H2B dimer and the H3–H4 tetramer. Additionally, H2A.Z nucleosomes have an altered surface that includes a metal ion, which may lead to changes in higher-order structure or the association of specific nuclear proteins with H2A.Z. Furthermore, we found that the incorporation of H2A.Z and H2A within the same nucleosome is unlikely due to significant changes in the interface between the two H2A.Z–H2B dimers.

title: Dendritic Cell KLF2 Expression Regulates T Cell Activation and Proatherogenic Immune Responses.
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) have been implicated as key regulators of innate and adaptive inflammation in various diseases, including atherosclerosis. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying DCs' role in modulating inflammation are not fully understood. Previous studies have shown that the transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) plays an important anti-inflammatory role in regulating the activation of different cell types involved in atherosclerotic lesion development, including endothelial cells, macrophages, and T cells. To investigate the role of KLF2 in DCs, we used a pan-DC, CD11c-specific cre-lox gene knockout mouse model. Our findings revealed that KLF2 deficiency led to increased surface expression of costimulatory molecules CD40 and CD86 on DCs, which in turn promoted enhanced T cell proliferation and apoptosis. Interestingly, bone marrow transplantation of mice with KLF2-deficient DCs into Ldlr-/- mice exacerbated atherosclerosis, likely due to heightened vascular inflammation characterized by increased DC presence within lesions, enhanced T cell activation and cytokine production, and elevated cell death in atherosclerotic lesions. These data suggest that KLF2 regulates the degree of DC activation, thereby influencing the intensity of proatherogenic T cell responses.

title: Targeting tumor-necrosis factor receptor pathways for tumor immunotherapy
text: With the success of ipilimumab and the promise of programmed death-1 pathway-targeted agents, the field of tumor immunotherapy is rapidly expanding. Newer targets for clinical development include select members of the tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) family. Agonist antibodies to these co-stimulatory molecules target both T and B cells, modulating T-cell activation and enhancing immune responses. In vitro and in vivo preclinical data have provided a basis for continued development of 4-1BB, OX40, glucocorticoid-induced TNFR-related gene, herpes virus entry mediator, and CD27 as potential therapies for patients with cancer. In this review, we summarize the immune response to tumors, consider preclinical and early clinical data on select TNFR family members, discuss potential translational challenges, and suggest possible combination therapies with the aim of inducing durable antitumor responses.

title: Plasma soluble corin in patients with heart failure.
text:
BACKGROUND: Corin is a transmembrane protease that plays a crucial role in the processing of natriuretic peptides in the heart. Like many membrane proteins, corin is also shed from the cell surface. In this study, we aimed to investigate the levels of soluble corin in plasma samples from healthy controls and patients with heart failure (HF) and acute myocardial infarction (AMI).
METHODS: We obtained plasma samples from 198 healthy adults and 291 patients with HF, as well as from 73 patients with AMI. Soluble corin levels in plasma were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method.
RESULTS: Our results showed that plasma corin levels were significantly lower in patients with HF compared to healthy controls (365 pg/mL [standard deviation (SD), 259] vs 690 pg/mL [SD, 260]; P<0.001). The reduction in plasma corin levels was found to correlate with the severity of HF, with lower levels observed in patients with New York Heart Association (NYHA) classes II, III, and IV compared to class II (450 pg/mL [SD, 281 pg/mL]; n=69), 377 pg/mL [SD, 270 pg/mL]; n=132], and 282 pg/mL [SD, 194 pg/mL]; n=90], respectively (P<0.001 class II vs class IV; P<0.05 class III vs class IV). In contrast, plasma corin levels in patients with AMI were similar to those of healthy controls (678 pg/mL [SD, 285 pg/mL]; P>0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that soluble corin is present in human plasma and that its levels are significantly reduced in patients with HF. These results suggest that corin deficiency may contribute to the pathogenesis of HF and that plasma corin may be used as a biomarker in the diagnosis of HF.

title: The NLRP3 inflammasome functions as a driver of the myelodysplastic syndrome phenotype.
text:
Despite genetic heterogeneity, myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs) share common features of cytological dysplasia and ineffective hematopoiesis. We found that a hallmark of MDSs is the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, which drives clonal expansion and pyroptotic cell death. Interestingly, MDS hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) overexpress inflammasome proteins and display activated NLRP3 complexes that trigger the activation of caspase-1, leading to the production of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-18, and ultimately, pyroptotic cell death.
We discovered that pyroptosis is triggered by the alarmin S100A9, which is overexpressed in MDS HSPCs and bone marrow plasma. Additionally, S100A9-induced signaling activates NADPH oxidase (NOX), leading to increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that initiate cation influx, cell swelling, and β-catenin activation.
Our findings suggest that knockdown of NLRP3 or caspase-1, neutralization of S100A9, and pharmacologic inhibition of NLRP3 or NOX can suppress pyroptosis, ROS generation, and nuclear β-catenin in MDSs, leading to the restoration of effective hematopoiesis. These results indicate that alarmins and founder gene mutations in MDSs activate a common redox-sensitive inflammasome circuit, which may provide new avenues for therapeutic intervention.

title: Structural Brain Correlates Associated with Professional Handball Playing
text:
Background:
Handball is a sport that requires exceptional bimanual performance, with the ability to control both the dominant and non-dominant hands being crucial for skilled play. The control of the non-dominant hand is particularly challenging, as it requires efficient catching and throwing, which are both dependent on the coordination of both hands.
Methodology/Hypotheses:
To investigate training-induced structural neuroplasticity in professional handball players, we employed various structural neuroimaging techniques and analytical approaches. Our study aimed to provide a comprehensive review of the literature on sport-induced structural neuroplastic alterations. We expected structural brain adaptations in regions relevant for motor and somatosensory processing, such as the grey matter (GM) of the primary/secondary motor (MI/supplementary motor area, SMA) and somatosensory cortex (SI/SII), basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum, as well as in the white matter (WM) of the corticospinal tract (CST) and corpus callosum. Specifically, we predicted stronger adaptations in brain regions controlling the non-dominant left hand.
Results:
Our results revealed increased GM volume in handball players compared to control subjects in the right MI/SI, bilateral SMA/cingulate motor area, and left intraparietal sulcus. Additionally, we found increased fractional anisotropy (FA) and axial diffusivity within the right CST in handball players compared to control women. Furthermore, we found a negative correlation between the age of handball training commencement and GM volume in the right and left MI/SI, and a negative correlation between years of handball training experience and radial diffusivity in the right CST. Finally, we observed tendencies for larger subcortical structures in handball players.
Discussion/Conclusion:
Our findings provide evidence of training-induced structural alterations in the somatosensory-motor network of handball players, with more pronounced adaptations in the right hemisphere controlling the non-dominant left hand. The correlations between handball training-related measures and anatomical differences suggest that these adaptations are the result of neuroplasticity rather than a genetic predisposition for a ball playing affinity. This study highlights the importance of investigating neuroplasticity in sportsmen to better understand the neural mechanisms of expertise in general.

title: The role of epigenetics in aging and age-related diseases
text: The significance of epigenetics in aging and age-related diseases is a crucial area of study in molecular physiology and medicine, as certain epigenetic factors are believed to play a mediating role in the relationship between the genome and the environment. In order to fully understand the role of epigenetics in aging, it is essential to meet two key conditions: there must be specific epigenetic changes that occur during aging, and these changes must be directly associated with the aged phenotype. If specific epigenetic modifications have a direct functional impact on aging, it is also important to determine whether they are influenced by genetic, environmental, or stochastic factors, and whether they can be transmitted to future generations. In this discussion, we will examine current knowledge in the field and outline potential future directions for research.

title: Effects of a high-fat diet exposure in utero on the metabolic syndrome-like phenomenon in mouse offspring through epigenetic changes in adipocytokine gene expression.
text: The relationship between parental obesity and the development of metabolic disorders in offspring, as well as the role of genetic and environmental factors, is not fully understood. Adipocytokines, such as leptin and adiponectin, play a crucial role in glucose and lipid metabolism. To investigate the potential epigenetic effects of prenatal exposure to a high-fat diet on adipocytokine gene expression, we compared the offspring of mice fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy (OH mice) to those of mice fed a control diet during pregnation (OC mice). Our results showed that OH mice were significantly heavier than OC mice from 14 weeks of age and exhibited hypertension, insulin resistance, and hyperlipidemia. Additionally, we found that OH mice had higher blood pressure and worse glucose tolerance than OC mice at 24 weeks of age. Furthermore, we observed changes in the expression of leptin and adiponectin in white adipose tissue, including lower adiponectin levels and higher leptin levels in OH mice. These changes were associated with epigenetic modifications, including lower acetylation and higher methylation levels of histone H3 at lysine 9 of the adiponectin promoter in adipose tissues of OH mice. In contrast, methylation of histone 4 at lysine 20 in the leptin promoter was significantly higher in OH compared with OC mice. These findings suggest that prenatal exposure to a high-fat diet may cause a metabolic syndrome-like phenomenon through epigenetic modifications of adipocytokine, adiponectin, and leptin gene expression.

title: Highly efficient miRNA-mediated reprogramming of mouse and human somatic cells to pluripotency.
text: Transcription factor-based cellular reprogramming has paved the way for converting somatic cells into a pluripotent state, but it has faced limitations due to the need for transcription factors and relatively low efficiency. We demonstrate here that expressing the miR302/367 cluster can rapidly and efficiently reprogram mouse and human somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) without the need for exogenous transcription factors. This miRNA-based reprogramming approach is two orders of magnitude more efficient than standard Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/Myc-mediated methods. Mouse and human miR302/367 iPSCs exhibit similar characteristics to Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/Myc-iPSCs, including expression of pluripotency markers, teratoma formation, and, for mouse cells, chimera contribution and germline contribution. We found that miR367 expression is essential for miR302/367-mediated reprogramming and activates Oct4 gene expression, and that suppressing Hdac2 is also required. Our data show that miRNA and Hdac-mediated pathways can cooperate effectively to reprogram somatic cells to pluripotency.

title: Unmet needs and depression among carers of people newly diagnosed with cancer.
text:
The primary objectives of this analysis were to:
1. Assess the prevalence of unmet needs among carers of individuals recently diagnosed with cancer.
2. Identify subgroups of carers who may be at a higher risk of depression.

To achieve these objectives, the study employed the following methods:

1. One hundred and fifty dyads of individuals with cancer and their carers, aged 18 years or older, were recruited from four Australian hospitals. Individuals with cancer who were receiving adjuvant cancer treatment with curative intent were eligible to participate.

2. Carers completed the Supportive Care Needs Survey-Partners & Caregivers (SCNS-P&C45), and both carers and patients completed the Centre of Epidemiologic-Depression Scale (CES-D).

3. The results showed that 57% of carers reported at least one unmet need, 37% reported at least three unmet needs, 31% reported at least five unmet needs, and 15% reported at least 10 unmet needs. The most commonly endorsed unmet needs were in the domains of information and healthcare service needs.

4. Thirty percent of carers and 36% of patients were at risk of clinical depression. A weak to moderate positive relationship was observed between unmet needs and carer depression (r=0.30, p<0.001).

5. Carer levels of unmet needs were significantly associated with carer age, hospital type, treatment type, cancer type, living situation, relationship status (in both uni- and multi-factor analysis); person with cancer age and carer level of education (in unifactor analysis only); but not with carer gender or patient gender (in both uni- and multi-factor analyses).


Conclusively, the findings highlight the importance of developing tailored programs to systematically assist carers who are supporting patients through the early stages of cancer treatment.

title: Glucose Sensing in L Cells: A Primary Cell Study
text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is an intestinal hormone that stimulates insulin secretion and improves glucose levels in type 2 diabetes. Currently available GLP-1-based treatments are limited by our lack of understanding of the underlying physiology of GLP-1 production in the intestine. To address this, we generated transgenic mice with L cells expressing a fluorescent protein, allowing us to study the characteristics of primary L cells using electrophysiology, fluorescence calcium imaging, and expression analysis. Our findings revealed that individual L cells are electrically excitable and respond to glucose, with sensitivity to the glucose stimulus being regulated by sodium glucose cotransporter 1 and ATP-sensitive K(+) channels. These pathways are consistent with their high expression levels in purified L cells, as revealed by quantitative RT-PCR. This approach has opened up new avenues for exploring the physiology and therapeutic potential of GLP-1 production in the intestine.

title: Total atherosclerotic burden by whole body magnetic resonance angiography predicts major adverse cardiovascular events.
text:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of the present study was to investigate the relationship between the Total Atherosclerotic Score (TAS), a measurement of the overall atherosclerotic burden of the arterial tree obtained through whole body magnetic resonance angiography (WBMRA), and the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), which includes cardiac death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and/or coronary revascularization. The study hypothesized that TAS would predict MACE.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, 305 randomly selected 70-year-old individuals (47% women) underwent WBMRA. The atherosclerotic burden of each subject was evaluated, and those with TAS values > 0 (i.e., atherosclerotic changes present) were found in 68% of the subjects. During a mean follow-up period of 4.8 years, MACE occurred in 25 subjects (8.2%). Adjusting for multiple risk factors, TAS was found to be significantly associated with MACE (odds ratio [OR] 8.86 for any degree of vessel lumen abnormality, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.14-69.11, p = 0.037). Additionally, the addition of TAS to the Framingham risk score (FRS) improved discrimination and reclassification, as evidenced by a rise in the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve from 0.681 to 0.750 (p = 0.0421).
CONCLUSION: In a population-based sample of 70-year-old men and women, WBMRA-derived TAS was found to predict MACE independently of major cardiovascular risk factors. These findings suggest that TAS may serve as a valuable tool in identifying individuals at high risk of MACE and informing personalized prevention and treatment strategies.

title: Regulation of ADMP and BMP2/4/7 at Opposite Embryonic Poles Generates a Self-Regulating Morphogenetic Field
text:
Embryonic self-regulation, the ability of an embryo to control its own development, is a complex process that involves the establishment of a morphogenetic field. This field is established through the interaction of various signaling molecules, including ADMP and BMP2/4/7. Our research has shown that the quadruple knockdown of ADMP and BMP2/4/7 in Xenopus embryos leads to the loss of self-regulation, resulting in ubiquitous neural induction throughout the ectoderm.
We have discovered that ADMP transcription in the Spemann organizer is activated at low BMP levels, and when ventral BMP2/4/7 signals are depleted, Admp expression increases, allowing for self-regulation. ADMP has BMP-like activity and signals via the ALK-2 receptor, but it is unable to signal dorsally due to inhibition by Chordin. The ventral BMP antagonists Sizzled and Bambi further refine the pattern.
Our experiments have also shown that both poles serve as signaling centers that can induce histotypic differentiation over considerable distances. We conclude that dorsal and ventral BMP signals and their extracellular antagonists, which are expressed under opposing transcriptional regulation, provide a molecular mechanism for embryonic self-regulation.
In summary, our research has shed light on the complex interplay of signaling molecules and their role in embryonic self-regulation. The establishment of a morphogenetic field is a crucial aspect of embryonic development, and our findings provide a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms that control this process.

title: Genetic control of mosquitoes.
text: Genetics may offer novel, species-specific, and environmentally friendly approaches to mosquito control through genetic modification. Genetic control strategies aim to either suppress target populations or introduce a harm-reducing trait that is not present in the wild. These approaches vary significantly in their properties, particularly between self-limiting strategies, which have a limited persistence, and self-sustaining strategies, which are designed to persist indefinitely within the target population and may spread to other populations. Several genetic modification techniques are currently under development, and initial field trials have been successful.

title: Colorectal Cancers from Distinct Ancestral Populations Show Variations in BRAF Mutation Frequency
text: Recent studies have shown that the frequency of somatic oncogenic mutations may vary among different ancestral populations for certain types of cancer. To investigate the frequency of key driver alterations in colorectal cancer, we used a high-throughput genotyping platform (OncoMap) to analyze 385 mutations across 33 known cancer genes in colorectal cancer DNA from 83 Asian, 149 Black, and 195 White patients. Our findings revealed that Asian patients had fewer canonical oncogenic mutations in the genes tested (60% vs Black 79% (P = 0.011) and White 77% (P = 0.015)), and that BRAF mutations occurred at a higher frequency in White patients (17% vs Asian 4% (P = 0.004) and Black 7% (P = 0.014)). These results suggest that using genomic approaches to identify the unique ancestral determinants present in different patient populations may lead to more effective and personalized treatments for colorectal cancer.

title: Direct neuronal reprogramming: learning from and for development.
text: The identification of key signaling pathways and transcriptional programs that direct neuronal diversity during development has made significant progress. In this Review, we explore how this knowledge has been used to successfully reprogram various cell types into a wide range of functional neurons. We discuss the extent to which direct neuronal reprogramming mimics embryonic development and the unique barriers to reprogramming that may arise due to a cell's developmental history. Finally, we examine a recently proposed model for cell specification, the 'Cook Islands' model, and evaluate its suitability based on recent findings from the direct reprogramming field.

title: Cell fusion hypothesis of the cancer stem cell.
text: Recent breakthroughs in cancer research have led to the discovery of tumor cells exhibiting stem cell-like properties, known as cancer stem cells (CSCs). CSCs are a rare subset of cells within the tumor mass that have the unique ability to initiate and sustain the growth of a diverse range of tumors. Despite significant progress, the origin of CSCs remains unclear and is likely to be cancer-specific. One intriguing theory is that CSCs may arise from the fusion of stem cells and differentiated cells, a mechanism that has the potential to explain the multifaceted roles of cell fusion in cancer development and progression. This hypothesis adds a valuable functional component to our understanding of the generation and maintenance of CSCs.

title: Antidepressant fluoxetine enhances glucocorticoid receptor function in vitro by modulating membrane steroid transporters.
text: 1. Incubation of LMCAT fibroblast cells with antidepressants enhances glucocorticoid receptor (GR)-mediated gene transcription when dexamethasone or cortisol are present, but not when corticosterone is present. We have shown that antidepressants achieve this by inhibiting the LMCAT cell membrane steroid transporter, which is similar to the multidrug resistance P-glycoprotein, and increasing the intracellular concentrations of dexamethasone or cortisol. However, previous experiments with the antidepressant fluoxetine in the presence of dexamethasone produced negative results (Pariante et al., 2001). 2. We have since re-examined the effects of fluoxetine on GR-mediated gene transcription in the presence of dexamethasone and compared its effects on GR-mediated gene transcription in the presence of cortisol and corticosterone. We have also examined the intracellular accumulation of radioactive cortisol and corticosterone. Additionally, we have examined the effects of fluoxetine on inhibition of P-glycoprotein activity in Caco-2 cells. 3. Our results show that fluoxetine (1-10 micro M) enhances GR-mediated gene transcription in the presence of dexamethasone and cortisol (by 140-170%) but not of corticosterone, and increases the intracellular accumulation of (3)H-cortisol (by 5-15%) but not of (3)H-corticosterone. Fluoxetine (10 micro M) also induces approximately 30% inhibition of PGP activity in Caco-2 cells. 4. Our findings suggest that antidepressants, including fluoxetine, inhibit membrane steroid transporters, similar to the multidrug resistance P-glycoprotein.

title: Physician knowledge levels and barriers to coronary risk prevention in women: survey results from the Women and Heart Disease Physician Education Initiative.
text: BACKGROUND Few studies have investigated whether physician knowledge, attitudes, or practice patterns may contribute to gender disparities in the primary prevention of coronary heart disease (CHD), including among physicians who treat the largest number of reproductive-age women, obstetricians and gynecologists (OB/GYNs). To identify barriers to the provision of recommended coronary risk factor therapies in women, we surveyed internists and OB/GYNs who attended Grand Rounds presentations developed for the New York State Women and Heart Disease Physician Education Initiative. This program aimed to improve screening and management of coronary risk factors in women. Participants were asked to complete a 7-minute questionnaire. RESULTS The mean age of the 529 respondents was 40.3 years (standard deviation = 12.3), with 75.1% of the participants being internists (n=378) and 42.7% (n=226) being women. Physicians correctly answered 71.5% of the 13 questions assessing their knowledge of coronary risk prevention (range, 4-13). Almost one-third of internists and half of the OB/GYNs were unaware that tobacco use is the leading cause of myocardial infarction in young women. For patients who smoked tobacco, only two-thirds of internists and 55.4% of OB/GYNs reported suggesting a quit date (p=0.007). After controlling for covariates, physicians who did not perceive time as a barrier were more likely to discuss smoking cessation (odds ratio=1.7 [1.1-2.7]). CONCLUSIONS Our findings suggest that time was perceived as a barrier to implementing risk prevention strategies among the internists and OB/GYNs surveyed. These physicians also underestimated the impact of tobacco use as a risk factor for CHD in young women. To address gender disparities in CHD prevention, both specialties require time-efficient educational programs that take into account specialty differences.

title: Separation of mother and daughter cells.
text:
Publisher Summary:
The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (S. cerevisiae) exhibits asymmetric cell division during vegetative growth. The position where the bud forms determines the plane of cell division. This chapter provides detailed protocols for separating and isolating mother and daughter cells, which have been used by researchers to study aging, bud site selection, and other aspects of asymmetric cell division. The protocols include methods for performing life span analysis through micromanipulation and large-scale collection of old cells.
At various stages of the life cycle, it can be challenging to distinguish between mothers and daughters due to the similarity in size between daughter cells and their mothers. Additionally, mother cells often bud again before their daughter cells form their first bud. To isolate virgin daughter cells from mother cells, a "baby machine" technique is employed, where mother cells are attached to a membrane and allowed to divide. Daughter cells from these attached cells are continuously eluted by washing the membrane. This method allows for effective isolation of daughter cells from mother cells, but not for recovering old mothers.

title: Postnatal development of adipocyte cellularity in the normal rat.
text: Several studies have demonstrated that the number of adipocytes remains stable in mature humans and certain species of rodents. While methods such as histometry and Coulter counting can measure the number of new cells entering the adipose depot, these methods cannot distinguish between the expansion of existing adipocytes and the synthesis of new adipocytes. The present study employs in vivo injection of [(3)H]thymidine to show that the synthesis of new adipocytes continues in the Sprague-Dawley rat after birth, but ceases before sexual maturity. Additionally, during the second and third postnatal weeks, a "bed" of preadipocytes is synthesized, which may take up to 30 days to mature into mature adipocytes.

title: Withdrawal Symptoms after Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor Discontinuation: A Systematic Review
text:
Background: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely prescribed in medical practice, yet their withdrawal symptoms have been associated with a range of clinically unappreciated symptoms.
Methods: Following the PRISMA guidelines, a systematic review of the literature was conducted using the following search terms: 'withdrawal symptoms', 'withdrawal syndrome', 'discontinuation syndrome', and 'discontinuation symptoms', in combination with 'SSRI', 'serotonin', 'antidepressant', 'paroxetine', 'fluoxetine', 'sertraline', 'fluvoxamine', 'citalopram', and 'escitalopram'. Electronic databases including CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, PubMed, and Web-of-Science were searched from inception to July 2014.
Results: A total of 15 randomized controlled studies, 4 open trials, 4 retrospective investigations, and 38 case reports were identified. The prevalence of the withdrawal syndrome varied across studies, and its estimation was hindered by a lack of case identification in many studies. Typically, symptoms occur within a few days of drug discontinuation and last for a few weeks, with gradual tapering. However, variations are possible, including late onset and/or longer persistence of disturbances. Symptoms may be easily misidentified as signs of impending relapse.
Conclusions: Clinicians should add SSRIs to the list of drugs that can induce withdrawal symptoms upon discontinuation, along with benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and other psychotropic drugs. The term 'discontinuation syndrome' used to describe SSRI withdrawal symptoms is inadequate and should be replaced with 'withdrawal syndrome'.

title: Sphingosine Kinase 1 Regulates the Akt/FOXO3a/Bim Pathway and Contributes to Apoptosis Resistance in Glioma Cells
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the mechanism by which Sphingosine kinase-1 (SPHK1) protects glioma cells from undergoing apoptosis. We found that dysregulation of SPHK1 leads to a decrease in glioma cells' sensitivity to apoptosis both in vitro and in vivo. Our mechanistic study revealed that overexpression of SPHK1 leads to downregulation of the pro-apoptotic protein Bim, and alterations in the transcriptional level of Bim in glioma cells. We also found a correlation between SPHK1 and Bim expression in primary glioma specimens. Moreover, we discovered that increasing SPHK1 expression in glioma cells leads to elevated Akt activity and inactivation of FOXO3a, which in turn results in the downregulation of Bim. A pharmacological approach revealed that these effects of SPHK1 are dependent on the PI3K pathway. Furthermore, we found that the effects of SPHK1 on the Akt/FOXO3a/Bim pathway can be reversed by SPHK1-specific RNA interference or SPHK1 inhibitors. Collectively, our results suggest that the regulation of the Akt/FOXO3a/Bim pathway may be a novel mechanism by which SPHK1 contributes to glioma tumorigenesis.

title: COX-2 and survivin are overexpressed and positively correlated in endometrial carcinoma.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the expression of survivin and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) in endometrial adenocarcinoma (EC) and their potential correlations with classical prognostic factors. Additionally, this study aimed to explore the possible relationship between these two genes and their impact on overall survival.
Methods:
An archival tissue sample of 50 EC, 30 endometrial hyperplasia, and 20 proliferative endometrium were immunohistochemically analyzed for survivin and COX-2 expression. The expression of these genes was compared between the different tissue types, and their correlation was analyzed.
Results:
Both survivin and COX-2 were overexpressed in hyperplasia and EC cases compared to proliferative endometrium, with statistical significance observed (p=0.01, p=0.02, respectively). Among EC cases, survivin and COX-2 were strongly positive in 38 (76%) and 30 (60%) patients, respectively. Furthermore, a positive correlation was found between survivin and COX-2 expression (p=0.0001, r=0.46). Neither survivin nor COX-2 expression was correlated with classical prognostic factors of endometrial carcinoma such as myometrial invasion, grade, or lymph node metastasis (p>0.05). Additionally, neither COX-2 nor survivin had an impact on overall survival (p>0.05).


Conclusion:
Both survivin and COX-2 are overexpressed in EC, and they seem to be early events in the occurrence of EC. Moreover, protein products of these two genes are positively correlated. COX-2 and survivin might share a common molecular pathway or enhance each other's actions in the developmental pathway of EC. Further investigation into the molecular basis of this relationship is warranted in endometrial carcinogenesis.

title: Structural plasticity of the adult brain: how animal models help us understand brain changes in depression and systemic disorders related to depression
text: The brain processes experiences and translates them into behavioral and physiological responses to promote adaptation through a mechanism called "allostasis." Stressful events, which are unexpected or threatening, trigger a cascade of chemical mediators, including cortisol and adrenaline from the adrenal glands, hormones, neurotransmitters, and immune system cytokines and chemokines. The brain's amygdala and hippocampus play crucial roles in identifying stressors and determining appropriate responses. The hippocampus, involved in memory formation, expresses receptors that allow it to respond to glucocorticoid hormones in the blood. Chronic stress can lead to atrophy of the hippocampus in psychiatric disorders, increased excitability, decreased dendritic branching, and reduced neuron number in the dentate gyrus. The amygdala, important for emotional memories, becomes hyperactive in post-traumatic stress disorder and depressive illness. In animal models of stress, there is evidence of nerve cell growth and hypertrophy in the amygdala. The changes in the brain after acute and chronic stressors resemble those seen in the metabolic, cardiovascular, and immune systems, with short-term adaptation followed by long-term damage, such as atherosclerosis, fat deposition, obesity, bone demineralization, and impaired immune function. The accumulation of this long-term damage, known as allostatic load, is also present in major depressive illness and may be a factor in other chronic anxiety and mood disorders.

title: CCR7 provides localized access to IL-2 and defines homeostatically distinct regulatory T cell subsets
text: Immune tolerance and activation rely on precise regulation of the number and function of immunosuppressive Foxp3(+) regulatory T (Treg) cells, and the importance of IL-2 in maintaining tolerance and preventing autoimmunity is well established. However, the homeostatic requirements for IL-2 among specific populations of peripheral Treg cells remain poorly understood. Our study shows that IL-2 selectively maintains a population of quiescent CD44(lo)CD62L(hi) Treg cells that have access to paracrine IL-2 produced in the T cell zones of secondary lymphoid tissues due to their expression of the chemokine receptor CCR7. In contrast, CD44(hi)CD62L(lo)CCR7(lo) Treg cells that reside in nonlymphoid tissues do not access IL-2-rich regions in vivo and are insensitive to IL-2 blockade; instead, their maintenance depends on continued signaling through the co-stimulatory receptor ICOS (inducible co-stimulator). Therefore, we have identified a fundamental homeostatic subdivision in Treg cell populations based on their localization, providing an integrated framework for understanding how Treg cell abundance and function are regulated by distinct signals in different tissue environments.

title: Assessing sequence comparison methods with reliable structurally identified distant evolutionary relationships.
text: In a study published in the Journal of Molecular Biology in 1995, the performance of various pairwise sequence comparison methods was evaluated using proteins with known reliable relationships based on their structures and functions, as documented in the SCOP database [Murzin, A. G., Brenner, S. E., Hubbard, T., & Chothia, C. (1995) J. Mol. Biol. 247, 536-540]. The methods tested included BLAST [Altschul, S. F., Gish, W., Miller, W., Myers, E. W., & Lipman, D. J. (1990) J. Mol. Biol. 215, 403-410], WU-BLAST2 [Altschul, S. F., & Gish, W. (1996) Methods Enzymol. 266, 460-480], FASTA [Pearson, W. R., & Lipman, D. J. (1988) Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 85, 2444-2448], and SSEARCH [Smith, T. F., & Waterman, M. S. (1981) J. Mol. Biol. 147, 195-197]. The study found that the error rate of all algorithms was significantly reduced when using statistical scores to evaluate matches rather than percentage identity or raw scores. The statistical scores of SSEARCH and FASTA were found to be reliable, with the number of false positives found in the tests agreeing well with the reported scores. However, the P-values reported by BLAST and WU-BLAST2 were found to exaggerate significance by orders of magnitude. SSEARCH, FASTA, and WU-BLAST2 performed best, and were capable of detecting almost all relationships between proteins with sequence identities greater than 30%. However, for more distantly related proteins, the methods performed less well, with only half of the relationships between proteins with 20-30% identity being found. The study concluded that while pairwise sequence comparison methods can identify some relationships between proteins, many homologs have low sequence similarity, and therefore, most distant relationships cannot be detected by any single method.

title: Evaluation of a mental health outreach service for homeless families.
text:
Objective:
To characterize the demographic and clinical features of homeless children and families encountered by the mental health outreach service (MHOS), evaluate the short-term psychosocial functioning of children and parents following intervention, and assess the perceptions and satisfaction of service users.
Methods:
Twenty-seven children from 23 families receiving MHOS and 27 children from 23 families residing in other hostels without access to the service were included in the study. The MHOS was provided by a clinical nurse specialist with expertise in child mental health, who offered assessment, brief treatment of mental health disorders in children, liaison with agencies, and training of homeless center staff.
Results:
Children in the experimental group showed a significantly higher decrease in Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) total scores. Receiving the intervention was the strongest predictor of improvement in SDQ total scores. There was no significant impact on parental mental health (General Health Questionnaire) scores. Homeless families and staff expressed high satisfaction with the MHOS.
Conclusion:
This MHOS for homeless families is an innovative intervention that addresses the complex and multiple needs of a vulnerable population unable to access mainstream mental health services. While the primary objective was to improve child mental health problems, the service adapted to meet social and practical needs of families in addition to its clinical role.

title: Evaluation of individuals with pulmonary nodules: when is it lung cancer? Diagnosis and management of lung cancer, 3rd ed: American College of Chest Physicians evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
text:
Objective:
The purpose of this article is to update and generate new evidence-based recommendations for the evaluation and management of individuals with solid and nonsolid pulmonary nodules.
Methods:
We updated prior literature reviews, synthesized the available evidence, and formulated recommendations using the methods outlined in the "Methodology for Development of Guidelines for Lung Cancer" in the American College of Chest Physicians Lung Cancer Guidelines, 3rd ed.

Results:
We developed recommendations for evaluating solid pulmonary nodules greater than 8 mm in diameter, solid nodules equal to or smaller than 8 mm in diameter, and subsolid nodules. The recommendations emphasize the importance of assessing the probability of malignancy, the utility of imaging tests, the need to weigh the benefits and harms of different management strategies (nonsurgical biopsy, surgical resection, and surveillance with chest CT imaging), and the significance of eliciting patient preferences.

Conclusions:
Individuals with pulmonary nodules should be evaluated and managed by estimating the probability of malignancy, performing imaging tests to better characterize the lesions, evaluating the risks associated with various management alternatives, and eliciting their preferences for management.

title: AgDscam, a Hypervariable Immunoglobulin Domain-Containing Receptor of the       Anopheles gambiae Innate Immune System
text: The activation of the insect innate immune system relies on a limited number of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) that can recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). In a recent study, we discovered a novel role for an alternatively spliced hypervariable immunoglobulin domain-encoding gene, Dscam, in generating a diverse range of PRRs involved in immune defense in the malaria vector Anopheles gambiae. The Anopheles gambiae Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule gene, AgDscam, has a complex genome organization with 101 exons that can produce over 31,000 potential alternative splice forms with different combinations of adhesive domains and interaction specificities. AgDscam responds to infection by producing pathogen challenge-specific splice form repertoires, and transient silencing of AgDscam compromises the mosquito's resistance to infections with bacteria and the malaria parasite Plasmodium. AgDscam mediates phagocytosis of bacteria through specific splice form-dependent mechanisms, and we found that it is a hypervariable PRR of the A. gambiae innate immune system.

title: Enterovirus-induced gene expression profile is critical for human pancreatic islet destruction
text: The onset of type 1 diabetes has been linked to viral infections, particularly those that induce inflammatory responses, beta cell destruction, and the release of beta cell autoantigens. The viral capabilities to induce beta cell death and the nature of the immune responses triggered by these infections are crucial factors in determining which viruses are diabetogenic. We hypothesized that enterovirus infection leads to a unique gene expression profile in primary human pancreatic islets, which ultimately results in islet destruction. To investigate this, we analyzed the global gene expression and secreted cytokine profiles induced by lytic or benign enterovirus infections using DNA microarrays and virus strains isolated from patients at the clinical onset of type 1 diabetes or capable of causing a diabetes-like condition in mice. Our findings revealed that the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes (IL-1-α, IL-1-β, and TNF-α) correlated with the lytic potential of the virus. Additionally, we detected temporally increasing gene expression levels of double-stranded RNA recognition receptors, antiviral molecules, cytokines, and chemokines for all studied virus strains. Notably, lytic coxsackievirus B5 (CBV-5)-DS infection also downregulated genes involved in glycolysis and insulin secretion. These results suggest a distinct, virus-strain-specific gene expression pattern leading to pancreatic islet destruction and pro-inflammatory effects after enterovirus infection. However, neither viral replication nor cytotoxic cytokine production alone are sufficient to induce necrotic cell death. Rather, the combined effect of these and possibly cellular energy depletion may contribute to the enterovirus-induced necrosis of islets.

title: Islet1 derivatives in the heart are of both neural crest and second heart field origin.
text:
RATIONALE: Islet1 (Isl1) has been proposed as a marker of cardiac progenitor cells derived from the second heart field and is used to identify and purify these progenitors from murine and human specimens for ex vivo expansion. However, the exclusive use of Isl1 as a second heart field marker is contingent upon its exclusion from other cardiac lineages, such as neural crest.
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether Isl1 is expressed by cardiac neural crest.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We employed an intersectional fate-mapping system using the RC::FrePe allele, which reports dual Flpe and Cre recombination. Combining Isl1(Cre/+), a second heart field driver, with Wnt1::Flpe, a neural crest driver, and Rc::FrePe revealed that some Isl1 derivatives in the cardiac outflow tract originate from Wnt1-expressing neural crest progenitors. In contrast, no overlap was observed between Wnt1-derived neural crest and an alternative second heart field driver, Mef2c-AHF-Cre.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings indicate that Isl1 is not exclusively expressed in second heart field progenitors but also labels cardiac neural crest. The overlap of Isl1 and Wnt1 lineages within the heart highlights a limitation in using Isl1 as an exclusive marker for second heart field cardiac progenitor cells and suggests that some Isl1-expressing progenitor cells derived from embryos, embryonic stem cultures, or induced pluripotent stem cultures may have a neural crest origin.

title: Review of the secondary injury theory of acute spinal cord trauma with emphasis on vascular mechanisms.
text:
In patients with spinal cord injuries, the primary or mechanical trauma rarely causes complete transection, despite resulting in complete functional loss. However, biochemical and pathological changes in the cord can worsen after the initial injury. To explain these observations, the concept of secondary injury has evolved, with numerous pathophysiological mechanisms proposed. This review focuses on vascular mechanisms, which have been extensively studied using various animal models of acute spinal cord injury.
Several systemic and local vascular effects have been identified as key mechanisms in the etiology of secondary injury. These include:
1. Hypotension and reduced cardiac output: These systemic effects can lead to decreased blood flow to the spinal cord, exacerbating the initial injury.
2. Loss of autoregulation in the injured segment of the spinal cord: The spinal cord's ability to regulate blood flow is disrupted after injury, leading to a significant reduction in microcirculation.
3. Reduction of the microcirculation in both gray and white matter: The microcirculation is particularly affected in hemorrhagic regions and adjacent zones, leading to a significant decrease in blood flow to the spinal cord.
4. Dose-dependent reduction of spinal cord blood flow: The severity of the injury determines the degree of reduction in spinal cord blood flow, which worsens over time after the initial injury.
5. Early hemorrhagic necrosis leading to major infarction at the injury site: Histological changes occur early after injury and can lead to significant tissue damage.

These vascular effects can be treated with various interventions, including:

1. Restoration of systemic normotension with volume expansion or vasopressors: This can improve blood flow to the spinal cord and counteract the effects of posttraumatic ischemia.
2. Improvement of spinal cord blood flow with dopamine, steroids, nimodipine, or volume expansion: These interventions can help restore blood flow to the spinal cord and improve functional outcomes.
3. Combination of nimodipine and volume expansion: This combination has been shown to improve posttraumatic spinal cord blood flow and functional outcomes, as measured by evoked potentials.

In conclusion, the concept of secondary injury has evolved to explain the observed phenomena in patients with spinal cord injuries. Vascular mechanisms, particularly posttraumatic ischemia, play a crucial role in the etiology of secondary injury. These mechanisms can be counteracted with various interventions, improving blood flow to the spinal cord and functional outcomes. Further research is needed to fully understand the pathophysiology of secondary injury and to develop effective treatments for this devastating condition.

title: Chronophin mediates an ATP-sensing mechanism for cofilin dephosphorylation and neuronal cofilin-actin rod formation.
text: In neurons under stress, actin and its key regulator cofilin are found in large, rod-shaped structures. These inclusions are also present in brains affected by Alzheimer's disease and appear in animal models of neurodegeneration. When neurons experience energy loss or oxidative stress, the pool of cofilin is rapidly dephosphorylated before being assembled into rod-shaped structures. While these events suggest a role for phosphatases in cofilin rod formation, the underlying mechanism has remained unclear. We have discovered an ATP-sensitive interaction between the cofilin phosphatase chronophin (CIN) and the chaperone hsp90, which forms a biosensor that regulates cofilin/actin rod formation. Our findings suggest a model whereby reduced interactions between CIN and hsp90 during ATP depletion enhance CIN-dependent cofilin dephosphorylation and subsequent rod assembly, providing a mechanism for the formation of pathological actin/cofilin aggregates during neurodegenerative energy flux.

title: Renal considerations in angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor therapy: a statement for healthcare professionals from the Council on the Kidney in Cardiovascular Disease and the Council for High Blood Pressure Research of the American Heart Association.
text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are now one of the most commonly used classes of antihypertensive drugs, with extended use in the long-term management of patients with congestive heart failure (CHF), diabetic and nondiabetic nephropathies. While ACE inhibitor therapy typically improves renal blood flow (RBF) and sodium excretion rates in CHF and reduces the rate of progressive renal injury in chronic renal disease, it can also be associated with a syndrome of "functional renal insufficiency" and/or hyperkalemia, leading to acute renal failure (ARF). This form of ARF most commonly develops shortly after initiation of ACE inhibitor therapy but can occur after months or years of therapy, even in the absence of prior adverse effects. The risk of ARF is higher when renal perfusion pressure cannot be sustained due to substantial decreases in mean arterial pressure (MAP) or when glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is highly dependent on angiotensin II (Ang II). Conditions that predict an adverse hemodynamic effect of ACE inhibitors in patients with CHF include preexisting hypotension and low cardiac filling pressures. The GFR is particularly dependent on Ang II during extracellular fluid (ECF) volume depletion, high-grade bilateral renal artery stenosis, or stenosis of a dominant or single kidney, as in a renal transplant recipient. Understanding the pathophysiological mechanisms and common risk factors for ACE inhibitor-induced functional ARF is crucial, as preventive strategies exist, and if effectively used, they may permit broader use of these compounds. Under normal physiological conditions, renal autoregulation adjusts renal vascular resistance, maintaining constant RBF and GFR over a wide range of MAPs. The intrinsic renal autoregulation mechanism is modulated by Ang II and the sympathetic nervous system. When renal perfusion pressure falls (as in hypotension or decreased Ang II), renal vascular resistance increases, reducing RBF and GFR.

title: Greater clinical benefit of more intensive oral antiplatelet therapy with prasugrel in patients with diabetes mellitus in the trial to assess improvement in therapeutic outcomes by optimizing platelet inhibition with prasugrel-Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 38.
text: In this study, we compared the effects of the antiplatelet drug prasugrel and clopidogrel on cardiovascular outcomes in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM). We found that prasugrel was associated with a significant reduction in cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, among patients with DM, compared to clopidogrel. This reduction in events was observed in both patients who were and were not taking insulin. However, there was no significant increase in major bleeding events with prasugrel in patients with DM. These findings suggest that prasugrel may be of particular benefit to patients with DM, as it provides more intensive oral antiplatelet therapy without an observed increase in bleeding risk.

title: Kinetics of early T cell receptor signaling regulate the pathway of lytic granule delivery to the secretory domain.
text: Cytolytic granules are involved in the killing of virus-infected cells by cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Our findings reveal that these granules can travel along either a short or long path to reach the secretory domain. Both paths involve the same intracellular molecular events, which have distinct spatial and temporal arrangements and are regulated by the kinetics of calcium-mediated signaling. Rapid signaling leads to the swift concentration of granules near the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) and subsequent delivery to the secretory domain, the shortest path. In contrast, indolent signaling results in late recruitment of granules that move along microtubules to the periphery of the synapse and then move tangentially to fuse at the outer edge of the secretory domain, a longer path. The short pathway is associated with faster granule release and more efficient killing, indicating that the kinetics of early signaling regulate the quality of the T cell cytolytic response.

title: Sirtuin-1 is a nutrient-dependent modulator of inflammation
text: Obesity is frequently accompanied by a host of comorbidities, including type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and atherosclerosis, and inflammation may play a role in their pathogenesis. However, the cellular mechanisms that connect nutrient sensing to inflammation are not yet fully understood. The deacetylase enzyme sirtuin-1 (SirT1), which is activated by energy depletion, has been shown to play a crucial role in the mammalian response to fasting and has more recently been implicated in the repression of inflammation. Interestingly, SirT1 mRNA and protein expression are decreased in obese rodent and human white adipose tissue, and experimental reduction of SirT1 in adipocytes and macrophages leads to low-grade inflammation that resembles that observed in obesity. These findings suggest that suppression of SirT1 during overnutrition may be a key factor in the development of obesity-related inflammation. This effect is likely due to multiple mechanisms, including direct deacetylation of the transcription factor NFκB and chromatin remodeling at inflammatory gene promoters. In this study, we investigate the impact of diet-induced obesity on SirT1 expression in macrophages, which are important contributors to the development of metabolic inflammation. Our findings suggest that SirT1 may serve as a common mechanism by which cells sense nutrient availability and modulate inflammatory signaling pathways in accordance with the organism's energy status.

title: A culture-independent sequence-based metagenomics approach to the investigation of an outbreak of Shiga-toxigenic Escherichia coli O104:H4.
text:
The Importance of Metagenomics in Outbreak Detection and Management
Traditional culture-based diagnosis can be a challenging and time-consuming process, particularly when dealing with novel or unknown strains. In the context of outbreaks of diarrheal disease, metagenomics offers a promising solution as an open-ended clinical discovery platform. By directly sequencing DNA from microbiologically complex samples, metagenomics can identify and characterize bacterial strains without the need for laboratory culture.
In a retrospective investigation, we analyzed 45 fecal samples collected during the 2011 outbreak of Shiga-toxigenic Escherichia coli (STEC) O104:H4 in Germany. We used high-throughput sequencing to obtain genome sequence data for the purposes of identification and characterization of the outbreak strain and other pathogens.
Our results demonstrate the potential of metagenomics as a culture-independent approach for outbreak detection and management. During phase 1, we developed a de novo assembly approach to obtain a draft genome of the outbreak strain. In phase 2, we determined the depth of coverage of the outbreak strain genome in each sample, and in phase 3, we compared sequences from each sample with sequences from known bacteria to identify pathogens other than the outbreak strain.
We recovered genome sequence data for the outbreak strain and identified other pathogens, including Clostridium difficile, Campylobacter jejuni, Campylobacter concisus, and Salmonella enterica. While challenges remain, such as improving diagnostic sensitivity, speeding up and simplifying workflows, and reducing costs, our findings suggest that metagenomics has the potential to revolutionize outbreak detection and management.

title: Biomarkers of endothelial dysfunction and risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text:
In this study, the authors investigated whether elevated levels of biomarkers reflecting endothelial dysfunction (E-selectin, intercellular adhesion molecule 1 [ICAM-1], and vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 [VCAM-1]) in nondiabetic women could predict the development of type 2 diabetes. The study was a prospective, nested case-control design within the Nurses' Health Study, an ongoing US study initiated in 1976. The authors analyzed blood samples from 737 women who developed incident diabetes by 2000 and 785 controls matched for age, fasting status, and race. The main outcome measure was the risk of confirmed clinically diagnosed type 2 diabetes based on baseline levels of the biomarkers.
The results showed that baseline levels of E-selectin, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 were significantly higher among cases than among controls. Elevated levels of E-selectin and ICAM-1 predicted incident diabetes in logistic regression models adjusted for body mass index (BMI), family history of diabetes, smoking, diet score, alcohol intake, activity index, and postmenopausal hormone use. The adjusted relative risks for incident diabetes in the top quintile vs the bottom quintiles were 5.43 for E-selectin, 3.56 for ICAM-1, and 1.12 for VCAM-1. Adjustment for waist circumference instead of BMI or further adjustment for baseline levels of C-reactive protein, fasting insulin, and hemoglobin A(1c) or exclusion of cases diagnosed during the first 4 years of follow-up did not alter these associations.
The study concluded that endothelial dysfunction predicts type 2 diabetes in women independent of other known risk factors, including obesity and subclinical inflammation.

title: Nrf2 protects human alveolar epithelial cells against injury induced by influenza A virus
text:
Background: Influenza A virus (IAV) infection primarily affects respiratory epithelial cells, leading to a range of clinical outcomes from mild upper respiratory infections to severe pneumonia. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of lung antioxidant defense systems in protecting against IAV-induced injury. Nuclear factor-erythroid 2 related factor 2 (Nrf2) is a crucial regulator of antioxidant gene expression, and its activation has been shown to protect against oxidative stress and inflammation.
Methods: We isolated alveolar type II (ATII) cells and alveolar macrophages (AM) from human lungs not suitable for transplantation and used them to study IAV infection. In some experiments, ATII cells were transdifferentiated into alveolar type I-like (ATI-like) cells. We analyzed PR8 virus production, influenza A nucleoprotein levels, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and the expression of antiviral genes in infected cells. Immunocytofluorescence was used to detect Nrf2 translocation, and western blotting was used to detect Nrf2, heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), and caspase 1 and 3 cleavage. We also examined the ability of AM to ingest PR8 virus-infected apoptotic ATII cells through efferocytosis, as well as cytokine levels, glutathione levels, necrosis, and apoptosis in infected cells. Additionally, we used adenovirus Nrf2 (AdNrf2) or Nrf2 small interfering RNA (siRNA) to overexpress or knockdown Nrf2, respectively.
Results: Our results showed that IAV infection induced oxidative stress, cytotoxicity, and apoptosis in ATI-like and ATII cells. We found that AM can ingest PR8 virus-infected apoptotic ATII cells through efferocytosis, but not viable cells. IAV infection increased ROS production, Nrf2, HO-1, Mx1, and OAS1 expression, and Nrf2 translocation to the nucleus. Nrf2 knockdown with siRNA sensitized ATI-like cells and ATII cells to injury induced by IAV, while overexpression of Nrf2 with AdNrf2 protected these cells. Furthermore, overexpression of Nrf2 followed by IAV infection decreased virus replication, influenza A nucleoprotein expression, antiviral response, and oxidative stress. However, AdNrf2 did not increase interferon-λ1 (IL-29) levels.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that IAV infection causes alveolar epithelial cell injury, and that Nrf2 protects these cells from the cytopathic effects of IAV by increasing the expression of antioxidant genes. Identifying the pathways involved in protecting cells from injury during influenza infection may be crucial for developing new therapeutic strategies.

title: Dynamics in the plasma membrane: how to combine fluidity and order.
text:
Cell membranes are remarkable supramolecular structures that not only act as a barrier between compartments but are also the site of numerous chemical reactions crucial to a cell's survival and function. In this review, we will delve into the molecular dynamics and mosaic organization of the plasma membrane, which are believed to have significant functional implications.
To begin, we will provide an overview of the basic concepts of Brownian diffusion and lipid domain formation in model membranes. We will then trace the evolution of ideas and techniques in this field, highlighting key discoveries made through the use of fluorescent labeling and imaging techniques to observe the dynamic processes at play in membrane structure and assembly.
One of the most significant findings in this field is the impact of lateral diffusion on cell signal transduction. We will provide examples of how lateral diffusion affects the transmission of signals across the membrane and outline some of the methodological challenges that must be addressed in order to fully understand this phenomenon.
Finally, we will discuss some of the future research directions in this field, including the development of new techniques for studying membrane dynamics and the integration of computational models with experimental data. By continuing to explore the complex dynamics of cell membranes, we can gain a deeper understanding of their role in cellular function and dysfunction, and ultimately develop new strategies for the diagnosis and treatment of diseases.

title: Management of chronic tension-type headache with tricyclic antidepressant medication, stress management therapy, and their combination: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Chronic tension-type headaches are a common and debilitating condition that can be challenging to manage in primary care settings. While behavioral and pharmacological therapies have been shown to be effective in reducing headache frequency and severity, the optimal combination of these therapies for chronic tension-type headaches remains unclear.
To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled trial at two outpatient sites in Ohio from August 1995 to January 1998. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either tricyclic antidepressant medication (amitriptyline or nortriptyline), placebo, stress management therapy (including relaxation and cognitive coping techniques), or a combination of stress management therapy and antidepressant medication.
The primary outcome measures included monthly headache index scores, number of days per month with at least moderate pain, analgesic medication use, and Headache Disability Inventory scores. Our results showed that tricyclic antidepressant medication and stress management therapy each produced larger reductions in headache activity, analgesic medication use, and headache-related disability compared to placebo. However, antidepressant medication yielded more rapid improvements in headache activity. Notably, combined therapy was more likely to produce clinically significant (>/=50%) reductions in headache index scores than antidepressant medication, stress management therapy, or placebo. On other measures, the combined therapy and its component therapies produced similar outcomes.
Our findings suggest that antidepressant medication and stress management therapy are each modestly effective in treating chronic tension-type headaches. However, combining these therapies may improve outcome relative to monotherapy. These results have important implications for the management of chronic tension-type headaches in primary care settings, where both behavioral and pharmacological therapies are commonly used.

title: Maximum likelihood estimates of species trees: how accuracy of phylogenetic inference depends upon the divergence history and sampling design.
text:
The understanding that gene trees, which represent the evolutionary relationships of genetic loci within a species, often disagree with the species tree, which represents the evolutionary relationships of all species in a clade, has led researchers to develop methods that incorporate the inherent stochasticity of genetic processes in the phylogenetic estimation procedure. Recent advances in species-tree estimation methods that consider the retention and sorting of ancestral polymorphism, as well as the actual probabilities of incomplete lineage sorting, are expected to provide a significant improvement over earlier summary-statistic based approaches that discard much of the information content of gene trees. However, these new methods have yet to be tested on truly challenging evolutionary histories, such as those marked by recent rapid speciation, where high levels of incomplete lineage sorting and discord among gene trees are prevalent.
In this study, we test a new maximum-likelihood method that incorporates stochastic models of both nucleotide substitution and lineage sorting for species-tree estimation. Using a simulation approach, we consider a broad range of species-tree topologies under two scenarios representing moderate and severe incomplete lineage sorting. Our results demonstrate that the maximum-likelihood method results in more accurate species trees than a summary-statistic based approach, highlighting the importance of incorporating the information contained in discordant gene trees. Additionally, we find that the shape of the original species tree has a significant impact on the accuracy of the species-tree estimates, with recent speciation events affecting the accuracy of the estimates. Furthermore, we show that sampling effort (number of individuals and/or loci) and sampling design (ratio of individuals to loci) are also important factors affecting the accuracy of species-tree estimates, which is again affected by the relative timing of divergence among species.
While these findings represent significant improvements over current methods, we acknowledge that recent radiations still pose daunting challenges for phylogenetics. Despite the increased sophistication of procedures that incorporate the process of gene lineage coalescence, recent speciation events can lead to high levels of incomplete lineage sorting and discord among gene trees, making it difficult to accurately estimate species relationships. Therefore, further research is needed to develop methods that can effectively handle these challenges and provide more accurate species-tree estimates.

title: Relationship of soft drink consumption to global overweight, obesity, and diabetes: a cross-national analysis of 75 countries.
text:
Objective:
This study aimed to investigate the relationship between soft drink consumption and the prevalence of obesity and diabetes globally.
Methods:
We employed multivariate linear regression to estimate the association between soft drink consumption and overweight, obesity, and diabetes prevalence in 75 countries, controlling for other food groups (cereals, meats, fruits and vegetables, oils, and total calories), income, urbanization, and aging. Data were obtained from the Euromonitor Global Market Information Database, the World Health Organization, and the International Diabetes Federation. Bottled water consumption, which increased parallel to soft drink consumption with per-capita income, served as a natural control group.
Results:
Soft drink consumption globally increased from 9.5 gallons per person per year in 1997 to 11.4 gallons in 2010. A 1% rise in soft drink consumption was associated with an additional 4.8 overweight adults per 100 (adjusted B; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.1, 6.5), 2.3 obese adults per 100 (95% CI = 1.1, 3.5), and 0.3 adults with diabetes per 100 (95% CI = 0.1, 0.8). These findings remained robust in low- and middle-income countries.
Conclusion:
Our study found a significant association between soft drink consumption and the prevalence of overweight, obesity, and diabetes worldwide, including in low- and middle-income countries. These findings suggest that soft drink consumption is a significant risk factor for these global health problems.

title: Extensive translation of circular RNAs driven by N6-methyladenosine
text: Extensive pre-mRNA back-splicing in the human transcriptome generates a diverse range of circular RNAs (circRNAs), yet the biological functions of these circRNAs remain largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most prevalent base modification of RNA, in the translation initiation of circRNAs in human cells. Our findings reveal that m6A promotes efficient translation initiation from circRNAs, with consensus m6A motifs enriched in these RNAs and a single m6A site sufficient to drive translation initiation. This m6A-driven translation requires the initiation factor eIF4G2 and the m6A reader protein YTHDF3, and is modulated by the methyltransferase METTL3/14 and the demethylase FTO. Furthermore, our analyses through polysome profiling, computational prediction, and mass spectrometry reveal that m6A-driven translation of circRNAs is widespread, with hundreds of endogenous circRNAs having translation potential. This study expands the coding landscape of the human transcriptome and suggests a role for circRNA-derived proteins in cellular responses to environmental stress.

title: Simvastatin reduces CD40 expression in an experimental model of early arterialization of saphenous vein graft.
text:
Background: Saphenous vein graft (VG) failure occurs more frequently than arterial grafts, and graft thrombosis is the main cause of early occlusion. The CD40-CD40L pathway has been identified as a potential culprit in this process, as it can link local inflammation to the coagulation cascade. In this study, we investigate the role of CD40 and its soluble ligand (sCD40L) in the immediate in vitro response of VG to arterial pressures, and explore the potential effects of Simvastatin supplementation.
Methods: We obtained samples of saphenous vein and internal mammary artery (IMA) from 16 patients without a history of statin therapy. We subjected these samples to pulsatile pressure distension and culture with or without Simvastatin supplementation. We measured CD40 and sCD40L expression in tissue lysate and culture supernatant, respectively, and also measured sCD40L levels in serum.
Results: Our results showed that CD40 expression was significantly lower in IMA samples compared to both distended and non-distended VG samples. Pressure distension up-regulated CD40 expression in VG segments after 24 and 48 hours. Simvastatin supplementation significantly reduced CD40 expression in both venous and arterial samples. This effect of Simvastatin was not affected by the addition of the nitric oxide synthase inhibitor L-NAME, but it was reversed by the addition of mevalonic acid. Mean sCD40L content in culture supernatants increased over time, suggesting that both platelets and the vessel wall are sources of CD40 and sCD40L.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that Simvastatin treatment modulates endothelial CD40-sCD40L in both venous and arterial grafts, and may represent a useful tool in pharmacological prevention of graft failure.

title: Cancer Cell Membrane-Coated Nanoparticles for Anticancer Vaccination and Drug Delivery
text: Cell-derived nanoparticles have gained attention due to their ability to mimic the natural properties of their cellular sources. This top-down engineering approach can be applied to develop novel therapeutic strategies by leveraging the unique interactions enabled through the retention of complex antigenic information. In this study, we report the biological functionalization of polymeric nanoparticles with a layer of membrane coating derived from cancer cells. The resulting core-shell nanostructures, which carry the full array of cancer cell membrane antigens, provide a robust platform with multiple applications in anticancer therapy. We demonstrate that coupling the particles with an immunological adjuvant can be used to promote a tumor-specific immune response in vaccine applications. Additionally, we show that taking advantage of the homotypic binding phenomenon frequently observed among tumor cells, the membrane functionalization allows for a unique cancer targeting strategy that can be utilized for drug delivery applications.

title: Autophagy deficiency leads to protection from obesity and insulin resistance by inducing Fgf21 as a mitokine
text: Despite growing interest and a recent surge in research, the role of autophagy in glucose and lipid metabolism remains unclear. To investigate, we generated mice with skeletal muscle-specific deletion of Atg7 (encoding autophagy-related 7). Unexpectedly, these mice exhibited reduced fat mass and were protected from diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance. This phenotype was accompanied by increased fatty acid oxidation and browning of white adipose tissue (WAT), which was mediated by the induction of fibroblast growth factor 21 (Fgf21). We found that mitochondrial dysfunction induced by autophagy deficiency increased Fgf21 expression through the activation of Atf4, a master regulator of the integrated stress response. Additionally, we observed that mitochondrial respiratory chain inhibitors also induced Fgf21 in an Atf4-dependent manner. Interestingly, we also found that autophagy deficiency in the liver, another insulin target tissue, led to Fgf21 induction, resistance to diet-induced obesity, and amelioration of insulin resistance. These findings suggest that autophagy deficiency and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction promote Fgf21 expression, which we term a 'mitokine', and together these processes promote protection from diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance.

title: Laboratory prediction of the requirement for renal replacement in acute falciparum malaria
