text: Background: Acute renal failure is a common complication of severe malaria in adults, with a poor prognosis if left untreated. Delaying renal replacement therapy (RRT) can increase mortality. Early identification of patients who will require RRT is crucial to improve outcomes. Objective: To determine the laboratory features that can predict a later requirement for RRT in adults with severe malaria. Methods: Prospectively collected data from two intervention studies were analyzed, focusing on laboratory indices of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and acute kidney injury (AKI) in adults with severe malaria. Results: Of 163 patients, 43 (26.4%) met criteria for dialysis, but only 19 (44.2%) received RRT due to limited availability. Patients with impaired renal function on admission (creatinine clearance < 60 ml/min) had their laboratory indices of ATN/AKI analyzed. Plasma creatinine level had the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for predicting a later requirement for RRT (AUC = 0.83, 95% CI = 0.74-0.92). The AUC for plasma creatinine was significantly better than those for urinary sodium level, urea to creatinine ratio (UCR), fractional excretion of urea (FeUN), and urinary neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalcin (NGAL) level. Conclusion: In adult patients with severe malaria and impaired renal function on admission, plasma creatinine level was the most accurate laboratory feature for predicting a later requirement for RRT, followed by urinary sodium level. These findings may help identify patients who require prompt RRT and improve outcomes.

title: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).
text: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are a sensitive and specific marker for ANCA-associated systemic vasculitis (AASV). Using indirect immunofluorescence on ethanol-fixed neutrophils, two major fluoroscopic patterns can be recognized: a diffuse cytoplasmic staining (C-ANCA) and a perinuclear/nuclear staining (P-ANCA). In patients with vasculitis, more than 90% of C-ANCA are directed against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA), while approximately 80-90% of P-ANCA recognize myelperoxidase (MPO-ANCA). However, it is important to note that C-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) is preferentially associated with Wegener's granulomatosis (WG), while P-ANCA (MPO-ANCA) is more commonly found in microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), idiopathic necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis (iNCGN), and Churg-Strauss syndrome (CSS). Nevertheless, there is not absolute specificity, and between 10-20% of patients with classical WG show P-ANCA (MPO-ANCA), and even a larger percentage of patients with MPA or CSS have C-ANCA (PR3-ANCA). Additionally, approximately 10-20% of patients with WG or MPA (and 40-50% of cases of CSS) have negative assays for ANCA. The best diagnostic performance is achieved when indirect immunofluorescence is combined with PR3 and MPO-specific ELISAs. ANCA with different and unknown antigen specificity are found in various conditions other than AASV, including inflammatory bowel diseases, other autoimmune diseases, and infections where their clinical significance is unclear. ANCA levels are useful for monitoring disease activity but should not be used alone to guide treatment. A significant increase in ANCA titers or the reappearance of ANCA should alert clinicians and lead to stricter patient control.

title: Emerging functional cross-talk between the Keap1-Nrf2 system and mitochondria
text: Nuclear factor erythroid-derived 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) was initially identified as a regulator of drug metabolizing enzyme gene expression in response to environmental electrophiles. Currently, it is recognized that Nrf2 controls the expression of over 200 cytoprotective genes to counteract endogenous or exogenous oxidative stress. Moreover, when activated in human tumors due to somatic mutations, Nrf2 confers growth advantages and chemotherapy resistance by regulating genes involved in various cellular processes, including the pentose phosphate pathway, nucleotide synthesis, and antioxidant proteins. Interestingly, recent studies have shown that Nrf2 is linked to mitochondrial biogenesis in certain tissues, such as the heart, under environmental stress conditions. Additionally, the functional homolog of Nrf2 in Caenorhabditis elegans, SKN-1, is activated by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and extends lifespan by promoting mitochondrial homeostasis (i.e., mitohormesis). Similarly, Nrf2 activation has been observed in the hearts of mice lacking Surf1, a protein involved in cellular respiration, which has cytochrome c oxidase defects. This review critically examines the relationship between Nrf2 and mitochondria and proposes that the Nrf2 stress pathway directly communicates with mitochondria to maintain cellular homeostasis during oxidative stress.

title: Regulation of pluripotency by RNA binding proteins.
text: The maintenance and exit of pluripotency rely on intricate coordination of a cell's molecular machinery. Significant progress has been made in unraveling the complex system, particularly in the realm of epigenetics, transcription, and non-coding RNAs. However, less attention has been devoted to post-transcriptional regulatory processes such as alternative splicing, RNA processing and modification, nuclear export, regulation of transcript stability, and translation. In this article, we delve into the RNA-binding proteins that facilitate post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression, summarizing current and ongoing research on their roles at various regulatory points and elucidating how they script the fate of pluripotent stem cells.

title: The ubiquitin ligase Drosophila Mind bomb promotes Notch signaling by regulating the localization and activity of Serrate and Delta.
text:
The Notch receptor and its ligands, belonging to the Delta/Serrate/LAG2 (DSL) family, are central components of the Notch signaling pathway, a crucial cellular communication system that regulates pattern formation during animal development. Delta is directly ubiquitinated by Drosophila and Xenopus Neuralized, as well as by zebrafish Mind bomb, which are unrelated RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligases with similar abilities to promote Delta endocytosis and signaling activity. Although orthologs of Neuralized and Mind bomb are present in most metazoans, their specific contributions to Notch signaling in any given organism have yet to be evaluated.
Our study reveals that a Drosophila homolog of Mind bomb (D-mib) is a positive regulator of Notch signaling that is required for multiple Neuralized-independent, Notch-dependent developmental processes. Additionally, we find that D-mib interacts physically and functionally with both Serrate and Delta. Our results demonstrate that D-mib uses its ubiquitin ligase activity to enhance DSL ligand activity, which is correlated with its ability to induce the endocytosis and degradation of both Delta and Serrate (Le Borgne et al., 2005). Furthermore, we show that D-mib can functionally replace Neuralized in multiple cell fate decisions that require endogenous Neuralized, highlighting the similar activities of these two unrelated ubiquitin ligases in regulating Notch signaling.
Our findings indicate that ubiquitination of Delta and Serrate by Neuralized and D-mib is a crucial requirement for DSL ligand activation throughout Drosophila development.

title: Myeloid differentiation factor-88/interleukin-1 signaling controls cardiac fibrosis and heart failure progression in inflammatory dilated cardiomyopathy.
text: The study aimed to investigate the role of the MyD88/IL-1 axis in the progression of acute myocarditis to end-stage heart failure. The researchers used a mouse model of experimental autoimmune myocarditis and induced myocarditis in wild-type and MyD88-deficient mice with similar distributions of heart-infiltrating cell subsets and comparable CD4+ T-cell responses. They found that injection of complete Freund's adjuvant or myocardial-specific peptide/CFA into diseased mice promoted cardiac fibrosis, ventricular dilation, and impaired heart function in wild-type mice but not in MyD88-deficient mice. The study also showed that bone marrow-derived cells from MyD88-deficient mice had reduced IL-1 receptor type I signaling, which contributed to the development of cardiac fibrosis during the progression to heart failure. Overall, the findings suggest that targeting the MyD88/IL-1 axis in the bone marrow compartment may be a novel therapeutic strategy against inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

title: Mechanisms of Life Span Extension by Rapamycin in the Fruit Fly Drosophila melanogaster
text: The target of rapamycin (TOR) signaling pathway is a crucial nutrient-sensing pathway that, upon genetic downregulation, leads to increased life span in a wide range of evolutionarily diverse organisms, including mammals. The central component of this pathway, TOR kinase, serves as the primary target of the drug rapamycin, a highly specific and well-characterized compound that has been approved for human use. Our findings demonstrate that feeding rapamycin to adult Drosophila results in life span extension, a phenomenon that is also observed in TOR mutants. This increase in life span is accompanied by enhanced resistance to both starvation and exposure to the toxic compound paraquat. Through a thorough analysis of the underlying mechanisms, we have discovered that rapamycin specifically extends life span through the TORC1 branch of the TOR pathway, by modulating both autophagy and translation. Additionally, our results indicate that rapamycin can increase life span in flies with mutations in the insulin/IGF signaling (IIS) pathway and in flies that have been subjected to dietary restriction, suggesting the presence of additional mechanisms.

title: Conversion of vascular endothelial cells into multipotent stem-like cells
text: Mesenchymal stem cells have the ability to differentiate into various cell types, but controversies persist regarding their effectiveness in clinical medicine due to differences in isolation methods and tissue sources. Our study reveals that vascular endothelial cells can transform into multipotent stem-like cells through an Activin-like kinase-2 (ALK2) receptor-dependent mechanism. In individuals with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), a disease characterized by excessive bone growth due to ALK2 mutations, or in transgenic mice expressing constitutively active ALK2, chondrocytes and osteoblasts exhibited endothelial markers. Using a Tie2-Cre construct, lineage tracing of heterotopic ossification in mice suggested an endothelial origin of these cell types. When endothelial cells were exposed to constitutively active ALK2 or treatment with TGF-β2 or BMP4, they underwent endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and acquired a stem cell-like phenotype. These stem-like cells could differentiate into osteoblasts, chondrocytes, or adipocytes. Our findings suggest that converting endothelial cells into stem-like cells may provide a novel approach to tissue engineering.

title: miR-302 Is Required for Timing of Neural Differentiation, Neural Tube Closure, and Embryonic Viability
text: The evolutionarily conserved miR-302 family of microRNAs plays a crucial role in early mammalian embryonic development. In this study, we investigate the function of miR-302a-d in mice and find that deletion of these microRNAs leads to a fully penetrant late embryonic lethal phenotype. Embryonic knockouts display an anterior neural tube closure defect, characterized by a thickened neuroepithelium. This abnormality is accompanied by increased progenitor proliferation, decreased cell death, and precocious neuronal differentiation. To gain insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects, we performed mRNA profiling at multiple time points during neurulation. Our results reveal a complex pattern of changing targets over time, including the identified target gene Fgf15. Interestingly, overexpression of Fgf15 in the neuroepithelium of the chick embryo leads to precocious neuronal differentiation. Moreover, we find that compound mutants between miR-302 and the related miR-290 locus exhibit a synthetic lethal phenotype prior to neurulation. Our findings suggest that miR-302 regulates neurulation by suppressing neural progenitor expansion and precocious differentiation. Additionally, our study uncovers redundant roles for miR-290 and miR-302 early in development.

title: Low copy number of the salivary amylase gene predisposes to obesity
text: Common multi-allelic copy number variants (CNVs) have been found to be enriched for associations with phenotypic traits compared to their biallelic counterparts. To investigate the influence of gene dosage effects on adiposity, we conducted a CNV association study of gene expression levels in adipose tissue. Our findings revealed a significant association between a multi-allelic CNV encompassing the salivary amylase gene (AMY1) and body mass index (BMI) and obesity. We replicated this association in a sample of 6,200 individuals. Our results showed that increased AMY1 copy number was positively associated with both amylase gene expression levels and serum enzyme levels, while reduced AMY1 copy number was associated with increased BMI and obesity risk. Specifically, we observed an eightfold difference in the risk of obesity between subjects in the top and bottom 10% of the copy number distribution. Our study demonstrates the power of integrated genomic approaches beyond genome-wide association studies and provides a genetic link between carbohydrate metabolism and BMI.

title: Loss, trauma, and human resilience: have we underestimated the human capacity to thrive after extremely aversive events?
text: Many people encounter loss or potentially traumatic events at some point in their lives, yet they continue to experience positive emotions and exhibit only minor and temporary disruptions in their ability to function. Unfortunately, much of psychology's understanding of how adults cope with loss or trauma has been shaped by research on individuals who sought treatment or displayed significant distress, leading some theorists to view resilience as a rare or pathological phenomenon. However, the author challenges these assumptions by examining evidence that resilience represents a distinct trajectory from the recovery process, that resilience in the face of loss or potential trauma is more common than is often acknowledged, and that there are multiple and sometimes unexpected pathways to resilience.

title: Role of boundary conditions in an experimental model of epithelial wound healing.
text: Coordinated cell movements in epithelial layers are crucial for proper tissue development and maintenance, yet our understanding of the mechanisms that regulate collective cell migration remains limited. Recent studies on Madin-Darby canine kidney epithelial monolayers have revealed a wave-like pattern of injury-induced MAPK activation, which is essential for collective cell migration after wounding. To investigate the effects of different wounding conditions on cell sheet migration, we developed a system that allowed us to dissect the classic wound healing assay. We examined Madin-Darby canine kidney sheet migration under three conditions: the classic wound healing assay, empty space induction, and injury via polydimethylsiloxane membrane peel-off. By tracking the motion of individual cells within the sheet under these conditions, we found that the dynamics of individual cell motion are responsible for coordinated migration of the sheet and are correlated with the activation of ERK1/2 MAPK. Additionally, we demonstrated that the propagation of waves of MAPK activation depends on the generation of reactive oxygen species at the wound edge.

title: Reproductive period and risk of dementia in postmenopausal women.
text: The study investigated the relationship between the length of a woman's reproductive period and her risk of developing dementia, specifically Alzheimer's disease (AD), in postmenopausal women. The study used data from the Rotterdam Study, a population-based prospective cohort study conducted in the Netherlands. The study included 3601 women aged 55 years or older who did not have dementia at baseline (1990-1993) and had information on age at menarche, age at menopause, and type of menopause. The study found that after adjusting for age and other covariates, women with natural menopause and more reproductive years had an increased risk of dementia, with an adjusted rate ratio (RR) of 1.78 for those in the highest quartile of reproductive years compared to those in the lowest quartile. The study also found that the risk of dementia associated with a longer reproductive period was most pronounced in women who carried the APOE epsilon4 gene, with adjusted RRs of 4.20 and 3.42 for dementia and AD, respectively, compared to those in the lowest quartile of reproductive years. However, in non-carriers, no clear association with dementia or AD was observed. The study did not support the hypothesis that a longer reproductive period reduces the risk of dementia in postmenopausal women.

title: Effects of growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 deficiency on ageing and longevity.
text: The current understanding of the effects of growth hormone (GH)/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) deficiency on the aging process and lifespan is reviewed. Evidence suggests that isolated GH deficiency (IGHD), multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (MPHD) including GH, as well as primary IGF1 deficiency (GH resistance, Laron syndrome) exhibit early aging signs, such as thin and wrinkled skin, obesity, hyperglycemia, and osteoporosis. These changes do not appear to impact lifespan, as patients reach old age. Animal models of genetic MPHD (Ames and Snell mice) and GH receptor knockout mice (primary IGF1 deficiency) have a statistically significant increase in longevity compared to normal controls. Conversely, mice transgenic for GH and acromegalic patients secreting large amounts of GH exhibit premature death. In conclusion, longstanding GH/IGF1 deficiency affects various aspects of the aging process without compromising lifespan, and as demonstrated in animal models, it prolongs longevity. In contrast, high GH/IGF1 levels accelerate mortality.

title: KLF1-null neonates display hydrops fetalis and a deranged erythroid transcriptome.
text:
In this study, we report a rare case of severe neonatal anemia with kernicterus resulting from compound heterozygosity for null mutations in the KLF1 gene, each inherited from asymptomatic parents. One of the mutations is novel and represents the first described case of a KLF1-null human. The phenotype of the patient is characterized by severe nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and marked erythroblastosis, which is more severe than that observed in congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type IV due to dominant mutations in the second zinc-finger of KLF1. Interestingly, the patient exhibited a high level of HbF expression into childhood (>70%), suggesting a crucial role for KLF1 in human hemoglobin switching.
Using RNA-seq analysis on circulating erythroblasts, we identified novel KLF1 target genes, including KIF23 and KIF11, which are essential for proper cytokinesis. Additionally, we discovered new functions for KLF1 in autophagy, global transcriptional control, and RNA splicing. Our findings suggest that loss of KLF1 may be a contributing factor in otherwise unexplained cases of severe neonatal NSHA or hydrops fetalis.
In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying severe neonatal anemia and highlights the importance of KLF1 in human red blood cell development and function. Further investigations into the role of KLF1 in human disease may lead to the identification of novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of severe anemia and other related disorders.

title: Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis.
text:
The degree of heterogeneity in a meta-analysis plays a significant role in determining the difficulty in drawing overall conclusions. This degree can be measured by estimating a between-study variance, but the interpretation of these measurements is specific to the chosen treatment effect metric. A test for heterogeneity exists, but its reliability depends on the number of studies in the meta-analysis. To address this limitation, we have developed new measures of the impact of heterogeneity on a meta-analysis, which are independent of the number of studies and the treatment effect metric. These measures include:
H = the square root of the chi-squared heterogeneity statistic divided by its degrees of freedom
R = the ratio of the standard error of the underlying mean from a random effects meta-analysis to the standard error of a fixed effect meta-analytic estimate
I2 = a transformation of (H) that describes the proportion of total variation in study estimates that is due to heterogeneity.
We discuss the interpretation, interval estimates, and other properties of these measures and examine them in five example data sets showing different amounts of heterogeneity. Our findings suggest that H and I2, which can usually be calculated for published meta-analyses, are the most useful summaries of the impact of heterogeneity. We recommend presenting these measures in published meta-analyses in preference to the test for heterogeneity.

title: Neurocognitive Development in Children Experiencing Intrauterine Growth Retardation and Born Small for Gestational Age: Pathological, Constitutional and Therapeutic Pathways
text:
Since the recent approval of growth hormone (GH) therapy for small for gestational age (SGA) children, there has been increased interest in the neurocognitive and psychosocial outcomes of this treatment. The primary goal of GH therapy in SGA children is to provide a symptomatic treatment for growth retardation, with the ultimate objective of reducing the risk of neurocognitive, psychological, social, or occupational impairment. Therefore, from a scientific perspective, assessing neurocognitive and psychosocial endpoints becomes crucial to determine the final treatment benefit experienced by the patient born SGA.
This article reviews recent studies on developmental risks in SGA and integrates the findings into a conceptual framework that outlines the sources and mediators of neurocognitive and psychosocial outcomes in intrauterine growth retardation and SGA. The framework highlights two distinct therapeutic pathways through which GH therapy may improve neurocognitive and behavioral outcomes:
1. Prevention of exposure to short-stature-related stressors via improved growth velocity and final height.
2. Potential metabolic and neurotropic effects of GH binding at receptors in the central nervous system, leading to changes in neuronal activity. While the existence and mechanisms of these physiologically mediated effects of GH on neurocognitive functioning in SGA patients remain hypothetical, further research is needed to fully understand their potential impact on treatment outcomes.

title: Gpr124 is essential for blood–brain barrier integrity in central nervous system disease
text: Although the blood-brain barrier (BBB) plays a crucial role in the etiology of various central nervous system (CNS) disorders, the endothelial receptor proteins that regulate BBB function are poorly understood. Recent studies have shown that the endothelial G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) Gpr124 is essential for normal forebrain angiogenesis and BBB function in mouse embryos. However, its role in adult animals remains unexplored. To investigate the function of Gpr124 in adult mice, we conditionally knocked out (CKO) the receptor in endothelial cells and observed the effects on BBB integrity. Our results showed that Gpr124 CKO did not affect homeostatic BBB integrity, but led to BBB disruption and microvascular hemorrhage in mouse models of both ischemic stroke and glioblastoma. These changes were accompanied by reduced cerebrovascular canonical Wnt–β-catenin signaling. Interestingly, constitutive activation of Wnt–β-catenin signaling fully corrected the BBB disruption and hemorrhage defects of Gpr124-CKO mice, restoring endothelial gene expression, pericyte coverage, and extracellular matrix integrity. These findings identify Gpr124 as an endothelial GPCR specifically required for endothelial Wnt signaling and BBB integrity under pathological conditions in adult mice. This discovery implicates Gpr124 as a potential therapeutic target for human CNS disorders characterized by BBB disruption.

title: Vegan proteins may reduce risk of cancer, obesity, and cardiovascular disease by promoting increased glucagon activity.
text: Amino acids play a crucial role in modulating the secretion of insulin and glucagon, with the composition of dietary protein having the potential to influence the balance of these hormones. Soy protein, along with other vegan proteins, is higher in non-essential amino acids than most animal-derived food proteins, which may preferentially favor glucagon production. This can have various health benefits, including lowering elevated serum lipid levels, promoting weight loss, and decreasing circulating IGF-I activity. Vegan diets, which are typically high in fiber and low in saturated fat, can also have insulin-sensitizing effects, further reducing insulin secretion. Additionally, the relatively low essential amino acid content of some vegan diets may decrease hepatic IGF-I synthesis. These factors can lead to a decrease in the risk of various degenerative diseases, such as cancer, coronary stenoses, and hemorrhagic stroke. However, it is important to note that an unnecessarily high intake of essential amino acids can be just as harmful as excessive fat intake, and may even cancel out the health benefits of a vegan diet. Therefore, it is crucial to consume the appropriate amount of amino acids to reap the benefits of a vegan diet.

title: AIR-2: An Aurora/Ipl1-related Protein Kinase Associated with Chromosomes and Midbody Microtubules Is  Required for Polar Body Extrusion and Cytokinesis  in Caenorhabditis elegans Embryos
text: A newly identified family of kinases related to the Drosophila Aurora and budding yeast Ipl1 proteins has been implicated in chromosome segregation and mitotic spindle formation in various organisms. Unlike other Aurora/Ipl1-related kinases, the Caenorhabditis elegans orthologue, AIR-2, is specifically associated with both meiotic and mitotic chromosomes. AIR-2 localizes to the most mature prophase I-arrested oocyte next to the spermatheca in the absence of sperm, and remains associated with chromosomes during meiotic divisions. During anaphase, AIR-2 is present between separating chromosomes, and also associates with both extruded polar bodies. In the embryo, AIR-2 is found on metaphase chromosomes, moves to midbody microtubules at anaphase, and persists at the cytokinesis remnant. Disruption of AIR-2 expression using RNA interference results in one-cell embryos that execute multiple cell cycles without undergoing cytokinesis, leading to the accumulation of excess DNA and microtubule asters. Polar bodies are not extruded, but remain in the embryo where they continue to replicate. The cytokinesis defect appears to occur late in the cell cycle, as transient cleavage furrows initiate at the proper location but regress before division is complete. Additionally, staining with a midbody microtubule marker reveals that some components of the midbody are not properly localized in the absence of AIR-2 activity. These findings suggest that AIR-2 may coordinate the congression of metaphase chromosomes with subsequent events of polar body extrusion and cytokinesis during each meiotic and mitotic division.

title: History of chronic comorbidity and risk of chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia in cancer patients not receiving G-CSF prophylaxis.
text:
Background: Chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia (FN) is a significant complication that can delay or reduce chemotherapy doses, ultimately affecting patient outcome. The risk of FN is influenced by both chemotherapy- and patient-level factors. This study aimed to investigate the impact of chronic comorbidities on the risk of FN in patients with various types of cancer.
Methods: A cohort study was conducted at Kaiser Permanente Southern California, examining the association between chronic comorbidities and the risk of FN in patients diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and six other types of cancer (breast, colorectal, lung, ovary, and gastric cancer) between 2000 and 2009. Electronic medical records were used to identify comorbidities and FN events. Cox models were employed, adjusting for propensity score, cancer type, and other variables, to determine the association between comorbid conditions and FN. Models were also created to account for cancer stage, baseline neutrophil count, chemotherapy regimen, and dose reduction.
Results: A total of 19,160 patients with a mean age of 60 years were included, and 963 (5.0%) developed FN in the first chemotherapy cycle. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (HR = 1.30, 1.07-1.57), congestive heart failure (HR = 1.43, 1.00-1.98), HIV infection (HR = 3.40, 1.90-5.63), autoimmune disease (HR = 2.01, 1.10-3.33), peptic ulcer disease (HR = 1.57, 1.05-2.26), renal disease (HR = 1.60, 1.21-2.09), and thyroid disorder (HR = 1.32, 1.06-1.64) were all found to be significantly associated with an increased FN risk.
Conclusions: This study demonstrates that a history of several chronic comorbidities increases the risk of FN, highlighting the importance of considering these factors when managing patients during chemotherapy.

title: Glioblastoma Subclasses Can Be Defined by Activity among Signal Transduction Pathways and Associated Genomic Alterations
text:
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a complex group of primary brain tumors, and various classification systems have been proposed based on clinical features, cellular resemblance, or signal transduction pathway activation. In this study, we aimed to identify and characterize distinct signaling subclasses of GBM using a targeted proteomic approach and integrate the results with genomic and transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).
Our results revealed three main signaling classes of GBM, each characterized by a specific pattern of activation and mutations in glioma-relevant signaling pathways. The EGFR signaling class was associated with high levels of Notch ligands, cleaved Notch receptor, and the downstream target Hes1, indicating prominent EGFR activation. The PDGF class showed high levels of PDGFB ligand and phosphorylation of PDGFRβ and NFKB, suggesting PDGF-pathway activation. In contrast, loss of the RAS regulator NF1 was associated with lower overall MAPK and PI3K activation and relative overexpression of the mesenchymal marker YKL40. These three signaling classes were found to correspond with distinct transcriptomal subclasses of primary GBM samples from TCGA, which were characterized by specific copy number aberrations and mutations in EGFR, PDGFRA, and NF1.
Our findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying GBM and may have important implications for the development of targeted therapies. The identification of distinct signaling subclasses of GBM could help guide the development of personalized treatments tailored to the specific molecular alterations present in each patient's tumor.

title: Loss of sex discrimination and male-male aggression in mice deficient for TRP2.
text: The mouse vomeronasal organ (VNO) is believed to play a role in mediating social behaviors and hormonal changes triggered by pheromonal cues. Despite significant progress in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the sensory response to pheromones and the behavioral repertoire induced through the VNO, there is still much to be learned. By leveraging the power of mouse genetics and multielectrode recording, our research team has made groundbreaking discoveries regarding the sensory activation of VNO neurons. Specifically, we have found that the sensory response to pheromones in VNO neurons requires the expression of TRP2, a member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) family of ion channels. Furthermore, our study has revealed that male mice lacking TRP2 expression fail to display typical male-male aggression and instead exhibit sexual and courtship behaviors towards both males and females. These findings suggest that the sensory activation of the VNO is crucial for sex discrimination of conspecifics and is essential for ensuring gender-specific behavior in mice.

title: Antibiotic-induced shifts in the mouse gut microbiome and metabolome increase susceptibility to Clostridium difficile infection
text: Antibiotics can have profound and long-lasting effects on the microbiota of the gastrointestinal tract, reducing the body's natural defenses against pathogens such as Clostridium difficile. Our study shows that antibiotic treatment leads to significant changes in the gut microbial community and the metabolome of mice susceptible to C. difficile infection. For example, levels of secondary bile acids, glucose, free fatty acids, and dipeptides decrease, while those of primary bile acids and sugar alcohols increase, reflecting the altered metabolic activity of the modified gut microbiome. In vitro and ex vivo experiments demonstrate that C. difficile can exploit specific metabolites that become more abundant in the mouse gut after antibiotics, such as the primary bile acid taurocholate for germination, and carbon sources like mannitol, fructose, sorbitol, raffinose, and stachyose for growth. Our findings suggest that antibiotic-induced alterations in the gut microbiome create an environment that favors C. difficile germination and growth.

title: Chemosensitization of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) following mobilization by the CXCR4 antagonist AMD3100.
text: The CXCR4-SDF-1 axis plays a central role in the migration and retention of both normal and malignant stem cells within the bone marrow (BM) microenvironment. To investigate the interaction between acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) cells and the BM microenvironment, we used a mouse model of APL and a small molecule competitive antagonist of CXCR4, AMD3100, in coculture and in vivo experiments. APL cells from a murine cathepsin G-PML-RARalpha knockin mouse were genetically modified with firefly luciferase (APL(luc)) to allow tracking by bioluminescence imaging. Coculture of APL(luc) cells with M2-10B4 stromal cells protected the leukemia cells from chemotherapy-induced apoptosis in vitro. Upon injection into syngeneic recipients, APL(luc) cells rapidly migrated to the BM followed by egress to the spleen and then to the peripheral blood, resulting in death due to leukostasis by day 15. Administration of AMD3100 to leukemic mice induced a 1.6-fold increase in total leukocytes and a 9-fold increase in circulating APL blast counts, which peaked at 3 hours and returned to baseline by 12 hours. Treatment of leukemic mice with chemotherapy plus AMD3100 resulted in decreased tumor burden and improved overall survival compared to mice treated with chemotherapy alone. These findings provide a proof-of-principle for targeting therapy directly to the critical tethers that promote AML-niche interactions.

title: Insights into G-quadruplex specific recognition by the DEAH-box helicase RHAU: Solution structure of a peptide-quadruplex complex.
text: Four-stranded nucleic acid structures known as G-quadruplexes have been implicated in a variety of important cellular processes, which are thought to require interactions between G-quadruplexes and proteins. However, the molecular basis for the specific recognition of G-quadruplexes by proteins remains unclear. The DEAH (Asp-Glu-Ala-His) box RNA helicase associated with AU-rich element (RHAU) (also referred to as DHX36 or G4R1) has been shown to specifically bind to and resolve parallel-stranded G-quadruplexes. In this study, we identified an 18-amino acid domain within RHAU that binds to parallel G-quadruplexes and determined the structure of this peptide complexed with a parallel DNA G-quadruplex. Our findings provide insight into the mechanism by which RHAU recognizes and binds to parallel G-quadruplexes, revealing a novel binding mode that is similar to that of ligands selected for specific G-quadruplex targeting. Specifically, the peptide binds to an exposed guanine tetrad (G-tetrad) through three electrostatic interactions between positively charged amino acids and negatively charged phosphate groups, resulting in a clamping effect that stabilizes the G-quadruplex structure. This binding mode represents a simple and efficient way to specifically target G-quadruplex structures, with potential implications for the regulation of G-quadruplex-mediated cellular processes.

title: IQ and non-clinical psychotic symptoms in 12-year-olds: results  from the ALSPAC birth cohort
text:
BACKGROUND: Non-clinical psychotic symptoms are common in children, but it is possible that a significant portion of reported symptoms are due to misinterpretation. There is a well-established association between low IQ score and schizophrenia. Psychosis-like symptoms in children may also be a risk factor for psychotic disorder, but their relationship with IQ is unclear.
AIMS: To investigate the prevalence, nature, and frequency of psychosis-like symptoms in 12-year-old children and to study their relationship with IQ.
METHOD: Longitudinal study using the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) birth cohort. A total of 6455 children completed screening questions for 12 psychotic symptoms followed by a semi-structured clinical assessment. IQ was assessed at 8 years of age using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (3rd UK edition).
RESULTS: The 6-month period prevalence for one or more symptoms was 13.7% (95% CI 12.8-14.5). After adjusting for confounding variables, there was a non-linear association between IQ score and psychosis-like symptoms, such that only children with below-average IQ scores had an increased risk of reporting these symptoms.
CONCLUSIONS: Non-clinical psychotic symptoms are common in 12-year-olds, and they are associated with low IQ scores. The pattern of association with IQ differs from that observed in schizophrenia.

title: Endothelin-1 is induced by cytokines in human vascular smooth muscle cells: evidence for intracellular endothelin-converting enzyme.
text: Endothelin-1 (ET-1) is the primary endothelin isopeptide produced by the vascular wall and appears to play a crucial role in regulating cardiovascular events. Elevations of ET-1 in the blood vessel wall are associated with various pathological conditions, many of which are cytokine-driven. To investigate the effects of cytokines on ET-1 production in human vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), we exposed VSMCs derived from internal mammary artery (IMA) and saphenous vein (SV) to tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) and interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) for up to 48 hours. Our results showed that the combination of TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma significantly increased the expression of mRNA for prepro-ET-1 and the release of ET-1 into the culture medium. This cytokine-stimulated release of ET-1 was inhibited by a series of dual endothelin-converting enzyme (ECE)/neutral endopeptidase inhibitors, including phosphoramidon, CGS 26303, and CGS 26393. These compounds also increased the release of big ET-1, but had no effect on the expression of mRNA for prepro-ET-1. Interestingly, ECE-1b/c mRNA was found in SV VSMCs, but no ECE-1a was present in these cells. These findings suggest that VSMCs, like endothelial cells, may contain an intracellular ECE responsible for the endogenous synthesis of ET-1. Under the influence of pro-inflammatory mediators, the vascular smooth muscle can therefore become an important site of ET-1 production, as has been established for the dilator mediators nitric oxide, prostaglandin I2, and prostaglandin E2.

title: Transposable elements have rewired the core regulatory network of human embryonic stem cells
text: Detecting new genomic control elements is crucial for comprehending the intricate transcriptional regulatory networks in their entirety. In this study, we investigated the genome-wide binding locations of three essential transcriptional regulators (POU5F1, also known as OCT4; NANOG; and CTCF) in human and mouse embryonic stem cells. Contrary to CTCF, we discovered that the binding profiles of OCT4 and NANOG exhibit significant differences, with only approximately 5% of the regions being homologously occupied. Our findings reveal that transposable elements contribute up to 25% of the bound sites in both humans and mice, and have integrated new genes into the core regulatory network of embryonic stem cells. These data suggest that species-specific transposable elements have significantly altered the transcriptional circuitry of pluripotent stem cells.

title: Cytomegalovirus microRNAs Facilitate Persistent Virus Infection in Salivary Glands
text:
Micro (mi)RNAs are small non-coding RNAs that regulate the expression of their targets' messenger RNAs (mRNAs) through both translational inhibition and regulation of target RNA stability. Recently, it has been discovered that many viruses, particularly of the herpesvirus family, express their own miRNAs to control both viral and cellular transcripts. However, the functions of these viral miRNAs in a physiologically relevant infection are still not well understood. As a result, no in vivo phenotype of a viral miRNA knock-out mutant has been described to date.
In this study, we investigate the first functional phenotype of a miRNA knock-out virus in vivo. We used a mutant mouse cytomegalovirus (MCMV) that lacks two viral miRNAs and infected mice with the virus. We found that virus production is selectively reduced in the salivary glands, an organ essential for virus persistence and horizontal transmission, during subacute infection. This phenotype depends on several factors, including viral load and mouse genetic background, and is abolished by combined but not single depletion of natural killer (NK) and CD4+ T cells.
Our results suggest that the viral miRNAs play a crucial role in immunoevasion, which is important for long-term virus persistence. This finding provides new insights into the mechanisms of virus infection and immune evasion, and may lead to the development of new antiviral therapies.

title: Coxibs and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in animal models of cancer chemoprevention.
text:
Coxibs, including celecoxib, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin, are among the most promising cancer chemopreventive agents under development today. This study examines the effectiveness of these agents in animal model studies of cancer prevention conducted by the authors. The studies evaluated here are limited to rodent models of colon/intestinal, bladder, and nonmelanoma skin cancer, in which celecoxib and other NSAIDs were administered as either cancer preventive or therapeutic agents. These studies may provide insights into several questions, including:
1. Is celecoxib unique compared to other NSAIDs, and what implications would this have for human use?
2. Are standard NSAIDs (which inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2) as effective as celecoxib in animal studies?
3. Is the efficacy of celecoxib in particular or NSAIDs in general due to their off-target effects or to their effects on COX-1 and COX-2?
4. What is the likely efficacy of low-dose aspirin?

Some questions raised by human trials and epidemiology are discussed and related to our observations in animal model studies. We also discuss the problem of cardiovascular (CV) events associated with coxibs and certain other NSAIDs and whether results in animal models are predictive of efficacy in humans. On the basis of epidemiologic studies and its CV profile, aspirin seems to be the most promising NSAID for preventing human colorectal, bladder, and skin cancer, although the animal data for aspirin are less clear. A comprehensive understanding of the results of coxibs and other NSAIDs in animal studies may help inform and shape human trials of these commonly employed, relatively inexpensive, and highly effective compounds.

title: The porphyrias: advances in diagnosis and treatment.
text: The inborn errors of heme biosynthesis, known as the porphyrias, are a group of 8 genetically distinct metabolic disorders that can be categorized into three main types: "acute hepatic," "hepatic cutaneous," and "erythropoietic cutaneous" diseases. Recent progress in understanding the pathogenesis and molecular genetic heterogeneity of the porphyrias has led to improved diagnostic techniques and therapeutic options. These advances include the development of DNA-based diagnostics for all porphyrias, a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of the acute hepatic porphyrias, the identification of an iron overload-induced inhibitor of hepatic uroporphyrin decarboxylase activity that causes the most common porphyria, porphyria cutanea tarda, and the discovery of an X-linked form of erythropoietic protoporphyria resulting from gain-of-function mutations in erythroid-specific 5-aminolevulinate synthase (ALAS2). Furthermore, new and experimental treatments for the erythropoietic porphyrias, such as chronic erythrocyte transfusions, bone marrow or hematopoietic stem cell transplants, and pharmacologic chaperone and stem cell gene therapies for congenital erythropoietic protoporphyria, are being developed and reviewed. These advances are of particular relevance to hematologists, who play a crucial role in the management of these disorders, including the administration of hematin infusions for acute attacks in patients with acute hepatic porphyrias, chronic phlebotomies for iron overload reduction and dermatologic lesion clearance in porphyria cutanea tarda, and diagnosis and treatment of the erythropoietic porphyrias. This review aims to provide hematologists with an update on the latest developments in these complex disorders.

title: Neutrophilic infiltration within the airway smooth muscle in patients with COPD.
text:
Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is an inflammatory disorder characterized by chronic airflow limitation, but the extent to which airway inflammation contributes to functional abnormalities is still unclear. The interaction between inflammatory cells and airway smooth muscle may play a crucial role.
Methods: To investigate the localization of inflammatory cells within airway smooth muscle in COPD, surgical specimens from 26 subjects undergoing thoracotomy (8 smokers with COPD, 10 smokers with normal lung function, and 8 non-smoking controls) were examined using immunohistochemical analysis. The number of neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, CD4+ and CD8+ cells within the smooth muscle of peripheral airways was quantified.
Results: Smokers with COPD had an increased number of neutrophils and CD8+ cells in the airway smooth muscle compared to non-smokers. Smokers with normal lung function also had a neutrophilic infiltration in the airway smooth muscle, but to a lesser extent. When all subjects were analyzed together, neutrophilic infiltration was inversely related to forced expiratory volume in 1 second (% predicted).
Conclusions: The microlocalization of neutrophils and CD8+ cells in the airway smooth muscle in smokers with COPD suggests a possible role for these cells in the pathogenesis of smoking-induced airflow limitation.

title: Characteristics of service users and provider organisations associated with experience of out of hours general practitioner care in England: population based cross sectional postal questionnaire survey.
text:
Objective: To investigate the experiences of users of out-of-hours general practitioner services in England, UK.
Design: Population-based cross-sectional postal questionnaire survey.
Setting: General Practice Patient Survey 2012-13.
Main Outcome Measures: Examine the potential associations between sociodemographic factors (including ethnicity and ability to take time away from work during working hours to attend a healthcare consultation) and provider organization type (not-for-profit, NHS, or commercial) and service users' experience of out-of-hours care (timeliness, confidence, and trust in the out-of-hours clinician, and overall experience of the service), rated on a scale of 0-100.
Results: The overall response rate was 35%; 971,232/2,750,000 patients returned surveys. Data from 902,170 individual service users were mapped to one of 86 providers of out-of-hours GP care with known organization type. Commercial providers of out-of-hours GP care were associated with poorer reports of overall experience of care, with a mean difference of -3.13 (95% confidence interval -4.96 to -1.30) compared with not-for-profit providers. Asian service users reported lower scores for all three experience outcomes than white service users (mean difference for overall experience of care -3.62, -4.36 to -2.89), as did service users who were unable to take time away from work compared with service users who did not work (mean difference for overall experience of care -4.73, -5.29 to -4.17).
Conclusions: Commercial providers of out-of-hours GP care were associated with poorer experience of care. Targeted interventions aimed at improving experience for patients from ethnic minorities and patients who are unable to take time away from work might be warranted.

title: Activating mutations in the NT5C2 nucleotidase gene drive chemotherapy resistance in relapsed ALL
text:
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), a malignancy of the hematopoietic system, is characterized by the uncontrolled proliferation of immature white blood cells. Despite aggressive chemotherapy, approximately 20% of pediatric patients and over 50% of adult patients with ALL do not achieve a complete remission or relapse after intensified chemotherapy, posing a significant challenge in the treatment of this disease.
Using whole-exome sequencing, we identified mutations in the cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase II gene (NT5C2) in 20/103 (19%) relapse T cell ALLs and 1/35 (3%) relapse B-precursor ALLs. The NT5C2 gene encodes a 5'-nucleotidase enzyme that plays a critical role in the inactivation of nucleoside-analog chemotherapy drugs. Our findings indicate that mutations in NT5C2 lead to increased nucleotidase activity in vitro, resulting in resistance to chemotherapy with 6-mercaptopurine and 6-thioguanine when expressed in ALL lymphoblasts.
Our results provide strong evidence for the prominent role of activating mutations in NT5C2 and increased nucleoside-analog metabolism in the progression of ALL and chemotherapy resistance. These findings have significant implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting NT5C2 mutations and improving treatment outcomes in ALL patients.

title: Ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation.
text: An increasing number of cellular processes are being found to be regulated by protein modification through ubiquitination. These include key cell cycle transitions, class I antigen processing, signal transduction pathways, and receptor-mediated endocytosis. In most cases, ubiquitination leads to the degradation of the modified protein by the 26S proteasome. After ubiquitin attachment to a substrate and binding to the proteasome, the bound substrate must be unfolded and translocated through a narrow channel to the proteasome interior, where it is cleaved into short peptides. Both ubiquitination and deubiquitination are mediated by large enzyme families, and the proteasome itself consists of multiple related but functionally distinct particles. This diversity allows for high substrate specificity and the regulation of a wide range of cellular processes.

title: A novel molecular mechanism of dual resistance to nucleoside and nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
text: Recently, mutations in the connection subdomain (CN) and RNase H domain of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT) have been observed to confer dual resistance to both nucleoside and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs and NNRTIs). To investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon, we hypothesized that these mutations reduce RNase H cleavage, providing more time for the NNRTI to dissociate from the RT, leading to the resumption of DNA synthesis and enhanced NNRTI resistance. Our findings showed that the reduction in RNase H cleavage has a dependent effect on NNRTI resistance, with the affinity of each NNRTI to the RT playing a significant role. Specifically, mutants such as D549N, Q475A, and Y501A, which reduce RNase H cleavage, enhance resistance to nevirapine (NVP) and delavirdine (DLV), but not to efavirenz (EFV) and etravirine (ETR), consistent with their increased affinity for the RT. Combining these mutants with NNRTI binding pocket (BP) mutants further increased NNRTI resistance by 3- to 30-fold, supporting our NNRTI resistance model. Additionally, we found that CNs from treatment-experienced patients, which were previously shown to enhance NRTI resistance, also reduce RNase H cleavage and enhance NNRTI resistance in both the context of the patient RT pol domain or a wild-type pol domain. These results confirm our predictions and provide evidence for a unifying mechanism by which CN and RH mutations can confer dual NRTI and NNRTI resistance.

title: Location Coding by Opponent Neural Populations in the Auditory Cortex
text: The auditory cortex plays a crucial role in sound localization, yet physiological investigations within the cortex have revealed inhomogeneous sampling of auditory space that is challenging to reconcile with localization behavior under the assumption of local spatial coding. Most neurons respond maximally to sounds located far to the left or right side, with few neurons tuned to the frontal midline. Contrary to expectations, psychophysical studies have shown optimal spatial acuity across the frontal midline. In this investigation, we revisit the issue of inhomogeneous spatial sampling in three regions of the cat auditory cortex. Our findings reveal that neural responses tend to be maximum for lateral positions, but exhibit the greatest modulation for near-midline source locations. Moreover, identification of source locations based on cortical responses displays sharp discrimination between left and right locations but relatively inaccurate discrimination within each half of space. Inspired by these observations, we propose an opponent-process theory, where sound-source locations are represented by differences in the activity of two broadly tuned channels formed by contra- and ipsilaterally preferring neurons. Furthermore, we present a simple model, based on spike-count differences across cortical populations, that provides bias-free, level-invariant localization and thus also resolves the "binding problem" of associating spatial information with other non-spatial attributes of sounds.

title: MLL1 Inhibition Reprograms Epiblast Stem Cells to Naive Pluripotency.
text: The conversion between naive and primed pluripotent states is accompanied by significant epigenetic changes. However, it is unclear whether epigenetic events alone can drive reprogramming to naive pluripotency, or if different chromatin states simply reflect different pluripotent states. Here, we demonstrate that inhibiting histone H3K4 methyltransferase MLL1 in mouse epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs) leads to efficient and synchronized reprogramming to naive pluripotency. More than 50% of treated EpiSCs exhibit features of naive embryonic stem cells (ESCs) within 3 days. Reverted ESCs also reactivate the silenced X chromosome and contribute to embryos following blastocyst injection, generating germline-competent chimeras. Interestingly, blocking MLL1 leads to a global redistribution of H3K4me1 at enhancers and represses lineage determinant factors and EpiSC markers, which indirectly regulate ESC transcription circuitry. These findings suggest that discrete perturbation of H3K4 methylation is sufficient to drive reprogramming to naive pluripotency.

title: MafB/c-Maf deficiency enables self-renewal of differentiated functional macrophages.
text: In multicellular organisms, terminal differentiation is typically linked to the end of the cell cycle, while pluripotent stem cells have the ability to self-renew without limit. Here, we report that combining the inactivation of two transcription factors, MafB and c-Maf, allows for the extended culture of mature monocytes and macrophages without loss of their differentiated phenotype or function. When transplanted into living organisms, these cells remain non-tumorigenic and contribute to functional macrophage populations. Our findings suggest that MafB/c-Maf deficiency makes self-renewal compatible with terminal differentiation, allowing for the amplification of functional differentiated cells without the formation of malignant stem cell intermediates.

title: Macropinocytosis: an endocytic pathway for internalising large gulps.
text: Macropinocytosis is a controlled form of endocytosis that facilitates the non-selective uptake of various molecules, nutrients, and antigens. This actin-dependent process begins with surface membrane ruffles that develop into large endocytic vacuoles called macropinosomes. Macropinocytosis is crucial in various physiological processes, including the capture of antigens in macrophages and dendritic cells, cell migration, and tumor metastasis. Additionally, this endocytosis pathway serves as a means for pathogens to enter cells. Despite significant progress in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying macropinosome formation and maturation, further research is needed to fully elucidate this process in vivo. Here, we will discuss the general characteristics of macropinocytosis, identify regulators of this pathway, and highlight strategies to explore its in vivo relevance.

title: KDM5B regulates embryonic stem cell self-renewal and represses cryptic intragenic transcription.
text: Although the regulation of histone methylation is believed to play a crucial role in embryonic stem cell (ESC) self-renewal, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Our study reveals that the histone H3 trimethyl lysine 4 (H3K4me3) demethylase, KDM5B, is a downstream target of the transcription factor Nanog and is essential for ESC self-renewal. Contrary to its previously believed function as a repressor, we find that KDM5B acts as an activator of a gene network involved in self-renewal. ChIP-Seq analysis shows that KDM5B predominantly targets intragenic regions and interacts with the chromodomain protein MRG15 to recruit it to H3K36me3. Depletion of KDM5B or MRG15 leads to increased intragenic H3K4me3, cryptic transcription initiation, and inhibition of transcriptional elongation of KDM5B target genes. We propose that KDM5B activates self-renewal-associated gene expression by repressing cryptic transcription initiation and maintaining an H3K4me3 gradient that promotes productive transcriptional elongation.

title: Increased CDK1 activity determines the timing of kinetochore-microtubule attachments in meiosis I
text:
The process of chromosome segregation during cell division relies on the stable attachment of kinetochores to spindle microtubules. In most cases, mitotic spindle formation and kinetochore-microtubule capture occur within minutes of nuclear envelope breakdown. However, in the case of meiosis I in mouse oocytes, the formation of the acentrosomal bipolar spindle takes 3-4 hours, and the stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule attachments is delayed by an additional 3-4 hours. The mechanism behind this delay, which likely prevents the formation of erroneous attachments during spindle formation, is currently unknown.
Our study reveals that during meiosis I, attachments are regulated by CDK1 activity, which gradually increases throughout prometaphase and metaphase I. Reducing CDK1 activity delayed the formation of stable attachments, while prematurely increasing CDK1 activity led to precocious formation of stable attachments and eventually lagging chromosomes at anaphase I. These findings suggest that the slow increase in CDK1 activity in meiosis I acts as a timing mechanism, allowing stable kinetochore-microtubule attachments to form only after bipolar spindle formation, thereby preventing attachment errors.

title: Discontinuation and non-publication of surgical randomised controlled trials: observational study
text:
Objective: To determine the rate of early discontinuation and non-publication of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving patients undergoing surgery.
Design: Cross-sectional observational study of registered and published RCTs.
Setting: Randomized controlled trials of interventions in patients undergoing a surgical procedure.
Data sources: The ClinicalTrials.gov database was searched for interventional trials registered between January 2008 and December 2009 using the keyword "surgery". Recruitment status was extracted from the ClinicalTrials.gov database. A systematic search for studies published in peer-reviewed journals was performed; if they were not found, results posted on the ClinicalTrials.gov results database were sought. Email queries were sent to trial investigators of discontinued and unpublished completed trials if no reason for the respective status was disclosed.
Main outcome measures: Trial discontinuation before completion and non-publication after completion. Logistic regression was used to determine the effect of funding source on publication status, with adjustment for intervention type and trial size.
Results: Of 818 registered trials found using the keyword "surgery," 395 met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 21% (81/395) were discontinued early, most commonly due to poor recruitment (44%, 36/81). The remaining 314 (79%) trials proceeded to completion, with a publication rate of 66% (208/314) at a median time of 4.9 (interquartile range 4.0-6.0) years from study completion to publication search. A further 6% (20/314) of studies presented results on ClinicalTrials.gov without a corresponding peer-reviewed publication. Industry funding did not affect the rate of discontinuation (adjusted odds ratio 0.91, 95% confidence interval 0.54 to 1.55) but was associated with a lower odds of publication for completed trials (0.43, 0.26 to 0.72). Investigators' email addresses for trials with an uncertain fate were identified for 71.4% (10/14) of discontinued trials and 83% (101/122) of unpublished studies. Only 43% (6/14) and 20% (25/122) replies were received. Email responses for completed trials indicated 11 trials in press, five published studies (four in non-indexed peer-reviewed journals), and nine trials remaining unpublished.
Conclusions: One in five surgical RCTs are discontinued early, one in three completed trials remain unpublished, and investigators of unpublished studies are frequently not contactable. This represents a waste of research resources and raises ethical concerns regarding hidden clinical data and futile participation by patients with its attendant risks. To promote future efficiency and transparency, changes are proposed to research governance frameworks to overcome these concerns.

title: Efficient Generation of Fully Reprogrammed Human iPS Cells via Polycistronic Retroviral Vector and a New Cocktail of Chemical Compounds
text: Direct reprogramming of human somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells using defined transcription factors (TFs) holds great promise for regenerative medicine and biomedical research. However, this procedure faces several challenges, including low reprogramming efficiency, the presence of partially reprogrammed colonies, and genetic mutations in the somatic cells' genome. To overcome these challenges, we describe a simple and efficient approach for generating fully reprogrammed human iPS cells. Our method involves the use of a single polycistronic retroviral vector that expresses four human TFs in a single open reading frame (ORF), in combination with a cocktail of three small molecules (Sodium butyrate, SB431542, and PD0325901). Our results demonstrate that human iPS cells generated by this approach exhibit the characteristic markers of human embryonic stem cells and exhibit pluripotency as demonstrated by their ability to differentiate into the three germ layers both in vitro and in vivo. Notably, this approach significantly accelerates the reprogramming process and reduces the number of partially reprogrammed iPS cell colonies, making it easier to isolate desired fully reprogrammed iPS cell colonies.

title: Prevalence, severity, and unmet need for treatment of mental disorders in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys.
text:
Little is known about the extent and severity of untreated mental disorders in developing countries, but a recent study aimed to change that by estimating the prevalence, severity, and treatment of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV) mental disorders in 14 countries across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia.
The study used a face-to-face household survey of 60,463 community adults conducted between 2001 and 2003 to assess the prevalence of DSM-IV disorders, their severity, and treatment using the World Health Organization (WHO) Composite International Diagnostic Interview (WMH-CIDI).
The study found that the prevalence of any DSM-IV disorder in the past year varied widely, from 4.3% in Shanghai to 26.4% in the United States, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 9.1%-16.9%. Between 33.1% (Colombia) and 80.9% (Nigeria) of 12-month cases were mild (IQR, 40.2%-53.3%). Serious disorders were associated with substantial role disability. However, despite the high prevalence of mild and subthreshold cases, only 35.5% to 50.3% of serious cases in developed countries and 76.3% to 85.4% in less-developed countries received no treatment in the 12 months before the interview.
The study suggests that reallocation of treatment resources could significantly reduce the problem of unmet need for treatment of mental disorders among serious cases. However, structural barriers exist to this reallocation. Therefore, careful consideration needs to be given to treating some mild cases, especially those at risk of progressing to more serious disorders.

title: Successful '9-month Bangladesh regimen' for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis among over 500 consecutive patients.
text:
Title: Outcome and Determinants of First-Line Treatment for Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis in Bangladesh: A Standardized Regimen Study
Background: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health burden in Bangladesh, with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) being a significant challenge. This study aimed to evaluate the outcome and determinants of the first treatment for MDR-TB patients using a standardized regimen consisting of a minimum 9-month duration.
Methods: This was a prospective, observational study of a gatifloxacin (GFX)-based directly observed regimen, with initial hospitalization. The 4-month intensive phase was extended until sputum smear conversion. Patients were monitored using culture for up to 2 years after treatment completion.
Results: Of the 515 patients enrolled from 2005 to 2011, 84.4% had a bacteriologically favorable outcome. However, only half of the patients completed treatment within 9 months, while 95% completed treatment within 12 months. Eleven patients failed or relapsed, and 93.1% of the 435 successfully treated patients completed at least 12 months of post-treatment follow-up. The strongest risk factor for a bacteriologically unfavorable outcome was high-level fluoroquinolone (FQ) resistance, particularly when compounded by initial pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance. Low-level FQ resistance had no unfavorable effect on treatment outcome. Amplification of drug resistance occurred only once, in a patient strain that was initially only susceptible to kanamycin and clofazimine.
Conclusion: The excellent outcome of the Bangladesh regimen was largely maintained, with bacteriological treatment failures and relapses being rare, except among patients with high-level GFX resistance, particularly in the presence of PZA resistance. These findings highlight the importance of early detection and management of drug resistance to optimize treatment outcomes in MDR-TB patients.

title: A Null Mutation in Inositol Polyphosphate 4-Phosphatase Type I Causes Selective Neuronal Loss in Weeble Mutant Mice
text: Weeble mutant mice exhibit profound locomotor instability and substantial neuronal degeneration in the cerebellum and hippocampal CA1 region. Using genetic mapping, we localized the mutation to the gene encoding inositol polyphosphate 4-phosphatase type I (Inpp4a), where a solitary nucleotide deletion results in a likely null allele. Inpp4a is involved in a pathway that regulates intracellular calcium release, as well as cell cycle progression by interacting with the Akt protooncogene. Dysfunction in either of these processes may underlie the neuronal loss observed in weeble mice. While other mutations in phosphoinositide enzymes have been linked to synaptic defects without neuronal loss, our findings suggest that Inpp4a is crucial for the survival of a specific subset of neurons during postnatal development in mice.

title: The myeloid transcription factor KLF2 regulates the host response to polymicrobial infection and endotoxic shock.
text: Optimal host defense requires precise control over myeloid cell activation, yet uncontrolled activation can lead to unchecked inflammation. Our findings identify Kruppel-like transcription factor 2 (KLF2) as a crucial regulator of myeloid cell activation in vivo. Under hypoxic or bacterial stimulation, KLF2 expression is reduced, leading to increased HIF-1α expression. In human septic patients, this pattern was observed, highlighting the importance of KLF2 in the immune response. We discovered that myeloid KLF2 functions as a potent inhibitor of NF-κB-dependent HIF-1α transcription, thereby determining the outcome of polymicrobial infections and endotoxemia. These results demonstrate that KLF2 acts as a tonic repressor of myeloid cell activation in vivo and a crucial regulator of the innate immune system.

title: PQBP1 Is a Proximal Sensor of the cGAS-Dependent Innate Response to HIV-1
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) play a crucial role in the immune response to viral infections by promoting both cell-intrinsic antiviral activity and the activation of adaptive immunity. Upon HIV-1 infection of DCs, an IRF3-dependent innate immune response is triggered, which requires the activity of cyclic GAMP synthase (cGAS). To identify immune regulators that interact directly with HIV-1-encoded features and initiate this innate response, we performed a targeted RNAi screen using primary human monocyte-derived DCs (MDDCs). Our findings revealed polyglutamine binding protein 1 (PQBP1) as a strong candidate, which directly binds to reverse-transcribed HIV-1 DNA and interacts with cGAS to initiate an IRF3-dependent innate response. Interestingly, MDDCs derived from Renpenning syndrome patients, who carry mutations in the PQBP1 locus, exhibit a severely impaired innate immune response to HIV-1 challenge, underscoring the critical role of PQBP1 as a proximal innate sensor of HIV-1 infection.

title: Malaria biology and disease pathogenesis: insights for new treatments
text: Plasmodium falciparum malaria, an infectious disease caused by a parasitic protozoan, claims the lives of nearly one million innocent children annually in Africa alone and remains a pressing public health concern. mounting evidence suggests that resistance to artemisinin derivatives, the current frontline therapy for the asexual blood stage of the infection, is emerging in southeast Asia. To combat this resurgent threat, renewed initiatives to eradicate malaria will benefit from an expanded arsenal of antimalarial agents, including novel drugs that target circulating P. falciparum gametocytes, thereby preventing transmission. Our current knowledge of the biology of asexual blood-stage parasites and gametocytes, as well as the ability to cultivate them in vitro, provides a foundation for optimism that high-throughput screenings of extensive chemical libraries will lead to the discovery of a new generation of antimalarial drugs. Furthermore, there is a pressing need for novel therapies to reduce the alarmingly high mortality rate associated with severe malaria. An in-depth understanding of the pathophysiology of severe disease may reveal rational targets for drugs that can improve survival rates.

title: Mutations among Italian mucopolysaccharidosis type I patients
text: A study screened 27 Italian patients for α-L-iduronidase mucopolysaccharidosis type I mutations, identifying 18 patients with 28 different mutations. The two most common mutations in northern Europeans, W402X and Q70X, accounted for 11% and 13% of the mutations, respectively. The R89Q mutation, which is uncommon in Europeans, was found in only one patient, accounting for 1.9% of the total mutations. The other mutations, P533R, A327P, and G51D, accounted for 11%, 5.6%, and 9.3% of the total mutations, respectively. Notably, the high frequency of the P533R mutation was found to be specific to Sicily and was higher than the 3% reported in a previous study of British/Australian individuals.

title: Radiation-Related Cancer Risks at Low Doses among Atomic Bomb Survivors
text: In an effort to better understand the cancer risks associated with low levels of radiation exposure, this study focuses on atomic bomb survivors who received doses less than 0.5 Sv. To provide more accurate risk estimates, the analysis is limited to survivors within 3,000 meters of the hypocenter of the bombs. The study examines solid cancer incidence among 7,000 cancer cases among 50,000 survivors in this dose and distance range from 1958 to 1994. The results indicate that there is a statistically significant increase in cancer risk in the range of 0-0.1 Sv, and an upper confidence limit on any possible threshold is estimated to be around 0.06 Sv. It is also found that modifying the neutron dose estimates does not significantly alter the conclusions of the study.

title: Barriers and facilitators to implement shared decision making in multidisciplinary sciatica care: a qualitative study
text:
The Dutch multidisciplinary sciatica guideline recommends that healthcare professionals and patients work together to decide on surgical or prolonged conservative treatment (shared decision making, SDM). However, SDM is not yet integrated into sciatica care. Existing research has focused on barriers and facilitators to SDM implementation from a single discipline's perspective, but multidisciplinary care may involve additional challenges. This qualitative study aimed to identify barriers and facilitators perceived by patients and professionals for SDM implementation in multidisciplinary sciatica care.
The study included 40 semi-structured interviews with healthcare professionals and three focus groups with patients. The interviews and focus groups were audio-recorded and transcribed. The barriers and facilitators identified by professionals and patients were categorized using the framework of Grol and Wensing. The software package Atlas.ti 7.0 was used for analysis.
Professionals reported 53 barriers and 5 facilitators to SDM, with most barriers related to the organizational context. Patients reported 35 barriers and 18 facilitators, with most barriers and facilitators related to the individual professional. Many of the new barriers identified by both professionals and patients were related to the multidisciplinary setting, such as lack of visibility, lack of trust in other disciplines, and lack of communication between disciplines.
The study found that more barriers than facilitators are perceived for SDM implementation in sciatica care. Newly identified barriers and facilitators are related to the multidisciplinary care setting. Therefore, an effective implementation strategy for SDM in a multidisciplinary setting, such as in sciatica care, should focus on these barriers and facilitators.

title: Molecular characterization of long-term survivors of glioblastoma using genome- and transcriptome-wide profiling.
text: The prognosis for glioblastoma, the most aggressive type of glioma, remains poor, with only a minority of patients surviving beyond three years after diagnosis. To investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying long-term survival in glioblastoma, we conducted genome- and transcriptome-wide profiling of glioblastoma samples from 94 patients, including 28 long-term survivors with over 36 months of overall survival (OS), 20 short-term survivors with less than 12 months of OS, and 46 patients with intermediate OS. Integrative bioinformatic analyses revealed that long-term survivors were younger and more frequently had IDH1/2 mutations and MGMT promoter methylation compared to short-term survivors. Gene expression profiling showed that long-term survivors had an over-representation of a proneural-like expression signature, which was linked to IDH1/2 mutations. However, IDH1/2-wildtype glioblastomas from long-term survivors did not have distinct gene expression profiles and included proneural, classical, and mesenchymal subtypes. Genomic imbalances also differed between IDH1/2-mutant and IDH1/2-wildtype tumors, but not between survival groups of IDH1/2-wildtype patients. These findings suggest that MGMT promoter methylation and IDH1/2 mutation play a crucial role in glioblastoma long-term survival, and that IDH1/2-wildtype glioblastomas in this cohort of long-term survivors may have other factors contributing to their long survival.

title: Impact of aortic stiffness on survival in end-stage renal disease.
text:
Background: Damage to large arteries is a significant contributor to the high cardiovascular morbidity and mortality observed in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Arterial stiffness and increased pulse pressure are the primary arterial alterations, but the relationship between aortic pulse-wave velocity (PWV) and mortality in these patients has not been previously investigated.
Methods and Results: A cohort of 241 patients with ESRD underwent hemodialysis between 1987 and 1998, with a mean follow-up duration of 72 months. The study found that 73 deaths occurred, including 48 cardiovascular and 25 non-cardiovascular fatal events. At the time of entry, patients underwent echocardiography and aortic PWV measurement by Doppler ultrasonography. Using Cox analyses, two factors emerged as predictors of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: age and aortic PWV. After adjusting for confounding factors, an odds ratio (OR) for PWV >12.0 versus <9.4 m/s was 5.4 (95% CI, 2.4-11.9) for all-cause mortality and 5.9 (95% CI, 2.3-15.5) for cardiovascular mortality. For each 1 m/s increase in PWV, the adjusted OR for all-cause mortality was 1.39 (95% CI, 1.19-1.62).
