title: Frailty Syndrome: A Transitional State in a Dynamic Process
text:
Frailty has traditionally been viewed as a synonym for disability and comorbidity, with a high prevalence in older age groups and a significant impact on falls, hospitalization, and mortality. However, there is growing recognition that frailty may be a distinct clinical syndrome with a biological basis. The frailty process is characterized as a transitional state between robustness and functional decline, marked by a decrease in total physiological reserves and an increased likelihood of insufficiency for maintaining and repairing the aging body. While no single altered system alone defines frailty, multiple systems are involved in its clinical presentation.
Clinical consensus defines the phenotype of frailty as encompassing wasting (loss of muscle mass and strength, as well as weight loss), loss of endurance, decreased balance and mobility, slowed performance, relative inactivity, and potentially, decreased cognitive function. Frailty is a distinct entity that can be easily recognized by clinicians, with multiple manifestations that may include appearance, nutritional status, subjective health rating, performance, sensory/physical impairments, and current care. Although the early stages of the frailty process may be clinically silent, when depleted reserves reach a critical threshold, the syndrome may become detectable through clinical, functional, behavioral, and biological markers.
An updated understanding of the clinical changes and underlying mechanisms of the frailty process, particularly in the pre-frail state, may support the belief held by many geriatricians that increasing frailty is distinguishable from aging and potentially reversible. Therefore, this article provides an update on the physiopathology and clinical and biological characteristics of the frailty process and speculates on possible preventative approaches.

title: Progression of preclinical diastolic dysfunction to the development of symptoms.
text: BACKGROUND: Preclinical diastolic dysfunction (PDD) is characterized by normal systolic function and diastolic dysfunction without symptoms of heart failure (HF). Despite its prevalence, the clinical phenotype and natural history of PDD remain poorly defined. This study aimed to investigate the clinical characteristics and progression to HF in patients with PDD. METHODS: The study population consisted of 82 patients who underwent echocardiography in 2005 and met the criteria for PDD (moderate or severe diastolic dysfunction and ejection fraction [EF] >50%). Patients were excluded if they had a diagnosis of HF or any HF symptoms (dyspnoea, oedema, or fatigue) at the time of echocardiography. The medical chart of the selected patients was reviewed, and the primary endpoint was the time to the development of HF according to the Framingham criteria or any symptoms of dyspnoea, oedema, or fatigue. RESULTS: The study population had a mean age of 69 years, with a female preponderance (67%). Hypertension was present in 76% of patients, and coronary artery disease was found in 29%. Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was present in 26% of patients, and estimated creatinine clearance was <60 ml/min in 51%. Over a 2-year follow-up, the cumulative probability of development of HF according to the Framingham criteria was low (1.9%), but the probability of development of any symptoms was higher (31.1%). The 2-year cumulative probability of cardiac hospitalisation was 21.2%. Hypertension and peripheral vascular disease were independently associated with the progression to the development of symptoms. CONCLUSION: The study found that patients with PDD have a high prevalence of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, coronary artery disease, and renal dysfunction. Although the progression to HF over 2 years was low, there was a moderate degree of progression to the development of symptoms and cardiac hospitalisations. The authors speculate that ventricular-arterial interaction may play a role in the progression of diastolic dysfunction to symptoms.

title: Aspirin in the chemoprevention of colorectal neoplasia: an overview.
text: There is substantial evidence supporting the effectiveness of aspirin in chemoprevention of colorectal cancer (CRC) in addition to its well-established benefits in the prevention of vascular disease. Epidemiological studies have consistently shown an inverse association between aspirin use and the risk of CRC. A recent pooled analysis of a long-term post-trial follow-up of nearly 14,000 patients from four randomized cardiovascular disease prevention trials found that daily aspirin treatment for approximately five years was associated with a 34% reduction in 20-year CRC mortality. A separate meta-analysis of nearly 3,000 patients with a history of colorectal adenoma or cancer in four randomized adenoma prevention trials showed that aspirin reduced the occurrence of advanced adenomas by 28% and any adenoma by 17%. Aspirin has also been shown to be beneficial in a clinical trial of patients with Lynch syndrome, a hereditary CRC syndrome, with a 50% or more reduction in the risk of CRC commencing five years after randomization and after aspirin had been discontinued. Some observational studies have also demonstrated an increase in survival among patients with CRC who use aspirin. Taken together, these findings strengthen the case for considering long-term aspirin use in CRC prevention. However, there is currently a lack of consensus on the balance of risks and benefits associated with long-term aspirin use, particularly in low-risk populations. Further research is needed to determine the optimal dose for cancer prevention and to elucidate the underlying mechanism of aspirin's anticancer effect.

title: Chemokine receptor trio: CXCR3, CXCR4 and CXCR7 crosstalk via CXCL11 and CXCL12.
text: Although chemokines have been well-established in immunity and endothelial cell activation, a rapidly growing body of literature suggests that the CXC Chemokine receptors CXCR3, CXCR4, and CXCR7 play a critical role in the development and progression of solid tumors. These receptors interact with shared ligands I-TAC (CXCL11) and SDF-1 (CXCL12) to mediate their effect on tumorigenesis. Over the past decade, CXCR4 has been extensively studied due to its overexpression in most human solid tumors and its potential role in cancer metastasis. As a result, many inhibitors of the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis have emerged as potential anti-cancer agents, with some in preclinical and clinical development stages. However, the recent discovery of CXCR7 as another receptor for CXCL12 with high binding affinity has raised questions about the potential of "selective blockade" of CXCR4 as cancer chemotherapy. Interestingly, CXCR7 can also bind CXCL11, which is a ligand for CXCR3. Both CXCR3 and CXCR7 are overexpressed in different solid tumors, and their ligands regulate tumor growth and metastasis. Therefore, understanding the interactions and crosstalk between these three chemokine receptors and their ligands is crucial for developing effective anti-cancer therapies. Additionally, these receptors are differentially expressed in tumor endothelial cells and cancer stem cells, suggesting their direct role in regulating tumor angiogenesis and metastasis. In this review, we will focus on the signals mediated by this receptor trio via their shared ligands and their role in tumor growth and progression.

title: Human Cyclin a Is Required for Mitosis until Mid Prophase
text: Using microinjection and time-lapse video microscopy, we have investigated the role of cyclin A in mitosis. By injecting purified, active cyclin A/cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) into synchronized cells at specific points in the cell cycle, we found that it can drive G2 phase cells into mitosis within 30 minutes of injection, even up to 4 hours before control cells enter mitosis. However, this premature mitosis is often abnormal, with non-condensed chromosomes and fusion of daughter cells. In contrast, microinjecting cyclin A/CDK2 into S phase cells has no effect on their progression through the following G2 phase or mitosis. To further investigate the role of cyclin A/CDK2, we also microinjected the amino terminus of p21Cip1/Waf1/Sdi1 (p21N) into cells to inhibit its activity. Our results show that p21N can prevent S phase or G2 phase cells from entering mitosis and cause early prophase cells to return to interphase. These findings suggest that cyclin A/CDK2 is a rate-limiting component required for entry into mitosis and progression through mitosis until late prophase, and may also be the target of the recently described prophase checkpoint.

title: Brief, four-session group CBT reduces binge eating behaviors among bariatric surgery candidates.
text:
Background: This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a brief, 4-session cognitive behavioral group psychotherapy in reducing binge eating among bariatric surgery candidates at an academic medical center. Binge eating has been linked to poorer outcomes among bariatric surgery patients, and some programs have mandated preoperative binge eating treatment as a contraindication. However, no previous studies have examined whether a preoperative binge eating intervention can successfully reduce binge eating behaviors among severely obese bariatric surgery candidates.
Methods: A total of 243 bariatric surgery candidates completed a brief cognitive behavioral group treatment for binge eating behaviors and were assessed on the Binge Eating Scale and the number of weekly binge eating episodes at the initial psychological evaluation and again after the group sessions. The study employed a pre-post intervention design.
Results: The results indicated significant reductions in both binge eating behaviors and cognitions and binge eating episodes after the group intervention. The intervention's effectiveness did not vary according to gender or ethnicity (black versus white).
Conclusion: A brief cognitive behavioral intervention can reduce binge eating behaviors among bariatric surgery candidates. Given the potential influence of binge eating on outcomes, bariatric surgery programs could benefit by treating binge eating before surgery.

title: Influence of smoking cessation after diagnosis of early stage lung cancer on prognosis: systematic review of observational studies with meta-analysis
text:
Objective: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the impact of smoking cessation after lung cancer diagnosis on prognostic outcomes.
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis.
Data sources: CINAHL (from 1981), Embase (from 1980), Medline (from 1966), Web of Science (from 1966), and CENTRAL (from 1977) up to December 2008, as well as reference lists of included studies.
Study selection: Randomized controlled trials or observational longitudinal studies that measured the effect of quitting smoking after lung cancer diagnosis on prognostic outcomes, regardless of stage at presentation or tumor histology, were included.
Data extraction: Two researchers independently identified studies for inclusion and extracted data.
Results: Nine out of 10 included studies found that continued smoking was associated with a significantly increased risk of all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 2.94, 95% confidence interval 1.15 to 7.54) and recurrence (1.86, 1.01 to 3.41) in early-stage non-small cell lung cancer and of all-cause mortality (1.86, 1.33 to 2.59), development of a second primary tumor (4.31, 1.09 to 16.98), and recurrence (1.26, 1.06 to 1.50) in limited-stage small cell lung cancer. No study contained data on the effect of quitting smoking on cancer-specific mortality or on the development of a second primary tumor in non-small cell lung cancer. Life table modeling based on these data estimated 33% five-year survival in 65-year-old patients with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer who continued to smoke compared with 70% in those who quit smoking. In limited-stage small cell lung cancer, an estimated 29% of continuing smokers would survive for five years compared with 63% of quitters on the basis of the data from this review.
Conclusions: This review provides preliminary evidence that smoking cessation after lung cancer diagnosis improves prognostic outcomes. From life table modeling, the estimated number of deaths prevented is larger than would be expected from the reduction of cardiorespiratory deaths after smoking cessation, so most of the mortality gain is likely to be due to reduced cancer progression. These findings indicate that offering smoking cessation treatment to patients presenting with early-stage lung cancer may be beneficial.

title: Epigenetic reprogramming and induced pluripotency.
text: The cloning of animals from adult cells has shown that the mature cells can be reprogrammed to behave like embryonic cells by unknown factors present in the oocyte. Recently, specific transcription factors have been identified that can induce pluripotency in adult cells without the need for oocytes, creating induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. iPS cells offer a valuable tool for investigating the molecular mechanisms involved in epigenetic reprogramming. Additionally, iPS cells can provide insights into normal development and disease, and may ultimately lead to personalized cell therapy for patients.

title: Sex differences in mortality following acute coronary syndromes.
text:
In this study, the authors investigated the relationship between sex and 30-day mortality in patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACS), and whether this relationship was modified by clinical syndrome or coronary anatomy. The study included a convenience sample of patients from 11 international randomized clinical trials between 1993 and 2006, with a total of 136,247 patients, of whom 38,048 (28%) were women. The main outcome measure was 30-day mortality following ACS.
The results showed that 30-day mortality was higher among women (9.6%) compared to men (5.3%), with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.91 and a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.83-2.00. However, after multivariable adjustment, the mortality difference between women and men was not significant (adjusted OR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.99-1.15). The authors found a significant sex by type of ACS interaction, with higher mortality among women in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and lower mortality among women in non-STEMI (NSTEMI) and unstable angina. In a cohort of 35,128 patients with angiographic data, women had less severe coronary disease, with fewer obstructive coronary arteries and more non-obstructive coronary artery disease. After adjustment for angiographic disease severity, the mortality difference between women and men was not significant, regardless of ACS type.
The authors concluded that sex-based differences in 30-day mortality among patients with ACS exist, but are largely explained by clinical differences at presentation and severity of angiographically documented disease.

title: Membrane topology of the 60-kDa Oxa1p homologue from Escherichia coli.
text: We have investigated the membrane structure of a 60-kDa inner membrane protein from Escherichia coli that shares similarities with the recently identified Oxa1p protein in Saccharomyces cerevisiae mitochondria, which is involved in the assembly of mitochondrial inner membrane proteins. Using hydrophobicity and alkaline phosphatase fusion analyses, we have determined that this E. coli protein has six transmembrane segments, including an N-terminal signal sequence that is not present in the mitochondrial Oxa1p. In contrast to previous attempts with partial N-terminal fusion protein constructs, we found that the full-length protein folds into a protease-resistant conformation, indicating that important folding determinants are located in the C-terminal region of the molecule.

title: Identifying and Characterizing Interplay between Hepatitis B Virus X Protein and Smc5/6
text: Hepatitis B X protein (HBx) plays a crucial role in the hepatitis B virus (HBV) replication cycle, but its function has been elusive until recently. It was discovered that HBx inhibits transcription from the HBV genome (covalently-closed circular DNA, cccDNA) by redirecting the DNA-damage binding protein 1 (DDB1) E3 ubiquitin ligase to target the structural maintenance of chromosome 5/6 complex (Smc5/6). By doing so, HBx alleviates transcriptional repression by Smc5/6 and stimulates HBV gene expression. In this review, we delve into the details of how the interplay between HBx and Smc5/6 was uncovered and characterized. We also discuss what is known about the repression of cccDNA transcription by Smc5/6, the timing of HBx expression, and the potential role of HBx in promoting hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

title: Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Vertical Transmission in 12-Month-Old Infants Born to HCV-Infected Women and Assessment of Maternal Risk Factors
text:
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is an often overlooked cause of pediatric liver disease, typically acquired through vertical transmission (VT) from infected mothers. Current guidelines recommend screening infants for HCV RNA at 1-2 months, based on earlier testing methods. Previous studies have shown VT rates ranging from 4% to 15% and a correlation with high maternal viral loads. In a prospective cohort study conducted in Cairo, Egypt, we evaluated HCV RNA in infants with VT and assessed maternal risk factors for transmission.
Methods: Pregnant women were screened for HCV from December 2012 to March 2014. Infants of viremic mothers were tested for HCV RNA at 12 months using real-time PCR. Maternal risk factors, including HCV RNA levels, mode of delivery, and IL28B genotype, were analyzed for their potential association with transmission.
Results: Of 2514 screened women, 54 (2.1%) were viremic and delivered 56 infants. Forty-nine infants were tested at 12 months, of which 7 were viremic, resulting in an HCV vertical transmission rate of 14.3% (7 of 49). The median HCV RNA level in the infants was 2100 IU/mL. None of the analyzed maternal risk factors were found to be associated with transmission.
Conclusions: In Egypt, where HCV is highly endemic, we observed an overall 12-month HCV VT rate of 14.3%. Further research should focus on identifying pregnant women more likely to transmit HCV and testing infants earlier to detect those at risk of developing chronic infection.

title: Long-term follow-up of cervical disease in women screened by cytology and HPV testing: results from the HART study
text:
Background: Several studies have demonstrated that testing for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types results in improved sensitivity for the detection of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2 or more (CIN2+), compared to cytology, although with a lower specificity.
Methods: We obtained follow-up results for women who participated in the HART study, which compared HPV testing (HC-II) with cytology as a primary screening modality. The study had a median follow-up time of 6 years.
Results: A total of 42 additional cases of CIN2+ were identified during the follow-up period, with women who were HPV positive at baseline being more likely to develop CIN2+ than those who were HPV negative (hazard ratio (HR) 17.2; 95% confidence interval (CI) (9.3-31.6)). The risk of developing CIN2+ increased with increasing viral load. Compared to HPV-negative women (relative light unit (RLU) <1), the HR (95% CI) was 5.4 (1.6, 18.2) for RLU of 1-10 and 25.5 (13.6, 47.9) for RLU > or = 10. Positive cytology (borderline or worse compared to negative) was also predictive of developing CIN2+, although to a lesser extent (HR 8.7; 95% CI (4.5-17.1)). Only one case of CIN3 and three cases of CIN2 were found in women who showed a positive cytology result but were HPV negative at baseline.
Conclusion: After 5 years of follow-up, CIN2+ occurred in 0.23% of women who were HPV negative at baseline compared to 0.48% of women who showed a negative cytology result, indicating a much longer low-risk interval for CIN2+ after HPV testing.

title: The Burden of Trachoma in Ayod County of Southern Sudan
text: In Ayod County, Jonglei State, Southern Sudan, a survey was conducted to assess the need for interventions to eliminate blinding trachoma. The survey found that trachoma is a significant cause of blindness in the area, with a high prevalence of signs of active trachoma and trichiasis (a condition where the eyelashes turn inward and scratch the cornea).

title: A Century of Cholesterol and Coronaries: From Plaques to Genes to Statins
text: Approximately one-fourth of all deaths in industrialized nations are due to coronary heart disease, a century of research has shown. The primary culprit behind this devastating condition is cholesterol-carrying low-density lipoprotein (LDL), which is regulated by specific receptors (LDLRs) in the liver that remove it from the bloodstream. Mutations that impair the function of these receptors lead to elevated LDL levels and an increased risk of heart attacks, often in childhood. Conversely, mutations that enhance the function of LDLRs result in lower LDL levels and a reduced risk of heart attacks. To effectively combat coronary disease, reducing LDL levels should be the primary focus. Fortunately, several effective strategies are currently available to achieve this goal. The key challenges are identifying which individuals to target, determining the optimal timing and duration of treatment.

title: Perinatal mortality in rural China: retrospective cohort study.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the use of local civil registration data to assess perinatal mortality in a typical rural county in a less developed province in China during 1999-2000.
Design:
Retrospective cohort study, following pregnancies from registration to outcome of infant seven days after birth.
Setting:
Routine family planning records in 20 rural townships in eastern China.
Subjects:
3697 pregnancies registered by the local family planning system during 1999.
Main Outcome Measures:
Abortions, stillbirths, early neonatal mortality, and perinatal mortality.
Results:
Only three cases were lost to follow-up. The average age of the women at pregnancy was 25.9 years. Three hundred and twelve pregnancies were aborted, and 240 ended in miscarriage (total 552, 15%). The perinatal mortality rate was 69 per 1000 births, the rate of stillbirth was 24 per 1000 births, and the early neonatal mortality was 46 per 1000 live births. The early neonatal mortality was 29 in boys and 69 in girls per 1000 live births. The perinatal mortality rate increased significantly with parity and was higher in townships with lower income per capita.
Conclusions:
The family planning system at the most local level is a valuable data source for studying perinatal mortality in rural China. The perinatal mortality rate in the study county was higher than previously reported for both rural and urban areas in China. The results by parity and sex of the infant raise concerns about the impact of the one-child policy.

title: Genetic disruption of aurora B uncovers an essential role for aurora C during early mammalian development.
text: Mitosis is regulated by multiple kinases that control cell cycle progression and prevent chromosome mis-segregation. Aurora kinase B interacts with survivin, borealin, and incenp to form the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC), which is involved in regulating microtubule-kinetochore attachments and cytokinesis. Unlike genetic ablation of survivin, borealin, or incenp, which results in early lethality at the morula stage, we show that aurora B is dispensable for CPC function during early cell divisions. This is due to the crucial function of aurora C during these early embryonic cycles. Expression of aurora C decreases during late blastocyst stages, resulting in post-implantation defects in aurora B-null embryos. These defects are characterized by abundant prometaphase figures and apoptotic cell death of the aurora B-deficient inner cell mass. Conditional deletion of aurora B in somatic cells that do not express aurora C results in chromosomal misalignment and lack of chromosome segregation. Re-expression of wild-type, but not kinase-dead, aurora C rescues this defect, suggesting functional overlap between these two kinases. Finally, aurora B-null cells partially arrest in the presence of nocodazole, suggesting that this kinase is not essential for the spindle assembly checkpoint.

title: NuSAP is essential for chromatin-induced spindle formation during early embryogenesis.
text:
Mitotic spindle formation is mediated by two distinct pathways: a centrosomal and a chromosomal route. RanGTP regulates the latter process by releasing microtubule-associated proteins from inhibitory complexes. NuSAP, a protein that binds to both microtubules and DNA, is a target of RanGTP and promotes the formation of microtubules near chromosomes. However, the role of NuSAP in cell proliferation in vivo remains unexplored.
Our study reveals that the expression of NuSAP is highly correlated with cell proliferation during embryonic development and adult life, making it a reliable marker of proliferating cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NuSAP deficiency in mice leads to embryonic lethality due to impaired spindle assembly. In NuSAP-deficient cells, spindle formation is inefficient, and chromosomes remain dispersed in the mitotic cytoplasm. As a result, the cells fail to progress through mitosis, leading to sustained spindle checkpoint activity and ultimately caspase-mediated apoptotic cell death.
Our findings highlight the essential role of NuSAP in proliferation of embryonic cells and underscore the importance of chromatin-induced spindle assembly.

title: E2F-6: a novel member of the E2F family is an inhibitor of E2F-dependent transcription
text:
The E2F family of transcription factors plays a crucial role in regulating the expression of genes necessary for proper cell cycle progression. Previous studies have identified five members of this family, including E2F1-5. These proteins can be grouped into two categories based on their function: those that induce S-phase progression when overexpressed in quiescent cells (E2Fs 1-3) and those that do not (E2Fs 4-5).
In this study, we report the identification of a novel member of the E2F family, which we refer to as E2F-6. E2F-6 shares significant homology with E2Fs 1-5, particularly in the DNA binding, heterodimerization, and transcriptional activation domains. However, unlike the other E2F family members, E2F-6 lacks a transactivation and pocket protein binding domain, thereby forming a distinct subcategory within the E2F family.
E2F-6 is a nuclear protein that can form heterodimers with the DP proteins (both DP-1 and DP-2) in vitro and in vivo. Our results demonstrate that the E2F-DP complex exhibits high DNA binding activity, with a preference for a TTTCCCGC E2F recognition site, which is distinct from the E2F consensus site derived from the E2 promoter (TTTCGCGC). In contrast to the other E2F family members, ectopic expression of E2F-6 inhibits transcription from promoters containing E2F recognition sites rather than activating transcription. Furthermore, overexpression of E2F-6 suppresses the transactivational effects of co-expression of E2F-1 and DP-1. The inhibitory effect of E2F-6 is dependent on its DNA binding activity and its ability to form heterodimers with the DPs.
Interestingly, ectopic expression of E2F-6 leads to an accumulation of cells in S-phase. Our data suggest that E2F-6 expression delays the exit from S-phase rather than inducing S-phase, further highlighting the functional distinction between E2F-6 and the previously identified E2F family members.
In conclusion, the present study identifies a novel member of the E2F family, E2F-6, which exhibits distinct functional properties compared to the previously known E2F family members. The results provide new insights into the regulation of cell cycle progression and highlight the complexity of the E2F family in controlling gene expression during the cell cycle.

title: Enhancement of hippocampal pyramidal cell excitability by the novel selective slow-afterhyperpolarization channel blocker 3-(triphenylmethylaminomethyl)pyridine (UCL2077).
text: The slow afterhyperpolarization (sAHP) in hippocampal neurons has been linked to learning and memory, yet its role in cell excitability and central nervous system function remains unclear due to two limitations: 1) there are currently no selective inhibitors that can effectively reduce the underlying current in vivo or in intact in vitro tissue preparations, and 2) the molecular identity of the small conductance K(+) channel that underlies the sAHP is unknown. To address these limitations, we investigated the effects of 3-(triphenylmethylaminomethyl)pyridine (UCL2077), a novel compound, on the sAHP in hippocampal neurons in culture and in slices. Our results show that UCL2077 selectively suppressed the sAHP with an IC(50) value of 0.5 microM in culture and approximately 10 microM in slices, with minimal effects on Ca(2+) channels, action potentials, input resistance, and the medium afterhyperpolarization. Additionally, UCL2077 had little effect on heterologously expressed small conductance Ca(2+)-activated K(+) (SK) channels. Interestingly, UCL2077 and apamin, a selective SK channel blocker, affected spike firing in hippocampal neurons in different ways. These findings suggest that SK channels are unlikely to underlie the sAHP. This study demonstrates that UCL2077, the most potent and selective sAHP blocker described to date, is a valuable pharmacological tool for exploring the role of sAHP channels in the regulation of cell excitability in intact tissue preparations and, potentially, in vivo.

title: Lessons from sudden coronary death: a comprehensive morphological classification scheme for atherosclerotic lesions.
text: This review aims to challenge the current understanding of the final stages of atherosclerosis progression. The traditional paradigm, largely based on observations by Davies and colleagues,1,2 suggests that death in atherosclerotic coronary artery disease results from the rupture of an advanced atherosclerotic lesion. However, recent autopsy studies suggest that this assumption may be incomplete. To reassess this paradigm, we reevaluated the morphological classification scheme proposed by the American Heart Association (AHA).3,4 This scheme is complex, with a long list of roman numerals modified by letter codes that are difficult to remember, and it implies a linear progression of lesion development. We found this approach to be ambiguous, as it is unclear whether there is a single sequence of events during the progression of all lesions. Therefore, we have developed a simpler classification scheme that is consistent with the AHA categories but easier to use, able to accommodate a wide range of morphological variations, and not overly burdened by mechanistic implications. The current understanding is based on the belief that type IV lesions, or "atheromas," described by the AHA are stable due to the fatty, necrotic core being contained by a smooth muscle cell-rich fibrous cap. Virchow's analysis in 1858 highlighted that the term "atheroma" originally referred to a dermal cyst (“Grutzbalg”), a fatty ...

title: Loss of allergen 1 confers a hypervirulent phenotype that resembles mucoid switch variants of Cryptococcus neoformans.
text: Microbial survival within a host often relies on the ability of a pathogen to undergo changes that evade the host's defense mechanisms. The human-pathogenic fungus Cryptococcus neoformans has been shown to undergo phenotypic switching in vivo, leading to persistence in tissue. Through microarray and real-time PCR analyses, the ALL1 gene was found to be downregulated in the hypervirulent mucoid switch variant, both during logarithmic growth and intracellular growth in macrophages. The ALL1 gene encodes a small cytoplasmic protein involved in capsule formation. Growth of an all1Delta gene deletion mutant was normal, and cells of the mutant produced a larger polysaccharide capsule than cells of the smooth parent and the complemented strain. The enlarged capsule inhibited macrophage phagocytosis, and the mutant exhibited a modest defect in capsule induction compared to other variants. In animal models, the all1Delta mutant exhibited a phenotype similar to that of the hypervirulent mucoid switch variant, characterized by decreased host survival and elevated intracranial pressure. Decreased survival is likely due to both an impaired cell-mediated immune response and ineffective phagocytosis by macrophages. These findings suggest that loss of the ALL1 gene enhances virulence by altering the host-pathogen interaction and impairing clearance, making it the first cryptococcal gene associated with elevated intracranial pressure. Our data support the hypothesis that an environmental opportunistic pathogen has modified its virulence in vivo through epigenetic downregulation of gene function.

title: Lessons from more than 80 structures of the GluA2 ligand-binding domain in complex with agonists, antagonists and allosteric modulators.
text: Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs), a family of ligand-gated ion channels, play a crucial role in fast synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. These receptors are essential for the development and function of the nervous system, and their dysfunction has been implicated in various brain disorders, including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia. Since the first publication of the structure of a recombinant soluble protein comprising the ligand-binding domain of GluA2 in 1998, extensive research has led to the determination of crystal structures of wildtype and mutant proteins, including different ligands. This structural information, combined with functional data, has enabled the development of models for receptor activation and desensitization by agonists, inhibition by antagonists, and block of desensitization by positive allosteric modulators. Moreover, the structural and functional studies have provided a powerful platform for the design of new selective compounds.

title: Diaphragm Atrophy and Contractile Dysfunction in a Murine Model of Pulmonary Hypertension
text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) leads to weight loss and dysfunction of the inspiratory (diaphragm) muscles. A widely used mouse model of PH, induced by the drug monocrotaline (MCT), has been examined to understand the underlying mechanisms of cachexia and diaphragm abnormalities in PH. However, it is unclear if this mouse model accurately reproduces the weight loss and diaphragm muscle dysfunction seen in human patients. To address this, we measured body and soleus muscle weight, food intake, and diaphragm contractile properties in mice after 6-8 weeks of saline (control) or MCT (600 mg/kg) injections. Our findings show that PH mice exhibited progressive weight loss, similar food intake compared to controls, and decreased diaphragm muscle strength, as evidenced by decreased maximal isometric specific force, maximal shortening velocity, and peak power. Additionally, protein carbonyls in whole-diaphragm lysates and the abundance of select myofibrillar proteins were unchanged by PH. These results suggest that the murine model of PH induced by MCT mimics the loss of body weight and diaphragm muscle weakness observed in human PH patients.

title: Identification of an anti-inflammatory protein from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a commensal bacterium deficient in Crohn's disease.
text:
Background: Crohn's disease (CD)-associated dysbiosis is characterized by a loss of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, which has been shown to exert an anti-inflammatory effect both in vitro and in vivo. However, the chemical nature of the anti-inflammatory compounds produced by F. prausnitzii has not been fully elucidated.
Methods: To identify and characterize the anti-inflammatory peptides produced by F. prausnitzii, we performed a peptidomic analysis using mass spectrometry. The anti-inflammatory effects of the identified peptides were then tested in vitro using intestinal epithelial cell lines and cell lines transfected with a plasmid construct encoding the candidate protein. In vivo, the cDNA of the candidate protein was delivered to the gut of mice using recombinant lactic acid bacteria to prevent dinitrobenzene sulfonic acid (DNBS)-induced colitis.
Results: Our analysis revealed seven peptides in the F. prausnitzii culture supernatant, which were derived from a single microbial anti-inflammatory molecule (MAM). The MAM protein was found to be 15 kDa in size and composed of 53% non-polar residues, which made it difficult to directly characterize the putative anti-inflammatory activity of the MAM-derived peptides. Transfection of MAM cDNA in epithelial cells led to a significant decrease in the activation of the nuclear factor (NF)-κB pathway with a dose-dependent effect. Finally, the use of a food-grade bacterium, Lactococcus lactis, delivering a plasmid encoding MAM was able to alleviate DNBS-induced colitis in mice.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that a 15 kDa protein produced by F. prausnitzii has anti-inflammatory properties and can inhibit the NF-κB pathway in intestinal epithelial cells. Additionally, the use of a food-grade bacterium to deliver the protein to the gut was able to prevent colitis in an animal model, providing a potential therapeutic approach for CD.

title: Calcium store sensor stromal-interaction molecule 1-dependent signaling plays an important role in cervical cancer growth, migration, and angiogenesis.
text: Store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) is the primary Ca(2+) entry mechanism in non-excitable cells. Stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) is an endoplasmic reticulum Ca(2+) sensor that triggers SOCE activation. However, the role of STIM1 in regulating cancer progression remains controversial, and its clinical relevance is unclear. Here, we demonstrate that STIM1-dependent signaling is crucial for cervical cancer cell proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis. STIM1 is overexpressed in 71% of early-stage cervical cancer tissues, and its expression level is significantly associated with the risk of metastasis and survival. EGF stimulation of cancer cells leads to increased interaction between STIM1 and Orai1 in juxta-membrane areas, resulting in Ca(2+) influx. STIM1 activates Ca(2+)-regulated protease calpain and Ca(2+)-regulated cytoplasmic kinase Pyk2, which regulate focal-adhesion dynamics in migratory cervical cancer cells. Silencing STIM1 in cervical cancer cells leads to a decrease in cell proliferation, an increase in p21 protein levels, and a decrease in Cdc25C protein levels, resulting in cell cycle arrest at the S and G2/M phases. Additionally, STIM1 regulates VEGF production in cervical cancer cells. Inhibition of STIM1 expression or blockade of SOCE activity inhibits tumor angiogenesis and growth in animal models, highlighting the crucial role of STIM1-mediated Ca(2+) influx in promoting tumor development in vivo. These findings make STIM1-dependent signaling an attractive therapeutic target.

title: A feasibility study for a randomised controlled trial of the Positive Reappraisal Coping Intervention, a novel supportive technique for recurrent miscarriage
text:
Introduction:
Recurrent miscarriage (RM) is defined as the occurrence of three or more miscarriages. The emotional toll of RM on women can be significant, with increased levels of distress and anxiety during the waiting period of any subsequent pregnancy. However, limited support and therapy are available for these women, leaving them to cope alone. The Positive Reappraisal Coping Intervention (PRCI) is a novel, self-administered supportive technique that has shown promise in improving the psychological well-being of patients awaiting the outcome of in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatment. The primary objective of this study is to assess the feasibility and effectiveness of the PRCI in improving quality of life in the difficult waiting period that women with previous RM endure before an ongoing pregnancy can be confirmed.
Methods and Analysis:
This study will employ a randomized controlled trial (RCT) feasibility design to establish the viability of conducting a multicenter RCT to definitively test the effects of the PRCI on the psychological well-being of women who have experienced RM during the initial waiting period of a subsequent pregnancy. A second component of the study will consist of a qualitative process evaluation exploring the initial experience of pregnancy following repeated miscarriages. Participants (n=50) will be randomized into one of two groups: the PRCI intervention group, which will receive the PRCI card and weekly questionnaires to assess their psychological well-being during the waiting period of their new pregnancy, and the non-intervention group, which will be asked to complete the same weekly questionnaires. Semistructured interviews (n=20) will be conducted with participants in the PRCI intervention group to gather qualitative data on their experiences.
Ethics and Dissemination:
Ethics approval has been obtained from the National Research Ethics Service Committee South Central-Hampshire A, and participating centers have given National Health Service Research and Development approval. Study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed journals, national and international conferences, and lay user groups. The study was registered with the ISRCTN registry (number ISRCTN43571276) on 18/02/2014, following adoption onto the United Kingdom Clinical Research Network (UKCRN) portfolio, with recruitment of the first participant occurring on 04/02/2014.

title: Report of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Workshop on Lipoprotein(a) and Cardiovascular Disease: recent advances and future directions.
text:
According to estimates, approximately 37% of the US population deemed high-risk for developing coronary artery disease (CAD) based on National Cholesterol Education Program guidelines have elevated plasma lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)], whereas Lp(a) is increased in only 14% of those deemed low-risk. Therefore, there is a pressing need to better comprehend the relative contribution of Lp(a) to the risk burden for CAD and other forms of vascular disease, as well as the underlying mechanisms. However, the complexity and size heterogeneity of Lp(a) have hindered the development of reliable immunoassays to measure Lp(a) concentrations in plasma, leading to significant intermethod variation in Lp(a) values and making it challenging to compare data from different clinical studies and achieve a uniform interpretation of clinical data.
To address these challenges, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) recently convened a workshop to evaluate the current understanding of Lp(a) as a risk factor for atherosclerotic disorders, determine how future studies could be designed to more clearly define the extent to which and mechanisms by which Lp(a) participates in these processes, and present the results of the NHLBI-supported program for the evaluation and standardization of Lp(a) immunoassays. This report summarizes the most recent data presented by workshop participants and provides practical and research recommendations.

title: Classification, functions, and clinical relevance of extracellular vesicles.
text:
Both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells release small, phospholipid-enclosed vesicles into their environment. The release of vesicles by cells serves various purposes, including the removal of obsolete cellular molecules, the exchange of biomolecules through transmembrane receptors, and the transportation of genetic information. While the release of vesicles can be beneficial to the cell, it can also pose a danger to the environment, such as in the case of blood, where vesicles can contribute to coagulation.
Evessels are cargo containers used by eukaryotic cells to exchange biomolecules and genetic information with other cells. This intercellular communication via extracellular cargo carriers appears to be conserved throughout evolution, making vesicles a highly efficient, robust, and economic means of exchanging information between cells. Additionally, vesicles protect cells from the accumulation of waste or drugs, contribute to physiology and pathology, and have a wide range of potential clinical applications, including biomarkers and anticancer therapy.
Unfortunately, vesicles can also be used by tumors and infectious diseases to facilitate spreading and evade immune surveillance. In this review, we will discuss the different types, nomenclature, functions, and clinical relevance of vesicles.

title: Estimating the sample mean and standard deviation from the sample size, median, range and/or interquartile range
text:
In systematic reviews and meta-analyses, researchers often combine the results of multiple clinical trials by calculating the sample mean and standard deviation. However, some trials may report the study results using different measures, such as the median, minimum, maximum, and first and third quartiles. To address this challenge, we propose new methods for estimating the sample mean and standard deviation in meta-analysis.
Our first contribution is to recognize the limitations of the existing method proposed by Hozo et al. (2005) for estimating the sample standard deviation. We demonstrate that this method can be less satisfactory in practice, and we propose a new estimation method that takes into account the sample size.
Our second contribution is to extend the existing methods for sample mean and standard deviation estimation to more general settings where the first and third quartiles are also available for the trials. Through simulation studies, we show that our proposed methods significantly improve the existing methods and provide a more comprehensive guidance for performing meta-analysis.
To summarize, our work provides a new and improved approach to sample mean and standard deviation estimation in meta-analysis, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods through simulation studies. Our proposed methods provide a more comprehensive guidance for researchers to perform meta-analysis in different situations, and they have important implications for the accuracy and reliability of meta-analytic results.

title: Fascin protein is critical for transforming growth factor β protein-induced invasion and filopodia formation in spindle-shaped tumor cells.
text: Fascin, an actin-binding protein overexpressed in all carcinomas, has been linked to poor prognosis, shorter survival, and more aggressive metastatic disease. It is believed that fascin facilitates tumor metastasis by promoting the formation of invasive membrane protrusions. However, the mechanisms underlying fascin overexpression in tumors are not fully understood. TGFβ, a cytokine secreted by tumor and mesenchymal cells, has been shown to promote metastasis in many late-stage tumors. While the pro-metastasis mechanisms of TGFβ are not yet fully elucidated, our study demonstrates that TGFβ induces fascin expression in spindle-shaped tumor cells through the canonical Smad-dependent pathway. Fascin plays a critical role in TGFβ-mediated filopodia formation, migration, and invasion in spindle tumor cells. Furthermore, our results show that fascin expression significantly correlates with TGFβ1 and TGFβ receptor I levels in a cohort of primary breast tumor samples. Our findings suggest that elevated TGFβ levels in the tumor microenvironment may contribute to fascin overexpression in some metastatic tumors. Additionally, our data suggest that fascin may play a central role in TGFβ-mediated tumor metastasis.

title: DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types
text:
BACKGROUND:
While DNA methylation levels have been shown to be associated with aging in various tissues and cell types, it remains unclear whether these levels can accurately predict age across a broad spectrum of human tissues and cell types. Moreover, it is unknown whether the resulting age prediction is a biologically meaningful measure.
RESULTS:
In this study, I developed a multi-tissue predictor of age that allows for the estimation of DNA methylation age in most tissues and cell types. This predictor was developed using 8,000 samples from 82 Illumina DNA methylation array datasets, covering 51 healthy tissues and cell types. The results showed that:
1. DNA methylation age is close to zero in embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells.
2. DNA methylation age correlates with cell passage number.
3. DNA methylation age gives rise to a highly heritable measure of age acceleration.
4. The predictor is applicable to chimpanzee tissues.

ANALYSIS OF CANCER SAMPLES:

Analysis of 6,000 cancer samples from 32 datasets revealed that all of the considered 20 cancer types exhibit significant age acceleration, with an average of 36 years. Low age-acceleration of cancer tissue is associated with a high number of somatic mutations and TP53 mutations, while mutations in steroid receptors greatly accelerate DNA methylation age in breast cancer.
FINAL RESULTS:

I propose that DNA methylation age measures the cumulative effect of an epigenetic maintenance system. This novel epigenetic clock can be used to address a host of questions in developmental biology, cancer, and aging research.

title: Whole-body MR vascular screening detects unsuspected concomitant vascular disease in coronary heart disease patients
text:
Coronary heart disease (CHD) patients often exhibit atherosclerotic vascular disease in other vascular territories beyond the coronary arteries. In this study, we investigated the frequency of concomitant arterial pathologies detected by whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in CHD patients, as well as the number of previously undiagnosed cases.
Of the 4,814 participants in the population-based Heinz Nixdorf Recall Study, 327 reported a history of CHD (e.g., previous coronary bypass surgery or angioplasty). Of these, 160 patients (mean age 66.4 years) underwent whole-body MRI, including imaging of the brain, heart (excluding the coronary arteries), and whole-body MRI angiography. The prevalence of various vascular pathologies was assessed and correlated with each other, as well as compared to patients' histories.
The study found that 16 (10%) of the 160 CHD patients showed signs of stroke on MRI, while 77 (48.1%) had a stenosis of >50% in at least one extracerebral peripheral artery (other than the coronaries), including 28 (17.5%) with relevant renal artery stenoses and 20 (12.5%) with relevant extracerebral internal carotid artery stenoses. In addition, false negative histories were reported in 12 of 81 cases with myocardial infarctions and in 11 of 16 cases with cerebrovascular infarctions.
The findings suggest that a whole-body atherosclerosis MRI screening program can detect previously undiagnosed concomitant vascular disease in CHD patients. Further studies are needed to assess the program's prospective value.

title: Key role of Ubc5 and lysine-63 polyubiquitination in viral activation of IRF3.
text: The mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS; also known as IPS-1, VISA, and CARDIF) is crucial for the innate immune response against RNA viruses. MAVS receives signals from the cytosolic RIG-I-like receptors, which recognize viral RNAs. However, the mechanism by which MAVS triggers the activation of downstream transcription factors, such as IRF3, to produce type-I interferons is not well understood. To investigate this, we established a cell-free system in which mitochondria derived from virus-infected cells activate IRF3 in the cytosol. Through fractionation of the cytosol, we identified Ubc5 as a ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2) required for IRF3 activation. Using an inducible RNAi strategy, we demonstrated that catalytically active Ubc5 is essential for IRF3 activation by viral infection. Additionally, we found that the activation of IRF3 also requires two ubiquitin-binding domains of NEMO. Furthermore, we showed that replacing endogenous ubiquitin with its K63R mutant abrogates viral activation of IRF3, indicating that K63 polyubiquitination plays a critical role in IRF3 activation.

title: Profiling of residual breast cancers after neoadjuvant chemotherapy identifies DUSP4 deficiency as a mechanism of drug resistance
text: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) can achieve a pathological complete response (pCR) in approximately 30% of breast cancer patients. However, many patients still have residual cancer after chemotherapy, which is associated with a higher risk of metastatic recurrence and poorer outcomes. We hypothesized that molecular profiling of tumors after NAC could identify genes involved in drug resistance. Using digital transcript counting, we profiled surgically resected breast cancers after NAC and found that low levels of dual specificity protein phosphatase 4 (DUSP4), an ERK phosphatase, were associated with high post-NAC tumor cell proliferation and basal-like breast cancer (BLBC) status. BLBC had higher DUSP4 promoter methylation and gene expression patterns of Ras-ERK pathway activation compared to other breast cancer subtypes. Overexpression of DUSP4 increased chemotherapy-induced apoptosis, while depletion of DUSP4 dampened the response to chemotherapy. Low DUSP4 expression in primary tumors after NAC was associated with treatment-refractory high Ki-67 scores and shorter recurrence-free survival. Finally, inhibition of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK) synergized with docetaxel treatment in BLBC xenografts, suggesting that DUSP4 downregulation activates the Ras-ERK pathway in BLBC, leading to an attenuated response to anti-cancer chemotherapy.

title: Age-related behaviors have distinct transcriptional profiles in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text:
There has been a significant amount of interest in identifying potential biomarkers of aging. Biomarkers of aging would be valuable in predicting an individual's potential vulnerabilities before they are expected to occur chronologically. Prior attempts to identify biomarkers of aging have often relied on comparisons between long-lived animals and a wild-type control. However, the effects of interventions in model systems that prolong lifespan, such as single gene mutations or caloric restriction, can be difficult to interpret due to the manipulation itself having unforeseen consequences on physiology, unrelated to aging. The search for predictive biomarkers of aging is challenging, and identifying metrics that can predict either physiological or chronological age would be of great value.
One methodology that has been used to identify biomarkers for various pathologies is gene expression profiling. In this study, we used whole-genome expression profiles of individual wild-type Caenorhabditis elegans across their entire lifespan. We scored individual nematodes for age-related behavioral phenotypes or survival and then associated their gene expression profiles with their age. This approach enabled the identification of transcriptional profiles highly associated with either physiological or chronological age. Our method serves as a paradigm for identifying potential biomarkers of aging in higher organisms that can be repeatedly sampled throughout their lifespan.

title: Synchronization of Diffusively-Connected Nonlinear Systems: Results Based on Contractions with Respect to General Norms
text: Contraction theory offers a sophisticated means of analyzing the behavior of nonlinear dynamical systems. In this paper, we explore the application of contraction principles to the synchronization of diffusively interconnected components described by nonlinear differential equations. We present estimates on the convergence of the difference in states between components, for various graph topologies such as lines, complete graphs, star graphs, and Cartesian products of these graphs. Our approach relies on contraction theory, which utilizes matrix measures derived from norms that are not induced by inner products. While these norms are commonly used in practice, the traditional Lyapunov-like linear matrix inequalities cannot be employed in our proofs. Instead, we employ alternative techniques, such as the Perron-Frobenius Theorem, when working with L1 or L∞ norms.

title: GeneTrack--a genomic data processing and visualization framework.
text: In today's era of high-throughput sequencing technologies, the generation of large datasets from techniques such as 'ChIP-chip' and 'ChIP-seq' presents significant informatics challenges, particularly for research groups with limited computational resources. To overcome this obstacle, we have developed a software platform specifically designed to store, analyze, and visualize high-resolution genome-wide binding data. GeneTrack streamlines several stages of the typical data processing pipeline, including smoothing and peak detection, and provides an easy-to-use web interface for disseminating results. Our software is freely available for use through the Google Project Hosting environment at <http://genetrack.googlecode.com>.

title: Multisite optical recording of excitability in the enteric nervous system.
text: A novel multisite optical recording technique utilizing an array of 464 photodiodes was employed to measure dynamic changes in transmembrane potentials (Vm) of guinea-pig and mouse enteric neurons stained with the voltage-sensitive dye Di-8-ANEPPS. Optical recordings of Vm changes in enteric neurons elicited by depolarizing current pulses or synaptic activation mirrored the Vm changes measured intracellularly in the same neuron. Action potentials exhibited a fractional change in fluorescence of -0.09 ± 0.06% and a peak-to-peak noise level of 20 ± 14% of the action potential amplitude. Following electrical stimulation of interganglionic nerve strands, slow excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs), nicotinic supra- and subthreshold fast EPSPs, and action potential propagation along interganglionic strands were observed. Local application of acetylcholine to a single ganglion induced reproducibly and dose dependently action potential discharge, demonstrating the feasibility of neuropharmacological studies. The optical mapping technique enabled simultaneous recording of action potentials in a large number of neurons with high spatiotemporal resolution, which is unattainable with conventional techniques. This technique provides a powerful tool to investigate excitability spread within enteric circuits and to assess the differential activation of enteric populations in response to various stimuli that modulate neuronal activity directly or through synaptic mechanisms.

title: Telomere-bound TRF1 and TRF2 stall the replication fork at telomeric repeats.
text: Vertebrate telomeres are composed of tandem repeats of T2AG3 and associated proteins, including telomeric DNA-binding proteins TRF1 and TRF2. It has been proposed that telomeres exist in two interswitchable states: the open state, which is accessible to various trans-acting factors, and the closed state, which excludes those factors. TRF1 and TRF2 are believed to promote the formation of the closed state. However, the mechanisms by which these states influence DNA replication are not well understood. To investigate, we analyzed the effects of TRF1 and TRF2 on telomeric replication both in vitro and in vivo. Using an in vitro replication system of linear SV40 DNA, we found that telomeric repeats are a poor replication template. Additionally, the addition of recombinant TRF1 and TRF2 significantly slowed the progression of the replication fork at telomeric repeats. When TRF1 was overexpressed in HeLa cells, cells with 4N DNA content were accumulated. Furthermore, cytological analyses revealed that the replication focus overlapped with telomere signals at a higher frequency in TRF1-overexpressing cells than in control cells, suggesting that TRF1 and TRF2 exert inhibitory effects on replication fork progression.

title: Margination of white blood cells in microcapillary flow.
text: The margination of white blood cells (WBCs) towards the walls of blood vessels is a crucial prerequisite for their effective adhesion to the vascular endothelium. To investigate the dependence of WBC margination on hydrodynamic interactions with the vessel walls, as well as on collective behavior and deformability, we conducted numerical simulations using a two-dimensional blood flow model. Our findings reveal that WBC margination is optimal in intermediate ranges of red blood cell (RBC) volume fractions and flow rates, while it is significantly reduced beyond these ranges. RBC aggregation enhances WBC margination, while WBC deformability has the opposite effect. These results are presented in state diagrams that provide a comprehensive overview of WBC margination for a wide range of flow and cell suspension conditions.

title: Lung cancer treatment waiting times and tumour growth.
text: In this study, we conducted a prospective audit of 29 lung cancer patients who were awaiting potentially curative radiotherapy at a single center. The patients were assessed as suitable for radical treatment by one consultant during 1999, and underwent both diagnostic and planning CT scans. We measured the tumor size on both scans and compared them to determine if there was any progression during the waiting period. Unfortunately, 21% of the patients became incurable due to tumor progression while on the waiting list. The delay between diagnostic and planning CT scans ranged from 18 to 131 days (median 54), with increases in cross-sectional tumor size over that period ranging from zero to 373%. The delay between the first hospital visit and starting treatment was 35-187 days (median 94), and between the date of the radiotherapy request and the starting date for treatment it was 23-61 days (median 44). Our findings suggest that even for patients who have specialist referral and are deemed suitable for potentially curative treatment, the outcome is prejudiced by waiting times that allow tumor progression. Limited access to specialists is often cited as the reason for the poor performance of the UK in treating lung cancer, and this study highlights the impact of waiting times on treatment outcomes.

title: Functional coupling of RNAP II transcription to spliceosome assembly.
text: In higher eukaryotes, the pathway of gene expression involves a complex network of physical and functional interactions among various molecular machines. To investigate the functional coupling of RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) transcription and pre-mRNA splicing, we established an efficient in vitro system. Our findings reveal that RNAP II-synthesized pre-mRNA is immediately and quantitatively directed into the spliceosome assembly pathway, whereas pre-mRNA synthesized by T7 RNA polymerase is assembled into a nonspecific H complex, which inhibits spliceosome assembly. As a result, RNAP II transcription leads to a significant increase in both the kinetics of splicing and overall yield of spliced mRNA compared to T7 transcription. Our findings suggest that RNAP II mediates the functional coupling of transcription to splicing by directing the nascent pre-mRNA into spliceosome assembly, thereby bypassing the inhibitory interaction with hnRNP proteins.

title: Calicum microdomains form within neutrophils at the neutrophil–tumor cell synapse: role in antibody-dependent target cell apoptosis
text:
Calcium (Ca2+) signals are crucial in cellular signal transduction, and their importance is particularly evident in immune cells. In particular, Ca2+ signaling plays a vital role in many forms of activation in immune cells. One such form is neutrophil-mediated antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), which is a key mechanism of tumor cell killing both in vitro and in patient care.
Using fluorescence techniques, we discovered that neutrophils exhibit Ca2+ signals during ADCC against breast fibrosarcoma cells. These signals are localized to specific microdomains at the interface between the neutrophil and tumor cell, where they display dynamic behaviors such as movement, fusion, and fission. The presence of these signals was blocked by the intracellular Ca2+ buffer BAPTA.
At the neutrophil-tumor cell synapse, we found that the neutrophil's cytoplasm is enriched in STIM1, a crucial mediator of Ca2+ signaling. In contrast, the Ca2+-binding proteins calbindin and parvalbumin were not affected. Our findings suggest that the Ca2+ microdomains observed in neutrophils are the result of an active signaling process.
Moreover, our results indicate that Ca2+ signals within neutrophils are essential for specific tumor cell apoptosis, suggesting a central role for microdomains in leukocyte-mediated tumor cell destruction. In conclusion, our findings highlight the importance of Ca2+ microdomains in neutrophil-mediated immune responses and their potential as a therapeutic target for cancer treatment.

title: Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors reduce mortality in diabetic patients with non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndromes.
text:
Background: Diabetes mellitus is a significant risk factor for adverse outcomes following acute coronary syndromes (ACS). It is hypothesized that platelet aggregation may play a role in the increased risk of adverse outcomes in diabetic patients with ACS. Therefore, the present meta-analysis aimed to investigate the potential benefit of platelet glycoprotein (GP) IIb/IIIa receptor inhibition in diabetic patients with ACS.
Methods and Results: The present meta-analysis pooled data from 6 large-scale platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor ACS trials (PRISM, PRISM-PLUS, PARAGON A, PARAGON B, PURSUIT, and GUSTO IV) including 6458 diabetic patients and 23 072 nondiabetic patients. The use of platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors was associated with a significant reduction in mortality at 30 days in diabetic patients (OR 0.74; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.92; P=0.007), but not in nondiabetic patients (3.0% versus 3.0%). The interaction between platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibition and diabetic status was statistically significant (P=0.036). Among 1279 diabetic patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) during index hospitalization, the use of these agents was associated with a significant reduction in mortality at 30 days (OR 0.30; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.69; P=0.002).
Conclusions: The present meta-analysis suggests that the use of platelet GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors may significantly reduce mortality at 30 days in diabetic patients with ACS, particularly in those undergoing PCI. These findings support the use of these agents in the medical management of non-ST-segment-elevation ACS in diabetic patients.

title: Glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and alterations in mitogen-activated protein kinase activation are mediated by oxidative stress in multidrug-resistant human breast carcinoma cells.
text: In our previous study, we found that glucose deprivation led to cell death in multidrug-resistant human breast carcinoma cells (MCF-7/ADR). As a follow-up, we aimed to investigate whether metabolic oxidative stress was the underlying cause or at least a contributing factor to this cytotoxicity. Our results show that within 3 minutes of being placed in glucose-free medium, the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway was activated and remained active for 3 hours. Glucose deprivation for 2-4 hours also led to oxidative stress, as evidenced by a 3-fold increase in the steady state concentration of oxidized glutathione and a 3-fold increase in pro-oxidant production. Treatment with glucose and glutamate rapidly suppressed MAPK activation and rescued cells from cytotoxicity, while glutamate and the peroxide scavenger, pyruvate, rescued cells from cell killing and suppressed pro-oxidant production. Additionally, the thiol antioxidant, N-acetyl-L-cysteine, rescued cells from glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and suppressed MAPK activation. These findings suggest that glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity and alterations in MAPK signal transduction in MCF-7/ADR cells are mediated by oxidative stress. These results also support the hypothesis that a common mechanism of glucose deprivation-induced cytotoxicity in mammalian cells may involve metabolic oxidative stress.

title: A structural basis for kinetochore recruitment of the Ndc80 complex via two distinct centromere receptors.
text: The Ndc80 complex is the primary microtubule-binding component of the kinetochore, whereas little is known about how the Spc24-25 heterodimer interacts with centromeric chromatin. Here, we provide molecular details of Spc24-25 in complex with the histone-fold protein Cnn1/CENP-T, which illustrates how this connection ultimately links microtubules to chromosomes. The conserved Ndc80 receptor motif of Cnn1 is bound as an α helix in a hydrophobic cleft at the interface between Spc24 and Spc25. Point mutations that disrupt the Ndc80-Cnn1 interaction also abrogate binding to the Mtw1 complex and are lethal in yeast. We identify a Cnn1-related motif in the Dsn1 subunit of the Mtw1 complex, which is necessary for Ndc80 binding and essential for yeast growth. Replacing this region with the Cnn1 peptide restores viability, demonstrating the functionality of the Ndc80-binding module in different molecular contexts. Finally, phosphorylation of the Cnn1 N-terminus coordinates the binding of the two competing Ndc80 interaction partners. Our data provide structural insights into the modular binding mechanism of the Ndc80 complex to its centromere recruiters.

title: Feedback Circuit among INK4 Tumor Suppressors Constrains Human Glioblastoma Development
text: We have developed a novel genome topography scan (GTS) algorithm to identify patterns of genomic alterations in human glioblastoma (GBM). Through the use of this algorithm, we discovered frequent codeletion of the genes p18(INK4C) and p16(INK4A) in GBM tumors. Functional studies revealed that restoring p18(INK4C) in GBM cells lacking both p16(INK4A) and p18(INK4C) resulted in impaired cell-cycle progression and reduced tumorigenic potential. Conversely, depleting p18(INK4C) in p16(INK4A)-deficient primary astrocytes or established GBM cells led to enhanced tumorigenicity in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, acute suppression of p16(INK4A) in primary astrocytes resulted in a concomitant increase in p18(INK4C). These findings uncover a regulatory circuit in the astrocytic lineage and demonstrate a tumor suppressor role for p18(INK4C) in human GBM, where it functions cooperatively with other INK4 family members to restrict inappropriate cell proliferation.

title: The SMC5/6 complex maintains telomere length in ALT cancer cells through SUMOylation of telomere-binding proteins
text: Most cancer cells activate telomerase to extend telomeres and achieve unlimited replicative potential. However, some cancer cells are unable to activate telomerase and instead use a mechanism called alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), which involves the recruitment of telomeres to specialized structures called PML bodies (termed APBs). Here, we demonstrate that the SMC5/6 complex localizes to APBs in ALT cells and plays a crucial role in targeting telomeres to these structures. Specifically, the MMS21 SUMO ligase component of the SMC5/6 complex SUMOylates multiple telomere-binding proteins, including TRF1 and TRF2. Inhibition of TRF1 or TRF2 SUMOylation prevents APB formation. Furthermore, depletion of SMC5/6 subunits by RNA interference inhibits telomere homologous recombination (HR) in ALT cells, leading to telomere shortening and senescence. Therefore, the SMC5/6 complex facilitates telomere HR and elongation in ALT cells by promoting APB formation through SUMOylation of telomere-binding proteins.

title: Dynein pulls microtubules without rotating its stalk.
text: Dynein is a microtubule motor protein that powers the movement of cilia and flagella. Recent research has suggested that the sliding of doublet microtubules is due to a conformational change in the motor domain, which moves a microtubule bound to the end of an extension called the stalk. However, the stalks themselves have been difficult to observe. To address this, the authors used a new method called "cryo-positive stain" electron microscopy to study sea urchin outer arm dynein molecules bound to microtubules. The results showed that the dynein molecules were active in in vitro motility assays and that the stalk angles relative to the microtubules did not change significantly between the ADP.vanadate and no-nucleotide states. However, the heads, together with their stalks, shifted with respect to their A-tubule attachments. These findings contradict models that suggest the stalk acts as a lever arm to amplify structural changes, and instead propose a new mechanism in which dynein uses its stalk as a grappling hook, catching a tubulin subunit 8 nm ahead and pulling on it by retracting a part of the tail (linker).

title: The INO80 chromatin remodeling complex in transcription, replication and repair.
text: The Ino80 ATPase is a member of the SNF2 family of ATPases and serves as a crucial component of ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes. Although Ino80 complexes from yeast and higher eukaryotes share a common set of conserved subunits, they have undergone significant evolutionary divergence and have acquired unique subunits with species-specific functions. Recent research has demonstrated that the Ino80 complex plays a key role in a wide range of chromatin-related nuclear processes, including transcription, DNA repair, and DNA replication.

title: VEX1 controls the allelic exclusion required for antigenic variation in trypanosomes.
text: Allelic exclusion is a crucial mechanism that enables African trypanosomes to evade the host immune system by rapidly changing their surface glycoproteins. These bloodstream parasites employ RNA polymerase-I (pol-I) to transcribe a single telomeric variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) gene at a time, resulting in an abundance of switchable VSG coats. Through a genetic screen, we identified the trypanosome VSG exclusion-1 (VEX1), which plays a pivotal role in regulating telomere-exclusive expression of VSG genes. VEX1 was found to be sequestered by the active VSG, leading to both positive and negative regulation of VSG expression. Specifically, VEX1 positively regulates VSGs and non-telomeric pol-I-transcribed genes, while negatively regulating VSGs. Interestingly, VEX1-mediated silencing also affects telomeric pol-I-transcribed reporter constructs, but only when they contain blocks of sequence sharing homology with a pol-I-transcribed locus. Our findings suggest that the restricted positive regulation mediated by VEX1 sequestration, combined with VEX1-dependent, possibly homology-dependent silencing, drives a "winner-takes-all" mechanism of allelic exclusion.

title: Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) regulates monocyte differentiation and functions in mBSA and IL-1β-induced arthritis.
text: Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) plays a crucial role in regulating various immune cell types, including monocytes. Our previous research has shown that KLF2 inhibits the pro-inflammatory activation of monocytes. However, the role of KLF2 in arthritis has yet to be explored. In this study, we found that KLF2 hemizygous mice had a significant increase in the recruitment of inflammatory CD11b(+)F4/80(+)Ly6C+ monocytes to inflamed sites, accompanied by enhanced expression of inflammatory mediators, such as MCP-1, Cox-2, and PAI-1, in bone marrow-derived monocytes from KLF2 hemizygous mice, compared to wild-type controls. Moreover, methylated-BSA and IL-1β-induced arthritis was more severe in KLF2 hemizygous mice than in littermate wild-type controls. Consistently, monocytes from KLF2 hemizygous mice showed an increased number of mature and differentiated cells towards the osteoclastic lineage, which may contribute to the exacerbation of cartilage and bone damage in arthritic mice. The severity of arthritis was associated with lower expression levels of proteins such as HSP60, HSP90, and MMP13, and higher levels of pPTEN, p21, p38, and HSP25/27 molecules in bone marrow cells from arthritic KLF2 hemizygous mice compared to littermate wild-type controls. These findings provide new insights into the KLF2-mediated transcriptional regulation of arthritis by modulating monocyte differentiation and function.

title: Relationship of collegiate football experience and concussion with hippocampal volume and cognitive outcomes.
text:
The study investigated the long-term effects of concussions and years of football experience on the brain volume and cognitive performance of collegiate football players. The study included 25 football players with a history of clinically diagnosed concussion, 25 football players without a history of concussion, and 25 non-football-playing healthy controls. The researchers used high-resolution anatomical magnetic resonance imaging to quantify brain volumes and baseline scores on a computerized concussion-related cognitive battery to assess cognitive performance.
The results showed that players with a history of concussion had smaller hippocampal volumes compared to healthy controls and players without a concussion history. Additionally, there was a significant inverse relationship between years of football played and hippocampal volume, as well as an inverse correlation between years of football played and reaction time.
The study suggests that repeated head trauma, such as concussions, may have long-term effects on the brain, including reduced volume of the hippocampus, a region important for memory and cognitive function. The study also found that years of football experience were associated with slower reaction time. These findings have important implications for the prevention and management of concussions in football players. Further research is needed to determine the temporal relationships of these findings and to better understand the effects of repeated head trauma on the brain.

title: STING and the innate immune response to nucleic acids in the cytosol
text: The detection of pathogen-derived nucleic acids in the cytosol is crucial for the initiation of the innate immune response against a wide range of bacterial, viral, and eukaryotic pathogens. However, inappropriate responses to cytosolic nucleic acids can lead to severe autoimmune disorders. The host protein STING has been identified as a central signaling molecule in the innate immune response to cytosolic nucleic acids, particularly in responses to cytosolic DNA and unique bacterial nucleic acids called 'cyclic dinucleotides'. Despite significant progress in understanding STING and its role in the innate immune response, many questions remain unresolved in the field.

title: Global Assessment of Genomic Regions Required for Growth in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
text: Understanding the genomic elements essential for the survival of bacterial pathogens is crucial to unlocking their basic physiology. Recent advances in high-density mutagenesis and deep sequencing have enabled the identification of indispensable and conditionally necessary genes in various bacteria. However, these genes only represent a portion of the complex genomes of important pathogens like Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a major global health threat.
