text: By leveraging the nuclear DNA of the African rice species Oryza glaberrima as a reference genome, researchers were able to uncover the timing, nature, mechanisms, and specificities of recent genetic evolution in the indica and japonica subspecies of Oryza sativa. The analysis revealed that both indica and japonica have experienced significant increases in genome size, with increases of >2% and >6%, respectively, since their divergence from a common ancestor. This expansion is primarily attributed to the amplification of LTR-retrotransposons. However, the genome has also undergone losses of various DNA sequences through unequal homologous recombination and illegitimate recombination, leading to a reduction in genome size. Small deletions were found to be particularly prevalent throughout the genome. In the analyzed regions of orthologous DNA, no instances of complete gene acquisition or loss were observed in either indica or japonica, nor were any examples of precise transposon excision detected. The sequences between genes showed a high rate of divergence, indicating a molecular clock for transposable elements that is at least 2-fold faster than synonymous base substitutions within genes. Additionally, regions prone to insertions and deletions exhibited higher levels of point mutations. These findings suggest a highly dynamic rice genome with competing processes for the generation and removal of genetic variation.

title: Detection of an autoreactive T-cell population within the polyclonal repertoire that undergoes distinct autoimmune regulator (Aire)-mediated selection.
text: The autoimmune regulator (Aire) plays a crucial role in central tolerance by promoting the display of tissue-specific antigens in the thymus. To investigate the impact of Aire on thymic selection in a physiological setting, we used tetramer reagents to detect autoreactive T cells specific for the Aire-dependent tissue-specific antigen interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP) in the polyclonal T-cell repertoire. Two class II tetramer reagents were designed to identify T cells specific for two different peptide epitopes of IRBP. Surprisingly, our analyses revealed a high frequency of activated T cells specific for both IRBP tetramers in Aire(-/-) mice, but not in Aire(+/+) mice. Interestingly, while one tetramer-binding T-cell population was efficiently deleted in the thymus in an Aire-dependent manner, the second tetramer-binding population was not deleted and could be detected in both the Aire(-/-) and Aire(+/+) T-cell repertoires. Our findings suggest that Aire-dependent thymic deletion of IRBP-specific T cells relies on intercellular transfer of IRBP between thymic stroma and bone marrow-derived antigen-presenting cells. Additionally, our data indicate that Aire-mediated deletion relies not only on thymic expression of IRBP, but also on proper antigen processing and presentation of IRBP by thymic antigen-presenting cells.

title: Spatial and temporal heterogeneity of Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum transmission along the Kenyan coast.
text: For one year, entomological surveys were conducted in 30 villages across Malindi, Kilifi, and Kwale districts along Kenya's coast to study the seasonal dynamics and spatial distributions of Anopheles mosquitoes and Plasmodium falciparum parasites. Mosquitoes were collected inside homes every two months, and malaria parasite prevalence was assessed among local schoolchildren at the end of the survey. A total of 5,476 Anopheles gambiae s.l. and 3,461 An. funestus were collected, with the An. gambiae complex comprising 81.9% An. gambiae s.s., 12.8% An. arabiensis, and 5.3% An. merus. An. gambiae s.s. was the primary vector of P. falciparum along the coast, while An. funestus accounted for over 50% of transmission in Kwale District. The transmission intensity varied significantly across sites, with some areas experiencing as few as one to 120 infective bites per person per year. Thirty-two percent of sites with malaria prevalences ranging from 38% to 70% had entomologic inoculation rates (EIR) below five infective bites per person per year. Anopheles gambiae s.l. and An. funestus densities in Kwale were not significantly influenced by rainfall, but were positively correlated with rainfall one and three months prior in Malindi and Kilifi Districts, respectively. These findings suggest that environmental heterogeneity in the predominant aquatic habitats in each district may play a role in the variation in transmission intensity. The study highlights that the highly non-linear relationship between EIRs and prevalence indicates that high prevalence may be governed by substantial variation in transmission intensity, and that field-based estimates of entomological parameters may not provide a sensitive indicator of transmission intensity.

title: Myelodysplasia and leukemia of Fanconi anemia are associated with a specific pattern of genomic abnormalities that includes cryptic RUNX1/AML1 lesions.
text: Fanconi anemia (FA) is a genetic disorder associated with bone marrow (BM) failure, myelodysplasia (MDS), and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). In a study of 57 FA patients with hypoplastic or aplastic anemia (n=20), MDS (n=18), AML (n=11), or no BM abnormality (n=8), BM samples were analyzed using karyotype, high-density DNA arrays compared to paired fibroblasts, and selected oncogene sequencing. A specific pattern of chromosomal abnormalities was found in MDS/AML, including 1q+ (44.8%), 3q+ (41.4%), -7/7q (17.2%), and 11q- (13.8%). Additionally, cryptic RUNX1/AML1 lesions (translocations, deletions, or mutations) were observed for the first time in FA (20.7%). Rare mutations of NRAS, FLT3-ITD, MLL-PTD, ERG amplification, and ZFP36L2-PRDM16 translocation were found, but no TP53, TET2, CBL, NPM1, and CEBPα mutations were observed. Homozygosity regions were found to be related to consanguinity rather than somatic copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, suggesting that homologous recombination is not a common progression mechanism in FA. Notably, the RUNX1 and other chromosomal/genomic lesions were found at the MDS/AML stages, except for 1q+, which was found at all stages. These findings have implications for staging and therapeutic management in FA patients and provide insights into the mechanisms of clonal evolution and oncogenesis in a background of genomic instability and BM failure.

title: Molecular and Cellular Approaches for Diversifying and Extending Optogenetics
text: Optogenetic technologies harness the power of light to control biological processes within targeted cells in vivo with unparalleled temporal precision. By employing molecular trafficking principles, we have significantly expanded the optogenetic toolkit in several key areas. Firstly, we have developed strategies that enable optical regulation at the far-red/infrared border, allowing for control across the entire visible spectrum. Additionally, we have improved the potency of optical inhibition without increasing the light power requirement, leveraging nanoampere-scale chloride-mediated photocurrents that maintain the light sensitivity and reversible, step-like kinetic stability of earlier tools. Furthermore, we have developed generalizable strategies for targeting cells based not only on genetic identity, but also on morphology and tissue topology, enabling versatile targeting in genetically intractable organisms. These advancements demonstrate the power of cellular principles in expanding the versatile fast optogenetic technologies, paving the way for their use in intact-systems biology and behavior.

title: An analysis of the Caenorhabditis elegans lipid raft proteome using geLC-MS/MS.
text:
Lipid rafts are specialized microdomains within the phospholipid bilayer of cells, proposed to function as platforms for various crucial cellular processes. These rafts are composed of specific types of phospholipids and proteins, including signaling proteins and Glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins. While proteomic studies of lipid rafts have primarily been conducted in mammalian cell lines and simple organisms, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans offers a unique opportunity for investigating this subcellular structure in a complex developmental context.
In this study, we aimed to investigate the lipid raft proteome of C. elegans, a model organism with a well-defined developmental profile. Using geLC-MS/MS, we identified a total of 44 proteins in the lipid raft fraction, of which 40 were determined to be likely raft proteins based on their predicted functions. Furthermore, we predicted that 21 of these proteins may be GPI-anchored, and experimentally confirmed the GPI-anchoring status of two of them.
Our findings demonstrate that lipid raft proteins, including GPI-anchored proteins, may play a variety of important roles within the nematode. This study provides a valuable starting point for further investigating the functions of lipid rafts in C. elegans, and may ultimately lead to the nematode becoming a useful model organism for studying these specialized microdomains.

title: Geographic distribution of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus soft tissue infections.
text:
The aim of this study is to investigate the geographic patterns of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections in the local pediatric population and determine if specific areas are at increased risk.
Methods:
We conducted a retrospective chart review of 614 patients who underwent incision and drainage of an abscess at a single pediatric surgical practice from January 2004 to December 2008. Additionally, we reviewed previously published data from 195 patients who underwent incision and drainage of an abscess from January 2000 to December 2003.
Results:
Our study found that S aureus was the most commonly cultured organism in the pediatric population undergoing incision and drainage, with 258 (66%) of the isolates being methicillin-resistant. This represents a 21% increase in the rate of MRSA cultures from 2000 to 2003. Using geographic information system space-time analysis, we identified clusters of MRSA cases within a 1.44-km radius between 2000 and 2003, and 5 separate clusters of more than 20 MRSA infection cases each were identified in 3 separate cities over the 8-year time span. The P value associated with these findings was 0.001.

Conclusion:
Our study shows that MRSA has become the most prevalent organism isolated from cultures of community-acquired abscesses requiring incision and drainage in the pediatric population in our local region. Significant clustering of MRSA infections has been identified in several different cities within our geographic region.

title: The right place at the right time: chaperoning core histone variants.
text: Histone proteins play a crucial role in maintaining cell homeostasis by dynamically regulating chromatin structure and epigenetic signaling. This is achieved through the controlled deposition and eviction of histones, which is mediated by specialized chaperones. With the evolution of histone variants, a complex network of functionally specific histone chaperones has emerged. While the molecular details of chaperone specificity for different histone variants are still being uncovered, a complete understanding of these processes is essential to elucidate the biological roles of histone variants, their chaperones, and their impact on chromatin dynamics.

title: Phosphorylation site mutations in heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) reduce or eliminate silencing activity.
text:
Introduction:
Heterochromatin-associated protein 1 (HP1) is an essential protein in Drosophila that plays a crucial role in the silencing of euchromatic genes mislocalized to heterochromatin. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of HP1 phosphorylation on its biological activity and biochemical properties.
Methods:
To identify sites of HP1 phosphorylation in vivo and determine the effect of phosphorylation on HP1's biochemical properties, we expressed Drosophila HP1 in lepidopteran cultured cells using a recombinant baculovirus vector. Phosphopeptides were identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization/time of flight mass spectrometry, and their sequences contained target sites for casein kinase II, protein tyrosine kinase, and PIM-1 kinase. Purified HP1 from bacterial (unphosphorylated) and lepidopteran (phosphorylated) cells were analyzed for their secondary structure, and their DNA binding properties were examined using electrophoretic mobility shift assays. To investigate the effect of phosphorylation on HP1's silencing activity, we generated mutant HP1 proteins with serine-to-alanine or serine-to-glutamate substitutions at consensus protein kinase motifs and evaluated their silencing activity in transgenic flies.
Results:
Our results show that HP1 is multiply phosphorylated in vivo, and hyperphosphorylation is correlated with heterochromatin assembly during development. Phosphorylation does not affect HP1's self-association but alters its DNA binding properties, suggesting that phosphorylation regulates HP1-dependent interactions. Moreover, serine-to-alanine and serine-to-glutamate substitutions at consensus protein kinase motifs in HP1 resulted in a reduction or loss of silencing activity in transgenic flies, indicating that dynamic phosphorylation/dephosphorylation regulates HP1 activity in heterochromatic silencing.
Discussion:
Our findings provide evidence that phosphorylation of HP1 plays a crucial role in regulating its activity in heterochromatic silencing. The alteration in DNA binding properties of phosphorylated HP1 suggests that phosphorylation may differentially regulate HP1-dependent interactions. The loss of silencing activity in transgenic flies with mutant HP1 proteins suggests that phosphorylation of HP1 is essential for its function in heterochromatic silencing. These results have implications for our understanding of the regulation of chromatin structure and gene expression.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that phosphorylation of HP1 regulates its activity in heterochromatic silencing. The alteration in DNA binding properties of phosphorylated HP1 suggests that phosphorylation may differentially regulate HP1-dependent interactions. These findings provide new insights into the regulation of chromatin structure and gene expression, and highlight the importance of phosphorylation in the function of HP1 in heterochromatin.

title: Elimination of paternal mitochondria in mouse embryos occurs through autophagic degradation dependent on PARKIN and MUL1
text: A distinctive characteristic of mitochondria is their transmission through the maternal lineage. However, the mechanism by which paternal mitochondria, inherited from sperm, are eliminated from early mammalian embryos is poorly understood. While autophagy has been implicated in nematodes, its conservation in mammals has been debated. Our study reveals that both cultured mouse fibroblasts and pre-implantation embryos employ a shared pathway for the removal of mitochondria through a process called mitophagy. In this process, mitochondria are engulfed by autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes for degradation. The E3 ubiquitin ligases PARKIN and MUL1 play redundant roles in eliminating paternal mitochondria. The process is accompanied by the depolarization of paternal mitochondria and requires the mitochondrial outer membrane protein FIS1, the autophagy adaptor P62, and the PINK1 kinase. Our findings demonstrate that the strict transmission of mitochondria through the maternal line relies on mitophagy and uncover a collaboration between MUL1 and PARKIN in this process.

title: Ribosome Profiling Provides Evidence that Large Noncoding RNAs Do Not Encode Proteins
text:
Large non-coding RNAs are gaining recognition as crucial players in cellular regulation. While earlier studies suggested that these transcripts primarily act as functional RNAs without a corresponding protein product, a recent investigation into ribosome occupancy revealed that many long intergenic non-coding RNAs (lincRNAs) are bound by ribosomes, raising the possibility of protein translation. However, our findings challenge this notion by demonstrating that classical non-coding RNAs and 5' untranslated regions (UTRs) exhibit the same ribosome occupancy as lincRNAs, indicating that ribosome occupancy alone is not sufficient to classify transcripts as coding or non-coding.
Instead, we propose a novel metric based on the known property of translation, where translating ribosomes are released upon encountering a bona fide stop codon. Using this metric, we demonstrate that it accurately distinguishes between protein-coding transcripts and all classes of known non-coding transcripts, including lincRNAs. These results suggest that the majority of lincRNAs do not function through encoded proteins.
In summary, our findings challenge the notion that lincRNAs are translated into proteins, and instead support the idea that they primarily act as functional RNAs. This study highlights the complexity of non-coding RNA regulation and the need for further investigation into their mechanisms of action.

title: Isolation of a Fusion Transcript, AMLl IETO, With Similarity to
text: We have created a genetic map of the chromosome 21 breakpoint region involved in t(8;21)(q22;q22.3) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and isolated a genomic fragment containing material from both chromosomes 8 and 21. Using probes from these regions, we have identified rearrangements in each of nine cases of t(8;21) AML examined. Additionally, we have isolated cDNA clones from a t(8;21) AML cDNA library that contain fused sequences from chromosomes 8 and 21. The chromosome 8 component, referred to as ETO (for eight twenty-one), spans a large genomic region, as suggested by the analysis of corresponding yeast artificial chromosomes (YACs). The DNA sequence of the chromosome 21 portion of the fusion transcript is derived from the normal AML1 gene. We have found a striking similarity (67% identity over 387 bp, with a corresponding 69% amino acid identity) between AML1 and the Drosophila segmentation gene, runt. The result of the translocation is the juxtaposition of 5' sequences of AML1 to 3' sequences of ETO, oriented telomere to centromere on the der(8) chromosome.

title: Treatment of spondyloarthropathy with 5-aminosalicylic acid (mesalazine): an open trial.
text:
OBJECTIVE: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and spondyloarthropathy (SpA) are inflammatory diseases of unknown etiology, and various exogenous and endogenous (inherited) factors contribute to their development. Sulfasalazine (SSZ) is generally accepted as a disease-modifying drug in the treatment of AS and SpA, but the specific component responsible for its efficacy is unclear. Some research suggests that 5-acetylsalicylic acid (5-ASA, mesalazine) may be the active moiety, given its similarity to the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease. To investigate this further, an open pilot study was conducted in two groups of patients with SpA.
METHODS: Twenty patients with SpA who were already taking SSZ were switched to 5-ASA (Pentasa), while 19 patients with active SpA were treated with 5-ASA without previous SSZ administration.
RESULTS: In the first group, 17 (85%) patients showed improved physician global clinical assessment compared to their previous SSZ treatment period. In contrast, the second group showed a statistically significant improvement in erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
CONCLUSION: The results of this study support the hypothesis that 5-ASA may be the active moiety of SSZ in the treatment of SpA.

title: Relationship of physical activity and television watching with body weight and level of fatness among children: results from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
text:
In this study, the relationship between physical inactivity and weight gain in children of different ethnic groups was investigated. The study used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III, which included 4063 children aged 8-16 years. The study found that:
* Only 80% of children reported engaging in vigorous physical activity for at least 3 days per week, with lower rates among non-Hispanic black and Mexican American girls (69% and 73%, respectively).
* Twenty percent of children participated in 2 or fewer bouts of vigorous physical activity per week, with a higher rate among girls (26%) than boys (17%).
* Overall, 26% of children watched 4 or more hours of television per day, with non-Hispanic black children having the highest rate (42%).
* Boys and girls who watched 4 or more hours of television per day had greater body fat and a higher body mass index than those who watched less than 2 hours per day (P < 0.001).

The study's findings suggest that many US children are inactive and that intervention strategies are needed to promote lifelong physical activity and prevent adverse health consequences. The study also highlighted the importance of considering the unique needs and experiences of different ethnic groups in such interventions.

title: Vascular Calcification in Chronic Kidney Disease is Induced by Bone Morphogenetic Protein-2 via a Mechanism Involving the Wnt/β-Catenin Pathway
text:
Background: Vascular calcification (VC), where vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) undergo a transformation into osteoblast-like cells, is a significant risk factor for accelerated atherosclerosis in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Phosphate plays a crucial role in regulating VC.
Methods: We investigated the expression of smooth muscle cell or osteogenesis markers in response to high phosphate concentrations or exogenous bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP-2) in rat VSMCs using qRT-PCR and western blotting. We also measured osteocalcin secretion by radioimmunoassay, differentiated and calcified VSMCs using alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity assay and Alizarin staining, and examined the involvement of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in VSMC calcification and osteoblastic differentiation induced by high phosphate or BMP-2 using short hairpin RNA-mediated silencing of β-catenin. Apoptosis was determined by TUNEL assay and immunofluorescence imaging.
Results: Our results showed that BMP-2 serum levels were significantly higher in CKD patients than in controls. High phosphate concentrations and BMP-2 induced VSMC apoptosis and upregulated the expression of β-catenin, Msx2, Runx2, and the phosphate cotransporter Pit1, while a BMP-2 neutralization antibody reversed these effects. Knockdown of β-catenin abolished the effect of high phosphate and BMP-2 on VSMC apoptosis and calcification.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that BMP-2 plays a crucial role in calcium deposition in VSMCs and VC in CKD patients via a mechanism involving the Wnt/β-catenin pathway.

title: Advances in brain tumor surgery.
text: Advancements in molecular and translational research, oncology, and surgery have given the medical community hope that intrinsic brain tumors may be treatable. Intraoperative imaging and brain mapping enable surgeons to perform operations with increased confidence and safety near sensitive areas of the brain. However, the infiltrating edge of a tumor and microscopic satellite lesions located far from the primary site will never be completely removed by surgery. It is through ongoing research into the delivery of an effective chemotherapy agent that we will eventually find a way to manage the primary cause of treatment failure.

title: Systematic review of controlled clinical trials of gastric lavage in acute organophosphorus pesticide poisoning.
text:
BACKGROUND:
Organophosphorus pesticide (OP) self-poisoning is a significant health problem in developing rural areas worldwide. However, there is limited clinical trial data to guide therapy for OP poisoning, which hinders the identification of the most effective treatment. Despite recognition of adverse effects, gastric lavage is commonly performed in Asia, but its effectiveness has not been extensively studied.
METHOD:
We conducted a systematic search of the literature to identify controlled clinical studies that evaluated the effectiveness of gastric lavage in OP pesticide self-poisoning. We included studies that reported the outcome of gastric lavage in patients with OP poisoning and assessed the quality of the studies using standardized criteria.
RESULTS:
Our search identified 56 studies, all of which were conducted in China. While the majority of studies reported benefits from the intervention, the quality of the studies was poor, with inadequate methodology to assess their quality. The patient population and study treatment protocol were not well-defined, and there was significant variation in case fatality rates between studies (ranging from 4.5% to 93%). None of the studies compared an intervention with no gastric lavage or provided data on the amount of poison removed.
CONCLUSION:
Despite widespread use of gastric lavage for OP pesticide poisoning in Asia, there is currently no high-quality evidence to support its clinical effectiveness. Further research is needed to determine which patients and for how long gastric lavage is effective in removing significant quantities of poison. Large clinical trials will be required to address the safety and effectiveness of gastric lavage, either single or multiple, in acute OP pesticide poisoning.

title: Integrin activation by Fam38A uses a novel mechanism of R-Ras targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum.
text: The integrin family of heterodimeric cell-surface receptors are crucial for cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion. Changes in either integrin-ligand affinity or integrin gene expression are involved in various diseases, including inflammation, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. In our search for novel activators of integrin-ligand affinity, we discovered the previously uncharacterized multi-transmembrane domain protein Fam38A, located at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Silencing Fam38A in epithelial cells leads to reduced cell adhesion by inactivating endogenous beta1 integrin. Fam38A mediates integrin activation by recruiting the small GTPase R-Ras to the ER, which activates the calcium-activated protease calpain by increasing calcium release from cytoplasmic stores. Fam38A-induced integrin activation is blocked by inhibiting either R-Ras or calpain activity or by silencing talin, a well-known calpain substrate. This study uncovers a novel mechanism for integrin activation by Fam38A, involving calpain and R-Ras signaling from the ER. These findings provide the first description of a novel spatial regulator of R-Ras, an alternative integrin activation-suppression pathway based on direct relocalization of R-Ras to the ER, and a mechanism linking R-Ras and calpain signaling from the ER with modulation of integrin-ligand affinity.

title: Convergence of 9-cis retinoic acid and peroxisome proliferator signalling pathways through heterodimer formation of their receptors
text:
Peroxisomes are cytoplasmic organelles that play a crucial role in mammalian lipid metabolism, particularly in the breakdown of long-chain fatty acids and the conversion of cholesterol to bile salts (as reviewed in Refs 1 and 2). Amphipathic carboxylates, such as clofibric acid, have been used in humans as hypolipidemic agents, and in rodents, these compounds stimulate the proliferation of peroxisomes. These agents, known as peroxisome proliferators, along with all-trans retinoic acid, activate genes involved in peroxisomal-mediated β-oxidation of fatty acids (1-4).
Our study shows that the receptor activated by peroxisome proliferators and the retinoid X receptor-α (RXR-α) form a heterodimer that regulates acyl-CoA oxidase gene expression in response to either clofibric acid or RXR-α ligand, 9-cis retinoic acid, a metabolite of all-trans retinoic acid (7,8). Simultaneous exposure to both activators results in a synergistic induction of gene expression, demonstrating the coupling of the peroxisome proliferator and retinoid signaling pathways. These findings provide evidence for a physiological role for 9-cis retinoic acid in modulating lipid metabolism.

title: The Utilization of Extracellular Proteins as Nutrients Is Suppressed by mTORC1
text: Despite the presence of various nutrients, mammalian cells preferentially metabolize glucose and free amino acids for energy and building blocks. Recent research has shown that Ras-induced macropinocytosis of extracellular proteins can reduce the dependence of transformed cells on extracellular glutamine. In this study, we investigate the potential of protein macropinocytosis as a source of essential amino acids. Our findings reveal that lysosomal degradation of extracellular proteins can support cell survival and activate mTORC1, but fail to induce significant cell accumulation. Contrary to its growth-promoting effects under amino-acid-replete conditions, we discovered that mTORC1 activation suppresses proliferation when cells rely on extracellular proteins as an amino acid source. Inhibiting mTORC1 leads to increased catabolism of endocytosed proteins and enhanced cell proliferation during nutrient-depleted conditions in vitro and within vascularly compromised tumors in vivo. These findings suggest that mTORC1 coupling to the availability of free amino acids may have important implications for the use of mTOR inhibitors as therapeutics.

title: A general model to explore complex dominance patterns in plant sporophytic self-incompatibility systems.
text: We created a comprehensive model of sporophytic self-incompatibility under negative frequency-dependent selection, allowing for intricate patterns of dominance among alleles. Using this model, we investigated the impact of various factors on equilibrium allelic frequencies, including the number of dominance classes, the number of alleles per class, the asymmetry in dominance expression between pollen and pistil, and whether selection acts on male or both male and female fitnesses. We discovered that the so-called "recessive effect" occurs in a wide range of situations. Our findings included emerging properties of finite population models with multiple alleles per class, such as higher maintenance of alleles in more dominant classes and the potential evolution of the number of dominance classes. Additionally, we examined the occurrence of homozygous genotypes and found that substantial proportions of these can occur for the most recessive alleles. We applied the model to two species with complex dominance patterns to test whether their allelic frequencies in natural populations match the distribution predicted by our model. Finally, we suggest that the model can be used to explicitly test for additional, allele-specific, selective forces.

title: Metabolic Reprograming in Macrophage Polarization
text: Recent research on the metabolism of immune cells has revealed the close connection between the metabolic state and the phenotype of these cells. Macrophages, in particular, provide a good example of this relationship. The way in which macrophages obtain their energy, either through glycolysis or oxidative metabolism, can lead to different phenotypes. Classically activated or M1 macrophages, which play a key role in the first line of defense against bacterial infections, rely on glycolysis for energy. In contrast, alternatively activated or M2 macrophages, which are involved in tissue repair and wound healing, use oxidative metabolism to fuel their longer-term functions. However, metabolic intermediates are not just a source of energy but can also directly influence the macrophage phenotype. For example, in M1 macrophages, the Krebs cycle intermediate succinate regulates the expression of HIF1α, which in turn drives the sustained production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL1β. In M2 macrophages, the carbohydrate kinase-like protein is critical for regulating the pentose phosphate pathway. The potential to target these events and impact disease is a promising area of research.

title: Characterization of constitutive CTCF/cohesin loci: a possible role in establishing topological domains in mammalian genomes
text:
BACKGROUND: Recent studies have proposed that human and mammalian genomes are divided into large, discrete domains that serve as units of chromosome organization. CTCF, a CCCTC-binding factor, has been shown to play a multifaceted role in genome regulation, including transcriptional regulation, chromosome-boundary insulation, DNA replication, and chromatin packaging. However, it remains unclear whether a subset of CTCF binding sites plays a functional role in establishing and maintaining chromatin topological domains.
RESULTS: To systematically investigate the functional role of CTCF binding sites in establishing and maintaining chromatin topological domains, we analyzed the genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenetic profiles of CTCF binding sites in 56 human cell lines from the ENCODE dataset. We identified approximately 24,000 CTCF binding sites (referred to as constitutive sites) that were bound in more than 90% of the cell lines. Our analysis revealed several key findings:
1. Constitutive CTCF loci were primarily located in constitutive open chromatin regions and often co-localized with constitutive cohesin loci.
2. Most constitutive CTCF loci were distant from transcription start sites and lacked CpG islands, but were enriched with full-spectrum CTCF motifs, including a recently reported 33/34-mer and two potentially novel (22/26-mer) motifs.
3. Notably, most constitutive CTCF loci were present in CTCF-mediated chromatin interactions detected by ChIA-PET, and these pair-wise interactions occurred predominantly within, but not between, topological domains identified by Hi-C.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that constitutive CTCF sites may play a role in organizing and maintaining the recently identified topological domains that are common across most human cells. These results provide new insights into the functional role of CTCF in genome organization and highlight the importance of further investigating the mechanisms underlying chromatin topological domains.

title: Regulation of Bcl-2 expression by HuR in HL60 leukemia cells and A431 carcinoma cells.
text:
The overexpression of the proto-oncogene bcl-2 is known to promote abnormal cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis. The expression of bcl-2 is, in part, regulated by mechanisms that control the stability of its mRNA. Previous studies have identified elements in the 3'-untranslated region of bcl-2 mRNA that play a role in regulating its stability. Specifically, RNA binding proteins such as nucleolin and Ebp1 have been shown to stabilize bcl-2 mRNA in HL60 cells.
In this study, we identify HuR as a component of bcl-2 messenger ribonucleoprotein (mRNP) complexes. RNA coimmunoprecipitation assays demonstrate that HuR binds to bcl-2 mRNA in vivo. Furthermore, we observe an RNA-dependent coprecipitation of HuR and nucleolin, suggesting that these proteins are present in common mRNP complexes. Additionally, in vitro binding assays reveal that nucleolin and HuR bind concurrently to the AU-rich element (ARE) RNA of bcl-2.
Knockdown of HuR in A431 cells leads to a decrease in bcl-2 mRNA and protein levels, and a decreased ratio of bcl-2 mRNA to heterogeneous nuclear RNA in HuR knockdown cells suggests a positive role for HuR in regulating bcl-2 mRNA stability. Recombinant HuR also retards exosome-mediated decay of bcl-2 ARE RNA in extracts of HL60 cells, supporting a role for HuR in the regulation of bcl-2 mRNA stability in these cells. Moreover, the addition of nucleolin and HuR to HL60 cell extracts produces a synergistic protective effect on decay of bcl-2 ARE RNA. Finally, HuR knockdown leads to a redistribution of bcl-2 mRNA from polysomes to monosomes, suggesting a role for HuR in both the regulation of bcl-2 mRNA translation and mRNA stability.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that HuR plays a positive role in regulating the stability of bcl-2 mRNA, and that it may be involved in both the regulation of mRNA translation and mRNA stability. These results provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying the regulation of bcl-2 expression and its role in cancer cell survival.

title: The Worldwide Variation in Avian Clutch Size across Species and Space
text: Across species and environmental gradients, traits such as clutch size exhibit significant variability. Historically, these variations have been investigated through either a comparative or geographic lens, respectively. In this study, we aimed to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the global variation in clutch size by analyzing the trait across 5,290 bird species, excluding brood parasites and pelagic species. We employed a combined model that integrated intrinsic (morphological, behavioral), extrinsic (environmental), and phylogenetic effects to predict up to 68% of the interspecific variation in clutch size. Subsequently, we applied the same species-level model to predict mean clutch size across 2,521 assemblages worldwide, which explained the observed eco-geographic pattern with remarkable accuracy. Our findings highlight the importance of offspring and adult mortality, which are jointly expressed through intrinsic and extrinsic correlates, in shaping clutch size across different species and environmental conditions. This study offers a novel integration of macroecology and comparative biology, providing a global and integrative understanding of the eco-geographic and cross-species variation in a fundamental life-history trait.

title: Diastolic heart failure--abnormalities in active relaxation and passive stiffness of the left ventricle.
text:
BACKGROUND: Patients exhibiting signs and symptoms of heart failure, despite having a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, are categorized as having diastolic heart failure. However, the underlying pathophysiological mechanism responsible for heart failure in these patients remains unclear.
METHODS: We prospectively identified 47 patients who met the diagnostic criteria for definite diastolic heart failure, all of whom exhibited signs and symptoms of heart failure, had a normal ejection fraction, and experienced increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. Ten healthy individuals without any cardiovascular disease served as controls. Left ventricular diastolic function was evaluated using cardiac catheterization and echocardiography.
RESULTS: Our findings revealed that patients with diastolic heart failure exhibited abnormal left ventricular relaxation and increased left ventricular chamber stiffness. Specifically, the mean (+/-SD) time constant for the isovolumic-pressure decline (tau) was longer in the diastolic heart failure group compared to the control group (59+/-14 msec vs. 35+/-10 msec, P=0.01). Additionally, the diastolic pressure-volume relation was shifted up and to the left in the diastolic heart failure group compared to the controls. Furthermore, the corrected left ventricular passive-stiffness constant was significantly higher in the diastolic heart failure group compared to the control group (0.03+/-0.01 vs. 0.01+/-0.01, P<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Our study suggests that patients with heart failure and a normal ejection fraction exhibit significant abnormalities in active relaxation and passive stiffness. These findings indicate that the pathophysiological cause of elevated diastolic pressures and heart failure in these patients is likely due to abnormal diastolic function.

title: The lncRNAs PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are not implicated in castration resistant prostate cancer
text: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been implicated in cancer biology, particularly in prostate cancer, where they contribute to essential cellular functions such as proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. Previous studies have identified lncRNAs, including PCGEM1 and PRNCR1, as potential actors in prostate cancer pathogenesis. However, recent concerns have been raised about the robustness of these findings. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of RNA-sequencing data to investigate whether PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are associated with prostate cancer. Our results show that only PCGEM1, but not PRNCR1, is significantly associated with prostate cancer. We also analyzed a large cohort of over 230 high-risk prostate cancer patients with long-term outcomes data and found that neither gene is associated with poor patient outcomes. Furthermore, we did not observe any evidence of PCGEM1 or PRNCR1 interacting with the androgen receptor (AR), which is a key regulator of prostate cancer growth. Our findings conclusively demonstrate that PCGEM1 and PRNCR1 are not prognostic lncRNAs in prostate cancer and refute suggestions that they interact in AR signaling.

title: p38MAPK controls expression of multiple cell cycle inhibitors and islet proliferation with advancing age.
text: Aging is a multifaceted process that is influenced by genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Recent research has implicated various cell cycle inhibitors in the aging process, but little is known about the upstream signals that trigger their expression. To investigate the role of p38MAPK in aging, we generated a dominant-negative allele (p38(AF)) by mutating the activating phosphorylation sites Thr180 and Tyr182. Heterozygous p38(AF) mice exhibited attenuated p38-dependent signaling and reduced expression of cell cycle inhibitors in various organs, including the pancreatic islets. As a result, aged p38(AF/+) mice showed enhanced proliferation and regeneration of islets compared to wild-type littermates. Concurrently, we observed an age-related decline in the expression of the p38-specific phosphatase Wip1. Wip1-deficient mice displayed decreased islet proliferation, while Wip1 overexpression restored aging-related decline in proliferation and regenerative capacity. These findings suggest that modulating p38MAPK activity may provide novel therapeutic strategies for treating certain age-related degenerative diseases.

title: ACTA PSYCHIATRICA
text:
Objective:
This study aimed to investigate the subjective effects associated with various antipsychotic medications, including olanzapine, risperidone, and older antipsychotics, as reported by individuals who have taken these drugs.
Method:
A content analysis of an internet database of comments about prescribed medications was conducted to identify and analyze the subjective effects of these antipsychotic medications. A total of 223 comments on risperidone, 170 on olanzapine, and 46 relating to three older antipsychotics were analyzed.
Results:
The analysis revealed that the predominant subjective effects associated with all drugs were sedation, cognitive impairment, and emotional flattening or indifference. Additionally, connections were found between these effects and Parkinsonian-like symptoms with the older drugs, sexual impairment with risperidone, and metabolic effects with olanzapine. The experience of akathisia was frequently linked to suicidal thoughts. Some respondents also reported that the drugs' subjective effects helped to reduce symptoms of mania, psychosis, and anxiety.
Conclusion:
While the generalizability of internet data may be uncertain, the findings of this study suggest that adverse subjective effects are a central aspect of the experience of taking antipsychotic medications and may be related to the desired therapeutic benefits. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the complex relationship between subjective effects and therapeutic outcomes in antipsychotic treatment.

title: White matter hyperintensities are a core feature of Alzheimer's disease: Evidence from the dominantly inherited Alzheimer network.
text:
Objective: To investigate the severity and distribution of white matter hyperintensities (WMHs) in presymptomatic individuals with genetic mutations that predispose them to develop Alzheimer's disease (AD).
Methods: The study included 299 participants from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network, with 184 carrying mutations associated with AD and 115 noncarrier controls. MRI data were analyzed to assess total and regional WMH volumes, and mixed-effects piece-wise linear regression was used to examine differences between carriers and noncarriers with respect to estimated years from expected symptom onset (EYO).
Results: Mutation carriers had greater total WMH volumes, which appeared to increase approximately 6 years before expected symptom onset. The effects were most prominent in the parietal and occipital lobes, which showed divergent effects as early as 22 years before estimated onset.
Interpretation: The findings suggest that WMHs may be a core feature of AD, a potential therapeutic target, and a factor that should be integrated into pathogenic models of the disease. These results indicate that WMHs may contribute to the development of AD well before expected symptom onset, and highlight the importance of considering WMHs in the diagnosis and treatment of AD.

title: Maternal and child undernutrition: consequences for adult health and human capital
text: In this study, we investigate the associations between maternal and child undernutrition and their long-term effects on adult health and disease in low-income and middle-income countries. We analyzed data from five prospective cohort studies in Brazil, Guatemala, India, the Philippines, and South Africa and found that indices of maternal and child undernutrition, such as maternal height and birthweight, were linked to adult outcomes such as height, schooling, income, and offspring birthweight. We also conducted systematic reviews of studies from low-income and middle-income countries for various adult disease indicators, including blood lipids, cardiovascular disease, lung and immune function, cancers, osteoporosis, and mental illness. Our findings suggest that undernutrition in childhood is associated with increased risk of adult disease, including high blood pressure, glucose concentrations, and harmful lipid profiles. Additionally, we found that rapid postnatal weight gain, particularly after infancy, is linked to these conditions. We also noted that birthweight is positively associated with lung function and the incidence of some cancers, and undernutrition may be associated with mental illness. Our study suggests that preventing undernutrition in early life can have important health, educational, and economic benefits.

title: Ubiquitin-dependent intramembrane rhomboid protease promotes ERAD of membrane proteins.
text: The ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway acts as a crucial cellular defense mechanism by directing misfolded and unassembled proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the proteasome. However, the components involved in ERAD of membrane proteins remain largely unexplored. Our study reveals that the evolutionarily conserved rhomboid family protein RHBDL4 functions as a ubiquitin-dependent ER-resident intramembrane protease, which is upregulated upon ER stress. RHBDL4 specifically targets single-spanning and polytopic membrane proteins with unstable transmembrane helices, leading to their degradation through the conventional ERAD machinery. Interestingly, RHBDL4 binds the AAA+-ATPase p97, suggesting that proteolytic processing and cytosolic dislocation are functionally linked. The evolutionary relationship between rhomboids and the ERAD factor derlin suggests that substrates for intramembrane proteolysis and protein dislocation are recruited through a shared mechanism.

title: Detection and function of nitric oxide during the hypersensitive response in Arabidopsis thaliana: where there's a will there's a way.
text: Twenty years ago, nitric oxide (NO) was identified as a crucial player in plant defense responses. Since then, a substantial amount of evidence has accumulated, supporting NO's role as a signaling molecule. However, there are still discrepancies in current NO detection assays, and the enzymatic pathways responsible for its synthesis remain unclear. This has led to heated debates regarding the function of NO in plants, with some questioning its existence in planta. To address these questions, we analyzed data obtained using the model pathosystem Arabidopsis/Pseudomonas, which demonstrates NO production during the hypersensitive response and confirms its role as a trigger of hypersensitive cell death and a mediator of defense gene expression. Additionally, we explored potential sources of NO synthesis, with a focus on the role of nitrite as the primary substrate for NO production during incompatible interactions.

title: The Cytosolic Chaperonin CCT/TRiC and Cancer Cell Proliferation
text: The molecular chaperone CCT/TRiC plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular proteostasis by facilitating the folding of key cytoskeletal proteins, such as tubulins and actins. Additionally, CCT/TRiC is involved in the folding of oncoproteins like cyclin E, Von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein, cyclin B, and p21(ras). These findings suggest that CCT/TRiC may play a role in cell proliferation and tumorigenesis. To investigate this further, we analyzed the expression levels and activity of CCT/TRiC in 18 cancer and one non-cancer human cell lines, as well as in a non-cancer human liver tissue. Our results show that CCT/TRiC expression levels are higher in cancer cell lines compared to normal cells, but its activity does not always correlate with expression levels. We also examined the expression levels of CCT/TRiC modulators and partners, such as PhLP3, Hop/P60, prefoldin, and Hsc/Hsp70. Our findings reveal a complex interplay between molecular chaperones that may contribute to the precise regulation of CCT/TRiC activity in cell proliferation by modulating the availability of client proteins. Our study provides novel insights into the role of CCT/TRiC-mediated protein folding machinery in cancer cell development.

title: RBP2 Belongs to a Family of Demethylases, Specific for Tri-and Dimethylated Lysine 4 on Histone 3
text:
Histone methylation has long been considered a stable epigenetic marker that defines the cell's transcriptional program. However, recent discoveries have challenged this notion, revealing that histone demethylases can erase these marks and reprogram gene expression. Here, we investigate the role of the JARID1 protein family in histone demethylation and its impact on development.
We demonstrate that the JARID1 proteins RBP2, PLU1, and SMCX are histone demethylases that specifically target di- and trimethylated histone 3 lysine 4 (H3K4). These findings are consistent with the known role of the JARID1 homolog Lid in regulating expression of homeotic genes during Drosophila development. In embryonic stem (ES) cells, we show that RBP2 is displaced from Hox genes during differentiation, coinciding with an increase in H3K4me3 levels and expression. Similarly, mutation or RNAi depletion of the C. elegans JARID1 homolog rbr-2 leads to increased H3K4me3 levels during larval development and defects in vulva formation.
Taken together, these results suggest that H3K4me3/me2 demethylation regulated by the JARID1 family plays a crucial role in developmental processes. This challenges the notion of histone methylation as a stable epigenetic marker and highlights the dynamic nature of epigenetic regulation.

title: Mitochondria: Dynamic Organelles in Disease, Aging, and Development
text: Mitochondria are the primary energy-producing structures in most eukaryotic cells, and they also play a role in various other cellular processes, including calcium signaling and programmed cell death (apoptosis). Given their essential functions, it would be reasonable to assume that mitochondrial dysfunction would lead to a consistent and predictable set of defects across all tissues. However, the effects of mitochondrial dysfunction in multicellular organisms are actually quite complex and far-reaching. Despite significant progress in understanding the basic biology of mitochondria, much remains to be discovered. Recent research has highlighted the importance of mitochondrial dynamics, including fusion and fission, in both development and disease.

title: Persistence of HIV-1 Receptor-Positive Cells after HSV-2 Reactivation: A Potential Mechanism for Increased HIV-1 Acquisition
text: To investigate the mechanism by which herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 infection contributes to HIV-1 acquisition, we conducted in-situ analysis of the cellular infiltrate from sequential biopsies of HSV-2 lesions from patients treated and untreated with antiviral therapy. Our findings revealed that CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells, as well as a mixture of plasmacytoid and myeloid dendritic cells (DCs), including those expressing the C-type lectin receptor DC-SIGN, persisted at sites of HSV-2 reactivation for extended periods of time, even with daily antiviral therapy. Of particular note, the CD4(+) T cells that persisted were found to recognize HSV-2 antigen, were enriched for expression of the chemokine receptor CCR5, and were in close proximity to DCs expressing the interleukin-3 receptor CD123 or DC-SIGN. Ex vivo infection with a CCR5-tropic strain of HIV-1 revealed higher levels of integrated HIV-1 DNA in cells derived from healed genital lesion biopsies compared to cells from control skin biopsies. These findings suggest that the persistence and concentration of HIV receptor-positive inflammatory cells in the genital area may contribute to the inability of anti-HSV-2 therapy to reduce HIV acquisition.

title: Chronic daily headache in Taipei, Taiwan: prevalence, follow-up and outcome predictors.
text: In Taipei, Taiwan, we conducted a two-stage, population-based survey of individuals aged 15 or older to investigate chronic daily headaches (CDH). Among the 3377 participants, 108 (3.2%) met the criteria for CDH, with a higher prevalence among women (4.3%) than men (1.9%). The most common subtype was tension-type headache (TM, 55%), followed by chronic tension-type headache (CTTH, 44%). Forty-three percent of CDH subjects overused analgesics. At the 2-year follow-up, 35% of CDH subjects still had CDH, with older age (>40 years, RR = 2.4), CDH onset after 32 years (RR = 1.8), CDH duration >6 years (RR = 2.0), medication overuse (RR = 1.8), and "daily" headache (RR = 2.1) as significant predictors for persistent CDH. Our findings suggest that CDH is not uncommon in the general population and that older individuals and those who overuse medication may have a more prolonged illness course.

title: In vivo microtubules are copolymers of available beta-tubulin isotypes: localization of each of six vertebrate beta-tubulin isotypes using polyclonal antibodies elicited by synthetic peptide antigens
text: In higher animals, the gene encoding beta-tubulin is composed of a small multigene family containing approximately seven functional genes. These genes produce a family of closely related but distinct polypeptide isotypes, each distinguished by specific sequences within the carboxy-terminal 15 amino acid residues. By immunizing rabbits with synthetic peptides corresponding to these variable domain sequences, we have now generated polyclonal antibodies specific for each of six distinct isotypes. The specificity of each antiserum has been unequivocally demonstrated through binding to bacterially produced, cloned proteins representing each isotype, as well as through the inhibition of binding by preincubation with the immunizing peptide but not with heterologous peptides. Quantitative measurement of the amount of each beta-tubulin isotype present in soluble and polymer forms in various cells has been achieved through protein blotting using cloned, isotypically pure polypeptides. However, no bias towards preferential assembly of any isotype has been observed. Indirect immunofluorescence localization of each isotype in three different cell types has revealed that in vivo, each class of microtubules visible by light microscopy is composed of copolymers of all isotypes expressed in a single cell.

title: Topiramate for smoking cessation: a randomized, placebo-controlled pilot study.
text:
INTRODUCTION: Topiramate (TOP) is a drug that blocks glutamate receptors and enhances GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) neurotransmission, which may help with smoking cessation. In this study, we compared the effects of behavioral counseling combined with TOP, TOP/nicotine patch (TOP/NIC), or placebo (PLC) on smoking cessation.
METHODS: We conducted a 10-week randomized trial in which subjects and research personnel were blinded to TOP versus PLC, but not to the TOP/NIC patch condition. In groups receiving TOP, the medication dosage was gradually titrated up to 200 mg/day. The smoking quit date (QD) was scheduled after 2 weeks of medication treatment, and nicotine patches (21 mg) were started on the QD in subjects randomized to the TOP/NIC condition. The main outcome measure was the end-of-treatment, 4-week continuous abstinence rate (CAR), which was biochemically confirmed.
RESULTS: A total of 57 subjects were randomized to treatment. The 4-week CAR was 5% in the PLC group, 26% in the TOP group, and 37% in the TOP/NIC group (p = .056). Pairwise comparisons showed a significant difference between TOP/NIC and PLC (p = .042) and a nonsignificant difference between TOP and PLC (p = .18). The PLC group gained 0.37 lb/week, while the TOP group lost 0.41 lb/week, and the TOP/NIC group lost 0.07 lb/week (p = .004). Pairwise comparisons showed a significant difference between TOP and PLC (p < .001) and between TOP/NIC and PLC (p = .035). Paresthesia was more frequent in subjects on TOP than PLC (p = .011).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that TOP, either alone or in combination with the NIC, resulted in a numerically higher quit rate than PLC and decreased weight. However, a larger, PLC-controlled trial is needed to confirm these findings.

title: Break-induced DNA replication.
text: Recombination-dependent DNA replication, also known as break-induced replication (BIR), was initially thought to be a mechanism exclusive to bacteriophage, but recent discoveries have shown that it plays a crucial role in repairing double-strand chromosome breaks in eukaryotes. This mechanism appears to be essential in restarting stalled and broken replication forks and maintaining the integrity of eroded telomeres. While BIR helps preserve genome integrity during replication, it also leads to genome instability through the production of loss of heterozygosity, nonreciprocal translocations, and complex chromosomal rearrangements.

title: The state of US health, 1990-2010: burden of diseases, injuries, and risk factors.
text:
Understanding the major health problems in the United States and how they change over time is crucial for informing national health policy. To measure the burden of diseases, injuries, and leading risk factors in the US from 1990 to 2010 and compare them with those of 34 countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), we used a systematic analysis of descriptive epidemiology that included 291 diseases and injuries, 1160 sequelae, and 67 risk factors or clusters of risk factors.
We found that life expectancy at birth and healthy life expectancy (HALE) in the US increased from 1990 to 2010, with a slight increase in the number of years lived with disability (YLDs). However, the US ranked 27th out of 34 OECD countries in terms of age-standardized death rate, 28th in terms of age-standardized YLL rate, 6th in terms of age-standardized YLD rate, 27th in terms of life expectancy at birth, and 26th in terms of HALE.
The leading risk factors related to DALYs were dietary risks, tobacco smoking, high body mass index, high blood pressure, high fasting plasma glucose, physical inactivity, and alcohol use. As the US population has aged, YLDs have comprised a larger share of DALYs than have YLLs.
Our findings suggest that while the US has made substantial progress in improving health, morbidity and chronic disability now account for nearly half of the US health burden, and improvements in population health in the US have not kept pace with advances in population health in other wealthy nations.

title: Malaria risk perception, knowledge and prophylaxis practices among travellers of African ethnicity living in Paris and visiting their country of origin in sub-Saharan Africa.
text: An observational prospective cohort study investigated malaria risk perception, knowledge, and preventive practices among African ethnic individuals living in Paris and traveling to their country of origin to visit friends or relatives (VFR). The study compared two groups of VFR who had visited a travel clinic (TC; n=122) or a travel agency (TA; n=69) before departure. Of the 47% of VFR who perceived malaria as a health concern, 75% recognized that malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes and that bed nets are an effective preventive measure. Perception of high malaria risk was higher in the TA group (33%) than in the TC group (7%). Only 35% of VFR mentioned the availability of a malaria vaccine, with many confusing it with yellow fever vaccine. Twenty-nine percent of VFR took adequate chemoprophylaxis with complete adherence, which was higher among the TC group (41%) than the TA group (12%). Effective antivector protection measures used included bed nets (16%), wearing long clothes at night (14%), and air conditioning (8%), with no significant differences between the study groups except for the use of impregnated bed nets (11% of the TC group and none of the TA group). The study suggests that improving media coverage, malaria chemoprophylaxis repayment, and cultural adaptation of preventive messages can help reduce the high rate of inadequate malaria prophylaxis in VFR.

title: Effect modification by population dietary folate on the association between MTHFR genotype, homocysteine, and stroke risk: a meta-analysis of genetic studies and randomised trials
text:
The MTHFR 677C→T polymorphism has been linked to elevated homocysteine levels and an increased risk of stroke. Previous research showed that the effects were most pronounced in areas with low dietary folate intake, but it was difficult to disentangle the effects of folate and small study bias. To address this limitation, we conducted a genetic analysis and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to investigate whether folate status modifies the association between MTHFR 677C→T and stroke risk.
We collaborated with 237 genetic studies that included 59,995 individuals and 20,885 stroke events. We compared the genetic findings with a meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials of homocysteine-lowering treatments and stroke risk (45,549 individuals, 2314 stroke events, 269 transient ischemic attacks).
Our findings revealed that the effect of the MTHFR 677C→T variant on homocysteine levels was larger in areas with low folate intake (Asia) than in regions with folate fortification (America, Australia, and New Zealand). The odds ratio (OR) for stroke was also higher in Asia than in these regions. Most randomized trials took place in areas with high or increasing population folate concentrations. The summary relative risk (RR) of stroke in trials of homocysteine-lowering interventions was similar to that predicted for the same extent of homocysteine reduction in large genetic studies in populations with similar folate status. However, the predicted effect of homocysteine reduction from large genetic studies in low folate regions (Asia) was larger (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.90), suggesting that lowering homocysteine levels may have a greater protective effect in these areas.
However, no trial has evaluated the effect of lowering homocysteine levels on stroke risk exclusively in a low folate region. In regions with increasing levels or established policies of population folate supplementation, the evidence from genetic studies and randomized trials suggests that there is no benefit from lowering homocysteine levels for preventing stroke. Further large-scale genetic studies of the association between MTHFR 677C→T and stroke in low folate settings are needed to distinguish effect modification by folate from small-study bias. If future randomized trials of homocysteine-lowering interventions for stroke prevention are undertaken, they should take place in regions with low folate consumption.
Funding for this research was provided by full funding sources listed at the end of the paper (see Acknowledgments).

title: Porcine circovirus type 2 DNA influences cytoskeleton rearrangements in plasmacytoid and monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
text: Functional disruption of dendritic cells (DC) by viral pathogens is a crucial strategy employed by these microorganisms to evade host immune defenses. In particular, porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2), a single-stranded DNA virus, impairs the activation of both plasmacytoid DC (pDC) and conventional DC by certain viruses or Toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands. This inhibitory capacity is attributed to the viral DNA, although the impairment does not affect all signaling cascades; TLR7 ligation by small chemical molecules will still induce the secretion of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α, but not interferon-α or IL-12. In this investigation, the molecular mechanisms underlying silencing were explored. PP2, a potent inhibitor of the Lyn and Hck kinases, produced a similar profile to the PCV2 DNA interference with cytokine secretion by pDC, effectively inhibiting cell activation induced through TLR9 ligation, but not through TLR7 ligation. Confocal microscopy and cytometry analysis strongly suggested that PCV2 DNA impairs actin polymerization and endocytosis in pDC and monocyte-derived DC, respectively. This study provides the first insight into the particular molecular mechanisms involved in PCV2 interference with DC danger recognition, which may be responsible for the virus-induced immunosuppression observed in infected pigs.

title: Sympathetic neural and cardiovascular responses during static handgrip exercise in women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy
text:
Women who have had hypertensive pregnancies are at a higher risk of experiencing cardiovascular events in the future, but the underlying mechanisms are unknown. However, research suggests that an exercise challenge can reveal hidden hypertensive tendencies, putting individuals at the greatest risk of developing cardiovascular disease. In a recent study, the authors examined whether women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy exhibit an enhanced exercise pressor response compared to women with a history of healthy pregnancies.
The study included 9 normotensive women with a history of healthy pregnancy (the "CON" group) and 12 women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy (the "HP+" group) who were studied during the mid-luteal phase of their menstrual cycle. The researchers measured heart rate (HR), systolic and diastolic blood pressure (SBP, DBP), and muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) during a cold pressor test (CPT), as well as after a period of recovery, during static handgrip to fatigue (SHG), and post-exercise circulatory arrest (PECA).
The results showed that the BP, HR, and MSNA responses to the CPT were similar between groups. However, during the SHG and PECA tests, the DBP and HR were significantly higher in the HP+ group compared to the CON group (both p < 0.05). Additionally, MSNA burst frequency tended to be elevated in the HP+ group during the stressor (peak Δ from baseline 31 ± 13 vs. 23 ± 13 bursts/min; p = 0.06). These findings suggest that women with a history of hypertensive pregnancy exhibit an enhanced cardiovascular reactivity to an exercise stimulus, which may indicate impaired cardiovascular control that precedes the clinical manifestation of hypertension or cardiovascular events.

title: Exercise and the immune system: regulation, integration, and adaptation.
text: Stress-induced immunological responses to exercise have prompted extensive research in the fields of stress immunology and neuroimmunology. It is suggested that exercise can serve as a model of temporary immunosuppression that occurs after severe physical stress, and this model can be easily manipulated in experimental settings to study the interactions between the nervous, endocrine, and immune systems. This review focuses on the mechanisms underlying exercise-induced immune changes, including neuroendocrinological factors such as catecholamines, growth hormone, cortisol, beta-endorphin, and sex steroids. Additionally, the review examines the metabolic link between skeletal muscles and the lymphoid system and discusses the mechanisms of exercise-associated muscle damage and the initiation of the inflammatory cytokine cascade. Given the ability of exercise to modulate the immune system in healthy individuals, the review also considers the clinical implications of exercise in the prevention of diseases for which the immune system plays a role. Drawing on both experimental, clinical, and epidemiological literature, the review addresses the interactions between exercise and infectious diseases as well as exercise and neoplasia within the context of aging and nutrition.

title: Positive feedback between PU.1 and the cell cycle controls myeloid differentiation.
text:
Regulatory gene circuits with positive-feedback loops play a crucial role in controlling stem cell differentiation. However, the mechanisms underlying positive feedback in these circuits can vary. In this study, we investigate the feedback mechanisms by which the transcription factor PU.1 regulates lymphoid and myeloid differentiation.
Using quantitative live-cell imaging, we found that developing B cells exhibit a decrease in PU.1 levels through a decrease in PU.1 transcription, while developing macrophages display an increase in PU.1 levels through elongation of their cell cycles, resulting in stable PU.1 accumulation. Interestingly, exogenous PU.1 expression in progenitors leads to increased endogenous PU.1 levels by inducing cell cycle lengthening, suggesting a positive feedback loop between the regulatory factor and the cell cycle.
Mathematical modeling revealed that this cell cycle-coupled feedback architecture is effective in stabilizing a slow-dividing differentiated state. These findings demonstrate that cell cycle duration serves as an integral component of a positive autoregulatory circuit, controlling cell fate.
In summary, our results provide insight into the mechanisms of positive feedback in regulatory gene circuits, highlighting the importance of cell cycle duration in controlling stem cell differentiation. The findings also suggest that positive feedback loops play a crucial role in maintaining the differentiated state of cells, and may be a general mechanism for controlling cell fate in various biological processes.

title: Peripheral B cell subsets.
text: Our comprehension of the origins and biological functions of distinct peripheral B cell subsets is still evolving. While some progress has been made in elucidating the synergy between B cell receptor (BCR)-derived signals and other receptors and signaling pathways that regulate the development of follicular, marginal zone, and B-1 B cells, this complex issue remains poorly understood. Recent research has shed light on the origins of B-1 and B-2 B cells, the ability of follicular B cells to mature in both the bone marrow and spleen, the existence of a defined precursor for marginal zone B cells, and the dual niche occupancy of follicular B cells.

title: Human IL-10 is produced by both type 1 helper (Th1) and type 2 helper (Th2) T cell clones and inhibits their antigen-specific proliferation and cytokine production.
text: In this study, the expression of the IL-10 gene and protein was investigated in both Th1 and Th2 CD4+ T cell clones using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), respectively. Although Th2 clones showed higher levels of IL-10 mRNA, IL-10 mRNA was consistently found in Th1 clones as well. Both Th1 and Th2 clones also produced measurable levels of IL-10 in their supernatants. The effect of human IL-10 (h-IL-10) and viral IL-10 (v-IL-10) on the proliferative response and cytokine production of Th1 and Th2 clones was then investigated. Addition of h-IL-10 and v-IL-10 to culture significantly reduced the proliferation of both Th1 and Th2 clones in response to specific antigen (Ag) and phytohemagglutinin (PHA), but had no inhibitory effect on the proliferative response of Th1 and Th2 clones to interleukin-2 (IL-2). h-IL-10 and v-IL-10 also inhibited the Ag-induced production of interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) by Th1 clones and the production of interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-5 (IL-5) by Th2 clones, whereas they had no effect on cytokine synthesis by the same clones stimulated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) plus anti-CD3 antibody. Interestingly, preincubation of antigen-presenting cells (APC) with h-IL-10 resulted in the inhibition of Ag-induced proliferation of both Th1 and Th2 clones, suggesting that h-IL-10 primarily affects APC. These findings demonstrate that, unlike the murine system where IL-10 is primarily produced by Th2 cells and inhibits the Th1 response, in the human system, IL-10 is produced by and inhibits the function of both Th1 and Th2 cells.

title: Evaluating strategies for improving ovarian response of the poor responder undergoing assisted reproductive techniques.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of various controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) regimens in improving fertility outcomes in women who have been defined as poor responders in previous cycles of assisted reproductive techniques (ART).
Design: Literature review
Patients: Women who have been identified as poor responders to standard COH regimens and are preparing for ART.
Intervention: A range of COH regimens are reviewed, including:
* Increased gonadotropin doses
* Change of gonadotropins
* Adjunctive growth hormone (GH)
* Luteal phase (long) GnRH agonist (GnRH-a) initiation
* Early follicular phase (flare) GnRH-a initiation
* Low-dose luteal phase (ultrashort) GnRH-a initiation
* Progestin pretreatment
* Microdose flare GnRH-a initiation

Main Outcome Measures:

* Maximum serum E2 levels
* Follicular development
* Dose and duration of gonadotropin therapy
* Cycle cancellation rates
* Oocytes retrieved
* Embryos transferred
* Clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates

Results: The lack of a standard definition of poor responders and the absence of large-scale prospective randomized trials make it challenging to draw definitive conclusions. However, the strategies that appear to be more consistently beneficial are microdose GnRH-a flare and late luteal phase initiation of a short course of low-dose GnRH-a discontinued before COH.

Conclusion(s): No single COH regimen will benefit all poor responders. Establishing uniform definitions and conducting large-scale prospective randomized trials are crucial. Developing a reliable precycle screen will enable the effective differentiation of normal responders, poor responders, and those who will not conceive with their own oocytes.

title: Identification and Functional Characterization of N-Terminally Acetylated Proteins in Drosophila melanogaster
text: Protein modifications play a crucial role in various biological processes across living organisms. Amino-terminal acetylation of proteins is a ubiquitous modification found throughout the tree of life, where the N-terminus of a nascent polypeptide chain is co-translationally acetylated after the removal of the initiating methionine residue. Despite extensive research on the enzymes and protein complexes involved in these processes, little is known about the biological function of these N-terminal modification events. To uncover common principles of N-terminal acetylation, we analyzed the amino-terminal peptides from proteins extracted from Drosophila Kc167 cells, detecting over 1,200 mature protein N-termini. Our findings revealed that N-terminal acetylation occurs with similar frequency in insects as in humans. As the sole determinant for N-terminal acetylation, we extracted the (X)PX rule, which indicates the prevention of acetylation under all circumstances. This rule can be used to genetically engineer a protein to study the biological relevance of the presence or absence of an acetyl group, thereby generating a generic assay to probe the functional importance of N-terminal acetylation. We applied the assay by expressing mutated proteins as transgenes in cell lines and in flies, providing a straightforward strategy to systematically study the functional relevance of N-terminal acetylations in cells and whole organisms. Since the (X)PX rule appears to be of general validity in both lower and higher eukaryotes, we propose that it can be used to investigate the function of N-terminal acetylation in all species.

title: Bax translocation and mitochondrial fragmentation induced by Helicobacter pylori.
text:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Previous in vitro and in vivo studies have shown an association between Helicobacter pylori infection and apoptosis in gastric epithelial cells. However, the exact mechanisms underlying this process are not fully understood, particularly with regards to the role of the mitochondria. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate whether Bax translocation and mitochondrial fragmentation occur in gastric epithelial cells upon exposure to H pylori, leading to cell death.
METHODS: The study used human gastric adenocarcinoma (AGS) cells, AGS cells transfected with the HPV-E6 gene (which inactivates p53 function), AGS-neo cells (transfected with the backbone construct), mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), and p19(ARF) null (ARF(-/-)) MEFs. Cells were incubated with a cag positive H pylori strain for up to 24 hours, and cytoplasmic and mitochondrial membrane fractions were analyzed by western blot for Bax translocation.
RESULTS: Bax translocation was detected in AGS, AGS-neo, and normal MEF cells after exposure to H pylori for three hours, but not in ARF(-/-) MEFs cells. Translocation of Bax after H pylori incubation was also detected in AGS-E6 cells (inactive p53 gene) but to a lesser degree than in AGS-neo cells. In parallel studies, the mitochondrial morphology of living cells infected with H pylori was assessed by confocal microscopy. Mitochondrial fragmentation was detectable after 10 hours of H pylori incubation with AGS cells and after seven hours with MEF cells. In wild-type MEFs, mitochondrial fragmentation was significantly increased in comparison with ARF null MEFs (43% v 10.4%, respectively). Furthermore, mitochondrial depolarisation and caspase-3 activity were initiated within four hours in cells incubated with H pylori, and these events were inhibited by forced expression of Bcl-2.
CONCLUSIONS: These data suggest that during H pylori-induced apoptosis, Bax translocates to the mitochondria, which subsequently undergo depolarization and profound fragmentation. Functional ARF and p53 proteins may play an important role in H pylori-induced mitochondrial modification.

title: Cancer chemoprevention: a rapidly evolving field
text: Cancer chemoprevention involves the long-term administration of synthetic, natural, or biological agents to prevent or delay the onset of cancer. Recent trials have shown the effectiveness of this approach in breast, prostate, and colon cancer.
