The way new chemopreventive agents are developed has changed significantly over the past decade, with a greater emphasis on thorough preclinical testing of agents before moving to clinical trials, and a focus on identifying biomarkers of activity that can be used to predict early efficacy. This review will provide an overview of the current state of chemoprevention and highlight potential new developments in the field.

title: Dengue is still an imported disease in China: a case study in Guangzhou.
text:
Dengue virus, consisting of four serotypes (DENV 1-4), infects approximately 390 million people worldwide annually, with the majority of cases occurring in tropical and subtropical regions. Due to continuous introductions of DENV from epidemic areas and favorable weather conditions, many regions have transitioned from hypo-endemicity to hyper-endemicity over the past few decades. Since the first dengue outbreak in 1978, it is crucial to assess the current situation in China over nearly 40 years. The purpose of this study was to determine whether dengue is endemic in China, which is essential for implementing effective dengue control and prevention strategies.
The study combined epidemiological data from the disease notification system, phylogenetic, and phylogeographic analyses in Guangzhou, China, which revealed the presence of all four serotypes. The Maximum Likelihood tree analysis showed that the viruses detected in Guangzhou were grouped into different clades, except for the viruses from 2002 and 2003, which clustered together. There was evidence of mutual introductions between Guangzhou and Southeast Asia, with most of the viruses being imported from Southeast Asia, and the sources of outbreaks in Guangzhou primarily originating from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
The study indicates that dengue in China remains an imported disease, with the possibility of localization.

title: The UNAIDS Estimation and Projection Package: a software package to estimate and project national HIV epidemics.
text: This paper outlines the Estimation and Projection Package (EPP), a software tool for estimating and projecting HIV prevalence levels in countries with generalized epidemics. The paper provides an overview of the software's interface and functionality, as well as the process of defining and modeling a national epidemic using locally relevant sub-epidemics and four epidemiological parameters to fit a curve and produce prevalence trends. The paper also includes an example of using the EPP in a country with a generalized epidemic and discusses the software's strengths and limitations, as well as future development plans.

title: Oncolytic adenovirus armed with IL-24 Inhibits the growth of breast cancer in vitro and in vivo
text:
Background: Interleukin-24 (IL-24) is a cytokine belonging to the IL-10 family, which has been shown to selectively induce cancer cell apoptosis, making it a promising strategy for cancer gene therapy.
Methods: To investigate the potential of IL-24 as a cancer treatment, we constructed a recombinant type five adenovirus (CNHK600-IL24) containing the IL-24 gene. The virus was tested for its ability to replicate only in tumor cells by assessing its replication in breast tumor cells (MDA-MB-231) and normal fibroblasts (MRC-5) using TCID50 and MTT assays. Additionally, the secretion of IL-24 was measured using ELISA and western blotting. The in vivo anti-tumor effect of CNHK600-IL24 was evaluated in nude mice carrying orthotopic or metastatic breast tumors.
Results: Our results showed that CNHK600-IL24 could efficiently replicate and result in high levels of IL-24 expression, leading to massive cell death in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells but not in MRC-5 normal fibroblasts. In addition, administration of CNHK600-IL24 to nude mice with orthotopic breast tumors significantly suppressed tumor growth, while treatment of mice with metastatic breast tumors resulted in improved survival compared to mice treated with a virus expressing EGFP. This effect was also observed in mice with metastatic tumors injected into the left ventricle.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that the oncolytic adenovirus armed with IL-24 is a promising candidate for virotherapy of breast cancer, exhibiting enhanced anti-tumor activity and improved survival compared to the virus expressing EGFP. Further studies are warranted to fully explore the potential of IL-24 as a cancer treatment.

title: Brain stem and cerebellar hyperintense lesions in migraine.
text:
Background and Purpose:
Migraineurs are at a higher risk of developing cerebellar infarcts and supratentorial white matter lesions. However, the prevalence, frequency, and distribution of infratentorial hyperintense lesions in migraine remain unknown.
Methods:
We conducted an MRI study on 295 migraineurs (161 with aura, 134 without aura, and 140 controls) aged 30-60 years from a population-based sample. Infratentorial hyperintensities were identified in 4.4% of migraineurs and 0.7% of controls (P=0.04). The majority of the hyperintensities were bilateral and located in the dorsal basis pontis. Migraineurs with infratentorial hyperintensities were found to have supratentorial white matter lesions more frequently.
Results:
We found an increased prevalence of infratentorial (predominantly pontine) hyperintensities in migraineurs from the general population. This extends the understanding of vulnerable brain regions and types of lesions in migraine brains. A hemodynamic ischemic pathogenesis is likely, but further research is needed.
Conclusions:
Our study revealed an increased prevalence of infratentorial hyperintensities in migraineurs from the general population. This finding suggests that the brain regions in migraineurs are more susceptible to ischemic damage, which may be related to hemodynamic changes. Further research is needed to elucidate the underlying pathophysiology.

title: NDRG1 promotes growth of hepatocellular carcinoma cells by directly interacting with GSK-3β and Nur77 to prevent β-catenin degradation
text: The N-myc downstream regulated gene 1 (NDRG1) is significantly associated with advanced tumor stages and poor survival in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), suggesting it as a potential therapeutic target. To further elucidate its role in hepatocarcinogenesis, we employed the ProtoArray® Human Protein Microarrays to identify interaction partners of NDRG1. We found that glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK-3β) and the orphan nuclear receptor (Nur77) interact with NDRG1. These interactions were validated in HCC cell lines through co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence staining. Additionally, we discovered that high levels of NDRG1 disrupt the degradation of β-catenin by competing with GSK-3β and Nur77, leading to increased expression of downstream oncogenic genes. In vivo, suppression of NDRG1 in HCC xenografts resulted in decreased β-catenin levels and tumor growth inhibition. Furthermore, we observed a positive correlation between NDRG1 expression and GSK-3β, Nur77, and β-catenin expressions in HCC patient samples. Our findings identify GSK-3β and Nur77 as novel interaction partners of NDRG1 and suggest that these protein-protein interactions play a crucial role in regulating β-catenin signaling in HCC cells. These findings provide potential targets for future therapeutic interventions.

title: A tutorial on statistical methods for population association studies
text: Although genetic association studies have been around for decades, there is still a lack of consensus on the most appropriate statistical procedures to use, even for the simplest analyses. In this overview, I will provide an overview of the various statistical approaches used in population association studies, including preliminary analyses such as Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium testing, inference of phase and missing data, and SNP tagging. I will also discuss single-SNP and multipoint tests for association, along with the key problems associated with these methods, including population structure and multiple testing. My goal is to outline the main methods used in genetic association studies, with a brief discussion of the challenges and ongoing developments in the field.

title: Identification and Characterization of Multiple TRIM Proteins That Inhibit Hepatitis B Virus Transcription
text: Tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins are a large family of over 100 members that share conserved motifs and have diverse biological functions. Some TRIM proteins have been shown to restrict viral infections and regulate host cellular innate immune responses. To identify TRIM proteins that modulate hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, we tested 38 human TRIMs for their effects on HBV gene expression, capsid assembly, and DNA synthesis in human hepatoma cells (HepG2). The study revealed that ectopic expression of eight TRIM proteins in HepG2 cells significantly reduced the amounts of secreted HBV surface and e antigens, as well as intracellular capsid and capsid DNA. Mechanistic analyses showed that these TRIM proteins not only reduced HBV mRNA expression but also inhibited HBV enhancer I and enhancer II activities. Specifically, studies focused on TRIM41 revealed that a specific HBV DNA segment was essential for TRIM41-mediated inhibition of HBV enhancer II activity, and this inhibition depended on the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of TRIM41 as well as the integrity of TRIM41's C-terminal domain. Additionally, knockdown of endogenous TRIM41 in a HepG2-derived stable cell line led to an increase in HBV preC/C RNA, resulting in higher levels of viral core protein, capsid, and capsid DNA. These findings identify eight TRIM proteins that inhibit HBV transcription and provide strong evidence for the endogenous role of TRIM41 in regulating HBV transcription in human hepatoma cells.

title: A mouse Mecp2-null mutation causes neurological symptoms that mimic Rett syndrome
text: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare inherited neurodevelopmental disorder that affects females, occurring in approximately 10,000 to 15,000 births. Typically, affected females develop normally for 6 to 18 months before losing voluntary movements, including speech and hand skills. The majority of RTT cases are caused by mutations in the X-linked gene MECP2, which encodes a protein that binds to methylated sites in genomic DNA and regulates gene expression. Previous studies using Mecp2-null embryonic stem cells suggested that MeCP2 is essential for mouse embryogenesis. To further investigate the role of MeCP2 in mice, researchers generated mice lacking Mecp2 using Cre-loxP technology. Both Mecp2-null mice and mice in which Mecp2 was deleted in the brain exhibited severe neurological symptoms at around six weeks of age. Interestingly, compensation for the absence of MeCP2 in other tissues by MeCP1 was not observed in genetic or biochemical tests. Heterozygous female mice also showed behavioral symptoms after several months, suggesting that the stability of brain function may be compromised by the absence of MeCP2, rather than brain development per se. The concurrent delay in symptom onset in both humans and mice raises the possibility that brain function may be more susceptible to disruption than previously thought.

title: The p38/MK2-Driven Exchange between Tristetraprolin and HuR Regulates AU–Rich Element–Dependent Translation
text: The translation of Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) in macrophages is tightly regulated by a complex mechanism involving the p38 Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK)/Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase Kinase (MK2) pathway and the AU-rich Element (ARE) in the TNF mRNA. In this study, we aim to elucidate the molecular mechanism of phosphorylation-regulated translation of TNF. Our findings reveal that translation of the TNF-precursor in the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) requires the expression of the ARE-binding and -stabilizing factor, Human Antigen R (HuR), in combination with either the activity of the p38 MAPK/MK2 pathway or the absence of the ARE-binding and -destabilizing factor, Tristetraprolin (TTP). We demonstrate that phosphorylation of TTP by MK2 leads to a decrease in its affinity for the ARE, impairing its ability to replace HuR and allowing HuR to initiate translation of TNF mRNA. Additionally, we show that translation of TTP's own mRNA is also regulated by this mechanism, resulting in an intrinsic feedback control of the inflammatory response. The phosphorylation-regulated exchange of TTP and HuR at target mRNAs provides a reversible switch between unstable/non-translatable and stable/efficiently translated mRNAs.

title: miR-205 hinders the malignant interplay between prostate cancer cells and associated fibroblasts.
text: The tumor microenvironment plays a crucial role in the acquisition of metastatic potential by cancer cells. In our recent study, we found that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) induce an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in prostate cancer (PCa) cells through a redox-dependent pathway involving cycloxygenase-2/hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1)/nuclear factor-κB. To identify potential tools to counteract oxidative stress and metastasis dissemination, we investigated the involvement of microRNAs (miRNAs) in tumor-stroma interplay. Our results showed that miR-205 is the most downregulated miRNA in PCa cells upon CAF stimulation, due to direct transcriptional repression by HIF-1. Ectopic miR-205 overexpression in PCa cells counteracted CAF-induced EMT, impairing cell invasion, acquisition of stem cell traits, tumorigenicity, and metastatic dissemination. Additionally, miR-205 blocked tumor-driven activation of surrounding fibroblasts by reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion. These findings suggest that miR-205 acts as a brake against PCa metastasis by blocking both the afferent and efferent arms of the circuit between tumor cells and associated fibroblasts, thereby interrupting the pro-oxidant and pro-inflammatory circuitries engaged by reactive stroma. Our findings provide a rationale for developing miRNA-based approaches to prevent and treat metastatic disease.

title: The prevention of type 2 diabetes
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) affects over 7% of adults in the US, resulting in significant personal and economic burdens. In prediabetic states, insulin secretion and action, which could be targeted by preventive interventions, are impaired. In trials, lifestyle modifications such as weight loss and exercise have proven effective in preventing incident T2DM in high-risk groups, with weight loss having the greatest impact. Various medications, including metformin, thiazolidinediones, and acarbose, can also prevent or delay T2DM onset. However, it is unclear whether diabetes-prevention strategies can also prevent the development of diabetic vascular complications. Despite this uncertainty, cardiovascular risk factors have been shown to be favorably affected by preventive strategies. These strategies can be implemented in routine clinical settings, but their widespread application has been limited by local financial considerations, even though they may be cost-effective at the population level.

title: The transcriptional landscape of the mammalian genome.
text: This research paper focuses on the comprehensive analysis of transcription start and termination sites, as well as the identification of previously unidentified full-length complementary DNA (cDNA) derived from the mouse genome. The study reveals extensive variation in transcripts arising from alternative promoter usage, splicing, and polyadenylation, resulting in 181,047 transcripts with 5' and 3' boundaries identified. Additionally, the study uncovers 16,247 new mouse protein-coding transcripts, including 5154 encoding previously unidentified proteins. The genomic mapping of the transcriptome reveals transcriptional forests with overlapping transcription on both strands, separated by regions with few transcripts. The data provide a comprehensive platform for comparative analysis of mammalian transcriptional regulation in differentiation and development.

title: The Protein Data Bank
text: The Protein Data Bank (PDB; Berman et al., 2000; Nucleic Acids Research, 28, 235-242; http://www.pdb.org/) is the sole global repository of primary structural data for biological macromolecules. A wealth of secondary data is derived from the PDB. It serves as the foundation for research in structural bioinformatics. This article aims to acquaint readers with the PDB's objectives, the systems in place for data submission and access, how to obtain additional information, and future plans for the resource's development. By the end of this article, readers should have a clear understanding of the PDB's scope and the range of data it provides.

title: Cell-State-Specific Metabolic Dependency in Hematopoiesis and Leukemogenesis
text: The balance between oxidative and non-oxidative glucose metabolism is crucial for various physiological processes. By selectively deleting enzymes involved in aerobic glycolysis, we investigated how modulating glucose metabolism impacts hematopoietic and leukemic cell populations. Our findings reveal that a deficiency in the M2 pyruvate kinase isoform (PKM2) reduces the levels of metabolic intermediates essential for biosynthesis and impairs progenitor function without affecting hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), whereas deletion of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) significantly inhibits the function of both HSCs and progenitors during hematopoiesis. In contrast, leukemia initiation by transforming alleles potentially affecting either HSCs or progenitors is impaired in the absence of either PKM2 or LDHA, suggesting that the cell-type-specific responses to metabolic manipulation in hematopoiesis do not apply to the context of leukemia. These findings suggest that fine-tuning the level of glycolysis may be a therapeutic strategy for treating leukemia while preserving HSC function.

title: A transition in brain state during propofol-induced unconsciousness.
text: Cortical dynamics are shaped by rhythmic oscillations during various states of consciousness, including active behavior, sleep, and general anesthesia. A prominent feature of these oscillations is cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling, which remains poorly understood in terms of its role in organizing conscious and unconscious brain states. By combining high-density EEG and intracranial electrocorticography recordings during gradual propofol induction in humans, we uncovered distinct states with opposing phase-amplitude coupling and different cortical source distributions. One state, present during unconsciousness, resembles slow oscillations observed in sleep. The other state, appearing at the loss or recovery of consciousness, exhibits an enhanced slow cortical potential. These findings provide objective electrophysiological markers of distinct unconscious brain states, which could be leveraged to improve EEG-based monitoring for general anesthesia.

title: Cohesins and condensins orchestrate the 4D dynamics of yeast chromosomes during the cell cycle
text:
The dynamics of chromosome structure during cell division are complex and involve the reorganization of chromosomes at multiple scales. While studies have investigated the roles of conserved architectural proteins, such as cohesin and condensin, in maintaining chromosome structure, a comprehensive view of chromosome architecture at both small and large scales during cell division is still lacking.
In this study, we provide the first genome-wide analysis of chromosome dynamics in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae during cell division. Using advanced imaging techniques, we observed the higher-order organization of the yeast genome at multiple stages of the cell cycle, from replication to segregation. Our findings reveal that cohesin and condensin play critical roles in controlling structural transitions during cell division.
During replication, cohesin helps establish long-range intra-chromosomal contacts, leading to the individualization of chromosomes. As the cell progresses through mitosis, the chromosomes are suddenly reorganized by mechanical forces exerted by the mitotic spindle, resulting in their separation. Our data suggest that condensin-mediated forces may also play a direct role in segregation, as evidenced by the formation of a condensin-dependent loop connecting the centromere cluster and the rDNA loci.
Our study provides a comprehensive view of chromosome dynamics in a unicellular eukaryote, but also uncovers new features of chromosome structural reorganization during cell division. Our findings have important implications for understanding the mechanisms of chromosome segregation and their role in maintaining genome stability.

title: Genome-wide patterns of divergence and gene flow across a butterfly radiation.
text: The Heliconius butterflies constitute a recent radiation exhibiting multiple levels of divergence, with ongoing gene flow between species. The recently sequenced genome of Heliconius melpomene has enabled us to investigate the genomic evolution of this group through dense RAD marker sequencing. Phylogenetic analysis of 54 individuals has provided robust support for the reciprocal monophyly of H. melpomene and Heliconius cydno, refuting previous phylogenetic hypotheses that H. melpomene may be paraphyletic with respect to H. cydno. Additionally, Heliconius timareta forms a monophyletic clade closely related to but distinct from H. cydno, with Heliconius heurippa falling within this clade. Our findings also reveal evidence for genetic admixture between sympatric populations of the sister clades H. melpomene and H. cydno/timareta, particularly between H. cydno and H. melpomene from Central America and between H. timareta and H. melpomene from the eastern slopes of the Andes. Furthermore, we find that divergence between races is primarily explained by isolation by distance, and there is no detectable genetic population structure between parapatric races, suggesting that hybrid zones between races are not zones of secondary contact. Our results also support previous findings that colour pattern loci are shared between populations and species with similar colour pattern elements, with this pattern being almost unique to these genomic regions, and only a very small number of other loci showing significant similarity between populations and species with similar colour patterns.

title: Randomized, double-blind study of the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of tafenoquine versus mefloquine for malaria prophylaxis in nonimmune subjects.
text: This clinical trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of tafenoquine as a malaria prophylaxis in Australian soldiers deployed to East Timor. The study was conducted in a randomized, double-blinded manner, with 492 subjects receiving 200 mg of tafenoquine per week for 6 months, while 162 subjects received 250 mg of mefloquine per week. After returning to Australia, the tafenoquine group received a placebo, while the mefloquine group received 30 mg of primaquine daily for 14 days. There were no significant differences in hematological and biochemical parameters between the two groups. Treatment-related adverse events were similar between the two groups, with 13.4% of tafenoquine subjects and 11.7% of mefloquine subjects experiencing adverse events. Three subjects on tafenoquine and none on mefloquine discontinued prophylaxis due to possible drug-related adverse events. No cases of malaria occurred during deployment, but 4 cases (0.9%) of Plasmodium vivax infection occurred among the tafenoquine group and 1 case (0.7%) occurred among the mefloquine group after discontinuation of medication. In a subset of subjects, mild vortex keratopathy was detected in 93% of tafenoquine subjects, but none of the mefloquine subjects. The vortex keratopathy resolved fully in all subjects within 1 year without affecting visual acuity. Overall, tafenoquine appears to be safe and well-tolerated as a malaria prophylaxis, with high efficacy.

title: Domain-wide regulation of DNA replication timing during mammalian development
text: Studies of replication timing have offered a window into the previously inaccessible higher-order levels of chromosome organization, revealing their plasticity during development. Although the mechanisms regulating replication timing are still unclear, recent genome-wide studies have provided a comprehensive survey of how replication timing is regulated during key early cell fate transitions in mammals, showing coordinated changes in a defined set of 400-800 kb chromosomal segments that affect nearly half of the genome. These changes are linked to alterations in sub-nuclear organization and domain-wide transcriptional potential, and the replication timing profiles of different tissues are surprisingly conserved from mouse to human, suggesting that the program has important developmental implications. As a result, these studies have laid the groundwork for connecting megabase-level chromosome structure to function, and suggest that replication plays a central role in organizing the genome at the domain level.

title: PU.1-mediated upregulation of CSF1R is crucial for leukemia stem cell potential induced by MOZ-TIF2
text: Leukemias and other cancers harbor self-renewing stem cells that contribute to the persistence of cancer. Eradication of these stem cells is crucial for effective cancer therapy. Using an acute myeloid leukemia (AML) model induced by the leukemia-associated monocytic leukemia zinc finger (MOZ)-TIF2 fusion protein, we demonstrate that AML can be cured by ablating leukemia stem cells. MOZ fusion proteins MOZ-TIF2 and MOZ-CBP interact with the transcription factor PU.1 to enhance the expression of macrophage colony–stimulating factor receptor (CSF1R, also known as M-CSFR, c-FMS or CD115). Our findings in PU.1-deficient mice reveal that PU.1 is essential for the ability of MOZ-TIF2 to establish and maintain AML stem cells. We identified CSF1Rhigh cells, which exhibit potent leukemia-initiating activity, and used transgenic mice expressing a drug-inducible suicide gene controlled by the CSF1R promoter to cure AML by ablation of CSF1Rhigh cells. Moreover, inhibition of CSF1R using transgenic mice or pharmacological inhibitors slowed the progression of MOZ-TIF2–induced leukemia. Our results suggest that targeting PU.1-mediated upregulation of CSF1R expression may be a promising therapeutic approach for this subtype of AML.

title: Pharmacological blockage of fibro/adipogenic progenitor expansion and suppression of regenerative fibrogenesis is associated with impaired skeletal muscle regeneration.
text: Acute muscle injury triggers the proliferation and differentiation of fibro/adipogenic progenitors (FAPs), leading to the deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) and a temporary phase of fibrogenesis. While the prolongation of this phase can result in permanent tissue scarring, the consequences of suppressing it are not fully understood. Using a model of acute muscle damage, we found that pharmacological inhibition of FAP expansion using Nilotinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor with antifibrotic activity, has a detrimental effect on myogenesis during regeneration. Our results suggest that Nilotinib inhibits the damage-induced expansion of satellite cells in vivo, but does not affect their proliferation in vitro, indicating a non-cell-autonomous effect. Furthermore, we discovered that Nilotinib impairs regenerative fibrogenesis by preventing the injury-induced expansion and differentiation of resident CD45(-):CD31(-):α7integrin(-):Sca1(+) mesenchymal FAPs. Our findings support the idea that the expansion of FAPs and transient fibrogenesis during regeneration play an important trophic role in promoting tissue-specific stem cell proliferation.

title: Deregulation of Scribble Promotes Mammary Tumorigenesis and Reveals a Role for Cell Polarity in Carcinoma
text:
The loss of cell polarity proteins, such as Scribble, can lead to the development of cancer in both Drosophila and mammals. In Drosophila, the loss of Scribble promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation, disrupting the normal structure and function of tissues. Similarly, in mammals, the role of polarity proteins in tumorigenesis is not well understood, but our study demonstrates that depletion of Scribble in mammary epithelia leads to the disruption of cell polarity, inhibition of three-dimensional morphogenesis, and the induction of dysplasia in vivo, which can progress to tumors after a long latency.
We found that loss of Scribble cooperates with oncogenes, such as c-myc, to transform epithelial cells and induce tumors in vivo by blocking the activation of an apoptosis pathway. Interestingly, both depletion and mislocalization of Scribble were sufficient to promote cell transformation. Moreover, spontaneous mammary tumors in mice and humans have been found to have downregulated and mislocalized Scribble, suggesting that the inhibition of Scribble promotes breast cancer formation.
Our study demonstrates that the deregulation of polarity pathways leads to the disruption of morphogenesis and inhibition of cell death, promoting dysplastic and neoplastic growth in mammals. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer development and progression.

title: The Polymeal: a more natural, safer, and probably tastier (than the Polypill) strategy to reduce cardiovascular disease by more than 75%.
text:
OBJECTIVE:
The Polypill concept, proposed in 2003, has shown promise in reducing cardiovascular risk management. However, its potential costs and adverse effects are significant limitations. This study aimed to identify a tastier and safer alternative to the Polypill, known as the Polymeal.
METHODS:
Data on the ingredients of the Polymeal were obtained from the literature. An evidence-based recipe consisting of wine, fish, dark chocolate, fruits, vegetables, garlic, and almonds was developed. Data from the Framingham Heart Study and the Framingham Offspring Study were used to create life tables to model the benefits of the Polymeal in the general population from age 50, assuming multiplicative correlations.
RESULTS:
Combining the ingredients of the Polymeal resulted in a significant reduction in cardiovascular disease events, with a 76% decrease in events observed. For men, taking the Polymeal daily resulted in an increase in total life expectancy of 6.6 years, an increase in life expectancy free from cardiovascular disease of 9.0 years, and a decrease in life expectancy with cardiovascular disease of 2.4 years. Corresponding differences for women were 4.8, 8.1, and 3.3 years, respectively.
CONCLUSION:
The Polymeal offers a promising, non-pharmacological, safe, cost-effective, and tasty alternative to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and increase life expectancy in the general population.

title: Islet-Like Clusters Derived from Mesenchymal Stem Cells in Wharton's Jelly of the Human Umbilical Cord for Transplantation to Control Type 1 Diabetes
text:
Background:
There is a growing interest in developing alternative sources of islet-replacement tissue for the treatment of type I diabetes mellitus. One promising source is human mesenchymal cells isolated from the Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord (HUMSCs). These cells have shown potential as a source of insulin-producing cells due to their stem cell properties and ease of obtainance compared to embryonic and bone marrow stem cells.
Methodology and Principal Findings:
In this study, HUMSCs were induced to form islet-like cell clusters in vitro through stepwise culturing in neuron-conditioned medium. These cell clusters were then transplanted into the liver of streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats via laparotomy. Glucose tolerance was measured 12 weeks after transplantation, along with immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy analysis. The islet-like cell clusters were found to contain human C-peptide and release human insulin in response to physiological glucose levels. Real-time RT-PCR analysis detected the expression of insulin and other pancreatic beta-cell-related genes (Pdx1, Hlxb9, Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1, and Glut-2) in these islet-like cell clusters. The hyperglycemia and glucose intolerance in the diabetic rats were significantly alleviated after transplantation of the islet-like cell clusters, without the use of immunosuppressants. In addition to the presence of islet-like cell clusters in the liver, some special fused liver cells were also found, characterized by human insulin and nuclei-positive staining and the presence of secretory granules.
Conclusions and Significance:
In this study, we successfully differentiated HUMSCs into mature islet-like cell clusters that possess insulin-producing ability both in vitro and in vivo. The use of HUMSCs in Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord as a source of stem cells for islet-replacement tissue shows great promise due to the large potential donor pool, rapid availability, lack of discomfort for the donor, and low risk of rejection.

title: Use of perioperative hydroxyethyl starch 6% and albumin 5% in elective joint arthroplasty and association with adverse outcomes: a retrospective population based analysis
text:
Objective: To investigate whether the use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% and albumin 5% in the perioperative setting of elective joint arthroplasties is associated with an increased risk of perioperative complications.
Design: Retrospective cohort study using population-based data from 2006 to 2013.
Setting: Data from 510 hospitals across the United States participating in the Premier Perspective database.
Participants: 1,051,441 patients undergoing elective total hip and knee arthroplasties.
Exposures: Perioperative fluid resuscitation with hydroxyethyl starch 6% or albumin 5%, or neither.
Main Outcome Measures: Acute renal failure and thromboembolic, cardiac, and pulmonary complications.
Results: Compared to patients who did not receive either colloid, perioperative fluid resuscitation with hydroxyethyl starch 6% or albumin 5% was associated with an increased risk of acute renal failure (odds ratios 1.23 (95% confidence interval 1.13-1.34) and 1.56 (1.36-1.78), respectively) and most other complications. A recent decrease in hydroxyethyl starch 6% use was noted, while that of albumin 5% increased.
Conclusions: Similar to findings in critically ill patients, this study shows that the use of hydroxyethyl starch 6% in the elective perioperative orthopedic setting is associated with an increased risk of acute renal failure and other complications. This increased risk also applies to albumin 5%. These findings raise concerns about the widespread use of these colloids in elective joint arthroplasty procedures.

title: BMAL1 and CLOCK, Two Essential Components of the Circadian Clock, Are Involved in Glucose Homeostasis
text: The molecular clock, a unique series of autoregulatory interactions, generates circadian timing in the body. Behavioral rhythms are regulated by the molecular clock, and we demonstrate a crucial role for Bmal1 and Clock in the control of glucose homeostasis. Inactivation of these clock components leads to a suppression of the diurnal variation in glucose and triglycerides. Gluconeogenesis is abolished in Bmal1-deficient mice and is reduced in Clock mutants, but the counterregulatory response of corticosterone and glucagon to insulin-induced hypoglycaemia is preserved. Additionally, a high-fat diet amplifies circadian variations in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, and mutation of Clock restores the chow-fed phenotype. Bmal1 and Clock, which function in the core molecular clock, exert profound control over recovery from insulin-induced hypoglycaemia. Furthermore, asynchronous dietary cues may modulate glucose homeostasis by interacting with peripheral molecular clocks.

title: Mechanisms of progression and regression of renal lesions of chronic nephropathies and diabetes.
text: The prevalence of chronic kidney diseases is rising globally, posing a significant public health concern. While genetic factors contribute to susceptibility and disease progression, proteinuria has been identified as an independent predictor of disease outcome. Treatment with medications and a low-protein diet can slow the decline of renal function in individuals with nondiabetic and diabetic nephropathies, potentially leading to remission and regression of renal lesions. In animal models, regression of glomerular structural changes is associated with glomerular remodeling, which can be quantified through 3D reconstruction studies of the glomerular capillary tuft. The contribution of resident cells in capillary regeneration is thought to play a role, but the involvement of renal or extrarenal progenitor cells may also be important. This review summarizes recent advances in our understanding of the mechanisms and mediators underlying renal tissue repair and its potential to reverse renal injury.

title: Contemporary type 1 diabetes pregnancy outcomes: impact of obesity and glycaemic control.
text:
Objective: To compare the outcomes of pregnancies in women with type 1 diabetes to those without, and to investigate the effects of obesity and glycemic control on these outcomes.
Design and Setting: Historical cohort study in a specialist diabetes and maternity network in Victoria, Australia.
Participants: All singleton births (at least 20 weeks gestation) from 2010 to 2013 were analyzed, including 107 pregnancies in women with type 1 diabetes and 27,075 pregnancies in women without diabetes. Women with type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes were excluded.
Methods: Data were extracted from the Birthing Outcomes System database and associations between type 1 diabetes and pregnancy outcomes were analyzed using multivariable regression.
Main Outcome Measures: Mode of birth, maternal and neonatal outcomes.
Results: Women with type 1 diabetes had a higher mean body mass index (BMI) than women without diabetes (mean BMI 27.3 kg/m2 [SD 5.0] vs 25.7 kg/m2 [SD 5.9]; P = 0.01). The median gestation period for their babies was shorter (median 37.3 weeks [IQR 34.6-38.1] vs 39.4 weeks [IQR 38.4-40.4]; P < 0.001) and they were more likely to be large for gestational age (LGA) (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 7.9; 95% CI 5.3-11.8). Women with type 1 diabetes were more likely to have had labor induced (aOR 3.0; 95% CI 2.0-4.5), a cesarean delivery (aOR 4.6; 95% CI 3.1-7.0), or a preterm birth (aOR 6.7; 95% CI 4.5-10.0); their babies were more likely to have shoulder dystocia (aOR 8.2; 95% CI 3.6-18.7), hypoglycemia (aOR 10.3; 95% CI 6.8-15.6), jaundice (aOR 5.1; 95% CI 3.3-7.7), respiratory distress (aOR 2.5; 95% CI 1.4-4.4), or to suffer perinatal death (aOR 4.3; 95% CI 1.9-9.9). In women with type 1 diabetes, greater obesity was associated with increased odds for an LGA baby or congenital malformation, and increased HbA1c levels were associated with preterm birth and perinatal death.
Conclusion: Women with type 1 diabetes, even when managed in a specialist setting, still experience adverse obstetric and neonatal outcomes. Poor glycemic control is not wholly responsible for adverse outcomes, reinforcing the importance of other risk factors, such as obesity and weight gain.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Vitamin D Action
text: The hormonal metabolite of vitamin D, 1α,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (1,25D), triggers biological responses by binding to the vitamin D receptor (VDR). When 1,25D binds to VDR, it forms a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) that recognizes and binds to specific DNA sequences in vitamin D-responsive genes. This complex recruits either coactivators or corepressors to modulate the transcription of genes involved in the traditional functions of vitamin D, such as calcium and phosphate absorption, and bone mineral metabolism. For example, 1,25D regulates the expression of genes involved in bone remodeling, such as RANKL, SPP1 (osteopontin), and BGP (osteocalcin), and also promotes intestinal calcium absorption through the regulation of genes such as TRPV6, CaBP9k, and claudin 2. Additionally, VDR can function independently of 1,25D in keratinocytes to regulate mammalian hair cycling by controlling genes involved in Wnt signaling. Furthermore, alternative, non-vitamin D VDR ligands, such as lithocholic acid, docosahexaenoic acid, and curcumin, have been identified. The combination of these ligands and 1,25D/VDR control of gene expression may help delay chronic diseases associated with aging, such as osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

title: Quantitative Temporal Viromics: An Approach to Investigate Host-Pathogen Interaction
text:
A comprehensive, quantitative analysis of the temporal changes in host and viral proteins throughout the course of a productive infection could provide valuable insights into the complex interactions between viruses and their hosts. To address this, we developed a cutting-edge proteomic technique called "quantitative temporal viromics" (QTV), which utilizes multiplexed tandem-mass-tag-based mass spectrometry. By employing this technique, we were able to investigate the dynamics of virus-host interaction in great detail, using human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) as a paradigmatic example.
HCMV is not only a significant pathogen but also a master of immune evasion, capable of manipulating the expression of over 8,000 cellular proteins to evade the host's immune system. Through the use of QTV, we were able to identify and characterize the viral proteins that are expressed at the cell surface, including 29 potential therapeutic targets. Additionally, we defined temporal profiles of over 80% of HCMV's canonical genes and 14 noncanonical open reading frames, providing a comprehensive understanding of the virus's life cycle.
The power of QTV lies in its ability to provide dynamic insights into viral infection, making it applicable to any virus with a robust in vitro model. By employing this technique, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between viruses and their hosts, ultimately leading to the development of novel therapeutic strategies and treatments.

title: Interactions between sleep, circadian function, and glucose metabolism: implications for risk and severity of diabetes.
text: Sleep disruptions, including insufficient sleep and fragmented rest, have been linked to an increased risk of developing diabetes. Laboratory studies have provided valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms. Large-scale prospective studies have shown that these sleep disturbances are associated with an elevated risk of diabetes onset. Obstructive sleep apnea, which combines sleep fragmentation and low oxygen levels, is a significant risk factor for insulin resistance and possibly diabetes. The question of whether improving glycemic control in type 2 diabetes patients through sleep apnea treatment remains controversial. Recently, there has been growing attention to sleep disturbances during pregnancy and their connection to gestational diabetes and high blood sugar levels, with potential consequences for maternal and fetal health. Animal studies have also suggested that disruptions to the body's internal clock may contribute to unfavorable metabolic outcomes. This review aims to provide a comprehensive update on the current state of knowledge regarding the connections between sleep disruptions, circadian dysfunction, and glucose metabolism, including both experimental, prospective, and interventional studies.

title: Antibody-Based HIV-1 Vaccines: Recent Developments and Future Directions
text:
In May 2007, the Global HIV Vaccine Enterprise convened a two-day workshop to discuss humoral immune responses to HIV and approaches to design vaccines that induce viral neutralizing and other potentially protective antibody responses. The workshop aimed to identify key scientific issues, gaps, and opportunities that have emerged since the Enterprise Strategic Plan was first published in 2005, and to make recommendations that Enterprise stakeholders can use to plan new activities.
Most effective viral vaccines work by generating antibodies that inactivate or neutralize the invading virus, and existing data strongly suggest that an optimally effective HIV-1 vaccine should elicit potent antiviral neutralizing antibodies. However, HIV-1 chronically replicates in the host and evades the antibody response, posing major obstacles to vaccine development. Current HIV vaccine candidates do not elicit neutralizing antibodies against most circulating virus strains, and thus the induction of a protective antibody response remains a major priority for HIV-1 vaccine development.
The workshop identified four areas that, if given proper attention, could provide key information that would bring the field closer to an effective antibody-based HIV-1 vaccine:
1. Structure-assisted immunogen design: Using the three-dimensional structure of HIV-1 envelope proteins to design immunogens that can elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies.
2. Role of Fc receptors and complement: Understanding the role of Fc receptors and complement in mediating antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) and complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), which are important mechanisms of antibody-based immunity against HIV-1.
3. Assay standardization and validation: Developing and standardizing assays to measure neutralizing antibody responses to HIV-1, including the use of primary cells and tissues, and validating these assays to ensure their accuracy and reproducibility.
4. Immunoregulation of B cell responses: Understanding the regulatory mechanisms that control B cell responses to HIV-1, including the role of regulatory T cells and the presence of autoantibodies, and using this knowledge to optimize vaccine-induced B cell responses.
Overall, the workshop highlighted the need for a comprehensive approach to vaccine development that takes into account the complexities of HIV-1 immunology and the challenges posed by the virus's ability to evade the immune response. By addressing these challenges and leveraging the latest scientific knowledge, the field can make significant progress towards developing an effective antibody-based HIV-1 vaccine.

title: Targeted therapy for cancer stem cells: the patched pathway and ABC transporters
text: Data from certain types of cancer, including leukemia and brain and breast cancer, suggest that a small subset of tumor cells exhibit stem cell-like properties and the ability for self-renewal. These cancer stem cells, which make up a small percentage of the total tumor cells (1% or less), share many characteristics with normal stem cells and have been termed "cancer stem cells." However, they are difficult to detect and study due to their limited number. Like normal stem cells, cancer stem cells are resistant to traditional cancer chemotherapy and radiation therapy, owing to their high levels of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) drug transporters, relative quiescence, enhanced DNA repair, and reduced ability to undergo apoptosis. Combining cancer therapy approaches that target both the cancer stem cells and the non-stem cells may lead to more effective treatments. Efforts to target the Hedgehog/Patched pathway, which is crucial during embryonic growth and differentiation, and the ABCG2 drug efflux transporter will be discussed.

title: Increased in vivo amyloid-β42 production, exchange, and loss in presenilin mutation carriers.
text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is believed to result from an imbalance in the production or clearance of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides in the central nervous system (CNS). Autosomal dominant AD (ADAD) caused by mutations in the presenilin (PSEN) gene is thought to occur due to increased Aβ42 production compared to Aβ40 in the CNS. While this has been demonstrated in rodent models of ADAD, it has not been observed in human mutation carriers.
To investigate the pathophysiological effects of PSEN1 and PSEN2 mutations on Aβ isoform production and turnover, we employed compartmental modeling of stable isotope labeling kinetic (SILK) studies in human carriers of PSEN mutations and related noncarriers. We compared the findings based on mutation status and the amount of fibrillar amyloid deposition as measured by positron emission tomography (PET) using the amyloid tracer Pittsburgh compound B (PIB).
Our results showed that CNS Aβ42 to Aβ40 production rates were 24% higher in mutation carriers compared to noncarriers, and this was independent of fibrillar amyloid deposits quantified by PET PIB imaging. Additionally, the fractional turnover rate of soluble Aβ42 relative to Aβ40 was 65% faster in mutation carriers, and this correlation was observed in individuals with varying levels of amyloid deposition. These findings support the hypothesis that Aβ42 is overproduced in the CNS of humans with PSEN mutations that cause AD, and demonstrate that soluble Aβ42 turnover and exchange processes are altered in the presence of amyloid plaques, leading to reduced recovery of Aβ42 in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Furthermore, we observed reversible exchange of Aβ42 peptides with preexisting unlabeled peptide in the presence of plaques.
In conclusion, our study provides evidence that the overproduction of Aβ42 in the CNS of humans with PSEN mutations is a key feature of AD, and that soluble Aβ42 turnover and exchange processes are altered in the presence of amyloid plaques. These findings have important implications for the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at reducing Aβ42 levels in the CNS and slowing down the progression of AD.

title: Basic residues in the T-cell receptor ζ cytoplasmic domain mediate membrane association and modulate signaling.
text: The T-cell receptor (TCR) is composed of a TCRαβ heterodimer, a TCRζ homodimer, and CD3γε and CD3δε heterodimers. Despite extensive research, the exact mechanism of T-cell activation following TCR ligand binding remains unclear. Previous studies suggested that the cytoplasmic tail of CD3ε binds to the plasma membrane through a basic residue-rich stretch (BRS) and proposed that dissociation from the membrane is necessary for phosphorylation. In this study, we demonstrate that BRS motifs within the cytoplasmic tail of TCRζ mediate association with the plasma membrane, and TCR engagement leads to TCRζ dissociation from the membrane. This dissociation requires phosphorylation of the TCRζ immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs by lymphocyte cell-specific protein tyrosine kinase (Lck) but not ζ-chain-associated protein kinase 70 binding. Mutations of the TCRζ BRS motifs that disrupt this membrane association attenuate both proximal and distal responses induced by TCR engagement. These mutations appear to alter the localization of TCRζ with respect to Lck and the mobility of the TCR complex. Our findings reveal that tyrosine phosphorylation of the TCRζ cytoplasmic domain regulates its association with the plasma membrane and highlight the functional importance of TCRζ BRS motifs.

title: Policies for alcohol restriction and their association with interpersonal violence: a time-series analysis of homicides in Cali, Colombia.
text:
In the city of Cali, Colombia, there is a high incidence of interpersonal violence deaths, including homicides. To address this issue, various alcohol control policies have been implemented, but their effectiveness in reducing alcohol-related problems is not well understood. This study aimed to determine whether different alcohol control policies are associated with changes in the incidence rate of homicides.
The study was conducted as an ecological study over a five-year period (2004-2008) using a time-series design. The policies implemented varied in terms of the hours of restriction of sales and consumption of alcohol, with the most restrictive policies prohibiting alcohol between 2 a.m. and 10 a.m. for 446 non-consecutive days, moderately restrictive policies prohibiting alcohol between 3 a.m. and 10 a.m. for 1277 non-consecutive days, and lax policies prohibiting alcohol between 4 a.m. and 10 a.m. for 104 non-consecutive days. The rates of homicides and unintentional injury deaths (excluding traffic events) were compared between different periods of days when different policies were in effect using conditional autoregressive negative binomial regressions.
The results showed that there was an increased risk of homicides in periods when the moderately restrictive policies were in effect compared to periods when the most restrictive policies were in effect (incidence rate ratio (IRR) 1.15, 90% confidence interval (CI) 1.05-1.26, P = 0.012). Additionally, there was an even higher risk of homicides in periods when the lax policies were in effect compared to periods when the most restrictive policies were in effect (IRR 1.42, 90% CI 1.26-1.61, P < 0.001). In contrast, less restrictive policies were not associated with an increased risk of unintentional injury deaths.
The study concluded that extended hours of sales and consumption of alcohol are associated with an increased risk of homicides in communities where homicides are high. Strong restrictions on alcohol availability could reduce the incidence of interpersonal violence events.

title: Effects of SNF1 on Maltose Metabolism and Leavening Ability of Baker's Yeast in Lean Dough.
text:
Introduction:
Maltose metabolism in baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) in lean dough is hindered by glucose repression, leading to delayed fermentation. To enhance maltose metabolism and leavening ability, it is essential to alleviate glucose repression. The Snf1 protein kinase has been identified as a crucial factor in responding to glucose repression and is required for the transcription of glucose-repressed genes, including the maltose-utilization genes (MAL).
Objectives:
To investigate the effect of SNF1 overexpression and deletion on maltose utilization, growth, and fermentation characteristics, as well as mRNA levels of MAL genes (MAL62 encoding the maltase and MAL61 encoding the maltose permease) and enzyme activities in industrial baker's yeast strains.
Methods:
Construction of SNF1 overexpression and deletion industrial baker's yeast strains and characterization of their maltose utilization, growth, and fermentation characteristics, as well as mRNA levels of MAL genes and enzyme activities.
Results:
Overexpression of SNF1 was found to be effective in glucose derepression, leading to increased MAL expression levels and enzyme activities. These enhancements resulted in an 18% increase in maltose metabolism in LSMLD medium (the low sugar model liquid dough fermentation medium) containing glucose and maltose and a 15% increase in leavening ability in lean dough.
Discussion:

These findings provide valuable insights into the breeding of industrial baker's yeast for rapid fermentation, highlighting the importance of alleviating glucose repression in enhancing maltose metabolism and leavening ability. The Snf1 protein kinase emerges as a key player in this process, underscoring its potential as a target for improving industrial baker's yeast strains.
Conclusion:

In conclusion, this study demonstrates the significance of glucose repression in maltose metabolism and leavening ability in baker's yeast, and the potential of SNF1 overexpression as a means of alleviating this repression. These findings have important implications for the breeding of industrial baker's yeast for rapid fermentation, and highlight the need for further research into the molecular mechanisms underlying maltose metabolism in this organism.

title: Review article
text: Ribosomopathies are a group of disorders characterized by genetic abnormalities that affect the biogenesis and function of ribosomes, leading to specific clinical phenotypes. Congenital mutations in genes encoding ribosomal proteins, such as RPS19, can cause Diamond-Blackfan anemia, a disorder marked by hypoplastic, macrocytic anemia. Other rare congenital syndromes, including Schwachman-Diamond syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita, cartilage-hair hypoplasia, and Treacher Collins syndrome, have also been linked to mutations in genes required for normal ribosome biogenesis. In addition, a somatically acquired deletion of chromosome 5q can lead to haploinsufficiency of the ribosomal protein RPS14 and an erythroid phenotype similar to Diamond-Blackfan anemia, resulting in the 5q- syndrome, a subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome. Acquired abnormalities in ribosome function have been implicated in human malignancies, and the p53 pathway, which provides a surveillance mechanism for protein translation and genome integrity, appears to play a critical role in the clinical features of ribosomopathies. Elucidating the mechanisms underlying the specific clinical syndromes caused by selective abnormalities in ribosome biogenesis may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for these diseases.

title: PD-L1 expression in human cancers and its association with clinical outcomes
text: PD-L1 is an immune checkpoint molecule that inhibits T cell activation, leading to tumor progression. Overexpression of PD-L1 in various cancers, including gastric, hepatocellular, renal cell, esophageal, pancreatic, ovarian, and bladder cancer, is associated with poor clinical outcomes. In contrast, PD-L1 expression is linked to better outcomes in breast cancer and Merkel cell carcinoma. The prognostic value of PD-L1 expression in lung cancer, colorectal cancer, and melanoma is controversial. Blocking antibodies that target PD-1 and PD-L1 have shown remarkable response rates in cancer patients with PD-L1-overexpressing tumors. However, relying solely on PD-L1 as a predictive biomarker for cancer immunotherapy is uncertain due to the limited accuracy of PD-L1 immunohistochemistry staining. Factors affecting the accuracy of PD-L1 immunohistochemistry staining include the use of different antibodies, varying cut-off values, and non-uniform PD-L1 expression in tumors, which can be influenced by sampling time and location. A better understanding of the tumor microenvironment and the use of additional biomarkers, such as gene markers and combined indexes, are necessary to more effectively identify patients who will benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade therapy.

title: Primate cytomegaloviruses encode and express an IL-10-like protein.
text:
An open reading frame (ORF) with homology to interleukin-10 (IL-10) has been discovered in rhesus cytomegalovirus (RhCMV). The IL-10-like protein is generated from a multispliced, polyadenylated early gene transcript that spans part of the UL111A ORF of human CMV (HCMV). Immunological assays confirm the expression of the IL-10-like protein in both tissue culture and RhCMV-infected rhesus macaques. Subsequent identification of conserved ORFs in human, baboon, and African green monkey CMV suggests that the protein may play a crucial role in the persistence and pathogenesis of primate CMV.
In this study, researchers identified an open reading frame (ORF) in rhesus cytomegalovirus (RhCMV) that shares homology with interleukin-10 (IL-10). This ORF is derived from a multispliced, polyadenylated early gene transcript that spans part of the UL111A ORF of human CMV (HCMV). The IL-10-like protein is expressed in both tissue culture and RhCMV-infected rhesus macaques, suggesting its potential role in the pathogenesis of primate CMV. The discovery of this ORF is significant because it highlights the conservation of this protein across different primate species, indicating its potential importance in the persistence of CMV.
In this investigation, scientists discovered an ORF in RhCMV that has homology to IL-10. This ORF is generated from a multispliced, polyadenylated early gene transcript that overlaps the UL111A ORF of HCMV. The IL-10-like protein is expressed in both tissue culture and RhCMV-infected rhesus macaques, suggesting its potential role in the pathogenesis of primate CMV. The identification of this ORF is noteworthy because it reveals the conservation of this protein across different primate species, implying its potential significance in the persistence of CMV.

title: Genome Sequencing and Analysis of the Tasmanian Devil and Its Transmissible Cancer
text: The Tasmanian devil (Sarcophilus harrisii), the largest marsupial carnivore, is endangered due to a transmissible facial cancer that is spread through direct transfer of living cancer cells through biting. In this study, we sequenced, assembled, and annotated the Tasmanian devil genome and whole-genome sequences of two geographically distant subclones of the cancer. Genomic analysis revealed that the cancer originated from a female Tasmanian devil and has since genetically diverged as it spread across Tasmania. The devil cancer genome contains over 17,000 somatic base substitution mutations, indicating a distinct mutational process. By genotyping somatic mutations in 104 tumors from different geographic and temporal locations, we uncovered the pattern of evolution and spread of this parasitic clonal lineage, with evidence of a selective sweep in one geographic area and persistence of parallel lineages in other populations.

title: A Temporarily Distinct Subpopulation of Slow-Cycling Melanoma Cells Is Required for Continuous Tumor Growth
text: Melanomas are highly diverse tumors, yet the functional significance of their various subpopulations remains unclear. By using the H3K4 demethylase JARID1B (KDM5B/PLU-1/RBP2-H1) as a biomarker, we have identified a small subset of slow-cycling melanoma cells that cycle at a rate of >4 weeks within the rapidly proliferating main population. Isolated JARID1B-positive melanoma cells produce a highly proliferative progeny. Depleting JARID1B leads to an initial acceleration of tumor growth followed by exhaustion, suggesting that the JARID1B-positive subpopulation is crucial for sustained tumor growth. JARID1B expression is dynamically regulated and does not conform to a hierarchical cancer stem cell model, as both JARID1B-negative and single melanoma cells can become positive and even single cells can be tumorigenic. These findings challenge the traditional understanding of melanoma heterogeneity and suggest a novel mechanism for tumor maintenance as a dynamic process mediated by a transiently distinct subpopulation.

title: A map of human circular RNAs in clinically relevant tissues
text:
Cellular circular RNAs (circRNAs) are generated through head-to-tail splicing and are present in all multicellular organisms studied to date. Recently, circRNAs have emerged as a distinct class of RNA molecules with post-transcriptional regulatory functions. It has been shown that many circRNAs are specifically expressed in certain tissues and developmental stages. The unique stability and tissue-specific expression of circRNAs make them promising candidates for clinical biomarker research.
To further investigate the role of circRNAs in human disease, we have generated a comprehensive circRNA expression resource of 20 clinically relevant tissues. These tissues include vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), human umbilical vein cells (HUVECs), artery endothelial cells (HUAECs), atrium, vena cava, neutrophils, platelets, cerebral cortex, placenta, and samples from mesenchymal stem cell differentiation. Our analysis revealed highly tissue-specific circRNA expression in these samples, with many circRNAs expressed at higher levels than their linear host transcripts.
Using RNA sequencing and bioinformatic analysis, we identified 71 validated circRNAs in our dataset. Of these, we found potential biomarkers for certain diseases, including adenosine deaminase-deficient, severe combined immunodeficiency (ADA-SCID) and Wiskott-Aldrich-Syndrome (WAS). Differential circRNA expression was observed in genes involved in the molecular pathogenesis of these diseases in patient samples compared to normal tissues.
Our findings highlight the importance of investigating circRNAs in human disease mechanisms and underscore the need for further research into their potential as clinical biomarkers.

title: Arp2/3 complex inhibition radically alters lamellipodial actin architecture, suspended cell shape, and the cell spreading process
text: Recent studies have investigated the dendritic actin cytoskeleton of the cell edge's lamellipodial (LP) region by experimentally decreasing the activity of the actin filament nucleator and branch former, the Arp2/3 complex. In this study, we extend these findings by pharmacologically inhibiting the Arp2/3 complex in sea urchin coelomocytes, which have an unusually broad LP region and display exaggerated centripetal flow. Using light and electron microscopy, we demonstrate that inhibition of the Arp2/3 complex via the drug CK666 significantly alters the LP actin architecture, slows centripetal flow, induces a lamellipodial-to-filopodial shape change in suspended cells, and leads to a novel actin structural organization during cell spreading. A common feature of the CK666 phenotype in coelomocytes is the formation of transverse actin arcs, and arc generation is arrested by a formin inhibitor. Additionally, we demonstrate that CK666 treatment produces actin arcs in other cells with broad LP regions, such as fish keratocytes and Drosophila S2 cells. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that the actin arcs visible upon Arp2/3 complex inhibition in coelomocytes may represent an exaggerated manifestation of elongated mother filaments that could potentially serve as a scaffold for the formation of the dendritic actin network.

title: Synergistic Activation of HIV-1 Expression by Deacetylase Inhibitors and Prostratin: Implications for Treatment of Latent Infection
text: The persistence of transcriptionally silent but replication-competent HIV-1 reservoirs in individuals on Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy (HAART) poses a significant barrier to virus eradication. Activating HIV-1 gene expression in these cells, along with the use of an efficient HAART, has been proposed as an adjuvant therapy to decrease the pool of latent viral reservoirs. In this study, we investigated the synergy between histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACIs) and prostratin, a non-tumor-promoting nuclear factor (NF)-κB inducer, on HIV-1 production in the latently-infected U1 monocytic cell line and latently-infected J-Lat T-cell clones. We found that the combination of prostratin and HDACI exhibited a strong synergistic activation of HIV-1 production, which was mediated by the synergistic recruitment of unresponsive cells into the expressing cell population. The combined treatment also showed a more pronounced nucleosomal remodeling in the U1 viral promoter region, which correlated with a synergistic reactivation of HIV-1 transcription. The physiological relevance of the prostratin+HDACI synergism was demonstrated in CD8(+)-depleted peripheral blood mononuclear cells from HAART-treated patients with undetectable viral load, as well as in resting CD4(+) T cells isolated from similar patients, where the combination treatment reactivated viral replication. Our findings suggest that combining different types of proviral activators may have important implications for reducing the size of latent HIV-1 reservoirs in HAART-treated patients.

title: Centrosome aberrations: cause or consequence of cancer progression?
text: Most human tumors exhibit aberrant centrosomes, indicating an underlying disturbance in the regulation of centrosome structure, duplication, or segregation. Centrosomes play a crucial role in organizing microtubule arrays throughout the cell cycle, thereby influencing both the architecture of the tissue and the accuracy of chromosome segregation. However, the origins of centrosomal abnormalities in tumors remain unclear, and their impact on the generation of invasive, genetically unstable cells during cancer progression is still being studied.

title: Autonomic neuropathy, QT interval lengthening, and unexpected deaths in male diabetic patients
text: In this study, the authors measured the QT intervals of 38 male diabetic subjects (13 with and 25 without autonomic neuropathy) over a range of 500-1000 milliseconds during resting state. They found a close linear relationship between QT and RR intervals in all subjects, with a significantly greater slope in the autonomic neuropathy group. Thirty-two of these subjects had repeat QT measurements 3-6 years later, and found that QT and QTC lengths significantly increased at the second visit, unrelated to age or time between recordings. Among the 71 male diabetic subjects under 60 years of age followed for 3 years, 13 had died, with all of those with autonomic neuropathy having longer QT and QTC intervals compared to those without neuropathy, despite similar ages and duration of diabetes. The authors conclude that there is an alteration in the QT/RR interval relationship in diabetic autonomic neuropathy, and that changes in QT length over time parallel changes in autonomic function. They suggest that there may be an association between QT interval prolongation and the risk of unexpected death in diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

title: Incidence of cancer after immunosuppressive treatment for heart transplantation.
text: Prolonged or intense immunosuppressive therapy following organ transplantation is associated with an elevated risk of cancer, particularly in heart and heart-lung transplant recipients compared to renal transplant patients. Notably, the incidence of lymphomas was significantly higher in cardiac recipients compared to renal patients. Furthermore, there was a nearly twofold increase in all neoplasms and a nearly sixfold increase in visceral tumors in cardiac recipients. Several factors may contribute to these disparities. In cardiac allograft recipients, intensive immunosuppression is often employed to treat acute rejection, and this era of polypharmacy, typically consisting of triple therapy, has resulted in the highest number of cardiac transplants.

title: Nucleating actin for invasion
text: The entry of cancer cells into surrounding tissue is a crucial step in the metastatic process, which is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths. This process involves the migration of cancer cells through the formation of structures such as invadopodia and pseudopodia, which rely on actin assembly regulated by specialized actin nucleation factors. There is a diverse range of actin nucleators present in human cells, including formins, spire, and Arp2/3-regulating proteins, and the discovery of additional factors may lead to the development of novel treatments for invasive and metastatic cancer.

title: GFI1 and GFI1B control the loss of endothelial identity of hemogenic endothelium during hematopoietic commitment.
text: Recent research has revealed that during embryonic development, hematopoietic progenitors and stem cells arise from hemogenic endothelium precursors through a process called endothelial to hematopoietic transition (EHT). Transcription factor RUNX1 is essential for this process, but the specific downstream regulators remain largely unknown. In this study, we identified Gfi1 and Gfi1b as direct targets of RUNX1 and critical regulators of EHT. GFI1 and GFI1B can induce the down-regulation of endothelial markers and the formation of round cells, a characteristic of EHT, in the absence of RUNX1. Conversely, blood progenitors in Gfi1- and Gfi1b-deficient embryos maintain the expression of endothelial genes and fail to release from the yolk sac and disseminate into embryonic tissues. Our findings demonstrate a crucial and specific role of the GFI1 transcription factors in the initial stages of the process leading to the generation of hematopoietic progenitors from hemogenic endothelium.

title: An RNA-directed nuclease mediates post-transcriptional gene silencing in Drosophila cells.
text: In a diverse group of organisms, including Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, planaria, hydra, trypanosomes, fungi, and plants, the introduction of double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) inhibits gene expression in a sequence-specific manner, a phenomenon known as RNA interference (RNAi) or post-transcriptional gene silencing (PTGS). This response may provide anti-viral defense, modulate transposition, or regulate gene expression. To elucidate the mechanisms underlying this genetic phenomenon, we have taken a biochemical approach. Here, we show that "loss-of-function" phenotypes can be created in cultured Drosophila cells by transfection with specific dsRNAs. This coincides with a significant reduction in the level of cognate cellular messenger RNAs (mRNAs). Extracts of transfected cells contain a nuclease activity that specifically degrades exogenous transcripts homologous to the transfected dsRNA. This enzyme contains an essential RNA component. After partial purification, the sequence-specific nuclease co-fractionates with a discrete, approximately 25-nucleotide RNA species, which may confer specificity to the enzyme through homology to the substrate mRNAs.

title: Expression of basal cell keratin 15 and keratin 19 in oral squamous neoplasms represents diverse pathophysiologies.
text: Human epithelial tissues contain keratin, which is upregulated during differentiation. The expression of various keratins differs depending on the target cell type, and these alterations are believed to reflect changes in cellular properties. The basal cells of oral epithelium express keratins 5 (K5), 14 (K14), 15 (K15), and 19 (K19), but the changes in these proteins during tumorigenesis are not well understood. To address this gap in knowledge and explore potential diagnostic applications, we investigated the expression of these keratins in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and squamous intraepithelial neoplasm (SIN). cDNA microarray analysis of 43 OSCC revealed a slight upregulation of keratin 14 (KRT14), a downregulation of keratin 15 (KRT15) and 19 (KRT19), and unchanged expression of keratin 5 (KRT5). Notably, there were significant variations in KRT15 and KRT19 expression across each cancer. Well-differentiated OSCC tend to express more KRT15 and less KRT19 compared to moderately- or poorly-differentiated OSCC. KRT15 was positively correlated with differentiation-related keratin, KRT13. These findings were further validated through immunohistochemical examination. K5 and K14 were ubiquitously expressed in all 50 OSCC and 50 SIN examined, while K15 and K19 were generally downregulated, but were retained in approximately half of the cases and exhibited diverse expression patterns. K15-positive cancers tended to display a well-differentiated phenotype, while K19-positive cancers tended to exhibit more invasive tumor fronts. Most K19-positive cancers showed little association with SIN. K19 was consistently downregulated in high-grade SIN, while K15 was downregulated mainly in high-grade SIN. In summary, K15 and K19, unlike K5 or K14, exhibit variable expression in both SIN and OSCC, reflecting their distinct pathogeneses and biological behaviors, suggesting their potential as markers for subclassifying OSCC and SIN.

title: Exosomes in Plasma of Patients with Ovarian Carcinoma: Potential Biomarkers of Tumor Progression and Response to Therapy.
text:
Background:
Ovarian cancer (OvCa) patients' plasma contains exosomes released by tumor cells, which may contribute to tumor progression. This study investigates the association between exosome presence/protein content in plasma and disease outcome, response to standard therapy, and resistance to therapies in OvCa patients at diagnosis and during treatment.
Methods:
Exosomes were isolated from OvCa patients' plasma (n=22), patients with benign tumors (n=10), and healthy controls (NC) using ultracentrifugation. Exosomes were visualized using scanning electron microscopy, and their protein content was measured. Western blots were used to evaluate the presence of MAGE 3/6 and TGF-β1 in exosomes.
Results:
OvCa patients' plasma contained higher levels of exosomal proteins compared to plasma from patients with benign tumors or NC (p<0.05). Exosomes isolated from OvCa patients' plasma carried TGF-β1 and MAGE3/6, which distinguished OvCa patients from those with benign tumors and NC. High protein levels of exosomes were observed in newly diagnosed patients, but the protein content of isolated exosomes was significantly higher in advanced stages of OvCa patients. Exosome levels varied during/after chemotherapy, and correlations between the changes in exosomal protein levels and clinical data suggested that the protein content of exosomes might be useful in predicting responses to therapy and prognosis in OvCa patients.
Conclusion:
Analysis of plasma exosomes offers a novel approach to diagnosis and monitoring response to therapies in OvCa patients.

title: Insecticide impregnated curtains to control domestic transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis in Venezuela: cluster randomised trial.
text:
Objective: To assess the impact of insecticide-impregnated curtains on the transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis in urban settings.
Design: Cluster randomized controlled trial with a household interview survey, observational study of people's behavior, and entomological study using light traps to capture sandflies inside homes.
Setting: 14 urban sectors in Trujillo, Venezuela.
Participants: 2913 inhabitants of 569 houses.
Intervention: Sectors were paired based on their 12-month cumulative incidence of cutaneous leishmaniasis, with one sector in each pair randomly allocated to receive polyester curtains impregnated with lambdacyhalothrin (intervention group) while the other sector received curtains without insecticide or no curtains (control group). After 12 months, a follow-up household survey was conducted.
Main Outcome Measures: Reduction in the abundance of sandflies indoors and 12-month incidence of clinical cases of cutaneous leishmaniasis.
Results: Transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis primarily occurred in the domestic setting, with an incidence of 4% over 12 months. The mean number of sandflies per trap per night was 16. After the follow-up survey, the 12-month incidence of cutaneous leishmaniasis was 0% in the intervention group and 8% in the six pairs of control groups that received unimpregnated curtains (mean difference 8, 95% confidence interval 4.22 to 11.78; P=0.001). There were significantly fewer sandflies in the intervention group (2 vs 15, mean difference 13 sandflies per trap; 95% confidence interval 4.22 to 11.78; P<0.001).
Conclusion: Insecticide-impregnated curtains provide a high degree of protection against indoor transmission of cutaneous leishmaniasis.

title: Chronic pancreatitis is essential for induction of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by K-Ras oncogenes in adult mice.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA), one of the most deadly forms of cancer in humans, is often characterized by the activation of oncogenes, specifically K-Ras. In this study, we investigate the role of K-Ras in the development of PDA by selectively expressing an endogenous K-Ras(G12V) oncogene in embryonic cells of acinar/centroacinar lineage. Our findings show that this leads to the formation of pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs) and invasive PDA, suggesting that PDA may arise from the differentiation of acinar/centroacinar cells or their precursors into ductal-like cells.
