In this study, we investigated the mechanisms of resistance to rociletinib in patients with T790M-positive lung cancers by performing biopsies at the time of progression. Our findings reveal that approximately half of the T790M-positive cancers had T790-wild-type clones that emerged as the dominant source of resistance to rociletinib. Moreover, we observed that the pretreatment fraction of T790M-positive cells influenced the response to rociletinib, and longitudinal analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) revealed an increase in plasma EGFR-activating mutations, which sometimes heralded rociletinib resistance. These findings underscore the importance of tumor heterogeneity when targeted therapies are used and highlight the need for combination regimens that also target T790-wild-type clones to improve outcomes.
In summary, our study demonstrates that T790-wild-type clones can emerge as a major mechanism of resistance to rociletinib in T790M-positive lung cancers, and that plasma ctDNA analysis can sometimes predict emerging resistance mechanisms. These findings have significant clinical implications and underscore the need for combination therapies to overcome tumor heterogeneity and improve outcomes.

title: Extrathymic Generation of Regulatory T Cells in Placental Mammals Mitigates Maternal-Fetal Conflict
text: Regulatory T (Treg) cells, whose development and function are governed by the X-encoded transcription factor Foxp3, are generated in the thymus (tTreg) and extrathymically (peripheral, pTreg), and their deficiency leads to fatal autoimmune disorders. In this study, we demonstrate that a Foxp3 enhancer, conserved noncoding sequence 1 (CNS1), which is essential for pTreg cell generation but dispensable for tTreg cell development, is present exclusively in placental mammals. CNS1 is primarily composed of mammalian-wide interspersed repeats (MIR) that have undergone retrotransposition during early mammalian evolution. During pregnancy, pTreg cells specific to a model paternal alloantigen are generated in a CNS1-dependent manner and accumulate in the placenta. Furthermore, when mated with allogeneic, but not syngeneic, males, CNS1-deficient females exhibit increased fetal resorption accompanied by increased immune cell infiltration and defective remodeling of spiral arteries. Our findings suggest that, during evolution, a CNS1-dependent mechanism of extrathymic differentiation of Treg cells emerged in placental animals to ensure maternal-fetal tolerance.

title: Acquired EGFR C797S mutation mediates resistance to AZD9291 in non–small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR T790M
text: Here, we investigated cell-free plasma DNA (cfDNA) from individuals with advanced lung cancer who had developed resistance to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) AZD9291. We initially performed next-generation sequencing on cfDNA from seven subjects and identified an acquired EGFR C797S mutation in one individual. We then used a cell line to express this mutant EGFR construct and demonstrated that it was resistant to AZD9291. Subsequently, we performed droplet digital PCR on serial cfDNA samples from 15 AZD9291-treated subjects and found that all were positive for the T790M mutation before treatment, but upon developing resistance, three distinct molecular subtypes emerged: six cases acquired the C797S mutation, five cases maintained the T790M mutation without acquiring the C797S mutation, and four cases lost the T790M mutation despite retaining the underlying EGFR activating mutation. Our findings provide insight into the diversity of mechanisms by which tumors develop resistance to AZD9291 and highlight the need for therapies that can overcome resistance mediated by the EGFR C797S mutation.

title: The Translation Initiation Factor 3f (eIF3f) Exhibits a Deubiquitinase Activity Regulating Notch Activation
text:
The activation of the mammalian Notch receptor after ligand binding involves a series of events, including metalloprotease-cleavage, endocytosis, monoubiquitination, and processing by the gamma-secretase, resulting in a soluble, transcriptionally active molecule. Notch1 receptor monoubiquitination is proposed to occur before its gamma-secretase cleavage, with the targeted lysine localized to its submembrane domain. Investigating the regulation of this step by a deubiquitinase (DUB) activity could provide new insights into Notch receptor activation and downstream signaling.
An immunofluorescence-based screening of an shRNA library identified eIF3f, previously known as a subunit of the translation initiation factor eIF3, as a DUB targeting the activated Notch receptor. eIF3f has an intrinsic DUB activity, and knocking down eIF3f leads to an accumulation of monoubiquitinated forms of activated Notch, which is counteracted by murine WT eIF3f but not by a catalytically inactive mutant. eIF3f is also recruited to activated Notch on endocytic vesicles by the putative E3 ubiquitin ligase Deltex1, which serves as a bridging factor.
Catalytically inactive forms of eIF3f as well as shRNAs targeting eIF3f repress Notch activation in a coculture assay, suggesting that eIF3f is a new positive regulator of the Notch pathway. Our results support two novel conclusions: (1) The activated form of Notch needs to be deubiquitinated before being processed by the gamma-secretase activity and entering the nucleus, where it fulfills its transcriptional function. (2) The enzyme responsible for this deubiquitinase activity is eIF3f, which is previously known as a translation initiation factor. These findings improve our understanding of Notch signaling and open new avenues of research on the Zomes family and the translation initiation factors.

title: Focal contacts as mechanosensors: externally applied local mechanical force induces growth of focal contacts by an mDia1-dependent and ROCKindependent mechanism
text: The transition of cell-matrix adhesions from initial punctate focal complexes to mature elongated forms, known as focal contacts, requires GTPase Rho activity. Specifically, activation of myosin II-driven contractility by a Rho target, Rho-associated kinase (ROCK), was shown to be essential for focal contact formation. To investigate the mechanism of Rho-dependent focal contact induction and to elucidate the role of cell contractility, we applied mechanical force to vinculin-containing dot-like adhesions at the cell edge using a micropipette. Local centripetal pulling led to local assembly and elongation of these structures, resulting in the formation of streak-like focal contacts, as revealed by the dynamics of green fluorescent protein-tagged vinculin or paxillin and interference reflection microscopy. Inhibition of Rho activity by C3 transferase suppressed force-induced focal contact formation. However, constitutively active mutants of another Rho target, the formin homology protein mDia1 (Watanabe et al., 1999), were sufficient to restore force-induced focal contact formation in C3 transferase-treated cells. Force-induced focal contact formation still occurred in cells subjected to myosin II and ROCK inhibition, indicating that mDia1 activity bypasses the requirement for ROCK-mediated myosin II contractility in the induction of focal contacts. Our experiments demonstrate that integrin-containing focal complexes behave as individual mechanosensors, assembling directionally in response to local force.

title: Maternal Protein Restriction Affects Postnatal Growth and the Expression of Key Proteins Involved in Lifespan Regulation in Mice
text: In a previous study, we found that maternal protein restriction in rodents during early life influenced growth rate and ultimately affected lifespan. Low birth weight due to maternal protein restriction followed by catch-up growth (recuperated animals) was associated with a shorter lifespan, while protein restriction and slow growth during lactation (postnatal low protein: PLP animals) increased lifespan. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we examined the effects of maternal diet on organ growth, metabolic parameters, and the expression of insulin/IGF1 signaling proteins and Sirt1 in the muscle of male mice at weaning. PLP mice, which experienced protein restriction during lactation, had improved insulin sensitivity, as evidenced by lower fasting glucose and insulin levels. PLP mice also had higher relative weights of brain and thymus, suggesting enhanced functional capacity of these tissues, which may contribute to their longer lifespan. Additionally, PLP mice had increased expression of insulin receptor substrate 1 and protein kinase C zeta. In contrast, recuperated animals had decreased levels of several insulin signaling proteins, including PI3 kinase subunits p85alpha, p110beta, and protein kinase C zeta, which may predispose them to insulin resistance. Sirt1 protein expression was also reduced in recuperated offspring. These findings suggest that maternal protein restriction can affect major metabolic pathways involved in the regulation of lifespan, which may explain the impact of maternal diet on longevity.

title: ‘Short stature in children - a questionnaire for parents’: a new instrument for growth disorder-specific psychosocial adaptation in children
text:
Recent research has shown that children with growth disorders, such as achondroplasia and growth hormone deficiency, exhibit comparable psychosocial adaptation as those without a growth disorder. However, there is a lack of sensitive and specific techniques for analyzing and comparing the quality of life of these children. To address this gap, we developed a new questionnaire for parents of short-statured children, which provides both qualitative and quantitative information on individual stress factors and sources of help.
We administered the questionnaire to 442 parents of children with growth retardation resulting from different causes. The analysis revealed four dimensions of psychosocial adaptation: suffering, future anxieties, behavioral problems, and coping efforts. The questionnaire demonstrated sufficient reliability and was able to distinguish between growth disorder groups. Specifically, we found that children with achondroplasia had more physical restrictions and a different profile of psychosocial adaptation compared to those with growth hormone deficiency.
Our findings suggest that the new questionnaire is a valuable tool for obtaining growth disorder-specific information on individual stress factors, resources, and psychosocial adaptation. This study provides evidence for the construct validity and specificity of the questionnaire, and highlights the importance of considering the unique needs and experiences of children with growth disorders.

title: Alphavirus-derived small RNAs modulate pathogenesis in disease vector mosquitoes.
text:
Mosquito-borne viruses cause significant health problems in both humans and domesticated animals, with a biological transmission cycle that relies on alternating virus replication in susceptible vertebrates and mosquito hosts. Although the vertebrate infection is typically acute and associated with disease, the continuous transmission of these viruses in nature depends on the establishment of a persistent, non-pathogenic infection in the mosquito vector. Previous studies have shown that an antiviral RNAi response can limit the replication of RNA viruses in flies, but the importance of this pathway as an antiviral defense in mammals is not well understood. One possible explanation for this discrepancy is the differences in immune responses between mammals and mosquitoes, which may allow viruses to persist in the invertebrate host without causing disease.
We recently identified small interfering RNAs (viRNAs) in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes infected with the mosquito-borne virus, Sindbis (SINV). These viRNAs were found to be 21 nucleotides in length and had an asymmetric distribution throughout the SINV genome. To investigate their role in controlling the pathogenic potential of these viruses, we infected mosquitoes with recombinant alphaviruses expressing suppressors of RNA silencing. Our results showed that decreased survival was observed in mosquitoes in which the accumulation of viRNAs was suppressed, suggesting that an exogenous siRNA pathway is essential for the survival of mosquitoes infected with alphaviruses and, therefore, the maintenance of these viruses in nature.

title: Nuclear RNAi maintains heritable gene silencing in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text: RNA interference (RNAi) is a heritable phenomenon in Caenorhabditis elegans, where the offspring of animals exposed to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) inherit the ability to silence genes that were targeted by RNAi in the previous generation. To investigate the mechanism of RNAi inheritance in C. elegans, we examined the expression of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and the deposition of histone 3 lysine 9 methylation (H3K9me) marks in progeny. Our findings indicate that exposure of animals to dsRNA leads to the heritable expression of siRNAs, but the deposition of H3K9me marks is not directly inherited. Instead, H3K9me marks are reestablished in inheriting progeny, and their appearance is more pronounced in progeny than in directly exposed animals. Additionally, we demonstrate that the nuclear RNAi (Nrde) pathway maintains heritable RNAi silencing in C. elegans. The Argonaute (Ago) NRDE-3 associates with heritable siRNAs and, in conjunction with the nuclear RNAi factors NRDE-1, NRDE-2, and NRDE-4, promotes siRNA expression in inheriting progeny. These results provide evidence that siRNA expression is heritable in C. elegans and define an RNAi pathway that maintains RNAi silencing and siRNA expression in the progeny of animals exposed to dsRNA.

title: Cancer survivors in the United States: prevalence across the survivorship trajectory and implications for care.
text:
BACKGROUND: Cancer survivors are a growing demographic, characterized by diverse needs for medical care, psychosocial support, and practical assistance. To inform survivorship research and practice, this study aims to provide an overview of the prevalent population of cancer survivors in terms of their overall numbers and prevalence by cancer site and time since diagnosis.
METHODS: Incidence and survival data from 1975 to 2007 were obtained from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program, while population projections for 2012 and beyond were obtained from the United States Census Bureau. Cancer prevalence for 2012 and beyond was estimated using the Prevalence Incidence Approach Model, which assumes constant future incidence and survival trends but dynamic projections of the U.S. population.
RESULTS: As of January 1, 2012, approximately 13.7 million cancer survivors were living in the United States, with projected prevalence reaching 18 million by 2022. Sixty-four percent of this population have survived 5 years or more after diagnosis; 40% have survived 10 years or more; and 15% have survived 20 years or more. Over the next decade, the number of people who have lived 5 years or more after their cancer diagnosis is projected to increase by approximately 37% to 11.9 million.
CONCLUSIONS: These prevalence estimates will inform the national research agenda and future projections regarding the health service needs of cancer survivors across the survivorship trajectory. A coordinated agenda for research and practice is necessary to address the long-term medical, psychosocial, and practical needs of this growing population.
IMPACT: The findings of this study will have a significant impact on the healthcare community, policymakers, and cancer survivors themselves, providing valuable insights into the changing landscape of cancer survivorship and the need for tailored support and care.

title: Human aneuploidy: mechanisms and new insights into an age-old problem
text: Approximately 10% of human pregnancies involve trisomic (three copies of a chromosome) or monosomic (one copy of a chromosome) embryos, with the incidence increasing to over 50% for women nearing the end of their reproductive years. Despite extensive research, the underlying molecular causes of aneuploidy (having an abnormal number of chromosomes) remain elusive. Recent studies in humans and model organisms have shed light on the intricate nature of meiotic defects, suggesting that the age-related increase in errors in the human female is not caused by a single factor but rather the result of a complex interplay between oogenesis-specific features and various endogenous and exogenous factors.

title: The Drosophila hindgut lacks constitutively active adult stem cells but proliferates in response to tissue damage.
text: Recent studies have suggested that the adult Drosophila hindgut contains active, tissue-replenishing stem cells, similar to those found in the midgut, but located within an anterior ring to form a single large crypt. However, our own research has found that there are no active stem cells and little cell turnover in adult hindgut tissue, based on clonal marking and BrdU incorporation studies. Contrary to previous proposals, we have shown that the adult hindgut is not generated by anterior stem cells during larval/pupal development. Nevertheless, we observed that severe damage to the hindgut can elicit cell proliferation within a ring of putative quiescent stem cells at the anterior of the pylorus. Therefore, the hindgut does not provide a model of tissue maintenance through constantly active stem cells, but it has the potential to shed light on mechanisms of stress-induced tissue repair.

title: Vitamin d deficiency in postmenopausal women - biological correlates.
text:
Introduction:
Low levels of vitamin D (VD) have been linked to secondary hyperparathyroidism and the resulting consequences of reduced bone mineral density (BMD), increased risk of fractures and falls. In this study, we aimed to investigate the VD status and related biological factors in a group of postmenopausal women.
Methods:
We evaluated 123 postmenopausal women referred to our institution for BMD evaluation by their general practitioner. Our study included serum measurements of total and ionized calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD), parathyroid hormone (PTH), osteocalcin, and bone mineral density (BMD) using central DXA osteodensitometry. VD insufficiency was defined as serum levels below 30 ng/ml, while deficiency was defined as levels below 20 ng/ml.
Results:
Our findings revealed that 91.9% of participants had VD levels below 30 ng/ml, with 74.8% having VD deficiency and 17.1% having insufficiency. Only 8.1% of the women had sufficient VD levels. A history of fragility fractures was present in 45.83% of osteoporotic patients, 27.27% of osteopenic patients, and 15.15% of women with normal BMD. Among the 32 women taking VD supplements at the time of evaluation, the 25OHD level was significantly higher in those with prior fragility fractures (p=0.018) and osteoporosis (p=0.008). 25OHD concentration negatively correlated with PTH, ALP, and osteocalcin. The bone markers evaluated had a significant inverse correlation with the radius BMD, T, and Z scores (p=0.004). Moreover, 27.17% of the cases with VD deficiency had secondary hyperparathyroidism, and the 25OHD concentration was significantly lower in these cases (p=0.000).

title: CD44v6 is a marker of constitutive and reprogrammed cancer stem cells driving colon cancer metastasis.
text: Colorectal cancer stem cells (CR-CSCs) are the driving force behind tumor formation and metastasis, but the mechanisms by which they acquire metastatic traits are not fully understood. In this study, we discovered that all CR-CSCs express the protein CD44v6, which is essential for their migration and the generation of metastatic tumors. Interestingly, CD44v6 expression is low in primary tumors but is highly expressed in clonogenic CR-CSC populations. We found that cytokines, such as hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), osteopontin (OPN), and stromal-derived factor 1α (SDF-1), secreted by tumor-associated cells, increase CD44v6 expression in CR-CSCs by activating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, which promotes migration and metastasis. Moreover, we found that CD44v6-negative progenitor cells do not give rise to metastatic lesions, but when treated with cytokines, they can acquire CD44v6 expression and metastatic capacity. Importantly, inhibition of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) selectively killed CD44v6-expressing CR-CSCs and reduced metastatic growth. Finally, we found that low levels of CD44v6 expression in patient tumors were associated with improved survival outcomes, suggesting that CD44v6 may serve as a functional biomarker and therapeutic target for metastatic colorectal cancer.

title: Senescent Cells, Tumor Suppression, and Organismal Aging: Good Citizens, Bad Neighbors
text: Cells from organisms with renewable tissues have the ability to permanently exit the cell cycle in response to various stressors, including damaged telomeres, DNA damage, strong growth signals, and disrupted chromatin. This response, known as cellular senescence, is regulated by the p53 and RB tumor suppressor proteins and serves as a powerful anticancer mechanism. However, as senescent cells age, they undergo changes that may contribute to aging and certain age-related diseases, such as late-life cancer. Therefore, the senescence response can be considered antagonistically pleiotropic, as it promotes early-life survival by preventing the development of cancer but may ultimately limit longevity by accumulating dysfunctional senescent cells.

title: Advances in high-resolution imaging--techniques for three-dimensional imaging of cellular structures.
text: A central objective in biology is to elucidate the connection between cellular organization and function. To achieve this, a deeper understanding of the composition and structure of organelles is essential. Although visualization of cellular organelles through fluorescence or electron microscopy (EM) has become a common tool for cell biologists, recent advances have significantly improved the clarity of cellular structures. In particular, advanced light-microscopy techniques are now capable of achieving resolutions below the diffraction limit, while EM tomography provides high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) images of cellular structures. The ability to perform both fluorescence and electron microscopy on the same sample (correlative light and electron microscopy, CLEM) enables the identification of fluorescently labeled proteins in relation to organelle structures visualized by EM. In this review, we will discuss the current state of the art in 3D biological imaging techniques, with a focus on recent advances in electron microscopy and fluorescence super-resolution techniques.

title: Quercetin attenuates vascular calcification by inhibiting oxidative stress and mitochondrial fission.
text: Vascular calcification is a strong predictor of increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, and has a high prevalence among patients with chronic kidney disease. The present study investigated the effects of quercetin on vascular calcification caused by oxidative stress and abnormal mitochondrial dynamics, both in vitro and in vivo. Quercetin was shown to block the calcification of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) by inhibiting oxidative stress and decreasing mitochondrial fission, which leads to mitochondria-dependent apoptotic events. Quercetin also significantly ameliorated aortic calcification in a rat model. In summary, our findings suggest that quercetin attenuates vascular calcification by reducing apoptosis of VSMCs through its inhibitory effects on oxidative stress and mitochondrial fission.

title: The M/GP5 Glycoprotein Complex of Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome Virus Binds the Sialoadhesin Receptor in a Sialic Acid-Dependent Manner
text: The porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) poses a significant threat to swine health worldwide and is currently the most prevalent viral disease affecting the swine industry. In the past, research has identified essential virus receptors and entry mediators, but the viral counterparts for these molecules have remained elusive, hindering the development of new-generation vaccines. The primary objective of this study was to identify the viral counterparts for sialoadhesin, a crucial PRRSV receptor found on macrophages. To achieve this, we constructed a soluble form of sialoadhesin and validated its ability to bind PRRSV in a sialic acid-dependent manner. We also demonstrated that sialoadhesin can neutralize PRRSV infection of macrophages, confirming its role as an essential PRRSV receptor. Our findings revealed that the M/GP(5) glycoprotein complex of PRRSV is the ligand for sialoadhesin, and the interaction is dependent on the sialic acid binding capacity of sialoadhesin and the presence of sialic acids on GP(5). This study not only advances our understanding of PRRSV biology but also provides valuable insights and tools for the development of new-generation PRRSV vaccines.

title: A versatile zero background T-vector system for gene cloning and functional genomics.
text:
With the recent surge in the availability of complete genomic sequences of various organisms, there is a growing demand for high-throughput and cost-effective systems for gene cloning and functional analysis. Although site-specific recombination-based cloning systems, such as Gateway cloning technology, offer efficient transfer of DNA fragments into multiple destination vectors, the two-step cloning process involved can be time-consuming and expensive.
To address this challenge, we have developed a zero background TA cloning system that enables simple and high-efficiency direct cloning of PCR-amplified DNA fragments with minimal self-ligation background. The improved T-vector system leverages the restriction enzyme XcmI to generate a T-overhang after digestion and the negative selection marker gene ccdB to eliminate self-ligation background after transformation.
We demonstrate the versatility and potential of the zero background TA cloning system by creating a range of transient and stable transformation vectors for constitutive gene expression, gene silencing, protein tagging, protein subcellular localization detection, and promoter fragment activity analysis in plants. The system's adaptability allows it to be easily customized for developing specialized expression vectors for other organisms, making it a valuable complement to the Gateway cloning system for gene cloning and functional genomics.

title: GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-Cortactin Pathway Frequently Used in Cancer Invasion Is Activated by VEGFR2 to Promote Angiogenesis
text: The collaboration between angiogenesis and cancer invasiveness significantly contributes to the malignancy of cancer. Arf6 and its effector, AMAP1, are frequently overexpressed in breast cancer and play a central role in inducing invasion and metastasis. In this pathway, Arf6 is activated by EGFR through GEP100. Arf6 is also highly expressed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and is involved in angiogenesis. Interestingly, we found that HUVECs highly express AMAP1, and VEGFR2 recruits GEP100 to activate Arf6. AMAP1 functions by binding to cortactin in cancer invasion and metastasis. Our study demonstrates that the same GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-cortactin pathway is essential for angiogenesis activities, including cell migration and tubular formation, as well as for the enhancement of cell permeability and VE-cadherin endocytosis of VEGF-stimulated HUVECs. Moreover, we found that components of this pathway are highly expressed in pathologic angiogenesis, and blocking this pathway effectively inhibits VEGF- or tumor-induced angiogenesis and choroidal neovascularization. The GEP100-Arf6-AMAP1-cortactin pathway, activated by receptor tyrosine kinases, appears to be a common pathway in angiogenesis and cancer invasion and metastasis, providing new therapeutic targets.

title: Dynamics of Cryptococcus neoformans-Macrophage Interactions Reveal that Fungal Background Influences Outcome during Cryptococcal Meningoencephalitis in Humans
text: Cryptococcosis is a complex fungal infection with diverse clinical manifestations and outcomes. While host factors have been implicated in the variability of cryptococcosis, the role of the fungal isolate itself remains unclear. To investigate the impact of clinical isolates on the interaction with host cells and disease outcome, we developed and validated novel flow cytometry-based assays using J774 macrophages. We analyzed the phenotype of 54 Cryptococcus neoformans clinical isolates recovered from cerebrospinal fluids (CSF) from 54 unrelated patients, and found significant variation in their interaction with macrophages. Isolates with low phagocytic index (PI) and high intracellular proliferation index (IPH2) were associated with nonsterilization of CSF at week 2 and death at month 3, respectively. A subset of 9 isolates with different phenotypes exhibited variable virulence in mice and displayed distinct patterns of intracellular gene expression, including the LAC1, APP1, VAD1, IPC1, PLB1, and COX1 genes. These findings suggest that, in addition to host factors, the patient's outcome can be influenced by fungal determinants. Deciphering the molecular events involved in cryptococcosis pathogenesis is crucial for understanding the disease mechanisms and developing effective therapies.

title: Angiopoietin-2 at high concentration can enhance endothelial cell survival through the phosphatidylinositol 3′-kinase/Akt signal transduction pathway
text: The Angiopoietin-Tie2 system in endothelial cells plays a crucial role in regulating vasculogenesis and vascular integrity. High levels of Ang2 mRNA are observed during tumorigenesis, although the specific function of Ang2 remains unclear. In this study, we discovered that high concentrations of Ang2 (800 ng/ml) act as an apoptosis survival factor for endothelial cells during serum deprivation-induced apoptosis. This survival effect was blocked by pre-treatment with a soluble Tie2 receptor and inhibitors of the PI 3'-kinase signaling pathway, including wortmannin and LY294002. Our findings indicate that at high concentrations, Ang2, like Ang1, can activate the Tie2 receptor, PI 3'-kinase, and serine-threonine kinase Akt, leading to endothelial cell survival. These results suggest that Ang2 may play a positive role in tumor angiogenesis.

title: Lipoxin a4 analogs attenuate induction of intestinal epithelial proinflammatory gene expression and reduce the severity of dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis.
text: The anti-inflammatory lipid mediators lipoxin A(4) (LXA(4)), aspirin-triggered 15-epi-LXA(4), and their stable analogs inhibit the secretion and recruitment of neutrophils by intestinal epithelial cells. To investigate the mechanism by which these lipid mediators modulate inflammatory responses, we analyzed global epithelial gene expression using cDNA microarrays. While LXA(4) analog alone did not significantly affect gene expression, pretreatment with LXA(4) analog attenuated the induction of approximately 50% of the genes up-regulated in response to the gastroenteritis-causing pathogen Salmonella typhimurium. A major subset of these genes is regulated by the transcription factor NF-κB, suggesting that LXA(4) analog is influencing NF-κB activity. We found that nanomolar concentrations of LXA(4) analog inhibited NF-κB-mediated transcriptional activation in a LXA(4) receptor-dependent manner and prevented the degradation of the inhibitory protein IκBα. LXA(4) analog did not affect earlier signaling events that lead to IκBα degradation, such as Ca(2+) mobilization or IκBα phosphorylation. To evaluate the in vivo relevance of these findings, we administered LXA(4) analog to mice with DSS-induced inflammatory colitis. Oral administration of LXA(4) analog significantly reduced weight loss, hematochezia, and mortality in these mice. These results suggest that LXA(4) analog-mediated inhibition of NF-κB activity can be therapeutic for diseases characterized by mucosal inflammation.

title: Serum plant and other noncholesterol sterols, cholesterol metabolism and 22-year mortality among middle-aged men.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the long-term prognostic value of serum non-cholesterol sterols, including plant sterols, in middle-aged men with high cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk, without statins at baseline.
Methods: This was a prospective study of 232 men (mean age 60 years) at high risk of CVD in 1985-1986. Most were hypercholesterolemic, 29 (12%) had a history of CVD or cancer, 6 (3%) had diabetes, and 46 (20%) had metabolic syndrome (MS). Measured non-cholesterol sterols (expressed as absolute concentrations or ratios to serum cholesterol to standardize for cholesterol concentrations) included lathosterol and desmosterol (reflecting cholesterol synthesis), and plant sterols (campesterol and sitosterol) and cholestanol (reflecting cholesterol absorption). The main outcome measure was total mortality.
Results: At baseline, markers of cholesterol synthesis and absorption showed expected inverse associations. During the 22-year follow-up, 101 men (43%) died. At baseline, non-survivors smoked more, exercised less, and had more components of MS (although not meeting strict criteria), whereas traditional risk factors of CVD were not significantly different. Of the non-cholesterol sterols (either absolute or ratio), only sitosterol was significantly higher in survivors than in non-survivors (P=0.02). In multivariable analyses, the highest sitosterol-to-cholesterol tertile was associated with significantly lower mortality risk (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30-0.87) compared to the lowest tertile. Other associations were nonsignificant, although a "global" index of cholesterol metabolism (desmosterol-to-sitosterol ratio) suggested higher cholesterol synthesis and lower absorption to be associated with higher total and CVD mortality.
Conclusion: Higher serum plant sterol levels in middle-aged men predicted lower long-term mortality risk, possibly reflecting an association between higher cholesterol synthesis/lower absorption and mortality.

title: Intracoronary autologous cardiac progenitor cell transfer in patients with hypoplastic left heart syndrome: the TICAP prospective phase 1 controlled trial.
text:
RATIONALE: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) remains a lethal congenital cardiac defect, with a high mortality rate. Recent studies have suggested that intracoronary administration of autologous cardiosphere-derived cells (CDCs) may improve ventricular function in patients with HLHS.
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of intracoronary delivery of CDCs in patients with hypoplastic left heart syndrome after staged surgical procedures.
METHODS: Between January 5, 2011, and January 16, 2012, 14 patients (1.8±1.5 years) were prospectively assigned to receive intracoronary infusion of autologous CDCs 33.4±8.1 days after staged procedures (n=7), with 7 controls receiving standard palliation alone. The primary end point was to assess the safety of the procedure, and the secondary end point included the preliminary efficacy of CDCs in improving right ventricular ejection fraction.
RESULTS: Manufacturing and intracoronary delivery of CDCs were found to be feasible, with no serious adverse events reported within the 18-month follow-up period. Patients treated with CDCs showed significant improvement in right ventricular ejection fraction from baseline to 3-month follow-up (46.9%±4.6% to 52.1%±2.4%; P=0.008). Compared with controls at 18 months, cardiac MRI analysis of CDC-treated patients showed higher right ventricular ejection fraction (31.5%±6.8% versus 40.4%±7.6%; P=0.049), improved somatic growth (P=0.0005), reduced heart failure status (P=0.003), and lower incidence of coil occlusion for collaterals (P=0.007).
CONCLUSIONS: Intracoronary infusion of autologous CDCs appears to be feasible and safe in children with hypoplastic left heart syndrome after staged surgery. Large phase 2 trials are warranted to evaluate the potential effects of cardiac function improvements and the long-term benefits of clinical outcomes.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: URL http://www.clinicaltrials.gov. Unique identifier: NCT01273857.

title: A Whole Brain Staining, Embedding, and Clearing Pipeline for Adult Zebrafish to Visualize Cell Proliferation and Morphology in 3-Dimensions
text:
The field of macro-imaging has experienced significant growth with the emergence of innovative clearing methods and confocal microscopes with lasers capable of penetrating deeper into tissue. This advancement enables visualization and modeling of the growth of entire organs from birth or with manipulation, disease, or injury, providing new insights into development, tissue-wide signaling, and cell-to-cell interactions. The zebrafish (Danio rerio) has evolved from a primarily developmental model to a leading adult model of tissue regeneration, with its unparalleled neurogenic and regenerative capacity in the mature central nervous system receiving particular attention. However, there are limited tools to investigate the adult brain, making it challenging to visualize changes in the entire adult brain in three dimensions (3D) to analyze systemic patterns of cell proliferation or specific cell populations under physiological, injury, or disease conditions.
To address this gap, we present a novel method that offers a straightforward pipeline from intraperitoneal injections of the proliferative marker 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) to whole brain labeling, followed by embedded and cleared brain samples suitable for 3D imaging using optical projection tomography (OPT). This method allows for imaging of GFP-reporter lines and cell-specific antibodies in the presence or absence of EdU, thanks to the small size of the adult zebrafish brain and the consistent degree of EdU labeling. The use of basic clearing agents, benzyl benzoate, and benzyl alcohol, makes this method accessible to most laboratories interested in understanding the vertebrate central nervous system in health and disease.
Post-processing of OPT-imaged adult zebrafish brains injected with EdU reveals proliferative patterns in EdU can be easily observed and analyzed using IMARIS and/or FIJI/IMAGEJ software. This protocol will provide a valuable tool to unlock new insights into systemic patterns in cell proliferation in the healthy and injured brain, brain-wide cellular interactions, stem cell niche development, and changes in brain morphology.

title: Single-Construct Polycistronic Doxycycline-Inducible Vectors Improve Direct Cardiac Reprogramming and Can Be Used to Identify the Critical Timing of Transgene Expression
text:
Direct reprogramming is a promising approach in regenerative medicine, which involves the conversion of fibroblasts into cardiomyocyte-like cells (iCMs) through the overexpression of specific transcription factors. However, the optimal timing and molecular mechanisms of cardiac reprogramming remain unclear.
Conventional doxycycline (Dox)-inducible temporal transgene expression systems require the simultaneous transduction of two vectors (pLVX-rtTA/pLVX-cDNA) carrying the reverse tetracycline transactivator (rtTA) and the tetracycline response element (TRE)-controlled transgene, respectively. This approach has been shown to be inefficient in cardiac reprogramming.
To address this limitation, we developed a single-construct-based polycistronic Dox-inducible vector (pDox-cDNA) that expresses both the rtTA and TRE-controlled transgenes. We used fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS), quantitative RT-PCR, and immunostaining to evaluate the efficiency of cardiac reprogramming using pDox-GMT. Our results showed that pDox-GMT increased cardiac reprogramming three-fold compared to the conventional pLVX-rtTA/pLVX-GMT.
Furthermore, we co-transduced pDox-Hand2 with retroviral pMX-GMT, which resulted in a three-fold increase in cardiac reprogramming compared to pMX-GMT alone. Temporal Dox administration revealed that Hand2 transgene expression is critical during the first two weeks of cardiac reprogramming. Microarray analyses demonstrated that Hand2 represses cell cycle-promoting genes and enhances cardiac reprogramming.
In conclusion, we have developed an efficient temporal transgene expression system that could be invaluable in the study of cardiac reprogramming. This system allows for the precise control of transgene expression during the critical early stages of cardiac reprogramming, which may lead to improved efficiency and accuracy in the generation of iCMs.

title: Increasing microtubule acetylation rescues axonal transport and locomotor deficits caused by LRRK2 Roc-COR domain mutations
text:
Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) mutations are the most common genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. LRRK2 is a multifunctional protein that affects various cellular processes, and it has been shown to bind microtubules. However, it remains unclear whether LRRK2 mutations impact microtubule-based axonal transport and contribute to the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease. In this study, we investigate the effect of LRRK2 containing Roc-COR domain mutations (R1441C, Y1699C) on microtubule-based axonal transport in primary neurons and Drosophila, and explore potential interventions for Parkinson's disease.
Our results show that LRRK2 mutations preferentially associate with deacetylated microtubules and inhibit axonal transport in primary neurons and Drosophila, leading to locomotor deficits in vivo. In vitro, we found that increasing microtubule acetylation using deacetylase inhibitors or the tubulin acetylase αTAT1 prevents association of mutant LRRK2 with microtubules, and restores axonal transport. In vivo, knockdown of the deacetylases HDAC6 and Sirt2, or administration of TSA rescues both axonal transport and locomotor behavior.
Our findings reveal a pathogenic mechanism of LRRK2 mutations in Parkinson's disease, and provide a potential therapeutic target for intervention. By increasing microtubule acetylation, we can restore axonal transport and locomotor function in Parkinson's disease, suggesting a new avenue for drug development.

title: G1 arrest and differentiation can occur independently of Rb family function
text: The capacity of progenitor cells to exit the cell cycle is crucial for proper embryonic development and homeostasis, yet the mechanisms that govern cell cycle exit remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the role of the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein and its family members p107 and p130 in G0/G1 arrest and differentiation in mammalian cells. Our findings revealed that triple knockout (TKO) mouse embryos survive until embryonic day 9-11. Interestingly, some TKO cells, including those in epithelial and neural lineages, are able to exit the cell cycle in G0/G1 and differentiate in teratomas and in culture. This ability of TKO cells to arrest in G0/G1 is associated with the repression of key E2F target genes. Our results demonstrate that G1 arrest is not solely dependent on Rb family members, highlighting the robustness of cell cycle regulatory networks during differentiation and providing a means to identify potential pathways for inhibiting the proliferation of cancer cells with mutations in the Rb pathway.

title: Induction of ectopic eyes by targeted expression of the eyeless gene in Drosophila.
text: The Drosophila gene "eyeless" (ey) encodes a transcription factor with both a paired domain and a homeodomain. It shares significant sequence similarity with the mouse "Small eye" (Pax-6) gene and the human "Aniridia" gene, which are involved in eye development. These genes exhibit conserved splicing patterns and expression patterns in the developing nervous system and eye during morphogenesis. Mutations in either the insect or mammalian genes result in reduced or absent eye structures, suggesting that ey plays a crucial role in eye morphogenesis. By expressing the ey complementary DNA in specific imaginal disc primordia of Drosophila, ectopic eye structures were induced on the wings, legs, and antennae. These ectopic eyes were morphologically normal and consisted of groups of fully differentiated ommatidia with a complete set of photoreceptor cells. These findings support the idea that ey is the master control gene for eye morphogenesis, as it is present in a wide range of metazoans, including vertebrates, ascidians, insects, cephalopods, and nemerteans.

title: mir-1-mediated paracrine effect of cancer-associated fibroblasts on lung cancer cell proliferation and chemoresistance.
text:
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with an overall 5-year survival rate of only 15%. Of all lung cancer cases, nearly 80% are non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) have been found to be prevalent in a significant number of NSCLCs, and they have been shown to promote tumor progression, metastasis, and resistance to therapy through paracrine signaling in various solid tumors.
In this study, we isolated CAFs from patient tissues and demonstrated that they enhanced cell proliferation and chemoresistance to cisplatin in lung cancer cell lines A549 and 95D through paracrine mechanisms. Subsequent analyses using ELISA and quantitative PCR revealed that CAFs exhibited higher levels of stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1) compared to normal fibroblasts (NFs). SDF-1 was found to facilitate lung cancer cell proliferation and drug resistance through the CXCR4-mediated signaling pathway, which involved NF-κB and Bcl-xL. Additionally, we discovered that the expression of SDF-1 in CAFs was negatively regulated by microRNA mir-1 through microRNA overexpression and quantitative PCR.
Our findings provide insight into the mechanisms by which CAFs contribute to lung cancer progression, highlighting the potential of targeting CAFs in tumor treatment. Overall, this study sheds light on the complex interplay between lung cancer cells and the surrounding stroma, and suggests new avenues for cancer therapy.

title: Genome-wide association analyses in East Asians identify new susceptibility loci for colorectal cancer
text: To identify new genetic factors for colorectal cancer (CRC), we conducted a comprehensive genome-wide association study in east Asians. By analyzing genome-wide data from 2,098 cases and 5,749 controls, we identified 64 promising single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) for replication in an independent set of samples. Our analysis revealed four SNPs with association P values of 8.58 × 10(-7) to 3.77 × 10(-10) in the combined analysis of all east Asian samples. Surprisingly, three of these SNPs were successfully replicated in a study of 26,060 individuals of European descent, with combined P values of 1.22 × 10(-10) for rs647161 (5q31.1), 6.64 × 10(-9) for rs2423279 (20p12.3), and 3.06 × 10(-8) for rs10774214 (12p13.32 near the CCND2 gene). These findings identify three new CRC susceptibility loci and provide valuable insights into the genetic and biological mechanisms underlying CRC.

title: Long non-coding RNAs as novel players in β cell function and type 1 diabetes
text:
Background:
Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as pivotal regulators of gene expression in various pathophysiological conditions, including autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. LncRNAs exhibit remarkable versatility, exerting their functions through interactions with RNA, DNA, or proteins. An extensive body of evidence has underscored the role of lncRNAs in immune and islet β cell function, particularly in the context of type 1 diabetes (T1D).
This review aims to highlight the emerging roles of lncRNAs in the pathogenesis of T1D and its complications, as well as the challenges and opportunities in understanding their mechanisms of action.
Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that lncRNAs within T1D-associated regions, in conjunction with regulatory variants and enhancer clusters, orchestrate chromatin remodeling in β cells, thereby serving as both cis- and trans-regulatory determinants of islet cell transcriptional programs. This complex interplay of lncRNAs, regulatory elements, and chromatin structure underscores the intricate mechanisms underlying the development and progression of T1D. Further investigations into the molecular mechanisms of lncRNAs in T1D may provide valuable insights into the development of novel therapeutic strategies for this debilitating disease.

title: Costs of the COPD. Differences between intensive care unit and respiratory intermediate care unit.
text:
INTRODUCTION:
To determine whether respiratory intermediate care units (RICUs) are cost-effective alternatives to intensive care units (ICUs) for patients with exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
PATIENTS AND METHODS:
A multi-centre, prospective, bottom-up cost study was conducted in 15 ICUs and 6 RICUs. COPD patients staying longer than 48 hours were recruited, with exclusions for those with immune deficiency or stroke. After standardizing the ICU sample to the RICU distribution of reasons for admission and vasoactive drug use on admission, 60 ICU patients and 65 RICU patients remained, of the original 164 recruited. Daily information on resources consumed was recorded and analyzed in terms of costs.
RESULTS:
Total cost per patient was significantly lower in RICUs compared to ICUs (754 vs. 1507 Euro; P < 0.0001). In all categories except drugs and nutrition, RICUs had lower costs. Notably, dead patients had significantly different disease severity between ICUs and RICUs, while surviving patients showed no differences.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our study suggests that some less severe COPD patients with pure respiratory failure could be successfully and cost-effectively treated in RICUs.

title: eRNAs are required for p53-dependent enhancer activity and gene transcription.
text: The p53 tumor suppressor protein regulates cell proliferation and survival by binding to specific genes involved in these processes and modulating their transcription. Using genome-wide chromatin-binding profiles, we discovered that p53 also binds to regions located far away from any known p53 target genes. Surprisingly, these distant regions share characteristics of enhancers, including conserved p53-binding sites. We term these p53-bound enhancer regions (p53BERs) and demonstrate that they exhibit enhancer activity, interacting with multiple neighboring genes to regulate transcription in a p53-dependent manner. Furthermore, p53BERs produce enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) that are essential for efficient transcriptional enhancement of interacting target genes and p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest. Our findings reveal a novel mechanism of transcription enhancement by p53, where it can regulate multiple genes from a single genomic binding site. Additionally, eRNA production from p53BERs is crucial for efficient p53-mediated transcription enhancement.

title: Induction of pluripotent stem cells from mouse embryonic fibroblasts by Oct4 and Klf4 with small-molecule compounds.
text: Somatic cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) using a combination of four transcription factors, Oct4/Sox2/Klf4/c-Myc or Oct4/Sox2/Nanog/LIN28. This approach offers a versatile platform for generating patient-specific cells for various therapeutic and research applications. However, limitations remain in this method due to issues with efficiency and viral genome integration. Recently, it was shown that neural progenitor cells (NPCs) transduced with Oct4/Klf4 can be reprogrammed into iPSCs, and NPCs naturally express Sox2, which may facilitate reprogramming in the absence of exogenous Sox2. In this study, we identified a small-molecule combination, BIX-01294 and BayK8644, that can efficiently reprogram Oct4/Klf4-transduced mouse embryonic fibroblasts, which do not endogenously express the factors necessary for reprogramming. This finding demonstrates that small molecules identified through a phenotypic screen can compensate for the need for viral transduction of critical factors, such as Sox2, and improve reprogramming efficiency.

title: Vps22/EAP30 in ESCRT-II mediates endosomal sorting of growth factor and chemokine receptors destined for lysosomal degradation.
text: The ubiquitin-binding protein Hrs and the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT)-I and ESCRT-III are involved in the sorting of endocytosed and ubiquitinated receptors to lysosomes for degradation and efficient termination of signaling. In this study, we investigated the role of the ESCRT-II subunit Vps22/EAP30 in the degradative protein sorting of ubiquitinated receptors. Vps22 was detected in endosomes containing endocytosed epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFRs) as well as Hrs and ESCRT-I and ESCRT-III in transiently expressed HeLa cells. Depletion of Vps22 by small interfering RNA resulted in decreased levels of other ESCRT-II subunits and greatly reduced degradation of EGFR and its ligand EGF as well as the chemokine receptor CXCR4. In contrast, depletion of Hrs or the ESCRT-I subunit Tsg101 resulted in sustained phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of extracellular-signal-regulated kinase1/2 downstream of the EGF-activated receptor. These results suggest an important role for Vps22 in ligand-induced EGFR and CXCR4 turnover and indicate that termination of EGF signaling occurs prior to ESCRT-II engagement.

title: XPG stabilizes TFIIH, allowing transactivation of nuclear receptors: implications for Cockayne syndrome in XP-G/CS patients.
text: Mutations in the human XPG gene underlie an inherited photosensitive disorder known as xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), which often co-occurs with Cockayne syndrome (XP-G/CS). The clinical features of CS in XP-G/CS patients are challenging to explain solely on the basis of a defect in nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway. Our findings reveal that XPG forms a stable complex with TFIIH, an essential transcription and NER factor. Mutations in XPG found in XP-G/CS patient cells that disrupt the association with TFIIH lead to the dissociation of CAK and XPD from the core TFIIH complex. As a consequence, the phosphorylation and transactivation of nuclear receptors are impaired in XP-G/CS cells and xpg(-/-) mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), which can be restored by expressing wild-type XPG. These findings provide insight into the role of XPG in stabilizing TFIIH and regulating gene expression, and offer an explanation for some of the clinical features of XP-G/CS.

title: Metabolic cycling in single yeast cells from unsynchronized steady-state populations limited on glucose or phosphate.
text: Oscillations in the expression of a large fraction of yeast genes are linked to the "metabolic cycle," which is typically observed only in prestarved, continuous cultures of yeast. To investigate whether these oscillations occur in individual cells from unsynchronized cultures growing exponentially in chemostats, we employed fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to detect mRNA in individual cells. By using gene-expression data from synchronized cultures to predict the coincident appearance of mRNAs from pairs of genes in unsynchronized cells, we found that individual cells growing slowly due to glucose or phosphate limitation exhibit the predicted oscillations. Our findings suggest that the yeast metabolic cycle is an intrinsic property of yeast metabolism and is not dependent on either synchronization or external limitation of growth by the carbon source.

title: in polyploid species
text:
We have developed the Yeast Gene Order Browser (YGOB) to facilitate visual comparisons and computational analysis of synteny relationships in yeast species. The data presented in YGOB, currently covering seven species, were manually curated by our team to identify homologous genes based on both sequence similarity and genomic context. We have reconciled different laboratories' lists of paralogous gene pairs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, resulting in a near-exhaustive list of 551 ohnolog pairs retained in this species, including 22 previously unidentified pairs. Similarly, we have identified 599 ohnolog pairs in Saccharomyces castellii and 404 pairs in Candida glabrata.
In this context, "synteny" refers to the similarity in gene order and organization between different species, and "ohnologs" are gene pairs that are derived from a recent genome duplication event. By manually curating these data, we have created a comprehensive resource for researchers to compare and analyze the synteny relationships between different yeast species.

title: Immune complex relay by subcapsular sinus macrophages and non-cognate B cells drives antibody affinity maturation
text: Subcapsular sinus (SCS) macrophages play a crucial role in the immune system by capturing antigens from lymphatic fluid and presenting them to B cells for follicular delivery. However, the properties of SCS macrophages have been poorly understood. Our study reveals that the development of SCS macrophages depends on lymphotoxin-alpha1beta2, and these cells exhibit distinct characteristics compared to other macrophage populations. Specifically, SCS macrophages have low levels of lysosomal enzymes and retain opsonized antigens on their surface, allowing them to present intact antigens to B cells. Intravital imaging experiments showed that immune complexes move along macrophage processes into the follicle, and non-cognate B cells play a key role in relaying opsonized antigens from the subcapsular region to the germinal center. Furthermore, our findings suggest that disruption of the transport process impairs affinity maturation, highlighting the importance of SCS macrophages in promoting humoral immunity. In summary, we characterize SCS macrophages as specialized antigen-presenting cells at the apex of an antigen transport chain that facilitates the immune response.

title: Promoter decoding of transcription factor dynamics involves a trade-off between noise and control of gene expression
text: Many transcription factors (TFs) encode information about upstream signals in the dynamics of their activation, but the mechanisms by which downstream genes decode these dynamics are poorly understood. To address this question, we used microfluidics to control the nucleocytoplasmic translocation dynamics of the budding yeast TF Msn2 and elucidated the principles governing how different promoters convert dynamical Msn2 input into gene expression output in single cells. By combining modeling and experiments, we classified promoters according to their signal-processing behavior and revealed that multiple, distinct gene expression programs can be encoded in the dynamics of Msn2. We found that both oscillatory TF dynamics and slow promoter kinetics lead to higher noise in gene expression, and that the promoter activation timescale is related to nucleosome remodeling. Our findings suggest a fundamental trade-off: while the cell can exploit different promoter classes to differentially control gene expression using TF dynamics, gene expression noise fundamentally limits how much information can be encoded in the dynamics of a single TF and reliably decoded by promoters.

title: GaAs nanopillar-array solar cells employing in situ surface passivation
text: Arrays of III-V direct-bandgap semiconductor nanopillars, such as GaAs, hold great promise as photovoltaic candidates due to their inherent high optical absorption coefficients and minimized reflection through light trapping, efficient charge collection in the radial direction, and the ability to synthesize them on low-cost platforms. However, the increased surface area of these nanopillars leads to surface states that hinder the power conversion efficiency. In this study, we demonstrate the first use of GaAs nanopillar-array photovoltaics, with epitaxial passivation and high-bandgap InGaP shells grown in situ to alleviate surface-state effects. Under light, the devices exhibit open-circuit voltages of 0.44 V, short-circuit current densities of 24.3 mA cm(-2), and fill factors of 62% with high external quantum efficiencies exceeding 70% across the spectral range of interest. We also utilize a novel titanium/indium tin oxide annealed alloy as a transparent ohmic anode.

title: Roles of histone acetylation and chromatin remodeling factor in a meiotic recombination hotspot.
text: Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling factors (ADCRs) play a crucial role in regulating gene expression by modifying local chromatin structure. In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the recombination hotspot ade6-M26 is activated by a cAMP responsive element (CRE)-like sequence, M26, and a heterodimeric ATF/CREB transcription factor, Atf1.Pcr1. Chromatin remodeling occurs meiotically around M26, and we investigated the roles of HATs and ADCRs in this process. Our results show that histones H3 and H4 around M26 are hyperacetylated in an M26- and Atf1-dependent manner early in meiosis. The S. pombe homolog of Gcn5p, SpGcn5, is required for the majority of histone H3 acetylation around M26 in vivo. Deletion of gcn5+ caused a significant delay in chromatin remodeling but only partial reduction of M26 meiotic recombination frequency. Deletion of the ADCR homolog snf22+, along with the snf22+ gcn5+ double deletion, abolished chromatin remodeling and significant reduction of meiotic recombination around M26. These findings suggest that HATs and ADCRs cooperate to alter local chromatin structure in a site-specific manner, similar to selective transcription activation, to activate meiotic recombination at M26.

title: The Somatic Genomic Landscape of Glioblastoma
text: In this study, we present a comprehensive characterization of the landscape of somatic genomic alterations in over 500 glioblastoma tumors (GBMs). Through multidimensional analysis, we identify novel mutated genes and complex rearrangements of signature receptors, including EGFR and PDGFRA. Additionally, we demonstrate a correlation between TERT promoter mutations and elevated mRNA expression, supporting a role in telomerase reactivation. Correlative analyses also reveal that the survival advantage of the proneural subtype is conferred by the G-CIMP phenotype, and MGMT DNA methylation may serve as a predictive biomarker for treatment response in classical subtype GBM. Furthermore, integrative analysis of genomic and proteomic profiles challenges the notion of targeting a pathway through inhibition of a downstream target, rather than directly inhibiting the target itself. These findings will facilitate the discovery of therapeutic and diagnostic target candidates, validate existing research and clinical observations, and generate novel hypotheses that advance our molecular understanding of this aggressive cancer.

title: Radioiodine treatment of multinodular non-toxic goitre.
text:
Objective: To investigate the long-term effects of radioactive iodine on thyroid function and size in patients with non-toxic multinodular goitre.
Design: Consecutive patients with multinodular non-toxic goitre were selected for radioactive iodine treatment and followed for a minimum of 12 months (median 48 months) after an intended dose of 3.7 MBq/g thyroid tissue corrected to a 100% uptake of iodine-131 in 24 hours.
Patients: 69 patients with a growing multinodular non-toxic goitre causing local compression symptoms or cosmetic inconveniences were included in the study. The treatment was chosen due to a high operative risk, previous thyroidectomy, or refusal to be operated on.
Main Outcome Measurements: Standard thyroid function variables and ultrasonically determined thyroid volume were measured before treatment and at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months after treatment, and then once a year.
Results: Of the 69 patients, 56 were treated with a single dose of 131I, 12 with two doses, and one with four doses. In 45 patients treated with one dose, the median thyroid volume was reduced from 73 (interquartile range 50-106) ml to 29 (23-48) ml at 24 months in the 39 patients in whom this was measured during follow-up. The median reduction was 40 (22-48) ml (60% reduction, p < 0.0001), with half of the reduction occurring within three months. Patients treated with two doses as well as those developing hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism had a significant reduction in thyroid volume. Eleven patients developed hypothyroidism (cumulative five-year risk 22%, 95% confidence interval 4.8% to 38.4%). Side effects were few, with three cases of hyperthyroidism and two cases of radiation thyroiditis. Only one patient was dissatisfied with the result and was referred for operation six months after treatment.
Conclusions: The use of radioactive iodine in selected cases of non-toxic multinodular goitre resulted in a substantial reduction in thyroid volume, with a low incidence of hypothyroidism and few side effects. This alternative to surgery is an attractive option for patients with a high operative risk, previous thyroidectomy, or refusal to be operated on.

title: Alterations in microRNA-124 and AMPA receptors contribute to social behavioral deficits in frontotemporal dementia
text: Neurodegenerative disorders, such as frontotemporal dementia (FTD), are often linked to behavioral abnormalities, yet the underlying anatomical and molecular causes remain poorly understood. In this study, we discovered that expressing a mutated form of the protein CHMP2B in mice leads to various age-related neurodegenerative changes, including social behavioral impairments. These deficits were accompanied by alterations in the composition of AMPA receptors (AMPARs), specifically an imbalance between permeable and impermeable AMPARs. We found that the abundance of the brain-specific microRNA miR-124, which regulates AMPAR subunit expression, was significantly decreased in the superficial layers of the cerebral cortex of mice expressing the mutant CHMP2B. Remarkably, we observed similar changes in miR-124 and AMPAR levels in the frontal cortex and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons from individuals with behavioral variant FTD. Moreover, ectopic miR-124 expression in the medial prefrontal cortex of mutant mice reduced AMPAR levels and partially restored behavioral deficits. Interestingly, knockdown of the AMPAR subunit Gria2 also alleviated social impairments. Our findings uncover a previously unappreciated mechanism involving miR-124 and AMPARs in regulating social behavior in FTD and suggest a potential therapeutic strategy.

title: Activated AMPK boosts the Nrf2/HO-1 signaling axis—A role for the unfolded protein response
text: In light of the emerging interplay between redox and metabolic signaling pathways, we investigated the potential crosstalk between nuclear factor E2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and AMP-activated kinase (AMPK), key regulators of cellular redox and energy balance, respectively. Utilizing xanthohumol (XN) as a dual activator of both AMPK and Nrf2 signaling pathways, we demonstrate that AMPK exerts a positive influence on Nrf2/heme oxygenase (HO-1) signaling in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. Genetic ablation or pharmacological inhibition of AMPK blunts Nrf2-dependent HO-1 expression induced by XN at the mRNA level. XN activates AMPK through interference with mitochondrial function and activation of liver kinase B1 as an upstream AMPK kinase, leading to enhanced Nrf2/HO-1 response. This enhancement does not depend on inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin, glycogen synthase kinase 3β, or altered abundance of Nrf2 (total and nuclear). Instead, we identify reduced endoplasmic reticulum stress as a key step in the AMPK-augmented Nrf2/HO-1 response. Our findings shed light on the previously incompletely understood cross talk between the LKB1/AMPK and Nrf2/HO-1 axes, revealing the unfolded protein response as an additional player and highlighting the tight cooperation between signaling pathways regulating cellular redox, energy, or protein homeostasis.

title: The IDEAL recommendations and urological innovation
text:
Like other surgical specialties, Urology has faced challenges in aligning its research processes with the principles of Evidence-Based Medicine. This article explains the IDEAL framework and recommendations, and illustrates how they can improve the evaluation of controversial urological procedures. From an insider's perspective, we provide an overview of the IDEAL Working Group's efforts and their impact on the field of Urology.
There are significant differences between drugs and interventions in the development and evaluation of new treatments. The conventional framework for conducting trials of new treatments is often inadequate for surgical innovations, leading to difficulties in conducting randomized controlled trials of surgical techniques. The persistence of case series in the scientific literature has been a contentious issue due to the mismatch between the subject of research and the methodology used.
The IDEAL framework provides a comprehensive description of the process of innovation and development for surgical trials, and the associated recommendations offer a suggested alternative approach to study design that is tailored to the unique challenges of new techniques. The IDEAL framework has the potential to transform the way urologists conduct clinical research, providing a more effective and efficient approach to evaluating new treatments.

title: Prolonged conservative care versus early surgery in patients with sciatica caused by lumbar disc herniation: two year results of a randomised controlled trial.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of early lumbar disc surgery compared to prolonged conservative care in treating sciatica over a two-year follow-up period.
Design: Randomized controlled trial
Setting: Nine hospitals in the Netherlands.
Participants: 283 patients with sciatica lasting 6-12 weeks.
Interventions: Early surgery or continued conservative treatment for six months, with delayed surgery if necessary.
Main Outcome Measures: Disability scores (Roland Disability Questionnaire for sciatica), leg pain (visual analogue scale), and self-rated global recovery (Likert scale).
Results: Of the 141 patients assigned to early surgery, 125 (89%) underwent microdiscectomy. Of the 142 patients assigned to conservative treatment, 62 (44%) eventually required surgery, seven in the second year of follow-up. There was no significant overall difference between treatment arms in disability scores during the first two years (P=0.25). Improvement in leg pain was faster for patients randomized to early surgery, with a significant difference between "areas under the curves" over two years (P=0.05). This short-term benefit of early surgery was no longer significant by six months and continued to narrow between six months and 24 months. Patient satisfaction decreased slightly between one and two years for both groups. At two years, 20% of all patients reported an unsatisfactory outcome.
Conclusions: Early surgery provided more rapid relief of sciatica than conservative care, but outcomes were similar by one year and did not change during the second year.
Trial Registry: ISRCT No 26872154.

title: Human papillomavirus testing for the detection of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cancer: final results of the POBASCAM randomised controlled trial.
text:
The study investigated the effectiveness of incorporating human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing into cervical cancer screening. The study randomly assigned 45,000 women aged 29-56 years to either receive HPV DNA and cytology co-testing or cytology testing alone. The primary endpoint was the number of women with high-grade cervical lesions (CIN grade 3 or worse) detected in the second screening round, 5 years after the first screening.
The results showed that the number of women with CIN grade 3 or worse was significantly lower in the group that received HPV DNA testing in the first screening round (88 cases) compared to the control group (122 cases). Additionally, the number of women with cervical cancer was also lower in the intervention group (4 cases) compared to the control group (14 cases).
The study also found that HPV DNA testing in the first screening round significantly improved the detection of CIN grade 2 or worse (267 cases in the intervention group vs 215 cases in the control group) and CIN grade 3 or worse (259 cases in the intervention group vs 272 cases in the control group). However, the cumulative detection of CIN grade 3 or worse and CIN grade 2 or worse did not differ significantly between the study arms.
The study suggests that incorporating HPV DNA testing into cervical cancer screening leads to earlier detection of clinically relevant CIN grade 2 or worse, which when adequately treated, improves protection against CIN grade 3 or worse and cervical cancer. Early detection of high-grade cervical legions caused by HPV16 was a major component of this benefit. The study lends support to the use of HPV DNA testing for all women aged 29 years and older.
Funding: Zorg Onderzoek Nederland (Netherlands Organisation for Health Research and Development).

title: Epigenetic therapy activates type I interferon signaling in murine ovarian cancer to reduce immunosuppression and tumor burden.
text:
Ovarian cancer is the most lethal of all gynecological malignancies, and there is an urgent need for the development of novel therapeutic strategies. Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and the response of ovarian cancers to immunotherapies has been disappointingly limited thus far. However, recent findings in a mouse model of EOC suggest that clinically relevant doses of DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase inhibitors (DNMTi and HDACi, respectively) can reduce the immunosuppressive microenvironment through type I interferon signaling, leading to improved response to immune checkpoint therapy. These data indicate that the type I interferon response is essential for the in vivo antitumorigenic actions of DNMTi, specifically the compound 5-azacytidine (AZA).
Through type I interferon signaling, AZA increases the numbers of CD45+ immune cells and the percentage of active CD8+ T and natural killer (NK) cells in the tumor microenvironment, while reducing tumor burden and extending survival. AZA also increases viral defense gene expression in both tumor and immune cells, and reduces the percentage of macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells in the tumor microenvironment. The addition of an HDACi to AZA further enhances the modulation of the immune microenvironment, specifically increasing T and NK cell activation and reducing macrophages compared to AZA treatment alone, while further extending survival. Finally, a triple combination of DNMTi/HDACi plus the immune checkpoint inhibitor α-PD-1 provides the most effective antitumor effect and longest overall survival, and may be a promising candidate for future clinical trials in ovarian cancer.

title: IGF2 is parentally imprinted during human embryogenesis and in the Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome
text: The phenomenon of parental imprinting, where one parental allele of a subset of chromosomal genes is preferentially expressed, has been observed primarily in mice. However, our study reveals that this phenomenon also occurs in humans, specifically in the insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) gene. By analyzing sequence polymorphisms in exon nine of the IGF2 gene from first trimester pregnancies, we found that only the paternally inherited allele is active in embryonic and extra-embryonic cells. Furthermore, only the paternal allele is expressed in tissues from a patient with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, a genetic disorder that is thought to result from parental imprinting dysregulation. These findings suggest that the parental imprinting of IGF2 is evolutionarily conserved from mice to humans and has important implications for the development of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

title: Safety and reliability of Radio Frequency Identification Devices in Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Computed Tomography
text:
BACKGROUND:
Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) devices are becoming increasingly important for ensuring patient safety in hospitals. The purpose of this study was to investigate the impact of RFID devices on patient safety, data reliability, and signal loss during Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT) scans.
METHODS:
Sixty RFID tags of the type I-Code SLI, 13.56 MHz, ISO 18000-3.1 were tested: Thirty type 1, with a 76 x 45 mm aluminum-etched antenna, and thirty type 2, with a 31 x 14 mm copper-etched antenna. Signal loss, material movement, and heat tests were performed in 1.5 T and 3 T MR systems. Additionally, the tags were tested during CT scanning to evaluate data integrity. Standardized function tests were performed with all transponders before and after all imaging studies.
RESULTS:
No memory loss or data alteration was observed in the RFID tags after MRI and CT scanning. The heating effect (maximum of 3.6 degrees C) and device movement (below 1 N/kg) had no significant impact on the RFID tags. However, signal loss (artifacts 2-4 mm) resulted in impaired interpretability of MR images when assessing superficial structures such as skin, subcutaneous tissues, or tendons.
CONCLUSIONS:
Patients wearing RFID wristbands are safe in 1.5 T and 3 T MR scanners using normal operation mode for RF fields. The findings of this study are specific to the RFID tags tested.

title: LXR-Dependent Gene Expression Is Important for Macrophage Survival and the Innate Immune Response
text: The liver X receptors (LXRs) are nuclear receptors that play a crucial role in regulating lipid metabolism. Recent studies have revealed that LXR signaling not only affects lipid metabolism but also impacts antimicrobial responses. Mice lacking LXRs are highly susceptible to infection with the intracellular bacteria Listeria monocytogenes (LM). Bone marrow transplant studies have shown that altered macrophage function is the primary factor contributing to this susceptibility. LXR-deficient macrophages undergo accelerated apoptosis when challenged with LM and exhibit impaired bacterial clearance in vivo. These defects are, in part, due to the loss of regulation of the antiapoptotic factor SPalpha, a direct target of LXRalpha. By expressing LXRalpha or SPalpha in macrophages, we have found that apoptosis can be inhibited in the presence of LM infection. Our findings demonstrate that LXR-dependent gene expression plays a previously unappreciated role in innate immunity and suggest that common nuclear receptor pathways mediate macrophage responses to modified lipoproteins and intracellular pathogens.

title: Alterations on peripheral B cell subsets following an acute uncomplicated clinical malaria infection in children
text:
Background: The impact of Plasmodium falciparum infection on B-cell homeostasis has not been well characterized. This study aimed to investigate whether a bout of acute malaria in young children leads to changes in the peripheral B-cell phenotype.
