Methods: We used flow-cytofluorimetric analysis to examine the B-cell phenotypes in the peripheral blood of children aged 2-5 years during an episode of acute uncomplicated clinical malaria and four weeks post-recovery, as well as in healthy age-matched controls.
Results: Our findings revealed a significant decrease in CD19+ B lymphocytes during acute malaria. Analysis of the CD19+ B cell subsets in the peripheral blood based on expression of IgD and CD38 showed a significant decrease in the numbers of naive CD38-IgD+ B cells, while there was an increase in CD38+IgD- memory 3 B cells during acute malaria. Additionally, we identified an expansion of transitional CD10+CD19+ B cells in children following an episode of acute malaria, with up to 25% of the total CD19+ B cell pool residing in this subset.
Conclusion: Our study shows that children experiencing an episode of acute uncomplicated clinical malaria experience profound disruptions in B-cell homeostasis.

title: SETD2: an epigenetic modifier with tumor suppressor functionality
text:
Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in understanding the epigenetic regulatory machinery. It has become evident that genetic alterations in multiple epigenetic modifier proteins are associated with various types of cancer. Moreover, targeting the epigenome has emerged as a novel approach to treat cancer patients. Recently, the first drugs have been developed that specifically target SETD2-negative tumors. In this review, we delve into the studies on Set domain containing 2 (SETD2), a histone modifier whose mutations have only recently been linked to cancer development.
We begin by examining the structural characteristics of SETD2 and its functional implications. We combine studies on SETD2 from yeast, Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, mice, and humans to gain a comprehensive understanding of its role. SETD2 is now recognized as the sole human gene responsible for trimethylation of lysine 36 of Histone H3 (H3K36). The readers of H3K36me3, which recruit protein complexes to carry out specific processes such as transcription elongation, RNA processing, and DNA repair, determine the impact of this histone modification.
We then explore the prevalence of SETD2-inactivating mutations in cancer, with the highest frequency observed in clear cell Renal Cell Cancer. We investigate how SETD2-inactivation might contribute to tumor development.
In conclusion, this review provides a comprehensive overview of the current understanding of SETD2 and its role in cancer development, highlighting the potential of targeting the epigenome as a novel approach to cancer treatment.

title: Updated energy budgets for neural computation in the neocortex and cerebellum.
text: The brain's energy supply plays a crucial role in determining its information processing capabilities, and accordingly, functional imaging signals are generated. Previous estimates of the energy expenditure on neural computation in the grey matter of the cerebral and cerebellar cortex have been reevaluated in light of recent findings that suggest action potentials in mammalian neurons are more energy efficient than previously thought. This study provides revised estimates of energy expenditure on neural computation in a simplified model of the cerebral cortex and a detailed model of the cerebellar cortex. In the cerebral cortex, the majority of energy (50%) is expended on postsynaptic glutamate receptors, followed by action potentials (21%), resting potentials (20%), presynaptic transmitter release (5%), and transmitter recycling (4%). In contrast, in the cerebellar cortex, excitatory neurons account for 75% of energy expenditure, while inhibitory neurons account for 25%. The majority of energy use in the cerebellar cortex is on the maintenance of resting potentials (54%) and postsynaptic receptors (22%), while action potentials account for only 17% of energy use. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying information processing in the brain.

title: Plasma homocysteine is a risk factor for recurrent vascular events in young patients with an ischaemic stroke or TIA
text:
Young patients who experience an ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA) often have no established vascular risk factors. However, hyperhomocysteinaemia has been identified as a risk factor for stroke in elderly patients, but its significance in young patients is unclear. To investigate, we examined the potential impact of plasma homocysteine levels on the risk of recurrent vascular events in patients between 18 and 45 years of age.
Our study included 161 consecutive patients with a recent cerebral infarction or TIA. We collected data on the primary event and homocysteine levels retrospectively from hospital records, and then contacted patients and general practitioners by phone to gather information on vascular events and medication use during the follow-up period. Vascular events included cerebral infarction, TIA, pulmonary embolism, venous thrombosis, myocardial infarction, and peripheral arterial disease.
We found a significant association between plasma homocysteine levels and the risk of recurrent vascular events in young patients, with a dose-effect relationship evident in the data. After adjusting for homocysteine-lowering treatment, the Cox hazard ratio was 1.7 (95% CI, 1.1-2.8) for any vascular outcome event, 1.9 (95% CI, 1.1-3.0) for arterial outcome events, and 1.8 (95% CI, 1.1-2.9) for cerebral outcome events. These findings are similar in magnitude to those observed in elderly patients.
Despite the small number of outcome events in our study, we were able to demonstrate a significant association between plasma homocysteine levels and the risk of recurrent vascular events in young patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA. This association is comparable in magnitude to that observed in elderly patients, suggesting that hyperhomocysteinaemia may play a role in the pathophysiology of vascular disease across different age groups.

title: LDL inhibits the mediation of cholesterol efflux from macrophage foam cells by apoA-I-containing lipoproteins. A putative mechanism for foam cell formation.
text: Although the accumulation of cholesterol in macrophages is an initial step in atherogenesis, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), a major risk factor for atherosclerosis, does not directly promote cholesterol accumulation in macrophages in its native form. On the other hand, apolipoprotein (apo) A-I-containing lipoprotein can remove cholesterol from cholesterol-loaded macrophages (foam cells) and prevent cholesterol from accumulating in the cells. We investigated the effect of LDL on cholesterol removal by two species of apoA-I-containing lipoproteins, one containing only apoA-I (LpA-I) and the other containing apoA-I and apoA-II (LpA-I/A-II). When foam cells were incubated with LpA-I or LpA-I/A-II, the cellular cholesterol mass was reduced. In contrast, when LDL was added, the cholesterol-reducing capacities of these lipoproteins were dose-dependently inhibited by LDL. In the presence of LDL, LpA-I and LpA-I/A-II removed free cholesterol preferentially from LDL rather than from the plasma membrane of foam cells. Additionally, a significant amount of cellular cholesterol was directly transferred to LDL rather than to LpA-I or LpA-I/A-II. The cellular cholesterol that moved to LDL was completely compensated for by the cholesterol influx from LDL to foam cells. Therefore, net cholesterol efflux (a combination of influx and efflux) from foam cells was inhibited by LDL. These findings suggest that LDL may accelerate foam cell formation by inhibiting cholesterol removal from the cells and that elevated levels of plasma LDL may become a risk factor for atherosclerosis by inhibiting the function of LpA-I and LpA-I/A-II at the cellular level.

title: Sugar-sweetened beverages, weight gain, and incidence of type 2 diabetes in young and middle-aged women.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages and weight change, as well as the risk of developing type 2 diabetes, in a cohort of women. We analyzed data from the Nurses' Health Study II, a prospective cohort study conducted from 1991 to 1999.
We found that women who consumed higher amounts of sugar-sweetened beverages, such as soft drinks and fruit punch, experienced greater weight gain over a 4-year period compared to those who consumed less of these beverages. Specifically, women who increased their consumption of sugar-sweetened soft drinks from 1 or fewer drinks per week to 1 or more drinks per day experienced a greater weight gain of 4.69 kg (or 10.3 lbs) over a 4-year period, compared to those who decreased their intake. Similarly, women who consumed higher amounts of fruit punch also experienced greater weight gain.
In addition, we found that higher consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages was associated with an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Specifically, women who consumed 1 or more sugar-sweetened soft drinks per day had a relative risk of type 2 diabetes of 1.83, compared to those who consumed less than 1 of these beverages per month. Similarly, consumption of fruit punch was associated with an increased diabetes risk.
Our findings suggest that higher consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages is associated with both greater weight gain and an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes in women. These results may be due to the high calorie content and rapid absorption of sugars in these beverages, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of metabolic disorders.
In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of monitoring and reducing consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages in order to promote healthy weight management and reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes in women.

title: Pancreatic stellate cells: partners in crime with pancreatic cancer cells.
text: Pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs) play a crucial role in the stromal reaction of pancreatic cancer, but their involvement in cancer progression remains inadequately understood. To investigate the influence of PSCs on pancreatic cancer growth, we employed two experimental approaches: an orthotopic model of pancreatic cancer and in vitro cultures of human PSCs (hPSCs) and human pancreatic cancer cell lines MiaPaCa-2 and Panc-1. Athymic mice were injected with saline, hPSCs, MiaPaCa-2 cells, or hPSCs in combination with MiaPaCa-2 cells. After 7 weeks, tumor size, metastases, and tumor histology were evaluated. In addition, in vitro studies were conducted to assess the effect of cancer cell secretions on PSC migration and the effect of hPSC secretions on cancer cell proliferation, apoptosis, and migration. The potential mediators of the effects of hPSC secretions on cancer cell proliferation were also examined using neutralizing antibodies. Our findings revealed that compared to mice receiving MiaPaCa-2 cells alone, mice injected with hPSCs in combination with MiaPaCa-2 exhibited (a) significantly larger tumors and more extensive regional and distant metastases, (b) the formation of fibrotic bands (desmoplasia) containing activated PSCs within tumors, and (c) increased tumor cell numbers. In vitro studies showed that, in the presence of pancreatic cancer cells, PSC migration was significantly enhanced. Moreover, hPSC secretions promoted the proliferation and migration of MiaPaCa-2 and Panc-1 cells, but inhibited their apoptosis. The proliferative effect of hPSC secretions on pancreatic cancer cells was inhibited in the presence of neutralizing antibody to platelet-derived growth factor. Our results suggest a substantial interaction between pancreatic cancer cells and stromal cells (PSCs) and imply that pancreatic cancer cells recruit stromal cells to create an environment that fosters cancer progression.

title: Preoperative statin treatment reduces systemic inflammatory response and myocardial damage in cardiac surgery.
text:
Objective: To investigate whether preoperative statin treatment is associated with a reduction in systemic inflammatory response (SIR) and myocardial damage markers after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB).
Methods: A prospective cohort of 138 patients underwent coronary and valvular surgery with CPB, and their plasma levels of pro-inflammatory interleukins (tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), interleukin (IL)-6, IL-8, and IL-2R), creatine phosphokinase (CPK), CPK-MB, and troponin I were measured before and at 1, 6, 24, and >72 hours after surgery. The study group was divided into two: patients who received (group A, n=72) or did not receive (group B, n=66) statins before surgery.
Results: The baseline, operative, and postoperative morbidity and mortality characteristics were similar between the two groups. Group A had significantly lower postoperative levels of IL-6 at 6 hours (68.8±5 pg/mL vs 108.9±108 pg/mL, p=0.01), 24 hours (71.7±7 pg/mL vs 110.4±106 pg/mL, p=0.01), and before hospital discharge (21.6±12 pg/mL vs 32.8±27 pg/mL, p=0.005) compared to group B, as well as lower average IL-6 levels in the first 24 hours after surgery (71.8±5 pg/mL vs 112.8±82 pg/mL, p=0.002). Additionally, group A had significantly lower postoperative CPK-MB at 24 hours (19.7±23 ng/mL vs 33.1±32 ng/mL, p=0.02) and troponin I levels at the end of the intervention (2.2±2.2 ng/mL vs 3.3±3.1 ng/mL, p=0.03) and at 24 hours (4.1±3.5 ng/mL vs 6.6±8 ng/mL, p=0.04) compared to group B.
Conclusion: Preoperative statin treatment is associated with lower biochemical parameters of systemic inflammatory response and myocardial damage after cardiac surgery with CPB, regardless of whether it is coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) or valvular surgery.

title: MEGA7: Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis Version 7.0 for Bigger Datasets.
text:
We are pleased to announce the latest version of the Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis (Mega) software, which includes a range of advanced methods and tools for phylogenomics and phylomedicine. This major upgrade has been optimized for use on 64-bit computing systems, allowing for the analysis of larger datasets with greater efficiency. Researchers can now utilize Mega to explore and analyze tens of thousands of sequences, thanks to its enhanced performance.
The new version of Mega includes an advanced wizard for building timetrees, as well as a novel functionality to automatically predict gene duplication events in gene family trees. Users have the option to utilize Mega in two interfaces: a graphical user interface (GUI) and a command line interface. The GUI is a native Microsoft Windows application that can also be used on Mac OS X, while the command line Mega is available as native applications for Windows, Linux, and Mac OS X. These interfaces are designed to cater to different user preferences and analysis needs, with the command line interface being particularly useful for high-throughput and scripted analysis.
Both versions of Mega are available for download free of charge from the Mega Software website.

title: DNA replication fidelity
text: DNA replication accuracy is a crucial factor in maintaining genome stability and has significant implications for the evolution of species and the origins of human diseases. Recent studies have provided new insights into the mechanisms that govern DNA replication fidelity, focusing on the structural and biochemical properties of DNA polymerases. These investigations have revealed the importance of hydrogen bonding, base pair geometry, and substrate-induced conformational changes in determining the accuracy of DNA replication. Additionally, these studies have shown how polymerase interactions with the DNA minor groove at and upstream of the active site influence nucleotide selectivity, the efficiency of exonucleolytic proofreading, and the rate of forming errors via strand misalignments. By highlighting common features that are relevant to the fidelity of any DNA synthesis reaction, these findings shed light on why fidelity can vary depending on the enzymes, the error, and the local sequence environment.

title: Viable neutrophils release mitochondrial DNA to form neutrophil extracellular traps
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are extracellular structures that can bind and kill microorganisms. It is believed that these structures are generated by living neutrophils undergoing cellular priming with granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and subsequent stimulation with toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) or complement factor 5a (C5a) receptors. Our findings show that viable neutrophils can generate NETs after priming and stimulation, and these structures contain mitochondrial DNA but no nuclear DNA. Additionally, we found that NET formation is dependent on the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and that neutrophil populations stimulated with GM-CSF and C5a have increased survival compared to resting neutrophils that do not generate NETs. In conclusion, our results suggest that NET formation by living neutrophils does not require cell death and does not limit the lifespan of these cells.

title: ATP-driven exchange of histone H2AZ variant catalyzed by SWR1 chromatin remodeling complex.
text: The conserved histone variant H2AZ plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and maintaining a barrier against the spread of silent heterochromatin. However, the process by which histone variants like H2AZ are incorporated into nucleosomes has been shrouded in mystery. Our research has uncovered a multisubunit enzyme, comprising the catalytic core Swr1, which is responsible for efficiently replacing conventional histone H2A with H2AZ in nucleosome arrays. Swr1 is essential for the deposition of H2AZ at specific locations on chromosomes in vivo, and it and H2AZ collaborate to regulate a subset of yeast genes. These findings shed light on an unappreciated function of the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling machinery.

title: FACT Disrupts Nucleosome Structure by Binding H2A-H2B with Conserved Peptide Motifs.
text:
FACT, a heterodimer of Spt16 and Pob3, is a crucial histone chaperone that plays a central role in the regulation of chromatin structure and function. Our studies have revealed that the H2A-H2B binding activity that is essential for FACT function resides in short acidic regions located near the C-terminal ends of each subunit. Mutations in these regions can have a profound impact on binding affinity and lead to a range of phenotypes, from mild to lethal, with the most significant effects unexpectedly coming from aromatic and carboxylate residues within each domain.
Spt16 and Pob3 bind to overlapping sites on H2A-H2B, and Spt16-Pob3 heterodimers simultaneously interact with two H2A-H2B dimers, adopting the same stoichiometry as the components of a nucleosome. Our crystal structure of Spt16:H2A-H2B provides a molecular explanation for the biochemical and genetic data, offers a model for Pob3 binding, and suggests a mechanism by which FACT reorganizes nucleosomes. Moreover, our findings highlight a surprising degree of similarity in the binding of diverse H2A-H2B chaperones, such as ANP32E and Swr1, to H2A.Z-H2B, which suggests that these proteins use common mechanisms to regulate nucleosome functions.

title: Role of AMP-activated protein kinase in mechanism of metformin action.
text: Metformin, a widely used drug for treating type 2 diabetes, lacks a defined cellular mechanism of action. However, its glucose-lowering effect is attributed to decreased hepatic glucose production and increased glucose utilization. Metformin's beneficial impact on circulating lipids has been linked to reduced fatty liver. AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a crucial cellular regulator of lipid and glucose metabolism, plays a key role in mediating metformin's effects. Our findings reveal that metformin activates AMPK in hepatocytes, leading to a reduction in acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) activity, induction of fatty acid oxidation, and suppression of lipogenic enzyme expression. Activation of AMPK by metformin or an adenosine analogue also suppresses the expression of sterol regulatory element-binding protein-1 (SREBP-1), a fundamental lipogenic transcription factor. In metformin-treated rats, hepatic expression of SREBP-1 and other lipogenic mRNAs and proteins is significantly reduced, and activity of the AMPK target, ACC, is also diminished. Using a novel AMPK inhibitor, we found that AMPK activation is essential for metformin's inhibition of glucose production by hepatocytes. Moreover, metformin stimulates glucose uptake in isolated rat skeletal muscles, which is accompanied by AMPK activation. Our results provide a unified explanation for the multifaceted beneficial effects of metformin and suggest that alternative means of modulating AMPK may be useful for treating metabolic disorders.

title: Interferon alfa therapy for chronic hepatitis B in children: a multinational randomized controlled trial.
text:
BACKGROUND & AIMS:
Interferon alfa (IFN-alpha) is not approved for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B in children. This study aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of IFN-alpha in children with chronic hepatitis B and elevated transaminase levels.
METHODS:
One hundred forty-nine children were enrolled in the study, with 70 receiving IFN-alpha2b (6 megunits/m2 thrice weekly for 24 weeks) and 74 serving as controls. The clearance of viral replication markers was evaluated 24 weeks after therapy and after 48 weeks of observation in the control group.
RESULTS:
Of the 144 evaluable children, 26% had a negative serum hepatitis B e antigen and viral DNA after treatment, compared to 11% of the control group (P < 0.05). Additionally, 26% of the treated children had normalized serum aminotransferase levels and improved liver histology, compared to 11% of the controls. Hepatitis B surface antigen became undetectable in 10% of the treated children and 1% of the controls. Female gender and IFN-alpha treatment were the only significant predictors of response. Ethnic origin, baseline aminotransferase level, initial DNA levels, and histology did not correlate with response. Most adverse reactions were mild or moderate, and the dose was reduced in 24% of the children.
CONCLUSIONS:
IFN-alpha therapy promotes the loss of viral replication markers and surface antigen in children with chronic hepatitis B, as well as improves aminotransferases and histology. IFN-alpha is a potential treatment option for children with chronic hepatitis B and elevated transaminase levels. However, further studies are needed to determine the long-term safety and efficacy of IFN-alpha in this population.

title: ImmTACs for targeted cancer therapy: Why, what, how, and which.
text: Overcoming immunosuppression and activating a cytotoxic T cell response has the potential to halt the progression of cancer and, in some cases, eradicate it. However, designing therapeutic interventions that achieve this goal has proven challenging. Recently, there have been notable breakthroughs in understanding the complexities of immune responses, leading to the development of new therapies. ImmTACs (immune-mobilising monoclonal TCRs against cancer) are a novel class of bispecific reagents that have shown promise in overcoming the problem of low affinity tumour-specific T cells. These reagents are engineered to have extremely high affinity for cognate tumour antigens, allowing them to bind to tumour cells and recruit polyclonal T cells to the tumour site. This leads to a potent redirected T cell response and tumour cell destruction. In vitro testing and early clinical data have provided a better understanding of ImmTAC function in vivo and their potential therapeutic benefit, including a durable response and the breaking of T cell tolerance. This review introduces ImmTACs as a promising immunotherapy approach, outlining their design, construction, and mechanism of action, as well as discussing target selection and preclinical safety testing.

title: Angiopoietin-like protein 3 supports the activity of hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow niche.
text: The current understanding of the physiological roles of angiopoietin-like proteins (Angptls) in the hematopoietic system is limited. However, our study has uncovered new insights into the role of Angptl3 in the hematopoietic system. We found that hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in Angptl3-deficient mice are fewer in number and more quiescent. When HSCs from Angptl3-deficient mice were transplanted into recipient mice, they showed impaired repopulation ability. Interestingly, we discovered that bone marrow sinusoidal endothelial cells express high levels of Angptl3 and are in close proximity to HSCs. Moreover, we found that bone marrow stromal cells or endothelium lacking Angptl3 have a significantly reduced capacity to support the expansion of repopulating HSCs. Our findings suggest that Angptl3 plays a crucial role in supporting the stemness of HSCs in the bone marrow niche. Specifically, Angptl3 represses the expression of the transcription factor Ikaros, which, when unregulated, can diminish the repopulation activity of HSCs. Therefore, Angptl3 acts as an extrinsic factor to promote the survival and function of HSCs in the bone marrow microenvironment.

title: Subsequent chemotherapy reverses acquired tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and restores response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer
text: BACKGROUND Patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) often develop resistance to epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as erlotinib and gefitinib after prolonged treatment. In this study, we report the successful treatment of two cases of advanced NSCLC that developed resistance to TKIs with a novel approach involving alternating chemotherapy and TKI therapy. CASE PRESENTATION Two patients with advanced or metastatic NSCLC were initially treated with palliative chemotherapy followed by erlotinib/gefitinib. When TKI therapy failed, they received two cycles of chemotherapy, followed by re-challenge with erlotinib or gefitinib. CONCLUSION Our findings suggest that patients with acquired TKI resistance in NSCLC may benefit from aggressive treatment strategies, including chemotherapy and targeted therapy. The use of alternating chemotherapy and TKI therapy may be a reasonable approach for those with an initial dramatic clinical response to TKI treatment. Further research is needed to confirm the efficacy of this approach and to better understand the mechanisms of resistance to TKIs in NSCLC.

title: Epigenetic Therapy Ties MYC Depletion to Reversing Immune Evasion and Treating Lung Cancer
text: Combining DNA-demethylating agents (DNMTis) with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACis) has the potential to significantly enhance cancer immunotherapy. In this study, we investigate the pharmacologic and isoform-specific properties of HDACis to optimize their combination with DNMTis. By developing a low-dose, sequential regimen, we aim to elicit a robust anti-tumor response in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients. Using in-vitro-treated NSCLC cell lines, we uncover an interferon α/β-mediated transcriptional program that enhances antigen presentation machinery, including the induction of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). This leads to the suppression of MYC signaling and a concomitant increase in the T cell chemoattractant CCL5. In mouse models of NSCLC, this combination treatment schema reverses tumor immune evasion and modulates T cell exhaustion towards memory and effector T cell phenotypes. Key correlative science metrics have emerged for an upcoming clinical trial, which will test the enhancement of immune checkpoint therapy for NSCLC.

title: The Role of PPARγ in Advanced Glycation End Products-Induced Inflammatory Response in Human Chondrocytes
text:
Objective:
Advances in the past decade have highlighted the protective properties of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors gamma (PPARγ) in the pathophysiology of osteoarthritis (OA). The aim of this study was to investigate the roles of PPARγ in the inflammatory response induced by advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) in human chondrocytes.
Methods:
Primary human chondrocytes were stimulated with AGEs in the presence or absence of neutralizing antibody against RAGE (anti-RAGE), MAPK specific inhibitors, and PPARγ agonist pioglitazone. The expression of inflammatory mediators, including interleukin-1 (IL-1), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and matrix metalloproteinase-13 (MMP-13), as well as PPARγ, nuclear nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) p65, and cytosol inhibitor of kappa B alpha (IκBα), was determined through western blotting and real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
Results:
AGEs enhanced the expression of IL-1, TNF-α, and MMP-13, but decreased PPARγ expression in a time- and dose-dependent manner, which was inhibited by anti-RAGE, SB203580 (p38 MAPK specific inhibitor), and SP600125 (selective inhibitor of JNK). PPARγ agonist pioglitazone inhibited the effects of AGEs-induced inflammatory response and PPARγ down-regulation. In human chondrocytes, AGEs induced cytosol IκBα degradation and increased the level of nuclear NF-κB p65, which was inhibited by PPARγ agonist pioglitazone.

Conclusions:
In primary human chondrocytes, AGEs down-regulated PPARγ expression and increased inflammatory mediators, which could be reversed by PPARγ agonist pioglitazone. Activation of RAGE by AGEs triggers a cascade of downstream signaling, including MAPK JNK/p38, PPARγ, and NF-κB. Therefore, PPARγ could be a potential target for pharmacologic intervention in the treatment of OA.

title: Surgical versus medical treatment with cyclooxygenase inhibitors for symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants.
text: The article discusses the comparison of surgical ligation and medical treatment with cyclooxygenase inhibitors (using indomethacin, ibuprofen, or mefenamic acid) as the initial treatment for symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in preterm infants. The study found that there was no significant difference in mortality during hospital stay, chronic lung disease, other bleeding, necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, creatinine level, or intraventricular hemorrhage between the two groups. However, there was a statistically significant increase in the surgical group in incidence of pneumothorax and retinopathy of prematurity stage III and IV compared to the indomethacin group. Additionally, there was a statistically significant decrease in failure of ductal closure rate in the surgical group. The authors conclude that the data are insufficient to make a conclusion as to whether surgical ligation or medical treatment with indomethacin is preferred as initial treatment for symptomatic PDA in preterm infants. They suggest that the duration of the "waiting-time" and transport to another facility with surgical capacity to have the PDA ligated could adversely affect outcomes, as could the perioperative care.

title: The Effect of Collinearity on Parameter Estimates in Nonlinear Mixed Effect Models
text:
Purpose:
To investigate the impact of correlations among predictor variables in a population pharmacokinetic model on the accuracy and precision of parameter estimates, and to determine the threshold level of correlation beyond which the inclusion of covariates in the structural pharmacokinetic model becomes problematic.
Methods:
A Monte Carlo simulation approach was used to generate concentration-time data similar to those observed in a Phase III clinical trial, with the drugs' pharmacokinetics dependent on two covariates. Five data sets were created with increasing correlation between the two covariates. Each data set was analyzed using NONMEM both with and without the inclusion of the covariates in the structural pharmacokinetic model. Summary measures of ill-conditioning and sensitivity analysis were employed to evaluate how increasing correlations among predictor variables affect the accuracy and precision of parameter estimates.
Results:
As the correlation between covariates increased, the standard errors of parameter estimates grew, and the estimates themselves became increasingly biased. When the correlation between predictor variables was 0.75, the standard errors of the parameter estimates were too large to determine statistical significance.

Conclusions:
Correlations among predictor variables exceeding 0.5 when entered into the model simultaneously should serve as a warning to researchers, as both the accuracy of the parameter estimates and the precision of the estimates may be compromised due to ill-conditioning.

title: An analysis of age and gender influences on the relative risk for suicide and psychotropic drug self-poisoning.
text:
The relationship between psychiatric illness, psychotropic medications, and suicide is complex, and clinicians face the challenge of balancing the benefits of treatment against the risk of drug overdose. To better understand this relationship, the present study compared the demographics of patients prescribed psychotropic drugs with those who attempted or completed suicide using these drugs. Data was obtained from the Australian census and studies of general practitioner prescribing, as well as patients who presented with self-poisoning in a defined geographic area.
The study found that the odds of attempting or completing suicide with psychotropic drugs were higher for those under the age of 45, despite this age group being the least likely to be prescribed these drugs. Men were found to have a significantly higher rate of completed suicide using more lethal methods. After correcting for prescription rates, the odds ratios for self-poisoning and suicide with psychotropic drugs were 11.1 and 1.7, respectively, for those aged 15-24, 4.9 and 4.3 for those aged 25-44, and 0.03 and 0.03 for those over 75. Women were found to be slightly more likely to poison themselves with psychotropic drugs, but this increased risk disappeared after correcting for prescription rates.
The study's findings suggest that greater caution should be exercised in prescribing psychotropic medications to individuals under the age of 45, as they are at a higher risk of drug overdose. Additionally, the study suggests that the least toxic compounds should be used, particularly among the elderly, as the risk of self-poisoning may have been overstated, potentially denying some patients adequate treatment.

title: Cell death and immune privilege.
text: The host's response to pathogens involves intricate inflammatory processes and immune reactions, which are crucial for protecting the body against infections. While these responses are essential for clearing infections, they can sometimes result in damage to surrounding tissue. Fortunately, most organ systems can recover from these injuries without lasting harm. However, there are certain areas of the body that are particularly vulnerable to inflammation, such as the eye, brain, and reproductive organs (testis, ovary). In these sensitive areas, even minor episodes of inflammation can have long-term consequences for the survival of the organism. In contrast to other parts of the body, the immune system in these areas operates differently, and a functioning immune response can sometimes lead to disease.

title: Niche-Independent Symmetrical Self-Renewal of a Mammalian Tissue Stem Cell
text: Pluripotent mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells multiply in simple monoculture through symmetrical cell divisions. However, in vivo, stem cells are believed to rely on specialized cellular microenvironments and undergo predominantly asymmetric divisions. Attempts to expand pure populations of tissue stem cells ex vivo have proven elusive. Neural progenitor cells are propagated in combination with differentiating progeny in floating clusters called neurospheres, but the proportion of stem cells in these neurospheres is low, and they cannot be directly observed or interrogated. Here, we demonstrate that the complex neurosphere environment is dispensable for stem cell maintenance, and that the combination of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF-2) and epidermal growth factor (EGF) is sufficient for the derivation and continuous expansion of pure cultures of neural stem (NS) cells. NS cells were derived from mouse ES cells and neural lineage induction was followed by growth factor addition in basal culture media. In the presence of only EGF and FGF-2, resulting NS cells proliferate continuously, are diploid, and clonogenic. After prolonged expansion, they remain able to differentiate efficiently into neurons and astrocytes in vitro and upon transplantation into the adult brain. Colonies generated from single NS cells all produce neurons upon growth factor withdrawal. NS cells uniformly express morphological, cell biological, and molecular features of radial glia, developmental precursors of neurons and glia. Consistent with this profile, adherent NS cell lines can readily be established from fetal mouse brain, and similar NS cells can be generated from human ES cells and human fetal brain. The extrinsic factors EGF plus FGF-2 are sufficient to sustain pure, symmetrical self-renewing divisions of NS cells, resulting in cultures that are the first known example of tissue-specific stem cells that can be propagated without accompanying differentiation. These homogeneous cultures will enable the delineation of molecular mechanisms that define a tissue-specific stem cell and allow direct comparison with pluripotent ES cells.

title: A Bivalent Chromatin Structure Marks Key Developmental Genes in Embryonic Stem Cells
text: The most highly conserved non-coding elements (HCNEs) in mammalian genomes are found to cluster within regions enriched for genes encoding transcription factors (TFs) involved in developmental processes. This observation suggests that these regions may harbor critical regulatory controls that govern development. To investigate this, we conducted an analysis of histone methylation in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells across 56 large HCNE-rich loci. Our findings revealed a distinct modification pattern, termed "bivalent domains," characterized by extensive H3 lysine 27 methylation interspersed with smaller regions of H3 lysine 4 methylation. Bivalent domains tend to coincide with TF genes expressed at low levels. We propose that these domains serve to silence developmental genes in ES cells while maintaining their poised state for activation. Furthermore, our study revealed striking correspondences between genome sequence and histone methylation in ES cells, which become less pronounced in differentiated cells. These results underscore the importance of DNA sequence in shaping the initial epigenetic landscape and suggest a novel chromatin-based mechanism for maintaining pluripotency.

title: Ovarian Surface Epithelium in Patients with Severe Ovarian Infertility: A Potential Source of Cells Expressing Markers of Pluripotent/Multipotent Stem Cells
text: The purpose of this research was to investigate the presence of stem cells in the ovarian surface epithelium of women with premature ovarian failure and no mature follicles or oocytes. During the study, small, round cells of unknown origin were found to express the SOX-2 marker of pluripotency among the epithelial cells after scraping the ovarian surface. These cells were an integral part of the ovarian surface epithelium. When the scraped cells were cultured in a medium with added follicular fluid to mimic the ovarian environment, primitive oocyte-like cells and round-shaped cell clusters were observed, which stained positively for alkaline phosphatase and pluripotency markers, such as SOX-2 and SSEA-4. These markers were expressed early and persistently in the culture. Single oocyte-like cells also expressed genes characteristic of pluripotent stem cells, including OCT4A, SOX-2, NANOG, NANOS, STELLA, CD9, LIN28, KLF4, GDF3, and MYC. The findings of this study confirmed the presence of putative stem cells in the ovarian surface epithelium of these patients and provided a basis for establishing a stem cell line in the future.

title: Structural Homeostasis: Compensatory Adjustments of Dendritic Arbor Geometry in Response to Variations of Synaptic Input
text: As the nervous system develops, there is inherent variability in the connections formed between differentiating neurons. Despite this variability, neural circuits form that are functional and remarkably robust. One way in which neurons cope with input variability is through homeostatic changes in electrical properties. Here, we investigate the development of dendrites in a specific central neuron (aCC) in the late Drosophila embryo, when it first receives connections and becomes electrically active. Simultaneously, we track the distribution of presynaptic sites on the developing postsynaptic arbor. Genetic manipulations of the presynaptic partners reveal that the postsynaptic dendritic arbor adjusts its growth to compensate for changes in the activity and density of synaptic sites. Blocking neurotransmitter synthesis or release results in increased dendritic extension, while an increase in presynaptic release sites leads to a reduction in dendritic arbor size. These growth adjustments occur locally within the arbor and are mediated by the postsynaptic activity state of protein kinase A, which modifies dendritic growth in response to synaptic activity. These findings suggest that the dendritic arbor acts as a homeostatic device, adjusting its size and geometry to balance input variability and ensure appropriate input levels.

title: Nutrition and physical activity guidelines for cancer survivors.
text: Cancer survivors are often eager to learn about nutrition and physical activity strategies to enhance their treatment outcomes, quality of life, and overall survival. In response, the American Cancer Society (ACS) assembled a team of experts in nutrition, physical activity, and cancer survivorship to evaluate the scientific evidence and best clinical practices related to optimal nutrition and physical activity after a cancer diagnosis. This report summarizes their findings and aims to provide healthcare providers with the most up-to-date information to help cancer survivors and their families make informed decisions regarding nutrition and physical activity. The report focuses on guidelines for nutrition and physical activity throughout the cancer care continuum, including important considerations during treatment and for patients with advanced cancer, while primarily addressing the needs of individuals who are disease-free or have stable disease following treatment. Additionally, the report discusses key nutrition and physical activity issues such as body weight, food choices, food safety, and dietary supplements, as well as specific concerns related to different types of cancer.

title: The role of protein clearance mechanisms in organismal ageing and age-related diseases.
text: As we age, our body's ability to maintain a functional proteome, or proteostasis, declines. This leads to the accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins, which disrupt cell function and tissue homeostasis, contributing to various age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, or Huntington's disease. These damaged proteins are typically degraded through the ubiquitin-proteasome system or through autophagy-lysosome, key components of the proteostasis network. Modulating either proteasome activity or autophagic-lysosomal potential has been shown to extend lifespan and protect organisms from the symptoms associated with proteostasis disorders, suggesting that protein clearance mechanisms are directly linked to aging and age-related diseases.

title: A distinctive DNA damage response in human hematopoietic stem cells reveals an apoptosis-independent role for p53 in self-renewal.
text: Highly regenerative tissues, such as blood, require effective DNA damage responses (DDR) to balance long-term regeneration with protection from cancer development. Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are responsible for life-long blood production, yet their response to DNA damage remains poorly understood. Our study reveals that human HSCs exhibit delayed DNA double-strand break rejoining, persistent gammaH2AX foci, and enhanced p53- and ASPP1-dependent apoptosis after exposure to gamma radiation compared to progenitors. Inactivation of p53 or overexpression of Bcl-2 reduced radiation-induced apoptosis and preserved in vivo repopulating HSC function. Interestingly, only Bcl-2-overexpressing HSCs showed higher self-renewal capacity, indicating that intact p53 positively regulates self-renewal independently of apoptosis. Conversely, HSCs with inactivated p53 had reduced self-renewal capacity and accumulated more spontaneous gammaH2AX foci in secondary transplants. Our findings demonstrate distinct physiological roles of p53 in ensuring optimal HSC function: regulation of apoptosis and prevention of gammaH2AX foci accumulation during HSC self-renewal.

title: Behavioral characterization of neuropeptide Y knockout mice.
text: An extensive characterization of behavior was conducted on mice lacking the gene for neuropeptide Y (NPY), including responses to 24 and 48 hour fasts and challenges with small molecule antagonists of NPY receptors implicated in mediating the feeding effects of NPY (i.e., Y1 and Y5). In addition, wildtype (WT) and NPY knockout (KO) mice were tested in a variety of behavioral assays, including locomotor monitors, elevated plus maze, inhibitory avoidance, acoustic startle, prepulse inhibition, and hot plate assays. One of the key findings was that the NPY KO mice had reduced food intake compared to WT controls in response to fasting. Furthermore, the data from these studies suggest that the NPY KO mice may have an anxiogenic-like phenotype and appear to be hypoalgesic in the hot plate paradigm, providing further evidence of the involvement of NPY in energy balance, anxiety, and possibly nociception.

title: Epigenetic-induced repression of microRNA-205 is associated with MED1 activation and a poorer prognosis in localized prostate cancer
text: Deregulation of microRNA (miRNA) expression has been shown to play a critical role in the development and progression of prostate cancer. In this study, we found that the expression of miRNA-205 (miR-205) is commonly repressed and the MIR-205 locus is hypermethylated in prostate cancer. The host gene of unknown function, LOC642587, is also inactivated in conjunction with miR-205. We discovered that miR-205 targets mediator 1 (MED1), also known as TRAP220 and PPARBP, for transcriptional silencing in normal prostate cells, leading to decreased MED1 mRNA levels and reduced levels of total and active phospho-MED1 protein. Overexpression of miR-205 in prostate cancer cells resulted in decreased cell viability, suggesting a tumor suppressor function. We found that hypermethylation of the MIR-205 locus was significantly associated with decreased miR-205 expression and increased MED1 expression in primary tumor samples, and this association was also observed in an expanded patient cohort. These results suggest that miR-205 is an epigenetically regulated tumor suppressor that may provide a potential biomarker in prostate cancer management.

title: Th2 cytokine response in Major Depressive Disorder patients before treatment
text: In Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), there are impairments in the interactions between the neuroendocrine and immune systems. To investigate this further, we compared the pro/anti-inflammatory Th1/Th2 cytokine balance in MDD patients and non-depressed controls. Our findings revealed that MDD subjects had higher levels of cortisol and TNF-alpha, increased percentages of CD3+CD8+ and NK cells, decreased B cell counts, and no significant changes in CD3+CD4+ lymphocyte counts. Additionally, we observed higher levels of IL-4 and IL-13 (Th2) cytokines and significantly lower levels of IL-2 and IFN-gamma (Th1) cytokines in the MDD group. These changes may be related to the elevated cortisol levels seen in MDD patients. Further research is needed to explore these findings and their implications for future therapeutic approaches in MDD patients.

title: CDD: conserved domains and protein three-dimensional structure
text: CDD, a component of NCBI's Entrez query and retrieval system, can be accessed through <http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Structure/cdd/cdd.shtml>. CDD provides annotation of protein sequences by identifying conserved domain footprints and functional sites based on these footprints. Pre-computed annotation is available through Entrez, and interactive search services accept single protein or nucleotide queries, as well as batch submissions of protein query sequences, using RPS-BLAST to rapidly identify potential matches. CDD maintains a collection of protein domain and full-length protein models, and its curation effort aims to provide detailed classifications for major and well-characterized protein domain families, supported by available 3D structure and the published literature. To date, the majority of protein 3D structures are represented by models tracked by CDD, and CDD curators are characterizing novel families emerging from protein structure determination efforts.

title: Extensive diversity of Ig-superfamily proteins in the immune system of insects.
text: The remarkable diversification of immune receptors in higher vertebrates is a distinctive feature. However, it remains unclear whether this molecular diversity provides immune protection in invertebrates. Our study reveals that immune cells in Drosophila have the potential to produce over 18,000 different isoforms of the Ig-superfamily receptor Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule (Dscam). These isoforms are secreted into the hemolymph and play a crucial role in phagocytic bacterial uptake, with hemocyte-specific Dscam loss resulting in reduced bacterial binding and impaired immune function. Notably, the high degree of molecular diversity in Dscam transcripts, generated through a mechanism of alternative splicing, is conserved across major insect orders, suggesting an unexpected level of complexity in the innate immune system of insects.

title: Preparing the outbreak assistance laboratory network in the Netherlands for the detection of the influenza virus A(H1N1) variant.
text:
In April 2009, the emergence of a variant influenza virus A(H1N1)v in the Northern Americas posed a potential threat of a pandemic. To prepare laboratories in the Netherlands for surge capacity in molecular diagnosis of A(H1N1)v infections, a study was conducted to evaluate the ability of laboratories to detect and identify the virus using a panel of blinded specimens.
The study involved 10 laboratories, which were provided with influenza virus A (M-gene), swine influenza virus A (NP-gene), and A(H1N1)v (H1v-gene) specific primers and probes, as well as a protocol developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, USA. The laboratories were asked to implement and test the protocol.
The results showed that all of the laboratories were able to detect A(H1N1)v using the CDC M-gene reagents, with similar sensitivity as their in-house M-gene based assays. However, RT-PCRs used in routine diagnostic settings in the laboratories did not or only showed low levels of cross-reactivity with A(H1N1)v. The CDC swine NP-gene and H1v-gene RT-PCRs showed reduced sensitivity compared to the CDC and in-house M-gene RT-PCRs, while in-house developed A(H1N1)v specific H1v-gene and N1v-gene RT-PCRs showed equal sensitivity to CDC and in-house M-gene RT-PCRs.
The study concluded that the Dutch laboratories are prepared to detect and specifically identify A(H1N1)v, although some level of cross-reactivity was observed with seasonal influenza viruses. The study also recommended the use of M-gene based generic influenza A virus detection in routine settings to be able to detect emerging influenza A viruses.

title: Averting Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes in India through Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Taxation: An Economic-Epidemiologic Modeling Study
text: In high-income countries, taxing sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) has been proposed as a strategy to reduce obesity and type 2 diabetes. However, the effectiveness of this approach in middle-income countries like India, where there is heterogeneity in SSB consumption and patterns of substitution between SSBs and other beverages, is less clear. Using data from a nationally representative survey of 100,855 Indian households, we estimated the potential health effects of a 20% SSB excise tax on various Indian subpopulations. We found that the tax could reduce overweight and obesity prevalence by 3.0% (95% CI 1.6%-5.9%) and type 2 diabetes incidence by 1.6% (95% CI 1.2%-1.9%) over the period 2014-2023, assuming that SSB consumption continues to increase linearly. However, if SSB consumption accelerates due to industry marketing, the tax could avert 4.2% (95% CI 2.5-10.0%) of prevalent overweight/obesity and 2.5% (95% CI 1.0-2.8%) of incident type 2 diabetes from 2014-2023. Our results suggest that the largest relative effect would be expected among young rural men, contradicting our initial hypothesis that urban populations would be the primary beneficiaries of SSB taxation. However, there are limitations to our estimation approach, including the assumption that consumer behavior will reflect future trends and potential underreporting of consumption in dietary recall data. Overall, our findings suggest that sustained SSB taxation at a high tax rate could mitigate rising obesity and type 2 diabetes in India among both urban and rural subpopulations.

title: Acute myopericarditis after multiple vaccinations in an adolescent: case report and review of the literature.
text: We present a case of postvaccination acute myopericarditis in an adolescent patient. The patient experienced sudden onset of chest pain, along with diffuse ST-segment elevation and elevated cardiac enzyme levels. Cardiac MRI revealed acute myocarditis. Fortunately, the patient recovered within a few days with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory treatment and is now clinically stable, with improved MRI findings at the 10-week follow-up. This case highlights the importance of considering myopericarditis as a potential complication of vaccination in adolescents, as reported in the pediatric literature.

title: Cardiovascular protection with antihypertensive drugs in dialysis patients: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Epidemiological studies have shown that lower blood pressure and decline in blood pressure over time are associated with higher mortality rates in dialysis patients. However, randomized controlled trials lack the power to establish the benefits of antihypertensive therapy in these patients. In this meta-analysis, we included patients on long-term dialysis who were randomized to receive antihypertensive drug therapy and compared their outcomes to those in a control or placebo group. We found that the overall benefit of antihypertensive therapy was significant, with a combined hazard ratio for cardiovascular events of 0.69 (95% CI: 0.56-0.84) using a fixed-effects model and 0.62 (95% CI: 0.45-0.86) using a random-effects model. In a sensitivity analysis, we found that the hypertensive group had a pooled hazard ratio of 0.49 (95% CI: 0.35-0.67), but when normotensives were included in the trial, the cardiovascular protection was less (pooled hazard ratio of 0.86 [95% CI: 0.67-1.12]). There was evidence of publication bias in the results. Randomized controlled trials suggest that antihypertensive therapy may be beneficial for hemodialysis patients, but adequately powered trials are needed to confirm these findings, particularly among those with hypertension.

title: Protoplasmic astrocytes in CA1 stratum radiatum occupy separate anatomical domains.
text:
Protoplasmic astrocytes are increasingly recognized as playing a crucial role in interacting with neuronal elements in the brain and influencing their activity. Recent studies have also suggested that these cells may exhibit diverse forms in the central nervous system (CNS). Our current understanding of astrocyte structure and distribution is primarily based on techniques that use the astrocytic marker glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and metal-impregnation methods. However, these techniques have limitations in visualizing the interactions among these complex cells.
In this study, we used intracellular injection combined with immunohistochemistry for GFAP to investigate the interactions among protoplasmic astrocytes in the CA1 stratum radiatum. Our findings reveal that GFAP only delineates approximately 15% of the total volume of the astrocyte, leading to incorrect conclusions regarding the interaction of processes of neighboring astrocytes. To gain a more detailed understanding of these interactions, we used fluorescent intracellular tracers of distinctive emissive wavelengths and analyzed them using three-dimensional (3D) confocal analysis and electron microscopy. Our results show that protoplasmic astrocytes establish primarily exclusive territories, providing important insights into the complex morphology of these cells and their 3D relationships with other astrocytes, oligodendroglia, neurons, and vasculature in the brain. This knowledge has significant implications for our understanding of nervous system function.

title: Leptin-receptor-expressing mesenchymal stromal cells represent the main source of bone formed by adult bone marrow.
text: Research on the identity and physiological function of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) has been hindered by a lack of markers that allow for both prospective identification and fate mapping in vivo. However, we have discovered that the Leptin Receptor (LepR) is a marker that highly enriches bone marrow MSCs. Our findings show that approximately 0.3% of bone marrow cells are LepR(+), with 10% of these cells being colony-forming unit fibroblastic (CFU-Fs), which account for 94% of bone marrow CFU-Fs. LepR(+) cells are capable of forming bone, cartilage, and adipocytes in culture and upon transplantation in vivo. Additionally, LepR(+) cells are also positive for other markers such as Scf-GFP(+), Cxcl12-DsRed(high), and Nestin-GFP(low), which highly enrich CFU-Fs. However, LepR(+) cells are negative for Nestin-CreER and NG2-CreER, markers that are unlikely to be found in CFU-Fs. Fate-mapping studies showed that LepR(+) cells arise postnatally and give rise to most bone and adipocytes formed in adult bone marrow, including bone regenerated after irradiation or fracture. Furthermore, LepR(+) cells are quiescent but can proliferate after injury. Therefore, LepR(+) cells are the major source of bone and adipocytes in adult bone marrow.

title: High-resolution sperm typing of meiotic recombination in the mouse MHC Ebeta gene.
text: Meiotic crossovers in the mouse Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) cluster were detected through pedigree analysis, which revealed the presence of hotspots. To investigate the properties of these hotspots, we conducted high-resolution sperm crossover analysis on the class II E(beta) gene. Our findings confirm the existence of a highly localized hotspot within the second intron of E(beta), spanning 1.0-1.6 kilobases (kb). This hotspot is flanked by nearly completely recombinationally inert DNA. Heterozygous mice for different MHC haplotypes exhibit variable crossover rates, but always the same hotspot, even when crossed with the highly diverged p haplotype. Crossovers in reciprocal orientations occur at similar frequencies but show different distributions across the hotspot, with the center points in the two orientations shifted on average by 400 base pairs (bp). This asymmetry leads to biased gene conversion in favor of hotspot markers from the non-initiating haplotype, supporting the double-strand break repair model of recombination, with haplotype s as the most efficient crossover initiator. The behavior of the E(beta) hotspot, including the localized nature of recombination initiation, is strikingly similar to that observed in human hotspots.

title: Long-term survival of beta thalassemia major patients treated with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation compared with survival with conventional treatment.
text: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in thalassemia remains a challenging treatment option. In a single-center case-control study involving 516 children and adult patients, 258 patients underwent sibling (67%) or unrelated (33%) HSCT, while 97 patients were adults (age ≥ 16 years). The median follow-up after HSCT was 11 years (range 1-30). The conditioning regimen consisted of busulfan (80.6%) or treosulfan-based (19.4%). A cohort of 258 age-sex matched conventionally treated (CT) patients was randomly selected. The 30-year overall survival (OS) and thalassemia-free survival (TFS) in transplanted patients were 82.6 ± 2.7% and 77.8 ± 2.9%, respectively, which were similar to the OS of 85.3 ± 2.7% in CT patients (P = NS). The incidence of grade II-IV acute and chronic graft versus host disease (GvHD) was 23.6% and 12.9%, respectively. The probability of rejection was 6.9%. Transplant-related mortality (TRM) (13.8%) was similar to the probability of dying of cardiovascular events in CT patients (12.2%). A high-risk Pesaro score (class 3) was associated with lower OS (odds ratio [OR] = 1.99, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.31-3.03) and TFS (OR = 1.54, 95% CI = 1.12-2.12). In adult patients, the 23-year OS and TFS after HSCT were 70 ± 5% and 67.3 ± 5%, respectively, which were similar to the OS of 71.2 ± 5% in CT patients (P = NS). Finally, treosulfan was associated with a lower risk of acute GvHD (P = .004; OR = 0.28, 95% CI = 0.12-0.67). In conclusion, the 30-year survival rate of ex-thalassemia patients after HSCT was similar to that expected in CT thalassemia patients, with the majority of HSCT survivors cured from thalassemia.

title: Global analysis of ATM polymorphism reveals significant functional constraint.
text: The ATM gene, which is mutated in ataxia-telangiectasia, has been found to be associated with various clinical manifestations, including cerebellar degeneration, abnormal proliferation of small blood vessels, and cancer. To investigate the genetic variation in the ATM gene, we conducted a comprehensive survey of sequence variation in the gene in diverse human populations. The protein-encoding exons and adjacent intron and untranslated sequences were analyzed in 93 individuals from seven major human populations. Additionally, the coding sequence was analyzed in four non-human primate species. Our study identified 88 variant sites in the human ATM gene using denaturing high-performance liquid chromatography, which had a sensitivity of 96%-100% for detecting DNA sequence variation. We compared the nucleotide diversity of the ATM gene to 14 other autosomal genes and found that the non-coding regions of the gene had diversity values comparable to those of other genes, while the coding regions had very low diversity, particularly in the last 29% of the protein sequence. Using the Hudson/Kreitman/Aguadé statistic, we found that the coding region of the ATM gene was significantly constrained relative to that of the orangutan, the Old World monkey, and the mouse, but not relative to that of the chimpanzee or the gorilla. Our results also showed extensive linkage disequilibrium in the ATM gene, which may be due to suppression of meiotic recombination at this locus. We defined seven haplotypes in the gene. Two haplotypes accounted for 82% of all chromosomes analyzed in all major populations, while two others carrying the same D126E missense polymorphism accounted for 33% of chromosomes in Africa but were never observed outside of Africa. The high frequency of this polymorphism may be due to a population expansion within Africa or selective pressure.

title: Ablation and regeneration of tolerance-inducing medullary thymic epithelial cells after cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone treatment.
text: Immunosuppressive drugs and cytotoxic chemotherapy agents are designed to target and eliminate specific immune cells, such as autoreactive, alloaggressive, or hyperinflammatory T cells, or malignant cells. However, these treatments can also have unintended consequences on the immune system, including severe immunological side effects. For instance, cyclosporine A, a commonly used immunosuppressive drug, has been linked to a rare autoimmune syndrome in some patients. Our study shows that this drug has a significant impact on murine thymic epithelial cells (TECs), which are crucial for rebuilding the immune system after treatment. We found that cyclosporine A causes extensive loss of autoimmune regulator (Aire(+)) tolerance-inducing MHC class II(high) medullary TECs (mTEC(high)). However, Aire expression was restored within 7 days, and full recovery of the mTEC(high) subset occurred within 10 days, accompanied by a decrease in a relatively resistant MHC class II(low) mTEC subset (mTEC(low)). Similarly, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone caused more extensive ablation of thymocytes and stromal cells, leading to severe depletion of tolerance-inducing mTEC(high). Our findings suggest that Aire(+) mTECs are highly sensitive to damage and that mTEC regeneration follows a conserved pattern regardless of the treatment regimen used.

title: GATA-3 regulates hematopoietic stem cell maintenance and cell-cycle entry.
text: Maintaining the quiescence of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) is crucial for their life-long function in generating blood cells. Approximately 75% of cells in a highly enriched long-term repopulating HSC (LT-HSC) pool are quiescent, with only a small percentage of LT-HSCs in cycle. Transcription factor GATA-3 plays a vital role in the development of T cells in the thymus and Th2 differentiation in peripheral organs. Although GATA-3 is expressed in HSCs, its role in prethymic progenitor cells has not been established. In this study, we found that Gata3-null mice have fewer LT-HSCs and fewer of these cells in cycle. Additionally, Gata3-null hematopoietic progenitor cells fail to enter an increased cycling state after myelosuppression induced by 5-fluorouracil. These findings demonstrate that GATA-3 is essential for maintaining a normal number of LT-HSCs and for their entry into the cell cycle.

title: CpG island methylator phenotype predicts progression of malignant melanoma.
text:
The purpose of this study is to investigate the presence of a specific epigenetic pattern, known as the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP), in cutaneous melanoma progression. CIMP is characterized by the coordinated inactivation of tumor suppressor and tumor-related genes (TRGs) and the methylation of multiple non-coding regions (MINT loci). The study aims to determine if CIMP is associated with advancing clinical tumor stage and disease outcome in melanoma.
The study analyzed the methylation status of TRGs and MINT loci in primary and metastatic tumors of different clinical stages (n=122). The results show an increase in hypermethylation of TRGs, such as WIF1, TFPI2, RASSF1A, and SOCS1, with advancing clinical tumor stage. Additionally, the study found a significant positive association between the methylation status of MINT17, MINT31, and TRGs. The methylation status of MINT31 was found to be associated with disease outcome in stage III melanoma.
Overall, these findings suggest that the presence of a CIMP pattern is associated with advancing clinical stage of malignant melanoma. Future prospective large-scale studies may determine if CIMP-positive primary melanomas are at high risk of metastasis or recurrence.

title: SLC1A5 mediates glutamine transport required for lung cancer cell growth and survival.
text:
PURPOSE: In a previous shotgun proteomic analysis of stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), we identified solute-linked carrier family A1 member 5 (SLC1A5) as an overexpressed protein in cancer tissues compared to matched controls. We hypothesized that the overexpression of SLC1A5 is a mechanism to meet the increased metabolic demand for lung cancer cell growth and survival.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: To test our hypothesis, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of SLC1A5 protein expression in archival lung cancer tissues (N = 98) and cell lines (N = 36) using immunohistochemistry and immunoblotting. Additionally, we examined the role of SLC1A5 in amino acid transportation by conducting kinetic analysis of l-glutamine (Gln) uptake in lung cancer cell lines in the presence and absence of a pharmacologic inhibitor of SLC1A5, gamma-l-Glutamyl-p-Nitroanilide (GPNA). Finally, we investigated the effect of Gln deprivation and uptake inhibition on cell growth, cell-cycle progression, and growth signaling pathways of five lung cancer cell lines.
RESULTS: Our findings revealed that (i) SLC1A5 protein is expressed in 95% of squamous cell carcinomas (SCC), 74% of adenocarcinomas (ADC), and 50% of neuroendocrine tumors; (ii) SLC1A5 is predominantly localized at the cytoplasmic membrane and is significantly associated with SCC histology and male gender; (iii) approximately 68% of Gln is transported in a Na(+)-dependent manner, with 50% of this transport attributed to SLC1A5 activity; and (iv) pharmacologic and genetic targeting of SLC1A5 resulted in a significant decrease in cell growth and viability in lung cancer cells, an effect mediated in part by mTOR signaling.
CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest that SLC1A5 plays a crucial role in Gln transport, controlling lung cancer cells' metabolism, growth, and survival.

title: Eic1 links Mis18 with the CCAN/Mis6/Ctf19 complex to promote CENP-A assembly
text: The foundation of kinetochore assembly is laid by CENP-A chromatin. The incorporation of CENP-A at centromeres is independent of replication and relies on the chaperone HJURP(Scm3) and Mis18 in vertebrates and fission yeast. The recruitment of Mis18 and HJURP(Scm3) to centromeres is regulated by the cell cycle. In vertebrates, Mis18 associates with Mis18BP1(KNL2), which is crucial for the recruitment of Mis18 and HJURP(Scm3). We identified two novel fission yeast Mis18-interacting proteins, Eic1 and Eic2, which are components of the Mis18 complex. Eic1 is essential for maintaining Cnp1(CENP-A) at centromeres and is crucial for kinetochore integrity, while Eic2 is dispensable. Eic1 also interacts with Fta7(CENP-Q/Okp1), Cnl2(Nkp2), and Mal2(CENP-O/Mcm21), components of the constitutive CCAN/Mis6/Ctf19 complex. Since no Mis18BP1(KNL2) orthologue has been identified in fission yeast, it remains unclear how the key Cnp1(CENP-A) loading factor Mis18 is recruited. Our findings suggest that Eic1 serves a function analogous to that of Mis18BP1(KNL2), connecting a module within the CCAN/Mis6/Ctf19 complex to temporally regulate the recruitment of the Mis18/Scm3(HJURP) Cnp1(CENP-A) loading factors. The novel interactions identified between CENP-A loading factors and the CCAN/Mis6/Ctf19 complex are likely to contribute to CENP-A maintenance in other organisms.

title: INTRANASAL INSULIN IMPROVES COGNITION AND MODULATES β-AMYLOID IN EARLY AD
text: Background: Reduced brain insulin signaling and low levels of insulin in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) have been observed in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Intravenous or intracerebroventricular insulin administration has been shown to improve memory, alter electroencephalography (EEG) patterns, and modulate neurotransmitters, possibly by increasing low brain insulin levels. Intranasal insulin administration has been shown to reach the brain within 15 minutes. Objective: To investigate the effectiveness of daily intranasal insulin treatment in patients with early AD or its prodrome, amnestic mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods: Twenty-five participants were randomly assigned to receive either placebo or 20 IU of intranasal insulin treatment using an electronic atomizer, and 24 participants completed the study. Participants, caregivers, and clinical evaluators were blinded to treatment assignment. Cognitive measures and blood samples were collected at baseline and after 21 days of treatment. Results: Fasting plasma glucose and insulin levels remained unchanged with treatment. The insulin-treated group showed better retention of verbal information after a delay compared to the placebo-assigned group (p = 0.0374). Insulin-treated participants also exhibited improved attention (p = 0.0108) and functional status (p = 0.0410). Insulin treatment increased fasting plasma levels of the short form of the β-amyloid peptide (Aβ40) (p = 0.0471), without affecting the longer isoform (Aβ42), resulting in an increased Aβ40/42 ratio (p = 0.0207). Conclusions: The results of this pilot study suggest that daily intranasal insulin treatment may be beneficial for patients with early AD or MCI, and provide a novel approach to the treatment of neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Maternal alloantigens promote the development of tolerogenic fetal regulatory T cells in utero.
text: As the immune system matures, T cells are selectively regulated to recognize and respond to foreign antigens while ignoring self-antigens. In mice, this process involves the elimination of self-reactive T cells. However, in humans, a unique mechanism is employed: the generation of regulatory T cells (Tregs) that suppress fetal immune responses. We have found that a significant number of maternal cells cross the placenta and reside in fetal lymph nodes, leading to the development of CD4+CD25highFoxP3+ Tregs that suppress fetal antimaternal immunity and persist until early adulthood. These findings reveal a form of antigen-specific tolerance in humans, induced in utero and likely playing a role in regulating immune responses after birth.

title: β-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme 1(BACE1) inhibitor treatment induces Aβ5-X peptides through alternative amyloid precursor protein cleavage
text:
INTRODUCTION:
The β-secretase enzyme, β-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1), plays a crucial role in the production of β-amyloid (Aβ) peptides, which are a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD). In a previous study, we found that treatment with a BACE1 inhibitor resulted in decreased levels of Aβ1-34 and increased levels of Aβ5-40, suggesting that these Aβ species may serve as novel pharmacodynamic biomarkers in clinical trials. To further investigate this finding, we conducted a randomized, placebo-controlled, and investigator-blind study in healthy subjects to examine the effects of BACE1 inhibition on CSF Aβ levels.
METHODS:
We randomly assigned 18 healthy subjects to receive a single dose of either 30 mg or 90 mg of LY2811376 (a BACE1 inhibitor) or placebo. CSF samples were collected before and after treatment, and Aβ levels were measured using hybrid immunoaffinity-mass spectrometry (HI-MS) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs).
RESULTS:
Our results demonstrate dose-dependent changes in CSF Aβ1-34, Aβ5-40, and Aβ5-X after treatment with LY2811376. Specifically, Aβ5-40 and Aβ5-X increased dose-dependently, as reflected by two independent methods, while Aβ1-34 decreased dose-dependently.
CONCLUSION:
Our findings confirm that CSF Aβ1-34 may be a useful marker for monitoring target engagement in clinical trials of BACE1 inhibitors. Since it is less hydrophobic than longer Aβ species, it is less susceptible to preanalytical confounding factors and may thus be a more stable marker. Additionally, our results suggest that BACE1 inhibition in humans is associated with APP-processing into N-terminally truncated Aβ peptides via a BACE1-independent pathway.
TRIAL REGISTRATION:

The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00838084) on January 23, 2009, and was last updated on July 14, 2009.

title: Cardiovascular diseases in Chinese, Malays, and Indians in Singapore. I. Differences in mortality.
text:
Study Objective:
The aim of this study was to investigate and compare the mortality rates from the three major cardiovascular diseases (ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive disease, and cerebrovascular disease) among the three main ethnic groups in Singapore, specifically the Chinese, Malays, and Indians.
Design:
The study used national death registration data in Singapore from 1980 to 1984, covering a population of 2.53 million people (76.5% Chinese, 14.8% Malays, 6.4% Indians, and 2.3% Others). The underlying cause of death, coded according to the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-9), was used for analysis.
Setting:
The study was conducted in the independent island state of Singapore, which has a population of approximately 2.53 million people.
Subjects:
The study analyzed all registered deaths in the age range of 30-69 years during the study period, by ethnic group.
Measurements and Main Results:

Indians had higher mortality rates from ischaemic heart disease compared to the other ethnic groups in both males and females, with age-standardized relative risks of Indian compared to Chinese (males: 3.8, females: 3.4). The excess mortality in Indians decreased with age.
For hypertensive disease, Malays had the highest mortality rates, with age-standardized relative risks of Malay compared to Chinese (males: 3.4, females: 4.4), Malay compared to Indian (males: 2.0, females: 2.5), and Indian compared to Chinese (males: 1.6, females: 1.6).
For cerebrovascular disease, there were minimal ethnic differences except for lower rates in Chinese females, with age-standardized relative risks of Malay compared to Chinese (males: 1.1, females: 1.9), Malay compared to Indian (males: 1.0, females: 1.1), and Indian compared to Chinese (males: 1.1, females: 1.7).


Conclusions:

The study found significant differences in mortality rates from the three main cardiovascular diseases among the three ethnic groups in Singapore. These findings highlight the importance of tailoring prevention and treatment strategies to the specific needs of each ethnic group.

title: Protein localization in electron micrographs using fluorescence nanoscopy
text:
A comprehensive understanding of a cell requires a detailed description of its molecular landscape, including the precise arrangement of proteins and their association with specific organelles. However, current techniques for imaging proteins at the nanoscale have limitations, such as low-quality fixation, limited availability of antibodies, and inaccessibility of antigens. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a novel approach called correlative fluorescence electron microscopy (CFEM), which allows for the nanoscopic localization of proteins in electron micrographs.
In CFEM, we use fluorescent proteins to label proteins of interest and express them in live Caenorhabditis elegans. We then fix the worms, embed them in plastic, and image the tagged proteins from ultrathin sections using either stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy or photoactivated localization microscopy (PALM). By correlating the fluorescence signals with the organelles imaged in electron micrographs from the same sections, we can determine the precise location of proteins within the cell.
We have applied CFEM to localize histones, a mitochondrial protein, and a presynaptic dense projection protein in electron micrographs.
