Our results demonstrate the power of CFEM for studying the molecular landscape of cells at the nanoscale, and its potential to reveal new insights into cellular structure and function.

title: The flavonoid component isorhamnetin in vitro inhibits proliferation and induces apoptosis in Eca-109 cells.
text:
Isorhamnetin, a flavonoid component, has been investigated for its anti-cancer effects on human esophageal squamous carcinoma cells (Eca-109). In vitro experiments were conducted to assess the drug's impact on cell viability, proliferation, and apoptosis.
Isorhamnetin exhibited a cytostatic effect on Eca-109 cells with an IC50 value of 40±0.08 μg/ml, as determined by MTT assay. The drug also inhibited cell proliferation, as evidenced by trypan blue exclusion assay, clone formation test, immunocytochemical assay of PCNA, and (3)H-thymidine uptake analysis. Cell cycle distribution was analyzed using flow cytometry, revealing a significant increase in the population of cells in the G(0)/G(1) phase and a decrease in the G(2)/M phase.
In addition to its cytostatic effect, isorhamnetin also stimulated apoptosis in Eca-109 cells, as observed through transmission electron microscopy and flow cytometry. The apoptosis rate increased from 6.3% to 16.3% in the treated group compared to the control group. To elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms, the expressions of six proliferation- and death-related genes were analyzed by flow cytometry. The expressions of bcl-2, c-myc, and H-ras were downregulated, while Bax, c-fos, and p53 were upregulated.
While these in vitro findings suggest that isorhamnetin may be a potent anti-cancer drug against Eca-109 cells, further in vivo experiments are needed to confirm these results.

In summary, isorhamnetin appears to have the potential to inhibit the growth of esophageal cancer cells (Eca-109) through both cytostatic and apoptotic mechanisms.

title: Arachidonic Acid in the Diabetic Rat Kidney
text: In the isolated perfused rat kidney, arachidonic acid elicits cyclooxygenase-dependent vasoconstriction, with enhanced responses in kidneys from diabetic rats. This study investigated the roles of cyclooxygenase-1 and -2 in the augmented vasoconstrictor effect of arachidonic acid in streptozotocin-diabetic rats. We also determined the release of 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (20-HETE), an eicosanoid that can elicit cyclooxygenase-dependent vasoconstriction. Our findings showed that vasoconstrictor responses to arachidonic acid were significantly enhanced in diabetic rat kidneys, associated with a 2-fold increase in the release of 6-keto-prostaglandin F1 alpha (6-keto-PGF1 alpha), a marker of cyclooxygenase activity. Inhibition of both cyclooxygenase isoforms with indomethacin abolished the vasoconstrictor response to arachidonic acid in both diabetic and control rat kidneys, while inhibition of cyclooxygenase-2 with nimesulide reduced perfusion pressure responses to 1 and 3 micrograms of arachidonic acid only in the diabetic rat kidney, consistent with a 3-fold increase in the renal cortical expression of cyclooxygenase-2. Interestingly, 20-HETE release from the diabetic rat kidney was reduced almost 6-fold and was not increased in response to arachidonic acid. These results demonstrate that the renal vasoconstrictor effect of arachidonic acid is solely dependent on cyclooxygenase activity, with no contribution from 20-HETE; in the diabetic rat, cyclooxygenase-2 activity contributes to the renal vasoconstrictor effect of arachidonic acid.

title: Two sequence motifs from HIF-1alpha bind to the DNA-binding site of p53.
text: There is evidence suggesting that the protein hypoxia-inducible factor-1alpha (HIF-1alpha) interacts with the tumor suppressor p53. To investigate this putative interaction, we mapped the binding of the core domain of p53 (p53c) to an array of immobilized HIF-1alpha-derived peptides and found two peptide-sequence motifs that bound to p53c with micromolar affinity in solution. One of these motifs was located adjacent to and the other coincided with the two proline residues (P402 and P564) that regulate the oxygen-dependent degradation of HIF-1alpha. Interestingly, the binding affinity was independent of the hydroxylation state of P564. Using NMR spectroscopy, we found that these sequence motifs bind to the DNA-binding site of p53c. Since the two sequences are similar and separated by 120 residues, and one is located in a largely unstructured transactivation domain, we propose that each sequence motif in HIF-1alpha binds to a different subunit of the p53 tetramer, leading to very tight binding. The binding data support the idea that p53 provides a mechanism for the degradation of HIF-1alpha in hypoxic tumor cells that are not hydroxylated at the two proline residues.

title: A functionally characterized test set of human induced pluripotent stem cells
text: Human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) hold great promise for studying development and creating in vitro disease models, but their variability has raised concerns about their reliability. To address this, we established a diverse set of 16 iPSC lines from seven individuals with different ages, sexes, and health statuses. We extensively characterized these lines for pluripotency and their ability to differentiate into motor neurons in two independent laboratories. Surprisingly, 13 of the iPSC lines generated functional motor neurons with similar efficiency to human embryonic stem cells (ESCs). Although three lines were initially resistant to neural differentiation, early neuralization rescued their performance. Notably, all 16 iPSC lines passed a rigorous test of differentiation capacity, despite variations in karyotype and early pluripotency marker expression. This iPSC and ESC test set serves as a valuable resource for researchers studying stem cell biology and its applications.

title: Differential regulation of MAP kinase activation by a novel splice variant of human MAP kinase phosphatase-2.
text:
Introduction:
MAP kinase phosphatase-2 (MKP-2) is a member of the dual specificity phosphatase family that plays a crucial role in inactivating the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathways. In this study, we identify a novel human MKP-2 variant (MKP-2-S) that lacks the MAP kinase binding site but retains the phosphatase catalytic domain.
Methods:
We used PC3 prostate and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells, as well as human prostate biopsies, to detect endogenous MKP-2-S transcripts and proteins. Cellular transfection of MKP-2-S resulted in the expression of a 33kDa nuclear protein with phosphatase activity comparable to the long form of MKP-2 (MKP-2-L). To investigate the differences between MKP-2-S and MKP-2-L, we analyzed their ability to bind ERK and JNK, as well as their susceptibility to proteosomal-mediated degradation.
Results:
Our results show that MKP-2-S lacks the kinase interacting motif (KIM) required for binding to ERK and JNK, and therefore does not bind to these kinases. In contrast, MKP-2-L bound ERK and to a lesser extent JNK. We found that protein turnover of adenoviral expressed MKP-2-S was accelerated relative to MKP-2-L, with a greater susceptibility to proteosomal-mediated degradation. MKP-2-S retained its ability to deactivate JNK in a similar manner as MKP-2-L and was an effective inhibitor of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) induction. However, unlike MKP-2-L, MKP-2-S was unable to reverse serum-induced ERK activation or significantly inhibit endothelial cell proliferation.
Discussion:
Our findings reveal the existence of a novel splice variant of MKP-2, MKP-2-S, which lacks the MAP kinase binding site and may play a role in the dysregulation of MAP kinase activity in certain disease states, particularly in breast and prostate cancers. The inability of MKP-2-S to bind ERK may contribute to its reduced ability to inhibit endothelial cell proliferation and reverse serum-induced ERK activation. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer development and progression.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study identifies a novel human MKP-2 variant (MKP-2-S) that lacks the MAP kinase binding site but retains the phosphatase catalytic domain. Our findings suggest that MKP-2-S may play a role in the dysregulation of MAP kinase activity in certain disease states, particularly in breast and prostate cancers. Further research is needed to fully understand the molecular mechanisms underlying the function of MKP-2-S and its potential as a therapeutic target for cancer treatment.

title: Myeloperoxidase acts as a profibrotic mediator of atrial fibrillation
text:
Observational and experimental studies have shown a strong association between atrial fibrillation and inflammation. However, the question of whether inflammation causes or is caused by atrial fibrillation, as well as which specific inflammatory mediators are involved, remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the role of myeloperoxidase (MPO), a heme enzyme abundantly expressed by neutrophils, in the pathophysiology of atrial fibrillation.
Using experimental and clinical evidence, we demonstrate that MPO is mechanistically involved in the development of atrial fibrillation. MPO-deficient mice pretreated with angiotensin II (AngII) to provoke leukocyte activation had lower atrial tissue abundance of the MPO product 3-chlorotyrosine, reduced activity of matrix metalloproteinases, and blunted atrial fibrosis compared to wild-type mice. Upon right atrial electrophysiological stimulation, MPO-deficient mice were protected from atrial fibrillation, which was reversed when MPO was restored. In humans, plasma concentrations of MPO were higher in individuals with atrial fibrillation compared to those without, and MPO colocalized with increased formation of 3-chlorotyrosine in the atria.
Our data suggest that MPO is a crucial factor in the development of structural remodeling of the myocardium, leading to increased vulnerability to atrial fibrillation. These findings have important implications for the development of new therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of atrial fibrillation.

title: Knowledge and use of secondary contraception among patients requesting termination of pregnancy.
text: A survey of 769 patients attending the St. James's University Fertility Control Clinic in England found that those who saw general practitioners were less knowledgeable about contraception than those who attended specialist clinics. The survey revealed a need for counseling on pill and condom use and protection against sexually transmitted diseases. Patients' knowledge of postcoital methods was also found to be lacking. The survey was conducted between April 1, 1991, and January 31, 1992, and included minority groups such as Afro-Caribbean (8%) and Asian (9%). Of the 307 patients using a less effective form of contraception at the time of conception, 93 reported a split or leaking condom, 13 reported a condom falling off during intercourse, and 32 reported inconsistent use of condoms. Only 20 of the 171 patients who had conceived while using condoms recognized a potential condom failure, and only 30% of the 171 patients with recognized condom failure and 12% of the 210 who had not used any contraception had adequate knowledge of postcoital pills. Only 2% of the 171 and 2% of the 381 patients had knowledge of postcoital insertion of an intrauterine contraceptive device. The majority (718 out of 769) of patients preferred using postcoital contraception. Contraceptive information was provided to 501 patients by a general practitioner, to 102 by a community family planning clinic, and to 163 patients with no medical advice. The survey found variable knowledge of postcoital contraceptive methods among patients, with 19% of the 372 patients treated by general practitioners providing 4 correct answers, compared to 50% of the 50 patients in community family planning clinics. The differences could not be explained by other demographic characteristics.

title: Domestication and Divergence of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Beer Yeasts
text: Although the domestication of livestock, pets, and crops has been well-documented, the extent to which microorganisms used in food production, such as yeast, have also undergone human selection is unclear. In this study, we investigate the genomes and phenotypes of 157 industrial Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeasts and reveal that they can be divided into five sublineages that are distinct from wild strains and originate from a limited number of ancestors through complex patterns of domestication and local divergence. Our analyses show strong industry-specific selection for traits such as stress tolerance, sugar utilization, and flavor production, while sexual cycle and other traits related to survival in nature have decayed, particularly in beer yeasts. These findings shed light on the origins, evolutionary history, and phenotypic diversity of industrial yeasts and provide a valuable resource for selecting superior strains. PAPERCLIP.

title: The ascendancy of Amblyomma americanum as a vector of pathogens affecting humans in the United States.
text: Until the 1990s, Amblyomma americanum was viewed primarily as a nuisance species with minimal impact on human health. However, with the discovery of pathogens such as Ehrlichia chaffeensis, Ehrlichia ewingii, and "Borrelia lonestari," the tick's role as a vector of zoonotic diseases has become increasingly evident. As a result, the public health significance of lone star ticks is no longer in doubt. In the next 25 years, the number of cases of human disease caused by A. americanum-associated pathogens is expected to rise. This increase will be driven by both biological and environmental factors that affect the distribution and transmission of zoonotic pathogens, as well as sociological and demographic changes that increase the likelihood of humans coming into contact with infected ticks. Improved diagnostic capabilities and national surveillance efforts will also contribute to the anticipated rise in recognized cases of disease.

title: Biallelic mutations in PALB2 cause Fanconi anemia subtype FA-N and predispose to childhood cancer
text: Recently, PALB2 has been identified as a nuclear partner of BRCA2. Biallelic mutations in BRCA2 are known to cause Fanconi anemia subtype FA-D1 and increase the risk of childhood cancers. In seven families with Fanconi anemia and early-onset cancer, we found pathogenic mutations in PALB2 (also known as FANCN), indicating that biallelic PALB2 mutations lead to a new subtype of Fanconi anemia, FA-N. Similar to biallelic BRCA2 mutations, these mutations significantly increase the risk of childhood cancer.

title: Long tandem arrays of complex repeat units in Chironomus telomeres.
text: A DNA fragment of 340 base pairs (bp) cloned from the Chironomus pallividittatus genome using EcoRI has been localized to the telomeres through in situ hybridization and connective regions between telomeres. No hybridization was observed in other areas of the chromosomes. Another EcoRI fragment, 525 bp long, has also been studied, representing a partial duplication of the 340-bp sequence. Genomic blot hybridization experiments revealed that the 340-bp sequence is a single, repeated unit that makes up approximately 1.2% of the Chironomus genome, with each telomere containing approximately 300 kilobases (kb) of this sequence. The repeat unit consists of two subrepeats, each present twice per repeat unit. Northern blot hybridization experiments showed that the telomere-associated sequences are transcribed into a distinct RNA species approximately 20 kb in size. The evolution of these telomere-associated DNA sequences is discussed.

title: Localization of Na+ channel isoforms at the atrioventricular junction and atrioventricular node in the rat.
text:
Background: The electrical activity of the atrioventricular node (AVN) is characterized by functional heterogeneity, but the relationship between this heterogeneity and the 3-dimensional structure of the AVN remains unclear. To address this gap in knowledge, we investigated the expression of Na(V)1.5 and other Na+ channel isoforms in the AVN.
Methods and Results: We used immunohistochemistry with isoform-specific Na+ channel antibodies to investigate Na+ channel expression in the rat AVN. Our results showed that Na(V)1.1 was distributed similarly to Na(V)1.5, while Na(V)1.2 was not detected. Na(V)1.3 labeling was observed in nerve fibers and cell bodies, but not myocytes, and was abundant in the penetrating atrioventricular (AV) bundle and the common bundle. In contrast, Na(V)1.5 labeling was abundant in the atrial and ventricular myocardium and the left bundle branch, but was absent in the open node, penetrating AV bundle, AV ring bundle, and common bundle. Na(V)1.6 was not detected.
Conclusions: Our findings provide molecular evidence of multiple electrophysiological cell types at the AV junction. These cell types are characterized by distinct patterns of Na+ channel expression, which are likely to play a crucial role in the regulation of AV conduction. Impaired AV conduction resulting from mutations in or loss of Na(V)1.5 must be the result of impaired conduction in the AVN inputs or output, rather than the AVN itself.

title: Follicular B cell trafficking within the spleen actively restricts humoral immune responses.
text: Follicular (FO) and marginal zone (MZ) B cells are maintained in distinct regions of the spleen, but the genetic basis for this segregation remains unclear. Our study reveals that B cell migration is regulated by lineage-specific transcription factors, specifically Klf2, which controls the expression of migratory receptors. Using gene-targeted mice, we found that altering splenic B cell migration leads to a significant in vivo gain-of-function phenotype in FO B cells, allowing them to quickly respond to MZ-associated antigens and pathogens in a T cell-dependent manner. This work shows that in wild-type animals, naive FO B cells are actively removed from the MZ, thereby limiting their ability to respond to blood-borne pathogens.

title: Interleukin-2 and inflammation induce distinct transcriptional programs that promote the differentiation of effector cytolytic T cells.
text: Interleukin-2 (IL-2) and inflammation play a crucial role in regulating the generation of effector and memory cytolytic T-lymphocytes (CTLs) during infection. Our study demonstrates a complex interplay between IL-2 and inflammatory signals during CTL differentiation. IL-2 stimulation leads to the upregulation of the transcription factor eomesodermin (Eomes), which in turn induces the expression of perforin (Prf1) and represses the re-expression of memory CTL markers Bcl6 and IL-7Ralpha. The binding of Eomes and STAT5 to the Prf1 cis-regulatory regions correlates with transcriptional initiation, resulting in increased recruitment of RNA polymerase II to the Prf1 promoter. Inflammation, such as CpG and IL-12, enhances the expression of IL-2Ralpha and the transcription factor T-bet, but counteracts late Eomes and perforin induction while preventing IL-7Ralpha repression by IL-2. In mice infected with lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, IL-2Ralpha-deficient effector CD8(+) T cells exhibit reduced expression of Bcl6 and increased expression of granzyme B, form fewer KLRG-1(+) and T-bet-expressing CTLs, and display impaired cytotoxic activity. These findings demonstrate that inflammation influences both effector and memory CTL differentiation, while persistent IL-2 stimulation promotes effector cell development at the expense of memory CTL development.

title: Neighbourhood risk factors for tuberculosis in Hong Kong.
text: Background: Tuberculosis (TB) has been linked to poverty, particularly in developing countries. However, there are few industrialized areas with high TB incidence, such as Hong Kong, where the relationship between poverty and TB is not well understood. Objective: To investigate the spatial distribution of TB and its association with neighborhood-level risk factors in Hong Kong. Methods: A total of 17,294 TB cases reported from 2005 to 2007 were mapped to the District Council Constituency Area (DCCA) level and standardized by age and sex using 2006 census population data. The standardized TB ratio was correlated with neighborhood risk factors categorized into family, ethnicity, economic, and environmental domains. Results: The indirectly standardized TB ratio showed a spatially varied pattern and was significantly associated with all neighborhood factors on univariate analysis. Only low household income was independently associated with the standardized TB ratio on multivariate analysis. Conclusion: Despite Hong Kong's well-developed social assistance scheme, which has virtually eliminated absolute poverty, low household income in the neighborhood remained significantly associated with TB, independent of place of birth, marital status, and other risk factors.

title: Genomic stability and tumour suppression by the APC/C cofactor Cdh1
text: The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), a ubiquitin protein ligase, collaborates with Cdc20 or Cdh1 to target and degrade cell-cycle proteins during mitosis and G1 phase. The absence of Cdh1 in embryonic development leads to lethality due to defects in trophoblast cell endoreduplication and placental dysfunction. However, when Cdh1 is expressed in the placenta, this lethality is averted. Cells lacking Cdh1 exhibit impaired proliferation and accumulate numerical and structural chromosomal aberrations, indicating that Cdh1 plays a crucial role in maintaining genomic stability. Heterozygous animals for Cdh1 show increased susceptibility to spontaneous tumors, suggesting that Cdh1 functions as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor. These animals also display behavioral defects associated with excessive proliferation of stem cells in the nervous system, indicating that Cdh1 is essential for preventing unscheduled proliferation of specific progenitor cells and protecting mammalian cells from genomic instability.

title: Developing primary palliative care.
text:
Although 65% of people with cancer want to die at home, only about 30% are successful in doing so.1,2 A government committed to choice for patients must improve this figure.3 Developing palliative care services in primary care is essential for realizing the expectations of dying people. Such services could also offer important opportunities for extending supportive humane care at an earlier stage, and to people not only with cancer but with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, motor neurone disease, and cardiac failure, for example, who also often have palliative care needs. Primary care professionals have the potential and ability to provide end-of-life care for most patients, given adequate training, resources, and, when needed, specialist advice.4,5 They share common values with palliative care specialists—holistic, patient-centered care, delivered in the context of families and friends.6 However, until recently, apart from Macmillan general practitioners and nurse facilitators, few comprehensive workforce initiatives have been undertaken in primary care that focus on end-of-life care.
Many cancer patients and their carers experience existential distress long before they die.7 Recognizing and alleviating such suffering is important, but it often goes unrecognized or is overlooked by services focusing on the terminal phase of illnesses. Primary care teams may know patients over long periods of time. They can readily identify patients from cancer and chronic disease registers who might benefit from an early palliative care approach. Such patients could be identified by clinicians asking one simple question of themselves: “Would I be surprised if my patient were to die in the next 12 months?”8 By identifying such patients proactively, we could deliver, simultaneously, active treatment and patient-centered supportive care, through a team with whom many patients have a valued long-term relationship. Palliative care services need to be extended to patients with non-malignant conditions who have comparable concerns and in some cases even greater unmet needs than cancer patients.9 Progress by palliative medicine specialists is hampered by issues such as uncertainty about the most effective models of care, lack of non-cancer expertise, and concerns about pressure on specialist services. General practitioners and community nurses can lead the way in providing a palliative care approach for patients with terminal organ failure illness. The first step in such an approach is for the goals of care to be discussed and agreed. Management plans are adjusted accordingly. Effective control of symptoms and maintaining quality of life are prioritized.
In light of these important opportunities, it is regrettable that the new general medical services contract has not prioritized palliative care. By day, other developments to achieve the quality indicators are taking precedence. By night and at weekends, the new unscheduled care services (which are responsible for providing care for 75% of the hours in the week) are even less well configured than previous out-of-hours provision to facilitate dying at home. Such services specialize in dealing with acute emergencies and often struggle to meet the medical, nursing, and social care needs of dying people and their families. These changes will greatly affect care for dying people and may increase the number of hospital admissions. However, one important initiative is gaining momentum within primary care. The Gold Standards Framework is a resource for organizing proactive palliative care in the community and is supported by funding from the Cancer Services Collaborative, Macmillan Cancer Relief, and the National Lottery.10 The framework provides a detailed guide to providing holistic, patient-centered care and thereby facilitates effective care in the community. Other recently initiated mechanisms for developing primary palliative care include the training of general practitioners with a special interest in palliative care and the new end-of-life initiative in England to improve palliative care provision by generalists and to share examples of good practice. To support such developments, it is essential that primary palliative care is supported by an adequate academic base. This is admittedly a challenging arena in which to undertake research, but progress has been made in recent years in developing conceptual models and research architectures for studying end-of-life issues. Now we need to build on this work to ensure that the understanding and insights gleaned can be translated into effective interventions. Every person with a progressive illness has a right to palliative care.12 Patients desire a reassuring professional presence in the face of death. General practitioners and community nurses are trusted by patients and are in a position to provide effective, equitable, and accessible palliative care. This will happen only if they have adequate time and resources and work in a system that encourages such care. Patients who receive holistic support in the community may be less likely to require expensive admission to hospital and often futile treatments at the end of their lives.

title: The effects of self-administering emergency contraception.
text:
Background: Emergency postcoital contraception is a means of preventing pregnancy after unprotected sexual intercourse. While it is currently only available with a prescription, there has been a proposal to make it available over-the-counter. To investigate the potential impact of this change, we conducted a study to assess how women would use emergency contraceptive pills if they were made available for self-administration.
Methods: We randomly assigned 553 women to either a treatment group, where they were provided with a supply of hormonal emergency contraceptive pills to keep at home, or a control group, where they had to visit a doctor to obtain emergency contraception. The frequency of use of emergency contraception, as well as the use of other contraceptives and the incidence of unwanted pregnancy, were assessed in both groups of women one year later.
Results: Of the 549 women in the treatment group and 522 women in the control group who provided detailed information at follow-up, 379 (69%) and 326 (62%), respectively, used emergency contraception at least once. Among those who returned the study questionnaire, 98% of the women in the treatment group used emergency contraception correctly. There were no serious adverse effects. Compared to the control group, the treatment group had a lower rate of emergency contraception use (47% vs 27%, P<0.001). However, the women in the treatment group did not use emergency contraception more frequently than the control group. The treatment group's use of other contraceptive methods was similar to that of the control group. There were 18 unintended pregnancies in the treatment group and 25 in the control group (relative risk, 0.7; 95% confidence interval, 0.4 to 1.2).
Conclusions: Making emergency contraception more easily accessible does not appear to have any adverse effects and may reduce the rate of unwanted pregnancies.

title: A coactivator of pre-mRNA splicing.
text: The nuclear matrix antigen recognized by the monoclonal antibody (mAb) B1C8 is a novel protein called SRm160 (SR-related matrix protein of 160 kD). SRm160 is rich in serine (S) and arginine (R) residues and is associated with splicing complexes. Unlike other proteins in the SR family of splicing factors, SRm160 lacks an RNA recognition motif. SRm160 and a related protein called SRm300 (the 300-kD nuclear matrix antigen recognized by mAb B4A11) form a complex that is essential for the splicing of specific pre-mRNAs. The SRm160/300 complex interacts with splicing complexes and enhances splicing through interactions with SR family proteins. The binding of SRm160/300 to pre-mRNA is normally dependent on U1 snRNP and is stabilized by U2 snRNP, indicating that the complex forms multiple interactions with components bound directly to important sites within pre-mRNA. These findings suggest that a complex of nuclear matrix proteins, including SRm160 and SRm300, functions as a coactivator of pre-mRNA splicing.

title: Comparison of pioglitazone vs glimepiride on progression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients with type 2 diabetes: the PERISCOPE randomized controlled trial.
text: In this study, researchers compared the effects of two medications, pioglitazone and glimepiride, on the progression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease. The study found that treatment with pioglitazone resulted in a significantly lower rate of progression of coronary atherosclerosis compared to glimepiride. Specifically, the study found that the mean percent atheroma volume (PAV) increased by 0.73% in the glimepiride group and decreased by 0.16% in the pioglitazone group over an 18-month period. Additionally, the study found that pioglitazone was associated with significant increases in high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels and decreases in triglyceride levels compared to glimepiride. On the other hand, glimepiride was associated with a higher incidence of hypoglycemia. The study included 543 patients at 97 academic and community hospitals in North and South America, and the results suggest that pioglitazone may be a more effective treatment option for slowing the progression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease.

title: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII coordinately represses the synthesis of virulence factors and the transcription regulator Rot by an antisense mechanism.
text: Staphylococcus aureus's intracellular effector RNAIII plays a crucial role in the quorum-sensing system, controlling the expression of numerous virulence genes. We demonstrate that the 3' domain of RNAIII functions as an antisense RNA, binding to specific mRNAs and repressing their translation initiation. This leads to rapid depletion of the mRNA pool and the activation of downstream genes, including the synthesis of exoproteins. Our findings highlight the complex regulatory network established by RNAIII and its 3' domain, which coordinates the expression of virulence factors in S. aureus.

title: Human Cytomegalovirus Latency-Associated Proteins Elicit Immune-Suppressive IL-10 Producing CD4+ T Cells
text:
Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a common virus that infects many people and stays in their bodies for life. In healthy individuals, the immune system can keep the virus under control. One way the virus does this is by establishing a state of "latency," which means the virus is not actively multiplying but is still present in the body.
We studied the immune response to HCMV in healthy individuals and found that there are specialized T cells that can recognize and attack both latently infected cells and cells infected with the virus during an active infection. These T cells are able to kill infected cells and produce a protein called interferon gamma (IFNγ), which helps to fight off the infection.
Interestingly, we found that some of these T cells produce a different protein called interleukin-10 (IL-10), which can suppress the immune response. This means that the virus may be able to evade the immune system by producing proteins that dampen the immune response to latency-associated antigens.
Overall, our findings suggest that HCMV has evolved to skew the immune response to latency-associated antigens in order to maintain a persistent infection in the body. This is a new and important discovery that could lead to a better understanding of how HCMV infects and persists in the body, and could potentially lead to the development of new treatments for HCMV infection.

title: Pamidronate induced anti-proliferative, apoptotic, and anti-migratory effects in hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
BACKGROUND/AIMS:
The Ras and Rho small GTPases are widely implicated in human tumorigenesis and metastasis. Recent studies have shown that pamidronate inhibits the mevalonate pathway, which is essential for the prenylation of these small GTPases. Given the potential of pamidronate to target these key players in tumor progression, we investigated its therapeutic potential in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
METHODS:
To evaluate the anti-proliferative effects of pamidronate on HCC cells, we analyzed cell growth using MTT assays with five hepatoma cell lines. Apoptosis was evaluated using DAPI and histone ELISA assays, and cell migration was assessed using a Modified Boyden Chamber assay. To assess the anti-proliferative effects of pamidronate in vivo, we injected PLC/PRF/5 cells into nude mice and monitored tumor volumes after treatment with pamidronate.
RESULTS:
Our results demonstrate that pamidronate inhibited cell growth in all HCC cell lines tested. Treatment with pamidronate led to a reduction in membrane-associated Ras and phosphorylated extracellular signal-regulated kinase 2 (ERK2). Additionally, pamidronate increased apoptosis and cleavage of Caspase-3 and -9, and suppressed membrane-associated RhoA and cell motility. In vivo, pamidronate significantly suppressed tumor growth at three weeks (P<0.03).
CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings suggest that pamidronate has potential as a therapeutic agent in the treatment of HCC by inducing anti-proliferative, apoptotic, and anti-migratory effects. These results provide a rationale for further investigating the use of pamidronate in the treatment of HCC.

title: Defective regulation of adipose tissue autophagy in obesity
text:
Objectives:
Autophagy is a highly regulated process that plays a crucial role in controlling various cellular functions, including organelle recycling, nutrient availability, and tissue differentiation. Recent studies have shown increased autophagic activity in the adipose tissue of obese individuals, suggesting a potential role for autophagy in obesity-related insulin resistance. However, the impact of weight loss on adipose tissue autophagy is unclear.
Study Design:
The study evaluated adipose tissue autophagy in mice and humans. In the first part of the study, mice were fed a high-fat diet for 15 days, leading to obesity and insulin resistance. The mice were then subjected to 40% caloric restriction for 15 days, and autophagy was evaluated. In the second part of the study, autophagy was evaluated in the subcutaneous adipose tissue of obese and non-diabetic subjects undergoing bariatric surgery for body mass reduction.
Methods:
Adipose tissue autophagy was evaluated using immunoblotting and immunofluorescence analysis. Systemic inflammation markers, including tumor necrosis factor-1α, interleukin (IL)-6, and IL-1β, were also evaluated.
Results:
In the mouse model, autophagy was increased in obese mice compared to lean controls, and caloric restriction increased autophagy in lean mice but decreased it in obese mice. Reintroduction of ad libitum feeding reduced autophagy in lean mice and increased it in obese mice. In human subjects, autophagy was increased in obese individuals compared to non-diabetic controls, and body mass reduction led to a decrease in autophagy.
Conclusion:
Obesity and caloric overfeeding are associated with defective regulation of autophagy in adipose tissue. The study in human subjects suggests that autophagy and inflammation are regulated independently. The findings suggest that weight loss may have a positive impact on adipose tissue autophagy, which could contribute to improved insulin sensitivity and metabolic health.

title: Recovery of visual response of injured adult rat optic nerves treated with transglutaminase.
text: The inability of axons in the central nervous system of adult mammals to spontaneously regenerate after injury is attributed, in part, to the presence of inhibitory molecules associated with oligodendrocytes. In contrast, the regeneration of central nervous system axons in fish is correlated with the presence of a transglutaminase enzyme. This enzyme dimerizes interleukin-2, and the resulting product is cytotoxic to oligodendrocytes in vitro. In a study, application of this nerve-derived transglutaminase to rat optic nerves, where injury had resulted in the loss of visual evoked potential response to light, led to the recovery of that response within 6 weeks after injury. Transmission electron microscopy analysis revealed the simultaneous appearance of axons in the distal stump of the optic nerve.

title: Cell survival during complete nutrient deprivation depends on lipid droplet-fueled β-oxidation of fatty acids.
text: Cells exposed to various forms of stress produce triacylglycerols and lipid droplets (LD), but the functional significance of this response is unclear. To investigate the protective role of lipid droplet biogenesis in cells committed to die, we employed a simple culture model of complete nutrient deprivation. Using human LN18 glioblastoma and HeLa cells, as well as CHO and rat primary astrocytes, we found that nutrient deprivation induced the synthesis of lipid droplets. Notably, death of these cells was accompanied by depletion of lipid droplets and was accelerated when we blocked lipid droplet biogenesis after inhibiting Group IVA phospholipase A2 (cPLA2α) or down-regulating ceramide kinase. Additionally, nutrient deprivation triggered β-oxidation of fatty acids, which was sensitive to cPLA2α inhibition. Remarkably, cell survival in these conditions became entirely dependent on fatty acid catabolism. These findings demonstrate that, during nutrient deprivation, cell viability is sustained by the degradation of fatty acids stored in lipid droplets.

title: Molecular and cytogenetic changes involved in the immortalization of nasopharyngeal epithelial cells by telomerase.
text: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a common cancer in Hong Kong and southern China, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is believed to play a crucial role in its development. Previous studies on the transformation mechanism of EBV genes were mostly conducted in either NPC or non-nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, which may not accurately represent premalignant nasopharyngeal epithelial cells. To address this limitation, we established an immortalized nasopharyngeal epithelial cell line, NP460hTert, using telomerase, which is largely diploid in karyotype. Interestingly, this cell line harbors genetic alterations previously identified in premalignant and malignant nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, including inactivation of p16 by homozygous deletion of the p16(INK4A) locus and downregulation of RASSF1A expression. The deletion of the p16(INK4A) locus appears to be the most crucial event for immortalization of nasopharyngeal epithelial cells by telomerase, and it occurs before RASSF1A downregulation. Additionally, we observed a gain of a 17q21-q25 fragment on chromosome 11p15 in all NP460hTert cells, which is a common genetic alteration in NPC. Furthermore, activation of NF-κB was observed in immortalized NP460hTert cells at later population doublings, and may play a role in the survival of immortalized NP epithelial cells. Finally, we found that the upregulation of Id1, a gene commonly expressed in various human cancers, including NPC, in the immortalized NP460hTert cells. Our findings suggest that the establishment of an immortalized nasopharyngeal epithelial cell line harboring common genetic alterations present in premalignant and cancerous nasopharyngeal epithelial cells may provide a valuable tool to investigate early events involved in NPC carcinogenesis, particularly the role of EBV infection in NPC development.

title: Cellular nucleic acid binding protein suppresses tumor cell metastasis and induces tumor cell death by downregulating heterogeneous ribonucleoprotein K in fibrosarcoma cells.
text:
Background: Cellular nucleic acid binding protein (CNBP) has been implicated in various diseases, including craniofacial development and myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) and sporadic inclusion body myositis (sIBM). CNBP regulates cell proliferation and survival by controlling nucleic acid secondary structure rearrangements, acting as a nucleic acid chaperone.
Methods: A range of techniques were employed, including cell viability assays, wound-scratch assays, chemotaxis assays, invasion assays, circular dichroic (CD) spectroscopy, NMR spectroscopy, chromatin immunoprecipitation, expression and purification of recombinant human CNBP, electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), surface plasmon resonance (SPR), fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) analyses, luciferase reporter assay, Western blotting, and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).
Results: Overexpression of CNBP led to increased cell death and suppression of cell motility and invasiveness in human fibrosarcoma cells. It was found that CNBP transcriptionally downregulated the expression of heterogeneous ribonucleoprotein K (hnRNP K) by forming a G-quadruplex in the hnRNP K promoter. The G-quadruplex stabilizing ligand tetra-(N-methyl-4-pyridyl) porphyrin (TMPyP4) could interact with and stabilize the G-quadruplex, leading to downregulation of hnRNP K transcription.
Conclusions: The present study demonstrated that CNBP overexpression increased cell death and suppressed cell metastasis by inducing G-quadruplex formation in the hnRNP K promoter, leading to downregulation of hnRNP K expression. This finding provides a new approach for controlling hnRNP K expression, which may shed light on the development of new anticancer drugs.

title: The DHR96 nuclear receptor regulates xenobiotic responses in Drosophila.
text: Exposure to foreign substances, such as plant toxins, pollutants, or prescription drugs, triggers a defense mechanism in organisms, leading to the activation of genes that encode crucial enzymes for detoxification. Although the study of xenobiotic responses has been extensive in vertebrates, little attention has been paid to exploring a simple genetic system for understanding the molecular basis of this coordinated transcriptional response. We investigated the effect of phenobarbital treatment on gene expression in Drosophila and found that approximately 1000 transcripts were significantly altered. Additionally, we identified the Drosophila ortholog of the human SXR and CAR xenobiotic receptors, DHR96, which plays a crucial role in this response. A DHR96 null mutant displayed increased sensitivity to the sedative effects of phenobarbital and the pesticide DDT, as well as defects in the expression of many phenobarbital-regulated genes. Furthermore, DHR96 was found to control metabolic and stress-response genes, highlighting its role in coordinating multiple response pathways. This work establishes a novel model system for elucidating the genetic regulation of xenobiotic stress responses.

title: A primate virus generates transformed human cells by fusion
text: A model proposing the origin and sporadic nature of cancer suggests that cancer cells are a chance result of random events leading to genetic and epigenetic variations. The prevailing view holds that these events are caused by mutations affecting chromosome segregation or stability. However, genomic and epigenetic variations can also be triggered by cell fusion, which is often induced by viruses. Contrary to popular belief, fused cells are not always harmless, as they can produce transformed, proliferating human cells. We provide evidence that a primate virus uses both viral and exosomal proteins involved in cell fusion to produce oncogenically transformed human cells. Our findings challenge the notion that cells fused by viruses are always destined to die, as expression of an oncogene or a mutated tumor suppressor p53 in just one of the fusion partners is sufficient to produce heterogeneous progeny. Additionally, we demonstrate that this virus can produce viable oncogenically transformed cells by fusing cells that are otherwise destined to die, thereby highlighting the role of viruses in carcinogenesis through cell fusion.

title: TAA1-Mediated Auxin Biosynthesis Is Essential for Hormone Crosstalk and Plant Development
text: Plants have evolved remarkable capabilities to adapt to changing environmental conditions by modulating their growth and development through complex hormonal and developmental signaling pathways. One such mechanism is the interaction between hormonal and developmental signals, which plays a critical role in generating the remarkable plasticity of plant growth and development. A case in point is the response of plants to the hormone ethylene, which depends on the type of tissue, developmental stage, and environmental conditions. By investigating the Arabidopsis wei8 mutant, we have discovered that a small family of genes mediates tissue-specific responses to ethylene. Biochemical analyses revealed that WEI8 encodes a long-sought tryptophan aminotransferase, TAA1, which is involved in the essential yet genetically uncharacterized indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPA) branch of the auxin biosynthetic pathway. Our findings establish a link between local auxin production, tissue-specific ethylene effects, and organ development, highlighting the key role of the IPA route in generating robust auxin gradients in response to environmental and developmental cues.

title: A research agenda for public health workforce development.
text: In recent decades, public health research has primarily focused on categorical rather than cross-cutting or systems issues. There has been a lack of research conducted on the infrastructure required to support public health programs. This article presents the findings of an interactive process to develop a research agenda for public health workforce development, aimed at informing all stakeholders in the public health system. This research is defined as a multidisciplinary field of inquiry that examines the public health workforce through various lenses, including costs, quality, accessibility, delivery, organization, financing, and outcomes of public health services. The research agenda was developed through meetings of expert panels between 2000 and 2003, resulting in a logic model and five priority research areas. To advance cross-cutting and systems-focused research, innovative partnerships between public and private sectors will be necessary.

title: Parallel processing in the mammalian retina
text: Our eyes process visual information in a parallel manner, transmitting different "images" of the outside world to the brain. These images can be line drawings (contours), watercolor paintings (color images), or even moving videos (motion images). This parallel processing begins as early as the first synapse of the retina, specifically at the cone pedicle. The molecular composition of the transmitter receptors on the postsynaptic neurons determines which images are transmitted to the inner retina. Within the second synaptic layer, the inner plexiform layer, complex inhibitory and excitatory interactions create filters that select which "images" are sent to the brain.

title: Oxymetholone Therapy of Fanconi Anemia Suppresses Osteopontin Transcription and Induces Hematopoietic Stem Cell Cycling
text: Androgens are commonly used to treat Fanconi anemia (FA) and other bone marrow failure syndromes, but the exact mechanism of their action is not fully understood. To investigate the therapeutic efficacy and mechanism of action of oxymetholone (OXM), aged Fancd2(-/-) mice were used. These mice recapitulate key human FA phenotypes, including reduced bone marrow cellularity, red blood cell macrocytosis, and peripheral pancytopenia, similar to those observed in humans. Interestingly, chronic OXM treatment significantly improved these hematological parameters and stimulated the proliferation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. RNA-Seq analysis revealed that downregulation of osteopontin may play a crucial role in the drug's action. Consistently, competitive repopulation assays showed that chronic OXM therapy eventually resulted in stem cell exhaustion. These findings expand our understanding of the regulation of hematopoietic stem cell proliferation and have direct clinical implications for the treatment of bone marrow failure.

title: A point mutation in KINDLIN3 ablates activation of three integrin subfamilies in humans
text:
Monogenic deficiency diseases offer a unique opportunity to investigate the role of individual molecules in human physiology and to identify the causes of disease arising from their dysfunction. In this study, we describe a rare genetic disorder affecting two human siblings who exhibited severe bleeding, frequent infections, and osteopetrosis at a young age. These symptoms are similar to, but more severe than those seen in individuals with leukocyte adhesion deficiency III (LAD-III). We found that the siblings had an inability to activate integrins on hematopoietic cells, including platelets and leukocytes, leading to the development of these symptoms.
To investigate the genetic basis of this disease, we analyzed immortalized lymphocyte cell lines isolated from the two individuals and found that several proteins involved in integrin activation, including Ras-associated protein-1 (RAP1) and calcium and diacylglycerol-regulated guanine nucleotide exchange factor-1 (CALDAG-GEF1), were present and functional. Further analysis revealed a point mutation in the coding region of the KINDLIN3 (official gene symbol FERMT3) gene, which was responsible for the disease. When wild-type KINDLIN-3 was expressed in the immortalized lymphocytes, their integrins became responsive to activation signals, demonstrating the essential role of KINDLIN-3 in integrin activation in humans. Finally, we found that allogeneic bone marrow transplantation could alleviate the symptoms of the disease, highlighting the potential for this approach in treating similar disorders.
In summary, this study provides insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying a rare genetic disorder and identifies a crucial role for KINDLIN-3 in integrin activation in humans. The findings also suggest that allogeneic bone marrow transplantation may be a viable therapeutic option for treating similar diseases.

title: Fasting Activation of AgRP Neurons Requires NMDA Receptors and Involves Spinogenesis and Increased Excitatory Tone
text: AgRP neuron activity is responsible for promoting feeding and weight gain, whereas the activity of nearby POMC neurons has the opposite effect. However, the role of excitatory glutamatergic input in regulating these neurons remains unclear. To address this question, we generated mice lacking NMDA receptors (NMDARs) on either AgRP or POMC neurons. Our findings revealed that deletion of NMDARs from AgRP neurons significantly reduced weight, body fat, and food intake, whereas deletion from POMC neurons had no effect. We also found that activation of AgRP neurons by fasting, as assessed by c-Fos, Agrp, and Npy mRNA expression, AMPA receptor-mediated EPSCs, depolarization, and firing rates, requires NMDARs. Additionally, AgRP neurons, but not POMC neurons, have dendritic spines, and increased glutamatergic input onto AgRP neurons induced by fasting is paralleled by an increase in spines. These findings suggest that glutamatergic synaptic transmission and its modulation by NMDARs play a crucial role in controlling AgRP neurons and determining the cellular and behavioral response to fasting.

title: Prevalence and Causes of Blindness and Low Vision in Southern Sudan
text: In southern Sudan, it is believed that background blindness and low vision are prevalent. However, the scope and geographical distribution of these conditions are largely unquantified. Our study aimed to determine the incidence of blindness and low vision, identify the primary causes of blindness and low vision, and estimate targets for blindness prevention programs in Mankien payam (district), southern Sudan.

title: Origin of nitrite and nitrate in nasal and exhaled breath condensate and relation to nitric oxide formation.
text:
Background: Elevated levels of nitrate and nitrite have been detected in exhaled breath condensate (EBC) in individuals with airway diseases, suggesting increased nitric oxide (NO) metabolism. However, the origin of these compounds in the airways has not been adequately studied.
Methods: We measured the fraction of exhaled NO (FE(NO)) and nitrite and nitrate in EBC, nasal condensate, and saliva from 17 tracheostomized and 15 non-tracheostomized subjects, all of whom were non-smokers without respiratory disease. Tracheal and oral samples were collected from the tracheostomized subjects, and nasal (during velum closure) and oral samples were collected from the non-tracheostomized subjects. Measurements were performed before and after sodium nitrate ingestion (10 mg/kg) and use of antibacterial mouthwash (chlorhexidine 0.2%).
Results: In tracheostomized subjects, oral FE(NO) increased by 90% after nitrate ingestion (p<0.01), while tracheal FE(NO) remained unchanged. Oral EBC nitrite levels were increased 23-fold at 60 minutes after nitrate ingestion (p<0.001), while the nitrite levels in tracheal EBC showed only a minor increase (fourfold, p<0.05). Nitrate was increased the same amount in oral and tracheal EBC at 60 minutes (2.5-fold, p<0.05). In non-tracheostomized subjects, oral FE(NO) and EBC nitrite increased after nitrate ingestion and after chlorhexidine mouthwash, and approached baseline levels again after 60 minutes (p<0.001). Nasal NO, nitrate, and nitrite were not affected by nitrate intake or mouthwash. At baseline, mouthwash with deionized water did not affect nitrite in oral EBC or saliva, but significant reductions were seen after antibacterial mouthwash (p<0.05 and p<0.001, respectively).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that besides the salivary glands, plasma nitrate is taken up by the lower airways but not the nasal airways. Nitrate levels in EBC are therefore influenced by dietary intake. Nitrate is reduced to nitrite by bacterial activity primarily in the oropharyngeal tract of healthy subjects. Only oropharyngeal nitrite seems to contribute to exhaled NO in non-inflamed airways, and there is also a substantial contribution of nitrite from the oropharyngeal tract during standard collection of EBC.

title: AZD9150, a next-generation antisense oligonucleotide inhibitor of STAT3 with early evidence of clinical activity in lymphoma and lung cancer
text:
Next-generation sequencing technologies have significantly advanced our understanding of cancer genetics, providing a wealth of information on the genetic mutations driving cancer growth and progression. Antisense technology, in particular, holds great promise as a platform for translating these advances into improved cancer therapeutics. By designing antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) inhibitors based solely on gene sequence information, we can target specific genes involved in cancer development and progression.
Recent clinical data have demonstrated the potent activity of systemically administered ASOs targeting genes expressed in the liver, highlighting the potential of this approach for treating a wide range of cancers. In this study, we investigate the preclinical activity and initial clinical evaluation of a class of ASOs containing constrained ethyl modifications for targeting the gene encoding the transcription factor STAT3, a notoriously difficult protein to inhibit therapeutically.
Using systemic delivery of the unformulated ASO, AZD9150, we observed decreased STAT3 expression in a broad range of preclinical cancer models, and showed antitumor activity in lymphoma and lung cancer models. Encouragingly, this preclinical activity translated into single-agent antitumor activity in patients with highly treatment-refractory lymphoma and non–small cell lung cancer in a phase 1 dose-escalation study.
Overall, these findings highlight the potential of antisense technology to revolutionize cancer treatment by targeting specific genes involved in cancer development and progression. By harnessing the power of next-generation sequencing technologies to identify key cancer genes, we can develop highly targeted and effective therapies that offer new hope for cancer patients.

title: Evidence of a pluripotent human embryonic stem cell line derived from a cloned blastocyst.
text: Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) technology has recently been used to create animals with a shared genetic makeup. In this study, we report the generation of a pluripotent embryonic stem (ES) cell line, called SCNT-hES-1, from a cloned human blastocyst. The SCNT-hES-1 cells exhibited typical ES cell morphology and surface markers and were able to differentiate into embryoid bodies in vitro and form teratomas in vivo containing cell derivatives from all three embryonic germ layers in severe combined immunodeficient mice. After continuous proliferation for over 70 passages, the SCNT-hES-1 cells maintained normal karyotypes and were genetically identical to the somatic nuclear donor cells. While it is possible that the cells may have originated through a parthenogenetic process, imprinting analyses suggest that the derived human ES cells are the result of SCNT.

title: Ultrarapid drug metabolism: PCR-based detection of CYP2D6 gene duplication.
text: The enzyme debrisoquine 4-hydroxylase (CYP2D6), which metabolizes a wide range of drugs, exhibits significant genetic variability among individuals. The activity of this enzyme can vary greatly between subjects, ranging from ultrafast to complete inactivity. As a result, the metabolic capacity of individuals can differ significantly, leading to intersubject differences in therapeutic efficacy and side effects even at standard recommended doses. Approximately 7% of Caucasians may possess a genetic mutation that results in ultrarapid drug metabolism (UM), leading to an increased expression of the CYP2D6 enzyme. Identifying UM subjects is clinically important for adjusting drug dosages and avoiding misdiagnosis of noncompliance. In our study, we employed newly developed PCR assays to detect the UM genotype in a population of 202 psychiatric patients. We found that approximately 3.5% of the population carried duplicate active CYP2D6 genes, indicating ultrarapid drug metabolism.

title: The Actions of Synaptically Released Zinc at Hippocampal Mossy Fiber Synapses
text: Zn2+ is abundantly present in high concentrations within synaptic vesicles of hippocampal mossy fibers. To investigate the physiological role of Zn2+ in this pathway, we employed the use of Zn2+ chelators and the mocha mutant mouse. Our findings indicate that Zn2+ is not directly involved in the unique presynaptic plasticities observed at mossy fiber synapses. However, Zn2+ is co-released with glutamate from these synapses, both spontaneously and in response to electrical stimulation, where it exerts a significant modulatory effect on NMDA receptors. Zn2+ occupies the high-affinity binding site of NMDA receptors at mossy fiber synapses in a tonic manner, while the lower affinity voltage-dependent Zn2+ binding site is occupied during action potential-driven release. Our results suggest that Zn2+ acts as a modulatory neurotransmitter released from mossy fiber synapses, playing a crucial role in shaping the NMDA receptor response at these synapses.

title: Association between folate intake from different food sources in Norway and homocysteine status in a dietary intervention among young male adults.
text: The present study aimed to investigate the impact of a dietary intervention that combined nutrition education with increased access to vegetables, fruits, and whole-grain bread on the participants' nutrient intake and plasma total homocysteine (p-tHcy) levels. The study included 376 male recruits from the Norwegian National Guard, with 176 participants in the intervention group and 105 participants in the control group. The 5-month intervention resulted in significant increases in the total consumption of vegetables, fruits, berries, and juice (P < 0.001) and whole-grain bread (P < 0.001). The intervention group showed a higher increase in dietary fiber and folate intake compared to the control group (P < 0.001 for both). The relative contribution of folate intake from fruits, vegetables, and whole-grain bread was higher in the intervention group compared to the control group (P < 0.001 for all). Furthermore, the study found that the increased intake of folate from whole-grain bread was inversely associated with a reduced concentration of p-tHcy (P = 0.017). In summary, the dietary intervention led to increased intakes of vegetables, fruits, and whole-grain bread, resulting in higher folate intake from these food components. The reduction in p-tHcy concentration was significantly related to the increased folate intake from whole-grain bread.

title: Beta interferon controls West Nile virus infection and pathogenesis in mice.
text: Research with mice lacking the plasma membrane receptor for type I interferon (IFN-αβR) has shown that IFN signaling restricts the tropism, dissemination, and lethality of viral infections, including West Nile virus (WNV) and other pathogenic viruses. However, the specific functions of individual IFN subtypes remain unclear. In this study, we used IFN-β-deficient mice to investigate the antiviral and immunomodulatory functions of this IFN subtype in restricting WNV infection. IFN-β-deficient mice were more susceptible to WNV infection, with greater overall mortality and enhanced viral replication in various tissues compared to wild-type mice. Although the quality and quantity of WNV-specific antibodies and CD8+ T cells were similar in both groups, we observed an altered CD4+ CD25+ FoxP3+ regulatory T cell response in IFN-β-deficient mice, with increased numbers of regulatory T cells after infection. These results suggest that IFN-β controls WNV pathogenesis by restricting infection in key cell types and modulating T cell regulatory networks.

title: Frontrunners of T cell activation: Initial, localized Ca2+ signals mediated by NAADP and the type 1 ryanodine receptor
text: The activation of T cells is the pivotal trigger for the adaptive immune system. Calcium (Ca2+) signaling is crucial for T cell activation, and it begins with brief, localized Ca2+ signals that occur initially. The second messenger nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) rapidly forms upon T cell activation and stimulates early Ca2+ signaling. To investigate the channels involved in NAADP-dependent Ca2+ signals, we developed a high-resolution imaging technique using multiple fluorescent Ca2+ indicator dyes to characterize these early signaling events in both primary murine T cells and human Jurkat cells. In the initial seconds of activation, we detected Ca2+ signals with diameters close to the detection limit and located near the activation site at the plasma membrane. In Jurkat cells where the ryanodine receptor (RyR) was knocked down or in primary T cells from RyR1−/− mice, either these early Ca2+ signals were not detected or their number was significantly reduced. Local Ca2+ signals observed within 20 ms upon microinjection of Jurkat cells with NAADP were also sensitive to RyR knockdown. In contrast, TRPM2 (transient receptor potential channel, subtype melastatin 2), a potential NAADP target channel, was not essential for the formation of initial Ca2+ signals in primary T cells. Through our high-resolution imaging method, we characterized early Ca2+ release events in T cells and obtained evidence for the involvement of RyR and NAADP in such signals.

title: A missense LAMB2 mutation causes congenital nephrotic syndrome by impairing laminin secretion.
text: Laminin β2 is a crucial component of laminin-521, a vital component of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). Mutations in LAMB2, the gene encoding laminin β2, can lead to Pierson syndrome, a severe congenital nephrotic syndrome accompanied by ocular and neurological defects. In contrast, individuals with missense mutations in LAMB2, such as R246Q, may exhibit less severe extrarenal abnormalities but still experience congenital nephrotic syndrome. To investigate how these missense mutations cause proteinuria, we generated three transgenic mouse lines in which R246Q-mutant rat laminin β2 replaced the wild-type mouse laminin β2 in the GBM. These transgenic mice displayed significantly less severe proteinuria compared to their non-transgenic Lamb2-deficient littermates, and the level of proteinuria correlated inversely with R246Q-LAMB2 expression. At the onset of proteinuria, the expression and localization of proteins associated with the slit diaphragm and foot processes were normal, and there were no obvious ultrastructural abnormalities. Low transgene expressors developed heavy proteinuria, foot process effacement, GBM thickening, and renal failure by 3 months, while high expressors developed only mild proteinuria by 9 months. In vitro studies revealed that the R246Q mutation impairs the secretion of laminin-521 from podocytes into the GBM. These findings suggest that the R246Q mutation causes nephrotic syndrome by disrupting the secretion of laminin-521 from podocytes into the GBM, but increased expression of the mutant protein can partially overcome this secretion defect and improve glomerular permselectivity.

title: Interleukin-33 prevents apoptosis and improves survival after experimental myocardial infarction through ST2 signaling.
text:
Background:
ST2 (IL-1 receptor family member) has both membrane-bound (ST2L) and soluble (sST2) isoforms, with sST2 serving as a biomarker for poor outcome in patients with myocardial infarction (MI). Recently, IL-33, a ligand for ST2, was discovered, and it was found to activate nuclear factor kappaB, potentially regulating apoptotic cell death. The present study aimed to investigate the cardioprotective role of IL-33 in MI through ST2 signaling.
Methods and Results:
IL-33 protected cultured cardiomyocytes from hypoxia-induced apoptosis, and this cardioprotection was partially inhibited by sST2. IL-33 induced the expression of antiapoptotic factors XIAP, cIAP1, and survivin. To evaluate the cardioprotective role of IL-33 in vivo, a blinded and randomized study of ischemia/reperfusion in rats was performed. IL-33 reduced cardiomyocyte apoptosis, suppressed caspase-3 activity, and increased expression of IAP family member proteins. IL-33 decreased both infarct and fibrosis volumes at 15 days, and both echocardiographic and hemodynamic studies revealed that IL-33 improved ventricular function. To determine whether cardioprotection by IL-33 is mediated through ST2 signaling, a randomized and blinded study of ST2(-/-) versus wild-type mice was performed in 98 mice subjected to MI. At 4 weeks after MI, IL-33 reduced ventricular dilation and improved contractile function in wild-type mice but not in ST2(-/-) mice. Finally, IL-33 improved survival after MI in wild-type but not in ST2(-/-) mice.
Conclusions:
IL-33 prevents cardiomyocyte apoptosis and improves cardiac function and survival after MI through ST2 signaling. These findings suggest that IL-33 may be a potential therapeutic target for the prevention and treatment of MI.

title: The impact of open versus closed format ICU admission practices on the outcome of high risk surgical patients: a cohort analysis
text:
In 2000, the organizational structure of the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) at the Zaandam Medical Centre (ZMC) transitioned from an open to a closed format. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of this change on the outcome of high-risk surgical patients.
Medical records of all consecutive high-risk surgical patients admitted to the ICU from 1996 to 1998 (open format) and from 2003 to 2005 (closed format) were reviewed. High-risk patients were defined based on the Identification of Risk in Surgical patients (IRIS) score. The study parameters included mortality, morbidity, ICU length of stay (LOS), and hospital LOS.
The mortality rate in the ICU patients was 25.7% in the open format group and 15.8% in the closed format group (p = 0.01). Morbidity decreased from 48.6% to 46.1% (p = 0.6). The average length of hospital stay was 17 days in the open format group and 21 days in the closed format group (p = 0.03).
Our findings suggest that high-risk surgical patients in the ICU benefit from a closed format setting, which can minimize the effects of high-risk surgery and ensure optimal care.

title: Induction therapy with autologous mesenchymal stem cells in living-related kidney transplants: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Context: Antibody-based induction therapy plus calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) have been shown to reduce acute rejection rates in kidney transplant recipients, but opportunistic infections and toxic CNI effects remain a challenge. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been successfully used to treat graft-versus-host disease, and this study aimed to assess the use of autologous MSCs as an alternative to antibody induction therapy in end-stage renal disease patients undergoing ABO-compatible, cross-match-negative kidney transplants from living-related donors.
Objective: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of autologous MSCs as an alternative to anti-IL-2 receptor antibody induction therapy in end-stage renal disease patients undergoing kidney transplantation.
Design, Setting, and Participants: This single-site, prospective, open-label, randomized study enrolled 159 patients from February 2008 to May 2009.
Intervention: Patients were randomly assigned to receive either autologous MSCs (1-2 x 106/kg) at kidney reperfusion and two weeks later, or standard-dose (80% of standard) or low-dose CNIs.
Main Outcome Measures: The primary outcome measure was the incidence of acute rejection and renal function (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR]) at 1 year. Secondary outcomes included patient and graft survival and incidence of adverse events.
Results: At 13 to 30 months post-transplant, patient and graft survival was similar among all groups. After 6 months, 4 of 53 patients (7.5%) in the autologous MSC plus standard-dose CNI group and 4 of 52 patients (7.7%) in the low-dose group had biopsy-confirmed acute rejection, compared to 11 of 51 controls (21.6%). None of the patients in either MSC group had glucorticoid-resistant rejection, while 4 patients in the control group did. Renal function recovered faster among both MSC groups, showing increased eGFR levels during the first month after surgery compared to the control group. Patients receiving standard-dose CNI had a mean difference of 6.2 mL/min per 1.73 m(2) in eGFR levels, and those in the low-dose CNI group had a mean difference of 10.0 mL/min per 1.73 m(2) in eGFR levels, compared to the control group. Additionally, the combined analysis of MSC-treated groups revealed a significantly decreased risk of opportunistic infections compared to the control group (hazard ratio, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.20-0.85; P = 0.02).
Conclusion: The use of autologous MSCs compared to anti-IL-2 receptor antibody induction therapy resulted in lower incidence of acute rejection, decreased risk of opportunistic infections, and better estimated renal function at 1 year.
Trial Registration: clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00658073.

title: Cerebral cortex assembly: generating and reprogramming projection neuron diversity
text: The mammalian cerebral cortex is the seat of the most advanced associative, cognitive, and motor functions within the central nervous system (CNS). The cortex boasts an impressive array of neuronal diversity, with excitatory projection neurons (PNs) and inhibitory interneurons (INs) serving as the primary cellular components. In this review, we will delve into recent advances in our understanding of the mechanisms that govern PN diversification during embryonic development, and explore the postnatal maintenance of these cell classes. Furthermore, we will ponder the intriguing possibility that PNs may be subject to reprogramming to enhance cortical plasticity in the adult.

title: Mechanical modulation of receptor-ligand interactions at cell-cell interfaces.
text:
Cell surface receptors have been extensively studied due to their role in initiating and regulating signal transduction cascades, leading to various cellular outcomes. However, a particular class of immune receptors, such as T-cell antigen receptors, whose ligands are anchored to the surfaces of other cells, remain poorly understood. The mechanism by which ligand binding initiates receptor phosphorylation, termed "receptor triggering," is controversial. Recent measurements of the (two-dimensional) receptor-ligand complex lifetimes at the cell-cell interface revealed that these lifetimes are smaller than (three-dimensional) lifetimes in solution, but the underlying mechanism is unknown. At the cell-cell interface, the receptor-ligand complex spans a short intermembrane distance (15 nm) compared to long surface molecules (LSMs) whose ectodomains span >40 nm, and these LSMs include phosphatases (e.g., CD45) that dephosphorylate the receptor. It has been proposed that size-based segregation of LSMs from a receptor-ligand complex is a mechanism of receptor triggering, but it is unclear whether the mechanochemistry supports such small-scale segregation.
To investigate this mechanism, we developed a nanometer-scale mathematical model that couples membrane elasticity with the compressional stiffness and lateral mobility of LSMs. Our findings reveal robust supradiffusive segregation of LSMs from a single receptor-ligand complex. The model predicts that LSM redistribution will result in a time-dependent tension on the complex, leading to a decreased two-dimensional lifetime. Interestingly, the model predicts a nonlinear relationship between the three- and two-dimensional lifetimes, which can enhance the ability of receptors to discriminate between similar ligands.
In summary, our study provides a novel mechanism for receptor triggering, where the redistribution of LSMs from a receptor-ligand complex leads to a decrease in the two-dimensional lifetime, allowing receptors to differentiate between similar ligands. This finding has important implications for our understanding of cellular signaling and the development of new therapeutic strategies for diseases that involve dysregulation of cell surface receptors.

title: High-performance neuroprosthetic control by an individual with tetraplegia.
text:
Background:
Loss of hand function due to paralysis or amputation can significantly impact an individual's ability to perform daily activities. Brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) have shown promise in restoring lost functions, particularly in individuals with tetraplegia. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of BMI training in restoring neurological control of a high-performance prosthetic limb in a tetraplegic individual.
Methods:
We implanted two 96-channel intracortical microelectrodes in the motor cortex of a 52-year-old individual with tetraplegia and conducted BMI training for 13 weeks. The goal was to enable the participant to control an anthropomorphic prosthetic limb with seven degrees of freedom (three-dimensional translation, three-dimensional orientation, one-dimensional grasping) using their neural signals. Clinical measures of upper limb function were used to assess the participant's ability to control the prosthetic limb.
Findings:
The participant was able to move the prosthetic limb freely in the three-dimensional workspace on the second day of training and demonstrated robust seven-dimensional movements after 13 weeks of training. The participant's success rate in target-based reaching tasks improved significantly, from 6.2% (chance level) to 91.6% (mean, SD 4.4). Improvements were also seen in completion time (decreased from 148 s to 112 s) and path efficiency (increased from 0.30 to 0.38). The participant was able to use the prosthetic limb to perform skilful and coordinated reach and grasp movements, resulting in clinically significant gains in tests of upper limb function. No adverse events were reported.
Interpretation:
The findings of this study suggest that BMI training can enable individuals with tetraplegia to recover the natural and intuitive command signals for hand placement, orientation, and reaching, allowing them to perform daily activities with greater ease and independence. With continued development of neuroprosthetic limbs, the potential for individuals with long-term paralysis to recover lost functions is promising.
Funding:
This study was funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, National Institutes of Health, Department of Veterans Affairs, and UPMC Rehabilitation Institute.

title: Phase locking and multiple oscillating attractors for the coupled mammalian clock and cell cycle.
text: Daily synchronous patterns of cell division at the tissue or organism level are observed in many species, suggesting that the circadian clock and cell cycle oscillators are coupled. However, the mechanistic interactions between these two systems in mammals are not well understood, particularly in terms of how the temporal organization of cell division at the single-cell level gives rise to the daily rhythm at the tissue level.
