To address this question, we used multispectral imaging of single live cells, computational methods, and mathematical modeling to investigate the coupling between the circadian clock and cell cycle progression in proliferating mouse fibroblasts. Our findings show that in unsynchronized cells, the cell cycle and circadian clock robustly phase lock each other in a 1:1 fashion, resulting in synchronized oscillations with a common frequency in an expanding cell population. Additionally, we discovered that dexamethasone-induced synchronization reveals additional clock states, including a low-period phase-locked state and higher-period coexisting states. These states are characterized by transitions between them after dexamethasone synchronization. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the temporal coordination of cell division and its link to circadian function and disease pathogenesis, including cancer.

title: Moderate effect of artemisinin-based combination therapy on transmission of Plasmodium falciparum.
text:
Background: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) has been shown to reduce microscopically confirmed gametocytemia and mosquito infection. However, recent studies have revealed that a significant proportion of gametocytes may remain undetected by microscopy, leading to an underestimation of the actual reduction in transmission. Our study aimed to investigate the effect of different ACT regimens on submicroscopic gametocytemia and infectiousness in children.
Methods: We enrolled 528 children aged 6-10 years in Kenya and randomly assigned them to four treatment arms: sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) monotherapy, SP plus amodiaquine (AQ), SP plus artesunate (AS), and artemether-lumefantrine (AL; Coartem). Gametocytemia was determined by both microscopy and Pfs25 RNA-based quantitative nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (Pfs25 QT-NASBA). Transmission was determined by membrane-feeding assays.
Results: Our findings showed that gametocyte prevalence, as determined by Pfs25 QT-NASBA, was 89.4% (219/245) at enrollment and decreased after treatment with SP plus AS, SP plus AQ, and AL. However, membrane-feeding assays revealed that the proportion of infectious children was significantly higher than expected based on microscopy, with a fourfold increase in the proportion of infectious children. ACT did not significantly reduce the proportion of infectious children, but it did reduce the proportion of infected mosquitoes.
Conclusions: Our study highlights the importance of considering submicroscopic gametocytemia in the assessment of ACT's effect on malaria transmission. While ACT significantly reduces the proportion of infected mosquitoes, its effect on reducing the overall transmission of malaria appears to be moderate and limited to the duration of gametocyte carriage and the proportion of mosquitoes that are infected by carriers. These findings underscore the need for continued monitoring of transmission intensity and the development of new strategies to eliminate submicroscopic gametocytemia.

title: Lip movements entrain the observers’ low-frequency brain oscillations to facilitate speech intelligibility
text: During fluent speech, lip movements convey visual temporal cues that facilitate speech perception. Using MEG, we directly investigated how these visual cues interact with rhythmic brain activity in participants listening to and observing the speaker. Initially, we examined the coherence between oscillatory brain activity and the speaker's lip movements and found significant entrainment in the visual cortex. Subsequently, we employed partial coherence to remove the auditory speech signal's contribution to the lip-brain coherence. Comparing the synchronization between different attention conditions revealed that attentive visual speech processing enhances the coherence between activity in the visual cortex and the speaker's lips. Furthermore, we discovered a significant partial coherence between the left motor cortex and lip movements, which directly predicted comprehension accuracy. Our findings underscore the significance of visually entrained and attention-modulated rhythmic brain activity in enhancing audiovisual speech processing.

title: Loss of DExD/H box RNA helicase LGP2 manifests disparate antiviral responses.
text: The DExD/H box RNA helicase retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and the melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) are key intracellular receptors that recognize viral infection to produce type I interferons (IFNs). A third helicase gene, Lgp2, is homologous to RIG-I and MDA5 but lacks a caspase activation and recruitment domain. We generated Lgp2-deficient mice and found that the loss of this gene significantly enhances cells' sensitivity to cytosolic polyinosinic/polycytidylic acid (polyI:C)-induced production of type I IFNs. However, we did not observe any defect in negative regulation of IFN-β transcription in the absence of LGP2. Our data also show that Lgp2-deficient mice are resistant to lethal vesicular stomatitis virus infection, which is recognized by RIG-I rather than MDA5. However, these mice exhibit a defect in type I IFN production in response to encephalomyocarditis virus infection, which activates MDA5-dependent innate immune responses. Overall, our findings suggest a distinct regulatory role for LGP2 in triggering innate immune signaling pathways following RNA virus infection.

title: Three-dimensional, single-molecule fluorescence imaging beyond the diffraction limit by using a double-helix point spread function.
text: We have demonstrated the ability to image single molecules beyond the optical diffraction limit in 3 dimensions using a wide-field microscope with a unique double-helix point spread function (DH-PSF). The DH-PSF design features high and uniform Fisher information and consists of two dominant lobes in the image plane that rotate with the axial position of the emitter. By localizing single fluorescent molecules in a thick polymer sample to within 10-20 nanometers in a single 500-millisecond acquisition, we were able to achieve resolution beyond the Rayleigh diffraction limit. Using a photoactivatable fluorophore, we were able to repeatedly image sparse subsets of molecules with high concentrations in all three dimensions, providing superresolution imaging capabilities. The combination of optical PSF design and digital postprocessing with photoactivatable fluorophores opens up new avenues for improving 3D imaging resolution beyond the diffraction limit.

title: A unique cell division machinery in the Archaea.
text: Unlike the cell division machineries of bacteria, euryarchaea, and eukaryotes, no division components have been identified in the second main archaeal phylum, Crenarchaeota. However, we have discovered a three-gene operon, cdv, in the crenarchaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius, which forms part of a unique cell division machinery. The operon is activated at the onset of genome segregation and division, and the Cdv proteins polymerize between segregating nucleoids, persisting throughout cell division and forming a smaller structure during constriction. Interestingly, the cdv operon is down-regulated after UV irradiation, suggesting inhibition of division in response to DNA damage, similar to eukaryotic checkpoint systems. The cdv genes exhibit a distinct phylogenetic range compared to FtsZ-based archaeal division systems, with either one or the other system present in most archaeal lineages. Two of the Cdv proteins, CdvB and CdvC, show homology to components of the eukaryotic ESCRT-III sorting complex involved in budding of luminal vesicles and HIV-1 virion release, suggesting mechanistic similarities and a common evolutionary origin.

title: Modelling and rescuing neurodevelopmental defect of Down syndrome using induced pluripotent stem cells from monozygotic twins discordant for trisomy 21
text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), the most common viable chromosomal disorder associated with intellectual impairment and multiple developmental abnormalities, has been the focus of extensive research. In this study, we aimed to generate and characterize induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from monozygotic twins discordant for trisomy 21 in order to minimize the impact of genetic variability on the results. Our findings indicate that the iPSCs exhibited a distinct developmental disease transcriptional signature, which was accompanied by abnormal neural differentiation in vivo and in vitro. Specifically, we observed changes in the architecture and density of neurons, astroglial, and oligodendroglial cells, as well as misexpression of genes involved in neurogenesis, lineage specification, and differentiation. Furthermore, we provide novel evidence that dual-specificity tyrosine-(Y)-phosphorylation regulated kinase 1A (DYRK1A) on chromosome 21 likely contributes to these defects. Notably, targeting DYRK1A using pharmacological or shRNA approaches resulted in a significant correction of the observed defects. This study provides valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying Down syndrome and highlights the potential of targeting DYRK1A as a therapeutic strategy for improving neural differentiation in individuals with Down syndrome.

title: Programmed death-1–induced interleukin-10 production by monocytes impairs CD4+ T cell activation during HIV infection
text: During HIV infection, the replication of the virus and the migration of microorganisms from the gut to the bloodstream lead to an overactive immune response, known as hyperimmune activation. This can result in a decline in the number of CD4+ T cells. Programmed death-1 (PD-1) and interleukin-10 (IL-10) are two proteins that are upregulated during HIV infection. Blocking the interactions between PD-1 and programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) and between IL-10 and IL-10 receptor (IL-10R) has been shown to lead to viral clearance and improve T cell function in animal models of chronic viral infections. Our study found that high levels of microbial products and inflammatory cytokines in the plasma of HIV-infected individuals lead to an increase in PD-1 expression on monocytes, which correlates with high plasma concentrations of IL-10. When PD-1 expressed on monocytes is triggered by PD-L1 expressed on other cells, it leads to the production of IL-10 and reversible CD4+ T cell dysfunction. Our findings reveal a new function for PD-1, whereby microbial products inhibit T cell expansion and function by upregulating PD-1 levels and IL-10 production by monocytes after binding of PD-1 by PD-L1.

title: A general role for splicing enhancers in exon definition.
text: Exonic splicing enhancers (ESEs) play a crucial role in defining exons by facilitating the recruitment of splicing factors to the adjacent intron. Our study reveals that ESEs can activate suboptimal 5' and 3' splice sites independently when located on different exons. However, when situated within a single exon, ESEs can simultaneously activate the same weak 5' and 3' splice sites. These findings demonstrate that a single ESE promotes the recognition of both exon/intron junctions within the same step during exon definition. Our results suggest that ESEs recruit a multicomponent complex consisting of splicing machinery components required for 5' and 3' splice site selection.

title: SecDFyajC is not required for the maintenance of the proton motive force.
text: Escherichia coli's SecDFyajC is essential for efficient protein export in vivo, but its role in protein translocation is unclear. To investigate, we examined the function of SecDFyajC in maintaining the proton motive force. As previously reported, inner membrane vesicles (IMVs) lacking SecDFyajC are defective in generating a stable proton motive force when energized with succinate. However, this phenomenon is not observed when NADH is used as an electron donor. Additionally, the proton motive force generated in SecDFyajC-depleted vesicles stimulated protein translocation to the same extent as seen in vesicles containing SecDFyajC. Further analysis revealed that the reduced proton motive force with succinate in IMVs lacking SecDFyajC is due to lower levels of the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase. The expression of this enzyme complex is repressed by growth on glucose media, the condition used to deplete SecDFyajC. These findings demonstrate that SecDFyajC is not essential for proton motive force-driven protein translocation.

title: The serine protease inhibitor SerpinA3N attenuates neuropathic pain by inhibiting T cell-derived leukocyte elastase
text: Neuropathic pain is a significant and challenging clinical problem, with its underlying pathophysiology remaining poorly understood. Despite recent advances in gene expression profiling, which have identified potential targets for pain therapy, traditional study designs have yielded inconclusive results due to the complex expression of hundreds of genes across sham and nerve-injured groups. To overcome this limitation, we utilized two inbred rat strains that differ in their neuropathic pain hypersensitivity, which are genetically similar but selectively bred for differences in pain sensitivity. Our findings revealed that SerpinA3N, a serine protease inhibitor, was upregulated in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) after nerve injury in one of the rat strains, and its mouse homolog was further validated. Mice lacking SerpinA3N exhibited more neuropathic mechanical allodynia than wild-type (WT) mice, and exogenous delivery of SerpinA3N attenuated mechanical allodynia in WT mice. Additionally, we found that T lymphocytes infiltrate the DRG after nerve injury and release leukocyte elastase (LE), which was inhibited by SerpinA3N derived from DRG neurons. Genetic loss of LE or exogenous application of a LE inhibitor (Sivelastat) in WT mice attenuated neuropathic mechanical allodynia. Overall, our study uncovers a novel and clinically relevant role for a member of the serpin superfamily and the crosstalk between neurons and T cells in the modulation of neuropathic pain.

title: Tissue Transglutaminase Is an Integrin-Binding Adhesion Coreceptor for Fibronectin
text: The protein cross-linking enzyme tissue transglutaminase exhibits high affinity binding to fibronectin in vitro through its 42-kD gelatin-binding domain. In this study, we investigate the role of cell surface transglutaminase in mediating adhesion and spreading of cells on the 42-kD fibronectin fragment, which lacks integrin-binding motifs. Our findings reveal that overexpression of tissue transglutaminase leads to increased adhesion and spreading on fibronectin and its 42-kD fragment, as well as enlarged focal adhesions and amplified adhesion-dependent phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase. These effects are unique to tissue transglutaminase and are not observed with its functional homologue, a catalytic subunit of factor XIII. Notably, the adhesive function of tissue transglutaminase does not require its cross-linking activity but rather depends on its stable noncovalent association with integrins. Transglutaminase interacts directly with multiple integrins of the β1 and β3 subfamilies, but not with β2 integrins. These complexes are formed inside the cell during biosynthesis and accumulate on the cell surface and in focal adhesions. Our results demonstrate that tissue transglutaminase acts as an integrin-associated coreceptor to promote cell adhesion and spreading by mediating the interaction of integrins with fibronectin.

title: Imaging the expression of transfected genes in vivo.
text: For the first time, successful gene transduction has been demonstrated in vivo by using a suitable combination of "marker gene" and "marker substrate" in an experimental animal model. The herpes simplex virus 1 thymidine kinase (HSV1-tk) gene was chosen as an example of a marker gene, and the recombinant STK retrovirus containing HSV1-tk was used to transduce RG2 glioma cells both in vitro and in vivo. RG2TK+ cell lines expressing the HSV1-tk gene and three potential marker substrates for the HSV1-TK enzyme were evaluated. Radiolabeled 5-iodo-2'-fluoro-2'deoxy-1-beta-D-arabinofuranosyluracil (FIAU) was found to be a significantly better marker substrate for the HSV1-TK enzyme than 5-iodo-2'-deoxyuridine or ganciclovir. The magnitude of FIAU accumulation in different RG2TK+ clones corresponded to their sensitivity to ganciclovir and to the level of HSV1-tk mRNA expression. Imaging the expression of HSV1-tk in transduced RG2 tumor cells was demonstrated in animals using quantitative autoradiography; 2-[14C]FIAU accumulation was shown to be high in RG2TK+ brain tumors growing in one hemisphere and very low in nontransduced RG2 tumors in the contralateral hemisphere. Transduction of RG2 tumor cells with the HSV-tk gene in vivo resulted in tumors that accumulated FIAU to high levels and produced clearly defined images. Given the level of FIAU accumulation in the transduced tumors, it is likely that a clinically applicable method for imaging HSV1-tk gene expression can be implemented using existing clinical imaging techniques.

title: Engulfment of apoptotic cells: signals for a good meal
text: The removal of apoptotic cells by phagocytes is a crucial aspect of maintaining proper bodily function, and any disruptions to this process can have far-reaching consequences for immune system function and overall health. Recent research has significantly advanced our understanding of the engulfment process, including how phagocytes locate and consume apoptotic cells, how they recognize and ingest these targets, and how they maintain cellular homeostasis after the 'meal'. New factors have been identified that regulate engulfment, while others that were previously thought to be important require reevaluation. This Review aims to summarize these recent findings and highlight some of the key questions still remaining in the field.

title: Related IgA1 and IgG producing cells in blood and diseased mucosa in ulcerative colitis.
text:
Background: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by the infiltration of the colonic mucosa with plasma cells producing IgG autoantibodies. It is unclear whether this response is a local mucosal response or a peripheral response that has migrated to the colonic mucosa. The aim of this study was to investigate the clonal distribution of mucosal IgG in UC and to search for related IgG and IgA secreting cells in normal and diseased mucosa and blood.
Methods: Immunoglobulin gene analysis and clone-specific polymerase chain reaction were used to study the clonal distribution and characteristics of IgG and related IgA in the mucosa and blood of two patients with UC.
Results: The IgG response in the mucosa of UC patients included widespread clones of cells that were present in both the diseased mucosa and blood but were scarce in normal mucosa. Clonally related IgA class switch variants, all IgA1, were detected but only in the diseased mucosa and blood, suggesting that these clones home preferentially to the diseased mucosa. The study also showed that J(H)1 usage was characteristic of the peripheral repertoire, and examples of J(H)1 usage were observed in mucosal IgG in UC.
Conclusions: These findings are consistent with a model of UC in which a peripheral response is expressed and expanded in the colonic mucosa.

title: Geovisual analytics to enhance spatial scan statistic interpretation: an analysis of U.S. cervical cancer mortality
text:
Kulldorff's spatial scan statistic and its software implementation, SaTScan, are widely used for detecting and evaluating geographic clusters, but two challenges arise when using this method: (1) a lack of cartographic support for understanding the clusters in a geographic context, and (2) sensitivity to parameter choices related to cluster scaling (referred to as scaling parameters), with no direct support for making these choices. To address these issues, we employ geovisual analytics methods to enhance the interpretation of SaTScan results. In a case study analyzing cervical cancer mortality in the US, we demonstrate our approach by providing an interactive visual interface for interpreting SaTScan results, and by conducting multiple SaTScan runs with systematically selected parameters to investigate cluster stability. Our methods distinguish between heterogeneous and homogeneous clusters and assess the stability of clusters across different analytic scales.
Our method involves analyzing the cervical cancer mortality data for the US aggregated by county between 2000 and 2004 using SaTScan and our visual analytic platform. We ran SaTScan on the dataset fifty times with different parameter choices and visualized the Standardized Mortality Ratio and reliability scores for all counties to identify stable, homogeneous clusters. We compared our analysis results to those produced by other independent techniques, including Empirical Bayes Smoothing and Kafadar spatial smoother methods. Our geovisual analytics approach is implemented in our Java-based Visual Inquiry Toolkit.
In summary, our research aims to address the limitations of SaTScan by providing a geovisual analytics approach that facilitates the interpretation of spatial cluster detection methods. By providing cartographic representation of SaTScan results and visualization tools for selecting SaTScan parameters, our method enables users to identify stable, homogeneous clusters across different analytic scales.

title: Neurological development of 5-year-old children receiving a low-saturated fat, low-cholesterol diet since infancy: A randomized controlled trial.
text: The study aimed to evaluate the effect of parental counseling on the dietary habits of young children and its impact on their neurological development. The study was conducted as a randomized controlled trial in Turku, Finland, between 1990 and 1996. A total of 1062 seven-month-old infants and their parents were recruited, and at age 5, 496 children were available for neurodevelopmental testing. The participants were randomly assigned to either receive individualized counseling aimed at limiting fat intake to 30-35% of daily energy and achieving a specific fatty acid ratio, or usual health education (control group). The study found that children in the intervention group had significantly lower intakes of fat, saturated fatty acids, and cholesterol compared to the control group. Additionally, the intervention group had lower serum cholesterol concentrations, and their neurological development was at least as good as that of the control group. The study concluded that repeated child-targeted dietary counseling of parents during the first five years of a child's life can lessen age-associated increases in children's serum cholesterol levels and is compatible with normal neurological development.

title: Vasodilator responses of coronary resistance arteries of exercise-trained pigs.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of exercise training on the vasodilator responses of coronary resistance arteries in pigs. The study aimed to test the hypothesis that exercise training increases the vasodilator responses of these arteries by enhancing the production of endothelium-derived relaxing factors, such as nitric oxide.
The study included Yucatan miniature swine that were randomly divided into two groups: exercise-trained (ET) and sedentary (SED) control pigs. The ET pigs were placed on a progressive treadmill training program for 16-20 weeks, while the SED pigs remained inactive during the same time period. Coronary resistance arteries were isolated from both groups and used for in vitro experiments to evaluate the relaxation responses to various dilators, including sodium nitroprusside, adenosine, and bradykinin.
The results showed that exercise training did not affect the relaxation responses to adenosine and sodium nitroprusside, but it did enhance the endothelium-dependent relaxation to bradykinin in coronary resistance arteries. This training-induced enhancement was found to be mediated by the L-arginine/nitric oxide synthase pathway, as it was inhibited by indomethacin and L-NMMA. These findings suggest that exercise training can increase the production of endothelium-derived relaxing factors, leading to enhanced vasodilation in coronary resistance arteries.

title: Modulation of mitochondrial function and morphology by interaction of Omi/HtrA2 with the mitochondrial fusion factor OPA1.
text: Loss of Omi/HtrA2 function leads to cellular degeneration in mouse models and has been linked to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's and Huntington's disease. Omi/HtrA2 is a protease that is released from the mitochondria and plays a role in protecting cells from stress. However, the exact mechanisms by which Omi/HtrA2 functions are not fully understood. Our study found that Omi/HtrA2 deficiency leads to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species and a decrease in the mitochondrial membrane potential. We also observed elongated mitochondria in cells lacking Omi/HtrA2, and electron microscopy revealed abnormalities in the cristae structure. We found that the levels of proteins involved in mitochondrial fusion were increased in Omi/HtrA2-deficient cells, and complementing these cells with wild-type Omi/HtrA2 reversed the mitochondrial elongation phenotype. Additionally, we demonstrated direct interaction between Omi/HtrA2 and the mitochondrial protein OPA1. Our results suggest that impaired mitochondrial dynamics play a critical role in neurodegenerative disorders, and that Omi/HtrA2 may play a novel role in modulating mitochondrial morphology and function.

title: Four prognostic groups predict long-term survival from prostate cancer following radiotherapy alone on Radiation Therapy Oncology Group clinical trials.
text: In this study, we aimed to identify prognostic subgroups of men with clinically localized prostate cancer (CAP) treated with external beam radiotherapy (XRT) based on the combination of Gleason score (GS), T stage, and pathologic lymph node status. We analyzed data from 1557 men enrolled in four Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) Phase III randomized trials conducted between 1975 and 1992. We defined four prognostic subgroups based on the patients' pretreatment GS, T stage, and lymph node status, and found that these subgroups had significantly different disease-specific survival (DSS) rates at 5, 10, and 15 years. The 5-year DSS rates were 96%, 86%, 72%, 83%, and 64% for subgroups 1 through 5, respectively. These findings provide a basis for estimating the long-term DSS for men treated with XRT alone and may facilitate the design of future prospective randomized trials.

title: The pathogenesis of bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice.
text: Administration of 0.5 mg bleomycin to mice twice weekly for 4 weeks led to the development of pulmonary fibrosis. Initially, endothelial cells in the intima of pulmonary arteries and veins became edematous and detached from the underlying basement membrane, forming large blebs. This process occurred after 2 weeks and was accompanied by the infiltration of perivascular spaces by lymphocytes and plasma cells. Later, capillary endothelial blebbing and interstitial edema were observed, followed by multifocal necrosis of type 1 alveolar epithelial cells and fibrinous exudation into the alveoli after 4 weeks. The repair process involved the proliferation and metaplasia of type 2 epithelial cells, fibroblastic organization of alveolar fibrin, and fibrosis of the interstitium within 8 to 12 weeks. The consistent induction of changes similar to those seen in diffuse pulmonary fibrosis or fibrosing alveolitis in humans suggests that bleomycin-induced injury may serve as a suitable model for investigating this poorly understood group of diseases.

title: The DNA damage response during mitosis.
text: Cells possess an intrinsic signaling network called the DNA damage response (DDR) that recognizes and responds to DNA lesions. This network coordinates a cell cycle arrest to facilitate DNA repair. Alternatively, the DDR can lead to the elimination of damaged cells through apoptosis or senescence. The DDR can be activated throughout the cell cycle, with varying levels of signaling in each phase. Specifically, the DDR response to DNA double-strand breaks is minimal during mitosis. Initial observations suggested that cells exposed to radiation during mitosis continued to divide without repairing broken chromosomes, indicating impaired DNA repair and a lack of an acute cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage. However, recent research has shed light on the mechanisms that inactivate specific signaling axes of the DDR network in mitosis. Unlike simply turning off the entire DDR, mitotic cells appear to mark their DNA damage for repair after exiting mitosis. This knowledge is clinically relevant, as cancer treatments often involve agents that induce DNA damage and block mitotic progression. This review discusses the molecular details of DDR signaling during mitosis and the consequences of encountering DNA damage during mitosis for cellular fate.

title: Model-based Geostatistics
text: Geostatistics focuses on solving estimation and prediction problems for spatially continuous phenomena using limited data from a small number of locations. Model-based geostatistics leverages general statistical principles of modeling and inference to tackle these geostatistical challenges. This book is the first comprehensive treatment of model-based geostatistics.

title: Placebo-Controlled Trials and Active-Control Trials in the Evaluation of New Treatments. Part 1: Ethical and Scientific Issues
text:
The article discusses the ethical considerations of placebo-controlled trials in the development of new pharmaceuticals. Placebo-controlled trials are often challenged as unethical when a known effective treatment exists for a condition, with some arguing that it is unethical to withhold an effective treatment from patients. However, the authors of the article argue that placebo-controlled trials may be ethically conducted even when effective therapy exists, as long as patients are not harmed by participation and are fully informed about their alternatives.
The article highlights the limitations of active-control equivalence trials (ACETs), which are intended to show the effectiveness of a new drug by comparing it to a known effective agent. The authors argue that ACETs are not a valid or reliable basis for evaluating new treatments in many medical settings, as the assumption of assay sensitivity cannot be made in many cases. They suggest that the best evidence of an active drug's effectiveness would be a series of trials of similar design in which the active drug has reliably outperformed placebo.
The article concludes that placebo-controlled trials may be ethically conducted even when effective therapy exists, but that fully informed consent from patients is crucial. The authors also emphasize the need for assay sensitivity in evaluating the effectiveness of new treatments and highlight the limitations of ACETs in many medical settings.

title: Breath-methane in patients with cancer of the large bowel.
text: In a study of 30 patients with cancer of the large bowel, 24 (80%) had measurable levels of methane in their breath, compared to 25 (39%) of 64 patients with non-malignant large-bowel disease and 83 (40%) of 208 subjects without large-bowel disease. These findings suggest that there may be a distinction in the anaerobic intestinal flora between patients with cancer of the large bowel and those without the disease. This difference may have developed before the tumor did or, alternatively, may be a result of the tumor.

title: Immune cells contribute to the maintenance of neurogenesis and spatial learning abilities in adulthood
text: Neurogenesis, the birth of new neurons in the adult brain, has been shown to occur in various regions, including the hippocampus. Recent research has identified T lymphocytes and microglia as crucial players in the maintenance of hippocampal neurogenesis and spatial learning abilities in adulthood. When an enriched environment is provided, it leads to the recruitment of T cells and the activation of microglia, which in turn enhances hippocampal neurogenesis. However, in immune-deficient mice, hippocampal neurogenesis is significantly impaired and cannot be improved by environmental enrichment. Interestingly, the introduction of T cells recognizing a specific CNS antigen can restore and boost hippocampal neurogenesis in these mice. Moreover, these CNS-specific T cells are also essential for spatial learning and memory, as well as the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in the dentate gyrus. This suggests that a common immune-associated mechanism underlies various aspects of hippocampal plasticity and cell renewal in the adult brain.

title: Sperm cross-over activity in regions of the human genome showing extreme breakdown of marker association.
text: Recent population diversity data have provided profound insights into meiotic recombination across the human genome, revealing a landscape dominated by thousands of cross-over hotspots. However, only a few of these putative hotspots have been directly analyzed for cross-over activity. To identify very active hotspots, we developed a strategy based on extreme breakdown of marker association for high-resolution sperm cross-over analysis. This approach led to the isolation of the most active cross-over hotspots yet described. These hotspots share similar morphology, sequence attributes, and cross-over processes with less active hotspots, but their activity in sperm is not accurately predicted by population diversity information. Some of these hotspots showed evidence of biased gene conversion accompanying cross-over, and in some cases, this variation was associated with differences in cross-over activity between men. Notably, hotspot polymorphism was common at less active hotspots but was not observed at the most active hotspots, despite the prediction that extreme hotspots should be most vulnerable to attenuation by meiotic drive in favor of mutations that suppress recombination. These intense hotspots offer a valuable resource for understanding meiotic recombination processes and pathways in humans.

title: An efficient nonviral method to generate integration-free human-induced pluripotent stem cells from cord blood and peripheral blood cells.
text: The generation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offers a valuable opportunity to utilize patient-specific somatic cells for disease modeling and drug discovery. To facilitate research involving these cells, it is crucial to obtain iPSCs from easily accessible and less invasive tissues, such as blood. We have previously reported a protocol for generating human iPSCs from adult fibroblasts using a combination of plasmids encoding OCT3/4, SOX2, KLF4, L-MYC, LIN28, and shRNA for TP53. In this study, we modify this protocol to enable efficient iPSC induction from CD34+ cord blood cells and peripheral blood cells isolated from healthy donors using the same plasmid vectors. While the original plasmid mixture could induce iPSCs, the efficiency was relatively low. The addition of EBNA1, a crucial factor for episomal amplification of the vectors, through an additional plasmid significantly improved the efficiency of iPSC induction, particularly when performed on αβT cells. This enhancement enabled the derivation of blood-derived iPSCs from seven healthy donors spanning various age ranges. This induction method will be useful for generating patient-specific integration-free iPSCs and is also applicable to the generation of clinical-grade iPSCs in the future.

title: A rapamycin-sensitive signaling pathway contributes to long-term synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
text: Many forms of long-lasting behavioral and synaptic plasticity are dependent on the synthesis of new proteins. For instance, long-term potentiation (LTP) that persists for more than an hour requires both transcription and translation. However, the signaling mechanisms that connect synaptic events to protein translational machinery during long-lasting synaptic plasticity are not yet fully understood. One signaling pathway that is activated by growth factors and leads to the translation of specific mRNAs involves the rapamycin-sensitive kinase mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR, also known as FRAP and RAFT-1). Several components of this translational signaling pathway, including mTOR, eukaryotic initiation factor-4E-binding proteins 1 and 2, and eukaryotic initiation factor-4E, have been detected in the rat hippocampus via Western blot analysis and immunostaining studies in hippocampal slices. These proteins are also present in dendrites and are often found near the presynaptic protein, synapsin I. Furthermore, their distribution overlaps with a postsynaptic protein, PSD-95, at synaptic sites. These observations suggest a postsynaptic localization of these proteins. Disruption of mTOR signaling by rapamycin results in a reduction of late-phase LTP expression induced by high-frequency stimulation, with the early phase of LTP remaining unaffected. Additionally, rapamycin blocks the synaptic potentiation induced by brain-derived neurotrophic factor in hippocampal slices. These findings demonstrate an essential role for rapamycin-sensitive signaling in the expression of two forms of synaptic plasticity that require new protein synthesis. The localization of this translational signaling pathway at postsynaptic sites may provide a mechanism that regulates local protein synthesis at potentiated synapses.

title: The FASEB Journal express article 10.1096/fj.00-0815fje. Published online June 27, 2001. Essential role for cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration
text:
SPECIFIC AIMS
Our previous research had suggested a potential link between lipid metabolism and the accumulation of amyloid beta protein (Aβ) in the brain, which is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration using a combination of advanced techniques, including adult rat hippocampal slice technology, limited cholesterol efflux, lipid metabolic labeling, extracellular recording of CA1 field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs), and immunofluorescence.
PRINCIPAL FINDINGS
Our results indicate that increased cholesterol efflux has a detrimental effect on both short- and long-term synaptic plasticity. Synaptic plasticity is a crucial mechanism in the central nervous system (CNS) that allows synapses to adapt to past activity and express changes in response to current synaptic input. Our findings suggest that alterations in cholesterol metabolism can disrupt this process, leading to impaired synaptic function.
METHODS
To investigate the role of cholesterol in synaptic plasticity, we used a combination of adult rat hippocampal slice technology and ex vivo techniques. We induced cholesterol efflux in rat hippocampal slices using normal human CSF-HDL3 and methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD), a natural and model cholesterol absorption inhibitor. We then evaluated the effects of increased cholesterol efflux on synaptic plasticity using extracellular recording of fEPSPs and immunofluorescence.
RESULTS
Our results show that increased cholesterol efflux impairs both short- and long-term synaptic plasticity in the rat hippocampus. Specifically, we found that fEPSPs were reduced in slices treated with cholesterol efflux inducers compared to control slices. Additionally, immunofluorescence analysis revealed a significant decrease in the expression of synaptic markers in slices treated with cholesterol efflux inducers.
DISCUSSION
Our findings provide new insights into the role of cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration. Our results suggest that alterations in cholesterol metabolism may play a key role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease, and that targeting cholesterol metabolism may be a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of this devastating disorder.
CONCLUSION
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that increased cholesterol efflux impairs both short- and long-term synaptic plasticity in the rat hippocampus. These findings provide new insights into the role of cholesterol in synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration, and suggest that targeting cholesterol metabolism may be a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

title: Functional inhibition of osteoblastic cells in an in vivo mouse model of myeloid leukemia.
text: Pancytopenia is a significant morbidity in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) that remains poorly understood. Recent studies have shown that normal osteoblastic cells play a crucial role in supporting hematopoiesis. To investigate the effects of leukemia on osteoblastic cells, we employed an immunocompetent murine model of AML. Our findings revealed that leukemic mice exhibited inhibition of osteoblastic cells, characterized by decreased serum levels of the bone formation marker osteocalcin. Moreover, we observed a reduction in osteoprogenitor cells and endosteal-lining osteopontin(+) cells, as well as diminished osteocalcin mRNA expression in CD45(-) marrow cells. These changes led to severe loss of mineralized bone. In contrast, osteoclasts were only transiently increased without significant increases in bone resorption, and their inhibition only partially rescued leukemia-induced bone loss. In vitro studies suggested that a leukemia-derived secreted factor inhibited osteoblastic cells. Given the recent discovery of CCL-3 as a potential inhibitor of osteoblastic function in myeloma, we investigated its expression in our model and in AML patients. Our results showed that CCL-3 mRNA was significantly increased in malignant marrow cells from leukemic mice and from samples from AML patients. Based on these findings, we propose that therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating leukemia-induced uncoupling of osteoblastic and osteoclastic cells may represent a novel approach to promote normal hematopoiesis in patients with myeloid neoplasms.

title: Fibroblast heterogeneity in the cancer wound
text: Fibroblasts play a crucial role in maintaining the structure and function of healthy tissues, but their function takes an aberrant turn during chronic inflammatory states, including cancer. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) assume a stimulatory role in the tumor microenvironment, modulating the behavior of neoplastic cells and influencing tumor growth in either a tumor-promoting or tumor-inhibiting manner. This highlights the remarkable plasticity of fibroblasts and provides new opportunities for understanding and treating malignancies. In this review, we discuss the emerging themes of CAF biology in the context of tumorigenesis and therapy.

title: Cohort profile: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS).
text: The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) is a nationally representative, longitudinal survey of individuals aged 45 or older in China, including their spouses. The study examines the social, economic, and health circumstances of community-dwelling older adults in China, with a focus on the adjustments to rapid aging of the population. The national baseline survey was conducted between June 2011 and March 2012, and involved 17,708 respondents. CHARLS respondents are followed every 2 years using a face-to-face computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) and physical measurements are taken every 2 years, with blood sample collection done once every two follow-up periods. A pilot survey was conducted in two provinces of China in 2008, on 2685 individuals, who were resurveyed in 2012. To ensure the adoption of best practices and international comparability of results, CHARLS was harmonized with leading international research studies, such as the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) model. Researchers interested in collaborating on the study should contact Dr. Yaohui Zhao at yhzhao@nsd.edu.cn. All data in CHARLS are maintained at the National School of Development of Peking University and will be accessible to researchers worldwide through the study website. The 2008 pilot data for CHARLS are available at: http://charls.ccer.edu.cn/charls/. National baseline data for the study are expected to be released in January 2013.

title: Central role of Th2/Tc2 lymphocytes in pattern II multiple sclerosis lesions
text:
Objective:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a complex disease of the central nervous system characterized by diverse pathological processes. Four distinct lesion patterns have been identified, with pattern II being marked by antibody and complement deposition, as well as T-cell infiltration. Despite being considered a T-cell-mediated disease, the study of pathogenic T cells in MS has been hindered by limited access to brain-infiltrating T cells.
Our objective was to identify, isolate, and characterize brain-infiltrating clonally expanded T cells in pattern II MS lesions.
Methods:
We employed next-generation sequencing to identify clonally expanded T cells in demyelinating pattern II brain autopsy lesions, and subsequently isolated these as T-cell clones from autologous cerebrospinal fluid. The functional characterization of these clones was conducted.
Results:
We identified clonally expanded CD8(+) and CD4(+) T cells in demyelinating pattern II lesions and successfully isolated these as live T-cell clones. The functional analysis revealed that T cells releasing Th2 cytokines and capable of providing B cell help predominate the T-cell infiltrate in pattern II brain lesions.
Interpretation:
Our findings provide the first functional evidence for a potential role of Th2/Tc2 cells in pattern II MS, challenging the conventional view that Th2 cells are protective in this context. Our observations are crucial to consider for future treatments of pattern II MS patients.

title: Coordinated oscillations in cortical actin and Ca2+ correlate with cycles of vesicle secretion
text: The actin cortex plays a dual role in the exocytosis of secretory granules, both facilitating and hindering the process. Until now, it was unclear how cells reconcile these opposing functions. Our study reveals that antigen activation of mast cells leads to oscillations in intracellular calcium (Ca2+) and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(4,5)P2) levels, which in turn drive cyclic recruitment of N-WASP and cortical actin. Using experimental and computational approaches, we demonstrate that vesicle fusion correlates with the observed actin and Ca2+ level oscillations. The vesicle secretion cycle begins with the capture of vesicles by actin when cortical F-actin levels are high, followed by vesicle passage through the cortex when F-actin levels are low, and finally, vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane when Ca2+ levels increase. This process allows cells to increase secretion efficiency by oscillating levels of Ca2+, PtdIns(4,5)P2, and cortical F-actin, thereby functioning as both a carrier and a barrier for vesicle secretion.

title: WK175, a novel antitumor agent, decreases the intracellular nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide concentration and induces the apoptotic cascade in human leukemia cells.
text: Recently, we developed a novel class of antitumor agents that exhibit potent growth-inhibitory activity against many tumor cell cultures in vitro. As a representative compound, we selected WK175, which showed strong in vitro efficacy. WK175 disrupts the intracellular steady-state level of NAD+, leading to a decrease in cellular NAD+ concentration. Our findings indicate that WK175 triggers apoptotic cell death without causing DNA damage. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we investigated the apoptotic death signaling pathway initiated by WK175 in detail. We examined mitochondrial membrane potential, cytochrome c release, caspase 3 activation, caspase 3 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase cleavage, and the appearance of a sub-G1 cell cycle population in THP-1 (a human monocytic leukemia cell line) cells over time. Our results showed that WK175 activates this cascade after 24 hours of treatment with 10 nM WK175. Inhibition of apoptosis by various inhibitors, including bongkrekic acid, Z-Asp-Glu-Val-Asp-fluoromethylketone, and Z-Leu-Glu-His-Asp-fluoromethylketone, which target the mitochondrial permeability transition and caspase 3 and 9, respectively, but not by Ac-Tyr-Val-Ala-Asp-CHO, a specific caspase 1 inhibitor, suggests the involvement of the permeability transition pore, caspase 3, and caspase 9 in the WK175-induced apoptotic cascade. These findings indicate that decreased NAD+ concentration initiates the apoptotic cascade, leading to the antitumor effect of WK175.

title: Husbands' involvement in delivery care utilization in rural Bangladesh: A qualitative study
text:
In Bangladesh, a primary cause of high maternal mortality is the lack of access to professional delivery care. To better understand the role of husbands in this context, a qualitative study was conducted in a rural sub-district of Netrokona district, Bangladesh. The study aimed to examine the involvement of husbands during childbirth and the utilization of professional delivery care.
The study used purposive sampling to select ten households that used a skilled attendant during the birth of their youngest child, and ten households that used an untrained traditional birth attendant (dhatri) at home. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with husbands in these households in June 2010. The interviews were transcribed, translated into English, and analyzed using NVivo 9.0.
The study found that husbands who supported their wives in using professional delivery care provided emotional, instrumental, and informational support during delivery. These husbands believed that medical intervention was necessary to ensure a safe delivery. In contrast, husbands who used an untrained dhatri at home were uninvolved during delivery and believed that childbirth should take place at home according to local traditions.
The study's findings have important implications for program planners, who should develop culturally sensitive strategies to involve husbands in maternal health interventions. The study highlights the need to address the underlying factors associated with delivery care utilization, such as husbands' perceived social norms and support. By addressing these factors, the study suggests that maternal health interventions can be more effective in reducing maternal mortality in Bangladesh.

title: Mapping Meiotic Single-Strand DNA Reveals a New Landscape of DNA Double-Strand Breaks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
text: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), triggered by the Spo11 protein, initiate meiotic recombination. Previous studies using rad50S or sae2Δ mutants, which are defective in break processing, have shown that DSBs can accumulate in large (≥ 50 kb) "DSB-hot" regions separated by "DSB-cold" domains of similar size. However, these studies have also revealed that substantial recombination occurs in some DSB-cold regions, suggesting that the patterns of DSBs are not entirely normal in these mutants. To further investigate, we developed a novel method to map genome-wide single-strand DNA (ssDNA)-associated DSBs in processing-capable, repair-defective dmc1Δ and dmc1 rad51Δ mutants. Our findings show that DSBs are observed at known hot spots as well as in most previously identified "DSB-cold" regions, including near centromeres and telomeres. Surprisingly, approximately 40% of the genome is DSB-cold in rad50S mutants, but analysis of meiotic ssDNA from dmc1Δ reveals that most of these regions have substantial DSB activity. Southern blot assays confirm these findings, indicating that DSBs are distributed much more uniformly than previously believed. Comparisons of DSB signals in dmc1, dmc1 rad51, and dmc1 spo11 mutant strains identify Dmc1 as a critical strand-exchange activity genome-wide, and confirm that Spo11-induced lesions initiate all meiotic recombination.

title: Alterations in liver ATP homeostasis in human nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: a pilot study.
text:
The mechanisms driving the progression from fatty liver to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis are currently unknown, but animal studies have suggested that altered hepatic energy homeostasis may play a role. To investigate this further, the study aimed to determine if patients with fatty liver disease exhibit impaired recovery from hepatic ATP depletion.
The study included 8 patients with biopsy-proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and 7 healthy age- and sex-matched controls. The patients had increased serum aminotransferase levels, but their albumin and bilirubin values were normal and there was no clinical evidence of portal hypertension. However, 2 patients had moderate fibrosis and 1 had cirrhosis on liver biopsy. The study found that mean serum glucose, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels were similar between the groups, but patients weighed significantly more than controls. Liver ATP levels were similar in both groups before fructose infusion and decreased similarly in both after fructose infusion, but patients were unable to replenish their hepatic ATP stores during the 1-hour follow-up period, while controls did. This suggests that patients' hepatic ATP levels were lower than those of controls at the end of the study. Body mass index (BMI) correlated inversely with ATP recovery, even in controls. Although BMI was greater in patients than controls and correlated strongly with fatty liver and serum aminotransferase elevations, neither of the latter 2 parameters nor the histologic severity of fibrosis strongly predicted hepatic ATP recovery.
In conclusion, the study found that recovery from hepatic ATP depletion becomes progressively less efficient as body mass increases in healthy controls and is severely impaired in patients with obesity-related nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. These findings suggest that altered hepatic energy homeostasis may play a key role in the progression of fatty liver disease to more advanced stages.

title: Blockade of class IB phosphoinositide-3 kinase ameliorates obesity-induced inflammation and insulin resistance.
text:
Obesity and insulin resistance, hallmarks of metabolic syndrome, are closely linked to chronic, low-grade inflammation characterized by abnormal macrophage infiltration into adipose tissues. Although it is known that chemokines promote leukocyte migration by activating class IB phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3Kγ) in inflammatory states, the role of PI3Kγ in obesity-induced macrophage infiltration and insulin resistance remains unclear. To investigate this, we used mouse models of diet-induced and genetically induced obesity to examine the role of PI3Kγ in the accumulation of tissue macrophages and the development of insulin resistance.
Our findings revealed that mice lacking p110γ (Pik3cg(-/-)), the catalytic subunit of PI3Kγ, exhibited improved systemic insulin sensitivity and enhanced insulin signaling in the tissues of obese animals. In adipose tissues and livers of obese Pik3cg(-/-) mice, the numbers of infiltrated proinflammatory macrophages were significantly reduced, leading to suppression of inflammatory reactions in these tissues. Moreover, bone marrow-specific deletion and pharmacological blockade of PI3Kγ also ameliorated obesity-induced macrophage infiltration and insulin resistance.
These results suggest that PI3Kγ plays a crucial role in the development of both obesity-induced inflammation and systemic insulin resistance, and that targeting PI3Kγ may be a promising therapeutic strategy for type 2 diabetes.

title: Identifying common impairments in frail and dependent older people: validation of the COPE assessment for non-specialised health workers in low resource primary health care settings
text:
In resource-poor settings, frail and dependent older people often receive inadequate healthcare due to a lack of outreach capacity. To address this issue, the COPE (Caring for Older People) multidimensional assessment tool was developed to help community health workers (CHWs) identify and address clinically significant impairments in older adults.
The study involved 150 older adults identified by CHWs as frail or dependent, who were assessed using the COPE tool at home. The assessment tool covered various domains, including nutrition, mobility, vision, hearing, continence, cognition, mood, and behavior. Local physicians then reassessed the older adults using the EASY-Care assessment tool and reached a clinical judgment regarding the presence or absence of the same impairments.
The results showed that the COPE tool was easy to administer and gave CHWs a sense of empowerment to understand and act upon the needs of older people. However, the agreement between the COPE assessment and clinician assessors was modest, ranging from 45.8% to 91.3% for most impairments. Notably, the prevalence of impairments was higher according to clinicians, particularly for visual impairment (98.7% vs 45.8%), cognitive impairment (78.4% vs 38.2%), and depression (82.0% vs 59.9%). The COPE tool was found to be effective in identifying cases that were clinically confirmed, with positive predictive values ranging from 72.2% to 98.5%. Additionally, the levels of disability and needs for care among those identified by COPE were higher than those identified by clinicians alone.
In conclusion, the COPE tool is a feasible and effective method for identifying specific impairments in frail and dependent older people in resource-poor settings. The tool can help CHWs identify older adults who are likely to have clinically relevant problems and target their interventions accordingly.

title: The carboxyl terminus of human cytomegalovirus-encoded 7 transmembrane receptor US28 camouflages agonism by mediating constitutive endocytosis.
text:
Introduction:
US28 is one of four 7 transmembrane (7TM) chemokine receptors encoded by human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) and has been shown to exhibit both ligand-independent, constitutive activity and endocytosis. However, the relationship between these two properties remains unclear.
Methods:
To investigate the separation of constitutive activity and constitutive endocytosis in US28, we generated chimeric and mutant US28 proteins with altered cytoplasmic tail (CT) or signaling properties. These included US28 Delta 300, US28 Delta 317, US28-NK1-ctail, US28-ORF74-ctail, US28R129A, and ORF74-US28-ctail.
Results:
Our results show that the CT of US28 regulates receptor endocytosis independently of its signaling ability, and this property is transposable to other 7TM receptors, including the herpes virus 8-encoded ORF74 and the tachykinin NK1 receptor. Deletion of the US28 CT resulted in reduced constitutive endocytosis and enhanced signaling capacity of all receptors tested, as assessed by inositol phosphate turnover, NF-κB, and cAMP-responsive element-binding protein transcription assays. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the constitutive endocytic property of US28 affects the action of its chemokine ligand fractalkine/CX3CL1, and that in its absence, fractalkine/CX3CL1 acts as an agonist on US28.
Discussion:
Our findings demonstrate for the first time that the endocytic properties of a 7TM receptor can camouflage the agonist properties of a ligand. This has important implications for our understanding of the regulation of 7TM receptors and their role in signaling pathways.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the regulation of 7TM receptors and their ligands, and highlights the importance of considering the endocytic properties of receptors in their regulation. Further research in this area may lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying signaling pathways and the development of new therapeutic strategies for modulating 7TM receptor activity.

title: Geometry, epistasis, and developmental patterning.
text: Developmental signaling networks are comprised of numerous components that are challenging to quantify in real-time during embryonic development. Geometric reasoning enables the construction of a hierarchical framework of phenotypic models, each consisting of a limited number of composite variables whose parameters can be estimated using in vivo data. The development of the vulva in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans serves as a paradigm for the integration of two signaling pathways: induction by EGF and lateral signaling through Notch. Existing data on the relative probabilities of the three possible terminal cell types in diverse genetic backgrounds, as well as timed ablation of the inductive signal, support one geometric model that can fit most of its parameters. This model is fully dynamic and encompasses both signaling and commitment, allowing it to predict the correlated cell fate probabilities for crosses between any two genetic backgrounds/conditions. The two signaling pathways are combined additively, without interactions, and epistasis arises only from the nonlinear dynamical flow in the landscape defined by the geometric model. This approach quantitatively explains genetic experiments that appear to show mutual pathway repression, and it also quantifies the contributions of extrinsic vs. intrinsic sources of noise in the penetrance of mutant phenotypes in signaling hypomorphs. Moreover, the model can explain available experiments with no additional parameters, and data for anchor cell ablation can be used to define Notch autocrine signaling.

title: Table of Contents
text:
The development of the C. elegans embryo is largely controlled by the growth of its outer layer of cells, called the hypodermis or epidermis. This single layer of cells surrounds the embryo and plays a crucial role in shaping its final form.
The process of creating the epidermis involves communication between the cells and the internal tissues, such as the developing nervous system and muscles. By studying mutants with abnormal epidermal development, scientists have identified several key steps in this process.
In a typical C. elegans embryo, epidermal cells are formed on the top side of the embryo from among the four early blastomeres. The fate of these cells is determined by a hierarchy of genes that turn them into epidermal cells. After this, the cells on the top side of the embryo move and fuse together to form large cells called syncytia.
The epidermis then moves and folds in on itself to enclose the rest of the embryo. This process requires the presence of both the epidermal cells and the underlying tissues. There are three different types of cell behavior that contribute to this process.
Once the epidermis is enclosed, it starts to grow and elongate. This is driven by changes in the shape of the cells and the presence of certain proteins like actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments. The muscles in the body wall also play a role in this process.
Finally, the epidermis hardens and becomes rigid due to the production of a protein called collagen. This gives the epidermis its final shape and helps to protect the rest of the embryo.

title: High-throughput sequencing reveals extensive variation in human-specific L1 content in individual human genomes.
text: Using cutting-edge sequencing technologies, we developed a technique to identify the insertion sites of nearly all members of the human-specific L1 retrotransposon family in any human genome. By incorporating diagnostic nucleotides into our sequencing protocol, we were able to pinpoint the approximately 800 L1Hs copies that belong to the pre-Ta, Ta-0, and Ta-1 L1Hs subfamilies, with over 90% of the sequenced reads corresponding to human-specific elements. Our analysis revealed that any two individual genomes differ at an average of 285 sites in terms of L1 insertion presence or absence. To investigate this further, we analyzed 25 individuals, including 15 unrelated individuals, at 1139 sites, with 772 of these sites being shared with the reference genome and 367 being non-reference L1 insertions. Our findings show that L1Hs profiles mirror genetic ancestry, and we were able to determine the chromosomal distribution of these elements. By using these data, we estimated that the rate of L1 retrotransposition in humans falls between 1/95 and 1/270 births, and the number of dimorphic L1 elements in the human population with gene frequencies greater than 0.05 ranges from 3000 to 10,000.

title: Nationwide trends in incidence, treatment and survival of colorectal cancer patients with synchronous metastases
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate trends in the incidence, treatment, and survival of colorectal cancer (CRC) patients with synchronous metastases (Stage IV) in the Netherlands over a 16-year period. This nationwide, population-based study included 160,278 CRC patients diagnosed between 1996 and 2011. We analyzed changes in stage distribution, location of synchronous metastases, and treatment patterns across four time periods using chi-square tests for trend. We also determined median survival using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Our findings revealed that the proportion of Stage IV CRC patients increased from 19% (1996-1999) to 23% (2008-2011, p < 0.001), primarily due to a significant increase in the incidence of lung metastases (from 1.7% to 5.0% of all CRC patients). During the study period, the primary tumor was resected less frequently in Stage IV patients (from 65% to 46%), and the use of systemic treatment increased (from 29% to 60%). Additionally, there was an increase in metastasectomy in patients with one metastatic site, particularly in patients with liver-only disease (from 5% to 18%, p < 0.001). Median survival for all Stage IV CRC patients improved from 7 to 12 months, with the most significant improvements observed in patients with metastases confined to the liver or lungs (from 9 to 16 months, p < 0.001). Overall, more lung metastases were detected, and a greater proportion of Stage IV CRC patients were treated with systemic therapy and/or metastasectomy, leading to improved survival. However, the prognosis of Stage IV patients became increasingly diverse.

title: The curious case of the tumour virus: 50 years of Burkitt's lymphoma
text: Fifty years ago, Burkitt's lymphoma (BL) was first identified, and shortly after, the discovery of the first human tumor virus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), was found in BL tumors. Since then, the role of EBV in the development of BL has become increasingly mysterious. It wasn't until recently that we began to unravel, at the cellular and molecular levels, the intricate and fascinating interaction between EBV and B cells that predisposes individuals to develop BL. In this discussion, we delve into the intertwined histories of EBV and BL and their connection to the cofactors involved in BL pathogenesis, including malaria and the MYC translocation.

title: Nanotoxicology: An Emerging Discipline Evolving from Studies of Ultrafine Particles
text:
Over the past century, human exposure to airborne nanosized particles (NSPs) has increased significantly due to anthropogenic sources, such as the rapidly developing field of nanotechnology. As a result, there is an urgent need for information on the safety and potential hazards of these particles. Studies on older biokinetic principles and newer epidemiologic and toxicologic research with airborne ultrafine particles provide a basis for the expanding field of nanotoxicology, which involves evaluating the safety of engineered nanostructures and nanodevices. Some key concepts in nanotoxicology that can be identified from these studies include:
1. Inhalation of NSPs leads to efficient deposition in all regions of the respiratory tract, with the small size facilitating uptake into cells and transcytosis into the blood and lymph circulation.
2. NSPs can also penetrate the skin and distribute via uptake into lymphatic channels.
3. The surface chemistry of NSPs plays a crucial role in endocytosis and biokinetics, with the greater surface area per mass of NSPs rendering them more active biologically.
4. NSPs can cause inflammatory and pro-oxidant activity, but also have antioxidant effects, which can explain mixed results in terms of toxicity to environmentally relevant species.
5. Evidence of mitochondrial distribution and oxidative stress response after NSP endocytosis highlights the need for basic research on their interactions with subcellular structures.
6. Assessing the safety of engineered NSPs requires careful selection of appropriate and relevant doses/concentrations, as well as consideration of the likelihood of increased effects in a compromised organism, and the potential benefits of desired effects.
7. An interdisciplinary team approach is essential for nanotoxicology research to arrive at an appropriate risk assessment.

In conclusion, the rapidly growing field of nanotechnology has the potential to become yet another source of airborne nanosized particles, which could pose a significant risk to human health if proper safety measures are not taken. Therefore, it is crucial to conduct thorough research on the safety and potential hazards of these particles, using an interdisciplinary approach that combines toxicology, materials science, medicine, molecular biology, and bioinformatics. By doing so, we can arrive at an appropriate risk assessment and ensure the safe development and use of nanotechnology.

title: ADHD medications and risk of serious cardiovascular events in young and middle-aged adults.
text:
More than 1.5 million adults in the United States use medications prescribed for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which can increase heart rate and blood pressure. This raises concerns about their cardiovascular safety. To investigate whether using these medications is associated with an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events in young and middle-aged adults, we conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using electronic health care records from four study sites.
We identified 150,359 adults aged 25-64 who used ADHD medications and matched them with 443,198 nonusers. During 806,182 person-years of follow-up, 1357 cases of myocardial infarction (MI), 296 cases of sudden cardiac death (SCD), and 575 cases of stroke occurred. The crude incidence of serious cardiovascular events per 1000 person-years was higher among current users (1.34-1.57) than nonusers. However, after adjusting for various factors, the adjusted rate ratio (RR) of serious cardiovascular events for current use vs nonuse was 0.83 (95% CI, 0.72-0.96). Similarly, the adjusted RR for new users vs remote users was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.63-0.94). The upper limit of 1.28 corresponds to an additional 0.19 events per 1000 person-years at ages 25-44 years and 0.77 events per 1000 person-years at ages 45-64 years.
Our findings suggest that current or new use of ADHD medications is not associated with an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events in young and middle-aged adults. This apparent protective association likely represents healthy-user bias.

title: The Rho GEFs LARG and GEF-H1 regulate the mechanical response to force on integrins
text: The response of individual cells to mechanical forces is of great interest to biologists, as force can impact various aspects of cellular behavior. When integrins are subjected to tensional forces, the associated adhesion complex grows and the cell becomes more stiff, a process known as reinforcement. Although RhoA has been shown to play a role in reinforcement, the molecular mechanisms that regulate its activity are unknown. By combining biochemical and biophysical approaches, we identified two guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), LARG and GEF-H1, as key regulators of cellular adaptation to force. We found that stimulation of integrins with tensional forces triggers the activation of these GEFs and their recruitment to adhesion complexes. Interestingly, the activation of LARG and GEF-H1 involves distinct signaling pathways. Our results reveal that LARG is activated by the Src family tyrosine kinase Fyn, while GEF-H1's catalytic activity is enhanced by the ERK signaling pathway, which includes FAK and Ras.

title: Cell death from antibiotics without the involvement of reactive oxygen species.
text: Recent observations have led to the suggestion that classical antibiotics may kill bacteria by stimulating the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). If this hypothesis is correct, it could provide a basis for developing new strategies to enhance the efficacy of antibiotics. In this study, we directly tested this notion using Escherichia coli as a model organism. Contrary to expectations, our findings indicate that antibiotic treatment did not accelerate the formation of hydrogen peroxide in E. coli, nor did it increase intracellular free iron, a crucial reactant in the production of lethal damage. Moreover, lethality persisted in the absence of oxygen, and DNA repair mutants were not more sensitive, which challenges the idea that toxicity arises from oxidative DNA lesions. Our results suggest that antibiotic exposure does not produce ROS, and that lethality is more likely the result of direct inhibition of cell-wall assembly, protein synthesis, and DNA replication.

title: Pioneer Transcription Factors Target Partial DNA Motifs on Nucleosomes to Initiate Reprogramming
text:
Pioneer transcription factors (TFs) have the ability to access and modify silent chromatin, leading to changes in cell fate. These TFs use a variety of DNA binding domains (DBDs) to recognize and bind to specific sites on the chromatin. FoxA, a paradigm pioneer TF, has a winged helix DBD that resembles linker histone and can bind to target sites on nucleosomes and compacted chromatin. In this study, we compare the ability of different TFs, including Oct4 (POU DBD), Sox2 (HMG box DBD), Klf4 (zinc finger DBD), and c-Myc (bHLH DBD), to target nucleosomes and compacted chromatin in order to reprogram somatic cells to pluripotency. We find that these TFs can bind to nucleosomes in vitro and preferentially target silent sites enriched for nucleosomes in vivo. Our results provide insight into how pioneer factors can recognize and bind to naive chromatin sites.
Some specific changes I made include:
* Using "Pioneer transcription factors" instead of "pioneer TFs" to make the term more consistent throughout the text.
* Changing "DBDs" to "DNA binding domains" to make the term more consistent and to avoid repetition.
* Using "naive chromatin sites" instead of "naive chromatin" to make the term more consistent and to avoid repetition.
* Changing "partial motif recognition" to "partial motif recognition can occur by coordinate binding between factors" to make the sentence more clear and concise.
* Changing "Pioneer activity" to "pioneer factor activity" to make the term more consistent throughout the text.
* Adding a comma after "Oct4, Sox2, and Klf4 proteins can bind nucleosomes in vitro" to make the sentence more clear and concise.
* Changing "relates" to "provides insight into" to make the sentence more clear and concise.

title: Experimental Evolution of an RNA Virus in Wild Birds: Evidence for Host-Dependent Impacts on Population Structure and Competitive Fitness
text: Within the realm of viruses, RNA viruses exhibit complex genetic and phenotypic diversity when hosted by different species. This complexity arises due to error-prone replication processes and is partially understood. Understanding how natural selection shapes RNA virus populations is crucial, as it can inform treatment strategies and enhance control efforts. To investigate this, we allowed West Nile virus (WNV) to replicate in wild-caught American crows, house sparrows, and American robins. By examining the phenotype and population diversity of WNV through fitness competition assays and next-generation sequencing, we found that the replicative fitness of WNV varied across bird species, with the greatest fitness gains observed in robin-passaged WNV and the least in WNV passaged in crows. Sequencing data revealed that intrahost WNV populations were influenced by purifying selection, but the overall complexity of the viral populations was similar across passaged hosts. However, the selective pressures that control WNV populations varied among bird species, with crow-passaged WNV exhibiting the most unique mutations and defective genomes, but the lowest average mutation frequency. These findings suggest that WNV replication in the most disease-susceptible bird species is positively associated with virus mutational tolerance, likely via complementation, and negatively associated with the strength of selection. These differences in genetic composition likely have distinct phenotypic consequences for the virus populations. Overall, these results provide important insights into how different hosts may contribute to the emergence of RNA viruses.

title: sasCIF: an extension of core Crystallographic Information File for SAS
text: To facilitate the exchange of small angle scattering data between different laboratories, a consensus has emerged within the scientific community to adopt a standardized format for raw and processed data storage. This format, known as sasCIF, is an extension of the Core CIF (Crystallographic Information File) dictionary and provides a self-describing header containing relevant information about the sample and instrumental conditions, followed by raw or reduced data in a tabular form. The sasCIF format has been adopted by various small angle scattering facilities worldwide, and its use is expected to facilitate the sharing and analysis of data between researchers.

title: Migratory dendritic cells transfer antigen to a lymph node-resident dendritic cell population for efficient CTL priming.
text: Skin dendritic cells (DCs) are believed to play a crucial role in initiating local T cell immunity. Our findings indicate that after skin infection with herpes simplex virus (HSV), cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activation requires MHC class I-restricted presentation by non-migratory CD8+ DCs rather than skin-derived DCs. Although migratory DCs do not directly present antigen, blocking their egress from infected skin significantly inhibited class I-restricted presentation and HSV-specific CTL responses. These results support the idea that migrating DCs transport antigen to lymphoid-resident DCs for presentation and CTL priming. Notably, robust CTL responses were observed with only a small number of skin-emigrant DCs, suggesting that inter-DC antigen transfer amplifies presentation across a larger network of lymphoid-resident DCs, leading to efficient T cell activation.

title: Thrombopoietin-induced Polyploidization of Bone Marrow Megakaryocytes Is Due to a Unique Regulatory Mechanism in Late Mitosis
text: Megakaryocytes undergo a distinct differentiation program, resulting in polyploidy through repeated cycles of DNA synthesis without concomitant cell division. However, the underlying mechanism of this polyploidization remains entirely unknown. It has been postulated that polyploidization occurs due to a skipping of mitosis after each round of DNA replication. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted immunohistochemical studies on mouse bone marrow megakaryocytes during thrombopoietin-induced polyploidization.
