Our findings revealed that megakaryocytes enter mitosis and progress through the normal prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, and up to anaphase A, but not to anaphase B, telophase, or cytokinesis. Notably, multiple spindle poles were formed as the polyploid megakaryocytes entered mitosis, and the nuclear membrane broke down during prophase. The sister chromatids were aligned on a multifaced plate, and the centrosomes were symmetrically located on either side of each face of the plate at metaphase. Furthermore, a set of sister chromatids moved into the multiple centrosomes during anaphase A. Interestingly, the pair of spindle poles in anaphase were located in close proximity to each other, suggesting that the lack of outward movement of spindle poles during anaphase B may result in the reassembling nuclear envelope encircling all sister chromatids in a single nucleus at anaphase. These observations imply that polyploidization of megakaryocytes is not solely due to a skipping of mitosis and suggest the presence of unique regulatory mechanisms in anaphase, such as factors controlling anaphase progression, including microtubule motor proteins, which may be involved in this polyploidization process.

title: Unifying Viral Genetics and Human Transportation Data to Predict the Global Transmission Dynamics of Human Influenza H3N2
text:
The information on global human movement patterns is crucial for developing spatial epidemiological models that predict the spread of infectious diseases, including influenza. However, it is challenging to determine which modes of dispersal drive pathogen spread using standard epidemiological data alone. Evolutionary analyses of pathogen genome sequences provide valuable insights into the spatial dynamics of influenza viruses, but they have largely neglected the wealth of information on human mobility. To address this gap, we developed a phylogeographic approach that combines empirical data on human movement with viral gene sequences to elucidate the global spread of human influenza subtype H3N2.
Our framework estimates the migration history of human influenza while simultaneously testing and quantifying a range of potential predictive variables of spatial spread. We found that the global dynamics of influenza H3N2 are driven by air passenger flows, while at more local scales, spread is also determined by processes that correlate with geographic distance. Our analyses confirmed the central role of mainland China and Southeast Asia in maintaining a source population for global influenza diversity. By comparing model output with the known pandemic expansion of H1N1 in 2009, we demonstrated that predictions of influenza spatial spread are most accurate when data on human mobility and viral evolution are integrated.
In conclusion, the global dynamics of influenza viruses are best explained by combining human mobility data with the spatial information inherent in sampled viral genomes. The integrated approach introduced here offers great potential for epidemiological surveillance through phylogeographic reconstructions and for improving predictive models of disease control.

title: Microtubule sliding activity of a kinesin-8 promotes spindle assembly and spindle length control
text: Molecular motors play crucial roles in the formation of mitotic spindles by controlling the stability of individual microtubules or by crosslinking and sliding microtubule arrays. Kinesin-8 motors, in particular, have been shown to play a regulatory role in controlling microtubule dynamics. These motors have microtubule-destabilizing activities and restrict spindle length in a wide variety of cell types and organisms. Here, we investigate the antiparallel microtubule-sliding activity of Kip3, a kinesin-8 motor from budding yeast. We find that the in vivo importance of this sliding activity is established through the identification of complementary Kip3 mutants that separate the sliding activity and microtubule-destabilizing activity. In conjunction with Cin8, a kinesin-5 family member, the sliding activity of Kip3 promotes bipolar spindle assembly and maintains genome stability. We propose a "slide-disassemble" model, where the sliding and destabilizing activities of Kip3 balance during pre-anaphase, facilitating normal spindle assembly. However, the destabilizing activity of Kip3 dominates in late anaphase, inhibiting spindle elongation and ultimately promoting spindle disassembly.

title: A Pharmacological Map of the PI3-K Family Defines a Role for p110α in Insulin Signaling
text: Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3-Ks) are an emerging class of drug targets, but the distinct roles of PI3-K isoforms remain poorly understood. To address this, we developed a strategy to investigate the PI3-K family through pharmacological interrogation. A diverse panel of PI3-K inhibitors was synthesized and their target selectivity was biochemically evaluated, revealing unexpected similarities across targets and chemical structures. Crystal structures of three inhibitors bound to p110γ revealed a mobile region that is selectively exploited by certain compounds. This chemical array was then used to delineate the PI3-K isoforms required for insulin signaling. Our findings show that p110α is the primary insulin-responsive PI3-K in cultured cells, while p110β is dispensable but sets a threshold for p110α activity. In vivo, compounds targeting p110α block the acute effects of insulin treatment, whereas a p110β inhibitor has no effect. These results demonstrate the power of systematic target validation using a matrix of inhibitors spanning a protein family.

title: Identification of Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen 1 protein domains that direct interactions at a distance between DNA-bound proteins.
text: The EBNA1 protein of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) interacts with and stimulates DNA replication at the latent origin of replication, oriP, through a direct connection with the two noncontiguous subelements of oriP. The EBNA1 molecules bound to the oriP subelements interact efficiently with one another through a DNA looping mechanism. We have previously identified a region of EBNA1 (termed the looping region) that is essential for mediating these interactions. Now, we demonstrate that two fragments of this region, containing an eight amino acid repeat, can facilitate homotypic interactions when transferred to another DNA-binding protein. The interactions mediated by the EBNA1 looping region appear to rely on DNA binding, as they are only observed when the proteins are bound to DNA.

title: Primary prevention of hypertension: clinical and public health advisory from The National High Blood Pressure Education Program.
text: In 1993, the National High Blood Pressure Education Program Coordinating Committee published its first statement on primary hypertension prevention. This updated report, drawing on the latest scientific literature, provides current recommendations for preventing hypertension through a population-based approach and an intensive targeted strategy tailored to individuals at high risk. These two strategies are complementary and emphasize six evidence-based approaches to prevent hypertension: engaging in moderate physical activity, maintaining a healthy body weight, limiting alcohol consumption, reducing sodium intake, consuming a potassium-rich diet, and eating a diet low in saturated and total fat and high in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy products. By implementing these strategies in public health and clinical practice, we can help prevent blood pressure from rising and reduce elevated blood pressure levels in individuals with high normal blood pressure or hypertension.

title: Formins: intermediates in signal-transduction cascades that affect cytoskeletal reorganization.
text: The regulation of cell growth and polarity is mediated by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton that can adapt to developmental and environmental cues. In animals and fungi, formins are one of four major classes of poly-L-proline-containing (PLP) proteins involved in the signaling cascade that reorganizes the actin cytoskeleton. Analysis of the Arabidopsis genome sequence reveals that formins are the only conserved profilin-binding PLP proteins in plants, and they show significant structural differences compared to their animal and fungal counterparts, suggesting that plant formins may be subject to unique mechanisms of regulation or perform distinct functions in plant cells.

title: Genetic variability in GLP-1 receptor is associated with inter-individual differences in weight lowering potential of liraglutide in obese women with PCOS: a pilot study
text: The study investigated the inter-individual differences in the weight-lowering potential of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs) in obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The researchers found that the genetic variability of the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) may play a role in the body weight response to GLP-1 RAs. Specifically, they found that carriers of at least one polymorphic allele of the GLP-1R gene (rs10305420) had a poor treatment response compared to carriers of two wild type alleles. On the other hand, carriers of at least one polymorphic allele of another GLP-1R gene (rs6923761) tended to have a stronger treatment response compared to carriers of two wild type alleles. The study also found that both groups showed comparable improvements in fasting glucose and glucose tolerance after oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) compared to baseline. However, there were no significant differences in gastrointestinal adverse events between the two groups. The study suggests that genetic variations in the GLP-1R gene may explain some of the inter-individual differences in response to GLP-1 RAs for weight loss in obese PCOS women.

title: Cost-effectiveness of aromatase inhibitor co-treatment for controlled ovarian stimulation.
text:
Background:
To compare the clinical outcomes and cost-effectiveness of using letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, in combination with follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), versus FSH alone for controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) in patients undergoing intrauterine insemination (IUI) for various indications.
Methods:
Four hundred and thirty-two consecutive patients who underwent 872 IUI cycles were included in the study. The patients were divided into two groups: Group I (308 patients) who received letrozole and FSH for anovulation, male factor infertility, unexplained infertility, endometriosis, and combined indications; and Group II (124 patients) who received FSH only for ovarian factor infertility, male factor infertility, unexplained infertility, endometriosis, and other indications. The main outcome measures were the number of mature follicles >16 mm in diameter, FSH dose per cycle, clinical pregnancy rate, and cost-effectiveness ratio per pregnancy.
Results:
The FSH dose required for ovarian stimulation was significantly lower when letrozole was used (P < 0.0001). Although a significantly higher number of follicles >16 mm and endometrial thickness at the day of hCG administration were observed in Group II, the pregnancy rate per started and per completed cycles was the same in both groups (14.4% and 15.9% in Group I, and 15.77% and 18.07% in Group II, respectively). The IUI cancellation rate was significantly lower with letrozole treatment (P = 0.05%). The cost per cycle was significantly lower in Group I versus Group II (468.93 Canadian dollars +/- 418.18 versus 1067.28 +/- 921.43; P < 0.0001). The cost-effectiveness ratio was 3249.42 dollars in the letrozole group and 6712.00 dollars in the FSH-only group.


Conclusion:

A letrozole-FSH combination could be an effective ovarian stimulation protocol in IUI cycles, and may be more cost-effective than FSH alone due to the difference in FSH dose and cost. A randomized controlled trial is needed to further substantiate this finding.

title: The cost effectiveness of stereotactic radiosurgery versus surgical resection in the treatment of solitary metastatic brain tumors.
text: The study compares the economic efficiency of surgical resection and stereotactic radiosurgery (SR) in treating metastatic brain tumors. The analysis includes a review of medical literature from 1974 to 1994 and finds that SR is more cost-effective than surgical resection. The study includes three surgical resection studies and one SR study that met the inclusion criteria. The authors developed a model to estimate typical resource usage for both treatment options and used a survey of capital and operating costs from five sites to estimate radiosurgery costs. The analysis reveals that SR has lower uncomplicated procedure costs, average complication costs per case, and total costs per procedure compared to surgical resection. SR is also found to be more cost-effective and has a better incremental cost-effectiveness than surgical resection. A sensitivity analysis shows that large changes in key assumptions would be required to change the analysis outcome. The study concludes that elimination of all surgical resection morbidity costs would still result in superior incremental cost-effectiveness for SR.

title: Trans-ancestry mutational landscape of hepatocellular carcinoma genomes
text: Diverse epidemiological factors are linked to the prevalence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in different populations. However, the global landscape of genetic changes in HCC genomes across various ancestral backgrounds remains unexplored. By analyzing data from 503 liver cancer genomes from diverse populations, we identified 30 candidate driver genes and 11 core pathway modules. Our study also compared the trans-ancestry substitution signatures in 608 liver cancer cases and uncovered unique mutational signatures that predominantly contribute to Asian cases. This work reveals previously unexplored ancestry-associated mutational processes in HCC development. We found that a combination of hotspot TERT promoter mutation, TERT focal amplification, and viral genome integration occurs in over 68% of cases, highlighting TERT as a central and ancestry-independent node of hepatocarcinogenesis. Additionally, we identified new alterations in genes encoding metabolic enzymes, chromatin remodelers, and a high proportion of mTOR pathway activations, which offer potential therapeutic and diagnostic opportunities.

title: Organization of the mitotic chromosome.
text: Mitotic chromosomes are among the most conspicuous structures within the cell, yet their internal organization has remained largely elusive for over a century. To address this longstanding puzzle, we employed chromosome conformation capture techniques, including 5C and Hi-C, across the cell cycle. Our findings reveal two distinct three-dimensional folding states of the human genome during the cell cycle. Specifically, we discovered that the highly compartmentalized and cell type-specific organization observed in nonsynchronous cells is restricted to the interphase phase. In contrast, metaphase chromosomes exhibit a homogeneous folding state that is locus-independent, common to all chromosomes, and consistent among cell types. Using polymer simulations, we found that the metaphase Hi-C data are not compatible with traditional hierarchical models and are instead best described by a linearly organized, longitudinally compressed array of consecutive chromatin loops.

title: Compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome.
text:
In 1997, Roger Bone proposed the concept of Compensatory Anti-Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CARS) to describe the unintended consequences of the body's counter-regulatory mechanisms aimed at limiting an overactive inflammatory response in patients with infectious (sepsis) or non-infectious Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS). One of the key consequences of CARS is the alteration of the immune status, which can increase the susceptibility of intensive care patients to nosocomial infections. This observation is supported by animal studies, where a first insult often leads to enhanced sensitivity to infection. However, the experimental procedures used in these studies can significantly impact the results.
Circulating leukocytes undergo alterations in sepsis and SIRS patients, as well as in animal models of these conditions. While these changes may appear to be a global defect in immune cell function, they are actually a reprogramming of circulating leukocytes. Within tissues, leukocytes are primed or activated rather than immunosuppressed. Therefore, CARS can be viewed as an adapted compartmentalized response aimed at silencing certain acute pro-inflammatory genes and maintaining the expression of genes involved in the anti-infectious process.

title: Quantum dots spectrally distinguish multiple species within the tumor milieu in vivo
text:
A solid tumor is composed of a mixture of cancer and host cells embedded in an extracellular matrix, nourished by a network of blood vessels. To fully understand the complex dynamics of tumor growth and progression, it is essential to be able to distinguish and monitor each component in real-time. However, conventional fluorescent dyes often hinder the simultaneous imaging of these components, limiting our ability to study tumor pathophysiology.
To overcome this limitation, we employed advanced multiphoton microscopy techniques and genetically modified mice that expressed green fluorescent protein. By combining these methods with the use of customized quantum dot preparations, we were able to simultaneously image and differentiate between tumor vessels, perivascular cells, and the extracellular matrix. This allowed us to measure the ability of particles of different sizes to access the tumor and monitor the recruitment of quantum dot–labeled bone marrow–derived precursor cells to the tumor vasculature.
Our findings demonstrate the versatility of quantum dots as a tool for studying tumor pathophysiology and identifying potential avenues for treatment. By leveraging their unique properties, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between tumor cells, vessels, and the surrounding microenvironment, ultimately leading to the development of more effective cancer therapies.

title: Arginase I: a limiting factor for nitric oxide and polyamine synthesis by activated macrophages?
text: Arginase hydrolyzes arginine into ornithine and urea, making it a potential regulator of nitric oxide (NO) and polyamine synthesis. To investigate whether cytosolic arginase isoform (arginase I) expression limits NO or polyamine production in activated RAW 264.7 macrophage cells, we overexpressed arginase I or beta-galactosidase in these cells and treated them with interferon-gamma to induce type 2 NO synthase or with lipopolysaccharide or 8-bromo-cAMP (8-BrcAMP) to induce ornithine decarboxylase. Our findings showed that overexpression of arginase I had no effect on NO synthesis, but cells overexpressing arginase I produced twice as much putrescine and more spermidine after treatment with 8-BrcAMP than cells expressing beta-galactosidase. These results suggest that endogenous levels of arginase I are limiting for polyamine synthesis, but not for NO synthesis, in activated macrophage cells. This study also demonstrates that it is possible to modulate arginase I levels enough to impact polyamine synthesis without affecting induced NO synthesis.

title: Opposing Effects of PKCθ and WASp on Symmetry Breaking and Relocation of the Immunological Synapse
text: The immunological synapse (IS) is a critical interface between T cells and antigen-presenting cells, characterized by the formation of supramolecular activation clusters (SMACs). To date, no studies have investigated the dynamics of naive T cell IS formation during antigen recognition. Our findings reveal that IS formation is a cyclical process, consisting of periods of stable IS formation and autonomous naive T cell migration. The migration phase is mediated by PKCtheta, which is localized to the F-actin-dependent peripheral (p)SMAC. Interestingly, PKCtheta-deficient T cells exhibit hyperstable IS in vitro and in vivo, accompanied by increased fast oscillations in the distal SMAC but reduced slow oscillations in pSMAC integrity. IS reformation is mediated by the Wiscott Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASp), which displays normal IS formation but is unable to reform IS after migration unless PKCtheta is inhibited. Our findings suggest that PKCtheta and WASp exert opposing control over IS stability through pSMAC symmetry breaking and reformation.

title: Integrins regulate microtubule nucleating activity of centrosome through mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (MEK/ERK) signaling.
text: Microtubule nucleation is a crucial step in the formation of the microtubule cytoskeleton, and recent studies have shown that androgen and Src promote microtubule nucleation and γ-tubulin accumulation at the centrosome. In this study, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms by which androgen and Src regulate these processes and investigate the potential role of integrins in these processes. To achieve this, we employed a tyrosine-to-alanine substitution in the membrane-proximal NPIY motif of the integrin β1 tail, which significantly decreased microtubule nucleation and γ-tubulin accumulation at the centrosome. Our findings indicate that the formation of the androgen receptor-Src complex and the activation of downstream signaling pathways are significantly suppressed when cells are adhered by the mutant integrin. Inhibitor studies revealed that microtubule nucleation requires MEK/ERK signaling but not PI3K/AKT signaling. Interestingly, the expression of activated RAF-1 was sufficient to rescue microtubule nucleation inhibited by the mutant integrin by promoting the centrosomal accumulation of γ-tubulin. Our data establish a novel integrin signaling paradigm, where integrins regulate microtubule nucleation by promoting the formation of androgen receptor-Src signaling complexes to activate the MEK/ERK signaling pathway.

title: Consumption of added sugars from liquid but not solid sources predicts impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance among youth at risk of obesity.
text: Little is known about the long-term associations between added sugar consumption (both solid and liquid sources) and glucose-insulin homeostasis in children. In a cohort of 630 Caucasian children aged 8-10 years with at least one obese biological parent, added sugar intake was assessed through three 24-hour dietary recalls at baseline. Two years later, the cohort was followed up with 564 participants, and changes in added sugar intake were examined in multivariate linear regression models adjusting for baseline level, age, sex, Tanner stage, energy intake, fat mass (using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry), and physical activity (measured through 7 days of accelerometry). Consumption of added sugars in either liquid or solid sources was not significantly related to changes in adiposity measures (fat mass, body mass index, or waist circumference). However, a higher consumption of added sugars from liquid sources (10 g/day) was associated with a 0.04 mmol/L increase in fasting glucose, a 2.3 pmol/L increase in fasting insulin, a 0.1 unit increase in homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), and a 0.4 unit decrease in Matsuda-insulin sensitivity index (Matsuda-ISI) in all participants (P < 0.01). No associations were observed between solid sources of added sugar consumption and these measures. Overweight/obese children at baseline had greater increases in adiposity indicators, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR, and decreases in Matsuda-ISI during the two-year period compared to normal-weight children. Consumption of added sugars from liquid sources was a risk factor for the development of impaired glucose homeostasis and insulin resistance over two years among youth at risk of obesity.

title: Towards an improved investment approach for an effective response to HIV/AIDS.
text: Significant changes are required to adopt a more targeted and strategic approach to investment in response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic, leading to long-term benefits. The current advocacy for resources has relied on a commodity-based approach, scaling up numerous strategies without considering their relative effectiveness. We propose a strategic investment framework that aims to improve the management of national and international HIV/AIDS responses. Our framework incorporates efficiency gains through community mobilization, synergies between program elements, and the extension of antiretroviral therapy for HIV transmission prevention. It categorizes investments into three categories: six basic programmatic activities, interventions creating an enabling environment, and programmatic efforts in other health and development sectors related to HIV/AIDS. Achieving universal access to HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support by 2015 would require an estimated annual investment of at least US$22 billion. Implementing the new investment framework would avert 12·2 million new HIV infections and 7·4 million AIDS deaths between 2011 and 2020 compared to continuing current approaches, resulting in 29·4 million life-years gained. The framework is cost-effective, with an estimated cost of $1060 per life-year gained, and the additional investment proposed would be largely offset by savings in treatment costs alone.

title: Pivotal Roles of T-Helper 17-Related Cytokines, IL-17, IL-22, and IL-23, in Inflammatory Diseases
text: T-helper 17 (Th17) cells are defined by their production of interleukin-17 (IL-17, also known as IL-17A), IL-17F, IL-21, and IL-22, as well as potentially tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and IL-6 upon certain stimulation. IL-23, which promotes Th17 cell development, plays a crucial role in this process, along with IL-17 and IL-22 produced by these cells, in various inflammatory diseases such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, colitis, and Concanavalin A-induced hepatitis. In this review, we will focus on the functional role of Th17 cells and their cytokines, including IL-17, IL-22, and IL-23, in both mouse models and human inflammatory diseases.

title: LXRS and FXR: the yin and yang of cholesterol and fat metabolism.
text: Liver X receptors (LXRs) and farnesoid X receptor (FXR) are nuclear receptors that serve as intracellular sensors for sterols and bile acids, respectively. Upon recognition of their ligands, these receptors trigger transcriptional responses that maintain a delicate, finely tuned balance in the metabolism of cholesterol and bile acids. LXRs also facilitate the efficient storage of energy derived from carbohydrates and fats, whereas FXR activation leads to a decrease in triglyceride levels and modulation of glucose metabolism. The intricate, dual interaction between these two receptor systems suggests that they have coevolved to form a highly sensitive and efficient system for maintaining total body fat and cholesterol homeostasis. Recent research has also highlighted the tissue-specific actions of these receptors, which are essential for proper functioning of various organ systems, including the cardiovascular, immune, reproductive, endocrine pancreas, renal, and central nervous systems. As such, LXRs and FXR represent promising therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of a wide range of metabolic and lipid-related disorders.

title: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus/human herpesvirus type 8-positive solid lymphomas: a tissue-based variant of primary effusion lymphoma.
text: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), also known as human herpesvirus type 8, is consistently identified in Kaposi's sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma (PEL), and multicentric Castleman's disease. In this study, we report four cases of KSHV-positive solid lymphomas that occurred in AIDS patients (cases 1-3) and in a HIV-seronegative individual (case 4). The patients presented with extranodal masses in the abdomen (cases 1, 3, and 4) or skin (case 2), as well as nodal involvement, including Kaposi's sarcoma (case 3). The gastrointestinal tract was also affected in two patients (cases 1 and 3). Unlike KSHV-positive lymphomas, these patients did not develop a lymphomatous effusion. KSHV was detected in the tumor cells of all cases through immunohistochemistry and polymerase chain reaction. Epstein-Barr virus was detected in two of the HIV-related cases. All KSHV-positive solid lymphomas exhibited PEL-like cell morphology. To investigate the relationship between these disorders and PEL, KSHV-positive solid lymphomas were analyzed for the expression of a set of genes previously shown to define PEL tumor cells through gene profiling analysis. The results showed that the expression of these genes in KSHV-positive lymphomas was similar to that of PEL but distinct from KSHV-negative AIDS-associated diffuse large cell lymphomas. Given the similar pathobiological features of KSHV-positive solid lymphomas to PEL, our findings suggest that these tumors should be considered as a tissue-based variant of classical PEL, regardless of HIV status.

title: STAR: ultrafast universal RNA-seq aligner.
text:
MOTIVATION:
The accurate alignment of high-throughput RNA-seq data is a challenging and unresolved problem due to the non-contiguous nature of transcripts, relatively short read lengths, and the constantly increasing throughput of sequencing technologies. Current RNA-seq aligners suffer from high mapping error rates, slow mapping speeds, read length limitations, and mapping biases.
RESULTS:
To align our large (>80 billion reads) ENCODE Transcriptome RNA-seq dataset, we developed the Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference (STAR) software, leveraging a novel RNA-seq alignment algorithm that utilizes sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching. STAR outperforms other aligners by a factor of >50 in mapping speed, aligning 550 million 2 × 76 bp paired-end reads per hour on a modest 12-core server, while improving alignment sensitivity and precision. STAR can detect both canonical and non-canonical splices, as well as chimeric (fusion) transcripts, and can map full-length RNA sequences. Experimentally validating 1960 novel intergenic splice junctions using Roche 454 sequencing of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction amplicons, we observed an 80-90% success rate, confirming the high accuracy of the STAR mapping strategy.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION:
STAR is implemented as a standalone C++ code and is available under the GPLv3 license. It can be downloaded from http://code.google.com/p/rna-star/.

title: Effect of alendronate on risk of fracture in women with low bone density but without vertebral fractures: results from the Fracture Intervention Trial.
text:
The study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of alendronate sodium in reducing the risk of clinical and vertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with low bone mineral density (BMD) but no vertebral fractures. The study was a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trial conducted at 11 community-based clinical research centers. A total of 4432 women aged 54-81 years with a femoral neck BMD of 0.68 g/cm2 or less were randomly assigned to either alendronate or placebo. All participants received a supplement containing calcium and vitamin D, and those in the alendronate group received 5 mg/d of alendronate sodium for 2 years followed by 10 mg/d for the remainder of the trial. The primary outcome measures were clinical fractures confirmed by x-ray reports, new vertebral deformities detected by morphometric measurements on radiographs, and BMD measured by dual x-ray absorptiometry.
The results showed that alendronate increased BMD at all sites studied and reduced clinical fractures from 312 in the placebo group to 272 in the intervention group, but not significantly so. Alendronate also reduced clinical fractures by 36% in women with baseline osteoporosis at the femoral neck, but there was no significant reduction among those with higher BMD. Additionally, alendronate decreased the risk of radiographic vertebral fractures by 44% overall. The study found that alendronate did not increase the risk of gastrointestinal or other adverse effects.
In conclusion, the study found that 4 years of alendronate sodium safely increased BMD and decreased the risk of first vertebral deformity in postmenopausal women with low BMD but no vertebral fractures. Alendronate significantly reduced the risk of clinical fractures among women with osteoporosis but not among women with higher BMD.

title: AP-1/sigma1B-adaptin mediates endosomal synaptic vesicle recycling, learning and memory.
text:
Synaptic vesicle recycling is a crucial process that involves the mediator protein AP-2/clathrin, but the extent to which the endosomal pathway is involved in this process remains unclear. Previous studies have shown that mice lacking the tissue-specific AP-1-sigma1B complex exhibit impaired synaptic vesicle recycling in hippocampal synapses. The ubiquitously expressed AP-1-sigma1A complex, on the other hand, mediates protein sorting between the trans-Golgi network and early endosomes in vertebrates. Interestingly, the expressions of sigma1A and sigma1B are highest in the brain.
Recent studies have shed light on the molecular mechanism underlying a severe human X-chromosome-linked mental retardation. In cultured neurons from sigma1B-deficient mice, synaptic vesicle reformation is reduced upon stimulation, and large endosomal intermediates accumulate. Moreover, sigma1B-deficient mice exhibit reduced motor coordination and severely impaired long-term spatial memory. These findings provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying neurological disorders.

title: Update of the FANTOM web resource: high resolution transcriptome of diverse cell types in mammals
text: Upon the initial release of the fifth iteration of the Functional Annotation of Mammalian Genomes (FANTOM5) collaborative project, we compiled a comprehensive collection of primary data and database systems within the FANTOM web resource (<http://fantom.gsc.riken.jp>). This centralized platform enables researchers to investigate the complex realm of transcriptional regulation and cellular states. Through the course of our collaboration, we have continued to expand and enhance the database systems, making them invaluable resources for the scientific community. We believe that the recent update to FANTOM5 will deepen the understanding of mammalian cellular organization and enable new discoveries. In this article, we detail the contents of FANTOM5, highlight recent developments in the web resource, and provide insights into future directions.

title: Adverse Events Associated With the Treatment of Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
text:
Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) poses a significant challenge to public health, requiring long-duration treatment with multiple second-line drugs. Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a crucial clinical consideration in patients undergoing anti-MDR-TB treatment, as they can significantly impact treatment outcomes. To investigate the frequency and type of ADEs associated with MDR-TB therapy, we conducted a systematic review of the literature.
Using the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, we searched for studies published from inception to October 1, 2012, with additional manual search of the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. We included studies that reported ADEs in MDR-TB patients treated with a regimen containing second-line drugs. Pooled estimates of incidence were calculated for each specific type of ADE using a random-effects model, with 95% confidence intervals.
Our analysis included 5346 MDR-TB patients, of whom 2602 (57.3%) experienced at least one ADE. The three most common side effects were gastrointestinal disorders (32.1%), ototoxicity (14.6%), and psychiatric disorders (13.2%). Subgroup analyses based on study population, previous tuberculosis treatment, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) prevalence, and length of treatment did not reveal any significant differences between groups. Among 1519 patients who developed ADEs with available data on impact on MDR-TB therapy, 70.4% required modification of MDR-TB treatment.
Our findings highlight the need for close monitoring and aggressive management of ADEs in MDR-TB patients, particularly for ototoxicity and psychiatric disorders. The high incidence of ADEs in this patient population underscores the importance of careful drug selection and dosing, as well as ongoing monitoring and supportive care.

title: Presynaptically Localized Cyclic GMP-Dependent Protein Kinase 1 Is a Key Determinant of Spinal Synaptic Potentiation and Pain Hypersensitivity
text:
The article discusses the role of Protein Kinase G1 (PKG-I) in the expression of synaptic long-term potentiation (LTP) in the spinal cord, which is implicated in pain hypersensitivity. Previous studies have shown that the NMDA receptor-NO pathway and the downstream second messenger, cGMP, are involved in these processes. However, the specific identity of cGMP targets mediating spinal LTP, their mechanisms of action, and their locus in the spinal circuitry are still unclear.
The study found that PKG-I localized presynaptically in nociceptor terminals plays a crucial role in the expression of spinal LTP. Using the Cre-lox P system, the researchers generated nociceptor-specific knockout mice lacking PKG-I specifically in presynaptic terminals of nociceptors in the spinal cord, but not in post-synaptic neurons or elsewhere (SNS-PKG-I(-/-) mice). Patch clamp recordings showed that activity-induced LTP at identified synapses between nociceptors and spinal neurons projecting to the periaqueductal grey (PAG) was completely abolished in SNS-PKG-I(-/-) mice, although basal synaptic transmission was not affected. Analyses of synaptic failure rates and paired-pulse ratios indicated a role for presynaptic PKG-I in regulating the probability of neurotransmitter release. Inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor 1 and myosin light chain kinase were recruited as key phosphorylation targets of presynaptic PKG-I in nociceptive neurons. Finally, behavioral analyses in vivo showed marked defects in SNS-PKG-I(-/-) mice in several models of activity-induced nociceptive hypersensitivity, and pharmacological studies identified a clear contribution of PKG-I expressed in spinal terminals of nociceptors.
In conclusion, the study demonstrates that presynaptic mechanisms involving an increase in release probability from nociceptors are operational in the expression of synaptic LTP on spinal-PAG projection neurons, and that PKG-I localized in presynaptic nociceptor terminals plays an essential role in this process to regulate pain sensitivity.

title: A Sleeping Beauty mutagenesis screen reveals a tumor suppressor role for Ncoa2/Src-2 in liver cancer.
text: The Sleeping Beauty (SB) transposon mutagenesis system is a powerful tool that enables the identification of mutations that accelerate tumor growth. In this study, we aimed to identify genes that cooperate with MYC, a frequently dysregulated gene in human cancer, to promote liver tumorigenesis. We conducted a forward genetic screen using a mouse model of MYC-induced liver cancer and SB-mediated mutagenesis. We analyzed 63 liver tumor nodules and identified at least 16 genes/loci that contribute to accelerated tumor development. To validate these findings, we employed RNAi-mediated knockdown in a liver progenitor cell line, which revealed three genes, Ncoa2/Src-2, Zfx, and Dtnb, as tumor suppressors in liver cancer. Additionally, we found that deleting Ncoa2/Src-2 in mice increases susceptibility to diethylnitrosamine-induced liver tumorigenesis. These findings highlight genes and pathways that restrain MYC-mediated liver tumorigenesis, providing potential targets for cancer therapy.

title: Protein-Protein Interaction Inhibition (2P2I)-Oriented Chemical Library Accelerates Hit Discovery.
text: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) hold immense potential for therapeutic intervention, and recent breakthroughs have identified key principles for identifying the next generation of innovative drugs. We utilized these rules to create an oriented chemical library consisting of diverse "PPI-like" modulators with cores identified as privileged structures in therapeutics. We then evaluated the resulting 1664 structurally diverse compounds on a series of representative protein-protein interfaces using homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF) technology. Our findings revealed significant enrichment factors for certain PPI classes, which correlated with the predicted "druggability" of the targets. As a proof-of-concept, we focused on selectivity profiles, 3D molecular modes of action resolved by X-ray crystallography, and biological activities of identified hits targeting the well-defined "druggable" bromodomains of the bromo and extraterminal (BET) family. Our study demonstrates the power of machine learning-based oriented chemical libraries in accelerating the identification of hits targeting PPIs. A broader application of this methodology to a larger set of compounds will expedite the discovery of novel and potent probes for this challenging class of targets.

title: Molecular characterization of endometrial cancer: a correlative study assessing microsatellite instability, MLH1 hypermethylation, DNA mismatch repair protein expression, and PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, and BRAF mutation analysis.
text: In this study, the authors aimed to comprehensively analyze the molecular genetic alterations in a large cohort of endometrial cancers using multiple techniques. They examined 96 cases for genomic alterations, including microsatellite instability (MSI), MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, p53 and mismatch repair protein expression, and mutations in PTEN, PIK3CA, KRAS, and BRAF. The study found that at least one alteration was identified in 48 of 87 (55%) specimens tested for PTEN, making it the most common abnormality. A PIK3CA alteration was observed in 16 (17%) specimens, and 29 of 94 (31%) MSI-tested tumors exhibited an MSI-H phenotype. Of the 29 MSI-H cases, 24 (83%) were positive for methylation of the MLH1 promoter region. Immunohistochemistry results showed loss of expression of MLH1/PMS2 in 23 (82%) of the 28 MSI-H cases, and KRAS mutations were identified in 12 (13%) of the cases. No BRAF V600E mutations were found. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the molecular genetic alterations in endometrial cancers, highlighting the importance of MLH1 promoter hypermethylation and PTEN mutations as potential therapeutic targets.

title: Identification of indole-3-carboxylic acid as mediator of priming against Plectosphaerella cucumerina.
text:
Plant resistance to the necrotrophic pathogen Plectosphaerella cucumerina is mediated by a combination of several hormonal-controlled signaling pathways. The priming agent β-aminobutyric acid (BABA) can effectively induce resistance against this pathogen by stimulating the deposition of callose-rich cell walls. In the current research, it is demonstrated that BABA-Induced Resistance (BABA-IR) against P. cucumerina in Arabidopsis has additional components, including the induction of defenses mediated by indolic derivatives.
A chromatographic approach for detecting and characterizing metabolites enhanced by BABA compared to water-treated plants only when the challenge is present has been developed. The metabolites that match this criteria are considered to be primed by BABA. The analytical procedure involves the combination of liquid chromatography (LC) with a triple quadrupole (TQD) detector in a precursor ion scanning mode. Using this analytical system, a signal at m/z 160 in negative electro-spray mode is primed by BABA in infected plants. Subsequent exact mass analysis in a quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer revealed that this ion is the indole-derivative metabolite indole-3-carboxylic acid (I3CA). The identity of I3CA was definitively confirmed by comparing its retention time and fragmentation spectra with a commercial standard. Quantification of I3CA in primed plants showed that this indolic metabolite is specifically primed by BABA upon P. cucumerina infection, while other indolic compounds such as IAA and camalexin are not.
Taking these observations together with the known role of callose in priming against this pathogen, suggests that priming is not a single mechanism but rather a multicomponent defense.

title: Evaluation of networks of randomized trials.
text: Randomized trials can be analyzed and interpreted as individual experiments or as part of a broader body of evidence. The amount and complexity of available randomized data vary depending on the topic. Systematic reviews can help identify gaps in the existing evidence, highlight discrepancies between trials, and inform future trials. A relatively new and controversial extension of systematic reviews, mixed treatment comparison (MTC) meta-analysis, has gained popularity recently. MTC meta-analysis can provide valuable insights into the available randomized evidence from multiple trials by ranking many treatments beyond simple pairwise comparisons. However, evaluating networks of trials also presents unique challenges and limitations. This article focuses on the statistical methodology for MTC meta-analysis, addressing inconsistency evaluation methods, methodological gaps, network geometry, and asymmetry metrics. We also discuss the implications of these factors in informing future trial planning.

title: Metabolic regulation by the mitochondrial phosphatase PTPMT1 is required for hematopoietic stem cell differentiation.
text:
The regulation and coordination of mitochondrial metabolism with hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) self-renewal and differentiation are not fully understood. Our study reveals that depletion of PTPMT1, a PTEN-like mitochondrial phosphatase, in inducible or hematopoietic-cell-specific knockout mice led to hematopoietic failure due to changes in the cell cycle and a block in the differentiation of HSCs. Interestingly, the HSC pool was increased by approximately 40-fold in PTPMT1 knockout mice. Reintroduction of wild-type PTPMT1, but not catalytically deficient PTPMT1 or truncated PTPMT1 lacking mitochondrial localization, restored differentiation capabilities of PTPMT1 knockout HSCs. Our findings demonstrate that PTPMT1 plays a crucial role in the metabolic regulation of HSC function.
Mitochondrial metabolism is essential for HSC function, and our study shows that PTPMT1 plays a critical role in this process. We found that depletion of PTPMT1 altered mitochondrial metabolism, leading to changes in the cell cycle and a block in the differentiation of HSCs. Additionally, we discovered that PTPMT1 deficiency directly enhances the activity of mitochondrial uncoupling protein 2, which is involved in the regulation of mitochondrial metabolism.
Our study also reveals that PTPMT1 is essential for the proper functioning of HSCs in different lineages, including myeloid, T lymphoid, and B lymphoid progenitors. However, depletion of PTPMT1 from these progenitors did not cause any defects in lineage-specific knockout mice. These findings suggest that PTPMT1 plays a unique role in regulating HSC function and metabolism.
In conclusion, our study establishes a crucial role of PTPMT1 in the metabolic regulation of HSC function. The regulation and coordination of mitochondrial metabolism with HSC self-renewal and differentiation are complex processes that are not fully understood. Further research is needed to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying these processes and to identify potential therapeutic targets for hematopoietic disorders.

title: GSK-3-mediated phosphorylation enhances Maf-transforming activity.
text:
The Maf oncoproteins are b-Zip transcription factors belonging to the AP-1 superfamily, which are involved in various cellular processes, including development, metabolism, and tumorigenesis. Studies have shown that Maf proteins are overexpressed in approximately 50% of human multiple myelomas. Our research has uncovered a novel mechanism by which Maf oncoproteins are regulated, involving GSK-3-dependent phosphorylation. Specifically, we have found that phosphorylation of Maf proteins by GSK-3 can increase their oncogenic activity, and we have identified a gene-expression subprogram regulated by GSK-3-mediated Maf phosphorylation that is involved in extracellular matrix remodeling and relevant to cancer progression.
Our findings indicate that GSK-3 triggers the sequential phosphorylation of MafA on residues S61, T57, T53, and S49, leading to its ubiquitination and degradation. However, this phosphorylation event paradoxically increases MafA-mediated transcriptional activity through the recruitment of the coactivator P/CAF. We have further demonstrated that P/CAF protects MafA from ubiquitination and degradation, suggesting that upon the release of the coactivator complex, MafA becomes polyubiquitinated and degraded to terminate the response.
In summary, our study has uncovered a novel mechanism by which Maf oncoproteins are regulated, involving GSK-3-dependent phosphorylation and ubiquitination. Our findings provide new insights into the complex regulatory networks that control cellular processes and have important implications for our understanding of cancer development and progression.

title: NETs are a source of citrullinated autoantigens and stimulate inflammatory responses in rheumatoid arthritis.
text: The early stages of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are not well understood, but the formation of autoantibodies against citrullinated protein antigens (ACPAs) is believed to be a key event in the disease's pathogenesis. Neutrophils from patients with various autoimmune diseases exhibit enhanced neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, which exposes autoantigens in the context of immunostimulatory molecules. To investigate the role of NETosis in RA, we examined its occurrence in circulating and synovial fluid neutrophils from RA patients compared to healthy controls and patients with osteoarthritis (OA). We found that neutrophils from RA patients exhibited enhanced NETosis compared to those from healthy controls and OA patients. Furthermore, we observed that NETs infiltrated RA synovial tissue, rheumatoid nodules, and skin. NETosis was found to correlate with the presence and levels of ACPA and with systemic inflammatory markers. RA sera and immunoglobulin fractions from RA patients with high levels of ACPA and/or rheumatoid factor significantly enhanced NETosis, and the NETs induced by these autoantibodies displayed distinct protein content. Notably, during NETosis, neutrophils externalized the citrullinated autoantigens implicated in RA pathogenesis, and anti-citrullinated vimentin antibodies potently induced NET formation. Additionally, the inflammatory cytokines interleukin-17A (IL-17A) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) induced NETosis in RA neutrophils. In turn, NETs significantly augmented inflammatory responses in RA and OA synovial fibroblasts, including the induction of IL-6, IL-8, chemokines, and adhesion molecules. These findings suggest that accelerated NETosis plays a key role in RA pathogenesis by externalizing citrullinated autoantigens and immunostimulatory molecules, which may promote aberrant adaptive and innate immune responses in the joint and periphery, perpetuating pathogenic mechanisms in the disease.

title: Is autoimmunity the Achilles' heel of cancer immunotherapy?
text: The advent of immuno-oncology as a groundbreaking strategy for metastatic cancer treatment will require clinicians to integrate this innovative approach with traditional therapies such as chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted small-molecule compounds. Simultaneously, it is crucial to comprehend the constraints and side effects of immunotherapy, as they are becoming increasingly apparent as the treatment becomes more widespread, particularly as first- and second-line therapies. Initially, immunotherapy was perceived as a relatively less toxic cancer treatment compared to others available, but as its use becomes more common, immunotoxicity and autoimmunity are emerging as significant challenges. In this Perspective, we examine evidence that suggests the occurrence of immunotoxicity is a positive sign for patients, explore potential mechanisms related to the induction of autoimmunity, and discuss strategies to mitigate immunotoxicity. Finally, we outline the need for ongoing research and reporting to minimize these side effects and optimize the benefits of immuno-oncology.

title: Trophoblast differentiation defect in human embryonic stem cells lacking PIG-A and GPI-anchored cell-surface proteins.
text:
Human embryonic stem (hES) cells have the ability to differentiate into various cell types, including those from the three embryonic germ layers and extraembryonic tissues such as trophoblasts. However, the mechanisms that govern the lineage choices of hES cells are not well understood. In this study, we generated two independent hES cell clones that lack a specific group of cell surface molecules called glycosyl-phosphatidyl-inositol-anchored proteins (GPI-APs). We found that the GPI-AP deficiency in these two hES clones is due to a deficiency in the gene expression of PIG-A (phosphatidyl-inositol-glycan class A), which is necessary for the first step of GPI synthesis.
Despite the GPI-AP deficiency, the hES cells were able to form embryoid bodies and initiate cell differentiation into the three embryonic germ layers. However, they failed to form trophoblasts after differentiation induction by embryoid body formation or by adding exogenous BMP4. We discovered that the defect in trophoblast formation was due to the lack of GPI-anchored BMP coreceptors, which resulted in impaired full BMP4 signaling activation in the GPI-AP-deficient hES cells. These findings reveal that GPI-AP-enhanced full activation of BMP signaling is essential for human trophoblast formation.

title: CRISPR Interference Limits Horizontal Gene Transfer in Staphylococci by Targeting DNA
text: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in bacteria and archaea can occur through various mechanisms, including phage transduction, transformation, and conjugation. Of particular importance is the latter, as it plays a significant role in the dissemination of antibiotic resistance. Clustered, regularly interspaced, short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) loci, in turn, provide sequence-directed immunity against phages. A clinical isolate of Staphylococcus epidermidis harbors a CRISPR spacer that matches the nickase gene present in the vast majority of staphylococcal conjugative plasmids. Our findings demonstrate that CRISPR interference prevents conjugation and plasmid transformation in S. epidermidis. Intriguingly, insertion of a self-splicing intron into the nickase gene blocks interference, even though the target sequence is reconstituted in the spliced mRNA, indicating that the interference machinery directly targets DNA. These results suggest that CRISPR loci can counteract multiple routes of HGT and potentially limit the spread of antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria.

title: Development of leukemia in donor cells after allogeneic stem cell transplantation--a survey of the European Group for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (EBMT).
text: Leukemia in donor cells (donor cell leukemia; DCL) is a rare but severe complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation (SCT) that has been poorly characterized. To address this gap in knowledge, a questionnaire survey was conducted among European Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group (EBMT) centers, which included 91 centers and 10489 allogeneic SCT cases between 1982 and 2003. The survey identified 14 cases of DCL, most of which had a myeloid phenotype (7 cases of acute myeloid leukemia, 3 cases of acute lymphocytic leukemia, and 1 case of chronic myeloid leukemia). Molecular analysis of chimerism was used to demonstrate the donor cell origin in most cases. The type and cytogenetic alterations of DCL were found to be independent of the original disease. The median time between transplantation and diagnosis of DCL was 17 months (4-164), and no specific risk factors for DCL were identified, including conditioning, donor, graft manipulation, graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis, or subsequent complications. Chemotherapy induced remissions in DCL, and 2 of 5 patients remain alive in remission after a second transplant. Notably, none of the stem cell donors developed hematologic malignancies during the median follow-up period of 9 years (range 6-30 years). These findings suggest that DCL is an extremely rare complication of allogeneic SCT, and treatment attempts with chemotherapy and a second SCT are justified. Additionally, donors are not at an increased risk of developing hematologic malignancies.

title: Lack of evidence of transfusion transmission of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in a US surveillance study.
text:
Since 2004, there have been reports of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) transmissions through blood transfusions in the United Kingdom, raising concerns about the potential risk of non-variant or classic forms of CJD transmission through blood donations. To investigate this further, researchers conducted a study to identify and follow up blood donors who developed CJD and the recipients of their blood components.
The study included 36 blood donors who later developed CJD and 436 recipients of their blood components. The researchers identified the recipients' vital status and cause of death by matching their personal identifiers with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Death Index database. They conducted these searches after recipients were enrolled in the study and annually thereafter for those who remained alive.
The study found that the recipients of blood components from donors who developed CJD survived a total of 2096.0 person-years after transfusion, with 144 recipients surviving 5 years or longer and 68 of them receiving blood donated 60 or fewer months before the onset of CJD in the donor. However, the researchers did not identify any recipients with CJD.
The results of this large, ongoing lookback study provide no evidence of transfusion transmission of CJD and reinforce the conclusion that the risk of transfusion transmission of prion disease by CJD donors is significantly lower than the comparable risk of transmission by vCJD donors.

title: Large-scale hypomethylated blocks associated with Epstein-Barr virus-induced B-cell immortalization.
text: Alterations in DNA methylation are ubiquitous in human cancer across all stages of development, providing a crucial insight into the mechanisms of carcinogenesis. A systematic approach to understanding the timing and nature of these alterations can be achieved by analyzing them in the context of a defined oncogenic agent, such as the human oncogenic herpesvirus Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). In this study, we employed whole-genome bisulfite sequencing to investigate the impact of EBV immortalization on the methylome of normal B-cells, activated B-cells, and EBV-immortalized B-cells from the same three individuals. Our findings were unexpected, as we observed large-scale hypomethylated blocks comprising approximately two-thirds of the genome that were induced by EBV immortalization but not by B-cell activation per se. These regions largely corresponded to hypomethylated blocks observed in human cancer and were associated with gene-expression hypervariability, similar to human cancer, and consistent with a model of epigenomic change promoting tumor cell heterogeneity. Additionally, we identified small-scale changes in DNA methylation near CpG islands. These results suggest that disruption of methylation is an early and critical step in malignant transformation.

title: Stem cell self-renewal specified by JAK-STAT activation in response to a support cell cue.
text: Stem cells produce a wide range of differentiated cell types throughout adulthood, such as blood, skin, and sperm. These stem cells have the ability to divide and produce daughter cells that either self-renew or differentiate. Although the microenvironment surrounding the stem cells, known as the "niche," can influence their fate decisions, few signals from the niche have been identified that specifically promote stem cell self-renewal. Here, we investigate the role of apical hub cells in the Drosophila testis as a niche that supports stem cell self-renewal. These hub cells produce the ligand Unpaired (Upd), which activates the JAK-STAT pathway in adjacent germ cells, specifying self-renewal and the continual maintenance of the germ line stem cell population.

title: Effects of interventions in pregnancy on maternal weight and obstetric outcomes: meta-analysis of randomised evidence
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effects of dietary and lifestyle interventions during pregnancy on maternal and fetal weight, and to quantify the effects of these interventions on obstetric outcomes.
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
Data sources: Major databases from inception to January 2012 without language restrictions.
Study selection: Randomized controlled trials that evaluated any dietary or lifestyle interventions with potential to influence maternal weight during pregnancy and outcomes of pregnancy.
Data synthesis: Results were summarized as relative risks for dichotomous data and mean differences for continuous data.
Results: A total of 44 relevant randomized controlled trials (7278 women) were identified, evaluating three categories of interventions: diet, physical activity, and a mixed approach. Overall, there was a 1.42 kg reduction (95% confidence interval 0.95 to 1.89 kg) in gestational weight gain with any intervention compared to control. With all interventions combined, there were no significant differences in birth weight (mean difference -50 g, -100 to 0 g) and the incidence of large for gestational age (relative risk 0.85, 0.66 to 1.09) or small for gestational age (1.00, 0.78 to 1.28) babies between the groups, though physical activity was associated with reduced birth weight (mean difference -60 g, -120 to -10 g). Interventions were also associated with a reduced risk of pre-eclampsia (0.74, 0.60 to 0.92) and shoulder dystocia (0.39, 0.22 to 0.70), with no significant effect on other critically important outcomes. Dietary intervention resulted in the largest reduction in maternal gestational weight gain (3.84 kg, 2.45 to 5.22 kg), with improved pregnancy outcomes compared to other interventions. The overall evidence rating was low to very low for important outcomes such as pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, and preterm delivery.
Conclusion: Dietary and lifestyle interventions during pregnancy can reduce maternal gestational weight gain and improve outcomes for both mother and baby. Among the interventions, those based on diet are the most effective and are associated with reductions in maternal gestational weight gain and improved obstetric outcomes.

title: Tetraspanin 3 Is Required for the Development and Propagation of Acute Myelogenous Leukemia.
text: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a fierce and often unresponsive cancer that affects both adults and children. Therefore, identifying key factors involved in AML growth is crucial for developing novel treatment strategies. Our study reveals that Tetraspanin 3 (Tspan3) is a target of the RNA-binding protein Musashi 2, which plays a pivotal role in AML. To investigate the functional significance of Tspan3 in AML, we generated Tspan3 knockout mice that showed no obvious defects at birth. However, Tspan3 deletion impaired the self-renewal and disease propagation of leukemia stem cells, leading to significantly improved survival in mouse models of AML. Moreover, Tspan3 inhibition also suppressed the growth of AML patient samples in vitro, indicating that Tspan3 is a crucial regulator of aggressive leukemias. Our findings further suggest that Tspan3 deficiency disrupts responses to the chemokine CXCL12/SDF-1 and leads to defects in AML localization within the niche, highlighting a role for Tspan3 in oncogenesis.

title: Reorganization of enhancer patterns in transition from naive to primed pluripotency.
text: Naive and primed pluripotency are characterized by distinct signaling pathways, gene expression profiles, and developmental potentials, but they share common transcription factors: Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog. Our study reveals that the transition between these two pluripotent states is associated with the redistribution of Oct4 protein and global reorganization of enhancer chromatin landscapes. Through genomic and biochemical analyses, we identified candidate mediators of primed state-specific Oct4 binding, including Otx2 and Zic2/3. Interestingly, premature overexpression of Otx2 can drive the exit from the naive state, leading to the expression of a subset of primed pluripotency-associated genes and reprogramming Oct4 to new enhancer sites. However, the ability of Otx2 to access new enhancer regions is influenced by its levels, the cis-encoded properties of the sites, and the signaling environment. Our findings shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying pluripotency and highlight the context-dependent nature of transcription factor function.

title: Topoisomerase II plays an essential role as a swivelase in the late stage of SV40 chromosome replication in vitro.
text: The effects of topoisomerases I and II on the replication of SV40 DNA were investigated using an in vitro replication system consisting of purified proteins that mimic the monopolymerase reaction. In the presence of both topoisomerases, two distinct nascent DNA strands were formed. One product arising from the replication of the leading template strand was approximately half the size of the template DNA, while the other product derived from the lagging template strand consisted of shorter DNA fragments. These products were synthesized using both naked SV40 DNA and SV40 chromosomes. For the replication of naked SV40 DNA, either topoisomerase I or II maintained replication fork movement and supported complete leading strand synthesis. However, when SV40 chromosomes were replicated with the same proteins, reactions containing only topoisomerase I produced shorter leading strands. In contrast, reactions supplemented with topoisomerase II resulted in the accumulation of mature-sized DNA products. The addition of VP-16, a specific inhibitor of topoisomerase II, blocked elongation of the nascent DNA during the replication of SV40 chromosomes in the presence of crude extracts from HeLa cells, further supporting the role of topoisomerase II as a swivelase in the late stage of SV40 chromosome replication in vitro.

title: Bromodomain Proteins Contribute to Maintenance of Bloodstream Form Stage Identity in the African Trypanosome
text:
Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite responsible for African sleeping sickness, is transmitted to mammalian hosts through the bite of the tsetse fly. Once inside the host, the parasite assumes two distinct forms: the bloodstream form (BF) and the insect form. The BF resides in the host's bloodstream and is covered with a highly immunogenic protein called Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG), which helps the parasite evade the host's immune system. In contrast, the insect form is found in the tsetse fly and has a different surface composition.
To better understand how trypanosomes maintain their BF cell fate and evade the host's immune system, we investigated the role of bromodomain proteins in these processes. Bromodomain proteins are known to play a role in maintaining stem cell fate, and we hypothesized that they may also be involved in maintaining the BF cell fate in trypanosomes. Using small-molecule inhibitors and genetic mutants, we found that bromodomain proteins are indeed essential for maintaining the BF cell fate and immune evasion in trypanosomes.
Our studies revealed that bromodomain proteins disrupt two major immune evasion mechanisms used by trypanosomes to evade the host's immune system. First, they disrupt monoallelic expression of the highly variable VSG protein, which allows the parasite to evade the host's immune response. Second, they block rapid internalization of antibodies bound to VSG on the surface of the trypanosome, preventing the host's immune system from recognizing and eliminating the parasite.
Importantly, our findings also showed that inhibition of bromodomain proteins leads to a decrease in virulence in a mouse model of infection, establishing these proteins as potential therapeutic drug targets for trypanosomiasis. To further understand the mechanism of action of bromodomain inhibitors, we determined the crystal structure of a trypanosome bromodomain in complex with the inhibitor I-BET151. Our structure reveals a novel binding mode of the inhibitor, providing a promising starting point for the development of new drugs against trypanosomiasis.
In summary, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms of trypanosome immune evasion and identifies bromodomain proteins as potential therapeutic targets for trypanosomiasis. The determination of the crystal structure of a trypanosome bromodomain in complex with I-BET151 provides a valuable tool for the development of new drugs against this devastating disease.

title: Timing requirements for insulin/IGF-1 signaling in C. elegans.
text: The insulin/IGF-1 signaling pathway plays a crucial role in various physiological processes across many organisms, including longevity, reproduction, and diapause. Given its central importance in animal biology, we investigated when during an organism's life this pathway is activated to regulate these different processes. Our findings in Caenorhabditis elegans reveal that the pathway acts during adulthood, up until relatively advanced ages, to influence aging. In contrast, it regulates diapause during development. Furthermore, we found that the pathway controls longevity and reproduction independently of one another, suggesting that life-span regulation can be temporally dissociated from other physiological processes that may seem to compromise an organism's quality of life.

title: Predominance of Type 1 Innate Lymphoid Cells in the Rectal Mucosa of Patients With Non-Celiac Wheat Sensitivity: Reversal After a Wheat-Free Diet
text:
Objective:
Non-celiac wheat sensitivity (NCWS) is defined as a reaction to ingested wheat after excluding celiac disease and wheat allergy. Despite its prevalence, the pathogenesis of NCWS is not fully understood, and this study aimed to investigate the inflammatory response in the rectal mucosa of patients with well-defined NCWS.
Methods:
A prospective study included 22 patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)-like clinical presentation, diagnosed with NCWS through a double-blind placebo-controlled challenge. Eight IBS patients who did not improve on a wheat-free diet were used as controls. Two weeks after oral challenge with 80 grams of wheat daily, cells were isolated from rectal biopsies and characterized using fluorescence-activated cell sorting analysis for intracellular cytokines and surface markers.
Results:
Rectal biopsies from wheat-challenged NCWS patients showed a significant mucosal CD45(+) infiltrate consisting of CD3(+) and CD3(-) lymphocytes, with the latter producing more interferon (IFN)-γ than IBS controls. Approximately 30% of IFN-γ-producing CD45(+) cells were T-bet(+), CD56(-), NKP44(-), and CD117(-), indicating the presence of type-1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1). IFN-γ-producing ILC1 cells significantly decreased in 10 patients analyzed 2 weeks after they resumed a wheat-free diet.


Conclusion:
These findings suggest that, in patients with active NCWS, IFN-γ-producing ILC1 cells infiltrate the rectal mucosa, providing evidence for the role of this innate lymphoid cell population in the pathogenesis of NCWS.

title: Folding and Self-Assembly of the TatA Translocation Pore Based on a Charge Zipper Mechanism
text: We present a novel concept for the folding and self-assembly of pore-forming proteins, including the TatA complex from the Twin-arginine translocase, based on electrostatic "charge zippers." Each subunit of TatA consists of a transmembrane segment, an amphiphilic helix (APH), and a C-terminal densely charged region (DCR). The sequence of charges in the DCR is complementary to the charge pattern on the APH, suggesting that the protein can be "zipped up" by a ladder of seven salt bridges. The resulting hairpin structure is found to be of a length that matches the lipid bilayer thickness, thus allowing for the self-assembly of a transmembrane pore through intra- and intermolecular salt bridges. The feasibility of this concept was rationalized through molecular dynamics simulations, and experimental evidence was obtained by monitoring the monomer-oligomer equilibrium of specific charge mutants. Furthermore, the concept is extended to other membrane-associated proteins, such as the biofilm-inducing peptide TisB, the human antimicrobial peptide dermcidin, and the pestiviral E(RNS) protein, which are also found to exhibit similar "charge zippers."

title: Molecular mechanisms of ribosomal protein gene coregulation.
text: The 137 ribosomal protein gene (RPG) set in Saccharomyces cerevisiae serves as a model for the study of gene co-regulation. In this work, we employed a combination of chromatin immunoprecipitation exo (ChIP-exo) and near-base-pair resolution analysis to investigate the positional and functional organization of the regulators (Rap1, Fhl1, Ifh1, Sfp1, and Hmo1) and the transcription machinery (TFIIB, TFIID, and RNA polymerase II) that interact with the RPGs. Our findings reveal that the regulators Hmo1, Fhl1, Ifh1, and Sfp1 cross-link to promoter DNA in a RPG-specific manner and demarcate specific regions of the chromatin structure. Notably, Hmo1 extends 20-50 base pairs (bp) downstream of Fhl1, and upon RPG repression, Fhl1 remains in place while Hmo1 dissociates, leading to an upstream shift of the +1 nucleosome. These observations suggest that Hmo1 and Fhl1 may form two distinct regulatory barriers that influence the positioning of the +1 nucleosome and the assembly of transcription complexes. Additionally, our results demonstrate that specific TFIID subunits cross-link to Rap1 sites, providing insight into the native interactions between Rap1 and TFIID. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of sequence-specific DNA binding and its impact on nucleosome positioning and transcription complex assembly, highlighting the co-evolution of coregulation with coding sequences.

title: Lipoatrophy and severe metabolic disturbance in mice with fat-specific deletion of PPARγ.
text: Adipose tissue is a crucial metabolic organ, and its dysfunction is linked to the development of obesity, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease. The nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) is considered the primary regulator of adipocyte differentiation and function. Although its cell-autonomous role in adipogenesis has been demonstrated in cell culture, previous fat-specific knockouts of the murine PPARγ gene did not exhibit a significant in vivo phenotype. To create a unique fat-specific PPARγ knockout (PPARγ FKO) mouse model, we used Adipoq-Cre mice to drive adipose-specific recombination. Surprisingly, PPARγ FKO mice had almost no visible brown and white adipose tissue at 3 months of age. As a consequence, they had enlarged pancreatic islets, massive fatty livers, and dramatically elevated levels of blood glucose and serum insulin, accompanied by extreme insulin resistance. PPARγ FKO mice also exhibited delayed hair coat formation due to the absence of dermal fat, disrupted mammary gland development with loss of mammary fat pads, and high bone mass with loss of bone marrow fat, indicating the critical roles of adipose PPARγ in these tissues. Our findings reveal the essentiality of fat PPARγ in adipose formation, whole-body metabolic homeostasis, and the normal development of fat-containing tissues.

title: Fluconazole prophylaxis: can we eliminate invasive Candida infections in the neonatal ICU?
text: The primary objective of preventing invasive Candida infections in extremely preterm infants should be a top priority for each neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to the high mortality and risk of neurodevelopmental impairment associated with these infections. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy and safety of fluconazole prophylaxis in preventing invasive Candida infections in high-risk infants, with a 91% reduction in incidence in infants <1000 g and an 85% reduction in infants <1500 g. Additionally, these studies have shown that targeting fluconazole prophylaxis to infants who are either <1000 g or < or =27 weeks is highly effective, safe, and inexpensive, and can eliminate these infections as a cause of neurodevelopmental impairment and mortality.

title: Fumarase deficiency in dichorionic diamniotic twins.
text:
Fumarase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive inherited disorder of metabolism that affects the Krebs Tricarboxylic Acid cycle. This condition is characterized by a significant neurological disease burden, which typically presents with symptoms such as microcephaly, dystonia, global developmental delay, seizures, and early mortality in infancy. Heterozygous carriers of the deficiency also have an increased risk of developing hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma.
We report on a non-consanguineous family in which a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy resulted in twin boys who were diagnosed with fumarase deficiency through biochemical, enzymatic, and molecular testing. The clinical phenotype of these individuals included hepatic involvement. A novel mutation in the fumarate hydratase gene was identified in this family.

title: Angiopoietin-2 is increased in sepsis and inversely associated with nitric oxide-dependent microvascular reactivity
text:
Introduction:
Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), a peptide released from endothelial cell Weibel-Palade bodies (WPBs), promotes endothelial activation and vascular permeability. However, the mechanisms underlying the increase in Ang-2 levels during severe sepsis are not well understood. Nitric oxide (NO) has been shown to inhibit WPB exocytosis, and decreased endothelial NO bioavailability has been observed in sepsis. Therefore, we hypothesized that the concentration of Ang-2 in sepsis would be inversely correlated with endothelial NO bioavailability.
Methods:
Plasma Ang-2, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and endothelial-active cytokines were measured in 83 patients with early sepsis and 41 healthy controls. The relationship between Ang-2 levels and reactive hyperemia-peripheral arterial tonometry (RH-PAT), a measure of endothelial NO bioavailability, was investigated.
Results:
Plasma Ang-2 levels were significantly elevated in sepsis patients compared to controls (median [interquartile range (IQR)]: severe sepsis, 12.4 [8.5-33.4] ng/ml; sepsis without organ failure, 6.1 [5.0-10.4] ng/ml; controls, 2.7 [2.2-3.6] ng/ml; P < 0.0001).
