Pharmacovigilance is a critical component of this monitoring system, as it enables national authorities to evaluate the safety and efficacy of biological medicines in real-world settings. The Americas Health Foundation brought together a group of experts to discuss the challenges and gaps in pharmacovigilance in Latin America, with a particular focus on the traceability and pharmacovigilance of biosimilars after approval. The recommendations developed by the group aim to provide countries with the tools they need to accurately document the safety and performance of biosimilars in real-life settings, ultimately leading to the successful implementation of pharmacovigilance for these medications throughout the region.

title: Coordinated regulation of sulfur and phospholipid metabolism reflects the importance of methylation in the growth of yeast
text: A yeast strain lacking Met4p, the primary transcriptional regulator of the sulfur assimilation pathway, is unable to produce methionine. This seemingly simple auxotroph fails to grow well in rich media supplemented with excess methionine, forming small colonies on yeast extract/peptone/dextrose plates. However, faster-growing large colonies are observed when overnight cultures are plated, suggesting that spontaneous suppressor mutations arise at a high frequency. To identify these suppressor mutations, we employed genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism and standard genetic analyses. The most common suppressors were found to be loss-of-function mutations in OPI1, which encodes a transcriptional repressor involved in phospholipid metabolism. Using a novel system that enables rapid and specific degradation of Met4p, we investigated the dynamic expression of genes following loss of Met4p. Our experiments revealed that Met4p activates genes involved in S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) maintenance, while Opi1p represses these genes. Cells lacking Met4p can grow normally when SAM is added to the media or one of the SAM synthetase genes is overexpressed. SAM serves as a methyl donor in three Opi1p-regulated reactions, ultimately leading to the synthesis of the abundant membrane phospholipid, phosphatidylcholine. Our findings demonstrate that rapidly growing cells require significant methylation, likely for the biosynthesis of phospholipids.

title: Glossary of reference terms for alternative test methods and their validation.
text:
This glossary was created to serve as a comprehensive reference source for professionals working in the field of alternatives to animal testing. It was compiled from a variety of existing reference documents from different sources and is intended to be a central point of reference for understanding alternative test methods. With the rapid growth of new alternative test methods and approaches over the past few decades, it became apparent that a consolidated, revised, and harmonized collection of terms used in the validation of these methods was necessary. The need for an updated glossary arose from the recognition that new words have emerged as new approaches have been developed, while others have become obsolete, and the meanings of some terms have evolved over time.
This glossary aims to provide guidance on validation issues related to new or updated testing methods, in line with current approaches. Additionally, due to ongoing developments and technologies, this glossary will be a living, constantly updated document. An internet-based version of this compilation can be found at <http://altweb.jhsph.edu>, allowing for the addition of new material.

title: Combinatorial transcriptional control in blood stem/progenitor cells: genome-wide analysis of ten major transcriptional regulators.
text:
Combinatorial transcription factor (TF) interactions play a crucial role in determining cellular phenotypes, and thus, are essential for stem cell formation, maintenance, and differentiation. In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of the genome-wide binding patterns and combinatorial interactions of ten key regulators of blood stem/progenitor cells (SCL/TAL1, LYL1, LMO2, GATA2, RUNX1, MEIS1, PU.1, ERG, FLI-1, and GFI1B). Through genome-wide computational analysis of complex binding patterns, followed by functional validation, we uncovered several novel insights into the transcriptional control of stem and progenitor cells.
Firstly, we identified a previously unappreciated combinatorial interaction between a group of seven TFs (SCL, LYL1, LMO2, GATA2, RUNX1, ERG, and FLI-1), which plays a crucial role in regulating the expression of genes involved in hematopoiesis. Secondly, we demonstrated that direct protein-protein interactions between four key regulators (RUNX1, GATA2, SCL, and ERG) are essential for stabilizing complex binding to DNA. Finally, we showed that compound heterozygosity for Runx1 and Gata2 results in severe hematopoietic defects and lethality at mid-gestation, highlighting the importance of these regulators in maintaining proper hematopoiesis.
Overall, this study underscores the power of genome-wide analysis in revealing novel functional insights into the transcriptional control of stem and progenitor cells. The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying hematopoiesis and stem cell biology, and may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for blood disorders.

title: Influence of CYP2D6 Polymorphisms on Serum Levels of Tamoxifen Metabolites in Spanish Women with Breast Cancer
text:
Background: Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer tumors rely on estrogen signaling for growth and proliferation, and can be treated with anti-estrogen therapy, such as tamoxifen. However, some patients may have reduced sensitivity to tamoxifen due to genetic polymorphisms in genes involved in its metabolism. The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of genetic variations in CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 on the pharmacokinetics of tamoxifen and its metabolites in Spanish women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer who were candidates for tamoxifen therapy.
Methods: We evaluated 90 women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer using the AmpliChip CYP450 test to determine their CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 gene variants. Plasma levels of tamoxifen and its metabolites were quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography.
Results: The CYP2D6 phenotype was found to be extensive metabolizer in 80% of patients, intermediate metabolizer in 12.2%, ultra-rapid metabolizer in 2.2%, and poor metabolizer in 5.6%. The allele frequency was 35.0% for allele (*)1, 21.0% for *2, and 18.9% for *4. All poor metabolizers in this series were *4/*4, and their endoxifen and 4-hydroxy tamoxifen levels were 25% lower than those of extensive metabolizers. The CYP2C19*2 allele, which has been associated with breast cancer outcomes, was detected in 15.6% of the studied alleles.
Conclusion: The present study suggests that genetic variations in CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 are associated with reduced metabolism of tamoxifen and its metabolites in Spanish women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. The results suggest that genotyping for these genes may be useful in predicting response to tamoxifen therapy and guiding treatment decisions.

title: Role of tumor associated macrophages in tumor angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis
text: Tumor angiogenesis is crucial for the growth and spread of cancer cells, as it provides them with essential nutrients and oxygen. An angiogenic switch, triggered by tumor cells, allows for the formation of new blood vessels, which in turn supports the tumor's rapid growth and metastasis. Macrophages, which are recruited and reprogrammed by tumor cells, play a key role in this process by secreting angiogenic factors, such as angiopoietin-2 and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A). These factors stimulate the recruitment of TIE2 receptor-expressing monocytes (TEM) into the tumor site, further promoting angiogenesis. Additionally, tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) sense hypoxia in avascular areas of the tumor and produce angiogenic factors, such as VEGFA, which stimulates chemotaxis of endothelial cells (EC) and macrophages. Elevated expression of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) by TAM mediates extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation and the release of bioactive VEGFA, promoting both angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis. Other angiogenic factors released by TAM include basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), thymidine phosphorylase (TP), urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA), and adrenomedullin (ADM). These factors also support lymphangiogenesis by inducing the formation of new lymphatic vessels. TAM can also express the lymphatic endothelial cell marker LYVE-1, indicating their role in tumor lymphangiogenesis. Furthermore, TAM can trans-differentiate into lymphatic endothelial cells, further contributing to the formation of new lymphatic vessels. The newly discovered factor YKL-40, which belongs to a family of mammalian chitinase-like proteins (CLP), has been shown to induce angiogenesis in vitro and in animal tumor models. Neutralizing the activity of YKL-40 with a monoclonal antibody blocks tumor angiogenesis and progression. The role of YKL-39 and SI-CLP in tumor angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis remains to be investigated.

title: The HIV Treatment Gap: Estimates of the Financial Resources Needed versus Available for Scale-Up of Antiretroviral Therapy in 97 Countries from 2015 to 2020
text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) revised its guidelines in 2015, recommending that all individuals living with HIV, regardless of their CD4 count, should start antiretroviral therapy (ART) immediately upon diagnosis. However, few studies have examined the global resources required to rapidly scale up ART. Under the Health Policy Project, we conducted modeling analyses for 97 countries to estimate the eligibility for and numbers on ART from 2015 to 2020, along with the facility-level financial resources required.
We found that:
* 25.7 million adults and 1.57 million children could be on ART by 2020 if countries maintain their current eligibility policies and increase coverage based on historical trends.
* 26.5 million adults and 1.53 million children could be on ART by 2020 if countries adopt aspects of the WHO 2013 guidelines.
* 30.4 million adults and 1.68 million children could be on ART by 2020 under the 90-90-90 scenario, which aims to have 90% of people living with HIV know their status, 90% of those diagnosed with HIV be on ART, and 90% of those on ART have viral suppression.
The facility-level financial resources needed for scaling up ART in these countries from 2015 to 2020 are estimated to be US$45.8 billion under the current scenario, US$48.7 billion under the WHO 2013 scenario, and US$52.5 billion under the 90-90-90 scenario. After projecting recent external and domestic funding trends, the estimated 6-year financing gap ranges from US$19.8 billion to US$25.0 billion, depending on the costing scenario and the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief contribution level, with the gap for ART commodities alone ranging from US$14.0 to US$16.8 billion.
Our findings suggest that countries are unlikely to meet the 90-90-90 treatment target unless they adopt a test-and-offer approach and increase ART coverage. The projected number of people receiving ART across three scenarios suggests that future resource needs for ART scale-up are significantly threatening the sustainability of the global HIV response without additional resource mobilization from domestic or innovative financing sources or efficiency gains. As the world moves towards adopting the WHO 2015 guidelines, advances in technology, including the introduction of lower-cost, highly effective antiretroviral regimens, may prove to be "game changers" that allow more people to be on ART with the resources available.

title: Distinction and relationship between elongation rate and processivity of RNA polymerase II in vivo.
text: A number of proteins and drugs have been linked to the transcriptional elongation process catalyzed by RNA polymerase II (Pol II), yet the factors that control the rate of nucleotide addition per minute (elongation rate) and the number of nucleotides added per initiation event (processivity) in living organisms are poorly understood. In this study, we discovered that a mutation in the Rpb2 subunit of Pol II significantly reduces both the elongation rate and processivity in vivo. In contrast, none of the putative elongation factors tested had an effect on the elongation rate, although mutations in the THO complex and in Spt4 significantly reduced processivity. The drugs 6-azauracil and mycophenolic acid also reduced both the elongation rate and processivity, and this processivity defect was exacerbated by mutations in Spt4, TFIIS, and CTDK-1. Our findings suggest that, in living organisms, a slower rate of Pol II elongation leads to premature dissociation along the chromatin template, and that Pol II processivity can be decoupled from elongation rate.

title: Neurite sprouting and synapse deterioration in the aging Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system.
text: Caenorhabditis elegans, a nematode species, has emerged as a powerful model organism for the investigation of the conserved mechanisms that modulate healthy aging in the nervous system. While neuronal death and/or loss of processes are not readily apparent in the aging C. elegans nervous system, dendrite restructuring and synaptic integrity decline are hypothesized to contribute to brain decline and dysfunction in humans. To investigate these changes at high resolution, we combined fluorescence microscopy and electron microscopy (EM) in the aging C. elegans nervous system. Our findings reveal two major components of morphological change: the accumulation of novel outgrowths from specific neurons and physical decline in synaptic integrity. Novel outgrowth phenotypes, including branching from the main dendrite or new growth from somata, occur at a high frequency in some aging neurons, but not all. Mitochondria are often associated with age-associated branch sites. Lowered insulin signaling maintains some structural integrity of ALM and PLM neurons into old age, and both DAF-16/FOXO and heat shock factor transcription factor HSF-1 exert neuroprotective functions. HSF-1 can act cell autonomously in this capacity. EM evaluation in synapse-rich regions reveals a striking decline in synaptic vesicle numbers and a diminution of presynaptic density size. Interestingly, old animals that maintain locomotory prowess exhibit less synaptic decline than same-age decrepit animals, suggesting that synaptic integrity correlates with locomotory healthspan. Our findings demonstrate similarities between the aging C. elegans nervous system and mammalian brain, highlighting the conserved neuronal responses to age. Dissection of neuronal aging mechanisms in C. elegans may thus inform the development of brain healthspan-extending therapies.

title: Determinants of adolescent physical activity and inactivity patterns.
text:
Despite recognition of the crucial role of environmental factors in shaping physical activity patterns among adolescents, limited research has been conducted to investigate the impact of these factors. This study aimed to investigate the environmental and sociodemographic determinants of physical activity and inactivity among subpopulations of US adolescents.
We defined environmental determinants as modifiable factors in the physical environment that directly influence the opportunity to engage in physical activity. Our study examined the relationship between environmental and sociodemographic factors and physical activity and inactivity among adolescents, with the implication that these findings could inform societal-level intervention strategies to increase physical activity and reduce inactivity.
The study population consisted of nationally representative data from the 1996 National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health, which included 17,766 US adolescents enrolled in middle and high schools. We collected data on hours spent on inactivity (TV/video viewing and video/computer games) and times spent on moderate to vigorous physical activity per week using a questionnaire. We categorized physical activity into three levels: low (0-2 times/week), medium (3-4 times/week), and high (>5 times/week), and inactivity into three categories: low (0-10 hours/week), medium (11-24 hours/week), and high (>25 hours/week).
We used logistic regression models to investigate sex and ethnic interactions in relation to environmental and sociodemographic factors to examine the potential impact of physical education and recreation programs and sociodemographic factors on physical activity and inactivity patterns.
Our results showed that moderate to vigorous physical activity was lower and inactivity higher among non-Hispanic black and Hispanic adolescents. Participation in school physical education programs was low among these adolescents and decreased with age. Participation in daily school physical education (PE) program classes and use of a community recreation center were associated with an increased likelihood of engaging in high levels of moderate to vigorous physical activity. Maternal education was inversely associated with high inactivity patterns, while high family income was associated with increased moderate to vigorous physical activity and decreased inactivity. High neighborhood serious crime level was associated with a decreased likelihood of falling in the highest category of moderate to vigorous physical activity.
These findings suggest that modifiable environmental factors, such as participation in school physical education and community recreation programs, play an important role in shaping physical activity patterns among adolescents. Despite the significant impact of participation in school physical education programs on physical activity patterns, few adolescents participated in such programs. Our findings highlight the need for intervention strategies that promote participation in these programs to increase physical activity and reduce inactivity among adolescents.

title: Suicide prevention strategies: a systematic review.
text:
The study included relevant publications from 1966 to June 2005, identified through electronic searches of MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and PsychINFO. The studies evaluated interventions in six major domains: education and awareness for the general public and professionals, screening tools for at-risk individuals, treatment of psychiatric disorders, restricting access to lethal means, and responsible media reporting of suicide. The study included 3 types of studies: systematic reviews and meta-analyses, quantitative studies (randomized controlled trials and cohort studies), and ecological or population-based studies.
The study found that education of physicians and restricting access to lethal means were effective in preventing suicide. Other interventions, such as public education, screening programs, and media education, require more testing. The study concluded that ascertaining which components of suicide prevention programs are effective in reducing suicide rates is essential to optimize the use of limited resources.
Here is a rewritten version of the text with some changes to improve readability and clarity:
In 2002, an estimated 877,000 people died by suicide worldwide. While some developed nations have implemented national suicide prevention plans, the effectiveness of these interventions is often not evaluated. This study aimed to examine the evidence for the effectiveness of specific suicide-prevention interventions and make recommendations for future prevention programs and research.
We conducted a comprehensive review of relevant publications from 1966 to June 2005, identifying them through electronic searches of MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and PsychINFO. We included studies that evaluated interventions in six major domains: education and awareness for the general public and professionals, screening tools for at-risk individuals, treatment of psychiatric disorders, restricting access to lethal means, and responsible media reporting of suicide. We included three types of studies: systematic reviews and meta-analyses, quantitative studies (randomized controlled trials and cohort studies), and ecological or population-based studies.
Our findings showed that education of physicians and restricting access to lethal means were effective in preventing suicide. Other interventions, such as public education, screening programs, and media education, require more testing. We concluded that identifying which components of suicide prevention programs are most effective in reducing suicide rates is crucial to optimize the use of limited resources.
Overall, the study highlights the need for more research on suicide prevention interventions to determine their effectiveness and inform the development of evidence-based programs. By improving our understanding of what works and what doesn't, we can better allocate resources and save lives.

title: Oxidative damage of DNA confers resistance to cytosolic nuclease TREX1 degradation and potentiates STING-dependent immune sensing.
text: Immune sensing of DNA is crucial for the body's defense against viruses, but it can also lead to autoimmune diseases such as lupus erythematosus (LE). Our research has uncovered evidence of the involvement of a specific DNA modification in the detection of cytosolic DNA. The oxidized base 8-hydroxyguanosine (8-OHG), a marker of oxidative DNA damage, enhances the immune system's recognition of cytosolic DNA by reducing its susceptibility to degradation by the enzyme 3' repair exonuclease 1 (TREX1). This modification arises naturally in pathogen DNA during exposure to reactive oxygen species (ROS) in lysosomes, as well as in neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) DNA during the oxidative burst. 8-OHG is also abundant in UV-exposed skin lesions of LE patients and colocalizes with type I interferon (IFN). Injecting oxidized DNA into the skin of lupus-prone mice leads to the formation of lesions that resemble those found in patients. These findings suggest that oxidized DNA serves as a prototypical damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) with significant implications for infection, sterile inflammation, and autoimmunity.

title: IL-18 induction of osteopontin mediates cardiac fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction in mice.
text:
Osteopontin (OPN), a key component of the extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in the fibrotic process during tissue remodeling. Previous studies have shown that OPN and the cytokine interleukin (IL)-18 are overexpressed in a variety of human cardiac pathologies. In this study, we aimed to investigate the regulatory role of IL-18 in the expression of cardiac OPN and its subsequent impact on interstitial fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction.
To achieve this, we first examined the expression of IL-18 and OPN in murine models of left ventricular pressure and volume overload. Our results showed parallel increases in IL-18 and OPN expression, as well as interstitial fibrosis, in these models. Next, we administered exogenous recombinant (r)IL-18 to mice for two weeks and observed a significant increase in cardiac OPN expression, interstitial fibrosis, and diastolic dysfunction.
We also investigated the role of the T helper (Th)1 lymphocyte phenotype in the regulation of cardiac OPN expression. Stimulation of Th1 lymphocytes with a selective toll-like receptor (TLR)9 agonist led to increased cardiac IL-18 and OPN expression, which was associated with increased cardiac fibrillar collagen concentrations and interstitial fibrosis, resulting in diastolic dysfunction.
Furthermore, we examined the direct effects of IL-18 on cardiac OPN expression in primary cardiac fibroblast cultures. Our results showed that rIL-18 induced OPN expression and protein levels in these cells. Conditioned media from TLR9-stimulated T lymphocyte cultures also induced IL-18 and OPN expression in cardiac fibroblasts, while blockade of the IL-18 receptor with a neutralizing antibody abolished the increase in OPN expression.
Finally, we investigated the role of the transcriptional factor interferon regulatory factor (IRF)1 in the regulation of IL-18 and OPN expression in cardiac fibroblasts. Our results showed that mutation of IRF1 or treatment with IRF1 small interfering RNA (siRNA) led to decreased expression of IL-18 and OPN in these cells. Interestingly, mice with a mutation in IRF1 showed reduced cardiac fibrotic development and increased left ventricular function compared to wild-type mice, suggesting that IRF1 plays a critical role in the regulation of cardiac fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction.
In conclusion, our results provide direct evidence that the induction of IL-18 regulates OPN-mediated cardiac fibrosis and diastolic dysfunction. These findings have important implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of cardiac fibrosis and related diseases.

title: Hematopoietic stem cell: self-renewal versus differentiation.
text: The mammalian blood system, comprising over 10 distinct mature cell types, is anchored by a single cell type: hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Within this system, HSCs are the only cells capable of both multipotency and self-renewal. Multipotency allows HSCs to differentiate into all blood cell types, while self-renewal enables them to reproduce themselves without differentiating. Since mature blood cells (MBCs) have a short lifespan, HSCs must constantly produce more differentiated progenitors while maintaining their own pool size throughout an organism's lifetime. This is achieved by balancing self-renewal and differentiation. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms of HSC self-renewal and differentiation has been a crucial area of research. This review focuses on the hierarchical structure of the hematopoietic system, current knowledge of the microenvironment and molecular cues regulating HSC self-renewal and differentiation, and emerging systems approaches to elucidate HSC biology.

title: RSEM: accurate transcript quantification from RNA-Seq data with or without a reference genome
text:
Background:
RNA-Seq is revolutionizing the field of transcriptomics by providing a high-throughput approach for measuring transcript abundances. However, one of the major challenges in transcript quantification from RNA-Seq data is the handling of reads that map to multiple genes or isoforms. This issue is particularly important when working with de novo transcriptome assemblies, as it is difficult to determine which transcripts are isoforms of the same gene.
Results:
We present RSEM, a user-friendly software package for quantifying gene and isoform abundances from single-end or paired-end RNA-Seq data. RSEM outputs abundance estimates, 95% credibility intervals, and visualization files, and can also simulate RNA-Seq data. Unlike other existing tools, RSEM does not require a reference genome, making it particularly useful for quantification with de novo transcriptome assemblies. On simulated and real data sets, RSEM has superior or comparable performance to quantification methods that rely on a reference genome.
Conclusions:
RSEM is an accurate and user-friendly software tool for quantifying transcript abundances from RNA-Seq data. Its ability to effectively use ambiguously-mapping reads enables accurate gene-level abundance estimates with large numbers of short single-end reads. On the other hand, estimates of the relative frequencies of isoforms within single genes may be improved through the use of paired-end reads, depending on the number of possible splice forms for each gene. RSEM has also provided valuable guidance for cost-efficient design of quantification experiments with RNA-Seq, which is currently relatively expensive.

title: A synthetic Escherichia coli predator–prey ecosystem
text: We have designed and constructed a synthetic ecosystem, consisting of two populations of Escherichia coli, which communicate and interact through quorum sensing and regulate each other's gene expression and survival through engineered gene circuits. This synthetic ecosystem exhibits logical dynamics similar to those of canonical predator-prey systems, with the predator cells inducing the expression of a killing protein in the prey, while the prey rescue the predators by eliciting the expression of an antidote protein in the predator. The long-term culturing of the system in microchemostats has experimentally validated the possibility of extinction, coexistence, and oscillatory dynamics of the predator and prey populations, depending on the operating conditions. To capture the system dynamics, a simple mathematical model has been developed, which enables a systematic exploration of the interactions between the populations in a predictable manner. The integration of experimental and mathematical approaches provides a comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between the populations in the synthetic ecosystem.

title: Funnel trap for the capture of phlebotomine sand flies (Diptera: Psychodidae) from tree holes.
text: A funnel trap specifically designed to fit over holes leading into hollow trees was used to capture adult phlebotomine sand flies, Lutzomyia shannoni Dyar, on Ossabaw Island in Chatham County, Georgia. These insects typically rested in hollow trees during the day and were collected by the funnel trap as they emerged from the tree holes at night. The trap is lightweight, durable, inexpensive, waterproof, and highly effective, with over 100 healthy L. shannoni ++ individuals captured per night by a single investigator during July and August 1988, when adult flies were abundant on the island.

title: Cystine/glutamate exchange regulates metabotropic glutamate receptor presynaptic inhibition of excitatory transmission and vulnerability to cocaine seeking.
text: Withdrawal from chronic cocaine use leads to a decrease in extracellular glutamate levels in the nucleus accumbens by inhibiting the cystine/glutamate exchange (xc-) process. Activating xc- with N-acetylcysteine can restore extracellular glutamate levels and prevent cocaine-induced drug seeking. It was hypothesized that the activation of xc- would increase glutamatergic tone on presynaptic group II metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR2/3), thereby inhibiting excitatory transmission and preventing drug seeking. In the first experiment, the capacity of glutamate derived from xc- to regulate excitatory transmission via mGluR2/3 was investigated. Physiological levels of cystine (100-300 nm) were restored to acute tissue slices from the nucleus accumbens or prefrontal cortex. Cystine increased glutamate efflux and decreased miniature EPSC (mEPSC) and spontaneous EPSC (sEPSC) frequency, as well as evoked EPSC amplitude. These effects of cystine were presynaptic, as there was no change in mEPSC or sEPSC amplitude, and an increase in the evoked EPSC paired-pulse facilitation ratio. The cystine-induced reduction in EPSCs was reversed by blocking either xc- or mGluR2/3. In the second experiment, blocking mGluR2/3 prevented the ability of N-acetylcysteine to inhibit the reinstatement of drug seeking in rats trained to self-administer cocaine. These data demonstrate that non-synaptic glutamate derived from xc- modulates synaptic glutamate release and regulates cocaine-induced drug seeking.

title: Survival analysis: time-dependent effects and time-varying risk factors.
text: In traditional Kaplan-Meier or Cox regression analysis, a risk factor measured at baseline is often associated with mortality over time. However, things can change during follow-up, such as the effect of a fixed baseline risk factor may vary over time, resulting in a weakening or strengthening of associations, or the risk factor itself may change over time. This paper focuses on short-term versus long-term effects (time-dependent effects) of a fixed baseline risk factor. An example is provided showing that underweight is a strong risk factor for mortality in dialysis patients, particularly in the short run. In contrast, overweight is a risk factor for mortality, which is stronger in the long run than in the short run. Additionally, the analysis of how time-varying risk factors (time-dependent risk factors) are related to mortality is demonstrated by avoiding the pitfall of adjusting for sequelae. The proper analysis of effects over time should be driven by a clear research question. Both types of research questions, those related to time-dependent effects as well as those related to time-dependent risk factors, can be analyzed using time-dependent Cox regression analysis. It will be shown that using time-dependent risk factors typically means focusing on short-term effects only.

title: Control of interneuron dendritic growth through NRG1/erbB4-mediated kalirin-7 disinhibition
text:
Neuregulin 1 (NRG1) is a secreted growth factor that activates the postsynaptic erbB4 receptor tyrosine kinase. Both NRG1 and erbB4 have been implicated in schizophrenia, but the downstream targets of this interaction are not well understood. ErbB4 is abundant in interneurons, and NRG1-mediated erbB4 activation has been shown to modulate interneuron function. However, the role of NRG1-erbB4 signaling in regulating interneuron dendritic growth is not well characterized.
Our study reveals that NRG1/erbB4 promote the growth of dendrites in mature interneurons through kalirin, a key regulator of dendritic morphogenesis. Recent research has linked the KALRN gene to schizophrenia, and our findings suggest that phosphorylation of kalirin's C-terminal region is critical for the effects of NRG1-erbB4 signaling on dendritic growth. Reduced interneuron dendrite length has been observed in individuals with schizophrenia, and understanding how NRG1-erbB4 signaling modulates interneuron dendritic morphogenesis may provide insight into the underlying mechanisms of this disease.
In summary, our study uncovers a novel mechanism by which NRG1-erbB4 signaling regulates interneuron dendritic growth through kalirin, and highlights the importance of this pathway in the development of cortical circuits. These findings may have implications for the understanding and treatment of schizophrenia, a disorder characterized by abnormalities in cortical function.

title: Use of gene-expression profiling to identify prognostic subclasses in adult acute myeloid leukemia.
text:
Background: The diagnosis and treatment of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are complex and challenging due to the molecular heterogeneity of the disease. The current classification system does not fully capture the diversity of AML, particularly for patients with intermediate-risk AML and a normal karyotype. Gene expression profiling offers a promising approach to improve the molecular classification of AML and identify novel prognostic markers.
Methods: We performed complementary DNA microarray analysis on peripheral blood or bone marrow samples from 116 adult AML patients (including 45 with a normal karyotype) to determine the levels of gene expression. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis was used to identify molecular subgroups with distinct gene expression signatures. A novel supervised learning algorithm was applied to a training set of samples from 59 patients to develop a gene expression-based clinical outcome predictor. The predictor was then tested using an independent validation group comprising the remaining 57 patients.
Results: Unsupervised analysis identified novel molecular subtypes of AML, including two prognostically relevant subgroups in AML with a normal karyotype. Using the supervised learning algorithm, we constructed an optimal 133-gene clinical outcome predictor that accurately predicted overall survival among patients in the independent validation group (P=0.006), including the subgroup of patients with AML with a normal karyotype (P=0.046). In multivariate analysis, the gene expression predictor was a strong independent prognostic factor (odds ratio, 8.8; 95% confidence interval, 2.6-29.3; P<0.001).
Conclusions: Our findings demonstrate the potential of gene expression profiling to improve the molecular classification of adult AML. The use of gene expression profiling can identify novel prognostic markers and improve treatment stratification for patients with AML, particularly those with a normal karyotype. Further validation and refinement of these methods are needed to fully realize their clinical potential.

title: Perspectives on public health workforce research.
text: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Office of Workforce and Career Development is dedicated to cultivating a skilled, sustainable, and diverse public health workforce through evidence-based training, career development, and strategic workforce planning to enhance population health outcomes. This article examines previous research efforts in identifying key areas of focus for public health workforce development, which are consolidated into eight primary themes. We propose a comprehensive framework for public health workforce research, encompassing six functional areas: definition and standards, data, methodology, evaluation, policy, and dissemination and translation. To prioritize the development of an actionable research agenda, we constructed a matrix of key challenges in workforce analysis by public health workforce categories. Our review of existing literature revealed valuable methods, models, and approaches for public health workforce research, and we explore new tools and approaches for addressing priority areas. Finally, we assess how interdisciplinary approaches from the social sciences can inform the development of a research framework for advancing public health workforce research and policy.

title: Gene targeting using zinc finger nucleases
text: The capacity to specifically manipulate the mammalian genome at the site of interest has far-reaching implications for both basic and applied research. Gene targeting involves introducing a DNA molecule into a cell, which replaces the corresponding chromosomal segment through homologous recombination, providing a precise means of manipulating the genome. However, the application of gene targeting to mammalian cells has been limited by its low efficiency in the past. Zinc finger nucleases (ZFNs) show promise in enhancing the efficiency of gene targeting by introducing DNA double-strand breaks in target genes, which then trigger the cell's endogenous homologous recombination machinery. Recent studies have demonstrated that ZFNs can achieve targeting frequencies of up to 20% in a human disease-causing gene. Further research is needed to translate these in vitro findings into in vivo applications and to determine whether ZFNs may introduce unwanted genomic instability.

title: relative expression results in real-time
text: Real-time reverse transcription followed by polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is the most suitable method for detecting and quantifying mRNA. It offers high sensitivity, good reproducibility, and a wide quantification range. Today, relative expression analysis is increasingly used, where the expression of a target gene is standardized by a non-regulated reference gene. Several mathematical algorithms have been developed to calculate an expression ratio based on real-time PCR efficiency and the crossing point deviation of an unknown sample versus a control. However, these equations and models can only determine a single transcription difference between one control and one sample. To address this limitation, a new software tool called REST (relative expression software tool) was developed. REST compares two groups, with up to 16 data points in a sample and 16 in a control group, for reference, and up to four target genes. The mathematical model used is based on PCR efficiencies and the mean crossing point deviation between the sample and control group. The expression ratio results of the four investigated transcripts are then tested for significance using a randomization test. The development and application of REST, as well as the usefulness of relative expression in real-time PCR using REST, are explained in this article. The latest software version of REST and examples for correct use can be downloaded at <http://www.wzw.tum.de/gene-quantification/>.

title: Pain attacks in non-complicated and complicated gallstone disease have a characteristic pattern and are accompanied by dyspepsia in most patients: the results of a prospective study.
text:
Objective: To characterize the pain pattern and associated symptoms of gallstone disease, and to determine the extent to which post-cholectectomy symptoms can be attributed to persistence of preoperative symptoms or new pathology.
Methods: A total of 220 patients with symptomatic gallstone disease, including complicated cases (acute cholecystitis and common bile duct stones), were interviewed using detailed questionnaires to identify pain patterns and symptoms of indigestion.
Results: The majority of patients experienced pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ), including the upper midline epigastrium. Pain was localized to the right subcostal area in 20% and to the upper epigastrium in 14%, while the rest (66%) had more evenly distributed pain. An area of maximal pain could be defined in 90% of patients, with maximal pain located under the costal arch in 51% and in the epigastrium in 41%. Pain was referred to the back in 63% of patients, with a mean visual analogue scale (VAS) score of very high (90 mm on a 0-100 scale). A pattern of incipient or low-grade warning pain with a subsequent relatively steady state until subsiding in the same fashion was present in 90% of patients. An urge to walk around was experienced by 71%. Pain attacks usually occurred in the late evening or at night (77%), with 85% of attacks lasting for more than one hour and almost never less than half an hour. Sixty-six percent of patients were intolerant to at least one type of food, but only 48% to fatty foods. Symptoms of functional indigestion (gastroesophageal reflux, dyspepsia, or irritable bowel symptoms) were seen in the vast majority in association with attacks.
Conclusions: Gallstone-associated pain follows a distinct pattern in the majority of patients, characterized by location in a defined area with a point of maximum intensity, referral, and occurrence mainly at night with duration of more than one hour. The majority of patients experience functional indigestion, mainly of the reflux type or dyspepsia. These findings suggest that post-cholecystectomy symptoms may not be entirely due to persistence of preoperative symptoms, but may also be related to new pathology.

title: Prevalence and cardiovascular disease correlates of low cardiorespiratory fitness in adolescents and adults.
text:
According to population surveys, physical activity levels are low in the United States. One consequence of inactivity is low cardiorespiratory fitness, which is a well-established risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD) morbidity and mortality. However, there is a lack of data on the prevalence of low fitness in representative US population samples.
To address this gap, we conducted an inception cohort study using data from the cross-sectional National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999-2002. Our sample included 3110 adolescents (ages 12-19) and 2205 adults (ages 20-49) who were free from previously diagnosed CVD and underwent submaximal graded exercise treadmill testing to estimate their maximum oxygen consumption (VO2max). We defined low fitness using percentile cut points from existing external referent populations and measured various CVD risk factors according to standard methods.
Our results showed that low fitness was present in 33.6% of adolescents and 13.9% of adults, with similar prevalence in males and females (P = .40). Non-Hispanic blacks and Mexican Americans had lower fitness levels than non-Hispanic whites. In all age-sex groups, body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference were inversely associated with fitness, and age- and race-adjusted odds ratios of overweight or obesity (BMI > or =25) ranged from 2.1 to 3.7 (P<.01 for all), comparing persons with low fitness with those with moderate or high fitness. Additionally, total cholesterol levels and systolic blood pressure were higher, and levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol were lower, among participants with low vs high fitness.
Our findings indicate that low fitness is a common problem in the US population and is associated with an increased prevalence of CVD risk factors. These findings highlight the importance of promoting physical activity and improving fitness levels in adolescents and adults to reduce the burden of CVD morbidity and mortality.

title: In situ regulation of DC subsets and T cells mediates tumor regression in mice.
text: Vaccines are largely ineffective for patients with advanced cancer, as the disease requires a robust and sustained activation of CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) to eliminate tumor cells and clear the disease. Recent studies have shown that specific subsets of dendritic cells (DCs) specialize in antigen cross-presentation and the production of cytokines, which regulate both CTLs and T regulatory (Treg) cells that suppress immune responses. To address this hypothesis, we investigated the role of coordinating the regulation of a DC network, including plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs) and CD8+ DCs, in enhancing host immunity in mice. We used functionalized biomaterials that incorporated various combinations of an inflammatory cytokine, immune danger signal, and tumor lysates to control the activation and localization of host DC populations in situ. We found that the numbers of pDCs and CD8+ DCs, as well as the endogenous production of interleukin-12, were strongly correlated with the magnitude of protective antitumor immunity and the generation of potent CD8+ CTLs. Vaccination by this method maintained local and systemic CTL responses for extended periods while inhibiting FoxP3 Treg activity during antigen clearance, resulting in complete regression of distant and established melanoma tumors. The efficacy of this vaccine as a monotherapy against large invasive tumors may be due to the local activity of pDCs and CD8+ DCs induced by persistent danger and antigen signaling at the vaccine site. These results suggest that a specific pattern of DC subsets correlates with the evolution of therapeutic antitumor responses and provide a framework for future vaccine design.

title: VEGF inhibits tumor cell invasion and mesenchymal transition through a MET/VEGFR2 complex.
text: Inhibition of VEGF signaling in mouse models of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) and a subset of GBM patients treated with bevacizumab leads to a proinvasive phenotype. Our findings demonstrate that VEGF directly and negatively regulates tumor cell invasion by enhancing the recruitment of protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) to a MET/VEGFR2 heterocomplex, thereby suppressing HGF-dependent MET phosphorylation and tumor cell migration. Conversely, VEGF blockade restores and increases MET activity in GBM cells in a hypoxia-independent manner, accompanied by a program reminiscent of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition characterized by a T-cadherin to N-cadherin switch and enhanced mesenchymal features. Inhibition of MET in GBM mouse models blocks mesenchymal transition and invasion provoked by VEGF ablation, resulting in a significant survival benefit.

title: Interaction between Oct3/4 and Cdx2 Determines Trophectoderm Differentiation
text:
Trophectoderm (TE), the earliest differentiated cell lineage in mammalian embryogenesis, gives rise to the placenta, a unique structure in mammalian development. The differentiation of TE cells is a pivotal event in early mammalian development, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood.
Embryonic stem (ES) cells can be induced to differentiate into the TE lineage through the forced repression of the POU-family transcription factor, Oct3/4. Our study demonstrates that overexpression of Caudal-related homeobox 2 (Cdx2) can also generate proper trophoblast stem (TS) cells. Cdx2 is dispensable for trophectoderm differentiation induced by Oct3/4 repression, but essential for TS cell self-renewal.
In preimplantation embryos, Cdx2 is initially coexpressed with Oct3/4 and they form a complex that reciprocally represses their target genes in ES cells. This suggests that reciprocal inhibition between lineage-specific transcription factors may play a role in the first differentiation event of mammalian development.
Overall, this study sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the differentiation of TE cells and highlights the importance of reciprocal inhibition between transcription factors in the regulation of cell fate decisions.

title: SSEA-1 is an enrichment marker for tumor-initiating cells in human glioblastoma.
text:
The expression of CD133+ in human glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) cells has been linked to tumor stem cells (TSCs) or tumor-initiating cells (TICs). However, approximately 40% of freshly isolated GBM specimens lack CD133+ tumor cells, raising the possibility that CD133 may not be a universal enrichment marker for GBM TSCs/TICs. In this study, we investigate the functional properties of stage-specific embryonic antigen 1 (SSEA-1/LeX)+ GBM cells, which are enriched for TSCs/TICs.
We found that SSEA-1+ GBM cells are highly tumorigenic in vivo, unlike SSEA-1- cells. Additionally, SSEA-1+ cells can give rise to both SSEA-1+ and SSEA-1- cells, establishing a cellular hierarchy. Furthermore, SSEA-1+ cells have self-renewal and multilineage differentiation potentials. Interestingly, a distinct subpopulation of SSEA-1+ cells was present in all but one of the primary GBMs examined (n = 24), and most CD133+ tumor cells were also SSEA-1+, suggesting that SSEA-1 may be a general TSC/TIC enrichment marker in human GBMs.
In summary, our findings suggest that SSEA-1/LeX+ GBM cells are a good enrichment marker for TSCs/TICs in human GBMs, and may be a more reliable marker than CD133 for identifying these cells.

title: Temporal regulation of topoisomerase IV activity in E. coli.
text: We have identified a mutant allele of the DNAX gene, which encodes the tau and gamma subunits of the DNA polymerase III holoenzyme, that exhibits extreme cell filamentation without affecting cell growth or DNA replication. This phenotype is attributed to a defect in the proper decatenation of daughter chromosomes during rapid cell growth. In contrast to wild-type cells, where ParC, one subunit of topoisomerase IV, is associated with the replication factory, the mutant cells exhibit a uniform distribution of ParC on the nucleoid. The distribution of ParE, the other subunit of topoisomerase IV, remains unchanged. Furthermore, the majority of topoisomerase IV activity in synchronized cell populations is observed at late stages of the cell cycle, when replication is almost complete. These findings suggest that the in vivo activity of topoisomerase IV may be dependent on the release of ParC from the replication factory.

title: Molecularly targeted therapy based on tumour molecular profiling versus conventional therapy for advanced cancer (SHIVA): a multicentre, open-label, proof-of-concept, randomised, controlled phase 2 trial.
text: The study assessed the effectiveness and safety of using molecularly targeted agents in patients with advanced cancer who had not responded to standard treatment. The agents were chosen based on the specific molecular alterations present in the patients' tumors, but were used off-label, meaning outside of their approved indications. The study found that the use of molecularly targeted agents did not improve progression-free survival compared to treatment at the discretion of the physician in this patient population. While the use of these agents was associated with a higher incidence of grade 3-4 adverse events, the difference was not statistically significant. The study suggests that off-label use of molecularly targeted agents should be discouraged and that enrollment in clinical trials is necessary to identify predictive biomarkers of efficacy.

title: CRTC2 (TORC2) contributes to the transcriptional response to fasting in the liver but is not required for the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.
text: The liver plays a crucial role in maintaining glucose homeostasis through the regulation of glucose storage and production. The cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is a key transcription factor involved in coordinating the hepatic response to fasting, but the mechanisms underlying its gene activation remain unclear. To investigate the contribution of CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 2 (CRTC2) to hepatic glucose metabolism, we generated CRTC2-deficient mice and evaluated their glucose metabolism in vivo. Our findings revealed that CRTC2-deficient hepatocytes exhibited reduced glucose production in response to glucagon, which was associated with decreased CREB binding to several genes involved in gluconeogenesis. However, despite reduced expression of CREB target genes, including phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase), and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 alpha (PGC-1alpha), no hypoglycemia was observed in mutant mice. These results provide genetic evidence supporting a role for CRTC2 in the transcriptional response to fasting, but suggest only a limited contribution of this cofactor to the maintenance of glucose homeostasis.

title: Ancient Hybridization and an Irish Origin for the Modern Polar Bear Matriline
text:
Background: Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are among the most vulnerable species to the rapidly changing Arctic climate, with their survival of global concern. However, there is a significant lack of knowledge regarding the evolutionary history of polar bears. Future conservation strategies would greatly benefit from an understanding of basic evolutionary information, such as the timing and conditions of their initial divergence from brown bears (U. arctos) or their response to previous environmental changes.
Results: We employed a spatially explicit phylogeographic model to estimate the dynamics of 242 brown bear and polar bear matrilines sampled across the last 120,000 years and throughout their present and past geographic ranges. Our findings reveal that the present distribution of these matrilines was shaped by a combination of regional stability and rapid, long-distance dispersal from ice-age refugia. Additionally, we identified multiple instances of hybridization between polar bears and brown bears throughout the Late Pleistocene.
Conclusions: The reconstructed matrilineal history of brown and polar bears exhibits two distinct features. Firstly, it is marked by dramatic and discrete climate-driven dispersal events. Secondly, opportunistic mating between these two species as their ranges overlapped has resulted in a strong genetic imprint, with a likely genetic exchange with extinct Irish brown bears forming the origin of the modern polar bear matriline. This suggests that interspecific hybridization may be more common than previously considered and may serve as a mechanism by which species adapt to marginal habitats during periods of environmental deterioration.

title: FBW7 ubiquitin ligase: a tumour suppressor at the crossroads of cell division, growth and differentiation
text: FBW7 (F-box and WD repeat domain-containing protein 7) serves as the substrate recognition component of an evolutionarily conserved SCF-type ubiquitin ligase complex, which is composed of SKP1, CUL1, and an F-box protein. FBW7 mediates the ubiquitination and degradation of various proto-oncogenes involved in cellular growth and division pathways, including MYC, cyclin E, Notch, and JUN. As a tumor suppressor, the regulatory network of FBW7 is disrupted in many human malignancies. Investigations have identified numerous cancer-associated mutations in FBW7 and its substrates, and loss of FBW7 function leads to chromosomal instability and tumorigenesis. This review focuses on the structural and functional aspects of FBW7 and its role in cancer development.

title: Hypoglycemic episodes and risk of dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text: Although acute hypoglycemia may be associated with cognitive impairment in children with type 1 diabetes, no studies have investigated whether hypoglycemia is a risk factor for dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a longitudinal cohort study of 16,667 older patients with type 2 diabetes from an integrated healthcare delivery system in northern California, following them for 27 years. Our findings indicate that hypoglycemic episodes severe enough to require hospitalization are associated with an increased risk of dementia. Specifically, compared to patients with no history of hypoglycemia, those with a single or multiple episodes had a graded increase in risk, with fully adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.26, 1.80, and 1.94, respectively. The attributable risk of dementia between individuals with and without a history of hypoglycemia was 2.39% per year. These findings suggest that hypoglycemic episodes may be a risk factor for dementia in older patients with type 2 diabetes, and that further research is needed to determine whether minor hypoglycemic episodes also increase this risk.

title: Defective mast cell effector functions in mice lacking the CRACM1 pore subunit of store-operated calcium release–activated calcium channels
text: CRACM1 (also known as Orai1) forms the pore subunit of store-operated calcium release-activated calcium channels. A mutation in the gene encoding CRACM1 has been linked to severe combined immunodeficiency disease in humans. To investigate the role of CRACM1 in mice, we generated mice lacking the gene for CRACM1 and examined their phenotype. We found that CRACM1-deficient mice were smaller in size and had impaired mast cell function, including defective degranulation and cytokine secretion. In addition, allergic reactions in vivo were inhibited in CRACM1-deficient mice. We observed robust CRACM1 expression in skeletal muscles, certain regions of the brain, heart, and kidney, but not in lymphoid regions such as the thymus and spleen. In contrast, CRACM2 was more abundant in mouse T cells. Consistent with these findings, store-operated calcium influx and T cell development and proliferation were unaltered in CRACM1-deficient T cells. Thus, CRACM1 is essential for mast cell effector function, but calcium release-activated calcium channels in mouse T cells are functional even in the absence of CRACM1.

title: MicroRNA-7: A miRNA with expanding roles in development and disease.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of small, non-coding RNA molecules (averaging 22 nucleotides in length) that play a crucial role in post-transcriptional gene regulation. By pairing with target mRNA transcripts through complementary base pairing, miRNAs can either accelerate mRNA degradation or inhibit protein translation, thereby influencing the expression of genes involved in various cellular processes. Given the pivotal role of miRNAs in regulating normal cellular physiology and pathological processes, their potential as therapeutic agents and diagnostic tools in human health is substantial. MicroRNA-7 (miR-7) is a highly conserved miRNA that exhibits restricted spatiotemporal expression during development and adulthood in humans and mice. The generation of mature miR-7 from three distinct genes in humans and mice underscores the importance of this miRNA in regulating fundamental cellular processes and its potential as a therapeutic target. This review aims to delve into the expanding role of miR-7 in health and disease, with a focus on organ differentiation and development, as well as various mammalian diseases such as the brain, heart, endocrine pancreas, and skin, and cancer. As our understanding of miR-7's regulation and functional potential grows, so too does the complexity of its potential applications as a biomarker and therapeutic agent.

title: Integration-free induced pluripotent stem cells model genetic and neural developmental features of down syndrome etiology.
text: Down syndrome (DS), the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability, is characterized by cognitive impairments that result from disruptions in normal cellular processes during development and adulthood. Despite significant research efforts, the underlying mechanisms of DS etiology remain poorly understood. To investigate the potential of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) in modeling DS phenotypes, we generated bona fide DS and wild-type (WT) nonviral iPSCs by episomal reprogramming. Surprisingly, DS iPSCs selectively overexpressed chromosome 21 genes, consistent with gene dosage, which led to deregulation of thousands of genes throughout the genome. DS and WT iPSCs were efficiently neurally converted, and showed similar lineage potency, differentiation kinetics, proliferation, and axon extension at early time points. However, at later time points, DS cultures displayed a twofold bias towards glial lineages. Additionally, DS neural cultures were found to be more sensitive to oxidative stress-induced apoptosis, which could be prevented by the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine. Our findings reveal a complex interplay of genetic alterations caused by trisomy 21, which are likely to contribute to the developmental phenotypes in DS brains. Moreover, the observed oxidative stress sensitivity may contribute to the accelerated neurodegeneration seen in DS, and our results provide a proof of concept for screening corrective therapeutics using DS iPSCs and their derivatives. Nonviral DS iPSCs can therefore serve as a valuable in vitro model for complex human diseases, offering a renewable and ethically unencumbered platform for discovery.

title: In Vivo CRISPR/Cas9 Gene Editing Corrects Retinal Dystrophy in the S334ter-3 Rat Model of Autosomal Dominant Retinitis Pigmentosa
text: Reliable genome editing via Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 may offer a means to correct inherited diseases in patients. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9 can be used in vivo to selectively ablate the rhodopsin gene carrying the dominant S334ter mutation (Rho(S334)) in rats that model severe autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. A single subretinal injection of guide RNA/Cas9 plasmid, combined with electroporation, resulted in allele-specific disruption of Rho(S334), preventing retinal degeneration and improving visual function.

title: Vitamin D insufficiency and the blunted PTH response in established osteoporosis: the role of magnesium deficiency
text:
Vitamin D insufficiency is common, but not all individuals with this deficiency exhibit the same biochemical responses. Specifically, some individuals may have a blunted response to parathyroid hormone (PTH) excess. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between magnesium (Mg) deficiency and the calcium-PTH endocrine axis in patients with established osteoporosis, with a focus on differing degrees of vitamin D and PTH status.
The study included 30 patients (10 women) who were divided into three groups based on their vitamin D and PTH levels. The groups were: low vitamin D and low PTH, low vitamin D and raised PTH, and vitamin replete. The study measured the participants' calcium, PTH, Mg retention (using the standard Mg loading test), dietary nutrient intake (calcium, vitamin D, Mg), and bone turnover markers (serum CTX & P1CP) at baseline and after oral Mg supplementation. Multivariate analysis was used to control for potential confounding baseline variables.
The results showed that all subjects within the low vitamin D and low PTH group had evidence of Mg depletion, as evidenced by a low Mg retention rate (mean = 70.3%, SD = 12.5). Additionally, these subjects showed an increase in calcium levels (mean = 0.06 mmol/l, SD = 0.01) and a rise in PTH levels (mean = 13.3 ng/l, SD = 4.5) compared to baseline. Following oral Mg supplementation, bone turnover increased, as evidenced by a rise in CTX (mean = 0.16 mcg/l, SD = 0.06) and P1CP (mean = 13.1 mcg/l, SD = 5.7) levels.
In contrast, subjects with a low vitamin D and raised PTH level had a lower Mg retention rate (mean = 55.9%, SD = 14.8) compared to the low vitamin D and low PTH group. Moreover, there was little change in both acute markers of calcium homeostasis and bone turnover markers following both the Mg loading test and oral supplementation.
The study's findings confirm that in patients with established osteoporosis, there is a distinct group with a low vitamin D and blunted PTH level, and that Mg deficiency is an important contributing factor. These results suggest that Mg supplementation may be beneficial in improving bone turnover in individuals with low vitamin D and blunted PTH levels, but further research is needed to confirm these findings.

title: Novel syndromes associated with JC virus infection of neurons and meningeal cells: no longer a gray area.
text:
The recent surge in the availability of immunomodulatory medications has led to the recognition of novel JC virus (JCV)-associated brain syndromes in patients with autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis, Crohn's disease, and psoriasis. This review focuses on the three newly discovered syndromes that are caused by JCV infection of neurons and meningeal cells, which were not previously recognized as predisposing factors for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
Recent findings have expanded our understanding of JCV infection, revealing that JCV-infected glial cells are frequently located at the gray-white matter junction or exclusively within the gray matter, leading to demyelination in the cortex. Mutations in JCV can also trigger a change in tropism, resulting in involvement of other cell types, such as neurons and meningeal cells, causing distinct clinical entities. These new features of JCV infection pose challenges for clinicians and investigators, highlighting the need for increased awareness and further research to better understand JCV pathogenesis and develop effective therapies.
In summary, we hope that increased awareness of these syndromes will lead to early diagnosis and pave the way for new research opportunities. However, we must remain vigilant and open to the possibility of additional JC variants or unknown polyomaviruses associated with neurological diseases.

title: Phosphoinositide 3-kinase signalling pathways in tumor progression, invasion and angiogenesis.
text:
The PI3K Signaling Pathway in Cancer: A Review of Mechanisms and Therapeutic Implications
Introduction:
The PI3K signaling pathway has emerged as a crucial player in cancer, with evidence suggesting that its dysregulation is involved in the progression of many common cancers. This review aims to provide an overview of the current understanding of the mechanisms by which the PI3K pathway contributes to tumor progression, and to discuss the potential of targeting this pathway for cancer therapy.
Evidence and Mechanisms:
Studies have shown that misregulation of the PI3K pathway is a hallmark of many cancer types, including breast, lung, and colon cancer. This misregulation can occur through loss of the tumor suppressor protein PTEN, or through constitutive activation of PI3K isoforms or downstream elements such as AKT and mTOR. Activation of the PI3K pathway promotes cell survival, proliferation, cytoskeletal deformability, and motility, as well as angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels that supply the growing tumor. The PI3K pathway also regulates the expression of angiogenic cytokines, such as VEGF, FGF, and Tie-2, which promote angiogenesis by signaling through receptors on endothelial cells.
Clinical Implications:
The involvement of the PI3K pathway in cancer has significant clinical implications. Targeting this pathway with specific inhibitors could potentially interfere with tumor progression at several pivotal points, including cell survival, invasion, and angiogenesis. In addition, the PI3K pathway is often overactive in cancer, making it an attractive target for cancer therapy.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, the PI3K signaling pathway plays a critical role in cancer, and targeting this pathway has the potential to be a valuable adjunct to conventional cancer therapies. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms by which the PI3K pathway contributes to cancer, and to develop specific inhibitors that can effectively target this pathway.

title: Complementary foods for infant feeding in developing countries: their nutrient adequacy and improvement
text:
Objective: To assess the nutritional adequacy of various plant-based complementary foods consumed in developing countries, specifically in Africa, India, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, and Thailand.
Methodology: The energy, nutrient, and anti-nutrient (dietary fiber and phytic acid) content of 23 plant-based complementary foods was calculated based on chemical analysis and literature values. These values were then compared to the estimated nutrient needs of infants aged 9-11 months, assuming average breast milk intake and three complementary feedings per day, each of 250g.
Results: The study found that complementary foods should provide approximately 25-50% of the daily requirements for protein, riboflavin, and copper, 50-75% for thiamin, calcium, and manganese, and 75-100% for phosphorus, zinc, and iron. While most of the foods met the estimated daily nutrient needs for protein, thiamin, and copper, they did not meet the requirements for calcium, iron, and in some cases zinc, even with moderate bioavailability assumed. Some of the foods based on rice were also inadequate in riboflavin (per day; per 100kcal).
Conclusion: The study suggests that even with strategies to improve iron and zinc bioavailability, the deficits in calcium, iron, and zinc are likely to persist. Therefore, research on the feasibility of fortifying plant-based complementary foods in developing countries with calcium, iron, and zinc is urgently needed.
Sponsorship: The study was supported by the Micronutrient Initiative through the Canadian International Development Agency.

title: Early aging and age-related pathologies in mice deficient in BMAL1, the core componentof the circadian clock.
text: Mice lacking the circadian transcription factor BMAL1 (brain and muscle ARNT-like protein) exhibit impaired circadian behavior and a loss of rhythmicity in the expression of target genes. In this study, we found that Bmal1-deficient mice have shorter lifespans and display premature aging symptoms, including sarcopenia, cataracts, reduced subcutaneous fat, organ shrinkage, and others. Interestingly, these aging phenotypes are associated with elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in certain tissues of the Bmal1-deficient animals. These findings, combined with previous research on the CLOCK/BMAL1-regulated control of stress responses, may offer an explanation for the early onset of age-related diseases in the absence of BMAL1.

title: A self-inactivating lentiviral vector for SCID-X1 gene therapy that does not activate LMO2 expression in human T cells.
text: To develop safer and more effective vectors for gene therapy of X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID-X1), we evaluated new self-inactivating lentiviral vectors based on the HIV virus. We created two vectors, CL20i4-hgamma(c)-Revgen and CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT, which contain the entire human common gamma chain (gamma(c)) genomic sequence driven by the gamma(c) promoter, and a promoter fragment from the eukaryotic elongation factor alpha (EF1alpha) gene, respectively. Both vectors also contain a 400-bp insulator fragment from the chicken beta-globin locus within the self-inactivating long-terminal repeat. In mouse SCID-X1 transplantation models, transduction of bone marrow cells with either vector restored T, B, and natural killer lymphocyte development and function. In addition, transduction of human CD34(+) bone marrow cells from SCID-X1 patients with either vector restored T-cell development in an in vitro assay. In safety studies using a Jurkat LMO2 activation assay, only the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector lacked the ability to transactivate LMO2 protein expression, while the CL20i4-hgamma(c)-Revgen vector significantly activated LMO2 protein expression. Furthermore, the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector has not caused any tumors in transplanted mice. Based on these preclinical demonstrations of efficacy and safety, we conclude that the CL20i4-EF1alpha-hgamma(c)OPT vector may be suitable for testing in a clinical trial.

title: Genetic Variants at Newly Identified Lipid Loci Are Associated with Coronary Heart Disease in a Chinese Han Population
text:
Background: Recent genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several novel loci associated with blood lipid levels in Caucasians. We aimed to investigate whether these genetic variants are also associated with coronary heart disease (CHD) susceptibility in a Chinese Han population.
Methods/Principal Findings: We conducted a two-stage case-control study in a Chinese Han population, consisting of 1,376 CHD cases and 1,376 sex- and age-matched controls, and validated significant single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in a second stage of 1,269 cases and 2,745 controls. We also examined associations between SNPs within the five novel loci and blood lipid levels in 4,121 controls. We identified two novel SNPs (rs599839 in CELSR2-PSRC1-SORT1 and rs16996148 in NCAN-CILP2) that were significantly associated with reduced CHD risk in Chinese (odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) in the dominant model: 0.76 (0.61-0.90; P = 0.001), 0.67 (0.57-0.77; P = 3.4 × 10(-8)), respectively). Multiple linear regression analyses using the dominant model showed that rs599839 was significantly associated with decreased low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels (P = 0.022), while rs16996148 was significantly associated with increased LDL and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels (P = 2.9 × 10(-4) and 0.001, respectively).
Conclusions/Significance: Our findings identify two novel SNPs (rs599839 and rs16996148) at newly identified lipid-associated loci that are significantly associated with CHD susceptibility in a Chinese Han population. These findings provide new insights into the genetic basis of CHD susceptibility in this population and may have implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for CHD prevention.

title: Spare respiratory capacity rather than oxidative stress regulates glutamate excitotoxicity after partial respiratory inhibition of mitochondrial complex I with rotenone.
text: According to a recent study, partial inhibition of mitochondrial complex I by rotenone in rodents reproduces certain aspects of Parkinson's disease. The study aimed to investigate whether the enhancement of neuronal cell death by rotenone is due to oxidative stress. To test this hypothesis, the researchers used primary cultures of rat cerebellar granule neurons in an acute glutamate excitotoxicity model. They found that even at low concentrations (5 nM), rotenone increased mitochondrial superoxide levels and potentiated glutamate-induced cytoplasmic calcium deregulation, which is the first irreversible stage of necrotic cell death. However, the use of a cell-permeant O2*- trap failed to prevent the effects of the inhibitor. The study also quantified the bioenergetic consequences of rotenone addition by monitoring cell respiration. The results showed that glutamate activation of NMDA receptors used up the full respiratory capacity of the in situ mitochondria, and over 80% of the glutamate-stimulated respiration was due to increased cellular ATP demand. Rotenone at 20 nM inhibited basal and carbonyl cyanide p-trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone-stimulated cell respiration and caused respiratory failure in the presence of glutamate. In addition, oligomycin, an inhibitor of ATP synthase, was also toxic in the presence of glutamate. The study concluded that the cell vulnerability in the rotenone model of partial complex I deficiency under these specific conditions is primarily determined by spare respiratory capacity rather than oxidative stress.

title: Isolated liver perfusion for non-resectable liver tumours: a review.
text: Over the past four decades, numerous treatments have been proposed for non-resectable primary or secondary hepatic cancer, but the outcomes have been largely disappointing. Isolated Hepatic Perfusion (IHP) was first attempted in the past, but it gained acceptance only recently after remarkable tumor responses were achieved through isolated limb perfusion with melphalan and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) for melanomas and sarcomas. The surgical isolation of the liver is a technically challenging operation that enables the safe administration of high doses of chemotherapeutics and TNF. In contrast, percutaneous techniques using balloon occlusion catheters are simpler but result in higher leakage rates from the perfusion circuit into the systemic circulation. Several phase I-II trials have demonstrated that IHP can achieve high tumor response rates, even in the presence of resistance to systemic chemotherapy. However, no significant advantage in overall survival has been shown thus far. IHP offers distinct pharmacokinetic advantages for locoregional chemotherapy and biotherapy, and it may also allow gene therapy with minimal systemic exposure and toxicity. At present, IHP remains an experimental treatment modality that should only be used in controlled trials.

title: Combinatorial control of exon recognition.
text: Pre-mRNA splicing is a crucial process in the expression of most metazoan genes, as it allows for the removal of non-coding intronic sequences and the assembly of exons into mature mRNAs prior to translation. This process is carried out by the spliceosome, a complex machine that catalyzes the precise removal of introns and the formation of mature mRNAs. Given the complexity of higher eukaryotic genes and the relatively low level of splice site conservation, the accuracy of the splicing machinery in recognizing and pairing splice sites is remarkable. Introns ranging in size from a few hundred to over 100,000 base pairs are efficiently removed during splicing. Moreover, alternative splicing events are observed between different cell types, during development, or during other biological processes, indicating a significant flexibility of the spliceosome in identifying and processing exons within a given pre-mRNA. To achieve this flexibility, splice site selection in higher eukaryotes has evolved to depend on multiple factors, including splice site strength, the presence or absence of splicing regulators, RNA secondary structures, the exon/intron architecture, and the pre-mRNA synthesis process itself. The relative contributions of each of these factors influence how efficiently splice sites are recognized and flanking introns are removed.
