In contrast, vaccine targeted to the small intestine induced only small intestinal immunity and failed to provide rectal or vaginal protection, highlighting the functional compartmentalization within the gut mucosal immune system. Therefore, using this oral vaccine delivery system to target the large intestine, but not the small intestine, may represent a feasible new strategy for immune protection of rectal and vaginal mucosa.

title: Timing of menarche and first full-term birth in relation to breast cancer risk.
text: The age at which a woman reaches menarche (her first menstrual period) and the interval between this age and the age at which she gives birth for the first time are established risk factors for breast cancer. However, few studies have investigated the relationship between these reproductive events and breast cancer risk. In a large, population-based study of White and African-American women in the United States, the authors used logistic regression to evaluate the association between the timing of these events and breast cancer risk among 4,013 cases and 4,069 controls. The results showed that among parous (having given birth) premenopausal and postmenopausal White women, those who had an interval of greater than or equal to 16 years between the ages of menarche and first birth had a 1.5-fold (95% confidence interval: 1.0, 2.2) and 1.4-fold (95% CI: 1.1, 1.8) increased risk of breast cancer, respectively, compared to those who had an interval of less than or equal to 5 years. Adjusting for age at first birth slightly altered these risk estimates, with odds ratios of 1.5 (95% CI: 0.8, 2.9) and 1.0 (95% CI: 0.6, 1.5), respectively. These associations were stronger for lobular and hormone-receptor-positive tumors, but were absent among premenopausal African-American women. The authors conclude that the interval between age at menarche and age at first birth is associated with the risk of hormonally sensitive types of breast cancer, particularly among White women.

title: Prognostic Value of Late Gadolinium Enhancement Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in Cardiac Amyloidosis
text:
Background: The prognosis and treatment of the two main types of cardiac amyloidosis, immunoglobulin light chain (AL) and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, are significantly influenced by the extent of cardiac involvement. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is a reference standard for the diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis, but its potential for stratifying risk is unknown.
Methods and Results: In this study, 250 prospectively recruited subjects, including 122 patients with ATTR amyloid, 9 asymptomatic mutation carriers, and 119 patients with AL amyloidosis, underwent LGE cardiovascular magnetic resonance. Subjects were followed up for a mean of 24±13 months. LGE was performed using phase-sensitive inversion recovery (PSIR) and without (magnitude only) and was compared with extracellular volume measured with T1 mapping. PSIR was found to be superior to magnitude-only inversion recovery LGE as it always nulled the tissue with the longest T1 (either blood or myocardium). LGE was classified into three patterns: none, subendocardial, and transmural, which were associated with increasing amyloid burden as defined by extracellular volume (P<0.0001), with transitions from none to subendocardial LGE occurring at an extracellular volume of 0.40 to 0.43 (AL) and 0.39 to 0.40 (ATTR) and to transmural LGE at 0.48 to 0.55 (AL) and 0.47 to 0.59 (ATTR). Sixty-seven patients (27%) died during the follow-up period. Transmural LGE was found to predict death (hazard ratio, 5.4; 95% confidence interval, 2.1-13.7; P<0.0001) and remained independent after adjustment for N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide, ejection fraction, stroke volume index, E/E', and left ventricular mass index (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 1.3-13.1; P<0.05).
Conclusions: There is a continuum of cardiac involvement in systemic AL and ATTR amyloidosis, with transmural LGE being determined reliably by PSIR and representing advanced cardiac amyloidosis. The PSIR technique provides incremental information on outcome even after adjustment for known prognostic factors.

title: Global, regional, and national comparative risk assessment of 79 behavioural, environmental and occupational, and metabolic risks or clusters of risks, 1990–2015: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2015
text:
The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2015 provides a comprehensive assessment of the burden of various risks on global health. The study uses a comparative risk assessment framework to estimate the attributable deaths, disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and trends in exposure to 79 different risks across different age groups, sex, years, and geographic locations from 1990 to 2015.
The study found that while some risks, such as unsafe sanitation and household air pollution, have decreased by more than 25% over the past 25 years, others, such as high BMI, high fasting plasma glucose, and drug use, have increased by more than 25% during the same period. The study also found that these risks jointly accounted for 57.8% of global deaths and 41.2% of DALYs in 2015.
The study identified the top 10 contributors to global DALYs among Level 3 risks, which are smoking, high systolic blood pressure, high fasting plasma glucose, high BMI, childhood undernutrition, ambient particulate matter, high total cholesterol, household air pollution, and alcohol use. The study also found that while some risks, such as micronutrient deficiencies and childhood undernutrition, have seen significant declines in attributable DALYs, others, such as rising exposure to high BMI, high fasting plasma glucose, and drug use, have contributed to notable increases in attributable DALYs.
The study also found that environmental risks and childhood undernutrition declined steadily with the Socio-demographic Index (SDI), while low physical activity, high BMI, and high fasting plasma glucose increased with SDI. In 119 countries, metabolic risks, such as high BMI and fasting plasma glucose, contributed the most attributable DALYs in 2015.
Overall, the study highlights the need for public policy makers to pay attention to the risks that are increasingly major contributors to global burden, such as high BMI, high fasting plasma glucose, and drug use. The study also underscores the importance of addressing these risks through interventions and policies aimed at reducing exposure and promoting healthy behaviors.

title: Human RecQ helicases in DNA repair, recombination, and replication.
text: RecQ helicases are a vital family of genome surveillance proteins that have been conserved throughout evolution, from bacteria to humans. These proteins play critical roles in maintaining genome stability and are often referred to as the "guardians of the genome." There are five human RecQ helicases, each with unique functions in genome maintenance, including DNA repair, recombination, replication, and transcription. These proteins interact with a variety of protein partners, which dictate their specialized functions. Interestingly, defects in certain RecQ helicases have been linked to heritable human disease syndromes. Future research aims to better understand the division of labor among the human RecQ helicases and how they collaborate to enhance genome stability. By gaining a deeper understanding of these proteins and their functions, researchers hope to uncover new avenues for the prevention and treatment of genetic disorders.

title: Metabolomics study of the therapeutic mechanism of Schisandra Chinensis lignans in diet-induced hyperlipidemia mice
text:
Background: Schisandra chinensis, a globally distributed plant, has been traditionally used in China to treat diseases such as hyperlipidemia, fatty liver, and obesity. In this study, we investigated the anti-hyperlipidemic effect of Schisandra chinensis lignans (SCL) using a rapid resolution liquid chromatography coupled with quadruple-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (RRLC-Q-TOF-MS)-based metabolomics approach.
Methods: Hyperlipidemic mice were orally administered with SCL (100 mg/kg) once a day for 4 weeks. Serum biochemistry assays were conducted to evaluate the treatment's effect on lipid levels, including triglyceride (TG), total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-c), and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-c). Metabolomics analysis was performed on serum samples, and principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) were used for pattern recognition and characteristic metabolite identification. The expression levels of critical regulatory factors of liver lipid metabolism, sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs) and its related gene expressions, were measured by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).
Results: Oral administration of SCL significantly decreased the serum levels of TC, TG, and LDL-c and increased the serum level of HDL-c in the hyperlipidemic mice, with no effect on lipid levels in control mice. Serum samples were scattered in the PCA scores plots in response to the control, HFD, and SCL groups. A total of 13 biomarkers were identified, and 9 of them were recovered to normal levels after SCL treatment. Based on KEGG pathway analysis, the anti-hyperlipidemic mechanisms of SCL may involve the TCA cycle, cholesterol synthesis, choline metabolism, and fatty acid metabolism. SCL also significantly inhibited the mRNA expression levels of hepatic lipogenesis genes, including SREBP-1c, fatty acid synthase (FAS), and acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), and decreased the mRNA expression of liver X receptor α (LXRα). Additionally, SCL significantly decreased the expression levels of SREBP-2 and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR) in the liver of hyperlipidemic mice.
Conclusion: The anti-hyperlipidemic effect of SCL was confirmed by both serum biochemistry and metabolomics analysis. The mechanism may involve the down-regulation of LXRα/SREBP-1c/FAS/ACC and SREBP2/HMGCR signaling pathways.

title: Tet1 and Tet2 regulate 5-hydroxymethylcytosine production and cell lineage specification in mouse embryonic stem cells.
text: TET family enzymes convert 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) in DNA. Our findings show that Tet1 and Tet2 are regulated by Oct4 and together maintain 5hmC in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs). During the reprogramming of fibroblasts to induced pluripotent stem cells, Tet1 and Tet2 are induced simultaneously with 5hmC. ESCs depleted of Tet1 through RNAi exhibit diminished expression of the Nodal antagonist Lefty1 and display hyperactive Nodal signaling, leading to an imbalance in differentiation towards the endoderm-mesoderm lineage in embryoid bodies in vitro. In culture conditions supplemented with Fgf4 and heparin, Tet1-depleted ESCs activate the trophoblast stem cell lineage determinant Elf5 and can colonize the placenta in midgestation embryo chimeras. Consistently, Tet1-depleted ESCs form aggressive hemorrhagic teratomas with increased endoderm, reduced neuroectoderm, and ectopic appearance of trophoblastic giant cells. These findings suggest that 5hmC is an epigenetic modification associated with pluripotency, and Tet1 regulates the lineage differentiation potential of ESCs.

title: Polycomb Associates Genome-wide with a Specific RNA Polymerase II Variant, and Regulates Metabolic Genes in ESCs
text: Polycomb repressor complexes (PRCs) play a crucial role in shaping the chromatin landscape and are implicated in both pluripotency and cancer. While it is known that PRCs can silence gene expression, the relationship between PRCs and RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is not well understood. To investigate this, we used ChIP-seq to map PRC repression markers and RNAPII states in embryonic stem cells (ESCs). Our findings reveal that PRC targets exhibit a range of RNAPII variants, including unproductive RNAPII (S5p(+)S7p(-)S2p(-)) genome-wide in developmental PRC targets. Interestingly, we found that PRCs and RNAPII-S5p physically bind to the same chromatin and functionally synergize. Additionally, we identified a cohort of genes marked by PRC and elongating RNAPII (S5p(+)S7p(+)S2p(+)), which produce mRNA and protein and exhibit increased expression upon PRC1 knockdown. These genes switch between active and PRC-repressed states within the ESC population and many have roles in metabolism. Our study sheds light on the complex interplay between PRCs and RNAPII in regulating gene expression in ESCs.

title: Chemokine-like receptor 1 (CMKLR1) and chemokine (C-C motif) receptor-like 2 (CCRL2); two multifunctional receptors with unusual properties.
text:
Chemokine-like receptor 1 (CMKLR1), also known as ChemR23, and chemokine (C-C motif) receptor-like 2 (CCRL2), are 7-transmembrane receptors that were first identified in the late 1990s due to their similarity to G-protein-coupled receptors. Initially, these receptors were considered orphan receptors without any known biological functions. However, recent studies have revealed that they have ligands and play important roles in various cellular processes.
Plasma protein-derived chemoattractant chemerin is a ligand for CMKLR1, and activating CMKLR1 with chemerin leads to the migration of macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs) in vitro, suggesting a proinflammatory role. However, in vivo studies using CMKLR-deficient mice indicate an anti-inflammatory role for this receptor, possibly due to the recruitment of tolerogenic plasmacytoid DCs. Chemerin/CMKLR1 interaction also promotes adipogenesis and angiogenesis. The anti-inflammatory lipid mediator, resolving E1, is another CMKLR1 ligand that inhibits leukocyte infiltration and proinflammatory gene expression. These divergent results suggest that CMKLR1 is a multifunctional receptor.
Chemokine CCL5 and CCL19 are reported to bind to CCRL2. Unlike Duffy antigen for chemokine receptor (DARC), D6 and CCX-CKR, CCRL2 does not signal, but it constitutively recycles, potentially reducing local concentration of CCL5 and CCL19 and subsequent immune responses. Interestingly, chemerin, a ligand for CMKLR1, is also a ligand for CCRL2. CCRL2 binds chemerin and increases local chemerin concentration to efficiently present it to CMKLR1 on nearby cells, providing a link between CCRL2 and CMKLR1. Although these findings suggest an anti-inflammatory role, a recent study using CCRL2-deficient mice indicates a proinflammatory role; thus, CCRL2 may also be multifunctional. Further studies using CMKLR1- or CCRL2-deficient mice are needed to further define the role of these receptors in immune responses and other cellular processes.

title: Identification of vitronectin as an extrinsic inducer of cancer stem cell differentiation and tumor formation.
text: There is an increasing body of evidence suggesting that cancer stem cells (CSCs), a rare subset of cells, play a crucial role in tumor initiation. CSCs are typically quiescent, self-renew, and form tumors at low frequencies, while also giving rise to the diverse cell types present within a tumor. Despite extensive research, the factors responsible for CSC differentiation remain unknown. Here, we uncover a novel mechanism of CSC differentiation, revealing that vitronectin, a component of human serum, drives stem cell differentiation through an integrin alpha V beta 3-dependent pathway. When CSCs are cultured on vitronectin, we observe a downregulation of stem cell genes, modification of differentiation markers, and loss of beta-catenin nuclear localization. Inhibition of integrin alpha V beta 3 impedes differentiation and subsequent tumor formation, highlighting the importance of this axis in novel therapies targeting both extrinsic and intracellular pathways.

title: STIM1 Is a Calcium Sensor Specialized for Digital Signaling
text: When cells are stimulated by calcium-mobilizing agonists at low, physiological concentrations, the resulting calcium signals typically take the form of repetitive, regenerative discharges of stored calcium, known as calcium oscillations [1]. These intracellular calcium fluctuations have long fascinated biologists as a form of digital intracellular signaling. Recent research has highlighted the importance of calcium influx as a crucial component of calcium oscillations [2]. This influx is mediated by a process called store-operated calcium entry, which is triggered by calcium sensor proteins, STIM1 and STIM2, in the endoplasmic reticulum [3]. STIM2 is activated by changes in endoplasmic reticulum calcium near the resting level, while a threshold of calcium depletion is required for STIM1 activation [4]. Our findings reveal that, unexpectedly, STIM1 is the exclusive calcium entry protein during calcium oscillations, leading to a transient drop in endoplasmic reticulum calcium with each oscillation. This drop is sufficient to transiently activate STIM1, which can be observed in some cells using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy. This arrangement provides a clear and unambiguous signaling system, translating a digital calcium release signal into calcium influx that can signal to downstream effectors.

title: Trends in the use of complementary health approaches among adults: United States, 2002-2012.
text:
This report presents national estimates of complementary health approach usage among adults in the United States across three time points: 2002, 2007, and 2012. Trends in the use of specific complementary health approaches are compared, and differences in usage are examined by demographic characteristics.
The study analyzed data from 88,962 adults aged 18 and over collected through the National Health Interview Survey in 2002, 2007, and 2012. The data were weighted to produce national estimates representative of the civilian, non-institutionalized U.S. adult population. Significance tests were used to evaluate differences between percentages at a 0.05 level.
The results showed that non-vitamin, non-mineral dietary supplements were the most commonly used complementary health approach, while the use of yoga, tai chi, and qi gong increased linearly across the three time points. Yoga accounted for approximately 80% of the prevalence among these three approaches. The study also found differences in complementary health approach usage by age and Hispanic or Latino origin and race.

title: Histone structure and nucleosome stability.
text: Histone proteins are crucial for the dynamic transition between active and inactive chromatin states. Despite their high degree of conservation due to evolutionary pressures to maintain the nucleosomal octameric core structure, histones have evolved diverse variants with distinct roles in gene regulation and epigenetic silencing. These variants, along with post-translational modifications and interactions with chromatin remodeling complexes, significantly impact DNA replication, transcription, repair, and recombination. Recent studies on chromatin structure have confirmed previous observations of interparticle interactions revealed through crystal structures, highlighting the complex interplay between histones and other chromatin components.

title: Cerebral palsy among term and postterm births.
text:
Although preterm delivery is a well-established risk factor for cerebral palsy (CP), preterm births account for only a minority of CP cases. However, there is limited information on the relationship between CP risk and gestational age in the term range, where most CP cases occur. This study aimed to investigate whether the timing of birth in the term and postterm period is associated with the risk of CP.
The study was a population-based follow-up study conducted in Norway using the Medical Birth Registry. The cohort consisted of 1,682,441 singleton children born between 1967 and 2001 with a gestational age of 37-44 weeks and no congenital anomalies. The cohort was followed up through 2005 by linking to other national registries. The main outcome measures were the absolute and relative risk of CP for children surviving to at least 4 years of age.
Of the cohort of term and postterm children, 1938 were registered with CP in the National Insurance Scheme. The risk of CP was lowest for children born at 40 weeks, with a prevalence of 0.99/1000 (95% CI, 0.90-1.08). The risk of CP increased with earlier or later delivery, with a prevalence at 37 weeks of 1.91/1000 (95% CI, 1.58-2.25) and a relative risk (RR) of 1.9 (95% CI, 1.6-2.4), a prevalence at 38 weeks of 1.25/1000 (95% CI, 1.07-1.42) and an RR of 1.3 (95% CI, 1.1-1.6), a prevalence at 42 weeks of 1.36/1000 (95% CI, 1.19-1.53) and an RR of 1.4 (95% CI, 1.2-1.6), and a prevalence after 42 weeks of 1.44/1000 (95% CI, 1.15-1.72) and an RR of 1.4 (95% CI, 1.1-1.8). These associations were even stronger in a subset with gestational age based on ultrasound measurements: at 37 weeks the prevalence was 1.17/1000 (95% CI, 0.30-2.04) and the relative risk was 3.7 (95% CI, 1.5-9.1). At 42 weeks the prevalence was 0.85/1000 (95% CI, 0.33-1.38) and the relative risk was 2.4 (95% CI, 1.1-5.3). Adjustment for infant sex, maternal age, and various socioeconomic measures had little effect.
The study found that compared to delivery at 40 weeks' gestation, delivery at 37 or 38 weeks or at 42 weeks or later was associated with an increased risk of CP. These findings suggest that the timing of birth in the term and postterm period may be an important factor in the development of CP.

title: 53BP1 Inhibits Homologous Recombination in Brca1-Deficient Cells by Blocking Resection of DNA Breaks
text: Defective DNA repair through homologous recombination (HR) is believed to be a significant factor in tumor development in individuals with Brca1 mutations. Our findings reveal that DNA breaks in Brca1-deficient cells are aberrantly joined into complex chromosome rearrangements through a process dependent on nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) factors, including 53BP1 and DNA ligase 4. Notably, loss of 53BP1 alleviates the hypersensitivity of Brca1 mutant cells to PARP inhibition and restores error-free repair through HR. Mechanistically, the deletion of 53BP1 promotes ATM-dependent processing of broken DNA ends to produce recombinogenic single-stranded DNA that can be repaired by HR. In contrast, the deficiency of Lig4 does not rescue the HR defect in Brca1 mutant cells but prevents the joining of chromatid breaks into chromosome rearrangements. Our results demonstrate that HR and NHEJ compete to process DNA breaks that arise during DNA replication, and that modulating this balance can be exploited to selectively protect or kill cells harboring Brca1 mutations.

title: The genetics of Mexico recapitulates Native American substructure and affects biomedical traits
text: Mexico boasts a rich cultural and ethnic diversity, yet the fine-scale patterns of human genome-wide variation within this region remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we analyzed genomic variation in over 1000 individuals from 20 indigenous and 11 mestizo populations across Mexico. Our findings revealed striking genetic stratification among indigenous groups, with some showing degrees of genetic differentiation comparable to that between Europeans and East Asians. Pre-Columbian genetic substructure was also evident in the ancestry of admixed mestizo individuals across the country. Moreover, two independent cohorts of Mexicans and Mexican Americans showed a significant association between subcontinental ancestry and lung function. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for fine-scale ancestry patterns in medical and population genetic studies within Mexico, as well as in other populations worldwide.

title: COPI Complex Is a Regulator of Lipid Homeostasis
text: Lipid droplets are ubiquitous organelles that play a crucial role in energy storage homeostasis and biosynthesis. Although the mechanisms of lipid droplet formation and regulation are not fully understood, it is known that the PAT protein family, which includes perilipin, adipocyte differentiation-related protein, and tail interacting protein of 47 kDa, coats the droplet surface and mediates interactions with lipases that remobilize stored lipids. To identify key regulatory genes in Drosophila, we used an image segmentation-based optical read-out system for RNA interference (RNAi) screening. Our findings indicate that the vesicle-mediated Coat Protein Complex I (COPI) transport complex is an evolutionarily conserved regulator of lipid homeostasis, and that COPI components regulate the composition of the PAT protein surface and promote the association of adipocyte triglyceride lipase (ATGL) with the lipid droplet surface to mediate lipolysis. Two compounds that inhibit COPI function, Exo1 and Brefeldin A, phenocopy COPI knockdowns, and RNAi inhibition of ATGL and simultaneous drug treatment indicate that COPI and ATGL function in the same pathway. These data highlight an interaction between vesicle transport systems and lipid droplets and suggest that the COPI complex plays a crucial role in regulating lipid homeostasis.

title: Differentiation of effector CD4 T cell populations (*).
text: CD4 T cells are crucial for the body's adaptive immune system, as they help fight off a wide range of pathogens. They also play a role in autoimmune diseases, such as asthma and allergies, as well as in cancer. When activated in a specific cytokine environment, naive CD4 T cells can differentiate into different types of T helper (Th) cells, including Th1, Th2, Th17, and iTreg, each with its own distinct pattern of cytokine production and function. This review summarizes the discovery, functions, and relationships among Th cells, as well as the cytokine and signaling requirements for their development, the transcription factors involved in their differentiation, and the epigenetic regulation of their key cytokines and transcription factors. Additionally, the review discusses human diseases caused by defects in CD4 T cell differentiation.

title: Homocysteine and other thiols in plasma and urine: automated determination and sample stability.
text: We have developed an enhanced version of our previously reported fully automated column-switching HPLC method for determining total plasma homocysteine using single-column reversed-phase separation. This modified method allows for the simultaneous analysis of homocysteine, cysteine, and cysteinylglycine in plasma, as well as acid-precipitated plasma and urine. The automated sample processing includes derivatization and chromatography, which were optimized to achieve accurate separations within 15 minutes. The optimal pH of the mobile phase for maximum fluorescence yield was found to be 3.65 for plasma and 3.50 for acid-precipitated plasma and urine. The method demonstrated high sensitivity (detection limit approximately 0.05 pmol) and precision (CV < 5%), with the ability to analyze approximately 70 samples in 24 hours. Additionally, serum and heparin plasma can also be analyzed using this method. Hemolysis up to approximately 2.0 g/L of hemoglobin did not interfere with the analytical recovery of homocysteine or cysteine. Standardization of blood-sampling procedures has significantly improved the method and expanded its applications.

title: Induced pluripotent stem cells in Alzheimer’s disease: applications for disease modeling and cell-replacement therapy
text: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia in individuals aged 65 and older. Despite the identification of numerous genetic and risk factors, the underlying mechanisms of AD remain poorly understood due to the inability to test theoretical hypotheses on non-postmortem and patient-specific research systems. Recent advances in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) technology offer a promising platform for creating reliable models of AD, as well as for efficient drug screening. Additionally, human-sourced iPSCs may provide a valuable tool for cell-replacement therapy against AD. While significant progress has been made, several key challenges must be addressed in iPSCs research, including the identification of robust disease phenotypes in AD modeling and the clinical availability of iPSCs-based cell-replacement therapy in humans. This review highlights recent advances in iPSCs research and discusses the translational challenges of using AD patients-derived iPSCs in disease modeling and cell-replacement therapy.

title: Nitrite protects against morbidity and mortality associated with TNF- or LPS-induced shock in a soluble guanylate cyclase–dependent manner
text: Nitrite (NO2(-)), previously considered an inert metabolite and biomarker of endogenous nitric oxide (NO), has been identified as a crucial biological NO reservoir in tissues and vasculature, contributing to hypoxic signaling, vasodilation, and cytoprotection following ischemia-reperfusion injury. Enzymatic reduction of nitrite to NO can occur at low pH and oxygen levels through deoxyhemoglobin, deoxymyoglobin, xanthine oxidase, mitochondrial complexes, or NO synthase (NOS). Our findings reveal that nitrite treatment exhibits contrasting effects compared to NOS inhibition, significantly attenuating hypothermia, mitochondrial damage, oxidative stress, tissue infarction, and mortality in a mouse shock model induced by a lethal tumor necrosis factor challenge. Mechanistically, nitrite-dependent protection is not associated with inhibition of mitochondrial complex I activity, as previously demonstrated for ischemia-reperfusion, but is largely abolished in mice lacking the soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) alpha1 subunit, a key intracellular NO receptor and signal transducer in the cardiovasculature. Additionally, nitrite provides protection against toxicity induced by Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide, although higher doses are required. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that nitrite can protect against toxicity in shock through sGC-dependent signaling, which may involve hypoxic vasodilation necessary to maintain microcirculation and organ function, as well as cardioprotection.

title: Mammographic density and the risk and detection of breast cancer.
text:
Background: Extensive mammographic density has been linked to an increased risk of breast cancer and hinders the accuracy of mammography in detecting cancer. However, the impact of density on cancer risk across different detection methods remains unclear.
Methods: We conducted three nested case-control studies in screened populations, comprising 1112 matched case-control pairs. We investigated the association between the percentage of density in the baseline mammogram and breast cancer risk, considering the method of cancer detection, time since screening initiation, and age.
Results: Compared to women with density in less than 10% of the mammogram, those with density in 75% or more had a significantly higher risk of breast cancer (odds ratio [OR] 4.7, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.0-7.4), regardless of whether detected by screening (OR 3.5, 95% CI 2.0-6.2) or within 12 months of a negative screening examination (OR 17.8, 95% CI 4.8-65.9). The increased risk of breast cancer persisted for at least 8 years after study entry and was higher in younger than older women. For women younger than the median age of 56 years, 26% of all breast cancers and 50% of cancers detected within 12 months of a negative screening test were attributable to density in 50% or more of the mammogram.
Conclusions: Extensive mammographic density is strongly associated with the risk of breast cancer detected by screening or between screening tests, and a substantial proportion of breast cancers can be attributed to this risk factor.

title: Pooled analysis of prospective cohort studies on height, weight, and breast cancer risk.
text: The study analyzed the relationship between anthropometric indices and the risk of breast cancer using pooled data from seven prospective cohort studies, involving 337,819 women and 4,385 incident invasive breast cancer cases. In multivariate analyses adjusting for reproductive, dietary, and other risk factors, the pooled relative risk (RR) of breast cancer per height increment of 5 cm was found to be 1.02 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.96, 1.10) in premenopausal women and 1.07 (95% CI: 1.03, 1.12) in postmenopausal women. Body mass index (BMI) showed significant inverse and positive associations with breast cancer among pre- and postmenopausal women, respectively, with the associations being nonlinear. Specifically, compared to premenopausal women with a BMI of less than 21 kg/m2, women with a BMI exceeding 31 kg/m2 had an RR of 0.54 (95% CI: 0.34, 0.85). In postmenopausal women, the RRs did not increase further when BMI exceeded 28 kg/m2, with an RR of 1.26 (95% CI: 1.09, 1.46). The authors found little evidence for interaction with other breast cancer risk factors. The study suggests that height is an independent risk factor for postmenopausal breast cancer, while the relation is less clear in premenopausal women. The association between BMI and breast cancer varies by menopausal status, with weight control potentially reducing the risk among postmenopausal women.

title: Cost effectiveness of ward based non-invasive ventilation for acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: economic analysis of randomised controlled trial.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of standard treatment versus non-invasive ventilation in patients hospitalized with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Design: Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis of a randomized controlled trial.
Setting: Medical wards in 14 hospitals across the United Kingdom.
Participants: A total of 236 patients admitted to hospital with an acute exacerbation of COPD and mild to moderate acidosis (pH 7.25-7.35) due to respiratory failure.
Main Outcome Measure: Incremental cost per in-hospital death.
Results: Of the 118 patients randomized to standard treatment, 24 died (20.5%), while 12 of the 118 patients (10.1%) in the non-invasive ventilation group died (P=0.05). The allocation to the non-invasive ventilation group was associated with a reduction in costs of £49,362 (approximately $78,741 or €73,109), primarily due to reduced use of intensive care units. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was -£645 ($-$2310 or €-$386) per death avoided, indicating a dominant (more effective and less costly) strategy. Modeling of these data suggests that a typical UK hospital providing a non-invasive ventilation service will avoid six deaths and three to nine admissions to intensive care units per year, with an associated cost reduction of £12,000-£53,000 per year.
Conclusions: Non-invasive ventilation is a highly cost-effective treatment that both reduced total costs and improved mortality in hospitalized patients with acute exacerbations of COPD.

title: Persistent human papillomavirus infection and cervical neoplasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: The detection of persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA in cervical tissue is used as a marker for assessing cervical cancer risk in clinical trials. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the authors evaluated the robustness of HPV persistence as a clinical marker by examining its association with high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2-3), high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), and invasive cervical cancer (collectively referred to as CIN2-3/HSIL+). The authors analyzed data from 41 studies that included over 22,500 women and found that the risk of CIN2-3/HSIL+ was consistently and strongly associated with HPV persistence, regardless of the duration of persistence or testing interval. The magnitude of the association varied depending on the specific comparison group used. These findings validate HPV persistence as a clinical marker and endpoint, and highlight the need for precise definition and standardization of HPV testing, sampling procedure, and test interval for reliable clinical testing.

title: Post-transcriptional Wnt Signaling Governs Epididymal Sperm Maturation
text: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway plays a crucial role in both development and disease. However, the upstream cascade of this pathway has remained largely unexplored due to the dominant role of β-catenin in transcriptional regulation. To address this gap in knowledge, we investigated the physiological functions of the upstream cascade in sperm maturation. Our findings reveal that Wnt signals released from the epididymis can induce responses in transcriptionally silent spermatozoa, and that mice lacking the Wnt regulator Cyclin Y-like 1 are male sterile due to defects in sperm motility and morphology. We also discovered that post-transcriptional Wnt signaling regulates sperm maturation through three distinct mechanisms: (1) reducing global protein poly-ubiquitination to maintain protein homeostasis; (2) inhibiting septin 4 phosphorylation to establish a membrane diffusion barrier in the sperm tail; and (3) inhibiting protein phosphatase 1 to initiate sperm motility. These findings challenge the prevailing view of Wnt signaling as solely transcriptional and invite reevaluation of its role in somatic cells as well.

title: CD28 Costimulation: From Mechanism to Therapy.
text: Ligation of the CD28 receptor on T cells provides a crucial second signal alongside T cell receptor (TCR) ligation for the activation of naive T cells. Here, we delve into the expression, structure, and biochemistry of CD28 and its ligands. CD28 signals play a pivotal role in various T cell processes, including cytoskeletal reorganization, cytokine production, survival, and differentiation. Unlike TCR ligation alone, CD28 ligation leads to distinct epigenetic, transcriptional, and post-translational modifications in T cells. We explore the function of CD28 and its ligands in both effector and regulatory T cells, highlighting their critical role in maintaining immune homeostasis. We also discuss the clinical efficacy of drugs that target CD28 ligands, despite the centrality of CD28 and its family members in immune function, many aspects of CD28 biology remain unclear. The translation of basic CD28 research into immunomodulatory therapeutics has been uneven, with both successes and failures. Factors contributing to these outcomes include complex receptor-ligand interactions among CD28 family members, differences between mouse and human CD28 families, and cell-type specific roles of CD28 family members.

title: Recommended diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis: guidelines from the International Panel on the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.
text: The International Panel on MS Diagnosis has revised the diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis (MS). The revised criteria prioritize the objective demonstration of lesion dissemination in both time and space through Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) integration with clinical and other paraclinical diagnostic methods. The revised criteria aim to facilitate the diagnosis of MS in patients presenting with a range of symptoms, including "monosymptomatic" disease resembling MS, typical relapsing-remitting disease, and insidious progression without clear attacks and remissions. The use of outdated terms such as "clinically definite" and "probable MS" has been discontinued. Instead, the diagnostic evaluation outcome is categorized as either MS, "possible MS" (for individuals at risk of MS but with equivocal diagnostic evaluation), or "not MS."

title: Regulation of radial glial survival by signals from the meninges.
text: Radial glial cells (RGCs) in the developing cerebral cortex act as progenitors for both neurons and glia, and their processes serve as guides for migrating neurons. While it was previously unknown whether RGC processes directly regulate the function of RGCs, our study reveals that the absence of beta1 integrins in RGCs leads to a reduction in RGC numbers and cortical size. Using TUNEL stains and time-lapse video recordings, we found that beta1-deficient RGC processes detach from the meningeal basement membrane (BM) and undergo apoptotic death. Similarly, surgical removal of the meninges also induces apoptosis in RGCs. Furthermore, mice lacking the BM components laminin alpha2 and alpha4 display defects in the attachment of RGC processes at the meninges, resulting in a smaller cortical size and increased apoptosis of RGC cells. Our findings demonstrate that the attachment of RGC processes at the meninges is crucial for RGC survival and the regulation of cortical size.

title: The sterol regulatory element binding proteins are essential for the metabolic programming of effector T cells and adaptive immunity
text: Newly activated CD8(+) T cells undergo metabolic reprogramming to meet the heightened biosynthetic demands of clonal expansion; however, the signaling mechanisms involved in this process are poorly understood. Our study reveals an essential role for sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs) in the acquisition of effector-cell metabolism. Without SREBP signaling, CD8(+) T cells are unable to undergo blastogenesis, resulting in attenuated clonal expansion during viral infection. Mechanistic studies demonstrate that SREBPs are essential for meeting the increased lipid requirements of membrane synthesis during blastogenesis. Interestingly, SREBPs are dispensable for homeostatic proliferation, suggesting a context-specific requirement for these proteins in effector responses. Our findings provide insights into the molecular signals that drive the metabolic reprogramming of CD8(+) T cells during the transition from quiescence to activation.

title: Human contribution to the European heatwave of 2003
text: The summer of 2003 was one of the hottest on record in Europe since at least the 16th century, with an unprecedented number of heat-related deaths reported in France, Germany, and Italy. It is difficult to determine whether the 2003 heatwave was caused by a specific climate modification, such as increased greenhouse gas emissions, as such events could occur by chance in an unaltered climate. However, researchers can estimate the extent to which human activities may have increased the likelihood of a heatwave of this magnitude. Using a specific framework, the authors estimate that human-induced increases in atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations and other pollutants have at least doubled the risk of a heatwave exceeding a certain temperature threshold in a large region of continental Europe. With a confidence level of over 90%, they conclude that human influence is the likely cause of this increased risk.

title: Do Antidepressants Cure or Create Abnormal Brain States?
text:
The term "antidepressant" refers to a drug that aims to correct specific biological abnormalities that contribute to the symptoms of depression, in line with the "disease-centred" model of psychotropic drug action. This model, inspired by similar approaches in general medicine, suggests that antidepressants work by restoring normal functioning by targeting the neuropathology of depression or depressive symptoms. In contrast, we propose an alternative "drug-centred" model, which suggests that psychotropic drugs can cause abnormal states that may coincidentally relieve psychiatric symptoms, rather than rectifying a hypothetical biochemical imbalance.
For instance, alcohol's disinhibiting effects may alleviate symptoms of social phobia, but this does not imply that alcohol corrects a chemical imbalance underlying social phobia. Similarly, sedation may reduce high arousal in acute psychiatric situations, while drugs that induce indifference, such as neuroleptics or opiates, may help reduce the distress of acute psychotic symptoms. Low-dose stimulants may improve attention and concentration in the short term.
The "disease-centred" model in psychiatry relies on inferring antidepressant effects from patients' scores on symptom rating scales, which are assumed to assess the manifestations of the disease. In contrast, the "drug-centred" model suggests that the physiological and subjective effects of drugs should be examined in their own right, including various forms of sedation, stimulation, and biopsychological states. While some drugs may produce euphoria or mood elevation, tolerance develops with long-term use, and these effects are not necessarily diminished by a person's emotional state upon drug ingestion. If antidepressants or other psychotropic drugs could be shown to have mood-elevating effects that persist and are not diminished by depression, this could distinguish them from drugs that cause euphoria and may prove uniquely useful in depressed patients.

title: Cancer exosomes trigger fibroblast to myofibroblast differentiation.
text: There is a growing interest in the cell-to-cell communication roles of cancer cells through the release of small vesicles called exosomes. In this study, we investigated whether exosomes produced by cancer cells could transmit information to normal stromal fibroblasts and trigger a cellular response. We found that certain cancer-derived exosomes could induce the expression of α-smooth muscle actin and other changes indicative of fibroblast differentiation into myofibroblasts. We discovered that TGF-β is present on the surface of exosomes in association with the transmembrane proteoglycan betaglycan. Although TGF-β is typically latent, this complex was fully functional in eliciting SMAD-dependent signaling. Inhibiting either signaling or betaglycan expression reduced differentiation. Notably, the kinetics and overall magnitude of the response were similar to those achieved with soluble TGF-β, but we identified unique qualitative differences in the exosomal delivery route, such as a significant increase in fibroblast FGF2 production. This previously unappreciated mechanism of cellular differentiation has significant implications for the underlying mechanisms of cancer-recruited stroma, fibrotic diseases, and wound-healing responses.

title: A model of multiple myeloma: culture of 5T33 murine myeloma cells and evaluation of tumorigenicity in the C57BL/KaLwRij mouse.
text:
The 5T33 multiple myeloma cell line is one of a series of transplantable murine myelomas that spontaneously arise in C57BL/KaLwRij mice. This study aims to characterize the in vitro properties of the 5T33 myeloma cell line, including its morphology, growth rate, paraprotein expression, and tumorigenicity in syngeneic animals.
The 5T33 cell line has been continuously cultured for over 10 months and has undergone more than 34 passages. In culture, the 5T33 myeloma cells grow as single cells or in small clusters of loosely adherent cells on an adherent stromal cell layer. The maximum doubling time is approximately 25 hours, and over 90% of the cells express cytoplasmic IgG2b paraprotein. The cultured 5T33 myeloma cells are highly tumorigenic in C57BL/KaLwRij mice, with as few as 500 cells inducing paralysis and death as early as day 36 post-tumor inoculation. The kinetics of tumor development and IgG2b paraprotein detection are dose dependent. Two weeks following intravenous inoculation of 5 x 105 cultured 5T33 myeloma cells, tumor cells are readily identified in the bone marrow. By 3 weeks post-tumor inoculation, 5T33 myeloma cells are found in various tissues throughout the animal. Current studies are focused on determining the sensitivity of this cell line to various therapeutic modalities.

title: HIV Treatment as Prevention: Systematic Comparison of Mathematical Models of the Potential Impact of Antiretroviral Therapy on HIV Incidence in South Africa
text:
Background:
Several mathematical models have investigated the impact of expanding access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) on new HIV infections. However, comparing the results and conclusions of these models is challenging due to differences in the questions they address and the outcome metrics they report. This study aims to compare the predictions of multiple models simulating the same ART intervention programs to determine the extent to which models agree on the epidemiological impact of expanded ART.
Methods and Findings:
Twelve independent mathematical models evaluated a standardized set of ART intervention scenarios in South Africa and reported a common set of outputs. The scenarios systematically varied the CD4 count threshold for treatment eligibility, access to treatment, and program retention. For a scenario in which 80% of HIV-infected individuals start treatment on average 1 year after their CD4 count drops below 350 cells/μl and 85% remain on treatment after 3 years, the models projected that HIV incidence would be 35% to 54% lower 8 years after the introduction of ART compared to a counterfactual scenario with no ART. There was more variation in the estimated long-term (38-year) reductions in incidence. The impact of optimistic interventions, including immediate ART initiation, varied widely across models, maintaining substantial uncertainty about the theoretical prospect for eliminating HIV from the population using ART alone over the next four decades. The number of person-years of ART per infection averted over 8 years ranged between 5.8 and 18.7. Considering the actual scale-up of ART in South Africa, seven models estimated that current HIV incidence is 17% to 32% lower than it would have been in the absence of ART. Differences between model assumptions about CD4 decline and HIV transmissibility over the course of infection explained only a modest amount of the variation in model results.
Conclusions:
Mathematical models evaluating the impact of ART vary substantially in structure, complexity, and parameter choices, but all suggest that ART, at high levels of access and with high adherence, has the potential to substantially reduce new HIV infections. There was broad agreement regarding the short-term epidemiologic impact of ambitious treatment scale-up, but more variation in longer-term projections and in the efficiency with which treatment can reduce new infections. Differences between model predictions could not be explained by differences in model structure or parameterization that were hypothesized to affect intervention impact.

title: Self-harm in prisons in England and Wales: an epidemiological study of prevalence, risk factors, clustering, and subsequent suicide
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the prevalence of self-harm and suicide in prisoners in England and Wales. We conducted a case-control study of all prisoners in these countries between 2004 and 2009, gathering data on self-harm incidents and associated risk factors. We also used a Bayesian approach to examine clustering of self-harm incidents and compared prisoners who self-harmed and subsequently died by suicide in prison with other inmates who self-harmed.
Our findings revealed that approximately 5-6% of male prisoners and 20-24% of female inmates self-harmed every year. Self-harm rates were significantly higher in female prisoners than in male inmates. The majority of prisoners who self-harmed (102 prisoners) accounted for 17,307 episodes of self-harm, with a significant proportion of these incidents occurring in women and teenage girls. Self-harm was associated with younger age, white ethnic origin, prison type, and a life sentence or being unsentenced in both sexes. In female inmates, committing a violent offence against an individual was also a risk factor. Clustering of self-harm incidents was observed in both sexes, with a significant intra-class correlation of 0·15 (95% CI 0·11-0·18).
Sadly, 109 prisoners died by suicide in prison after self-harming, with a higher risk of suicide in prisoners who self-harmed than in the general prison population. In male prisoners, older age and a previous self-harm incident of high or moderate lethality were associated with subsequent suicide. In female inmates, a history of more than five self-harm incidents within a year was associated with subsequent suicide.
Our findings highlight the urgent need for prevention and treatment of self-harm in prisoners to reduce the risk of suicide in this vulnerable population.

title: Elimination of HIV in South Africa through Expanded Access to Antiretroviral Therapy: A Model Comparison Study
text:
Background:
The implementation of universal test and treat (UTT) strategies has been proposed as a means of eliminating HIV in South Africa within 7 years, based on a influential mathematical modeling study. However, the underlying deterministic model was criticized for its simplicity and lack of realism, and other modeling studies have yielded conflicting results. This study aims to investigate the implications of different model structures and assumptions on the long-term impact of UTT and the possibility of HIV elimination.
Methods and Findings:
Nine different mathematical models of the South African HIV epidemic were developed in a stepwise approach of increasing complexity and realism. The simplest model resembles the initial deterministic model, while the most comprehensive model is the stochastic microsimulation model STDSIM, which includes sexual networks and HIV stages with different degrees of infectiousness. UTT was defined as annual screening and immediate ART for all HIV-infected adults, starting at 13% in January 2012 and scaled up to 90% coverage by January 2019. All models predict elimination, with the most comprehensive model predicting elimination at a later point in time, after 20 to 25 years. Additionally, the current ART treatment policy alone could drive HIV incidence to low levels, making UTT a cost-effective intervention. However, the study's limitations include the definition of elimination as incidence below 1/1,000 person-years rather than 0% prevalence, and the lack of drug resistance modeling.
Conclusions:
Our results confirm previous predictions that the HIV epidemic in South Africa can be eliminated through UTT at 90% coverage. However, more realistic models suggest that elimination is likely to occur at a later point in time than previously suggested. Additionally, UTT is a cost-effective intervention, although less cost-effective than previously predicted. The study's findings highlight the importance of considering the complexity of the HIV transmission dynamics when modeling the impact of UTT and other interventions.

title: Bile acid receptor TGR5 agonism induces NO production and reduces monocyte adhesion in vascular endothelial cells.
text:
Objective:
The TGR5 receptor, a G-protein-coupled receptor for bile acids, has been found to play a significant role in vascular endothelial cells. However, the function of TGR5 in these cells remains largely unknown.
Approach and Results:
In bovine aortic endothelial cells, treatment with a high-affinity TGR5 agonist, taurolithocholic acid (TLCA), led to a significant increase in nitric oxide (NO) production. This effect was abolished when TGR5 was depleted using small interfering RNA. Similarly, TLCA-induced NO production was observed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells, which was accompanied by increased phosphorylation of endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) serine 1177 and Akt serine 473, as well as intracellular calcium increase. Inhibition of these signals significantly decreased TLCA-induced NO production.
We further examined the effect of TGR5-mediated NO production on inflammatory responses in endothelial cells. In human umbilical vein endothelial cells, TLCA significantly reduced tumor necrosis factor-α-induced monocyte adhesion, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 expression, and nuclear factor-κB activation. TLCA also inhibited lipopolysaccharide-induced monocyte adhesion to mesenteric venules in vivo. These inhibitory effects of TLCA were abolished when NO synthase was inhibited.
Conclusions:
Our findings demonstrate that TGR5 agonism induces NO production via Akt activation and intracellular calcium increase in vascular endothelial cells, which in turn inhibits monocyte adhesion in response to inflammatory stimuli.

title: Structural insights into calicivirus attachment and uncoating.
text: The Caliciviridae family consists of positive-sense RNA viruses of medical and veterinary significance. In humans, caliciviruses are a primary cause of acute gastroenteritis, while in animals, they can lead to respiratory illness, conjunctivitis, stomatitis, and hemorrhagic disease. Due to the limited availability of culture systems for many viruses in this family, research into virus-host interactions is restricted. Fortunately, feline calicivirus (FCV), a member of the Vesivirus genus, can be propagated in cell culture, providing a manageable model for study. Recently, feline junctional adhesion molecule 1 (fJAM-1) was identified as a functional receptor for FCV. By combining cryo-electron microscopy, three-dimensional image reconstruction, and homology modeling, we have obtained the first structural view of a native calicivirus-protein receptor complex. Our findings reveal that domain 1 of fJAM-1 binds to the outer face of the P2 domain of the FCV capsid protein VP1, inducing conformational changes in the viral capsid. This study provides valuable insights into the mechanisms of virus attachment and uncoating.

title: Human SNP Links Differential Outcomes in Inflammatory and Infectious Disease to a FOXO3-Regulated Pathway
text: The clinical course and ultimate outcome, or prognosis, of complex diseases vary greatly between affected individuals. This variability is crucial in determining the impact a disease has on a patient's life, yet it is poorly understood. In this study, we leverage existing genome-wide association study data to gain insights into the role of genetics in prognosis. We identify a non-coding polymorphism in the FOXO3A gene (rs12212067: T > G) where the minor (G) allele, despite not being associated with disease susceptibility, is linked to a milder disease course in Crohn's disease and rheumatoid arthritis, and an increased risk of severe malaria. Carrying the minor allele is shown to limit inflammatory responses in monocytes through a FOXO3-driven pathway, which, in turn, reduces production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNFα, and increases production of anti-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-10. Therefore, we uncover a shared genetic contribution to prognosis across distinct diseases that operates via a FOXO3-driven pathway modulating inflammatory responses.

title: Patient Outcomes with Teaching Versus Nonteaching Healthcare: A Systematic Review
text:
There is ongoing debate among healthcare professionals regarding the quality of medical care provided at teaching hospitals compared to non-teaching hospitals. To investigate this topic, we systematically reviewed the available evidence.
Methods and Findings:
We searched PubMed, consulted with experts, and cross-referenced literature to identify studies that compared mortality and other patient outcomes between teaching and non-teaching healthcare facilities. We included studies that reported adjusted estimates of the mortality ratio and found 132 eligible studies, of which 93 focused on mortality and 61 addressed other outcomes. Our analysis found a summary relative risk of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.93-1.00) for teaching versus non-teaching healthcare facilities and 1.04 (95% CI: 0.99-1.10) for minor teaching versus non-teaching facilities. There was significant heterogeneity between studies (I2 = 72% for the main analysis). Results were similar across studies using clinical and administrative databases. We found no significant differences in outcomes between teaching and non-teaching facilities after adjusting for volume/experience, severity, and comorbidity (relative risk: 1.01). Smaller studies did not differ significantly from larger studies, and differences were observed for some diagnoses, such as better survival rates for breast cancer and cerebrovascular accidents in teaching hospitals and better survival rates from cholecystectomy in non-teaching hospitals. However, other outcomes were diverse, and teaching healthcare facilities did not generally perform better or worse than non-teaching facilities.
Conclusions:
While the available data are limited by their non-randomized design, they suggest that the teaching status of a healthcare facility does not significantly improve or worsen patient outcomes overall. Differences in outcomes for specific diseases cannot be ruled out, but are likely to be small.

title: DNA damage and Repair Modify DNA methylation and Chromatin Domain of the Targeted Locus: Mechanism of allele methylation polymorphism
text: We investigate the changes in chromatin structure, DNA methylation, and transcription that occur during and after homologous DNA repair (HR). Our findings reveal that HR alters the DNA methylation pattern of the repaired segment. Additionally, HR affects local histone H3 methylation and chromatin structure by forming DNA-chromatin loops connecting the 5' and 3' ends of the repaired gene. Over a two-week period following repair, transcription-associated demethylation promoted by Base Excision Repair enzymes further modifies the methylation of the repaired DNA. As a result, the repaired genes display stable but diverse methylation profiles that determine the levels of expression in each clone. Our data suggest that the DNA methylation and chromatin remodeling induced by HR may serve as a source of permanent variation in gene expression in somatic cells.

title: DNA repair factor APLF is a histone chaperone.
text: Poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation plays a pivotal role in the repair of damaged DNA, where it regulates chromatin relaxation as a crucial step in the repair process. However, the molecular mechanism by which poly(ADP-ribose) modulates chromatin remains inadequately understood. In this study, we identify a poly(ADP-ribose)-regulated protein, APLF, as a DNA-damage-specific histone chaperone. APLF selectively binds to the histone H3/H4 tetramer through its C-terminal acidic motif, which shares similarity with the motif found in the histone chaperones of the NAP1L family (NAP1L motif). We demonstrate that APLF exhibits histone chaperone activities that are dependent on its acidic domain, and that the NAP1L motif is essential for the repair capacity of APLF in vivo. Furthermore, we identify structural analogs of APLF in lower eukaryotes that can bind histones and localize to sites of DNA damage-induced poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation. These findings elucidate the involvement of histone chaperones in poly(ADP-ribose)-regulated DNA repair reactions.

title: Regulation of sympathetic nerve activity during the cold pressor test in normotensive pregnant and nonpregnant women.
text:
In this study, we investigated the changes in neurovascular transduction during normotensive pregnancy, specifically during periods of heightened sympathetic activation. We tested the hypothesis that despite an exacerbated muscle sympathetic nerve activity (microneurography) response to cold pressor stimulation, the blunting of neurovascular transduction in normotensive pregnant women would result in similar changes in vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure (Finometer) relative to nonpregnant controls.
Baseline neurovascular transduction was reduced in pregnant women compared to controls, expressed as the quotient of total resistance and mean arterial pressure and sympathetic burst frequency (0.32±0.07 versus 0.58±0.16 mm Hg/L/min/bursts/min, P<0.001 and 2.4±0.7 versus 3.6±0.8 mm Hg/bursts/min, P=0.001). Sympathetic activation was greater across all 3 minutes of cold pressor stimulation in the pregnant women compared to the nonpregnant controls. Peak sympathoexcitation was also greater in pregnant than in nonpregnant women, whether expressed as sympathetic burst frequency (+17±13 versus +7±8 bursts/min, P=0.049), burst incidence (+17±9 versus +6±11 bursts/100 hb, P=0.03), or total activity (+950±660 versus +363±414 arbitrary units, P=0.04). However, neurovascular transduction during peak cold pressor-induced sympathoexcitation remained blunted in pregnant women (0.25±0.11 versus 0.45±0.08 mm Hg/L/min/bursts/min, P<0.001 and 1.9±1.0 versus 3.2±0.9 mm Hg/bursts/min, P=0.006). Therefore, mean arterial pressure (93±21 versus 99±6 mm Hg, P=0.4) and total peripheral resistance (12±3 versus 14±3 mm Hg/L/min) were not different between pregnant and nonpregnant women during peak sympathoexcitation. These data indicate that the third trimester of normotensive pregnancy is associated with reductions in neurovascular transduction, which result in the dissociation of sympathetic outflow from hemodynamic outcomes, even during cold pressor-induced sympathoexcitation.

title: The Germ Cell Determinant Blimp1 Is Not Required for Derivation of Pluripotent Stem Cells
text: Blimp1 (Prdm1), a key regulator of primordial germ cells (PGCs), collaborates with Prdm14 during PGC specification from postimplantation epiblast cells. Together, they initiate epigenetic reprogramming in early germ cells, leading to a pluripotent state equivalent to embryonic stem cells (ESCs). While Prdm14 can promote reprogramming and is essential for maintaining the pluripotent state, it is unclear whether Blimp1 plays a similar role. To investigate, we employed a genetic approach and found that Blimp1 is dispensable for the derivation and maintenance of ESCs and postimplantation epiblast stem cells (epiSCs). Interestingly, Blimp1 is also dispensable for reprogramming epiSCs to ESCs. These findings suggest that reprogramming, including the conversion of somatic cells to ESCs, may not necessarily involve an obligatory passage through a Blimp1-positive PGC-like state.

title: A Nexus for Gene Expression—Molecular Mechanisms of Spt5 and NusG in the Three Domains of Life
text: Evolutionary related multisubunit RNA polymerases (RNAPs) transcribe the genomes of all living organisms, with the core subunits of these enzymes exhibiting universal conservation across the three domains of life, indicative of a shared evolutionary ancestry. However, one RNAP-associated transcription factor, Spt5, also known as NusG in bacteria, displays a unique degree of conservation across all domains of life. All other factors that assist RNAP during the transcription cycle are specific to individual domains or are only conserved between archaea and eukaryotes. Spt5 and its bacterial homologue NusG play a crucial role in regulating gene expression through various mechanisms, including modulating transcription processivity and promoter proximal pausing, coupling transcription and RNA processing or translation, and recruiting termination factors to silence laterally transferred DNA and protect the genome against double-stranded DNA breaks. This review aims to discuss recent findings that highlight Spt5-like factors as evolutionarily conserved hubs for the coordination and regulation of the cellular machineries responsible for information processing.

title: Haplotype estimation using sequencing reads.
text:
High-throughput sequencing technologies generate short sequence reads that contain phase information if they span two or more heterozygous genotypes. However, current methods for inferring haplotypes from genotype data typically do not utilize this information. To address this limitation, we have developed an extension of the SHAPEIT2 method that incorporates phase-informative sequencing reads to improve phasing accuracy. Our approach incorporates base quality scores within each read to probabilistically model the information provided by the read. The method is primarily designed for high-coverage sequence data or data sets that already have genotypes called, and it has an important application in phasing single samples sequenced at high coverage for use in medical sequencing and studies of rare diseases. Additionally, our method can use existing panels of reference haplotypes.
We evaluated the method by using a mother-father-child trio sequenced at high coverage by Illumina, along with low-coverage sequence data from the 1000 Genomes Project (1000GP). Our results showed that using phase-informative reads increases the mean distance between switch errors by 22% from 274.4 kb to 328.6 kb. To further assess the performance of our method, we simulated sequencing reads with varying insert sizes, read lengths, and base error rates using male chromosome X haplotypes from the 1000GP samples. Our results showed that using a mixture of insert sizes produced the best results when using short 100 bp paired-end reads. However, when using longer reads with high error rates (5-20 kb reads with 4%-15% error per base), phasing performance was substantially improved.

title: Time and Money: The True Costs of Health Care Utilization for Patients Receiving "Free" HIV/Tuberculosis Care and Treatment in Rural KwaZulu-Natal.
text: In sub-Saharan African countries, HIV and tuberculosis (TB) treatment is often provided free of charge, but patients still incur significant costs. A study conducted in rural South Africa found that patients receiving antiretroviral treatment (ART) and TB treatment incurred average monthly health expenditures of ZAR 164 (approximately USD 11) and ZAR 122 (approximately USD 9), respectively. These expenditures included costs for transportation, time spent traveling to and using services, and financing through borrowing or selling assets. The study found that patients receiving pre-ART treatment incurred higher costs than those receiving ART, with a significant portion of these costs going towards traditional healers and chemists. The study suggests that providing subsidized transportation, reducing the number of clinic visits, and establishing drug pick-up points closer to home could help reduce costs for ART patients, potentially improving retention and adherence. The findings also suggest that transitioning patients to ART earlier, as under HIV treatment-as-prevention policies, may not substantially increase patients' financial burden.

title: A new system for naming ribosomal proteins.
text: A novel system for naming ribosomal proteins has been proposed, which the authors aim to implement in the future. They emphasize the need to eliminate the confusion arising from the assignment of identical names to unrelated ribosomal proteins from different species. In this system, homologous ribosomal proteins are given the same name, regardless of species, allowing for a clear distinction between these proteins. The new system features a format for naming new proteins that is similar enough to the old names to be easily recognizable, yet unambiguously identifies them as part of the new system.

title: COSMIC: mining complete cancer genomes in the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer
text: The COSMIC (Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer) database, maintained by the Sanger Institute, curates a comprehensive collection of somatic mutations in human cancer. The latest release, v48 (July 2010), contains over 136,000 coding mutations in nearly 542,000 tumor samples, with 4803 genes (26%) harboring one or more mutations. The database includes full scientific literature curation for 83 major cancer genes and 49 fusion gene pairs, with ongoing updates and new additions. Key among these is TP53, now available through a collaboration with the IARC p53 database. In addition to data from the Cancer Genome Project and The Cancer Genome Atlas, large systematic screens are also curated. The website has undergone significant upgrades, providing improved data mining capabilities through new selection filters and graphics, as well as an enhanced Biomart for automated data mining and integration with other biological databases. Annotation of genomic features has become a major focus, with COSMIC now curating full-genome resequencing experiments and developing new web pages, export formats, and graphics styles. With all genomic information updated to GRCh37, COSMIC integrates diverse types of mutation information and strengthens ties with Ensembl and other data resources.

title: Quantitative imaging assay for NF-κB nuclear translocation in primary human macrophages
text: Quantitative measurement of NF-κB nuclear translocation is a crucial tool in cellular immunology research. Existing methods, however, have limitations such as low sensitivity, high cost, or dependence on cell lines. To address these challenges, novel imaging techniques are being developed, but they also have limitations, including the need for specialized imaging equipment or image analysis software. In this study, we present a simple and cost-effective method for quantifying NF-κB RelA nuclear translocation using immunofluorescence microscopy and the publicly available image analysis software ImageJ. This method can be easily adopted by researchers without specialized image analysis expertise, and it provides accurate and reliable results. We validate the method by demonstrating the time course and dose response of NF-κB nuclear translocation in primary human macrophages stimulated with LPS, as well as by comparing the results with those obtained using a commercial NF-κB activation reporter cell line.

title: An RNA-sequencing transcriptome and splicing database of glia, neurons, and vascular cells of the cerebral cortex.
text:
The major cell types of the brain exhibit distinct differences in their developmental processes, metabolism, signaling, and function. To gain a deeper understanding of the unique characteristics and interactions of these cell types, we purified and analyzed representative populations of neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, newly formed oligodendrocytes, myelinating oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, and pericytes from mouse cerebral cortex.
We generated a comprehensive transcriptome database for these eight cell types by RNA sequencing and employed a sophisticated algorithm to identify novel cell type-specific genes and splicing isoforms. Through bioinformatic analysis, we uncovered thousands of new markers for cell identification, tools for genetic manipulation, and insights into the brain's biology. For example, our findings reveal how neurons and astrocytes differ in their ability to dynamically regulate glycolytic flux and lactate generation due to distinct splicing of the PKM2 gene, which encodes the glycolytic enzyme pyruvate kinase.
This dataset will provide a valuable resource for understanding the development and function of the brain, and to ensure its widespread dissemination, we have created a user-friendly website (<http://web.stanford.edu/group/barres_lab/brain_rnaseq.html>) that enables researchers to analyze and compare transcription and alternative splicing profiles across various cell classes in the brain.

title: C9orf72 repeat expansions cause neurodegeneration in Drosophila through arginine-rich proteins
text:
Introduction:
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are devastating neurodegenerative disorders that are often caused by expansions of the C9orf72 gene. Specifically, an expanded GGGGCC repeat in C9orf72 is the most common genetic cause of these diseases. While the mechanisms underlying C9orf72-mediated neurodegeneration are not fully understood, one key question is whether the repeat RNA itself or dipeptide repeat proteins generated by repeat-associated, non-ATG translation are primarily responsible for toxicity.
To address this question, we developed in vitro and in vivo models to dissect repeat RNA and dipeptide repeat protein toxicity.
Methods:
We used in vitro models to express pure repeats and stop codon–interrupted "RNA-only" repeats in Drosophila, and observed that expanded repeats caused adult-onset neurodegeneration, while RNA-only repeats did not. We also expressed individual dipeptide repeat proteins with non-GGGGCC RNA sequences in Drosophila, and found that both poly(glycine-arginine) and poly(proline-arginine) proteins caused neurodegeneration.
Results:
Our findings indicate that both repeat RNA and dipeptide repeat proteins contribute to C9orf72-mediated neurodegeneration, suggesting a dual toxicity mechanism. Specifically, the expanded GGGGCC repeat in C9orf72 promotes the generation of toxic dipeptide repeat proteins, which in turn cause neurodegeneration.
Discussion:
Our study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying C9orf72-mediated neurodegeneration. The finding that both repeat RNA and dipeptide repeat proteins contribute to disease pathology suggests a complex interplay between these two types of molecules. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of C9orf72-mediated neurodegeneration and to identify potential therapeutic targets for these devastating diseases.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study has shown that expanded GGGGCC repeats in C9orf72 promote the generation of toxic dipeptide repeat proteins, which in turn cause neurodegeneration. These findings support a dual toxicity mechanism, whereby both repeat RNA and dipeptide repeat proteins contribute to C9orf72-mediated neurodegeneration. Further research is needed to fully understand the molecular mechanisms underlying C9orf72-mediated neurodegeneration and to identify potential therapeutic targets for these devastating diseases.

title: Targeted nanoparticles containing the proresolving peptide Ac2-26 protect against advanced atherosclerosis in hypercholesterolemic mice
text: Chronic, non-resolving inflammation is a crucial factor in the progression of advanced atherosclerotic lesions. In the normal inflammatory response, resolution is mediated by various agonists, including the glucocorticoid-regulated protein annexin A1. The proresolving actions of annexin A1, which are mediated through its receptor N-formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2/ALX), can be mimicked by an amino-terminal peptide encompassing amino acids 2-26 (Ac2-26). Collagen IV (Col IV)–targeted nanoparticles (NPs) containing Ac2-26 were evaluated for their therapeutic effect on chronic, advanced atherosclerosis in fat-fed Ldlr−/− mice. When administered to mice with preexisting lesions, Col IV–Ac2-26 NPs were targeted to lesions and led to significant improvements in key advanced plaque properties, including an increase in the protective collagen layer overlying lesions (which was associated with a decrease in lesional collagenase activity), suppression of oxidative stress, and a decrease in plaque necrosis. In mice lacking FPR2/ALX in myeloid cells, these improvements were not observed. These findings suggest that administration of a resolution-mediating peptide in a targeted NP activates its receptor on myeloid cells to stabilize advanced atherosclerotic lesions, supporting the concept that defective inflammation resolution plays a role in advanced atherosclerosis and providing a new therapeutic approach.

title: Interleukin-2 gene variation impairs regulatory T cell function and causes autoimmunity
text: Autoimmune diseases are believed to arise from abnormalities in the normal functioning of the immune system, and research suggests that genetic variations on mouse chromosome 3 (Idd3) may play a role in determining susceptibility to these diseases. Specifically, we have found that certain genetic variants on Idd3 are associated with differences in the expression of interleukin-2 (IL-2), a key immune regulatory cytokine.
