To investigate whether the observed correlations are causal, we engineered mice with reduced IL-2 production and observed that they exhibited similar autoimmune dysregulation as mice with naturally occurring susceptibility alleles of Il2. Reduced IL-2 production in both genetic and engineered mice was associated with decreased function of CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells, which are crucial for maintaining immune homeostasis.

title: GRSF1 Regulates RNA Processing in Mitochondrial RNA Granules
text: Various specialized domains have been identified within the cytosol and nucleus, but little is known about the compartmentalization of RNA within the mitochondrial matrix. GRSF1 (G-rich sequence factor 1), an RNA binding protein, was previously localized to the cytosol. However, our study revealed that an isoform of GRSF1 accumulates in distinct foci within the mitochondrial matrix. These foci are composed of newly synthesized mitochondrial RNA and also contain RNase P, an enzyme involved in mitochondrial RNA processing. GRSF1 was found to interact with RNase P and is essential for the processing of both classical and tRNA-less RNA precursors. In the absence of GRSF1, the cleavage of primary RNA transcripts is abnormal, leading to reduced expression of mitochondrially encoded proteins and mitochondrial dysfunction. Our findings suggest that the GRSF1-RNase P complexes in the mitochondrial matrix correspond to sites where primary RNA transcripts converge to be processed. We have termed these large ribonucleoprotein structures "mitochondrial RNA granules."

title: Midlife Serum Cholesterol and Increased Risk of Alzheimer’s and Vascular Dementia Three Decades Later
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between midlife serum total cholesterol levels and the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease (AD) and vascular dementia (VaD) in a large, multiethnic cohort of men and women.
Methods: We analyzed data from 9,844 participants in the Kaiser Permanente Northern California Medical Group who underwent detailed health evaluations between 1964 and 1973 at ages 40-45 years and were still members of the health plan in 1994. AD and VaD were ascertained through medical records between January 1, 1994, and June 1, 2007. We used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, education, race/ethnic group, sex, midlife diabetes, hypertension, body mass index (BMI), and late-life stroke to estimate the hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for AD and VaD.
Results: A total of 469 participants had AD, and 127 had VaD. Compared to desirable cholesterol levels (<200 mg/dl) as a reference, hazard ratios (HR) and 95% CI for AD were 1.23 (0.97-1.55) and 1.57 (1.23-2.01) for borderline (200-239 mg/dl) and high cholesterol (≥240 mg/dl), respectively. HR and 95% CI for VaD were 1.50 (1.01-2.23) for borderline and 1.26 (0.82-1.96) for high cholesterol. Further analyses for AD (cholesterol quartiles, 1st quartile reference) indicated that cholesterol levels >220 mg/dl were a significant risk factor: HR were 1.31 (1.01-1.71; 3rd quartile, 221-248 mg/dl) and 1.58 (1.22-2.06; 4th quartile, 249-500 mg/dl).
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that midlife serum total cholesterol levels are associated with an increased risk of developing AD and VaD. Even moderately elevated cholesterol levels increase the risk of dementia. Dementia risk factors should be addressed as early as midlife, before underlying disease(s) or symptoms appear.

title: "The contribution of chronic diseases to the prevalence of dependence among older people in Latin America, China and India: a 10/66 Dementia Research Group population-based survey"
text:
The number of older people is expected to rise significantly worldwide, leading to an increase in age-related chronic diseases and dependence. Dependence is a crucial aspect of disability, yet it remains understudied. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence and correlates of dependence among older people in middle-income countries.
A cross-sectional survey was conducted at 11 sites in seven countries, including urban and rural areas in Peru, Mexico, China, and India. A total of 15,022 interviews were conducted with informants, and the full 10/66 Dementia Research Group survey protocol was applied, including assessments of depression, dementia, physical impairments, and self-reported diagnoses. Dependence was rated by informants based on open-ended questions on the participant's needs for care. The prevalence of dependence was analyzed, and the independent contribution of underlying health conditions was estimated.
The prevalence of dependence increased with age at all sites, with a tendency for lower prevalence in men than in women. The age-standardized prevalence was lower at all sites than in the USA. Dementia made the largest independent contribution to dependence, with a median population attributable prevalence fraction (PAPF) of 34% (range 23%-59%). Other substantial contributors were limb impairment (9%, 1%-46%), stroke (8%, 2%-17%), and depression (8%, 1%-27%).
The findings suggest that the demographic and health transitions will lead to a large increase in the number of dependent older people, particularly in middle-income countries. Urgent priorities include the prevention and control of chronic neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases and the development of long-term care policies and plans.

title: An actomyosin-based barrier inhibits cell mixing at compartmental boundaries in Drosophila embryos
text:
The proper formation of tissues and organs in animal embryos requires the separation of cells into distinct compartments. While several theories have been proposed to explain how cells are sorted into different compartments, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that maintain cell separation at boundaries remain unclear. In this study, we investigate the role of actomyosin-based barriers in maintaining compartmental cell separation in early Drosophila embryos.
We find that cells can temporarily invade neighboring compartments during cell division, but are then pushed back into their original compartment. Actomyosin cytoskeletal components are enriched at compartmental boundaries, forming cable-like structures when the epidermis is mitotically active. When we inhibit the function of non-muscle myosin II (MyoII) in live embryos using chromophore-assisted laser inactivation (CALI), dividing cells are no longer pushed back, leading us to propose that local regulation of actomyosin contractibility is the primary mechanism for sorting cells at compartmental boundaries.
In summary, our findings demonstrate that actomyosin-based barriers play a crucial role in maintaining compartmental cell separation in early Drosophila embryos, and suggest that local regulation of actomyosin contractility is the primary mechanism for sorting cells at these boundaries.

title: Clinical algorithms for malaria diagnosis lack utility among people of different age groups.
text: In a study conducted in Kilifi District, Kenya, we aimed to determine the usefulness of clinical algorithms in malaria diagnosis among different age groups. A total of 1602 participants, including children and adults, were enrolled in the study. We collected smears and recorded clinical signs and symptoms (both prompted and spontaneous) of all individuals presenting to the clinic with a fever. A malaria case was defined as a person with a fever and concurrent parasitaemia. We selected the most sensitive and specific clinical signs and symptoms (algorithms) for diagnosing malaria in each age group (<5 years, 6-14 years, and >15 years). These age-optimized derived algorithms were able to identify approximately 66% of malaria cases in children under 5 years of age, 23% in children aged 6-14 years, and 66% in adults. If these algorithms were used to guide treatment decisions, 16% of children under 5 years, 44% of children aged 6-14 years, and 66% of adults with a history of fever and parasitaemia >/=5000 parasites/microl of blood would be sent home without treatment. Our findings suggest that clinical algorithms have limited utility in malaria diagnosis, particularly in older age groups where avoiding unnecessary use of anti-malarials is crucial to make more drugs available to the truly needy population of young children.

title: Large-scale genetic fine mapping and genotype-phenotype associations implicate polymorphism in the IL2RA region in type 1 diabetes
text: Genome-wide association studies have identified disease-related regions on chromosomes. However, to localize the causal variant(s), comprehensive resequencing, extensive genotyping, and sophisticated statistical analyses are required on large sample sets, leading to targeted functional studies. In this study, we localized the association with type 1 diabetes (T1D) to two independent groups of SNPs in the interleukin 2 receptor alpha (IL2RA) gene region, spanning overlapping regions of 14 and 40 kb, encompassing IL2RA intron 1 and the 5' regions of IL2RA and RBM17. The odds ratio for the association was 2.04, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.70-2.45, and a P-value of 1.92 × 10^-28. Additionally, we found that IL2RA T1D susceptibility genotypes were associated with lower levels of the biomarker, soluble IL-2RA, suggesting that an inherited lower immune responsiveness increases the risk of T1D.

title: Maternal obesity epigenetically alters visceral fat progenitor cell properties in male offspring mice.
text:
KEY POINTS:
1. Maternal obesity (MO) reduces the density of adipogenic progenitor cells in the adipose tissue of offspring.
2. The ability of adipose tissue to expand in the offspring of obese mothers is limited, and this limitation is associated with metabolic dysfunction when challenged with a high-fat diet.
3. MO induces epigenetic changes in the promoter of zinc finger protein 423 (zfp423), a key transcription factor in adipogenesis, leading to increased adipogenic differentiation in progenitor cells.
4. The long-term effects of MO on the adipogenic capacity of progenitor cells in offspring adipose tissue demonstrate a developmental programming effect.
ABSTRACT:
Maternal obesity (MO) programs offspring obesity and metabolic disorders, although the underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. Progenitor cells are the source of new adipocytes. The present study aimed to test whether MO epigenetically predisposes adipocyte progenitors in the fat of offspring to adipogenic differentiation and subsequent depletion, which leads to a failure of adipose tissue plasticity under positive energy balance, contributing to adipose tissue metabolic dysfunction.
C57BL/6 female mice were fed either a control diet (10% energy from fat) or a high-fat diet (45% energy from fat) for 8 weeks before mating. Male offspring of control (Con) and obese (OB) dams were weaned onto a regular (Reg) or obesogenic (Obe) diet until 3 months of age. At weaning, male OB offspring had higher expression of Zinc finger protein 423 (zfp423), a key transcription factor in adipogenesis, as well as lower DNA methylation of its promoter in progenitors of epididymal fat compared to Con offspring, which was correlated with enhanced adipogenic differentiation. At 3 months of age, progenitor density was 30.9 ± 9.7% lower in OB/Obe compared to Con/Obe mice, accompanied by a limited expansion of the adipocyte number when challenged with a high-energy diet. This difference was associated with lower DNA methylation in the zfp423 promoter in the epididymal fat of OB/Obe offspring, which was correlated with greater macrophage chemotactic protein-1 and hypoxia-inducible factor 1α expression. In summary, MO epigenetically limits the expansion capacity of offspring adipose tissue, providing an explanation for the adipose metabolic dysfunction of male offspring in the setting of MO.

title: Quality Testing of Artemisinin-Based Antimalarial Drugs in Myanmar.
text: Artemisinin-based combination therapies are the primary treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. However, the proliferation of counterfeit and substandard artemisinin-based antimalarials in Southeast Asia poses a significant challenge to malaria elimination efforts. To assess the situation, we purchased 153 artemisinin-containing antimalarials from various private drug stores in Myanmar as convenience samples. The quality of these drugs was evaluated using specific dipsticks for artemisinin derivatives as point-of-care devices. A subset of the samples was further tested using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Our survey revealed that > 35% of the collected drugs were oral artesunate and artemether monotherapies. All but one of the samples tested with the dipsticks showed detectable artemisinin derivative content, indicating that the labeled contents were roughly equivalent. However, one artesunate injection sample was found to be devoid of any active ingredient using both the dipstick assay and HPLC analysis. The continued circulation of oral monotherapies and the discovery of falsified parenteral artesunate raises concerns about the quality of antimalarial drugs in Myanmar during the malaria elimination phase, a situation that warrants increased regulatory oversight.

title: LINE-1 Retrotransposition Activity in Human Genomes
text: The human genome is characterized by a high abundance of long interspersed element-1 (LINE-1 or L1) sequences, which are known to be highly active (i.e., "hot") and responsible for a significant portion of retrotransposition activity in the genome. However, the distribution and diversity of these hot L1s within the human population remain largely unexplored. To address this gap in knowledge, we employed a fosmid-based, paired-end DNA sequencing strategy to identify full-length L1s in a set of individuals. Our results reveal 68 full-length L1s that are differentially present among individuals and absent from the human genome reference sequence. Notably, the majority of these L1s were found to be highly active in a cultured cell retrotransposition assay. Genotyping 26 of these elements revealed that two L1s are exclusive to Africa and that two others are absent from the H952 subset of the Human Genome Diversity Panel. These findings suggest that hot L1s are more abundant in the human population than previously appreciated, and that ongoing L1 retrotransposition continues to contribute significantly to interindividual genetic variation.

title: Immune cell promotion of metastasis
text: Metastatic cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths, and conventional immunotherapy and chemotherapy have shown limited success in halting its progression. Recent studies in mouse models have revealed that the presence of immunosuppressive cells in tumors protects metastatic cancer cells from being eliminated by killer cells, thereby undermining the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Moreover, the majority of immune cells present in the tumor typically differentiate into cells that promote each stage of the metastatic cascade, making them potential targets for therapy. In this review, we delve into the role of tumor-infiltrating immune cells in the metastatic cascade and explore potential therapeutic strategies to target these cells.

title: PICH: a DNA translocase specially adapted for processing anaphase bridge DNA.
text: The Plk1-interacting checkpoint helicase (PICH) protein is found at ultrafine anaphase bridges (UFBs) in mitosis, where it interacts with a group of DNA repair proteins, including the Bloom's syndrome protein (BLM). However, the function of PICH and how it is recruited to UFBs is poorly understood. To investigate the properties of PICH in an in vitro model of an anaphase bridge, we employed a combination of microfluidics, fluorescence microscopy, and optical tweezers. Our findings reveal that PICH exhibits a remarkable affinity for duplex DNA, resulting in ATP-dependent protein translocation and extension of the DNA. Most notably, the affinity of PICH for DNA binding increases with tension-induced DNA stretching, mimicking the effect of the mitotic spindle on a UFB. Additionally, PICH binding appears to reduce force-induced DNA melting. Based on these observations, we propose a model in which PICH recognizes and stabilizes DNA under tension during anaphase, thereby facilitating the resolution of entangled sister chromatids.

title: The Dynamics of Genome-wide DNA Methylation Reprogramming in Mouse Primordial Germ Cells
text: Genome-wide DNA methylation reprogramming is a process that occurs in mouse primordial germ cells (PGCs) and preimplantation embryos, although the intricate dynamics and biological consequences of this process are still poorly understood. To investigate this phenomenon, we conducted whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (BS-Seq) and RNA-Seq across key stages spanning from E6.5 epiblast to E16.5 PGCs. Our findings reveal that global loss of methylation occurs during PGC expansion and migration, with evidence suggesting a passive demethylation mechanism. However, certain sequences that carry long-term epigenetic memory (such as imprints, CpG islands on the X chromosome, and germline-specific genes) only undergo demethylation upon PGCs' entry into the gonads. Notably, the transcriptional profile of PGCs is tightly regulated despite global hypomethylation, with a transient expression of the pluripotency network, suggesting that reprogramming and pluripotency are intimately linked. Our results provide a framework for elucidating the epigenetic ground state of pluripotency in the germline.

title: Major histocompatibility complex associations of ankylosing spondylitis are complex and involve further epistasis with ERAP1
text: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a common, inherited inflammatory arthritis that is significantly influenced by genetics. The major genetic risk factor for AS is HLA-B*27, but the exact mechanisms by which it contributes to the development of the disease are not fully understood. To gain a better understanding of the genetic basis of AS susceptibility, we analyzed 7,264 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) gene in a sample of 22,647 individuals with AS and controls of European descent. We used imputation to identify SNPs, classical HLA alleles, and amino acid residues within HLA proteins, and tested their association with AS status. Our findings indicate that in addition to the well-established role of HLA-B*27 alleles, several other HLA-B alleles also contribute to susceptibility to AS. After controlling for associated haplotypes in HLA-B, we observed independent associations with variants in the HLA-A, HLA-DPB1, and HLA-DRB1 loci. Furthermore, we found that the ERAP1 SNP rs30187 is associated with AS risk in both HLA-B*27 and HLA-B*40:01 carriers, independent of their HLA-B genotype.

title: RNA sequencing identifies dysregulation of the human pancreatic islet transcriptome by the saturated fatty acid palmitate.
text: The pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes (T2D) is characterized by pancreatic β-cell dysfunction and death, which are significantly influenced by saturated fatty acids, particularly palmitate. In this study, we employed RNA sequencing to investigate the transcriptome of human islet preparations exposed to palmitate, and identified 1,325 modified genes. Our findings revealed that palmitate induces fatty acid metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, leading to the modulation of genes involved in ubiquitin and proteasome function, autophagy, and apoptosis. Inhibition of autophagic flux and lysosome function contributes to lipotoxicity, while palmitate also inhibits transcription factors that control β-cell phenotype, including PAX4 and GATA6. Furthermore, we identified 59 T2D candidate genes that were expressed in human islets, and 11 of these were modified by palmitate. Additionally, we found that palmitate modified the expression of 17 splicing factors and shifted the alternative splicing of 3,525 transcripts. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of modified transcripts and genes revealed that the top changed functions related to cell death. Finally, we analyzed transcription factor binding sites in palmitate-modified transcripts and found a role for PAX4, GATA, and the ER stress response regulators XBP1 and ATF6. Overall, this study uncovered novel mechanisms of palmitate-induced β-cell dysfunction and death, highlighting the cross talk between metabolic stress and candidate genes at the β-cell level.

title: The Ratio of Monocytes to Lymphocytes in Peripheral Blood Correlates with Increased Susceptibility to Clinical Malaria in Kenyan Children
text:
Background: Plasmodium falciparum malaria remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, with young children bearing the brunt of the disease. While older children and adults experience fewer clinical attacks, they are still susceptible to asymptomatic P. falciparum infection. Understanding the host factors associated with immunity to clinical malaria and the ability to maintain asymptomatic infection is crucial for the development of improved strategies for disease prevention.
Methods and Findings: In this study, we investigate the potential of full differential blood counts to predict susceptibility to clinical malaria among Kenyan children sampled at five annual cross-sectional surveys. Our results show that the ratio of monocytes to lymphocytes in peripheral blood at the time of survey is directly correlated with the risk of clinical malaria during follow-up, with a hazard ratio of 2.7 (95% CI: 1.42, 5.01, P = 0.002) observed among children with asymptomatic P. falciparum infection at the time of measurement. However, this association is not present in children without detectable parasitaemia (HR = 1.0, 95% CI: 0.74, 1.42, P = 0.9).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that the monocyte to lymphocyte ratio, which can be easily derived from routine full differential blood counts, may serve as a useful marker of an individual's immune response to P. falciparum infection. This study highlights the potential of this simple and inexpensive diagnostic tool for identifying children at risk of clinical malaria and informing the development of targeted interventions to prevent disease.

title: Dynamic analysis of filopodial interactions during the zippering phase of Drosophila dorsal closure.
text: Dorsal closure is a crucial epithelial fusion event that takes place late in Drosophila embryogenesis, resulting in the sealing of a midline hole by the bonding of two opposing epithelial sheets. During this process, leading edge epithelial cells exhibit filopodial behavior, with the formation of adhesions depending on the interdigitation of these filopodia. To ensure accurate alignment of the opposing epithelia, we employed a genetic approach to label mutually exclusive stripes of RFP-Moesin and GFP-Moesin in each segment using the engrailed and patched promoters. Our observations reveal mutually exclusive interactions between the filopodia of engrailed and patched cells, leading to the formation of tethers between them. These tethers can realign misaligned epithelial sheets. We also observe this behavior during repair of laser wounds in the ventral epithelium, indicating that it is not limited to leading edge cells during dorsal closure. Furthermore, we characterize the behavior of a patched-expressing cell located within the engrailed region of segments A1-A5 and provide evidence that this cell contributes to cell matching.

title: Expression of Versican 3′-Untranslated Region Modulates Endogenous MicroRNA Functions
text:
Background:
Mature microRNAs (miRNAs) are single-stranded RNAs that play a crucial role in post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating the expression of target genes. In our previous study, we demonstrated that the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of the non-coding transcript versican can antagonize the function of miR-199a-3p, leading to increased expression of the matrix proteins versican and fibronectin, and enhanced cell-cell adhesion and organ adhesion. However, the impact of this non-coding fragment on tumorigenesis remains unclear.
Methods and Findings:
Using a combination of computational prediction and in vitro and in vivo experiments, we investigated the effect of versican 3'UTR on miR-199a-3p function and tumorigenesis. Our results showed that expression of versican 3'UTR not only antagonizes miR-199a-3p but also reduces its steady-state expression. We found that overexpression of versican 3'UTR in a mouse breast carcinoma cell line, 4T1, resulted in decreased levels of miR-199a-3p, which in turn led to differences in tumor growth. Computational analysis revealed that both miR-199a-3p and miR-144 target the cell cycle regulator Rb1, while miR-144 and miR-136 also target the phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN). Expression of Rb1 and PTEN was up-regulated synergistically in vitro and in vivo, suggesting that the 3'UTR binds and modulates miRNA activities, leading to the release of these mRNAs for translation. In tumor formation assays, cells transfected with the 3'UTR formed smaller tumors compared to cells transfected with a control vector.
Conclusion:
Our findings demonstrate that a 3'UTR fragment can be used to modulate miRNA functions. Additionally, our study suggests that miRNAs in cancer cells are more susceptible to degradation due to their interaction with non-coding 3'UTRs. This non-coding component of mRNA may be used retrospectively to modulate miRNA activities, providing a potential therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment.

title: Prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy of the epitope vaccine CTB-UA against Helicobacter pylori infection in a BALB/c mice model
text: Epitope vaccine based on the enzyme urease of Helicobacter pylori holds promise as a prophylactic and therapeutic vaccine against H. pylori infection. In our previous study, an epitope vaccine called CTB-UA was constructed by combining the mucosal adjuvant cholera toxin B subunit (CTB) with an epitope (UreA183–203) from the H. pylori urease A subunit (UreA). This vaccine demonstrated good immunogenicity and immunoreactivity, and was able to induce specific neutralizing antibodies that effectively inhibited the enzymatic activity of H. pylori urease. In this study, the prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy of the epitope vaccine CTB-UA was evaluated in a BALB/c mouse model. The results showed that oral prophylactic or therapeutic immunization with CTB-UA significantly reduced H. pylori colonization compared to oral immunization with PBS. Additionally, the protection was found to be correlated with antigen-specific IgG, IgA, and mucosal secretory IgA antibody responses. These findings suggest that CTB-UA may be a promising vaccine candidate for controlling H. pylori infection.

title: Spatial co-distribution of neglected tropical diseases in the east African great lakes region: revisiting the justification for integrated control.
text:
Objective:
To identify the spatial patterns of co-endemicity between Schistosoma mansoni and soil-transmitted helminths (STHs), including Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and hookworm, in the Great Lakes region of East Africa, in order to inform integrated neglected tropical disease control programs in the area.
Methodology:
Parasitological surveys were conducted in Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, and Burundi among 28,213 children in 404 schools. Bayesian geostatistical models were used to interpolate prevalence data across the study area, and interpolated prevalence maps were overlaid to identify areas of co-endemicity.
Results:
In the Great Lakes region, the prevalence of Schistosoma mansoni was 18.1%, hookworm infection was ubiquitous (50.0%), A. lumbricoides infection was 6.8%, and T. trichiura infection was 6.8%. Hookworm infection was highly focal, while S. mansoni, A. lumbricoides, and T. trichiura were highly focal. Most areas were endemic (prevalence >or=10%) or hyperendemic (prevalence >or=50%) for one or more STHs, while endemic areas for schistosomiasis mansoni were limited to foci adjacent large perennial water bodies.
Conclusion:

Because of the widespread distribution of hookworm infection in the region, treatment programs are necessary for STH control throughout the area. However, efficient schistosomiasis control should only be targeted at limited high-risk areas, and integration of schistosomiasis control with STH control is only indicated in limited foci in East Africa.

title: Direct conversion of patient fibroblasts demonstrates non-cell autonomous toxicity of astrocytes to motor neurons in familial and sporadic ALS.
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) leads to the degeneration of motor neurons, paralysis, and ultimately death. Accurate modeling of the disease, identifying its underlying mechanisms, and developing effective treatments are urgently needed. In our previous work, we demonstrated motor neuron toxicity in postmortem ALS spinal cord-derived astrocytes. However, these cells can only be obtained after death, and their expansion is limited.
In this study, we report a novel method to convert adult human fibroblasts from living ALS patients into induced neuronal progenitor cells (i-astrocytes) and then differentiate them into astrocytes (i-astrocytes). This approach provides a rapid, highly reproducible means of disease modeling and drug screening.
Using this method, we found that non-cell autonomous toxicity to motor neurons is present when i-astrocytes from familial ALS patients with mutations in superoxide dismutase or hexanucleotide expansion in C9orf72 (a gene on chromosome 9) are cocultured with motor neurons. Remarkably, i-astrocytes from sporadic ALS patients also exhibit this toxicity, suggesting a common mechanism.
The ease of producing and expanding i-astrocytes now enables rapid disease modeling and high-throughput drug screening to alleviate astrocyte-derived toxicity, which is a hallmark of ALS. This breakthrough could lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for this devastating disease.

title: Combined Single-Cell Functional and Gene Expression Analysis Resolves Heterogeneity within Stem Cell Populations
text: The diversity within the self-renewal capacity of adult hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) has challenged our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying HSC function. Gene expression studies have been hindered by the presence of multiple HSC subtypes and non-HSCs in bulk HSC populations, making it difficult to gain a deeper understanding of the gene expression program of murine HSCs. To overcome these challenges, we combined single-cell functional assays with flow cytometric index sorting and single-cell gene expression assays. By integrating these datasets through bioinformatic analysis, we developed an unbiased sorting strategy that separates non-HSCs from HSCs, and single-cell transplantation experiments using the enriched population were combined with RNA-seq data to identify key molecules associated with long-term durable self-renewal. This approach produced a single-cell molecular dataset that is linked to functional stem cell activity. Finally, we demonstrated the broader applicability of this approach by linking key molecules with defined cellular functions in another stem cell system.

title: Acids: Structures, Properties, and Functions (University Science Books, Sausalito, CA, 2000).
text: Humans who exhibit a defective form of the transcription factor AIRE (autoimmune regulator) are prone to developing multiorgan autoimmune diseases. To investigate this phenomenon, we employed aire-deficient mice and hypothesized that this transcription factor regulates autoimmunity by promoting the ectopic expression of peripheral tissue-restricted antigens in medullary epithelial cells of the thymus. Our findings confirmed this hypothesis, as the mutant animals displayed a distinct profile of autoimmune diseases that was dependent on the absence of aire in stromal cells of the thymus. Analysis of aire-deficient thymic medullary epithelial cells revealed a specific reduction in the ectopic transcription of genes encoding peripheral antigens. These findings underscore the crucial role of thymically imposed "central" tolerance in controlling autoimmunity.

title: Directed Actin Polymerization Is the Driving Force for Epithelial Cell–Cell Adhesion
text: Recent research has revealed that epithelial cells engage in a process of intercellular adhesion mediated by cadherin proteins, which involves unexpected mechanisms involving calcium and actin polymerization. Calcium stimulation leads to the formation of filopodia that penetrate and embed into neighboring cells, with E-cadherin complexes clustering at the tips of these filopodia to form a two-rowed zipper of embedded puncta. Desmosomes are also involved in clamping opposing cell surfaces, while the recruitment of proteins such as vinculin, zyxin, VASP, and Mena to adhesion zippers requires the presence of alpha-catenin. Actin reorganization and polymerization play a crucial role in merging puncta into a single row and sealing cell borders, but in cells lacking alpha-catenin or blocked in VASP/Mena function, filopodia embed but actin reorganization/polymerization is prevented, and membranes cannot seal. Overall, this study unveils a dynamic mechanism for intercellular adhesion involving calcium-activated filopodia penetration and VASP/Mena-dependent actin reorganization/polymerization.

title: Ribosomal DNA copy number loss and sequence variation in cancer
text:
Ribosomal DNA (rDNA) is one of the most variable regions in the human genome with respect to copy number, presenting a significant challenge for understanding its regulation and functional implications. Despite its crucial role in cellular function, the mechanisms governing rDNA copy number, stability, and sequence in the mammalian genome remain largely unexplored. To address this knowledge gap, we employed computational and droplet digital PCR approaches to investigate rDNA copy number in both normal and cancer states across the human and mouse genomes. Our findings reveal that rDNA copy number and sequence can undergo changes in cancer genomes, with a notable loss of copies accompanied by global copy number co-variation in human cancer genomes. Contrary to expectations, cancer genomes with lower rDNA copies exhibit mutational evidence of mTOR hyperactivity, suggesting a potential link between rDNA copy number and cancer development.
The PTEN phosphatase, a tumor suppressor critical for genome stability and negative regulator of the mTOR kinase pathway, was found to be involved in this process. Interestingly, hematopoietic cancer stem cells from a Pten-deficient mouse model for leukemia display lower rDNA copy number despite increased proliferation, rRNA production, and protein synthesis, indicating that loss of rDNA copies may be a recurrent feature in cancers associated with mTOR activation. Furthermore, our results suggest that rDNA copy number may serve as a simple and useful indicator of whether a cancer will be sensitive to DNA damaging treatments.
In summary, our study uncovers the complex dynamics of rDNA copy number in the human genome, highlighting its potential as a predictive biomarker for cancer sensitivity to DNA damaging therapies. The findings also underscore the importance of further investigating the regulatory mechanisms governing rDNA copy number and its relationship with cancer development and progression.

title: The association of Red cell distribution width and in-hospital mortality in older adults admitted to the emergency department
text:
BACKGROUND:
The aim of this study was to investigate whether elevated red blood cell distribution width (RDW) at admission is associated with an increased risk of mortality in older patients presenting to the emergency department (ED).
METHODS:
We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients aged 65 years or older who visited the ED with any medical issues between May 2013 and October 2013. RDW values were measured at the time of admission. The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to determine the relationship between RDW and mortality.
RESULTS:
A total of 1,990 patients were included in the study, with a mean age of 75 years (standard deviation [SD] 7) and 936 (47%) male patients. The in-hospital mortality rate was 3.76% (74 patients). Compared to survivors, non-survivors had higher RDW values (15.9 ± 2.5 vs. 13.8 ± 1.7, p < 0.001). Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that RDW was independently associated with all-cause in-hospital mortality after adjusting for other confounding factors.
DISCUSSION:
Our findings suggest that RDW at admission is a predictor of all-cause in-hospital mortality among patients older than 65 years. After adjusting for multiple confounders, the all-cause in-hospital mortality rate increased by 21.8% for each 1% increase in RDW.
CONCLUSION:
These results indicate that RDW at admission is associated with in-hospital mortality among patients older than 65 years. Therefore, RDW at admission may serve as a surrogate marker of disease severity. However, we caution against using these findings to inform clinical decision-making until they are validated in external studies.

title: Gene regulation by the act of long non-coding RNA transcription
text: Long non-protein-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are believed to be the most abundant transcript class in the mouse and human transcriptomes. Two key questions regarding lncRNAs are whether all of them are functional and how they exert their function. While some lncRNAs have been shown to function through their product, it is not the only possible mechanism. In this review, we focus on the possibility that lncRNA transcription itself, rather than the lncRNA product, plays a role in regulating protein-coding gene activity in cis. We examine instances where lncRNA transcription leads to either gene silencing or activation, and discuss methods for determining whether the lncRNA product or its transcription is responsible for the regulatory effect.

title: Life and death of cardiac stem cells: a paradigm shift in cardiac biology.
text:
The realization that myocyte mitosis occurs in various stages of life, including fetal, neonatal, adult, and hypertrophied heart, has challenged the long-held view that the mammalian heart is incapable of regenerating its parenchymal cells. This new perspective suggests that myocyte formation is preserved throughout life, revealing a remarkable growth potential of the heart. This review summarizes the significant findings accumulated over the past two decades, which support the notion that the heart has the inherent ability to replace its parenchymal cells. This unexpected characteristic has important implications for understanding myocardial homeostasis, cardiac aging, and tissue repair.
The dogma that the heart is a postmitotic organ, incapable of regenerating parenchymal cells, was established in the 1970s and has significantly influenced basic and clinical research in cardiology for the past three decades. According to this paradigm, cardiomyocytes undergo cellular hypertrophy, but they cannot enter the cell cycle or be replaced by a pool of primitive cells. The only response of cardiomyocytes to stress is hypertrophy or death. Therefore, extensive research has focused on identifying the molecular mechanisms of myocyte hypertrophy and their genetic control. Significant progress has been made in understanding the biology of hypertrophic myocyte growth, and various new technologies have led to a scientific revolution in the field. However, despite this significant progress, very little is known about the mechanisms of myocyte regeneration in the adult heart.
In conclusion, the recognition that myocyte mitosis occurs throughout life has challenged the traditional view of the heart's biology and highlighted the need for further research into the mechanisms of myocyte regeneration. This review provides an overview of the significant findings accumulated over the past two decades and emphasizes the importance of understanding the mechanisms of myocyte regeneration in the adult heart.

title: Paraneoplastic thrombocytosis: the secrets of tumor self-promotion.
text: Paraneoplastic thrombocytosis, a condition characterized by an excessive increase in platelet count, is frequently observed in individuals with solid tumors. This association is often associated with poorer prognosis. Recent research suggests that a complex feedback loop may exist between platelets and tumor cells, with reciprocal interactions between tumor growth, metastasis, and platelet activation. Specifically, tumors can stimulate platelet production and activation, which in turn can promote tumor growth and metastasis. These findings open up promising new avenues for therapeutic intervention.

title: Perceived age as clinically useful biomarker of ageing: cohort study.
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between perceived age and survival in a population-based twin cohort, as well as the correlation between perceived age and various age-related phenotypes.
Design: Longitudinal follow-up study with survival data up to January 2008, when 675 (37%) of the 1826 twins had died.
Setting: Population-based twin cohort in Denmark.
Participants: 20 nurses, 10 young men, and 11 older women (assessors); 1826 twins aged >or=70.
Main Outcome Measures: Assessors' perceived age of twins based on photographs, as well as physical and cognitive tests and molecular biomarker of ageing (leucocyte telomere length) for twins.
Results: For all three groups of assessors, perceived age was significantly associated with survival, even after adjustment for chronological age, sex, and rearing environment. Perceived age remained significantly associated with survival after further adjustment for physical and cognitive functioning. The likelihood that the older-looking twin of the pair died first increased with increasing discordance in perceived age within the twin pair, suggesting that common genetic factors influence both perceived age and survival. Perceived age, controlled for chronological age and sex, also correlated significantly with physical and cognitive functioning as well as with leucocyte telomere length.
Conclusion: Perceived age, which is commonly used by clinicians as a general indicator of a patient's health, is a robust biomarker of ageing that predicts survival among individuals aged >or=70 and correlates with important functional and molecular ageing phenotypes.

title: Inflammatory Reaction as Determinant of Foreign Body Reaction Is an Early and Susceptible Event after Mesh Implantation
text: Objective: To investigate and compare the short-term and long-term courses of determinants for foreign body reaction as biocompatibility predictors for meshes in an animal model. Materials and Methods: Three different meshes (TVT, UltraPro, and PVDF) were implanted in sheep, with native and plasma-coated meshes placed bilaterally in various locations (interperitoneally, fascia onlay, and muscle onlay/fascia sublay). Meshes were explanted at 5 minutes, 20 minutes, 60 minutes, and 120 minutes, and histochemically investigated for inflammatory infiltrate, macrophage infiltration, vessel formation, myofibroblast invasion, and connective tissue accumulation. The results were compared to long-term values over 24 months. Results: Macrophage invasion reached highest levels (up to 60%) in the short term and decreased within 24 months to about 30%. Inflammatory infiltrate increased within the first 2 hours, with stable levels and ranking among the meshes observed during long-term follow-up. No activity was detected for myofibroblasts, connective tissue, and CD31+ cells during the first 120 minutes. Conclusion: The local inflammatory reaction is an early and susceptible event after mesh implantation, which cannot be influenced by prior plasma coating and does not depend on the location of implantation.

title: Riesz pyramids for fast phase-based video magnification
text: We introduce a novel compact image pyramid representation, called the Riesz pyramid, which enables real-time phase-based motion magnification with improved efficiency and quality. Our new representation is less overcomplete than even the smallest two orientation, octave-bandwidth complex steerable pyramid, and can be implemented using simple, spatially-oriented linear filters. Motion-magnified videos produced with the Riesz pyramid exhibit comparable quality to those produced with the complex steerable pyramid, while also offering improved efficiency and reduced computational complexity. Unlike the complex steerable pyramid, the Riesz pyramid phase-shifts image features along only their dominant orientation, resulting in faster and more accurate motion estimation.

title: Alpha-Synuclein Induces Lysosomal Rupture and Cathepsin Dependent Reactive Oxygen Species Following Endocytosis
text: α-synuclein dysregulation is a crucial aspect of Parkinson's disease pathology. Recent studies have shown that α-synuclein aggregates are toxic to cells in culture and can spread between them, but the underlying mechanisms are not well understood. By studying viruses and bacteria that enter cells by rupturing intracellular vesicles, researchers have found that α-synuclein aggregates can induce the breakdown of lysosomes in neuronal cell lines. This breakdown can be triggered by direct addition of α-synuclein aggregates to cells or by transferring them between cells. The rupture of lysosomes leads to an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) in target cells, which is known to contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation, both of which are hallmarks of Parkinson's disease. Furthermore, α-synuclein aggregates can activate the inflammasome in THP-1 cells, another cellular mechanism linked to Parkinson's disease. These findings provide insight into the mechanisms underlying the propagation of α-synuclein pathology in cells and its connection to the disease processes in Parkinson's disease.

title: Mechanistic Fracture Criteria For The Failure Of Human Cortical Bone
text:
A comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying bone fracture is crucial for predicting the risk of fracture associated with aging and disease. Despite significant research, a mechanistic framework for explaining how the microstructure affects the failure of bone remains elusive. Although micromechanical models incorporating local failure criteria have been developed for metallic and ceramic materials, few such models exist for biological materials. In fact, there is little evidence to support the widely held belief that fracture in bone is locally strain-controlled, as is typically observed in ductile fracture in metallic materials.
To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a novel series of experiments using a double-notch-bend geometry, designed to shed light on the critical failure events in bone. By examining how the propagating crack interacts with the bone microstructure, we aimed to provide a mechanistic understanding of fracture and to determine how properties vary with orientation. Our findings revealed that fracture in human cortical bone is consistent with strain-controlled failure, and the influence of the microstructure can be described using several toughening mechanisms. We also estimated the relative importance of these mechanisms, including uncracked-ligament bridging.
Our study provides a significant step forward in understanding the mechanisms of bone fracture, and our findings have important implications for the development of new treatments and interventions to prevent and treat fractures in aging and diseased bone. By shedding light on the complex interplay between the microstructure and the propagating crack, we have laid the foundation for the development of more accurate and predictive models of bone fracture, which can be used to improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: Inhibition of limb regeneration in the axolotl after treatment of the skin with actinomycin D.
text: In this experiment, actinomycin D was used to investigate the role of the epidermis in underlying tissue regeneration during limb regeneration in axolotls. The skin was removed from the forelimbs of axolotls, from the elbow to the shoulder, and divided into two groups: one was soaked in actinomycin D (5.0 or 10.0 μg/ml 0.6% NaCl) for three hours, while the other was soaked in 0.6% NaCl for the same period of time (control). Each piece of skin was then orthotopically replanted, and both limbs were amputated through the treated skin, proximal to the elbow. After an initial healing period, the control limbs regenerated normally, with a slightly paler color than the untreated limbs. In contrast, limbs bearing actinomycin-treated skin did not display any visible signs of regeneration during the first week following amputation, although histological analysis revealed that dedifferentiation was occurring. However, by 35-40 days, blastemas had formed on most of the experimental limbs, which developed rapidly and attained levels of development close to the controls. Actinomycin D temporarily inhibits the formation of the apical epidermal cap and the subsequent aggregation of dedifferentiated cells into a blastema, but once the effect wears off, a new apical cap forms, and the dedifferentiated cells quickly organize into a blastema and begin to differentiate.

title: Retinoic acid-related orphan receptors α and γ: key regulators of lipid/glucose metabolism, inflammation, and insulin sensitivity
text:
Retinoic acid-related orphan receptors RORα and RORγ play a crucial role in regulating lipid and glucose metabolism, as well as immune functions. Research has shown that RORα-deficient mice are protected against age- and diet-induced obesity, hepatosteatosis, and insulin resistance. The reduced expression of genes involved in lipid synthesis, transport, and storage in adipose tissue is thought to contribute to this protection. Additionally, RORα-deficient mice exhibit decreased adipose tissue-associated inflammation, as evidenced by reduced infiltration of M1 macrophages and decreased expression of proinflammatory genes.
Similarly, deficiency in RORγ also protects against diet-induced insulin resistance through a distinct mechanism. Recent studies have suggested that RORs play a key role in linking the circadian clock machinery to the regulation of metabolic genes and metabolic syndrome. As ligand-dependent transcription factors, RORs may provide novel therapeutic targets for the management of obesity and associated metabolic diseases, including hepatosteatosis, adipose tissue-associated inflammation, and insulin resistance.

title: ERS/ESTS clinical guidelines on fitness for radical therapy in lung cancer patients (surgery and chemo-radiotherapy).
text:
A collaborative effort between multidisciplinary experts from the European Respiratory Society (ERS) and the European Society of Thoracic Surgery (ESTS) has resulted in the development of guidelines for the functional evaluation of lung cancer patients. The goal of these guidelines is to provide clear and up-to-date recommendations for clinicians to determine the fitness of patients for surgery and chemo-radiotherapy.
To achieve this, the subject was divided into various topics, each assigned to at least two experts. The authors conducted their own literature searches, without a centralized review. The draft reports written by the experts were then reviewed, discussed, and voted upon by the entire panel of experts. The evidence supporting each recommendation was summarized and graded using the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network Grading Review Group method.
The resulting guidelines provide a functional algorithm for risk stratification of lung resection candidates, emphasizing the importance of cardiological evaluation, forced expiratory volume in 1 second, systematic carbon monoxide lung diffusion capacity, and exercise testing. In contrast, the lack of data makes it impossible to recommend specific tests, cut-off values, or algorithms for patients undergoing chemo-radiotherapy before lung resection.
The guidelines also emphasize the importance of managing lung cancer patients in specialized settings by multidisciplinary teams. This approach ensures that patients receive comprehensive and coordinated care from a team of experts, leading to better outcomes and improved quality of life.

title: The Ran GTPase regulates mitotic spindle assembly
text: Ran is a ubiquitous nuclear GTPase with a well-established role in interphase nuclear transport, but its functions in mitosis are less clear. The GTPase state of Ran is regulated by RanGAP1 and RCC1, and it interacts with RanBP1, a guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitor. RanBP1 has a high affinity for GTP-bound Ran and enhances the activity of RanGAP1, leading to increased GTP hydrolysis. RanBP1 levels fluctuate during the cell cycle, and elevated concentrations of RanBP1 have been shown to prolong mitosis in mammalian cells and Xenopus egg extracts (unpublished observations). To investigate the effects of increased RanBP1 levels on mitosis, we examined spindle assembly in Xenopus egg extracts treated with exogenous RanBP1 during M phase. Our findings indicate that Ran's role in spindle assembly is independent of nuclear transport and is likely mediated by changes in microtubule dynamics.

title: A summary of the effects of antihypertensive medications on measured blood pressure.
text:
Background: Epidemiological studies analyzing family data on blood pressure (BP) are often hindered by the effects of antihypertensive medications. In this review, we synthesized the results of clinical trials investigating the effects of BP-lowering medications.
Methods: We conducted a systematic review of 137 clinical trials with monodrug therapies and 28 clinical trials of combination drug therapies, involving a total of 11,739 participants, from PubMed. The six major classes/groups of antihypertensive medications were categorized by ethnicity: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, alpha1-blockers, cardioselective beta-blockers (beta1-blockers), calcium channel blockers, thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics, and loop diuretics.
Results: Using sitting or supine BP measurements, monodrug therapy with ACE inhibitors resulted in a weighted average decrease of 12.5/9.5 mm Hg in systolic and diastolic BP for ethnic groups combined. Similarly, alpha1-blockers, beta1-blockers, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and loop diuretics showed BP-lowering effects of 15.5/11.7 mm Hg, 14.8/12.2 mm Hg, 15.3/10.5 mm Hg, 15.3/9.8 mm Hg, and 15.8/8.2 mm Hg, respectively. However, ACE inhibitors, alpha1-blockers, and beta1-blockers were less effective in African Americans than in non-African Americans, while calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and loop diuretics were more effective in African Americans than in non-African Americans. For two-drug combination therapy with ethnic groups combined, the BP-lowering effect of the second medication was 84% and 65% for systolic and diastolic BP, respectively.
Conclusions: The BP-lowering effects reported here can be used to impute the pretreatment BP levels, which can improve the information content and hence the power of epidemiological analysis in studies where use of antihypertensive medications is a confounding factor in BP measurements.

title: Stem Cells and Early Lineage Development
text: The recent generation of pluripotent stem cell lines from various sources, including reprogrammed adult somatic cells, has sparked debate about the equivalence of these different pluripotent states. At least two distinct states have been identified in the early embryo: the epiblast progenitors in the blastocyst and the pluripotent progenitors of the later gastrulating embryo. Determining the initial developmental stage of these pluripotent lines is crucial for establishing the optimal conditions for differentiating them into therapeutically relevant cell types.

title: Divergent clonal evolution of castration resistant neuroendocrine prostate cancer
text: An increasingly recognized mechanism of resistance to androgen receptor (AR)-directed therapy in prostate cancer involves the phenomenon of epithelial plasticity, where tumor cells exhibit low to absent AR expression and often display neuroendocrine features. Despite progress in understanding the etiology and molecular basis of this "alternative" treatment-resistant cell state, its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. To investigate, we analyzed whole-exome sequencing data from metastatic biopsies from patients and observed significant genomic overlap between castration-resistant tumors histologically characterized as prostate adenocarcinomas (CRPC-Adeno) and neuroendocrine prostate cancer (CRPC-NE). Analysis of biopsy samples from the same individuals over time revealed a model consistent with divergent clonal evolution. Genome-wide DNA methylation analysis revealed substantial epigenetic differences between CRPC-NE tumors and CRPC-Adeno, and also identified samples of CRPC-Adeno with clinical features of AR independence as CRPC-NE, suggesting that epigenetic modifiers may play a role in the induction and/or maintenance of this treatment-resistant state. This study supports the emergence of an alternative, "AR-indifferent" cell state through divergent clonal evolution as a mechanism of treatment resistance in advanced prostate cancer.

title: S-phase-promoting cyclin-dependent kinases prevent re-replication by inhibiting the transition of replication origins to a pre-replicative state
text:
In the process of DNA replication and cell division, the activation of kinase complexes made up of cyclin and cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) triggers these processes. It was previously believed that the association of Cdks with different classes of cyclins determined whether S phase (replication) or M phase (mitosis) would occur. However, recent findings in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae have cast doubt on this notion.
In S. cerevisiae strains lacking C1b1-C1b4, cells undergo DNA replication once but fail to enter mitosis. By isolating mutations in two genes, SIM1 and SIM2 (which is identical to SEC72), researchers were able to allow such cells to undergo an extra round of DNA replication without mitosis. The Clb5 kinase, which promotes S phase, remains active during the G2-phase arrest of cells in the parental strain, but its activity declines rapidly in sim mutants. Increased expression of the CLB5 gene prevents re-replication. Therefore, a cyclin B-kinase that promotes DNA replication in G1-phase cells can prevent re-replication in G2-phase cells.
Inactivation of C1b kinases by expression of the specific C1b-Cdk1 inhibitor p40SIC1 is sufficient to induce a prereplicative state at origins of replication in cells blocked in G2/M phase by nocodazole. Re-activation of C1b-Cdk1 kinases induces a second round of DNA replication.
Based on these findings, the authors propose a new model for how S-phase-promoting cyclin B--Cdk complexes prevent re-replication during S, G2, and M phases by inhibiting the transition of replication origins to a pre-replicative state. This model can explain why origins "fire" only once per S phase and why S phase is dependent on the completion of the preceding M phase.

title: E-cadherin engagement stimulates proliferation via Rac1
text: E-cadherin has been shown to play a crucial role in the suppression of tumor growth and the inhibition of cell proliferation in vitro. Our studies have revealed that reducing the seeding density of normal rat kidney-52E (NRK-52E) or MCF-10A epithelial cells from confluence can lead to the release of cells from growth arrest. However, unexpectedly, further decreasing the seeding density to the point where cells are isolated from their neighbors actually leads to a decrease in proliferation. Microengineered substrate experiments revealed that E-cadherin engagement can stimulate peak proliferation at intermediate seeding densities, and that the proliferation arrest at high densities is not due to E-cadherin, but rather results from a crowding-dependent decrease in cell spreading against the underlying substrate. Additionally, our findings showed that Rac1 activity, which is induced by E-cadherin engagement specifically at intermediate seeding densities, is required for the cadherin-stimulated proliferation, and that the control of Rac1 activation by E-cadherin is mediated by p120-catenin. These results demonstrate a stimulatory role for E-cadherin in proliferative regulation and provide insight into the mechanisms by which cell–cell contact can modulate epithelial cell proliferation in different settings.

title: Structure of Actin-related protein 8 and its contribution to nucleosome binding
text:
Nuclear actin-related proteins (Arps) have been identified as subunits of various chromatin remodeling complexes, yet their molecular functions within these complexes remain unclear. To elucidate the role of Arp8, a subunit of the INO80 complex, we have determined the crystal structure of Arp8 in its ATP-bound form. Our findings reveal that human Arp8 contains several insertions in the conserved actin fold, which preclude its ability to polymerize. Interestingly, one of these insertions spans the active site cleft and appears to rigidify the domain architecture, while features shared with actin suggest an allosterically controlled ATPase activity. Through quantitative binding studies with nucleosomes and histone complexes, we have found that Arp8 and the Arp8-Arp4-actin-HSA sub-complex of INO80 exhibit a strong preference for nucleosomes and H3-H4 tetramers over H2A-H2B dimers, indicating that Arp8 functions as a nucleosome recognition module. In contrast, Arp4 appears to prefer binding to (dis)assembly intermediates in the remodeling reaction, rather than nucleosomes.
In summary, our study provides new insights into the molecular functions of Arp8 within the INO80 complex. Through structural and functional analysis, we have identified a nucleosome recognition module and revealed the binding preferences of Arp8 and its subunits. These findings shed light on the mechanisms of chromatin remodeling and provide a framework for further investigations into the role of Arps in nucleosome dynamics.

title: Regulation of β-Adrenergic Receptor Signaling by S-Nitrosylation of G-Protein-Coupled Receptor Kinase 2
text:
Beta-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs), which are prototypical G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), play a crucial role in controlling various physiological processes. However, the G-protein signaling pathway is curtailed by G-protein kinases (GRKs), which target receptors for internalization. Nitric oxide (NO) and/or S-nitrosothiols (SNOs) can prevent the loss of β-AR signaling in vivo, but the molecular details are unclear. Here, we investigate the effect of SNOs on β-AR signaling in mice and cells.
Our findings show that SNOs increase β-AR expression and prevent agonist-stimulated receptor downregulation in mice. In cells, SNOs decrease GRK2-mediated β-AR phosphorylation and subsequent recruitment of β-arrestin to the receptor, resulting in the attenuation of receptor desensitization and internalization. GRK2 is S-nitrosylated by SNOs as well as by NO synthases, and GRK2 S-nitrosylation increases following stimulation of multiple GPCRs with agonists. We identify Cys340 of GRK2 as the principal locus of inhibition by S-nitrosylation. Our studies reveal a central molecular mechanism through which GPCR signaling is regulated.
In summary, our research uncovers a critical molecular mechanism by which GPCR signaling is regulated through the interaction of SNOs with GRK2. This finding provides new insights into the complex interplay between GPCR signaling and the regulation of physiological processes.

title: Electroporation enables the efficient mRNA delivery into the mouse zygotes and facilitates CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing
text: Recent advancements in the CRISPR/Cas9 system have significantly reduced the time required to generate mutant mice, yet the need for a time-consuming microinjection step hinders its widespread application in high-throughput genetic analysis. To address this limitation, we have developed a simple, efficient, and large-scale genome editing method that replaces microinjection with electroporation of RNAs encoding the CRISPR/Cas9 system. We used this method to perform single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN)-mediated knock-in in mouse embryos, facilitating large-scale genetic analysis in the mouse.

title: Summary
text: The genetic disorders Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) and restrictive dermopathy (RD) are caused by the accumulation of farnesylated prelamin A due to defects in the lamin A maturation pathway. Both conditions exhibit symptoms resembling accelerated aging. The mechanism by which farnesylated prelamin A leads to these accelerated aging phenotypes is not understood. Our study found that in HGPS and RD fibroblasts, DNA damage checkpoints are persistently activated due to compromised genomic integrity. Inactivation of checkpoint kinases ataxia-telangiectasia-mutated (ATM) and ATR (ATM- and Rad3-related) in these patient cells can partially overcome their early replication arrest. Treatment of patient cells with a protein farnesyltransferase inhibitor (FTI) did not reduce DNA double-strand breaks and damage checkpoint signaling, although the treatment improved the abnormal nuclear morphology of the cells. These findings suggest that DNA damage accumulation and abnormal nuclear morphology are independent phenotypes resulting from prelamin A accumulation in these progeroid syndromes. Since DNA damage accumulation is a significant contributor to the symptoms of HGPS, our results question the effectiveness of treating HGPS with FTIs alone.

title: The Buccaneer software for automated model building. 1. Tracing protein chains.
text: A novel approach for automated protein chain tracing in experimental electron density maps is presented. The method leverages the application of an oriented electron density likelihood target function to identify likely Cα positions. This function is applied in two stages: (1) to locate a few initial "seed" positions in the map, and (2) to grow these seed positions into extended chain fragments using the target function. Techniques for assembling the chain fragments into a preliminary chain trace are also discussed.

title: Expression profile of genes modulated by Aloe emodin in human U87 glioblastoma cells.
text:
Glioblastoma, the most aggressive and malignant form of glioma, appears to be resistant to various chemotherapeutic agents. Therefore, researchers have intensively investigated potential targets to modulate specific molecular pathways involved in glioblastoma development and progression. Aloe emodin has been identified as a potential therapeutic agent, believed to modulate gene expression in cancer cells. In this study, the molecular mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effect of Aloe emodin on gene expression profiles in the human U87 glioblastoma cell line were investigated using microarray technology.
The gene expression analysis revealed a total of 8,226 gene alterations out of 28,869 genes, with 34 genes showing statistically significant changes (p<0.05) after treatment with 58.6 μg/ml of Aloe emodin for 24 hours. These genes were grouped into several clusters based on their biological functions, revealing the induction of expression of genes involved in apoptosis (programmed cell death) and tissue remodeling in U87 cells. Specifically, genes such as SHARPIN, BCAP31, FIS1, RAC1, and TGM2 from the apoptotic cluster were confirmed by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). These results provide valuable insights into the molecular targets of Aloe emodin and could serve as a guidance for further studies to discover potential cancer therapies based on its treatment.

title: The miniature genome of a carnivorous plant Genlisea aurea contains a low number of genes and short non-coding sequences
text:
BACKGROUND: Genlisea aurea (Lentibulariaceae) is a carnivorous plant with an unusually small genome size of 63.6 megabases (Mb), which is one of the smallest known among higher plants. The genomic data of Genlisea suggests that this condition is a derived state within the genus, making it an ideal model organism for investigating the evolutionary mechanisms of genome contraction.
RESULTS: In this study, we report the sequencing and de novo draft assembly of the G. aurea genome. The assembly consists of 10,687 contigs with a total length of 43.4 Mb, and includes 17,755 complete and partial protein-coding genes. A comparison of the G. aurea genome with that of Mimulus guttatus, another representative of the higher core Lamiales clade, reveals significant differences in gene content and the length of non-coding regions.
CONCLUSIONS: The genome contraction in G. aurea was a complex process involving gene loss and reduction in length of introns and intergenic regions, but not intron loss. The gene loss is more pronounced in genes that belong to multigenic families, indicating that genetic redundancy is a crucial factor in genome size reduction.

title: Abnormal Spine Morphology and Enhanced LTP in LIMK-1 Knockout Mice
text: In vitro studies suggest a role for the LIM kinase (LIMK) family in regulating cofilin phosphorylation and actin dynamics. Additionally, abnormal expression of LIMK-1 has been linked to Williams syndrome, a mental disorder characterized by severe visuospatial cognitive impairments. However, the in vivo function of these kinases remains unclear. To investigate, we employed LIMK-1 knockout mice, which revealed a crucial in vivo role for LIMK-1 in regulating cofilin and the actin cytoskeleton. Our findings also showed that the knockout mice exhibited significant abnormalities in spine morphology and synaptic function, including enhanced hippocampal long-term potentiation. The knockout mice also displayed altered fear responses and spatial learning. These results indicate that LIMK-1 plays a critical role in dendritic spine morphogenesis and brain function.

title: Wdr5 Mediates Self-Renewal and Reprogramming via the Embryonic Stem Cell Core Transcriptional Network
text: The transcriptional and epigenetic networks of embryonic stem (ES) cells are crucial for self-renewal maintenance, but their functional interplay remains unclear. Our study reveals that WD repeat domain 5 (Wdr5), a key component of the mammalian Trithorax (trxG) complex, positively correlates with the undifferentiated state and regulates ES cell self-renewal. We demonstrate that Wdr5, an "effector" of histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methylation, interacts with the pluripotency transcription factor Oct4. Genome-wide protein localization and transcriptome analyses show overlapping gene regulatory functions between Oct4 and Wdr5. The Oct4-Sox2-Nanog circuitry and trxG complex cooperate in activating transcription of self-renewal regulators, and Wdr5 expression is essential for efficient induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell formation. We propose an integrated model of transcriptional and epigenetic control, mediated by select trxG members, for the maintenance of ES cell self-renewal and somatic cell reprogramming.

title: Neurons derived from reprogrammed fibroblasts functionally integrate into the fetal brain and improve symptoms of rats with Parkinson's disease.
text: The long-term objective of nuclear transfer or alternative reprogramming techniques is to generate patient-specific donor cells for transplantation therapy, avoiding the rejection complication that is prevalent in current transplantation medicine. Recently, it was shown that the four transcription factors Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc can induce pluripotency in mouse fibroblasts. However, the therapeutic potential of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells for neural cell replacement strategies remained unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that iPS cells can be efficiently differentiated into neural precursor cells, which then differentiate into neuronal and glial cell types in culture. Following transplantation into the fetal mouse brain, the cells migrate to various brain regions and differentiate into glia and neurons, including glutamatergic, GABAergic, and catecholaminergic subtypes. Electrophysiological recordings and morphological analysis revealed that the grafted neurons exhibited mature neuronal activity and were functionally integrated into the host brain. Additionally, iPS cells were induced to differentiate into dopamine neurons of midbrain character and were able to improve behavior in a rat model of Parkinson's disease following transplantation into the adult brain. To minimize the risk of tumor formation from the grafted cells, we separated contaminating pluripotent cells and committed neural cells using fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Our results demonstrate the therapeutic potential of directly reprogrammed fibroblasts for neuronal cell replacement in the animal model.

title: Responses of primate frontal cortex neurons during natural vocal communication.
text:
The controversial history of the role of primate frontal cortex in vocal communication and its implications for language evolution can be traced back to the ongoing debate over the neural basis of vocalization processing. While some studies suggest that vocalization processing occurs in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex neurons, others propose that vocal-motor activity is primarily subcortical and distinct from the neural architecture of humans. However, direct evidence of neural activity during natural vocal communication is limited due to the use of chair-restrained animals in previous studies.
To address this limitation, we recorded the activity of single neurons across multiple regions of prefrontal and premotor cortex in freely moving marmosets engaged in a natural vocal behavior known as antiphonal calling. Our goal was to determine whether neurons in marmoset frontal cortex exhibited responses during vocal-signal processing and/or vocal-motor production during active, natural communication.
Our findings revealed motor-related changes in single neuron activity during vocal production, but relatively weak sensory responses for vocalization processing during this natural behavior. Vocal-motor responses occurred both prior to and during call production and were typically coupled to the timing of each vocalization pulse. Despite the relatively weak sensory responses, a population classifier was able to distinguish between neural activity that occurred during presentations of vocalization stimuli that elicited an antiphonal response and those that did not.
These findings provide important insights into the role that nonhuman primate frontal cortex neurons play in natural communication and lay the groundwork for more explicit tests of the functional contributions of these neocortical areas during vocal behaviors.

title: Salt-inducible kinase 2 links transcriptional coactivator p300 phosphorylation to the prevention of ChREBP-dependent hepatic steatosis in mice.
text:
The text can be rewritten with simpler language and a more conversational tone as follows:
Obesity and type 2 diabetes are linked to increased fat production in the liver. This leads to fat accumulation in liver cells, known as hepatic steatosis, which is a common liver problem in the US. A protein called Carbohydrate-responsive element-binding protein (ChREBP) plays a key role in the development of hepatic steatosis in mice. However, the exact mechanisms that make ChREBP more active are not well understood.
In this study, we found two proteins, p300 and SIK2, that regulate ChREBP's activity. In cultured mouse liver cells, we showed that glucose can activate p300, which in turn acetylates ChREBP on a specific spot (Lys672). This makes ChREBP more effective at controlling genes involved in fat production. SIK2, on the other hand, can decrease ChREBP's activity by phosphorylating p300 on a different spot (Ser89). When we blocked SIK2's activity, ChREBP became more active, leading to increased fat production in the liver.
We also found that mice lacking SIK2 or overexpressing p300 had similar liver problems, including hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance, and inflammation. Furthermore, low SIK2 activity was linked to increased p300 activity and fat accumulation in the liver in mice with type 2 diabetes and obesity.
Our findings suggest that reducing p300 activity may help treat hepatic steatosis in obesity and type 2 diabetes. We also identified SIK2 activators and specific p300 inhibitors as potential targets for pharmaceutical intervention.

title: A Role for NuSAP in Linking Microtubules to Mitotic Chromosomes
text: The spindle apparatus is a microtubule (MT)-based machinery that attaches to and separates chromosomes during mitosis and meiosis. Self-organization of the spindle around chromatin involves the assembly of MTs, their attachment to the chromosomes, and their organization into a bipolar array. One regulator of spindle self-organization is RanGTP, which is generated at chromatin and activates a set of soluble, Ran-regulated spindle factors such as TPX2, NuMA, and NuSAP. However, the mechanisms by which these spindle factors direct and attach MTs to the chromosomes remain unclear. Recently, the nucleolar and spindle-associated protein (NuSAP) was identified as an essential MT-stabilizing and bundling protein that is enriched at the central part of the spindle. Our study shows that NuSAP efficiently adsorbs to isolated chromatin and DNA and can directly produce and retain high concentrations of MTs in the immediate vicinity of chromatin or DNA. Additionally, we found that NuSAP-chromatin interaction is subject to Ran regulation and can be suppressed by Importin alpha (Impalpha) and Imp7. Based on these findings, we propose that the presence of MT binding agents such as NuSAP, which can be directly immobilized on chromatin, are critical for targeting MT production to vertebrate chromosomes during spindle self-organization.

title: Molecular features of cellular reprogramming and development
text: During ontogeny, somatic cells undergo progressive specialization, but they can be redirected to form other cell types through experimental manipulation, including those with embryonic potential. Early attempts at nuclear reprogramming, such as somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) and cell fusion, faced significant technical challenges in dissecting the regulatory programs governing cell identity. However, the discovery of direct reprogramming, which involves ectopic expression of a defined set of transcription factors, has provided a more tractable platform for understanding the molecular mechanisms of cellular specification, differentiation, cell type stability, and pluripotency. By studying direct reprogramming, we can gain insights into the control and maintenance of cellular identity during developmental transitions, with a focus on transcriptional and epigenetic regulation.

title: Small molecule modifiers of circadian clocks
text: Circadian clocks orchestrate 24-hour cycles of vital physiological and behavioral processes in response to daily environmental changes. These clocks exhibit remarkable precision under constant conditions yet demonstrate remarkable responsiveness to resetting signals.
