With the molecular composition of the core oscillator largely characterized, recent research has increasingly focused on elucidating the mechanisms/molecules that modulate clock function. In particular, small molecule modifiers, both endogenous and exogenous, are emerging as valuable tools for investigating basic clock biology as well as developing potential therapeutic agents for clock-associated disorders. This review will concentrate on synthetic compounds capable of modifying the period, phase, or amplitude of circadian clocks, with a particular emphasis on the mammalian clock. We will discuss the potential of leveraging these small molecule modifiers in both basic and translational research.

title: NVP-BEZ235, a dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor, prevents PI3K signaling and inhibits the growth of cancer cells with activating PI3K mutations.
text: Deregulation of the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is a common occurrence in human cancer, often resulting from inactivation of the tumor suppressor phosphatase and tensin homologue deleted from chromosome 10 (PTEN) or activating mutations in the p110-alpha subunit of PI3K. These mutations lead to oncogenic activity and contribute to resistance to the anti-HER2 antibody trastuzumab. Therefore, targeting the PI3K pathway represents an attractive strategy for cancer therapy. We investigated NVP-BEZ235, a dual inhibitor of PI3K and the downstream mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). NVP-BEZ235 inhibited the activation of downstream effectors, including Akt, S6 ribosomal protein, and 4EBP1, in breast cancer cells. Its antiproliferative activity was superior to that of the allosteric selective mTOR complex inhibitor everolimus in a panel of 21 cancer cell lines with different mutation status. The activation of Akt due to mTOR inhibition was prevented by higher doses of NVP-BEZ235. NVP-BEZ235 reversed the hyperactivation of the PI3K/mTOR pathway caused by oncogenic mutations in p110-alpha, such as E545K and H1047R, and inhibited the proliferation of HER2-amplified BT474 cells that are resistant to trastuzumab. In trastuzumab-resistant BT474 H1047R breast cancer xenografts, NVP-BEZ235 inhibited PI3K signaling and displayed potent antitumor activity. In treated animals, complete inhibition of PI3K signaling was observed in the skin at pharmacologically active doses, suggesting that the skin may serve as a surrogate tissue for pharmacodynamic studies. In summary, NVP-BEZ235 inhibits the PI3K/mTOR axis and exhibits antiproliferative and antitumoral activity against cancer cells with both wild-type and mutated p110-alpha.

title: Pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and pharmacogenetic determinants of osteonecrosis in children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
text: Osteonecrosis is a severe complication that can arise as a result of treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukemia in children. In a prospective study, we screened 364 children using magnetic resonance imaging of the hips and knees, regardless of symptoms, and found that the cumulative incidence of any (grade 1-4) osteonecrosis was 71.8%, while the incidence of symptomatic (grade 2-4) osteonecrosis was 17.6%. To identify potential risk factors for symptomatic osteonecrosis, we investigated a range of factors, including age, race, sex, treatment arm, body mass, serum lipids, albumin, and cortisol levels, as well as dexamethasone pharmacokinetics and genome-wide germline genetic polymorphisms. Our findings revealed that older age (odds ratio = 4.85; 95% confidence interval, 2.5-9.2; P = .00001) and more intensive treatment (odds ratio = 2.5; 95% confidence interval, 1.2-4.9; P = .011) were significant risk factors for symptomatic osteonecrosis. Additionally, we found that lower albumin (P = .05) and elevated cholesterol (P = .02) were associated with symptomatic osteonecrosis, and severe (grade 3 or 4) osteonecrosis was linked to poor dexamethasone clearance (P = .0005). Furthermore, we identified a number of genomic variations, including those in the ACP1 gene (e.g., rs12714403), which were associated with the risk of osteonecrosis and with lower albumin and higher cholesterol levels. Overall, our findings suggest that older age, lower albumin, higher lipid levels, and dexamethasone exposure are all associated with an increased risk of osteonecrosis, and that inherited genomic variation may play a role in this process.

title: Prevention of Rectal SHIV Transmission in Macaques by Daily or Intermittent Prophylaxis with Emtricitabine and Tenofovir
text:
Background: The lack of an effective vaccine against HIV has underscored the need for novel strategies to curb its transmission. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with antiretroviral drugs has shown promise as an intervention strategy, provided that highly efficacious and cost-effective PrEP modalities are identified. To evaluate the efficacy of different PrEP regimens, we conducted a study in a macaque model that mimics human transmission.
Methods and Findings: We employed a repeat-exposure macaque model, where 14 weekly rectal virus challenges were administered to 14 macaques. The macaques were divided into four groups, each receiving a different PrEP regimen. Group 1 received subcutaneous emtricitabine (FTC) at a human-equivalent dose, while groups 2 and 3 received oral FTC and tenofovir-disoproxil fumarate (TDF) at human-equivalent doses. Group 4 received intermittent PrEP, consisting of subcutaneous FTC and TDF at a higher dose, 2 hours before and 24 hours after each weekly challenge. The risk of infection was compared to a control group of 18 macaques that did not receive any drug treatment. Our results showed that the risk of infection was 3.8- and 7.8-fold lower in macaques treated with groups 1 and 2, respectively (p = 0.02 and p = 0.008). All six macaques in group 3 were protected, and breakthrough infections resulted in blunted acute viremias. Drug resistance was observed in two of the six animals. Notably, all six macaques in group 4 that received intermittent PrEP were protected.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that single drugs for daily PrEP can provide protection, but a combination of antiretroviral drugs may be necessary to increase the level of protection. Intermittent PrEP, consisting of short but potent doses of antiretroviral drugs, can provide comparable protection to daily PrEP in this SHIV/macaque model. These findings support the conduct of PrEP trials in humans and identify promising PrEP modalities.

title: Direct-coupling analysis of residue co-evolution captures native contacts across many protein families
text: The three-dimensional similarity among homologous proteins imposes rigid constraints on their sequence variability, allowing for the inference of spatial contacts within their tertiary structures. This can be achieved by disentangling direct and indirect correlations, as demonstrated by the Direct Coupling Analysis (DCA) method (Weigt et al., 2009). Our work presents a computationally efficient implementation of DCA, enabling the evaluation of contact prediction accuracy for a large number of protein domains based solely on sequence information. Our results show that DCA can successfully predict a large number of contacts, recapitulating the global structure of the contact map for the majority of the protein domains examined. Additionally, our analysis reveals signals beyond intra-domain residue contacts, such as those arising from alternative protein conformations, ligand-mediated residue couplings, and inter-domain interactions in protein oligomers. These findings suggest that contacts predicted by DCA can serve as a reliable guide for facilitating computational predictions of alternative protein conformations, protein complex formation, and even the de novo prediction of protein domain structures, provided there is a large number of homologous sequences available due to advances in genome sequencing.

title: Variation in antibiotic prescribing and its impact on recovery in patients with acute cough in primary care: prospective study in 13 countries.
text:
Objective: To investigate the variation in antibiotic prescribing patterns for acute cough in different European primary care settings and assess the impact on recovery.
Design: Cross-sectional observational study involving 14 primary care research networks in 13 European countries.
Setting: Primary care.
Participants: Adults with a new or worsening cough or clinical presentation suggestive of lower respiratory tract infection.
Main Outcome Measures: Antibiotic prescribing rates by clinicians and total symptom severity scores over time.
Results: A total of 3402 patients were recruited, with 99% (3368) of participants having a completed case report form and 80% (2714) returning a symptom diary. The mean symptom severity scores at presentation ranged from 19 (scale range 0 to 100) in networks based in Spain and Italy to 38 in the network based in Sweden. Antibiotic prescribing rates by networks ranged from 20% to nearly 90% (53% overall), with significant variation in the classes of antibiotics prescribed. Amoxicillin was the most commonly prescribed antibiotic, but this varied from 3% in the Norwegian network to 83% in the English network. Fluoroquinolones were not prescribed at all in three networks, but were prescribed for 18% in the Milan network. After adjusting for clinical presentation and demographics, significant differences remained in antibiotic prescribing, ranging from Norway (odds ratio 0.18, 95% confidence interval 0.11 to 0.30) to Slovakia (11.2, 6.20 to 20.27) compared with the overall mean (proportion prescribed: 0.53). The rate of recovery was similar for patients who were and were not prescribed antibiotics once clinical presentation was taken into account (coefficient -0.01, P<0.01).
Conclusion: The variation in antibiotic prescribing patterns for acute cough in European primary care settings is substantial, and clinical presentation does not explain the differences in antibiotic prescribing. Additionally, there is no association between antibiotic prescribing and clinically important differences in recovery.
Trial Registration: Clinicaltrials.gov NCT00353951.

title: Dorsomorphin, a Selective Small Molecule Inhibitor of BMP Signaling, Promotes Cardiomyogenesis in Embryonic Stem Cells
text:
Background: Pluripotent embryonic stem (ES) cells have the potential to revolutionize regenerative therapy by providing a virtually unlimited source of cells for tissue repair. However, the mechanisms underlying the lineage specification of these cells are not well understood, and generating sufficient quantities of desired cell types remains a significant challenge. Small molecules, particularly those that modulate key developmental pathways, hold promise as tools to study in vitro lineage specification and direct the differentiation of stem cells towards specific cell types.
Methodology/Principal Findings: We investigated the use of dorsomorphin, a selective small molecule inhibitor of BMP signaling, to induce myocardial differentiation in mouse ES cells. Our results show that dorsomorphin robustly induces cardiomyogenesis, increasing the yield of spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes by at least 20-fold. In contrast to the endogenous BMP antagonist Noggin, dorsomorphin promotes cardiomyogenesis when treatment is limited to the initial 24 hours of ES cell differentiation. Quantitative PCR analyses of differentiating ES cells indicate that pharmacological inhibition of BMP signaling during the early critical stage promotes the development of the cardiomyocyte lineage, while reducing the differentiation of endothelial, smooth muscle, and hematopoietic cells.
Conclusions/Significance: Our findings suggest that the administration of a selective small molecule BMP inhibitor during the initial stages of ES cell differentiation significantly promotes the differentiation of primitive pluripotent cells towards the cardiomyocytic lineage, apparently at the expense of other mesodermal lineages. These results demonstrate the potential of small molecule modulators of developmental pathways, such as dorsomorphin, as versatile pharmacological tools for stem cell research and regenerative medicine.

title: Cineradiography of Monkey Lip-Smacking Reveals Putative Precursors of Speech Dynamics
text: A distinctive feature of speech is its characteristic 5 Hz rhythm, which has been the subject of much theoretical speculation. One hypothesis posits that this rhythm evolved through the modification of rhythmic facial movements in ancestral primates. To test this idea, we employed cineradiography (X-ray movies) to quantify and characterize the internal dynamics of the macaque monkey vocal tract during lip-smacking (a rhythmic facial expression) and chewing. Previous studies in humans have shown that speech movements are faster than chewing movements, and the functional coordination between vocal tract structures is distinct between the two behaviors. If rhythmic speech evolved from a rhythmic ancestral facial movement, then it is reasonable to expect that monkey lip-smacking versus chewing should also exhibit these differences. Our findings reveal that the lips, tongue, and hyoid move with a speech-like 5 Hz rhythm during lip-smacking, but not during chewing. Moreover, the functional coordination between these structures was found to be distinct for each behavior, providing empirical support for the hypothesis that the human speech rhythm evolved from the rhythmic facial expressions of ancestral primates.

title: Interneuronal DISC1 regulates NRG1-ErbB4 signalling and excitatory-inhibitory synapse formation in the mature cortex.
text: Neuregulin-1 (NRG1) and its receptor ErbB4 play a significant role in various aspects of neurodevelopment, but the underlying mechanisms in the mature brain are not well understood. DISC1, a multifunctional scaffold protein, mediates multiple cellular processes. In this study, we uncover a functional relationship between DISC1 and NRG1-ErbB4 signaling in mature cortical interneurons. By using cell type-specific gene modification in vitro and in vivo, including in a mutant DISC1 mouse model, we demonstrate that DISC1 inhibits NRG1-induced ErbB4 activation and signaling. This effect is likely mediated by competitive inhibition of ErbB4 binding to PSD95. Furthermore, we show that interneuronal DISC1 influences NRG1-ErbB4-mediated phenotypes in the fast spiking interneuron-pyramidal neuron circuit. Post-mortem brain analyses and some genetic studies have suggested that interneuronal deficits and the involvement of the DISC1, NRG1, and ErbB4 genes may contribute to schizophrenia. Our findings suggest a mechanism by which cross-talk between DISC1 and NRG1-ErbB4 signaling may contribute to these deficits.

title: The Proto-Oncogene c-maf Is Responsible for Tissue-Specific Expression of Interleukin-4
text: The molecular mechanism underlying the unique cytokine expression of CD4+ T helper 1 (Th1) and Th2 subsets remains unclear. In this study, we discovered that the proto-oncogene c-maf, a basic region/leucine zipper transcription factor, regulates tissue-specific expression of interleukin-4 (IL-4). c-Maf is specifically expressed in Th2 cells but not Th1 clones and is induced during normal precursor cell differentiation along a Th2 lineage. We found that c-Maf binds to a c-Maf response element (MARE) in the proximal IL-4 promoter, adjacent to a site footprinted by extracts from Th2 cells but not Th1 clones. Ectopic expression of c-Maf in Th1 cells, B cells, and nonlymphoid cells can transactivate the IL-4 promoter, a function that maps to the MARE and Th2-specific footprint. Additionally, c-Maf works in conjunction with the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NF-ATp) to initiate endogenous IL-4 production by B cells. Our findings suggest that manipulating c-Maf may be a potential strategy for altering Th subset ratios in human disease.

title: hClock gene expression in human colorectal carcinoma.
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate changes in the expression of the human Clock (hClock) gene, a key component of the circadian gene family, in colorectal carcinomas (CRCs) and to explore the potential implications of these changes. Previous research has shown that disruptions to the body's circadian rhythms can contribute to the development of CRCs. However, the molecular alterations to the circadian genes involved in CRCs have not been well characterized. Using immunofluorescence and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis, we examined the expression of the hCLOCK protein and gene in 30 cases of CRC. Our findings showed that the hCLOCK protein was expressed in all patient samples, with higher levels of expression observed in CRC tissues compared to non-cancerous tissues. Specifically, the highest levels of hCLOCK expression were found in poorly differentiated or late-stage Dukes' grade tumors and in 64.3% of tumors with lymph node metastasis. We also observed a significant positive correlation between hClock gene expression and protein expression in CRCs, as well as with other genes involved in circadian regulation, such as ARNT, HIF-1α, and VEGF. Conversely, there was no significant correlation between hClock expression and genes involved in apoptosis, such as Bak, Bax, and Bid. Our results suggest that the circadian gene hClock is stably expressed in human colorectal mucosa and plays a role in regulating the expression of downstream clock-controlled genes. Furthermore, we propose that hCLOCK may interact with HIF-1α/ARNT and activate VEGF to promote tumor angiogenesis and metastasis.

title: The Antiretroviral Therapy in Lower Income Countries (ART-LINC) Collaboration and ART Cohort Collaboration (ART-CC) groups Summary
text:
Background:
Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) is being scaled up in developing countries, yet there are concerns about the outcomes of HIV-infected patients starting treatment in low-income settings compared to high-income countries. This study aimed to compare the baseline characteristics and outcomes of patients starting HAART in low-income and high-income settings.
Methods:
The study included 4810 treatment-naïve adult patients starting HAART in 18 programs in Africa, Asia, and South America (low-income settings) and 22,217 patients in 12 HIV cohort studies from Europe and North America (high-income settings). All patients from high-income settings and 2725 patients from low-income settings were actively followed-up and included in survival analyses.
Findings:
Compared to high-income countries, patients starting HAART in low-income settings had lower CD4 cell counts, were more likely to be female, and more likely to start treatment with a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). However, at 6 months, the median number of CD4 cells gained and the percentage of patients reaching HIV-1 RNA levels lower than 500 copies/mL were similar in both settings. Mortality was higher in low-income settings (124 deaths during 2236 person-years of follow-up) than in high-income settings (414 deaths during 20,532 person-years). The adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of mortality comparing low-income with high-income settings fell from 4.3 (95% CI 1.6-11.8) during the first month to 1.5 (0.7-3.0) during months 7-12. The provision of treatment free of charge in low-income settings was associated with lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.23; 95% CI 0.08-0.61).
Interpretation:
Patients starting HAART in resource-poor settings have increased mortality rates in the first months on therapy compared to those in developed countries. Timely diagnosis and assessment of treatment eligibility, coupled with free provision of HAART, might reduce this excess mortality.

title: A family of phosphoinositide 3-kinases in Drosophila identifies a new mediator of signal transduction
text:
Introduction:
Mammalian phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) play crucial roles in receptor-mediated signal transduction and have been implicated in various cellular processes, including transformation and mitogenesis, by elevating cellular phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate levels. In contrast, yeast PI3Ks have been shown to be essential for protein trafficking.
Results:
We have identified a family of three distinct PI3Ks in Drosophila using a PCR-based approach that targets the conserved catalytic domain of PI3Ks. One of these family members, PI3K_92D, is closely related to the prototypical PI3K p110α, while PI3K_59F is homologous to Vps34p. The third member, PI3K_68D, is a novel PI3K that is ubiquitously expressed throughout the Drosophila life cycle and encodes a protein of 210 kDa lacking sequences involved in linking p110 PI3Ks to p85 adaptor proteins. The PI3K_68D cDNA contains an amino-terminal proline-rich sequence and a carboxy-terminal C2 domain, which could interact with SH3 domains. In vitro biochemical assays revealed that PI3K_68D has a novel substrate specificity, preferring phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate, and is unable to phosphorylate phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate, the putative in vivo substrate for p110.
Discussion:
Our findings describe a family of PI3Ks in Drosophila, including a novel class represented by PI3K_68D. PI3K_68D lacks p85-adaptor-binding sequences and has a Ca(2+)-independent phospholipid-binding domain, suggesting that it could define a novel signal transduction pathway. The potential to bind to signalling molecules containing SH3 domains and the restricted in vitro substrate specificity of PI3K_68D suggest that it may play a distinct role in Drosophila signal transduction.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study identifies a novel PI3K in Drosophila, PI3K_68D, which has the potential to define a novel signal transduction pathway. Further investigations into the molecular mechanisms of PI3K_68D may provide insights into the regulation of signal transduction in Drosophila and other organisms.

title: Mammalian RAD52 Functions in Break-Induced Replication Repair of Collapsed DNA Replication Forks
text: Human cancers are characterized by the presence of oncogene-induced DNA replication stress (DRS), which renders them dependent on repair pathways such as break-induced replication (BIR) for the repair of damaged DNA replication forks. To elucidate the mechanisms underlying BIR, we conducted a targeted siRNA screen for genes whose depletion impedes G1 to S phase progression upon oncogenic cyclin E overexpression. Among the top hits was RAD52, a gene that is non-essential in mice. In cells where DNA replication forks were intentionally collapsed by oncogenes or chemicals, the Rad52 protein was observed to localize to DRS foci. Depletion of Rad52 by siRNA or genetic knockout of the gene resulted in impaired restart of collapsed forks and accumulation of DNA damage in cells experiencing DRS. Moreover, in cancer-prone, heterozygous APC mutant mice, homozygous deletion of the Rad52 gene was found to suppress tumor growth and prolong lifespan. These findings suggest that mammalian RAD52 plays a crucial role in repairing collapsed DNA replication forks in cancer cells.

title: Neural crest cell lineage segregation in the mouse neural tube.
text: Neural crest (NC) cells originate in the dorsal neural tube (NT) and migrate throughout the embryo to develop into various cell types. A significant unresolved question is when and how the fate of NC cells is determined. There is extensive evidence for multipotent NC cells, whose fate is decided during or after migration. Some evidence suggests that the NC is already divided into subpopulations of distinct precursors within the NT. To investigate this, we examined the mouse embryo. We found that a specific subpopulation of cells on the most dorsomedial aspect of the NT expresses the receptor tyrosine kinase Kit (previously known as c-kit), emigrates exclusively into the developing dermis, and then expresses definitive markers of the melanocyte lineage, thereby identifying themselves as melanocyte progenitor cells. These cells are generated predominantly at the midbrain-hindbrain junction and cervical trunk, with significant numbers also found in the lower trunk. In contrast, other cells within the dorsal NT that are Kit-, migrate ventrally, and from embryonic day 9.5, express the neurotrophin receptor p75. These cells are likely to give rise to ventral NC derivatives, such as neurons and glia. The p75+ cells are located ventrolateral to the Kit+ cells in areas of the NT where these two cell types are found. These findings provide direct in vivo evidence for NC lineage segregation within the mouse neural tube.

title: How absolute is zero? An evaluation of historical and current definitions of malaria elimination
text: The complexity of decisions to eliminate malaria from a country is compounded by ambiguity surrounding key terminology, particularly "control" and "elimination." Accurate forecasting of resource and operational requirements is impossible without clear definitions of these terms. Despite the Global Malaria Eradication Program's debate over the precise definition of "eradication," similar deliberations regarding the meanings of "elimination" and "control" are largely absent today, hindering programme planning. To advance the contemporary debate, this paper presents a historical review of commonly used terms, including control, elimination, and eradication, and analyzes their underlying mathematical concepts through simple branching process models. The importance of pragmatic definitions is emphasized, and it is argued that current conceptions of elimination fail to provide practical strategic milestones. New conceptual definitions are suggested to more precisely describe the old goals of "control" (now called "controlled low-endemic malaria") and "elimination," and a third state, "controlled non-endemic malaria," is proposed to describe the epidemiological condition in which endemic transmission has been interrupted but malaria resulting from onward transmission continues to occur at a sufficiently high level. Finally, guidelines are discussed for deriving operational definitions and metrics that will make these concepts relevant, measurable, and achievable for a particular environment.

title: Fission Yeast Scm3: A CENP-A Receptor Required for Integrity of Subkinetochore Chromatin
text:
The mechanisms by which CENP-A is specifically incorporated into centromeres are not well understood. However, research has shown that proteins such as Mis16 and Mis18 play a crucial role in the localization of CENP-A at centromeres. These proteins form a conserved complex from fission yeast to human, and are essential for the proper localization of CENP-A at centromeres.
In fission yeast, the protein Sim1 is involved in the localization of Scm3 (orthologous to budding yeast Scm3) to centromeres. Scm3 is required for the proper localization of CENP-A at centromeres, and it is thought to act as a receptor or assembly factor for CENP-A. This process is mediated by the interaction between Scm3 and Mis16/18, which are responsible for receiving CENP-A from an escort protein called Sim3. Once received, CENP-A is assembled into subkinetochore chromatin through the cooperation of Mis16/18 and Scm3.
While Scm3 has been proposed to form a unique hexameric nucleosome with CENP-A and histone H4 at budding yeast point centromeres, our current understanding suggests that Scm3 acts as a CENP-A receptor/assembly factor, working in conjunction with Mis16 and Mis18 to facilitate the incorporation of CENP-A into centromeres.

title: The Molecular Basis for Oat Intolerance in Patients with Celiac Disease
text:
Background:
Celiac disease is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the small intestine that affects the body's ability to absorb nutrients from food. It is caused by an inappropriate immune response to dietary gluten, and is treated by following a strict gluten-free diet. Recent studies have shown that oats are safe for celiac disease patients, and they are now often included in the diet. However, there is limited understanding of whether oat intolerance exists in celiac disease and the underlying mechanisms.
Methods and Findings:
We selected nine adults with celiac disease who had a history of oats exposure and studied their response to oats. Four of the patients experienced clinical symptoms on an oats-containing diet, and three of these patients had intestinal inflammation typical of celiac disease at the time of oats exposure. We established T-cell lines from these patients and compared them to T-cell lines from patients who appeared to tolerate oats. We found that the T-cell lines from the patients who experienced symptoms recognized avenin peptides, which are similar to wheat gluten epitopes, and this recognition was mediated by tissue transglutaminase-mediated deamidation.
Conclusions:
Our study suggests that some celiac disease patients may have avenin-reactive mucosal T-cells that can cause mucosal inflammation, even if they are eating a strict gluten-free diet that includes oats. This may be a reason for villous atrophy and inflammation in patients with celiac disease who are eating oats. Further clinical follow-up of celiac disease patients eating oats is advisable to better understand the relationship between oat intolerance and celiac disease.

title: A comparison of continuous and bi-level positive airway pressure non-invasive ventilation in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: a meta-analysis
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the comparative effectiveness of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP) noninvasive ventilation in patients with cardiogenic pulmonary edema. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to determine if there were any significant differences in clinical outcomes between the two treatment modalities.
Our search strategy yielded seven RCTs that included a total of 290 patients with cardiogenic pulmonary edema. We found that the hospital mortality and risk of requiring invasive ventilation were not significantly different between patients treated with CPAP and those treated with BiPAP. Additionally, the duration of noninvasive ventilation required until pulmonary edema resolved and length of hospital stay were also not significantly different between the two groups. However, there was a trend towards an increase in new onset acute myocardial infarction in patients treated with BiPAP.
Our findings suggest that BiPAP does not offer any significant clinical benefits over CPAP in patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Given the limited data available, the choice of modality will depend mainly on the equipment available until further research provides conclusive evidence of the superiority of one modality over the other.

title: CaMKII induces permeability transition through Drp1 phosphorylation during chronic β-AR stimulation
text:
Chronic stimulation of β-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs) can lead to dysfunction in the heart through a mechanism involving the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). The exact mechanism by which this occurs is not fully understood, but our study shows that chronic administration of isoproterenol (ISO) leads to a persistent increase in mPTP openings, resulting in mitochondrial damage and cardiac dysfunction.
We found that this effect is mediated by the phosphorylation of the mitochondrial fission protein, dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) at a specific serine site (S616). Inhibiting this phosphorylation site or Drp1 activity blocked the mPTP opening and myocyte death in vitro and rescued heart hypertrophy in vivo. Interestingly, we also found that in human failing hearts, Drp1 phosphorylation at the same serine site (S616) is increased, providing further evidence for the role of this pathway in heart dysfunction.
Overall, our findings uncover a novel pathway downstream of chronic β-AR stimulation that links cytosolic stress signals to mitochondrial dysfunction in the heart, providing new insights into the mechanisms underlying cardiac dysfunction in various diseases.

title: MicroRNA Response of Primary Human Macrophages to Arcobacter Butzleri Infection
text: The role of microRNAs (miRNAs) in infectious diseases is becoming increasingly evident, and their use as a diagnostic tool and therapeutic application are the primary areas of focus in ongoing research. In this study, we aimed to identify miRNAs involved in the immune signaling of macrophages in response to Arcobacter (A.) butzleri infection, an emerging foodborne pathogen that causes gastroenteritis. To achieve this, we isolated primary human macrophages and analyzed miRNA expression through RNA sequencing. Our findings revealed the expression of several miRNAs previously associated with bacterial infections, including miR-155, miR-125, and miR-212, which play a crucial role in fine-tuning the immune response through Toll-like receptor signaling. Additionally, we identified novel miRNAs, such as miR-3613, miR-2116, miR-671, miR-30d, and miR-629, that were differentially regulated in A. butzleri-infected cells. These miRNAs target pathways involved in processes such as apoptosis and endocytosis, which may be relevant to A. butzleri pathogenesis. Our study contributes new insights into the interaction between A. butzleri and human innate immune cells, shedding light on the underlying regulatory mechanisms in macrophages during infection.

title: The circadian factor Period 2 modulates p53 stability and transcriptional activity in unstressed cells
text:
Human Period 2 (hPer2) is a transcriptional regulator at the core of the circadian clock mechanism, playing a crucial role in generating the negative feedback loop that sustains the clock. Its significance in human disease is underscored by alterations in its function, which can impact a wide range of biochemical and physiological processes. When hPer2 is absent, it can lead to the development of various cancers and increase the cell's susceptibility to genotoxic stress. Therefore, we sought to identify a previously uncharacterized checkpoint node in which circadian components integrate environmental stress signals with the DNA-damage response.
Our findings reveal that hPer2 interacts with the C-terminal half of human p53 (hp53) and forms a stable trimeric complex with hp53's negative regulator, Mdm2. We discovered that hPer2 binding to hp53 prevents Mdm2 from being ubiquitinated and targeted for degradation by the proteasome. Decreased hPer2 expression directly affects hp53 levels, while its overexpression influences both hp53 protein stability and the transcription of target genes. Our findings position hPer2 at the center of the hp53-mediated response, ensuring that basal levels of hp53 are maintained to facilitate a rapid, hp53-mediated transcriptional response when needed.

title: Properties of Commelina yellow mottle virus's complete DNA sequence, genomic discontinuities and transcript suggest that it is a pararetrovirus.
text:
The second group of plant viruses known to possess a genome composed of circular double-stranded DNA are the non-enveloped bacilliform viruses. In this study, we have characterized the viral transcript and determined the complete sequence of the genome of Commelina mellow mottle virus (CoYMV), a member of this group.
Our analysis of the viral transcript revealed that CoYMV encodes a single terminally-redundant genome-length plus 120 nucleotide transcript, with a fraction of the transcripts being polyadenylated, although the majority of the transcript is not polyadenylated. Furthermore, our analysis of the genome sequence revealed that the genome is 7489 base pairs in size, and that the transcribed strand contains three open reading frames capable of encoding proteins of 23, 15, and 216 kDa. The function of the 25 and 15 kDa proteins is currently unknown. Interestingly, the 216 kDa polypeptide shares similarities with the coat protein and protease/reverse transcriptase polyprotein of the cauliflower mosaic virus, suggesting that the 216 kDa polypeptide is a polyprotein that is proteolytically processed to yield the virion coat protein, a protease, and replicase (reverse transcriptase and ribonuclease H).
Notably, each strand of the CoYMV genome is interrupted by site-specific discontinuities, and the locations of these discontinuities, as well as the presence of a region on the CoYMV transcript capable of annealing with the 3'-end of cytosolic initiator methionine tRNA, are consistent with replication by reverse transcription. To test this hypothesis, we constructed a construct containing 1.3 CoYMV genomes and introduced it into Commelina diffusa, the host plant for CoYMV, using Agrobacterium-mediated infection. Our results demonstrate that this construct is infective, providing further evidence for the role of reverse transcription in the replication of non-enveloped bacilliform viruses like CoYMV.

title: The Glucocorticoid Receptor Inhibits
text: Glucocorticoids suppress the activation of pro-inflammatory genes, such as interleukin-8 (IL-8) and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), by inhibiting the activity of the transcription factor NFκB. Our experiments suggest that the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) achieves this by interacting with NFκB through protein-protein interactions, specifically the Zinc binding region (ZBR) of the GR, which includes the DNA binding and dimerization functions of the receptor. We found that the ZBR binds directly to the dimerization domain of the RelA subunit of NFκB in vitro and that the ZBR is sufficient to associate with RelA bound at NFκB response elements in vivo. Additionally, we showed that GR does not disrupt DNA binding by NFκB, and that the GR ligand binding domain is essential for repression of NFκB but not for association with it. To investigate the mechanism by which GR represses NFκB-activated transcription, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation assays in untransfected A549 cells and found that the inflammatory signal TNFα stimulates the assembly of preinitiation complexes (PICs) at the IL-8 and ICAM-1 promoters, and that the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II (pol II) in these complexes becomes phosphorylated at serines 2 and 5 in its carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) heptapeptide repeats (YSPTSPS). Remarkably, GR interferes with phosphorylation of serine 2 of the pol II CTD, but does not inhibit PIC assembly under repressing conditions.

title: Regulation of myeloid cell function through the CD200 receptor.
text: Myeloid cells play a crucial role in chronic inflammatory diseases due to their ability to produce pro-inflammatory, destructive, and remodeling factors. CD200 is expressed on various cell types, while the recently discovered CD200R is found on myeloid cells and T cells. Deletion of CD200 in vivo leads to myeloid cell dysregulation and increased susceptibility to autoimmune inflammation, suggesting that the CD200-CD200R interaction is involved in immune suppression. In this study, we demonstrate that CD200R agonists suppress myeloid cell function in vitro in both mice and humans, and define a dose-response relationship between receptor expression and cellular inhibition. We also show that CD200R agonists inhibit cytokine secretion from mouse peritoneal macrophages stimulated with IFN-gamma and IL-17, but not with LPS. Inhibition of cytokine production correlates with CD200R expression levels, and is only observed in low CD200R expressing cells when the CD200R agonists are further cross-linked. Additionally, we find that CD200R agonists inhibit IL-5 and IL-13 secretion from human PBMCs, with inhibition occurring only when the CD200R is cross-linked on monocytes and not on CD4+ T cells. Overall, our findings provide direct evidence that the CD200-CD200R interaction regulates monocyte/macrophage function in both murine and human systems, supporting the potential clinical application of CD200R agonists for the treatment of chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Management of hepatitis C disease among VA patients with schizophrenia and substance use disorders.
text:
Objective: To compare the rates of hepatitis C (HCV) infection, testing, and treatment among patients with schizophrenia, a substance use disorder, or co-occurring schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and a substance use disorder, and a control group.
Methods: Data from 293,445 patients of the Northwest Veterans Healthcare Administration were analyzed.
Results: The study found that the substance use disorder group comprised 13.6% of the sample, while the schizophrenia group constituted 1.6% and the co-occurring disorders group constituted 1.4%. The results showed that these groups were approximately four, two, and six times more likely than the control group to receive HCV testing, and about seven, two, and eight times more likely to be infected with HCV. However, the rate of interferon (IFN) therapy was significantly lower for the substance use group and the group with co-occurring disorders, but the magnitude of the differences was not substantial, suggesting that these high-risk groups were not excluded from IFN therapy.

title: Equity in adherence to antiretroviral therapy among economically vulnerable adolescents living with HIV in Uganda
text: According to studies conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, children who are vulnerable due to poverty are disproportionately affected by HIV, with many contracting the virus through mother-to-child transmission. For adolescents living with HIV, adherence to life-saving treatment regimens can be impacted by the complex set of economic and social circumstances that affect their families and exacerbate health problems. Using data from the National Institute of Child and Human Development (NICHD) funded Suubi+Adherence study, we examined the relationship between individual and composite measures of equity and self-reported adherence among Ugandan adolescents aged 10-16 living with HIV (n = 702). Our findings showed that greater asset ownership, specifically the possession of seven or more tangible assets by the family, was associated with higher odds of self-reported adherence (OR 1.69, 95% CI: 1.00-2.85). Additionally, we found that distance to the nearest health clinic impacted adherence, with youth living closest to a clinic being more likely to report optimal adherence (OR 1.49, 95% CI: 0.92-2.40). Furthermore, we found that adolescents with greater economic advantage in household assets, financial savings, and caregiver employment had higher odds of adherence by a factor of 1.70 (95% CI: 1.07-2.70). These findings suggest that addressing economic and social inequities through interventions may be beneficial to increase antiretroviral therapy (ART) uptake among economically vulnerable youth, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. This study is one of the first to investigate the relationship between equity and adherence to ART among economically vulnerable youth with HIV.

title: High-Resolution Phenotypic Profiling Defines Genes Essential for Mycobacterial Growth and Cholesterol Catabolism
text: The intricate networks of cellular metabolism are highly interconnected, and alterations in individual enzymes can have far-reaching consequences. As a result, global gene expression profiling methods have limited value in predicting how the loss of a single function will affect the cell. In this study, we employed a novel approach to global phenotypic profiling to directly identify the genes required for the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. By combining high-density mutagenesis and deep-sequencing, we characterized the composition of complex mutant libraries exposed to different conditions, allowing us to unambiguously identify the genes essential for Mtb growth in vitro. This approach proved to be a significant improvement over previous methods. To further explore functions necessary for persistence in the host, we investigated the pathways involved in the utilization of cholesterol, a critical carbon source during infection. Our findings revealed that few of the genes we identified had been implicated in this adaptation through transcriptional profiling, and only a fraction were encoded in the chromosomal region known to encode sterol catabolic functions. Surprisingly, these genes comprise a large percentage of those previously shown to be required for bacterial growth in mouse tissue, highlighting the significance of this single nutritional change in the adaptation to the host. This work provides the most comprehensive genetic characterization of a sterol catabolic pathway to date, suggests putative roles for uncharacterized virulence genes, and precisely maps genes encoding potential drug targets.

title: Tyrosine phosphorylation regulates the endocytosis and surface expression of GluN3A-containing NMDA receptors.
text: Selective control of receptor trafficking allows for the remodeling of excitatory synapse receptor composition, supporting synaptic transmission, plasticity, and development. GluN3A (formerly NR3A), a non-conventional NMDA receptor subunit, has unique properties that limit the plasticity and maturation of excitatory synapses, making its removal a critical step in neuronal circuit development. However, the molecular signals involved in GluN3A endocytic removal are unclear. Here, we identify a novel endocytic motif (YWL) within the cytoplasmic C-terminal tail of GluN3A that mediates its binding to the clathrin adaptor AP2. We found that alanine mutations within the GluN3A endocytic motif inhibited clathrin-dependent internalization and led to increased cell-surface expression of GluN3A-containing NMDARs, while mimicking phosphorylation of the tyrosine residue promoted internalization and reduced cell-surface expression. We also demonstrate that the tyrosine residue is phosphorylated by Src family kinases, which in turn limits surface GluN3A expression in neurons. Our results provide a new molecular signal for GluN3A internalization and reveal a mechanism by which the functional surface expression of GluN3A-containing receptors is coupled to the phosphorylation state of GluN3A subunits. These findings have implications for synaptic plasticity and neurodevelopment.

title: Myeloid-specific Krüppel-like factor 2 inactivation increases macrophage and neutrophil adhesion and promotes atherosclerosis.
text:
RATIONALE: Previous studies have shown that hemizygous deficiency of the transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) can augment atherosclerosis in hypercholesterolemic mice. However, the specific cell type responsible for the increased atherosclerosis due to KLF2 deficiency has not been identified. This study aimed to investigate the consequence of myeloid cell-specific KLF2 inactivation in atherosclerosis.
METHODS AND RESULTS: To achieve cell-specific knockout of KLF2, Cre/loxP recombination was used to generate myeloid-specific KLF2 knockout (myeKlf2(-/-)) mice. Macrophages isolated from myeKlf2(-/-) mice were found to be similar to myeKlf2(+/+) macrophages in terms of response to activation, polarization, and lipid accumulation. However, myeKlf2(-/-) macrophages adhered more strongly to endothelial cells compared to myeKlf2(+/+) macrophages. Additionally, neutrophils from myeKlf2(-/-) mice adhered more strongly to endothelial cells, and fewer myeKlf2(-/-) neutrophils survived in culture over a 24-hour period compared to myeKlf2(+/+) neutrophils. When myeKlf2(-/-) mice were bred with Ldlr(-/-) mice and fed a high-fat and high-cholesterol diet, significant increases in atherosclerosis were observed in the myeKlf2(-/-)Ldlr(-/-) mice compared to myeKlf2(+/+)Ldlr(-/-) littermates. The increased atherosclerosis in myeKlf2(-/-)Ldlr(-/-) mice was associated with elevated presence of neutrophils and macrophages, as well as corresponding increases in myeloperoxidase, chlorinated, and nitrosylated tyrosine epitopes in their lesion areas compared to myeKlf2(+/+)Ldlr(-/-) mice.
CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates a role for myeloid KLF2 expression in modulating atherosclerosis. The increased neutrophil accumulation and atherosclerosis progression in myeloid-specific KLF2-deficient mice underscore the importance of neutrophils in promoting vascular oxidative stress and atherosclerosis. These findings suggest that elevating KLF2 expression may be a novel strategy for prevention and treatment of atherosclerosis.

title: Epidemiology of Staphylococcus aureus blood and skin and soft tissue infections in the US military health system, 2005-2010.
text:
Background:
The incidence rates of hospital-onset methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections have been reported to be decreasing, but there is limited information on the rates of community-onset S. aureus infections. This study aimed to characterize the overall and annual incidence rates of community-onset and hospital-onset S. aureus bacteremia and skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) in a national healthcare system and to evaluate trends in the incidence rates of S. aureus bacteremia and SSTIs, as well as the proportion due to MRSA.
Methods:
This was an observational study of all Department of Defense TRICARE beneficiaries from January 2005 through December 2010. Medical record databases were used to identify and classify all annual first-positive S. aureus blood and wound or abscess cultures as methicillin-susceptible S. aureus or MRSA, and as community-onset or hospital-onset infections (isolates collected >3 days after hospital admission). The unadjusted incidence rates per 100,000 person-years of observation, the proportion of infections that was due to MRSA, and annual trends for 2005 through 2010 were examined using the Spearman rank correlation test or the Mantel-Haenszel χ2 test for linear trend.
Results:
During 56 million person-years (nonactive duty: 47 million person-years; active duty: 9 million person-years), there were 2643 blood and 80,281 wound or abscess annual first-positive S. aureus cultures. The annual incidence rates varied from 3.6 to 6.0 per 100,000 person-years for S. aureus bacteremia and 122.7 to 168.9 per 100,000 person-years for S. aureus SSTIs. The annual incidence rates for community-onset MRSA bacteremia decreased from 1.7 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 1.5-2.0 per 100,000 person-years) in 2005 to 1.2 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 0.9-1.4 per 100,000 person-years) in 2010 (P = .005 for trend). The annual incidence rates for hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia also decreased from 0.7 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 0.6-0.9 per 100,000 person-years) in 2005 to 0.4 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 0.3-0.5 per 100,000 person-years) in 2010 (P = .005 for trend). Concurrently, the proportion of community-onset SSTIs due to MRSA peaked at 62% in 2006 before decreasing annually to 52% in 2010 (P < .001 for trend).

Conclusion:
In the Department of Defense population consisting of men and women of all ages from across the United States, the rates of both community-onset and hospital-onset MRSA bacteremia decreased in parallel, while the proportion of community-onset SSTIs due to MRSA has more recently declined. These findings suggest that the decreasing trend in MRSA bacteremia and SSTIs observed in this study may be due to a combination of factors, including improved infection control practices and changes in population demographics. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to identify the most effective strategies for preventing and controlling MRSA infections in different populations.

title: Potentiation of NMDA currents by pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide in neonatal rat sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
text: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were conducted on sympathetic preganglionic neurons (SPNs) in the intermediolateral cell column of thoracolumbar spinal cord slices from 12- to 16-day-old rats. The effects of pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide (PACAP)-38 on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)- and kainate (KA)-induced inward currents were investigated. PACAP, in concentrations (10-30 nM) that did not significantly affect holding currents, reversibly increased NMDA-induced currents but not KA-induced currents. At higher concentrations (>30 nM), the peptide produced a sustained inward current. The potentiating effect of PACAP was blocked by prior incubation of the slices with the adenylate cyclase inhibitor MDL-12,330A (25 μM). Additionally, superfusing the slices with the membrane-permeable cyclic AMP analogue N6,2'-O-dibutyryladenosine 3':5'-cyclic monophosphate (100-300 μM) in the presence of the phosphodiesterase inhibitor 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (700 μM) increased the NMDA currents. These findings suggest that PACAP selectively enhances NMDA receptor-mediated responses in rat SPNs, likely through a cyclic AMP-dependent mechanism, providing evidence that the peptide may be involved in synaptic plasticity.

title: Aberrant Expression of RCAN1 in Alzheimer’s Pathogenesis: A New Molecular Mechanism and a Novel Drug Target
text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD), a devastating neurodegenerative disorder, is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly. Characterized by three hallmarks of neuropathology - neuritic plaque deposition, neurofibrillary tangle formation, and neuronal loss - AD is a complex and multifactorial disorder. Recent evidence suggests that dysregulation of regulator of calcineurin 1 (RCAN1) plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of AD. RCAN1 dysregulation leads to neuronal apoptosis and Tau hyperphosphorylation, contributing to neuronal loss and neurofibrillary tangle formation. This review aims to provide an overview of the recent advances in the regulation of RCAN1 expression and its physiological functions, as well as the role of AD risk factors in inducing RCAN1 dysregulation. Furthermore, we summarize the effects of RCAN1 dysregulation on APP processing, Aβ generation, and neuritic plaque formation, and discuss the potential of targeting RCAN1 as a new therapeutic approach.
Keywords: Alzheimer's disease, regulator of calcineurin 1, RCAN1, neuronal loss, neurofibrillary tangle formation, APP processing, Aβ generation, neuritic plaque formation, therapeutic approach.

title: Congruent Visual Speech Enhances Cortical Entrainment to Continuous Auditory Speech in Noise-Free Conditions.
text:
The impact of audiovisual speech on our ability to comprehend a speaker is a topic of significant interest in the field of cognitive neuroscience. Previous research has shown that the presentation of congruent auditory and visual information can enhance our ability to understand speech, even in noise-free conditions. However, incongruent auditory and visual information can hinder our perception and lead to the perception of false information. While efforts to investigate the neural basis of these effects have primarily focused on the case of discrete audiovisual syllables, recent studies have demonstrated that cortical response measures to continuous auditory speech can be obtained using multivariate analysis methods.
In this study, we aim to investigate the effects of temporal and contextual congruency on the cortical encoding of the speech envelope in humans using electroencephalography (EEG). Specifically, we examine how the presentation of congruent audiovisual speech affects the cortical representation of the speech envelope in noise-free conditions. Our results show that the cortical representation of the speech envelope is enhanced when the auditory and visual streams are temporally and contextually congruent. This enhancement is most pronounced at the temporal scale corresponding to syllabic rate (2-6 Hz). Furthermore, our data suggest that neural entrainment to the speech envelope is inhibited when the auditory and visual streams are incongruent both temporally and contextually.
Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying multisensory integration in the context of continuous speech. They demonstrate that the temporal and contextual congruency of audiovisual speech plays a crucial role in the cortical encoding of speech, and that this effect is most pronounced at the temporal scale corresponding to syllabic rate. These findings have important implications for the development of new methods for investigating the neural basis of multisensory integration in the context of continuous speech.

title: Telomere tethering at the nuclear periphery is essential for efficient DNA double strand break repair in subtelomeric region
text: In the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which lacks lamins, the nuclear pore complex (NPC) has been proposed to play a role in chromatin organization. Using fluorescence microscopy on living cells, we have found that nuclear pore proteins within the Nup84 core complex, including Nup84p, Nup145Cp, Nup120p, and Nup133p, act as anchors to position telomere XI-L at the nuclear periphery. The integrity of this complex is essential for repressing the expression of a URA3 gene located in the subtelomeric region of a chromosome end. Moreover, altering the integrity of this complex reduces the efficiency of repairing a DNA double-strand break (DSB) only when it occurs in the subtelomeric region, even though the repair machinery is functional. These findings confirm and expand the role of the NPC, through the Nup84 complex, in organizing chromatin function. They also demonstrate that anchoring telomeres is crucial for efficient repair of DSBs occurring in these regions and is essential for maintaining genome integrity.

title: p63 Regulates adult neural precursor and newly born neuron survival to control hippocampal-dependent Behavior.
text: The molecular mechanisms governing the survival of adult neural precursor cells (NPCs) and their role in maintaining adult neurogenesis are not well understood. To investigate the function of p63, a member of the p53 family, in adult NPCs, we conducted experiments in mice. We found that conditional ablation of p63 in adult NPCs or p63 haploinsufficiency led to a decrease in the number of NPCs and newborn neurons in the neurogenic zones of the hippocampus, lateral ventricles, and olfactory bulb. These reductions were attributed to increased apoptosis of NPCs and newborn neurons, which were rescued by inhibiting caspase activity, p53, or the p53 apoptotic effector PUMA (p53-upregulated modulator of apoptosis). Moreover, these cellular deficits had functional consequences, leading to impairments in hippocampus-dependent memory formation. These findings suggest that p63 regulates the number of adult NPCs and adult-born neurons, as well as neural stem cell-dependent cognitive functions, and that it does so, at least in part, by inhibiting p53-dependent cell death.

title: Tyrosine-Phosphorylated Caveolin-1 Blocks Bacterial Uptake by Inducing Vav2-RhoA-Mediated Cytoskeletal Rearrangements
text: Certain bacterial adhesins may promote a pathogen's extracellular lifestyle rather than entry into host cells, but little is known about the stimuli that occur during these interactions. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms by which type IV pili (Tfp)-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae (P(+)GC) interact with host cells and prevent bacterial internalization. We find that P(+)GC induces an immediate recruitment of caveolin-1 (Cav1) in host cells, which triggers cytoskeletal rearrangements via downstream phosphotyrosine signaling. Through a broad and unbiased analysis of potential interaction partners for tyrosine-phosphorylated Cav1, we identify a direct interaction between Cav1 and the Rho-family guanine nucleotide exchange factor Vav2. Both Vav2 and its substrate, the small GTPase RhoA, play a direct role in the Cav1-mediated prevention of bacterial uptake. Our findings demonstrate how Tfp-producing bacteria avoid host cell uptake and provide insight into the mechanisms of caveolin function. Additionally, our data have been extended to enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, highlighting the generality of these mechanisms.

title: Effects of GC Bias in Next-Generation-Sequencing Data on De Novo Genome Assembly
text:
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) has revolutionized genome assembly due to its significantly higher data throughput and lower cost compared to traditional Sanger sequencing. However, NGS presents new computational challenges for de novo genome assembly, including the impact of GC bias on assembly quality. While GC bias has been known to affect genome assembly, the extent of its impact remains unclear. In this study, we conducted a systematic analysis to investigate the effects of GC bias on genome assembly.
Our results reveal that GC bias can lower assembly completeness only when the degree of bias exceeds a certain threshold. At high levels of GC bias, the assembly fragmentation observed in these regions can be attributed to the low coverage of reads in GC-poor or GC-rich areas of the genome. This effect was observed across all assemblers studied. Increasing the total amount of NGS data can rescue the assembly fragmentation caused by GC bias, but the required amount of data depends on the distribution of GC contents.
Interestingly, both low and high coverage depths due to GC bias also lower the accuracy of assembly. These findings provide valuable insights for improving de novo genome assembly in the presence of GC bias. In summary, our study demonstrates that while NGS has greatly improved genome assembly, it is crucial to consider the impact of GC bias on assembly quality to achieve optimal results.

title: Cancer inhibition through circadian reprogramming of tumor transcriptome with meal timing.
text: Circadian disruption has been shown to accelerate cancer progression, while circadian reinforcement has the potential to halt it. In a study conducted on mice with P03 pancreatic adenocarcinoma (n = 77), the effect of meal timing (MT) on tumor growth was investigated. The mice were synchronized and fed ad libitum (AL) or with meal timing from Zeitgeber time (ZT) 2 to ZT6 with either a normal or high-fat diet. Tumor gene expression profiling was conducted using DNA microarrays at endogenous circadian time (CT) 4 and CT16. The study found that MT inhibited cancer growth by approximately 40% compared to AL (P = 0.011), regardless of calorie intake. However, clock gene transcription remained arrhythmic in tumors, indicating that the circadian clock system is not the primary mechanism underlying the growth inhibition. MT did, however, upregulate or downregulate the expression of 423 tumor genes according to the circadian cycle, with 36 genes involved in cellular stress, cell cycle, and metabolism showing circadian expression patterns. MT also induced >10-fold circadian expression of Hspa8, Cirbp, and Ccna2 in tumors. The study suggests that targeting circadian clocks may represent a novel potential challenge for cancer therapeutics.

title: Role of chicken melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 in induction and activation of innate and adaptive immune responses to infectious bursal disease virus in cultured macrophages
text: The present study aimed to investigate the role of chicken melanoma-differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) in recognizing and responding to infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) infection in chicken macrophages. Our findings showed that IBDV infection in HD11 cells led to a significant increase in IBDV titers and RNA loads, as well as the upregulation of various immune genes, including MDA5, interferon-β (IFN-β), dsRNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR), 2', 5'-oligoadenylate synthetase (OAS), myxovirus resistance gene (Mx), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), IL-6, IL-8, IL-12(p40), IL-18, IL-10, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), and major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC class I). Notably, chMDA5 knockdown led to higher IBDV RNA loads and lower nitric oxide production, as well as reduced expression levels of chicken MDA5, IFN-β, PKR, OAS, Mx, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12(p40), IL-18, IL-10, iNOS, MHC class I, and CD86 at 24 hours post-infection (hpi). Conversely, overexpression of chMDA5 resulted in lower IBDV titers and RNA loads, as well as higher nitric oxide production and expression levels of chicken MDA5, IFN-β, PKR, OAS, Mx, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12(p40), IL-18, IL-10, iNOS, MHC class I, and CD86 at 2 hpi. These findings suggest that chMDA5 plays a crucial role in sensing IBDV infection and initiating an innate immune response that in turn activates the adaptive immune response and limits IBDV replication.

title: Age-Associated Sperm DNA Methylation Alterations: Possible Implications in Offspring Disease Susceptibility
text:
Recent research has revealed a link between paternal aging and the susceptibility of offspring to various diseases. It is well established that certain neuropsychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, as well as trinucleotide expansion associated diseases like myotonic dystrophy and Huntington's disease, and even some forms of cancer, have a higher incidence in the offspring of older fathers. Despite the strong epidemiological evidence supporting this association, the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. However, it is believed that epigenetic changes, particularly DNA methylation alterations, play a role.
In this study, we investigated the impact of aging on DNA methylation in mature human sperm. Using a methylation array approach, we analyzed the sperm DNA methylation patterns of 17 fertile donors at two time points, separated by 9-19 years. We identified 139 regions of significantly hypomethylated DNA and 8 regions of significantly hypermethylated DNA with age. A subset of these alterations was confirmed in an independent cohort. A total of 117 genes are associated with these regions of methylation alterations, including genes previously linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. While our findings do not establish a causal relationship, they suggest that the age-related changes in sperm DNA methylation may contribute to the increased incidence of neuropsychiatric and other disorders in the offspring of older males. Further research is needed to determine whether these methylation changes play a causal role in the development of these diseases.

title: Mutations in the nuclear bile acid receptor FXR cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis
text:
Neonatal cholestasis is a critical condition that requires prompt diagnosis, as it can be life-threatening. While some cases of familial cholestasis have been linked to mutations in specific genes, there are still unexplained cases that remain. In this study, we report on four individuals from two unrelated families who exhibited neonatal cholestasis and mutations in the NR1H4 gene, which encodes the farnesoid X receptor (FXR). FXR is a nuclear hormone receptor that plays a crucial role in regulating bile acid metabolism.
The clinical features of severe, persistent NR1H4-related cholestasis in these individuals included neonatal onset with rapid progression to end-stage liver disease, vitamin K-independent coagulopathy, low-to-normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase activity, elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein, and undetectable liver bile salt export pump (ABCB11) expression. These findings highlight the essential role of FXR in maintaining bile acid homeostasis and liver protection.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that mutations in NR1H4 can lead to severe and persistent neonatal cholestasis, underscoring the importance of this gene in liver function. Further research into the genetic basis of cholestasis may lead to improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for this condition.

title: Phase II study of panobinostat in combination with bevacizumab for recurrent glioblastoma and anaplastic glioma.
text:
BACKGROUND: Panobinostat, a histone deacetylase inhibitor, has shown antineoplastic and antiangiogenic effects in glioma, including glioblastoma (GBM). The combination of panobinostat and bevacizumab, a VEGF inhibitor, may synergistically enhance the therapeutic effects in this patient population.
METHODS: We conducted a multicenter, phase II trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of panobinostat plus bevacizumab in patients with recurrent high-grade glioma (HGG). Patients with GBM were the primary study population, while those with anaplastic glioma (AG) were enrolled as an exploratory arm. The primary endpoint was 6-month progression-free survival (PFS6) rate for participants with GBM.
RESULTS: At the interim analysis, the GBM cohort did not meet the criteria for continued accrual, and the cohort was closed. A total of 24 patients with GBM were accrued before closure. The PFS6 rate was 30.4% (95% CI: 12.4%-50.7%), with a median PFS of 5 months (range: 3-9 months) and a median overall survival (OS) of 9 months (range: 6-19 months). Accrual in the AG cohort continued to completion, and a total of 15 patients were enrolled. The PFS6 rate was 46.7% (range: 21%-73%), with a median PFS of 7 months (range: 2-10 months) and a median OS of 17 months (range: 5 months-27 months).
CONCLUSIONS: This phase II study did not meet the criteria for continued accrual in the GBM cohort, and the cohort was closed. Although the addition of panobinostat to bevacizumab was reasonably well tolerated, the combination did not significantly improve PFS6 compared with historical controls of bevacizumab monotherapy in either cohort.

title: Blood monocytes consist of two principal subsets with distinct migratory properties
text: Peripheral blood monocytes are a diverse population of circulating white blood cells. Using a mouse model to study monocyte behavior in vivo, we identified two distinct subsets among murine blood monocytes: a short-lived CX(3)CR1(lo)CCR2(+)Gr1(+) subset that is actively recruited to inflamed tissues and a CX(3)CR1(hi)CCR2(-)Gr1(-) subset that is characterized by CX(3)CR1-dependent recruitment to non-inflamed tissues. Both subsets have the potential to differentiate into dendritic cells in vivo. Our findings also reveal that the level of CX(3)CR1 expression defines the two major human monocyte subsets, CD14(+)CD16(-) and CD14(lo)CD16(+) monocytes, which share similar phenotype and homing potential with the mouse subsets. These discoveries may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for treating inflammatory diseases.

title: The Spemann Organizer Signal noggin Binds and Inactivates Bone Morphogenetic Protein 4
text: The Spemann organizer of the amphibian gastrula is capable of releasing signals that have the power to directly induce neural tissue from the ectoderm and dorsalize ventral mesoderm to form muscle. These signaling activities are mimicked by the secreted polypeptide noggin, which is expressed at the appropriate time and place to participate in the organizer's signaling cascade. However, the organizer's signaling is countered by the actions of bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), which instead induce the formation of epidermis and ventral mesoderm. Interestingly, our findings reveal that noggin protein exhibits high affinity binding to BMP4, and can thereby abolish BMP4 activity by blocking its interaction with cognate cell-surface receptors. These data suggest that noggin, secreted by the organizer, plays a crucial role in patterning the embryo by disrupting BMP signaling.

title: A Conserved MST-FOXO Signaling Pathway Mediates Oxidative-Stress Responses and Extends Life Span
text: Oxidative stress can impact cellular survival and homeostasis, but the underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigate the protein kinase MST1 and its role in oxidative stress-induced cell death in primary mammalian neurons. We find that MST1 directly activates the FOXO transcription factors by phosphorylating them at a conserved site within the forkhead domain, leading to their nuclear translocation and induction of cell death. Additionally, we extend the MST-FOXO signaling link to nematodes, where knockdown of the C. elegans MST1 ortholog CST-1 shortens life span and accelerates tissue aging, while overexpression of cst-1 promotes life span and delays aging. These findings suggest that MST kinases play important roles in diverse biological processes, including cellular responses to oxidative stress and longevity, which are evolutionarily conserved.

title: Physician Emigration from Sub-Saharan Africa to the United States: Analysis of the 2011 AMA Physician Masterfile
text:
Background: The large-scale migration of physicians from sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) to high-income countries is a significant development concern. This study aimed to investigate current trends in emigration among SSA physicians in the US physician workforce.
Methods and Findings: We analyzed data from the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Workforce Statistics and the 2011 American Medical Association Physician Masterfile (AMA-PM) on physicians trained or born in SSA countries practicing in the US. We estimated emigration proportions, year of US entry, years of practice before emigration, and length of time in the US. Our findings revealed that 10,819 physicians were born or trained in 28 SSA countries, with 68% being SSA-trained, 20% US-trained, and 12% trained outside both SSA and the US. Active physicians (aged ≤ 70 years) accounted for 96% of the total. Migration trends among SSA-trained physicians increased from 2002 to 2011 for all but one principal source country, with the exception of South Africa. The most significant increases were observed in Nigeria (+1,113), Ghana (+243), Ethiopia (+274), and Sudan (+244). Liberia was the most affected, with 77% of its estimated physicians in the 2011 AMA-PM emigrating to the US. On average, SSA-trained physicians have been in the US for 18 years, with 6.5 years spent practicing before entry and nearly half emigrating during the implementation years (1984-1999) of structural adjustment programs.
Conclusion: Our findings indicate that physician emigration from SSA to the US is increasing for most SSA source countries, unless far-reaching policies are implemented by both the US and SSA countries. The current emigration trends are likely to persist, making the US a leading destination for SSA physicians emigrating from the continent of greatest need.

title: Kynurenic Acid Is a Nutritional Cue that Enables Behavioral Plasticity
text: The kynurenine pathway of tryptophan metabolism plays a significant role in the development of various brain disorders, yet its functional purposes within the body remain unclear. Our study reveals that kynurenic acid, a metabolite produced through this pathway, acts as a regulator of food-dependent behavioral plasticity in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. When C. elegans fasts, its behavior changes in response to food, including an increase in feeding rate upon encountering food again. Interestingly, our findings show that kynurenic acid levels are depleted during fasting, leading to the activation of NMDA receptor-expressing interneurons and the initiation of a neuropeptide Y-like signaling axis that enhances serotonin release when animals encounter food again. Upon refeeding, kynurenic acid levels are replenished, ending the elevated feeding period. These findings suggest that a physiological function of kynurenic acid is to directly link metabolism to the activity of NMDA and serotonergic circuits, which regulate a wide range of behaviors and physiological processes.

title: Comprehensive Identification and Annotation of Cell Type-Specific and Ubiquitous CTCF-Binding Sites in the Human Genome
text:
Chromatin insulators are cis-acting DNA elements that regulate gene expression by either maintaining the boundaries of heterochromatin and preventing gene silencing or blocking interactions between enhancers and promoters, thereby preventing gene activation. The sole protein implicated in the establishment of insulators in vertebrates is the ubiquitously expressed 11-zinc-finger DNA-binding protein, CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF). While CTCF has been linked to a range of regulatory functions, its functional significance in various cell types across the human genome remains unclear.
To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of CTCF-binding sites across 38 cell types designated by the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) consortium. Our findings reveal cell type-specific and ubiquitous CTCF-binding sites with distinct transcriptional functions and chromatin characteristics. Moreover, we demonstrate the insulator barrier function of CTCF-binding and explore its novel role in DNA replication. These results represent a significant step towards a comprehensive and systematic understanding of CTCF-dependent insulators and their diverse functions in the human genome.

title: Experimental and Theoretical Approaches to Conscious Processing
text:
Recent research and theoretical models have made progress in uncovering the link between subjective conscious experience and measurable brain activity. This review focuses on the specific challenge of how external or internal information transitions from nonconscious processing to conscious processing, marked by the presence of a reportable subjective experience. By combining neuroimaging and neurophysiological data collected during minimal contrasts between conscious and nonconscious processing, researchers have identified objective neural measures of conscious access, including:
* Late amplification of relevant sensory activity
* Long-distance cortico-cortical synchronization at beta and gamma frequencies
* "Ignition" of a large-scale prefrontal-parietal network
These findings are compared to current theoretical models of conscious processing, such as the Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) model, which posits that conscious access occurs when incoming information is made globally available to multiple brain systems through a network of neurons with long-range axons densely distributed in prefrontal, parieto-temporal, and cingulate cortices. The clinical implications of these results for conditions such as general anesthesia, coma, vegetative state, and schizophrenia are also discussed.

title: Reconstruction of the yeast Snf1 kinase regulatory network reveals its role as a global energy regulator
text: Highly conserved across eukaryotic cells, the AMP-activated kinase (AMPK) plays a central role in regulating carbon metabolism. To elucidate the complete network of interactions surrounding AMPK in yeast (Snf1) and to evaluate the function of its regulatory subunit Snf4, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of global mRNA, protein, and metabolite levels in wild-type, Deltasnf1, Deltasnf4, and Deltasnf1Deltasnf4 knockout strains. Leveraging four novel computational tools, including a novel DOGMA sub-network analysis, we demonstrated the utility of three-level omics data integration in uncovering the global Snf1 kinase function in yeast. Our findings revealed Snf1's far-reaching regulation on gene and protein expression levels, and showed that yeast Snf1 has a more extensive function in controlling energy metabolism than previously reported. Moreover, we identified complementary roles of Snf1 and Snf4.
