Similarly to the function of AMPK in humans, our findings established Snf1 as a low-energy checkpoint, and demonstrated that yeast can be utilized more extensively as a model system for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying the global regulation of AMPK in mammals, failure of which leads to metabolic diseases.

title: Influence of Steroid Hormone Signaling on Life Span Control by Caenorhabditis elegans Insulin-Like Signaling
text:
Sterol-sensing nuclear receptors and insulin-like growth factor signaling have evolved to play crucial roles in controlling aging. In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, bile acid-like steroid hormones called dafachronic acids (DAs) regulate longevity by binding to and modulating the activity of the conserved nuclear receptor DAF-12, which is similar to the insulin receptor (InsR) ortholog DAF-2. However, the interplay between the DA/DAF-12 pathway and DAF-2/InsR signaling in controlling life span is not well understood. To investigate this, we specifically examined the roles of liganded and unliganded DAF-12 in life span control in the context of reduced DAF-2/InsR signaling.
Our findings reveal that in animals with reduced daf-2/InsR activity, either reducing DA biosynthesis or completely abrogating DAF-12 activity shortens life span, suggesting that liganded DAF-12 promotes longevity. In contrast, in animals with reduced DAF-2/InsR activity induced by daf-2/InsR RNAi, both liganded and unliganded DAF-12 promote longevity. However, in daf-2/InsR mutants, liganded and unliganded DAF-12 act in opposition to control life span. These findings establish new roles for a conserved steroid signaling pathway in life span control and elucidate interactions among DA biosynthetic pathways, DAF-12, and DAF-2/InsR signaling in aging.

title: Asymmetric Cell Divisions Sustain Long-Term  Hematopoiesis from Single-sorted Human Fetal Liver Cells
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in adult bone marrow are thought to originate from fetal liver precursors. To investigate the cellular dynamics involved in long-term hematopoiesis, we studied single-sorted candidate HSCs from fetal liver that were cultured in the presence of a mix of stimulatory cytokines. After 8-10 days, the number of cells in primary cultures varied from 10,000 cells. Single cells in slow-growing colonies were then recloned when they reached a 100-200 cell stage. Notably, the number of cells in subclones differed significantly again. These findings suggest that primitive hematopoietic cells divide asymmetrically, with uneven distribution of proliferative potential and cell cycle properties among daughter cells. The continuous generation of functional heterogeneity among the clonal progeny of HSCs supports the idea of intrinsic control of stem cell fate and provides a model for the long-term maintenance of hematopoiesis both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Reprogramming factor expression initiates widespread targeted chromatin remodeling.
text: Despite significant progress in characterizing the transcription factor-driven reprogramming of somatic cells to an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) state, numerous mechanistic questions remain unanswered. To gain a deeper understanding of the early events in the reprogramming process, we conducted a systematic analysis of the transcriptional and epigenetic changes that occur during early factor induction after discrete numbers of cell divisions. Our findings revealed rapid, genome-wide changes in euchromatic histone modification, H3K4me2, at over a thousand loci, including large subsets of pluripotency-related or developmentally regulated gene promoters and enhancers. In contrast, patterns of the repressive H3K27me3 modification remained relatively unchanged, with focused depletion specifically at positions where H3K4 methylation is gained. These chromatin regulatory events occurred prior to transcriptional changes within the corresponding loci, providing evidence for an early, organized, and population-wide epigenetic response to ectopic reprogramming factors. Our data shed light on the temporal order through which somatic identity is reset during reprogramming.

title: Stroke and migraine--the spectrum of cause and effect.
text: The connection between migraine and stroke is intricate. While stroke may occur simultaneously with migraine, migraine can also increase the risk of stroke in women under 45 years old and possibly in men who experience migraine with aura. However, stroke can mimic migraine, and some migraine symptoms may be indicative of underlying cerebrovascular disorders. Rarely, migraine can cause an actual stroke, and the mechanisms behind this phenomenon are not yet fully understood, likely involving an interaction between the dynamic changes in cerebral blood flow and stroke risk factors.

title: MicroRNA Regulation of Cbx7 Mediates a Switch of Polycomb Orthologs during ESC Differentiation
text: The Polycomb Group (PcG) of chromatin-modifying enzymes plays a crucial role in regulating pluripotency and differentiation in mammalian cells. Mammalian genomes contain multiple homologs of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1) components, including five orthologs of the Drosophila Polycomb protein (Cbx2, Cbx4, Cbx6, Cbx7, and Cbx8). Our studies have identified Cbx7 as the primary Polycomb ortholog of PRC1 complexes in embryonic stem cells (ESCs). Interestingly, the expression of Cbx7 is downregulated during ESC differentiation, preceding the upregulation of Cbx2, Cbx4, and Cbx8, which are directly repressed by Cbx7. Notably, ectopic expression of Cbx7 inhibits differentiation and X chromosome inactivation, while concurrently enhancing ESC self-renewal. Conversely, Cbx7 knockdown induces differentiation and derepresses lineage-specific markers. In a functional screen, we identified the miR-125 and miR-181 families as regulators of Cbx7 that are induced during ESC differentiation. Ectopic expression of these miRNAs accelerates ESC differentiation by regulating Cbx7. These findings establish a critical role for Cbx7 and its regulatory miRNAs in determining pluripotency.

title: Differences in the Clinical Effects of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers: A Critical Review of the Evidence
text: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of hypertension and related cardiovascular events, such as heart disease and stroke. Although both ACE inhibitors and ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) are effective in treating hypertension, recent research suggests that they may have different cardiovascular protective effects. Our growing understanding of their distinct mechanisms of action may help explain these differences. As more studies investigate these mechanisms, we can expect to see an increase in research on the relative benefits and drawbacks of ACE inhibitors and ARBs for hypertension treatment, particularly in patients with cardiological comorbidities. ACE inhibitors are a safe and promising therapeutic option for these patients.

title: A talin-dependent LFA-1 focal zone is formed by rapidly migrating T lymphocytes
text: Cells such as fibroblasts and endothelial cells migrate through coordinated responses involving discrete integrin-containing focal adhesions and complexes. In contrast, the organization of integrins on highly motile T lymphocytes is poorly understood. To investigate the distribution, activity, and cytoskeletal linkage of integrin lymphocyte function associated antigen-1 (LFA-1) on human T lymphocytes migrating on endothelial cells and ligand intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), we examined the pattern of total LFA-1, which varies from low expression in lamellipodia to high expression in the uropod. However, high-affinity, clustered LFA-1 is restricted to a mid-cell zone that remains stable over time and across different ICAM-1 densities. Talin is essential for the stability and formation of this LFA-1 zone, and disruption of the talin-integrin link leads to loss of zone integrity and a significant decrease in migration speed on ICAM-1. This unique adhesive structure, which differs from previously described integrin-containing attachments in other cell types, has been termed the "focal zone."

title: Tricyclic antidepressants and headaches: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of tricyclic antidepressants in treating migraine, tension-type, and mixed headaches through a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Design: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Data sources: Medline, Embase, Cochrane Trials Registry, and PsycLIT.
Study selection: Randomized controlled trials of adults receiving tricyclics as monotherapy for at least four weeks.
Data extraction: Frequency of headaches (number of headache attacks for migraine and number of days with headache for tension-type headaches), headache intensity, and headache index.
Results: A total of 37 studies met the inclusion criteria. Tricyclics significantly reduced the number of days with tension-type headache and number of headache attacks from migraine compared to placebo (standardized mean difference -1.29, 95% confidence interval -2.18 to -0.39 and -0.70, -0.93 to -0.48), but not compared to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (-0.80, -2.63 to 0.02 and -0.20, -0.60 to 0.19). The effect of tricyclics increased with longer duration of treatment (β=-0.11, 95% confidence interval -0.63 to -0.15; P<0.0005). Tricyclics were also more likely to reduce the intensity of headaches by at least 50% than either placebo (tension-type: relative risk 1.41, 95% confidence interval 1.02 to 1.89; migraine: 1.80, 1.24 to 2.62) or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (1.73, 1.34 to 2.22 and 1.72, 1.15 to 2.55). Tricyclics were more likely to cause adverse effects than placebo (1.53, 95% confidence interval 1.11 to 2.12) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (2.22, 1.52 to 3.32), including dry mouth (P<0.0005 for both), drowsiness (P<0.0005 for both), and weight gain (P<0.001 for both), but did not increase dropout rates (placebo: 1.22, 0.83 to 1.80, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: 1.16, 0.81 to 2.97).
Conclusion: Tricyclic antidepressants are effective in preventing migraine and tension-type headaches and are more effective than selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, although with greater adverse effects. The effectiveness of tricyclics seems to increase over time.

title: Functional Consequences of Splicing of the Antisense Transcript COOLAIR on FLC Transcription
text: Antisense transcription, which is widespread in many genomes, has been the subject of much debate regarding its functional significance. We are currently investigating the functionality of a set of long noncoding antisense transcripts, collectively called COOLAIR, produced at the Arabidopsis FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC). COOLAIR initiates downstream of the major sense transcript poly(A) site and terminates either early or extends into the FLC promoter region. Our findings reveal that the splicing of COOLAIR is functionally important. This was discovered through analysis of a hypomorphic mutation in the core spliceosome component PRP8, which perturbs a cotranscriptional feedback mechanism linking COOLAIR processing to FLC gene body histone demethylation and reduced FLC transcription. Our results suggest that altered splicing of a long noncoding transcript can quantitatively modulate gene expression through cotranscriptional coupling mechanisms.

title: Nuclear Factor-�B Affects Tumor Progression in a Mouse Model of Malignant Pleural Effusion
text: In this study, we developed a novel mouse model of malignant pleural effusion (MPE) by directly injecting Lewis lung cancer (LLC) cells into the pleural space of syngeneic C57B/6 mice. The resulting pleural effusions exhibited similar cellular and biochemical features to those found in human MPEs. The growth and implantation of pleural tumors triggered a host inflammatory response, characterized by the infiltration of mixed inflammatory cells into the pleural fluid. Interestingly, LLC cells exhibited high basal nuclear factor (NF)-κB activity in vitro and in vivo, which we used to drive the expression of a NF-κB–dependent green fluorescent protein-firefly luciferase fusion reporter construct. This allowed for intravital tracing of pleural tumors. Our findings indicate that tumor NF-κB activity plays a crucial role in the development and progression of MPE. Specifically, inhibition of NF-κB in LLC cells did not affect cell viability in culture, but injection of LLC cells expressing a dominant NF-κB inhibitor resulted in decreased tumor burden, decreased pleural effusion volume, and decreased pleural effusion tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) levels. These results suggest that targeting NF-κB may be a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of MPE.

title: A phase I study of PF-04449913, an oral hedgehog inhibitor, in patients with advanced solid tumors.
text:
Objective: To determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of PF-04449913, an orally administered single-agent, and to evaluate its safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and preliminary antitumor activity in patients with advanced tumors.
Design: An open-label, multicenter, phase I study employing a 3+3 design with dose escalation/de-escalation until the MTD was identified. PF-04449913 was administered once daily for 28 days in continuous cycles, starting at 80 mg/day.
Results: A total of 23 patients were enrolled, of whom 19 were evaluable for first-cycle dose-limiting toxicity (DLT). The first-cycle DLT rate at the 640 mg dose level was 33.3%, indicating that the MTD was estimated to be 320 mg once daily. The recommended phase II dose was not determined. PF-04449913 was generally well tolerated at doses of 80 to 320 mg once daily, with the most common treatment-related adverse events (AEs) being grade 1-2 dysgeusia, fatigue, decreased appetite, nausea, dizziness, dehydration, and diarrhea. Treatment-related grade 3 AEs occurred only in patients receiving the 640 mg dose once daily, and no grade 4-5 AEs were reported. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed generally dose-proportional kinetics with biphasic elimination, supporting once-daily dosing. PF-04449913 modulated hedgehog signaling at the dose levels tested, as demonstrated by >80% downregulation of GLI1 expression in the skin of treated patients. Eight patients (34.8%) achieved stable disease, and three patients with disease progression at enrollment had prolonged disease stabilization (≥6 months).
Conclusions: The results of this study support further evaluation of PF-04449913 in patients with advanced solid tumors, with the identified MTD of 320 mg once daily providing a basis for future clinical trials.

title: Histone levels are regulated by phosphorylation and ubiquitylation dependent proteolysis
text: Histone levels are tightly regulated to prevent adverse effects such as genomic instability and hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents due to the accumulation of highly basic proteins when DNA replication slows down or stops. Although chromosomal histones are stable, excess (non-chromatin bound) histones are rapidly degraded in a Rad53 (radiation sensitive 53) kinase-dependent manner in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Here, we demonstrate that excess histones associate with Rad53 in vivo and undergo modifications such as tyrosine phosphorylation and polyubiquitylation before their proteolysis by the proteasome. We identify the Tyr 99 residue of histone H3 as critical for efficient ubiquitylation and degradation of this histone. Additionally, we identify the ubiquitin conjugating enzymes (E2) Ubc4 and Ubc5, as well as the ubiquitin ligase (E3) Tom1 (temperature dependent organization in mitotic nucleus 1), as enzymes involved in the ubiquitylation of excess histones. Regulated histone proteolysis has significant implications for maintaining epigenetic marks on chromatin, genomic stability, and the packaging of sperm DNA.

title: TLR-activated B cells suppress T cell-mediated autoimmunity.
text:
TLRs (toll-like receptors) on immune cells, such as dendritic cells, macrophages, and B lymphocytes, recognize microbial infections and trigger immune responses. MyD88, a TLR-signaling adaptor protein, is expressed on these cells and plays a crucial role in activating immune responses. However, the impact of TLR-activated B cells on T cell-mediated inflammation is not well understood.
In this study, we investigated the role of TLR-activated B cells in a T cell-mediated autoimmune disease called experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). We found that TLR signaling in B cells suppresses inflammatory T cell responses (both Th1 and Th17) and promotes recovery from EAE. Interestingly, only certain TLR are required on B cells for resolution of EAE, and these TLR are dispensable for disease initiation. This suggests that a category of TLR agonists preferentially triggers a suppressive function in B cells, limiting autoimmune disease.
We also found that the regulatory function of B cells is provided by components of Mycobacterium tuberculosis present in the adjuvant. This suggests that MyD88 signaling in B cells antagonizes MyD88 signaling in other cells, which drives differentiation of Th17 cells and is required for induction of EAE.
Overall, our data indicate that B cells play a crucial role in linking recognition of microbial products via TLR to suppression of a T cell-mediated autoimmune disease. This highlights the importance of B cells in regulating immune responses and preventing autoimmune diseases.

title: Successful expansion of functional and stable regulatory T cells for immunotherapy in liver transplantation
text: Investigations into strategies to prevent organ transplant rejection while minimizing long-term immunosuppression are underway, with a focus on regulatory T cells (Tregs) nearing clinical application. A clinical trial, ThRIL, recently launched at King's College London, aims to use Treg cell therapy to induce tolerance in liver transplant recipients, with the potential to revolutionize the management of these patients and enable a future of drug-free transplants. This study marks the first attempt to manufacture clinical-grade Tregs from prospective liver transplant recipients using a CliniMACS-based GMP isolation technique and expansion with anti-CD3/CD28 beads, IL-2, and rapamycin. The protocol successfully enriched a pure, stable population of Tregs (>95% CD4+CD25+FOXP3+), achieving adequate numbers for clinical application. Notably, the method prevented the conversion of Tregs to Th17 cells under pro-inflammatory conditions, resulting in the expansion of superior functional Tregs compared to freshly isolated cells. The final Treg product was manufactured in the clinical research facility (CRF), a crucial step towards clinical application. The data presented in this manuscript, combined with anticipated clinical results from ThRIL, will significantly impact the management of liver transplant recipients.

title: A framework for improving microRNA prediction in non-human genomes
text:
Recent attention has focused on predicting novel pre-microRNAs (miRNAs) from genomic sequences, with most studies concentrated on the human genome. Previous studies have demonstrated that human-trained methods retain accuracy when applied to other species, but have failed to report the significant decrease in specificity (the ability to correctly reject non-miRNA sequences) in non-human genomes. Given that the ratio of true miRNA sequences to pseudo-miRNA sequences is approximately 1:1000, low specificity hinders the application of existing tools to non-human genomes due to the large number of false positives.
To address this issue, we introduce a framework called SMIRP, which leverages sequence conservation and phylogenetic distance information to create species-specific miRNA prediction systems. Our framework shows substantial improvements in specificity and precision for four non-human test species when applied to three different prediction systems representing two types of classifiers (support vector machine and Random Forest), based on three different feature sets, with both human-specific and taxon-wide training data. The SMIRP framework is potentially applicable to all miRNA prediction systems, and we expect significant improvements in precision and specificity, while maintaining sensitivity, regardless of the machine learning technique chosen.

title: CD8 Cells of Patients with Diffuse Cutaneous Leishmaniasis Display Functional Exhaustion: The Latter Is Reversed, In Vitro, by TLR2 Agonists
text: Leishmania mexicana (Lm) infection causes two forms of cutaneous leishmaniasis: localized (LCL) and diffuse (DCL). DCL patients have a poor cellular immune response, leading to chronicity of the infection. It has been proposed that CD8 T lymphocytes (CD8) play a crucial role in infection clearance, although the role of CD8 cytotoxicity in disease control has not been fully elucidated. Lesions of DCL patients have been shown to have lower numbers of CD8 cells compared to patients with LCL, and leishmanicidal treatment restores CD8 numbers. The enhanced response of CD8 towards Leishmania parasites led us to compare the functional properties of CD8 cells from patients with LCL and DCL. We analyzed IFNγ production, antigen-specific proliferation, and cytotoxicity of CD8 cells purified from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) against autologous macrophages (MO) infected with Leishmania mexicana (MOi). Additionally, we examined tissue biopsies from both groups of patients for evidence of cytotoxicity associated with apoptotic cells in the lesions. We found that CD8 cells from DCL patients exhibited low cytotoxicity, low antigen-specific proliferation, and low IFNγ production when stimulated with MOi, compared to LCL patients. Furthermore, DCL patients had significantly fewer TUNEL+ cells in their lesions, which is a hallmark of cellular exhaustion. We aimed to restore the functional capacity of CD8 cells from DCL patients by preincubating them with TLR2 agonists: Leishmania lipophosphoglycan (LPG) or Pam3Cys. Cytotoxicity against MOi, antigen-specific proliferation, and IFNγ production were restored with both stimuli, while the expression of the exhaustion marker PD-1 was reduced. Our findings suggest that the CD8 response is crucial for controlling Lm infection in LCL patients, and that chronic infection in DCL patients leads to a state of CD8 functional exhaustion, which may facilitate disease progression. This is the first report showing the presence of functionally exhausted CD8 T lymphocytes in DCL patients, and that pre-stimulation with TLR2 ligands can restore the effector mechanisms of CD8 T lymphocytes from DCL patients against Leishmania mexicana-infected macrophages.

title: Enhancer Evolution across 20 Mammalian Species
text: The mammalian radiation has been accompanied by significant changes in non-coding regions of the genome, yet a comprehensive understanding of regulatory evolution in these organisms remains elusive. To address this knowledge gap, we investigated the evolution of promoters and enhancers active in liver across 20 mammalian species from six diverse orders by profiling the genomic enrichment of H3K27 acetylation and H3K4 trimethylation. Our findings reveal that the rapid evolution of enhancers is a universal feature of mammalian genomes, with the majority of recently evolved enhancers arising from ancestral DNA exaptation rather than lineage-specific expansions of repeat elements. In contrast, liver promoters exhibit a high degree of conservation across these species, with only a limited number of changes observed. Furthermore, our data demonstrate that recently evolved enhancers can be associated with genes under positive selection, highlighting the potential of this approach for annotating regulatory adaptations in genomic sequences. These results provide important insights into the functional genetics underlying mammalian regulatory evolution.

title: IDH1 mutations alter citric acid cycle metabolism and increase dependence on oxidative mitochondrial metabolism.
text: Oncogenic mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IDH1/2) are prevalent in various types of cancer, yet the metabolic consequences of these genetic alterations remain incompletely understood. In this study, we performed (13)C metabolic flux analysis on a panel of isogenic cell lines harboring heterozygous IDH1/2 mutations. Our findings revealed that under hypoxic conditions, IDH1-mutant cells exhibited increased oxidative tricarboxylic acid metabolism, accompanied by decreased reductive glutamine metabolism, in contrast to IDH2-mutant cells. However, selective inhibition of mutant IDH1 enzyme function failed to restore the impaired reductive carboxylation activity. Moreover, this metabolic reprogramming resulted in increased sensitivity of IDH1-mutant cells to hypoxia or electron transport chain inhibition in vitro. Finally, IDH1-mutant cells showed poor growth as subcutaneous xenografts within a hypoxic in vivo microenvironment. Our results suggest potential therapeutic strategies to exploit the unique metabolic vulnerabilities associated with IDH1 mutations.

title: The assessment of the prognostic value of tumor markers and cytokines as SCCAg, CYFRA 21.1, IL-6, VEGF and sTNF receptors in patients with squamous cell cervical cancer, particularly with early stage of the disease
text: The purpose of this study is to investigate the predictive value of various tumor markers, including squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCCAg), cytokeratin-19 fragment (CYFRA 21.1), interleukin 6 (IL-6), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor I (sTNF RI), and sTNF RII, in patients with squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. The study included 138 patients with stages I-IVA, as determined by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) classification, who were followed for 10 years. During this time, 56 relapses and 53 deaths occurred, and recurrent disease was confirmed in 45% of patients. The researchers measured the pretreatment serum levels of these markers in all patients and evaluated their ability to predict disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) using the log-rank test and Cox regression model. Additionally, the researchers analyzed the ROC curve for patients with recurrence and found that the largest area under the curve was demonstrated for SCCAg and IL-6, and for patients who died, the largest area under the curve was demonstrated for SCCAg and VEGF. Cox analysis revealed that independent prognostic factors for DFS were only SCCAg and IL-6, but for OS, the prognostic value was IL-6 and SCCAg, but in patients with early stage, VEGF, IL-6, and CYFRA 21.1 were prognostic factors for OS. The study suggests that the serum levels of VEGF, CYFRA 21.1, and IL-6 before treatment in patients with early stage cervical cancer are important prognostic factors.

title: Combination of platelet count and mean platelet volume (COP-MPV) predicts postoperative prognosis in both resectable early and advanced stage esophageal squamous cell cancer patients
text: The purpose of this study is to identify the most powerful prognostic factor from routine blood tests for esophageal squamous cell cancer (ESCC) patients. We evaluated various laboratory tests, including red blood cell parameters (hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, and red blood cell distribution width), platelet morphological parameters (mean platelet volume and platelet count), blood coagulation status (D-dimer), and tumor biomarker (CA19-9). Additionally, we calculated the combination of preoperative platelet and mean platelet volume (COP-MPV) and found it to be an independent prognostic factor for overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) in multivariate analyses. In subgroup analyses for early (stages I and II) and locally (stage III) advanced stage patients, COP-MPV was significantly associated with OS and DFS in each group. Our findings suggest that COP-MPV is a promising predictor for postoperative survival in ESCC patients.

title: Dementia incidence and mortality in middle-income countries, and associations with indicators of cognitive reserve: a 10/66 Dementia Research Group population-based cohort study
text:
Background: Few cohort studies from low- or middle-income countries have reported lower incidences of dementia compared to high-income countries. This study aimed to investigate the incidence of dementia according to criteria from the 10/66 Dementia Research Group and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) IV, as well as the effect of dementia at baseline on mortality and the independent effects of age, sex, socioeconomic position, and cognitive reserve.
Methods: This was a population-based cohort study of individuals aged 65 years and older living in urban and rural sites in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Venezuela, and urban and rural sites in Peru, Mexico, and China. Participants were interviewed at baseline and again 3-5 years later, and incidence of dementia was determined using criteria from the 10/66 Dementia Research Group and DSM-IV. Mortality hazards were also assessed, and informant reports of dementia before death were obtained for participants who had died.
Findings: A total of 12,887 participants were interviewed at baseline, of whom 11,718 were free of dementia. The incidence of 10/66 dementia varied between 18.2 and 30.4 per 1000 person-years, and was 1.4-2.7 times higher than the incidence of DSM-IV dementia (9.9-15.7 per 1000 person-years). Mortality hazards were 1.56-5.69 times higher in individuals with dementia at baseline than in those who were dementia-free. Informant reports suggested a high incidence of dementia before death, and the overall incidence might be 4-19% higher if these data were included. 10/66 dementia incidence was independently associated with increased age (HR 1.67; 95% CI 1.56-1.79), female sex (HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.61-0.84), and low education (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.81-0.97), but not with occupational attainment (HR 1.04; 95% CI 0.95-1.13).
Interpretation: The results of this study provide support for the cognitive reserve hypothesis, suggesting that education, literacy, verbal fluency, and motor sequencing confer substantial protection against the onset of dementia in middle-income countries as in high-income countries. The study was funded by the Wellcome Trust Health Consequences of Population Change Programme, WHO, US Alzheimer's Association, and FONACIT/CDCH/UCV.

title: Regulation of immune responses by extracellular vesicles
text: Extracellular vesicles, including exosomes, are small membrane-bound vesicles derived from multivesicular bodies or the plasma membrane. Most, if not all, cell types release these vesicles, which then enter the bodily fluids. These vesicles contain a subset of proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids derived from the parent cell. It is believed that extracellular vesicles play important roles in intercellular communication, both locally and systemically, by transferring their contents between cells. Extracellular vesicles are involved in various physiological processes and have important roles in immune regulation, with vesicles from both non-immune and immune cells. Additionally, extracellular vesicle-based therapeutics are being developed and clinically tested for the treatment of inflammatory diseases, autoimmune disorders, and cancer. Given the significant therapeutic potential of extracellular vesicles, this Review focuses on their role in modulating immune responses and their potential therapeutic applications.

title: Risk of cancer after low doses of ionising radiation: retrospective cohort study in 15 countries.
text:
Objective:
To provide accurate estimates of the risk of cancer following prolonged exposure to low levels of ionizing radiation and to enhance the scientific basis of radiation protection standards for environmental, occupational, and medical diagnostic exposures.
Design:
Multinational retrospective cohort study of cancer mortality among workers in the nuclear industry in 15 countries.
Participants:
407,391 workers were individually monitored for external radiation exposure over a total follow-up period of 5.2 million person-years.
Main Outcome Measures:
Estimates of excess relative risks per sievert (Sv) of radiation dose for mortality from cancers other than leukaemia and from leukaemia excluding chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, which are the primary causes of death considered by radiation protection authorities.
Results:
The excess relative risk for cancers other than leukaemia was found to be 0.97 per Sv (95% confidence interval: 0.14 to 1.97). Analyses of causes of death related or unrelated to smoking suggest that while confounding by smoking may be present, it is unlikely to fully explain this increased risk. The excess relative risk for leukaemia excluding chronic lymphocytic leukaemia was found to be 1.93 per Sv (<0 to 8.47). Based on these estimates, it is estimated that 1-2% of cancer deaths among workers in this cohort may be attributable to radiation exposure.
Conclusions:
These estimates, derived from the largest study of nuclear workers ever conducted, are higher than, but statistically compatible with, the risk estimates used in current radiation protection standards. The findings suggest that there is a small excess risk of cancer, even at the low doses and dose rates typically received by nuclear workers in this study.

title: Gamma-Secretase Represents a Therapeutic Target for the Treatment of Invasive Glioma Mediated by the p75 Neurotrophin Receptor
text: The multifunctional signaling protein p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75(NTR)) plays a central role in the highly invasive nature of malignant gliomas. Our findings reveal that neurotrophin-dependent regulated intramembrane proteolysis (RIP) of p75(NTR) is essential for p75(NTR)-mediated glioma invasion, and we identify a novel therapeutic approach for targeting glioma cells. By expressing cleavage-resistant chimeras of p75(NTR) or treating animals with clinically applicable gamma-secretase inhibitors, we observed a significant decrease in glioma invasion and prolonged survival. Importantly, we observed proteolytic processing of p75(NTR) in p75(NTR)-positive patient tumor specimens and brain tumor initiating cells, highlighting the potential of p75(NTR) as a therapeutic target. These findings suggest that gamma-secretase inhibitors may have direct clinical application for the treatment of malignant glioma.

title: Preliminary assessment of inhaled nitric oxide for acute vaso-occlusive crisis in pediatric patients with sickle cell disease.
text:
The article discusses the potential benefits of inhaled nitric oxide (INO) therapy for the treatment of vaso-occlusive crises in pediatric patients with sickle cell disease. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 20 patients aged 10 to 21 years with severe acute vaso-occlusive crisis were randomly assigned to receive either INO (80 ppm with 21% final concentration of inspired oxygen) or placebo (21% inspired oxygen) for 4 hours. The primary outcome measure was the change in pain intensity at 4 hours compared to preinhalation pain, assessed using a 10-cm visual analog scale (VAS). Secondary outcome measures included pain over 6 hours, parenteral narcotic use over 24 hours, duration of hospitalization, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and methemoglobin concentration.
The results showed that while there was no significant difference in pain intensity at 4 hours between the INO and placebo groups, there was a trend towards greater pain relief in the INO group over the first 4 hours of inhalation. Additionally, morphine use over 6 hours was significantly less in the INO group, but there was no difference in pain relief over 4 hours or 24 hours. The duration of hospitalization was similar in both groups. No adverse effects of INO were observed. The study suggests that INO may be beneficial for acute vaso-occlusive crisis in pediatric patients with sickle cell disease, warranting further investigation.

title: Corresponding author:
text: Over the years, cytogenetic analysis techniques have evolved and become an integral part of routine laboratory testing, providing valuable diagnostic and prognostic information in hematologic disorders. Karyotypic aberrations contribute to understanding the molecular pathogenesis of disease, which in turn informs the rational application of therapeutic modalities. While metaphase cytogenetics (MC) has been the primary method of analysis, recent advances in molecular technologies have complemented MC and overcome many of its limitations, including the need for cell culture. Whole genome scanning using comparative genomic hybridization and single nucleotide polymorphism arrays (CGH-A; SNP-A) can analyze somatic or clonal unbalanced chromosomal defects. In SNP-A, the combination of copy number detection and genotyping enables the diagnosis of copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, a lesion that cannot be detected by MC but may have important pathogenetic implications. Whole genome scanning arrays, despite their inability to detect balanced translocations, enable the detection of chromosomal defects in a higher proportion of patients with hematologic malignancies. Newly detected chromosomal aberrations, including somatic uniparental disomy, may lead to more precise prognostic schemes in many diseases.

title: Rare Variants Create Synthetic Genome-Wide Associations
text:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified over 2,000 common variants associated with various diseases or traits (<http://www.genome.gov/gwastudies>). While it is generally believed that these associated variants reflect the effect of nearby common causal sites, we propose an alternative explanation: uncommon or rare variants may create "synthetic associations" by occurring more frequently in association with one of the alleles at a common site compared to the other allele. Despite being a theoretical possibility, synthetic associations have never been systematically explored as a possible explanation for GWAS findings.
Using simple computer simulations, we show that synthetic associations can arise under specific conditions and may account for or contribute to many identified signals in GWAS. We demonstrate this using real datasets, where rare causal mutations responsible for both hearing loss and sickle cell anemia create genome-wide significant synthetic associations, spanning a 2.5-Mb interval with scores of associated variants. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the possibility of synthetic associations in the interpretation and follow-up of GWAS signals.

title: Decoding of Cytoplasmic Ca2+ Oscillations through the Spatial Signature Drives Gene Expression
text: Cytoplasmic Ca(2+) oscillations are a ubiquitous signaling mode that triggers a wide range of cellular responses (1, 2). These oscillations are considered the primary mechanism of Ca(2+) signaling due to their ability to occur at low levels of stimulus intensity (3). Ca(2+) oscillations are thought to convey information through their amplitude and frequency, leading to the activation of specific downstream targets (4-6). Our findings reveal that the spatial Ca(2+) gradient within the oscillation is crucial. When mast cells were stimulated with varying concentrations of agonists in the presence or absence of external Ca(2+), Ca(2+) oscillations were indistinguishable. However, only oscillations accompanied by Ca(2+) entry through store-operated CRAC channels triggered gene expression. In contrast, increased cytoplasmic Ca(2+) buffering prevented oscillations but not gene activation. These results suggest that local Ca(2+) influx, rather than global Ca(2+) oscillations, drives gene expression at physiological levels of stimulation. Furthermore, our findings imply that the role of Ca(2+) oscillations may be to activate CRAC channels, thereby generating spatially restricted Ca(2+) signals that drive gene activation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the spatial profile of a Ca(2+) oscillation provides a novel mechanism by which a pleiotropic messenger specifically activates gene expression.

title: Effect of glucosamine on pain-related disability in patients with chronic low back pain and degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Chronic low back pain (LBP) with degenerative lumbar osteoarthritis (OA) is a common condition affecting a large portion of the adult population. Despite the increasing use of glucosamine supplements by patients with chronic LBP, there is limited research on its effectiveness in this context. To investigate the effect of glucosamine in patients with chronic LBP and degenerative lumbar OA, we conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at Oslo University Hospital Outpatient Clinic in Norway.
The study included 250 patients aged 25 years or older with chronic LBP (lasting over 6 months) and degenerative lumbar OA. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 1500 mg of oral glucosamine per day or a placebo for 6 months, with assessments of effect at the end of the intervention period and at 1 year (6 months postintervention). The primary outcome measure was pain-related disability, assessed using the Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ). Secondary outcomes included numerical scores from pain-rating scales at rest and during activity, as well as quality-of-life measures using the EuroQol-5 Dimensions (EQ-5D) instrument. Data were collected at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 and 6 months, and again at 1 year.
At baseline, the mean RMDQ score was similar for the glucosamine and placebo groups (9.2 and 9.7, respectively). At 6 months, the mean RMDQ score was unchanged for both groups (5.0 for glucosamine and 5.5 for the placebo group). At 1 year, the mean RMDQ scores were 4.8 for glucosamine and 5.5 for the placebo group. There were no statistically significant differences in change between groups when assessed after the 6-month intervention period and at 1 year: RMDQ (P = .72), LBP at rest (P = .91), LBP during activity (P = .97), and quality-of-life EQ-5D (P = .20). Mild adverse events were reported in 40 patients in the glucosamine group and 46 in the placebo group (P = .48).
Our findings suggest that 6-month treatment with oral glucosamine did not result in reduced pain-related disability among patients with chronic LBP and degenerative lumbar OA. These results provide little support for the use of glucosamine in this patient population. TRIAL REGISTRATION: clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT00404079.

title: Adult cervicocerebral artery dissection: a single-center study of 301 Finnish patients.
text:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE:
There is a scarcity of small-scale studies examining potential risk factors, comorbidities, and prognostic indicators in adults with spontaneous cervicocerebral artery dissections (CAD). This study aims to investigate the prognostic factors and associations of CAD with vascular risk factors in a large, hospital-based cohort of Finnish patients.
METHODS:
We conducted a retrospective analysis of 301 consecutive patients diagnosed with CAD between 1994 and 2007. The patients were recruited from a single hospital in Finland, and the study included both men and women. The patients' medical records were reviewed to collect data on demographics, vascular risk factors, and clinical outcomes.
RESULTS:
Our findings indicate that two-thirds of the patients were male (68%), and women were significantly younger than men. Migraine, particularly with visual aura, was more common in patients with CAD compared to the general Finnish population (36% of all patients). Smoking was also more prevalent in patients with CAD. At 3 months, 83% of patients achieved a favorable outcome. Occlusion of the dissected artery, internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD), and recent infection in infarction patients were associated with a poorer outcome. ICAD patients had fewer brain infarctions, but the strokes they experienced were more severe. During the 4-year follow-up period, seven patients (2.3%) died, and six patients (2%) had verified CAD recurrences.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our study provides evidence for the association of CAD with male sex and possible association with smoking and migraine. The study also suggests that occlusion of the dissected artery, ICAD, and infection may be associated with poorer outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of identifying and managing potential risk factors and comorbidities in patients with CAD to improve clinical outcomes.

title: Genetic variation and gastric cancer risk: a field synopsis and meta-analysis.
text: Background: The study of genetic susceptibility to sporadic gastric carcinoma has seen a significant increase in published data, yet a comprehensive and quantitative overview remains lacking. Objective: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of the evidence on the association between DNA variation and the risk of developing stomach cancer. Methods: We conducted a systematic search of the literature to identify studies investigating the relationship between genetic polymorphisms and gastric cancer risk. We graded the summary evidence according to the Venice criteria and calculated the false positive report probability (FPRP) to validate the significance of the findings. Subgroup meta-analyses were conducted for ethnicity, tumour histology, tumour site, and Helicobacter pylori infection status. Results: Our search identified 824 eligible studies comprising 2,530,706 subjects (cases: 261,386 (10.3%)). We performed 456 primary and subgroup meta-analyses on 156 variants involving 101 genes. Eleven variants were significantly associated with disease risk and had a high level of summary evidence: MUC1 rs2070803 at 1q22 (diffuse carcinoma subgroup), MTX1 rs2075570 at 1q22 (diffuse), PSCA rs2294008 at 8q24.2 (non-cardia), PRKAA1 rs13361707 at 5p13 (non-cardia), PLCE1 rs2274223 at 10q23 (cardia), TGFBR2 rs3087465 at 3p22 (Asian), PKLR rs3762272 at 1q22 (diffuse), PSCA rs2976392 (intestinal), GSTP1 rs1695 at 11q13 (Asian), CASP8 rs3834129 at 2q33 (mixed), and TNF rs1799724 at 6p21.3 (mixed). We also identified polymorphisms with lower quality significant associations (n=110). Conclusion: Our findings identify several high-quality biomarkers of gastric cancer susceptibility. These data will form the basis of an annually updated online resource that will be integral to the study of gastric carcinoma genetics and may inform future screening programmes.

title: Structure and function of the blood–brain barrier
text: The central nervous system (CNS) relies on a highly regulated microenvironment to facilitate neural signaling. At the interface between the blood and CNS, three key barriers exist: the blood-brain barrier (BBB), blood-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) barrier, and arachnoid barrier. The BBB, located at the microvessel endothelium of the brain, is the primary site of blood-CNS exchange. The BBB is composed of endothelial tight junctions, which form a physical barrier, and membrane transporters and vesicular mechanisms that create a transport barrier. Astrocytic glial cells, pericytes, and microglia play crucial roles in maintaining the structure and function of the BBB. The embryonic development and changes in the BBB due to pathology are also described. The BBB is subject to short- and long-term regulation, which may be disrupted in disease. Any drug discovery or delivery program aiming to target or avoid the CNS must consider the unique features of the BBB.

title: Golli protein negatively regulates store depletion-induced calcium influx in T cells.
text: Calcium influx is essential for the activation and differentiation of T cells, but the intricate mechanisms governing this process are still unclear. Our study uncovers a critical role of the golli protein in regulating calcium influx in T cells. Golli, an alternatively spliced product of the myelin basic protein gene, regulates calcium entry in T cells by inhibiting the store depletion-induced calcium influx. We found that golli-deficient T cells exhibit hyperproliferation and enhanced calcium entry upon T cell receptor stimulation. Interestingly, the myristoylation site on golli plays a crucial role in its inhibitory action on calcium influx, as mutation of this site disrupts golli's association with the plasma membrane and reverses its inhibitory effect. These findings suggest that golli functions in a unique manner to regulate T cell activation through a mechanism involving the modulation of calcium homeostasis.

title: Extracellular vesicles derived from renal cancer stem cells induce a pro-tumorigenic phenotype in mesenchymal stromal cells
text: Renal carcinomas have been shown to harbor a population of cancer stem cells (CSCs) with self-renewal capacity and tumor-promoting potential. These CSCs secrete large amounts of extracellular vesicles (EVs) that can transfer various molecules, including proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids, and induce epigenetic changes in target cells. Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (MSCs) are susceptible to tumor-derived signals and can be recruited to the tumor microenvironment. However, the precise role of MSCs in tumor development is still debated, as they have been reported to exhibit both pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects. In this study, we investigated the participation of renal CSC-derived EVs in the interaction between tumor and MSCs. Our findings revealed that CSC-derived EVs promoted persistent changes in MSCs, characterized by increased expression of genes involved in cell migration (CXCR4, CXCR7), matrix remodeling (COL4A3), angiogenesis (IL-8, Osteopontin, Myeloperoxidase), and tumor growth. EV-stimulated MSCs exhibited enhanced migration towards the tumor conditioned medium in vitro and promoted migration of renal tumor cells in vivo. Moreover, EV-stimulated MSCs induced vessel-like formation in vivo, supporting tumor growth and vascularization. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that CSC-derived EVs can induce phenotypical changes in MSCs that promote tumor growth.

title: In vivo effect of chronic hypoxia on the neurochemical profile of the developing rat hippocampus.
text:
The study investigated the impact of chronic postnatal hypoxia on the developing hippocampus in a rat model. Using in vivo 1H NMR spectroscopy at 9.4 T, the researchers evaluated the neurochemical profile of the hippocampus in rats exposed to 10% O2 from postnatal day (P) 3 to P28. The study found that chronic hypoxia affected the concentrations of several neurochemicals in the hippocampus, including aspartate, creatine, phosphocreatine, GABA, glutamate, glutamine, glutathione, myoinositol, N-acetylaspartate (NAA), phosphorylethanolamine, and the glutamate/glutamine (Glu/Gln) ratio. The increased phosphocreatine/creatine (PCr/Cr) ratio was also observed, which suggests decreased brain energy consumption. The altered neurochemical profile during hippocampal development may underlie some of the cognitive deficits present in human infants at risk of chronic hypoxia.
The study found that chronic hypoxia affected the neurochemical profile of the hippocampus in rats, with changes in the concentrations of several neurochemicals. These changes may be related to the well-established link between excitatory neurotransmission and brain energy metabolism. The study suggests that elevated glutamate, GABA, and Glu/Gln ratios may indicate suppressed excitatory neurotransmission in an energy-limited environment, while decreased NAA and phosphorylethanolamine suggest reduced neuronal integrity and phospholipid metabolism. These findings may have implications for understanding the cognitive deficits observed in children with cyanotic congenital heart disease.

title: Noncoding Transcription by RNA Polymerase Pol IVb/Pol V Mediates Transcriptional Silencing of Overlapping and Adjacent Genes
text: Nuclear transcription extends beyond gene-coding regions and permeates the intergenic and noncoding space of eukaryotic genomes. The enigmatic significance of this ubiquitous noncoding transcription remains largely unexplored. However, recent findings have illuminated the role of Arabidopsis RNA polymerase IVb/Pol V, a multisubunit nuclear enzyme, in transcribing intergenic and noncoding sequences. This facilitates the formation of heterochromatin and silencing of adjacent and overlapping genes. Pol IVb/Pol V transcription is dependent on the chromatin-remodeling protein DRD1, yet operates independently of siRNA biogenesis. Notably, both Pol IVb/Pol V transcription and siRNA production are essential for transposon silencing, suggesting that Pol IVb/Pol V generates RNAs or chromatin structures that serve as scaffolds for siRNA-mediated heterochromatin-forming complexes. This discovery provides a novel solution to a longstanding paradox in epigenetic control: the apparent contradiction between the need for transcription to silence the same region.

title: Intestinal microbiota metabolism of L-carnitine, a nutrient in red meat, promotes atherosclerosis
text:
The intestinal microbiota metabolizes choline and phosphatidylcholine in the gut, producing trimethylamine (TMA). This compound is further metabolized to trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), which has been linked to an increased risk of atherosclerosis. Our study shows that the intestinal microbiota's metabolism of dietary L-carnitine, a compound found in red meat, also leads to the production of TMAO and accelerates atherosclerosis in mice. Interestingly, we found that omnivorous humans produced more TMAO than vegans or vegetarians after consuming L-carnitine, suggesting that the gut microbiome plays a key role in this process. We also found that the presence of specific bacterial taxa in the gut was associated with both TMAO levels and dietary status. Our results suggest that high levels of TMAO in the blood may be a marker of increased CVD risk, and that the intestinal microbiota may contribute to this risk through the metabolism of dietary L-carnitine.
In mice, chronic dietary L-carnitine supplementation led to increased synthesis of TMA and TMAO, as well as enhanced atherosclerosis. However, this effect was only observed when the intestinal microbiota was not suppressed. In contrast, dietary supplementation with TMAO or either carnitine or choline reduced in vivo reverse cholesterol transport in mice with an intact intestinal microbiota. These findings suggest that the intestinal microbiota may play a key role in the link between high levels of red meat consumption and CVD risk.

title: Hepatotoxicity associated with antiretroviral therapy in adults infected with human immunodeficiency virus and the role of hepatitis C or B virus infection.
text: The use of antiretroviral drugs, including protease inhibitors, to treat human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection has been associated with hepatotoxicity, particularly in individuals co-infected with hepatitis C or B virus. To investigate this further, a prospective cohort study was conducted at an urban HIV clinic, including 298 patients who started new antiretroviral therapies between January 1996 and January 1998. Of these, 211 (71%) received protease inhibitors as part of combination therapy, and 87 (29%) received dual nucleoside analog regimens. The study found that severe hepatotoxicity occurred in 31 (10.4%) of the 298 patients, with ritonavir use associated with a higher incidence of toxicity. However, there was no significant difference in hepatotoxicity incidence among the different treatment groups. Chronic viral hepatitis was associated with an increased risk of severe hepatotoxicity among patients prescribed non-ritonavir regimens, but most patients with chronic hepatitis C or B virus infection did not experience significant toxic effects. The use of any protease inhibitor in patients with hepatitis C infection was associated with a 12.2% incidence of severe hepatotoxicity. The study concluded that while ritonavir may increase the risk of severe hepatotoxicity, withholding protease inhibitor therapy from individuals coinfected with hepatitis B or C virus is not justified.

title: Mutations in the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase pathway predict for antitumor activity of the inhibitor PX-866 whereas oncogenic Ras is a dominant predictor for resistance.
text: The novel phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor PX-866 was evaluated against 13 experimental human tumor xenografts derived from various cell lines. Mutations in PI3K (PIK3CA) and loss of PTEN activity were not necessarily predictive of sensitivity to PX-866, while mutant oncogenic Ras was a dominant determinant of resistance, even in tumors with coexisting PIK3CA mutations. The level of PI3K signaling activation, as measured by phosphorylated Ser(473)-Akt, did not predict in vivo antitumor response to PX-866. Reverse-phase protein array analysis revealed that Ras-dependent downstream targets, such as c-Myc and cyclin B, were elevated in cell lines resistant to PX-866 in vivo. Studies using an H-Ras construct showed that mutant Ras can use multiple pathways for tumorigenesis, leading to resistance to PI3K inhibition. The identification of Ras and downstream signaling pathways driving resistance to PI3K inhibition may serve as a guide for patient selection in clinical trials and for the development of rational combinations with other targeted agents.

title: Changing mortality patterns in East and West Germany and Poland. II: short-term trends during transition and in the 1990s.
text:
Objectives:
Examine trends in life expectancy at birth and age-specific mortality patterns in the former German Democratic Republic (GDR) and Poland during the political transition period and throughout the 1990s in both parts of Germany and in Poland.
Methods:
Decompose life expectancy by age and cause of death. Analyze changes in life expectancy during transition using data from 1988/89 and 1990/91 for the GDR and Poland, and examine life expectancy changes after transition based on 1992-97 data for Germany and 1991-96 data for Poland.
Results:
In both the GDR and Poland, male life expectancy at birth declined by almost one year during transition, primarily due to rising death rates from external causes and circulatory diseases. Female life expectancy in Poland deteriorated by 0.3 years, largely attributable to increasing circulatory mortality among the elderly, while in East Germany, rising death rates in children and young adults were nearly balanced by declining circulatory mortality among those over 70. Between 1991/92 and 1996/97, male life expectancy at birth increased by 2.4 years in the former GDR, 1.2 years in the old Federal Republic, and 2.0 years in Poland (women: 2.3, 0.9, and 1.2 years). In East Germany and Poland, the overall improvement was largely due to falling mortality among men aged 40-64, while those over 65 contributed the largest proportion to life expectancy gains in women. The change in deaths among men aged 15-39 accounted for 0.4 of a year to life expectancy at birth in East Germany and Poland, primarily due to greater decreases from external causes. Among those over 40, absolute contributions to changing life expectancy were greater in the former GDR than in the other two entities in both sexes, largely due to circulatory diseases. A persisting East-west life expectancy gap in Germany of 2.1 years in men in 1997 was largely due to external causes, diseases of the digestive system, and circulatory diseases. Higher death rates from circulatory diseases among the elderly largely explain the female life expectancy gap of approximately one year.

title: 0021-972X/06/$15.00/0 The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism 91(3):760–771 Printed in U.S.A. Copyright © 2006 by The Endocrine Society doi: 10.1210/jc.2005-1923 REVIEW: Aromatase Inhibitors for Ovulation Induction
text:
For the past four decades, clomiphene citrate (CC) has been the primary treatment for anovulation in infertile women. However, CC is associated with common side effects, such as antiestrogenic effects on the endometrium and cervix, which can hinder pregnancy success. Additionally, there is a higher risk of multiple pregnancies with CC compared to natural cycles. To address these issues, the concept of aromatase inhibition was proposed as a new method of ovulation induction that could avoid many of CC's adverse effects. This review aims to compare the physiological mechanisms of action and efficacy of CC and aromatase inhibitors (AIs) for ovulation induction.
We conducted a systematic review of published studies comparing CC and AI treatment, either alone or in combination with gonadotropins, for ovulation induction or augmentation. Our search yielded few controlled studies, but pilot and preliminary comparisons suggested that AIs are as effective as CC in inducing ovulation, without the antiestrogenic side effects. AIs also result in lower serum estrogen concentrations and are associated with good pregnancy rates and a lower incidence of multiple pregnancy compared to CC. When combined with gonadotropins for assisted reproductive technologies, AIs reduce the dose of FSH required for optimal follicle recruitment and improve the response to FSH in poor responders.
Preliminary evidence suggests that AIs may replace CC in the future due to their similar efficacy and reduced side effect profile. However, definitive studies in the form of randomized controlled trials comparing CC with AIs are currently lacking. Further research is needed to fully understand the benefits and limitations of AIs for ovulation induction.

title: Patent ductus arteriosus: lack of evidence for common treatments.
text: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a common diagnosis in extremely premature infants, particularly those with lung disease. Despite decades of research, the question of whether the benefits of treatments to prevent ductal patency or promote closure outweigh the risks remains unanswered. The authors tend to avoid using treatments designed to close the PDA. This review highlights three reasons for this cautious approach: the natural tendency of the ductus arteriosus to close spontaneously; the potential adverse effects of persistent ductal patency; and the benefits and risks of treatments for closure.

title: Gene therapy of arthritis with TCR isolated from the inflamed paw.
text:
In recent years, advancements in the treatment of autoimmune diseases have been significantly improved by the use of biological agents. However, some of these biologics are accompanied by severe side effects, such as tuberculosis and other types of infections. As a result, there is a pressing need for non-systemic and lesion-specific methods of delivering therapeutic agents. To address this challenge, we attempted to treat a mouse model of arthritis by using T cells that expressed a regulatory molecule and were specifically targeted to the inflamed paw.
To achieve this, we first identified the TCR alpha-beta genes present in the inflamed paw of mice with collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) through a combination of single-strand chain polymorphism analysis of TCR and single-cell sorting. We identified an expanded clone B47, which is autoreactive but not specific to type II collagen. In vivo, TCR genes from B47-transduced T cells accumulated in the inflamed paw. Injection of cells cotransduced with the B47 and soluble TNFRIg genes resulted in a significant suppression of CIA. The suppression was correlated with the amount of TNFRIg transcripts in the hind paw, rather than the serum concentrations of TNFRIg. Moreover, T cells cotransduced with the B47 and intracellular Foxp3 genes significantly suppressed CIA by reducing the expression of TNF-alpha, IL-17A, and IL-1beta, as well as bone destruction. These cells also suppressed the progression of established CIA. Therefore, immunosuppressive therapy using autoreactive TCRs is a promising therapeutic strategy for arthritis, whether the TCRs are used to deliver soluble or intracellular suppressive molecules.

title: Melatonin: A Mitochondrial Targeting Molecule Involving Mitochondrial Protection and Dynamics
text: Melatonin has been hypothesized to be primarily synthesized within mitochondria. This hypothesis is supported by the recent discovery that aralkylamine N-acetyltransferase/serotonin N-acetyltransferase (AANAT/SNAT) is localized in the mitochondria of oocytes, and isolated mitochondria are capable of generating melatonin. Additionally, it has been postulated that melatonin acts as a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant, accumulating within mitochondria despite a concentration gradient. This is likely facilitated by the presence of mitochondrial melatonin transporters, which mediate active transport of melatonin into mitochondria. Once inside mitochondria, melatonin protects these organelles by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), inhibiting the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP), and activating uncoupling proteins (UCPs). This maintains the optimal mitochondrial membrane potential and preserves mitochondrial functions. Furthermore, melatonin has been shown to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics, reducing mitochondrial fission and elevating fusion. Mitochondrial dynamics exhibit an oscillatory pattern that corresponds to the melatonin circadian secretory rhythm in pinealeocytes and likely in other cells. Recent studies have also demonstrated that melatonin promotes mitophagy and maintains homeostasis of mitochondria.

title: Self-reported health status and access to health services in a sample of prisoners in Italy
text:
In Italy, there has been limited research on the self-reported health status of prisoners, particularly among underserved populations. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted among male prisoners to assess their self-reported health, quality of life, and access to health services.
The study included 908 prisoners who completed a self-administered, anonymous questionnaire covering demographic and detention characteristics, as well as their self-reported health status and quality of life. Of the 650 prisoners who participated in the study, 31.6% and 43.5% reported poor perceived health status and quality of life, respectively. Additionally, 60% of prisoners reported that their health had worsened or greatly worsened during their time in prison.
Older age, lower education, psychiatric disorders, self-reported health problems on prison entry, and suicide attempts within prison were found to be significantly associated with a worse perceived health status. The study also found that prisoners encountered general practitioners an average of six times in the previous year, with the frequency of medical encounters being significantly associated with older age, sentenced prisoners, psychiatric disorders, and self-reported health problems on prison entry.
The findings of the study suggest that prisoners have a perceived poor health status, highlighting the need for specific care needs and health promotion programs. The study emphasizes the importance of addressing the long-term effects of incarceration on prisoners' health and the need for programs to correct risk behaviors and prevent these effects.

title: BH3-only Protein Noxa Is a Mediator of Hypoxic Cell Death Induced by Hypoxia-inducible Factor 1α
text: Hypoxia, a common cause of cellular demise, is implicated in various diseases such as stroke and chronic degenerative disorders. In response to hypoxia, cells exhibit adaptive mechanisms by expressing a range of genes, which enable them to cope with altered metabolic demands, reduce oxygen consumption, and eliminate damaged cells. Using PCR-based suppression subtractive hybridization, we identified the BH3-only Bcl-2 family protein Noxa as a differentially expressed gene in hypoxia. Noxa functions as a mediator of p53-induced apoptosis and is regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α). Our findings demonstrate that suppression of Noxa expression by antisense oligonucleotides protects cells from hypoxia-induced death and reduces infarction volumes in an animal model of ischemia. Additionally, we showed that reactive oxygen species (ROS) and cytochrome c release contribute to Noxa-mediated hypoxic cell death. Overall, our results indicate that Noxa is induced by HIF-1α and plays a crucial role in hypoxic cell death.

title: Neutrophil extracellular chromatin traps connect innate immune response to autoimmunity
text:
Autoantibodies to DNA and histones (chromatin) are the defining antigen specificity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and related musculoskeletal disorders, but the mechanisms responsible for their induction remain unclear. However, the discovery of neutrophil extracellular chromatin traps (NETs) has significantly advanced our understanding of the mechanisms underlying autoimmune diseases. NETs are a conserved feature of innate immune responses to a wide range of microbial pathogens, and they play a crucial role in immobilizing and degrading microbial pathogens at the site of infection.
In the context of autoimmune diseases, NETs have been implicated as a source of nuclear antigens that trigger autoantibody production. While apoptotic bodies have also been proposed as a source of nuclear antigens, the evidence suggests that NETs are a more likely source. Furthermore, the presence of NET chromatin in immune deposits has been implicated in the pathogenesis of glomerulonephritis in SLE and other autoimmune immune complex diseases.
In this review, we critically evaluate the available evidence supporting the role of NETs as a source of nuclear antigens in autoimmunity, and discuss the potential implications of this mechanism in the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases.

title: Bcl2 Regulation by the Melanocyte Master Regulator Mitf Modulates Lineage Survival and Melanoma Cell Viability
text: Kit/SCF signaling and Mitf-dependent transcription are crucial for the development and pigmentation of melanocytes. To identify Mitf-dependent Kit transcriptional targets in primary melanocytes, microarray analysis was conducted. Among the identified targets was BCL2, which, when deleted in its germline form, leads to melanocyte loss and exhibits synergy with Mitf in mice. The regulation of BCL2 by Mitf was confirmed in melanocytes and melanoma cells, as well as through chromatin immunoprecipitation of the BCL2 promoter. Additionally, Mitf regulates BCL2 in osteoclasts, and both Mitf(mi/mi) and Bcl2(-/-) mice display severe osteopetrosis. Disruption of Mitf in melanocytes or melanoma leads to profound apoptosis, which can be rescued by BCL2 overexpression. Notably, primary human melanoma expression microarrays revealed close proximity between MITF and BCL2, providing insight into the essential roles of both Mitf and Bcl2 in the melanocyte lineage and the treatment resistance of melanoma.

title: YOKO HONDA AND SHUJI HONDA 1
text: The daf-2 gene network in Caenorhabditis elegans regulates longevity by controlling the expression of genes involved in antioxidant defense systems. Mutations in the daf-2 gene, which encodes a member of the insulin receptor family, lead to life extension and the formation of a specialized larval stage called the constitutive dauer. Two additional mutations in the clk-1 gene, which is homologous to yeast CAT5/COQ7 and regulates ubiquinone biosynthesis, further enhance life extension and oxidative stress resistance (Oxr). The insulin-like signaling pathway from daf-2 to the daf-16 gene, a homologue of the HNF-3/forkhead transcription factor, regulates the expression of genes involved in antioxidant defense systems, including the sod-3 gene, which encodes Mn-superoxide dismutase (SOD). The daf-2 mutation leads to increased sod-3 gene expression, which is further enhanced by the clk-1 mutation. These findings suggest that the daf-2 gene network controls longevity by regulating the Mn-SOD-associated antioxidant defense system, which plays a role in efficient life maintenance at the dauer stage.

title: Brown Fat and Browning for the Treatment of Obesity and Related Metabolic Disorders
text: Brown fat is a specialized fat depot that can boost metabolism and generate heat. Recent discoveries of active brown fat in adult humans and new transcription factors controlling brown adipocyte differentiation have reignited interest in the field of brown fat research, which is rapidly expanding. Brown fat expansion or activation leads to increased energy expenditure and a negative energy balance in mice, preventing weight gain. Brown fat can also utilize glucose and lipids and improve glucose metabolism and blood lipids, even without weight loss. Exposure to cold temperatures and certain medications can induce the browning of white adipose tissue, transforming it into a more efficient fat-burning tissue. Brown adipocytes that arise from the thermogenic activation of white adipose tissue share characteristics with classical brown adipocytes, such as high mitochondrial content and UCP1 expression, but have a distinct origin and molecular signature. Increasing browning in brown fat may also enhance its overall activity. Human studies have shown that findings in mice can be replicated, making brown fat a promising target for treating obesity and related disorders.

title: Hypoxia-induced energy stress regulates mRNA translation and cell growth.
text: Oxygen (O2) deprivation, or hypoxia, has profound effects on cellular metabolism and growth. Cells can adapt to low O2 levels by activating hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), which plays a crucial role in regulating cellular responses to hypoxia. However, recent studies have shown that hypoxia can also inhibit mRNA translation by suppressing multiple key regulators, including eIF2alpha, eEF2, and the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) effectors 4EBP1, p70S6K, and rpS6, independent of HIF. These effects are mediated by energy starvation and activation of the AMPK/TSC2/Rheb/mTOR pathway, which leads to eEF2 inhibition. Moreover, the long-term effects of hypoxia on cellular bioenergetics and mTOR inhibition can have significant consequences for cellular survival. Interestingly, mutation of the TSC2 tumor suppressor gene can confer a growth advantage to cells by repressing hypoxic mTOR inhibition and hypoxia-induced G1 arrest, highlighting the complex interplay between cellular responses to hypoxia and cellular survival. Overall, eIF2alpha, eEF2, and mTOR inhibition represent important HIF-independent mechanisms of energy conservation that promote cellular survival under low O2 conditions.

title: The dystonia-associated protein torsinA modulates synaptic vesicle recycling.
text: The loss of a glutamic acid residue in the AAA-ATPase torsinA is primarily responsible for early onset autosomal dominant primary dystonia. In this study, we discovered that snapin, which binds SNAP-25 and enhances the association of the SNARE complex with synaptotagmin, interacts with both wild type and mutant torsinA. Snapin co-localized with endogenous torsinA on dense core granules in PC12 cells and was recruited to perinuclear inclusions containing mutant DeltaE-torsinA in neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells. To investigate the role of torsinA in synaptic vesicle recycling, we analyzed synaptic vesicle endocytosis using the lipophilic dye FM1-43 and an antibody directed against an intravesicular epitope of synaptotagmin I. Our findings showed that overexpression of wild type torsinA inhibits synaptic vesicle endocytosis, while overexpression of DeltaE-torsinA increases FM1-43 uptake. Knockdown of snapin and/or torsinA using small interfering RNAs had a similar inhibitory effect on the exo-endocytic process. Additionally, down-regulation of torsinA leads to the persistence of synaptotagmin I on the plasma membrane, which is similar to the effect observed with the overexpression of the DeltaE-torsinA mutant. These findings suggest that torsinA plays a role in regulated exocytosis, and that DeltaE-torsinA exerts its pathological effects through a loss of function mechanism. This may impair neuronal uptake of neurotransmitters, such as dopamine, contributing to the development of dystonic movements.

title: In vivo electroporation in the embryonic mouse central nervous system
text: This protocol outlines a straightforward approach for in vivo electroporation in the nervous system of embryonic mice. By microinjecting DNA into the brain ventricle or spinal cord central canal and subsequently delivering electrical pulses using forceps-type electrodes, efficient gene transfection into the nervous system is achieved. This method allows for the operation on multiple embryos (>10) within a 30-min time frame, with a high survival rate (>90%) and efficient gene expression (>90% of survivors express the transfected genes). Importantly, gene expression in neurons persists for an extended period, even after birth, making this technique suitable for investigating the roles of genes in both embryonic development and higher-order nervous system functions, such as learning.

title: Hierarchical phylogenetic models for analyzing multipartite sequence data.
text:
There is ongoing debate in the field of phylogenetics regarding the most effective approach for incorporating information from multiple sequence datasets in phylogenetic analyses. Two main strategies have been proposed: (1) strict combined-data approaches, which involve concatenating all partitions and estimating a single evolutionary history, and (2) consensus/independence approaches, which involve analyzing each partition independently and then combining the results. However, these methods have limitations, and researchers have developed alternative methods, such as mixtures across the model space of a strict combined-data approach and a priori independent parameters, to address these limitations.
Our research proposes a middle ground approach, which involves constructing a Bayesian hierarchical phylogenetic model. This framework enables researchers to pool information across data partitions to improve the precision of individual parameter estimates while allowing for the estimation and testing of across-partition quantities, such as the distribution from which individual topologies are drawn. We use standard hierarchical priors on continuous evolutionary parameters across partitions, and the structure on topologies varies depending on the research problem. We demonstrate our model with three examples: (1) the evolutionary history of the guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) using alignments of 13 mitochondrial genes, (2) the frequency of horizontal gene transfer using 50 prokaryotic genes, and (3) the evolution of HIV sequences longitudinally sampled from HIV+ patients. Our results show that the hierarchical model provides more precise continuous parameter estimates than an independent parameter approach without losing the salient features of the data.
In conclusion, the debate over how to incorporate information from multipartite sequence data in phylogenetic analyses is ongoing, and our proposed middle ground approach offers a promising solution.
