By constructing a Bayesian hierarchical phylogenetic model, researchers can pool information across data partitions to improve estimate precision while permitting the estimation and testing of across-partition quantities. Our approach has the advantage of being flexible and adaptable to different research problems, and we demonstrate its effectiveness with three examples.

title: Up-to-date catalogues of yeast protein complexes
text:
Gold standard datasets of protein complexes are crucial for inferring and validating protein-protein interactions. Although significant progress has been made in characterizing protein complexes in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, many researchers still rely on the manually curated complexes catalogued by the Munich Information Center of Protein Sequences database. However, this catalogue has become outdated and does not reflect the current state of knowledge. Here, we present two newly curated catalogues of yeast protein complexes: CYC2008 and YHTP2008.
CYC2008 is a comprehensive catalogue of 408 manually curated heteromeric protein complexes supported by small-scale experiments reported in the current literature. This catalogue serves as an up-to-date reference set for biologists interested in discovering protein interactions and complexes. YHTP2008, on the other hand, comprises 400 high-throughput complexes annotated with current literature evidence. Among them, 262 complexes overlap with CYC2008, while 68 complexes have only partial or no overlap. Evidence for interacting subunits is collected for 68 complexes that have only partial or no overlap with CYC2008 complexes, and no literature evidence was found for 100 complexes. Some of these partially supported and unsupported complexes may be interesting candidates for experimental follow-up. Both catalogues are freely available at: <http://wodaklab.org/cyc2008/>.

title: Synergistic Mechanisms of DNA Demethylation during Transition to Ground-State Pluripotency
text: Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) exist in a spectrum of reversible molecular states, ranging from a naive ground state in 2i to metastable embryonic stem cells (ESCs) in serum, to lineage-primed epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs). To investigate the role of DNA methylation (5mC) across these pluripotent states, we mapped genome-wide 5mC and 5-hydroxymethycytosine (5hmC) in multiple PSCs. Ground-state ESCs display an altered distribution of 5mC and 5hmC at regulatory elements, with reduced absolute levels compared to ESCs in serum. In contrast, EpiSCs exhibit increased promoter 5mC and reduced 5hmC, contributing to their developmental restriction. Upon switching to 2i, there is a rapid onset of both the ground-state gene expression program and global DNA demethylation. Mechanistically, repression of de novo methylases by PRDM14 leads to slow kinetics of DNA demethylation, while TET1/TET2-mediated 5hmC conversion enhances the rate and extent of hypomethylation. These processes act synergistically during transition to ground-state pluripotency to establish a robustly hypomethylated state.

title: Febrile seizures in the developing brain result in persistent modification of neuronal excitability in limbic circuits
text: Febrile seizures, which affect approximately 3-5% of infants and young children, are a common occurrence. However, the relationship between these early life seizures and the development of epilepsy later in life has been the subject of ongoing debate. To better understand this association, we employed a novel rat model of complex febrile seizures and patch clamp techniques to investigate the effects of hyperthermia-induced seizures on the hippocampus in immature rats. Our findings revealed a selective and long-lasting increase in inhibitory synaptic transmission in the hippocampus, which persists into adulthood. These alterations in synaptic communication following early life seizures challenge the prevailing view of benign nature of early-life febrile convulsions.

title: Identification of an allele of VAM3/SYP22 that confers a semi-dwarf phenotype in Arabidopsis thaliana.
text: The short stem and midrib (ssm) mutants of Arabidopsis thaliana exhibit both semi-dwarf and wavy leaf phenotypes due to defects in the elongation of stem internodes and leaves. These abnormalities cannot be restored by exogenous phytohormones. Initially identified as a single recessive mutant in the ecotype Columbia (Col-0), genetic crossing experiments revealed that the mutant phenotype is actually restored by another gene that is functional in the ecotype Landsberg erecta (Ler) and not in Col-0. Map-based cloning of the gene responsible for the ssm mutation uncovered a small deletion in the sixth intron of a gene encoding a syntaxin, VAM3/SYP22, which has been implicated in vesicle transport to the vacuole. This mutation leads to a peptide insertion in the deduced VAM3/SYP22 polypeptide sequence due to defective splicing of the shortened sixth intron. Interestingly, comparison of the wild-type Ler genome to the wild-type Col-0 genome revealed a single base pair deletion causing a frameshift mutation in SYP23, a gene with high homology to VAM3/SYP22. These findings suggest that VAM3/SYP22 and SYP23 have overlapping functions and that the vesicle transport mediated by these syntaxins is crucial for shoot morphogenesis.

title: Class Ia MHC-deficient BALB/c mice generate CD8+ T cell-mediated protective immunity against Listeria monocytogenes infection.
text: CD8(+) T cells are essential for immunity against intracellular pathogens like Listeria monocytogenes. In this study, we investigated the protective capacity of class Ib MHC-restricted T cells during L. monocytogenes infection in mice with a reduced number of CD8(+) T cells. We used class Ia MHC-deficient mice, which have a lower number of circulating CD8(+) T cells, to determine the protective potential of class Ib MHC-restricted T cells. We found that C.B10 K(b-/-)D(b-/-) mice, which have a BALB/c genetic background and are more susceptible to Listeria infection, were fully protected against a lethal Listeria infection after immunization with a sublethal dose of the pathogen. Adoptive transfer of Listeria-immune splenocyte subsets into naive K(b-/-)D(b-/-) mice revealed that CD8(+) T cells were the primary immune cells responsible for this protection. A CD8(+) T cell line isolated from a Listeria-infected class Ia MHC-deficient mouse was shown to specifically recognize Listeria-infected cells in vitro and provided significant protection against L. monocytogenes challenge when transferred alone. These findings suggest that even a limited number of class Ib MHC-restricted T cells are sufficient to trigger the rapid recall response required for protection against secondary Listeria infection.

title: Upregulated PD-1 Expression Is Associated with the Development of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, but Not the PD-1.1 Allele of the PDCD1 Gene
text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex autoimmune disease with multisystem involvement, and its genetic inheritance is not fully understood. Programmed death 1 (PD-1), a negative regulator of T cells, has been identified as a candidate gene in SLE pathogenesis. To investigate the role of PD-1 in SLE, we measured the expression levels of PD-1 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 30 SLE patients and 30 healthy controls using flow cytometry and quantitative real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Our results showed that PD-1 expression levels were significantly higher in SLE patients compared to controls. Furthermore, we found that the upregulated PD-1 expression levels in SLE patients were strongly associated with SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) scores. No significant difference was observed between PD-1 expression levels and the variant of the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs36084323. These findings suggest that increased PD-1 expression may contribute to the pathogenesis of SLE, and upregulated PD-1 expression may serve as a biomarker for SLE diagnosis. Additionally, PD-1 inhibitors may be a promising therapeutic approach for treating SLE.

title: Endothelial cell membranes contain podocalyxin--the major sialoprotein of visceral glomerular epithelial cells
text:
Podocalyxin is the primary sialoprotein found in the glycocalyx of glomerular podocytes. In this study, we investigated the extraglomerular localization of podocalyxin using a monospecific antibody obtained through affinity purification of IgG on nitrocellulose transfers of glomerular podocalyxin. Through indirect immunofluorescence, we found that podocalyxin was present in the blood vessels of various organs, including the lung, heart, kidney, small intestine, brain, pancreas, aorta, and peripheral blood vessels in the liver. However, it was not detected in the endothelial cells that line the sinusoids of these organs.
Using immunoelectron microscopy in both pre-embedding and post-embedding procedures, we localized podocalyxin to the luminal membrane domain of endothelial cells. The distribution of podocalyxin was found to be patchy on the endothelial cell surface. To confirm the presence of podocalyxin in lung tissue, we performed immunoblotting using SDS extracts of lung tissue. Our findings indicate that (a) podocalyxin is a ubiquitous component of endothelial plasma membranes, (b) it is specifically restricted to the luminal membrane domain, and (c) its distribution on the endothelial cell surface is uneven.

title: Teratogen-Induced Oxidative Stress Targets Glyceraldehyde-3-Phosphate Dehydrogenase in the Organogenesis Stage Mouse Embryo
text: Exposure of mouse embryos to the teratogen hydroxyurea (HU) during the organogenesis stage leads to the induction of curly tail and limb malformations. Oxidative stress, which results from the interaction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) with polyunsaturated bilipid membranes, contributes to the developmental toxicity of HU. Specifically, the formation of α,β-unsaturated reactive aldehydes, such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), occurs in the embryo following HU exposure. The goal of the current study is to investigate the formation of 4-HNE-protein adducts in the embryo after HU exposure and to identify the proteins targeted. The study found that HU exposure on gestation day 9 in CD1 mice resulted in elevated formation of 4-HNE-protein adducts in the caudal region of the embryo. Interestingly, three of the 4-HNE-modified proteins, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase 2, and aldolase 1, A isoform, are involved in energy metabolism. The study also showed that the formation of 4-HNE-GAPDH protein adducts reduced GAPDH enzymatic activity by 20% and attenuated lactate production by 40%. Furthermore, HU exposure induced the nuclear translocation of GAPDH in the caudal region of exposed embryos, which may be associated with the reactivation of oxidized proteins involved in DNA repair, such as apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease-1, and the stimulation of E1A-associated P300 protein/creb-binding protein (p300/CBP) activity, leading to cell death in a p53-dependent pathway. The study suggests that GAPDH is a redox-sensitive target in the embryo and may play a role in a stress response during development.

title: Recurrent venous thromboembolism and bleeding complications during anticoagulant treatment in patients with cancer and venous thrombosis.
text: A small proportion of patients with deep vein thrombosis (DVT) experience recurrent venous thromboembolic complications or bleeding during anticoagulant treatment, and this risk is higher in patients with cancer. A prospective follow-up study aimed to determine whether patients with cancer have a higher risk of recurrent thromboembolism or bleeding during anticoagulant treatment compared to those without cancer. The study included 842 patients, of whom 181 had known cancer at entry. The 12-month cumulative incidence of recurrent thromboembolism in cancer patients was 20.7% (95% CI, 15.6%-25.8%), compared to 6.8% (95% CI, 3.9%-9.7%) in patients without cancer, resulting in a hazard ratio of 3.2 (95% CI, 1.9-5.4). Similarly, the 12-month cumulative incidence of major bleeding was higher in cancer patients (12.4%, 95% CI, 6.5%-18.2%) compared to patients without cancer (4.9%, 95% CI, 2.5%-7.4%), with a hazard ratio of 2.2 (95% CI, 1.2-4.1). The risk of recurrence and bleeding was found to be related to the severity of cancer and occurred predominantly during the first month of anticoagulant therapy, but could not be explained by sub- or overanticoagulation. The study suggests that cancer patients with venous thrombosis are more likely to develop recurrent thromboembolic complications and major bleeding during anticoagulant treatment, and that these risks are correlated with the extent of cancer. The study highlights the need for new treatment strategies to address these risks.

title: Fitting multilevel models in complex survey data with design weights: Recommendations
text:
BACKGROUND: Multilevel models (MLM) offer a powerful approach for analyzing complex survey data, allowing researchers to account for both individual-level and contextual determinants of public health outcomes. However, there is a lack of summarized guidance on how to fit MLMs in survey data with design weights. Simulation studies have suggested that scaling design weights using two methods can improve the accuracy of MLM estimates. This study aims to evaluate the performance of scaled-weighted and unweighted MLM analyses across various software programs and outcome types.
METHODS: Using data from the 2005-2006 National Survey of Children with Special Health Care Needs (NS-CSHCN), which collected data from children clustered within states, this study compares the performance of scaled-weighted and unweighted MLM analyses across different outcome types (categorical vs. continuous), model types (level-1, level-2, or combined), and software programs (Mplus, MLwiN, and GLLAMM). The study examines the differences between scaled weighted estimates and standard errors, and evaluates the impact of scaling on inferential conclusions.
RESULTS: The results show that scaled weighted estimates and standard errors differed slightly from unweighted analyses, but the differences were minimal and did not lead to different inferential conclusions. Additionally, the study found that there were minimal differences in results across software programs, which increases confidence in the accuracy of the results and inferential conclusions, regardless of software choice.
CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that when using MLMs in survey data with design weights, it is important to scale the weights and use software that properly includes the scaled weights in the estimation process. This study highlights the need for summarized guidance on fitting MLMs in survey data with design weights, and provides evidence that scaling design weights can improve the accuracy of MLM estimates.

title: Functional outcomes of multi-condition collaborative care and successful ageing: results of randomised trial
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of integrated care for chronic physical diseases and depression in reducing disability and improving quality of life among middle-aged and elderly individuals.
Design: A randomized controlled trial comparing multi-condition collaborative care for depression and poorly controlled diabetes and/or risk factors for coronary heart disease with usual care in 14 primary care clinics in Seattle, Washington.
Participants: Patients with diabetes or coronary heart disease, or both, and blood pressure above 140/90 mm Hg, low density lipoprotein concentration >3.37 mmol/L, or glycated haemoglobin 8.5% or higher, and PHQ-9 depression scores of ≥ 10.
Intervention: A 12-month intervention combining self-management support, monitoring of disease control, and pharmacotherapy to control depression, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia.
Main Outcome Measures: Social Role Disability (Sheehan Disability Scale), Global Quality of Life Rating, and World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS-2) scales to measure disabilities in activities of daily living (mobility, self-care, household maintenance).
Results: Of 214 patients enrolled (106 intervention and 108 usual care), disability and quality of life measures were obtained for 97 intervention patients at six months (92%) and 92 at 12 months (87%), and for 96 usual care patients at six months (89%) and 92 at 12 months (85%). Improvements from baseline on the Sheehan Disability Scale (-0.9, 95% confidence interval -1.5 to -0.2; P = 0.006) and global quality of life rating (0.7, 0.2 to 1.2; P = 0.005) were significantly greater at six and 12 months in patients in the intervention group. There was a trend toward greater improvement in disabilities in activities of daily living (-1.5, -3.3 to 0.4; P = 0.10).
Conclusions: Integrated care that covers chronic physical disease and comorbid depression can reduce social role disability and enhance global quality of life.
Trial Registration: Clinical Trials NCT00468676.

title: A Comparison of Cost Effectiveness Using Data from Randomized Trials or Actual Clinical Practice: Selective Cox-2 Inhibitors as an Example
text: The article discusses the limitations of using data from randomized clinical trials (RCTs) in cost-effectiveness analyses, particularly when evaluating the use of selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs). The authors analyzed data from the UK General Practice Research Database (GPRD) to estimate the exposure characteristics and individual probabilities of upper gastrointestinal (GI) events during current exposure to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or coxibs. They developed a basic cost-effectiveness model comparing two alternative strategies: prescription of a conventional NSAID or coxib. The study population included over 1 million patients prescribed conventional NSAIDs or coxibs, and the results showed that only a minority of patients used the drugs long-term and daily, whereas coxib RCTs required daily use for at least 6-9 months. The mean cost of preventing one upper GI event as recorded in GPRD was US$104k (ranging from US$64k with long-term daily use to US$182k with intermittent use), and US$298k for hospitalizations. The mean costs over calendar time were US$58k during 1990-1993 and US$174k during 2002-2005. The authors found that using RCT data rather than GPRD data for event probabilities resulted in significantly higher mean costs, with the VIGOR RCT and CLASS RCT showing mean costs of US$16k and US$20k, respectively. The study highlights the limitations of relying solely on RCT data in cost-effectiveness analyses and the need for external validity in these analyses.

title: 7α, 25-dihydroxycholesterol-mediated activation of EBI2 in immune regulation and diseases
text: In 1993, EBI2, also known as GPR183, was first identified as one of the main genes induced in Burkitt's lymphoma cell line BL41 by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. Later, in 2009, it was discovered that EBI2 plays a crucial role in regulating B cell migration and responses. As a result, an effort was made to find its endogenous ligand. In 2011, two groups reported the identification of 7α, 25-dihydroxyxcholesterol (7α, 25-OHC), an oxysterol, as the likely physiological ligand of EBI2. Subsequent studies further elucidated how 7α, 25-OHC binds to EBI2 and how a gradient of 7α, 25-OHC can be generated in vivo, regulating the migration, activation, and functions of B cells, T cells, dendritic cells (DCs), monocytes/macrophages, and astrocytes. The discovery of 7α, 25-OHC as a G protein-coupled receptor ligand revealed a previously unknown signaling system of oxysterols, a class of molecules with profound biological functions. Dysregulation of oxysterol synthesis or functions is believed to contribute to various diseases, including inflammation, autoimmune diseases, cardiovascular diseases, neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, and metabolic diseases such as diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Therefore, EBI2 may represent a promising target for therapeutic interventions for human diseases.

title: PrimPol Bypasses UV Photoproducts during Eukaryotic Chromosomal DNA Replication
text: DNA damage can hinder the DNA replication machinery, leading to genetic instability. To overcome this challenge, various mechanisms exist to complete genome duplication without a pristine DNA template, but the enzymes involved are not fully understood. Here, we investigate the role of Primase-Polymerase (PrimPol; CCDC111), an archaeal-eukaryotic primase found in eukaryotic cells, in chromosomal DNA replication. Our findings reveal that PrimPol is essential for replication fork progression on damaged DNA templates, particularly those exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light. This is achieved through its ability to catalyze translesion synthesis (TLS) of UV lesions, bypassing the Pol η-dependent pathway. Interestingly, this pathway is not epistatic with the Pol η-dependent pathway, and as a result, PrimPol protects xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) patient cells from UV-induced cytotoxicity. Additionally, we demonstrate that PrimPol is also crucial for efficient replication fork progression during an unperturbed S phase. These findings suggest that PrimPol is a vital player in replication fork progression in eukaryotic cells.

title: The novel immunosuppressive enzyme IL4I1 is expressed by neoplastic cells of several B-cell lymphomas and by tumor-associated macrophages
text: In our previous study, we discovered a strong expression of the IL4I1 gene in primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and identified the protein as a secreted L-phenylalanine oxidase that inhibits T-cell proliferation in vitro. Here, we investigated the expression pattern of IL4I1 protein in 315 human malignancies, including lymphoid and non-lymphoid tumors. Our results showed that IL4I1 expression was frequent in tumors, with tumor-associated macrophages expressing the protein in most cases. IL4I1 was also detected in neoplastic cells from follicular lymphoma, classic and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, and small lymphocytic lymphoma, which are all germinal center derived. Additionally, we found IL4I1-positive tumor cells in rare cases of solid cancers, such as mesothelioma. Enzymatic activity was observed in parallel with protein expression, suggesting that IL4I1 is functional in vivo. Depending on the tumor type, IL4I1 may impact different infiltrating lymphocyte populations, which can have consequences on tumor evolution. In the case of follicular lymphoma cells, which are susceptible to antitumor cytotoxic T cells killing but depend on interactions with local T helper cells for survival, high levels of IL4I1 expression were associated with the absence of bone marrow involvement and a better outcome. These findings suggest that IL4I1 may be a useful prognosis factor.

title: Poor prognosis in carcinoma is associated with a gene expression signature of aberrant PTEN tumor suppressor pathway activity.
text: The future of cancer management lies in pathway-specific therapy, and the oncogenic phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is a prime target. Despite its prevalence in solid tumors, there is currently no reliable test for PI3K pathway activation in human tumors. However, by taking advantage of the observation that loss of the negative regulator PTEN leads to robust activation of the PI3K pathway, we developed and validated a microarray gene expression signature for immunohistochemistry (IHC)-detectable PTEN loss in breast cancer (BC). Our findings indicate that PTEN mRNA levels are the primary determinant of PTEN protein levels in BC, and some PTEN IHC-positive BCs exhibited the signature of PTEN loss, which was associated with moderately reduced PTEN mRNA levels and specific types of PIK3CA mutations and/or amplification of HER2. This signature is more sensitive than PTEN IHC for identifying tumors with pathway activation, and its prediction of poor patient outcome in independent data sets of breast, prostate, and bladder carcinoma highlights its clinical utility. Furthermore, stathmin, encoded by the signature gene STMN1, was found to be an accurate IHC marker of the signature and had prognostic significance in BC. Stathmin also demonstrated pathway-pharmacodynamic activity in vitro and in vivo, suggesting that the signature or its components may be useful tests for stratifying patients for anti-PI3K pathway therapy and monitoring therapeutic efficacy. This study underscores the enormous potential impact of pathway inhibition on patient survival, particularly in metastatic cancer, highlighting the urgent need for further research and clinical application of these findings.

title: Suppression of subtelomeric VSG switching by Trypanosoma brucei TRF requires its TTAGGG repeat-binding activity
text:
Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite responsible for human African trypanosomiasis, has evolved a strategy to evade the host immune system by constantly changing its major surface antigen (VSG) in the bloodstream of its mammalian host. VSGs are expressed from subtelomeric loci, and previous studies have shown that telomere proteins TbTIF2 and TbRAP1 play important roles in VSG switching and VSG silencing regulation, respectively. Our latest discovery reveals that another telomere protein, TbTRF, also plays a critical role in VSG switching regulation.
We have solved the structure of the DNA-binding Myb domain of TbTRF, which folds into a conserved helix-loop-helix structure similar to that of mammalian TRF proteins. Surprisingly, the TbTRF Myb domain can tolerate the bulky J base found in T. brucei telomere DNA, and its DNA-binding affinity is not affected by the presence of J both in vitro and in vivo. Furthermore, we found that point mutations in the Myb domain of TbTRF that reduce its in vivo DNA-binding affinity also lead to increased VSG switching frequencies, indicating that the telomere DNA-binding activity of TbTRF is essential for its role in VSG switching regulation.
In summary, our findings suggest that TbTRF plays a critical role in regulating VSG switching in T. brucei by binding to telomere DNA and modulating the expression of VSGs. The structure of the TbTRF Myb domain provides insights into the mechanism of VSG switching regulation and highlights the importance of telomere DNA-binding proteins in the parasite's evasion strategy.

title: CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity eliminates primary tumor cells in metastatic melanoma through high MHC class II expression and can be enhanced by inhibitory receptor blockade
text: Metastatic melanoma is a rapidly progressing and deadly disease with limited treatment options. Immunotherapy based on tumor-targeting cytotoxic T cell responses holds promise, and we investigated the potential of using CD4+ cytotoxic T cells in this context. We also examined the regulatory mechanisms that control CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Our findings revealed that CD4+ cytotoxic T cells from metastatic melanoma patients exhibit elevated frequencies compared to healthy controls and can kill autologous tumor cells independently of CD8+ T cells. However, several restrictive factors were identified, including the requirement for high MHC class II expression on melanoma cells, which was not satisfied in a subset of melanomas. Additionally, the granzyme B and perforin release by activated CD4+ cytotoxic T cells was reduced after coculturing with autologous melanoma cells, which exhibited low LAMP-1 expression and low granzyme B and perforin secretion in the supernatant. These findings suggest that inhibitory mechanisms are present to suppress CD4+ cytotoxic T cells. Interestingly, blockade of PD-1 and CTLA-4 enhanced the cytolytic activity of CD4+ T cells, but this effect was only observed in MHC class II high melanomas and not in MHC class II low melanomas. Overall, our study demonstrates that CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity can eliminate primary melanoma cells, but the efficacy depends on MHC class II expression.

title: The epidemiology and iatrogenic transmission of hepatitis C virus in Egypt: a Bayesian coalescent approach.
text: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a significant contributor to liver cancer and cirrhosis, with Egypt possibly having the highest prevalence worldwide. In this study, we utilize a novel Bayesian inference framework to estimate the transmission dynamics of HCV in Egypt by analyzing viral gene sequences from sampled individuals. Our findings reveal that the number of HCV infections in Egypt experienced rapid exponential growth between 1930 and 1955, providing strong genetic evidence that the Egyptian HCV epidemic was initiated and spread through extensive antischistosomiasis injection campaigns. Although the transmission rate has decreased since then, we predict that HCV will continue to be prevalent in Egypt for several decades. Our combined population genetic and epidemiological analysis provides detailed estimates of historical changes in Egyptian HCV prevalence, which are consistent with a demographic scenario specified a priori. Moreover, our results offer an objective test of inference methods based on the coalescent process.

title: Improving population representation through geographic health information systems: mapping the MURDOCK study.
text: This paper explores methods for evaluating and optimizing recruitment strategies to ensure that study populations are representative of the target area. We apply these methods to the Measurement to Understand Reclassification of Disease of Cabarrus/Kannapolis (MURDOCK) study, a longitudinal population health study focusing on Kannapolis and Cabarrus County, NC. Although efforts have been made to create a representative participant registry, biases in recruitment are unavoidable. By geospatially referencing participants at entry, we can monitor and improve recruitment efforts. We assess the representativeness of the MURDOCK participant population using chi-squared tests compared to 2010 Census data for the entire 18 ZIP code catchment area and individual Census tracts. A logistic regression model is fit to identify Census tracts with low recruitment, defined as fewer than 56 participants from those tracts. We also calculate the median distance to the enrollment site and find that tracts with low recruitment rates have higher minority and younger populations, suggesting targeted recruitment strategies. Additionally, we find that areas farther away from enrollment sites have lower representation, indicating that distance to the site may be a barrier. These findings have broader implications for improving recruitment efforts and representative sampling in other population-based studies.

title: Haplotype-based variant detection from short-read sequencing
text: To directly detect haplotypes from short-read DNA sequencing data, current small-variant detection methods need to be modified. Here, we propose a Bayesian statistical framework that can effectively model multiallelic loci across sets of individuals with varying copy number. We then detail the implementation of this framework in a haplotype-based variant detector, FreeBayes.

title: Longitudinal Genome-Wide Association of Cardiovascular Disease Risk Factors in the Bogalusa Heart Study
text:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, and recent genome-wide association studies (GWA) have identified numerous loci associated with CVD risk factors in adults. However, it remains unclear whether these loci predict trait levels at all ages, how they contribute to the development of CVD risk factors over time, or whether they could be used to identify individuals who are pre-symptomatic and provide the opportunity for preventive measures before disease onset.
To address these questions, we conducted a GWA study on participants in the longitudinal Bogalusa Heart Study (BHS) and characterized the association between genetic factors and the development of CVD risk factors from childhood to adulthood. We identified 7 genome-wide significant associations involving CVD risk factors, two of which have been previously reported. We then tested these regions for replication in the Young Finns Study (YF) and found two strong associations: rs247616 in CETP with HDL levels (combined P = 9.7 x 10(-24)), and rs445925 at APOE with LDL levels (combined P = 8.7 x 10(-19)).
Our findings indicate that SNPs identified in adult cross-sectional studies tend to have age-independent effects in the BHS, with effect sizes consistent with previous reports. Additionally, we found that previously identified variants were associated with adult trait levels above and beyond those seen in childhood, but variants with time-dependent effects were also promising predictors.
Our study is the first GWA study to evaluate the role of common genetic variants in the development of CVD risk factors in children as they advance through adulthood, highlighting the utility of using longitudinal studies to identify genetic predictors of adult traits in children.

title: Actin and serum response factor transduce physical cues from the microenvironment to regulate epidermal stem cell fate decisions
text: Homeostasis of the epidermis relies on a balance between stem cell renewal and differentiation, which is regulated by external signals from the extracellular matrix (ECM). To investigate the underlying pathways, we employed a cutting-edge approach of creating individualized microenvironments for single cells, allowing for precise control of variables. Using micropatterned surfaces, we identified the signaling pathways that trigger human epidermal stem cells to differentiate upon restricted ECM contact. Notably, keratinocytes remained rounded on small islands (20 μm in diameter) and differentiated at a higher frequency compared to cells that could spread on larger islands (50 μm in diameter). Differentiation did not depend on ECM composition or density, but rather, the actin cytoskeleton mediated shape-induced differentiation by regulating serum response factor (SRF) transcriptional activity. We found that SRF and its co-factor MAL play a crucial role in differentiation, with SRF knockdown or MAL knockdown inhibiting differentiation, while overexpression of MAL stimulated SRF activity and involucrin expression. Additionally, we discovered that SRF target genes FOS and JUNB are also essential for differentiation, with c-Fos mediating serum responsiveness, and JunB being regulated by actin and MAL. Our findings demonstrate how biophysical cues are translated into transcriptional responses that determine epidermal cell fate.

title: Reproducibility and automatic measurement of QT dispersion.
text: This study evaluated the reproducibility of QT dispersion measurements obtained from abnormal electrocardiograms (ECGs) in patients with previous myocardial infarction, using both observer-based and automated methods. The study included 70 patients and used standard 12-lead ECGs recorded at 25 mm/s. The ECGs were digitized and analyzed using specialized software that allowed for either manual ( observer-based) or automated (algorithm-based) measurements. The results showed excellent reproducibility for the RR interval (mean absolute error 3-4 ms, relative error 0.3-0.5%), good reproducibility for the mean QT interval (intrasubject error 6 ms, relative error 1.4%, interobserver error 7 ms, relative error 1.8%), and moderate reproducibility for the QTc dispersion (intrasubject error 12 ms, 17.3%, interobserver error 15 ms, 22.1%, observers' vs automatic measurement errors 30-28 ms, 35.4-31.9%). However, the reproducibility of QT dispersion measurements was found to be limited due to the difficulty in measuring the most challenging QT intervals, which hinders its clinical usefulness as a predictor of events. Any automated system must be able to recognize both common and difficult T wave morphologies to be effective in measuring QT dispersion.

title: Inhibition of LSD1 sensitizes glioblastoma cells to histone deacetylase inhibitors.
text:
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a particularly aggressive brain tumor that remains a significant clinical challenge despite advances in cancer therapy. Despite efforts to improve patient outcomes, there has been little change in survival rates over the past decade. Enzymes involved in epigenetic alterations have emerged as promising targets for cancer therapy due to their critical roles in cellular processes that contribute to oncogenesis. HDAC inhibitors have shown moderate success in treating GBM, but the underlying mechanisms of their action are not fully understood.
Our study aimed to investigate the effects of inhibiting LSD1, a lysine-specific demethylase, in combination with HDAC inhibitors on GBM cell lines. We found that co-inhibition of LSD1 and HDACs resulted in increased apoptosis in GBM cells, with the most significant effects observed in cells treated with both inhibitors. To validate these findings, we used pharmacological inhibition of LSD1 with tranylcypromine and observed synergistic apoptotic cell death in GBM cells. In contrast, normal human astrocytes were not affected by this combination treatment.
Our results suggest that LSD1 and HDACs cooperate to regulate key pathways of cell death in GBM cell lines, but not in normal cells. These findings validate the use of combined LSD1 and HDAC inhibitors as a potential therapeutic approach for GBM. Further investigation into the mechanisms underlying this synergy may lead to the development of more effective and targeted cancer therapies.

title: Challenges for malaria elimination in Zanzibar: pyrethroid resistance in malaria vectors and poor performance of long-lasting insecticide nets
text:
BACKGROUND: Long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) and indoor residual house spraying (IRS) are the primary interventions for controlling malaria vectors in Zanzibar. The aim of this study was to assess the resistance status of malaria vectors to the insecticides used in LLINs and IRS and to evaluate the durability and efficacy of LLINs on the island.
METHODS: Mosquitoes were collected from Pemba and Unguja islands in 2010-2011 for use in World Health Organization (WHO) susceptibility tests. One hundred and fifty LLINs were collected from households on Unguja Island and their physical state was recorded. The LLINs were then tested for efficacy and total insecticide content.
RESULTS: Species identification revealed that over 90% of the Anopheles gambiae complex was An. arabiensis, with a small number of An. gambiae sensu stricto and An. merus present. Susceptibility tests showed that An. arabiensis on Pemba was resistant to the pyrethroids used in LLINs and IRS. Mosquitoes from Unguja Island, however, were fully susceptible to all pyrethroids tested. A physical examination of 150 LLINs showed that two-thirds were damaged after only three years in use. All used nets had a significantly lower (p < 0.001) mean permethrin concentration of 791.6 mg/m2 compared to 944.2 mg/m2 for new nets. Their efficacy decreased significantly against both susceptible An. gambiae s.s. colony mosquitoes and wild-type mosquitoes from Pemba after just six washes (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The sustainability of the gains achieved in malaria control in Zanzibar is seriously threatened by the resistance of malaria vectors to pyrethroids and the short-lived efficacy of LLINs. This study highlights that even in relatively well-resourced and logistically manageable areas like Zanzibar, malaria elimination will be challenging to achieve with the current control measures.

title: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen acts as a cytoplasmic platform controlling human neutrophil survival
text: Neutrophil apoptosis, a crucial process in resolving inflammation, is not fully understood at the molecular level. In this study, we uncover a survival pathway controlled by proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), a nuclear factor involved in DNA replication and repair of proliferating cells. We found that mature neutrophils, despite their inability to proliferate, express high levels of PCNA in their cytosol, which is constitutively associated with procaspases. Interestingly, cytosolic PCNA abundance decreased during apoptosis, and increased during exposure to the survival factor granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). Peptides derived from the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, which compete with procaspases to bind PCNA, triggered neutrophil apoptosis, suggesting that specific modification of PCNA protein interactions affects neutrophil survival. Moreover, overexpression of PCNA rendered neutrophil-differentiated PLB985 myeloid cells more resistant to TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand- or gliotoxin-induced apoptosis, while a decrease in PCNA expression after PCNA small interfering RNA transfection sensitized these cells to apoptosis. Finally, a mutation in the PCNA interdomain-connecting loop, the binding site for many partners, significantly decreased the PCNA-mediated antiapoptotic effect. These findings identify PCNA as a regulator of neutrophil lifespan, highlighting a novel target to potentially modulate pathological inflammation.

title: Development of the Human Infant Intestinal Microbiota
text: Immediately after birth, a new microbial ecosystem is established in a human being's gastrointestinal tract, a universal and essential part of human biology. However, the process of this ecosystem's development, including the sources of the microbes, how it varies from one infant to another, and its impact on human physiology, growth, and disease, is still poorly understood. To investigate these questions, we designed a microarray to detect and quantify the small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA) gene sequences of various bacterial species and taxonomic groups. Using this microarray, along with sequencing of cloned libraries of PCR-amplified SSU rDNA, we analyzed the microbial communities in an average of 26 stool samples from 14 healthy, full-term infant participants, including a pair of dizygotic twins, at defined intervals throughout the first year of life. To investigate the origins of the infant microbiota, we also profiled vaginal and milk samples from most of the mothers, as well as stool samples from all of the mothers, most of the fathers, and two siblings. Our findings revealed that the composition and temporal patterns of the microbial communities varied significantly from baby to baby, with distinct features of each baby's microbial community recognizable for intervals of weeks to months. The striking parallel temporal patterns of the twins suggested that incidental environmental exposures play a major role in determining the unique characteristics of each baby's microbial community. By the end of the first year of life, the idiosyncratic microbial ecosystems in each baby had converged towards a profile characteristic of the adult gastrointestinal tract.

title: Combinatorial modulation of galP and glk gene expression for improved alternative glucose utilization
text:
Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) is a crucial precursor for anaerobic production of succinate and malate. However, inactivating PEP/carbohydrate phosphotransferase systems (PTS) can increase PEP availability, but the resulting strain may have a low glucose utilization rate. To enhance anaerobic glucose utilization rate for efficient production of succinate and malate, combinatorial modulation of galactose permease (galP) and glucokinase (glk) gene expression was carried out in the chromosome of an Escherichia coli strain with inactivated PTS.
To construct libraries of artificial regulatory parts, including promoter and messenger RNA stabilizing region (mRS), λ-Red recombination was used in the E. coli chromosome in front of the β-galactosidase gene (lacZ). Most of the regulatory parts selected from the mRS library had constitutive activity under different cultivation conditions. A one-step recombination method was then employed to modulate galP and glk gene expression with different regulatory parts. Glucose utilization rates of the strains modulated with either galP or glk increased, and the rates showed a positive correlation with the expression strength of both genes. Combinatorial modulation had a synergistic effect on glucose utilization rate. The highest glucose utilization rate (1.64 g/L h) was 10-fold higher than that of the PTS-deficient strain and 39% higher than the wild-type E. coli. These modulated strains can be used for efficient anaerobic production of succinate and malate.

title: Matrix eQTL: Ultra fast eQTL analysis via large matrix operations
text:
Expression Quantitative Trait Loci (eQTL) mapping is the process of identifying specific genomic regions that influence the expression of genes. This technique is used to study the regulatory mechanisms of normal tissues and to identify genetic factors contributing to complex diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and cystic fibrosis. With the advent of high-throughput genomic and transcriptomic data, eQTL analysis has become increasingly complex, requiring the analysis of millions of SNPs and thousands of transcripts across hundreds of samples. This computational challenge has limited the popularity of eQTL analysis, often forcing researchers to focus on a subset of transcripts and SNPs. However, with the availability of larger genotype and gene expression datasets, there is a growing need for fast and efficient eQTL analysis tools.
To address this need, we have developed a new method called Matrix eQTL, which uses linear models to efficiently analyze large-scale eQTL datasets. Matrix eQTL can model and test for association using both linear regression and ANOVA models, and can include covariates to account for factors such as population structure, gender, and clinical variables. Additionally, it supports testing of heteroscedastic models and models with correlated errors.
In our experiments, Matrix eQTL was found to be thousands of times faster than existing popular software for QTL/eQTL analysis. This makes it an ideal tool for analyzing large-scale eQTL datasets. Matrix eQTL is implemented as both Matlab and R packages, allowing it to be easily run on Windows, Mac OS, and Linux systems. The software is freely available at the following address: <http://www.bios.unc.edu/research/genomic_software/Matrix_eQTL>.

title: The structure of DdrB from Deinococcus: a new fold for single-stranded DNA binding proteins
text: Deinococcus spp. have gained recognition for their remarkable ability to rapidly repair genomic damage caused by exposure to high levels of ionizing radiation or desiccation. Despite being first characterized over 50 years ago, the underlying mechanism of this repair process remains poorly understood. In this study, we report the 2.8 Å structure of DdrB, a unique single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein found only in Deinococcus spp. DdrB forms a pentameric ring that selectively binds to single-stranded DNA, but not double-stranded DNA. Surprisingly, the crystal structure of DdrB reveals a novel fold that is distinct from all other single-stranded binding (SSB) proteins previously characterized. The discovery of this unique ssDNA binding function suggests that DdrB may play a more specialized role in damage recovery, potentially involving protein recruitment or DNA architecture maintenance. We discuss possible mechanisms of DdrB action in damage repair.

title: N348I in the Connection Domain of HIV-1 Reverse Transcriptase Confers Zidovudine and Nevirapine Resistance
text:
Background:
The catalytically active 66-kDa subunit of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) reverse transcriptase (RT) is composed of DNA polymerase, connection, and ribonuclease H (RNase H) domains. While most known RT inhibitor resistance mutations have been identified in the polymerase domain, the connection and RNase H domains are not routinely analyzed in clinical samples. In this study, we aimed to investigate the in vivo relevance of an N348I mutation in the RT connection domain and its role in drug resistance.
Methods and Findings:
We analyzed the prevalence of N348I in clinical isolates, its emergence under selective drug pressure, and its association with changes in viral load, specific drug treatment, and known drug resistance mutations from the Centre's database. N348I increased in prevalence from 1% in treatment-naive individuals to 12.1% in treatment-experienced patients (p = 7.7 x 10-12). N348I emerged early in therapy and was highly associated with thymidine analogue mutations (TAMs), lamivudine resistance mutations M184V/I, and non-nucleoside RTI (NNRTI) resistance mutations K103N and Y181C/I. The association with TAMs and NNRTI resistance mutations was consistent with the selection of N348I in patients treated with regimens containing both zidovudine and nevirapine. The appearance of N348I was associated with a significant increase in viral load, which was as large as the viral load increases observed for any of the TAMs. Introduction of N348I into HIV-1 molecular clones with different genetic backbones showed that it decreased zidovudine susceptibility 2- to 4-fold, and combined with TAMs, it also decreased susceptibility to nevirapine and efavirenz. Biochemical analyses of recombinant RT containing N348I provided supporting evidence for its role in zidovudine and NNRTI resistance and gave some insight into the molecular mechanism of resistance.

title: Dual Targeting of PDGFRα and FGFR1 Displays Synergistic Efficacy in Malignant Rhabdoid Tumors
text: The subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex are frequently mutated in a sizable proportion of human cancers. Specifically, malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs), which are aggressive and lethal pediatric cancers, often exhibit a deficiency in the SWI/SNF subunit SMARCB1. To investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms in MRTs, we employed an integrated molecular profiling and chemical biology approach. Our findings revealed that the receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) PDGFRα and FGFR1 are coactivated in MRT cells, and that dual blockade of these receptors exhibits synergistic efficacy. Inhibitor combinations targeting both receptors and the dual inhibitor ponatinib effectively suppress the AKT and ERK1/2 signaling pathways, leading to apoptosis. Remarkably, MRT cells that have developed resistance to the PDGFRα inhibitor pazopanib are susceptible to FGFR inhibitors. Our study also demonstrated that PDGFRα levels are regulated by SMARCB1 expression, and clinical specimens were found to express both PDGFRα and FGFR1 in rhabdoid tumor patients. These findings support a therapeutic strategy in cancers with SWI/SNF deficiencies by exploiting the coactivation dependencies of RTKs.

title: A nano-positioning system for macromolecular structural analysis
text: Frequently, the positions of flexible domains within macromolecules or complexes cannot be determined using standard structural biology techniques. To address this challenge, we developed a method that leverages probabilistic data analysis to combine single-molecule measurements with X-ray crystallography data. This approach not only provides the most likely position of a fluorescent dye molecule attached to the domain but also generates a three-dimensional probability distribution that reflects the experimental uncertainty. As a result, single-pair fluorescence resonance energy transfer measurements can now be used as a quantitative tool for investigating the position and dynamics of flexible domains within macromolecular complexes. We applied this method to determine the position of the 5′ end of the nascent RNA exiting transcription elongation complexes of yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) RNA polymerase II and investigated the influence of transcription factor IIB on the position of the RNA.

title: Tumor-associated macrophages correlate with the clinicopathological features and poor outcomes via inducing epithelial to mesenchymal transition in oral squamous cell carcinoma
text:
BACKGROUND:
Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of cancer cells play crucial roles in the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). However, the role of TAMs in inducing EMT in OSCC remains unclear.
RESULTS:
We investigated the expression of macrophage markers CD68 and CD163, epithelial marker E-cadherin, and mesenchymal marker vimentin in 127 OSCC patients using semi-quantitative immunohistochemistry. Our findings revealed that CD68 and CD163 expression was not limited to infiltrating TAMs but was also detected in cancer cells themselves. High levels of CD68-positive macrophages were associated with poor overall survival, while the expression of CD163 in both macrophages and cancer cells was linked to poor overall survival and had a significant prognostic impact in OSCC. Notably, the expression of CD163 in cancer cells was significantly related to E-cadherin and vimentin. Furthermore, incubation of TAMs-conditioned medium led to a fibroblast-like appearance of cancer cells (HN4, HN6, and SCC9) accompanied by decreased/increased expression of E-cadherin/vimentin, which were correlated with enhanced migratory and invasive abilities.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings suggest that TAMs can promote EMT in OSCC, contributing to the progression of oral cancer.

title: Geometric cues for directing the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells.
text: Significant research has been dedicated to understanding the factors that influence the lineage commitment of stem cells. This study demonstrates that cell shape, independent of soluble factors, has a significant impact on the differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from bone marrow. When exposed to competing soluble differentiation signals, cells cultured in rectangles with increasing aspect ratio and in shapes with pentagonal symmetry but with different subcellular curvature, and with each occupying the same area, display different adipogenesis and osteogenesis profiles. The results reveal that geometric features that increase actomyosin contractility promote osteogenesis and are consistent with the in vivo characteristics of the microenvironment of the differentiated cells. Pharmacological agents that disrupt the cytoskeleton modulate shape-based trends in lineage commitment, verifying the critical role of focal adhesion and myosin-generated contractility during differentiation. Microarray analysis and pathway inhibition studies suggest that contractile cells promote osteogenesis by enhancing c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) and extracellular related kinase (ERK1/2) activation in conjunction with elevated wingless-type (Wnt) signaling. Overall, this work highlights the role that geometric shape cues can play in orchestrating the mechanochemical signals and paracrine/autocrine factors that direct MSCs to appropriate fates.

title: Amyloid accumulation is a late event in sporadic Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in nontransgenic rats
text: The amyloid cascade hypothesis proposes that the deposition of the amyloid beta (Aβ) peptide in the brain is a pivotal event in the onset of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, recent findings suggest that amyloid toxicity may not be the primary cause of sporadic AD, which leads to cognitive decline. Using accelerated senescence nontransgenic OXYS rats, we investigated the timing of Aβ aggregation in relation to other age-dependent changes in the brain. Our results showed that increases in Aβ1-42 levels and extracellular Aβ deposits occur later than synaptic losses, neuronal cell death, mitochondrial structural abnormalities, and hyperphosphorylation of the tau protein. We identified genetic variants associated with the risk of either late-onset or early-onset AD, including App, Apoe4, Bace1, Psen1, Psen2, and Picalm. Our findings indicate that OXYS rats may serve as a model for sporadic AD. It is possible that multiple age-related pathological processes may precede the toxic amyloid accumulation, which in turn triggers the final stage of the sporadic form of AD and becomes a hallmark event of the disease.

title: Estimating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol by the Friedewald equation is adequate for classifying patients on the basis of nationally recommended cutpoints.
text: In this study, we compared the accuracy of estimated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol values obtained using the Friedewald formula (total cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol minus VLDL cholesterol, estimated as triglycerides divided by 5) with those obtained through lipoprotein fractionation in a sample of 4736 individuals. Our findings showed that when triglycerides were less than 2.0 g/L, more than 90% of estimated LDL values were within +/- 10% of the measured values. However, this proportion decreased to 72% and 39% at triglyceride concentrations of 2.0-4.0 g/L and 4.0-6.0 g/L, respectively. Additionally, we found that LDL values derived from an alternative formula, which estimates VLDL as triglycerides divided by 6, were even less accurate. Nevertheless, the use of estimated LDL for risk classification based on the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel cutpoints of 1.30 and 1.60 g/L was considered acceptable. At triglyceride concentrations less than or equal to 5.0 g/L, 88% of classifications based on estimated LDL were concordant with those by measured LDL. Only 11% of classifications were shifted across one cutpoint, and fewer than 1% of classifications were misclassified two cutpoints high. Refinements in the estimation model did not substantially improve LDL estimation or concordance of risk classification.

title: Conditional Kif3a ablation causes abnormal hedgehog signaling topography, growth plate dysfunction, and excessive bone and cartilage formation during mouse skeletogenesis.
text: The motor protein Kif3a and primary cilia play crucial roles in regulating developmental processes, particularly in the formation of the cranial base and synchondroses. However, the specific mechanisms by which they contribute to these processes are not fully understood. To investigate, we generated mice lacking Kif3a in cartilage and focused on the cranial base and synchondroses. Our findings revealed that Kif3a deficiency led to growth retardation and dysmorphogenesis of the cranial base, which were evident through anatomical and micro-computed tomography (microCT) analysis in neonatal animals. Additionally, Kif3a deficiency altered the growth plate organization and function of synchondroses, with the severity of these changes increasing over time. By postnatal day (P)7, mutant growth plates displayed abnormal zones of chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy, characterized by strong collagen II (Col2a1) gene expression but minimal expression of Indian hedgehog (Ihh), collagen X (Col10a1), vascular endothelial growth factor (Vegf), matrix metalloproteinase-13 (Mmp13), and osterix (Sp7). Concurrently, unexpected developmental events occurred in perichondrial tissues, including excessive intramembranous ossification along the perichondrial border and the formation of ectopic cartilage masses. To identify the underlying mechanisms, we analyzed hedgehog signaling topography and intensity in mutant growth plates and perichondrial tissues, using the expression of the hedgehog effectors Patched 1 and Gli1, as well as the hedgehog-binding cell-surface component syndecan 3. Our findings revealed that hedgehog signaling was feeble within mutant growth plates as early as P0, but was actually higher and widespread in mutant perichondrial tissues. Finally, we studied postnatal mice deficient in Ihh in cartilage, which displayed minimal cranial base defects compared to Kif3a-deficient mice. In summary, Kif3a and primary cilia contribute uniquely to cranial base development and synchondrosis growth plate function, leading to abnormal topography of hedgehog signaling, growth plate dysfunction, and unphysiologic responses and processes in perichondrial tissues, including ectopic cartilage formation and excessive intramembranous ossification.

title: Morin Attenuates Ovalbumin-Induced Airway Inflammation by Modulating Oxidative Stress-Responsive MAPK Signaling.
text:
Asthma is a common inflammatory disease characterized by airway hyperresponsiveness, inflammation, and remodeling. Morin, a bioactive compound derived from certain plant species, has shown promise in reducing inflammation in various conditions. However, its impact on pulmonary diseases, particularly asthma, remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether morin can alleviate airway inflammation in chronic asthma by modulating oxidative stress.
In vivo experiments involved administering morin or dexamethasone to ovalbumin-sensitized mice before challenge. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and lung tissues were collected for cell counting, histological analysis, and protein detection. In vitro, human bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) were exposed to tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) and the supernatant was collected for protein analysis.
Severe inflammation and remodeling were observed in the airways of the sensitized mice. Treatment with morin significantly attenuated the infiltration of inflammatory cells into the BALF and around the respiratory tracts and vessels. Morin also reduced goblet cell hyperplasia and collagen deposition/fibrosis, and dose-dependently inhibited the increases in IgE, TNF-α, interleukin- (IL-) 4, IL-13, matrix metalloproteinase-9, and malondialdehyde. In human BECs challenged with TNF-α, morin consistently decreased the levels of proteins such as eotaxin-1, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, IL-8, and intercellular adhesion molecule-1. Western blotting and 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein assay revealed that morin abolished the increases in intracellular ROS and MAPK phosphorylation, suggesting that ROS/MAPK signaling contributes to the relief of airway inflammation.
Our findings indicate for the first time that morin alleviates airway inflammation in chronic asthma, likely through the oxidative stress-responsive MAPK pathway. This suggests that morin may be a potent agent for asthma management.

title: Spontaneous autoimmunity prevented by thymic expression of a single self-antigen
text: The expression of self-antigens in the thymus is believed to play a crucial role in the deletion of autoreactive T cells, ensuring the body's unresponsiveness to its own tissues. The Autoimmune regulator (Aire) gene, which is defective in autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, has been shown to promote thymic expression of self-antigens. However, a direct link between specific thymic self-antigens and a single autoimmune phenotype in this model has been elusive. Our findings reveal that autoimmune eye disease in aire-deficient mice develops as a result of the loss of thymic expression of a single eye antigen, interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP). Moreover, we demonstrate that lack of IRBP expression solely in the thymus, even in the presence of aire expression, is sufficient to trigger spontaneous eye-specific autoimmunity. These results suggest that the failure of thymic expression of a selective single self-antigen can lead to organ-specific autoimmune disease in otherwise self-tolerant individuals.

title: Preventing bacterial DNA release and absent in melanoma 2 inflammasome activation by a Legionella effector functioning in membrane trafficking.
text:
Legionella pneumophila, the pathogen responsible for Legionnaires' disease, resides within a specialized membrane structure called the Legionella-containing vacuole (LCV). The LCV is protected from fusion with lysosomes, allowing the bacteria to replicate efficiently within host macrophages. To facilitate this process, L. pneumophila employs a type IVB secretion system called Dot/Icm. One of the key effectors of this system is the protein SdhA, which plays a crucial role in preventing host cell death and promoting bacterial growth within macrophages.
Our studies have shown that the absence of SdhA leads to increased activation of caspase-1 and the secretion of interleukin-1β (IL-1β), as well as macrophage pyroptosis during Legionella infection. These inflammasome activation phenotypes are independent of the established flagellin-NAIP5-NLRC4 axis and rely on the DNA-sensing AIM2 inflammasome. We have also found that Legionella DNA is released into macrophage cytosol, and this effect is significantly enhanced in the absence of SdhA. Interestingly, SdhA bears a functional Golgi-targeting GRIP domain that is required for preventing AIM2 inflammasome activation. Ectopic expression of SdhA has also revealed a unique ring-shape membrane structure, suggesting a role in membrane trafficking and maintaining LCV membrane integrity.
Our findings suggest a possible link between LCV trafficking and maturation, and the suppression of host innate immune detection. Specifically, SdhA appears to play a critical role in maintaining the integrity of the LCV and preventing the activation of the AIM2 inflammasome, thereby allowing Legionella to evade the host immune response.

title: Cytosolic viral sensor RIG-I is a 5'-triphosphate-dependent translocase on double-stranded RNA.
text: Retinoic acid inducible-gene I (RIG-I) is a cytosolic protein with multiple domains that detects viral RNA and triggers an antiviral immune response. Two N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domains (CARDs) transmit the signal, while a regulatory domain prevents signaling in the absence of viral RNA. RIG-I can recognize two molecular patterns, 5'-triphosphate and double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), to distinguish between pathogenic and self-RNA. However, the function of the DExH box helicase domain, which is also essential for activity, is less clear. Using single-molecule protein-induced fluorescence enhancement, we discovered that RIG-I has a robust adenosine 5'-triphosphate-powered dsRNA translocation activity. The CARDs significantly suppress translocation in the absence of 5'-triphosphate, and the activation by 5'-triphosphate triggers RIG-I to translocate preferentially on dsRNA in cis. This integrated response to two RNA molecular patterns may provide a means to specifically detect and combat replicating viruses.

title: Human Cytomegalovirus-Encoded Interleukin-10 Homolog Inhibits Maturation of Dendritic Cells and Alters Their Functionality
text: Interleukin-10 (IL-10), a cytokine produced by dendritic cells (DCs), plays a crucial role in regulating adaptive immunity by suppressing the maturation and cytokine production of DCs, thereby preventing the activation and polarization of naïve T cells towards protective gamma interferon-producing effectors. We hypothesized that human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), a viral pathogen, utilizes its viral IL-10 homolog (cmvIL-10) to attenuate DC functionality, thereby subverting the efficient induction of antiviral immune responses. Through RNA and protein analyses, we demonstrated that the cmvIL-10 gene is expressed with late gene kinetics in HCMV-infected cultures. Treatment of immature DCs (iDCs) with supernatant from HCMV-infected cultures inhibited both the lipopolysaccharide-induced DC maturation and proinflammatory cytokine production, effects that were specifically mediated through the IL-10 receptor and were not observed when DCs were treated with supernatant from cells infected with a cmvIL-10-knockout mutant. Incubation of iDCs with recombinant cmvIL-10 recapitulated the inhibition of maturation. Furthermore, cmvIL-10 had pronounced long-term effects on those DCs that could overcome this inhibition of maturation, including enhanced migration towards the lymph node homing chemokine and reduced cytokine production. Notably, cmvIL-10 potentiates these anti-inflammatory effects, at least partially, by inducing endogenous cellular IL-10 expression in DCs. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that cmvIL-10 causes long-term functional alterations at all stages of DC activation.

title: Model for unidirectional movement of axonemal and cytoplasmic dynein molecules
text: A novel model for the unidirectional movement of dynein is proposed based on both structural observations and biochemical experimental results. In this model, the binding affinity of dynein for microtubules is independent of their nucleotide state, and the transition between strong and weak microtubule binding is naturally determined by the variation in relative orientation between the stalk and microtubule as the stalk rotates during nucleotide-state transitions. Therefore, the enigmatic communication from the ATP binding site in the globular domain to the far MT-binding site in the tip of the stalk, which is a key component of conventional models, is not required. Using this model, the previously observed experimental results, such as the effect of ATP and ADP bindings on the dissociation of dynein from microtubules, the processive movement of single-headed axonemal dyneins at saturating ATP concentrations, the load dependence of step size for the processive movement of two-headed cytoplasmic dyneins, and the dependence of stall force on ATP concentration, can be well explained.

title: The inflammasome component NLRP3 impairs antitumor vaccine by enhancing the accumulation of tumor-associated myeloid-derived suppressor cells.
text: The inflammasome is a protein complex that plays a crucial role in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) and interleukin-18 (IL-18), in response to microbial and non-microbial stimuli. However, the role of the NLRP3 inflammasome in antitumor immunity has remained unclear. To investigate this, we evaluated the function of the NLRP3 inflammasome in the immune response using dendritic cell vaccination against the poorly immunogenic melanoma cell line B16-F10. Our findings showed that vaccination of Nlrp3-deficient mice led to a 4-fold improvement in survival compared to control animals, indicating that NLRP3 plays a critical role in impeding antitumor immune responses. We found that this effect was dependent on CD8+ T cells and exhibited both immune specificity and memory. Interestingly, we also observed that the absence of NLRP3 resulted in a 5-fold reduction in the number of tumor-associated myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) found in host mice, and adoptive transfer experiments showed that NLRP3-deficient MDSCs were less efficient in reaching the tumor site. These findings suggest that NLRP3 plays a critical role in accumulating MDSCs in tumors and inhibiting antitumor T-cell immunity after dendritic cell vaccination. Our study establishes an unexpected role for NLRP3 in impeding antitumor immune responses and suggests novel approaches to improve the response to antitumor vaccines by limiting NLRP3 signaling.

title: Natural Killer Cells for Immunotherapy – Advantages of the NK-92 Cell Line over Blood NK Cells
text: Natural killer (NK) cells are highly effective cytotoxic immune cells that hold promise for cancer therapy and potentially for severe viral infections. However, isolating sufficient numbers of functionally active NK cells from a patient's blood can be challenging due to their low representation (approximately 10%) among lymphocytes, and they are often impaired in their activity. An alternative approach is to obtain NK cells from healthy donors, but this requires depletion of allogeneic T cells to prevent graft-versus-host reactions. Cytotoxic cell lines have been established from patients with clonal NK-cell lymphoma, which can be expanded in culture in the presence of IL-2. While several NK cell lines have shown some antitumor activity, only the NK-92 cell line has consistently and reproducibly demonstrated high cytotoxicity against tumors. Additionally, NK-92 cells can be genetically modified to recognize specific tumor antigens or to enhance the effectiveness of monoclonal antibodies through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Importantly, NK-92 cells have been safely infused into patients with advanced cancer, with clinical benefit observed in some cases.

title: Differential activation of DNA-PK based on DNA strand orientation and sequence bias
text:
DNA-PKcs and Ku are crucial components of the complex responsible for non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Ku, a heterodimeric protein, binds to DNA ends and facilitates the recruitment of the catalytic subunit, DNA-PKcs. Our research has focused on investigating the impact of DNA strand orientation and sequence bias on the activation of DNA-PK. Furthermore, we have assessed the effect of the position and strand orientation of cisplatin adducts on kinase activation.
To achieve this, we prepared a series of duplex DNA substrates with site-specific cisplatin–DNA adducts placed in three different orientations on the duplex DNA. Terminal biotin modification and streptavidin (SA) blocking were employed to direct DNA-PK binding to the unblocked termini with a specific DNA strand orientation and cisplatin–DNA adduct position. Kinase activity was measured, and the results revealed that DNA strand orientation and sequence bias significantly influence kinase activation, only a portion of which could be attributed to Ku-DNA binding activity. Additionally, the position of cisplatin–DNA adducts resulted in varying degrees of inhibition depending on distance from the terminus as well as strand orientation.
These findings highlight the importance of local variations in DNA structure, chemistry, and sequence on DNA-PK activation and potentially NHEJ.

title: Regulators of Trypanosoma brucei Cell Cycle Progression and Differentiation Identified Using a Kinome-Wide RNAi Screen
text: The African trypanosome, Trypanosoma brucei, maintains a crucial connection between cell cycle regulation and differentiation throughout its complex life cycle. While significant changes in phosphorylation have been observed between the mammalian bloodstream form and the insect procyclic form, relatively little is known about the parasite's protein kinases (PKs) involved in cellular proliferation and differentiation regulation. To address this knowledge gap, a T. brucei kinome-wide RNAi cell line library was generated, allowing for independent and inducible knockdown of each of the parasite's 190 predicted PKs. Screening this library using a cell viability assay identified at least 42 PKs that are essential for normal bloodstream form proliferation in culture. A secondary screen revealed 24 PKs whose RNAi-mediated depletion resulted in various cell cycle defects, including those in G1/S, kinetoplast replication/segregation, mitosis, and cytokinesis. Of these, 15 are novel cell cycle regulators. Additionally, two PKs, named repressor of differentiation kinase (RDK1 and RDK2), were identified as essential for bloodstream to procyclic form differentiation. RDK1 is a membrane-associated STE11-like PK, while RDK2 is a NEK PK that is critical for parasite proliferation. RDK1 works in conjunction with the PTP1/PIP39 phosphatase cascade to prevent uncontrolled bloodstream to procyclic form differentiation, while RDK2 is a PK whose depletion efficiently induces differentiation in the absence of known triggers. Therefore, the RNAi kinome library provides a valuable tool for functional analysis of cell signaling pathways in African trypanosomes, as well as for identifying and validating drug targets.

title: Chemotherapy options in elderly and frail patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (MRC FOCUS2): an open-label, randomised factorial trial
text:
The FOCUS2 clinical trial aimed to investigate reduced-dose chemotherapy options for elderly and frail patients with advanced colorectal cancer who were considered unfit for full-dose chemotherapy. The study was conducted in 61 UK centers and included 459 patients who were randomly assigned to one of four treatment groups: 48-hour intravenous fluorouracil with levofolinate (group A), oxaliplatin and fluorouracil (group B), capecitabine (group C), or oxaliplatin and capecitabine (group D). The primary outcome measures were progression-free survival (PFS) and change from baseline to 12 weeks in global quality of life (QoL) in each treatment group.
The results of the study showed that the addition of oxaliplatin to chemotherapy did not significantly improve PFS, but the substitution of fluorouracil with capecitabine did not improve QoL. The risk of having any grade 3 or worse toxic effects was not significantly increased with oxaliplatin, but was higher with capecitabine than with fluorouracil. Baseline symptoms, widespread disease, and use of oxaliplatin were predictive of better overall treatment utility (OTU).
The study demonstrates that with an appropriate design, including reduced starting doses of chemotherapy, frail and elderly patients can participate in a randomized controlled trial. The findings suggest that a combination including oxaliplatin may be preferable to single-agent fluoropyrimidines, although the primary endpoint of PFS was not met. The study also highlights the importance of comprehensive baseline assessment as an objective predictor of treatment benefit.
The FOCUS2 trial was funded by Cancer Research UK and the Medical Research Council.

title: Whole-genome sequencing of Oryza brachyantha reveals mechanisms underlying Oryza genome evolution
text: The wild species of the genus Oryza harbor a vast, untapped reservoir of genes with agronomic potential for rice improvement. In this study, we present the de novo assembled genome sequence of Oryza brachyantha, spanning 261 megabases. Notably, the genome of Oryza brachyantha displays a compact structure due to the low activity of long-terminal repeat retrotransposons and the deletion of ancient long-terminal repeat elements. We identified 32,038 protein-coding genes in the Oryza brachyantha genome, of which only 70% are located in collinear positions relative to the rice genome. Our analysis of non-collinear genes suggests that double-strand break repair through non-homologous end joining plays a crucial role in gene movement and the erosion of collinearity in the Oryza genomes. Additionally, we observed segmental and tandem duplications in the rice genome, which are further expanded by transposable element insertions. The high-quality reference genome sequence of Oryza brachyantha provides a valuable resource for functional and evolutionary studies in the genus Oryza.

title: Ultrasound imaging for lumbar punctures and epidural catheterisations: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
Objective: To determine whether ultrasound imaging can improve the success rate of lumbar punctures and epidural catheterizations compared to standard palpation methods, and to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ultrasound imaging in these procedures.
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Data Sources: Ovid Medline, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials up to May 2012, without restriction by language or publication status.
Review Methods: Randomized trials that compared ultrasound imaging with standard methods in the performance of lumbar punctures or epidural catheterizations were identified.
Results: 14 studies with a total of 1334 patients were included (674 patients assigned to the ultrasound group, 660 to the control group). Five studies evaluated lumbar punctures, and nine evaluated epidural catheterizations.
