Ultrasound imaging reduced the risk of failed procedures (risk ratio 0.21 (95% confidence interval 0.10 to 0.43), P<0.001). Subgroup analysis showed similar risk reduction for lumbar punctures (risk ratio 0.19 (0.07 to 0.56), P=0.002) and epidural catheterizations (0.23 (0.09 to 0.60), P=0.003). Ultrasound imaging also significantly reduced the risk of traumatic procedures (risk ratio 0.27 (0.11 to 0.67), P=0.005), the number of insertion attempts (mean difference -0.44 (-0.64 to -0.24), P<0.001), and the number of needle redirections (mean difference -1.00 (-1.24 to -0.75), P<0.001).
Conclusions: Ultrasound imaging can reduce the risk of failed or traumatic lumbar punctures and epidural catheterizations, as well as the number of needle insertions and redirections. Ultrasound may be a useful adjunct for these procedures.

title: Guidance of B cells by the orphan G protein-coupled receptor EBI2 shapes humoral immune responses.
text: Humoral immunity relies on both rapid and long-term antibody production against invading pathogens. This is achieved through the generation of distinct B cell populations, including extrafollicular plasmablasts and follicular germinal center (GC) B cells. However, the signals that guide B cells to these alternative compartments have not been fully understood. Our study reveals that the orphan G protein-coupled receptor Epstein-Barr virus-induced gene 2 (EBI2, also known as GPR183) plays a crucial role in B cell migration. We found that EBI2 expression on activated B cells is essential for their movement to extrafollicular sites and the induction of early plasmablast responses. Conversely, downregulation of EBI2 enables B cells to access the center of follicles and promotes efficient GC formation. Our findings provide a previously uncharacterized dimension to B cell migration that is crucial for coordinating rapid versus long-term antibody responses.

title: SIRT1 is required for long-term growth of human mesenchymal stem cells
text: Human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) hold great therapeutic potential due to their ability to self-renew and differentiate into various tissues. However, MSCs often undergo senescence when cultured in vitro, and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we discovered that the NAD-dependent protein deacetylase SIRT1 is differentially expressed in human bone marrow-derived MSCs (B-MSCs) and adipose tissue-derived MSCs after multiple passages in cell culture. Using lentiviral shRNA, we found that selectively knocking down SIRT1 in human MSCs at an early passage slows down cell growth and accelerates cellular senescence. Conversely, overexpressing SIRT1 delays senescence in B-MSCs that have undergone prolonged in vitro culturing, and the cells retain their adipogenic and osteogenic potential. We also discovered that the delayed accumulation of the protein p16 is involved in the SIRT1-mediated effect. Interestingly, resveratrol, a compound known to activate SIRT1 deacetylase activity, only transiently promotes the proliferation of B-MSCs. Our findings provide valuable insights into the role of SIRT1 in the aging of normal diploid cells and may contribute to the prevention of human MSCs senescence, which is crucial for MSCs-based tissue engineering and therapies.

title: Rapid and persistent modulation of actin dynamics regulates postsynaptic reorganization underlying bidirectional plasticity
text: The synapse, a highly specialized cellular structure, undergoes reorganization in response to changes in input signal strength. While the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, actin, a key component of the cytoskeleton and scaffold for synapses, is a plausible locus for reorganization. Using a novel FRET-based imaging technique to monitor the equilibrium between F-actin and G-actin in dendritic spines of rat hippocampal neurons, we demonstrate that tetanic stimulation leads to a rapid and persistent shift in actin equilibrium towards F-actin, resulting in enlarged spines and increased postsynaptic binding capacity. In contrast, prolonged low-frequency stimulation shifts the equilibrium towards G-actin, leading to a loss of postsynaptic actin and structural plasticity. This bidirectional regulation of actin is crucial for protein assembly and disassembly and provides a substrate for bidirectional synaptic plasticity.

title: Sublime Microglia: Expanding Roles for the Guardians of the CNS
text: Recent research has challenged the long-held belief that microglia in the central nervous system (CNS) solely play a role in disease states. Instead, emerging evidence suggests that these immune cells actively shape the structure of the CNS, refine neuronal connections, and contribute to plasticity. These physiological functions of microglia in the normal CNS begin during development and persist into adulthood. This article aims to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the diverse roles of microglia beyond their traditional association with neuroinflammation, and to explore the complex signaling and communication mechanisms that underlie their normal physiology in the CNS.

title: Cancer after pre-eclampsia: follow up of the Jerusalem perinatal study cohort.
text:
Objective: To compare the incidence of cancer among women with and without a history of pre-eclampsia.
Design: Cohort study.
Setting: Jerusalem perinatal study of women who delivered in three large hospitals in West Jerusalem during 1964-76.
Participants: 37,033 women.
Main Outcome Measures: Age-adjusted and multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios for cancer incidence for the entire cohort and for women who were primiparous at study entry.
Results: Cancer developed in 91 women who had pre-eclampsia and 2204 who did not (hazard ratio 1.27, 95% confidence interval 1.03 to 1.57). The risk of site-specific cancers was increased, particularly of the stomach, ovary epithelium, breast, and lung or larynx. The incidence of cancer of the stomach, breast, ovary, kidney, and lung or larynx was increased in primiparous women at study entry who had a history of pre-eclampsia.
Conclusions: A history of pre-eclampsia is associated with increased overall risk of cancer and incidence at several sites. This may be explained by environmental and genetic factors common to the development of pre-eclampsia and cancer in this population.

title: Keeping your senescent cells under control
text: Cellular senescence is a state of permanent cell cycle arrest that can occur in response to various forms of cellular damage or stress. While initially thought to be a mere culture phenomenon, recent in vivo studies have shown that cellular senescence plays a crucial role in limiting tumorigenesis and contributes to the cytotoxicity of certain anticancer agents. Senescent cells have also been observed in aged or damaged tissues, and their senescence checkpoints can affect the regenerative reserve of tissues and organismal aging. However, the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) can have both pro-tumorigenic and anti-tumor effects, depending on the context. The SASP can enhance the tumorigenicity of surrounding breast cancer cells, but it can also induce apoptosis of tumor cells. The regulatory pathways controlling the SASP are complex and involve microRNAs, such as miR-146a/b, which negatively regulate the secretion of inflammatory cytokines. The work of Bhaumik et al. highlights the importance of modulating the SASP in aging and cancer, and suggests that miR-146a/b may be a promising therapeutic target.

title: Role for insulin signaling in catecholaminergic neurons in control of energy homeostasis.
text: Dopaminergic midbrain neurons play a crucial role in integrating sensory information on the palatability and rewarding properties of food into the complex regulation of energy homeostasis. To investigate the involvement of insulin receptor (IR) signaling in this circuitry, we inhibited IR signaling in tyrosine hydroxylase (Th)-expressing cells of mice (IR(ΔTh)). Our findings revealed that IR inactivation in Th-expressing cells led to increased body weight, fat mass, and hyperphagia in mice. Interestingly, insulin failed to stimulate firing frequency in 50% of dopaminergic ventral tegmental area/substantia nigra (VTA/SN) neurons in IR(ΔTh) mice, suggesting a critical role of IR signaling in catecholaminergic neurons for food intake regulation. Moreover, these mice exhibited altered responses to cocaine under food-restricted conditions, further supporting the importance of IR signaling in this context. Taken together, these in vivo findings provide compelling evidence for the essential role of insulin signaling in catecholaminergic neurons for the control of energy homeostasis.

title: [New guidelines to evaluate the response to treatment in solid tumors].
text: Anticancer drugs undergo a process of evaluation to assess their effectiveness in shrinking tumors. In the 1970s, the International Union Against Cancer and the World Health Organization (WHO) established criteria for evaluating tumor response to treatment. However, these criteria were reviewed and updated in 1994 by several organizations involved in clinical cancer research, as they recognized the need for more comprehensive and accurate assessment methods. This led to the development of new guidelines that replace the previous WHO criteria. Meanwhile, one of the participating groups proposed a novel approach to response evaluation, which involves measuring tumor lesions in a unidimensional manner instead of the traditional bidimensional method. This new concept, known as the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST), has been extensively validated and integrated into the current guidelines. This article provides a philosophical background to explain the various purposes of response evaluation and proposes a model that combines the assessment of all existing lesions, including target lesions and nontarget lesions, to estimate an overall response to treatment. The article also codifies methods of assessing tumor lesions and provides a comprehensive review of all aspects of response evaluation, including tumor shrinkage, and amends them where necessary.

title: Structural Rearrangements of NR1/NR2A NMDA Receptors during Allosteric Inhibition
text:
The N-terminal domain (NTD) of ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits plays a crucial role in subunit oligomerization, but the molecular mechanisms by which it influences the receptor's activity remain unclear. In N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors (NMDARs), the NTDs of NR2A and NR2B subunits also bind to the endogenous inhibitor zinc (Zn(2+)). Although these binding sites have been well-characterized, the mechanisms by which the NTDs communicate with the rest of the receptor to modulate its activity are still unknown.
To address this question, we focused on the ABD dimer interface, which is a critical structural element that connects the NTDs and the channel gate of the receptor. Our findings reveal that this interface is a major determinant of allosteric modulation of NMDARs, and that its strength controls both proton inhibition and Zn(2+) binding.
Conformational changes at the ABD dimer interface appear to be a conserved mechanism across all iGluR subfamilies, but have evolved to serve different functions. For example, fast desensitization occurs at AMPA and kainate receptors, while allosteric inhibition occurs at NMDARs.
In summary, our study sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying allosteric modulation of iGluRs, and highlights the importance of the ABD dimer interface in mediating these effects. These findings have implications for our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying synaptic plasticity and learning, and may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for a range of neurological disorders.

title: The role of iron in Mycobacterium smegmatis biofilm formation: the exochelin siderophore is essential in limiting iron conditions for biofilm formation but not for planktonic growth
text: Many species of mycobacteria are known to form structured biofilm communities at liquid-air interfaces and on solid surfaces. The full development of Mycobacterium smegmatis biofilms requires the addition of supplemental iron above 1 μM ferrous sulphate, although planktonic growth is not dependent on iron addition. Microarray analysis of the M. smegmatis transcriptome reveals that iron-responsive genes, particularly those involved in siderophore synthesis and iron uptake, are strongly induced during biofilm formation, suggesting a response to iron deprivation even when 2 μM iron is present. The acquisition of iron under these conditions is specifically dependent on the exochelin synthesis and uptake pathways, and the strong defect of an iron-exochelin uptake mutant suggests a regulatory role of iron in the transition to biofilm growth. In contrast, although the expression of mycobactin and iron ABC transport operons is highly upregulated during biofilm formation, mutants in these systems form normal biofilms in low-iron (2 μM) conditions. A close correlation between iron availability and matrix-associated fatty acids suggests a possible metabolic role in the late stages of biofilm maturation, in addition to the early regulatory role. Notably, M. smegmatis surface motility is also dependent on iron availability, requiring both supplemental iron and the exochelin pathway to acquire it.

title: Plasma lipids and prolactin in patients with breast cancer.
text: In a comparative study of pre- and postmenopausal women with benign and malignant breast disease, notable differences were observed in circulating plasma prolactin and lipid concentrations. Plasma lipids, phospholipids, triglycerides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids were found to be higher in blood samples collected from breast cancer patients prior to surgery compared to non-cancer patients. Specifically, HDL-Cholesterol levels were significantly lower in cancer patients. These differences persisted when the patient groups were sub-divided according to menopausal status. Interestingly, plasma prolactin concentrations were higher in cancer patients compared to non-cancer patients, with a more pronounced effect observed in premenopausal than postmenopausal patients. Within the premenopausal group, patients with invasive or poorly differentiated disease had significantly higher prolactin levels than those with non-invasive disease. No correlations were observed between plasma prolactin and any of the lipid fractions.

title: expression by oxidized linoleic
text:
Hypercholesterolemia is associated with impaired endothelium-dependent vascular relaxations, paradoxically, endothelial production of nitrogen oxides is increased in the early stages of hypercholesterolemia. Prior research has shown that oxidized low-density lipoprotein (LDL) has both stimulatory and inhibitory effects on endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) expression, with a focus on lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) as a component of oxidized LDL, which may modulate this effect. Another biologically active component of oxidized LDL is 13-hydroperoxyoctadecadienoic acid (13-HPODE), an oxidized form of linoleic acid. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of 13-HPODE on eNOS expression in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs).
Twenty-four hour treatment of endothelial cells with 13-HPODE resulted in a dose-dependent increase in eNOS mRNA levels, as determined by Northern analysis. Time-response studies showed that 13-HPODE treatment significantly increased eNOS mRNA levels at 12 and 24 hours. Concomitant with the increase in eNOS mRNA levels, 20 μM 13-HPODE treatment significantly increased eNOS protein content and enzyme activity. Nuclear run-on studies indicated that the rate of transcription of the eNOS gene was significantly elevated 4 hours after 13-HPODE treatment compared to control cultures. Additionally, actinomycin D studies demonstrated that the half-life of eNOS mRNA was increased from 6 hours to 12 hours by 13-HPODE treatment. These observations suggest that endothelial cells may attempt to compensate for oxidative injury by increasing eNOS expression in early stages of hypercholesterolemia.

title: Specific killing of multiple myeloma cells by (-)-epigallocatechin-3-gallate extracted from green tea: biologic activity and therapeutic implications.
text:
Green tea polyphenol, epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), exhibits antioxidant and chemopreventive properties, making it a promising candidate for cancer treatment. In this study, we investigated the efficacy of EGCG in multiple myeloma (MM) cells. Our results show that EGCG induces dose- and time-dependent growth arrest and apoptotic cell death in MM cell lines, including those dependent on interleukin-6 (IL-6), without significantly affecting the growth of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) or normal fibroblasts. Treatment with EGCG also led to significant apoptosis in human myeloma cells grown as tumors in SCID mice.
We found that EGCG interacts with the 67-kDa laminin receptor 1 (LR1), which is overexpressed in myeloma cell lines and patient samples compared to normal PBMCs. Silencing LR1 using RNA interference (RNAi) abrogated EGCG-induced apoptosis in myeloma cells, indicating that LR1 plays a crucial role in mediating EGCG's antimyeloma effects while sparing PBMCs.
Our analysis of gene expression changes revealed that EGCG treatment activates distinct pathways of growth arrest and apoptosis in MM cells, including the expression of death-associated protein kinase 2, Fas ligand, Fas, caspase 4, p53-like proteins (p73, p63), positive regulators of apoptosis (CARD10, CARD14), and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (p16 and p18). These findings provide a rationale for the clinical evaluation of EGCG as a potential treatment for MM.
In summary, our study demonstrates the potent and specific antimyeloma activity of EGCG, highlighting its potential as a cancer treatment.

title: Pharmacologic inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 arrests the growth of glioblastoma multiforme intracranial xenografts.
text: Activation of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (cdk4/6) is prevalent in most glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) tumors, making them an attractive target for the development of small molecule inhibitors. In this study, we investigated the molecular determinants and in vivo response of diverse GBM cell lines and xenografts to PD-0332991, a cdk4/6-specific inhibitor. Our findings reveal that PD-0332991 exhibits potent G(1) cell cycle arrest and induction of senescence in all 16 retinoblastoma protein (Rb)-proficient GBM cell lines, regardless of other genetic lesions. However, five cell lines with homozygous inactivation of Rb were completely resistant to treatment. We also found that Rb is essential for sensitivity to cdk4/6 inhibition, as short hairpin RNA depletion of Rb expression conferred resistance to PD-0332991. Notably, PD-0332991 efficiently crossed the blood-brain barrier and showed significant growth suppression in intracranial GBM xenograft tumors, including those that had recurred after initial therapy with temozolomide. Importantly, no mice receiving PD-0332991 died due to disease progression while on therapy. Furthermore, the combination of PD-0332991 and radiation therapy resulted in a significantly increased survival benefit compared to either therapy alone. These results support the evaluation of PD-0332991 in clinical trials for both newly diagnosed and recurrent GBM, and suggest that Rb status is the primary determinant of potential benefit from this therapy.

title: Choosing Haplotype-Tagging SNPS Based on Unphased Genotype Data Using a Preliminary Sample of Unrelated Subjects with an Example from the Multiethnic Cohort Study
text: We present an approach for selecting haplotype-tagging single nucleotide polymorphisms (htSNPs) that is currently being applied in two large, nested case-control studies within a multiethnic cohort (MEC). The goal of these studies is to identify genetic variations associated with the risk of prostate and breast cancer by analyzing common genetic variations in candidate genes. To estimate haplotype frequencies in a preliminary sample of 70 control subjects from each of the 5 ethnic groups in the MEC, we employed a variant of the Excoffier-Slatkin E-M algorithm after genotyping a high-density of SNPs selected every 3-5 kilobases in and around the candidate genes. To evaluate the performance of a set of candidate htSNPs, we assumed known haplotype frequencies from the preliminary sample and calculated the uncertainty of the number of copies of common haplotypes carried by an individual using a coefficient of determination, R2h. We chose a set of htSNPs of a given size to maximize the minimum value of R2h over the common haplotypes, h.

title: A model for the role of gut bacteria in the development of autoimmunity for type 1 diabetes
text: Several lines of evidence suggest a connection between the gut microbiome and type 1 diabetes. Studies have shown that treating diabetes-prone rodents with probiotics or antibiotics can prevent the development of the disorder. These rodents also have distinct differences in their gut microbiomes compared to healthy rodents. Recent studies in children with a high genetic risk for type 1 diabetes have found significant differences in the gut microbiomes of children who develop autoimmunity for the disease and those who remain healthy. However, these differences are not consistent across all studies due to strong environmental influences on microbiome composition, particularly diet and geography. By controlling for these confounding factors, researchers have discovered bacterial associations with disease, such as a strong association between the dominant bacterial species, Bacteroides dorei, and type 1 diabetes in a human cohort from a single Finnish city. Additionally, recent DNA methylation analyses suggest that a thorough epigenetic analysis of the gut microbiome may be warranted. This suggests a possible model whereby a diet high in fat and gluten and low in resistant starch may be the primary driver of gut dysbiosis, leading to a lack of butyrate production by gut bacteria and the development of a permeable gut, which in turn may lead to autoimmunity. The bacterial community responsible for these changes in butyrate production may vary around the world, but bacteria of the genus Bacteroides are thought to play a key role.

title: METHODS AND RESULTS
text: Cytoscape is an open-source software platform for integrating complex biomolecular networks with high-throughput expression data and other molecular states into a unified conceptual framework. While applicable to any system of molecular components and interactions, Cytoscape is particularly powerful when used in conjunction with large databases of protein-protein, protein-DNA, and genetic interactions that are increasingly available for humans and model organisms. The core software provides basic functionality for visualizing and querying the network, as well as integrating it with expression profiles, phenotypes, and other molecular states. Additionally, the Core is extensible through a straightforward plug-in architecture, allowing for rapid development of new computational analyses and features. Several case studies of Cytoscape plug-ins are surveyed, including a search for interaction pathways correlating with changes in gene expression, a study of protein complexes involved in cellular recovery to DNA damage, inference of a combined physical/functional interaction network for Halobacterium, and an interface to detailed stochastic/kinetic gene regulatory models.

title: Dual Regulation of miRNA Biogenesis Generates Target Specificity in Neurotrophin-Induced Protein Synthesis
text:
Control of translation is a fundamental mechanism of regulation in gene expression, and the induction of protein synthesis by brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays a critical role in enduring modifications of synaptic function. However, the mechanisms by which BDNF selectively regulates only a subset of expressed mRNAs remain poorly understood.
Our study reveals that BDNF rapidly induces the levels of Dicer, leading to increased levels of mature microRNAs (miRNAs) and the formation of RNA processing bodies in neurons. Additionally, BDNF rapidly induces the expression of Lin28, resulting in the loss of Lin28-regulated miRNAs and a corresponding increase in translation of their target mRNAs. The binding sites for Lin28-regulated miRNAs are necessary and sufficient to confer BDNF responsiveness to a transcript.
Importantly, our findings demonstrate that the specificity of BDNF-regulated translation is dependent on a two-part posttranscriptional control of miRNA biogenesis, which enhances mRNA repression in association with GW182 while selectively derepressing and increasing translation of specific mRNAs. These mechanisms provide a novel insight into the regulation of gene expression by BDNF and have important implications for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying synaptic plasticity and neuronal function.

title: A Viral microRNA Cluster Strongly Potentiates the Transforming Properties of a Human Herpesvirus
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a oncogenic human herpesvirus, induces cell proliferation in resting B lymphocytes, its reservoir in vivo, after infection. The viral latent proteins are necessary for permanent B cell growth, but it is unknown if they are sufficient. Recently, EBV was found to encode microRNAs (miRNAs) that are expressed in infected B cells and some EBV-associated lymphomas. EBV miRNAs are grouped into two clusters located near the BHRF1 gene or within viral BART transcripts. To investigate the role of the BHRF1 miRNA cluster, we constructed a virus mutant lacking all three members (Δ123) and a revertant virus. Our results show that the B cell transforming capacity of the Δ123 EBV mutant is reduced by more than 20-fold compared to wild type or revertant viruses. B cells exposed to the knock-out virus grew slower and had a two-fold reduction in the percentage of cells entering the cell cycle S phase. Additionally, they had higher levels of latent gene expression and protein production than their wild type counterparts. These findings suggest that the BHRF1 miRNAs accelerate B cell expansion at lower latent gene expression levels, potentially facilitating persistence of the virus in the infected host. Therefore, the EBV BHRF1 miRNAs may represent new therapeutic targets for the treatment of some EBV-associated lymphomas.

title: EMSY overexpression disrupts the BRCA2/RAD51 pathway in the DNA-damage response: implications for chromosomal instability/recombination syndromes as checkpoint diseases
text:
EMSY has been shown to link the BRCA2 pathway to sporadic breast/ovarian cancer, as it encodes a nuclear protein that interacts with the BRCA2 N-terminal domain, which is involved in chromatin/transcription regulation. However, when EMSY is amplified/overexpressed, it can repress BRCA2 transactivation potential and induce chromosomal instability, mimicking the effects of BRCA2 mutations in the development of hereditary breast/ovarian cancer. In addition to its role in chromatin/transcription regulation, EMSY may also play a part in the DNA-damage response, as it can localize to sites of DNA damage/repair. This suggests that EMSY overexpression may repress BRCA2 in DNA-damage replication/checkpoint and recombination/repair processes, which are coordinated and require the interaction of EMSY with other proteins such as PALB2, RPA, and RAD51.
Using a well-characterized recombination/repair assay system, we have demonstrated that a slight increase in EMSY level can indeed repress these processes independently of transcriptional interference/repression. These findings support a scenario where EMSY amplification may mimic BRCA2 deficiency by overriding the function of RPA and PALB2, crippling the BRCA2/RAD51 complex at DNA-damage and replication/transcription sites. Additionally, BRCA2/RAD51 may coordinate these processes by employing EMSY, PALB2, and RPA.
Our findings have significant implications for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer predisposition, as they suggest that EMSY may play a role in a novel recombination mechanism that is conceived as a checkpoint rather than a DNA repair system for cell division, survival, death, and human diseases. The tissue specificity of cancer predisposition may also provide new insights into targeted therapy and prevention.

title: Original Article
text:
The consumption of fruits and vegetables has been shown to reduce the risk of chronic diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular disease. This is attributed to the various protective antioxidants, carotenoids, and phytonutrients found in these foods. The present study aimed to investigate the effect of supplementing with dehydrated concentrates from mixed fruit and vegetable juices (Juice Plus+R) on various biomarkers of health.
A double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted on 60 Japanese adults (age 27.8 years, BMI 22.1) and randomly divided into two groups of 30, matched for sex, age, BMI, and smoking status (39 males, 22 smokers; 21 females, 13 smokers). Subjects were given encapsulated supplements containing mixed fruit and vegetable juice concentrates or a matching placebo for 28 days, and blood and urine samples were collected at baseline, day 14, and day 28 for analysis.
The results showed that 28-day supplementation with the fruit and vegetable juice concentrate capsules significantly increased the levels of serum beta-carotene by 528% (p < 0.0001), lycopene by 80.2% (p < 0.0005), and alpha-tocopherol by 39.5% (p < 0.0001). Additionally, serum folate levels increased by 174.3% (p < 0.0001), and plasma homocysteine levels decreased by 19.9% (p < 0.03). Furthermore, measures of oxidative stress, such as serum lipid peroxides and urine 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8OHdG), decreased significantly. When the data was analyzed separately for smokers (n = 17), comparable changes were observed.
In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that supplementation with the fruit and vegetable juice concentrate capsules is a highly bioavailable source of phytonutrients, which can elevate desirable levels of antioxidants associated with a reduced risk of disease. Additionally, the supplementation led to a decrease in markers of oxidative stress and an improvement in folate status, with a concomitant decrease in homocysteine levels, in both smokers and non-smokers. These findings suggest that supplementation with the fruit and vegetable juice concentrate capsules may be a useful adjunct to a healthy diet in maintaining optimal health.

title: NCBI GEO: archive for functional genomics data sets—update
text: The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO, <http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/>) is a global public repository for high-throughput microarray and next-generation sequence functional genomic data sets contributed by the research community. The platform supports the archiving of raw data, processed data, and metadata, which are meticulously indexed, cross-linked, and searchable. All data are freely accessible for download in various formats. Additionally, GEO offers a range of web-based tools and strategies to facilitate user querying, analysis, and visualization of the data. This article provides an update on the current status and recent database developments, including the release of GEO2R, an R-based web application that enables users to efficiently analyze GEO data.

title: Viral Paratransgenesis in the Malaria Vector Anopheles gambiae
text:
Paratransgenesis, the genetic manipulation of symbiotic microorganisms in insects, is being explored as a potential method to control vector-borne diseases such as malaria. However, the lack of suitable symbiotic microorganisms for the major malaria vector, Anopheles gambiae, has hindered the feasibility of paratransgenic malaria control. In contrast, densonucleosis viruses (DNVs) are attractive agents for viral paratransgenesis in other insect systems due to their ability to infect important vector insects, be genetically manipulated, and transmit to subsequent generations. However, An. gambiae has been shown to be resistant to DNV dissemination.
We recently discovered, cloned, and characterized the first DNV (AgDNV) capable of infecting and disseminating in An. gambiae. We developed a versatile AgDNV-based expression vector to express any gene of interest in An. gambiae using a two-plasmid helper-transducer system. To demonstrate the potential of this viral paratransgenesis strategy, we used this system to transduce expression of an exogenous gene (enhanced green fluorescent protein; EGFP) in An. gambiae mosquitoes. Wild-type and EGFP-transducing AgDNV virions were highly infectious to An. gambiae larvae, disseminated EGFP to and expressed it in epidemiologically relevant adult tissues such as midgut, fat body, and ovaries, and were transmitted to subsequent mosquito generations. These proof-of-principle data suggest that AgDNV could be used as part of a paratransgenic malaria control strategy by transducing anti-Plasmodium peptides or insect-specific toxins in Anopheles mosquitoes. AgDNV will also be a valuable and easy-to-use laboratory tool for transient gene expression or RNAi in An. gambiae.

title: The polycomb group protein L3mbtl2 assembles an atypical PRC1-family complex that is essential in pluripotent stem cells and early development.
text: L3mbtl2 has been implicated in the repression of transcription and the compacting of chromatin, but its biological function remains uncharacterized. Our study reveals that disrupting L3mbtl2 leads to embryonic lethality during gastrulation, accompanied by impaired proliferation and abnormal differentiation of L3mbtl2-deficient embryonic stem (ES) cells. L3mbtl2 functions as a regulatory complex that recruits a Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1)-related complex, including G9A, Hdac1, and Ring1b, and regulates gene expression by modulating histone modifications such as H3K9 dimethylation, low histone acetylation, and H2AK119 ubiquitination. Genome-wide analysis reveals that the L3mbtl2-dependent complex primarily regulates genes not bound by canonical PRC1 and PRC2, but some developmental regulators are repressed by the combined activity of all three complexes. Our findings uncover a selective and essential role for an atypical PRC1-family complex in ES cells and early development.

title: Long-term effect of aspirin on cancer risk in carriers of hereditary colorectal cancer: an analysis from the CAPP2 randomised controlled trial
text:
BACKGROUND Observational studies have shown that regular aspirin consumption is associated with a reduced risk of colorectal cancer. However, previous randomized controlled trials have not specifically investigated the preventive effects of aspirin on colorectal cancer. The CAPP2 trial aimed to evaluate the antineoplastic effects of aspirin and resistant starch in individuals with Lynch syndrome, the most common inherited colorectal cancer syndrome. We now report the long-term follow-up of participants randomly assigned to aspirin or placebo.
METHODS In the CAPP2 randomized trial, individuals with Lynch syndrome were randomly assigned in a two-by-two factorial design to receive either 600 mg of aspirin or aspirin placebo, or 30 g of resistant starch or starch placebo, for up to 4 years. Randomization was in blocks of 16 with provision for optional single-agent randomization and extended postintervention double-blind follow-up. Participants and investigators were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint was the development of colorectal cancer. Analysis was conducted using intention-to-treat and per-protocol methods. This trial is registered with ISRCTN59521990.
RESULTS A total of 861 participants were randomly assigned to aspirin or aspirin placebo. At a mean follow-up of 55.7 months, 48 participants had developed 53 primary colorectal cancers (18 in the aspirin group and 30 in the placebo group). Using intention-to-treat analysis, the hazard ratio for time to first colorectal cancer was 0.63 (95% CI 0.35-1.13, p=0.12). Using Poisson regression to account for multiple primary events, the incidence rate ratio was 0.56 (95% CI 0.32-0.99, p=0.05). For participants who completed 2 years of intervention (258 aspirin and 250 aspirin placebo), per-protocol analysis yielded a hazard ratio of 0.41 (95% CI 0.19-0.86, p=0.02) and an incidence rate ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.18-0.78, p=0.008). No data on adverse events were available postintervention, but during the intervention, adverse events did not differ between the aspirin and placebo groups.
INTERPRETATION Our findings suggest that 600 mg of aspirin per day for a mean of 25 months significantly reduced cancer incidence after 55.7 months in individuals with hereditary colorectal cancer. Further studies are needed to determine the optimal dose and duration of aspirin treatment. Funding for this study was provided by the European Union, Cancer Research UK, Bayer Corporation, National Starch and Chemical Co, UK Medical Research Council, Newcastle Hospitals trustees, Cancer Council of Victoria Australia, THRIPP South Africa, The Finnish Cancer Foundation, SIAK Switzerland, and Bayer Pharma.

title: Drosophila CPEB Orb2A Mediates Memory Independent of Its RNA-Binding Domain
text: Long-term memory and synaptic plasticity are thought to involve the synthesis of new proteins at active synapses, with the CPEB family of RNA binding proteins, including Drosophila Orb2, implicated in this process. Despite understanding the role of these molecules in memory formation, the precise mechanism is poorly understood. To investigate the role of endogenous Orb2 in long-term memory formation, we used gene targeting and site-specific transgenesis to specifically modify the Orb2 gene. Our findings reveal that the Orb2A and Orb2B isoforms, both essential for memory formation, have distinct functions. While both isoforms contain glutamine-rich and RNA-binding domains, Orb2A requires the former and Orb2B the latter. We show that Orb2A induces Orb2 complexes in a manner dependent on both its glutamine-rich region and neuronal activity. Our findings suggest that Orb2B acts as a conventional CPEB, regulating transport and/or translation of specific mRNAs, while Orb2A forms stable complexes that are essential for memory persistence in an unconventional manner.

title: Functional hemichannels in astrocytes: a novel mechanism of glutamate release.
text: Little is known about the functional properties of unopposed gap junction hemichannels in the brain, but recent evidence suggests that these hemichannels can act as standalone channels in astrocytes. Using immunocytochemistry, dye uptake, and HPLC measurements, we found that astrocytes in vitro express functional hemichannels that can mediate the efflux of glutamate and aspartate. These functional hemichannels were confirmed by demonstrating the passage of extracellular lucifer yellow (LY) into astrocytes in a nominal divalent cation-free solution (DCFS) and the ability to block this passage with gap junction blocking agents. We also found that glutamate/aspartate release in DCFS was blocked by multivalent cations (Ca2+, Ba2+, Sr2+, Mg2+, and La3+) and gap junction blocking agents (carbenoxolone, octanol, heptanol, flufenamic acid, and 18alpha-glycyrrhetinic acid) with affinities similar to those reported for blockade of gap junction intercellular communication. In addition, glutamate efflux via hemichannels was accompanied by reduced glutamate uptake, but glutamate release in DCFS was not significantly mediated by the reversal of the glutamate transporter. Control experiments excluded the possibility that glutamate release was mediated by volume-sensitive anion channels, P2X7 purinergic receptor pores, or general purinergic receptor activation. Furthermore, blocking intracellular Ca2+ mobilization by BAPTA-AM or thapsigargin did not inhibit glutamate release in DCFS. Our findings suggest that astrocyte hemichannels may play a role in regulating extracellular glutamate levels in the brain, with implications for normal and pathological brain function.

title: Human Rad52 binds and wraps single-stranded DNA and mediates annealing via two hRad52–ssDNA complexes
text: Rad52 plays a crucial role in the repair of DNA through discrete repair pathways by promoting the annealing of complementary strands of DNA bound by replication protein A (RPA). To investigate the mechanism by which human Rad52 (hRad52) interacts with and mediates annealing of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA)-RPA complexes, we employed a fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) assay that incorporated two fluorescent dyes into DNA substrates. Our results revealed that hRad52 bound to ssDNA or ssDNA-RPA complexes in two distinct modes, depending on the concentration of hRad52. At low concentrations, hRad52 wrapped ssDNA around its protein ring, while at higher concentrations, ssDNA was stretched between multiple hRad52 rings. Our findings suggest that efficient annealing by hRad52 occurs when each complementary DNA strand or each ssDNA-RPA complex is bound by hRad52 in a wrapped configuration, indicating that homology search and annealing occur via two hRad52-ssDNA complexes. In contrast, mutants of hRad52 with impaired binding to hRPA protein (hRad52(RQK/AAA) and hRad52(1-212)) failed to compete with hRPA for binding to ssDNA and did not counteract hRPA-mediated duplex destabilization, highlighting the crucial role of hRad52-hRPA interactions in promoting efficient DNA annealing.

title: Mendelian Randomization Study of B-Type Natriuretic Peptide and Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence of Causal Association from Population Studies
text:
Background: Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested an inverse association between levels of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) in the blood and the risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the prospective relationship between BNP levels and T2D incidence is uncertain, and it is unclear whether this association is confounded.
Methods and Findings: We conducted a prospective case-cohort study and genotyped the BNP variant rs198389 in three T2D case-control studies. We combined our results with existing data from 11 case-control studies in a meta-analysis. Using a Mendelian randomization approach, we compared the observed association between rs198389 and T2D to that expected based on the relationship between NT-pro-BNP levels and T2D. In participants of our case-cohort study who were free of T2D and cardiovascular disease at baseline, we observed a 21% (95% CI 3%-36%) decrease in the risk of incident T2D per one standard deviation (SD) higher log-transformed NT-pro-BNP levels after adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, systolic blood pressure, smoking, family history of T2D, history of hypertension, and levels of triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. The association between rs198389 and T2D observed in case-control studies was similar to that expected based on the pooled estimate for the log-NT-pro-BNP level to T2D association and the difference in NT-pro-BNP levels per C allele of rs198389. No significant associations were observed between the rs198389 genotype and potential confounders.
Conclusions: Our findings provide evidence for a potential causal role of the BNP system in the etiology of T2D. Further studies are needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and explore possibilities for preventive interventions.

title: brain organization
text: During the perinatal period, the activation of estrogen receptors (ER) in the developing brain plays a crucial role in the defeminization of neural control of reproductive function and sexual behavior. Two main ER isoforms, ERalpha and ERbeta, are present in neural circuits that regulate ovarian cycle and sexual behavior. This study provides the first evidence that individual ER isoforms contribute differently to the process of estrogen-dependent defeminization. Neonatal activation of ERalpha in female rats resulted in the abrogation of cyclic ovarian activity and female sexual behavior in adulthood, accompanied by male-like alterations in the morphology of the anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) and sexually dimorphic nucleus of the preoptic area (SDN-POA). In contrast, exposure to an ERbeta-selective agonist induced persistent estrus and had a strong defeminizing effect on the hypothalamic gonadotropin "surge generator" AVPV, but failed to alter female sexual behavior, responsiveness to estrogens, and morphometric features of the behaviorally relevant SDN-POA. These findings suggest that ER isoforms convey different, and probably not synergistic, chemical signals in the course of neonatal sex-specific brain organization.

title: Thresholds for the cost–effectiveness of interventions: alternative approaches
text:
Many countries rely on the cost-effectiveness thresholds recommended by the World Health Organization's Choosing Interventions that are Cost-Effective (WHO-CHOICE) project when evaluating health interventions. According to WHO-CHOICE, an intervention is considered cost-effective if the cost per disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted is less than three times the country's annual gross domestic product (GDP) per capita. Interventions that meet this threshold are defined as highly cost-effective, with a threshold of once the annual GDP per capita per DALY averted. However, we argue that relying on these thresholds can be misleading and limit the usefulness of cost-effectiveness analyses in public health decision-making.
Firstly, the use of these thresholds has little theoretical justification. The WHO-CHOICE thresholds were developed based on a simplistic analysis of the economic burden of disease, without considering the broader social and economic context in which health interventions are implemented. As a result, the thresholds may not accurately reflect the relative values of different interventions in different settings.
Secondly, the thresholds skirt the difficult but necessary task of ranking the relative values of locally-applicable interventions. By setting a single threshold for cost-effectiveness, decision-makers are unable to fully consider the trade-offs between different interventions, such as the potential benefits and harms of each intervention, as well as the resource constraints and priorities of the health system.
Finally, the WHO-CHOICE thresholds are set so low that very few interventions with evidence of efficacy can be ruled out. This can lead to a situation where the most effective interventions are not prioritized, as they may not meet the threshold for cost-effectiveness.
To address these limitations, we propose alternative approaches for applying cost-effectiveness criteria to choices in the allocation of health-care resources. These approaches prioritize the consideration of the relative values of different interventions, taking into account the broader social and economic context, as well as the resource constraints and priorities of the health system. By adopting these approaches, decision-makers can make more informed and nuanced decisions about the allocation of health-care resources, and ensure that the most effective interventions are prioritized.

title: Effect of low doses of ionising radiation in infancy on cognitive function in adulthood: Swedish population based cohort study.
text:
Objective: To investigate whether exposure to low doses of ionizing radiation in infancy affects cognitive function in adulthood.
Design: Population-based cohort study.
Setting: Sweden.
Participants: 3094 male individuals who received radiation for cutaneous hemangioma before the age of 18 months between 1930 and 1959.
Main Outcome Measures: Radiation dose to the frontal and posterior parts of the brain, and the association between dose and intellectual capacity at the age of 18 or 19 years, measured through cognitive tests (learning ability, logical reasoning, spatial recognition) and high school attendance.
Results: The proportion of boys who attended high school decreased with increasing doses of radiation to both the frontal and posterior parts of the brain, from approximately 32% among those not exposed to around 17% in those who received more than 250 mGy. For the frontal dose, the multivariate odds ratio was 0.47 (95% confidence interval 0.26 to 0.85, P for trend 0.0003), and for the posterior dose, it was 0.59 (0.23 to 1.47, 0.0005). A negative dose-response relation was also evident for the three cognitive tests for learning ability and logical reasoning but not for the test of spatial recognition.
Conclusions: Low doses of ionizing radiation to the brain in infancy have a significant impact on cognitive abilities in adulthood.

title: Differential effects of charybdotoxin on the activity of retinal ganglion cells in the dark- and light-adapted mouse retina
text: Patch-clamp recordings were conducted on retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in the mouse retina to investigate the effects of blockade of BK(Ca) channels on the electrical activity of these cells. Under dark adaptation, blockade of BK(Ca) channels resulted in increased spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and light-evoked On-EPSCs, while simultaneously decreasing the light-evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs). However, under light adaptation, blockade of BK(Ca) channels led to a decrease in the light-evoked On-EPSCs, as well as the spontaneous IPSCs and light-evoked On- and Off-IPSCs. The blockade of BK(Ca) channels significantly altered the outputs of RGCs by transforming their light-evoked responses into a bursting pattern and increasing the light-evoked depolarization of the membrane potentials, while not significantly affecting the peak firing rates of light-evoked responses.

title: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome: review of the phenotype
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is a rare and well-known disorder characterized by extreme short stature, low body weight, early hair loss, lipodystrophy, scleroderma, decreased joint mobility, osteolysis, and facial features resembling an aged individual. Cardiovascular problems lead to early death. Cognitive development is normal. Data from 10 cases in the present study and 132 cases from the literature are presented. The incidence in the Netherlands over the past century was 1:4,000,000, with a sex ratio of 1.2:1. The main initial symptoms were failure to thrive (55%), hair loss (40%), skin problems (28%), and lipodystrophy (20%). The mean age of diagnosis was 2.9 years, and growth was more disturbed than height, with growth delay starting during fetal development. The mean height at over 13 years of age was 109 cm, and the mean weight was 14.5 kg. Osteolysis was widespread but limited to the viscerocranium, and lipodystrophy was generalized, with the exception of intra-abdominal fat deposits. Cardiovascular problems are highly variable, with both early onset and diverse nature. Stroke and coronary dysfunction are the most common. Pathological findings in coronaries and aorta resemble those of elderly individuals, but can also be more limited. Loss of smooth muscle cells is the most notable finding. The mean age of death was 12.6 years. Patients can be classified into two groups: classical HGPS, which follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance and is characterized by spontaneous mutations, and non-classical progeria, in which growth is less retarded, scalp hair remains for a longer time, lipodystrophy progresses more slowly, osteolysis is more pronounced except in the face, and survival into adulthood is possible. The inheritance pattern of non-classical progeria is likely autosomal recessive. The cause of HGPS is an abnormal Lamin A, either through a mutated LMNA gene or abnormal posttranslational processing (ZMPSTE24 gene mutations). Of 34 LMNA mutations found in progeria patients, 26 were classical p. G608G mutations (76%). The pathogenesis is likely to involve multiple pathways, and potential therapeutic strategies include RNA interference techniques and inhibition of the dominant-negative influence of abnormally formed Lamin A on polymerization with normally formed Lamin A.

title: Identification of an autoantigen demonstrates a link between interstitial lung disease and a defect in central tolerance.
text:
Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a prevalent manifestation of systemic autoimmunity, characterized by progressive inflammation or scarring of the lungs. This can result in significantly impaired gas exchange, leading to hypoxemia, pulmonary hypertension, and even death. Unfortunately, the underlying mechanisms of ILD remain poorly understood, including the role of specific defects in immune tolerance. Another key question is whether autoimmune responses targeting the lung parenchyma are essential to ILD pathogenesis, particularly in isolated idiopathic forms.
Our research has shed light on the etiology of ILD by demonstrating that a specific defect in central tolerance, caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator gene (Aire), leads to an autoreactive T cell response to a lung-specific antigen named vomeromodulin. This results in the development of ILD in both mice and humans with Aire deficiency. Our findings establish the AIRE-deficient model of autoimmunity as a suitable translational system for investigating the fundamental mechanisms of ILD pathogenesis.

title: In vivo role of ER-associated peptidase activity in tailoring peptides for presentation by MHC class Ia and class Ib molecules
text: Endoplasmic reticulum-associated aminopeptidase (ERAP1) has been implicated in the final proteolytic processing of peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules. To investigate the in vivo role of ERAP1, we generated ERAP1-deficient mice. Our findings revealed a significant reduction in cell surface expression of MHC class Ia molecules H-2Kb and H-2Db, as well as of class Ib molecule Qa-2, in these animals. Although cells from mutant animals exhibited reduced capacity to present several self- and foreign antigens to Kb-, Db-, or Qa-1b–restricted CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, presentation of some antigens was unaffected or significantly enhanced. Moreover, mice generated defective CD8+ T cell responses against class I–presented antigens. These findings demonstrate an essential in vivo role of ER-associated peptidase activity in tailoring peptides for presentation by MHC class Ia and class Ib molecules.

title: PD 0332991, a selective cyclin D kinase 4/6 inhibitor, preferentially inhibits proliferation of luminal estrogen receptor-positive human breast cancer cell lines in vitro
text:
Introduction:
Alterations in cell cycle regulators have been implicated in the development of human malignancies, including breast cancer. PD 0332991 is an orally active, highly selective inhibitor of the cyclin D kinases (CDK)4 and CDK6, with the ability to block retinoblastoma (Rb) phosphorylation in the low nanomolar range. To identify predictors of response to PD 0332991, we determined the in vitro sensitivity to the drug across a panel of molecularly characterized human breast cancer cell lines.
Methods:
Forty-seven human breast cancer and immortalized cell lines representing the known molecular subgroups of breast cancer were treated with PD 0332991 to determine IC50 values. These data were analyzed against baseline gene expression data to identify genes associated with PD 0332991 response.
Results:
Cell lines representing the luminal estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) subtype (including those that are HER2 amplified) were found to be most sensitive to growth inhibition by PD 0332991, while nonluminal/basal subtypes were most resistant. Analysis of variance identified 450 differentially expressed genes between sensitive and resistant cells. PD 0332991 was found to elevate pRb and cyclin D1 and decrease CDKN2A (p16) in the most sensitive lines. Cell cycle analysis showed G0/G1 arrest in sensitive cell lines, and Western blot analysis demonstrated that Rb phosphorylation was blocked in sensitive lines but not resistant lines. PD 0332991 was synergistic with tamoxifen and trastuzumab in ER+ and HER2-amplified cell lines, respectively. PD 0332991 also enhanced sensitivity to tamoxifen in cell lines with conditioned resistance to ER blockade.
Conclusions:
These studies suggest a role for CDK4/6 inhibition in some breast cancers and identify criteria for patient selection in clinical studies of PD 0332991.

title: Identification of secreted proteins that mediate cell-cell interactions in an in vitro model of the lung cancer microenvironment.
text: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells with K-ras mutations recruit various stromal cells (including macrophages, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts) to the tumor microenvironment, which can either promote or inhibit tumor growth through mechanisms that are not fully understood. To investigate this phenomenon, we developed an in vitro model where we cocultured a murine K-ras mutant lung adenocarcinoma cell line (LKR-13) with murine lung stromal cells. Our findings revealed that stromal cells enhance LKR-13 cell tumorigenicity by altering the tumor cell secretome, including proteins involved in angiogenesis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. Specifically, we found that the proteins CXCL1 and IL-18 play a crucial role in this process. Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of these proteins revealed that stromal cell migration, LKR-13 cell proliferation, and LKR-13 cell tumorigenicity are dependent on CXCL1 and IL-18. Our results suggest that targeting tumor/stromal cell interactions may be a promising therapeutic approach for NSCLC patients.

title: Tightrope act: autophagy in stem cell renewal, differentiation, proliferation, and aging
text: Autophagy is a natural process in which cells break down and recycle damaged or dysfunctional cellular components, such as organelles and protein aggregates. Stem cells, which are characterized by self-renewal, pluripotency, and quiescence, have a unique requirement for autophagy due to their limited capacity to dilute cellular waste and spent organelles, as well as their need for remodeling to differentiate. Here, we review the current literature on the role of autophagy in embryonic and adult stem cells, including hematopoietic, mesenchymal, and neuronal stem cells, highlighting the diverse and contrasting roles autophagy plays in their biology. Additionally, we discuss the few available studies on stem cells, lysosomal activity, and autophagy, and the need for novel techniques to detect autophagy in primary cells in order to fully understand its importance in stem cells during transplantation, a promising therapeutic approach for many diseases.

title: Variant Histone H2A.Z Is Globally Localized to the Promoters of Inactive Yeast Genes and Regulates Nucleosome Positioning
text: Histone H2A.Z is an evolutionarily conserved histone variant that plays a crucial role in transcriptional regulation, antisilencing, silencing, and genome stability. However, the mechanisms by which H2A.Z regulates these various biological functions remain poorly understood, in part due to the limited knowledge of its spatial distribution along chromosomes and its role in regulating chromatin structure. To address this gap in knowledge, we employed chromatin immunoprecipitation combined with tiling microarrays (ChIP-seq) to map H2A.Z across the yeast genome at an approximately 300-bp resolution. Our analysis identified 4,862 small regions, typically one or two nucleosomes wide, that are decorated with H2A.Z. These regions, termed "H2A.Z loci," were found predominantly within specific nucleosomes in the promoter regions of inactive genes throughout the genome. Furthermore, we demonstrated that H2A.Z can regulate nucleosome positioning at the GAL1 promoter. Within HZAD domains, where H2A.Z exhibits an antisilencing function, H2A.Z is localized in a broader pattern, suggesting that the variant histone regulates silencing and transcriptional activation through distinct mechanisms. Our findings suggest that the incorporation of H2A.Z into specific promoter-bound nucleosomes configures chromatin structure to poise genes for transcriptional activation. The implications of these findings for higher eukaryotes are discussed.

title: Collective trauma in northern Sri Lanka: a qualitative psychosocial-ecological study
text:
BACKGROUND: Complex situations arising from war and natural disasters have a profound psychosocial impact on individuals, families, communities, and society as a whole. The mental health effects on individuals can range from non-pathological distress to various psychiatric disorders, while massive and widespread trauma and loss can alter family and social processes at multiple levels.
METHOD: This qualitative, ecological study employed participatory observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions with community-level relief and rehabilitation workers and government and non-governmental officials in Northern Sri Lanka, where the researcher was actively involved in psychosocial and community mental health programs among the Tamil community. The study compared the effects of chronic war on community functioning with those observed after the tsunami.
RESULTS: The study revealed fundamental changes in family and community dynamics, including single-parent families, lack of trust among members, changes in significant relationships, and child-rearing practices at the family level. Communities became more dependent, passive, and silent, with a breakdown in traditional structures, institutions, and familiar ways of life, as well as a deterioration in social norms and ethics. Various community-level interventions were attempted to address these issues.
CONCLUSION: Exposure to conflict, war, and disaster situations leads to profound changes in family and community dynamics, affecting individuals, families, communities, and society as a whole. Effective relief, rehabilitation, and development programs must address the problem of collective trauma through integrated, multi-level approaches.

title: Guidelines for the selection of highly effective siRNA sequences for mammalian and chick RNA interference.
text: In the current study, we investigated the relationship between short interfering RNA (siRNA) sequence and RNA interference (RNAi) effect using 62 targets of four exogenous and two endogenous genes in three mammalian and Drosophila cells. Our findings reveal the rules that govern siRNA sequence preference, which can be used to design highly effective siRNAs for systematic mammalian functional genomics. These rules indicate that siRNAs that satisfy all four conditions are capable of inducing highly effective gene silencing in mammalian cells: (i) A/U at the 5' end of the antisense strand; (ii) G/C at the 5' end of the sense strand; (iii) at least five A/U residues in the 5' terminal one-third of the antisense strand; and (iv) the absence of any GC stretch of more than 9 nt in length. In contrast, siRNAs with different features in relation to the first three conditions show little or no gene silencing in mammalian cells. The same rules for siRNA sequence preference were found applicable to DNA-based RNAi in mammalian cells and in ovo RNAi using chick embryos. However, little siRNA sequence preference could be detected in Drosophila in vivo RNAi.

title: Overview of the CCP4 suite and current developments
text: The CCP4 (Collaborative Computational Project, Number 4) software suite is a comprehensive collection of programs, data, and software libraries designed for macromolecular structure determination through X-ray crystallography. The suite is designed to be highly flexible, allowing users to employ various methods to achieve their goals. The programs originate from diverse sources, but are united through a standardized infrastructure of file formats, data objects, and graphical interfaces. Automation pipelines are also included in the suite, further streamlining the structure solution process. After providing a brief overview of the CCP4 suite's evolution over the past 30 years, this article provides an extensive overview of the current suite, highlighting how each program contributes to a complete software package.

title: Histone Demethylase Expression Enhances Human Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Efficiency and Promotes Derivation of Pluripotent Stem Cells.
text: The inefficient derivation of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) using somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) limits their potential use. The formation of blastocysts from human SCNT embryos occurs at a low rate, and only some oocyte donors are capable of supporting this process. Previous research in mice revealed that reducing histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) through ectopic expression of the H3K9me3 demethylase Kdm4d improves SCNT embryo development. Building on this finding, we demonstrate that overexpressing a related H3K9me3 demethylase, KDM4A, improves human SCNT. Our results show that H3K9me3 in the human somatic cell genome serves as a reprogramming barrier in SCNT, and that overexpression of KDM4A significantly enhances blastocyst formation in human SCNT embryos. This discovery has implications for improving SCNT in various contexts, including regenerative medicine, by facilitating transcriptional reprogramming and enabling the efficient derivation of SCNT-derived ESCs using adult Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) patient somatic nuclei donors.

title: Interface Contractility between Differently Fated Cells Drives Cell Elimination and Cyst Formation
text: Although extensive research has been conducted on cellular mechanisms that suppress tumors, little is known about the mechanisms that operate at the tissue level to prevent the formation of aberrant cells in epithelial tissues. Our findings in Drosophila imaginal discs reveal that ectopic expression of transcription factors that determine cell fate leads to the formation of abnormal epithelial cysts. These cysts do not form cell autonomously but rather result from the juxtaposition of two cell populations with different fates. The juxtaposition of wild-type and aberrantly specified cells leads to the accumulation of actomyosin at their shared interface, both at adherens junctions and along basolateral interfaces. Experimental validation of 3D vertex model simulations demonstrates that enhanced interface contractility is sufficient to explain many morphogenetic behaviors, including cyst formation by intermediate-sized clusters and segregation of large cell populations by formation of smooth boundaries or apical constriction in small groups of cells. Furthermore, we find that single cells experiencing lateral interface contractility are eliminated from tissues through apoptosis. The formation of cysts occurs when the elimination of single, aberrantly specified cells fails, and cells proliferate to intermediate cell cluster sizes. Our results provide a novel perspective on morphogenetic mechanisms, which arise from cell-fate heterogeneities within tissues and maintain or disrupt epithelial homeostasis.

title: Resonating circadian clocks enhance fitness in cyanobacteria.
text: In certain organisms, the combination of a light/dark cycle and the endogenous circadian clock can enhance longevity, growth rate, and development. However, there is limited evidence to suggest that the resonance between the endogenous clock and the environmental cycle directly improves reproductive fitness. To investigate the adaptive significance of circadian programming, we evaluated the relative fitness of various strains of cyanobacteria under competition, with different circadian periods. Our findings suggest that circadian programming may act through soft selection, favoring strains with a circadian period similar to that of the light/dark cycle.

title: Stromal Fibroblasts Present in Invasive Human Breast Carcinomas Promote Tumor Growth and Angiogenesis through Elevated SDF-1/CXCL12 Secretion
text: Fibroblasts are a predominant component of the stromal cells within breast carcinomas, yet their functional involvement in tumorigenesis remains poorly understood. To investigate the contributions of carcinoma-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) to tumor growth, we employed a coimplantation tumor xenograft model. Our findings demonstrate that CAFs isolated from human breast carcinomas exhibit a myofibroblastic phenotype and significantly enhance the growth of admixed breast carcinoma cells compared to normal mammary fibroblasts derived from the same patients. CAFs promote angiogenesis by recruiting endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) into carcinomas, an effect mediated in part by the secretion of stromal cell-derived factor 1 (SDF-1). Additionally, CAF-secreted SDF-1 directly stimulates tumor growth through its cognate receptor, CXCR4, which is expressed on carcinoma cells. Our findings indicate that fibroblasts within invasive breast carcinomas play a significant role in tumor promotion, primarily through the secretion of SDF-1.

title: Embryonic Origin of Postnatal Neural Stem Cells
text: Adult neural stem/progenitor cells located within the walls of the lateral ventricles generate a diverse array of neurons for the olfactory bulb (OB). The spatial distribution of these cells determines the types of OB neurons they produce. Our study reveals that the majority of mouse B1 cell precursors are generated between embryonic days (E) 13.5 and 15.5 and remain quiescent until they are reactivated postnatally. Using a retroviral library containing over 100,000 genetic tags, we found that B1 cells share a common progenitor with embryonic cells of the cortex, striatum, and septum, although this lineage relationship is lost before E15.5. Regional specification of B1 cells becomes evident as early as E11.5 and is spatially associated with the production of neurons that populate distinct areas of the forebrain. This investigation uncovers an early embryonic regionalization of postnatal neural stem cells and the lineage relationship between them and embryonic progenitor cells.

title: The Opa1-Dependent Mitochondrial Cristae Remodeling Pathway Controls Atrophic, Apoptotic, and Ischemic Tissue Damage
text:
Mitochondrial morphological and ultrastructural changes occur during apoptosis and autophagy, but their in vivo relevance for tissue response to damage is unclear. To investigate, we focused on the optic atrophy 1 (OPA1)-dependent cristae remodeling pathway in vivo and found that it regulates the response of multiple tissues to apoptotic, necrotic, and atrophic stimuli. Genetic inhibition of the cristae remodeling pathway in vivo did not affect development but protected mice from various forms of tissue damage, including denervation-induced muscular atrophy, ischemic heart and brain damage, and hepatocellular apoptosis. Our results suggest that the OPA1-dependent cristae remodeling pathway is a fundamental, targetable determinant of tissue damage in vivo.
Mechanistically, OPA1-dependent mitochondrial cristae stabilization enhances mitochondrial respiratory efficiency, blunts mitochondrial dysfunction, cytochrome c release, and reactive oxygen species production. These findings demonstrate that the OPA1-dependent cristae remodeling pathway plays a crucial role in maintaining mitochondrial function and preventing tissue damage in vivo. Our study provides evidence that targeting this pathway may be a promising therapeutic strategy for various forms of tissue damage.

title: First Proposal of Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay for Regenerative Medicine
text:
Advances in stem cell research have led to an increase in studies on regenerative medicine globally, with numerous institutions and companies involved. However, the lack of a standardized format for experimentation hinders reproducibility and data exchange among laboratories or cell banks. To address this challenge, we propose Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay for Regenerative Medicine (MIACARM), a standardized format for describing cellular assay data, to facilitate practical regenerative medicine. Building on the existing Minimum Information About a Cellular Assay, MIACARM provides a platform for exchanging cellular assay data among cell banks or registries at over 20 sites worldwide.
Currently, there are numerous human cell information storage sites globally, but reproducibility and data exchange among different laboratories or providers are often inadequate or non-existent due to the lack of a standardized format for experiments. This collaborative study, involving scientists from stem cell banks and cellular information registries worldwide, including those in the US, the UK, Europe, and Japan, aims to address this issue by proposing new minimum information guidelines for cellular assay data deposition. MIACARM is designed to promote data exchange and facilitate practical regenerative medicine.

title: The PAR proteins: fundamental players in animal cell polarization.
text: The discovery of the PAR genes dates back to genetic screens for regulators of cytoplasmic partitioning in the early embryo of C. elegans, where they were found to encode six different proteins essential for asymmetric cell division in the worm zygote. Some of these PAR proteins are localized asymmetrically and form physical complexes with one another, a striking observation that has led researchers to propose that they play a crucial role in cell polarization. Intriguingly, the PAR proteins have been found to regulate cell polarization in a wide range of contexts across many different animal species, suggesting that they may be part of an ancient and fundamental mechanism for cell polarization. While much remains to be learned about how the PAR proteins function, recent advances in cell biology and biochemistry are beginning to shed light on the mechanisms by which they polarize cells.

title: Prions Adhere to Soil Minerals and Remain Infectious
text: An unidentified environmental reservoir of infectivity contributes to the natural transmission of prion diseases (transmissible spongiform encephalopathies [TSEs]) in sheep, deer, and elk. Prion infectivity may enter soil environments through shedding from diseased animals and the decomposition of infected carcasses. Burial of TSE-infected cattle, sheep, and deer as a means of disposal has led to the unintentional introduction of prions into subsurface environments. In this study, we investigated the potential of soil to serve as a TSE reservoir by examining the interaction between the disease-associated prion protein (PrPSc) and common soil minerals. We found that PrPSc adsorbed substantially to two clay minerals, quartz, and four whole soil samples. We quantified the PrPSc-binding capacities of each mineral and observed that PrPSc desorbed from montmorillonite clay was cleaved at an N-terminal site, resulting in a strong interaction between PrPSc and Mte. Despite cleavage and avid binding, PrPSc bound to Mte remained infectious. Our findings suggest that PrPSc released into soil environments may be preserved in a bioavailable form, perpetuating prion disease epizootics and exposing other species to the infectious agent.

title: Regulated Accumulation of Desmosterol Integrates Macrophage Lipid Metabolism and Inflammatory Responses
text: In atherosclerosis, inflammation and macrophage foam cells are prominent features, but the connections between cholesterol accumulation and inflammation, as well as the LXR-dependent signaling pathways, are poorly understood. To investigate these relationships, we employed lipidomic and transcriptomic approaches to evaluate the impact of diet and LDL receptor genotype on macrophage foam cell formation in the peritoneal cavities of mice. Surprisingly, foam cell formation was associated with significant changes in hundreds of lipid species, rather than the expected activation of inflammatory gene expression. Our findings suggest that regulated desmosterol accumulation underlies many homeostatic responses, including activation of LXR target genes, inhibition of SREBP target genes, selective reprogramming of fatty acid metabolism, and suppression of inflammatory response genes in macrophage foam cells. These observations indicate that macrophage activation in atherosclerotic lesions results from extrinsic, pro-inflammatory signals generated within the artery wall, which suppress homeostatic and anti-inflammatory functions of desmosterol.

title: A JOURNAL OF NEUROLOGY
text:
Brain glial cells, comprising approximately five times the number of neurons, have recently gained attention for their potential involvement in epileptic seizures. Specifically, microglia and astrocytes, which are responsible for surveillance of brain damage and inflammatory responses, have been implicated in the facilitation and potential triggering of seizures. While recent evidence suggests that innate immune responses play a role in lowering the seizure threshold in experimental models of epilepsy, it remains unclear whether these responses can independently initiate seizures in vivo.
Our study demonstrates that cortical innate immune responses can produce profound increases in brain excitability, leading to focal seizures. We found that cortical application of lipopolysaccharide, which binds to toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), triples evoked field potential amplitudes and produces focal epileptiform discharges. These effects are prevented by pre-application of interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. Our results indicate that the innate immune response may play a significant role in acute seizures by increasing neuronal excitability through interleukin-1 release in response to TLR4 detection of danger signals associated with central nervous system infections and brain injury. These findings suggest an important role of innate immunity in epileptogenesis and highlight the potential of glial inhibition, through pharmacological blockade of TLR4 and the pro-inflammatory mediators released by activated glia, in the study and treatment of seizure disorders in humans.

title: Sequential domain assembly of ribosomal protein S3 drives 40S subunit maturation.
text: Eukaryotic ribosomes are assembled through the association of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) with ribosomal proteins, forming nuclear precursor particles that undergo a complex maturation pathway guided by non-ribosomal assembly factors. In this study, we provide insights into the mechanisms that promote the maturation of the 40S ribosomal subunit by examining the role of ribosomal protein S3. We show that S3 dimerizes and is imported into the nucleus in a rotated conformation, associated with the chaperone Yar1. Initial assembly of S3 with 40S precursors occurs through its C-domain, while the N-domain protrudes from the 40S surface. Subsequent replacement of Yar1 by the assembly factor Ltv1 fixes the S3 N-domain in its rotated orientation, preventing its association with 40S ribosomes. Finally, Ltv1 release, triggered by phosphorylation, and the subsequent flipping of the S3 N-domain into its final position result in the stable integration of S3, representing a novel assembly mechanism for the incorporation of ribosomal proteins.
