title: Assaying proliferation and differentiation capacity of stem cells using disaggregated adult mouse epidermis
text: In this protocol, we detail the process of isolating and characterizing keratinocytes from adult mouse epidermis, and examining their function in an in vivo skin reconstitution assay using neonatal dermal cells. We also describe how to subject the isolated keratinocytes to clonal analysis in vitro and in vivo, and how to enrich for hair follicle-inducing dermal papilla cells in the dermal preparation. By using these approaches, we can compare the ability of different populations of adult epidermal stem cells to proliferate and differentiate into different lineages. The isolation and preparation of cells for the skin reconstitution assay typically takes 2 days, while clonal growth in culture is assessed after 14 days, and evaluation of the grafts is performed after 4-5 weeks.

title: Telomerase-negative immortalized human cells contain a novel type of promyelocytic leukemia (PML) body.
text:
Telomerase-negative immortalized human cells maintain their telomeres through an alternative mechanism known as alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT). In this study, we investigate the presence of a novel nuclear structure in ALT cells, which we term ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs). APBs are large, donut-shaped structures composed of PML protein, telomeric DNA, and the telomere-binding proteins human telomere repeat binding factors 1 and 2. Immunostaining revealed that APBs also contain replication factor A, RAD51, and RAD52, proteins involved in DNA synthesis and recombination. Notably, the appearance of APBs coincides with the activation of ALT, and they are exclusively found in ALT tumors and cell lines, but not in mortal cell strains or in telomerase-positive cell lines or tumors.
In this investigation, we uncover the presence of a novel nuclear structure in telomerase-negative immortalized human cells, which we term ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs). APBs are large, donut-shaped structures composed of PML protein, telomeric DNA, and the telomere-binding proteins human telomere repeat binding factors 1 and 2. Through immunostaining, we further reveal that APBs also contain replication factor A, RAD51, and RAD52, proteins involved in DNA synthesis and recombination. Our findings indicate that APBs are a distinctive feature of ALT cells and are closely associated with the activation of this alternative telomere-lengthening mechanism. Moreover, our results show that APBs are exclusive to ALT tumors and cell lines, but not found in mortal cell strains or in telomerase-positive cell lines or tumors, highlighting their potential as a diagnostic marker for ALT.

title: Prediction of coronary artery disease by a systemic atherosclerosis score index derived from whole-body MR angiography
text: The present study aimed to investigate the relationship between whole-body magnetic resonance angiography (WB-MRA) findings, including a systemic atherosclerosis score index (ASI), and the presence of significant coronary artery disease (CAD). WB-MRA was performed on 50 patients scheduled to undergo elective cardiac catheterization for suspected CAD. In each patient, 40 extra-cardiac vessel segments were evaluated and assigned scores based on their luminal narrowing. The ASI was generated as the ratio of the summed scores to analyzable segments. The results showed that patients with significant CAD (n = 27) had higher ASI values compared to those without CAD (n = 22) (1.56 vs. 1.28, p = 0.004). The ASI correlated with established cardiovascular risk scores, including the PROCAM and Framingham risk scores. A ROC-derived ASI of > 1.54 was found to be a strong predictor of significant CAD, with a sensitivity of 59%, specificity of 86%, and positive predictive value of 84%. Additionally, the study found that patients with CAD were more likely to have extra-cardiac stenoses compared to those without CAD (55% vs. 14%, p = 0.003). These findings suggest that WB-MRA-derived ASI is a useful tool for assessing the risk of coronary disease in patients with extra-cardiac manifestations of atherosclerosis.

title: Analysis of re-replication from deregulated origin licensing by DNA fiber spreading
text:
Each human cell division cycle poses a significant challenge: preventing the initiation of DNA replication origins more than once, a phenomenon known as re-replication. Acute deregulation of replication control can lead to extensive DNA damage, cell-cycle checkpoint activation, and cell death, while moderate deregulation can promote genome instability and tumorigenesis. However, detecting re-replication in the absence of noticeable increases in cellular DNA content has proven difficult, making it challenging to determine if the ability to re-replicate is restricted to a particular cell-cycle phase.
To address this challenge, we developed an adaptation of DNA fiber spreading, allowing for the direct detection of re-replication on single DNA molecules from human chromosomes. Using this method, we demonstrate substantial re-replication within 1 hour of S phase entry in cells overproducing the replication factor, Cdt1. Furthermore, a comparison of the HeLa cancer cell line to untransformed fibroblasts reveals that HeLa cells exhibit low-level re-replication in otherwise unperturbed cell cycles. Interestingly, depletion of the Cdt1 inhibitor, geminin, in an untransformed fibroblast cell line results in undetectable re-replication by standard assays but is readily quantifiable by DNA fiber spreading analysis.
This study highlights the importance of direct evaluation of re-replicated DNA molecules in understanding the events that promote or perturb genome stability. By employing this novel approach, we gain valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying genome maintenance and disease progression, paving the way for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

title: Liver receptor homolog-1 is essential for pregnancy
text: Successful pregnancy requires the coordination of various signals and factors from different tissues. One key element involved in this process is liver receptor homolog-1 (Lrh-1), an orphan nuclear receptor that regulates metabolism and hormone synthesis. Lrh-1 is highly expressed in granulosa cells of ovarian follicles and in the corpus luteum of rodents and humans. Germline ablation of the Nr5a2 gene, which encodes Lrh-1, leads to embryonic lethality at gastrulation in mice. Depletion of Lrh-1 in ovarian follicles shows that it regulates genes necessary for both steroid synthesis and ovulation. To investigate the role of Lrh-1 in mouse gestation, we disrupted its expression in the corpus luteum, resulting in luteal insufficiency. Hormone replacement allowed embryo implantation, but was followed by gestational failure, with impaired endometrial decidualization, compromised placental formation, fetal growth retardation, and fetal death. Lrh-1 is also expressed in the mouse and human endometrium, and in a primary culture of human endometrial stromal cells. Reduction of NR5A2 transcript abundance through RNA interference abrogated decidualization in these cells. These findings demonstrate that Lrh-1 plays essential roles in maintaining the corpus luteum, promoting decidualization, and forming the placenta, making it a crucial element in establishing and sustaining pregnancy.

title: Transcriptional Signature and Memory Retention of Human-Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
text: Genetic reprogramming of somatic cells to a pluripotent state, known as induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), has been achieved using mouse and human cells through the over-expression of specific genes. However, the similarity between human iPSCs and human Embryonic Stem Cells (hESCs) remains unclear. In this study, we investigated the transcriptional profile of human iPSCs generated without the use of viral vectors or genomic insertions. Our results show that human iPSCs are similar to hESCs in general, but there are significant differences between the two. To generate human iPSCs without viral vectors or genomic insertions, we used pluripotent factors Oct4 and Nanog cloned in episomal vectors and transfected into human fetal neural progenitor cells. The transient expression of these factors, or Oct4 alone, resulted in efficient generation of human iPSCs. Our reprogramming strategy revealed a potential transcriptional signature for human iPSCs while retaining the gene expression of donor cells in reprogrammed cells free of viral and transgene interference. Additionally, the episomal reprogramming strategy represents a safe way to generate human iPSCs for clinical purposes and basic research.

title: A CXCL1 Paracrine Network Links Cancer Chemoresistance and Metastasis
text: Metastasis and chemoresistance in cancer are intricately linked, yet the molecular underpinnings of this connection remain elusive. Our research uncovered a complex network of paracrine signals between cancer, myeloid, and endothelial cells that drives both processes in breast cancer. Cancer cells that overexpress CXCL1 and 2 through transcriptional hyperactivation or 4q21 amplification are better equipped to survive in metastatic sites. CXCL1/2 attract CD11b(+)Gr1(+) myeloid cells into the tumor, which produce chemokines such as S100A8/9, further enhancing cancer cell survival. However, chemotherapeutic agents used to treat cancer do not directly kill cancer cells, but instead trigger a concurrent stromal reaction in which endothelial and other stromal cells produce TNF-α. TNF-α, in turn, enhances CXCL1/2 expression in cancer cells, thereby amplifying the CXCL1/2-S100A8/9 loop and leading to chemoresistance. By blocking the CXCR2 receptor, we were able to break this cycle and enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy against breast tumors and metastases. This network of endothelial-carcinoma-myeloid signaling interactions provides a crucial link between chemoresistance and metastasis, offering potential targets for intervention.

title: Prophylaxis of postoperative vomiting in children undergoing tonsillectomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text:
Introduction:
Postoperative vomiting (POV) remains a significant cause of morbidity in children undergoing tonsillectomy. Various prophylactic anti-emetic interventions have been studied, but there has been limited systematic review in this patient population. This systematic review aims to evaluate the effectiveness of different prophylactic anti-emetic strategies in preventing POV in children undergoing tonsillectomy.
Methods:
A systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, MEDLINE, and EMBASE to identify double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials of prophylactic anti-emetic interventions in children undergoing tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy. The outcome of interest was POV in the first 24 hours. Summary estimates of the effect of each prophylactic anti-emetic strategy were derived using fixed-effect meta-analysis. Dose-response effects were estimated using logistic regression where appropriate. A total of 22 articles were identified.
Results:
Good evidence was found for the prophylactic anti-emetic effect of dexamethasone (odds ratio (OR) 0.23, 95% CI 0.16-0.33), and the serotinergic antagonists ondansetron (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.29-0.46), granisetron (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.06-0.19), tropisetron (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.06-0.35), and dolasetron (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.1-0.59). Metoclopramide was also found to be efficacious (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.34-0.77). However, insufficient evidence was found to suggest that dimenhydrinate, perphenazine, or droperidol, in the doses studied, are efficacious. Additionally, gastric aspiration or acupuncture were not found to be effective.
Conclusion:
Dexamethasone and the anti-serotinergic agents appear to be the most effective agents for the prophylaxis of POV in children undergoing tonsillectomy. These findings suggest that these interventions may be useful in reducing the incidence of POV in this patient population. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the optimal dosing and timing of these interventions.

title: A method of comparing the areas under receiver operating characteristic curves derived from the same cases.
text:
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves are a widely used tool in medical diagnostics to evaluate and compare the performance of different diagnostic technologies or algorithms. In this paper, we propose a novel method to refine the statistical comparison of the areas under two ROC curves derived from the same set of patients by taking into account the correlation between the areas that is induced by the paired nature of the data.
To achieve this, we utilize the correspondence between the area under an ROC curve and the Wilcoxon statistic, which is a widely used measure of non-parametric significance. By assuming binormal distributions for the underlying data, we are able to create a table that converts the observed correlations in paired ratings of images into a correlation between the two ROC areas. This correlation can then be used to reduce the standard error (uncertainty) about the observed difference in areas, resulting in a considerable increase in the statistical sensitivity (power) of the comparison.
For studies involving multiple readers, this method provides a valuable measure of a component of the sampling variation that is otherwise difficult to obtain. By taking into account the paired nature of the data, our approach can provide more accurate and reliable results than traditional methods, which do not account for this important aspect of the data.

title: Transient inactivation of Rb and ARF yields regenerative cells from postmitotic mammalian muscle.
text:
An intriguing biological conundrum is the limited capacity for tissue regeneration in mammals, in contrast to the remarkable regenerative abilities of urodele amphibians and teleost fish. This disparity has sparked interest in the underlying mechanisms, with recent studies suggesting that cell cycle reentry may play a crucial role in regeneration. Specifically, upon inactivation of the retinoblastoma (Rb) protein, proliferation of postmitotic urodele skeletal muscle cells is induced, a mechanism that does not exist in mammalian muscle.
Building on these findings, we postulated that a tumor suppressor present in mammals but absent in regenerative vertebrates, the Ink4a product ARF (alternative reading frame), may function as a regeneration suppressor. Consistent with this hypothesis, concomitant inactivation of Arf and Rb led to mammalian muscle cell cycle reentry, loss of differentiation properties, and upregulation of cytokinetic machinery.
To investigate this further, we employed laser micro-dissection-catapulting to isolate single postmitotic myocytes, and transiently suppressed Arf and Rb. Remarkably, myoblast colonies were generated that retained the ability to differentiate and fuse into myofibers upon transplantation in vivo. These findings support the hypothesis that Arf evolved at the expense of regeneration, and provide insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying tissue regeneration in different organisms.

title: CENP-B Controls Centromere Formation Depending on the Chromatin Context
text: The centromere is a crucial region of chromatin that directs the accurate inheritance of eukaryotic chromosomes during cell division. However, the mechanism by which the centromere assembles and stabilizes at a specific genomic location is not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the role of the centromeric protein CENP-B in de novo centromere formation on human/mammalian artificial chromosomes (HAC/MACs). We find that the de novo formation of a HAC/MAC with a functional centromere requires the presence of alpha-satellite DNA containing CENP-B binding motifs. Interestingly, we observe that CENP-B plays a dual role in centromere formation, as it enhances histone H3-K9 trimethylation and DNA methylation on integration sites, thereby stimulating heterochromatin formation. In contrast, centromere formation is suppressed in cells expressing CENP-B when alpha-satellite DNA is integrated into a chromosomal site. These findings suggest that CENP-B plays a critical role in ensuring the de novo formation of centromeres on DNA lacking a functional centromere, while preventing the formation of excess centromeres on chromosomes.

title: Improved tools for biological sequence comparison.
text: We have created three computer programs for analyzing protein and DNA sequences: FASTA, FASTP, and RDF2. FASTA is a more advanced version of FASTP, which can search protein or DNA sequence databases and compare a protein sequence to a DNA sequence database by translating the DNA data base as it is searched. FASTA includes an additional step in the calculation of the initial pairwise similarity score that allows multiple regions of similarity to be combined to increase the score of related sequences. RDF2 can evaluate the significance of similarity scores using a shuffling method that preserves local sequence composition. LFASTA can display all regions of local similarity between two sequences with scores greater than a threshold, using the same scoring parameters and a similar alignment algorithm. These programs have been modified to allow comparison of DNA or protein sequences based on various alternative scoring matrices.

title: The adverse consequences of unmet need among older persons living in the community: dual-eligible versus Medicare-only beneficiaries.
text:
Objective:
To estimate and compare the prevalence of specific adverse consequences associated with unmet need for assistance among a vulnerable subgroup of older adults who are dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, compared to those eligible for Medicare only.
Methodology:
Using data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), a representative survey of the older Medicare population, we calculated the prevalence of disability-related need for assistance with self-care, household tasks, and mobility activities, as well as the prevalence of adverse consequences of unmet need by dually eligible and Medicare only status.
Results:
Over 2 million community-dwelling older persons experienced an adverse consequence due to unmet need for assistance with self-care (e.g., soiled their clothes), over 2 million experienced adverse consequences due to unmet need for assistance with household tasks (e.g., went without groceries), and over 3 million persons experienced at least one adverse consequence of unmet need for assistance with mobility-related activities (e.g., had to stay in bed) in the month prior to the NHATS interview. Dually eligible persons experienced higher rates of 6 of the 11 adverse consequences studied and were more likely to have at least one adverse consequence in all 3 domains than others.
Discussion:
Several care models are emerging with the goal of integrating medical care, behavioral health, and long-term services for the dual eligible population. Indicators of adverse consequences of unmet need could be used to monitor the quality and adequacy of such care systems. The findings of this study highlight the importance of addressing the unmet need for assistance among this vulnerable population, and the need for more comprehensive and integrated care models to address their complex needs.

title: Supplementary information: ‘MesoRD User’s Guide ’ and other
text:
MesoRD: A Tool for Stochastic Simulation of Chemical Reactions and Diffusion
MesoRD is a software tool designed for stochastic simulation of chemical reactions and diffusion. Specifically, it is an implementation of the next subvolume method, which is an exact method for simulating the Markov process corresponding to the reaction-diffusion master equation.
AVAILABILITY
MesoRD is free and open-source software, written in C++ and licensed under the GNU General Public License (GPL). It is compatible with Linux, Mac OS X, NetBSD, Solaris, and Windows XP operating systems, and can be downloaded from the MesoRD website at <http://mesord.sourceforge.net>.
CONTACT
For more information or assistance with using MesoRD, please contact one of the following developers:
* Johan Elf: <johan.elf@icm.uu.se>
* Johan Hattne: <johan.hattne@embl-hamburg.de>

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
Additional documentation, including a user's guide, is available on the MesoRD website at <http://mesord.sourceforge.net>.

title: Functional anatomy of T cell activation and synapse formation.
text: T cell activation and function rely on the ordered interaction between T cells and antigen-presenting cells (APCs). In vivo, these interactions occur through two distinct dynamics: transient contacts mediated by promigratory junctions called immunological kinapses or prolonged contacts facilitated by stable junctions called immunological synapses. Kinapses are maintained in a steady state to enable reference to self-peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) and search for pathogen-derived pMHC, while synapses are induced by T cell receptor (TCR) interactions with agonist pMHC under specific conditions. These interactions lead to robust immune responses that generate effector and memory T cells. High-resolution imaging has revealed that the synapse is highly organized, integrating cell adhesion, TCR recognition of pMHC complexes, and an array of activating and inhibitory ligands to promote or prevent T cell signaling. This review aims to elucidate the molecular components, geometry, and timing underlying kinapses and synapses, and to provide a comprehensive understanding of these interactions. By integrating recent molecular and physiological data, we hope to shed light on the mechanisms underlying T cell activation and function, and to suggest potential avenues for future research.

title: Modulation of Replicative Lifespan in Cryptococcus neoformans: Implications for Virulence
text:
The fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans exhibits replicative aging, characterized by advanced generational age and phenotypic changes that contribute to enhanced resistance to host and antifungal-based killing. Based on these findings, we hypothesized that altering the generational age of the pathogenic yeast population would impact its vulnerability to the host and virulence. SIR2, a well-conserved histone deacetylase, was identified as a potential target for anti-aging drugs.
We generated a mutant C. neoformans strain (sir2Δ) and observed a shortened replicative lifespan (RLS) in sir2Δ cells, consistent with its known role in aging. RLS analysis revealed that treatment with Sir2p-agonists prolonged RLS, while treatment with a Sir2p-antagonist shortened RLS. These effects were dependent on SIR2 and not observed in sir2Δ cells. Since loss of SIR2 resulted in slightly impaired fitness, we could not compare the effects of genetic RLS modulation on virulence between wild-type and sir2Δ cells. Instead, we chemically modulated RLS by treating C. neoformans cells with Sir2p agonists or antagonists in a Galleria mellonella infection model. Our findings suggest that prolonging RLS by treatment with Sir2p agonists decreased virulence in the Galleria host, while shortening RLS with a Sir2p antagonist enhanced virulence. Additionally, combination therapy with Sir2p agonists and antifungal therapy significantly enhanced the antifungal's effect. Importantly, no difference in virulence was observed when sir2Δ cells were used for infection, confirming target specificity and ruling out non-specific effects of the drugs on the Galleria host. These results suggest that RLS modulating drugs, such as Sir2p agonists, may be a promising new class of antifungal drug targets that can enhance antifungal efficacy.

title: Pf4-Cre transgenic mice allow the generation of lineage-restricted gene knockouts for studying megakaryocyte and platelet function in vivo.
text: To generate transgenic mice that express Cre-recombinase exclusively in the megakaryocytic lineage, we modified a mouse BAC clone through homologous recombination and replaced the first exon of the platelet factor 4 (Pf4), also known as CXCL4, with an improved Cre cDNA. Several strains expressing the transgene were generated and one strain, Q3, was further studied. By crossing Q3 mice with a ROSA26-lacZ reporter strain, we found that Cre-recombinase activity was confined to megakaryocytes. These results were confirmed by crossing Q3 mice with a strain containing loxP-flanked integrin beta1. Conditional deletion of the integrin beta1 protein in megakaryocytes was complete at the DNA level, and platelets were almost devoid of the integrin beta1 protein. The Pf4-Cre transgenic strain will be a valuable tool for investigating megakaryopoiesis, platelet formation, and platelet function.

title: LIN-44/Wnt Directs Dendrite Outgrowth through LIN-17/Frizzled in C. elegans Neurons
text: The proper development of the nervous system relies on the proper formation and morphology of two key components of neurons: axons and dendrites. Although both are essential for signal transmission, our understanding of dendrite development is still limited. In the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, we have found that the Wnt ligand LIN-44 and its Frizzled receptor LIN-17 play a crucial role in regulating dendrite development of the PQR oxygen sensory neuron. In lin-44 and lin-17 mutants, dendrites fail to form, grow abnormally, or are misdirected. By manipulating the temporal and spatial expression of LIN-44 and using cell-ablation experiments, we have found that this molecule is patterned during embryogenesis and acts as a attractive cue to determine the site from which the dendrite emerges. Additionally, we have discovered that LIN-44 signaling is transmitted through the LIN-17 receptor, which acts cell autonomously in PQR neurons. Furthermore, we have found that LIN-17 interacts with another Wnt molecule, EGL-20, and functions in parallel to MIG-1/Frizzled in this process. Our results reveal a crucial role for Wnt and Frizzled molecules in regulating dendrite development in vivo.

title: Why do general practitioners prescribe antibiotics for upper respiratory tract infections to meet patient expectations: a mixed methods study
text:
Objective: To investigate the role of patient expectations in general practitioners' (GPs) antibiotic prescribing for upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) in Australia.
Methods: A concurrent explanatory mixed-methods approach using a cross-sectional survey and semistructured interviews was employed. The study setting was primary care GPs in Australia, and 584 GPs completed the survey (response rate of 23.6%). Thirty-two GPs were interviewed individually. The outcome measure was the prescribing of antibiotics for URTIs.
Results: More than half of the GP respondents to the survey reported that they would prescribe antibiotics for URTIs to meet patient expectations. Qualitative findings revealed that 'patient expectations' may be the primary reason for inappropriate prescribing, but it encompasses other factors, including limited time, poor doctor-patient communication, and diagnostic uncertainty. The study identified three role archetypes to explain the behavior of GPs regarding antibiotic prescribing for URTIs. The main themes emerging from the qualitative component were that many GPs did not think that antibiotic prescribing in primary care was responsible for the development of antibiotic resistance nor that their individual prescribing would make any difference in light of larger issues like hospital prescribing or veterinary use. For them, there were negligible negative consequences from their inappropriate prescribing.
Conclusion: There is a need to raise awareness about the scope and magnitude of antibiotic resistance and the role of primary care prescribing in contributing to the problem, as well as the contribution of individual prescribing decisions.

title: Migraine and cardiovascular disease: systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Objective: To investigate the association between migraine and cardiovascular disease, including stroke, myocardial infarction, and death due to cardiovascular disease. Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Data sources: Electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library) and reference lists of included studies and reviews published until January 2009. Selection criteria: Case-control and cohort studies investigating the association between any migraine or specific migraine subtypes and cardiovascular disease. Review methods: Two investigators independently assessed the eligibility of identified studies using a two-step approach. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Studies were grouped according to a priori categories on migraine and cardiovascular disease. Data extraction: Two investigators extracted data. Pooled relative risks and 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Results: The studies were heterogeneous in terms of participant characteristics and definition of cardiovascular disease. Nine studies investigated the association between any migraine and ischaemic stroke, with a pooled relative risk of 1.73 (95% CI 1.31-2.29). Additional analyses revealed a significantly higher risk among people who had migraine with aura (2.16, 1.53-3.03) compared to people who had migraine without aura (1.23, 0.90-1.69; meta-regression for aura status P=0.02). Furthermore, the results suggested a greater risk among women (2.08, 1.13-3.84) compared to men (1.37, 0.89-2.11). Age less than 45 years, smoking, and oral contraceptive use further increased the risk. Eight studies investigated the association between migraine and myocardial infarction, with a pooled relative risk of 1.12 (95% CI 0.95-1.32). Five studies investigated the association between migraine and death due to cardiovascular disease, with a pooled relative risk of 1.03 (95% CI 0.79-1.34). Only one study investigated the association between women who had migraine with aura and myocardial infarction and death due to cardiovascular disease, showing a twofold increased risk. Conclusion: Migraine is associated with a twofold increased risk of ischaemic stroke, which is only apparent among people who have migraine with aura. Our results also suggest a higher risk among women and risk was further magnified for people with migraine who were aged less than 45, smokers, and women who used oral contraceptives. We did not find an overall association between any migraine and myocardial infarction or death due to cardiovascular disease. Too few studies are available to reliably evaluate the impact of modifying factors, such as migraine aura, on these associations.

title: Effect of Duration and Intermittency of Rifampin on Tuberculosis Treatment Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
text:
Background: Treatment regimens for active tuberculosis (TB) that are intermittent or use rifampin only during the initial phase have been proposed as practical alternatives, but their efficacy has been questioned. To assess the effect of duration and intermittency of rifampin use on TB treatment outcomes, we conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
Methods and Findings: We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane CENTRAL database for clinical trials published in English, French, or Spanish between 1965 and June 2008. Randomized controlled trials that used standardized treatment with rifampin-containing regimens were included. Studies reported bacteriologically confirmed failure and/or relapse in previously untreated patients with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB. Pooled cumulative incidences of treatment outcomes and association with risk factors were computed using stratified random effects meta-analyses. Meta-regression was performed using a negative binomial regression model. A total of 57 trials with 312 arms and 21,472 participants were included in the analysis. Regimens that used rifampin only for the first 1-2 months had significantly higher rates of failure, relapse, and acquired drug resistance compared to regimens that used rifampin for 6 months. This was particularly evident when there was initial drug resistance to isoniazid, streptomycin, or both. However, there was little evidence of difference in failure or relapse with daily or intermittent schedules of treatment administration, although there was insufficient published evidence to support administration of treatment twice weekly throughout therapy.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that TB treatment outcomes are significantly worse with shorter duration of rifampin use, or with initial drug resistance to isoniazid and/or streptomycin. Treatment outcomes were similar with all intermittent schedules evaluated, but there is insufficient evidence to support administration of treatment twice weekly throughout therapy.

title: A novel set of DNA methylation markers in urine sediments for sensitive/specific detection of bladder cancer.
text: This study aims to identify a set of DNA methylation markers in urine sediments that can accurately detect bladder cancer. The study analyzed the methylation status of 59 tumor-associated genes in bladder cancer cell lines, a small cohort of cancer biopsies, and urine sediments from 132 bladder cancer patients, as well as 23 age-matched patients with noncancerous urinary lesions, 6 neurologic diseases, and 7 healthy volunteers. The results showed that cancer-specific hypermethylation was observed in 15 genes in urine sediments, with a sensitivity of 91.7% and an accuracy of 87%. The study also found that the methylation markers identified in this study were different from those identified in previous studies in the United States, suggesting a possible epigenetic disparity between the American and Chinese cases. Overall, the study suggests that methylation profiling of an 11-gene set in urine sediments can be a sensitive and specific method for detecting bladder cancer, particularly in early stages of the disease.

title: Posttranslational Acetylation of α-Tubulin Constrains Protofilament Number in Native Microtubules
text:
Background: Microtubules are composed of linear polymers of α-β tubulin dimers (protofilaments) that self-assemble into a quinary structure. In vitro studies have shown that microtubules assembled from purified tubulin contain between 10 and 16 protofilaments, yet such structural polymorphisms are not observed in cells. This discrepancy suggests that factors other than tubulin are involved in regulating protofilament number.
Results: In this study, we investigate the role of acetylation of MEC-12 α-tubulin in constraining protofilament number in C. elegans touch receptor neurons (TRNs). We find that mutants lacking α-tubulin acetyltransferase activity have short microtubules with rampant lattice defects and variable protofilament number. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that acetylation of lysine 40 promotes the formation of interprotofilament salt bridges, thereby stabilizing lateral interactions between protofilaments and constraining quinary structure to produce stable, structurally uniform microtubules in vivo.
Conclusions: Our findings demonstrate that acetylation of α-tubulin is a crucial constraint on protofilament number in vivo. We propose a structural model in which this posttranslational modification promotes the formation of lateral salt bridges that fine-tune the association between adjacent protofilaments and enable the formation of uniform microtubule populations in vivo.

title: A KEY ROLE FOR OREXIN IN PANIC ANXIETY
text: Panic disorder is a severe anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, debilitating panic attacks, which are accompanied by decreased central gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) activity and exaggerated autonomic and respiratory responses to intravenous infusions of hypertonic sodium lactate. In a rat model of panic disorder, chronic inhibition of GABA synthesis in the dorsomedial-perifornical hypothalamus leads to the development of anxiety-like states and an increased vulnerability to cardioexcitatory responses induced by sodium lactate. The dorsomedial-perifornical hypothalamus is rich in neurons containing orexin (ORX), which play a crucial role in arousal, vigilance, and central autonomic mobilization, all of which are essential components of panic. Our findings demonstrate that activation of ORX-synthesizing neurons is necessary for the development of a panic-prone state in the rat panic model, and either silencing of the hypothalamic gene encoding ORX (Hcrt) with RNAi or systemic ORX-1 receptor antagonists block the panic responses. Furthermore, we have found that individuals with panic anxiety exhibit elevated levels of ORX in their cerebrospinal fluid compared to those without panic anxiety, suggesting that the ORX system may be involved in the pathophysiology of panic anxiety and that ORX antagonists may represent a promising new treatment strategy for panic disorder.

title: Local Increases in Mechanical Tension Shape Compartment Boundaries by Biasing Cell Intercalations
text:
During tissue development in animals, mechanical forces play a crucial role in organizing tissues into distinct, non-mixing groups of cells, known as compartments. The boundaries between these compartments are characterized by straight morphologies and are associated with signaling centers that regulate tissue growth and patterning. Recent studies have shown that local increases in mechanical tension at cell junctions along compartment boundaries can prevent cell mixing and maintain straight boundaries. However, the cellular mechanisms underlying this process are not well understood.
To investigate the mechanisms by which local increases in mechanical tension maintain compartment boundaries, we used live imaging and quantitative image analysis to study the dynamics of cell intercalation at the anteroposterior compartment boundaries of the Drosophila pupal abdominal epidermis. Our results show that cell mixing within compartments involves multiple cell intercalations, and that the frequency and orientation of these intercalations are unchanged along the compartment boundaries. Instead, we found that an asymmetry in the shrinkage of junctions during intercalation is biased, resulting in cell rearrangements that suppress cell mixing.
Using simulations of tissue growth, we were able to demonstrate that local increases in mechanical tension can account for this bias in junctional shrinkage. Our findings suggest that local increases in mechanical tension play a crucial role in maintaining cell populations separate by influencing junctional rearrangements during cell intercalation.
In summary, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms by which mechanical forces regulate tissue organization during development. By studying the dynamics of cell intercalation at compartment boundaries in the Drosophila pupal abdominal epidermis, we have identified a novel mechanism by which local increases in mechanical tension maintain straight boundaries and prevent cell mixing.

title: MDA5 and PTPN2, two candidate genes for type 1 diabetes, modify pancreatic β-cell responses to the viral by-product double-stranded RNA
text:
In type 1 diabetes (T1D), beta-cell destruction is believed to be triggered by a complex interplay between the immune system and beta cells. Recent studies have suggested that genetic factors may play a role in modulating this dialogue. To investigate this further, we evaluated the impact of two candidate genes, MDA5 and PTPN2, on beta-cell responses to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), a byproduct of viral replication.
We used INS-1E cells and primary rat beta cells to examine the effects of small interference RNAs (siRNAs) targeting MDA5 or PTPN2 on gene and protein expression, as well as viability, after exposure to intracellular synthetic dsRNA (polyinosinic-polycitidilic acid-PIC). Our results showed that PIC increased MDA5 and PTPN2 mRNA expression, which was inhibited by specific siRNAs. PIC also triggered apoptosis in both cell types, with augmentation by PTPN2 knockdown (KD), although inhibition of MDA5 did not modify PIC-induced apoptosis. In contrast, MDA5 silencing decreased PIC-induced cytokine and chemokine expression, although inhibition of PTPN2 induced minor or no changes in these inflammatory mediators.
Our findings suggest that changes in MDA5 and PTPN2 expression can modify beta-cell responses to dsRNA. MDA5 regulates inflammatory signals, while PTPN2 may function as a defense mechanism against pro-apoptotic signals generated by dsRNA. These two candidate genes for T1D may thus modulate beta-cell apoptosis and/or local release of inflammatory mediators in the course of a viral infection by acting, at least in part, at the pancreatic beta-cell level.
In conclusion, our study provides evidence that the dialogue between beta cells and the immune system is influenced by genetic factors, and that modulation of MDA5 and PTPN2 may play a role in beta-cell destruction in T1D. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms involved and to identify potential therapeutic targets for the prevention or treatment of T1D.

title: Tumor necrosis factor signaling mediates resistance to mycobacteria by inhibiting bacterial growth and macrophage death.
text: Tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a crucial player in controlling tuberculosis, is believed to protect against the disease by directing the formation of organized aggregates of immune cells, known as granulomas. However, when TNF signaling is lost, tuberculosis progresses more rapidly in humans, and the increased mortality of Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infected mice is associated with disorganized, necrotic granulomas. The specific roles of TNF signaling before this endpoint remain unclear. To better understand the mechanisms of TNF in mycobacterial pathogenesis, we monitored the progression of Mycobacterium marinum infection in transparent zebrafish. Our findings revealed that loss of TNF signaling leads to increased mortality, even when only the innate immune response is involved. In the absence of TNF, mycobacterial growth and granuloma formation are accelerated, followed by the necrotic death of overloaded macrophages and breakdown of the granuloma. These results suggest that TNF is not essential for granuloma formation, but rather maintains granuloma integrity by restricting mycobacterial growth within macrophages and preventing their necrosis.

title: Loss of negative regulation by Numb over Notch is relevant to human breast carcinogenesis
text: The biological conflict between Notch and Numb regulates the balance between proliferation and differentiation during development and homeostasis. Although altered Notch signaling has been linked to various human diseases, including cancer, evidence for a significant role of Notch in human tumors has remained elusive. Here, we reveal that the loss of Numb-mediated control over Notch signaling occurs in approximately 50% of human mammary carcinomas, resulting from specific ubiquitination and degradation of Numb. Mechanistically, Numb functions as an oncsuppressor, as its ectopic expression in Numb-negative, but not in Numb-positive, tumor cells inhibits proliferation. Increased Notch signaling is observed in Numb-negative tumors, but returns to basal levels upon Numb restoration. Conversely, Numb silencing enhances Notch signaling in normal breast cells and Numb-positive breast tumors. Finally, inhibition of Notch pharmacologically in Numb-negative, but not Numb-positive, breast tumors leads to growth suppression. Therefore, the Numb/Notch biological conflict is essential for the homeostasis of the normal mammary gland and its disruption contributes to human mammary carcinogenesis.

title: Cortical Dynein Controls Microtubule Dynamics to Generate Pulling Forces that Position Microtubule Asters
text: Dynein at the cortex plays a crucial role in positioning processes, such as spindle positioning during embryonic cell division and centrosome positioning during fibroblast migration. To investigate how cortical dynein interacts with microtubule ends to generate force and impact positioning, we have reconstituted the 'cortical' interaction between dynein and dynamic microtubule ends in an in vitro system using microfabricated barriers. Our findings show that barrier-attached dynein captures microtubule ends, inhibits growth, and triggers microtubule catastrophes, thereby controlling microtubule length. The subsequent interaction with shrinking microtubule ends generates pulling forces up to several pN. By combining experiments in microchambers with a theoretical description of aster mechanics, we demonstrate that dynein-mediated pulling forces lead to the reliable centering of microtubule asters in simple confining geometries. Our results highlight the intrinsic ability of cortical microtubule-dynein interactions to regulate microtubule dynamics and drive positioning processes in living cells.

title: Breast cancer risk factors in relation to breast density (United States)
text: In this study, we examined the relationship between known breast cancer risk factors and mammographic breast density in a large cohort of New Hampshire women. We analyzed data from 144,018 women with at least one mammogram recorded in a statewide registry, and assessed the influence of various risk factors on breast density using the BI-RADS classification. Our initial analyses revealed an inverse association between age and breast density, as well as a negative association between BMI and breast density. We also found that women who had late age at menarche, premenopausal status, and current hormone therapy (HT) use tend to have higher breast density, while those with greater parity tend to have lower breast density. Stratified analyses revealed interactions between age, BMI, and HT use, with a stronger positive effect of age at first birth in postmenopausal women. The multivariable model showed a slight positive influence of family history of breast cancer. However, the influence of age at menarche and reproductive factors on breast density was less evident in women with high BMI. Interestingly, we found that density is reduced in young women using HT, but increased in HT users aged 50 or more.

title: Perspective: repression of competition and the evolution of cooperation.
text: Repression of competition within groups emerges as a crucial force in shaping the evolution of cooperation, joining kin selection as the second major factor in the history of life. When opportunities for competition against neighbors are limited within groups, individuals can enhance their own success only by boosting the efficiency and productivity of their group. As a result, characters that suppress competition within groups promote cooperation and enhance group success. This idea was first proposed in the context of fair meiosis, where each chromosome has an equal chance of transmission via gametes. By understanding how repression of competition in fair meiosis leads to increased group success, Alexander developed his theories on the evolution of human sociality. He argued that human social structures spread when they repress competition within groups and promote successful group-against-group competition. Buss later added a new example, suggesting that metazoan success depended on repressing competition between cellular lineages. Maynard Smith then synthesized these ideas, and in this paper, I provide simple mathematical models to illustrate the key processes by which repression of competition evolves. I first clarify the concepts, then delve into the history of the idea, and finally summarize recent developments and promising areas for future research.

title: Article
text: The study aimed to investigate the effects of RA, a ligand of RARalpha, on immune responses in human and murine colitis. The study used colonic biopsies from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and induced colitis in mice by administering TNBS intrarectally. The cells were cultured and treated with RA or LE135, an antagonist of RARalpha, and the expressions of IL-17 and FOXP3 were detected through immunohistochemistry. The study also measured cytokine levels in the cultures of mouse lamina propria mononuclear cells (LPMCs) and detected the expressions of FOXP3 and IL-17 in colon tissues and mesenteric lymph nodes (MLN) through immunohistological analysis. The study found that RA treatment up-regulated FOXP3 expression and down-regulated IL-17 expression in colon biopsies of patients and in colon tissues and MLN of mice with colitis compared to controls. Additionally, LPMCs from RA-treated mice produced lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-17) but more regulatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-beta) compared to untreated mice. LE135 had the opposite effect of RA. Furthermore, RA ameliorated TNBS-induced colitis in a dose-dependent manner, as seen by improved body weight and colon inflammation. The study suggests that RA down-regulates colon inflammatory responses in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) both in vitro and in vivo, representing a potential therapeutic approach in IBD treatment.

title: Multiple RNA surveillance pathways limit aberrant expression of iron uptake mRNAs and prevent iron toxicity in S. cerevisiae.
text: The tight regulation of mRNA expression encoding iron uptake proteins is crucial to maintain iron homeostasis and prevent intracellular iron toxicity. Our findings indicate that many mRNAs encoding iron uptake or mobilization proteins are expressed in iron-replete conditions even in the absence of the S. cerevisiae RNase III ortholog Rnt1p or the nuclear exosome component Rrp6p. Furthermore, extended forms of these mRNAs accumulate in the absence of Rnt1p or the 5'-->3' exonucleases Xrn1p and Rat1p, suggesting that multiple degradative pathways collaborate in surveilling aberrant transcripts. RNase III-deficient cells exhibit heightened sensitivity to high iron concentrations, implying that Rnt1p-mediated RNA surveillance is essential to prevent iron toxicity. These results demonstrate that multiple ribonucleolytic pathways play a vital role in iron homeostasis in yeast, ensuring the avoidance of potentially toxic consequences arising from the expression of the iron starvation response in iron-replete conditions.

title: Differential regulation of adherens junction dynamics during apical-basal polarization.
text: Adherens junctions (AJs) in epithelial cells undergo constant turnover to modulate adhesion properties in response to various physiological and developmental cues, but the mechanisms regulating AJ dynamics during apical-basal polarization remain unclear. To investigate, we employed novel GFP markers of Drosophila E-cadherin (DE-cadherin) and β-catenin (Armadillo, Arm) to quantify in vivo dynamics of biosynthetic turnover and membrane redistribution using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) assays. Our findings revealed that membrane DE-Cad and Arm in AJs of polarizing epithelial cells exhibited significantly faster biosynthetic turnover than in polarized cells. Fast biosynthetic turnover of membrane DE-Cad was found to be microtubule-dependent, whereas Arm in AJs of polarizing cells showed a faster and diffusion-based membrane redistribution that was distinct from the slower and exchange-based DE-Cad membrane distribution. Biochemical assays revealed that the binding of Arm to DE-Cad was weaker in polarizing cells compared to polarized cells. Our data suggest that the molecular interaction between DE-Cad and Arm is modulated during apical-basal polarization, revealing a novel mechanism crucial for establishing apical-basal polarity through regulating AJ dynamics.

title: Phylogenetic analysis of mRNA polyadenylation sites reveals a role of transposable elements in evolution of the 3′-end of genes
text: mRNA polyadenylation is a crucial step in the maturation of the majority of eukaryotic mRNAs, and is closely linked with the termination of transcription in determining the 3' end of genes. An abundance of human and mouse genes harbor alternative polyadenylation sites (poly(A) sites), which lead to the generation of mRNA variants containing distinct 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) or alternative protein-coding sequences. In this study, we investigated the conservation and divergence of different types of alternative poly(A) sites across human, mouse, rat, and chicken. Our findings revealed that the 3' most poly(A) sites tend to be more conserved than those located upstream, while poly(A) sites situated upstream of the 3' most exon, also known as intronic poly(A) sites, are significantly less conserved. Genes with a longer evolutionary history are more likely to exhibit alternative polyadenylation, suggesting the acquisition of poly(A) sites through evolution. Moreover, we found that non-conserved poly(A) sites are more frequently associated with transposable elements (TEs) than conserved ones, although the utilization of these sites is less frequent. Different classes of TEs exhibit distinct characteristics in their association with poly(A) sites through the exaptation of TE sequences into polyadenylation elements. Our results establish a conservation pattern for alternative poly(A) sites in several vertebrate species and highlight the dynamic modification of the 3' end of genes through evolutionary processes involving TEs.

title: Inter- and Intra-Host Viral Diversity in a Large Seasonal DENV2 Outbreak
text:
BACKGROUND:
High genetic diversity at both inter- and intra-host levels is a hallmark of RNA viruses due to their error-prone nature during genome replication. Several studies have investigated the extent of viral variability using different RNA virus deep sequencing methods, with a focus on pathogens that cause chronic infections in humans. However, there is a lack of research on arthropod-borne, acute viral infections.
METHODS AND PRINCIPAL FINDINGS:
In this study, we used two different deep sequencing approaches to analyze the complete genome of ten DENV2 isolates from representative classical and severe cases in a large outbreak in Brazil. Our analysis of the consensus genomes revealed a larger extent of the 2010 epidemic compared to a previous epidemic in another city two years earlier (genetic distance = 0.002 and 0.0008, respectively). Within the host, we found a high level of conservation across the viral populations. Excluding homopolymer regions of 454/Roche generated sequences revealed 10 to 44 variable sites per genome population at a frequency of >1%, resulting in very low intra-host genetic diversity. Interestingly, while up to 60% of all variable sites at the intra-host level were non-synonymous changes, only 10% of inter-host variability resulted from non-synonymous mutations, indicating purifying selection at the population level.
CONCLUSIONS AND SIGNIFICANCE:
Our findings suggest that despite the error-prone nature of RNA-dependent RNA-polymerase, dengue viruses maintain low levels of intra-host variability. This is consistent with the idea that purifying selection acts on the viral population at the population level, limiting the accumulation of non-synonymous mutations. These results have important implications for our understanding of the evolution and transmission of RNA viruses, and highlight the need for further research on arthropod-borne, acute viral infections.

title: Serum Soluble Corin Deficiency Predicts Major Disability within 3 Months after Acute Stroke
text:
OBJECTIVE:
Stroke patients with low levels of serum soluble corin have been associated with an increased risk of poor outcomes. However, the relationship between serum soluble corin and stroke prognosis has yet to be investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to determine whether serum soluble corin levels are associated with the risk of major disability or death within 3 months after stroke.
METHODS:
This study included 522 stroke patients who were followed for 3 months to identify major disability, death, and vascular events. Serum soluble corin levels were measured at baseline for all participants. Logistic regression analysis was used to examine the associations between baseline serum soluble corin levels and outcomes of stroke, adjusting for age, sex, baseline NIHSS score, hours from onset to hospitalization, smoking, drinking, hypertension, diabetes, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation, family history of stroke, and stroke subtype.
RESULTS:
Patients with high levels of serum soluble corin had a significantly lower crude risk for the composite outcome of major disability or death (odds ratio [OR] = 0.64, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.43-0.96) compared to patients with low levels of corin (the lowest tertile). After adjusting for age and baseline NIHSS score, patients with high levels of corin still had a significantly lower risk for the composite outcome of major disability or death (OR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.36-0.99). This association became statistically significant after adjusting for other conventional factors (OR = 0.61, P = 0.058). No significant association was found between serum soluble corin and other composite outcomes.
CONCLUSION:
Our findings suggest that low levels of serum soluble corin may predict the risk of major disability within 3 months after stroke, independent of baseline neurological deficits. These results suggest a potential role of corin in stroke prognosis.

title: Altered PTEN expression; a diagnostic marker for differentiating normal, hyperplastic and neoplastic endometrium
text:
Background:
Molecular alterations have been identified in endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (EECA), with loss of the PTEN protein being the most common alteration. The aim of this study was to investigate the expression pattern of the PTEN gene in normal, hyperplastic, and neoplastic endometrium.
Methods:
This study was conducted in a referral gynecologic hospital in Tehran, Iran, and included 87 consecutive specimens. The samples were divided into three groups: group A (normal proliferative endometrium, n = 29), group B (hyperplastic endometrium, including simple hyperplasia without atypia, n = 21, and complex hyperplasia with atypia, n = 8), and group C (EECA, n = 29). Immunohistochemical (IHC) evaluation of PTEN was performed, and the results were analyzed using arbitrary quantitative methods based on the staining area and intensity of the color reaction.
Results:
PTEN immunoreactivity was present in all normal proliferative endometrium, all simple hyperplasia, 75% of atypical complex hyperplasia, and in 48% of EECA (P < 0.001). The intensity of PTEN reaction was significantly higher in the group with proliferative endometrium compared to hyperplastic endometrium and EECA (P < 0.001).

Conclusion:
The results of this study suggest that PTEN expression is significantly higher in cyclical endometrium compared to atypical hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma. These findings may have implications for the diagnosis and treatment of endometrial cancer.

title: Care Seeking for Neonatal Illness in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review
text:
Despite recent progress in reducing child mortality, neonatal deaths continue to account for 41% of all deaths in children under five years of age worldwide, with over 90% of these deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Infections are a leading cause of neonatal deaths, and limitations in care seeking for ill neonates contribute to high mortality rates. However, there is a lack of data on care-seeking behaviors in LMICs, particularly regarding the type of care sought.
To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of studies that reported on care-seeking behaviors for ill or suspected ill neonates in LMICs. Our search yielded 784 studies, of which 22 provided relevant data from community household surveys, facility-based surveys, and intervention trials. The majority of studies were from South Asia (n = 17/22), set in rural areas (n = 17/22), and published within the last 4 years (n = 18/22).
Our analysis found that among 9,098 neonates who were ill or suspected to be ill, 4,320 caregivers sought some type of care, including care from a health facility (n = 370) or provider (n = 1,813). Care seeking ranged between 10% and 100% among caregivers, with a median of 59%. Care seeking from a health care provider yielded a similar range and median, while care seeking at a health care facility ranged between 1% and 100%, with a median of 20%.
Our findings indicate that there is a paucity of data on newborn care-seeking behaviors, particularly in urban settings and regions outside of South Asia. Moreover, there was a lack of consistency in definitions of illness, care-seeking, and care providers.
To address these gaps, we recommend the collection of representative data on care-seeking patterns in different geographic regions and the development of interventions to enhance care seeking during this vulnerable time period. This could involve improving healthcare infrastructure, increasing access to healthcare services, and promoting awareness campaigns to educate caregivers about the importance of seeking medical attention for ill newborns.
In conclusion, our findings highlight the need for more research on newborn care-seeking behaviors in LMICs, particularly in terms of care sought from health care facilities and medically trained providers. By better understanding the factors that influence care seeking, we can develop targeted interventions to improve newborn survival rates in these regions.

title: Synaptic Incorporation of AMPA Receptors during LTP Is Controlled by a PKC Phosphorylation Site on GluR1
text: The incorporation of GluR1-containing AMPA receptors into synapses is essential for various forms of neural plasticity, including long-term potentiation (LTP). While several signaling pathways involved in this process have been identified, the specific modifications that control GluR1 incorporation into synapses remain unclear. Here, we uncover that the phosphorylation of GluR1 by PKC at a highly conserved serine 818 residue is increased during LTP and plays a critical role in LTP expression. In vitro and in vivo studies reveal that GluR1 is phosphorylated by PKC at this site, and acute phosphorylation or a phosphomimetic mutation promotes GluR1 incorporation into synapses. Conversely, inhibiting GluR1 S818 phosphorylation reduces LTP and blocks PKC-driven synaptic incorporation of GluR1. Our findings demonstrate that the phosphorylation of GluR1 S818 by PKC is a crucial event in the plasticity-driven incorporation of AMPA receptors into synapses.

title: The Bloom's syndrome helicase promotes the annealing of complementary single-stranded DNA
text: The product of the gene mutated in Bloom's syndrome, BLM, is a 3'-5' DNA helicase belonging to the highly conserved RecQ family, which also exhibits a unique ability to promote single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) annealing. This activity, which does not require Mg2+, is inhibited by ssDNA binding proteins and ATP, and is dependent on DNA length. Through the analysis of various truncation mutants of BLM, we have identified the C-terminal domain as essential for strand annealing and have pinpointed a 60 amino acid stretch within this domain as being crucial for both ssDNA binding and strand annealing. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the ssDNA annealing activity of BLM and its significance in the repair of damaged replication forks.

title: Bayesian selection of continuous-time Markov chain evolutionary models.
text: We develop a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (RJMCMC) approach to estimating the posterior distribution of phylogenies based on aligned DNA/RNA sequences under various hierarchical evolutionary models. By using a proper, yet non-truncated and uninformative prior, we demonstrate the advantages of the Bayesian approach to hypothesis testing and estimation in phylogenetics by comparing different models for the infinitesimal rates of change among nucleotides, the number of rate classes, and the relationships among branch lengths. We compare the relative probabilities of these models and the appropriateness of a molecular clock using Bayes factors. Our most general model, first proposed by Tamura and Nei, involves parameterizing the infinitesimal change probabilities among nucleotides (A, G, C, T/U) into six parameters, including three parameters for the nucleotide stationary distribution, two rate parameters for nucleotide transitions, and another parameter for nucleotide transversions. Nested models include the Hasegawa, Kishino, and Yano model with equal transition rates and the Kimura model with a uniform stationary distribution and equal transition rates. To illustrate our methods, we examine simulated data, 16S rRNA sequences from 15 contemporary eubacteria, halobacteria, eocytes, and eukaryotes, 9 primates, and the entire HIV genome of 11 isolates. Our findings reveal that the Kimura model is too restrictive, that the Hasegawa, Kishino, and Yano model can be rejected for some data sets, and that there is evidence for more than one rate class and a molecular clock among similar taxa. Additionally, we find that a molecular clock can be rejected for more distantly related taxa.

title: The intersection between aging and cardiovascular disease.
text: As the average human lifespan continues to rise, the proportion of individuals aged 65 and older is growing rapidly and will continue to do so in the next two decades. Within this age group, cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death, and the associated treatment costs are expected to increase. Aging is an inevitable part of life, and unfortunately, it poses the largest risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Despite significant research in both the cardiovascular field and the molecular biology of aging, many questions remain unanswered regarding how genetic pathways that regulate aging in model organisms influence cardiovascular aging. Similarly, few studies have fully assessed the role of these aging pathways in cardiovascular health. However, this gap is beginning to close, and these two fields are merging together. This review provides an overview of key genes involved in regulating lifespan and health span, including sirtuins, AMP-activated protein kinase, mammalian target of rapamycin, and insulin-like growth factor 1, and their roles in regulating cardiovascular health. We also discuss a series of review articles that will appear in succession, providing a more comprehensive analysis of studies linking genes of aging and cardiovascular health, and offering perspectives on future directions in these intimately linked fields.

title: Single-RNA counting reveals alternative modes of gene expression in yeast
text: Proper execution of transcriptional programs is crucial for gene expression regulation, requiring precise control over timing and amplitude. However, the extent to which the transcription machinery fulfills this requirement remains unclear. To address this question, we employed an in situ hybridization approach that allows for the detection of individual mRNA molecules within single cells. Our findings reveal that expression levels for certain genes are higher than previously reported, and that mRNA abundance can vary significantly among cells. Notably, variability in expression levels for most constitutively expressed genes is surprisingly low. By combining single-transcript measurements with computational modeling, we discovered that low expression variation is achieved through the use of single transcription-initiation events that are temporally distinct, rather than through transcriptional bursts. In contrast, the gene PDR5, which is regulated by the transcription coactivator complex SAGA, is expressed through transcription bursts, resulting in greater variation in expression levels. These data provide direct evidence for the existence of multiple expression modes used to modulate the transcriptome.

title: A complete landscape of post-transcriptional modifications in mammalian mitochondrial tRNAs
text:
In mammalian mitochondria, 22 distinct types of transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules encoded in mitochondrial DNA play critical roles in the translation of 13 essential subunits of the respiratory chain complexes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. Following transcription, these mitochondrial tRNAs (mt tRNAs) are modified by nuclear-encoded tRNA-modifying enzymes, which are essential for their proper functioning. However, the information available on these modifications has been incomplete, and this study aimed to address this issue by isolating and comprehensively determining the post-transcriptional modifications of all 22 species of mt tRNAs from bovine liver using mass spectrometry.
The study described the primary structures with post-transcriptional modifications of seven previously uncharacterized mt tRNAs and provided revised information on base modifications in five other mt tRNAs. The analysis revealed 15 species of modified nucleosides at 118 positions (7.48% of total bases) in the complete set of bovine mt tRNAs. This finding provides insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying the decoding system in mammalian mitochondria and enables the prediction of candidate tRNA-modifying enzymes responsible for each modification of mt tRNAs.

title: Preventing coronary heart disease: B vitamins and homocysteine.
text: The list of modifiable risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease continues to expand. Well-established risk factors include cigarette smoking, high blood pressure, physical inactivity, elevated cholesterol, underlying lipoprotein abnormalities, lipoprotein(a), diabetes, overweight, male gender, and age. Recent studies have also linked elevated plasma homocysteine levels to an increased risk of arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and dietary and supplemental folic acid has been shown to reduce homocysteine levels. A study published in this issue of Circulation provides further evidence of the importance of homocysteine and suggests that plasma folate and plasma pyrixodal-l-phosphate (vitamin B6) are protective factors. The study, conducted as part of the European Concerted Action Project, involved 750 patients younger than age 60 with diagnoses of coronary, cerebrovascular, or peripheral vascular disease and 800 healthy control subjects. The study found that men in the highest quintile for fasting total homocysteine (tHcy) had an estimated relative risk of 2.2 for vascular disease, with a striking dose-response relationship and a more-than-multiplicative interaction with cigarette smoking and high blood pressure. The study also examined the effects of three B vitamins on fasting and post-methionine-loading tHcy levels and any independent effects on cardiovascular disease.

title: Relationship between serum parathyroid hormone levels, vitamin D sufficiency, and calcium intake.
text:
In recent years, there has been increased recognition of the importance of adequate vitamin D status for optimal bone health. However, there is no universally agreed upon ideal intake level. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is commonly used as an indicator of vitamin D status, but a universal reference level has not been established. This study aimed to investigate the relative importance of high calcium intake and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D for calcium homeostasis, as determined by serum intact parathyroid hormone (PTH).
The study was a cross-sectional design that included 2310 healthy Icelandic adults aged 30-85 years. Participants completed a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire that assessed vitamin D and calcium intake. They were divided into groups based on calcium intake (<800 mg/d, 800-1200 mg/d, and >1200 mg/d) and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (<10 ng/mL, 10-18 ng/mL, and >18 ng/mL). Serum PTH was the primary outcome measure.
The study found that among healthy participants, serum PTH was lowest in the group with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of more than 18 ng/mL, but highest in the group with a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of less than 10 ng/mL. At a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of <10 ng/mL, calcium intake of less than 800 mg/d was significantly associated with higher serum PTH (P = .04), and at a calcium intake of more than 1200 mg/d, there was a significant difference between the lowest and highest vitamin D groups (P = .04).
The study's findings suggest that as long as vitamin D status is adequate, calcium intake levels of more than 800 mg/d may not be necessary for maintaining calcium metabolism. Vitamin D supplements are necessary for adequate vitamin D status in northern climates.

title: Sex-specific effects of the DAF-12 steroid receptor on aging in Caenorhabditis elegans.
text:
Throughout the animal kingdom, there are noticeable differences in longevity and aging between males and females. These differences are likely due in part to variations in endocrinology between the sexes. In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, males have a longer lifespan compared to females. To investigate the possible role of sex differences in insulin/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and steroid endocrinology in this sex difference in aging, we studied C. elegans populations in liquid culture. Our findings suggest that sex differences in steroid endocrinology may play a significant role in aging in C. elegans, similar to mammals.
In hermaphrodite populations, mutational loss of the DAF-12 steroid receptor had a significant impact on lifespan, as previously observed in plate-culture studies. However, in males, mutation of daf-12 had little to no effect on aging, regardless of the strength of the daf-2 insulin/IGF-1 receptor mutation. In contrast, mutation of daf-12 marginally reduced lifespan in daf-2(+) hermaphrodites, but not in daf-2(+) males. These results suggest that sex differences in steroid endocrinology may contribute to sex differences in aging in C. elegans, as seen in mammals.

title: Nonclassical binding of formylated peptide in crystal structure of the MHC class lb molecule H2-M3
text: H2-M3 is a class Ib MHC molecule from mouse with a remarkable 10(4)-fold preference for binding N-formylated peptides. To investigate the basis of this unique specificity, we expressed and crystallized a soluble form of M3 in combination with a formylated nonamer peptide, fMYFINILTL, and determined its structure through X-ray crystallography. At a resolution of 2.1 Å, the crystal structure of M3 revealed a close resemblance to class la MHC molecules in overall structure, but with significant differences in the peptide-binding groove. Specifically, the A pocket, which normally accommodates the free N-terminus of a bound peptide, is closed, and the peptide is shifted one residue, resulting in the P1 side chain being positioned in the B pocket. The formyl group is coordinated by His-9 and a bound water molecule on the floor of the groove.

title: Sequential signals toward podosome formation in NIH-src cells
text:
Podosomes (also referred to as invadopodia in cancer cells) are actin-rich adhesion structures that play a crucial role in various cellular processes. Despite their importance, the molecular mechanisms underlying podosome formation are not fully understood. In this study, we aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms of podosome formation in Src-transformed NIH3T3 (NIH-src) cells.
Our findings revealed that podosomes in NIH-src cells are enriched with PtdIns(3,4)P2, a phosphoinositide that plays a crucial role in podosome formation. Live-cell imaging analysis showed that Src expression stimulated podosome formation at focal adhesions of NIH3T3 cells after PtdIns(3,4)P2 accumulation.
We also found that the adaptor protein Tks5/FISH, which is essential for podosome formation, forms a complex with Grb2 at adhesion sites in an Src-dependent manner. Additionally, we discovered that N-WASP binds to all SH3 domains of Tks5/FISH, which facilitates circular podosome formation. These results suggest that the augmentation of the N-WASP-Arp2/3 signal is accomplished on the platform of Tks5/FISH-Grb2 complex at focal adhesions, which is stabilized by PtdIns(3,4)P2.
In conclusion, our findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms of podosome formation and highlight the importance of PtdIns(3,4)P2, Tks5/FISH, Grb2, and N-WASP in this process. These findings may have implications for our understanding of cellular migration and invasion in various diseases, including cancer.

title: Forebrain engraftment by human glial progenitor cells enhances synaptic plasticity and learning in adult mice.
text: Human astrocytes are larger and more complex than those of infraprimate mammals, suggesting that their role in neural processing has evolved over time. To investigate the cell-autonomous and species-specific properties of human glial cells, we transplanted human glial progenitor cells (GPCs) into neonatal immunodeficient mice. Following maturation, the recipient brains exhibited a significant increase in both human glial progenitors and astrocytes. Notably, the engrafted human glia were found to be gap-junction-coupled to host astroglia, yet retained the size and pleomorphism of human astroglia, and exhibited enhanced Ca2+ signaling propagation. Moreover, we observed a significant enhancement of long-term potentiation (LTP) and learning in mice that received human glial chimeras, compared to mice allografted with murine GPCs. These findings suggest that human glia differentially contribute to activity-dependent plasticity and learning in mice.

title: Reprogramming of human fibroblasts to pluripotency with lineage specifiers.
text: Since the initial discovery that OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC overexpression can induce pluripotency in somatic cells, numerous methodologies have been developed to enhance our understanding of the reprogramming process. However, unlike in mice, it has proven challenging to replace OCT4 during the reprogramming of human cells. In this study, we report a strategy to accomplish this replacement. Through a combination of transcriptome and bioinformatic analysis, we identified factors previously characterized as lineage specifiers that can replace OCT4 and SOX2 in the reprogramming of human fibroblasts. Our results demonstrate that it is possible to simultaneously replace OCT4 and SOX2 with alternative lineage specifiers in the reprogramming of human cells. At a broader level, these findings support a model in which counteracting lineage specification networks underlies the induction of pluripotency.

title: Mechanisms of endocytosis.
text: Endocytic mechanisms play a crucial role in regulating the composition of the plasma membrane, thereby influencing how cells interact with their surroundings. In this review, we provide an overview of mammalian endocytic mechanisms, with a particular focus on the cellular proteins involved in these processes. We delve into the well-characterized clathrin-mediated endocytic pathways and discuss alternative endocytic pathways that operate independently of clathrin, including the CLIC/GEEC endocytic pathway, arf6-dependent endocytosis, flotillin-dependent endocytosis, macropinocytosis, circular doral ruffles, phagocytosis, and trans-endocytosis. Additionally, we critically evaluate the role of caveolae and caveolin1 in endocytosis.
