Measuring bone mass through densitometry is a crucial aspect of diagnosing osteoporosis and determining an appropriate treatment plan. Bone mineral densitometry (BMD) has become more widely available and commonly used in clinical practice. This review aims to evaluate the clinical applications of BMD in various patient populations.
We conducted a MEDLINE search to update previous meta-analyses on the relationship between BMD and fracture risk. We also used data from the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures to estimate fracture risk based on BMD and age in postmenopausal women. Our review emphasizes meta-analyses and systematic reviews when available.
Our analysis found that BMD predicts fracture risk and can be combined with age to estimate absolute fracture risk in postmenopausal white women. Hip BMD is a stronger predictor of hip fracture than other BMD measurements. However, there is insufficient data to translate BMD results into fracture risk for men and non-white women. The benefits of fracture prevention treatments depend on BMD, with individuals with osteoporosis having a higher fracture risk and greater benefit from treatment compared to those without osteoporosis.
Guidelines based on systematic reviews and a cost-effectiveness analysis suggest that measuring BMD in white women over 65 years old and potentially selecting younger postmenopausal women for densitometry based on risk factors is worthwhile. However, other potential clinical applications of BMD that require further study include screening men and non-white women, monitoring BMD in patients receiving treatment, and identifying patients with secondary causes of osteoporosis.
In conclusion, BMD is a valuable tool in diagnosing and managing osteoporosis. While there are limitations to its application, measuring BMD can help predict fracture risk and guide treatment decisions. Further research is needed to fully understand the clinical applications of BMD in various patient populations.

title: Vascular Calcifying Progenitor Cells Possess Bidirectional Differentiation Potentials
text:
Vascular calcification is a complex and advanced feature of atherosclerosis for which no effective treatment options are currently available. To investigate the potential for modulating or reversing calcification, we identified and characterized calcifying progenitor cells in the aortas of mice. Using markers such as Sca-1 and PDGFRα, we sorted cells into four distinct populations: Sca-1(+) cells that expressed both Sca-1 and PDGFRα, Sca-1(+) cells that expressed only PDGFRα, Sca-1(-) cells that expressed only PDGFRα, and Sca-1(-) cells that did not express either marker.
We found that Sca-1(+) progenitor cells in the aorta originated from the bone marrow (BM) and could be clonally expanded. Interestingly, we discovered that among the Sca-1(+) progenitor populations, Sca-1(+)/PDGFRα(-) cells possessed bidirectional differentiation potentials towards both osteoblastic and osteoclastic lineages, while Sca-1(+)/PDGFRα(+) cells differentiated into an osteoblastic lineage unidirectionally.
To evaluate the potential of modulating in vivo calcification, we established models of ectopic and atherosclerotic calcification in mice. Our results showed that Sca-1(+) progenitor cells increased the volume and calcium scores of ectopic calcification, but treatment with a PPARγ agonist decreased bone formation in atherosclerotic plaques. Furthermore, systemic infusion of Sca-1(+)/PDGFRα(-) cells into Apoe(-/-) mice increased the severity of calcified atherosclerotic plaques, but activation of PPARγ in these cells led to a significant decrease in plaque severity.
Our findings suggest that a subtype of BM-derived and vessel-resident progenitor cells may offer a therapeutic target for the prevention of vascular calcification, and that PPARγ activation may be an option to reverse calcification. These findings have important implications for the development of new therapies for vascular calcification, a common complication of cardiovascular disease.

title: Physiological relevance of cell cycle kinases.
text: The early study of cell division cycle regulation and its control by protein kinases primarily focused on genetic and biochemical research in yeast and other model organisms. Key regulatory mechanisms identified in these pioneering studies have been found to be conserved in mammals. However, recent investigations in various cell types or genetic models have provided a fresh perspective on the function of these major cell cycle regulators in different tissues. Here, we review the physiological significance of mammalian cell cycle kinases, including cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks), Aurora and Polo-like kinases, and mitotic checkpoint regulators (Bub1, BubR1, and Mps1), as well as less-studied enzymes such as Cdc7, Nek proteins, or Mastl. These proteins play crucial roles in development, tissue homeostasis, and human disease, including the control of self-renewal or asymmetric cell division in stem/progenitor cells and the ability to regenerate injured tissues. Moreover, many of these proteins have unexpected functions in metabolism, cardiovascular function, or neuron biology, and their modulation may have multiple therapeutic benefits in human disease.

title: Matrix Metalloproteinase 1 Is Necessary for the Migration of Human Bone Marrow-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells Toward Human Glioma
text: Human mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been increasingly used as cellular vectors for delivering therapeutic genes to tumors. However, the mechanism of mobilization remains poorly understood. In this study, we isolated MSCs from various donors that expressed similar cell surface markers and had multilineage differentiation potential. We found that different MSC isolates displayed varying migration abilities towards human glioma cells. We hypothesized that distinct molecular signals may be involved in the different tumor tropisms exhibited by these MSC isolates. To test this hypothesis, we compared the gene expression profiles of tumor-trophic MSCs with those of non-tumor-trophic MSCs. We found that the MMP1 gene was highly expressed and its protein activity was increased by 27-fold and 21-fold, respectively, in highly migrating MSCs compared to poorly migrating MSCs. Functional inactivation of MMP1 abrogated the migratory potential of MSCs towards glioma-conditioned medium. Conversely, the non-migratory phenotype of poorly migrating MSCs could be rescued in the presence of either recombinant MMP1 or conditioned medium from highly migrating MSCs. Ectopic expression of MMP1 in poorly migrating cells also rendered them responsive to the signaling cues from glioma cells in vivo. However, blocking the interaction of MMP1 and its cognate receptor PAR1 diminished the migratory ability of MSCs. Taken together, this study provides the first evidence that MMP1 is critical in the migration capacity of MSCs, acting through the MMP1/PAR1 axis.

title: Bullying in school: are short pupils at risk? Questionnaire study in a cohort.
text:
Bullying remains a persistent issue in schools, causing significant stress for victims. It may also have long-term consequences for bullies, including the persistence of antisocial behavior into adulthood. Notably, victims tend to be weaker than their bullies, which could suggest that shorter students are more likely to be targeted and less likely to engage in bullying behavior.
To investigate this phenomenon, the Wessex growth study examined the prevalence of bullying among students of different heights. The study included 92 short normal adolescents who were below the third centile for height at school entry, as well as 117 controls matched for age and sex. The results showed that the mean height SD scores for short pupils were -1.90 (-3.53 to -0.01), while the controls had a mean height SD score of 0.31 (-1.41 to 0.30). There were no significant differences in sex or social class between the groups, and the mean age of the participants was 14.7 (13.4-15.7) years.
The study used a bullying questionnaire, derived from work by Whitney and Smith,5 to assess the experiences of bullying among the participants. The results showed that short pupils were more likely to be victims of bullying than controls. These findings suggest that height may play a role in the prevalence of bullying, with shorter students being more vulnerable to bullying behavior.

title: Inflammasome-induced IL-1β secretion in microglia is characterized by delayed kinetics and is only partially dependent on inflammatory caspases.
text: Inflammasomes are multi-protein complexes that connect pathogen recognition and cellular stress to the processing of the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β (IL-1β). Although inflammasome-mediated activation has been extensively studied in hematopoietic macrophages and dendritic cells, less is known about microglia, the resident tissue macrophages of the brain that originate from a distinct progenitor. To compare inflammasome-mediated activation in different types of macrophages, we isolated primary microglia and hematopoietic macrophages from adult, healthy rhesus macaques and analyzed the expression profile of NOD (nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain)-like receptors, adaptor proteins, and caspases. We characterized inflammasome activation and regulation in detail. Our findings demonstrate that primary microglia can respond to the same innate stimuli as hematopoietic macrophages, but microglial responses are more persistent due to a lack of negative regulation on pro-IL-1β expression. Additionally, we show that while caspase 1, 4, and 5 activation is essential for inflammasome-induced IL-1β secretion by hematopoietic macrophages, microglial secretion of IL-1β is only partially dependent on these inflammatory caspases. These results highlight key cell type-specific differences that may inform the development of strategies to modulate innate immune responses in the brain.

title: microRNA-29a suppresses cell proliferation by targeting SPARC in hepatocellular carcinoma.
text: In this study, we generated a lentivirus vector encoding the miR-29a precursor and established two stable cell lines, PLC-29a and 97L-29a, to investigate the role of miR-29a in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) growth. We found that overexpressing miR-29a significantly suppressed the growth of HCC cell lines MHCC-97L and PLC, and dual-luciferase reporter assays revealed that miR-29a directly targeted the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of the SPARC mRNA. Silencing SPARC expression by RNAi knockdown resulted in a similar effect as miR-29a overexpression on HCC cell growth regulation. Interestingly, we found that anti-miR-29a oligonucleotides (AMOs) upregulated the levels of SPARC in HCC cells. Furthermore, we observed that the phosphorylation of AKT/mTOR downstream of SPARC was inhibited in miR-29a-overexpressing HCC cells. To investigate the expression of miR-29a in HCC tissues, we examined the expression levels of miR-29a in 110 HCC tissues and the corresponding nearby non-cancerous liver tissues using qRT-PCR, and found significantly lower expression of miR-29a in the tissues affected by HCC. Our findings suggest that the expression of miR-29a is important in the regulation of the SPARC-AKT pathway and HCC growth.

title: Another Barrier to Regeneration in the CNS: Activated Macrophages Induce Extensive Retraction of Dystrophic Axons through Direct Physical Interactions
text: Injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons undergo a prolonged process of retraction after spinal cord injury, which is accompanied by the infiltration of macrophages. While the correlation between macrophage infiltration and axonal retraction has been observed, the direct involvement of these inflammatory cells in the process has not been definitively demonstrated. In this study, we investigated the role of macrophages in axonal retraction within the dorsal columns of the spinal cord using in vivo experiments and found that axonal retraction occurred between days 2 and 28 after injury and was associated with the presence of ED-1+ cells, a marker of macrophages. We also used clodronate liposome-mediated depletion of infiltrating macrophages to reduce axonal retraction and observed a significant decrease in the extent of axonal retraction. However, we did not observe any evidence of regeneration. In an in vitro model of the glial scar, we used time-lapse imaging of adult dorsal root ganglion neurons to examine macrophage-axon interactions and found that adhesive contacts and physical interplay between macrophages and dystrophic axons led to extensive axonal retraction. Our results indicate that activated macrophages play a direct role in axonal retraction through physical cell-cell interactions with injured axons, and that this process is dependent on the growth state of the axon and the activation state of the macrophage. Unlike intrinsically active cell lines, both primary macrophages and microglia require activation to induce axonal retraction. Additionally, our findings suggest that contact with astrocytes does not have a deleterious effect on adult dystrophic axons, indicating that the induction of extensive retraction is specific to phagocytic cells.

title: Large-Scale Movements of IF3 and tRNA during Bacterial Translation Initiation
text: In the initiation process of bacterial translation, three initiation factors (IFs) play a crucial role in selecting the initiator tRNA and identifying the start codon on the 30S ribosomal subunit. Recently, we have obtained 11 single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) reconstructions of the complex formed between the 30S subunit, initiator tRNA, mRNA, and IFs 1-3, which represent different stages of the initiation pathway. IF1 acts as an anchor for IF2 and IF3, enhancing their activities. IF2 adopts an extended conformation that allows it to capture the formylmethionyl group on tRNA, while IF3 and tRNA undergo significant conformational changes to accommodate the formylmethionyl-tRNA (fMet-tRNA(fMet)) into the P site for start codon recognition.

title: Corresponding Author:
text: In higher eukaryotes, introns are removed from protein-coding mRNAs through the splicing process, which involves a large complex called the spliceosome. This complex consists of five non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) and approximately 200 proteins. By comparing the differences in spliceosomal proteins among various basal eukaryotic lineages, it is possible to infer properties of the splicing system in the last common ancestor of extant eukaryotes, the eukaryotic ancestor. Initially, we hypothesize that the spliceosome has evolved in complexity throughout eukaryotic evolution, similar to the increase in intron length in multicellular eukaryotes. However, upon examining the distribution of spliceosomal components, we find that not only was a spliceosome present in the eukaryotic ancestor, but it also contained most of the key components found in modern eukaryotes, including all small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) protein components and many splicing-related proteins. Both major and trans-splicing are likely to have been present, and the spliceosome had already formed connections with other cellular processes such as transcription and capping. However, there is no evidence to suggest that minor (U12-dependent) splicing was present in the eukaryotic ancestor. While the last common ancestor of extant eukaryotes exhibits much of the molecular complexity seen today, we cannot infer any properties of the earlier "first eukaryote" from this work.

title: 2D and 3D Stem Cell Models of Primate Cortical Development Identify Species-Specific Differences in Progenitor Behavior Contributing to Brain Size.
text: The size and complexity of the cerebral cortex are thought to contribute to differences in cognitive abilities between humans and other animals. To investigate this, we compared cortical progenitor cell output in humans and three nonhuman primates using directed differentiation of pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) in adherent two-dimensional (2D) and organoid three-dimensional (3D) culture systems. Clonal lineage analysis revealed that primate cortical progenitors proliferate for a longer period of time than rodent progenitors, resulting in more early-born neurons. This difference in progenitor expansion leads to a greater number of neurons generated by each progenitor cell in primates. Interestingly, this mechanism for regulating cortical size is regulated cell autonomously in culture, suggesting that the size of the primate cerebral cortex is at least partially controlled at the level of individual cortical progenitor cell clonal output.

title: Multicolor “DiOlistic” Labeling of the Nervous System Using Lipophilic Dye Combinations
text: We present a technique for rapidly labeling a large number of cells in the nervous system with multiple colors. By using a "gene gun" to deliver lipophilic dye-coated particles to neuronal preparations, individual neurons and glia that come into contact with the particles are quickly labeled. By using particles coated with different combinations of lipophilic dyes, many cells within a complex neuronal network can be simultaneously labeled with a wide range of colors. This technique is most effective in living tissue, but it also works on previously fixed material. In living tissue, labeled neurons continue to exhibit normal synaptic activity and undergo dendritic remodeling. This technique therefore provides a valuable tool for studying the structural plasticity of neuronal circuits in living preparations. Additionally, the Golgi-like labeling of neurons with multiple colors offers a novel approach to investigating neuronal connectivity.

title: A DNA test to sex most birds.
text: Birds are challenging to determine their sex. Young birds rarely display sex-linked physical characteristics, and we estimate that adult females resemble males in over 50% of bird species worldwide. This difficulty can hinder both evolutionary studies and human-assisted breeding of birds. DNA-based sex identification provides a solution. We describe a test based on two conserved CHD (chromo-helicase-DNA-binding) genes located on the avian sex chromosomes of all birds, with the possible exception of ratites (ostriches, etc.). The CHD-W gene is located on the W chromosome, making it unique to females. The other gene, CHD-Z, is found on the Z chromosome and occurs in both sexes (female, ZW; male, ZZ). The test involves PCR with a single set of primers, which amplify homologous sections of both genes and incorporate introns whose lengths differ. On a gel, males exhibit a single CHD-Z band, while females display a second, distinctive CHD-W band.

title: Evidence that Embryonic Neurons Regulate the Onset of Cortical Gliogenesis via Cardiotrophin-1
text:
The development of the embryonic cortex involves the sequential generation of neurons and glial cells. However, the mechanisms that control the transition from neurogenesis to gliogenesis are not well understood. To investigate this process, we used cultures of cortical precursor cells that mimic the in vivo differentiation pattern. We found that cortical neurons produce and secrete a protein called cardiotrophin-1, which triggers a signaling pathway that is essential for the timely formation of astrocytes. Our results suggest that a similar process occurs in vivo, and that the neurotrophic cytokine cardiotrophin-1 plays a key role in regulating the balance between neurogenesis and gliogenesis in the developing cortex.
In further experiments, we found that electroporating neurotrophic cytokines into the environment of embryonic cortical precursors leads to premature gliogenesis, while disrupting the gp130-JAK-STAT pathway delays the normal timed appearance of astrocytes. Additionally, we observed that the cortex of neonatal cardiotrophin-1-deficient mice has fewer astrocytes. These findings suggest that there is a feedback mechanism in place, where newly born neurons produce cardiotrophin-1, which instructs multipotent cortical precursors to generate astrocytes, thereby ensuring that gliogenesis does not occur until neurogenesis is complete.

title: The Inhibition of TDP-43 Mitochondrial Localization Blocks Its Neuronal Toxicity
text:
Genetic alterations in the TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TARDBP), also known as TDP-43, have been implicated in the development of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). An increase in the cytoplasmic presence of TDP-43 is a prominent histopathological feature of degenerating neurons in various neurodegenerative diseases. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying TDP-43's contribution to ALS pathophysiology remain unclear.
Our study has uncovered a novel role for TDP-43 in the mitochondria of neurons in ALS and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) patients. We found that disease-associated mutations in TDP-43 lead to increased mitochondrial localization of the protein. In mitochondria, wild-type (WT) and mutant TDP-43 preferentially bind to mRNAs encoding respiratory complex I subunits ND3 and ND6, leading to their impaired expression and the disassembly of complex I.
Our findings suggest that the suppression of TDP-43 mitochondrial localization can abolish the mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal loss caused by WT and mutant TDP-43, and improve phenotypes in transgenic mutant TDP-43 mice. These results link TDP-43 toxicity directly to mitochondrial bioenergetics and provide a promising therapeutic approach for neurodegeneration.
In summary, our study reveals a critical role for TDP-43 in mitochondrial function and provides a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Effect on the quality of peer review of blinding reviewers and asking them to sign their reports: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
Contextual concerns regarding bias, a lack of accountability, and poor quality of peer review have led to questions about the balance between anonymity for reviewers and authors.
Objective: To evaluate the impact of blinded reviewer identities and signed reports on the quality of peer review.
Design: Randomized controlled trial.
Setting: A general medical journal.
Participants: A total of 420 reviewers from the journal's database.
Intervention: We modified a paper accepted for publication to identify 8 areas of weakness. Reviewers were randomly assigned to 5 groups. Groups 1 and 2 had their authors' names and affiliations removed, while groups 3 and 4 were aware of the authors' identities. Groups 1 and 3 were requested to sign their reports, while groups 2 and 4 were requested to return their reports unsigned. The fifth group received the paper in the standard manner of the journal, with the authors' identities revealed and a request to provide anonymous feedback. Group 5 differed from group 4 only in that its members were unaware they were participating in a study.
Main Outcome Measure: The number of weaknesses in the paper identified by reviewers.
Results: A total of 221 reviewers (53%) provided reports. The mean number of weaknesses identified was 2 (1.7, 2.1, 1.8, and 1.9 for groups 1, 2, 3, and 4 and 5 combined, respectively). There were no statistically significant differences between groups in their performance. Reviewers who were blinded to the authors' identities were less likely to recommend rejection than those who were aware of the authors' identities (odds ratio, 0.5; 95% confidence interval, 0.3-1.0).
Conclusions: Neither blinded reviewer identities nor requiring signed reports had a significant impact on the rate of error detection. Such measures are unlikely to improve the quality of peer review reports.

title: 2001. Comparison of three management strategies for patients with atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. Baseline results from a randomized trial
text:
More than 2 million US women receive an uncertain cervical cytology diagnosis (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance [ASCUS]) annually. Effective colposcopy triage strategies are needed to identify the minority of women with clinically significant disease while avoiding unnecessary follow-up evaluations for others.
The ASCUS/LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) Triage Study (ALTS) is a multicenter, randomized trial comparing the sensitivity and specificity of three management strategies to detect cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 (CIN3): immediate colposcopy (considered the reference standard), triage based on HPV results from Hybrid Capture 2(TM) (HC 2) and thin-layer cytology results, or triage based on cytology results alone. This article summarizes the enrollment results for 3488 women with a referral diagnosis of ASCUS.
Among participants with ASCUS, the underlying prevalence of histologically confirmed CIN3 was 5.1%. The sensitivity to detect CIN3 or above by testing for cancer-associated HPV DNA was 96.3%, with 56.1% of women referred to colposcopy. Sensitivity of a single repeat cytology specimen with a triage threshold of HSIL or above was 44.1%, with 6.9% referred. Sensitivity of a lower cytology triage threshold of ASCUS or above was 85.3%, with 58.6% referred.
HC 2 testing for cancer-associated HPV DNA is a viable option in the management of women with ASCUS. It has greater sensitivity to detect CIN3 or above and specificity comparable to a single additional cytologic test indicating ASCUS or above.

title: Cell Stem Cell Article In Vivo Fate Analysis Reveals the Multipotent and Self-Renewal Capacities of Sox2 + Neural Stem Cells in the Adult Hippocampus
text: To investigate the properties of adult neural stem cells (NSCs), we generated and analyzed Sox2-GFP transgenic mice. In these mice, Sox2-GFP cells in the subgranular zone (SGZ) express markers characteristic of progenitors, but we found that they represent two distinct populations with different proliferation levels. Using lentivirus- and retrovirus-mediated fate-tracing studies, we discovered that Sox2-positive cells in the SGZ have the potential to give rise to both neurons and astrocytes, indicating their multipotency at both the population and single-cell levels. A subpopulation of Sox2-positive cells also gives rise to cells that retain Sox2, highlighting Sox2-positive cells as a primary source of adult NSCs. When exposed to mitotic signals, the proliferation of Sox2-positive cells is increased, leading to the generation of Sox2-positive NSCs and neuronal precursors. Our findings suggest that an asymmetric contribution of Sox2-positive NSCs may play a crucial role in maintaining the constant size of the NSC pool and producing new neurons during adult neurogenesis.

title: Past exposure to sun, skin phenotype, and risk of multiple sclerosis: case-control study.
text:
Objective: To investigate whether past high sun exposure is associated with a lower risk of developing multiple sclerosis.
Design: Population-based case-control study.
Setting: Tasmania, latitudes 41-3 degrees South.
Participants: 136 cases with multiple sclerosis and 272 controls randomly selected from the community and matched on sex and year of birth.
Main Outcome Measure: Multiple sclerosis was defined by both clinical and magnetic resonance imaging criteria.
Results: Higher sun exposure during the ages of 6-15 years (averaging 2-3 hours or more per day during summer weekends and holidays) was associated with a decreased risk of multiple sclerosis (adjusted odds ratio 0.31, 95% confidence interval 0.16-0.59). Greater sun exposure in winter seemed more protective than in summer. Additionally, higher actinic damage was independently associated with a decreased risk of multiple sclerosis (odds ratio 0.32, 95% confidence interval 0.11-0.88 for grades 4-6 disease). A dose-response relationship was observed between multiple sclerosis and decreasing sun exposure during childhood and early adolescence, as well as with actinic damage.
Conclusion: Higher sun exposure during childhood and early adolescence is associated with a lower risk of developing multiple sclerosis. This suggests that insufficient ultraviolet radiation may play a role in the development of multiple sclerosis.

title: Endocytic Trafficking of Rac Is Required for the Spatial Restriction of Signaling in Cell Migration
text: The small GTPases Rab5 and Rac play critical roles in endocytosis and actin remodeling, respectively, and their coordinated regulation is essential for the spatial restriction of intracellular signaling, which is crucial for various polarized cellular functions. Our findings demonstrate that clathrin- and Rab5-mediated endocytosis are necessary for the activation of Rac induced by motogenic stimuli. Rac activation occurs on early endosomes, where the Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Tiam1 is also recruited. Subsequent recycling of Rac to the plasma membrane ensures localized signaling, leading to the formation of actin-based migratory protrusions. Therefore, membrane trafficking of Rac is essential for the spatial resolution of Rac-dependent motogenic signals. Furthermore, we provide evidence that a Rab5-to-Rac circuitry regulates the morphology of motile mammalian tumor cells and primordial germinal cells during zebrafish development, suggesting that this circuitry may be relevant for the regulation of migratory programs in various cells in both in vitro settings and whole organisms.

title: Significance of stem cell marker Nanog gene in the diagnosis and prognosis of lung cancer
text:
The purpose of the current study was to investigate the potential of the Nanog gene as a diagnostic and prognostic marker for lung cancer. Specifically, the study aimed to:
1. Analyze the expression of the Nanog gene in lung cancer tissues and adjacent normal tissues.
2. Compare the expression of Nanog gene in lung cancer patients with different clinical stages and histological subtypes.
3. Evaluate the expression of Nanog gene in lung cancer stem cells and its correlation with the clinical features of lung cancer patients.

In total, 100 patients diagnosed with lung cancer between April 2013 and May 2015 were included in the study. The patients were randomly divided into two groups: group A (lung cancer) and group B (squamous cell lung carcinoma). RT-PCR was used to detect the expression of the Nanog gene in both cancer and adjacent tissues. The results showed that the expression of Nanog gene in the two groups of patients varied to different degrees. There was no significant difference between the two groups in terms of age, gender, disease stage, and lymph node metastasis. However, the expression of Nanog gene in patients with carcinoma was significantly higher than in the adjacent tissues (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the expression of Nanog gene was significantly higher in differentiated and well-differentiated carcinoma tissues than in poorly differentiated and undifferentiated carcinoma (p < 0.05). Additionally, the expression of Nanog gene was significantly higher in CD44+ cells than in other cell populations. The study concluded that the Nanog gene may serve as a useful diagnostic and prognostic marker for lung cancer, particularly in terms of disease stage and cell differentiation.

title: Current knowledge and future directions of TLR and NOD signaling in sepsis
text: Over time, the incidence of sepsis has been on the rise, accompanied by a heightened risk of mortality from the condition. In the United States, sepsis care costs billions of dollars annually. Sepsis is a complex condition that results from an imbalance in the body's immune system, leading to multi-organ failure. The Toll-like receptor (TLR) family, which was first identified in Drosophila, plays a crucial role in recognizing microbial pathogens. These pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) activate intracellular signal transduction pathways upon sensing invading microorganisms. NOD signaling is also involved in the recognition of bacteria and works synergistically with the TLR family in initiating an efficient immune response to eliminate invading microbial pathogens. TLRs and NOD1/NOD2 respond to different pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Research into modulating TLR and NOD signaling has generated significant excitement and debate as a potential therapeutic strategy for managing sepsis. However, despite the existence of molecules targeting these signaling pathways, none have proven efficacy in clinical trials thus far.

title: Concentration Sensing by the Moving Nucleus in Cell Fate Determination: A Computational Analysis
text:
During the development of the vertebrate neuroepithelium, the nucleus of neural progenitor cells (NPCs) undergoes a dynamic migration pattern, moving from the apex towards the base and then returning to the apex (known as interkinetic nuclear migration). As the nucleus migrates, it samples a spatial concentration profile of the cytoplasmic Notch intracellular domain (NICD). However, the nucleus also exhibits complex stochastic motions, including random waiting and back-and-forth movements, which can result in randomly varying levels of NICD in the cytoplasm. Despite this stochastic nature of nuclear migration, the position of the nucleus can still determine the fate of the resulting daughter cells.
To investigate how nuclear position can influence fate determination in this context, we developed a mathematical model that accounts for reaction, diffusion, and nuclear accumulation of NICD in NPCs during interkinetic nuclear migration. Using experimentally measured trajectory-dependent probabilities of nuclear turning, waiting times, and average nuclear speeds in NPCs in the developing zebrafish retina, we performed stochastic simulations to compute the nuclear trajectory-dependent probabilities of NPC differentiation. By comparing these probabilities with experimentally measured nuclear NICD concentrations and trajectory-dependent probabilities of differentiation, we were able to estimate the NICD cytoplasmic gradient.
Our computational studies reveal that spatially polarized production of NICD, rapid cytoplasmic consumption, and the time-averaging effect of nuclear import/export kinetics are sufficient to explain the experimentally observed differentiation probabilities. These findings provide quantitative support for the nuclear concentration-sensing mechanism for NPC fate determination in zebrafish retina. In summary, our study demonstrates that the position of the nucleus during interkinetic nuclear migration can influence the fate of daughter cells, even in the presence of stochastic motions and varying levels of NICD.

title: Odorant-specific adaptation pathways generate olfactory plasticity in C. elegans
text:
Following prolonged exposure to an odorant, the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans exhibits a reduced response to the odorant for an extended period of time, typically several hours. This olfactory adaptation is specific to the odorant and is mediated by the AWC neurons, which are responsible for sensing the odorant. Interestingly, animals can adapt independently to different odorants sensed by the same pair of olfactory neurons, indicating that the mechanism of olfactory adaptation is highly specific and complex.
Studies have shown that the adaptation process is genetically determined, with different genes playing a critical role in adaptation to different odorants. For example, animals lacking the gene adp-1 are unable to adapt to a subset of AWC-sensed odorants, suggesting that adp-1 plays a crucial role in a calcium-dependent process required for adaptation. Similarly, mutations in the gene osm-9 affect adaptation to a different but overlapping subset of AWC-sensed odorants, further highlighting the complexity of the adaptation process.
Notably, mutations in adp-1 and osm-9 do not impair the ability of unadapted animals to respond to odorants, indicating that odorant sensation and odorant adaptation are distinct processes. This suggests that the adaptation process is a specialized response that allows the animal to better detect and respond to specific odorants, while still maintaining the ability to detect and respond to other odorants.

title: Genome-wide dFOXO targets and topology of the transcriptomic response to stress and insulin signalling
text: FoxO transcription factors, inhibited by insulin/insulin-like growth factor signaling (IIS), play a crucial role in various organismal processes, including lifespan. Using genomic tools, we identified over 700 direct targets of dFOXO in adult female Drosophila. dFOXO is essential for the transcription of several IIS components and interacting pathways, such as TOR, in the wild-type fly. The genomic locations occupied by dFOXO in adults differ from those observed in larvae or cultured cells, and remain unchanged upon exposure to stress or reduced IIS. However, the binding of dFOXO to its targets is increased, and additional targets are activated, upon genetic reduction in IIS. We uncovered the part of the IIS transcriptional response directly controlled by dFOXO and the indirect effects, and showed that some parts of the transcriptional response to IIS reduction do not require dFOXO. Promoter analyses revealed GATA and other forkhead factors as potential mediators of the indirect and dFOXO-independent effects. Furthermore, we found genome-wide evolutionary conservation of dFOXO targets between Drosophila and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, enriched for a second tier of regulators, including the dHR96/daf-12 nuclear hormone receptor.

title: Stable partnership and progression to AIDS or death in HIV infected patients receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy: Swiss HIV cohort study.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the association between a stable romantic partnership and clinical outcomes in HIV-infected patients receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
Design:
Prospective cohort study of adults with HIV (Swiss HIV cohort study) conducted at seven outpatient clinics across Switzerland.
Participants:
3736 patients in the cohort who started HAART before 2002 (median age 36 years, 29% female, median follow-up time of 3.6 years).
Main Outcome Measures:
Time to AIDS or death (primary endpoint), death alone, increases in CD4 cell count of at least 50 and 100 above baseline, optimal viral suppression (a viral load below 400 copies/ml), and viral rebound.
Results:
Of the 3736 participants, 2985 (80%) reported a stable partnership on at least one occasion. When starting HAART, 52% (545/1042) of participants reported a stable partnership, and after five years of follow-up, 46% (190/412) of participants reported a stable partnership. In an analysis stratified by previous antiretroviral therapy and clinical stage when starting HAART, the adjusted hazard ratio for progression to AIDS or death was 0.79 (95% confidence interval 0.63 to 0.98) for participants with a stable partnership compared to those without. Adjusted hazards ratios for other endpoints were 0.59 (0.44 to 0.79) for progression to death, 1.15 (1.06 to 1.24) for an increase in CD4 cells of 100 counts/microl or more, and 1.06 (0.98 to 1.14) for optimal viral suppression.
Conclusions:
A stable romantic partnership is associated with a slower rate of progression to AIDS or death in HIV-infected patients receiving HAART.

title: Specific deficit of the ON response in visual transmission by targeted disruption of the mGIuR6 gene
text: Leveraging the restricted expression of metabotropic glutamate receptor subtype 6 (mGluR6) in retinal ON bipolar cells, we generated knockout mice lacking mGluR6 expression. The homozygous mutant mice exhibited a loss of ON responses to light, but preserved OFF responses, in comparison to wild-type controls. Despite the absence of mGluR6, the retinal structure and projection of optic fibers to the brain remained unchanged. Additionally, behavioral responses to light stimulation were observed in the mGluR6-deficient mice through shuttle box avoidance behavior experiments using light exposure as a conditioned stimulus. These findings demonstrate that mGluR6 plays a critical role in synaptic transmission to ON bipolar cells, and that the OFF response serves as an essential means of transmitting visual information.

title: Common BRCA1 variants and susceptibility to breast and ovarian cancer in the general population.
text: Most cases of young-onset breast cancer and ovarian cancer are thought to be caused by rare, highly penetrant mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. However, these mutations are uncommon in the general population and are estimated to account for only a small percentage of breast cancer cases. A larger proportion of breast cancer may be due to common variants that confer more modest individual risks. We have investigated the frequency of four common polymorphisms in the BRCA1 gene (Gln356Arg, Pro871Leu, Glu1038Gly, and Ser1613Gly) in large series of breast and ovarian cancer cases and controls. Due to linkage disequilibrium, these polymorphisms form three haplotypes with a frequency greater than 1.3%. The most common haplotypes, defined by the alleles Gln356Pro871Glu1038Ser1613 and Gln356Leu871Gly1038Gly1613, have frequencies of 0.57 and 0.32, respectively, and do not differ significantly between patient and control groups. However, our data suggest that the Arg356 allele may have a different genotype distribution in breast cancer patients compared to controls (Arg356 homozygotes are more frequent in the control groups, P = 0.01), which may indicate that it may provide protection against breast cancer. If this finding can be confirmed, it may provide insight into the structural features of the BRCA1 protein that are important for its function.

title: Exercise causes a tissue-specific change of NO production in the kidney and lung.
text: Nitric oxide (NO) is produced in the vascular endothelium and plays a crucial role in regulating local vascular tone. Exercise causes changes in systemic and regional blood flow, leading to an increase in blood flow to working muscles and a decrease in blood flow to certain organs, such as the kidneys and intestine. We hypothesized that exercise would lead to changes in NO production in specific organs. To investigate this, we studied the expression of NO synthase (NOS) mRNA and protein, NOS activity, and tissue levels of nitrite/nitrate (stable end products of NO) in the kidneys and lungs of rat after exercise. Rats were made to run on a treadmill for 45 minutes at a speed of 25 m/min, and immediately after exercise, the kidneys and lungs were removed. Control rats remained at rest during the same period. Our results showed that expression of endothelial NOS (eNOS) mRNA in the kidneys was significantly lower in exercise rats compared to control rats, while expression in the lungs was significantly higher in exercise rats compared to control rats. Western blot analysis confirmed these findings. In contrast, neither the expression of neuronal NOS (nNOS) mRNA and protein nor inducible NOS (iNOS) mRNA and protein in the kidneys and lungs differed between exercise and control rats. NOS activity in the kidneys was significantly lower in exercise rats, while activity in the lungs was significantly higher in exercise rats. However, iNOS activity in both organs did not differ between exercise and control rats. Tissue levels of nitrite/nitrate in the kidneys were significantly lower in exercise rats, while levels in the lungs were significantly higher in exercise rats. Our findings show that exercise leads to tissue-specific changes in NO production in the kidneys and lungs.

title: Ballistic labeling and dynamic imaging of astrocytes in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures
text: In vivo, protoplasmic astrocytes in mammalian central nervous system (CNS) tissues exhibit a highly complex three-dimensional (3D) morphology. However, when dissociated and cultured in vitro, these cells often assume a flattened, fibroblast-like morphology with only a few simple processes. Using fluorescent labeling and confocal reconstruction techniques, we demonstrate that many astrocytes in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures exhibit a more native, complex cytoarchitecture. While astrocytes at the surface of slice cultures exhibit a reactive form with several thick glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)-positive processes, astrocytes situated in deeper regions of the tissue retain a highly complex 3D morphology with many fine spine- or veil-like protrusions. Using gene gun-mediated ballistic delivery of gold or tungsten particles carrying cDNAs (Biolistics), lipophilic dyes (DiOlistics), or fluorescent intracellular calcium indicators (Calistics), we can label dozens of astrocytes in single slice cultures. Expression of a membrane-targeted form of enhanced green fluorescent protein (Lck-GFP) is found to be superior to soluble eGFP for resolving fine astrocytic processes. Time-lapse confocal imaging of Lck-GFP transfected astrocytes or "calistically" labeled astrocytes shows structural remodeling and calcium transients, respectively. This approach provides an in vitro system for investigating the functional architecture, development, and dynamic remodeling of astrocytes and their relationships to neurons and glia in live mammalian brain tissues.

title: A bipotential precursor population for pancreas and liver within the embryonic endoderm.
text: The pancreas differentiates independently from the dorsal and ventral domains of embryonic gut endoderm during embryonic development. Gene inactivation studies in mice have identified factors crucial for the development of the dorsal pancreas, but the factors responsible for the emergence of the ventral pancreas have remained elusive. In this investigation, we explored the hypothesis that the emergence of the ventral pancreas is linked to the emergence of the liver. Our findings indicate that the liver and ventral pancreas are specified at the same time and within the same general domain of cells. Using embryo tissue explantation experiments, we discovered that the default fate of the ventral foregut endoderm is to activate the pancreas gene program. However, FGF signaling from the cardiac mesoderm diverts this endoderm to express genes for liver instead of those for pancreas. Our findings do not suggest that the choice of cell type for pancreas or liver is based on growth or viability. Cardiac mesoderm or FGF induces the local expression of Sonic Hedgehog, which in turn inhibits the expression of pancreas genes but not liver genes. The bipotential precursor cell population for pancreas and liver in embryonic development and its fate selection by FGF share features that appear to be recapitulated in the adult pancreas and reflect the evolution of these organs.

title: ErbB4-neuregulin signaling modulates synapse development and dendritic arborization through distinct mechanisms.
text: Research has linked perturbations in the NRG1/ErbB4 system to schizophrenia, with affected patients exhibiting altered levels of these proteins and impaired glutamatergic synaptic function. However, the role of NRG1/ErbB4 in regulating synapse maturation and neuronal circuitry has been largely unexplored. Our study found that ErbB4 is expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory interneurons at postsynaptic sites, and overexpression of ErbB4 enhances the size of presynaptic inputs without affecting their number. Conversely, knockdown of ErbB4 using shRNA reduces the size of presynaptic inputs. We also found that ErbB4-mediated synapse maturation requires its extracellular domain, but its tyrosine kinase activity is dispensable for this process. Additionally, we discovered that depletion of ErbB4 leads to a decrease in the number of primary neurites, and stimulation of ErbB4 using a soluble form of NRG1 results in exuberant dendritic arborization through activation of the tyrosine kinase domain of ErbB4 and the phosphoinositide 3-kinase pathway. These findings suggest that NRG1/ErbB4 signaling regulates synapse maturation and dendritic morphology through two distinct mechanisms: trans-synaptic signaling and tyrosine kinase activity.

title: Dynamic Helix Interactions in Transmembrane Signaling
text: Investigating how protein transmembrane domains transmit signals across membranes is fraught with distinct challenges. Despite these obstacles, we will examine the factors that have contributed to success in this field and reflect on the insights gained from these studies. These findings imply that some of the most intriguing properties of transmembrane helix interactions may be the most difficult to investigate using current techniques.

title: Association between smoking and risk of bladder cancer among men and women.
text:
Background: Previous studies have shown that tobacco smoking is responsible for approximately 50-65% of bladder cancer cases in men and 20-30% in women. However, these estimates may need to be revised due to changes in smoking prevalence and cigarette composition.
Objective: To evaluate the association between tobacco smoking and bladder cancer in a large, contemporary cohort.
Methods: We analyzed data from 281,394 men and 186,134 women in the National Institutes of Health-AARP (NIH-AARP) Diet and Health Study, who were followed up for 4.5 million person-years. We calculated the hazard ratios (HRs) and population attributable risks (PARs) for bladder cancer according to smoking status.
Results: During follow-up, 3896 men and 627 women developed bladder cancer. Former smokers and current smokers had higher risks of bladder cancer than never smokers, with HRs of 2.22 and 4.06, respectively. The PAR for ever smoking was 0.50 in men and 0.52 in women.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that the association between smoking and bladder cancer may be stronger than previously thought, with a PAR of 0.50 in women and 0.52 in men. These results highlight the need for continued efforts to reduce smoking prevalence and bladder cancer incidence.

title: Leptin regulates glutamate and glucose transporters in hypothalamic astrocytes.
text:
Glial cells play a crucial role in modulating the metabolism and activity of neurons, and there is growing interest in their involvement in appetite and energy balance. Previous studies have shown that leptin, a key regulator of appetite and metabolism, can influence glial structural proteins and morphology. Our findings expand on these discoveries by demonstrating that metabolic status and leptin levels also impact astrocyte-specific glutamate and glucose transporters, indicating that metabolic signals have a direct impact on synaptic efficiency and glucose uptake, ultimately affecting neuronal function.
We observed alterations in the basal and glucose-stimulated electrical activity of hypothalamic proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons in mice whose mothers were fed a high-fat diet during pregnancy. In adulthood, increased body weight and fasting also led to changes in the expression of glucose and glutamate transporters. These results suggest that the metabolic state of the entire organism can influence hypothalamic glial cell activity, implicating these cells in the development of obesity.

title: Metabolic phenotyping of human blood plasma: a powerful tool to discriminate between cancer types?
text:
Background:
Emerging evidence has demonstrated that cancer cell metabolism differs from that of normal cells. However, the extent to which different cancer types are characterized by distinct metabolic profiles remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether the plasma metabolic phenotype can be used to differentiate between lung and breast cancer.
Methods:
The proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectrum of plasma was divided into 110 integration regions, each representing the metabolic phenotype. These regions were used to train a classification model to discriminate between 80 female breast cancer patients and 54 female lung cancer patients, all with adenocarcinoma. The model's validity was evaluated through permutation testing and by classifying an independent validation cohort of 60 female breast cancer patients and 81 male lung cancer patients, all with adenocarcinoma.
Results:
The model achieved 99% accuracy in classifying breast cancer patients and 93% accuracy in classifying lung cancer patients, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.96. The model was validated in the independent cohort with a sensitivity of 89%, specificity of 82%, and AUC of 0.94. Decreased levels of sphingomyelin and phosphatidylcholine (phospholipids with choline head group) and increased levels of phospholipids with long, saturated fatty acid chains were found to indicate that cell membranes of lung tumors are more rigid and less sensitive to lipid peroxidation. The other discriminating metabolites pointed to a more pronounced response of the body to the Warburg effect in lung cancer.
Conclusion:
Metabolic phenotyping of plasma allows for the distinction between lung and breast cancer, suggesting that the metabolite profile reflects more than a general cancer marker.

title: Direct in vivo assessment of microcirculatory dysfunction in severe falciparum malaria.
text: This study aimed to investigate microcirculatory changes in the mucosal surfaces of patients with severe malaria using direct in vivo observation with orthogonal polarization spectral (OPS) imaging. The study included 43 adult patients with severe falciparum malaria, as well as comparison groups of patients with uncomplicated malaria, patients with bacterial sepsis, and healthy individuals. The study found that the microcirculation in the rectal mucosa of patients with severe malaria was significantly disturbed, with heterogeneous obstruction that was proportional to the severity of the disease. Blocked capillaries were found in 29 patients (67%), and were associated with concurrent hyperdynamic blood flow in adjacent vessels in 27 patients (93%). The proportion of blocked capillaries correlated with the base deficit in plasma and with the concentration of lactate. The study also found that abnormalities in the microcirculation disappeared when the patients recovered. In contrast, healthy individuals and patients with uncomplicated malaria or sepsis did not show stagnant erythrocytes, and hyperdynamic blood flow was prominent in patients with sepsis. These findings underscore the prominent role of microvascular obstruction in the pathophysiology of severe malaria, and highlight the fundamental difference between the microvascular pathophysiology of malaria and that of bacterial sepsis.

title: Multiple archaeal groups mediate methane oxidation in anoxic cold seep sediments.
text: No microorganism capable of anaerobic growth on methane as the sole carbon source has been cultivated yet, so our knowledge of these microbes is mainly based on geochemical and microbiological observations of field samples. Using combined fluorescent in situ hybridization and secondary ion mass spectrometry, we have identified anaerobic methanotrophs in marine methane-seep sediments for the first time. Our findings show that at least two distinct archaeal groups (ANME-1 and ANME-2) are involved in the anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM) at methane seeps. These archaeal groups often coexist with bacteria, but they can also be found as single cells or in monospecific aggregations. Isotopic analysis suggests that both monospecific archaeal cells and cell aggregates are active in anaerobic methanotrophy, along with multispecies consortia. Our data indicate that the microbial species and biotic interactions mediating anaerobic methanotrophy are diverse and complex, and that highly structured ANME-2/Desulfosarcina consortia are not the only entities responsible for AOM at marine methane seeps. Other microbial groups, including ANME-1 archaea, can also consume anaerobic methane either as single cells, in monospecific aggregates, or in multispecies consortia.

title: N-cadherin in the spotlight of cell-cell adhesion, differentiation, embryogenesis, invasion and signalling.
text: Cell migration is a crucial process that occurs throughout embryonic development, adulthood, and in certain pathological conditions. Cadherins, particularly the neural cell adhesion molecule N-cadherin, play a significant role in this process. During embryonic development, N-cadherin is essential for gastrulation and neural crest development. N-cadherin-mediated contacts activate various signaling pathways, including Rho GTPases and tyrosine kinase signaling (e.g., through the fibroblast growth factor receptor). In cancer, cadherins regulate the balance between suppression and promotion of invasion. E-cadherin functions as an invasion suppressor and is downregulated in most carcinomas, while N-cadherin, an invasion promoter, is frequently upregulated. Expression of N-cadherin in epithelial cells leads to changes in morphology, transforming them into more motile and invasive cells. However, in some cancers, such as osteosarcoma, N-cadherin may function as a tumor suppressor. N-cadherin can have multiple functions, promoting adhesion or inducing migration depending on the cellular context.

title: Role of fascin in filopodial protrusion
text: In this study, the researchers investigated the mechanisms of actin bundling in filopodia. They analyzed the localization of known actin cross-linking proteins in mouse melanoma B16F1 cells and found that fascin was specifically localized along the entire length of all filopodia, whereas other actin cross-linkers were not. RNA interference of fascin led to a reduction in the number of filopodia, and remaining filopodia had abnormal morphology with wavy and loosely bundled actin organization. The researchers also found that dephosphorylation of serine 39 in fascin determined the frequency of cellular filopodia. The constitutively active fascin mutant S39A increased the number and length of filopodia, while the inactive fascin mutant S39E reduced filopodia frequency. Using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching of GFP-tagged wild-type and S39A fascin, the researchers found that dephosphorylated fascin underwent rapid cycles of association to and dissociation from actin filaments in filopodia, with a t1/2 of less than 10 seconds. The study proposes that fascin is a key specific actin cross-linker that provides stiffness for filopodial bundles, and its dynamic behavior allows for efficient coordination between actin filament elongation and bundling in filopodia.

title: TOR Signaling in Growth and Metabolism
text: The target of rapamycin (TOR) is a crucial protein that regulates cell growth and metabolism in response to environmental cues. Through studies in model organisms, we have gained a deeper understanding of mammalian TOR complexes and the signaling pathways they mediate. TOR is part of two distinct multiprotein complexes: TOR complex 1 (TORC1), which is sensitive to the drug rapamycin, and TORC2, which is not. Dysregulation of mammalian TORC1 has significant physiological consequences, suggesting that inhibitors of mammalian TOR may be useful in the treatment of various diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, autoimmunity, and metabolic disorders.

title: Self-Organization of the Escherichia coli Chemotaxis Network Imaged with Super-Resolution Light Microscopy
text: The Escherichia coli chemotaxis network serves as a model system for the study of biological signal processing. In E. coli, transmembrane receptors responsible for signal transduction aggregate into large clusters consisting of thousands of proteins. These sensory clusters have been observed at the cell poles and future division sites. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms behind chemotaxis cluster formation, cluster size regulation, and the robust maintenance of cluster location in dividing cells remain unclear. To investigate these processes, we employed photoactivated localization microscopy (PALM) to map the cellular locations of three key chemotaxis proteins (Tar receptor, CheY, and CheW) with unprecedented resolution of 15 nm. Our findings reveal that cluster sizes are approximately exponentially distributed, with no characteristic cluster size, and that one-third of Tar receptors are part of smaller lateral clusters rather than the large polar clusters. By analyzing the spatial distribution of over 1 million individual proteins from 326 cells, we suggest that stochastic self-assembly is the primary mechanism for cluster formation, without the involvement of the cytoskeleton or active transport. Our super-resolution PALM maps provide evidence that stochastic self-assembly can create and maintain approximately periodic structures in biological membranes, highlighting the importance of this process in bacterial chemotaxis.

title: Ciliary Extracellular Vesicles: Txt Msg Organelles
text:
Cilia, sensory organelles found on the surface of cells, play a crucial role in monitoring the surrounding environment. In addition to their role as sensory receivers, cilia also release extracellular vesicles (EVs), which are small, sub-micron sized organelles that are used for intercellular communication in all three kingdoms of life. These EVs are released from ciliated cells and can coordinate systemic responses within an organism, both in normal and diseased states. However, despite their importance, the relationship between cilia and EVs, as well as the fundamental biology of EVs, is still not well understood.
Recent studies in model organisms such as Chlamydomonas and Caenorhabditis elegans have begun to shed light on the role of cilia in EV biogenesis and reception. In Chlamydomonas, EVs are shed from the tips of flagella and are bioactive, while in Caenorhabditis elegans, EVs are released by ciliated sensory neurons in an intraflagellar transport-dependent manner. These EVs play a role in modulating animal-to-animal communication, and their bioactivity is dependent on the content of the EV cargo.
Abnormalities in EV shedding or cilia-EV interactions have been linked to ciliopathies, a group of diseases characterized by defects in cilia structure or function. As research into these organelles continues to advance, a new field of cell biology may emerge, with the cilium being recognized as a dedicated organelle for EV biogenesis and reception. Understanding the mechanisms by which EVs exert bioactivity and the insights that can be gained from studying EV biogenesis and function in model organisms may provide valuable insight into the treatment and management of ciliopathies in humans.

title: The NOD-like receptor NLRP12 attenuates colon inflammation and tumorigenesis.
text: NLRP12 is a member of the intracellular Nod-like receptor (NLR) family that has been implicated in the regulation of inflammatory responses. Despite its potential role in downregulating the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, the physiological function of NLRP12 in maintaining intestinal homeostasis and preventing colorectal tumorigenesis remains poorly characterized. To investigate the role of NLRP12 in inflammatory diseases, we generated mice lacking the gene encoding this protein and analyzed their susceptibility to colon inflammation and tumorigenesis. Our findings indicate that NLRP12-deficient mice are highly susceptible to colon inflammation and tumor development, which is characterized by increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and tumorigenic factors. We also observed that the failure of NLRP12 to dampen the activation of nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) in macrophages contributes to the enhanced colon inflammation and colorectal tumor development in these mice. These results provide insight into the critical role of NLRP12 in maintaining intestinal homeostasis and protecting against colorectal tumorigenesis.

title: Ionic mechanism of ouabain-induced concurrent apoptosis and necrosis in individual cultured cortical neurons
text: Energy deficiency and dysfunction of the Na+, K+-ATPase are common consequences of various pathological insults, but the mechanisms of cellular injury induced by impaired Na+, K+-ATPase function are not well understood. To investigate this, we used cultured cortical neurons to examine the hypothesis that blocking the Na+, K+-ATPase leads to cell death through depletion of intracellular potassium ions and increase in intracellular calcium and sodium ions, resulting in both apoptotic and necrotic cell death. Our results show that the Na+, K+-ATPase inhibitor ouabain induces concentration-dependent neuronal death, accompanied by cell swelling, intracellular calcium and sodium increase, potassium decrease, cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation, and DNA laddering. Electron microscopy revealed the coexistence of ultrastructural features of both apoptosis and necrosis in individual cells. Treatment with the caspase inhibitor Z-Val-Ala-Asp(OMe)-fluoromethyl ketone (Z-VAD-FMK) blocked >50% of ouabain-induced neuronal death, while potassium channel blockers or high potassium medium, but not calcium channel blockade, prevented cytochrome c release, caspase activation, and DNA damage. Combining K+ channel blockade with Ca2+ or Na+ channel blockade or high K+ medium resulted in additional protection. Furthermore, coapplication of Z-VAD-FMK and nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, produced virtually complete neuroprotection. These findings suggest that the neuronal death associated with Na+, K+-pump failure consists of concurrent apoptotic and necrotic components, mediated by intracellular depletion of potassium ions and accumulation of calcium and sodium ions, respectively. The ouabain-induced hybrid death may represent a distinct form of cell death related to the brain injury of inadequate energy supply and disrupted ion homeostasis.

title: Potential consequences of replacing a retail alcohol monopoly with a private licence system: results from Sweden.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the potential impact of replacing Sweden's state-controlled alcohol retail system with a private licensing system on alcohol consumption and related harm.
Design: Two scenarios were analyzed: (1) replacing the current alcohol monopoly with private licensed stores specializing in alcohol sales, and (2) making all alcohol available in grocery stores. A multiplicative model was used to project the effects of changes in key factors, including hours of sale, retail prices, promotion, and advertising, on alcohol consumption. The projected consumption increase was then used to estimate the impact on a set of harm indicators, with values obtained from the literature.
Findings: According to the projections, scenario 1 would result in a 17% increase in consumption (1.4 liters/capita), leading to an additional 770 deaths, 8500 assaults, 2700 drinking driving offenses, and 4.5 million sick days per year. Scenario 2 would result in a 37.4% increase in consumption (3.1 liters/capita), resulting in an additional 2000 deaths, 20,000 assaults, 6600 drinking driving offenses, and 11.1 million days of sick leave per year.
Conclusions: The projections suggest that privatization of Sweden's alcohol retail market would significantly increase alcohol consumption and related harm, based on the research literature.

title: A comprehensive genomic binding map of gene and chromatin regulatory proteins in Saccharomyces.
text: In Saccharomyces, hundreds of different proteins regulate and implement transcription on a large scale. However, the interrelationships between these proteins have not been thoroughly investigated. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a comprehensive study to determine the genome-wide binding locations of 200 transcription-related proteins under both normal and acute heat-shock conditions. Our findings reveal a greater diversity and specialization of regulation associated with the SAGA transcription pathway compared to the TFIID pathway. We also identify new regulators enriched at tRNA genes and uncover a global co-occupancy network of over 20,000 unique regulator combinations that show a high degree of regulatory interconnections among lowly expressed genes. Additionally, we find that regulators of the SAGA pathway are located largely distal to the core promoter, while regulators of the TFIID pathway are located proximally. Finally, we observe distinct mobilization of SAGA- versus TFIID-linked regulators during acute heat shock.

title: Tie2/Angiopoietin-1 Signaling Regulates Hematopoietic Stem Cell Quiescence in the Bone Marrow Niche
text: The dormant state is believed to be an essential characteristic of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) for their survival and function in the bone marrow (BM). The interaction between HSCs and their specific microenvironments, known as stem cell niches, is crucial for adult hematopoiesis in the BM. Our study reveals that HSCs expressing the receptor tyrosine kinase Tie2 are in a dormant state and resistant to apoptosis, and comprise a subpopulation of HSCs (side-population, SP) that adhere to osteoblasts (OBs) in the BM niche. The interaction between Tie2 and its ligand Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) induces the formation of HSCs in vitro and maintains their long-term repopulating activity in vivo. Additionally, Ang-1 enhances the ability of HSCs to become quiescent and adhere to bone, providing protection to the HSC compartment from myelosuppressive stress. These findings suggest that the Tie2/Ang-1 signaling pathway plays a vital role in maintaining HSCs in a dormant state within the BM niche.

title: Thirty-One Novel Biomarkers as Predictors for Clinically Incident Diabetes
text:
The prevalence of diabetes is increasing globally, making it a pressing public health concern. Despite this, the underlying factors that contribute to diabetes risk are not fully understood. In this study, we aimed to identify novel biomarkers that could help predict the risk of developing diabetes.
We evaluated 31 potential biomarkers in two large cohorts: the FINRISK97 cohort (n = 7,827) and the Health 2000 cohort (n = 4,977). We used Cox proportional hazards models to assess the relationship between each biomarker and the risk of diabetes, while adjusting for classic risk factors. We also used receiver operating characteristic curves and other statistical measures to evaluate the discriminatory ability of each biomarker.
Our findings revealed that a score consisting of adiponectin, apolipoprotein B, C-reactive protein, and ferritin almost doubled the risk of diabetes in the validation cohort. This score also improved the model's discrimination and reclassification of diabetes risk. Interestingly, we found that the best score for men and women differed, with the best results among men being a score of four biomarkers (adiponectin, apolipoprotein B, ferritin, and interleukin-1 receptor antagonist), and among women, a score that included adiponectin, apolipoprotein B, C-reactive protein, and insulin.
Our study provides new insights into the pathogenesis of diabetes and may help with targeting prevention and treatment. The identification of novel biomarkers for diabetes risk could lead to improved early detection and intervention, ultimately reducing the burden of this disease.

title: Exploiting lymphatic transport and complement activation in nanoparticle vaccines
text: Researchers have explored the use of antigen targeting and adjuvancy schemes to enhance the delivery of antigens to dendritic cells and activate them in vaccine development. In this study, we investigate the potential of nanoparticles as a vaccine platform by targeting dendritic cells in the lymph nodes through interstitial flow and activating them in situ using complement activation. We found that ultra-small nanoparticles (25 nm) were highly efficient in transporting into lymphatic capillaries and targeting half of the dendritic cells in the draining lymph nodes, compared to larger nanoparticles (100 nm) which were only 10% as efficient. The surface chemistry of these nanoparticles also activated the complement cascade, generating a danger signal that potently activated dendritic cells. Using nanoparticles conjugated to the model antigen ovalbumin, we demonstrated the ability to generate both humoral and cellular immunity in mice in a size- and complement-dependent manner.

title: The sheddase ADAM10 is a potent modulator of prion disease
text: The prion protein (PrP(C)) is highly expressed in the nervous system and plays a critical role in prion diseases, where it misfolds into pathogenic PrP(Sc). Some research has suggested that PrP(C) may also serve as a receptor for neurotoxicity in common neurodegenerative proteinopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease. PrP(C) is shed from the plasma membrane by the enzyme ADAM10, but the impact of this process on prion disease is not fully understood. To investigate, we used conditional knockout mice to deplete ADAM10 in forebrain neurons and examined the effects on PrP(C) levels and prion disease progression. Our findings reveal that lack of ADAM10 leads to increased levels of PrP(C) and reduced incubation times for prion infection, suggesting a dual role for ADAM10-mediated shedding in prion disease. Additionally, our data indicate that the absence of shedding impairs the spread of prion pathology, highlighting the importance of proteolytic processing in prion disease.

title: High-affinity zinc inhibition of NMDA NR1-NR2A receptors
text: Micromolar concentrations of extracellular zinc ions (Zn2+) have been shown to antagonize native N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors through a dual mechanism involving both voltage-independent and voltage-dependent inhibition. To elucidate the relative importance of these mechanisms and their subunit specificity, we investigated recombinant NMDA receptors expressed in HEK 293 cells and Xenopus oocytes. Our findings indicate that the voltage-dependent inhibition is comparable between NR1a-NR2A and NR1a-NR2B receptors, while the voltage-independent inhibition occurs at lower Zn2+ concentrations in NR1a-NR2A receptors (IC50 in the nanomolar range) than in NR1a-NR2B receptors (IC50 in the micromolar range). The pronounced effect observed on NR1a-NR2A receptors is attributed to the slow dissociation of Zn2+ from its binding site. By examining the effects of Zn2+ on various combinations of NR1 (NR1a or NR1b) and NR2 (NR2A, NR2B, NR2C) subunits, we demonstrate that both the NR1 and NR2 subunits contribute to the voltage-independent Zn2+ inhibition. Moreover, we discovered that in control conditions (i.e., in zero nominal Zn2+ solutions), the addition of low concentrations of heavy metal chelators significantly potentiates the responses of NR1a-NR2A receptors, but not of NR1a-NR2B receptors. This observation suggests that trace amounts of a heavy metal (probably Zn2+) contaminate standard solutions and tonicly inhibit NR1a-NR2A receptors. Furthermore, chelation of a contaminant metal may account for the rapid NR2A subunit-specific potentiations produced by reducing agents like DTT or glutathione.

title: PrimPol, an Archaic Primase/Polymerase Operating in Human Cells
text: We have identified and characterized a novel primase in human cells, known as PrimPol, which demonstrates the ability to initiate DNA synthesis with deoxynucleotides, a process that is distinct from the exclusive use of ribonucleotides by regular primases. Furthermore, PrimPol has been found to be a DNA polymerase that is particularly adept at bypassing the most common oxidative DNA damage, such as abasic sites and 8-oxoguanine, in both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA compartments. Using subcellular fractionation and immunodetection techniques, we have determined that PrimPol is present in both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA compartments in human and mouse cells. However, our findings indicate that PrimPol is absent from mitochondria derived from PRIMPOL knockout mice, suggesting a critical role for this enzyme in mitochondrial DNA replication. In addition, we have found that silencing or ablating the PRIMPOL gene in human and mouse cells leads to impaired mitochondrial DNA replication. Based on the synergistic interactions observed between PrimPol and replicative DNA polymerases Polγ and Polε, we propose that PrimPol functions as a translesion DNA polymerase or a specific DNA primase that reinitiates DNA synthesis downstream of lesions that obstruct replication fork progression during both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA replication.

title: Predictors of Attrition and Academic Success of Medical Students: A 30-Year Retrospective Study
text:
Objective: To identify factors contributing to academic failure and predict academic success among medical students at the University of Split in Croatia.
Methods: We analyzed academic records of 2054 students enrolled between 1979 and 2008. We found that 26% (533/2054) of enrolled students did not graduate, with the most common reasons being personal issues (36.4%), transfer to another medical school (35.6%), and dismissal due to unsatisfactory academic performance (21.2%). We also analyzed the academic performance of 1126 graduates, including 395 men and 731 women, and found that their average graduation GPA was 3.67±0.53 and study duration was 7.6±2.44 years. Additionally, we found that only 6.4% (42/654) of students graduated in time during the 5-year curriculum, and 55% (240/472) of students graduated in time after the curriculum was extended to 6 years. We identified variables that predicted whether a student would graduate or not, including high school grades, entrance exam score, and year of enrollment. Specifically, high school grades and entrance exam score were significant predictors of graduation grades, while entrance exam score predicted the length of studying.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that pre-admission academic qualifications and year of enrollment are important predictors of academic success in medical school. The high attrition rate highlights the need for more attention to be devoted to this issue.

title: Mechanical regulation of cell function with geometrically modulated elastomeric substrates
text: We have established a library of micromolded elastomeric micropost arrays to independently manipulate the rigidity of the substrate, without affecting the surface properties of adhesives or other materials. Our experiments showed that the rigidity of the microposts has a significant impact on cell morphology, focal adhesions, cytoskeletal contractility, and stem cell differentiation. Additionally, we found that early changes in cytoskeletal contractility can predict later stem cell fate decisions in individual cells.

title: THE EMBO JOURNAL
text: Glutamate-gated ion channels, also known as ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs), are activated by the extracellular environment through an extensive extracellular domain composed of two clamshell-shaped segments. The distal, N-terminal domain (NTD) of iGluRs has been found to exhibit allosteric potential in N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) type iGluRs, which has not been observed in analogous domains of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors (AMPARs). In this study, we present new structural data that reveal the dynamic properties of the GluA2 and GluA3 AMPAR NTDs. GluA3 exhibits a unique zipped-open dimer interface with unconstrained lower clamshell lobes, similar to those found in metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs). This labile interface enables interprotomer rotations, which can be transmitted to downstream receptor segments.
