Additionally, we found that high frequencies of new somatic L1 insertions occur in human lung cancer genomes, and genome-wide analysis suggests that altered DNA methylation may be responsible for the observed L1 mobilization in these tumors. Our findings indicate that transposon-mediated mutagenesis is a significant factor in human genomes and is likely to have a profound impact on human biology and disease.

title: Knowledge of young African American adults about heart disease: a cross-sectional survey
text:
Background: African Americans have a higher prevalence of cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality compared to other ethnic groups. Young adults are a critical target population for intervention strategies to prevent and reduce CVD risk. This study aimed to assess the level of knowledge regarding lifestyle risk factors for CVD among young African American adults in Phoenix, Arizona, using the Health Belief Model as a conceptual framework.
Methods: A convenience sample of 172 African American men and women aged 18-26 years completed a questionnaire adapted from the American Heart Association's national surveys. Descriptive statistics were analyzed by age, gender, education level, and health status variables, including body mass index (BMI), smoking status, and physical activity.
Results: The study found that some aspects of heart disease were well-known among young adult African Americans, while knowledge of other important risk factors and preventive behaviors varied. Education level, gender, and self-efficacy (the belief in one's ability to change behaviors) were identified as predictors of CVD knowledge. Specifically, higher education, female gender, and high self-efficacy were associated with higher CVD knowledge scores. Additionally, predictors of self-efficacy in changing CVD risk included higher education and perceived low risk of CVD, but these characteristics explained only a small proportion of the variance.
Conclusions: Evaluating baseline knowledge of CVD is crucial before designing and implementing health promotion programs. Identifying strengths and weaknesses in knowledge can help tailor programs to be more effective. Future research should aim to identify additional characteristics that influence knowledge and risk perception.

title: Recent insights into the role of Notch signaling in tumorigenesis
text: Members of the Notch family of transmembrane receptors play a crucial role in determining cell fate. Over the past decade, evidence has emerged suggesting that Notch signaling is involved in the development and progression of both hematologic and solid malignancies. Notch signaling regulates a wide range of cellular functions and microenvironmental cues that are important for tumorigenesis, including cell proliferation, apoptosis, adhesion, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and angiogenesis. Contrary to previous beliefs, recent findings suggest that Notch signaling can act both as an oncogene and a tumor suppressor, depending on the context. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of the molecular and functional aspects of Notch-mediated neoplastic transformation and explore the cellular mechanisms that underlie its complex role in tumorigenesis.

title: BRIEFINGS IN FUNCTIONAL GENOMICS AND PROTEOMICS. VOL 5. NO 3. 209^221 doi:10.1093/bfgp/ell028 Histone acetylation in gene regulation
text: Genetic information is encased in the highly dynamic nucleoprotein structure known as chromatin. Many biological processes are regulated through modifications made to key proteins after translation. One of the most well-studied covalent modifications influencing gene regulation in eukaryotic cells is the acetylation of lysine residues on the N-terminal histone tails. This review will examine the role of enzymes involved in controlling both histone and non-histone proteins acetylation levels in the cell, with a particular focus on their impact on cancer.

title: Efficacy of monthly tafenoquine for prophylaxis of Plasmodium vivax and multidrug-resistant P. falciparum malaria.
text: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, we evaluated the efficacy of monthly doses of tafenoquine in preventing Plasmodium vivax and multidrug-resistant P. falciparum malaria in Thai soldiers. A total of 205 soldiers received either a loading dose of tafenoquine 400 mg per day for 3 days, followed by single monthly 400-mg doses (n = 104), or placebo (n = 101), for up to 5 consecutive months. Among volunteers who completed follow-up (96 tafenoquine and 91 placebo recipients), there were 22 P. vivax, 8 P. falciparum, and 1 mixed infection. Notably, all infections except one P. vivax occurred in placebo recipients, indicating a protective efficacy of 97% for all malaria (95% confidence interval [CI], 82%-99%), 96% for P. vivax malaria (95% CI, 76%-99%), and 100% for P. falciparum malaria (95% CI, 60%-100%). The study found that monthly tafenoquine was safe, well tolerated, and highly effective in preventing P. vivax and multidrug-resistant P. falciparum malaria in Thai soldiers during 6 months of prophylaxis.

title: Headache, migraine, and structural brain lesions and function: population based Epidemiology of Vascular Ageing-MRI study
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between various types of headaches and the volume of white matter hyperintensities (WMH), brain infarcts, and cognitive function in a population-based study.
Design: Cross-sectional study.
Setting: Epidemiology of Vascular Ageing study in Nantes, France.
Participants: 780 participants (mean age 69, 58.5% women) with detailed headache assessment.
Main Outcome Measures: Brain scans were evaluated for volume of WMH (using fully automated imaging processing) and classification of infarcts (using a standardized assessment grid). Cognitive function was assessed by a battery of tests, including the mini-mental state examination.
Results: Of the 780 participants, 163 (20.9%) reported a history of severe headaches, and 116 had migraine, of whom 17 (14.7%) reported aura symptoms. An association was found between any history of severe headache and increasing volume of WMH. The adjusted odds ratio for being in the highest third for total volume of WMH was 2.0 (95% confidence interval 1.3 to 3.1, P for trend 0.002) for participants with any history of severe headache compared to those without severe headache in the lowest third. The association pattern was similar for all headache types. Migraine with aura was the only headache type strongly associated with volume of deep WMH (highest third odds ratio 12.4, 1.6 to 99.4, P for trend 0.005) and with brain infarcts (3.4, 1.2 to 9.3). The location of infarcts was predominantly outside the cerebellum and brain stem. No evidence was found for cognitive impairment for any headache type with or without brain lesions.
Conclusions: In this population-based study, any history of severe headache was associated with an increased volume of WMH. Migraine with aura was the only headache type associated with brain infarcts. No evidence was found to suggest that headache of any type, either alone or in combination with brain lesions, was associated with cognitive impairment.

title: Characterization of adipocytes derived from fibro/adipogenic progenitors resident in human skeletal muscle
text:
A recent study has revealed the existence of fibro/adipogenic progenitors located between skeletal muscle fibers. The aim of this investigation was to determine the extent to which these progenitors differentiate into fully functional adipocytes. The characterization of muscle progenitor-derived adipocytes is crucial in understanding muscle homeostasis, as they are believed to be the cellular origin of intermuscular adipose tissue that develops in various pathophysiological situations.
To isolate these progenitors, the researchers used a panel of 15 human muscle biopsies based on their specific cell-surface immunophenotype, which included CD15+/PDGFRα+CD56-. This allowed them to investigate their differentiation into adipocytes and the cellular functions of terminally differentiated adipocytes. The study found that adipogenic differentiation was regulated by the same effectors as those regulating differentiation of progenitors derived from white subcutaneous adipose tissue. Moreover, basic adipocyte functions, such as triglyceride synthesis and lipolysis, occurred at levels similar to those observed with subcutaneous adipose tissue progenitor-derived adipocytes.
However, the study also found a surprising feature of muscle progenitor-derived adipocytes: they are insensitive to insulin-induced glucose uptake, which is associated with the impairment of phosphorylation of key insulin-signaling effectors. These findings suggest that muscle adipogenic progenitors give rise to bona fide white adipocytes that have an unexpected insulin-resistance phenotype.

title: Membrane lipids in invadopodia and podosomes: Key structures for cancer invasion and metastasis
text: Invadopodia are protrusions that cancer cells extend outside of their cell membranes to degrade the extracellular matrix (ECM). Podosomes are similar structures found in oncogene-transformed fibroblasts and immune cells, including macrophages and osteoclasts, which play a crucial role in remodeling the ECM during cancer invasion and metastasis. While significant research has focused on identifying the molecular components and regulators of invadopodia/podosomes, the mechanisms by which these components are assembled into these structures and how assembly is spatially and temporally regulated remain poorly understood. This review aims to summarize recent progress on the molecular mechanisms of invadopodia/podosome formation, with a particular emphasis on the roles of lipid rafts and phosphoinositides.

title: CCR2 and CXCR4 regulate peripheral blood monocyte pharmacodynamics and link to efficacy in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis
text:
Background: CCR2 has been a focus of interest as a target for inflammatory disease due to its key role in regulating monocyte trafficking to sites of inflammation.
Methods: In this study, we examined the pharmacodynamic consequences of CCR2 blockade on the peripheral blood monocyte compartment in the context of acute and chronic inflammatory processes. We used a potent small molecule antagonist to block CCR2 in vivo and measured the effects on circulating Ly6Chi monocytes.
Results: Our results demonstrate that CCR2 antagonism led to a rapid decrease in the number of circulating Ly6Chi monocytes, which was largely due to the CXCR4-dependent sequestration of these cells in the bone marrow. Additionally, we found that CCR2 antagonism led to an accumulation of circulating CCL2 and CCL7 levels in the blood, indicating a role for CCR2 in regulating the levels of its ligands under homeostatic conditions. Finally, we showed that the pharmacodynamic changes due to CCR2 antagonism were apparent after chronic dosing in a mouse model of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, which demonstrated a dramatic reduction in disease severity.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that CCR2 antagonism in vivo has tractable pharmacodynamic effects that can be used to align target engagement with biologic effects on disease activity. These results provide a basis for further investigation into the therapeutic potential of CCR2 blockade in inflammatory diseases.

title: Displacement of a DNA binding protein by Dda helicase
text: Bacteriophage T4 Dda helicase has recently been shown to be active as a monomer in unwinding short duplex oligonucleotides and displacing streptavidin from 3'-biotinylated oligonucleotides. However, its activity for streptavidin displacement and DNA unwinding increases with the number of Dda molecules bound to the substrate molecule. To investigate the ability of Dda to displace DNA binding proteins, a substrate was designed with a DNA binding site for the Escherichia coli trp repressor and a single-stranded overhang. Our results show that a single Dda molecule is insufficient to displace the E. coli trp repressor from double-stranded DNA under single turnover conditions, although the substrate is unwound and the repressor is displaced when the single-stranded overhang is long enough to accommodate two Dda molecules. The amount of product formed increases when the substrate can accommodate more than two Dda molecules. These findings suggest that multiple Dda molecules work together to displace DNA binding proteins in a manner that correlates with the DNA unwinding activity and streptavidin displacement activity. We propose a cooperative "inchworm" model to describe the activities of Dda helicase.

title: Control of Developmental Regulators by Polycomb in Human Embryonic Stem Cells
text: Polycomb group proteins are crucial for the early development of metazoans, yet their involvement in human development remains inadequately understood. To investigate the role of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) subunit SUZ12 in human development, we mapped its distribution across the entire non-repeat portion of the genome in human embryonic stem (ES) cells. Our findings reveal that SUZ12 is dispersed across a significant portion of over two hundred genes encoding key developmental regulators. These genes are characterized by histone H3K27 trimethylation, transcriptional repression, and high conservation across the genome. Interestingly, we discovered that PRC2 target genes are preferentially activated during ES cell differentiation, and that ES cell regulators OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG co-occupy a notable subset of these genes. These results suggest that PRC2 occupies a distinct set of developmental genes in ES cells that must be repressed to maintain pluripotency and are poised for activation during ES cell differentiation.

title: PAD4 is essential for antibacterial innate immunity mediated by neutrophil extracellular traps
text: Neutrophils capture and eliminate bacteria by forming highly condensed chromatin structures called neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). Previous research revealed that histone hypercitrullination, catalyzed by peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4), correlates with chromatin decondensation during NET formation. However, the function of PAD4 in NET-mediated bacterial entrapment and killing has yet to be investigated. To address this, we used PAD4 knockout mice to demonstrate that PAD4 is essential for NET-mediated antibacterial function. Unlike PAD4(+/+) neutrophils, PAD4(-/-) neutrophils are unable to form NETs after stimulation with chemokines or exposure to bacteria, and are impaired in bacterial killing through NETs. In a mouse model of necrotizing fasciitis, PAD4(-/-) mice are more susceptible to bacterial infection than PAD4(+/+) mice due to a lack of NET formation. Additionally, we found that citrullination of histones and nucleosomes decreases their bacterial killing activity, suggesting that PAD4 primarily contributes to chromatin decondensation to form NETs rather than increasing histone-mediated bacterial killing. Our results provide insight into the role of histone hypercitrullination in the innate immune response during bacterial infection.

title: Human ‘brite / beige’ adipocytes develop from capillary networks and their implantation improves metabolic homeostasis in mice
text:
Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) is highly expressed in brown adipose tissue, where it uncouples electron transport from ATP production, generating heat. UCP1 is also found in adipocytes outside classical brown adipose tissue depots, termed "brite" (brown-in-white) or "beige". In humans, the presence of brite or beige adipocytes is associated with a lean, metabolically healthy phenotype, but whether these adipocytes play a causal role is unclear. Here, we investigate the proliferation and differentiation of human brite/beige adipocyte progenitors in response to pro-angiogenic factors, and their impact on systemic glucose homeostasis.
We find that brite/beige adipocyte progenitors proliferate in association with expanding capillary networks, and adipocytes formed from these progenitors display uncoupled respiration. When implanted into normal chow-fed or high-fat diet (HFD)-fed glucose-intolerant NOD-scid IL2rg(null) (NSG) mice, brite/beige adipocytes enhance systemic glucose tolerance. These adipocytes also express neuroendocrine and secreted factors, including the pro-protein convertase PCSK1, which is strongly associated with human obesity.
Our findings suggest that pro-angiogenic conditions drive the proliferation of human beige/brite adipocyte progenitors, and activated beige/brite adipocytes can affect systemic glucose homeostasis through a neuroendocrine mechanism. These findings have important implications for the development of novel therapies for metabolic disorders.

title: Mindfulness meditation and improvement in sleep quality and daytime impairment among older adults with sleep disturbances: a randomized clinical trial.
text:
The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a mindfulness meditation intervention, called Mindful Awareness Practices (MAPs), in improving sleep quality among older adults with moderate sleep disturbances. The study was a randomized controlled trial conducted from January to December 2012 at a medical research center. Participants were randomly assigned to either the MAPs intervention or a sleep hygiene education (SHE) intervention. The MAPs intervention consisted of six weekly sessions of 2 hours each, with assigned homework, while the SHE intervention included a similar number of sessions with a focus on sleep hygiene practices. The primary outcome measure was the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), which was used to assess sleep quality at baseline and post-intervention. Secondary outcomes included measures of insomnia symptoms, depression, anxiety, stress, and fatigue, as well as inflammatory signaling via nuclear factor (NF)-κB.
The results showed that participants in the MAPs group had significant improvements in sleep quality compared to those in the SHE group, as measured by the PSQI. Specifically, the mean PSQI scores were 10.2 (1.7) at baseline and 7.4 (1.9) at post-intervention in the MAPs group, compared to 10.2 (1.8) at baseline and 9.1 (2.0) at post-intervention in the SHE group. The between-group difference in PSQI scores was 1.8 (95% CI, 0.6-2.9), with an effect size of 0.89. The MAPs group also showed significant improvements in secondary outcomes, including insomnia symptoms, depression symptoms, fatigue interference, and fatigue severity, compared to the SHE group. However, no significant differences were observed between the groups for anxiety, stress, or NF-κB. Notably, NF-κB concentrations significantly declined over time in both groups. The study suggests that a community-accessible MAPs intervention may be an effective way to improve sleep quality among older adults with moderate sleep disturbances, and that this effect may carry over into reducing sleep-related daytime impairment, which has implications for quality of life.

title: THE ORIGIN AND DIFFERENTIATION OF MICROGLIAL CELLS DURING DEVELOPMENT
text: Some researchers believe that microglia originate from the neural epithelium, but most now think that these cells are of mesodermal origin and belong to the monocyte/macrophage lineage. During central nervous system (CNS) development, microglial cells enter the CNS from the bloodstream, ventricular space, or meninges. Once inside, they migrate throughout the nervous parenchyma in a stereotyped manner, with long-distance tangential migration occurring before radial migration of individual cells. As they move through the nervous tissue, microglial cells exhibit both ameboid and ramified forms, with ramified cells thought to be the final differentiated state. The factors that control microglial invasion, migration, and differentiation are not well understood, but are believed to involve environmental factors such as soluble or cell-surface bound molecules and components of the extracellular matrix. Microglial cells play important roles in the developing CNS, including clearing cell debris, withdrawing misdirected or transitory axons, and supporting cell survival and neurite growth.

title: Integrin αvβ8-Mediated TGF-β Activation by Effector Regulatory T Cells Is Essential for Suppression of T-Cell-Mediated Inflammation
text: Regulatory T (Treg) cells play a crucial role in preventing self-destructive T cell responses, but the mechanisms by which they maintain immune homeostasis and limit responses during inflammation are not fully understood. In this study, we found that effector Treg cells express high levels of the integrin αvβ8, which allows them to activate latent transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β). Surprisingly, Treg-cell-specific deletion of integrin αvβ8 did not lead to spontaneous inflammation, suggesting that this pathway is not essential for Treg cells to maintain immune homeostasis. However, Treg cells lacking expression of integrin αvβ8 were unable to suppress pathogenic T cell responses during active inflammation, highlighting the importance of this mechanism in suppressing self-destructive T cell responses. Our findings identify a key role for effector Treg-cell-mediated activation of latent TGF-β in the suppression of self-harmful T cell responses during active inflammation.

title: Effects of treatment for intestinal helminth infection on growth and cognitive performance in children: systematic review of randomised trials.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the impact of anthelmintic drug treatment on growth and cognitive performance in children.
Data Sources: Electronic databases including Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group controlled trial register, Cochrane controlled trials register, Embase, and Medline, as well as citations of identified trials and contact with the World Health Organization and field researchers.
Review Methods: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials in children aged 1-16 that compared anthelmintic treatment with placebo or no treatment. Assessment of trial validity and data abstraction conducted independently by two reviewers.
Main Outcome Measures: Growth and cognitive performance.
Results: Thirty randomized controlled trials involving over 15,000 children were identified. The effects of anthelmintic treatment on mean weight were unremarkable, with significant heterogeneity observed across trials. Some positive effects were observed in trials reporting weight change outcomes, including a single dose of any anthelmintic resulting in a pooled estimate of 0.24 kg (95% CI 0.15 kg to 0.32 kg; fixed effects model assumed) and 0.38 kg (0.01 kg to 0.77 kg; random effects model assumed). Trials of multiple doses showed mean weight change of up to one year of follow-up of 0.10 kg (0.04 kg to 0.17 kg; fixed effects) or 0.15 kg (0.00 to 0.30 kg; random effects). At more than one year of follow-up, mean weight change was 0.12 kg (-0.02 kg to 0.26 kg; fixed effects) and 0.43 kg (-0.61 kg to 1.47 kg; random effects). Cognitive performance outcomes were inconclusive.
Conclusions: There is limited evidence to suggest that routine anthelmintic treatment of children in areas where helminths are common has an effect on weight gain, but this is not consistent across trials. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether this intervention improves cognitive performance.

title: Choosing appropriate substitution models for the phylogenetic analysis of protein-coding sequences.
text: Although the majority of phylogenetic inference studies on protein-coding sequences still rely on traditional methods, few analyses have incorporated evolutionary models that consider the genetic code. This oversight is further exacerbated by the exclusion of codon-based models from commonly employed model selection techniques, likely due to the perceived computational cost associated with these models. To address this issue, we investigated an efficient alternative to standard nucleotide substitution models that incorporates codon position (CP). We evaluated the most appropriate model for alignments of 177 RNA virus genes and 106 yeast genes using 11 substitution models, including one codon model and four CP models. Our results show that the majority of analyzed gene alignments are best described by CP substitution models, rather than by standard nucleotide models, and without the significant computational burden of full codon models. These findings have important implications for phylogenetic inference of coding sequences, as they demonstrate that incorporating CPs into substitution models can not only significantly reduce computational costs but may also frequently result in more accurate phylogenetic reconstructions.

title: Polycomb Proteins Remain Bound to Chromatin and DNA during DNA Replication In Vitro
text:
During development, the transcriptional status of a gene can be maintained through multiple rounds of cell division, an epigenetic effect that is believed to reflect heritable changes in chromatin folding and histone modifications or variants at target genes. However, little is known about how these chromatin features are inherited through cell division. A particular challenge for maintaining transcription states is DNA replication, which can disrupt or dilute chromatin-associated proteins and histone modifications.
Polycomb group protein complexes, such as PRC1-class Polycomb complexes, are essential for development and are thought to heritably silence transcription by altering chromatin folding and histone modifications. It is not known whether these complexes and their effects are maintained during DNA replication or subsequently re-established. Interestingly, when PRC1-class Polycomb complex-bound chromatin or DNA is replicated in vitro, Polycomb complexes remain bound to replicated templates. This retention of Polycomb proteins through DNA replication may contribute to the maintenance of transcriptional silencing through cell division.

title: Control of CNS Cell-Fate Decisions by SHP-2 and Its Dysregulation in Noonan Syndrome
text:
Within the developing mammalian central nervous system (CNS), growth factors direct multipotent precursors to differentiate into neurons or glia, a process that can be disrupted leading to neural dysfunction. For instance, genetic mutations that result in the constitutive activation of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2 have been linked to Noonan Syndrome (NS), a disorder characterized by learning disabilities and mental retardation. Here, we investigate the role of SHP-2 in the development of the CNS and its potential contribution to the cognitive impairments in NS patients.
We demonstrate that genetic knockdown of SHP-2 in cultured cortical precursors or in the embryonic cortex inhibits basal neurogenesis and leads to an increase in astrocyte formation. Conversely, expression of an NS-associated SHP-2 mutant promotes neurogenesis and inhibits astrogenesis. Similar results are observed in a mouse knockin model that mimics the human NS phenotype. These findings suggest that SHP-2 instructs precursors to differentiate into neurons rather than astrocytes during the neurogenic period, and alterations in the relative ratios of these two cell types upon constitutive SHP-2 activation may contribute to the cognitive impairments in NS patients.

title: Global Regulation of H2A.Z Localization by the INO80 Chromatin-Remodeling Enzyme Is Essential for Genome Integrity
text: INO80 is an evolutionarily conserved chromatin-remodeling enzyme that plays critical roles in transcription, DNA repair, and replication. Our findings demonstrate that the yeast INO80 protein regulates these diverse processes, at least in part, by controlling the genome-wide distribution of the histone variant H2A.Z. In the absence of INO80, H2A.Z nucleosomes are mislocalized, and H2A.Z levels at promoters exhibit reduced responsiveness to transcriptional changes, suggesting that INO80 controls H2A.Z dynamics. Furthermore, we provide evidence that INO80 possesses a histone-exchange activity, allowing the enzyme to replace nucleosomal H2A.Z/H2B with free H2A/H2B dimers. Additionally, genetic interactions between INO80 and Htz1 support a model in which INO80 catalyzes the removal of unacetylated H2A.Z from chromatin as a mechanism to promote genome stability.

title: Rho GTPase signalling in cell migration
text: Cells migrate through various mechanisms, influenced by their surroundings, including the composition of the extracellular matrix, interactions with other cells, and chemical signals. Rho GTPases are essential for all types of cell migration, although the specific contribution of each Rho GTPase varies depending on the environment and cell type. In this review, I will discuss recent advances in our understanding of how Rho GTPases contribute to different types of migration, comparing lamellipodium-driven versus bleb-driven migration modes. Additionally, I will explore how cells migrate across the endothelium and discuss the roles of other less-well characterized members of the Rho family beyond Rho, Rac, and Cdc42.

title: A Novel Adaptor Protein Orchestrates Receptor Patterning and Cytoskeletal Polarity in T-Cell Contacts
text: The recognition of antigens by T cells involves the formation of a specialized junction between the T cell and the antigen-presenting cell, which is generated by the recruitment and exclusion of specific proteins to the contact area. Despite being crucial, the mechanisms that regulate these events are still unknown. In this study, we investigate the role of the adhesion molecule CD2 in the recognition of antigens by T cells. We demonstrate that the ligand engagement of CD2 initiates a process of protein segregation, CD2 clustering, and cytoskeletal polarization. Interestingly, protein segregation is not dependent on the cytoplasmic domain of CD2, but CD2 clustering and cytoskeletal polarization require an interaction between the CD2 cytoplasmic domain and a novel SH3-containing protein called CD2AP. CD2AP likely facilitates receptor patterning in the contact area by linking specific adhesion receptors to the cytoskeleton, thereby playing a crucial role in the recognition of antigens by T cells.

title: Operable non-small cell lung cancer diagnosed by transpleural techniques : do they affect relapse and prognosis?
text:
Study Objective:
We investigated whether transpleural methods for diagnosing peripheral lung cancer, such as needle aspiration or tumor excision, impact relapse and prognosis, as these techniques have the potential to disseminate malignant cells from the tumor.
Design:
We conducted a retrospective study at a national referral hospital.
Patients:
We reviewed 239 patients who underwent surgery between 1990 and 1998 and had non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) of less than 3 cm in diameter that was completely resected. The duration of postoperative follow-up ranged from 12 to 105 months, with a median period of 45 months.
Interventions:
We categorized the transbronchial method as using a bronchoscope, and the transpleural method as using needle aspiration cytology or tumor excision. Dichotomous variables included gender, histologic type of squamous cell carcinoma or other type of carcinoma, pathologic stage, and whether the diagnostic method was the transbronchial type only (first-line method) or the transpleural type (second-line method).
Results:
Lung cancer was diagnosed in 45 patients using the transpleural technique and 194 patients using the transbronchial technique. There were no significant statistical differences in age, gender, histologic type, pathologic stage, or tumor size between the two groups. There were 42 relapses, with 7 occurring in the transpleural technique group and 35 in the transbronchial technique group (p = 0.90). Of the 7 patients in the transpleural group, there were 4 distant metastases and 3 local relapses, while in the transbronchial group, there were 20 distant metastases and 15 local relapses (p = 0.99). Pleural carcinomatosis occurred in none of the 45 patients in the transpleural group and in 1 case (0.5%) in the 194 patients in the transbronchial group (p = 0.99). Patients in the transpleural group had a statistically better 5-year survival rate than patients in the transbronchial group (79.4% vs 60.3%, p = 0.04). This finding was also confirmed as an independent prognostic factor in a multivariate analysis.
Conclusions:
Our study suggests that transpleural methods may be a suitable approach for diagnosing operable lung cancer that is difficult to diagnose using bronchoscopy, as these methods did not affect relapse and prognosis in the patients in our study.

title: Characterization of the adipocyte cellular lineage in vivo
text: Mature adipocytes are generated through the proliferation and differentiation of precursor cells. Previous studies conducted by our research group have identified adipocyte progenitors in white adipose tissue (WAT) as Lin(-):CD29(+):CD34(+):Sca-1(+):CD24(+) (CD24(+)) cells, which are capable of generating functional WAT (reference). In this study, we employ several Cre recombinase mouse models to investigate the adipocyte cellular lineage in vivo. While it has been proposed that white adipocytes originate from endothelial and haematopoietic lineages, our findings indicate that neither of these lineages label white adipocytes. However, platelet-derived growth factor receptor α (PdgfRα)-Cre tracing labels all white adipocytes. Analysis of WAT from PdgfRα-Cre reporter mice reveals CD24(+) and Lin(-):CD29(+):CD34(+):Sca-1(+):CD24(-) (CD24(-)) cells as adipocyte precursors. Our results show that CD24(+) cells give rise to the CD24(-) population in vivo, and the CD24(-) cells express late markers of adipogenesis. Based on these findings, we propose a model where CD24(+) adipocyte progenitors undergo further commitment to the adipocyte lineage, resulting in the loss of CD24 expression and the generation of CD24(-) preadipocytes. This characterization of the adipocyte cellular lineage will facilitate the study of the mechanisms that regulate WAT formation in vivo and WAT mass expansion in obesity.

title: Reducing Plasmodium falciparum Malaria Transmission in Africa: A Model-Based Evaluation of Intervention Strategies
text: Over the past decade, there has been a significant scale-up of malaria interventions across Africa. However, it remains unclear what level of reduction in transmission is achievable using currently available tools. To address this question, we developed a simulation model that accounts for the three major vector species in Africa (Anopheles gambiae s.s., An. arabiensis, and An. funestus) and incorporated the impact of artemisinin-combination therapy (ACT) and long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) from 2000 onwards. We then explored the impact of continued roll-out of LLINs, additional rounds of indoor residual spraying (IRS), mass screening and treatment (MSAT), and a future RTS,S/AS01 vaccine in six representative settings with varying transmission intensity, vector-species combinations, and patterns of seasonality. Our findings suggest that interventions using current tools can result in major reductions in Plasmodium falciparum malaria transmission and the associated disease burden in Africa. In low- to moderate-transmission settings where vectors are primarily endophilic, a comprehensive and sustained intervention program can lead to reductions in parasite prevalence below a 1% threshold. However, in high-transmission settings and those with exophilic vectors, additional new tools will be required to achieve this level of reduction. Our findings highlight the need for continued investment in malaria control efforts and the development of new tools to combat this persistent disease.

title: Golgi Export of the Kir2.1 Channel Is Driven by a Trafficking Signal Located within Its Tertiary Structure
text: The mechanisms by which newly synthesized proteins are directed to the cell surface from the Golgi apparatus are not well understood. In this study, we investigate the transport of the potassium channel Kir2.1 from the Golgi to the cell surface. We find that Kir2.1 is selected as cargo into Golgi export carriers in an unusual manner, dependent on specific residues within the protein's tertiary structure. These residues form a recognition site for interaction with the AP1 adaptor complex, which marks Kir2.1 for incorporation into clathrin-coated vesicles at the trans-Golgi. The identification of a trafficking signal in the tertiary structure of Kir2.1 reveals a quality control step that links protein conformation to Golgi export, providing insight into how mutations in Kir2.1 can lead to the arrest of channels at the Golgi.

title: Characteristics of Body Fat, Body Fat Percentage and Other Body Composition for Koreans from KNHANES IV
text: The accurate measurement of body fat mass has become increasingly crucial due to the rising prevalence of obesity. In this study, we utilized dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry to assess body composition in a sample of 10,456 individuals aged 20-85 years (4,476 men and 5,980 women) from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey IV (KNHANES IV). Reference values for body composition were obtained using the LMS method. We found that the fat mass index (FMI, body fat mass/height(2); kg/m(2)) of Korean men did not exhibit a significant correlation with age (P = 0.452), whereas the ratio of percentage of fat in the trunk and legs was positively related to age in both genders. In contrast, the appendicular lean mass/height(2) (kg/m(2)) of Korean men showed a negative correlation with age (P < 0.001). In contrast, the ratio of appendicular lean mass/height(2) in women increased with age (P < 0.001). When we defined obesity based on the FMI classification, the rates of obesity were 6.1% (FMI > 9 kg/m(2)) in men and 2.7% (FMI > 13 kg/m(2)) in women. Our findings suggest that muscle mass decreases and obesity increases with aging in Korean men, whereas both fat mass and obesity increase with aging in Korean women.

title: The Evolution of Dominance in Sporophytic Self-Incompatibility Systems. II. Mate Availability and Recombination
text: Sporophytic self-incompatibility (SSI) is a self-pollen recognition system that promotes outcrossing in plants. In SSI systems, recognition is typically controlled by a complex locus (5-locus) with separate genes determining pollen and stigma specificity. The dominance level of an S-allele can vary depending on whether pollen or stigma specificity is examined, and can be dominant, recessive, or codominant. In this study, the evolution of dominance in single-locus SSI is explored using numerical models and simulation. The models suggest that limitation in the number of compatible mates is required for the evolution of S-allele dominance in the stigma, but not in the pollen. Additionally, tight linkage between the S-locus and modifier locus promotes the evolution of S-allele dominance hierarchies. The models are interpreted with respect to published information on the molecular basis of dominance in SSI systems and reported S-allele dominance relationships in various species. These studies indicate that dominant S-alleles are more common in the pollen than in the stigma, which may suggest that mate limitation is relatively infrequent in natural populations with SSI.

title: Neurological outcomes of animal models of uterine artery ligation and relevance to human intrauterine growth restriction: a systematic review
text:
This review investigates the molecular, neurological, and behavioral outcomes in animal models of uterine artery ligation. We analyze the similarity of these outcomes to the pathological and functional phenotypes found in cerebral palsy and its associated developmental disorders in humans.
METHODS:
We conducted a literature search of the PubMed database for studies published between 1990 and 2013 that used the uterine artery ligation model. From the included studies, we summarized and analyzed the relevant neuroanatomical and behavioral deficits.
RESULTS:
Our review included 25 studies, and we found several significant outcomes. Fetuses with growth restriction exhibited a gradient of reduced body weight, with sparing of brain mass. The somatosensory cortex, hippocampus, and corpus callosum were significantly reduced in size. The motor cortex appeared to be spared of identifiable deficits. Upregulation of apoptotic proteins and downregulation of proteins important to neuronal survival, growth, and differentiation were observed. Neuronal apoptosis and astrogliosis occurred throughout the brain regions, and white matter injury involved oligodendrocyte precursor maturation arrest, hypomyelination, and aberrant myelin organization. Animals with growth restriction displayed deficits in gait, memory, object recognition, and spatial processing.
INTERPRETATION:
Our findings suggest that uterine artery ligation in animal models leads to neuronal death, white matter injury, motor abnormalities, and cognitive deficits, which are similar to the deficits found in human cerebral palsy. Therefore, this animal model is clinically relevant and can help us understand the underlying pathophysiology of cerebral palsy.

title: The fidelity of the ligation step determines how ends are resolved during Nonhomologous end joining
text: Nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) is a crucial mechanism for repairing chromosomal breaks, despite the diverse structures of the ends involved. However, the exact steps employed by NHEJ to resolve these breaks are not well understood. To address this question, we investigated the cellular NHEJ of ends with systematically mispaired and damaged termini. Our findings reveal that NHEJ is highly proficient at bypassing subtle terminal mispairs and radiomimetic damage through direct ligation. However, the ability of NHEJ to bypass these structures varies widely, with a gradual reduction in bypass products from 85% to 6% as the severity of the mispair increases. Notably, end processing by nucleases and polymerases is increased to compensate for the reduced bypass efficiency, with the pathways that require the fewest number of steps to generate a suitable substrate for ligation being favored. This suggests that both the frequency and nature of end processing are tailored to meet the demands of the ligation step. Based on our findings, we propose a model where the ligase organizes all the steps involved in NHEJ within a stable paired-end complex to limit end processing and associated errors.

title: Laminin-based cell adhesion anchors microtubule plus ends to the epithelial cell basal cortex through LL5α/β
text: LL5beta has been identified as a microtubule-anchoring factor that attaches EB1/CLIP-associating protein (CLASP)-bound microtubule plus ends to the cell cortex. In this study, we demonstrate that LL5beta and its homologue LL5alpha (LL5s) co-localize with autocrine laminin-5 and its receptors, integrins alpha3beta1 and alpha6beta4, at the basal side of fully polarized epithelial sheets. Depletion of both laminin receptor integrins abolishes the cortical localization of LL5s, whereas LL5 depletion reduces the amount of integrin alpha3 at the basal cell cortex. Activation of integrin alpha3 is sufficient to initiate LL5 accumulation at the cell cortex. LL5s form a complex with the cytoplasmic tails of these integrins, although the nature of their interaction may be indirect. Analysis of the three-dimensional distribution of microtubule growth by visualizing EB1-GFP in epithelial sheets in combination with RNA interference reveals that LL5s are essential for maintaining the density of growing microtubules selectively at the basal cortex. These findings demonstrate that signaling from laminin-integrin associations attaches microtubule plus ends to the epithelial basal cell cortex.

title: DNA topoisomerases: structure, function, and mechanism.
text: DNA topoisomerases address the topological challenges associated with DNA replication, transcription, recombination, and chromatin remodeling by introducing temporary single- or double-strand breaks in the DNA. In addition, these enzymes fine-tune the steady-state level of DNA supercoiling to facilitate protein interactions with the DNA and prevent excessive supercoiling, which is detrimental. Recent crystal structures of topoisomerase fragments from various classes of enzymes have provided valuable insights into their mechanisms, complementing previous conclusions based on biochemical analyses. Surprisingly, despite limited sequence homology, the structural folds of type IA and type IIA topoisomerases from prokaryotes and type IIA enzymes from eukaryotes share functional motifs in critical regions of the enzymes. The structurally distinct type IB enzymes are similar to a class of enzymes known as tyrosine recombinases. Common structural themes among topoisomerases include hinged clamps that open and close to bind DNA, DNA binding cavities for temporary storage of DNA segments, and the coupling of protein conformational changes to DNA rotation or DNA movement. For type II topoisomerases, the binding and hydrolysis of ATP modulate conformational changes in the enzymes to affect changes in DNA topology.

title: Pilot testing of dipsticks as point-of-care assays for rapid diagnosis of poor-quality artemisinin drugs in endemic settings
text: Background: High-quality artemisinin drugs are crucial for the effective management of malaria cases, yet the increasing prevalence of low-quality counterfeit drugs in many endemic regions poses a significant challenge to malaria treatment. To address this issue, we developed a point-of-care assay for the rapid identification of counterfeit and substandard artemisinin drugs in resource-limited areas. Methods: We employed specific monoclonal antibodies against artemether and artesunate to create prototypes of lateral flow dipstick assays. In this pilot study, we evaluated the feasibility of these dipsticks under various endemic settings and their performance when used by untrained personnel. Results: Our findings demonstrated that the dipstick tests can be successfully performed by different investigators with the provided instruction sheet. None of the artemether and artesunate drugs collected from public pharmacies in different endemic countries failed the test. Conclusion: It is conceivable that the simple dipstick assays, with potential future optimization of test conditions and sensitivity, could serve as a qualitative and semi-quantitative screening tool for rapid detection of counterfeit artemisinin drugs in endemic regions.

title: Increased Microerythrocyte Count in Homozygous α+-Thalassaemia Contributes to Protection against Severe Malarial Anaemia
text:
The hereditary hemoglobinopathy alpha(+)-thalassemia is caused by a reduced synthesis of alpha-globin chains, which are essential for normal adult hemoglobin (Hb). Individuals who are homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia have microcytosis and an increased red blood cell count. This genetic condition provides significant protection against severe malaria, including severe malarial anemia (SMA), characterized by a hemoglobin concentration of less than 50 grams per liter. However, it does not affect the number of parasites in the blood.
We reanalyzed data from children living on the north coast of Papua New Guinea who participated in a case-control study to determine whether the erythrocyte indices associated with alpha(+)-thalassemia homozygosity provide a hematological benefit during acute malaria. We found that children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia have a reduction in median red blood cell count of approximately 1.5 x 10^12 cells/L during acute falciparum malaria compared to values in community children (p < 0.001). We developed a simple mathematical model that predicts that children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia lose less hemoglobin than children of normal genotype for a reduction in red blood cell count of >1.1 x 10^12 cells/L due to the reduced mean cell hemoglobin in homozygous alpha(+)-thalassemia. In addition, children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia require a 10% greater reduction in red blood cell count than children of normal genotype (p = 0.02) for hemoglobin concentration to fall to 50 grams per liter, the cutoff for SMA. We estimated that the hematological profile in children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia reduces the risk of SMA during acute malaria compared to children of normal genotype (relative risk 0.52; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24-1.12, p = 0.09).
Our findings suggest that the increased red blood cell count and microcytosis in children homozygous for alpha(+)-thalassemia may contribute significantly to their protection against SMA. A lower concentration of hemoglobin per red blood cell and a larger population of red blood cells may be a biologically advantageous strategy against the significant reduction in red blood cell count that occurs during acute infection with the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. This hematological profile may reduce the risk of anemia by other Plasmodium species, as well as other causes of anemia. Other host polymorphisms that induce an increased red blood cell count and microcytosis may confer a similar advantage.

title: Construction of Escherichia coli K-12 in-frame, single-gene knockout mutants: the Keio collection
text: We have systematically deleted all non-essential genes in Escherichia coli K-12 using a precise, one-step method involving the replacement of open-reading frame coding regions with a kanamycin cassette flanked by FLP recognition target sites. This resulted in the inactivation of 4288 genes, of which 3985 were successfully mutated. To address issues encountered in high-throughput studies, we generated two independent mutants for every deleted gene, which we have collectively termed the 'Keio collection'. This resource provides a valuable tool not only for investigating unknown gene functions and gene regulatory networks but also for genome-wide testing of mutational effects in a standardized E. coli K-12 background. Unfortunately, we were unable to disrupt 303 genes, including 37 of unknown function, which are now identified as potential essential genes. The Keio collection is available for distribution through GenoBase (http://ecoli.aist-nara.ac.jp/).

title: Validated RealTime reverse transcriptase PCR methods for the diagnosis and pathotyping of Eurasian H7 avian influenza viruses
text:
Avian influenza (AI) caused by H7 AI viruses (AIVs) of both low pathogenicity (LP) and high pathogenicity (HP) are notifiable poultry diseases. The objective of this study was to design and validate two Real-Time reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reactions (RRT PCRs) for the detection and pathotyping of Eurasian H7 AIVs.
The study used two RRT PCRs that amplified the HA2 and cleavage site CS (CS) regions of the haemagglutinin gene. The RRT PCRs were validated against 65 H7 AIVs, 57 non-H7 AIVs, and 259 poultry swabs, as well as against the M gene (AI generic) RRT PCR and virus isolation (VI). An additional 38 swabs and 20 tissue specimens were used to extend the validation of the M gene RRT PCR.
The results showed that both H7 RRT PCRs amplified all 61 Eurasian lineage H7 AIVs, but none of the 57 non-H7 AIVs. The sensitivity and specificity of the H7 HA2 RRT PCR were 95.4% and 64.6%, respectively, while the specificity was 97.9% and 99.6% for the H7 CS RRT PCR. The H7 HA2 RRT PCR was more sensitive than virus isolation, while the H7 CS RRT PCR provided an opportunity for rapid pathotyping of H7 AIVs.
In conclusion, the high sensitivity of the H7 HA2 RRT PCR makes it suitable for use in poultry surveillance and disease diagnosis. The H7 CS RRT PCR provides an opportunity for rapid pathotyping of H7 AIVs.

title: Interleukin-6 receptor pathways in coronary heart disease: a collaborative meta-analysis of 82 studies
text:
Background: Persistent inflammation has been implicated in the development and progression of cardiovascular disease. The interleukin-6 receptor (IL6R) signaling pathway is a key player in the inflammatory response, and genetic variations in this pathway have been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. To investigate the potential causal relationship between IL6R-related pathways and coronary heart disease, we conducted a large-scale genetic and biomarker analysis.
Methods: We performed a collaborative meta-analysis of 125,222 participants, including 51,441 cases with coronary heart disease and 136,226 controls. We genotyped the Asp358Ala (rs2228145) variant in the IL6R gene and assessed its association with a panel of conventional risk factors and inflammation biomarkers. We also evaluated the effect of the Asp358Ala variant on localized gene expression and postlipopolysaccharide stimulation of interleukin 6.
Findings: Our results showed that the minor allele frequency of Asp358Ala was 39%. However, we found no significant associations between the Asp358Ala variant and lipid concentrations, blood pressure, adiposity, dysglycaemia, or smoking. In contrast, the presence of one or more copies of the Asp358Ala allele was associated with increased mean concentrations of IL6R and interleukin 6, as well as reduced mean concentrations of C-reactive protein and fibrinogen. Additionally, we observed a 3.4% reduction in the risk of coronary heart disease for every copy of the Asp358Ala allele inherited. We did not observe any significant relationships between the Asp358Ala variant and IL6R mRNA levels or interleukin-6 production in monocytes.
Interpretation: Our findings provide evidence for a causal association between IL6R-related pathways and coronary heart disease. The large-scale human genetic and biomarker data suggest that genetic variations in the IL6R pathway may play a key role in the development and progression of cardiovascular disease. Funding: The study was supported by the British Heart Foundation, UK Medical Research Council, UK National Institute of Health Research, Cambridge Biomedical Research Centre, and BUPA Foundation.

title: Plasma exosomes can deliver exogenous short interfering RNA to monocytes and lymphocytes
text: Despite the promise of RNA interference (RNAi) in various therapeutic applications, including cancer treatment, several technical challenges must be addressed first. One of the major hurdles is delivering nucleic acids across the cell membrane. This study demonstrates that exosome vesicles derived from human cells can effectively deliver short interfering RNA (siRNA) to human mononuclear blood cells. Exosomes are small, endocytic vesicles involved in cell-to-cell communication, including antigen presentation, tolerance development, and RNA transport. The study tested different methods for introducing siRNA into exosomes and optimized the process using electroporation. Plasma exosomes (exosomes from peripheral blood) were used as a gene delivery vector (GDV) to transport exogenous siRNA to human blood cells. The results showed that the vesicles effectively delivered the administered siRNA into monocytes and lymphocytes, leading to selective gene silencing of mitogen-activated protein kinase 1. These findings suggest that human exosomes can be used as a GDV to deliver therapeutic siRNAs to cells.

title: Quantitative analysis of tumor-derived methylated p16INK4a sequences in plasma, serum, and blood cells of hepatocellular carcinoma patients.
text:
PURPOSE AND EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the clinical usefulness and effectiveness of real-time quantitative methylation-specific PCR (RTQ-MSP) for detecting and monitoring hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) after treatment using peripheral blood samples. RTQ-MSP was used to quantify methylated p16INK4a sequences in plasma, serum, and peripheral blood cells collected from 49 HCC patients preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively.
RESULTS:
The results of the study demonstrated the sensitivity of RTQ-MSP in detecting methylated p16INK4a sequences in peripheral blood, with the ability to detect down to 10 genome-equivalents of methylated p16INK4a sequences. Quantitative MSP data were expressed as the methylation index, which was the percentage of bisulfite converted unmethylated and methylated p16INK4a sequences that consisted of methylated p16INK4a sequences. The study found that methylated p16INK4a sequences were present in the peripheral circulation of 80% (23 of 29) of HCC patients. No significant difference was seen in the detectability and concentrations of methylated p16INK4a sequences between preoperative plasma and serum samples from HCC patients. Preoperatively, the p16INK4a methylation indices ranged from 0.2 to 100% and from 0.012 to 0.075% in the patients' plasma and buffy coat samples, respectively. After surgical resection, the median p16INK4a methylation indices in plasma and buffy coat concordantly decreased 12- and 15-fold, respectively. These results demonstrated the clinical usefulness and effectiveness of peripheral blood RTQ-MSP for detecting and monitoring HCC after treatment. Furthermore, none of the intraoperative plasma samples and only two of the intraoperative buffy coat samples were p16INK4a methylation positive.
CONCLUSIONS:
The study concluded that quantification of epigenetic changes in peripheral blood by RTQ-MSP is useful for the detection and monitoring of HCC. The results suggest that RTQ-MSP may be a valuable tool for non-invasive monitoring of HCC after treatment, and may help to identify patients who are at high risk of recurrence.

title: Dynamic control of excitatory synapse development by a Rac1 GEF/GAP regulatory complex.
text: The small GTPase Rac1 plays a crucial role in orchestrating actin-dependent remodeling, which is essential for various cellular processes, including synapse development. However, the mechanisms that govern the regulation of Rac1 signaling remain poorly understood. Specifically, little is known about the interactions between Rac1 activators (GEFs) and inhibitors (GAPs) that control Rac1 activity. To address this knowledge gap, we identified a regulatory complex composed of a Rac-GEF (Tiam1) and a Rac-GAP (Bcr) that collaborate to regulate excitatory synapse development. Our findings reveal that disruption of Bcr function within this complex leads to increased Rac1 activity and dendritic spine remodeling, resulting in excessive synaptic growth that can be rescued by Tiam1 inhibition. Notably, EphB receptors utilize the Tiam1-Bcr complex to control synaptogenesis, with Tiam1 inducing Rac1-dependent spine formation, while Bcr prevents Rac1-mediated receptor internalization, thereby promoting spine growth over retraction. Our findings highlight the importance of a Rac-specific GEF/GAP complex in maintaining optimal levels of Rac1 signaling, providing valuable insights into the regulation of small GTPases.

title: 4-1BB Costimulation Ameliorates T Cell Exhaustion Induced by Tonic Signaling of Chimeric Antigen Receptors
text: Chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) targeting CD19 have demonstrated remarkable antitumor responses in hematologic malignancies, with tumor regression occurring infrequently when CARs target other antigens. The reasons for this discrepancy are unclear, whether it be due to the greater susceptibility of hematologic malignancies to CAR therapies or the superior functionality of the CD19 CAR itself. Our findings indicate that tonic CD3-ζ phosphorylation, triggered by antigen-independent clustering of CAR single-chain variable fragments, can lead to early exhaustion of CAR T cells, which limits their antitumor efficacy. This activation is observed in all CARs studied, except for the highly effective CD19 CAR. Additionally, we determine that CD28 costimulation enhances, while 4-1BB costimulation reduces, exhaustion induced by persistent CAR signaling. These results provide biological insights into the antitumor effects of CD19 CARs and the observations that CD19 CAR T cells incorporating the 4-1BB costimulatory domain are more persistent in clinical trials.

title: Ultrafast Evolution and Loss of CRISPRs Following a Host Shift in a Novel Wildlife Pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum
text: Measurable rates of genome evolution are well-documented in human pathogens, but less is understood about bacterial pathogens in the wild, particularly during and after host switches. Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG), a pathogenic bacterium, has evolved primarily in poultry and recently jumped to wild house finches (Carpodacus mexicanus), a common North American songbird. For the first time, we have characterized the genome and measured rates of genome evolution in House Finch isolates of MG, as well as in poultry outgroups. Using whole-genome sequences of 12 House Finch isolates across a 13-year serial sample and an additional four newly sequenced poultry strains, we estimate a nucleotide diversity in House Finch isolates of only approximately 2% of the ancestral poultry strains and a nucleotide substitution rate of 0.8-1.2 x 10^-5 per site per year in both poultry and House Finches, which is an exceptionally fast rate comparable to some of the highest estimates reported for bacteria. We also found high diversity and complete turnover of CRISPR arrays in poultry MG strains prior to the switch to the House Finch host, but after the invasion of House Finches, there is progressive loss of CRISPR repeat diversity, and recruitment of novel CRISPR repeats ceases. Recent (2007) House Finch MG strains retain only approximately 50% of the CRISPR repertoire found in (1994-1995) strains and have lost the CRISPR-associated genes required for CRISPR function. Our results suggest that genome evolution in bacterial pathogens of wild birds can be extremely rapid and is often accompanied by the apparent loss of CRISPR function.

title: Inducing Tumor Immunity through the Selective Engagement of Activating Fcγ Receptors on Dendritic Cells
text: The process of inducing tumor-specific immunity relies on the efficient capture and presentation of tumor antigens by dendritic cells (DCs), leading to the expansion and activation of tumor-specific cytotoxic T cells. However, this process requires a maturation signal, which can be lacking in the absence of tolerance. While immune complexes (ICs) can enhance antigen capture, they often fail to induce DC maturation, naive T cell activation, and protective immunity. We have found that interfering with the inhibitory signal delivered by FcγRIIB on DCs converts ICs into potent maturation agents, leading to T cell activation. By using this approach in combination with immunization with DCs pulsed ex-vivo with ICs, we have generated antigen-specific CD8+ T cells in vivo and achieved efficient protective immunity in a murine melanoma model. These findings suggest that ICs may normally function to maintain tolerance through the binding to inhibitory FcγRs on DCs, but they can be converted to potent immunogenic stimuli by selective engagement of activating FcγRs. This mechanism provides a novel approach to the development of tumor vaccines.

title: Homocysteine and the risk of ischemic stroke in a triethnic cohort: the NOrthern MAnhattan Study.
text:
Background and Purpose:
The exact level of total homocysteine (tHcy) that increases the risk of ischemic stroke is still unknown, and no large-scale prospective studies have included sufficient elderly minority subjects. To investigate the association between mild to moderate fasting tHcy levels and the incidence of ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and vascular death, we conducted a multiethnic prospective study.
Methods:
We followed a population-based cohort of 2939 subjects (mean age 69 ± 10 years; 61% women, 53% Hispanics, 24% blacks, and 20% whites) for vascular events (stroke, myocardial infarction, and vascular death) over time. Baseline measurements of tHcy and methylmalonic acid were taken among the subjects. Using Cox proportional models, we calculated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between tHcy categories and vascular events after adjusting for age, race, education, renal insufficiency, B12 deficiency, and other risk factors.
Results:
Our adjusted HR for a tHcy level of ≥15 micromol/L compared to <10 micromol/L was highest for vascular death (HR = 6.04; 95% CI, 3.44 to 10.60), followed by combined vascular events (HR = 2.27; 95% CI, 1.51 to 3.43), ischemic stroke (HR = 2.01; 95% CI, 1.00 to 4.05), and nonvascular death (HR = 2.02; 95% CI, 1.31 to 3.14). Mild to moderate elevations of tHcy of 10 to 15 micromol/L were not significantly predictive of ischemic stroke, but increased the risk of vascular death (HR = 2.27; 95% CI, 1.44 to 3.60) and combined vascular events (HR = 1.42; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.88). The effect of tHcy was stronger among whites and Hispanics, but not a significant risk factor for blacks.
Conclusions:
Total Hcy elevations above 15 micromol/L are an independent risk factor for ischemic stroke, whereas mild elevations of tHcy of 10 to 15 micromol/L are less predictive. The vascular effects of tHcy are greatest among whites and Hispanics, and less among blacks.

title: Expression and purification of recombinant methylated HBHA in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
text: The Heparin-Binding Haemagglutinin (HBHA) is a mycobacterial adhesin involved in the dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from the site of primary infection and a potential candidate for the development of a new vaccine against tuberculosis. A novel post-translational modification, methylation, confers important immunological properties to HBHA. To investigate the possibility of producing recombinant methylated HBHA in fast-growing mycobacteria for use in immunological and biochemical studies, we cloned the complete coding sequence of HBHA in the plasmid pMV206 under the control of a strong promoter (hsp60) or its own promoter. The constructs were electroporated into Mycobacterium smegmatis and the recombinant strains were analyzed for the presence of the HBHA protein using monoclonal antibodies D2 and E4. Our results showed that high levels of intact protein expression can be toxic to the mycobacteria, and that methylated HBHA can only be obtained in M. smegmatis using a weaker promoter sequence. Additionally, the expression of the complete structural gene is required to obtain methylated HBHA. To overcome these limitations, we constructed a recombinant M. smegmatis strain (pMV3-38) that expresses a histidine-tagged methylated HBHA that can be easily purified. This strategy should be effective for evaluating a new HBHA-based vaccine candidate for tuberculosis.

title: Detection of alternative lengthening of telomeres by telomere quantitative PCR
text: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is one of the two well-established mechanisms of telomere length maintenance that are crucial for the unlimited proliferative potential of cancer cells. However, existing methods for detecting ALT in tumors are time-consuming and labor-intensive, hindering the study of the prevalence and prognostic significance of ALT in large tumor cohorts. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel diagnostic strategy based on telomere quantitative PCR, which enables the rapid detection of ALT in tumors with minimal requirements for tumor material. This protocol simultaneously assesses two key characteristics of ALT cells: their exceptionally long telomeres and the presence of C-circles (partially double-stranded circles of telomeric C-strand DNA). By requiring only 30 ng of genomic DNA, this approach will facilitate large-scale investigations of ALT in tumors and can be easily adapted by clinical laboratories.

title: Noise and interlocking signaling pathways promote distinct transcription factor dynamics in response to different stresses
text: All cells have complex networks that detect and respond to environmental stresses. Yeast cells use diverse signaling pathways to sense stress, which ultimately lead to the activation of transcription factors Msn2 and Msn4. To better understand the role of Msn2/4's nuclear dynamics, we combined time-lapse imaging of Msn2-GFP in living cells with computational modeling of stress-sensing networks. Our findings reveal that various signaling pathways, including Ras/protein kinase A, AMP-activated kinase, the high-osmolarity response mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway, and protein phosphatase 1, regulate Msn2 activation in different ways in response to different stresses. Additionally, we discovered that brief periods of nuclear localization lead to a more robust transcriptional response compared to sustained nuclear localization. Using stochastic modeling, we replicated the responses of Msn2 to different stresses and found that the noise in the signaling pathways, amplified by the limited number of Msn2 molecules in the cell, gives rise to bursts of nuclear localization. This noise allows genetically identical cells to respond differently to environmental cues, enabling them to adapt to an uncertain future and balance growth and survival in an unpredictable environment.

title: Long-term financing needs for HIV control in sub-Saharan Africa in 2015-2050: a modelling study.
text:
Objectives:
To estimate the current and future funding required for HIV treatment and prevention in 9 sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries, which account for 70% of the HIV burden in Africa, under different scenarios of intervention scale-up.
To analyze the gaps between current expenditures and funding obligations and discuss the policy implications of future financing needs.

Design:
We used the Goals module from Spectrum to provide a range of estimates for future financing obligations, using the most up-to-date cost and coverage data. Four different scale-up scenarios were applied, varying by treatment initiation threshold and service coverage level. The model projections were compared to current domestic and international financial sources available in selected SSA countries.
Results:
The estimated resources required for HIV prevention and treatment in 2015-2050 for the 9 SSA countries range from US$98 billion to maintain current coverage levels for treatment and prevention with eligibility for treatment initiation at CD4 count of <500/mm(3) to US$261 billion if treatment were to be extended to all HIV-positive individuals and prevention scaled up. With the addition of new funding obligations for HIV, which arise implicitly through commitment to achieve higher than current treatment coverage levels, overall financial obligations (sum of debt levels and the present value of the stock of future HIV funding obligations) would rise substantially.
Conclusions:
Investing upfront in the scale-up of HIV services to achieve high coverage levels will reduce HIV incidence, prevention, and future treatment expenditures by realizing long-term preventive effects of ART to reduce HIV transmission. Future obligations are too substantial for most SSA countries to be met from domestic sources alone. New sources of funding, in addition to domestic sources, include innovative financing. Debt sustainability for sustained HIV response is an urgent imperative for affected countries and donors.

title: Cell-mediated immunity and antibody responses elicited by attenuated Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhi strains used as live oral vaccines in humans.
text: The urgent need for improved typhoid vaccines is hindered by a lack of understanding about the specific factors that contribute to immunity against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) infections in humans. Although antibodies to S. Typhi O, H, and Vi are believed to play a role in protection, it is unclear whether these antibodies act alone or in conjunction with other immune responses, such as cell-mediated immunity (CMI). CMI responses induced by oral vaccines in humans include the production of type 1 cytokines (e.g., interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha), lymphoproliferation, and CD8(+) cytotoxic T cell responses restricted by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class Ia and nonclassical MHC class Ib (HLA-E) molecules. In summary, the immune response to S. Typhi vaccination is surprisingly complex and multifaceted, but the specific immune mechanisms that confer protection remain poorly understood.

title: Extensive Promoter-Centered Chromatin Interactions Provide a Topological Basis for Transcription Regulation
text: Higher-order chromosomal organization for transcription regulation remains poorly understood in eukaryotes, despite significant progress in the field. To address this knowledge gap, we employed genome-wide Chromatin Interaction Analysis with Paired-End-Tag sequencing (ChIA-PET) to map long-range chromatin interactions associated with RNA polymerase II in human cells. Our findings revealed a wealth of previously unappreciated interactions between promoters, including intragenic, extragenic, and intergenic interactions. These interactions were further organized into higher-order clusters, where proximal and distal genes were connected through promoter-promoter interactions. Most genes with promoter-promoter interactions were found to be actively transcribed and cooperatively regulated, suggesting a combinatorial complexity in transcriptional control. Comparative analyses of different cell lines revealed that cell-specific chromatin interactions could provide structural frameworks for cell-specific transcription, and enrichment of enhancer-promoter interactions was observed for cell-specific functions. Additionally, genetically-identified disease-associated noncoding elements were found to be spatially engaged with corresponding genes through long-range interactions. Overall, our study provides new insights into transcription regulation by three-dimensional chromatin interactions for both housekeeping and cell-specific genes in human cells.

title: Resazurin microtiter assay plate: simple and inexpensive method for detection of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
text: A novel method for detecting multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis is presented, which involves measuring the reduction of resazurin. Eighty clinical isolates were tested against isoniazid and rifampin, and the results at 7 days were compared to those of the proportion method. The method showed excellent specificity and sensitivity. Additionally, it is simple, cost-effective, and quick, and could potentially be used to detect resistance to other antituberculosis drugs.

title: The pervasiveness and plasticity of circadian oscillations: the coupled circadian-oscillators framework.
text:
MOTIVATION: Circadian oscillations have been observed in various biological systems, including animals, plants, fungi, and cyanobacteria, and play a crucial role in regulating the homeostasis and behavior of these systems. Genetically encoded molecular clocks, which are based on negative transcription/translation feedback loops and involve only a small number of genes, are central to maintaining these oscillations. However, high-throughput gene expression experiments have revealed that a much larger fraction of transcripts in a typical tissue oscillate with the day-night cycle, and the oscillating species vary across tissue types, suggesting that a larger fraction of transcripts and potentially other molecular species may exhibit circadian oscillations.
RESULTS: To quantify the pervasiveness and plasticity of circadian oscillations, we conducted a large-scale analysis of 18 circadian transcriptomic studies and 10 circadian metabolomic studies conducted in mice using different tissues and conditions. Our findings indicate that over half of protein-coding genes in the cell can produce transcripts that exhibit circadian oscillations in at least one set of conditions, and similar results were observed for measured metabolites. Genetic or environmental perturbations can disrupt existing oscillations by altering their amplitudes and phases, suppressing them, or giving rise to novel circadian oscillations. The oscillating species and their oscillations provide a characteristic signature of the physiological state of the corresponding cell/tissue. Molecular networks comprise many oscillator loops that have been shaped by evolution over two trillion day-night cycles to have an intrinsic circadian frequency. These oscillating loops are connected by shared nodes in a large network of coupled circadian oscillators, with the clock genes forming a major hub. Cells can program and reprogram their circadian repertoire through epigenetic and other mechanisms.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: High-resolution and tissue/condition-specific circadian data and networks are available at http://circadiomics.igb.uci.edu. For more information, please contact pfbaldi@ics.uci.edu.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Gene–environment interactions in 7610 women with breast cancer: prospective evidence from the Million Women Study
text:
Background: Limited information is available on the combined effects of low-penetrance genetic susceptibility polymorphisms and environmental factors on breast cancer incidence. To investigate potential gene-environment interactions, we analyzed the effects of 12 polymorphisms in relation to prospectively collected information on 10 established environmental risk factors in a large UK prospective study.
Methods: We genotyped 7610 breast cancer cases and 10,196 controls for 12 polymorphisms (FGFR2-rs2981582, TNRC9-rs3803662, 2q35-rs13387042, MAP3K1-rs889312, 8q24-rs13281615, 2p-rs4666451, 5p12-rs981782, CASP8-rs1045485, LSP1-rs3817198, 5q-rs30099, TGFB1-rs1982073, and ATM-rs1800054) and compared genotypic relative risks across the environmental risk factors.
Results: After multiple testing correction, none of the 120 comparisons revealed significant evidence of a gene-environment interaction. Contrary to previous suggestions, there was little evidence that the genotypic relative risks were affected by use of hormone replacement therapy, either overall or for oestrogen-receptor-positive disease. Only one of the 12 polymorphisms (MAP3K1-rs889312) was correlated with any of the 10 other risk factors, with carriers of the high-risk C allele being significantly shorter than non-carriers (mean height 162.4 cm [95% CI 162.1-162.7] vs 163.1 cm [162.9-163.2]; p=0.01 after multiple testing correction).
Interpretation: The risks of breast cancer associated with low-penetrance susceptibility polymorphisms do not vary significantly with these 10 established environmental risk factors.
Funding: This study was funded by Cancer Research UK and the UK Medical Research Council.

title: Thrombocytopenia as an Indicator of Malaria in Adult Population
text:
Objective: To assess the predictive value of thrombocytopenia in malaria diagnosis.
Patients and Methods: This was a prospective observational study conducted at the Medical Unit of Hayat Abad Medical Complex from November 2008 to November 2010, including all adult patients with fever and thrombocytopenia.
Results: Of the total 228 patients with fever and thrombocytopenia, 121 (53%) were diagnosed with malaria. Among them, 82 (68%) had falciparum malaria, while 39 (32%) had vivax infection. The platelet counts of these 121 malaria patients ranged between 25,000 and 150,000/dL, with a mean value of 101,000/dL (SD ± 47,500) and a median of 75,000/dL.
