Reversible inhibition of both isoforms in culture with blebbistatin enriches for long-term hematopoietic multilineage reconstituting cells by 5-fold or more as assessed in vivo, and megakaryocytes become more polyploid, producing 4-fold more platelets. MII thus plays a multifunctional role in polarized division and niche sensing.

title: Critical Role of the Virus-Encoded MicroRNA-155 Ortholog in the Induction of Marek's Disease Lymphomas
text:
Despite the well-established roles of certain oncogenes in cancer development, microRNAs (miRNAs) are increasingly implicated in various human cancers. The discovery of miRNAs in oncogenic herpesviruses, such as KSHV, highlights their potential to contribute to the oncogenic capabilities of these viruses. However, demonstrating the direct in vivo role of virus-encoded miRNAs in neoplastic diseases like those induced by KSHV is challenging due to the lack of suitable models. To address this, we used excellent natural disease models of rapid-onset Marek's disease (MD) lymphomas in chickens, which allow for the examination of the oncogenic potential of virus-encoded miRNAs.
We found that deleting the six-miRNA cluster 1 from the viral genome abolished the oncogenicity of the virus, with a single miRNA within the cluster, miR-M4, being the primary contributor to this loss of oncogenicity. This was confirmed by the rescue of oncogenic phenotype by revertant viruses that expressed either the miR-M4 or the cellular homolog gga-miR-155. This is the first demonstration of the direct in vivo role of a virus-encoded miRNA in inducing tumors in a natural infection model. Additionally, the use of viruses deleted in miRNAs as effective vaccines against virulent MDV challenge offers the prospect of generating genetically defined attenuated vaccines.

title: Functional insights into the role of nuclear-retained long noncoding RNAs in gene expression control in mammalian cells
text:
The mammalian genome contains a vast array of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) genes, which have been implicated in the regulation of gene expression. Recent studies have shown that several of these lncRNAs play crucial roles in various biological processes, including epigenetic gene regulation, transcriptional control, and post-transcriptional regulation. These lncRNAs are localized in different subcellular compartments, with the majority being retained in the cell nucleus and classified as nuclear-retained lncRNAs (nrRNAs).
nrRNAs have been shown to execute diverse functions, such as providing structural support to the hierarchical organization of the nucleus and influencing the recruitment of chromatin modifier factors to specific chromatin sites. In this review, we will summarize the recently described roles of mammalian nrRNAs in controlling gene expression by affecting chromatin organization, transcription, pre-mRNA processing, nuclear organization, and their involvement in disease.
By influencing chromatin organization, nrRNAs can affect the accessibility of transcription factors to DNA, leading to changes in gene expression. They can also regulate pre-mRNA processing by modulating the splicing and polyadenylation of mRNAs, leading to changes in gene expression. Additionally, nrRNAs have been shown to play a role in nuclear organization, with some acting as organizers of chromatin structures and others influencing the localization of other proteins and RNAs.
Furthermore, nrRNAs have been implicated in various diseases, including cancer, where they can act as oncogenes or tumor suppressors. For example, some nrRNAs have been shown to promote the proliferation of cancer cells by regulating key genes involved in cell cycle progression and apoptosis. In contrast, other nrRNAs have been shown to inhibit the growth of cancer cells by suppressing the expression of oncogenes.
In conclusion, the study of mammalian nrRNAs has revealed a complex and multifaceted system of gene regulation that plays a crucial role in controlling gene expression. Further research into the functions of these non-coding RNAs may lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying gene regulation and disease, and may ultimately lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of diseases.

title: Downregulation of TAP1 in B lymphocytes by cellular and Epstein-Barr virus-encoded interleukin-10.
text: Virally infected cells degrade intracellular viral proteins through proteolytic degradation and present the resulting peptides to CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) through major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules. However, some viruses have evolved strategies to evade the immune system by interfering with the antigen presentation pathway. For example, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) expresses a late protein, BCRF1, which is similar to human interleukin-10 (hIL-10). We found that hIL-10 and EBV's BCRF1 downregulate the expression of two transporter proteins (TAPs) involved in antigen presentation, LMP2 and TAP1. This results in a decrease in the transport of peptide antigens into the endoplasmic reticulum, their loading onto MHC I molecules, and subsequent surface presentation. As a consequence, IL-10 and BCRF1 cause a general reduction in surface MHC I molecules on B lymphocytes, which may also affect the recognition of EBV-infected cells by CTLs.

title: TGF-β and Insulin Signaling Regulate Reproductive Aging via Oocyte and Germline Quality Maintenance
text:
Reproductive decline is one of the earliest signs of aging in both humans and the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans. While research on somatic aging has been extensive in both species, the underlying mechanisms that regulate reproductive aging remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the role of two key signaling pathways, TGF-β signaling and insulin/IGF-1 signaling, in regulating reproductive aging in C. elegans.
Our findings reveal that TGF-β signaling plays a crucial role in regulating reproductive aging in C. elegans, modulating multiple aspects of the reproductive process, including embryo quality, oocyte fertilizability, chromosome segregation fidelity, DNA damage resistance, and oocyte and germline morphology. Interestingly, TGF-β activity regulates reproductive span and germline/oocyte quality non-cell-autonomously, and is temporally and transcriptionally distinct from its regulation of growth.
We also identify a set of genes involved in chromosome segregation, cell cycle, and DNA damage response that are upregulated in TGF-β mutant oocytes, decline with age in mammalian oocytes, and are critical for oocyte quality maintenance. These findings suggest that C. elegans and humans share many aspects of reproductive aging, including the correlation between reproductive aging and declining oocyte quality, as well as the underlying mechanisms that determine oocyte quality.
In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms that regulate reproductive aging in C. elegans and highlights the conservation of these mechanisms in humans. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for the development of interventions aimed at improving reproductive health and fertility in both species.

title: The Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition Generates Cells with Properties of Stem Cells
text: The epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a crucial developmental program that is often activated during cancer progression and metastasis. In this study, we investigate the effect of EMT induction on immortalized human mammary epithelial cells (HMLEs) and its impact on the acquisition of mesenchymal traits and stem cell markers. Our results show that EMT induction in HMLEs leads to the expression of stem cell markers and an increased ability to form mammospheres, a property associated with mammary epithelial stem cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate that stem cells isolated from HMLE cultures also exhibit EMT markers and form mammospheres, indicating a direct link between EMT and the gain of epithelial stem cell properties. Additionally, we show that stem cells isolated from mouse or human mammary glands or mammary carcinomas also express EMT markers, further supporting our findings. Finally, we demonstrate that transformed human mammary epithelial cells that have undergone EMT form mammospheres, soft agar colonies, and tumors more efficiently, highlighting the potential of EMT-induced cells as a source of cancer stem cells. Overall, our findings provide strong evidence for the direct link between EMT and the gain of epithelial stem cell properties.

title: NEMO Prevents RIP Kinase 1-Mediated Epithelial Cell Death and Chronic Intestinal Inflammation by NF-κB-Dependent and -Independent Functions
text: Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) play a crucial role in maintaining gut immune homeostasis, and impaired epithelial responses are implicated in the development of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). IEC-specific ablation of nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) essential modulator (NEMO) leads to Paneth cell apoptosis and impaired antimicrobial factor expression in the ileum, as well as colonocyte apoptosis and microbiota-driven chronic inflammation in the colon. Interestingly, combined deficiency of RelA, c-Rel, and RelB in IECs does not lead to colitis, suggesting that NEMO prevents colon inflammation through NF-κB-independent functions. Inhibition of receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) kinase activity or combined deficiency of Fas-associated via death domain protein (FADD) and RIPK3 prevents epithelial cell death, Paneth cell loss, and colitis development in mice with epithelial NEMO deficiency. These findings suggest that NEMO inhibits intestinal inflammation by blocking RIPK1 kinase activity-mediated IEC death, which could have implications for the treatment of colitis in patients with NEMO mutations and possibly IBD.

title: Suppression of Myc oncogenic activity by ribosomal protein haploinsufficiency
text: The Myc oncogene regulates the expression of several components of the protein synthesis machinery, including ribosomal proteins, initiation factors, RNA polymerase III, and ribosomal DNA. While it is known that increasing protein synthesis capacity can lead to cancer, the specific mechanisms by which this occurs are not fully understood. Here, we use ribosomal protein heterozygote mice as a genetic tool to restore normal protein synthesis levels in Emu-Myc/+ transgenic mice, and show that the oncogenic potential of Myc is suppressed. Our findings demonstrate that Myc's ability to increase protein synthesis directly enhances cell size and accelerates cell cycle progression, independent of known cell cycle targets transcriptionally regulated by Myc. Additionally, when protein synthesis is restored to normal levels, Myc-overexpressing precancerous cells are more efficiently eliminated by programmed cell death. Our findings reveal a new mechanism that links increases in general protein synthesis rates to a specific impairment in translation initiation, leading to reduced mitotic-specific expression of the endogenous IRES-dependent form of Cdk11 (also known as Cdc2l and PITSLRE). This impairment results in cytokinesis defects, increased centrosome numbers, and genome instability in Emu-Myc/+ mice. When accurate translational control is re-established, genome instability is suppressed. Our findings demonstrate the importance of translational control in cancer initiation and highlight the specific molecular mechanisms by which perturbations in translational control lead to cancer.

title: Susceptibility to exacerbation in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text: Background: Despite the significance of exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), there is a lack of understanding regarding their frequency, determinants, and consequences. Objective: To investigate the phenomenon of frequent exacerbations in COPD and its association with disease severity and other clinical variables. Methods: In this large observational cohort study, we analyzed the frequency and correlates of exacerbations in 2138 patients with COPD enrolled in the Evaluation of COPD Longitudinally to Identify Predictive Surrogate Endpoints (ECLIPSE) study. Exacerbations were defined as events leading to antibiotic or corticosteroid prescription or hospitalization. Exacerbation frequency was assessed over a 3-year period. Results: Exacerbation rates increased with disease severity, with a higher frequency observed in patients with more advanced stages of COPD (p < 0.001). Specifically, 22% of patients with stage 2 COPD, 33% with stage 3, and 47% with stage 4 experienced frequent exacerbations (defined as two or more in the first year of follow-up). A history of exacerbations was the strongest predictor of future exacerbations across all stages of COPD (odds ratio, 2.37; 95% confidence interval, 1.84-3.06). Other factors associated with frequent exacerbations included a history of gastroesophageal reflux or heartburn, poorer quality of life, and elevated white-cell count. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that frequent exacerbations in COPD are a distinct phenotype that is independent of disease severity and can be predicted by a combination of clinical variables. These findings have implications for the targeting of exacerbation-prevention strategies across the spectrum of disease severity. (Funded by GlaxoSmithKline; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00292552.)

title: Sympathetic baroreflex gain in normotensive pregnant women.
text: During normotensive pregnancy, there is an increase in muscle sympathetic nerve activity while mean arterial pressure is maintained or reduced, suggesting a resetting of the baroreflex. We hypothesized that sympathetic baroreflex gain would be reduced in normotensive pregnant women compared to nonpregnant controls. We measured integrated muscle sympathetic burst incidence, total sympathetic activity, blood pressure, and R-R interval in 11 pregnant women (age 33 ± 1 weeks gestation, BMI 23.5 ± 0.9 kg/m2) and 11 nonpregnant controls (age 29 ± 1 year, BMI 25.2 ± 1.7 kg/m2). Pregnant women had higher baseline sympathetic burst incidence and total sympathetic activity compared to controls. Despite similar mean and diastolic blood pressures between the two groups, the baroreflex set point was reset upward in pregnant women. Baroreflex gain, calculated as the linear relationship between sympathetic burst incidence and diastolic blood pressure, was reduced in pregnant women compared to controls. Additionally, sympathetic and cardiovagal gains were negatively correlated in pregnant women. These findings suggest that the sympathetic nervous system's influence over arterial blood pressure is reduced in normotensive pregnancy, likely through a baroreceptor-dependent mechanism.

title: Facilitators and Impediments of the Pluripotency Reprogramming Factors' Initial Engagement with the Genome
text: The ectopic expression of transcription factors can reprogram cell fate, yet the mechanisms underlying this process are not fully understood, particularly in regards to the initial binding of factors to the genome. To investigate this, we generated a map of Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc (O, S, K, and M) binding on the human genome during the first 48 hours of reprogramming fibroblasts to pluripotency. Our findings reveal three key aspects of the initial chromatin binding events: (1) c-Myc plays an unexpected role in facilitating the engagement of OSK chromatin, (2) O, S, and K act as pioneer factors at enhancers of genes that promote reprogramming, and (3) megabase-scale chromatin domains marked by H3K9me3, including many genes required for pluripotency, are present and impede the efficiency of reprogramming. These findings highlight the complexity of the initial factor binding events that must be overcome in the minority of cells that successfully undergo reprogramming.

title: Fibrillar Collagen Inhibits Arterial Smooth Muscle Proliferation through Regulation of Cdk2 Inhibitors
text: Arterial smooth muscle cells (SMCs) are arrested in the G1 phase of the cell cycle when they come into contact with polymerized type I collagen fibrils, while monomer collagen promotes SMC proliferation. The expression of cyclin E-associated kinase and cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (cdk2) is inhibited on polymerized collagen, and levels of the cdk2 inhibitors p27Kip1 and p21Cip1/Waf1 are increased compared to SMCs on monomer collagen. p27Kip1 associates with the cyclin E-cdk2-p21Cip1/Waf1 complex in SMCs on polymerized collagen. Monovalent blocking antibodies to alpha2 integrins, which mediate adhesion to both forms of collagen, mimic these effects on monomer collagen. Additionally, polymerized collagen rapidly suppresses p70 S6 kinase, a potential regulator of p27Kip1. These findings suggest that fibrillar collagen specifically regulates early integrin signaling, leading to up-regulation of cdk2 inhibitors and inhibition of SMC proliferation.

title: Memory CD4+ T cells induce innate responses independently of pathogen
text: Recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by the immune system can trigger a robust inflammatory response. We investigated whether the adaptive immune system can also influence the type and intensity of the innate inflammatory response. Our findings show that the response of memory, but not naive, CD4+ T cells enhances the production of multiple innate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (IICs) in the lung. This leads to early control of the virus during influenza infection. The memory CD4+ T cell-induced IICs and viral control require cognate antigen recognition and are optimal when memory cells are either TH1 or TH17 polarized, but are independent of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) production. This mechanism allows memory CD4+ T cells to induce an early innate response that enhances immune protection against pathogens, a previously unrecognized function.

title: Direct Upregulation of STAT3 by MicroRNA-551b-3p Deregulates Growth and Metastasis of Ovarian Cancer.
text:
Introduction:
Ovarian cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths in women, and high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is the most aggressive and difficult-to-treat subtype. Amplification of chromosome 3q26.2 is a common feature of HGSOC, and it has been associated with poor clinical outcome. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that play a critical role in regulating gene expression and have been implicated in cancer development and progression. In this study, we investigated the role of miRNA-551b-3p in HGSOC and its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.
Methods:
We used a combination of bioinformatics and experimental approaches to investigate the expression of miRNA-551b-3p in HGSOC and its potential mechanisms of action. We analyzed the expression of miRNA-551b-3p in HGSOC tissues and cell lines and evaluated its impact on cell proliferation, apoptosis, and survival. We also used in vitro and in vivo experiments to investigate the direct targeting of miRNA-551b-3p on the STAT3 promoter and its downstream effects on cellular processes.
Results:
Our results showed that miRNA-551b-3p is highly amplified in HGSOC and is associated with poor clinical outcome. We found that miRNA-551b-3p upregulates the expression of STAT3 protein by binding to its promoter and recruiting RNA polymerase II and the TWIST1 transcription factor. This direct activation of STAT3 transcription by miRNA-551b-3p was confirmed in vitro and in vivo using cell lines and xenograft models. Furthermore, we showed that anti-miRNA-551b treatment reduced STAT3 expression and ovarian cancer growth in vivo.
Discussion:
Our findings provide new insights into the role of miRNA-551b-3p in HGSOC and its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target. The direct activation of STAT3 transcription by miRNA-551b-3p is a novel mechanism of action and highlights the complexity of miRNA-mediated regulation of gene expression. The use of anti-miRNA-551b therapy as a potential treatment for HGSOC is promising and warrants further investigation.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study demonstrates the critical role of miRNA-551b-3p in HGSOC and its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target. The direct activation of STAT3 transcription by miRNA-551b-3p is a novel mechanism of action and highlights the complexity of miRNA-mediated regulation of gene expression. Further investigation into the mechanisms of miRNA-551b-3p and its potential as a therapeutic target is warranted.

title: Human albumin administration in critically ill patients: systematic review of randomised controlled trials.
text:
Objective: To determine the effect of administering human albumin or plasma protein fraction on mortality in critically ill patients.
Design: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials comparing administration of albumin or plasma protein fraction with no administration or with administration of crystalloid solution in critically ill patients with hypovolaemia, burns, or hypoalbuminaemia.
Subjects: A total of 30 randomized controlled trials involving 1419 patients were included in the review.
Main Outcome Measure: The primary outcome measure was mortality from all causes at the end of follow-up for each trial.
Results: The results showed that in each patient category, the risk of death in the albumin-treated group was higher than in the comparison group. Specifically, the relative risk of death after albumin administration was 1.46 (95% CI: 0.97-2.22) for hypovolaemia, 2.40 (95% CI: 1.11-5.19) for burns, and 1.69 (95% CI: 1.07-2.67) for hypoalbuminaemia. The pooled relative risk of death with albumin administration was 1.68 (95% CI: 1.26-2.23), with a fixed effects model indicating a 6% (95% CI: 3%-9%) increase in the risk of death with albumin.
Conclusions: The findings of this systematic review suggest that there is no evidence to support the use of human albumin in critically ill patients with hypovolaemia, burns, or hypoalbuminaemia, and that it may actually increase mortality. These results indicate that the use of human albumin in critically ill patients should be urgently reviewed and that it should not be used outside the context of rigorously conducted, randomized controlled trials.

title: A fine-scale map of recombination rates and hotspots across the human genome.
text:
Genetic maps, which provide a detailed picture of how recombination rates vary across a genome, are a crucial tool for various genetic analyses. In this study, we have generated a high-resolution genetic map of the human genome using statistical methods to analyze genetic variation data. This map reveals over 25,000 recombination hotspots, along with specific motifs and sequence contexts that contribute to their activity. Our findings suggest a two-stage model for recombination, where hotspots are random features within a larger framework that constrains long-range recombination rates.
In this model, the behavior of recombination rates differs significantly between large (megabase) and small (kilobase) scales. By identifying and characterizing these hotspots, we can gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that control recombination and their impact on genetic variation. This knowledge can be used to improve the accuracy of genetic association studies, forensic analysis, and other applications that rely on the study of genetic variation.

title: Mental Health Support Provided Throughout the Bariatric Surgery Clinical Pathway in French Specialized Care Centers for Obesity
text: According to international guidelines, pre-operative psychological assessment is recommended for bariatric surgery candidates. As a result, healthcare teams caring for bariatric patients should include at least one mental health provider, such as a psychologist or psychiatrist. To evaluate the psychology and psychiatry resources and practices in France's 37 specialized obesity centers (CSOs), created by the French Ministry of Health, the study aimed to collect information on the centers' psychology and psychiatry resources and practices. The study found significant differences and shortages in the available psychology/psychiatry resources. Most psychologists and psychiatrists surveyed stated that they only meet new patients before surgery (56%) or both before and after the operation (30%), while some do not meet all patients (before and/or after surgery). However, all professionals provide psychology assessments, and around 75% offer a psychological follow-up, indicating similar practices among psychologists and psychiatrists. The results highlight the importance of psychological/psychiatric evaluations in French CSOs and the lack of mental health providers in some services. Additionally, post-operative psychological follow-up is not usually provided, suggesting the need for clear recommendations for long-term follow-up.

title: Calcium: Regulation of cell death: the calcium–apoptosis link
text: The fundamental question of whether to live or die is poignantly reflected in the dual nature of calcium (Ca2+) in living organisms – a survival factor or a ruthless killer. For centuries, it has been recognized that Ca2+ signals play a crucial role in regulating a wide range of essential cellular functions, making them indispensable for cell survival. However, more recent research has revealed that excessive or disrupted intracellular Ca2+ compartmentalization can lead to cytotoxicity and trigger either apoptotic or necrotic cell death, highlighting the dual and potentially deadly impact of Ca2+ on cellular function.

title: Breaking the code of DNA binding specificity of TAL-type III effectors.
text: Many bacteria rely on injecting effector proteins into eukaryotic cells through the type III secretion process to manipulate cellular processes. TAL (transcription activator-like) effectors from plant pathogenic Xanthomonas are key virulence factors that function as transcriptional activators in the plant cell nucleus by directly binding to DNA with a central domain of tandem repeats. In this study, we investigate how the target DNA specificity of TAL effectors is encoded. We found that each repeat in the TAL effector recognizes one base pair in the target DNA, with two hypervariable amino acid residues in each repeat responsible for recognizing the target base pair. We used computational predictions and experimental validation to identify the recognition sequences of TAL effectors and demonstrate their specificity. Our findings reveal the modular protein architecture of TAL effectors, enabling the design of artificial effectors with new specificities. This study highlights the functionality of a distinct type of DNA binding domain and provides insights into the design of DNA binding domains for biotechnology applications.

title: Interferon-Gamma at the Crossroads of Tumor Immune Surveillance or Evasion
text: Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) is a multifaceted cytokine with both pro- and antitumor effects. As a key player in the immune response, IFN-γ has been used to treat various diseases, despite its adverse effects. Although there is evidence implicating IFN-γ in tumor immune surveillance, IFN-γ-based therapies have had limited success in clinical trials. Recent findings suggest that IFN-γ may also promote tumor growth through mechanisms such as insensitivity to IFN-γ signaling, downregulation of major histocompatibility complexes, and upregulation of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase and checkpoint inhibitors, including programmed cell death ligand 1. However, IFN-γ-mediated responses are still positively associated with patient survival in several cancers. To improve therapies that exploit IFN-γ signaling pathways, it is crucial to understand the intricate and highly regulated effects of IFN-γ in the tumor microenvironment. This review discusses the current knowledge on the pro- and antitumorigenic effects of IFN-γ and its relevance to identifying IFN-γ-responsive patients.

title: Role of antioxidants in paraquat toxicity.
text:
Paraquat, a tetranitrogen herbicide, is a highly toxic compound for both humans and animals, resulting in numerous cases of acute poisoning and fatalities over the past few decades. The mechanisms of toxicity involve the generation of the superoxide anion, leading to the formation of more harmful reactive oxygen species, such as hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radical. Additionally, the oxidation of cellular NADPH, the primary source of reducing equivalents for the intracellular reduction of paraquat, disrupts important NADPH-dependent biochemical processes. The primary cause of death in paraquat poisoning is respiratory failure due to an oxidative insult to the alveolar epithelium, resulting in obliterating fibrosis.
Currently, management of paraquat poisoning remains largely supportive and involves modifying the toxicokinetics of the poison. Unfortunately, there are no true pharmacological antagonists for paraquat, and no chelating agents capable of binding the poison in the blood or other tissues. Given that paraquat induces its toxic effects through oxidative stress-mediated mechanisms, innovations in the management of paraquat poisoning are focused on the use of antioxidants. This review aims to present the current status of antioxidants in ameliorating or treating the toxic effects produced by paraquat.

title: Nucleation of nuclear bodies by RNA
text: The genesis of the various functional compartments within the mammalian cell nucleus remains largely unexplored. In particular, the initial step in forming these compartments, known as nuclear bodies, is poorly understood. Here, we uncover a novel role for RNA in the formation of these structures. Our findings demonstrate that RNA can act as both a structural element and a nucleator of nuclear bodies. We show that multiple types of coding and non-coding RNAs are sufficient to de novo assemble and are enriched in histone locus bodies, nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, and nuclear stress bodies. The formation of these nuclear bodies occurs through the recruitment and accumulation of proteins resident within them, which are primed by RNA. These results highlight the importance of transcription in nuclear body formation and suggest that RNA transcripts can function as a scaffold for the formation of major nuclear bodies. Overall, our findings establish RNA-primed biogenesis of nuclear bodies as a general principle of nuclear organization.

title: Evaluation of human papillomavirus testing in primary screening for cervical abnormalities: comparison of sensitivity, specificity, and frequency of referral.
text: The study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade 3 or higher, compared to traditional Pap smear testing. The study included 4075 women who attended Planned Parenthood clinics in Washington State and were screened simultaneously using both HPV DNA testing by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and liquid-based RNA-DNA hybridization capture with signal amplification (signal amplification). Women who were positive for high-risk HPV types or had Pap results of atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS) or higher were referred for colposcopy and biopsy. The study found that HPV DNA testing had higher sensitivity but lower specificity than traditional Pap smear testing for detecting CIN 3 or higher. The estimated prevalence of CIN 3 or higher was 3.2%. The sensitivity of thin-layer Pap (with a result of > or = ASCUS) for identifying women with CIN 3 or higher was only 61.3%, compared to 88.2% for HPV testing by PCR and 90.8% by signal amplification. The specificities of the tests were also different, with HPV testing showing higher specificities than Pap smear testing. The study also found that signal amplification testing of women with ASCUS and referral of those with a positive result was about as sensitive and more specific than referral for colposcopy of all women with ASCUS or higher. The strategy requiring repeat positive PCR tests on 2 visits had a sensitivity of 84.2% and a specificity of 86.2%. The study concluded that HPV DNA testing may be a reasonable alternative to cytology-based screening of reproductive-age women in certain settings, particularly where screening intervals are long or haphazard.

title: Breaking the chains: structure and function of the deubiquitinases
text: Ubiquitination is a reversible protein modification that plays a crucial role in various cellular functions. Recent advances have led to a deeper understanding of a superfamily of enzymes known as deubiquitinases (DUBs), which remove ubiquitin from proteins. Contrary to their uniform structure and function, DUBs exhibit a diverse range of mechanistic features. Despite the small number (less than 100) of DUBs, these enzymes are subject to multiple layers of regulation that control their activity and specificity. Given their involvement in critical regulatory processes, DUBs may represent promising new therapeutic targets.

title: Replication protein A: a heterotrimeric, single-stranded DNA-binding protein required for eukaryotic DNA metabolism.
text: Replication protein A (RPA), also known as replication factor A (RFA) or human single-stranded DNA-binding protein, is a single-stranded DNA-binding protein that plays a crucial role in multiple processes in eukaryotic DNA metabolism, including DNA replication, DNA repair, and recombination. RPA homologues have been identified in all eukaryotic organisms examined and are composed of three subunits of approximately 70, 30, and 14 kDa. These proteins bind nonspecifically to single-stranded DNA and interact with and/or modify the activities of multiple proteins. In cells, RPA is phosphorylated by DNA-dependent protein kinase when bound to single-stranded DNA (during S phase and after DNA damage), which may play a role in coordinating DNA metabolism in the cell. Additionally, RPA may also have a role in modulating gene expression.

title: Internal fixation versus nonoperative treatment of displaced 3-part proximal humeral fractures in elderly patients: a randomized controlled trial.
text: BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to evaluate the 2-year outcomes of elderly patients with a displaced 3-part fracture of the proximal humerus who were randomized to treatment with a locking plate or nonoperative management. PATIENTS AND METHODS: We included 60 patients, with a mean age of 74 years (range, 56-92), in the study. The majority of patients (81%) were women. The primary outcome measures were the Constant and Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) scores, as well as health-related quality of life (HRQoL) assessed using the EuroQol EQ-5D index. RESULTS: At the final 2-year follow-up, the results for range of motion (ROM), function, and HRQoL were all in favor of the locking plate group. The mean flexion in the locking plate group was 120°, compared to 111° in the nonoperative group (P = .36), and the mean abduction was 114° compared to 106° (P = .28). The corresponding values for the Constant score were 61 versus 58 (P = .64), for DASH 26 versus 35 (P = .19), and the mean EQ-5D index score was 0.70 compared to 0.59 (P = .26). Despite good primary reduction in 86% of the fractures in the locking plate group, 13% of the patients experienced a fracture complication requiring a major reoperation, and 17% had a minor reoperation. CONCLUSION: The results of our study suggest that treatment with a locking plate leads to better functional outcomes and HRQoL in elderly patients with a displaced 3-part fracture of the proximal humerus, but at the cost of additional surgery in approximately 30% of patients.

title: Good and bad consequences of altered fatty acid metabolism in heart failure: evidence from mouse models.
text: The transition from relying on fatty acid oxidation (FAO) to increased glucose utilization in heart failure has long been interpreted as an oxygen-sparing mechanism. However, recent findings suggest that this shift may actually be detrimental for the failing heart. This review aims to provide new insights into metabolic adaptations in heart failure by examining data from mouse models that have undergone modifications in cardiac FA metabolism at various levels of the FA metabolic pathway. These studies have shed light on whether and when modulations in FA metabolism are protective against heart failure, particularly in the context of ischaemic and non-ischaemic heart failure.

title: Pericytes of human skeletal muscle are myogenic precursors distinct from satellite cells
text: Cells derived from the blood vessels of human skeletal muscle have the ability to regenerate skeletal muscle, similar to embryonic mesoangioblasts. However, these adult cells do not express endothelial markers, but instead express markers of pericytes, such as NG2 proteoglycan and alkaline phosphatase (ALP). These cells can be isolated from freshly dissociated ALP-positive cells and have the potential to be used in cell therapy protocols for patients. Unlike canonical myogenic precursors (satellite cells), pericyte-derived cells express myogenic markers only in differentiated myotubes, which they form spontaneously with high efficiency. When transplanted into severe combined immune deficient–X-linked, mouse muscular dystrophy (scid–mdx) mice, pericyte-derived cells colonize host muscle and generate numerous fibers expressing human dystrophin. Similar cells isolated from Duchenne patients and engineered to express human mini-dystrophin also give rise to many dystrophin-positive fibers in vivo. These findings suggest that myogenic precursors, distinct from satellite cells, are associated with microvascular walls in human skeletal muscle and may represent a correlate of embryonic 'mesoangioblasts' present after birth. These cells may be a promising candidate for future cell-therapy protocols in patients.

title: Ten years' experience with alendronate for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women.
text:
BACKGROUND: Antiresorptive agents are widely used to treat osteoporosis, a condition characterized by the progressive loss of bone mass and density. In this study, we report the results of a multinational, randomized, double-blind clinical trial investigating the long-term efficacy and safety of alendronate, a commonly used antiresorptive agent, in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.
METHODS: The study consisted of four phases, with the initial three-year phase comparing three daily doses of alendronate (5 mg, 10 mg, or 20 mg) with placebo. Women in the original placebo group received alendronate in years 4 and 5 and were then discharged, while women in the original active-treatment groups continued to receive alendronate during the initial extension (years 4 and 5). In two further extensions (years 6 and 7, and 8 through 10), women who had received 5 mg or 10 mg of alendronate daily continued on the same treatment. Women in the discontinuation group received 20 mg of alendronate daily for two years and then 5 mg daily in years 3, 4, and 5, followed by five years of placebo. Randomized group assignments and blinding were maintained throughout the 10-year study period.
RESULTS: The study included 247 postmenopausal women who participated in all four phases of the study. Treatment with 10 mg of alendronate daily for 10 years resulted in significant increases in bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine (13.7%, 95% CI: 12.0-15.5%), trochanter (10.3%, 95% CI: 8.1-12.4%), femoral neck (5.4%, 95% CI: 3.5-7.4%), and total proximal femur (6.7%, 95% CI: 4.4-9.1%) compared to baseline values. In contrast, the group given 5 mg of alendronate daily exhibited smaller gains in BMD. Discontinuation of alendronate resulted in a gradual loss of its effects, as measured by BMD and biochemical markers of bone remodeling. Safety data, including fractures and stature, did not suggest that prolonged treatment resulted in any loss of benefit.
CONCLUSIONS: The results of this study demonstrate that alendronate is effective and well tolerated over a 10-year period, with sustained therapeutic effects observed in women treated with 10 mg of alendronate daily. Discontinuation of alendronate resulted in a gradual loss of its effects, suggesting that prolonged treatment may be necessary to maintain bone health in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

title: UCP1-independent signaling involving SERCA2b-mediated calcium cycling regulates beige fat thermogenesis and systemic glucose homeostasis
text: Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) plays a central role in brown fat-mediated nonshivering thermogenesis, but its function in beige fat remains unclear. In this study, we discovered a novel, UCP1-independent thermogenic mechanism in beige fat that involves enhanced ATP-dependent calcium (Ca2+) cycling through the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase 2b (SERCA2b) and ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2). Inhibition of SERCA2b impairs UCP1-independent beige fat thermogenesis in humans, mice, and pigs, a species that lacks UCP1. Conversely, activating α1- and/or β3-adrenergic receptors or the SERCA2b-RyR2 pathway stimulates UCP1-independent thermogenesis in beige adipocytes. Without UCP1, beige fat functions as a 'glucose sink,' dynamically expending glucose through enhanced glycolysis, tricarboxylic acid metabolism, and pyruvate dehydrogenase activity to generate ATP for thermogenesis through the SERCA2b pathway. This novel thermogenic mechanism allows beige fat to control whole-body energy homeostasis independently of body weight loss. Our findings uncover a noncanonical thermogenic pathway through which beige fat regulates energy metabolism.

title: Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN) mediates 3′-end maturation of the telomerase RNA component
text: Mutations in the PARN gene, which encodes poly(A)-specific ribonuclease, are associated with telomere diseases such as familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and dyskeratosis congenita. However, the mechanism by which PARN deficiency impairs telomere maintenance remains unclear. To investigate, we used somatic cells and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patients with dyskeratosis congenita harboring PARN mutations. Our findings reveal that PARN is essential for the maturation of the telomerase RNA component (TERC) at the 3' end. Patient-derived cells and cells with disrupted PARN exhibit decreased levels of TERC, which is accompanied by an increase in the proportion of oligo(A) forms of TERC. Using deep sequencing of TERC RNA 3' termini, we demonstrate that PARN is required for the removal of post-transcriptionally acquired oligo(A) tails that target nuclear RNAs for degradation. Restoring PARN function normalizes TERC levels and the proportion of oligo(A) forms of TERC, providing a mechanism linking PARN mutations to telomere diseases.

title: Folic acid supplementation and dietary folate intake, and risk of preeclampsia
text:
Background/Objectives:
Previous studies have suggested that folic acid supplementation may reduce the risk of preeclampsia, a pregnancy-related complication characterized by high blood pressure and damage to organs. However, the results of these studies have been inconsistent, and the evidence is not conclusive. Our study aimed to investigate the hypothesis that folic acid supplementation and dietary folate intake before conception and during pregnancy can reduce the risk of preeclampsia.
Subjects/Methods:
We conducted a birth cohort study in 2010-2012 at the Gansu Provincial Maternity & Child Care Hospital in Lanzhou, China, enrolling 10,041 pregnant women without chronic hypertension or gestational hypertension. Participants were categorized based on their use of folic acid supplements and dietary folate intake during pregnancy.
Results:
Our findings showed that compared to non-users, folic acid supplement users had a significantly reduced risk of preeclampsia (OR=0.61, 95% CI: 0.43-0.87). A dose-response relationship was observed among women who used folic acid supplements during pregnancy only, with the reduced risk increasing with duration of use (P-trend=0.007). The association between folic acid supplementation and reduced risk of preeclampsia was similar for mild or severe preeclampsia and for early- or late-onset preeclampsia, although the statistical significance was only observed for mild (OR=0.50, 95% CI: 0.30-0.81) and late-onset (OR=0.60, 95% CI: 0.42-0.86) preeclampsia. In contrast, the reduced risk associated with dietary folate intake during pregnancy was only seen for severe preeclampsia (OR=0.52, 95% CI: 0.31-0.87, for the highest quartile of dietary folate intake compared to the lowest).
Conclusions:
Our study suggests that folic acid supplementation and higher dietary folate intake during pregnancy may reduce the risk of preeclampsia. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq (MACS)
text: We introduce Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq data (MACS), a powerful tool for analyzing ChIP-Seq data generated by next-generation sequencing technologies such as Solexa's Genome Analyzer. MACS employs a novel approach to modeling the shift size of ChIP-Seq tags, allowing for improved spatial resolution in predicted binding sites. In addition, MACS utilizes a dynamic Poisson distribution to account for local biases in the genome, resulting in more robust predictions. Comparative evaluations with other ChIP-Seq peak-finding algorithms demonstrate the superiority of MACS. Notably, MACS is freely available for use.

title: Familial obesity and leanness.
text: Using the Princeton School District Family Study cohort, our research aimed to estimate the prevalence of suspected familial ponderosity (obesity) and leanness, provide empirical risk estimates for the proportion of probands' first-degree relatives affected, and investigate the contributions of diseases, drugs, and caloric intake to relative obesity and leanness. We analyzed 379 probands, including 125 whites and 52 blacks from a random recall group and 147 whites and 55 blacks from a hyperlipidemic recall group. Suspected familial obesity was identified in 2.4% and 6% of random and hyperlipidemic recall group whites, respectively, and suspected familial leanness was found in 2.4% and 1.4% of random and hyperlipidemic recall whites and 3.8% of randomly recalled blacks. Notably, approximately twice as many first-degree relatives of top Quetelet index decile probands themselves had top decile Quetelet indices, while approximately three times as many first-degree relatives of bottom decile Quetelet index probands themselves had bottom decile Quetelet indices. Furthermore, 19% and 31% of top decile Quetelet index white probands from random and hyperlipidemic recall groups came from families where at least two other first-degree relatives were similarly obese, while 18% and 20% of white random and hyperlipidemic recall group probands with bottom decile Quetelet indices had suspected familial leanness. Interestingly, none of the subjects with familial obesity or leanness had overt metabolic or pharmacological explanations for their body habitus. Additionally, within-family clustering of hypertension was common in kindreds with suspected familial obesity, but absent in kindreds with suspected familial leanness. These findings suggest that marked within-family clustering of both obesity and leanness is useful diagnostically, and family-wide therapeutic intervention may be most effective in reducing obesity in many kindreds.

title: In-hospital switching of oral P2Y12 inhibitor treatment in patients with acute coronary syndrome undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention: prevalence, predictors and short-term outcome.
text:
In clinical practice, the use of P2Y12 inhibitor switching has become more prevalent in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) due to the availability of prasugrel and ticagrelor in addition to clopidogrel. The Greek AntiPlatelet REgistry (GRAPE) study aimed to investigate the prevalence, predictive factors, and short-term outcomes of in-hospital P2Y12 inhibitor switching in 1794 ACS patients undergoing PCI.
The study found that switching occurred in 636 (35.5%) patients, with the majority (90.4%) switching between prasugrel and ticagrelor. Predictive factors of switching included presentation to a non-PCI-capable hospital, bivalirudin use, age ≥75 years, and regional trends. In a propensity-matched analysis, no significant differences in major adverse cardiovascular (MACE) or bleeding events were observed between switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent versus novel agent constant administration. However, there were more Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) type 1, 2, and any type events, and fewer MACE when switching from clopidogrel to a novel agent versus only clopidogrel administration.
In conclusion, in-hospital P2Y12 inhibitor switching is a common clinical practice in ACS patients undergoing PCI, influenced by clinical factors and regional practice differences. Switching to a novel agent may be associated with a higher risk of bleeding, highlighting the need for careful consideration and close monitoring of patients receiving these medications.

title: Structural basis of allosteric and synergistic activation of AMPK by furan-2-phosphonic derivative C2 binding.
text: The metabolic stress-sensing enzyme AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) plays a crucial role in regulating metabolism in response to energy supply and demand. Activating AMPK through drugs may be a promising approach for treating metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes. We have crystallized AMPK in complex with its activator 5-(5-hydroxyl-isoxazol-3-yl)-furan-2-phosphonic acid (C2), revealing two C2-binding sites in the γ-subunit distinct from nucleotide sites. Interestingly, C2 acts synergistically with the drug A769662 to activate AMPK α1-containing complexes independent of upstream kinases. Our findings suggest that combining drugs that target AMPK could be an effective strategy for treating metabolic diseases.

title: Validity of age at menarche self-reported in adulthood.
text:
Objective: To assess the accuracy of self-reported age at menarche in adulthood and examine the impact of socioeconomic position, education, gynaecological events, and psychological symptoms on the validity of recall.
Design: Prospective birth cohort study.
Setting: England, Scotland, and Wales.
Participants: 1050 women from the Medical Research Council National Survey of Health and Development, with two measures of age at menarche (one recorded in adolescence and the other self-reported at age 48) were included in the study.
Results: The study found that the validity of self-reported age at menarche in middle age compared to that recorded in adolescence was moderate (kappa = 0.35, r = 0.66, n = 1050). The validity was improved by categorizing age at menarche into three groups: early, normal, and late (kappa = 0.43). The agreement was influenced by educational level and having had a stillbirth or miscarriage.
Conclusions: The study's findings suggest that the accuracy of self-reported age at menarche in middle age is limited, and researchers should use such measures with caution. The study highlights the importance of considering the potential sources of error and bias when using self-reported measures of age at menarche in epidemiological research.

title: Seroepidemiologic survey of captive Old-World primates for antibodies to human and simian retroviruses, and isolation of a lentivirus from sooty mangabeys (Cercocebus atys).
text: From a sample of 526 Old World monkeys and apes housed in US zoos and vivaria, serum samples were tested for antibodies to HTLV-I, HTLV-III/LAV, and simian-AIDS retrovirus, type I (SRV-I). The initial screening was conducted using ELISA, and ELISA-positive samples, as well as those from cage contacts, were further tested by Western blotting. A significant number of false-positive and false-negative results were identified. However, most true positive reactions were directed towards a single retrovirus, and a few individuals from four species were positive for more than one retrovirus. Specifically, 39 out of 526 (7%) animals tested positive for HTLV-I, 21 out of 516 (4%) animals tested positive for SRV-I, and 23 out of 526 (4%) animals tested positive for HTLV-III/LAV. Many of the HTLV-III/LAV seropositive animals were from a mixed-species zoo exhibit containing sooty mangabeys, mandrills, Kolb's guenons, and talapoins. A type D virus was isolated from the blood of three out of ten SRV-I antibody-positive Tonkeana macaques, but not from any of the seropositive talapoins. A lentivirus was isolated from the blood of four out of seven HTLV-III/LAV seropositive sooty mangabeys, but not from seropositive talapoins in the same exhibit or from two seropositive colobus from another zoo. The sooty mangabey lentivirus caused generalized lymphadenopathy, leukopenia, and decreased levels of T4 lymphocytes in two experimentally infected rhesus macaques.

title: Coronary plaque disruption.
text:
Coronary atherosclerosis is the most common cause of ischemic heart disease, and plaque disruption with superimposed thrombosis is the primary culprit behind acute coronary syndromes such as unstable angina, myocardial infarction, and sudden death.1-5 Therefore, understanding why atherosclerosis progresses suddenly and life-threateningly is crucial for event-free survival. While the volume and severity of stenosis have been considered important factors, recent research has shown that the composition and vulnerability of the plaque are the most critical determinants of thrombus formation.6 Lipid-rich and soft plaques are more prone to rupture and thrombosis than collagen-rich and hard plaques.
Atherosclerosis is a complex interaction between blood elements, disturbed flow, and vessel wall abnormalities, involving inflammation, growth, degeneration, necrosis, calcification, and thrombosis.9-23 These processes lead to the formation of mature plaques, which are prone to disruption and thrombosis. Thrombotic factors may play a role early in atherogenesis, but a flow-limiting thrombus does not develop until mature plaques are present, which is why thrombosis is considered a complication rather than a fundamental component of atherosclerosis.
Mature plaques are characterized by atherosis and sclerosis, which are the result of a complex interplay between inflammation, growth, degeneration, necrosis, calcification, and thrombosis. These processes lead to the formation of a mature plaque, which is prone to disruption and thrombosis. Understanding the mechanisms responsible for the sudden conversion of a stable atherosclerotic plaque to an unstable and life-threatening atherothrombotic lesion is crucial for event-free survival.
In conclusion, coronary atherosclerosis is the most common cause of ischemic heart disease, and plaque disruption with superimposed thrombosis is the primary culprit behind acute coronary syndromes. The composition and vulnerability of the plaque are the most critical determinants of thrombus formation, and understanding these mechanisms is crucial for event-free survival.

title: p16INK4A is a robust in vivo biomarker of cellular aging in human skin.
text: The gene p16INK4A, which encodes an inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6, has been identified as a key regulator of cellular aging and premature senescence. While there is evidence of an age-dependent increase in p16INK4A expression in human fibroblasts in vitro, little is known about its expression in vivo. To investigate the relationship between p16INK4A expression and donor age in human skin, we analyzed p16INK4A expression by immunohistochemistry and compared it to the expression of the p16INK4A repressor BMI1 in skin samples from three age groups: 0-20, 21-70, and 71-95 years. Our results showed that the number of p16INK4A-positive cells was significantly higher in elderly individuals compared to younger age groups, with both epidermis and dermis showing increased expression. In contrast, BMI1 gene expression was significantly downregulated with increasing donor age. Furthermore, co-expression studies revealed that Ki67-positive cells were negative for both p16INK4A and BMI1, suggesting that these genes are involved in distinct cellular processes. Our findings provide the first in vivo evidence that p16INK4A expression directly correlates with chronological aging of human skin, making it a biomarker for human aging in vivo. These data also suggest a model for changes in regulatory gene expression that drive aging in human skin.

title: hPrimpol1/CCDC111 is a human DNA primase-polymerase required for the maintenance of genome integrity.
text: Recently, a novel DNA primase-polymerase, termed Prim-pol, has been identified as a member of the archaeal-eukaryotic primase (AEP) superfamily. In this study, we characterize a previously uncharacterized Prim-pol in human cells, which we designate hPrimpol1 (human primase-polymerase 1). Our findings demonstrate that hPrimpol1 exhibits both primase and DNA polymerase activities in vitro, and interacts directly with the RPA1 protein in an RPA1-dependent manner. Furthermore, we show that depletion of hPrimpol1 leads to increased levels of spontaneous DNA damage and defects in the restart of stalled replication forks. Notably, both RPA1 binding and the primase activity of hPrimpol1 are essential for its cellular function during DNA replication. Our results suggest that hPrimpol1 plays a novel role in the response to DNA replication stress.

title: Functional proteomics identifies miRNAs to target a p27/Myc/phospho-Rb signature in breast and ovarian cancer
text: The myc oncogene is overexpressed in approximately half of all breast and ovarian cancers, yet attempts to develop therapeutic strategies against myc have proven challenging. Myc regulates multiple cellular processes, including the cell cycle, which is associated with cell proliferation and tumor progression. We identified a protein signature characterized by high levels of myc, low levels of the protein p27, and high levels of phosphorylated retinoblastoma protein (Rb) in breast and ovarian cancers, which is significantly correlated with poor patient survival. Using a functional proteomics approach, we screened a library of microRNAs (miRNAs) in multiple cell lines and integrated data from patient tumors, identifying a panel of five miRNAs (miR-124, miR-365, miR-34b*, miR-18a, and miR-506) that have potential as tumor suppressors. Mechanistic studies revealed that miR-124 induces the direct transcriptional activation of p27 protein levels by binding to and inducing the p27 promoter region, leading to a subsequent G1 cell cycle arrest. In vivo studies using a xenograft model demonstrated that nanoparticle-mediated delivery of miR-124 can reduce tumor growth and sensitize cells to etoposide, suggesting a potential clinical application of miRNAs as therapeutics to target the functional effects of myc on tumor growth.

title: The potential role of miRNAs 21 and 199-a in early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common types of cancer worldwide, and early detection is crucial for improving patient outcomes. One of the major challenges in HCC diagnosis is the lack of sensitive biomarkers for early detection. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have been identified as promising biomarkers for HCC, as they can regulate gene expression and are present in small amounts of serum and tissue. This study aimed to investigate the serum and tissue expression of miR-21 and miR-199-a as potential early detectors for HCC.
A total of 40 serum and tissue samples (17 from chronic hepatitis and 23 from HCC patients) were collected and analyzed for miR-21 and miR-199-a expression using real-time quantitative reverse-transcriptase PCR (RT-qPCR). The results showed that the expression of serum miR-21 was significantly increased in HCC compared to chronic hepatitis (P<0.001), while miR-199-a was significantly decreased in HCC compared to chronic hepatitis (P<0.001). Additionally, the median of miR-21 was found to be higher in malignant tissues than in adjacent non-malignant tissues, although the difference was not statistically significant (P=0.191). In contrast, miR-199-a was significantly decreased in malignant tissues compared to adjacent non-malignant tissues (P<0.001). ROC analysis revealed that miR-21 and miR-199-a had reasonable sensitivity and specificity for disease progression, making them potential circulating biomarkers for HCC.
In conclusion, this study demonstrated that the expression of miR-21 is significantly up-regulated and miR-199-a is significantly down-regulated in serum of patients with HCC, suggesting their potential use as early detectors for HCC. The results provide evidence for the clinical utility of miR-21 and miR-199-a as biomarkers for HCC diagnosis and prognosis.

title: Tex10 Coordinates Epigenetic Control of Super-Enhancer Activity in Pluripotency and Reprogramming.
text: Super-enhancers (SEs) are clusters of transcriptional enhancers that are occupied by multiple lineage-specific transcription factors, driving the expression of genes that define cell identity. In embryonic stem cells (ESCs), SEs are highly enriched for the core pluripotency factors Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog. In this study, we aimed to elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying SE activity in pluripotency and reprogramming. By analyzing a protein interaction network surrounding Sox2, we identified Tex10 as a key pluripotency factor that plays a crucial role in ESC self-renewal, early embryo development, and reprogramming. Tex10 is enriched at SEs in a Sox2-dependent manner and regulates histone acetylation and DNA demethylation at these regions. Our findings also demonstrate that Tex10 is essential for pluripotency and reprogramming in human cells, highlighting its importance as a core component of the pluripotency network. This study sheds light on the epigenetic control of SE activity and its role in determining cell fate.

title: Value of whole brain re-irradiation for brain metastases--single centre experience.
text:
AIMS: There is ongoing debate in the medical literature regarding the role of repeat whole brain radiation (WBRT) for previously irradiated brain metastases. Our study aimed to investigate the practice at Princess Margaret Hospital regarding the re-irradiation of patients with progressive or recurrent brain metastatic disease after initial WBRT.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients treated for brain metastases with more than one course of WBRT between 1997 and 2003. Using a comprehensive computerised database, we identified 72 patients who were retreated with WBRT at a later date. We reviewed the medical records of these patients to gather information on their demographics, treatment doses, and outcomes.
RESULTS: The median age of the study population was 56.5 years, with the most common primary tumor sites being lung (51 patients) and breast (17 patients). The most frequently used dose for initial WBRT was 20 Gy/5 fractions (62 patients). The doses used for re-irradiation ranged from 25 Gy/10 fractions (22 patients) to 20 Gy/8 fractions (10 patients). Thirty-one percent of patients experienced a partial clinical response after re-irradiation, while 27% remained stable, and 32% deteriorated. Patients with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0-1 at the time of retreatment had longer survival. In responders, the mean duration of response was 5.1 months, and the median survival after re-irradiation was 4.1 months. One patient experienced memory impairment and pituitary insufficiency after 5 months of progression-free survival.
CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that repeat WBRT may be a useful treatment option for carefully selected patients with progressive or recurrent brain metastases. With improved survival and systemic treatment options for patients with metastatic disease, more patients may be candidates for consideration of repeat WBRT. However, prospective studies are needed to further clarify the outcomes of this treatment approach.

title: Bisphosphonates in oncology: rising stars or fallen heroes.
text: The introduction of bisphosphonates in oncology has significantly transformed the management of patients with metastatic bone disease. In this manuscript, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the clinical trials supporting the use of bisphosphonates in this setting and review recent and ongoing research. We also summarize the evidence demonstrating the benefits of bisphosphonate use in preventing treatment-induced bone loss and explore the intriguing emerging data on their antitumor potential when used in the adjuvant setting. Furthermore, we discuss the need for a careful balancing of the potential benefits and risks of bisphosphonate therapy, including the recently recognized late-toxicity of osteonecrosis of the jaw.

title: IL-33, a recently identified interleukin-1 gene family member, is expressed in human adipocytes.
text: Inflammation in adipose tissue is a hallmark of obesity. To investigate the role of IL-33, a recently identified member of the IL-1 gene family, in this process, we examined its expression in human adipocytes and preadipocytes. Our results show that IL-33, IL-1RL1, and IL-1RAP are expressed in human visceral white fat, as well as in preadipocytes and adipocytes (SGBS cells). Treatment with TNFα for 24 hours led to a 6-fold increase in IL-33 mRNA levels in preadipocytes and adipocytes. Time-course studies revealed that the increase in IL-33 mRNA with TNFα was maximized (>55-fold) at 12 hours, which is distinct from the responses to IL-1β (peak mRNA increase at 2 hours; 5.4-fold) and IL-18 (peak mRNA increase at 6 hours; >1500-fold). Interestingly, exposure of adipocytes to hypoxia (1% O2, 24 hours) did not alter IL-33 mRNA levels in adipocytes, while a 3-fold increase was observed in preadipocytes. Our findings suggest that human adipocytes and preadipocytes express IL-33, but the various IL-1 family members exhibit distinct differences in their responsiveness to TNFα.

title: Imaging techniques for assaying lymphocyte activation in action
text: Advances in imaging techniques have significantly enhanced our comprehension of lymphocyte activation. Recent breakthroughs in spatial and temporal resolution, as well as the development of novel labeling tools, have enabled researchers to directly observe the activation process in real-time. As a result, the use of imaging techniques to study lymphocyte activation has expanded, providing an unparalleled level of cellular and molecular detail in the field. Consequently, certain models of lymphocyte activation have been validated, others have been revised, and some have been entirely replaced with new concepts. In this review, we will discuss the current imaging techniques used to assess lymphocyte activation in various contexts, ranging from whole animals to single molecules, and evaluate their advantages and limitations.

title: Extending healthy life span--from yeast to humans.
text: When the food intake of organisms such as yeast and rodents is reduced (dietary restriction), they exhibit increased longevity compared to those on a standard diet. Similarly, reducing the activity of nutrient-sensing pathways through mutations or chemical inhibitors also leads to longer lifespans. In rodents, both dietary restriction and decreased nutrient-sensing pathway activity have been shown to reduce the incidence of age-related decline in function and disease, including tumors and neurodegeneration. Dietary restriction has also been found to increase lifespan and protect against diseases such as diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease in rhesus monkeys, and in humans, it has been shown to cause changes that protect against these age-related pathologies. Additionally, mutations in the growth hormone receptor and natural genetic variants in nutrient-sensing pathways have been linked to increased human lifespan. These findings suggest that dietary restriction and reduced activity of nutrient-sensing pathways may slow aging through similar mechanisms, which have been conserved throughout evolution. However, there is also the potential for negative side effects, which must be carefully considered in any attempts to apply these findings to human health.

title: Hospital and 1-year survival of patients admitted to intensive care units with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
Objective: To investigate the outcomes and identify variables associated with hospital and 1-year survival in patients admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Design: Prospective, multicenter, inception cohort study.
Setting: Forty-two ICUs at 40 US hospitals.
Patients: A total of 362 admissions for COPD exacerbation selected from the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) III database of 17,440 ICU admissions.
Measurements and Results: Hospital mortality for the 362 admissions was 24%. For the 167 patients aged 65 years or older, mortality was 30% at hospital discharge, 41% at 90 days, 47% at 180 days, and 59% at 1 year. Median survival for all patients was 224 days, and median survival for the patients who died within 1 year was 30.5 days. On multiple regression analysis, variables associated with hospital mortality included age, severity of respiratory and nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction, and hospital length of stay before ICU admission. Development of nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction was the major predictor of hospital mortality (60% of total explanatory power) and 180-day outcomes (54% of explanatory power). Respiratory physiological variables (respiratory rate, serum pH, PaCO2, PaO2, and alveolar-arterial difference in partial pressure of oxygen [PAO2-PaO2]) indicative of advanced dysfunction were more strongly associated with 180-day mortality rates (22% of explanatory power) than hospital death rates (4% of explanatory power). After controlling for severity of illness, mechanical ventilation at ICU admission was not associated with either hospital mortality or subsequent survival.
Conclusions: Patients with COPD admitted to an ICU for an acute exacerbation have a substantial hospital mortality (24%). For patients aged 65 years or older, mortality doubles in 1 year from 30% to 59%. Hospital and longer-term mortality is closely associated with development of nonrespiratory organ system dysfunction; severity of the underlying respiratory function substantially influences mortality following hospital discharge. The need for mechanical ventilation at ICU admission did not influence either short- or long-term outcomes. Physicians should be aware of these relationships when making treatment decisions or evaluating new therapies.

title: Kindlin-3 is essential for integrin activation and platelet aggregation
text: Integrin-mediated platelet adhesion and aggregation are crucial for the maintenance of vascular integrity and the prevention of blood loss. However, excessive platelet aggregation can lead to the formation of thrombi, which can cause cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarctions and cerebral strokes. To ensure that platelets only aggregate at sites of injury, integrins on circulating platelets are in a low-affinity state and undergo a process known as integrin activation or priming upon contact with a wounded vessel. This process is mediated by the binding of the cytoskeletal protein Talin to the β subunit cytoplasmic tail of integrins. Our findings demonstrate that platelets lacking the adhesion plaque protein Kindlin-3 are unable to activate integrins, despite normal Talin expression. As a direct consequence, Kindlin-3 deficiency leads to severe bleeding and resistance to arterial thrombosis. Mechanistically, Kindlin-3 can directly bind to distinct regions of β-integrin tails, leading to integrin activation. Our study identifies Kindlin-3 as a novel and essential element in platelet integrin activation in hemostasis and thrombosis.

title: Opening of compacted chromatin by early developmental transcription factors HNF3 (FoxA) and GATA-4.
text: In embryonic liver precursor cells, the transcription factors HNF3 (FoxA) and GATA-4 are the earliest known to bind the albumin gene enhancer. To investigate how these factors access inactive chromatin, we created nucleosome arrays containing albumin enhancer sequences and compacted them with linker histone. Surprisingly, HNF3 and GATA-4 bound their sites in compacted chromatin even in the absence of ATP-dependent enzymes, whereas other transcription factors like NF-1, C/EBP, and GAL4-AH did not. We found that the ability of HNF3 to open chromatin is due to a high-affinity DNA binding site and the C-terminal domain of the protein, which binds histones H3 and H4. These findings suggest that transcription factors that promote gene expression during development are also capable of initiating chromatin opening events.

title: N- and E-cadherins in Xenopus are specifically required in the neural and non-neural ectoderm, respectively, for F-actin assembly and morphogenetic movements.
text: Transmembrane cadherins are calcium-dependent intercellular adhesion molecules that play a crucial role in the development of tissues. Recent studies have revealed that these molecules are also involved in actin assembly during adhesive contact formation. However, the specific roles of actin assembly in transmembrane cadherins during development are not fully understood. To investigate this, we used the developing ectoderm of the Xenopus embryo as a model and found that both N-cadherin in the neural ectoderm and E-cadherin in the non-neural (epidermal) ectoderm are essential for the characteristic morphogenetic movements of these tissues. However, depletion of either N-cadherin or E-cadherin did not lead to dissociation of the tissues at the neurula stage, likely due to the expression of C-cadherin in each tissue. Interestingly, depletion of each cadherin was not rescued by the other or by the expression of C-cadherin, suggesting that each cadherin has a unique domain of expression on the cell membrane. These findings highlight the combinatorial nature of cadherin function and demonstrate how cell adhesion and motility can be combined in morphogenetic tissue movements to generate the form and shape of embryonic organs.

title: Mutation of the fumarase gene in two siblings with progressive encephalopathy and fumarase deficiency.
text: In this study, we report the identification of fumarase deficiency, an inborn error of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, in two siblings born to first cousin parents. The children presented with progressive encephalopathy, dystonia, leucopenia, and neutropenia. Elevated levels of lactate in the cerebrospinal fluid and high fumarate excretion in the urine prompted us to investigate the activities of the respiratory chain and the Krebs cycle, leading to the definitive diagnosis of fumarase deficiency. Our findings revealed a profound and widespread deficiency of fumarase in all tissues examined, affecting both the cytosolic and mitochondrial isoenzymes. Analysis of fumarase cDNA revealed that both patients were homozygous for a missense mutation, a G-955-->C transversion, which predicts a Glu-319-->Gln substitution in a highly conserved region of the fumarase cDNA. Both parents, who were found to be heterozygous for this substitution, exhibited reduced fumarase activity in their lymphocytes. To our knowledge, this is the first molecular characterization of tricarboxylic acid deficiency, a rare inherited inborn error of metabolism in childhood.

title: Adult Neurogenesis Is Sustained by Symmetric Self-Renewal and Differentiation.
text: Somatic stem cells have been identified in various adult tissues, and understanding how they self-renew is crucial for understanding long-term stem cell maintenance and the generation of progeny for cell replacement. In the adult mouse brain, neural stem cells (NSCs) reside in the walls of the lateral ventricles (ventricular-subventricular zone [V-SVZ]). The mechanism by which these cells are retained in adulthood for lifelong neurogenesis is unknown. Using multiple clonal labeling techniques, we have found that the majority of NSCs divide symmetrically. While approximately 20%-30% of these cells self-renew symmetrically and remain in the niche for several months before generating neurons, the remaining 70%-80% undergo consuming divisions, generating progeny, leading to the depletion of NSCs over time. This cellular mechanism decouples self-renewal from the generation of progeny, and limited rounds of symmetric self-renewal and consuming symmetric differentiation divisions can explain the observed levels of neurogenesis throughout life.

title: A common missense variant in NUDT15 confers susceptibility to thiopurine-induced leukopenia
text: Thiopurine therapy, commonly used to treat autoimmune conditions, can lead to life-threatening leukopenia in some individuals. This adverse effect is associated with genetic variations in TPMT (encoding thiopurine S-methyltransferase), particularly in individuals of European descent. However, despite a lower frequency of TPMT mutations in Asians, the incidence of thiopurine-induced leukopenia is higher in Asian populations. In this study, we used an Immunochip-based 2-stage association study in 978 Korean subjects with Crohn's disease treated with thiopurines to identify genetic variants associated with thiopurine-induced early leukopenia. We found a nonsynonymous SNP in NUDT15 (encoding p. Arg139Cys) that was strongly associated with thiopurine-induced early leukopenia (odds ratio (OR) = 35.6; Pcombined = 4.88 × 10−94). In Koreans, this variant demonstrated sensitivity and specificity of 89.4% and 93.2%, respectively, for thiopurine-induced early leukopenia (compared to 12.1% and 97.6% for TPMT variants). Interestingly, this SNP was also strongly associated with thiopurine-induced leukopenia in subjects with inflammatory bowel disease of European descent (OR = 9.50; P = 4.64 × 10−4). Therefore, NUDT15 is a pharmacogenetic determinant for thiopurine-induced leukopenia in diverse populations.

title: Induction of cell cycle entry eliminates human leukemia stem cells in a mouse model of AML
text: Cancer stem cells have been implicated in the initiation, progression, and recurrence of various types of cancer, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Our previous research has shown that CD34+CD38− AML stem cells in the endosteal region of the bone marrow are relatively resistant to chemotherapy. Using a NOD/SCID/IL2rγnull mouse model of human AML, we have now demonstrated that these stem cells are cell cycle quiescent and can be induced to enter the cell cycle by treatment with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). In combination with cell cycle-dependent chemotherapy, G-CSF treatment significantly enhances the induction of apoptosis and elimination of primary AML stem cells in vivo. This combination therapy leads to improved survival of secondary recipients after transplantation of leukemia cells compared to chemotherapy alone.

title: Reconstitution of the immune system after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in humans
