text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is intricately linked to an elevated susceptibility to infections, due to the profound immune deficiency that ensues. As a consequence, the patient is exposed to a heightened risk of infectious complications. Fortunately, the innate immune system, encompassing epithelial barriers, monocytes, granulocytes, and natural killer cells, begins to recover within a matter of weeks after transplantation. In contrast, the adaptive immune system, comprising B and T cells, experiences a slower rate of recovery, with T-cell counts normalizing during the initial months after transplantation, yet T-cell immunity may persistently impaired for extended periods of time. Over the past decade, significant strides have been made in elucidating the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon, which may potentially lead to the development of novel therapeutic interventions to accelerate the recovery process.

title: Vision tests in the mouse: Functional phenotyping with electroretinography.
text: Electroretinography (ERG) is a widely used diagnostic tool in clinical ophthalmology, providing objective information about retinal function. In addition, ERG is also applied in basic research, where animal models of inherited retinal diseases have significantly contributed to our understanding of the composition of ERG responses and how retinal degenerative pathologies affect retinal function. For instance, electrophysiological assessment of genetically engineered mice, which mimic human mutations that lead to retinal diseases, can be compared with clinical data. The limitations of examining human patients are significantly reduced when assessing mice. Proper measurement and analysis of retinal responses require careful consideration of several important aspects. This paper focuses on these aspects and provides exemplary ERG data obtained from normal wild-type mice and transgenic mice with specific functional properties, such as Rho-/- (rod opsin knockout, cone function only) and Cnga3-/- (cone CNG channel deficient, rod function only), to illustrate the contributions of rod and cone systems to ERG responses.

title: Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 is essential for meiosis but not for mitotic cell division in mice
text: We used homologous recombination in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells to target the gene encoding cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2). Interestingly, embryonic fibroblasts lacking CDK2 can proliferate normally and become immortal after continuous passage in culture. However, eliminating a conditional CDK2 allele in immortal cells does not significantly affect their proliferation. Notably, CDK2-deficient mice are viable and can survive for up to two years, indicating that CDK2 is dispensable for the proliferation and survival of most cell types. However, we discovered an unexpected role for CDK2 in the completion of prophase I during meiotic cell division in male and female germ cells.

title: Capsaicin-sensitive sensory nerve fibers contribute to the generation and maintenance of skeletal fracture pain.
text: Although skeletal pain can significantly impact a patient's functional status and quality of life, there is limited knowledge on the specific populations of peripheral nerve fibers that drive non-malignant bone pain. In the present study, neonatal male Sprague-Dawley rats were treated with capsaicin or vehicle and subjected to femoral fracture at young adulthood (15-16 weeks old). Capsaicin treatment resulted in a significant (>70%) depletion in the density of calcitonin-gene related peptide (CGRP+) sensory nerve fibers in the periosteum, but not 200 kDa neurofilament H (NF200+) sensory nerve fibers. The periosteum plays a crucial role in driving fracture pain, and the reduction in CGRP+ fibers in the periosteum was associated with a 50% reduction in the severity of fracture-induced skeletal pain-related behaviors, such as spontaneous flinching, guarding, and weight bearing. These findings suggest that both capsaicin-sensitive (primarily CGRP+) and capsaicin-insensitive (primarily NF200+) sensory nerve fibers contribute to the generation and maintenance of skeletal fracture pain. Skeletal pain can significantly hinder functional recovery following trauma-induced fracture, osteoporosis-induced fracture, and orthopedic surgery procedures such as knee and hip replacement. Understanding the specific populations of sensory nerve fibers involved in skeletal pain may lead to the development of more targeted and effective mechanism-based therapies to attenuate acute and chronic skeletal pain.

title: Surgical therapy for dystonia.
text: Surgical interventions for dystonia have evolved since the early 20th century, with advancements in technology and a deeper understanding of the basal ganglia's role in the disorder. Dystonia is a descriptive term for a movement disorder characterized by involuntary muscle contractions, which can affect various regions of the body or be generalized. It is crucial to differentiate between primary dystonias, which are caused by genetic or idiopathic factors, and secondary dystonias, which result from structural, metabolic, or neurodegenerative disorders. Secondary dystonias are more common than primary dystonias, and the latter typically respond well to pallidotomy or deep brain stimulation of the internal segment of the globus pallidum. However, limited historical and current data suggest that the thalamus may be a promising target for the treatment of secondary dystonias, but further, prospective, randomized studies are required. Currently, combinations of bilateral targets are possible with the existing deep brain stimulation (DBS) technology, but such procedures are not widely used due to surgical morbidity and expense. This review focuses on the surgical treatment of dystonia, with a distinction between primary and secondary dystonias, as well as generalized and cervical dystonia.

title: MEG3 imprinted gene contribution in tumorigenesis.
text: Maternally Expressed Gene 3 (MEG3) is a maternally expressed, imprinted gene that encodes a large non-coding RNA molecule. This gene also hosts microRNAs (miRNAs) and small nucleolar RNAs. MEG3 plays a crucial role in cell proliferation regulation by interacting with cyclic AMP, p53, murine double minute 2 (MDM2), and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15). The expression of MEG3 is regulated by epigenetic mechanisms, including aberrant CpG methylation, which has been observed in various types of cancer. Additionally, gene copy number loss has been reported as another mechanism associated with tumorigenesis. MEG3 deletion appears to upregulate paternally expressed genes while downregulating the expression of maternally expressed genes and tumor suppressor miRNAs, although there is conflicting data on this topic. MEG3 is believed to be a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 14q32, and its association with tumorigenesis is rapidly growing.

title: Uptake of rosuvastatin by isolated rat hepatocytes: comparison with pravastatin.
text:
The liver is the primary target organ for the lipid-lowering effects of rosuvastatin, a newly developed 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase inhibitor. To optimize its efficacy, it is desirable for rosuvastatin to be selectively taken up by the liver. In this study, we investigated the uptake kinetics of rosuvastatin and its comparison with that of pravastatin, another lipid-lowering drug, using isolated rat hepatocytes.
Both rosuvastatin and pravastatin were found to undergo uptake through a combination of active transport and passive diffusion processes. However, rosuvastatin had a lower Michaelis constant (Km) for uptake rate (9.17 micro M) compared to pravastatin (16.5 micro M), indicating a greater affinity for the transport system. Additionally, rosuvastatin had a higher maximum uptake rate (Vmax) and carrier-mediated uptake clearance (Vmax/Km) compared to pravastatin, indicating a greater efficiency in being transported into hepatocytes.
Sodium and chloride ions did not play a significant role in the uptake of either drug, but both drugs were inhibited by depletion of cellular ATP and organic anions such as bromosulfophthalein. Interestingly, rosuvastatin also inhibited the uptake of pravastatin, with an inhibition constant (Ki) similar to its Km.
Our results suggest that an organic anion transport protein is the primary mediator of hepatic uptake for both rosuvastatin and pravastatin. However, rosuvastatin exhibited a greater affinity and efficiency for this transport system compared to pravastatin. These findings provide insight into the mechanisms underlying the hepatic uptake of rosuvastatin and may help optimize its design and development as a lipid-lowering drug.

title: Junctophilin-4, a component of the endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane junctions, regulates Ca2+ dynamics in T cells.
text: In immune cells, Orai1 and STIM1 play a crucial role in store-operated Ca(2+) entry (SOCE) through their interaction at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-plasma membrane (PM) junctions. However, the molecular composition of these junctions in T cells is not well understood. Our study reveals that junctophilin-4 (JP4), a junctional protein in excitable cells, is expressed in T cells and localized at the ER-PM junctions, where it regulates Ca(2+) signaling. Silencing or genetic manipulation of JP4 leads to decreased ER Ca(2+) content and SOCE, which in turn impairs activation of the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) signaling pathways, and reduces expression of activation markers and cytokines. Mechanistically, JP4 interacts with STIM1 via its cytoplasmic domain, facilitating STIM1 recruitment into the junctions. Additionally, JP4 forms a complex with junctate, a Ca(2+)-sensing ER-resident protein that mediates STIM1 recruitment into the junctions. We propose that the cooperative interaction between the junctate-JP4 complex and STIM1 maintains ER Ca(2+) homeostasis and mediates SOCE in T cells.

title: The PI3K inhibitor arsenal: choose your weapon!
text: Due to its widespread involvement in inflammation and cancer, there has been a growing recognition of the therapeutic potential of inhibitors of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway, leading to increased interest in compounds with suitable pharmacological profiles. These are primarily focused on inhibiting PI3K itself. However, as class I PI3Ks are also essential for a range of normal physiological processes, broad-spectrum PI3K inhibition may be poorly tolerated. In recent years, patents have emerged for a new generation of PI3K inhibitors, with a particular emphasis on developing compounds with enhanced isoform selectivity for use as anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory therapies. Nevertheless, challenges persist in targeting this enzyme family successfully through pharmacology.

title: Infralimbic BDNF/TrkB enhancement of GluN2B currents facilitates extinction of a cocaine-conditioned place preference.
text: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) regulates synaptic activity and behavioral flexibility, and a decrease in BDNF has been linked to psychiatric disorders and cognitive impairments. However, BDNF has limited clinical utility due to its pharmacokinetics. Here, we demonstrate that activating a primary BDNF target, tropomyosin-related kinase B (TrkB) receptor, enhances the amplitude and prolongs the decay kinetics of N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor currents in male rat infralimbic prefrontal pyramidal neurons. These effects are mediated by the bidirectional regulation of extinction of a cocaine-induced conditioned place preference (CPP), a task that requires behavioral flexibility. Blockade of infralimbic TrkB receptors or NMDA receptors containing the GluN2B subunit disrupts consolidation of extinction of the CPP, while potentiation of TrkB receptor activity with infralimbic infusions of BDNF or systemic injections of 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8DHF), a newly synthesized TrkB receptor agonist, strengthens extinction of the CPP. The 7,8DHF-induced enhancement of extinction is prevented by infralimbic infusions of a GluN2B-specific receptor antagonist, demonstrating that TrkB receptor activation enhances extinction learning via GluN2B-containing NMDARs. These findings suggest that infralimbic TrkB receptor activation may be a useful pharmacological adjunct for extinction-based therapies for the treatment of psychiatric disorders associated with reduced BDNF activity.

title: Compaction of chromatin by diverse Polycomb group proteins requires localized regions of high charge.
text: Polycomb group (PcG) proteins are essential for the epigenetic maintenance of developmental genes in a repressed state. Specifically, proteins in the Polycomb-repressive complex 1 (PRC1) class of the PcG are conserved across species, from flies to humans, and inhibit transcription. One hypothesis regarding the mechanism of PRC1 is that it compacts chromatin, as supported by electron microscopy experiments demonstrating that Drosophila PRC1 compacts nucleosomal arrays. Our findings show that this function is conserved between Drosophila and mouse PRC1 complexes and requires a region with an overrepresentation of basic amino acids. Interestingly, while the active region is located in the Posterior Sex Combs (PSC) subunit in Drosophila, it is unexpectedly found in a different PRC1 subunit, a Polycomb homolog called M33, in mice. We provide experimental support for the general importance of a charged region by predicting the compacting capability of PcG proteins from other species and testing several of these proteins using solution assays and microscopy. Our results suggest that the ability of PcG proteins to compact chromatin in vitro can be predicted by the presence of domains of high positive charge, and that PRC1 components from a variety of species conserve this highly charged region. This supports the hypothesis that compaction is a crucial aspect of PcG function.

title: Angiopoietin-like proteins stimulate ex vivo expansion of hematopoietic stem cells
text: The successful ex vivo expansion of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) would significantly benefit the treatment of diseases and advance our understanding of crucial stem cell biology questions. In this study, we employed microarray analysis to identify the HSC-supportive mouse fetal liver CD3+ cells that express the proteins angiopoietin-like 2 (Angptl2) and angiopoietin-like 3 (Angptl3). Our findings indicate that the co-culture of highly enriched HSCs with Angptl2 or Angptl3, along with saturating levels of other growth factors, led to a 24- or 30-fold net expansion of long-term HSCs through reconstitution analysis. Additionally, the coiled-coil domain of Angptl2 was found to stimulate the expansion of HSCs. Furthermore, other proteins, including angiopoietin-like 5, angiopoietin-like 7, and microfibril-associated glycoprotein 4, were also identified as supportive factors for HSC expansion in culture.

title: Balancing co-stimulation and inhibition with BTLA and HVEM
text: The interaction between B- and T-lymphocyte attenuator (BTLA), an inhibitory receptor belonging to the immunoglobulin superfamily, and herpesvirus-entry mediator (HVEM), a co-stimulatory tumour-necrosis factor receptor, is distinctive in that it is the only instance of a receptor-ligand interaction that connects these two families of receptors. This unique association has sparked questions about how receptors from different families can interact and what downstream signaling events might occur following receptor activation. Recent studies have shown that engagement of HVEM with its endogenous ligand (LIGHT) from the tumour-necrosis factor family elicits a robust immune response, whereas HVEM interactions with BTLA negatively regulate T-cell responses.

title: Lin28b is sufficient to drive liver cancer and necessary for its maintenance in murine models.
text: Lin28a/b are RNA-binding proteins that play a crucial role in regulating stem cell maintenance, metabolism, and oncogenesis. While poorly differentiated, aggressive cancers often exhibit elevated Lin28 expression, its precise role in tumor initiation and progression remains unclear. To investigate this, we employed murine models and found that overexpression of Lin28b is sufficient to initiate hepatoblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. Moreover, we observed that Lin28b is overexpressed in MYC-driven hepatoblastomas and that liver-specific deletion of Lin28a/b leads to reduced tumor burden, extended latency, and prolonged survival. Our findings were corroborated by both intravenous siRNA against Lin28b and conditional Lin28b deletion, which also resulted in decreased tumor burden and improved survival. Interestingly, we found that Igf2bp proteins are upregulated in the context of Lin28b overexpression, with Igf2bp3 being particularly important for promoting cell growth. Taken together, our results demonstrate that Lin28b is both necessary and sufficient to initiate and maintain liver cancer in murine models.

title: Nanoenzymology of the 20S proteasome: proteasomal actions are controlled by the allosteric transition.
text: The proteasome is a crucial cytosolic proteolytic complex found in eukaryotic cells, and its structure and enzymatic properties have been well-studied. However, elucidating the mechanism of its enzymatic actions has proven challenging despite long-standing interest. Recently, we employed tapping mode atomic force microscopy (AFM) in liquid to observe the alpha-rings of the proteasome in a top-view position, which repeatedly switched between their open and closed conformations, potentially controlling access to the central channel. In this study, we utilized AFM to investigate the molecules in a side-view position and found that they acquired two stable conformations. The 20S particles were classified as either barrel-like or cylinder-like, and the relative abundance of the two conformers depended on the nature of their interactions with ligands. In control or inhibited molecules, the barrels predominated, while the cylinders and open molecules prevailed when the proteasome was observed in the presence of peptide substrates. Based on these data, we developed a two-state model of allosteric transitions to explain the dynamics of proteasomal structure. This model provides a better understanding of the observed properties of the 20S molecule and sets the foundation for further studies of the structural dynamics of the proteasome.

title: Changes in plasma copeptin, the c-terminal portion of arginine vasopressin during water deprivation and excess in healthy subjects.
text:
The measurement of arginine vasopressin (AVP) is often challenging due to its short half-life, making it difficult to accurately measure in clinical settings. However, a larger precursor peptide, copeptin, has been shown to be a useful tool for assessing AVP levels in critically ill patients. The objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical usefulness of copeptin as a new marker in disordered states of blood volume and plasma osmolality.
This prospective observational study was conducted in a university hospital, and involved 24 healthy adults undergoing three different interventions designed to manipulate plasma osmolality and volume: 28 hours of water deprivation, 17 hours of hypertonic saline infusion combined with thirsting, and hypotonic saline infusion with iv desmopressin administration during free water intake. The results showed that water deprivation led to significant weight loss, increased plasma osmolality, and a corresponding increase in copeptin levels from 4.6 to 9.2 pmol/liter (P < 0.0001). During hypertonic saline infusion and thirsting, copeptin levels increased from 4.9 to 19.9 pmol/liter (P < 0.0001). Conversely, during hypotonic saline infusion, plasma osmolality decreased, and copeptin levels decreased from 6.2 to 2.4 pmol/liter (P < 0.01).
The study concluded that copeptin shows identical changes during disordered water states as previously shown for AVP, suggesting that it may be a reliable marker of AVP secretion and a potential substitute for measuring circulating AVP levels in clinical practice.

title: Propagation and recovery of intact, infectious Epstein-Barr virus from prokaryotic to human cells.
text: Current genetic manipulation techniques face challenges when dealing with the large genomes of herpesviruses, such as gamma-herpesviruses. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a system that enables the cloning of any gamma-herpesvirus in Escherichia coli using an F factor-derived plasmid. This approach has successfully established immortalized B cell lines with recombinant Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), demonstrating that the F factor-cloned EBV genome possesses all the characteristics of wild-type EBV. The versatility of E. coli as a host allows for any genetic modification, thus enabling the comprehensive analysis of EBV functions. Moreover, it is now possible to generate attenuated EBV strains in vitro, paving the way for the development of vaccine strains. By incorporating genes for hygromycin resistance and green fluorescent protein onto the E. coli cloned EBV genome, we can investigate the EBV target cells beyond B lymphocytes.

title: Chemosensitivity profile assay of circulating cancer cells: prognostic and predictive value in epithelial tumors.
text: The detection of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in metastatic breast cancer using the CellSearch technology has raised additional questions regarding the biological significance of this information. We hypothesized that a drug-resistance profile of CTCs may predict response to chemotherapy in cancer patients and could be used for patient selection. In a prospective trial involving 105 patients with carcinoma, CTCs were isolated from peripheral blood and evaluated for the expression of genes involved in drug resistance. The drug-resistance profile was correlated with disease-free survival (DFS) and time to progression (TTP) in a 24-month follow-up. As a secondary endpoint, the objective response correlation was also evaluated. Notably, 51% of patients were found positive for CTCs, while all blood samples from healthy donors were negative. The drug-resistance profile correlated significantly with DFS and TTP (p < 0.001 in both). The test had a sensitivity of 98% in predicting treatment response and a specificity of 100%, with a positive predictive value of 96.5% and a negative predictive value of 100%. These findings suggest that a drug-resistance profile of CTCs may represent a first step towards individualizing chemotherapy in cancer patients.

title: Trends in heart failure incidence and survival in a community-based population.
text: The epidemiological investigation into heart failure has yet to be comprehensively explored, with limited data available on incidence, survival rates, and sex-specific temporal trends in community-based populations. To investigate this, a population-based cohort study was conducted in Olmsted County, Minnesota, using the resources of the Rochester Epidemiology Project. The study included 4537 Olmsted County residents (57% women; mean age 74 years) diagnosed with heart failure between 1979 and 2000. The diagnosis was validated using both Framingham criteria and clinical criteria. The main outcome measures were the incidence of heart failure and survival after heart failure diagnosis. The results showed that the incidence of heart failure was higher among men (378/100,000 persons; 95% confidence interval [CI], 361-395 for men; 289/100,000 persons; 95% CI, 277-300 for women) and did not change over time among men or women. After a mean follow-up of 4.2 years (range, 0-23.8 years), 3347 deaths occurred, including 1930 among women and 1417 among men. Survival after heart failure diagnosis was worse among men than women (relative risk, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.24-1.43) but overall improved over time (5-year age-adjusted survival, 43% in 1979-1984 vs 52% in 1996-2000, P<.001). However, men and younger persons experienced larger survival gains, contrasting with less or no improvement for women and elderly persons. In conclusion, this community-based cohort study found that the incidence of heart failure has not declined during 2 decades, but survival after onset of heart failure has increased overall, with less improvement among women and elderly persons.

title: Doxycycline induces apoptosis in PANC-1 pancreatic cancer cells.
text:
Background: Tetracyclines, such as doxycycline, have been reported to exhibit cytotoxic activity against mammalian tumor cells, but the mechanism underlying their effects on cell proliferation remains unclear.
Materials and Methods: In this study, the antitumor effect of doxycycline was investigated in the human pancreatic cancer cell line, PANC-1. Additionally, the effect of doxycycline on the expression of interleukin (IL)-8, a potent proangiogenic factor, was examined.
Results: Our results demonstrate that doxycycline exhibits cytotoxic effects on PANC-1 cells at concentrations greater than 20 microg/ml, which are accompanied by G(1)-S cell cycle arrest and DNA fragmentation. Doxycycline consistently activates the transcription of p53, p21, and Fas/FasL-cascade-related genes, while reducing the expression of Bcl-xL and Mcl-1. Furthermore, doxycycline at a concentration of 5 microg/ml, which is below the cytotoxic level, suppresses endogenous and paclitaxel-induced IL-8 expression. In the mouse xenograft model, doxycycline treatment resulted in a 80% suppression of tumor growth.
Conclusion: These findings suggest that doxycycline exerts its antitumor effect by activating proapoptotic genes, inhibiting IL-8 expression, and suppressing antiapoptotic genes.

title: Orientationally invariant indices of axon diameter and density from diffusion MRI.
text: This study proposes and tests a novel technique for measuring orientationally invariant indices of axon diameter and density in white matter using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These indices have the potential to provide more specific markers of white matter microstructure than traditional indices from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). The technique utilizes a four-compartment tissue model combined with an optimized multishell high-angular-resolution pulsed-gradient-spin-echo acquisition. The method is tested in simulation experiments on fixed monkey brains and on live human brains using a clinical 3T scanner. The human data acquisition takes approximately one hour. The simulation experiments demonstrate that both the monkey and human protocols are able to distinguish distributions of axon diameters that occur naturally in white matter. The axon diameter index is compared to the mean axon diameter weighted by axon volume, and the results show that the index is protocol-dependent, but correlation is good for the monkey protocol and weaker, but discernible, for the human protocol. Maps of axon diameter and density indices from the monkey and human data in the corpus callosum and corticospinal tract reflect known trends from histology. This demonstration shows that it is possible to measure orientationally invariant sensitivity to natural axon diameter distributions using both specialist and clinical hardware for the first time. These findings motivate further refinement, validation, and evaluation of the precise nature of the indices and the influence of potential confounds.

title: IFI16 and cGAS cooperate in the activation of STING during DNA sensing in human keratinocytes
text: Many human cells have the ability to detect the presence of foreign DNA during infection through the cytosolic DNA receptor cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS), which produces the second messenger cyclic GMP-AMP (cGAMP). While other potential DNA receptors have been identified, it is unclear whether their functions are redundant, tissue-specific, or integrated into the cGAS-cGAMP pathway. Here, we demonstrate that interferon-γ inducible protein 16 (IFI16) collaborates with cGAS in DNA sensing in human keratinocytes, as both cGAS and IFI16 are necessary for a full innate immune response to exogenous DNA and DNA viruses. Additionally, IFI16 is required for the activation of STING, a key player in the antiviral response, and interacts with STING to promote STING phosphorylation and translocation. We propose that the two DNA sensors IFI16 and cGAS cooperate to prevent the inappropriate activation of the type I interferon response.

title: Oncostatic effects of the indole melatonin and expression of its cytosolic and nuclear receptors in cultured human melanoma cell lines.
text: Melatonin has been shown to have anti-tumor effects on malignant melanoma in both in vitro and in vivo studies. In this study, we investigated the growth-inhibitory effects of melatonin on four melanoma cell lines (SBCE2, WM-98, WM-164, and SKMEL-188) with different growth patterns and phenotypes. We found that melatonin suppressed proliferation in all melanoma cell lines, with the highest efficacy in the SKMEL-188 cells cultured in serum-free media. The effects of melatonin were confirmed in a clonogenic assay. We also analyzed the expression of cytosolic quinone oxidoreductases NQO1, NQO2 (also known as MT3 receptor), and nuclear receptor RORalpha by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Our results showed that NQO1 was expressed in all cell lines, while NQO2 and nuclear receptor RORalpha (including its isoform RORalpha4) were only detected in SBCE2, WM-164, and WM-98 cells. These findings suggest that melatonin differentially suppresses proliferation in melanoma cell lines of different behavior, and the intensity of the anti-tumor response may be related to the cell-line specific pattern of melatonin cellular receptors and cytosolic binding protein expression.

title: Lysosomal localization of TRPML3 depends on TRPML2 and the mucolipidosis-associated protein TRPML1.
text:
Mucolipidosis type IV is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder characterized by severe neurodegeneration, achlorhydria, and visual impairments such as corneal opacity and strabismus. The disease is caused by mutations in the group 2 transient receptor potential (TRP)-related cation channel, TRPML1. Mammals encode two additional TRPML proteins, TRPML2 and TRPML3, but there is limited information available on their properties. Our study aimed to investigate the interactions between these proteins and their subcellular distribution.
Our results demonstrate that TRPMLs interact to form homo- and heteromultimers. Specifically, TRPML1 and TRPML2 homomultimers are lysosomal proteins, while TRPML3 homomultimers are located in the endoplasmic reticulum. However, when either TRPML1 or TRPML2 is coexpressed with TRPML3, the localization of TRPML3 shifts to lysosomes. Conversely, TRPML3 does not affect the localization of TRPML1 or TRPML2 in the endoplasmic reticulum. These findings indicate a hierarchy in the subcellular distribution of the TRPMLs, with TRPML1 and TRPML2 dictating the localization of TRPML3.
In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the interactions between the TRPML proteins and their subcellular distribution. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying mucolipidosis type IV and other lysosomal storage disorders.

title: Evolution of metastasis revealed by mutational landscapes of chemically induced skin cancers
text: Human tumors exhibit a high degree of genetic heterogeneity, but the mechanisms that govern the timing and route of metastatic dissemination of subclones remain unclear. To investigate these processes, we used whole-exome sequencing of 103 matched benign, malignant, and metastatic skin tumors from genetically diverse mice. Our findings suggest that most metastases disseminate synchronously from the primary tumor, supporting the parallel rather than linear evolution model of metastasis. Shared mutations between primary carcinomas and their matched metastases bear the A-to-T signature of the initiating carcinogen dimethylbenzanthracene, while non-shared mutations are predominantly G-to-T, a signature associated with oxidative stress. The presence of carcinomas that either did or did not metastasize in the same host animal suggests that tumor-intrinsic factors play a role in metastatic seeding. We also demonstrate the importance of germline polymorphisms in determining allele-specific mutations and identify somatic genetic alterations that are specifically related to the initiation of carcinogenesis by Hras or Kras mutations. The use of mouse tumors that mimic the genetic heterogeneity of human cancers can provide valuable insights into the clonal evolution of metastasis and inform the development of novel therapies.

title: A specific inhibitor of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, 2-(4-morpholinyl)-8-phenyl-4H-1-benzopyran-4-one (LY294002).
text: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PtdIns 3-kinase) is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in growth factor signal transduction by interacting with both receptor and non-receptor tyrosine kinases, including the platelet-derived growth factor receptor. Investigating the inhibitors of PtdIns 3-kinase can provide valuable insights into the function and regulatory mechanisms of the enzyme. Quercetin, a natural bioflavonoid, was previously shown to inhibit PtdIns 3-kinase with an IC50 value of 1.3 micrograms/ml (3.8 microM), and its inhibition appeared to be directed at the ATP-binding site of the kinase. Analogs of quercetin were then investigated as PtdIns 3-kinase inhibitors, with the most potent ones exhibiting IC50 values in the range of 1.7-8.4 micrograms/ml. In contrast, genistein, a potent tyrosine kinase inhibitor of the isoflavone class, did not significantly inhibit PtdIns 3-kinase (IC50 > 30 micrograms/ml). To further investigate PtdIns 3-kinase inhibitors, other chromones were evaluated, and one such compound, 2-(4-morpholinyl)-8-phenyl-4H-1-benzopyran-4-one (also known as 2-(4-morpholinyl)-8-phenylchromone, LY294002), completely and specifically abolished PtdIns 3-kinase activity (IC50 = 0.43 microgram/ml; 1.40 microM) without affecting PtdIns 4-kinase or selected protein and lipid kinases. Analogs of LY294002 demonstrated a very selective structure-activity relationship, with slight changes in structure causing marked decreases in inhibition. LY294002 was shown to completely abolish PtdIns 3-kinase activity in fMet-Leu-Phe-stimulated human neutrophils, as well as inhibit proliferation of smooth muscle cells in cultured rabbit aortic segments. Given the central role of PtdIns 3-kinase in growth factor signal transduction, the development of specific inhibitors against the kinase may be beneficial in the treatment of proliferative diseases, as well as in elucidating the biological role of the kinase in cellular proliferation and growth factor response.

title: A simple two-step protocol for the purification of human pancreatic beta cells
text: Isolating pure human beta cells would be beneficial for various research purposes. However, the lack of specific surface antigens has been a significant challenge. To overcome this, we aimed to develop a straightforward method for human beta cell isolation by initially eliminating ductal cells through their expression of carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9), followed by positive selection of beta cells based on their expression of polysialic acid–neural cell adhesion molecule (PSA-NCAM). We investigated the cell type-specific expression of CA19-9, NCAM, and PSA-NCAM in sections of adult human pancreas and cultured primary endocrine and exocrine cells. Dispersed human islet cells were purified in two steps, after 4 days of suspension culture, by binding to magnetic microbeads coupled to antibodies against CA19-9 and PSA-NCAM. NCAM expression was observed in ducts and islets in the human pancreas, while PSA-NCAM immunoreactivity was only detected in islets. PSA-NCAM staining in dispersed cells revealed that the marker is expressed in all endocrine cell types, but not in duct cells. Although purification of dispersed islet cells using PSA-NCAM microbeads alone did not completely eliminate contaminating duct cells, elimination of the duct cells by CA19-9 microbeads followed by positive sorting of the PSA-NCAM-positive cells in five consecutive islet preparations resulted in 90 to 98% pure endocrine cells, of which 89 to 97% were beta cells. We have thus described a simple and reliable method for isolating viable human pancreatic beta cells devoid of exocrine acini and ducts.

title: Prev | Table of Contents Reports Embryonic Stem Cell Lines Derived from Human
text: Human blastocyst-derived, pluripotent cell lines have been established, characterized by their normal karyotypes, high levels of telomerase activity, and expression of cell surface markers typical of primate embryonic stem cells but not other early lineages. Following 4-5 months of undifferentiated proliferation in vitro, these cells retain their developmental potential to form trophoblast and derivatives of all three embryonic germ layers, including endoderm (gut epithelium), mesoderm (cartilage, bone, smooth muscle, and striated muscle), and ectoderm (neural epithelium, embryonic ganglia, and stratified squamous epithelium). These cell lines have the potential to be valuable in human developmental biology, drug discovery, and transplantation medicine.

title: Ascorbic-acid transporter Slc23a1 is essential for vitamin C transport into the brain and for perinatal survival
text: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) has only been proven to be essential for preventing scurvy, likely due to its role as a cofactor for enzymes involved in post-translational modifications that stabilize collagen. To investigate the importance of a specific transporter for ascorbic acid transport, we created mice lacking the ortholog of a rat ascorbic acid transporter, Slc23a1. In cultured embryonic fibroblasts from these mice, we found that ascorbic acid uptake was significantly reduced to less than 5% of normal levels. Moreover, ascorbic acid levels were undetectable or reduced in the blood and tissues of Slc23a1-deficient mice. Prenatal supplementation of pregnant females did not increase blood ascorbic acid levels in Slc23a1-deficient fetuses, suggesting that Slc23a1 is crucial for ascorbic acid transport across the placenta. Slc23a1-deficient mice died shortly after birth due to respiratory failure and intraparenchymal brain hemorrhage. Surprisingly, the lungs of these mice showed no postnatal expansion despite normal levels of surfactant protein B. The brain hemorrhage was unlikely to be caused by scurvy, as Slc23a1-deficient mice did not exhibit hemorrhage in any other tissues and their skin had normal levels of 4-hydroxyproline. Our findings reveal that Slc23a1 is essential for the transport of ascorbic acid into various tissues and across the placenta, and its deficiency leads to lethal consequences in newborn mice, highlighting a previously unappreciated requirement for ascorbic acid during the perinatal period.

title: MVP-mediated exosomal sorting of miR-193a promotes colon cancer progression
text: Exosomes are emerging as key players in intercellular communication, with their release having the potential to impact both the donor cells and the recipient cells. However, the extent to which the release of exosomes affects the donor cells themselves has yet to be thoroughly investigated. In this study, we investigate the exosomal miRNA expression profiles in primary mouse colon tumors, liver metastases of colon cancer, and normal colon tissues. Our findings reveal that in more advanced disease, higher levels of tumor suppressor miRNAs are encapsulated in the exosomes. We also identify a novel mechanism by which miR-193a interacts with the major vault protein (MVP) and demonstrate that knockout of MVP leads to the accumulation of miR-193a in the exosomal donor cells, rather than the exosomes themselves. This results in the inhibition of tumor progression. Furthermore, we show that miR-193a causes cell cycle G1 arrest and cell proliferation repression by targeting Caprin1, which upregulates Ccnd2 and c-Myc. Our findings suggest that MVP-mediated selective sorting of tumor suppressor miRNAs into exosomes promotes tumor progression.

title: Casual blood pressure and neurocognitive function in children with chronic kidney disease: a report of the children with chronic kidney disease cohort study.
text:
Background and Objectives:
Children with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at increased risk of cognitive impairment, with approximately 50% of this population also experiencing hypertension. However, the specific contribution of hypertension to CKD-related neurocognitive deficits in children remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between elevated blood pressure (EBP) and neurocognitive test performance in children with CKD.
Design, Setting, Participants, and Measurements:
This was a cross-sectional analysis of the relationship between auscultatory blood pressure and neurocognitive test performance in children aged 6-17 years enrolled in the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) project. A total of 383 subjects were included in the analysis.
Results:
Of the 383 subjects, 132 (34%) had EBP (systolic BP and/or diastolic BP ≥90th percentile). Subjects with EBP had significantly lower mean (SD) scores on Wechsler Abbreviated Scales of Intelligence (WASI) Performance IQ and Full Scale IQ compared to those with normal BP (normal BP versus EBP: WASI Performance IQ, 96.1 (16.7) vs. 92.4 (14.9), P = 0.03; WASI Full Scale IQ, 97.0 (16.2) vs. 93.4 (16.5), P = 0.04). There was a significant inverse correlation between BP index (subject's BP/95th percentile BP) and Performance IQ score (systolic, r = -0.13, P = 0.01; diastolic, r = -0.19, P < 0.001). On multivariate analysis, the association between lower Performance IQ score and increased BP remained significant after controlling for demographic and disease-related variables (EBP, β = -3.7, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -7.3 to -0.06; systolic BP index, β = -1.16 to 95% CI: -2.1, -0.21; diastolic BP index, β = -1.17, 95% CI: -1.8 to -0.55).
Conclusions:
This study found that higher BP was independently associated with decreased WASI Performance IQ scores in children with mild-to-moderate CKD. These findings suggest that hypertension may play a significant role in the cognitive impairment observed in children with CKD. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the underlying mechanisms.

title: Bone marrow failure and developmental delay caused by mutations in poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN).
text:
BACKGROUND:
Deadenylation, the process by which poly(A) tail length is regulated, plays a crucial role in the function and fate of RNA molecules. Poly(A)-specific ribonuclease (PARN) is a key enzyme involved in this process, and its dysfunction has been implicated in various diseases. However, the biological significance of germline mutations in PARN remains poorly understood.
METHODS:
To investigate the role of PARN in human disease, we identified mutations in PARN in patients with haematological and neurological manifestations. We employed genomic, biochemical, and knockdown approaches in human marrow cells and zebrafish to clarify the mechanisms underlying the disease.
RESULTS:
Our analysis revealed large monoallelic deletions in PARN in four patients with developmental delay or mental illness. One patient in particular exhibited a severe neurological phenotype, central hypomyelination, and bone marrow failure, and had an additional missense mutation on the non-deleted allele, resulting in severely reduced PARN protein and deadenylation activity. Interestingly, cells from this patient displayed impaired oligoadenylation of specific H/ACA box small nucleolar RNAs. Moreover, PARN-deficient patient cells displayed short telomeres and an aberrant ribosome profile, similar to those observed in some variants of dyskeratosis congenita. Knocking down PARN in human marrow cells and zebrafish led to impaired haematopoiesis, further supporting a causal link with the human disease.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings suggest that large monoallelic mutations in PARN can underlie developmental/mental illness, while biallelic mutations can lead to severe bone marrow failure and central hypomyelination. These results highlight the importance of PARN in human health and disease, and underscore the need for further investigations into the molecular mechanisms underlying these phenotypes.

title: The changing epidemiology of malaria in Ifakara Town, southern Tanzania.
text: Between 1995 and 2000, significant changes occurred in the epidemiology of malaria in Ifakara, southern Tanzania. We documented these changes through parasitological and clinical data from community- and hospital-based studies involving children up to the age of 5 years. There was a rightward shift and decrease in the age-specific parasite prevalence in community-based cohort studies. The incidence of clinical malaria in placebo-receiving infants in additional study cohorts decreased from 0.8 episodes per infant per year in 1995 to 0.43 episodes per year in 2000, with an incidence rate ratio of 0.53 (95% confidence interval: 0.404, 0.70, P<0.0001). Concurrently, there was an increase in the total number of malaria admissions and a notable rightward shift in the age distribution of these admissions (median age in 1995: 1.55 years vs. 2.33 years in 2000, P<0.0001). However, the burden of malaria deaths remained disproportionately high in infants. We discuss how these dramatic changes in the epidemiology of malaria may have resulted from the use of existing malaria control tools. Caution is warranted when interpreting hospital-based data, as it is likely to underestimate the impact of anemia on mortality in the community, where most pediatric deaths occur. Even in low/moderate malaria transmission settings, targeting effective malaria control at infants may lead to substantial reductions in infant mortality caused by malaria.

title: MicroRNA-192 in diabetic kidney glomeruli and its function in TGF-beta-induced collagen expression via inhibition of E-box repressors.
text: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins, such as collagen 1-alpha 1 and -2 (Col1a1 and -2). Transforming growth factor beta1 (TGF-beta), a key regulator of these extracellular matrix genes, is upregulated in mesangial cells (MC) in DN. Using microarray profiling, we observed that TGF-beta increased Col1a2 mRNA in mouse MC (MMC) and decreased the expression of an E-box repressor, deltaEF1. TGF-beta treatment or short hairpin RNAs targeting deltaEF1 increased the enhancer activity of upstream E-box elements in the Col1a2 gene. Additionally, TGF-beta decreased the expression of Smad-interacting protein 1 (SIP1), another E-box repressor similar to deltaEF1. Interestingly, we found that SIP1 is a target of microRNA-192 (miR-192), a microRNA (miR) that is highly expressed in the kidney. MiR-192 levels were also increased by TGF-beta in MMC. TGF-beta treatment or transfection with miR-192 decreased endogenous SIP1 expression as well as reporter activity of a SIP1 3' untranslated region (UTR)-containing luciferase construct in MMC. Conversely, a miR-192 inhibitor enhanced the luciferase activity, confirming SIP1 to be a miR-192 target. Furthermore, miR-192 synergized with deltaEF1 short hairpin RNAs to increase Col1a2 E-box-luc activity. Importantly, the in vivo relevance of these findings was demonstrated by the observation that miR-192 levels were significantly enhanced in glomeruli isolated from streptozotocin-injected diabetic mice as well as diabetic db/db mice relative to corresponding nondiabetic controls, in parallel with increased TGF-beta and Col1a2 levels. These results uncover a role for miRs in the kidney and DN in controlling TGF-beta-induced Col1a2 expression by down-regulating E-box repressors.

title: Activation of PAR(2) receptors sensitizes primary afferents and causes leukocyte rolling and adherence in the rat knee joint.
text:
Background and Purpose:
The PAR2 receptors have been implicated in the development of chronic arthritis, but the underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigated the activation of PAR2 receptors in the rat knee joint and their role in the inflammatory response.
Experimental Approach:
We used immunohistochemistry to examine the expression of PAR2 receptors in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) cells in the rat knee joint. Electrophysiological recordings were used to assess the effects of stimulating PAR2 receptors on nerve fibers in the knee joint. Leukocyte kinetics were monitored using intravital microscopy. The role of TRPV1 and NK1 receptors in the PAR2 responses was assessed using selective antagonists.
Key Results:
We found that PAR2 receptors were expressed in 59% of FG-positive DRG cells. Stimulation of PAR2 receptors with the activating peptide 2-furoyl-LIGRLO-NH(2) increased joint nerve firings during both normal and noxious rotation. This effect was maximal at 3 minutes and was accompanied by increased leukocyte rolling and adhesion. The effects of 2-furoyl-LIGRLO-NH(2) were blocked by pre-treatment with the selective antagonists SB366791 and RP67580.
Conclusions and Implications:
Our findings suggest that PAR2 receptors play an acute inflammatory role in the knee joint via TRPV1- and NK1-dependent mechanisms involving both PAR2-mediated neuronal sensitization and leukocyte trafficking. These results provide new insights into the pathogenesis of chronic arthritis and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of this condition.

title: Polyphosphate kinase 1, a central node in the stress response network of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, connects the two-component systems MprAB and SenX3-RegX3 and the extracytoplasmic function sigma factor, sigma E.
text:
The regulation of polyphosphate (poly P) metabolism in Mycobacterium tuberculosis is critical for the bacterium's response to stress, particularly phosphate starvation. In this study, we investigate the regulatory architecture of the signal transduction system involved in poly P metabolism, including the two-component system (TCS) SenX3-RegX3, the extracytoplasmic function sigma factor SigE, and the poly P-synthesizing enzyme polyphosphate kinase 1 (PPK1).
We identify a regulatory element in the ppk1 promoter that is activated under phosphate starvation, which is attenuated upon deletion of an imperfect palindrome likely representing a binding site for the response regulator RegX3. We confirm the binding of phosphorylated RegX3 to this site using an electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Additionally, we find that the activity of the ppk1 promoter is abrogated upon deletion of a putative SigE binding site.
To further investigate the role of SigE in ppk1 transcription, we perform in vitro transcription experiments and observe that SigE is involved in ppk1 transcription. Furthermore, overexpression of RseA (anti-SigE) attenuates ppk1 expression under phosphate starvation, supporting the role of SigE in ppk1 transcription.
Our findings suggest the presence of multiple positive-feedback loops in the signalling circuit involving poly P metabolism, which could contribute to the persistence of M. tuberculosis. This is consistent with our earlier observation that PPK1 is capable of regulating sigE expression via the MprAB TCS.
In summary, our study reveals the regulatory architecture of the signal transduction system involved in poly P metabolism in M. tuberculosis, which is critical for the bacterium's response to stress. The identification of the regulatory elements involved in ppk1 transcription provides insights into the mechanisms of persistence in M. tuberculosis.

title: Natural history of asymptomatic unruptured cerebral aneurysms evaluated at CT angiography: growth and rupture incidence and correlation with epidemiologic risk factors.
text: Objective: To investigate the relationship between aneurysm size and epidemiological risk factors using computed tomographic (CT) angiography. Methods: In this HIPAA-compliant, institutional review board-approved study, patients with known asymptomatic unruptured intracerebral aneurysms were followed up longitudinally with CT angiographic examinations. Growth was defined as an increase in one or more dimensions by 5% or more, and associations of epidemiological factors with aneurysm growth and rupture were analyzed using logistic regression analysis. Inter- and intra-observer agreement coefficients for dimension, volume, and growth were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient and difference of means with 95% confidence intervals, the agreement statistic, and the McNemar χ(2) test. Results: A total of 165 patients with 258 aneurysms were included, with a mean follow-up time of 2.24 years from diagnosis. Forty-six of 258 aneurysms (18%) grew larger during follow-up. Spontaneous rupture occurred in four of 228 intradural aneurysms (1.8%). The risk of aneurysm rupture per patient-year was 2.4% (95% CI: 0.5%, 7.12%) with growth and 0.2% (95% CI: 0.006%, 1.22%) without growth (P = 0.034). There was a 12-fold higher risk of rupture for growing aneurysms (P < 0.002), with high intra- and interobserver correlation coefficients for size, volume, and growth. Tobacco smoking (P < 0.015) and initial size (P < 0.051) were independent covariates that predicted 78.4% of growing aneurysms. Conclusion: These findings support imaging follow-up of all patients with aneurysms, including those with smaller aneurysms than the current 7-mm treatment threshold. Aneurysm growth, size, and smoking were associated with increased rupture risk.

title: A search for the presence of the enteroviral capsid protein VP1 in pancreases of patients with Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes and pancreases and hearts of infants who died of coxsackieviral myocarditis
text: Using an antiserum raised against a recombinant Coxsackie virus B3 capsid protein (VP1), an immunocytochemical technique was developed that could detect the presence of all Coxsackie B viruses in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded infected tissue culture cells. This technique was applied to autopsy heart and pancreas tissue from 21 patients who were thought to have died of acute Coxsackievirus B myocarditis, and cardiac myocytes were positive for VP1 in 12 of 20 cases where the heart was available for study. Insulitis was present in the pancreas in seven of these cases, and all seven islet endocrine cells containing VP1 were found. In contrast, VP1 was rarely found in exocrine pancreas. In heart and pancreas tissue, cells positive for VP1 often showed signs of necrosis. Autopsy pancreases from 88 patients who had died at clinical presentation of Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus showed no evidence of VP1 presence. The ongoing destruction of insulin-secreting B cells seen at the time of death in the diabetic pancreas is unlikely to be due to a direct cytopathic effect of a Coxsackie B virus, but this study does not rule out the possibility that a persistent infection of B cells by a defective enterovirus may lead to their destruction through an autoimmune mechanism.

title: Direct reprogramming of mouse fibroblasts to cardiomyocyte-like cells using Yamanaka factors on engineered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) hydrogels.
text: Direct reprogramming techniques enable the rapid conversion of somatic cells into cardiomyocytes or cardiomyocyte-like cells without passing through the pluripotent state. A recently described protocol combines Yamanaka factor induction with pluripotency inhibition followed by BMP4 treatment to rapidly reprogram mouse fibroblasts into beating cardiomyocyte-like cells. The original study was conducted using Matrigel-coated tissue culture polystyrene (TCPS), a stiff material that also non-specifically adsorbs serum proteins. To overcome this limitation, protein adsorption-resistant poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) materials can be covalently modified to present precise concentrations of adhesion proteins or peptides without unintended effects of non-specifically adsorbed proteins. Here, we describe an improved protocol that incorporates custom-engineered materials. We first reproduced the Efe et al. protocol on Matrigel-coated TCPS, reprogramming adult mouse tail-tip mouse fibroblasts (TTF) and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) into cardiomyocyte-like cells that displayed striated sarcomeric α-actinin staining, spontaneous calcium transients, and visible beating. We then designed PEG culture substrates to promote MEF adhesion via laminin and RGD-binding integrins. PEG hydrogels improved proliferation and reprogramming efficiency, as evidenced by increased beating patch number and area, gene expression, and flow cytometry, resulting in almost twice the number of sarcomeric α-actinin positive cardiomyocyte-like cells compared to the original substrate. These findings demonstrate that cellular reprogramming can be enhanced using custom-engineered materials.

title: Effects of risedronate treatment on vertebral and nonvertebral fractures in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis: a randomized controlled trial. Vertebral Efficacy With Risedronate Therapy (VERT) Study Group.
text: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of daily oral risedronate treatment (2.5 or 5 mg/d) for 3 years in postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis, to reduce the risk of vertebral and other fractures. The study included 2458 ambulatory women aged 50-85 years with at least one vertebral fracture at baseline, who were randomly assigned to receive risedronate or placebo. The primary outcome measures were the incidence of new vertebral fractures, nonvertebral fractures, and changes in bone mineral density (BMD) as determined by dual x-ray absorptiometry. The study found that treatment with 5 mg/d of risedronate significantly reduced the cumulative incidence of new vertebral fractures by 41% over 3 years, compared to placebo (11.3% vs 16.3%; P=0.003). Additionally, there was a 65% reduction in the incidence of nonvertebral fractures after the first year (2.4% vs 6.4%; P<0.001). BMD increased significantly at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, femoral trochanter, and midshaft of the radius compared to placebo. The overall safety profile of risedronate was similar to that of placebo, with regard to gastrointestinal safety. These findings suggest that risedronate therapy is effective and well tolerated in the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis.

title: Hypoxia — a key regulatory factor in tumour growth
text: Cells exhibit a range of biological responses when exposed to hypoxic conditions, such as the activation of signaling pathways that regulate cellular proliferation, angiogenesis, and survival. Cancer cells have evolved to exploit these pathways, allowing tumors to persist and even grow under hypoxic conditions. This tumor hypoxia is linked to poor prognosis and resistance to radiation therapy. As a result, many components of the hypoxia-response pathway are potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: Loss of fibronectin from the aged stem cell niche affects the regenerative capacity of skeletal muscle in mice
text: Age-related changes in the muscle tissue have long been believed to impair the function of stem cells. Our study reveals that the aged stem cell niche in skeletal muscle has reduced levels of fibronectin (FN), leading to detrimental consequences for the function and maintenance of muscle stem cells (MuSCs). We found that deleting the gene encoding FN from young regenerating muscles recreates the aging phenotype, resulting in a loss of MuSC numbers. Using an extracellular matrix (ECM) library screen and pathway profiling, we identified FN as the preferred adhesion substrate for MuSCs and demonstrated that integrin-mediated signaling through focal adhesion kinase and the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway is significantly de-regulated in MuSCs from aged mice due to insufficient attachment to the niche. Replenishing FN levels in the aged niche rejuvenates stem cells and restores youthful muscle regeneration. In conclusion, our findings uncover the loss of stem cell adhesion to FN in the niche ECM as a previously unknown aging mechanism.

title: Monitoring starvation-induced reactive oxygen species formation.
text: Reactive oxygen species (ROS), which have the potential to harm cells by oxidizing their constituents such as DNA, proteins, and lipids, can also act as potent modulators in various signal transduction pathways, including autophagy. Autophagy was previously believed to be associated with oxidative stress, with a focus on the degradation of oxidized proteins and organelles. However, recent research has suggested that ROS also play a signaling role in the regulation of autophagy, leading to either cell survival or death, depending on the circumstances. To investigate the effects of ROS on this pathway, it is essential to determine the localization, intensity, kinetics, and importance of the oxidative signal in autophagy. Once these factors are characterized, methods for detecting and manipulating ROS formation can be employed to monitor and control autophagic activity. In this chapter, we will discuss approaches for examining ROS in the context of autophagy.

title: Why do patients with multimorbidity in England report worse experiences in primary care? Evidence from the General Practice Patient Survey
text:
Objective: To investigate the primary care experiences of individuals with multiple long-term conditions in England, focusing on the impact of comorbidity on patient satisfaction.
Design and Methods: We analyzed data from 906,578 respondents to the 2012 General Practice Patient Survey in England, including 583,143 patients with one or more long-term conditions. We employed mixed effect logistic regressions to analyze data on six items covering three care domains (access, continuity, and communication) and a single item on overall primary care experience. We controlled for sociodemographic characteristics and general practice using random effects, and further explored the importance of health-related quality of life measured using the EuroQoL (EQ-5D) scale.
Results: The majority of patients with long-term conditions reported a positive experience of care at their general practice (range 74.0-93.1%), with only modest variation by type of condition. However, the number of comorbid conditions was associated with a reducing percentage of patients reporting a positive experience of care, with the OR for reporting a positive experience decreasing from 0.83 (95% CI 0.80-0.87) for respondents with no long-term condition to 0.31 (95% CI 0.27-0.35) for respondents with four or more long-term conditions. This relationship was no longer observed after adjusting for health-related quality of life, with pain making the greatest difference among five quality of life variables included in the analysis.
Conclusions: Patients with multiple long-term conditions more frequently report worse experiences in primary care, but patient-centred measures of health-related quality of life, especially pain, are more important than the number of conditions in explaining why patients with multiple long-term conditions report worse experiences of care.

title: The rice FISH BONE gene encodes a tryptophan aminotransferase, which affects pleiotropic auxin-related processes.
text:
Auxin is a crucial plant hormone that plays a central role in plant growth and development. The localization of auxin within organs has been shown to be instrumental in regulating various physiological processes. Through the analysis of Arabidopsis mutants, it has been revealed that the indole-3-pyruvic acid (IPA) pathway, catalyzed by the TRYPTOPHAN AMINOTRANSFERASE OF ARABIDOPSIS (TAA) and YUCCA (YUC) families, is the primary biosynthetic pathway of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) in plants. However, limited information is available regarding the molecular mechanisms of auxin biosynthesis in rice.
In this study, we identified a rice mutant, fish bone (fib), which encodes an orthologue of the TAA gene family. Loss of FIB function resulted in a range of pleiotropic abnormal phenotypes, including small leaves with large lamina joint angles, abnormal vascular development, small panicles, abnormal organ identity, and defects in root development, accompanied by a reduction in internal IAA levels. Furthermore, we observed alterations in auxin sensitivity and polar transport activity in the fib mutant. These findings suggest that FIB plays a pivotal role in IAA biosynthesis in rice, and that the biosynthesis, transport, and sensitivity of auxin are closely interrelated.

title: Successful mouse cloning of an outbred strain by trichostatin A treatment after somatic nuclear transfer.
text: Despite the widespread use of somatic cloning techniques for various applications and basic research in different species, including mice, extremely low success rates have persisted for over a decade. In mice, the most clonable strains have been limited to hybrid F1 strains such as B6D2F1. However, we have recently developed a new and efficient cloning technique using trichostatin A (TSA), which leads to a 2-5 fold increase in success rates for cloning mouse cumulus cells from B6D2F1. To further validate this TSA cloning technique, we attempted to clone the adult ICR mouse, an outbred strain that has never been directly cloned before. Surprisingly, we were able to obtain both male and female cloned mice from cumulus and fibroblast cells of adult ICR mice using TSA, with a success rate of 4-5%, which is comparable to the 5-7% success rate observed in B6D2F1. This demonstrates that the TSA treatment not only improves the success rates of cloning from hybrid strains, but also enables cloning from previously "unclonable" strains.

title: A Genome-wide CRISPR Death Screen Identifies Genes Essential for Oxidative Phosphorylation.
text: Oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is the primary mechanism for ATP production in humans, and deficiencies in this process can arise from mutations in either the mitochondrial or nuclear genome, comprising the largest collection of inborn errors of metabolism. Currently, we lack a comprehensive inventory of human genes and pathways essential for OXPHOS. To address this gap, we have developed a genome-wide CRISPR "death screen" that selectively targets and eliminates cells lacking the ability to undergo OXPHOS, allowing us to identify genes essential for this process. Inspired by the observation that human cells lacking OXPHOS are more likely to survive in glucose but die in galactose, we screened for cells that could survive in the absence of glucose and identified 191 high-confidence hits essential for OXPHOS, including 72 known OXPHOS diseases. Our screen also revealed a functional module consisting of NGRN, WBSCR16, RPUSD3, RPUSD4, TRUB2, and FASTKD2, which regulates the mitochondrial 16S rRNA and intra-mitochondrial translation. Our work provides a comprehensive catalog of genes required for OXPHOS and demonstrates the power of death screening for functional genomic analysis.

title: RecQ helicases: caretakers of the genome
text: RecQ helicases are highly conserved across the evolutionary spectrum, from bacteria to humans. Germline mutations in three of the five known family members in humans have been linked to debilitating disorders that are characterized by, among other things, an increased susceptibility to cancer. One of these disorders, Bloom's syndrome, is particularly associated with a predisposition to all types of cancer. So, how do RecQ helicases safeguard against cancer? It appears that they play a crucial role in maintaining genomic stability by functioning at the interface between DNA replication and DNA repair.

title: Mortality from causes amenable and non-amenable to medical care: the experience of eastern Europe.
text:
Objective:
To investigate and compare national trends in mortality rates from conditions that can be improved through timely and appropriate medical care, and those that are less responsive to medical interventions, across different regions of Europe.
Design:
An analysis of trends in direct age-standardized mortality rates from the 1950s to 1987 in four Eastern European countries (Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and the German Democratic Republic) and two Western European countries (the Federal Republic of Germany and England and Wales), as well as two North American countries (the United States and Canada).
Population:
The total populations of the relevant countries during the study period.
Main Outcome Measures:

Proportional changes over time in age-standardized mortality rates. Mortality rates were divided into two categories: amenable and non-amenable causes, and the trends were analyzed for the age group of 0-64 years.
Results:

A significant divergence in trends in all-cause mortality was observed between Eastern Europe and Western countries around 1970, with Western countries experiencing a steady decline in mortality rates while Eastern Europe's rates remained relatively static. In the age group of 0-64 years, mortality rates from amenable causes of death declined more slowly in Eastern Europe than in the West, particularly after 1970. In contrast, mortality rates from non-amenable causes of death rose in Eastern European countries from the late 1960s compared to substantial declines in such mortality in the West.
Conclusions:

Non-amenable causes of death are the primary, but not exclusive, reason for the lack of improvement in trends in all-cause mortality in Eastern Europe from 1970. The health agenda in Eastern Europe should prioritize lifestyle improvements and environmental improvements, while also focusing on enhancements in the quality and efficiency of direct health services.

title: Dynamic regulation of heterochromatin function via phosphorylation of HP1-family proteins.
text: Heterochromatin is defined by the methylation of histone H3 at lysine 9, which is recognized by a group of highly conserved proteins belonging to the HP1 family. Heterochromatin plays a crucial role in various chromosomal functions, including transcriptional gene silencing and sister-chromatid cohesion. These functions are carried out by a range of effector proteins that interact with HP1-family proteins, although the mechanisms underlying their association are not yet fully understood. Recent studies have shown that phosphorylation of the fission-yeast HP1 homolog Swi6 regulates the association of transcriptional regulators in a differential manner, leading to changes in the transcriptional activity of heterochromatin without affecting sister-chromatid cohesion. These findings, along with those obtained using other systems, suggest that phosphorylation of HP1/Swi6 provides a dynamic pathway for the differential regulation of heterochromatin in response to both intracellular and intercellular signals.

title: Modeling neurogenesis impairment in Down syndrome with induced pluripotent stem cells from Trisomy 21 amniotic fluid cells.
text: Down syndrome (DS), also known as Trisomy 21 (T21) syndrome, is a common chromosomal abnormality caused by an extra duplication of chromosome 21. In the context of neuron development research, experimental models derived from human cells are considered the most desirable and accurate for basic research. The generation of diseased induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells is a crucial step in understanding the developmental stages of complex neuronal diseases. In this study, we generated human DS iPS cell lines from second trimester amniotic fluid (AF) cells using lentiviral delivery of Yamanaka factors and subsequently differentiated them into neuronal progenitor cells (NPCs) for further analysis. The T21 AF-iPS cells were characterized for the expression of pluripotent markers and their ability to differentiate into all three germ layers by forming embryoid bodies in vitro and teratomas in vivo. Notably, the T21 AF-iPS cells maintained their unique karyotype, consisting of three pairs of chromosome 21. Additionally, we observed increased levels of amyloid precursor protein in NPCs derived from T21 AF-iPS cells compared to NPCs from normal AF-iPS cells. Furthermore, we found that T21 iPS-NPCs generated fewer neurons than controls and exhibited developmental defects during neurogenesis. These findings suggest that T21 AF-iPS cells may serve as a valuable tool to elucidate the impairment of neurogenesis in Down syndrome and the onset of Alzheimer's disease.

title: Control over DNA replication in time and space.
text: DNA replication is precisely regulated in both time and space to ensure genome integrity. In eukaryotic cells, replication begins at multiple sites along the genome, known as origins of replication, and propagates in both directions. The regulation of these origins is mediated by dynamic complexes called origin bound complexes, which determine the timing and location of replication. During late mitosis and G1 phase, potential origins are recognized and become "licensed" through the assembly of pre-replicative complexes (pre-RCs) containing the MCM2-7 helicases. As the cell enters the G1/S phase transition, a subset of these pre-RCs are activated, leading to the establishment of replication forks. The location of these origins is influenced by the organization of chromatin and the nuclear environment, and the selection of origins exhibits stochastic properties. The regulatory mechanisms that control these events rely on the periodic fluctuations of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity throughout the cell cycle.

title: MYC/MIZ1-dependent gene repression inversely coordinates the circadian clock with cell cycle and proliferation
text: The circadian clock and cell cycle are two critical cellular systems that regulate global physiology according to a temporal schedule. While these systems may seem to have conflicting functions, our findings suggest that they are actually coordinated through the actions of a central regulator: MYC. We demonstrate that overexpressing MYC in U2OS cells leads to a weakening of the circadian clock and an increase in cell proliferation, while reducing MYC levels strengthens the clock and slows down cell growth. The inhibition of the circadian clock is dependent on the formation of repressive complexes between MYC and MIZ1, leading to the downregulation of core clock genes such as BMAL1 (ARNTL), CLOCK, and NPAS2. Furthermore, we find that BMAL1 expression levels are inversely correlated with MYC levels in 102 human lymphomas, suggesting that MYC acts as a master regulator that modulates the impact of cell cycle and circadian clock on gene expression.

title: Relevance of asystole during head-up tilt testing.
text: The prognostic value of prolonged asystole during head-up tilt testing is unclear. In a study of 209 patients with a history of syncope and positive head-up tilt tests, 19 patients experienced asystole lasting over 5 seconds (mean duration of 15 ± 10 seconds). Compared to patients without asystole (group 1b), group 1a patients were younger (32 ± 12 vs 47 ± 21 years, p < 0.005), but the clinical manifestations were not more severe (7 ± 5 vs 8 ± 6 episodes of syncope, p = NS; and 2 vs 13 patients with injury during syncope, p = NS). During follow-up (mean of 2 ± 1 year), 11% and 8% of group 1a patients experienced recurrence of symptoms, which was not significantly different from group 1b (p = NS). None of the patients in the asystole group underwent pacemaker implantation. In contrast, of 75 normal volunteers (group 2) without a history of syncope who underwent tilt tests to evaluate the specificity of the test, 3 had asystole (mean duration of 10 seconds). During over one year of follow-up, all 3 individuals were asymptomatic. Therefore, prolonged asystole during head-up tilt testing does not predict a more severe outcome or poor response to pharmacological therapy. Moreover, an asystolic response does not increase the specificity of the head-up tilt test, as it may occur in asymptomatic "normal" volunteers.

title: Increasing informed uptake and non-uptake of screening: evidence from a systematic review.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of interventions aimed at improving informed uptake of screening tests.
Search Strategy: Electronic databases, bibliographies, and expert opinions were searched to identify published and unpublished studies up to August 2000.
Inclusion Criteria: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and controlled trials of interventions aimed at increasing informed uptake of screening tests. All participants were eligible as defined by the entry criteria of individual programs. Studies had to report actual uptake and meet three out of four criteria used to define informed uptake.
Data Extraction and Synthesis: Relevant studies were identified, data extracted, and validity assessed by two reviewers independently. Outcome data included screening uptake, knowledge, informed decision-making, and attitudes towards screening. A random-effects model was used to calculate individual relative risks and 95% confidence intervals.
Main Results: Six controlled trials (five RCTs and one quasi-RCT) focusing on antenatal and prostate-specific antigen screening were included. All reported risks/benefits of screening and assessed knowledge. Two also assessed decision-making. Two reported risks/benefits to all randomized groups and evaluated different ways of presenting information. However, neither found that interventions such as videos, information leaflets with decision trees, or touch screen computers conveyed any additional benefits over well-prepared leaflets.
Conclusions: While there is some evidence suggesting that changing the format of informed choice interventions in screening does not significantly affect knowledge, satisfaction, or decisions about screening, it is unclear whether informed choice affects uptake. Further research is needed to develop a valid instrument for measuring all components of informed choice in screening, as well as to conduct more well-designed RCTs.

title: Mitochondrial RNA Granules Are Centers for Posttranscriptional RNA Processing and Ribosome Biogenesis.
text: Mitochondrial RNA granules play a pivotal role in the posttranscriptional processing of mRNAs, yet the significance of cytoplasmic RNA granules has been largely overlooked. Through a proteomic characterization of mitochondrial RNA granules, we identified a diverse array of proteins dedicated to RNA metabolism. Investigation of four uncharacterized putative RNA-binding proteins, including two RNA helicases (DHX30 and DDX28) and two members of the Fas-activated serine-threonine kinase (FASTKD) family (FASTKD2 and FASTKD5), revealed that both helicases and FASTKD2 are essential for mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis showed that DDX28 and FASTKD2 bind the 16S rRNA, while FASTKD5 is involved in the maturation of precursor mRNAs that cannot be processed by the canonical mRNA maturation pathway. Silencing FASTKD5 resulted in a near-complete loss of mature COX I mRNA, which significantly impaired the synthesis of COX I and led to a defect in complex IV assembly.
