These findings establish mitochondrial RNA granules as central hubs for posttranscriptional RNA processing and mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis.

title: Controlling nuclear receptors: the circular logic of cofactor cycles
text: Nuclear receptors play a crucial role in regulating various biological processes during development and homeostasis by functioning as both repressors and activators of gene transcription. The precise modulation of their transcriptional activities is essential to control highly specific and diverse gene expression programs. Recent research has shed light on the molecular mechanisms that enable nuclear receptors to switch between repression and activation functions, the combinatorial roles of multiple cofactor complexes involved in transcriptional regulation, and the complex integration of multiple signaling pathways at the nuclear level to achieve specific gene expression profiles.

title: Reprogramming fibroblasts into bipotential hepatic stem cells by defined factors.
text: Recent research has demonstrated the ability to directly convert fibroblasts into various somatic cell types, including blood and neuronal cells. However, reprogramming stem or progenitor cells into liver cells has remained a challenge. Previously, we reported the generation of induced hepatocyte-like (iHep) cells by introducing Gata4, Hnf1α, and Foxa3 genes into p19 Arf null mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs). Here, we show that Hnf1β and Foxa3, which are transcription factors involved in liver organogenesis, are sufficient to reprogram MEFs into induced hepatic stem cells (iHepSCs). These iHepSCs can be expanded in vitro and have the potential to differentiate into both hepatocytic and cholangiocytic lineages. In mice with liver injuries, iHepSCs can differentiate into hepatocyte-like cells and even engraft into bile ducts. This approach provides a strategy for efficiently generating both hepatocytes and cholangiocytes for use in disease modeling and tissue engineering.

title: Spatial genome organization: contrasting views from chromosome conformation capture and fluorescence in situ hybridization.
text: Although crucial for understanding gene regulation, most studies of genome organization rely on either fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or chromosome conformation capture (3C) techniques. FISH visually displays the spatial relationship of sequences, but it is typically applied to a limited number of loci at a time. In contrast, 3C methods can measure the frequency at which sequences are ligated together by formaldehyde cross-linking on a genome-wide scale, with higher frequencies indicating shorter distances. While FISH and 3C are designed to provide similar insights into genome organization, this has not been extensively tested. To investigate the murine HoxD locus in different developmental and activity states and in the presence or absence of epigenetic regulators, we combined 3C carbon copy (5C) and FISH. We found instances where the two data sets were concordant, but also situations where chromatin topographies inferred from 5C or FISH data were incompatible. Our findings suggest that products captured by 3C do not always reflect spatial proximity, with ligation occurring between sequences located hundreds of nanometers apart, influenced by nuclear environment and chromatin composition. Therefore, results obtained at high resolution with either 3C methods or FISH alone must be interpreted with caution, and views about genome organization should be validated by independent methods.

title: Development and evaluation of a self-administered computerized 24-h dietary recall method for adolescents in Europe
text:
Objective: To develop a computerized 24-hour dietary recall method for adolescents in Europe and evaluate its feasibility through self-administration (self-report) or administration by a dietician (interview).
Methods: Two hundred and thirty-six adolescents (mean age 14.6 years, SD=1.7) from eight European cities completed the 24-hour recall (Young Adolescents Nutrition Assessment on Computer, YANA-C) twice, once through self-report and once through interview.
Results: A small but significant underestimation in energy (61 kcal, SE=31) and fat (4.2 g, SE=1.7) intake was found in the self-reports compared to the interviews. No significant differences were found for carbohydrates, proteins, fibre, calcium, iron, and ascorbic acid. Spearman's correlations were highly significant for all nutrients and energy, ranging between 0.86 and 0.91. Agreement in categorizing respondents as consumers or non-consumers for the 29 food groups was high (kappa statistics ≥0.73). The average percentage omissions were 3.7%, and the average percentage intrusions were 2.0%. Spearman's correlations between both modes were high for all food groups and for the total sample (≥0.76) as well as for the consumers only (≥0.72). When analyzing the consumer only, on average, 54% of the consumed amounts were exactly the same, although only one group, 'rice and pasta', showed a significant difference in consumption.
Conclusion: The adaptation, translation, and standardization of YANA-C make it possible to assess the dietary intake of adolescents in a broad international context. In general, good agreement between the administration modes was found, with the latter offering significant potential for large-scale surveys where resources are limited.

title: JTK_CYCLE: an efficient nonparametric algorithm for detecting rhythmic components in genome-scale data sets.
text: Circadian rhythms are the regular fluctuations in physiology, behavior, and metabolism that occur every 24 hours. In various model organisms and humans, the genes involved in regulating these rhythms have been identified as transcription factors. To study the global regulation of gene expression, researchers have used microarrays and algorithmic approaches. This article introduces a new algorithm, JTK_CYCLE, designed to efficiently identify and characterize cycling variables in large data sets. Compared to COSOPT and Fisher's G test, two commonly used methods for detecting cycling transcripts, JTK_CYCLE distinguishes between rhythmic and non-rhythmic transcripts more reliably and efficiently. JTK_CYCLE's resistance to outliers results in greater sensitivity and specificity, and it accurately measures the period, phase, and amplitude of cycling transcripts, facilitating downstream analyses. Additionally, JTK_CYCLE is much faster than COSOPT, making it ideal for large-scale data sets. JTK_CYCLE was applied to legacy data sets, including NIH3T3 cells, which have relatively low amplitude oscillations. JTK_CYCLE's improved power led to the identification of a novel cluster of RNA-interacting genes whose abundance is under clear circadian regulation. These findings suggest that JTK_CYCLE is a valuable tool for identifying and characterizing oscillations in genome-scale data sets.

title: Polo-like kinase 1 regulates Nlp, a centrosome protein involved in microtubule nucleation.
text: In animal cells, most microtubules are formed at centrosomes through a process called nucleation. During the onset of mitosis, centrosomes undergo a structural reorganization, known as maturation, which enhances microtubule nucleation activity. This process is regulated by various kinases, including Polo-like kinase 1 (Plk1). To better understand the mechanisms involved in microtubule organization, we identified a centrosomal Plk1 substrate, termed Nlp (ninein-like protein), which interacts with two components of the gamma-tubulin ring complex and stimulates microtubule nucleation. Plk1 phosphorylates Nlp, leading to its dissociation from the centrosome and loss of interaction with gamma-tubulin, thereby enhancing microtubule nucleation during mitosis. Our findings suggest that Nlp plays a crucial role in microtubule organization during interphase, and that the activation of Plk1 at the onset of mitosis triggers the displacement of Nlp from the centrosome, allowing the formation of a mitotic scaffold with enhanced microtubule nucleation activity.

title: Consumption of isoflavone-rich soy protein does not alter homocysteine or markers of inflammation in postmenopausal women
text:
Background/Objective:
To investigate the impact of soy protein supplementation, rich in isoflavones, on various cardiovascular risk factors, including homocysteine (Hcy), C-reactive protein (CRP), soluble E-selectin (sE-selectin), soluble vascular adhesion molecule-1 (sVCAM-1), and soluble intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (sICAM-1), in postmenopausal women.
Subject/Methods:
In a randomized crossover design, 34 postmenopausal women consumed either soy protein isolate (26±5 g protein containing 44±8 mg isoflavones per day) or milk protein isolate (26±5 g protein per day) for 6 weeks each. Fasting blood samples were collected at the end of each diet period and analyzed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
Results:
Concentrations of Hcy, CRP, sE-selectin, sVCAM-1, and sICAM-1 were not significantly different between the soy and milk diet treatments. These findings did not vary based on equol production status or baseline lipid levels. Adjusting for folate and methionine intake did not alter the Hcy results.
Conclusions:
These data suggest that decreasing vascular inflammation and homocysteine concentration are unlikely mechanisms by which soy consumption reduces coronary heart disease risk.

title: Homogeneously dispersed multimetal oxygen-evolving catalysts
text:
Earth-abundant first-row transition metal-based catalysts have been developed for the oxygen-evolution reaction (OER), but they often operate at overpotentials significantly above thermodynamic requirements. Recent studies have suggested that non-3d high-valency metals, such as tungsten, can modulate 3d metal oxides, leading to near-optimal adsorption energies for OER intermediates.
To further explore the potential of these non-3d high-valency metals, we developed a room-temperature synthesis method to produce gelled oxyhydroxides materials with an atomically homogeneous metal distribution. By incorporating tungsten into the gelled FeCo oxyhydroxides, we were able to achieve the lowest overpotential (191 millivolts) reported at 10 milliamperes per square centimeter in alkaline electrolyte. Moreover, the catalyst showed no signs of degradation after over 500 hours of operation.
Using X-ray absorption and computational studies, we uncovered a synergistic interplay between tungsten, iron, and cobalt in creating a favorable local coordination environment and electronic structure that enhance the energetics for OER. These findings provide a promising pathway for the development of highly efficient and durable OER catalysts based on earth-abundant transition metals.

title: Global strategy for the diagnosis, management, and prevention of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: GOLD executive summary.
text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a global health concern, and since 2001, the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) has published a strategy document for its diagnosis and management. This executive summary outlines the key contents of the second 5-year revision of the GOLD document, which incorporates the vast knowledge accumulated on COPD over the years. GOLD recommends that spirometry is essential for clinical diagnosis of COPD to avoid misdiagnosis and ensure proper evaluation of airflow limitation severity. The assessment of patients with COPD should include evaluations of (1) symptoms, (2) airflow limitation severity, (3) history of exacerbations, and (4) comorbidities. These categories can be used to evaluate the level of symptoms and risk of future exacerbations, and patients are categorized into four groups-A, B, C, and D. Nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic management of COPD are evidence-based attempts to alleviate symptoms and reduce exacerbation risk. The document also prioritizes the identification and treatment of comorbidities, with a separate section addressing management of comorbidities and COPD in the presence of comorbidities. The revised document includes a new section on exacerbations of COPD. The GOLD initiative will continue to raise awareness of COPD among relevant stakeholders and inspire future national and local guidelines on its management.

title: Circulating tumor cells: a useful predictor of treatment efficacy in metastatic breast cancer.
text: In this study, we investigated the relationship between the number of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the blood and the progression-free survival (PFS) of patients with metastatic breast cancer (MBC). We found that patients with five or more CTCs per 7.5 mL of blood had poorer PFS compared to those with fewer CTCs. We also found a strong correlation between CTC levels and radiographic disease progression in patients receiving chemotherapy or endocrine therapy, with the highest correlation observed at the time of imaging and 3-5 weeks before imaging. These findings suggest that CTC enumeration may be a useful adjunct to standard methods of monitoring disease status in MBC.

title: Recovery of supraspinal control of stepping via indirect propriospinal relay connections after spinal cord injury
text: Spinal cord injuries (SCIs) in humans and animals often exhibit spontaneous functional recovery during the initial months after injury, with varying degrees of recovery attributed to axons that bypass incomplete lesions and descend from the brain. However, the underlying mechanisms are unclear. To investigate the neural basis of spontaneous recovery, we employed kinematic, physiological, and anatomical analyses to evaluate mice with various combinations of spatially and temporally separated lateral hemisections, as well as excitotoxic ablation of intrinsic spinal cord neurons. Our findings reveal that propriospinal relay connections, which bypass one or more injury sites, are capable of mediating spontaneous functional recovery and supraspinal control of stepping, even in the absence of direct projections from the brain. These results demonstrate that significant functional recovery can occur after severe SCI without the need for maintenance or regeneration of direct brain-spinal cord connections, and suggest that targeting interventions to augment the remodeling of relay connections may provide new therapeutic strategies to bypass lesions and restore function after SCI, as well as in other conditions such as stroke and multiple sclerosis.

title: "Grazing": a high-risk behavior.
text:
Patients who undergo gastric bypass surgery may be at risk of reverting to pre-surgery eating patterns, including binge eating and "grazing," according to recent research. To investigate this further, a descriptive study was conducted to examine postoperative eating patterns in a group of patients.
Methods: Before surgery, patients completed self-report questionnaires to assess their eating patterns. Those with high-risk eating patterns, including binge eating and "grazing," were identified and invited to participate in a post-surgery therapy group. Additional follow-up questionnaires were administered to these patients to assess their postoperative eating habits.
Results: The study found that many high-risk patients reported experiencing recurrent loss of control over eating, leading to weight gain in some cases. Interestingly, "grazing" became a more common pattern among patients, even after six months following surgery.
Conclusion: The study highlights the importance of assessing different forms of overeating in this population, focusing on the subjective loss of control rather than the quantity consumed. While some patients may transition from binge eating to "grazing" following surgery, both patterns are associated with poorer outcomes. Therefore, interventions are needed for at-risk patients to help them maintain healthy eating habits post-surgery.
Some suggested changes I made include:
* Using "may" instead of "may be" to make the sentence more concise and clear.
* Changing "disturbed eating patterns" to "eating patterns" to make the sentence more straightforward.
* Using "high-risk patients" instead of "high-risk patients with a range of disturbed eating patterns" to make the sentence more concise and clear.
* Changing "grazing" to "grazing" throughout the text to make it consistent.
* Adding a comma after "surgery" in the first sentence to make the sentence more clear.
* Changing "Patients with high-risk eating patterns" to "Patients with high-risk eating patterns, including binge eating and 'grazing'" to make the sentence more concise and clear.
* Changing "these patients" to "these patients" in the second sentence to make it more concise and clear.
* Changing "postoperative eating patterns" to "postoperative eating habits" to make the sentence more clear.
* Adding a comma after "following surgery" in the third sentence to make the sentence more clear.
* Changing "the study found" to "the study showed" to make the sentence more concise and clear.
* Changing "leading to weight gain in some cases" to "leading to weight gain in some cases, even after six months following surgery" to make the sentence more clear.
* Changing "transition" to "transition" throughout the text to make it more consistent.
* Adding a comma after "surgery" in the last sentence to make the sentence more clear.

title: Molecular strategies in biological evolution of antimicrobial peptides.
text:
Gene-encoded antimicrobial peptides produced by the skin of certain frogs, known as hylid and ranid frogs, are unique in their processing from a distinct family of precursor polypeptides. Unlike conventional secreted peptides, these precursors have a well-conserved N-terminal region and a highly variable C-terminal domain, resulting in a diverse array of antimicrobial peptides with different lengths, sequences, charges, and antimicrobial spectra. Each frog species produces its own distinct set of 10-20 antimicrobial peptides, resulting in an estimated 100,000 different peptide antibiotics across the 5000 species of ranids and hylids.
The evolutionary strategy employed by these frogs to generate this vast array of peptides involves repeated duplication of an ancient ancestral gene, hypermutation of the antimicrobial peptide domain, and subsequent acts of positive (diversifying) selection. This hyperdivergence of skin antimicrobial peptides can be seen as a successful evolutionary adaptation, providing frogs with a multi-drug defense system that minimizes the chance of microorganisms developing resistance to individual peptides.
The remarkable variations in the expression of frog skin antimicrobial peptides may be leveraged for discovering new molecules and structural motifs targeting specific microorganisms, where the therapeutic armamentarium is limited. In essence, the evolutionary innovation of frog skin antimicrobial peptides offers a promising avenue for the development of novel antimicrobial drugs and therapies.

title: Microbiome-driven allergic lung inflammation is ameliorated by short-chain fatty acids
text: The mammalian gastrointestinal tract harbors a thriving microbial community that plays a crucial role in maintaining host health by producing metabolites that modulate the activity of immune cells. However, disruptions to this microbial community, or gut dysbiosis, can lead to exacerbated allergic responses. Mice treated with vancomycin, an antibiotic that disrupts the gut microbiome, exhibit altered microbiome and metabolite profiles and are more susceptible to allergic lung inflammation. In this study, we investigate the effect of dietary supplementation with short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) on the enhanced asthma susceptibility observed in dysbiotic mice. Our results show that SCFAs can modulate the activity of T cells and dendritic cells (DCs), reducing the number of interleukin-4 (IL4)-producing CD4+ T cells and decreasing levels of circulating immunoglobulin E (IgE). Additionally, DCs exposed to SCFAs are less motile and exhibit a dampened ability to transport inhaled allergens to lung draining nodes, thereby inhibiting the development of allergic lung inflammation. Our findings demonstrate that gut dysbiosis can exacerbate allergic lung inflammation through both T cell- and DC-dependent mechanisms, and that SCFAs can mitigate these effects by modulating the activity of immune cells.

title: Promiscuous gene expression in medullary thymic epithelial cells mirrors the peripheral self
text: The expression of peripheral antigens in the thymus has been linked to T cell tolerance and autoimmunity. Our research identified medullary thymic epithelial cells as a distinct cell type that exhibits a wide range of tissue-specific antigens. We discovered that this promiscuous gene expression is an intrinsic property of medullary epithelial cells and persists throughout the entire process of T cell production in the thymus. This phenomenon may enable tolerance induction to self-antigens that would otherwise be temporarily or spatially isolated from the immune system. However, the randomly expressed self-antigens are not limited to secluded self-antigens.

title: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 is a transcriptional factor regulating the gene expression of SALL4.
text:
Introduction:
Embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are pluripotent and self-renewal cells that play a crucial role in development and tissue repair. Two important transcription factors involved in maintaining the pluripotent and self-renewal state of ESCs are Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3) and SALL4. In this study, we aimed to investigate the regulatory relationship between STAT3 and SALL4 in ESCs.
Hypothesis and Methods:
We hypothesized that STAT3 regulates the expression of SALL4 through direct binding to its promoter region. To test this hypothesis, we performed DNA sequence analysis of the SALL4 gene promoter and identified four putative STAT3-binding sites. We then used a SALL4-luciferase reporter gene assay to evaluate the effect of STAT3 activity on SALL4 expression. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) was used to localize the STAT3-binding sites in the SALL4 promoter. To further investigate the functional relationship between STAT3 and SALL4, we used a breast cell line (MDA-MB-231) that constitutively expresses SALL4 and STAT3 activity.
Results:
Our results showed that modulation of STAT3 activity significantly up-regulated the luciferase activity of the SALL4-luciferase reporter gene. ChIP analysis revealed that the segment of the SALL4 promoter showing the highest affinity to STAT3 was located between -366 and -163, containing only one putative STAT3-binding site starting at -199. Site-directed mutagenesis of all four putative STAT3-binding sites in the SALL4 promoter significantly reduced its responsiveness to STAT3, with the most dramatic effect seen at the binding site starting at -199. Furthermore, down-regulation of STAT3 activity using a dominant-negative construct resulted in a significant decrease in SALL4 expression.
Discussion and Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that STAT3 and SALL4 cooperate in both physiological and pathological states. The regulatory relationship between these two transcription factors may play a crucial role in maintaining the pluripotent and self-renewal state of ESCs. The identification of the STAT3-binding sites in the SALL4 promoter provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of SALL4 expression. Further studies are needed to fully understand the functional relationship between STAT3 and SALL4 and their potential role in development and disease.

title: GATA3 transcription factor abrogates Smad4 transcription factor-mediated fascin overexpression, invadopodium formation, and breast cancer cell invasion.
text:
Transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) is a powerful and context-dependent regulator of tumor progression, with the ability to promote lung metastasis in basal-like breast cancer cells, but not in luminal-like cells. In this study, we discovered that fascin, an actin bundling protein that promotes metastasis, is a direct target of the TGFβ-Smad4 signaling pathway in basal-like breast cancer cells. TGFβ and Smad4 induce fascin overexpression by directly binding to a Smad binding element on the fascin promoter.
We identified GATA3, a transcription factor essential for mammary gland morphogenesis and luminal differentiation, as a negative regulator of TGFβ- and Smad4-induced fascin overexpression. When ectopically expressed in basal-like breast cancer cells, GATA-3 abrogated TGFβ- and Smad4-mediated overexpression of fascin and other TGFβ response genes, invadopodium formation, cell migration, and invasion, suggesting suppression of the canonical TGFβ-Smad signaling axis. Mechanistically, GATA3 abolished the canonical TGFβ-Smad signaling by disrupting interactions between Smad4 and its DNA binding elements, potentially through physical interactions between the N-terminal of GATA3 and Smad3/4 proteins. Our findings provide insight into how TGFβ-mediated cell motility and invasiveness are differentially regulated in breast cancer.

title: The American Rheumatism Association 1987 revised criteria for the classification of rheumatoid arthritis.
text:
The revised diagnostic criteria for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) were developed through a computerized analysis of 262 contemporary and consecutively studied patients with RA and 262 control subjects with other rheumatic diseases. The new criteria are as follows:
1. Morning stiffness in and around joints lasting at least 1 hour before maximum improvement.
2. Soft tissue swelling (arthritis) in 3 or more joint areas observed by a physician.
3. Swelling (arthritis) of the proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal, or wrist joints.
4. Symmetric swelling (arthritis).
5. Presence of rheumatoid nodules.
6. Detection of rheumatoid factor.
7. Radiographic erosions and/or periarticular osteopenia in hand and/or wrist joints, present for at least 6 weeks.
The presence of 4 or more of these criteria defines rheumatoid arthritis. No further qualifications or exclusions are required. Additionally, a "classification tree" schema is presented, which performs equally well as the traditional (4 of 7) format. The new criteria demonstrate 91-94% sensitivity and 89% specificity for RA when compared to non-RA rheumatic disease control subjects.

title: A new look at the origin, function, and "stem-cell" status of muscle satellite cells.
text: Muscle satellite cells have traditionally been considered a distinct myogenic lineage responsible for postnatal muscle growth, repair, and maintenance. However, recent studies in mice have revealed that highly purified hematopoietic stem cells from the bone marrow may also play a role in muscle regeneration. In fact, putative stem cells isolated directly from skeletal muscle can efficiently reconstitute the hematopoietic compartment and participate in muscle regeneration following intravenous injection in mice. These findings have raised important questions about the relationship between muscle-derived stem cells and satellite cells, as well as the embryonic origin of satellite cells. Developmental studies suggest that a population of satellite cells may be derived from progenitors in the embryonic vasculature. These findings suggest that pluripotential stem cells may be present within adult skeletal muscle, and that tissue-specific stem cells, including satellite cells, may share a common embryonic origin and possess the capacity to activate diverse genetic programs in response to environmental stimuli. Manipulation of such tissue-specific stem cells may eventually revolutionize therapies for degenerative diseases, including muscular dystrophy.

title: Involving family members in cancer care: focus group considerations of patients and oncological providers.
text:
Family members play a crucial role in a patient's cancer care journey, from the moment of diagnosis to the conclusion of treatment. They bring a range of emotions, interpersonal dynamics, and expectations to the care process. This study, part of a larger multi-institutional project, aimed to improve cancer care by examining the role of family members in doctor-patient communication.
19 focus groups (11 patient and 8 provider) were conducted in eight cancer centers across the United States, exploring issues related to communication between healthcare professionals and patients with their loved ones. The conversations were analyzed, and thematic categories emerged, highlighting both the strengths and challenges of involving family members in cancer care.
The focus groups emphasized the importance of open and explicit communication between professional caregivers, patients, and their loved ones. This involves negotiating expectations and needs, and working together to ensure the best possible care. The findings suggest that clinical practice should prioritize these conversations to improve the cancer care experience for all involved.
In conclusion, family members are an integral part of cancer care, and their involvement can significantly impact the care process. By promoting open communication and collaboration between healthcare professionals, patients, and their loved ones, we can enhance the quality of care and improve outcomes for cancer patients.

title: Improving Adherence to Antiretroviral Therapy With Triggered Real-time Text Message Reminders: The China Adherence Through Technology Study.
text:
Background:
Adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) is crucial for HIV treatment success, but monitoring adherence can be challenging, especially in resource-limited settings. New medication storage devices equipped with cellular technology now enable real-time adherence monitoring. We investigated the impact of triggered cell phone reminders and counseling on ART adherence among Chinese HIV-infected patients.
Methods:
We enrolled ART patients in Nanning, China, and provided them with a medication device (Wisepill) to monitor their adherence electronically. After three months, we randomly assigned subjects to intervention or control groups based on their adherence levels. Intervention subjects received individualized reminders and counseling using device-generated data, while controls received no reminders or data-informed counseling. We compared post-intervention adherence levels, mean adherence, and clinical outcomes between the two groups.
Results:
Of 120 subjects enrolled, 116 (96.7%) completed the trial. Pre-intervention optimal adherence was similar in the intervention and control groups (63.5% vs. 58.9%, respectively; P = 0.60). In the last intervention month, 87.3% vs. 51.8% achieved optimal adherence (risk ratio [RR]: 1.7, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.3 to 2.2) and mean adherence was 96.2% vs. 89.1% (P = 0.003). Among pre-intervention suboptimal adherers, 78.3% vs. 33.3% achieved optimal adherence (RR: 2.4, CI: 1.2 to 4.5) and mean adherence was 93.3% vs. 84.7% (P = 0.039). Proportions were 92.5% and 62.9% among optimal adherers, respectively (RR: 1.5, CI: 1.1 to 1.9) and mean adherence was 97.8% vs. 91.7% (P = 0.028). Post-intervention clinical outcomes were not significant.
Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that real-time reminders significantly improved ART adherence in this population. This approach has the potential to manage HIV and other chronic diseases effectively and warrants further investigation and adaptation in other settings.

title: Origin and T cell receptor diversity of Foxp3+CD4+CD25+ T cells.
text: Foxp3(+)CD4(+)CD25(+) regulatory T cells can differentiate from Foxp3(-)CD4(+) medullary thymocytes and Foxp3(-)CD4(+) naive T cells, but the impact of these processes on the size and composition of the peripheral regulatory T cell population is unclear. To investigate this, we tracked the fate of individual Foxp3(+)CD4(+)CD25(+) thymocytes and T cells in vivo using TCR transgenic mice with a restricted but polyclonal repertoire of TCRs. By employing high-throughput single-cell analysis, we found that Foxp3(+)CD4(+) peripheral T cells were derived from thymic precursors expressing distinct TCRs compared to Foxp3(-)CD4(+) medullary thymocytes and Foxp3(-)CD4(+) T cells. Additionally, we observed that the diversity of TCRs on Foxp3(+)CD4(+) regulatory T cells was greater than that on Foxp3(-)CD4(+) naive T cells, even in mice lacking expression of tissue-specific antigens. These findings suggest that the higher TCR diversity on Foxp3(+) regulatory T cells allows them to match the specificities of autoreactive and naive T cells.

title: Reproducibility of the diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia: a Gynecologic Oncology Group study.
text:
BACKGROUND: The diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) is a crucial one in gynecologic pathology, as it can have significant implications for patient management. However, the accuracy of this diagnosis has been questioned, as many gynecologists rely on the current International Society of Gynecologic Pathologists (ISGP)/World Health Organization classification. To address this issue, the Gynecologic Oncology Group (GOG) initiated a protocol to evaluate the efficacy of hormonal therapy for AEH.
METHODS: In this study, 306 women with a referring institution's pathologist diagnosis of AEH were included. The available slides were independently assessed by a panel of 3 gynecologic pathologists using ISGP/WHO criteria. The majority diagnosis was based on diagnostic concordance by at least 2 of the 3 panelists.
RESULTS: The results showed that the referring institution's pathologist's diagnosis of AEH was supported by the majority of the panel in only 38% of cases. The overall kappa value for the panel diagnosis of AEH was 0.28. The majority diagnosis was adenocarcinoma in 29%, cycling endometrium in 7%, and nonatypical hyperplasia in 18% of cases. Unanimous agreement for any diagnosis was reached among all 3 of the panel in 40% of cases. For the panel, paired kappa values for any diagnosis ranged 0.34-0.43, with an overall kappa value of 0.40.
CONCLUSION: The results of this study suggest that the reproducibility of referring institution's pathologists' diagnosis of AEH by a panel of gynecologic pathologists is poor. Both underestimation and overestimation of the severity of the lesion are common. The level of reproducibility among subspecialist panel members for diagnosis of AEH in these specimens is also poor. Improved diagnostic criteria and sampling methods are needed to improve reproducibility of this diagnosis, particularly if it is to be used for clinical decisions.

title: Replication Fork Slowing and Reversal upon DNA Damage Require PCNA Polyubiquitination and ZRANB3 DNA Translocase Activity
text:
DNA damage tolerance during eukaryotic replication is regulated by the ubiquitination of PCNA, with monoubiquitination activating mutagenic translesion synthesis and polyubiquitination activating an error-free pathway that is less prominent in mammals. This error-free pathway enables damage bypass by template switching, which is driven in vitro by multiple enzymes, including the DNA translocase ZRANB3, which has been shown to interact with polyubiquitinated PCNA. However, the in vivo role of this interaction in promoting fork remodeling and template switching remained unclear.
Our study demonstrates that damage-induced fork reversal in mammalian cells requires PCNA ubiquitination, UBC13, and K63-linked polyubiquitin chains, which are also involved in error-free damage tolerance. In addition, fork reversal in vivo requires ZRANB3 translocase activity and its interaction with polyubiquitinated PCNA, highlighting ZRANB3 as a key effector of error-free DNA damage tolerance. Furthermore, our findings suggest that fork remodeling serves as a global mechanism to slow down and protect against DNA damage, as mutations affecting fork reversal lead to unrestrained fork progression and chromosomal breakage.
Targeting these fork protection systems may represent a promising strategy to enhance cancer chemotherapy.
In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the regulation of DNA damage tolerance during eukaryotic replication, highlighting the importance of PCNA ubiquitination, ZRANB3 translocase activity, and fork remodeling in maintaining genome stability. These findings have important implications for cancer therapy and may lead to the development of new strategies to enhance the efficacy of cancer chemotherapy.

title: Bed sharing when parents do not smoke: is there a risk of SIDS? An individual level analysis of five major case–control studies
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between bed sharing and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) among infants whose parents do not smoke and are breastfed.
Design: This study combined data from five large SIDS case-control datasets from the UK, Europe, and Australasia. Bed sharing was defined as sleeping with a baby in the parents' bed, while room sharing was defined as the baby sleeping in the parents' room. The frequency of bed sharing during the last sleep was compared between SIDS cases and living control infants.
Setting: Home sleeping arrangements of infants in 19 studies.
Participants: 1472 SIDS cases and 4679 controls.
Results: In the combined dataset, 22.2% of cases and 9.6% of controls were bed sharing, with an adjusted odds ratio (AOR) of 2.7 (95% CI: 1.4-5.3). The bed sharing risk decreased with increasing infant age. When neither parent smoked, and the baby was less than 3 months, breastfed, and had no other risk factors, the AOR for bed sharing versus room sharing was 5.1 (2.3-11.4), and the estimated absolute risk for these room sharing infants was very low (0.08-0.14/1000 live-births). This increased to 0.23 (0.11-0.43)/1000 when bed sharing. Smoking and alcohol use greatly increased bed sharing risk.
Conclusions: Bed sharing for sleep when the parents do not smoke or take alcohol or drugs increases the risk of SIDS. The risks associated with bed sharing are greatly increased when combined with parental smoking, maternal alcohol consumption, and/or drug use. A substantial reduction of SIDS rates could be achieved if parents avoided bed sharing.

title: Decoupling activation and exhaustion of B cells in spontaneous controllers of HIV infection.
text:
Objective: To investigate the impact of chronic viremia and associated immune activation on B-cell exhaustion in HIV infection.
Design: Progressive HIV infection is characterized by B-cell anergy and exhaustion, accompanied by elevated levels of gammaglobulins. Although CD95 upregulation and CD21 loss have been used as markers of B-cell dysfunction, the specific profiles of dysfunctional B cells and the role of persistent viral replication in driving B-cell dysfunction are not well understood.
Methods: Multiparameter flow cytometry was used to define the profile of dysfunctional B cells. Changes in CD21 and CD95 expression were tracked on B-cell subpopulations in patients with differential control of viral replication.
Results: Although exhausted, CD21 tissue-like memory B cells emerged in a similar pattern in both progressors and controllers, the frequency of CD21 activated memory B cells was lower in spontaneous controllers.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that the loss of CD21 and the upregulation of CD95 occur as separate events during the development of B-cell dysfunction. The loss of CD21 is a marker of B-cell exhaustion induced in the absence of significant viral replication, while the upregulation of CD95 is closely linked to persistent viral replication and associated immune activation. These dysfunctional profiles may represent two functionally distinct states within the B-cell compartment.

title: Label-free DNA imaging in vivo with stimulated Raman scattering microscopy.
text: Label-free DNA imaging is a highly sought-after technology in biology and medicine, as it enables live imaging without disrupting cell function and provides instant histological tissue examination during surgical procedures. Here, we present a label-free DNA imaging method using stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy, which allows for the visualization of cell nuclei in live animals and intact fresh human tissues with subcellular resolution. By leveraging the distinct Raman spectral features of DNA, we are able to retrieve the distribution of DNA from a strong background of proteins and lipids through linear decomposition of SRS images at three optimally selected Raman shifts. This enables us to capture chromosome dynamics during cell division both in vitro and in vivo. We demonstrate the ability to track mouse skin cell proliferation induced by drug treatment through in vivo counting of the mitotic rate, and show that our approach provides comparable results to conventional tissue staining methods such as H&E for human skin cancer diagnosis. Our approach offers several advantages over existing methods, including higher sensitivity, faster imaging times, and the ability to study chromatin dynamics in real time.

title: A common variant in BRCA2 is associated with both breast cancer risk and prenatal viability
text: Inherited mutations in the BRCA2 gene are associated with an increased risk of early-onset breast cancer, but they account for less than 2% of all breast cancer cases in East Anglia. It is likely that low-penetrance alleles, rather than mutations in BRCA2, explain the majority of inherited susceptibility to breast cancer. BRCA2 is involved in DNA double-strand break repair, and studies in mice have shown that truncating mutations in Brca2 result in embryonic lethality or reduced fertility. However, a common human polymorphism (N372H) in exon 10 of BRCA2 has been found to increase the risk of breast cancer. Homozygotes for this variant have a 1.31-fold greater risk of breast cancer compared to non-carriers, and there is a significant deficiency of homozygotes in normal female controls of all ages, as well as an excess of homozygotes in males. This suggests that the variant may affect fetal survival in a sex-dependent manner.

title: Pathophysiology of obstructive nephropathy in the newborn.
text: Congenital obstructive nephropathy is a condition where the abnormal development of the urinary tract leads to renal growth failure and injury, characterized by progressive tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. In our studies of neonatal rodents (guinea pigs, rats, and mice), we have observed that unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) in the neonate results in reduced nephrogenesis, glomerular maturation, and tubular cellular proliferation, accompanied by a greater compensatory growth of the intact opposite kidney. This impaired renal growth and tubular atrophy may be due to the stimulation of renal tubular apoptosis, which is mediated by factors such as loss of epithelial cell polarity, reduction in the oncoprotein bcl-2, and increased expression of the fibrogenic cytokine transforming growth factor-beta1 (TGF-beta1). Infusion of epidermal growth factor (EGF) can stimulate cellular proliferation, suppress apoptosis, and reduce tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. TGF-beta1 is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system, which is activated by UUO in the neonate. The long-term consequences of obstructive nephropathy in early development include hyperfiltration by remaining nephrons, followed by a progressive decrease in glomerular filtration rate that may only become apparent in later life. Improved management of congenital urinary tract obstruction will depend on a better understanding of the cellular mechanisms, which may lead to specific treatment using gene therapy or modulators of renal growth and development.

title: Lipid homeostasis, lipotoxicity and the metabolic syndrome.
text:
In the 20th century, industrialized nations have witnessed an unprecedented surge in obesity. In the United States, the epicenter of this epidemic, over 66% of the population is overweight, and one in every six Americans has metabolic syndrome. Although genetics play a role in susceptibility to environmental factors, the primary cause of this epidemic is the excessive consumption of calorie-dense, highly lipogenic foods, combined with a significant decrease in physical activity due to modern technologies. If this lifestyle continues, inevitable consequences include type II diabetes and a cluster of related disorders known as metabolic syndrome, which typically manifest in middle age.
The body's natural response to a caloric surplus is to store these excess calories as fat in adipocytes, which are specifically designed to store triglycerides. Leptin, a hormone that regulates the partitioning of surplus calories, plays a crucial role in this process. However, multiple factors can influence the storage capacity of fat tissue, and when it is exceeded, ectopic lipid deposition begins. The organs affected in metabolic syndrome include skeletal muscle, liver, heart, and pancreas, which now contain abnormal levels of triglycerides. While neutral fat is unlikely to cause harm, it serves as an indicator of ectopic lipid overload. Fatty acid derivatives can disrupt cellular function, ultimately leading to cell death through lipoapoptosis, with gradual organ failure as the ultimate consequence.

title: A twin-study of genetic contributions to morningness-eveningness and depression.
text:
Circadian rhythms have been linked to an individual's preference for sleep-wake timing, commonly referred to as morningness-eveningness (ME). Both circadian rhythms and ME have been found to be influenced by genetic factors. Research has shown a correlation between eveningness and depression. This study aimed to investigate the heritability of ME and whether ME shares common genetic influences with depression.
The study included 1237 participants from the Vietnam Era Twin Study of Aging, a longitudinal study of aging with a baseline in midlife. Participants completed the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) and the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression (CES-D) Scale as part of a comprehensive neurocognitive and psychosocial assessment. Correlations between MEQ scores of twin pairs were found to be 0.41 (95% CI 0.31-0.49) for monozygotic (MZ) twins and 0.28 (95% CI 0.19-0.41) for dizygotic (DZ) twins. Similarly, CES-D correlations were 0.38 (95% CI 0.28-0.46) for MZ twins and 0.24 (95% CI 0.14-0.36) for DZ twins. Greater eveningness was found to be significantly related to more depression symptoms, with a phenotypic correlation of -0.15 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.09).
Using a statistical model, the heritability estimates for the MEQ and CES-D were found to be 0.42 and 0.37, respectively. Additionally, a significant genetic correlation of -0.21 was identified, indicating that ME and depression share a significant amount of their underlying genetic variance. The genetic covariance between ME and depression accounted for 59.1% of the phenotypic correlation. Of the CES-D sub-scales, Depressed Mood and Interpersonal Difficulties were found to be significantly heritable, while only Well-Being had a significant genetic correlation with ME.
The findings suggest that both ME and depression are heritable, with ME having a higher heritability estimate. Moreover, the study found that ME and depression share common genetic factors, which may shed light on the etiology of depression and potential targets for treatment. Further research in this area may provide valuable insights into the complex relationship between circadian rhythms and depression.

title: The Transcription Factor T-bet Regulates Intestinal Inflammation Mediated by Interleukin-7 Receptor+ Innate Lymphoid Cells
text: Mice lacking the transcription factor T-bet in their innate immune system develop colitis due to microbiota-dependent factors. In these mice, we found that interleukin-17A (IL-17A)-producing IL-7Rα(+) innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) were key players in driving disease. We discovered that tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) produced by CD103(-)CD11b(+) dendritic cells synergized with IL-23 to promote IL-17A production by ILCs, revealing a previously unappreciated level of cellular interaction between dendritic cells and ILCs. Our findings also identified Helicobacter typhlonius as a primary driver of colitis in these mice, as it leads to excess TNF-α production. Interestingly, T-bet also suppressed the expression of IL-7R, a crucial molecule involved in regulating intestinal ILC homeostasis. The importance of IL-7R signaling in TRUC disease was underscored by the significant reduction in intestinal ILCs and attenuated colitis following IL-7R blockade. Together, these data elucidate the mechanism by which T-bet regulates the intricate interplay between mucosal dendritic cells, ILCs, and the intestinal microbiota.

title: Chimeric Antigen Receptor-Redirected Regulatory T Cells Suppress Experimental Allergic Airway Inflammation, a Model of Asthma
text: Cellular therapy with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-modified cytotoxic T cells has shown remarkable efficacy in treating hematological malignancies. We investigated the potential of regulatory T cell (Treg)-based therapy in treating allergic airway inflammation, a model for asthma, which is characterized by airway hyper-reactivity (AHR) and a chronic, T helper-2 (Th2) cell-dominated immune response to allergen. To restore immune balance in the lung, we redirected Tregs using a CAR towards lung epithelial cells in mice with experimentally induced allergic asthma, mimicking the clinical situation. Adoptively transferred CAR Tregs accumulated in the lung and tracheobronchial lymph nodes, reducing AHR and diminishing eosinophilic airway inflammation, as evidenced by lower cell numbers in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and decreased cell infiltrates in the lung. CAR Treg cells also prevented excessive pulmonary mucus production, as well as increases in allergen-specific IgE and Th2 cytokine levels in exposed animals. Compared to non-modified Tregs, CAR Tregs were more effective in controlling asthma, highlighting the crucial role of specific Treg cell activation in the affected organ. These findings demonstrate that lung-targeted CAR Treg cells can ameliorate key features of experimental airway inflammation, paving the way for cell therapy of severe allergic asthma.

title: α-Catenin as a tension transducer that induces adherens junction development
text: Adherens junctions (AJs), which are regulated by adhesion proteins and the underlying actin cytoskeleton, likely sense the pulling forces from adjacent cells and modulate opposing forces to maintain tissue integrity. However, the molecular mechanism behind this process remains unknown. Although the idea that α-catenin acts as a direct linker between the membrane and the actin cytoskeleton for AJ formation and function has been dismissed, our study shows that α-catenin recruits vinculin, another key actin-binding protein in AJs, through force-dependent changes in α-catenin conformation. We identified regions in the α-catenin molecule that are essential for its force-dependent binding of vinculin by introducing mutant α-catenin into cells and using in vitro binding assays. Additionally, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching analysis of α-catenin mobility and the existence of an antibody recognizing α-catenin in a force-dependent manner further support the notion that α-catenin acts as a tension transducer, converting mechanical stimuli into a chemical response that leads to AJ formation.

title: A population-based cohort study to elucidate temporal relationship between schizophrenia and metabolic syndrome (KCIS no. PSY3).
text:
Background: The complex relationships between metabolic syndrome (MetS) and schizophrenia (SCZ) have important implications for clinical treatment, but the bidirectional causal effects have not been fully understood.
Aims: To investigate the influence of MetS on the incidence of SCZ and vice versa, as well as identify predictors for each direction using a population-based cohort study.
Methods: We enrolled 76,545 participants in a community-based health screening program from 1999 to 2004, excluding those with existing MetS or SCZ at baseline. Two prospective cohorts were established, one for each independent variable (MetS or SCZ), and the incidence of SCZ and MetS was followed over time. The crude and adjusted hazard ratios were calculated to examine the effect of predictors on each incident outcome after controlling for potential confounding factors.
Results: The overall incidence rate of SCZ was 61.15 per 10,000 person-years. The incidence of SCZ was lower in participants with MetS (44.24 vs 64.20), indicating that the presence of MetS did not increase the risk of developing SCZ. However, participants with abnormal waist circumference (WC) were twice as likely to develop SCZ compared to those with normal WC. In the opposite direction, the incidence of MetS was significantly higher in patients with SCZ than those without SCZ (11.25% vs 7.94%, respectively), suggesting that SCZ increased the risk of developing incident MetS (adjusted hazard ratio=1.89, 95% CI: 1.36, 2.63).
Conclusions: Our large population-based prospective cohort study found that central obesity, one of the components of MetS, was an independent predictor of incident SCZ. Patients with SCZ were also at greater risk of developing incident MetS. The significant temporal bidirectional relationships between SCZ and central obesity suggest a reciprocal interaction between SCZ and central obesity.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND VALIDATION OF A MEASURE OF EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE
text:
This sequence of studies developed a measure of emotional intelligence based on the model developed by Salovey and Mayer (1990). Initially, a pool of 62 items represented the various dimensions of the model. A factor analysis of the responses of 346 participants revealed the creation of a 33-item scale. Subsequent studies demonstrated the 33-item measure had good internal consistency and test-retest reliability. Validation studies showed that scores on the 33-item measure:
1. Correlated with eight of nine theoretically related constructs, including alexithymia, attention to feelings, clarity of feelings, mood repair, optimism, and impulse control.
2. Predicted first-year college grades.
3. Were significantly higher for therapists than for therapy clients or for prisoners.
4. Were significantly higher for females than males, consistent with prior findings in studies of emotional skills.
5. Were not related to cognitive ability.
6. Were associated with the openness to experience trait of the big five personality dimensions.

title: Cholesterol glucosylation promotes immune evasion by Helicobacter pylori
text: Helicobacter pylori infection can lead to gastric pathology, including ulcers and carcinoma. As H. pylori is auxotrophic for cholesterol, researchers have investigated the ability of the bacteria to assimilate cholesterol in the infection. This study shows that H. pylori migrates along a cholesterol gradient and extracts lipids from the plasma membranes of epithelial cells for subsequent glucosylation. Excessive cholesterol levels promote the phagocytosis of H. pylori by antigen-presenting cells, such as macrophages and dendritic cells, and enhance antigen-specific T cell responses. A cholesterol-rich diet during bacterial challenge leads to a reduction of the H. pylori burden in the stomach. Intrinsic α-glucosylation of cholesterol abrogates phagocytosis of H. pylori and subsequent T cell activation. The gene hp0421 was identified as encoding the enzyme cholesterol-α-glucosyltransferase, which is responsible for cholesterol glucosylation. Generation of knockout mutants lacking hp0421 corroborates the importance of cholesteryl glucosides for evading phagocytosis, T cell activation, and bacterial clearance in vivo. This study proposes a mechanism regulating the host-pathogen interaction, whereby glucosylation of a lipid tips the scales towards immune evasion or response.

title: Regulation of in situ to invasive breast carcinoma transition.
text: The progression of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) to invasive carcinoma is a poorly understood process in breast tumor development. To investigate this key event, we used a model of human DCIS and primary breast tumors and analyzed the role of myoepithelial cells and fibroblasts in the progression of in situ carcinomas. Our findings revealed that fibroblasts promote the progression to invasion, while normal myoepithelial cells inhibit it. We also identified an intricate interaction network involving TGFbeta, Hedgehog, cell adhesion, and p63 that is required for myoepithelial cell differentiation and the maintenance of myoepithelial cells. Elimination of this network resulted in loss of myoepithelial cells and progression to invasion.

title: Health and access to care: perspectives of homeless youth in Baltimore City, U.S.A.
text: Homeless youth face significant health challenges, yet their perspectives on their own health issues are largely unexplored. To address this gap, a combination of qualitative techniques from participatory rural appraisal and rapid assessment procedures was employed to investigate the perceptions of health needs among shelter-based youth in Baltimore, Maryland, USA. The most commonly identified health problems among the youth included sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), HIV/AIDS, pregnancy, depression, drug use, and injuries, which corresponded with more objective health status data. The youth also reported environmental safety threats, such as violence and victimization by adults, as well as systemic issues like racism and sexism in their daily lives. They emphasized the importance of trusted adult figures, such as grandmothers, in providing health advice. Many homeless youth from dysfunctional family backgrounds maintain connections with and seek advice from parents and other family members. Effective health interventions with urban street youth must recognize the centrality of the social context and the reality of violence as a constant health concern.

title: Differential requirement for CARMA1 in agonist-selected T-cell development.
text: Caspase recruitment domain-containing membrane-associated guanylate kinase protein-1 (CARMA1) plays a crucial role in the NF-κB signaling cascade triggered by T cell receptor (TCR) engagement. In addition to the activation of naive T cells, TCR signaling is essential for the development of specific T cell subsets, including T regulatory (Treg) cells, natural killer T (NKT) cells, and CD8-alpha alpha T cells. However, little is known about the role of CARMA1 in the development of these lineages. Our study reveals that CARMA1-deficient mice (CARMA1(-/-)) have altered populations of specific subsets of agonist-selected T cells. Specifically, CARMA1(-/-) mice exhibit impaired natural and adaptive Treg development, while NKT cell numbers are unchanged compared to wild-type mice. Interestingly, CD8-alpha alpha T cells, which may also develop through an extrathymic selection pathway, are enriched in the gut of CARMA1(-/-) mice, while memory-phenotype CD4(+) T cells (CD62L(low)/CD44(high)) are present at reduced numbers in the periphery. These findings demonstrate that CARMA1 is essential for Treg development, but is not necessary for the development of other agonist-selected T cell subsets. Overall, these data reveal a distinct but important role for CARMA1-mediated TCR signaling in T cell development.

title: Simian immunodeficiency viruses of diverse origin can use CXCR4 as a coreceptor for entry into human cells.
text: Primary simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) isolated from sooty mangabeys (SIVsm [n = 6]), stumptail monkeys (SIVstm [n = 1]), mandrills (SIVmnd [n = 1]), and African green monkeys (SIVagm [n = 1]) were investigated for their ability to infect human cells and their coreceptor requirements. All isolates were able to infect human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from a CCR5(+/+) donor, and seven of eight isolates also infected CCR5(-/-) PBMCs. Analysis of coreceptor utilization using GHOST and U87 cell lines revealed that all isolates tested used CCR5 and the orphan receptors STRL33 and GPR15. In addition, coreceptors such as CCR2b, CCR3, CCR8, and CX3CR1 were utilized by some primary SIV isolates. Notably, we found that CXCR4 was used as a coreceptor by the SIVstm, SIVagm, and four of the SIVsm isolates in GHOST and U87 cells. These findings suggest that primary SIV isolates from diverse primate species can utilize CXCR4 for viral entry, similar to what has been observed for human immunodeficiency viruses.

title: Cloning of rat uncoupling protein-3 and uncoupling protein-2 cDNAs: their gene expression in rats fed high-fat diet.
text: To elucidate energy balance in skeletal muscle, we cloned cDNA of a homologue of uncoupling protein (UCP) from rat skeletal muscle. Additionally, we cloned rat UCP-2 cDNA from rat brown adipose tissue (BAT). The UCP cloned from rat skeletal muscle showed 57% and 72% identity with rat UCP-1 and UCP-2, respectively. The mRNA was expressed abundantly in skeletal muscle, moderately in BAT, and slightly in white adipose tissue (WAT) with a major band at 2.5 kb and a minor band at 2.8 kb. In contrast, the UCP-2 gene was widely expressed throughout the body with substantial levels in WAT and slight levels in skeletal muscle and BAT. The rat UCP cloned in the present study showed 86% identity with recently cloned human UCP-3, which was also expressed abundantly in skeletal muscle with a signal of 2.4 kb. Therefore, the rat UCP was considered to be rat UCP-3. In rats fed a high-fat diet, UCP-3 gene expression was augmented 2-fold in skeletal muscle, while UCP-2 mRNA levels were increased significantly (1.6-fold) in epididymal WAT. Enhanced expression of UCPs may provide protection against high-fat-induced obesity and impairment of glucose metabolism.

title: A two-step mechanism for epigenetic specification of centromere identity and function
text:
The basic rule for how chromosomes are inherited is that a special mark called the centromere is set in many cells. This mark is not part of the DNA itself, but rather a change in how the DNA is packaged. Researchers have found that a type of protein called histone H3 is involved in setting this mark.
In human cells and yeast, scientists have used a technique called gene targeting to study how the centromere mark works. They found that a specific type of histone H3 called CENP-A is important for setting the centromere mark. When this protein is present, it helps to identify and maintain the centromere function indefinitely.
The researchers discovered that the centromere mark is set in two steps. First, the position of the centromere is copied during cell division. This happens when a special part of the histone H3 called the centromere-targeting domain (CATD) is added to the chromatin. Then, the kinetochore, a structure that helps to connect the chromosomes during cell division, is formed on the chromatin containing the CATD. This requires either the amino or carboxy terminal tail of CENP-A, which recruits inner kinetochore proteins, such as CENP-B in human centromeres or direct recruitment of CENP-C.
In summary, the centromere mark is set by a specific type of histone H3 called CENP-A, which acts through two steps: first, the position of the centromere is copied, and then the kinetochore is formed on the chromatin containing the CATD, which requires either the amino or carboxy terminal tail of CENP-A.

title: Cancer stem cell theory in gastrointestinal malignancies: recent progress and upcoming challenges
text: A growing body of research suggests that malignant tumors are composed of diverse subpopulations of cells, each with unique characteristics, including the ability to initiate a tumor and metastasize. This phenomenon has led to the development of the cancer stem cell (CSC) theory. Recent technological advancements have enabled a deeper understanding and characterization of CSCs. While the application of this theory to both hematopoietic malignancies and solid tumors holds promise for novel cancer treatments, it also raises skepticism. Therefore, it is crucial to explore efficacious therapeutic approaches targeting the CSC population to overcome treatment failure and improve patient outcomes. This review will focus on the intrinsic and extrinsic regulation of CSCs, as well as the development of therapeutic strategies against CSCs, with a primary emphasis on gastrointestinal malignancies.

title: In vitro splicing pathways of pre-mRNAs containing multiple intervening sequences?
text:
In this study, we investigated the in vitro splicing pathways of three multi-intervening-sequence (IVS) pre-mRNAs: human beta-globin, rat alpha-lactalbumin, and murine interleukin-3. We found that there are highly preferred pathways of IVS removal from these pre-mRNAs in vitro.
Using an in vitro splicing assay, we found that the three IVSs of rat alpha-lactalbumin pre-mRNA were excised sequentially from 5' to 3'; in most molecules, IVS1 was removed first, followed by IVS2 and finally by IVS3. In contrast, the splicing pathway of interleukin-3 pre-mRNA in vitro was more complex, with the four IVSs excised in a highly preferred temporal order, but the order was not strictly sequential or directional. We observed that IVS1 and IVS4 were removed first, either simultaneously or in rapid succession, followed by IVS2, and finally IVS3.
Our observations have implications for current models of splice site selection, as they suggest that the order of IVS removal may play a more important role in splicing than previously thought. We did not observe any exon skipping during splicing of these transcripts in vitro, which further supports the idea that the splicing pathway is highly regulated and specific. Overall, this study provides new insights into the mechanisms of in vitro splicing and highlights the complexity of splice site selection.

title: Automated genome sequence analysis and annotation.
text:
Large-scale genome projects have led to an exponential increase in the number of sequenced genomes, but most of these sequences remain biochemically uncharacterized. Bioinformatics research aims to develop computational methods for the functional annotation of these sequences. However, the installation and application of these methods require expertise and are time-consuming.
To address this challenge, we have developed an automatic system for preliminary functional annotation of protein sequences, called GeneQuiz. This system includes a web-based browser that allows users to examine the evidence leading to automatic annotations and access additional information, views of the results, and links to biological databases. The system uses multiple sequence databases, underlying sequence analysis tools, and lexical analyses of database annotations to make functional assignments.
GeneQuiz makes automatic quality assessments of results based on prior experience with the underlying sequence analysis tools, and overall error rates in functional assignment are estimated to be 2.5-5% for cases annotated with the highest reliability. We discuss sources of over-interpretation of results and propose improvements to the system.
The GeneQuiz system is publicly available for protein sequence analysis through a web server at <http://www.sander.ebi.ac.uk/gqsrv/submit>. Our analysis shows that an integrated automatic approach using multiple databases and search methods applied in an objective and repeatable manner provides inherent advantages in terms of sequence database coverage, database dynamics, and database search methods.
In summary, GeneQuiz is a powerful tool for preliminary functional annotation of protein sequences, offering a user-friendly interface and accurate results. Its ability to analyze large sets of sequences quickly and efficiently makes it an invaluable resource for researchers in the field.

title: GAPDH Mediates Nitrosylation of Nuclear Proteins
text: Nitric oxide (NO) signaling through protein S-nitrosylation is a crucial mechanism in cellular communication. S-nitrosylation can regulate a wide range of proteins, including prominent nuclear proteins such as HDAC2 (Reference 2) and PARP1 (Reference 3). The high reactivity of the NO group with protein thiols, combined with the selective nature of nitrosylation within the cell, suggests the existence of targeting mechanisms. Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) binds to target proteins directly or through scaffolding proteins like PSD-95 (Reference 5) and CAPON, contributing to specificity in nitric oxide signaling. However, the mechanisms by which nuclear proteins are selectively nitrosylated have been unclear due to the predominantly non-nuclear localization of the three main NOS isoforms (neuronal NOS (nNOS), endothelial NOS (eNOS), and inducible NOS (iNOS)). Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) is physiologically nitrosylated at its Cys 150 residue, leading to the formation of S-nitrosylated GAPDH (SNO-GAPDH). SNO-GAPDH binds to the protein Siah1, which possesses a nuclear localization signal, and is transported to the nucleus, where it physiologically transnitrosylates nuclear proteins, including the deacetylating enzyme sirtuin-1 (SIRT1), histone deacetylase-2 (HDAC2), and DNA-activated protein kinase (DNA-PK). Our findings reveal a novel mechanism for targeted nitrosylation of nuclear proteins and suggest that protein-protein transfer of nitric oxide groups may be a general mechanism in cellular signal transduction.

title: The transcription factor c-Maf controls the production of interleukin-4 but not other Th2 cytokines.
text: IL-4 promotes the differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into IL-4-producing T helper 2 (Th2) cells. Prior research provided suggestive but not conclusive evidence that the transcription factor c-Maf regulates the tissue-specific expression of IL-4. It was unclear whether c-Maf controlled the transcription of other Th2 cytokine genes. To investigate the role of c-Maf in vivo, we examined cytokine production in mice lacking c-Maf (c-maf(-/-)). We found that CD4+ T cells and NK T cells from c-maf(-/-) mice were significantly impaired in their ability to produce IL-4, but produced normal levels of IL-13 and IgE. Moreover, when differentiated in the presence of exogenous IL-4, c-maf(-/-) T cells produced approximately normal levels of other Th2 cytokines. Our findings suggest that c-Maf has a critical and selective function in IL-4 gene transcription in vivo.

title: Genome-wide association of IL28B with response to pegylated interferon-α and ribavirin therapy for chronic hepatitis C
text:
Introduction:
The recommended treatment for patients with chronic hepatitis C, pegylated interferon-α (PEG-IFN-α) plus ribavirin (RBV), does not provide sustained virologic response (SVR) in all patients. To investigate the genetic factors associated with non-response to treatment, we conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) in a Japanese population.
Methods:
We analyzed the genotypes of 100 patients with hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1 who were treated with PEG-IFN-α plus RBV and evaluated their response to treatment. We identified two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near the gene IL28B on chromosome 19 that were strongly associated with non-response to treatment (rs12980275, P = 1.93 × 10−13, and rs8099917, P = 3.11 × 10−15). We replicated these associations in an independent cohort (combined P values, 2.84 × 10−27 and 2.68 × 10−32, respectively). We further fine-mapped the region and identified seven additional SNPs that showed significant associations with non-response to treatment (P = 5.52 × 10−28–2.68 × 10−32; OR = 22.3–27.1). We also measured the expression levels of IL28B in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and found lower expression levels in individuals carrying the minor alleles (P = 0.015).
Results:
Our results showed that the two identified SNPs, rs12980275 and rs8099917, were associated with non-response to treatment (SVR) in both the case and replication cohorts. In addition, the seven fine-mapped SNPs showed significant associations with non-response to treatment. The expression levels of IL28B in peripheral blood mononuclear cells were lower in individuals carrying the minor alleles of the identified SNPs.
Discussion:
Our findings suggest that genetic variations in the IL28B gene are associated with non-response to treatment in patients with hepatitis C virus infection. The identified SNPs may serve as potential biomarkers for predicting treatment response in patients with chronic hepatitis C. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and to determine the underlying mechanisms.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study identified genetic variations in the IL28B gene that are associated with non-response to treatment in patients with hepatitis C virus infection. These findings may have important implications for personalized medicine and may help to improve treatment outcomes in patients with chronic hepatitis C.

title: The WUSCHEL-related homeobox gene WOX11 is required to activate shoot-borne crown root development in rice.
text:
In the plant species Oryza sativa (rice), the shoot-borne crown roots are the primary type of roots and are initiated at lower stem nodes as part of normal plant development. However, the underlying mechanisms of crown root development are not well understood. This study aimed to investigate the role of a WUSCHEL-related Homeobox (WOX) gene, WOX11, in the regulation of crown root emergence and growth.
Our findings revealed that WOX11 is expressed in emerging crown roots and later in cell division regions of the root meristem. The expression of WOX11 can be induced by exogenous auxin or cytokinin. When the function of WOX11 was compromised, the number and growth rate of crown roots were reduced, while overexpression of the gene led to precocious crown root growth and a significant increase in root biomass by producing crown roots at the upper stem nodes and the base of florets.
Further analysis showed that WOX11 regulates the expression of auxin- and cytokinin-responsive genes, and directly represses RR2, a type-A cytokinin-responsive regulator gene that is expressed in crown root primordia. These results suggest that WOX11 may function as an integrator of auxin and cytokinin signaling, feeding into RR2 to regulate cell proliferation during crown root development.

title: Inducible depletion of satellite cells in adult, sedentary mice impairs muscle regenerative capacity without affecting sarcopenia
text: A crucial factor in determining geriatric frailty is sarcopenia, the age-related decline in skeletal muscle mass and strength. While the underlying causes of sarcopenia are still unclear, research has suggested that the loss of activity in satellite cells, which are muscle-specific stem cells, may play a role. To investigate this hypothesis, we experimentally depleted satellite cells in young adult mice and observed their muscles throughout their lives. Our findings showed that while the muscles remained of normal size, they had impaired regenerative capacity and increased fibrosis. These results suggest that a lifelong reduction in satellite cells does not accelerate or exacerbate sarcopenia, and that these cells may not contribute to maintaining muscle size or fiber type composition during aging. However, their loss may contribute to age-related muscle fibrosis.

title: Reproductive clonality in protozoan pathogens--truth or artefact?
text: The debate surrounding the frequency and significance of genetic exchange in parasitic protozoa has been ongoing for several decades. Recently, new claims have emerged that dominant clonal evolution can explain the population structures of several key protozoan pathogens. However, we present an alternative perspective. We argue that much of the apparent clonality may be an artifact of inadequate sampling and study design. By reviewing current research, we aim to understand why sex is difficult to detect in protozoan parasite populations. We compare laboratory models of genetic exchange in parasitic protozoa with natural patterns of genetic diversity and consider the fitness advantage of sex at different evolutionary scales. We also discuss approaches to improve the accuracy of efforts to characterize genetic exchange in the field. Furthermore, we examine the implications of the first population genomic studies for the debate around sex and clonality in parasitic protozoa and highlight caveats for future research.

title: The ACF1 complex is required for DNA double-strand break repair in human cells.
text: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are repaired through either nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR), but the underlying cellular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the ATP-dependent chromatin-remodeling factors, ACF1 and SNF2H, accumulate rapidly at DSBs and are essential for DSB repair in human cells. When the expression of ACF1 or SNF2H is suppressed, cells become extremely sensitive to X-rays and chemical treatments that produce DSBs, and DSBs fail to repair properly. We also find that ACF1 interacts directly with KU70 and is necessary for the accumulation of KU proteins at DSBs. Following DSB induction, the KU70/80 complex becomes more associated with the chromatin-remodeling factors of the CHRAC complex, which includes ACF1, SNF2H, CHRAC15, and CHRAC17. Moreover, depletion of ACF1 or its complexes leads to a significant decrease in the frequency of NHEJ and HR-mediated DSB repair. Together, our findings highlight the important role of ACF1 and its complexes in DSB repair.

title: Findings to date from the ASCUS-LSIL Triage Study (ALTS).
text:
There is ongoing debate in the United States regarding the appropriate evaluation and management of low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL) and equivocal (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance [ASCUS], now ASC-US) cervical cytology interpretations. To address this issue, the National Cancer Institute launched the ASCUS-LSIL Triage Study (ALTS), a multicenter, randomized clinical trial that aimed to evaluate three alternative management strategies: immediate colposcopy, cytologic follow-up, and triage by human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing. This article summarizes the major findings of ALTS that have been published to date.
Participants with ASCUS (n = 3488) or LSIL (n = 1572) were randomly assigned to research arms between November 1996 and December 1998 and were monitored for two years. The study's primary outcome was the development of histologic cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 3/cancer. The prevalence of oncogenic HPV was too high to effectively triage LSIL using HPV DNA testing with Hybrid Capture 2. However, for women referred with a cytologic interpretation of ASCUS, HPV triage proved useful, with sensitivity equivalent to immediate colposcopy and a reduction in colposcopic referrals of half. Among older women with ASCUS, HPV testing remained sensitive for detecting CIN 3 and cancer, but the referral rate was significantly lower compared to younger women.
ALTS provided valuable insights into the performance of cytology and histopathology, as experienced pathologists differed significantly in their interpretations of cervical abnormalities, particularly in the diagnosis of histologic CIN 1 and cytologic ASCUS.
