Nonetheless, it was possible to identify a relatively rare subtype of ASCUS that has a high positive predictive value for identifying women with underlying high-grade CIN. Additional analyses are ongoing.

title: Marine organisms as a source of new anticancer agents.
text: Throughout the past four decades, various active anticancer agents have been derived from both plant and terrestrial microorganisms. The isolation of C-nucleosides from the Caribbean sponge, Cryptotheca crypta, in the 1970s served as the foundation for the synthesis of cytarabine, the first marine-derived anticancer agent to be developed for clinical use. Cytarabine is currently used in the treatment of patients with leukaemia and lymphoma. Additionally, gemcitabine, one of its fluorinated derivatives, has been approved for use in patients with pancreatic, breast, bladder, and non-small-cell lung cancer. In recent years, several new experimental anticancer agents derived from marine sources have entered preclinical and clinical trials, expanding the field significantly due to advancements in deep-sea collection, extraction, and large-scale production through aquaculture and synthesis. This paper provides examples of marine-derived experimental agents currently undergoing preclinical and early clinical evaluation, along with a summary of available information on the results of phase I and II trials of agents such as aplidine, ecteinascidin-734 (ET-734), dolastatin 10, and bryostatin 1.

title: A randomized, placebo-controlled trial of diindolylmethane for breast cancer biomarker modulation in patients taking tamoxifen
text: Diindolylmethane (DIM), a metabolite of indole-3-carbinol found in cruciferous vegetables, has been proposed to have cancer chemopreventive activity in the breast. However, there is limited evidence of both clinically relevant activity and long-term safety data for DIM. To investigate the activity and safety of combined DIM use with tamoxifen in breast cancer patients, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was conducted. One hundred thirty women taking tamoxifen were randomly assigned to receive either oral BR-DIM at 150 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 months. The primary study endpoint was the change in urinary 2/16α-hydroxyestrone (2/16α-OHE1) ratio. Secondary endpoints included changes in 4-hydroxyestrone (4-OHE1), serum estrogens, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), breast density, and tamoxifen metabolites. Compliance with treatment was greater than 91%. BR-DIM significantly increased the 2/16α-OHE1 ratio compared to placebo (-0.7 [−1.7, 0.8], P < 0.001). Additionally, serum SHBG levels increased with BR-DIM compared to placebo (+25 ± 22 and +1.1 ± 19 nmol/L, respectively). No significant changes in breast density were observed using mammography or MRI. Plasma tamoxifen metabolites (endoxifen, 4-OH tamoxifen, and N-desmethyl-tamoxifen) were reduced in women receiving BR-DIM compared to placebo (P < 0.001). Minimal adverse events were reported and did not differ by treatment arm. In conclusion, this study suggests that daily BR-DIM supplementation in tamoxifen-treated breast cancer patients promotes favorable changes in estrogen metabolism and circulating levels of SHBG. Further research is warranted to determine whether BR-DIM-associated decreases in tamoxifen metabolites, including effects on endoxifen levels, may attenuate the clinical benefit of tamoxifen. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01391689).

title: Intracellular coenzymes as natural biomarkers for metabolic activities and mitochondrial anomalies.
text:
Mitochondria are crucial for energy metabolism, programmed cell death, and oxidative stress. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA can impair the structure and function of key enzyme complexes, leading to a variety of health issues, including cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, and aging. Early detection of mitochondrial and metabolic abnormalities is essential for effective diagnosis and therapeutic intervention.
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) play important roles in various cellular oxidation-reduction reactions. Notably, NADH and FAD are naturally fluorescent, allowing for non-invasive imaging of metabolic activities in living cells and tissues. The autofluorescence of NADH and FAD can be excited using distinct wavelengths for complementary imaging methods, and is sensitive to protein binding and local environment. This article highlights recent advancements in using intracellular NADH and FAD as potential biomarkers for metabolic and mitochondrial activities.

title: Biochemical differences in the alphabeta T cell receptor.CD3 surface complex between CD8+ and CD4+ human mature T lymphocytes.
text: In this study, we investigated the differences in the T cell receptor (TCR) complex between CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from individuals lacking the CD3gamma chain (gamma(-)) and compared them to primary T cells from normal (gamma+) donors. We found that the surface TCR.CD3 components from CD4+ gamma- T cells were similar in size to those from CD4+ gamma+ controls, except for a different stoichiometry of the alpha-beta-delta-epsilon (2)zeta (2) complex. In contrast, the surface TCRalpha, TCRbeta, and CD3delta chains of CD8+ gamma- T cells were not present in their usual sizes. Using confocal immunofluorescence and blue native gel electrophoresis (BN-PAGE), we observed a heterogeneous population of TCR.CD3 in these cells. Our results also showed that the monoclonal antibody RW2-8C8 stained CD8+ T cells more strongly than CD4+ T cells, and this difference was dependent on the glycosylation of the TCR.CD3 complex but independent of T cell activation or differentiation. Additionally, we found that RW2-8C8 staining of CD8+ T cells was more dependent on lipid raft integrity than that of CD4+ T cells. Finally, immunoprecipitation studies on purified primary CD4+ and CD8+ T cells revealed TCR glycosylation differences between the two. Taken together, these findings suggest that there are conformational or topological lineage-specific differences in the TCR.CD3 from CD4+ and CD8+ wild-type T cells, which may be relevant for cis interactions during antigen recognition and signal transduction.

title: Circulating mitochondrial DNA in serum of patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
text: Neutrophils play a crucial role in the pathophysiology of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and recent studies have shown that neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are involved in the disease. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is also released during NET formation. In this study, we measured the levels of circulating cell-free mtDNA and genomic DNA in the serum of patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. We enrolled 14 active patients and 11 in remission, along with 10 healthy controls. Using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), we found that both fragments of mtDNA (79 base pairs and 230 base pairs) and genomic DNA were significantly elevated in patients compared to controls. Only the shorter 79 base pair mtDNA fragment correlated with the active stage of the disease and clinical symptoms. Our findings suggest that the extracellular release of mtDNA accompanies the active stage of the disease, and circulating mtDNA levels are high in untreated patients. These results demonstrate the potential of mtDNA as a biomarker for monitoring treatment response.

title: Estrogen receptor-alpha promotes alternative macrophage activation during cutaneous repair.
text: Efficient local recruitment of monocytes/macrophages is crucial for tissue repair. Once recruited, these cells are polarized towards either classical (pro-inflammatory) or alternative (pro-healing) activation, depending on the cytokine environment. Estrogen plays a significant role in regulating this process, acting as an anti-inflammatory regulator of cutaneous healing. However, the understanding of how estrogen/estrogen receptor (ER) contributes to macrophage polarization and its local effects on wound healing is limited. Our study identifies a novel role for ERα signaling in polarizing macrophages towards an alternative phenotype. Cell-specific ER ablation studies demonstrate an in vivo role for inflammatory cell ERα, but not ERβ, in poor healing associated with altered cytokine profiles and reduced numbers of alternatively activated macrophages. Additionally, we reveal intrinsic changes in ERα-deficient macrophages that impair their ability to respond to alternative activation signals in vitro. Overall, our findings demonstrate that ERα-expressed in inflammatory cells promotes alternative macrophage polarization, which is beneficial for timely healing. Given the diverse roles of ERs, these findings are likely to be relevant to many pathologies involving excessive inflammation.

title: Disturbance in cerebral spinal fluid sphingolipid content is associated with memory impairment in subjects infected with the human immunodeficiency virus
text:
Despite the widespread use of antiretroviral therapies to control the replication of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), cognitive dysfunctions known as HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) continue to affect approximately 50% of individuals infected with the virus. Currently, there is no biomarker that can identify HIV-infected individuals at risk of developing HAND. Previous studies have identified specific sphingolipid species that are dysregulated in HAND, but the neurocognitive correlates of these biochemical findings are not well understood.
To address this question, we compared levels of sphingomyelin, ceramide, and sterol species in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with performance on standard neurological tests designed to assess the function of multiple cognitive and motor domains in HIV-infected subjects. Our findings revealed that sphingomyelin:ceramide ratios for specific acyl chain lengths (C16∶0, C18∶0, C22∶0, and C24∶0) were associated with worse performance on several indices of memory. The most significant association was found for the acyl chain of C18∶0, which consistently correlated with performance on multiple tests of memory. These findings suggest that the sphingomyelin:ceramide ratio for C18∶0 may serve as a reasonable surrogate marker for memory dysfunction in HIV-infected individuals.

title: An observational study fluid balance and patient outcomes in the Randomized Evaluation of Normal vs. Augmented Level of Replacement Therapy trial.
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between daily fluid balance during intensive care unit (ICU) stay and clinical outcomes in patients enrolled in the Randomized Evaluation of Normal vs. Augmented Level (RENAL) replacement therapy study.
Design: Statistical analysis of data from multicenter, randomized, controlled trials.
Setting: Thirty-five ICUs in Australia and New Zealand.
Patients: Cohort of 1453 patients enrolled in the RENAL study.
Interventions: We examined the association between daily fluid balance and clinical outcomes using multivariable logistic regression, Cox proportional hazards, time-dependent analysis, and repeated measure analysis models.
Measurements and Main Results: During ICU stay, mean daily fluid balance among survivors was -234 mL/day compared to +560 mL/day among nonsurvivors (p < .0001). Mean cumulative fluid balance over the same period was -1941 vs. +1755 mL (p = .0003). A negative mean daily fluid balance during study treatment was independently associated with a decreased risk of death at 90 days (odds ratio 0.318; 95% confidence interval 0.24-0.43; p < .0001) and with increased survival time (p < .0001). In addition, a negative mean daily fluid balance was associated with significantly increased renal replacement-free days (p = .0017), ICU-free days (p < .0001), and hospital-free days (p = .01). These findings were unaltered after the application of different statistical models.
Conclusions: In the RENAL study, a negative mean daily fluid balance was consistently associated with improved clinical outcomes. Fluid balance may be a target for specific manipulation in future interventional trials of critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy.

title: Prison health care: a review of the literature.
text: The growing prison population and the significant health issues faced by inmates pose a challenge to the dual goals of punishment, rehabilitation, and community reintegration. A literature review highlighted the key health concerns in prison settings, including mental health disorders, substance abuse, and infectious diseases. The unique needs of women prisoners and older inmates must also be taken into account. In addition to providing basic health care, prison health services should prioritize health promotion and community reintegration to ensure the well-being of both prisoners and the broader society. Collaboration between health and prison authorities is crucial to delivering effective health care, and telemedicine is one potential strategy for achieving this goal.

title: A Brief History of Long-Term Potentiation
text: Since the initial discovery of long-term potentiation (LTP) in 1973, a vast array of research has been conducted on this captivating phenomenon, serving as a foundational cellular model for learning and memory. Despite experiencing significant growth pains throughout the years, LTP has finally reached a point of maturity. In this review, we delve into the rich history of LTP and the exciting current state of research. These are indeed thrilling times, with an unprecedented pace of discovery.

title: Tumor-Induced IL-6 Reprograms Host Metabolism to Suppress Anti-tumor Immunity
text: In cancer patients, cachexia, or wasting syndrome, is characterized by caloric deficiency. Our study reveals that tumors manipulate the host's metabolic response to caloric deprivation, leading to immune suppression. In mice with transplanted colorectal cancer or autochthonous pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA), we found that IL-6 reduces the liver's ability to produce ketones by suppressing PPARalpha, the key regulator of ketogenesis. When these mice are subjected to caloric deficiency, their relative hypoketonemia triggers a significant increase in glucocorticoid levels. This hormonal stress response suppresses multiple immune pathways within the tumor. Interestingly, administering corticosterone to raise plasma corticosterone levels to a level lower than that observed in cachectic mice abolishes the response of mouse PDA to an immunotherapy that is currently in clinical trials. Our findings suggest that tumor-induced IL-6 impairs the ketogenic response to reduced caloric intake, leading to a systemic metabolic stress response that hinders anti-cancer immunotherapy.

title: Chaperoning stem cells: a role for heat shock proteins in the modulation of stem cell self-renewal and differentiation?
text: Self-renewal and differentiation of stem cells are closely regulated processes that are influenced by both internal (intrinsic) and external (extrinsic) signals. Molecular chaperones and co-chaperones, including heat shock proteins (Hsp), are ubiquitous proteins that play a crucial role in modulating protein conformation and complex formation. While the function of Hsp is well understood in differentiated cells, its role in stem cells remains unclear. Interestingly, embryonic stem cells exhibit enhanced stress tolerance and high levels of chaperone expression. This review aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of stem cell research from a molecular chaperone perspective, and propose a model of chaperone-mediated self-renewal in mouse embryonic stem cells.

title: How much alcohol and how often? Population based case-control study of alcohol consumption and risk of a major coronary event.
text:
Objective: To investigate the impact of alcohol consumption quantity and frequency on the risk of acute myocardial infarction and coronary death.
Design: A case-control study was conducted in the Lower Hunter region of New South Wales, Australia, from 1983 to 1994.
Subjects: The study included 11,511 men and women aged 35-69 years, with 6077 controls randomly selected from the same population.
Main Outcome Measure: The primary outcome measures were acute myocardial infarction or coronary death.
Results: The study found that men and women who consumed one or two drinks of alcohol on five or six days a week had a lower risk of a major coronary event compared to non-drinkers, after adjusting for age, smoking, and medical history. This reduction in risk was observed in both men and women. Additionally, an acute protective effect of alcohol consumption was found for regular drinkers who consumed one or two drinks in the 24 hours preceding the onset of symptoms.
Conclusion: The study suggests that the frequency and quantity of alcohol consumption are important factors in assessing the risk of a major coronary event. The lowest risk was observed among men who reported drinking one to four drinks daily on five or six days a week and among women who reported drinking one or two drinks daily on five or six days a week.

title: Tracking adipogenesis during white adipose tissue development, expansion and regeneration
text: White adipose tissue exhibits remarkable plasticity, allowing it to adapt and change in response to various stimuli. To investigate this phenomenon, we developed a novel system for the inducible and permanent labeling of mature adipocytes, which we called the AdipoChaser mouse. Using this system, we monitored adipogenesis during development, high-fat diet (HFD) feeding, and cold exposure. Our findings reveal that during cold-induced "browning" of subcutaneous fat, the majority of "beige" adipocytes arise from de novo-differentiated adipocytes. In contrast, epididymal fat initiates adipogenesis after 4 weeks of HFD feeding, while subcutaneous fat undergoes hypertrophy for a period of up to 12 weeks. Interestingly, gonadal fat develops postnatally, while subcutaneous fat develops between embryonic days 14 and 18. Our results highlight the significant differences in adipogenic potential among various fat depots.

title: Blockade of adrenoreceptors inhibits the splenic response to stroke.
text:
Recent research has highlighted the involvement of the immune system in the delayed cellular degeneration that occurs after a stroke. In the permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model of stroke, the spleen shrinks in size, and this reduction is caused by the release of immune cells from the spleen. Systemic treatment with human umbilical cord blood cells (HUCBC) 24 hours after a stroke can block the reduction in spleen size while significantly reducing the size of the affected area in the brain. Splenectomy, or the removal of the spleen, two weeks before a stroke can also reduce the size of the affected area in the brain. This suggests that the spleen plays a detrimental role in the neurodegeneration that occurs after a stroke.
After a stroke, the sympathetic nervous system is activated, leading to increased levels of catecholamines, such as norepinephrine, in the spleen and throughout the body. These catecholamines bind to receptors on the spleen, including alpha and beta receptors. This study aimed to determine whether catecholamines regulate the spleen's response to a stroke.
The study used male Sprague-Dawley rats that were either denervated, or had their nerves to the spleen removed, two weeks before a stroke, or received injections of various drugs to block or activate different types of adrenergic receptors. Denervation did not affect the size of the affected area in the brain or the reduction in spleen size, but treatment with a drug that blocks alpha receptors, prazosin, or a drug that blocks beta receptors, carvedilol, prevented the reduction in spleen size and significantly reduced the size of the affected area in the brain. These results suggest that circulating catecholamines regulate the spleen's response to a stroke through the activation of both alpha and beta adrenergic receptors.

title: Effects of Thiazolidinediones on Stroke Recovery: A Case-Matched Controlled Study
text: Anti-inflammatory therapy has been shown to decrease infarct size and enhance stroke recovery. Thiazolidinedione peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)gamma agonists, such as pioglitazone and rosiglitazone, have potent anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing effects, making them a promising treatment option for stroke patients with type 2 diabetes. In a recent study, 30 stroke patients with type 2 diabetes who were admitted for inpatient stroke rehabilitation were randomly assigned to receive either pioglitazone or rosiglitazone, and their outcomes were compared to a control group of 30 stroke patients with type 2 diabetes who did not receive thiazolidinediones. The results showed that the thiazolidinedione-treated group exhibited significantly greater improvement in functional independence measure (FIMTM) scores compared to the control group (25.6 ± 10.2 SD vs. 19.8 ± 10.5, respectively, P = 0.015). There was no significant difference in length of rehabilitation hospital stay or final discharge destination between the two groups. These findings suggest that the use of thiazolidinediones may be associated with enhanced functional recovery in stroke patients with type 2 diabetes.

title: Crosstalk between tumor and endothelial cells promotes tumor angiogenesis by MAPK activation of Notch signaling.
text: Although significant progress has been made in understanding the induction of tumor vasculature by secreted angiogenic factors, little is known about the role of direct cell-to-cell contact in promoting tumor angiogenesis. In this study, we investigate the potential of Notch ligand Jagged1, induced by growth factors via mitogen-activating protein kinase (MAPK) in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) cells, to promote angiogenesis. Our findings reveal that Jagged1 activation in HNSCC cells leads to the formation of capillary-like sprouts in nearby endothelial cells (ECs), resulting in enhanced neovascularization and tumor growth in vivo. Furthermore, we found a significant correlation between the level of Jagged1 expression and tumor blood vessel content, as well as an association with the development of HNSCC. Our results provide insight into a novel mechanism by which the direct interaction between tumor cells and ECs promotes angiogenesis through the MAPK and Notch signaling pathways.

title: A Sequential splicing mechanism promotes selection of an optimal exon by repositioning a downstream 5' splice site in preprotachykinin pre-mRNA.
text: To investigate the molecular basis of alternative splicing, we analyzed the splicing of pre-mRNAs containing an optional exon, E4, from the preprotachykinin gene. This gene encodes substance P and related tachykinin peptides through alternative splicing of a common pre-mRNA. Our findings reveal that the skipping of E4 is the predominant mechanism of alternative splicing in this gene. However, the incorporation of E4 into the final spliced RNA is constrained by an initial block to splicing of the upstream intervening sequence (IVS), IVS3. This block is relieved by sequential splicing, which removes the downstream IVS4, resulting in a structural change that promotes IVS3 splicing. To identify the structural changes that promote IVS3 splicing, we examined the effects of various mutations on splicing activity. The most significant effect was observed when a 2-nucleotide substitution was made at the 5' splice site of E4, converting it to an exact consensus match, GUAAGU. Interestingly, the inclusion of exon 5 sequences alone was not sufficient to promote splicing, but when a 15-nucleotide segment containing GUAAGU was inserted into a splicing-defective mutant just downstream of the hybrid exon segment E4E5, splicing activity was restored. Additionally, we found that the 72-nucleotide L2 exon of adenovirus, without its associated 5' splice site, can activate splicing when juxtaposed to E4. These findings suggest that RNA structural changes play a crucial role in the regulation of alternative splicing.

title: Melatonin and the circadian regulation of sleep initiation, consolidation, structure, and the sleep EEG.
text: The endogenous melatonin rhythm, regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, exhibits a close association with the endogenous sleep propensity rhythm and the EEG oscillations that occur during sleep, such as sleep spindles and slow waves. This association persists even when the sleep-wake cycle is desynchronized from the melatonin endogenous circadian rhythm. Administration of melatonin during the day leads to increased daytime sleep propensity, as evidenced by shorter sleep onset latency and improved sleep consolidation. The EEG during daytime sleep after melatonin administration resembles the EEG patterns observed during nocturnal sleep, with increased sleep spindle activity and decreased slow-wave sleep and slow-wave activity, as detected by quantitative EEG analysis. Higher doses of melatonin (5 mg or more) administered before nocturnal sleep result in increased REM sleep. These findings demonstrate that melatonin has a significant impact on the main characteristics of human sleep, including latency to sleep onset, sleep consolidation, slow waves, sleep spindles, and REM sleep. Further studies using physiologically relevant doses and delivery systems that generate physiological plasma melatonin profiles are needed to fully elucidate the role of the endogenous circadian rhythm of melatonin in the circadian regulation of sleep.

title: Long-term survival, quality of life, and quality-adjusted life-years among critically ill elderly patients.
text:
Objective: To evaluate mortality, quality of life (QOL), and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) in critically ill elderly patients.
Design: Cross-sectional survey.
Setting: A ten-bed medical-surgical intensive care unit (ICU) in a tertiary care university hospital.
Patients: The study included 882 elderly patients (aged 65 years or older) and 1,827 controls (younger than 65 years) treated between 1995 and 2000.
Intervention: None.
Measurements and Main Results: Mortality was assessed during ICU and hospital stays, as well as 12, 24, and 36 months after ICU discharge. The cumulative 3-year mortality rate among the elderly (57%) was higher than that among the controls (40%). The majority (66%) of elderly nonsurvivors died within one month after ICU discharge. All elderly patients with day-1 Sequential Organ Failure (SOFA) scores >15 died during the ICU stay. QOL was assessed using EQ-5D and RAND-36 measures from 10 months to 7 years after discharge. The majority (88%) of elderly survivors reported good or satisfactory health state, with 66% finding it similar or better than 12 months earlier, and 48% similar or better than their pre-admission state. QOL measures by RAND-36 revealed that aging decreased competencies most in physical functioning, physical role limitations, and vitality, but the elderly had better values in mental health than the controls. However, QALYs of the elderly respondents were 21% to 35% lower than the mean QALY minus 2 sd units of the age- and gender-adjusted general population.
Conclusions: While high age alone is not a valid reason to refuse intensive care, the benefits perceived by intensive care seem to decrease with aging, if reflected as QALYs. However, 97% of elderly survivors lived at home, and 88% of them considered their QOL satisfactory or good after hospital discharge, highlighting the need for more reliable information on the outcome for the elderly.

title: Recent developments and complexities in neutrophil transmigration.
text: The purpose of this review is to highlight recent advances in the understanding of the mechanisms that govern neutrophil migration from the bloodstream to inflamed tissues, which is a crucial component of the innate immune response and a key factor in the development of inflammatory disorders. This field of research has seen significant progress in recent years, particularly in the areas of leukocyte luminal crawling, cellular and molecular changes in leukocytes and endothelial cells, and neutrophil migration through the endothelial barrier. The review will cover the prerequisites for neutrophil migration, including the formation of protrusions on endothelial cells, and the regulation of endothelial cell luminal and junctional adhesion molecules. Additionally, the review will discuss neutrophil migration through the vascular pericyte coverage and basement membrane. Overall, a better understanding of the mechanisms that mediate neutrophil migration may lead to the development of more specific anti-inflammatory interventions.

title: Exploring the epidemiological characteristics of cancers of unknown primary site in an Australian population: implications for research and clinical care.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the trends in incidence, mortality, and survival rates of cancer of unknown primary site (CUP) in South Australia and to identify clinical implications.
Methodology:
The study used data from the South Australian Cancer Registry to calculate age-standardized incidence and mortality rates from 1977 to 2004. The study also investigated disease-specific survival, socio-demographic, histological, and secular predictors of CUP compared to cancers of known primary site and CUP histological types using multivariable logistic regression.
Results:
The incidence and mortality rates of CUP increased by approximately 60% between 1977-80 and 1981-84, with rates peaking in 1993-96. The male to female incidence and mortality rate ratios were approximately 1.3:1. The incidence and mortality rates increased with age, and the odds of unspecified histological type were higher for males than females, non-metropolitan residents, low socio-economic areas, and for the period 1977-88 compared to subsequent diagnostic periods. CUP represented a higher proportion of cancers in Indigenous patients. The case survival rate was 7% at 10 years from diagnosis, and factors predictive of lower case survival included older age, male sex, Indigenous status, lower socio-economic status, and unspecified histology type.
Conclusion:
The study found poor outcomes for CUP, with a modest improvement in survival. The study identified socio-demographic groups at elevated risk of CUP and worse treatment outcomes, highlighting the need for increased research and clinical attention in these groups.

title: Alkylating agent melphalan augments the efficacy of adoptive immunotherapy using tumor-specific CD4+ T cells.
text:
In recent years, the immune-enhancing properties of certain chemotherapy drugs have gained increasing attention. This has led to the exploration of combining conventional chemotherapy with immunotherapy strategies to achieve sustained therapeutic benefits. Previous studies have shown that melphalan, a commonly used alkylating agent for treating multiple myeloma, has immunomodulatory effects. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
In this study, we investigated the impact of melphalan on endogenous immune cells and adoptively transferred tumor-specific CD4+ T cells in tumor-bearing mice. We found that melphalan treatment led to a rapid release of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines during the cellular recovery phase after myelodepletion and leukodepletion. Additionally, tumor cells exhibited characteristics of immunogenic cell death, including the translocation of the endoplasmic reticulum-resident calreticulin and the extracellular release of high-mobility group box 1. Furthermore, there was enhanced tumor antigen uptake by dendritic cells in the tumor-draining lymph node.
Our findings provide mechanistic insights into the immunostimulatory effects of melphalan and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of combining melphalan with adoptive cell therapy using tumor-specific CD4+ T cells. We found that the combination of melphalan and CD4+ T cell adoptive cell therapy was more effective than either treatment alone in prolonging the survival of mice with advanced B cell lymphomas or colorectal tumors. These results suggest that combining chemotherapy with immunotherapy may be a promising strategy for treating various types of cancer.

title: Influence of cigarette smoking on inhaled corticosteroid treatment in mild asthma.
text:
BACKGROUND: Although inhaled corticosteroids have been established as a treatment for asthma, there is a lack of research on the impact of cigarette smoking on their effectiveness. This study aimed to investigate the effect of active cigarette smoking on the response to treatment with inhaled corticosteroids in patients with mild asthma.
METHODS: In a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study, 38 adult asthmatic patients (21 non-smokers) were given inhaled fluticasone propionate (1000 microg/day) or placebo for three weeks. Efficacy was assessed using morning and evening peak expiratory flow (PEF) readings, spirometric parameters, bronchial hyperreactivity, and sputum eosinophil counts. The study compared the responses to treatment in non-smoking and smoking asthmatic patients.
RESULTS: The results showed a significantly greater increase in mean morning PEF in non-smokers compared to smokers following inhaled fluticasone (27 l/min vs -5 l/min). Non-smokers also had a statistically significant increase in mean morning PEF (27 l/min), mean forced expiratory volume in 1 second (0.17 l), and geometric mean PC20 (2.6 doubling doses), as well as a significant decrease in the proportion of sputum eosinophils (-1.75%) after fluticasone compared to placebo. No significant changes were observed in the smoking asthmatic patients for any of these parameters.
CONCLUSIONS: The study found that active cigarette smoking impairs the efficacy of short-term inhaled corticosteroid treatment in mild asthma. These findings have important implications for the management of patients with mild asthma who smoke.

title: Hitting the target: emerging technologies in the search for kinase substrates.
text:
Through phosphorylation, protein kinases can modulate the activity, localization, protein interactions, and stability of their target proteins. Despite the significance of identifying these substrates in understanding cellular processes, progress has been slow due to the challenges associated with identifying bona fide substrates of specific protein kinases. Traditional methods, such as genetic screens, yeast two-hybrid assays, and biochemical purification, are often time-consuming and unreliable. However, recent advances have led to the development of novel approaches that have successfully identified genuine in vivo substrates of certain protein kinases. These methods include:
1. Screening for phosphorylation of proteins from phage expression libraries: This approach involves using a phage library containing a diverse range of proteins and screening for those that are phosphorylated by a specific kinase.
2. Peptide library screens to determine optimal motifs favored by specific kinases: This method involves creating a library of peptides containing different sequences and testing their ability to be phosphorylated by a particular kinase.
3. Use of phospho-motif antibodies: These antibodies are specific to phosphorylated sequences and can be used to identify proteins that are phosphorylated by a particular kinase.
4. An approach that uses structurally altered kinases and allele-specific adenosine triphosphate analogs and kinase inhibitors: This method involves using mutated kinases that are unable to phosphorylate their normal substrates, and instead, phosphorylate a specific substrate of interest.
We discuss the advantages and limitations of each approach and highlight their potential applications in understanding protein kinase function and regulation.

title: Histone phosphorylation: a chromatin modification involved in diverse nuclear events.
text:
Histone posttranslational modifications play a crucial role in modulating chromatin structure and are involved in various cellular processes. These modifications act as signals for the recruitment, assembly, or retention of chromatin-associated factors and are essential for chromatin remodeling linked to nuclear processes. While histone phosphorylation is best known for its role in cellular response to DNA damage, such as demarcating large chromatin domains around the site of DNA breakage, it also plays important roles in other chromatin-based events, including DNA repair, transcription, and chromatin compaction during cell division and apoptosis.
Several kinases and phosphatases regulate histone phosphorylation, and the interplay between these enzymes and other histone modifications allows for intricate control over chromatin remodeling processes. This complex regulatory network enables cells to fine-tune their chromatin structure and function in response to various stimuli, ensuring proper cellular function and maintaining genome stability.
In this review, we summarize the current knowledge of histone phosphorylation and its key roles in various cellular processes. We discuss the different kinases and phosphatases involved in regulating histone phosphorylation and their impact on chromatin remodeling. Additionally, we highlight the intricate crosstalk between phosphorylation and other histone modifications, which allows for sophisticated control over chromatin remodeling processes.
In summary, histone posttranslational modifications are essential for chromatin structure and function, and histone phosphorylation plays a crucial role in various cellular processes. The complex regulatory network involving histone phosphorylation and other modifications allows for intricate control over chromatin remodeling, ensuring proper cellular function and maintaining genome stability.

title: Neurodevelopmental Outcome After a Single Course of Antenatal Steroids in Children Born Preterm: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
text:
Objective: To systematically review and integrate data on the neurodevelopmental outcome of children after administration of a single course of antenatal corticosteroids for threatened preterm labor.
Data Sources: Medline, Scopus, CENTRAL, and clinicaltrials.gov (inception to August 2014) using combinations of terms such as "prenatal," "antenatal," "cortico*," "*steroid*," "betamethasone," "dexamethasone," "neurodevelopment*," "*development*," and "follow-up." We perused the references of the retrieved articles.
Methods of Study Selection: We included randomized and nonrandomized trials reporting on the neurodevelopmental outcomes of children whose mothers were administered a single course of betamethasone or dexamethasone antenatally for threatened preterm birth as opposed to placebo or no treatment.
Results: Summary risk ratio (RR) was calculated for dichotomous data; standardized mean difference was calculated for trials that measured the same outcome but used different methods. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I statistic. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were planned according to study design, specific steroid, and mean gestational age at birth. A single course of antenatal corticosteroids was associated with reduced risk for cerebral palsy (seven studies; treated: 390 of 5,199, untreated: 146 of 1,379; RR 0.678, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.564-0.815), psychomotor development index less than 70 (two studies; treated: 783 of 3,049, untreated: 258 of 969; RR 0.829, 95% CI 0.737-0.933), and severe disability (five studies; treated: 1,567 of 4,840, untreated: 475 of 1,211; RR 0.787, 95% CI 0.729-0.850). Steroid treatment increased the rates of intact survival (six studies; treated: 1,082 of 2,013, untreated: 273 of 561; RR 1.186, 95% CI 1.056-1.332). Betamethasone was found to significantly decrease the risk for severe disability and increase the rate of intact survival. Dexamethasone increased the rate of intact survival; however, data for dexametasone and the other planned subgroup analyses were limited (fewer than 1,000 children at most). The major limitations involved inclusion of nonrandomized studies and scarcity of data on finer neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Conclusion: A single course of antenatal corticosteroids in women at high risk for preterm birth appears to improve most neurodevelopmental outcomes in offspring born before 34 weeks of gestation.

title: Prognostic impact of minimal pleural effusion in non-small-cell lung cancer.
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the clinical significance of minimal pleural effusion (PE) in patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Although minimal PE may represent an early phase of malignant PE, its prognostic implications have rarely been explored. Therefore, we examined the prevalence of minimal PE in our patient population and its impact on survival. We also considered possible accumulation mechanisms in our data set.
Our study included 2,061 patients with NSCLC, of whom 272 (13.2%) had minimal PE. The distribution of patients by stage was as follows: 5.2% stage I, 10.9% stage II, 13.2% stage IIIA, 23.8% stage IIIB, and 13.9% stage IV. Minimal PE was found to significantly correlate with shorter survival time compared to no PE (median survival time, 7.7 months vs 17.7 months; log-rank P < .001), even after adjusting for all variables. The prognostic impact of minimal PE was higher in early-stage disease (Pinteraction = .001). In patients with minimal PE (n = 237), pleural invasion or attachment as a direct mechanism was observed in 87.8%, and it emerged as an independent factor predicting poorer survival (P = .03).
In conclusion, our findings suggest that minimal PE is a common and prognostically significant finding in NSCLC patients. Its presence is particularly important in early-stage disease, where it may indicate poorer survival outcomes. Further investigation into the mechanisms of minimal PE accumulation may lead to improved diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for NSCLC patients.

title: Fusion proteins for versatile antigen targeting to cell surface receptors reveal differential capacity to prime immune responses.
text: Targeting proteins to antigen-presenting cells (APCs) is a promising approach to elicit adaptive immune responses. However, the relationship between the choice of targeted receptor and the quality and quantity of responses remains poorly understood. We describe a strategy for expressing antigens, including hydrophobic proteins, as soluble fusion proteins that are optimized for proteasome-dependent major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I-restricted cross-presentation and form stable complexes with a wide variety of targeting antibodies. Upon subcutaneous immunization, these complexes were initially taken up by CD169+ lymph node subcapsular sinus macrophages. In the ovalbumin (OVA) model system, receptor-targeted antigenic complexes primed specific T and B cell responses in vitro and in vivo at least 100-fold more efficiently than antigen alone. Comparing 10 targeting receptors allowed us to establish a ranking with respect to priming of CD8+ T cell responses and demonstrated striking differences with respect to the relative efficacy of CD8+ and CD4+ T cell subset and B cell priming. The described fusion proteins should help in developing optimized strategies for targeted delivery of protein antigens in the context of tolerization or vaccination.

title: A sequential model for peptide binding and transport by the transporters associated with antigen processing.
text: The TAP proteins facilitate the translocation of antigenic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). However, investigations into the specificity of this process have been hindered by TAP-independent factors that influence the amount of peptide accumulation in the ER during transport assays. To overcome this challenge, we have developed an overexpression system that allows for the separate quantification of peptide binding to the TAP substrate-binding site and peptide transport by TAP. Our findings reveal that the efficiency of peptide accumulation in the ER is directly proportional to the affinity of the peptide for the TAP substrate-binding site. However, this process can be modulated by interactions with the glycosylation system within the ER and, likely, peptide efflux. Interestingly, random peptide mixtures of 9-16 amino acids exhibit significantly higher affinity for the TAP substrate-binding site compared to shorter or longer peptides. Additionally, our results suggest a model for TAP function, in which peptides bind to TAP heteromers in the absence of ATP and are released upon the binding of ATP.

title: Outcome of repeated radiosurgery for recurrent metastatic brain tumors.
text:
Objective: We investigated the outcomes of repeat gamma knife radiosurgery (GKS) in patients who experienced local or distant recurrence after initial radiosurgery.
Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 204 patients who underwent GKS, of whom 43 (21%) underwent repeat radiosurgery for recurrence at the original treatment site or new lesions at remote sites. The second GKS was given to 16 patients for local recurrence, 13 for new lesions at remote sites, and 14 for both local recurrence and new lesions.
Results: The median survival time from the first GKS was 36 weeks (7-190 weeks) in all patients and 68 weeks (16-156 weeks) in patients who underwent repeat GKS. The median time between the first and second GKS was 37 weeks. The median survival time after the second radiosurgical intervention was 32 weeks (7-132 weeks). The local control rate at 6 months after salvage GKS was 90.7%. The most significant prognostic factor in both initial and salvage GKS was the RPA class.
Conclusion: Recurrence is common in patients with metastatic brain tumors after initial radiosurgery. The survival time and local control rate after salvage GKS are comparable to those after initial radiosurgery. GKS as a salvage treatment may provide additional survival benefit in select patients.

title: Human CYP3A4 and murine Cyp3A11 are regulated by equol and genistein via the pregnane X receptor in a species-specific manner.
text:
Introduction:
The Pregnane X receptor (PXR) is a crucial component of the body's adaptive defense system, responsible for eliminating harmful xenobiotics. PXR activation by endogenous and exogenous chemicals, including steroids, antibiotics, bile acids, and herbal compounds, leads to the induction of drug metabolism. In this study, we investigated the ability of isoflavones, including genistein, daidzein, and the metabolite equol, to activate human and mouse PXR in vitro and in vivo.
Methods:
We conducted cell-based transient transfection studies using primary hepatocytes and a mammalian 2-hybrid assay to evaluate the activation of PXR by isoflavones. The expression of the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) promoter was also examined in human hepatocytes treated with equol.
Results:
Our results showed that isoflavones, particularly equol, are able to activate PXR in both human and mouse systems. In vitro studies revealed that equol was the most potent activator of human PXR, while genistein and daidzein were less effective. In vivo studies demonstrated that equol induced the expression of CYP3A11 mRNA and protein in mice fed a soy protein-containing diet. Conversely, treatment of wild-type, but not PXR(-/-), mouse hepatocytes with genistein and daidzein resulted in the induction of Cyp3A11 mRNA.
Discussion:
Our findings suggest that there is a species-specific difference in the activation of PXR by isoflavones, with equol being the most potent activator in both human and mouse systems. These results have important implications for the development of new drugs and therapies that target PXR, as well as for the understanding of the mechanisms underlying the effects of isoflavones on drug metabolism.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study provides evidence that isoflavones, including equol, are able to activate PXR in both human and mouse systems. These findings have important implications for the development of new drugs and therapies that target PXR, as well as for the understanding of the mechanisms underlying the effects of isoflavones on drug metabolism. Further research is needed to fully understand the complex interactions between isoflavones and PXR, and to explore the potential therapeutic applications of these findings.

title: Metabolism of glucose, glutamine, long-chain fatty acids and ketone bodies by murine macrophages.
text: In this study, the activities of key enzymes involved in metabolism were investigated in elicited (inflammatory) macrophages of mice and lymph node lymphocytes of rats. The results showed that hexokinase activity in macrophages was very high, comparable to any other major tissue in the body, and higher than phosphorylase or 6-phosphofructokinase activity, suggesting that glucose is a more important fuel source than glycogen and that the pentose phosphate pathway is also important in these cells. However, when macrophages were incubated in vitro, the rate of glucose utilization was significantly lower than the activity of 6-phosphofructokinase, indicating that the rate of glycolysis increases dramatically during phagocytosis or increased secretory activity. Macrophages had higher activities of citrate synthase and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase than lymphocytes, suggesting that the tricarboxylic acid cycle is important for energy generation in these cells. The activity of 3-oxoacid CoA-transferase was higher in macrophages, but that of 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase was significantly lower in lymphocytes. Additionally, the activity of carnitine palmitoyltransferase was higher in macrophages, suggesting that both fatty acids and acetoacetate can provide acetyl-CoA as a substrate for the tricarboxylic acid cycle. No detectable rate of acetoacetate or 3-hydroxybutyrate utilization was observed during incubation of resting macrophages, but the rate of oleate utilization was 1.0 nmol/h per mg of protein or about 2.2% of the activity of palmitoyltransferase. The activity of glutaminase was found to be about 4-fold higher in macrophages than in lymphocytes, indicating that the rate of glutamine utilization could be very high. The rate of glutamine utilization by resting macrophages was similar to that reported for rat lymphocytes, but was considerably lower than the activity of glutaminase.

title: TGF-beta inhibition of endothelial cell proliferation: alteration of EGF binding and EGF-induced growth-regulatory (competence) gene expression.
text: Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) inhibits the growth of endothelial cells derived from various sources, including human umbilical vein, bovine aorta, and rat heart. Prolonged exposure of rat heart endothelial cells to TGF-beta leads to significant changes in cell morphology that are characteristic of senescent cells. These changes are accompanied by a decrease in the number of high-affinity receptors for epidermal growth factor (EGF), with minimal alteration in total receptor number. Furthermore, the expression of specific competence genes (c-myc, JE, KC) induced by EGF is reduced, while the induction of c-fos gene expression by EGF remains unchanged in response to TGF-beta treatment. These findings suggest that growth inhibitors like TGF-beta may modulate the cell's response to growth-stimulatory factors.

title: Human NK cells in acute myeloid leukaemia patients: analysis of NK cell-activating receptors and their ligands
text: NK cell activation is tightly regulated to protect healthy cells while eliminating cancerous or virally infected cells. NK cells have a diverse array of surface receptors that enable them to discriminate between normal and abnormal cells. The expression of certain receptors on NK cells can determine whether they become activated and kill target cells. In this study, we found that NKp46, NKp30, DNAM-1, CD244, and CD94/NKG2C activating receptors were reduced on NK cells from acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients. This reduction may be caused by chronic exposure to ligands on leukemic blasts. We identified ligands for NK cell-activating receptors on leukemic blasts, including DNAM-1 ligands, which are frequently expressed, and the NKG2D ligand MICA/B, which is present in half of the patients. Only one-fourth of the patients expressed the CD48 ligand, which is also a target for CD244. The decreased expression of activating receptors and/or the variable expression of ligands on leukemic blasts can impair NK cell-mediated immunosurveillance, leading to inadequate tumor immunity. Understanding the activating receptor repertoire on NK cells and their ligands on leukemic blasts will provide new opportunities for immunotherapy against leukemia.

title: Production of interleukin-6 in contracting human skeletal muscles can account for the exercise-induced increase in plasma interleukin-6.
text:
In this study, we investigated the contribution of skeletal muscle to the accumulation of interleukin-6 (IL-6) in the blood during prolonged exercise. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether the IL-6 production by contracting skeletal muscle is sufficient to account for the increase in IL-6 concentration in the blood.
To address this question, we conducted a series of experiments in six healthy male participants who performed one-legged dynamic knee extensor exercise for 5 hours at a moderate intensity (25 W, representing 40% of peak power output). Blood samples were collected from the artery and vein of both legs at regular intervals throughout the exercise, and IL-6 concentrations were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
Our results showed that arterial plasma concentrations of IL-6 increased 19-fold compared to rest, and the difference in IL-6 concentration between the exercising and resting legs followed the same pattern. However, there was no significant difference in IL-6 release between the two legs. Furthermore, the median IL-6 production by the muscle over the last 2 hours of exercise was found to be 6.8 ng min-1 (kg active muscle)-1 (range, 3.96-9.69 ng min-1 kg-1).
Notably, the net IL-6 release from the muscle over the last 2 hours of exercise was found to be 17-fold higher than the elevation in arterial IL-6 concentration, indicating a very high turnover of IL-6 during muscular exercise. These findings suggest that IL-6 produced by skeletal contracting muscle plays a significant role in maintaining glucose homeostasis during prolonged exercise.

title: Symptoms of hypoglycemia in children with IDDM.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the symptoms of hypoglycemia in children with insulin-dependent diabetes from both the child's and parents' perspectives, and to compare the symptom reporting of diabetic children with that of adult diabetic patients.
Research Design and Methods:
Interviews were conducted with 100 parents and 43 of their children, and the frequency and intensity of hypoglycemia symptoms were documented using a structured interview. The symptoms were then classified into groups using Principal Components Analysis (PCA).
Results:
Diabetic children and their parents showed similar agreement on the relative frequency and intensity of hypoglycemia symptoms reported. PCA of the symptom reports revealed that diabetic children and their parents identified the same distinct subgroups of hypoglycemia-related symptoms, including behavioral disturbance and autonomic-neuroglycopenic subgroups.
Conclusions:
Hypoglycemic symptoms in children with diabetes are distinct from those experienced by insulin-treated adults, with behavioral changes being the primary features of low blood glucose. These findings have important implications for parental education on hypoglycemia.

title: Comparative Protein Structure Modeling Using MODELLER.
text: Comparative protein structure modeling is a technique used to predict the three-dimensional structure of a target protein based on its alignment to one or more known protein structures (templates). This process involves four main steps: fold assignment, target-template alignment, model building, and model evaluation. In this unit, we will describe how to use the program MODELLER to calculate comparative models and how to utilize the ModBase database of such models. We will also discuss common errors and applications of comparative modeling, using the example of modeling lactate dehydrogenase from Trichomonas vaginalis (TvLDH). Additionally, we will provide instructions on how to download and install the MODELLER software. © 2016 John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

title: IL-6 as a keystone cytokine in health and disease
text: Interleukin 6 (IL-6) exerts a wide range of effects on immune and non-immune cells, displaying hormone-like characteristics that influence homeostatic processes. IL-6 exhibits context-dependent pro- and anti-inflammatory properties and is now considered a key target for therapeutic intervention. However, the complex signaling pathway controlling IL-6 activity presents challenges for developing effective interventions. Clinical experience with IL-6 antagonists has raised new questions about the optimal timing and method of blocking this cytokine to improve disease outcomes and patient wellbeing. Here, we explore the impact of IL-6 on innate and adaptive immunity and discuss the potential benefits of various IL-6 antagonists, considering how the immunobiology of IL-6 may inform clinical decision-making.

title: Chaperoning 5S RNA assembly.
text:
In eukaryotic cells, three of the four ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs)—the 5.8S, 18S, and 25S/28S rRNAs—are generated from a single pre-rRNA transcript and subsequently assembled into ribosomes. The fourth rRNA, the 5S rRNA, is transcribed by RNA polymerase III and forms a separate ribonucleoprotein particle (RNP) containing ribosomal proteins Rpl5/uL18 and Rpl11/uL5, before being incorporated into preribosomes. In mammals, the 5S RNP also plays a crucial role in regulating the homeostasis of the tumor suppressor p53. The processing and assembly of the 5S RNP are mediated by a specialized complex composed of Rpf2 and Rrs1 in yeast or Bxdc1 and hRrs1 in humans.
Our study focuses on the structural and functional characterization of the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex, both alone and in complex with the 5S RNA, as well as its interactions within pre-60S ribosomes. We have found that the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex contains a unique 5S RNA E-loop-binding module, which interacts with the Rpl5 protein and also contacts the ribosome assembly factor Rsa4 and the 25S RNA. We propose that the Rpf2-Rrs1 complex establishes a network of interactions that guide the incorporation of the 5S RNP into preribosomes in their initial conformation before they rotate to form the central protuberance of the mature large ribosomal subunit.

title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and neutrophil infiltration: role of cigarette smoke and cyclooxygenase products.
text: Cigarette smoke is the primary cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which can lead to airway inflammation. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) is produced within human airways and has been found to have both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory effects. In this study, we measured PGE2 concentrations in induced sputum supernatants from various subject groups and correlated these values with neutrophil infiltration and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression. Cigarette smoke extract (CSE) was used to evaluate the effect of smoking on COX-2 and PGE2 receptor expression, as well as PGE2 release in neutrophils and alveolar macrophages (AM) obtained from normal donors. The effects of PGE2 and PGE receptor agonists and antagonists on neutrophil adhesion to a human bronchial epithelial cell line (16HBE) were also evaluated. Our results showed that PGE2 levels, COX-2 expression, and neutrophil infiltration were significantly higher in normal smokers and COPD smokers compared to controls and COPD former smokers (P < 0.0001). Induced sputum supernatant caused neutrophil adhesion to 16HBE that was significantly reduced in COPD smokers only when PGE2 was immunoprecipitated. In vitro experiments confirmed that CSE increased PGE2 release and COX-2 and PGE2 receptor expression in neutrophils and AM. PGE2 enhanced neutrophil adhesion to 16HBE, and a specific E-prostanoid 4 (EP4) receptor antagonist blunted its effect. These findings suggest that CSE promotes the induction of COX-2 and contributes to the pro-inflammatory effects of PGE2 in the airways of COPD subjects.

title: Non-receptor tyrosine kinase Etk is involved in the apoptosis of small cell lung cancer cells.
text: The study investigated the role of Etk (also known as Bmx), a tyrosine kinase that plays a crucial role in apoptosis of epithelial cells, in the apoptosis of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) cells. The study analyzed the expression levels of Etk, Bcl-2, Bcl-X(L), and p53 in 171 lung cancer specimens, including 71 SCLCs and 100 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases. The study found that high expression of Etk occurred in 74.6% of SCLC cases, but only in 40% of NSCLC cases, and there was a significant difference in the expression levels of Bcl-2, Bcl-X(L), and p53 between Etk-positive and Etk-negative SCLC cases. The study also found that the levels of Bcl-2 and Bcl-X(L) significantly increased in cells overexpressing Etk (H446-Etk) than in parental H446 cells after doxorubicin treatment, and were positively associated with Etk expression. However, p53 did not correspond with Etk expression, although its expression decreased significantly with apoptosis in both H446-Etk and H446 cells. The study also found that downregulation of Etk by Etk siRNA sensitized H446 cells to doxorubicin. The results suggest that upregulation of tyrosine kinase Etk may be a new mechanism involved in protecting SCLC cells from apoptosis, and that Bcl-2 and Bcl-X(L) but not p53 may contribute to doxorubicin-induced apoptosis through the Etk pathway.

title: No Pasaran! Role of the axon initial segment in the regulation of protein transport and the maintenance of axonal identity.
text: The transmission of information in the brain relies on the highly organized structure of neurons, which is supported by various cellular transport processes. These processes include the active transport of proteins and the passive movement of molecules between compartments. The axon initial segment (AIS), located at the junction between the somatodendritic and axonal compartments, plays a crucial role in neuronal function, serving as both the initiation site of action potentials and the regulator of axonal arborization. Over time, the components and interactions within the AIS have been progressively elucidated, as well as their role in AIS assembly and maintenance. Two mechanisms have been identified that contribute to the regulation of protein transport at the AIS: a surface diffusion barrier and an intracellular traffic filter. However, a detailed understanding of these processes is still lacking. In light of recent findings on the AIS cytoskeleton structure, this review aims to explore how a better understanding of the AIS architecture can shed light on its role in regulating protein transport and maintaining axonal identity.

title: The effectiveness of right heart catheterization in the initial care of critically ill patients. SUPPORT Investigators.
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between the use of right heart catheterization (RHC) in the intensive care unit (ICU) during the first 24 hours of care and subsequent patient outcomes, including survival, length of stay, intensity of care, and cost of care.
Design: Prospective cohort study.
Setting: Five US teaching hospitals between 1989 and 1994.
Subjects: A total of 5735 critically ill adult patients receiving care in an ICU for one of nine prespecified disease categories.
Main Outcome Measures: Survival time, cost of care, intensity of care, and length of stay in the ICU and hospital, determined from clinical records and the National Death Index. A propensity score for RHC was constructed using multivariable logistic regression. Case-matching and multivariable regression modeling techniques were used to estimate the association of RHC with specific outcomes after adjusting for treatment selection using the propensity score. Sensitivity analysis was used to estimate the potential effect of an unidentified or missing covariate on the results.
Results: By case-matching analysis, patients with RHC had an increased 30-day mortality (odds ratio, 1.24; 95% confidence interval, 1.03-1.49). The mean cost per hospital stay was $49,300 ($17,000-$30,500) with RHC and $35,700 ($11,300-$20,600) without RHC. Mean length of stay in the ICU was 14.8 (5-9-17) days with RHC and 13.0 (4-7-14) days without RHC. These findings were all confirmed by multivariable modeling techniques. Subgroup analysis did not reveal any patient group or site for which RHC was associated with improved outcomes. Patients with higher baseline probability of surviving 2 months had the highest relative risk of death following RHC. Sensitivity analysis suggested that a missing covariate would have to increase the risk of death 6-fold and the risk of RHC 6-fold for a true beneficial effect of RHC to be misrepresented as harmful.
Conclusion: In this observational study of critically ill patients, after adjustment for treatment selection bias, RHC was associated with increased mortality and increased utilization of resources. The cause of this apparent lack of benefit is unclear. The results of this analysis should be confirmed in other observational studies. These findings justify reconsideration of a randomized controlled trial of RHC and may guide patient selection for such a study.

title: Natural history of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and approaches to therapy
text: After cell-to-cell transmission, HTLV-I increases its viral genome through de novo infection and the proliferation of infected cells. In vivo, the proliferation of infected cells is clonal and persistent, and infected cells are selected by the host's immune system, the genetic and epigenetic environment of proviral integration sites, and other factors. In leukemic cells, Tax gene expression is often impaired by genetic and epigenetic mechanisms, allowing ATL cells to evade the host immune system. Conversely, ATL cells acquire the ability to proliferate without Tax through intracellular genetic and epigenetic changes. Despite advances in supportive care and the development of novel treatment agents, the prognosis for ATLL remains poor. However, several therapies have been shown to improve prognosis compared to CHOP (VEPA), including interferon-α plus zidovudine, intensive chemotherapy with G-CSF support and Allo-SCT, and emerging novel approaches such as HDAC inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, and proteasome inhibitors. However, comparison between different therapeutic approaches is complicated by the diverse natural history of ATLL, the different recruitment of naïve-to-therapy, refractory or relapsed patients, and variations in the reporting of outcomes that often exclude difficult-to-evaluate patients. Moreover, results from small proof-of-principle studies have not been extended with randomized, controlled trials. Therefore, large, randomized, controlled trials involving multicenter, international collaborations are necessary to identify optimal therapy as rapidly as possible and to avoid further unnecessary patient suffering.

title: Hierarchical organization of the plasma membrane: investigations by single-molecule tracking vs. fluorescence correlation spectroscopy.
text: Advances in single-molecule tracking and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) have enabled groundbreaking observations of the plasma membrane in living cells, revolutionizing our understanding of molecular diffusion, interaction, and signal transduction at the membrane. It is becoming increasingly evident that the plasma membrane is a complex, heterogeneous structure composed of diverse structures on the nanoscale to mesoscale (2-200 nm) with varying lifetimes, during which certain membrane molecules temporarily associate. These interactions occur within the time-dependent, inhomogeneous two-dimensional liquid environment of the plasma membrane, which may be a key factor in determining its functions.

title: Stability of the antimalarial drug dihydroartemisinin under physiologically relevant conditions: implications for clinical treatment and pharmacokinetic and in vitro assays.
text: Artemisinins are a class of antimalarial drugs known for their potency, but they are also highly unstable due to their chemical composition. They degrade quickly in the presence of ferrous iron, Fe(II)-heme, or biological reductants. While the stability of these drugs has been studied in vitro, there is less information on how it translates to clinical situations. Dihydroartemisinin (DHA), a metabolite of other artemisinins, was chosen for study because it is an antimalarial drug on its own. The stability and antimalarial activity of DHA were examined in phosphate-buffered saline, plasma, and erythrocyte lysate at different temperatures and pH levels. The extent of DHA decomposition was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography with electrochemical detection. The role of Fe(II)-heme in DHA instability was investigated by blocking its reactivity with carbon monoxide (CO). The results showed a significant reduction in DHA's antimalarial activity after incubation in plasma and to a lesser extent in erythrocyte lysate. Activity was reduced by half after 3 hours and almost completely abolished after 24 hours. Serum-enriched media also affected DHA activity. The effects were temperature and pH dependent, with increased decomposition occurring at higher temperatures and in plasma. These findings suggest that in vitro studies may not accurately reflect the clinical efficacy of artemisinin drugs, as disorders such as fever, hemolysis, or acidosis associated with malaria severity can contribute to their instability.

title: Modulation of anxiety through blockade of anandamide hydrolysis
text:
The psychoactive compound found in cannabis, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol, produces subjective responses in humans that are mediated by the CB1 cannabinoid receptor. These responses suggest that endogenous cannabinoids may play a role in regulating emotions. However, the inconsistent effects of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol limit the therapeutic potential of direct cannabinoid agonists. An alternative approach may involve the development of drugs that enhance the effects of endogenous cannabinoids by preventing their degradation.
In this study, we describe a class of potent, selective, and systemically active inhibitors of fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), the enzyme responsible for breaking down the endogenous cannabinoid anandamide. Like clinically used anti-anxiety drugs, these inhibitors exhibit benzodiazepine-like effects in the elevated zero-maze test and suppress isolation-induced vocalizations in rats. These effects are accompanied by increased brain levels of anandamide and are prevented by CB1 receptor blockade. Our findings suggest that anandamide plays a role in modulating emotional states and that FAAH inhibition may represent a novel approach to anti-anxiety therapy.

title: Familial clustering of reflux symptoms
text:
Objective:
Several case reports have described multiple family members with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and Barrett's esophagus. However, the extent to which familial factors contribute to GERD remains unclear. To investigate this, we conducted a postal questionnaire study among first-degree relatives of patients with documented GERD.
Methods: We recruited 418 first-degree relatives of six groups of patients, including those with no dyspeptic symptoms, reflux symptoms and a normal pH study, reflux symptoms and an abnormal pH study, reflux symptoms and a low lower esophageal sphincter (LOS) pressure, Barrett's esophagus, and peptic stricture. Relatives completed a questionnaire on their reflux symptoms and medication use.
Results: Our findings showed that infrequent reflux symptoms were equally common among all groups of relatives, while frequent reflux symptoms were more common among relatives of patients with an abnormal pH study and either normal (p= 0.007) or low LOS pressure (p= 0.01) or Barrett's esophagus (p= 0.003) compared to relatives of nondyspeptic patients (9%). Frequent reflux symptoms were also more common among relatives of patients with Barrett's esophagus (30%) than among those with a normal pH study (16%). Similarly, reflux medication use showed a similar pattern.
Conclusions: Our study found that familial clustering of reflux symptoms is seen in relatives of patients with reflux symptoms and increased esophageal acid exposure, as well as in relatives of patients with Barrett's esophagus. These findings suggest that familial factors may play a role in the development of GERD and Barrett's esophagus.

title: Histone chaperones: 30 years from isolation to elucidation of the mechanisms of nucleosome assembly and disassembly
text: Over three decades have passed since the discovery of nucleosomes in 1974 and the isolation of the first histone chaperone in 1978. While various types of histone chaperones have been studied and their functions understood, the fundamental processes of nucleosome assembly and disassembly have been less well characterized. Recently, the three-dimensional structure of a hetero-trimeric complex composed of the histone chaperone CIA/ASF1 and the histone H3-H4 dimer was determined, and this complex was proposed to be an intermediate in nucleosome assembly and disassembly reactions. Additionally, CIA was shown to biochemically dissociate the (H3-H4)2 tetramer into two histone H3-H4 dimers, suggesting that CIA regulates the semi-conservative replication of nucleosomes. Our goal is to provide an overview of prominent histone chaperones and elucidate the mechanisms that preserve and modify epigenetic information. We will also discuss the reactions involved in nucleosome assembly and disassembly.

title: Specificity of the dRP/AP lyase of Ku promotes nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) fidelity at damaged ends.
text: Nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) is a crucial process for the efficient repair of chromosomal breaks. However, the ligation step of NHEJ is often hindered by break-associated nucleotide damage, including base loss, which can result in abasic sites or 5'-dRP/AP sites. Ku, a 5'-dRP/AP lyase, plays a critical role in excising these damaged bases at the ends of the break, preparing them for ligation. Our findings demonstrate that the activity of Ku is most pronounced when the abasic site is located within a short 5' overhang, as this allows for efficient preparation of the termini for ligation. In contrast, Ku is less active near 3' strand termini, where excision would result in a ligation-blocking α,β-unsaturated aldehyde. Furthermore, we show that the activity of Ku is strongly suppressed by as little as two paired bases 5' of the abasic site, indicating that this site is essential for the excision process. Interestingly, in vitro end joining experiments reveal that abasic sites embedded in double-stranded DNA do not block the NHEJ ligation step, suggesting that suppression of the excision activity of Ku in this context is not essential for ligation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the DNA between the 5' terminus and the abasic site can also be retained in junctions formed by cellular NHEJ, indicating that these sites are at least partly resistant to other abasic site-cleaving activities. Our findings suggest that high levels of the 5'-dRP/AP lyase activity of Ku are restricted to substrates where excision of an abasic site is required for ligation, thereby promoting more accurate joining.

title: Gut-expressed gustducin and taste receptors regulate secretion of glucagon-like peptide-1.
text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is released from gut endocrine L cells in response to glucose and regulates appetite, insulin secretion, and gut motility. However, the mechanism by which glucose stimulates GLP-1 secretion from gut L cells is unknown. We discovered that human duodenal L cells express taste receptors, including gustducin, and other taste transduction elements. Mouse intestinal L cells also express gustducin. When alpha-gustducin null mice were given glucose, they showed deficiencies in GLP-1 secretion and the regulation of plasma insulin and glucose levels. Isolated small bowel and intestinal villi from alpha-gustducin null mice had impaired GLP-1 secretion in response to glucose. The human L cell line NCI-H716 expresses gustducin, taste receptors, and other taste signaling elements. GLP-1 release from NCI-H716 cells was enhanced by sugars and the noncaloric sweetener sucralose, and inhibited by the sweet receptor antagonist lactisole or siRNA against alpha-gustducin. Our findings suggest that gut L cells "taste" glucose through the same mechanisms as taste cells in the tongue. Modulating GLP-1 secretion in gut "taste cells" may provide a promising treatment for obesity, diabetes, and abnormal gut motility.

title: Apoptosis in breast cancer: relationship with other pathological parameters.
text: Apoptosis is a prevalent occurrence in breast cancer, which can be detected through light microscopy in conventional histopathological sections or via specialized staining techniques. The percentage of apoptotic cells among the total cell population or the number of apoptotic cells per square millimeter of neoplastic tissue is typically described as the apoptotic index (AI). In breast cancer, the AI is not correlated with tumor size, axillary lymph node metastasis, or distant metastasis at diagnosis. However, the AI is higher in invasive ductal carcinomas compared to other histological types. Additionally, high AI is associated with high histological grade, high nuclear grade, comedo-type necrosis, lack of tubule formation, and dense infiltration of the tumor by lymphocytes. Notably, sex steroid receptor-negative tumors exhibit higher AIs than sex steroid receptor-positive ones. Furthermore, aneuploid breast cancers with high S-phase fractions (SPFs) display higher AI values compared to diploid tumors with low SPFs. Interestingly, p53-positive breast cancers have high AIs, while tumors that are Bcl-2 positive have low AIs. The AI demonstrates a strong positive correlation with various direct or indirect indicators of cell proliferation, including the mitotic index and Ki67 immunolabeling. Univariate survival analyses reveal that a high AI is linked to unfavorable disease outcome in both axillary lymph node-negative and -positive breast cancer. However, multivariate analyses indicate that AI is not an independent prognostic factor. In conclusion, a high AI is closely associated with malignant cellular features and indicators of invasiveness and cell proliferation in breast cancer.

title: Dietary flavonoids: bioavailability, metabolic effects, and safety.
text: Flavonoids, the most prevalent group of plant polyphenols, are responsible for the distinct flavors and colors of various fruits and vegetables. To date, over 5000 different flavonoids have been identified.
