The flavonoid subclassification can be broadly categorized into six main groups: flavones (e.g., apigenin, luteolin), flavonols (e.g., quercetin, myricetin), flavanones (e.g., naringenin, hesperidin), catechins or flavanols (e.g., epicatechin, gallocatechin), anthocyanidins (e.g., cyanidin, pelargonidin), and isoflavones (e.g., genistein, daidzein). Most flavonoids in plants are attached to sugars (glycosides), although some may exist as aglycones. The growing interest in the potential health benefits of flavonoids is attributed to their potent antioxidant and free-radical scavenging activities observed in vitro. While some human feeding studies have suggested that the absorption and bioavailability of specific flavonoids may be higher than previously thought, the results of epidemiologic studies investigating the role of flavonoid consumption in human health have been inconsistent. Some studies suggest a protective effect of flavonoid consumption in cardiovascular disease and cancer, while others have found no association or even potential harm. Given the diverse range of biological activities attributed to flavonoids, further research is warranted to fully understand their potential benefits and risks in both laboratory and population-based settings.

title: Virus-specific cytotoxic T-lymphocyte responses select for amino-acid variation in simian immunodeficiency virus Env and Nef
text: Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL) responses to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) emerge early after infection, but ultimately fail to prevent disease progression to AIDS. HIV may evade the CTL response by incorporating mutations within CTL epitopes. We investigated 10 CTL epitopes during the course of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) disease progression in three related macaques. All 10 of these epitopes accumulated mutations and showed evidence of positive selection by the time the macaques died. Many of these mutations reduced or eliminated major histocompatibility complex class I binding and/or CTL recognition, providing strong support for the CTL 'escape' hypothesis.

title: TRICHOME BIREFRINGENCE and its homolog AT5G01360 encode plant-specific DUF231 proteins required for cellulose biosynthesis in Arabidopsis.
text: The Arabidopsis thaliana trichome birefringence (tbr) mutant exhibits a significant reduction in crystalline cellulose in trichomes, despite the molecular mechanism underlying TBR remaining unknown. Through our investigation, we discovered that TBR belongs to the plant-specific DUF231 domain gene family, comprising 46 members in Arabidopsis with unknown functions. These genes also harbor the TBL domain, which contains a conserved GDSL motif found in some esterases/lipases. TBR and TBL3 (TBR-like3) are transcriptionally coordinated with primary and secondary CELLULOSE SYNTHASE (CESA) genes, respectively. The tbr and tbl3 mutants display lower levels of crystalline cellulose and altered pectin composition in trichomes and stems, respectively, which are tissues typically rich in secondary wall crystalline cellulose. In contrast, primary wall cellulose levels remain unchanged in both mutants as measured in etiolated hypocotyls, while the amount of esterified pectins is reduced and pectin methylesterase activity is increased in this tissue. Furthermore, etiolated tbr hypocotyls exhibit reduced length with swollen epidermal cells, a phenotype characteristic of primary CESA mutants or the wild type treated with cellulose synthesis inhibitors. Our findings demonstrate that two TBL genes contribute to the synthesis and deposition of secondary wall cellulose, likely by influencing the esterification state of pectic polymers.

title: Genetic predictors of taxane-induced neurotoxicity in a SWOG phase III intergroup adjuvant breast cancer treatment trial (S0221)
text: Taxanes have improved survival rates for breast cancer patients, but often cause neurological toxicities. Identifying biomarkers related to these toxicities could help tailor treatment plans. In a study of 888 patients from the SWOG0221 phase III adjuvant trial for breast cancer, we investigated the relationship between single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the Fanconi Anemia (FA)/BRCA pathway and grade 3/4 neurotoxicities. We found that 4 out of 20 FANCD2 SNPs were significantly associated with an almost two-fold increased risk of toxicity. Two FANCD2 haplotypes were also linked to neurological toxicity, with odds ratios (OR) of 1.8 and 1.7 in the overall population. Additionally, an African-American-specific haplotype was associated with a nearly 3-fold increase in the risk of neurological toxicity. Expression analyses revealed that significant FANCD2 SNPs were associated with FANCD2 expression levels. In contrast, no associations were found between SNPs in BRCA1 and neurotoxicities. These findings suggest that SNPs in FANCD2, but not in BRCA1, are associated with a 70-80% increase in the odds of grade 3/4 neurological toxicities and increased expression of the gene. If replicated, women with these genotypes should be closely monitored for toxicities and could be targeted for preventive measures or alternative therapeutic approaches.

title: Preoperative C-reactive protein predicts mid-term outcome after cardiac surgery.
text:
Background: C-reactive protein (CRP) is a recognized risk factor for cardiovascular events in both healthy populations and patients with coronary artery disease. However, the role of CRP after discharge home after cardiac surgery remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of CRP on short-term and mid-term outcomes after cardiac surgery.
Methods: From August 2000 to May 2004, CRP values were available for 597 unselected patients undergoing cardiac operations. Based on their CRP levels, the cohort was divided into two groups: a low inflammatory status (LHS) group of 354 patients with CRP levels of less than 0.5 mg/dL, and a high inflammatory status (HIS) group of 243 patients with CRP levels of 0.5 mg/dL or higher. Follow-up lasted a maximum of 3 years (median, 1.8 ± 1.5 years) and was 92.6% complete.
Results: In-hospital mortality was 8.2% in the HIS group and 3.4% in the LHS group (odds ratio [OR], 2.61; p = 0.02). The incidence of postoperative infections was 16.5% in the HIS group and 5.1% in the LHS group (OR, 3.25; p = 0.0001). Sternal wound infections were also more frequent in the HIS group (10.7% versus 2.8%; OR, 3.43; p = 0.002). During follow-up, the HIS group had worse survival (88.5% ± 2.9% versus 91.9% ± 2.5%; OR, 1.93; p = 0.05) and a higher need for hospitalization for cardiac-related causes (73.6% ± 6% versus 86.5% ± 3.2%; OR, 1.82; p = 0.05).
Conclusions: Patients undergoing cardiac surgery with a CRP level of 0.5 mg/dL or higher are at a higher risk of in-hospital mortality and postoperative infections, even after surgical correction of cardiac disease. Despite these findings, a high preoperative CRP value remains an independent risk factor for mid-term survival and hospitalization for cardiac causes.

title: Inhibition of Hedgehog signaling enhances delivery of chemotherapy in a mouse model of pancreatic cancer.
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is among the most aggressive and lethal human cancers due to its intrinsic resistance to various chemotherapeutic agents. To investigate the underlying mechanisms of chemoresistance in this disease, we utilized a mouse model of PDA that is refractory to the clinically used drug gemcitabine. Our findings revealed that the tumors in this model exhibited poor perfusion and vascularization, which are also characteristic of human PDA. We then evaluated the potential of coadministering IPI-926, a drug that targets the Hedgehog cellular signaling pathway, with gemcitabine to enhance drug delivery and therapeutic efficacy in this mouse model. Our results showed that the combination therapy led to a transient increase in intratumoral vascular density and gemcitabine concentration, resulting in a transient stabilization of disease. These findings suggest that inefficient drug delivery may be a significant contributor to chemoresistance in pancreatic cancer.

title: Mutant SOD1 inhibits ER-Golgi transport in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
text:
Misfolded Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase (SOD1) is implicated in both familial and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but the mechanism by which it triggers downstream cellular events is not fully understood. In this study, we investigate the subcellular localization of mutant SOD1 (mSOD1) in neuronal cells and its impact on secretory protein transport from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi apparatus.
Our findings reveal that mSOD1 is predominantly localized in the cytoplasm of neuronal cells, and that it inhibits the transport of secretory proteins from the ER to the Golgi apparatus. This inhibition of ER-Golgi transport is linked to the activation of endoplasmic reticulum stress, Golgi fragmentation, and axonal transport. Furthermore, we show that the inhibition of ER-Golgi trafficking precedes the formation of protein aggregates, Golgi fragmentation, and apoptosis in cells expressing mSOD1.
Interestingly, we found that restoring ER-Golgi transport by over-expressing coatomer coat protein II subunit Sar1 can protect against inclusion formation and apoptosis in mSOD1-expressing cells. This suggests that dysfunction in ER-Golgi transport is a key early event in the pathogenesis of ALS.
Taken together, our findings provide a novel mechanism linking several cellular events in ALS, suggesting that early dysfunction in ER-Golgi transport may play a critical role in the pathogenesis of this devastating disease.

title: High spatial resolution mapping of malaria transmission risk in the Gambia, west Africa, using LANDSAT TM satellite imagery.
text: Understanding local variability in malaria transmission risk is crucial when designing intervention or vaccine trials. By combining field data, satellite image analysis, and GIS modeling, we created a high-resolution map of malaria entomological inoculation rates (EIR) in The Gambia, West Africa, with a resolution of 48 villages in 1996 and 21 villages in 1997. Our analyses revealed that the EIR varied from 0 to 166 infective bites per person per rainy season, highlighting the significant local variability in malaria transmission risk. Through detailed field surveys, we identified the primary breeding habitats of the Anopheles gambiae s.l. mosquito species, which were then mapped with an overall accuracy of 85% using a LANDSAT TM satellite image. We found that village EIRs decreased as a power function of the size and proximity of the breeding areas, and used this relationship to map the variation in EIR across the entire 2500-square-kilometer study area.

title: Functional analysis of repressor binding sites in the iab-2 regulatory region of the abdominal-A homeotic gene.
text: Spatial boundaries of homeotic gene expression are established and maintained by two sets of transcriptional repressors: the gap gene products and the Polycomb group proteins. Previous studies have implicated the Hunchback (HB) protein in setting the anterior expression limit of the Ubx homeotic protein in parasegment 6. In this study, we investigate the DNA elements and trans-acting repressors that control the spatial expression of the Abdominal-A (ABD-A) homeotic protein. We analyze a 1.7-kb enhancer element, iab-2(1.7), from the iab-2 regulatory region, which shows that both HB and Krüppel (KR) are required to set the ABD-A anterior boundary in parasegment 7. Using DNase I footprinting and site-directed mutagenesis, we demonstrate that HB and KR are direct regulators of this iab-2 enhancer. Interestingly, we find that KR repression occurs through a local quenching mechanism, and that the gap repressor Giant (GT) initially establishes a posterior expression limit at parasegment 9, which shifts posteriorly after the blastoderm stage. Additionally, we show that the iab-2 enhancer contains multiple binding sites for the Polycomb group protein Pleiohomeotic (PHO), which are required in vivo for chromosome pairing-dependent repression of a mini-white reporter. However, these PHO sites are not sufficient to maintain repression of a homeotic reporter gene anterior to parasegment 7. Full maintenance at late embryonic stages requires additional sequences adjacent to the iab-2(1.7) enhancer.

title: Apolipoprotein E: high-avidity binding to beta-amyloid and increased frequency of type 4 allele in late-onset familial Alzheimer disease.
text: Apolipoprotein E (APOE) is specifically located within the senile plaques, vascular amyloid, and neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's disease (AD). In vitro, APOE in cerebrospinal fluid strongly binds to synthetic beta-A4 peptide (the primary component of senile plaques), with high affinity requiring amino acids 12-28 of the beta-A4 peptide. The APOE gene is located on chromosome 19q13.2, within a region previously linked to late-onset familial AD. Analysis of APOE alleles in AD patients and controls revealed a highly significant association between the APOE-epsilon 4 allele and late-onset familial AD. The allele frequency of APOE-epsilon 4 was 0.50 ± 0.06 in 30 randomly selected AD patients from different families, compared to 0.16 ± 0.03 in 91 age-matched unrelated controls (Z = 2.44, P = 0.014). These findings suggest a functional role of the APOE-E4 isoform in the pathogenesis of late-onset familial AD.

title: Unmarked gene deletion and host–vector system for the hyperthermophilic crenarchaeon Sulfolobus islandicus
text: Sulfolobus islandicus is being utilized as a model organism for the study of archaeal biology, geo-biology, and evolution. However, due to the lack of a genetic system, researchers were unable to perform genetic analyses on this organism. To overcome this challenge, the team screened for colonies with a spontaneous pyrEF mutation, and successfully obtained one mutant with a truncated pyrE sequence. This mutant was then used to delete the β-glycosidase (lacS) gene. Two unmarked gene deletion methods, plasmid integration and segregation, and marker replacement and looping out, were employed to generate unmarked lacS mutants. Additionally, a new alternative recombination mechanism, marker circularization and integration, was identified and used to obtain the desired deletion mutation. To further expand the genetic toolkit for S. islandicus, Sulfolobus–E. coli plasmid shuttle vectors were constructed, which were able to complement the ΔpyrEFΔlacS mutation after transformation. This work established a complete set of genetic tools for S. islandicus, with pyrEF and lacS serving as genetic markers.

title: ADAM13 disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains bind to the second heparin-binding domain of fibronectin.
text:
Adam13 is a member of the disintegrin and metalloprotease protein family that is expressed on the surface of cranial neural crest cells and plays a crucial role in their migration. Adam13 is a functional protease that can cleave fibronectin in vitro and remodel its substrate in vivo. By using a recombinant secreted protein containing both the disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains of Adam13, we demonstrate that this "adhesive" region of the protein binds directly to fibronectin. Fibronectin fusion proteins containing various functional domains were used to identify the ADAM13 binding site as the second heparin-binding domain. Mutation of the syndecan-binding site (PPRR --> PPTM) within this domain abolishes binding of the recombinant disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains of Adam13.
We further show that the adhesive disintegrin and cysteine-rich domain of Adam13 can promote cell adhesion via beta(1) integrins. This adhesion requires integrin activation and can be inhibited by antibodies to the cysteine-rich domain of Adam13 and beta(1) integrin. Interestingly, we find that wild-type Adam13 can be shed from the cell surface, releasing the metalloprotease domain associated with the disintegrin and cysteine-rich domains. This suggests that Adam13 shedding may involve its own metalloprotease activity and that the released protease may interact with both integrins and extracellular matrix proteins.

title: Clinical epidemiology of heart failure.
text: The purpose of this paper is to examine the clinical epidemiology of heart failure. The last comprehensive review of the epidemiology of heart failure was published in 2000, and since then, there has been an increase in manuscripts exploring the epidemiological aspects of heart failure. However, despite this growth, there is still a need for more information, as highlighted by various editorials.

title: Toll-like receptor 7 agonist GS-9620 induces prolonged inhibition of HBV via a type I interferon-dependent mechanism.
text:
Background and Aims:
GS-9620, an oral agonist of toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7), is currently in clinical development for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B (CHB). Previous studies have shown that GS-9620 can induce prolonged suppression of serum viral DNA and antigens in animal models of CHB. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its antiviral activity were not fully understood.
Methods:
Cryopreserved primary human hepatocytes (PHH) and differentiated HepaRG (dHepaRG) cells were infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and treated with GS-9620, conditioned media from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells treated with GS-9620 (GS-9620-CM), or other innate immune stimuli. The antiviral and transcriptional response to these agents was determined using various assays.
Results:
GS-9620 had no antiviral activity in HBV-infected PHH, consistent with low levels of TLR7 mRNA expression in human hepatocytes. In contrast, GS-9620-CM induced prolonged reduction of HBV DNA, RNA, and antigen levels in PHH and dHepaRG cells via a type I interferon (IFN)-dependent mechanism. GS-9620-CM did not reduce covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) levels in either cell type. Transcriptional profiling demonstrated that GS-9620-CM strongly induced various HBV restriction factors, including the immunoproteasome subunits, but not APOBEC3A or the Smc5/6 complex. Moreover, established HBV infection did not modulate innate immune sensing or signaling in cryopreserved PHH. GS-9620-CM also induced expression of an immunodominant viral peptide in HBV-infected PHH.

title: Depletion of glutathione induces 4-hydroxynonenal protein adducts and hydroxyurea teratogenicity in the organogenesis stage mouse embryo.
text: Glutathione (GSH) homeostasis plays a crucial role during organogenesis, and its disruption can lead to oxidative stress and teratogenicity. To investigate the impact of GSH depletion on organogenesis, l-buthionine-S,R-sulfoximine (BSO) was administered to timed pregnant CD-1 mice 4 hours before exposure to a model teratogen, hydroxyurea (HU). Treatment with BSO or HU alone did not affect the GSH/glutathione disulfide (GSSG) ratio in the embryo, but the combination of BSO and HU at the higher dose (HU-600) resulted in increased oxidative stress in the embryos, as evidenced by the induction of 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) protein adducts. BSO pretreatment increased the severity of external and skeletal malformations, such as curly tail, hind limb malformations, hydrocephaly, exencephaly, open eye, spina bifida, and gastroschisis, induced by HU-400 and HU-600. The formation of 4-HNE protein adducts was localized to regions of the embryo that are highly susceptible to insult, such as the somites and caudal neural tube, suggesting that disruption of pattern formation during organogenesis is involved in the teratogenic effects of HU.

title: Nonproductive human immunodeficiency virus type 1 infection in nucleoside-treated G0 lymphocytes.
text: Productive infection by human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) requires the activation of target cells, and infection of quiescent peripheral CD4 lymphocytes by HIV-1 leads to incomplete, unstable reverse transcripts. Previous studies have identified G1b as the cell cycle stage required for the optimal completion of the reverse transcription process in T lymphocytes, but the mechanisms involved in the blockage of reverse transcription remain unclear. In this study, we investigated whether changes in nucleotide levels influence viral reverse transcription in G0 cells. To bypass the role of ribonucleotide reductase, we added exogenous deoxyribonucleosides to highly purified T cells in the G0 or G1a phase of the cell cycle. Our results showed a significant increase in the efficiency of reverse transcription following the addition of deoxyribonucleosides. To evaluate the stability and functionality of these full reverse transcripts, we used an HIV-1 reporter virus that expresses the murine heat-stable antigen on the surfaces of infected cells. After activating quiescent cells treated with exogenous nucleosides, no increased rescue of productive infection was observed, indicating an additional non-reversible blockage of productive infection in quiescent T cells. These findings have important implications in the gene therapy field, as they suggest ways to improve the ability of lentivirus vectors to enter metabolically inactive cells, such as hematopoietic stem cells.

title: Imported malaria in children: a national surveillance in the Netherlands and a review of European studies.
text:
BACKGROUND: Falciparum malaria, also known as malaria tropica, is a leading cause of childhood mortality worldwide. According to estimates, approximately 365 million clinical cases of Plasmodium falciparum malaria occur annually in sub-Saharan Africa, where the majority of malaria-related deaths occur. In contrast, imported malaria cases in Europe are more prevalent among returning travelers or immigrants from African countries, with children being at a higher risk than adults. The objective of this study was to identify high-risk groups for imported childhood malaria in Europe in order to inform strategies for prevention, early recognition, and management.
METHODS: This study reviewed all cases of pediatric malaria notified by the Dutch Paediatric Surveillance System (Nederland Signalerings Centrum Kindergeneeskunde, NSCK) in the Netherlands from May 2003 to January 2005, as well as literature published between 1996 and 2006 on imported malaria in children in Europe.
RESULTS: The majority of pediatric malaria cases (n = 15, 47%) occurred in long-term and new immigrants, with the majority of cases acquired in sub-Saharan Africa. P. falciparum was the dominant species in these cases. Only one quarter of children had received adequate malaria chemoprophylaxis. Complicated disease occurred in 10 (31%) of the cases reviewed. A literature review revealed 6082 reported cases of imported malaria among children in Europe, with four deaths and only one case of neurological sequelae reported.
CONCLUSION: Imported malaria in children remains a significant public health concern in Europe, and addressing the underlying reasons for inadequate prophylaxis is crucial to preventing malaria-related deaths.

title: Respiratory and cardiovascular responses to walking down a traffic-polluted road compared with walking in a traffic-free area in participants aged 60 years and older with chronic lung or heart disease and age-matched healthy controls: a randomised, crossover study
text: The study aimed to investigate the impact of short-term exposure to traffic pollution on respiratory and cardiovascular responses in older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or ischaemic heart disease, as well as healthy volunteers. The study found that walking along a busy street with high levels of pollution had adverse effects on lung function, including an increase in the rate of decline of lung function in older individuals and those with COPD. In contrast, walking in a traffic-free area with lower pollution levels led to an increase in lung function and a decrease in pulse wave velocity and augmentation index in all participants, including those with COPD. The study also found that exposure to traffic pollution was associated with an increase in the risk of adverse cardiovascular effects, such as an increase in the risk of ischaemic heart disease. The study suggests that policies should aim to control ambient levels of air pollution along busy streets to mitigate the negative health effects of traffic pollution.

title: Overall and cancer related mortality among patients with ocular inflammation treated with immunosuppressive drugs: retrospective cohort study.
text:
The study aimed to investigate whether immunosuppressive drugs used to treat ocular inflammatory diseases are associated with increased mortality rates. The study design was a retrospective cohort analysis of patients from five tertiary ocular inflammation clinics in the United States. The cohort included 7957 patients with non-infectious ocular inflammation, of whom 2340 received immunosuppressive drugs during follow-up. The main outcome measures were overall and cancer mortality.
The study found that overall mortality rates were similar among patients who used immunosuppressive drugs and those who did not, with a standardized mortality ratio of 1.02 (95% CI: 0.94-1.11) and 1.10 (95% CI: 0.93-1.29), respectively. Similarly, cancer mortality rates were also similar between the two groups, with a standardized mortality ratio of 1.10 (95% CI: 0.93-1.29). However, the study did find that tumor necrosis factor inhibitors were associated with increased overall and cancer mortality, with adjusted hazard ratios of 1.99 (95% CI: 1.00-3.98) and 3.83 (95% CI: 1.13-13.01), respectively.
In conclusion, the study found that most commonly used immunosuppressive drugs do not increase overall or cancer mortality rates. However, the study's findings regarding tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are less robust and require further investigation.

title: Ephrin B1–mediated repulsion and signaling control germinal center T cell territoriality and function
text: Follicular T helper (TFH) cells play a crucial role in orchestrating the germinal center (GC) reaction locally. However, the mechanisms that regulate their dynamics and helper functions within the GC are not well understood. Our study uncovered a novel mechanism that regulates TFH cell function in the GC. We found that GC-expressed ephrin B1 (EFNB1) inhibits T cell-B cell adhesion and TFH retention in the GC by signaling through TFH-expressed EPHB6 receptor. Interestingly, EFNB1 also promotes interleukin-21 production from GC TFH cells by signaling primarily through EPHB4. Consequently, EFNB1-deficient GCs exhibited defective production of plasma cells despite having an excess of TFH cells. In a competitive GC reaction, EFNB1-deficient B cells more efficiently interacted with TFH cells and produced more bone-marrow plasma cells, likely due to increased contact-dependent help. Our findings reveal a local, contact-dependent guidance system that controls GC TFH dynamics and effector functions.

title: Molecular profiling and predictive value of circulating tumor cells in patients with metastatic breast cancer: an option for monitoring response to breast cancer related therapies
text:
Purpose: We investigated the use of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the blood of metastatic breast cancer patients (n = 42) to predict therapy response.
Methods: We analyzed CTCs before and during therapy for EpCAM, MUC1, and HER2 transcripts using the AdnaTest BreastCancer assay. Additionally, we evaluated the expression of ER and PR receptors by RT-PCR.
Results: Our analysis revealed a detection rate of 52% for CTCs (86% for EpCAM, 86% for MUC1, 32% for HER2, 35% for ER, and 12% for PR). Notably, 45% of patients with ER-positive tumors, 78% of patients with PR-positive tumors, and 60% of patients with HER2-negative tumors had CTCs that were negative for ER, PR, and HER2. Furthermore, 29% of patients with HER2-negative tumors had HER2-positive CTCs. The test accurately predicted therapy response in 78% of cases. Interestingly, the persistence of CTCs was found to significantly correlate with shorter overall survival (P = 0.005).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that molecular profiling of CTCs may provide superior prognostic information regarding risk assessment for recurrence and predictive judgment of therapeutic regimens.

title: Alternate-day wheel access: effects on feeding, body weight, and running.
text: Access to a running wheel in rats leads to a temporary but pronounced suppression of feeding. The underlying reasons for this phenomenon are unclear. To investigate, we examined the effects of alternate-day wheel access on feeding and running behavior in 25 male Sprague-Dawley rats. We found that when rats had access to the wheel only on certain days, their food intake was suppressed on wheel days and increased on non-wheel days throughout the 32-day experiment. Contrarily, body weight decreased on wheel days and showed a significant increase on non-wheel days. Interestingly, the rats' running behavior remained consistent across both wheel groups and plateaued at a similar level, but running was elevated in the alternate-day wheel group during the first few hours after returning to the wheel. These findings suggest that the suppression of feeding is not due to the novelty of the wheel and can be extended by providing periods without wheel access. The temporary nature of feeding suppression in chronic wheel access conditions may be attributed to longer-term motivational changes.

title: Evaluation of the association between the first observation and the longitudinal change in C-reactive protein, and all-cause mortality.
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between vascular inflammation, as measured by subacute C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, and all-cause mortality, as well as the association between changes in CRP status and mortality.
Methods: We used probabilistic record linkage to match hospital episode data, laboratory reports, and mortality statistics in a large urban population. Survival was evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression models.
Results: Of the 22,962 patients who had their first CRP measurement in the subacute range (1-10 mg/l), a 7.3% (95% CI 5.4%-9.2%) increase in the hazard ratio (HR) of death was observed for each additional unit increase in CRP across the subacute range after controlling for confounding factors (p<0.001). In patients whose CRP changed from normal (<or=3 mg/l) to elevated (>3 mg/l), the HR increased 6.7-fold (p<0.001) after controlling for confounding factors, compared to cases whose CRP remained normal. Conversely, among those whose CRP was reduced from elevated to normal, the hazard ratio halved to 3.5 (p = 0.018). An identical pattern of risk emerged in an underpowered analysis of time to cardiovascular events.
Conclusions: CRP level predicted all-cause mortality, and additional inclusion of prior change in CRP level and current CRP level more so. Increasing vascular inflammation, as measured by CRP, increases the likelihood of death.

title: Research Priorities in Sudden Unexpected Infant Death: An International Consensus.
text: Despite the progress made in reducing sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) through safe sleep campaigns, the rate of reduction has slowed in many developed countries. To tackle this persistent problem, it is crucial to identify the areas of research that should be prioritized to reduce SUID deaths globally. The Global Action and Prioritization of Sudden Infant Death Project was an international consensus process that brought together experts and lay members of the SUID community from 25 countries to identify research priorities. Through two online surveys and workshops held in the UK, US, and Australia, the project established 10 priority areas for research, with three main themes emerging: (1) understanding the underlying mechanisms of SUID, (2) ensuring best practices in data collection, management, and sharing, and (3) better understanding of target populations and more effective communication of risk. This project provides the international SUID community with a shared list of research priorities to work towards reducing the number of sudden infant deaths globally.

title: Modification of the Constant-Murley shoulder score-introduction of the individual relative Constant score Individual shoulder assessment.
text: The Constant-Murley shoulder assessment score has been found to be a reliable diagnostic tool in various studies. However, its clinical accuracy can vary when comparing patients in larger, heterogeneous groups. To address this limitation, the "relative Constant score" (CS(rel)) was developed by using reference parameters from healthy age and gender-related control groups. In this study, the authors aimed to further improve the accuracy of the assessment by using the functional performance of the uninjured collateral shoulder of the same individual as a reference. This led to the development of the "individual relative Constant score" (CS(indiv)). The CS(indiv) and CS(rel) were compared in 125 consecutive patients with shoulder disorders and a control group of 125 healthy volunteers. The results showed that the CS(indiv) outperformed the CS(rel) in discriminating between patients and healthy volunteers (p=0.004). This suggests that the individual relative Constant score provides a more accurate assessment of functional results for shoulder disorders. Its use is expected to be more reliable in larger and more diverse patient populations, as it eliminates interindividual differences in age, gender, and constitution, as well as other individual physiological parameters.

title: Celiac disease screening by immunochromatographic visual assays: results of a multicenter study.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the efficiency of two immunochromatographic visual stick assays, based on human recombinant tissue transglutaminase (tTG), for screening celiac disease (CD).
Patients and Methods: In a multicenter, prospective study, 72 control children with normal small bowel mucosa and 113 untreated patients with CD (Marsh type 3 lesions) were enrolled from pediatric gastroenterology units in Spain and Latin America. The results were evaluated by gastroenterologists and two independent observers at the coordination center, and the interobserver variability was found to be low.
Results: The AtTGA stick displayed a sensitivity of 96.5% and specificity of 98.6%, while the AtTGA/AGA stick showed a sensitivity of 94.5% and specificity of 98.6% for AtTGA and a sensitivity of 63.1% and specificity of 95.2% for AGA. The highest efficiency and positive likelihood ratio was obtained for the AtTGA stick, which was higher than for IgA AtTGA by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Additionally, the IgA AtTGA/AGA stick, with an efficiency of 95.1%, compared to 89.2% when the combined results of the two ELISAs were considered, proved to be an excellent diagnostic tool for infants without IgA deficiency.
Conclusion: These two assays are highly efficient for CD screening, combining high diagnostic accuracy with simplicity and rapidity of visual methods.

title: Down-regulation of keratin 4 and keratin 13 expression in oral squamous cell carcinoma and epithelial dysplasia: a clue for histopathogenesis.
text:
Objective:
This study aimed to identify specific keratin subtypes that may be associated with the development of oral epithelial neoplasms.
Methods:
We used cDNA microarray analysis to examine the expression of all keratin subtypes in 43 oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) cases. Immunohistochemical analysis was then performed on 100 OSCC and oral epithelial dysplasia (OED) cases to examine the expression of the major keratins. Changes in keratin expression were observed and consistent down-regulation of keratin 4 (K4) and K13 expression was found. These changes were associated with morphological changes in the affected oral epithelium.
Cell culture experiments were also conducted using transfection of various keratin subtypes to investigate the effects of altered keratin expression on cell shape and movement.
Results:
Our results showed that aberrant expression of K4 and K13, which are the dominant pair of differentiation-related keratins in oral keratinocytes, is associated with dysregulation of epithelial differentiation in OSCC and OED. These keratins, especially K4, may be useful for pathological diagnosis. We propose that the aberrant expression of K4 and K13 and concomitant up-regulation of other keratins may contribute to morphological alterations in the affected epithelium.

title: Identification of short-lived long non-coding RNAs as surrogate indicators for chemical stress response.
text:
Abiotic and biotic stressors in human cells often result from sudden or frequent changes in environmental factors, leading to elaborate molecular responses that are crucial for maintaining homeostasis, ecological balance, and evolutionary adaptability. While signaling pathways and protein networks have been the primary focus of stress research, recent studies have highlighted the importance of long non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) in mediating cellular stress responses.
In this study, we identified six novel short-lived long ncRNAs (MIR22HG, GABPB-AS1, LINC00152, IDI2-AS1, SNHG15, and FLJ33630) that are involved in the molecular mechanisms associated with cellular stress responses in HeLa Tet-off cells exposed to chemical stressors (cisplatin, cycloheximide, and mercury (II) oxide). Our findings indicate that these short-lived long ncRNAs respond to both general and specific chemical stressors, with elevated expression levels due to prolonged decay rates and interruption of RNA degradation pathways.
Based on these findings, we propose that these long ncRNAs have the potential to serve as surrogate indicators of cellular stress responses, providing a novel avenue for understanding the complex molecular mechanisms underlying stress responses in human cells.

title: Isolation of a gene encoding a functional zinc finger protein homologous to erythroid Krüppel-like factor: identification of a new multigene family.
text: We have identified and characterized a novel zinc finger transcription factor gene, termed lung Krüppel-like factor (LKLF). Using a hybridization probe based on the zinc finger domain of erythroid Krüppel-like factor (ELKF), we isolated LKLF and found that it is closely related to ELKF. LKLF is expressed in a limited number of tissues, with the highest levels in the lungs and spleen. The gene is developmentally regulated, with expression detected in the 7-day embryo followed by a decrease at 11 days and subsequent reexpression. LKLF and ELKF share a high degree of similarity in their zinc finger regions, but their sequences diverge significantly elsewhere in the protein. The putative transactivation domains of both proteins are proline-rich regions. In the DNA-binding domain, the three zinc finger motifs are conserved to the point that the predicted DNA contact sites are identical, suggesting that both proteins may bind to the same core sequence. This was confirmed through transactivation assays in which mouse fibroblasts were transiently transfected with a human beta-globin reporter gene in the absence and presence of an LKLF cDNA construct. Expression of the LKLF gene activated the human beta-globin promoter, which contains a CACCC sequence that is recognized by EKLF. Mutation of this site resulted in a significant decrease in reporter gene expression. LKLF and ELKF are therefore members of a unique family of transcription factors that have distinct patterns of expression in different tissues and appear to recognize the same DNA-binding site.

title: A small molecule restores function to TRPML1 mutant isoforms responsible for mucolipidosis type IV.
text: Mucolipidosis type IV (MLIV), an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder, is characterized by severe neurodevelopmental abnormalities and neuro-retinal degeneration. Mutations in the TRPML1 gene are the primary cause of MLIV. To identify small-molecule activators that could potentially restore TRPML1 mutant channel function, we employed lead optimization strategies and tested MLIV patient fibroblasts. Using the whole-lysosome planar patch-clamp technique, we found that the endogenous ligand PI(3,5)P2 had reduced activity in MLIV mutant isoforms, while synthetic ligands could increase channel activity. Interestingly, the F465L mutation rendered TRPML1 pH insensitive, while the F408Δ mutation impacted synthetic ligand binding. Our findings also revealed that small molecule treatment could rescue trafficking defects and zinc accumulation in lysosomes of MLIV mutant fibroblasts. Overall, our data suggest that small molecules have the potential to restore channel function and alleviate disease-associated abnormalities in patient cells harboring specific MLIV point mutations.

title: Characterization of a murine monoclonal antibody to Cryptococcus neoformans polysaccharide that is a candidate for human therapeutic studies.
text: The murine monoclonal antibody (MAb) 18B7, an immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) kappa, is currently in preclinical development for the treatment of Cryptococcus neoformans infections. In preparation for its potential use in humans, we have thoroughly investigated the serological and biological properties of MAb 18B7. Structural analysis of MAb 18B7 revealed striking similarities to the related protective MAb 2H1, despite several amino acid differences. In vitro studies demonstrated that MAb 18B7 binds to all four serotypes of C. neoformans, opsonizes C. neoformans serotypes A and D, enhances both human and mouse effector cell antifungal activity, and activates the complement pathway, leading to the deposition of complement component 3 (C3) on the cryptococcal capsule. In vivo studies showed that administration of MAb 18B7 to mice resulted in rapid clearance of serum cryptococcal antigen and deposition in the liver and spleen. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that MAb 18B7 bound to capsular glucuronoxylomannan in infected mouse tissues. Importantly, no reactivity of MAb 18B7 was detected with normal human, rat, or mouse tissues. These findings suggest that both the variable and constant regions of MAb 18B7 are biologically functional and support its potential use in human therapeutic trials.

title: Treatment with cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors enables repeated administration of vaccinia virus for control of ovarian cancer.
text: Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of death among women with gynecologic malignancies in the United States, and there is a pressing need for effective treatments. One promising new approach is cancer therapy using oncolytic viruses, which selectively infect and destroy cancer cells. Vaccinia virus has been shown to preferentially target tumor cells while sparing healthy tissue, but its effectiveness can be limited by the development of neutralizing antibodies. In this study, we discovered that cox-2 inhibitors can overcome this limitation by preventing the generation of these antibodies, allowing for repeated administration of vaccinia virus without loss of infectivity. We evaluated the antivaccinia antibody response using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and neutralization assays and found that treatment with Cox-2 inhibitors inhibited the generation of neutralizing antibodies. Additionally, we found that combination therapy with Cox-2 inhibitors and vaccinia virus was more effective in treating MOSEC/luc tumor-bearing mice than either treatment alone. This combination represents a potential innovative approach to controlling ovarian tumors.

title: Ser-752-->Pro mutation in the cytoplasmic domain of integrin beta 3 subunit and defective activation of platelet integrin alpha IIb beta 3 (glycoprotein IIb-IIIa) in a variant of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
text: Integrins are transmembrane receptors that mediate cell-cell or cell-matrix adhesion. Integrin alpha IIb beta 3 (glycoprotein IIb-IIIa) acts as a fibrinogen receptor on platelets, promoting platelet aggregation. However, the mechanisms involved in the transition from an inactive to an active conformation are not well understood. We investigated a case of Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a congenital bleeding disorder characterized by the absence of platelet aggregation and fibrinogen binding. The patient's platelets did not bind fibrinogen even though they expressed alpha IIb beta 3. Further studies revealed that isolated alpha IIb beta 3 could bind to an Arg-Gly-Asp-Ser affinity column, and the binding of soluble fibrinogen to the patient's platelets could be triggered by modulators of alpha IIb beta 3 conformation, such as the Arg-Gly-Asp-Ser peptide and alpha-chymotrypsin. These findings suggested that a functional Arg-Gly-Asp binding site was present within alpha IIb beta 3, and that the patient's defect was not due to a blockade of alpha IIb beta 3 in an inactive conformational state. We then sequenced the cytoplasmic domain of beta 3 and found a T-->C mutation at nucleotide 2259, resulting in a Ser-752-->Pro substitution. This mutation is likely responsible for the uncoupling of alpha IIb beta 3 from cellular activation, as it is the only mutation in the entire alpha IIb beta 3 sequence, and genetic analysis of the family showed that the absence of the Pro-752 beta 3 allele was associated with the normal phenotype. Our findings identify the C-terminal portion of the cytoplasmic domain of beta 3 as an intrinsic element in the coupling between alpha IIb beta 3 and platelet activation.

title: Crossover and noncrossover pathways in mouse meiosis.
text:
During meiosis, the recombination of homologous chromosomes generates two types of products: crossover (CR) and noncrossover (NCR) products. CRs form connections between homologous chromosomes, while intermediates leading to NCRs are thought to play a role in homologous pairing. However, the mechanisms by which these events are differentiated and regulated are not yet fully understood.
To address this question, we have developed a strategy to detect, quantify, and map NCRs in parallel with CRs at the Psmb9 meiotic recombination hot spot in male and female mouse germ lines. Our results provide direct molecular evidence for distinct CR and NCR pathways of DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair in mouse meiosis, based on three key observations:
1. Both CRs and NCRs require the presence of Spo11, a key enzyme involved in the meiotic recombination process.
2. NCR products have shorter conversion tracts than CRs, indicating that they may be generated through a different repair pathway.
3. Only CRs require the presence of the MutL homolog Mlh1, which is involved in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks.

Our findings show that both CRs and NCRs are formed from middle to late pachytene of meiotic prophase, and provide evidence for an Mlh1-independent CR pathway, where mismatch repair does not require Mlh1. These results shed light on the complex interplay of mechanisms involved in meiotic recombination and provide new insights into the regulation of DNA repair in the germline.

title: IAP regulation of metastasis.
text: Inhibitor-of-Apoptosis (IAP) proteins play a role in tumor progression, but the mechanisms underlying this process are not fully understood. Our study reveals that cooperation between XIAP and survivin promotes tumor cell invasion and metastasis. This pathway is distinct from IAP-mediated inhibition of cell death, as it involves the activation of NF-κB, leading to increased fibronectin gene expression, signaling by β1 integrins, and activation of cell motility kinases FAK and Src. These findings demonstrate that IAPs are direct metastasis genes, and targeting these proteins with antagonists could provide a new approach to antimetastatic therapy in cancer treatment.

title: 15-Hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase is down-regulated in colorectal cancer.
text: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) can promote tumor growth by modulating multiple oncogenic pathways, including cell proliferation, angiogenesis, migration, invasion, and apoptosis. Although the levels of PGE2 in tissues are maintained through a balance between biosynthesis and degradation, most studies have focused solely on the cyclooxygenase-dependent formation of this lipid. The enzyme responsible for the degradation of PGE2 is NAD+-dependent 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (15-PGDH). Our study found high levels of 15-PGDH in the human and mouse large intestine, while its expression is decreased in several colorectal carcinoma cell lines and other human malignancies, such as breast and lung cancers. We also observed decreased expression of 15-PGDH in ApcMin+/- mouse adenomas. Enzymatic activity of 15-PGDH correlates with expression levels, and genetic disruption of 15-Pgdh completely blocks production of the urinary PGE2 metabolite. Furthermore, our results showed that 15-PGDH expression and activity are significantly down-regulated in human colorectal carcinomas compared to matched normal tissue, suggesting a novel tumor suppressor role for 15-PGDH due to loss of expression during colorectal tumor progression.

title: Stimulation of CD25+CD4+ regulatory T cells through GITR breaks immunological self-tolerance
text: In healthy animals, CD25+CD4+ regulatory T cells are crucial for maintaining immunological self-tolerance. Our findings reveal that the glucocorticoid-induced tumor necrosis factor receptor family–related gene (GITR), also known as TNFRSF18, is predominantly expressed on CD25+CD4+ T cells and CD25+CD4+CD8− thymocytes in naïve mice. We discovered that stimulating GITR impaired the suppression abilities of CD25+CD4+ T cells. Moreover, eliminating GITR-expressing T cells or administering a monoclonal antibody to GITR led to the development of organ-specific autoimmune diseases in otherwise healthy mice. These results suggest that GITR plays a vital role in the dominant immunological self-tolerance maintained by CD25+CD4+ regulatory T cells and could be a promising target for preventing or treating autoimmune diseases.

title: The missing cases of tuberculosis in Malawi: the contribution from cross-border registrations.
text: Low case detection rates of new smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) patients globally are a cause for concern, and this is particularly true in Malawi, where the aim of a recent study was to investigate the number and percentage of patients registered for TB who lived in neighboring countries and the registration, recording, and reporting practices for these "foreign" patients. The study visited all 44 non-private hospitals in Malawi, which register and treat all TB patients in the public health sector, and found that only 10 (23%) of the hospitals maintained a separate register for cross-border TB cases in 2001, and 14 (32%) in 2002. The patients recorded in these registers were not formally reported to the Malawi National TB Programme (NTP), the neighboring country's NTP, or to the World Health Organization (WHO). As a result, these cases were considered "missing." The study found that in Malawi, there were 77 cross-border new smear-positive PTB cases in 2001 and 91 in 2002, which constituted about 3% of the missing smear-positive cases in hospitals with cross-border registers and about 1% of the missing cases nationally.

title: Parathyroid hormone induces E4bp4 messenger ribonucleic acid expression primarily through cyclic adenosine 3',5'-monophosphate signaling in osteoblasts.
text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) binding to its receptor triggers the activation of protein kinase A (PKA), protein kinase C (PKC), and calcium signaling pathways, leading to the transcription of primary response genes in osteoblasts. One of these genes, adenovirus E4 promoter-binding protein/nuclear factor regulated by IL-3 (E4BP4/NFIL3), is induced by PTH in primary mouse osteoblasts (MOBs). To investigate the signaling pathways involved in PTH-induced E4bp4 expression, we examined the effects of various signaling molecules on E4bp4 mRNA levels in MOBs. Our results show that forskolin (FSK), an adenylate cyclase inducer, and 8-bromo-cAMP, a cAMP analog, increase E4bp4 mRNA levels, while ionomycin, a calcium ionophore, has no effect. Pretreatment of cells with a PKA inhibitor strongly inhibited PTH- and FSK-induced E4bp4 expression, while overnight pretreatment with a PKC inhibitor did not alter PTH and FSK effects. Additionally, PTH (3-34), which does not activate cAMP signaling, did not increase E4bp4 expression. Prostaglandin E(2), which signals through cAMP, increased E4bp4 mRNA at all doses, while prostaglandin F(2alpha), which primarily activates PKC and calcium signaling, induced E4bp4 only at high doses. Finally, PTH (1-34) injection induced E4bp4 mRNA expression in mice at 1 hour post-injection. Our data suggest that PTH-induced E4bp4 mRNA expression is mediated primarily through cAMP-PKA signaling in vitro and in vivo, and may play a role in attenuating the transcription of osteoblastic genes possessing E4bp4 promoter binding sites.

title: Managing finances of shipping living donor kidneys for donor exchanges.
text:
Kidney donor exchanges allow recipients with immunologically incompatible donors to receive compatible living donor grafts, but managing the financial aspects of these exchanges can be complex and may hinder the broader implementation of donor exchange programs. Transplant centers that utilize the National Kidney Registry database to facilitate donor exchange transplants have developed a financial model that addresses the costs associated with paired donor exchanges and donor chain transplants.
The first principle of this model is to eliminate financial liability for the donor. The model then accounts for various costs, including donor evaluation, hospital costs for donor nephrectomy, physician fees, organ transportation, and recipient inpatient services. Billing between hospitals is based on Medicare cost report-defined costs rather than charges, ensuring compliance with current federal regulations. We believe that this financial framework could serve as a model for the United Network for Organ Sharing's managed donor exchange program.

title: Human herpesvirus 8 infection and Kaposi's sarcoma among human immunodeficiency virus-infected and -uninfected women.
text: Little is known about the prevalence of human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) infections among women, particularly in high-risk populations. To address this gap in knowledge, a cross-sectional study was conducted among HIV-infected and high-risk HIV-uninfected women in a multisite cohort. The study included 2483 participants and used serological tests to detect HHV-8 infection. The results showed that 4.1% of women were reactive to latent HHV-8 antigens, while 12.0% were reactive to induced antigens. Among women who reported Kaposi's sarcoma, 7 out of 8 had HHV-8 antibodies. The study also found that HHV-8 infection was associated with various risk factors, including HIV infection, drug use, and risky sexual behavior. Specifically, HHV-8 infection was more common among HIV-positive women who used crack, cocaine, or heroin (76% vs. 65%; P<.001), had a past syphilis infection (29% vs. 20%; P<.001), had an injection drug-using male sex partner (61% vs. 53%; P=.014), were black (P=.010), and enrolled at certain sites (P=.015). In multivariate analysis, HIV infection, older age, past syphilis, black race, and enrollment site were independently associated with HHV-8 infection. Overall, the study highlights the importance of investigating HHV-8 infections among high-risk populations, including women, and identifying the factors that contribute to their susceptibility to infection.

title: Cloning of three novel neuronal Cdk5 activator binding proteins.
text: Neuronal Cdk5-like kinase (Nclk) regulates neuronal differentiation and cytoskeleton dynamics. Previous studies showed that Nclk consists of a catalytic subunit, Cdk5, and an activator protein (p25nck5a) derived from a larger neuronal-specific protein (p35nck5a). In this study, we isolated three additional novel p35nck5a-associated proteins using a yeast two-hybrid screen. These proteins, designated C42, C48, and C53, have molecular masses of 66, 24, and 57 kDa, respectively. Northern blot analysis revealed that these proteins are expressed in various human tissues, including the brain, heart, skeletal muscle, placenta, lung, liver, kidney, and pancreas. Bacterially expressed GST-fusion forms of these proteins co-precipitated p35nck5a complexed with Cdk5 from insect cell lysate. Among these proteins, only C48 and C53 could be phosphorylated by Nclk, suggesting that they may be its substrates. Sequence similarity searches revealed that C48 is distantly related to the restin protein, while C42 has homologs of unknown function in Caenorhabditis elegans and Arabidopsis thaliana.

title: The Artemis:DNA-PKcs endonuclease cleaves DNA loops, flaps, and gaps.
text: In eukaryotic cells, the nonhomologous DNA end joining (NHEJ) pathway is the primary mechanism for repairing double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs). Artemis and the 469kDa DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PKcs) collaborate to execute this process in vertebrate organisms. Artemis harbors a unique structure-specific endonuclease activity that is activated by DNA-PKcs-mediated binding and phosphorylation. To comprehend the scope of structural features recognized by the Artemis:DNA-PKcs complex, we investigated various DNA substrates. Our findings reveal that all substrates containing single-to-double-strand transitions can be cleaved by the Artemis:DNA-PKcs complex near the transition region. These cleaved substrates include heterologous loops, stem-loops, flaps, and gapped substrates, demonstrating the versatility of the Artemis:DNA-PKcs nuclease in processing single-/double-strand transition regions. This flexibility is crucial in understanding how reconstituted NHEJ systems lacking DNA polymerases can effectively join incompatible DNA ends while preserving 3' overhangs. Moreover, the ability of the Artemis:DNA-PKcs complex to remove secondary structures that hinder DNA end processing during NHEJ may be essential.

title: A promoter derived from taro bacilliform badnavirus drives strong expression in transgenic banana and tobacco plants
text: Taro bacilliform virus (TaBV) is a pararetrovirus belonging to the genus Badnavirus, which infects the monocotyledonous plant Colocasia esculenta, commonly known as taro. A specific region of the TaBV genome, spanning nucleotides 6,281 to 12 (T1200), was investigated for its promoter activity in various plant cells. This region includes the 3' end of open reading frame 3 (ORF3) and the intergenic region up to the end of the tRNAmet-binding site. In transient assays, three of the four 5' deletion fragments tested (T600, T500, and T250) showed promoter activity in taro leaf, banana suspension cells, and tobacco callus. When these promoters were evaluated in stably transformed, in vitro-grown transgenic banana and tobacco plants, they were found to drive near-constitutive expression of either the green fluorescent protein (GFP) or β-glucuronidase (GUS) reporter gene in the stem (or pseudostem), leaves, and roots, with the strongest expression observed in vascular tissue. In transgenic banana leaves, the T600 promoter directed fourfold greater GUS activity than the T1200, T500, and maize polyubiquitin-1 promoters. In contrast, the levels of GUS expression directed by the three promoters were found to be between four- and ten-fold lower in transgenic tobacco leaves compared to the double Cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter. These findings suggest that the TaBV-derived promoters may be useful for constitutive expression of transgenes in either monocotyledonous or dicotyledonous species.

title: Age of ovary determines remaining life expectancy in old ovariectomized mice.
text: We examined the ability of young ovaries, transplanted into old ovariectomized CBA mice, to enhance the remaining lifespan of the hosts. We used donor females that were sexually mature at 2 months of age, and recipients that were prepubertally ovariectomized at 3 weeks of age. The transplants were performed at 5, 8, or 11 months of age. Compared to ovariectomized control females, the life expectancy of 11-month recipient females was increased by 60%, while the life expectancy of intact control females was increased by 40%. Only 20% of the 11-month transplant females died within a 300-day period following ovarian transplantation, compared to nearly 65% of the ovariectomized control females. The 11-month-old recipient females resumed estrus and continued to cycle for several months beyond the age of control female reproductive senescence. Our findings are consistent with recent discoveries on the gonadal influence on aging in Caenorhabditis elegans and may provide insights into how the mammalian gonad, including the human gonad, can regulate aging and influence longevity.

title: Use of macrolides in mother and child and risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: nationwide cohort study
text:
Objective: To investigate the association between maternal use of macrolide antibiotics during pregnancy and the postnatal period, and the risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) in infants.
Design: Nationwide register-based cohort study.
Setting: Denmark, 1996-2011.
Participants: 999,378 liveborn singletons and linked individual-level information on macrolide prescriptions (maternal use during pregnancy, n=30,091; maternal use after birth, n=21,557; use in infants, n=6591), surgery for IHPS, and potential confounders.
Main Outcome Measures: Surgery for IHPS categorized by maternal macrolide use during pregnancy, after birth, and in infants after birth.
Results: Of 880 infants with IHPS, 29.8% (95% CI: 16.4-54.1) had exposure to macrolides during days 0-13 after birth, and 3.24% (1.20-8.74) had exposure during days 14-120 after birth. Compared to infants with no macrolide use, the adjusted rate ratio for IHPS was 24.4 (95% CI: 13.0-44.1) and 0.65 (0.06-2.21) cases per 1000 infants exposed to macrolides, respectively. The rate ratio for maternal macrolide use during days 0-13 after birth was 3.49 (1.92-6.34), and during days 14-120 was 0.70 (0.26-1.90). The rate ratios for maternal macrolide use during pregnancy were 1.02 (0.65-1.59) for weeks 0-27 and 1.77 (0.95-3.31) for weeks 28 to birth; the corresponding absolute risk differences were 0.01 (-0.31 to 0.50) and 0.67 (-0.06 to 2.02).
Conclusions: Treatment of young infants with macrolide antibiotics was strongly associated with IHPS, and should only be administered if potential treatment benefits outweigh the risk. Maternal use of macrolides during the first two weeks after birth was also associated with an increased risk of IHPS. A possible association was also found with use during late pregnancy.

title: The psychiatric manifestations of mitochondrial disorders: a case and review of the literature.
text:
Mitochondrial disorders can cause a range of psychiatric symptoms, including mood disorders, cognitive impairment, psychosis, and anxiety. Despite the potential significance of these findings, mitochondrial disorders have received little attention in the literature, and the diagnosis is often overlooked or misdiagnosed in patients with psychiatric illness.
To investigate this issue further, we describe a patient who presented with borderline personality disorder and treatment-resistant depression and were ultimately diagnosed with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS). We also conducted a systematic review of the literature to identify all case reports of patients with mitochondrial disorders who initially present with prominent psychiatric symptoms.
Our search identified 50 cases of mitochondrial disorders with psychiatric symptoms, the most common of which were mood disorders, cognitive deterioration, psychosis, and anxiety. The most common diagnosis (52% of cases) was a MELAS mutation, followed by other genetic mitochondrial diagnoses such as polymerase gamma mutations, Kearns-Sayre syndrome, mitochondrial DNA deletions, point mutations, twinkle mutations, and novel mutations.
These findings have important implications for the diagnosis and treatment of patients with psychiatric illness. Psychiatrists should be aware of the clinical features that are indicative of a mitochondrial disorder and investigate patients with suggestive presentations. Additionally, psychiatrists should be knowledgeable about the treatment implications of the diagnosis, including the use of targeted therapies and the potential benefits of genetic testing.
In conclusion, mitochondrial disorders can cause a range of psychiatric symptoms, and psychiatrists should be aware of the potential significance of these findings in their patients. Further research is needed to better understand the relationship between mitochondrial disorders and psychiatric illness, and to develop effective treatments for these conditions.

title: Polo kinase and Asp are needed to promote the mitotic organizing activity of centrosomes
text: Interfering with the activity of polo-like kinases can lead to the formation of abnormal spindles, characterized by monopolar structure. These kinases also regulate various crucial steps in mitosis, including mitotic entry, activation of the anaphase-promoting complex, and the necessary conditions for cytokinesis. The similarities between the phenotypes of Drosophila mutants asp and polo suggest a common role in spindle pole function. The abnormal spindles of asp mutants are bipolar but have disorganized broad poles, where γ-tubulin displays an abnormal distribution. Moreover, the synergistic effect of polo1 aspE3 double mutants suggests a possible involvement of these genes in a shared process. Asp is a protein of approximately 220,000 molecular mass (Mr 220K) located at the centrosome face that interacts with spindle microtubules. In partially purified centrosomes, it co-purifies with γ-tubulin to organize microtubule asters. Our findings reveal that Asp is the previously identified Mr 220K substrate of Polo kinase, which phosphorylates Asp in vitro, converting it into an MPM2 epitope. Polo and Asp proteins co-immunoprecipitate and exist as part of a 25–38S complex. Centrosome extracts from polo-derived embryos are unable to restore the ability of salt-stripped centrosomes to nucleate microtubule asters, which can be rescued by addition of phosphorylated Asp or active Polo kinase.

title: How long will long-term potentiation last?
text: The paramount quality of long-term potentiation (LTP) as a memory mechanism is its enduring nature over time. Although the fundamental characteristics of LTP persistence were first identified 30 years ago, recent research has provided new insights into the duration of LTP persistence and its regulation by activity and experience. It is now evident that LTP, specifically in the dentate gyrus, can either decay rapidly, lasting from hours to weeks, or persist stably, lasting months or longer. The mechanisms that govern LTP induction also influence its subsequent persistence, but the maintenance of LTP is also influenced by post-induction activity patterns, whether experimentally induced or generated by experience. These findings establish the dentate gyrus LTP as a valuable model system for investigating the mechanisms that govern the induction, maintenance, and interference with long-term memory, including very long-term memory lasting months or longer. The challenge is to extend these studies to other brain areas and to explore the relationship, if possible, between the properties and regulation of LTP maintenance and the properties of the information stored in those regions.

title: An IL-13 inhibitor blocks the development of hepatic fibrosis during a T-helper type 2-dominated inflammatory response.
text: In schistosomiasis, chronic parasite egg-induced granuloma formation can lead to tissue destruction and fibrosis, causing significant morbidity and mortality. Our study highlights the crucial role of interleukin-13 (IL-13) in the pathogenesis of schistosomiasis and demonstrates the therapeutic potential of IL-13 inhibitors in controlling hepatic fibrosis. Previous studies have shown that T-helper type 2 (Th2) cytokines, including IL-13 and IL-4, dominate the immune response in mice infected with Schistosoma mansoni. However, the specific contributions of these cytokines to the development of fibrosis were not well understood. Our findings demonstrate that both IL-13 and IL-4 play redundant roles in granuloma formation, but IL-13 is the dominant Th2 cytokine regulating fibrosis. IL-13 stimulates collagen production in fibroblasts and decreases procollagen I and III mRNA expression in mice treated with an IL-13 inhibitor, sIL-13Ralpha2-Fc. In contrast, the reduction in fibrosis observed in IL-4-deficient mice is less pronounced than in sIL-13Ralpha2-Fc-treated animals. Fibrosis is a common pathological feature of various allergic, autoimmune, and infectious diseases, and our findings suggest that IL-13 inhibitors may have broader therapeutic applications in preventing damaging tissue fibrosis resulting from Th2-dominated inflammatory responses.

title: Validity and reliability of observational methods for studying medication administration errors.
text: The study investigated the accuracy and consistency of observational methods used to detect medication administration errors (MAEs) in a UK hospital. Between January and June 1998, two pharmacists observed and recorded MAEs observed by nurses on two hospital wards. The observers intervened in cases of potentially harmful errors. The study analyzed the percentage of omitted doses for which a reason was documented during both observation and non-observation periods. Error rates were also analyzed based on the number of observed rounds for each nurse. The study found that there was no significant difference in the percentage of omitted doses between observation and non-observation periods, and no change in error rates with repeated observations. Additionally, there was no difference in error rates before and after the first intervention for each nurse, and no difference in error detection between the two observers. The study concluded that observation of nurses during drug administration did not significantly affect the MAE rate, and tactful interventions by the observers also had no impact. The study also found that observer reliability was high, suggesting that concerns about the validity and reliability of observational methods may be unfounded.

title: Directly reprogrammed fibroblasts show global epigenetic remodeling and widespread tissue contribution.
text: The expression of four transcription factors, Oct4, Sox2, c-Myc, and Klf4, is sufficient to reprogram the genome of fibroblasts into a pluripotent state, generating induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. However, it remains unclear whether this process globally resets epigenetic differences between differentiated and pluripotent cells. To investigate this, we used novel selection approaches to generate iPS cells from fibroblasts and characterized their epigenetic state. Our findings showed that female iPS cells exhibited reactivation of a silenced X chromosome and random X inactivation upon differentiation, while genome-wide analysis of histone modifications revealed that iPS cells were highly similar to embryonic stem (ES) cells. Additionally, iPS cells gave rise to viable high-degree chimeras with contribution to the germline, indicating that transcription factor-induced reprogramming leads to the global reversal of the somatic epigenome to an ES-like state. These results provide a framework for studying epigenetic modifications during nuclear reprogramming and suggest that abnormal epigenetic reprogramming does not pose a problem for the therapeutic potential of iPS cells.

title: Exocrine ontogenies: on the development of pancreatic acinar, ductal and centroacinar cells.
text: This review provides an overview of the current understanding of pancreas development, including the formation of acinar, ductal, and centroacinar cells. We discuss the transcription factors involved in various stages of exocrine differentiation, from multipotent progenitor cells to fully differentiated acinar and ductal cells. The branching epithelial tree of the embryonic pancreas undergoes a process of progressive restriction, where multipotent pancreatic progenitor cells are directed to either a central "trunk" domain that gives rise to the islet and ductal lineages, or a peripheral "tip" domain that gives rise to acinar cells. Additionally, we examine the role of soluble morphogens and other signaling pathways in influencing these events. Finally, we explore the enigmatic centroacinar cells, whose lineage remains uncertain and whose possible progenitor capacities are still being investigated.

title: The history of SIVS and AIDS: epidemiology, phylogeny and biology of isolates from naturally SIV infected non-human primates (NHP) in Africa.
text: Simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) naturally infects non-human primates in Africa, with 40 different strains identified to date. These viruses are highly diverse and cluster into six distinct phylogenetic lineages. At least eight SIVs are considered recombinant viruses, based on different clustering patterns in different genomic regions. The three known types of genomes are characterized by the presence of vpr, vpx, or vpu genes. vpx is a result of a gene duplication event and is specific to SIVs infecting the Papionini tribe of monkeys and HIV-2 in humans. vpu is found in SIVcpz and HIV-1 and may have originated from a recombination involving SIVs from cercopitecini monkeys. SIV is generally non-pathogenic in its natural hosts, likely due to virus-host adaptation, which allows the virus to replicate without causing disease. However, SIVs have a high propensity for cross-species transmission, and the outcome in the new host can vary from inapparent infection to highly pathogenic. The high diversity of SIVs is attributed to a high mutation rate due to low fidelity of the reverse-transcriptase, active viral and host cell turnover, and host-dependent evolution and recombination. Cross-species transmission is not rare, but preferential host switching may drive the majority of cross-species transmissions. Many SIVs have been shown to grow in vitro on human PBMC, leading to the suggestion that SIV represents a threat for infection of humans in Central Africa and that AIDS is a zoonosis. However, there is no evidence to suggest that AIDS is acquired like a zoonosis. SIV may adapt to the new human host, leading to emergence in the general population. Studying SIV in its natural hosts can provide important clues to the real threat to human populations and elucidate the mechanisms associated with long-term persistent viral infection without clinical consequences for the host.

title: The association between common physical impairments and dementia in low and middle income countries, and, among people with dementia, their association with cognitive function and disability. A 10/66 Dementia Research Group population-based study.
text:
OBJECTIVE:
Chronic physical comorbidities are prevalent in dementia, yet there is a lack of evidence to support evidence-based guidelines for their management. Our study aimed to investigate the extent of these comorbidities and their impact on cognitive function and disability in population-based studies in low- and middle-income countries, where chronic diseases and impairments are likely to be both common and undertreated.
METHODS:
We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional survey of all individuals aged 65 years and older in 11 catchment areas across China, India, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Mexico, and Peru. We estimated the prevalence of pain, incontinence, hearing, and visual impairments, and mobility impairment, and undernutrition among individuals with and without dementia, and assessed the independent contribution of these impairments to cognitive function and disability, adjusting for age, gender, education, and dementia severity.
RESULTS:
We found that incontinence, hearing impairment, mobility impairment, and undernutrition were consistently associated with the presence and severity of dementia across regions. Among individuals with dementia, incontinence, hearing impairment, and mobility impairment were independently associated with disability in all regions, while the contributions of pain, visual impairment, and undernutrition were inconsistent. Notably, hearing impairment made a significant independent contribution to cognitive impairment.
CONCLUSIONS:
Our findings highlight the urgent need for clinical trials of the feasibility, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of regular physical health checks and remediation of identified pathologies, given the high prevalence of comorbidities identified in our population-based studies and the strong evidence for their independent impact on functioning.

title: Serum biomarkers as predictors of lung function decline in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text:
BACKGROUND: Recent studies have shown that patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exhibit low-grade systemic inflammation, which is associated with faster declines in lung function. We aimed to investigate the correlation between serum biomarkers and the decline of lung function in COPD patients.
METHOD: We measured the baseline levels of 9 serum biomarkers (TIMP-1, alpha1-antitrypsin, MMP-9, TNF-alpha, TGF-beta, IL-6, IL-8, neutrophil elastase, and CRP), fibrinogen, and white blood cell counts (WCC) in 96 COPD patients. Lung function was measured at the time of blood sampling and every 3-6 months during the observation period (median 25.0 months). We identified 20 patients as rapid decliners of lung function and 53 patients as non-decliners.
RESULTS: Our results showed that neutrophil counts, serum CRP, and MMP-9 levels were significantly higher in the rapid decliners compared to the non-decliners (p<0.05). The annual change of % predicted FEV(1) was inversely correlated with MMP-9 (r=-0.288; p<0.01) and CRP (r=-0.354; p<0.005) (partial correlation coefficients adjusted for age, sex, cardiovascular disease, smoking history, and baseline % predicted FEV(1)). None of the other biomarkers were correlated with the annual change of % predicted FEV(1).
CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that serum CRP and MMP-9 levels are associated with the decline of lung function in COPD patients. These markers may be useful as predictors of rapid decline of FEV(1) in COPD patients. Further large-scale and long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings and to determine the exact roles of these biomarkers in COPD progression.

title: Phosphorylation of ATM by Cdk5 mediates DNA damage signaling and regulates neuronal death
text: The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase-like kinase ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated) plays a central role in coordinating DNA damage responses, including cell-cycle checkpoint control, DNA repair, and apoptosis. Mutations of ATM lead to a range of defects, from neurodegeneration to cancer predisposition. However, the mechanism by which DNA damage activates ATM is poorly understood. Here, we uncover that the cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5), activated by DNA damage, directly phosphorylates ATM at Ser 794 in post-mitotic neurons.
