title: Systemic arterial hypertension in children following renal transplantation: prevalence and risk factors.
text:
Background: Blood pressure (BP) control after renal transplantation is crucial for optimal allograft and patient outcomes. Our study aimed to investigate the distribution of BP and the prevalence of hypertension in pediatric kidney transplant recipients over the first five years after transplantation, as well as to identify clinical and center-specific factors associated with hypertension.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective chart review of all pediatric kidney transplant patients in the UK, with data collected at 6 months, 1, 2, and 5 years after transplantation. We defined hypertension as systolic and/or diastolic BP > 95th percentile. We analyzed the prevalence of hypertension in both hypertensive and non-hypertensive subjects and evaluated the effectiveness of anti-hypertensive therapy.
Results: Of the 428 patients included in the study, 27.3%, 27.6%, 26.0%, and 25.6% were hypertensive at 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and 5 years after transplantation, respectively. At each time point, approximately 58% of patients were receiving anti-hypertensive therapy, with 31-36% remaining hypertensive. When subjects were identified as hypertensive, on anti-hypertensive medication, or had untreated hypertension, 66.4%, 61.0%, 56.4%, and 55.9% were hypertensive at each time point, respectively. Multivariate analysis revealed odds ratios for systolic hypertension of 4.16 (deceased versus living donor), 2.65 (lowest versus highest quartile of height z-score), and 2.07 (if on anti-hypertensive medication; yes versus no). Significant variation in prevalent rates of hypertension was observed between centers (P < 0.0001), which remained significant after adjustment for all factors in the multivariate model (P = 0.003).
Conclusions: Our study found that control of BP after kidney transplantation remains suboptimal in pediatric centers in the UK, with approximately 25% of patients remaining hypertensive five years after transplantation. Significant differences in hypertension prevalence were observed between centers, which may reflect differences in assessment and management of hypertension. Further investigation is needed to identify effective strategies for improving BP control in this patient population.

title: Coupling cAMP signaling to transcription in the liver: pivotal role of CREB and CREM.
text: Transcriptional factors that bind to cAMP-responsive elements (CREs) in the promoters of various genes belong to the basic domain-leucine zipper superfamily and are composed of three genes in mammals: CREB, CREM, and ATF-1. These proteins are generated through posttranscriptional events, such as alternative splicing, and regulate gene expression by acting as activators or repressors. Activation is triggered by signaling-dependent phosphorylation of a key acceptor site (Ser133 in CREB) by various kinases, including PKA, CamKIV, and Rsk-2. This phosphorylation event leads to the interaction with CBP (CREB-binding protein), a co-activator that also has histone acetyltransferase activity. Repression may involve the dephosphorylation of the activators, leading to decreased association with CBP. Another pathway of transcriptional repression on CRE sites involves the inducible repressor ICER (inducible cAMP early repressor), a product of the CREM gene. ICER is an inducible repressor that is involved in autoregulatory feedback loops of transcription, regulating the down-regulation of early response genes, such as c-fos. The liver represents a unique physiological setting where cAMP-responsive signaling plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression. Following partial hepatectomy, a finely tuned program of gene expression is triggered, leading to specific checkpoints that coordinate a coordinated regeneration of the tissue. Temporal kinetics of transcriptional activation after hepatectomy reveal an early induction pattern for several genes, some of which are controlled by the CREB/CREM transcription factors. The robust induction of ICER after partial hepatectomy suggests an important role of CREM in liver physiology. The delay in tissue regeneration in CREM-deficient mice confirms the crucial function of this factor in regulating hepatocyte proliferation. The study of the specific modification codes that histones display during liver regeneration and physiology will provide exciting new insights into the dynamics of chromatin architecture.

title: Comparison of dietary assessment methods in a Southern French population: use of weighed records, estimated-diet records and a food-frequency questionnaire
text: Objective: The study aimed to develop and validate dietary assessment instruments for the French Mediterranean region. Methods: A sample of 150 male and female volunteers completed three different assessment methods: a 4-day weighed dietary record (PETRA), a 7-day estimated-diet record (S7) based on a checklist and a set of photographs, and a semi-quantitative (standard portion) food-frequency questionnaire (FFQ). The days when PETRA was used to evaluate food consumption coincided with the first 4 days of S7 (S4). Results: Validation was based on nutrients and foods. Energy-adjusted Pearson correlation coefficients between S4 and PETRA ranged from 0.32 for vitamin E to 0.81 for vitamin C (mean: 0.65 for 21 nutrients). There was practically no misclassification in opposite extreme quartiles. Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.63 for fish and seafood to 0.90 for wine (mean: 0.76 for 16 food groups). There was practically no misclassification in opposite extreme quartiles. De-attenuated energy-adjusted Pearson correlation coefficients between FFQ and S7 ranged from 0.22 for proteins and monounsaturated fatty acids to 0.80 for iron (mean: 0.45). 10% or less of subjects were misclassified in opposite extreme quartiles (except for vitamin C, 12%). Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.25 for green-yellow-red raw vegetables to 0.76 for wine (mean: 0.42). 8% or less of subjects were misclassified in opposite extreme quartiles (except for citrus fruit, 11%). Conclusions: Portion estimation using the set of photographs was validated by the correlation between S4 and PETRA for both nutrients and foods. The FFQ provides a reasonably reliable measure of macronutrient intake and a good measure of micronutrient intake when compared with the data in the literature. It performs less well for food intake. Better results can be achieved for FFQ by using the set of photographs instead of standard portions and by adding further questions on foods which are insufficiently covered. Sponsorship: The study was financially supported by INSERM contract 91-1006 and the Ardèche and Hérault Committees of the ‘Ligue contre le cancer’.

title: Substrate fate in activated macrophages: a comparison between innate, classic, and alternative activation.
text:
Macrophages play a crucial role in both innate and adaptive immunity, and their activation can be divided into three main modes: innate, classic, and alternative pathways. These different stimuli result in the expression of specific sets of genes involved in the release of pro- or anti-inflammatory stimuli. In this study, we investigated whether the metabolic patterns of activated macrophages depend on the signaling pathway activated.
To achieve this, we used a [1,2-(13)C(2)]glucose tracer-based metabolomics approach to characterize the metabolic flux distributions in macrophages stimulated through the classic, innate, and alternative pathways. By combining this methodology with mass isotopomer distribution analysis of the newly formed metabolites, our data revealed that activated macrophages are predominantly glycolytic cells, with a clear distinction between the classic/innate activation and the alternative pathway. Interestingly, macrophage activation through LPS/IFN-gamma or TLR-2, -3, -4, and -9 leads to similar metabolic flux distribution patterns, regardless of the pathway activated. However, stimulation through the alternative pathway has minimal metabolic effects.
The molecular basis for the differences between these two types of behavior involves a switch in the expression of 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase (PFK2) from the liver type-PFK2 to the more active ubiquitous PFK2 isoenzyme. This switch is triggered by Hif-1alpha activation and leads to increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate concentration and glycolytic flux. However, using macrophages targeted for Hif-1alpha, we found that the switch of PFK2 isoenzymes still occurs in LPS/IFN-gamma-activated macrophages, suggesting that this pathway regulates ubiquitous PFK2 expression through Hif-1alpha-independent mechanisms.

title: The effect of folic acid supplementation on plasma homocysteine in an elderly population.
text:
BACKGROUND: Elevated levels of plasma homocysteine have been linked to an increased risk of coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and venous thrombosis. Folic acid is the most effective means of reducing homocysteine levels, but the optimal dosage for this population is unknown, particularly among the elderly who are most affected.
AIM: To investigate the effects of various daily folic acid supplements (0, 50, 100, 200, 400, and 600 microg) on plasma homocysteine levels in an elderly population.
DESIGN: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
METHODS: Participants aged 65-75 years (n=368) were randomly assigned to receive one of the treatments for 6 weeks. Plasma homocysteine levels were measured after 3 and 6 weeks of supplementation.
RESULTS: Only the 400 and 600 microg groups showed significantly lower homocysteine levels compared to the placebo group (p=0.038 and p<0.001, respectively). Using multiple linear regression analysis and considering each individual's total folic acid intake (diet plus supplement), a total daily folic acid intake of 926 microg would be required to ensure that 95% of the elderly population is free of cardiovascular risk due to folate deficiency.
DISCUSSION: Achieving a daily folic acid intake of 926 microg through diet alone is unlikely, and supplementation or fortification of food with folic acid may be necessary to reach this target.

title: Central obesity and hyperinsulinaemia in women are associated with polymorphism in the 5' flanking region of the human insulin gene.
text:
Obesity is a complex disease characterized by a multitude of genetic and environmental factors. The distribution of body fat is heterogeneous, with different regions of the body (e.g. central and lower body) being affected to varying degrees. Furthermore, the distribution of fat within these regions shows a stronger genetic component compared to total body fat. Central obesity, in particular, is associated with hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance, which are also features of non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and atherosclerosis.
To investigate the molecular genetics of central obesity, we examined 56 severely obese (mean body mass index 40), unrelated British Caucasoid young women for associations between restriction fragment length polymorphisms of candidate genes and anthropometric measurements and indices of insulin secretion and resistance. The candidate genes studied were the insulin receptor, insulin-sensitive glucose transporter, and insulin gene. We found an association between the class 3 allele of the hypervariable region in the 5' flanking region of the insulin gene and upper segment obesity (P = 0.005). Additionally, this allele was associated with fasting hyperinsulinaemia (P = 0.01), stimulated insulin secretion (P = 0.01), and insulin resistance as calculated from the homeostatic model of assessment (HOMA; P = 0.008). No such associations were observed with the other candidate genes studied.
Our findings suggest that polymorphisms in the 5' flanking region of the insulin gene may influence the expression of the gene and, in turn, modulate insulin production in severely obese female subjects.

title: Population density profiles of nasopharyngeal carriage of 5 bacterial species in pre-school children measured using quantitative PCR offer potential insights into the dynamics of transmission.
text: Bacterial vaccines have the potential to reduce the prevalence of carriage in healthy individuals. Carriage is typically evaluated as a binary endpoint, with individuals either colonized or not colonized. However, the use of real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) allows for the quantification of bacterial DNA in mucosal samples over a wide range, providing a more nuanced understanding of carriage dynamics. By combining culture and species-specific qPCR assays for Streptococcus pneumoniae (lytA), Streptococcus pyogenes (ntpC), Moraxella catarrhalis (ompJ), Haemophilus influenzae (hdp), and Staphylococcus aureus (nuc) with standard curves generated against log-phase reference strain broth cultures, we were able to describe the frequency and peak density distributions of carriage in nasopharyngeal swabs from 161 healthy 2-4 year old children. Our findings indicate that both qPCR and culture methods were generally consistent in their detection of carriage, although there was some discordance at lower detection thresholds, particularly for S. pyogenes and S. aureus. Additionally, we observed a wide range of bacterial DNA concentrations in healthy children carrying these bacteria, which may indicate that different individuals vary greatly in their infectiousness at different times. Understanding the interplay between host, microbial, and environmental factors that influence colonization density is crucial for accurately predicting the effectiveness of vaccines.

title: Circadian mechanisms in murine and human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells following dexamethasone exposure.
text: A small group of regulatory factors control the circadian rhythms in mammalian cells. While the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain acts as the central circadian oscillator, circadian clocks are also present in peripheral tissues and cells. Recent studies have shown that over 20% of mRNAs in bone and adipose tissues exhibit a circadian pattern of expression. This study investigates the presence of the core circadian transcriptional machinery in primary cultures of murine and human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs). Exposure to dexamethasone synchronized the expression of mRNAs encoding the albumin D binding protein (dbp), brain-muscle arnt-like 1 (bmal1), period 3 (per3), rev-erb alpha (Rev A), and rev-erb beta (Rev B) in BMSCs. The genes exhibited a mean oscillatory period of 22.2 to 24.3 hours. The peak expression of mRNAs encoding "positive" (bmal1) and "negative" (per3) components of the circadian regulatory apparatus were found to be out of phase with each other by approximately 8-12 hours, consistent with in vivo observations. In vivo, phosphorylation by glycogen synthase kinase 3beta (GSK3β) regulates the turnover of per3 and components of the core circadian regulatory apparatus. In vitro addition of lithium chloride, a GSK3β inhibitor, significantly shifted the acrophase of all genes by 4.2-4.7 hours in BMSCs, with only male murine BMSCs displaying a significant increase in the length of the period of oscillation. These findings suggest that human and murine BMSCs provide a valid in vitro model for investigating circadian mechanisms in bone metabolism and stem cell biology.

title: Herpesvirus-encoded GPCRs: neglected players in inflammatory and proliferative diseases?
text: Herpesviruses have evolved to encode membrane-associated G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) within their viral genomes, which bear a structural resemblance to chemokine receptors. These viral GPCRs exploit the host cell's GPCR-mediated signaling networks for their survival, replication, and pathogenesis. Of particular interest are the herpesvirus-encoded chemokine receptors ORF74, BILF1, and US28, which are found at inflammatory sites and tumor cells. These virus-specific targets offer promising opportunities for directed therapies, given the druggability of GPCRs in general.

title: Midbody accumulation through evasion of autophagy contributes to cellular reprogramming and tumorigenicity
text: The midbody, a singular organelle formed during cytokinesis, plays a crucial role in the final separation of daughter cells. However, the fate of midbodies (MBds) after cell division remains unclear. Our study reveals that MBds are inherited asymmetrically by daughter cells, with the older centrosome preferentially transmitting MBds to the younger cell. MBds are specifically accumulated in stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, and potential cancer 'stem cells' both in vivo and in vitro. Notably, loss of MBds accompanies stem-cell differentiation and is mediated by the binding of the autophagic receptor NBR1 to the midbody protein CEP55. In contrast, differentiating cells and normal dividing cells do not accumulate MBds and exhibit high autophagic activity. Strikingly, MBd enrichment enhances reprogramming to induced pluripotent stem cells and increases the in vitro tumorigenicity of cancer cells. These findings uncover unexpected roles for MBds in stem cells and cancer 'stem cells'.

title: Integrated genomic analysis identifies clinically relevant subtypes of glioblastoma characterized by abnormalities in PDGFRA, IDH1, EGFR, and NF1.
text: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network (TCGA) has recently identified recurrent genetic abnormalities in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). In this study, we classify GBM into four molecular subtypes based on gene expression patterns: Proneural, Neural, Classical, and Mesenchymal. By integrating multiple types of genomic data, we identify distinct patterns of somatic mutations and DNA copy number alterations for each subtype. For example, the Classical subtype is characterized by mutations in EGFR, NF1, and PDGFRA/IDH1, while the Mesenchymal subtype shows a different gene expression profile and mutational landscape. We also find that the response to aggressive therapy varies by subtype, with the greatest benefit observed in the Classical subtype and little to no benefit in the Proneural subtype. Our findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the molecular diversity of GBM and have important implications for future research.

title: Chronic Hepatitis B Infection: A Review
text: More than 240 million individuals globally are infected with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV), with a significant proportion of these individuals progressing to cirrhosis, which may lead to liver failure and liver cancer. Observational studies have shown that treatment with pegylated interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogues (such as lamivudine, adefovir, entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, and tenofovir alafenamide) can suppress HBV DNA replication and improve liver inflammation and fibrosis. Long-term viral suppression is associated with regression of liver fibrosis and a reduced risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in cohort studies. However, the cure rates after treatment remain low (3%-7% with pegylated interferon and 1%-12% with nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy). While pegylated interferon therapy can be completed in 48 weeks without the development of resistance, its use is limited by poor tolerability and adverse effects such as bone marrow suppression and exacerbation of existing neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression. Newer agents (entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil, and tenofovir alafenamide) may be associated with a significantly reduced risk of drug resistance compared with older agents (lamivudine and adefovir) and should be considered as the first-line treatment. In conclusion, antiviral treatment with either pegylated interferon or a nucleos(t)ide analogue should be offered to patients with chronic HBV infection and liver inflammation in an effort to reduce progression of liver disease. Nucleos(t)ide analogues should be considered as first-line therapy, and most patients will require indefinite therapy due to the low cure rates.

title: CD64 expression distinguishes monocyte-derived and conventional dendritic cells and reveals their distinct role during intramuscular immunization.
text: Although most vaccines are administered intramuscularly (i.m.), little is known about the dendritic cells (DCs) that reside within skeletal muscles. In this study, we investigated the distinct DC subsets that inhabit muscles and their migratory counterparts in draining lymph nodes (LNs). We used the expression of CD64, a high-affinity IgG receptor, to distinguish between conventional DCs (cDCs) and monocyte-derived DCs (mo-DCs). Our findings revealed that alum-injected muscles contain large numbers of cDCs that belong to the CD8α+ and CD11b+ subtypes, which are capable of capturing antigens (Ag) and migrating to draining LNs, where they efficiently activate naive T cells. In contrast, mo-DCs were as numerous as cDCs in alum-injected muscles, but only a small fraction migrated to draining LNs. Notably, the addition of small amounts of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to alum enhanced mo-DC migration. Our results demonstrate that the migratory and functional behavior of muscle DCs and mo-DCs plays a crucial role in the overall immunogenicity of i.m. vaccination, and that a full understanding of the role of adjuvants during this type of vaccination must take into account the heterogeneous behavior of these cells.

title: T-cell-antigen recognition and the immunological synapse
text: Over the past five years, there has been significant excitement in the field of T-cell-antigen recognition, with the immunological synapse - a complex cellular structure that forms at the interface of a T cell and a cell expressing the appropriate peptide-MHC complexes - at the center of attention. Advances in imaging technologies have allowed us to gain a deeper understanding of the role of cell-surface molecules and their associated signaling modules in cell-to-cell communication. The pace of progress has been so rapid that T-cell-antigen recognition may be the first system in which the molecular basis of cell-cell recognition is fully understood.

title: Key interactions by conserved polar amino acids located at the transmembrane helical boundaries in Class B GPCRs modulate activation, effector specificity and biased signalling in the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor.
text:
Class B GPCRs have the potential to exhibit biased agonism in response to ligand stimulation, where multiple signalling effectors are activated. Previous studies highlighted key polar amino acids in the GLP-1 receptor, a key therapeutic target for diabetes and obesity. This study identifies additional conserved polar residues in Class B GPCRs that are important for receptor stability and signalling specificity, using a combination of mutagenesis, pharmacological characterization, molecular modeling, and computational analysis.
The study identifies three positively charged residues (R3.30227, K4.64288, R5.40310) located at the extracellular boundaries of TMs 3, 4, and 5, which are predicted to stabilize extracellular loop 2, a crucial domain for ligand affinity and receptor activation. Additionally, a predicted hydrogen bond network between residues located in TMs 2 (R2.46176), 6 (R6.37348), and 7 (N7.61406 and E7.63408) at the cytoplasmic face of the receptor is important for stabilizing the inactive receptor and directing signalling specificity. Furthermore, residues at the bottom of TM 5 (R5.56326) and TM6 (K6.35346 and K6.40351) are crucial for receptor activation and downstream signalling. Finally, residues predicted to be involved in stabilization of TM4 (N2.52182 and Y3.52250) also influence cell signalling.
In summary, this work expands our understanding of peptide-mediated signalling by the GLP-1 receptor and highlights the importance of these conserved polar residues in Class B GPCRs for receptor stability and signalling specificity.

title: Influence of lifestyle modification on arterial stiffness and wave reflections.
text: Arterial stiffness and wave reflections have deleterious effects on cardiovascular function and disease risk, and are associated with an increased rate of mortality in patients with end-stage renal failure and essential hypertension. Therefore, the prevention and treatment of arterial stiffness are of utmost importance. As arterial stiffening is increasingly recognized as a key predictor of cardiovascular disease (CVD), it is essential to elucidate the role of lifestyle modifications in preventing and reversing arterial stiffening. The available evidence suggests that lifestyle modifications, particularly aerobic exercise and sodium restriction, demonstrate clinical efficacy as therapeutic interventions for preventing and treating arterial stiffening. Consequently, there is sufficient evidence to recommend lifestyle modifications as a primary therapeutic approach for arterial stiffening. However, further research is needed to fully comprehend the mechanisms of lifestyle modifications and to optimize their use in the management of arterial stiffening.

title: Effect of exercise-induced ischemia on QT interval dispersion.
text: An increased dispersion of ventricular repolarization duration (QT dispersion) is associated with an increased risk of arrhythmias. This study aimed to investigate the effect of exercise on QT dispersion in patients with ischemic heart disease (IHD). QT dispersion, corrected QT dispersion, and the percentage change in uncorrected and corrected QT dispersion between rest and peak exercise were measured in 14 control subjects, 17 patients with IHD, and 14 patients with IHD receiving beta-blockers (IHD-B). All subjects underwent a standard Bruce protocol exercise test, and QT intervals were measured at rest and peak exercise using a digitizing tablet interfaced to a personal computer. Compared to the control and IHD-B groups, QT dispersion at rest was significantly increased in the IHD group (corrected QT dispersion: 74 ± 7 vs 40 ± 4 and 49 ± 5 msec, respectively, p < 0.03). At peak exercise, the corrected QT dispersion was greater in the IHD group compared to the control group (57 ± 5 vs 26 ± 3 msec, p < 0.03). Moreover, the percentage change in QT dispersion with exercise was significantly higher in the IHD group (52% ± 5%) compared to the control group (28% ± 4%, p < 0.002) and the IHD-B group (30% ± 3%, p < 0.01). These findings suggest that a larger mean QT dispersion at peak exercise and an increased percentage change in QT dispersion with exercise may contribute to the increased susceptibility of the IHD group to arrhythmias. The cardioprotective effects of beta-blockers may be attributed to their ability to blunt exercise-related changes in QT dispersion.

title: Effects of powered mobility on self-initiated behaviors of very young children with locomotor disability.
text: This research examines the impact of powered mobility on the spontaneous behavior of six young children with diverse disabilities who learned to use motorized wheelchairs in less than three weeks. Using a multiple baseline design, two-hour observation periods were recorded on video at 10-day intervals before and after they achieved independent mobility. The study analyzed the frequency of self-initiated interactions with objects, spatial exploration, and communication with caregivers. Results showed that three children exhibited increased behavior in all three categories, while one child increased in two categories but decreased in interactions with objects. The remaining two children only showed increased spatial exploration.

title: BCR/ABL modifies the kinetics and fidelity of DNA double-strand breaks repair in hematopoietic cells.
text: The oncogenic BCR/ABL tyrosine kinase promotes the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Following exposure to gamma radiation, BCR/ABL-positive leukemia cells exhibit an increased accumulation of DSBs compared to normal cells. These lesions are repaired through a time-dependent process involving non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination repair (HRR) mechanisms. However, our findings reveal that mutations and large deletions are present in the HRR and NHEJ products, respectively, in BCR/ABL-positive leukemia cells. We propose that unreliable repair of DSBs may contribute to genomic instability in Philadelphia chromosome-positive leukemias.

title: Bone morphogenetic protein signaling in nephron progenitor cells
text: Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling is crucial for various aspects of kidney development and plays a significant role in determining the outcome of kidney injury. BMP treatment is also an essential component of protocols for differentiating nephron progenitors from pluripotent stem cells. This review will delve into the role of BMP signaling in directing nephron progenitor cells in these different contexts.

title: Computational analysis of 3'-ends of ESTs shows four classes of alternative polyadenylation in human, mouse, and rat.
text: Alternative initiation, splicing, and polyadenylation are crucial mechanisms employed by many organisms to generate diversity among mature mRNA transcripts originating from the same transcription unit. While previous computational analyses of alternative polyadenylation have primarily focused on polyadenylation activities within or downstream of the normal 3'-terminal exons, our study presents the results of the first genome-wide analysis of patterns of alternative polyadenylation in the human, mouse, and rat genomes across the entire transcribed regions of mRNAs using 3'-ESTs with poly(A) tails aligned to genomic sequences. Four distinct classes of patterns of alternative polyadenylation emerge from this analysis: tandem poly(A) sites, composite exons, hidden exons, and truncated exons. We estimate that at least 49% (human), 31% (mouse), and 28% (rat) of polyadenylated transcription units exhibit alternative polyadenylation. A portion of these alternative polyadenylation events lead to the creation of new protein isoforms.

title: Epigenetic instability in ES cells and cloned mice.
text: Cloning through nuclear transfer (NT) is a challenging process, resulting in a high mortality rate among clones before birth and growth abnormalities in survivors. To investigate the underlying causes of these issues, we examined imprinted gene expression in both cloned mice and the embryonic stem (ES) cell donor populations from which they were derived. Our findings revealed that the epigenetic state of the ES cell genome was highly unstable, and variation in imprinted gene expression was observed in most cloned mice, even those derived from the same subclone of ES cells. Despite these abnormalities, many of the animals survived to adulthood, suggesting that mammalian development may be surprisingly resilient to epigenetic aberrations in the genome. These findings imply that even seemingly normal cloned animals may harbor subtle abnormalities in gene expression.

title: Successful three-way kidney paired donation with cross-country live donor allograft transport.
text: Offering transplantation opportunities to patients with incompatible live donors through kidney paired donation (KPD) is considered a crucial strategy to address the organ shortage crisis. It is estimated that implementing a national KPD program in the United States could lead to an additional 1000-2000 transplants per year. While most of these transplants could be performed within the participants' local or regional area, patients with rare blood types or broad HLA sensitization may benefit from larger geographic matching. In this case, either the patients or organs would need to travel to optimize the benefits of a national program. Our study demonstrates how a triple KPD enabled a highly sensitized patient (PRA 96%) to receive a well-matched kidney from a live donor on the opposite coast. The kidney was removed in San Francisco and transported to Baltimore, where it was reperfused 8 hours later. The patient experienced prompt function and has maintained a serum creatinine level of 1.1 mg/dl one year later. This case provides a model for addressing the complexities involved in implementing a national KPD program in a large country like the United States.

title: Role of PACAP and VIP in astroglial functions.
text: Astrocytes constitute a substantial proportion of the human brain, comprising at least half of its volume. In addition to their supporting functions, astrocytes play a crucial role in the regulation of stem cell proliferation, synaptic plasticity, and neuroprotection. These cells are also involved in the response to neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, and they release regulatory factors known as gliotransmitters that modulate neuronal physiology. Of particular interest is the expression of the Pituitary Adenylate Cyclase-Activating Polypeptide (PACAP)-specific receptor PAC1-R and the PACAP/Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide (VIP) mutual receptors VPAC1-R and VPAC2-R by astrocytes during development and/or in the adult. Recent studies have demonstrated that PACAP and VIP modulate a range of astrocyte activities, including proliferation, plasticity, glycogen production, and biosynthesis of neurotrophic factors and gliotransmitters.

title: A subset of 26S proteasomes is activated at critically low ATP concentrations and contributes to myocardial injury during cold ischemia.
text: The molecular mechanisms underlying myocardial injury during warm or cold ischemia remain inadequately understood. Although proteasomes are believed to contribute to myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury, their roles during the ischemic period are still unclear. Given that donor hearts are frequently exposed to prolonged global cold ischemia prior to cardiac transplantation, we investigated the role and regulation of the proteasome during cold ischemic storage of rat hearts in relation to myocardial ATP content. Our findings revealed that cardiac proteasome peptidase activity increased by 225% as ATP levels declined during cold ischemic storage of hearts in University of Wisconsin (UW) solution for up to 48 hours. The addition of the specific proteasome inhibitor epoxomicin to the UW solution significantly reduced edema formation and preserved the ultrastructural integrity of the cardiomyocyte. Using purified 20S/26S proteasome enzyme preparations, we demonstrated that this activation can be attributed to a subset of 26S proteasomes that are stable at ATP concentrations far below physiological levels. Furthermore, our data showed that ATP negatively regulates the activity of this subset of proteasomes, with maximal activation occurring at ATP concentrations in the low micromolar range. These findings suggest that proteasome activation is a pathophysiologically relevant mechanism of cold ischemic myocardial injury, and that a subset of 26S proteasomes may function as a cell-destructive protease that is activated as ATP levels decline. Notably, proteasome inhibition during cold ischemia preserved the ultrastructural integrity of the cardiomyocyte.

title: Coping and satisfaction with growth hormone treatment among short-stature children.
text: The impact of children's ability to cope with a chronic medical condition requiring prolonged treatment on their quality of life and that of their parents serves as a measure of the quality of treatment. This study specifically examines the coping abilities and satisfaction with treatment of children who were two or more standard deviations below average in height for their age and gender, and were receiving growth hormone (GH) treatment for at least a year. The study population consisted of 96 patients, including 53 males, who were treated with daily injections at home for 12 to 66 months. A self-administered questionnaire was used to assess the patients' ability to cope and their degree of satisfaction and compliance with treatment. No significant differences were found in coping abilities, satisfaction, or compliance based on gender, presence of an underlying disease, age at which treatment began, or duration of treatment. Despite the fact that the long-term effects of GH treatment on final height are still unknown, the patients' satisfaction and compliance with treatment were high.

title: Risk for breast cancer development determined by mammographic parenchymal pattern.
text:
A classification system for breast cancer risk based solely on mammographic parenchymal patterns has been developed. The study analyzed mammography images of over 30-year-old women who were examined at Hutzel Hospital in Detroit over a five-year period, with an average follow-up time of approximately 2.5 years. The study identified four groups of patients with varying incidences of breast cancer, including:
Group 1: 0.1% incidence of breast cancer
Group 2: 0.4% incidence of breast cancer
Group 3: 1.7% incidence of breast cancer
Group 4: 2.2% incidence of breast cancer
Each group was characterized by distinct mammographic parenchymal patterns, which were described and criteria for their identification were provided.

title: Accurate coarse-grained modeling of red blood cells.
text: We establish a systematic coarse-graining method for modeling red blood cells (RBCs) based on mean-field theory. Our three-dimensional RBC membrane model considers the bending energy, in-plane shear energy, and constraints of fixed surface area and fixed enclosed volume. The coarse-graining method is versatile and can be applied at any level of coarse-graining without requiring any fitting parameters. We investigate the sensitivity of the coarse-grained model and validate its behavior against both experimental data and dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations of RBCs in various flow conditions, including capillary and shear flows.

title: Mice deficient in CD4 T cells have only transiently diminished levels of IFN-gamma, yet succumb to tuberculosis.
text: CD4 T cells play a crucial role in the protective immune response against tuberculosis. To investigate the mechanism of this protection, two mouse models lacking CD4 T cells were used to examine the impact of CD4 T cells on resistance to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Transgenic mice lacking either major histocompatibility complex class II (MHC class II) or CD4 molecules were found to be more susceptible to M. tuberculosis infection than wild-type mice, as measured by survival following infection. However, the relative resistance of CD4-deficient mice was not attributed to increased numbers of double-negative (CD4-8-) T cells. Analysis of in vivo interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) production in the lungs of infected mice revealed that both mutant mouse strains were transiently impaired in their ability to produce IFN-gamma following infection. At 2 weeks post-infection, IFN-gamma production in the mutant mice was reduced by over 50% compared to wild-type mice. However, by 4 weeks post-infection, both mutant and wild-type mice had similar levels of IFN-gamma mRNA and protein production. In CD4 T cell-deficient mice, IFN-gamma production was found to be due to CD8 T cells. These findings suggest that early events in M. tuberculosis infection are crucial determinants of the course of infection and support the hypothesis that CD4 T cells play an important role in the protective immune response against tuberculosis.

title: Treatment and management of graft-versus-host disease: improving response and survival.
text:
Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a significant clinical challenge in the field of allogenic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, with a high morbidity and mortality rate. Despite significant advances in understanding the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and predisposing factors, a standardized therapeutic strategy for GVHD is still lacking.
Corticosteroid therapy has shown good evidence for initial treatment of both acute and chronic forms of GVHD. However, the most effective approach to steroid-refractory disease remains controversial, with current practice varying significantly between institutions. Early diagnosis, multidisciplinary collaboration, and adequate supportive care, including infection prophylaxis, are crucial in optimizing outcomes for patients with GVHD.
The aim of this review is to provide an overview of existing treatment options and management strategies for acute and chronic GVHD, in the hope of improving patient outcomes in the future.

title: The value of self-report assessment of adherence, rhinitis and smoking in relation to asthma control.
text: Objective: To investigate the utility of self-report measures of inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) adherence, rhinitis, and smoking status in predicting asthma control. Methods: Patients prescribed ICS for asthma at 85 UK practices completed validated questionnaires assessing asthma control (Asthma Control Questionnaire; ACQ) and adherence (Medication Adherence Report Scale), as well as a two-item measure of smoking status and a single-item measure of rhinitis. Complete anonymized questionnaires were available for 3916 participants. Results: Poor asthma control (ACQ >1.5) was associated with reported rhinitis (OR = 4.62; 95% CI: 3.71-5.77), smoking (OR = 4.33; 95% CI: 3.58-5.23), and low adherence to ICS (OR = 1.35; 95% CI: 1.18-1.55). The degree of rhinitis was also significant, with those reporting severe rhinitis experiencing the worst asthma control, followed by those reporting mild rhinitis and then those reporting no rhinitis symptoms (F(2, 3913) = 128.7, p < 0.001). Additionally, there was a significant relationship between the number of cigarettes smoked each day and asthma control (F(5, 655) = 6.08, p < 0.001). Conclusions: This study demonstrates that self-report measures of ICS adherence, rhinitis, and smoking status can identify potentially modifiable predictors of poor asthma control. These findings suggest that incorporating these measures into routine asthma reviews could help improve asthma control and reduce symptoms.

title: Development of a syngeneic mouse model for events related to ovarian cancer.
text: In this study, researchers isolated mouse ovarian surface epithelial cells (MOSEC) from virgin, mature mice and cultured them in vitro. They found that early passage cells (<20 passages) had a cobblestone morphology and exhibited contact inhibition of growth, but this was lost after approximately 20 passages in vitro. When injected into athymic and syngeneic mice, early passage MOSEC did not form tumors in vivo, while late passage MOSEC formed tumors throughout the abdominal cavity and produced hemorrhagic ascitic fluid. The tumors were found to be highly malignant and contained both carcinomatous and sarcomatous components. The researchers also established ten clonal lines from late passage MOSEC, which formed multiple peritoneal tumors and ascitic fluid after injection into mice. The clonal cell lines were found to have polyploid modal chromosome numbers, with common chromosomal abnormalities including +5, +15, +19 and -X, -3, -4. One cell line had a clonal translocation between chromosomes 15 and 18, while another had a small marker chromosome. These findings demonstrate the development of a mouse model for studying events related to ovarian cancer in humans, with the ability to form extensive tumors within the peritoneal cavity and produce tumors in mice with intact immune systems. This model provides a unique opportunity for investigating molecular and immune interactions in ovarian cancer development.

title: Hypoxia in cancer: significance and impact on clinical outcome
text: Hypoxia, a hallmark of advanced solid tumors, has emerged as a crucial factor in tumor progression and resistance to therapy. This condition presents a paradoxical "Janus face," as it can both slow down tumor growth and promote an aggressive phenotype. Despite being independent of traditional prognostic factors such as tumor stage and nodal status, hypoxia has been suggested as an unfavorable prognostic indicator for patient outcomes. Studies using direct oxygenation assessment have shown that patients with hypoxic cervical cancers or soft tissue sarcomas have poorer disease-free survival. In head and neck cancers, hypoxia has been linked to poorer survival and local control. However, technical limitations of direct oxygen sensing have led to the use of surrogate markers, such as hypoxia-related endogenous proteins (e.g., HIF-1α, GLUT-1, CA IX) or exogenous bioreductive drugs. While endogenous markers have shown prognostic significance in some studies, the prognostic value of exogenous markers appears limited. Non-invasive imaging techniques, such as PET or SPECT detection of radiolabeled tracers or MRI techniques (e.g., BOLD), can also be used to assess hypoxia. However, the clinical experience with these methods is currently limited, and inconsistencies in the endpoints used to characterize oxygenation status and methodological differences (e.g., different immunohistochemical staining procedures) may impact the accuracy of the prognostic parameter used.

title: Knowledge and Practice of Standard Precautions and Awareness Regarding Post-Exposure Prophylaxis for HIV among Interns of a Medical College in West Bengal, India.
text:
Objective:
To assess the knowledge of interns regarding standard precautions and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, and identify the gap between knowledge and practice, as well as determine the perceived barriers against adherence to standard precautions.
Methods:
A study was conducted among 130 interns of the 2010-11 batch from a government-run medical college in Kolkata, India, using a self-administered questionnaire that covered basic components of standard precautions and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV. The questionnaire also included open-ended questions regarding reasons for non-adherence to standard precautions and additional space for specific comments.
Results:
The study found that while interns had good knowledge of personal protective equipment, hand washing, safe handling, and disposal of needles and sharp objects, they had poor adherence to these practices. The main reasons for non-adherence were found to be clumsiness in handling needles, wearing gloves, feeling uncomfortable when wearing aprons, impracticality of regular hand-washing, and non-availability of equipment. Although most respondents were aware of washing sites of injured with soap and water, approximately 32.3% did not know that antiseptics could cause more damage. Additionally, only 63.8% of respondents were aware of reporting any incidence of occupational exposure, and knowledge on post-exposure prophylaxis regimens was generally found to be poor.
Conclusion:
The study highlighted a significant gap between knowledge and practice of standard precautions and inadequate knowledge of post-exposure prophylaxis, emphasizing the need for continuous on-site training of interns with supportive supervision and monitoring of their activities.

title: Viruses and microRNAs
text: The discovery of RNA interference (RNAi) and cellular microRNAs (miRNAs) has revolutionized the field of biological research and uncovered a previously unknown level of post-transcriptional gene regulation. Recently, virally encoded miRNAs have been identified in several pathogenic human viruses, and their potential functions are being explored. I propose that cellular miRNAs may have played a significant role in shaping the evolution of these viruses and continue to influence their in vivo behavior. As our understanding of viral miRNA function grows, it may provide new insights into how latent viruses, such as herpesviruses, evade the host immune system. Additionally, research into viral miRNA function may lead to novel approaches for treating diseases caused by these viruses.

title: Economic impact of primary open-angle glaucoma in Australia.
text:
Background: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, posing significant public health and economic concerns.
Design: A systematic review of published randomized trials and population-based studies since 1985 was conducted to assess the economic impact of primary open-angle glaucoma.
Methods: A dynamic model was used to estimate the cost-effectiveness of different interventions to prevent vision loss from primary open-angle glaucoma in Australia, taking into account changes in detection rates and management strategies. The main outcome measures were financial cost (in Australian dollars) and disability-adjusted life years.
Results: The prevalence of glaucoma in Australia is expected to increase from 208,000 in 2005 to 379,000 in 2025 due to the aging population. Health system costs over the same time period are estimated to increase from $AU355 million to $AU784 million. Total costs (health system costs, indirect costs, and costs of loss of well-being) will increase from $AU1.9 billion to $AU4.3 billion in Australia.
Conclusion: Primary open-angle glaucoma poses a substantial economic burden, which will significantly increase by 2025. This dynamic model provides a valuable tool for ongoing policy formulation and determining the economic impact of interventions to prevent visual impairment and blindness from glaucoma.

title: The LIM domain-containing homeo box gene Xlim-1 is expressed specifically in the organizer region of Xenopus gastrula embryos.
text: A novel protein motif, named LIM, has been identified in the homeobox genes lin-11, Isl-1, and mec-3 in Caenorhabditis elegans, which determine cell lineages during embryonic development. We isolated related LIM class homeobox genes from Xenopus laevis, including Xlim-1, and investigated its expression pattern. Xlim-1 mRNA is present at low levels in the unfertilized egg, with a major expression phase during the gastrula stage, followed by a decrease and subsequent increase during the tadpole stage. The brain exhibits the highest abundance of Xlim-1 mRNA in adult tissues. The maternal and late expression phases of the Xlim-1 gene suggest that it has multiple functions at different stages of the Xenopus life cycle. In the gastrula embryo, Xlim-1 mRNA is localized in the dorsal lip and dorsal mesoderm, which is consistent with its role in establishing body pattern during gastrulation. Explant experiments revealed that Xlim-1 mRNA is induced by the mesoderm-inducing factor activin A and retinoic acid, which is not a mesoderm inducer but affects patterning during Xenopus embryogenesis. Combining activin A and retinoic acid leads to synergistic induction of Xlim-1 mRNA. The structure, inducibility, and localized expression in the organizer of the Xlim-1 gene suggest that it plays a role in establishing body pattern during gastrulation.

title: Signal transduction proteins that associate with the platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) receptor mediate the PDGF-induced release of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase from permeabilized cells.
text:
In a study published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 1991, researchers investigated the signal transduction pathways involved in the release of glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) from permeabilized rat kidney cells. The study found that G6PD release was significantly increased in cells transfected with wild type platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) receptors (PDGFR) following stimulation with peptide growth factors, but not in cells transfected with tyrosine kinase-deficient PDGFR. The study also found that the PDGF-stimulated release of G6PD was partially restored in PDGFR mutants that could associate with either phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase or phospholipase C gamma 1. The study concluded that the release of G6PD:
1. Requires intrinsic PDGFR tyrosine kinase activity
2. Requires PDGFR autophosphorylation
3. Is mediated by signaling proteins that associate with the PDGFR
4. Is not mediated by direct phosphorylation of G6PD.

title: Microarrays for the study of viral gene expression during human cytomegalovirus latent infection.
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is one of the largest known DNA viruses, with a ubiquitous presence in the human host. Following the resolution of primary productive infection, HCMV establishes a lifelong latent infection in myeloid lineage cells, such as monocytes and their progenitors. While most adults with HCMV infection are asymptomatic, the virus can cause neurological deficits in infants and remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in immunosuppressed individuals. Microarray-based studies have provided valuable insights into the genes that are transcriptionally active during both the productive and latent phases of HCMV infection. This chapter details the methods used to investigate genes in HCMV using microarrays, with a focus on two cell types: productively infected human foreskin fibroblasts and latently infected primary human myeloid progenitor cells.

title: Physiological implications of hydrogen sulfide: a whiff exploration that blossomed.
text: The crucial life-sustaining role of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) has evolved from microorganisms to plants, invertebrates, vertebrates, and finally to mammals. However, for centuries, H2S was primarily known for its toxicity and environmental hazards. Only in the past decade has its physiological importance been recognized. The discovery of endogenous H2S production in mammalian cells and its subsequent typification as a gasotransmitter have led to a deeper understanding of its multifaceted physiological functions. H2S-catalyzing enzymes are differentially expressed in various organ systems, including the cardiovascular, nervous, immune, renal, respiratory, gastrointestinal, reproductive, liver, and endocrine systems. These enzymes modulate the functions of these systems by producing H2S, which in turn affects a variety of molecular targets, such as ion channels and signaling proteins. Abnormalities in H2S metabolism have been implicated in a wide range of pathological conditions, including hypertension, atherosclerosis, heart failure, diabetes, cirrhosis, inflammation, sepsis, neurodegenerative disease, erectile dysfunction, and asthma. To address these challenges, novel technologies have been developed to detect endogenous H2S production, and novel H2S-delivery compounds have been invented to aid therapeutic intervention of diseases related to abnormal H2S metabolism. As research in this field continues to expand, it is entering an exponential era of exploration and discovery.

title: TatC is a specificity determinant for protein secretion via the twin-arginine translocation pathway.
text: The recent discovery of a ubiquitous translocation pathway, specifically required for proteins with a twin-arginine motif in their signal peptide, has shifted attention to its membrane-bound components, including TatC. Unlike most organisms whose genomes have been completely sequenced, the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis harbors two tatC-like genes, tatCd and tatCy. The corresponding TatCd and TatCy proteins may be involved in the translocation of 27 proteins with putative twin-arginine signal peptides, with approximately 6-14 predicted to be secreted into the growth medium. Using a proteomic approach, we found that PhoD of B. subtilis, a phosphodiesterase belonging to a novel protein family, is secreted via the twin-arginine translocation pathway. Notably, TatCd is crucial for the secretion of PhoD, while TatCy is not required. These findings suggest that TatC acts as a specificity determinant for protein secretion via the Tat pathway. Based on our observations, we propose that the TatC-determined pathway specificity is due to specific interactions between TatC-like proteins and other pathway components, such as TatA, of which three paralogues are present in B. subtilis.

title: Function and regulation of SUMO proteases
text: Covalent attachment of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) to proteins is highly dynamic, and both SUMO conjugation and cleavage can be regulated. Protein desumoylation is mediated by SUMO proteases, which play a crucial role in controlling various cellular mechanisms, including transcription, cell division, and ribosome biogenesis. Recent breakthroughs have led to the discovery of two novel classes of SUMO proteases, improved understanding of SUMO protease specificity, and the revelation of previously unappreciated SUMO protease functions in key cellular pathways. These advances, combined with new connections between SUMO proteases and the recently identified SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligases (STUbLs), make this an exciting time to study these enzymes.

title: Review article: prebiotics in the gastrointestinal tract.
text:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are short-chain carbohydrates that alter the composition or metabolism of the gut microbiota in a beneficial manner, potentially leading to improved health outcomes. Unlike probiotics, which are live microorganisms, prebiotics are non-living and are expected to be cheaper and carry less risk, making them easier to incorporate into the diet.
AIM: To review the published evidence for the effects of prebiotics on gut function and human health.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of the Science Citation Index was conducted using the terms "prebiotic," "microbiota," "gut bacteria," "large intestine," "mucosa," "bowel habit," "constipation," "diarrhea," "inflammatory bowel disease," "Crohn's disease," "ulcerative colitis," "pouchitis," "calcium," and "cancer," focusing primarily on studies in humans and reports in the English language. The Cochrane Library was also searched, but no clinical studies or meta-analyses were identified on this topic.
RESULTS: Three prebiotics - oligofructose, galacto-oligosaccharides, and lactulose - were found to clearly alter the balance of the large bowel microbiota by increasing the numbers of bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus. These carbohydrates are fermented and produce short-chain fatty acids and intestinal gas, although the effects on bowel habit are relatively small. Randomized-controlled trials of their effect in a clinical context are limited, although animal studies have shown anti-inflammatory effects in inflammatory bowel disease and increased calcium absorption.
CONCLUSIONS: While it is still early days for prebiotics, they offer the potential to modify the gut microbial balance in a way that brings direct health benefits at a relatively low cost and with minimal risk.

title: Pain catastrophizing and general health status in a large Dutch community sample.
text: The current study aimed to investigate the relationship between pain catastrophizing and overall health status in a Dutch adult community sample, including various subgroups of individuals with musculoskeletal pain. As part of this study, we also replicated previous studies on the factor structure, reliability, and validity of the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS). Our findings showed that across different pain subgroups, catastrophizing uniquely contributed to the prediction of various aspects of general health status beyond the variance explained by pain intensity, age, gender, and chronicity. Strongest associations were found between catastrophizing and mental health, general health perception, social functioning, and vitality. Additionally, the association between catastrophizing and general health status was not moderated by the chronicity of the pain. Our results from confirmatory factor analysis confirmed a three-factor model of the PCS, which was invariant across different subgroups of people with musculoskeletal pain. The inter-factor correlations were high, and the incremental explanatory power of the three-factor model over a one-factor model was only marginal, suggesting that a one-factor model might be justifiable as well. The reliability of the PCS total and subscales was adequate across various pain subgroups, and we also found evidence for the concurrent validity of the PCS.

title: Variability in risk of gastrointestinal complications with individual non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: results of a collaborative meta-analysis.
text:
Objective: To compare the relative risks of serious gastrointestinal complications associated with different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
Design: Systematic review of controlled epidemiological studies that investigated the relation between NSAID use and admission to hospital for haemorrhage or perforation.
Setting: Hospital and community-based case-control and cohort studies.
Main Outcome Measures:
(a) Estimated relative risks of gastrointestinal complications with use of individual drugs, with exposure to ibuprofen used as the reference; (b) ranking of the relative risks observed in the studies to summarize the sequence of risk.
Results: 12 studies met the inclusion criteria, providing comparative data on ibuprofen and other NSAIDs. Ibuprofen ranked lowest or equal lowest for risk in 10 of the 11 studies, and the pooled relative risks calculated with exposure to ibuprofen as the reference were all significantly greater than 1.0 (interval of point estimates 1.6 to 9.2). Overall, ibuprofen was associated with the lowest relative risk, followed by diclofenac. Azapropazone, tolmetin, ketoprofen, and piroxicam ranked highest for risk, and indomethacin, naproxen, sulindac, and aspirin occupied intermediate positions. Higher doses of ibuprofen were associated with relative risks similar to those with naproxen and indomethacin.
Conclusions: The low risk of serious gastrointestinal complications associated with ibuprofen is primarily due to the low doses used in clinical practice. In higher doses, ibuprofen is associated with a similar risk to other NSAIDs. Using low-risk drugs in low doses as first-line treatment would significantly reduce morbidity and mortality due to serious gastrointestinal toxicity from these drugs.

title: Accuracy of weighed dietary records in studies of diet and health.
text:
Objective:
To conduct an independent evaluation of the accuracy of seven-day weighed dietary records in assessing habitual dietary intake, as the most commonly used method in studies examining the relationship between diet and health.
Design:
Subjects from the Northern Ireland Diet and Health Study, who were randomly selected by stratified sampling, were re-evaluated to represent the range of energy intakes in the study.
Setting:
Northern Ireland.

Subjects:
31 free-living adults (16 men and 15 women).

Main Outcome Measures:
Energy intake measured by seven-day weighed dietary records and total energy expenditure estimated concurrently using the doubly labeled water technique.

Results:
The average recorded energy intake was significantly lower than the measured expenditure in the overall group (9.66 MJ/day vs 12.15 MJ/day, 95% confidence interval of 1.45 to 3.53 MJ/day). Among those in the upper third of energy intakes, the mean (SE) ratio of intake to expenditure was close to 1.0, indicating accurate records (men: 1.01 (0.11), women: 0.96 (0.08). In the middle and lower thirds, the ratios for men were 0.74 (0.05) and 0.70 (0.07), respectively, and for women, 0.89 (0.07) and 0.61 (0.07).


Conclusions:
These findings suggest a significant bias in reporting habitual energy intake, which may have far-reaching implications for the interpretation of many nutritional studies.

title: A novel family of sequence-specific endoribonucleases associated with the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats.
text: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPRs) work in conjunction with associated CAS proteins to protect microbial cells from foreign genetic elements using unknown molecular mechanisms. All CRISPR systems contain proteins of the CAS2 family, suggesting that these uncharacterized proteins play a central role in this process. In this study, we demonstrate that CAS2 proteins are a novel family of endoribonucleases. We found that six purified CAS2 proteins from different organisms cleaved single-stranded RNAs preferentially within U-rich regions. A representative CAS2 enzyme, SSO1404 from Sulfolobus solfataricus, specifically cleaved the phosphodiester linkage on the 3'-side and generated 5'-phosphate- and 3'-hydroxyl-terminated oligonucleotides. The crystal structure of SSO1404 was resolved at 1.6 Å resolution, revealing the first ribonuclease with a ferredoxin-like fold. Mutagenesis of SSO1404 identified key residues (Tyr-9, Asp-10, Arg-17, Arg-19, Arg-31, and Phe-37) that are essential for enzymatic activity, and suggested that Asp-10 may be the primary catalytic residue. Therefore, CAS2 proteins are sequence-specific endoribonucleases, and we propose that their role in the CRISPR-mediated anti-phage defense involves degradation of phage or cellular mRNAs.

title: Menstrual and reproductive factors in relation to mammographic density: the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation (SWAN)
text:
In this study, we investigated the relationship between menstrual and reproductive factors and mammographic density in pre- and early perimenopausal women. We analyzed data from 801 participants in the Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN) and found that certain menstrual and reproductive factors were associated with mammographic density. Specifically, we found that:
* Older age at menarche was associated with higher mammographic density (β = 10.3, P < 0.01 for >13 vs. <12 years).
* Premenstrual cravings and bloating were associated with lower mammographic density (β = -3.36, P = 0.02).
* Younger age at first full-term birth was associated with lower mammographic density (β = -8.12, P < 0.01 for ≤23 years versus no births).
* Greater number of births was associated with lower mammographic density (β = -6.80, P < 0.01 for ≥3 births versus no births).
* Premenopausal status was associated with higher mammographic density (β = 3.78, P < 0.01 versus early perimenopausal).

We also found that the association between number of births and mammographic density was only significant in women with a low body mass index (BMI).

Our findings suggest that a mechanism for the association between parity and breast cancer may involve mammographic density among pre- and early perimenopausal women, which may be modified by body size.

In conclusion, our study provides evidence that menstrual and reproductive factors may play a role in the development of breast cancer by affecting mammographic density. Specifically, we found that older age at menarche, premenstrual cravings and bloating, younger age at first full-term birth, greater number of births, and premenopausal status were associated with mammographic density. Additionally, we found that the association between number of births and mammographic density was only significant in women with a low BMI. These findings may have implications for breast cancer prevention and treatment.

title: Genetic and environmental determinants of 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels in Hispanic and African Americans.
text: Background: Vitamin D deficiency is linked to various adverse health outcomes, yet the genetic epidemiology of vitamin D and its metabolites is poorly understood. Objective: To investigate the relationship between three genes related to vitamin D and levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D) in Hispanic Americans (HAs) and African Americans (AAs). Design and Setting: Cross-sectional study of 1,534 individuals from three study centers: Los Angeles, California (AAs, n=513); San Luis Valley, Colorado (HAs, n=513); and San Antonio, Texas (HAs, n=504). Main Outcome Measures: Plasma levels of 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D were measured. Results: 25(OH)D levels were highest in the San Luis Valley HAs (18.3±7.7 ng/ml), lower in San Antonio HAs (14.6±6.4 ng/ml), and lowest in AAs (11.0±5.4 ng/ml). Similarly, levels of 1,25(OH)2D were similar in AAs (43.5±13.9 pg/ml) and San Luis Valley HAs (43.2±13.3 pg/ml), but higher in San Antonio HAs (48.6±17.0 pg/ml). After adjusting for gender and age within each study center, two single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the vitamin D binding protein gene (DBP), rs4588 and rs7041, were associated with 25(OH)D, and one SNP in the DBP, rs4588, was associated with 1,25(OH)2D at all three study centers. Conclusion: SNPs in the DBP are associated with levels of 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D in HA and AA participants in the Insulin Resistance Atherosclerosis Family Study.

title: Changes in the levels of inositol phosphates after agonist-dependent hydrolysis of membrane phosphoinositides.
text:
In this study, the formation of inositol phosphates in response to agonists was investigated in three different tissues: brain slices, parotid gland fragments, and insect salivary glands. The tissues were first incubated with [3H]inositol, which was incorporated into the phosphoinositides. The researchers then used various chromatographic techniques, such as anion-exchange and high-resolution anion-exchange chromatography, high-voltage paper ionophoresis, and paper chromatography, to identify and quantify the different inositol phosphates present in each tissue.
The results showed that all three tissues contained glycerophosphoinositol, inositol 1-phosphate, inositol 1,4-bisphosphate, and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate. However, there was no evidence of the existence of inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate. The most significant change observed was an enormous increase in inositol 1,4-bisphosphate in the insect salivary gland and parotid gland after stimulation with 5-hydroxytryptamine and carbachol, respectively. Carbachol also induced a large increase in the level of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate in the parotid gland. Stimulation of brain slices with carbachol resulted in a modest increase in the levels of bis- and tris-phosphate.
Interestingly, the researchers found that in all three tissues, there was a significant agonist-dependent increase in the level of inositol 1-phosphate. This may indicate that the earliest event in the stimulus-response pathway is the hydrolysis of polyphosphoinositides by a phosphodiesterase to yield inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and inositol 1,4-bisphosphate, which are subsequently hydrolyzed to inositol 1-phosphate and inositol. The absence of inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate could suggest that, at very short times after stimulation, phosphatidylinositol is not catabolized by its specific phosphodiesterase, or that any cyclic derivative liberated is rapidly hydrolyzed by inositol 1:2-cyclic phosphate 2-phosphohydrolase.
In summary, this study provides evidence for the formation of inositol phosphates in response to agonists in three different tissues, and suggests that the earliest event in the stimulus-response pathway is the hydrolysis of polyphosphoinositides to yield inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and inositol 1,4-bisphosphate.

title: RNA editing in brain controls a determinant of ion flow in glutamate-gated channels.
text:
L-glutamate, the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, regulates ion channel activity through specific receptors. Recent studies have characterized the subunit components of two related classes of glutamate receptor channels using cDNA cloning. These subunits contain either an arginine or a glutamine residue in a specific position, which significantly impacts ion flow properties. Our previous research showed that the arginine residue in this position dominates ion flow properties for one channel class.
Our latest findings reveal that the genomic DNA sequences encoding the channel segment of all subunits contain a glutamine codon (CAG), despite the presence of an arginine codon (CGG) in the mRNAs of three subunits. We excluded the possibility that alternative genes or exons were responsible for the arginine codon. Therefore, we propose that RNA editing is responsible for altering the subunit transcripts of the two glutamate receptor classes with different efficiency and selectivity.

title: Post-translational modifications of the beta-1 subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase affect enzyme activity and cellular localization.
text:
The AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a ubiquitous mammalian enzyme that plays a crucial role in cellular adaptation to metabolic stress. Comprised of a catalytic alpha subunit and regulatory beta and gamma subunits, AMPK is a heterotrimer that is allosterically regulated by AMP and phosphorylation of the alpha subunit. The beta subunit is post-translationally modified by myristoylation and multi-site phosphorylation, which in turn affects enzyme activity, heterotrimer assembly, and subcellular localization.
In the present study, we employed site-directed mutagenesis and mammalian cell expression to investigate the impact of beta subunit post-translational modifications on AMPK function. Specifically, we examined the effects of removing the myristoylation site (G2A mutant) and mutating the serine-108 phosphorylation site (S108A) on enzyme activity, beta subunit localization, and heterotrimer assembly. Our results showed that removal of the myristoylation site resulted in a 4-fold activation of AMPK and a relocalization of the beta subunit from a particulate extranuclear distribution to a more homogenous cell distribution. In contrast, mutation of the serine-108 phosphorylation site had no effect on enzyme activity but resulted in nuclear redistribution of the beta subunit. Interestingly, mutations at other phosphorylation sites (SS24, 25AA, and S182A) did not affect enzyme activity but were associated with nuclear redistribution of the beta subunit.
Taken together, these findings demonstrate that both myristoylation and phosphorylation of the beta subunit of AMPK modulate enzyme activity and subunit cellular localization, thereby increasing the complexity of AMPK regulation.

title: Caloric restriction delays age-related methylation drift
text: In mammals, caloric restriction has consistently been shown to lead to a longer lifespan. Epigenetic information encoded by DNA methylation is tightly regulated, but there is a striking drift that occurs with age, resulting in both gains and losses of DNA methylation at various sites. Interestingly, this epigenetic drift is conserved across species and correlates with lifespan when comparing mice, rhesus monkeys, and humans. For example, rhesus monkeys exposed to 30% caloric restriction from a young age (7-14 years) showed a significant attenuation of age-related methylation drift compared to ad libitum-fed controls, resulting in a blood methylation age that appeared 7 years younger than their chronologic age. Similarly, mice exposed to 40% caloric restriction from a young age (0.3 years) showed even more pronounced effects, with their blood methylation age appearing 7-10 years younger than their chronologic age. These findings suggest that epigenetic drift is a determinant of lifespan in mammals, and that caloric restriction may have a significant impact on this process.

title: Structural analysis of multiprotein complexes by cross-linking, mass spectrometry, and database searching.
text: The majority of protein complexes are inaccessible to high-resolution structural analysis using conventional methods. In this study, we employed a novel combination of cross-linking, mass spectrometry, and bioinformatics to investigate two human complexes containing large coiled-coil segments: the NDEL1 homodimer and the NDC80 heterotetramer. A significant challenge in cross-linking analysis is the identification of cross-linked peptides from fragmentation spectra. To overcome this limitation, we developed a purpose-built database to match spectra with cross-linked peptides, established a scoring system to evaluate the quality of identifications, and estimated false positive rates. Our approach revealed important structural parameters, such as the directionality of the homodimeric coiled coil of NDEL1, the register of the heterodimeric coiled coils of the NDC80 complex, and the organization of a tetramerization region in the NDC80 complex. This novel approach is particularly useful for analyzing complexes that are difficult to study using standard structural methods.

title: The long non-coding RNA H19-derived miR-675 modulates human gastric cancer cell proliferation by targeting tumor suppressor RUNX1.
text: Recent research has implicated the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) H19 in the tumorigenesis of gastric cancer, with studies showing its upregulation in this context. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the role of H19 and its mature product microRNA-675 (miR-675) in gastric cancer development remain unclear. In this investigation, we discovered that miR-675 was co-expressed with H19 and played a pivotal role in promoting gastric cancer cell growth. Subsequent experiments confirmed that RUNX1, a tumor suppressor, was a direct target of miR-675. Using a luciferase reporter assay and Western blotting analyses, we demonstrated that RUNX1 mediated the effects of H19/miR-675 on gastric cancer cell phenotypes. Furthermore, our findings revealed an inverse relationship between the expression of RUNX1 and H19/miR-675 in gastric cancer tissues and cell lines. Taken together, our study suggests that the novel pathway H19/miR-675/RUNX1 regulates gastric cancer development and may serve as a potential therapeutic target for this disease.

title: Methylphenidate-induced erections in a prepubertal child.
text: Methylphenidate is commonly used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, we report a case of a prepubescent child who experienced unexpected and unwanted erections after starting a response-adjusted dosing regimen of sustained-release methylphenidate. Although priapism is a rare adverse reaction associated with methylphenidate, it is essential that physicians and parents are aware of this potential side effect, as it can have serious long-term consequences.

title: Mechanism of NO-mediated oxidative and nitrative DNA damage in hamsters infected with Opisthorchis viverrini: a model of inflammation-mediated carcinogenesis.
text: Infection-mediated inflammation plays a crucial role in the development of cholangiocarcinoma (CHCA), and Opisthorchis viverrini (OV) infection is a significant risk factor for CHCA. In this study, we investigated the formation of 8-nitroguanine and 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-oxodG) in the liver of hamsters infected with OV, as well as the expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1). We developed a specific antibody against 8-nitroguanine without cross-reactivity and performed double immunofluorescence staining to evaluate the distribution of these DNA adducts in the liver and bile ducts. Our results showed that 8-oxodG and 8-nitroguanine were primarily localized in the same inflammatory cells and epithelium of bile ducts, with the strongest immunoreactivity observed on days 21 and 30, respectively. Notably, these DNA adducts persisted in the epithelium of bile ducts even after 180 days, suggesting a long-term effect. Furthermore, we found that the expression of iNOS was associated with the formation of 8-nitroguanine, and that HO-1 expression might contribute to the enhancement of oxidative DNA damage in the epithelium of small bile ducts. Overall, our findings suggest that nitrative and oxidative DNA damage via iNOS expression may play a role in the carcinogenesis of CHCA.

title: Monte Carlo tests for associations between disease and alleles at highly polymorphic loci.
