The gelatinases (MMPs 2 and 9) were also detected, but less prominently. IL-1β- and TNFα-positive chondrocytes were also observed in a proportion of cells in the superficial zones of OA specimens. Minimal immunostaining for MMPs and cytokines was observed in the deep zone of all OA specimens, where the cartilage matrix and chondrocyte morphology appeared normal. In contrast, virtually no immunostaining was observed in full-thickness normal cartilage specimens. In vitro studies confirmed that chondrocytes can produce these 6 MMPs. Dual immunolocalization studies demonstrated the coexpression of IL-1β with MMP-8 in individual chondrocytes in situ. Conclusion: These results suggest that the superficial zone of OA cartilage specimens, characterized by fibrillations, chondrocyte clusters, and degenerative matrix changes, contains a variable proportion of cells that immunostain for IL-1β, TNFα, and 6 different MMPs. These observations support the notion that cytokine-MMP associations reflect a modified chondrocyte phenotype and an intrinsic process of cartilage degradation in OA.

title: β-catenin-independent WNT signaling in basal-like breast cancer and brain metastasis.
text: A recent study has shed light on the role of WNT signaling in primary breast cancers of the basal-like subtype and its potential as a predictor of brain metastasis. However, the responsible WNT ligand remains unidentified. To investigate this further, the researchers compared the expression of WNT5A and B in two human breast cancer cell lines, MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7, which represent the basal-like and luminal A subtypes, respectively. They found that WNT5A and B were overexpressed in MDA-MB-231 cells compared to MCF-7, and that inhibition of WNT signaling reduced MDA-MB-231 invasiveness. Conversely, recombinant WNT5B enhanced MCF-7 invasion, and this effect was abolished by WNT and Jun-N-terminal kinase antagonists. The study also found that β-catenin was not localized in the nuclei of brain metastases, and that expression of WNT5A/B and alternative WNT receptors ROR1 and 2 was present in both basal-like primaries and brain metastases. These findings were validated using external gene expression datasets and hierarchical cluster analysis revealed a close relation between basal-like cancers and brain metastases. Gene set enrichment analyses confirmed WNT pathway enrichment in basal-like primaries and cerebral metastases of all subtypes. In conclusion, the study suggests that WNT signaling plays a significant role in basal-like and other subtypes of breast cancers metastasizing to the brain, with β-catenin-independent WNT signaling possibly mediated by ROR1-2.

title: Retinal attenuates inflammatory arthritis by reciprocal regulation of IL-17-producing T cells and Foxp3(+) regulatory T cells and the inhibition of osteoclastogenesis.
text: Retinoids, such as vitamin A and its derivatives, have the ability to regulate immune responses. The aim of this study was to determine whether all-trans retinaldehyde (retinal), a vitamin A derivative, could inhibit inflammatory responses and joint destruction in DBA/1J mice with collagen-induced arthritis (CIA). The study found that mice treated with retinal had lower arthritis scores and a lower incidence of arthritis compared to those treated with cottonseed oil. Histopathological evidence of joint damage was also reduced in mice treated with retinal, along with a decrease in the infiltration of immune cells. Additionally, the expression of proinflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress proteins, and osteoclast markers was significantly reduced in mice treated with retinal. In vitro, retinal increased Foxp3 expression and inhibited Th17 development. The proportion of Foxp3(+) Treg cells was increased in the spleens of mice treated with retinal, while the proportion of Th17 cells was reduced. In both mice and a human culture system, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) positive mononuclear cells and multinucleated cells were significantly reduced after treatment with retinal. The expression of osteoclast differentiation markers was dramatically decreased upon addition of retinal. These findings suggest that retinal has profound immunoregulatory functions and potential value for the treatment of autoimmune inflammatory disorders.

title: NRAGE promotes the malignant phenotype of hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a deadly disease due to the limited effectiveness of available treatments for patients with advanced or recurrent stages of the disease. To improve patient outcomes, it is essential to identify a valuable biomarker for HCC progression and a molecular target for therapy. Neurotrophin receptor-interacting melanoma antigen-encoding protein (NRAGE), a member of the type II melanoma-associated antigen family, regulates apoptosis and cell death by interacting with various proteins, and its role in HCC is currently unknown. Therefore, the present study aimed to elucidate the functional role of NRAGE in HCC tumorigenesis.
The study analyzed resected tumor and non-cancerous liver tissues from 151 HCC patients, along with HCC cell lines, using polymerase chain reaction and immunohistochemical techniques to determine NRAGE expression levels and the expression levels of potential interacting proteins. The results showed that NRAGE mRNA expression levels significantly correlated with those of apoptosis-antagonizing transcription factor (AATF), and were not affected by cirrhosis in non-cancerous liver tissues compared to elevated levels in HCC tissues. The expression patterns of NRAGE protein and mRNA were consistent among 30 representative specimen pairs. Furthermore, increased NRAGE expression in HCC patients correlated significantly with a shorter disease-specific survival time and was identified as an independent prognostic factor via multivariate analysis (hazard ratio, 2.23; 95% confidence interval, 1.06-3.83; P=0.020).
The study's findings indicate that increased NRAGE expression affects HCC progression via its interaction with AATF, and may serve as a novel biomarker and molecular target for the treatment of HCC.

title: Regulation of ISW2 by concerted action of histone H4 tail and extranucleosomal DNA.
text: The interaction of ISW2 with nucleosomal DNA near the dyad was confirmed through DNA footprinting and photoaffinity labeling using recombinant histone octamers, indicating that the histone H4 N-terminal tail is essential for stable contact between ISW2 and this internal nucleosomal site. Additionally, the study found that efficient ISW2 remodeling requires the H4 N-terminal tail, although the lack of this tail can be partially compensated for by increasing the incubation time or concentration of ISW2. Similarly, the length of extranucleosomal DNA affects the stable contact of ISW2 with this same internal nucleosomal site, with the optimal length being approximately 70-85 bp. These findings suggest that the histone H4 tail, in conjunction with an optimal length of extranucleosomal DNA, recruits and orients ISW2 properly onto the nucleosome for efficient nucleosome remodeling. This property of ISW2 may also contribute to its previously observed ability to affect nucleosome spacing.

title: Embryonic Stem Cells for Severe Heart Failure: Why and How?
text: The experience gained in cardiac cell therapy suggests that the regeneration of extensively necrotic myocardial areas cannot be achieved solely through the paracrine effects of grafted cells, but rather requires the conversion of these cells into functional cardiomyocytes. This approach has a strong rationale, as demonstrated by encouraging experimental results in animal models of myocardial infarction. However, before clinical applications can be pursued, several critical issues must be addressed, including optimizing the cardiac specification of human embryonic stem cells, purifying the resulting progenitor cells to ensure a pure graft without any contamination by residual pluripotent cells that carry the risk of tumorigenesis, and controlling expected allogeneic rejection through clinically acceptable methods. If these challenges can be overcome, the therapeutic success of this approach will depend on the ability to efficiently deliver the cells to the target tissue, maintain their survival once engrafted, and enable them to spatially organize in a way that contributes to the contractile function of the heart.

title: A comparison of letrozole to gonadotropins for ovulation induction, in subjects who failed to conceive with clomiphene citrate.
text:
Objective: To compare the pregnancy rates (PR) of letrozole and gonadotropins in individuals who failed to conceive with clomiphene citrate (CC).
Design: Retrospective cohort study.
Setting: University reproductive center.
Patients: Individuals treated with letrozole or gonadotropins who failed to conceive with CC.
Intervention(s): Controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH), transvaginal ultrasound, ovulation induction, intrauterine insemination (IUI).
Main outcome measure(s): Pregnancy rates per cycle.
Results: Among patients who failed to conceive with at least three cycles of CC, gonadotropins had a higher PR per cycle than letrozole. However, among individuals who failed to conceive with less than three cycles of CC and whose medications were changed due to thin uterine lining or intolerable side effects, the average PR per cycle for letrozole and gonadotropin treatments were equivalent. All patients conceived within three stimulation cycles with either gonadotropins or letrozole.
Conclusion(s): In patients who failed to conceive with CC, gonadotropins have higher PR for ovulation induction than letrozole. However, PR were high enough with letrozole to justify its use in this population of patients. Letrozole and gonadotropins should not be used for more than three cycles without a conception.

title: Epigenetic mechanisms in neurological disease
text: The exploration of brain epigenomes, encompassing various forms of DNA methylation and covalent histone modifications, is yielding groundbreaking insights into the mechanisms underlying neural development, neurological disorders, and aging. Historically, chromatin abnormalities in the brain were perceived as static lesions that occurred during early development in the context of rare genetic syndromes. However, it is now evident that epigenetic machinery mutations and malfunctions span a broader continuum, including adult-onset neurodegenerative diseases. This article delves into how recent advances in neuroepigenetics have enhanced our understanding of developmental and degenerative brain disorders and discusses their potential implications for the development of future therapeutic strategies.

title: Reversal of the cellular phenotype in the premature aging disease Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome
text: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is a rare childhood disease characterized by premature aging, caused by a spontaneous point mutation in the lamin A (LMNA) gene. This mutation leads to the production of a truncated lamin A protein and a corresponding reduction in the levels of wild-type lamin A. The resulting morphological abnormalities in nuclear envelope structure are most pronounced in fibroblasts from individuals with HGPS. Our study demonstrates that the cellular disease phenotype of HGPS is reversible, but the introduction of wild-type lamin A protein does not rescue the symptoms. Instead, we have found that the mutant LMNA mRNA and lamin A protein can be efficiently eliminated through the correction of an aberrant splicing event using a targeted oligonucleotide. Following splicing correction, HGPS fibroblasts exhibit normal nuclear morphology, with restored distribution and levels of lamina-associated proteins, corrected histone modifications specific to heterochromatin, and reestablished expression of misregulated genes. Our findings provide proof of principle for the correction of the premature aging phenotype in individuals with HGPS, opening up new avenues for the treatment of this rare and debilitating disease.

title: Agouti-related peptide–expressing neurons are mandatory for feeding
text: Despite the fact that multiple hormones are involved in regulating energy homeostasis in the hypothalamus, the expression of neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) in the arcuate nucleus is not significantly affected. However, inactivating the genes encoding NPY and AgRP has no impact on food intake in mice. Contrary to this, we have found that selectively ablating AgRP-expressing neurons in adult mice leads to a sudden decrease in feeding, providing direct evidence for the critical role of these neurons in regulating energy homeostasis.

title: Predictors of survival after acute paraquat poisoning.
text: Acute paraquat poisoning is often fatal, and there is currently no standard treatment available. To identify predictors of survival after acute paraquat poisoning, a study was conducted on 602 patients. The study assessed the amount of ingested paraquat and the level of paraquat in the urine to determine the severity of exposure. Initial clinical parameters, such as vital signs, hemoglobin, white blood cell count, pH, PaCO2, PaO2, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, total bilirubin, amylase, and glucose, were also measured at the time of arrival at the emergency room. The outcomes were categorized as survivors and nonsurvivors. Multiple logistic regression analysis was used to identify the predictors of survival after acute paraquat poisoning. The study found that young age, exposure through the percutaneous or inhalational route, and lower levels of paraquat exposure were associated with better survival outcomes. Additionally, lower degrees of leukocytosis, acidosis, and renal, hepatic, and pancreatic failures on admission were also good prognostic factors of survival after acute paraquat poisoning. In conclusion, the study highlights the importance of early identification and treatment of acute paraquat poisoning, particularly in young individuals and those exposed through the percutaneous or inhalational route.

title: Decreased neurogenesis after cholinergic forebrain lesion in the adult rat.
text: Adult neurogenesis is regulated by various extracellular cues, including hormones, growth factors, and neurotransmitters. The cholinergic system of the basal forebrain is a key transmitter system involved in learning and memory, and its input plays a crucial role in adult neurogenesis. To investigate the role of cholinergic input in adult neurogenesis, we used an immunotoxin approach to selectively lesion cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain of adult rats. Five weeks after lesioning, we observed a significant decline in neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus and olfactory bulb, as measured by the number of cells colocalized with the markers BrdU and NeuN. Additionally, we found increased numbers of apoptotic cells in the subgranular zone, the progenitor region of the dentate gyrus, and within the periglomerular layer of the olfactory bulb. These findings suggest that the cholinergic system plays a survival-promoting role for neuronal progenitors and immature neurons in regions of adult neurogenesis, similar to its role during brain development. We propose that loss of cholinergic input within the basal forebrain may not only lead to cognitive deficits but may also alter the functionality of the dentate gyrus, which may exacerbate cognitive deficits.

title: DNA Methylation in Major Depressive Disorder.
text: Epigenetic processes play a crucial role in regulating gene expression, which in turn affects protein production and ultimately shapes an organism's phenotype. However, both random epigenetic variations and environmental changes to the epigenome can impact neurodevelopment and aging, potentially contributing to the origins of mental health disorders. Investigating the role of epigenetic mechanisms is complex, as it involves accounting for genotype, tissue, and cell type-specific epigenetic changes, while also addressing the challenges of linking mental disorders to biological profiles. In this chapter, we will summarize the current evidence suggesting the importance of DNA methylation as a key epigenetic mechanism in major depressive disorder.

title: Consensus structural features of purified bacterial TatABC complexes.
text:
The twin-arginine translocation (Tat) system is a crucial mechanism for the transport of folded proteins across the plasma membranes of bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Salmonella typhimurium, and Agrobacterium tumefaciens. In this study, we aimed to investigate the composition and structural organization of purified Tat complexes from these three bacterial species. To achieve this, we first evaluated the functional activity of these Tat systems in vivo by expressing the tatABC operons from S.typhimurium or A.tumefaciens in an E.coli tat null mutant strain, which resulted in efficient export of an E.coli cofactor-containing substrate, TMAO reductase, via the Tat pathway.
Using affinity-tagged Tat complexes isolated from each bacterial species, we found that the TatA, TatB, and TatC subunits were present in each complex, indicating a strong interaction between these subunits. Single-particle electron microscopy studies revealed that the isolated Tat complexes had oval-shaped, asymmetric particles with dimensions up to 13 nm, characterized by the presence of stain-excluding densities surrounding more or less central pools of stain, suggesting protein-lined pores or cavities. Notably, the size variation among the particles suggested a modular form of assembly and/or the recruitment of varying numbers of TatBC/TatA units.
Despite low levels of sequence homology between the Tat systems of these three bacterial species, our combined data indicate both structural and functional conservation in these systems. This study provides valuable insights into the composition and organization of the Tat complexes in these bacteria, which can inform our understanding of their mechanisms of protein transport and their potential as targets for antimicrobial therapy.

title: Advances in graft-versus-host disease biology and therapy
text: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used to treat a range of disorders, but its effectiveness is often limited by the occurrence of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in our understanding of the interplay between the donor and host immune systems that contributes to GVHD. Advances in basic immunology, preclinical models, and clinical studies have led to the development of novel strategies for preventing and treating GVHD. This Review highlights the recent breakthroughs in our understanding of GVHD pathogenesis and the potential for immune-based interventions that can be translated into clinical practice.

title: Ly6Chi monocytes direct alternatively activated profibrotic macrophage regulation of lung fibrosis.
text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a devastating disease with no known cure. Despite the lack of efficacy of anti-inflammatory therapies, the role of monocytes and macrophages in lung fibrogenesis and resolution remains controversial. To investigate this, we employed multiple in vivo depletion strategies and adoptive transfer techniques, as well as analyzed samples from IPF patients. Our findings demonstrate the crucial role of circulating monocytes and lung macrophages in pulmonary fibrosis, with the alternatively activated macrophage phenotype playing a significant part. We discovered that depletion of lung macrophages during fibrogenesis reduced pulmonary fibrosis, as evidenced by decreased collagen deposition, fibrosis score, and expression of fibrosis-related genes. Conversely, depletion of Ly6Chi circulating monocytes also reduced pulmonary fibrosis and the number of alternatively activated lung macrophages. Interestingly, adoptive transfer of Ly6Chi monocytes exacerbated fibrosis, but the transferred cells were not observed in the lungs of recipient mice. Our study highlights the importance of these cells in the progression of pulmonary fibrosis and suggests that they may also play a role in the reversible phase of bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis.

title: A single RNA-dependent RNA polymerase assembles with mutually exclusive nucleotidyl transferase subunits to direct different pathways of small RNA biogenesis.
text: Members of the conserved family of eukaryotic RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (Rdrs) play a crucial role in the synthesis of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) intermediates in various pathways of small RNA (sRNA) biogenesis and RNA-mediated silencing. Despite their importance, the Rdr-dependent pathways of sRNA production are less well-characterized compared to Rdr-independent pathways, and the Rdr enzymes themselves are less well-studied compared to their viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase counterparts. Previously, we described a physical and functional coupling of the Tetrahymena thermophila Rdr, Rdr1, and a Dicer enzyme, Dcr2, in the production of approximately 24-nucleotide (nt) sRNA in vitro. Here, we investigate the endogenous complexes that harbor Rdr1, termed RDRCs. We find that RDRCs assemble into distinct subunits, with two subunits, Rdn1 and Rdn2, possessing noncanonical ribonucleotidyl transferase motifs. We show that Rdn1 and Rdn2 are uridine-specific polymerases of separate RDRCs, and that two additional RDRC subunits, Rdf1 and Rdf2, are present only in RDRCs containing Rdn1. Our results demonstrate that Rdr1 catalytic activity is retained in RDRCs purified from cell extracts lacking any of the nonessential RDRC subunits or if the RDRC harbors a catalytically inactive Rdn. However, specific disruption of each RDRC imposes distinct loss-of-function consequences at the cellular level, leading to a previously unanticipated complexity in Rdr-dependent sRNA biogenesis in vivo.

title: Identification of T6SS-dependent effector and immunity proteins by Tn-seq in Vibrio cholerae.
text:
The Type VI protein secretion system (T6SS) plays a crucial role in bacterial competition through contact-dependent killing of competitors. T6SS delivers effectors to neighboring cells, which are then neutralized by immunity proteins produced by the recipient cells. Although T6SS has been found in over 100 gram-negative bacteria, including many human pathogens, the specific immunity proteins involved in T6SS-mediated immunity are not well understood.
To address this gap in knowledge, we employed a high-throughput approach using transposon mutagenesis and deep sequencing (Tn-seq) to identify T6SS immunity proteins in Vibrio cholerae. We performed saturating transposon mutagenesis in both wild-type and T6SS-deficient V. cholerae, and analyzed the relative abundance of each transposon mutant in the mutant library using deep sequencing. This allowed us to identify genes encoding immunity proteins that are essential in the wild-type strain but dispensable in the T6SS mutant.
Our results revealed three immunity proteins that provide protection against killing by T6SS-predatory cells. We also identified their cognate T6SS-secreted effectors, which are involved in both antibacterial and antieukaryotic activities, as well as the assembly of the T6SS apparatus. Interestingly, the lipase and muramidase T6SS effectors identified in this study highlight the diversity of T6SS-secreted substrates and the distinct mechanisms used by the dynamic T6SS organelle to target these substrates for secretion.
In summary, our study provides new insights into the T6SS-mediated immunity mechanism in V. cholerae, and highlights the importance of this system in bacterial competition and pathogenesis. The identification of immunity proteins and their cognate effectors provides a valuable resource for further investigating the complex interplay between bacteria and their environment.

title: Immunotherapy of metastatic kidney cancer.
text: From April 1986 to September 2000, 122 patients with Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma (MRCC) were treated with monthly intralymphatic injections of Interleukin-2 (IL-2) and interferon (IFN), along with intra-muscular (i.m.) administration of IL-2 and tumor necrosis factor (TF). Of these patients, 71 also received a 3-day cycle of monthly IL-2 inhalations with a mean of 998 daily U. A total of 89 MRCC cases that were not treated with immunotherapy served as historical controls. The adverse clinical side effects associated with treatment were minimal. CR (n = 11) and PR (n = 13) were observed in 24/122 patients, with 17 of these patients resuming tumor growth and 7 remaining in remission for 11-69 months. The overall median survival of treated patients was 28 months, which is 3.5-fold higher than the median survival of historical controls (7.5 months). A Kaplan-Meier curve showed that 25% of responding patients were still alive 11 years after the start of immunotherapy. The addition of IL-2 by inhalation appeared to improve survival. The current immunotherapy protocol is found to be effective, safe, and less costly compared to other treatments, while providing a good quality of life to MRCC patients. If confirmed in a multicenter trial, it could serve as the basis for developing low-dose immunomodulatory treatments.

title: Autoimmune T cell responses in the central nervous system
text: "Autoimmune T cell responses play a critical role in central nervous system (CNS) diseases such as multiple sclerosis. Recent research has shown that CNS autoimmunity can be mediated by two distinct populations of CD4+ T cells, each producing a different cytokine: interferon-γ or interleukin-17. These CD4+ T cell subsets within the CNS have a significant impact on the disease pathology and clinical course. New animal models have also revealed that myelin-specific CD8+ T cells can also contribute to CNS autoimmunity. This Review aims to summarize the latest advances in understanding the mechanisms of CNS autoimmunity, including the regulation and interplay between these different T cell subsets."

title: Effects of FXR in foam-cell formation and atherosclerosis development.
text: Farnesoid X receptor (FXR), a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily activated by bile acids, plays a crucial role in regulating bile acid, cholesterol, and triglyceride homeostasis. Disruption of the FXR gene in mice leads to an unfavorable lipid profile with elevated serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels. However, the mechanisms by which FXR contributes to foam-cell formation and atherosclerosis development remain unclear. Our study found that peritoneal macrophages isolated from FXR-deficient mice exhibited reduced uptake of oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL-C), which was accompanied by a decrease in CD36 expression in these cells. This effect was deemed FXR-independent, as FXR was not detectable in the peritoneal macrophages. To investigate the extent to which FXR modulates atherosclerosis development, FXR/apolipoprotein E (ApoE) double-deficient mice were generated, with female mice used for atherosclerosis analysis. Compared to ApoE-deficient mice, the FXR/ApoE double-deficient mice displayed less atherosclerotic lesion area in the aorta, despite elevated serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels. Our findings suggest that disrupting the FXR gene may attenuate atherosclerosis development, likely due to reduced oxLDL-C uptake by macrophages. Our study highlights the limitations of relying on serum lipid levels as a surrogate marker for evaluating the efficacy of FXR modulators in treating hyperlipidemia.

title: Purkinje cell compartments in the reeler mutant mouse as revealed by Zebrin II and 90-acetylated glycolipid antigen expression
text: The cerebellum is organized into parallel bands that can be visualized histologically in adult mice using specific immunostaining techniques. The Purkinje cell sets can be identified with monoclonal antibodies Zebrin II (ZII) and P-path (PP), which target different antigens. In the reeler mutant (rl/rl), where most Purkinje cell migration is blocked beneath the cerebellar white matter, the staining pattern is compared to that of normal adult mice. The results show that Purkinje cells in the mutant exhibit a tendency to distribute into alternating zones that stain for either Zebrin II or P-path, with transition zones of mixed labeling. However, the number of zones is lower in the mutant than in normal mice, with roughly 7-9 zones per side compared to 14 major divisions in wild type mice. These findings suggest that the migration of neurons destined to express these markers may be segregated, and that the final phase of migration into the cortex may involve further splitting or interdigitation between cell sets expressing the two antigens.

title: Awake craniotomy with brain mapping as the routine surgical approach to treating patients with supratentorial intraaxial tumors: a prospective trial of 200 cases.
text:
In a prospective trial of 200 patients undergoing surgical treatment for supratentorial intraaxial tumors at a single institution, an awake craniotomy was performed as the standard approach regardless of the involvement of eloquent cortex. The study aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of this technique.
The patient population consisted of 195 (97.5%) patients who underwent brain mapping, with a total of 33 (16.5%) patients experiencing complications. There were two deaths in the series, resulting in a mortality rate of 1%. New postoperative neurological deficits were observed in 13% of patients, but were permanent in only 4.5% of them. The study found that complication rates were higher in patients with gliomas, preoperative neurological deficits, prior radiation therapy or surgery. Notably, none of the patients who entered the operating room neurologically intact experienced a permanent neurological deficit postoperatively.
In the most recent 50 patients treated, three (6%) required a stay in the intensive care unit, and the median total hospital stay was 1 day. The study concluded that the use of awake craniotomy can significantly reduce resource utilization without compromising patient care by minimizing intensive care time and total hospital stay. The technique provides an effective and practical alternative to craniotomy performed with the patient in a state of general anesthesia, allowing for brain mapping and avoiding general anesthesia.

title: Reactive Oxygen Species Localization Programs Inflammation to Clear Microbes of Different Size
text: The number of immune cells recruited to sites of infection is determined and adjusted based on the differences in cellular stoichiometry between the host and pathogen, but the underlying mechanisms are currently unknown. Our research has uncovered a novel role for reactive oxygen species (ROS) as sensors of microbe size. We found that neutrophils use ROS to detect the differential localization of ROS generated in response to microbes of different size, and adjust their interleukin (IL)-1β expression accordingly. Small microbes trigger ROS production intracellularly, suppressing IL-1β expression and limiting neutrophil recruitment, while large microbes trigger ROS production extracellularly, amplifying IL-1β expression and recruiting numerous neutrophils to form cooperative clusters. Defects in ROS-mediated microbe size sensing lead to large neutrophil infiltrates and clusters in response to small microbes, contributing to inflammatory diseases. These findings highlight the importance of ROS localization in signal transduction.

title: Helicobacter pylori infection triggers aberrant expression of activation-induced cytidine deaminase in gastric epithelium
text: Infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) increases the risk of developing gastric cancer. Our study shows that infection of gastric epithelial cells with 'cag' pathogenicity island (cagPAI)-positive H. pylori leads to abnormal expression of activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), a member of the cytidine-deaminase family that functions as a DNA and RNA editing enzyme. This occurs through the IκB kinase-dependent nuclear factor-κB activation pathway. H. pylori infection leads to an increase in AID expression, which results in the accumulation of nucleotide alterations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene in gastric cells in vitro. Our findings suggest that aberrant AID expression caused by H. pylori infection may be a mechanism of mutation accumulation in the gastric mucosa during H. pylori-associated gastric carcinogenesis.

title: The role of the immune response during SIVagm infection of the African green monkey natural host.
text: The African green monkey (AGM) is one of many African species naturally infected with simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV). Unlike other hosts, AGMs do not develop AIDS, and understanding the basis for this resistance could have significant theoretical and practical implications. Early studies by our group focused on identifying immune mechanisms that might keep the virus under control, but these efforts failed to identify any obvious candidates. It was later discovered that SIVagm replicates with the same intensity in AGMs as HIV-1 does in humans, leading to a shift in focus towards identifying immunological features present in susceptible hosts but absent in the AGM natural host. The apparent immunological tolerance of AGMs to the SIVagm core protein led to the hypothesis that anti-Gag antibodies may play a role in immune complex formation, virus trapping in lymph nodes, and immune dysfunction. However, testing this hypothesis in vivo has proven challenging, and the current research focuses on the possibility that T-cell tolerance to the Gag protein may play a crucial role in preventing the immune system's collapse characteristic of immunodeficiency virus infection in heterologous primate hosts.

title: The S-LANSS score for identifying pain of predominantly neuropathic origin: validation for use in clinical and postal research.
text: This study aimed to develop and validate a self-report version of the Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs (LANSS) pain scale, known as the S-LANSS. The S-LANSS was designed to identify pain of predominantly neuropathic origin without the need for clinical examination. Two hundred patients with chronic pain completed the S-LANSS unaided, and a researcher then administered the scale and the Neuropathic Pain Scale (NPS) in an interview format. An independent clinician determined the pain type (neuropathic versus nociceptive) and rated their certainty about the diagnosis. The S-LANSS scale was also incorporated into a chronic pain questionnaire that was sent to 160 community patients and 150 newly referred patients waiting for pain clinic assessment. The results showed that the S-LANSS correctly identified 75% of pain types when self-completed and 80% when used in interview format. The sensitivity of the self-completed S-LANSS scores ranged from 74% to 78%, depending on the cutoff score. There were significant associations between NPS items and total score with S-LANSS scores. In the postal survey, completed questionnaires were returned by 57% of patients (n = 174). The internal consistency and convergent validity of the survey S-LANSS scores were confirmed. The findings support the S-LANSS scale as a valid and reliable self-report instrument for identifying neuropathic pain, and it is also acceptable for use in postal survey research. Establishing valid measures of symptoms and signs in neuropathic pain will allow standardized comparisons with other investigational measures, leading to new insights into the relationship between pathophysiologic mechanisms and clinical manifestations of pain.

title: Bias in meta-analysis detected by a simple, graphical test.
text:
Funnel plots (plots of effect estimates against sample size) may be useful in detecting bias in meta-analyses that were later contradicted by large trials. We investigated whether a simple test of funnel plot asymmetry can predict discordance between meta-analyses and large trials, and assessed the prevalence of bias in published meta-analyses.
Design: We conducted a Medline search to identify pairs of meta-analyses and large trials, and analyzed funnel plots from 37 meta-analyses identified from a hand search of four leading general medicine journals from 1993 to 1996 and 38 meta-analyses from the second issue of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 1996.
Main outcome measure: We measured the degree of funnel plot asymmetry using the intercept from a regression of standard normal deviates against precision.
Results: In the eight pairs of meta-analysis and large trial identified (five from cardiovascular medicine, one from diabetic medicine, one from geriatric medicine, and one from perinatal medicine), there were four concordant and four discordant pairs. In all cases, discordance was due to meta-analyses showing larger effects. Funnel plot asymmetry was present in three out of four discordant pairs, but not in any of the concordant pairs. In 14 (38%) journal meta-analyses and 5 (13%) Cochrane reviews, funnel plot asymmetry indicated bias.
Conclusions: A simple analysis of funnel plots provides a useful test for the likely presence of bias in meta-analyses, but the capacity to detect bias will be limited when meta-analyses are based on a limited number of small trials, and the results from such analyses should be treated with considerable caution.

title: Exploring Metabolic Configurations of Single Cells within Complex Tissue Microenvironments.
text: Over the past few years, a significant amount of evidence has emerged highlighting the crucial role of metabolism in various cellular processes, including cell differentiation and fate. Here, we present a novel method for assessing the metabolic profile of individual cells within their native tissue microenvironment. This approach involves visualizing and quantifying multiple enzymatic activities at saturating substrate conditions, followed by cell type identification. We thoroughly validated the method to demonstrate its potential and applied it to study the metabolic configurations of different human immune cell populations in healthy and tumor colon tissue. Additionally, we investigated the intercellular metabolic relationships between cancer cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts in a breast cancer tissue array. Our findings demonstrate that analyzing the metabolic profiles of individual cells can provide a valuable complement to existing research methods, shedding light on the complex metabolic networks that exist within cells in situ.

title: Twenty-four hour and early morning blood pressure control of olmesartan vs. ramipril in elderly hypertensive patients: pooled individual data analysis of two randomized, double-blind, parallel-group studies.
text:
Objective: To compare the antihypertensive efficacy of olmesartan medoxomil and ramipril on 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure (ABP) in elderly hypertensive patients through a pooled data analysis of two studies with identical designs (one Italian and one European).
Methods: After a 2-week placebo wash-out, 1453 elderly hypertensive patients (65-89 years; sitting office DBP 90-109 mmHg and/or sitting office SBP 140-179 mmHg) were randomly assigned to a 12-week double-blind treatment with olmesartan medoxomil 10 mg or ramipril 2.5 mg once-daily, up-titrated (20 and 40 mg olmesartan medoxomil; 5 and 10 mg ramipril) after 2 and 6 weeks in patients without normalized office BP. 24-hour ABP was recorded at randomization and after 12 weeks.
Results: In 715 patients with valid baseline and end-of-treatment recordings, baseline-adjusted 24-hour SBP and DBP reductions were greater with olmesartan medoxomil (n = 356) than with ramipril (n = 359) [between-treatment differences and 95% confidence interval (CI), SBP: 2.2 (3.8, 0.6), P = 0.006; DBP: 1.3 (2.2, 0.3), P = 0.009]. Olmesartan medoxomil showed larger BP reductions in the last 6 hours from the dosing interval and higher smoothness indices than ramipril. Olmesartan medoxomil reduced the SBP morning rise [-2.8 (-4.9, -0.8) mmHg], whereas ramipril did not [+1.5 (-0.6, +3.6) mmHg; P = 0.004 between-treatments]. In 582 patients with sustained hypertension (office and 24-hour ambulatory hypertension), the largest antihypertensive effect was observed, with between-treatment differences still in favor of olmesartan medoxomil [SBP: 2.1 (3.9, 0.4), P = 0.019; DBP: 1.2 (2.3, 0.1), P = 0.032].
Conclusions: Olmesartan medoxomil provides a more effective and sustained 24-hour BP control than ramipril in elderly hypertensive patients, particularly in the hours farthest from last intake.

title: Abi1 is essential for the formation and activation of a WAVE2 signalling complex
text: WAVE2 is a protein that plays a crucial role in reorganizing actin filaments by transmitting signals from Rac to the Arp2/3 complex, leading to lamellipodia protrusion. WAVE2 exhibits actin nucleation activity in vitro, but it does not directly bind to Rac. Instead, it forms complexes with other proteins that regulate its activity. The assembly, localization, and activation of these complexes in vivo are not well understood. In this study, we used tandem mass spectrometry to identify an Abi1-based complex containing WAVE2, Nap1 (Nck-associated protein), and PIR121. Abi1 interacts directly with the WHD domain of WAVE2, enhances WAVE2's actin polymerization activity, and mediates the assembly of a WAVE2-Abi1-Nap1-PIR121 complex. This complex is as active as a WAVE2-Abi1 sub-complex in stimulating Arp2/3 and is re-localized to the leading edge of ruffles in vivo after Rac activation. Inhibition of Abi1 by RNA interference (RNAi) abrogates Rac-dependent lamellipodia protrusion, demonstrating that Abi1 orchestrates the proper assembly and activation of the WAVE2 complex in vivo.

title: The dendritic cell lineage: ontogeny and function of dendritic cells and their subsets in the steady state and the inflamed setting.
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) form an impressive cellular network that orchestrates adaptive immune responses based on cues from the periphery. Over the past four decades, significant progress has been made in understanding the origin and unique characteristics of DCs, which are distinct from other leukocytes and form a distinct hematopoietic branch. Recent research has also revealed that tissue DCs are composed of different subsets with distinct developmental and functional properties, which play a crucial role in regulating T lymphocyte function. This review summarizes the major advances in our understanding of the regulation of DC lineage commitment, differentiation, diversification, and function in situ.

title: IL-15 Receptor Deletion Results in Circadian Changes of Locomotor and Metabolic Activity
text:
Interleukin-15 (IL-15) is a cytokine produced in the brain that acts on its specific receptor IL-15Rα and co-receptors IL-2Rβ and IL-2Rγ in neuronal cells. However, the functional significance of the cerebral IL-15 system is not yet fully understood. To investigate this, we employed a knockout mouse model to test the hypothesis that IL-15Rα regulates metabolic activity and body temperature.
We first quantified the specific metabolic phenotype of IL-15Rα knockout mice and found that they were leaner with lower fat composition compared to normal mice. Interestingly, these knockout mice displayed a significantly higher acrophase in locomotor activity and heat dissipation throughout the circadian cycle. During the light phase, there was a significant increase in food intake, oxygen consumption, and carbon dioxide production in the knockout mice, indicating adaptive thermogenesis. Notably, the difference in metabolic activity between the light and dark phases suggests that IL-15Rα plays a role in circadian rhythm regulation.
Furthermore, we observed that the body temperature of the knockout mice was significantly higher than that of the control mice, particularly during the light phase. This increase in body temperature was primarily due to a large difference in temperature occurring between 0600 and 0900 h.
To further investigate the mechanisms underlying these observations, we performed qPCR analysis of hypothalamic homogenates and found that IL-15Rα activation in the wild-type mice led to increased mRNA expression of orexin and transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 cation channels. These findings suggest a direct role of IL-15Rα in the hypothalamus.
In conclusion, our results demonstrate that activation of hypothalamic neurons by IL-15 in mice contributes to thermoregulation and modifies the metabolic phenotype. These findings provide new insights into the functional significance of the cerebral IL-15 system and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for metabolic disorders.

title: Vaginal progesterone, cerclage or cervical pessary for preventing preterm birth in asymptomatic singleton pregnant women with a history of preterm birth and a sonographic short cervix.
text:
Objective: To compare the outcomes of pregnancy in women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth and short cervical length, managed with different treatment protocols, including cerclage, vaginal progesterone, and cervical pessary.
Methods: This study compared the perinatal outcomes of 142 women treated with cerclage (USA), 59 with vaginal progesterone (UK), and 42 with cervical pessary (Spain), all of whom had a prior spontaneous preterm birth before 34 weeks and a shortened cervical length detected by transvaginal ultrasound.
Results: There were no significant differences in perinatal losses, neonatal morbidity, and preterm births among the three groups, except for a higher rate of preterm birth before 34 weeks' gestation in the vaginal progesterone group compared to the cervical pessary group (32% vs 12%; relative risk (RR) = 2.70; 95% CI, 1.10-6.67). When only the subgroups of women with cervical length < 25 mm, irrespective of gestational age, were compared, the difference between these two cohorts was not statistically significant (RR = 2.21; 95% CI, 0.83-5.89).
Conclusion: Cerclage, vaginal progesterone, and pessary appear to have similar effectiveness as management strategies in women with singleton pregnancy, previous spontaneous preterm birth, and short cervix. Direct randomized comparisons of these strategies, or combinations thereof, are needed to determine the optimal management.

title: The oxytocinase subfamily of M1 aminopeptidases.
text: The placental leucine aminopeptidase (P-LAP), adipocyte-derived leucine aminopeptidase (A-LAP), and leukocyte-derived aminopeptidase (L-RAP) belong to a distinct group within the M1 family of aminopeptidases, which we term the "Oxytocinase subfamily." This subfamily shares a common feature of HEXXH(X)18E Zn-binding and GAMEN motifs that are essential for enzymatic activity. A unique characteristic of the subfamily members is their intracellular localization. P-LAP is translocated from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane in a stimulus-dependent manner, while A-LAP and L-RAP are retained in the endoplasmic reticulum. These enzymes contain sequences that enable their specific localization within the cell. It is becoming evident that the subfamily members play important roles in maintaining homeostasis, including the maintenance of normal pregnancy, memory retention, blood pressure regulation, and antigen presentation. In this review, we summarize the current state of knowledge on this newly identified subfamily.

title: Myc represses primitive endoderm differentiation in pluripotent stem cells.
text: The generation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offers a novel means to investigate the underlying mechanisms that govern stem cell pluripotency and self-renewal. Myc, a transcription factor previously implicated in murine embryonic stem cell (mESC) maintenance and directed reprogramming of fibroblasts, remains poorly understood in terms of its role in pluripotency. Our study reveals that codeletion of c- and N-MYC in iPSCs and embryonic stem cells (ESCs) leads to their spontaneous differentiation into primitive endoderm. We demonstrate that Myc sustains pluripotency by repressing the expression of the primitive endoderm master regulator GATA6, while also contributing to cell cycle control through regulation of the miR-17-92 miRNA cluster. Our findings highlight the essential requirement for c- or N-myc in pluripotency beyond proliferative and metabolic control.

title: [Vitamin D and latitude as environmental factors in multiple sclerosis].
text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) exhibits a significant increase in prevalence as one moves closer to the poles, both north and south of the equator. One potential explanation for this phenomenon is the role of vitamin D, as the strength of ambient ultraviolet light, which is essential for vitamin D production, decreases with increasing latitude. It is well established that vitamin D has immunomodulatory functions and has been shown to suppress an animal model of MS. Additionally, it is believed that genes related to vitamin D are critical susceptibility genes for MS. An interdisciplinary approach, combining environmental and genetic factors, is necessary to investigate the association between vitamin D and MS.

title: Type 2 cytokines: mechanisms and therapeutic strategies
text: Type 2 immune responses are defined by the cytokines interleukin-4 (IL-4), IL-5, IL-9, and IL-13, which can have both protective and harmful effects. Type 2 immunity promotes anti-parasitic immunity, suppresses autoimmune diseases caused by type 1 immunity, neutralizes toxins, maintains metabolic homeostasis, and regulates wound repair and tissue regeneration following infection or injury. However, when type 2 responses are dysregulated, they can become a major factor in disease development. Type 2 immunity triggers a complex inflammatory response involving eosinophils, mast cells, basophils, type 2 innate lymphoid cells, IL-4- and/or IL-13-conditioned macrophages, and T helper 2 (TH2) cells, which are crucial to the pathogenesis of many allergic and fibrotic disorders. As chronic type 2 immune responses contribute to disease, mechanisms that regulate their maintenance are thought to function as essential disease-modifying strategies. This Review discusses the various endogenous negative regulatory mechanisms that counteract type 2 immunity and highlights how therapies targeting some of these pathways are being developed to treat type 2-mediated diseases.

title: Implanted microvessels progress through distinct neovascularization phenotypes.
text:
In our previous work, we demonstrated that implanted microvessels form a new microcirculation with minimal host-derived vessel investment. Our goal was to characterize the vascular phenotypes present during neovascularization in these implants and identify post-angiogenesis events. Using morphological, functional, and transcriptional assessments, we identified three distinct vascular phenotypes in the implants: sprouting angiogenesis, neovascular remodeling, and network maturation.
The first phenotype, sprouting angiogenesis, was characterized by high proliferation and low mural cell coverage. This was followed by a neovascular remodeling phenotype, which featured a perfused, poorly organized neovascular network, reduced proliferation, and re-associated mural cells. The last phenotype, network maturation, included a vascular network organized into a stereotypical tree structure, with vessels containing normal perivascular cell associations. Additionally, proliferation was low and restricted to the walls of larger microvessels. The transition from angiogenesis to neovascular remodeling coincided with the appearance of blood flow in the implant neovasculature.
Our analysis of vascular-specific and global gene expression revealed that the intermediate, neovascular remodeling phenotype is transcriptionally distinct from the other two phenotypes. Therefore, this vascular phenotype likely represents a distinct vascular process involving unique cellular and vascular mechanisms. Furthermore, this neovascular remodeling phase may be a normal aspect of the general neovascularization process. Given that this phenotype is arguably dysfunctional, many of the microvasculatures present within compromised or diseased tissues may not represent a failure to progress appropriately through a normally occurring neovascularization phenotype.

title: Characterization of a highly variable eutherian microRNA gene.
text: Mouse microRNAs (miRNAs) miR-290-miR295 are encoded by a cluster of partially homologous pre-miRNA hairpins and are likely to be functionally important in embryonic stem (ES) cells and preimplantation embryos. We demonstrate that a spliced, capped, and polyadenylated primary transcript spans this entire Early Embryonic microRNA Cluster (EEmiRC). Processing by Drosha yields additional large nuclear RNA intermediates. A conserved promoter element containing a TATA-box directs EEmiRC transcription. Sequence analysis reveals that the EEmiRC transcription unit is remarkably variable and can only be identified bioinformatically in placental (eutherian) mammals. Consistent with eutherian-specific function, EEmiRC is expressed in trophoblastic stem (TS) cells. When examining evolutionary and functional relationships, it is important to consider the organization of the entire miRNA locus in addition to the mature miRNA sequences. Applying this concept suggests that EEmiRC is a recently acquired rapidly evolving gene important for eutherian development.

title: The function of follicular helper T cells is regulated by the strength of T cell antigen receptor binding
text: The differentiation of follicular helper T cells (TFH cells) is crucial for effective protein vaccination. In this study, we identify and characterize three distinct subsets of TFH cells based on their expression of the transcription factor T-bet. These subsets have distinct migratory properties, developmental programming, and functions in vivo. We find that the expression of the transcriptional repressor Blimp-1 distinguishes T zone 'lymphoid' effector helper T cells (CD62LhiCCR7hi) from CXCR5lo 'emigrant' effector helper T cells and CXCR5hi 'resident' TFH cells expressing the transcriptional repressor Bcl-6 (CD62LloCCR7lo). Our results demonstrate that helper T cells with the highest specific binding of peptide–major histocompatibility complex class II and the most restricted T cell antigen receptor junctional diversity 'preferentially' develop into the antigen-specific effector TFH compartment. Our findings highlight the central role of differences in T cell antigen receptor binding strength in the antigen-specific mechanisms that 'program' specialized effector TFH function in vivo.

title: Disruption of tumor necrosis factor-alpha gene diminishes the development of atherosclerosis in ApoE-deficient mice.
text: Inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), have been implicated in the development of atherosclerosis. However, the specific role of TNF-alpha in this process remains unclear. To investigate the effect of TNF-alpha on atherogenesis, we generated mice lacking both apolipoprotein E (apoE) and TNF-alpha (apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/-) and compared them with apoE-/- mice. Although serum total cholesterol levels were elevated in both groups, there were no significant differences in atherosclerotic plaque area between the two groups. The atherosclerotic lesion size in the aortic sinus of apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- mice was significantly smaller than that of apoE-/- mice. RT-PCR analysis revealed that the expression levels of intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) were higher in apoE-/- mice than in apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- mice. Macrophages from apoE(-/-) mice showed higher levels of oxidized LDL uptake and increased expression of scavenger receptor class A (SRA) compared to those from apoE-/-/TNF-alpha-/- mice. These findings suggest that TNF-alpha plays an atherogenic role by upregulating the expression of adhesion molecules and chemoattractants in the vascular wall, and by inducing SRA expression and oxidized LDL uptake in macrophages.

title: Differential expression of bcl-2 and susceptibility to anti-Fas-mediated cell death in peripheral blood lymphocytes, monocytes, and neutrophils.
text: The recently identified Fas antigen (Ag) is a cell surface molecule that can induce programmed cell death, or apoptosis. The cytoplasmic product of the proto-oncogene bcl-2 has been shown to prolong the survival of cells by inhibiting apoptosis. To investigate the significance of expressing both molecules, we examined the expression of Fas Ag and bcl-2 on blood leukocyte populations and evaluated their sensitivity to the cytolytic action of anti-Fas antibody. Our findings revealed that Fas Ag was expressed on a subset of lymphocytes, while neutrophils and monocytes expressed Fas Ag constitutively. In contrast, there was a significant difference in bcl-2 expression among these leukocytes, with lymphocytes expressing bcl-2 intensely, monocytes showing weaker expression, and neutrophils being almost absent for bcl-2 expression. This lack of bcl-2 expression was associated with increased sensitivity of neutrophils to apoptotic cell death in vitro, as compared to monocytes and lymphocytes. Our results suggest that the ability of anti-Fas antibody to induce apoptosis in Fas+ lymphoid and hematopoietic cells may be influenced by the expression of bcl-2.

title: Foxp2 and Foxp1 cooperatively regulate lung and esophagus development.
text: The lung's airways develop through a complex process of branching morphogenesis, resulting in the extensive and intricate surface area required for postnatal respiration. Two forkhead transcription factors, Foxp2 and Foxp1, are expressed in multiple foregut-derived tissues, including the lung and intestine. In this study, we found that loss of Foxp2 in mice leads to defective postnatal lung alveolarization, contributing to postnatal lethality. Using in vitro and in vivo assays, we showed that T1alpha, a gene specifically expressed in lung alveolar epithelial cells, is a direct target of Foxp2 and Foxp1. Interestingly, loss of a single Foxp1 allele in addition to complete loss of Foxp2 results in more severe morphological defects in mutant lungs and leads to perinatal loss of all Foxp2(-/-);Foxp1(+/-) mice. Furthermore, expression of N-myc and Hop, crucial regulators of lung development, is compromised in Foxp2(-/-);Foxp1(+/-) mutants. In addition to defects in lung development, we also observed disruptions in esophageal muscle development in Foxp2(-/-);Foxp1(+/-) embryos, a tissue where Foxp2 and Foxp1 are co-expressed. These findings demonstrate the essential roles of Foxp2 and Foxp1 in the development of anterior foregut-derived tissues, including the lung and esophagus.

title: Crystal structure of the eukaryotic 60S ribosomal subunit in complex with initiation factor 6.
text: Ribosomes are the catalysts of protein synthesis in all living organisms, with eukaryotic ribosomes being significantly larger and more complexly regulated than their prokaryotic counterparts. The large subunit of eukaryotic ribosomes (60S) is responsible for peptide bond formation and contains the nascent polypeptide exit tunnel. In this study, we present the crystal structure of the 60S ribosomal subunit from Tetrahymena thermophila in complex with eukaryotic initiation factor 6 (eIF6) and the antibiotic cycloheximide, at a resolution of 3.5 angstroms. This structure reveals the intricate network of interactions between eukaryotic-specific ribosomal protein features and RNA expansion segments within the eukaryotic 60S subunit, and provides insights into the roles of eukaryotic ribosomal protein elements in the active site and other functional regions of the subunit. Furthermore, the structure elucidates the molecular basis of the interaction with eIF6 and provides a structural framework for further investigations into ribosome-associated diseases and the initiation of protein synthesis.

title: Hedgehog signaling regulates brain tumor-initiating cell proliferation and portends shorter survival for patients with PTEN-coexpressing glioblastomas.
text: The identification of brain tumor stem-like cells (BTSCs) has suggested a role for self-renewal mechanisms in the initiation and progression of brain tumors. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the tumor-forming capacity of BTSCs remain unclear. In this study, we generated gene expression profiles of BTSCs and identified both Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling-dependent and -independent BTSCs, as well as their respective glioblastoma surgical specimens. We found that BTSC proliferation could be inhibited in a pathway-dependent manner in vitro and in an intracranial tumor model in athymic mice. Both SHH-dependent and -independent brain tumor growth required phosphoinositide 3-kinase-mammalian target of rapamycin (PI3K-mTOR) signaling. Interestingly, we found that the levels of SHH and phosphatase and tensin homolog 1 (PTCH1) expression were significantly higher in PTEN-expressing tumors than in PTEN-deficient tumors. Moreover, we showed that hyperactive SHH-GLI signaling in PTEN-coexpressing human glioblastoma (GBM) was associated with reduced survival time. These findings suggest that distinct proliferation signaling dependence may underlie glioblastoma propagation by BTSCs, and modeling these mechanisms may provide a rationale for individualized GBM treatment.

title: Stress and host immunity amplify Mycobacterium tuberculosis phenotypic heterogeneity and induce nongrowing metabolically active forms.
text: Non-replicating and metabolically inactive bacteria are believed to play a role in latent tuberculosis infections and relapse following "sterilizing" chemotherapy. However, there is limited evidence to support this idea. In this study, we used quantitative time-lapse microscopy and a reporter of ribosomal RNA gene expression to investigate the single-cell dynamics of Mycobacterium tuberculosis replication and ribosomal activity. Our findings reveal that even under standard growth conditions, M. tuberculosis exhibits significant heterogeneity among individual cells. This heterogeneity is further amplified when the bacteria are exposed to stressful conditions such as nutrient limitation, stationary phase, intracellular replication, and growth in mouse lungs. Interestingly, we found that the lungs of chronically infected mice harbor a subpopulation of non-growing but metabolically active bacteria, which are absent in mice lacking interferon-γ, a cytokine essential for antituberculosis immunity. These cryptic bacterial forms are particularly prominent in mice treated with the antituberculosis drug isoniazid, suggesting a role in post-chemotherapeutic relapses. Our results suggest that the amplification of bacterial phenotypic heterogeneity in response to host immunity and drug pressure may play a significant role in tuberculosis persistence.

title: Proteomic analysis reveals Warburg effect and anomalous metabolism of glutamine in pancreatic cancer cells.
text: In this current study, we employed mass spectrometry using LTQ-Orbitrap technology to characterize the proteomes of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell line PANC-1 and normal pancreatic duct cells. Through label-free quantification analysis based on spectra count, we identified over 1700 proteins from each sample, including a large number of differentially expressed metabolic enzymes and proteins involved in various cellular processes such as cytoskeleton, cell adhesion, transport, transcription, translation, and cell proliferation. Our findings revealed that metabolic pathways were altered in PANC-1, consistent with the Warburg effect, and also uncovered anomalous metabolism of glutamine, suggesting that glutamine was primarily utilized as a nitrogen donor in nucleotide and amino acid biosynthesis in PANC-1. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the metabolic changes in PANC-1, which may serve as a basis for the development of new diagnostics and treatments for PDAC.

title: Prevalence of attempting weight loss and strategies for controlling weight.
text:
In the United States, overweight and obesity rates are increasing among adults. To investigate weight control strategies and prevalence of weight loss and maintenance attempts, a random-digit telephone survey was conducted in 1996 as part of the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS). The survey included 107,804 adults aged 18 and older from 49 states and the District of Columbia.
The survey found that 28.8% of men and 43.6% of women reported attempting to lose weight, while 35.1% of men and 34.4% of women reported attempting to maintain their weight. Among those attempting to lose weight, the most common strategy was reducing fat intake, but not calories (34.9% of men and 40.0% of women). Only 21.5% of men and 19.4% of women reported using the recommended combination of reducing calorie intake and engaging in at least 150 minutes of leisure-time physical activity per week.
Among men attempting to lose weight, the median weight was 90.4 kg with a goal weight of 81.4 kg, while among women, the median weight was 70.3 kg with a goal weight of 59.0 kg. These findings suggest that weight loss and weight maintenance are common concerns for men and women in the US, and that many individuals are not using the recommended strategies for weight control.

title: Antibodies specific for Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen-1 cross-react with human heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L.
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) has been linked to multiple sclerosis (MS), and elevated levels of antibodies against the EBV nuclear antigen-1 (EBNA-1) are commonly observed in MS patients. The aim of this study was to investigate whether anti-EBNA-1 antibodies in MS patients cross-react with a self-antigen. We purified anti-EBNA-1 antibodies from human plasma, used them to immunoprecipitate antigens from human brain tissue, and identified the bound antigens using mass spectrometry. We found that anti-EBNA-1 consistently bound to heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L (HNRNPL). We then expressed both the long and short isoforms of HNRNPL and confirmed that the long isoform cross-reacts with EBNA-1 using Western blots and ELISA. Immunohistochemistry also revealed that anti-EBNA-1 bound to an antigen in the nucleus of cultured rat central nervous system cells. Interestingly, we found that antibodies to HNRNPL were present in both healthy controls and MS patients, but the levels were not increased in MS patients. Based on these findings, we conclude that HNRNPL is an autoantigen that cross-reacts with EBNA-1. Further research is needed to determine the relevance of this autoantigen to MS and other autoimmune diseases.

title: Roles of chromatin remodellers in DNA double strand break repair.
text: With a solid grasp of the DNA double strand break (DSB) repair mechanisms and the signaling processes triggered by DSBs, attention is shifting to the chromatin environment's role in facilitating efficient repair. Mutations in chromatin remodeling complexes have been linked to cancer, highlighting the importance of understanding how these changes affect genomic stability. Our current knowledge of DSB repair pathways suggests that each one has unique requirements for chromatin remodeling. Additionally, restricting the extent of chromatin modifications may play a crucial role in determining which repair pathway is utilized. In this review, we will examine the distinct DSB repair pathways and their potential need for chromatin remodeling, while also discussing the roles of ATP-driven chromatin remodelers in these pathways.

title: Epstein-Barr virus and virus human protein interaction maps.
text: A comprehensive mapping of interactions among Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) proteins and interactions between EBV proteins and human proteins should provide specific hypotheses and a broad perspective on EBV strategies for replication and persistence. Using a rigorous high-throughput yeast two-hybrid system, interactions of EBV proteins with each other and with human proteins were assessed, resulting in the identification of 43 interactions between EBV proteins and 173 interactions between EBV and human proteins. The resulting "interactome" maps provided a framework for hypotheses regarding protein function. For example, the EBV protein LF2, whose function is unknown, was found to interact with the EBV immediate early R transactivator (Rta) and inhibit Rta transactivation. From a broader perspective, EBV genes can be divided into two evolutionary classes: "core" genes, which are conserved across all herpesviruses, and "noncore" genes. The EBV-EBV interactome map was found to be enriched for interactions among proteins in the same evolutionary class. Additionally, human proteins targeted by EBV proteins were enriched for highly connected or "hub" proteins and for proteins with relatively short paths to all other proteins in the human interactome network. Targeting of hubs may represent an efficient mechanism for EBV reorganization of cellular processes.

title: Relation between Medicare screening reimbursement and stage at diagnosis for older patients with colon cancer.
text:
In 1998 and 2001, Medicare's reimbursement policy for colonoscopies was changed to provide coverage for high-risk patients and all individuals, respectively. This study aimed to investigate whether these policy changes were associated with an increase in colonoscopy use and early-stage colon cancer diagnosis among Medicare beneficiaries.
The study included patients aged 67 and older who were diagnosed with colon cancer between 1992 and 2002, as well as a control group of Medicare beneficiaries who did not have cancer. The researchers found that colonoscopy use among Medicare beneficiaries without cancer increased significantly from an average rate of 285 per 100,000 quarterly in the no-coverage period (1992-1997) to 889 and 1919 per 100,000 quarterly in the limited coverage period (January 1998-June 2001) and universal coverage period (July 2001-December 2002), respectively (P<.001 for each pairwise comparison). During the study period, 44,924 eligible patients were diagnosed with colorectal cancer, and the proportion of patients diagnosed at an early stage increased from 22.5% in the no-coverage period to 25.5% in the limited coverage period and 26.3% in the universal coverage period (P<.001 for each pairwise comparison).
The study found that the expansion of Medicare reimbursement was strongly associated with an increased probability of early-stage diagnosis for patients with proximal colon lesions but weakly associated, if at all, for patients with distal colon lesions. The selective effect of the coverage change on proximal colon lesions suggests that increased use of whole-colon screening modalities such as colonoscopy may have played a pivotal role.
In conclusion, the study found that the expansion of Medicare reimbursement for colonoscopies was associated with an increased use of colonoscopy among Medicare beneficiaries and an increased probability of early-stage diagnosis among those diagnosed with colon cancer. The findings suggest that increasing access to colonoscopy through Medicare reimbursement can lead to improved cancer outcomes.

title: Direct visualization of the endomitotic cell cycle in living megakaryocytes: differential patterns in low and high ploidy cells.
text: Endomitosis in megakaryocytes (MKs) involves repeated DNA replication without cytokinesis, a crucial step in MK development. However, the dynamics of chromosomes during endomitosis have never been observed in living MKs. To address this gap in knowledge, we developed a new transgenic mouse model in which a green fluorescent protein is fused to the human histone H2B and targeted to MKs. Using ex vivo time-lapse microscopy, we found that chromosomal condensation occurs at early mitosis in all MKs. In high ploidy MKs (>8N), late anaphase is characterized by a ring-like alignment of chromosomes with multiple territories formed between them. In contrast, in low ploidy MKs, mitotic chromosomes segregate to form two distinct groups separated by a clear space before re-joining to form a single cluster. This study is the first to document chromosomal segregation patterns during endomitosis ex vivo and to demonstrate their potential differential regulation in low and high ploidy cells.

title: Aberrant expression and altered cellular localization of desmosomal and hemidesmosomal proteins are associated with aggressive clinicopathological features of oral squamous cell carcinoma
text: Disruption of cell adhesion plays a central role in the progression of various cancers, including oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). The desmosome and hemidesmosome are critical structures that regulate cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion, respectively. To investigate their contributions in the biology of OSCC, we conducted immunohistochemical analyses of 51 cases of OSCC for proteins involved in these junctions, including desmoglein 1 (DSG1), DSG2, DSG3, desmocollin 2 (DSC2), integrin beta 4 (ITGB4), laminin gamma chain 2 (LAMC2), and collagen type 17 alpha 1 (COL17A1). Our findings revealed that in OSCC, the expression of DSG1, DSG3, DSC2, and COL17A1 decreased and internalized to the cytoplasm, while ITGB4 and mature LAMC2 were induced in the cancer cells facing the stroma. We correlated these findings with clinicopathological parameters, including histologic differentiation, pattern of invasion, and presence of lymph node metastasis. Our results showed that decreased expression of DSG3 and DSC2 was associated with more aggressive clinicopathological features, including less differentiated and more invasive histologic features and a higher incidence of nodal metastasis. Lower COL17A1 expression and higher LAMC2 expression were also linked to a more aggressive phenotype. These findings reinforce the notion that disruption of the keratin-associated anchoring junctions confers aggressive features to cancer cells.

title: Histone/protein deacetylase inhibitors increase suppressive functions of human FOXP3+ Tregs.
text: Histone/protein deacetylases (HDACs) reduce histone and protein acetylation, leading to the repression of gene transcription and modulation of various protein functions. Our study revealed significant differences in HDAC expression before and after stimulation of human T regulatory (Treg) and T effector cells, suggesting the potential for targeting Tregs with HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) in the future. Treatment with various HDACi small molecules enhanced, by up to 4.5-fold (average 2-fold), the suppressive functions of both freshly isolated and expanded human Tregs, consistent with our previous murine data. The use of HDACi increased Treg expression of CTLA-4, a key negative regulator of immune response, and we found a direct and significant correlation between CTLA-4 expression and Treg suppression. Therefore, HDACi compounds are promising pharmacological tools to enhance Treg suppressive functions, which may have potential therapeutic applications in patients with autoimmunity or post-transplantation.

title: Enhanced pathological angiogenesis in mice lacking β3 integrin or β3 and β5 integrins
text: Inhibition of αvβ3 or αvβ5 integrin function has been shown to suppress tumor growth and neovascularization, suggesting that these integrins play a critical role in angiogenesis. However, our study found that mice lacking β3 integrins or both β3 and β5 integrins not only support tumorigenesis, but also exhibit enhanced tumor growth and angiogenesis. Furthermore, we observed that the absence of β3 integrins leads to augmented angiogenic responses to hypoxia and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). We did not observe any changes in the expression or functions of other integrins, but found elevated levels of VEGF receptor-2 (also called Flk-1) in β3-null endothelial cells. These findings suggest that αvβ3 and αvβ5 integrins are not essential for vascular development or pathological angiogenesis, and highlight the need for further investigation into the mechanisms of action of αv-integrin antagonists in anti-angiogenic therapeutics.

title: A lineage of myeloid cells independent of Myb and hematopoietic stem cells.
text: Macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs) are crucial components of the immune system, and it was previously believed that they originate and renew from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). However, some macrophages develop in the embryo before the appearance of definitive HSCs, which led us to reinvestigate their development. Our findings reveal that the transcription factor Myb is essential for the development of both HSCs and all CD11b(high) monocytes and macrophages. Surprisingly, Myb is dispensable for the development of yolk sac (YS) macrophages and the subsequent persistence of these cells in adult tissues, including liver Kupffer cells, epidermal Langerhans cells, and microglia. These results demonstrate a distinct lineage of tissue macrophages that arise from the YS and are genetically distinct from HSC progeny.

title: Heterogenic Loss of the Wild-Type BRCA Allele in Human Breast Tumorigenesis
text: For individuals genetically predisposed to breast and ovarian cancer due to a mutant BRCA allele, somatic loss of heterozygosity in the wild-type allele is considered essential for cancer initiation and progression. However, several lines of evidence suggest that haploinsufficiency of the BRCA gene may also lead to phenotypic effects. We analyzed archival fixed and embedded tissue samples from women with germ line deleterious mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2, and identified focal areas of normal breast epithelium, atypical ductal hyperplasia, ductal carcinoma-in-situ, and invasive ductal carcinoma in 14 BRCA1-linked and 9 BRCA2-linked breast cancers. We also studied 10 BRCA-linked prophylactic mastectomy specimens and 12 BRCA-linked invasive ovarian carcinomas. Using laser catapult microdissection, we isolated cells from the various pathologic lesions and corresponding normal tissues, and performed real-time polymerase chain reaction assays to quantify the proportion of wild-type to mutant BRCA alleles in each tissue sample. Our results showed a high level of heterogeneity in loss of heterozygosity within and between preinvasive lesions and invasive cancers from BRCA1 and BRCA2 heterozygotes with breast cancer. In contrast, all BRCA-associated ovarian cancers displayed complete loss of the wild-type BRCA allele. These findings suggest that loss of the wild-type BRCA allele is not essential for BRCA-linked breast tumorigenesis, which has important implications for the genetic mechanism of BRCA tumor suppression and for the clinical management of this patient population.

title: Targeted therapies in urothelial carcinoma.
text: The purpose of this review is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of targeted therapies for urothelial carcinoma, with a focus on the molecular targets and clinical trials underway. Greater understanding of the biology and genetics of urothelial carcinoma is enabling the identification and definition of appropriate molecular targets for novel-targeted therapies.
