This review summarizes the targeted therapies being investigated in clinical trials, including immunotherapy and agents targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, and other molecular targets. The majority of these agents are being studied in the second-line setting, with new targets emerging, such as CD105, polo-like kinase-1, phosphatidylinositide 3-kinases (PI3K), transforming growth factor β receptor/activin receptor-like kinase β, estrogen receptor, and the hepatocyte growth factor receptor (HGFR or MET). While there have been no major therapeutic advances to date, the proliferation of clinical trials holds promise for significant advances in treatment strategies for urothelial carcinoma.

title: H2S and HS− donor NaHS releases nitric oxide from nitrosothiols, metal nitrosyl complex, brain homogenate and murine L1210 leukaemia cells
text: Nitrosoglutathione (GSNO), 500 nmol/l relaxed precontracted rat aortic rings. The relaxation effect was significantly enhanced by H2S- and HS−-donor NaHS (30 μmol/l) at pH 7.5 but not at pH 6.3. To investigate the molecular mechanism of this effect, we examined whether NaHS can release nitric oxide (NO) from NO donors. Using an electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy method and measuring the NO oxidation product (nitrite) by the Griess reaction, we found that NaHS released NO from nitrosothiols, including GSNO, S-nitroso-N-acetyl-dl-penicillamine (SNAP), nitroprusside (SNP), and rat brain homogenate and murine L1210 leukaemia cells. Our observation that the releasing effect was more pronounced at pH 8.0 than at pH 6.0 suggests that HS−, rather than H2S, is responsible for the NO-releasing effect. Since H2S and HS− are endogenously produced in mammals, we propose that their ability to release NO from nitrosothiols and metal nitrosyl complexes may contribute to some of their biological activities and play a role in S-nitrosothiol signaling reactions.

title: Amitriptyline is effective in chronic but not in episodic tension-type headache: pathogenetic implications.
text: The tricyclic antidepressant drug amitriptyline has been found to be effective in treating both chronic tension-type headaches and other chronic pain syndromes. However, its efficacy in treating episodic tension-type headaches, a different type of headache, remains unclear. In an open-label study of 82 non-depressed patients with either chronic or episodic tension-type headaches, amitriptyline was found to significantly reduce the frequency and duration of headaches, as well as analgesic consumption, in patients with chronic tension-type headaches, but not in those with episodic tension-type headaches. Further placebo-controlled trials, possibly using higher doses of amitriptyline, may help clarify the different response patterns to the drug between the two types of headaches, and whether they are related to differences in central nociception or peripheral myofascial factors.

title: Kruppel-like factor 2 is required for trafficking but not quiescence in postactivated T cells.
text: The transcription factor Kruppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) was proposed to regulate genes involved in cell cycle entry and T cell trafficking; however, the specific role of KLF2 expression in post-activated T cells remains unclear. Previous studies suggested that cytokines such as IL-2 and IL-15 regulate KLF2 re-expression in post-activation T cells and influence effector versus memory T cell differentiation. To investigate the role of KLF2 in activated CD8+ T cells, we used conditional and inducible KLF2-knockout model systems and cultured them with these cytokines. Our findings revealed that KLF2 was required for the effective transcription of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor-1 (S1P1) and CD62L in post-activation T cells. However, different cytokines had varying effects on the expression of cell-cycle-related genes, and endogenous KLF2 had a minimal impact. Surprisingly, KLF2-deficient T cells showed dysregulated trafficking but not altered proliferative characteristics following in vivo responses to antigen. These data help define KLF2-dependent and -independent aspects of activated CD8+ T cell differentiation and argue against a physiological role in cell cycle regulation.

title: Hypoalbuminemia in acute illness: is there a rationale for intervention? A meta-analysis of cohort studies and controlled trials.
text: OBJECTIVE: To determine whether hypoalbuminemia is an independent risk factor for poor outcomes in acutely ill patients and to evaluate the potential of exogenous albumin administration for improving outcomes in hypoalbuminemic patients. SUMMARY: Hypoalbuminemia, or low levels of albumin in the blood, has been associated with poor outcomes in acutely ill patients, but the causal relationship between the two remains unclear. While some trials have investigated the use of albumin therapy to correct hypoalbuminemia, the results have been inconclusive. This meta-analysis aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the relationship between hypoalbuminemia and poor outcomes, as well as the potential benefits of albumin therapy in hypoalbuminemic patients. METHODS: A meta-analysis of 90 cohort studies and nine prospective controlled trials was conducted to evaluate the association between hypoalbuminemia and poor outcomes. RESULTS: Hypoalbuminemia was found to be a strong, dose-dependent independent predictor of poor outcome in acutely ill patients. Each 10-g/L decline in serum albumin concentration significantly increased the odds of mortality, morbidity, prolonged hospital stay, and increased resource utilization. The association between hypoalbuminemia and poor outcome was found to be independent of both nutritional status and inflammation. Analysis of dose-dependency in controlled trials of albumin therapy suggested that complication rates may be reduced when the serum albumin level attained during albumin administration exceeds 30 g/L. CONCLUSIONS: Hypoalbuminemia is strongly associated with poor clinical outcomes in acutely ill patients. While the results of this meta-analysis suggest that albumin therapy may have potential benefits in hypoalbuminemic patients, further well-designed trials are needed to fully characterize its effects. In the interim, there is no compelling basis to withhold albumin therapy if it is judged clinically appropriate.

title: Methionine restriction decreases visceral fat mass and preserves insulin action in aging male Fischer 344 rats independent of energy restriction.
text: Reduced dietary methionine intake (0.17% methionine, MR) and caloric restriction (CR) have been shown to prolong lifespan in male Fischer 344 rats. Although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear, both interventions are characterized by lower body weight and reductions in adiposity. CR-induced preservation of insulin responsiveness in older animals is linked to the reduction in fat deposition. These studies aim to elucidate the relationship between insulin sensitivity and visceral fat in MR animals and determine whether the decreased visceral fat accumulation and preserved insulin sensitivity observed in MR animals are secondary to CR. To achieve this, rats were pair-fed a control diet (0.86% methionine, CF) to match the food intake of MR animals for 80 weeks, resulting in similar insulin, glucose, and leptin levels and comparable amounts of visceral fat. Conversely, MR animals exhibited significantly reduced visceral fat compared to CF and PF, accompanied by decreases in basal insulin, glucose, and leptin levels and increases in adiponectin and triiodothyronine. Notably, daily energy expenditure in MR animals was found to significantly exceed that of both PF and CF. In a separate cohort, the insulin responses of older MR animals, as measured by oral glucose challenge, were found to be similar to those of young animals. Longitudinal assessments of MR and CF from 112 weeks of age revealed that MR prevented age-associated increases in serum lipids. Interestingly, MR animals showed a 40% reduction in insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels by 16 weeks, which was sustained throughout life, whereas CF IGF-1 levels declined much later, beginning at 112 weeks. Taken together, these findings suggest that MR reduces visceral fat and preserves insulin activity in aging rats independent of energy restriction.

title: Generation of T cell receptor–retrogenic mice: improved retroviral-mediated stem cell gene transfer
text:
The use of retrogenic mice provides a rapid and adaptable method for generating T cell receptor (TCR)-transgenic mice. By employing a retrovirus to transduce bone marrow progenitor cells with a specific TCR-α/β subunit, TCR-retrogenic mice can be generated in a relatively short period of time, typically within 4-6 weeks, compared to conventional TCR transgenics which can take 6 months or longer.
In this updated protocol, we have optimized the efficiency of bone marrow transduction and bone marrow reconstitution compared to our previously published method. The main modification from the previous protocol involves the use of spin transduction with viral supernatant instead of coculture with the viral producer cell line. These changes result in improved bone marrow viability, increased consistency of bone marrow transduction and engraftment, and a reduced ratio of bone marrow donor mice to bone marrow recipients.

title: Transient delivery of modified mRNA encoding TERT rapidly extends telomeres in human cells.
text: Telomere extension has been proposed as a means to enhance cell culture and tissue engineering, as well as to treat diseases. However, nonviral, nonintegrating methods for telomere extension have been inefficient. We report that delivering modified mRNA encoding TERT to human fibroblasts and myoblasts leads to a transient increase in telomerase activity and rapid telomere extension, followed by resumption of telomere shortening. Three consecutive transfections over a 4-day period extended telomeres by up to 0.9 kb in a cell type-specific manner in fibroblasts and myoblasts, and conferred additional 28 ± 1.5 and 3.4 ± 0.4 population doublings (PDs), respectively. The proliferative capacity of treated cells increased in a dose-dependent manner. Interestingly, the refractory period observed after the second and third transfections was transient, as a later fourth transfection increased fibroblast proliferative capacity by an additional 15.2 ± 1.1 PDs, similar to the first transfection. Overall, these treatments led to an increase in absolute cell number of more than 10(12)-fold. Notably, unlike immortalized cells, all treated cell populations eventually stopped increasing in number and expressed senescence markers to the same extent as untreated cells, indicating that the rapid method of extending telomeres and increasing cell proliferative capacity without the risk of insertional mutagenesis has broad utility in disease modeling, drug screening, and regenerative medicine.

title: The death receptor CD95 activates adult neural stem cells for working memory formation and brain repair.
text: Adult neurogenesis persists in the subventricular zone and the dentate gyrus, and can be induced following central nervous system (CNS) injury. However, the final contribution of newly generated neurons to neuronal networks is limited. In contrast, our findings reveal that stimulation of the "death receptor" CD95 does not induce apoptosis in neural stem cells, but instead leads to increased stem cell survival and neuronal specification. These effects are mediated by the activation of the Src/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, resulting in enhanced protein translation. We demonstrate that CD95-mediated neurogenesis is also observed in the ischemic CA1 region, the naive dentate gyrus, and when CD95L is overexpressed in the adult subventricular zone. Conversely, lack of hippocampal CD95 leads to a reduction in neurogenesis and working memory deficits. Following global ischemia, CD95-mediated brain repair can rescue behavioral impairment. Therefore, we identify the CD95/CD95L system as a crucial instructive signal for ongoing and injury-induced neurogenesis.

title: Umbilical Cord Blood Therapy Potentiated with Erythropoietin for Children with Cerebral Palsy: A Double-blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial
text:
Allogeneic umbilical cord blood (UCB) has shown potential as a therapeutic option for cerebral palsy (CP), and the addition of recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEPO) may enhance its efficacy due to its neurotrophic effects. The aim of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of allogeneic UCB potentiated with rhEPO in children with CP.
This randomized, controlled trial enrolled 96 children with CP, who were assigned to one of three parallel groups: the pUCB group, which received allogeneic UCB potentiated with rhEPO; the EPO group, which received rhEPO and placebo UCB; and the Control group, which received placebo UCB and placebo rhEPO. All participants underwent rehabilitation therapy. The primary outcome measures were changes in scores on the Gross Motor Performance Measure (GMPM), Gross Motor Function Measure, and Bayley Scales of Infant Development-II (BSID-II) Mental and Motor scales over a 6-month treatment period. Additionally, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were conducted at baseline and follow-up to assess changes in brain structure and function.
The results showed that compared to the EPO (n = 33) and Control (n = 32) groups, the pUCB (n = 31) group exhibited significantly higher scores on the GMPM and BSID-II Mental and Motor scales at 6 months. DTI revealed significant correlations between the GMPM increment and changes in fractional anisotropy in the pUCB group. 18F-FDG-PET/CT showed differential activation and deactivation patterns between the three groups. There were no significant differences in the incidence of serious adverse events between the groups.
In conclusion, this study suggests that UCB treatment improved motor and cognitive function in children with CP undergoing active rehabilitation, accompanied by structural and metabolic changes in the brain. These findings support the potential of UCB as a therapeutic option for CP.

title: Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP(1-38)) enhances N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor function and brain-derived neurotrophic factor expression via RACK1.
text:
In a recent study, we discovered a novel mechanism by which the scaffolding protein RACK1 modulates the phosphorylation state and function of the N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. We found that RACK1 binds both the NR2B subunit of the NMDA receptor and the nonreceptor protein-tyrosine kinase, Fyn. RACK1 inhibits Fyn phosphorylation of NR2B, leading to decreased NMDA receptor-mediated currents in CA1 hippocampal slices.
To further investigate this mechanism, we identified the signaling cascade that occurs upon RACK1 release from the NMDA receptor complex. We discovered that activation of the cAMP/protein kinase A (PKA) pathway in hippocampal slices leads to the release of RACK1 from NR2B and Fyn. This results in the induction of NR2B phosphorylation and enhancement of NMDA receptor-mediated activity via Fyn.
We also identified the neuropeptide, pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide (PACAP(1-38)), as a ligand that induces phosphorylation of NR2B and enhances NMDA receptor potentials. Furthermore, we found that activation of the cAMP/PKA pathway leads to the movement of RACK1 to the nuclear compartment in dissociated hippocampal neurons. In the nucleus, RACK1 regulates the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) induced by PACAP(1-38).
In summary, our results suggest that activation of adenylate cyclase by PACAP(1-38) leads to the release of RACK1 from the NMDA receptor and Fyn, resulting in NMDA receptor phosphorylation, enhanced activity mediated by Fyn, and the induction of BDNF expression by RACK1.

title: MUC1 oncoprotein activates the IκB kinase β complex and constitutive NF-κB signalling
text: Nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) is consistently activated in various human malignancies due to mechanisms that are not fully understood. The oncoprotein MUC1 is overexpressed in most human carcinomas, blocking apoptosis and inducing transformation. This study demonstrates that overexpression of MUC1 in human carcinoma cells leads to constitutive activation of NF-κB p65. We found that MUC1 interacts with the high-molecular-weight IκB kinase (IKK) complex in vivo, and the MUC1 cytoplasmic domain binds directly to IKKβ and IKKγ. Interaction of MUC1 with both IKKβ and IKKγ is necessary for IKKβ activation, leading to phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα. In non-malignant epithelial cells, MUC1 is recruited to the TNF-R1 complex and interacts with IKKβ–IKKγ in response to TNFα stimulation. TNFα-induced recruitment of MUC1 is dependent on TRADD and TRAF2, but not the death-domain kinase RIP1. Additionally, MUC1-mediated activation of IKKβ is dependent on TAK1 and TAB2. These findings suggest that MUC1 plays a crucial role in physiological activation of IKKβ and that overexpression of MUC1 in human cancers leads to sustained induction of the IKKβ–NF-κB p65 pathway.

title: Lipoxins: novel series of biologically active compounds formed from arachidonic acid in human leukocytes.
text: In a recent study, researchers isolated a novel series of oxygenated derivatives of arachidonic acid in human leukocytes, known as trihydroxytetraenes. The structure of the major compound, 5,6,15L-trihydroxy-7,9,11,13-icosatetraenoic acid, was previously established. In this study, the structure of a second member of the trihydroxytetraene series, 5D,14,15L-trihydroxy-6,8,10,12-icosatetraenoic acid, was determined. When added to human neutrophils, both compounds stimulated superoxide anion generation and degranulation at submicromolar concentrations without inducing a significant aggregation response. The results suggest that the 5- and 15-lipoxygenase pathways of human leukocytes interact to form new oxygenated derivatives of arachidonic acid, which may play a role in regulating specific cellular responses. The trivial names lipoxin A and lipoxin B are proposed for the new compounds.

title: Nitric oxide synthase generates superoxide and nitric oxide in arginine-depleted cells leading to peroxynitrite-mediated cellular injury.
text: In addition to synthesizing nitric oxide (NO), purified neuronal NO synthase (nNOS) can produce superoxide (.O2-) at lower concentrations of the amino acid L-Arg. Using electron paramagnetic resonance spin-trapping techniques, we monitored NO and .O2- formation in nNOS-transfected human kidney 293 cells. In control cells transfected with nNOS, the addition of the Ca2+ ionophore A23187 led to the production of NO, but not .O2-. However, when cells were grown in L-Arg-free medium, we observed the formation of .O2- in the absence of A23187, which increased as the cytosolic L-Arg levels decreased. This increase in .O2- formation was virtually abolished by the specific NOS blocker, N-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME). Furthermore, we observed the accumulation of nitrotyrosine, a specific nitration product of peroxynitrite, in L-Arg-depleted cells but not in control cells. Activation by A23187 led to cytotoxicity in L-Arg-depleted cells, but not in control cells, with marked lactate dehydrogenase release. This cytotoxicity was largely prevented by either superoxide dismutase or L-NAME. These findings suggest that with reduced L-Arg availability, nNOS can elicit cytotoxicity by generating .O2- and NO, which interact to form the potent oxidant peroxynitrite. Regulating arginine levels may provide a therapeutic approach to disorders involving .O2-/NO-mediated cellular injury.

title: Sudden infant death syndrome and unclassified sudden infant deaths: a definitional and diagnostic approach.
text: In 1969, the initial definition of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) was established. Over the next two decades, significant additional information emerged, leading to the refinement of the definition in 1984. Since then, an expert panel of pediatric and forensic pathologists and pediatricians has continually evaluated and updated the definition of SIDS to incorporate new epidemiologic, pathologic, and ancillary test findings. As a result, a revised general definition of SIDS was developed for administrative and vital statistics purposes. To facilitate research into sudden infant death, the new definition was stratified into distinct categories. A separate category, referred to as unclassified sudden infant deaths, was also introduced for cases that do not meet the criteria for a diagnosis of SIDS and for which alternative diagnoses of natural or unnatural causes are uncertain. It is anticipated that the definitions will continue to evolve in the future as new knowledge and understanding of SIDS and sudden infant death emerge.

title: Inter-viral conflicts that exploit host CRISPR immune systems of Sulfolobus.
text: Infection of Sulfolobus islandicus REY15A with a mixture of different Sulfolobus viruses, including STSV2, did not induce the acquisition of new spacers by the host CRISPR immune system. However, coinfection with the tailed fusiform viruses SMV1 and STSV2 resulted in the hyperactive acquisition of spacers in both CRISPR loci, exclusively from STSV2, leading to the loss of STSV2 but not SMV1. Interestingly, SMV1 was found to activate adaptation while being resistant to CRISPR-mediated adaptation and DNA interference. An exceptional single clone, S-1, isolated from an SMV1 + STSV2-infected culture, acquired STSV2-specific spacers and lost STSV2 but not SMV1. This effect was also reproducible when reinfecting wild-type host cells with a variant SMV1 isolated from the S-1 culture. The variant SMV1 lacked a virion protein ORF114 that was shown to bind DNA. This study also provided evidence for the following conclusions: (i) there are limits to the maximum sizes of CRISPR loci, (ii) spacer uptake significantly retards the growth of infected cultures, (iii) protospacer selection is random and non-directional, and (iv) the reversible uptake of spacers from STSV2 and SMV1. A hypothesis is proposed to explain the complex interactions between SMV1 and the host CRISPR immune system.

title: Lung Carcinogenesis by Diesel Exhaust Particles and the Carcinogenic Mechanism Via Active Oxygens.
text: In an experiment to investigate the role of oxygen radicals in lung cancer development induced by diesel exhaust particles (DEP), we found a strong correlation between the response of lung tumors and the formation of 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) in lung DNA of mice exposed to DEP through repeated intratracheal instillation. Additionally, we observed increased activity of cytochrome P-450 reductase in the lungs, which is a representative enzyme of superoxide generation, as well as the expression of two types of nitric oxide (NO) synthases, cNOS and iNOS, in the lungs. On the other hand, the activities of CuZn-superoxide dismutase (SOD) and Mn-SOD antioxidant enzymes were decreased after DEP instillation. These findings suggest that the generation of superoxide, hydroxyl radical, and nitric oxide is increased in epithelial cells in the airways, and that these reactive species react easily to form peroxynitrite (ONOO(-)), which can also produce hydroxyl radicals. The hydroxyl radical may play a crucial role in the carcinogenic effects of DEP.

title: Prion-induced amyloid heart disease with high blood infectivity in transgenic mice.
text: We examined the distribution of prion protein (PrP) in transgenic mice that express a mutated form of the protein lacking the glycophosphatydylinositol (GPI) membrane anchor. In the brain, blood, and heart, we detected both abnormal protease-resistant PrP (PrPres) and prion infectivity using immunoblotting and inoculation of non-transgenic mice. The level of infectious scrapie in blood plasma was found to be above 10(7) 50% infectious doses per milliliter. Additionally, we observed PrPres-positive amyloid deposits in the hearts of these transgenic mice, which led to cardiac stiffness and disease.

title: Circulating plasma microRNAs as a screening method for detection of colorectal adenomas.
text:
The study aimed to investigate the potential of using circulating plasma microRNAs (miRNAs) as a screening tool for colorectal polyps and adenomas. The study included 210 patients, including those with polyps (n=117), cancer (n=12), and healthy controls (n=81) who were positive for faecal occult blood testing (FOBt). The researchers analyzed the expression levels of 19 miRNAs in the plasma of these patients and compared them to endoscopy reports and histology results.
The results showed that the miRNA panel showed significant differences in expression levels between patients with polyps, cancer, or both, and between patients with polyps and healthy controls. Specifically, the miRNAs miR-19a, miR-98, miR-146b, miR-186, and miR-625 showed significant differences in expression levels between these groups. The receiver operating characteristic analysis showed that the sensitivity and specificity of the panel were 60% or more and 86% or more, respectively, for detecting polyps and adenomas in both men and women.
The study suggests that the use of circulating plasma miRNAs as a screening test for colorectal polyps and adenomas has potential. However, further research is needed to validate these findings and to determine the clinical utility of this test.

title: Short term persistence of human papillomavirus and risk of cervical precancer and cancer: population based cohort study
text:
Objective: To determine the cumulative incidence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) II or worse (grade II+) or CIN grade III+ over a 3-year and 5-year period in women with persistent prevalence of carcinogenic human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.
Design: Population-based cohort study.
Setting: Guanacaste, Costa Rica.
Participants: 2282 sexually active women actively followed after enrollment.
Main Outcome Measures: Primary endpoints include the 3-year and 5-year cumulative incidence of histologically confirmed CIN grade II+ (n=70). Cervical specimens collected at each visit were tested for over 40 HPV genotypes. HPV 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68, 73, and 82 were considered the primary carcinogenic genotypes.
Results: Women who tested positive for a carcinogenic HPV at enrollment and after approximately one year (9-21 months) (positive/positive) had a 3-year cumulative incidence of CIN grade II+ of 17.0% (95% confidence interval 12.1% to 22.0%). Those who tested negative/positive (3.4%, 0.1% to 6.8%), positive/negative (1.2%, -0.2% to 2.5%), and negative/negative (0.5%, 0.1% to 0.9%) were at a significantly lower risk. There was little difference in the cumulative incidence of CIN grade II+ between testing positive twice for any carcinogenic HPV genotype (same genotype or different genotypes) compared to testing positive twice for the same carcinogenic genotype (17.0% vs 21.3%, respectively). Short-term persistence of HPV 16 strongly predicted CIN grade II+, with a 3-year cumulative incidence of 40.8% (26.4% to 55.1%). Similar patterns were observed for the 5-year cumulative incidence of grade II+ and for 3-year and 5-year cumulative incidence of grade III+.
Conclusions: Short-term persistence of a prevalently detected carcinogenic HPV infection, especially HPV 16, strongly predicts a subsequent diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia II+ over the next few years.

title: Nature and anisotropy of cortical forces orienting Drosophila tissue morphogenesis
text: The development of embryos and organs relies on cells' ability to modify their connections with neighboring cells. By employing quantitative modeling and laser nano-dissection, we investigated the mechanics of a morphogenetic process, the elongation of Drosophila melanogaster embryos, which arises from the exchange of polarized cell neighbors. Our findings reveal that the anisotropy of cortical tension at apical cell junctions is sufficient to drive tissue elongation. We estimated this value by comparing in silico and in vivo data using various tissue descriptors. Nano-dissection of the actomyosin network showed that tension is anisotropically distributed and depends on myosin II accumulation. Additionally, relaxation of junctions after nano-dissection revealed that cortical elastic forces are the dominant factor in this process. Interestingly, fluctuations in vertex positions (points where three or more cells meet) facilitate neighbor exchanges. Our study delineates the contribution of subcellular tensile activity in polarizing junction remodeling and the permissive role of vertex fluctuations during tissue elongation.

title: The influence of some metabolic inhibitors on phagocytic activity of mouse macrophages in vitro.
text: The study investigated the impact of various metabolic inhibitors on phagocytosis in macrophages cultured in vitro from mouse peritoneal exudate. The following inhibitors were tested at a concentration of 10(-3) M: sodium iodoacetate, sodium fluoride, sodium fluoroacetate, sodium malonate, 2-4-dinitrophenol, sodium azide, ouabain, and cycloheximide. Iodoacetate significantly inhibited phagocytosis, suggesting that glycolysis is the primary source of energy for this process. In contrast, fluoride, although it inhibits glycolysis, did not affect phagocytosis. This discrepancy may be due to the fact that sodium fluoride blocks anaerobic glycolysis only at an unphysiological temperature (0°C). Fluoroacetate and malonate, which interfere with the Krebs cycle, did not inhibit phagocytosis, as the Krebs cycle is underdeveloped in macrophagic cells. Sodium azide and 2-4-dinitrophenol, inhibitors of oxidative phosphorylation, showed an effect on phagocytosis only after 3 hours of cell exposure. Ouabain, which blocks Na+ and K+ transport across the plasma membrane, likely inhibited phagocytosis by disrupting cell membrane movements. The mode of action of cycloheximide on phagocytosis remains unclear, as it inhibits protein synthesis and may prevent the renewal of the cell membrane.

title: Two-tiered coupling between flowing actin and immobilized N-cadherin/catenin complexes in neuronal growth cones.
text: Neuronal growth cones move forward by dynamically connecting their actin-based motility to substrate adhesion, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. To investigate these mechanisms, we cultured primary neurons on N-cadherin-coated micropatterned substrates and used single particle tracking combined with photoactivated localization microscopy (sptPALM) to image adhesion and cytoskeletal proteins at the ventral surface of growth cones. We discovered transient interactions between flowing actin filaments and immobilized N-cadherin/catenin complexes on the second timescale, resulting in a local reduction of actin retrograde flow. To rescue normal actin flow on micropatterns, we expressed a dominant negative N-cadherin construct that competed with endogenous N-cadherin for actin binding. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments confirmed the differential kinetics of actin and N-cadherin, and revealed a 20% population of actin filaments confined to N-cadherin micropatterns, contributing to local actin accumulation. Computer simulations using relevant kinetic parameters validated this mechanism, suggesting that a two-tiered clutch mechanism involving short- and long-lived interactions between the motile actin network and spatially restricted adhesive complexes may sustain dynamic environment sensing and provide the necessary force for growth cone migration.

title: Cloning of factors related to HIV-inducible LBP proteins that regulate steroidogenic factor-1-independent human placental transcription of the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, P450scc.
text: The enzyme cytochrome P450scc is essential for the synthesis of all steroid hormones in the body. The adrenal and gonadal glands use the same strategy to transcribe this enzyme, which involves the orphan nuclear receptor steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1). However, the placenta has a unique strategy for transcribing P450scc that is independent of SF-1 and requires different cis-acting elements. To identify the factors that regulate P450scc transcription in the placenta, we performed a yeast one-hybrid screen using cDNA clones from human placental cells. We identified two transcription factors, LBP-1b and LBP-9, that bind specifically to the -155/-131 region of the P450scc promoter in the placenta. LBP-1b is already known to be induced by HIV infection and type I infection of lymphocytes, while LBP-9 is a new factor that shares 83% amino acid sequence identity with LBP-1b. When expressed in yeast, both factors bound to the -155/-131 DNA, and antisera to LBP proteins supershifted the LBP-9.DNA complex and inhibited the formation of the LBP-1b.DNA complex. Our results suggest that LBP transcription factors play a crucial role in regulating P450scc transcription in the placenta, and their modulation of placental but not adrenal P450scc transcription highlights the distinctiveness of placental strategies for steroidogenic enzyme gene transcription.

title: Functional reprogramming of polyploidization in megakaryocytes.
text: Polyploidization is a natural process that often occurs alongside cell differentiation, and its deregulation has been linked to genomic instability and cancer. Despite its importance, the reasons why cells choose specific polyploidization mechanisms are still unknown. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive genetic analysis of endomitosis, a process by which megakaryocytes become polyploid by entering mitosis but aborting anaphase. We found that ablation of the APC/C cofactor Cdc20 leads to mitotic arrest and severe thrombocytopenia, while lack of the kinases Aurora-B, Cdk1, or Cdk2 does not affect megakaryocyte polyploidization or platelet levels. Interestingly, ablation of Cdk1 leads to a switch to endocycles without mitosis, while polyploidization in the absence of Cdk1 and Cdk2 occurs through aberrant re-replication events. Notably, ablation of these kinases rescues the defects in Cdc20-null megakaryocytes. These findings suggest that endomitosis can be functionally replaced by alternative polyploidization mechanisms in vivo, providing a cellular basis for therapeutic approaches aimed at distinguishing between mitotic and polyploid cells.

title: Histone methyltransferase activity associated with a human multiprotein complex containing the Enhancer of Zeste protein.
text: Enhancer of Zeste (E(z)) is a Polycomb-group transcriptional repressor and a founding member of the SET domain-containing protein family. Although several SET-domain proteins exhibit intrinsic histone methyltransferase (HMT) activity, recombinant E(z) protein was found to be inactive in a HMT assay. In this study, we report the isolation of a multiprotein E(z) complex termed Polycomb repressive complex (PRC) 2, which consists of extra sex combs, suppressor of zeste-12 (Su(z)12), and histone binding proteins RbAp46/RbAp48. PRC2 possesses HMT activity specific to Lys 9 (K9) and Lys 27 (K27) of histone H3, and this activity is dependent on the intact SET domain in the E(z) protein. We propose that transcriptional repression by the E(z) protein involves methylation-dependent recruitment of PRC1. The presence of Su(z)12, a potent suppressor of position effect variegation, in PRC2 suggests that PRC2 may play a widespread role in heterochromatin-mediated silencing.

title: Simvastatin reduces platelet-endocardium adhesion in atrial fibrillation.
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between the CD40/CD40L system and increased thrombogenesis in atrial fibrillation (AF), and to evaluate the effects of simvastatin treatment on this relationship.
Methods: An in vitro study using human tissue from University Hospital (tertiary referral center) involved experiments on right atrial segments obtained before cardiopulmonary bypass in either the presence or absence of 5 microM simvastatin. Two groups of patients in either chronic atrial fibrillation or sinus rhythm at the time of cardiac surgery were also studied. The endocardial expression of CD40, the release of CD40L, and adhesion of platelets to the endocardium were evaluated, as well as the thickness of platelet aggregates and the platelet distribution on the endocardium.
Results: Atrial fibrillation was associated with a significant increase in endocardial CD40 expression compared to sinus rhythm (293.1+/-55.1 pg/ml vs. 230.9+/-53.3 pg/ml, p<0.01), and platelet-endocardial adhesion was higher in fibrillating atria than in sinus rhythm atria (10.8+/-2.2 vs. 5.2+/-1.3 platelet CD41 AU, p<0.01). Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that about 62% of fibrillating endocardium was covered by platelets, compared to 12% of non-sinus rhythm atria. Addition of simvastatin significantly reduced CD40 expression as well as platelet adhesion to fibrillating atria, and this effect was not reversed by the addition of mevalonic acid.
Conclusions: Chronic atrial fibrillation acutely upregulates CD40 expression as well as platelet adhesion to the endocardium. Simvastatin is effective in modulating this expression, suggesting that it may contribute to reducing the risk of intra-atrial thrombus formation.

title: Transmission of sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease by blood transfusion: risk factor or possible biases.
text:
BACKGROUND The recent occurrence of transfusion-related cases of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) has renewed attention to the potential risk of other forms of CJD transmission through blood transfusions.
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS We included 741 patients with sporadic CJD, 175 patients with genetic CJD, and 482 no-CJD patients with a definite alternative diagnosis in our study, all of whom had available blood transfusion history. We evaluated the risk of exposure to blood transfusions occurring more than 10 years before disease onset and potential confounding factors using crude odds ratios (ORs) in univariate analyses. Variables with significant ORs were included in multivariate logistic regression analyses.
RESULTS In the univariate model, blood transfusion occurring more than 10 years before clinical onset was found to be 4.1 times more frequent in sporadic CJD patients than in other neurological disorders. However, this significance was lost when the 10-year lag time was not considered. Multivariate analyses revealed that the risk of developing sporadic CJD after transfusion increased significantly (OR = 5.05) after adjusting for potential confounding factors. Analysis of patients with genetic CJD did not reveal any significant risk factors associated with transfusion.
CONCLUSION This case-control study is the first to demonstrate a significant risk of transfusion occurring more than 10 years before clinical onset in sporadic CJD patients. While the biological plausibility of these findings is uncertain, they suggest that previous epidemiological studies may have overestimated the safety of blood transfusions in sporadic CJD.

title: Advantages and pitfalls of fructosamine and glycated albumin in the diagnosis and treatment of diabetes.
text: The accurate diagnosis and monitoring of diabetic patients are crucial in reducing the risk of complications. Currently, the primary diagnostic and prognostic tools in diabetes are plasma glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) tests. However, these measures have limitations and can be affected by various clinical and analytical factors. The introduction of alternative indices of glucose homeostasis, such as fructosamine and glycated albumin (GA), may provide a more reliable alternative, particularly in patients with rapid glucose fluctuations, red blood cell disorders, or renal disease. According to available evidence, GA has a higher diagnostic efficiency than fructosamine across a broad range of clinical settings. The current method for measuring GA is also more standardized and less susceptible to preanalytical variables than those used for fructosamine assessment. Additionally, GA has a lower reagent cost and can be automated on many conventional laboratory instruments, making it a more practical option. While further studies are needed to definitively establish GA as a reliable alternative to HbA1c, it may offer valuable insights into glucose homeostasis in patients where HbA1c values may be unreliable.

title: Catalytic-Independent Functions of PARP-1 Determine Sox2 Pioneer Activity at Intractable Genomic Loci.
text: Pioneer transcription factors (TFs) serve as genomic first responders by binding to inaccessible regions of chromatin, thereby promoting enhancer formation. However, the mechanism by which pioneer TFs gain access to chromatin remains an unresolved question. Our study investigates the role of PARP-1, a nucleosome-binding protein, in facilitating the binding of the pioneer TF Sox2 to inaccessible genomic loci in embryonic stem cells. We found that PARP-1 cooperates with the intrinsic properties of Sox2 to enhance its binding to difficult-to-reach genomic regions. These actions of PARP-1 are independent of its poly(ADP-ribosyl) transferase activity. Our results identify specific features of the genome that determine Sox2's pioneer activity, including the presence of PARP-1-dependent binding sites in euchromatic regions with high nucleosome occupancy and low co-occupancy by other transcription factors. Additionally, we demonstrate that PARP-1 stabilizes Sox2 binding to nucleosomes at suboptimal sites through cooperative interactions on DNA. Our findings provide insights into the intrinsic and extrinsic factors that govern pioneer TF activity, and suggest that the conditional pioneer activity observed with Sox2 at certain binding sites may be a common feature of other pioneer TFs operating at intractable genomic loci.

title: Steroid regulation of C. elegans diapause, developmental timing, and longevity.
text: Hormones are instrumental in guiding significant developmental milestones and timing events across various species. In the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, the steroid hormone receptor DAF-12 plays a pivotal role in integrating environmental and physiological cues to regulate life history traits. DAF-12 acts as a central hub, connecting pathways that control developmental timing, stage specification, and longevity. This complex system has provided valuable insights into the regulation of biological time by steroid hormones. Here, we will delve into the molecular mechanisms, intricate circuitry, and signaling pathways involved in life stage transitions in the worm and explore how they have shed light on the steroid hormone regulation of developmental processes.

title: A core subunit of Polycomb repressive complex 1 is broadly conserved in function but not primary sequence.
text: Polycomb Group (PcG) proteins mediate heritable gene silencing by modifying chromatin structure through noncovalent interactions. An essential PcG complex, PRC1, compacts chromatin and inhibits chromatin remodeling, and the intrinsically disordered C-terminal region of PSC (PSC-CTR) in Drosophila melanogaster plays a crucial role in these processes. However, the significance of the PSC-CTR sequence's effects on chromatin outside of Drosophila was unclear due to its poor conservation. To investigate the mechanistic basis and extent of conservation of PSC-CTR activity, we identified 17 metazoan PSC-CTRs spanning chordates to arthropods and examined their sequence features and biochemical properties. Our findings reveal that PSC-CTR sequences are poorly conserved but highly charged and structurally disordered, and that active PSC-CTRs are distinguished from less active ones by the absence of extended negatively charged stretches. We also found that PSC-CTR activity can be increased by dispersing its contiguous negative charge, confirming the importance of this property. Using the sequence properties defined as important for PSC-CTR activity, we predicted the presence of active PSC-CTRs in additional diverse genomes. Our analysis reveals broad conservation of PSC-CTR activity across metazoans, suggesting that a disordered domain with dispersed negative charges underlies PRC1 activity and is conserved across metazoans and plants.

title: Dietary status of trained female cyclists.
text: In this study, the dietary habits of eight highly trained female cyclists were evaluated. Each cyclist kept a 3-day food record, which was analyzed using a computerized software package to determine the nutrient content of their diets. Blood samples were also collected to assess hemoglobin, hematocrit, and albumin levels. The results showed that the cyclists' diets were low in energy (85% of the Recommended Daily Allowance, or RDA) and carbohydrates (4.4 grams per kilogram of body weight per day). The diets were also found to be deficient in several micronutrients, including folic acid (76% of the RDA), magnesium (81%), iron (59%), and zinc (48%). In addition, more than one-third of the cyclists did not consume enough of the following micronutrients: pyridoxine, folic acid, cobalamin, vitamin E, magnesium, iron, and zinc. Despite normal hemoglobin (135 grams per liter), hematocrit (0.39), and albumin (45 grams per liter) levels, the hemoglobin values were in the lower 50% of normal range. The study suggests that these athletes could benefit from nutrition education and diet counseling to improve their dietary quality, particularly in terms of consuming more foods high in protein, such as meats, poultry, fish, beans, peas, and nuts.

title: Regulation of Pax-3 expression in the dermomyotome and its role in muscle development.
text: The segmented mesoderm in vertebrates gives rise to a diverse range of cell types during embryonic development, including the axial skeleton and muscle. A number of transcription factors containing a paired domain (Pax proteins) are expressed in the segmented mesoderm during embryogenesis, including Pax-3 and a closely related gene, Pax-7, which are both expressed in the segmental plate and dermomyotome. In this study, we investigate the role of signals from the notochord in patterning the expression of Pax-3, Pax-7, and Pax-9 in somites and the subsequent differentiation of cell types derived from the somitic mesoderm. To assess the functional significance of Pax-3 in the differentiation of cell types derived from the dermomyotome, we analyze the development of muscle in splotch mouse embryos, which lack a functional Pax-3 gene. Our findings reveal that a population of Pax-3-expressing cells derived from the dermomyotome that normally migrate into the limb are absent in homozygous splotch embryos, resulting in the loss of limb muscles. Interestingly, no abnormalities were detected in the trunk musculature of splotch embryos, suggesting that Pax-3 is specifically required for the development of limb muscles but not trunk muscle.

title: Angiopoietin 2 is a partial agonist/antagonist of Tie2 signaling in the endothelium.
text:
Original Text:
Angiopoietin 2 (Ang2) was initially shown to be a competitive antagonist of Ang1, a receptor tyrosine kinase that is essential for endothelial cell (EC) function. However, subsequent studies have yielded conflicting results regarding the role of Ang2 in Tie2 signaling. Our findings reveal that Ang2 acts as both an agonist and an antagonist of Tie2, depending on the presence of Ang1. Exogenous Ang2 activates Tie2 and the pro-survival PI3K/Akt pathway in ECs, but with lower potency and affinity compared to exogenous Ang1. Endogenous Ang2, on the other hand, maintains Tie2, PI3K, and Akt activities and promotes EC survival, migration, and tube formation. However, when ECs are stimulated with Ang1 and Ang2, Ang2 inhibits Ang1-induced Tie2 phosphorylation, Akt activation, and EC survival in a dose-dependent manner. Our findings suggest that Ang2 is both an agonist and an antagonist of Tie2, with endogenous Ang2 maintaining a critical level of Tie2 activation for EC function. These findings may reconcile conflicting reports on Ang2's effect on Tie2, deepen our understanding of receptor tyrosine kinase signal transduction mechanisms, and inform the targeting of Ang2 and Tie2 in conditions such as sepsis and cancer.

title: Bacteremia caused by a strain of Desulfovibrio related to the provisionally named Desulfovibrio fairfieldensis.
text: Over a period of 5 years, eight isolates of Desulfovibrio spp. were obtained from various sources, including abdominal or brain abscesses and blood. Of these, seven isolates were part of a mixed flora, while one strain was isolated in pure culture from the blood of a patient with peritonitis of appendicular origin. Analysis of the 16S rRNA gene sequences revealed that this strain was closely related to Desulfovibrio fairfieldensis. This report presents the fourth isolate of this recently described species to be isolated in pure culture or as a predominant part of the flora, and associated with infectious processes. These findings suggest that D. fairfieldensis may have a higher pathogenic potential than other Desulfovibrio species.

title: Vitamin D: The "sunshine" vitamin.
text: Vitamin D insufficiency affects almost half of the global population, with an estimated 1 billion people worldwide experiencing a deficiency (VDD). This widespread issue can be attributed to lifestyle factors such as reduced outdoor activities and environmental factors like air pollution, which limit exposure to sunlight and hinder the skin's ability to produce vitamin D through UVB-induced synthesis. The high prevalence of vitamin D insufficiency is a significant public health concern, as it is an independent risk factor for total mortality in the general population. Current research suggests that more vitamin D may be needed to prevent chronic diseases, as the number of people with VDD continues to rise. Vitamin D deficiency is common in all age groups, and guidelines recommend supplementation at suggested daily intake and tolerable upper limit levels. Measuring serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels is also recommended as an initial diagnostic test in patients at risk of deficiency. Treatment with either vitamin D2 or vitamin D3 is recommended for deficient patients. A 2007 meta-analysis showed that vitamin D supplementation was associated with significantly reduced mortality, highlighting the importance of understanding the mechanisms underlying the relationship between vitamin D and overall health. This review aims to summarize the biology and clinical implications of vitamin D deficiency.

title: Cyclin D1 activation in B-cell malignancy: association with changes in histone acetylation, DNA methylation, and RNA polymerase II binding to both promoter and distal sequences.
text:
Introduction:
Cyclin D1 expression is aberrantly regulated in mantle cell lymphoma and a subset of multiple myeloma due to chromosomal translocations. Despite significant progress in understanding the molecular mechanisms involved in this deregulation, the underlying processes remain largely elusive. In this study, we aimed to investigate the patterns of DNA methylation and histone acetylation at the cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11q13 in B-cell malignancies.
Methods:
We analyzed the patterns of DNA methylation and histone acetylation at the cyclin D1 locus in B-cell malignancies using cell lines and patient samples. We used immunoprecipitation and ChIP-seq to identify the regions of hyperacetylated histones and hypomethylated DNA. We also examined the binding of RNA polymerase II at the cyclin D1 promoter and 3' immunoglobulin heavy-chain regulatory regions in malignant B-cell lines with deregulated cyclin D1 expression.
Results:
Our results showed that the cyclin D1 promoter was hypomethylated and hyperacetylated in expressing cell lines and patient samples, while the upstream major translocation cluster region was methylated and hypoacetylated. Interestingly, hypomethylated DNA and hyperacetylated histones were also found at the cyclin D1 promoter in nonexpressing cell lines and nontumorigenic B and T cells. Furthermore, RNA polymerase II binding was demonstrated both at the cyclin D1 promoter and 3' immunoglobulin heavy-chain regulatory regions only in malignant B-cell lines with deregulated cyclin D1 expression. Our findings suggest a model where RNA polymerase II bound at IgH regulatory sequences can activate the cyclin D1 promoter by either long-range polymerase transfer or tracking.
Discussion:
Our study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the deregulation of cyclin D1 expression in B-cell malignancies. The findings suggest that RNA polymerase II binding at the cyclin D1 promoter and 3' immunoglobulin heavy-chain regulatory regions may play a critical role in the activation of the cyclin D1 promoter in these malignancies. The observed patterns of DNA methylation and histone acetylation at the cyclin D1 locus also provide important clues into the underlying mechanisms of deregulation. Overall, our results highlight the complex interplay between epigenetic modifications and transcriptional regulation in B-cell malignancies and suggest potential new targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: The physiological regulation of toll-like receptor expression and function in humans.
text: Eleven mammalian Toll-like receptors (TLRs) have been identified, and they play a crucial role in regulating immune responses. However, the factors that regulate TLR expression and function in vivo are poorly understood. To investigate the physiological regulation of TLR expression and function in humans, we collected peripheral venous blood samples from healthy volunteers at different times of day and examined the expression of TLRs on CD14(+) monocytes. We found that the upregulation of costimulatory and antigen-presenting molecules on CD14(+) monocytes following activation with specific TLR ligands was greater in samples collected in the evening compared to the morning. To examine the influence of physical stress on TLR expression and function, we collected peripheral venous blood samples from healthy volunteers at rest and following 1.5 hours of strenuous exercise in the heat. We found that strenuous exercise resulted in a decrease in the expression of TLRs 1, 2, and 4 on CD14(+) monocytes. Additionally, the upregulation of CD80, CD86, MHC class II, and interleukin-6 by CD14(+) monocytes following activation with specific TLR ligands was decreased in samples obtained following exercise compared to at rest. These results demonstrate that TLR function is modulated under physiological conditions in vivo and provide evidence for the role of immunomodulatory hormones in the regulation of TLR function.

title: A review of psychosocial needs of breast-cancer patients and their relatives.
text:
Objective: To identify the psychosocial needs of breast cancer patients and their relatives, as well as the factors that influence these needs, and to develop a preliminary model to guide future research and support in clinical practice.
Background: Women diagnosed with breast cancer face a life-threatening illness that can be emotionally and physically demanding. Treatment and recovery can be challenging for both patients and their relatives. Conducting a need assessment can help clinicians prioritize providing appropriate support.
Methodology: A literature review was conducted using electronic databases and specific research terms. Twenty articles were analyzed.
Results: The needs identified by patients include:
1. Treatment-related physical and social impairments, such as fatigue, menopausal symptoms, and changed body image.
2. Emotional distress, including fear of recurrence, anxiety, and depression.
Partners also have needs, including:
1. Help to protect themselves and the patient from various threats.
2. Information about the patient's condition and prognosis, as well as their own emotional distress.
There is a lack of knowledge about the needs of relatives. The interaction between patients and their partners is influenced by factors such as mutual familial support, women's and partners' health, and emotional distress.
Conclusion: A preliminary family-based model is proposed to guide future research and clinical support. Further research is needed to determine which psychosocial factors may influence the patients' and relatives' needs.
Relevance to Clinical Practice: The proposed model can provide a framework for healthcare professionals to evaluate patients' and relatives' met and unmet needs and the real demand for support, guiding care planning, counseling, and education.

title: Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase 1 Represses Liver X Receptor-mediated ABCA1 Expression and Cholesterol Efflux in Macrophages.
text: Liver X receptors (LXR) are nuclear receptors that play a pivotal role in the reverse cholesterol transport pathway by up-regulating ATP-binding cassette transporters (ABCA1 and ABCG1) that mediate cellular cholesterol efflux. While mouse models of atherosclerosis have shown reduced atherosclerosis and enhanced regression of established plaques upon LXR activation, the coregulatory factors that modulate LXR-dependent gene activation in macrophages remain to be elucidated. To identify novel regulators of LXR, we employed affinity purification and mass spectrometry to analyze nuclear LXRα complexes and identified poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase-1 (PARP-1) as an LXR-associated factor. Our findings revealed that PARP-1 interacts with both LXRα and LXRβ and that depletion or inhibition of PARP-1 activity augmented LXR ligand-induced ABCA1 expression in RAW 264.7 macrophages and primary bone marrow-derived macrophages, without affecting LXR-dependent expression of other target genes, such as ABCG1 and SREBP-1c. Chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments further confirmed PARP-1 recruitment to the LXR response element in the promoter of the ABCA1 gene. Additionally, we demonstrated that LXR is poly(ADP-ribosyl)ated by PARP-1, providing a potential mechanism by which PARP-1 influences LXR function. Importantly, the PARP inhibitor 3-aminobenzamide enhanced macrophage ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux to the lipid-poor apolipoprotein AI, highlighting the crucial role of PARP-1 in LXR-regulated lipid homeostasis. Elucidating the interplay between PARP-1 and LXR may offer insights into the development of novel therapeutics for treating atherosclerosis.

title: Emergency contraception: advance provision in a young, high-risk clinic population.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the impact of providing advance emergency contraception on its use and potential secondary effects on regular contraceptive use.
Methods: We conducted a controlled trial among female clients aged 16-24 years at a publicly funded family planning clinic. Participants were randomly assigned to receive advance emergency contraception and education (treatment) or education only (control). Follow-up was conducted among 263 participants (133 treatment, 130 control) and the main outcome measures were emergency contraception knowledge and use, frequency of unprotected sex, and patterns of contraceptive use in the past 4 months.
Results: Participants demonstrated knowledge of emergency contraception at follow-up, with the treatment group being three times more likely to use it compared to the control group (P =.006). However, the treatment group did not report higher frequencies of unprotected sex than the control group. Notably, women in the treatment group (28%) were more likely than those in the control group (17%) to report using less effective contraception at follow-up compared to enrollment (P =.05). Both groups showed an increase in consistent pill use from enrollment to follow-up (34% versus 45%), but the control group (58%) was more likely than the treatment group (32%) to report consistent pill use at follow-up (P =.03).
Conclusion: Providing advance emergency contraception resulted in increased use of emergency contraception, but not solely through education. Additionally, there were potentially negative effects on regular contraceptive use, such as a shift towards less effective methods. These findings highlight the importance of considering the potential impact of advance emergency contraception provision on regular contraceptive use.

title: Immunophenotypic analysis of AIDS-related diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and clinical implications in patients from AIDS malignancies consortium clinical trials 010 and 034
text:
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in patients with HIV infection is a clinically heterogeneous disease, and immunohistochemical markers can predict clinical outcome. In this study, we analyzed the immunophenotype of 81 DLBCLs from patients with AIDS in two clinical trials and compared it with survival data, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) positivity, and CD4 counts.
Our results showed that the germinal center (GC) and non-GC subtypes of DLBCL did not significantly differ in terms of overall survival or CD4 count at cancer presentation. EBV was found in both subtypes of DLBCL, although less frequently in the GC subtype, and did not affect survival. Expression of FOXP1, Blimp-1/PRDM1, or BCL-2 was not correlated with the outcome in patients with AIDS-related DLBCL.
Our findings suggest that with current treatment strategies for lymphoma and control of HIV infection, commonly used immunohistochemical markers may not be clinically relevant in HIV-infected patients with DLBCL. The only predictive immunohistochemical marker identified was Ki-67, where a higher proliferation index was associated with better survival, suggesting a better response to therapy in patients whose tumors had higher proliferation rates.
In summary, our study indicates that immunohistochemical markers may not be useful in predicting clinical outcome in HIV-infected patients with DLBCL, and that Ki-67 may be a useful marker for predicting response to therapy.

title: Prion-like activity of Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase: implications for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
text: Neurodegenerative diseases belong to a larger category of protein misfolding disorders, known as proteinopathies. Experimental evidence suggests that prion-like mechanisms play a role in many common neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, tauopathies, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). These diseases are characterized by the misfolding and aggregation of specific proteins, which can lead to neurotoxicity. ALS, a fatal disease marked by progressive motor neuron degeneration, is a classical proteinopathy. The disease is characterized by the formation of protein aggregates within and around motor neurons, which contribute to neurodegeneration. Misfolded/oxidized superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) protein is highly toxic to motor neurons and plays a key role in ALS pathology. Recent research has revealed prion-like properties in both mutant and wild-type SOD1, which may provide the molecular basis for the clinically observed spread of the disease through the nervous system. This review examines the current understanding of the prion-like properties of SOD1 and discusses proposed mechanisms of intercellular transmission.

title: Analysis of Epstein-Barr virus-regulated host gene expression changes through primary B-cell outgrowth reveals delayed kinetics of latent membrane protein 1-mediated NF-κB activation.
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is an oncogenic human herpesvirus that significantly alters host gene expression to immortalize primary B cells. In this study, we investigated EBV-regulated host gene expression changes during primary B-cell infection, from initial proliferation to the formation of lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs). While most EBV-regulated mRNAs were altered during the transition from resting, uninfected B cells to initial B-cell proliferation, a notable number of mRNAs changed uniquely from early proliferation to LCL outgrowth. We identified consistently and dynamically EBV-regulated biological processes, protein classes, and targets of specific transcription factors. Initially, genes associated with proliferation, stress responses, and the p53 pathway were highly enriched. However, the transition from early to long-term outgrowth was characterized by genes involved in the inhibition of apoptosis, the actin cytoskeleton, and NF-κB activity. It was previously believed that the primary viral protein responsible for NF-κB activation, latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1), is expressed within 2 days after infection. Our data indicate that while this is true, LCL-level LMP1 expression and NF-κB activity are not evident until 3 weeks after primary B-cell infection. Furthermore, heterologous NF-κB activation during the first week after infection increased the transformation efficiency, while early NF-κB inhibition had no effect on transformation. Rather, inhibition of NF-κB was not toxic to EBV-infected cells until LMP1 levels and NF-κB activity were high. These findings collectively highlight the dynamic nature of EBV-regulated host gene expression and support the notion that early EBV-infected proliferating B cells have a fundamentally distinct growth and survival phenotype from that of LCLs.

title: Clinical and laboratory features of adult T-cell leukaemia lymphoma in Barbados.
text: In this study, we investigated the clinical and pathological features of 23 Afro-Caribbean patients with adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) admitted to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Barbados over a 5-year period. The patients included 9 males and 14 females, with a median age of 38 years (range 14-84). Of the patients, 12 had acute leukaemia, 10 had lymphoma (including 4 with solitary extra-nodal lesions), and 1 had the smouldering subtype. Two patients had a past history of tropical spastic paraparesis/HTLV-I associated myelopathy (TSP/HAM). The prognosis was poor, with only 3 complete responses to chemotherapy (CHOP) lasting from 9 to 36 months. Our findings suggest that ATLL in Barbados shares similarities with the disease in other Caribbean islands and Japan, with the notable exception that the age of onset in Barbados is significantly younger than in Japan.

title: Acoustic landmarks drive delta-theta oscillations to enable speech comprehension by facilitating perceptual parsing.
text:
A growing body of research suggests that slow (less than 10 Hz) neuronal oscillations in the auditory cortex are involved in tracking incoming speech and other complex auditory signals. Recent studies have identified specific acoustic features, such as temporal envelopes, that are reflected in the phase of these oscillations. However, the exact mechanism by which this alignment influences intelligibility is not fully understood.
Our study aims to investigate the role of the 'sharpness' of temporal fluctuations in the critical band envelope in speech perception. We hypothesize that these sharp events in the stimulus cause cortical rhythms to re-align and parse the stimulus into syllable-sized chunks for further decoding, leading to improved intelligibility.
Using magnetoencephalographic (MEG) recordings, we found that removing temporal fluctuations at the syllabic rate resulted in reduced envelope-tracking activity. Conversely, artificially reinstating these fluctuations led to a regain of envelope-tracking activity, which in turn correlated with the intelligibility of the stimulus.
Our findings suggest that the sharpness of fluctuations in the stimulus, as reflected in the cochlear output, drive cortical oscillatory activity to track and entrain to the stimulus at its syllabic rate. This process likely facilitates parsing of the stimulus into meaningful chunks appropriate for subsequent decoding, enhancing perception and intelligibility.
In summary, our study provides evidence that the alignment between speech acoustics and neural oscillations in the auditory cortex is crucial for speech perception, and that the sharpness of temporal fluctuations in the stimulus plays a key role in this process.

title: Crystal structures of complexes of the small ribosomal subunit with tetracycline, edeine and IF3.
text: The small ribosomal subunit plays a pivotal role in the decoding of genetic information and the initiation of protein synthesis. Through X-ray crystallography, we investigated the structures of three different complexes of the small ribosomal subunit of Thermus thermophilus in the presence of various inhibitors: tetracycline, edeine, and the C-terminal domain of translation initiation factor IF3. Our crystal structure analysis revealed the functionally important site responsible for the blockage of the A-site upon binding of tetracycline. Additionally, we identified five additional tetracycline binding sites that help resolve controversial biochemical data on the location of tetracycline. Our findings also highlight the role of edeine in inhibiting initiation and its interaction with the P-site tRNA. Furthermore, the location of the C-terminal domain of IF3 on the solvent side of the platform provides insight into the formation of the initiation complex and suggests that the anti-association activity of IF3 is due to its influence on the conformational dynamics of the small ribosomal subunit.

title: Plasmid-encoded proinsulin preserves C-peptide while specifically reducing proinsulin-specific CD8⁺ T cells in type 1 diabetes.
text:
In type 1 diabetes (T1D), an intense inflammatory response leads to the destruction of β cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, where insulin is produced and released. A long-sought therapy for T1D is one that targets the specific autoimmune response in this disease while sparing the rest of the immune system. Proinsulin is a major target of the adaptive immune response in T1D. We hypothesized that an engineered DNA plasmid encoding proinsulin (BHT-3021) would preserve β cell function in T1D patients by reducing the number of insulin-specific CD8+ T cells.
We conducted a study involving 80 subjects aged 18 years or older who were diagnosed with T1D within the past 5 years. Subjects were randomly assigned to receive intramuscular injections of BHT-3021 or a placebo, weekly for 12 weeks, and were monitored for safety and immune responses in a blinded manner. Four dose levels of BHT-3021 were evaluated: 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, and 6.0 mg. C-peptide was used as both an exploratory efficacy measure and a safety measure. Islet-specific CD8+ T cell frequencies were assessed using multimers of monomeric human leukocyte antigen class I molecules loaded with peptides from pancreatic and unrelated antigens.
No serious adverse events related to BHT-3021 were observed. C-peptide levels improved relative to the placebo at all doses, with the greatest improvement observed at the 15-week time point (+19.5% BHT-3021 versus -8.8% BHT-placebo, P < 0.026). Proinsulin-reactive CD8+ T cells declined in the BHT-3021 arm (P < 0.006), but not against unrelated islet or foreign molecules. No significant changes were noted in interferon-γ, interleukin-4 (IL-4), or IL-10 production in CD4 T cells.
Our findings demonstrate that a plasmid encoding proinsulin reduces the frequency of CD8+ T cells reactive to proinsulin while preserving C-peptide over the course of dosing.

title: Dexamethasone and risk of nausea and vomiting and postoperative bleeding after tonsillectomy in children: a randomized trial.
text:
In this study, researchers investigated the effectiveness of dexamethasone in preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in pediatric patients undergoing tonsillectomy. The study was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted at a major public teaching hospital in Switzerland between February 2005 and December 2007. A total of 215 children were enrolled in the study and randomly assigned to receive dexamethasone (at doses of 0.05, 0.15, or 0.5 mg/kg) or placebo intravenously after anesthesia induction. The primary outcome measure was the prevention of PONV at 24 hours after surgery, and secondary outcome measures included the reduction in the need for ibuprofen at 24 hours and the evaluation of adverse effects.
The results showed that dexamethasone dose-dependently reduced the risk of PONV at 24 hours after tonsillectomy, with the highest dose (0.5 mg/kg) showing the greatest effect. However, dexamethasone was associated with an increased risk of postoperative bleeding, with 26 bleeding episodes occurring in 22 children. Eight children required emergency reoperation due to bleeding, all of whom had received dexamethasone. The study was stopped early due to safety concerns.
In conclusion, while dexamethasone was effective in preventing PONV in pediatric tonsillectomy patients, it was associated with an increased risk of postoperative bleeding. The study highlights the importance of carefully weighing the benefits and risks of medications used to prevent PONV in pediatric patients undergoing surgery.

title: Detection of sweet and umami taste in the absence of taste receptor T1r3.
text: According to recent research, the taste receptors T1r2 and T1r3 are believed to be responsible for detecting sweet flavors, while T1r1 and T1r3, as well as a truncated form of the type 4 metabotropic glutamate receptor (taste-mGluR4), are thought to be involved in detecting umami flavors. In this study, mice lacking T1r3 were found to have diminished but not completely eliminated responses to sugars and umami compounds in both behavioral and neural tests. These findings suggest that there may be T1r3-independent receptors or pathways in taste cells that are responsible for detecting sweet and umami flavors.

title: Cyclin A1 is required for meiosis in the male mouse
text: The mammalian A-type cyclin family consists of two members, cyclin A1 (encoded by Ccna1) and cyclin A2 (encoded by Ccna2). Cyclin A2 regulates both G1/S and G2/M transitions, and deletion of Ccna2 in mice is embryonically lethal. In contrast, cyclin A1 is specifically expressed in the germ cell lineage of mice and humans, with highest levels found in the testis and certain myeloid leukemia cells. To investigate the role of cyclin A1 and potential redundancy among the cyclins in vivo, we generated mice with a null mutation of Ccna1. Ccna1-null males were sterile due to a block in spermatogenesis before the first meiotic division, while females were normal. In Ccna1-null males, meiosis arrest was associated with increased germ cell apoptosis, desynapsis abnormalities, and reduced Cdc2 kinase activation at the end of meiotic prophase. Notably, cyclin A1 is essential for spermatocyte passage into the first meiotic division in male mice, a function that cannot be complemented by co-expressed B-type cyclins.

title: Metabolic effects of isoenergetic nutrient exchange over 24 hours in relation to obesity in women.
text: For 24 hours, whole-body indirect calorimetry was used to investigate the effects of feeding, during a sedentary test day, on isoenergetic diets varying in fat (3 or 40% of total energy) and carbohydrate (82 or 45%), on three groups of women: lean, obese, and "post-obese" after slimming. Energy expenditure was higher in absolute terms in the obese women. When fasting, 24-hour energy expenditure was lower by 3-7% compared to when energy balance was achieved. There were no significant differences in energy expenditure between the two diets or between the groups, but the thermogenic effect of the high-carbohydrate diet was significantly greater than that of the high-fat diet (5.8 vs 3.5% of energy expenditure: P < 0.01). The post-obese tended to have lower energy expenditure per kg of fat-free mass (FFM) than controls when fasting and when high-fat fed, but this pattern was not observed in the obese. Sleeping energy expenditure was particularly low in the post-obese group when high-fat fed. Daily variations in respiratory quotient (RQ) showed a more pronounced rise in morning RQ from the nocturnal minimum in the obese and post-obese, which may indicate an energy-saving mechanism through greater availability of stored dietary carbohydrate.

title: Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease: an integrated clinical syndrome.
text: The conventional belief that survivors of acute kidney injury (AKI) tend to fully recover renal function has been challenged. AKI can lead to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) directly, and increase the risk of developing incident chronic kidney disease (CKD) and worsening of underlying CKD. The severity, duration, and frequency of AKI are important predictors of poor patient outcomes. CKD is a significant risk factor for the development and progression of AKI. Experimental data support the clinical observations, and the bidirectional relationships between AKI and CKD are evident. Factors such as reduced renal mass, vascular insufficiency, cell cycle disruption, and maladaptive repair mechanisms contribute to the progression of AKI in patients with and without coexistent CKD. The distinction between AKI and CKD may be artificial, and a more integrated approach to understanding the clinical syndrome of diminished glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is warranted. This syndrome has both acute and chronic stages, and the outcome is determined by host factors, including the balance of adaptive and maladaptive repair mechanisms over time. Physicians should provide long-term follow-up to patients with initial episodes of AKI, even if they presented with normal renal function, to monitor for potential progression to CKD or ESRD.

title: Fatty acids as modulators of the immune response.
text: Abundant research has demonstrated the role of fatty acids as modulators of inflammation and immune responses. While many studies have focused on omega-3 fatty acids, the evidence from human clinical trials is more inconsistent. This review provides a historical context for understanding how fatty acids affect the immune system, highlights two recent landmark reports from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, and reviews the data from human clinical trials investigating the impact of various bioactive fatty acids on immune responses. Limitations in experimental design and immune assays are discussed, and recommendations are provided to improve future studies. Despite the discordance between expectation and evidence in this field, the potential of fatty acids as immunomodulators remains promising.

title: Common and rare variants in multifactorial susceptibility to common diseases
text: Here, we provide a historical overview of the quest for genetic variations that influence an individual's susceptibility to a chronic disease, from the groundbreaking work of R.A. Fisher to the current excitement surrounding whole-genome association studies (WGAS). We then delve into the underlying concepts of identifying common variants as disease causal factors and contrast them with the basic principles of the rare variant hypothesis. The identification of rare variants involves carefully selecting candidate genes, utilizing highly efficient resequencing techniques, and assessing the functional consequences of the implicated variant. We believe that this approach can be successfully applied currently to uncover the role of rare variants in the multifactorial inheritance of common diseases, which could lead to the development of much-needed preventative screening programs.
