title: Cell-cell adhesion and signalling.
text: Recent discoveries have unveiled signaling pathways triggered by Rho small GTPases, which orchestrate the assembly, stability, and function of junctions, as well as the interactions between adhesive complexes and the underlying cortical cytoskeleton. Of particular interest is the interplay between adherens junctions, Rho protein activation, and the dynamic interplay between microtubules, actin filaments, and intermediate filaments. This interplay has far-reaching implications for the functional regulation of cell-cell adhesion, and suggests a more integrated understanding of signaling processes.

title: Fibroblast growth factor 21 as an emerging metabolic regulator: clinical perspectives.
text: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a metabolic hormone produced primarily by the liver, regulates glucose and lipid metabolism through various actions in tissues and the brain. In mice, fasting leads to increased expression of FGF21 in the liver, where it stimulates gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and ketogenesis as an adaptive response to fasting and starvation. In the fed state, FGF21 acts as an autocrine factor in adipocytes, regulating the activity of PPAR-γ through a feed-forward loop mechanism. Administration of recombinant FGF21 has shown to confer metabolic benefits, including improved insulin sensitivity, blood glucose, lipid profile, and body weight, in obese mice and diabetic monkeys, without adverse effects. These findings suggest the potential of FGF21 as a therapeutic agent for obesity-related diseases. However, in human studies, high levels of circulating FGF21 are found in obesity and related cardiometabolic disorders, including metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and coronary artery disease. These findings may indicate FGF21 resistance or compensatory responses to underlying metabolic stress, and suggest the need for higher doses of FGF21 to achieve therapeutic efficacy. Additionally, serum FGF21 has been identified as a potential biomarker for the early detection of these cardiometabolic disorders. This review summarizes recent advances in understanding FGF21's physiological and clinical implications.

title: Assessment of the cerebral circulation in adults with coarctation of the aorta.
text:
Objective: To investigate the prevalence and risk factors of intracranial aneurysm (IA) in adults with coarctation of the aorta (CoA) through prospective screening with computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the intracranial vessels.
Methods: We prospectively enrolled adults aged ≥18 years with CoA in a screening program from January 2008 to February 2011. CTA of the intracranial vessels was performed, and the prevalence and risk factors of IA were analyzed.
Results: A total of 43 patients (58% female, 33.55 ± 10.21 years) with CoA completed CTA of the intracranial vessels. Five patients (11%) were found to have IA, and these patients were older than those without IA (45.6 ± 8.17 vs. 30.89 ± 7.89, P = 0.0003). No significant differences were found in fasting lipid profiles, C-reactive protein, brain natriuretic peptide, and homocysteine levels between CoA patients with and without IA (P = not significant).
Conclusion: Prospective screening of adults with CoA confirmed the increased prevalence of IA but also identified increased age as the sole risk factor. These data suggest that screening is justified particularly in the fourth and fifth decades of life. Further studies are required to investigate the development, natural history, and treatment of IA.

title: Bioenergetic aspects of apoptosis, necrosis and mitoptosis
text:
In this review, I examine the interplay between bioenergetic processes and programmed cell death phenomena, including apoptosis and necrosis, as well as mitochondrial suicide (mitoptosis). Based on my analysis, I draw the following conclusions:
(I) ATP and increased mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ) are essential for certain stages of apoptosis and necrosis.
(II) Apoptosis, even if it is accompanied by increases in ATP and ΔΨ at its early stages, ultimately leads to a collapse of ΔΨ and a decrease in ATP.
(III) A moderate (approximately threefold) decrease in ATP levels for short or long periods can induce apoptosis or necrosis, respectively. In some cases, cell death is mediated by a ΔΨ-dependent overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by the initial (Complex I) and middle (Complex III) segments of the respiratory chain. ROS trigger mitoptosis, which is thought to eliminate mitochondria that overproduce ROS from the intracellular population. Massive mitoptosis can result in cell death due to the release of cell death proteins normally sequestered in the mitochondrial intermembrane space.

title: Embryonic stem cells require Wnt proteins to prevent differentiation to epiblast stem cells
text:
Pluripotent stem cells exist in two states: naive and primed. Naive stem cells, such as mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs), have an open genome with minimal repressive epigenetic marks. In contrast, primed stem cells, such as epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs), have activated epigenetic machinery that supports differentiation into various cell types. The transition from naive to primed pluripotency is a critical event in cellular differentiation, but the signals that control this process are unclear.
We found that paracrine and autocrine Wnt signals are essential for self-renewal of ESCs and are required to prevent their differentiation into EpiSCs. Moreover, we discovered that Wnt proteins, in combination with the cytokine LIF, can support ESC self-renewal in the absence of any undefined factors and generate new ESC lines, including those from non-permissive mouse strains. Our results not only reveal that Wnt signals regulate the naive-to-primed pluripotency transition, but also identify Wnt as a crucial and limiting factor for ESC self-renewal.

title: CLIP identifies Nova-regulated RNA networks in the brain.
text: Nova proteins are neuron-specific antigens that are targeted in paraneoplastic opsoclonus myoclonus ataxia (POMA), an autoimmune neurological disorder characterized by abnormal motor inhibition. Nova proteins regulate neuronal pre-messenger RNA splicing by directly binding to RNA, and to identify Nova RNA targets, we developed a method called CLIP (cross-linking and immunoprecipitation) to purify protein-RNA complexes from mouse brain. Through CLIP, we identified 34 transcripts that were bound by Nova proteins multiple times. Of these, three-quarters encode proteins that function at the neuronal synapse, and one-third are involved in neuronal inhibition. Using CLIP in Nova-deficient mice, we confirmed the splicing targets c-Jun N-terminal kinase 2, neogenin, and gephyrin, which encodes a protein that clusters inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine receptors, two previously identified Nova splicing targets. Our findings reveal that Nova coordinately regulates a biologically coherent set of RNAs encoding multiple components of the inhibitory synapse, which may be related to the underlying cause of abnormal motor inhibition in POMA.

title: Anti-Angiogenic Activity of Selected Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors, PD166285 and PD173074: Implications for Combination Treatment with Photodynamic Therapy
text:
Angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels from existing ones, is essential for tumor growth. This process involves coordinated signaling between endothelial and tumor cells through angiogenic growth factor signaling. Disrupting these events can have significant implications for suppressing tumor growth. To evaluate the anti-angiogenic and anti-tumor activities of two compounds, PD166285 and PD173074, in combination with photodynamic therapy (PDT), various assays were conducted in vitro and in vivo.
PD166285, a broad-spectrum receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitor, inhibited the activity of multiple RTKs, including PDGFR-β, EGFR, and FGFR1TK, with an IC50 value of 7-85nM. In contrast, PD173074, a selective FGFR1TK inhibitor, displayed high selectivity towards FGFR1TK, with an IC50 value of 26nM. Notably, PD173074 showed >100-fold selective growth inhibitory action towards human umbilical vein endothelial cells compared to a panel of tumor cell lines. Both compounds inhibited the formation of microcapillaries on Matrigel-coated plastic, indicating anti-angiogenic activity.
In vivo anti-angiogenesis studies in mice revealed that oral administration of either PD166285 (1-25mg/kg) or PD173074 (25-100mg/kg) resulted in dose-dependent inhibition of angiogenesis. Treatment with PD166285 or PD173074 following PDT led to significantly prolonged tumor regressions compared to PDT alone (p<0.001). Many long-term survivors were also observed in combination treatment groups. PD166285 and PD173074 displayed potent anti-angiogenic and anti-tumor activity, prolonging the duration of anti-tumor response to PDT. These findings suggest that inhibitors of specific RTKs, such as FGFR1TK, may lead to the development of new chemotherapeutic agents capable of limiting tumor angiogenesis and regrowth following cytoreductive treatments like PDT.

title: The VirB type IV secretion system of Bartonella henselae mediates invasion, proinflammatory activation and antiapoptotic protection of endothelial cells.
text:
Bartonella henselae, a zoonotic pathogen, infects both felines and humans, causing intraerythrocytic bacteremia and a range of clinical manifestations in incidentally infected humans. Remarkably, this bacterium can colonize the human vascular endothelium, leading to inflammation and the formation of vasoproliferative lesions known as bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis. To study this interaction, cultured human endothelial cells provide an in vitro system. However, little is known about the bacterial virulence factors required for this pathogenic process. Recently, we identified the type IV secretion system (T4SS) VirB as an essential pathogenicity factor in Bartonella, required for establishing intraerythrocytic infection in the mammalian reservoir. Here, we demonstrate that the VirB T4SS mediates most of the virulence attributes associated with the interaction of B. henselae during its interaction with human endothelial cells. These include:
1. Massive rearrangements of the actin cytoskeleton, resulting in the formation of bacterial aggregates and their internalization by the invasome structure.
2. Nuclear factor kappaB-dependent proinflammatory activation, leading to cell adhesion molecule expression and chemokine secretion.
3. Inhibition of apoptotic cell death, resulting in enhanced endothelial cell survival.

Moreover, we show that the VirB system mediates cytostatic and cytotoxic effects at high bacterial titers, which interfere with a potent VirB-independent mitogenic activity. In conclusion, the VirB T4SS is a major virulence determinant of B. henselae, required for targeting multiple endothelial cell functions exploited by this vasculotropic pathogen.

title: Serum Cystatin C Is Related to Pulse Wave Velocity Even in Subjects with Normal Serum Creatinine
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate the relationship between serum cystatin C and arterial stiffness in individuals with normal serum creatinine levels. A total of 2,018 participants (1,120 males and 898 females) were enrolled, and their mean brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV) was measured as a marker of arterial stiffness. Our findings showed that serum cystatin C was positively related to baPWV in males (R² = 0.056, p < 0.001) and females (R² = 0.090, p < 0.001). In males, age, waist circumference, heart rate, cystatin C level, triglyceride level, and fasting glucose were independent contributors to baPWV, while in females, age, heart rate, cystatin C level, fasting glucose, and insulin level were the significant variables. Our results confirmed that serum cystatin C was related to pulse wave velocity even in subjects with normal serum creatinine levels, suggesting that it could be a more predictable marker of arterial stiffness than serum creatinine and creatinine-based glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

title: Screening for inhibition of Vibrio cholerae VipA-VipB interaction identifies small-molecule compounds active against type VI secretion.
text:
The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is the most prevalent bacterial secretion system and a crucial virulence mechanism employed by Gram-negative bacteria to target eukaryotic cells or other microorganisms. The components of T6SS exhibit significant variability, but some components are deemed essential for its function. In Vibrio cholerae, two homologous proteins, VipA and VipB, have been identified in all T6SSs studied so far. The interaction between VipA and VipB is essential for secretion, and disrupting this interaction could potentially abrogate T6S.
To investigate this possibility, a library of 9,600 small-molecule compounds was screened for their ability to block the binding of VipA to VipB in a bacterial two-hybrid system (B2H). After excluding compounds that showed cytotoxicity towards eukaryotic cells, inhibited growth of Vibrio, or inhibited an unrelated B2H interaction, 34 compounds were further investigated for their effects on T6SS-dependent secretion of hemolysin-coregulated protein (Hcp) or phospholipase A1 activity. Two compounds, KS100 and KS200, showed intermediate or strong effects in both assays. Analogues were generated, and compounds with potent inhibitory effects in the assays and desirable physicochemical properties as predicted by in silico analysis were identified.
Since these compounds specifically target a virulence mechanism without affecting bacterial replication, they have the potential to mitigate virulence with minimal risk of developing resistance.

title: Early life compartmentalization of human T cell differentiation and regulatory function in mucosal and lymphoid tissues
text: The early development and function of T cells in tissues during early life remain poorly understood, despite their crucial role in adaptive immunity. Recent studies in mice have shown that the localization of T cell subsets in tissues is essential for both protective immunity and immunoregulation. However, in humans, the early stages of T cell differentiation and function in tissues have not been explored. To address this gap in knowledge, we analyzed T cells derived from pediatric organ donors in the first two years of life, compared to adult organ donors. Our findings reveal early compartmentalization of T cell differentiation and regulation in pediatric tissues. In contrast to adult tissues, which predominantly contain memory T cells, pediatric blood and tissues are characterized by a higher proportion of naive recent thymic emigrants. Effector memory T cells (T(EM)) are also present in the lungs and small intestine, but at much lower frequencies than in adult tissues. Furthermore, regulatory T (T(reg)) cells comprise a significantly higher proportion of CD4(+) T cells in pediatric tissues compared to adult tissues (30-40% vs. 1-10%). Interestingly, pediatric tissue T(reg) cells are able to suppress endogenous T cell activation, and early T cell functionality is confined to mucosal sites with the lowest T(reg):T(EM) cell ratios. This suggests that there is in situ control of immune responses in early life, which may play a crucial role in the development of immune tolerance.

title: Circulating microRNAs as biomarkers for hepatocellular carcinoma.
text:
Objective: To investigate the potential of measuring serum levels of microRNAs (miRNAs) miR-16, miR-195, and miR-199a as a diagnostic tool for differentiating hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) from chronic liver diseases (CLDs).
Background: Recent studies have suggested a link between aberrant expression of miRNAs and HCC.
Methods: This retrospective analysis included sera from 105 HCC patients, 107 CLD patients, and 71 normal control subjects. The levels of miR-16, miR-195, and miR-199a were measured using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction. Conventional HCC markers, including α-fetoprotein (AFP), lens culinaris agglutinin-reactive AFP (AFP-L3%), and des-γ-carboxyprothrombin (DCP), were measured with commercial kits.
Results: The results showed that serum levels of miR-16 and miR-199a were significantly lower in HCC patients than in CLD patients or control subjects (P<0.01). As a single marker, miR-16 had the highest sensitivity for HCC, followed by miR-199a, AFP, DCP, AFP-L3%, and miR-195. The combination of miR-16, AFP, AFP-L3%, and DCP yielded the optimal combination of sensitivity (92.4%) and specificity (78.5%) for HCC, overall and when analysis was restricted to patients with tumors size smaller than 3 cm. As a second-line HCC marker, miR-16 yielded positive HCC predictions in 18 of the 26 (69.2%) HCC patients with negative results on all 3 conventional markers, most of whom had tumors size smaller than 3 cm; miR-16 was falsely positive in only 12 of 96 (12.5%) CLD patients.
Conclusion: The addition of miR-16 to conventional serum markers improved sensitivity and specificity for HCC. Use of miR-16 for second-line testing in cases considered negative on the basis of conventional HCC markers should be explored in larger, prospective studies.

title: Mitochondrial haplogroups and hypervariable region polymorphisms in schizophrenia: a case-control study.
text: Previous studies have identified associations between certain mitochondrial haplogroups and schizophrenia (SZ) in various populations. However, there is a lack of research on the relationship between major mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) haplogroups and SZ in the Chinese population. To address this gap, we conducted a case-control study to investigate the association between mtDNA haplogroups and SZ genesis in the Chinese Han population. We sequenced the mtDNA hypervariable regions (HVR1, HVR2, and HVR3) in a total of 298 SZ patients and 298 controls and classified the haplotypes into 10 major haplogroups. Our results showed that only haplogroup N9a was nominally significantly associated with protection from SZ, with a p-value of 0.004 and an odds ratio (OR) of 0.251 (0.092-0.680) after adjustment for age and sex. Additionally, we found that three HVR polymorphisms were significantly different between SZ patients and controls, all of which were linked to the N9a haplogroup. Our findings suggest that mtDNA haplogroup N9a may be a protective factor for SZ in the Chinese Han population.

title: Resolution of acute inflammation in the lung.
text: Acute inflammation in the lung is crucial for maintaining overall health, as it provides protection against invading microorganisms, noxious stimuli, and tissue injury. However, it is equally important for the resolution of inflammation to prevent further damage to healthy tissue. The lung has evolved specialized mediators, known as resolving mediators, to promote the resolution of acute inflammation. These include lipoxins, resolvins, protectins, and maresins, which are agonists for resolution that interact with specific receptors on leukocytes and structural cells to regulate inflammation and promote tissue repair. In contrast, defects in the resolution of acute inflammation have been implicated in several common lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and cystic fibrosis, which are characterized by excess or chronic inflammation. This review aims to delve into the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the resolution of acute inflammation in the lung.

title: The calcium sensor STIM1 is regulated by androgens in prostate stromal cells.
text:
Background: Prostate development and maintenance in the adult are mediated by an interplay between stromal and glandular components. Androgens exert a direct influence on the stroma, which plays a crucial role in this process. To investigate the direct link between androgens and stromal cells, we examined the effect of androgens on intracellular calcium ([Ca2+]i) in prostate stromal cells.
Methods: We used freshly obtained prostate stromal cells and cultures derived from patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Gene expression in dihydrotestosterone (DHT)-treated and untreated cells was compared using Affymetrix gene expression arrays, and Ca2+-regulated features were identified using Gene Ontology (GO). Changes in [Ca2+]i were determined in Fluo-4-loaded cells using fluorescence microscopy. Androgen regulation was confirmed using chromatin immunoprecipitation.
Results: We sorted prostate stromal cell cultures based on the expression of integrin α1 β1, which enriched for cells expressing the androgen receptor (AR). We identified key functional categories within the androgen-induced gene expression signature, focusing on genes involved in calcium signaling. STIM1 was identified as a significantly differentially expressed gene with four relevant associated GO terms. DNA sequence analysis revealed that the promoter region of STIM1 contained putative androgen response element sequences, and AR binding ability of STIM1 was confirmed. Androgens directly regulated STIM1 expression, and STIM1 effects on store-operated calcium entry were inhibited by STIM1 knockdown. Reduced STIM1 expression in prostate stromal cells led to a reduction in basal Ca2+ levels, the amount of Ca2+ released by thapsigargin, and a reduction in store filling following TG-induced store depletion.
Conclusions: These results indicate that androgens modulate [Ca2+]i through the direct regulation of the STIM1 gene by AR binding to the STIM1 promoter.

title: Role of soluble guanylate cyclase in dilator responses of the cerebral microcirculation.
text: The responses of cerebral blood vessels to nitric oxide (NO) are mediated by soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC)-dependent and potentially sGC-independent mechanisms. In these experiments, we investigated the hypothesis that the dilatation of cerebral microvessels in response to NO is dependent on the activation of sGC. We measured the diameters of cerebral arterioles in anesthetized rabbits using a closed cranial window, and found that the vasodilation produced by the NO-independent activator of sGC, YC-1, was blocked by ODQ, an inhibitor of sGC. These findings suggest that sGC is functionally important in cerebral arterioles. Additionally, we found that acetylcholine, which stimulates endogenous production of NO by the endothelium, produced dilatation of cerebral arterioles that was inhibited by ODQ. Furthermore, increases in arteriolar diameter in response to sodium nitroprusside, an NO donor, were inhibited by approximately 80% by ODQ, but were not affected by inhibitors of the cytochrome P450 pathway. These results indicate that the dilatation of the cerebral microcirculation in response to exogenously applied and endogenously produced NO is dependent, in large part, on the activation of sGC.

title: Noxa controls Mule-dependent Mcl-1 ubiquitination through the regulation of the Mcl-1/USP9X interaction.
text: The regulation of Mcl-1, a pro-survival protein, is tightly controlled, and its down-regulation promotes apoptosis. Mcl-1 interacts with various BH3-only proteins, including Noxa, which plays a crucial role in modulating Mcl-1 expression. In this study, we demonstrated that Noxa triggers the degradation of Mcl-1 at the mitochondria by exclusively localizing to this compartment. The Noxa-mediated degradation of Mcl-1 requires the E3 ligase Mule, which is responsible for the polyubiquitination of Mcl-1. Recently, USP9X, an E3 ligase, was shown to be involved in Mcl-1 protein turnover by preventing its degradation through the removal of conjugated ubiquitin. To investigate the impact of Noxa on the deubiquitination process, we examined the USP9X/Mcl-1 interaction and found that Noxa over-expression led to a decrease in this interaction, accompanied by an increase in the levels of Mcl-1 polyubiquitinated forms. Furthermore, Noxa over-expression triggered an increase in the Mule/Mcl-1 interaction, concurrent with a decrease in the Mule/USP9X complex formation. These modifications ultimately result in the degradation of Mcl-1 by the proteasome machinery. The involvement of Noxa in the regulation of Mcl-1 proteasomal degradation adds complexity to this process, which is governed by multiple interactions.

title: Paediatric HIV infection.
text: By the year 2000, there will be approximately six million pregnant women and five to ten million children infected with HIV-1. In response, intervention strategies have been developed and implemented in some cases. However, these strategies must be timely and cost-effective, taking into account that the majority of HIV-1 infected individuals reside in developing countries. Further research is needed to better understand the immunological and virological factors that contribute to HIV-1 transmission from mother to child, as well as the differential disease progression in infected children and the transient nature of some infections.

title: Potential role of NF-kappaB in adult neural stem cells: the underrated steersman?
text:
Neural stem cells are precursors of neurons and glial cells, and during brain development, these cells proliferate, migrate, and differentiate into specific lineages. Recently, neural stem cells within the adult central nervous system have been identified, and research is emerging on the regulation of stem cell proliferation, migration, and differentiation by various soluble factors, such as chemokines and cytokines. However, the signal transduction mechanisms downstream of these factors are not well understood. Here, we review potential evidence for a central role of the transcription factor nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) in these critical signal transduction processes.
NF-κB is an inducible transcription factor discovered in lymphocytes by David Baltimore's laboratory and is expressed in neurons, glia, and neural stem cells. NF-κB plays a crucial role in various biological processes, including inflammation, innate immunity, development, apoptosis, and anti-apoptosis. Recent studies have shown that members of the NF-κB family are widely expressed in neurons, glia, and neural stem cells in the nervous system. In the nervous system, NF-κB plays a crucial role in neuronal plasticity, learning, memory consolidation, neuroprotection, and neurodegeneration. Recent data suggest an important role of NF-κB in the proliferation, migration, and differentiation of neural stem cells.

NF-κB is composed of three subunits: two DNA-binding and one inhibitory subunit. Activation of NF-κB takes place in the cytoplasm and results in the degradation of the inhibitory subunit, allowing the nuclear import of the DNA-binding subunits. Within the nucleus, several target genes can be activated.


We propose a model explaining the multiple actions of NF-κB on neural stem cells. Furthermore, we discuss the potential role of NF-κB within the so-called brain cancer stem cells.

title: Intrauterine factors and risk of breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of current evidence.
text:
BACKGROUND: Emerging evidence suggests a potential association between prenatal experiences in women and their subsequent risk of developing breast cancer. The possible underlying mechanisms include variations in maternal endogenous sex hormone and growth hormone levels, germ-cell mutations, the formation of cancer stem cells, and other genetic or epigenetic events. To systematically review and summarize the available data on the relationship between perinatal factors and breast cancer risk, we conducted a comprehensive search of published studies.
METHODS: We systematically searched for studies that assessed the association between perinatal factors and breast cancer risk. We evaluated each perinatal factor separately, including birthweight, birth length, parental age at delivery, gestational age, intrauterine exposure to diethylstilbestrol, twin membership, maternal pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, and other factors.
FINDINGS: Our search yielded 57 studies published between October 1, 1980, and June 21, 2007. We found that increased birthweight (relative risk [RR] 1.15 [95% CI 1.09-1.21]), birth length (RR 1.28 [1.11-1.48]), higher maternal age (RR 1.13 [1.02-1.25]), and paternal age (RR 1.12 [1.05-1.19]) were associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. Conversely, maternal pre-eclampsia or eclampsia (RR 0.48 [0.30-0.78]) and twin membership (RR 0.93 [0.87-1.00]) were associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer. No significant association was found between breast cancer risk and gestational age at birth (RR 0.95 [0.71-1.26]) or maternal diethylstilbestrol treatment (RR 1.40 [0.86-2.28]).
INTERPRETATION: Our findings suggest that the intrauterine environment plays a significant role in the development of breast cancer in adulthood. Elucidating the underlying mechanisms responsible for this association is crucial for the development of prevention and treatment strategies.

title: Helicobacter hepaticus does not induce or potentiate colitis in interleukin-10-deficient mice.
text: Helicobacter hepaticus has been shown to cause colitis, hepatitis, and hepatocellular carcinoma in various mouse models. The aim of this study was to determine if H. hepaticus can induce colitis in mice lacking the interleukin-10 (IL-10) gene and enhance colitis in specific-pathogen-free (SPF) IL-10-deficient mice. IL-10-deficient mice were monoassociated with H. hepaticus ATCC 51448 through oral feeding and rectal enemas on either a mixed (C57BL/6 x 129/Ola) or inbred (129/SvEv) genetic background. In a second experiment, germfree IL-10-deficient mice were colonized with stool from SPF mice that either did or did not harbor endogenous H. hepaticus. After 7-9 weeks of colonization, weight loss and mortality were assessed, the colon was examined for histology, and mesenteric lymph node cells were evaluated for T-cell activation markers. The results showed that IL-10-deficient mice monoassociated with H. hepaticus for up to 16 weeks exhibited minimal histologic colitis or increased IL-12 production. SPF IL-10-knockout mice did not display significant differences in weight loss, mortality rate, histologic scores, colonic IL-12 secretion, or T-cell activation with or without H. hepaticus. Therefore, the study concluded that H. hepaticus does not induce or potentiate disease in IL-10-deficient mice and is not necessary to induce colitis in genetically susceptible hosts.

title: Metabolic interplay between glycolysis and mitochondrial oxidation: The reverse Warburg effect and its therapeutic implication.
text: The Warburg effect, a metabolic process characterized by increased glycolysis in cancer cells, may contribute to the aggressive nature of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, recent studies have revealed the limitations of the Warburg effect, including high mitochondrial respiration and low glycolysis rates in cancer cells. To reconcile these contradictory findings, the "reverse Warburg effect" has been proposed, which suggests that there is a metabolic interplay between glycolytic and oxidative cells. Additionally, aerobic glycolysis may occur in the stromal compartment surrounding the tumor, where stromal cells provide lactate to cancer cells, preventing the creation of an acidic tumor microenvironment. This concept highlights the heterogeneity of tumors, making it challenging to develop a single-agent cure. Understanding the flexibility of metabolism through lactate shuttles offers new opportunities to develop treatments that target the hypoxic tumor microenvironment and overcome the limitations of glycolytic inhibitors.

title: Enhanced waterlogging tolerance in barley by manipulation of expression of the N‐end rule pathway E3 ligase PROTEOLYSIS6
text: Enhancing crops' tolerance to low oxygen levels (hypoxia) during flooding is a crucial goal for ensuring food security. In Arabidopsis thaliana, the N-end rule pathway of targeted proteolysis regulates plant responses to hypoxia by controlling the stability of group VII ethylene response factor (ERFVII) transcription factors, which are influenced by the oxidation state of the amino terminal (Nt)-cysteine (Cys). Here, we demonstrate that the barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) ERFVII BERF1 is a substrate of the N-end rule pathway in vitro. Furthermore, we show that Nt-Cys acts as a sensor for hypoxia in vivo, as the stability of the oxygen-sensor reporter protein MCGGAIL-GUS increases in waterlogged transgenic plants. Transgenic RNAi barley plants with reduced expression of the N-end rule pathway N-recognin E3 ligase PROTEOLYSIS6 (HvPRT6) exhibit increased expression of hypoxia-associated genes and altered seed germination phenotypes. In addition, these plants show sustained biomass, enhanced yield, retention of chlorophyll, and enhanced induction of hypoxia-related genes in response to waterlogging. HvPRT6 RNAi plants also exhibit reduced chlorophyll degradation in response to continued darkness, which is often associated with waterlogged conditions. Barley Targeting Induced Local Lesions IN Genomes (TILLING) lines containing mutant alleles of HvPRT6 display increased expression of hypoxia-related genes and phenotypes similar to RNAi lines. Our findings suggest that the N-end rule pathway represents a promising target for plant breeding to enhance tolerance to waterlogging in barley and other cereals, thus improving food security.

title: A SUMO-Dependent Protein Network Regulates Chromosome Congression during Oocyte Meiosis
text: During the meiosis process in the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans, a multi-protein ring complex (RC) localizes between homologous chromosomes, promoting chromosome congression through the action of the chromokinesin KLP-19. While some RC components have been identified, the mechanism of RC assembly has remained unclear. Our study reveals that the SUMO E3 ligase GEI-17/PIAS is essential for KLP-19 recruitment to the RC, and proteomic analysis showed that KLP-19 is a SUMO substrate in vivo. In vitro analysis showed that KLP-19 is efficiently sumoylated in a GEI-17-dependent manner, while GEI-17 undergoes extensive auto-sumoylation. GEI-17 and another RC component, the kinase BUB-1, contain functional SUMO interaction motifs (SIMs), allowing them to recruit SUMO-modified proteins, including KLP-19, into the RC. These findings highlight the importance of SUMO-SIM networks in regulating the assembly of dynamic protein complexes.

title: Prediagnostic levels of C-peptide, IGF-I, IGFBP -1, -2 and -3 and risk of endometrial cancer.
text: Chronic hyperinsulinemia, characterized by elevated levels of insulin and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), has been linked to an increased risk of various cancers, including endometrial cancer. In this study, we investigated the association between pre-diagnostic blood concentrations of C-peptide (a marker of pancreatic insulin production), IGF-I, IGFBP-1, -2, and -3 and endometrial cancer risk in a prospective case-control study nested within three cohorts in New York (USA), Umeå (Sweden), and Milan (Italy). Our findings indicate that higher levels of C-peptide are associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.76 (95% confidence interval (CI): 1.91-11.8) observed in the highest quintile of C-peptide levels. This association remained significant after adjustment for body mass index (BMI) and other confounders. In contrast, levels of IGFBP-1 were inversely related to endometrial cancer risk, with an OR of 0.30 (95% CI: 0.15-0.62) in the upper quintile, but the association was weakened and lost statistical significance after adjustment for confounders. No significant associations were observed between endometrial cancer risk and levels of IGF-I, IGFBP-2, or IGFBP-3. These findings suggest that chronic hyperinsulinemia is a risk factor for endometrial cancer, and that reducing insulin levels through lifestyle modifications or medication may help prevent this disease.

title: Interactions between SRY and SOX genes in mammalian sex determination.
text: The SRY gene on the mammalian Y chromosome is believed to play a crucial role in determining testis development, but the exact mechanism by which it does so is still unclear. Initially, it was thought that SRY directly activates other genes in the testis-determining pathway. However, this paper presents an alternative hypothesis that SRY functions indirectly by interacting with related genes SOX3 (from which SRY evolved) and SOX9 (which is involved in vertebrate gonad differentiation). According to this hypothesis, in females, SOX3 inhibits SOX9 function, while in males, SRY inhibits SOX3 and allows SOX9 to play its role in testis determination. This hypothesis makes specific predictions about the phenotypes of individuals with deficiencies or excesses of any of the three genes, and can explain the unusual cases of XX(SRY-) males and transdifferentiation in the absence of SRY. Additionally, this hypothesis suggests a possible evolutionary origin of the dominant SRY sex-determining system in mammals, which may have arisen from an ancient system that relied on SOX3 dosage.

title: Chromatin immunoprecipitation and microarray-based analysis of protein location
text:
Genome-wide location analysis, also known as ChIP-Chip, is a powerful technique that combines chromatin immunoprecipitation and DNA microarray analysis to identify protein-DNA interactions in living cells. This approach involves chemical crosslinking of protein-DNA interactions in vivo, followed by cell lysis, DNA fragmentation, and immunoaffinity purification of the desired protein. The enriched DNA population is then labeled and combined with a differentially labeled reference sample before being applied to DNA microarrays to detect enriched signals.
To generate maps of protein-genome occupancy, various computational and bioinformatic approaches are used to normalize the enriched and reference channels, connect signals to specific portions of the genome represented on the microarrays, and provide confidence metrics. Here, we describe the experimental protocols used for crosslinking cells, labeling and hybridization, and provide insights into the factors that influence the results. These protocols typically take approximately one week to complete once sufficient numbers of cells have been obtained and have been used to produce high-quality ChIP-chip results in a variety of cell and tissue types.

title: Spatial and temporal clusters of Barmah Forest virus disease in Queensland, Australia.
text:
Objective: To identify spatial and temporal clusters of Barmah Forest virus (BFV) disease in Queensland, Australia, using geographical information systems and spatial scan statistics (SaTScan).
Methods: We obtained BFV disease cases, population, and statistical local areas (SLAs) boundary data from Queensland Health and Australian Bureau of Statistics during 1992-2008. A retrospective Poisson-based analysis using SaTScan software and method was conducted to identify purely spatial and space-time BFV disease high-rate clusters. The spatial cluster size was set to a proportion of the population, and time windows ranging from 1 to 12 months were used for the space-time analysis, with a 200 km radius.
Results: SaTScan detected a significant purely spatial cluster (including 23 SLAs) and a significant space-time cluster (including 24 SLAs) in approximately the same location. Additional secondary clusters were identified from both analyses in several locations.
Conclusions: This study demonstrates the existence of statistically significant BFV disease clusters in Queensland, Australia. The study also highlights the relevance and applicability of SaTScan in analyzing ongoing surveillance data to identify clusters to inform the development of effective BFV disease prevention and control strategies in Queensland, Australia.

title: Surfactant Protein B Suppresses Lung Cancer Progression by Inhibiting Secretory Phospholipase A2 Activity and Arachidonic Acid Production
text:
Background and Objectives: Radiotherapy is a common treatment for patients with inoperable cancer, including advanced stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, radioresistance is a major obstacle in radiotherapy, and its underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. This study aimed to investigate the role of surfactant protein B (SP-B) in radioresistance in NSCLC.
Methods: To investigate the mechanism of radioresistance regulated by SP-B, we established the ΔSFTPB A549 cell line and analyzed SP-B expression. We also analyzed the change in SP-B expression in response to ionizing radiation (IR) in A549 and NCI-H441 cell lines. Conditioned media (CM) from NSCLC cells were used to evaluate the downstream signaling pathway. The in vivo effects of SP-B were assessed through a mouse xenograft model with intratumoral injection of CM.
Results: Our results showed that in response to IR, NSCLC cell lines exhibited decreased SP-B expression, which was regulated by the TGF-β signaling pathway. Decreased SP-B expression inhibited cell survival and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Treatment with CM from irradiated cells activated sPLA2, enhanced protein kinase Cδ-MAPKs signaling pathway, and increased arachidonic acid production. We confirmed the in vivo roles of SP-B through a mouse xenograft model.
Conclusion: Our findings revealed that down-regulation of SP-B was involved in the radiation-induced metastatic conversion of NSCLC, and provided evidence that SP-B acted as a suppressor of NSCLC progression.

title: Liraglutide improves hippocampal synaptic plasticity associated with increased expression of Mash1 in ob/ob mice
text:
Objective: Consumption of a high-fat diet has detrimental effects on learning and memory formation, which is linked to impaired hippocampal function. Activation of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) signaling ameliorates these adverse effects, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of daily subcutaneous treatment with GLP-1 mimetic, Liraglutide, on synaptic plasticity, hippocampal gene expression, and metabolic control in adult obese diabetic (ob/ob) mice.
Results: Long-term potentiation (LTP) induced in the CA1 area was completely abolished in ob/ob mice compared to lean controls. However, Liraglutide treatment rescued these detrimental effects on LTP, and Liraglutide-treated mice exhibited a superior LTP profile compared to lean controls. Expression of hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor-type 2 was not significantly different between groups, but synaptophysin and Mash1 were decreased in ob/ob mice. Treatment with Liraglutide over 21 days increased expression of Mash1 in ob/ob mice (2.0-fold; P<0.01). These changes were associated with significantly reduced plasma glucose levels (21% reduction; P<0.05) and markedly improved plasma insulin concentrations (2.1- to 3.3-fold; P<0.05 to P<0.01). Liraglutide also significantly reduced the glycaemic excursion following an intraperitonal glucose load and markedly enhanced the insulin response to glucose. Oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, respiratory exchange ratio, and energy expenditure were not altered by Liraglutide therapy. On day 21, accumulated food intake (32% reduction; P<0.05) and number of feeding bouts (32% reduction; P<0.05) were significantly reduced, but simple energy restriction was not responsible for the beneficial actions of Liraglutide.
Conclusion: Liraglutide elicits beneficial effects on metabolic control and synaptic plasticity in mice with severe obesity and insulin resistance, mediated in part through increased expression of Mash1, which is believed to improve hippocampal neurogenesis and cell survival.

title: Post-transcriptional regulation of IME1 determines initiation of meiosis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: The IME1 gene of Saccharomyces cerevisiae is essential for the initiation of meiosis. The transcription of IME1 is detected under conditions that induce meiosis, such as starvation for nitrogen and glucose, and the presence of certain gene products. Our study shows that IME1 is also subject to translational regulation, meaning that its protein production can be controlled in addition to its transcription. Translation of IME1 mRNA can occur under different conditions, including nitrogen starvation, G1 arrest, and the presence of certain gene products. Specifically, we found that elevated transcription levels of IME1 on a multicopy plasmid, elevated transcription provided by a Gal-IME1 construct, G1 arrest due to alpha-factor treatment, and G1 arrest following mild heat-shock treatment of cdc28 diploids can all lead to the expression of Ime1 protein in vegetative cultures. These findings suggest that starvation is not only required for transcription and efficient translation of IME1, but also for the activation of Ime1 protein or the induction/activation of another factor that, either alone or in combination with Ime1, initiates meiosis.

title: Targeted proteomics reveals compositional dynamics of 60S pre-ribosomes after nuclear export
text: The construction and intracellular targeting of eukaryotic pre-ribosomal particles involve a multitude of diverse transiently associating trans-acting assembly factors, energy-consuming enzymes, and transport factors. The inability to rapidly and reliably measure the co-enrichment of multiple factors with maturing pre-ribosomal particles poses a significant biochemical bottleneck in understanding their function and the precise contribution of over 50 energy-consuming steps involved in ribosome assembly. To overcome this challenge, we developed a workflow that combines genetic trapping, affinity-capture, and selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry (SRM-MS) to study the dynamic proteome of pre-60S particles after nuclear export. By exploiting this approach, we uncovered assembly factors that travel with pre-60S particles from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, where they are released before initiating translation. Additionally, we identified a novel shuttling factor that facilitates the nuclear export of pre-60S particles. Our workflow provides a reliable discovery tool to unveil dynamic processes that contribute to the in vivo assembly and transport of macromolecular complexes.

title: Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea and incident stroke: the sleep heart health study.
text:
RATIONALE: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) has been linked to various physiological perturbations that increase the risk of hypertension and atherosclerosis, which are known risk factors for ischemic stroke. However, the relationship between OSA and ischemic stroke risk in the general population remains unclear.
OBJECTIVES: To determine the incidence of ischemic stroke among individuals with OSA in a community-based sample of men and women across a wide range of OSA severity.
METHODS: Baseline polysomnography (PSG) was conducted between 1995 and 1998 in a longitudinal cohort study. The primary exposure was the obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI), and the outcome was incident ischemic stroke.
RESULTS: A total of 5,422 participants without a history of stroke at baseline and untreated for OSA were followed for a median of 8.7 years. One hundred ninety-three ischemic strokes were observed. In covariate-adjusted Cox proportional hazard models, a significant positive association between ischemic stroke and OAHI was observed in men (P value for linear trend: P = 0.016). Specifically, men in the highest OAHI quartile (>19) had an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.86 (95% confidence interval, 1.1-7.4). In the mild to moderate range (OAHI, 5-25), each one-unit increase in OAHI was estimated to increase stroke risk by 6% (95% confidence interval, 2-10%). In contrast, stroke was not significantly associated with OAHI quartiles in women, but increased risk was observed at an OAHI greater than 25.
CONCLUSIONS: The present findings suggest that OSA is associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke in community-dwelling men, particularly in the mild to moderate range of OSA severity. These results provide evidence for the potential benefits of targeting OSA in stroke prevention trials.

title: Reproducibility of 31P cardiac magnetic resonance spectroscopy at 3 T.
text: The aim of this study was to leverage the enhanced clinical field strength of 3 Tesla (3T) to develop and optimize a chemical shift imaging (CSI) protocol, resulting in high-quality spectra with high specificity to the myocardium. The protocol was designed to produce spectra with minimal user bias, using an analysis method that relies solely on anatomical location. Twenty healthy male subjects were scanned on two separate occasions using the optimized CSI protocol at 3T, and the data was analyzed for intra- and inter-subject variability, as well as intra- and inter-observer variability. The results showed that the average phosphocreatine (PCr)/adenosine triphosphate (ATP) value was 2.07 +/- 0.38 and 2.14 +/- 0.46 for scan 1 and 2, respectively, indicating no significant difference between the two scans. Intra-subject variability was 0.43 +/- 0.35 (20%), while inter-subject coefficient of variation was 18%. Intra-observer variability, assessed by a single observer, was 0.14 +/- 0.24 with no significant difference between analyses. The inter-observer variability was also found to be insignificant, with an intra-class correlation coefficient of 0.763. The improved signal strength at 3T resulted in better spatial resolution and myocardial specificity without compromising reproducibility compared to previous studies at 1.5T. The developed acquisition protocol and analysis method provide high-quality spectra and are free from user bias.

title: Nuclear HuR accumulation through phosphorylation by Cdk1.
text: A predominantly cytoplasmic RNA-binding protein, HuR, translocates to the nucleus in response to stress and proliferative signals, where it stabilizes or modulates the translation of target mRNAs. Here, we demonstrate that HuR phosphorylation at S202 by the G2-phase kinase Cdk1 influences its subcellular localization. HuR is specifically phosphorylated in synchronous G2-phase cultures; its cytoplasmic levels increase upon Cdk1 inhibition and decrease upon Cdk1 activation. In contrast, the non-phosphorylatable point mutant HuR(S202A) remains predominantly nuclear. Using a novel anti-phospho-HuR(S202) antibody, we show that phospho-HuR(S202) is predominantly nuclear, while unphosphorylated HuR is more cytoplasmic. Our findings suggest that Cdk1 phosphorylates HuR during G2, thereby retaining it in the nucleus in association with 14-3-3 and hindering its post-transcriptional function and anti-apoptotic influence.

title: Surgical Resection for Patients with Solid Brain Metastases: Current Status
text: Brain metastases affect up to 40% of cancer patients. Recent advancements in imaging and detection, as well as improved treatment of underlying systemic disease, have led to an increase in the occurrence of metastases. These advancements have also improved surgical techniques, including image-guided surgery, which can effectively treat metastatic lesions. Class 1 data suggests that surgery is a better treatment option for metastases compared to whole brain radiation. Additionally, there is evidence to suggest that even metastases in sensitive areas can be safely removed. The complication rate is low, and the recurrence rate is less than 10%. Surgery is typically recommended for patients with a mass with an unknown primary, symptomatic masses in eloquent areas, masses with significant edema requiring high-dose steroids, masses larger than 3 cm, or when radiosurgery may also be an option. The decision to use radiosurgery or whole brain radiation in conjunction with surgical removal is still being evaluated.

title: Clinical features and treatment of peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum.
text:
Context: Peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum (PPG), a rare variant of pyoderma gangrenosum, has been primarily reported in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). However, there have been some cases where PPG has occurred in the absence of IBD. Objective: To better understand the clinical features, diagnosis, and management of PPG in both IBD and non-IBD patients.
Design, Setting, and Patients: This was a retrospective analysis of 7 patients with PPG seen at a university-affiliated community setting between 1988 and December 1999.
Main Outcome Measures: The clinical and histopathologic features, associated disorders, and microbiologic findings of the patients were evaluated.
Results: Of the 7 patients, 2 had Crohn's disease, 2 had ulcerative colitis, and 3 had abdominal cancer. Five patients experienced at least one relapse of PPG after initial healing. Interestingly, only one patient with IBD had a parallel course of PPG, while the other 3 patients with IBD did not. In addition, both patients whose stoma was relocated developed an ulcer at the new site. Effective treatments included topical superpotent corticosteroids, intralesional injection of triamcinolone acetonide at the ulcer margin, topical cromolyn sodium, oral dapsone, prednisone, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous infliximab.
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that PPG can occur in both IBD and non-IBD patients, and biopsy of the skin lesion is not diagnostic but can help rule out other causes. Relocation of the stoma may lead to a new ulceration, and trauma to the skin of a predisposed patient can trigger the pustules or ulcerations associated with pathergy. JAMA. 2000;284:1546-1548.

title: The Tof1p-Csm3p protein complex counteracts the Rrm3p helicase to control replication termination of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: The termination of replication forks at specific sites in the genome of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, known as the natural termini, is regulated in a sequence-specific and polar manner through the interaction of the Fob1p replication terminator protein with the tandem Ter sites located in the non-transcribed spacers. Our study reveals a second level of global control mediated by the intra-S-phase checkpoint protein complex of Tof1p and Csm3p, which protects stalled forks at Ter sites against the activity of the Rrm3p helicase ("sweepase"). The sweepase tends to release arrested forks by temporarily displacing the Ter-bound Fob1p. Consistently, very few replication forks were arrested at the natural replication termini in the absence of the two checkpoint proteins. In contrast, the absence of the Rrm3p helicase led to a slight enhancement of fork arrest at the Ter sites. Deleting the TOF1 (or CSM3) genes, which encode the checkpoint proteins, restored fork arrest by removing both the fork-releasing and fork-protection activities. Other genes, such as MRC1, WSS1, and PSY2, that are involved in the MRC1 checkpoint pathway, were not involved in this global control. This observation suggests that Tof1p-Csm3p function differently from MRC1 and the other genes. This mechanism is not limited to the natural Ter sites but was also observed at fork arrest caused by the meeting of a replication fork with transcription approaching from the opposite direction.

title: Association of hypomethylation of LINE-1 repetitive element in blood leukocyte DNA with an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
text: The study aimed to investigate the association between global DNA hypomethylation in blood leukocyte DNA and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). A total of 315 HCC cases and 356 age, sex, and HBsAg status-matched controls were included in the analysis. Global methylation in blood leukocyte DNA was measured using bisulfite-polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and pyrosequencing on LINE-1 repeats. The results showed that the median methylation level in HCC cases (77.7% 5-methylcytosine (5mC)) was significantly lower than that in controls (79.5% 5mC) (P=0.004, Wilcoxon rank-sum test). The odds ratios (ORs) of HCC for individuals in the third, second, and first (lowest) quartiles of LINE-1 methylation were 1.1, 1.4, and 2.6, respectively, compared to individuals in the fourth (highest) quartile (P for trend <0.001). Additionally, a 1.9-fold (95% CI 1.4–2.6) increased risk of HCC was observed among individuals with LINE-1 methylation below the median compared to individuals with higher (>median) LINE-1 methylation. These findings suggest that global hypomethylation detected in blood leukocyte DNA may serve as a potential biomarker for identifying individuals at risk of HCC.

title: The ketogenic diet for the treatment of childhood epilepsy: a randomised controlled trial.
text: The ketogenic diet has been a widely used and successful treatment for children with drug-resistant epilepsy since the 1920s. To evaluate the efficacy of the diet in a randomized controlled trial, 145 children aged 2-16 years who had daily seizures despite previous antiepileptic drug treatment were enrolled between 2001 and 2006. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either the ketogenic diet immediately or after a 3-month delay, with no other changes to their treatment (control group). The primary outcome measure was the reduction in seizures, and tolerability of the diet was assessed through questionnaires at 3 months. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00564915). Of the 103 children who provided complete data, 54 were in the diet group and 49 were in the control group. After 3 months, the mean percentage of baseline seizures was significantly lower in the diet group (62.0% vs 136.9%, 75% decrease, 95% CI 42.4-107.4%; p<0.0001). Twenty-eight children (38%) in the diet group had greater than 50% seizure reduction, compared to four (6%) controls (p<0.0001), and five children (7%) in the diet group had greater than 90% seizure reduction, compared to no controls (p=0.0582). There was no significant difference in the efficacy of the treatment between symptomatic generalised or symptomatic focal syndromes. The most common side effects reported at the 3-month review were constipation, vomiting, lack of energy, and hunger. The results of this trial support the use of the ketogenic diet in children with treatment-resistant epilepsy. Funding for the study was provided by the HSA Charitable Trust, Smiths Charity, Scientific Hospital Supplies, and the Milk Development Council.

title: Building-in biosafety for synthetic biology.
text: As synthetic biology advances, practical applications are transitioning from the realm of theoretical ideas and laboratory-based research to actual implementation. However, a pressing concern, particularly with microbial systems, is that self-replicating, re-engineered cells may have unintended consequences if they escape or multiply beyond their intended environment. To address this biosafety issue, various mechanisms for limiting microbial replication and horizontal gene transfer have been proposed. These include using host-construct dependencies such as toxin-antitoxin pairs, conditional plasmid replication, or the requirement for a specific metabolite to be present for cellular function. While the development of more sophisticated 'firewalls' through refactoring of the existing genetic code or tailoring of orthogonal systems, such as xeno nucleic acids, offers promise for the future, this article focuses on what can be achieved using current technology. The state-of-the-art in designing for biosafety is summarized, and general recommendations are provided (e.g., short environmental retention times) for current synthetic biology projects to better protect themselves against potential negative impacts.

title: Sustained active site rigidity during synthesis by human DNA polymerase μ
text: DNA polymerase μ (Pol μ) is the sole human DNA polymerase capable of repairing double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) with unpaired 3′ ends through nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ). To investigate this function, we structurally characterized the catalytic cycle of Pol μ for single-nucleotide incorporation. These structures revealed that, in contrast to other template-dependent DNA polymerases, Pol μ exhibits no significant large-scale conformational changes in protein subdomains, amino acid side chains, or DNA upon dNTP binding or catalysis. Instead, the only notable conformational change occurs earlier in the catalytic cycle, where the flexible loop 1 region repositioned upon DNA binding. Pol μ variants with alterations in loop 1 displayed altered catalytic properties and were partially defective in NHEJ. These findings suggest that specific loop 1 residues contribute to Pol μ's unique ability to catalyze template-dependent NHEJ of DSBs with unpaired 3′ ends.

title: Angiopoietin-1 requires p190 RhoGAP to protect against vascular leakage in vivo.
text:
Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1), a ligand of the endothelial receptor Tie-2, inhibits permeability in mature vessels, but the underlying mechanism remains unknown. Our study reveals that Ang-1 signals Rho family GTPases to organize the cytoskeleton in a way that enhances the permeability barrier function of endothelial cells. Specifically, Ang-1 phosphorylates Tie-2 and its downstream effector, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, leading to the activation of one GTPase, Rac1, and the inhibition of another, RhoA. We found that loss of either part of this dual effect abrogates the cytoskeletal and anti-permeability actions of Ang-1, suggesting that coordinated GTPase regulation is essential for its vessel-sealing effects.
p190 RhoGAP, a GTPase regulatory protein, plays a crucial role in this coordinating function. p190 RhoGAP is phosphorylated by Ang-1 treatment, requires Rac1 activation, and is necessary for RhoA inhibition. Interestingly, Ang-1 prevents the cytoskeletal and pro-permeability effects of endotoxin but requires p190 RhoGAP to do so.
To further investigate the role of p190 RhoGAP in Ang-1's protective effects, we treated mice with p190 RhoGAP small interfering RNA and observed that it completely abolished Ang-1's ability to rescue endotoxemia-induced pulmonary vascular leak and inflammation.
Our findings provide mechanistic evidence that targeting the endothelium through Tie-2 may offer specific therapeutic strategies in life-threatening endotoxemic conditions such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome. By modulating the endothelial cytoskeleton through coordinated regulation of Rho GTPases, Ang-1 offers a promising new approach to controlling vascular permeability.

title: Vesicular trafficking of semaphorin 3A is activity-dependent and differs between axons and dendrites.
text: Secreted semaphorins, acting as guidance cues during nervous system development, remain poorly understood in terms of their transport and secretion by neurons. Through cultured cortical neuron analysis, we discovered endogenous semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) displaying a punctate distribution in axons and dendrites. GFP-Sema3A exhibited a similar distribution and co-localized with secretory vesicle cargo proteins. Live-cell imaging revealed highly dynamic trafficking of GFP-Sema3A vesicles, displaying distinct properties in axons and dendrites regarding directionality, velocity, mobility, and pausing time. In axons, most GFP-Sema3A vesicles moved rapidly in an anterograde direction without interruption, while in dendrites, many vesicles were stationary and moved equally frequently in both directions. Disruption of microtubules, but not actin filaments, significantly impaired GFP-Sema3A transport. Interestingly, depolarization induced a reversible arrest of axonal transport of GFP-Sema3A vesicles, while having little effect on dendritic transport. Conversely, action potential blockade using tetrodotoxin (TTX) accelerated axonal transport, but not dendritic transport. These findings suggest that axons and dendrites regulate the trafficking of Sema3A and likely other secretory vesicles in distinct manners, with axons specializing in fast, uninterrupted anterograde transport. Moreover, neuronal activity regulates secretory vesicle trafficking in axons by a depolarization-evoked trafficking arrest.

title: Frequency of Intracranial Aneurysms Determined by Magnetic Resonance Angiography in Children (Mean Age 16) Having Operative or Endovascular Treatment of Coarctation of the Aorta (Mean Age 3).
text: Coarctation of the aorta (CofA) has been linked to an elevated risk of intracranial aneurysm (IA) in adults. However, little is known about the prevalence of IAs in children treated early in life for CofA. This magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) study aimed to investigate the incidence of IAs in 80 children who underwent treatment for CofA during early childhood. MRA scans were performed at an average age of 15.7 ± 7.1 years, with surgical or endovascular treatment for CofA occurring at an average age of 2.6 ± 4.4 years. Surprisingly, no IA was detected in the study participants. Contrary to previous findings in adult patients with late treatment for CofA, this study failed to confirm the association between CofA and IAs in very early treated children. Our results suggest that the developmental relationship between CofA and IAs may be influenced by modifiable risk factors such as hypertension, rather than the presence of CofA itself. In conclusion, our findings suggest that early treatment of CofA can reduce the formation of IAs in children, making MRA screening less necessary in this young population.

title: Transcriptional profiling of the heart reveals chamber-specific gene expression patterns.
text: The expression of genes specific to each cardiac chamber is crucial for the proper development and function of the heart. To investigate the genetic basis of cardiac chamber specialization, we conducted a comprehensive transcriptional profiling of the four heart chambers and the interventricular septum. Our rigorous statistical analysis identified known and novel members of gene families important for cardiac development and function, including LIM proteins, homeobox proteins, Wnt and T-box pathway proteins, and structural proteins like actins and myosins. Additionally, we identified thousands of differentially expressed genes for which there is limited structural or functional information. Clustering of these genes revealed essential signaling pathways for chamber-specific feature development and maintenance. To facilitate future research in this area, we constructed a searchable internet database that allows for the study of chamber-specific gene expression across all genes represented on our comprehensive microarray. We anticipate that further investigation of genes identified through this effort will provide insights into the specialization of heart chamber tissues and their specific roles in cardiac development, aging, and disease.

title: CD34+ hematopoietic stem-progenitor cell microRNA expression and function: a circuit diagram of differentiation control.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a recently discovered class of epigenetic elements that consist of small non-coding RNAs that bind to the 3' untranslated region of messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and down-regulate their translation into proteins. miRNAs play crucial roles in various cellular processes, including metabolism, apoptosis, differentiation, and development. In this study, we identified 33 miRNAs expressed in CD34+ hematopoietic stem-progenitor cells (HSPCs) from normal human bone marrow and mobilized human peripheral blood stem cell harvests. We combined these data with human HSPC mRNA expression data and miRNA-mRNA target predictions to create a novel miRNA:mRNA interaction database called the Transcriptome Interaction Database. In silico predictions from the database suggested that miRNAs control hematopoietic differentiation by translational control of mRNAs essential for hematopoiesis. Based on these predictions, we developed a model for miRNA control of hematopoiesis, in which many genes specifying hematopoietic differentiation are expressed by HSPCs but are regulated by miRNAs until differentiation occurs. We validated miRNA control of several target mRNAs by demonstrating that their translation is indeed decreased by miRNAs. Finally, we chose miRNA-155 for functional characterization in hematopoiesis, as we predicted that it would regulate both myelopoiesis and erythropoiesis. As expected, miRNA-155 transduction significantly reduced both myeloid and erythroid colony formation in normal human HSPCs.

title: Acute exercise activates nuclear factor (NF)-kappaB signaling pathway in rat skeletal muscle.
text: Two experiments were conducted to investigate the effects of an acute bout of physical exercise on the nuclear protein kappaB (NF-κB) signaling pathway in rat skeletal muscle. In Experiment 1, rats were subjected to a 1-hour treadmill run at 25 m/min, 5% grade, or until exhaustion (Ex), and compared to a control group (C) that received an injection of pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate (PDTC, 100 mg/kg, i.p.) 24 and 1 hour prior to the exercise bout. Additional groups of rats were injected with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 8 mg/kg, i.p.), t-butylhydroperoxide (tBHP, 1 mmol/kg, i.p.), or saline (C) and were killed at resting conditions. Exercise-induced increases in NF-κB binding and P50 protein content were observed in muscle nuclear extracts compared to C rats. In contrast, cytosolic IκBα and IκB kinase (IKK) contents were decreased, while phospho-IκBα and phospho-IKK contents were increased. The exercise-induced activation of the NF-κB signaling cascade was partially abolished by PDTC treatment. In Experiment 2, the time course of exercise-induced NF-κB activation was examined. Highest levels of NF-κB binding were observed at 2 hours post-exercise, while decreased cytosolic IκBα and increased phospho-IκBα content were found at 0-1 hour post-exercise. Peak levels of P65 were observed at 2-4 hours post-exercise. These findings suggest that the NF-κB signaling pathway can be activated in a redox-sensitive manner during muscular contraction, likely due to increased oxidant production. The cascade of intracellular events may be the precursor to elevated gene expression of manganese superoxide dismutase observed earlier (Pfluegers Arch. 442, 426-434, 2001).

title: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII and the endoribonuclease III coordinately regulate spa gene expression.
text: Staphylococcus aureus RNAIII is one of the largest regulatory RNAs, which controls multiple virulence genes encoding exoproteins and cell wall-associated proteins. Among its effects, RNAIII represses the expression of the spa gene (coding for the surface protein A) through a multi-step mechanism involving transcriptional repression, translation inhibition, and mRNA degradation by the double-strand-specific endoribonuclease III (RNase III). The 3' end domain of RNAIII, partially complementary to the 5' part of spa mRNA, forms an initial loop-loop interaction, which is sufficient to inhibit the formation of the translation initiation complex in vitro. However, in vivo, the coordinated action of RNase III is essential to degrade the mRNA and irreversibly arrest translation. Our findings further suggest that RNase III is recruited to target paired RNAs, adding complexity to the expression of the S. aureus virulon.

title: Fast calcium and voltage-sensitive dye imaging in enteric neurones reveal calcium peaks associated with single action potential discharge.
text: Slow changes in intracellular calcium (Ca(2+)) levels have been found to reflect increased neuronal activity. Our study utilized single-trial fast Ca(2+)(i) imaging with a sampling rate of at least 200 Hz to investigate the relationship between Ca(2+)(i) fluctuations and neuronal activity in enteric neurons and nerve fibers. Our findings revealed that fast Ca(2+)(i) imaging can detect peaks associated with single spike discharge, as recorded by consecutive voltage-sensitive dye (VSD) imaging. Additionally, fast Ca(2+)(i) imaging revealed subthreshold fast excitatory postsynaptic potentials. The effects of nicotine on Ca(2+)(i) peaks were reduced by -conotoxin and blocked by ruthenium red or tetrodotoxin. Furthermore, fast Ca(2+)(i) imaging can be used to directly record single action potentials in enteric neurons. The Ca(2+)(i) peaks observed in this study required the opening of voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, as well as Ca(2+) release from intracellular stores.

title: New colorimetric cytotoxicity assay for anticancer-drug screening.
text:
We have developed a rapid, sensitive, and cost-effective method for measuring cellular protein content in adherent and suspension cultures in 96-well microtiter plates. This method is suitable for both small-scale laboratory experiments and large-scale applications, such as the National Cancer Institute's disease-oriented in vitro anticancer drug discovery screen, which requires the analysis of millions of culture wells per year.
To measure cellular protein content, we used a sulforhodamine B (SRB) staining method. First, we fixed the cells with trichloroacetic acid, then stained them for 30 minutes with 0.4% (weight/volume) SRB dissolved in 1% acetic acid. We removed any unbound dye by washing the cells four times with 1% acetic acid. Finally, we extracted the protein-bound dye with 10 mM unbuffered Tris base (tris (hydroxymethyl)aminomethane) for determination of optical density in a computer-interfaced, 96-well microtiter plate reader.
Our SRB assay results were found to be linear with both the number of cells and cellular protein levels measured by the Lowry and Bradford assays over a range of cell densities from sparse subconfluence to multilayered supraconfluence. The signal-to-noise ratio at 564 nm was approximately 1.5 with 1,000 cells per well. Compared to other fluorescence assays, our SRB assay was found to be highly sensitive, with a signal-to-noise ratio that was superior to those of several other visible dyes.
One of the advantages of our SRB assay is that it provides a colorimetric end point that is nondestructive, indefinitely stable, and visible to the naked eye. This makes it a useful tool for measuring drug-induced cytotoxicity and quantitating clonogenicity. Additionally, the SRB dye can be measured quantitatively at the single-cell level by static fluorescence cytometry when excited with a laser at 488 nm.
In summary, we have developed a rapid, sensitive, and cost-effective method for measuring cellular protein content in adherent and suspension cultures in 96-well microtiter plates. Our SRB assay provides a colorimetric end point that is nondestructive, indefinitely stable, and visible to the naked eye, making it a useful tool for drug screening and cytotoxicity assays.

title: A murine model of human myeloma bone disease.
text: Myeloma causes a severe and distinctive form of osteolytic bone disease. Although osteoclast activation is responsible for bone destruction, the underlying mechanisms by which myeloma cells increase osteoclast activity remain unclear. To elucidate these mechanisms, we developed an animal model of human myeloma bone disease using mice. Multiple myeloma spontaneously occurs in aging C57BL/KaLwRij mice, exhibiting the same characteristics as the human disease, including bone lesions. However, this model is challenging to study due to variability in the number of myeloma cells in marrow-derived preparations. To create a more reliable animal model, we established and cloned a cell line from murine myeloma and found that it causes osteolytic bone lesions in mice similar to human myeloma bone disease. The cell line produces interleukin-6, but grows independently of exogenous interleukin-6. Inoculating mice intravenously with cultured cells predictably leads to an identical disease, including monoclonal gammopathy and radiographic bone lesions. Some mice became hypercalcemic, and the bone lesions showed increased osteoclast activity. Similar results were observed when we inoculated Nu/Bg/XID mice with cultured murine myeloma cells. Due to the ability to inoculate mice with precise numbers of cells and predict the onset of bone lesions, hypercalcemia, and death, this model should be a valuable tool for investigating the mechanisms by which myeloma cells activate osteoclasts in this animal model of human myeloma bone disease.

title: Ticagrelor vs. clopidogrel in patients with acute coronary syndromes and diabetes: a substudy from the PLATelet inhibition and patient Outcomes (PLATO) trial
text: Patients with diabetes mellitus (DM) have a higher risk of ischaemic events and bleeding after acute coronary syndromes (ACS). In the PLATelet inhibition and patient Outcomes (PLATO) trial, ticagrelor was shown to reduce the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke, but with similar rates of major bleeding compared to clopidogrel. To investigate the outcome of ticagrelor versus clopidogrel in patients with DM or poor glycaemic control, we analyzed a subset of patients with pre-existing DM (n = 4662), including 1036 patients on insulin, and compared them to a larger group of patients without DM (n = 13 951). We also analyzed subgroups based on admission levels of hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c; n = 15 150). In patients with DM, ticagrelor reduced the primary composite endpoint, all-cause mortality, and stent thrombosis, with no significant increase in major bleeding. These findings were consistent with the overall cohort and did not show any significant interactions between diabetes status and treatment. Additionally, ticagrelor reduced the primary endpoint, all-cause mortality, and stent thrombosis in patients with HbA1c above the median, with similar bleeding rates. These results suggest that ticagrelor may be a safe and effective treatment option for ACS patients with DM or poor glycaemic control, without an increase in major bleeding events.

title: Cardiovascular risk factors and migraine: the GEM population-based study.
text:
Background: Migraine, particularly with aura, has been identified as a risk factor for early-onset ischemic stroke. However, the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood, and it is unclear whether migraineurs have a higher risk profile for cardiovascular disease.
Methods: In this study, we compared the cardiovascular risk profile of adult migraineurs to that of non-migraineurs. Participants (n=5,755, 48% male, age 20-65) were from the Genetic Epidemiology of Migraine (GEM) study, a population-based study in the Netherlands. A total of 620 current migraineurs were identified, including 31% with aura (MA) and 5% unclassified. Controls were 5,135 individuals without lifetime migraine. Cardiovascular risk factors measured included blood pressure (BP), serum total and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (TC, HDL), smoking, oral contraceptive use, and the Framingham risk score for myocardial infarction or coronary heart disease (CHD) death.
Results: Compared to controls, migraineurs were more likely to smoke (odds ratio (OR) = 1.43, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.10-1.83), less likely to consume alcohol (OR = 0.58, 95% CI = 0.50-0.77), and more likely to report a parental history of early myocardial infarction. Migraineurs with aura were more likely to have an unfavorable cholesterol profile (TC ≥ 240 mg/dL, OR = 1.43, 95% CI = 0.97-2.13), have elevated BP (systolic BP ≥ 140 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥ 90 mm Hg, OR = 1.76, 95% CI = 1.04-3.07), and report a history of early onset CHD or stroke (OR = 3.96, 95% CI = 1.10-14.30).
