text: Nuclear extracts derived from HeLa and Drosophila melanogaster KC cell lines have been found to repair single base pair mismatches within open circular DNA heteroduplexes, which contain a specific, site-specific incision located 808 base pairs from the mismatch. Both extract systems exhibit strand-specific correction, with a high bias towards the incised DNA strand. The efficiency of correction varies among different mispairs within a homologous set of heteroduplexes, with G.T > G.G ≈ A.C > C.C. Correction is accompanied by localized DNA synthesis at the region spanning the mispair and the strand break, indicating that mismatch recognition is linked to the repair process. The abolition of correction by aphidicolin and relative insensitivity to high concentrations of ddTTP suggest the involvement of alpha and/or delta class DNA polymerases. These findings suggest that higher eukaryotic cells possess a general, strand-specific mismatch repair system similar to the Escherichia coli mutHLS and Streptococcus pneumoniae hexAB pathways, which play a major role in maintaining genetic stability in these bacterial species.

title: Renal outcomes with telmisartan, ramipril, or both, in people at high vascular risk (the ONTARGET study): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, controlled trial.
text:
Background: Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are known to reduce proteinuria in patients with various kidney diseases. However, the combination of these drugs has not been extensively studied in terms of its renal effects, particularly in older patients with established atherosclerotic vascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage.
Methods: We conducted a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group trial from 2001 to 2007, in which 25,620 patients aged 55 years or older with established atherosclerotic vascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage were randomly assigned to receive either ramipril (an ACE inhibitor), telmisartan (an ARB), or a combination of both drugs. The primary renal outcome was a composite of dialysis, doubling of serum creatinine, and death, and secondary outcomes included the rate of dialysis or doubling of serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
Results: During the trial, 784 patients permanently discontinued randomized therapy due to hypotensive symptoms, with a higher incidence in the combination therapy group (406 patients). The number of events for the primary renal outcome was similar for telmisartan (1147 events, 13.4%) and ramipril (1150 events, 13.5%), but higher with combination therapy (1233 events, 14.5%, HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.92-1.09, p=0.037). The secondary renal outcome, dialysis or doubling of serum creatinine, was similar between telmisartan (189 events, 2.21%) and ramipril (174 events, 2.03%), but more frequent with combination therapy (212 events, 2.49%, HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.01-1.51, p=0.038). Additionally, the rate of eGFR decline was less with ramipril compared to telmisartan or combination therapy. The increase in urinary albumin excretion was less with telmisartan or combination therapy compared to ramipril.
Interpretation: Our findings suggest that in older patients with established atherosclerotic vascular disease or diabetes with end-organ damage, the renal effects of telmisartan are similar to those of ramipril, while combination therapy worsens major renal outcomes. These results suggest that the combination of ARBs and ACE inhibitors may not be the most effective strategy for reducing proteinuria in this patient population.

title: Hypothermic preservation up-regulates calpain expression and increases ubiquitination in cultured vascular endothelial cells: influence of dopamine pretreatment.
text: The study aimed to investigate the effect of dopamine (DA) pretreatment on proteolysis in endothelial cells subjected to prolonged cold storage, which can negatively impact organ transplantation outcomes. The study used human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) and subjected them to hypothermic preservation or not. The results showed that HUVEC were sensitive to cold storage, leading to morphological changes, loss of viability, and significant changes in the cellular proteome. DA pretreatment prevented cell death during cold storage. Western blot analysis revealed that cold storage led to time-dependent up-regulation of calpain 1 and 2, which could be prevented by addition of EDTA. DA pretreatment abolished autoproteolysis of calpain 1. Ubiquitination analysis revealed an increase in ubiquitinated conjugates after cold storage, which was not prevented by DA pretreatment. Neither proteasome nor calpain inhibitors protected endothelial cells during cold storage. The study concluded that activation of the calpain pathway and the ubiquitin proteasome system occur in endothelial cells subjected to cold preservation, and DA pretreatment inhibits the former, but proteolysis is not the major cause of endothelial cell death.

title: The three 'C' s of chromosome conformation capture: controls, controls, controls
text: Transcriptional regulation in higher eukaryotes is governed by regulatory elements such as enhancers, which are recognized by transcription factors. These regulatory elements can be located far away from their target genes, often spanning distances of several megabases. Recent research has shown that long-range control of gene expression can occur through direct physical interactions between genes and these regulatory elements, a phenomenon known as looping. The chromosome conformation capture (3C) methodology can be used to detect these looping interactions. While 3C is relatively straightforward to perform, it is essential to carefully design experiments and use appropriate controls to draw meaningful conclusions. The guidelines provided here can help experimental design and minimize misinterpretation of 3C results.

title: Effects of exercise training of 8 weeks and detraining on plasma levels of endothelium-derived factors, endothelin-1 and nitric oxide, in healthy young humans.
text: The study investigated the effects of chronic exercise on the production of nitric oxide (NO) and endothelin-1 (ET-1) in humans. Eight healthy young subjects participated in the study, engaging in 1 hour of cycling on a leg ergometer at 70% of their maximum oxygen uptake (VO2max) three to four times a week for 8 weeks. Venous plasma concentrations of NO and ET-1 were measured before and after the exercise training, as well as after the 4th and 8th week after cessation of training. The results showed that chronic exercise significantly increased the plasma concentration of NO and decreased the plasma concentration of ET-1 in humans. Specifically, the plasma concentration of NOx (a stable end product of NO) significantly increased after exercise training, and the plasma concentration of ET-1 significantly decreased after exercise training. These changes lasted until the 4th week after cessation of exercise training, after which the levels returned to basal levels. There was also a significant negative correlation between plasma NOx concentration and plasma ET-1 concentration. The study suggests that chronic exercise may produce beneficial effects on the cardiovascular system by increasing production of NO and decreasing production of ET-1, which may have vasodilative and antiatherosclerotic effects.

title: Neuron-specific expression of CuZnSOD prevents the loss of muscle mass and function that occurs in homozygous CuZnSOD-knockout mice.
text: Deletion of copper-zinc superoxide dismutase (CuZnSOD) in Sod1(-/-) mice leads to accelerated loss of muscle mass and force during aging, but the decline does not occur in muscles specifically expressing CuZnSOD. To investigate the role of motor neurons in muscle degeneration, we generated transgenic Sod1(-/-) mice in which CuZnSOD was expressed under the control of the synapsin 1 promoter (SynTgSod1(-/-) mice). Unlike in Sod1(-/-) mice, SynTgSod1(-/-) mice did not exhibit reductions in muscle mass or isometric force, despite expressing CuZnSOD in brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. In contrast, muscles of age-matched Sod1(-/-) mice showed significant reductions in mass and force, accompanied by increased oxidative damage and adaptations in stress responses. Additionally, degeneration of neuromuscular junction (NMJ) structure and function occurred in Sod1(-/-) mice but not in SynTgSod1(-/-) mice. Our findings suggest that maintaining redox homeostasis in motor neurons is crucial for preserving NMJ and skeletal muscle structure and function during aging.

title: A developmental transition in definitive erythropoiesis: erythropoietin expression is sequentially regulated by retinoic acid receptors and HNF4.
text: The cytokine erythropoietin (Epo) plays a crucial role in promoting the proliferation and differentiation of erythropoietic progenitor cells during early fetal development. We have found that the Epo gene is a direct target of retinoic acid signaling in the fetal liver during this period, prior to embryonic day E12.5. Mouse embryos lacking the retinoic acid receptor gene RXR alpha have a similar morphological and histological phenotype to embryos with mutated Epo genes, and flow cytometric analysis reveals that RXR alpha-deficient embryos are deficient in erythroid differentiation. We show that the Epo gene is inducible by retinoic acid in embryos and contains a specific DNA sequence (DR2) that binds to retinoic acid receptors and regulates its expression. Unlike Epo-deficient embryos that die from anemia, the erythropoietic deficiency in RXR alpha-deficient embryos is transient, with Epo mRNA expression returning to normal levels by E12.5 and erythropoiesis and liver morphology recovering by E14.5. We also find that another nuclear receptor protein, HNF4, is abundantly expressed in fetal liver hepatocytes and competes with retinoic acid receptors for occupancy of the Epo gene enhancer DR2 element. Our findings suggest that Epo expression is regulated by RXR alpha and retinoic acid during the E9.5--E11.5 phase of fetal liver erythropoiesis, with expression then becoming dominated by HNF4 activity from E11.5 onward. This transition may explain why Epo expression is controlled by hypoxic rather than retinoic acid signaling later in development.

title: Tetraspanin 7 (TSPAN7) expression is upregulated in multiple myeloma patients and inhibits myeloma tumour development in vivo.
text:
BACKGROUND: Increased expression of the tetraspanin protein TSPAN7 has been observed in various types of cancer, including multiple myeloma (MM). However, the mechanisms by which TSPAN7 contributes to cancer progression are not fully understood.
METHODS: In this study, we investigated the expression of TSPAN7 in MM cells and evaluated its impact on adhesion, migration, and growth in vitro, as well as its role in bone marrow (BM) homing and tumor growth in vivo. Additionally, we characterized the association of TSPAN7 with cell surface partner molecules in vitro.
RESULTS: Our results showed that TSPAN7 was highly expressed at the RNA and protein levels in approximately 50% of MM patient samples. Overexpression of TSPAN7 in the murine myeloma cell line 5TGM1 led to a significant reduction in tumor burden in 5TGM1/KaLwRij mice 4 weeks after intravenous administration of 5TGM1 cells. While TSPAN7 overexpression did not affect cell proliferation in vitro, it increased 5TGM1 cell adhesion to BM stromal cells and transendothelial migration. Furthermore, TSPAN7 was found to associate with the molecular chaperone calnexin on the cell surface.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that elevated TSPAN7 expression may be associated with better outcomes for up to 50% of MM patients.

title: Association of body mass index with outcomes in patients with CKD.
text: Obesity has been linked to increased mortality in the general population, yet this association is reversed in patients undergoing dialysis. The nature of the relationship between obesity and adverse clinical outcomes in non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients, as well as the potential interaction between the severity of disease and this association, remains unclear. To investigate this, we analyzed data from a nationally representative cohort of 453,946 United States veterans with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 ml/min per 1.73 m(2). We examined the associations between body mass index (BMI) categories and all-cause mortality and disease progression (using multiple definitions, including incidence of end-stage renal disease, doubling of serum creatinine, and slopes of eGFR) in Cox proportional hazards models and logistic regression models, after adjusting for age, race, comorbidities, and medications, and baseline eGFR. Our findings revealed a relatively consistent U-shaped association between BMI and clinical outcomes, with the best outcomes observed in overweight and mildly obese patients. Conversely, BMI levels <25 kg/m(2) were associated with worse outcomes in all patients, independent of severity of CKD, while BMI levels ≥35 kg/m(2) were associated with worse outcomes in patients with earlier stages of CKD, but this association was attenuated in those with eGFR<30 ml/min per 1.73 m(2). These findings suggest that a cautious approach to weight management is warranted in this patient population until clinical trials establish the ideal BMI.

title: WRN, the protein deficient in Werner syndrome, plays a critical structural role in optimizing DNA repair.
text: Werner syndrome (WS), a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the WRN gene, predisposes individuals to both cancer and premature aging. The WRN protein is a RECQ-like helicase that plays a crucial role in DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair through non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR). Previous studies have shown that WS cells exhibit extensive deletions at non-homologous DNA ends during DSB repair, which can be complemented by wild-type (wt) WRN. WRN possesses both 3' --> 5' exonuclease and 3' --> 5' helicase activities. To investigate the relative contributions of these enzymatic activities to DSB repair, we examined the effects of complementing WS cells with mutants of WRN that lack either the exonuclease or helicase activity, or both. Our results suggest that balanced exonuclease and helicase activities of WRN are required for optimal HR, and that WRN may also play a structural role in optimizing HR and efficient NHEJ repair. Additionally, our findings suggest that mammalian RECQ helicases, including BLM, have distinct functions that can fine-tune recombination events.

title: In vitro generated antibodies specific for telomeric guanine-quadruplex DNA react with Stylonychia lemnae macronuclei.
text:
Most eukaryotic telomeres contain a repeating sequence with stretches of guanine residues that form a 3'-terminal overhang beyond the telomeric duplex region. The telomeric repeat of hypotrichous ciliates, d(T(4)G(4)), forms a 16-nucleotide 3'-overhang. These sequences can adopt either parallel-stranded or antiparallel-stranded quadruplex conformations in vitro. Although it has been proposed that guanine-quadruplex conformations may play important roles in cellular processes such as telomere function, recombination, and transcription, evidence for their existence in vivo has been difficult to obtain.
To investigate the in vivo structure of telomeres, we generated high-affinity single-chain antibody fragment (scFv) probes for the guanine-quadruplex formed by the Stylonychia telomeric repeat through ribosome display from the Human Combinatorial Antibody Library. Of the scFvs selected, one (Sty3) had an affinity of 125 pM for the parallel-stranded guanine-quadruplex and could distinguish between parallel or antiparallel quadruplex conformations with at least 1,000-fold specificity. A second scFv (Sty49) bound both the parallel and antiparallel quadruplexes with similar affinity (Kd = 3-5 nM). Indirect immunofluorescence studies showed that Sty49 specifically reacted with the macronucleus but not the micronucleus of Stylonychia lemnae. The replication band, where replication and telomere elongation occur, was also not stained, indicating that the guanine-quadruplex is resolved during replication.
Our results provide experimental evidence that the telomeres of Stylonychia macronuclei adopt in vivo a guanine-quadruplex structure, suggesting that this structure may play an important role in telomere function.

title: Incidence of skin cancer after renal transplantation in The Netherlands.
text: In a study of 764 patients who received a renal allograft at Leiden University Hospital between 1966 and 1988, the incidence of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and basal cell carcinoma (BCC) was examined separately. The mean follow-up period was 8.7 years (range 1-21 years), during which time 176 skin cancers were diagnosed in 47 patients. The risk of developing a first tumor increased from 10% after 10 years to 40% after 20 years of graft survival. Compared to the general Dutch population, the overall incidence of SCC was 250 times higher and that of BCC was 10 times higher in these long-term graft survivors. The location of SCCs and BCCs differed significantly. Solar radiation is believed to be a key risk factor for skin cancer development, but the occurrence of skin cancer in long-term graft survivors is also a major problem in countries with a higher latitude and moderate sun exposure, such as the Netherlands.

title: Myogenic and morphogenetic defects in the heart tubes of murine embryos lacking the homeo box gene Nkx2-5.
text: The mouse homeobox gene Nkx2-5 is expressed in precardiac mesoderm and the myocardium of embryonic and fetal hearts. Disrupting Nkx2-5 leads to abnormal heart morphogenesis, growth retardation, and embryonic lethality at around 9-10 days post-coitum (p.c.). Heart tube formation occurs normally in mutant embryos, but the critical process of looping morphogenesis, which determines heart form, is not initiated at the linear heart tube stage (8.25-8.5 days p.c.). Although commitment to the cardiac muscle lineage, expression of most myofilament genes, and myofibrillogenesis are not affected, the myosin light-chain 2V gene (MLC2V) is not expressed in mutant hearts or in mutant embryonic stem cell-derived cardiocytes. MLC2V expression normally occurs only in ventricular cells and is the earliest known molecular marker of ventricular differentiation. The regional expression of two other ventricular markers, myosin heavy-chain beta and cyclin D2, in mutant hearts suggests that not all ventricle-specific gene expression is dependent on Nkx2-5. The data demonstrate that Nkx2-5 is essential for normal heart morphogenesis, myogenesis, and function, and that it is a component of a genetic pathway required for myogenic specialization of the ventricles.

title: Hygiene hypothesis in inflammatory bowel disease: a critical review of the literature.
text: The hygiene hypothesis is believed to be a significant contributor to the increasing incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) worldwide, although the specific factors involved in this association are not well understood. To investigate, we conducted a systematic review of the literature to identify hygiene-related factors that may be associated with the development of IBD. Our search yielded publications from 1966 to 2007 on key terms related to the hygiene hypothesis and IBD, including H pylori exposure, helminths, cold chain hypothesis, measles infection and vaccination, antibiotic use, breastfeeding, family size, sibship, urban upbringing, day care attendance, and domestic hygiene. While the literature suggests that the hygiene hypothesis and decreased microbial exposure in childhood likely play a role in IBD, the supporting data vary in strength for each factor. The most promising factors associated with IBD development include H pylori exposure, helminths, breastfeeding, and sibship. However, most studies in this area are plagued by methodological shortcomings, such as relying on retrospective recall of information, which makes it difficult to determine the importance of the hygiene hypothesis in IBD. Further research is needed to fully understand the hygiene hypothesis in IBD and its potential role in the disease's aetiology.

title: Are dual eligibles admitted to poorer quality skilled nursing facilities?
text:
Dual eligibles, individuals who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid coverage, often receive lower quality care compared to other Medicare beneficiaries after being discharged from a skilled nursing facility (SNF). To investigate this disparity, we used a random utility maximization model and tested how dual eligibility status affects the discharge process.
Our study included 692,875 Medicare fee-for-service patients (22% of whom were dual eligibles), who were discharged from SNFs between July 2004 and June 2005. We used Medicare enrollment and Medicaid Analytic Extract files to determine dual eligibility status and measured the proportion of Medicaid patients and nursing staff characteristics as indicators of SNF quality.
Our findings revealed that dual eligibles were more likely to be discharged to SNFs with a higher proportion of Medicaid patients and fewer nurses. These results were robust when using an alternative subsample of patients based on primary diagnoses, propensity of being dual eligible, and likelihood of remaining in the nursing home.
Our study highlights the disparities in access to quality SNF care for dual eligibles. To address this issue, we recommend improving discharge planning processes to redirect patients to higher quality providers, regardless of Medicaid eligibility.

title: Quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis of acquired cancer drug resistance to pazopanib and dasatinib
text: The majority of patients treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) develop drug resistance, posing a significant challenge in modern cancer therapy. To address this unmet need, this study utilizes mass spectrometry to investigate the global phosphoproteomic changes that occur in response to TKI resistance in the A204 rhabdoid tumor cell line. Our analysis reveals that only a small percentage (6% and 9.7%) of the quantified phosphoproteome is altered upon acquisition of resistance to pazopanib and dasatinib, respectively. Interestingly, pazopanib-resistant cells exhibit increased phosphorylation in cytoskeletal regulatory pathways, while dasatinib-resistant cells show upregulation of the insulin receptor/IGF-1R signaling pathway. Drug response profiling rediscovers previously reported vulnerabilities associated with pazopanib and dasatinib resistance and identifies a new dependency on the second-generation HSP90 inhibitor NVP-AUY-922. This study provides a valuable resource for identifying candidate signalling determinants of TKI resistance and highlights the potential of inhibiting HSP90 function as a means of salvage therapy to overcome TKI resistance. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of new cancer therapies and advance our understanding of the mechanisms of TKI resistance.

title: Pandemic H1N12009 influenza and HIV: a review of natural history, management and vaccine immunogenicity.
text:
The purpose of this review is to assess the impact of the 2009 HIN1 influenza strain (H1N12009) on individuals with HIV. The H1N12009 strain was associated with more severe disease and increased risk of mortality, particularly among at-risk populations. As a result, there was a focused effort to evaluate the disease burden and vaccine efficacy in HIV patients.
Recent findings suggest that, similar to other immune-compromised individuals, most HIV-infected individuals recovered from H1N12009 infection without major complications. Although HIV infection was initially assumed to be a risk factor for more severe disease and death, the available literature does not support this hypothesis. Neuraminidase inhibitors were well tolerated by this population, and there was no evidence of clinically significant pharmacokinetic interactions with antiretroviral therapy. Immunogenicity was found to be increased with H1N12009 vaccine compared to historical results of non-pandemic vaccines, and booster dosing was also beneficial. The H1N12009 vaccine was generally well tolerated and did not have a detrimental effect on HIV status.
In summary, the worst-case scenario did not materialize for H1N12009 in either the general population or in individuals with HIV. Immunization with adjuvant represents a crucial measure to protect this population from H1N12009 and other future novel influenza strains.

title: Population genomics of the honey bee reveals strong signatures of positive selection on worker traits.
text: The majority of theories explaining the evolution of eusociality rely on two fundamental assumptions: mutations affecting the phenotype of sterile workers are driven by positive selection if they benefit fertile kin, and worker traits are the primary means by which social insects adapt to their environment. Despite the prevalent belief that positive selection shapes the evolution of worker traits, we know surprisingly little about the frequency of positive selection acting on the genomes of eusocial insects. To address this knowledge gap, we analyzed the genomes of 40 individual honey bees (Apis mellifera) and identified thousands of genes and regulatory sequences exhibiting signs of adaptive evolution across multiple time scales. Our findings reveal that Apoidea- and Apis-specific genes are enriched for signs of positive selection, indicating that novel genes play a disproportionate role in the adaptive evolution of eusocial insects. Additionally, we found that worker-biased proteins exhibit higher signs of adaptive evolution compared to queen-biased proteins, supporting the idea that worker traits are crucial for adaptation. Furthermore, genes involved in worker division of labor were also enriched for signs of positive selection. Finally, genes associated with worker behavior based on brain gene expression analysis were highly enriched for adaptive protein and cis-regulatory evolution. Our study highlights the significant contribution of worker phenotypes to adaptive evolution in social insects and provides a wealth of knowledge on the genetic loci that influence fitness in honey bees.

title: An acetylation switch in p53 mediates holo-TFIID recruitment.
text:
Posttranslational modifications play a crucial role in regulating gene expression by modulating the activity of transcription factors. For example, the acetylation of the p53 transcription factor can enhance its ability to activate target genes, such as p21. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms by which acetylation of p53 regulates the recruitment of transcriptional activators to the p21 promoter.
We find that the acetylation of two lysine residues in p53 (K373 and K382) leads to the recruitment of the TFIID subunit TAF1 to the p21 promoter through its bromodomains. UV irradiation of cells causes the acetylation of these lysine residues, which in turn recruits TAF1 to a distal p53-binding site on the p21 promoter prior to looping to the core promoter.
Inhibition of the acetyl-p53/bromodomain interaction prevents TAF1 recruitment to both the distal p53-binding site and the core promoter, suggesting that this interaction is essential for transcriptional activation. Furthermore, we observe that the TFIID subunits TAF4, TAF5, and TBP are present on the core promoter prior to TAF1, indicating that different subunits of TFIID may be recruited separately to the p21 promoter and that the transcriptional activation depends on posttranslational modification of the p53 transcription factor.
In summary, our findings demonstrate that posttranslational modifications of p53 play a critical role in regulating the recruitment of transcriptional activators to the p21 promoter and that this process is essential for transcriptional activation in response to DNA damage.

title: Dasatinib inhibits both osteoclast activation and prostate cancer PC-3-cell-induced osteoclast formation.
text:
Targeting Prostate Cancer Bone Metastases with Dasatinib
Prostate cancer bone metastases are a significant challenge in cancer treatment, and current therapies have limited effectiveness. New treatments are being developed that focus on the interaction between cancer cells, bone marrow cells, and the bone matrix. Osteoclasts play a crucial role in the development of bone tumors caused by prostate cancer. Since Src kinase has been shown to be essential for osteoclast function, we hypothesized that dasatinib, a Src family kinase inhibitor, would reduce osteoclast activity and prostate cancer cell-induced osteoclast formation.
Results:
Dasatinib inhibited RANKL-induced osteoclast differentiation of bone marrow-derived monocytes with an EC(50) of 7.5 nM. Prostate cancer cells, such as PC-3, can differentiate RAW 264.7 cells, a murine monocytic cell line, into osteoclasts, and dasatinib inhibited this differentiation. Conditioned medium from PC-3 cell cultures can also differentiate RAW 264.7 cells into osteoclasts, and dasatinib inhibited this process as well. Even the lowest concentration of dasatinib (1.25 nmol) inhibited osteoclast differentiation by 29%. Moreover, dasatinib inhibited osteoclast activity by 58% as measured by collagen 1 release.
Experimental Design:
We conducted in vitro experiments using the Src family kinase inhibitor dasatinib to target osteoclast activation as a means of inhibiting prostate cancer bone metastases.
Conclusion:
Dasatinib inhibits osteoclast differentiation of mouse primary bone marrow-derived monocytes and PC-3 cell-induced osteoclast differentiation. Dasatinib also inhibits osteoclast degradation activity, suggesting that targeting osteoclast differentiation and activity may be an effective targeted therapy for patients with prostate cancer bone metastases.

title: BMP receptor ALK3 controls collecting system development.
text: The molecular signals that regulate the growth and branching of the ureteric bud during the formation of the renal collecting system are still poorly understood. Previous studies have shown that members of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) family signal through the type I BMP receptor ALK3 to inhibit ureteric bud and collecting duct cell morphogenesis in vitro. To investigate the function of the BMP signaling pathway in vivo, we generated a murine model of ALK3 deficiency restricted to the ureteric bud lineage (Alk3(UB-/-) mice). At the onset of branching morphogenesis, Alk3(UB-/-) kidneys exhibit an abnormal primary (1 degree) ureteric bud branch pattern and an increased number of ureteric bud branches. However, during later stages of renal development, Alk3(UB-/-) kidneys have fewer ureteric bud branches and collecting ducts than wild-type kidneys. Postnatal Alk3(UB-/-) mice display a dysplastic renal phenotype characterized by hypoplasia of the renal medulla, a decreased number of medullary collecting ducts, and abnormal expression of beta-catenin and c-MYC in medullary tubules. In summary, our findings demonstrate that ALK3-dependent BMP signaling is essential for normal kidney development, particularly in the regulation of ureteric bud branching.

title: Increased release of ferritin and iron by iron-loaded alveolar macrophages in cigarette smokers.
text: In this study, we investigated the presence of iron in the lower respiratory tract of cigarette smokers and its potential release into the alveolar space. We found that the amount of iron in the lower respiratory tract of smokers is higher than in non-smokers, and a significant portion of this iron is sequestered within alveolar macrophages (AM). When we examined the in vitro release of iron, ferritin, and transferrin from AM recovered by bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from 27 healthy subjects, including nine nonsmokers (NS), nine light smokers (LS), and nine heavy smokers (HS), we found that the release of iron was significantly higher in AM from LS and HS compared to NS. Additionally, we found that AM from smokers contained greater than 10 nmol of iron per 10(6) cells, and released a greater percentage of cell ferritin stores in vitro over 4 h compared to AM from NS. These findings suggest that AM may be a source of iron in the alveolar space and that cigarette smoke may play a role in the release of iron from these cells, leading to oxidant injury.

title: The spectrum of retinopathy in adults with Plasmodium falciparum malaria
text: A specific type of retinopathy has been identified in African children with cerebral malaria, but there has been limited research on this topic in adults. Since the retinal vasculature is structurally and functionally similar to the cerebral vasculature, studying retinal changes can provide valuable insights into the pathophysiology of cerebral malaria. In a recent observational study, high-definition portable retinal photography was used to evaluate malarial retinopathy in adults in Bangladesh. The study found that retinopathy was present in 63% of adults with severe malaria and 70% of those with cerebral malaria. Moderate or severe retinopathy was more common in cerebral malaria (55%) than in uncomplicated malaria (20%), bacterial sepsis (0%), or healthy controls (0%). The retinal changes observed were similar to those previously described in African children, but no vessel discoloration was observed. The severity of retinal whitening was found to correlate with admission venous plasma lactate levels, suggesting that retinal ischemia represents systemic ischemia. These findings suggest that a compromised microcirculation has important pathophysiological significance in severe and cerebral malaria, and that portable retinal photography has potential as a valuable tool for studying malarial retinopathy.

title: Prospective randomized open blinded end-point (PROBE) study. A novel design for intervention trials. Prospective Randomized Open Blinded End-Point.
text: A novel study design, called the PROBE study (Prospective Randomized Open Blinded End-point), is presented, which offers several advantages over the traditional double-blind design. In the PROBE design, participants are randomly assigned to either the intervention or control group, and the end-points are evaluated by a blinded end-point committee. One of the key benefits of the PROBE design is its lower cost compared to the double-blind design, which should make the results more easily applicable in routine medical care. Additionally, the PROBE design more closely resembles standard clinical practice, which may improve the generalizability of the study findings. Despite the blinded end-point evaluation, there is no difference between the PROBE and double-blind designs in terms of end-point assessment.

title: PSGL-1 function in immunity and steady state homeostasis.
text:
The significance of P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL-1) in leukocyte migration has evolved beyond its initial characterization as a selectin ligand. PSGL-1 was initially perceived as a simple molecule with an extracellular mucin domain that acted as a flexible rod, facilitating leukocyte attachment to endothelial selectins. However, recent studies have revealed a more complex role for PSGL-1 in both innate and adaptive immune responses.
The interaction between leukocytes and endothelium mediated by PSGL-1 and selectins requires the presence of branched O-glycans on specific PSGL-1 amino acid residues. In some cell types, such as neutrophils, the enzymes responsible for O-glycosylation are constitutively expressed, while in others, such as T cells, they are only activated upon appropriate stimulation. As a result, PSGL-1 supports leukocyte recruitment in both inflammatory and homeostatic settings.
The selectins engage multiple sugar residues on the branched O-glycans of PSGL-1, forming velcro-like catch bonds that facilitate leukocyte rolling. These interactions also trigger signaling events that influence cell phenotype and function. The scrutiny of PSGL-1 has led to a deeper understanding of its function as a selectin ligand and has revealed unexpected insights into its role in homeostasis, including stem cell homing to the thymus and mature T-cell homing to secondary lymphoid organs.
PSGL-1 has been found to bind homeostatic chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 and to support the chemotactic response to these chemokines. However, the O-glycan modifications of PSGL-1 that support rolling mediated by selectins in inflammatory conditions can interfere with its binding to homeostatic chemokines, limiting the responsiveness of T cells to chemotactic cues in steady state conditions.
The multi-level influence of PSGL-1 on cell traffic in both inflammatory and steady state settings is determined by the orchestrated addition of O-glycans. While central to PSGL-1 function, the in vivo regulation of PSGL-1 glycosylation in T cells remains poorly understood. This review aims to update understanding of PSGL-1 functional scope and to highlight the current knowledge gaps in PSGL-1 glycosylation regulation in T cells.

title: Ligand binding determines whether CD46 is internalized by clathrin-coated pits or macropinocytosis.
text:
CD46 is a ubiquitous cell surface receptor found on human cells that plays a crucial role in the immune system. It interacts with complement components C3b and C4b, as well as various pathogens such as measles virus and human herpes virus 6. The binding of ligands to CD46 affects several cellular processes, including protection of autologous cells from complement attack, intracellular signaling, antigen presentation, and down-regulation of cell surface CD46. Recent research has shown that CD46 signaling can connect the innate and acquired immune systems. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these processes and the importance of intracellular trafficking of the receptor are still not well understood.
Our study demonstrates that CD46 is internalized in non-lymphoid cells through clathrin-coated pits, which then traffic to multivesicular bodies and are recycled to the cell surface. However, cross-linking of CD46 at the cell surface, either through multivalent antibody or measles virus, induces pseudopodia that engulf the ligand in a process similar to macropinocytosis. This leads to the degradation of cell surface CD46. We have identified two pathways for CD46 internalization, which are regulated by the valence of cross-linking and utilize either clathrin-coated pits or pseudopodial extension. This has important implications for CD46 signaling, antigen presentation, CD46 down-regulation, and the engulfment of pathogens.

title: A three-dimensional cell biology model of human hepatocellular carcinoma in vitro
text: We developed an in vitro three-dimensional (3D) model of metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) by culturing MHCC97H cells within a rotating wall vessel bioreactor on molecular scaffolds. Our morphological and biochemical analyses revealed that the 3D HCC model closely resembled many clinical and pathological features of HCC in vivo, including cancer cell morphology, tissue ultrastructure, protein production and secretion, glucose metabolism, tissue-specific gene expression, and apoptosis. When we transplanted these spheroids into the livers of nude mice, they formed tumors and even metastasized to distant sites. This 3D HCC model is a promising tool for studying HCC tumor biology, testing anticancer drugs, and establishing HCC animal models.

title: Patterns of age-specific mortality in children in endemic areas of sub-Saharan Africa.
text: Understanding the age- and season-specific mortality rates of malaria is crucial for developing effective epidemiological models of malaria immunity. However, most studies have aggregated their findings into broad age groups and across seasons, making it challenging to predict the impact of targeted interventions on specific age groups of children. To address this limitation, we present age-specific mortality rates for children under the age of 15 in seven demographic surveillance sites in sub-Saharan Africa with stable Plasmodium falciparum malaria transmission. Using verbal autopsies (VAs) to estimate the proportion of deaths attributed to malaria, we calculated malaria-specific mortality rates for each site, age group, and month of the year. Our findings reveal that a substantial proportion of deaths (ranging from 20.1% in Mozambique to 46.2% in Burkina Faso) were due to malaria. The overall age patterns of malaria mortality were similar across the different sites. Deaths in children under 3 months old were rarely attributed to malaria, while the proportion of deaths attributed to malaria increased with age, peaking in children over 1 year old. Interestingly, all-cause mortality rates peaked during the rainy season in most sites, but the seasonality in malaria transmission was not reflected in the proportion of deaths attributed to malaria, except in the two sites in Burkina Faso. Improving the specificity of VAs would enhance the accuracy of age- and season-specific malaria mortality rates, enabling more effective modeling of malaria immunity.

title: Obesity due to melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) deficiency is associated with increased linear growth and final height, fasting hyperinsulinemia, and incompletely suppressed growth hormone secretion.
text:
Context: Melanocortin receptor 4 (MC4R) deficiency is characterized by excessive linear growth, exceeding what would be expected based on the degree of obesity.
Objective: The objective of this investigation was to compare the somatotroph axis in obese MC4R-deficient patients and equally obese controls.
Patients and Methods: Anthropometric measurements and insulin concentrations were obtained from 153 MC4R-deficient subjects and 1392 controls matched for age and severity of obesity. A subset of 33 MC4R-deficient patients and 36 control subjects had their fasting IGF-I, IGF-II, IGF binding protein (IGFBP)-1, IGFBP-3, and acid-labile subunit levels measured. Pulsatile GH secretion was examined in six adult MC4R-deficient subjects and six obese controls.
Results: Height standard deviation score was significantly higher in MC4R-deficient children under the age of 5 compared to controls (mean ± SEM: 2.3 ± 0.06 vs. 1.8 ± 0.04, P < 0.001), with this effect persisting throughout childhood. Final height (cm) was greater in MC4R-deficient men (mean ± SEM: 173 ± 2.5 vs. 168 ± 2.1, P < 0.001) and women (mean ± SEM: 165 ± 2.1 vs. 158 ± 1.9, P < 0.001). Fasting IGF-I, IGF-II, acid-labile subunit, and IGFBP-3 concentrations were similar between the two groups. GH levels were significantly suppressed in obese controls, but pulsatile GH secretion was preserved in MC4R deficiency. The mean maximal GH secretion rate per burst and mass per burst were increased in MC4R deficiency, consistent with increased pulsatile and total GH secretion. Fasting insulin levels were markedly elevated in MC4R-deficient children.
Conclusions: In MC4R deficiency, increased linear growth in childhood leads to increased adult final height, exceeding what would be predicted by obesity alone. GH pulsatility is maintained in MC4R deficiency, consistent with animal studies, suggesting a role for MC4R in regulating hypothalamic somatostatinergic tone. Fasting insulin levels are significantly higher in children carrying MC4R mutations. Both of these factors may contribute to the accelerated growth phenotype characteristic of MC4R deficiency.

title: The selectivity of beta-adrenoceptor antagonists on isoprenaline-induced changes in heart rate, blood pressure, soleus muscle contractility and airways function in anaesthetized cats.
text: In this study, the activity of four beta-adrenoceptor antagonists (propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol, and butoxamine) was measured in anesthetized cats, and their effects on four parameters (heart rate, blood pressure, soleus muscle contractility, and airway reactance) were compared to the activity of four synthetic phenylethanolamine derivatives. The results showed that all of the antagonists caused parallel shifts in the dose-response curves for isoprenaline (a beta-adrenoceptor agonist) for all parameters except blood pressure. Propranolol was the most potent antagonist and showed some selectivity of action on soleus muscle compared to heart. Atenolol and metoprolol were approximately equipotent and were cardioselective at low doses only. Butoxamine was the least potent antagonist and had non-beta-adrenoceptor effects on the parameters measured. The new compounds tested, including 4'-bromo-2'-methoxy-N-isopropyl phenylethanolamine, the 4'-chloro- and 4'-methyl analogues, and 4'-methoxy-N-t-butyl phenylethanolamine, were all potent antagonists but did not exhibit any selectivity of action. The results suggest that there is no clear separation of beta-adrenoceptors into beta 1- and beta 2-subclasses in the organs of the cat, and that beta-adrenoceptor-mediated effects on skeletal muscle and airways are not clearly separated.

title: Breast cancer and obesity: an update.
text: Obesity has a complex relationship with breast cancer, both in terms of risk factors and clinical outcomes. In postmenopausal women, particularly the elderly, various measures of obesity have been positively associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. However, before menopause, increased body weight is inversely related to breast cancer risk. Both premenopausal and postmenopausal breast cancer are influenced by the mechanisms by which body weight and obesity affect estrogen levels, which in turn impact breast cancer risk. Obesity has also been linked to more advanced disease at diagnosis and poorer prognosis in both premenopausal and postmenopausal breast cancer. Notably, breast cancer in African-American women exhibits distinct differences in its relationship to obesity compared to white women, despite the high prevalence of obesity in African-American women contributing to a relatively poor prognosis. While estrogens are often emphasized as the primary factor explaining the effects of obesity on breast cancer, other factors, such as insulin, insulin-like growth factor-I, and leptin, may play a more significant role in the development of an aggressive tumor phenotype. This review highlights the importance of these factors and their relationship to angiogenesis and transcriptional factors.

title: Dietary saturated and unsaturated fats as determinants of blood pressure and vascular function.
text: For decades, the amount and type of dietary fat have been linked to the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Arterial stiffness and endothelial dysfunction are crucial factors in the development of heart disease (CHD). Various methods are used to assess vascular function in nutritional science, including clinic and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, pulse wave analysis, pulse wave velocity, flow-mediated dilatation, and venous occlusion plethysmography. The present review focuses on the impact of dietary fat quantity and type on blood pressure, arterial compliance, and endothelial function. In terms of fat quantity, habitual dietary fat consumption appears to have a limited influence on vascular function, although single high-fat meals postprandially impair endothelial function compared to low-fat meals. This is attributed to increased circulating lipoproteins and non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA), which may induce pro-inflammatory pathways and increase oxidative stress. In contrast, cross-sectional data suggest that saturated fat adversely affects vascular function, while polyunsaturated fat (predominantly linoleic acid, 18 : 2n-6, and n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA)) is beneficial. Specifically, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, 20 : 5n-3) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22 : 6n-3) can lower blood pressure, improve arterial compliance in type 2 diabetics and dyslipidaemics, and enhance endothelium-dependent vasodilation. The mechanisms underlying this vascular protection and the distinct physiological effects induced by EPA and DHA are areas of ongoing research. Due to the scarcity of good-quality observational or interventional data on dietary fatty acid composition and vascular function, no additional recommendations can be provided beyond current guidelines at present.

title: Very small embryonic-like stem cells with maximum regenerative potential get discarded during cord blood banking and bone marrow processing for autologous stem cell therapy.
text: The study investigated the loss of very small embryonic-like stem cells (VSELs) during cord blood banking and bone marrow (BM) processing for autologous stem cell therapy. VSELs are pluripotent stem cells with maximum regenerative potential, but they are lost during these procedures due to their small size. The study compared VSELs in human umbilical cord blood (UCB) and discarded red blood cells (RBC) fraction obtained after separation of mononuclear cells from human BM, and found that they settle along with the RBCs during Ficoll-Hypaque density separation. The study also detected a distinct population of slightly larger, round hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) with cytoplasmic Oct-4 in the "buffy" coat, which is usually banked or used during autologous stem cell therapy. Immunohistochemical studies on umbilical cord tissue (UCT) sections showed the presence of nuclear Oct-4-positive VSELs and many fibroblast-like mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) with cytoplasmic Oct-4. The results suggest that the true stem cells in adult body tissues are the VSELs, while HSCs and MSCs are actually progenitor stem cells that arise by asymmetric cell division of VSELs. The study may help explain the low efficacy reported during adult autologous stem cell trials, where unknowingly progenitor stem cells are injected rather than the pluripotent stem cells with maximum regenerative potential.

title: CNS repair requires both effector and regulatory T cells with distinct temporal and spatial profiles.
text: Monocyte-derived macrophages (mo-MΦs) and T cells have been shown to play a crucial role in spinal cord repair. Recent research has identified the remote brain choroid plexus epithelium (CP) as a key portal for monocyte recruitment, and found that IFN-γ is essential for its activation and leukocyte trafficking. Our study aimed to reconcile the need for effector T cells with the role of inflammation-resolving immune cells in the repair process. Using an acute spinal cord injury model, we found that mice lacking IFN-γ-producing T cells had limited recruitment of inflammation-resolving mo-MΦ to the spinal cord parenchyma. We also demonstrated that mo-MΦ locally regulated the recruitment of thymic-derived Foxp3(+) regulatory T (Treg) cells to the injured spinal cord parenchyma at the subacute/chronic phase. Interestingly, an ablation protocol that resulted in reduced Tregs at this stage interfered with tissue remodeling, while transient ablation of Tregs before the injury favored repair. Our findings suggest that reduced systemic immunosuppression at the time of the insult can enhance CNS repair. Overall, our data highlight a dynamic immune cell network that is essential for repair, involving effector and regulatory T cells, interconnected by mo-MΦ. Any dysregulation of these populations may hinder the repair process, emphasizing the need for temporally and spatially controlled therapeutic interventions.

title: Sperm function tests and fertility.
text: Historically, the diagnosis of male infertility has relied on a descriptive evaluation of semen, focusing on the number of sperm, their motility, and morphology. The underlying principle is that male fertility can be defined by a threshold concentration of motile, morphologically normal sperm that must be exceeded for conception. However, numerous studies have shown that this fundamental concept is flawed, and it is not necessarily the absolute number of sperm that determines fertility, but rather their functional competence. In light of this conclusion, various in vitro tests have been developed to assess sperm function, including their potential for movement, cervical mucus penetration, capacitation, zona recognition, the acrosome reaction, and sperm-oocyte fusion. These functional assays have been found to accurately predict the fertilizing capacity of human spermatozoa in vitro and in vivo. Recent advancements in the field include tests to assess oxidative stress and DNA integrity in sperm, providing information on both fertilizing capacity and embryonic development.

title: Isolation and characterization of the cDNA encoding BKLF/TEF-2, a major CACCC-box-binding protein in erythroid cells and selected other cells.
text: CACCC boxes are prevalent in regulatory elements of genes expressed in erythroid cells, as well as in select other cell types. While the erythroid cell-specific CACCC-box-binding protein EKLF has been shown to be essential in vivo for the proper expression of the adult beta-globin gene, it is dispensable for the regulation of several other globin and non-globin erythroid cell-expressed genes. In this study, we sought to identify additional CACCC-box transcription factors present in murine erythroid cells. We discovered a prominent gel shift activity (designated BKLF) in yolk sac and fetal liver erythroid cells, which could be distinguished from EKLF using specific antibodies. Through relaxed-stringency hybridization, we obtained the cDNA encoding BKLF, a highly basic, novel zinc finger protein related to EKLF and other Krüppel-like proteins in its DNA-binding domain but distinct elsewhere. BKLF, which is expressed widely but not ubiquitously in cell lines, is highly expressed in the midbrain region of embryonic mice and appears to correspond to the gel shift activity TEF-2, a transcriptional activator implicated in the regulation of the simian virus 40 enhancer and other CACCC-box-containing regulatory elements. Given its high affinity and preference for binding to many CACCC sequences of erythroid cell-expressed genes, BKLF is likely to play a significant role in the control of a wide range of genes whose expression is independent of EKLF's action.

title: Effect of osteoporosis treatments on risk of non-vertebral fractures: review and meta-analysis of intention-to-treat studies
text: The majority of osteoporosis treatments have been shown to reduce the risk of vertebral fractures, while evidence for preventing non-vertebral fractures is less conclusive. To provide a more comprehensive assessment of non-vertebral anti-fracture efficacy, this review and meta-analysis analyzed data from randomized, placebo-controlled phase III clinical trials with at least 3-year duration. The ITT population was the primary focus, with radiographs confirming the defined endpoint of non-vertebral fractures. Eleven clinical trials met the inclusion criteria, with three showing statistically significant (P ≤0.05) non-vertebral anti-fracture efficacy in the ITT population: two trials with risedronate and one trial with strontium. A meta-analysis revealed significant reductions in the relative risk of non-vertebral fracture for both alendronate (RR=0.86; 95% CI: 0.76–0.97, P =0.012) and risedronate (RR=0.81; 95% CI: 0.71–0.92, P =0.001). Risedronate and strontium ranelate were the only treatments to demonstrate non-vertebral anti-fracture efficacy in this rigorous assessment. Risedronate was the only agent shown to demonstrate efficacy in multiple trials. The meta-analysis also showed that both alendronate and risedronate provide non-vertebral anti-fracture efficacy.

title: Islet1 deletion causes kidney agenesis and hydroureter resembling CAKUT.
text:
Introduction:
Islet1 (Isl1) is a transcription factor that is transiently expressed in a subset of heart and limb progenitors during embryonic development. Recent studies have shown that conditional deletion of Isl1 in mice leads to unexpected kidney abnormalities, prompting further investigation into the role of Isl1 in kidney development.
Methods:
In situ hybridization was used to examine the expression of Isl1 in the kidneys of mice. Conditional deletion of Isl1 was also performed to assess the effect on kidney development.
Results:
Isl1 was found to be expressed in the mesenchymal cells surrounding the base of the ureteric bud in mice. Conditional deletion of Isl1 resulted in kidney agenesis or hypoplasia, as well as hydroureter, a phenotype resembling human congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT). The absence of Isl1 led to ectopic branching of the ureteric bud out from the nephric duct or the formation of accessory buds, both of which could lead to obstruction of the ureter-bladder junction and consequent hydroureter. Furthermore, the lack of Isl1 reduced the expression of Bmp4, a gene implicated in the CAKUT-like phenotype, in the metanephric region before ureteric budding.
Discussion:

Our findings suggest that Isl1 is essential for proper development of the kidney and ureter by repressing the aberrant formation of the ureteric bud. These observations highlight the potential of Isl1 as a causative gene for human CAKUT. Further studies are warranted to investigate the role of Isl1 in kidney development and its potential as a therapeutic target for CAKUT.
Conclusion:

In conclusion, our study demonstrates the critical role of Isl1 in kidney development and highlights its potential as a causative gene for human CAKUT. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms underlying CAKUT and to identify potential therapeutic targets for this debilitating disorder.

title: Tissue transglutaminase (TG2)--a wound response enzyme.
text:
The repair of damaged tissue after injury is a complex process that involves a series of coordinated events, including inflammation, re-epithelialization, neovascularization, and the synthesis and stabilization of a fibrous extracellular matrix (ECM) that is remodeled over time to resemble normal tissue. During this process, certain members of the transglutaminase (TG) family, including tissue transglutaminase (TG2), play a crucial role in promoting tissue repair. TG2 is the most widely expressed member of the TG family and is involved in wound healing through its ability to stabilize proteins and regulate the behavior of various cell types recruited to the damaged area.
In this article, we will explore the function of TG2 in wound repair, using both early and recent evidence from the literature to demonstrate how this multifunctional enzyme affects the stability of the ECM, cell-ECM interactions, and cell behavior during the different phases of wound healing. We will also discuss how TG2 itself might be exploited for therapeutic use, highlighting its potential as a novel class of wound-healing mediators.

title: Crystal structures of the glutamate receptor ion channel GluK3 and GluK5 amino-terminal domains.
text:
Ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) are responsible for the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. The assembly of these receptors into different subtypes, such as AMPA, kainate, and N-methyl-d-aspartic acid (NMDA) receptors, is regulated by their extracellular amino-terminal domains (ATDs). Kainate receptors are further divided into low-affinity receptor families (GluK1-GluK3) and high-affinity receptor families (GluK4-GluK5) based on their affinity for the neurotoxin kainic acid. These two families share a 42% sequence identity in the intact receptor but only a 27% sequence identity at the ATD level.
We have determined the high-resolution crystal structures of GluK3 and GluK5 ATDs, which crystallize as dimers. However, the dimer assembly of these receptors is different, with GluK3 forming a more compact dimer than GluK5. In contrast, both GluK3 and GluK5 have similar R2 domain dimer assembly to that reported for other non-NMDA iGluRs. This observation suggests that GluK4-GluK5 cannot form functional homomeric ion channels and require obligate coassembly with GluK1-GluK3. Our analysis also reveals that the relative orientation of domains R1 and R2 in individual non-NMDA receptor ATDs varies by up to 10°, which is different from the 50° difference observed in the NMDA receptor GluN2B subunit. This restricted domain movement in non-NMDA receptor ATDs is due to extensive intramolecular contacts between domain R1 and domain R2, as well as their assembly as dimers, which interact at both R1 and R2 domains. Our results provide the first insights into the structure and function of GluK4-GluK5, the least understood family of iGluRs.

title: Effectiveness of screening older people for impaired vision in community setting: systematic review of evidence from randomised controlled trials.
text:
Objective: To evaluate whether community-based screening for impaired vision among older adults leads to improvements in vision.
Design: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials that assessed the effectiveness of community-based screening for impaired vision among older adults, with at least 6-month follow-up.
Population: Adults aged 65 or older.
Main Outcome Measure: Proportions of individuals with visual impairment in intervention and control groups, as measured by various methods of assessing visual impairment.
Results: Five trials with a total of 3494 participants were included in the review. All trials used self-reported measures of visual impairment, both as screening tools and outcome measures. However, the inclusion of a visual screening component in the assessment did not result in significant improvements in self-reported visual problems (pooled odds ratio 1.04, 95% confidence interval 0.89-1.22). A small reduction (11%) in the number of older people with self-reported visual problems cannot be excluded.
Conclusions: Based on the present evidence, community-based screening for impaired vision among older adults is not justified. Visual impairment in this age group can usually be reduced with treatment. The lack of benefit seen in the review may be due to various factors, and further research is needed to determine the most appropriate interventions for older adults with unreported impairment of vision.

title: Protein interaction network of the mammalian Hippo pathway reveals mechanisms of kinase-phosphatase interactions.
text:
The Hippo signaling pathway regulates organ size and tissue homeostasis in response to various stimuli, including cell density and mechanosignaling. Pharmacological inhibition of phosphatases can also activate Hippo signaling in cell culture. To comprehensively map the Hippo protein-protein interaction network, we used okadaic acid to inhibit serine and threonine phosphatases and identified 749 protein interactions, including 599 previously unrecognized interactions. Our findings revealed that several interactions with phosphatases were phosphorylation-dependent and provided insights into the mechanism of Hippo pathway regulation.
We found that mutations in the T-loop of MST2 (mammalian STE20-like protein kinase 2), which prevented autophosphorylation, disrupted its association with STRIPAK (striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase complex). Deletion of the amino-terminal forkhead-associated domain of SLMAP (sarcolemmal membrane-associated protein), a component of the STRIPAK complex, prevented its association with MST1 and MST2. Phosphatase inhibition led to temporally distinct changes in proteins that interacted with MOB1A and MOB1B (Mps one binder kinase activator-like 1A and 1B) and promoted interactions with upstream Hippo pathway proteins, such as MST1 and MST2, and with the trimeric protein phosphatase 6 complex (PP6). Furthermore, mutation of three basic amino acids in the phospho-serine- and phospho-threonine-binding domain of human MOB1B prevented its interaction with MST1 and PP6 in cells treated with okadaic acid.
Our results suggest that changes in phosphorylation orchestrate interactions between kinases and phosphatases in Hippo signaling, providing a potential mechanism for pathway regulation. This study provides a comprehensive view of the Hippo protein-protein interaction network and highlights the importance of phosphorylation-dependent interactions in regulating Hippo signaling.

title: Differential Effects of N-Acetylcysteine, Theophylline or Bicarbonate on Contrast-Induced Rat Renal Vasoconstriction
text:
Background: Vasoconstriction and the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) following contrast media (CM) injection are key factors in the development of CM-induced nephropathy. To investigate the effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC), theophylline, or sodium bicarbonate on intrarenal vasoconstriction and ROS generation in a rat model of CM-induced nephropathy, we conducted a study.
Methods: Following a 3-day dehydration, Sprague-Dawley rats received CM (Telebrix) or sham 'CM' injection of 0.9% saline. Some of the rats received NAC, theophylline, or bicarbonate before the CM injection. Medullary renal blood flow was measured using laser Doppler. The animals were sacrificed 1, 15, or 30 minutes after the treatments, and their kidneys were removed for the assessment of intrarenal STAT-8 isoprostane, prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), and nitric oxide (NO) levels.
Results: NAC significantly attenuated vasoconstriction, while theophylline only mildly attenuated the perfusion drop at 15 minutes and was ineffective after 30 minutes. Unlike theophylline or bicarbonate, NAC significantly increased intrarenal PGE2 levels. NAC, theophylline, but not bicarbonate, gradually increased intrarenal NO levels. CM-induced ROS accumulation, as measured by STAT-8 isoprostane levels, progressed undisturbed in all experimental variables.
Conclusions: (1) CM-induced intrarenal vasoconstriction was efficiently prohibited by NAC but not bicarbonate or theophylline; (2) the vasodilatory effect of NAC was mediated via increased PGE2 synthesis; and (3) ROS accumulation was a primary renal response to CM-induced injury, not affected by any pharmacologic manipulations.

title: Induction of AMPK activity corrects early pathophysiological alterations in the subtotal nephrectomy model of chronic kidney disease.
text: The most commonly used model for studying nondiabetic chronic kidney disease (CKD) is the rat kidney ablation and infarction (A/I) model, which involves the removal of 5/6 of the kidney. At one week post-injury, the A/I kidney exhibits decreased kidney function and metabolic efficiency, as evidenced by lower glomerular filtration rate and oxygen consumption per sodium transport (QO2/TNa). Contrary to expectations, we found that AMPK activity in this model decreases over time, despite the progression of kidney damage. However, we found that inducing AMPK activity through the use of metformin or 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide can increase AMPK activity, improve kidney metabolic efficiency, and ameliorate kidney fibrosis and structural alterations. Our findings suggest that AMPK activity is reduced in the subtotal nephrectomy model of nondiabetic CKD, and that restoration of AMPK activity may prove an effective therapeutic target for the treatment of nondiabetic CKD.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging for volume estimation of large multinodular goitres: a comparison with scintigraphy.
text: In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in non-surgical treatments for reducing the size of large multinodular goitres. To evaluate the accuracy of magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for volume estimation in this context, 20 patients with a multinodular goitre larger than 100 ml were studied using both MR and scintigraphic (SC) imaging methods. The intraobserver and interobserver coefficients of variation (CV) for MR measurements were found to be 2.2% and 4.1%, respectively, indicating high precision. In contrast, the intraobserver and interobserver CVs for SC measurements were 7.5% and 10.1%, respectively, indicating lower precision. The correlation between the two methods was weak (r = 0.665), resulting in a combined CV of 17.3% for SC measurements. The study concluded that MR imaging can be used for in vivo thyroid volume estimation in large multinodular goitres, offering a more precise and detailed assessment of thyroid growth and mechanical complications compared to SC imaging.

title: Differential role of CbpA and PspA in modulation of in vitro CXC chemokine responses of respiratory epithelial cells to infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae.
text: Respiratory epithelial cells play a crucial role in the host response to respiratory pathogens, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, by releasing chemokines that attract neutrophils. To investigate the specific virulence factors of S. pneumoniae that trigger chemokine production, researchers infected epithelial cell lines (A549 and Detroit-562) with wild-type S. pneumoniae or mutants lacking certain virulence factors. The results showed that the choline-binding protein A (CbpA) and pneumococcal surface protein A (PspA) play distinct roles in regulating chemokine production. Infection with a CbpA deletion mutant (DeltaCbpA) led to a twofold increase in chemokine production, suggesting that CbpA inhibits chemokine induction. Similarly, infection with a PspA deletion mutant (DeltaPspA) resulted in a twofold decrease in chemokine production from A549 cells, but not Detroit-562 cells. Deletion of the N-terminal alpha-helical domain of PspA reduced the ability of S. pneumoniae to elicit a chemokine response, indicating that the N termini of CbpA and PspA have different effects on chemokine induction. These findings suggest that the N termini of these proteins exert differential effects on epithelial cells infected with S. pneumoniae, highlighting the complex interplay between pathogens and host cells during respiratory infections.

title: HIV-1 therapy with monoclonal antibody 3BNC117 elicits host immune responses against HIV-1
text: 3BNC117 is a broad and potent neutralizing antibody against HIV-1 that targets the CD4 binding site on the viral envelope spike. When administered passively, this antibody has been shown to prevent infection in animal models and suppress viremia in HIV-1–infected individuals. In this study, we investigate the effects of HIV-1 immunotherapy with a single injection of 3BNC117 on host antibody responses in viremic individuals. Our findings reveal that compared to untreated controls, 3BNC117 infusion significantly improves neutralizing responses to heterologous tier 2 viruses in nearly all study participants. These results suggest that 3BNC117-mediated immunotherapy enhances host humoral immunity to HIV-1.

title: Safety and efficacy of RNAi therapy for transthyretin amyloidosis.
text:
Transthyretin amyloidosis is caused by the accumulation of abnormal transthyretin proteins in the peripheral nerves and heart. A potential treatment approach is RNA interference (RNAi), which can reduce the production of transthyretin. In this study, we evaluated two RNAi formulations, ALN-TTR01 and ALN-TTR02, in patients with transthyretin amyloidosis and healthy volunteers.
We found that both formulations resulted in rapid and sustained reductions in transthyretin levels, with the highest dose of ALN-TTR01 reducing transthyretin levels by 38% compared to placebo (P=0.01). ALN-TTR02 showed similar reductions in transthyretin levels across different doses, with a mean reduction of 82-86% at 28 days (P<0.001 for all comparisons). These reductions were confirmed to be RNAi-mediated. While mild-to-moderate infusion-related reactions occurred in some participants, the overall safety profile was manageable.
Our findings demonstrate the potential of RNAi therapy targeting transthyretin messenger RNA to treat transthyretin amyloidosis. Further studies are needed to confirm these results and to determine the long-term safety and efficacy of this approach. (Funded by Alnylam Pharmaceuticals; ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT01148953 and NCT01559077.)

title: The mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 is inhibited by the peptide GsMTx4.
text: Cells can respond to mechanical stress by activating mechanosensitive ion channels (MSCs), which are crucial for cellular sensing and signaling. The cloning of Piezo1, a eukaryotic cation selective MSC, has enabled the study of mechanical transduction at the cellular level. Since Piezo1 shares electrophysiological properties with endogenous cationic MSCs, we investigated whether the peptide GsMTx4 targets Piezo1 activity. Our results show that extracellular GsMTx4 inhibited ∼80% of the mechanically induced current from transfected HEK293 cells with micromolar concentrations, and this inhibition was voltage insensitive. The binding and unbinding rate constants were found to be 7.0 × 10(5) M(-1) s(-1) and 0.11 s(-1), respectively, with a K(D) of ∼155 nM, similar to values reported for endogenous MSCs. GsMTx4 exhibited gating modifier behavior, shifting the pressure-gating curve to the right by ∼30 mmHg, and was active on closed channels. In contrast, streptomycin, a nonspecific inhibitor of cationic MSCs, showed use-dependent inhibition characteristic of open channel block. GsMTx4 did not block currents of the mechanical channel TREK-1 on outside-out patches. Whole-cell Piezo1 currents were also reversibly inhibited by GsMTx4, with similar on and off rates. These findings support the use of Piezo1 in high-throughput screens for pharmacological agents and diagnostic assays.

title: Thiazolidinediones improve beta-cell function in type 2 diabetic patients.
text:
Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) have been shown to improve glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Recent in vivo and in vitro studies have also suggested that TZDs may improve pancreatic beta-cell function. To investigate this further, we conducted a study in which T2DM patients were randomized to receive either a placebo or TZD treatment for 4 months.
We found that TZD treatment significantly improved fasting plasma glucose (FPG), mean plasma glucose during oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT), HbA1c, and insulin-mediated total body glucose disposal (Rd) in all TZD-treated groups, compared to the placebo groups. Additionally, TZD treatment significantly improved the insulin secretion/insulin resistance (disposition) index, which is a measure of the balance between insulin secretion and insulin resistance. This improvement was observed in all TZD-treated groups, regardless of their baseline insulin therapy.
Interestingly, we found that improved insulin secretion correlated positively with increased body weight, fat mass, and Rd, and inversely with decreased plasma glucose and free fatty acid (FFA) levels during OGTT. These findings suggest that TZDs may improve beta-cell function by promoting the growth and function of pancreatic beta cells.
In conclusion, our study provides evidence that TZD treatment leads to improved beta-cell function in T2DM patients, which is strongly correlated with improved glycemic control. These findings support the use of TZDs as a treatment for T2DM, particularly in patients who are obese or have a high risk of developing insulin resistance.

title: A novel Ku70 function in colorectal homeostasis separate from nonhomologous end joining
text: Ku70, a nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) factor, also plays a role in tumor suppression, although the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Previous studies showed that mice lacking DNA ligase IV (Lig4), another key NHEJ factor, developed aggressive lymphoma in the absence of tumor suppressor p53. However, introducing a hypomorphic mutant p53R172P, which impaired p53-mediated apoptosis but not cell-cycle arrest, abrogated the tumor phenotype in Lig4-deficient mice. Surprisingly, when we bred Ku70-deficient mice with p53R172P mice, the mice were free of diabetes, despite 80% of the mutant mice having enlarged colons with pronounced inflammation. Remarkably, most of these mutant mice progressed to dysplasia, adenoma, and adenocarcinoma, suggesting an NHEJ-independent function of Ku70. In contrast to Lig4-deficient mice, Ku70-deficient mice showed nuclear stabilization of β-catenin, higher expression of cyclin D1 and c-Myc in affected colon sections, and this phenotype was not due to the p53 mutation. Our findings not only uncover a novel function of Ku70 in colon homeostasis but also provide an excellent in vivo model to study how chronic inflammation and abnormal cellular proliferation contribute to tumorigenesis and tumor progression in the colon.

title: Association of Sickle Cell Trait With Hemoglobin A1c in African Americans
text: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between sickle cell trait (SCT) and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels among African Americans. The study included 4620 participants from two community-based cohorts, with a mean age of 52.3 years and 61.3% of participants being women. The study found that participants with SCT had lower HbA1c levels compared to those without SCT, even after adjusting for key risk factors. Specifically, for a given fasting glucose level, HbA1c values were statistically significantly lower in those with SCT (5.72%) compared to those without (6.01%). The difference in HbA1c levels was greater at higher fasting and 2-hour glucose concentrations. Additionally, the prevalence of prediabetes and diabetes was lower among participants with SCT when defined using HbA1c values. These findings suggest that HbA1c may underestimate past glycemia in black patients with SCT and require further evaluation.

title: PGAP2 mutations, affecting the GPI-anchor-synthesis pathway, cause hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome.
text:
Recently, mutations in genes involved in the synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor have been identified in a new group of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDGs) with distinct clinical features. To date, mutations have been found in six genes (PIGA, PIGL, PIGM, PIGN, PIGO, and PIGV) encoding proteins in the GPI-anchor synthesis pathway in individuals with severe neurological symptoms, including seizures, muscular hypotonia, and intellectual disability.
We developed a diagnostic gene panel targeting all known genes encoding proteins in the GPI-anchor synthesis pathway to screen individuals with these features, and detected three missense mutations in PGAP2 (c.46C>T, c.380T>C, and c.479C>T) in two unrelated individuals with hyperphosphatasia with mental retardation syndrome (HPMRS). The mutations were found to cosegregate in the investigated families. PGAP2 is involved in fatty-acid GPI-anchor remodeling, which occurs in the Golgi apparatus and is essential for stable association between GPI-anchored proteins and the cell-surface membrane rafts.
To further investigate the role of PGAP2 in HPMRS, we transfected altered protein constructs (p. Arg16Trp, p. Leu127Ser, and p. Thr160Ile) into PGAP2-null cells. While these constructs partially restored GPI-anchored marker proteins CD55 and CD59 on the cell surface, our findings suggest that an impairment in GPI-anchor remodeling is a key factor in the development of HPMRS.
Our study demonstrates that targeted sequencing of genes encoding proteins in the GPI-anchor synthesis pathway is a valuable diagnostic approach for this subgroup of CDGs.
