This approach can help identify individuals with HPMRS and other CDGs, and may lead to a better understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms and the development of new therapeutic strategies.

title: Screening for Lung Cancer: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
text:
The USPSTF (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force) recommends annual screening for lung cancer in adults aged 55-80 who have a 30 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years. This recommendation is based on the evidence of both the benefits and harms of screening, as well as an assessment of the balance between the two. The USPSTF does not consider the cost of providing screening in this assessment. Clinicians should understand the evidence but individualize decision-making to the specific patient or situation.
The USPSTF recognizes that clinical decisions involve more considerations than evidence alone. Similarly, the USPSTF notes that policy and coverage decisions involve considerations in addition to the evidence of clinical benefits and harms.
The benefits of lung cancer screening include:
* Preventing a substantial number of lung cancer-related deaths in persons at high risk
* Direct evidence from a large, well-conducted, randomized, controlled trial (RCT) provides moderate certainty of the benefit of lung cancer screening with LDCT in this population
* The magnitude of benefit to the person depends on that person's risk for lung cancer, as those who are at highest risk are most likely to benefit

The harms of lung cancer screening include:
* False-negative and false-positive results
* Incidental findings
* Overdiagnosis of lung cancer
* Radiation exposure
The USPSTF assessment found moderate certainty that annual screening for lung cancer with LDCT is of moderate net benefit in asymptomatic persons who are at high risk for lung cancer based on age, total cumulative exposure to tobacco smoke, and years since quitting smoking. The moderate net benefit of screening depends on limiting screening to persons who are at high risk, the accuracy of image interpretation being similar to that found in the NLST (National Lung Screening Trial), and the resolution of most false-positive results without invasive procedures.
Clinical considerations include:
* Patient population under consideration: the risk for lung cancer increases with age and cumulative exposure to tobacco smoke and decreases with time since quitting smoking
* Screening tests: low-dose computed tomography has shown high sensitivity and acceptable specificity for the detection of lung cancer in high-risk persons
* Treatment: surgical resection is the current standard of care for localized NSCLC. This type of cancer is treated with surgical resection when possible and also with radiation and chemotherapy.
* Other approaches to prevention: smoking cessation is the most important intervention to prevent NSCLC. Advising smokers to stop smoking and preventing nonsmokers from being exposed to tobacco smoke are the most effective ways to decrease the morbidity and mortality associated with lung cancer. Current smokers should be informed of their continuing risk for lung cancer and offered cessation treatments. Screening with LDCT should be viewed as an adjunct to tobacco cessation interventions.

Useful resources for smoking cessation include the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) website, which provides information on tobacco quit lines and other resources available in several languages.

title: Dual role of interleukin-10 in the regulation of respiratory syncitial virus (RSV)-induced lung inflammation.
text:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) are among the most common reasons for hospitalization in children, causing acute respiratory failure and sequelae such as secondary bacterial infections and reactive airway disease. One host response observed in severe RSV-induced LRTI and/or subsequent development of asthma is increased expression of interleukin (IL)-10. However, conflicting results have been reported regarding the role of IL-10 in regulating the host response to RSV LRTI, with some studies suggesting that IL-10 inhibits asthmatic responses, while others suggest that it intensifies the disease. To reconcile these discordant observations, we used a lung-specific, inducible IL-10 over-expression (OE) transgenic mouse model to investigate the role of IL-10 in regulating the host response to RSV LRTI.
Our results showed that the presence of IL-10 at the time of RSV infection not only attenuated acute inflammatory responses (within 24 hours post-infection), but also late inflammatory changes (characterized by Th2 cytokine and chemokine expression). However, when IL-10 OE was delayed until the late immune response to RSV infection, additive effects rather than inhibitory effects were observed. Interestingly, in non-infected IL-10 OE mice, IL-10 OE alone induced up-regulation of Th2 cytokine and Th2-related chemokine expression. We identified a subset of CD11b(+)CD11c(+)CD49b(+)F4/80(-)Gr-1(-) myeloid cells as the principal source of IL-10-induced IL-13 production. Therefore, the augmented pathological responses observed in our 'delayed' IL-10 over-expression model could be attributed to IL-10 OE alone.
Our study suggests that IL-10 has dual roles in regulating RSV-induced lung inflammation, which appear to depend on the timing of when elevated IL-10 is expressed in the lung. These findings may have implications for the development of novel therapies for RSV-induced LRTI and asthma.

title: Latent membrane protein 1 of Epstein–Barr virus coordinately regulates proliferation with control of apoptosis
text: Latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1), an oncogenic protein encoded by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), functions as a constitutively active receptor in the membrane of infected B cells. LMP1 plays a critical role in the induction and maintenance of B cell proliferation, and its signaling pathways mimic those of the CD40 receptor. To investigate the immediate-early cellular target genes regulated by LMP1, we generated a conditional LMP1 allele within the context of the intact EBV genome. Our findings revealed that LMP1 specifically induces mitogenic B cell activation through c-Myc and Jun/AP1 family members, and confirmed its direct role in upregulating the expression of multiple genes involved in cell survival. Notably, LMP1's signals are essential for the G1/S transition in human B cells, and cells lacking these signals are cell cycle arrested and survive quiescently. Our results suggest that LMP1's activities are not required to maintain survival in non-proliferating cells, as it induces both pro- and anti-apoptotic genes whose balance allows for survival during LMP1-mediated proliferation.

title: Crizotinib in ROS1-rearranged non-small-cell lung cancer.
text:
Background: Chromosomal rearrangements of the ROS1 proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase (ROS1) gene have been identified as a distinct molecular subgroup of non-small-cell lung cancers (NSCLCs). These rearrangements may confer sensitivity to ROS1 kinase inhibition, making ROS1-targeted therapies a promising treatment option.
Methods: In an expansion cohort of a phase 1 study, 50 patients with advanced NSCLC who tested positive for ROS1 rearrangement were treated with the small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor crizotinib at a standard oral dose of 250 mg twice daily. Safety, pharmacokinetics, and response to therapy were evaluated. ROS1 fusion partners were identified using next-generation sequencing or reverse-transcriptase-polymerase-chain-reaction assays.
Results: The objective response rate was 72% (95% confidence interval [CI], 58-84), with 3 complete responses and 33 partial responses. The median duration of response was 17.6 months (95% CI, 14.5-not reached), and median progression-free survival was 19.2 months (95% CI, 14.4-not reached), with 25 patients (50%) still in follow-up for progression. Seven ROS1 fusion partners were identified, including 5 known and 2 novel partner genes. No correlation was observed between the type of ROS1 rearrangement and the clinical response to crizotinib. The safety profile of crizotinib was similar to that seen in patients with ALK-rearranged NSCLC.
Conclusions: These findings suggest that crizotinib is highly active in patients with advanced ROS1-rearranged NSCLC, defining a second molecular subgroup of NSCLC for which ROS1-targeted therapies may be effective. Further studies are needed to confirm these results and to determine the long-term safety and efficacy of crizotinib in this patient population. (Funded by Pfizer and others; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00585195.)

title: The S. cerevisiae Rrm3p DNA helicase moves with the replication fork and affects replication of all yeast chromosomes.
text: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae DNA helicase Rrm3p is crucial for the normal progression of DNA replication through over 1000 discrete sites throughout the genome. Our findings show that the replication of all yeast chromosomes is significantly delayed in rrm3 cells, even in regions without any predicted Rrm3p-dependent sites. Interestingly, the rate of fork movement in rrm3 cells appears similar to wild-type except at known Rrm3p-dependent sites, suggesting that while Rrm3p has a global role in DNA replication, its activity is primarily required at specific, challenging-to-replicate sites. Using chromatin immunoprecipitation, we found that Rrm3p is associated with both Rrm3p-dependent and -independent sites and moves with the replication fork through both. Furthermore, we discovered that Rrm3p interacts with Pol2p, the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon, in vivo, indicating that Rrm3p is an integral part of the replication fork apparatus rather than simply being recruited to its sites of action when replication forks stall at these sites.

title: The pathophysiology of protein-overload proteinuria.
text:
In a rat model of protein overload nephrosis induced by intraperitoneal administration of bovine serum albumin (BSA), alterations in glomerular function and structure were investigated using fractional clearance studies with inulin and tracer proteins of different molecular size and charge. The results showed:
1. Unchanged glomerular filtration rate and renal plasma flow in proteinuric rats.
2. A 34-fold increase in the fractional clearance of rat serum albumin (C/GFR), reaching values similar to BSA.
3. A 2-fold increase in C/GFR for anionic horse radish peroxidase (HRP), but normal values for neutral and cationic HRP.
4. An 11- and 3-fold increase in the C/GFR for heterologous IgG and IgM, respectively.
Glomerular epithelial cells showed degenerative changes, but the distribution of anionic sites in the glomerular basement membrane was found to be unaltered, as determined by polyethyleneimine binding studies. In summary, an elevation of serum albumin concentration led to increased transcapillary albumin transport, which resulted in degenerative changes in glomerular epithelial cells and the development of large pore defects. These changes were completely reversible.

title: Effects of aging on central and peripheral mammalian clocks.
text: The circadian organization undergoes changes with age, yet the extent to which these alterations are due to modifications in the central pacemakers, peripheral oscillators, or coupling mechanisms that maintain the system remains unclear. To investigate the effects of aging on the rhythmic expression of the Period 1 (Per1) gene in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and peripheral tissues, we employed transgenic rats with a luciferase (luc) reporter. Young (2 months) and aged (24-26 months) Per1-luc transgenic rats, entrained to light-dark cycles, were sacrificed, and tissues were isolated and cultured. Per1-luc expression was measured in 10 tissues. In the SCN, the central mammalian pacemaker, Per1-luc expression exhibited robust rhythmicity for over 7 weeks in culture. The only notable difference between SCN rhythmicity in young and old rats was a slight but statistically significant shortening of the free-running period with aging. Circadian rhythmicity in some peripheral tissues remained unchanged by aging, while others displayed phase advancements relative to the light cycle or were completely arrhythmic. Interestingly, these arrhythmic tissues could be induced to oscillate by application of forskolin, suggesting that they retained the capacity to oscillate but were not being appropriately driven in vivo. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the effects of aging on the mammalian circadian system, suggesting that aging affects rhythms in some but not all tissues, and may primarily act on interactions among circadian oscillators, potentially attenuating the ability of the SCN to drive damped oscillators in the periphery.

title: CtBP3/BARS drives membrane fission in dynamin-independent transport pathways
text: Membrane fission is a crucial process in membrane transport, and until now, the only protein machinery known to be involved in in vivo transport is dynamin. However, our findings suggest that other fission mechanisms may exist. Here, we demonstrate that carboxy-terminal binding protein 3/brefeldin A-ribosylated substrate (CtBP3/BARS) regulates fission in basolateral transport from the Golgi to the plasma membrane and in fluid-phase endocytosis, whereas dynamin is not involved in these steps. Conversely, CtBP3/BARS is inactive in apical transport to the plasma membrane and in receptor-mediated endocytosis, which are controlled by dynamin. These findings indicate that CtBP3/BARS regulates membrane fission in both endocytic and exocytic transport pathways, distinct from those that require dynamin.

title: Influenza A myocarditis developing in an adult liver transplant recipient despite vaccination: a case report and review of the literature.
text: Individuals who have undergone solid organ transplants and are taking chronic immunosuppressive drugs are at a higher risk of contracting the influenza virus even after being vaccinated. Myocarditis, a rare but known complication of influenza infection, can occur in these individuals. We present the first case of an adult liver transplant recipient who received prophylactic vaccination but still developed influenza A myocarditis. This highlights the potential vulnerability of solid organ transplant recipients to infections, as they often have a reduced response to protein-based vaccines. Further research is needed to determine if administering antiviral chemoprophylaxis to solid organ transplant recipients during the influenza season would be an effective preventive measure against influenza in this high-risk population.

title: Extrapulmonary effects of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on physical activity: a cross-sectional study.
text:
The study aimed to investigate the relationship between extrapulmonary effects of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and its comorbidities with reduced physical activity in patients with COPD. The study included 170 outpatients with COPD (GOLD stages I-IV and BODE score 0-10) who wore a multisensor accelerometer armband to measure their physical activity over 5-6 consecutive days. In addition to assessing cardiovascular status using echocardiography, vascular Doppler sonography, and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels, the study also evaluated mental status, metabolic/muscular status, systemic inflammation, and anemia using Beck Depression Inventory, bioelectrical impedance analysis, handgrip strength, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein/fibrinogen, and hemoglobin levels, respectively.
The results showed that in a multivariate linear regression analysis, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels, echocardiographically measured left ventricular diastolic function, and systemic inflammation were independently associated with reduced physical activity in patients with COPD. These findings suggest that higher values of systemic inflammation and left cardiac dysfunction are associated with reduced physical activity in patients with COPD.
In conclusion, the study highlights the importance of considering the extrapulmonary effects of COPD and its comorbidities when assessing physical activity in patients with COPD. The findings suggest that measuring systemic inflammation and left cardiac function may help identify patients with COPD who are at risk of reduced physical activity, which can have a significant impact on their quality of life and overall health.

title: Cleavage efficient 2A peptides for high level monoclonal antibody expression in CHO cells.
text: Linking the heavy chain (HC) and light chain (LC) genes using a single cassette with 2A peptides allows for control of the LC and HC ratio and reduction of non-expressing cells. In this study, four different 2A peptides derived from foot-and-mouth disease virus (F2A), equine rhinitis A virus (E2A), porcine teschovirus-1 (P2A), and Thosea asigna virus (T2A) were compared for their ability to express three biosimilar IgG1 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell lines. The HC and LC were linked using different 2A peptides both in the absence and presence of GSG linkers. The insertion of a furin recognition site upstream of 2A allowed for the removal of 2A residues that would otherwise be attached to the HC. The study found that different 2A peptides exhibited different cleavage efficiencies, which correlated with the mAb expression level. The relative cleavage efficiency of each 2A peptide remained similar for the expression of different IgG1 mAbs in different CHO cells. While complete cleavage was not observed for any of the 2A peptides, GSG linkers did enhance the cleavage efficiency and thus the mAb expression level. The T2A peptide with a GSG linker (GT2A) exhibited the highest cleavage efficiency and mAb expression level. Stably amplified CHO DG44 pools generated using GT2A had titers of 357, 416, and 600 mg/L for the three mAbs in shake flask batch cultures. Incomplete cleavage likely resulted in incorrectly processed mAb species and aggregates, which were removed through a chromatin-directed clarification method and protein A purification. The vector and methods presented provide an easy process that is beneficial for both mAb development and manufacturing.

title: The complexity of human ribosome biogenesis revealed by systematic nucleolar screening of Pre-rRNA processing factors.
text: Mature ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are generated from polycistronic precursors through a complex processing scheme. Previous studies have extensively characterized rRNA processing in yeast and assumed conservation in humans. To functionally characterize the human rRNA processing machinery, we identified and characterized 625 nucleolar proteins in HeLa cells, of which 286 were essential for processing. Notably, 74 of these proteins lacked a yeast homolog, indicating unique strategies and recruitment of distinct trans-acting factors in human cells. We demonstrated that defects in pre-rRNA processing are conserved across different cell types, including primary cells, and are not due to activation of a p53-dependent nucleolar tumor surveillance pathway. Furthermore, we found that 3' end maturation of 18S rRNA involves the yeast ITS2 processing factor EXOSC10/Rrp6, highlighting the importance of this factor in human rRNA processing. Our findings have significant implications for understanding ribosomopathies at the molecular level and developing effective therapeutic agents.

title: Maximal aerobic capacity in African-American and Caucasian prepubertal children.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate differences in resting, submaximal, and maximal oxygen consumption (VO2) between African-American (n = 44) and Caucasian (n = 31) prepubertal children aged 5-10 years. VO2 was measured using indirect calorimetry in the fasted state, and submaximal and maximal VO2 were determined during a treadmill exercise test. The study also measured total fat mass (FM), soft lean tissue mass (LTM), and leg soft LTM using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, and total energy expenditure (TEE) and activity energy expenditure (AEE) using doubly labeled water. The results showed a significant effect of ethnicity on VO2max, with African-American children having an approximately 15% lower VO2max than Caucasian children (1.21 ± 0.032 vs. 1.43 ± 0.031 l/min, respectively). This lower VO2max persisted after adjusting for soft LTM, FM, leg LTM, TEE, and AEE. In conclusion, the study found that African-American and Caucasian children have similar VO2 levels at rest and during submaximal exercise, but VO2max is lower in African-American children, independent of various factors.

title: Penaeus monodon Dscam (PmDscam) has a highly diverse cytoplasmic tail and is the first membrane-bound shrimp Dscam to be reported.
text: The Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule (Dscam) is likely to play a crucial role in the "alternative adaptive immunity" observed in invertebrates. Dscam consists of a cytoplasmic tail involved in signal transduction and a highly variable extracellular region that may utilize a pathogen recognition mechanism similar to that of vertebrate antibodies. In a previous study, we isolated a unique tail-less form of Dscam from Litopenaeus vannamei. In this investigation, we report the first membrane-bound form of shrimp Dscam, PmDscam, which was isolated from Penaeus monodon. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that crustacean Dscams from shrimp and water fleas do not share a single subclade, but are distinct from invertebrate Dscam-like molecules and insect Dscams. The extracellular regions of PmDscam were located in N-terminal Ig2, N-terminal Ig3, and the entire Ig7 domain. The PmDscam extracellular variants and transmembrane domain variants were generated through mutually exclusive alternative splicing events, while the cytoplasmic tail variants were produced by exon inclusion/exclusion. Based on the genomic organization of Daphnia Dscam's cytoplasmic tail, we propose a model for how the shrimp Dscam genomic locus may use Type III polyadenylation to produce both tail-less and membrane-bound forms.

title: The different biological effects of telomestatin and TMPyP4 can be attributed to their selectivity for interaction with intramolecular or intermolecular G-quadruplex structures.
text: The existence of G-quadruplex structures in telomeres of Stylonychia macronuclei and the promoter of c-myc in human cells has been validated as potential targets for drug design. However, the next crucial step is to determine the selectivity of G-quadruplex-interactive agents for different types of G-quadruplex structures. In this study, we have investigated the selectivity of telomestatin, a natural product isolated from Streptomyces anulatus 3533-SV4, for intramolecular and intermolecular G-quadruplex structures formed in telomeres. Our results demonstrate that telomestatin interacts preferentially with intramolecular G-quadruplex structures and shows a 70-fold selectivity for intramolecular structures over duplex DNA. Importantly, telomestatin stabilizes G-quadruplex structures in the absence of monovalent cations, which is a unique characteristic among G-quadruplex-interactive compounds. At noncytotoxic concentrations, telomestatin suppresses the proliferation of telomerase-positive cells within several weeks. In contrast, TMPyP4, a compound that preferentially facilitates the formation of intermolecular G-quadruplex structures, suppresses the proliferation of alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT)-positive cells as well as telomerase-positive cells. We have also shown that TMPyP4 induces anaphase bridges in sea urchin embryos, whereas telomestatin did not have this effect, highlighting the importance of the selectivity of these compounds for different types of G-quadruplex structures in mediating distinct biological effects. Specifically, stabilization of intramolecular G-quadruplex structures produces telomerase inhibition and accelerated telomere shortening, whereas facilitation of the formation of intermolecular G-quadruplex structures induces the formation of anaphase bridges.

title: Targeting oxidative stress to treat endometriosis.
text:
Endometriosis, a condition affecting 10% of women of reproductive age, is characterized by the presence of implanted endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. Despite its prevalence, the underlying pathophysiology of endometriosis remains unclear, with various theories proposed. Given its frequency, there is a pressing need for a novel treatment approach. Recent studies have shed light on the pathological characteristics of endometriosis, revealing a vicious cycle involving oxidative stress (OS) and the implantation of ectopic endometrium. This cycle is further exacerbated by the generation of high levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which also contribute to OS.
The current review examines the evidence linking OS and endometriosis, and explores potential antioxidant agents that have been investigated specifically in endometriosis patients. These include vitamins C and E, melatonin, resveratrol, xanthohumol, and epigallocatechin-3-gallate. The review reveals a significant effect of these antioxidants on endometriosis.
While aiming to reduce OS as a treatment goal for endometriosis appears promising, most studies are either in vitro or animal-based, highlighting the need for further research in human subjects to fully elucidate the impact of OS reduction on patients with endometriosis.

title: Interferon alpha for the treatment of chronic hepatitis C in patients infected with human immunodeficiency virus. Hepatitis-HIV Spanish Study Group.
text:
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in individuals who have been infected parenterally with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) such as injection drug users, hemophiliacs, and transfused patients is a growing cause of morbidity and mortality. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of interferon (IFN) alpha therapy in these patients and identified predictors of response to this treatment.
A total of 119 patients with chronic hepatitis C (90 of whom were infected with HIV and 29 of whom were not) were included in a multicenter, prospective, open, non-randomized observational study. IFN-alpha was given subcutaneously in a dosage of 5 million units three times a week for 3 months, followed by a dose of 3 million units given subcutaneously three times a week for an additional 9 months. Complete response, defined as normalization of aminotransferases and negative HCV RNA in the blood, was observed in 26 (32.5%) of 80 HIV-infected patients and 10 (37.0%) of 27 non-HIV-infected patients (P = .666) after completion of the treatment.
Two variables were independently associated with a response in HIV-infected patients: a CD4+ T lymphocyte count of > 500 x 10(6)/L and a baseline HCV viremia level of < 10(7) copies/mL. Relapses occurred in 30.8% of the HIV-infected patients and 12.5% of non-HIV-infected patients (P = .403) in the 12 months following treatment.
In conclusion, IFN-alpha therapy was found to be effective in reducing HCV viral load in a subset of HIV-infected patients, but the response rate was lower compared to non-HIV-infected patients. The identification of predictors of response to IFN-alpha therapy may help guide treatment decisions in this patient population.

title: Vanishing cerebellar infarcts in a migraine patient.
text: Recent studies have suggested that migraine may be a risk factor for the development of infarct-like lesions in the posterior circulation territory. These lesions are thought to be true vascular infarcts based on their size, location, and MRI characteristics. However, since there have been no postmortem studies to identify the pathology of these MRI findings, the true cause of these lesions remains unknown. A case of a patient with migraine is presented, who developed MRI-visible cerebellar infarcts, but these lesions disappeared 16 days later, raising questions about their vascular ischemic origin.

title: A novel viral transcript with homology to human interleukin-10 is expressed during latent human cytomegalovirus infection.
text:
Human cytomegalovirus (CMV) establishes latent infections in hematopoietic cells, such as granulocyte-macrophage progenitors (GM-Ps), where the virus is sequestered in a non-replicating state. While limited transcriptional activity has been reported during latency, the study aimed to further investigate viral gene expression during this phase of infection.
Using an experimental model of latency and primary human GM-Ps, this study latently infected with CMV strain Toledo and extracted RNA subjected to reverse transcription-PCR (RT-PCR) using CMV gene-specific primers. The results showed the detection of transcription from the UL111.5A region of the viral genome, which was also observed in GM-Ps latently infected with AD169 and Towne strains, indicating strain independence. Interestingly, UL111.5A-region transcripts were also detected in mononuclear cells from healthy bone marrow and mobilized peripheral blood allograft donors, indicating expression during natural latent infection.
To further investigate, mapping experiments were conducted using RNA extracted from latently infected GM-Ps, which revealed the expression of a novel UL111.5A region transcript with a splicing pattern distinct from that observed during productive infection of permissive cells. This UL111.5A region transcript is predicted to encode a 139-amino-acid protein with homology to the potent immunosuppressor interleukin-10 (IL-10) and the viral IL-10 homolog expressed during productive CMV infection. The expression of a latency-associated cmvIL-10 may enable the virus to evade immune recognition and clearance during the latent phase of infection.

title: Treatments for somnambulism in adults: assessing the evidence.
text: Somnambulism, or sleepwalking, is a parasomnia that occurs during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, characterized by movement behaviors typically confined to wakefulness. In cases where sleepwalking causes distress or danger despite safety measures, medical or psychological intervention may be necessary. A comprehensive literature review was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and the Ovid Evidence-Based Medicine Reviews (EBM) multifile databases, yielding no high-quality, rigorously controlled trials for the treatment of sleepwalking in adults. Seven reports of small trials with control arms or retrospective case series involving 30 or more patients were found. Given the lack of robust evidence to inform treatment recommendations, a thorough discussion with patients is recommended. Well-designed, adequately powered clinical trials are now needed, and multi-center collaborations may be necessary to obtain the required sample sizes.

title: Premature chromosome condensation: evidence for in vivo cell fusion in human malignant tumours.
text: Premature chromosome condensation (PCC) was investigated in direct tissue preparations from patients with various haematological diseases and carcinomas using the GTG-technique. PCC was observed in 6 out of 166 malignancies (128 haematological cases, 35 carcinomas, and 3 malignant effusions) analysed. Chromosome analysis revealed that PCC occurred in S-phase and G1-phase in each case, with a frequency ranging from 1% to 8.6% of metaphases examined. These findings suggest that PCC chromosomes, which are thought to represent cell fusion in vivo, are not uncommon in naturally occurring human malignancies. Additionally, the authors propose that PCC may contribute to the heterogeneity of tumor cell populations, possibly in conjunction with other factors.

title: Blockade of the angiotensin system improves mental health domain of quality of life: A meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
text:
Objective: To investigate the impact of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) blockers on mental health quality of life in adults without physical symptoms.
Study Design: Meta-analysis of published literature.
Data Sources: PubMed and clinicaltrials.gov databases were searched in January 2017.
Study Selection: Randomized controlled trials comparing ACE inhibitors or AT1R blockers with placebo or other antihypertensive medications were included.
Data Synthesis: Eleven studies were analyzed, showing that ACE inhibitors and AT1R blockers were associated with improved overall quality of life (SMD = 0.11, 95% CI = [0.08, 0.14], p < 0.0001), positive wellbeing (SMD = 0.11, 95% CI = [0.05, 0.17], p < 0.0001), mental (SMD = 0.15, 95% CI = [0.06, 0.25], p < 0.0001), and anxiety (SMD = 0.08, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.16], p < 0.0001) domains of quality of life. However, no significant difference was found in the depression domain (SMD = 0.05, 95% CI = [0.02, 0.12], p = 0.15).
Conclusions: The use of ACE inhibitors and AT1R blockers for the treatment of hypertension in otherwise healthy adults is associated with improved mental health domains of quality of life. Further research is needed to properly evaluate the potential of drugs that block the angiotensin system as a novel psychiatric target.

title: The role of epigenetics in aging and autoimmunity.
text: The decline in immunological competence with age is concurrent with an increase in the incidence of autoimmune diseases. Aging of the immune system, or immunosenescence, is characterized by a decline in both T and B cell function, and paradoxically, the presence of low-grade chronic inflammation. There is a growing body of evidence suggesting that epigenetic modifications, the study of inherited changes in gene expression that are not encoded by the DNA sequence itself, undergo changes with aging. Interestingly, emerging research has implicated a key role for epigenetics in human pathologies, including inflammatory and neoplastic disorders. In this review, we will examine the potential mechanisms that contribute to the increase in autoimmune responses in aging. Specifically, we will explore how epigenetic alterations, particularly DNA methylation and histone acetylation, accumulate during aging and contribute to the risk of autoimmunity.

title: A framework for understanding and targeting residual disease in oncogene-driven solid cancers
text: Molecular targeted therapy has the potential to significantly enhance survival rates in cancer patients. However, achieving complete and sustained responses to targeted therapy remains a challenge, particularly in individuals with advanced-stage solid tumors. Even the most effective targeted treatments often fail to completely eliminate tumors, leading to residual disease and tumor progression that hinders patient survival. To address this challenge, we highlight the need to better comprehend the molecular mechanisms underlying residual disease, with the ultimate goal of designing therapeutic strategies to eradicate or significantly reduce residual disease. This would allow us to transition from temporary disease control to chronic management or, ideally, achieve a cure for patients with advanced-stage solid tumors. Currently, our approach to managing drug resistance focuses on reacting to the emergence of resistance mechanisms after treatment initiation. In contrast, we propose a proactive approach that involves identifying and targeting the underlying mechanisms that lead to residual disease before it becomes a significant problem. By taking a preemptive approach, we may be able to prevent or significantly reduce the development of drug resistance, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes.

title: Long-term inhibition of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 in Alzheimer's prone mice.
text: We investigated the impact of long-term inhibition of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) with sitagliptin on the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) in a transgenic mouse model. We found that daily injections of sitagliptin (at doses of 5, 10, or 20 mg/kg) for 12 weeks significantly improved memory performance in the contextual fear conditioning test. Additionally, sitagliptin increased the levels of the gut hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) in the brain, reduced nitrosative stress and inflammation, and decreased the number and area of amyloid-beta (Aβ) deposits in the brain. The most pronounced effects were observed at the highest dose of 20 mg/kg. Our findings suggest that inhibiting DPP-4 with sitagliptin can delay the progression of AD pathology, including Aβ deposition, when administered early in the disease course of a transgenic mouse model of AD.

title: Structural and mechanistic insights into phospholipid transfer by Ups1–Mdm35 in mitochondria
text: Eukaryotic cells are divided into distinct organelles, each with its own membrane-bound structure, and these organelles rely on the efficient transport of lipids to perform their respective functions. In particular, the Ups1-Mdm35 system plays a crucial role in the transfer of phosphatidic acid (PA) between the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes. To better understand the mechanism of this process, we determined the X-ray structures of Mdm35 and Ups1-Mdm35 with and without PA. Our findings reveal that the Ups1-Mdm35 complex forms a single domain with a unique pocket and flexible lid structure. Through structure-based mutational analysis, we identified key residues that are essential for PA extraction from the membrane upon Ups1 binding. Additionally, we found that the dissociation of Mdm35 enhances Ups1 binding to the membrane, and that basic residues near the pocket entrance are important for both Ups1 binding and PA extraction. These results provide a structural basis for understanding the mechanism of PA transfer between mitochondrial membranes.

title: Redox regulation of cell migration and adhesion.
text: Reactive oxygen species (ROS), particularly hydrogen peroxide, and the proteins that regulate them play crucial roles in the migration and adhesion of cells. Upon stimulation of cell surface receptors with growth factors and chemoattractants, ROS are generated, which transmit signals from the cell surface to key signaling proteins inside the cell. ROS then function within cells to promote migration and also influence the behavior of migrating cells in nonmigrating cells. Hydrogen peroxide has been proposed to act as a chemoattractant in its own right, attracting immune cells to wounds. Our discussion focuses on recent advances in understanding how organisms utilize ROS in the related processes of cell migration and adhesion.

title: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome, Quick Sequential Organ Function Assessment, and Organ Dysfunction: Insights From a Prospective Database of ED Patients With Infection
text:
Background: The recent revision of sepsis definitions has abandoned the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and instead focuses on the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) as a bedside indicator of organ dysfunction. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic impact of SIRS, compare the diagnostic accuracy of SIRS and qSOFA for organ dysfunction, and compare the standard (Sepsis-2) and revised (Sepsis-3) definitions for organ dysfunction in emergency department (ED) patients with infection.
Methods: This prospective study enrolled 8,871 ED patients with presumed infection over a period of 3 years. Sufficient observational data were collected to calculate SIRS, qSOFA, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA), comorbidity, and mortality.
Results: The study found that SIRS was associated with an increased risk of organ dysfunction (relative risk [RR] 3.5) and mortality (odds ratio [OR] 3.2) in patients without organ dysfunction. SIRS and qSOFA showed similar discrimination for organ dysfunction (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.72 vs 0.73). qSOFA was specific but poorly sensitive for organ dysfunction (96.1% and 29.7%, respectively). Mortality for patients with organ dysfunction was similar for Sepsis-2 and Sepsis-3 (12.5% and 11.4%, respectively), although 29% of patients with Sepsis-3 organ dysfunction did not meet Sepsis-2 criteria. Increasing numbers of Sepsis-2 organ system dysfunctions were associated with greater mortality.
Conclusions: The study suggests that SIRS remains a useful marker of organ dysfunction and mortality, and abandoning the concept may be premature. qSOFA showed high specificity but poor sensitivity as a bedside screening method. Although mortality for organ dysfunction was comparable between Sepsis-2 and Sepsis-3, more prognostic and clinical information is conveyed using Sepsis-2 regarding the number and type of organ dysfunctions. The SOFA score may require recalibration.

title: Requirement of NAD and SIR2 for life-span extension by calorie restriction in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: Calorie restriction has been shown to increase lifespan in a wide range of organisms. While it was once thought that reducing oxidative stress through calorie restriction might be the key to slowing aging, the exact mechanism by which this dietary regimen works is still unclear. To investigate, we used yeast as a model organism and experimented with physiological and genetic means to mimic calorie restriction. Our findings revealed a significant extension in lifespan, which was not observed in yeast strains lacking the SIR2 gene (which encodes the anti-aging protein Sir2p) or the NPT1 gene (involved in the synthesis of NAD, the oxidized form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide). These results suggest that the increased longevity induced by calorie restriction is dependent on the activation of Sir2p through NAD.

title: Pathways disrupted in human ALS motor neurons identified through genetic correction of mutant SOD1.
text: Although various genetic mutations have been identified as causative factors in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), the underlying mechanisms by which these mutations affect motor neuron biology remain poorly understood. In this study, we employed a combination of reprogramming and stem cell differentiation techniques, genome engineering, and RNA sequencing to investigate the transcriptional and functional changes that occur in human motor neurons as a result of mutant SOD1. Our findings indicate that mutant SOD1 leads to a distinct transcriptional signature, characterized by increased oxidative stress, impaired mitochondrial function, altered subcellular transport, and activation of the ER stress and unfolded protein response pathways. Functional studies revealed that these pathways are disrupted in a manner dependent on the SOD1 mutation. Moreover, analysis of stem-cell-derived motor neurons from ALS patients harboring a repeat expansion in C9orf72 revealed that some of these changes are more broadly conserved in ALS.

title: Effect of enalapril on 12-year survival and life expectancy in patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction: a follow-up study.
text: In the SOLVD (Studies of Left Ventricular Dysfunction) trials, enalapril reduced mortality in patients with symptomatic left ventricular dysfunction, but not in those with asymptomatic dysfunction. To determine if this mortality reduction was sustained over time, a 12-year follow-up of the SOLVD trials was conducted. The study included 5165 patients who were alive at the end of the original trials. The results showed that treatment with enalapril for 3-4 years led to a significant improvement in survival, with an increase in life expectancy. The hazard ratio for death was 0.90 for the enalapril group compared to the placebo group (95% CI 0.84-0.95, p=0.0003), and the median survival was extended by 9.4 months (95% CI 2.8-16.5, p=0.004). These findings suggest that treatment with enalapril for a longer period of time leads to a sustained improvement in survival in patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

title: TGFbeta/activin/nodal signaling is necessary for the maintenance of pluripotency in human embryonic stem cells.
text:
Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) have the ability to self-renew indefinitely and give rise to cells from all three primary germ layers, yet the signaling pathways that govern their pluripotency are not well understood. To investigate, we focused on the role of TGFbeta superfamily signaling in hESCs, as it plays a key role in early cell fate decisions during embryonic development.
Our findings reveal that in undifferentiated hESCs, the TGFbeta/activin/nodal signaling pathway is activated through the signal transducer SMAD2/3, while the BMP/GDF branch (SMAD1/5) is only active in isolated mitotic cells. Upon early differentiation, SMAD2/3 signaling is decreased, while SMAD1/5 signaling is activated. We found that TGFbeta/activin/nodal signaling is required for the maintenance of undifferentiated hESC markers. Additionally, we show that SMAD2/3 activation is required downstream of WNT signaling, which we previously demonstrated to be sufficient to maintain the undifferentiated state of hESCs. Remarkably, we found that SMAD2/3 signaling is also required to maintain the inner cell mass (from which stem cells are derived) in ex vivo mouse blastocyst cultures.
These findings reveal a crucial role for TGFbeta signaling in the earliest stages of cell fate determination and demonstrate an interconnection between TGFbeta and WNT signaling in these contexts. Our study sheds light on the complex network of signaling pathways that govern the pluripotency of hESCs and has important implications for the understanding of embryonic development and stem cell biology.

title: The structure and expression of a novel gene activated in early mouse embryogenesis.
text: In this study, we have cloned and determined the sequence of the mouse H19 gene. This gene is controlled by two trans-acting loci, raf and Rif, which regulate its expression in adult basal and inducible levels, respectively. By analyzing the sequence and structure of the H19 gene, we found that it is unrelated to the alpha-fetoprotein gene and must have acquired its regulation independently. The H19 gene has a unique structure, consisting of five exons and four small introns. The largest open reading frame of the gene, which encodes a protein of approximately 14 kd, is located within the first large exon and is followed by four ATG codons that may regulate translation initiation. The rest of the gene, which encompasses all five exons, is presumed to be untranslated, with the long 5' untranslated region possibly serving as a regulatory element. Our findings suggest that the gene is activated early during muscle cell differentiation, as demonstrated through experiments using tissue culture cell lines of the mesodermal lineage.

title: Diminished linear growth during intermittent calcitriol therapy in children undergoing CCPD.
text: Intermittent calcitriol therapy has been shown to improve linear growth in children with renal bone disease, with 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D playing a key role in regulating chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation. However, the impact of intermittent calcitriol therapy on linear growth in children is not well understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of intermittent calcitriol therapy on linear growth in 16 pre-pubertal patients with bone biopsy-proven secondary hyperparathyroidism. We found that Z-scores for height did not change during 12 months of daily calcitriol therapy, but Z-scores decreased from -1.8 +/- 0.32 to -2.0 +/- 0.33 during intermittent calcitriol therapy (P < 0.01). The largest reductions in Z-scores were seen in patients who developed adynamic bone lesions after 12 months of treatment. We also found that delta Z-scores for height correlated with serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) and alkaline phosphatase levels during intermittent calcitriol therapy, but not during daily calcitriol therapy. These findings suggest that high-dose intermittent calcitriol therapy may directly inhibit chondrocyte activity within the growth plate cartilage of children with end-stage renal disease, potentially adversely affecting linear growth.

title: Comparison of pain syndromes associated with nervous or somatic lesions and development of a new neuropathic pain diagnostic questionnaire (DN4)
text: Few studies have directly compared the clinical features of neuropathic and non-neuropathic pains. To address this gap, the French Neuropathic Pain Group developed a clinician-administered questionnaire named DN4, which combines sensory descriptors and signs from bedside sensory examination. This questionnaire was used in a prospective study of 160 patients with pain associated with a definite neurological or somatic lesion. The most common causes of nervous lesions (n=89) were traumatic nerve injury, post herpetic neuralgia, and post stroke pain. Non-neurological lesions (n=71) included osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthropathies, and mechanical low back pain. Each patient was evaluated independently by two experts to confirm the diagnosis of neuropathic or non-neuropathic pain. The study compared the prevalence of pain descriptors and sensory dysfunctions between the two groups of patients. The psychometric properties of the DN4 questionnaire were also analyzed, including face validity, inter-rater reliability, factor analysis, and logistic regression to identify the discriminant properties of items or combinations of items for the diagnosis of neuropathic pain. The study found that a small number of items in the questionnaire were sufficient to distinguish neuropathic pain. The 10-item questionnaire developed in the study may serve as a useful diagnostic instrument in both clinical research and daily practice.

title: Changing the density of alcohol outlets to reduce alcohol-related problems.
text: As legal and political debates surrounding the issuance of new liquor licenses continue to evolve, there is growing interest in understanding the impact of alcohol outlet density on alcohol consumption and related harm. However, a comprehensive review of the available evidence on this topic is lacking. In this Harm Reduction Digest, Livingston, Chikritzhs, and Room provide a critical analysis of the research literature on the effects of alcohol sales outlet density on alcohol consumption and related problems. They propose a novel framework for conceptualizing these relationships and discuss the implications for reducing alcohol-related harm.

title: [Pharmacokinetics and biotransformation of the antimycotic drug ciclopiroxolamine in animals and man after topical and systemic administration].
text:
1. After applying a 1% aqueous cream containing carbon-14-labelled broad-spectrum antimycotic ciclopiroxolamine (Hoe 296, Batrafen) to healthy human dorsal skin for 6 hours with an occlusive dressing for 5 hours, percutaneous absorption accounted for an average of 1.3% of the applied dose. Excretion occurred primarily through the kidneys, with biological half-lives of 1.7 hours. The highest concentrations of ciclopiroxolamine were found in the horny layer of the skin, with values ranging from 2300 to 4500 micrograms per square centimeter. These levels were maintained throughout the penetration period, which lasted for 1.5 hours. According to histoautoradiography studies, ciclopiroxolamine can penetrate the skin through the epidermis and hair follicles. When applied to fingernails, the radioactive-labelled compound penetrated through the nail as well. In contrast, the percutaneous absorption rate in dogs was higher, at 5-15% of the dose, than in humans.
2. After administering a 1% aqueous cream containing ciclopiroxolamine (Hoe 296, Batrafen) to bitches at a dose of 1 mg/kg, between 42 and 97% of the dose was recovered in the urine and faeces, with the remainder having penetrated into the tampon used to close the vagina.
3. Ciclopiroxolamine is primarily excreted in the urine of dogs and humans as a glucuronide, with a second glucuronide metabolite present in smaller amounts. The metabolite patterns after oral and dermal application were similar, and the binding of ciclopiroxolamine to serum proteins in humans was found to be 96 +/- 2% in a concentration range of 0.01-11.0 micrograms per milliliter.
4. Placental transfer of ciclopiroxolamine was low in rats, with good absorption by the mother animal but lower radioactivity in the foetal tissues compared to maternal blood.

title: Maximizing the diagnostic utility of endoscopic biopsy in dogs and cats with gastrointestinal disease.
text: Flexible endoscopy has become a crucial tool for the diagnosis of various small animal gastrointestinal (GI) diseases, but proper technique is essential to ensure accurate results. This review examines the current diagnostic utility of flexible endoscopy, including practical considerations for endoscopic biopsy, optimal instrumentation for collecting mucosal specimens, correlating endoscopic indices with clinical activity and histopathological findings, and recent advancements in endoscopic diagnosis of GI disease. Recent studies have established guidelines for endoscopic biopsy, highlighting the optimal number and quality of diagnostic specimens from different regions of the gut. These studies have also demonstrated the value of ileal biopsy in the diagnosis of canine and feline chronic enteropathies, as well as the utility of endoscopic biopsy specimens beyond routine histopathological analysis, including their use in immunohistochemical, microbiological, and molecular studies.

title: Age-structured red blood cell susceptibility and the dynamics of malaria infections.
text: Malaria parasites and the human immune system interact on a dynamic landscape, where a population of replicating parasites depletes a population of replenishing red blood cells (RBCs). This interaction receives relatively little attention, but it provides valuable insights into the mechanisms that control most malaria infections. Our focus is on the observation that three of the four malaria-parasite species infecting humans are restricted to particular age classes of RBCs. We incorporate this observation into models of infection dynamics to distinguish common from species-specific pressures on host immune responses. Our findings reveal that age structuring has profound effects on the course of infection. For all four species, conditions exist under which the parasites may persist at low densities or clear in the absence of an immune response. Catastrophic anemia can occur even with the two species that attack only the youngest RBCs, although only a small fraction of cells are parasitized at any point. Interestingly, with these two species, compensatory erythropoietic responses in the host can accelerate parasite population growth. A "basic reproduction rate" characterizes these differences in outcomes.

title: Helicobacter pylori AlpA and AlpB bind host laminin and influence gastric inflammation in gerbils.
text: Helicobacter pylori, a gram-negative bacterium, persistently colonizes the human gastric mucosa, leading to the development of gastritis, ulcers, and gastric cancer. Adherence to the gastric epithelium is a crucial step in the infection process, and various adhesins have been identified as key players in this process. However, the AlpAB locus, which encodes adhesins involved in adherence to human gastric tissue, has received limited attention. In this study, we investigated the role of AlpA and AlpB in H. pylori binding to laminin, a protein component of the gastric extracellular matrix. Our results demonstrate that abrogation of H. pylori AlpA and AlpB significantly reduces binding of the bacterium to laminin, while expression of plasmid-borne alpA or alpB confers laminin-binding ability to Escherichia coli. Moreover, an H. pylori strain lacking only AlpB is also deficient in laminin binding. These findings suggest that both AlpA and AlpB contribute to H. pylori laminin binding. Surprisingly, the H. pylori SS1 mutant deficient in AlpA and AlpB exhibited more severe inflammation in gerbils than the isogenic wild-type strain. The identification of laminin as the target of AlpA and AlpB provides a valuable opportunity for future investigations into the complex host-pathogen interactions that occur during H. pylori infection.

title: A quantitative analysis of kinase inhibitor selectivity
text: Kinase inhibitors are a promising new class of drugs that have the potential to target multiple biological pathways. However, the full range of their effects on the human body is not yet fully understood, particularly in terms of their interactions with other proteins in the kinome. To address this knowledge gap, we have generated comprehensive interaction maps for 38 kinase inhibitors across a panel of 317 kinases, representing over 50% of the predicted human protein kinome. This study represents the most detailed investigation of kinase inhibitor selectivity to date, revealing a wide variety of interaction patterns. To facilitate a global analysis of the results, we have developed a novel tool called a selectivity score, which allows us to quantify and differentiate the various interaction patterns observed. We also investigated the impact of panel size and found that smaller assay panels do not provide a reliable measure of selectivity.

title: Ribosomal protein S9 is a novel B23/NPM-binding protein required for normal cell proliferation.
text: B23 (NPM/nucleophosmin) is a multifunctional nucleolar protein belonging to the nucleoplasmin superfamily of acidic histone chaperones. B23 plays a crucial role in embryonic development, genomic stability, ribosome biogenesis, and anti-apoptotic signaling. Altered expression or mutations of B23 have been observed in various types of cancer. Despite its multifunctional nature, the molecular function of B23 remains poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate the association of B23 with a protein complex composed of ribosomal proteins and RNA helicases. Specifically, we explored the interaction between B23 and ribosomal protein S9 (RPS9). Our findings revealed that S9 binding to B23 requires an intact oligomerization domain of B23. Depletion of S9 by small interfering RNA led to decreased protein synthesis and G(1) cell cycle arrest, accompanied by the induction of p53 target genes. We found that S9 is a short-lived protein in the absence of ribosome biogenesis, and proteasomal inhibition significantly increased its protein level. Overexpression of B23 facilitated nucleolar storage of S9, while knockdown of B23 led to decreased levels of nucleolar S9. Our results suggest that B23 selectively stores and protects S9 in nucleoli, thereby facilitating ribosome biogenesis.

title: Vasculature-associated cells expressing nestin in developing bones encompass early cells in the osteoblast and endothelial lineage.
text: Nestin-positive (Nes(+)) cells are crucial components of adult bone marrow hematopoiesis, but their origin during endochondral bone development remains unknown. Recent studies using mice expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP) under the direction of the nestin promoter/enhancer (Nes-GFP) have shed light on the origins of these cells. In embryonic perichondrium, Nes(+) cells were found to be either endothelial or non-endothelial in nature, with the latter being early cells of the osteoblast lineage that descend from their progenitors upon Indian hedgehog signaling and Runx2 expression. During vascular invasion and ossification center formation, these Nes(+) cells were closely associated with each other and increased in number progressively. Interestingly, cells targeted by tamoxifen-inducible cre recombinase driven by the nestin enhancer (Nes-creER) in developing bone marrow were predominantly endothelial cells. Furthermore, Nes(+) cells in postnatal bones were found to be a heterogeneous population, consisting of cells in both the osteoblast and endothelial lineages. These findings reveal a previously unappreciated complexity in stromal populations, with Nes(+) cells functioning as vasculature-associated early cells in both the osteoblast and endothelial lineages.

title: Public health, academic medicine, and the alcohol industry's corporate social responsibility activities.
text: We delved into the evolving connections between the alcohol industry, academic medicine, and the public health community, examining these relationships through the lens of public health theory and corporate social responsibility. Our review encompassed sponsorship of scientific research, attempts to shape public perceptions of research findings, dissemination of scientific knowledge, and industry-funded policy initiatives. As the scientific evidence suggests that reducing alcohol consumption can be achieved through regulatory and legal measures, the academic community has found itself at odds with the views of the alcohol industry. Our analysis revealed that the alcohol industry has stepped up its scientific and policy-related activities under the guise of corporate social responsibility initiatives, with most of these efforts serving the industry's economic interests.

title: RET, ROS1 and ALK fusions in lung cancer
text: Using an integrated molecular and histopathology-based screening system, we evaluated 1,529 lung cancers for fusions of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) and c-ros oncogene 1, receptor tyrosine kinase (ROS1). We identified 44 ALK-fusion–positive and 13 ROS1-fusion–positive adenocarcinomas, including unidentified fusion partners for ROS1. In addition, we discovered novel kinase fusions that may be potential targets for molecular-targeted therapy, such as kinesin family member 5B (KIF5B)-ret proto-oncogene (RET) and coiled-coil domain containing 6 (CCDC6)-RET, in 14 adenocarcinomas. A multivariate analysis of 1,116 adenocarcinomas, including 71 kinase-fusion–positive adenocarcinomas, revealed four independent factors that are indicative of poor prognosis: age ≥50 years, male sex, high pathological stage, and negative kinase-fusion status.

title: Genetic and biochemical interactions among Yar1, Ltv1 and Rps3 define novel links between environmental stress and ribosome biogenesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text: In the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the assembly of ribosomes is tightly regulated by environmental conditions through the coordinated transcriptional control of genes involved in ribosome biogenesis. In this study, we investigate the roles of two nonessential stress-responsive genes, YAR1 and LTV1, in the production of 40S subunits. Our findings reveal that Yar1, a small ankyrin-repeat protein, physically interacts with RpS3, a component of the 40S subunit, and with Ltv1, a recently identified substoichiometric component of a 43S preribosomal particle. We demonstrate that cells lacking YAR1 or LTV1 are hypersensitive to specific protein synthesis inhibitors and exhibit abnormal polysome profiles, characterized by a reduced number of 40S subunits and an excess of free 60S subunits. Interestingly, both mutants are also sensitive to a range of environmental stress conditions. Overexpression of RPS3 suppresses both the stress sensitivity and the ribosome biogenesis defects of Deltayar1 mutants, but does not suppress either defect in Deltaltv1 mutants. Our findings suggest that YAR1 and LTV1 play distinct, nonessential roles in 40S subunit production. The stress-sensitive phenotypes of strains lacking these genes reveal a previously unappreciated connection between ribosome biogenesis factors and environmental stress sensitivity.

title: Rational design of acridine-based ligands with selectivity for human telomeric quadruplexes.
text: Structure-based modeling techniques have been employed to design a series of disubstituted triazole-linked acridine compounds with selectivity for human telomeric quadruplex DNA. A focused library of these compounds was synthesized using click chemistry, and the selectivity concept was validated against two promoter quadruplexes from the c-kit gene with known molecular structures, as well as with duplex DNA using a FRET-based melting method. Lead compounds were found to have reduced effects on the thermal stability of the c-kit quadruplexes and duplex DNA structures. These effects were further explored through competition experiments, which revealed that binding to duplex DNA is minimal even at high duplex:telomeric quadruplex ratios. Selectivity towards the c-kit quadruplexes is more complex, with some evidence of stabilization at increasing excess over human telomeric quadruplex DNA. The selectivity of these compounds is attributed to the dimensions of the triazole-acridine structure, particularly the separation of the two alkyl-amino terminal groups. Both lead compounds also exhibited selective inhibitory effects on the proliferation of cancer cell lines compared to a normal cell line, and one of them has been shown to inhibit the activity of the telomerase enzyme, which is selectively expressed in tumor cells where it plays a role in maintaining telomere integrity and cellular immortalization.

title: Hospital volume and the outcomes of mechanical ventilation.
text:
Background: An increase in patient volume has been linked to improved outcomes in various high-risk medical and surgical conditions. However, the relationship between hospital volume and patient outcomes among critically ill patients remains unclear.
Methods: We analyzed data from 20,241 nonsurgical patients receiving mechanical ventilation at 37 acute care hospitals between 2002 and 2003. Multivariate analyses were performed to account for differences in severity of illness and other case mix factors.
Results: Our findings indicate that an increase in hospital volume is associated with improved survival among patients receiving mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital. Specifically, admission to a hospital in the highest quartile according to volume (i.e., >400 patients receiving mechanical ventilation per year) was associated with a 37% reduction in adjusted odds of death in the ICU (P<0.001) and a 36% reduction in adjusted in-hospital mortality (P<0.001). Among survivors, there were no significant trends in length of stay in the ICU or hospital.
Conclusions: Our study suggests that mechanical ventilation of patients in a hospital with a high case volume is associated with reduced mortality. Further research is needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of this relationship.

title: A meta-analysis of depression during pregnancy and the risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and intrauterine growth restriction.
text:
The following is a rewritten version of the text with improved readability and clarity:
Background: Maternal depressive symptoms during pregnancy have been linked to an increased risk of preterm birth (PTB), low birth weight (LBW), and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) in some studies. Objective: To estimate the risk of PTB, LBW, and IUGR associated with antenatal depression. Methods: We conducted a systematic review of studies published between January 1980 and December 2009, searching multiple databases including MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Social Work Abstracts, Social Services Abstracts, and Dissertation Abstracts International. We included prospective studies that reported data on antenatal depression and at least one adverse birth outcome. Results: Of 862 reviewed studies, 29 met the selection criteria. Pooled relative risks (RRs) for the effect of antenatal depression on each birth outcome were calculated using random-effects methods. The estimates of risk for categorically defined antenatal depression and PTB and LBW remained significant after correcting for publication bias. The risk of LBW associated with antenatal depression was significantly higher in developing countries compared to the United States or European social democracies. Categorically defined antenatal depression tended to be associated with an increased risk of PTB among women of lower socioeconomic status in the United States. Conclusion: Women with depression during pregnancy are at increased risk for PTB and LBW, with the magnitude of the effect varying depending on depression measurement, country location, and socioeconomic status. Antenatal depression should be identified through universal screening and treated to reduce the risk of adverse birth outcomes.

title: ES cell pluripotency and germ-layer formation require the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling component BAF250a.
text: ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes, a prominent group of epigenetic modulators, harness the energy of ATP hydrolysis to alter the structure of chromatin, making it more or less accessible to nuclear factors. BAF250a (ARID1a), a unique and essential subunit of the BAF chromatin remodeling complex, plays a crucial role in early germ-layer formation during development. Our studies reveal that ablation of BAF250a in early mouse embryos leads to developmental arrest around embryonic day 6.5 and the absence of the mesodermal layer, indicating its critical function in early development. Moreover, BAF250a deficiency impairs ES cell pluripotency, significantly hinders self-renewal, and promotes differentiation into primitive endoderm-like cells under normal feeder-free culture conditions. Interestingly, this phenotype can be partially rescued by the presence of embryonic fibroblast cells. DNA microarray, immunostaining, and RNA analyses revealed that BAF250a-mediated chromatin remodeling contributes to the proper expression of key genes involved in ES cell self-renewal, including Sox2, Utf1, and Oct4. Furthermore, the pluripotency defects in BAF250a-mutant ES cells appear to be cell lineage-specific, as embryoid body-based analyses showed that BAF250a-deficient stem cells are impaired in differentiating into fully functional mesoderm-derived cardiomyocytes and adipocytes but can differentiate into ectoderm-derived neurons. Our findings suggest that BAF250a is a crucial component of the gene regulatory machinery in ES cells, controlling self-renewal, differentiation, and cell lineage decisions.

title: Metabolic shutdown in Escherichia coli cells lacking the outer membrane channel TolC.
text: The outer membrane protein TolC is a crucial component of multidrug efflux and type I secretion systems in Escherichia coli. Disabling TolC leads to increased susceptibility to antibiotics and defects in the secretion of toxic proteins. Contrary to expectations, we found that the absence of TolC significantly impairs cell division and growth in minimal glucose media, with the TolC-dependent phenotype being further exacerbated by the loss of ygiB and ygiC genes, which are expressed in the same operon as tolC and have homologs on other chromosomes. Our results indicate that this growth deficiency is caused by a depletion of the essential metabolite NAD+ and high NADH/NAD+ ratios. The increased amounts of PspA and decreased rates of NADH oxidation in TolC-deficient membranes suggest stress on the membrane and dissipation of a proton motive force. We conclude that inactivation of TolC triggers metabolic shutdown in E. coli cells grown in minimal glucose media. The TolC-dependent phenotype is partially rescued by YgiBC and YjfMC, which have parallel functions unrelated to TolC.

title: Acyl and total ghrelin are suppressed strongly by ingested proteins, weakly by lipids, and biphasically by carbohydrates.
text:
Ghrelin is an orexigenic hormone that plays a crucial role in regulating appetite and body weight. Its levels increase before meals and decrease after food ingestion. Understanding the effects of specific macronutrients on ghrelin regulation could help in the design of weight-reducing diets.
In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids on acyl and total ghrelin levels in human subjects. We hypothesized that lipids would suppress ghrelin levels to a lesser extent than carbohydrates or proteins.
We conducted a randomized, within-subjects cross-over study involving 16 healthy participants. The participants were provided with isocaloric, isovolemic beverages composed primarily of carbohydrates, proteins, or lipids. We measured the magnitude of postprandial suppression of total and acyl ghrelin levels using a novel acyl-selective, two-site ELISA.
Our results showed that all beverages suppressed plasma acyl and total ghrelin levels. However, we observed a significant effect of macronutrient class on the decremental area under the curve for both acyl and total ghrelin, with protein suppressing ghrelin levels more than carbohydrate and lipid. Additionally, we found that total ghrelin nadir levels were significantly lower after both carbohydrate and protein beverages compared to lipid beverages. Furthermore, in the first 3 postprandial hours, the rank order for acyl and total ghrelin suppression was carbohydrate more than protein more than lipid. However, in the subsequent 3 hours, there was a marked rebound above preprandial values of acyl and total ghrelin after carbohydrate ingestion alone.
Our findings suggest that the effects of high-protein/low-carbohydrate diets on weight loss and high-fat diets on weight gain may be related to the suppression of ghrelin levels. These results provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying the effects of different macronutrient compositions on ghrelin regulation and may help in the development of personalized weight-reducing diets.

title: Hydrogen sulfide increases nitric oxide production with calcium-dependent activation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase in endothelial cells.
text: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) was recently discovered to be synthesized in mammalian tissues by various enzymes. Numerous studies have shown that H2S has vasodilator and antihypertensive effects on the cardiovascular system, but the intracellular mechanisms of its vasodilation and interactions with other endothelium-derived relaxing factors, such as nitric oxide (NO), remain unclear. To investigate the direct regulation of endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) activity and NO production by H2S, we examined the effects of a H2S donor, NaHS, on cultured endothelial cells. Our results showed that NaHS dose-dependently increased NO production in endothelial cells, which was abolished by a calcium chelator (BAPTA-AM) but not by the absence of extracellular calcium. The NaHS-induced NO production was partially blocked by inhibitors of ryanodine receptor (dantrolene) or inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptor (xestospongin C). NaHS significantly increased intracellular calcium concentrations, which was attenuated by dantrolene or xestospongin C. NaHS also induced phosphorylation of eNOS at the activating phosphoserine residue 1179. The NaHS-induced eNOS phosphorylation and NO production were not affected by a PI3K/Akt inhibitor (wortmannin). Our findings suggest that H2S directly acts on endothelial cells to induce eNOS activation and NO production by releasing calcium from the intracellular store in the endoplasmic reticulum, which may explain one of the mechanisms of its vasodilator function.

title: Fear of falling and visual field loss from glaucoma.
text:
Objective: To investigate if visual field (VF) loss caused by glaucoma is associated with a greater fear of falling.
Design: A prospective, observational study.
Participants: 83 glaucoma patients with bilateral VF loss and 60 healthy controls without significant VF loss were recruited from patients with suspected glaucoma.
Methods: Participants completed the University of Illinois at Chicago Fear of Falling Questionnaire, and their ability to perform tasks without fear of falling was assessed using Rasch analysis.
Main Outcome Measures: The ability to perform tasks without fear of falling was expressed in logits, with lower scores indicating less ability and greater fear of falling.
Results: Glaucoma patients had greater VF loss than control subjects (median better-eye mean deviation [MD] of -8.0 decibels [dB] vs. +0.2 dB; P<0.001), but did not differ in terms of age, race, gender, employment status, the presence of other adults in the home, body mass index (BMI), grip strength, cognitive ability, mood, or comorbid illness (P ≥ 0.1 for all). In multivariate models, glaucoma subjects reported greater fear of falling as compared with controls (β = -1.20 logits; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.87 to -0.53; P = 0.001), and fear of falling increased with greater VF loss severity (β = -0.52 logits per 5-dB decrement in the better eye VF MD; 95% CI, -0.72 to -0.33; P<0.001). Other variables predicting greater fear of falling included female gender (β = -0.55 logits; 95% CI, -1.03 to -0.06; P = 0.03), higher BMI (β = -0.07 logits per 1-unit increase in BMI; 95% CI, -0.13 to -0.01; P = 0.02), living with another adult (β = -1.16 logits; 95% CI, -0.34 to -1.99 logits; P = 0.006), and greater comorbid illness (β = -0.53 logits/1 additional illness; 95% CI, -0.74 to -0.32; P<0.001).
Conclusions: Bilateral VF loss resulting from glaucoma is associated with greater fear of falling, with an impact that exceeds numerous other risk factors. Given the physical and psychological repercussions associated with fear of falling, significant quality-of-life improvements may be achievable in patients with VF loss by screening for, and developing interventions to minimize, fear of falling.

title: Repeat instability: mechanisms of dynamic mutations
text: Disease-causing repeat instability is a distinct and intriguing form of mutation that is associated with over 40 neurological, neurodegenerative, and neuromuscular disorders. DNA repeat expansion mutations are dynamic and ongoing within tissues and across generations, with patterns of inherited and tissue-specific instability determined by both gene-specific cis-elements and trans-acting DNA metabolic proteins. The mechanisms underlying repeat instability likely involve the formation of unusual DNA structures during DNA replication, repair, and recombination. Advances in experimental techniques have shed light on the underlying mechanisms of repeat instability, revealing novel ways in which metabolic pathways can either drive or protect against repeat instability.

title: Demographic Risk Factors for Alcohol-Related Aggression In and Around Licensed Venues.
text:
Few studies have examined the interplay between gender, area-level socio-economic status (SES), and individual SES (operationalized as occupational category) in predicting alcohol-related aggression (ARA) in and around licensed venues. The present study aimed to investigate these factors and their relationship with ARA in a sample of 697 men and 649 women aged 16-47. Participants completed a patron intercept survey as part of a larger study examining trends in harm and stakeholders' views surrounding local community level interventions in dealing with alcohol-related problems in the night-time economy.
Binary logistic regression analyses revealed that age, gender, occupational category, area-level SES, and level of intoxication at the time of interview were significant predictors of ARA involvement. Being male doubled the odds of involvement in ARA, while age was a protective factor. Blue collar workers had more than double the odds of ARA involvement compared to professionals, and individuals living in the most socio-economically disadvantaged areas were over twice as likely to report experiencing ARA compared to those living in the most advantaged areas.
