The study challenges the existing view that OSE is a bipotent source of oocytes and granulosa cells, instead suggesting that mammalian ovaries harbor distinct very small embryonic-like PSCs and tissue-committed progenitor stem cells populations that have the potential to differentiate into oocyte-like structures in vitro, while mesenchymal fibroblasts may form supporting granulosa-like somatic cells. Further research at the single-cell level, including complete gene expression profiling, is needed to confirm whether postnatal oogenesis is a conserved phenomenon in adult mammals.

title: Rearrangement of CRLF2 is associated with mutation of JAK kinases, alteration of IKZF1, Hispanic/Latino ethnicity, and a poor outcome in pediatric B-progenitor acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
text: Gene expression profiling of 207 children with high-risk B-progenitor acute lymphoblastic leukemia revealed 29 cases (14%) with significantly elevated expression of CRLF2 (cytokine receptor-like factor 2). In these cases, genomic rearrangements of CRLF2 were identified, including 18 cases (62%) with a translocation of the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene IGH@ on 14q32 to CRLF2 in the pseudoautosomal region 1 of Xp22.3/Yp11.3, and 10 cases (34%) with a 320-kb interstitial deletion centromeric of CRLF2, resulting in a P2RY8-CRLF2 fusion. One case had both IGH@-CRLF2 and P2RY8-CRLF2 rearrangements, and another had a novel CRLF2 rearrangement. Only two cases were Down syndrome. CRLF2 rearrangements were found to be significantly associated with activating mutations of JAK1 or JAK2, deletion or mutation of IKZF1, and Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (Fisher exact test, P < .001 for each). Notably, patients with CRLF2 rearrangements had poor treatment outcomes compared to those without these rearrangements (35.3% vs 71.3% relapse-free survival at 4 years; P < .001). These findings suggest that activation of CRLF2 expression, mutation of JAK kinases, and alterations of IKZF1 cooperate in the development and progression of B-cell leukemias, making these pathways important therapeutic targets in this disease.

title: Substrate requirements for ErmC' methyltransferase activity.
text: ErmC' is a methyltransferase that confers resistance to the macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B group of antibiotics by methylating 23S rRNA at a specific adenine residue (A-2085 in Bacillus subtilis and A-2058 in Escherichia coli). The gene for ErmC' was cloned and expressed in high levels in E. coli, and the protein was purified to near homogeneity. Substrate requirements studies showed that a 262-nucleotide RNA fragment within domain V of B. subtilis 23S rRNA can be used efficiently for methylation at A-2085. Kinetic studies of the monomethylation reaction revealed that the apparent Km of this 262-nucleotide RNA oligonucleotide was 26-fold higher than the value determined for full-size and domain V 23S rRNA, and the Vmax also rose sevenfold. Based on the kinetic data, a model of RNA-ErmC' interaction involving multiple binding sites is proposed.

title: Validity of the World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) Screener in a representative sample of health plan members.
text: The validity of the six-question World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) Screener was evaluated in a sample of individuals enrolled in a large US health plan. A subsample of 668 subscribers completed the ASRS Screener twice to assess test-retest reliability and then a third time with a clinical interviewer for DSM-IV adult ADHD diagnosis. The data were weighted to account for differences between the sample and the population in terms of socio-demographics and past medical claims. Internal consistency reliability of the continuous ASRS Screener ranged from 0.63 to 0.72, while test-retest reliability (Pearson correlations) ranged from 0.58 to 0.77. A four-category version of the ASRS Screener showed strong concordance with clinician diagnoses, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.90. The brief and ability to distinguish between DSM-IV cases and non-cases make the six-question ASRS Screener suitable for use in both community epidemiological surveys and clinical outreach and case-finding initiatives.

title: The body-mass index of twins who have been reared apart.
text: To determine the relative importance of genetic and environmental factors on body mass index (BMI), we analyzed data from identical and fraternal twins raised apart or together. Our sample consisted of 93 pairs of identical twins raised apart, 154 pairs of identical twins raised together, 218 pairs of fraternal twins raised apart, and 208 pairs of fraternal twins raised together. We found that the intraclass correlation coefficients for BMI among identical twins raised apart were 0.70 for men and 0.66 for women, indicating a significant genetic component to BMI. These estimates were similar to those obtained from maximum-likelihood model-fitting analyses, which suggested that genetic influences accounted for 0.74 of the variance in BMI among men and 0.69 among women. Additionally, we found that nonadditive genetic variance played a significant role in determining BMI, particularly among men. In contrast, unique environmental influences, such as those experienced by an individual and not shared within the family, contributed approximately 30% of the variance in BMI. Our results suggest that genetic factors have a substantial impact on BMI, while the shared childhood environment has little to no influence on BMI later in life. These findings corroborate and extend previous studies of twins and adoptees.

title: A study of high cell density cultivation process of recombinant Helicobacter pylori multi-epitope vaccine engineering bacteria.
text:
Objective:
To develop a high cell density cultivation process for recombinant Helicobacter pylori multi-epitope vaccine engineering bacteria BIB, resulting in increased expression and yield of the target protein.
Methods:
Building on the results of shake flask fermentation, the process was scaled up to a 50 L fermenter to optimize and validate the factors affecting protein yield, including fermentation medium, inoculum size, inducer concentration, induction time, induction duration, inducer addition method, and feeding strategy.
Results:
After 8 hours of incubation in modified TB medium at 37°C, the BIB working seed was inoculated at 5% (v/v) and induced for an additional 11 hours with a final lactose concentration of 5 mmol/L. During the growth phase, glucose was added at a rate of 80 ml/h as the carbon source, and in the induction phase, glycerol was added at a rate of 40 ml/h as the carbon source. Ammonia water was added dropwise to maintain a pH of around 7.0, and the revolution speed was adjusted to maintain a dissolved oxygen level above 30%. The final bacterial cell density was 70 g/L, and the protein expression amount was approximately 32%.
Conclusion:
The high cell density cultivation process significantly increased the expression and yield of the target protein rBIB. This approach can be used to produce large quantities of the recombinant vaccine for use in clinical trials and beyond.

title: Phorbol esters and cytokines regulate the expression of the NEMO-related protein, a molecule involved in a NF-kappa B-independent pathway.
text: The NF-κB signaling pathway plays a crucial role in immune, inflammatory, and apoptotic responses. Recently, we identified NEMO (NF-κB Essential Modulator) as a critical component of this pathway. NEMO is a structural and regulatory subunit of the IKK complex, which phosphorylates NF-κB inhibitors. Database searching led to the isolation of a cDNA encoding a protein similar to NEMO, called NRP (NEMO-related protein). We found that NRP is part of a novel high molecular weight complex that does not contain any known IKK complex members. Contrary to our expectations, we did not observe any effect of NRP on NF-κB signaling. However, we did find that treatment with phorbol esters leads to NRP phosphorylation and a decrease in its half-life, which can be inhibited by K-252a and stauroporin. We also demonstrated that de novo expression of NRP can be induced by interferon and tumor necrosis factor alpha, and that these stimuli have a synergistic effect on NRP expression. Additionally, we found that endogenous NRP is associated with the Golgi apparatus. Interestingly, we also observed that NRP is associated with two kinases, suggesting that it may play a similar role in another signaling pathway, similar to NEMO.

title: Tailoring Nutritional Advice for Mexicans Based on Prevalence Profiles of Diet-Related Adaptive Gene Polymorphisms
text:
The distribution of adaptive gene (DRAG) polymorphisms varies across different populations in Mexico, with higher frequencies of these polymorphisms observed in Amerindian (AM) groups compared to Mestizos, who have a mix of AM, European (EUR), and African ancestry. These findings were revealed through a study that aimed to provide a prevalence profile of several DRAG polymorphisms in the Mexican population, including Central West (CW) Mexico subpopulations.
Using geographic heat maps created with ArcGIS software, the study found that the MTHFR C677T, ABCA1 Arg230Cys, APOE T388C/C526T, and LCT C-13910T polymorphisms, as well as AMY1 copy number variation (CNV), exhibited a heterogeneous distribution across Mexico. Specifically, the highest frequencies of the MTHFR 677T, ABCA1 230C, and APOE ε4 adaptive alleles were observed in AM groups in the CW region, followed by Mestizos with intermediate AM ancestry. The LCT-13910T allele frequency was highest in Mestizos-EUR, but extremely low in AM, while the AMY1 diploid copy number was 6.82 ± 3.3 copies.
These genetic differences highlight the need for genome-based nutritional advice tailored to regional and individual differences in the Mexican population. By understanding the specific genetic adaptations of different populations, it may be possible to develop a healthier dietary pattern that takes into account the available foods and traditional food culture in each region. This approach could help reduce the risk of chronic diseases associated with DRAG polymorphisms in carriers of the adaptive alleles.

title: Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Through Inhibition of the Renin-Angiotensin System
text:
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is becoming a significant public health concern due to its high prevalence and associated morbidity and mortality. Given the rapid increase in the number of cases, prevention of the disease should be a priority in the near future. While lifestyle modifications are crucial, various pharmacological interventions have shown promise in preventing or delaying the onset of type 2 diabetes.
Antidiabetic drugs such as metformin, acarbose, and troglitazone have been proven effective in clinical trials. Additionally, antiobesity agents like orlistat have shown potential in reducing body weight and improving glucose tolerance. However, not all antihypertensive agents have the same effect on insulin sensitivity. While some, such as diuretics and β-adrenoceptor antagonists, may worsen insulin resistance, newer agents like ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists (ARAs) have shown neutral or even slightly positive metabolic effects.
Several clinical trials have investigated the impact of ACE inhibitors and ARAs on insulin sensitivity in hypertensive patients, with mixed results. While some studies found a slight increase in insulin sensitivity, others failed to reveal any significant changes. The mechanisms of improvement in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity through the inhibition of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) are complex and involve improved blood flow and microcirculation in skeletal muscles, enhanced insulin and glucose delivery to insulin-sensitive tissues, and improved insulin signaling and secretion.
Recent large-scale clinical studies have consistently shown that treatment with ACE inhibitors or ARAs for 3–6 years reduces the incidence of type 2 diabetes in hypertensive patients by an average of 14% (p = 0.034) in the CAPPP with captopril, 34% (p < 0.001) in the HOPE with ramipril, 30% (p < 0.001) in the ALLHAT with lisinopril, 25% (p < 0.001) in the LIFE with losartan, and 25% (p = 0.09) in the SCOPE with candesartan cilexetil. These findings have led to the initiation of two large, prospective, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials, the DREAM trial with ramipril and the NAVIGATOR trial with valsartan, with the primary outcome of preventing type 2 diabetes.
In conclusion, the recent consistent observations of a 14–34% reduction in the development of diabetes in hypertensive patients receiving ACE inhibitors or ARAs are encouraging and suggest a new strategy to reduce the ongoing epidemic and burden of type 2 diabetes. While there are still many aspects of the pathogenesis, prevention, and treatment of type 2 diabetes that need to be uncovered, these findings offer hope for a potential prevention and treatment strategy.

title: Randomized dose-finding clinical trial of oncolytic immunotherapeutic vaccinia JX-594 in liver cancer
text: Oncolytic viruses and immunotherapeutics have complementary mechanisms of action (MOA) that are both self-amplifying in tumors, yet the impact of dose on patient outcome is unclear. JX-594 (Pexa-Vec) is an oncolytic and immunotherapeutic vaccinia virus. To determine the optimal JX-594 dose in patients with advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), we conducted a randomized phase 2 dose-finding trial (n = 30). Radiologists infused low- or high-dose JX-594 into liver tumors on days 1, 15, and 29; infusions resulted in detectable intravascular JX-594 genomes. Objective intrahepatic Modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (mRECIST) (15%) and Choi (62%) response rates and intrahepatic disease control (50%) were equivalent in injected and distant non-injected tumors at both doses. JX-594 replication and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) expression preceded the induction of anticancer immunity. In contrast to tumor response rate and immune endpoints, patient survival duration was significantly related to dose (median survival of 14.1 months compared to 6.7 months on the high and low dose, respectively; hazard ratio 0.39; P = 0.020). JX-594 demonstrated oncolytic and immunotherapy MOA, tumor responses, and dose-related survival in patients with HCC.

title: Misread protein creates membrane channels: an essential step in the bactericidal action of aminoglycosides.
text: The pleiotropic effects of aminoglycosides have been attributed to their irreversible uptake and blockade of initiating ribosomes, but the mechanisms underlying their bactericidal action remain unclear. Recent evidence suggests that the incorporation of misread proteins into the membrane may account for the membrane damage observed in response to aminoglycoside exposure. According to this mechanism, the bactericidal action of aminoglycosides proceeds through a series of sequential steps, each of which is essential: (1) initial low levels of antibiotic entry; (2) interaction with chain-elongating ribosomes, leading to misreading; (3) incorporation of misread protein into the membrane, resulting in the formation of abnormal channels; (4) increased and irreversible entry through these channels; and (5) blockade of initiating ribosomes. This mechanism can explain several previously unexplained observations, including the requirement for protein synthesis during the lag phase before membrane damage, the ability of streptomycin-resistant cells to take up streptomycin after treatment with another aminoglycoside, and the acceleration of streptomycin uptake by puromycin at moderate concentrations. Furthermore, the findings suggest that normal membrane proteins must possess not only a hydrophobic anchoring surface but also a tight fit in the membrane.

title: Rate of cervical cancer, severe intraepithelial neoplasia, and adenocarcinoma in situ in primary HPV DNA screening with cytology triage: randomised study within organised screening programme.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the performance and impact of primary human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA screening with cytology triage compared to conventional cytology in detecting cervical cancer and severe pre-cancerous lesions in a population-based screening program.
Design: Randomized controlled trial.
Setting: Population-based screening program for cervical cancer in southern Finland from 2003 to 2005.
Participants: 58,076 women aged 30-60 years old invited to the routine population-based screening program for cervical cancer.
Interventions: Primary HPV DNA test (hybrid capture II) with cytology triage if the result was positive or conventional cytological screening (reference).
Main Outcome Measures: Rate of cervical cancer, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade III, and adenocarcinoma in situ (as a composite outcome referred to as CIN III+) during 2003-2007 through record linkage between files from the screening registry and the national cancer registry.
Results: There were 95,600 and 95,700 woman-years of follow-up and 76 and 53 cases of CIN III+, respectively (of which six and eight were cervical cancers), in the HPV and conventional arms, respectively. The relative rate of CIN III+ in the HPV arm versus the conventional arm was 1.44 (95% confidence interval 1.01 to 2.05) among all women invited for screening and 1.77 (1.16 to 2.74) among those who attended. Among women with a normal or negative test result, the relative rate of subsequent CIN III+ was 0.28 (0.04 to 1.17). The rate of cervical cancer between arms was 0.75 (0.25 to 2.16) among women invited for screening and 1.98 (0.52 to 9.38) among those who attended.
Conclusions: When incorporated into a well-established organized screening program, primary HPV screening with cytology triage was more sensitive than conventional cytology in detecting CIN III+ lesions. The number of cases of cervical cancer was small, but considering the high probability of progression of CIN III, the findings are of importance regarding cancer prevention.
Trial Registration: Current Controlled Trials ISRCTN23885553.

title: Metabolic syndrome as a risk factor for diabetes.
text: The metabolic syndrome was initially characterized as a condition marked by insulin resistance, which is characterized by a cluster of metabolic traits, including high triglycerides, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high blood pressure, abdominal obesity, and impaired glucose regulation. Although different definitions have been proposed by various consensus groups, epidemiological studies have shown that they all associate the metabolic syndrome with a similar increased risk of cardiometabolic disease, which ranges from three- to 20-fold higher risk of diabetes, depending on the number of components and the inclusion of impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance. The latter suggests that the beta cell may be unable to produce enough insulin to compensate for insulin resistance. There is a hyperbolic relationship between insulin production and insulin sensitivity, which can be calculated by the disposition index. When this is altered, there is an increased risk of developing Type 2 diabetes. There have been no clinical trials conducted specifically on individuals diagnosed with the metabolic syndrome, but structured lifestyle changes, such as weight loss and exercise, have been shown to reduce the incidence of Type 2 diabetes by almost 50% in people with impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance, as long as a weight loss of at least 5% is achieved. Oral antidiabetic and anti-obesity drugs have also been effective to a lesser degree. Some fibrates have reduced or delayed incident diabetes, while extended-release niacin has a neutral effect and statins are controversial. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are the antihypertensive agents least associated with incident diabetes.

title: The fallacy of the ecological fallacy: the potential misuse of a concept and the consequences.
text: Ecological studies have been criticized in epidemiological contexts due to the "ecological fallacy," despite evidence showing that correlations derived from ecological- and individual-level analyses are not comparable. While the conceptual meaning of the ecological fallacy remains unclear, this paper argues that issues in cross-level inference can be understood as validity problems, rather than being unique to ecological-level analyses. This approach acknowledges both the potential inference problems in individual-level studies and the unique contributions of ecological variables, thereby expanding the scope for identifying causes of disease and developing effective interventions to improve public health.

title: Blocking caspase-activated apoptosis improves contractility in failing myocardium.
text:
Cardiac myocyte apoptosis has been observed in end-stage heart failure in humans. The therapeutic potential of blocking apoptosis in congestive heart failure (CHF) remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the role of caspase activation in cardiac contractility and sarcomere organization in the development of CHF.
In a rabbit model of heart failure induced by rapid ventricular pacing, we demonstrated, using in vivo transcoronary adenovirus-mediated gene delivery of the potent caspase inhibitor p35, that caspase activation is associated with a decrease in contractile force of failing myocytes, resulting in disruption of sarcomeric structure. In this animal model, gene transfer of p35 prevented the increase in caspase 3 activity and DNA-histone formation. Genetically manipulated hearts expressing p35 showed a significant improvement in left ventricular pressure rise (+dp/dt), decreased end-diastolic chamber pressure (LVEDP), and delayed development of heart failure.
To further elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we examined the effects of caspase 3 on cardiomyocyte dysfunction in vitro. Microinjection of activated caspase 3 into the cytoplasm of intact myocytes led to sarcomeric disorganization and reduced contractility of the cells. These findings demonstrate a direct impact of caspases on cardiac function, suggesting potential therapeutic strategies via antiapoptotic regimens.

title: Development and validation of QRISK3 risk prediction algorithms to estimate future risk of cardiovascular disease: prospective cohort study
text:
Objective: To develop and validate updated QRISK3 prediction algorithms to estimate the 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in women and men, accounting for potential new risk factors.
Design: Prospective open cohort study.
Setting: General practices in England providing data for the QResearch database.
Participants: 1309 QResearch general practices in England, with 981 practices used to develop the scores and a separate set of 328 practices used to validate the scores. A total of 7.89 million patients aged 25-84 years were included in the derivation cohort, and 2.67 million patients in the validation cohort.
Methods: Cox proportional hazards models were used in the derivation cohort to derive separate risk equations for men and women for evaluation at 10 years. Risk factors considered included those already in QRISK2 (age, ethnicity, deprivation, systolic blood pressure, body mass index, total cholesterol: high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio, smoking, family history of coronary heart disease in a first-degree relative aged less than 60 years, type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, treated hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease (stage 4 or 5)), and new risk factors (chronic kidney disease (stage 3, 4, or 5), a measure of systolic blood pressure variability (standard deviation of repeated measures), migraine, corticosteroids, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), atypical antipsychotics, severe mental illness, and erectile dysfunction diagnosis or treatment in men). Calibration and discrimination measures were determined in the validation cohort for men and women separately and for individual subgroups by age group, ethnicity, and baseline disease status.
Main Outcome Measures: Incident CVD recorded on any of the following three linked data sources: general practice, mortality, or hospital admission records.
Results: A total of 363 565 incident cases of CVD were identified in the derivation cohort during follow-up, arising from 50.8 million person-years of observation. All new risk factors considered met the model inclusion criteria, except for HIV/AIDS, which was not statistically significant. The models had good calibration and high levels of explained variation and discrimination. In women, the algorithm explained 59.6% of the variation in time to diagnosis of CVD (R2, with higher values indicating more variation), and the D statistic was 2.48, and Harrell's C statistic was 0.88 (both measures of discrimination, with higher values indicating better discrimination). The corresponding values for men were 54.8%, 2.26, and 0.86. Overall performance of the updated QRISK3 algorithms was similar to the QRISK2 algorithms.
Conclusion: Updated QRISK3 risk prediction models were developed and validated. The inclusion of additional clinical variables in QRISK3 (chronic kidney disease, a measure of systolic blood pressure variability, migraine, corticosteroids, SLE, atypical antipsychotics, severe mental illness, and erectile dysfunction) can help enable doctors to identify those at most risk of heart disease and stroke.

title: The importance of engaging policy-makers at the outset to guide research on and introduction of vaccines: the use of policy-maker surveys.
text:
Conducting face-to-face surveys of policy-makers and other influential leaders can help identify key issues related to the introduction of new vaccines, including:
1. Major concerns regarding the introduction of a new vaccine.
2. Decision-makers and groups in a country who play a significant role in vaccine introduction.
3. Obstacles that may hinder the introduction of vaccines.
4. Data requirements necessary to overcome these obstacles.

By gathering the opinions and beliefs of those who will make or influence decisions on introducing a new vaccine, these studies can ensure that research activities align with the needs of policy-makers in endemic countries. These surveys can also inform vaccine introduction strategies by identifying feasible means of distributing, targeting, and financing vaccines.
This paper describes the methodology used in conducting such surveys and discusses methodological issues. It also presents lessons learned from two policy-maker surveys conducted in several Asian countries regarding new-generation vaccines against cholera, typhoid fever, and shigellosis; and future vaccines against dengue fever/dengue hemorrhagic fever.

title: Histone acetyltransferase PCAF regulates inflammatory molecules in the development of renal injury.
text:
Inflammation plays a crucial role in the development and progression of kidney diseases, including chronic kidney disease (CKD) and acute kidney injury (AKI). However, the underlying mechanisms that regulate inflammation in these renal injuries are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigated the role of p300/CBP-associated factor (PCAF), a histone acetyltransferase, in the regulation of inflammatory molecules in the kidneys of mice with CKD and AKI.
Our results showed that PCAF was overexpressed in the kidneys of db/db mice and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-injected mice, which are models of CKD and AKI, respectively. Additionally, we found elevated histone acetylation, such as H3K18ac, and up-regulation of some inflammatory genes, including intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), in the kidneys of these mice. Furthermore, we observed increased recruitment of H3K18ac to the promoters of ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and MCP-1 in the kidneys of LPS-injected mice.
In vitro studies revealed that PCAF knockdown in human renal proximal tubule epithelial cells (HK-2) led to decreased expression of inflammatory molecules, including VCAM-1, ICAM-1, p50 subunit of nuclear factor kappa B (p50), and MCP-1 mRNA and protein levels, as well as a decrease in H3K18ac levels. Conversely, overexpression of PCAF enhanced the expression of these inflammatory molecules. Moreover, PCAF deficiency reduced palmitate-induced recruitment of H3K18ac on the promoters of ICAM-1 and MCP-1, as well as inhibited palmitate-induced upregulation of these inflammatory molecules.
Taken together, our findings suggest that PCAF plays a crucial role in the regulation of inflammatory molecules through H3K18ac, which provides a potential therapeutic target for inflammation-related renal diseases.

title: T1 mapping for myocardial extracellular volume measurement by CMR: bolus only versus primed infusion technique.
text:
The aim of this study was to evaluate the accuracy of the "bolus only" T1 mapping cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) technique for measuring myocardial extracellular volume fraction (ECV). The study compared the bolus only technique with two independent standards: collagen volume fraction (CVF) from myocardial biopsy in aortic stenosis (AS), and the infusion technique in five representative conditions.
One hundred forty-seven subjects were included: healthy volunteers (n = 50), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (n = 25), severe AS (n = 22), amyloid (n = 20), and chronic myocardial infarction (n = 30). Both the bolus only and infusion ECV measurements were performed and compared. In 18 subjects with severe AS, the results were also compared with histological CVF.
The results showed a strong correlation between the two techniques (r² = 0.97) across healthy and diseased states. However, in diseases with high ECV (amyloid, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, late gadolinium enhancement, and infarction), the bolus only technique consistently measured higher ECV values compared to the infusion technique, with a mean difference of 0.040 ± 0.075 (p < 0.001).
The study concluded that the bolus only, T1 mapping-derived ECV measurement is sufficient for ECV measurement across a range of cardiac diseases, and this approach is histologically validated in AS. However, when ECV is >0.4, the bolus only technique consistently measures higher ECV values compared to the infusion technique.

title: Cytomegalovirus US2 destroys two components of the MHC class II pathway, preventing recognition by CD4+ T cells
text:
Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous herpesvirus that can cause severe disease in immunosuppressed individuals, such as those undergoing bone marrow or tissue transplantation, or those with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). HCMV establishes lifelong latent infections and periodically reactivates, using a range of immune evasion strategies to evade the host immune system. One such strategy involves the degradation of key proteins involved in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II antigen presentation pathway, which is crucial for the activation of CD4+ T lymphocytes.
We have discovered that the HCMV protein US2 specifically targets and degrades two essential proteins in the MHC class II antigen presentation pathway: HLA-DR-α and DM-α. This is surprising, as US2 has previously been shown to degrade MHC class I proteins, which have limited homology with class II proteins. The degradation of these proteins by US2 significantly reduces or eliminates the ability of infected cells to present antigens to CD4+ T lymphocytes.
This finding suggests that US2 may allow HCMV-infected macrophages to remain relatively "invisible" to CD4+ T cells, a property that would be advantageous after virus reactivation. By evading the host immune system, HCMV can persistently infect its hosts and cause persistent disease.
In summary, our study reveals a novel mechanism of immune evasion employed by HCMV, which involves the degradation of key proteins in the MHC class II antigen presentation pathway. This strategy allows HCMV-infected cells to evade CD4+ T cell recognition and activation, potentially contributing to the persistence of HCMV infection.

title: CD169-positive macrophages dominate antitumor immunity by crosspresenting dead cell-associated antigens.
text: The generation of tumor-targeted cytotoxic T lymphocytes is crucial for the induction of antitumor immunity. To activate these CD8(+) T cells, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) must first acquire tumor cell-associated antigens. While the major source of tumor antigens is dead tumor cells, little is known about how APCs in draining lymph nodes acquire and present these antigens. Our study reveals that CD169(+) macrophages phagocytose dead tumor cells transported via lymphatic flow and subsequently crosspresent tumor antigens to CD8(+) T cells. Subcutaneous immunization with irradiated tumor cells protects mice from syngenic tumors. However, tumor antigen-specific CD8(+) T cell activation and subsequent antitumor immunity are significantly impaired in mice depleted of CD169(+) macrophages. Unlike migratory dendritic cells (DCs) and lymph node-resident conventional DCs, CD169(+) macrophages are not essential for the crosspresentation of tumor antigens. Therefore, we have identified CD169(+) macrophages as the dominant lymph node-resident APCs responsible for early activation of tumor antigen-specific CD8(+) T cells.

title: Emerging mechanisms in morphogen-mediated axon guidance.
text:
During early animal development, various secreted morphogenic molecules, such as Sonic hedgehog (Shh), Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp family members, regulate cell proliferation and determine the fate and phenotype of target cells by activating well-characterized signaling pathways. These pathways ultimately control gene transcription and play an important and evolutionarily conserved role in neural circuit assembly. Shh, Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp signaling regulate neuronal polarization, axon and dendrite development, and synaptogenesis, processes that require rapid and local changes in cytoskeletal organization and plasma membrane components.
A key question is whether morphogen signaling at the growth cone uses similar mechanisms and intracellular pathway components as those described for morphogen-mediated cell specification. This review discusses recent advances towards understanding this problem, highlighting how Shh, Wnt, and TGFbeta/Bmp have adapted their "classical" signaling pathways or adopted alternative and novel molecular mechanisms to influence different aspects of neuronal circuit formation.

title: Lessons learnt from malaria epidemics in the Islamic Republic of Iran.
text: The Islamic Republic of Iran is currently in the preliminary stages of malaria control, although malaria outbreaks continue to pose a significant threat in the southern regions of the country. This retrospective study aims to investigate the epidemiological characteristics and underlying factors of 60 malaria outbreaks reported in Sistan va Baluchestan province between 2005 and 2009. A zero-truncated negative binomial model was employed to examine the relationship between potential predictor variables and the total number of malaria cases. The majority of malaria outbreaks occurred in the southern part of the province, primarily between July and October, with the peak occurring in August. The majority of outbreaks were small-scale (68.3% were fewer than 100 cases) and short-lived (51.7% lasted less than one month). Plasmodium falciparum was detected in 46.7% of the outbreaks. The most significant predictor variables were found to be increases in rainfall rates and population movements. These findings may contribute to the development of an epidemic investigation and reporting system as the country approaches the malaria elimination phase.

title: Autoradiography of chromosomal DNA fibers from Chinese hamster cells.
text: Ignorance of the actual length of DNA molecules within the chromosomes of higher organisms has long been a significant hindrance to comprehending chromosome structure. As a result, researchers have endeavored to estimate the size of DNA in higher organisms using various methods, including electron microscopy. One notable study by Solari (1) has yielded the longest measured DNA length to date - a DNA fiber from a sea urchin sperm measuring an impressive 93 micrometers in length.

title: Epigenetic memory and preferential lineage-specific differentiation in induced pluripotent stem cells derived from human pancreatic islet beta cells.
text: Human-induced pluripotent stem cells (HiPSCs) are comparable to human embryonic stem cells (HESCs) in terms of their pluripotency. Using two genetic lineage-tracing systems, we demonstrated the generation of iPSC lines from human pancreatic islet beta cells. These reprogrammed cells exhibited markers of pluripotency and differentiated into the three embryonic germ layers. However, beta cell-derived iPSCs (BiPSCs) maintained an open chromatin structure at key beta-cell genes, along with a unique DNA methylation signature that distinguishes them from other PSCs. BiPSCs also showed an enhanced ability to differentiate into insulin-producing cells both in vitro and in vivo, compared to ESCs and isogenic non-beta iPSCs. Our findings suggest that the epigenetic memory may predispose BiPSCs to differentiate more readily into insulin-producing cells. These results indicate that the phenotype of HiPSCs may be influenced by their cells of origin, and that their skewed differentiation potential may be advantageous for cell replacement therapy.

title: CCL2/monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 mediates enhanced transmigration of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected leukocytes across the blood-brain barrier: a potential mechanism of HIV-CNS invasion and NeuroAIDS.
text:
Introduction:
Encephalitis and dementia associated with Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) are characterized by leukocyte infiltration into the Central Nervous System (CNS), microglia activation, aberrant chemokine expression, disruption of the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB), and eventual loss of neurons. While it is known that HIV infection of leukocytes affects their ability to transmigrate in response to chemokines and alter BBB integrity, little is understood about the specific mechanisms involved.
Objective:
To investigate the effect of HIV infection of leukocytes on their ability to transmigrate across a tissue culture model of the human BBB in response to the chemokine CCL2, and to determine whether this process is associated with disruption of the BBB.
Methods:
We used a tissue culture model of the human BBB to evaluate the transmigration of HIV-infected leukocytes in response to CCL2. The BBB was disrupted by adding HIV-infected cells to the model, and the expression of tight junction proteins, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and chemokine receptors was evaluated.
Results:
Our results demonstrate that HIV infection of human leukocytes leads to increased transmigration across our tissue culture model of the human BBB in response to CCL2, as well as disruption of the BBB, as evidenced by enhanced permeability, reduction of tight junction proteins, and expression of MMP-2 and MMP-9. HIV-infected cells added to the model did not transmigrate in the absence of CCL2, nor did this condition alter BBB integrity. The chemokines CXCL10/interferon-gamma-inducible protein of 10 kDa, CCL3/macrophage inflammatory protein-1alpha, or CCL5/RANTES did not enhance HIV-infected leukocyte transmigration or BBB permeability. However, the increased capacity of HIV-infected leukocytes to transmigrate in response to CCL2 was found to correlate with their increased expression of CCR2, the chemokine receptor for CCL2.
Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that CCL2 plays a key role in the infiltration of HIV-infected leukocytes into the CNS and the subsequent pathology characteristic of NeuroAIDS. These data provide new insights into the mechanisms involved in the progression of HIV-associated neurological disorders and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of these conditions.

title: Prostaglandin E2 as an inhibitory modulator of fibrogenesis in human lung allografts.
text:
The study investigates the role of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) in modulating the fibrotic differentiation of human lung allograft-derived mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) in bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS). The research aims to elucidate the regulatory pathways involved in the suppression of fibrotic differentiation by PGE2.
The study employed various methods, including the assessment of PGE2's effects on MSC proliferation, collagen secretion, and α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) expression. The study found that PGE2 inhibited the proliferation, collagen secretion, and α-SMA expression of MSCs derived from normal lung allografts. The study also identified a PGE2/E prostanoid (EP)2/adenylate cyclase pathway as the underlying mechanism. The study further demonstrated that endogenous PGE2 secretion was associated with the amelioration of myofibroblast differentiation in vitro, while its inhibition augmented α-SMA expression. The study found that BOS MSCs secreted significantly less PGE2 than non-BOS MSCs and were defective in their ability to induce cyclooxygenase-2, which impaired their ability to up-regulate PGE2 synthesis in response to IL-1β. Additionally, BOS MSCs demonstrated resistance to the inhibitory actions of PGE2, which was associated with a reduction in the EP2/EP1 ratio.
The study's findings suggest that the PGE2 axis plays a crucial role in regulating the fibrotic differentiation of MSCs in BOS. The study's results provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying BOS and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of this debilitating lung disease.

title: Association of DNA polymerase mu (pol mu) with Ku and ligase IV: role for pol mu in end-joining double-strand break repair.
text: Mammalian DNA polymerase mu (pol mu) shares some similarities with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, but its functional significance in cells remains unclear. Our study reveals that exposure of cells to ionizing radiation (IR) leads to an increase in pol mu protein levels. Additionally, pol mu forms distinct nuclear foci following IR, which are largely coincident with foci of gammaH2AX, a previously characterized marker of sites of DNA double-strand breaks. These findings suggest that pol mu plays a role in the cellular response to DNA double-strand breaks. Furthermore, we have found that pol mu interacts with the nonhomologous end-joining repair factor Ku in cell extracts and requires both Ku and another end-joining factor, XRCC4-ligase IV, to form a stable complex on DNA in vitro. Pol mu also facilitates the stable recruitment of XRCC4-ligase IV to Ku-bound DNA and ligase IV-dependent end joining, whereas the related mammalian DNA polymerase beta does not form a complex with Ku and XRCC4-ligase IV and is less effective in facilitating joining mediated by these factors. Our data therefore support a crucial role for pol mu in the end-joining pathway for repair of double-strand breaks.

title: Stromal-epithelial metabolic coupling in cancer: integrating autophagy and metabolism in the tumor microenvironment.
text: Cancer cells do not exist as homogeneous populations in the body. Instead, they are embedded in "cancer cell nests" surrounded by stromal cells, including cancer-associated fibroblasts. This suggests that stromal fibroblasts may influence the metabolism of adjacent cancer cells, and vice versa. Our recent proposal suggests that the Warburg effect in cancer cells may be due to culturing them in isolation from their normal stromal context or tumor microenvironment. In fact, when cancer cells are co-cultured with fibroblasts, cancer cells increase their mitochondrial mass, while fibroblasts lose their mitochondria. A deeper analysis of this phenomenon reveals that aggressive cancer cells are "parasites" that use oxidative stress as a "weapon" to extract nutrients from surrounding stromal cells. Oxidative stress in fibroblasts induces the autophagic destruction of mitochondria, leading to the production of energy-rich nutrients (such as lactate and ketones) that feed cancer cells. This mechanism would allow cancer cells to survive and proliferate during metastasis without relying on blood vessels for nutrient supply. We propose that stromal catabolism, via autophagy and mitophagy, fuels the anabolic growth of tumor cells, promoting tumor progression and metastasis. This new paradigm, termed "The Autophagic Tumor Stroma Model of Cancer Metabolism" or the "Reverse Warburg Effect," also fits with the glutamine addiction (glutaminolysis) observed in many cancer cells, which promotes oxidative mitochondrial metabolism in aggressive cancer cells.

title: Oxidative stress in renal dysfunction: mechanisms, clinical sequelae and therapeutic options
text: Oxidative stress has been shown to play a significant role in the high incidence of cardiovascular events in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Despite the presence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors, the huge cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in this population group cannot be fully explained. Oxidative stress is increased in patients with renal impairment due to elevated oxidant activity and reduced antioxidant capacity, and this increase is proportional to the degree of renal dysfunction. The presence of inflammation in CKD further exacerbates the oxidant generation process. The two primary consequences of oxidative stress are endothelial dysfunction and left ventricular hypertrophy, both of which have adverse cardiovascular consequences. With our current understanding of oxidative stress, it is crucial to explore treatment options that target its reduction in the hope of reversing endothelial dysfunction and left ventricular hypertrophy, and thus mitigating the clinical sequelae of these abnormalities.

title: Effect of age, sex, and sites on the cellularity of the adipose tissue in mice and rats rendered obese by a high-fat diet.
text: In a study conducted on Swiss mice, the size and number of fat pads in the parametrium were determined in mice made obese through a high-fat diet (40% lard by weight) given ad libitum. This diet and a control diet were fed to two groups of mothers during gestation and lactation, and their suckling offspring were given the same diets throughout life. Two-week-old mice suckled by obese mothers had larger parametrial fat pads compared to those suckled by non-obese mothers. This difference was attributed solely to an increase in fat cell size. After weaning, the obese group showed a continuous increase in fat cell number until week 18, while the control group did not exhibit any change in cell number. When the high-fat diet was introduced to adult rats, it also triggered an increase in fat cell number. The study compared three sites of fat pads (perirenal, epididymal, and subcutaneous) in both sexes at 32 weeks of age, and found that all sites increased in weight in the high-fat fed group. The obese mice showed site-specific responses to the diet, with hyperplasia in the perirenal site, hypertrophy in the epididymal and subcutaneous sites, and hyperplasia plus hypertrophy in the parametrial site. The study concluded that the level of fat in a diet plays a role in both the formation and maturation of new fat cells, as well as the regulation of fat cell lipid content. The two processes may act together or separately depending on the adipose tissue site.

title: Transcriptional integration of mitochondrial biogenesis.
text: Gene regulatory factors encoded in the nucleus are crucial for mitochondrial function and development. Some of these factors operate exclusively within the mitochondria to regulate mitochondrial transcription, translation, and other processes. Others control the expression of genes in the nucleus that are necessary for mitochondrial metabolism and organelle formation. The PGC-1 family of transcriptional coactivators plays a key role in transmitting and integrating physiological signals that regulate metabolism, differentiation, and cell growth to the transcriptional machinery that controls mitochondrial function. As a result, the PGC-1 coactivators serve as a central component of the transcriptional regulatory circuitry that coordinately controls the energy-producing functions of mitochondria in response to changing physiological conditions, senescence, and disease.

title: RFID system evaluation against radiated transient noise
text: In this study, we evaluate the performance of a radiofrequency identification (RFID) system according to the ISO/IEC 14443 type-B standard in the presence of transient noise. The system operates at a frequency of 13.56 MHz and is exposed to interference from transient bursts with varying levels, frequencies, and durations in a controlled environment. To assess the impact of these transient noises on the digital communication system, we use two different methods: direct observation of an RFID device in the presence of transient signals and time-domain analysis of the interference using simulation. Our results show that the RFID system is susceptible to errors due to the transient noises, highlighting the importance of measuring and evaluating these phenomena in the time domain to ensure the system's reliability.

title: Musculoskeletal pain in Europe: its impact and a comparison of population and medical perceptions of treatment in eight European countries.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the impact of musculoskeletal pain (MP) on individuals and the management of MP by primary care physicians in eight European countries. Specifically, to:
* Describe the impact of MP on individuals
* Compare the management of MP by the population and primary care physicians
* Identify misconceptions about treatment

Methods:

* A total of 5803 people with MP and 1483 primary care physicians in eight European countries were randomly selected and interviewed by telephone using a structured questionnaire to gather information on usual management of MP and perceived benefits and risks of treatment.
* Current health status (SF-12) was also assessed.

Results:

* From primary care physicians' perspectives, MP appears to be well managed, with all presenting patients offered some form of treatment, and most doctors trying to improve patients' quality of life.
* However, from a population perspective, up to 27% of people with pain do not seek medical help, and of those who do, several wait months/years before seeing a doctor.
* Only 55% or fewer patients who have seen a doctor are currently receiving prescription treatment for their pain.
* Communication between doctors and patients is poor, with few patients given information about their condition, and many having misconceptions about treatment.

Conclusions:

* Management of MP is similar across eight European countries, but there is discordance between physician and patient perspectives of care.
* Some people with pain have never sought medical help despite being in constant/daily pain.
* Those who do seek help receive little written information or explanation, and many have misperceptions about the benefits and risks of treatment that limit their ability to actively participate in decisions about their care.

title: [Palliative care in Germany].
text: The delivery of palliative care in Germany still faces a significant undersupply for both inpatients and outpatients. However, over the past 15 years, progress has been made in Germany, which has drawn increasing attention to the situation of the incurably ill and dying. As a result, the first specialized palliative care structures have been established. While the situation for inpatients in hospitals and hospices is pleasing, albeit not yet fully covered, there is a more pressing need for outpatient care. Financial resources for palliative care, which have been addressed only partially to date, must be made more available to meet the growing demand. It is essential to recognize the needs of the incurably ill, their relatives, and friends, and to prioritize this issue on the healthcare agenda. The current developments in the federal government and individual states offer hope that the delivery of palliative care will improve further in the coming years.

title: A view to a kill: the bacterial type VI secretion system.
text: The bacterial type VI secretion system (T6SS) is an organelle that shares structural and mechanistic similarities with an intracellular membrane-attached contractile phage tail. Recent studies have revealed that a rapid conformational change in the structure of a sheath protein complex propels T6SS spike and tube components, along with antibacterial and antieukaryotic effectors, out of T6SS-containing cells and into surrounding prey cells. The contracted organelle is then recycled through an ATP-dependent process. T6SS is regulated at both transcriptional and posttranslational levels, with the latter involving detection of membrane perturbation in some species. In addition to targeting eukaryotic cells directly, the T6SS can also attack other bacteria co-infecting a mammalian host, underscoring its importance in both environmental ecosystems and infection and disease. This review summarizes recent advances in our understanding of the structure, mechanical function, assembly, and regulation of the T6SS.

title: Open Access Increases Citation Rate
text: PLoS Biology publishes a research article by Gunther Eysenbach that provides robust evidence that open-access articles are more immediately recognized and cited than non-OA articles. The study compared citations compiled by Thomson Scientific (formerly Thomson ISI) to individual articles published between June 2004 and December 2004 in the same journal, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), with an associated publication charge of US$1,000. The results show that OA articles gained a significant citation advantage over non-OA articles during the 4 to 16 months following publication, with OA articles being twice as likely to be cited 4 to 10 months after publication and almost three times as likely between 10 and 16 months. The analysis also looked at the impact of self-archiving non-OA articles and found that self-archived articles are also cited less often than OA articles from the same journal. The study highlights several potential challenges to the long-term future of open access, including varying attitudes of authors at different stages of their career, access to appropriate funds, and the potential for hybrid journals to dominate the market. However, the evidence from the current analysis argues most strongly for a time advantage in citation for OA articles, and open-access advocates should be emboldened by tangible evidence for what has seemed obvious all along.

title: Serum immunoglobulin A from patients with celiac disease inhibits human T84 intestinal crypt epithelial cell differentiation.
text:
BACKGROUND & AIMS:
Celiac disease is characterized by an abnormality in the biology of the jejunal crypt-villus axis, involving the deposition of immunoglobulin (Ig) A antibodies underneath the epithelium. The aim of this study was to investigate whether celiac disease serum IgA (specifically, reticulin/endomysial autoantibodies) interferes with the communication between mesenchymal cells and epithelial cells.
METHODS:
To achieve this goal, the study employed three-dimensional collagen gel cultures of T84 epithelial cells, which were differentiated with IMR-90 fibroblasts or transforming growth factor beta. The effects of purified celiac IgA and monoclonal tissue transglutaminase antibodies (CUB7402) on the cocultures were studied by adding the antibodies to the mixture.
RESULTS:
The study found that active celiac disease IgA, which reacts with tissue transglutaminase, significantly inhibited T84 epithelial cell differentiation (P < 0.001) and increased epithelial cell proliferation (P = 0.024). Similar effects were observed when antibodies against tissue transglutaminase were used.
CONCLUSIONS:
The primary finding of this study suggests that celiac disease-associated IgA class antibodies disrupt transforming growth factor beta-mediated fibroblast-epithelial cell cross-talk in this in vitro crypt-villus axis model. This discovery implies that celiac disease-specific autoantibodies may also contribute to the formation of the gluten-triggered jejunal mucosal lesion in celiac disease.

title: Pathogenesis of diseases associated with antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies.
text: Little is known about the underlying causes of diseases associated with circulating antineutrophil cytoplasm autoantibodies (ANCA), such as primary vasculitides and inflammatory bowel diseases. However, researchers are continuing to uncover the immune mechanisms involved in the development of these diseases. In this review, we will first examine the triggers that lead to the production of ANCA, including the potential role of microbial superantigens and any potential flaws in the process of apoptosis or the removal of apoptotic cells. We will then focus on the contribution of ANCA to clinical symptoms and its pathogenic role, including the accessibility of ANCA antigens as targets for circulating antibodies and the manner in which ANCA causes tissue damage. Additionally, we will explore the mechanisms by which ANCA activates neutrophils, including the engagement of Fcgamma receptors, the possible mechanisms of neutrophil-mediated tissue damage, and the neutrophil-endothelial interaction.

title: The common marmoset as a novel animal model system for biomedical and neuroscience research applications.
text:
The common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a tiny New World primate, has gained significant attention in the fields of biomedical science and neuroscience due to its unique characteristics. These include:
1. Cross-reactivity with human cytokines or hormones, making it an ideal model for studying human diseases.
2. Easy handling due to its small size, facilitating research and experimentation.
3. High reproductive efficiency, allowing for a steady supply of animals for research purposes.
4. Establishment of basic research tools, such as genetic manipulation, providing a solid foundation for studying the common marmoset.
5. Unique behavioral and cognitive characteristics, offering insights into the evolution of social behavior and cognitive processes.
Several neurological disease models have been developed in the common marmoset, including Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, stroke, multiple sclerosis, and spinal cord injury. Recently, we have also developed transgenic common marmosets with germline transmission, which is expected to provide a new and valuable animal model for studying human diseases. In this review, we will summarize the recent progress of biomedical research and neuroscience using the common marmoset as an excellent model system.

title: Liver receptor homolog-1 regulates the transcription of steroidogenic enzymes and induces the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into steroidogenic cells.
text:
Steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1, also known as Ad4BP) has been shown to be a primary transcriptional regulator of steroidogenic-related genes. However, our previous studies have revealed that liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1), a member of the NR5A nuclear receptor family, is expressed at much higher levels than SF-1 mRNA in the human gonad. We have also demonstrated that SF-1 can induce the differentiation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) into steroidogenic cells, such as Leydig or adrenocortical cells. The introduction of LRH-1 into human MSCs (hMSCs) using cAMP also led to the expression of steroidogenic enzymes, including CYP17, and their differentiation into steroid hormone-producing cells. Our results suggest that LRH-1 plays a crucial role in regulating the steroidogenic lineage in MSCs and may represent a key regulator of steroid hormone production in human Leydig cells.
To investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of CYP17 by LRH-1, we performed promoter analysis, EMSA, and chromatin immunoprecipitation assays using LRH-1-transduced hMSCs. Our findings revealed that three LRH-1 binding sites in the CYP17 promoter region were responsible for its transactivation. Immunohistochemical studies also showed that LRH-1 protein was expressed in human Leydig cells. Furthermore, we found that the CYP17 promoter region was highly methylated in hMSCs, but demethylation occurred upon introduction of LRH-1 and cAMP treatment.
Taken together, our results suggest that LRH-1 plays a critical role in regulating the steroidogenic program in MSCs and may represent a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of steroid hormone-related disorders.

title: Checkpoint responses to replication fork barriers.
text: The significance of DNA replication fidelity in maintaining genome integrity cannot be overstated. When an active replication fork is disrupted, various cellular pathways are activated to stabilize the replication apparatus and rectify the issue. However, if the problem persists, the fork may collapse, exposing free DNA ends to potentially harmful processing. In prokaryotes, replication fork collapse can trigger the activity of recombination proteins to restore the replication fork. Recent research has shown that recombination is also closely linked to replication in eukaryotic cells, with recombination proteins being recruited to collapsed, but not stalled, replication forks. This review aims to discuss the different types of replication fork barriers (RFBs) that can lead to distinct DNA structures at stalled replication forks. The DNA structure checkpoints that operate within S phase respond to different RFBs in different ways, and we will examine the processes that are regulated by the DNA replication checkpoints, with a particular focus on the function of the intra-S phase checkpoint that stabilizes the stalled fork.

title: Ecology, economics and political will: the vicissitudes of malaria strategies in Asia.
text:
The documented history of malaria in parts of Asia spans over 2,000 years, during which the disease has been a significant player in the socioeconomic landscape of many nations. On a smaller scale, the last half century has witnessed fluctuations in malaria prevalence and impact across the diverse ecosystems of the region, reflecting the changing social, economic, and political structures. While the majority of global malaria cases are currently found in Africa, Asia once had a higher incidence before successful malaria control programs were implemented. However, the region now faces a global threat in the form of the epicenter of multidrug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, which is gradually spreading across the tropical world. This reflects the impact of economic changes, such as population mobility in search of commerce and trade, as well as the effects of political instability.
The period from the 1950s to the 1990s saw near eradication of malaria in Sri Lanka, control and resurgence in India, the influence of war and post-war instability on drug resistance in Cambodia, an increase in severe and cerebral malaria in Myanmar during prolonged political turmoil, and the essential disappearance of the disease from most of Thailand except for forested border areas where it remains uncontrollable. Both positive and negative experiences offer lessons for the debate between eradication and control as strategies. China has long aimed for "basic elimination," or near eradication, with community organization, thorough case detection, management, and focus elimination, as well as political will at all levels of society. However, China has not succeeded in international border regions where unfettered population movement hinders the program. Thailand, Malaysia, and Vietnam have reached essential elimination in their rice field plains through vigorous vertical programs but fall short at their forested borders.
Economics plays a central role in the history of malaria, with the current love affair with free market economics limiting the involvement of communities in malaria management. The task of malaria control or elimination must be linked to the basic macroeconomic process that preoccupies governments, rather than being isolated in the health sector. Historically, malaria has had a significant negative impact on the productivity of nations, and economic models need to be revised with political aplomb and integrated with technical and demographic strategies. Recent decades in Chinese malaria history offer some relevant lessons for this context.

title: Global and regional risk of disabling sequelae from bacterial meningitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Limited data exist to assess the global and regional risk of sequelae following bacterial meningitis. To address this knowledge gap, we aimed to estimate the risks of major and minor sequelae caused by bacterial meningitis, as well as the distribution of different types of sequelae and compare risk by region and income. We conducted a systematic review of published papers from 1980 to 2008. We categorized sequelae into major (cognitive deficit, bilateral hearing loss, motor deficit, seizures, visual impairment, hydrocephalus) and minor (behavioural problems, learning difficulties, unilateral hearing loss, hypotonia, diplopia) types. Of the 132 papers selected for inclusion, the median (interquartile range) risk of at least one major or minor sequela after hospital discharge was 19.9% (12.3-35.3%). The risk of at least one major sequela was 12.8% (7.2-21.1%), and the risk of at least one minor sequela was 8.6% (4.4-15.3%). The median (interquartile range) risk of at least one major sequela was 24.7% (16.2-35.3%) in pneumococcal meningitis, 9.5% (7.1-15.3%) in Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) meningitis, and 7.2% (4.3-11.2%) in meningococcal meningitis. The most common major sequela was hearing loss (33.9%), and 19.7% of individuals had multiple impairments. In a random-effects meta-analysis, the all-cause risk of a major sequela was twice as high in the African (pooled risk estimate 25.1% [95% CI 18.9-32.0%]) and southeast Asian regions (21.6% [95% CI 13.1-31.5%]) compared to the European region (9.4% [95% CI 7.0-12.3%]; overall I(2)=89.5%, p<0.0001). The risks of long-term disabling sequelae were highest in low-income countries, where the burden of bacterial meningitis is greatest. Our findings suggest that vaccination with Hib, pneumococcal, and meningococcal vaccines could have averted many of the reported sequelae.

title: Efficacy of human papillomavirus testing for the detection of invasive cervical cancers and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia: a randomised controlled trial.
text:
Background:
Human papillomavirus (HPV) testing is more sensitive but less specific than cytology for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). We evaluated the effectiveness of cervical cancer screening policies based on HPV testing.
Methods:
Between March 2004 and December 2004, we randomly assigned women aged 25-60 years to conventional cytology or HPV testing in combination with liquid-based cytology (first phase) or alone (second phase). Randomization was done using computer in two screening centers and sequential opening of numbered sealed envelopes in the remaining seven centers. During the first phase, women who were HPV-positive and aged 35-60 years were referred to colposcopy, while women aged 25-34 years were referred to colposcopy only if cytology was also abnormal or HPV testing was persistently positive. During the second phase, women in the HPV group were referred for colposcopy if the HPV test was positive. Two rounds of screening occurred in each phase, and all women had cytology testing only at the second round. The primary endpoint was the detection of grade 2 and 3 CIN, and invasive cervical cancers during the first and second screening rounds. Analysis was conducted by intention to screen. This trial is registered, number ISRCTN81678807.
Findings:
In total, 47,001 women were randomly assigned to the cytology group and 47,369 to HPV testing. Of these, 33,851 women from the cytology group and 32,998 from the HPV-testing group had a second round of screening. We also retrieved histological diagnoses from screening done elsewhere. The detection of invasive cervical cancers was similar for the two groups in the first round of screening (nine in the cytology group vs seven in the HPV group, p=0.62); no cases were detected in the HPV group during round two, compared with nine in the cytology group (p=0.004). Overall, in the two rounds of screening, 18 invasive cancers were detected in the cytology group versus seven in the HPV group (p=0.028). Among women aged 35-60 years, at round one, the relative detection (HPV vs cytology) was 2.00 (95% CI 1.44-2.77) for CIN2, 2.08 (1.47-2.95) for CIN3, and 2.03 (1.60-2.57) for CIN2 and 3 together. At round two, the relative detection was 0.54 (0.23-1.28) for CIN2, 0.48 (0.21-1.11) for CIN3, and 0.51 (0.28-0.93) for CIN2 and 3 together. Among women aged 25-34 years, there was significant heterogeneity between phases in the relative detection of CIN3. At round one, the relative detection was 0.93 (0.52-1.64) in phase one and 3.91 (2.02-7.57) in phase two. At round two, the relative detection was 1.34 (0.46-3.84) in phase one and 0.20 (0.04-0.93) in phase two. Pooling both phases, the detection ratio of CIN2 for women aged 25-34 years was 4.09 (2.24-7.48) at round one and 0.64 (0.23-1.27) at round two.
Interpretation:
HPV-based screening is more effective than cytology in preventing invasive cervical cancer by detecting persistent high-grade lesions earlier and providing a longer low-risk period. However, in younger women, HPV screening leads to over-diagnosis of regressive CIN2. Funding: European Union, Italian Ministry of Health, Regional Health Administrations of Piemonte, Tuscany, Veneto, and Emilia-Romagna, and Public Health Agency of Lazio.

title: Microcytosis, iron deficiency and thalassaemia in a multi-ethnic community: a pilot study.
text: The high prevalence of microcytosis (defined as mean cell hemoglobin <27 pg) without any other abnormalities is a significant source of confusion in screening for hemoglobin disorders. In this small pilot study, we aimed to address this confusion by routinely proceeding to plasma ferritin and HPLC assay using the original sequestrene blood sample when microcytosis is detected. Our study included 1,302 individuals referred for a full blood count by their General Practitioner (GP) to a North London district general hospital serving a multi-ethnic inner-city population. We established the participants' ethnicity through a questionnaire. In North Europeans, microcytosis was present in 3% of males (half of which were iron-deficient) and 11% of females (most of which were iron-deficient). In contrast, among ethnic minorities, microcytosis was present in 35% of males (one-tenth of which were iron-deficient) and 45% of females (less than half of which were iron-deficient). Based on these findings, we were able to make an exclusion diagnosis of "probable alpha thalassaemia" in the remaining individuals. Our results suggest that when microcytosis is present, routinely analyzing the original sequestrene sample using plasma ferritin assay and hemoglobinopathy screening could lead to a more efficient and cost-effective laboratory service for primary care and maternity services.

title: Crystal structure of the human AAA+ protein RuvBL1.
text: RuvBL1 is a highly conserved eukaryotic protein belonging to the AAA(+)-family of ATPases, which are involved in various cellular processes. The protein plays important roles in signaling pathways such as c-Myc and Wnt pathways, as well as in chromatin remodeling, transcriptional regulation, and DNA repair. In this study, we present the three-dimensional structure of the selenomethionine variant of human RuvBL1, which was refined to 2.2 Å resolution using diffraction data. The crystal structure of the hexamer reveals that the monomers are formed of ADP-bound RuvBL1 proteins. The protein contains three domains, with the first and third domains involved in ATP binding and hydrolysis. Although previous studies have shown that ATPase activity is essential for RuvBL1's in vivo functions, we could only detect a marginal activity with the purified protein. Structural homology and DNA binding studies suggest that the second domain, which is unique among AAA(+) proteins and not present in the bacterial homolog RuvB, is a novel DNA/RNA-binding domain. We demonstrate that RuvBL1 interacts with single-stranded DNA/RNA and double-stranded DNA. The structure of the RuvBL1.ADP complex, combined with our biochemical results, suggest that while RuvBL1 possesses all the structural characteristics of a molecular motor, including those of an ATP-driven helicase, one or more as yet undetermined cofactors are required for its enzymatic activity.

title: Characteristics of a monoclonal antibody (RM124) against acute myelocytic leukemia cells.
text: A monoclonal antibody (MCA) was developed against cells from an experimental rat myelocytic leukemia (BNML) model. The characteristics of this rat leukemia model are similar to those of human acute myelocytic leukemia. The MCA, called RM124, was analyzed to determine its labeling pattern on BNML leukemia cells, normal rat bone marrow cells, and hemopoietic stem cells (HSC) using flow cytometry and complement-dependent cytotoxicity assays. Flow cytometry revealed a significantly higher labeling of leukemic cells by RM124 compared to normal bone marrow cells, including colonies forming units (CFU-S) and CFU-C. However, a smaller subpopulation of normal granulocytes showed cross-reactivity, but at a lower labeling density. The cytotoxicity assays showed that there was selective killing of leukemic cells compared to normal HSC (CFU-S).

title: Quantitative assessment of T-cell repertoire recovery after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
text: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) can lead to delayed T cell recovery and restricted T cell receptor (TCR) diversity, which are associated with increased risks of infection and cancer relapse. However, technical challenges have hindered the accurate measurement of TCR diversity after allo-HSCT. To overcome these challenges, we employed a novel approach that combines 5' rapid amplification of complementary DNA ends PCR (5' RACE-PCR) with deep sequencing to quantify TCR diversity in 28 recipients of allo-HSCT. By analyzing duplicate blood samples, we demonstrated the accuracy of our method in determining the frequency of individual TCRs. Our findings revealed that cord blood-graft recipients approximated the TCR diversity of healthy individuals after 6 months, while recipients of T cell-depleted peripheral-blood stem cell grafts exhibited significant deficiencies in CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cell diversities, with a 28-fold and 14-fold decrease, respectively, compared to healthy individuals. However, these deficiencies improved only for the CD4(+) T cell compartment after 12 months. Our approach provides an unprecedented view of T cell repertoire recovery after allo-HSCT and may identify patients at high risk of infection or relapse.

title: Silver sulfadiazine for the treatment of partial-thickness burns and venous stasis ulcers.
text:
BACKGROUND: For decades, silver-containing antibiotics such as silver sulfadiazine (SSD) have been used as standard topical treatment for patients with partial-thickness burns and venous stasis ulcers. This systematic review aims to answer the following research question: in ambulatory patients with partial-thickness burns or stasis dermatitis ulcers, does the use of topical SSD compared to non-antibiotic dressings improve mortality, wound healing, re-epithelialization, or infection rates?
METHODS: We conducted a systematic search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and other databases to identify randomized controlled trials that enrolled patients with partial-thickness burns or venous stasis ulcers and randomized them to either topical SSD or placebo, saline-soaked gauze, paraffin gauze, sterile dry dressing, or non-antibiotic moist dressing. Outcomes included mortality, wound healing, speed of re-epithelialization, and infection rates.
RESULTS: Our search yielded 400 potential articles for burns and 50 articles for stasis dermatitis ulcers. However, only seven animal studies (one mouse, four rat, and two pig) were relevant to the proposed question, providing conflicting results. While some studies support the use of SSD for treating partial-thickness burns, others question its effectiveness. The only human study found did not show a significant improvement in the rate of complete healing in the SSD group compared to placebo at 4 weeks or 1 year of follow-up.
CONCLUSION: Based on the available evidence, there is insufficient support to routinely use SSD for ambulatory patients with either partial-thickness burns or stasis dermatitis ulcers to reduce mortality, prevent infection, or accelerate wound healing in humans.

title: Putting p53 in Context
text: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer, with functional implications that are both complex and multifaceted. Upon activation by a variety of stress stimuli, p53 orchestrates an intricate transcriptional program that encompasses a wide range of biological responses. Despite the extensive characterization of the p53 network, a complete understanding of how and under what circumstances p53 exerts its diverse effects remains elusive. To gain insight into the mechanisms underlying p53's tumor-suppressive activities, it is essential to consider the interplay between cell type, mutation profile, and epigenetic cell state, and to explore strategies for restoring p53's tumor-suppressive functions in cancer.

title: Modeling the evolution of culture-adapted human embryonic stem cells.
text: The long-term evolution of human embryonic stem (ES) cells in culture is inevitable, as any mutant with a growth advantage will be selectively amplified. However, the impact of population size, mutation rate, and selection pressure on this evolution is often overlooked. To address this gap in understanding, we developed a Monte Carlo simulation model to predict how changes in these factors influence the emergence and spread of mutant ES cells. We validated the model by comparing its predictions with in vitro data. The simulation provides an estimate of the expected rate of generation of culture-adapted ES cells under different assumptions about the key parameters. Notably, it highlights the effect of population size, revealing that maintaining cells in smaller populations reduces the likelihood of abnormal cultures developing.

title: CD28 delivers a unique signal leading to the selective recruitment of RelA and p52 NF-kappaB subunits on IL-8 and Bcl-xL gene promoters.
text: CD28 is a crucial costimulatory receptor that plays a vital role in the full activation of T lymphocytes. The CD28 receptor can enhance T cell antigen receptor (TCR) signals and deliver independent signals, leading to the activation of IκB kinase and NF-κB.
