Our study demonstrates that the TCR-independent CD28 signal leads to the selective transcription of survival (Bcl-xL) and inflammatory (IL-8 and B cell activation factor, but not proliferative (IL-2), genes in a NF-κB-dependent manner. CD28-stimulated T cells actively secrete IL-8, and Bcl-xL up-regulation protects T cells from radiation-induced apoptosis. The transcription of CD28-induced genes is mediated by the specific recruitment of RelA and p52 NF-κB subunits to target promoters. In contrast, p50 and c-Rel, which preferentially bind NF-κB sites on the IL-2 gene promoter after anti-CD3 stimulation, are not involved. Therefore, we have identified CD28 as a key regulator of genes important for both survival and inflammation.

title: Netting neutrophils are major inducers of type I IFN production in pediatric systemic lupus erythematosus.
text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by a breakdown of tolerance to nuclear antigens and the formation of immune complexes. Recent genomic studies have shown that SLE leukocytes uniformly express type I interferon (IFN)-induced and neutrophil-related transcripts. Increased production and/or bioavailability of IFN-α and alterations in dendritic cell (DC) homeostasis have been linked to SLE pathogenesis. Although neutrophils have long been associated with SLE, their role in disease pathogenesis remains unclear. This study shows that mature SLE neutrophils are primed in vivo by type I IFN and die upon exposure to SLE-derived anti-ribonucleoprotein antibodies, releasing neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). SLE NETs contain DNA as well as large amounts of LL37 and HMGB1, neutrophil proteins that facilitate the uptake and recognition of mammalian DNA by plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs). Our findings reveal an unexpected role for neutrophils in SLE pathogenesis and identify a novel link between nucleic acid-recognizing antibodies and type I IFN production in this disease.

title: Assessment for selection for the health care professions and specialty training: consensus statement and recommendations from the Ottawa 2010 Conference.
text:
Assessment for selection in medicine and the health professions should adhere to the same quality assurance processes as in-course assessment. The literature on selection is limited and lacks theoretical or conceptual depth. For written testing, there is evidence of the predictive validity of the Medical College Admission Test (MCAT) for medical school and licensing examination performance. Additionally, there is evidence for the predictive validity of grade point average, particularly when combined with MCAT for graduate entry, although there is limited evidence on the predictive validity of school leaver scores. Interviews have not been shown to be reliable selection measures. Studies of multiple mini-interviews have demonstrated good predictive validity and reliability. The growing interest in personality testing is the only area that warrants further research.
Widening access to medical and health professional programs is a growing priority, and this aligns with the social accountability mandate of medical and health professional schools. While traditional selection measures disproportionately affect certain population groups, there is limited evidence on the effectiveness of non-traditional measures in widening access. Preparation and outreach programs show the most promise.
In summary, there are only a few areas of consensus for assessment for selection. Future actions should focus on adopting good assessment principles, aligning curricula, using multi-method programmatic approaches, developing interdisciplinary frameworks, and utilizing sophisticated measurement models. The social accountability mandate of medical and health professional schools requires that social inclusion, workforce issues, and widening access be embedded in the principles of good assessment for selection.

title: THE GLYOXAL BIS(2-HYDROXYANIL) METHOD MODIFIED FOR LOCALIZING INSOLUBLE CALCIUM SALTS.
text:
To enhance the staining of insoluble calcium salts with glyoxal bis(2-hydroxyanil) (GBHA), the original solution containing 2 ml of 0.4% GBHA in absolute ethanol and 0.3 ml of aqueous 5% NaOH was modified as follows:
Modification I:
* 1 or 2 drops of the modified solution (0.6 ml of 10% aqueous NaOH and 0.4% GBHA in absolute ethanol) were placed on the section and allowed to evaporate gradually to dryness, concentrating the GBHA and NaOH on the insoluble calcium salts.
Modification II:
* 0.1 gm GBHA in 2 ml of 3.4% NaOH in 75% ethanol was added to the section and allowed to stain for 5 minutes.
To prevent diffusion and loss of calcium, the tissues were processed using the freeze-substitution or freeze-dry method, and sections were stained without removing the paraffin. The stained slides were immersed for 15 minutes in 90% ethanol saturated with KCN and Na2CO3 to enhance specificity to calcium, rinsed, and counterstained in 95% ethanol containing 0.1% each of fast green and hematoxylin.

title: Detecting selective sweeps: a new approach based on hidden markov models.
text: Recent advancements in detecting and localizing selective sweeps through the analysis of SNP data have gained significant attention. In this study, we propose the use of hidden Markov models (HMMs) for identifying selective sweeps in DNA sequences. Similarly to other methods, our HMMs utilize the site frequency spectrum and the spatial distribution of diversity along the sequence to detect selection. However, our HMMs explicitly model the correlation structure between adjacent sites, which sets them apart from earlier approaches. The detection capabilities of our methods and their accuracy in estimating the location of the selected site are comparable to those of other methods for constant population sizes. In contrast, our HMMs often produce fewer false positives when dealing with population bottlenecks.

title: A Balance between Secreted Inhibitors and Edge Sensing Controls Gastruloid Self-Organization.
text:
The initial stages of human embryonic development remain largely enigmatic. To elucidate the mechanisms of patterning in the human embryo, we employed colonies of human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) cultured on micropatterned substrates and differentiated with BMP4. These gastruloids recapitulate the embryonic arrangement of the mammalian germ layers and provide a platform to investigate the structural and signaling mechanisms governing human gastrulation.
Structurally, high-density hESCs display a unique reorganization of their receptors, with lateral localization at the center of the colony and apical localization at the edge. This relocalization strategy insulates cells at the center from apically applied ligands while maintaining responsiveness to basally presented ones. Furthermore, BMP4 directly induces the expression of its own inhibitor, NOGGIN, creating a reaction-diffusion mechanism that underlies patterning.
To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we developed a quantitative model integrating edge sensing and inhibitors, which can predict human fate positioning in gastruloids and potentially in the human embryo. This approach provides a novel framework for understanding the complex processes governing human embryonic development.

title: Tenectin is a novel alphaPS2betaPS integrin ligand required for wing morphogenesis and male genital looping in Drosophila.
text:
The morphogenesis of adult structures in holometabolous insects, such as flies, is regulated by two key hormones: ecdysteroids and juvenile hormones. These hormones coordinate cell-cell interactions, which are mediated in part by cell surface integrin receptors and their extracellular matrix (ECM) ligands. While the role of these adhesion molecules in insect development has been studied, the regulation of these molecules by hormones is not well understood.
To investigate this further, we focused on a newly discovered ECM molecule called tenectin. We found that tenectin is a hormonally regulated ECM protein that plays a crucial role in the proper morphogenesis of adult wing and male genitalia. Our experiments showed that tenectin functions as a new ligand for the PS2 integrins, which are important for cell adhesion and signaling. The interaction between tenectin and the PS2 integrins is dependent on specific motifs, such as RGD and RGD-like sequences.
Our findings also revealed a novel role for PS integrins in the execution of left-right asymmetry during the development of the male genitalia. These results provide new insights into the complex interplay between hormones, adhesion molecules, and the ECM during insect development.
In summary, our study uncovered a previously unknown role for tenectin in insect morphogenesis and highlighted the importance of hormonal regulation of adhesion molecules in insect development. The findings also suggest a new mechanism for the execution of left-right asymmetry during development.

title: Schedule-dependent interaction between anticancer treatments
text: The oncogene MDMX is overexpressed in many cancers, leading to the suppression of the tumor suppressor protein p53. Inhibitors of MDMX could potentially reactivate p53 and enhance the effectiveness of drugs that damage DNA. However, we currently lack a comprehensive understanding of how inhibiting MDMX affects the p53 signaling pathway and the sensitivity of cancer cells to DNA damage. By using live cell imaging, we discovered that depleting MDMX in single cells leads to two distinct phases of p53 accumulation: an initial postmitotic pulse followed by low-amplitude oscillations. The response to DNA damage differed between these two phases, with MDMX depletion synergizing with DNA damage in causing cell death during the first phase, but inhibiting cell death during the second phase. Therefore, a quantitative understanding of signal dynamics and cellular states is crucial for designing an optimal schedule of dual-drug administration.

title: Potent, Selective, and Orally Bioavailable Inhibitors of VPS34 Provide Chemical Tools to Modulate Autophagy in Vivo.
text: Autophagy is a crucial cellular process that involves the degradation of damaged or dysfunctional cellular components through lysosomal-dependent mechanisms. Until recently, the study of autophagy was hindered by the lack of effective pharmacological tools, but recent advances have led to the development of selective inhibitors of the PI 3-kinase VPS34, which is essential for autophagy. In this study, we describe the discovery and characterization of potent and selective VPS34 inhibitors, their pharmacokinetic properties, and their ability to inhibit autophagy in both cellular and mouse models.

title: The role of neutrophils in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus.
text:
Recent advances have shed light on the pivotal role of neutrophils in the pathogenesis of systemic autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Neutrophils are now recognized as key regulators of innate and adaptive immunity, and their dysregulation can lead to the development of organ damage in SLE.
Several putative biomarkers for SLE have been identified as neutrophil-related, including neutrophil granular proteins and histones undergoing post-translational modifications during neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. In the bone marrow, lupus neutrophils can drive B and T cell abnormalities by producing excessive amounts of type-I interferons, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα), and B-cell stimulating factors such as B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL).
Lupus neutrophils and, in particular, low-density granulocytes (a distinct pathogenic subset) exhibit epigenetic modifications and genomic alterations that may contribute to their deleterious roles in SLE. The proteins and enzymes externalized by NETs can also affect vascular health by inducing endothelial apoptosis and oxidizing lipoproteins, leading to atherosclerosis.
Inhibiting NET formation through peptidylarginine deiminase inhibitors has been shown to abrogate the lupus phenotype and atherosclerosis in murine studies, highlighting the potential of targeting these immunostimulatory pathways in SLE.
In summary, recent discoveries underscore the importance of neutrophils, low-density granulocytes, and NET formation and clearance in SLE pathogenesis. Future research should focus on identifying specific targets for therapeutic intervention in these pathways to treat SLE.

title: Enhancement of proteasome function by PA28α overexpression protects against oxidative stress.
text: The primary function of the proteasome is the targeted degradation of intracellular proteins, and dysfunction of the proteasome has been implicated in various cardiac diseases, including experimental cardiomyopathies and human congestive heart failure. Currently, there are no effective measures to enhance proteasome function, but such interventions could be beneficial in elucidating the pathogenic role of proteasome dysfunction and may have significant therapeutic potential. The association of proteasome activator 28 (PA28) with the 20S proteasome may play a role in antigen processing, but it is unclear whether PA28 has any important functions outside of antigen presentation. However, our study shows that overexpressing PA28α (PA28αOE) in cultured neonatal rat cardiomyocytes leads to increased levels of 11S proteasomes and enhanced degradation of a validated proteasome surrogate substrate (GFPu). PA28αOE also attenuates the increases in protein carbonyls and suppresses apoptosis induced by hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in cardiomyocytes under basal conditions or when exposed to oxidative stress. Our findings suggest that PA28αOE can up-regulate 11S proteasomes, enhance the removal of misfolded and oxidized proteins, and protect against oxidative stress in cardiomyocytes, providing a potential means to increase proteasomal degradation of abnormal cellular proteins.

title: A unified concept of species and its consequences for the future of taxonomy
text: Contemporary species concepts are diverse, yet they all share a common foundation: the idea that species are segments of lineages at the population level of biological organization. However, different species concepts emphasize different secondary properties, such as intrinsic reproductive isolation, monophyly, and diagnosability, which are considered necessary for recognizing lineages as species. A unified species concept, on the other hand, can be achieved by viewing the common fundamental idea of a separately evolving lineage segment as the only necessary property of species, and interpreting the various secondary properties as lines of evidence relevant to assessing lineage separation or as properties that define different subcategories of the species category. This unified species concept has significant implications for taxonomy, including the recognition of undifferentiated and undiagnosable lineages as species, the possibility of species fusion, the nested nature of species within other species, and the rejection of the species category as a taxonomic rank. This shift in perspective reflects a broader conceptual change in the discipline of systematics, which has moved away from a utilitarian focus on classifying organisms towards a more scientific approach of testing hypotheses about lineage boundaries and phylogenetic relationships. The unified species concept is a natural outcome of this shift and represents a more complete acceptance of the idea that species are fundamental units of biology. As such, it is central to the future of taxonomy.

title: Regulation of the small GTP-binding protein Rho by cell adhesion and the cytoskeleton.
text: Soluble factors from serum, such as lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), are believed to activate the small GTP-binding protein Rho through their ability to induce actin stress fibers and focal adhesions in a Rho-dependent manner. However, the role of cell adhesion to extracellular matrices (ECM) in activating Rho has been controversial due to the difficulty in distinguishing changes in Rho activity from the structural contributions of ECM to the formation of focal adhesions. To address these questions, we developed an assay to measure GTP-bound cellular Rho. When Swiss 3T3 cells were plated on fibronectin-coated dishes, there was a transient inhibition of Rho, followed by a phase of Rho activation. The activation phase was significantly enhanced by serum. In serum-starved adherent cells, LPA induced a transient Rho activation, while suspended cells showed sustained Rho activation in the presence of serum. Furthermore, suspended cells had higher Rho activity than adherent cells in the presence of serum, indicating the existence of an adhesion-dependent negative-feedback loop. Interestingly, we also found that both cytochalasin D and colchicine, which have opposite effects on stress fibers and focal adhesions, can activate Rho. Our results demonstrate that ECM, cytoskeletal structures, and soluble factors all play a role in regulating Rho activity.

title: Core binding factors are necessary for natural killer cell development and cooperate with Notch signaling during T-cell specification.
text: CBFbeta is the non-DNA-binding subunit of core binding factors (CBFs), and its levels are crucial for T-cell development. Mice with reduced CBFbeta exhibit profound defects in T-cell development, but not in B-cell development. Our study shows that CBFbeta is also essential for early NK-cell development. Furthermore, we found that T-cell development abruptly halts during the specification stage, as the expression of Gata3 and Tcf7, which are key regulators of T lineage specification, is significantly reduced, along with the functional thymic progenitors. Neither constitutively active Notch signaling nor IL-7 signaling can restore T-cell expansion or differentiation in CBFbeta-deficient cells, nor can overexpression of Runx1 or CBFbeta overcome a lack of Notch signaling. Therefore, the prethymic cell's ability to respond appropriately to Notch signaling is dependent on CBFbeta, and both signals converge to activate the T-cell developmental program.

title: VEGF and podocytes in diabetic nephropathy.
text: Vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-A) is a protein produced by podocytes that is essential for the survival of endothelial cells, podocytes, and mesangial cells. VEGF-A regulates the function of slit diaphragms and podocyte shape by interacting with VEGF receptor 2, nephrin, and actin. Chronic high blood sugar levels can lead to an overproduction of VEGF-A in podocytes and a decrease in endothelial nitric oxide, which can contribute to the development and progression of diabetic nephropathy. The abnormal communication between VEGF-A and nitric oxide pathways is fueled by the diabetic environment, resulting in increased oxidative stress. Recent discoveries about these harmful molecular mechanisms provide new potential targets for treatment of diabetic kidney disease.

title: Detection and distribution patterns of telomerase activity in insects.
text: Telomeres of most insects are composed of pentanucleotide (TTAGG)n repeats, although this structure is absent in certain insect species, such as Diptera, where telomere maintenance may occur independently of telomerase. To elucidate the diverse mechanisms of telomere formation in insects, we conducted a comprehensive study of a putative insect telomerase that has not been previously described. Utilizing a modified telomeric repeat amplification protocol (TRAP), we initially detected telomerase activity in crickets, cockroaches, and two Lepidopteran insects. Our findings revealed that the telomerase from crickets and cockroaches requires dATP, dGTP, and dTTP as substrates, but not dCTP, and sequence analysis of the products of TRAP revealed that the (TTAGG)n repeats are synthesized by telomerase. Notably, the cockroach telomerase was detected in both somatic (fat body, muscle, and neural tissues) and germ line (testis) cells, indicating that the expression of this enzyme is not regulated in a tissue-specific manner at the adult stage. Conversely, we were unable to detect telomerase activity in all tissues and cell cultures of the silkworm, Bombyx mori, and in two Drosophila and one Sarcophaga cell lines, supporting the hypothesis that Dipteran insects maintain their telomeres independently of telomerase.

title: Conversion of the lac repressor into an allosterically regulated transcriptional activator for mammalian cells.
text: A novel mammalian regulatory system was created by modifying the Escherichia coli lac repressor to create a mammalian transcriptional activator. The lac repressor was altered by adding a nuclear localization signal from the simian virus 40 (SV40) large tumor antigen and the transcription activation domain from the herpes simplex virus type 1 virion protein 16. The resulting lac activator protein (LAP) fusions were potent activators of various promoters containing lac operator sequences placed either upstream or downstream of the transcription unit. A single lac operator was sufficient for transactivation, while multiple operators exhibited synergistic activity when separated by a small distance. Promoters containing 14 or 21 operator sequences were induced at least 1,000-fold in response to LAP, with levels of activity 20 to 30 times greater than that of the SV40 early promoter in HeLa cells. LAP activation was inhibited by isopropyl-beta-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG), indicating that it retained the functions necessary for allosteric regulation. LAP was also found to be bifunctional, acting as both a transcriptional activator and repressor of expression of an SV40 promoter containing an operator immediately downstream of the TATA box. Finally, genetic selection schemes were developed that allowed for the generation of LAP-expressing cell lines at high frequency from either established or primary cells in culture.

title: Antigen availability determines CD8⁺ T cell-dendritic cell interaction kinetics and memory fate decisions.
text: T cells are activated by antigen-bearing dendritic cells (DCs) in lymph nodes through three distinct phases. The initial phase, characterized by transient and serial interactions between DCs and T cells, is inversely correlated with the dose of antigen. However, our findings challenge this notion, as we have shown that CD8+ T cells interacting with DCs presenting low-dose, short-lived antigen did not transition to the second phase of activation, whereas higher antigen dose led to this transition. Both antigenic constellations promoted T cell proliferation and effector differentiation, but yielded different transcriptome signatures at 12 hours and 24 hours. T cells that experienced the second phase developed long-lived memory, whereas conditions without stable DC-T cell contacts led to immunological amnesia. These findings indicate that T cells make fate decisions within hours after antigen exposure, resulting in long-term memory or abortive effector responses, which are correlated with the kinetics of T cell-DC interactions.

title: BAX/BAK-independent mitoptosis during cell death induced by proteasome inhibition?
text: Proteasome inhibitors trigger rapid cell death in cancer cells. We found that in epithelial cancer cells, this death is accompanied by a dramatic and simultaneous increase in several BH3-only proteins, including BIK, BIM, MCL-1S, NOXA, and PUMA, as well as p53. These elevated levels are likely due to direct inhibition of proteasomal degradation, induction of transcription, and active translation. Unlike cell death triggered by BAX and BAK, this process is independent of these proteins and occurs through the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. By identifying the sequence of molecular events triggered by a typical proteasome inhibitor, MG132, we found that it starts with rapid accumulation of BH3-only proteins in the mitochondria, followed by mitochondrial membrane permeabilization and subsequent loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, leading to irreversible changes in mitochondrial ultrastructure, degradation of the mitochondrial network, and impairment of crucial mitochondrial functions. Our results also provide a rationale for broader use of proteasome inhibitors to kill apoptosis-resistant tumor cells that lack functional BAX/BAK proteins.

title: Site of action of a ribosomal RNA methylase responsible for resistance to erythromycin and other antibiotics.
text: The enzyme responsible for conferring resistance to erythromycin in the organism Streptomyces erythraeus modifies a single adenine residue in the 23S rRNA of Bacillus stearothermophilus. This adenine residue corresponds to position Ade 2058 in Escherichia coli 23S rRNA. Additionally, the same enzyme responsible for conferring resistance to macrolides, lincomycin, and streptogramin B-related antibiotics in Staphylococcus aureus also acts at this same site.

title: 53BP1 nuclear bodies form around DNA lesions generated by mitotic transmission of chromosomes under replication stress
text: The completion of genome duplication is hindered by structural and topological barriers that obstruct the progression of replication forks, posing a significant threat to genome integrity. However, the fate of DNA with unresolved replication intermediates remains unclear. Our study reveals that mild replication stress leads to an increase in the frequency of chromosomal lesions that are transmitted to daughter cells. These lesions are sequestered in nuclear compartments marked by p53-binding protein 1 (53BP1) and other chromatin-associated genome caretakers during G1 phase. Our findings indicate that the number of 53BP1 nuclear bodies increases after genetic ablation of BLM, a DNA helicase involved in the resolution of entangled DNA. Conversely, the number of 53BP1 nuclear bodies is partially suppressed by knocking down SMC2, a condensin subunit essential for the mechanical stability of mitotic chromosomes. Furthermore, our study provides evidence that 53BP1 nuclear bodies protect chromosomal fragile sites sequestered in these compartments from erosion. Taken together, these data suggest that the restoration of DNA or chromatin integrity at sites prone to replication errors requires transmission of mitotic information to the next cell generation.

title: Targeted inhibition of tumor-specific glutaminase diminishes cell-autonomous tumorigenesis.
text:
Glutaminase (GLS) plays a crucial role in cancer cell metabolism, growth, and proliferation. As a potential therapeutic target, GLS has been explored, but its impact on cancer cell-autonomous growth versus the host microenvironment remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the role of GLS in a mouse model of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and its potential as a cancer therapeutic target.
Our findings reveal that loss of one copy of the Gls gene (Gls) hinders tumor progression in an immune-competent MYC-mediated mouse model of HCC. Treatment with a GLS-specific inhibitor, bis-2-(5-phenylacetamido-1,3,4-thiadiazol-2-yl)ethyl sulfide (BPTES), prolonged survival without evident toxicities in mice with MYC-induced HCC. BPTES also inhibited the growth of a MYC-dependent human B cell lymphoma cell line (P493) by blocking DNA replication, leading to cell death and fragmentation. In mice bearing P493 tumor xenografts, BPTES treatment inhibited tumor cell growth, but P493 xenografts expressing a BPTES-resistant GLS mutant (GLS-K325A) or overexpressing GLS were not affected by BPTES treatment. Moreover, a customized Vivo-Morpholino that targets human GLS mRNA significantly inhibited P493 xenograft growth without affecting mouse Gls expression. In contrast, a Vivo-Morpholino directed at mouse Gls had no antitumor activity in vivo.
Our results demonstrate that GLS is essential for tumorigenesis and support targeting GLS with small molecule or genetic inhibitors as a potential cancer therapy approach.

title: Dominant optic atrophy, deafness, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, dystaxia, and myopathy. A new syndrome.
text: Twenty-three members of a 96-person family exhibited an autosomal dominant disorder that had not been previously described. This disorder presented with progressive optic atrophy, abnormal electroretinography without retinal pigment changes, and progressive sensorineural hearing loss that typically manifests in the first or second decade of life. As they reach midlife, individuals experience additional symptoms such as ptosis (drooping of the eyelid), ophthalmoplegia (weakness or paralysis of the muscles that control eye movement), dystaxia (involuntary eye movements), and a nonspecific myopathy (muscle weakness).

title: Dynein is required for polarized dendritic transport and uniform microtubule orientation in axons
text: Axons and dendrites exhibit distinct differences in microtubule organization and the organelles and proteins they contain. Our findings reveal that the microtubule motor dynein plays a crucial role in polarized transport and orientation of axonal microtubules in Drosophila melanogaster dendritic arborization (da) neurons. Changes in organelle distribution within the dendritic arbors of dynein mutant neurons are correlated with a proximal shift in dendritic branch position. Additionally, dynein is necessary for the dendrite-specific localization of Golgi outposts and the ion channel Pickpocket. Unlike axonal microtubules, which are normally oriented uniformly plus-end-distal, the absence of dynein leads to the presence of both plus- and minus-end distal microtubules in axons. These data suggest that dynein is essential for the unique properties of the axon and dendrites, as the absence of dynein causes dendritic organelles and proteins to enter the axon and disrupt the uniform polarity of axonal microtubules.

title: Small molecule screening in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived terminal cell types.
text: In recent years, there has been a growing need for improved clinical outcomes in drug discovery, leading to increased interest in the use of human cells that are more physiologically relevant. Patient-specific human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) offer a promising solution, providing a robust, scalable, and cost-effective model of human disease physiology. The use of hiPSCs in small molecule high throughput screening (HTS) is beginning to shape the drug discovery process, with the potential to identify novel therapeutic compounds. However, developing HTS assays using hiPSCs presents several challenges that must be addressed. This technology has the potential to revolutionize the way drugs are discovered and developed.

title: Gene expression during gonadogenesis in the chicken embryo.
text:
In this study, the expression of genes involved in vertebrate sex determination and differentiation was investigated in embryonic chicken gonads using reverse transcription and polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). The genes studied included anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), SOX9, SOX3, Wilms' tumor gene (WT1), and the orphan nuclear receptor genes, SF1 and DAX1. The results showed that some of these genes exhibited sexually dimorphic expression profiles during gonadal development, while others were expressed at similar levels in both sexes.
The gene encoding AMH was expressed in both sexes before and during sexual differentiation of the gonads, with higher levels of expression observed in males than in females. The expression of SOX9 was male-specific, and its levels were up-regulated after the detection of AMH transcripts. In contrast, SOX3 was expressed prior to the detection of SOX9 and was up-regulated in both sexes at the onset of gonadal sex differentiation, but its levels declined later in development. The WT1 gene was highly expressed in both sexes, while SF1 expression was higher in developing ovaries than in testes. DAX1 transcripts were observed in both sexes at all stages examined, but expression appeared higher in developing ovaries.
These expression profiles were analyzed in light of current theories of vertebrate sex determination, which propose that the sex of an individual is determined by the balance between genetic and environmental factors during early embryonic development. The results of this study provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying sex determination and differentiation in vertebrates, and may have implications for our understanding of sex-related disorders and diseases.

title: Organ-resident, nonlymphoid cells suppress proliferation of autoimmune T-helper lymphocytes.
text: Local presentation of autoantigens by resident cells inappropriately expressing self-antigen determinants has been implicated in organ-specific autoimmune diseases. Experimental autoimmune uveoretinitis, induced in rats by immunization with retinal soluble antigen, serves as a model of organ-specific autoimmunity. In an in vitro system derived from this model, uveitogenic rat T-helper lymphocytes specific to the retinal soluble antigen, or control T-helper lymphocytes reactive to the purified protein derivative of tuberculin, were cocultured with Ia-expressing syngeneic retinal glial cells (Müller cells) in the presence of specific antigen. Antigen presentation was not apparent under standard culture conditions, and the Müller cells significantly suppressed the proliferative response of primed T-helper lymphocytes to antigen presented on conventional antigen-presenting cells, as well as their subsequent interleukin-2 (IL-2)-dependent expansion. Suppression of proliferation was accompanied by inhibition of IL-2 production in response to antigen, as well as by reduction in high-affinity IL-2 receptor expression, and occurred via a direct cell-to-cell contact-dependent mechanism. These findings suggest a crucial role for local immune regulation mechanisms in maintaining tissue homeostasis.

title: Drug induced refractory headache--clinical features and management.
text:
In a study conducted among 200 patients who were taking daily symptomatic or immediate relief medications in excessive quantities, despite experiencing severe headaches on a daily or near-daily basis, it was found that 116 (58%) of them were also taking concomitant prophylactic medications that were ineffective. The patients were then instructed to follow a low-tyramine, low-caffeine diet and undergo biofeedback training. The effects of continuing symptomatic medications, discontinuing symptomatic medications, and modifying or changing prophylactic medications were evaluated in different treatment groups. The results indicate that:
1. Daily use of symptomatic or immediate relief medications is associated with the development of chronic daily headache.
2. Discontinuing daily symptomatic medications leads to improvement in headache symptoms.
3. Concurrent use of symptomatic medications neutralizes the effectiveness of prophylactic medications.
4. Discontinuing daily symptomatic medications enhances the beneficial effect of prophylactic medications.

In summary, the study suggests that the use of daily symptomatic or immediate relief medications can lead to the development of chronic daily headache, and discontinuing these medications can result in improvement in headache symptoms. Additionally, the study found that concomitant use of symptomatic medications can neutralize the effectiveness of prophylactic medications, and discontinuing daily symptomatic medications can enhance the beneficial effect of prophylactic medications.

title: Neuromodulation of neurons and synapses.
text: Neuromodulation is the underlying mechanism for the flexibility of neural circuits and behavior. Individual neuromodulators can have diverse effects within a neuron by targeting multiple physiological mechanisms, while multiple neuromodulators may have overlapping targets with convergent actions. The diverse actions of neuromodulators can be either synergistic or antagonistic, but they often involve a balanced adjustment of nonlinear membrane and synaptic properties through targeting ion channel and synaptic dynamics, rather than just excitability or synaptic strength. Additionally, neuromodulators can exert effects at multiple timescales, from short-term adjustments to long-term regulation. This review summarizes some of the key actions of neuromodulators on ion channel and synaptic properties.

title: Mutation frequency and specificity with age in liver, bladder and brain of lacI transgenic mice.
text: The frequency and specificity of mutations were examined in nuclear DNA from liver, bladder, and brain of Big Blue lacI transgenic mice at various ages, ranging from 1.5 to 25 months. Mutations increased with age in liver and bladder, while a small initial increase in mutation frequency was observed in young brain animals, followed by a lack of further increase in adult mice. To investigate the origin of these mutations, the mutational spectra were determined for each tissue and age group. DNA sequence analysis of mutant lacI transgenes revealed no significant changes in mutational specificity across different tissues and ages, suggesting that the mutations originated from a common set of DNA lesions that occur during DNA replication. The data also indicated that there were no significant age-related changes in mutational frequencies due to oxidative damage or errors arising from changes in DNA polymerase fidelity or DNA repair efficiency. Therefore, no evidence was found to support the hypothesis that oxidative damage or accumulation of errors in nuclear DNA contributes significantly to the aging process in these three somatic tissues.

title: Breaching the basement membrane: who, when and how?
text: The basement membrane (BM), a specialized network of extracellular matrix macromolecules, surrounds various cell types, including epithelial, endothelial, muscle, fat, and nerve cells. During development, immune surveillance, and disease states such as cancer and fibrosis, host cells penetrate the BM by activating specific programs, the identity of which are largely uncharacterized. While it is commonly assumed that all cells use similar mechanisms to cross BM barriers, emerging evidence suggests that cells may selectively employ protease-dependent or -independent invasion programs. Recent findings indicate that protease-dependent transmigration relies on a group of membrane-anchored enzymes called membrane-type matrix metalloproteinases, which irreversibly modify BM structure. In contrast, mechanisms facilitating protease-independent transmigration remain unexplored and may involve the reversible disassembly of the BM network. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying BM transmigration will provide valuable insights into pathological tissue remodeling events and pave the way for the development of novel therapeutics.

title: Soluble MD-2 is an acute-phase protein and an opsonin for Gram-negative bacteria.
text:
Myeloid differentiation factor-2 (MD-2) is a protein that plays a crucial role in the immune response to Gram-negative bacterial infections. It is typically coexpressed with and binds to Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), enabling immune cells to respond to lipopolysaccharides (LPS) on the surface of these bacteria. MD-2 can also exist as a soluble protein (sMD-2) in addition to its membrane-bound form. Interestingly, levels of sMD-2 in plasma and other inflamed tissues are significantly elevated in patients with severe infections, suggesting that this protein may play a key role in the host innate immune response.
We have found that sMD-2 is a type II acute-phase protein, meaning that its production is up-regulated in response to an acute-phase response, such as that induced by interleukin-6. In fact, sMD-2 mRNA and protein levels are up-regulated in mouse liver after the induction of an acute-phase response. Additionally, we have discovered that sMD-2 is secreted by human hepatocytic cells and is an essential cofactor for the activation of TLR4-expressing cells by Gram-negative bacteria.
Furthermore, we have shown that sMD-2 opsonization of Gram-negative bacteria accelerates and enhances phagocytosis, primarily by polymorphonuclear neutrophils. In summary, our findings suggest that sMD-2 plays a crucial role in the host innate immune response to Gram-negative infections, functioning as both an opsonin and a cofactor essential for TLR4 activation.

title: Division-coupled astrocytic differentiation and age-related depletion of neural stem cells in the adult hippocampus.
text: The production of new neurons in the adult hippocampus undergoes a decline with age, a phenomenon that may contribute to age-related cognitive impairment. Our findings suggest that the continuous depletion of the neural stem cell pool, as a result of their division, may play a role in the age-related decrease in hippocampal neurogenesis. By examining the dynamics of adult hippocampal stem cells, we have discovered that upon exiting their quiescent state, these cells undergo a series of asymmetric divisions, resulting in the production of dividing progeny destined to become neurons and eventually mature astrocytes. This division-coupled process is directly linked to the decrease in the number of neural stem cells, highlighting the intricate relationship between neurogenesis and the maintenance of the adult hippocampal stem cell pool. We propose a comprehensive scheme of the neurogenesis cascade in the adult hippocampus, which incorporates a "disposable stem cell" model and accounts for the disappearance of hippocampal neural stem cells, the emergence of new astrocytes, and the age-related decline in the production of new neurons.

title: P19 embryonal carcinoma cells.
text:
P19 cells are a type of pluripotent embryonal carcinoma cell line that can be grown continuously in media supplemented with serum. These cells are capable of differentiating into various cell types through the use of non-toxic drugs. Retinoic acid, for example, can effectively induce the differentiation of P19 cells into neurons, astroglia, and microglia, which are normally derived from the neuroectoderm. Additionally, exposure of P19 cell aggregates to dimethyl sulfoxide can lead to the differentiation of endodermal and mesodermal derivatives, including cardiac and skeletal muscle.
P19 cells can be easily transfected with DNA encoding recombinant genes, and stable lines expressing these genes can be isolated. This makes P19 cells an ideal material for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying the developmental decisions made by differentiating pluripotent cells.

title: Iguanas and Salmonella marina infection in children: a reflection of the increasing incidence of reptile-associated salmonellosis in the United States.
text:
Objective: To investigate the clinical aspects and risk factors for Salmonella serotype Marina infection in the United States, specifically focusing on exposure to iguanas.
Methods: We analyzed data from 32 patients with Salmonella Marina infection reported to the National Salmonella Surveillance System in 1994. Demographic information, clinical course, diet, travel history, and contact with reptiles before illness were collected through interviews with patients.
Results: Of the 32 patients, 81% were infants (<1 year of age) and 75% were male. This is in contrast to other Salmonella isolates reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 1994, where 14% of patients were infants and 49% were male. Eleven patients (34%) were hospitalized for a median of 3.5 days (range: 2-21 days), and one patient died. Of the 28 patients with reported iguana exposure, only 4 (14%) touched the reptile, and only 12 (43%) realized that it might have been the source of infection. Seven (32%) of 22 families who owned an iguana at the time of illness continued to own the pet when contacted a median of 28 weeks later. Individuals who believed that the iguana was the source of infection were more likely to have given away or sold the pet than those who did not. Four isolates (13%) were from blood, and bacteremia was associated with taking antibiotics during the 30 days before S Marina infection (odds ratio: 24; 95% confidence interval: 1.2-1309).
Conclusion: Salmonella serotype Marina infection is a potentially serious illness associated with exposure to iguanas, highlighting the larger problem of reptile-associated salmonellosis. Many parents are unaware of the risk of owning an iguana and the potential for Salmonella infection. Pediatricians, veterinarians, and pet store owners should educate their patients and customers about the risks of reptile ownership and provide appropriate preventive measures.

title: Siblings with opposite chromosome constitutions, dup(2q)/del(7q) and del(2q)/dup(7q).
text: Chromosome 7q36 microdeletion syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by underdeveloped brain, microcephaly, sexual organ abnormalities, and language difficulties. Key features of this syndrome include developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorders, BDMR syndrome, and distinctive facial features. High-resolution chromosomal analysis and subtelomeric multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification were used to screen two brothers with global developmental delay, revealing subtelomeric rearrangements on the same sites of 2q37.2 and 7q35, with reversed deletion and duplication. Both brothers displayed dysmorphic facial features, severe delays in physical and intellectual development, and abnormal genitalia with distinctive abnormalities in their phenotypes. The family did not exhibit any genetic abnormalities. According to the genetic analysis of their parents, adjacent-1 segregation from their mother's side was suggested as the mechanism of the gene mutation. By comparing the phenotypes of our patients with previous reports on similar patients, we aimed to identify related genes and their chromosomal locations.

title: Methods for quantifying follicular numbers within the mouse ovary.
text:
Accurate estimation of the number of ovarian follicles at various stages of development is crucial for understanding the process of folliculogenesis and the endocrine signals and paracrine/autocrine mechanisms that regulate oocyte growth and maturation. Previous studies have reported significant differences in follicular numbers per ovary, ranging from 10-fold to greater, using various methods. This study introduces unbiased and assumption-free stereological methods for quantifying early and growing follicular numbers in the mouse ovary.
Using a fractionator approach to sample histological sections of adult wild-type ovaries, primordial and primary follicles were counted independently using the optical and physical disector methods. These methods, which are unaffected by follicular size or shape, yielded estimates of 1930 +/- 286 and 2227 +/- 101 primordial follicles, and 137 +/- 25 and 265 +/- 32 primary follicles per ovary at 70 and 100 days of age, respectively. Secondary and later follicular numbers at 100 days of age were estimated at 135 per ovary through exact counts on serial sections. Remnants of zona pellucidae (a marker of previous follicular atresia) were estimated using a fractionator/physical disector approach and were approximately 500 per ovary.
The application of these quantitative methods will enable a more comprehensive understanding of follicular dynamics and the factors that regulate their growth and maturation, allowing for better comparisons between different studies.

title: Identification of functional cooperative mutations of SETD2 in human acute leukemia
text: Acute leukemia characterized by chromosomal rearrangements typically requires additional genetic alterations to progress to full-blown malignancy, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. By analyzing the genomes of monozygotic twins discordant for MLL (KMT2A) gene rearrangements, we identified a novel fusion gene (MLL-NRIP3) and biallelic mutations in SETD2 (a histone H3K36 methyltransferase). Surprisingly, loss-of-function mutations in SETD2 were found in 6.2% of 241 patients with acute leukemia and were associated with multiple chromosomal abnormalities. Our study also revealed a global loss of H3K36 trimethylation (H3K36me3) in leukemic cells with SETD2 mutations. In the presence of a genetic lesion, downregulation of SETD2 contributed to both leukemia initiation and progression by enhancing the self-renewal potential of leukemia stem cells. These findings provide strong evidence for SETD2 as a new tumor suppressor and suggest that disruption of the SETD2-H3K36me3 pathway is a distinct epigenetic mechanism underlying leukemia development.

title: Evidence regarding human papillomavirus testing in secondary prevention of cervical cancer.
text:
Clinicians need frequent updates on the latest research regarding innovative cervical cancer prevention methods, given the constantly increasing amount of new information. Recent meta-analyses and systematic reviews have summarized the results of 3 possible clinical applications of human papillomavirus (HPV) testing:
1. Triage of women with equivocal or low-grade cytologic abnormalities: HPV-triage with the Hybrid Capture(®) 2 assay (Qiagen Gaithersburg, Inc., MD, USA) is more accurate (higher sensitivity, similar specificity) than repeat cytology.
2. Prediction of the therapeutic outcome after treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) lesions: HPV testing can predict the likelihood of CIN persistence or progression after treatment.
3. Primary screening for cervical cancer and pre-cancer: HPV testing can detect more CIN2, CIN3, or cancer compared to cytology, but is less specific. Combined HPV and cytology screening provides a small gain in sensitivity but at the expense of a considerable loss in specificity.
The evidence base supports that HPV testing is advantageous in triage of women with equivocal abnormal cytology, in surveillance after treatment of CIN lesions, and in primary screening of women aged 30 years or older. However, a well-organized screening program with good compliance is necessary to fully benefit from HPV-based screening.

title: International standards for fetal growth based on serial ultrasound measurements: the Fetal Growth Longitudinal Study of the INTERGROWTH-21st Project.
text:
In 2006, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed growth standards for infants and children up to the age of 5 years based on expert committee recommendations. Building on this work, the Fetal Growth Longitudinal Study (FGLS), part of the INTERGROWTH-21(st) Project, aimed to establish international growth and size standards for fetuses using the same methods and conceptual approach.
The FGLS was a multicenter, population-based study that assessed fetal growth in geographically defined urban populations in eight countries where mothers had adequate health and nutritional needs and access to adequate antenatal care. Ultrasound measurements were taken prospectively from 14 weeks and 0 days of gestation until birth in a cohort of women with adequate health and nutritional status who were at low risk of intrauterine growth restriction. The five primary ultrasound measures of fetal growth - head circumference, biparietal diameter, occipitofrontal diameter, abdominal circumference, and femur length - were obtained every 5 weeks (within 1 week either side) from 14 weeks to 42 weeks of gestation. The best-fitting curves for each measure were selected using second-degree fractional polynomials and further modeled in a multilevel framework to account for the longitudinal design of the study.
We screened 13,108 women commencing antenatal care at less than 14 weeks and 0 days of gestation, of whom 4607 (35%) were eligible. Of these, 4321 (94%) had pregnancies without major complications and delivered live singletons without congenital malformations, making up the analysis population. We documented very low maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity, confirming that the participants were at low risk of adverse outcomes. For each of the five fetal growth measures, the mean differences between the observed and smoothed centiles for the 3rd, 50th, and 97th centiles, respectively, were small: 2·25 mm (SD 3·0), 0·02 mm (3·0), and -2·69 mm (3·2) for head circumference; 0·83 mm (0·9), -0·05 mm (0·8), and -0·84 mm (1·0) for biparietal diameter; 0·63 mm (1·2), 0·04 mm (1·1), and -1·05 mm (1·3) for occipitofrontal diameter; 2·99 mm (3·1), 0·25 mm (3·2), and -4·22 mm (3·7) for abdominal circumference; and 0·62 mm (0·8), 0·03 mm (0·8), and -0·65 mm (0·8) for femur length. We calculated the 3rd, 5th, 10th, 50th, 90th, 95th, and 97th centile curves according to gestational age for these ultrasound measures, representing the international standards for fetal growth.
We recommend these international fetal growth standards for the clinical interpretation of routinely taken ultrasound measurements and for comparisons across populations. Funding for the study was provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

title: Role of NF-kappa B in cell survival and transcription of latent membrane protein 1-expressing or Epstein-Barr virus latency III-infected cells.
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) latency III infection transforms B lymphocytes into lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) by expressing EBV nuclear and membrane proteins, EBNAs, and latent membrane proteins (LMPs), which regulate transcription through Notch and tumor necrosis factor receptor pathways. The study investigated the role of NF-κB in LMP1 and overall EBV latency III transcriptional effects by treating LCLs with BAY11-7082 (BAY11), a specific inhibitor of NF-κB. BAY11 rapidly and irreversibly inhibited NF-κB, leading to decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, apoptosis, and altered LCL gene expression. The study found that more than 80% of genes that were downregulated by an NF-κB inhibitor, Delta N-I kappa B alpha, were also downregulated by BAY11 treatment. Newly identified NF-κB-induced, LMP1-induced, and EBV-induced genes included pleckstrin, Jun-B, c-FLIP, CIP4, and I kappa B epsilon. The study also found that EBV latency III-regulated gene products mediate cell migration, antigen presentation, mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway, and interferon signaling. The expression of IRF-2, AIM1, ASK1, SNF2L2, and components of IFN signaling pathways distinguished EBV latency III-infected B cells from IgM-stimulated or germinal-center B cells.

title: Endotoxin tolerance: new mechanisms, molecules and clinical significance.
text: Prior exposure to minute amounts of endotoxin can render innate immune cells, such as monocytes/macrophages, resistant to subsequent endotoxin challenge, a phenomenon known as "endotoxin tolerance". This state has been linked to sepsis in clinical settings, where it contributes to "immunosuppression" and mortality. Despite significant research, the underlying molecular mechanisms of endotoxin tolerance remain unclear. Recent discoveries highlighting the self-regulating nature of inflammation, the relative importance of MyD88 versus TRIF signaling pathways in inducing activation or tolerance, the plasticity of NF-κB function, and the role of chromatin modification and microRNAs in LPS-induced gene reprogramming suggest a need to reassess endotoxin tolerance. This review aims to integrate these new findings into a comprehensive understanding of endotoxin tolerance, its molecular basis, and its clinical implications in various diseases.

title: Pancreatic tumor cells with mutant K-ras suppress ERK activity by MEK-dependent induction of MAP kinase phosphatase-2.
text: In human pancreatic carcinomas, mutations in the K-ras gene occur frequently. Previous studies showed that oncogenic, activated K-ras did not constantly activate extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK1 and ERK2) in pancreatic carcinoma cell lines. In the current study, the ERK signaling pathway was further characterized in pancreatic tumor cell lines to determine if it is subject to compensatory downregulation. The study found that the attenuation of serum-induced ERK activation was not due to a delay in the kinetics of ERK phosphorylation. Treatment with the tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor orthovanadate increased ERK phosphorylation, suggesting the presence of a vanadate-sensitive tyrosine phosphatase in the negative regulation of ERK. Additionally, expression of the dual specificity phosphatase MAP kinase phosphatase-2 (MKP-2) was found to be elevated in most pancreatic tumor cell lines, and its expression correlated with the presence of active MAP kinase kinase (MEK). These results suggest that pancreatic tumor cells with oncogenic K-ras may compensate, in part, by upregulating MKP-2 to repress the ERK signaling pathway.

title: E2F3 is a mediator of DNA damage-induced apoptosis.
text: The E2F transcription factors have emerged as pivotal regulators of programmed cell death, or apoptosis, following DNA damage. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms by which the E2F family member E2F3a is induced in response to DNA damage. Our findings reveal that E2F3a can be transcriptionally and posttranslationally regulated in response to DNA damage, with the latter mechanism relying on the checkpoint kinases. We demonstrate that E2F3a is a substrate for these kinases and that mutation of the phosphorylation site abolishes its ability to be induced by DNA damage. Additionally, we show that E2F1 and E2F2 are transcriptionally induced by DNA damage in an E2f3-dependent manner. Finally, using both in vitro and in vivo approaches, we demonstrate that E2f3 is essential for DNA damage-induced apoptosis, thereby establishing its role as a master regulator of the DNA damage response.

title: miR-294/miR-302 promotes proliferation, suppresses G1-S restriction point, and inhibits ESC differentiation through separable mechanisms.
text: The microRNAs miR-294 and miR-302 promote the abbreviated G1 phase of embryonic stem cell (ESC) cell cycle and suppress differentiation induced by let-7. To investigate the role of retinoblastoma (Rb) family proteins in these processes, we evaluated their involvement. Under normal growth conditions, miR-294 accelerates the rapid G1-S transition independently of the Rb family. Conversely, miR-294 inhibits the further accumulation of cells in G1 in response to nutrient deprivation and cell-cell contact in an Rb-dependent manner. We identified five additional microRNAs (miR-26a, miR-99b, miR-193, miR-199a-5p, and miR-218) that silence ESC self-renewal in the absence of other microRNAs, all of which are counteracted by miR-294 and miR-302. Of the six differentiation-inducing microRNAs, four also induce an Rb-dependent G1 accumulation. However, all six still silence self-renewal in the absence of the Rb proteins. These findings demonstrate that the miR-294/miR-302 family acts through both Rb-dependent and -independent pathways to regulate the G1 restriction point and the silencing of self-renewal, respectively.

title: Bacteriophage latent-period evolution as a response to resource availability.
text: Bacteriophages (phages) shape microbial communities by lysing hosts, transferring genetic material, and inducing lysogenic conversion. To accurately predict how natural communities are affected, it is crucial to develop predictive models. Here, we investigate how variations in model parameters, such as eclipse period, latent period, adsorption constant, burst size, and modeling strategy, can impact predictions. We compare two existing models of phage growth, which differ in their approach to modeling phage adsorption. At higher host densities (approximately 10(8) cells/ml), both models accurately predict experimentally determined phage population growth rates. However, at lower host densities (10(7) cells/ml), the computer simulation continues to accurately predict phage growth rates, while the explicit model fails to do so. Next, we focus on predictions of latent-period optima, which is the latent period that maximizes the population growth of a specific phage in the presence of a specific host cell density and quality. Both models predict similar latent-period optima at higher host densities (e.g., 17 min at 10(8) cells/ml). However, at lower host densities (e.g., 10(5) cells/ml), the computer simulation predicts much shorter latent-period optima than the explicit model (e.g., 90 versus 1,250 min). Finally, we explore the impact of host quality on phage latent-period evolution. By differentiating between latent-period phenotypic plasticity and latent-period evolution, we suggest that the impact of host quality on phage latent-period evolution may be relatively small.

title: Neutrophil elastase-mediated lung disease.
text: Elastases from both neutrophils and macrophages have been implicated in the initiation and progression of lung diseases. Although it is unlikely that these proteases evolved specifically to harm lung tissue, the elastin-rich connective tissue framework of the lungs appears to be particularly susceptible to their action. Assuming that neutrophil elastase plays a role in neutrophil migration towards sites of inflammation and degradation of proteins from invading organisms or other products of the inflammatory response, the role of inhibitors of this protease is to protect normal tissues from its harmful effects. In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, an experimental disruption of the protease-anti-protease balance leads to an increased risk of destructive lung disease.

title: Role of TRPML and two-pore channels in endolysosomal cation homeostasis.
text:
The transient receptor potential (TRP) channels TRPML1, TRPML2, and TRPML3 (also known as mucolipins 1-3 or MCOLN1-3) are nonselective cation channels that play a crucial role in various physiological processes. Mutations in the Trpml1 gene have been associated with mucolipidosis type IV in humans, characterized by psychomotor retardation, corneal clouding, and retinal degeneration. Similarly, mutations in the Trpml3 gene have been linked to deafness, circling behavior, and coat color dilution in mice. In contrast, no disease-causing mutations have been reported for the Trpml2 gene.
Like TRPML channels, which are primarily expressed in the endolysosmal pathway, two-pore channels (TPCs), including TPC1, TPC2, and TPC3, are found in intracellular organelles, such as endosomes and lysosomes. Both TRPML channels and TPCs may function as calcium/cation release channels in these organelles, with TRPMLs being activated by phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate and regulated by pH, and TPCs being activated by nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate in a calcium- and pH-dependent manner. They may also be involved in endolysosomal transport and fusion processes, such as intracellular calcium sources. However, the exact physiological roles of TRPML channels and TPCs remain unclear, and it is unclear whether TRPML channels are solely endolysosomal ion channels or may also be functional at the plasma membrane in vivo.

title: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma in London: clinical experience of 21 cases.
text: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a rare disease in the United Kingdom, primarily affecting individuals of Afro-Caribbean descent. Between 1981 and 1995, 21 cases were reported in two inner London teaching hospitals, where approximately 17% of the population is of Afro-Caribbean origin. The clinical presentations were similar to those seen in HTLV-I-endemic areas. Combination chemotherapy was effective in achieving major responses (CR + PR) in 10 out of 16 assessable patients (63%), with a median survival of 5.5 months. However, disease progression and opportunistic infections were the primary causes of treatment failure and death. Three patients (14%) relapsed in the central nervous system (CNS). The immunosuppression in ATLL was profound, highlighting the need for new and more effective treatment approaches, such as zidovudine and alpha-interferon, which should include prophylaxis against CNS disease and opportunistic infections.

title: Regeneration, tissue injury and the immune response.
text: The immune system's involvement in tissue repair has led to speculation about its potential influence on organ, tissue, or appendage regeneration following injury. While some suggest that inflammatory responses may hinder regeneration, there is evidence to suggest that immune components may play more positive roles. The immunoprivileged vertebrate eye provides an interesting case study, as inflammatory responses are inhibited by various immunomodulatory mechanisms. In some newt species, ocular tissues such as the lens are capable of regenerating, and recent research has shown that the response to local lens injury involves the activation of antigen-presenting cells, which migrate to the spleen, return to the damaged lens, and induce regeneration from the dorsal iris. The activation of thrombin in the dorsal iris is another key aspect of the injury response that contributes to the initiation of regeneration. The interplay between the immune response and regenerative response is examined across different phylogenetic lines, with a particular focus on lens regeneration in various species.

title: Poverty, Hunger, Education, and Residential Status Impact Survival in HIV
text: Despite combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV-infected individuals have higher mortality rates than non-infected individuals. Socioeconomic status (SES) is a predictor of mortality in many chronic illnesses, but data on its impact in HIV-infected individuals is limited. We analyzed 878 HIV-infected individuals followed from 1995 to 2005 and found that lower SES predicted higher mortality in univariate and multivariate analyses. The 200 individuals who died were older, had lower CD4 counts, and higher viral loads (VL) compared to the survivors. Age, transmission category, education, albumin, CD4 counts, VL, hunger, and poverty were predictive of death in univariate analyses, with age, CD4 counts, albumin, VL, and poverty remaining significant in the multivariable model. Mixed models revealed associations between CD4 counts and education, hunger, and albumin, and between albumin and education, homelessness, and poverty. VL was associated with education and hunger. Our findings suggest that SES contributes to mortality in HIV-infected individuals directly and indirectly, highlighting the importance of addressing SES in health policy for this population.

title: The INO80 ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex is a nucleosome spacing factor.
text: The INO80 ATP-dependent remodeler exhibits distinct differences in nucleosome mobilization compared to another remodeler, SWI/SNF, which is also involved in gene activation. Unlike SWI/SNF, INO80 is unable to disassemble nucleosomes when remodeling short nucleosomal arrays. Instead, INO80 more closely resembles the nucleosome spacing activity of ISW2 and ISW1a, which are typically involved in transcription repression. INO80 requires a minimum of 33-43 base pairs (bp) of extranucleosomal DNA for mobilizing nucleosomes, with 70 bp being optimal. INO80 preferentially moves mononucleosomes to the center of DNA, similar to ISW2 and ISW1a, but with higher precision. In contrast, ISW2/1a requires the H4 tail for nucleosome mobilization, whereas INO80 does not. INO80 moves arrays of two or three nucleosomes with 50 or 79 bp of linker DNA closer together, resulting in a final length of approximately 30 bp of linker DNA or a repeat length of approximately 177 bp. A minimum length of >30 bp of linker DNA is required for nucleosome movement and spacing by INO80 in arrays.

title: Concentrations of tenofovir and emtricitabine in saliva: implications for preexposure prophylaxis of oral HIV acquisition.
text: To prevent the transmission of HIV through oral sex, drugs used for pre-exposure prophylaxis (Prep) must be able to diffuse into the saliva. In a study of 41 HIV-infected patients on stable antiretroviral treatment, we measured the concentrations of tenofovir (TFV) and emtricitabine (FTC) in both plasma and saliva. The mean ratio of saliva to plasma concentration was 3% (±4%) for TFV and 86.9% (±124%) for FTC. These findings suggest that a combination of TDF (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) and FTC may be effective in preventing oral acquisition of HIV.

title: Increased lean body mass as an early indicator of olanzapine-induced weight gain in healthy men.
text: One of the primary limitations of many psychiatric medications is weight gain, which remains poorly understood. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we conducted a 2-week double-blind placebo-controlled study on weight gain with olanzapine, a medication frequently associated with this side effect. Healthy male volunteers were randomly assigned to receive either olanzapine (5 mg/day for 7 days, then 10 mg/day for 7 days) or a matching placebo. Of the 24 participants, 19 completed the study (olanzapine, n=13; placebo, n=6). We measured body weight, glucose, triglycerides, total cholesterol, lipid levels, leptin, insulin, and aldosterone levels, as well as resting metabolic rate, body composition, physical activity, and 24-hour dietary intake. We found that olanzapine significantly increased weight and triglyceride levels, as well as insulin and leptin levels, in the entire olanzapine group. In participants who actually gained weight (n=8), lean mass increased, while fat mass remained unchanged, and insulin, fasting glucose, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, and non-high-density lipoprotein levels increased, while aldosterone levels decreased. In contrast, there were no significant metabolic or endocrine changes in participants receiving placebo or in those receiving olanzapine who did not gain weight. These findings suggest that early metabolic changes associated with olanzapine use may be independent of fat accumulation.

title: QTc interval length and QT dispersion as predictors of mortality in patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes.
text: Patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM) are at an increased risk of cardiovascular death, but the underlying reasons are not fully understood. To investigate the impact of electrocardiogram (ECG) measures on mortality in a cohort of 324 Caucasian NIDDM patients, we recorded resting 12-lead ECGs at baseline and evaluated the corrected QT interval length (QTc) and QT dispersion (QT-disp). QTc was found to be 454 (376-671) ms(1/2) (median (range)), while QT-disp was 61 (0-240) ms. Prolonged QTc interval (PQTc), defined as QTc-max > 440 ms(1/2), was present in 67% of the patients, and prolonged QT-disp (PQT-disp), defined as QT-disp > 50 ms, was present in 51%. During the 9-year follow-up period, 100 patients died (52 from cardiovascular diseases). The Cox proportional hazard model revealed that QTc-max, age, albuminuria, retinopathy, HbA1c, insulin treatment, total cholesterol, serum creatinine, and presence of cardiac heart disease based on Minnesota coded ECG were independent predictors of all-cause mortality. However, QT-disp was not a predictor, but QTc-max interval was an independent predictor of cardiovascular mortality. Our study showed a high prevalence of QTc and QT-disp abnormalities and highlighted the importance of evaluating QTc-max in NIDDM patients for predicting mortality.

title: Repriming of DNA synthesis at stalled replication forks by human PrimPol
text: During the process of genomic duplication, DNA replication forks that fail to progress properly can lead to the formation of double-strand breaks, posing a threat to genomic stability. The likelihood of fork collapse increases when replication inhibitors are present or after exposure to UV radiation, which alters the structure of DNA. In these situations, the replisome may resort to error-prone translesion synthesis (TLS) DNA polymerases to facilitate fork progression. Alternatively, the replisome may bypass the damaged DNA, leaving an unreplicated gap that is later repaired. This mechanism relies on a priming event occurring downstream of the lesion. Our study reveals that PrimPol, a newly discovered human primase and TLS polymerase, plays a crucial role in maintaining uninterrupted fork progression after UV irradiation and in reinitiating DNA synthesis after dNTP depletion. As a key enzyme in tolerating DNA damage, PrimPol could potentially serve as a target for cancer therapy.

title: Recombinant human tumor necrosis factor administered as a five-day continuous infusion in cancer patients: phase I toxicity and effects on lipid metabolism.
text: Recombinant human tumor necrosis factor (rH-TNF) is a cytotoxic cytokine with diverse effects. In a Phase I trial, we administered rH-TNF via a five-day continuous intravenous (IV) infusion every 28 days to 19 patients, starting with a dose of 5 x 10^4 U/m2/d and escalating to 3.0 x 10^5 U/m2/d (the maximum tolerated dose). Mild and self-limiting systemic side effects occurred, including fever, chills, hypotension, fatigue, anorexia, and headaches. At the maximum tolerated dose, dose-limiting hematologic toxicity (transient thrombocytopenia and leukopenia) and elevated bilirubin levels were observed. Lipoprotein analysis revealed decreases in high-density lipoproteins and increases in triglycerides and very-low-density lipoproteins. Using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) test, we found that plasma rH-TNF levels remained below 0.2 U/mL. Based on these findings, the recommended Phase II dose of rH-TNF administered as a five-day continuous infusion is 2.4 x 10^5 U/m2/d.

title: Tissue-specific expression and regulation of sexually dimorphic genes in mice.
text: In this study, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of sex differences in gene expression across multiple somatic tissues of 334 mice derived from an intercross between inbred mouse strains C57BL/6J and C3H/HeJ. Leveraging the power of a large sample size, we were able to detect subtle differences in gene expression between the sexes, and the use of an intercross allowed for the genetic control of sexually dimorphic gene expression to be investigated. Using microarray analysis of 23,574 transcripts, we found that the extent of sexual dimorphism in gene expression was significantly greater than previously recognized, with thousands of genes showing sexual dimorphism in liver, adipose, and muscle tissues, and hundreds of genes exhibiting sexual dimorphism in the brain. These genes displayed highly tissue-specific patterns of expression and were enriched for distinct pathways represented in the Gene Ontology database. Additionally, we observed evidence of chromosomal enrichment of sexually dimorphic genes not only on the sex chromosomes, but also on several autosomes. Genetic analyses revealed that the transcript levels of a large number of sexually dimorphic genes were controlled by several expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) hotspots that exhibited tissue-specific control. Furthermore, many tissue-specific transcription factor binding sites were found to be enriched in the sexually dimorphic genes.

title: The role of prevention in oncology practice: results from a 2004 survey of American Society of Clinical Oncology members.
text: In 2004, the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Cancer Prevention Committee conducted a survey among its members to assess their involvement in cancer prevention activities. The survey was administered to a random sample of 2,000 domestic members and a convenience sample of 3,144 international members. A total of 49.7% of domestic members contacted and survey-eligible responded (n = 851), while 465 international members responded. The results showed that 35% of the respondents had received formal instruction in cancer prevention and control, and the majority expected an increase in prevention, screening, and risk reduction services in their practices in the next five years. The majority of respondents also reported caring for cancer survivors and providing general medical care, as well as referring patients for cancer prevention and control services such as cancer screening, tobacco and nutrition counseling, risk reduction, and chemoprevention. Multivariable modeling revealed that fewer perceived barriers to the inclusion of cancer prevention activities in clinical practice existed among those practicing in an academic setting, seeing a higher proportion of patients without a cancer diagnosis, having formal training in prevention and control, expecting an increase in prevention activities in the next five years, and providing community advice on prevention. Overall, the survey found that while barriers to cancer prevention and control activities in oncology clinical practice do exist, a significant proportion of ASCO members are interested in and willing to engage in these activities, with a desire for more specific educational programs in this emerging area of oncology practice.

title: Stress-dependent regulation of FOXO transcription factors by the SIRT1 deacetylase.
text: The Sir2 deacetylase has been shown to modulate organismal life-span across various species, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its longevity-promoting effects remain largely elucidated. In mammalian cells, our findings indicate that the Sir2 homolog, SIRT1, plays a crucial role in regulating the cellular response to stress by interacting with the FOXO family of Forkhead transcription factors. Specifically, SIRT1 was found to interact with the FOXO3 transcription factor in response to oxidative stress, leading to the deacetylation of FOXO3 in vitro and within cells. Our results demonstrate that SIRT1 has a dual impact on FOXO3 function, enhancing its ability to induce cell cycle arrest and resistance to oxidative stress while inhibiting its capacity to induce cell death. These findings suggest that members of the Sir2 family of proteins may promote organismal longevity by modulating FOXO-dependent responses away from apoptosis and towards stress resistance.

title: TLR-Mediated Innate Production of IFN-γ by CD8+ T Cells Is Independent of Glycolysis.
text: CD8(+) T cells can respond to unrelated infections without recognizing specific antigens (Ag), a process known as Ag-independent or bystander activation. This rapid innate-like immune response allows Ag-experienced T cells to alert other immune cell types to pathogenic intruders. In this study, we found that murine CD8(+) T cells can sense TLR2 and TLR7 ligands, leading to the rapid production of IFN-γ but not TNF-α or IL-2. Importantly, Ag-experienced T cells activated by TLR ligands produce sufficient IFN-γ to activate macrophages. Unlike Ag-specific reactivation, TLR-dependent production of IFN-γ by CD8(+) T cells relies exclusively on newly synthesized transcripts and does not induce mRNA stability. The activation of PI3K and serine-threonine kinase Akt, as well as protein synthesis, are also required for TLR-induced IFN-γ production. We investigated the energy source that drives TLR-induced IFN-γ production and found that mitochondrial respiration provides sufficient energy for TLR-induced IFN-γ production, rather than a glycolytic switch. This is the first report describing that TLR-mediated bystander activation elicits a helper phenotype of CD8(+) T cells, leading to a short boost of IFN-γ production that activates macrophages but keeps T cell responses limited to unrelated infections.

title: Recommendations for the presurgical psychosocial evaluation of bariatric surgery patients.
