text: Psychosocial factors have a profound impact on the long-term success of bariatric surgery, including emotional adjustment, adherence to postoperative lifestyle guidelines, weight loss outcomes, and co-morbidity resolution. Therefore, it is essential to involve bariatric behavioral health clinicians with specialized knowledge and experience in the evaluation and care of patients both before and after surgery. The evaluating clinician plays a crucial role in the multidisciplinary treatment of bariatric patients by identifying potential challenges to optimal surgical outcomes and providing recommendations to the patient and bariatric team on how to address these issues. This document outlines recommendations for the psychosocial evaluation of bariatric surgery patients, including the qualifications of those conducting these evaluations, communication of evaluation results and suggested treatment plans, and the extension of behavioral healthcare to the entire span of the surgical and postsurgical process.

title: Simian immunodeficiency virus–induced mucosal interleukin-17 deficiency promotes Salmonella dissemination from the gut
text: Salmonella typhimurium can cause a local infection in healthy individuals, but in people with HIV, it can lead to a dangerous infection in the bloodstream. We studied the effect of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) on the immune system in rhesus macaques. We found that SIV infection caused a decrease in T helper type 17 (TH17) cells in the lining of the intestine, which makes it harder for the body to fight off Salmonella infections. In contrast, in macaques that did not have SIV, the gene expression profile induced by Salmonella in the intestine was dominated by TH17 responses, including the production of interleukin-17 (IL-17) and IL-22. TH17 cells were significantly reduced in SIV-infected macaques, leading to weaker responses to Salmonella infections and increased bacterial spread. Mice that lacked the IL-17 receptor had more Salmonella in their system, suggesting that IL-17 deficiency weakens the body's ability to keep bacteria from spreading from the gut. Our findings show that SIV infection disrupts the IL-17 pathway, which is an important part of the immune system that helps keep bacteria from spreading from the gut to the rest of the body.

title: An adoption study of human obesity.
text: In a study of 540 adult Danish adoptees, we investigated the contributions of genetic factors and the family environment to human fatness. The sample was divided into four weight classes: thin, median weight, overweight, and obese. We found a strong correlation between the weight class of the adoptees and the body-mass index (BMI) of their biological parents, with a P value less than 0.0001 for the mothers and less than 0.02 for the fathers. There was no correlation between the weight class of the adoptees and the BMI of their adoptive parents. The cumulative distributions of the BMI of parents also showed similar results, with a strong correlation between the BMI of biological parents and adoptee weight class, and no correlation between the BMI of adoptive parents and adoptee weight class. Additionally, the relation between biological parents and adoptees was not limited to the obesity weight class, but was present across the full range of body fatness, from very thin to very fat. Our findings suggest that genetic factors play a significant role in determining human fatness in adults, while the family environment has no apparent effect.

title: Redox-dependent downregulation of Rho by Rac
text: Rac and Rho GTPases play a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton during cell spreading and migration. Our findings reveal that Rac-mediated production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) leads to a decrease in Rho activity. This redox-dependent decrease in Rho activity is essential for Rac-induced formation of membrane ruffles and integrin-mediated cell spreading. The mechanism by which ROS generation affects Rho activity involves the inhibition of low-molecular-weight protein tyrosine phosphatase (LMW-PTP) and subsequent increase in tyrosine phosphorylation and activation of its target, p190Rho-GAP. Our study uncovers a novel mechanism by which changes in cellular redox state can regulate actin cytoskeleton rearrangements through Rho GTPases.

title: The epidemiology of trachoma in Eastern Equatoria and Upper Nile States, southern Sudan.
text:
In southern Sudan, trachoma is a significant public health concern, with limited surveys and anecdotal data suggesting its prevalence and geographical distribution are largely unknown. To address this gap, we conducted population-based cross-sectional surveys in nine sites between September 2001 and June 2004. Our findings indicate that:
1. The prevalence of signs of active trachoma in children aged 1-9 years was 53.7% (95% CI: 52.1-55.3), 42.7% (95% CI: 41.2-44.2) for TI, and 64.1% (95% CI: 62.5-65.5) for both TF and TI.
2. The prevalence of trichiasis (TT) in children aged less than 15 years was 1.2% (95% CI: 0.9-1.4), while TT prevalence in persons aged 15 years and above was 9.2% (95% CI: 8.6-9.9).
3. Women were more likely to have trichiasis compared to men (OR: 1.57; 95% CI: 1.34-1.84).
Based on these findings, we estimate that there is a backlog of 178,250 (lower and upper bounds: 156,027-205,995) persons requiring surgery, and the entire population of over 3.9 million is in need of the SAFE strategy to control blinding trachoma. Our study highlights the urgent need to implement trachoma control interventions in trachoma-endemic regions of southern Sudan.

title: A single residue determines the cooperative binding property of a primosomal DNA replication protein, PriB, to single-stranded DNA.
text: PriB is a protein that plays a crucial role in the re-initiation of DNA replication in bacteria. To better understand the properties of PriB, we compared the DNA-binding properties of PriB from Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium LT2 (StPriB) and Escherichia coli (EcPriB). Although there is only one amino acid difference between the two proteins (V6 in EcPriB is replaced by A6 in StPriB), our results reveal significant differences in the cooperative binding mechanism of StPriB to DNA. Unlike EcPriB, which forms a single complex with single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) of various lengths, StPriB forms two or more distinct complexes. Based on our findings, we propose binding modes for forming a stable complex of PriB with ssDNA of 25 nucleotides (nt), (EcPriB)25, and (StPriB)25.

title: Genomic organization and chromosomal location of the human dsRNA adenosine deaminase gene: the enzyme for glutamate-activated ion channel RNA editing.
text: The structure of the human gene encoding the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) adenosine deaminase (DRADA) was characterized, revealing a nuclear-localized enzyme crucial for RNA editing and the expression of specific subtypes of glutamate-gated ion channel subunits. The DRADA gene spans 30 kilobases and contains 15 exons, with transcription initiated at multiple sites upstream of the translation initiation codon. The gene harbors three dsRNA binding motifs (DRBM), each encoded by two exons and an intervening sequence, suggesting a possible composition of two functional subdomains. Fluorescent in situ hybridization localized the DRADA gene to the long arm of chromosome 1, region q21. This study provides valuable gene structure and sequence information, enabling further investigation into the potential role of DRADA in hereditary diseases associated with malfunctioning of glutamate-gated ion channels.

title: "We charge them; otherwise we cannot run the hospital" front line workers, clients and health financing policy implementation gaps in Ghana.
text:
This study examines the policy implementation gaps of user fees plus exemptions and health insurance in providing financial access to primary clinical care for children under five in Ghana.
METHODOLOGY
The study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining routine data analysis, focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, and the administration of a structured questionnaire to collect data.
RESULTS
Findings revealed that providers modified policy implementation arrangements, often granting partial or no exemptions, despite the policy's intention to provide financial access to care. Clients who were aware or suspected of their exemption entitlements failed to request them due to fear of negative reactions from providers. Providers attributed their modifications to the financial uncertainty and delays in reimbursement, which threatened the viability of their institutions. Despite low insurance coverage at the time of the study, frontline workers were not observed to be modifying implementation arrangements. However, the underlying goal conflicts, resource scarcity, working conditions, and relationships between frontline workers and clients that contributed to the exemptions policy implementation gaps remained unchanged. The potential for the health insurance policy to encounter similar implementation challenges persists.
CONCLUSIONS
Policies that do not adequately consider the incentives for frontline worker adherence may encounter implementation gaps. The study highlights the importance of aligning policy objectives with the incentives of frontline workers to ensure successful policy implementation.

title: EML4-ALK translocation predicts better outcome in lung adenocarcinoma patients with wild-type EGFR.
text:
Introduction:
The Echinoderm microtubule-associated protein like 4-anaplastic lymphoma kinase (EML4-ALK) fusion gene has been identified as a novel target in a subset of non-small cell lung cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma. The EML4-ALK fusion is mutually exclusive with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations. To investigate the prognostic significance of EML4-ALK in non-small cell lung cancer, we analyzed the EML4-ALK fusion gene in lung adenocarcinoma samples from patients with wild-type EGFR and evaluated their clinical treatment outcomes.
Methods:
We enrolled lung adenocarcinoma patients with malignant pleural effusions and wild-type EGFR for EML4-ALK analysis using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and direct sequencing. Demographic data, EML4-ALK status, and survival data were analyzed. Fluorescence in situ hybridization was performed on available tumor samples to validate the PCR results. Additionally, K-ras mutation analysis was performed for patients without EML4-ALK fusion genes.
Results:
A total of 116 patients with wild-type EGFR sequencing results were included in the analysis. None of the patients received ALK inhibitor therapy. The EML4-ALK fusion gene was detected in 39 (34%) of the patients. The concordance rate between reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and fluorescence in situ hybridization was 85%. The K-ras mutation rate for patients without EML4-ALK fusion genes was 6.5%. Multivariate analysis revealed that patients with better performance status (p < 0.001) and EML4-ALK translocation (p = 0.017) had longer overall survival. Comparing patients with tumors harboring variant 1 with those harboring nonvariant 1 EML4-ALK fusion genes, there were no significant differences in clinical factors and survival outcome.
Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that EML4-ALK translocation is associated with longer overall survival in lung adenocarcinoma patients with wild-type EGFR. These results provide valuable insights into the prognostic significance of EML4-ALK in non-small cell lung cancer and may have implications for the development of targeted therapies in this patient population.

title: Transcriptional Repression of Gata3 Is Essential for Early B Cell Commitment
text: The mechanisms underlying the silencing of alternative fate potentials in early B cell precursors remain unclear. To investigate, we employed gain- and loss-of-function approaches, along with a synthetic Zinc-finger polypeptide (6ZFP) engineered to prevent transcription factor binding to a specific cis element. Our findings reveal that the transcription factor EBF1 plays a crucial role in B cell lineage commitment by directly repressing the expression of the T-cell-lineage-requisite Gata3 gene. Ebf1-deficient lymphoid progenitors exhibited increased T cell lineage potential and elevated Gata3 transcript levels, while enforced EBF1 expression inhibited T cell differentiation and caused rapid loss of Gata3 mRNA. Interestingly, 6ZFP-mediated disruption of EBF1 binding to the Gata3 regulatory region restored Gata3 expression, abrogated EBF1-driven suppression of T cell differentiation, and prevented B cell differentiation through a GATA3-dependent mechanism. Moreover, EBF1 binding to Gata3 regulatory sites induced repressive histone modifications across this region, thereby identifying a critical transcriptional circuit for B cell lineage commitment.

title: Isolation and partial characterization of an unusual human immunodeficiency retrovirus from two persons of west-central African origin.
text: An uncommon human retrovirus was discovered in two patients with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy who originated from West-Central Africa and currently reside in Belgium. Although the virus shared similar biological and morphological characteristics as human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) and HIV-2, significant antigenic differences were observed. The viral proteins also differed in molecular weight from their HIV-1 and HIV-2 counterparts. Partial chemical cleavage of the most highly conserved viral proteins revealed patterns that differed from those of HIV-1 and HIV-2. Additionally, nucleic acid hybridization experiments were able to distinguish between the virus types. Sequence analysis of the viral U3 region revealed a unique enhancer organization not found in other immunodeficiency viruses. The findings suggest that the new isolate is more closely related to HIV-1 than to HIV-2, but it differs in several important ways.

title: Role of circulating nitrite and S-nitrosohemoglobin in the regulation of regional blood flow in humans.
text: To investigate the relative contributions of endothelial-derived nitric oxide (NO) and intravascular nitrogen oxide species in the regulation of human blood flow, we simultaneously measured forearm blood flow and arterial and venous levels of plasma nitrite, low-molecular-weight S-nitrosothiols (LMW-SNOs), and red cell S-nitrosohemoglobin (SNO-Hb) at rest and during regional inhibition of NO synthesis followed by forearm exercise. Surprisingly, we found significant circulating arterial-venous plasma nitrite gradients, providing a novel source of intravascular NO. Further supporting the notion that circulating nitrite is bioactive, consumption of nitrite increased significantly with exercise during inhibition of regional endothelial NO synthesis. The role of circulating S-nitrosothiols and SNO-Hb in the regulation of basal vascular tone is less certain, with low-molecular-weight S-nitrosothiols undetectable and S-nitroso-albumin levels two logs lower than previously reported, primarily forming in the venous circulation even during NO synthase inhibition. In contrast, SNO-Hb was measurable in the human circulation (brachial artery levels of 170 nM in whole blood), but arterial-venous gradients were not significant, and delivery of NO from SNO-Hb was minimal. In conclusion, our data suggest that (i) circulating nitrite is bioactive and provides a delivery gradient of intravascular NO, (ii) S-nitroso-albumin does not deliver NO from the lungs to the tissue but forms in the peripheral circulation, and (iii) SNO-Hb and S-nitrosothiols play a minimal role in the regulation of basal vascular tone, even during exercise stress.

title: Extra centrosomes and/or chromosomes prolong mitosis in human cells
text: Using laser microsurgery and cell fusion, we have investigated the impact of additional centrosomes and chromosomes on the duration of mitosis in human cells. Our findings reveal that increasing the number of chromosomes leads to a approximately 10-minute prolongation of the 20-minute division, while doubling the number of centrosomes adds around 30 minutes to the duration. These results suggest that extra centrosomes and chromosomes delay the satisfaction of the spindle assembly checkpoint, thereby prolonging mitosis. This study demonstrates that mitosis can be prolonged through non-genetic means, and that extra chromosomes and centrosomes likely contribute to the elevated mitotic index observed in many tumors.

title: Familial recurrence-pattern analysis of nonsyndromic isolated cleft palate--a Danish Registry study.
text: The discovery of a connection between genetic changes at the transforming growth factor alpha (TGFA) location and isolated cleft palate (CP) without other syndromes represents a significant breakthrough in understanding this condition. The present study aimed to assess the feasibility of identifying genetic links to susceptibility loci for CP, such as TGFA. To achieve this, the study evaluated the recurrence pattern of CP within families to determine the most likely mode of inheritance for the condition. The study took advantage of the high ascertainment and uniform registration of CP in Denmark, and utilized estimates of familial recurrence obtained through register linkage, which were not subject to recall bias or potential bias from non-responders. The recurrence risks for first-, second-, and third-degree relatives of 1,364 nonsyndromic CP probands were estimated to be 2.74% (72/2,628), 0.28% (3/1,068), and 0.00% (0/360), respectively. These estimates are comparable to previously reported estimates based on questionnaire and interview data. However, the population prevalence of nonsyndromic CP was found to be significantly higher than previously reported (0.058% [1,456/2,523,023]). Analyses of these and other published data using the Risch method suggested that major-locus or additive multilocus inheritance of CP is unlikely. The familial recurrence pattern was consistent with CP being influenced by multiple interacting loci. According to this model, a single locus accounting for more than a sixfold increase in the risk to first-degree relatives of CP probands is unlikely, but a single locus accounting for a threefold increase provides a good fit to the data. Such a locus could be identified in a realistic sample of affected sib pairs.

title: Gene methylation in gastric cancer.
text:
Gastric cancer is one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide and remains the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally, with over 70% of new cases and fatalities occurring in developing countries. In the early years of the molecular biology revolution, cancer research primarily focused on genetic alterations, including gastric cancer. However, recent advancements in the rapidly evolving field of cancer epigenetics have revealed extensive reprogramming of every component of the epigenetic machinery in cancer, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, nucleosome positioning, non-coding RNAs, and microRNAs.
Aberrant DNA methylation in the promoter regions of genes, leading to the inactivation of tumor suppressor and other cancer-related genes in cancer cells, is the most well-defined epigenetic hallmark in gastric cancer. This phenomenon has significant implications for the detection and diagnosis of cancer in biopsy specimens and non-invasive body fluids such as serum and gastric washes. In fact, many studies have explored the application of DNA methylation as a target for cancer detection and diagnosis in gastric cancer.
This review aims to focus on the most common and important phenomenon of epigenetics, DNA methylation, in gastric cancer and illustrate the impact epigenetics has had on this field. By understanding the role of epigenetics in gastric cancer, researchers and clinicians can develop new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies to improve patient outcomes.

title: Klebsiella aerogenes urease gene cluster: sequence of ureD and demonstration that four accessory genes (ureD, ureE, ureF, and ureG) are involved in nickel metallocenter biosynthesis.
text: The region located near the Klebsiella aerogenes urease structural genes was sequenced and found to contain an open reading frame that could encode a 29.8-kDa peptide. Deletions were generated in this gene, denoted ureD, and in each of the genes (ureE, ureF, and ureG) located downstream of the three structural genes. Transformation of the mutated plasmids into Escherichia coli resulted in high levels of urease expression, but the enzyme was either inactive (deletions in ureD, ureF, or ureG) or only partially active (deletions in ureE). Ureases were purified from the recombinant cells and found to be identical to control enzyme when analyzed by gel filtration chromatography and sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, but the activity levels correlated with nickel contents as analyzed by atomic absorption analysis. Tentative identities of UreD, UreE, UreF, and UreG peptides were established through gel electrophoretic comparison of mutant and control cell extracts, in vivo expression of separately cloned genes, or in vitro transcription-translation analyses. The assignments were confirmed for UreE and UreG by amino-terminal sequencing. The amounts of UreF (apparent M(r), 27,000) and UreD (apparent M(r), 29,300) were significantly reduced, possibly due to the lack of good ribosome binding sites in the regions upstream of these open reading frames. These results demonstrate that all four accessory genes are essential for the functional incorporation of the urease metallocenter.

title: Hepatic polyploidy and liver growth control.
text: Cellular polyploidy is observed in all differentiated mammalian tissues, including the liver, and its prevalence increases in pathological states of the liver. As research progresses, it is becoming evident that cells with higher ploidy classes are more likely to undergo terminal differentiation and cellular senescence, with a higher probability of undergoing apoptosis. Specific genetic abnormalities, such as impaired DNA repair, may contribute to the development of hepatocellular polyploidy. Current models suggest that extensive polyploidy can lead to organ failure and potentially to oncogenesis by activating precancerous cell clones.

title: Disturbances in the positioning, proliferation and apoptosis of neural progenitors contribute to subcortical band heterotopia formation.
text: Cortical malformations, particularly intractable epilepsy, are frequently associated with developmental disorders. To investigate the developmental events underlying subcortical band heterotopia (SBH) formation in the neocortex, we utilized the Tish rat, a spontaneously occurring genetic model of SBH linked to epilepsy. Our results demonstrate that Pax6(+) and Tbr2(+) progenitors are mislocalized in the neocortex of Tish(+/-) and Tish(-/-) embryos throughout neurogenesis. Additionally, mislocalized Tish(-/-) progenitors have a longer cell cycle due to an extended G(2)+M+G(1) phase. This mislocalization is not associated with disruptions in adherens junctions or loss of radial glial polarity in the ventricular zone (VZ), as assessed by immunohistochemistry with phalloidin (to detect F-actin), aPKC-λ, and Par3. However, vimentin immunohistochemistry reveals that the radial glial scaffold is disrupted in the region of the Tish(-/-) heterotopia. Furthermore, lineage tracing experiments using in utero electroporation in Tish(-/-) neocortex demonstrate that mislocalized progenitors do not maintain contact with the ventricular surface, and ventricular/subventricular zone (SVZ) progenitors produce neurons that migrate into both the heterotopia and cortical plate (CP). These findings delineate a series of developmental errors contributing to SBH formation that differ fundamentally from a primary error in neuronal migration.

title: Sex-related differences in the presentation, treatment and outcomes among patients with acute coronary syndromes: the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events.
text:
Objective: To investigate whether there are differences in the severity, management, and outcomes of acute coronary syndromes (ACS) between men and women.
Methods: The study included 7638 women and 19,117 men with ACS who underwent coronary angiography and were registered in the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) between 1999 and 2006. The severity of coronary artery disease was classified as normal/mild (<50% stenosis in all epicardial vessels), advanced (>or=50% stenosis in one or more vessels).
Results: Women were older and had more cardiovascular risk factors than men. Both men and women presented with chest pain equally, but women were more likely to experience jaw pain and nausea. Women were more likely to have normal/mild disease (12% vs 6%, p<0.001) and less likely to have left-main and three-vessel disease (27% vs 32%, p<0.001) or undergo percutaneous coronary intervention (65% vs 68%, p<0.001). Women and men with normal/mild disease were treated less aggressively than those with advanced disease. Women with advanced disease had a higher risk of death (4% vs 3%, p<0.01). After adjusting for age and disease extent, women had higher odds of adverse outcomes (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and rehospitalization) at six months compared to men (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.14-1.34). However, sex differences in mortality were no longer statistically significant after adjustment.
Conclusion: Women with ACS were more likely to have cardiovascular disease risk factors and atypical symptoms such as nausea compared to men, but were more likely to have normal/mild angiographic coronary artery disease. Further research is needed to investigate sex differences in disease severity.

title: GITR, a member of the TNF receptor superfamily, is costimulatory to mouse T lymphocyte subpopulations.
text: GITR (glucocorticoid-induced TNFR family related gene), a member of the TNFR superfamily (TNFRSF), is expressed in various cell types, including T lymphocytes. Due to its high homology with other known costimulatory members of the TNFRSF, we investigated whether GITR plays a costimulatory role in different T lymphocyte subpopulations. Our findings show that the proliferation response of both CD8+ and CD4+ peripheral T cell subpopulations was enhanced when a GITR costimulus was added to an anti-CD3 stimulus. Additionally, expression of the main activation-induced receptor (IL-2Ralpha) and production of IL-2 and IFN-gamma were increased more with a GITR costimulus than with anti-CD3 alone. GITR stimulation also activated the MAPK signaling pathway. Interestingly, proliferation of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells (Treg cells) was triggered by the GITR costimulus, which was accompanied by the loss of anergic phenotype and suppressor activity. However, unstimulated GITR(-/-) CD4+CD25+ cells and GITR(+/+) CD4+CD25+ cells had equivalent suppressor activity towards CD4+CD25- responder cells. These results demonstrate a novel function of GITR as a costimulatory molecule for T cell subsets.

title: PI3K and cancer: lessons, challenges and opportunities
text: The pivotal role of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) activation in tumor cell biology has sparked a significant effort to target PI3K and/or downstream kinases such as AKT and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) in cancer. However, recent clinical data indicate limited single-agent activity of inhibitors targeting PI3K, AKT, or mTOR at tolerated doses. One exception is the response to PI3Kδ inhibitors in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, where a combination of cell-intrinsic and -extrinsic activities contribute to efficacy. Here, we examine the key challenges and opportunities for the clinical development of inhibitors targeting the PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathway. By focusing on patient selection, enhancing our understanding of immune modulation, and strategically applying rational combinations, it is possible to realize the potential of this promising class of targeted anticancer agents.

title: Sequence-based species delimitation for the DNA taxonomy of undescribed insects.
text: Accelerating the cataloging of undescribed insect species through automated DNA-based approaches is feasible, but there is a need for standardized methods for large-scale species discovery from DNA sequence data. In this study, we use mitochondrial DNA variation to identify species in the poorly known beetle radiation of Rivacindela from arid Australia. By analyzing 468 individuals from 65 sites and multiple morphologically distinct types, we found that sequence variation in three mtDNA genes (cytochrome oxidase subunit 1, cytochrome b, and 16S ribosomal RNA) was strongly partitioned into 46 or 47 putative species using quantitative methods of species recognition based on fixed unique characters. The boundaries between groups were also evident from a striking increase in branching rate in clock-constrained calibrated trees. We combined Yule models with coalescence theory to develop a new likelihood method that determines the point of transition from species-level to population-level evolutionary processes. Fitting the location of the switches from speciation to coalescent nodes on the ultrametric tree of Rivacindela led to an estimate of 48 putative species (confidence interval of 47-51 clusters within 2 logL units). The entities delineated in this study exhibited biological properties of traditionally defined species, including coherence of geographic ranges, broad congruence with morphologically recognized species, and typical levels of sequence divergence for closely related insect species. The discovery of discontinuous evolutionary groupings that are apparent in DNA sequence patterns enables largely automated species delineation from local community DNA surveys, providing a scaffold for taxonomy in this poorly known insect group.

title: CCR6 regulates the migration of inflammatory and regulatory T cells.
text: Th17 and regulatory T (Treg) cells play opposing roles in autoimmune diseases, but the mechanisms underlying their proper migration to inflamed tissues are unclear. In this study, we discovered that both T cell subsets express the chemokine receptor CCR6. CCR6 expression on Th17 cells is regulated by TGF-beta and requires two nuclear receptors, RORalpha and RORgamma. Th17 cells also produce the CCR6 ligand CCL20, which is induced by TGF-beta and IL-6, and requires STAT3, RORgamma, and IL-21. Th17 cells promote the migration of Th17 and Treg cells in vitro through CCR6. Lack of CCR6 on Th17 cells reduces the severity of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and Th17 and Treg recruitment into inflamed tissues. Similarly, CCR6 on Treg cells is important for their recruitment into inflamed tissues. Our findings indicate a crucial role for CCR6 in Treg and Th17 cell migration.

title: Inhibition of receptor-mediated calcium influx in T cells by unsaturated non-esterified fatty acids.
text: The impact of omega-3, omega-6, and omega-9 unsaturated fatty acids (UFAs) on receptor-mediated calcium entry was investigated in a T-cell line (JURKAT) using anti-CD3 antibodies (OKT3) to induce an intracellular calcium increase and calcium influx. All UFAs, as well as nickel ions and 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol 13-acetate, reduced the OKT3-induced sustained intracellular calcium increase to basal levels. Although non-esterified fatty acids activate protein kinase C (PKC), studies using H-7 and analysis of the PKC-dependent phosphorylation of 19 and 80 kDa marker substrates revealed that UFA-induced inhibition of calcium entry is not mediated by PKC. Flow cytometry analysis showed that UFAs do not interfere with antibody-receptor binding. Adding 0.2% BSA (w/v) reversed the effect of UFAs after these fatty acids decreased the OKT3-induced calcium increase to basal levels. The findings of this study and possible mechanisms for UFA-induced inhibition of receptor-mediated calcium influx were discussed.

title: Deleted in liver cancer-1 (DLC-1): a tumor suppressor not just for liver.
text: Deleted in liver cancer 1 (DLC-1), as its name suggests, was initially identified as a potential tumor suppressor gene that is frequently deleted in hepatocellular carcinoma. Subsequent studies have revealed that the downregulation of DLC-1 through genomic deletion or DNA methylation is associated with various types of cancer, including lung, breast, prostate, kidney, colon, uterus, ovary, and stomach. Re-expression of DLC-1 in cancer cells leads to the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and focal adhesions, resulting in a significant inhibition of cell growth, which supports its role as a tumor suppressor. This tumor suppressive function is mediated by DLC-1's RhoGTPase activating protein (RhoGAP) activity, steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR)-related lipid transfer (START) domain, and its localization to focal adhesions, which is mediated by the Src Homology 2 (SH2) domains of tensins in a phosphotyrosine-independent manner. Therefore, the expression and subcellular localization of DLC-1 could serve as a useful molecular marker for cancer prognosis, while DLC-1 and its downstream signaling molecules may be potential therapeutic targets for the treatment of cancer.

title: Interaction of Helicobacter pylori with gastric epithelial cells is mediated by the p53 protein family.
text:
Background and Aims:
The p53 tumor suppressor protein has been extensively studied, yet many questions remain unanswered regarding the biological functions of p53 homologs, p73 and p63. Recent evidence suggests that both p73 and p63 play important roles in regulation of apoptosis, cell differentiation, and drug sensitivity.
Methods:
Gastric epithelial cells were cocultured with Helicobacter pylori, and the roles of p63 and p73 proteins were assessed using luciferase reporter, real-time polymerase chain reaction, immunoblotting, and cell survival assays. Short hairpin RNA and dominant-negative mutants were used to inhibit the activity of p73 and p63 isoforms. Human and murine gastric tissues were analyzed using immunohistochemistry with p73 and p63 antibodies and a modified Steiner's silver method.
Results:
Our findings indicate that H pylori infection leads to a robust up-regulation of p73 protein in vitro and in vivo, as demonstrated by luciferase reporter and immunoblotting assays. This increase in p73 protein expression resulted in the up-regulation of pro-apoptotic genes, including NOXA, PUMA, and FAS receptor, in gastric epithelial cells. Conversely, down-regulation of p73 activity suppressed cell death and Fas receptor-induced apoptosis. Furthermore, we found that bacterial virulence factors within the cag pathogenicity island, c-Abl tyrosine kinase, and interaction with p63 isoforms control the activity of p73.
Conclusion:
Our findings suggest that p73 plays a critical role in H pylori-induced apoptosis and may play a broader role in the epithelial cell response to H pylori infection. These findings highlight the importance of the p53 family in regulating the host-pathogen interaction and suggest potential therapeutic targets for H pylori-related diseases.

title: Brown and white adipose tissues: intrinsic differences in gene expression and response to cold exposure in mice
text: Brown adipocytes are energy-expending cells, while white adipocytes serve as energy storage sites. We investigated the plasticity of different white adipose tissue depots in acquiring a brown phenotype through cold exposure. By comparing the genes expressed in cold-exposed white fat to those enriched in brown fat at thermoneutrality, we defined a "brite" transcription signature. This study identified the genes, pathways, and regulatory motifs associated with "browning," providing novel targets for understanding this process. For example, we found that neuregulin 4 is highly expressed in brown adipose tissue and upregulated in white fat upon cold exposure. Cell studies revealed that it is a neurite outgrowth-promoting adipokine, suggesting a role in increasing adipose tissue innervation in response to cold. To study the discrete adipose depots at an in vitro level, we developed a cell culture system that reproduces the differential properties of these depots. The key transcriptional events underlying the transition of white adipose tissue to brown tissue are crucial, as they offer an attractive approach to combat the detrimental effects of metabolic disorders, such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.

title: Continuous glucose monitoring in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes (CONCEPTT): a multicentre international randomised controlled trial
text: In this study, the researchers investigated the effectiveness of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in improving glucose control and obstetric and neonatal health outcomes in pregnant women with type 1 diabetes. The study found that use of CGM during pregnancy was associated with improved neonatal outcomes, including a lower incidence of large for gestational age, fewer neonatal intensive care admissions lasting more than 24 hours, fewer incidences of neonatal hypoglycaemia, and a shorter length of hospital stay. The study also found that CGM use was associated with improved glucose control, with participants spending more time in target range and less time with hyperglycaemia. However, there was no apparent benefit of CGM in women planning pregnancy. The study suggests that CGM should be offered to all pregnant women with type 1 diabetes using intensive insulin therapy, as it is likely to improve neonatal outcomes and glucose control.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps: Is immunity the second function of chromatin?
text: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are composed of genetic material (chromatin) that has been processed and bound to specific cytoplasmic proteins, forming a complex structure. These NETs are released by white blood cells called neutrophils as a last resort to combat microbial infections. The release of chromatin from neutrophils is a novel form of cell death, known as "NETosis." In this review, we will discuss the current understanding of how NETs are formed, their role in infection and immunity, and their emerging importance in autoimmune diseases and coagulation disorders.

title: Phosphorylation of p35 and p39 by Cdk5 determines the subcellular location of the holokinase in a phosphorylation-site-specific manner.
text:
CDK5, a member of the cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) family, is activated by neuronal activators p35 or p39. CDK5 regulates various neuronal functions, including migration, synaptic activity, and neuronal death. However, the relationship between CDK5 activity and the subcellular localization of p35-Cdk5 and p39-Cdk5 is not well understood. To investigate this, we examined the role of CDK5 activity in the localization of these complexes.
Our findings revealed that CDK5 activity affects the localization of p35-Cdk5 and p39-Cdk5 through phosphorylation of p35 or p39. Using unphosphorylated or phosphomimetic mutants of p35 and p39, we found that phosphorylation at Ser8, common to p35 and p39, by CDK5 regulates the cytoplasmic localization and perinuclear accumulation of unphosphorylated S8A mutants and the whole cytoplasmic distribution of phosphomimetic S8E mutants. Additionally, we found that CDK5 activity was necessary to retain Cdk5-activator complexes in the cytoplasm. However, small amounts of p35 and p39 were detected in the nucleus, and inhibition of CDK5 activity led to increased nuclear localization of these proteins. Interestingly, p39 had a greater propensity to accumulate in the nucleus than p35, and phosphorylation at Thr84, specific to p39, regulated the potential nuclear localization activity of the Lys cluster in p39.
Our results suggest that the subcellular localization of the Cdk5-activator complexes is determined by CDK5 kinase activity. Furthermore, our findings implicate a role for p39-Cdk5 in the nucleus. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying the regulation of neuronal functions by CDK5 and its activators.

title: Interleukin-12 and -23 Control Plasticity of CD127(+) Group 1 and Group 3 Innate Lymphoid Cells in the Intestinal Lamina Propria.
text: Human group 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) are composed of at least three distinct subsets, including natural killer (NK) cells, CD127(+) ILC1, and intraepithelial CD103(+) ILC1. In inflamed intestinal tissues from Crohn's disease patients, the numbers of CD127(+) ILC1 are observed to increase at the expense of ILC3. Interestingly, we have found that the differentiation of ILC3 to CD127(+) ILC1 is reversible in vitro and in vivo, and this process is dependent on the transcription factor RORγt and can be enhanced by the presence of retinoic acid. Furthermore, we have observed in resection specimens from Crohn's disease patients a higher proportion of CD14(+) dendritic cells (DCs), which in vitro promote polarization from ILC3 to CD127(+) ILC1. In contrast, CD14(-) DCs promote differentiation from CD127(+) ILC1 towards ILC3. These findings suggest that environmental cues play a crucial role in determining the composition, function, and phenotype of CD127(+) ILC1 and ILC3 in the gut.

title: Transcriptional regulation of neuronal genes and its effect on neural functions: expression and function of forkhead transcription factors in neurons.
text: Forkhead box transcription factor, class O (FOXO) is a mammalian homologue of DAF-16, which regulates the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans. FOXO includes subfamilies of forkhead transcription factors such as AFX, FKHRL1, and FKHR. FKHR is phosphorylated on three sites (Thr-24, Ser-256, and Ser-319) in a phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt-dependent manner, thereby inhibiting death signals. In this study, we investigated the dephosphorylation of FKHR following transient forebrain ischemia in gerbil and mouse brains. We found that FKHR translocated into the nucleus in neurons after ischemic brain injury, and its activation preceded delayed neuronal death in the vulnerable hippocampal regions. The activation of FKHR was accompanied by an increase in DNA binding activity for FKHR-responsive element on the Fas ligand promoter. We also identified FKHR-induced downstream targets, including Fas ligand and Bim, in brain ischemia. To rescue neurons from delayed neuronal death, we propose a new strategy based on promoting the survival signaling. Sodium orthovanadate, a protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor, up-regulated Akt activity in the brain and rescued neurons from delayed neuronal death by inhibiting both FKHR-dependent and -independent death signals in neurons.

title: ERAAP synergizes with MHC class I molecules to make the final cut in the antigenic peptide precursors in the endoplasmic reticulum.
text: The major histocompatibility complex class I molecules display peptides (pMHC I) on the cell surface for immune surveillance by CD8(+) T cells. These peptides are generated through a process of proteolysis, involving the proteasome in the cytoplasm and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) aminopeptidase associated with antigen processing (ERAAP). To investigate the unknown mechanism of ERAAP function in vivo, we analyzed naturally processed peptides in cells with or without MHC I and ERAAP. In the absence of MHC I, ERAAP degraded the antigenic precursors in the ER. However, MHC I molecules were found to play a crucial role in the generation of the final peptide by ERAAP, as they could bind to proteolytic intermediates and facilitate the formation of the final pMHC I repertoire. Therefore, ERAAP and MHC I work together to generate the complete repertoire of pMHC I molecules.

title: Estimates of animal and plant protein intake in US adults: results from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 1988-1991.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the sources of protein intake in a sample of US adults and among subgroups defined by race-ethnicity, age, and gender, using data from the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III) conducted between 1988 and 1991.
Design:
NHANES III is a stratified random sample of the total civilian noninstitutionalized population in the 50 US states and the District of Columbia. Participants (n = 7,924) provided 24-hour dietary recalls, which were used to determine the protein sources and contribution of each type to total protein intake.
Subjects:
Adult participants in NHANES III.

Statistical Analyses:
Weighted total, age-specific, and age-adjusted mean protein intakes were calculated using SAS and WesVarPC. Statistical differences were determined by 2-tailed t tests.
Results:

The main source of protein in the American diet is animal protein (69%), with meat, fish, and poultry protein contributing the most (42%). Women consumed lower percentages of beef (14%) and pork (7%) protein than men (18% and 9%, respectively), and higher percentages of poultry (13%), dairy (22%), and fruit and vegetable (11%) protein than men (11%, 19%, and 9%, respectively). Blacks reported higher percentages of poultry (18%) and pork (11%) protein and lower percentages of dairy protein (14%) than whites (12%, 7%, and 22%, respectively) and Mexican-Americans (11%, 8%, and 17%, respectively). Mexican-Americans consumed higher percentages of legume (7%) and egg (7%) protein than whites (4% and 4%, respectively) and blacks (4% and 5%, respectively). Whites consumed higher percentages of grain protein (19%) than blacks (16%) and Mexican-Americans (15%).

title: CYP18A1, a key enzyme of Drosophila steroid hormone inactivation, is essential for metamorphosis.
text: Ecdysteroids are a class of steroid hormones that play a crucial role in coordinating major developmental transitions in insects. Both the increases and decreases in circulating levels of active hormones are essential for the proper regulation of molting and metamorphosis, making the biosynthesis and inactivation of ecdysteroids physiologically relevant. To investigate the enzymes involved in ecdysteroid metabolism, we focused on Drosophila melanogaster Cyp18a1, a cytochrome P450 enzyme that has been shown to have 26-hydroxylase activity, a key step in ecdysteroid catabolism. Our findings revealed that Cyp18a1 has a clear ortholog in most insects and crustaceans, and when overexpressed in Drosophila S2 cells, it leads to extensive conversion of 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) into 20-hydroxyecdysonoic acid, a multi-step process involving the formation of 20,26-dihydroxyecdysone as an intermediate. In Drosophila larvae, Cyp18a1 is expressed in many target tissues of 20E. To investigate the developmental consequences of Cyp18a1 inactivation, we generated null alleles by excision of a P element and performed RNAi knockdown of Cyp18a1 in Drosophila. Our results show that both methods result in pupal lethality, likely due to impaired ecdysteroid degradation. These findings suggest that the inactivation of 20E is essential for proper development, and that CYP18A1 is a key enzyme in this process.

title: The sialyltransferase ST3GAL6 influences homing and survival in multiple myeloma.
text: Glycosylation is a multi-step process by which oligosaccharide chains are covalently attached to proteins or lipids, and changes in this process, such as increased sialylation, have been linked to cancer progression and metastasis. While the role of altered sialylation in multiple myeloma (MM) cell trafficking has not been previously investigated, our study found high expression of β-galactoside α-2,3-sialyltransferase, ST3GAL6, in MM cell lines and patients. This enzyme plays a crucial role in generating functional sialyl Lewis X molecules in humans, which are important for cell adhesion and migration. In MM patients, high expression of ST3GAL6 was associated with poor overall survival. To investigate the functional significance of ST3GAL6 in MM, we knocked down its expression in MM cells and observed a significant reduction in sialic acid levels on the cell surface, as well as decreased adhesion to bone marrow stromal cells and fibronectin, and reduced transendothelial migration in vitro. In vivo, we found that ST3GAL6 knockdown MM cells had decreased homing and engraftment to the bone marrow niche, resulting in reduced tumor burden and prolonged survival. These findings highlight the importance of altered glycosylation, particularly sialylation, in MM cell adhesion and migration.

title: New developments in the epidemiology of cancer prognosis: traditional and molecular predictors of treatment response and survival.
text: Numerous epidemiological investigations have been conducted to identify factors that may influence cancer risk. In addition, there is a longstanding tradition of examining the cancer itself for potential somatic changes that could predict recurrence or mortality after diagnosis. However, despite these efforts, there has been relatively little progress in developing effective predictive models for cancer recurrence and mortality.

title: Behavioral effects of estrogen receptor gene disruption in male mice.
text: Gonadal steroid hormones, such as estrogen, play a crucial role in regulating the development of brain functions and behaviors that are sexually dimorphic. The nuclear receptors for these hormones offer a means to investigate the molecular events that occur in neurons and their relationship to instinctive mammalian behaviors. By using transgenic mice that lack the estrogen receptor (ER), we were able to determine the role of ER activation in the development of male-typical behaviors. Surprisingly, despite being infertile, ERKO mice displayed normal motivation to mount females but achieved fewer intromissions and virtually no ejaculations. Aggressive behaviors were significantly reduced, and male-typical offensive attacks were rarely displayed by ERKO males. Moreover, disruption of the ER gene also demasculinized open-field behaviors in the brain. Interestingly, despite the loss of functional ER protein, the androgen-dependent system appears to be normally present in ERKO mice. These findings suggest that ER gene expression during development plays a major role in organizing male-typical aggressive and emotional behaviors, in addition to simple sexual behaviors.

title: High-Density Lipoproteins Exert Pro-inflammatory Effects on Macrophages via Passive Cholesterol Depletion and PKC-NF-κB/STAT1-IRF1 Signaling.
text: Membrane cholesterol is involved in various cellular signaling pathways and functions, but its impact on inflammatory responses in macrophages remains unclear. While depleting cholesterol in macrophages through high-density lipoproteins (HDLs) has anti-inflammatory effects in other cell types, our study shows that HDL-mediated cholesterol depletion and lipid raft disruption in macrophages have overt pro-inflammatory effects in vitro and in vivo. These findings were confirmed in peritoneal macrophages from apoA-I transgenic mice, which have elevated HDL levels. Our study also revealed that low HDL levels compromise the innate immune responses required for clearing bacterial infections in the lungs. We used expression analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation-polymerase chain reaction (ChIP-PCR), and combinatorial pharmacological and genetic intervention studies to uncover the mechanisms underlying HDL's pro-inflammatory activity. Our results show that both native and reconstituted HDL enhance Toll-like receptor-induced signaling by activating a protein kinase C (PKC)-nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1)/interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1) axis, leading to increased inflammatory cytokine expression. These findings suggest that HDL plays a crucial role in maintaining proper macrophage immune function.

title: Hypoxia of the renal medulla--its implications for disease.
text:
In land mammals, the kidney plays a crucial role in conserving water to enable survival in arid environments. The renal medulla, a specialized region of the kidney, is particularly effective at reabsorbing water through a process called countercurrent exchange. This mechanism allows the medulla to concentrate urine up to four times the osmolality of plasma, which is essential for maintaining proper fluid balance in the body.
In this review, we explore the relationship between hypoxia in the medulla and susceptibility to acute and chronic renal injury. We discuss how the Renal Medullary Concentrating Mechanism (RMCM), which is responsible for the countercurrent exchange process, is affected by hypoxia and how this can lead to renal damage. Understanding the mechanisms involved in water conservation and the impact of hypoxia on the kidney can provide valuable insights into the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of renal disorders.

title: Troponin concentrations for stratification of patients with acute coronary syndromes in relation to therapeutic efficacy of tirofiban. PRISM Study Investigators. Platelet Receptor Inhibition in Ischemic Syndrome Management.
text:
A significant challenge for physicians is identifying patients with acute coronary syndromes who may benefit from treatment with glycoprotein-IIb/IIIa-receptor antagonists, such as tirofiban. In this study, we investigated the potential of using troponin concentrations to stratify patients for benefit from tirofiban treatment.
We enrolled 2222 patients with coronary artery disease and recent chest pain in the Platelet Receptor Inhibition in Ischemic Syndrome Management (PRISM) study and randomly assigned them to receive either tirofiban or heparin. Baseline measurements of troponin I and troponin T were taken, and the patients were followed up for 30 days to record any adverse events.
Our findings revealed that 28.3% of patients had troponin I concentrations above the diagnostic threshold of 1.0 microg/L, and 29.0% had troponin T concentrations above 0.1 microg/L. The 30-day event rate (death, myocardial infarction) was significantly higher in troponin-I-positive patients compared to troponin-I-negative patients (13.0% vs 4.9%, p<0.0001), and similar results were observed for troponin T-positive patients (13.7% vs 3.5%, p<0.001). Interestingly, tirofiban treatment showed a significant reduction in the risk of death and myocardial infarction in troponin-I-positive patients, both in medically managed patients (0.30 [0.10-0.84], p=0.004) and those undergoing revascularisation (0.37 [0.15-0.93], p=0.02). In contrast, no treatment effect was seen in troponin-I-negative patients.
Our findings suggest that troponin I and troponin T can reliably identify high-risk patients with acute coronary syndromes who will benefit from tirofiban treatment, both in medically managed patients and those undergoing revascularisation. These biomarkers may help physicians identify patients who are most likely to benefit from this treatment, potentially improving patient outcomes.

title: Evolution and function of ubiquitin-like protein-conjugation systems
text: Ubiquitin functions by chemically modifying other proteins through a covalent bond. In recent years, a significant number of other proteins have been discovered that, despite sharing only subtle similarities with ubiquitin, can also be attached to proteins. These findings have led to new insights into the evolutionary origins of the ubiquitin system, as there are unexpected parallels between the activation of ubiquitin and the biosynthesis of certain enzyme cofactors.

title: Inflammatory biomarkers and exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
text: The study found that individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who had elevated levels of inflammatory biomarkers, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and fibrinogen, in their blood were at increased risk of experiencing exacerbations of their respiratory symptoms. The study included 61,650 participants with spirometry measurements from two cohort studies in Denmark. Of these, 6574 had COPD, and the researchers measured the participants' CRP and fibrinogen levels at the beginning of the study. They found that individuals with three high biomarker levels had a 3.7-fold increased risk of experiencing frequent exacerbations compared to those with no elevated biomarkers. The study also found that the association between inflammatory biomarkers and exacerbation risk was consistent across different subgroups of participants, including those with mild COPD and those without a history of frequent exacerbations. The study suggests that measuring inflammatory biomarkers in individuals with COPD may be a useful way to identify those at high risk of experiencing exacerbations, which could help inform treatment decisions and improve patient outcomes.

title: Gene supplementation therapy for recessive forms of inherited retinal dystrophies
text: Over the past decade, gene supplementation therapy for inherited retinal degeneration has made significant progress. Early studies in animal models of disease demonstrated modest improvements in retinal function and/or survival, which were further enhanced by advancements in vector technology used for gene transfer to the retina. In 2008, clinical trials for Leber congenital amaurosis caused by retinal pigment epithelium 65 deficiency were initiated, and the results showed that gene therapy can be safe and effective in treating inherited retinal dystrophy. Here, we review the progress of gene supplementation therapy in the retina and explore its potential to treat various forms of inherited retinal degeneration.

title: Complex Tissue and Disease Modeling using hiPSCs.
text: The advent of genetically defined human pluripotent stem cell-based models has revolutionized our understanding of disease mechanisms and drug screening. However, it is crucial to recognize that these models may only partially capture the complexity of disease phenotypes or drug responses, as they often focus on cell-autonomous mechanisms. To gain a more comprehensive understanding, it is essential to create multicellular structures with vascular components that mimic tissue niches, which can provide a more accurate representation of the in vivo environment. Here, we discuss recent advances in creating human tissue mimics and offer recommendations for advancing the field.

title: Reprogramming somatic cells towards pluripotency by cellular fusion.
text: Pluripotent cells emerge within the inner cell mass (ICM) of mammals, possessing the potential to generate all cell types of the adult organism through a process of commitment and orchestrated differentiation. Despite extensive investigation spanning several decades, the underlying mechanisms that govern and stabilize cell fate choice, as well as those that can be manipulated to reverse it, remain partially elucidated. Reprogramming of somatic cells towards a pluripotent-like state can be achieved through various experimental routes, including nuclear transfer, the provision of a defined cocktail of transcription factors, or fusion with a pluripotent stem cell partner. These approaches have been employed to demonstrate the remarkable epigenetic plasticity of terminally differentiated cell types, as well as to identify the factors essential for pluripotent conversion. In this review, we summarize recent advances in cell fusion-based studies, aiming to illuminate the basis of pluripotency and the epigenetic mechanisms that facilitate cell type interconversion.

title: Anorectic drugs and pulmonary hypertension from the bedside to the bench.
text: For over three decades, drugs used for weight reduction in obese individuals have been employed. The use of aminorex, an amphetamine analog that raises norepinephrine levels in the central nervous system, led to a surge in primary pulmonary hypertension (PPH) in Europe in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The use of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine, which inhibit the release and reuptake of 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) and increase 5-HT levels in the brain, was linked to a second epidemic of PPH. These drugs have been voluntarily withdrawn from the market due to their association with PPH. The exact cause of PPH in patients treated with these drugs is unknown, but recent evidence suggests that potassium channel abnormalities and the vasoactive and proliferative properties of 5-HT may play a role. Experimental evidence suggests that these drugs inhibit 4-aminopyridine-sensitive currents in potassium channels, leading to vasoconstriction in pulmonary resistance vessels and perhaps smooth muscle cell proliferation. High levels of 5-HT are known to be present in individuals with fenfluramine-induced PPH, but a direct cause-and-effect relationship has not been established. The epidemics of anorectic-related PPH may have provided valuable insights into the causes of PPH unrelated to these agents.

title: B-catenin deficiency, but not Myc deletion, suppresses the immediate phenotypes of APC loss in the liver.
text: Approximately 30% of hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs) exhibit dysregulated Wnt signaling, making it crucial to identify downstream pathways involved in the activation of Wnt signaling. Using cre-lox technology, we deleted the Apc gene in adult mouse livers and observed a rapid increase in nuclear β-catenin and c-Myc within 4 days of gene deletion, leading to induction of proliferation and hepatomegaly. To investigate the downstream pathways responsible for these phenotypes, we analyzed the impact of APC inactivation in the context of beta-catenin and c-Myc deficiency. Surprisingly, beta-catenin loss rescued both the proliferation and hepatomegaly phenotypes after APC loss, while c-Myc deletion had no effect on the phenotypes of APC loss in the liver. These findings suggest that the consequences of Wnt pathway deregulation within the liver are distinct from those observed in the intestine, with the majority of Wnt targets being beta-catenin-dependent but c-Myc-independent in the liver.

title: Uncoupling Mitochondrial Respiration for Diabesity.
text: Until recently, the mechanism of adaptive thermogenesis was believed to involve the expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in brown and beige adipocytes. UCP1 catalyzes a proton leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, leading to uncoupled oxidative metabolism and increased energy expenditure without ATP production. As such, increasing UCP1 expression in brown and beige adipose tissue was considered a viable target for obesity-related disorders. However, recent research has uncovered an UCP1-independent pathway to uncouple mitochondrial respiration. A secreted enzyme, PM20D1, predominantly found in UCP1-expressing adipocytes, exhibits both catalytic and hydrolytic activities, forming N-acyl amino acids. These endogenous uncouplers of mitochondrial respiration are produced at physiological concentrations and can reversibly uncouple mitochondrial respiration. In obese mice, administration of PM20D1 or its products leads to improved glucose tolerance and increased energy expenditure, resulting in 10% weight loss primarily in adipose tissue. These findings suggest that this metabolic pathway may hold promise as a novel therapy for diabesity, the disease state characterized by both diabetes and obesity.

title: A functional polymorphism in the prodynorphin gene promotor is associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.
text: The prodynorphin gene (PDYN), which encodes the anticonvulsant peptide dynorphin, is a strong candidate for a seizure suppressor gene and potential modulator of susceptibility to temporal lobe epilepsy. In a case-control association study involving 155 patients with non-lesional temporal lobe epilepsy and 202 controls, we found that low expression of the PDYN promoter in the L-allele form was associated with an increased risk of temporal lobe epilepsy in individuals with a family history of seizures. Interestingly, regardless of family history, individuals homozygous for the L-allele were found to have a higher risk of experiencing secondary generalized seizures and status epilepticus.

title: Cardiovascular and renal benefits of dry bean and soybean intake.
text: Dry beans and soybeans are nutrient-dense and fiber-rich, providing high-quality protein sources. Both have been shown to have protective and therapeutic effects, with studies demonstrating their potential to lower serum cholesterol concentrations, improve various aspects of diabetes, and offer metabolic benefits that aid in weight management. Soybeans are unique in their isoflavone content, particularly genistein and diadzein, which exhibit various biological functions. Soybeans and soy-based foods have been found to have multifaceted health-promoting effects, including cholesterol reduction, improved vascular health, preserved bone mineral density, and reduction of menopausal symptoms. While soy appears to have salutary effects on renal function, the mechanisms are not fully understood. Although populations consuming high amounts of soy have lower incidences of certain cancers, experimental data are insufficient to establish a definitive protective role of soy. As the availability of legume products and resources increases, incorporating dry beans and soyfoods into the diet can be both practical and enjoyable. With the shift towards a more plant-based diet, dry beans and soy will be valuable tools in the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases.

title: Nonuniform probability of glutamate release at a hippocampal synapse.
text:
A change in the likelihood of neurotransmitter release (Pr) is a crucial mechanism underlying synaptic plasticity. Contrary to the assumption that Pr remains constant across all terminals within a single synapse, our findings suggest that Pr can vary significantly between terminals, even those originating from the same axon. By analyzing the progressive block of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor-mediated synaptic currents using the irreversible open channel blocker MK-801, we found that release probability was nonuniform (ranging from 0.09 to 0.54) for terminals arising from a single axon, with the majority displaying a low Pr. However, terminals with higher Pr are more susceptible to activity-dependent modulation, which plays a critical role in long-term potentiation.
In this rewrite, I have attempted to make the language more concise and clear, while still conveying the same meaning as the original text. I have also added more technical terms and phrases to improve the readability of the text for a scientific audience.

title: An autoimmune disease, APECED, caused by mutations in a novel gene featuring two PHD-type zinc-finger domains
text: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED) is the solely recognized systemic autoimmune disease with a well-established monogenic background. Unlike other autoimmune disorders, APECED's primary biochemical abnormality remains unknown. Our research has led to the isolation of a novel gene, AIRE, which encodes a protein containing two PHD-type zinc-finger motifs, suggesting its role in transcriptional regulation. To date, five mutations in AIRE have been identified in individuals with APECED. This discovery represents the first instance of a single-gene defect causing a systemic human autoimmune disease, offering a valuable opportunity to delve into the molecular mechanisms underlying autoimmunity.

title: NuA4 lysine acetyltransferase Esa1 is targeted to coding regions and stimulates transcription elongation with Gcn5.
text: The major H4 lysine acetyltransferase (KAT) complex in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, NuA4, is recruited to promoters and enhances transcription initiation. NuA4 subunits contain domains that bind methylated histones, suggesting that histone methylation targets NuA4 to coding sequences during transcription elongation. We demonstrate that NuA4 is cotranscriptionally recruited, dependent on its physical association with elongating polymerase II (Pol II) phosphorylated on the C-terminal domain by cyclin-dependent kinase 7/Kin28, but independently of subunits required for NuA4 recruitment to promoters. While histone methylation by Set1 and Set2 is dispensable for NuA4's interaction with Pol II and targeting to some coding regions, it enhances NuA4-histone interaction and H4 acetylation in vivo. The NuA4 KAT, Esa1, mediates increased H4 acetylation and enhanced RSC occupancy and histone eviction in coding sequences, stimulating the rate of transcription elongation. Esa1 cooperates with the H3 KAT in SAGA, Gcn5, to enhance these functions. Our findings reveal a pathway for acetylation-mediated nucleosome remodeling and eviction in coding sequences that stimulates transcription elongation by Pol II in vivo.

title: Targeting mitotic exit leads to tumor regression in vivo: Modulation by Cdk1, Mastl, and the PP2A/B55α,δ phosphatase.
text: Targeting mitotic exit has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy against cancer. By employing genetically modified mice, our research demonstrates that the APC/C cofactor Cdc20 is essential for anaphase onset in vivo, including in embryonic and adult cells, as well as progenitor/stem cells. Ablation of Cdc20 leads to efficient regression of aggressive tumors, whereas current mitotic drugs have limited effects. Interestingly, Cdc20-deficient cells can undergo mitotic exit upon inactivation of Cdk1 and the kinase Mastl (Greatwall). This process relies on the activity of PP2A phosphatase complexes containing B55α or B55δ regulatory subunits. These findings highlight the importance of key players in mitotic exit in mammals and their implications in maintaining the balance between cell death and mitotic exit in tumor cells.

title: DrugBank 5.0: a major update to the DrugBank database for 2018
text:
DrugBank (www.drugbank.ca) is a comprehensive online database that provides detailed information on drugs, their mechanisms, interactions, and targets. First introduced in 2006, DrugBank has undergone significant updates over the past 12 years to keep pace with advances in web technologies and changing needs in drug research and development. The latest version, DrugBank 5.0, represents the most significant upgrade in over a decade, with many improvements made to the quantity, quality, and consistency of drug indications, drug binding data, drug-drug and drug-food interactions, and more.
New features in DrugBank 5.0 include:
* A 300% increase in the number of investigational drugs in the database
* A nearly 600% increase in the number of drug-drug interactions
* Over 3000% increase in the number of SNP-associated drug effects
* Addition of information on the influence of hundreds of drugs on metabolite levels (pharmacometabolomics)
* Addition of information on gene expression levels (pharmacotranscriptomics)
* Addition of information on protein expression levels (pharmacoprotoemics)
* Updates on the status of hundreds of new drug clinical trials and existing drug repurposing trials
In addition to these new features, the DrugBank website has undergone significant improvements to enhance its ease of use, utility, and potential applications in various areas of pharmacological research, pharmaceutical science, and drug education.

title: Analyzing mechanisms of alternative pre-mRNA splicing using in vitro splicing assays.
text:
The development of in vitro assays to study pre-mRNA splicing has led to significant advancements in understanding the fundamental features of splicing signals and the machinery involved in this process. The versatility of in vitro assays allows for manipulation of various biochemical factors, enabling the investigation of alternative splicing mechanisms. By modifying reaction conditions, researchers can accumulate, isolate, and characterize reaction intermediates, providing valuable insights into how the spliceosome removes introns and how regulatory elements influence splice site recognition and alternative exons. These advantages have made in vitro splicing assays a standard tool, despite being independent of RNA transcription and other RNA processing events, and in some cases deviating from the natural process of mRNA biogenesis.
In this chapter, we will outline the essential tools and techniques required to perform in vitro splicing assays. We will also present various experimental designs and approaches used to gain insights into the mechanisms of splice site recognition and activation, as well as methods to measure the kinetics of splicing, observe the formation of pre-spliceosomal complexes, and manipulate the in vitro system to resolve regulatory influences in alternative splicing.

title: New Roles for Pharmacists in Community Mental Health Care: A Narrative Review
text:
Medications are a crucial treatment modality for many mental health conditions, and as the burden of mental illnesses grows globally, pharmacists are well-positioned to play a more significant role in supporting individuals with mental health issues. This narrative review aims to explore the evidence for pharmacist-delivered services in mental health care and identify the barriers and facilitators to increasing their involvement as part of the broader mental health care team. The review is divided into three main sections:
1. The pharmacist's role in mental health care within multidisciplinary teams and in the early detection of mental illness: The review highlights new roles for pharmacists within multidisciplinary teams, such as case conferencing and collaborative drug therapy management. Additionally, there are new roles that would benefit from increased pharmacist involvement, including the early detection of mental health conditions, development of care plans, and follow-up of individuals with mental health problems.
2. The pharmacist's role in supporting quality use of medicines through medication review, strategies to improve medication adherence, and antipsychotic polypharmacy: The review describes the impact of pharmacist-led interventions designed to reduce inappropriate use of psychotropic medications and improve medication adherence. Other potential roles discussed include the management of antipsychotic polypharmacy and involvement in patient-centered care.
3. Barriers and facilitators to the implementation of mental health pharmacy services, including organizational culture and mental health stigma: The review identifies barriers related to pharmacists' attitudes, stigma, and skills in caring for patients with mental health problems. Additionally, barriers affecting pharmacist-physician collaboration are described, along with strategies to reduce mental health stigma.

In conclusion, this narrative review highlights the critical role that pharmacists can play in mental health care, both within multidisciplinary teams and through direct patient care. By addressing the barriers to implementation and promoting greater collaboration between pharmacists and other healthcare professionals, we can improve the quality of mental health care and support individuals with mental illnesses in their recovery.

title: UV light-induced DNA synthesis arrest in HeLa cells is associated with changes in phosphorylation of human single-stranded DNA-binding protein.
text: Our findings demonstrate that DNA replication activity in extracts of human HeLa cells decreases following exposure to UV radiation. The alterations in replication activity observed in vitro are parallel to the UV-induced block in cell cycle progression of these cells in culture. UV irradiation also induces specific changes in the phosphorylation pattern of the 34 kDa subunit of a DNA replication protein, human single-stranded DNA-binding protein (hSSB). The appearance of a hyperphosphorylated form of hSSB correlates with the reduced in vitro DNA replication activity in extracts of UV-irradiated cells. In vitro replication activity can be restored in these extracts by adding purified hSSB, suggesting that the UV-induced DNA synthesis arrest may be mediated in part by phosphorylation-related changes in the activity of hSSB, an essential component of the DNA replication machinery.

title: P446L-importin-beta inhibits nuclear envelope assembly by sequestering nuclear envelope assembly factors to the microtubules.
text: The P446L mutant of Drosophila importin-beta (P446L-imp-beta) has been reported to prevent nuclear envelope (NE) assembly in a dominant negative manner. To elucidate the mechanism of action of P446L-imp-beta, we investigated NE assembly on Sepharose beads in vitro. Our findings revealed that NE assembly does not occur in extracts supplemented with exogenous P446L-imp-beta, while a NE also forms on beads coated with importin-beta. Interestingly, when immobilized on Sepharose beads, P446L-imp-beta exhibits similar recruitment of NE vesicles as normal importin-beta. However, there is a discrepancy in the behavior of cytoplasmic and bead-bound P446L-imp-beta, which is attributed to its increased ability to bind microtubules (MTs) compared to normal importin-beta. While wild-type importin-beta can bind MTs and the binding decreases upon RanGTP interaction, P446L-imp-beta cannot be removed from MTs by RanGTP. P446L-imp-beta, like normal importin-beta, binds some nucleoporins required for NE assembly at the end of mitosis. Our findings suggest that the inhibitory effect of P446L-imp-beta on NE assembly is due to sequestering some of these nucleoporins to MTs.

title: Histone chaperones and nucleosome assembly.
text: Recent structural studies of the nucleosome core particle have provided insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying chromatin assembly and dynamics during replication and transcription. These structures have enabled a deeper understanding of the interactions between histones and DNA, as well as the role of histone chaperones and chromatin remodeling complexes in these processes. The nucleosome core, composed of the histone octamer, exhibits twofold symmetry, which may be exploited by histone chaperones to bind core histones. Recent research has also suggested that the nucleoplasmin pentamer may play a crucial role in histone storage, sperm chromatin decondensation, and nucleosome assembly by forming a decamer through dimerization. In this model, histone binding on the lateral surface of the chaperone involves stereospecific interactions and a shared twofold axis, providing a framework for understanding the mechanisms of chromatin regulation.

title: Intestinal methane production in obese individuals is associated with a higher body mass index.
text:
Background: Obesity is a widespread epidemic affecting approximately one-third of the population in the United States. Recent research suggests that the gut microbiome may play a crucial role in the development of obesity. This study aimed to investigate the association between methanogenic archaea and obesity in human subjects.
Methods: We recruited overweight and obese individuals from a weight loss program at a tertiary care medical center. Participants completed a questionnaire to assess bowel symptoms and provided a single end-expiratory breath sample to measure methane levels. We used bivariate and multivariate analyses to determine the association between methane levels and body mass index (BMI).
Results: A total of 58 participants were enrolled in the study, with 20% (n = 12) having breath test results indicating methane levels above 3 parts per million (ppm). The mean breath methane concentration was 12.2 ± 3.1 ppm.
