We also focused on the association between congenital malformations and maternal hyperglycemia in pregnant women with pregestational diabetes who had near-normal HbA1c levels in early pregnancy.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This literature review included original studies published in English after 1997, with data on congenital malformations and HbA1c in at least 250 women with pregestational diabetes. We searched electronic databases such as PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, and Web of Science. In total, 9 studies with 6225 women with type 1 diabetes and 2334 women with type 2 diabetes were included.
RESULTS: The prevalence of congenital malformations was 6.4% in women with type 1 diabetes and 4.3% in women with type 2 diabetes. When compared to the general population, the relative risk for congenital malformations was 3.2 for women with pregestational diabetes. In women with HbA1c levels below 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) in early pregnancy or between 53-64 mmol/mol (7.0-8.0%), the prevalence of congenital malformations was 4.3% and 3.7%, respectively, with relative risks of 2.2 and 1.9, respectively, compared to the background population.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that pregnant women with pregestational diabetes have a threefold higher risk of congenital malformations compared to the general population. Additionally, HbA1c levels below 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) in early pregnancy were associated with a twofold increased risk of congenital malformations compared to the background population.

title: Local and systemic insulin resistance resulting from hepatic activation of IKK-beta and NF-kappaB.
text: Our research demonstrates that obesity and a high-fat diet (HFD) lead to the activation of NF-κB and its downstream targets in the liver. To mimic this state of chronic, subacute inflammation in mice, we selectively expressed a constitutively active form of IKK-β in hepatocytes using transgenic mice, designated LIKK. These mice exhibit a type 2 diabetes phenotype characterized by hyperglycemia, severe hepatic insulin resistance, and moderate systemic insulin resistance, including effects in muscle. Similarly to HFD-fed wild-type mice, the hepatic production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, was increased in LIKK mice. We also observed parallel increases in cytokine signaling in the liver and muscle of these mice. Interestingly, insulin resistance was improved in LIKK mice by neutralizing IL-6 or inhibiting IKK-β using salicylate. Reversing hepatic IκBα superrepressor expression (LISR) restored the phenotype of both LIKK mice and HFD-fed wild-type mice. These findings suggest that lipid accumulation in the liver leads to subacute hepatic inflammation through NF-κB activation and downstream cytokine production, resulting in insulin resistance both locally in the liver and systemically.

title: Homelessness and health.
text: Homelessness has a profound impact on the health of tens of thousands of Canadians, with serious consequences for their well-being and life expectancy. Homeless individuals are disproportionately vulnerable to a range of health issues, including seizures, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, musculoskeletal disorders, tuberculosis, and skin and foot problems. Moreover, they face significant obstacles that hinder their access to adequate healthcare, exacerbating their already precarious situation. To address this pressing issue, more research is necessary to develop effective strategies for delivering healthcare to this marginalized population.

title: Serum metabolomics in animal models and human disease.
text:
The purpose of this study is to explore recent applications of serum metabolomics in both human and animal research. The main focus is on comprehending the intricate variations in human metabolism and utilizing serum metabolomics for disease profiling.
Recent studies have attempted to develop non-invasive biomarkers of disease and track the effects of nutritional and genetic interventions using serum metabolomics. While significant progress has been made, including identifying common changes in aging, menopause, and cancer, interpretation challenges have arisen due to small sample sizes in most human studies and differences between human and rodent metabolomes. However, a metabolic screen of over 1000 "healthy" humans (the Humsermet project) has shed light on numerous variables that can be used to refine the interpretation and design of future human studies, as well as data mining.
While some common serum metabolome alterations have been identified, inconsistencies remain. A comprehensive human serum metabolome database could be valuable in guiding future research in both humans and animals.

title: Differential Requirement of the Extracellular Domain in Activation of Class B G Protein-coupled Receptors.
text:
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) from the secretin-like (class B) family play a crucial role in hormonal homeostasis and are a prominent target for the treatment of metabolic disorders and neuronal diseases. These receptors are characterized by a large N-terminal extracellular domain (ECD) and a transmembrane domain (TMD) composed of seven transmembrane helices, which are hallmarks of GPCRs. Class B GPCRs are activated by peptide hormones, with their C termini bound to the receptor ECD and their N termini bound to the TMD. It is believed that the ECD functions as an affinity trap to bind and localize the hormone to the receptor, allowing the N terminus to insert into the TMD and induce conformational changes that activate downstream signaling.
However, recent studies have challenged the prevailing model of GPCR activation. We have found that human class B GPCRs exhibit significant variation in their requirement for the ECD in hormone binding and activation. For instance, receptors such as corticotrophin-releasing factor receptor 1 (CRF1R), parathyroid hormone receptor (PTH1R), and pituitary adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide type 1 receptor (PAC1R) can bypass the ECD requirement for high affinity hormone binding through induced proximity and mass action effects. In contrast, receptors such as glucagon receptor (GCGR) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) require the ECD for signaling even when the hormone is covalently linked to the TMD. Furthermore, our findings suggest a direct role of the ECD in GLP-1R activation by small molecules that interact with the intracellular side of the receptor.
In conclusion, our study highlights the complexity and variability of GPCR activation mechanisms, particularly in the class B family. These findings have important implications for the development of drugs targeting these receptors, as they suggest that the ECD may play a more direct and essential role in receptor activation than previously thought.

title: Genome-wide maps of histone modifications unwind in vivo chromatin states of the hair follicle lineage.
text: Using mouse skin as a model, we investigate how adult stem cells remodel their chromatin in response to signaling cues. By profiling global mRNA and chromatin changes in quiescent and activated hair follicle stem cells (HF-SCs) and their progeny, we reveal a prominent role for polycomb-group (PcG)-mediated histone H3K27 trimethylation in regulating HF-lineage progression. Unlike embryonic stem cells, PcG represses nonskin lineages and hair follicle differentiation in HF-SCs. In contrast, HF-SC regulators acquire H3K27me3 marks in their committed progeny, while nonskin regulators remain PcG-repressed. Interestingly, genes poised in embryonic stem cells and active in HF-SCs are also important for balancing HF-SC quiescence, highlighting the power of chromatin mapping in understanding stem cell behavior. Our findings demonstrate how HF-SCs cycle between quiescent and activated states without losing stemness, and define the role of PcG-mediated repression in governing a fate switch that is irreversible.

title: Two classes of endogenous small RNAs in Tetrahymena thermophila.
text: In Tetrahymena thermophila, small RNAs play a crucial role in RNA interference (RNAi) pathways, directing RNA degradation, translational repression, or DNA/chromatin methylation. The RNAi mechanism in Tetrahymena involves approximately 27-30-nucleotide (nt) RNAs, which are developmentally regulated and govern DNA elimination. In this study, we investigate the sequence features of these RNAs and identify a second RNAi pathway consisting of approximately 23-24-nt RNAs that accumulate strain-specifically and map to the genome in clusters antisense to predicted genes. Our findings demonstrate the existence of multiple endogenous RNAi pathways in the unicellular organism Tetrahymena, a complexity previously thought to be exclusive to multicellular organisms.

title: The binding of maize DHN1 to lipid vesicles. Gain of structure and lipid specificity.
text:
Dehydrins (DHNs; late embryogenesis abundant D-11) are a family of plant proteins that are induced in response to abiotic stresses such as drought, low temperature, and salinity, or during the late stages of embryogenesis. These proteins have been found to be intrinsically unstructured, but they contain a specific sequence called the "K segment" that resembles a class A2 amphipathic alpha-helical, lipid-binding domain. This raises the question of whether DHNs bind lipids, bilayers, or phospholipid vesicles.
In this study, we investigate the binding properties of maize (Zea mays) DHN DHN1 to lipid vesicles containing acidic phospholipids. We find that DHN1 binds more favorably to smaller vesicles than to larger ones, and that the association of DHN1 with vesicles results in an increase in the alpha-helicity of the protein. These findings suggest that DHNs, and potentially other plant stress proteins in the late embryogenesis abundant and cold-regulated classes, may undergo function-related conformational changes at the water/membrane interface, which could be related to the stabilization of vesicles or other endomembrane structures under stress conditions.

title: Requirement of heterochromatin for cohesion at centromeres.
text: Centromeres are characterized by heterochromatic properties in many organisms, yet the mechanisms underlying their mitotic function remain elusive. During cell division, newly replicated sister chromatids must cohere until anaphase, at which point Scc1/Rad21-mediated cohesion is disrupted. In metazoans, chromosome arm cohesins dissociate during prophase, leaving centromeres as the sole linkage before anaphase. The distinction between centromere cohesion and arm cohesion remains unresolved. Fission yeast Swi6, a homologue of Heterochromatin protein 1, is a component of silent heterochromatin. Our findings demonstrate that this heterochromatin is specifically required for the cohesion between sister centromeres. Swi6 is essential for the association of Rad21-cohesin with centromeres, but not along chromosome arms, highlighting its role in distinguishing centromere cohesion from arm cohesion. Therefore, one of the functions of centromeric heterochromatin is to attract cohesin, thereby ensuring proper sister centromere cohesion and chromosome segregation during cell division.

title: Gene expression in human skeletal muscle: alternative normalization method and effect of repeated biopsies
text: The reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) method has recently gained popularity in determining transcription and mRNA content in rodent and human muscle samples. However, the common practice of using endogenous controls to correct for variability in cDNA between samples is not optimal. To address this issue, we investigated (1) a novel normalization method based on measuring cDNA content using fluorescent dyes PicoGreen and OliGreen, (2) the impact of repeated muscle biopsies on mRNA gene expression, and (3) the spatial heterogeneity in mRNA expression across the muscle. Our results showed high sensitivity and linearity (R2>0.99) in both OliGreen and PicoGreen analyses using standard curves constructed from oligo standards, representative RT samples, or double-stranded lambda DNA. These findings suggest that PicoGreen and OliGreen may serve as potential alternatives for normalization in human gene expression studies. Additionally, our study found that multiple muscle biopsies obtained from the same muscle do not affect the mRNA response induced by an acute exercise bout for any of the genes examined.

title: The Impact of Location of Progressive Visual Field Loss on Longitudinal Changes in Quality of Life of Patients with Glaucoma.
text:
Purpose: To investigate the relationship between the rate of progressive loss in different regions of the visual field and the longitudinal changes in quality of life (QoL) in patients with glaucoma.
Design: Prospective, observational cohort study.
Participants: 236 patients with glaucomatous visual field loss followed for an average of 4.3±1.5 years.
Methods: All subjects had the 25-item National Eye Institute Visual Functioning Questionnaire (NEI VFQ-25) performed annually and standard automated perimetry (SAP) at 6-month intervals. Subjects were included if they had a minimum of 2 NEI VFQ-25 and 5 SAP tests during follow-up. The association between the change in NEI VFQ-25 Rasch-calibrated scores and the change in different regions of the visual field was investigated using a joint multivariable longitudinal linear mixed model.
Main Outcome Measures: The relationship between the change in QoL scores and the change in mean sensitivity in different regions of the visual field.
Results: There was a significant correlation between the change in NEI VFQ-25 Rasch scores during follow-up and the change in different regions of the visual field. Each 1 decibel (dB)/year change in binocular mean sensitivity of the central inferior area was associated with a decline of 2.6 units/year in the NEI VFQ-25 scores (R(2) = 35%; P < 0.001). Corresponding associations with change in QoL scores for the peripheral inferior, central superior, and peripheral superior areas of the visual field had R(2) values of 30%, 24%, and 19%, respectively. The association for the central inferior visual field area was statistically significantly stronger than those of the central superior area (P = 0.011) and peripheral superior area (P = 0.001), but not the peripheral inferior area (P = 0.171). Greater declines in NEI VFQ-25 scores were also seen in patients who had worse visual field sensitivity at baseline.
Conclusions: Progressive decline in sensitivity in the central inferior area of the visual field had the strongest association with longitudinal decline in QoL of patients with glaucoma.

title: Use of thiazolidinediones and the risk of bladder cancer among people with type 2 diabetes: a meta-analysis.
text:
Background: Patients with type 2 diabetes have a 40% increased risk of developing bladder cancer. Thiazolidinediones, particularly pioglitazone, have been linked to this increased risk. To investigate the association between thiazolidinedione use and bladder cancer incidence among adults with type 2 diabetes, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of published and unpublished studies.
Methods: We searched major biomedical databases and grey literature sources from inception to March 2012 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, and case-control studies that reported incident bladder cancer among individuals with type 2 diabetes who had ever (versus never) been exposed to pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, or any thiazolidinedione. We selected 4 RCTs, 5 cohort studies, and 1 case-control study, with a total of 2,657,365 patients, of whom 3643 developed bladder cancer, resulting in an overall incidence rate of 53.1 per 100,000 person-years.
Results: Our meta-analysis of the cohort studies found a significant association between thiazolidinedione use and bladder cancer incidence (pooled relative risk [RR] 1.15, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04-1.26, I(2) = 0%). Specifically, pioglitazone use was associated with an increased risk of bladder cancer (pooled RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.07-1.39, I(2) = 0%). In contrast, no significant association was observed between rosiglitazone use and bladder cancer incidence (pooled RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.34-2.23, I(2) = 0%). The limited evidence available supports the hypothesis that thiazolidinediones, particularly pioglitazone, are associated with an increased risk of bladder cancer among adults with type 2 diabetes.
Interpretation: Our findings suggest that thiazolidinediones, particularly pioglitazone, may increase the risk of bladder cancer among adults with type 2 diabetes. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to determine the underlying mechanisms.

title: Immune signaling by RIG-I-like receptors.
text: The RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), including RIG-I, MDA5, and LGP2, play a crucial role in detecting RNA viral infections and initiating antiviral immunity. These receptors reside in the cytoplasm and recognize viral RNA ligands or processed self-RNA to trigger innate immune responses and inflammation. RLRs also modulate the adaptive immune response through crosstalk networks with Toll-like receptors and other factors. The regulation of RLR signaling occurs at various levels, including autoregulation, ligand and cofactor interactions, and posttranslational modifications. Dysregulation of RLR expression or signaling has been implicated in the development of autoimmune diseases, highlighting the importance of understanding RLR signaling mechanisms to develop RLR-targeted therapeutics for antiviral and immune-modifying applications.

title: Ionizing radiation-induced long-term expression of senescence markers in mice is independent of p53 and immune status.
text: Exposure to ionizing radiation (IR) has been shown to trigger the formation of senescence markers, a state that coincides with the inability of irradiated tissues to repair and regenerate themselves properly over a lifetime. We hypothesized that these senescence markers could persist long-term in vivo, potentially contributing to the permanent decline in tissue function. To investigate this, we examined mouse tissues exposed to a sublethal dose of IR and found that they displayed persistent DNA damage foci and elevated levels of the senescence marker p16(INK4a) up to 45 weeks after exposure, the maximum time analyzed. Additionally, BrdU-labeling experiments revealed that the IR-induced damaged cells were preferentially eliminated, at least partially, in a tissue-dependent manner. Surprisingly, the accumulation of damaged cells occurred independently of the DNA damage response modulator p53 and the intact immune system, as their levels were similar in wild-type and Rag2(-/-) gammaC(-/-) mice, which lack T, B, and NK cells. Together, our findings provide strong evidence that exposure to IR leads to long-term expression of senescence markers in vivo, a phenomenon that may contribute to the reduced tissue functionality observed in cancer survivors.

title: Cranial neural crest and the building of the vertebrate head
text: The development of the head in vertebrates is a highly complex process involving a series of molecular and morphogenetic events that result in species-specific craniofacial morphologies. At the core of this process is a specialized cell type of neural origin, the neural crest, which plays a central role in generating the craniofacial mesenchyme. The degree of intrinsic patterning information present in the neural crest has been the subject of recent debate, with new findings highlighting the importance of environmental signals in coordinating craniofacial morphogenesis across space and time.

title: Tamoxifen resistance in MCF7 cells promotes EMT-like behaviour and involves modulation of beta-catenin phosphorylation.
text: In our previous research, we demonstrated that breast cancer cells that have developed resistance to endocrine therapy exhibit altered growth patterns and increased aggressiveness in vitro. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we focused on the integrity of the protein complex involved in cell-cell adhesion, as dysfunctional adhesion can promote an aggressive phenotype. Using a tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cell line (TamR), we found that these cells grew as loosely packed colonies with lost cell-cell junctions, exhibited altered morphology characteristic of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and had increased levels of tyrosine-phosphorylated beta-catenin and decreased serine/threonine-phosphorylated beta-catenin. Additionally, TamR cells showed loss of association between beta-catenin and E-cadherin, elevated cytoplasmic and nuclear beta-catenin, and increased transcription of beta-catenin target genes involved in tumour progression and EMT. Inhibition of EGFR kinase activity in TamR cells reduced beta-catenin tyrosine phosphorylation, increased beta-catenin-E-cadherin association, and promoted cell-cell adhesion. These findings suggest that homotypic adhesion in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells is dysfunctional due to EGFR-driven modulation of beta-catenin phosphorylation and may contribute to the enhanced aggressive phenotype and transition towards a mesenchymal phenotype in vitro.

title: Expression profiles of Toll-like receptors in non-small cell lung cancer and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
text:
The study investigated the expression of Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and control subjects. TLRs are key components of the innate immune system and play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) and lung cancer.
The study found that:
* TLR3, TLR4, TLR7, and TLR9 mRNA expression was significantly higher in NSCLC patients compared to IPF patients and controls.
* TLR3 mRNA expression was significantly higher in NSCLC patients compared to IPF patients and controls.
* TLR7 mRNA expression was significantly higher in both NSCLC and IPF groups compared to controls.
* TLR9 expression at the mRNA level was significantly higher in both NSCLC and IPF groups compared to controls.
* TLR2 mRNA expression was significantly higher in IPF patients compared to controls.

Flow cytometry analysis revealed that:
* TLR3 and TLR9 expression were decreased in IPF patients compared to the NSCLC group and controls.
* TLR9 expression was decreased in IPF patients compared to controls.

The study's main findings were:

* Increased expression of endosomal TLRs in NSCLC patients and elevated expression of TLR2 in pulmonary fibrosis.


These findings do not support a common TLR pathway hypothesis between NSCLC and IPF.

In conclusion, the study suggests that TLRs play a role in the pathogenesis of ILDs and lung cancer, and that there may be distinct mechanisms underlying the development of these diseases.

title: A protein farnesyltransferase inhibitor ameliorates disease in a mouse model of progeria.
text: Progerias are a class of rare genetic disorders characterized by accelerated aging. These conditions are often caused by mutations that result in the accumulation of a farnesylated form of prelamin A, a protein essential for maintaining the structural integrity of the cell nucleus. In progeria, the misfolded prelamin A disrupts the nuclear scaffolding, leading to abnormalities in nuclear shape and function. Previous studies have demonstrated that inhibitors of farnesyltransferase (FTIs) can reverse this cellular abnormality. To investigate the efficacy of FTIs in progeria, we evaluated the effects of ABT-100, an FTI, in Zmpste24-deficient mice, a mouse model of the disease. Our results showed that FTI treatment led to improved body weight, grip strength, bone density, and survival rate in mice at 20 weeks of age. These findings suggest that FTIs may have therapeutic potential in humans with progeria.

title: A rare mutation in UNC5C predisposes to late-onset Alzheimer's disease and increases neuronal cell death
text: We have identified a rare genetic mutation, T835M (rs137875858), in the UNC5C netrin receptor gene that is associated with late-onset Alzheimer's disease in two families and in four large case-control cohorts (odds ratio = 2.15, Pmeta = 0.0095). This mutation, located in the conserved hinge region of UNC5C, leads to increased cell death in human HEK293T cells and rodent neurons, as demonstrated through in vitro studies. Furthermore, neurons expressing T835M UNC5C are more susceptible to cell death from various neurotoxic stimuli, including β-amyloid (Aβ), glutamate, and staurosporine. Based on these findings and the high expression of UNC5C in the adult nervous system, we propose that one possible mechanism by which T835M UNC5C contributes to the risk of Alzheimer's disease is by increasing susceptibility to neuronal cell death, particularly in vulnerable regions of the disease brain.

title: Treatment of active tuberculosis in HIV-coinfected patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Background: Patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and tuberculosis (TB) are at increased risk of death, treatment failure, and relapse. Objective: To evaluate the impact of duration and dosing schedule of rifamycin and use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) on the treatment of active TB in HIV-positive patients through a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized, controlled trials and cohort studies. Methods: A comprehensive search of 5158 citations yielded 6 randomized trials and 21 cohort studies that met the inclusion criteria. Relapse rates were compared between regimens using rifamycin for 2 months versus at least 8 months, and between daily and thrice-weekly therapy in the initial phase. Results: The pooled cumulative incidence of treatment failure, death during treatment, and relapse were calculated using random-effects models, and multivariable meta-regression was performed using negative binomial regression. The results showed that relapse was more common with regimens using 2 months of rifamycin compared to those using rifamycin for at least 8 months. Additionally, thrice-weekly therapy in the initial phase was associated with higher rates of failure and relapse compared to daily therapy. There were trends towards higher relapse rates if rifamycins were used for only 6 months compared to >/=8 months, or if ART was not used. Conclusions: The findings of this review raise concerns about current treatment recommendations for HIV-TB coinfection. The data suggest that at least 8 months duration of rifamycin therapy, initial daily dosing, and concurrent ART may be associated with better outcomes. However, adequately powered randomized trials are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Crystal structure and association behaviour of the GluR2 amino-terminal domain.
text: Fast excitatory neurotransmission is primarily mediated by ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs), which are tetrameric, ligand-gated ion channel proteins composed of three subfamilies: AMPA, kainate, and NMDA receptors. Each subfamily shares a common modular-domain architecture, with active channels formed exclusively by assemblies of subunits within the same subfamily. The molecular basis for how the amino-terminal domain (ATD) guides subfamily-specific receptor assembly is not well understood. However, our study reveals that the ATDs of AMPA receptors (GluR1- and GluR2-ATDs) form tightly associated dimers, and through the analysis of crystal structures of the GluR2-ATD, we propose mechanisms by which the ATD guides subfamily-specific receptor assembly.

title: Deficiency in l-serine deaminase results in abnormal growth and cell division of Escherichia coli K-12.
text: The inability to deaminate l-serine severely hinders the growth and cell division of Escherichia coli K-12. A mutant strain lacking the three genes (sdaA, sdaB, tdcG) encoding its three l-serine deaminases grows well in glucose minimal medium, but upon subculture into medium containing glucose and casamino acids, it produces abnormally large and irregularly shaped cells, many of which lyse. When inoculated into Luria-Bertani (LB) broth with or without glucose, the mutant forms long filaments. Providing S-adenosylmethionine restores cell division in glucose-containing LB broth and alleviates the growth defect in medium containing casamino acids. We propose that the replication of E. coli is regulated by methylation, and that an elevated intracellular l-serine concentration, in the presence of other amino acids, depletes the cell of S-adenosylmethionine, leading to cell division failure.

title: Stem cell characteristics in prostate cancer cell lines.
text:
Background:
Recent studies have suggested the presence of a small, stem-like cell population in various human cancers, which is crucial for tumor (re)population.
Objective:
To investigate the stem cell properties of established prostate cancer (PCa) cell lines in vitro.
Design, Settings, and Participants:
Six established PCa cell lines (DU145, DuCaP, LAPC-4, 22Rv1, LNCaP, and PC-3) were examined for their stem cell properties using low-density plating and serial passaging. The expression of putative stem cell markers, including CD133 and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), was examined using flow cytometry and immunohistochemical staining.
Results and Limitations:
Five out of six cell lines formed clear holo-, mero-, and paraclones. Unlike paraclones, DU145 holoclones could be maintained in culture for several passages, indicating self-renewal ability. Using FACS analysis in DU145 cells, a small fraction (0.01%) of CD133(+) cells was detected, but these cells did not show more holoclone formation than marker-negative cells or unselected cells. Immunohistochemistry revealed alpha2-integrin and BCRP as potential stem cell markers, and CK5 with the combination of CK18 to distinguish transient amplifying cells.
Conclusions:
These results suggest the possible presence of stem-like cells in several established PCa cell lines. However, CD133 selection does not enrich for stem-like cells in PCa cell lines.

title: Resistance to antimicrobials in humans and animals.
text:
The notion that overusing antibiotics is the sole cause of antimicrobial resistance and reducing their use is the sole solution is oversimplified. While it is true that the excessive or inappropriate use of antibiotics in clinical medicine and their use in animal feed as growth promoters have contributed to the emergence of antimicrobial resistance, it is not the only factor.
Beginning in the mid-20th century, warning signs of antimicrobial resistance, or "chinks in the antimicrobial armor," began to appear. By the 1990s, various reports had highlighted the dangers of excessive or inappropriate antibiotic use in clinical medicine and its use in animal feed as growth promoters.1-3 However, the idea that reducing antibiotic use would automatically redress the problem has proven too simplistic.
The United Kingdom government's response to the House of Lords report included a public information campaign, surveillance of resistance along the food chain, targets for hospital-acquired infections, and the establishment of an overarching advisory body on all aspects of antibiotic use. However, the concept of overuse has proven too simplistic, as the evidence of overprescribing as the primary cause of antimicrobial resistance has been challenged.
In reality, the problem of antimicrobial resistance is more complex and multifaceted, involving factors such as the development of new antibiotics, the appropriate use of existing antibiotics, and the need for better infection control practices in healthcare settings. Therefore, a more comprehensive approach to addressing antimicrobial resistance is required, one that takes into account the various factors contributing to the problem and seeks to address them through a range of strategies.

title: Unmet needs and depressive symptoms among low--income older adults.
text: Previous research has identified several risk factors for late-life depression, including declining health, social isolation, and financial difficulties. On the other hand, social support from families and friends, as well as religiosity, have been found to be protective factors against depression. In this study, we aimed to investigate whether unmet needs for home- and community-based services among low-income older adults are associated with depressive symptoms, controlling for these known risk and protective factors. We conducted interviews with 213 community-residing older adults to assess their depressive symptoms using the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) and their unmet needs in the areas of personal assistance, instrumental and environmental support, emotional support, and other facilitative/enabling services. Our findings revealed a positive association between the number of unmet needs and depressive symptoms, although this association only explained a small proportion of the variance in GDS scores. We discuss the implications of these findings for future research and practice.

title: A key role for Ctf4 in coupling the MCM2-7 helicase to DNA polymerase alpha within the eukaryotic replisome.
text: The eukaryotic replisome plays a pivotal role in maintaining genome stability, yet its structural organization remains poorly understood. Previous studies have shown that regulatory proteins assemble around the MCM2-7 helicase at replication forks in yeast to form the replisome progression complex (RPC), which may connect MCM2-7 to other replisome components. Our current investigation reveals that the RPC interacts with DNA polymerase alpha, which primers each Okazaki fragment during lagging strand synthesis. Our findings suggest that a complex comprising the GINS and Ctf4 components of the RPC is essential for coupling MCM2-7 to DNA polymerase alpha. Recent studies have also demonstrated that the Mrc1 subunit of RPCs binds DNA polymerase epsilon, which synthesizes the leading strand at replication forks. Our data indicate that disruption of both Ctf4 and Mrc1 leads to chronic activation of the DNA damage checkpoint during chromosome replication, preventing cells from completing the cell cycle. These findings underscore the importance of coupling MCM2-7 to replicative polymerases in the regulation of eukaryotic chromosome replication and highlight the crucial role of Ctf4 in this process.

title: Data analysis methods for detection of differential protein expression in two-dimensional gel electrophoresis.
text: The recent advancement in microarray technology has prompted statisticians and bioinformaticians to create novel statistical approaches for comparing different biological samples. The ultimate goal is to identify a limited number of genes that are differentially expressed among thousands. In quantitative proteomics, the analysis of protein expression through two-dimensional gel electrophoresis shares some similarities with transcriptomic studies. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate various data analysis methodologies commonly used in array analysis using different proteomic data sets consisting of hundreds of proteins. Surprisingly, the significance analysis of microarrays method proved to be more powerful than the Student's t test in accurately identifying differentially expressed proteins, even with a limited number of replicates. This approach will help avoid wasting time and resources on false positives and prevent the loss of valuable information due to false negatives.

title: A clinical approach to circadian rhythm sleep disorders.
text:
Circadian rhythm sleep disorders are characterized by complaints of insomnia and excessive sleepiness resulting from alterations in the internal body clock or misalignment with the 24-hour social and physical environment. In addition to physiological and environmental factors, maladaptive behaviors often play a significant role in the development of these disorders. This review will focus on the clinical approach to diagnosing and managing various circadian rhythm sleep disorders, including delayed sleep phase disorder, advanced sleep phase disorder, non-entrained type, irregular sleep-wake rhythm, shift work sleep disorder, and jet lag disorder.
Diagnostic tools such as sleep diaries and wrist activity monitoring can help confirm the diagnosis. Because behavioral and environmental factors are often involved in the development of these conditions, a multimodal approach is usually necessary. Interventions may include sleep hygiene education, timed exposure to bright light, avoidance of bright light at the wrong time of day, and pharmacological approaches, such as melatonin. However, it is important to note that the use of melatonin is not an FDA-approved indication for the treatment of circadian rhythm sleep disorders.

title: SIVrcm infection of macaques.
text: In a previous report, we characterized SIVrcm, a unique primate lentivirus discovered in a Red-Capped Mangabey (RCM) pet in Gabon. SIVrcm is distinct from HIV-1 and HIV-2/SIV families of primate lentiviruses. This report presents additional in vitro replication studies and the results of SIVrcm infection in macaques. SIVrcm exhibited minimal cytopathic effects in Molt 4 Clone 8 cells and rhesus and human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). In vivo, SIVrcm was found to be non-pathogenic in rhesus macaques after 200 days and in cynomolgous macaques after one year, but it caused a chronic infection in both species.

title: Integrating nutrition security with treatment of people living with HIV: lessons from Kenya.
text: BACKGROUND: HIV-positive individuals have increased caloric requirements, which can be exacerbated by the side effects of antiretroviral treatment (ART) and lead to malnutrition. Nutritional support can alleviate these side effects and improve adherence to treatment, but there is a need for more comprehensive interventions to strengthen the nutrition security of individuals receiving ART. OBJECTIVE: To identify the benefits and challenges of interventions aimed at improving the nutrition security of people living with HIV who are receiving ART. METHODS: A qualitative study was conducted in western Kenya in 2005 and 2006 to evaluate the impact of a short-term nutrition intervention linked to the provision of free ART. RESULTS: Patients enrolled in the nutrition program reported improved adherence to their medication, reduced side effects, and increased ability to satisfy their appetite. Many clients also reported weight gain, recovery of physical strength, and resumption of work activities. These improvements were seen to have a positive impact on the support they received from family and community. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide further evidence for the need for a more holistic and comprehensive approach to addressing the coexistence of HIV and chronic nutrition insecurity. Future research should focus on bridging the gap between short-term nutritional support and longer-term livelihood security programming for communities affected by HIV. This will require interdisciplinary research and intersectoral action from the agriculture and health sectors in these environments.

title: Acylated and desacyl ghrelin stimulate lipid accumulation in human visceral adipocytes
text:
Objectives:
The study aimed to investigate the impact of obesity and obesity-related type 2 diabetes (T2D) on the circulating forms of the orexigenic hormone ghrelin, specifically acylated and desacyl ghrelin, and their potential role in regulating adipogenesis in humans.
Methods:
Plasma concentrations of acylated and desacyl ghrelin were measured in 80 subjects, and the expression of the ghrelin receptor (growth hormone secretagogue receptor, GHS-R) was analyzed in omental adipose tissue using western blot and immunohistochemistry. The effect of acylated and desacyl ghrelin on adipogenesis was determined in vitro in omental adipocytes using a range of concentrations (0.1-1000 pmol/l).
Results:
Circulating concentrations of acylated ghrelin were increased, while desacyl ghrelin levels were decreased, in obesity and obesity-related T2D. There were positive correlations between body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, insulin, and homeostasis model assessment (HOMA) index with acylated ghrelin levels. Obese individuals showed lower protein expression of GHS-R in omental adipose tissue. In differentiating omental adipocytes, incubation with both acylated and desacyl ghrelin significantly increased mRNA levels of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) and sterol-regulatory element binding protein 1 (SREBP1), as well as several fat storage-related proteins, including acetyl-CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthase, lipoprotein lipase, and perilipin. Consequently, both ghrelin forms stimulated intracytoplasmic lipid accumulation.
Conclusions:
Both acylated and desacyl ghrelin stimulate lipid accumulation in human visceral adipocytes. The elevation of acylated ghrelin concentrations in obese individuals may play a role in excessive fat accumulation in obesity.

title: Significant correlation between LKB1 and LGR5 gene expression and the association with poor recurrence-free survival in rectal cancer after preoperative chemoradiotherapy
text: The objective of the current study was to investigate whether the expression levels of LKB1 and LGR5 genes in rectal cancer tissues were associated with clinical outcomes in patients treated with preoperative chemoradiotherapy (CRT). To achieve this, we obtained residual cancer cells from 52 patients with locally advanced rectal cancer who underwent preoperative CRT. We isolated total RNA from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue samples using microdissection and measured the expression levels of LKB1 and LGR5 genes using real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction and immunohistochemistry. In addition, we performed in vitro studies using colon cancer cell lines to investigate the serial changes in LKB1, LGR5, and PRKAA1 (AMPK) gene expression after irradiation. Our findings revealed that tissue samples from patients with poor pathological response and tumor recurrence had significantly higher expression levels of LKB1 and LGR5 genes compared to those without them (P < 0.05). Furthermore, there was a significant positive correlation between LKB1 and LGR5 gene expression after CRT (Spearman's ρ: 0.429, P = 0.0023). Notably, patients with high expression levels of both LKB1 and LGR5 had a significantly lower recurrence-free survival compared to the other group (P = 0.0055, 95% confidence interval: 1.39–11.08). In vitro studies also showed a similar pattern of serial gene expression among LKB1, LGR5, and PRKAA1 after irradiation. These results suggest that LKB1 and LGR5 expression may play a role in resistance to CRT, contributing to tumor relapse in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer treated with preoperative CRT.

title: Evaluating the impact of pharmacists in mental health: a systematic review.
text:
Over the past 30 years, efforts to improve patient outcomes in mental health care have involved integrating the skills of various healthcare professionals into collaborative care models. Clinical pharmacists have played a significant role in these models, contributing in various capacities such as educators, consultants, and providers. This systematic review aims to evaluate the impact of pharmacists in mental health care by analyzing the medical literature from 1972 to 2003.
We identified approximately 35 publications that described the roles of clinical pharmacists in mental health care. However, only 16 studies met our criteria for scientific rigor, with half of them conducted in inpatient settings and the other half in outpatient settings across various healthcare organizations, including Veterans Administration, health maintenance organizations, community mental health clinics, and nursing homes.
The 16 studies demonstrated positive outcomes, including improved treatment recommendations, patient education, prescribing practices, patient satisfaction, and resource use. However, most of the studies were small, and limitations in study design hindered further comparison.
Given the long history and success of pharmacists in mental health care, further multicenter cost-effectiveness trials are warranted to support the role of the psychiatric pharmacist.

title: Multicenter phase II study of lapatinib in patients with brain metastases from HER2-positive breast cancer.
text:
Background: Brain metastases are a common complication in patients with advanced HER2+ breast cancer, with approximately one-third of patients developing them. Effective treatment options for patients with central nervous system (CNS) progression after cranial radiation are limited, posing a significant clinical challenge. Lapatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting both epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and HER2, has shown promise in reducing CNS lesions in a small phase 2 trial. This study aimed to further evaluate the CNS activity of lapatinib in patients with HER2+ breast cancer and CNS metastases.
Methods: Eligible patients had HER2+ breast cancer, progressive brain metastases, prior trastuzumab therapy, and cranial radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was CNS objective response, defined as a >or=50% volumetric reduction in CNS lesions without increasing steroid use, worsening neurological symptoms, or extra-CNS disease progression. An exploratory analysis was conducted to assess the association between volumetric reduction and improvement in progression-free survival and neurological signs and symptoms. Patients who progressed on lapatinib were given the option to receive lapatinib plus capecitabine as part of an extension study.
Results: Of the 242 patients enrolled, 6% exhibited CNS objective responses to lapatinib, and 21% experienced a >or=20% volumetric reduction in their CNS lesions. An association was observed between volumetric reduction and improvement in progression-free survival and neurological signs and symptoms. In the 50 evaluable patients who entered the lapatinib plus capecitabine extension, 20% achieved a CNS objective response and 40% experienced a >or=20% volumetric reduction in their CNS lesions.
Conclusion: This study confirms the modest CNS antitumor activity of lapatinib and suggests that the addition of capecitabine may improve outcomes. Further studies of lapatinib-based regimens for CNS metastases from HER2+ breast cancer are warranted.

title: Control of signaling-mediated clearance of apoptotic cells by the tumor suppressor p53
text: The inefficient removal of dying cells can lead to abnormal immune responses, such as unresolved inflammation and autoimmune conditions. Our research shows that the tumor suppressor p53 regulates the phagocytosis of apoptotic cells through its target, Death Domain1α (DD1α), which suggests that p53 promotes both the proapoptotic pathway and postapoptotic events. DD1α functions as an engulfment ligand or receptor that interacts with homophilic intermolecular interactions at intercellular junctions of apoptotic cells and macrophages, unlike other typical scavenger receptors that recognize phosphatidylserine on the surface of dead cells. Defects in DD1α in mice led to in vivo defects in clearing dying cells, resulting in multiple organ damage indicative of immune dysfunction. p53-induced expression of DD1α ensures efficient clearance of cell corpses and promotes precise immune responses.

title: Circulating tumor DNA as a non-invasive substitute to metastasis biopsy for tumor genotyping and personalized medicine in a prospective trial across all tumor types.
text: Cell-free tumor DNA (ctDNA) has the potential to revolutionize non-invasive diagnostic testing for personalized medicine by providing similar molecular information as invasive tumor biopsies. In the histology-independent phase II SHIVA trial, patients are matched with targeted therapeutics based on previous screening of multiple somatic mutations using metastatic biopsies. To evaluate the utility of ctDNA in this trial, an ancillary study was conducted to compare de novo detection of somatic mutations in plasma DNA versus metastasis biopsies in 34 patients with 18 different tumor types. The study analyzed 46 genes and over 6800 COSMIC mutations using a multiplexed next-generation sequencing panel. The results showed that in 27 patients, 28 of 29 mutations identified in metastasis biopsies (97%) were also detected in matched ctDNA. Additionally, one mutation was found only in ctDNA. In the seven other patients, mutation detection from metastasis biopsy failed due to insufficient biopsy material, but was successful in all plasma DNA samples, providing three additional potential actionable mutations. These findings suggest that ctDNA analysis could serve as an alternative or replacement to metastasis biopsies for multiplexed mutation detection in selecting personalized therapies based on the patient's tumor genetic content, regardless of cancer type or metastatic site.

title: TGF-beta suppresses tumor progression in colon cancer by inhibition of IL-6 trans-signaling.
text: Alterations in TGF-beta signaling have been observed in colorectal cancer, although the molecular consequences of these alterations remain poorly understood. To investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying TGF-beta signaling in colorectal cancer, we employed transgenic mice overexpressing TGF-beta or a dominant-negative TGF-betaRII. Our findings demonstrate that TGF-beta signaling in tumor-infiltrating T lymphocytes regulates the growth of dysplastic epithelial cells in experimental colorectal cancer, as determined by histological analysis and a novel high-resolution chromoendoscopy system. At the molecular level, TGF-beta signaling in T cells regulates STAT-3 activation in tumor cells through IL-6 signaling. Specifically, tumor cell-derived soluble IL-6R is required for IL-6 signaling, and inhibition of TGF-beta-dependent IL-6 trans-signaling prevents tumor progression in vivo. Our data provide novel insights into the role of TGF-beta signaling in colorectal cancer and suggest potential therapeutic strategies for colorectal cancer treatment based on inhibition of TGF-beta-dependent IL-6 trans-signaling.

title: New opportunities: the use of nanotechnologies to manipulate and track stem cells.
text: Nanotechnologies are novel platforms that hold great promise in measuring, comprehending, and manipulating stem cells. Examples of such include magnetic nanoparticles and quantum dots for the labeling and in vivo tracking of stem cells; nanoparticles, carbon nanotubes, and polyplexes for the intracellular delivery of genetic material/oligonucleotides and protein/peptides; and engineered nanometer-scale scaffolds for stem cell differentiation and transplantation. This review examines the application of nanotechnologies in stem cell tracking, differentiation, and transplantation, while also delving into their utility and the potential concerns surrounding their potential cytotoxicity.

title: The emergence of order in the Drosophila pupal retina.
text: During the pupal stage of development, the autonomously developing ommatidia in the Drosophila eye are organized into a long-range order through the emergence of eight additional cell types. These cells form an interweaving lattice with the ommatidia, with the lattice being refined through the removal of excess cells to bring neighboring ommatidia into register. Local cell-cell contacts play a crucial role in determining the fate of each cell, with cells making specific contacts predicting their cell type. For example, cells that contact the anterior or posterior cone cells in an ommatidium invariably become primary pigment cells, while cells that contact primary pigment cells from different ommatidia become secondary and tertiary pigment cells. In contrast, the development of bristles is distinct from ommatidial development, with the four cells of each bristle group arising from a single founder cell and differentiating in a center-radiating manner. During two stages of programmed cell death, the bristles are brought into their final position, and once all cells in the lattice have achieved their final position, a second stage of retinal development begins, resulting in the production of structures specific to each cell type. This paper provides a detailed account of these stages of pupal development and suggests how local cell-cell contacts may give rise to the functional retina.

title: Gene expression analysis by cDNA microarray in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
text:
Background:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a common type of cancer affecting humans, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its development are poorly understood. Comprehensive gene expression profiling is crucial for elucidating the underlying molecular mechanisms of OSCC.
Methods:
We performed cDNA microarray analysis to investigate the expression patterns of 16,617 genes in nine OSCC patients. We identified 47 genes with altered expression across all cases and classified their ontology into 10 categories. To validate the microarray data, we analyzed the expression of genes such as TGFBI, FADD, and DUSP1 by reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). We used hierarchical clustering analysis to divide the nine cases into two clusters.
Results:
Our results suggest that the 47 genes identified have a functional significance in oral squamous cell carcinogenesis. Additionally, the gene expression patterns identified by hierarchical clustering analysis may represent degrees of differentiation. The postoperative recovery was uneventful, and all patients were free from tumor after surgery.
Conclusions:
In conclusion, our findings suggest that comprehensive gene expression profiling can provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying OSCC. The identification of 47 genes with altered expression patterns may lead to the development of new diagnostic markers or therapeutic targets for OSCC. The use of hierarchical clustering analysis to identify distinct gene expression patterns in OSCC may also help to better understand the molecular mechanisms underlying this disease. Further accumulation of cases and long-term observation will enable the addition of 5-year survival rate data, which will enhance the ability to represent the malignancy of OSCC based on these gene expression patterns.

title: Risk factors associated with symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux.
text: BACKGROUND: Despite the prevalence of gastroesophageal reflux (GER) among patients, there is a lack of population-based data on the risk factors for this condition in the United States. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to investigate the risk factors for GER in an age- and gender-stratified random sample of the population of Olmsted County, Minnesota, using a valid self-report questionnaire. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study and mailed a questionnaire to residents aged 25-74 years. The questionnaire assessed reflux symptoms and potential risk factors, and logistic regression was used to estimate the odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for reflux symptoms associated with each risk factor. RESULTS: Of the 2,118 eligible subjects, 1,524 (72%) responded. The following risk factors were independently associated with frequent (at least weekly) reflux symptoms: body mass index (BMI) >30 kg/m2 (OR = 2.8; CI, 1.7-4.5), having an immediate family member with heartburn or esophageal/gastric disease (OR = 2.6; CI, 1.8-3.7), a past history of smoking (OR = 1.6; CI, 1.1-2.3), consuming more than seven drinks per week (OR = 1.9; CI, 1.1-3.3), and a higher psychosomatic symptom checklist score (OR per 5 units = 1.4; CI, 1.3-1.6). CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that obesity is a strong risk factor for GER, although the value of weight reduction remains to be proven. The finding that family history is also a risk factor suggests a possible genetic component to the disorder.

title: A mathematical investigation of the effects of inhibitor therapy on three putative phosphorylation cascades governing the two-component system of the agr operon.
text: Two-component systems (TCSs) are commonly used by bacteria to detect specific external signals and respond accordingly through a phosphorylation cascade within the cell. The TCS of the agr operon in Staphylococcus aureus, for example, plays a crucial role in a regulatory process known as quorum sensing, which is a cell-to-cell communication mechanism used to assess population density. By manipulating this "knowledge," S. aureus can coordinate the production of its arsenal of virulence factors, which are essential for promoting infection. To gain a deeper understanding of this process, we have developed three models of the agr operon, each incorporating a different phosphorylation cascade for the TCS. Using numerical and asymptotic techniques, we have examined the effects of inhibitor therapy, a novel approach to controlling bacterial infection by attenuating virulence, on each of these cascades. Our results provide insights into the potential effectiveness of such therapy and highlight the broad relevance of TCSs throughout the bacterial kingdom.

title: Coregulators in nuclear estrogen receptor action: from concept to therapeutic targeting.
text: Estrogens play a crucial role in regulating various physiological processes, including growth, differentiation, and function of various target tissues, such as the male and female reproductive systems, breast, skeletal, nervous, cardiovascular, digestive, and immune systems. The majority of these biological activities are mediated through two genetically distinct receptors, ERalpha and ERbeta, which function as hormone-inducible transcription factors. Recent research has shown that the recruitment of coregulatory proteins to these receptors is essential for their ability to respond to hormones or pharmacological ligands, interpret extracellular signals, catalyze chromatin condensation, and communicate with the general transcription apparatus at target gene promoters. Additionally, the presence of corepressors, which function as negative regulators of ER activity, adds an extra layer of complexity to ER action. This review also discusses current efforts to develop pharmaceutical agents that target ER-cofactor interactions as therapeutics for estrogen-associated pathologies.

title: Autophagy and mTORC1 regulate the stochastic phase of somatic cell reprogramming
text:
We have investigated the mechanisms underlying the induction of autophagy during the reprogramming of mouse fibroblasts to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by four reprogramming factors (Sox2, Oct4, Klf4, and c-Myc). Our findings indicate that autophagy is robustly induced during this process, which we refer to as 4F reprogramming. Notably, this induction occurs independently of p53 activation and is mediated by the coordinated downregulation of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and the upregulation of autophagy-related genes.
Our results reveal a complex interplay between the 4F factors in regulating autophagy during reprogramming. While Klf4 and c-Myc induce autophagy-related genes, Sox2 and Oct4 inhibit their expression. This bifurcation in the regulation of autophagy leads to a paradoxical situation where inhibition of mTORC1 facilitates reprogramming by promoting cell reshaping (mitochondrial remodeling and cell size reduction), while mTORC1 activation impairs reprogramming by triggering autophagy.
Interestingly, our findings also suggest that autophagy does not participate in cell reshaping during reprogramming, but instead degrades p62, a protein that facilitates reprogramming in autophagy-deficient cells. This delicate balance between mTORC1 inhibition and autophagy induction in the early phase of reprogramming ultimately determines reprogramming efficiency.
In conclusion, our study uncovers a complex signaling network involving mTORC1 inhibition and autophagy induction in the early phase of reprogramming, which is critical for efficient reprogramming of mouse fibroblasts to iPSCs. Further investigations into the mechanisms underlying this process may provide valuable insights into the development of novel therapeutic strategies for a variety of diseases.

title: Lithium Therapy Improves Neurological Function and Hippocampal Dendritic Arborization in a Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 1 Mouse Model
text:
Background: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1) is a dominantly inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor and cognitive dysfunction. The disease is caused by an expanded polyglutamine tract in the ataxin 1 (ATXN1) gene, leading to a multifactorial pathogenesis involving misfolding of ATXN1 and transcriptional dysregulation. Lithium, a compound with known neuroprotective effects, has been shown to improve motor coordination, learning, and memory in various conditions. Therefore, we investigated the efficacy of lithium treatment in a knock-in mouse model of SCA1 (Sca1154Q/2Q mice) to determine its potential as a therapeutic candidate for human SCA1 patients.
Methods and Findings: Sca1154Q/2Q mice and their wild-type littermates were fed either regular chow or chow supplemented with 0.2% lithium carbonate. Dietary lithium carbonate supplementation resulted in improved motor coordination, learning, and memory in Sca1154Q/2Q mice, with motor improvement seen both presymptomatically and after symptom onset. Neuropathologically, lithium treatment attenuated the reduction of dendritic branching in mutant hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Additionally, lithium treatment restored the levels of isoprenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase (Icmt; alternatively, Pccmt), a protein that is down-regulated early in the course of SCA1 pathogenesis.
Conclusions: The positive effect of lithium on multiple behavioral measures and hippocampal neuropathology in an authentic disease model, combined with its ability to restore an early marker of ATXN1 toxicity, makes it a promising candidate treatment for human SCA1 patients. Further research is warranted to fully explore the therapeutic potential of lithium in SCA1.

title: The progression from hypertension to congestive heart failure.
text:
Objective: To investigate the relationship between hypertension and the development of congestive heart failure (CHF), including the time course of progression and identifying risk factors that contribute to the development of overt heart failure in hypertensive subjects.
Design: Inception cohort study.
Setting: General community.
Participants: Original Framingham Heart Study and Framingham Offspring Study participants aged 40 to 89 years and free of CHF. The study began on January 1, 1970, to reflect contemporary experience.
Exposure Measures: Hypertension (defined as blood pressure of at least 140 mm Hg systolic or 90 mm Hg diastolic or current use of medications for hypertension treatment) and other potential CHF risk factors were assessed at periodic clinic examinations.
Outcome Measure: The development of CHF.
Results: A total of 5143 eligible subjects contributed 72422 person-years of observation. During up to 20.1 years of follow-up (mean, 14.1 years), there were 392 new cases of heart failure; in 91% (357/392), hypertension preceded the development of heart failure. Adjusting for age and heart failure risk factors in proportional hazards regression models, the hazard for developing heart failure in hypertensive compared with normotensive subjects was about 2-fold in men and 3-fold in women. Multivariable analyses revealed that hypertension had a high population-attributable risk for CHF, accounting for 39% of cases in men and 59% in women. Among hypertensive subjects, myocardial infarction, diabetes, left ventricular hypertrophy, and valvular heart disease were predictive of increased risk for CHF in both sexes. Survival following the onset of hypertensive CHF was bleak; only 24% of men and 31% of women survived 5 years.
Conclusions: Hypertension was the most common risk factor for CHF, and it contributed a large proportion of heart failure cases in this population-based sample. Preventive strategies directed toward earlier and more aggressive blood pressure control are likely to offer the greatest promise for reducing the incidence of CHF and its associated mortality.

title: Association of plasma resistin with glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria in hypertensive adults.
text:
A recently discovered pro-inflammatory cytokine, Resistin, has been linked to insulin resistance, inflammation, and renal dysfunction. In a study of 1575 hypertensive adults without known coronary heart disease or stroke (857 blacks and 718 non-Hispanic whites), we investigated the association between plasma Resistin levels and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and albuminuria.
We found that higher plasma Resistin levels were associated with lower eGFR in both ethnic groups after adjusting for coronary heart disease risk factors, use of renin-angiotensin blockers, and statins. This association remained significant after further adjusting for markers of insulin resistance (homeostasis model assessment for insulin resistance) and inflammation (plasma C-reactive protein). The association between Resistin and lower eGFR was seen in subjects with and without diabetes in both ethnic groups. Additionally, higher Resistin levels were associated with a higher urine albumin:creatinine ratio in black subjects with diabetes and non-Hispanic white subjects with diabetes, independent of coronary heart disease risk factors, hypertension medication use, and statin use.
Our findings suggest that Resistin may play a role in the development of kidney disease in adults with hypertension, particularly in the presence of concomitant diabetes. This association was independent of traditional risk factors for kidney disease and markers of insulin resistance and inflammation.

title: Large-scale candidate gene scan reveals the role of chemoreceptor genes in host plant specialization and speciation in the pea aphid.
text: Understanding the underlying drivers of speciation is crucial for comprehending the patterns of biodiversity. Identifying the genetic changes that lead to adaptation and reproductive isolation is essential to connecting barriers to gene flow with the causal origins of divergence. In this study, we present a novel approach to the genetics of speciation, which complements commonly used methods such as quantitative trait locus mapping and genome-wide scans for selection. We employ a large-scale candidate gene approach using sequence capture to identify the genetic changes underlying reproductive isolation in the pea aphid, a model system for the study of ecological speciation. By means of targeted resequencing, we scale up the candidate gene approach to test the role of chemosensory gene families in host plant specialization. Screening for the signature of divergence under selection at 172 candidate and noncandidate loci, we uncover a small number of loci that show high levels of differentiation among host races, which mostly correspond to odorant and gustatory receptor genes. This study provides the first indication that some chemoreceptor genes, often tightly linked together in the genome, may play a crucial role in local adaptation and reproductive isolation in the pea aphid and potentially other phytophagous insects. Our approach opens up a new avenue for the functional genomics of ecological speciation.

title: The cancer stem cell hypothesis: a guide to potential molecular targets.
text: Conventional cancer theories propose that tumors are the result of uncontrolled cell growth due to the accumulation of random mutations in genes that regulate cell division. However, contradictions to this theory have been reported in the past. These discrepancies may be resolved by the presence of residual tumor cells, known as Cancer Stem Cells (CSCs), which are responsible for tumorigenesis, tumor maintenance, tumor metastasis, and tumor relapse. In this review, we will summarize the current understanding of CSCs, with a focus on the potential to identify specific markers of CSCs and discuss the therapeutic potential of targeting these cells for cancer treatment.

title: Serum amyloid A: An acute-phase protein involved in tumour pathogenesis
text: The synthesis of acute-phase protein serum amyloid A (SAA) is primarily regulated by inflammatory cytokines, and elevated levels of SAA may serve as a marker for both acute and chronic inflammatory diseases. However, SAA is also produced in non-hepatic tissues, such as human carcinoma metastases and cancer cell lines. An growing body of in vitro research supports the idea that SAA plays a role in carcinogenesis and neoplastic diseases. The accumulation of evidence suggests that SAA may be included in a group of biomarkers to detect a pattern of physiological events that reflect the growth of malignancy and host response. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the various ways in which SAA may contribute to tumor development, progression, and metastasis, and to gain a deeper understanding of SAA as a potential link between chronic inflammation and neoplasia.

title: Body size and outcomes on peritoneal dialysis in the United States.
text:
Background: Being overweight has been cited as a relative contraindication to peritoneal dialysis. However, the actual mortality rates among overweight and obese patients undergoing dialysis have not been well-established.
Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 418,021 Medicare patients initiating dialysis between 1995 and 2000. We categorized patients based on their body mass index (BMI) at the time of dialysis initiation into underweight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m2), overweight (BMI 25.0-29.9 kg/m2), and obese (BMI > 29.9 kg/m2). We examined the association between BMI and the likelihood of initiating peritoneal dialysis, as well as the adjusted mortality hazards among peritoneal dialysis patients.
Results: Our findings indicate that while underweight patients were less likely to initiate peritoneal dialysis (odds ratio [OR] 0.70, p < 0.05), overweight (OR 1.12, p < 0.05) and obese (OR 0.87, p < 0.05) patients had higher adjusted mortality hazards in the first, second, and third year after dialysis initiation compared to normal-weight patients. After censoring for switch to hemodialysis, the associations remained significant. Similarly, for transplantation, the corresponding results were observed (underweight: OR 0.76, p < 0.05; overweight: OR 0.90, p < 0.05; obese: OR 0.88, p < 0.05). For switching to hemodialysis, the hazards ratios were also significant (underweight: HR 0.92, p < 0.05; overweight: HR 1.07, p < 0.05; obese: HR 1.28, p < 0.05).
Conclusion: Our study suggests that while overweight and obese patients are less likely to initiate peritoneal dialysis, they have longer survival than normal-weight patients after initiating dialysis. These findings challenge the conventional wisdom that being overweight is a relative contraindication to peritoneal dialysis.

title: The anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome: a machine designed to destroy
text: The anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) is a multifunctional ubiquitin ligase that plays a crucial role in both cellular processes within the eukaryotic cell cycle and outside of it. As the most complex enzyme known to catalyze ubiquitination reactions, the APC/C is composed of over a dozen subunits that come together to form a large 1.5-million-dalton complex. Recent research has uncovered a wealth of mechanisms that regulate APC/C activity, providing initial insights into how this unique ubiquitin ligase identifies its substrates.

title: Regulation of the expression of alkaline phosphatase in a human breast-cancer cell line.
text: Treatment of cultured human breast cancer cells BC-M1 with dexamethasone led to the induction of a placental-type alkaline phosphatase (ALP). Both the ALP activity and mRNA levels in the cells were found to increase in response to dexamethasone treatment, which was time- and dose-dependent. The induction of ALP activity by dexamethasone was shown to be a complex process involving other regulatory proteins, as the accumulation of ALP mRNA was inhibited by actinomycin D and cycloheximide. Contrary to dexamethasone, retinoic acid (RA) had opposing effects on ALP expression, reducing its induction. Additionally, thermostability and sensitivity analysis of the BC-M1 ALP revealed that it is most similar to the placental form. Northern hybridization analysis also showed that ALP mRNA transcripts in BC-M1 and term placenta are similar in size and distinct from that of the placental-like mRNA transcript in choriocarcinoma cells. Furthermore, the degradation of BC-M1 ALP mRNA had a similar half-life of 27 h in untreated and dexamethasone- or RA-treated cells, indicating that the induction of ALP in BC-M1 cells by dexamethasone is primarily due to an increase in the transcription of the ALP gene.

title: Declining tuberculosis notification trend associated with strengthened TB and expanded HIV care in Swaziland.
text:
This retrospective observational study examines the Swaziland National Tuberculosis (TB) Control Programme's efforts between 2004 and 2014. The aim is to identify the discrepancy between actual declines in TB case notifications and estimated incidence increases. The review of policies and practices reveals that the most significant factors contributing to the decrease in TB case notifications were:
1. Increased access to antiretroviral therapy for co-infected TB patients, leading to improved treatment outcomes and reduced transmission.
2. Successful integration of TB and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) services in the country, resulting in improved coordination and delivery of care.
3. Enhanced implementation of all components of directly observed treatment, active case finding, and rapid diagnosis using new technologies, leading to earlier detection and treatment of TB cases.
By analyzing these factors, the study provides valuable insights into the effective strategies employed by the Swaziland National TB Control Programme to combat TB and improve health outcomes in the country.

title: Advances in techniques of testing mycobacterial drug sensitivity, and the use of sensitivity tests in tuberculosis control programmes.
text: In 1961, a group of international experts convened an informal consultation to develop criteria and technical procedures for reliable tests of sensitivity to the three main antituberculosis drugs (isoniazid, streptomycin, and p-aminosalicylic acid). Seven years later, the group reconvened to review the latest advancements in the field and provide practical guidance on how to use these tests in tuberculosis control programs. The participants agreed on how to define drug sensitivity and resistance and emphasized the importance of using a discrimination approach to calibrate sensitivity tests. The paper also includes descriptions of sensitivity tests used by the Medical Research Council of Great Britain for first- and second-line drugs, as well as two variants of the proportion method developed by the Institut Pasteur in Paris, and a method for calibrating sensitivity tests.

title: Time from finding abnormality on mass-screening to final diagnosis of lung cancer.
text: In Japan, mass screening for lung cancer is a distinct system. This study examines the time frame from discovering an abnormality during mass screening to the final diagnosis of lung cancer. Of the 517 patients with lung cancer admitted to our hospital over a 10-year period ending in December 2001, 83 (16.1%) were detected through mass screening. We reviewed the medical records of these patients and calculated the intervals from mass screening to pathological diagnosis with clinical staging. The time from mass screening to the hospital visit was less than 2 months in 62 (74.7%) cases, while 5 (6.0%) patients visited the hospital more than 6 months after the mass screening. There was no significant difference in the interval between gender (p=0.0680) and age (p=0.1532). Among 60 patients referred from outside, the average time from initial medical attention at a nearby clinic to pathological diagnosis at our hospital was 0.5 months. Additionally, the interval was 0.5 months for patients diagnosed with lung cancer at our hospital. There was a statistically significant difference in survival between patients diagnosed within 4 months of the screening and those diagnosed more than 4 months later (p=0.0487). While the interval in most cases was acceptable, further improvements are needed to minimize delays and maximize the benefits of early cancer detection.

title: Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) regulates B-cell reactivity, subset differentiation, and trafficking molecule expression.
text: The transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2) is essential for the proper migration of T cells, but its function in B cells is unclear. Our study reveals that B cells lacking KLF2 exhibit decreased expression of the migration-related proteins CD62L and β7-integrin, yet the expression of the target protein sphingosine-1 phosphate receptor 1 (S1PR1) in T cells is only mildly affected. Surprisingly, deleting KLF2 led to a significant reduction in the B1 B-cell population and a corresponding increase in transitional and marginal zone B cells. Moreover, KLF2-deficient B cells showed enhanced apoptosis and impaired proliferation upon B-cell receptor cross-linking. Gene expression analysis revealed that KLF2-deficient follicular B cells exhibit characteristics similar to those of marginal zone B cells, including reduced expression of key signaling molecules that may contribute to the impaired activation of these cells. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that KLF2 plays a crucial role in determining the normal differentiation and functional responses of mature B cells.

title: Antibiotics and risk of subsequent first-time acute myocardial infarction.
text:
Context: Increasing evidence suggests a potential link between certain bacterial infections and an increased risk of developing acute myocardial infarction. If this association exists, individuals who have used antibiotics active against these bacteria may be at lower risk of developing acute myocardial infarction compared to non-users.
Objective: To investigate whether previous use of antibiotics decreases the risk of developing a first-time acute myocardial infarction.
Design: A population-based case-control analysis using the General Practice Research Database, which includes 350 general practices in the United Kingdom.
Participants: A total of 3315 case patients aged 75 years or younger with a diagnosis of first-time acute myocardial infarction between 1992 and 1997, and 13139 controls without myocardial infarction matched to cases for age, sex, general practice attended, and calendar time.
Main Outcome Measures: Use of antibiotics among individuals who developed a first-time acute myocardial infarction and those who did not.
Results: Cases were significantly less likely to have used tetracycline antibiotics (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.55-0.90) or quinolones (adjusted OR = 0.45, 95% CI = 0.21-0.95). No effect was found for previous use of macrolides (primarily erythromycin), sulfonamides, penicillins, or cephalosporins.
