Conclusions: The findings from this large case-control analysis provide further evidence for an association between bacterial infections with organisms susceptible to tetracycline or quinolone antibiotics and the risk of acute myocardial infarction. These results are preliminary and warrant further research to explore the role of infections in the etiology of acute myocardial infarction.

title: Thrombopoietin/MPL signaling regulates hematopoietic stem cell quiescence and interaction with the osteoblastic niche.
text: The maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) relies on their interactions with their niche in the bone marrow (BM). Our findings reveal that long-term HSCs (LT-HSCs) expressing the thrombopoietin (THPO) receptor, MPL, are a quiescent population in adult BM and are closely associated with THPO-producing osteoblastic cells. THPO/MPL signaling regulates the quiescence of LT-HSCs by upregulating beta1-integrin and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors. Inhibition or stimulation of the THPO/MPL pathway using neutralizing antibodies or THPO, respectively, has a reciprocal effect on the quiescence of LT-HSCs. Treatment with anti-MPL neutralizing antibody, AMM2, reduced the number of quiescent LT-HSCs and allowed for exogenous HSC engraftment without irradiation. In contrast, exogenous THPO transiently increased the quiescent HSC population and subsequently induced HSC proliferation in vivo. These observations suggest that THPO/MPL signaling plays a critical role in regulating LT-HSCs in the osteoblastic niche.

title: Interlaboratory reproducibility and proficiency testing within the human papillomavirus cervical cancer screening program in Catalonia, Spain.
text: In Catalonia, a screening protocol for cervical cancer, including human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing using the Digene Hybrid Capture 2 (HC2) assay, was implemented in 2006. To evaluate the reproducibility of the HC2 assay, a proficiency testing (PT) survey of HPV samples was conducted in 2008. Participating laboratories provided 20 samples annually, with random selection from four HC2 readings intervals: <0.5, 0.5-0.99, 1-9.99, and ≥10. Kappa statistics were used to assess agreement levels between original and PT readings. Bootstrapping was used to calculate the nature and origin of discrepant results. A total of 946 specimens were retested. The kappa values were 0.91 for categorical classification and 0.79 for the four HC2 intervals. Sample retesting yielded systematically lower HC2 values than the original test, regardless of the time elapsed (median 53 days). The probability of clinically discrepant results upon retesting was higher for samples with HC2 values in the 0.5-5 interval (10.80%, 95% CI: 7.86-14.33) compared to samples outside this interval (0.85%, 95% CI: 0.17-1.69). The HC2 assay showed high interlaboratory concordance. Differential confidence thresholds were identified, and guidelines for interlaboratory PT were suggested to ensure analytical quality assessment of HPV DNA detection in cervical cancer prevention.

title: The role of regulatory variation in complex traits and disease
text: We are currently experiencing an unparalleled phase of discovery in identifying genetic locations that influence traits across a wide range of organisms, from simple organisms to humans. However, a comprehensive understanding of how these locations impact traits remains elusive for the majority of them. Recent advances in the genetics of gene expression have emerged as a crucial tool for connecting genetic variations to phenotypes. Here, we provide an overview of the molecular nature of regulatory variants and their influence on the transcriptome and proteome. We highlight conceptual breakthroughs from studies in model organisms and illustrate concrete examples of how individual polymorphisms can lead to changes in gene expression, ultimately resulting in physiological changes and disease risk.

title: Adhesion disengagement uncouples intrinsic and extrinsic forces to drive cytokinesis in epithelial tissues.
text:
Cytokinesis involves the invagination of a cell by a contractile actomyosin ring, which is mediated by E-cadherin-mediated adhesion connections between adjacent cells in epithelial tissues. However, the mechanisms underlying invagination, the formation of new junctions, and the preservation of tissue integrity during epithelial division are not well understood.
Studies in Drosophila embryos have shown that apicobasal cleavage is polarized, with invagination occurring faster from the basal than from the apical side. The contraction of the actomyosin ring is controlled by septin filaments and Anillin, but the polarized constriction of the ring is not well understood.
Instead, the formation of the new junction during cytokinesis is due to the mechanical anchorage of the ring to E-cadherin complexes. The disengagement of E-cadherin complexes in the cleavage furrow is followed by the formation of new E-cadherin complexes at the new interface. The tension exerted by the cytokinetic ring and neighboring cells is essential for E-cadherin disengagement.
Our study uncovers the intrinsic and extrinsic forces necessary for cytokinesis and provides a framework for understanding how tissue cohesion is preserved during epithelial division.

title: The epithelial inward rectifier channel Kir7.1 displays unusual K+ permeation properties.
text: Rat and human cDNA sequences were analyzed to identify proteins that encoded a 360 amino acid polypeptide with a typical tertiary structure of inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Kir). The newly discovered proteins, termed Kir7.1, were found to be <37% identical to other Kir subunits and had unique residues at conserved sites, particularly in the pore region. High levels of Kir7.1 transcripts were detected in rat brain, lung, kidney, and testis, with strong expression in secretory epithelial cells of the choroid plexus. In situ hybridization of rat brain sections revealed that Kir7.1 mRNA was absent from neurons and glia but highly expressed in secretory epithelial cells. In Xenopus oocytes, Kir7.1 generated macroscopic Kir currents with a shallow dependence on external potassium concentration, which is distinct from other Kir channels. The methionine at position 125 in the pore region of Kir7.1 was found to be responsible for the unique K+ permeability characteristics. When this residue was replaced by the conserved arginine in mutant Kir7.1 channels, the pronounced dependence of K+ permeability on [K+]e and increased Ba2+ sensitivity were restored, indicating the importance of this site in regulating K+ permeability in Kir channels by extracellular cations.

title: Oral fingolimod (FTY720) for relapsing multiple sclerosis.
text: Fingolimod (FTY720), a novel oral immunomodulating agent, is currently being investigated for the treatment of relapsing multiple sclerosis. In this proof-of-concept study, we randomly assigned 281 patients to receive either oral fingolimod at doses of 1.25 mg or 5.0 mg, or a placebo, once daily, and followed them for 6 months with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical evaluations. The primary endpoint was the total number of gadolinium-enhanced lesions detected on T(1)-weighted MRI at monthly intervals over the 6-month period. In an extension study, patients who received placebo were randomly assigned to one of the fingolimod doses after completing the core study. A total of 255 patients completed the core study, and the median number of gadolinium-enhanced lesions on MRI was significantly lower with 1.25 mg and 5.0 mg of fingolimod compared to placebo (P<0.001 and P=0.006, respectively). The annualized relapse rate was also significantly lower in the fingolimod groups compared to the placebo group (P=0.009 and P=0.01, respectively). In the extension study, the number of gadolinium-enhanced lesions and relapse rates remained low in the fingolimod groups, and both measures decreased in patients who switched from placebo to fingolimod. Common adverse events included nasopharyngitis, dyspnea, headache, diarrhea, and nausea, and there were also clinically asymptomatic elevations of alanine aminotransferase levels in fingolimod-treated patients. One case of the posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome occurred in the 5.0-mg group. Fingolimod was also associated with a reduction in heart rate and a modest decrease in forced expiratory volume in 1 second. These findings suggest that fingolimod may be effective in reducing the number of lesions detected on MRI and clinical disease activity in patients with multiple sclerosis, and larger, longer-term studies are warranted to confirm these findings. (Clinicaltrials.gov numbers: NCT00333138 [core study] and NCT00235430 [extension].)

title: Nonoverlapping functions of DNA polymerases mu, lambda, and terminal deoxynucleotidyltransferase during immunoglobulin V(D)J recombination in vivo.
text: DNA polymerases mu (pol mu), lambda (pol lambda), and terminal deoxynucleotidyltransferase (TdT) are enzymes within the pol X family that share similarities in both sequence and functional domain organization. Previously, it was discovered that pol mu participates in light chain but not heavy chain gene rearrangement, despite being present during the process. This study reveals that immunoglobulin heavy chain junctions from pol lambda-deficient animals have shorter lengths with normal N-additions, indicating that pol lambda is recruited during heavy chain rearrangement at an earlier stage than TdT. In contrast to previous in vitro studies, analysis of animals with combined inactivation of these enzymes revealed no overlapping or compensatory activities for V(D)J recombination between pol mu, pol lambda, and TdT. This complex usage of polymerases with distinct catalytic specificities may correspond to the specific function that the third hypervariable region assumes for each immunoglobulin chain, with pol lambda maintaining a large heavy chain junctional heterogeneity and pol mu ensuring a restricted light chain junctional variability.

title: Moderate regular exercise increases basal production of nitric oxide in elderly women.
text: Vascular endothelial cells produce nitric oxide (NO), a potent vasodilator and antiatherosclerotic agent, which may help regulate vascular tone and prevent the progression of atherosclerosis. However, NO activity decreases with aging. Previous studies have shown that intense aerobic exercise training in healthy young individuals increases plasma nitrite/nitrate (NOx) concentrations. Given that even mild regular exercise can increase NO production, we hypothesized that a 3-month mild aerobic exercise training program would increase NOx concentrations in previously sedentary older adults. We measured plasma NOx and cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) concentrations in elderly women before and after a 3-month exercise training regimen (cycling on a leg ergometer at 80% ventilatory threshold for 30 min, 5 days/week). Our results showed that the individual ventilatory threshold increased significantly after exercise training, and blood pressure at rest decreased. The plasma concentration of NOx and cGMP both increased after exercise training, suggesting that even a mild regular aerobic-endurance exercise can increase NO production in previously sedentary older adults, which may have beneficial effects on the cardiovascular system, such as antihypertensive and antiatherosclerotic effects through endogenous NO.

title: Competition between target sites of regulators shapes post-transcriptional gene regulation
text: Post-transcriptional gene regulation (PTGR) of mRNA turnover, localization, and translation is mediated by microRNAs (miRNAs) and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). These regulators exert their effects by binding to specific sequences within their target mRNAs. Recent evidence suggests that competition for binding is a fundamental principle of PTGR. miRNAs can be neutralized and sequestered by their target mRNAs through a process termed "sponging," and competition between binding sites on different RNAs may lead to regulatory crosstalk between transcripts. Here, we use quantitative modeling to explore competition effects under physiological conditions and review the role of endogenous sponges in PTGR, taking into account the key features that have emerged.

title: Primary prevention of ischemic stroke: A statement for healthcare professionals from the Stroke Council of the American Heart Association.
text:
Stroke is the third leading cause of death in the United States, with an estimated 700,000 incident strokes occurring annually and 4.4 million stroke survivors. The economic burden of stroke was estimated to be $51 billion in 1999, with the majority of these costs being due to indirect expenses. Despite advances in treatment, such as tissue plasminogen activator for acute ischemic stroke, the best approach to reducing the burden of stroke remains prevention. High-risk or stroke-prone individuals can be identified and targeted for specific interventions.
The Stroke Council of the American Heart Association formed an ad hoc writing group to review the evidence on various established and potential stroke risk factors. The writing group used a literature review, reference to previously published guidelines, and expert opinion to summarize existing evidence and formulate recommendations. The risk factors were classified based on their potential for modification and the strength of evidence. The tables provide the estimated prevalence, population attributable risk, relative risk, and risk reduction with treatment for each factor when known. Population attributable risk reflects the proportion of ischemic strokes in the population that can be attributed to a particular risk factor.
For example, the table shows that high blood pressure is a modifiable risk factor for stroke, with a well-documented relative risk of 1.5 and a population attributable risk of 30%. This means that if high blood pressure is controlled, the number of strokes in the population can be reduced by 30%.
Overall, the writing group found that there is strong evidence for the association between many established and potential stroke risk factors, including high blood pressure, smoking, obesity, physical inactivity, and diabetes. The group also found that the prevalence of many of these risk factors has remained unchanged or has even increased in recent years, despite the availability of effective interventions.
In conclusion, stroke is a significant public health burden in the United States, and prevention is the most effective way to reduce its impact. High-risk individuals can be identified and targeted for specific interventions, and the writing group's recommendations provide a clear and concise overview of the evidence on various stroke risk factors.

title: Chimeric live, attenuated vaccine against Japanese encephalitis (ChimeriVax-JE): phase 2 clinical trials for safety and immunogenicity, effect of vaccine dose and schedule, and memory response to challenge with inactivated Japanese encephalitis antigen.
text: ChimeriVax-JE is a live, attenuated vaccine against Japanese encephalitis, using the yellow fever (YF) 17D vaccine as a vector. In a double-blind phase 2 trial, 99 adults received the vaccine, placebo, or YF 17D vaccine (YF-VAX). ChimeriVax-JE was well tolerated, with no significant differences in adverse events between the treatment groups. The vaccine also induced short-lived viremias in both ChimeriVax-JE and YF-VAX recipients, but 82 (94%) of 87 subjects who received graded doses of ChimeriVax-JE developed neutralizing antibodies. A second dose administered 30 days later had no booster effect. Previous inoculation with YF did not interfere with ChimeriVax-JE, but there was a trend (not statistically significant) suggesting that ChimeriVax-JE may have interfered with YF-VAX administered 30 days later. Another study investigated immunological memory in individuals who had received ChimeriVax-JE 9 months prior and in ChimeriVax-JE-naive subjects challenged with inactivated mouse-brain vaccine (JE-VAX). Anamnestic responses were observed in preimmune individuals. Overall, ChimeriVax-JE appears to be a safe and effective vaccine that provides protective levels of neutralizing antibody after a single dose.

title: Global prevalence of anxiety disorders: a systematic review and meta-regression.
text:
Background: The literature on the global prevalence of anxiety disorders has been characterized by significant variability, with estimates ranging widely across studies. To address this issue, a systematic review and meta-regression analysis were conducted to estimate the prevalence of anxiety disorders and identify factors influencing these estimates. The findings of this study will inform the forthcoming Global Burden of Disease study.
Method: A systematic search of electronic databases, reference lists, review articles, and monographs identified prevalence studies of anxiety disorders published between 1980 and 2009. Additionally, experts were contacted to identify any missing studies. Substantive and methodological factors associated with inter-study variability were identified through meta-regression analyses, and the global prevalence of anxiety disorders was calculated adjusting for study methodology.
Results: The study identified 87 prevalence studies across 44 countries, with estimates of current prevalence ranging from 0.9% to 28.3% and past-year prevalence ranging from 2.4% to 29.8%. Substantive factors, including gender, age, culture, conflict, and economic status, and urbanicity, accounted for the greatest proportion of variability. Methodological factors, such as prevalence period, number of disorders, and diagnostic instrument, explained an additional 13% of variance between studies. The global current prevalence of anxiety disorders adjusted for methodological differences was estimated to be 7.3% (4.8-10.9%), with estimates ranging from 5.3% (3.5-8.1%) in African cultures to 10.4% (7.0-15.5%) in Euro/Anglo cultures.
Conclusions: Anxiety disorders are common, and the factors identified in this study explain a significant portion of the variability in prevalence estimates. Specifically, cultural differences in responses to survey instruments for anxiety disorders should be taken into account. The findings of this study will inform the development of future research on anxiety disorders and their prevalence.

title: Expression of optineurin, a glaucoma-linked gene, is influenced by elevated intraocular pressure.
text: Recently, a protein called Optineurin (OPTN) has been linked to 16.7% of families with primary open-angle glaucoma. While the function of OPTN in the eye is still unknown, it is present in the trabecular meshwork, which plays a crucial role in maintaining intraocular pressure (IOP). To gain a better understanding of OPTN's role in the development of glaucoma, we investigated its expression in response to factors known to be associated with the disease, including elevated IOP, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFalpha), and dexamethasone (DEX). We conducted these studies in human organ cultures under conditions mimicking physiological pressure. Our findings show that OPTN is significantly upregulated after 2, 4, and 7 days of sustained elevated IOP. Additionally, OPTN expression is induced 2.3-fold by TNFalpha and 2.6-fold by prolonged DEX treatment. These results suggest that OPTN is part of the transcriptome responding to glaucomatous insults and support the protective role of this protein in the trabecular meshwork.

title: Prevention of malaria in long-term travelers.
text:
Long-term travelers (defined as those traveling for 6 months or longer) face unique challenges when it comes to malaria prevention. Current guidelines primarily focus on preventing Plasmodium falciparum infections in short-term travelers, leaving long-term travelers at a higher risk of malaria. To address this issue, this study aims to:
1. Examine the risk of malaria in long-term travelers
2. Evaluate recent developments in personal protective measures for long-term travelers
3. Assess the safety and tolerability of malaria chemoprophylaxis during long-term use
4. Consider various prevention strategies, including continuous chemoprophylaxis, stand-by emergency self-treatment, seasonal prophylaxis, and strategies to prevent primary infection and relapses from P vivax malaria.

The study conducted a comprehensive search of scientific publications, including MEDLINE via OVID and PubMed, to identify relevant studies and articles with a cutoff date of July 2006. Additional references were obtained from searching the bibliographies of the selected articles, dissertations, and conference proceedings on travel medicine. No language restrictions were applied.

The evidence synthesis revealed that long-term travelers underutilize personal protective measures and have poor adherence to continuous chemoprophylaxis regimens. Various strategies are used during long-term stays, including discontinuation of chemoprophylaxis after the initial period, sequential regimens with different medications, stand-by emergency self-treatment, and seasonal chemoprophylaxis targeting high-incidence periods or locations. Each strategy has advantages and drawbacks. The concern of counterfeit drugs sold in endemic countries poses a serious issue for long-term travelers who purchase medications overseas. Vivax malaria causes significant illness in travelers, but relapses of vivax malaria are not prevented with the current first-line chemoprophylaxis regimens. Consensus guidelines are needed for the prevention of malaria in long-term travelers.


In conclusion, prevention of malaria in long-term travelers is a complex issue that requires expert advice from travel medicine specialists. Recommendations for prevention of malaria in long-term travelers must be individualized.

title: Activation of AMPKα2 in adipocytes is essential for nicotine-induced insulin resistance in vivo
text: Cigarette smoking appears to promote weight loss in humans, yet it also leads to insulin resistance (IR) and hyperinsulinemia. However, the underlying mechanisms are unclear. Our study reveals that nicotine, a primary component of cigarette smoke, selectively activates AMP-activated protein kinase alpha 2 (AMPKα2) in adipocytes, leading to the degradation of MAP kinase phosphatase-1 (MKP1) through a nicotine-dependent pathway. This results in the aberrant activation of p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase and c-Jun N-terminal kinase, leading to increased phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1) at serine 307. The subsequent degradation of IRS1 inhibits protein kinase B, leading to the loss of insulin-mediated inhibition of lipolysis. As a result, nicotine increases lipolysis, which leads to weight loss, but this increase also raises the levels of circulating free fatty acids, contributing to IR in insulin-sensitive tissues. These findings establish AMPKα2 as a crucial mediator of nicotine-induced whole-body IR, despite reductions in adiposity.

title: Availability of evidence of benefits on overall survival and quality of life of cancer drugs approved by European Medicines Agency: retrospective cohort study of drug approvals 2009-13
text:
Objective: To assess the availability of data on the overall survival and quality of life benefits of cancer drugs approved in Europe.
Design: Retrospective cohort study.
Setting: Publicly accessible regulatory and scientific reports on cancer approvals by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) from 2009 to 2013.
Main outcome measures: Pivotal and postmarketing trials of cancer drugs based on their design features (randomization, crossover, blinding), comparators, and endpoints. The availability and magnitude of benefit on overall survival or quality of life were determined at the time of approval and after market entry. The validated European Society for Medical Oncology Magnitude of Clinical Benefit Scale (ESMO-MCBS) was used to assess the clinical value of the reported gains in published studies of cancer drugs.
Results: From 2009 to 2013, the EMA approved the use of 48 cancer drugs for 68 indications. Of these, eight indications (12%) were approved based on a single-arm study. At the time of market approval, there was significant prolongation of survival in 24 of the 68 (35%). The magnitude of the benefit on overall survival ranged from 1.0 to 5.8 months (median 2.7 months). At the time of market approval, there was an improvement in quality of life in seven of 68 indications (10%). Out of 44 indications for which there was no evidence of a survival gain at the time of market authorization, in the subsequent postmarketing period, there was evidence for extension of life in three (7%) and reported benefit on quality of life in five (11%). Of the 68 cancer indications with EMA approval, and with a median of 5.4 years' follow-up (minimum 3.3 years, maximum 8.1 years), only 35 (51%) had shown a significant improvement in survival or quality of life, while 33 (49%) remained uncertain. Of 23 indications associated with a survival benefit that could be scored with the ESMO-MCBS tool, the benefit was judged to be clinically meaningful in less than half (11/23, 48%).
Conclusions: This systematic evaluation of oncology approvals by the EMA in 2009-13 shows that most drugs entered the market without evidence of benefit on survival or quality of life. At a minimum of 3.3 years after market entry, there was still no conclusive evidence that these drugs either extended or improved life for most cancer indications. When there were survival gains over existing treatment options or placebo, they were often marginal.

title: A cluster randomized, controlled trial of breast and cervix cancer screening in Mumbai, India: methodology and interim results after three rounds of screening.
text:
Cervical and breast cancers are the most common malignancies affecting women globally, with a significant impact on developing countries. In May 1998, with funding from the National Cancer Institute (NCI, USA), the Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai, India, launched a cluster-randomized, controlled screening trial to address this issue. The study employed trained primary health workers to provide health education, visual inspection of the cervix using 4% acetic acid-VIA, and clinical breast examination in the screening arm, while the control arm received only health education. The trial involves four rounds of screening at 2-year intervals, followed by 8 years of monitoring for incidence and mortality from cervical and breast cancers.
The methodology and interim results after three rounds of screening are presented here. The screening arm comprised 75360 participants, while the control arm had 76178 participants. Key findings include:
* High screening participation rates in the screening arm
* Low attrition rates in both arms
* Good compliance to diagnostic confirmation in the screening arm
* Significant downstaging in the screening arm
* Excellent treatment completion rate in the screening arm
* Improving case fatality ratios in the screening arm

The ever-screened and never-screened participants in the screening arm exhibited significant differences in variables such as religion, language, age, education, occupation, income, and health-seeking behavior for gynecological and breast-related complaints. In contrast, the control arm showed excellent participation rates for health education, low attrition rates, and a good number of symptomatic referrals for both cervical and breast cancers.

title: Evidence for energy-dependent accumulation of paraquat into rat lung
text: The herbicide paraquat (N,N'-dimethyl 4,4'-bipyridinium) can cause widespread edema and fibrosis in the human lung following accidental ingestion, with death occurring in some cases several weeks later (1-3). Initially, there are no apparent pulmonary changes in the first few days after ingestion. In animal studies, the lung has been consistently identified as the primary target organ (4-6). Following administration of paraquat to animals, the lung exhibits a high initial concentration of the herbicide, which persists over time (7-9). The mechanism by which the lung retains paraquat is currently unknown.

title: Role of gut commensal microflora in the development of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
text: Mucosal tolerance has been considered a promising pathway for treating autoimmune diseases, including human multiple sclerosis and experimental conditions such as experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). While there is limited information on the ability of commensal gut bacteria to induce and maintain peripheral immune tolerance, our study found that reducing the gut microbiota through antibiotic treatment impaired the development of EAE in inbred SJL and C57BL/6 mice. In contrast, mice that received intraperitoneal antibiotics showed no significant decline in gut microflora and developed EAE similar to untreated mice, suggesting that the reduction in disease activity was due to changes in the gut bacterial population. We found that protection was associated with lower levels of proinflammatory cytokines and increased levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and IL-13. Additionally, adoptive transfer of low numbers of IL-10-producing CD25(+)CD4(+) T cells (>75% FoxP3(+)) purified from cervical lymph nodes of commensal bacteria reduced mice, and in vivo neutralization of CD25(+) cells suggested the role of regulatory T cells in maintaining peripheral immune homeostasis. Our data suggest that modifying gut commensal bacteria through antibiotic treatment can modulate peripheral immune tolerance, which may offer a new therapeutic approach in the treatment of multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune diseases.

title: Epidemiology of surgically managed pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence.
text:
Objective: To determine the incidence of surgically managed pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence in a population-based cohort and to describe their clinical characteristics.
Methods: This retrospective cohort study included all patients undergoing surgical treatment for prolapse and incontinence at Kaiser Permanente Northwest between 1995 and 2015. A standardized data-collection form was used to review all inpatient and outpatient charts of the 395 women identified. Variables examined included age, ethnicity, height, weight, vaginal parity, smoking history, medical history, and surgical history, including the preoperative evaluation, procedure performed, and details of all prior procedures. Analysis included calculation of age-specific and cumulative incidences and determination of the number of primary operations compared with repeat operations performed for prolapse or incontinence.
Results: The age-specific incidence of surgical intervention increased with advancing age. By age 80, the lifetime risk of undergoing a single operation for prolapse or incontinence was 11.1%. The majority of patients were older, postmenopausal, parous, and overweight, with nearly half being current or former smokers and one-fifth having chronic lung disease. Reoperation was common (29.2% of cases), with the time intervals between repeat procedures decreasing with each successive repair.
Conclusion: Pelvic floor dysfunction is a significant health issue for older women, as evidenced by the 11.1% lifetime risk of undergoing a single operation for pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence, as well as the large proportion of reoperations. Our findings support further epidemiologic research to determine the etiology, natural history, and long-term treatment outcomes of these conditions.

title: Antihypertensive classes, cognitive decline and incidence of dementia: a network meta-analysis.
text:
OBJECTIVES:
Preventing cognitive decline and dementia through blood pressure lowering treatments has yielded inconsistent results. To investigate the effectiveness of different classes of antihypertensive drugs on cognitive function and dementia incidence, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials (18,515 individuals) and 11 studies (831,674 individuals). Network meta-analysis was used to compare the effects of antihypertensive classes.
METHODS:
We analyzed the effects of antihypertensive treatment on overall cognition and specific cognitive functions, as well as the risk of all-cause dementia. Randomized trials and observational studies were combined (n = 15) and compared to randomized trials alone (n = 4). Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) were found to have larger benefits on overall cognition compared to placebo (adjusted effect size 0.60 ± 0.18, P = 0.02), with ARBs being more effective than β-blockers (0.67 ± 0.18, P = 0.01), diuretics (0.54 ± 0.19, P = 0.04), and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (0.47 ± 0.17, P = 0.04) in rank. The mean change in blood pressure did not significantly differ between the different antihypertensive drug classes.
RESULTS:
Our findings support the notion that antihypertensive treatment has beneficial effects on cognitive decline and dementia prevention, with ARBs possibly being the most effective.
CONCLUSION:
Our study suggests that antihypertensive treatment has a positive impact on cognitive function and dementia incidence, with ARBs emerging as the most effective class of drugs. These findings have important implications for the prevention of cognitive decline and dementia in hypertensive patients.

title: Abnormal hemoglobins in a quarter million people.
text: Hemolysates from over a quarter million people in Alabama were separated using cellulose acetate electrophoresis at pH 8.4, and those showing abnormalities were also separated in citrate agar at pH 6.0. The globin chains of non-Hb S and non-Hb C mutants were separated in urea-mercaptoethanol buffers at both pH 8.9 and pH 6.0, and 60 of these samples were structurally analyzed. Of approximately 6,000 samples from whites, only three contained abnormal hemoglobins, including Hb D Los Angeles, Hb J Baltimore, and one unidentified. In contrast, about 29,000 samples from blacks contained electrophoretically detectable abnormalities, most of which were associated with Hb S or C, present at frequencies of about 9% and 3%, respectively. Approximately 1,000 samples resolved into patterns with potential clinical significance. In addition, 20 other mutant hemoglobins were detected in various genetic combinations in 164 kindreds, including four previously unknown hemoglobins, Hb Alabama, Montgomery, Titusville, and Mobile. The methods used were rapid, economical, and well-suited for large-scale surveys, providing highly specific characterizations of many mutant hemoglobins. No discrepancies were found between the presumptive identifications based on these characterizations and the definitive identifications obtained from structural analyses.

title: Cellular adaptation to mechanical stress: role of integrins, Rho, cytoskeletal tension and mechanosensitive ion channels.
text: To gain insights into how cells perceive and adapt to mechanical stress, we applied tension forces to magnetic microbeads attached to cell-surface integrin receptors and measured changes in bead displacement with high resolution using optical microscopy. Our findings revealed four distinct mechanical responses in cells: (1) an immediate viscoelastic response, (2) early adaptive behavior characterized by attenuation of forces in response to oscillatory stress, (3) later adaptive cell stiffening with sustained (>15 seconds) static stress, and (4) a large-scale repositioning response with prolonged (>1 minute) stress. Notably, these adaptation responses were biochemically distinct, with the immediate and early responses influenced by dissipating cytoskeletal prestress (isometric tension), while the later adaptive response was not. The repositioning response was prevented by inhibiting tension through interference with Rho signaling, similar to the immediate and early responses, but it was also prevented by blocking mechanosensitive ion channels or inhibiting Src tyrosine kinases. Furthermore, cooling cells to 4°C slowed down biochemical remodeling and suppressed all adaptive responses. These findings demonstrate that cells employ multiple mechanisms to detect and respond to changes in mechanical stress applied to integrins.

title: Cutting edge: Candida albicans hyphae formation triggers activation of the Nlrp3 inflammasome.
text: The pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β plays a crucial role in antifungal immunity, but the mechanisms by which fungal pathogens trigger its secretion are unclear. In this study, we investigate the role of the Nlrp3 inflammasome in the activation of IL-1β production in response to Candida albicans infection. Our findings show that the ability of C. albicans to switch from a unicellular yeast form to a filamentous form is essential for the activation of the Nlrp3 inflammasome, as C. albicans mutants incapable of forming hyphae were defective in their ability to induce IL-1β secretion from macrophages. Furthermore, mice lacking the Nlrp3 gene were more susceptible to C. albicans infection, highlighting the importance of Nlrp3 in innate immune responses to this pathogen.

title: Type 2 diabetes and subsequent incidence of breast cancer in the Nurses' Health Study.
text: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to investigate the potential association between hyperinsulinemia and the development of mammary carcinogenesis. Insulin resistance has been linked to an increased risk of breast cancer, and type 2 diabetes is a common condition characterized by insulin resistance. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, we evaluated the association between type 2 diabetes and the incidence of invasive breast cancer in a population of 116,488 female nurses aged 30-55 years. Participants were followed up for 2.3 million person-years, during which time 6,220 women developed type 2 diabetes and 5,189 incident cases of invasive breast cancer were identified. RESULTS: The results of the study showed that women with type 2 diabetes had a modestly elevated incidence of breast cancer compared to women without diabetes (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.17; 95% CI 1.01-1.35). This association was observed primarily among postmenopausal women (1.16; 0.98-1.62) and was stronger among women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer (1.22; 1.01-1.47). CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that women with type 2 diabetes may have a slightly increased risk of developing breast cancer. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and to explore the underlying mechanisms.

title: Virus-encoded microRNAs.
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) have garnered significant interest due to their regulatory role in various cellular processes, including immune function, apoptosis, and tumorigenesis. It has been discovered that several virus families encode miRNAs, and their roles in the viral infectious cycle are continuously being elucidated. Despite the identification of over 225 viral miRNAs, a comprehensive understanding of their functions remains limited. In this article, we focus on a few well-characterized viral miRNAs and use them to extrapolate general themes of viral miRNA activity. These themes include the regulation of viral gene expression through autoregulation, evasion of host defenses, and a likely important role in maintaining latent and persistent infections. We hypothesize that while the molecular mechanisms and machinery of viral miRNAs may be similar to those of host miRNAs, they have evolved to target unique viral-encoded transcripts or networks of host genes. A significant proportion of viral miRNAs may regulate only a limited number of principal host genes. To advance the field, we propose the need for additional functional studies that utilize surgical viral miRNA mutants combined with relevant models of infection.

title: Wolfram syndrome 1 and adenylyl cyclase 8 interact at the plasma membrane to regulate insulin production and secretion
text: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress can lead to dysfunction and loss of pancreatic β-cells, contributing to the progression of type 2 diabetes. Wolfram syndrome 1 (WFS1) has been shown to play a crucial role in the ER stress signaling pathway, but its function in β-cell function remains unclear. Our study reveals that WFS1 is essential for glucose- and glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1)-stimulated cyclic AMP production and regulation of insulin biosynthesis and secretion. Upon glucose stimulation, WFS1 translocates from the ER to the plasma membrane, where it forms a complex with adenylyl cyclase 8 (AC8), an essential enzyme in β-cells that integrates glucose and GLP-1 signaling. However, ER stress and mutant WFS1 inhibit complex formation and AC8 activity, reducing cAMP synthesis and insulin secretion. These findings demonstrate that a protein involved in ER stress has a distinct function outside the ER, regulating both insulin biosynthesis and secretion. The reduction of WFS1 protein on the plasma membrane during ER stress is a contributing factor to β-cell dysfunction and the progression of type 2 diabetes.

title: Two Rice GRAS Family Genes Responsive to N-Acetylchitooligosaccharide Elicitor are Induced by Phytoactive Gibberellins: Evidence for Cross-Talk Between Elicitor and Gibberellin Signaling in Rice Cells
text: In this study, we investigate the response of two GRAS family genes, CIGR1 and CIGR2, in rice to the potent elicitor N-acetylchitooligosaccharide (GN). Our findings show that these genes are rapidly induced by exogenous gibberellins, with the induction pattern depending on the dose and biological activity of the gibberellins. This suggests that the induction of the genes by gibberellin is mediated by a specific receptor that can recognize and transduce the signal. Further analysis revealed that the induction of CIGR1 and CIGR2 by gibberellin is dependent on protein phosphorylation/dephosphorylation events. Interestingly, we found that these genes are not induced in rice calli derived from a constitutive gibberellin-responsive mutant or a mutant deficient in the α-subunit of the heterotrimeric G-protein. These results suggest that the signal transduction cascade from gibberellin is independent of that from the elicitor GN, and that CIGR1 and CIGR2 have dual, distinct roles in defense and development.

title: Ghrelin's second life: from appetite stimulator to glucose regulator.
text: Ghrelin, a 28-amino acid peptide hormone produced by the stomach, was the first orexigenic hormone to be discovered from the periphery. The octanoyl modification at Ser3, mediated by ghrelin O-acyltransferase (GOAT), is crucial for ghrelin's biological activity. Ghrelin stimulates food intake by binding to its receptor (GRLN-R) on neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus. Ghrelin is expressed throughout the body, which suggests its involvement in various physiological functions, including growth hormone release, gastric emptying, and body weight regulation. Interestingly, ghrelin and GRLN-R are also found in the pancreas, implying a local physiological role. Recent studies have highlighted an important role for ghrelin and its receptor in regulating blood glucose homeostasis, which is the main focus of this review. Several mechanisms of this regulation have been proposed, and one possibility is the inhibition of insulin secretion. Although there is some controversy, most studies suggest that ghrelin has an inhibitory effect on insulin secretion, leading to increased circulating glucose levels. This suggests that ghrelin may be a diabetogenic factor. Obesity-related type 2 diabetes has become a major health concern, with almost epidemic proportions worldwide. Therefore, targeting the ghrelin-GOAT signaling pathway with potential antagonists may be a promising new approach for treating this disease.

title: Histone acetylation and deacetylation in yeast
text: Histone acetylation and deacetylation in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae occur through the targeted action of acetyltransferase and deacetylase enzymes on gene promoters, as well as through a global and untargeted manner that affects most nucleosomes. Recent research has uncovered new roles for histone acetylation, including its involvement in transcription, DNA replication, repair, and heterochromatin formation. Additionally, specific acetylatable lysines can serve as binding sites for regulatory factors. Furthermore, histone deacetylation is not only repressive but can also be required for gene activation.

title: Neuroinflammation in spinal cord injury: therapeutic targets for neuroprotection and regeneration.
text: Traumatic spinal cord injury triggers a multifaceted inflammatory response at the injury site, which can both enhance repair and exacerbate pathology. The immune cascade that unfolds after injury changes over time and distance from the lesion, leading to the production of various cytokines, proteases, and growth factors. These molecules create dynamic environments that determine the fate of affected neurons and glia, either promoting repair or contributing to pathology. The microenvironmental cues generated by the cells in the injured area hold the key to harnessing the repair process. By manipulating the assembly and phenotype of cells in the neuroinflammatory response, it may be possible to promote outcomes such as pain relief, regeneration, and functional recovery. This review examines the potential of the neuroinflammatory response to achieve these goals.

title: Evaluation of systemic amyloidosis by scintigraphy with 123I-labeled serum amyloid P component.
text:
Background: Systemic amyloidosis is a complex disease characterized by the deposition of abnormal protein aggregates in various organs and tissues. Monitoring the progression and distribution of disease has been challenging due to the limitations of biopsy. Serum amyloid P component (SAP) is a normal plasma protein that exhibits specific binding affinity for amyloid fibrils, making it a potential marker for amyloid deposits.
Methods: In this study, we investigated the use of labeled SAP for imaging amyloid deposits in patients with systemic amyloidosis. Purified human SAP was labeled with iodine-123 and administered intravenously to 50 patients with biopsy-proven systemic amyloidosis (25 with the AL type and 25 with the AA type) and to 26 control patients with disease and 10 healthy subjects. Whole-body images and regional views were obtained after 24 hours and read in a blinded fashion.
Results: The 123I-SAP was rapidly and specifically localized in amyloid deposits in patients with systemic amyloidosis. Scintigraphic images obtained were characteristic and appeared to accurately identify the extent of amyloid deposition in all 50 patients. No uptake of the 123I-SAP was observed in control patients or healthy subjects. In patients with AA amyloidosis, the spleen was consistently affected, while the scans showed uptake in the heart, skin, carpal region, and bone marrow in patients with the AL type. Positive images were seen in six patients in whom biopsies had been negative or unsuccessful, and amyloid was subsequently found on biopsy or at autopsy. Amyloid deposition was observed to progress in nine of 11 patients studied serially.
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that scintigraphy after the injection of 123I-SAP can be a valuable tool for diagnosing, locating, and monitoring the extent of systemic amyloidosis.

title: The Neurovascular Unit Coming of Age: A Journey through Neurovascular Coupling in Health and Disease
text: The concept of the neurovascular unit (NVU), formalized at the 2001 National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke Stroke Progress Review Group meeting, highlights the intricate relationship between the brain and its blood vessels. Since then, the NVU has garnered significant attention from the neuroscience community, leading to substantial advancements in the field. This review will provide an update on the current state of knowledge of the NVU, with a focus on one of its most critical functions: the interaction between neural activity and blood flow. The available evidence suggests a shift in the mechanisms of neurovascular coupling, moving away from a unidimensional process involving neuronal-astrocytic signaling to local blood vessels towards a multidimensional process involving mediators released from multiple cells engaging distinct signaling pathways and effector systems across the entire cerebrovascular network in a highly coordinated manner. The recent recognition of NVU dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases, although still poorly understood, supports the emerging idea that maintaining neurovascular health is essential for brain health.

title: Effects of MAL61 and MAL62 overexpression on maltose fermentation of baker's yeast in lean dough.
text:
The primary fermentable sugar in lean dough is maltose. To enhance the leavening capabilities of baker's yeast in lean dough, maltose metabolism should be improved. Maltase (alpha-glucosidase, encoded by MAL62) and maltose permease (encoded by MAL61) are the key enzymes involved in maltose metabolism. However, the major rate-limiting factor in maltose metabolism and leavening ability of baker's yeast in lean dough remains unclear.
To investigate the decisive factor for maltose metabolism of industrial baker's yeast in lean dough, we constructed MAL61 and/or MAL62 overexpression strains. Our findings revealed that elevated maltose permease activity through MAL61 overexpression resulted in less improvement in maltose fermentation compared to elevated maltase activity through MAL62 overexpression. Specifically, significant increases in maltase activity through MAL62 overexpression led to a 44% increase in the leavening ability of industrial baker's yeast in lean dough and a 39% increase in maltose metabolism in a medium containing glucose and maltose.
These results demonstrate that maltase is the rate-limiting factor in maltose fermentation of industrial baker's yeast in lean dough. This study provides a foundation for the breeding of industrial baker's yeast for quick dough leavening.

title: Human papillomavirus genotype 31 does not express detectable microRNA levels during latent or productive virus replication.
text: It has recently come to light that several pathogenic DNA viruses produce virally encoded microRNAs within infected cells. Specifically, a range of human and animal herpesviruses, as well as members of the polyoma- and adenovirus families, have been found to harbor microRNAs. Despite the lack of understanding surrounding their functions, it is likely that these viral microRNAs play a crucial role in viral replication in vivo. In this study, we investigated the microRNAs expressed in human cells during the latent and productive phases of the human papillomavirus genotype 31 (HPV31) replication cycle. Surprisingly, we were unable to identify a single HPV31-specific microRNA among the over 500 cellular microRNAs cloned and identified. Based on these findings, we conclude that HPV31, and possibly all human papillomaviruses, do not express viral microRNAs.

title: Integrated genomic profiling of endometrial carcinoma associates aggressive tumors with indicators of PI3 kinase activation.
text: Although approximately 75% of endometrial cancers are diagnosed at an early stage, a significant proportion (15-20%) of these tumors recur. To identify features that predict recurrent disease, we conducted an integrated analysis of genome-wide expression and copy-number data from primary endometrial carcinomas, along with extensive clinical and histopathological data. Unsupervised analysis of the expression data revealed two distinct clusters with different phenotypes, which were associated with significant differences in disease-free survival. Using a global genomic survey of amplifications, deletions, and loss of heterozygosity, we identified 11 amplified regions and 13 deleted regions. Amplification of the oncogene PIK3CA on 3q26.3 was associated with poor prognosis and segregated with a transcriptional cluster of aggressive tumors. Moreover, samples with PIK3CA amplification showed signatures of in vitro PI3 kinase (PI3K) activation, which were also present in aggressive tumors without PIK3CA amplification. Tumors with loss of PTEN expression or PIK3CA overexpression without PIK3CA amplification also showed high expression of the PI3K pathway member STMN1 and an aggressive phenotype in test and validation datasets. However, mutations of PTEN or PIK3CA were not associated with the same expression profile or aggressive phenotype. STMN1 expression had independent prognostic value, highlighting the importance of systematic characterization of the cancer genome in clinically annotated specimens. Our findings suggest that the PI3K pathway may play a particularly important role in patients with aggressive endometrial cancer.

title: Alteration of the Antitumor Immune Response by Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts
text: Within the tumor microenvironment, a specific subset of cells known as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) play a pivotal role in the intricate process of tumor-stroma interaction. CAFs, one of the most prominent stromal cell populations in most types of human carcinomas, have been implicated in various aspects of tumor progression, including tumor growth, angiogenesis, cancer stemness, extracellular matrix remodeling, tissue invasion, metastasis, and even chemoresistance. Over the past decade, these activated tumor-associated fibroblasts have also been found to modulate the anti-tumor immune response on multiple levels. This review aims to provide an overview of our current understanding of how CAFs accomplish this task and their potential therapeutic implications.

title: Confusion and memory loss from capsular genu infarction: a thalamocortical disconnection syndrome?
text: We investigated six patients who experienced a sudden change in behavior after an infarction in the inferior genu of the internal capsule. The acute symptoms included fluctuating levels of alertness, inattention, memory loss, apathy, abulia, and psychomotor retardation, which suggested dysfunction in the frontal lobe. Contralateral hemiparesis and dysarthria were generally mild, except when the infarct extended into the posterior limb. Neuropsychological testing in five patients with left-sided infarcts revealed severe verbal memory loss, and additional cognitive deficits consistent with dementia occurred in four patients. A right-sided infarct caused transient impairment in visuospatial memory. Functional brain imaging in three patients showed a focal reduction in hemispheric perfusion that was most prominent in the ipsilateral inferior and medial frontal cortex. We inferred that the capsular genu infarct interrupted the inferior and anterior thalamic peduncles, leading to functional deactivation of the ipsilateral frontal cortex. These observations suggest that one mechanism for cognitive deterioration from a lacunar infarct is the disconnection of white-matter tracts, which in some instances can lead to "strategic-infarct dementia."

title: Neoadjuvant androgen ablation before radical prostatectomy in cT2bNxMo prostate cancer: 5-year results.
text:
PURPOSE: In the initial report of the Lupron Depot Neoadjuvant Prostate Cancer Study Group, patients who received 3 months of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) showed a significant decrease in positive surgical margins. We present the longest follow-up data of any neoadjuvant trial to date, monitoring these patients for 5 years.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This multi-institutional, prospective, randomized trial was conducted between February 1992 and April 1994, involving patients with stage cT2b prostate cancer. A total of 138 patients received 3 months of leuprolide plus flutamide before radical prostatectomy, while 144 patients underwent radical prostatectomy only. Patients were followed up every 6 months with serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing for 5 years. Biochemical recurrence was defined as PSA levels greater than 0.4 ng/ml.
RESULTS: At 5 years, there was no significant difference in the biochemical recurrence rate between the neoadjuvant androgen ablation plus prostatectomy group (64.8%) and the prostatectomy only group (67.6%) (p = 0.663).
CONCLUSIONS: Although 3 months of ADT before radical prostatectomy appeared to reduce positive surgical margins, our 5-year follow-up data do not suggest any improvement in the recurrence rate. Until further studies demonstrate improved outcomes with longer periods of ADT, induction ADT before radical prostatectomy is not justified.

title: Full-length transcriptome assembly from RNA-Seq data without a reference genome.
text: Massively parallel sequencing of cDNA has enabled the deep and efficient exploration of transcriptomes. Current methods for reconstructing transcripts from such data typically rely on aligning reads to a reference genome, which can be a limiting factor when working with samples that lack a complete or accurate reference genome. To address this challenge, we present the Trinity method for de novo assembly of full-length transcripts. We evaluate Trinity on transcriptome data from fission yeast, mouse, and whitefly, whose reference genomes are not yet available. By constructing and analyzing sets of de Bruijn graphs, Trinity efficiently recovers a large fraction of transcripts, including alternatively spliced isoforms and transcripts from recently duplicated genes. In comparison to other de novo transcriptome assemblers, Trinity recovers more full-length transcripts across a broad range of expression levels, with a sensitivity similar to methods that rely on genome alignments. Our approach provides a comprehensive solution for transcriptome reconstruction in any sample, particularly in the absence of a reference genome.

title: Growth restricted in vitro culture conditions alter the imprinted gene expression patterns of mouse embryonic stem cells.
text: Embryonic stem (ES) cell-derived clones and chimeras are frequently associated with growth abnormalities during fetal development, leading to the production of under/overweight offspring with elevated neonatal mortality and morbidity. The role of imprinted genes in controlling fetal growth is a significant factor in this phenomenon, with improper epigenetic reprogramming of cells used in the procedures often cited as the primary cause. To investigate this further, we analyzed the expression patterns of two growth regulatory imprinted genes, insulin-like growth factor II (Igf2) and H19, in mouse ES cells cultured under growth-restricted conditions and after in vitro aging. Our findings reveal that culturing ES cells under serum-depleted conditions (starvation) and at high cell density (confluence) leads to increased expression of both imprinted genes and aberrant methylation profiles in key regulatory sites of Igf2 and H19. These alterations in methylation and gene expression suggest a possible epigenetic mechanism underlying the loss of developmental potential in ES cell-derived clones and chimeras.

title: When is antipsychotic polypharmacy supported by research evidence? Implications for QI.
text:
BACKGROUND: The concurrent use of multiple standing antipsychotics (antipsychotic polypharmacy) has become increasingly common among both inpatients and outpatients. However, reviews of research evidence on antipsychotic polypharmacy have not distinguished between appropriate and inappropriate use.
METHODS: A systematic search of the MEDLINE database from 1966 to December 2007 was conducted to identify studies comparing changes in symptoms, functioning, and/or side effects between patients treated with multiple antipsychotics and patients treated with a single antipsychotic. The studies were then grouped based on whether prescribing was concordant with guideline recommendations for multiple-antipsychotic use.
RESULTS: A review of the literature, including three randomized controlled trials, found limited support for the use of antipsychotic polypharmacy in patients without a history of treatment resistance to multiple trials of monotherapy. In patients with a history of treatment resistance, limited data suggest that antipsychotic polypharmacy may be beneficial, primarily when clozapine is augmented with a second-generation antipsychotic.
DISCUSSION: The research evidence suggests that antipsychotic polypharmacy should be avoided in patients without guideline-recommended indications for its use. The Joint Commission is implementing a core measure set for Hospital-Based Inpatient Psychiatric Services, which includes two measures related to antipsychotic polypharmacy. The first measure assesses the overall rate of antipsychotic polypharmacy, while the second measure determines whether clinically appropriate justification has been documented to support the use of more than one antipsychotic medication.

title: The Liverpool uveal melanoma liver metastases pathway: outcome following liver resection.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the outcomes of patients who underwent liver resection for metastases from uveal melanoma.
Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 155 patients with uveal melanoma metastases referred for liver resection over a 9-year period. High-risk patients were offered 6-monthly non-contrast liver MRI surveillance after primary uveal melanoma treatment, and those with detected liver metastases underwent contrast-enhanced liver MRI, CT of the thorax, and staging laparoscopy.
Results: Of the 155 patients, 17 (11.0%) underwent liver resection, and one patient received percutaneous radio-frequency ablation. The majority of patients who underwent liver resection had multiple metastectomies (n = 8), and three patients had major liver resections. The overall median survival for patients treated with surgery/ablation was 27 months (14-90 months), which was significantly better than patients treated palliatively (median = 8 months, P < 0.001). Following surgery, 11 patients had recurrent disease (median = 13 months). Patients who underwent a major liver resection had a poorer disease-free survival (P = 0.037).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that patients who can undergo surgical resection for metastatic uveal melanoma have a more favorable survival compared to those who do not.

title: Smooth muscle lineage diversity in the chick embryo. Two types of aortic smooth muscle cell differ in growth and receptor-mediated transcriptional responses to transforming growth factor-beta.
text: In avian embryo lineage analysis studies, two types of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) in the tunica media of large elastic arteries have been identified: one that originates from the cardiac neural crest and is ectodermal in origin (Ect), and another that arises from local mesenchyme of mesodermal origin (Mes). To investigate whether differences in primary embryonic lineage can lead to differences in SMC growth and differentiation properties, we isolated Ect and Mes SMCs from the Day 14 chick embryo aorta. Our findings show that despite their different embryonic origins, Ect and Mes SMCs express similar levels of seven smooth muscle differentiation markers in vitro, indicating that they share a common smooth muscle developmental fate in vivo. However, we observed lineage-dependent differences in SMC growth properties, with Ect SMCs displaying a greater capacity for growth in serum-free medium under conditions that allow for short-range cell-cell interactions. The peptide growth factors tested, including PDGF-AA, PDGF-BB, basic FGF, EGF, and activin, stimulated DNA synthesis to similar extents in Ect and Mes SMCs. However, we found significant lineage-dependent differences in SMC responses to transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta), with Ect SMCs exhibiting a 12-fold increase in luciferase activity in response to TGF-beta 1 (0.4-400 pmole/liter), while Mes SMCs showed a 3-fold increase. Analysis of TGF-beta receptor phenotypes revealed that Ect and Mes SMCs expressed similar levels of types I, II, and III TGF-beta receptors. However, using a polyclonal antibody specific for the chick type II TGF-beta receptor subunit, we found that Mes SMCs produce a fully glycosylated form of this protein, while Ect SMCs elaborate only an unglycosylated type II TGF-beta receptor. These findings suggest that Ect and Mes SMCs exhibit lineage-dependent differences in growth and receptor-mediated transcriptional responses to at least one important class of SMC morphogens and growth modifiers, such as the TGF-betas. Our results imply that different SMC populations within a common vessel wall may respond differently to signals that direct formation of the tunica media in the embryo and to factors involved in the progression of vascular disease later in life.

title: THE USE OF LEAD CITRATE AT HIGH pH AS AN ELECTRON-OPAQUE STAIN IN ELECTRON MICROSCOPY
text:
Aqueous solutions of lead salts (1, 2) and saturated solutions of lead hydroxide (1) have been used as stains to enhance the electron-scattering properties of biological materials examined in the electron microscope. Saturated solutions of lead hydroxide (1) stain more intensely than either lead acetate or monobasic lead acetate (1, 2), but form insoluble lead carbonate upon exposure to air. To avoid contamination of sections during staining, elaborate procedures have been developed to exclude air or carbon dioxide (3, 4). Recently, several modifications of Watson's lead hydroxide stain (1) have been developed (5-7). These modified stains use a high pH (approximately 12) and may contain small amounts of tartrate (6), a relatively weak complexing agent (8), in addition to lead. These modified stains are less likely to contaminate sections with precipitated stain products.
The stain described here differs from previous alkaline lead stains in that the chelating agent, citrate, is present in sufficient excess to sequester all lead present. Lead citrate, soluble in high concentrations in basic solutions, is a chelate compound with an apparent association constant (log Ka) between ligand and lead ion of 6.5 (9). Tissue binding sites, presumably organophosphates, and other anionic species present in biological components following fixation, dehydration, and plastic embedding, have a greater affinity for this cation than lead citrate. As a result, alkaline lead citrate solutions are less likely to contaminate sections, and no precipitates form when fresh staining solution is exposed to air for up to 30 minutes. The resulting staining of sections is high in intensity in Araldite or Epon-embedded material. The stain can be used to stain cytoplasmic membranes, ribosomes, glycogen, and nuclear material (Figs. 1-3).
STAIN SOLUTION: Lead citrate is prepared by dissolving lead acetate trihydrate in a solution of sodium citrate trihydrate. The pH of the solution is adjusted to approximately 12 using 2N sodium hydroxide solution.

title: Amylase, Lipase, and Acute Pancreatitis in People With Type 2 Diabetes Treated With Liraglutide: Results From the LEADER Randomized Trial.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the changes in serum amylase and lipase levels and the incidence of acute pancreatitis in patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk treated with liraglutide or placebo over a period of 3.5-5 years.
Design and Methods: A total of 9,340 patients with type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to either liraglutide or placebo (median observation time of 3.84 years). Fasting serum lipase and amylase levels were monitored, and acute pancreatitis was adjudicated in a blinded manner.
Results: Compared to the placebo group, liraglutide-treated patients experienced increases in serum lipase and amylase levels of 28.0% and 7.0%, respectively. These increases were observed at 6 months and remained stable throughout the study. During the study period, 18 (0.4% [1.1 events/1,000 patient-years of observation]) liraglutide-treated and 23 (0.5% [1.7 events/1,000 PYO]) placebo patients developed acute pancreatitis, with most cases occurring after 12 months of randomization. Liraglutide-treated patients with a prior history of pancreatitis (n = 147) were not more likely to develop acute pancreatitis than similar patients in the placebo group (n = 120). Additionally, elevations in amylase and lipase levels did not predict future risk of acute pancreatitis (positive predictive value <1.0%) in patients treated with liraglutide.
Conclusions: In a population of patients with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk, there were fewer events of acute pancreatitis among liraglutide-treated patients compared to the placebo group. Liraglutide was associated with increases in serum lipase and amylase levels, but these increases were not predictive of an event of subsequent acute pancreatitis.

title: Zoledronic acid is unable to induce apoptosis, but slows tumor growth and prolongs survival for non-small-cell lung cancers.
text:
BACKGROUND: Zoledronic acid (ZOL), a third-generation nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate, has shown promise as a potential therapeutic agent against various types of cancer, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, multiple myeloma, and small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). However, there is limited information on the anti-tumor effect of ZOL on non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study aimed to investigate the effects of ZOL on the line-1 tumor cell line, a murine lung adenocarcinoma cell line similar to human lung adenocarcinoma, in vitro and in vivo.
METHODS: The anti-tumor effects of ZOL (ranging from 3 to 100 microM) were evaluated on line-1 tumor cells in vitro using an MTT assay, cell-cycle analysis by flow cytometry, and apoptosis detection by annexin V/propidium iodide (PI) and 4'-6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining. The growth and survival of line-1 tumor cells were also examined following ZOL treatment (1 microg/kg/week) using an animal model. In vivo cell-cycle pattern was evaluated using lacZ-expressing line-1 cells (line-1/lacZ).
RESULTS: ZOL significantly slowed the growth of line-1 tumors in a dose-dependent manner in vitro, with arrested cells typically in the S/G2/M phase of the cell cycle. However, no apoptotic cells were detected following ZOL exposure. Following drug removal, the drug-inhibited cells resumed proliferation, and the cell-cycle prolongation induced by ZOL earlier disappeared. In vivo studies showed that ZOL significantly slowed the growth of line-1 tumors, resulting in longer survival for mice. Using line-1/lacZ cells, the in vivo cell-cycle distribution of line-1 tumor cells following ZOL exposure revealed S/G2/M-phase arrest that was similar to the in vitro culture.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that ZOL has potential as a therapeutic agent for reducing tumor burden and prolonging survival in murine pulmonary adenocarcinoma. ZOL induces cell-cycle arrest without inducing apoptosis in line-1 tumor cells, and may be a useful combination therapy with chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy for the effective treatment of NSCLC in humans. Further clinical trials are needed to verify these findings.

title: A central role for central tolerance.
text: The recent clarification of the role of central tolerance in preventing organ-specific autoimmunity has significantly altered our understanding of self/nonself discrimination. This transformative shift is primarily due to the discovery of the widespread expression of tissue-restricted self-antigens (TRAs) by medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs). Notably, TRA expression in mTECs mirrors the entirety of the body's tissues, regardless of their developmental or spatial-temporal expression patterns. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying TRA expression in mTECs, as well as the various mechanisms of tolerance induction and their implications for the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases and other biological processes such as fertility, pregnancy, puberty, and tumor defense.

title: Contribution of traditional healers to a rural tuberculosis control programme in Hlabisa, South Africa.
text:
The study was conducted in the rural health district of Hlabisa, located in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The objective of the study was to assess the acceptability and effectiveness of traditional healers as supervisors of tuberculosis (TB) treatment in an existing directly observed treatment, short-course (DOTS) program.
The study design was an observational comparison of treatment outcomes among new TB patients in three intervention sub-districts that offered the additional option of traditional healers for DOT supervision, with those in the remainder of the district that offered the standard range of options for DOT supervision. The study also compared treatment outcomes between different options for DOT supervision.
A total of 3461 TB patients were registered in Hlabisa District from April 1999 to December 2000, of whom 2823 were discharged from hospital to the ambulatory DOT program. Treatment outcomes were known for 1816 patients in Hlabisa District, including 275 patients in the intervention area. There was no significant difference in treatment outcomes between the intervention and control areas (77% vs. 75%). Among 275 patients with known outcomes in the intervention area, 48 patients were supervised by traditional healers, and 227 patients were supervised by other categories of DOT supervisors. Treatment completion was not significantly higher among patients supervised by traditional healers than among patients supervised by other categories of DOT supervisors (88% vs. 75%, P = 0.3841). Interviews with 41 of 51 traditional healer patients who had completed treatment revealed high levels of satisfaction with the care received.
The study concluded that traditional healers make an effective contribution to TB program performance in this pilot scheme in Hlabisa district. Further evaluation will be necessary as this approach is scaled up.

title: Alzheimer's disease: the two-hit hypothesis.
text: There is a wealth of evidence indicating that oxidative stress and aberrant cellular changes play a significant role in the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, despite both of these processes occurring early in the disease progression, the relationship between them and their role in the pathophysiology of AD was previously unclear. Recent studies, however, have shed light on this relationship by examining the signaling pathways involved in mitogenic and oxidative stress processes in AD. Based on these findings, we propose a "two-hit hypothesis" that suggests that both oxidative stress and abnormalities in mitotic signaling are necessary to drive disease progression. In this paper, we review the evidence for oxidative stress and abnormal mitotic alterations in AD and explain the two-hit hypothesis by detailing how these mechanisms work together to contribute to the disease process.

title: Toll-like receptor 7 mediates pruritus
text: Toll-like receptors are typically found in immune cells to help regulate the body's first line of defense against infection. However, our research has discovered that Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) is also expressed in C-fiber primary sensory neurons, which are responsible for transmitting sensory information from the skin to the brain. We have found that TLR7 plays a crucial role in inducing itch (pruritus), but is not necessary for eliciting other types of pain, such as mechanical, thermal, inflammatory, and neuropathic pain in mice. These findings suggest that TLR7 may be a potential target for anti-itch treatments in skin diseases.

title: Antigen presentation by major histocompatibility complex class I-B molecules.
text: Majority of MHC class I loci are composed of Class I-b genes. These monomorphic or oligomorphic molecules have been characterized in various organisms, with the mouse providing a wealth of information due to its numerous potentially intact genes. Two key differences distinguish Class I-b molecules from Class I-a: limited polymorphism and lower surface expression on cells. These features suggest broader implications for the evolution and function of this class. Additionally, Class I-b proteins often have shorter cytoplasmic domains, may be secreted, or substitute a lipid anchor for the transmembrane domain. Some are also expressed in limited cell or tissue distribution. At least six mouse MHC class I-b molecules have been shown to present antigens to alpha beta or gamma delta T cells. Recent advances have shed light on the physiological function of H-2M3a and defined the natural peptide-binding motif of Qa-2. Significant progress has also been made towards understanding other Class I-b molecules, including Qa-1, TL, HLA-E, HLA-G, and the MHC-unlinked class I molecule CD1. However, we argue that categorizing MHC genes as Class I-a or I-b is conceptually misleading, despite its historical basis and practical utility. We then discuss antigen presentation by Class I-b molecules, focusing on their structure, polymorphism, peptide antigen binding requirements, and tissue expression.

title: Pdgfrβ+ Mural Preadipocytes Contribute to Adipocyte Hyperplasia Induced by High-Fat-Diet Feeding and Prolonged Cold Exposure in Adult Mice.
text: The expansion of white adipose tissue (WAT) in obesity involves the de novo differentiation of new adipocytes, but the cellular origin of these cells remains unclear. To investigate this, we utilized Zfp423(GFP) reporter mice to characterize adipose mural (Pdgfrβ(+)) cells with varying levels of the preadipocyte commitment factor Zfp423. Our findings reveal that adipose tissue contains distinct mural populations, with levels of Zfp423 distinguishing adipogenic from inflammatory-like mural cells. Using our "MuralChaser" lineage tracking system, we uncovered adipose perivascular cells as developmental precursors of adipocytes formed in obesity, with adipogenesis and precursor abundance regulated in a depot-dependent manner. Interestingly, Pdgfrβ(+) cells do not significantly contribute to the initial cold-induced recruitment of beige adipocytes in WAT; instead, it is only after prolonged cold exposure that these cells differentiate into beige adipocytes. These results provide genetic evidence for a mural cell origin of white adipocytes in obesity and suggest that beige adipogenesis may arise from multiple sources.

title: Effect of clinical guidelines on medical practice: a systematic review of rigorous evaluations.
text: Although interest in clinical guidelines has never been higher, there is ongoing debate about their effectiveness. Despite this, a comprehensive overview of the evidence has been lacking. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review of 59 published evaluations of clinical guidelines that met rigorous scientific standards. These evaluations assessed guidelines for specific clinical conditions (24 studies), preventive care (27 studies), and guidelines for prescribing or support services (8 studies). Our findings indicate that the majority of these studies detected significant improvements in the process of care after the introduction of guidelines, with 23 out of 24 studies showing improvements in specific clinical conditions and 25 out of 27 studies showing improvements in preventive care. Moreover, 11 studies that assessed the outcome of care reported significant improvements.
