Based on these findings, we conclude that explicit guidelines can indeed improve clinical practice when introduced in the context of rigorous evaluations. However, the magnitude of these improvements can vary significantly.

title: Threonine as a carbon source for Escherichia coli.
text: Threonine can serve as the sole source of carbon and energy for certain mutants of Escherichia coli K-12 through an aerobic pathway involving threonine dehydrogenase, resulting in the production of aminoketobutyric acid. This acid is then metabolized by aminoketobutyric acid ligase, leading to the formation of acetyl coenzyme A and glycine. A strain lacking serine transhydroxymethylase utilizes this pathway and eliminates glycine as a waste product. Evidence of aminoketobutyric acid ligase activity was obtained after treating crude extracts with Sephadex G100.

title: Protein S-nitrosylation: a physiological signal for neuronal nitric oxide
text: Nitric oxide (NO) has been linked to a wide range of physiological and pathophysiological processes that cannot be fully explained by its established effects on soluble guanylyl cyclase. While exogenous NO can S-nitrosylate cysteine residues in proteins, the importance of endogenous NO in this process is still unclear. To investigate, we employed a novel proteomic approach to identify proteins that are endogenously S-nitrosylated. We found that these proteins are lost in mice lacking neuronal NO synthase (nNOS), suggesting that protein S-nitrosylation is a physiological signaling mechanism for nNOS. Our findings implicate metabolic, structural, and signaling proteins as targets of NO, which may be influenced by neuronally generated NO. These discoveries demonstrate the importance of protein S-nitrosylation in nNOS-mediated signaling pathways.

title: Hypoxia‐Sensitive COMMD1 Integrates Signaling and Cellular Metabolism in Human Macrophages and Suppresses Osteoclastogenesis
text:
Summary:
Hypoxia enhances inflammatory responses and osteoclastogenesis through poorly understood mechanisms. We identified COMMD1 as a cell-intrinsic negative regulator of osteoclastogenesis that is suppressed by hypoxia. In human macrophages, COMMD1 inhibits the induction of NF-κB signaling and a transcription factor E2F1-dependent metabolic pathway triggered by the cytokine RANKL. Hypoxia-induced downregulation of COMMD1 protein expression amplifies RANKL-induced expression of inflammatory and E2F1 target genes, leading to enhanced osteoclastogenesis. E2F1 targets include genes involved in glycolysis and metabolic pathways, as well as inflammatory cytokine-driven target genes. Our findings link increased COMMD1 expression with reduced bone erosion in rheumatoid arthritis and provide a mechanism by which hypoxia exacerbates inflammation and bone loss. Myeloid deletion of Commd1 leads to increased osteoclastogenesis in arthritis and inflammatory osteolysis models. These results identify COMMD1 and an E2F-metabolic pathway as key regulators of osteoclastogenic responses under pathological inflammatory conditions, and provide a mechanism by which hypoxia amplifies inflammation and bone destruction.

title: Production of tyrosol by Candida albicans biofilms and its role in quorum sensing and biofilm development.
text: In this study, we investigated the production of tyrosol, a quorum-sensing molecule, by Candida albicans and its potential role in biofilm development. We found that both planktonic cells and biofilms of four C. albicans strains, including mutants with defects in the Efg 1 and Cph 1 morphogenetic signaling pathways, produced extracellular tyrosol during growth at 37°C. There was a positive correlation between tyrosol production and biomass for both cell types. However, biofilm cells produced significantly more tyrosol than planktonic cells, with a 50% increase in tyrosol production per cell dry weight. The addition of exogenous farnesol, another quorum-sensing molecule, inhibited biofilm formation by up to 33% after 48 hours. Interestingly, tyrosol stimulated hypha production during the early stages of biofilm development, but had no effect on biofilm formation when added simultaneously with farnesol. Our results suggest that farnesol has a dominant action on biofilm formation, and that biofilms formed in the presence of both compounds consist almost entirely of yeast cells. Furthermore, we found that tyrosol activity exceeds that of farnesol after 14 hours, but not after 24 hours, and that farnesol activity increases significantly during the later stages of biofilm development. Overall, our findings support the conclusion that tyrosol acts as a quorum-sensing molecule for both planktonic cells and biofilms, with its action most significant during the early and intermediate stages of biofilm formation.

title: Regulated nucleo/cytoplasmic exchange of HOG1 MAPK requires the importin beta homologs NMD5 and XPO1.
text:
The transduction of extracellular signals to the nucleus of eukaryotic cells is a crucial process mediated by MAP kinase signaling modules. However, the mechanisms underlying the crossing of the nuclear envelope remain poorly understood. Our study aimed to investigate the nuclear import of the HOG1 MAP kinase cascade in response to osmotic stress in yeast cells.
Using green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusions of the kinases involved in the HOG1 cascade, we observed that HOG1, PBS2, and STE11 localize to the cytoplasm of unstressed cells. Upon osmotic stress, HOG1 selectively translocates to the nucleus, a process that occurs rapidly, is transient, and correlates with the phosphorylation and activation of the MAP kinase by its upstream kinase. Our findings indicate that HOG1 phosphorylation is necessary and sufficient for its nuclear translocation, as a catalytically inactive kinase that is phosphorylated is translocated to the nucleus with equal efficiency as the wild-type.
Our results also demonstrate that the nuclear import of HOG1 under stress conditions requires the activity of the small GTP binding protein Ran-GSP1, but not the NLS-binding importin alpha/beta heterodimer. Instead, HOG1 import requires the activity of a novel importin beta homolog encoded by the gene NMD5. Similarly, the export of dephosphorylated HOG1 from the nucleus requires the activity of the NES receptor XPO1/CRM1.
Our findings provide insight into the requirements for the regulated nuclear transport of a stress-activated MAP kinase, highlighting the importance of the HOG1 cascade in mediating cellular responses to osmotic stress.

title: FBW7 regulates endothelial functions by targeting KLF2 for ubiquitination and degradation
text:
The protein F-box and WD repeat domain-containing 7 (FBW7) plays a crucial role in various physiological and pathological processes, including endothelial cell function. Although FBW7 is essential for vascular development, its function in endothelial cells has remained largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate the role of FBW7 in endothelial cell function and identify a novel target of FBW7, the zinc finger transcription factor Krüppel-like factor 2 (KLF2).
Using RNA interference, we found that depleting FBW7 significantly impairs angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo. We discovered that FBW7 regulates KLF2 stability through phosphorylation by glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3) at two conserved phosphodegrons. Mutating these phosphodegron motifs abolishes FBW7-mediated degradation and ubiquitination of KLF2. Our findings suggest that KLF2 is an essential target of FBW7 in the regulation of endothelial cell function. Moreover, we demonstrate that FBW7-mediated KLF2 degradation is critical for angiogenesis in teratomas and zebrafish development.
Our study reveals a novel role for FBW7 in endothelial cell migration, angiogenesis, inflammation, and barrier integrity. These findings provide new insights into the regulation of KLF2 stability in vivo and highlight the importance of FBW7 in endothelial cell function. Overall, our study sheds light on the complex interplay between FBW7 and KLF2 in endothelial cells and has important implications for our understanding of vascular biology and disease.

title: Role of RhoA-specific guanine exchange factors in regulation of endomitosis in megakaryocytes.
text: Polyploidization can occur before aneuploidy develops in cancer, whereas in megakaryocytes (Mks), polyploidization is a tightly regulated developmental process crucial for efficient platelet production through unknown mechanisms. Using primary cells, we discovered that guanine exchange factors GEF-H1 and ECT2, which are often overexpressed in cancer and necessary for RhoA activation during cytokinesis, must be downregulated for Mk polyploidization. The first (2N-4N) endomitotic cycle requires GEF-H1 downregulation, whereas subsequent cycles (>4N) require ECT2 downregulation. Exogenous expression of both GEF-H1 and ECT2 prevents endomitosis, resulting in proliferation of 2N Mks. Furthermore, we found that the mechanism by which polyploidization is prevented in Mks lacking Mkl1, which is mutated in megakaryocytic leukemia, is due to elevated GEF-H1 expression; shRNA-mediated GEF-H1 knockdown alone rescues this ploidy defect. These insights into the mechanisms of normal versus malignant megakaryocytopoiesis and aberrant mitosis in aneuploid cancers deepen our understanding of the complex processes involved in platelet production and cancer development.

title: Optimal therapy for reduction of lipoprotein(a).
text:
What is Known and Objective:
There is a growing body of evidence from both experimental and clinical studies demonstrating the atherogenic and pro-thrombotic potential of Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)], as well as its causative role in coronary heart disease and stroke. While most research has focused on identifying suitable therapies for hyperlipoproteinemia(a), novel strategies are emerging that target the "inflammatory pathways" by inhibiting Interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling with natural compounds such as Ginkgo biloba or the IL-6 receptor antibody Tocilizumab. These approaches have shown promising results in lowering Lp(a) levels and cardiovascular risk. In addition, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin may also decrease plasma Lp(a) concentrations and modulate its influence on platelets.
What is New and Conclusion:
While current approaches for lowering Lp(a) levels have been inadequate, novel insights into the underlying biological mechanisms are emerging that may lead to more effective treatment strategies. In particular, targeting the "inflammatory pathways" through the inhibition of IL-6 signaling with natural compounds or the IL-6 receptor antibody Tocilizumab shows promise in reducing Lp(a) levels and cardiovascular risk. Additionally, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin may also play a role in modulating Lp(a) levels and platelet function. Further research is needed to fully understand the potential of these novel approaches and to develop more effective treatments for hyperlipoproteinemia(a) and related cardiovascular diseases.

title: Early gastric cancer and dysplasia.
text: Since the initial description of early gastric cancer in Japan in 1962, its treatment has undergone significant advancements, transitioning from curative surgical resection to endoscopic resection. Initially, polypectomy was used, followed by the development of endoscopic submucosal dissection. As global experience with these endoscopic techniques grows and gains acceptance, studies have demonstrated their comparable effectiveness to historical surgical outcomes in carefully selected patients. The criteria for endoscopic resection have expanded to provide more patients with improved quality of life, avoiding the morbidity and mortality associated with surgery. This article reviews the evolutionary role of endoscopic and surgical therapy in early gastric cancer.

title: The impact of homelessness on children.
text: This article examines and evaluates the impact of homelessness on children, highlighting the significant threats to their well-being and future success. Homeless children face numerous challenges, including health issues, hunger and malnutrition, developmental delays, anxiety and depression, behavioral problems, and poor academic performance. The article also identifies factors that may contribute to these outcomes, such as inadequate living conditions, instability in shelters and residences, lack of access to necessary services, and barriers to accessing available resources. To address these issues, the article argues that public policy initiatives are necessary to support homeless children and ensure their basic needs are met.

title: Strategies of microbial cheater control.
text: The potential advantages of cooperation among microorganisms can be hindered by genetic conflict within social groups, which can manifest as "cheating." For cooperation to be a successful evolutionary strategy, the detrimental effects of this conflict must be either prevented or mitigated. To establish an interpretive framework for future research in microbial behavioral ecology, we outline a variety of hypothetical mechanisms by which cheaters might be restrained.

title: Golden Hours in Severe Paraquat Poisoning-The Role of Early Haemoperfusion Therapy.
text:
INTRODUCTION:
Paraquat, a widely used herbicide, is often ingested accidentally in Southern India, resulting in a high mortality rate due to its lack of an antidote. The usual causes of death are acute lung injury or multi-organ failure. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of early hemoperfusion as a treatment for paraquat poisoning.
MATERIALS AND METHODS:
This retrospective analysis was conducted at a Tertiary Medical College Hospital between January 2012 and December 2015, including patients with a history of paraquat ingestion. The study compared outcomes in patients who received only gastric lavage and symptomatic treatment with those who received hemoperfusion as a therapy. The role of early hemoperfusion (within 6 hours) versus late hemoperfusion (after 6 hours) in paraquat-poisoned patients was also evaluated. The data collected included age, sex, treatment modality, and outcome in patients who received early and late hemoperfusion.
RESULTS:
A total of 101 patients were analyzed, of which 62 died. The mortality rate was significantly higher in patients who received only gastric lavage and symptomatic treatment (92.1%) compared to those who received hemoperfusion (42.9%). Additionally, we found that early hemoperfusion resulted in a better survival rate.
CONCLUSION:
Our findings suggest that early hemoperfusion is a helpful treatment for severe paraquat poisoning, improving survival rates in these patients.

title: Changes in the prevalence of cerebral palsy for children born very prematurely within a population-based program over 30 years.
text: Although cerebral palsy (CP) among extremely premature infants has been reported as a significant morbidity outcome, there are challenges in comparing published CP rates across various birth years and locations. To investigate changes in population-based, gestational age-specific prevalence rates of CP among extremely premature infants over a 30-year period, we conducted a prospective, population-based longitudinal outcome study in Northern Alberta. Our study included 2318 infants born between 1974 and 2003, with birth weights ranging from 500 to 1249 grams and gestational ages between 20 and 27 weeks. By the age of 2, 1437 (62%) of the infants had died, 23 (1%) were lost to follow-up, and 858 (37%) had undergone multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental assessment. We determined the population-based prevalence rates of CP among survivors and confirmed the diagnosis for each child by age 3 or older. Our findings revealed that among those whose gestational age was 20 to 25 weeks, population-based survival increased from 4% to 31% (P<.001), while the CP prevalence per 1000 live births increased monotonically from 0 to 110 until the years 1992-1994 (P<.001) and decreased thereafter to 22 in the years 2001-2003 (P<.001). Similarly, among those whose gestational age was 26 to 27 weeks, population-based survival increased from 23% to between 75% and 80% (P<.001), while the CP prevalence per 1000 live births increased monotonically from 15 to 155 until the years 1992-1994 (P<.001) and then decreased to 16 in the years 2001-2003 (P<.001). For the survivors born in the years 2001-2003, the CP prevalence was 19 per 1000 live births. Our study suggests that population-based CP prevalence rates among children born prematurely have shown steady reductions in the last decade, with stable or reducing mortality, reversing trends prior to 1992-1994.

title: Desferrioxamine treatment of porphyria cutanea tarda in a patient with HIV and chronic renal failure.
text: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) can occur in HIV patients, and current research suggests that HIV infection may disrupt the hepatic cytochrome oxidase system, leading to impaired porphyrin metabolism. Furthermore, chronic hemodialysis in renal failure may increase the risk of developing PCT. In addition to the known factors that contribute to the development of PCT in HIV-infected individuals, it is possible that porphyrin accumulation due to renal failure may play a role in the expression of this disease. We present a case of PCT in an HIV-1 infected patient who was undergoing blood dialysis and was refractory to antimalarial treatment, but responded well to desferrioxamine therapy.

title: Mutations in G protein beta subunits promote transformation and kinase inhibitor resistance
text: Activating mutations in genes encoding G protein α (Gα) subunits are present in approximately 4-5% of all human cancers, while oncogenic alterations in Gβ subunits have not been characterized. Our study demonstrates that recurrent mutations in the Gβ proteins GNB1 and GNB2 lead to cytokine-independent growth and activate canonical G protein signaling. Specifically, multiple mutations in GNB1 affect the protein interface that binds Gα subunits as well as downstream effectors, disrupting Gα interactions with the Gβγ dimer. Interestingly, different mutations in Gβ proteins cluster according to tumor lineage, with all 11 GNB1 K57 mutations found in myeloid neoplasms and seven of eight GNB1 I80 mutations in B cell neoplasms. To further investigate the role of GNB1 in cancer, we expressed patient-derived GNB1 variants in Cdkn2a-deficient mouse bone marrow and observed either myeloid or B cell malignancies. Treatment with the dual PI3K-mTOR inhibitor BEZ235 suppressed GNB1-induced signaling and significantly improved survival. In addition, we found that mutations in the GNB1 gene often cooccur with oncogenic kinase alterations, such as the BCR-ABL fusion protein, the V617F substitution in JAK2, and the V600K substitution in BRAF. Coexpression of patient-derived GNB1 variants with these mutant kinases resulted in inhibitor resistance in each context. These findings suggest that GNB1 and GNB2 alterations confer transformed and resistance phenotypes across a range of human tumors and may be targetable with inhibitors of G protein signaling.

title: Isolation of major pancreatic cell types and long-term culture-initiating cells using novel human surface markers.
text: We have developed a groundbreaking panel of cell surface markers for isolating and studying all major cell types of the human pancreas. To identify these markers, we used a novel approach involving hybridoma selection and immunohistochemistry/flow cytometry. We identified antibodies that specifically bind to surface antigens on islet (panendocrine or alpha-specific) and non-islet pancreatic cell subsets (exocrine and duct). These antibodies were then used to isolate populations of alpha, beta, exocrine, or duct cells from primary human pancreas using FACS, and to characterize the detailed cell composition of human islet preparations. Additionally, we employed these antibodies to demonstrate that human islet expansion cultures originate from non-endocrine cells and that insulin expression levels can be increased up to 1% of normal islet cells by subpopulation sorting and overexpression of the transcription factors Pdx-1 and ngn3, an improvement over previous results with this culture system. These methods have the potential to enable the analysis and isolation of functionally distinct pancreatic cell populations, which could have significant implications for cell therapy.

title: Re-engineered CD40 receptor enables potent pharmacological activation of dendritic-cell cancer vaccines in vivo
text: The clinical outcomes of dendritic cell (DC) vaccine trials have been modest, highlighting the need for refinement in DC vaccine design. Despite the identification of numerous potential antigens, the development of methods to enhance antigen presentation by DCs has lagged. To address this challenge, we have engineered a potent, drug-inducible CD40 (iCD40) receptor, which enables temporally controlled, lymphoid-localized, and DC-specific activation. iCD40 is composed of a membrane-bound cytoplasmic domain of CD40 fused to drug-binding domains, allowing it to respond to a lipid-permeable, high-affinity dimerizer drug while bypassing ectodomain-dependent negative-feedback mechanisms. These modifications result in prolonged activation of iCD40-expressing DCs in vivo, leading to more potent CD8+ T-cell effector responses, including the eradication of previously established solid tumors. In contrast to activation of DCs ex vivo, iCD40-mediated DC activation exhibits enhanced potency both in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, iCD40-expressing DCs have a prolonged lifespan, which may lead to more effective vaccines, including those for use in immune-compromised patients.

title: Effect of homocysteine lowering on mortality and vascular disease in advanced chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease: a randomized controlled trial.
text: In this study, the authors investigated whether high doses of folic acid and B vitamins would reduce mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease. The study was a double-blind, randomized controlled trial conducted at 36 US Department of Veterans Affairs medical centers between 2001 and 2006. A total of 2056 participants aged 21 years or older with advanced chronic kidney disease (estimated creatinine clearance < or =30 mL/min) or end-stage renal disease (n = 751) and high homocysteine levels (> or = 15 micromol/L) were included in the study. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a daily capsule containing 40 mg of folic acid, 100 mg of pyridoxine hydrochloride (vitamin B6), and 2 mg of cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) or a placebo. The primary outcome measure was all-cause mortality, and secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, amputation of all or part of a lower extremity, a composite of these 3 plus all-cause mortality, time to initiation of dialysis, and time to thrombosis of arteriovenous access in hemodialysis patients. The results showed that mean baseline homocysteine levels were similar in both groups, but it was lowered by 6.3 micromol/L (25.8%; P < .001) in the vitamin group and 0.4 micromol/L (1.7%; P = .14) in the placebo group at 3 months. However, there was no significant effect of vitamin treatment on mortality (448 vitamin group deaths vs 436 placebo group deaths) or on secondary outcomes such as MI (129 vitamin group events vs 150 for placebo), stroke (37 vitamin group events vs 41 for placebo), and amputation (60 vitamin group events vs 53 for placebo). The composite of MI, stroke, and amputations plus mortality (P = .85), time to dialysis (P = .38), and time to thrombosis in hemodialysis patients (P = .97) did not differ between the vitamin and placebo groups. The study concluded that treatment with high doses of folic acid and B vitamins did not improve survival or reduce the incidence of vascular disease in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease or end-stage renal disease.

title: Treated individuals who progress to action or maintenance for one behavior are more likely to make similar progress on another behavior: coaction results of a pooled data analysis of three trials.
text: The purpose of this study was to investigate the phenomenon of coaction, which refers to the likelihood that taking action on one behavior will lead to taking action on a second behavior. The study compared treatment and control groups in three randomized trials of Transtheoretical Model (TTM) tailored interventions, involving a total of 9461 participants in the United States in 1999. The study analyzed the data to assess coaction in three behavior pairs (diet and sun protection, diet and smoking, and sun protection and smoking). The results showed that the treatment group had a higher likelihood of taking action on a second behavior compared to the control group, with two of the behavior pairs showing significant results at 12 and 24 months. The combined odds ratios (ORs) for the treatment and control groups at 12 and 24 months were 1.63 and 1.85 for the treatment group, and 1.20 and 1.10 for the control group. These findings were consistent with previous studies that applied TTM tailoring to energy balance behaviors. The study suggests that more research is needed to identify predictors of coaction in multiple behavior change interventions.

title: Trabecular bone score as an indicator for skeletal deterioration in diabetes.
text:
The novel texture index, Trabecular Bone Score (TBS), was developed to evaluate the gray-level variations in lumbar spine dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry images and was found to be related to bone microarchitecture independent of bone mineral density (BMD). In this study, the authors investigated the use of TBS as an indicator of skeletal deterioration in diabetes.
The study included 1229 men and 1529 postmenopausal women aged 50 years or older from the Ansung cohort, a ongoing prospective, community-based cohort study conducted from 2009 to 2010. The study measured biochemical parameters, TBS, and BMD from dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry images.
The results showed that TBS was lower in men with diabetes compared to non-diabetic men, and lumbar spine BMD was higher in men with diabetes. However, TBS was only lower in women with diabetes in an unadjusted model, but not after adjusting for covariates. Additionally, TBS was negatively correlated with glycated hemoglobin, fasting plasma glucose, fasting insulin, and homeostasis model assessment for insulin resistance in both genders.
The study found that the inverse association between TBS and insulin resistance may make it an indicator for determining skeletal deterioration in diabetic patients who have high BMD. These findings suggest that TBS may be a useful tool for assessing bone health in diabetic patients, particularly those with high BMD.

title: Full activation of the T cell receptor requires both clustering and conformational changes at CD3.
text: T cell receptor (TCR-CD3) triggering involves both receptor clustering and conformational changes within the cytoplasmic tails of the CD3 subunits. The mechanism by which TCR-CD3 ligand binding induces these conformational changes is currently unknown. Through the use of well-defined ligands, we have shown that the conformational change requires both multivalent engagement and the restricted mobility of the TCR-CD3 complexes imposed by the plasma membrane. This conformational change is elicited through cooperative rearrangements of two TCR-CD3 complexes and does not require alterations in the structure of the TCR-beta ectodomains. This conformational change within the CD3 subunits is reversible and requires ligand dissociation, and plays a crucial role in T cell activation. Our permissive geometry model provides a molecular mechanism that explains how the information from ligand binding to TCR-beta is transmitted to the CD3 subunits and the intracellular signaling machinery.

title: Class III PI3K Vps34 plays an essential role in autophagy and in heart and liver function.
text: A critical regulator of autophagy, Class III PI3K Vps34 (also known as PIK3C3), has been identified as an essential factor in mammalian autophagy. Although Vps34 has been well-characterized in yeast, its role in mammals remains unclear. To elucidate the physiological function of Vps34 and to determine its precise role in autophagy, we generated Vps34(f/f) mice, in which the expression of Cre recombinase leads to a deletion of exon 4 of Vps34 and a frameshift mutation resulting in a deletion of 755 of the 887 amino acids of Vps34. Acute ablation of Vps34 in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) upon adenoviral Cre infection leads to a diminished capacity for localized phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) generation and blockade of both endocytic and autophagic degradation. Starvation-induced autophagosome formation is also impaired in Vps34-null MEFs and liver. Liver-specific Albumin-Cre;Vps34(f/f) mice exhibit hepatomegaly and hepatic steatosis, as well as impaired protein turnover. Ablation of Vps34 in the heart of muscle creatine kinase-Cre;Vps34(f/f) mice leads to cardiomegaly and decreased contractility. Interestingly, while amino acid-stimulated mTOR activation is suppressed in the absence of Vps34, the steady-state level of mTOR signaling is not significantly affected in Vps34-null MEFs, liver, or cardiomyocytes. Taken together, our findings indicate that Vps34 plays a critical role in regulating functional autophagy and is essential for normal liver and heart function.

title: Sex-based differences in the effect of digoxin for the treatment of heart failure.
text:
Background: The Digitalis Investigation Group trial found that treatment with digoxin did not significantly reduce overall mortality among patients with heart failure and depressed left ventricular systolic function, although it did result in a slight decrease in hospitalizations. However, the study did not evaluate the potential sex-based differences in the effectiveness of digoxin therapy.
Methods: We conducted a post-hoc subgroup analysis of the 6800 patients in the Digitalis Investigation Group study to assess whether there were any sex-based differences in the effect of digoxin therapy on the primary end point of death from any cause. We used Mantel-Haenszel tests of heterogeneity and a multivariable Cox proportional-hazards model to evaluate the interaction between sex and digoxin therapy.
Results: Our analysis revealed an absolute difference of 5.8% (95% CI, 0.5-11.1) between men and women in the effect of digoxin on the rate of death from any cause (P=0.034 for the interaction). Specifically, women who were randomly assigned to digoxin had a higher rate of death than women who were randomly assigned to placebo (33.1% vs. 28.9%; absolute difference, 4.2%, 95% CI, -0.5-8.8). In contrast, the rate of death was similar among men randomly assigned to digoxin and men randomly assigned to placebo (35.2% vs. 36.9%; absolute difference, -1.6%, 95% CI, -4.2-1.0). In the multivariable analysis, digoxin was associated with a significantly higher risk of death among women (adjusted hazard ratio for the comparison with placebo, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.02-1.47), but it had no significant effect among men (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.85-1.02; P=0.014 for the interaction).
Conclusions: Our findings suggest that the effect of digoxin therapy differs between men and women with heart failure and depressed left ventricular systolic function. Specifically, digoxin therapy is associated with an increased risk of death from any cause among women, but not men. These sex-based differences in the effectiveness of digoxin therapy highlight the importance of considering gender when designing and interpreting clinical trials.

title: Recipient-type specific CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells favor immune reconstitution and control graft-versus-host disease while maintaining graft-versus-leukemia.
text: CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) play a crucial role in preventing autoimmune diseases of organs and in inducing tolerance to allogeneic organ transplants. Recent studies have shown that high numbers of Tregs can modulate graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) when administered with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in mice. However, it is challenging to obtain sufficient numbers of freshly purified Tregs from a single donor for therapeutic use in the clinic. To address this limitation, we expanded Tregs ex vivo by stimulating them with allogeneic antigen-presenting cells (APCs), which resulted in the production of alloantigen-specific regulatory T cells. Here, we demonstrate that Tregs specific for the recipient's alloantigens control GVHD while promoting immune reconstitution. In contrast, irrelevant Tregs only provide partial protection against GVHD. Notably, specific Tregs exhibited preferential survival in grafted animals, and their use was compatible with some form of graft-versus-tumor activity. These findings suggest that using recipient-type specific Tregs in the control of GVHD may be a promising approach for future clinical trials.

title: Expression of the gene encoding the chemorepellent semaphorin III is induced in the fibroblast component of neural scar tissue formed following injuries of adult but not neonatal CNS.
text: This study investigates the expression of the chemorepellent protein semaphorin III (D)/collapsin-1 (sema III) in the central nervous system (CNS) following various types of lesions. The research focuses on the scar tissue that forms after penetrating injuries to the lateral olfactory tract (LOT), cortex, perforant pathway, and spinal cord. The study finds that scar tissue contains numerous spindle-shaped cells that express high levels of sema III mRNA. These cells are located in the core of the scar and exhibit characteristics of fibroblast-like cells. The study also identifies the receptor neuropilin-1, which is expressed in injured neurons and projects to the lesion site, as well as in a subpopulation of scar-associated cells and blood vessels around the scar. The expression of sema III and neuropilin-1 in the scar suggests that these molecules play a role in CNS scar formation. The study also finds that the secreted chemorepellent sema III is expressed following CNS injury, and that this expression inhibits the outgrowth of injured neurites. The study suggests that inactivating sema III in scar tissue could be a means to promote long-distance regeneration in the adult CNS.

title: The relationship of the level of cyclic amp to differentiation in primary cultures of chick muscle cells.
text: "This study investigated the effect of elevated cAMP levels on the differentiation of primary chick myoblast cultures. At 24 hours after plating, the cultures were treated with either 0.1 mM but 2 cAMP or 1 mM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine and maintained throughout a 70-hour incubation period. Both reagents significantly delayed the fusion of myoblasts, but had no noticeable impact on the increase in creatine phosphokinase activity. Morphological analysis of the cells revealed no significant differences in the relative numbers of myoblasts and fibroblasts between the control, but 2 cAMP, and 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine cultures. However, the latter reagent appeared to inhibit cell proliferation to some extent."

title: Intact endothelial autophagy is required to maintain vascular lipid homeostasis.
text: The physiological role of autophagic flux within the vascular endothelial layer remains poorly understood, but recent studies have shed light on its importance in regulating excess lipids. In primary endothelial cells, oxidized and native low-density lipoprotein (LDL) stimulates autophagosome formation, and excess native or modified LDL is engulfed within autophagic structures. When the essential autophagy gene ATG7 is knocked down, there is a buildup of intracellular (125)I-LDL and oxidized LDL (OxLDL) in endothelial cells, suggesting that autophagy may play a crucial role in regulating lipid accumulation. To investigate the physiological importance of these observations, mice with a conditional deletion of ATG7 within the endothelium were used. In these mice, there was a prolonged retention of fluorescently labeled OxLDL within the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroidal endothelium of the eye following acute intravenous infusion of OxLDL. In a chronic model of lipid excess, the absence of endothelial autophagy significantly increased atherosclerotic burden. These findings suggest that strategies that stimulate autophagy or prevent the age-dependent decline in autophagic flux may be beneficial in treating atherosclerotic vascular disease.

title: Induction of circadian gene expression in human subcutaneous adipose-derived stem cells.
text:
OBJECTIVE:
To investigate the oscillatory expression of genes encoding the circadian transcriptional apparatus in murine adipose tissues and evaluate the suitability of human subcutaneous adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) as an in vitro model for studying circadian biology in human adipose tissue.
METHODS:
Primary cultures of undifferentiated or adipocyte-differentiated ASCs were treated with dexamethasone, rosiglitazone, or 30% fetal bovine serum. The response of undifferentiated ASCs to dexamethasone was further evaluated in the presence of lithium chloride, which inhibits glycogen synthase kinase 3, a key component of the circadian apparatus. Total RNA was harvested at 4-hour intervals over 48 hours and analyzed by real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).
RESULTS:
Adipocyte-differentiated cells exhibited a more rapid response to treatments than their undifferentiated counterparts, but the period of the circadian gene oscillation was longer in the adipocyte-differentiated cells. Dexamethasone induced circadian gene expression patterns with mean periods of 25.4 and 26.7 hours in undifferentiated and adipocyte-differentiated ASCs, respectively. Both rosiglitazone and serum shock resulted in a significantly longer period of circadian gene expression in adipocyte-differentiated ASCs compared to undifferentiated ASCs. The Bmal1 profile was phase-shifted by approximately 8 to 12 hours relative to Per1, Per3, and Cry2, consistent with their in vivo expression patterns. Lithium chloride inhibited adipogenesis and significantly lengthened the period of Per3 and Rev-erbalpha gene expression profiles by >5 hours in dexamethasone-activated undifferentiated ASCs.
DISCUSSION:

These findings support the initial hypothesis and validate ASCs as a suitable in vitro model for studying circadian biology in human adipose tissue. The results demonstrate that the circadian transcriptional apparatus exhibits oscillatory expression in murine adipose tissues and that human ASCs can be used to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying circadian rhythm regulation in adipose tissue. The study highlights the potential of ASCs as a valuable tool for exploring the complex interplay between circadian rhythm and adipose tissue function in human health and disease.

title: BCL9 promotes tumor progression by conferring enhanced proliferative, metastatic, and angiogenic properties to cancer cells.
text:
The Wnt signaling cascade has been implicated in the development and progression of various human cancers, with some components functioning as tumor suppressors while others behave as oncogenes. Our study aimed to investigate the role of the Wnt pathway component BCL9 in oncogenesis and its potential as a therapeutic target for cancer treatment.
Using expression profiling analysis and in vitro and in vivo functional studies, we found that BCL9 is a novel oncogene that is aberrantly expressed in human multiple myeloma and colon carcinoma. Our results show that BCL9 enhances the transcriptional activity of beta-catenin regardless of the mutational status of the Wnt signaling components, leading to increased cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and metastasis. Notably, BCL9 knockdown significantly reduced tumor load, metastasis, and host angiogenesis in xenograft mouse models of cancer by down-regulating c-Myc, cyclin D1, CD44, and vascular endothelial growth factor expression by tumor cells.
Our findings suggest that deregulation of BCL9 is a crucial contributor to tumor progression, underscoring its potential as a drug target for therapeutic intervention in various malignancies associated with aberrant Wnt signaling. The pleiotropic roles of BCL9 uncovered in this study highlight its value as a therapeutic target in multiple cancer types.

title: Programmed cell death pathways in cancer: a review of apoptosis, autophagy and programmed necrosis.
text: Programmed cell death (PCD), encompassing apoptosis, autophagy, and programmed necrosis, is proposed to be a cellular response to pathological stimuli, mediated by an intrinsic program. These three forms of PCD may collectively determine the fate of malignant cells; apoptosis and programmed necrosis consistently contribute to cell demise, while autophagy can exhibit either pro-survival or pro-death behaviors. Recent accumulation of evidence has significantly advanced our understanding of cancer initiation and progression, with the three distinct forms of cell death. Elucidating PCD signaling pathways may facilitate the development of novel, targeted anti-cancer therapeutic strategies. Therefore, in this review, we provide a concise overview of apoptosis, autophagy, and programmed necrosis pathways, as well as apoptosis-related microRNA regulation, in cancer. By comprehending the complex interplay between these three forms of PCD, scientists and clinicians may ultimately harness them for the discovery of novel drug targets, paving the way for future cancer treatments.

title: Loss of gametophytic self-incompatibility with evolution of inbreeding depression.
text:
In plants, gametophytic self-incompatibility (SI) is a widespread mechanism that prevents self-fertilization and the negative consequences of inbreeding, such as inbreeding depression. However, this mechanism can evolve into self-compatibility over time. By analyzing the genetic mechanisms behind the breakdown of gametophytic SI, we can gain insights into the evolution of plant reproduction.
There are two main mechanisms by which gametophytic SI can break down: a nonfunctional S-allele and an unlinked modifier locus that inactivates the S-locus. Under certain conditions, self-compatible alleles can invade a self-incompatible population, leading to the loss of SI. The likelihood of invasion depends on factors such as the selfing rate, the number of S-alleles, and pollen limitation.
High selfing rates and a small number of S-alleles can favor the spread of self-compatible genotypes, while pollen limitation can also contribute to the breakdown of SI. Observed parameter values suggest that the maintenance of gametophytic SI is due to a combination of high inbreeding depression in self-incompatible populations and intermediate selfing rates of the self-compatible genotypes, as well as sheltered load linked to the S-locus.
In summary, gametophytic SI is a common mechanism in plants that prevents self-fertilization and inbreeding depression. However, this mechanism can evolve into self-compatibility over time, leading to the loss of SI. The likelihood of invasion depends on various factors, including selfing rate, number of S-alleles, and pollen limitation. Understanding the genetic mechanisms behind the breakdown of gametophytic SI can provide insights into the evolution of plant reproduction.

title: The oncogenic microRNA miR-22 targets the TET2 tumor suppressor to promote hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal and transformation.
text: MicroRNAs are frequently altered in cancer, and we found that miR-22 is upregulated in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and leukemia, with poor prognosis. To investigate its role in hematopoietic stem cells and malignancy, we generated mice that conditionally express miR-22 in the hematopoietic compartment. These mice showed reduced levels of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) and increased hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal, accompanied by defective differentiation. Conversely, inhibiting miR-22 in leukemic cells blocked proliferation in both mice and humans. Over time, miR-22 transgenic mice developed MDS and hematological malignancies. We also identified TET2 as a key target of miR-22 in this context, with ectopic expression of TET2 suppressing the miR-22-induced phenotypes. Decreased TET2 protein levels correlated with poor clinical outcomes and miR-22 overexpression in MDS patients, suggesting that miR-22 is a potent oncogene and that disruptions in the miR-22/TET2 regulatory network are common in hematopoietic malignancies.

title: Transmission of atherosclerosis susceptibility with gut microbial transplantation.
text:
Recent studies suggest a link between the metabolism of certain dietary nutrients by the gut microbiome and the development of atherosclerotic heart disease. We investigate the hypothesis that gut microbial transplantation can transmit the ability of the microbiome to produce trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a compound associated with increased atherosclerosis susceptibility.
In a mouse model, we found a strong association between TMAO levels and atherosclerotic plaque burden, with one strain producing significantly more TMAO than another. When we transplanted the gut microbiome from the high TMAO-producing strain into mice lacking their own intestinal microbes, the recipients showed increased choline diet-dependent TMAO levels and atherosclerotic plaque burden compared to mice receiving the microbiome from a strain that produced less TMAO.
Microbial DNA analysis revealed that the transplanted microbiota from the high TMAO-producing strain was transmitted to the recipients, along with differences in the proportions of specific taxa that correlated with TMAO levels in both donors and recipients. These findings suggest that the gut microbiome may play a role in transmitting atherosclerosis susceptibility, and that targeting the gut microbiome may be a novel therapeutic approach for modulating atherosclerosis susceptibility.

title: The complete primary structure of the spermadhesin AWN, a zona pellucida-binding protein isolated from boar spermatozoa.
text: AWN is a protein derived from the male accessory glands that becomes associated with the surface of sperm upon ejaculation. It is believed to play a role in mediating sperm adhesion to the egg's zona pellucida through a carbohydrate-recognition mechanism, which may be involved in the initial events of fertilization in pigs. In this study, we have employed a combination of protein-chemical and mass spectrometric methods to determine the complete primary structure of AWN. Our findings reveal that AWN exists in two isoforms, AWN-1 and AWN-2, which differ in that AWN-2 is N-terminally acetylated. The amino acid sequence of AWN consists of 133 residues and contains two disulphide bridges between nearest-neighbour cysteine residues. Analysis of the amino acid sequence of the AWN proteins shows significant similarity only to AQN-1 and AQN-3, two other boar spermadhesins.

title: What influences government adoption of vaccines in developing countries? A policy process analysis.
text: This paper proposes a framework for examining the process by which governments in developing countries consider and adopt new vaccines. The paper focuses on the cases of Taiwan and Thailand, where the early adoption of the Hepatitis B vaccine was studied to identify the factors that influence the adoption process. The study finds that while the literature has identified several explanatory factors, a variable-centric approach may not fully capture the complexity of the adoption process. Instead, the paper argues that the policy context and process play a crucial role in determining the pace and extent of adoption. The cases suggest that modeling "causal diversity" - the complex set of necessary and sufficient conditions leading to particular decision outcomes - can help predict the institutionalization of new vaccines in a broad range of country contexts. A better understanding of how government decision-makers filter information and the arenas in which critical decisions are shaped and taken can assist both analysts and advocates in crafting targeted strategies to accelerate the diffusion of new vaccines.

title: Benzodiazepines and injurious falls in community dwelling elders.
text: Benzodiazepines are commonly used medications in older adults, but they are associated with an increased risk of falls, which can have serious consequences. To assess the impact of benzodiazepine-related injurious falls in elderly individuals, a nested case-control study was conducted using data from the French PAQUID (Personnes Agées QUID) community-based cohort over 10 years. The main outcome measure was the occurrence of an injurious fall, which was defined as a fall resulting in hospitalization, fracture, head trauma, or death. Controls (3:1) were frequency-matched to cases. Benzodiazepine exposure was defined as the use of benzodiazepines in the previous 2 weeks reported at the follow-up visit preceding the fall. The study found that benzodiazepine use was significantly associated with the occurrence of injurious falls, with a significant interaction with age. The adjusted odds ratio for injurious falls in subjects aged 80 years or older exposed to benzodiazepines was 2.2 (95% CI: 1.4-3.4), while the odds ratio for subjects aged <80 years was 1.3 (95% CI: 0.9-1.9). The population attributable risk for injurious falls in subjects exposed to benzodiazepines was 28.1% (95% CI: 16.7-43.2) for subjects aged 80 years or older. The incidence of injurious falls in subjects aged 80 years or older exposed to benzodiazepines in the PAQUID cohort was 2.8/100 person-years, and over 9% of these falls were fatal. Based on these findings and recent population estimates, benzodiazepine use could be responsible for almost 20,000 injurious falls in subjects aged 80 years or older every year in France, and nearly 1800 deaths. These results suggest that new methods are needed to limit the use of benzodiazepines in elderly individuals, as existing good practice guidelines have not been effective in preventing their misuse.

title: Effect of women's nutrition before and during early pregnancy on maternal and infant outcomes: a systematic review.
text:
According to current understanding of biological processes, the nutritional status of women before and during early pregnancy (less than 12 weeks gestation) plays a crucial role in determining fetal development and ensuring successful pregnancy outcomes. To investigate this further, we conducted a systematic review of the evidence on the impact of maternal nutrition before and during early pregnancy on maternal, neonatal, and child health outcomes. Our review included 45 articles, consisting of nine intervention trials and 32 observational studies, which were identified through database searches of PubMed and EMBASE, as well as review articles.
Our findings indicate that periconceptional folic acid supplementation (<12 weeks gestation) significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects. Observational studies also suggest that preconceptional and periconceptional intake of vitamin and mineral supplements is associated with a lower risk of delivering offspring who are low birthweight and/or small-for-gestational age (SGA) and preterm deliveries (PTD). Some studies have found that indicators of maternal prepregnancy size, such as low stature, underweight, and overweight, are associated with increased risks of PTD and SGA.
While the available data highlight the importance of women's nutrition prior to and during the first trimester of pregnancy, there is a need for well-designed prospective studies and controlled trials in developing country settings to examine relationships with low birthweight, SGA, PTD, stillbirth, and maternal and neonatal mortality. Specifically, we need to evaluate the effectiveness of periconceptional interventions such as food supplements, multivitamin-mineral supplements, and specific micronutrients (iron, zinc, iodine, vitamin B-6 and B-12) in improving pregnancy outcomes. Additionally, we need to investigate the relationship between measures of prepregnancy body size and composition and maternal, neonatal, and child health outcomes.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that women's nutritional status before and during early pregnancy plays a critical role in determining fetal development and pregnancy outcomes. Further research is needed to identify the most effective interventions and to address the knowledge gaps in this area.

title: Kinesin-2 controls development and patterning of the vertebrate skeleton by Hedgehog- and Gli3-dependent mechanisms.
text: Hedgehog signaling plays a crucial role in the patterning of the vertebrate skeleton. Our findings demonstrate that inhibiting the Kif3a subunit of the kinesin-2 intraflagellar transport motor in mesenchymal skeletal progenitor cells leads to severe patterning defects in the craniofacial region, including the formation of a split sternum and polydactyly. These deformities are similar to those observed in mice with disrupted hedgehog signaling. We show that in Kif3a-deficient tissues, both the repressor function of the Gli3 transcription factor and the activation of its downstream targets, Ptch and Gli1, are impaired. Quantitative analysis of gene expression reveals that the Gli1 transcript level is significantly reduced, while Gli3 expression remains unchanged. However, the motor appears to be essential for the efficient cleavage of the full-length Gli3 transcription factor into a repressor form.

title: Ablation of NF1 function in neurons induces abnormal development of cerebral cortex and reactive gliosis in the brain.
text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a prevalent genetic disorder that affects the growth properties of neural-crest-derived cell populations. Approximately one-half of NF1 patients exhibit learning disabilities. To investigate the function of NF1 in vitro and in vivo, we employed Cre/loxP technology to generate a conditional mutation in the NF1 gene. Introduction of a Synapsin I promoter-driven Cre transgenic mouse strain into the conditional NF1 background resulted in ablation of NF1 function in most differentiated neuronal populations. These mice displayed abnormal development of the cerebral cortex, indicating that NF1 plays an indispensable role in this aspect of central nervous system (CNS) development. Notably, although the mice were tumor-free, they exhibited extensive astrogliosis in the absence of conspicuous neurodegeneration or microgliosis. These findings suggest that NF1-deficient neurons can induce reactive astrogliosis through a non-cell autonomous mechanism.

title: Pathology of postprimary tuberculosis in humans and mice: contradiction of long-held beliefs.
text:
Tuberculosis remains one of the world's leading infectious causes of death, with approximately 80% of cases occurring in the lung due to postprimary (secondary) tuberculosis. Unfortunately, tissue samples from developing lesions are scarce, and there are no recognized animal models of postprimary tuberculosis. In the preantibiotic era, when tissue availability was more abundant, several investigators described early postprimary tuberculosis as a lipid pneumonia distinct from the caseating granulomas commonly observed today.
To better understand the progression of postprimary tuberculosis, we conducted a study using histopathologic, immunohistochemical, and acid fast staining techniques on tissue samples from individuals with untreated primary and postprimary tuberculosis, as well as mice with reactivation tuberculosis. Our findings confirmed that postprimary tuberculosis begins as a lipid pneumonia accompanied by bronchial obstruction, with infection restricted to foamy alveolar macrophages. The development of cavities is due to a combination of caseation of tuberculous pneumonia and microvascular occlusion, which is characteristic of delayed type hypersensitivity (DTH). Reactivation tuberculosis in mice also begins as a similar lipid pneumonia with bronchial obstruction, and there is evidence for participation of DTH. Both in humans and mice, developing necrosis is associated with localization of organisms within lipid droplets.
Our results suggest that the reactivation tuberculosis model in mice is a valuable model of developing human postprimary tuberculosis.

title: Secondary aerosolization of viable Bacillus anthracis spores in a contaminated US Senate Office.
text: In the aftermath of bioterrorist attacks involving letters and mail-handling systems in Washington, DC, which resulted in Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) spore contamination in the Hart Senate Office Building and other nearby facilities, this study aimed to investigate the secondary aerosolization of B anthracis spores indoors. The study collected air, surface dust, and swab samples under semiquiescent (minimal activities) and simulated active office conditions to estimate the reaerosolization of B anthracis spores. The results showed that viable B anthracis spores reaerosolized under semiquiescent conditions, with a significant increase in reaerosolization during simulated active office conditions. The study found that more than 80% of the B anthracis particles collected on stationary monitors were within the alveolar respirable size range of 0.95 to 3.5 micro meters. These findings have important implications for appropriate respiratory protection, remediation, and reoccupancy of contaminated office environments.

title: Fingolimod provides long-term protection in rodent models of cerebral ischemia.
text:
Objective:
The sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor agonist fingolimod (FTY720), which has shown efficacy in advanced multiple sclerosis clinical trials, was investigated for its potential to reduce reperfusion injury in various organs, including the heart, liver, and kidney. Given its success in clinical trials, we examined the therapeutic effects of fingolimod in rodent models of focal cerebral ischemia. To assess the translational significance of these findings, we evaluated whether fingolimod improved long-term behavioral outcomes, whether delayed treatment was still effective, and whether neuroprotection could be achieved in a second species.
Methods:
We used rodent models of middle cerebral artery occlusion and cell-culture models of neurotoxicity and inflammation to investigate the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of neuroprotection by fingolimod.

Results:
In a transient mouse model, fingolimod reduced infarct size, neurological deficit, edema, and the number of dying cells in the core and periinfarct area. Neuroprotection was accompanied by decreased inflammation, as fingolimod-treated mice had fewer activated neutrophils, microglia/macrophages, and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)-positive blood vessels. Fingolimod-treated mice showed a smaller infarct and performed better in behavioral tests up to 15 days after ischemia. Reduced infarct was observed in a permanent model even when mice were treated 4 hours after ischemic onset. Fingolimod also decreased infarct size in a rat model of focal ischemia. Fingolimod did not protect primary neurons against glutamate excitotoxicity or hydrogen peroxide, but decreased ICAM-1 expression in brain endothelial cells stimulated by tumor necrosis factor alpha.

Interpretation:

These findings suggest that anti-inflammatory mechanisms, rather than direct effects on neurons, underlie the beneficial effects of fingolimod after stroke. S1P receptors are a highly promising target in stroke treatment.

title: Induced regeneration—the progress and promise of direct reprogramming for heart repair
text: The regeneration of cardiac tissue has the potential to revolutionize cardiovascular medicine. Recent breakthroughs in stem cell biology and direct reprogramming, or transdifferentiation, have opened up new avenues for achieving this goal. In this Review, we delve into the latest advances in generating new cardiomyocytes in vitro, as well as the exciting progress made towards in vivo reprogramming of cardiac tissue. We also discuss the challenges and controversies that continue to hinder the field.

title: "Sandwich"-type immunoassay of carcinoembryonic antigen in patients receiving murine monoclonal antibodies for diagnosis and therapy.
text: Measurements of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) in blood significantly increased in some patients who received injections of monoclonal antibody. CEA levels were measured using a monoclonal antibody-based double-determinant enzyme immunoassay, where untreated plasma samples were diluted with an equal volume of buffer containing mouse serum. Rising CEA levels were accompanied by the appearance and simultaneous increase in titers of human antibody against mouse immunoglobulin (HAMA). Treatment of these sera with solid-phase anti-human IgG or Protein A restored CEA titers to pre-treatment values, suggesting that the serum factor responsible for false-positive CEA titers was most likely HAMA. Neither adding undiluted mouse serum to the assay mixture nor pre-treating plasma samples with heat (70 degrees C) was effective in abolishing HAMA interference. In contrast, protein precipitation with polyethylene glycol (130 g/L) or heating plasma samples to 90 degrees C eliminated false-positive titers caused by HAMA, while authentic CEA titers remained unaffected.

title: Mutant dynactin in motor neuron disease
text: Impaired axonal transport in motor neurons has been proposed as a mechanistic basis for neuronal degeneration in motor neuron disease. In this study, we investigate the genetic basis of a lower motor neuron disease and identify a linkage to a specific region of chromosome 2p13, spanning approximately 4 megabases (Mb). Through mutation analysis of a gene located within this interval, we identify a single base pair change resulting in an amino acid substitution that is predicted to disrupt the folding of the protein's microtubule-binding domain. Using binding assays, we demonstrate decreased binding of the mutant protein to microtubules, providing evidence that dysfunction of dynactin-mediated transport can lead to human motor neuron disease.

title: Thioredoxin mediates oxidation-dependent phosphorylation of CRMP2 and growth cone collapse.
text: Semaphorin3A (Sema3A) acts as a repulsive guidance molecule for axons by inducing growth cone collapse through the phosphorylation of collapsin response mediator protein 2 (CRMP2). In this study, we investigate the role of CRMP2 oxidation and thioredoxin (TRX) in regulating CRMP2 phosphorylation and growth cone collapse. We find that Sema3A stimulation generates hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) through the MICAL protein, which oxidizes CRMP2, leading to the formation of a disulfide-linked homodimer through cysteine-504. The oxidized CRMP2 then forms a transient disulfide-linked complex with TRX, which stimulates CRMP2 phosphorylation by glycogen synthase kinase-3, ultimately resulting in growth cone collapse. We also reconstitute oxidation-dependent phosphorylation of CRMP2 in vitro using a limited set of purified proteins, providing further evidence of the importance of H2O2 and CRMP2 oxidation in Sema3A-induced growth cone collapse. Additionally, our findings suggest an unappreciated role for TRX in linking CRMP2 oxidation to phosphorylation.

title: Pathologic indicators of degradation and inflammation in human osteoarthritic cartilage are abrogated by exposure to n-3 fatty acids.
text:
Objective: To investigate the effect of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation on the metabolism of osteoarthritic (OA) cartilage.
Methods: The metabolic profile of human OA cartilage was analyzed at the time of harvest and after 24-hour exposure to n-3 PUFAs or other classes of fatty acids, followed by explant culture for 4 days in the presence or absence of interleukin-1 (IL-1). Parameters measured included glycosaminoglycan release, aggrecanase and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity, and the expression of messenger RNA (mRNA) for inflammatory mediators, aggrecanases, MMPs, and their natural tissue inhibitors (tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases [TIMPs]).
Results: Supplementation with n-3 PUFA (but not other fatty acids) significantly reduced the endogenous and IL-1-induced release of proteoglycan metabolites from articular cartilage explants and abolished endogenous aggrecanase and collagenase proteolytic activity. Additionally, expression of mRNA for ADAMTS-4, MMP-13, and MMP-3 was specifically abolished with n-3 PUFA supplementation. Furthermore, n-3 PUFA supplementation abolished the expression of mRNA for inflammatory mediators (cyclooxygenase 2, 5-lipoxygenase, 5-lipoxygenase-activating protein, tumor necrosis factor alpha, IL-1alpha, and IL-1beta) without affecting the expression of message for several other proteins involved in normal tissue homeostasis.
Conclusion: These studies demonstrate that n-3 PUFA supplementation can significantly alter the pathologic indicators manifested in human OA cartilage, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for n-3 PUFAs in the management of OA.

title: Interactive effects of oligofructose and obesity predisposition on gut hormones and microbiota in diet-induced obese rats.
text:
Objective: Oligofructose (OFS) is a prebiotic that modifies gut hormones and microbiota, leading to reduced energy intake and fat mass. This study aimed to investigate the effects of OFS on diet-induced obese (DIO) and diet-resistant (DR) rats.
Methods: Adult, male DIO and DR rats were randomly assigned to a high-fat/high-sucrose (HFS) diet or HFS diet supplemented with 10% OFS for 6 weeks. Body composition, food intake, gut microbiota, plasma gut hormones, and cannabinoid CB(1) receptor expression in the nodose ganglia were measured.
Results: OFS reduced body weight, energy intake, and fat mass in both phenotypes (P < 0.05). OFS altered the gut microbiota profiles in DIO and DR rats, with the differences between the two phenotypes eliminated by OFS. OFS did not modify plasma ghrelin or CB(1) expression in nodose ganglia, but it reduced plasma levels of GIP and elevated PYY levels (P < 0.05).
Conclusions: OFS was able to reduce body weight and adiposity in both prone and resistant obese phenotypes. The changes in gut microbiota profiles and gut hormone levels induced by OFS likely contribute to the sustained lower body weights.

title: RKIKK motif in the intracellular domain is critical for spatial and dynamic organization of ICAM-1: functional implication for the leukocyte adhesion and transmigration.
text: No direct evidence has been reported on the relationship between the spatial organization of ICAM-1 on the cell surface and its physiological function in terms of leukocyte adhesion and transendothelial migration (TEM). However, our study found that ICAM-1 can directly regulate the de novo elongation of microvilli and is thereby clustered on the microvilli. In contrast, truncation of the intracellular domain resulted in a uniform distribution of ICAM-1 on the cell surface. Further analysis revealed that a specific segment of amino acids in the N-terminal third of the intracellular domain is essential for the proper localization and dynamic distribution of ICAM-1, as well as its association with F-actin, ezrin, and moesin. Notably, deletion of this segment significantly delayed LFA-1-dependent membrane projection and decreased leukocyte adhesion and TEM. Additionally, endothelial cells treated with cell-permeant penetratin-ICAM-1 peptides comprising ICAM-1 RKIKK sequences inhibited leukocyte TEM. Together, these findings suggest that the (507)RKIKK(511) motif is essential for microvillus ICAM-1 presentation and may play a novel regulatory role in leukocyte TEM.

title: Immunology of the tick-host interaction and the control of ticks and tick-borne diseases.
text: Sixty years have passed since the first experimental vaccine against ticks was administered. Since then, progress has been slow, although the recent commercial release of a recombinant vaccine against Boophilus microplus represents a significant breakthrough. Despite extensive research, the nature of naturally acquired protective immunity against ticks remains poorly understood, particularly in domesticated ruminant hosts. While some progress has been made in characterizing the antigens of naturally acquired immunity, more work is needed to fully understand this complex phenomenon. Additionally, crucial questions remain about the impact of tick-induced immunosuppression and the effect of immunity on the transmission of tick-borne diseases, despite some fascinating and important recent findings. Peter Willadsen and Frans Jongejan discuss these issues in their presentation.

title: Rapid method for the isolation of lipoproteins from human serum by precipitation with polyanions.
text: Procedures for isolating lipoproteins from human serum through precipitation with polyanions and divalent cations are described. A mixture of low and very low density lipoproteins can be prepared without ultracentrifugation by precipitating with heparin and either MnCl2 alone or MgCl2 plus sucrose. In both cases, the precipitation is reversible, selective, and complete. The highly concentrated isolated lipoproteins are free of other plasma proteins as determined by immunological and electrophoretic methods. The low density and very low density lipoproteins can then be separated from each other by ultracentrifugation. The advantage of this method is that large amounts of lipoproteins can be prepared with a single preparative ultracentrifugation. Polyanions other than heparin may also be used, such as dextran sulfate and MnCl2, or sodium phosphotungstate and MgCl2, which allow for the subsequent precipitation of high density lipoproteins by increasing the concentrations of the reagents. These lipoproteins, containing small amounts of protein contaminants, can be further purified by ultracentrifugation at a density of 1.22. With a single preparative ultracentrifugation, immunologically pure high density lipoproteins can be isolated from large volumes of serum.

title: The role of oral antidiabetic agents: why and when to use an early-phase insulin secretion agent in Type II diabetes mellitus
text:
Evidence from the 1990s strongly supports the notion that maintaining good glycaemic control is crucial for both Type I (insulin-dependent) and Type II (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes mellitus. While measurement of HbA1c is the standard for assessing the impact of glucose control on the development and prevention of diabetic complications, more recent research suggests that other glucose parameters, such as postchallenge and postprandial hyperglycaemic peaks, may also be important.
Currently, there is no universally accepted standard approach to pharmacological management of Type II diabetes. The United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study has shown that reaching near-normal glycaemic targets is critical, and the pharmacotherapy of this progressive disease can be challenging. Loss of endogenous insulin secretion has been confirmed to contribute to the progression of Type II diabetes in the United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study, and early insulinization was not found to be advantageous compared to other forms of therapy.
In recent years, the advent of polypharmacy has significantly strengthened the treatment of Type II diabetes. This has been further enhanced with the development of early-phase insulin secretion agents, such as nateglinide and repaglinide, which can reduce mealtime glucose excursions and HbA1c levels both as monotherapy and in combination with metformin. The antidiabetic potential of these agents is similar to that of the combination treatment with glibenclamide and metformin. Additional research is needed to confirm their long-term effect on improving life expectancy and reducing diabetic complications in Type II diabetic patients.

title: Layered hydrogels accelerate iPSC-derived neuronal maturation and reveal migration defects caused by MeCP2 dysfunction.
text: Investigating a wide range of cellular phenotypes in neurodevelopmental disorders using patient-derived neural progenitor cells (NPCs) can be facilitated by 3D assays, as 2D systems cannot fully replicate the organization of cells in the brain. To address this, we developed a novel 3D migration and differentiation assay in layered hydrogels to examine how these processes are affected in neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Rett syndrome. Our soft 3D system mimics the brain environment and accelerates the maturation of neurons from human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived NPCs, resulting in electrophysiologically active neurons within just 3 weeks. Using this platform, we uncovered a genotype-specific effect of methyl-CpG-binding protein-2 (MeCP2) dysfunction on iPSC-derived neuronal migration and maturation, resulting in reduced neurite outgrowth and fewer synapses, in 3D layered hydrogels. This 3D system expands the range of neural phenotypes that can be studied in vitro to include those influenced by physical and mechanical stimuli or requiring specific arrangements of multiple cell types.

title: Inducible gene expression: diverse regulatory mechanisms
text: The rapid activation of gene expression in response to stimuli is primarily mediated by the regulation of RNA polymerase II-dependent transcription. In this Review, we delve into the key events that occur during the transcription cycle in eukaryotes, which are crucial for the rapid and precise activation of gene expression in response to external stimuli. These events include the regulated recruitment of the transcription machinery to the promoter, as well as additional control steps such as chromatin remodeling and the release of paused polymerase. Recent research has also shown that certain components of signal transduction pathways play a direct role in activating transcription at target genes.

title: On the origins of ultra-fine anaphase bridges.
text: According to a study published in Nature Cell Biology in 2009, replication stress can induce the formation of sister-chromatid bridges at specific locations on the chromosomes, known as fragile site loci, during mitosis. The study, conducted by Chan et al., found that this phenomenon occurs as a result of the stress caused by the replication process, which can lead to the misalignment of the sister chromatids and their subsequent bridging. The study highlights the importance of understanding the mechanisms that govern chromosome segregation during cell division, as errors in this process can lead to genetic instability and the development of cancer.

title: Resistance to gefitinib in PTEN-null HER-overexpressing tumor cells can be overcome through restoration of PTEN function or pharmacologic modulation of constitutive phosphatidylinositol 3'-kinase/Akt pathway signaling.
text:
Introduction:
Tyrosine kinase (TK) inhibitors have emerged as a promising new approach to the treatment of HER overexpressing tumors. However, the optimal use of these agents awaits further elucidation of the downstream signaling pathways that mediate their effects. In our previous work, we reported that both EGFR- and Her2-overexpressing tumors are sensitive to the new EGFR-selective TK inhibitor gefitinib (ZD1839, "Iressa"), and sensitivity to this agent correlated with its ability to down-regulate Akt. However, EGFR-overexpressing MDA-468 cells, which lack PTEN function, are resistant to ZD1839, and ZD1839 is unable to down-regulate Akt activity in these cells.
Experimental Design:
To investigate the role of PTEN function in ZD1839 resistance, we generated MDA468 cells with tet-inducible PTEN expression.
Results:
We found that the resistance of MDA-468 cells to ZD1839 is attributable to EGFR-independent constitutive Akt activation caused by loss of PTEN function in these cells. Reconstitution of PTEN function through tet-inducible expression restores ZD1839 sensitivity to these cells and reestablishes EGFR-stimulated Akt signaling. Although restoration of PTEN function to tumors is challenging to implement clinically, much of the effects of PTEN loss are attributable to overactive PI3K/Akt pathway signaling, and this overactivity can be modulated by pharmacologic approaches. We found that pharmacologic down-regulation of constitutive PI3K/Akt pathway signaling using the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 similarly restores EGFR-stimulated Akt signaling and sensitizes MDA-468 cells to ZD1839.
Conclusion:
Sensitivity to ZD1839 requires intact growth factor receptor-stimulated Akt signaling activity. PTEN loss leads to uncoupling of this signaling pathway and results in ZD1839 resistance, which can be reversed with reintroduction of PTEN or pharmacologic down-regulation of constitutive PI3K/Akt pathway activity. These findings have important predictive and therapeutic clinical implications.

title: Transcriptome analysis reveals human cytomegalovirus reprograms monocyte differentiation toward an M1 macrophage.
text: Monocytes are the primary target cells for human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) infection, and they are believed to play a crucial role in the hematogenous dissemination of the virus. Upon infection, monocytes undergo a process of polarization, where they differentiate into either a proinflammatory M1 macrophage or an anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage. We hypothesized that HCMV infection induces a proinflammatory M1 macrophage in monocytes to promote viral dissemination, as a proinflammatory state provides the necessary tools for infected monocytes to migrate from the blood into tissues. To test this hypothesis, we used Affymetrix Microarray to analyze the transcriptional profile of HCMV-infected monocytes at a key temporal point following infection. Our results showed that HCMV significantly up-regulated 583 (5.2%) of the total genes and down-regulated 621 (5.5%) of the total genes with a fold change of 1.5 or greater. Ontology analysis revealed that genes involved in classical M1 macrophage activation were significantly stimulated by HCMV infection, with 65% of genes associated with M1 polarization being up-regulated, while only 4% of genes associated with M2 polarization were up-regulated. Additionally, analysis of the monocyte chemokinome at the transcriptional level showed that 44% of M1 and 33% of M2 macrophage chemokines were up-regulated. Proteomic analysis using chemokine Ab arrays confirmed the secretion of these chemotactic proteins from HCMV-infected monocytes. Overall, our findings indicate that the HCMV-infected monocyte transcriptome exhibited a unique M1/M2 polarization signature that was skewed towards the classical M1 activation phenotype.

title: Antithymocyte globulin treatment for patients with recent-onset type 1 diabetes: 12-month results of a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
text:
Type 1 diabetes is caused by the immune system attacking and destroying the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Preclinical studies and early clinical trials have suggested that antithymocyte globulin (ATG), a drug that depletes T cells, may be effective in reducing this autoimmune response. In this phase 2 clinical trial, we evaluated the safety and efficacy of rabbit ATG in preserving islet function in patients with recent-onset type 1 diabetes.
