We randomly assigned 38 patients to receive ATG and 20 patients to receive a placebo over a period of four days. The primary endpoint was the change in C-peptide levels, a measure of beta-cell function, from baseline to 12 months. We found no significant difference in C-peptide levels between the ATG and placebo groups, with a mean change of -0.195 pmol/mL in the ATG group and -0.239 pmol/mL in the placebo group. All but one participant in the ATG group experienced cytokine release syndrome and serum sickness, which was associated with a transient rise in interleukin-6 and acute-phase proteins. ATG treatment also resulted in general T-cell depletion, with slow reconstitution over 12 months, but effector memory T cells were not depleted, and the ratio of regulatory to effector memory T cells declined in the first 6 months and stabilized thereafter. There were more grade 3-4 adverse events in the ATG group than in the placebo group, but no significant difference in the incidence of infectious diseases.
Our findings suggest that a brief course of ATG is not effective in preserving beta-cell function in patients with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. The general depletion of T cells in the absence of specific depletion of effector memory T cells and the preservation of regulatory T cells may be an ineffective treatment for type 1 diabetes.

title: The nucleosome family: dynamic and growing.
text: Since the discovery of the nucleosome in 1974, scientists have discovered a range of discrete particles in which DNA is wrapped around histone complexes with varying stoichiometries, including octasomes, hexasomes, tetrasomes, "split" half-nucleosomes, and more recently, bona fide hemisomes. The question remains as to whether these particles exist in vivo, under what conditions, and what their physiological significance is in the complex DNA transactions within the eukaryotic nucleus. This review summarizes research spanning over three decades and provides a new understanding of the nucleosome, no longer viewed as a single static entity but rather as a family of particles with diverse structural and dynamic properties, leading to different functionalities.

title: Association between serum corin levels and risk of acute myocardial infarction.
text:
BACKGROUND: Emerging evidence suggests that corin plays a crucial role in regulating fluid balance, blood pressure, and cardiac function by activating natriuretic peptides. The present case-control study aimed to investigate the association between serum soluble corin levels and the risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI).
METHODS: We enrolled 856 AMI patients and 856 healthy controls and examined the potential relationship between serum corin levels and AMI risk using logistic regression analysis.
RESULTS: Compared to healthy controls, AMI patients had higher BMI, were less physically active, and were more likely to have histories of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and smoking. Serum levels of corin were significantly lower in AMI patients (825±263pg/ml) compared to healthy controls (1246±425pg/ml). The odds ratios of ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) decreased with increasing levels of serum corin in both men and women after adjusting for body mass index, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, and physical activity (P for trend <0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that serum levels of corin are significantly decreased in AMI patients, and this decrease is associated with an increased risk of STEMI and NSTEMI in both men and women.

title: Crosstalk between the estrogen receptor and the HER tyrosine kinase receptor family: molecular mechanism and clinical implications for endocrine therapy resistance.
text: Breast cancer development and progression are influenced by the intricate interactions between steroid receptors, such as the estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor, and growth factor receptor signaling. In recent years, cancer treatment has witnessed the emergence of various strategies targeting these specific cancer pathways and key molecules (ER and growth factor receptors) to slow or stop tumor growth. However, treatment success has been inconsistent, and both de novo (initial) and acquired resistance have been a challenge. Recent research on ER biology has provided new insights into ER function in breast cancer and highlighted the crucial role of a harmonious interplay between the ER and HER (human epidermal growth factor receptor) signaling pathways in the development of resistance to endocrine therapies targeting the ER pathway. The aim of this review article is to summarize the current understanding of the mechanisms of resistance of breast cancer cells to endocrine therapies due to the crosstalk between the ER and HER signaling pathways and to explore potential new therapeutic approaches that could extend the duration of response and prevent endocrine-resistant tumor growth.

title: Nuclear PTEN functions as an essential regulator of SRF-dependent transcription to control smooth muscle differentiation
text: Vascular disease progression is characterized by significant changes in the phenotype and function of vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs). The expression of contractile genes and differentiation of SMCs are directly regulated by the transcription factor serum response factor (SRF). However, the mechanisms that control the SMC phenotype are not fully understood. Our study reveals that the lipid and protein phosphatase, PTEN, plays a novel role in the nucleus by functioning as a crucial regulator of SRF-mediated differentiation of SMCs. PTEN interacts with the N-terminal domain of SRF and promotes SRF binding to essential promoter elements in SMC-specific genes. The loss of nuclear PTEN due to nucleo-cytoplasmic translocation leads to reduced myogenically active SRF, but enhanced SRF activity on target genes involved in proliferation. Notably, decreased expression of PTEN was observed in intimal SMCs of human atherosclerotic lesions, highlighting the potential clinical significance of these findings.

title: SEROSURVEY FOR FELINE LEUKEMIA VIRUS AND LENTIVIRUSES IN CAPTIVE SMALL NEOTROPIC FELIDS IN SÃO PAULO STATE, BRAZIL
text:
Abstract:
Feline leukemia virus (FeLV), Gammaretrovirus, and feline immunodeficiency virus, a Lentivirus, are members of the Retroviridae family and can establish persistent infections in domestic cats (Felis catus). These viruses can cause cytoproliferative and cytosuppressive disorders, resulting in high morbidity and mortality rates among domestic cats worldwide. The infection of endangered neotropic small felids with these viruses could have devastating consequences. To investigate the prevalence of FeLV and feline lentiviruses in neotropic small felids kept in captivity in São Paulo state, Brazil, serum samples from 104 animals belonging to the species Leopardus pardalis, Leopardus tigrinus, Leopardus wiedii, Herpailurus yaguarondi, and Oncifelis geoffroyi were tested using commercially available immunoassays. The results were negative, suggesting that retrovirus infection is not a significant clinical problem in these populations. Given that domestic cats in São Paulo city are naturally infected with these pathogens, and feral cats are commonly found in zoological facilities in Brazil, preventive measures should be taken to avoid transmission of retroviruses to naive populations of wild and captive neotropic felids in Brazil.
Introduction:
Feline leukemia virus (FeLV), Gammaretrovirus, and feline immunodeficiency virus, a Lentivirus, are members of the Retroviridae family and can establish persistent infections in domestic cats (Felis catus). These viruses can cause cytoproliferative and cytosuppressive disorders, resulting in high morbidity and mortality rates among domestic cats worldwide. The infection of endangered neotropic small felids with these viruses could have devastating consequences.
Methods:
Serum samples from 104 animals belonging to the species Leopardus pardalis, Leopardus tigrinus, Leopardus wiedii, Herpailurus yaguarondi, and Oncifelis geoffroyi kept in captivity in São Paulo state, Brazil, were tested for FeLV and feline lentiviruses using commercially available immunoassays.
Results:
All results were negative, suggesting that retrovirus infection is not a significant clinical problem in these populations.
Discussion:
Given that domestic cats in São Paulo city are naturally infected with these pathogens, and feral cats are commonly found in zoological facilities in Brazil, preventive measures should be taken to avoid transmission of retroviruses to naive populations of wild and captive neotropic felids in Brazil.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, the present study suggests that retrovirus infection is not a significant clinical problem in neotropic small felids kept in captivity in São Paulo state, Brazil. However, given the potential consequences of infection, preventive measures should be taken to avoid transmission of retroviruses to naive populations of wild and captive neotropic felids in Brazil.

title: Comparing the metabolism of quercetin in rats, mice and gerbils
text:
Several rodent species are used to investigate the metabolism of quercetin in vivo, but it is unclear if they are a suitable animal model. To address this, we compared the metabolism of quercetin in Wistar rats, Balb/c mice, and Mongolian gerbils. We measured the levels of quercetin metabolites, such as quercetin-3-glucuronide (Q3G), quercetin-3′-sulfate (Q3′S), and methyl-quercetin isorhamnetin (IH), in the plasma, lungs, and livers of these animals using high-performance liquid chromatography after acute and/or chronic quercetin administration. We also investigated the metabolic enzyme activities in the intestinal mucosal membrane and liver.
Our findings revealed that after acute quercetin administration, the Q3′S level was highest in gerbils. However, after long-term supplementation (20 weeks), Q3G became the dominant metabolite in all animals, followed by IH and Q3′S. Interestingly, the gerbils still had a higher Q3′S conversion ratio compared to the other animals. The average concentrations of total quercetin in the plasma of gerbils were the highest in both short- and long-term studies.
We also observed that the activities of uridine 5′-diphosphate-glucuronosyltransferase, phenolsulfotransferase, and catechol-O-methyltransferase were induced by quercetin in a dose- and tissue-dependent manner in all animals.
In conclusion, while the metabolism of quercetin is similar in all animals after long-term supplementation, the accumulation of quercetin and Q3′S conversion ratio in gerbils are higher than those in the other animals. Therefore, gerbils may be a more suitable animal model for studying the metabolism of quercetin in vivo.

title: Cytokinesis failure generating tetraploids promotes tumorigenesis in p53-null cells
text: A widely accepted theory in the field of tumorigenesis suggests that failure in cell division, leading to the formation of genetically unstable tetraploid cells, can contribute to the development of aneuploid malignancies. To test this hypothesis, we experimentally blocked cytokinesis in p53-null (p53-/-) mouse mammary epithelial cells (MMECs), allowing for the isolation of diploid and tetraploid cultures. Our findings revealed that the tetraploid cells had an increased frequency of whole-chromosome mis-segregation and chromosomal rearrangements. Only the tetraploid cells were transformed in vitro after exposure to a carcinogen, and when transplanted subcutaneously into nude mice, they gave rise to malignant mammary epithelial cancers that contained numerous non-reciprocal translocations and a 8–30-fold amplification of a chromosomal region containing a cluster of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) genes. MMP overexpression is known to be associated with mammary tumors in both humans and animal models, thus supporting the idea that tetraploidy enhances the frequency of chromosomal alterations and promotes tumor development in p53-deficient MMECs.

title: Claspin, a Chk1-regulatory protein, monitors DNA replication on chromatin independently of RPA, ATR, and Rad17.
text: Claspin is essential for the ATR-dependent activation of Chk1 in Xenopus egg extracts containing partially replicated DNA. Our findings show that Claspin interacts with chromatin in a regulated manner during S phase. The binding of Claspin to chromatin is dependent on the pre-replication complex (pre-RC) and Cdc45, but not on replication protein A (RPA). These dependencies suggest that Claspin binds to chromatin at the initiation of DNA unwinding, around replication origins. In contrast, both ATR and Rad17 require RPA for association with DNA. Notably, Claspin, ATR, and Rad17 can bind to chromatin independently. These results suggest that Claspin plays a crucial role in monitoring DNA replication during S phase. Moreover, these proteins may cooperate in checkpoint regulation by detecting distinct aspects of the DNA replication fork.

title: Cold-related respiratory symptoms in the general population.
text: The prevalence and threshold temperatures of self-reported respiratory symptoms related to cold exposure were investigated in a large population-based study. The study included 6,591 men and women aged 25-74 years from the national FINRISK study, with a focus on healthy individuals and those with respiratory diseases such as asthma and chronic bronchitis. The results showed that cold-related respiratory symptoms were more common among individuals with respiratory diseases, with a threshold temperature for symptom onset of -14°C for males and -15°C for females. The threshold temperature increased with age, and was higher among individuals with asthma and chronic bronchitis. The study suggests that cold-related respiratory symptoms may have a significant impact on health-related quality of life in cold climates, particularly among individuals with respiratory diseases.

title: Carvedilol for children and adolescents with heart failure: a randomized controlled trial.
text: Although beta-blockers have been shown to improve symptoms and survival in adults with heart failure, little is known about their effectiveness in children and adolescents. To investigate this, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was conducted among 161 children and adolescents with symptomatic systemic ventricular systolic dysfunction. The study found that carvedilol, a beta-blocker, did not significantly improve clinical heart failure outcomes in children and adolescents with symptomatic systolic heart failure. However, the study may have been underpowered, and there may be a differential effect of carvedilol based on ventricular morphology. Further research is needed to determine the safety and efficacy of beta-blockers in this population.

title: The circadian clock gene BMAL1 is a novel therapeutic target for malignant pleural mesothelioma.
text:
Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is a highly aggressive and poorly prognostic neoplasm that originates from the mesothelial cells lining the parietal pleura. Despite significant advances in MPM treatment, the development of more effective therapeutic strategies remains crucial. Recently, BMAL1, a core component of the circadian clock machinery, has been found to be overexpressed in MPM. In this study, we investigated the potential of BMAL1 as a molecular target for MPM.
Our results showed that BMAL1 is overexpressed in the majority of MPM cell lines and a subset of clinical specimens compared to a nontumorigenic mesothelial cell line (MeT-5A) and normal parietal pleural tissue, respectively. Interestingly, a serum shock induced a rhythmic BMAL1 expression change in MeT-5A, suggesting that the circadian rhythm pathway is deregulated in MPM cells.
To further investigate the role of BMAL1 in MPM, we conducted a knockdown experiment using two MPM cell lines (ACC-MESO-1 and H290). Our findings showed that BMAL1 knockdown suppressed proliferation and anchorage-dependent and independent clonal growth in both cell lines, but not in MeT-5A. Additionally, BMAL1 depletion resulted in cell cycle disruption, accompanied by upregulation of apoptotic and polyploidy cell populations, downregulation of Wee1, cyclin B, and p21(WAF1/CIP1), and upregulation of cyclin E expression. Notably, BMAL1 knockdown induced mitotic catastrophe, characterized by disruption of cell cycle regulators and induction of drastic morphological changes, including micronucleation and multiple nuclei, in ACC-MESO-1 cells that expressed the highest level of BMAL1.
In conclusion, our findings suggest that BMAL1 plays a critical role in MPM and could serve as an attractive therapeutic target for this aggressive neoplasm.

title: Mechanism and Regulation of DNA-Protein Crosslink Repair by the DNA-Dependent Metalloprotease SPRTN
text: Covalent DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs) are harmful DNA lesions that interfere with crucial chromatin processes, such as replication and transcription. Prior to the recent discovery of a DPC-processing enzyme in yeast, little was known about the specific repair mechanisms for DPCs. In higher eukaryotes, the existence of a DPC protease is inferred from data in Xenopus laevis egg extracts, but its identity remains elusive. Here, we identify the metalloprotease SPRTN as the DPC protease acting in metazoans. Loss of SPRTN function leads to an inability to repair DPCs and increased sensitivity to DPC-inducing agents. SPRTN accomplishes DPC processing through a unique DNA-induced protease activity, which is regulated by multiple sophisticated regulatory mechanisms. Cellular, biochemical, and structural studies reveal a DNA switch that triggers its protease activity, a ubiquitin switch that controls SPRTN chromatin accessibility, and regulatory autocatalytic cleavage. Our findings also provide a molecular explanation for how SPRTN deficiency causes the premature aging and cancer predisposition disorder Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome.

title: 'Zero is not good for me': implications of infertility in Ghana.
text: BACKGROUND In sub-Saharan Africa, children are highly valued, and as such, infertility has been found to increase the risk of psychological distress, marital conflict, and risky sexual behavior, while also depriving individuals and couples of an important source of economic and social capital. This study aims to explore the implications of infertility for women in Ghana, West Africa, through a qualitative analysis of semi-structured interview data collected from 107 women seeking treatment in gynecological and obstetric clinics in Accra, Ghana. METHODS The analysis of the interview data focused on mental health, marital stability, social interactions, and gendered experiences. RESULTS The findings reveal that infertile women in Ghana face significant social stigma, marital strain, and mental health difficulties. Many women feel that they are disproportionately blamed for infertility and its consequences, leading to greater social consequences for women than for male partners. Corroborative findings were also obtained from women who do not self-identify as infertile, who emphasize the severe social consequences of infertility, particularly for women. CONCLUSIONS Infertility in Ghana has significant implications for social interactions, marital stability, and mental health, with women bearing a disproportionate burden of these consequences. These findings highlight the need for greater awareness and support for individuals and couples affected by infertility in Ghana.

title: Ethical dilemmas in a randomized trial of asthma treatment: can Bayesian statistical analysis explain the results?
text:
Objective:
The original objective of this study was to determine whether the use of bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) ventilation would reduce the need for endotracheal intubation, the length of hospital stay, and hospital charges in patients with status asthmaticus. However, due to the development of physician treatment bias, patient enrollment became difficult, and the study was subsequently conducted using Bayesian statistics to explain the study results when this bias occurs.
Methods:
This study was a prospective, randomized controlled clinical trial conducted over a 34.5-month period at an urban university hospital with an emergency department census of 94,000 annual visits. Patients remaining in status asthmaticus after initial standard treatment with inhaled beta-agonists and steroids were randomized to receive BiPAP ventilation plus standard treatment versus standard treatment alone (non-BiPAP), with intubation for either group as needed. Patients with concurrent cardiac or other pulmonary diseases were excluded. The primary outcome measures were endotracheal intubation rate and length of hospital stay. Secondary outcome measures included vital signs (respiratory rate, pulse rate, blood pressure), changes in expiratory peak flow, changes in pulse oximetry values, and hospital charges. Data were analyzed using Fisher's exact test, Mann-Whitney tests, and Bayesian statistics. For patients enrolled in the study more than once, data analysis was performed on the first enrollment only.
Results:
Nineteen patients were enrolled in the BiPAP group and 16 patients in the non-BiPAP group. Patients were frequently enrolled more than once, and the data from the subsequent enrollments were excluded from the analysis. A marked decrease in enrollment due to physician treatment bias led to a premature termination of the study. Demographics showed that the groups were similar in age, sex, initial peak flow rate, and arterial blood gas measurements. There was a 7.3% increase (95% CI = -22 to +45) in the intubation rate in the non-BiPAP group (n = 2) compared with that for the BiPAP group (n = 1). No significant difference was seen in length of hospital stay or hospital charges, although there was a favorable trend toward the BiPAP group. Complications encountered in the BiPAP group included one patient with discomfort associated with the nasal BiPAP mask. Bayesian analysis demonstrated that in order for the collected data to be convincing at the 95% confidence level, the prior conviction among treating physicians that BiPAP was a successful treatment modality would have had to be 98.9%.

Conclusion:
In this study, BiPAP appeared to have no deleterious effects in patients with status asthmaticus, with a trend toward decreased endotracheal intubation rate, decreased length of hospital stay, and decreased hospital charges. Although further study with more patients is needed to determine the clinical and statistical significance of this intervention, ethical concerns regarding withholding BiPAP treatment from the patients in the control group forced a premature termination of the study in the authors' institution.

title: Mental health in prison populations. A review--with special emphasis on a study of Danish prisoners on remand.
text:
OBJECTIVE: To conduct a comprehensive review of the literature on mental health and psychiatric morbidity in prison populations, and to compare the findings with a Danish study on remand prisoners.
METHOD: The literature was systematically reviewed and categorized into the following sections:
1. Validity of psychometrics in prison populations
2. Prevalence of psychiatric disorders prior to imprisonment
3. Incidence of psychiatric disorders during imprisonment
4. Psychopathy related to psychiatric comorbidity
5. Dependence syndromes, with a focus on different administration of heroin use (smoke vs. injection)

RESULTS: The review revealed several key findings:

1. Prison populations worldwide are increasing, and this growth is expected to continue in the coming years.
2. Psychometrics may perform differently in prison populations compared to general populations, with the General Health Questionnaire-28 having low validity in remand prisoners.
3. Psychiatric morbidity, including schizophrenia, is higher and perhaps increasing in prison populations compared to general populations. Dependence syndromes are the most common disorders in this population.
4. The early phase of imprisonment is a vulnerable period with a moderately high incidence of adjustment disorders, and twice the incidence in solitary confinement (SC) compared to non-SC.
5. Prevalence of psychopathy is lower in European than North American prisons. Medium to high scores of psychopathy are related to higher psychiatric comorbidity.
6. Opioid dependence is the most common drug disorder, with subjects using injection representing a more dysfunctional group than subjects using smoke administration.

CONCLUSION: The findings of this review suggest that there is a growing population of mentally ill prisoners who are insufficiently detected and treated. This highlights the need for improved detection and treatment of mental health disorders in prison populations, particularly in the early phase of imprisonment.

title: Why females live longer than males: control of longevity by sex hormones.
text: Females generally exhibit a longer lifespan than males in various species, including humans. Research has identified a possible explanation for this phenomenon, which involves the beneficial effects of estrogens on longevity. Estrogens bind to estrogen receptors and upregulate the expression of genes associated with longevity, such as those encoding antioxidant enzymes like superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase. As a result, mitochondria from female cells produce fewer reactive oxygen species than those from male cells. While administering estrogens has potential benefits, such as increasing longevity, it also has limitations, including feminizing effects and an increased risk of diseases like uterine cancer in postmenopausal women. Phytoestrogens, found in soy or wine, may offer some of the favorable effects of estrogens without the adverse consequences. Investigating gender differences in longevity can provide valuable insights into the aging process and inform strategies to enhance the lifespan of both females and males.

title: The pre-B-cell receptor: selector of fitting immunoglobulin heavy chains for the B-cell repertoire
text:
In this Opinion piece, I delve into the role of the pre-B-cell receptor (pre-BCR) in the development of antigen-specific B cells, focusing on aspects such as IgH variable-region repertoire selection, precursor B-cell differentiation and proliferation, and IgH allelic exclusion. By comparing the pre-BCR with the pre-T-cell receptor (pre-TCR) in T-cell development, I raise intriguing questions about the similarities and differences between these two lymphocyte lineages.
Why do B- and T-cell lineages both utilize a surrogate chain – the surrogate light chain and the pre-TCR α-chain, respectively – during their development? What are the specific functions of the pre-BCR and pre-TCR in lymphocyte differentiation and antigen-receptor allelic exclusion? This article, in conjunction with the accompanying piece by Harald von Boehmer, aims to provide some insightful answers to these queries.

title: Helicobacter species methods and protocols. Introduction.
text: Helicobacter infection is a chronic and persistent condition that accounts for the majority of cases of gastric and duodenal ulcers, as well as gastric cancer. The study of this bacterium, its interaction with the host, and the host's immune response has greatly benefited from the standardization of culture techniques and the use of animal models. The following chapters will delve into the clinical aspects of infection and provide guidance on the most effective methods for investigating this infection.

title: Effectiveness of statin-eluting stent on early inflammatory response and neointimal thickness in a porcine coronary model.
text:
Background: Drug-eluting stents (DES) have become the standard of care during coronary revascularization due to their ability to significantly reduce rates of restenosis and target lesion revascularization compared to bare metal stents (BMS). However, DES have limitations, including delayed healing and persistent local inflammation, which can lead to late thrombosis. Statins have been shown to inhibit cell proliferation, inflammation, and restore endothelial function. The present study aimed to evaluate the potential of stent-based cerivastatin delivery to reduce stent-induced inflammatory responses and adverse effects on endothelial function, while inhibiting neointimal hyperplasia in a porcine coronary model.
Methods and Results: Nine pigs were randomly assigned to groups in which the coronary arteries (18 coronaries per group) received either a cerivastatin-eluting stent (CES) or a BMS. All animals survived without any adverse effects. Scanning electron microscopy revealed a significant decrease in inflammatory cell infiltration on day 3 after stenting in the treated vessels (inflammation score: 1.15±0.12 vs 2.43±0.34, p<0.0001). At day 28, endothelial function was preserved in both the CES and BMS groups, as evaluated by intracoronary bradykinin infusion. Volumetric intravascular ultrasound imaging revealed decreased intimal volume in the CES group (28.3±5.4 vs 75.9±4.2 mm3, p<0.0001). Histomorphometric analysis showed reduced neointimal area (1.74±0.45 vs 3.83±0.51 mm2, p<0.0001) in the CES group, despite similar injury scores (1.77±0.30 vs 1.77±0.22, p=0.97).
Conclusion: In porcine coronary arteries, CES significantly decreased neointimal hyperplasia with a decreased early inflammatory response and without endothelial dysfunction. These findings suggest that stent-based cerivastatin delivery may be a promising approach to reduce adverse effects associated with DES implantation.

title: Genetic variation in West Nile virus from naturally infected mosquitoes and birds suggests quasispecies structure and strong purifying selection.
text: In this study, the genetic diversity of West Nile virus (WNV) was examined in naturally infected mosquitoes and birds on Long Island, NY, during the peak transmission season of 2003. The researchers analyzed the WNV genome by cloning and sequencing a 1938 nucleotide fragment comprising the 3' end of the envelope (E) coding region and the 5' end of the non-structural protein 1 (NS1) coding region from 20 clones per specimen. The results showed that WNV infections are derived from a genetically diverse population of genomes in nature, with a mean nucleotide diversity of 0.016% within individual specimens and a mean of 19.5% of clones differing from the consensus sequence. The study found that WNV sequences in mosquitoes were more genetically diverse than in birds, and there was no host-dependent bias for particular types of mutations. Additionally, non-consensus clones obtained from two avian specimens had highly similar genetic signatures, suggesting that WNV genetic diversity may be maintained throughout the enzootic transmission cycle. The study also provided evidence of purifying selection in both intra- and interhost WNV populations. Overall, these findings support the idea that WNV populations may be structured as a quasispecies and demonstrate strong purifying natural selection in WNV populations.

title: Overlapping patterns of IGF2 and H19 expression during human development: biallelic IGF2 expression correlates with a lack of H19 expression.
text: The spatial distribution of IGF2 and H19 gene expression exhibits striking similarities during certain stages of human embryonic/fetal and early postnatal development. However, there are some notable exceptions, such as the ciliary anlage of the embryonic retina and the choroid plexus/leptomeninges, where IGF2 transcripts were detected but not H19. In contrast, the choroid plexus/leptomeninges expressed both parental IGF2 alleles, whereas RNase protection analysis revealed weak activity of the P1 promoter and active P2, P3, and P4 promoters throughout the tissue. These observations suggest a coordinated control of the reciprocally imprinted and closely linked IGF2 and H19 loci.

title: Intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation after balloon catheter injury. The role of basic fibroblast growth factor.
text: The study investigated the localization and synthesis of basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) in the rat carotid artery during periods of chronic smooth muscle cell proliferation. Immunocytochemical staining revealed the presence of bFGF in the uninjured arterial wall, and after balloon injury, this cellular staining decreased. Western and northern blot analyses also showed that the amount of bFGF protein and mRNA decreased after injury. To further explore the role of bFGF in chronic smooth muscle cell proliferation, a neutralizing antibody to bFGF was administered 4 and 5 days after injury, but this had no effect on intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation. These findings suggest that an increase in bFGF expression is not necessary for the chronic smooth muscle cell proliferation observed after balloon catheter injury, and that bFGF is not the primary mitogen responsible for intimal smooth muscle cell proliferation.

title: Prevention of central venous catheter-associated thrombosis: a meta-analysis.
text:
PURPOSE: Anticoagulant prophylaxis in patients with central venous catheters is a controversial topic. To address this, we conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to evaluate the effectiveness of anticoagulant prophylaxis in preventing catheter-associated deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive search of major databases, including MEDLINE and EMBASE, up to May 2006, supplemented by manual searches of conference proceedings and bibliographies. We included randomized controlled trials that evaluated the use of anticoagulant prophylaxis in patients with central venous catheters.
RESULTS: Our meta-analysis included 15 randomized controlled trials that evaluated the effectiveness of different anticoagulant regimens, including unfractionated heparin infusion, oral fixed low-dose vitamin K antagonist, and subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin. Our findings showed that anticoagulant prophylaxis is effective in preventing all catheter-associated DVT in patients with central venous catheters, with summary relative risks ranging from 0.31 to 0.73 across all trials (achieving statistical significance for all regimens). However, the effectiveness of anticoagulant prophylaxis in preventing symptomatic DVT, including pulmonary embolism, remains uncertain.
CONCLUSION: Our meta-analysis provides evidence that anticoagulant prophylaxis is effective in preventing catheter-associated DVT in patients with central venous catheters. However, further research is needed to determine the effectiveness of anticoagulant prophylaxis in preventing symptomatic DVT, including pulmonary embolism.

title: Long-term efficacy of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation in adolescents: a randomized controlled trial.
text:
A double-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted among Dutch adolescents to evaluate the short-term efficacy of nicotine patches compared to placebo patches in helping them quit smoking. The study found that nicotine patches were effective in reducing smoking at the end of treatment, but only among highly compliant participants. The study then examined whether the effects of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) held at 6- and 12-month follow-ups.
The study included 257 adolescents aged 12-18 years who smoked at least seven cigarettes a day and were motivated to quit smoking. Participants were randomly assigned to either a nicotine patch or placebo patch condition using a computer-generated list. The study consisted of an information meeting followed by a 6- or 9-week treatment. Smoking cessation, compliance, and potential covariates were measured using online questionnaires, and smoking cessation at T8 was biochemically validated by saliva cotinine.
The results showed that at T7, 8.1% and 5.7% of participants in the nicotine and placebo patch groups, respectively, were abstinent. At T8, abstinence was 4.4% and 6.6%, respectively. Intention-to-treat analyses revealed no significant effects of NRT on abstinence rates at T7 (odds ratio [OR] = 1.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.57, 4.16) and validated abstinence rates at T8 (OR = 0.64, 95% CI = 0.21, 1.93) neither after considering compliance nor after adjusting for covariates.
In conclusion, the study found that NRT fails in helping adolescents quit smoking at 6- and 12-month follow-ups. This suggests that a more intensive approach is needed to assist youngsters in their quit attempts.

title: Interferon gamma in autoimmunity: A complicated player on a complex stage.
text: Early perceptions of autoimmune disease viewed interferon gamma (IFNγ) as a prototypical pro-inflammatory factor. However, recent discoveries have revealed that IFNγ can exhibit both pro- and anti-inflammatory activities, with the final outcome depending on the physiological or pathological context being examined. In this review, we will discuss the major immune-modulatory activities of IFNγ and summarize current evidence for its impact on disease pathology and regulation in various autoimmune diseases and disease models.

title: The first gene of the Bacillus subtilis clpC operon, ctsR, encodes a negative regulator of its own operon and other class III heat shock genes.
text: The Bacillus subtilis clpC operon is regulated by two distinct stress response pathways, involving either σB or a class III stress response mechanism, which act on a σA-like promoter. When the clpC operon was placed under the control of an inducible Pspac promoter, we observed significant repression of the natural clpC promoters fused to a β-galactosidase (lacZ) reporter gene upon IPTG induction. This result suggests that one of the clpC gene products acts as a negative regulator of the operon. We identified the negative regulator, encoded by the first gene of the clpC operon, ctsR, which contains a predicted helix-turn-helix DNA-binding motif. Deletion of ctsR abolished negative regulation and resulted in high expression of both the clpC operon and the clpP gene under non-stressed conditions. However, we observed additional increases in clpC and clpP mRNA levels after heat shock, even in the absence of σB, suggesting a second induction mechanism at the vegetative promoter. Using two-dimensional gel analysis and mRNA studies, we found that the expression of other class III stress genes was at least partially influenced by the ctsR deletion. Further experiments using clpC promoter fragments fused to the reporter gene bgaB or used in gel mobility shift assays with the purified CtsR protein revealed a potential target region where the repressor binds in vivo and in vitro. Our data demonstrate that the CtsR protein acts as a global repressor of the clpC operon, as well as other class III heat shock genes, by preventing unstressed transcription from either the σB- or σA-dependent promoter, and may be inactivated or dissociate under inducing stress conditions.

title: Role for c-myc in activation-induced apoptotic cell death in T cell hybridomas.
text: Immature T cells and certain T cell hybridomas undergo programmed cell death, or apoptosis, when activated through their T cell receptor complex, a phenomenon that is likely linked to the negative selection of developing T cells induced by antigens. This activation-induced apoptosis requires the cells to be actively producing proteins and RNA, although the specific genes involved in this process have not been previously identified. Using antisense oligonucleotides targeting the c-myc gene, we found that inhibiting c-Myc protein expression in T cell hybridomas prevents all aspects of activation-induced apoptosis without affecting the production of lymphokines in these cells. These findings suggest that c-Myc expression is a crucial component of activation-induced apoptosis.

title: Examining BCL-2 family function with large unilamellar vesicles.
text:
The BCL-2 family of proteins, consisting of approximately 20 members, plays a crucial role in regulating cell survival and apoptosis. These proteins interact with each other to maintain cell survival or initiate apoptosis, a process of programmed cell death, in response to cellular stress. The BCL-2 family can be divided into two subgroups: pro-apoptotic proteins, such as BAK and BAX, which promote apoptosis by compromising the integrity of the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), and anti-apoptotic proteins, such as BCL-2 and BCL-xL, which inhibit apoptosis by tightly controlling the interactions between pro-apoptotic proteins and other BCL-2 family members.
In order for BAK/BAX to induce MOMP (mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization), they require transient interactions with BH3-only proteins, such as BID, which are also pro-apoptotic. Anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, such as BCL-2 related gene, long isoform, and MCL-1, regulate cellular survival by controlling the interactions between BAK/BAX and BH3-only proteins. Additionally, the availability of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins is also dictated by sensitizer/de-repressor BH3-only proteins, such as BAD or PUMA, which bind and inhibit anti-apoptotic members.
The cellular decision to maintain survival or induce MOMP is dictated by multiple BCL-2 family interactions at the OMM. Large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) are a biochemical model to explore relationships between BCL-2 family interactions and membrane permeabilization. LUVs are comprised of defined lipids that are assembled in ratios identified in lipid composition studies from solvent extracted Xenopus mitochondria. This model system allows for direct exploration of BCL-2 family function because the protein and lipid components are completely defined and tractable.
In this study, recombinant BCL-2 family protein combinations and controls are used in LUVs containing a polyanionic dye (ANTS: 8-aminonaphthalene-1,3,6-trisulfonic acid) and cationic quencher (DPX: p-xylene-bis-pyridinium bromide) to measure membrane permeabilization in real-time. As the LUVs permeabilize, ANTS and DPX diffuse apart, and a gain in fluorescence is detected. This protocol allows for kinetic analyses of protein interactions and real-time measurements of membrane permeabilization, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms of BCL-2 family function.

title: The Hippo pathway effector YAP controls mouse hepatic stellate cell activation.
text:
Hepatic stellate cell activation is a natural response to liver injury, but prolonged activation leads to excessive matrix production and the formation of scar tissue, ultimately causing fibrosis and cirrhosis. While several signaling pathways have been identified that promote stellate cell activation, the mechanisms that trigger and drive early activation are not well understood.
We discovered the Hippo pathway and its effector, YAP, as a crucial regulator of stellate cell activation. YAP is a transcriptional co-activator that drives early changes in gene expression during stellate cell activation. In vivo and in vitro activation of stellate cells leads to rapid YAP activation, as evidenced by its nuclear translocation and induction of YAP target genes. Similarly, YAP is activated in human fibrotic livers, as demonstrated by its nuclear localization. Importantly, inhibition of YAP expression or pharmacological inhibition of YAP prevents stellate cell activation in vitro and impedes fibrogenesis in mice.
Our findings suggest that inhibition of YAP presents a novel approach for the treatment of liver fibrosis.

title: Human Monocytes Engage an Alternative Inflammasome Pathway.
text: Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) is a cytokine whose activity is regulated by the inflammasome, a complex of proteins that triggers its release. However, in response to lipopolysaccharide, human monocytes produce IL-1β independently of classical inflammasome stimuli. This unique response was found to be species-specific and not observed in mice. In fact, lipopolysaccharide triggered an "alternative inflammasome" in human monocytes that relied on NLRP3-ASC-caspase-1 signaling, but lacked the classical inflammasome characteristics of pyroptosome formation, pyroptosis induction, and K(+) efflux dependency. By analyzing the underlying signaling pathway in a monocyte transdifferentiation system, researchers discovered that alternative inflammasome activation was propagated by TLR4-TRIF-RIPK1-FADD-CASP8 signaling upstream of NLRP3. Notably, this signaling cascade only played a role in alternative inflammasome activation and did not extend to classical NLRP3 activation. The findings suggest a crucial role for this signaling cascade in TLR4-driven, IL-1β-mediated immune responses and immunopathology in humans.

title: The use of biosimilars in immune-mediated disease: A joint Italian Society of Rheumatology (SIR), Italian Society of Dermatology (SIDeMaST), and Italian Group of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IG-IBD) position paper.
text: Biological agents are widely used in rheumatology, dermatology, and inflammatory bowel disease. Over the past decade, there has been a strengthening of evidence regarding their efficacy and safety across all therapeutic indications. Biosimilar agents are monoclonal antibodies similar to previously approved biologics. In the European Union, they have been approved for all indications in the management of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs), although data are currently available only for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. Direct evidence on the efficacy, safety, and immunogenicity of biosimilars is mandatory in psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease, as well as in children. Based on the current evidence in the literature, we present the joint official position of the Italian Societies of Rheumatology, Dermatology, and Inflammatory Bowel Disease on the use of biosimilars in IMIDs.

title: The coordination of cyclic microtubule association/dissociation and tail swing of cytoplasmic dynein.
text: The dynein motor domain is composed of three parts: the tail, head, and stalk. It is believed to generate force against microtubules by swinging the tail back and forth during its ATPase cycle. To do this, dynein must coordinate the tail swing with the association/dissociation of microtubules at the stalk tip. Although the former process is becoming clearer, the latter remains unknown. Using a single-headed recombinant dynein motor domain from Dictyostelium, we investigated how the motor domain interacts with microtubules, how the two mechanical cycles are coordinated, and which ATPase site regulates this coordination. Our findings show that the two mechanical cycles proceed simultaneously at most intermediate states in the ATPase cycle. The motor domain in the post-stroke state binds strongly to the microtubule with a dissociation constant (Kd) of approximately 0.2 microM, while most of the motor domains in the prestroke state bind weakly to the microtubule with a Kd of >10 microM. However, our results suggest that the timings of microtubule affinity changes and tail swings are staggered at the recovery stroke step in which the tail swings from the post-stroke to the prestroke position. The ATPase site in the AAA1 module of the motor domain is responsible for coordinating these two mechanical processes.

title: A conserved modified wobble nucleoside (mcm5s2U) in lysyl-tRNA is required for viability in yeast.
text:
Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) specific to Gln, Lys, and Glu from all organisms (except Mycoplasma) contain a 2-thiouridine derivative (xm(5)s(2)U) in the wobble position. These tRNAs read the A- and G-ending codons in the split codon boxes His/Gln, Asn/Lys, and Asp/Glu. In eukaryotic cytoplasmic tRNAs, the conserved constituent (xm(5)-) in position 5 of uridine is 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl (mcm(5)). A protein (Tuc1p) from yeast similar to the bacterial protein TtcA, which is required for the synthesis of 2-thiocytidine in position 32 of the tRNA, was found to be responsible for the synthesis of 2-thiouridine in the wobble position (position 34) in tRNAs from organisms from the domains Eukarya and Archaea. Deletion of the TUC1 gene along with a deletion of the ELP3 gene, which results in the lack of the mcm(5) side chain, removes all modifications from the wobble uridine derivatives of the cytoplasmic tRNAs specific for Gln, Lys, and Glu. Surprisingly, overexpression of the mcm(5)s(2)U-lacking tRNA(Lys) alone was sufficient to restore viability in the double mutant.
The study suggests that the primary function of mcm(5)s(2)U34 is to improve the efficiency of reading the cognate codons rather than to prevent mis-sense errors. The presence of the mcm(5) side chain in the wobble position enhances the ability of the tRNA to recognize and bind to the correct codon, leading to improved translation efficiency.

title: The molecular requirements for cytokinesis.
text: After anaphase, animal cells form an actomyosin contractile ring that constricts the plasma membrane to separate the two daughter cells. This process is completed through the severing of a cytoplasmic bridge, which is ultimately achieved through the coordinated action of a core set of approximately 20 proteins in most animal cells. These components are involved in the contractile ring, central spindle, RhoA signaling pathway, and on vesicles that expand the membrane and sever the bridge. While additional proteins may be involved in cytokinesis, their specific functions and conservation across animal cells are not as well-defined.

title: Ibuprofen for the treatment of patent ductus arteriosus in preterm or low birth weight (or both) infants.
text: The text discusses the effectiveness and safety of ibuprofen compared to indomethacin in closing a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in newborn infants. The authors analyzed 33 studies involving 2190 infants and found that ibuprofen was as effective as indomethacin in closing the PDA, with a reduced risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and transient renal insufficiency. The study also found that oral ibuprofen was as effective as iv administration and that high-dose iv ibuprofen was more effective than standard-dose iv ibuprofen. However, the authors noted that more research is needed to determine the optimal dosage and administration route of ibuprofen, as well as its long-term effects on infants with PDA.

title: A gradient of template dependence defines distinct biological roles for family X polymerases in nonhomologous end joining.
text: Three members of the Pol X family have been linked to nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) in mammals. Template-independent TdT promotes diversity during NHEJ-dependent repair of V(D)J recombination intermediates, but the roles of the template-dependent polymerases mu and lambda in NHEJ remain unclear. Our study shows that both pol mu and pol lambda are recruited by NHEJ factors to fill gaps when ends have partially complementary overhangs, suggesting equivalent roles in promoting accuracy in NHEJ. However, only pol mu promotes accuracy during immunoglobulin kappa recombination, a distinctive in vivo role that correlates with pol mu's TdT-like ability to act when primer termini lack complementary bases in the template strand. Unlike TdT, synthesis by pol mu in this context is primarily instructed by a template from another DNA molecule, resulting in an apparent gradient of template dependence that is largely attributable to a small structural element present in all three polymerases.

title: Involvement of sympathetic nervous system and brown fat in endotoxin-induced fever in rats.
text: The aim of this study was to investigate the role of brown adipose tissue (BAT) and the sympathetic nervous system in the increase in body heat production that occurs during endotoxin-induced fever. The study found that after two doses of endotoxin (Escherichia coli lipopolysaccharide) given 24 hours apart, oxygen consumption (VO2) increased by 28% over a 4-hour period. Injection of a mixed beta-adrenoceptor antagonist (propranolol) reduced VO2 by 14% in endotoxin-treated rats, while selective beta 1- (atenolol) or beta 2- (ICI 118551) antagonists suppressed VO2 by 10%. These drugs had no effect on VO2 in control animals. The study also found that BAT thermogenic activity, as measured by in vitro mitochondrial guanosine 5'-diphosphate (GDP) binding, was elevated by 54% in one BAT depot and by 171% in other BAT depots. Surgical denervation of one lobe of the interscapular depot prevented these responses. The study found that endotoxin failed to stimulate GDP binding in rats fed protein-deficient diets, which may have been due to either BAT thermogenic activity already being elevated in control rats fed these diets or endotoxin causing a significant suppression of food intake in protein-deficient animals. The results suggest that sympathetic activation of BAT is involved in the thermogenic responses to endotoxin and that these responses can be modified by dietary manipulation.

title: Metabolic, Epigenetic, and Transgenerational Effects of Gut Bacterial Choline Consumption.
text: Choline is a crucial nutrient and methyl donor that plays a vital role in epigenetic regulation. In this study, we investigated the impact of gut microbial choline metabolism on bacterial fitness and host biology by engineering a microbial community lacking a single choline-utilizing enzyme. Our findings indicate that choline-utilizing bacteria compete with the host for this nutrient, leading to significant alterations in plasma and hepatic levels of methyl-donor metabolites and recapitulating biochemical signatures of choline deficiency. Mice harboring high levels of choline-consuming bacteria exhibited increased susceptibility to metabolic disease in the context of a high-fat diet. Moreover, bacterially induced reduction of methyl-donor availability influenced global DNA methylation patterns in both adult mice and their offspring, leading to behavioral alterations. Our results demonstrate an unappreciated effect of bacterial choline metabolism on host metabolism, epigenetics, and behavior, highlighting the importance of considering interpersonal differences in microbial metabolism when determining optimal nutrient intake requirements.

title: Genome-wide analysis reveals SR protein cooperation and competition in regulated splicing.
text: SR proteins, which are well-characterized RNA binding proteins, play a crucial role in promoting exon inclusion by binding to exonic splicing enhancers (ESEs). However, it has been unclear whether the regulatory rules deduced from studies on model genes apply more broadly to the activities of SR proteins in the cell. To address this question, we conducted global analyses of two prototypical SR proteins, SRSF1 (SF2/ASF) and SRSF2 (SC35), using splicing-sensitive arrays and CLIP-seq on mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs). Surprisingly, we found that these SR proteins promote both inclusion and skipping of exons in vivo, despite their binding patterns not fully explaining such opposite responses. Further investigation revealed that loss of one SR protein is often accompanied by coordinated loss or compensatory gain in the interaction of other SR proteins at the affected exons. These findings suggest that specific effects on regulated splicing by one SR protein actually depend on a complex network of relationships with multiple other SR proteins in mammalian genomes.

title: Human tuberculous granulomas induce peripheral lymphoid follicle-like structures to orchestrate local host defence in the lung.
text: The human tuberculous granuloma provides a structural framework for local immune processes that determine the outcome of tuberculosis. Due to the limited understanding of these processes in human patients, the current study aimed to gain insights into the functional and structural properties of infected tissue. To achieve this, the study investigated the mycobacterial load in lesions and distribution to different tissue locations, as well as the distribution, functions, and interactions of host immune cells. Early granuloma formation in previously healthy lung tissue was analyzed to identify a spatio-temporal sequence of cellular infiltration to sites of mycobacterial infection. A general structure of the developing granuloma was identified, consisting of an inner cell layer with few CD8+ cells surrounding the necrotic center and an outer area of lymphocyte infiltration harboring mycobacteria-containing antigen-presenting cells, as well as CD4+, CD8+, and B cells in active follicle-like centers resembling secondary lymphoid organs. It is concluded that the follicular structures in the peripheral rim of granulomas serve as a morphological basis for the sustained host response in pulmonary tuberculosis.

title: Eosinophil pathogenicity mechanisms and therapeutics in neuromyelitis optica.
text:
Eosinophils are conspicuously abundant in inflammatory demyelinating lesions observed in neuromyelitis optica (NMO). To investigate the role of eosinophils in NMO pathogenesis and the potential therapeutic utility of eosinophil inhibitors, we employed a variety of experimental approaches, including cell culture, ex vivo spinal cord slices, and in vivo mouse models of NMO.
In vitro studies revealed that eosinophils isolated from mouse bone marrow exhibited antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) against cells expressing aquaporin-4 in the presence of NMO autoantibody (NMO-IgG). Moreover, the presence of complement significantly enhanced the cytotoxic activity of eosinophils through a complement-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (CDCC) mechanism. In ex vivo spinal cord slice cultures, NMO pathology was induced by the inclusion of eosinophils or their granule toxins, and the second-generation antihistamines cetirizine and ketotifen, which have eosinophil-stabilizing actions, significantly reduced NMO-IgG/eosinophil-dependent cytotoxicity and NMO pathology.
In vivo studies conducted in live mice demonstrated that demyelinating NMO lesions produced by continuous intracerebral injection of NMO-IgG and complement were characterized by marked eosinophil infiltration. Lesion severity was found to be increased in transgenic hypereosinophilic mice, but was reduced in mice made hypoeosinophilic by anti-IL-5 antibody or by gene deletion, and in normal mice receiving cetirizine orally.
Our findings suggest that eosinophils play a significant role in NMO pathogenesis through ADCC and CDCC mechanisms, and that approved eosinophil-stabilizing drugs may have therapeutic utility in the treatment of NMO.

title: Association of cystic fibrosis with abnormalities in fatty acid metabolism.
text:
Background: Patients with cystic fibrosis have been found to have altered levels of plasma fatty acids. Previous studies have demonstrated that arachidonic acid levels are increased and docosahexaenoic acid levels are decreased in tissues from cystic fibrosis-knockout mice. This study aimed to investigate whether similar fatty acid defects are present in humans with mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene.
Methods: Fatty acids were analyzed from nasal- and rectal-biopsy specimens, nasal epithelial scrapings, and plasma from 38 subjects with cystic fibrosis and compared with results in 13 obligate heterozygotes, 24 healthy controls, 11 subjects with inflammatory bowel disease, 9 subjects with upper respiratory tract infection, and 16 subjects with asthma.
Results: The ratio of arachidonic to docosahexaenoic acid was significantly increased in mucosal and submucosal nasal-biopsy specimens (P<0.001) and rectal-biopsy specimens (P=0.009) from subjects with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic sufficiency and subjects with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic insufficiency, compared with values in healthy control subjects. In nasal tissue, this change reflected an increase in arachidonic acid levels and a decrease in docosahexaenoic acid levels. In cells from nasal mucosa, the ratio of arachidonic to docosahexaenoic acid was significantly increased in subjects with cystic fibrosis (P<0.001), compared with healthy controls, with values in obligate heterozygotes intermediate between these two groups (P<0.001). The ratio was not increased in subjects with inflammatory bowel disease. Subjects with asthma and those with upper respiratory tract infection had values intermediate between those in subjects with cystic fibrosis and those in healthy control subjects.
Conclusions: These findings indicate that alterations in fatty acids similar to those in cystic fibrosis-knockout mice are present in CFTR-expressing tissue from subjects with cystic fibrosis, providing further evidence of the role of CFTR in regulating fatty acid metabolism.

title: Actin dynamics and cell-cell adhesion in epithelia.
text: Recent breakthroughs in the field of intercellular adhesion have underscored the crucial role of adherens junction association with the underlying actin cytoskeleton. In skin epithelial cells, a dynamic aspect of adherens junction formation involves the formation of filopodia, which extend into the membrane of adjacent cells, thereby clustering adherens junction protein complexes at their tips. This clustering, in turn, stimulates actin polymerization at the cytoplasmic interface of these complexes. While the underlying mechanism remains elusive, the VASP/Mena family of proteins appears to play a crucial role in organizing actin polymerization at these sites. In vivo, adherens junction formation relies on filopodia in processes where epithelial sheets need to be physically moved closer to form stable intercellular connections, such as during ventral closure in embryonic development or wound healing in the postnatal animal.

title: Lamin A-dependent nuclear defects in human aging.
text: Mutations in the nuclear structural protein lamin A are responsible for the premature aging syndrome known as Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS). It is unclear whether lamin A plays a role in normal aging. Our findings reveal that the same molecular mechanism underlying HGPS is active in healthy cells, leading to similar defects in histone modifications and increased DNA damage. We have discovered that age-related nuclear defects in healthy individuals are caused by spontaneous use of a cryptic splice site in lamin A, which when constitively activated, leads to HGPS. Inhibition of this splice site reverses the nuclear defects associated with aging, suggesting that lamin A plays a role in physiological aging.

title: Zmpste24 deficiency in mice causes spontaneous bone fractures, muscle weakness, and a prelamin A processing defect.
text: Zmpste24 is a membrane-bound metalloproteinase found in the endoplasmic reticulum of cells. Biochemical studies on tissues from Zmpste24-deficient mice (Zmpste24(-/-)) have revealed a role for Zmpste24 in the processing of CAAX-type prenylated proteins. In this study, we investigate the pathological consequences of Zmpste24 deficiency in mice. Zmpste24(-/-) mice exhibit a slow weight gain, malnutrition, and progressive hair loss. The most striking pathological feature is the spontaneous fracture of multiple bones, similar to those seen in mice with osteogenesis imperfecta. The volume of cortical and trabecular bone is significantly reduced in Zmpste24(-/-) mice. In addition, Zmpste24(-/-) mice display muscle weakness in the lower and upper extremities, similar to mice lacking the farnesylated CAAX protein prelamin A. Interestingly, prelamin A processing is defective in fibroblasts lacking Zmpste24, as well as in fibroblasts lacking the CAAX carboxyl methyltransferase Icmt, but is normal in fibroblasts lacking the CAAX endoprotease Rce1. Muscle weakness in Zmpste24(-/-) mice can be attributed to defective prelamin A processing, but the brittle bone phenotype suggests a broader role for Zmpste24 in mammalian biology.

title: Human and other faeces as breeding media of the trachoma vector Musca sorbens.
text: The fly Musca sorbens Wiedemann (Diptera: Muscidae) is believed to transmit Chlamydia trachomatis, leading to human trachoma. The literature suggests that M. sorbens breeds primarily on isolated human faeces on the soil surface, but not in covered pit latrines. To identify the breeding media of M. sorbens in a rural Gambian village endemic for trachoma, we conducted experiments where test breeding media were presented for oviposition on soil-filled buckets and monitored for adult emergence. Our results showed that M. sorbens emerged from human faeces (6/9 trials), calf faeces (3/9), cow faeces (3/9), dog faeces (2/9), and goat faeces (1/9), but not from horse faeces, composting kitchen scraps, or a soil control (0/9 of each). After adjusting for the mass of the medium, the greatest number of flies emerged from human faeces (1426 flies/kg). The median time for emergence was 9 (interquartile range = 8-9.75) days post-oviposition. Of the flies emerging from faeces, 81% were M. sorbens. Male and female flies emerging from human faeces were significantly larger than those from other media, indicating that they would be more fecund and live longer than smaller flies from other sources. Female flies caught from children's eyes were of a similar size to those from human faeces, but significantly larger than those from other media. Our findings suggest that human faeces are the preferred larval medium for M. sorbens, although some breeding also occurs in animal faeces. Removing human faeces from the environment through the provision of basic sanitation is likely to significantly reduce fly density, eye contact, and trachoma transmission. However, if faeces of other animals are present, M. sorbens will persist.

title: Current Health and Environmental Status of the Maasai People in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: As time passes, the AIDS pandemic continues to escalate, affecting an estimated 38.6 million people globally. In response, two Cal Poly students are designing a satellite health clinic to serve the Maasai people residing in the Kajiado district of Southern Kenya. The Maasai have traditionally lived as pastoralists, relying on their cattle for sustenance and water, which can lead to contamination. However, as Kenya's population grows, the Maasai's traditional grazing land is shrinking, causing some to turn to farming to sustain their livelihoods. This shift has contributed to the desertification and deforestation of their region. As the Maasai's lifestyle evolves, they are relying more on maize for nutrients, which has altered their culture. To better understand the Maasai and identify potential aid needed to support their survival, we will address these changes.

title: Identification and characterization of a widely expressed form of adenylyl cyclase.
text: A novel mammalian adenylyl cyclase was identified through the use of reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) with degenerate primers based on a conserved region of previously described adenylyl cyclases (Premont, R. T. (1994) Methods Enzymol. 238, 116-127). The full-length cDNA sequence obtained from mouse brain predicts a 1353-amino acid protein with a 12-membrane span topology and two regions of high similarity to the catalytic domains of adenylyl cyclases. Comparison of this novel adenylyl cyclase with the eight previously described mammalian enzymes revealed that it belongs to a sixth distinct subclass of mammalian adenylyl cyclases. The AC9 gene was localized to human chromosome band 16p13.3-13.2. The 8.5-kb mRNA encoding the type 9 adenylyl cyclase is widely distributed and found at high levels in skeletal muscle and brain, particularly in the hippocampus, cerebellum, and neocortex. An antiserum directed against the carboxyl terminus of the type 9 adenylyl cyclase detects native and expressed recombinant AC9 protein in tissue and cell membranes, with highest levels in mouse brain membranes. Characterization of expressed recombinant AC9 revealed that it is a functional adenylyl cyclase that is stimulated by Mg2+, forskolin, and mutationally activated Gsalpha. AC9 activity is not affected by Ca2+/calmodulin or by G protein betagamma-subunits. Therefore, AC9 represents a functional G protein-regulated adenylyl cyclase found in brain and most somatic tissues.

title: Expression of Golli mRNA during development in primary immune lymphoid organs of the rat
text: The gene-of-the-oligodendrocyte lineage (Golli)-MBP transcription unit contains three exons specific to the Golli protein, in combination with eight exons from the classic myelin basic protein (MBP) gene. This results in the production of alternatively spliced proteins that share amino acid sequences with MBP. Unlike MBP, which is expressed only in the nervous system late in development, Golli gene products are expressed both pre- and post-natally at multiple sites. In this study, we determined the sequence of Golli in rats using RT-PCR and 5' RACE, and found that Golli sequences are expressed in primary lymphoid organs as early as embryonic day 16.5 (e16.5), which may explain the anergic T cell response we observed in Golli-induced meningitis.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of single baseline measurement of Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay for diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction in emergency department: systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Objective: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies to evaluate the accuracy of a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay (Roche Diagnostics) for the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies.
Data sources: Medline, Embase, and other relevant electronic databases were searched from January 2006 to December 2013.
Study selection: Studies were included if they evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a single baseline measurement of Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay for the diagnosis of AMI in patients presenting to the ED with suspected ACS.
Study appraisal and data synthesis: Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts, and then the full texts, using the adapted QUADAS-2 tool for methodological quality assessment. If appropriate, meta-analysis was conducted using the hierarchical bivariate model.
Results: Twenty-three studies reported the performance of the evaluated assay at presentation. The results for 14 ng/L and 3-5 ng/L cut-off values were pooled separately. At 14 ng/L (20 papers), the summary sensitivity was 89.5% (95% confidence interval [CI] 86.3% to 92.1%) and the summary specificity was 77.1% (95% CI 68.7% to 83.7%). At 3-5 ng/L (six papers), the summary sensitivity was 97.4% (95% CI 94.9% to 98.7%) and the summary specificity was 42.4% (95% CI 31.2% to 54.5%). This means that if 21 of 100 consecutive patients have the target condition (21%, the median prevalence across the studies), 2 (95% CI 2 to 3) of 21 patients with AMI will be missed (false negatives) if 14 ng/L is used as a cut-off value and 18 (95% CI 13 to 25) of 79 patients without AMI will test positive (false positives). If the 3-5 ng/L cut-off value is used, <1 (95% CI 0 to 1) patient with AMI will be missed and 46 (95% CI 36 to 54) patients without AMI will test positive.
Conclusions: The results indicate that a single baseline measurement of the Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive assay could be used to rule out AMI if lower cut-off values such as 3 ng/L or 5 ng/L are used. However, this method should be part of a comprehensive triage strategy and may not be appropriate for patients who present less than three hours after symptom onset. Care must also be exercised because of the higher imprecision of the evaluated assay and the greater effect of lot-to-lot reagent variation at low troponin concentrations.
Systematic Review Registration: PROSPERO registration number CRD42013003926.

title: Pericyte differentiation.
text: Pericytes are identified in the body based on their location: they are embedded within the basement membrane of microvessels. They form an integral part of the microvascular wall and are believed to play a role in angiogenesis, although their specific function is not fully understood. Pericytes derived from the retinal microvasculature have been cultured and identified through a series of distinct characteristics that set them apart from other stromal cells, such as smooth muscle cells. In vitro, pericytes form multicellular nodules rich in extracellular matrix, which becomes mineralized in the presence of serum. These findings suggest that pericytes are primitive mesenchymal cells that can differentiate into an osteogenic phenotype. Pericyte differentiation is characterized by changes in their response to transforming growth factor beta 1 and the synthesis and/or deposition of various extracellular matrix proteins, such as laminin, Type IV collagen, tenascin, Type X collagen, osteonectin, and thrombospondin-1. Angiogenesis is often associated with mineralization, leading researchers to suggest that pericytes may contribute to mineralization in vivo.

title: Membrane association of the CD3ε signaling domain is required for optimal T cell development and function.
text: The T-cell receptor (TCR):CD3 complex transmits crucial signals that are essential for optimal T-cell development and adaptive immunity. In a resting T cell, the CD3ε cytoplasmic tail interacts with the plasma membrane through a proximal basic-rich stretch (BRS), which facilitates the transduction of signals that regulate T-cell development and function. In this study, we demonstrate that mice lacking a functional CD3ε-BRS exhibited significant reductions in thymic cellularity and a limited transition of CD4-CD8-double-negative (DN) thymocytes to DN4 thymocytes, resulting from enhanced DN4 TCR signaling that led to increased cell death and TCR downregulation in subsequent populations. Moreover, positive, but not negative, T-cell selection was affected in mice lacking a functional CD3ε-BRS, which resulted in limited peripheral T-cell function and a significantly reduced ability to respond to influenza infection. These findings collectively suggest that the association of the CD3ε signaling domain with the plasma membrane is essential for optimal T-cell development and peripheral T-cell function.

title: A new era in ovulation induction.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of aromatase inhibitors in ovulation induction, superovulation, and IVF.
Design: A literature search was conducted using MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Database of systematic reviews, with the keywords "aromatase inhibitor," "letrozole," "anastrazole," "ovulation induction," "ovulation," and "superovulation."
Results: Ovulation induction with letrozole resulted in an ovulation rate of 70%-84% and a pregnancy rate of 20%-27% per cycle. In comparison, ovulation and pregnancy rates with letrozole were higher than those of anastrazole. Superovulation with letrozole resulted in fewer developing follicles and a thicker endometrium. The use of letrozole for superovulation was associated with a higher pregnancy rate than with clomiphene citrate (CC) (16.7% vs. 5.6%). Additionally, the addition of letrozole to FSH treatment led to a decreased FSH requirement. The pregnancy rate for treatment with letrozole and FSH was similar to that for FSH alone.
Conclusion: Aromatase inhibitors are as effective as or superior to CC in ovulation induction and superovulation. Unlike CC, they do not have an antiestrogenic effect on the endometrium. Given their advantages, aromatase inhibitors can replace CC as ovulation-inducing drugs. Their role in IVF remains to be determined.

title: Of lineage and legacy: the development of mammalian hematopoietic stem cells
text: The hematopoietic system is one of the earliest complex tissues to form in the developing mammalian embryo. In the field of developmental hematopoiesis, there is particular interest in understanding the origin of adult bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells. However, tracing their origin is challenging due to the mobile nature of blood and the fact that hematopoietic cells emerge from multiple embryonic sites. The origin of the adult mammalian blood system remains a topic of ongoing research and debate. Additionally, there is a focus on identifying the developmental signals that induce the adult hematopoietic stem cell program, as these may provide valuable insights for expanding and generating these clinically important cell populations outside of the body (ex vivo). This review provides a historical overview of the current understanding of the developmental origins of hematopoiesis, as well as the latest research in this area.

title: Long crocidolite asbestos fibers cause polyploidy by sterically blocking cytokinesis.
text: Asbestos has been classified as a physical carcinogen due to its carcinogenic effects, which are primarily linked to fiber dimensions. It is hypothesized that long asbestos fibers may disrupt chromosome distribution during cell division, causing genetic changes that lead to cell transformation and cancer progression. Using advanced microscopy techniques, such as high-resolution time-lapse light microscopy and serial-section electron microscopy, we have tracked individual crocidolite asbestos fibers through the later stages of cell division in LLC-MK2 epithelial cells and observed their impact on cytokinesis. Our findings reveal that long fibers (15-55 micrometers), trapped by the cleavage furrow, can block cytokinesis, resulting in the formation of binucleated cells. The ends of these blocking fibers are often found within invaginations of the newly formed nuclei. We also observed nuclear envelope-fiber attachment, where a chromatin strand runs with the fiber into the intercellular bridge. These observations suggest that individual crocidolite fibers can cause genomic changes by sterically blocking cytokinesis, and that fiber length and affinity for the nuclear envelope are important factors. These genomic changes may be among the initial events leading to asbestos-induced cancers.

title: Neural induction and early patterning in vertebrates.
text:
In vertebrates, the development of the nervous system is initiated by signals from a specialized region of the early embryo during gastrulation, a process known as neural induction. This discovery was first made by experimental embryologists studying amphibian embryos, and subsequent research has shown that eliminating transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) signaling in the ectoderm is a key step in the acquisition of an anterior neural fate. This observation forms the basis of the "default" model of neural induction.
Endogenous neural inducers, such as secreted proteins, work to inhibit TGFβ ligands in the dorsal ectoderm, leading to the induction of a non-neural fate in the ventral ectoderm. Conversely, inhibition of the TGFβ pathway has been shown to be sufficient to directly induce neural fate in mammalian embryos, as well as pluripotent mouse and human embryonic stem cells. This suggests that the molecular mechanism underlying neural induction is conserved across a wide range of organisms in the evolutionary tree.
