Using acidotropic agents and inhibitors of a specific class of lysosomal proteases, coupled with metabolic labeling and immunoprecipitation, we found that APP is degraded within an acidic compartment to produce at least 12 COOH-terminal fragments. Of these, nine contain the entire beta/A4 domain and are potentially amyloidogenic. Treatment with E64 or Z-Phe-Ala-CHN2 irreversibly blocked the activities of lysosomal cysteine proteases cathepsins B and L, but did not inhibit the lysosomal aspartic protease cathepsin D or alter the production of potentially amyloidogenic fragments. Instead, the inhibitors prevented further degradation of the fragments. These findings suggest that large numbers of potentially amyloidogenic fragments of APP are generated in an acidic compartment by non-cysteine proteases and are then eliminated within lysosomes by cysteine proteases. Immunoblot and immunohistochemical analyses confirmed that chronic cysteine protease inhibition leads to accumulation of potentially amyloidogenic APP fragments in lysosomes. These results provide further support for the hypothesis that an acidic compartment may be involved in amyloid formation and begin to define the proteolytic events that may be important for amyloidogenesis.

title: Pharmaceutical Public-Private Partnerships in the United States and Europe: Moving from the Bench to the Bedside
text: To address unmet medical needs and enhance industry competitiveness, regulators in both the US and EU have taken steps to bridge the gap between academic research and patient care. A pharmaceutical public-private partnership (PPPP), a legally binding contract between a private pharmaceutical enterprise and a public or private research university, can be a valuable tool for ensuring a more efficient return on investment in the highly regulated pharmaceutical industry. By framing a binding contract with respect for positive social norms, PPPPs can move parties away from an inefficient Nash Equilibrium and towards the Pareto Optimal Frontier. Effective coordination of interdependent actors is also crucial, as PPPPs can flip the parties' incentives compared to traditional contracts, enhancing the likelihood of successful commercialization. This article provides an annotated roadmap for universities, private firms, and EU policy makers to create efficient PPPPs in Europe, with a secondary purpose of suggesting amendments to US laws governing the patenting of government-funded technology to prevent undue burdens on the sharing of upstream medical discoveries and research tools. Our analysis combines game theory and law and management approaches to for-profit PPPPs.

title: Chronic stress and psychological well-being: evidence from Thailand on household crowding.
text: This study investigates the impact of household crowding, a specific form of chronic stress, on psychological well-being. Using data from a large (n = 2017) random sample of households in Bangkok, Thailand, we find that objective household crowding (i.e., living in a crowded space) negatively affects psychological well-being, even after controlling for various background characteristics. This effect is mediated by subjective crowding (i.e., perceived crowding), which consistently and directly harms well-being. We also find no evidence of a gender effect. Interestingly, the effects of objective and subjective crowding are similar across different household structures, including two- and three-generation households and one- and multiple-couple households. Our findings challenge the idea that subjective crowding is simply an effect of psychological well-being, instead suggesting that crowding constitutes a major source of chronic stress that can undermine well-being. Although our analysis is based on data from one city, we place our findings in a broader historical and theoretical context to suggest that household crowding is likely to have detrimental effects on psychological well-being in many cultural settings.

title: Age- and sex-specific genomic profiles in non-small cell lung cancer.
text: In this study, the authors aimed to investigate differences in the underlying biology of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) based on patient age and sex. The study included 787 patients with early-stage NSCLC who were divided into subgroups based on age (< 70 vs > or = 70 years old) or sex. The authors analyzed the patients' lung tumor samples and clinical data to identify patterns of oncogenic pathway activation and tumor biology/microenvironment status. They found that low- and high-risk patient clusters/cohorts were identified based on 5-year recurrence-free survival, with the longest and shortest survival times, respectively, within the age and sex NSCLC subgroups. These cohorts demonstrated similar patterns of pathway activation. In patients younger than 70 years, high-risk patients had increased activation of the Src and tumor necrosis factor pathways, while high-risk patients aged 70 years or older had increased activation of the wound healing and invasiveness pathways. In women, high-risk patients had increased activation of the invasiveness and STAT3 pathways, while high-risk men had increased activation of the STAT3, tumor necrosis factor, EGFR, and wound healing pathways. Multivariate analyses confirmed the independent clinical relevance of the pathway-based subphenotypes in women and patients younger than 70 years. These findings suggest that oncogenic pathway activation profiles may be useful in predicting recurrence-free survival in NSCLC patients. However, these findings require validation in independent patient data sets.

title: Amelioration of colitis by genetically engineered murine regulatory T cells redirected by antigen-specific chimeric receptor.
text:
Background and Aims:
The use of regulatory T cells (Tregs) for the treatment of inflammatory diseases is limited by the scarcity of antigen-specific Tregs. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that involves using chimeric immune receptors to redirect effector T cells (Teff) to sites of inflammation. This approach has the potential to alleviate a broad range of diseases characterized by an uncontrolled inflammatory response.
Methods:
To enable the use of this approach in a clinical setting, we have developed a novel protocol for the efficient retroviral transduction and expansion of murine naturally occurring regulatory T cells (nTregs) with a 2,4,6-trinitrophenol-specific tripartite chimeric receptor.
Results:
Our results demonstrate that transduced nTregs maintain their Foxp3 level, can undergo repeated expansion upon ex vivo encounter with their cognate antigen in a major histocompatibility complex-independent, costimulation-independent, and contact-dependent manner, and specifically suppress Teff cells. Adoptive transfer of small numbers of the transduced nTregs was associated with antigen-specific, dose-dependent amelioration of trinitrobenzenesulphonic acid colitis.
Conclusions:
This study demonstrates that nTregs can be efficiently transduced to express functional, antigen-specific chimeric receptors that enable the specific suppression of effector T cells both in vitro and in vivo. This approach may enable future cell-based therapeutic applications in inflammatory bowel disease, as well as other inflammatory disorders.

title: Purification and activation properties of UreD-UreF-urease apoprotein complexes.
text: In this study, the assembly of the Klebsiella aerogenes urease nickel metallocenter in vivo was investigated, and the presence of UreD, UreF, and UreG accessory proteins was found to be essential for its formation. Previous research had shown that the urease apoprotein exists in both uncomplexed form and as complexes with UreD, UreF, and UreG. However, this study revealed the existence of a novel series of complexes consisting of UreD, UreF, and urease apoprotein, which exhibited distinct activation properties compared to urease and UreD-urease complexes. Unlike the previously described species, the UreD-UreF-urease complexes were resistant to inactivation by nickel chloride (NiCl2). Additionally, the bicarbonate concentration dependence for UreD-UreF-urease apoenzyme activation was significantly decreased compared to that of urease and UreD-urease apoproteins. Using western blot (immunoblot) analyses with polyclonal anti-urease and anti-UreD antibodies, it was found that UreD is masked in the UreD-UreF-urease complexes, likely due to the binding of UreF. The study proposes that the binding of UreF modulates the UreD-urease apoprotein activation properties by excluding nickel ions from binding to the active site until after formation of the carbamylated lysine metallocenter ligand.

title: Coordinate regulation of the IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 cytokine cluster in Th2 clones revealed by allelic expression patterns.
text: The cytokines IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 are markers for the Th2 subset of effector T cells and are often co-expressed. These cytokine genes are located within a genomic region of approximately 140 kilobases in both mouse and human. Using IL-4-expressing CD4+ T cell clones derived from F1 mice, we identified allelic polymorphisms for each of these cytokines and determined the parental origin of the cytokine mRNAs. Both monoallelic and biallelic expression was observed for each gene, as well as for an additional gene, IL-3, located approximately 450 kilobases telomeric on the same chromosome. Interestingly, when these cytokines were co-expressed in T cell clones, IL-4 was expressed from the same allele as IL-13 or IL-5 in approximately 81% of instances, while there was only 52% concordance of these three cytokines at the allelic level among clones that expressed IL-3. Our findings suggest that independent expression of the cytokine alleles occurs frequently in T cells, but the clustered locus encompassing IL-4, IL-13, and IL-5 is subject to coordinated regulation.

title: T-cell activation.
text:
INTRODUCTION
T-cell activation is a complex process that involves the recognition of antigens by the T-cell receptor (TCR) complex on the surface of T cells. The TCR complex is composed of two main chains (alpha and beta) and a CD3 complex, which are non-covalently linked to form a heterodimer. The TCR complex recognizes antigens presented on the surface of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) through the binding of peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) molecules.
CELLULAR AND MOLECULAR REQUIREMENTS FOR T-CELL ACTIVATION
T-cell activation requires the interaction of the TCR complex with pMHC molecules on the surface of APCs. This interaction triggers a signaling cascade that leads to the activation of T cells. The activation of T cells involves the engagement of the TCR complex with pMHC molecules, which leads to the activation of the CD3 complex and the recruitment of signaling molecules, such as Lck and ZAP-70, to the TCR complex. The activation of T cells also involves the expression of activation markers, such as CD25 and CD69, and the upregulation of the expression of TCR alpha and beta chains.
THE T-CELL ANTIGEN RECEPTOR COMPLEX
The TCR complex is composed of two main chains (alpha and beta) and a CD3 complex, which are non-covalently linked to form a heterodimer. The TCR complex recognizes antigens presented on the surface of APCs through the binding of pMHC molecules. The TCR complex is composed of several domains, including the variable region, the constant region, and the transmembrane domain. The variable region is responsible for recognizing the antigen, while the constant region is involved in the binding of the TCR complex to the CD3 complex.
T-CELL ACTIVATION BY ANTIBODies AND LECTINS
In addition to the TCR complex, T cells can also be activated by antibodies and lectins. Antibodies can activate T cells through the binding of the antibody to the TCR complex, which leads to the activation of the T cell. Lectins, on the other hand, can activate T cells by binding to the TCR complex and triggering the activation of the T cell.
OTHER CELL SURFACE STRUCTURES (ACCESSORY MOLECULES) INVOLVED IN ANTIGEN RECOGNITION AND ACTIVATION
In addition to the TCR complex, several other cell surface structures are involved in antigen recognition and activation of T cells. These include the CD40 ligand, which is involved in the activation of T cells through the binding of CD40 ligand to CD40 on the surface of APCs. Other accessory molecules involved in T-cell activation include CD80 and CD86, which are involved in the activation of T cells through the binding of CD80 and CD86 to CD28 on the surface of T cells.
MINIMAL REQUIREMENTS FOR T-CELL ACTIVATION
T-cell activation requires several minimal requirements, including the binding of the TCR complex to pMHC molecules, the expression of activation markers, and the upregulation of the expression of TCR alpha and beta chains. In addition, T-cell activation also requires the expression of the CD3 complex and the presence of signaling molecules, such as Lck and ZAP-70.
CONSEQUENCES OF T-CELL ACTIVATION
T-cell activation has several consequences, including the expression of activation markers, the upregulation of the expression of TCR alpha and beta chains, and the acquisition of cytolytic activity. T-cell activation also leads to the production of cytokines, such as interleukin-2 (IL-2), which are involved in the activation and proliferation of T cells.
MECHANISMS OF SIGNAL TRANSMISSION VIA THE TCR COMPLEX
The TCR complex transmits signals through several mechanisms, including the binding of the TCR complex to pMHC molecules, the recruitment of signaling molecules to the TCR complex, and the activation of the CD3 complex. The TCR complex also transmits signals through the activation of the ZAP-70 protein, which is involved in the activation of T cells.
MODE OF CONTROL OF GENE EXPRESSION DURING T-CELL ACTIVATION
T-cell activation involves the regulation of gene expression through several mechanisms, including the activation of transcription factors, such as NF-κB, and the expression of cytokines, such as IL-2. The expression of these molecules is involved in the activation and proliferation of T cells.
MECHANISM OF ACTION OF IL-2
IL-2 is involved in the activation and proliferation of T cells through several mechanisms, including the activation of transcription factors, such as NF-κB, and the upregulation of the expression of TCR alpha and beta chains. IL-2 also plays a role in the differentiation of T cells into effector cells, such as cytotoxic T cells and T helper 1 cells.
ACQUISITION OF CYTOLYTIC ACTIVITY
T-cell activation also involves the acquisition of cytolytic activity through the expression of cytolytic molecules, such as granzymes and perforin. These molecules are involved in the lysis of target cells and are activated through the binding of the TCR complex to pMHC molecules.
ANALOGIES WITH IMMATURE T CELLS
T-cell activation also has several analogies with immature T cells, including the expression of CD45RA and CD27, which are involved in the activation and differentiation of T cells. Immature T cells also express high levels of CD62L, which is involved in the activation and differentiation of T cells.
In conclusion, T-cell activation is a complex process that involves the recognition of antigens by the TCR complex on the surface of T cells. The activation of T cells requires the binding of the TCR complex to pMHC molecules, the expression of activation markers, and the upregulation of the expression of TCR alpha and beta chains. T-cell activation also involves the expression of cytokines, such as IL-2, and the acquisition of cytolytic activity through the expression of cytolytic molecules, such as granzymes and perforin.

title: Effect of hydroxyethyl starch on bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass: a meta-analysis of randomized trials.
text:
Objective: To determine the effects of hydroxyethyl starch on bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass through a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
Methods: A meta-analysis of postoperative blood loss in randomized clinical trials of hydroxyethyl starch versus albumin for fluid management in adult cardiopulmonary bypass surgery was performed. The impact of hydroxyethyl starch molecular weight and molar substitution was also assessed. Additionally, randomized trials comparing different hydroxyethyl starch solutions were included.
Results: Eighteen trials with 970 total patients were included in the analysis. Compared to albumin, hydroxyethyl starch increased postoperative blood loss by 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 18.2%-48.3%; P < .001). The risk of reoperation for bleeding was found to be more than doubled by hydroxyethyl starch (relative risk, 2.24; 95% confidence interval, 1.14-4.40; P = .020). Hydroxyethyl starch also increased transfusion of red blood cells by 28.4% (95% confidence interval, 12.2%-44.6%; P < .001), fresh-frozen plasma by 30.6% (95% confidence interval, 8.0%-53.1%; P = .008), and platelets by 29.8% (95% confidence interval, 3.4%-56.2%; P = .027). No significant differences were found between hydroxyethyl starch 450/0.7 and 200/0.5. Insufficient data were available for hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.4 versus albumin, but no significant differences were detected in head-to-head comparisons of hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.4 with 200/0.5. Albumin improved hemodynamics, but there were no differences in fluid balance, ventilator time, intensive care unit stay, or mortality.
Conclusion: Hydroxyethyl starch increased blood loss, reoperation for bleeding, and blood product transfusion after cardiopulmonary bypass. No evidence was found to suggest that these risks could be mitigated by lower molecular weight and substitution.

title: Downstream of Mutant KRAS, the Transcription Regulator YAP Is Essential for Neoplastic Progression to Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a malignancy with poor prognosis and frequently harbors oncogenic KRAS mutations. Despite extensive research, KRAS has remained an elusive therapeutic target. However, our study uncovered an unexpected association between the abundance of YAP mRNA, which encodes Yes-associated protein (YAP), and PDAC. We found that YAP expression was elevated in human PDAC tissues compared to normal pancreatic epithelia. In genetically engineered KrasG12D and KrasG12D:Trp53R172H mouse models, pancreas-specific deletion of Yap halted the progression of early neoplastic lesions to PDAC without affecting normal pancreatic development and endocrine function. Our findings indicate that YAP is critically required for the proliferation of mutant Kras or Kras:Trp53 neoplastic pancreatic ductal cells in culture and for their growth and progression to invasive PDAC in mice. YAP functions as a downstream effector of the oncogenic KRAS–mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, promoting the expression of genes encoding secretory factors that cumulatively sustain neoplastic proliferation, a tumorigenic stromal response in the tumor microenvironment, and PDAC progression in Kras and Kras:Trp53 mutant pancreas tissue. Our study identifies YAP as a critical oncogenic KRAS effector and a potential therapeutic target for PDAC and possibly other KRAS-mutant cancers.

title: Rho, Rac and Cdc42 regulate actin organization and cell adhesion in macrophages.
text:
Introduction:
Rho family proteins have been shown to regulate actin organization in fibroblasts, but their functions in cells of haematopoietic origin have not been extensively studied. In this study, we investigate the role of Rho family proteins in Bac1.2F5 cells, a colony-stimulating factor-1 (CSF-1)-dependent murine macrophage cell line.
Methods:
We used microinjection of constitutively activated (V12)Rac1, dominant inhibitory Rac mutant (N17Rac1), V12Cdc42, and Rho inhibitor (C3 transferase) to study the role of Rho family proteins in CSF-1-induced actin reorganization in Bac1 cells. We also analyzed the composition of focal complexes, which are cell-to-substratum adhesion sites containing beta1 integrin, pp125FAK, paxillin, vinculin, and tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins.
Results:
Our results show that CSF-1 rapidly induces actin reorganization in Bac1 cells, leading to the formation of filopodia, lamellipodia, and membrane ruffles at the plasma membrane, as well as the appearance of fine actin cables within the cell interior. Microinjection of V12Rac1 stimulated lamellipodium formation and membrane ruffling, while dominant inhibitory Rac mutant N17Rac1 inhibited CSF-1-induced lamellipodium formation and induced cell rounding. V12Cdc42 induced the formation of long filopodia, while N17Cdc42 prevented CSF-1-induced formation of filopodia but not lamellipodia. V14RhoA stimulated actin cable assembly and cell contraction, while Rho inhibitor C3 transferase induced the loss of actin cables. Bac1 cells had cell-to-substratum adhesion sites containing beta1 integrin, pp125FAK, paxillin, vinculin, and tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins. These 'focal complexes' were present in growing and CSF-1-starved cells, but were disassembled in cells injected with N17Cdc42 or N17Rac1. Interestingly, beta1 integrin did not disperse until long after focal phosphotyrosine and vinculin staining had disappeared.
Discussion:
Our findings suggest that in Bac1 macrophages, Cdc42, Rac, and Rho regulate the formation of distinct actin filament-based structures, and that Cdc42 and Rac are also required for the assembly of adhesion sites to the extracellular matrix. These results provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying actin-based cellular processes in haematopoietic cells.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study demonstrates the importance of Rho family proteins in regulating actin organization and adhesion in Bac1 macrophages. The findings provide a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying actin-based cellular processes in haematopoietic cells and have implications for the study of cellular processes in general.

title: Visualizing the function and fate of neutrophils in sterile injury and repair
text: Neutrophils have been linked to harmful inflammatory responses in various conditions, where they cause tissue damage and ultimately perish, only to be engulfed by other immune cells like monocytes and macrophages. However, in the context of a fully healing sterile thermal injury to the liver, neutrophils play a crucial role in the repair process by entering the injury site and dismantling damaged vessels, creating channels for new blood vessel growth. Once these tasks are completed, they do not die at the injury site nor are they consumed by other immune cells. Instead, many of these neutrophils embark on a preprogrammed journey, first migrating to the lungs where they upregulate the expression of CXCR4 (C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4), and then entering the bone marrow, where they undergo programmed cell death, or apoptosis.

title: The effect of mass screening on incidence and mortality of squamous and adenocarcinoma of cervix uteri.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of the Finnish national cervical cancer screening program in reducing incidence and mortality rates, particularly for squamous cell carcinomas.
Methods: Obtained cervical cancer incidence and mortality data from the Finnish Cancer Registry, covering the period from 1953 (when the registry was established) to 1991. Analyzed data from women aged 30-60 years who were notified for screening every 5 years.
Results: Found a significant decrease in cervical carcinoma incidence, from 15.4 per 10(5) woman-years in the early 1960s to 2.7 per 10(5) woman-years in 1991. Correspondingly, mortality rates have also decreased, from 6.6 to 1.4 per 10(5) woman-years. However, the decrease in incidence is primarily seen in squamous cell carcinomas, while the mortality caused by adenocarcinoma has decreased in screened birth cohorts but the incidence rate has remained the same.
Conclusions: The Finnish national cervical cancer screening program has been effective in reducing incidence and mortality rates, particularly for squamous cell carcinomas. Continuation of the program is crucial. In the future, more attention should be given to glandular cell atypias in cervical smears to potentially decrease the incidence of cervical adenocarcinoma.

title: Role of 5-HT in the regulation of the brain-pituitary-adrenal axis: effects of 5-HT on adrenocortical cells.
text: Serotonin (5-HT) plays a crucial role in regulating the brain-pituitary-adrenal axis, particularly by controlling the activity of hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) neurons and pituitary corticotropes through activation of 5-HT1A and (or) 5-HT2A/2C receptor subtypes. 5-HT can also stimulate the renin-angiotensin system by activating renin secretion and enhancing aldosterone production. Locally, 5-HT produced in the adrenal gland stimulates the secretory activity of adrenocortical cells through a paracrine mode of communication. Immunohistochemical and biochemical studies have demonstrated the presence of 5-HT in the adrenal glands of various species, including humans. In vitro and in vivo studies have shown that 5-HT stimulates corticosteroid secretion in various species, with the mechanism of action differing between species. For example, in frogs and humans, the stimulatory effect of 5-HT on adrenocortical cells is mediated through a 5-HT4 receptor subtype positively coupled to adenylyl cyclase and calcium influx. In contrast, in rats, the effect of 5-HT on aldosterone secretion is mediated via activation of 5-HT7 receptors. Clinical studies have shown that 5-HT4 receptor agonists stimulate aldosterone secretion in healthy volunteers and in patients with corticotropic insufficiency and primary hyperaldosteronism. Local serotonergic control of corticosteroid production may play a role in the physiological regulation of the adrenal cortex and in the pathophysiology of cortisol and aldosterone disorders.

title: Effect of interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor/cachectin on glucose turnover in the rat.
text: In this study, we investigated the effects of recombinant human interleukin-1 beta (IL-1) and recombinant human tumor necrosis factor alpha/cachectin (TNF) on glucose metabolism in healthy rats. We used a primed constant infusion of D-(6-3H)glucose and D-[U-14C]glucose to measure glucose kinetics. During the 6-hour isotope and 4-hour monokine infusion, we determined plasma levels of glucagon and insulin and correlated them with changes in glucose metabolism. Our results showed that IL-1, but not TNF, increased the rates of glucose appearance (Ra) and disappearance (Rd), and were associated with an increase in glucagon and a decrease in the ratio of insulin to glucagon. Plasma glucose concentration was elevated early after IL-1 administration, coinciding with the peak in Ra. The augmentation of the metabolic clearance rate (MCR) and the percent of flux oxidized by IL-1 suggest that this monokine induces the utilization of glucose as a substrate. TNF administration failed to modify the Ra or Rd, percent of flux oxidized, or MCR. TNF-treated rats increased the percent of glucose recycling, but not the total rate of glucose production. Our findings suggest that endogenous macrophage products, such as IL-1, play a role in the diverse alterations of carbohydrate metabolism seen during injury and/or infection.

title: Human and murine very small embryonic-like cells represent multipotent tissue progenitors, in vitro and in vivo.
text: The aim of this research was to investigate the developmental progression of human and mouse very small embryonic-like (HuVSEL or MuVSEL) cells in both in vitro and in vivo environments. In vitro, these cells differentiated into cells from all three embryonic germ layers. In contrast to controls, HuVSEL cells produced robust mineralized tissue of human origin in calvarial defects. Immunohistochemistry revealed that HuVSEL cells gave rise to neurons, adipocytes, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts within the calvarial defects. MuVSEL cells were also able to differentiate into similar lineages. In the first round of serial transplants of MuVSEL cells into irradiated osseous sites, approximately 60% of the cells maintained their VSEL cell phenotype, while other cells differentiated into multiple tissues at 3 months. However, secondary transplants did not identify donor VSEL cells, suggesting limited self-renewal, but did demonstrate VSEL cell derivatives in situ for up to 1 year without identifying teratomas. These findings demonstrate that VSEL cells produce multiple cellular structures both in vitro and in vivo and provide a foundation for future cell-based regenerative therapies for osseous, neural, and connective tissue disorders.

title: High frequency of p16 (CDKN2/MTS-1/INK4A) inactivation in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
text: The tumor suppressor gene p16 (CDKN2/MTS-1/INK4A) can be inactivated through multiple genetic mechanisms, including homozygous deletion, point mutation, and promoter methylation. To investigate these mechanisms in head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCC), we analyzed 29 invasive primary HNSCC tumors using immunohistochemistry with a new monoclonal antibody (mAb), DCS-50. We found that 24 of 29 (83%) tumors lacked nuclear staining for p16. Further genetic analysis revealed that 16 (67%) of these tumors had homozygous deletions, 5 (21%) were methylated, 1 had a rearrangement at the p16 locus, and 1 had a frameshift mutation in exon 1. These findings suggest that: (a) inactivation of the p16 tumor suppressor gene is a common event in HNSCC; (b) p16 is inactivated through multiple mechanisms, including homozygous deletion, point mutation, and promoter methylation; and (c) immunohistochemical analysis for p16 expression is a reliable and relatively simple method for evaluating p16 gene inactivation.

title: Genome-wide RNAi screen of Ca(2+) influx identifies genes that regulate Ca(2+) release-activated Ca(2+) channel activity.
text:
Recent studies conducted by our group and others have demonstrated a crucial and conserved role of Stim in store-operated calcium influx and calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channel activity. Through an unbiased genome-wide RNA interference screen in Drosophila S2 cells, we have identified 75 hits that significantly inhibit calcium influx upon store depletion by thapsigargin. Of these, 11 predicted transmembrane proteins, including Stim, and one protein, olf186-F, were found to play a key role in regulating CRAC channel activity.
Our findings show that olf186-F is a critical component of the CRAC channel complex, as RNA interference-mediated knockdown of olf186-F resulted in a profound reduction of thapsigargin-evoked calcium entry and CRAC current. Conversely, overexpression of olf186-F led to a 3-fold increase in CRAC current. Interestingly, when olf186-F was co-transfected with Stim, CRAC currents were found to increase to 8-fold higher than control and developed more rapidly.
Our results suggest that olf186-F is a member of a highly conserved family of four-transmembrane spanning proteins, with homologs from Caenorhabditis elegans to human. Furthermore, we found that the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) calcium pump, sarco/ER calcium ATPase (SERCA), and the single transmembrane-soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive (NSF) attachment receptor (SNARE) protein Syntaxin5 are also required for CRAC channel activity. Together, these findings suggest a signaling pathway in which Stim senses calcium depletion within the ER, translocates to the plasma membrane, and interacts with olf186-F to trigger CRAC channel activity.

title: Wedelolactone induces growth of breast cancer cells by stimulation of estrogen receptor signalling.
text: Wedelolactone, a plant-derived compound, has been shown to exhibit anti-cancer properties against breast and prostate carcinomas in both in vitro and in vivo studies. This compound targets multiple cellular proteins, including androgen receptors, 5-lipoxygenase, and topoisomerase IIα. In this study, a novel biological activity of wedelolactone at nanomolar (nM) doses was observed, where it acts as an agonist of estrogen receptors (ER) α and β. This was demonstrated through transactivation of estrogen response elements (ERE) in cells transiently expressing either ERα or ERβ, as well as through molecular docking of wedelolactone into the ligand binding pocket of both ERα and ERβ. In breast cancer cells, wedelolactone stimulates the growth of estrogen receptor-positive cells, activates rapid non-genomic estrogen signaling, and induces the expression of estrogen-responsive genes. These effects can be inhibited by pretreatment with a pure ER antagonist, ICI 182,780, and are not observed in ER-negative breast cancer cells. Therefore, we conclude that wedelolactone acts as a phytoestrogen in breast cancer cells by stimulating both genomic and non-genomic estrogen signaling pathways.

title: Subpopulations of mouse blood monocytes differ in maturation stage and inflammatory response.
text: Blood monocytes serve as well-characterized precursors for both macrophages and dendritic cells in humans. However, compared to humans, the monocyte subsets in mice have been minimally characterized. In this study, we identified three distinct subpopulations of mouse monocytes based on their differential expression of Ly-6C, CD43, CD11c, MBR, and CD62L. These subsets share similar phagocytic capabilities, expression of the M-CSF receptor (CD115), and ability to differentiate into macrophages upon M-CSF stimulation. By depleting blood monocytes using dichloromethylene-bisphosphonate-loaded liposomes and monitoring their repopulation, we found that the subsets have a developmental relationship. Monocytes were maximally depleted 18 hours after liposome application and subsequently reappeared in the circulation, exclusively of the Ly-6C(high) subset, which resembles bone marrow monocytes. Serial flow cytometric analyses of newly released Ly-6C(high) monocytes revealed that their Ly-6C expression decreased while in circulation. Under inflammatory conditions induced by acute infection with Listeria monocytogenes or chronic infection with Leishmania major, there was a significant increase in immature Ly-6C(high) monocytes, similar to the inflammatory left shift of granulocytes. Additionally, acute peritoneal inflammation recruited preferentially Ly-6C(med-high) monocytes. These findings identify distinct subpopulations of mouse blood monocytes that differ in maturation stage and capacity to migrate to inflammatory sites.

title: Proteogenomics to discover the full coding content of genomes: a computational perspective.
text: Proteogenomics, a field that intersects genomics and proteomics, has emerged as a powerful tool for identifying and characterizing protein-coding genes. This technology involves searching tandem mass spectra against genomic databases, providing valuable information for gene annotation that is difficult or impossible to obtain through standard methods. Examples of the information gained through proteogenomics include confirmation of translation, determination of reading frames, identification of gene and exon boundaries, evidence for post-translational processing, identification of splice-forms including alternative splicing, and prediction of novel genes. However, to fully realize the potential of proteogenomics, several technological hurdles must be overcome, such as improving the speed and accuracy of peptide identification, constructing and searching specialized databases, correcting sampling bias, and others. This article reviews the current state of the field, highlighting its successes and the role of computation in overcoming these challenges. We discuss how technological and algorithmic advances have enabled large-scale proteogenomic studies in various model organisms, including Arabidopsis, yeast, fruit flies, and humans. Additionally, we provide a glimpse into the future of the field, outlining early efforts to tackle the challenges of complex gene structures, searching against genomes of related species, and immunoglobulin gene reconstruction.

title: The in vitro phosphorylation of p53 by calcium-dependent protein kinase C--characterization of a protein-kinase-C-binding site on p53.
text: In vitro studies have shown that Ca2+-dependent protein kinase C (PKC) phosphorylates the recombinant murine p53 protein on specific residues in a conserved basic region of 25 amino acids located in the C-terminal part of the protein. Using a synthetic p53 peptide (357-381), we found that PKC phosphorylates the peptide at multiple Ser and Thr residues, including Ser360, Thr365, Ser370, and Thr377. Interestingly, the ability of the peptide to stimulate sequence-specific DNA binding by p53 is lost upon phosphorylation by PKC. To further investigate the mechanisms of PKC-dependent phosphorylation of p53, we compared the phosphorylation of full-length p53 and the p53 peptide (357-381) by PKC. Our results suggest that the accessibility of the phosphorylation sites on full-length p53 is important for PKC-dependent phosphorylation, and that a domain on p53 distinct from the peptide (357-381) is involved in binding PKC. We have identified a conserved 27-amino-acid peptide (p53-(320-346)-peptide) within the C-terminal region of p53 that interacts with PKC in vitro. This peptide inhibits PKC autophosphorylation and the phosphorylation of substrates, including the p53 peptide (357-381), neurogranin, and histone H1. Our findings suggest that p53-(320-346)-peptide may play a role in regulating the in vivo phosphorylation of p53 by PKC.

title: Role of ocular pigment epithelial cells in immune privilege
text: The ocular microenvironment is characterized by both immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory properties. Pigment epithelial (PE) cells isolated from the eye have the ability to suppress the activation of T cells and the induction of regulatory T cells in vitro, through the production of inhibitory molecules such as CD86 (B7-2), TGF-β, thrombospondin-1, PD-L1/B7-H1, and cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen 2α. These cells can be isolated from different parts of the eye, including the iris, ciliary body, and retina, and each has its own unique mechanism of T-cell suppression. Additionally, PE-derived regulatory T cells acquire functions that contribute to immune regulation in the eye. The eye employs multiple strategies to control immune-mediated inflammation, known as immune privilege, to prevent extensive damage to bystander cells and maintain vision. This review focuses on the immunosuppressive properties of ocular PE cells in immune privileged sites.

title: Drug-resistant Salmonella in the United States: an epidemiologic perspective.
text: Salmonellosis poses a significant health threat in the United States, with over 40,000 reported cases and 500 deaths each year, resulting in financial costs exceeding $50 million. Moreover, there is a growing concern about antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella strains, which has important implications for public health. Although the transmission chain of the bacteria can be complex, combining epidemiological and laboratory studies with advanced molecular biology techniques allows researchers to trace antimicrobial-resistant Salmonellae back to their primary source: animal-derived foods. These findings suggest that the antimicrobial drugs to which food animals are exposed create selective pressure that leads to the emergence and persistence of resistant strains.

title: Glutamine-specific N-terminal amidase, a component of the N-end rule pathway.
text: Deamidation of the N-terminal Glutamine (Gln) by Nt(Q)-amidase, an N-terminal amidohydrolase, is part of the N-end rule pathway of protein degradation. We detected the activity of Ntaq1, the gene product of which was purified from bovine brains, in mouse tissues, and began analyzing this enzyme. Ntaq1 is highly conserved across animals, plants, and some fungi, but its sequence differs from that of other amidases. An earlier mutant in the Drosophila Cg8253 gene, which we show here encodes Nt(Q)-amidase, has defects in long-term memory. Other studies have identified protein ligands of the uncharacterized human C8orf32 protein, which we show here to be the Ntaq1 Nt(Q)-amidase. Remarkably, recent "high-throughput" studies have solved the crystal structure of C8orf32 (Ntaq1). Our site-directed mutagenesis of Ntaq1 and its crystal structure reveal that the active site and catalytic mechanism of Nt(Q)-amidase are similar to those of transglutaminases.

title: Brahma-related gene 1-dependent STAT3 recruitment at IL-6-inducible genes.
text:
Introduction:
Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a multifunctional cytokine that plays a crucial role in immunoregulation, hemopoiesis, proliferation, and tumorigenesis. IL-6 signaling involves the activation of signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), which is mediated by phosphorylation, dimerization, and nuclear translocation. Brahma-related gene 1 (BRG1) is an essential component of the yeast-mating type-switching and sucrose-nonfermenting chromatin-remodeling complex, and has been shown to be involved in the recruitment of STAT1 or STAT1/STAT2-containing complexes to interferon (IFN) targets. In this study, we investigate the role of BRG1 in the recruitment of STAT3 to IFN regulatory factor 1 (IRF1) promoter and its downstream effects on chromatin remodeling and gene expression.
Methods:
We used a combination of chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) and gene expression analysis to investigate the role of BRG1 in IL-6-induced gene expression. We found that BRG1 is constitutively present at a subset of IL-6-responsive genes and is required for STAT3 recruitment, downstream histone modifications, and IL-6-induced chromatin remodeling. We also observed that IL-6-induced recruitment of STAT3 to the IRF1 promoter is BRG1 dependent, despite the fact that STAT1 recruitment to this locus is BRG1 independent.
Results:
Our results show that BRG1 plays a broad role in mediating STAT accessibility at multiple cytokine-responsive promoters, and that there are promoter-specific differences in the effect of BRG1 on basal chromatin accessibility and STAT protein recruitment. We found that BRG1 increases basal expression of IFN-induced transmembrane protein 3 (IFIT3) and IFN-gamma-induced protein 16 (IP-16), and enhances basal chromatin accessibility at the promoter of IRF1. Furthermore, we observed that the effect of BRG1 on basal expression is STAT3 independent, as revealed by small interfering RNA (siRNA) knockdown.
Discussion:
Our findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying IL-6-induced gene expression and chromatin remodeling. We demonstrate that BRG1 plays a critical role in recruiting STAT3 to cytokine-responsive promoters, and that this process is independent of STAT1. Our results also highlight the promoter-specific differences in the effect of BRG1 on basal chromatin accessibility and STAT protein recruitment. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying cytokine signaling and gene expression, and may lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of diseases associated with dysregulated cytokine signaling.

title: High and low fat consumers, their macronutrient intake and body mass index: further analysis of the National Diet and Nutrition Survey of British Adults.
text:
Objective: To investigate the differences in macronutrient intake and body mass index (BMI) between individuals classified as high and low fat consumers, using data from the Dietary and Nutritional Survey of British Adults.
Design: Reanalysis of 7-day weighed food records collected from 1240 adults in Great Britain between 1986 and 1987.
Setting: Private households in Great Britain.
Subjects: A total of 1240 adults, with 10.8% (6.1% of the total population) classified as low fat consumers and 15.4% (8.7% of the total population) classified as high fat consumers.
Main Outcome Measures: Macronutrient consumption and BMI.
Results: The study found that 30% of the subjects changed fat group classification when the criteria for defining high and low fat groups were altered from fat percentage to fat grams (FATg). Nutrient intakes differed according to the definition of the groups, with the high fat FATg group consuming significantly more of all nutrients than the low fat FATg group. However, this was not seen for the fat percentage analysis, with the high fat group consuming more fat and less carbohydrate. The average BMI tended to be higher in the high fat than the low fat groups, particularly in the FATg analysis, but the high fat group contained a wide range of BMIs. Further exploration of BMI in the high fat groups showed that age was the only variable that distinguished individuals in the top and bottom quartiles of BMI.
Conclusions: The study found that high and low fat consumers differ according to various variables, and this is affected by how these groups are defined. High fat consumers tend to have a higher BMI than low fat consumers, but not all high fat consumers are overweight or obese.

title: Quantitative, genome-wide analysis of eukaryotic replication initiation and termination.
text: Many fundamental aspects of DNA replication, such as the precise locations where synthesis is initiated and terminated, the frequency of origin usage, and the influence of transcription on fork progression, remain poorly understood. Through the comprehensive deep sequencing of Okazaki fragments, we have systematically documented replication fork directionality throughout the S. cerevisiae genome, enabling the analysis of initiation, origin efficiency, fork progression, and termination. Our findings reveal that leading-strand initiation preferentially occurs within a nucleosome-free region at replication origins. Using a strain that allows for the induction of early firing of late origins, we demonstrate that replication termination is primarily a passive process that does not rely on cis-acting sequences or replication fork pausing. The replication profile is primarily determined by the kinetics of origin firing, allowing us to reconstruct chromosome-wide timing profiles from an asynchronous culture.

title: The murine H19 gene is activated during embryonic stem cell differentiation in vitro and at the time of implantation in the developing embryo.
text: The in vitro differentiation of murine embryonic stem cells into embryoid bodies recapitulates the events that occur in vivo during the early stages of embryonic development, including the time period around implantation. Using this system in combination with differential cDNA cloning, we have identified genes whose expression is regulated during early embryogenesis. As part of this study, we isolated several cDNA clones, including one that corresponds to the gene H19. This gene is expressed in extraembryonic cell types at the time of implantation and is later expressed in all cells of the mid-gestation embryo, with the exception of most cells of the developing central and peripheral nervous systems. After birth, expression of this gene is either reduced or ceases in all tissues.

title: Localization of Sir2p: the nucleolus as a compartment for silent information regulators.
text: In wild-type budding yeast strains, the proteins encoded by SIR3, SIR4, and RAP1 co-localize with telomeric DNA in a limited number of foci within interphase nuclei. Immunostaining of Sir2p reveals an additional punctate staining pattern that overlaps with Rap1 foci, as well as a subdomain localization within the nucleolus. Using formaldehyde cross-linking and immunoprecipitation with anti-Sir2p antibodies, the presence of Sir2p at both the spacer of the rDNA repeat and at telomeres is confirmed. In strains lacking Sir4p, Sir3p becomes concentrated in the nucleolus through a pathway that requires SIR2 and UTH4, a gene that regulates life span in yeast. The unexpected nucleolar localization of Sir2p and Sir3p is associated with observed effects of sir mutations on rDNA stability and yeast longevity, identifying a new site of action for silent information regulatory factors.

title: Optogenetics reveal delayed afferent synaptogenesis on grafted human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural progenitors.
text:
The reprogramming of somatic cells into a pluripotent stem cell state has opened up new avenues for cell replacement therapy and disease modeling in various neurological disorders. However, it remains unclear to what extent the grafted human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) differentiate into functional neurons and integrate into the host circuitry. To investigate this, we used an in vitro model of hyperexcitable epileptic tissue, organotypic hippocampal slice cultures (OHSCs), and adult rats in vivo.
We first differentiated the hiPSCs into long-term self-renewing neuroepithelial stem (lt-NES) cells, which are known to form primarily GABAergic neurons. When differentiated in OHSCs for 6 weeks, lt-NES cell-derived neurons displayed neuronal properties such as tetrodotoxin-sensitive sodium currents and action potentials (APs), as well as both spontaneous and evoked postsynaptic currents, indicating functional afferent synaptic inputs. The grafted cells had a distinct electrophysiological profile compared to host cells in the OHSCs, with higher input resistance, lower resting membrane potential, and APs with lower amplitude and longer duration.
To investigate the origin of synaptic afferents to the grafted lt-NES cell-derived neurons, the host neurons were transduced with Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) and optogenetically activated by blue light. Simultaneous recordings of synaptic currents in grafted lt-NES cell-derived neurons using whole-cell patch-clamp technique at 6 weeks after grafting revealed limited synaptic connections from host neurons. Longer differentiation times, up to 24 weeks after grafting in vivo, revealed more mature intrinsic properties and extensive synaptic afferents from host neurons to the lt-NES cell-derived neurons, suggesting that these cells require extended time for differentiation/maturation and synaptogenesis. However, even at this later time point, the grafted cells maintained a higher input resistance. These data indicate that grafted lt-NES cell-derived neurons receive ample afferent input from the host brain. Since the lt-NES cells used in this study show a strong propensity for GABAergic differentiation, the host-to-graft synaptic afferents may facilitate inhibitory neurotransmitter release, and normalize hyperexcitable neuronal networks in brain diseases, for example, such as epilepsy.

title: Anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody in new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus.
text:
Background: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by the destructive action of T lymphocytes on insulin-producing beta cells. Previous clinical studies have shown that continuous immune suppression can temporarily slow the loss of insulin production. Preclinical studies have suggested that a monoclonal antibody against CD3 could reverse hyperglycemia at presentation and induce tolerance to recurrent disease.
Methods: We investigated the effects of a non-activating humanized monoclonal antibody against CD3, hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala), on the loss of insulin production in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Within 6 weeks of diagnosis, 24 patients were randomly assigned to receive either a single 14-day course of treatment with the monoclonal antibody or no antibody, and were followed for at least 1 year.
Results: Treatment with hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala) maintained or improved insulin production in 9 of the 12 patients in the treatment group after 1 year, compared to 2 of the 12 controls (P=0.01). The treatment effect on insulin responses lasted for at least 12 months after diagnosis. Glycosylated hemoglobin levels and insulin doses were also reduced in the monoclonal-antibody group. No severe side effects occurred, and the most common side effects were fever, rash, and anemia. Clinical responses were associated with a change in the ratio of CD4+ T cells to CD8+ T cells 30 and 90 days after treatment.
Conclusions: Treatment with hOKT3gamma1(Ala-Ala) mitigates the deterioration in insulin production and improves metabolic control during the first year of type 1 diabetes mellitus in the majority of patients. The mechanism of action of the anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody may involve direct effects on pathogenic T cells, the induction of populations of regulatory cells, or both.

title: Establishment and in vitro differentiation of a new embryonic stem cell line from human blastocyst.
text: Embryonic stem cells have the unique ability to remain unchanged and divide indefinitely in a laboratory dish while maintaining the potential to develop into different types of cells. These cells have significant potential for use in various studies, such as gene function and differentiation. The goal of this study was to create a human embryonic stem cell line. Researchers separated the inner cell mass of a human blastocyst and cultured it on mouse embryonic fibroblasts in a special medium containing additives. The established cell line was evaluated using various methods, including morphology, passaging, freezing and thawing, alkaline phosphatase expression, Oct-4 expression, and the presence of surface markers such as Tra-1-60 and Tra-1-81. Additionally, the cell line's karyotype and spontaneous differentiation were evaluated. Differentiated cardiomyocytes and neurons were also examined using transmission electron microscopy and immunocytochemistry. The results of this study demonstrate the derivation of a new human embryonic stem cell line, Royan H1, which remains undifferentiated in morphology after continuous passaging for over 30 passages, has a normal XX karyotype, is viable after freezing and thawing, and expresses alkaline phosphatase, Oct-4, Tra-1-60, and Tra-1-81. These cells can also differentiate in vitro in the absence of feeder cells and produce embryoid bodies that can further differentiate into beating cardiomyocytes as well as neurons. These findings establish Royan H1 cells as a new human embryonic stem cell line.

title: Lactate Metabolism in Human Lung Tumors
text: Cancer cells consume glucose and produce lactate in culture, but it is unclear whether lactate plays a role in energy metabolism in living tumors. Previous studies have shown that human non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) use glucose in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Here, we investigate the use of lactate in the TCA cycle by NSCLCs. We found that lactate is also a TCA cycle carbon source for NSCLC, and its utilization is more pronounced in tumors with high glucose uptake and aggressive behavior. In human NSCLC patients, infusing 13C-lactate revealed extensive labeling of TCA cycle metabolites. Deleting monocarboxylate transporter-1 (MCT1) from tumor cells in mice eliminated lactate-dependent metabolite labeling, confirming that lactate uptake is tumor-cell-autonomous. Surprisingly, our in vivo data indicate that lactate's contribution to the TCA cycle is more significant than previously thought, suggesting that tumors, including bona fide human NSCLC, can use lactate as a fuel in vivo.

title: Increased lipid peroxidation as a mechanism of methionine-induced atherosclerosis in rabbits.
text: Methionine is converted into homocysteine through the transmethylation/transsulfuration pathway, which may lead to atherogenic effects through various mechanisms, including lipid peroxidation. Therefore, consuming excessive dietary methionine may contribute to the development of atherosclerosis. To investigate this hypothesis, we measured plasma and aortic thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), as well as activities of aortic and erythrocyte superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase (GPX) in rabbits fed a methionine-enriched diet for 6 or 9 months. Histological examinations of aortas were also performed. Our results show that feeding rabbits a methionine-enriched diet for 6 or 9 months resulted in significant increases in plasma and aortic TBARS levels and aortic antioxidant enzyme activities, but a decrease in plasma antioxidant activity (AOA). In erythrocytes, SOD activity increased, catalase remained normal, and GPX decreased in the treated animals. Histological examination of aortas revealed typical atherosclerotic changes, such as intimal thickening, deposition of cholesterol, and calcification, in methionine-fed rabbits. These findings confirm that a high-methionine diet may induce atherosclerosis in rabbits and suggest that disturbances in lipid peroxidation and antioxidant processes may be involved in its atherogenic influence.

title: Sex differences in sex chromosome gene expression in mouse brain.
text:
A fundamental question in the field of sex chromosome biology is whether genes encoded on the sex chromosomes (X and Y) act directly in non-gonadal tissues to influence sex differences in development and function, or whether all sex differences in somatic tissues are induced by gonadal secretions. As part of this question, we investigated whether mouse X-Y homologous gene pairs are expressed in the brain in a sex-specific manner.
Using RT-PCR and northern blot analysis, we evaluated mRNA expression in the brain of eight Y-linked genes and their X-linked homologues at three ages: 13.5 days post coitum (dpc), the day of birth (P1), and adulthood. Our results showed that transcripts of six Y genes were expressed in the brain at one or more ages, including Usp9y, Ube1y, Smcy, Eif2s3y, Uty, and Dby. Notably, these genes were also expressed in XY female brains, indicating that they do not require testicular secretions for their expression. In contrast, six X-linked homologues (Usp9x, Ube1x, Smcx, Eif2s3x, Utx, and Dbx) were expressed in the brain, with all of these transcripts exhibiting significantly higher levels of expression in female brains than in male brains, regardless of their X-inactivation status. Interestingly, for five of these gene pairs, the expression of the Y-linked homologue in males was not sufficient to compensate for the female bias in X gene expression. Furthermore, we found that three X-Y gene pairs (Usp9x/y, Ube1x/y, and Eif2s3x/y) showed differential regulation, with their expression patterns differing in the brain or in different tissues. These findings suggest several mechanisms by which these genes may contribute to sex differences in brain development and function.

title: Genome architecture, rearrangements and genomic disorders.
text: An increasing number of human diseases have been found to result from recurrent DNA rearrangements involving unstable genomic regions. These are termed genomic disorders, where the clinical phenotype is a consequence of abnormal gene dosage due to the rearrangement of genomic fragments. Both intrachromosomal and interchromosomal rearrangements are facilitated by the presence of region-specific low-copy repeats (LCRs), which are sequences that span approximately 10-400 kilobases of genomic DNA, share at least 97% sequence identity, and provide the substrates for homologous recombination, thus predisposing the region to rearrangements. Additionally, it has been suggested that higher-order genomic architecture involving LCRs plays a significant role in karyotypic evolution and primate speciation.

title: painDETECT: a new screening questionnaire to identify neuropathic components in patients with back pain.
text:
Objective: To develop and validate a simple, validated screening tool to detect neuropathic pain (NeP) components in chronic low back pain (LBP) patients, and to determine the prevalence of NeP components in a large-scale survey.
Methods: In collaboration with the German Research Network on Neuropathic Pain, a painDETECT questionnaire (PD-Q) was developed and validated in a prospective, multicentre study. The PD-Q was applied to approximately 8000 LBP patients.
Results: The PD-Q is a reliable screening tool with high sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive accuracy. In an unselected cohort of chronic LBP patients, 37% were found to have predominantly neuropathic pain. Patients with NeP had higher ratings of pain intensity, more (and more severe) co-morbidities such as depression, panic/anxiety, and sleep disorders, which also affected functionality and use of health-care resources. Based on the prevalence of LBP in the general population, it is estimated that 14.5% of female and 11.4% of male Germans suffer from LBP with a predominant NeP component.
Conclusion: Simple, patient-based, easy-to-use screening questionnaires can determine the prevalence of NeP components in individual LBP patients and in heterogeneous cohorts of such patients. Accurate diagnosis of NeP is crucial in choosing appropriate therapy, as NeP correlates with more intense pain, more severe co-morbidities, and poorer quality of life.

title: Scoring of dual fluorescein and ICG inflammatory angiographic signs for the grading of posterior segment inflammation (dual fluorescein and ICG angiographic scoring system for uveitis)
text:
Purpose:
The aim of this study is to propose a semiquantitative dual fluorescein angiography (FA) and indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) scoring system for uveitis, which can assist in monitoring disease progression and treatment response.
Methods:
The proposed scoring system was developed based on existing FA scoring systems, a standardized ICGA protocol, and schematic interpretation of ICGA findings in posterior uveitis. The scores assigned to the fluorescein and ICG angiographic signs reflect the ongoing inflammatory process in the posterior segment. To enable direct comparison between FA and ICGA, the ICGA scores were multiplied by a coefficient of 2 to adjust the total score to that of FA.
Results:
A total maximum score of 40 was assigned to the FA signs, including optic disc hyperfluorescence, macular edema, retinal vascular staining and/or leakage, capillary leakage, retinal capillary nonperfusion, neovascularization of the optic disc, neovascularization elsewhere, pinpoint leaks, and retinal staining and/or subretinal pooling. A total maximum score of 20 was assigned to the ICGA signs, including early stromal vessel hyperfluorescence, choroidal vasculitis, dark dots or areas (excluding atrophy), and optic disc hyperfluorescence.
Conclusion:
The proposed combined fluorescein and ICG angiographic scoring system may help estimate the magnitude of retinal versus choroidal inflammation, monitor disease progression, and assess treatment response. Its applicability and reliability need to be tested in clinical settings, and intra- and interobserver variations need to be determined.

title: Improving outcomes of acute kidney injury: report of an initiative
text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a multifaceted disorder involving various etiological factors and occurring in diverse settings. The disorder presents with a range of clinical manifestations, from mild elevations in serum creatinine levels to anuric renal failure. To address the complexity of AKI, we have established a collaborative network, the Acute Kidney Injury Network (AKIN), comprising experts from multiple disciplines. The AKIN has proposed standardized diagnostic and classification criteria for AKI, which will require validation through future studies. The AKIN provides a platform for knowledge sharing and collaboration, ultimately aiming to improve patient outcomes.

title: A Screen for Endocytic Motifs
text: Sorting signals for cargo selection into coated vesicles are typically in the form of short linear motifs. Three well-characterized motifs for clathrin-mediated endocytosis have been identified: YXXPhi, [D/E]XXXL[L/I], and FXNPXY. To expand the repertoire of endocytic motifs, we generated a library of CD8 chimeras with random sequences in their cytoplasmic tails and used a novel fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-based assay to select for endocytosed constructs. Of the five tails that were most efficiently internalized, only one contained a conventional motif. Two of the tails harbored dileucine-like sequences that appear to be variations on the [D/E]XXXL[L/I] motif. Surprisingly, another tail contained a novel internalization signal, YXXXPhiN, which was able to function in cells expressing a mutant mu2 that cannot bind YXXPhi, indicating that it is not a variation on the YXXPhi motif. Notably, similar sequences are present in endogenous proteins, including a functional YXXXPhiN (in addition to a classical YXXPhi) in cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4). These findings suggest that the repertoire of endocytic motifs is more extensive than previously thought, with potentially many more yet to be identified.

title: Microtubule stabilization reduces scarring and causes axon regeneration after spinal cord injury.
text: Hypertrophic scarring and limited intrinsic axon growth are significant hindrances to spinal cord repair. These processes are tightly regulated by microtubule dynamics. In rodents, moderate microtubule stabilization after spinal cord injury led to a decrease in scar formation through various cellular mechanisms, including dampening of transforming growth factor-β signaling. This resulted in a decrease in the accumulation of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and made the lesion site more conducive to axon regeneration of growth-competent sensory neurons. Additionally, microtubule stabilization promoted the growth of central nervous system axons in the Raphe-spinal tract and led to functional improvements. Overall, microtubule stabilization reduces fibrotic scarring and enhances the capacity of axons to grow.

title: Histone tails: Directing the chromatin response to DNA damage.
text: A significant amount of energy is devoted to altering large sections of chromatin near DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) after they occur. This is done to create a platform for the inducible and modular assembly of DNA repair protein complexes in the vicinity of the DNA lesion. This complex signaling network is crucial for repairing DNA damage and communicating with cellular processes that occur both directly (cis) and indirectly (trans) to the genomic lesion. Failure to properly execute these DNA damage-induced chromatin changes has been linked to a range of developmental abnormalities, immunodeficiency, and cancer in both humans and genetically engineered mouse models. This review will discuss the current understanding of the histone modifications that occur in mammalian cells in response to DNA damage, highlighting their role in maintaining genome integrity.

title: Sestrin2 inhibits uncoupling protein 1 expression through suppressing reactive oxygen species.
text: Uncoupling protein 1 (Ucp1), located in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mammalian brown adipose tissue (BAT), generates heat by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation. Upon cold exposure or nutritional abundance, sympathetic neurons stimulate BAT to express Ucp1, leading to energy dissipation and thermogenesis. Increased Ucp1 expression reduces obesity in mice and is associated with leanness in humans. However, there is limited understanding of how Ucp1 expression is regulated at the molecular level. Here, we investigate the involvement of Sestrin2 and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in regulating Ucp1 expression. Transgenic overexpression of Sestrin2 in adipose tissues inhibited both basal and cold-induced Ucp1 expression in interscapular BAT, leading to decreased thermogenesis and increased fat accumulation. Endogenous Sestrin2 is also important for suppressing Ucp1 expression, as BAT from Sestrin2-deficient mice showed a high level of Ucp1 expression. The redox-inactive mutant of Sestrin2 was incapable of regulating Ucp1 expression, suggesting that Sestrin2 inhibits Ucp1 expression primarily by reducing ROS accumulation. Consistently, ROS-suppressing antioxidants, such as butylated hydroxyanisole and N-acetylcysteine, inhibited cold- or cAMP-induced Ucp1 expression. p38 MAPK, a signaling mediator required for cAMP-induced Ucp1 expression, was inhibited by either Sestrin2 overexpression or antioxidant treatments. These results suggest that Sestrin2 and antioxidants inhibit Ucp1 expression by suppressing ROS-mediated p38 MAPK activation, highlighting a critical role of ROS in proper BAT metabolism.

title: The non-catalytic function of XPG protein during dual incision in human nucleotide excision repair.
text: XPG is a member of the FEN-1 structure-specific endonuclease family and has 3'-junction cutting activity on bubble substrates, making the 3'-incision in the human dual incision (excision nuclease) repair system. To investigate the role of XPG in nucleotide excision repair, we mutated two key amino acid residues involved in DNA binding and catalysis, overexpressed the mutant proteins using a baculovirus/insect cell system, and characterized the mutant proteins. The mutation D77A had a modest effect on junction cutting and excision activity, resulting in uncoupled 5'-incision by mammalian cell-free extracts. The D812A mutation completely abolished the junction cutting and 3'-incision activities of XPG, but the excision nuclease reconstituted with XPG (D812A) carried out normal 5'-incision at the 23rd-24th phosphodiester bonds 5' to a (6-4) photoproduct without producing any 3'-incision. These findings suggest that Asp-812 is an active site residue of XPG and that the physical presence of XPG in the protein-DNA complex is required non-catalytically for subsequent 5'-incision by XPF-ERCC1.

title: A 40-Hz auditory potential recorded from the human scalp.
text: Computer analysis of brainwave activity can extract a sequential pattern of brain potentials that are synchronized to sound stimuli, with the potentials appearing between 8 and 80 milliseconds after the stimulus. These potentials exhibit a consistent waveform resembling 3 or 4 cycles of a 40-Hz sine wave when the sounds are repeated at a rate of around 40 per second. This phenomenon, known as the 40-Hz event-related potential (ERP), displays several interesting properties. Firstly, it has been observed that the 40-Hz ERP disappears with the administration of anesthesia, suggesting that adequate processing of sensory information may require cyclical brain events in the 30- to 50-Hz range, similar to phenomena observed in the visual and olfactory systems. Secondly, measurements of latency and amplitude of the 40-Hz ERP suggest that it may contain useful information on the number and location of auditory nerve fibers that are excited by a given tone. Finally, the presence of the 40-Hz ERP is observed at sound intensities very close to normal adult thresholds for the audiometric frequencies, which could have practical applications in clinical hearing testing.

title: Bile acids: natural ligands for an orphan nuclear receptor.
text: Bile acids play a crucial role in regulating the transcription of genes involved in cholesterol metabolism through a poorly understood molecular mechanism. In physiological concentrations, free and conjugated forms of chenodeoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid, and deoxycholic acid activate the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), a nuclear receptor that was previously considered an orphan receptor. As ligands, these bile acids and their conjugates modulate the interaction between FXR and a peptide derived from steroid receptor coactivator 1, providing evidence for a nuclear bile acid signaling pathway that may regulate cholesterol homeostasis.

title: The yeast ribosomal protein L32 and its gene.
text:
The Saccharomyces cerevisiae ribosomal protein gene RPL32 is of particular interest for two reasons:
1. It is located near another ribosomal protein gene, RP29, whose divergent transcription may be regulated by the same control sequences.
2. The splicing of RPL32's transcript is regulated by the protein it encodes, ribosomal protein L32. RPL32 has been extensively studied. It is essential for cell growth, and its sequence suggests that L32 is a protein of 105 amino acids with a basic NH2 terminus and acidic COOH terminus, and is homologous to ribosomal protein L30 of mammals. The reading frame of L32 has been confirmed through partial NH2-terminal analysis, and the nucleotide sequence predicts an intron of 230 nucleotides with a unique GTCAGT sequence at the 5' end and a polyadenylation site 100 nucleotides downstream of the termination codon. Transcription initiates 58 nucleotides upstream of the AUG initiation codon. Analysis of the intergenic region between RP29 and RPL32 reveals three copies of a consensus sequence linked to transcriptional regulation, and a deletion removing all three sequences reduces synthesis of a L32-LacZ fusion protein by more than 90%, with some residual activity remaining.

title: Derivation conditions impact X-inactivation status in female human induced pluripotent stem cells.
text: Female human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines exhibit variability in X-inactivation status, with the majority maintaining one transcriptionally active X (Xa) and one inactive X (Xi) chromosome from donor cells. However, at a low frequency, hiPSC lines with two Xas are produced, suggesting sporadic epigenetic alterations of the Xi during reprogramming. Our findings demonstrate that the derivation conditions of hiPSC lines have a significant impact on X-inactivation status. hiPSC lines generated using the Kyoto method (retroviral or episomal reprogramming), which utilizes leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF)-expressing SNL feeders, frequently exhibit two Xas. In contrast, early passage Xa/Xi hiPSC lines generated on non-SNL feeders are converted into Xa/Xa hiPSC lines after several passages on SNL feeders, and supplementation with recombinant LIF can reactivate some X-linked genes. These findings highlight the significance of feeders in affecting X-inactivation status, and the efficient production of Xa/Xa hiPSC lines provides unprecedented opportunities to investigate human X-reactivation and -inactivation.

title: Loss of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine and ten-eleven translocation 2 protein expression in malignant melanoma.
text: Several research groups have recently reported a significant decrease in 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) levels in various types of cancer, including breast, liver, lung, pancreatic, colon, prostate, brain, and myeloid cancers. In this study, we investigated the levels of 5hmC in benign compound nevi (BCN), dysplastic compound nevi (DCN), superficial spreading melanomas (SSM), and cutaneous metastatic disease (CMD). We used immunohistochemistry to detect 5hmC, 5-methylcytosine (5mC), and ten-eleven translocation 2 protein (TET2). Our results showed that the median 5hmC levels were significantly higher in BCN and DCN compared to thin SSM, thick SSM, and CMD. In contrast, the levels of 5mC did not differ significantly between nevi and melanoma. The intensity of TET2 expression was predominantly weak, but it was found to be significantly more frequent in nevi than in thin SSM, thick SSM, and CMD. Our findings suggest that 5hmC and TET2 may play an important role in the epigenetic regulation of melanoma development and progression.

title: Estimation of the dietary requirement for vitamin D in healthy adults.
text:
Background:
Knowledge gaps regarding the optimal dietary intake of vitamin D have contributed to the variability in international dietary recommendations for this nutrient.
Objective:
To determine the range of dietary vitamin D intakes required to maintain serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) concentrations above various proposed cutoffs (ie, 25, 37.5, 50, and 80 nmol/L) during wintertime after adjusting for the effect of summer sunshine exposure and diet.
Design:
A randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind 22-week intervention study was conducted in men and women aged 20-40 years (n = 238) by using different supplemental doses (0, 5, 10, and 15 microg/d) of vitamin D(3) throughout the winter. Serum 25(OH)D concentrations were measured using enzyme-linked immunoassay at baseline (October 2006) and endpoint (March 2007).
Results:
There were clear dose-related increments (P < 0.0001) in serum 25(OH)D with increasing supplemental vitamin D(3) intake. The slope of the relation between vitamin D intake and serum 25(OH)D was 1.96 nmol x L(-1) x microg(-1) intake. The vitamin D intake that maintained serum 25(OH)D concentrations of >25 nmol/L in 97.5% of the sample was 8.7 microg/d. This intake ranged from 7.2 microg/d in those who enjoyed sunshine exposure, 8.8 microg/d in those who sometimes had sun exposure, and 12.3 microg/d in those who avoided sunshine. Vitamin D intakes required to maintain serum 25(OH)D concentrations of >37.5, >50, and >80 nmol/L in 97.5% of the sample were 19.9, 28.0, and 41.1 microg/d, respectively.
Conclusion:
The range of vitamin D intakes required to ensure maintenance of wintertime vitamin D status (as defined by incremental cutoffs of serum 25(OH)D) in the vast majority (>97.5%) of 20-40-year-old adults, considering a variety of sun exposure preferences, is between 7.2 and 41.1 microg/d.

title: Rapid purification of homodimer and heterodimer HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by metal chelate affinity chromatography.
text: We have modified an Escherichia coli vector to express both 66-kDa HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (p66) and the pol-coded protease simultaneously. This twin expression cassette results in high levels of both reverse transcriptase and protease, but under these conditions, approximately 50% of the over-expressed p66 reverse transcriptase is processed, leading to the accumulation of large quantities of p66/p51 enzyme. To facilitate the purification of these enzymes, we added a poly(histidine) affinity label to the amino terminus of the reverse-transcriptase-coding sequence (His-p66). This allows for simple and rapid purification of milligram quantities of either p66 or p66/p51 enzyme from a crude lysate using metal chelate affinity chromatography. Purified His-p66 and His-p66/His-p51 reverse transcriptase exhibit both reverse transcriptase and RNase H activity. Additionally, the purification of a p66/p51 enzyme where only the p66 component is labeled provides further evidence for the existence of a heterodimer.

title: Polyphenols of Cocoa: Inhibition of Mammalian 15-Lipoxygenase
text: Some cocoa and chocolate products contain high levels of epicatechin and related oligomers, known as procyanidins. These compounds were found to inhibit the activity of isolated rabbit 15-lipoxygenase-1 in a dose-dependent manner, with the larger oligomers being more effective. The decamer fraction had an IC50 value of 0.8 M, while the monomeric flavanols, epigallocatechin gallate and epicatechin gallate, were more potent than epicatechin and procyanidin nonamer. These compounds also inhibited the formation of 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid from arachidonic acid in rabbit smooth muscle cells transfected with human 15-lipoxygenase-1. However, inhibition of the lipoxygenase pathway in J774A.1 cells transfected with porcine leukocytetype 12-lipoxygenase was only observed when the cells were sonicated, suggesting a membrane barrier for flavanols in these cells. Additionally, epicatechin and the procyanidin decamer inhibited recombinant human platelet 12-lipoxygenase.
