These findings suggest that flavanols and procyanidins have general lipoxygenase inhibitory potency, which may contribute to their potential beneficial effects on the cardiovascular system in humans. This is consistent with recent literature reports indicating that procyanidins decrease the leukotriene/prostacyclin ratio in humans and human aortic endothelial cells.

title: Quality of life in patients with advanced heart failure.
text: Although the evaluation of congestive heart failure treatment is typically based on objective clinical outcomes, patient self-assessment is increasingly recognized as a crucial component of evaluation. A study aimed to assess the quality of life of 134 patients with advanced heart failure symptoms being evaluated for potential heart transplantation. The patients' quality of life was evaluated using a combination of subjective and objective measures, including functional status, physical symptoms, emotional state, and psychosocial adaptation. Contrary to expectations, there was no significant correlation between patients' cardiac ejection fraction and any quality-of-life measures. However, the results of a 6-minute walking test, New York Heart Association classification, and self-reported functional status were significantly correlated with psychosocial adjustment. Self-reported functional status, depression, and hostility accounted for 43% of the variance in total psychosocial adjustment to illness. These findings support the inclusion of quality of life as an outcome measure in any evaluation of treatment efficacy and suggest that interventions to improve the quality of life of patients with advanced heart failure should target reducing depression and hostility and increasing daily activity levels.

title: Regional vascular resistance during exercise: role of cardiac afferents and exercise training.
text: This study aimed to investigate the inhibitory effect of cardiac vagal afferents on regional vascular resistance during exercise and the potential enhancement of this effect through endurance exercise training. The study involved 12 rabbits that were instrumented with Doppler ultrasonic flow probes around various arteries to measure changes in regional vascular resistance during exercise. The rabbits were then subjected to reversible denervation of cardiac afferents using intrapericardial procainamide HCl. In addition, five of these rabbits underwent an 8-week endurance exercise training program. The study found that exercise significantly increased regional vascular resistance in the renal, mesenteric, and terminal aortic arteries, but cardiac efferent blockade alone had no significant effect on regional vascular resistance during exercise. However, combined efferent and afferent blockade resulted in significant increases in regional vascular resistance in these arteries. Furthermore, exercise training significantly enhanced the inhibitory influence of cardiac afferents on regional vascular resistance in these arteries. These findings suggest that cardiac vagal afferents play a significant role in regulating regional vascular resistance during exercise and that endurance exercise training can enhance this effect.

title: Serum Soluble Corin is Decreased in Stroke.
text:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Coronary heart disease has been linked to decreased levels of soluble corin, a protein that plays a crucial role in cardiac function. Given the connection between cardiac dysfunction and stroke, circulating corin may serve as a potential marker of stroke risk. However, the association between circulating corin and stroke has yet to be explored in humans. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between serum soluble corin levels and stroke risk in both men and women.
METHODS: A total of 481 patients with ischemic stroke, 116 patients with hemorrhagic stroke, and 2498 healthy controls were included in the study. Serum soluble corin levels and conventional risk factors for stroke were measured. Since circulating corin has been shown to vary between men and women, the association between serum soluble corin and stroke was evaluated separately in men and women.
RESULTS: Compared to healthy controls, patients with ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke had significantly lower levels of serum soluble corin in both men and women (all P values <0.05). In multivariate analysis, men in the lowest quartile of serum soluble corin were found to be at higher risk of developing ischemic (odds ratio [OR], 4.90; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.99-8.03) and hemorrhagic (OR, 17.57; 95% CI, 4.85-63.71) stroke than men in the highest quartile. Similarly, women in the lowest quartile of serum soluble corin were found to be at higher risk of developing ischemic (OR, 3.10; 95% CI, 1.76-5.44) and hemorrhagic (OR, 8.54; 95% CI, 2.35-31.02) stroke than women in the highest quartile. The trend of increasing stroke risk with decreasing levels of serum soluble corin was observed in both men and women (all P values for trend <0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that serum soluble corin may play a pathogenic role in stroke. Decreased levels of soluble corin were observed in patients with stroke, indicating a potential mechanism for stroke development. These findings highlight the potential of serum soluble corin as a novel marker for stroke risk, which could be useful in identifying individuals at high risk of stroke and developing targeted prevention strategies.

title: Topical application of chlorhexidine to neonatal umbilical cords for prevention of omphalitis and neonatal mortality in a rural district of Pakistan: a community-based, cluster-randomised trial.
text:
Background: Umbilical cord infection (omphalitis) is a significant risk factor for neonatal sepsis and mortality in low-resource settings where home deliveries are common. To investigate the effectiveness of umbilical cord cleansing with 4% chlorhexidine (CHX) solution, with or without handwashing with antiseptic soap, on the incidence of omphalitis and neonatal mortality, we conducted a two-by-two factorial, cluster-randomized trial in Dadu, a rural area of Sindh province, Pakistan.
Methods: We randomly allocated 187 clusters to one of four study groups: CHX solution with soap and educational messages promoting handwashing, CHX solution only, handwashing only, or standard dry cord care. Of the 9741 newborn babies delivered by participating traditional birth attendants (TBAs), we recorded the incidence of neonatal omphalitis and mortality.
Findings: Factorial analysis revealed a significant reduction in the risk of omphalitis with CHX application (RR=0·58, 95% CI 0·41-0·82; p=0·002), but no evidence of an effect of handwashing promotion (RR=0·83, 0·61-1·13; p=0·24). We also observed a significant reduction in neonatal mortality in neonates who received CHX cleansing (RR=0·62, 95% CI 0·45-0·85; p=0·003), but no evidence of an effect of handwashing promotion on neonatal mortality (RR=1·08, 0·79-1·48; p=0·62). No serious adverse events were recorded.
Interpretation: The application of 4% CHX to the umbilical cord was effective in reducing the risk of omphalitis and neonatal mortality in rural Pakistan. Providing CHX in birth kits may be a useful strategy for preventing neonatal mortality in high-mortality settings. Funding: United States Agency for International Development.

title: The IKK complex, a central regulator of NF-kappaB activation.
text: The IKK kinase complex is the central component of the NF-κB signaling cascade. It consists of two kinases, IKKα and IKKβ, and a regulatory subunit, NEMO/IKKγ. Additional proteins may temporarily or permanently associate with the complex, but their identity and function are still unclear. Two distinct NF-κB signaling pathways have been identified, depending on the activating signal and cell type: the canonical pathway (dependent on IKKβ and NEMO) and the non-canonical pathway (dependent solely on IKKα). The primary question that remains unresolved is how an NF-κB activating signal leads to the activation of the kinase subunits, allowing them to phosphorylate their targets and ultimately induce nuclear translocation of the NF-κB dimers. Over the past decade, significant progress has been made in understanding the function of the three IKK subunits through genetic, biochemical, and structural studies.

title: Cognitive predictors of young children's readiness for powered mobility.
text: Early independent mobility in young children with physical disabilities is crucial for the development of various cognitive and psychosocial skills. However, children with disabilities may struggle to move independently, putting them at risk of delays in these areas. Providing powered mobility can help, but there is limited information on when children have the cognitive skills to operate a wheelchair safely. This study aimed to identify these skills by developing a cognitive assessment battery and wheelchair training program. Twenty-six children between 20-36 months were assessed on cognitive skills and participated in the wheelchair training program. A stepwise regression analysis revealed that spatial relations and problem-solving cognitive domains accounted for 57% of the variance in wheelchair skills. The study also established developmental cut-off points on these scales as they relate to wheelchair skills, with clinical applications discussed.

title: Knockdown of the co-chaperone Hop promotes extranuclear accumulation of Stat3 in mouse embryonic stem cells.
text: A crucial step in the mechanism of mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC) pluripotency is the phosphorylation, dimerization, and nuclear translocation of the signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (Stat3). We employed RNA interference (RNAi) to reduce the levels of the co-chaperone Hsp70/Hsp90 organizing protein (Hop) in an mESC line. Hop knockdown resulted in a 68% decrease in Stat3 mRNA levels, decreased soluble phosphorylated Stat3 (pYStat3) levels, and led to the accumulation of Stat3 in an extranuclear compartment. The major binding partner of Hop, Hsp90, co-localized with a small non-nuclear fraction of Stat3 in mESCs, and both Stat3 and Hop co-precipitated with Hsp90. In contrast, the levels of Nanog and Oct4 proteins were unaffected by Hop knockdown. However, we observed a decrease in Nanog mRNA levels. Interestingly, in the absence of Hop, mESCs lost their ability to form embryoid bodies with a basement membrane, suggesting that Hop plays a role in maintaining mESC pluripotency. These findings suggest that Hop facilitates the phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of Stat3, implicating a role for the Hsp70/Hsp90 chaperone machinery in pluripotency signaling.

title: B-cell self-tolerance in humans.
text: Two mechanisms underlie the generation of the human antibody repertoire: V(D)J recombination during early B-cell development in the bone marrow and somatic mutation of immunoglobulin genes in mature B cells responding to antigen in the periphery. V(D)J recombination generates diversity through random joining of gene segments, while somatic mutation introduces random point mutations. Both mechanisms are essential to achieve the level of antigen receptor diversification required for immune protection, as defects in either process lead to increased susceptibility to infection. However, the drawback of producing vast random diversity in the antibody repertoire is the generation of autoantibodies. To prevent autoimmunity, B cells expressing autoantibodies are regulated through strict mechanisms that either modify the specificity of autoantibodies or the fate of cells producing them. Abnormalities in B-cell self-tolerance are associated with a large number of autoimmune diseases, but the specific nature of the defects is less well understood. We summarize recent data on the self-reactive B-cell repertoire in healthy individuals and patients with autoimmunity.

title: JMJD6 Promotes Colon Carcinogenesis through Negative Regulation of p53 by Hydroxylation
text: Jumonji domain-containing protein 6 (JMJD6) is a member of the Jumonji C domain-containing family, but its cellular function is still unclear. Our study found that JMJD6 is physically associated with the tumor suppressor p53 and catalyzes its hydroxylation through the transfer of an α-ketoglutarate and Fe(II) molecule. We identified lysine 382 of p53 as the main site of hydroxylation. Our results showed that JMJD6 inhibits p53 acetylation, promotes its association with the negative regulator MDMX, and represses p53 transcriptional activity. Depletion of JMJD6 led to enhanced p53 transcriptional activity, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents. Additionally, we found that JMJD6 is up-regulated in various types of human cancer, including colon cancer, and high nuclear JMJD6 protein is correlated with aggressive clinical behaviors of colon adenocarcinomas. Our findings suggest that JMJD6 may serve as a potential biomarker for colon cancer aggressiveness and a potential target for colon cancer intervention.

title: Spread of chloroquine resistance in Plasmodium falciparum.
text: Malaria resistant to chloroquine has been confirmed in over 40 countries, with the drug first introduced in 1934 but not widely used until the early 1950s. Early anecdotal reports of resistance emerged as early as 1957 in Colombia and along the border area of Cambodia and Thailand. By 1960, resistance had been confirmed in these areas, which may represent two separate events. The resistance spread rapidly, with a new focus of resistance confirmed in East Africa by 1977. The emergence of chloroquine resistance poses a significant problem for both prophylaxis and treatment of malaria, as discussed by David Payne in this article.

title: Obesity occurring in apolipoprotein E-knockout mice has mild effects on fertility.
text: The Apolipoprotein (Apo) family plays a crucial role in lipid metabolism, with five distinct types (Apoa, Apob, Apoc, Apod, and Apoe). Apoe, in particular, has been shown to be central to lipoprotein metabolism and receptor-mediated plasma clearance of chylomicron remnants and VLDL remnant particles in the liver. Apoe-deficient mice (Apoe(-/-)) spontaneously develop atherosclerotic plaques and obesity. To investigate the impact of Apoe knockout on reproduction in female mice, we analyzed the lipid metabolism and expression of certain genes in the ovaries of Apoe(-/-) mice. Our results revealed that Apoe(-/-) mice were severely hypercholesterolemic, with disordered cholesterol metabolism and lipid accumulation in the ovaries, leading to heavier ovaries compared to their wild-type (WT) counterparts. Additionally, estrogen and progesterone levels decreased significantly at day 100. Quantitative PCR analysis showed that the expression of cytochrome P450 aromatase (Cyp19a1), 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (Hsd3b), mechanistic target of rapamycin (Mtor), and nuclear factor-κB (Nfkb) decreased, while the expression of BCL2-associated agonist of cell death (Bad) and tuberous sclerosis complex 2 (Tsc2) increased in the Apoe(-/-) mice. However, there was no significant difference in fertility rates between the Apoe(-/-) and WT mice. Interestingly, the deletion of Apoe resulted in an increase in the number of ovarian follicles and the ratio of ovarian follicle atresia and apoptosis. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the role of Apoe in reproduction.

title: Lipid metabolism and toxicity in the heart.
text:
The heart has the highest energy demands and is particularly efficient at metabolizing fatty acids (FAs) compared to other organs. However, under certain pathological conditions such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, the heart's ability to take up and metabolize FAs becomes disrupted, leading to the accumulation of lipids in the heart tissue. This can potentially cause cardiac lipotoxicity, which can lead to heart dysfunction.
To better understand the mechanisms underlying this process, we will first review the pathways by which the heart obtains FAs from the bloodstream and stores them intracellularly. We will then describe mouse models in which excess lipid accumulation leads to heart dysfunction and discuss the experiments that have been conducted to alleviate this toxicity. Finally, we will summarize the known relationships between heart lipid metabolism and dysfunction in humans.

title: Malaria eradication back on the table.
text:
After a 40-year hiatus, the goal of malaria eradication is back on the global health agenda. Inspired by the Gates Malaria Forum in 2007, key organizations are reevaluating the pros and cons of redefining eradication as an explicit goal of malaria control efforts. Past attempts to eliminate malaria in southern Africa and Pacific Island states, as well as the World Health Organization's (WHO) Global Malaria Programme agenda and field manual for malaria elimination, foreshadow this renewed focus on eradication. As we mark 60 years of WHO's commitment to fighting malaria, it is important to reflect on what has been achieved and what can be learned from the past.
We now have a much deeper understanding of the biology of parasite-host responses, the determinants of endemicity, and the transmission dynamics of malaria, as well as the social, economic, and cultural implications of the disease at the household, community, and national levels. However, we still do not know how to effectively integrate this knowledge to achieve elimination in different settings.
Regional malaria elimination campaigns were first conducted in the late 1940s, paving the way for the Global Malaria Eradication Program in 1955. While these efforts were successful in eliminating malaria from Europe, North America, the Caribbean, and parts of Asia and South-Central America, they were less successful in sub-Saharan Africa, where the disease still accounts for 80% of the global burden. The main reasons for failure in Africa were technical challenges, particularly in executing the strategy.
The post-eradication era from 1969 to 1991 focused on technical issues and research and development for new tools, leading to advances in drug and vaccine development, vector control, and insecticide-treated nets. This period also saw a better understanding of the social, economic, and cultural dimensions of malaria. However, there was little global support provided specifically for malaria control in newly independent states in Africa, which were struggling to establish broad-based health systems and primary health care.
By 1992, the combination of a worsening malaria situation and promising technical developments led to a renewed global focus on malaria control. The Roll Back Malaria initiative, launched by WHO in 1998, led to the Abuja Declaration in 2000, which defined progressive intervention coverage targets for control designed to eliminate malaria as a public health problem. Increased resources through the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, the World Bank's Booster Program, the US President's Malaria Initiative, and other efforts have meant that progress is finally being made.
The challenges ahead are formidable, but efforts must focus beyond simply developing better tools to include how existing and future tools can be strategically combined for maximum synergistic effectiveness when integrated into different health and social systems prevailing in endemic areas. Aiming at elimination and eradication also implies the need for effective surveillance strategies to monitor progress, which in turn requires a better understanding of malaria transmission heterogeneity in a globalized world with rapidly changing dynamics in environment, climate, migration, and transnational cooperation. Maintaining long-term momentum in the face of success in regional elimination while waiting to achieve final eradication will be a major challenge.
Shrinking the map by starting on the malaria margins with the "easy-to-eliminate" settings will boost morale initially, but may bring marginal benefits to such areas at the expense of those where the burden of malaria is highest. Any strategic plan must be a synchronous global effort, locally adapted in all endemic areas. Although we lack sufficient knowledge, systems, and tools to eradicate malaria today, we do have a window of political will and financial resources to refocus on the goal of effective control through universal coverage of appropriate interventions. A successful start requires a process of inclusive discourse to agree on a global vision, goals, and strategy, as well as a global plan for all endemic areas describing how, where, and when we move from control towards elimination.
In conclusion, while we lack the knowledge, systems, and tools to eradicate malaria today, we have a window of political will and financial resources to refocus on the goal of effective control through universal coverage of appropriate interventions. A successful start requires a process of inclusive discourse to agree on a global vision, goals, and strategy, as well as a global plan for all endemic areas describing how, where, and when we move from control towards elimination. The prerequisites for a successful start are: (i) a process of inclusive discourse to agree on global vision, goals, and strategy; and (ii) a global plan for all endemic areas describing how, where, and when we move from control towards elimination.

title: CI-994 (N-acetyl-dinaline) in combination with conventional anti-cancer agents is effective against acute myeloid leukemia in vitro and in vivo.
text: N-acetyl-dinaline (CI-994) is an experimental anti-cancer drug that targets histone deacetylases. We investigated the potential of CI-994 to enhance the effectiveness of conventional chemotherapeutics used in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) treatment. In a rat model of AML, we found that CI-994 combined with cytarabine (ara-C), daunorubicin, and mitoxantrone resulted in moderate synergy in vitro. In vivo, higher doses of CI-994 led to complete remissions. CI-994/ara-C was particularly effective against Brown Norway rat acute myelocytic leukemia (BNML), while the combinations of CI-994/daunorubicin and CI-994/mitoxantrone also showed activity against BNML. These findings suggest that CI-994 may have favorable interactions with conventional anti-cancer drugs used to treat AML.

title: CTCF and Cohesin in Genome Folding and Transcriptional Gene Regulation.
text:
The dynamic structural organization of chromosomes plays a crucial role in various cellular processes, including genome function, replication, integrity, and propagation, during the cell cycle. The folding of chromosomes in interphase provides regulatory segmentation for appropriate transcriptional control, facilitates ordered genome replication, and contributes to genome integrity by limiting illegitimate recombination. Recent high-resolution chromosome conformation capture and functional studies have provided insights into the spatial and regulatory compartmentalization of mammalian genomes, and mechanistic models have been proposed to explain how CTCF and cohesin control the functional architecture of mammalian chromosomes.
In this review, we will discuss the current understanding of the dynamic structural organization of chromosomes in mammalian cells, including the role of CTCF and cohesin in maintaining the functional architecture of chromosomes. We will also highlight recent studies that have shed light on the mechanisms underlying the spatial and regulatory compartmentalization of mammalian genomes, and discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of genome function and regulation.
Chromosome folding in interphase is a dynamic process that plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and genome stability. The folding of chromosomes into higher-order structures, such as chromatin loops and topologically associating domains (TADs), provides a regulatory framework for the organization of genes and regulatory elements. These higher-order structures can bring distant regulatory elements into close proximity with their target genes, facilitating the recruitment of transcription factors and other regulatory proteins.
The maintenance of the functional architecture of chromosomes is also crucial for genome stability. Chromosomal breaks and rearrangements can lead to genome instability, which can contribute to the development of cancer and other diseases. CTCF and cohesin are two key proteins that play a crucial role in maintaining the functional architecture of chromosomes. CTCF is a transcriptional repressor that is involved in the regulation of gene expression and the maintenance of chromosome stability. Cohesin is a chromatin-binding protein that helps to maintain the structural integrity of chromosomes by holding together the sister chromatids.
Recent studies have provided new insights into the mechanisms underlying the spatial and regulatory compartmentalization of mammalian genomes. For example, chromosome conformation capture (3C) and related techniques have shown that chromosomes are organized into a network of loops and TADs, with distant regulatory elements and gene loci brought into close proximity by these higher-order structures. These studies have also highlighted the importance of CTCF and cohesin in maintaining the functional architecture of chromosomes, and have provided insights into the mechanisms underlying their action.
In conclusion, the dynamic structural organization of chromosomes plays a crucial role in genome function, replication, integrity, and propagation. Recent studies have provided new insights into the mechanisms underlying the spatial and regulatory compartmentalization of mammalian genomes, and have highlighted the importance of CTCF and cohesin in maintaining the functional architecture of chromosomes. Further research in this area will continue to shed light on the complex processes underlying genome function and regulation, and will inform the development of new therapeutic strategies for the treatment of genome-related diseases.

title: Melatonin synthesized by T lymphocytes as a ligand of the retinoic acid-related orphan receptor.
text:
Melatonin has a wide range of physiological effects on the immune system, modulating various biological functions through multiple mechanisms. While the significance of specific melatonin receptors has been well established for different immune processes, recent studies have suggested that retinoic acid-related orphan receptor alpha (RORα) may play a crucial role in nuclear melatonin signaling. However, it is unclear whether melatonin directly interacts with RORα or if there are other downstream effects.
Our study found that RORα is primarily localized in the nucleus of human Jurkat T-cells, and it co-immunoprecipitates with melatonin. Immunocytochemistry analysis also revealed co-localization of melatonin and RORα. Melatonin was shown to cause a time-dependent decrease in nuclear RORα levels, suggesting a role in regulating RORα transcriptional activity.
Interestingly, RORα acts as a molecular switch that regulates the generation of two important immune cell types: Th17 cells and Treg cells. These cells play a crucial role in maintaining a balance between immune harm and protection, making RORα a potential therapeutic target for various clinical disorders.
Our findings suggest that melatonin may modulate RORα activity, providing a new avenue for the treatment of immune-related disorders. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms of melatonin-RORα interaction and its potential therapeutic applications.

title: Age- and infection intensity-dependent cytokine and antibody production in human trichuriasis: the importance of IgE.
text: The study investigated the cytokine and antibody response to Trichuris trichiura infection in 96 individuals living in an area where the parasite is highly prevalent and infection follows a convex age-intensity profile. Upon stimulation with T. trichiura antigen, a small proportion of the study participants produced interleukin (IL)-4 (7%), IL-9 (5%), and IL-13 (17%). In contrast, a larger proportion produced IL-10 (97%), tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha (93%), and interferon (IFN)-gamma (32%). The levels of TNF-alpha (P = 0.016) and IFN-gamma (P = 0.012) significantly increased with age, indicating a shift towards a more chronic infection phenotype. The primary parasite-specific antibodies produced were IgG1, IgG4, IgA, and IgE. Notably, IgE was the only subclass that correlated negatively with infection intensity, as defined by egg output (P = 0.008), and positively with host age (P = 0.010). These findings suggest a mixed cytokine response in trichuriasis and an IgE-associated level of protection.

title: The cryoprotective effect of trehalose supplementation on boar spermatozoa quality.
text: To enhance the quality of frozen-thawed boar sperm, the impact of trehalose on the success of cryopreservation was investigated. We evaluated the effect of different trehalose concentrations (0, 25, 50, 100, and 200 mmol/l) on the freeze-thawing tolerance of boar spermatozoa in a basic cooling extender. Our results showed that the optimum concentration of trehalose for improving cryopreservation capacity was 100 mmol/l. We used motility, acrosome integrity, membrane integrity, and cryocapacitation as parameters to evaluate the cryopreservation capacity of boar spermatozoa. Our findings revealed that the addition of 100 mmol/l trehalose to the extender significantly improved sperm motility, membrane integrity, and acrosome integrity, while freeze-thawing tolerance was reduced for the highest concentration of trehalose (200 mmol/l). Before and after capacitation, the CTC score for semen diluted by the 100 mmol/l trehalose extender was 3.68% and 43.82%, respectively. In conclusion, trehalose supplementation in a basic extender with a concentration of 100 mmol/l can significantly improve the cryoprotective capacity of boar spermatozoa during the cryopreservation process.

title: Roads to polyploidy: the megakaryocyte example.
text: Polyploidy, characterized by multiple copies of the haploid chromosome number, has been observed in various organisms, including plants, insects, and mammalian cells such as platelet precursors and megakaryocytes. These cell types achieve high ploidy through distinct cell cycles. Megakaryocytes undergo an endomitotic cell cycle, which involves an S phase interrupted by a gap, leading to mitosis without anaphase B and cytokinesis. Here, we review the mechanisms that drive polyploidy in megakaryocytes and compare them to those observed in other systems where high ploidy is achieved. Polyploidy is often associated with changes in gene expression, including both genes that may be determinants of new cell physiology and genes that induce polyploidization. Future studies will aim to further investigate these two groups of genes.

title: Central memory and effector memory T cell subsets: function, generation, and maintenance.
text: The memory T cell pool serves as a dynamic reservoir of antigen-experienced T cells that accumulate throughout an individual's lifetime. Recent research has revealed that memory T cells comprise distinct populations of central memory (TCM) and effector memory (TEM) cells, each with unique homing capabilities and effector functions. This review aims to delve into the heterogeneity of TCM and TEM, their developmental stages, and the current theories on their generation and maintenance in both humans and mice.

title: The Werner and Bloom syndrome proteins help resolve replication blockage by converting (regressed) holliday junctions to functional replication forks.
text: Cells have evolved mechanisms to deal with obstacles in DNA replication, allowing for the completion of DNA synthesis and minimizing genomic instability. One such mechanism involves the formation of Holliday junction structures, which can be resolved through the action of helicases like WRN and BLM. These helicases are critical for maintaining genomic stability and are thought to play a role in resolving replication blockages. Our study examines the actions of WRN and BLM on a special Holliday junction substrate that mimics a regressed replication fork. We found that both WRN and BLM convert this Holliday junction substrate into a four-stranded replication fork structure, suggesting that they target the Holliday junction to initiate branch migration. The Holliday junction binding protein RuvA inhibits this conversion process. Importantly, the resulting conversion product is suitable for replication with its leading daughter strand readily extended by DNA polymerases. Our findings suggest that WRN and BLM can re-establish functional replication forks to overcome fork blockages, a function that is consistent with the phenotypes associated with WRN- and BLM-deficient cells.

title: Do Montelukast Sodium and N-Acetylcysteine Have a Nephroprotective Effect on Unilateral Ureteral Obstruction? A Placebo Controlled Trial in a Rat Model.
text:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate the nephroprotective effects of montelukast sodium and N-acetylcysteine on secondary renal damage caused by unilateral ureteral obstruction in a rat model.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this experiment, 30 male Wistar albino rats were randomly divided into three groups: placebo, N-acetylcysteine, and montelukast sodium. Three rats served as the control group. The left ureter of the rats was surgically obstructed with 4-zero polyglactin sutures, and the rats received medication for 3 days before obstruction and for 15 days thereafter. Dimercaptosuccinic acid renal scintigraphy was performed before obstruction and on day 15. The rats were sacrificed on day 15, and histopathological examinations were conducted. Biochemical assessments of oxidative stress markers (myeloperoxidase and malondialdehyde), sulfhydryl levels, and total nitrite for lipid peroxidation were performed, as well as assessments of oxidative protein damage and antioxidant levels.
RESULTS: On pathological examination, inflammation and tubular epithelial damage were found to be less severe in the N-acetylcysteine and montelukast sodium groups compared to the placebo group (p <0.05). No significant differences were observed in normal kidneys. Myeloperoxidase, malondialdehyde, and total nitrite levels were found to be lower in the N-acetylcysteine group and myeloperoxidase and malondialdehyde levels were lower in the montelukast sodium group compared to the placebo group (p <0.05). No significant differences were observed in sulfhydryl levels among the three groups (p >0.05). No pathological, chemical, or scintigraphic differences were observed among the N-acetylcysteine, montelukast sodium, and sham-treated groups (p >0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: The results of this study suggest that N-acetylcysteine and montelukast sodium have a protective effect against obstructive damage to the kidney. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings.

title: Oxidative phosphorylation: synthesis of mitochondrially encoded proteins and assembly of individual structural subunits into functional holoenzyme complexes.
text: In higher eukaryotes, the majority of ATP produced through cellular processes is generated by five protein complexes (I-V) embedded within the inner mitochondrial membrane through a process called oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Maintaining energy homeostasis under typical conditions relies on OXPHOS's ability to adapt to changing cellular energy demands. However, a chronic failure to do so is a common cause of human disease. Unlike Complex II, the structural subunits of OXPHOS complexes are encoded by both the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes. Due to the physical separation of the two genomes, the expression of the 13 mitochondrially encoded polypeptides must be coordinated with that of relevant nuclear-encoded partners to assemble functional holoenzyme complexes. The assembly of these complexes is a highly regulated process, and several nuclear-encoded factors have been identified that function at distinct stages in the assembly of individual OXPHOS complexes.

title: Familial gastroesophageal reflux and development of Barrett's esophagus.
text: The family of an elderly man with Barrett's esophagus underwent examination for gastroesophageal reflux and the development of Barrett's esophagus. All five living children have either gastroesophageal reflux or esophagitis, or both, and three have definitive Barrett's esophagus. Two third-generation descendants also have gastroesophageal reflux. This pattern suggests that the trait of gastroesophageal reflux is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Additionally, the family has a high incidence of cancer, which may indicate the presence of the cancer family syndrome.

title: The effect of folate fortification on folic acid-based homocysteine-lowering intervention and stroke risk: a meta-analysis.
text:
OBJECTIVE: Folate and vitamin B12 play crucial roles in the metabolic process of homocysteine, a risk factor for atherothrombotic events. Low folate intake or low plasma folate levels are associated with increased stroke risk. Previous randomized controlled trials have yielded conflicting results on the effect of folic acid supplementation on homocysteine reduction and stroke risk. This meta-analysis aimed to investigate the impact of different folate fortification statuses on the effects of folic acid supplementation on homocysteine reduction and stroke risk.
DESIGN: Relevant randomized controlled trials were identified through a systematic literature search. Homocysteine reduction was compared among subgroups stratified by folate fortification status. Relative risks with 95% confidence intervals were used to assess the association between folic acid supplementation and stroke risk.
SETTING: The meta-analysis included 14 randomized controlled trials with a total of 39,420 participants.
RESULTS: Homocysteine reductions were 26.99% (SD 1.91), 18.38% (SD 3.82), and 21.30% (SD 1.98), respectively, in the subgroups without folate fortification, with folate fortification, and with partial folate fortification. A significant difference was observed between the subgroups with folate fortification and without folate fortification (P=0.05). The relative risk of stroke was 0.88 (95% CI 0.77, 1.00, P=0.05) in the subgroup without folate fortification, 0.94 (95% CI 0.58, 1.54, P=0.82) in the subgroup with folate fortification, and 0.91 (95% CI 0.82, 1.01, P=0.09) in the subgroup with partial folate fortification.
CONCLUSIONS: Folic acid supplementation may have a modest benefit in stroke prevention in regions without folate fortification.

title: On the origin and impact of mesenchymal stem cell heterogeneity: new insights and emerging tools for single cell analysis.
text: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) exhibit significant cell-to-cell variation, which is evident across different donors, tissue sources, and within cell populations. This heterogeneity complicates the use of MSCs in regenerative applications and may limit their therapeutic efficacy. Conventional assays that measure MSC properties in bulk mask this cell-to-cell variation, as they do not account for the extensive variability present amongst and within clonal MSC populations. Recent studies have revealed that MSCs exhibit differences in functional differentiation capacity, molecular state (including epigenetic, transcriptomic, and proteomic status), and biophysical properties. The origins of these variations are still unclear, but potential mechanisms include in vivo micro-anatomical heterogeneity, epigenetic bistability, and transcriptional fluctuations. Emerging tools for single-cell analysis of MSC gene and protein expression may provide further insight into the mechanisms and implications of single-cell variation amongst these cells, ultimately improving the clinical utility of MSCs in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications. This review outlines the dimensions of MSC heterogeneity, discusses the known mechanisms that govern it, and highlights emerging technologies that may refine our understanding and enhance clinical application of this unique cell type.

title: Altered microRNA expression in bovine skeletal muscle with age.
text: As individuals age, skeletal muscle function declines, leading to various inherited and acquired muscular disorders. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), which play a crucial role in muscle maintenance and repair, may be altered during these processes. To investigate miRNA expression in bovine skeletal muscle during different stages of development and aging, we performed a comprehensive next-generation small RNA sequencing analysis. Our study identified 511 miRNAs, including one putatively novel miRNA, in five different periods of bovine skeletal muscle development. Differential expression analysis revealed 36 miRNAs that were differentially expressed between prenatal and postnatal stages of muscle development, including several myomiRs (miR-1, miR-206, and let-7 families). Additionally, we found that 14 miRNAs were up-regulated and 22 miRNAs were down-regulated in the muscle of postnatal stage compared to different muscle tissues. Furthermore, we predicted and submitted a novel miRNA, bta-mir-10020, to the miRBase database. Using a dual luciferase reporter assay, we demonstrated that bta-mir-10020 directly targeted the 3'-UTR of the bovine ANGPT1 gene. Our findings also predicted that differentially expressed miRNAs targeted 3609 bovine genes, which were enriched in functionality for muscle growth and disease. Our study significantly expands the repertoire of bovine miRNAs expressed in muscle and could contribute to further studies on growth and developmental disorders in this tissue type.

title: Apoptosis occurs predominantly in bystander cells and not in productively infected cells of HIV- and SIV-infected lymph nodes
text: Despite the 13-year discovery of human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) as the cause of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), the mechanism of how HIV kills its primary target, the T cell carrying the CD4 antigen, remains unknown. Previous studies have shown an increase in the percentage of apoptotic cells among circulating CD4+ (and CD8+) T cells of HIV-seropositive individuals and an increase in frequency of apoptosis with disease progression. However, it is unclear whether this apoptosis occurs in infected or uninfected T cells. To investigate this further, we used in situ labeling of lymph nodes from HIV-infected children and simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV)-infected macaques to determine whether apoptosis occurs in productively infected cells or bystander cells. Our findings suggest that apoptosis occurs predominantly in bystander cells and not in the productively infected cells themselves, which has important implications for the pathogenesis and therapy of HIV infection. Specifically, these data support the idea that rational drug therapy may involve combination agents targeting both viral replication in infected cells and apoptosis of uninfected cells.

title: Neuronal origin of a cerebral amyloid: neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's disease contain the same protein as the amyloid of plaque cores and blood vessels.
text: The protein component of Alzheimer's disease amyloid, specifically the aggregated polypeptide A4, is composed of subunits with a mass of approximately 4 kDa. The deposition of amyloid begins within neurons, followed by extracellular accumulation. Using antibodies raised against synthetic peptides, we have identified epitopes located in the N-terminal region (residues 1-11) and the inner region (residues 11-23) of the A4 monomer, which are specific to neurofibrillary tangles and plaque cores/vascular amyloid, respectively. Additionally, the non-protein component of the amyloid, aluminum silicate, may play a role in the deposition or amplification of the aggregated protein. The amyloid of Alzheimer's disease shares similarities in subunit size and composition, but not sequence, with the scrapie-associated fibril and its constituent polypeptides. The NFT component does not exhibit homology with any known components of normal neurofilaments.

title: Pregnancy characteristics and maternal risk of breast cancer.
text:
During pregnancy, hormone levels are significantly higher than at other times in a woman's life. The placenta is the primary source of these hormones, and changes in placental function may serve as indirect markers of hormone exposure during pregnancy. While the relationship between these markers and breast cancer risk in mothers has been inconsistent, this study aimed to investigate the association between indirect hormone exposure measures, such as placental weight and other pregnancy characteristics, and the risk of breast cancer in mothers.
The study used data from the Swedish Birth Register, Cancer Register, Cause of Death Register, and Population Register to identify women who delivered singletons between 1982 and 1989 and were followed up until the occurrence of breast cancer, death, or the end of follow-up in 2001. Of the 314,019 women in the cohort, 2216 (0.7%) developed breast cancer during the follow-up period, with 2100 (95%) diagnosed before the age of 50. Compared to women with placentas weighing less than 500 grams in two consecutive pregnancies, those whose placentas weighed between 500 and 699 grams in their first pregnancy and at least 700 grams in their second pregnancy (or vice versa) had an increased risk of breast cancer (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.07-3.08). The risk was doubled among women whose placentas weighed at least 700 grams in both pregnancies (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.05; 95% CI, 1.15-3.64). A high birth weight (> or =4000 grams) in two consecutive births was associated with an increased risk of breast cancer before adjusting for placental weight and other covariates (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.76-1.59).
In conclusion, this study found that placental weight is positively associated with the risk of breast cancer in mothers. These findings further support the hypothesis that hormones produced during pregnancy play a crucial role in modifying breast cancer risk in mothers.

title: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a category or a continuum? Genetic analysis of a large-scale twin study.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the heritability of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) using a large-scale twin sample, and to compare the continuum versus categorical approaches to ADHD.
Method:
A cohort of 1,938 families with twins and siblings aged 4 to 12 years were assessed for ADHD using a DSM-III-R-based maternal rating scale. Probandwise concordance rates and correlations in monozygotic and dizygotic twins and siblings were calculated, and heritability was examined using the De Fries and Fulker regression technique.
Results:
There was a moderate to high heritability of ADHD (0.75 to 0.91), which was robust across different types of familial relationships (twin, sibling, and twin-sibling) and across different definitions of ADHD (as part of a continuum or as a disorder with various symptom cutoffs). No evidence was found for non-additive genetic variation or for shared family environmental effects.
Conclusions:
These findings suggest that ADHD can be best viewed as the extreme of a behavior that varies genetically throughout the entire population, rather than as a disorder with discrete determinants. This has implications for the classification of ADHD and for the identification of genes for this behavior, as well as implications for diagnosis and treatment.

title: Antiapoptotic BCL-2 is required for maintenance of a model leukemia.
text: Resistance to programmed cell death, often achieved through overexpression of anti-apoptotic proteins, is a common occurrence in cancer. However, it remains unclear whether these defects are essential for tumor maintenance. To investigate, we generated mice with a conditional BCL-2 gene and constitutive c-myc, which leads to lymphoblastic leukemia. Eliminating BCL-2 resulted in rapid loss of leukemic cells and significantly prolonged survival, providing strong evidence that BCL-2 is a valid target for cancer therapy. Surprisingly, loss of this single molecule led to cell death, even in the presence of other oncogenic events. This suggests a generalizable model in which cancer-specific alterations trigger persistent death signals that would otherwise cause cell death if not countered by a necessary apoptotic defect.

title: Cellular and histopathological changes in the infrapatellar fat pad in the monoiodoacetate model of osteoarthritis pain.
text:
Objective:
The infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) has been identified as a source of anterior knee pain, and its role in the progression of degenerative joint disease (DJD) has been studied using the monoiodoacetate (MIA) model of DJD in rats. This study aimed to investigate changes in the IPFP of rats undergoing the MIA model and to determine whether these changes contribute to the pain observed in the early stages of the disease.
Methods:
Rats were injected intra-articularly with MIA and the development of weight bearing asymmetry was followed for 21 days compared to vehicle-injected animals. In addition, IPFPs were removed from both ipsilateral and contralateral joints, and inflammatory infiltrate and histopathological changes were analyzed.
Results:
The MIA injection caused marked weight bearing asymmetry, and ipsilateral IPFP wet weights were significantly increased on days 1 and 3 in MIA-treated animals. MIA treatment also resulted in significant increases in IPFP total white blood cells and monocytes on days 1, 3, and 7, and neutrophils on days 1 and 3. Histopathological findings at early time points progressed to adipocyte necrosis, IPFP fibrosis, patellar cartilage, and subchondral bone necrosis with synovial hyperplasia at later timepoints.


Conclusions:
The current study demonstrated that marked inflammatory changes in the IPFP occur during the early stages of the MIA model of OA, which may contribute to the pain observed at this early stage. Further research is needed to explore the role of the IPFP in later stages of the disease.

title: Angiogenesis therapy: amidst the hype, the neglected potential for serious side effects.
text:
Although relatively unknown as a therapeutic concept a decade ago, angiogenesis therapy has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential to revolutionize the treatment of patients with atherosclerotic lesions obstructing arteries that supply the myocardium or legs. However, as with any potent therapeutic intervention, there is a risk of harmful effects. Despite this, there has been a lack of in-depth discussion of the potential dangers inherent in angiogenesis interventions, particularly in the scientific community.
Recently, a tragic death due to injection of large amounts of an adenoviral vector into the hepatic artery has raised concerns about the safety of angiogenesis therapy. This event has led to a shift from unbridled enthusiasm to profound skepticism in the lay media. However, for the scientific community, there has been a general lack of discussion of the potential dangers inherent in angiogenesis interventions.
As we know more about the underlying biological activities of potent angiogenic cytokines, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF), we can identify specific side effects that may occur as potential complications of angiogenesis therapy. These side effects are important to consider, not only because of the recent tragic event but also because they are inherent in the mechanisms of angiogenesis itself.
In summary, while angiogenesis therapy has the potential to revolutionize the treatment of atherosclerotic lesions, it is important to consider the potential side effects that may occur. A thorough understanding of the underlying biological activities of angiogenic cytokines can help us anticipate and mitigate these complications.

title: Body mass index and magnetic resonance markers of brain integrity in adults.
text:
OBJECTIVE:
Adult obesity and overweight have been consistently linked to an increased risk of developing dementia, particularly Alzheimer's disease, later in life. These conditions have also been associated with cognitive impairments and structural alterations in the brain, even among otherwise healthy adults. While proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) can distinguish between neuronal and glial components of the brain and provide insights into the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of brain atrophy and cognitive changes, no spectroscopic studies have investigated the relationships between adiposity and brain metabolites.
METHODS:
We conducted a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and proton MRS study on 50 healthy middle-aged participants (mean age: 41.7 ± 8.5 years; 17 women) who were also scanned as control subjects in another study.
RESULTS:
After adjusting for age and sex, greater body mass indices (BMIs) were found to be associated with:
1. Lower concentrations of N-acetylaspartate (a spectroscopic marker of neuronal viability) in frontal (p = 0.001), parietal (p = 0.006), and temporal (p = 0.008) white matter.
2. Lower N-acetylaspartate levels in frontal gray matter (p = 0.01).
3. Lower concentrations of choline-containing metabolites (associated with membrane metabolism) in frontal white matter (p = 0.05).
INTERPRETATION:
These findings suggest that increased BMI at midlife is associated with neuronal and/or myelin abnormalities, primarily in the frontal lobe. As the frontal white matter is more susceptible to the effects of aging than other lobes, our results may indicate accelerated aging in individuals with high levels of adiposity, which could increase the likelihood of developing age-related diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease.

title: Characteristics of medial temporal lobe epilepsy: II. Interictal and ictal scalp electroencephalography, neuropsychological testing, neuroimaging, surgical results, and pathology.
text:
In this study, the authors retrospectively evaluated 67 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy without any obvious, potentially epileptogenic lesions, who underwent intracranial electrodes, temporal lobectomy, and subsequent pathology analysis. The study found that:
* Interictal scalp EEG showed paroxysmal abnormalities in 96% of patients, primarily in the anterior temporal region.
* Bilateral independent paroxysmal activity was observed in 42% of patients, with a preponderance over the side of seizure origin in half of the cases.
* Ictal EEG changes were rarely detected during seizure onset, but lateralized buildup of rhythmic seizure activity occurred in 80% of patients. In 13% of cases, the scalp EEG seizure buildup was contralateral to the side of seizure origin as confirmed by depth EEG and surgical findings.
* Lateralized postictal slowing was observed in 73% of patients, providing a reliable lateralizing finding.
* Neuropsychological testing revealed lateralizing findings concordant with the side of seizure origin in 73% of patients, while 26 patients (37%) had bilaterally intact memory.
* Intracarotid amobarbital (Amytal) testing demonstrated absent or marginal memory functions on the side of seizure onset in 63% of patients.
* Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was highly sensitive in detecting subtle medial temporal abnormalities, which were present in 23 of 28 MRI scans and corresponded with mesial temporal sclerosis on pathological examination in all but 2 patients.

In conclusion, the study found that interictal and ictal EEG findings, neuropsychological testing, and MRI can provide valuable lateralizing information in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy, which can help guide surgical resection and improve seizure outcomes.

title: OPA1-dependent cristae modulation is essential for cellular adaptation to metabolic demand.
text: The structural organization of mitochondrial cristae, which are invaginations of the inner membrane, is dynamically regulated in response to the cell's energetic demands. However, the mechanisms by which this regulation occurs and the consequences of these changes are largely unknown. Optic atrophy 1 (OPA1) is a mitochondrial GTPase that plays a crucial role in maintaining the structure of cristae, and our study shows that it responds dynamically to changes in energetic conditions. Specifically, we found that OPA1's ability to regulate cristae structure is independent of its role in mitochondrial fusion, as an OPA1 mutant that can still oligomerize but has no fusion activity was able to maintain cristae structure. Additionally, we found that OPA1 is required for resistance to starvation-induced cell death, mitochondrial respiration, growth in galactose media, and maintenance of ATP synthase assembly, regardless of its fusion activity. Our results also suggest that mitochondrial solute carriers (SLC25A) interact with OPA1 and play a role in regulating its function. We propose that OPA1 senses energy substrate availability through these interactions, which modulates its function in the regulation of mitochondrial architecture.

title: Phenylpropanolamine and the risk of hemorrhagic stroke.
text:
Background: Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) is a commonly used ingredient in appetite suppressants and cough or cold remedies. Case reports have linked the use of products containing PPA to hemorrhagic stroke, often after the first use of these products. To investigate the potential association, we conducted a case-control study.
Methods: We recruited 702 patients aged 18-49 years from 43 US hospitals who had suffered a subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage within 30 days before enrollment, and randomly selected two control subjects per patient from the general population using random-digit dialing. Eligibility criteria included the absence of a previously diagnosed brain lesion.
Results: Our findings showed an increased risk of hemorrhagic stroke associated with the use of appetite suppressants containing PPA in women, with an adjusted odds ratio of 16.58 (95% CI, 1.51-182.21; P=0.02). The association was also observed in women who used cough or cold remedies containing PPA, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.13 (95% CI, 0.86-11.46; P=0.08). However, no increased risk was observed in men who used cough or cold remedies containing PPA.
Discussion: Our results suggest that PPA in appetite suppressants, and possibly in cough and cold remedies, is an independent risk factor for hemorrhagic stroke in women. These findings have important implications for the safety of these products and highlight the need for further research to better understand the potential risks and benefits of PPA use.

title: The safety of intravenous fluorescein for confocal laser endomicroscopy in the gastrointestinal tract.
text: BACKGROUND: Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) is rapidly gaining traction as a valuable tool for gastrointestinal endoscopic imaging. To optimize imaging with CLE, fluorescent contrast agents are employed, with intravenous fluorescein being the most commonly used. However, despite its widespread use in diagnostic angiography of the retina, the safety profile of fluorescein for CLE has not been extensively evaluated. AIMS: To determine the incidence of serious and total adverse events associated with intravenous fluorescein use in gastrointestinal CLE. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 16 leading academic medical centers with active CLE research protocols that involved intravenous fluorescein. Centers that actively monitored adverse events during CLE procedures were included. RESULTS: A total of 2272 gastrointestinal CLE procedures were performed at the 16 centers, with the most common dose of contrast agent being 2.5-5 mL of 10% sodium fluorescein. No serious adverse events were reported, while mild events occurred in 1.4% of individuals, including nausea/vomiting, transient hypotension without shock, injection site erythema, diffuse rash, and mild epigastric pain. The limitation of the study is that only immediate post-procedure adverse events were actively monitored. CONCLUSIONS: The use of intravenous fluorescein for gastrointestinal CLE appears to be relatively safe, with few acute complications observed.

title: Metabolic DNA as the origin of spontaneously released DNA?
text:
A fraction of DNA is released spontaneously from living, but not dead or dying, human, other mammalian, avian, amphibian, and plant cells. This released DNA fraction has been shown to be present in both actively dividing and nondividing cell populations, and is labile. It is also associated with DNA-dependent RNA or DNA polymerase, and has a lower molecular weight than the typical genetic DNA fraction. In contrast, earlier studies identified a DNA fraction that was present in both actively dividing and nondividing cell populations, was labile, and had a lower molecular weight than the typical genetic DNA fraction. This DNA fraction was termed metabolic DNA (m-DNA) and was proposed as possibly forming extra gene copies for the rapid production of m-RNA, which would be destroyed subsequently. Therefore, we suggest that the metabolic DNA fraction may be the precursor to the spontaneously released DNA fraction.
In this rewrite, I have tried to make the language more concise and clear, while still conveying the same information as the original text. I have also reorganized the paragraphs to make the flow of ideas more logical and easier to follow. Let me know if you have any further questions or if there is anything else I can help you with!

title: The flavivirus precursor membrane-envelope protein complex: structure and maturation.
text: Many viruses undergo a final assembly stage involving maturation before being transmitted to a new host. The maturation process of flaviviruses is regulated by proteolytic cleavage of the precursor membrane protein (prM), which converts inactive virus particles into infectious ones. We have determined the high-resolution crystal structure of a recombinant protein consisting of the dengue virus prM linked to the envelope glycoprotein E. The structure represents the prM-E heterodimer and aligns well with the cryo-electron microscopy density of immature virus at neutral pH. The pr peptide beta-barrel structure covers the fusion loop in E, preventing fusion with host cell membranes. The structure provides a framework for identifying the stages of its pH-dependent conformational transformation during maturation, culminating in the release of pr upon budding from the host.

title: Peptide and non-peptide G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) in skeletal muscle.
text: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) constitute a significant portion of cell surface receptors that play a crucial role in various cellular processes. Despite the extensive research on GPCRs in other muscle tissues such as cardiac and vascular smooth muscle cells, there has been limited systematic analysis of these receptors in skeletal muscle. In this study, we have compiled a comprehensive list of GPCRs expressed in skeletal muscle and review their known functions in both muscle tissue and cultured skeletal muscle cells.

title: Characterization of complete genome and small RNA profile of pagoda yellow mosaic associated virus, a novel badnavirus in China.
text: A newly discovered badnavirus was identified in pagoda trees displaying yellow mosaic symptoms on their leaves through high-throughput sequencing of small RNAs. The complete genome of this virus was found to consist of 7424 nucleotides, with 40.4-45.1% sequence identity to other badnaviruses. The genome encodes five open reading frames (ORFs) on the plus strand, including three conserved badnaviral ORFs. These findings suggest that this virus is a new member of the genus Badnavirus in the family Caulimoviridae. The virus has been tentatively named pagoda yellow mosaic associated virus (PYMAV). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that PYMAV forms a distinct group with gooseberry vein banding virus (GVBV) and grapevine vein-clearing virus (GVCV) when compared to other well-characterized badnaviral groups. Additionally, the viral-derived small RNA (vsRNA) profile of PYMAV was analyzed and compared to that of viruses within the same family. The most abundant PYMAV vsRNAs were found to be 21-nt in length, whereas other viruses in the same family have a predominance of 22- or 24-nt vsRNA. The percentage of sense PYMAV vsRNA was almost equal to that of antisense vsRNA, whereas vsRNAs of other viruses in the family display preferences toward the sense strand of their genome. Furthermore, PYMAV vsRNAs were symmetrically distributed along the genome with no obvious vsRNA generating hotspots.

title: Experimental approaches for the treatment of malignant gliomas.
text: Malignant gliomas, including glioblastomas and anaplastic astrocytomas, are the most common primary brain tumors. Over the past three decades, treatment for these tumors has evolved to include surgical resection, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy with temozolomide. Although the median survival of patients with glioblastomas has increased from six months to 14.6 months, these tumors remain deadly for the majority of patients. However, recent significant progress has been made in understanding the molecular mechanisms of tumor growth and development. This knowledge is being translated into clinical trials to develop new therapies.

title: Reversal of hyperglycemia in mice by using human expandable insulin-producing cells differentiated from fetal liver progenitor cells.
text: Beta-cell replacement therapy is widely regarded as the most promising approach for treating type 1 diabetes. However, the limited availability of cells for transplantation is a significant hindrance to its widespread application. To address this challenge, we explored the potential of inducing stem/progenitor cells to differentiate into insulin-producing cells. We focused on fetal human progenitor liver cells (FH) and investigated their ability to differentiate into beta cells after the introduction of the pancreatic duodenal homeobox 1 (Pdx1) gene. Our findings demonstrated that FH cells possess a significant replication capacity and can be further expanded by introducing the gene for the catalytic subunit of human telomerase. Immortalized FH cells expressing Pdx1 exhibited enhanced beta-cell gene expression, insulin production, and insulin storage capabilities, as well as regulated insulin release in response to glucose stimulation. When transplanted into diabetic mice, the cells were able to restore and maintain euglycemia for extended periods, as evidenced by the presence of human C-peptide in the mouse serum. These results suggest that this approach may offer a novel source of cells for transplantation in patients with type 1 diabetes, providing a potential solution to the current cell shortage hindering the widespread application of beta-cell replacement therapy.

title: A review of the methods for human iPSC derivation.
text: The capacity to reprogram somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) provides a potential avenue for creating patient-specific cell lines that can aid in the study of human diseases and the development of therapeutic interventions. Various methods exist for generating iPSC lines, but those best suited for use in these applications must be efficient enough to produce iPSCs from limited sample sizes, capable of reprogramming cells from both skin fibroblasts and blood, and free of unwanted genetic material. Several reprogramming techniques meet these criteria and can be used to derive iPSCs in projects with both basic scientific and therapeutic objectives. Combining these reprogramming methods with small molecule modulators of signaling pathways can lead to successful generation of iPSCs from even the most difficult-to-reprogram patient-derived somatic cells.

title: EB virus-encoded RNAs are recognized by RIG-I and activate signaling to induce type I IFN.
text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-encoded small RNAs (EBERs) are non-polyadenylated, untranslated RNAs that are most abundant in latently EBV-infected cells and are expected to form secondary structures with numerous short stem-loops. In contrast, Retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) is a cytosolic protein that detects viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) inside the cell and initiates signaling pathways leading to the induction of protective cellular genes, including type I interferons (IFNs). In this study, we investigated whether EBERs are recognized by RIG-I as dsRNA. Our results show that transfection of RIG-I plasmid induced IFNs and IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) in EBV-positive Burkitt's lymphoma (BL) cells, but not in their EBV-negative counterparts or EBER-knockout EBV-infected BL cells. Furthermore, transfection of EBER plasmid or in vitro-synthesized EBERs induced expression of type I IFNs and ISGs in RIG-I-expressing, EBV-negative BL cells, but not in RIG-I-minus counterparts. Additionally, we found that EBERs activated RIG-I's substrates, NF-κB and IFN regulatory factor 3, which are essential for type I IFN activation. Finally, we showed that EBERs co-precipitated with RIG-I, providing further evidence for their recognition by RIG-I. Taken together, these findings indicate that EBERs are recognized by RIG-I and activate signaling to induce type I IFN in EBV-infected cells.

title: Pregnancy in dialysis patients: a review of outcomes, complications, and management.
text: Although rare, pregnancy can occur in women on chronic dialysis. According to studies conducted between 1992 and 2003, pregnancy occurred in approximately 1-7% of women on chronic dialysis. Interestingly, intensive dialysis of 16-24 hours per week has been associated with improved infant survival. This article reviews the incidence, duration, fetal and maternal complications, and outcomes of pregnancy in women on chronic dialysis, as well as the management of anemia, hypertension, electrolytes, bone minerals, and acid-base parameters in these patients. Additionally, recommendations are made regarding the dialysis prescription for pregnant women on hemodialysis (HD) or peritoneal dialysis (PD). The complex and fragile nature of pregnancy in dialysis patients requires close collaboration between the patient, nephrologist, dialysis staff, obstetrician, and neonatologist to maximize the chances of a successful pregnancy.

title: Potent immunosuppressive activities of cytomegalovirus-encoded interleukin-10.
text: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) has developed sophisticated mechanisms to evade the host immune system. Recently, a novel gene composed of noncontiguous open reading frames was identified in the genomes of human and primate CMV. This gene shares limited homology with endogenous cellular interleukin-10 (IL-10). We investigated the biological activities of the CMV IL-10-like gene product and found it to possess potent immunosuppressive properties. Both purified recombinant CMV IL-10 and CMV IL-10 expressed in supernatants of human cells inhibited the proliferation of mitogen-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), with comparable activity to recombinant human IL-10. Additionally, CMV IL-10 expressed from human cells inhibited cytokine synthesis, as treatment of stimulated PBMCs and monocytes with CMV IL-10 led to a significant decrease in the production of proinflammatory cytokines. Furthermore, CMV IL-10 decreased the expression of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and class II molecules on the surface of cells, while increasing the expression of the nonclassical MHC allele HLA-G. These findings demonstrate for the first time that CMV has a biologically active IL-10 homolog that may contribute to immune evasion during virus infection.

title: Evidence for the presence of urease apoprotein complexes containing UreD, UreF, and UreG in cells that are competent for in vivo enzyme activation.
text: In vivo activation of Klebsiella aerogenes urease, a nickel-containing enzyme, requires the presence of functional UreD, UreF, and UreG accessory proteins, and is further facilitated by UreE. These accessory proteins are believed to be involved in metallocenter assembly. A series of three UreD-urease apoprotein complexes are present in cells that express high levels of ureD, and these complexes are thought to be essential for in vivo activation of the enzyme. In this study, we investigated the effect of accessory gene deletions on urease complex formation. We found that the ureE, ureF, and ureG gene products were not required for formation of the UreD-urease complexes, but the complexes from the ureF deletion mutant exhibited delayed elution during size exclusion chromatography. We propose that UreF alters the conformation of the UreD-urease complexes. Additionally, we discovered a new series of urease apoprotein complexes present only in cells containing ureD, ureF, and ureG, along with the urease subunit genes. These complexes contain urease, UreD, UreF, and UreG, and we propose that they represent the activation-competent form of urease apoprotein in the cell.

title: Human somatic cell nuclear transfer using adult cells.
text: Derivation of personalized human pluripotent stem cells through somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) holds promise for various therapeutic applications. However, achieving successful SCNT with human cells has proven challenging, and so far, it has only been accomplished with fetal or infant somatic cells. In this study, we describe the use of a novel methodology to generate human embryonic stem cells (ESCs) through SCNT using dermal fibroblasts from 35- and 75-year-old male donors. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of SCNT for adult human cells and underscore the need for further investigation into the potential of SCNT for regenerative medicine.

title: "Natural" killer cells in the mouse. I. Cytotoxic cells with specificity for mouse Moloney leukemia cells. Specificity and distribution according to genotype.
text: In the spleens of young adult mice, there are naturally occurring killer lymphocytes with specificity for mouse Moloney leukemia cells. These cells exhibit lytic activity against both syngeneic and allogeneic Moloney leukemia cells, but show a higher level of activity against in vitro grown leukemia cells. Interestingly, two leukemias of non-Moloney origin and the mastocytoma line P815 were resistant to lysis, while the killer cells showed a high degree of specificity for Moloney leukemia cells, as demonstrated by competition experiments using unlabeled Moloney or other tumor cells as inhibitors in the cytotoxic assays. Moreover, the capacity to compete and sensitivity to lysis were found to be highly positively correlated. The kinetics of the cytotoxic assay revealed a rapid induction of lysis within one to four hours, suggesting that the lytic activity is not induced in vitro. No evidence was found of soluble factors playing any role in the cytolytic assay.

title: Dose-response study on thyrotoxic patients undergoing positron emission tomography and radioiodine therapy
text: With acknowledged limitations in assessing thyroid function and radiation exposure, our previous policy involved administering 75 MBq of iodine-131 at 6-monthly intervals to patients with Graves' disease until they became euthyroid. However, with the introduction of positron emission tomography (PET) at our hospital, we have been able to estimate thyroid radiation doses with an accuracy of approximately 20%. Using iodine-124 PET scans, we have determined the thyroid mass and calculated the radiation dose to the thyroid gland. A dose-response study was conducted on 65 patients who received radiation doses of less than 80 Gy, and the results showed that patients who received a low radiation dose (less than 20 Gy) at their first treatment had a high probability of remaining toxic at 12 months. In contrast, patients who received higher radiation doses (more than 40 Gy) at their first treatment had a high probability of achieving remission. The probability of becoming euthyroid increased more rapidly with increasing radiation dose than the probability of becoming hypothyroid. Based on these findings, we have introduced a new treatment protocol. Before receiving iodine-131 therapy, a 124I PET tracer study will be performed to deliver a prescribed thyroid dose of 50 Gy to patients with Graves' disease. Additional 131I therapy will only be considered if patients are still toxic at 12 months.

title: Increased serum soluble corin in mid pregnancy is associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
text: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between serum soluble corin levels in mid-pregnancy and the risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP). The study included 68 pairs of HDP patients and age- and gestational weeks-matched controls. Serum soluble corin levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay methods, and the relationship between soluble corin and HDP was examined using conditional logistic regression models. The results showed that serum soluble corin levels were significantly higher in HDP patients compared to controls (median [interquartile range]: 1968 [1644-2332] pg/mL vs. 1700 [1446-2056] pg/mL, p=0.002). Participants were categorized into quartiles of serum soluble corin levels in controls, and participants in the highest quartile had a significantly increased risk of HDP (odds ratio [OR], 4.21; 95% confidence interval [95% CI], 1.31-13.53) after multivariate adjustment. The first three quartiles were merged as a reference group, and participants in the highest quartile had a significantly increased risk of HDP (OR, 2.28, 95% CI, 1.02-5.06). The study suggests that increased serum soluble corin levels in mid-pregnancy may be an indicator of HDP.

title: The in vitro effect of dandelions antioxidants on microsomal lipid peroxidation.
text: Dandelions have been used in herbal medicine for centuries due to their diverse therapeutic properties. These include choleretic, diuretic, anti-inflammatory, appetite-stimulating, and laxative effects. Additionally, there is evidence to suggest that the antioxidant properties of dandelions play a key role in their therapeutic effects. To better understand how dandelions work, researchers examined the effects of natural extracts on a microsomal fraction of rat liver. The results showed that the extracts reduced lipid peroxidation and inhibited cytochrome c activity, both with and without NADPH, in a concentration-dependent manner.

title: Local Ca2+ influx through Ca2+ release-activated Ca2+ (CRAC) channels stimulates production of an intracellular messenger and an intercellular pro-inflammatory signal.
text: The entry of Ca2+ through store-operated Ca2+ channels in mast cells triggers the production of the pro-inflammatory molecule leukotriene C4 (LTC4) through a signaling pathway involving Ca2+-dependent protein kinase C, mitogen-activated protein kinases ERK1/2, phospholipase A2, and 5-lipoxygenase. In this study, we investigate the role of local Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels in the plasma membrane in stimulating this signaling pathway.
