We find that manipulating the amplitude and spatial extent of Ca2+ entry by altering chemical and electrical gradients for Ca2+ influx or changing the Ca2+ buffering of the cytoplasm affects protein kinase C and ERK activation, arachidonic acid generation, and LTC4 secretion, with little change in the bulk cytoplasmic Ca2+ rise. Interestingly, despite similar bulk cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentrations, protein kinase C activation and LTC4 secretion are larger in conditions with higher external Ca2+ and La3+ (an inhibitor of CRAC channels) than in conditions with lower external Ca2+. This suggests that a subplasmalemmal Ca2+ rise is central to the signaling pathway. We also find that the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase Syk couples CRAC channel opening to protein kinase C and ERK activation, and that recombinant TRPC3 channels also activate protein kinase C, indicating that subplasmalemmal Ca2+ rather than a microdomain exclusive to CRAC channels is the trigger. Overall, our findings demonstrate the versatility of subplasmalemmal Ca2+ increase in mast cells, which can trigger both cytoplasmic responses through intracellular messengers and long-distance changes through increased secretion of paracrine signals.

title: Cytokine production patterns and lymphoproliferative responses in volunteers orally immunized with attenuated vaccine strains of Salmonella typhi.
text: Newly developed recombinant strains of attenuated Salmonella typhi, used as live oral vaccines, elicit robust immune responses. This study investigated the patterns of cytokine production and proliferation in response to specific S. typhi antigens in individuals immunized orally with attenuated S. typhi vaccines CVD 906, CVD 908, and CVD 908 expressing the circumsporozoite protein of Plasmodium falciparum. Following immunization, lymphocytes in the blood of subjects showed significantly enhanced proliferative responses and interferon-gamma production in response to purified S. typhi flagella compared to pre-immunization levels. Correlations were also observed between interleukin-4 production and both interferon-gamma production and proliferation to S. typhi flagella, indicating a negative correlation between these variables. These findings demonstrate that oral immunization with attenuated S. typhi strains or those carrying a foreign gene leads to the development of strong systemic cell-mediated immunity to purified S. typhi antigens, including the production of cytokines consistent with T1-type responses.

title: Molecular interplay of the noncoding RNA ANRIL and methylated histone H3 lysine 27 by polycomb CBX7 in transcriptional silencing of INK4a.
text: The expression of the INK4b/ARF/INK4a tumor suppressor locus in normal and cancerous cell growth is regulated by the modification of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27me) through the action of the Polycomb group proteins. The antisense noncoding RNA ANRIL, located within the INK4b/ARF/INK4a locus, also plays a crucial role in the expression of protein-coding genes in cis, although its mechanisms have remained unclear. In this study, we uncover the unexpected interaction between the noncoding RNA ANRIL and the chromobox 7 (CBX7) protein within the polycomb repressive complex 1. We find that both ANRIL and CBX7 are overexpressed in prostate cancer tissues, and their interaction plays a crucial role in the ability of CBX7 to repress the INK4b/ARF/INK4a locus and control cellular senescence. Through structure-guided analysis, we reveal the molecular interplay between noncoding RNA and H3K27me as mediated by the conserved chromodomain. Our findings suggest a mechanism by which noncoding RNA participates directly in epigenetic transcriptional repression.

title: Tumor necrosis factor alpha mediates apoptosis of brown adipocytes and defective brown adipocyte function in obesity.
text: Obesity frequently exhibits severe quantitative and qualitative defects in brown adipocytes. To determine whether aberrant TNF-alpha expression in obesity contributes to functional brown fat atrophy, we investigated genetically obese (ob/ob) mice with targeted null mutations in the genes encoding the two TNF receptors. Our findings revealed that the absence of both TNF receptors or p55 receptor alone led to a significant reduction in brown adipocyte apoptosis and an increase in beta(3)-adrenoreceptor and uncoupling protein-1 expression in obese mice. Additionally, we observed increased numbers of multilocular functionally active brown adipocytes and improved thermoregulation in obese animals lacking TNF-alpha function. These results suggest that TNF-alpha plays a crucial role in multiple aspects of brown adipose tissue biology and mediates the abnormalities that occur at this site in obesity.

title: Engineered FGF19 eliminates bile acid toxicity and lipotoxicity leading to resolution of steatohepatitis and fibrosis in mice
text:
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a growing chronic liver condition with no approved treatments. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms that drive NAFLD's development and progression are poorly understood. However, emerging evidence suggests that dysregulated bile acid metabolism may play a novel role in NAFLD pathogenesis. Interestingly, NAFLD patients often exhibit low levels of fibroblast growth factor 19 (FGF19), an endocrine hormone in the gut-liver axis that regulates de novo bile acid synthesis, lipogenesis, and energy homeostasis.
To investigate the potential therapeutic benefits of FGF19, we developed a mouse model that recapitulates the clinical progression of human NAFLD, including simple steatosis, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and advanced "burnt-out" NASH with hepatocellular carcinoma. Treatment with either FGF19 or an engineered nontumorigenic FGF19 analogue, M70, significantly reduced liver enzymes, histological features of NASH, and improved insulin sensitivity, energy homeostasis, and lipid metabolism. Notably, while FGF19 induced hepatocellular carcinoma formation in these mice following prolonged exposure, animals expressing M70 showed no evidence of liver tumorigenesis in this model.
Our findings suggest that engineered FGF19 represents a potentially promising therapeutic for patients with NASH. By regulating multiple pathways, including antisteatotic, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic activities, FGF19 may offer a novel approach to treating this prevalent and debilitating liver disease. (Hepatology Communications 2017;1:1024-1042)

title: Leptin deficiency contributes to the pathogenesis of alcoholic fatty liver disease in mice.
text: White adipose tissue (WAT) produces and secretes adipokines, which play a crucial role in regulating lipid metabolism. The present study aimed to investigate the effects of alcohol consumption on adipokine levels and the underlying mechanisms involved in the development of alcoholic fatty liver disease. To achieve this, mice were fed alcohol for varying periods of time (2, 4, or 8 weeks) to assess changes in adipokine levels over time. Alcohol exposure was found to reduce WAT mass and body weight, concurrent with the accumulation of lipids in the liver. Interestingly, plasma adiponectin concentrations were observed to increase at 2 weeks of alcohol exposure, but subsequently declined to normal levels by 4 and 8 weeks. In contrast, alcohol exposure suppressed leptin gene expression in WAT and led to decreased plasma leptin levels at all time points measured. Notably, there exists a positive correlation between plasma leptin concentrations and WAT mass or body weight. To investigate the potential role of leptin deficiency in alcohol-induced hepatic lipid dysregulation, mice were fed alcohol for 8 weeks with or without leptin administration for the final 2 weeks. Leptin administration normalized plasma leptin concentrations and reversed alcoholic fatty liver disease. Furthermore, leptin administration attenuated alcohol-induced changes in genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, very low-density lipoprotein secretion, and transcriptional regulation, as well as reduced phosphorylation levels of signal transducer Stat3 and adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase. These findings demonstrate for the first time that leptin deficiency, concurrent with reductions in WAT mass, contributes to the pathogenesis of alcoholic fatty liver disease.

title: Three-dimensional chemical imaging of skin using stimulated Raman scattering microscopy
text:
Abstract:
Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy was employed to generate three-dimensional images of native skin, providing insights into the microanatomical features of the skin and the penetration of topically applied materials. SRS microscopy allowed for the collection of image depth stacks at distinct wavelengths, which corresponded to vibrational modes of proteins, lipids, and water in the skin. Observations revealed that corneocytes in the stratum corneum were grouped together in clusters, ranging in diameter from 100 to 250 μm, separated by microanatomical skin-folds called canyons. These canyons occasionally extended down to depths comparable to that of the dermal–epidermal junction below the flat surface regions in both porcine and human skin. SRS imaging revealed the distribution of chemical species within cell clusters and canyons, with water being predominantly located within cell clusters and its concentration increasing rapidly at the transition from stratum corneum to viable epidermis. Conversely, canyons were found to be devoid of detectable levels of water and rich in lipid material. The application of oleic acid-d34 to the skin surface resulted in the lining of canyons down to a depth of 50 μm below the skin surface. These findings have implications for the evaluation of penetration profiles of bioactive materials measured using traditional methods, such as tape-stripping.

title: Familial amyloidosis: a study of 52 North American-born patients examined during a 30-year period.
text: Between 1961 and 1990, 52 patients with biopsy-confirmed familial amyloidosis residing in North America were evaluated at the Mayo Clinic. At the time of diagnosis, 83% of these patients had peripheral neuropathy, 33% had autonomic neuropathy, and 27% had cardiomyopathy. Renal disease was uncommon, and liver involvement was rare. The median age at diagnosis was 64 years. The sensitivity of various diagnostic biopsies was similar to that for primary amyloidosis, with deposits of amyloid found in 77-78% of subcutaneous fat aspirates or rectal biopsy specimens and in 41% of bone marrow specimens. The median survival time for patients with inherited amyloidosis was 5.8 years, which was longer than that for patients with primary amyloidosis. When patients were grouped according to organ involvement, the survival of those with familial amyloidosis remained superior. The presence of cardiomyopathy and an interaction variable of age and the presence of autonomic neuropathy were strong predictors of survival. Of the 52 patients, 22 died, with 12 (55%) dying of cardiac failure or cardiac arrhythmia. Nine patients (41%) died of inanition due to progressive peripheral or autonomic neuropathy. Transthyretin was identified by immunohistochemical studies in 31 of 34 tissue samples, and a transthyretin mutation was found in 24 of these. Additionally, a transthyretin mutation was identified in five additional patients for whom tissue was unavailable for immunostaining.

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the environment within the phagosome.
text: Once past the epithelial barrier, macrophages serve as the primary defense against microbial invasion. For most microorganisms, the acidic and enzymatically active environment of the phagolysosome is lethal to them. Although we have a good understanding of the events that regulate phagosome maturation, our knowledge of the phagosome's lumenal environment is only now being elucidated through real-time functional assays. These assays measure pH changes, phagosome/lysosome fusion, proteolysis, lipolysis, and beta-galactosidase activity. This information is crucial for understanding pathogens that have adapted to the endosomal/lysosomal system. Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects macrophages by halting the normal phagosome maturation process, retaining its acidic vacuole at pH 6.4, which resembles an early endosome. Current research focuses on the transcriptional response of the bacterium to the changing environment in the macrophage phagosome. By manipulating these environmental cues, such as preventing the pH drop to pH 6.4 with concanamycin A, we have found that the bacterium's transcriptional response is largely abrogated, indicating that pH is the primary signal that the bacterium senses and responds to. These approaches represent our ongoing efforts to unravel the complex dialogue between the pathogen and its host cell.

title: High density DNA methylation array with single CpG site resolution.
text: We have developed a cutting-edge genome-wide DNA methylation microarray, termed the "Next-Generation DNA Methylation BeadChip," which enables high-throughput analysis of methylation patterns across the human genome. This novel platform boasts an unprecedented density of over 480,000 CpG sites that can be assessed simultaneously in twelve samples, providing a comprehensive view of genome-wide methylation. The innovative design of the BeadChip includes the coverage of 99% of RefSeq genes with multiple probes per gene, 96% of CpG islands from the UCSC database, as well as CpG island shores and additional content selected from whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data and input from leading DNA methylation experts. The well-established Infinium® Assay is used for the analysis of CpG methylation using bisulfite-converted genomic DNA. By employing this technology, we investigated DNA methylation patterns in both normal and tumor DNA samples and compared the results with whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) data obtained for the same samples. Our findings revealed highly comparable DNA methylation profiles between the array and sequencing methods (average R2 of 0.95), demonstrating the potential of the BeadChip for rapidly advancing methylation research. The ability to comprehensively analyze genome-wide methylation patterns will significantly enhance our understanding of the complex interplay between DNA methylation and gene expression.

title: Acentrosomal Microtubule Assembly in Mitosis: The Where, When, and How.
text: During mitosis, the cell assembles a bipolar spindle, a microtubule (MT)-based structure that separates the duplicated chromosomes into two daughter cells. Most animal cells initiate mitosis with duplicated centrosomes, which provide a source of dynamic MTs. However, recent research has shown that spindle assembly actually relies on the formation of acentrosomal MTs around the chromosomes after the breakdown of the nuclear envelope. These acentrosomal MTs are thought to nucleate through a mechanism that is independent of the centrosomes. The exact mechanisms of chromosome-dependent MT nucleation, MT amplification, and the interaction between these two pathways are still not fully understood and have generated some controversy. In this study, we aim to reconcile the available data and present an integrated model that accounts for the acentrosomal MT assembly process in dividing cells.

title: Molecular mechanisms of mammalian DNA repair and the DNA damage checkpoints.
text:
DNA damage is a common occurrence in the life of a cell, and it can lead to mutations, cancer, and ultimately, cellular or organismic death. When DNA is damaged, the cell responds with various mechanisms to either repair the damage or eliminate cells with potentially harmful mutations. These responses include:
1. Removing DNA damage and restoring the continuity of the DNA duplex.
2. Activating a DNA damage checkpoint, which halts cell cycle progression to allow for repair and prevent the transmission of damaged or incompletely replicated chromosomes.
3. Changes in the transcription profile, which may be beneficial to the cell.
4. Eliminating heavily damaged or seriously deregulated cells through apoptosis.
Different mechanisms are employed for DNA repair, including direct repair, base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair, double-strand break repair, and cross-link repair. The DNA damage checkpoints rely on damage sensor proteins, such as ATM, ATR, Rad17-RFC, and 9-1-1, to detect DNA damage and initiate signal transduction cascades that involve Chk1 and Chk2 Ser/Thr kinases and Cdc25 phosphatases. These signal transducers activate p53 and inhibit cyclin-dependent kinases to halt cell cycle progression at the G1/S, intra-S, or G2/M checkpoints.
In this review, we will delve into the molecular mechanisms of DNA repair and the DNA damage checkpoints in mammalian cells.

title: Characterization of serotonin 5-HT2C receptor signaling to extracellular signal-regulated kinases 1 and 2.
text: Serotonin 5-HT2C receptors (5-HT(2C)Rs), primarily expressed in the central nervous system (CNS), have been implicated in various neuropsychiatric disorders, including obesity, depression, and schizophrenia. To investigate the mechanisms underlying the coupling of 5-HT(2C)Rs to extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) 1/2, we employed a Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cell line stably expressing the receptor at levels comparable to those found in the brain. Utilizing the non-RNA-edited isoform of the 5-HT(2C)R, we observed constitutive ERK1/2 phosphorylation and demonstrated that this process is modulated by full, partial, and inverse agonists. Interestingly, we observed agonist-directed trafficking of the receptor stimulus, leading to differences in the effects on phosphoinositide accumulation and intracellular calcium elevation compared to ERK1/2 phosphorylation. Through subsequent molecular characterization, we found that 5-HT-stimulated ERK1/2 phosphorylation in this cellular background requires phospholipase D, protein kinase C, and activation of the Raf/MEK/ERK module, while being independent of both receptor- and non-receptor tyrosine kinases, phospholipase C, phosphoinositide 3-kinase, and endocytosis. Our findings highlight the potential for selectively modulating signaling pathways in the differential regulation of neuronal signaling, with implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: Short-term medical service trips: a systematic review of the evidence.
text: Short-term medical service trips (MSTs) aim to address unmet healthcare needs in low- and middle-income countries. However, a lack of empirical evidence on the effectiveness of these trips is a significant concern. To address this issue, systematic research reviews are essential to develop evidence-based recommendations for healthcare delivery. I focused on MST publications with empirical results and conducted searches in May 2013, identifying 67 studies published since 1993. Unfortunately, only 6% of these studies were published in the past 20 years, with nearly 80% reporting on surgical trips. Despite the growing popularity of MSTs, the medical literature remains limited, with the majority of scholarly publications lacking significant data collection. By incorporating data collection into service trips, organizations can validate their practices and provide valuable insights into areas that require improvement.

title: Comparison of Beck Depression Inventories -IA and -II in psychiatric outpatients.
text: The revised Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-IA; Beck & Steer, 1993b) and the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II; Beck, Steer, & Brown, 1996) were administered to 140 psychiatric outpatients with various psychiatric disorders. The coefficient alphas of the BDI-IA and the BDI-II were, respectively, .89 and .91. The BDI-IA and BDI-II differed in their mean ratings for certain symptoms, with the BDI-II rating higher on symptoms such as Sadness, Past Failure, Self-Dislike, Change in Sleeping Pattern, and Change in Appetite. The BDI-II also had a higher mean total score and more endorsed symptoms than the BDI-IA. However, the correlations between the two inventories and various variables, such as sex, ethnicity, age, mood disorder diagnosis, and the Beck Anxiety Inventory (Beck & Steer, 1993a), were within 1 point of each other for the same variables.

title: Tumor engraftment in nude mice and enrichment in stroma- related gene pathways predict poor survival and resistance to gemcitabine in patients with pancreatic cancer.
text:
Objective: To evaluate the engraftment rate, factors influencing engraftment, and predictability of clinical outcome of low-passage xenografts from patients with resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) and establish a bank of PDA xenografts.
Methods: Patients with resectable PDA undergoing surgery at Johns Hopkins Hospital were enrolled in the study. Representative tumor pieces were implanted in nude mice, and the status of the SMAD4 gene and content of tumor-generating cells were determined by immunohistochemistry. Gene expression was analyzed using a U133 Plus 2.0 array. Patients were followed for progression and survival.
Results: A total of 94 patients with PDA were resected, and 69 tumors were implanted in nude mice, resulting in 42 (61%) engrafted carcinomas. Engrafted carcinomas were more often SMAD4 mutant and had a metastatic gene expression signature, indicating a worse prognosis. Tumors from patients resistant to gemcitabine were enriched in stroma-related gene pathways, while tumors sensitive to gemcitabine were enriched in cell cycle and pyrimidine gene pathways. The time to progression for patients who received treatment with gemcitabine for metastatic disease was double in patients with xenografts sensitive to gemcitabine.
Conclusion: A successful xenograft was generated in 61% of patients attempted, resulting in a pool of 42 PDA xenografts with significant biological information and annotated clinical data. Patients with PDA and SMAD4 inactivation had a better engraftment rate. Engraftment was a poor prognosis factor, and engrafted tumors had a metastatic gene expression signature. Tumors from gemcitabine-resistant patients were enriched in stromal pathways.

title: The MCM8-MCM9 complex promotes RAD51 recruitment at DNA damage sites to facilitate homologous recombination.
text: Previous studies have implicated the minichromosome maintenance proteins MCM8 and MCM9 in DNA replication elongation and prereplication complex (pre-RC) formation, respectively. Our findings demonstrate that these proteins physically associate with each other and that MCM8 is essential for the stability of MCM9 in mammalian cells. Depletion of MCM8 or MCM9 in human cancer cells or the loss of function MCM9 mutation in mouse embryo fibroblasts renders cells more susceptible to the DNA interstrand cross-linking agent cisplatin. Consistent with their role in the repair of interstrand cross-links (ICLs) through homologous recombination (HR), knockdown of MCM8 or MCM9 significantly reduces the efficiency of HR repair. Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis using human DR-GFP cells or Xenopus egg extracts revealed that MCM8 and MCM9 proteins are rapidly recruited to sites of DNA damage and promote the recruitment of RAD51. These findings suggest that these metazoan-specific MCM homologs are novel components of HR and may represent potential targets for cancer treatment in combination with DNA cross-linking agents.

title: The 5TMM series: a useful in vivo mouse model of human multiple myeloma.
text:
The present invention provides a novel combination sink and dishwashing apparatus, where a sink shares a common side wall with a cabinet that encloses a closed space. The cabinet features a wire basket for holding and washing multiple dishes within the cabinet. The common side wall, which forms one side of the sink, can be opened to allow the wire basket to slide in and out of the sink for loading and unloading dishes.
Inside the cabinet, the invention incorporates a motor-powered pump that sprays water through a rotating spray arm to wash dishes, similar to traditional dishwashing machines. Additionally, the invention may include a motor-powered garbage disposal.
In an alternative embodiment, the invention can consist of two adjacent cabinets, each located on opposite sides of the sink, providing additional storage and washing capacity.

title: Ionic protein-lipid interaction at the plasma membrane: what can the charge do?
text: Phospholipids are the primary components of cell membranes, but they play a more significant role than just forming lipid bilayers. In particular, acidic phospholipids create microdomains in the plasma membrane and can interact with proteins through ionic interactions, which can have a profound impact on protein function. The list of proteins affected by these interactions has been rapidly expanding, and now includes membrane proteins, cytoplasmic soluble proteins, and viral proteins. In this review, we will explore how acidic phospholipids in the plasma membrane regulate protein structure and function through ionic interactions, and how calcium ions (Ca2+) modulate these interactions via both direct and indirect mechanisms.

title: A20 is overexpressed in glioma cells and may serve as a potential therapeutic target.
text:
Objective A20 is a tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-inducible primary response gene that has been found to have antiapoptotic functions in various cancer cells. This study investigates the expression of A20 in human glioma tissues and four glioma cell lines, and its impact on the tumorigenesis of glioma cells and a mouse tumor model.
Methods:
Human glioma tissue samples and cells were subjected to reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), western blotting, and immunohistochemistry. Glioma cells were analyzed by flow cytometry. A xenograft tumor model in mice was used to evaluate the knockdown effect of specific A20 small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) on tumorigenesis.
Results:
A20 was overexpressed in clinical glioma tissue samples (63.9%) and correlated with clinical staging. All four human glioma cell lines expressed A20, with U87 displaying the strongest expression signals. Inhibiting A20 expression with siRNAs in vitro reduced the growth rates of glioma cells and caused G1/S arrest and increased apoptosis. In a mouse tumor model, local administration of siRNA significantly suppressed solid tumor growth.
Conclusions:
A20 was overexpressed in both human glioma tissues and cell lines, and inhibiting A20 expression significantly slowed tumor cell growth in culture and in mice. These findings suggest that A20 is involved in the tumorigenesis of human glioma and may serve as a future therapeutic target.

title: Prevalence and size of directly detected patent foramen ovale in migraine with aura.
text:
Background: Transcranial contrast Doppler studies have shown an increased prevalence of right-to-left shunts in patients with migraine with aura compared to controls. However, the anatomy and size of these shunts have never been directly assessed.
Methods: In a cross-sectional case-control study, the authors performed transesophageal contrast echocardiography on 93 consecutive patients with migraine with aura and 93 healthy controls.
Results: The study found that 47% of patients with migraine with aura had a patent foramen ovale, which is a significantly higher prevalence compared to 17% of controls (odds ratio [OR] 4.56, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.97-10.57, p < 0.001). Additionally, the study found that small shunts were equally prevalent in both groups (10% in migraineurs and 10% in controls), but moderate-sized or large shunts were more common in the migraine group (38% vs 8% in controls, p < 0.001). The presence of more than a small shunt increased the odds of having migraine with aura by 7.78-fold (95% CI 2.53-29.30, p < 0.001). No other echocardiographic differences were found between the study groups, and headache and baseline characteristics did not differ in migraine patients with and without shunt.
Conclusions: The study found that nearly half of patients with migraine with aura have a right-to-left shunt due to a patent foramen ovale. The size of these shunts is larger in migraineurs than controls. The clinical presentation of migraine is identical in patients with and without a patent foramen ovale. These findings suggest that patent foramen ovale may play a role in the pathophysiology of migraine with aura.

title: A Live Attenuated Chimeric West Nile Virus Vaccine, rWN/DEN4&Dgr;30, Is Well Tolerated and Immunogenic in Flavivirus-Naive Older Adult Volunteers
text: West Nile virus (WNV) is a significant cause of mosquito-borne illness in the United States, with human disease ranging from mild fever to severe neurological infection. Adults aged 60 years and older are more susceptible to severe neurological disease, with a high mortality rate or long-lasting sequelae. A chimeric live attenuated WNV vaccine, rWN/DEN4&Dgr;30, has been shown to be safe and immunogenic in healthy adults aged 18-50 years. This study evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of rWN/DEN4&Dgr;30 in flavivirus-naive adults aged 50-65 years and found it to be safe and immunogenic. Unpredictable outbreaks of WNV infection highlight the need for a safe and effective vaccine as a public health tool.

title: Localization and requirement for Myosin II at the dorsal-ventral compartment boundary of the Drosophila wing.
text: As organisms develop, cell populations within tissues can become segregated into distinct groups through the formation of barriers, known as compartment boundaries. While compartment boundaries have been observed in various tissues, the molecular mechanisms that drive their formation are often poorly understood. In the Drosophila wing, for example, a strip of Notch activation helps maintain the dorsal-ventral compartment boundary, which is dependent on the actin cytoskeleton. Our study reveals that the dorsal-ventral boundary exhibits a unique accumulation of Myosin II, which is regulated by Notch signaling. Conversely, the dorsal-ventral boundary is depleted of the Par-3 homologue Bazooka. We also found that mutations in the Myosin heavy chain subunit encoded by zipper can impair dorsal-ventral compartmentalization without affecting anterior-posterior compartmentalization. These findings highlight a specific requirement for Myosin activity in dorsal-ventral compartmentalization and suggest a novel mechanism in which contractile tension along an F-actin cable at the compartment boundary contributes to compartmentalization.

title: The cause of hepatic accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate on fructose loading.
text:
The metabolic changes that occur in livers of fed rats when perfused with 10mmol/L fructose have been examined.
1. Fructose loading resulted in a significant accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate, reaching up to 8.7μmol/g liver within 10 minutes, a loss of total adenine nucleotides (up to 35% after 40 minutes) with a corresponding decrease in ATP content to 23% within 10 minutes, a sevenfold increase in the concentration of IMP to 1.1μmol/g, and an eightfold increase in the concentration of alpha-glycerophosphate to 1.1μmol/g.
2. There was a transient decrease in Pi from 4.2 to 1.7μmol/g, which recovered to normal values within 40 minutes, likely due to uptake of Pi from the perfusion medium.
3. The degradation of adenine nucleotides beyond the stage of AMP can be accounted for by the decrease in ATP and Pi. Since ATP inhibits 5-nucleotidase, and Pi inhibits AMP deaminase, any AMP arising in the tissue is susceptible to dephosphorylation or deamination under the conditions occurring after fructose loading.
4. The content of lactate increased to 4.3μmol/g at 80 minutes, while pyruvate also increased, and the lactate/pyruvate ratio remained within physiological limits.
5. The concentration of free fructose within the liver remained significantly lower than that in the perfusion medium, indicating that the rate of fructose penetration into the tissue was lower than the rate of utilization.
6. The fission of fructose 1-phosphate by liver aldolase is inhibited by several phosphorylated intermediates, especially by IMP, with a K(i) of 0.1mm.
7. The maximal rates of enzymes synthesizing and splitting fructose 1-phosphate are approximately equal, and the accumulation of fructose 1-phosphate on fructose loading is due to the inhibition of the fission of fructose 1-phosphate by the IMP arising from the degradation of adenine nucleotides.

title: Reported side effects to chloroquine, chloroquine plus proguanil, and mefloquine as chemoprophylaxis against malaria in Danish travelers.
text:
Background: The study aimed to investigate the frequency of reported symptoms among travelers taking chloroquine, chloroquine plus proguanil, or mefloquine as malaria prophylaxis.
Method: The study was an open, non-randomized observational study conducted at two travel clinics in Copenhagen, Denmark. Participants were recruited consecutively and completed a questionnaire on their symptoms and compliance with their medication.
Results: A total of 5,446 travelers were included in the study, with 4,158 (76.3%) completing the questionnaire. Compliance was significantly higher among mefloquine users (83.3%), compared to chloroquine plus proguanil users (76.3%). Additionally, 84.8%, 59.3%, and 69.5% of travelers using chloroquine, chloroquine plus proguanil, and mefloquine, respectively, reported no symptoms, while 0.6%, 1.1%, and 2.8% reported "unacceptable" symptoms. Compared to chloroquine, mefloquine users had a higher risk of reporting depression (RR 5.06, 95% CI 2.71-9.45), "strange thoughts" (RR 6.36, 95% CI 2.52-16.05), and altered spatial perception (RR 3.00, 95% CI 1.41-6.41).
Conclusion: Overall, mefloquine was found to be at least as well tolerated as chloroquine plus proguanil, with better compliance. However, travelers taking mefloquine were more likely to experience symptoms related to the central nervous system, which were perceived as more severe when they occurred.

title: Ubiquitinylation of the cytosolic domain of a type I membrane protein is not required to initiate its dislocation from the endoplasmic reticulum.
text: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) US2 and US11 proteins target newly synthesized class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) heavy chains for rapid degradation through a process termed dislocation. US2 induces the formation of class I MHC heavy chain conjugates of increased molecular weight, which are recognized by a conformation-specific monoclonal antibody, W6/32, suggesting that these class I MHC molecules retain their proper tertiary structure. These conjugates are properly folded and glycosylated heavy chains modified by attachment of an estimated one, two, and three ubiquitin molecules. In contrast to US11, which targets class I MHC heavy chains for dislocation in a manner that requires the conformation of the heavy chain molecule, US2 shows different requirements in terms of the conformation of the heavy chain molecule. Although ubiquitin conjugation may occur on the cytosolic tail of the class I MHC molecule, replacement of lysines in the cytosolic tail of heavy chains with arginine does not prevent their degradation by US2. In an in vitro system that recapitulates US2-mediated dislocation, heavy chains that lack these lysines still occur in an ubiquitin-modified form, but in the soluble (cytoplasmic) fraction. Such ubiquitin conjugation can only occur on the class I MHC lumenal domain and is likely to take place once class I MHC heavy chains have been discharged from the endoplasmic reticulum. Our findings suggest that ubiquitinylation of class I MHC heavy chain is not required during the initial step of the US2-mediated dislocation reaction.

title: The adaptor protein Tks5/Fish is required for podosome formation and function, and for the protease-driven invasion of cancer cells.
text: Tks5/Fish is a scaffolding protein that contains five SH3 domains and one PX domain. In Src-transformed cells, Tks5/Fish localizes to podosomes, which are distinct protrusions on the ventral membrane. To investigate the role of Tks5/Fish in podosome formation and cellular invasion, we reduced Tks5/Fish levels in Src-transformed cells. These cells were no longer able to form podosomes, degrade gelatin, or invade surrounding tissues. We observed Tks5/Fish expression in podosomes in invasive cancer cells, as well as in human breast cancer and melanoma samples. Additionally, we found that Tks5/Fish expression was necessary for protease-driven matrigel invasion in human cancer cells. Furthermore, coexpression of Tks5/Fish and Src in epithelial cells led to the formation of podosomes. These findings suggest that Tks5/Fish plays a crucial role in podosome formation, extracellular matrix degradation, and cancer cell invasion.

title: Corticosteroid injections for shoulder pain.
text:
BACKGROUND:
Corticosteroid injections have been widely used to treat shoulder pain, but there is limited evidence to support their efficacy. This review aims to determine the effectiveness and safety of corticosteroid injections in adults with shoulder pain.
OBJECTIVES:
To evaluate the efficacy and safety of corticosteroid injections in the treatment of shoulder pain in adults.
SEARCH STRATEGY:
A comprehensive search of various databases including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and Science Citation Index was conducted up to June 2002.
SELECTION CRITERIA:
Randomized and pseudo-randomized trials that compared corticosteroid injections to placebo or another intervention in adults with shoulder pain were included. Specific exclusions included shoulder pain of less than three weeks duration, rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and fracture.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS:
Two independent reviewers assessed trial inclusion and methodological quality using predetermined criteria. Results were presented separately for rotator cuff disease, adhesive capsulitis, full-thickness rotator cuff tear, and mixed diagnoses, and meta-analysis was performed where possible.
MAIN RESULTS:
Twenty-six trials met the inclusion criteria, with varying numbers, sites, and dosages of injections. The number of participants per trial ranged from 20 to 114 (median 52 participants). Methodological quality was variable. For rotator cuff disease, subacromial steroid injection showed a small benefit over placebo in some trials, but no benefit of subacromial steroid injection over nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) was demonstrated based on the pooled results of three trials. For adhesive capsulitis, two trials suggested a possible early benefit of intra-articular steroid injection over placebo, but there was insufficient data for pooling of any of the trials. One trial suggested a short-term benefit of intra-articular corticosteroid injection over physiotherapy in the short term (success at seven weeks: relative risk [RR] = 1.66 [1.21, 2.28]).
REVIEWER'S CONCLUSIONS:
Despite numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of corticosteroid injections for shoulder pain, their small sample sizes, variable methodological quality, and heterogeneity make it difficult to draw conclusions about their efficacy. Subacromial corticosteroid injection for rotator cuff disease and intra-articular injection for adhesive capsulitis may be beneficial, although their effect may be small and not well-maintained. Further RCTs are needed to investigate the efficacy of corticosteroid injections for shoulder pain, as well as to determine the factors that influence their efficacy, such as needle placement, anatomical site, frequency, dose, and type of corticosteroid.

title: IL-2 receptor signaling is essential for the development of Klrg1+ terminally differentiated T regulatory cells.
text: Thymic-derived natural T regulatory cells (Tregs) exhibit functional and phenotypic heterogeneity. Recently, a small subset of peripheral Tregs has been found to express the protein Klrg1, but it remains unclear how this defines a unique Treg subset. In this study, we demonstrate that Klrg1(+) Tregs represent a distinct terminally differentiated subset derived from Klrg1(-) Tregs. This subset is a recently activated and highly proliferative population that resides primarily in mucosal tissues and expresses elevated levels of suppressive molecules. Additionally, the development of Klrg1(+) Tregs requires extensive IL-2R signaling, which functions independently of its role in Treg homeostasis and competitive fitness. These findings suggest a parallel with terminally differentiated short-lived CD8(+) T effector cells, implying an important pathway driving Ag-activated conventional T lymphocytes also operates for Tregs.

title: The aurora B kinase promotes inner and outer kinetochore interactions in budding yeast.
text: The kinetochore, a macromolecular protein complex, plays a crucial role in chromosome segregation. Specifically, the Dsn1 component is essential for kinetochore assembly and is phosphorylated by the Aurora B kinase. Our research has shown that Aurora B phosphorylation of Dsn1 promotes the interaction between outer and inner kinetochore proteins in budding yeast.

title: AMP-activated/SNF1 protein kinases: conserved guardians of cellular energy
text: The SNF1/AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) family plays a crucial role in maintaining the delicate balance between ATP production and consumption in all eukaryotic cells. These kinases are composed of a catalytic subunit and regulatory subunits that sense cellular energy levels, forming heterotrimers. When energy levels are compromised, the AMPK system activates catabolic pathways, inhibiting protein, carbohydrate, and lipid biosynthesis, as well as cell growth and proliferation. Interestingly, recent findings have also highlighted the importance of AMPK in functions beyond energy homeostasis, such as maintaining cell polarity in epithelial cells.

title: Mammographic density, plasma vitamin D levels and risk of breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
text: Mammographic density is a significant risk factor for breast cancer, yet the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. Some studies suggest that vitamin D may reduce breast cancer risk, and dietary vitamin D intake has been associated with lower breast density. To investigate the potential relationship between vitamin D and mammographic density, we conducted a case-control study within the Nurses' Health Study cohort. Our sample consisted of 463 postmenopausal cases and 497 controls. We measured the association between mammographic density and plasma levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)(2)D]. We also examined whether plasma vitamin D metabolites modify the association between breast density and breast cancer risk. Mammographic density was measured from digitized film mammograms, and generalized linear models were used to determine the mean percent breast density per quartile of vitamin D metabolite. Logistic regression models were used to calculate relative risks and confidence intervals, and all models were adjusted for matching variables and potential confounders. Our findings revealed no significant cross-sectional association between circulating levels of 25(OH)D or 1,25(OH)(2)D and mammographic density. Women in the highest tertile of mammographic density and lowest tertile of plasma 25(OH)D had a 4-fold greater risk of breast cancer compared to women with the lowest mammographic density and highest plasma 25(OH)D levels (RR = 3.8; 95% CI: 2.0-7.3). The overall interaction between mammographic density and plasma 25(OH)D was not significant (p-het = 0.20). These results suggest that the association between mammographic density and breast cancer is independent of plasma vitamin D metabolites in postmenopausal women. Further research is warranted to explore the relationship between vitamin D, mammographic density, and breast cancer risk.

title: Finding the right niche: B-cell migration in the early phases of T-dependent antibody responses.
text: Humoral immune responses rely on B cells encountering antigen, interacting with helper T cells, proliferating, and differentiating into either low-affinity plasma cells or, after organizing into a germinal center (GC), high-affinity plasma cells and memory B cells. Notably, each of these events occurs in association with distinct stromal cells in separate subcompartments of lymphoid tissue. B cells must rapidly and highly regulate their migration between niches to successfully mount an immune response. The chemokine CXCL13 plays a central role in guiding B cells to follicles, while T-zone chemokines direct activated B cells to the T zone. Additionally, sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) promotes cell egress from tissue and marginal-zone B-cell positioning in the spleen. Recent studies have also revealed a role for the orphan receptor, EBV-induced molecule 2 (EBI2; GPR183), in guiding activated B cells to inter and outer follicular niches, and down-regulation of this receptor is essential for organizing cells into GCs. This review aims to discuss the current understanding of the roles played by chemokines, S1P, and EBI2 in the migration events that underlie humoral immune responses.

title: Arginine Starvation Impairs Mitochondrial Respiratory Function in ASS1-Deficient Breast Cancer Cells
text: Autophagy, the primary catabolic response to nutrient deprivation, is essential for eliminating damaged or dysfunctional organelles. However, excessive autophagy can be detrimental and contribute to cell death. The availability of enzymes involved in molecule biosynthesis can influence a cell's dependence on exogenous nutrient uptake. Argininosuccinate synthetase 1 (ASS1) is a crucial enzyme in arginine biosynthesis, and its reduced abundance is common in many solid tumors. We demonstrated that prolonged arginine starvation, induced by exposure to ADI-PEG20 (pegylated arginine deiminase), resulted in autophagy-dependent death of ASS1-deficient breast cancer cells. These cells are arginine auxotrophs, requiring extracellular arginine for their survival. In vitro and in vivo experiments showed that arginine starvation led to mitochondrial oxidative stress, impairing mitochondrial bioenergetics and integrity. Furthermore, only autophagy-competent breast cancer cells were susceptible to the lethal effects of prolonged arginine starvation. ASS1 was found to be low in abundance or absent in over 60% of 149 random breast cancer biosamples, suggesting that patients with such tumors may be candidates for arginine starvation therapy.

title: A prospective natural-history study of coronary atherosclerosis.
text: In a prospective study of 697 patients with acute coronary syndromes, the authors found that major adverse cardiovascular events occurring during follow-up were equally attributable to recurrence at the site of culprit lesions and to nonculprit lesions. Although nonculprit lesions responsible for unanticipated events were often angiographically mild, they were more likely to be characterized by a large plaque burden, a small luminal area, or some combination of these characteristics, as determined by gray-scale and radiofrequency intravascular ultrasonography. The study found that nonculprit lesions associated with recurrent events were more likely to be classified as thin-cap fibroatheromas. These findings suggest that even angiographically mild coronary lesions can be a source of future cardiovascular events, and that the assessment of plaque characteristics using intravascular ultrasonography may be useful in predicting this risk. (Funded by Abbott Vascular and Volcano; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00180466.)

title: What do medical schools teach about women's health and gender differences?
text:
Objective: To investigate the inclusion of women's health and gender-specific content in the curricula of US medical schools and identify institutional factors associated with its presence.
Methodology: Using data from the Association of American Medical Colleges' Curriculum Management and Information Tool (CurrMIT), the authors conducted a curriculum search of schools that entered course/clerkships in CurrMIT from November 2003 to February 2004. They identified interdisciplinary women's health or gender-specific courses/clerkships and searched a subset of schools for specified women's health topics and gender-specific content on any topic. Statistical analyses were performed to assess the relationship between the frequency of topics and school characteristics.
Results: The authors identified 95 schools that entered related courses/clerkships, with ten interdisciplinary women's health courses/clerkships at nine schools. In the subset of 60 schools with comprehensive CurrMIT information, 18 specified women's health topics and 24 gender-specific content topics were identified, for a total of 42 topics. The number of topics taught ranged from zero to 26 (mean = 11). More than 50% of the schools taught 11 of the 18 specified topics, while fewer than 30% included gender-specific topics. There was no association between the mean number of topics taught and school characteristics in bivariate analysis, but a women's health program (p= .01) and female dean (p= .06) were positively associated in a regression model.
Conclusion: Few schools offer interdisciplinary women's health courses/clerkships or include gender-specific information in their curricula. A designated women's health program may increase this content in schools' curricula.

title: A molecular framework for plant regeneration.
text:
Plants and certain animals possess an impressive capacity for organ regeneration, where adult tissues are able to differentiate into new cell types. Despite this remarkable ability, the molecular mechanisms underlying regeneration have remained largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate the local regeneration response in Arabidopsis root tips, with a focus on the hormone auxin and its role in cell fate determination.
Using laser-induced wounding, we disrupt the flow of auxin in root tips and demonstrate that this leads to changes in cell fate, which are dependent on the expression of the transcription factors PLETHORA, SHORTROOT, and SCARECROW. These transcription factors regulate the expression and polar position of PIN auxin efflux-facilitating membrane proteins, which are essential for the reconstitution of auxin transport in renewed root tips. Our findings reveal a novel regeneration mechanism that involves the use of embryonic root stem-cell patterning factors to first respond to and subsequently stabilize a new hormone distribution.

title: Cocoa flavonols and procyanidins promote transforming growth factor-beta1 homeostasis in peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
text:
New research suggests that certain flavan-3-ols and procyanidins (FP) may have a positive impact on cardiovascular health. Previous studies have shown that FP isolated from cocoa can modulate the levels and production of signaling molecules involved in immune function and inflammation, including cytokines and eicosanoids. In this study, the researchers examined whether FP fractions, ranging from monomers to decamers, could modulate the secretion of the cytokine transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta(1) from resting human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC).
The study involved 13 healthy subjects, who were grouped according to their baseline levels of TGF-beta(1). When PBMCs from individuals with low baseline levels of TGF-beta(1) were stimulated with individual FP fractions (25 microg/ml), TGF-beta(1) release was enhanced by 15%-66% compared to baseline (P < 0.05; monomer, dimer, and tetramer). The low-molecular-weight FP fractions (<or=pentamer) were more effective at augmenting TGF-beta(1) secretion than larger fractions (>or=hexamer), with the monomer and dimer inducing the greatest increases (66% and 68%, respectively). In contrast, TGF-beta(1) secretion from high TGF-beta(1) baseline subjects was inhibited by individual FP fractions (P < 0.05; trimer through decamer). The inhibition was most pronounced with trimeric through decameric fractions (28%-42%), and monomers and dimers moderately inhibited TGF-beta(1) release (17% and 23%, respectively).
These findings suggest that in healthy individuals, the homeostatic modulation of TGF-beta(1) production by FP may offer an additional mechanism by which FP-rich foods can benefit cardiovascular health. TGF-beta(1) plays a crucial role in vascular function and inflammation, and its dysregulation has been implicated in various cardiovascular diseases. The study provides evidence that FP may have a positive impact on cardiovascular health by modulating the production of TGF-beta(1) in a manner that depends on the individual's baseline levels of the cytokine.

title: BMP receptor IA is required in mammalian neural crest cells for development of the cardiac outflow tract and ventricular myocardium.
text: The neural crest, a multipotent and migratory cell population arising from the boundary between the neural and surface ectoderm, undergoes induction and regulation by bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) in mouse embryos. Specifically, BMP2 and BMP4 have been implicated as regulators of neural crest cell induction, maintenance, migration, differentiation, and survival. In mouse, there are three known BMP2/4 type I receptors, with Bmpr1a being expressed in the neural tube early enough to participate in neural crest development from the outset. However, earlier roles in other domains have obscured its requirement in the neural crest. To investigate the role of Bmpr1a in neural crest development, we ablated it specifically in the neural crest cells, starting at the five-somite stage. Our findings suggest that BMPRIA is dispensable for many aspects of early neural crest biology, but it is essential for outflow tract development and perinatal viability. Specifically, mutant embryos display a shortened cardiac outflow tract with defective septation, which is a critical process that relies on neural crest cells and is essential for perinatal survival. Moreover, these embryos die in mid-gestation due to acute heart failure, which may result from reduced BMP signaling in a novel, minor population of neural crest derivatives in the epicardium, a known source of ventricular myocardial proliferation signals. These findings demonstrate that BMP2/4 signaling in mammalian neural crest derivatives is crucial for outflow tract development and may regulate a critical proliferation signal for the ventricular myocardium.

title: Early intermittent noninvasive ventilation for acute chest syndrome in adults with sickle cell disease: a pilot study
text: Alveolar hypoxia and hypoxic vasoconstriction can lead to the entrapment of sickle cells within the pulmonary vasculature, which can worsen the outcome of acute chest syndrome (ACS). Improving alveolar ventilation and oxygenation may improve the outcome of ACS. A prospective, randomized, single-center, open study was conducted from November 1998 to February 2002 to evaluate the effectiveness of noninvasive ventilation (NIV) in improving oxygenation in adults with ACS. Seventy-one consecutive ACS episodes in 67 patients were randomly assigned to either oxygen therapy (n = 36) or NIV (n = 35) for 3 days in a medical step-down unit. At baseline, the NIV group had a higher respiratory rate and pain score compared to the oxygen group. NIV promptly lowered the respiratory rate, increased PaO2, and decreased the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-aDO2), which remained unchanged with oxygen therapy. PaCO2 significantly worsened only in the oxygen group. On day 3, the groups did not differ in the proportion of episodes with normal PaO2 or A-aDO2. However, patient satisfaction and compliance were lower with NIV. No differences were noted in pain relief, transfusions, or length of stay. In the subgroup of patients with severe hypoxemia (PaO2 ≤ 65 mmHg), physiological variables improved faster with NIV, with slightly more pronounced differences. Respiratory rate and gas exchange improved faster with NIV, but NIV failed to significantly reduce the number of patients remaining hypoxemic at day 3, and was associated with greater patient discomfort.

title: Serum Exosome MicroRNA as a Minimally-Invasive Early Biomarker of AML
text: Relapse remains the primary cause of mortality in patients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Enhanced tracking of minimal residual disease (MRD) holds the potential for timely treatment adjustments to prevent relapse. Current surveillance techniques detect circulating blasts that coincide with advanced disease and poorly reflect MRD during early relapse. In this study, we investigate the use of exosomes as a minimally invasive platform for a microRNA (miRNA) biomarker. We identify a set of miRNAs enriched in AML exosomes and track levels of circulating exosome miRNA that distinguish leukemic xenografts from both non-engrafted and human CD34+ controls. We develop biostatistical models that reveal circulating exosomal miRNA at low marrow tumor burden and before circulating blasts can be detected. Notably, both leukemic blasts and marrow stroma contribute to serum exosome miRNA. We propose the development of serum exosome miRNA as a platform for a novel, sensitive compartment biomarker for prospective tracking and early detection of AML recurrence.

title: Human cytomegalovirus encodes an MHC class I-like molecule (UL142) that functions to inhibit NK cell lysis.
text: Clinical and low passage strains of human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) encode an additional MHC class I-related molecule, UL142, in addition to the previously described UL18. The open reading frame for UL142 is located within the ULb' region, which is absent in several common high passage laboratory strains of HCMV. To investigate the function of UL142, cells were transfected with UL142 or infected with a recombinant adenovirus expressing UL142, and then used to screen both polyclonal natural killer (NK) cells and NK cell clones in a completely autologous system. Analysis of 100 NK cell clones derived from five donors revealed 23 clones that were inhibited by fibroblasts expressing UL142 alone. Furthermore, small interfering RNA-mediated knockdown of UL142 mRNA expression in HCMV-infected cells resulted in increased sensitivity to lysis. These findings suggest that UL142 is a novel HCMV-encoded MHC class I-related molecule that inhibits NK cell killing in a clonally dependent manner.

title: Identification of the conserved serine/threonine residues important for gibberellin-sensitivity of Arabidopsis RGL2 protein.
text:
Introduction:
The DELLA proteins GAI, RGA, RGL1, and RGL2 in Arabidopsis have been identified as plant growth repressors, repressing various developmental processes. Previous studies have shown that gibberellin (GA) can attenuate the repressive function of DELLA proteins by triggering their degradation through the proteasome pathway. However, it remains unclear if GA-induced protein degradation is the sole mechanism for regulating the bioactivity of DELLA proteins.
To investigate this further, we used tobacco BY2 cells as a suitable system for studying GA signaling. Our findings revealed that RGL2 exists in a phosphorylated form in BY2 cells and undergoes GA-induced degradation, which is blocked by proteasome inhibitors and serine/threonine phosphatase inhibitors. However, serine/threonine kinase inhibitors had no detectable effect, suggesting that dephosphorylation of serine/threonine is a prerequisite for degradation of RGL2 via the proteasome pathway.
To further elucidate the mechanisms involved, we conducted site-directed mutagenesis of all 17 conserved serine and threonine residues in RGL2. Our results showed that six mutants (RGL2(S441D), RGL2(S542D), RGL2(T271E), RGL2(T319E), RGL2(T411E), and RGL2(T535E)) mimicking constitutive phosphorylation are resistant to GA-induced degradation. This suggests that these sites may be potential phosphorylation sites.
To evaluate the functional effects of these mutations, we developed a functional assay based on the expression of GA 20-oxidase. Our findings showed that RGL2(T271E) is likely a null mutant, while RGL2(S441D), RGL2(S542D), RGL2(T319E), RGL2(T411E), and RGL2(T535E) only retained 4-17% of the activity of the wild-type RGL2, respectively. However, expression of GA 20-oxidase in BY2 cells expressing these mutant proteins is still responsive to GA, indicating that the stabilization of RGL2 protein is not the only pathway for regulating its bioactivity.
Conclusion:
Our study provides new insights into the regulation of DELLA protein bioactivity in Arabidopsis. We demonstrate that GA-induced degradation of RGL2 is a key mechanism for regulating its bioactivity, and that dephosphorylation of serine/threonine residues may be a prerequisite for this process. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the stabilization of RGL2 protein is not the only pathway for regulating its bioactivity, and that other mechanisms, such as changes in protein-protein interactions or post-translational modifications, may also play a role. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the complex signaling pathways involved in plant growth and development.

title: A chart review of cyproheptadine for stimulant-induced weight loss.
text: Youths with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often experience weight loss when taking stimulants, which can limit optimal dosing and compliance. However, cyproheptadine, a medication commonly used to promote weight gain, has been shown to be effective in this context. In a retrospective chart review of 28 pediatric psychiatry outpatients, we found that 4 patients did not consistently take cyproheptadine, and 3 discontinued it within the first 7 days due to intolerable side effects. Data were analyzed for 21 patients (age range 4-15 years) who continued taking 4-8 mg of cyproheptadine nightly (mean final dose = 4.9 mg/day) for at least 14 days (mean duration = 104.7 days). These patients had lost weight on stimulant alone (mean weight loss was 2.1 kg, mean weight velocity was -19.3 g/day). However, when taking cyproheptadine, all 21 patients gained weight, with a mean gain of 2.2 kg (paired t = 6.87, p < 0.0001) and a mean weight velocity of 32.3 g/day. Additionally, 11 of 17 patients who had reported initial insomnia on stimulant alone noted significant improvements in sleep with cyproheptadine added. Based on these findings, we conclude that concomitant cyproheptadine may be a useful adjunct in treating weight loss in youths with ADHD, pending further randomized controlled trials.

title: Life course breast cancer risk factors and adult breast density (United Kingdom)
text:
Objective: To investigate whether risk factors in childhood and early adulthood are associated with later mammographic breast density.
Methods: This study analyzed data from 628 women who underwent a medical examination at the University of Glasgow Student Health Service between 1948 and 1968, completed a questionnaire in 2001, and had a screening mammogram in Scotland between 1989 and 2002. Mammograms were classified using a six-category classification system (SCC) of breast density percent. Logistic regression was used to determine the associations between risk factors and having a high-risk mammogram (≥25 dense).
Results: In multivariate analyses, high-risk mammograms were associated with parity (adjusted odds ratio (OR) per child: 0.77, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.61-0.99), age at first birth, OR per year: 1.05, 0.99-1.11, smoking at university, OR smokers versus non-smokers: 0.58, 0.36-0.92, and body mass index (BMI) while at university, OR per 1kg/m2: 0.75, 0.69-0.82. No significant associations were found for age at menarche, birth weight, oral contraceptive (OC) use, height, leg length, or exercise at age 20.
Conclusions: This study confirms previous findings that breast density is influenced by reproductive events and some anthropometric measures. However, the majority of the risk factors examined in this study were not closely related to adult breast density.

title: Osteoclast nuclei of myeloma patients show chromosome translocations specific for the myeloma cell clone: a new type of cancer-host partnership?
text: A hallmark of multiple myeloma is the destruction of bone, which is not attributed to the malignant cells themselves but rather to osteoclasts, multinucleated cells of monocytic origin that are the only cells capable of bone resorption. The present study provides evidence that bone-resorbing osteoclasts from myeloma patients contain nuclei with translocated chromosomes of myeloma B-cell clone origin, in addition to nuclei without these translocations, as revealed through the combination of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and immunohistochemistry on bone sections. These malignant nuclei are transcriptionally active and appear to be fully integrated within the normal osteoclast population. The contribution of malignant nuclei to the osteoclast population analyzed in this study was found to be greater than 30%. Osteoclast-myeloma clone hybrids, which contain more nuclei than normal osteoclasts, were found to occur in close proximity to myeloma cells. Similar hybrid cells were generated in co-cultures of myeloma cells and osteoclasts, as evidenced by the tracing of myeloma nuclei using translocations, bromo-deoxyuridine, or the Y chromosome of male myeloma cells in female osteoclasts. These findings suggest that malignant cells can directly participate in the formation of bone-resorbing osteoclasts through fusion between myeloma cells and osteoclasts, thereby contributing significantly to bone destruction in multiple myeloma. The possibility that malignant cells may corrupt host cells by transferring malignant DNA has been underestimated in cancer research to date.

title: Frequency modulation entrains slow neural oscillations and optimizes human listening behavior.
text:
The human brain's ability to continuously track dynamic environmental stimuli, particularly speech, is believed to be enhanced through a process called "entrainment," where endogenous neural oscillations are reorganized to align with expected critical events. Previous studies have focused on the role of abrupt onsets in entraining neural oscillations, but this experiment goes beyond those findings by addressing two key questions: (1) Can neural oscillations be entrained by the temporal dynamics of ongoing rhythmic stimuli without abrupt onsets? and (2) Does neural entrainment improve the performance of the perceptual system?
To investigate, the experiment used human electroencephalography (EEG) recordings of listeners detecting short gaps in a 3-Hz frequency-modulated sound. The results showed that listeners' ability to detect gaps was not evenly distributed in time, but rather clustered in certain preferred phases of the modulation. Furthermore, the optimal stimulus phase was found to be individually determined by the neural delta oscillation entrained by the stimulus. Interestingly, delta phase (a measure of the brain's neural activity in the 0.5-4 Hz range) was found to predict behavior better than stimulus phase or the event-related potential after the gap, suggesting that phase realignment in response to frequency-modulated auditory stimuli has behavioral benefits.
Overall, these findings suggest that frequency fluctuations in natural environmental input serve as a pacing signal for endogenous neural oscillations, influencing perceptual processing. This study provides evidence for the importance of entrainment in improving perception and highlights the dynamic nature of neural processing in response to environmental stimuli.

title: Interventions by pharmacists in out-patient pharmaceutical care.
text:
Pharmacist interventions have long been recognized as a valuable contribution to the patient care process, reducing medication errors, rationalizing therapy, and lowering treatment costs. The primary objective of this study was to determine the number and types of medication errors intervened by dispensing pharmacists at the OPD pharmacy of Khoula Hospital during 2009. The interventions filed by pharmacists and assistant pharmacists in the OPD pharmacy were collected, categorized, and analyzed after a detailed review.
The findings reveal that 72.3% of the interventions were minor, with 40.5% related to changes in medication orders. A higher number of interventions were observed in female patients compared to male patients. Notably, 98.2% of the interventions were accepted by prescribers, indicating the importance of pharmacy practice among healthcare professionals. In this study, 688 interventions were due to prescribing errors, with 40.5% related to changing medication orders or clarifying medications. Administrative issues accounted for 14.9% of interventions, while selection of medications and ignorance of patient history accounted for 8.7% and 8.2%, respectively. Pharmacists also intervened to address overdoses of medications (14.9%). Moderately significant interventions were observed in 19.4% of cases, with 7.5% having a significant impact on major medication errors. Pharmacists intervened in 20.8% of prescriptions to prevent complications, 25.1% to rationalize treatment, and 7.9% to improve compliance.
Based on these findings, we conclude that the role of pharmacists in improving the healthcare system is crucial. We recommend conducting more research-based studies to raise awareness among healthcare professionals, provide solutions to prescription and dispensing issues, improve documentation systems, emphasize the importance of pharmacy practice, reduce prescribing errors, and update the knowledge of pharmacists and other healthcare professionals.

title: Biochemical studies on Mycobacterium tuberculosis UreG and comparative modeling reveal structural and functional conservation among the bacterial UreG family.
text:
Nickel, a micronutrient essential for cellular life, can be toxic in soluble form at non-physiological concentrations. To address this paradox, living organisms have evolved efficient systems for nickel utilization and homeostasis. One such system involves the incorporation of nickel into the active site of urease, a multistep process that requires the interplay of various accessory proteins. Understanding this activation mechanism may lead to medical applications against ureolytic bacteria, including the deadly pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This study focuses on UreG, an essential chaperone that activates urease in vivo by inserting nickel ions into the active site.
Using both experimental and computational approaches, the soluble M. tuberculosis UreG (MtUreG) was overexpressed in E. coli, purified to homogeneity, and its identity was confirmed by mass spectrometry. On-line size-exclusion chromatography and light scattering revealed that MtUreG exists as a dimer in solution, with a disulfide bond present in the dimer. The free thiol concentration was determined, showing that MtUreG has low GTPase activity under native conditions, with a kcat of 0.01 min-1. Circular dichroism spectroscopy revealed a well-defined secondary structure (8% alpha-helices, 29% beta-strands) in MtUreG, while NMR spectroscopy indicated that this protein does not have a rigid three-dimensional fold and can be classified as an intrinsically unstructured polypeptide. A molecular model of MtUreG in its fully folded and functional form was built using fold recognition algorithms. An extensive similarity search was performed to identify conserved patterns in all known bacterial UreG sequences, leading to the recognition of key residues and motifs important for protein function. A structural database containing homology-built models of the most representative UreG proteins was created, confirming structural analogies among the UreG family. A flexible region, likely important for protein function, was identified. The structural conservation among this class of GTPases was discussed based on their function in the urease assembly process.

title: (99m)Tc-HisoDGR as a Potential SPECT Probe for Orthotopic Glioma Detection via Targeting of Integrin α5β1.
text:
Integrins, a large family of cell adhesion receptors, have been shown to play a significant role in glioma proliferation and invasion. Among the various integrin receptors, αvβ3, αvβ5, and α5β1 have garnered clinical interest for glioma diagnosis and antitumor therapy. Of these, integrin α5β1 has been highlighted as a prognostic and diagnostic marker in glioma, with expression correlated to a poorer prognosis in high-grade gliomas. However, compared to extensively studied integrins αvβ3 and αvβ5, few integrin α5β1-specific radiotracers have been reported. Developing α5β1-specific radiotracers could provide alternative diagnostic and evaluation options, as well as add new insights into tumor progression.
To investigate the selective targeting of integrin α5β1 in vivo, we fabricated a novel probe, (99m)Tc-HisoDGR, for SPECT imaging of glioma. In mouse models of α5β1-positive U87MG human glioma, SPECT/CT scans, biodistribution experiments, and blocking studies were conducted. Small-animal SPECT/CT imaging experiments demonstrated that the tumors were clearly visualized in both subcutaneous and orthotopic glioma tumor models with minimal background activity at 0.5, 1, and 2 hours post-injection (p.i.). The tumor accumulation of (99m)Tc-HisoDGR was significantly reduced when excess cold isoDGR peptide was coinjected, indicating that the tumor uptake was specifically mediated by integrin α5β1. Our findings indicate that (99m)Tc-HisoDGR represents a powerful molecular probe for imaging integrin α5β1-positive cancer, and may be a promising tool for evaluating malignancy, predicting prognosis, identifying patients sensitive to integrin α5β1-targeted drugs, and monitoring response to these drugs in clinical trials.

title: Effect of cyclic AMP-dependent protein phosphorylating conditions on the pH-dependent activity of tyrosine hydroxylase from beef and rat striata.
text: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH, EC 1.14.16.2) from beef brain striata was purified 23-fold from an acetone-dried extract using a series of chromatographic steps. When this enzyme preparation is subjected to a cyclic AMP-dependent protein phosphorylation system, there is a notable change in the pH dependence of its enzymatic activity. Specifically, the pH optimum at saturating tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) concentration shifts from below pH 6 to approximately pH 6.7. At pH 7, activation is primarily observed as an increase in the maximum velocity (Vmax), whereas at pH 6, activation is primarily observed as a decrease in the Michaelis constant (Km) for the pterin cofactor. Furthermore, even with the control enzyme, the Km for pterin cofactor exhibits a precipitous decline as the pH is increased from 6 towards neutrality. Similar results were obtained using G-25 Sephadex-treated rat striatal TH. In situ activation of TH by phosphoryling conditions in rat striatal synaptosomes was found to primarily result in an increase in the maximum rate of dopamine synthesis. These findings suggest that changes in TH activity induced by cyclic AMP-dependent protein phosphorylation will be largely dependent on the pH environment of the enzyme.

title: Interaction of TNF with TNF receptor type 2 promotes expansion and function of mouse CD4+CD25+ T regulatory cells.
text: Although TNF is known to be a major pro-inflammatory cytokine, recent evidence suggests that it also has immunosuppressive feedback effects. In this study, we found that mouse peripheral CD4+CD25+ T regulatory cells (Tregs) expressed significantly higher levels of TNFR2 compared to CD4+CD25(-) T effector cells (Teffs). In cocultures of Tregs and Teffs, inhibition of Teff proliferation by Tregs was initially transiently abrogated by TNF, but longer exposure to TNF restored suppressive effects. Teff cytokine production remained continually suppressed by Tregs. The anergy of Tregs in response to TCR stimulation was overcome by TNF, which expanded the Treg population. Additionally, TNF expanded Tregs even more when combined with IL-2, up-regulating expression of CD25 and FoxP3, and enhancing suppressive activity. Unlike TNF, IL-1β and IL-6 did not up-regulate FoxP3-expressing Tregs. Furthermore, the number of Tregs increased in wild-type mice but not in TNFR2-deficient mice following sublethal cecal ligation and puncture. Depletion of Tregs significantly decreased mortality following cecal ligation and puncture. These findings suggest that the stimulatory effect of TNF on Tregs is more pronounced due to the higher expression of TNFR2 by Tregs. Moreover, the slower response of Tregs to TNF results in delayed immunosuppressive feedback effects.

title: The basics of epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
text: The origins of the mesenchymal cells involved in tissue repair and pathological processes, such as tissue fibrosis, tumor invasiveness, and metastasis, are not well understood. However, recent research suggests that epithelial-mesenchymal transitions (EMTs) may play a crucial role in the emergence of these cells. As we will discuss, processes similar to those involved in embryonic development, such as implantation, embryogenesis, and organ formation, are co-opted and distorted by chronic inflammation and neoplastic diseases. The identification of the signaling pathways that drive EMT programs during these diseases has provided new insights into the versatility of cellular phenotypes and potential therapeutic interventions.

title: Child maltreatment, other trauma exposure, and posttraumatic symptomatology among children with oppositional defiant and attention deficit hyperactivity disorders.
text: In a study examining the relationship between child psychiatric outpatient admissions and trauma exposure, four distinct groups were identified using a retrospective case-control design: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD), comorbid ADHD-ODD, and adjustment disorder controls. The study found that ODD and ADHD were associated with a history of physical or sexual maltreatment, while PTSD symptoms were most severe when ADHD and maltreatment co-occurred or when ODD and accident/illness trauma co-occurred. The association between ODD and PTSD Criterion D (hyperarousal/hypervigilance) symptoms remained significant after controlling for overlapping symptoms, while the association between ADHD and PTSD symptoms was largely due to an overlapping symptom. These findings suggest that screening for maltreatment, other trauma, and PTSD symptoms may be beneficial in preventing, treating, and researching childhood disruptive behavior disorders.

title: Exercise-induced asthma screening of elite athletes: field versus laboratory exercise challenge.
text: The purpose of this study was to compare the effectiveness of a laboratory-based exercise challenge (LBC) and a field-based exercise challenge (FBC) for screening elite athletes for exercise-induced asthma (EIA). Twenty-three elite athletes who tested positive for EIA using a field-based challenge (FBC) were compared to 23 gender and sport-matched controls (non-asthmatics) to establish normal reference values for pulmonary function tests (PFTs). Before the FBC, athletes completed a medical history questionnaire to assess EIA symptoms.
