Subgroup analysis revealed the most notable effects in patients with psoriatic arthritis, with significant improvements in all primary and secondary outcome variables. Adverse events were more common in the SSZ group, but were transient or reversible after treatment cessation.
Conclusion: The results of this study demonstrate that SSZ is more effective than placebo in treating active spondylarthropathy, particularly in patients with psoriatic arthritis. While SSZ was associated with more adverse events, the benefits of treatment outweigh the risks.

title: A randomized trial of aspirin to prevent colorectal adenomas in patients with previous colorectal cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: Animal and observational studies have suggested that regular aspirin use may decrease the risk of colorectal adenomas, which are precursors to most colorectal cancers. To investigate this association further, we conducted a randomized, double-blind clinical trial.
METHODS: We randomly assigned 635 patients with a history of colorectal cancer to receive either 325 mg of aspirin per day or a placebo. We determined the proportion of patients with adenomas, the number of recurrent adenomas, and the time to adenoma detection between randomization and subsequent colonoscopic examinations. Relative risks were adjusted for age, sex, cancer stage, the number of colonoscopic examinations, and the time to a first colonoscopy. The study was terminated early by an independent data and safety monitoring board when statistically significant results were reported during a planned interim analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 517 randomized patients had at least one colonoscopic examination a median of 12.8 months after randomization. The incidence of adenomas was significantly lower in the aspirin group (17%) compared to the placebo group (27%) (P=0.004). The mean (+/-SD) number of adenomas was also lower in the aspirin group (0.30+/-0.87) compared to the placebo group (0.49+/-0.99) (P=0.003 by the Wilcoxon test). The adjusted relative risk of any recurrent adenoma in the aspirin group was 0.65 (95% CI, 0.46-0.91). The time to the detection of a first adenoma was longer in the aspirin group (hazard ratio for the detection of a new polyp, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.43-0.94; P=0.022).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that daily aspirin use is associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of colorectal adenomas in patients with a history of colorectal cancer. These results provide further evidence of the potential benefits of aspirin in colorectal cancer prevention.

title: The Wilms tumour suppressor protein WT1 (+KTS isoform) binds alpha-actinin 1 mRNA via its zinc-finger domain.
text: Mutations in the WT1 gene are associated with a range of developmental disorders affecting the urinary and reproductive systems, as well as an increased risk of certain cancers, including Wilms tumor, acute myeloid leukemia, and breast and prostate cancers. The WT1 protein belongs to the early growth response family of zinc-finger transcription factors, and has a unique feature in which an alternatively spliced tripeptide insertion (KTS) between zinc fingers 3 and 4 modulates its transcriptional activity. While -KTS isoforms bind DNA and regulate gene expression, +KTS isoforms have reduced DNA binding affinity and interact with splice factors and RNA in vitro and in vivo. Despite efforts to identify candidate DNA targets, the physiological mRNA targets of WT1 remain to be fully characterized. To investigate the molecular interactions of WT1, we examined the distribution of WT1 in ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes in nuclear extracts from M15 cells, a mouse mesonephric fetal kidney cell line. We found that WT1 co-fractionated with the splice factor PSF in large RNP particles greater than or equal to 2 megadaltons. Additionally, we found that PSF co-immunoprecipitated with WT1, suggesting a functional interaction between these two multifunctional proteins. Using a yeast three-hybrid library constructed from the co-immunoprecipitated RNA, we identified the alpha-actinin 1 (ACTN1) mRNA as a likely physiological target of WT1. In vitro band shift assays confirmed the ability of the WT1 zinc-finger domain (+KTS) to bind to this sequence. ACTN1 is the first identified physiological target of WT1, highlighting the importance of this protein in regulating gene expression.

title: How safe are psychiatric medications after a voluntary overdose?
text:
The study suggests that psychiatric medications, particularly benzodiazepines, new antidepressants, and antipsychotics, are relatively safe when used for self-poisoning. The study's findings indicate that patients with mental illnesses who are under-treated are at a higher risk of suicide. The study concludes that it is better to prescribe psychiatric medications, particularly the new ones, rather than withhold them due to an exaggerated fear of a lethal overdose.
Here is a rewritten version of the text with some changes to improve readability and clarity:
This study examined the use of psychiatric medications in suicide attempts and their potential lethality. The study analyzed 563 suicide attempts in a general hospital in Madrid between 1996 and 1998, finding that 81% of the attempts involved medication overdose. The most commonly used medications were benzodiazepines (65%), followed by new antidepressants (11%), tricyclic antidepressants (10%), and antipsychotics (8%). The study found that patients who overdosed on these medications were more likely to have been prescribed them. However, the study also found that all patients who overdosed on psychiatric medications recovered well and were discharged without any sequelae.
The study suggests that psychiatric medications, particularly benzodiazepines, new antidepressants, and antipsychotics, are relatively safe when used for self-poisoning. The study's findings indicate that patients with mental illnesses who are under-treated are at a higher risk of suicide. The study concludes that it is better to prescribe psychiatric medications, particularly the new ones, rather than withhold them due to an exaggerated fear of a lethal overdose.

title: Health benefits, costs, and cost-effectiveness of earlier eligibility for adult antiretroviral therapy and expanded treatment coverage: a combined analysis of 12 mathematical models.
text:
Background:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has recently revised its guidelines for Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) initiation for HIV-positive individuals, recommending initiation for those with CD4 cell counts ≤500 cells/µL, a higher threshold than the previous recommendation of CD4 counts ≤350 cells/µL. As a result, country decision makers must now consider whether to expand ART eligibility beyond the previous threshold.
Methods:
To evaluate the potential health impact, costs, and cost-effectiveness of different adult ART eligibility criteria, we used multiple independent mathematical models in four settings: South Africa, Zambia, India, and Vietnam. We projected the results over 20 years and analyzed the costs from a health system perspective. We calculated the incremental cost per Disability-Adjusted Life Year (DALY) averted to compare competing strategies, and considered strategies to be 'very cost-effective' if the cost per DALY was less than the country's per capita gross domestic product (GDP), and 'cost-effective' if the cost per DALY was less than three times per capita GDP.
Findings:
Our findings indicate that expanding ART eligibility to individuals with CD4 cell counts ≤500 cells/µL is cost-effective in all four settings, with the cost per DALY averted ranging from $237 to $1691 in South Africa, $749 in Zambia, $131 to $241 in India, and $290 in Vietnam. Expanding treatment coverage in the general population was also found to be cost-effective. In concentrated epidemics, expanded access among key populations was also cost-effective.
Interpretation:
Our findings suggest that expanding ART eligibility to individuals with CD4 cell counts ≤500 cells/µL is a cost-effective strategy in low- and middle-income settings. However, these findings should be revisited as further information becomes available. Scaling-up ART should be considered as one of the high-priority health interventions competing for health budgets.
Funding:
The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and World Health Organization provided funding for this study.

title: Chronic daily headache: long-term prognosis following inpatient treatment with repetitive IV DHE.
text: In this study, we retrospectively analyzed the long-term outcomes of 50 patients with chronic daily headache (CDH) who were admitted to an inpatient headache program. The patients had been detoxified, received repetitive intravenous dihydroergotamine (IV DHE) and prophylactic medications, and became headache-free on this regimen. At the time of admission, 37 patients had transformed migraine (TM), 12 had new daily persistent headache (NDPH), and 1 had chronic tension-type headache. The patients had abused various substances, including caffeine, acetaminophen, aspirin, ibuprofen, narcotics, and ergotamine. Twenty patients were using preventive medication at the time of admission. Follow-up evaluations were conducted at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after discharge. At 3 months, 44% of the patients had an excellent or good result, and 28% had a fair result. At 24 months, 59% of the patients had a good or excellent result, and 28% had a fair result. Five patients were overusing analgesics, and four of them were doing poorly.

title: Survival in a case of massive paraquat ingestion.
text: Paraquat exposure can result in fatal outcomes, primarily due to gastrointestinal lesions, shock, and acute respiratory distress syndrome, as well as the progressive development of pulmonary fibrosis associated with refractory hypoxemia. We present a case of suicidal paraquat ingestion in a 59-year-old male, where most poor prognostic indicators were observed. Treatment involved early digestive decontamination and hemodialysis, followed by antioxidant therapy, including the administration of deferoxamine (100 mg/kg over 24 hours) and a continuous infusion of acetylcysteine (300 mg/kg/day for 3 weeks). Although the patient only experienced nonoliguric acute renal failure, mild liver test abnormalities, and a CO transfer factor impairment without respiratory symptoms, renal and hepatic disturbances resolved within 1 month, while CO transfer factor remained altered 14 months later. This observation suggests that early administration of antioxidant therapy, including deferoxamine and acetylcysteine, in combination with measures to prevent digestive absorption or enhance elimination, may limit systemic toxicity in potentially fatal paraquat poisoning.

title: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase is a cytosolic DNA sensor that activates the type I interferon pathway.
text: The presence of DNA in the cytoplasm of mammalian cells serves as a potent danger signal, triggering host immune responses such as the production of type I interferons. Specifically, cytosolic DNA induces interferons through the production of cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cyclic GMP-AMP, or cGAMP), which interacts with and activates the adaptor protein STING. Through the use of biochemical fractionation and quantitative mass spectrometry, we identified a cGAMP synthase (cGAS), a member of the nucleotidyltransferase family, as a key player in this process. Overexpression of cGAS led to the activation of the transcription factor IRF3 and the induction of interferon-β in a STING-dependent manner. Conversely, knockdown of cGAS inhibited IRF3 activation and interferon-β induction in response to DNA transfection or DNA virus infection. Notably, cGAS was found to bind to DNA in the cytoplasm and catalyze cGAMP synthesis, thereby functioning as a cytosolic DNA sensor that triggers interferon production through the cGAMP signaling pathway. These findings provide insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying the host defense response to DNA and highlight the importance of cGAS in the early detection of viral infections.

title: Eating pathology, emotion regulation, and emotional overeating in obese adults with Binge Eating Disorder.
text:
Objective:
The current study aimed to investigate the relationship between emotional regulation, emotional overeating, and general eating pathology in a sample of adults with Binge Eating Disorder (BED) seeking treatment.
Methodology:
The sample consisted of 326 adults (248 women and 78 men) who were obese and met the DSM-IV-TR criteria for BED. Prior to treatment, participants completed the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), Emotional Overeating Questionnaire (EOQ), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and Eating Disorder Examination-Questionnaire (EDE-Q) as part of a comprehensive assessment battery.
Results:
Hierarchical regression analyses revealed that difficulties with emotion regulation accounted for unique variance in both emotional overeating and general eating pathology above and beyond sex and negative affect.
Discussion:
Emotion regulation may play a significant role in the maintenance of emotional overeating and eating pathology in obese adults with BED. These findings highlight the importance of addressing emotion regulation difficulties in the treatment of BED.

title: Monoallelic expression and methylation of imprinted genes in human and mouse embryonic germ cell lineages.
text: Imprinting, an epigenetic modification, leads to the monoallelic expression of certain genes, and disrupted imprinting is believed to hinder human stem cell transplantation, as studies have shown that epigenetic marks are unstable in mouse embryonic germ (EG) and embryonic stem (ES) cells. However, the imprinting of stem cells in humans has not been directly examined. Our study found that three imprinted genes, TSSC5, H19, and SNRPN, exhibit monoallelic expression in in vitro differentiated human EG-derived cells, while a fourth gene, IGF2, shows partially relaxed imprinting with a ratio ranging from 4:1 to 5:1, similar to that observed in normal somatic cells. Additionally, we found normal methylation of an imprinting control region (ICR) that regulates H19 and IGF2 imprinting, suggesting that imprinting may not be a significant epigenetic barrier to human EG cell transplantation. Furthermore, we were able to generate an in vitro mouse model of genomic imprinting by deriving EG cells from 8.5-day embryos of an interspecific cross, resulting in cells that exhibit biallelic expression and preferential expression of the parental allele after differentiation. This model will allow for the manipulation of epigenetic modifications in cultured EG cells, which may not be possible in human stem cell studies.

title: Functional in vivo interactions between JNK1 and JNK2 isoforms in obesity and insulin resistance.
text: The c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNKs) play a crucial role in regulating inflammation and insulin action in both cultured cells and whole animals. Obesity has been shown to increase total JNK activity, with JNK1 being the primary isoform involved. Interestingly, studies have revealed that JNK2 also plays a role in metabolic homeostasis, although the exact nature of this involvement has been unclear due to regulatory crosstalk between the two isoforms. To investigate the specific role of JNK2 in metabolic regulation, we generated mice with combined deletions of the Jnk1 and Jnk2 genes and examined body weight and glucose metabolism in these mutant mice. Our findings revealed that only mice lacking both Jnk1 and Jnk2 genes exhibited reduced body weight and increased insulin sensitivity, along with decreased total JNK activity and cytokine expression in liver tissue. These data suggest that JNK2 is also involved in metabolic regulation, although its function is modulated by the presence of JNK1.

title: The immunological synapse of CTL contains a secretory domain and membrane bridges.
text: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) rapidly eliminate their targets through a process that involves the formation of an immunological synapse, similar to that observed in CD4 cells. Within 5 minutes of contact between a CTL and its target cell, an adhesion ring of proteins surrounds an inner domain containing signaling molecules. Lytic granule secretion occurs in a separate domain within the adhesion ring, maintaining the organization of signaling proteins during exocytosis. As the cells separate, target cell plasma membrane markers are transferred to the CTL, as evidenced by both live and fixed cell studies. Electron microscopy reveals the formation of membrane bridges between the CTL and target cell membranes, providing a possible mechanism for this transfer.

title: Compromised intestinal epithelial barrier induces adaptive immune compensation that protects from colitis.
text: Mice lacking the junctional adhesion molecule A (JAM-A, encoded by F11r) exhibit enhanced intestinal epithelial permeability, bacterial translocation, and elevated colonic lymphocyte numbers, yet do not develop colitis. To investigate the contribution of adaptive immune compensation in response to increased intestinal epithelial permeability, we examined the susceptibility of F11r(-/-)Rag1(-/-) mice to acute colitis. While negligible contributions of adaptive immunity were observed in F11r(+/+)Rag1(-/-) mice, F11r(-/-)Rag1(-/-) mice exhibited increased microflora-dependent colitis. Elimination of T cell subsets and cytokine analyses revealed a protective role for TGF-β-producing CD4(+) T cells in F11r(-/-) mice. Additionally, loss of JAM-A resulted in elevated mucosal and serum IgA that was dependent upon CD4(+) T cells and TGF-β. Interestingly, absence of IgA in F11r(+/+)Igha(-/-) mice did not affect disease, whereas F11r(-/-)Igha(-/-) mice displayed markedly increased susceptibility to acute injury-induced colitis. These findings establish a role for adaptive immune-mediated protection from acute colitis under conditions of intestinal epithelial barrier compromise.

title: Apoptosis and chemoresistance in transgenic cancer models
text:
Despite decades of effort, multidrug resistance remains a persistent challenge in clinical oncology. Initial studies from over a decade ago demonstrated that genes encoding cellular efflux pumps can confer resistance to a wide range of unrelated anticancer drugs, even before they reach their intracellular targets. More recent research has revealed that many drugs induce a common apoptotic program, leading to speculation that mutations in this program may also contribute to multidrug resistance. However, a thorough evaluation of the role of apoptosis in drug-resistant cancer cells has been complicated by technical limitations, including the presence of unknown background mutations in patient biopsy samples and the potential for biased results from cancer cell lines.
To address these challenges, we sought to develop a more reliable and tractable model system for studying the impact of apoptosis on treatment outcome. We discuss the potential limitations of cell culture-based assays and highlight the advantages of genetically engineered mouse models. We also describe a novel transgenic mouse model that allows us to examine the effects of drug treatment on primary lymphomas with genetically defined lesions, treated at their natural site. This approach offers a more physiologically relevant system for studying drug resistance and may provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying this complex phenomenon.

title: NC-100717: a versatile RGD peptide scaffold for angiogenesis imaging.
text: Targeting the molecular pathways involved in angiogenesis holds great promise for detecting disease pathology using in vivo imaging technologies. The process of angiogenesis requires the activation and migration of endothelial cells, which are critical for the formation of new blood vessels. Endothelial cells interact with the extracellular matrix through specific interactions with a variety of cell adhesion receptors known as integrins. Peptides containing the tripeptide sequence RGD have been shown to bind with high affinity to integrins associated with angiogenesis, such as alphavbeta3 and alphavbeta5. In this study, we describe the synthesis and in vitro binding affinity of the RGD-containing peptide NC-100717 and a range of molecular probes derived from this intermediate.

title: Dose-dependent effect of statins on the incidence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery.
text:
BACKGROUND: Acute kidney injury (AKI) following cardiac surgery is associated with increased morbidity and mortality.
METHODS: We investigated whether statin treatment is associated with a lower incidence of postoperative AKI in 2,104 consecutive patients who underwent coronary artery bypass graft or valve surgery at the Minneapolis Veterans Administration Medical Center. AKI was defined as an absolute increase in serum creatinine of greater than 0.3 mg/dL or a relative increase of greater than 50% from baseline within 48 hours after surgery or requiring postoperative hemodialysis according to the AKI network criteria. Propensity scores were used to adjust for differences between the statin and no-statin treatment groups. All statins were converted to equivalent-dose simvastatin and divided at the median to construct high-dose (≥40 mg) and low-dose (<40 mg) statin groups.
RESULTS: Of the 2,104 patients, 1,435 (68%) were taking statins (638 high-dose), and 495 (24%) developed AKI (25% high-dose vs 40% low-dose vs 35% no-statin; p = 0.014). Independent predictors of AKI included estimated preoperative glomerular filtration rate (p = 0.003), diabetes mellitus (p = 0.02), valve surgery with or without coronary artery bypass graft (p = 0.024), cardiopulmonary bypass time (p = 0.001), and intraaortic balloon pump (p = 0.055). After propensity adjustment, statin treatment was not associated with postoperative AKI (odds ratio 0.79; 95% confidence interval 0.59 to 1.06; p = 0.11 for high-dose vs no-statin). After full adjustment for all independent predictors of AKI, the results did not change. Statins also had no effect on the incidence of postoperative hemodialysis (0.8% high-dose vs 1.9% low-dose vs 1% no-statin; p = 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that statin treatment is not associated with a lower incidence of AKI after cardiac surgery.

title: Comparison of allogeneic vs autologous bone marrow–derived mesenchymal stem cells delivered by transendocardial injection in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy: the POSEIDON randomized trial.
text:
The POSEIDON study compared the safety and efficacy of allogeneic and autologous mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) in patients with left ventricular (LV) dysfunction due to ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM). The study was a phase 1/2 randomized trial conducted at a US tertiary-care referral hospital between April 2, 2010, and September 14, 2011, with 13-month follow-up.
Thirty patients were enrolled in the study, with 10 LV sites per patient receiving 20 million, 100 million, or 200 million cells (in 5 patients per dose level). The primary outcome measures included the incidence of treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs) within 30 days of the procedure, as well as efficacy assessments such as the 6-minute walk test, exercise peak VO2, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ), New York Heart Association class, LV volumes, ejection fraction (EF), early enhancement defect (EED; infarct size), and sphericity index.
The results showed that within 30 days of the procedure, one patient in each group (allogeneic and autologous) experienced a treatment-emergent SAE (6.7% and 6.7%, respectively), which was less than the prespecified stopping event rate of 25%. At 1 year, there were no ventricular arrhythmia SAEs observed among allogeneic recipients compared with 4 patients (26.7%) in the autologous group (P = .10). Relative to baseline, autologous but not allogeneic MSC therapy was associated with an improvement in the 6-minute walk test and the MLHFQ score, but neither improved exercise VO2 max. Allogeneic and autologous MSCs reduced mean EED by −33.21% (95% CI, −43.61% to −22.81%; P < .001) and sphericity index but did not increase EF. Allogeneic MSCs reduced LV end-diastolic volumes, and low-dose concentration MSCs (20 million cells) produced the greatest reductions in LV volumes and increased EF.
The study found that allogeneic MSCs did not stimulate significant donor-specific alloimmune reactions. In conclusion, the study suggested that both allogeneic and autologous MSCs were safe and associated with favorable effects on patient functional capacity, quality of life, and ventricular remodeling, without significant immunologic reactions. However, the study had some limitations, such as the small sample size and the lack of a placebo control group. Further studies with larger sample sizes and more rigorous designs are needed to confirm these findings and establish the safety and efficacy of MSCs for the treatment of ICM.

title: Periosteal bone formation--a neglected determinant of bone strength.
text: Organisms with lower body masses are capable of hunting for sustenance on the undersides of branches or along sheer cliff faces without being significantly impeded by gravity. In contrast, larger organisms require rapid movement to obtain food and avoid becoming prey, which is facilitated by the lever function of long bones. These three-dimensional structures are masterful examples of biomechanical engineering, combining the seemingly contradictory properties of stiffness and flexibility, strength and lightness through their material composition and structural design. The stiffness of long bones is derived from the triple-helical structure of collagen type I, which is encrusted with hydroxyapatite crystals, providing enhanced mechanical stability and resistance to deformation.

title: Triglyceride depletion of brown adipose tissue enables analysis of mitochondrial respiratory function in permeabilized biopsies.
text: The research on mitochondrial functions in adipocytes has shown that mitochondria play a crucial role in the onset and progression of obesity and related disorders. Traditional methods for assessing mitochondrial function in brown adipose tissue (BAT) involve measuring enzyme levels or respiration in isolated mitochondria, which can be time-consuming and require significant amounts of tissue. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a novel and efficient protocol for analyzing mitochondrial respiratory states in BAT biopsies. This protocol involves depleting intracellular triglycerides followed by tissue permeabilization, which significantly reduces the amount of tissue required for analysis (approximately 17 mg wet weight). Additionally, the protocol enables the analysis of all mitochondrial respiratory states, including phosphorylation (OXPHOS), non-phosphorylation (LEAK), and uncoupled (ETS) states, as well as the use of substrates for complex I, complex II, and cytochrome c. These features validate the preparation efficiency and demonstrate mitochondrial integrity, making the protocol ideal for studying small BAT regions in human and animal models. With this protocol, we can gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that regulate mitochondrial function in health and disease, which is crucial for developing effective treatments for obesity and related disorders.

title: HES-1 preserves purified hematopoietic stem cells ex vivo and accumulates side population cells in vivo.
text: Mouse long-term hematopoietic reconstituting cells are found in the c-Kit+Sca-1+Lin- (KSL) cell population, with CD34(low/-) cells representing the most highly purified population of hematopoietic stem cells in the adult bone marrow. We have demonstrated that retrovirus-mediated transduction of CD34(low/-)c-Kit+Sca-1+Lin- (34-KSL) cells with the HES-1 gene, which encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor involved in the growth phase of neural stem cells in the embryo, preserves the long-term reconstituting activity of these cells in vitro. Additionally, we found that cells derived from the HES-1-transduced 34-KSL population produce progenies characterized by negative Hoechst dye staining, which defines the side population, and by CD34(low/-) profile in the bone marrow KSL population in each recipient mouse at ratios 3.5- and 7.8-fold those produced by non-transduced 34-KSL-derived competitor cells. Our findings suggest that HES-1 preserves the long-term reconstituting hematopoietic activity of 34-KSL stem cells ex vivo. Furthermore, up-regulation of HES-1 protein in the 34-KSL population without retrovirus transduction, that is, without unnecessary cell division, may represent a potent approach to absolute expansion of hematopoietic stem cells.

title: Measuring Absolute RNA Copy Numbers at High Temporal Resolution Reveals Transcriptome Kinetics in Development.
text: Transcript regulation is crucial for cellular function, and dysregulation can lead to disease. Despite advances in transcriptome surveillance, we lack a comprehensive understanding of transcript dynamics, which hinders quantitative biology. This is particularly evident in embryonic development, where rapid changes in gene expression determine cell fate decisions. By employing ultra-high-frequency sampling and absolute normalization of sequence reads, we have generated detailed gene expression trajectories in absolute transcript numbers during the first 8 weeks of human gestation. Our findings reveal that transcript kinetics vary by eight orders of magnitude during this period. By grouping genes based on expression dynamics, we discovered that "temporal synexpression" predicts shared gene function. Remarkably, a single parameter, the characteristic timescale, can categorize transcript kinetics globally and distinguish genes involved in development from those involved in cellular metabolism. Our analysis provides unprecedented insights into the reorganization of maternal and embryonic transcripts and revolutionizes our ability to perform quantitative biology.

title: Inflammasome activation by adenylate cyclase toxin directs Th17 responses and protection against Bordetella pertussis.
text:
The inflammasome plays a crucial role in the immune response to infection, particularly in the production of interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). While it is known that inflammasome-mediated IL-1β production is involved in the development of autoinflammatory diseases, its role in promoting adaptive immunity to infection has not been well-studied. In this article, we investigate the role of inflammasome-mediated IL-1β in promoting T cell responses to infection.
Using a murine respiratory challenge model, we found that the course of Bordetella pertussis infection was significantly exacerbated in mice lacking the interleukin-1 receptor type I (IL-1R1). We discovered that the bacterial toxin adenylate cyclase toxin (CyaA) induced robust IL-1β production by dendritic cells through activation of the caspase-1-containing NALP3 inflammasome complex. Interestingly, we found that CyaA-mediated activation of caspase-1 was not dependent on adenylate cyclase enzyme activity but was dependent on the pore-forming capacity of CyaA.
Furthermore, we observed that CyaA promoted the induction of antigen-specific T helper 17 (Th17) cells in wild-type mice but not in IL-1R1-deficient mice. Additionally, the bacterial load was enhanced in IL-17-defective mice. Our findings suggest that CyaA promotes IL-1β-mediated Th17 cells, which contribute to the clearance of the bacteria from the respiratory tract.
Our study demonstrates that the inflammasome plays a critical role in promoting adaptive immunity to infection by polarizing T cell responses towards the Th17 subtype. These findings have important implications for our understanding of the mechanisms of infection and immunity, and may lead to the development of new strategies for the treatment of infectious diseases.

title: Infection and apoptosis as a combined inflammatory trigger.
text: While research has focused extensively on the phagocytosis of microbial pathogens and non-inflammatory phagocytosis of apoptotic cells, the consequences of innate immune recognition of host cells undergoing apoptosis as a direct result of infection remain unclear. In this scenario, the innate immune system encounters a complex mix of signals, including those from apoptotic cells and the infecting pathogen. Activation of nuclear receptors has been implicated in the response to apoptotic cells, while Toll-like receptors are the prototypical inflammatory receptors involved in infection. When these signals intersect, a unique set of events unfolds, beginning with the repression of a subset of inflammatory genes and culminating in the induction of a T helper-17 adaptive immune response. This response is optimally suited for eliminating the infecting pathogen and repairing the damage caused to host tissue during infection.

title: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia with t(14;19)(q32;q13) is characterized by atypical morphologic and immunophenotypic features and distinctive genetic features.
text: The t(14;19)(q32;q13) cytogenetic abnormality, involving the IGH@ and BCL3 loci, is a rare occurrence in B-cell malignancies, specifically chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL). We analyzed the clinicopathologic, cytogenetic, and molecular genetic characteristics of 14 cases of CLL/SLL with this abnormality. All patients (10 men and 4 women) had lymphocytosis, and 10 had lymphadenopathy. The neoplastic cells in the blood and bone marrow were predominantly small, but showed cytological and immunophenotypic abnormalities. In all cases, the t(14;19) abnormality was present in the neoplastic stem cell line, and it was the sole abnormality in 4 cases. Additional cytogenetic abnormalities, such as trisomy 12 and complex karyotypes, were present in 10 cases. Fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed the IGH@/BCL3 fusion gene in all cases. The IGHV genes were unmutated in all cases, but only 7 expressed the ZAP70 protein. Seven cases preferentially used IGHV4-39. Our findings suggest that t(14;19)(q32;q13) identifies a subset of CLL/SLL with distinct clinicopathologic and genetic features. Moreover, t(14;19) may represent an early, potentially primary, genetic event.

title: Risk factors for the development of gallstone recurrence following medical dissolution. The British-Italian Gallstone Study Group.
text:
Objective: To identify risk factors for gallstone recurrence following non-surgical treatment in a multicentre cohort of post-dissolution gallstone patients.
Design: A prospective follow-up study of 163 patients with confirmed gallstone dissolution treated with bile acids or lithotripsy plus bile acids, followed up by ultrasound scans and clinical assessments at 6-monthly intervals for up to 6 years.
Setting: Six gastroenterology units in the UK and Italy.
Participants: One hundred and sixty-three patients with confirmed gallstone dissolution following non-surgical therapy (bile acids or lithotripsy plus bile acids).
Outcome Measures: Subject-related variables (sex, age, height, weight, body mass index), gallstone-related variables (number, diameter, presence of symptoms, months to complete stone clearance), treatment modalities (bile acid therapy, extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy), and follow-up related variables (weight change, use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, statins, pregnancies and/or use of oestrogens) were assessed using univariate and multivariate analysis to identify potential risk factors for gallstone recurrence.
Results: Forty-five gallstone recurrences were observed during the follow-up period. Multiple primary gallstones and length of time to achieve gallstone dissolution were the only variables associated with a significant increase in the recurrence rate. The appearance of biliary sludge during follow-up was also significantly related to the development of gallstone recurrence. Use of statins or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents did not provide protection against recurrence.
Conclusions: Patients with primary single stones are the best candidates for non-surgical treatment of gallstones, as they have a low risk of gallstone recurrence. The positive association of recurrence with biliary sludge formation and time to dissolution of primary stones suggests that impaired gallbladder motility may play a role in the pathogenesis of this condition.

title: Deletion of the developmentally essential gene ATR in adult mice leads to age-related phenotypes and stem cell loss.
text: The DNA damage response (DDR) has been implicated in various developmental abnormalities, cancers, and premature aging. Specifically, mutations in the ATR checkpoint regulator have been linked to developmental defects in both mice and humans, including pregastrulation lethality and Seckel syndrome. Our findings demonstrate that deleting ATR in adult mice leads to defects in tissue homeostasis and the rapid onset of age-related phenotypes, such as hair graying, alopecia, kyphosis, osteoporosis, thymic involution, fibrosis, and other abnormalities. Using histological and genetic analyses, we have shown that ATR deletion causes acute cellular loss in tissues where continuous cell proliferation is necessary for maintenance. Notably, thymic involution, alopecia, and hair graying in ATR-knockout mice were found to be associated with significant reductions in tissue-specific stem and progenitor cells and a decline in tissue renewal and homeostatic capacity. These results suggest that a reduction in regenerative capacity in adults due to the deletion of a developmentally essential DDR gene is sufficient to cause the premature appearance of age-related phenotypes.

title: Conventional and monocyte-derived CD11b(+) dendritic cells initiate and maintain T helper 2 cell-mediated immunity to house dust mite allergen.
text: Dendritic cells (DCs) are essential for the development of allergic airway inflammation, but it remains unclear which specific subset of DCs is responsible for this task. To investigate, we used CD64 and MAR-1 staining to separate CD11b(+) monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs) from conventional DCs (cDCs) and evaluated their antigen uptake, migration, and presentation abilities in response to inhaled house dust mite (HDM) in both lung and lymph node (LN) DCs. Our findings revealed that mainly CD11b(+) cDCs, but not CD103(+) cDCs, induced T helper 2 (Th2) cell immunity in HDM-specific T cells in vitro and asthma in vivo. Interestingly, studies in Flt3l(-/-) mice, which lack all cDCs, showed that moDCs were also capable of inducing Th2 cell-mediated immunity, but only when high-dose HDM was administered. Our results indicate that migratory CD11b(+) cDCs are the primary subset responsible for inducing Th2 cell-mediated immunity in the LN, while moDCs play a key role in orchestrating allergic inflammation in the lung through the production of proinflammatory chemokines and allergen presentation.

title: Interplay between the dividing cell and its neighbors regulates adherens junction formation during cytokinesis in epithelial tissue.
text: The formation of adherens junctions (AJs) during cell division is largely unexplored. Our study reveals that AJ formation is closely linked to cytokinesis and involves an intricate interplay between the dividing cell and its neighboring cells. During the contraction of the cytokinetic ring, neighboring cells accumulate Myosin II and generate the necessary cortical tension to establish the initial geometry of the daughter cell interface. However, the neighboring cell membranes hinder AJ formation. As the midbody forms and the neighboring cells withdraw, Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization oriented by the midbody maintains AJ geometry and regulates AJ final length and the arrangement of epithelial cells during division. We propose that cytokinesis in epithelia is a multicellular process that involves the cooperative actions of the dividing cell and its neighbors, resulting in a two-tiered mechanism that spatially and temporally controls AJ formation while maintaining tissue cohesiveness.

title: Cancer stem cells in solid tumours: accumulating evidence and unresolved questions
text: Solid tumors pose a significant cancer burden and represent a major challenge in cancer treatment. The cancer stem cell (CSC) hypothesis offers a promising explanation for the therapeutic resistance and dormant behavior exhibited by many of these tumors. Emerging evidence suggests that various solid tumors are organized in a hierarchical manner, sustained by a distinct subpopulation of CSCs. Recent studies in mouse models of epithelial tumorigenesis have provided direct evidence for the CSC hypothesis, although alternative models of tumor heterogeneity also exist. The clinical relevance of CSCs remains a crucial question, but initial findings suggest that targeting these cells may be a viable strategy.

title: The structure of the follistatin:activin complex reveals antagonism of both type I and type II receptor binding.
text: TGF-beta ligands stimulate a wide range of cellular responses by signaling through both Type I and Type II receptors. However, the activity of these ligands can be regulated by antagonists, such as follistatin, which bind to the ligand and prevent it from interacting with its receptors. In this study, we have determined the structure of activin A, a TGF-beta ligand, complexed with the high-affinity follistatin antagonist. Our findings reveal that two follistatin molecules encircle activin, neutralizing one-third of its residues and receptor binding sites. Previous studies suggested that Type I receptor binding would not be affected by follistatin, but our crystal structure shows that the N-terminal domain of follistatin has an unexpected fold that mimics a universal Type I receptor motif, occupying the receptor binding site. The formation of follistatin:BMP:Type I receptor complexes can be explained by the stoichiometric and geometric arrangement of the activin:follistatin complex. The mode of ligand binding by follistatin has important implications for its ability to neutralize homodimeric and heterodimeric ligands of this growth factor family.

title: The activity of siRNA in mammalian cells is related to structural target accessibility: a comparison with antisense oligonucleotides.
text: The biological activity of siRNA is influenced by local characteristics of the target RNA, including local RNA folding. In this study, we investigated the relationship between local target accessibility and the extent of inhibition of the target gene by siRNA. We used a computational approach to assess target accessibility and chose two sites of ICAM-1 mRNA predicted to be accessible motifs and one site predicted to adopt an inaccessible structure to test siRNA constructs for suppression of ICAM-1 gene expression in ECV304 cells. Our results showed that the local target-dependent effectiveness of siRNA was significantly different from that of antisense oligonucleotides (asON). The concentration dependency of siRNA-mediated suppression indicated a >1000-fold difference between active siRNAs (IC50 approximately 0.2-0.5 nM) and an inactive siRNA (IC50 > or = 1 microM). The extremely high activity of the siRNA si2B (IC50 = 0.24 nM) suggests that not all siRNAs shown to be active at usual concentrations of >10-100 nM belong to this highly active species. Our findings suggest an approach to assess target accessibility for siRNA and support the design of active siRNA constructs. This approach can be automated, work at high throughput, and is open to include additional parameters relevant to the biological activity of siRNA.

title: Rapid accumulation of mutations during seed-to-seed propagation of mismatch-repair-defective Arabidopsis.
text: During the numerous cell divisions that occur before the formation of plant gametes, their apical-meristem and floral antecedents are constantly exposed to both endogenous and environmental mutagenic threats. Although some deleterious recessive mutations may be eliminated during the growth of haploid gametophytes and functionally haploid early embryos ("haplosufficiency quality-checking"), the diversity of plant genome-maintenance systems suggests that quality control is aggressive during prior diploid growth. To test this hypothesis in Arabidopsis, we propagated 36 MMR-defective (Atmsh2-1) lines in parallel with 36 wild-type lines. The Atmsh2-1 lines quickly accumulated a wide range of mutations, with fifth-generation (G5) plants showing abnormalities in morphology and development, fertility, germination efficiency, seed/silique development, and seed set. In contrast, only two Atmsh2-1 lines appeared normal at G5, while all 36 wild-type lines were normal. Analyses of insertion/deletion mutations at six repeat-sequence (microsatellite) loci revealed that each Atmsh2-1 line had evolved its own unique "fingerprint," resulting from as many as 10 microsatellite mutations in a single line. These findings demonstrate that MMR during diploid growth is essential for plant genomic integrity.

title: Archaeal chromatin and transcription.
text: Archaea have a diverse array of sequence-independent DNA binding proteins that suggest the evolution of multiple, sometimes overlapping and interchangeable solutions to the challenge of compacting genomes. Some of these proteins undergo post-translational modifications, such as lysine acetylation or methylation, which may be analogous to the histone modifications that regulate eukaryotic chromatin structure and transcription. Archaeal transcription initiation is most similar to the eukaryotic RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) system, but Archaea lack homologues of the multisubunit complexes that remodel eukaryotic chromatin and activate RNAPII initiation. Instead, they have sequence-specific regulators that repress and possibly activate archaeal transcription through mechanisms similar to the bacterial paradigm of regulating promoter binding by RNAP. Repressors compete with archaeal TATA-box binding protein (TBP) and TFB for the TATA-box and TFB-recognition elements (BRE) of the archaeal promoter, or with archaeal RNAP for the site of transcription initiation. Transcript-specific regulation by repressors binding to sites of transcript initiation is consistent with these sites having little sequence conservation. However, most Archaea have only one TBP and/or TFB that must therefore bind to similar TATA-box and BRE sequences upstream of most genes. Repressors that function by competing with TBP and/or TFB binding must also make additional contacts with transcript-specific regulatory sites adjacent or remote from the TATA-box/BRE region. The fate of the archaeal TBP and TFB following transcription initiation remains unclear, but based on functional homology with their eukaryotic RNAPII-system counterparts, archaeal TBP and possibly also TFB should remain bound to the TATA-box/BRE region after transcription initiation. However, this seems unlikely as it might limit repressor competition at this site to only the first round of transcription initiation.

title: Temporal segregation of 4-1BB versus CD28-mediated costimulation: 4-1BB ligand influences T cell numbers late in the primary response and regulates the size of the T cell memory response following influenza infection.
text: In this report, we demonstrate that CD28-deficient mice exhibit a severe impairment in the initial expansion of D(b)/NP366-374-specific CD8 T cells in response to influenza virus infection, whereas 4-1BB ligand (4-1BBL)-deficient mice show no defect in primary T cell expansion to influenza virus. In contrast, 4-1BBL-deficient mice exhibit a decrease in D(b)/NP366-374-specific T cells later in the primary response. Upon secondary challenge with influenza virus, 4-1BBL-deficient mice show a decrease in the number of D(b)/NP366-374-specific T cells compared to wild-type mice, resulting in a reduction of the CD8 T cell expansion during the in vivo secondary response. This is accompanied by a concomitant reduction of CTL effector function. In contrast, Ab responses and secondary CD4 T cell responses to influenza are unaffected by 4-1BBL deficiency. These findings suggest that CD28 is critical for initial T cell expansion, while 4-1BB/4-1BBL signaling affects T cell numbers later in the response and is essential for the survival and/or responsiveness of the memory CD8 T cell pool.

title: Functional role of high-affinity anandamide transport, as revealed by selective inhibition.
text: Anandamide, an endogenous ligand for central cannabinoid receptors, is released from neurons upon depolarization and rapidly deactivated. The mechanisms of anandamide inactivation are not fully understood, but it is believed to occur through transport into cells or enzymatic hydrolysis. The compound N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)arachidonylamide (AM404) was shown to inhibit the accumulation of anandamide in rat neurons and astrocytes in vitro, suggesting that this accumulation is mediated by carrier-mediated transport. Although AM404 did not activate cannabinoid receptors or inhibit anandamide hydrolysis, it enhanced receptor-mediated anandamide responses in vitro and in vivo. These findings suggest that carrier-mediated transport may play a crucial role in terminating the biological effects of anandamide, and could potentially be targeted for therapeutic purposes.

title: Silibinin inhibits the invasion of IL-6-stimulated colon cancer cells via selective JNK/AP-1/MMP-2 modulation in vitro.
text: Silibinin, a flavonoid with antihepatotoxic and pleiotropic anticancer properties, was investigated for its ability to inhibit cell invasion in IL-6-stimulated LoVo colon cancer cells. This study demonstrated that silibinin down-regulated matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) expression via attenuation of activator protein-1 (AP-1) binding activity. Western blot analysis revealed that silibinin treatment reduced MMP-2 protein expression by 1.6- or 1.7-fold compared to the control. Similar results were observed in zymography and confocal microscopy. Furthermore, pretreatment with silibinin abolished the binding activity of AP-1 and MMP-2 promoter activity via AP-1 binding, as demonstrated by EMSA and luciferase assay. Additionally, a [(3)H]-thymidine incorporation proliferation assay and cell migration assay showed that silibinin inhibited IL-6-stimulated LoVo cell proliferation and invasion. These findings suggest that silibinin inhibits LoVo cell invasion by reducing MMP-2 presentation through the attenuation of AP-1 binding activity, providing a novel antimetastatic application for silibinin in colon cancer chemoprevention.

title: Immigration cohorts and residential overcrowding in southern California
text: To what extent do immigrants reduce their high rates of residential overcrowding as they spend more time in the United States? This question is addressed by using a "double cohort" method that examines birth cohorts within immigration cohorts. This approach allows for the separation of duration effects from aging effects as cohorts progress through different life stages, during which family sizes may be expanding or contracting. The analysis reveals that cohort trends differ significantly from the cross-sectional pattern observed at a single point in time. Income growth among cohorts is found to contribute substantially to the decline in overcrowding over time. However, cohort trends among Hispanic immigrants diverge from those among other immigrants, indicating a less pronounced decrease in overcrowding and even small increases in certain age ranges.

title: Expression of green fluorescent protein in the ureteric bud of transgenic mice: a new tool for the analysis of ureteric bud morphogenesis.
text: The development and branching of the ureteric bud is a complex process that ultimately determines the organization of the collecting duct system and the number of nephrons in the metanephric kidney. While progress has been made in identifying the genes involved in this process, the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying ureteric bud morphogenesis remain poorly understood. To address these questions, we generated transgenic mice in which a green fluorescent protein (GFP) is expressed in the ureteric bud under the control of the Hoxb7 promoter. In these mice, GFP is expressed in every branch of the ureteric bud throughout renal development and in its derivative epithelia in the adult kidney. The ability to visualize GFP fluorescence in living tissue allows for the dynamic study of ureteric bud growth and branching over several days in cultured kidneys using confocal microscopy. This powerful tool enables the investigation of normal ureteric bud morphogenesis patterns and the response of the bud to growth factors, matrix elements, and other regulatory agents.

title: Biological properties of herpes simplex virus 2 replication-defective mutant strains in a murine nasal infection model.
text: In this study, we used a mouse nasal model of Herpes Simplex Virus 2 (HSV-2) infection to investigate the biological properties of wild-type (wt), TK-negative, and replication-defective strains of the virus in vivo. We found that the wt virus caused lethal encephalitis in mice at high doses, while lower doses failed to establish latent infection in neurons of the trigeminal ganglia. In contrast, the TK-negative mutant virus replicated in nasal tissue but showed limited replication in the trigeminal ganglia. The replication-defective mutant virus did not replicate in nasal tissue or persist at the inoculation site or in the trigeminal ganglia. However, inoculation of mice with these mutant viruses at distant sites reduced the acute replication and latent infection of the wt virus following intranasal challenge. This infection model provides a useful system for studying the properties of HSV-2 strains and demonstrates that replication-defective mutant strains do not persist at sites of inoculation or in sensory ganglia but can induce immune protection that reduces the latent viral load of a challenge virus.

title: The sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor agonist FTY720 modulates dendritic cell trafficking in vivo.
text: The investigational drug FTY720 is currently undergoing Phase III clinical trials for the prevention of organ rejection. FTY720 works by binding to the G protein-coupled sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1PR1) on immune cells, specifically lymphocytes, which inhibits their migration to inflammatory sites. However, the impact of FTY720 on dendritic cell (DC) trafficking has not been evaluated. In this study, we found that murine DCs express all five subtypes of the S1PR receptor (S1PR1-5). Administration of FTY720 to mice resulted in a significant reduction in circulating T and B cells within 24 hours, but not in blood-borne DCs, which were increased for up to 96 hours. Additionally, the numbers of adoptively transferred, fluorochrome-labeled syngeneic or allogeneic DCs in the blood were increased in FTY720-treated animals, while donor-derived DCs and allostimulatory activity for host naïve T cells within the spleen were reduced. Administration of the selective S1PR1 agonist SEW2871 significantly enhanced circulating DC numbers. Flow analysis revealed that the expression of CD11b, CD31/PECAM-1, CD54/ICAM-1, and CCR7 on blood-borne DCs was downregulated following FTY720 administration. Furthermore, transendothelial migration of FTY720-P-treated immature DCs to the CCR7 ligand CCL19 was reduced. These findings suggest that modulation of DC trafficking by FTY720 may contribute to its immunosuppressive effects.

title: Sustained survivin expression from OX40 costimulatory signals drives T cell clonal expansion.
text: The sustained activation of the T cell receptor (TCR) and costimulatory molecules is believed to be essential for generating large numbers of effector T cells. Our research has shown that Survivin, a protein involved in cell survival, is regulated in peripheral T cells through OX40 cosignaling, which leads to sustained activation of the PI3K and PKB pathways. Survivin is induced by OX40 signaling independent of mitotic progression in late G1 phase, and its blockade leads to suppression of T cell division and induction of apoptosis. Interestingly, Survivin expression alone is sufficient to restore proliferation and prevent apoptosis in costimulation-deficient T cells, and can even rescue T cell expansion in vivo. This suggests that sustained Survivin expression from costimulatory signaling maintains T cell division over time and regulates the extent of clonal expansion. However, Bcl-2 family proteins are also required for T cell survival after the phase of active division, highlighting the complex interplay between different signaling pathways in T cell homeostasis.

title: The Combination of Exercise and Respiratory Training Improves Respiratory Muscle Function in Pulmonary Hypertension
text: In this study, we aimed to investigate the impact of exercise and respiratory training on respiratory muscle strength and 6-min walking distance (6MWD) in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). We included seven PAH patients (four women) with a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 45 ± 11 mmHg and median World Health Organization (WHO) functional class of 3.1 ± 0.4, with either idiopathic or associated PAH. The patients underwent three weeks of in-hospital exercise and respiratory training, which was continued at home for another 12 weeks, while their medication remained constant. Respiratory muscle function was assessed using twitch mouth pressure (TwPmo) during nonvolitional supramaximal magnetic phrenic nerve stimulation, and 6MWD was measured at baseline and after 3 and 15 weeks. Our results showed that both TwPmo (+0.41 ± 0.34 kPa, +56 ± 39%) and 6MWD (+81 ± 30 m, +20 ± 9%) significantly increased between baseline and the final assessment (pairwise comparison: p = 0.012/<0.001; RM-ANOVA considering I, II, III: p = 0.037/<0.001). These findings suggest that exercise and respiratory training may be an effective adjunct to medical therapy in improving respiratory muscle strength and exercise capacity in PAH patients. Future randomized, controlled trials should be carried out to further investigate these findings.

title: Dual role of the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis in the development of autoimmune myocarditis: induction by IL-12 and protection by IFN-gamma.
text: The interplay between IL-12 and IFN-gamma plays a crucial role in the development of autoimmune diseases, including myocarditis. Our study investigated the role of the IL-12/IFN-gamma (Th1) axis in the development of autoimmune myocarditis. We found that IL-12-deficient mice on a susceptible background were resistant to myocarditis, while IFN-gamma-deficient mice developed fatal autoimmune disease. Interestingly, blocking IL-4R signaling did not confer susceptibility to myocarditis in IL-12-deficient mice, suggesting that IL-12 triggers autoimmunity through a mechanism independent of IFN-gamma and IL-4. Our findings indicate that the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis is a double-edged sword in the development of autoimmune myocarditis, as IL-12 mediates disease through the induction and expansion of Th1-type cells, while IFN-gamma production from these cells limits disease progression.

title: Somatic and Germline Diversification of a Putative Immunoreceptor within One Phylum: Dscam in Arthropods.
text:
Arthropod Dscam, a homologue of the human Down Syndrome cell adhesion molecule, is a receptor utilized by both the nervous and immune systems. Unlike in vertebrates, evolutionary pressures have resulted in a vast diversity of Dscam isoforms in arthropods, which play a crucial role in specifying neuronal identity during nervous system differentiation. This chapter examines the different modes of Dscam diversification in the context of arthropod evolution and its immune system, where its role is still a subject of controversy.
In insects and crustaceans, the single Dscam gene undergoes mutually exclusive alternative splicing, resulting in over 10,000 isoforms. In more basal arthropods, such as centipedes, Dscam diversity is generated through a combination of many germline genes (over 80) with the possibility of alternative splicing affecting only one exon cluster in about half of these genes. In even more basal arthropods, such as chelicerates, no splicing possibility is detected, but there are dozens of germline Dscam genes. Compared to controlling the expression of multiple germline genes, the somatic mutually alternative splicing within a single gene may offer a simplified way of expressing a large Dscam repertoire.
Expressed on the surface of hemocytes, Dscam acts as a phagocytic receptor and is also found in solution. Further research is needed to fully understand its binding to pathogens, its role in phagocytosis, its potential role in specifying hemocyte identity, its expression kinetics, and the regulation of its RNA splicing to elucidate how its diversity is linked to immunity.

title: Epidemiology, health-related quality of life and economic burden of binge eating disorder: a systematic literature review
text: Objective: To conduct a systematic review of the epidemiology, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and economic burden of binge eating disorder (BED). Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted using Medline, Embase, PsycINFO, PsycARTICLES, Academic Search Complete, CINAHL Plus, Business Source Premier, and Cochrane Library. The search included English-language articles published between 2009 and 2013, and the epidemiology data were limited to studies published during this time period. The included studies were assessed for quality, and the data on HRQoL and economic burden were extracted and analyzed. Results: Forty-nine articles were included in the review, with data on epidemiology reported in 31 studies, HRQoL burden in 16 studies, and economic burden in 7 studies. The lifetime prevalence of BED in the general population was found to be 1.1-1.9%, according to the 4th Edition of The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV). BED was associated with significant impairment in aspects of HRQoL, including both physical and mental health, and was related to increased healthcare utilization and costs. The annual direct healthcare costs per BED patient ranged between $2,372 and $3,731. Conclusions: BED is a serious eating disorder that significantly impairs HRQoL and is associated with increased healthcare utilization and costs. Further research is needed to better understand the long-term HRQoL and economic burden of BED.

title: Subcellular steroid/nuclear receptor dynamics.
text: Steroid hormones, thyroid hormones, retinoic acids, and vitamin D bind to their receptors, now referred to as steroid/nuclear receptors, which are ligand-dependent transcription factors. These receptors can be divided into three categories based on their unliganded distribution: those primarily in the nucleus, those in the cytoplasm, and those with mixed cytoplasmic and nuclear distributions. However, upon ligand binding, the receptors undergo almost complete nuclear translocation. The addition of a ligand leads to the recruitment of cofactors and the redistribution of receptor complexes in the nucleus, potentially involving more complex events than simple DNA binding sites for transcription. Using green fluorescent protein (GFP) and its color variants, the subcellular distribution of steroid/nuclear receptors has been found to be more dynamic than previously thought, with some receptors shuttling between the cytoplasm and nucleus. By imaging and localizing protein activities and interactions of steroid/nuclear receptors in a single cell, a more complete understanding of their function can be gained.

title: EMT, the cytoskeleton, and cancer cell invasion
text: The metastatic process, or the spread of cancer cells throughout the body to form secondary tumors at distant sites, requires cancer cells to leave the primary tumor and acquire migratory and invasive capabilities. This process, known as epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), involves changes in the adhesive properties of cancer cells, as well as the development of migratory and invasive properties through a dramatic reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and the formation of membrane protrusions necessary for invasive growth. Despite significant research, the molecular mechanisms underlying these cellular changes are still poorly understood, and the various migratory organelles, including lamellipodia, filopodia, invadopodia, and podosomes, require further functional and molecular characterization. Additionally, there is a lack of direct experimental evidence linking the formation of migratory membrane protrusions to the process of EMT and tumor metastasis. In this review, we have summarized recent insights into the molecular processes and players involved in EMT on one side and the formation of invasive membrane protrusions on the other side.

title: Different response of human glioma tumor-initiating cells to epidermal growth factor receptor kinase inhibitors.
text: Given the crucial role of cancer stem cells (CSCs), specifically tumor-initiating cells (TICs), in the development, progression, and recurrence of various tumors, we investigated the in vitro sensitivity of human glioma TICs to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) kinase inhibitors (erlotinib and gefitinib). To achieve this, we isolated and characterized cells from seven glioblastomas (GBM 1-7) using neural stem cell permissive conditions, which confirmed that these cultures were enriched in TICs. Subsequently, TIC cultures were exposed to increasing concentrations of erlotinib and gefitinib, and their survival was evaluated after 1-4 days. Our findings revealed a time- and concentration-dependent cell death response in most cases, with GBM 2 displaying complete resistance to both drugs, and GBM 7 showing sensitivity only at the highest concentrations tested. Using a radioligand binding assay, we demonstrated that all GBM TICs express EGFR. Notably, erlotinib and gefitinib inhibited EGFR and ERK1/2 phosphorylation/activation in all GBMs, regardless of the antiproliferative response observed. However, under basal conditions, GBM 2 exhibited high Akt phosphorylation that was insensitive to both drugs, whereas GBM 7 was insensitive to gefitinib, and Akt inactivation occurred only at the highest erlotinib concentration tested, indicating a precise relationship between the antiproliferative effects of the drug and Akt inhibition. Of interest, down-regulation of phosphatase and tensin homolog expression was observed in GBM 2, which may contribute to its insensitivity to the drugs. In conclusion, our findings suggest that glioma TICs are responsive to anti-EGFR drugs, but the expression of phosphatase and tensin homolog and Akt inhibition are crucial for such an effect.

title: Structural features of the interaction of the 3'-untranslated region of mRNA containing exosomal RNA-specific motifs with YB-1, a potential mediator of mRNA sorting.
text: In our previous work, we demonstrated that YB-1 is the only protein in the cytoplasmic (S100) extract of HEK293 cells that specifically interacts with RNA hairpins containing specific motifs, which are often found in exosomal RNA and proposed to target RNAs into exosomes. Here, we investigated the interactions between YB-1 and a fragment of the 3'-untranslated region (UTR) of septin 14 mRNA (SEPT14 RNA), which contains all three motifs. We found that YB-1 can bind to SEPT14 RNA in a cooperative manner, with up to 5 moles of protein per mole of RNA, and that the presence of the motifs 1 and 2 in the RNA hairpin competes with SEPT14 RNA for binding to YB-1, while motif 3 is less competitive. Our findings suggest that the specific environments of these motifs contribute significantly to the YB-1 binding. We also analyzed the environments of motifs 1-3 in the 3' UTRs of HEK293 cell mRNAs gained from RNA-seq data and found that the primary binding sites of YB-1 are hairpins containing some part of the motif along with its specific surroundings. We derived the consensus sequences of these hairpins and conclude that our findings provide a new understanding of the structural basis of the interactions between YB-1 and mRNAs carrying these motifs.

title: Periodic screening for breast cancer: the HIP Randomized Controlled Trial. Health Insurance Plan.
text: This paper presents the findings of the first breast cancer screening trial, initiated in December 1963, to evaluate the effectiveness of screening. Participants were women aged 40-64 years enrolled in the Health Insurance Plan (HIP) of Greater New York, randomly assigned to study or control groups. Women in the study group underwent screening, including film mammography (cephalocaudal and lateral views of each breast) and clinical breast examination, every year for three years. The study compared breast cancer incidence and mortality between the study and control groups, as well as within age subgroups. By the end of 18 years, the study group had a 25% lower breast cancer mortality rate among women aged 40-49 and 50-59 at entry compared to the control group. However, the majority of this reduction occurred among women in the 40-49 age subgroup who were diagnosed with breast cancer after turning 50. The utility of screening women in their forties is therefore questionable.

title: Staphylococcus aureus infections.
text: Micrococcus, when limited in its scope and activity, can cause acute suppurative inflammation (phlegmon), but when more extensive and intense in its impact on the human body, it can lead to the most virulent forms of septicaemia and pyaemia. In a series of elegant clinical observations and laboratory studies published in 1880 and 1882, Ogston described the nature of staphylococcal disease and its role in sepsis and abscess formation. Despite being first identified over 100 years ago, Staphylococcus aureus remains a formidable pathogen in humans, with both community-acquired and hospital-acquired infections on the rise. However, the mortality rates associated with these infections have remained relatively unchanged. Treatment of these infections poses a significant challenge, and new strategies are needed to combat this persistent pathogen.

title: Structural overview of the nuclear receptor superfamily: insights into physiology and therapeutics.
text: As ligand-regulated transcription factors, nuclear hormone receptors offer a nearly ideal target for drug development, with internal pockets that bind to hydrophobic, drug-like molecules and well-characterized ligand-induced conformational changes that recruit transcriptional coregulators to promoter elements. However, the challenge lies in identifying ligands with gene-selective actions, which impact disease outcomes through a narrow subset of target genes rather than the entire gene-regulatory repertoire. Here, we summarize the concepts and progress made in the development of steroidal and nonsteroidal receptor ligands, including the use of crystal structures, high-throughput screens, and rational design approaches for identifying useful therapeutic molecules. The lack of selective receptor modulators stems from a deeper understanding of receptor interdomain communications, posttranslational modifications, and receptor-protein interactions that can be exploited for target gene selectivity.

title: Differential assembly of inwardly rectifying K+ channel subunits, Kir4.1 and Kir5.1, in brain astrocytes.
text: The inwardly rectifying potassium channel subunit Kir5.1 is highly expressed in the brain, but its precise distribution and function are still largely unknown. To investigate the distribution and properties of Kir5.1 in the brain, we compared the biochemical and immunological properties of Kir5.1 with those of its co-expressed subunit Kir4.1 in mouse brain tissue. Our results showed that brain-expressed Kir channels can be divided into at least two subsets: heteromeric Kir4.1/5.1 and homomeric Kir4.1. Heteromeric Kir4.1/5.1 was found in the neocortex and olfactory bulb, while homomeric Kir4.1 was confined to the hippocampus and thalamus. Interestingly, we did not observe any homomeric Kir5.1 expression. The expression of Kir4.1 and Kir5.1 was found to occur only in astrocytes, specifically in the membrane domains facing the pia mater and blood vessels or in the processes surrounding synapses. Additionally, we found that both Kir4.1/5.1 and Kir4.1 could be associated with PDZ domain-containing syntrophins, which may play a role in the subcellular targeting of these astrocyte Kir channels. Since heteromeric Kir4.1/5.1 and homomeric Kir4.1 have distinct ion channel properties (Tanemoto et al., 2000; Tucker et al., 2000), it is possible that these channels play differential physiological roles in the K+ -buffering action of brain astrocytes in a region-specific manner.

title: Low-grade serous ovarian cancer: a unique disease.
text: Low-grade serous carcinomas account for approximately 10% of all ovarian serous carcinomas. A substantial body of research has elucidated notable differences in the clinical and molecular features of these tumors compared to high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas. Notably, patients with low-grade serous ovarian tumors are typically diagnosed at a younger age, exhibit longer overall survival, and experience lower response rates to conventional chemotherapy. Additionally, low-grade serous ovarian carcinomas display distinct pathological and molecular characteristics when compared to high-grade serous carcinomas, yet share similarities with serous tumors of low malignant potential. This observation suggests a common pathogenic mechanism and a continuum of disease progression from serous tumors of low malignant potential to low-grade serous carcinomas. Further investigation, focusing specifically on low-grade serous carcinomas, is warranted to determine the potential benefits of utilizing alternative chemotherapeutic agents, hormonal therapies, or targeted biologic agents in the treatment of this disease.

title: Renal outcomes with different fixed-dose combination therapies in patients with hypertension at high risk for cardiovascular events (ACCOMPLISH): a prespecified secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial.
text:
Background:
The Avoiding Cardiovascular Events through Combination Therapy in Patients Living with Systolic Hypertension (ACCOMPLISH) trial demonstrated that initial antihypertensive therapy with benazepril plus amlodipine was superior to benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide in reducing cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. In this study, we investigated the effects of these drug combinations on the progression of chronic kidney disease.
Methods:
ACCOMPLISH was a double-blind, randomized trial conducted in five countries (USA, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, and Finland). A total of 11 506 patients with hypertension at high risk for cardiovascular events were randomly assigned via a central, telephone-based interactive voice response system in a 1:1 ratio to receive benazepril (20 mg) plus amlodipine (5 mg) or benazepril (20 mg) plus hydrochlorothiazide (12.5 mg). Drug doses were force-titrated to attain recommended blood pressure goals. Progression of chronic kidney disease, a prespecified endpoint, was defined as doubling of serum creatinine concentration or end-stage renal disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate <15 mL/min/1.73 m(2) or need for dialysis). Analysis was conducted using intention-to-treat (ITT) methodology. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT00170950.
Findings:
The trial was terminated early (mean follow-up 2.9 years [SD 0.4]) due to the superior efficacy of benazepril plus amlodipine compared with benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide. At trial completion, vital status was not known for 143 (1%) patients who were lost to follow-up (benazepril plus amlodipine, n=70; benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide, n=73). All randomized patients were included in the ITT analysis. There were 113 (2.0%) events of chronic kidney disease progression in the benazepril plus amlodipine group compared with 215 (3.7%) in the benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide group (HR 0.52, 0.41-0.65, p<0.0001). The most common adverse event in patients with chronic kidney disease was peripheral oedema (benazepril plus amlodipine, 189 of 561, 33.7%; benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide, 85 of 532, 16.0%). In contrast, angio-oedema was more frequent in the benazepril plus amlodipine group than in the benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide group in patients without chronic kidney disease. In addition, dizziness, hypokalaemia, and hypotension were more common in the benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide group than in the benazepril plus amlodipine group in patients without chronic kidney disease.
Interpretation:
Our findings suggest that initial antihypertensive treatment with benazepril plus amlodipine should be considered as the preferred option over benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide, as it slows the progression of nephropathy to a greater extent.
Funding:
The study was funded by Novartis.

title: Effects of exercise training on health status in patients with chronic heart failure: HF-ACTION randomized controlled trial.
text:
In this study, the researchers aimed to investigate the effects of exercise training on health status among patients with heart failure. The study was a randomized, controlled trial involving 2331 medically stable outpatients with heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less. The participants were randomized into two groups: usual care plus aerobic exercise training, and usual care alone. The exercise training program consisted of 36 supervised sessions followed by home-based training, while the usual care group received no exercise intervention. The primary outcome measure was the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) overall summary scale and key subscales, which were assessed at baseline, every 3 months for 12 months, and annually thereafter for up to 4 years.
The results of the study showed that the exercise training group experienced a greater improvement in KCCQ overall summary score compared to the usual care group at 3 months, with an additional 1.93-point increase in the exercise training group (95% confidence interval, 0.84 to 3.01). This improvement was statistically significant (P < .001). After 3 months, there were no further significant changes in KCCQ score for either group, resulting in a sustained, greater improvement overall for the exercise group (P < .001). Similar results were observed on the KCCQ subscales, and no subgroup interactions were detected.
In conclusion, the study found that exercise training conferred modest but statistically significant improvements in self-reported health status compared to usual care without training. These improvements occurred early and persisted over time. The study highlights the potential benefits of exercise training for improving health status among patients with heart failure.

title: Acute respiratory failure in patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia: a prospective randomized evaluation of noninvasive ventilation.
text:
