This process occurs within 5-60 minutes and is independent of oxidants. Mitochondrial DNA is not a significant component of these NETs, but they do have some proteolytic activity and can kill Staphylococcus aureus. As time passes, the nuclear envelope ruptures, and DNA fills the cytoplasm, potentially for later lytic NET production. Panton-Valentine leukocidin, autolysin, and a lipase were identified in the supernatants as NET-inducing factors, with Panton-Valentine leukocidin being the dominant inducer. We have discovered a novel, rapid mechanism of NET release that contributes to the trapping and killing of S. aureus.

title: 131-I radioiodine therapy for hyperthyroidism in patients with Graves' disease, uninodular goitre and multinodular goitre.
text:
We analyzed 201 patients who received a standardized dose of radioiodine (131-I) for the treatment of hyperthyroidism between 1981 and 1986. The patients were categorized into three groups based on the type of thyroid disorder: Graves' disease (170 patients), uninodular goiter (10 patients), and multinodular goiter (21 patients).
For patients with Graves' disease, the mean (standard error) dose of 131-I was 369 (10) MBq, and the remission rate at 6 months was 94%, with a cumulative relapse rate of 12% at 1 year and 21% at 5 years. The incidence of hypothyroidism was 26% at 3 months, 55% at 6 months, 61% at 1 year, and 66% at 5 years.
For patients with uninodular goiter, the mean (standard error) dose of 131-I was 438 (85) MBq, and the remission rate at 6 months was 100%, with no relapses observed at 1 year but a relapse rate of 17% at 5 years. The incidence of hypothyroidism was 26% at 3 months, 30% at 6 months, 40% at 1 year, and 40% at 5 years.
For patients with multinodular goiter, the mean (standard error) dose of 131-I was 613 (77) MBq, and the remission rate at 6 months was 79%, with a relapse rate of 26% at 1 year and 39% at 5 years. The incidence of hypothyroidism was 5% at 3 months, 14% at 6 months, 24% at 1 year, and 24% at 5 years.
In conclusion, our study shows that the standardized dose of radioiodine (131-I) is effective in treating hyperthyroidism, with high remission rates and low relapse rates observed in patients with Graves' disease. However, patients with multinodular goiter have a higher relapse rate compared to those with uninodular goiter. The incidence of hypothyroidism also varies depending on the type of thyroid disorder and the dose of radioiodine used.

title: Enteral nutrition in the critically ill patient.
text: The timing and route of nutrition provided to critically ill patients can significantly impact their outcome. Early enteral nutrition has been shown to reduce infectious morbidity in these patients. However, there is a subset of patients who are malnourished upon admission to the intensive care unit, and in these cases, parenteral nutrition can be beneficial.

title: Genomewide analysis of nucleosome density histone acetylation and HDAC function in fission yeast.
text: We have conducted a comprehensive investigation of the enzymatic specificity, expression profiles, and binding locations of four histone deacetylases (HDACs) in fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe), representing the three major phylogenetic classes. By comparing nucleosome density, histone acetylation patterns, and HDAC binding in both intergenic and coding regions with gene expression profiles, we discovered unique roles for each HDAC in regulating gene expression.

title: In vitro antimicrobial activity of mangrove plant Sonneratia alba.
text:
Objective:
To investigate the antimicrobial properties of Sonneratia alba (S. alba) using various extraction methods and microdilution and disc diffusion assays against six microorganisms.
Methods:
The antimicrobial activity of S. alba was evaluated using disc diffusion and microdilution methods against six microorganisms, including gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) and Bacillus cereus (B. cereus), gram-negative Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the yeast Cryptococcus neoformans. The antimicrobial activities were also evaluated using n-hexane, ethyl acetate, and methanol as solvents for plant extracts.
Results:
The results showed that the methanol extract of S. alba was the most effective extract against all six microorganisms, with the highest antimicrobial activity. In contrast, the n-hexane extract showed no activity against any of the microorganisms. The antimicrobial activities of the methanol extract were observed against S. aureus, B. cereus, E. coli, and C. neoformans, with the most sensitive strain being E. coli (17.5 mm).
Conclusions:

Based on the results of this study, it can be concluded that S. alba exhibits antimicrobial activities against certain microorganisms, with the methanol extract showing the highest antimicrobial activity. These findings suggest that S. alba may be a potential source of antimicrobial compounds with potential applications in medicine and agriculture. However, further research is needed to fully understand the antimicrobial properties of S. alba and to identify the active compounds responsible for its antimicrobial activity.

title: Obesity induces a phenotypic switch in adipose tissue macrophage polarization.
text: Adipose tissue macrophages (ATMs) infiltrate adipose tissue during obesity and contribute to insulin resistance. We hypothesized that macrophages migrating to adipose tissue upon high-fat feeding may differ from those that reside there under normal diet conditions. Our findings revealed a novel population of ATMs in adipose tissue of obese mice, characterized by the expression of the F4/80 and CD11c markers, which was not observed in lean mice. ATMs from lean mice exhibited markers of M2 or "alternatively activated" macrophages, including Ym1, arginase 1, and Il10. In contrast, diet-induced obesity led to a decrease in the expression of these M2 markers and an increase in the expression of genes characteristic of M1 or "classically activated" macrophages, such as TNF-alpha and iNOS. Interestingly, ATMs from obese C-C motif chemokine receptor 2-KO (Ccr2-KO) mice maintained their M2 phenotype at levels similar to those of lean mice. The anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10, which was overexpressed in ATMs from lean mice, protected adipocytes from TNF-alpha-induced insulin resistance. Our findings suggest that diet-induced obesity leads to a shift in the activation state of ATMs from an M2-polarized state in lean animals that may protect adipocytes from inflammation to an M1 pro-inflammatory state that contributes to insulin resistance.

title: Psychological Outcome 4 Years after Restrictive Bariatric Surgery
text:
Obesity is associated with severe psychiatric and somatic comorbidities, as well as impaired psychosocial functioning. Bariatric surgery is the most effective treatment for weight loss and obesity-related illnesses, and has been shown to improve psychological and psychosocial outcomes. However, the long-term impact of bariatric surgery on these outcomes is not well understood. This study aimed to evaluate the relationship between weight loss and psychological variables, including depression, anxiety, health-related quality of life (HRQOL), and self-esteem, up to 4 years after obesity surgery.
Using standardized questionnaires, the study assessed 148 patients (47 males and 101 females, mean age 38.8 ± 10.2 years) before surgery (T1), and 1 year (T2), 2 years (T3), and 4 years (T4) after surgery. The participants lost an average of 24.6%, 25.1%, and 22.3% of their initial weight at T2, T3, and T4, respectively. Statistical analysis revealed significant improvements in depressive symptoms, physical HRQOL, and self-esteem, with peak improvements observed 1 year after surgery. These improvements were largely maintained over time. Significant correlations were found between weight loss and improvements in depression, physical HRQOL, and self-esteem. However, as weight regain occurred, psychological improvements showed a slow but not significant decline over time.
In conclusion, this study found that bariatric surgery leads to significant improvements in psychological variables, including depression, anxiety, HRQOL, and self-esteem, up to 4 years after surgery. However, these improvements may decline over time as weight regain occurs. Therefore, it is important to monitor psychological outcomes and provide ongoing support to patients after bariatric surgery.

title: Dynamics of Microvillus Extension and Tether Formation in Rolling Leukocytes.
text:
The binding of P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL-1) to P-selectin mediates the rolling of leukocytes, particularly neutrophils, under flow conditions. In human neutrophils, PSGL-1 molecules are located on the surface of the cell, specifically on the microvilli, which are small protrusions on the cell membrane. When a new P-selectin-PSGL-1 bond forms, it exerts a pulling force on the microvillus, causing it to deform. Depending on the strength of the bond, the microvillus can either be extended or a thin membrane cylinder (tether) can form at its tip.
To better understand the mechanics of microvillus deformation, we propose a Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic material model. Using a modified version of our Event-Tracking Model of Adhesion (ETMA), we demonstrate how P-selectin-PSGL-1 load-bearing bonds shape microvillus deformation during neutrophil rolling at low shear rates (50 s(-1)) and P-selectin site density (150 molecules μm(-2)). We also explore the impact of microvillus deformability on neutrophil rolling and find that the average microvillus extension accounts for 65% of the total microvillus-tether complex extension. Additionally, we show that the rolling neutrophil may never fully rest due to the ability of the microvillus to deform, which stabilizes cell rolling.
Our results provide a quantitative comparison between the deformable and non-deformable microvilli cases, supporting the concept that the ability of the microvillus to deform plays a crucial role in stabilizing cell rolling. This study contributes to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying leukocyte trafficking and inflammation, which are essential for maintaining tissue homeostasis and responding to infection and injury.

title: Female Gender and Reproductive Factors Affecting Risk, Relapses and Progression in Multiple Sclerosis
text: Multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic inflammatory demyelinating and degenerative disease of the central nervous system, is a leading cause of neurological disability in young adults. Notably, the female gender carries a higher risk of developing relapsing remitting MS, yet being female and of childbearing age may provide some protection against cognitive decline and progressive onset MS, an adverse predictive factor for long-term disability. The risk of MS in women has been linked to an earlier age of menarche. While parity does not significantly impact MS risk, a recent association between higher parity and offspring number and reduced risk of a first demyelinating event suggests a potential suppressive effect. Pregnancy in MS patients is associated with a reduced relapse rate and alleviation of neurological symptoms, particularly during the third trimester. Childbirth itself does not appear to have a detrimental effect on the long-term course of MS. Fertility treatment in MS patients has been linked to an increased relapse risk in the following 3-month period, particularly when the procedure did not result in pregnancy and gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonists were used. Overall, there is substantial evidence to suggest that sex steroid hormones play a regulatory role in MS. Given the lack of correlations between single hormone blood levels and the underlying mechanisms are unclear. In conclusion, the increased MS risk in women and the fluctuations in relapse and progression risk associated with reproductive events suggest complex interactions between the immune, neuroendocrine, and reproductive systems in MS.

title: Spatial release from masking based on binaural processing for up to six maskers.
text: Spatial Release from Masking (SRM) was measured to identify a female target word spoken in the presence of male masker words. The target words were presented from a single loudspeaker located at midline, while two, four, or six masker words were played from either the same source or spatially separated locations around the target source. The masker words were presented in three different masking conditions: speech-in-speech, speech-in-noise, and filtered speech-in-filtered speech. The results were summarized in three-point psychometric functions, which related the proportion of correct word identification to the target-to-masker ratio (in decibels) for both co-located and spatially separated target and masker sources. SRM was calculated by comparing the slopes and intercepts of these functions, and the results showed that SRM decreased as the number of symmetrically placed masker sources increased from two to six. This decrease was independent of the type of masking, with almost no SRM measured for six masker sources. These findings suggest that when SRM is primarily dependent on binaural processing, it is limited to fewer than six sound sources.

title: Nephrin mutations cause childhood- and adult-onset focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
text: Mutations in the NPHS1 gene are associated with congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type, which typically presents before the age of 3 months. Recent studies have also identified NPHS1 mutations in childhood-onset steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and milder forms of the disease. However, the role of these mutations in adults with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis remains unclear. To address this question, we developed a computational scoring matrix to evaluate the pathogenicity of amino acid substitutions in the NPHS1 gene. This matrix considers biophysical and biochemical differences between wild-type and mutant amino acids, evolutionary conservation of the amino acid residue in orthologs, and defined domains. We applied this approach to a cohort of 97 patients from 89 unrelated families, including 52 patients with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome after the age of 18. We identified compound heterozygous or homozygous NPHS1 mutations in five familial and seven sporadic cases, including one patient aged 27 at onset of disease. Using our computational approach, we classified these mutations as either 'severe' or 'mild.' Our findings suggest that patients with two 'severe' mutations have an earlier onset of disease compared to patients with at least one 'mild' mutation. Additionally, our study indicates that NPHS1 analysis may be useful in patients with later-onset focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

title: Use of clomifene during early pregnancy and risk of hypospadias: population based case-control study.
text:
Clomifene is commonly used to induce ovulation, but its use has been linked to an increased risk of hypospadias in male offspring. This is concerning, as little is known about the potential risks of using clomifene in women who are trying to conceive.
Clomifene is structurally related to diethylstilbestrol, a drug that has been associated with vaginal and cervical clear cell adenocarcinoma in women exposed in utero. While the adverse effects on daughters are severe, links to testicular cancer and urogenital anomalies, such as epididymal cysts, have been reported in sons exposed in utero. A recent study also found an increased risk of hypospadias in the sons of women exposed to diethylstilbestrol in utero.
Clomifene has a half-life of approximately five days, but its metabolites have been detected in blood samples up to six weeks after administration and in faeces for several weeks. The incidence of hypospadias may be increasing, which is a concern for women who use clomifene to induce ovulation.
Our case-control study was conducted in the Danish counties of North Jutland, Aarhus, Viborg, and Randers to investigate the potential risks of hypospadias in male offspring of women who have used clomifene. The results showed that the risk of hypospadias was significantly higher in the offspring of women who had used clomifene compared to those who had not. These findings suggest that clomifene may pose a risk to male fertility and reproductive health.
In conclusion, while clomifene is commonly used to induce ovulation, its use has been linked to an increased risk of hypospadias in male offspring. Further research is needed to fully understand the potential risks of clomifene and to determine the appropriate measures to minimize these risks.

title: Association of aspirin and NSAID use with risk of colorectal cancer according to genetic variants.
text:
The use of aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) has been associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer. To identify genetic markers that may confer differential benefit from aspirin or NSAID chemoprevention, we conducted a case-control study of colorectal cancer cases and controls across the United States, Canada, Australia, and Germany. We tested gene × environment interactions between regular use of aspirin and/or NSAIDs and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in relation to risk of colorectal cancer.
Our results showed that regular use of aspirin and/or NSAIDs was associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer (odds ratio [OR], 0.69 [95% CI, 0.64-0.74]; P = 6.2 × 10(-28)). We identified two SNPs, rs2965667 at chromosome 12p12.3 near the MGST1 gene and rs16973225 at chromosome 15q25.2 near the IL16 gene, that showed a genome-wide significant interaction with aspirin and/or NSAID use. Specifically, aspirin and/or NSAID use was associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among individuals with the TT genotype of rs2965667 (OR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.61-0.70]; P = 7.7 × 10(-33)), but with a higher risk among those with rare (4%) TA or AA genotypes (OR, 1.89 [95% CI, 1.27-2.81]; P = .002). In contrast, regular use was associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among individuals with the AA genotype of rs16973225 (OR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.62-0.71]; P = 1.9 × 10(-30)), but not among those with less common (9%) AC or CC genotypes (OR, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.78-1.20]; P = .76).
Our findings suggest that the association between aspirin and/or NSAID use and colorectal cancer risk may vary according to genetic variation at specific loci. Validation of these findings in additional populations may facilitate targeted colorectal cancer prevention strategies.

title: Intravaginal ring eluting tenofovir disoproxil fumarate completely protects macaques from multiple vaginal simian-HIV challenges.
text: Topical pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) can prevent HIV transmission at the site of mucosal exposure. Intermittent dosing of vaginal gels containing the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase inhibitor tenofovir has shown protection in animal studies, but clinical trials have yielded modest or no protection. Intravaginal rings (IVRs) may improve efficacy by providing long-term, sustained drug delivery and enhancing adherence. Although some IVRs are in the clinical pipeline, 100% efficacy in a repeated macaque vaginal challenge model has not been achieved. Here, we describe a reservoir IVR technology that delivers the tenofovir prodrug tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) continuously for 28 days in a repeated challenge model. In this study, TDF IVRs generated reproducible and protective drug levels, and all treated macaques remained seronegative and simian-HIV RNA negative after 16 weekly vaginal exposures to 50 tissue culture infectious dose SHIV162p3. In contrast, 11/12 control macaques became infected, with a median of four exposures assuming an eclipse of 7 days from infection to virus RNA detection. Protection was associated with TDF levels in vaginal fluid and ex vivo antiviral activity of cervicovaginal lavage samples. These findings support the advancement of TDF IVRs and the concept of extended duration drug delivery devices delivering topical antiretrovirals for preventing sexual transmission of HIV in humans.

title: Epithelial and mesenchymal subpopulations within normal basal breast cell lines exhibit distinct stem cell/progenitor properties.
text:
The proposed study aims to investigate the role of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in mammary epithelial cells and breast cancer cells, specifically in regards to stem cell features. It is proposed that EMT in claudin-low breast tumors may reveal their origin in basal stem cells, but it remains unclear whether EMT is an inherent property of normal basal stem cells. To address this question, the study will use nontumorigenic basal cell lines as models of normal stem cells/progenitors and examine the spontaneous generation of mesenchymal-like cells through EMT. The study will also investigate the stem cell/progenitor properties of these cells and determine whether a mesenchymal-like phenotype is required for the maintenance of all stem cell properties.
The study will use gene expression profiling and inhibition of Slug and Zeb1 EMT-inducers to determine the progenitor and mesenchymal-like phenotype in EpCAM+ cells and Fibros, respectively. The findings suggest that nontumorigenic basal cell lines have an intrinsic capacity for EMT, but a mesenchymal-like phenotype does not necessarily correlate with the acquisition of global stem cell/progenitor features. The study proposes that EMT in normal basal cells and claudin-low breast cancers may reflect aberrant/incomplete myoepithelial differentiation.

title: Involvement of members of the Rab family and related small GTPases in autophagosome formation and maturation
text: Macroautophagy, the process by which cytosolic components and organelles are engulfed and degraded by a double-membrane structure, can be viewed as a specialized, multistep membrane transport process that intersects with the exocytic and endocytic membrane trafficking pathways. Various Rab GTPases, which regulate secretory and endocytic membrane traffic, have been shown to play critical or accessory roles in autophagy. For instance, the biogenesis of the pre-autophagosomal isolation membrane (or phagophore) relies on the functionality of Rab1. Additionally, a non-canonical, Atg5/Atg7-independent mode of autophagosome generation from the trans-Golgi or endosome requires Rab9. Other Rabs, such as Rab5, Rab24, Rab33, and Rab7, have been shown to be required or involved at various stages of autophagosomal genesis and maturation. Furthermore, recent studies have demonstrated that the small GTPase RalB can induce isolation membrane formation and maturation via its engagement of the exocyst complex, a known Rab effector. Here, we summarize the current understanding of the involvement of Rabs in autophagy and propose possible mechanisms with future perspectives.

title: Comparative risk of new-onset diabetes mellitus for antihypertensive drugs: A network meta-analysis.
text: New-onset diabetes mellitus (NOD) arises in some individuals during the treatment of other diseases, such as hypertension. In this study, we conducted a network meta-analysis to compare the effects of various antihypertensive drugs on NOD. By analyzing the odd ratios and confidence intervals, we found that both angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers were associated with a lower risk of developing NOD compared to placebo, with ranking probabilities of 79.81% and 72.77%, respectively. On the other hand, β-blockers and calcium channel blockers may significantly increase the probability of NOD (β-blockers: odds ratio, 2.18 [95% credible intervals: 1.36-3.50]; calcium channel blockers: odds ratio, 1.16 [95% credible intervals, 1.05-1.29]). Our findings suggest that angiotensin receptor blockers have a significant advantage in preventing NOD compared to other treatments.

title: Transformation of mammalian cells by constitutively active MAP kinase kinase.
text: Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MAPKK) plays a crucial role in signal transduction pathways that regulate cellular responses to growth and differentiation factors. Oncogenes, such as ras, src, raf, and mos, have been implicated in cell transformation by prolonging the active state of MAPKK and downstream signaling components. To investigate this hypothesis, we generated constitutively active MAPKK mutants with basal activities up to 400 times greater than that of the unphosphorylated wild-type kinase. We found that expression of these mutants in mammalian cells led to enhanced activation of AP-1-regulated transcription, resulting in the formation of transformed foci, efficient growth in soft agar, and high tumorigenicity in nude mice. These findings support the idea that constitutive activation of MAPKK is sufficient to promote cell transformation.

title: Psychological treatment of malignant vasovagal syncope due to bloodphobia.
text: A 17-year-old adolescent with recurrent faints due to a blood-injury phobia was investigated. During a cardiovascular reflex examination in our syncope unit, a duration of 50 seconds of asystole was recorded. He was subsequently treated using a combination of systematic desensitization techniques, including muscular tension and cognitive methods, provided by the Pediatric Psychosocial Department. As a result of this treatment, the individual has not experienced any further syncopal events.

title: QT and QTc dispersion are accurate predictors of cardiac death in newly diagnosed non-insulin dependent diabetes: cohort study.
text:
Patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus are at an increased risk of dying from cardiovascular disease. A small study suggested that a prolonged QT interval may predict cardiac death in patients with diabetic nephropathy who have received insulin treatment. The question now is whether the same is true in newly diagnosed diabetes patients who have no apparent complications. Additionally, QT dispersion, a related electrocardiographic variable, has been shown to predict cardiac death in patients with chronic heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, or essential hypertension. To investigate this further, we studied a group of 182 patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (103 men, mean age 52.8 years, SD 8.5) from the Dundee cohort of the United Kingdom prospective diabetes study, recruited between 1982 and 1988. The patients were followed up for a mean of 10.3 years.
In this study, we aimed to determine whether QT dispersion can predict cardiac death in diabetic patients without any apparent complications. Our findings suggest that QT dispersion may be a useful predictor of cardiac death in this population, highlighting the importance of monitoring and managing cardiovascular risk factors in diabetes patients.

title: Recombinant human IL-10 prevents the onset of diabetes in the nonobese diabetic mouse.
text: The study investigated the role of interleukin-10 (IL-10) in the pathogenesis of autoimmune diabetes mellitus in the nonobese diabetic (NOD) mouse model. The research aimed to evaluate the effect of IL-10 on three key parameters of diabetes: the development of hyperglycemia, insulitis, and insulin production by beta cells. Initial experiments involved assessing the impact of anticytokine antibodies on disease progression. The results showed that monoclonal anti-interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) antibody significantly reduced the incidence of hyperglycemia in female NOD mice, while anti-IL-4, IL-5, and IL-10 were ineffective. Subsequent studies demonstrated that daily subcutaneous administration of IL-10, a potent inhibitor of IFN-gamma production by TH1 T cells, to 9 and 10-week-old NOD mice delayed the onset of disease and significantly reduced the incidence of diabetes. Histopathology of pancreatic tissue revealed that IL-10 treatment reduced the severity of insulitis, prevented cellular infiltration of islet cells, and promoted normal insulin production by beta cells. These findings suggest that IL-10 suppresses the induction and progression of autoimmune pathogenesis associated with diabetes mellitus and may have a potential therapeutic role in this autoimmune disease.

title: Arterial hypertension and progression of chronic kidney disease in children during 10-year ambulatory observation.
text: The primary objective of this investigation was to conduct a comprehensive, long-term retrospective analysis of the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in children, with a particular focus on the role of hypertension (HTN) in this process. Our findings revealed that the average rate of CKD progression was significantly higher in individuals with HTN compared to those without HTN. Moreover, we found that the treatment of hypertension in these patients requires a multidrug approach that should be intensified over time as the duration of CKD increases.

title: Exercise blood flow patterns within and among rat muscles after training.
text:
This study aimed to investigate the impact of a long-term, moderate-intensity treadmill training program on the distribution of blood flow within and among muscles in rats during exercise. One group of male Sprague-Dawley rats (T) underwent 1 hour of daily training for 13-17 weeks at a speed of 30 m/min on a motor-driven treadmill, while a second group of rats (UT) received 10 minutes of daily training for 4 weeks at the same speed. Muscle succinate dehydrogenase activities were higher in the trained rats (T), indicating a significant training effect. Blood flows (BFs) in 32 hindlimb muscles or muscle parts, as well as other selected organs, were measured in both groups using radiolabeled microspheres during pre-exercise and while the rats ran for 30 seconds, 5 minutes, or 15 minutes at 30 m/min on the treadmill. The results showed:
1. There were no differences in total hindlimb muscle BF between the UT and T rats at any time point.
2. Trained rats (T) had higher pre-exercise heart rates and higher muscle BFs in the deep red extensor muscles, suggesting a greater anticipatory response to the impending exercise.
3. Trained rats (T) demonstrated more rapid elevations in BF in the red extensor muscles at the commencement of exercise.
4. Trained rats (T) had higher BFs in red extensor muscles during exercise, while untrained rats (UT) had higher BFs in white muscles.
5. Trained rats (T) maintained higher BFs in visceral organs during exercise.

These findings indicate that exercise training leads to changes in the distribution of BF within and among muscles and among organs during exercise. Specifically, the study found that the high-oxidative motor units that are primarily recruited in the muscles during the initial stages of moderate treadmill exercise receive higher blood flows in the trained rats, which likely contributes to increased resistance to fatigue.

title: Serious infections after unrelated donor transplantation in 136 children: impact of stem cell source.
text: The comparison of infection risks after umbilical cord blood (UCB) and bone marrow (BM) transplantation is not well established. To investigate, we analyzed the incidence of serious infections in pediatric patients who underwent myeloablative unrelated donor transplantation with unmanipulated BM (n = 52), T cell-depleted BM (n = 24), or UCB (n = 60) for the treatment of hematologic malignancy. Our findings revealed that the cumulative incidence of 1 or more serious infections was comparable among the 3 groups (BM, 81%; TCD, 83%; UCB, 90%; P = .12). Multivariate analysis showed no significant differences in infection risk between groups, with the exception of a greater risk of viral infections in the first 42 days after transplantation in TCD recipients (RR, 3.5; P = .02). Interestingly, after day 180, TCD recipients had a significantly increased infection risk (RR, 3.1; P = .03), while the risk in UCB recipients (RR, 0.5; P = .23) was comparable to that in BM recipients. Other factors associated with an increased infection risk included age > or = 8 years, graft failure, and severe acute graft-versus-host disease. These data suggest that the risk of serious infection after pediatric UCB transplantation is comparable to that with unmanipulated BM.

title: The NBS1–Treacle complex controls ribosomal RNA transcription in response to DNA damage
text:
Chromosomal breakage triggers transient silencing of ribosomal RNA synthesis, but the underlying mechanisms remained obscure. In this study, we uncover an in trans signaling mechanism that leads to pan-nuclear silencing of rRNA transcription in response to DNA damage. This is accompanied by transient recruitment of the Nijmegen breakage syndrome protein 1 (NBS1), a central regulator of DNA damage responses, into the nucleoli. We identify TCOF1 (also known as Treacle), a nucleolar factor involved in ribosome biogenesis and mutated in Treacher Collins syndrome, as a key interaction partner of NBS1. Our findings demonstrate that Treacle-mediated NBS1 recruitment into the nucleoli regulates rRNA silencing in trans in the presence of distant chromosome breaks.
In this investigation, we explore the mechanisms underlying the silencing of ribosomal RNA synthesis in response to chromosomal breakage. Previous studies have shown that this process is transient and reversible, but the underlying mechanisms remained unclear. By employing a combination of biochemical, genetic, and cellular approaches, we uncover an in trans signaling mechanism that triggers pan-nuclear silencing of rRNA transcription in response to DNA damage.
Our findings reveal that the Nijmegen breakage syndrome protein 1 (NBS1) plays a central role in this process. NBS1 is a key regulator of DNA damage responses and has been implicated in the maintenance of genome stability. We demonstrate that NBS1 translocation and accumulation in the nucleoli is dependent on the interaction with TCOF1 (also known as Treacle), a nucleolar factor involved in ribosome biogenesis. Treacle has been implicated in the development of Treacher Collins syndrome, a genetic disorder characterized by craniofacial abnormalities and hearing loss.
Our results provide evidence that Treacle-mediated NBS1 recruitment into the nucleoli regulates rRNA silencing in trans in the presence of distant chromosome breaks. This mechanism is likely to play a crucial role in maintaining genome stability in response to DNA damage. Overall, our findings shed light on the complex interplay between chromosomal breakage and gene expression, and highlight the importance of the nucleolus in regulating these processes.

title: Inflammatory T cells rapidly induce differentiation of human bone marrow stromal cells into mature osteoblasts.
text: Activated T cells secrete multiple cytokines that play a crucial role in the bone destruction associated with rheumatoid arthritis. While the role of T cells in osteoclastogenesis has been extensively studied, their impact on osteoblast formation and activity remains poorly understood. In this investigation, we tested the hypothesis that activated T cells contribute to enhanced bone turnover by promoting osteoblastic differentiation. Our findings revealed that T cells produce soluble factors that induce alkaline phosphatase activity in bone marrow stromal cells and elevate the expression of Runx2 and osteocalcin mRNA. These data suggest that T cell-derived factors have the potential to stimulate the differentiation of bone marrow stromal cells into the osteoblast lineage. Interestingly, both bone marrow stromal cells and osteoblasts expressed RANK mRNA, which was strongly up-regulated by activated T cell conditioned medium. However, the inhibitory effects of osteoprotegerin, a RANKL decoy receptor, may be mitigated by the simultaneous rise in the osteoprotegerin competitor TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand. Based on our findings, we propose that during chronic inflammation, T cells regulate bone loss through a dual mechanism involving both direct stimulation of osteoclastogenesis and indirect induction of osteoblast differentiation and up-regulation of bone turnover via coupling.

title: Prevention of coronary heart disease with pravastatin in men with hypercholesterolemia. West of Scotland Coronary Prevention Study Group.
text:
Background: Lowering blood cholesterol levels has been shown to reduce the risk of coronary heart disease. This double-blind study aimed to determine the effectiveness of pravastatin in reducing the incidence of nonfatal myocardial infarction and death from coronary heart disease in men with hypercholesterolemia and no history of myocardial infarction.
Methods: We randomly assigned 6595 men aged 45-64 years with a mean plasma cholesterol level of 272 ± 23 mg/dL to receive either 40 mg of pravastatin or placebo orally once daily for a mean follow-up period of 4.9 years. Medical records, electrocardiographic recordings, and national death registry data were used to identify clinical endpoints.
Results: Pravastatin significantly lowered plasma cholesterol levels by 20% and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels by 26%, compared to placebo. There were 248 definite coronary events in the placebo group, and 174 in the pravastatin group, resulting in a relative reduction in risk of 31% (95% CI, 17-43%, P < 0.001). Similar reductions were observed in the risk of nonfatal myocardial infarctions (31% reduction, P < 0.001), death from coronary heart disease (definite cases alone: 28% reduction, P = 0.13; definite plus suspected cases: 33% reduction, P = 0.042), and death from all cardiovascular causes (32% reduction, P = 0.033). There was no significant increase in the risk of death from noncardiovascular causes in the pravastatin group. Additionally, there was a 22% reduction in the risk of death from any cause in the pravastatin group (95% CI, 0-40%, P = 0.051).
Conclusions: Treatment with pravastatin significantly reduced the incidence of myocardial infarction and death from cardiovascular causes without adversely affecting the risk of death from noncardiovascular causes in men with moderate hypercholesterolemia and no history of myocardial infarction.

title: Validation of a migraine-specific questionnaire for use in family studies.
text: The availability of reliable migraine-specific questionnaires is crucial when analyzing large numbers of migraine patients. The Finnish Migraine-Specific Questionnaire has undergone validation in two stages. In the first stage, clinical diagnosis of migraine was established in 100 consecutive patients using International Headache Society criteria. Migraine was then diagnosed independently based on responses to the questionnaire. In the second stage, responses from 100 questionnaires collected in a family study were analyzed, and respondents were interviewed by phone for diagnosis confirmation. Six cases were unable to be contacted. The questionnaire's sensitivity for migraine was 0.99 (167 out of 168; combined validation stages 1 and 2) and specificity was 0.96 (25 out of 26 cases; validation stage 2). The questionnaire also allowed for the differentiation between migraine with and without aura based on responses, with chance-corrected agreement (Cohen's kappa) of 0.804 when comparing diagnoses reached based on the questionnaire and clinical diagnoses, and 0.858 when combining questionnaire responses with telephone interviews. A Cohen's kappa value above 0.75 indicates good agreement, thus justifying the use of the Finnish Migraine-Specific Questionnaire in research on migraine genetics.

title: Defining early lineage specification of human embryonic stem cells by the orchestrated balance of canonical Wnt/beta-catenin, Activin/Nodal and BMP signaling.
text: The canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway has diverse roles in embryonic development, stem cell self-renewal, and cancer progression. In this study, we found that stabilized expression of β-catenin in human embryonic stem (hES) cells disrupted their self-renewal, leading to the formation of primitive streak (PS)/mesoderm progenitors, similar to early mammalian embryogenesis. The cooperative action of β-catenin, Activin/Nodal, and BMP signaling pathways was essential for the formation of PS/mesoderm progenitors. Interestingly, blocking BMP signaling completely abolished mesoderm generation, and instead induced a cell fate change towards anterior PS progenitors. The phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt signaling pathway played a crucial role in the specification of anterior PS progenitors, at least in part by enhancing β-catenin stability. Additionally, Activin/Nodal and Wnt/β-catenin signaling synergistically induced the generation and specification of anterior PS/endoderm progenitors. Our findings demonstrate that the coordinated balance of Activin/Nodal and BMP signaling determines the cell fate of the nascent PS induced by canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling in hES cells.

title: Sphingosine can pre- and post-condition heart and utilizes a different mechanism from sphingosine 1-phosphate.
text:
Introduction:
Sphingosine, a sphingolipid metabolite, has been shown to have cardioprotective effects in various studies. However, its mechanism of action remains unclear, particularly in comparison to its phosphorylated form, sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P). In this study, we investigate the cardiotoxicity and cardioprotective effects of sphingosine at physiologic concentrations and explore its mechanism of action.
Methods:
Ex vivo rat heart experiments were performed to evaluate the cardiotoxicity and cardioprotective effects of sphingosine at physiologic concentrations. The hearts were subjected to ischemia/reperfusion injury, and the infarct size and left ventricular developed pressure were measured. The effects of VPC23019, an S1P(1and3)G-protein coupled receptor antagonist, on S1P-induced protection were also investigated. Additionally, the role of protein kinase C, PI3 kinase, and protein kinase A in sphingosine preconditioning was examined using specific inhibitors.
Results:
Our results show that sphingosine at a high concentration (5 microM) is cardiotoxic, leading to increased infarct size in response to ischemia/reperfusion. However, at a physiologic concentration (0.4 microM), sphingosine is cardioprotective, with a >75% recovery of left ventricular developed pressure during reperfusion and a decrease in infarct size from 45% of the risk area to less than 8%. In contrast, S1P at 5 microM is cardioprotective, but at a physiologic concentration (0.4 microM), it is not effective in protecting the heart from ischemia/reperfusion injury. The addition of VPC23019 to the preconditioning or postconditioning medium completely blocks S1P-induced protection. Interestingly, VPC23019 does not affect the ability of 0.4 microM sphingosine to either precondition or postcondition hearts. Our results also reveal that inhibition of protein kinase C with GF109203X blocks sphingosine preconditioning, but does not affect preconditioning by 0.4 microM sphingosine. Similarly, cotreatment with the PI3 kinase inhibitor wortmanin blocks sphingosine preconditioning, but does not affect preconditioning by S1P. On the other hand, inhibition of protein kinase G with KT5823 has no effect on S1P preconditioning, but completely eliminates preconditioning by sphingosine. Additionally, the protein kinase A inhibitory peptide 14-22 amide blocks sphingosine preconditioning, but not S1P preconditioning.
Discussion:
Our findings demonstrate that sphingosine is not toxic at physiologic concentrations and is a potent cardioprotectant that utilizes a completely different mechanism than S1P. Unlike S1P, which activates G-protein coupled receptors, sphingosine acts through cyclic nucleotide-dependent pathways. The results of this study provide new insights into the mechanisms of cardioprotection and suggest that sphingosine may be a useful therapeutic agent for the prevention and treatment of ischemia/reperfusion injury.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study shows that sphingosine is a cardioprotective agent that acts through a unique mechanism independent of G-protein coupled receptors. The results provide new insights into the mechanisms of cardioprotection and suggest that sphingosine may be a useful therapeutic agent for the prevention and treatment of ischemia/reperfusion injury. Further studies are needed to fully understand the mechanisms of sphingosine-mediated cardioprotection and to evaluate its potential as a therapeutic agent.

title: Coordination of p300-mediated chromatin remodeling and TRAP/mediator function through coactivator PGC-1alpha.
text: Transcriptional coactivators that interact with the nuclear receptor peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) include the protein acetyltransferase p300, the TRAP/Mediator complex, which interacts with the general transcription machinery, and the highly regulated PGC-1α. Our findings demonstrate that PGC-1α directly interacts with TRAP/Mediator through the PPARγ-interacting subunit TRAP220, and stimulates TRAP/Mediator-dependent function on DNA templates. Additionally, while ineffective on its own, PGC-1α enhances p300-dependent histone acetylation and transcription on chromatin templates in response to PPARγ. These functions are mediated by distinct interaction domains in PGC-1α, which are occupied by PPARγ, p300, and TRAP220 in a ligand-dependent manner. Our results also suggest a crucial role for PGC-1α in coordinating these steps through dynamic and concerted interactions, highlighting its importance in both chromatin remodeling and preinitiation complex formation or function (transcription).

title: Phospholipid synthesis and lipid composition of subcellular membranes in the unicellular eukaryote Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
text:
Isolation and Characterization of Subcellular Membranes from Saccharomyces cerevisiae
In this study, we isolated and analyzed the lipid composition of various subcellular membranes from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, including mitochondria, microsomes, plasma membranes, secretory vesicles, vacuoles, nuclear membranes, peroxisomes, and lipid particles. Our improved isolation procedures allowed us to investigate the capacity of these membranes to synthesize phospholipids and to catalyze sterol delta 24-methylation.
The microsomal fraction was found to be heterogeneous in terms of density and the distribution of phospholipid-synthesizing enzymes. The specific activity of phosphatidylserine synthase was highest in a subfraction of microsomes that was distinct from heavier microsomes containing phosphatidylinositol synthase and the phospholipid N-methyltransferases. Interestingly, phosphatidylserine decarboxylase was exclusively located in mitochondria, confirming previous findings. Additionally, we observed that CDO-diacylglycerol synthase was present in both mitochondria and microsomal membranes.
The lipid particle fraction showed the highest specific activities of glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase and sterol delta 24-methyltransferase, indicating that these membranes are enriched in lipid-synthesizing enzymes. In contrast, nuclear and plasma membranes, vacuoles, and peroxisomes contained only marginal activities of these enzymes. The plasma membrane and secretory vesicles were found to be enriched in ergosterol and phosphatidylserine, while lipid particles were characterized by their high content of ergosterol esters.
To further investigate the structure and function of these membranes, we measured the fluorescence anisotropy of trimethylammonium diphenylhexatriene, which probes the rigidity of the plasma membrane and secretory vesicles. Our results showed that the high content of ergosterol in these membranes contributes to their rigidity.
In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the lipid composition and the capacity of subcellular membranes from Saccharomyces cerevisiae to synthesize phospholipids and to catalyze sterol delta 24-methylation. Our findings highlight the heterogeneity of the microsomal fraction and the specific location of lipid-synthesizing enzymes in different membranes. Additionally, our results demonstrate the importance of ergosterol in determining the rigidity of the plasma membrane and secretory vesicles.

title: Use of health services by prison inmates: comparisons with the community.
text: The future organization of prison healthcare recommends that the National Health Service (NHS) and the Prison Service should collaborate to plan and provide healthcare services for inmates. Previously, the Prison Service had sole responsibility for providing healthcare, but the NHS will now need to assess the current level of healthcare demand and provision. To inform joint planning, a key component of the information base is data on current service utilization. This paper compares primary care and inpatient health service utilization data for UK prisoners with health service utilization data for comparable community populations. In the community, primary care is primarily provided by general practitioners and professions allied to medicine (mostly nurses). Community residents have access to the full range of NHS outpatient and inpatient facilities. Within prisons, primary care is provided by medical officers (some of whom are general practitioners), nursing grades, and healthcare officers (who have received some training in healthcare). Some prisons have their own inpatient facilities (healthcare center beds), which provide a limited level of inpatient care and do not have a direct equivalent in the community. Prisoners also have access to NHS outpatient and inpatient facilities and to visiting specialists. The prison population has a high turnover and varies daily, so the prison population is expressed as an average daily population over a one-year period.

title: Regulation of p53 in response to DNA damage
text: Activation of p53 can occur in response to various cellular stresses, including DNA damage, hypoxia, and nucleotide deprivation. Multiple forms of DNA damage, such as those caused by ionizing radiation (IR), radio-mimetic drugs, ultraviolet light (UV), and chemicals like methyl methane sulfonate (MMS), have been shown to activate p53. Under normal conditions, p53 levels are maintained at low levels due to its short half-life, and it exists in an inactive state with limited ability to bind DNA and activate transcription. Upon DNA damage, p53 levels rapidly increase, and its ability to bind DNA and mediate transcriptional activation enhances, leading to the activation of genes that trigger cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, or DNA repair. Recent research suggests that this regulation is primarily achieved through a series of phosphorylation, dephosphorylation, and acetylation events on the p53 polypeptide. Here, we delve into the nature of these modifications, the enzymes responsible for them, and how changes in p53 modification lead to its activation.

title: Hydrogen sulphide regulates intracellular pH in vascular smooth muscle cells.
text: In this study, we investigated the role of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) in regulating intracellular pH (pH(i)) in vascular smooth muscle cells and its contribution to vasodilation. We found that exposure to the H2S donor sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS) decreased pH(i) in a concentration-dependent manner, with effects observed at concentrations ranging from 10 microM to 1 mM. Interestingly, inhibition of the Na(+)/H(+) exchanger with 5-(N-ethyl-N-isopropyl) amiloride (EIPA, 10 microM) or plasmalemmal Ca(2+)-ATPase with cadmium chloride (CdCl2, 20 nM) did not affect the pH(i) lowering effect of NaHS. However, blockade of the Cl(-)/HCO3- exchanger with 4,4'-diisothiocyanatostilbene-2,2'-disulfonic acid (DIDS) significantly attenuated the pH(i) lowering effect of NaHS. Additionally, NaHS significantly increased the activity of the Cl(-)/HCO3- exchanger when measured with NH4Cl prepulse method. Notably, DIDS also attenuated the vasorelaxation induced by NaHS, while EIPA and CdCl2 did not have any effect. Our findings suggest that H2S-induced intracellular acidification is, at least partially, responsible for H2S-mediated vasorelaxation.

title: Cell and biomolecule delivery for tissue repair and regeneration in the central nervous system.
text:
Tissue engineering often involves the use of cells and scaffolds to replace damaged or diseased tissue. This field has evolved from a means of delivering biomolecules such as insulin or neurotrophic factors, as cells are natural producers of these therapeutic agents. As a result, cell delivery is an essential aspect of tissue engineering. The controlled release of biomolecules is also crucial, as it can facilitate cell engraftment, modulate inflammatory responses, or enhance the behavior of delivered cells. Here, we discuss advances in cell and biomolecule delivery for tissue regeneration, with a particular focus on the central nervous system (CNS).
In the first section, we explore encapsulated cell therapy, where cells are protected within a biodegradable matrix to prevent immune rejection and promote cell survival. In the second section, we examine the use of polymeric nano/microspheres and hydrogels to deliver biomolecules for nerve regeneration and endogenous cell stimulation. These biomaterials can provide a protective environment for cells and biomolecules, while also promoting cell attachment and proliferation.
In the third section, we discuss combination strategies involving neural stem/progenitor cells or mesenchymal stem cells, which can differentiate into various cell types, and biomolecule delivery. By combining these approaches, we can enhance tissue regeneration and repair. However, challenges associated with delivering therapeutic agents to the CNS, such as the blood-brain barrier, must be addressed to ensure effective treatment.
In summary, tissue engineering involves the use of cells and scaffolds to replace damaged or diseased tissue, and cell delivery is an essential aspect of this field. The controlled release of biomolecules can facilitate cell engraftment, modulate inflammatory responses, or enhance the behavior of delivered cells. By combining cell and biomolecule delivery strategies, we can enhance tissue regeneration and repair, particularly in the CNS. However, challenges associated with delivering therapeutic agents to the CNS must be addressed to ensure effective treatment.

title: The angiotensin II type 1 receptor blocker olmesartan preferentially improves nocturnal hypertension and proteinuria in chronic kidney disease
text:
Title: Olmesartan Add-on Therapy Improves Ambulatory Blood Pressure Profile and Renal Function in Hypertensive Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease: A Randomized Controlled Trial
Background: Accumulated evidence suggests that an altered ambulatory blood pressure (BP) profile, particularly elevated nighttime BP, reflects target organ injury and is a better predictor of further cardiorenal risk than clinic BP or daytime BP in hypertensive patients complicated by chronic kidney disease (CKD). This study aimed to investigate the beneficial effects of olmesartan, an angiotensin II type 1 receptor blocker (ARB), on ambulatory BP profiles and renal function in hypertensive CKD patients.
Methods: Forty-six patients were randomly assigned to the olmesartan add-on group (n=23) or the non-ARB group (n=23). Ambulatory BP monitoring was performed at baseline and after the 16-week treatment period, and renal function parameter measurements were collected.
Results: Although the baseline clinic BP levels and the after-treatment/baseline (A/B) ratios of clinic BP levels were similar in the olmesartan add-on and non-ARB groups, the A/B ratios of ambulatory 24-h and nighttime BP levels in the olmesartan add-on group were significantly lower. Furthermore, the A/B ratios of urinary protein, albumin, and type IV collagen excretion in the olmesartan add-on group were significantly lower than those in the non-ARB group (urinary protein excretion, 0.72±0.41 vs. 1.45±1.48, P=0.030; urinary albumin excretion, 0.73±0.37 vs. 1.50±1.37, P=0.005; urinary type IV collagen excretion, 0.87±0.42 vs. 1.48±0.87, P=0.014) despite comparable A/B ratios for the estimated glomerular filtration rate in the two groups. These results indicate that in hypertensive patients with CKD, olmesartan add-on therapy improves the ambulatory BP profile via a preferential reduction in nighttime BP with concomitant renal injury inhibition.
Conclusion: The present study suggests that olmesartan add-on therapy may be a useful strategy for improving the ambulatory BP profile and renal function in hypertensive patients with CKD. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings and to determine the long-term efficacy and safety of olmesartan add-on therapy in this patient population.

title: Surgical vs nonsurgical treatment of adults with displaced fractures of the proximal humerus: the PROFHER randomized clinical trial.
text: The study compared the clinical effectiveness of surgical and nonsurgical treatments for adults with displaced fractures of the proximal humerus involving the surgical neck. The study found that there was no significant difference in patient-reported clinical outcomes between the two groups over a two-year period following fracture occurrence. Specifically, the Oxford Shoulder Score, a measure of clinical outcome, did not significantly differ between the surgical and nonsurgical groups. The study also found that there were no significant between-group differences in secondary outcomes such as complications, subsequent therapy, and mortality. These findings suggest that surgical treatment may not be necessary for all patients with displaced proximal humeral fractures involving the surgical neck, and that nonsurgical treatment may be a viable alternative.

title: Kinetics and Fidelity of the Repair of Cas9-Induced Double-Strand DNA Breaks
text: The RNA-guided DNA endonuclease Cas9 is a potent tool for genome editing, but little is known about the mechanisms of DNA repair following Cas9-mediated double-strand breaks (DSBs) in living cells. To address this knowledge gap, we developed a strategy to measure the kinetics of DSB repair at specific loci in human cells. By analyzing the repair of DSBs over time using a time series of DNA samples, we found that the repair process is variable and slow, with half-life times ranging from several hours to over 10 hours. Additionally, we observed that the repair process is prone to errors, with both classical and microhomology-mediated end joining pathways contributing to erroneous repair. Our approach provided quantitative insights into the kinetics and fidelity of DSB repair at specific loci, revealing that Cas9-induced DSBs are repaired in an atypical manner.

title: Network meta-analysis for indirect treatment comparisons.
text: In situations where two treatments have not been directly compared in a randomized trial, I present methods for evaluating their relative effectiveness using network meta-analysis techniques. These methods allow for the estimation of both heterogeneity in the effect of any given treatment and inconsistency (incoherence) in the evidence from different pairs of treatments. A straightforward estimation procedure using linear mixed models is provided and applied in a meta-analysis of treatments for acute myocardial infarction.

title: Liver transplantation and opioid dependence.
text:
Chronic hepatitis C is the leading cause of liver transplantation in the United States, with intravenous drug use as the primary risk factor for transmission. However, there is a lack of information on substance use among liver transplantation patients in the United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS) database. To address this gap, a mail survey was conducted among all 97 adult liver transplantation programs in the US in 2000, with telephone follow-up in May and June of the same year.
The survey found that all 90% of the programs accept patients with a history of alcoholism or other addictions, including heroin dependence. However, most programs require at least 6 months of abstinence from alcohol (88%) and illicit drugs (83%). Additionally, 94% of the programs have addiction treatment requirements. Consultations from substance abuse specialists are obtained by 86% of the programs. While 56% of the programs accept patients receiving methadone maintenance, approximately 180 patients receiving methadone maintenance have undergone liver transplantation.
The study's findings suggest that most liver transplantation programs have established policies for patients with substance use disorders. However, there is a lack of representation of opioid-dependent patients receiving opioid replacement therapy in transplantation programs. While there is limited anecdotal evidence for negative impacts of opioid replacement therapy on liver transplantation outcomes, policies requiring discontinuation of methadone in 32% of programs may result in relapse of previously stable patients.

title: RIG-I-mediated antiviral responses to single-stranded RNA bearing 5'-phosphates.
text: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) produced during viral replication is thought to be the primary trigger for the activation of antiviral immunity mediated by enzymes known as RNA helicases, including retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5). Our research has shown that infection with influenza A virus does not result in the production of dsRNA, and instead, RIG-I is activated by viral genomic single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) bearing 5'-phosphates. This activation is blocked by the influenza protein nonstructured protein 1 (NS1), which forms a complex with RIG-I in infected cells. These findings designate RIG-I as a sensor of ssRNA and a potential target of viral immune evasion, and suggest that its ability to detect 5'-phosphorylated RNA evolved in the innate immune system as a means of distinguishing between self and non-self.

title: In-hospital switching between adenosine diphosphate receptor inhibitors in patients with acute myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention: Insights into contemporary practice from the TRANSLATE-ACS study.
text:
The TRANSLATE-ACS study, a large observational study conducted at 230 hospitals in 12 countries, aimed to investigate the frequency, effectiveness, and safety of switching between adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor inhibitors in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) who were initially treated with clopidogrel. The study included 11,999 patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and were discharged from the hospital.
The study found that more than 1 in 10 patients (11.4%) were switched from clopidogrel to prasugrel or ticagrelor during their hospital stay, primarily after PCI (60.9%) and at hospital discharge (26.7%). Similarly, among patients initially treated with prasugrel or ticagrelor, 13.6% were switched to clopidogrel, with the majority of switches occurring after PCI (48.2%) and at hospital discharge (48.0%).
The study found that switching to prasugrel or ticagrelor was not associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) or bleeding when compared with continuation on clopidogrel. Specifically, switching from prasugrel or ticagrelor to clopidogrel was not associated with an increased risk of MACE (8.9% vs. 7.7%, adjusted hazard ratio 1.06, 95% confidence interval 0.75-1.49, p=0.76), and switching from clopidogrel to prasugrel or ticagrelor was not associated with an increased risk of bleeding (2.7% vs. 3.3%, adjusted hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval 0.64-1.42, p=0.82).
In conclusion, the study found that in-hospital ADP receptor inhibitor switching is common in contemporary clinical practice, occurring in more than 1 in 10 AMI patients. The study also found that switching between ADP receptor inhibitors does not appear to be significantly associated with increased MACE or bleeding, suggesting that clinicians may have adequate flexibility in their treatment strategies for AMI patients.

title: Platelet activation in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text: The abnormal metabolic state associated with diabetes renders blood vessels vulnerable to atherosclerosis, which can alter the functional properties of various cell types, including endothelium and platelets. Specifically, alterations in platelet metabolism and intraplatelet signaling pathways may contribute to the development of atherothrombotic complications in diabetes. Multiple mechanisms may be responsible for enhanced platelet aggregation, including hyperglycemia, which can directly activate platelets in vivo and lead to non-enzymatic glycation of platelet glycoproteins, causing changes in their structure and conformation, as well as alterations in membrane lipid dynamics. Additionally, hyperglycemia-induced oxidative stress can lead to increased peroxidation of arachidonic acid, resulting in the formation of biologically active isoprostanes, which acts as a key biochemical link between poor glycemic control and persistent platelet activation. Furthermore, oxidative stress can activate transcription factors and lead to the expression of redox-sensitive genes, resulting in a phenotypic shift of endothelium towards an adhesive and pro-thrombotic state, leading to initial platelet activation, adhesion, and subsequent platelet aggregate formation. The significance of these findings is underscored by the results of clinical trials demonstrating the beneficial effects of metabolic control on platelet function, as well as the finding that aspirin treatment may be more effective in diabetic than non-diabetic patients. Proper medical management of diabetes can have a significant impact on long-term outcomes in this high-risk population.

title: Nicotinic receptor-mediated neuroprotection in neurodegenerative disease models.
text: Multiple lines of evidence, ranging from molecular and cellular to epidemiological, have implicated nicotinic transmission in the pathology of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). This review article presents evidence for the protective effects of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) stimulation and the signal transduction pathways involved in this mechanism. Our studies using rat-cultured primary neurons provide the basis for this review. Nicotine-induced protection was found to be mediated by the alpha7 nAChR, which activates downstream signaling pathways involving phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), Src, and Akt. Specifically, nicotine administration led to increased levels of phosphorylated Akt, an effector of PI3K, Bcl-2, and Bcl-x. Our hypothesis for the mechanism of nAChR-mediated survival signal transduction is that the alpha7 nAChR activates the Src family, which in turn activates PI3K to phosphorylate Akt, leading to the up-regulation of Bcl-2 and Bcl-x. This up-regulation could prevent neuronal death induced by beta-amyloid (Aβ), glutamate, and rotenone, suggesting that nicotinic transmission may provide a potential therapeutic target for delaying the progression of neurodegenerative diseases such as AD and PD.

title: High-throughput parallel proteogenomics: a bacterial case study.
text:
In recent years, a new approach to genome annotation known as "proteogenomics" has emerged, which leverages mass spectrometry (MS) to annotate a genome. This approach involves mapping peptides to a six-frame translation of the genome, including available splice databases, to refine gene models. By using this method, it is possible to improve the accuracy of gene regions such as exon boundaries, novel genes, gene boundaries, frame shifts, reverse strands, translated UTRs, and novel splice junctions. However, there are challenges associated with assigning confidence to the resulting annotations and applying these refinements to gene models.
One of the main challenges is determining the best approach for assigning confidence to the annotations and applying the refinements to gene models. This is not a straightforward process, as many gene prediction tools have been trained on and refined with model organisms such as Arabidopsis thaliana and Escherichia coli, and may not be suitable for niche genomes. In this study, we outline a suitable approach for preprocessing mass spectra and optimizing the MS/MS search for a given dataset, and discuss future challenges and better strategies for tackling them.
We use Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens (nitrogen-fixing bacteria) as a case study, utilizing the latest second-generation proteogenomics tools with multiple gene models for cross-validation of proteogenomics annotations. By leveraging these tools, we aim to improve the accuracy of gene annotation and better understand the complexities of the genome.

title: Keratinocyte-specific transglutaminase of cultured human epidermal cells: relation to cross-linked envelope formation and terminal differentiation.
text: The predominant form of the cross-linking enzyme, transglutaminase, in cultured normal human epidermal keratinocytes is primarily located in cellular particles and can be solubilized using nonionic detergents. Upon anion-exchange or gel-filtration chromatography, it elutes as a single peak. Monoclonal antibodies raised against the particulate enzyme recognize two transglutaminases in the cell cytosol, with the second cytosolic transglutaminase showing distinct kinetic and physical properties from the first and not being essential for the formation of the keratinocyte cross-linked envelope in vitro. The anti-transglutaminase antibodies stain the more differentiated layers of the epidermis in a pattern similar to that seen with anti-involucrin antiserum, supporting the idea that the identified transglutaminase is involved in cross-linked envelope formation in vivo.

title: The effects of genetic and pharmacological blockade of the CB1 cannabinoid receptor on anxiety.
text: The purpose of this study was to compare the impact of genetic and pharmacological disruption of the CB1 cannabinoid receptor on anxiety levels in mice. In the first experiment, the behavior of CB1-knockout mice and wild-type mice was contrasted. In the second experiment, the cannabinoid antagonist SR141716A (0, 1, and 3 mg/kg) was administered to both CB1-knockout and wild-type mice. Unexpectedly, SR141716A reduced anxiety in both wild-type and CB1-knockout mice, despite only marginally affecting locomotion. Recent research suggests the existence of a novel cannabinoid receptor in the brain, and SR141716A has been shown to bind to both the CB1 and this novel receptor. The findings presented here support these discoveries, suggesting that the cannabinoid receptor antagonist affected anxiety in both wild-type and CB1-knockout mice, implying that the novel receptor may play a role in anxiety. It is possible that the discrepancy between the effects of genetic and pharmacological blockade of the CB1 receptor may indicate the involvement of the novel receptor in anxiety.

title: Immune activation and HIV persistence: implications for curative approaches to HIV infection.
text: Despite the effective suppression of HIV replication with combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), both the virus and chronic inflammation/immune dysfunction persist indefinitely. Unraveling the relationship between HIV and the host immune environment during therapy may lead to novel interventions aimed at either curing the infection or preventing the development of inflammation-associated organ damage. Chronic inflammation and immune dysfunction may contribute to HIV persistence by promoting virus production, generating new target cells, infecting both activated and resting cells, altering the migration patterns of susceptible cells, increasing the proliferation of infected cells, and impairing normal HIV clearance mechanisms. In turn, chronic HIV production or replication may exacerbate inflammation and immune dysfunction, creating a vicious cycle that perpetuates the persistence of the virus. The rapidly evolving data on these issues suggest that understanding this complex relationship is crucial for developing effective strategies to cure HIV infection.

title: Tissue-specific alterations in the glucocorticoid sensitivity of immune cells following repeated social defeat in mice
text:
Endogenous glucocorticoids (GC) play a crucial role in terminating the inflammatory response following infection and tissue injury. However, recent findings suggest that stress can impair the anti-inflammatory effects of these hormones. To investigate this further, we studied the impact of social disruption (SDR) stress on the immunosuppressive effects of corticosterone (CORT) in mice. We found that splenocytes from SDR-stressed mice were less sensitive to the immunosuppressive effects of CORT, leading to increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and enhanced cell survival. Myeloid cells expressing the marker CD11b were found to play a key role in this process.
To explore the potential source of GC-insensitive cells, we investigated the bone marrow as a possible source. Our results showed that bone marrow cells were virtually GC-resistant and retained high levels of cell viability even after treatment with CORT. However, repeated exposure to the acute stressor over a period of 2, 4, or 6 days led to an increase in the GC sensitivity of the bone marrow cells. This increase in GC sensitivity was associated with enhanced mRNA expression of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), an increase in the number of myeloid progenitors, and a decrease in the proportion of mature CD11b+ cells. The changes in the cellular composition of the bone marrow were accompanied by an increase in splenic CD11b+ cell numbers. Interestingly, we found a significant negative correlation between the GC sensitivity of bone marrow and spleen cells, suggesting that social stress causes the redistribution of GC-insensitive myeloid cells from the bone marrow to the spleen.
In summary, our findings suggest that stress can impair the anti-inflammatory effects of endogenous glucocorticoids, and that the bone marrow may play a key role in this process. The redistribution of GC-insensitive myeloid cells from the bone marrow to the spleen may contribute to the exacerbation of inflammation in response to stress.

title: Delays in the diagnosis of lung cancer.
text:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer patients often experience delays in diagnosis, which can lead to advanced stage at diagnosis and poor long-term survival. This study aims to investigate the delays experienced by patients referred to a regional cancer center with lung cancer.
METHODS: A prospective cohort of patients referred with newly diagnosed lung cancer were surveyed over a 3-month period to assess delays in diagnosis. Patients were asked when they first experienced symptoms, saw their doctor, underwent tests, and started treatment. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the different time intervals.
RESULTS: Of the 73 patients referred, 56 (77%) consented to participate, and 52 (30 males, 22 females) were interviewed, as two patients died before being interviewed and two could not be contacted. The median age of the patients was 68 years, and the stage distribution was as follows: IB/IIA (10%), stage IIIA (20%), IIIB/IV (70%). Patients waited a median of 21 days (interquartile range [IQR] 7-51 days) before seeing a doctor and a further 22 days (IQR 0-38 days) to complete any investigations. The median time from presentation to specialist referral was 27 days (IQR 12-49 days), and a further 23.5 days (IQR 10-56 days) to complete investigations. The median wait to start treatment once patients were seen at the cancer center was 10 days (IQR 2-28 days). The overall time from development of first symptoms to starting treatment was 138 days (IQR 79-175 days).
CONCLUSIONS: Lung cancer patients experience significant delays from the development of symptoms to first initiating treatment. These findings highlight the need to raise awareness of lung cancer symptoms and establish rapid assessment clinics for patients with suspected lung cancers.

title: Calcium and peak bone mass.
text:
Based on previous epidemiological, clinical, and experimental studies, it has been demonstrated that adequate calcium intake during growth can influence peak bone mass/density and prevent postmenopausal and senile osteoporosis. Calcium intake during adolescence appears to affect skeletal calcium retention directly, and a calcium intake of up to 1600 mg/day may be required for optimal prevention. Adolescent females at the time of puberty are considered the optimal population for early prevention of osteoporosis through calcium intake. Young individuals must be in a state of positive calcium balance to provide the necessary calcium for skeletal modeling and consolidation, although the exact degree of balance required to achieve peak bone mass and density is unknown.
To determine calcium requirements in young individuals and evaluate the determinants of calcium metabolism during peak bone mass acquisition, a review of 487 calcium balances from published reports was conducted according to developmental phase and calcium intake. The analysis showed that calcium intake and skeletal modeling/turnover are the most important determinants of calcium balance during growth, with the highest requirements during infancy, adolescence, and young adulthood. Infants and adolescents have higher calcium absorption than children and young adults to meet their high calcium needs. The absorption of calcium during periods of rapid bone modeling/turnover is likely mediated by Nicolaysen's endogenous factor. Urinary calcium levels increase with age, reaching a maximum by the end of puberty, and calcium intake has little effect on urinary calcium excretion during the period of most rapid skeletal formation.
Based on these studies, it is suggested that the Recommended Daily Allowance (RDA) for calcium should be higher than currently established for children, adolescents, and young adults to ensure sufficient skeletal retention of calcium for optimal peak bone mass formation. In addition to nutrition, heredity (both parents) and endocrine factors (sexual development) also appear to have a significant impact on peak bone mass formation, with most skeletal mass accumulated by late adolescence indicating an early timing of peak bone mass.

title: Most clinical tests cannot accurately diagnose rotator cuff pathology: a systematic review.
text:
Question: Do clinical tests accurately diagnose rotator cuff pathology?
Design: Systematic review of investigations into the diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests for rotator cuff pathology.
Participants: People with shoulder pain who underwent clinical testing to diagnose rotator cuff pathology.
Outcome Measures: The diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests was determined using likelihood ratios.
Results: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria, evaluating 14 clinical tests in 89 separate assessments of diagnostic accuracy. Only one evaluation, palpation for supraspinatus ruptures, resulted in significant positive and negative likelihood ratios. Eight of the 89 evaluations resulted in either significant positive or negative likelihood ratios, but none of these were found in other studies. Of the 89 evaluations, 71 (80%) did not result in either significant positive or negative likelihood ratio evaluations across different studies.
