title: Subversion of Systemic Glucose Metabolism as a Mechanism to Support the Growth of Leukemia Cells.
text: From a biological standpoint, cancer cells can be viewed as parasitic entities that compete with the host for essential resources such as glucose. In this context, we investigated the phenomenon of adaptive homeostasis in leukemia models and human leukemia samples, where malignant cells manipulate systemic physiology to prioritize their glucose needs. Specifically, we found that tumor cells induce excessive production of IGFBP1 from adipose tissue to impair insulin sensitivity, while also disrupting gut microbiota, serotonin production, and incretin function to suppress insulin secretion. Notably, disrupting the adaptive homeostasis of leukemia cells leads to attenuated disease progression and prolonged survival. Our findings offer a novel approach to managing leukemic disease at a systemic level.

title: Tumor-derived exosomes induce N2 polarization of neutrophils to promote gastric cancer cell migration
text:
Background: Exosomes are extracellular vesicles that play a crucial role in intercellular communication, both in health and disease. Tumor-derived exosomes have been shown to modulate the immune response and contribute to tumor progression. However, the mechanisms by which tumor-derived exosomes regulate neutrophil function are not fully understood.
Methods: In this study, we investigated the effects of gastric cancer cell-derived exosomes (GC-Ex) on the pro-tumor activation of neutrophils and elucidated the underlying mechanisms. We used a variety of techniques, including cell viability assays, western blotting, and immunofluorescence staining, to evaluate the effects of GC-Ex on neutrophil function.
Results: Our results showed that GC-Ex prolonged neutrophil survival and induced expression of inflammatory factors in neutrophils. In turn, GC-Ex-activated neutrophils promoted gastric cancer cell migration. We found that GC-Ex transported high mobility group box-1 (HMGB1), which activated the NF-κB pathway through interaction with TLR4, leading to an increased autophagic response in neutrophils. Blocking HMGB1/TLR4 interaction, NF-κB pathway, and autophagy reversed GC-Ex-induced neutrophil activation. Silencing HMGB1 in gastric cancer cells confirmed HMGB1 as a key factor for GC-Ex-mediated neutrophil activation. Furthermore, HMGB1 expression was upregulated in gastric cancer tissues, and increased HMGB1 expression was associated with poor prognosis in patients with gastric cancer. Finally, we showed that gastric cancer tissue-derived exosomes acted similarly as exosomes derived from gastric cancer cell lines in neutrophil activation.
Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that gastric cancer cell-derived exosomes induce autophagy and pro-tumor activation of neutrophils via HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling, providing new insights into mechanisms for neutrophil regulation in cancer and shedding light on the multifaceted role of exosomes in reshaping tumor microenvironment.

title: ROS-induced R loops trigger a transcription-coupled but BRCA1/2-independent homologous recombination pathway through CSB
text: Active genome regions are safeguarded by transcription-coupled DNA repair mechanisms, including transcription-coupled homologous recombination (TC-HR). We employed reactive oxygen species (ROS) to induce and investigate TC-HR at a transcribed locus in human cells. As with canonical HR, TC-HR requires RAD51. However, RAD51 localization to damage sites during TC-HR does not rely on BRCA1 and BRCA2, but rather on RAD52 and Cockayne Syndrome Protein B (CSB). During TC-HR, RAD52 is recruited by CSB through an acidic domain. CSB, in turn, is recruited by R loops, which are strongly induced by ROS in transcribed regions. Interestingly, CSB exhibits a strong affinity for DNA:RNA hybrids in vitro, suggesting that it acts as a sensor of ROS-induced R loops. Therefore, TC-HR is initiated by R loops, carried out by the CSB-RAD52-RAD51 axis, and establishes a BRCA1/2-independent alternative HR pathway that protects the transcribed genome.

title: Autophagy and its potent modulators from phytochemicals in cancer treatment
text:
Autophagy is a fundamental cellular process that helps remove damaged or harmful components within cells, ultimately leading to cellular self-digestion and recycling. This process is crucial in cancer treatment, as it can help prevent cancer cells from growing and dividing uncontrollably. Therapy-induced autophagy can act as a pro-survival mechanism, but excessive or uncontrolled autophagy can lead to non-apoptotic cell death, also known as autophagic cell death.
Natural compounds found in plants and herbs have been used for centuries to treat various types of cancers. Recent evidence suggests that these compounds can target the autophagic pathway, making them promising agents for cancer treatment. However, these compounds have different effects on autophagy, and their dynamic role in regulating this process must be evaluated.
In this review, we discuss the role of autophagy in cancer development and therapy, with a focus on the anti-cancer activities of autophagic modulators, particularly phytochemicals. We also propose a novel premise that the dynamic role of phytochemicals in regulating autophagy should be evaluated in cancer treatment. By understanding the complex interplay between autophagy and cancer, we can develop more effective and targeted cancer therapies.

title: Exosomal miR-99a-5p is elevated in sera of ovarian cancer patients and promotes cancer cell invasion by increasing fibronectin and vitronectin expression in neighboring peritoneal mesothelial cells
text:
This study aimed to investigate the potential of using circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) in the blood, specifically exosomal miRNAs, as a diagnostic marker for ovarian cancer. The study also explored the functional role of exosomal miRNAs in ovarian cancer progression.
Methods:
The study used exosomes collected from serous ovarian cancer cell lines, TYK-nu and HeyA8 cells, and analyzed the expression of miRNAs in these exosomes using an exosomal miRNA microarray. The expression levels of serum miR-99a-5p were determined in 62 patients with ovarian cancer, 26 patients with benign ovarian tumors, and 20 healthy volunteers using miRNA quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). The study also investigated the effect of exosomal miR-99a-5p on human peritoneal mesothelial cells (HPMCs) and analyzed the potential target genes of miR-99a-5p using proteomic analysis with the tandem mass tag method.
Results:
The study found that the serum levels of miR-99a-5p were significantly higher in patients with ovarian cancer compared to benign tumor patients and healthy volunteers. A receiver operating characteristic curve analysis showed that a cut-off of 1.41 had a sensitivity and specificity of 0.85 and 0.75, respectively, for detecting ovarian cancer. The study also found that the expression levels of miR-99a-5p were significantly decreased after ovarian cancer surgery, indicating that miR-99a-5p may reflect tumor burden. Treatment with exosomes from ovarian cancer cells increased the expression of miR-99a-5p in HPMCs, which promoted ovarian cancer invasion by upregulating fibronectin and vitronectin.

Conclusions:
The study suggests that serum miR-99a-5p may be a promising diagnostic marker for ovarian cancer, with a sensitivity and specificity of 0.85 and 0.75, respectively. The study also found that exosomal miR-99a-5p from ovarian cancer cells promotes ovarian cancer invasion by affecting HPMCs through fibronectin and vitronectin upregulation, and may serve as a target for inhibiting ovarian cancer progression.

title: The Pfam protein families database.
text: Pfam is a widely utilized database of protein families, currently boasting over 13,000 manually curated protein families as of version 26.0. Pfam is accessible through servers located in the UK (http://pfam.sanger.ac.uk/), the USA (http://pfam.janelia.org/), and Sweden (http://pfam.sbc.su.se/). Here, we provide an update on the changes that have occurred since our 2010 NAR paper (version 24.0). Over the past two years, we have created 1840 new families and increased the coverage of the UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) to nearly 80%. To further engage the Wikipedia community, we have linked Pfam families to relevant Wikipedia pages and encouraged the Pfam and Wikipedia communities to improve and expand those pages. We continue to enhance the Pfam website and add new visualizations, such as the 'sunburst' representation of the taxonomic distribution of families. In this work, we also address two topics of particular interest to the Pfam community. First, we explain the definition and use of family-specific, manually curated gathering thresholds. Second, we discuss the features of domains of unknown function (also known as DUFs), which constitute a rapidly growing class of families within Pfam.

title: Exercise as a therapeutic approach to improve blood pressure in patients with peripheral arterial disease: current literature and future directions.
text:
INTRODUCTION:
Patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) often exhibit reduced functional capacity and increased mortality due to cardiovascular disease. Despite the importance of exercise in improving walking capacity in these patients, the effects of exercise on cardiovascular parameters have been inadequately explored. This review aims to examine the role of exercise in reducing blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD and to summarize the current evidence on the acute and chronic effects of walking and resistance exercise on blood pressure and its determinants.
AREAS COVERED:
This review will focus on the following areas:
1. The acute and chronic effects of exercise on blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD.
2. The specific effects of walking and resistance exercise on blood pressure and its determinants.
3. The potential benefits and limitations of exercise interventions in patients with symptomatic PAD.
EXPERT COMMENTARY:
The findings of this review suggest that exercise promotes both acute and chronic reductions in blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD. These effects were observed primarily after walking and resistance exercise. While the current evidence suggests that exercise interventions may be beneficial for patients with symptomatic PAD, further research is needed to investigate the effects of other exercise modalities, particularly non-painful exercises, on cardiovascular function in this population.
By summarizing the current evidence on the effects of exercise on blood pressure in patients with symptomatic PAD, this review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the potential benefits and limitations of exercise interventions in this population. The findings of this review may inform the development of exercise programs tailored to the specific needs of patients with symptomatic PAD, with the goal of improving cardiovascular function and reducing mortality risk.

title: Morin Exhibits Anti-Inflammatory Effects on IL-1β-Stimulated Human Osteoarthritis Chondrocytes by Activating the Nrf2 Signaling Pathway
text:
Background/Aims: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a complex disease characterized by joint inflammation, which can lead to the degradation of cartilage and bone. Morin, a flavonoid compound, has been shown to have anti-inflammatory properties. The aim of this study was to investigate the anti-inflammatory activity and mechanism of morin on human osteoarthritis chondrocytes stimulated by interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β).
Methods: The study used human osteoarthritis chondrocytes stimulated by IL-1β to evaluate the anti-inflammatory activity of morin. The levels of nitric oxide (NO) and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) were measured using the Griess method and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), respectively. The levels of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) 1, 3, and 13 were also measured using ELISA.
Results: The results showed that IL-1β significantly increased the production of NO, PGE2, MMP1, MMP3, and MMP13. Treatment with morin significantly attenuated these increases. Additionally, IL-1β-induced nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation was suppressed by morin. Furthermore, the expression of Nrf2 and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) were increased by morin, and knockdown of Nrf2 could prevent the anti-inflammatory effects of morin.
Conclusion: In conclusion, this study suggests that morin attenuates IL-1β-induced inflammation by activating the Nrf2 signaling pathway, which leads to the suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and matrix degrading enzymes. These findings provide evidence for the potential use of morin as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of osteoarthritis.

title: Impact of blood pressure variability on cardiovascular events in elderly patients with hypertension.
text: In elderly hypertensive patients, blood pressure variability is a characteristic feature of hypertension. However, its clinical significance remains unclear. To investigate the impact of blood pressure variability on the development of cardiovascular events in elderly hypertensive patients, we conducted a study on 106 consecutive patients aged 60 years or older (mean age: 73.9 ± 8.1 years; male: 54%). All patients underwent 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and were followed up for a median of 34 months (range: 3-60 months). During the follow-up period, 39 cardiovascular events occurred, including 14 cases of cerebral infarction and 7 cases of acute myocardial infarction. We used the coefficient of variation (CV) of 24-hour systolic blood pressure (SBP) values as an index of blood pressure variability and divided the patients into two groups according to their mean CV value (a cut-off point of 10.6%). The results showed that the rate of cardiovascular events was significantly higher in the high CV group than in the low CV group (p < 0.05). In addition, Cox's proportional hazards analysis revealed that increased blood pressure variability was an independent predictive variable for cardiovascular events. Furthermore, the CV value of daytime SBP and the SD value of both 24-hour SBP and daytime SBP were found to have positive correlations with the onset of cardiovascular events. These findings suggest that increased blood pressure variability may be an independent risk factor for cardiovascular events in elderly hypertensive patients.

title: Reprogramming committed murine blood cells to induced hematopoietic stem cells with defined factors.
text: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are responsible for maintaining blood production throughout a person's lifetime, and they are the primary cells used in bone marrow transplantation. We have discovered that briefly expressing six transcription factors (Run1t1, Hlf, Lmo2, Prdm5, Pbx1, and Zfp37) in otherwise committed lymphoid and myeloid progenitors and myeloid effector cells can grant these cells the ability to differentiate into multiple blood cell types. The inclusion of additional factors such as Mycn and Meis1, as well as the use of polycistronic viruses, significantly enhances the efficiency of reprogramming. The resulting cells, which we have designated as induced-HSCs (iHSCs), possess the ability to differentiate into multiple blood cell types in a clonal manner, reconstitute the stem/progenitor compartments, and can be serially transplanted. Using single-cell analysis, we found that iHSCs derived under optimal conditions exhibit a gene expression profile that is remarkably similar to that of endogenous HSCs. These findings demonstrate that the expression of a specific set of transcription factors is sufficient to activate the gene networks that govern HSC functional identity in committed blood cells. Our results suggest that blood cell reprogramming may be a viable strategy for generating transplantable stem cells for clinical applications.

title: Genetic variability in a frozen batch of MCF-7 cells invisible in routine authentication affecting cell function
text:
Cell line authentication, annotation, and quality control measures often fall short in addressing genetic heterogeneity within cell lines. In the Human Toxome Project, we found that there can be significant cellular and phenotypic heterogeneity within a single batch of the human breast adenocarcinoma cell line MCF-7, even when obtained directly from a cell bank. STR profiling, a common method used for cell authentication, only serves to detect cross-contamination and misidentification of cell lines, but does not reveal the full extent of heterogeneity within a cell line.
Our findings demonstrate that heterogeneity in cell lines can have serious consequences for the reproducibility of experiments. For example, we observed differences in morphology, estrogenic growth response, whole genome gene expression, and untargeted mass-spectroscopy metabolomics between MCF-7 cells. Using Comparative Genomic Hybridization (CGH), we traced these differences back to genetic heterogeneity present in the cells from the original frozen vials, even from the same ATCC lot. However, STR markers did not reveal any differences between the samples and the ATCC reference.
These findings highlight the need for additional quality assurance measures in Good Cell Culture Practice and cell characterization, particularly using methods such as CGH to detect possible genomic heterogeneity and genetic drifts within cell lines. By improving our understanding of the genetic diversity within cell lines, we can better ensure the reliability and accuracy of research results.

title: The Mammalian-Specific Protein Armcx1 Regulates Mitochondrial Transport during Axon Regeneration
text: Mitochondrial transport plays a vital role in the physiology of neurons and their axons, but its impact on neuronal injury responses, such as survival and regeneration, remains largely unexplored. In a mouse model with robust axon regeneration, we discovered that Armcx1, a gene encoding a mitochondria-localized protein, is upregulated after axotomy in this high regeneration condition. Overexpressing Armcx1 in adult retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) enhances mitochondrial transport, and both neuronal survival and axon regeneration are promoted after injury. These effects are dependent on the mitochondrial localization of Armcx1. In contrast, silencing Armcx1 hinders both neuronal survival and axon regeneration in this high regeneration model, further supporting the key role of Armcx1 in regulating neuronal injury responses in the adult central nervous system (CNS). Our findings suggest that Armcx1 regulates mitochondrial transport during neuronal repair.

title: A diversity of beta diversities: straightening up a concept gone awry. Part 1. Defining beta diversity as a function of alpha and gamma diversity
text: The term "beta diversity" has been used to encompass a wide range of phenomena, each capturing a different aspect of compositional heterogeneity between locations. However, these concepts are not necessarily related or interconnected. This two-part review aims to provide a unified framework for understanding the various definitions of beta diversity and what they measure. In this first part, we focus on defining the beta component of diversity, which involves determining what diversity means and how it is partitioned into alpha (a) and beta (b) components. Different definitions of "beta diversity" have been used in the ecological literature, but true beta diversity is obtained when the total effective number of species in a dataset (true gamma diversity g) is multiplicatively partitioned into the effective number of species per compositionally distinct community.

title: A cross-cultural study of wine consumers with respect to health benefits of wine
text: The current study aimed to investigate consumer preferences and consumption habits regarding the health benefits of wine among two culturally and demographically diverse groups: Koreans and Australians. Participants were required to be wine drinkers aged 18 or older. Data was collected through an online questionnaire, which revealed that perceived health benefits of red wine were higher in the Australian sample than the Korean sample. Additionally, Australian consumers had more knowledge about health benefits of wine compared to Korean consumers. Red wine was the preferred wine style for both groups, but the proportion of preference for red wine was significantly higher in the Korean sample. In terms of expenditure on wine products, both groups preferred a price range of AUD$11-$19. The findings also showed that health-oriented wine was more appealing to Korean consumers than Australian consumers. Interestingly, Korean women preferred red wine as much as men, while Australian women consumed significantly more white wine than men. These results provide valuable insights for winemakers and wine marketers on the importance of emphasizing health aspects in wine production and marketing to maximize consumer appeal.

title: DIASPORA BONDS: TAPPING THE DIASPORA DURING DIFFICULT TIMES
text: India and Israel have collectively raised over US$35 billion by leveraging the financial resources of their diaspora communities. These diaspora bonds represent a reliable and cost-effective source of external funding, often when countries face difficulties accessing international capital markets. For diaspora investors, these bonds offer a unique opportunity to support their country of origin while also providing a valuable investment opportunity. The potential for diaspora bonds is substantial for many countries with large diaspora populations abroad. However, for countries with weak governance and high sovereign risk, diaspora bond issuance may require support for institutional capacity building and credit enhancement from international organizations or bilateral agencies. For instance, Haiti could potentially raise several hundred million dollars through diaspora bond issuance if a suitable guarantee structure is put in place to reassure investors in the country's public institutions.

title: Peroxisome Proliferator Activated Receptor gamma (PPARγ) Agonist Rosiglitazone Ameliorate Airway Inflammation by Inhibiting Toll-Like Receptor 2 (TLR2)/Nod-Like Receptor with Pyrin Domain Containing 3 (NLRP3) Inflammatory Corpuscle Activation in Asthmatic Mice
text:
The purpose of this study was to investigate the function and mechanism of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) agonist rosiglitazone in the toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2)/nod-like receptor with pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammatory corpuscle pathway in asthmatic mice.
MATERIALS AND METHODS:
Eighteen female mice (C57) were randomly divided into four groups: control, asthma model group challenged with ovalbumin (OVA), rosiglitazone group, and PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone treatment group. The study observed the infiltration of peribronchial inflammatory cells and the proliferation and mucus secretion of bronchial epithelial goblet cells through hematoxylin and eosin and periodic acid-Schiff staining. Western blots were used to detect the expression levels of TLR2, PPARγ, nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), NLRP3, and ASC [apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing C-terminal caspase recruitment domain (CARD)].
RESULTS:
The study found that the number of inflammatory cells and eosinophils, as well as the levels of OVA-specific IgE, interleukin-4 (IL-4), and IL-13, were significantly higher in the C57 asthma group compared to the C57 control group and the treatment group (P<0.05). The infiltration of peribronchiolar inflammatory cells, wall thickening, goblet cell hyperplasia, and mucus secretion in the treatment group were all significantly decreased compared to those in the asthma group. PPARγ expression in the treatment group was significantly higher compared to the asthma group and the control group (P<0.05). The protein expression levels of TLR2, NF-κB, NLRP3, and ASC were significantly lower in the asthma group but were higher in the control group (P<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS:
The study concluded that PPARγ rosiglitazone ameliorates airway inflammation by inhibiting NF-κB expression in asthmatic mice, and further inhibits the activation of TLR2/NLRP3 inflammatory corpuscles.

title: Omi/HtrA2 Participates in Age-Related Autophagic Deficiency in Rat Liver
text:
The liver is a vital organ with numerous essential functions, and the preservation of normal hepatic function is crucial for overall health. As an integral mechanism for maintaining cellular homeostasis, autophagy plays a pivotal role in ensuring proper organ function. Research has shown that decline in hepatic function is often associated with deficiencies in autophagy in aging livers. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. The serine protease Omi/HtrA2 belongs to the HtrA family and promotes apoptosis through either the caspase-dependent or caspase-independent pathway. Mice lacking Omi/HtrA2 exhibit progeria symptoms (premature aging), which are similar to the characteristics of autophagic insufficiency.
In this study, we demonstrated that both the protein level of Omi/HtrA2 in the liver and hepatic function decline with age in rats, and there is a positive correlation between them. Furthermore, several autophagy-related proteins (LC3II/I, Beclin-1, and LAMP2) in rat liver were significantly decreased with increasing age. Finally, inhibition of Omi/HtrA2 resulted in reduced autophagy and hepatic dysfunction. These findings suggest that Omi/HtrA2 participates in age-related autophagic deficiency in rat liver, offering a novel insight into the mechanisms involved in liver aging.

title: Macrosomia and Hyperinsulinaemic Hypoglycaemia in Patients with Heterozygous Mutations in the HNF4A Gene
text: Macrosomia, characterized by an excessively large fetus, is associated with a higher risk of neonatal and maternal complications. Despite the prevalence of this condition, the underlying factors remain poorly understood. However, recent studies have implicated increased foetal insulin secretion as a key mediator of macrosomia in offspring of diabetic mothers and those with congenital hyperinsulinemia. To investigate the in utero and neonatal role of two crucial regulators of pancreatic insulin secretion, we conducted a study examining the birthweight and incidence of neonatal hypoglycaemia in patients with heterozygous mutations in the maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) genes HNF4A (encoding HNF-4α) and HNF1A/TCF1 (encoding HNF-1α), as well as the effect of pancreatic deletion of Hnf4a on foetal and neonatal insulin secretion in mice.

title: ART adherence clubs: A long-term retention strategy for clinically stable patients receiving antiretroviral therapy
text: The ART adherence club model described here offers patient-friendly access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) for clinically stable patients, reducing the burden on healthcare facilities while increasing resources for new and at-risk patients. Under the model, 30 patients are grouped together in an ART club, meeting every 2 months for less than an hour at a facility or community location. A lay club facilitator leads the group, providing quick clinical assessments, referrals as needed, and pre-packed ART. From 2011 to 2012, after adoption by the Western Cape Government, over 600 ART clubs were established in Cape Town, providing care to over 16,000 patients. This extensive and rapid rollout demonstrates strong patient and facility support, suggesting that a similar model could be successfully implemented nationally.

title: Exercise-linked FNDC5/irisin rescues synaptic plasticity and memory defects in Alzheimer’s models
text: Defective hormonal signaling in the brain has been implicated in the development of Alzheimer's disease (AD), a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by synaptic failure and memory loss. Irisin, an exercise-induced myokine, is produced through the cleavage of the membrane-bound precursor protein fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5). Our findings demonstrate that FNDC5/irisin levels are reduced in the hippocampi and cerebrospinal fluid of AD individuals, as well as in experimental AD models. Moreover, we have shown that knockdown of brain FNDC5/irisin impairs long-term potentiation and novel object recognition memory in mice, while boosting brain levels of FNDC5/irisin rescues synaptic plasticity and memory in AD mouse models. Interestingly, peripheral overexpression of FNDC5/irisin also rescues memory impairment, while blockade of either peripheral or brain FNDC5/irisin attenuates the neuroprotective actions of physical exercise on synaptic plasticity and memory in AD mice. Our findings suggest that FNDC5/irisin plays a crucial role in mediating the beneficial effects of exercise on synaptic plasticity and memory in AD models, thereby positioning it as a potential therapeutic agent for the treatment of AD.

title: Influence of antidepressant therapy on sick leave in primary care: ADAS, a comparative observational study
text:
Sweden's yearly sick leave expenditures are relatively modest compared to other European countries, with common mental disorders (CMD) accounting for 10-15% of the adult population. A Swedish register-based study found that antidepressant therapy for patients on long-term sick leave for CMD resulted in longer sick leave and higher frequency of non-time-limited sickness compensation compared to psychotherapy, work-oriented rehabilitation, and other therapies.
The aim of this study was to determine if patients treated with antidepressants while on long-term sick leave for depression, anxiety, and stress-related mental disorders had longer sick leave than those treated with other therapies.
This prospective, observational study included 192 patients from 28 primary health care centers in the Region Västra Götaland, Sweden, who were on sick leave for CMD. The outcome measures were gross and net sick leave days.
The results showed that there were no significant differences in sick leave days (gross or net) due to CMD between the patients treated and not treated with antidepressants during the 12-month observation period. However, the groups differed at baseline in terms of frequency of exhaustion disorder, with a higher frequency of exhaustion disorder in the group without antidepressants.
Analysis of other possible factors associated with shorter or longer sick leave revealed that the patient's own perception of possibility of returning to work in the near and distant future was a significant factor associated with longer sick leave. Specifically, the patient's perception of possibility of returning to their present workplace was associated with longer sick leave.
Given the significant impact of CMD on sick leave and sick leave costs, the patient's perception of possibility of returning to work in the near and distant future should be highlighted in future research on the rehabilitation process.

title: CDX2 inhibits the proliferation and tumor formation of colon cancer cells by suppressing Wnt/β-catenin signaling via transactivation of GSK-3β and Axin2 expression
text:
Introduction:
Caudal-related homeobox transcription factor 2 (CDX2) is an intestine-specific nuclear transcription factor that has been implicated in the tumorigenesis of various human cancers. However, the functional role of CDX2 in the development and progression of colorectal cancer (CRC) remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to investigate the role of CDX2 in CRC cell proliferation and tumor formation.
Methods:
We used CDX2 knockdown and overexpression in colon cancer cells to evaluate its effect on cell proliferation and tumor formation in vitro and in vivo. We also used TOP/FOP-Flash reporter assay to evaluate the effect of CDX2 on Wnt signaling activity, and western blot assay to evaluate the expression of downstream targets of Wnt signaling. In addition, we used dual-luciferase reporter and quantitative chromatin immunoprecipitation (qChIP) assays to investigate the direct binding of CDX2 to the promoter of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) and axis inhibition protein 2 (Axin2).
Results:
Our results showed that CDX2 knockdown in colon cancer cells promoted cell proliferation in vitro and accelerated tumor formation in vivo, while CDX2 overexpression inhibited cell proliferation. We also found that CDX2 knockdown or overexpression significantly increased or decreased Wnt signaling activity, respectively. Furthermore, we found that downstream targets of Wnt signaling, including β-catenin, cyclin D1, and c-myc, were up-regulated or down-regulated in CDX2-knockdown or CDX2-overexpressing colon cancer cells. Additionally, we found that suppression of Wnt signaling by XAV-939 led to a marked suppression of the cell proliferation enhanced by CDX2 knockdown, while activation of this signaling by CHIR-99021 significantly enhanced the cell proliferation inhibited by CDX2 overexpression.
Discussion:
Our results indicate that CDX2 inhibits the proliferation and tumor formation of colon cancer cells by suppressing Wnt/β-catenin signaling. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the tumorigenesis of CRC and suggest that CDX2 may be a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of CRC.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, our study demonstrates that CDX2 inhibits the proliferation and tumor formation of colon cancer cells by suppressing Wnt/β-catenin signaling. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the tumorigenesis of CRC and suggest that CDX2 may be a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of CRC.

title: Prostaglandin E2 mediates sensory nerve regulation of bone homeostasis
text: The question remains whether sensory nerves can detect changes in bone density or metabolic activity to regulate bone homeostasis. Our research has uncovered a novel mechanism by which sensory nerves are involved in bone formation and remodeling. We found that prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) secreted by osteoblastic cells activates EP4 receptors in sensory nerves, leading to inhibition of sympathetic activity through the central nervous system and regulation of bone formation. Our findings suggest that PGE2 secreted by osteoblasts increases when bone density decreases, as demonstrated in osteoporotic animal models. Ablation of sensory nerves leads to erosion of skeletal integrity. Knockout of the EP4 gene in sensory nerves or cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2) in osteoblastic cells significantly reduces bone volume in adult mice. Sympathetic tone is increased in sensory denervation models, and propranolol, a β2-adrenergic antagonist, rescues bone loss. Moreover, injection of SW033291, a small molecule that increases PGE2 levels locally, significantly boosts bone formation, while the effect is blocked in EP4 knockout mice. Our results demonstrate that PGE2 mediates the sensory nerve's control over bone homeostasis and promotes regeneration.

title: The Bone and Joint Decade 2000-2010.
text: According to the World Health Organization, the period between 2000 and 2010 was declared the Bone and Joint Decade. This designation is timely and appropriate, as hundreds of millions of people worldwide are afflicted with disabilities caused by trauma, aging, and degenerative conditions affecting the musculoskeletal system. Advances in orthopedic surgery and rheumatology have significantly benefited patients through improvements in pharmacology, imaging techniques, surgical methods, and the use of artificial materials to replace damaged bone and cartilage. However, these man-made materials are prone to wear and tear and loosening within the host bone. As we enter the Bone and Joint Decade, further progress in treating bone and joint diseases depends on more fundamental research into cartilage and bone. The Human Genome Project has provided a better understanding of disease genes and the potential for gene manipulation to prevent and treat specific diseases. Cartilage cell culture and transplantation are already a reality, and tissue engineering, which involves growing cells in three-dimensional collagen or synthetic biodegradable polymers, is expected to be used in the future to replace damaged bone and cartilage with living and bone and cartilaginous tissues, respectively. While significant progress has been made, more research is needed to achieve a breakthrough in the treatment of bone and joint diseases by the end of this decade.

title: Prevalence of late-life depression and gap in mental health service use across European regions.
text:
In this study, we aimed to investigate the prevalence and disparities in the use of mental health services among older adults with late-life depression in four European regions (Western Europe, Scandinavia, Southern Europe, and Central and Eastern Europe). We also examined various socio-demographic, social, and health-related factors that might be associated with mental health service use.
Our study was based on data from the Survey on Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, which included a population-based sample of 28,796 individuals (53% women, mean age 74 years) living in Europe. We estimated the prevalence of late-life depression in the whole sample and compared the results across the four regions. We also identified factors that were most strongly associated with depression, including the number of chronic diseases, pain, limitations in instrumental activities of daily living, grip strength, and cognitive impairment.
Our findings revealed that the prevalence of late-life depression was highest in Southern Europe (35%), followed by Central and Eastern Europe (32%), Western Europe (26%), and lowest in Scandinavia (17%). The gap in mental health service use was significant, with 79% of individuals with depression not seeking professional help.
We concluded that interventions aimed at reducing the burden of late-life depression should focus on individuals with chronic somatic comorbidities and limitations in mental and physical functioning. Strategies to promote help-seeking among older adults, reduce stigma associated with mental illness, and educate general practitioners could help narrow the gap in mental health service utilization.

title: Impedance and Interface Properties of Al/Methyl-Red/p-InP Solar Cell
text: An Al/methyl-red/p-InP solar cell was fabricated using a solution-processing method and characterized using current-voltage (I-V) and capacitance-voltage-frequency (C-V-f) measurements at room temperature. From the dark I-V characteristics, the ideality factor and barrier height of the device were calculated as 1.11 eV and 2.02, respectively. The device exhibited good photovoltaic behavior with a maximum open circuit voltage of 0.38 V and short-circuit current of 2.8 nA under low light intensity of 200 lx. The barrier height and acceptor carrier concentration values for the Al/methyl-red/p-InP devices were extracted as 1.27 eV and from the linear region of its characteristics, respectively. The difference between the I-V and C-V measurements was attributed to the different nature of the two types of measurements. Additionally, the energy distribution curves of the interface states and their time constants were obtained from the experimental conductance properties of the Al/methyl-red/p-InP structure at room temperature. The interface state densities and their relaxation times of the device ranged from 1.11 eV to 0.79 eV, and decreased with bias voltage from the experimental results.

title: R: A Language for Data Analysis and Graphics
text: In this article, we detail our experience in creating and implementing a novel statistical computing language. Drawing inspiration from two existing programming languages, we sought to integrate their most valuable features into our new language. Our innovation offers significant advantages in the realms of portability, computational efficiency, memory management, and scoping.

title: The Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates
text:
The most widely used and cited atlas of the mouse brain, "The Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates," provides researchers and students with accurate stereotaxic coordinates for laboratory use and detailed delineations and indexing of structures for reference. The accompanying DVD offers drawings of brain structures that can be used as templates for publication figures. The third edition is both a significant revision and expansion of previous editions.
New features include:
* High-resolution digital color photography of tissue sections in the horizontal plane of section, complementing the coronal and sagittal series.
* All tissue sections are now shown in high resolution digital color photography.
* Photographs of sections and intermediate sections are provided on the accompanying DVD in high-resolution JP 2000 format.
* Revised delineations and naming conventions consistent with Paxinos and Watson's "Rat Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates, 6th Edition."
* The atlas is now in a more practical 14"x11" format for convenient lab use.
* Full color throughout.
* Includes a CD of all plates and diagrams, as well as Adobe Illustrator files of the diagrams, and a variety of additional useful material.
* Coronal and sagittal diagrams are completely reworked and updated.
* Rhombomeric borders are included in sagittal figures for the first time in mammals.
* Microscopic plates are scanned with a new method in much higher quality.

title: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis
text: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis is the latest addition to the esteemed UseR! series by Springer, which has emerged as the most rapidly expanding resource for computational statistics at present. The books in this series are all interconnected with R, either showcasing a novel package created by the authors themselves or providing a comprehensive guide to applying statistical techniques using the diverse packages available in R. ggplot2 represents an implementation of The Grammar of Graphics (Wilkinson, 2005) in R, a systematic approach to the design of statistical graphics that was first introduced in a book reviewed in the Journal of Statistical Software by Cox (2007). This implementation has been developed by Hadley Wickham, who is also the author of the book under review.

title: Multiple Imputation For Nonresponse In Surveys
text: "Our book collection boasts a comprehensive treatment of multiple imputation for nonresponse in surveys, accessible to you through public online access. With instant download capabilities, you can conveniently retrieve the desired text from our servers, strategically located in various locations to minimize latency and ensure seamless access. Moreover, this work is compatible with a wide range of devices, ensuring a smooth reading experience regardless of the device you choose to use."

title: Inhibition of the dipeptidyl peptidase DPP4 (CD26) reveals IL-33-dependent eosinophil-mediated control of tumor growth
text: Inhibition of the dipeptidyl peptidase DPP4 (CD26) has been shown to enhance T cell migration and tumor immunity by preserving functional chemokine CXCL10. Building on these findings, we investigated the effect of DPP4 inhibition on tumor immunity in pre-clinical models of hepatocellular carcinoma and breast cancer. Our results revealed a distinct mechanism by which inhibition of DPP4 improves anti-tumor responses. Treatment with the DPP4 inhibitor sitagliptin led to increased levels of the chemokine CCL11 and enhanced migration of eosinophils into solid tumors. Enhanced tumor control was preserved in mice lacking lymphocytes and was ablated after depletion of eosinophils or treatment with degranulation inhibitors. We also demonstrated that tumor-cell expression of the alarmin IL-33 was necessary and sufficient for eosinophil-mediated anti-tumor responses, and this mechanism contributed to the efficacy of checkpoint-inhibitor therapy. These findings provide insight into the role of IL-33- and eosinophil-mediated tumor control, which is revealed when endogenous mechanisms of DPP4 immunoregulation are inhibited. Eosinophils, which were previously known mainly in allergy settings, are increasingly recognized as playing a role in other aspects of immunity. By using a clinically approved DPP4 inhibitor, we were able to facilitate the recruitment of eosinophils to mouse tumors, where they are essential for tumor destruction.

title: Cycling Quiescence in Temozolomide Resistant Glioblastoma Cells Is Partly Explained by microRNA-93 and -193-Mediated Decrease of Cyclin D
text:
Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a deadly brain tumor that often develops resistance to chemotherapy, particularly to the alkylating agent Temozolomide (TMZ). Despite extensive research, the mechanisms underlying TMZ resistance remain poorly understood. Our study aimed to investigate the mechanisms of TMZ resistance in GBM cells and identify potential therapeutic strategies to reverse chemoresistance.
We found that TMZ resistance in GBM cells is associated with upregulation of mismatch repair genes, ABC-targeted drug efflux, and cell cycle alterations. However, the mechanism by which TMZ induces cell cycle arrest in GBM cells has not been well-established. To investigate this further, we analyzed the expression of microRNAs (miRNAs) in TMZ-resistant GBM cells and found that miR-93 and -193 are significantly upregulated in these cells.
Computational analyses suggested that these miRNAs may target Cyclin D1, a key regulator of cell cycle progression. To validate these findings, we performed experiments to investigate the effects of miR-93 and -193 on Cyclin D1 expression. Our results showed that these miRNAs blunt the effects of TMZ on Cyclin D1 expression, leading to increased cell cycling quiescence and resistance to TMZ.
Furthermore, we found that miR-93 and -193 also decrease the sensitivity of GBM cells to TMZ. These findings provide a mechanism by which GBM cells can develop resistance to TMZ through miRNA-mediated targeting of Cyclin D1.
Our study also identified potential therapeutic approaches to reverse chemoresistance at the miRNA, exosomal, and cell cycle levels. These findings suggest that targeting miR-93 and -193 or their downstream targets may be a promising strategy to enhance the effectiveness of TMZ in treating GBM. Additionally, our findings highlight the importance of considering the complex interplay between GBM cells and their microenvironment in the development of chemoresistance.
In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms of TMZ resistance in GBM cells and identifies potential therapeutic strategies to overcome chemoresistance. Further research is needed to validate these findings and to explore their clinical implications.

title: Longitudinal changes in maternal corin and mid-regional proatrial natriuretic peptide in women at risk of pre-eclampsia
text:
Objectives: This study aimed to investigate the longitudinal changes in maternal plasma levels of corin and midregional proatrial natriuretic peptide (MR-PANP) in pregnancies that develop preeclampsia (PE) and gestational hypertension (GH).
Methods: A nested case-control study was conducted among a larger prospective longitudinal study of singleton pregnancies at high risk for PE. Blood samples were collected every four weeks until delivery. The distribution of maternal plasma corin and PANP was analyzed, and repeated measures were performed using a multilevel mixed-effects linear model.
Results: A total of 471 samples were analyzed from 122 women, including 85 that remained normotensive, 12 with GH, 13 term-PE, and 12 preterm-PE. In the normotensive group, log10 corin levels were associated with gestational age (p < 0.001). In the GH and term-PE groups, corin levels did not differ significantly from the normotensive group (p = 0.64 and p = 0.16, respectively). Compared to the normotensive group, MR-PANP levels were significantly higher in the preterm-PE and GH groups (p = 0.046 and p = 0.019, respectively), but not in the term-PE group (p = 0.47).
Conclusions: Maternal plasma corin and MR-PANP may be useful biomarkers for the prediction of preterm-PE. Disclosures: A. Khalil has received research support and has commercial interests in USCOM, Roche, Alere, NICOM, and Q-fFN. He has also served as a speaker for Roche.

title: Children's Exercise Physiology
text:
The newly revised and updated "Children's Exercise Physiology, Second Edition" offers the most current research, methodologies, and approaches related to children's physiological responses to exercise. This book examines not only the current gaps that separate children from adults, but also the underlying mechanisms of these differences. Readers will gain an understanding of what makes children distinct from adults physiologically, such as their smaller size, biochemical differences, neuromuscular differences, and lack of sexual and hormonal maturity, as well as the reasons for these differences. This book is particularly useful for individuals involved in young athlete development, disease management, and health promotion, as it provides valuable insights into the physiological determinants of exercise performance.
Since the first edition of this book was published eight years ago, the field of children's exercise physiology has rapidly evolved. This streamlined second edition contains 13 chapters, an introduction, and updated features to enhance learning, including:
* Chapter objectives, discussion questions, and research directions to facilitate comprehension
* A reorganized table of contents for improved flow between chapters
* A new final chapter dedicated to the role of the central nervous system
* In-depth discussion of the determinants of aerobic fitness and VO2 kinetics, as well as the significance of maximal aerobic power in children
* Enhanced chapters on thermoregulation and metabolic and endocrinologic responses to exercise
With this updated edition, readers can be confident they are receiving the most current information on children's exercise physiology.

title: Cost-effectiveness in health and medicine
text:
Chapter 1: Cost-Effectiveness Analysis as a Guide to Resource Allocation in Health - Roles and Limitations
Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) is a decision-making tool that evaluates the efficiency of health interventions by comparing their costs and outcomes. CEA plays a crucial role in guiding resource allocation in healthcare, as it helps policymakers and healthcare providers to identify interventions that provide the best value for money. However, CEA has several limitations that need to be considered when using it to inform healthcare decisions.
Chapter 2: Theoretical Foundations of Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
CEA is based on the concept of opportunity cost, which is the value of the next best alternative use of resources. The theoretical foundations of CEA are rooted in microeconomics, which provides a framework for understanding how individuals and organizations make decisions about how to allocate resources.
Chapter 3: Framing and Designing the Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
The design of a CEA study depends on the research question being addressed. The study should be framed in a way that addresses the key questions and identifies the relevant costs and outcomes. The study design should also take into account the perspective of the decision-maker and the time horizon of the analysis.
Chapter 4: Identifying and Valuing Outcomes
Outcomes are the benefits or harms associated with an intervention. Identifying and valuing outcomes is a critical step in CEA, as it helps to determine the costs and benefits of an intervention. The valuation of outcomes should be based on the preferences of the decision-maker, and the outcomes should be expressed in a way that is comparable across different interventions.
Chapter 5: Assessing the Effectiveness of Health Interventions
The effectiveness of an intervention is a critical factor in CEA. The effectiveness of an intervention should be measured in terms of its impact on outcomes, and the measurement of effectiveness should be based on the best available evidence. The assessment of effectiveness should also take into account the variability in outcomes and the uncertainty associated with the estimates.
Chapter 6: Estimating Costs in Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
Estimating costs is a critical step in CEA, as it provides the basis for comparing costs and outcomes. The estimation of costs should be based on the best available evidence, and the costs should be expressed in a way that is comparable across different interventions. The estimation of costs should also take into account the variability in costs and the uncertainty associated with the estimates.
Chapter 7: Time Preference
Time preference is the preference for receiving benefits or costs in the present or in the future. Time preference can affect the results of CEA, as different time preferences can lead to different conclusions about the relative efficiency of interventions. The time preference of the decision-maker should be taken into account when conducting CEA.
Chapter 8: Reflecting Uncertainty in Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
Uncertainty is a critical consideration in CEA, as it can affect the accuracy of the results. The uncertainty associated with CEA can arise from various sources, including the variability in outcomes, the uncertainty in the estimates of costs and effects, and the uncertainty in the preferences of the decision-maker. The uncertainty in CEA should be reflected in the results, and the decision-maker should be aware of the uncertainty when making decisions.
Chapter 9: Reporting Cost-Effectiveness Studies and Results
The reporting of CEA studies and results is critical to ensure that the findings are transparent and reproducible. The reporting of CEA studies should follow a standard format, and the results should be presented in a way that is easy to understand. The reporting of CEA results should also take into account the perspective of the decision-maker and the time horizon of the analysis.

title: Weight gain during pregnancy: reexamining the guidelines.
text: As women of childbearing age have become heavier, the balance between the health of the mother and the child during pregnancy has become more challenging to manage. This is due to the variation in gestational weight gain, which has created a need for a reevaluation of the 1990 Institute of Medicine guidelines for weight gain during pregnancy. The book "Weight Gain During Pregnancy" addresses this need by providing a comprehensive review of the literature and independent analyses of existing databases. It builds upon the conceptual framework established in the 1990 guidelines and explores the relationships between weight gain during pregnancy and various factors, such as the mother's weight and height before pregnancy. The book also presents specific, updated target ranges for weight gain during pregnancy and guidelines for proper measurement, including a specific range of recommended gain for obese women. The intended audience for this book includes practitioners who care for women of childbearing age, policy makers, educators, researchers, and pregnant women themselves, as it provides them with the knowledge and tools necessary to promote optimal pregnancy outcomes.

title: To err is human. Building a safer health system
text:
Human beings are prone to making errors, and the healthcare industry is no exception. According to the Institute of Medicine (IOM) Report [1], healthcare services are a complex system susceptible to accidents. In fact, some systems are more prone to accidents than others, and when a system fails, there are often multiple factors at play. In healthcare, human errors are the leading contributors to accidents, but these errors often stem from failures within the system itself. These failures can be difficult to identify, as they may be hidden within complex computer systems or within various managerial layers.
To prevent errors, it's essential to design systems that make it challenging for people to engage in wrongful behavior and easy for them to follow the right procedures. In healthcare, this means creating processes that prioritize patient safety and prevent accidental injuries. As the healthcare industry becomes more complex, the opportunities for errors multiply. The IOM report "To Err is Human" proposes a framework for reducing medical errors and improving patient safety.
The environment in which these efforts occur has a significant impact on quality. This impact can be broken down into two dimensions: the first involves the domain of quality, which encompasses medical practices that align with current knowledge. The second dimension involves external forces that can drive quality improvement within the delivery system. Although the risk of dying due to a medical error significantly exceeds the risk of dying in an airline accident, public attention has been more focused on improving safety in the airline industry than in healthcare systems.
To clarify, an error refers to the failure of a planned action to be completed as intended or the use of a wrong plan to achieve a goal. An adverse event, on the other hand, is an injury caused by medical management rather than the patient's underlying condition. An adverse event attributable to error is considered a "preventable adverse event."
In conclusion, human error is an inherent part of the healthcare industry, and it's essential to address these errors to improve patient safety. By designing systems that promote correct behavior and prevent mistakes, we can reduce the risk of accidents and provide better care for our patients.

title: Excess risk of lymphomas, leukemia and myeloma in patients with rheumatoid arthritis
text: The study examined the incidence of malignant neoplasms among 11,483 male and 34,618 female individuals with rheumatoid arthritis using two nationwide data registers in Finland. The Social Insurance Institution's Population Data Register provided information on medication for chronic diseases, while the Finnish Cancer Registry contained data on all cancer patients diagnosed in Finland. The total follow-up period was 213,911 person-years. The study found that the incidence of all malignant neoplasms was higher in males and at a level expected in females. The expected number of cases of leukemia, lymphomas, Hodgkin's disease, and myeloma in both sexes was 59.6, compared to the 130 observed cases. This difference was statistically highly significant (p).

title: Advanced Human Nutrition
text:
Advanced Human Nutrition, Second Edition offers a comprehensive and in-depth exploration of the human body and the essential nutrients that it requires for optimal function. The book delves into the biochemical, physiological, and molecular aspects of nutrition, providing readers with a detailed understanding of why these nutrients are crucial for maintaining good health.
To enhance the reader's comprehension, the text is accompanied by a range of figures and diagrams that illustrate the complex pathways and molecular functions of nutrients. These visual aids help to break down the information into manageable chunks, making it easier for students to grasp the material.
The book covers a wide range of topics, including cell aging, damage, and repair systems; human nutrition, digestion, and absorption; microflora and satiety/hunger mechanisms; macronutrients during exercise and the role of liquids and sports drinks; and prevalent diseases in western cultures such as coronary heart disease, cancer, and osteoporosis.
In addition to the comprehensive text, an Instructor's Manual, PowerPoint Presentations, and a TestBank are available as free downloads, providing instructors with additional resources to enhance their teaching and assessment of students. Overall, Advanced Human Nutrition, Second Edition is an essential resource for anyone looking to gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between nutrition and human health.

title: The Endothelium: Modulator of Cardiovascular Function
text:
Introduction:
The endothelium, a layer of cells that lines the blood vessels, plays a crucial role in regulating vascular tone and blood flow. Endothelium-dependent responses, such as relaxation and dilation, are critical for maintaining proper blood flow and oxygen delivery to tissues. In this chapter, we will discuss the methods used to study endothelium-dependent responses, the endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF), the physiological actions of EDRF, other relaxing substances released by the endothelium, the production of contracting agents, local regulation of endothelium-dependent responses, neurohumoral regulation, heterogeneity and chronic modulation, disease, and therapeutic implications.
Methods to Study Endothelium-Dependent Responses:
Several methods have been developed to study endothelium-dependent responses, including:
* Isolated blood vessels: Isolated blood vessels are used to study the direct effects of endothelial cells on vascular tone.
* In vitro experiments: In vitro experiments are used to study the effects of endothelial cells on vascular tone in the absence of other cell types.
* In vivo experiments: In vivo experiments are used to study the effects of endothelial cells on vascular tone in the presence of other cell types.
* Imaging techniques: Imaging techniques, such as intravital microscopy and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), are used to visualize and measure changes in vascular tone in real-time.
Endothelium-Derived Relaxing Factor (EDRF):
EDRF is a relaxing substance released by the endothelium that can cause relaxation and dilation of blood vessels. EDRF is a potent vasodilator that can cause relaxation of blood vessels in the presence of vasoconstrictors.
Physiological Actions:
EDRF has several physiological actions, including:
* Relaxation of blood vessels: EDRF can cause relaxation and dilation of blood vessels, leading to increased blood flow and oxygen delivery to tissues.
* Anti-inflammatory effects: EDRF has anti-inflammatory effects, which can help to reduce inflammation and improve vascular function.
* Neuroprotective effects: EDRF has neuroprotective effects, which can help to protect against neurodegenerative diseases.
Other Relaxing Substances Released By the Endothelium:
In addition to EDRF, the endothelium releases other relaxing substances that can cause relaxation and dilation of blood vessels. These substances include:
* Nitric oxide (NO): NO is a potent vasodilator that can cause relaxation and dilation of blood vessels.
* Prostacyclin (PGI2): PGI2 is a potent vasodilator that can cause relaxation and dilation of blood vessels.
Production of Contracting Agents:
In addition to releasing relaxing substances, the endothelium also produces contracting agents that can cause vasoconstriction. These agents include:
* Endothelin-1 (ET-1): ET-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor that can cause vasoconstriction and reduce blood flow to tissues.
Local Regulation of Endothelium-Dependent Responses:
The endothelium regulates endothelium-dependent responses locally through the release of relaxing and contracting substances. This local regulation of endothelium-dependent responses is critical for maintaining proper blood flow and oxygen delivery to tissues.
Neurohumoral Regulation:
Neurohumoral regulation of endothelium-dependent responses involves the interaction between the endothelium and the nervous system. This interaction can affect endothelium-dependent responses and play a role in the regulation of blood flow and vascular tone.
Heterogeneity and Chronic Modulation:
The endothelium is a heterogeneous structure that can be modulated by a variety of factors, including aging, inflammation, and disease. Chronic modulation of the endothelium can lead to changes in endothelium-dependent responses and the development of disease.
Disease:
Disease can affect endothelium-dependent responses by altering the function of the endothelium and the release of relaxing and contracting substances. This can lead to changes in blood flow and vascular tone, which can have a significant impact on overall health and well-being.
Therapeutic Implications:
Understanding the mechanisms of endothelium-dependent responses and the factors that affect them has important therapeutic implications. This knowledge can be used to develop new treatments for a variety of diseases, including cardiovascular disease, pulmonary disease, and neurological disorders.
